p.seg: Number Five
The "Explanations of the Book of Documents" states:
Heaven has five appellations:
When revered as a ruler,
it is called August Heaven;
When its primordial energy is vast and expansive,
it is referred to as Vast Heaven;
When its benevolence shelters and pities those below,
it is termed Compassionate Heaven;
When overseeing from above,
it is named Sovereign Heaven;
When viewed from afar,
appearing deep blue,
it is called Azure Heaven.
The "Commentary on the Rites of Zhōu"
four names
The Erya says:
Spring is called the azure sky,
summer the vast sky,
autumn the compassionate sky,
and winter the lofty sky.
Lǐ Xún's commentary states:
In spring, all things begin to grow,
their color is azure,
hence it is called the azure sky;
in summer, all things are robust and flourishing,
their energy is vast,
hence it is called the vast sky;
in autumn, all things mature,
each possessing patterns,
hence it is called the compassionate sky.
Mín
means pattern.
In winter, the yin energy is above,
and all things are hidden and stored,
hence it is called the lofty sky.
Tàiqīng
The virtue of the sage,
extends upward to the supreme clarity,
downward to the supreme tranquility,
and in the middle to all spirits,
then the light of the auspicious star becomes radiant,
sweet dew descends,
vermilion grass grows,
and sweet springs emerge.
《Hè Guànzǐ》
At the beginning of human life
Heaven is
the origin of man;
parents are
the foundation of man.
When in distress, man returns to his foundation,
thus in toil, hardship, exhaustion, and extremity, he never fails to cry out to Heaven;
in sickness, pain, sorrow, and distress, he never fails to cry out to his parents.
． "Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of Qū Yuán"
The essence of all yang energies
Heaven,
the essence of all yang energies,
combines to form the Great Unity,
and divides into distinct names.
"Chūnqiū Shuōtící"
The Ancestor of All Things
Heaven and Earth are
born of the primordial energy,
the ancestor of all things.
The Lǐ Tǒng states:
Dǒng Zhòngshū said:
Heaven is
the ancestor of all beings.
Thus it universally covers and embraces without distinction,
establishing the sun, moon, wind, and rain to harmonize them,
and regulating yin and yang, cold and heat to complete them.
From his biography.
Dàgāo
When offering sacrifices to the great and lofty, pigs are considered the superior sacrificial animal.
． "Huáinánzǐ: Fàn Lùn Xià"
To solemnly serve the highest.
"Chén Shū: Shìzǔ Zhào"
Essence of the Multitude of Deities
Heaven is
the essence of the assembly of spirits,
with the sun, moon, and stars manifesting their positions.
Zhèng Xuán's "Annotations on the Rites of Zhōu"
Qīngmíng
"Chǔ Cí":
Leaning against the azure firmament to unfurl rainbows.
Annotation:
Azure firmament,
means the sky.
It speaks of the deep and distant blue clouds.
Tàiyuán
Only Tàiyuán is revered,
the goddess of earth bestows blessings.
Note:
Tàiyuán
refers to Heaven.
The goddess of earth
refers to Earth.
From the "Hànshū"
Shàng Xuán
Praying for blessings from the Supreme Mystery,
Thinking how to be devout.
Píngzǐ's "Eastern Capital Rhapsody"
Tàihào
Láng Yǐ submitted a memorial stating:
Eliminate calamities and manifest blessings,
comply with Heaven to achieve harmony,
dismiss and remove cruel harms,
in order to pacify the common people,
then Tàihào will be pleased and harmonious,
and the sound of thunder will arise.
Annotation:
Tàihào,
refers to Heaven.
From the "Later Han Dynasty, Original Biography."
Líng Yào
Cài Bójiē's "Epitaph for Chén Tàiqiū" states:
He received the essence of mountains and rivers,
embodying the purity of the celestial brilliance.
Annotation states:
Celestial brilliance,
refers to Heaven.
The "Apocryphal Texts of the Shangshu" contains verification.
Celestial brilliance,
according to Zhāng Héng's "Celestial Constitution and Armillary Sphere," states:
The root of all that covers and supports,
originates from nothing before the primordial energy,
the foundation of celestial brilliance,
divides the energy to form the primordial images.
Master of All Deities
Heaven is
the master of all deities;
virtue, morality, benevolence, and righteousness
are the ways of Heaven;
trembling and fear
are the heart of Heaven.
To abandon the Way and destroy virtue
is to despise the ways of Heaven;
to be treacherous, narrow-minded, and unrestrained
is to defy the will of humanity.
． 《Lùn Héng Biàn Chóng》
All living beings greatly look up to
Heaven is
that which revolves,
that which is balanced,
accumulated yang, pure and firm;
its substance rotates,
the great object of reverence for all living beings.
It is also said:
That which establishes heaven and earth
is water;
that which completes heaven and earth
is qì.
The qì of water and soil ascends to become heaven.
Yáng Quán's "Discourse on the Principles of Things"
Dàyuán
The *Wénxuǎn* includes Shù Xī's "Poem to Fill Omissions," which says:
Vast and immense is the great circle,
Boundless and obscure are the nine realms.
Lǚ Xiàng's commentary states:
The great circle
refers to heaven.
Note:
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
The great circle is above,
the great square is below.
The *Guǎnzǐ* says:
If a person can be tranquil and upright,
then they can uphold the great circle and tread upon the great square.
Shàng Líng
The *Wénxuǎn*, Yán Yánnián's "Preface to the Qu River Poems," states:
Reflecting on the heart of the Supreme Spirit,
To bestow blessings upon the wishes of the common people.
Liú Liáng's annotation says:
Supreme Spirit,
Refers to Heaven.
Note:
Cáo Zǐjiàn's "Lament for Emperor Wén of Wèi" states:
The Supreme Spirit descended with auspicious signs,
The Huángchū era was thus blessed.
The *Sòng Zhì*, Fù Xuán's "Sacrificial Songs of Jìn," states:
I, day and night,
Reverently serve the Supreme Spirit.
The *Nán Qí Shū*, Xiè Zhuāng's "Ascension Song Lyrics" of Sòng, states:
Brightly serving the former sages,
Cherishing and moistening the Supreme Spirit.
Also states:
Initiating the succession and sacrificial pairing,
Able to face the Supreme Spirit.
The "Edict Deposing Hǎilíng Wáng by the Empress Dowager":
The reason the Supreme Spirit bestows favor and mandate,
Is why the millions place their trust and hearts.
The *Liáng Shū*, Emperor Wǔ's "Edict of Abdication," states:
Reverently fearing the Supreme Spirit,
To bear the illustrious enterprise.
The *Wèi Shū, Péngchéng Wáng Xié Biography* states:
The Supreme Spirit shows no discernment,
The imperial body is unwell.
Yuán Zǐgōng's memorial states:
Suburban sacrifice to Heaven and honoring the Emperor,
Is to face and respond to the Supreme Spirit.
Gāo Lǘ's "Ode to Ultimate Virtue" states:
The Supreme Spirit descended with discernment,
Thinking the emperor would restore righteousness.
Thus favored Yǒu Wèi,
To match Heaven and receive the mandate.
Jǔqú Méngxùn's memorial states:
The Supreme Spirit descended with blessings,
The throne returned to the virtuous.
The *Língzhēng Zhì*, memorial by the officials, states:
The Supreme Spirit bestowed care,
Auspicious signs and virtues gathered abundantly.
The *Běi Qí Shū*, Gāo Yáng's "Edict of Abdication," states:
The Supreme Spirit grew weary of virtue,
Rightfully returning the great mandate.
The *Běi Shǐ, Wáng Shào Biography, Dì Tōng Jì* states:
Harmonizing with the spirit of the emperor,
Means the great Suí's virtue aligns with the Supreme Spirit.
The *Suí Shū, Yuè Zhì* states:
The Supreme Spirit accumulates a hundred blessings,
Circular Instrument
. The "Song Dynasty Calendar Treatise" records Zǔ Chōngzhī's memorial stating:
The initial nine of the yang lines,
marks the qi beginning due north,
where the seven constellations of the Dark Warrior,
position Xū at the zi direction.
If the circular instrument determines directions
with the sun as reference,
the winter solstice's lodging
should be in Xuánxiāo,
yet the current southern extreme
resides in the eastern quadrant.
Yuán Líng
Xiè Zhuāng's "Rhapsody on the Moon" says:
The gentle earth is congealed like snow,
The round heaven is a watery mirror.
Lǐ Shàn comments:
"Gentle earth"
refers to the earth,
"round heaven"
refers to the sky.
The Round Essence
Yán Yánnián's "Writ of Condolence for Empress Wényuán" states:
The round essence first blazed,
The square divinity began to congeal.
Lǐ Jì comments:
Round essence
refers to heaven.
The "Old Book of Táng" records Guō Zǐyí's "Memorial on the Enshrinement of Emperor Sùzōng's Empress Wú in the Ancestral Temple" stating:
The round essence manifested its substance,
The square divinity embodied its elegance.
Cānglíng
Sēng Yán's "Reply to Liú Shànmíng" states:
In his advanced years,
he directed affairs with authority,
which was truly bestowed by the Azure Spirit, achieving success through borrowed hands.
In the "Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism,"
Emperor Wǔ of the Zhōu dynasty's "Edict on Executing Yǔwén Hù and Posthumously Honoring Xiàomǐn" says:
Above, it aligns with the blessings of the Azure Spirit,
below, it manifests the gifts of the Earth Deity.
"Book of Zhōu"
Xuán Yí
The Book of Northern Qi records the imperial edict as saying:
Above, it aligns with the celestial principles;
below, it corresponds with the rivers and mountains.
The Lord of All Deities
Emperor Xuánzōng had not yet performed the suburban sacrifice ceremony in person.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng submitted a memorial stating:
Heaven is
the sovereign of all deities,
and that from which the king receives his mandate.
Since ancient times, rulers who inherited the throne
must have the ritual of suburban sacrifice,
which is to revere the Mandate of Heaven and repay what they have received.
Old Book of Táng
The Ancestor of Humanity
Lí Gàn's "Jiāo Jì Nán" states:
The beginning of all things
is Heaven;
the beginning of humanity,
is ancestors.
"New Book of Tang" biography, "Old Records of Rites and Ceremonies"
Earth as a Canopy, Stars as Highways
Wáng Biāo's "Ode to Heaven" states:
Vast is the earth as a canopy,
Boundless are the stars as highways.
"Qīng Yì Lù"
Hàoqióng
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Fēngshàn Shū":
At the dawn of high antiquity's beginning,
from the vast heavens came forth humankind.
Yán Shígǔ comments:
"Hào qióng"
both refer to Heaven.
"Hào" speaks of the vapor's vast expanse,
"qióng" speaks of the form's vaulted dome.
Hào Cāng
Bān Gù's "Response to a Guest's Jest":
He roused his divine virtue,
joining winds and clouds,
transcending the vast wilderness,
and trod the azure heavens.
Yán Shìgǔ notes:
Hàohào
refers to Heaven.
The primordial breath is vast and boundless,
hence called the Vast Heaven;
its color is azure,
hence called the Azure Heaven.
Hào Qián
Mǎ Róng's "Guǎngchéng Sòng":
To emulate creation with Earth,
And match divine works with Heaven.
Hòu Hàn Shū
Jiǔ Cāng
Ruǎn Jí's "Letter to Fú Yì" states:
The height of the nine heavens,
even swift-feathered birds cannot reach its summit;
the depth of the four seas,
even deep-sea creatures cannot fathom its bottom.
Wáng Jiǎn's "Stele Inscription at Qītóutuó Temple":
Those who gaze at the azure color above
cannot comprehend its distance.
The "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
The blue of the sky—
is that its true color?
Or is it because of its infinite distance?
Jiǔ Yě
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" states:
Heaven has nine fields:
the central one is Jūn Tiān,
the eastern one is Cāng Tiān,
the northeastern one is Biàn Tiān,
the northern one is Xuán Tiān,
the northwestern one is Yōu Tiān,
the western one is Mín Tiān,
the southwestern one is Zhū Tiān,
the southern one is Yán Tiān,
the southeastern one is Yáng Tiān.
Also, the "Guǎngyǎ" says:
Nine Heavens:
the eastern one is Hào Tiān,
the southern one is Chì Tiān,
the western one is Chéng Tiān,
the rest are the same.
Furthermore, the "Tàixuán Jīng" states:
Nine Heavens:
first, Zhōng Tiān,
second, Xiàn Tiān,
third, Cóng Tiān,
fourth, Gēng Tiān,
fifth, Zuì Tiān,
sixth, Kuò Tiān,
seventh, Jiǎn Tiān,
eighth, Chén Tiān,
ninth, Chéng Tiān.
The Six Qi
The Zuo Zhuan says:
Heaven has six qi,
which descend to produce the five flavors.
Du Yu comments:
The six qi
refer to yin, yang, wind, rain, darkness, and brightness.
Nine Passes
The "Summoning the Soul" says:
Do not ascend to heaven.
Tigers and leopards guard the nine passes,
Pecking and harming those below.
Wáng Yì notes:
The heavenly gate has nine layers,
With divine tigers and leopards controlling its opening and closing,
Pecking to kill those who wish to ascend.
Eight Pillars
The "Heavenly Questions" states:
Where stand the eight pillars,
Why is the southeast deficient?
The commentary says:
It means heaven has eight mountains as pillars,
Where do they all stand?
The southeast is insufficient,
Who caused this deficiency?
"Chǔ Cì"
Jiǔ Chóng
The "Heavenly Questions" states:
Heaven, being round, has nine layers;
Who measured and planned them?
The annotation says:
It means that heaven is round and has nine layers;
Who could have measured and known this?
"The Songs of Chǔ"
Jiǔ Qián
Cuī Yīn's "Dá Zhì" states:
Looking up, one explores as far as the nine heavens.
Note:
Nine layers.
"Hòu Hàn"
Eight Dimensions
Dōngfāng Shuò's "Seven Admonitions" states:
Drawing upon the eight dimensions to guide myself,
I ingest the ethereal vapors to prolong life.
Annotation:
Heaven has eight dimensions,
which serve as its guiding principles.
The "Guǎnzǐ" says:
Heaven is upheld by something,
Earth is borne by something.
If nothing upheld it,
Heaven would have already collapsed,
how much more so for humans?
Jiǔ Líng
Wáng Bāo's "Nine Laments" says:
I ascend the nine heavens to let my spirit roam.
Annotation:
It means to imagine ascending the nine heavens to release one's spirit.
Nine Heavens
. "Treatise on Music of the Book of Hàn":
With focused spirit and determined will, he traversed the nine gāi.
Annotation:
Gāi,
means layers,
referring to the heights of the nine heavens.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Fēng Shàn Memorial" states:
The virtue of the great Hàn flows upward to the nine gāi,
and downward to the eight yán.
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
The boundaries of the nine heavens are called the nine yín,
and beyond the nine heavens lies the nine gāi.
Annotation:
Yín,
means brink or edge.
Gāi,
means steps or tiers.
It indicates there are nine tiers in sequence.
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
Ruòshì said to Lú Áo:
I have an appointment with the vast and boundless at the heights of the nine gāi.
Qī Héng
The "Xiaojing Yuanshenqi" states:
The celestial sphere has seven rings and six intervals.
Annotation:
Although heaven has seven rings, it mentions intervals because
from the inner ring to the middle ring,
and from the middle ring to the outer ring,
the distance between them totals 117,000 li.
Jiǔ Hóng
Yáng Xióng's "Jiě Nàn" states:
The emerald hornless dragon and the crimson hornless dragon,
without ascending on floating clouds,
or riding swift winds,
cannot soar to the Nine Gates.
Annotation:
The Nine Gates,
are the gates of the Nine Heavens.
"Hàn Shū"
Ten Cardinal Relationships
Heaven has ten aspects,
heaven, earth, yang, yin, water, soil, humans, metal, wood, and fire,
making ten aspects in total.
Heaven also possesses joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure,
corresponding to humans,
uniting them by category,
thus heaven and humanity are one.
"Chūnqiū Fánlù"
Jiǔxiāo
Wèi Zhāng Yuān's "Ode to Observing Celestial Phenomena" says:
Ascending the beautiful peak to gaze afar,
Beholding the divine phenomena across the Nine Heavens.
Annotation:
The Nine Heavens,
refer to the nine layers of heaven.
The "Dào Shū" records:
The Nine Heavens,
are named Shénxiāo, Qīngxiāo, Bìxiāo, Dānxiāo, Jǐngxiāo, Yùxiāo, Lángxiāo, Zǐxiāo, and Tàixiāo.
The "Chǔ Cí" contains:
Soaring on crimson heavens to approach the Grand Purity.
the four borders
Beyond the twenty-eight lunar mansions, each extends fifteen thousand li,
forming the extreme boundaries of the four wanderings,
called the four extremities.
The "Kǎo Líng Yào" states:
Heaven has four extremities,
to distribute the essence and spirit;
Earth has four great rivers,
to bring forth charts and writings.
The "Hé Tú" says:
Heaven has four extremities and three paths.
The four extremities refer to
the constellation Fáng;
the three paths refer to
the three paths between the stars of Fáng:
the southern gap is the upper path,
the central is the middle path,
and the northern gap is the lower path.
The "Tiān Jìng Jīng"
Sìhé
"Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng":
Heaven has four harmonies.
On the four sides of Kūnlún,
the atmosphere is mild and warm,
which is called harmony.
The way of heaven turns leftward,
over one day and one night,
it rotates by one degree.
The sun and moon move leftward across the sky,
and in one day and one night,
they complete a cycle around the four harmonies.
"Zhōu Bì" states:
Heaven and earth have four poles and four harmonies.
Annotation:
The so-called four harmonies
are referred to as the poles.
Zǐ, wǔ, mǎo, yǒu
represent the centers of east, west, south, and north.
Sān Biàn
. "Hàn Tiānwén Zhì" states:
The movement of heaven undergoes a minor change every thirty years,
a moderate change in a century,
a major change every five hundred years,
three major changes form one cycle,
and three cycles complete the grand preparation.
Nine Positions
Heaven has nine positions,
Earth has nine domains,
Heaven has three luminaries,
Earth has three forms.
"Líng Xiǎn"
Eight Regulations
Heaven has essence,
earth has form;
heaven has eight solar terms,
earth has five geographical divisions.
Thus they can be the parents of all things.
"Sùwèn"
tempering stones to mend the firmament
The Liezi says:
Heaven and Earth
are also things.
Things have deficiencies,
so in ancient times, Nǚwā Shì smelted five-colored stones to mend their gaps,
and cut off the legs of the giant sea turtle to set up the four pillars.
The Huainanzi says:
In the distant past,
the four pillars collapsed,
the nine provinces split apart;
Heaven could no longer cover all,
Earth could no longer support fully.
Fires blazed fiercely and were not extinguished,
waters flooded vastly and did not cease.
Thereupon, Nǚwā Shì smelted five-colored stones to repair the azure sky,
cut off the turtle's legs to set up the four pillars,
slew the black dragon to save Jìzhōu,
and piled up reed ashes to stop the flooding waters.
Tiānzhù
Gònggōng and Zhuānxū contended to become emperor,
and in his rage he struck Mount Bùzhōu.
He broke the pillars of heaven,
and severed the cords of the earth.
Thus heaven tilted to the northwest,
and the sun, moon, and stars moved there;
the earth became unfilled in the southeast,
so all rivers and waters flow there.
"Lièzǐ"
Táng Lè's "Ode to Greatness" says:
"The mighty warrior, indignant, severed heaven's cords;
the Northern Dipper slanted and Mount Tài was leveled."
Tiāngōng
Those who follow the Way claim that the Yellow Emperor rode a dragon, ascending through the clouds,
mounted the morning clouds and mist,
climbed up to the celestial palaces,
and passed by the heavenly palace with inverted reflections.
The celestial sphere is like a chariot,
with a canopy to which the sun and moon are suspended—
how could one ascend to it?
from "Imperial Survey of Tombs and Graves Records"
With Táng
Shū Yú's mother dreamed that Heaven said to King Wǔ:
"I command you to bear a son,
named Yú,
and I will give him Táng."
When the child was born,
there was a character on his palm,
reading "Yú",
so they named him accordingly.
Records of the Grand Historian
bestowed upon Chǔ
Gōngsūn Guīfù met with the King of Chǔ in Sòng.
The people of Sòng reported their urgent situation to Jìn,
and the Marquis of Jìn wished to rescue them.
Bó Zōng said:
"It cannot be done.
Heaven is currently favoring Chǔ,
we cannot contend with them.
Although Jìn is strong,
can we defy Heaven?"
Zuǒ Zhuàn
Looking Up
Duke Huán of Qí said:
"What does a ruler hold in highest regard?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"He regards Heaven as highest."
Duke Huán looked upward.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The Heaven I speak of
is not the vast blue firmament.
One who rules over others
should regard the common people as Heaven."
From "Shuō Yuàn"
Dream oppression
Initially,
Mùzǐ left the Shūsūn clan,
went to Qí,
married a woman from the Guó clan,
and begot Mèng Bǐng and Zhòng Rén.
He dreamed that the sky was pressing down on him and he could not withstand it.
Looking around, he saw a man,
with a black face and a hunched back,
deep-set eyes and a snout-like mouth,
who shouted to him, "Niú, help me!"
Only then did he overcome it.
"Zuǒ Zhuàn"
Tiān Zuì
The "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states:
In the past, the Heavenly Emperor was pleased with Duke Mù of Qín and granted him an audience,
entertaining him with the grand music of the celestial sphere.
The Emperor became intoxicated,
and then made a golden decree,
bestowing this land,
cutting off the portion of the Quail's Head constellation.
The "Rhapsody on Lamenting the South of the River" states:
To grant Qín the Quail's Head,
why was Heaven so intoxicated?
Yú Xǐ's "Records of Anecdotes" says:
A proverb states:
The Heavenly Emperor was drunk, and Qín became tyrannical,
gold mistakenly fell as meteorites.
It is said that Duke Mù of Qín dreamed of the Heavenly Emperor performing the celestial music,
and this proverb already existed.
Lǐ Wénráo said:
In the past, the golden decree during the Qín era was called "Heaven's intoxication."
How could Heaven be constantly drunk!
"Selections of Refined Literature"
When Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào fell ill,
for five days he remained unconscious.
After two days,
he half-awoke and told his officials:
"I was at the Emperor's abode and very happy.
I roamed the celestial sphere with a hundred deities,
listening to the grand music with nine performances and myriad dances,
unlike the music of the Three Dynasties,
its sound moved people's hearts."
Biǎn Què told Dǒng Ānyú:
"In the past, Duke Mù of Qín once experienced this,
awakening after seven days,
and told Gōngsūn Zhī and Zǐyú:
'The reason I stayed so long at the Emperor's abode, where I was very happy,
was because I happened to be learning something.'"
"Records of the Grand Historian"
The man of Qǐ feared the sky might fall
In the State of Qǐ there was a man
who worried that heaven and earth might collapse,
leaving him no place to survive,
and he neglected sleep and food.
Another person, concerned about his anxiety,
went to enlighten him.
Saying:
"Heaven is merely accumulated vapor.
There is no place without vapor,
like bending, stretching, and breathing.
We move and rest within it all day long,
why worry about its collapse?"
The man replied:
"If heaven is indeed accumulated vapor,
shouldn't the sun, moon, and stars fall down?"
The enlightener said:
"The sun, moon, and stars are merely the shining parts within this accumulated vapor.
Even if they fell,
they couldn't cause any harm."
《Lièzǐ》
Discourse on Heaven
The "General Meaning of the Five Classics" states:
Zōu Yǎn spoke grandly about celestial matters,
thus he was called "Discourser on Heaven."
Liú Xiàng's "Separate Records" says:
What Zōu Yǎn discussed regarding the cycles of the Five Virtues,
the vastness of heaven and earth,
and his writings on celestial affairs,
led to him being called "Zōu the Discourser on Heaven."
The "Records of the Grand Historian" states:
Yǎn was grandiose and profoundly eloquent,
thus the people of Qí praised him as "Yǎn the Discourser on Heaven."
Dreaming of Ascending to Heaven
In Rǔnán there was formerly the Hóngxìbēi reservoir,
during the reign of Emperor Chéng,
Zhái Fāngjìn memorialized to have it destroyed.
Emperor Chéng dreamed that he ascended to heaven,
where the Celestial Emperor angrily said:
"Why have you destroyed my Zhuólóng Abyss?"
． from "The Biography of Xǔ Yáng in the Book of the Later Hàn"
Groping the heavens
Empress Héxī Dèng once dreamed of touching the sky,
where the celestial sphere stretched vast and pure blue,
smooth as malt sugar,
with shapes resembling stalactites.
She then looked up and sipped from it.
She consulted a dream interpreter,
who recounted that Emperor Yáo dreamed of climbing up to heaven,
and Emperor Tāng dreamed of reaching the sky and licking it.
These were omens from the sagely kings of old,
auspicious beyond words.
《Hòu Hàn Shū》
Tiāntóu Tiāněr Tiānzú Tiānxìng
The envoy of Wú, Zhāng Wēn, came on a diplomatic mission,
and all the officials went to bid him farewell,
but Qín Mì arrived late.
He asked Mì,
"Does Heaven have a head?"
Mì replied,
"It does."
Wēn said,
"In which direction is it?"
He said,
"In the west.
The Book of Songs says:
'He turns His gaze westward.'
From this, we infer
the head is in the west."
Wēn said,
"Does Heaven have ears?"
Mì said,
"Heaven dwells on high but hears the lowly.
The Book of Songs says:
'The crane cries in the ninefold marsh,
its voice is heard by Heaven.'
If it had no ears,
how could it hear?"
Wēn said,
"Does Heaven have feet?"
Mì said,
"It does.
The Book of Songs says:
'Heaven's steps are difficult,
this man is not as good.'
If it had no feet,
how could it walk?"
Wēn said,
"Does Heaven have a surname?"
Mì said,
"It does."
Wēn said,
"What surname?"
Mì said,
"The surname Liú."
Wēn said,
"How do you know that?"
Mì said,
"The Son of Heaven's surname is Liú,
therefore I know it."
Wēn said,
"Is the sun born in the east?"
Mì said,
"Though it is born in the east,
it sets in the west."
His answers came as swiftly as an echo following a sound,
whereupon Wēn greatly admired and respected him.
Records of Shǔ
Mèng Mù Pò Tiān
Xǔ Zhēnjūn, Wú Měng, and Guō Pú together visited Wáng Dūn,
Dūn said:
"Last night I dreamed of breaking through the heavens with a piece of wood,
would my succession to the throne be perfect?"
Xǔ Zhēnjūn said:
"This dream is certainly not auspicious.
Breaking through the heavens with wood,
forms the character 'wèi' (未).
You should not act recklessly,
for the Jìn dynasty's fortune has certainly not declined yet."
"Biographies of the Twelve True Lords"
Zhāng Bīn was recommended as Filially Pious and Incorrupt,
and dreamed of erecting a pole.
Suǒ Dǎn said:
"This is the character 'wèi' (未)."
"Records of Former Liáng"
Heavenly Grandfather
In the first year of the Jiànwǔ era,
the Year Star trespassed against Tiānguān.
Yǔ Yì wrote to Yǔ Bīng, saying:
"The Year Star trespassing against Tiānguān
portends that 'passages and bridges shall be obstructed.'
Lately, there have been no unusual events in Jiāngdōng,
nor has river travel been particularly difficult;
yet Shí Hǔ has for years closed his borders and severed diplomatic communications.
This indeed is another sign of Heaven's confusion, failing to distinguish black from white."
． "Astronomical Records of the Book of Sòng"
Knocking at the door
Táo Kǎn dreamed he grew eight wings,
flying up to heaven,
where he saw nine celestial gates.
He had ascended eight of them,
but could not enter the final gate,
beating his wings against the sky.
The gatekeeper struck him with a staff,
causing him to fall to the ground,
breaking his left wing.
Upon waking,
his left armpit still ached.
Later, as commander of eight provinces,
he secretly harbored ambitions for the throne,
yet whenever he recalled the omen of the broken wing,
he restrained himself and desisted.
"History of the Jin Dynasty"
The Heavenly Emperor's face is one chi square.
During the Xiánkāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
there was a scholar named Zhōu Wèi
who died and came back to life.
He said the Heavenly Emperor summoned him,
led him up to the hall,
and when he looked up at the Emperor,
he saw a face one foot square.
He asked the attendants:
"Is this the ancient Heavenly Emperor Zhāng?"
They replied:
"The ancient Heavenly Emperor
has long since passed away as a sage.
This is the recent Cáo Míngdì."
The Heavenly Gate opens
Records of the Book of Jin:
Féng Bá, ruler of Northern Yan, once saw the heavenly gate open at night,
with divine radiance blazing brilliantly,
illuminating the courtyard.
Book of Northern Qi:
Emperor Wénxuān Gāo Yáng, while traveling with Shìzōng past Mount Liáoyáng,
alone witnessed the heavenly gate open,
with no others seeing it.
Records of Preserved Light:
Yáng Xíjí saw the sky split open in his youth,
revealing billowing clouds and mist within,
tiered pavilions rising and falling,
their brilliance shining down upon the mountains,
before slowly closing again.
Surviving Accounts of Wáng Wéngōng:
Dàn saw the heavenly gate open in his childhood,
with his own name inscribed inside.
Liú Xióngfēi, Military Commissioner of Sìchuān, also witnessed the heavenly gate open.
Dreaming of the Heavenly Gate Opening
Sòng Xuē Āndū initially campaigned in Guǎnshǎn,
arriving at Jiùkǒu,
he dreamed of looking up at the sky,
and saw the heavenly gate open.
He said to his attendants:
"Do you see the heavenly gate opening?"
When Xiàowǔ suppressed the rebellion and ascended the throne,
he sighed and said:
"Could the dream of the heavenly gate opening be an omen of restoration?"
For his achievements, he was enfeoffed as Nánxiāng Nán.
"History of the Southern Dynasties"
Glory
During the Yǒngmíng era,
the sky suddenly cast a yellow radiance upon the earth,
which none could explain.
The Minister of Justice presented the "Ode to the Golden Heaven."
Wáng Chī remarked:
This is not the Golden Heaven,
but what is called glorious light.
Emperor Shìzōng was greatly pleased
and appointed him as the Governor of Yǒngyáng.
(Book of Qí)
Tiān zhōng zì
Liáng Shěn Yǔ was close friends with Fàn Yún,
and in the late Qí dynasty, he once stayed overnight at Yún's place.
He dreamed of sitting on the beam pillar of the house,
looking up to see the characters "Fàn's Residence" in the sky.
Yǔ recounted this dream to Emperor Gāozǔ,
and Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"Yún will not die,
this dream can be verified."
From "Liáng Yǔ's Biography."
Yúntíng Gōng
Suí Wàn Bǎocháng was born intelligent and clever,
exquisitely versed in the principles of bells and pitch pipes.
He once encountered about ten extraordinary individuals in the wilderness,
who summoned him forward,
and said:
"The Supreme Deity, considering your heaven-endowed nature for music and pitch,
has sent the officials of the钧天 Palace to reveal the profound and subtle essentials."
They commanded him to sit,
instructed him for a long while,
then all ascended into the sky and departed.
When Bǎocháng returned home,
five days had already passed.
From then on, regarding the music of the human world,
there was none he did not master thoroughly.
Suddenly one evening,
the immortals he had previously met descended to his home,
and said:
"Do you remember the gathering at the云亭 Palace?"
Bǎocháng was bewildered for a long time,
then he comprehended.
Another day, he said to his neighbors:
"I was temporarily banished from the immortal palace to the human world,
and am about to leave now."
After ten days, no one knew where he had gone.
"Collected Accounts of Immortals"
Báiyù Lóu
Lǐ Hè once fell ill and saw a man in crimson clothing riding a red dragon,
with a young boy holding a tablet
inscribed with what resembled ancient seal script,
saying:
"The Supreme God has newly built a White Jade Tower,
now completed,
summoning you to compose its record,
for heavenly life is rather pleasant."
Hè then breathed his last.
From "Basic Biography"
After Hè's death,
his mother dreamed of Hè saying:
"The Supreme God,
ruler of immortals,
recently moved the capital to the Moon Garden,
where he built the White Jade Palace.
Because I am skilled in poetry,
he summoned me along with several other literary scholars
to jointly compose the record for the new palace.
The Emperor also built the Condensed Void Hall,
appointing us to compile musical compositions.
Now I have become one of the celestial beings,
and am very happy!
I hope you, mother, will not worry about me."
From "Records of the Xuan Room"
From "Records Beyond the Dust"
Five Virtues
Emperor Shìzōng of the Zhōu dynasty observed the great flood in Sìzhōu,
and recorded it to ask Dòu Yǎn.
Yǎn replied:
"Heaven and Earth possess five virtues—
moistening, parching, generating, completing, and moving."
(Yùhǎi Gànzhū yī)
Holding up
Hán Qí was governing Qínzhōu when,
after lying ill for several days,
he suddenly said:
"I just dreamed twice that I was holding up the heavens with my hands."
Later, he supported Emperor Yīngzōng while he was still a feudal lord,
and assisted Emperor Shénzōng when he was crown prince.
From "Juànyóu Lù"
The celestial phenomenon formed a text.
When Páng Jí commanded Yán'ān,
on the winter solstice at midnight,
in a trance,
he saw the celestial phenomenon form a text,
which said:
"Páng Jí will become chancellor in ten years,
and shall assist the Son of Heaven with benevolence."
He gazed at it for a long time before it vanished.
Ten years later, he indeed became chancellor.
From "Old Tales of Qǔ Wěi"
Jade Capital and Golden Palace
Wáng Sù once dreamed of arriving at the Jade Capital's golden palace,
where in the hall stood a figure wearing purple robes and an emerald crown,
who said:
"I am the Vice Minister of the East Gate,
while you, sir, are the Vice Minister of the West Gate.
We once submitted a memorial reprimanding Lord Shì."
Upon waking from the dream,
he composed a poem that read:
"As if returning from the land of Huáxū,
through deep clouds and mist, towers appeared.
The bright moon cast a lonely chill, the rooster's call urgent,
startling this floating life—one dream's end."
In his later years, recalling the dream of the Jade Capital,
he wrote another poem:
"Hidden in the azure void, the White Jade Capital,
my dream soul flew into the Phoenix City.
When shall I tread beyond the clouds and mist again?
The bright-toothed, blue-pupiled one has already promised."
"Talks on Poetry Past and Present"
The library of the Supreme Sovereign
In the early years of the Zhènghé era,
a certain Fāng Cháosàn from Pútián served as the magistrate of Wùyuán.
He fell ill with a fever and lay bedridden,
awakening after three days
and said:
"I arrived at a city,
where a Daoist priest bowed and said:
'You, sir, are a man of the Táng dynasty,
who once performed hidden merits. The Emperor summoned you to the White Jade Tower,
which is where Lǐ Chángjí composed his records.
When tested on the Great Way of Non-Action,
you, sir, wrote a verse containing these striking lines:
"The Emperor drilled holes and lost his soul,
The snake added legs and lost the cup."
The Emperor, upon reading it, was greatly pleased,
appointed you as a Xiūwén Láng,
with the sole duty of writing,
and later promoted you to Yùhuá Shìláng.
Subsequently, due to your arrogance in talent, you were envied by many,
and demoted to Qúnyù Outer Supervisor.
The Qúnyù Hall is the Emperor's library of texts and charts.
From then on, your audiences with him became less frequent.
One day,
while the Emperor was touring the Jade Garden, he summoned you.
You were boating on the pond with Sòng Dàohuá
and entertained thoughts of mortal husband and wife,
for which you were impeached by the messenger,
banished,
and fell into the human world,
but you shall return before long.'"
Yí Jiān Zhì
Chānghé
The "Lí Sāo" says:
I commanded the heavenly gatekeeper to open the gates,
but he leaned against the Chāng Hé and stared at me.
The "Huái Nán Zǐ" states:
Pushed open the Chāng Hé,
and entered the heavenly gate.
The annotation explains:
Chāng Hé
is the gate where one begins to ascend to heaven.
The heavenly gate
is the gate of the Purple Tenuity Palace, where the Supreme Deity resides.
Zhāng Yuān's "Ode on Observing Celestial Phenomena" says:
Majestically, the Chāng Hé stands wide open.
The annotation explains:
Between the two flanking walls of the palace,
the southern opening, shaped like a gate, is called the Chāng Hé Gate.
Zhāng Héng's ode says:
I called to the heavenly gatekeeper to open the door,
and beheld the Celestial Emperor in his jade palace.
Tiānmén
The "Hetu Kuodixiang" states:
The northwest is the Gate of Heaven,
the southeast is the Door of Earth.
Annotation:
Heaven is insufficient in the northwest,
thus it is the Gate of Heaven;
Earth is not full in the southeast,
thus it is the Door of Earth.
. The "Hanshu Yue Zhi" says:
The Gate of Heaven opens,
vast and expansive.
Annotation:
The celestial body,
is in a firm and clear state.
In the "Shenyi Jing," in the great wilderness of the northwest,
there is a golden palace a thousand zhang high,
on top of which is a bright moon pearl,
three zhang in diameter,
illuminating a thousand li,
inside there are golden steps,
and the two palaces are called the Gate of Heaven.
The Way of Heaven
Méichéng's Music Bureau poem says:
A beauty is atop the clouds,
The celestial road separates us with no fixed date.
Tiāndǒu
The Book of Documents states:
Heaven's work is to be carried out by humans.
The Commentary says:
Those who accomplish the work of Heaven and Earth
never fail to flourish.
From this perspective,
if rulers of the age wish to forcibly enrich those who have achieved nothing,
they are contending with Heaven,
and to desire long-lasting stability
has never been possible.
Qiánfū Lùn
Heaven's Teaching
Common people say:
When the former rulers intended to issue an amnesty,
they would first send horses to patrol the markets and neighborhoods,
listening at street corners,
and all would say:
There will be an amnesty.
This was how they understood Heaven's instruction.
But if a benevolent ruler truly hears this
and immediately follows it as Heaven's instruction,
no mistake could be greater.
Alas!
Tiānyǔ
The lofty mountains stand vast and blue,

From "Xú Líng's Stele of the Temple of Filial Piety"
Zhāng Gōng
Is not the way of heaven like the stretching of a bow?
The high it presses down,
the low it lifts up;
the excessive it takes from,
the deficient it gives to.
The way of heaven
is to reduce the excessive and supplement the deficient.
"Lǎozǐ"
A circle not conforming to the compass.
《Lǎozǐ》 says:
The greatest simplicity has no form,
the greatest Dào has no measure.
Thus, the circle of heaven does not conform to the compass,
the square of earth does not conform to the set square.
《Wénzǐ》
Without beginning or end,
heaven is round and endless,
thus none can behold its form;
earth is square and boundless,
thus none can peer through its gate.
Heaven's transformations follow no fixed shape,
earth's growth and life have no measure.
《Wénzǐ》
Qīngmíng
The Way of Heaven is without partiality,
thus it is eternally upright;
Heaven?
Constantly upright,
thus it is clear and bright.
"Shēnzǐ"
Zhèng's commentary:
"Kǎolíngyào" states:
Heaven,
is pure yang, clear and bright, without form.
The sage takes it as the model,
and creates the jade celestial sphere to measure its phenomena.
Yīnyáng
From the pole southward,
is the yang of heaven;
from the pole northward,
is the yin of heaven.
From "Discourses on the Principles of Things"
Qīng yáng
accumulates to form Heaven,
thus Heaven is qīng yáng.
Huángdì Sùwèn
Rising from the Ox constellation
The "Hetu Kuodi Xiang" states:
The heavens move leftward,
starting from the Ox;
the earth moves rightward,
starting from the Net.
The "Shizi" states:
The heavens extend leftward and rise from the Ox,
the earth opens rightward and rises from the Net and the Hairy Head.
Insufficient in the northwest
The "Sùwèn" states:
Heaven is deficient in the northwest,
thus the northwest is yin,
and a person's right ear and eye are not as sharp as the left;
Earth is not full in the southeast,
thus the southeast is yang,
and a person's left hand and foot are not as strong as the right.
It also says:
Heaven is deficient in the northwest,
so it is cold on the left and cool on the right;
Earth is not full in the southeast,
so it is hot on the right and warm on the left.
The annotation explains:
In the terrain of the Central Plains,
the northwest is high,
and the southeast is low.
Now, all rivers flow eastward to the vast sea,
so the heights and lows of east, west, north, and south can be understood.
The Qi of the Four Directions
The qi of the east is thunder,
the qi of the south is lightning,
the qi of the west is the rainbow,
the qi of the north is clouds, rain, hail, and sleet,
the qi of the center is dew.
"Zàohuà Quányú"
Heaven's officials, Heaven's messengers, Heaven's seasons, Heaven's taboos
The four seasons are
Heaven's officials;
the sun and moon are
Heaven's messengers;
the stars and constellations are
Heaven's seasons;
rainbows and comets are
Heaven's taboos.
． Huáinánzǐ: Tiānwén Xùn
like a bamboo hat
The sky's form arches like a bamboo hat,
covering the surface of the earth.
It floats above the primordial qi,
like pressing down on water with an overturned toilet case to keep it from flowing—
this is because qi fills the space within.
Yǔ Sǒng's "Discussion on Probing the Heavens"
The canopy cover
theory states:
Zhuānxū created the armillary sphere,
Huángdì made the canopy heaven,
both taking heaven as a canopy cover.
． "Liú Shì Lì Zhèng Wèn"
tilted canopy
The ancients said:
There are three theories on the shape of heaven and earth:
First is the Sphere-Heaven theory,
second is the Canopy-Heaven theory,
third is the Infinite Empty Night theory.
As for the Infinite Empty Night theory,
none have ever heard it explained.
Later, Yú Bǐng wrote "The Theory of Vaulted Heaven",
Yáo Xìn wrote "The Theory of Dawn Heaven",
Yú Xǐ wrote "The Theory of Stable Heaven",
with various forms and different appearances,
each differing among them.
The Canopy-Heaven theory further has three versions:
One says heaven is like a carriage canopy,
moving within the eight extremes.
One says the shape of heaven is like a bamboo hat,
high in the center and low at the four edges;
one says heaven is like a tilted carriage canopy,
high in the south and low in the north.
"Records of Astronomy"
Fúpén
The celestial sphere is level,
no different from the earth,
resembling the shape of an overturned bowl.
． From the "Explanations" chapter of Lùn Héng
Wheel
The sky is like a wheel,
ending and beginning again,
reaching the extreme and then reversing.
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū"
"Língxiàn" states:
Heaven revolves with yang,
Earth halts its wheel with yin.
Chicken egg
The heavens are like an egg,
the earth like the yolk within,
solitary and dwelling inside the heavens.
The heavens are vast and the earth small,
with water both inside and outside the heavens.
The heavens each ride on qì and stand,
carrying water and floating.
The circumference of the heavens is three hundred sixty-five and one-quarter degrees,
divided again in the middle,
so half covers the earth above,
and half encircles below the earth.
Thus, the twenty-eight constellations are half visible and half hidden,
as the heavens revolve like the turning of a carriage wheel hub.
Húntiānyí
Ant Mill
The Zhōubì school says:
The heavens are round like a spread canopy,
the earth is square like a chessboard.
The heavens revolve sideways like a turning millstone moving leftward,
while the sun and moon move rightward.
As the heavens rotate leftward,
the sun and moon actually travel eastward,
but are pulled westward by the heavens.
This is likened to an ant crawling on a millstone:
the millstone turns left while the ant moves right,
but since the millstone moves faster and the ant slower,
the ant inevitably follows the millstone's leftward rotation.
Tiānjūn
The various states and towns of Mǎhán,
each had one person in charge of sacrifices,
worshipping a deity known as "Tiānjūn."
From the "Later Records of the Four Barbarians."
to regard Heaven as an elder brother
The King of the State of Wō considered Heaven his elder brother,
and the Sun his younger brother.
At dawn, he would emerge to attend to governance,
sitting cross-legged,
but when the sun rose, he would cease handling affairs,
saying:
"I entrust them to my younger brother."
From the History of the Northern Dynasties
The Name of the Heavenly Spirit
The "Comprehensive Meaning of the Five Classics" states:
The greatest of the celestial deities is called Haótiān Shàngdì,
which is Yàopòbǎo,
also known as Tiānhuáng Dàdì,
and also called Tàiyī.
His assistants are the Five Deities:
the Green Deity of the east, Wēilíngyǎng,
the Red Deity of the south, Chìbiāonù,
the White Deity of the west, Báizhāojù,
the Black Deity of the north, Yèguāngjì,
and the Yellow Deity of the center, Hánshūniǔ.
Another theory states that the Azure Deity is named Língfú,
the Red Deity is named Wénzǔ,
the White Deity is named Xiǎnjì,
the Black Deity is named Xuánjǔ,
and the Yellow Deity is named Shéndǒu.
The "River Chart" says:
Their essences manifest in the east as the Azure Dragon,
in the south as the Vermilion Bird,
in the center as the Qilin,
in the west as the White Tiger,
and in the north as
the Black Tortoise
Mù Gōng,
also known as Dōng Wáng Fù,
also called Dōng Wáng Gōng,
also titled Yù Huáng Jūn,
resides among cloudy chambers,
using purple clouds as canopies,
and azure clouds as walls.
"Xiān Zhuàn Shí Yí"
recounts that in early Hàn times, four or five children
were drawing on the ground playing,
when one child sang:
"Wearing blue skirts, enter the Heavenly Gate,
bow to Jīn Mǔ and salute Mù Gōng."
Zhāng Zǐfáng went and paid respects, saying:
"These are the jade attendants of Dōng Wáng Gōng.
What is called Jīn Mǔ
is Xī Wáng Mǔ.
Mù Gōng
is Dōng Wáng Gōng.
Immortals bow to Wáng Gōng and salute Wáng Mǔ."
"Zhēn Gào"
"Lǎo Jūn Zhōng Jīng" states:
Dōng Wáng Fù
is the essence of pure yang,
preceding all deities.
He governs the East,
residing below at Pénglái Mountain,
with the surname Wúwéi,
and the courtesy name Jūnjiě.
Xī Wáng Mǔ
is the essence of supreme yin.
With the surname Zìrán,
and the courtesy name Jūnsī,
she governs below at the golden city of Kūnlún,
where nine-layered clouds display five colors,
atop peaks reaching ten thousand zhàng.
Above aligns with the Northern Dipper, flowery canopies, purple chambers beneath the North Star.
Another account says Dōng Wáng Gōng's personal name is Ní,
courtesy name Jūnmíng.
Xī Wáng Mǔ's surname is Yáng, personal name Huí.
Zhū Rú Asks Heaven
A dwarf asked a tall man about the height of the sky,
and the tall man replied:
"I don't know."
The dwarf said:
"Though you don't know,
you are closer to it than I am."
Therefore, when inquiring about matters,
one must ask those who know.

The Heavenly Emperor Summons a Song
Sòng Hè Dàoyǎng was skilled in the art of divination through milfoil stalks.
Once he encountered a professional singing woman who had fallen ill and was near death,
so he performed a divination for her and said:
"This is not death,
but the Heavenly Emperor summoning her to sing."
He then placed a lump of earth over her heart,
and she revived shortly after.
From the History of the Southern Dynasties, regarding Hè
Yùdì jū
The Jade Emperor's abode is always embraced by crimson clouds,
making even true immortals unable to see his face.
"Biography of Assisting the Sage"
records Sū Shì's verse:
Attending ministers stand like swans in the Palace of Universal Brightness,
where a single crimson cloud upholds
the Jade Emperor.
Yùjīng
The Classic of the Five Stars states:
In heaven is the White Jade Capital,
the Golden Palace.
． The Inner Classic of the Divine Pivot and Golden Light records:
the upper realm's Jade Capital.
A commentary explains:
the Jade Capital
is the Heaven of Non-Action.
Thirty-six Heavens
From the Mystic Metropolis and Jade Capital downward,
there are altogether thirty-six heavens,
of which twenty-eight are within the Three Realms.
The six heavens of Huánglǔ Heaven, Yùwán Heaven, Hétóng Heaven, Píngyù Heaven, Wénjǔ Heaven, and Qīyào Móyí Heaven constitute the Realm of Desire;

the eighteen heavens of Yuèhéng Heaven, Méngyì Heaven, Héyáng Heaven, Gōnghuá Heaven, Zōngpiāo Heaven, Huángjiā Heaven, Tángyào Heaven, Duānjìng Heaven, Gōngqìng Heaven, Jíyáo Heaven, Yuánzǎi Kǒngshēng Heaven, Huángyá Heaven, Jífēng Heaven, Xiàománg Heaven, Wēngchóng Fúróng Heaven, Jiāngyóu Heaven, Ruǎnyuè Heaven, and Tánshì Heaven constitute the Realm of Form;
the four heavens of Xiāodù Heaven, Yuándòng Heaven, Hànchǒng Miàochéng Heaven, and Xiùlè Jìnshàng Heaven constitute the Formless Realm.

Beyond the Three Realms are called the Four Human Heavens, Chángróng Heaven, Yùlóng Téngshèng Heaven, Fàndù Heaven, and Píngyù Jiǎyì Heaven, named the Heavens of Seed People, also called the Four Brahma Heavens.
Beyond the Four Human Heavens are the Three Pure Realms:
Jade Pure, Great Pure, and Supreme Pure,
also named the Three Heavens:
Qīngwēi Heaven, Yǔyú Heaven, and Dàchì Heaven.
The uppermost is the Great Lofty Heaven,
making a total of thirty-six heavens.
"Lingbao Benyuan Jing, Yunji Qiqian"
Great Luo
The Great Canopy is in the Mystic Metropolis,
above the Jade Capital, where purple subtlety and golden towers, seven treasures, qilin, and lions transform and arise within it,
with the Celestial Venerables of the Three Worlds governing therein.
The Yuánshǐ Scripture states:
In the realm of the Great Canopy, there is no true ruler,
only the qi of the Great Brahma,
encompassing all heavens.
Above the great void, there are natural five-colored clouds,
their hue azure-yellow, called the Yellow Heaven.
Above the Yellow Heaven, its color azure-blue is called the Cāng Heaven.
Above the Cāng Heaven, its color profound and empty, tinged with blue, is called the Green Heaven.
Hence, the ode says:
Above the Three Realms,
vast and boundless is the Great Canopy.
Above, there are no roots of color,
cloud layers towering majestically.
Ninth Heaven
The first heaven among the nine heavens is named Yùdān Wúliàng Heaven,

Tiānwēng
Tiānwēng's surname was Zhāng,
given name Jiān,
courtesy name Làkě.
He was from Yúyáng.
In his youth, he was uninhibited,
with no restraints or taboos.
He once set a net and caught a white sparrow,
which he loved and kept.
He dreamed that the Heavenly Elder Liú was reproaching him angrily,
often wanting to kill him,
but the white sparrow would always inform Jiān,
who prepared various methods to await him,
so he could never be harmed.
The Heavenly Elder then descended to observe him,
and Jiān lavishly hosted him as a guest,
then secretly rode the Heavenly Elder's chariot,
mounted a white dragon,
and, whipping the reins, ascended to heaven.
The Heavenly Elder mounted another dragon to pursue him,
but could not catch up.
Once Jiān reached the Mysterious Palace,
he replaced all officials,
blocked the northern gate,
enfeoffed the white sparrow as Marquis of Shàngqīng,
and decreed that the white sparrow's descendants would not be born on the earthly realm.
Liú Wēng, having lost his governance,
wandered among the Five Peaks causing disasters,
which troubled Jiān,
so he appointed Liú Wēng as Grand Administrator of Tàishān,
in charge of the registers of life and death.

"Buddhist Scriptures"
Yáng Bèi
The heavens are round with twelve guiding principles,
the earth is square with twelve governing records.
The celestial principles revolve with three hundred and sixty cycles as one complete rotation,
the terrestrial records operate with three hundred and thirty cycles as one degree.
When the heavens complete three thousand six hundred rotations, it is called a yang surge,
when the earth turns three thousand three hundred degrees, it is called a yin eclipse.
The celestial qi reaches its extreme at the Great Yin,
the terrestrial qi exhausts itself at the Great Yang,
thus when yang is agitated, it surges,
when yin is obstructed, it eclipses,
when both yin and yang surge and eclipse,
the qi of heaven and earth reverses.
When the qi of heaven and earth reverses,
this is called a minor kalpa.
When the heavens complete nine thousand nine hundred rotations, it is called a yang eclipse,
when the earth turns nine thousand three hundred degrees, it is called a yin surge,
during yang eclipse the qi exhausts itself at the Great Yin,
during yin surge the qi reaches its extreme at the Great Yang,
thus when yin is obstructed, it eclipses,
when yang is agitated, it surges,
when both yin and yang eclipse and surge, then heaven and earth transform,
the transformation of heaven and earth is called a great kalpa.

Heaven's Adversity
The Lingbao naturally cycles through its phases,

and the Great Hundred Six;
the Lesser Yang Nine
and the Lesser Hundred Six.
Every three thousand three hundred years marks a Lesser Yang Nine and Lesser Hundred Six,
while nine thousand nine hundred years marks a Great Yang Nine and Great Hundred Six.
Heaven's calamity is called Yang Nine,
and Earth's deficiency is called Hundred Six.
After the era of Jīntiān Shì,
in the year of Jiǎshēn,
it is when the cycles of Heaven and Earth reach their end of adversity and prosperity,
and the Yang Nine and Hundred Six converge.
At that time, the Dao and virtue will shine forth,
while malevolence and chaos will erupt violently,
and a sage ruler will receive the mandate in the year of Rénchén.
"Lingbao Tiāndì Yùndù Jīng"
Heaven does not revolve to the left.
The learned Yáng Zǐyún, following popular belief,
considered heaven as a canopy constantly rotating leftward,
with the sun, moon, and stars following it east and west.
He thus illustrated their forms, paths, and movements in relation to the four seasons,
calculating times of dusk, dawn, day, and night,
intending to establish rules for the world and leave a model for posterity.
I challenged him,
saying:
"During the spring and autumn equinoxes, day and night should be equal;
at dawn, the sun rises due east at the Mao direction,
and at dusk, it sets due west at the You direction.
Now, observing from the perspective of people under heaven,
this is the human Mao-You, not heaven's;
heaven's Mao-You should correspond to the Northern Dipper's pole.
The Northern Dipper's pole is the pivot of heaven, the axis of the sky.
It is like a canopy having a central hub.
Although the canopy rotates, the hub does not move;
heaven also rotates completely,
yet the Dipper's pole remains constant,
indicating it is the center of heaven.
Looking up, it appears in the north,
not directly above people,
and during the equinoxes,
the sun rises and sets south of the Dipper.
If it were like a rotating canopy,
then the northern path would be longer,
and the southern path shorter;
how could the lengths of day and night be equal then?"
Zǐyún had no answer.
Later, while reporting affairs with Zǐyún, we sat under the corridor of the White Tiger Hall;
due to the cold, I turned my back to the sun to warm it.
After a while,
the sunlight moved away,
and my back was no longer warmed.
I used this to show Zǐyún, saying:
"If heaven is a rotating canopy and the sun moves westward,
its light and shadow should still illuminate this corridor, only shifting slightly eastward;
it should not withdraw completely.
If it withdraws, isn't that consistent with the theory of the celestial sphere?"
Zǐyún immediately abandoned his established principles,
and Confucian scholars realized that the idea of heaven's leftward rotation was incorrect.

Ten Glows
The Rites of Zhōu:
The Shìjìn official was in charge of the ten atmospheric phenomena method,
to observe ominous signs and distinguish good and bad fortune.
The first is called jìn,
referring to the five-colored qi of yīn and yáng,
where jìn and excess encroach upon each other.
Some say it is bào,
such as earrings and back jades,

The second is called xiàng,
referring to clouds resembling qi,
forming shapes and images,
such as clouds like red birds,
flying alongside the sun.
The third is called xī,
qi beside the sun piercing it,
shaped like the xī worn by children.
The fourth is called jiān,
referring to clouds and qi hovering above the sun.
The fifth is called àn,
referring to solar or lunar eclipses or dim sunlight.
The sixth is called méng,
referring to dim and unclear brightness.
The seventh is called mí,
referring to a white rainbow spanning the sky and piercing the sun.
The eighth is called xù,
referring to qi resembling mountains above the sun,
or it is said:
crowns, earrings, and back jades,
layered in order,
appear beside the sun.
The ninth is called jī,
referring to halo qi.
Or it is said:
a rainbow.
As mentioned in the Book of Songs: "A morning jī in the west."
The tenth is called xiǎng,
referring to five-colored qi,
with tangible forms,
green indicates famine,
red indicates war,
white indicates mourning,
black indicates sorrow,
yellow indicates harvest.
Or it is said:
xiǎng,
means thought.
Red qi taking the shape of humans or beasts,
can be contemplated to discern good or bad fortune.

Dreaming of Fighting
Jié acted without virtue,
so Tāng ordered Yī Yǐn to go and observe.
He spied on Xià by listening through Mò Xǐ.
Mò Xǐ said:

and a sun in the east.
The two suns fought each other.
The western sun won,
while the eastern sun was defeated."
Yī Yǐn reported this to Tāng,
who then ordered his army to march out from the east of the capital,
advancing westward. Before their blades even crossed, Jié fled.

"Records of the Emperors and Kings"
Competing in governance
King Wén of Zhōu asked Yùzǐ:
"May I ask, when a gentleman is about to assume his office,
how should he be towards his people?"
Yùzǐ replied:
"When a gentleman is about to assume his office,
he should be towards his people
bright and radiant,
like the sun at its first rising.
Once he has assumed his office,
he should be towards his people brilliantly shining,
like the sun at high noon.
After he has left his office,
he should be towards his people dim and fading,
like the sun after it has set.
Therefore, when a gentleman is about to assume office and is radiant,
it means righteousness is heard first.
When he has assumed office and shines brilliantly,
it means the people preserve their blessings.
When he has left office and becomes dim,
it means the people lose his teachings."
King Wén said:
"I accept this instruction."

On Distinguishing the Distance of the Sun
Confucius was traveling east when he saw two children arguing,
and asked them the reason.
One child said,
"I believe the sun is closer to people at sunrise,
and farther away at noon."
The other child believed the sun is farther at sunrise and closer at noon.
Confucius asked,
"How do you know this?"
One child said,
"When the sun first rises, it's as big as a carriage canopy;
by noon, it's like a plate or bowl.
Isn't this because distant things appear small while nearby things appear large?"
The other child said,
"At sunrise, the weather is cool and refreshing;
by noon, it feels like dipping into hot soup.
Isn't this because nearby things feel hot while distant things feel cool?"

King Nán'è asked Nàgāsīnuó:

its substance is one,
why is it extremely hot in summer,
and extremely cold in winter?
In summer the days are long,
in winter the days are short?"

the road is long and its movement slow,
shining upon the golden mountains,

in winter it travels the lower path,
the road is short and its movement fast,
shining upon the ocean waters,
hence the days are short and extremely cold."

while clouds obscure it

even if the capital does not witness it,
other regions are certain to see it.
This represents a profound heavenly warning
that must not be overlooked.
I have heard that during the first year of the Yǒngshǐ era of Emperor Chéng of Hàn, a solar eclipse occurred in the ninth month,
which was not visible in the regions,
but was seen in the capital.
Gǔ Yǒng interpreted this as indicating indulgence in wine,
with the disaster lying within.
In the second year, second month,
another solar eclipse occurred,
visible in the regions,
but not in the capital,
and Gǔ Yǒng interpreted this as indicating the exhaustion of the common people,
with the disaster lying outside.
In my humble opinion, Gǔ Yǒng's interpretation
does not seem to align with heavenly intent.
When the regions do not see it
but the capital does,
the disaster is still minor.
When the regions see it
but the capital does not,
the disaster grows deeper.
The sun
symbolizes the ruler,
and heaven's intent suggests that if the ruler is obscured
by yin and evil influences, with calamities clearly manifested,
so that all under heaven know of the worry and danger,
while the court alone remains unaware.
From this perspective,
the ruler should particularly engage in self-reflection,
maintain vigilance, and concern himself with the state,
yet the officials instead begin to congratulate one another.
How can this not be called mutual deception between superior and subordinate,
deceiving and inviting severe reprimand?
Moreover, the eclipse was not total,
which indicates the inaccuracy of the astronomical officials' calculations.
They should be held accountable for their faults,
and this is also no reason for congratulations."

and when easy to verify, wisdom becomes clear,

for there is a man in the moon wearing a straw raincoat and carrying a sword."

His son asked:

In the West, a month is divided into white and black.

Bright Half and Dark Half
According to Indian custom, the period from new moon to full moon is called the Bright Half,
while the period from full moon to new moon is called the Dark Half,
which may consist of fourteen days
or fifteen days,
due to the variation in the length of the lunar month.
The Dark Half followed by the Bright Half together form one month,
and six months constitute one ayana,
when the sun moves northward (Uttarāyaṇa),
and when the sun moves southward (Dakṣiṇāyana),
these two ayanas together make one year.

The Glory of Yáng
The term "star" signifies essence,
the splendor of yang,
the yang essence becomes the sun,
and the sun divides to form stars,
hence the character is formed by "sun" giving birth to "star".
"Chūnqiū Shuōtící"
The essence of primordial energy
The stars are
the essence of primordial energy.
The Three Calendars
The essence of all things,
ascends to form the arrayed stars.
"Shuōwén"
The virtue of Kūn spreads its essence,
ascending to become the multitude of stars.
"Hétú"
The qi of water and earth,
ascends to form the layered cosmos,
the essence of all things,
condenses into the arrayed constellations,

"Dù Mù's Commentary on Sūnzǐ"
Jīn zhī sàn qì
Stars are
the dispersed qi of metal.

when there are many human stars,
the state is auspicious;
if few, then inauspicious.
Mèng Kāng said:
Stars
are stone.
Metal and stone generate each other,
and humans correspond with the qi of the stars.
"Qián Astronomical Records"
The essence of mountains and rivers
The earth consists of mountains and rivers,
the essence of mountains and rivers,
ascends to form stars,
each corresponding to its respective province and city,
dividing territories into states,
creating spiritual talismans for verification.
"State Essence Talisman"
The vital energy of mountains and rivers ascends to form constellations.
"Biography of Táng Yánsīshàn"
Forms originate from the earth,
the earth has mountains, river valleys, wells and springs, rivers, cave lakes, ponds and marshes, reservoirs and wetlands, ditches and ravines, to express and release its energy.
Heaven has three hundred forty-eight constellations and stars,
also formed by the coagulation of celestial essence.
Condensed and luminous, they become stars.
Stars,
their forms originate from the earth,
their essence completes in heaven,
arranged in positions, interlocking and standing firm,
each having its own affiliations,
in the wilderness they symbolize creatures,
at court they symbolize officials,
among humans they symbolize affairs,
those distinguished by divinity,
are arranged in five columns.
These constitute thirty-five names,
one residing in the center called the Northern Dipper,
four distributed in the directions forming the twenty-eight mansions,
officials both internal and external that are constantly bright,
number one hundred twenty-four,
those that can be named are three hundred twenty,
making two thousand five hundred stars in number,
the total roughly eleven thousand five hundred twenty,
all creatures bustling with activity,
all receive their tied destinies.
"Língxiàn"
The substance of all things
Stars are
the essence of yīn and yáng,
the substance of all things,
the forms of the five elements.
Their substance is below,
while their brilliant light is in the heavens.
The fates of all officials
each follow their origin.
When they fly and move, the people become unsettled.

Xiàng Guān
The Correct Meaning of the Book of Documents states:
Heaven has the sun and moon,
shining over day and night,
just as the chief among the king's officials leads the feudal lords.
The Northern Dipper encircles the North Star,
just as the high ministers surround and guard the Son of Heaven.
The five planets move among the constellations,
just as the regional inspectors oversee the feudal lords.
The twenty-eight constellations are distributed across the four directions,
just as the feudal lords guard the territory for the Son of Heaven.
Fixed stars and various stars
The constant stars are like the high ministers and nobles,
the multitude of stars are like the common people.
When the ranked stars are in order, the multitude of stars are aligned;
when the constant stars are in disorder, the multitude of stars fall.
The Discourses on Salt and Iron

the brightest among them,
is where Tàiyǐ constantly resides.

The Three Dukes attend beside it,
feudal lords encircle and support it,
the Jade Sight-Tube and Jade Sighting-Tube,

its symbol is the pivot,

the place for all regions,

The Azure Dragon governs the east,

the positions of various states and their officials,

Běidǒu
Heaven and earth each have their own dominions;
the Northern Dipper has seven stars,
just as the Son of Heaven has seven administrative affairs.
The "Chūnqiū Héchéng Tú"
states: The seven stars of the Northern Dipper, known as Xuánjī and Yùhéng, regulate the seven administrative affairs;
the handle points to the Dragon Horn, the beam aligns with the Southern Dipper, and the bowl rests near the head of Orion.
This is called the Emperor's Chariot operating at the center,
overseeing the four directions,
dividing yin and yang,
establishing the four seasons,
balancing the five phases and their shifts,
setting the rhythms and determining all cycles,
all are connected to the Dipper.

records: The first star is Tiānshū,
the second is Xuán,
the third is Jī,
the fourth is Quán,
the fifth is Héng,
the sixth is Kāiyáng,
and the seventh is Yáoguāng.
The first to the fourth form the bowl,
the fifth to the seventh form the handle,
combined they make up the Dipper,
residing in yin and spreading yang, hence called the Northern Dipper.

The Voice and Tongue of Heaven
The Dipper serves as
the mouth and tongue of Heaven,
with the Jade Balance forming the handle and the Pivot as the Jade Sighting-Tube.
In the "Wenyao Jun,"
Lǐ Gù responded to an imperial edict, saying,
"Your Majesty has the Imperial Secretariat,
just as Heaven has the Northern Dipper.
The Dipper acts as Heaven's mouth and tongue,
and the Imperial Secretariat likewise serves as Your Majesty's mouth and tongue.
The Dipper regulates the primordial energy and balances the four seasons,
while the Imperial Secretariat issues royal decrees and governs the administration,
making it the minister who controls the energy throughout the four seas."
The "Book of the Later Han" states:
"The Heavenly principle resides in the Dipper, governing the Three Dukes,
much like the human throat in the pharynx,
managing the tongue's speech."
Sòng Jūn annotated:
"The Dipper is Heaven's mouth and tongue,
primarily responsible for issuing governance and teachings.
The Three Dukes guide and proclaim the ruler's commands,
which, when compared to humans,
should resemble the throat in the pharynx,
managing the mouth and tongue
to ensure speech is orderly and coherent."

Zhèng Xuán states that the Dipper
is the essence of the center of heaven;
when heaven loses its balance,

The Dipper's Handle

responsible for the Dipper's governance,

therefore the Dipper's Handle is also lost,
no longer visible.

shaped like a pair of eyes,
layered into three tiers,
covering the Dipper's bowl,
named the Celestial Stairs.

Sāntái
Below the Kui star are six stars,
arranged in pairs close to each other, named the Sāntái.
When the colors of the Sāntái are uniform, the ruler and ministers are in harmony;
if uneven, it indicates discord.

Tàijiē
Huángdì's Taijiē "Six Talismans Classic" states:
The Taijiē refers to
the three celestial steps.
The upper star of the upper step represents the male ruler,
the lower star represents the female ruler,
the upper star of the middle step represents the feudal lords,
the lower star represents the high ministers and officials,
the upper star of the lower step represents the senior scholars,
the lower star represents the common people.
When the three steps are level, yin and yang harmonize,
winds and rains come timely, and the gods of the land and grain all receive their proper offerings,
the harvest is abundant,
the people rest, and the world is greatly peaceful—
this is called great peace.
If they are not level, the five gods lack sacrifices,
solar eclipses occur,
water sources dry up and do not moisten the land,
crops fail to mature,
winter thunder and summer frost appear,
the common people are unsettled,
thus the way of governance collapses,
the Son of Heaven enforces tyrannical decrees,
fond of raising armies,
building palaces and towers,
expanding parks and hunting grounds—
then the upper step becomes dim and widely spaced.
Wénchāng
The six stars of the Dipper's bowl supporting the frame are called the Wénchāng Palace,
the first is called the Supreme General,
the second is called the Second General,
the third is called the Honored Minister,
the fourth is called the Director of Destinies,
the fifth is called the Director of Medium Affairs,
the sixth is called the Director of Emoluments.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Land of Abundance
The Wén Yào Gōu states:
The Wénchāng Palace serves as the celestial treasury.

the convergence of essence,

to promulgate the celestial order.

The six stars of Wénchāng lie before the Big Dipper's bowl,
serving as the six treasuries of heaven.
They govern the collective calculation of the heavenly way.
Sāngōng
The three stars south of the Dipper's handle and the three stars west of the first star of the Dipper's bowl,
are all called Sān Gōngzhǔ,
who propagate virtuous teachings and harmonies,
officials harmonizing the seven regulators and balancing yīn and yáng.

Shàng
Eastern Wall
The two stars of the Eastern Wall govern literature,
serving as the secret repository of all books under heaven.
If they appear bright in divination,
then collected texts will embody the Way,
crafty techniques will recede as petty men withdraw,
and noble persons will advance.
Otherwise,
the Son of Heaven will favor military officials,
disdain scholars of culture,
cause upright ministers who study antiquity to retreat into obscurity,
and employ those who form cliques and engage in crooked practices.

Píng Xīng
The Classic of Filial Piety: Internal Affairs states:
When the king distances himself from suspicion and distinguishes subtleties,
differentiates the noble from the base,
restrains arrogant ministers,
and pacifies rebellious sons,
then the Screen Star shines brightly for him,
moistening the Emperor's Throne and making its brilliance great.

The Screen Star and the Five Emperor's Thrones shine with moisture,
making their brilliance great.
Gōu Yǔ
The Classic of Filial Piety: Inner Affairs states:
When brothers are close,
the grace of their closeness causes the Hooked Latch not to leave the chamber.
