and because he was the emperor's maternal uncle,
he wielded court authority internally,
which Wáng Dǎo could not tolerate.
At the time, Wáng was sitting in Yěchéng,
a strong wind raised dust,
and Wáng immediately raised his fan to brush away the dust, saying:
"Yuánguī's dust sullies people."
(From "Shì Shuō")
Benevolent Influence
The Jin Yang Qiu states:
When Yuán Hóng was the governor of Dong Commandery,
Xiè Ān took Yuán Hóng's hand and presented him with a fan,
to which Yuán Hóng said:
"I shall reverently uphold and spread your benevolent influence,
to comfort the common people."
A refreshing breeze
Xiè Ān said:
When I was young, I met Prime Minister Wáng in the palace court,
and immediately felt
a refreshing breeze
gently brushing against people.
The Blue Bird Holds a Talisman
Wú Zhēnjūn once encountered a great wind,
he wrote a talisman and placed it on the roof,
where a blue bird carried it away,
and the wind immediately ceased.
"Continued Biographies of Immortals"
Sīfēng Lìngshǐ
Emperor Míng, being corpulent and detesting the wind,
would often wear a light leather garment in the summer.
He appointed two attendants as Wind-Watching Officials,
tasking them to promptly report whenever the wind arose from any direction.
From "The Book of Sòng"
Long Wind
The Book of Sòng records:
Zōng Què, whose courtesy name was Yuángàn,
when young, followed his father.
The recluse scholar Bǐng asked about his aspirations,
to which he replied:
"I wish to ride the long wind and break through the waves of ten thousand miles."
◇The "Gāotáng Fu" states:
"When the long wind arrives, the waves rise."
The "Western Capital Fu":
"The long wind strikes against the separate towers,
stirring up great billows and raising waves."
The "River Fu":
"The long wind, blowing fiercely, increases its force."
The petty man's demeanor
During the reign of Qí Shénwǔ,
in the Battle of Mángshān, wind blew from the west into the camp.
Lǐ Yèxīng said:
"When the wind comes from the direction of petty men, we shall achieve a great victory."
Shénwǔ declared:
"If we win,
I will appoint you as the governor of Běnzhōu."
Later, it indeed came true.
(From "The History of the Northern Dynasties")
The Overbearing General
Emperor Suí Yáng was boating,
when suddenly a dark wind stirred the waves.
He sighed and said:
"This wind could be called an overbearing general."
From "Qīng Yì Lù"
As if scorched by fire
After Hóu Jūnjí pacified Gāochāng,
Tàizōng intended to establish it as a commandery and county,
Chǔ Suìliáng said:
"The roads of Gāochāng,
with deserts stretching a thousand miles,
have winter winds icy and biting,
and summer winds as if scorched by fire.
Travelers encountering these often perish."
From "Essentials of Governance from the Zhēnguàn Era"
Shèngfēng
The hermit Bāo Chāomíng served Emperor Xuánzong,
and was ordered to accompany Gēshū Hàn on the western campaign.
In every battle, he always gained the advantage.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Xùn Èr Raises the Wind
Xiāo Zhìzhōng, in the first year of the Jǐngyún era, served as the governor of Jìn Prefecture.
He intended to go hunting on the day of the Là festival.
The day before,
a woodcutter on Huò Mountain saw a tall man facing the valley and letting out a long cry.
Soon, rhinoceroses, deer, boars, foxes, rabbits, pheasants, and wild geese gathered around him, numbering about a hundred.
The tall man said:
"I am the messenger of Xuánmíng,
sent by the Northern Emperor with an order.
Tomorrow, Governor Xiāo will hunt you all down.
Some of you will die by his falcon,
some by his arrows."
The herd of animals trembled with fear and begged for their lives.
An old elk knelt down and pleaded for rescue.
The messenger said:
"Yán Sì of the Eastern Valley is good at strategizing.
You may go to him and seek help."
The herd of animals followed him.
The woodcutter secretly observed them arriving at the Eastern Valley,
where there was a Taoist priest.
The old elk pleaded sorrowfully.
The Taoist priest said:
"If you ask Téng Liù to bring snow
and Xùn Èr to summon the wind,
then Governor Xiāo will not go hunting."
"Yesterday, Téng Liù lost his spouse.
If you offer him a beautiful woman,
he will immediately bring snow."
"Xùn Èr loves to drink.
If you bribe him with fine wine,
he will immediately summon the wind."
Two foxes claimed they could obtain these things.
The herd of animals dispersed. The next day, before dawn,
a fierce storm of wind and snow arrived,
lasting the entire day before it ceased.
Governor Xiāo did not go hunting.
"Records of the Mysterious and Strange"
Yínpíng Zhǐ Fēng
During the Tiānbǎo era,
one day a great wind suddenly arose.
The emperor ordered Amoghavajra to suppress it through prayer.
He requested a silver vase to perform rituals and empower it,
and shortly after, the wind calmed down.
Suddenly, a goose in the pond accidentally knocked over the vase,
and the wind resumed even more violently than before.
The emperor commanded him to stop it again,
and it ceased immediately upon his action.
The emperor then bestowed upon him the title:
Knower of the Treasury.
From "The Song Dynasty Biographies of Eminent Monks."
Fēng Shíbā Yí
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Cuī Yuánwēi one spring night in the garden encountered maidens in blue attire named:
Yáng shì, Lǐ shì, Táo shì,
and a young girl in crimson called Shí Cùcù.
Suddenly came news of Fēng Jiā Shíbā Yí's arrival,
her speech crisp and cool,
carrying an air of woodland elegance.
Cùcù said:
"We maidens in the garden
are often harassed by ill winds,
constantly seeking Eighteenth Aunt's protection.
If you, recluse, would each New Year's dawn make a vermilion banner
bearing patterns of the sun, moon, and five planets,
then at dawn on the first day of February, when the east wind stirs, erect it east of the garden -
thus shall we avoid calamity."
Cuī the following year on this day raised the banner,
that day the east wind scoured the earth, breaking trees and scattering blossoms,
yet the garden's profuse flowers remained unmoved.
Only then did Cuī realize the maidens were spirits of the flowers,
and Aunt Fēng was the wind deity.
"Records of the Unusual"
Wind-Predicting Chimes
In the Táng Qíwáng's palace, within a bamboo grove, shattered jade pieces were hung.
Every night, the sound of the jade pieces striking each other would indicate the presence of wind,
earning the name "Wind-Predicting Chimes."
From "Kāiyuán Anecdotes."
Wind-Observing Banner
In the palaces of the five kings, each erected a tall pole in their courtyards,
hanging a five-colored banner from the top of the pole.
Small golden bells were attached to the four corners of the banner,
so that when they made a sound, attendants would immediately observe the direction the banner pointed,
allowing them to discern the wind conditions from all directions.
"Kāiyuán Yíshì"
Ode to the Warm Breeze
Liǔ Gōngquán accompanied Emperor Wénzong on an excursion to the rear garden,
where they composed linked verses.
The emperor said:
"Everyone suffers from the sweltering heat,
but I love the long summer days."
Liǔ responded:
"When the warm breeze blows from the south,
the palace halls are filled with a gentle coolness."
From "The Official Biography."
Greedy Wolf Wind
In the Former Shǔ,
in the tenth month of the first year of the Xiánníng era, Wáng Yǎn visited Qínzhōu.
Upon reaching Zǐtóng, a great wind arose,
tearing off roofs and uprooting trees.
The Grand Astrologer said:
"This is the Greedy Wolf Wind.
It signifies that there will be defeated armies and slain generals."
Wáng Yǎn paid no heed.
When he reached Miángǔ, the Táng army entered his territory.
Wáng Yǎn grew fearful and hastily turned back.
The prefectures and counties wherever the Táng army reached all surrendered in welcome.
The eastern direction generates wind.
The east is where the sun begins,
the wind is the start of teachings,
acting as heaven's envoy,
issuing commands and decrees,
thus originating from the eastern direction.
When clearing skies leave mountains dusky,
and pale dust merges with horizons,
making cliffs and valleys appear as one—
this marks the wind from rocky peaks.
With yellow-white dim dust
veiling the evening sky like a wall,
only heaven's canopy remains visible—
this signals the wind from rivers and marshes.
When yellow, black, and white dust descend together,
it heralds fierce storms over mountains and wetlands.
The Inner Classic: Treatise on Five Movements states:
"Whistling chaos and splitting openings manifest wind's transformations,
while shaking, pulling, breaking, and uprooting demonstrate wind's functions."
Wind Master
The Annals of Lü Bùwéi states:
The Wind Master is called Fēi Lián.
Yìng Shào explains:
Fēi Lián is a divine bird,
capable of summoning winds.
The Songs of Chǔ records:
"Then Fēi Lián was sent to hasten and join."
The Comprehensive Records of Customs notes:
The Rites of Zhōu prescribes offering sacrifices to the Wind Master with willow torches.
The Wind Master
is the constellation Jī,
which governs winnowing and scattering,
able to bring forth winds.
Yǎng Xùn corresponds to the eldest daughter.
The eldest is the chief.
Hence it is said:
The spirit of the Wind Chief is Wù.
Therefore, the Wind Chief is worshipped on the Bǐng Xū day in the northwest,
as fire overcomes metal and acts as wood's assistant.
The Astronomical Records of Jìn states:
Jī is also called the Heavenly Rooster, governing the eight winds.
Whenever the sun and moon lodge in Jī, Bì, Zhěn, or Yì,
winds arise.
Sūnzǐ's methods of fire attack state:
When setting fires, observe the sun and moon;
if the moon is in Jī, Bì, Zhěn, or Yì,
these four lodgings are days when winds arise.
The Chūnqiū Wěi text says:
If the moon deviates from its course
and separates from Jī,
winds will raise sand.
The annotation in the Treatise on Sacrifices
by Yán Shīgǔ states:
The Wind Chief is Fēi Lián, and the Rain Master is Píng Yì.
Some interpreters consider them to be the stars Jī and Bì.
Since the records mention the twenty-eight lunar mansions
and also include the Wind Chief and Rain Master,
it is understood they are not Jī and Bì.
The Wind
Chief's name
is Fāng Dàozhāng.
The Seven Tablets
Dismemberment
The Erya says:
The sacrifice to the wind is called:
Zhé. Sun Yán explains:
After the sacrifice, the offering is torn apart,
and the sacrificial animal is scattered by the wind.
Lǐ Xún says:
For the sacrifice to the wind, the head, hooves, and skin of the sacrificial animal are broken apart,
and used in the sacrifice, hence it is called:
Zhé.
Guō Pú comments:
Nowadays, it is customary
to tear apart a dog in the middle of the main road,
saying it is to stop the wind,
which reflects this practice.
Yángjiǎo
Zhuāngzǐ said:
The back of the Peng is like Mount Tài,
its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky,
it soars ninety thousand lǐ spiraling like a sheep's horn,
piercing through the clouds,
bearing the blue sky.
Sīmǎ's annotation:
Sheep's horn,
refers to the wind spiraling upward like a sheep's horn.
Luò Bīnwáng's petition:
Spiraling like a sheep's horn to touch the heavens,
spreading the steed's hooves to soar with brilliance.
Wáng Bó's petition:
The ox's hooves are already weary,
facing the great abyss, the dragon scales rise;
the sheep's horn may be encountered,
envisioning the high road, one strokes its wings.
Alternative Names
The Erya says:
The south wind is called the kǎifēng
(as in the Odes of Bèi: "The kǎifēng comes from the south")
The east wind is called the gǔfēng
(as in the Odes of Bèi: "Gently blows")
the gǔfēng
The north wind is called the liángfēng
(as in the Odes of Bèi: "The north wind is cool")
The west wind is called the qínfēng
(as in the Greater Odes: "There is a path for the great wind")
Fénlún is called tuí
(Guǒ notes:
"A violent wind descending from above,"
as in the Minor Odes: "Only the wind and tuí")
A wind descending from above is called biāo
(the Shuōwén explains:
"Biāo is a swift wind")
It is also called fúyáo, a whirlwind
(as in the Chǔcí: "Lamenting the whirlwind")
. Piāo is the wind that arises with the sun,
bào is the wind that arises when it is overcast,
yì is the wind that brings rain and dust,
mái is as in the Monthly Orders: a swift wind is called huāngfēng,
the Fēngsútōng says:
a fierce wind is called liè,
a cool wind is called liú,
a gentle breeze is called liáo,
a light wind is called sōu,
a light wind coming from a hole is called.
The branches do not rustle.
Confucian scholars discussing the auspicious signs of great peace all mention five phenomena,
one being winds that do not cause branches to whistle.
Winds do not make branches sing.
In *Lùnhéng*,
Dǒng Zhòngshū states that in an era of great peace, winds do not sway branches,
but only open buds and break sprouts.
The *Xījīng Zájì* records
that in times of peace, yin and yang harmonize, and winds and rains are uniformly balanced,
with no regional disparities across the land.
Yet terrain has steepness and levelness, hence winds vary in speed;
even under peaceful governance, some inequalities persist.
Only when equilibrium is achieved do branches cease to whistle.
As stated in *Yì Jī Lǎn Tú*.
The demeanor of a noble person
When a wind arrives clear and bright,
and for a long time does not shake the branches and leaves of trees,
remaining two or three zhàng above the ground,
this indicates the virtue of a dragon is in the downwind direction.
If it is clear and bright but does not reach two or three chǐ,
this is the wind of a noble person.
"Fēngsú Tōng"
High and Low
When the wind is high, its path is far-reaching;
when low, its path is near.
Generally, when an extraordinary gale
lasts three days and three nights,
it affects the entire world.
If it lasts two days and two nights, it affects half the world;
if one day and one night, it extends a thousand miles.
From Bàopǔzǐ
Fast and Slow
When wind begins slowly and later accelerates, it comes from afar;
when it starts swiftly and later moderates, it originates nearby.
Generally, when wind rustles leaves, it travels ten lǐ;
when it causes branches to whistle, one hundred lǐ;
when it sways branches, two hundred lǐ;
when it sheds leaves, three hundred lǐ;
when it breaks small branches, four hundred lǐ;
when it breaks large branches, five hundred lǐ;
when it sends sand and stones flying, one thousand lǐ;
when it uproots large trees, five thousand lǐ;
all winds from whistling branches upward are winds of one hundred lǐ or more.
"Yǐ Sǐ Zhàn"
The bird's nest supports the branch.
Birds and magpies know that the year will be windy,
so they leave the tall trees and nest on side branches.
Note:
Fú,
means "side."
From Huáinánzǐ.
Birds stand facing the wind,
fish swim against the current.
Birds face into the wind,
to let their feathers lie smooth.
When a light breeze comes from an unknown direction,
one can observe which way the birds are facing.
"Suǒ Suì Lù"
The wine overflows.
The Huainanzi says:
The mutual responses among categories of things,
are mysterious and profoundly subtle,
beyond resolution by debate and argument.
Thus, when the east wind arrives, wine ferments and overflows;
this is the primordial power of creation.
It is said that clouds are the qi of the eastern direction, which is wind.
Therefore, ice cannot melt without the east wind,
and fermentation cannot overflow without the east wind.
The tiger roars.
The Chunqiu Yuanming Bao says:
When a fierce tiger roars in the valley, the wind rises—things of the same kind activate each other.
The Huainanzi says:
When a tiger roars, the valley wind arrives.
Annotation:
The tiger is a yang creature,
and belongs to the same category as the wind.
Chéng Gōngsuǐ's "Ode to the Roar" states:
Feilián drums in the deep tunnel,
and a fierce tiger responds in the central valley.
A kite cries.
When there is dust ahead, a kite is mounted and made to sound.
Annotation:
When the kite sounds, wind arises.
From "Book of Rites: Qu Li"
A Pleasant Breeze
"Rhapsody on the Capital of Wei":
The benevolent wind is like fragrant air.
Biàn Ràng's "Rhapsody on the Flowery Terrace" states:
The benevolent wind spreads in spring.
Xiè Hùn's poem "Roaming the Western Pond" says:
The benevolent wind sweeps through the lush garden.
Lǚ Xiàng comments:
It refers to the spring breeze.
Yuán Yáng of the Jin dynasty said:
Have you ever seen a bright mirror,
Weary from repeated reflections in clear streams,
Fearful of the benevolent wind?
Guāngfēng
Summoning the Soul says:
"The gentle breeze stirs the fragrant plants,
wafting over the lofty orchids."
Annotation:
"Guang feng"
refers to when the rain has ceased, the sun emerges with wind,
and the vegetation appears radiant.
The lingering wind
The Songs of Chǔ:
“The lingering winds of autumn and winter.”
The annotation states:
“Lingering means remaining.”
Xiè Língyùn’s poem:
“The early sunlight dispels the lingering winds,
The new warmth replaces the former chill.”
Yán Yánzhī’s response to Xiè’s poem says:
“Leaning on the cliff, I listen to the lingering winds.”
Lì Fēng
Zhuāngzǐ says:
A gentle breeze brings a small harmony,
a gusting wind brings a great harmony,
when a fierce wind ceases, all the apertures become empty,
yet do you alone not see how the swaying things are quivering?
Note:
A gentle breeze is a small wind,
a fierce wind is a great wind.
The Leaf-Hunting Wind
Zhōu Shēng's "Lièzǐ" says: The wind that hunts leaves does not accord with the eight seasonal nodes.
Shí Yóu Fēng
Emperor Xiaowu of Song's "Song of Supervisor Dīng" says:
I wish to become a stone wind,
cutting off travelers from all directions.
Chén Zǐ'áng's "Delayed by Wind Entering the Gorge" says:
Today in my hometown, friends
should be joyfully gathering together,
who would know the road through Bā Gorge
is made arduous by the stone wind.
Dài Shùlún's "Poem Presented to Prefect Péi":
Knowing I cannot yet depart,
I feel ashamed before the stone wind.
Láng Shìyuán's poem for Lú Qínqīng staying behind:
Though aware of our future meeting,
hard to part on this night.
Do not let this wine for an old friend
be less than the stone wind.
Lǐ Yìshān's poem:
The coming wind stores the fragrant breeze of Stone Post.
Wáng Zǐnián's "Records of Omissions" states:
In Yíngzhōu, fragrant winds occasionally arise,
cool and gentle as they start.
Spreading sleeves to catch them makes them linger for years without fading,
touching skin to make it soft and smooth.
Dust-Dispelling Wind
Mount Kūnlún has winds from all four directions,
meaning winds from east, south, west, and north arise simultaneously.
There is also a dust-dispelling wind;
if one's clothes are soiled with dust and this wind arrives to blow on them,
the garments become as clean as if washed.
"Records of Omissions"
The Plum Blossom Wind
In the fifth month, there is the Plum Blossom Wind,
which is regarded by the Jiānghuái region as the seasonal wind.
There is also continuous rain called the Plum Rain,
which ruins any clothing it touches.
"Fēngtǔ Jì"
Huángquè Wind
In the south in the sixth month, there is a prolonged southeasterly wind,
commonly called the Yellow Sparrow Wind,
for at that time sea fish transform into yellow sparrows,
hence the name.
"Records of Local Conditions"
Carp Wind
《Summary Record》:
The carp wind is the wind of the ninth month.
Lǐ Hè's poem reads:
Before the gate, the flowing water leads to Jiānglíng's way,
As the carp wind rises, the lotus blooms wither.
Additionally, an ancient lyric states:
Auspicious clouds form brocade, reflecting on the skiff,
While the carp wind rises.
Trade Wind
Boats on the Yangtze and Huai Rivers sailing upstream
often wait for the northeast wind, called the trade wind.
In the seventh and eighth months there is the early trade wind,
in the third month the bird trade wind,
and in the fifth month the wheat trade wind.
"Supplement to the National History"
Flower Message Wind
Xú Kǎi's "Records of the Year" states:
Flowers bloom in the third month,
called Flower Message Wind.
"Miscellaneous Records of Dōnggāo":
In Jiangnán, from early spring to early summer, every five days there is a period of wind known as Flower Message Wind.
The plum blossom wind comes first,
the chinaberry blossom wind comes last.
There are twenty-four periods in total, marking the end of cold.
Later, a poet wrote:
After the chinaberry blooms, the scenery is lovely,
When plums turn yellow, the rain is heavy.
Xú Shīchuān wrote:
On the 105th day, Cold Food Festival rain,
Twenty-four periods of Flower Message Wind.
Another ancient poem says:
Early rice glistens after rain clears,
Bitter chinaberry flower wind blows as days grow long.
Hurricane
The "Lingnan Lu" states:
In Lingnan, the powerful winds of autumn and summer are called jù,
which start at noon and cease by midnight.
They topple houses and stiffen trees, and in severe cases, lift roof tiles like flying butterflies,
occurring once every few years or two to three times a year.
The "Nanyue Zhi" states:
During the Xī'ān period, jù winds were frequent,
and jù refers to a wind that blows from all four directions.
It is also said:
These fearsome winds often occur in the sixth and seventh months,
and three days before they arrive,
even chickens and dogs become restless.
The larger ones may last up to seven days,
while the smaller ones last one or two days.
Foreigners refer to them as the "Black Wind Ridge."
The "Biaolu Yiyun" records that in the South Sea during autumn and summer,
sometimes the clouds appear turbid,
with a halo like a rainbow,
six to seven feet long.
This phenomenon signals the imminent arrival of a jù wind, hence it is called the jù.
If a sudden clap of thunder is heard, the jù wind will not occur.
Sailors often use this as a sign
to prepare in advance.
The "Pānyú Zá Jì" states:
Before a jù wind strikes,
there is a light breeze and drizzling rain,
starting gently and then intensifying,
which is called the "tempering wind."
Sailing Wind
In Wúzhōng, the rainy season had just passed,
when a refreshing breeze arrived abruptly.
This wind, lasting for about ten days, is called the "merchant ship wind."
It is said that when merchant ships first return from overseas, this wind brings them back.
According to the "Suǒsuì Lù,"
in Wúzhōng, every summer, the southeast wind blows for several days,
sometimes even lasting over ten days before stopping.
The people of Wúzhōng call it the "merchant ship wind."
It is believed that overseas ships pray to the gods to obtain this wind,
riding it to reach the Zhèjiāng region.
In Sū Dōngpō's "Poem of Wúzhōng," he wrote:
"Thirty days have passed since the rainy season ended,
and the merchant ship wind arrives from afar."
As recorded in the "Táng Xī Shīhuà."
Ancient Airs
A wind that tears off roofs and breaks trees is called a furious wind,
one that raises sand and rolls stones is called a wild wind,
one that swirls and turns repeatedly is called a chaotic wind,
a sudden, violent wind,
appearing and vanishing abruptly is called a tempest.
A wind that rises vigorously and swirls alone is called a surging wind,
one that spirals upward like a whirlwind is called a whirlwind.
A wind that comes cool, gentle, and mild,
without stirring up dust, is called a harmonious wind.
"Yǐsī Zhàn"
The Four Winds
The "Nányuè Zhì" states: The Xī'ān region is often windy, commonly known as the wind from all directions.
Wǔ Fēngxìn
In Wú custom, the fifth day of the tenth month is considered the birthday of the Five Winds.
Over a thousand fishing families from Tài Lake prepare grand offerings of livestock and wine to feast the various gods in the lakeside temples and pray.
If there is wind on this day, then wind and rain will arrive as expected every five days,
continuing this way throughout the year,
allowing them to set sail and catch fish.
This is called the Five Winds prophecy.
Sea breeze
The perils of sea routes are called the foolish wind,
and the black wind.
When the foolish wind arises,
it howls furiously for days on end without cease.
The four directions become indistinguishable.
The black wind, however, darkens the sky,
blurring the distinction between day and night.
"The Illustrated Classic"
Jùnfēng
In the first month, there is a Jun wind,
Jun means
great,
a great wind,
the south wind.
Why is the south wind considered great?
Ice must melt with the south wind,
life must begin with the south wind,
and harvest must come with the south wind.
Therefore, it is called great.
From the "Da Dai Li"
Gāngfēng
Kites and sparrowhawks spreading their wings cannot move,
forty li above the ground,
the wind's force is fierce and strong, verifiable,
there exists a world of violent winds.
Bàopǔzǐ
Fēngshān
Ten miles west of the old city of Běiwū County lies Fēngshān,
where there is a cave as round as a wheel,
from which winds blow ceaselessly, creating a desolate atmosphere.
Fēngmén Shān
On Fēngmén Mountain there is a stone gate,
over a hundred zhang above the ground.
When wind is about to arise,
this gate faintly emits black vapor rising upward,
and within moments a black wind spreads across the sky.
"Records of Wǔlíng"
Fēng Mǔ
The wind mother emerges from Jiǔdé County,
resembling an ape.
Upon seeing people, it appears ashamed,
but extends its neck to strike and kill.
If it obtains wind, it revives.
"Liú Xīnqī's Records of Jiāozhōu"
Wind Well
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Records of Jīngzhōu" states:
In Yíyōu Hěngshān County,
there is a mountain with a wind cave,
its opening several feet wide,
named Wind Well.
In summer, wind blows out,
in winter, wind blows in.
When the wind enters or exits,
it cleanses the surroundings constantly.
Passing by in hot months, one feels a chill.
Someone wearing fur garments thought Yuán Shānsōng said:
Wind emerges in summer and enters in winter,
remaining still at the spring and autumn equinoxes.
I went to observe it,
at the time in the fourth month,
standing several zhang away from the cave, in a moment,
I shivered from cold.
It is said that by the middle of the sixth month,
it becomes even more unbearable to visit.
Someone passing by in winter left a bamboo hat in the cave,
the wind drew it in, and after a full day it returned,
retrieved at Bùyáng Creek,
thus revealing its hidden connection.
"Water Classic"
Fēngxué
On Lóngshān's stones there are often traces of immortals and dragons,
hence the mountain's name.
On its four slopes there are large caves,
each as large as a carriage wheel.
In spring, wind emerges from the east,
in autumn from the west,
in summer from the south,
and in winter from the north.
They never disrupt this order.
A monk named Fǎměng once entered the eastern cave in summer,
and saw stone chambers and stone figures.
Wishing to explore all the caves,
he suddenly heard someone sternly say:
"Reverend, the other caves are like the eastern one, you should not come to see them."
Fǎměng was startled,
and found himself outside the cave without realizing how.
From "Xíng Zǐlì's Geographical Records"
A dog emerges from a burrow.

Seeing Clouds, Knowing Wind
To the right of Bái'á Shān there is a huge cave like a well,

Around the mouth of the cave, moisture glistens like sweat,
occasionally emitting vapor
that rises into the sky, forming white clouds.
In a short while, the wind begins to roar like thunder.
The villagers, upon seeing the clouds, know the wind is coming; when the vapor disperses, the wind calms.
If the vapor is fine, the wind is small;
if abundant, the wind is fierce.
If the cave is blocked, though the wind lessens, the people suffer more from miasma;
if opened, the wind returns as before and the miasma also diminishes.
Wind Wheel

Purifying,

Thunder,
is the drum of Heaven.

When yin and yang combine, they form thunder.

When the qi of yin and yang gather together, they become thunder.

Accumulated wind becomes thunder.

The Gǔliáng Zhuàn

"Tíng"
is the lingering sound of thunder,

The Wǔjīng Tōngyì explains:
Both "zhèn" and "tíng" refer to thunderclaps.

The Eldest Son of Heaven and Earth
Thunder is the firstborn between heaven and earth,
because it leads all things in their emergence and withdrawal.
When yang is active for one hundred and eighty-three days, it ends;
when yin is active for one hundred and eighty-three days, it also ends.
Thunder emerges from the earth in the second month,
for one hundred and eighty-three days;
when thunder emerges, all things emerge.
In the eighth month, it withdraws into the earth for one hundred and eighty-three days;
when thunder withdraws, all things withdraw.
This is its constant pattern.
Thus, if thunder is at peace, all things are at peace;
if thunder is harmful, all things are harmed.
It is like a state:
if the ruler is at peace, the state is at peace;
if the ruler is harmful, the state is harmed.
"Hóng Fàn Lùn"
In the Yì, thunder emerges in the second month,
its hexagram is called Yù,
signifying that all things follow thunder out of the earth,
all in ease and comfort.
It enters in the eighth month,
its hexagram is called Guī Mèi,
signifying thunder returns.
Entering the earth, it nurtures roots and kernels,
protects and stores hibernating insects,
avoiding the harm of extreme yīn,
emerging from the earth, it fosters the growth of blossoms and fruits,
develops and reveals what is hidden,
spreading the virtue of abundant yáng.
Entering, it can eliminate harm,
emerging, it can promote benefit,
symbolizing the ruler.
"Wǔ Xíng Zhuàn"
states thunder arises in the eleventh month with Huáng Zhōng,
peaks in the second month,

Warding off Yin and eliminating harm
Confucius said:
When thunder first arises, it signifies the beginning of vigor, where the ruler is weak and the ministers strong.
Starting from the hexameter Jiě:
Thunder is
that which initiates the sprouting of buds,
expels the yin and eliminates harm.
All things depend on thunder to break free,
and rely on rain for moisture.
Thus, the classic states:
Thunder stirs them,
rain moistens them.
If the king honors leniency and follows the spring ordinances, thunder will respond in season;
otherwise, it will erupt in winter,
when it should be dormant instead.
Therefore, the Yì Zhuàn says:
When thunder should sound but does not,
it is because the sun is weak.

Order

Thunder is
a command,

thunder shakes and dispels stagnation.

To fend off difficulties and turn the tide
Why do the five stars observe clouds, thunder, and lightning killing people?
Thunder is Heaven's minister who repels calamities and resolves conflicts.
If the ruler adheres to regulations, thunder will restrain violence accordingly;
if humans usurp the power of reward and punishment, then thunder and lightning will kill people.
"Jīng Fáng's Commentary on the Yì Jīng"
Thunder is the agitated energy of the sun.
Thunder is the agitated energy of the sun.
In the first month, yang energy stirs, so thunder begins in the first month.
In the fifth month, yang energy is at its peak, so thunder is rapid in the fifth month.
In autumn and winter, yang energy declines, so thunder lies dormant in autumn and winter.
During the height of summer, the sun governs affairs.
Yin energy takes advantage of this.
When yin and yang struggle against each other, they clash and contend.
Clashing and contending leads to violent ejection.
Violent ejection produces poison.
If it strikes a person, the person dies immediately.
If it strikes a tree, the tree breaks.
If it strikes a house, the house collapses.
If a person is under a tree or inside a house and is accidentally struck, they die.

Shocking a Hundred Miles
The Apocrypha on the Analects says:
Thunder shakes a hundred lǐ,
its sound reaches accordingly.
Sòng Jūn annotates:
Because thunder moves across a hundred lǐ, it is thus used to model the state's governance;
the sound of thunder represents how far the policies and teachings of the feudal lords extend,
reaching those nearby.
Lì Yán's Response to Matters states:
Someone asked, "Thunder's shock is said to alarm a hundred lǐ—
how do we know this?"
Yán replied:
"We know it by its numerical principle.
Yang in motion corresponds to nine,
its number being thirty-six;
yin in stillness corresponds to eight,
its number being thirty-two.
When one yang moves, two yin follow—
hence it is called a hundred lǐ."
The Discourses Weighed in the Balance states:
Winds differ across a thousand lǐ;
thunder is not shared within a hundred lǐ.
Storing Ice and Discarding Ice
When ice is stored in accordance with the season, thunder occurs without causing shock,
but if stored ice is discarded unused, thunder will not manifest yet cause shock.

Yángshēng

The Wrath of Heaven
The Lùn Héng states:
People call thunder and lightning the wrath of heaven,

is the voice of heaven's anger.

Thunder shatters and lightning flashes—that is heaven's wrath,
yet it cannot last a full morning.
With a sage ruler on the throne,
how could there be wrath against a minister lasting an entire generation!

Attacking the Qí Platform
The Huainanzi says:
A commoner woman cried out to Heaven, and thunder and lightning struck down at Duke Jǐng,
causing the terrace to collapse, his limbs to be injured and broken,
and the sea to flood greatly.
Xǔ Shèn's commentary states:
She was a lowly woman,
a widow from Qí,
childless,
who did not remarry but served her mother-in-law,
with diligence and respect.
She had no sons but had a daughter,
and the daughter coveted her mother's wealth,
urging her mother to remarry.
The widow firmly refused,
so the daughter killed her mother and falsely accused the widow.
The widow, unable to clear her name, cried out to Heaven in grievance,
and Heaven responded with thunder and lightning,
striking down at Duke Jǐng's terrace,
causing it to collapse and be destroyed,
injuring Duke Jǐng's limbs,
and making the sea flood greatly as a result.

In Húyáng County,

Clearing False Accusations
In Hénán, Lǐ Shūqīng served as an official,
and was recommended for the Filial and Incorrupt examination.
A fellow candidate envied him.
He had a maidservant spread rumors that Shūqīng had committed adultery with his widowed sister.
His sister, grieved by the accusation of adultery,
went to the government office and committed suicide.
Shūqīng also took his own life to prove his innocence.
He had done nothing wrong.
Three years later, a thunderbolt struck the one who had harmed Shūqīng,
placing his corpse before Shūqīng's grave.
His family retrieved and buried it,
but in autumn, thunder again struck open the tomb.

Unfazed by an earthquake

yet his expression remained unchanged,

when Liú Yào was eight years old,

when lightning struck the tree,
all others nearby fell to the ground,
but Yào remained calm and unperturbed,

Moving the cypress to avert disaster
Prime Minister Wáng ordered Guō Pú to perform a divination for him.
When the hexagram was completed,
Guō's expression turned very grim, and he said:
"Your Excellency is facing the calamity of being struck by lightning."
Wáng asked if there was any way to avert or overcome it.
Guō replied:
"Take a carriage and head west for several miles.
There you will find a cypress tree.
Cut a section equal to your height,
and place it on the bed where you usually sleep.
Then the disaster can be averted."
Wáng followed his advice.
A few days later, the cypress was indeed struck and shattered by lightning,
and his family members all celebrated.
The Grand General remarked:
"So you simply shifted the blame onto a tree."

Attack the large vessel
Gù Xié served as the Transmission Secretary,
when in the second year of the Datong era, thunder struck the Grand Bridge,
and the magistrate of Jiankang County immediately submitted a report.
Xié considered this inauspicious
and did not promptly present it to the emperor.
When the emperor later learned of this, he said:

and secondly to reveal my own faults.

Pīlì Yǔn
Shénwǔ once inspected horses at the northern pasture road,

so Shénwǔ ordered Xuē Gūyán to investigate it.

"Miscellaneous Records of Exile to the Wilderness"
by Dīng Wèi records:
Old accounts say seven li south of Qīnzhōu there was a thunder that lifted water,
now known as Nándù.
Originally, a local named Chén had no son,
but while hunting, he obtained a large egg,
over a foot in circumference,
and brought it home.
Not knowing what it was,
one day it suddenly cracked open with a clap of thunder,
immediately giving birth to a son.
They nurtured and raised him, and he continued their family line.
The villagers regarded it as extraordinary and called him:
"Thunder Seed" in the second year of Chén Tiānjiàn.
Léigōngjiā Shù
About ten li west of the state in the Táng Dynasty, there was a large locust tree,
struck by a thunderbolt,
split open several zhàng wide,
with the thunder god trapped within the tree,
roaring like a thunderclap.
At that time, Dí Rénjié was the military governor,
and with his guests and attendants, he went to observe.
The crowd all recoiled in fear,
none daring to advance.
Rénjié alone rode straight forward on horseback,
approached and questioned him.
He then explained that a rebellious dragon was in the tree,
and he had been ordered to pursue it but lost his power and could not endure,
thus getting trapped by the tree.
If someone would rescue him,
he would richly repay the kindness.
Rénjié ordered sawyers to cut the tree open, and only then did he emerge.
Afterward, he would always report in advance on matters of fortune and misfortune.
Division of Boundaries
During the Kāiyuán era, the boundary between Zhāngzhōu and Quánzhōu was unfairly divided,
leading to mutual lawsuits filed at the central government.
For years, imperial envoys were unable to resolve the dispute.
One day, a sudden great thunderstorm occurred,
with a clap of thunder,
causing a cliff to split open in the middle.
The contested land expanded into a path,
which then became an official road.
Inside the cliff were six lines of square seal script comprising twenty-four characters,
each several feet wide, which no one could decipher.
At the beginning of the Zhēnyuán era, an exile named Lǐ Biàn interpreted them, saying:
"Zhāngzhōu and Quánzhōu,
divide the land in great peace,
Yǒng'ān and Lóngxī,
with lofty mountains and clear air,
unconfused for a thousand years,
serving as a model for all eternity."
The mentioned Yǒng'ān and Lóngxī
are the names of border villages in the two prefectures.
From "Records of Strange Events in Zhāngzhōu and Quánzhōu."
Fāngshì Summoning Thunder
Emperor Xuánzōng once summoned the mountain hermit Bāo Chāo on a winter day,
ordering him to summon thunder.
Chāo responded:
"Tomorrow around noon there will be thunder."
The emperor then ordered Gāo Lìshì to oversee this,
and Chāo performed rituals and magic throughout the night.
By dawn until late morning,
the sky remained completely clear without a trace of clouds.
Lìshì grew fearful,
but Chāo said:
"General, look at the southern mountains—
there should be black energy like a plate forming."
Lìshì looked and it was as Chāo had said;
shortly afterward, wind arose,
the black energy spread everywhere,
and several claps of fierce thunder sounded.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Thunderbolt Vehicle
Lǐ Yōng was in Jièxiū County of the Northern Capital,
where commoners delivering documents stopped overnight at the Jìn Temple.
At midnight, someone knocked on the door, saying:
"The King of Jièxiū temporarily requests the Thunderbolt Chariot,
to harvest wheat in Jièxiū on a certain day."
After a long while, several people were seen carrying an object like a banner pole,
with flags and streamers attached in a ring on top,
the streamers having a total of twenty-eight leaves,
each leaf glowing like lightning.
They raised it and handed it over.
The commoners informed all neighboring villages,
but the villagers did not believe it.
On that day, clouds and mist covered the sky over Jiè Mountain,
pouring rain like ropes,
with roaring winds and thundering, damaging over a thousand qǐng of wheat.
Several villages sued the commoners for sorcery.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Léi Gōng's appearance
In the fourth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
in Xuānzhōu, there was suddenly a great thunderstorm,
and a creature fell to the ground.
It had a pig's head, hands and feet with two digits each, holding a red snake,
which it was biting.
Soon, the clouds darkened and it disappeared.
People made drawings of it and circulated them.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
In Léizhōu, there are frequent thunderstorms in spring and summer,
occurring daily without fail.
In autumn, they burrow into the ground,
their appearance resembling that of a pig,
and people capture and eat them.
"Guóshǐ Bǔ"
There was once a resident of Léizhōu
who, during a great thunderstorm,
saw a creature in the air
with a pig's head and scaly body,
of very strange appearance.
The man swung his knife and struck the creature, causing it to fall to the ground.
Blood flowed on the road, and the thunder grew even more violent.
That night, it ascended into the sky and departed.
Afterward, the house of the man who wielded the knife
was frequently struck by heavenly fire.
Among the residents of Léizhōu who draw images of thunder for worship,
all depict it with a pig's head and scaly body.
"Tóuhuāng Zálù"
Zhèn Línfǔ
In June of the first year of the Yuánhé era,
a courtesan in Huìzhōu was struck dead by lightning in the city street,
with vermilion characters inscribed under her arm,
reading "Lǐ Línfǔ",
who abused power through cruelty and manipulation of authority,
and was ordered by the Emperor to be struck dead by lightning.
"Records of Lóngchéng"
Suppress the rebellious minister in the palace.
During the Yuánhé period, Lǐ Shīdào occupied Qīng and Qí,
neither paying tribute nor making visits to the court. Emperor Xiànzōng ordered a general to campaign against him.
The imperial army was unsuccessful, and Lǐ Shīdào became increasingly arrogant.
He then constructed a new palace, imitating the emperor's main courtyard,
and chose an auspicious day to reside there.
That evening, clouds and darkness swiftly gathered,
with wind and rain like a tumult,
followed by thunderous strikes,
causing collapse and ruin.
Shortly after, it was further engulfed by heavenly fire,
leaving nothing behind.
The people of Qīng and Qí looked at one another and said,
"A minister rebelling against the ruler
is punished by heaven.
How can his transgressions be forgiven?"
A little over ten days later,
Lǐ Shīdào was indeed executed.
"Xuānshì Zhì"
Zhèn Temple
When Xiāo Huàn first arrived in Suìzhōu,
he had two banner poles made,
which he donated to the temple for its vegetarian feast.
After the celebration concluded with music,
suddenly a violent thunderclap struck the poles,
shattering them into dozens of pieces.
The following year,
on the day of the thunderclap, Huàn died.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The urn is placed on the beam.
Yuán Zhěn had an estate in Jiǎqiàn, Xiāngzhōu, Jiāngxià.
Just as the roof beam was completed in the newly built hall,
during a fierce wind and heavy rain, estate tenants were delivering six or seven jars of oil.
Suddenly, a thunderclap sounded,
and all the oil jars lined up on the beam,
without a single drop spilled.
That year, Yuán passed away.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Splitting mountains and filling valleys
Dōngyáng Commandery borders the Zhè River,
where a mountain spans several hundred lǐ in circumference.
The river curved and encircled it,
causing delays and difficulties for boat traffic, which troubled people greatly.
During the Tàihé era, the Regular Attendant Jìng Xīn was appointed as its governor.
One evening, the clouds darkened at dusk,
and violent winds, thunder, and lightning stirred tumultuously.
Houses and the river surged and overflowed,
leaving everyone in fear and confusion.
By dawn, it finally cleared.
People went to see the scene
and found the mountain had been split down the middle,
separated by several hundred paces,
allowing the river to flow straight through it.
The curved sections were filled with stones,
thus eliminating the problem of winding obstruction.
(Records from the Xuānshì Hall)
Five brothers
Yè Qiānsháo once took shelter from the rain,
and rescued the Thunder God trapped between trees.
The next day, the Thunder God gave him a scroll of ink script, saying:
"By following this, you can summon thunderstorms,
cure illnesses and suffering,
and achieve merits by saving people.
I have four brothers,
and if you need to hear thunder,
just call for Thunder Two.
Thunder Five has a fierce and impatient nature—
unless it's a critical emergency,
do not summon him."
From then on, Yè used talismans to summon rain,
all with remarkable effects.
Once, while drunk in Jízhōu,
he was insulted by the governor.
He then loudly called for Thunder Five.
At that time, the commandery was suffering from a severe drought,
but suddenly, violent thunder and lightning erupted.
The governor descended the steps to greet him respectfully,
begging him to bring rain.
Within two days, the land was thoroughly soaked,
and this incident became widely known.
"Biographies of Divine Immortals' Responses"
Léi Shén Yí Chuáng
Wú Chái Zàiyòng was in Guāngzhōu,
when one day there was a great clap of thunder.
His family members all crouched and hid,
but Zàiyòng remained in the doorway,
sitting upright without moving.
Soon, four figures in short jackets and trousers appeared,
carrying Zàiyòng on a broken bed out into the courtyard.
Amidst another great clap of thunder,
the house split open and a dragon emerged.
From "Jiǔ Guó Zhì"
Léi Gōng Lù
In the region of Bāshǔ,
on high mountain peaks or clean grounds,
they built altars to the Lord of Heaven,
to pray for rain during droughts.
These were established according to the rituals and methods descended from the Supreme Deity during the Kāiyuán era,
to instruct people.
If the altars were desecrated by cattle or sheep,
or if those preparing for the fast drank alcohol or ate meat,
they were often struck dead by lightning.
Wáng Ráo of Xīnfán,
while visiting his other estate,
was hosted by villagers who cooked pork for him.
A man returning from the Lord of Heaven fast
joined the feast and ate meat.
Wáng asked him:
"Aren't you afraid of thunder?"
The man replied:
"I am brothers with thunder,
what is there to fear?"
Intrigued, Wáng inquired further,
and the man said:
"I possess the Register of Léigōng,
sharing the same duties as thunder."
Wáng examined his register and
found it to be true.
There were also several scrolls—
one depicted a strong man
punching the ground to create a well,
named the Fist-Well;
another showed a scholar carrying firewood,
called the Valley of Firewood;
and one with seven hands scooping and winnowing,
titled the Seven-Mountain Winnow.
At the residence of Lǐ the Daoist in the eastern village of Jiānglíng,
such a register was also kept,
said to be
the Jade Cavern Method Register.
(From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán")
Mistaken Strike
In Jiāngxī Village, someone was struck dead by lightning,
and then a voice from the sky called out:
"A mistake has been made,
you can pound earthworms into a paste and apply it to the navel,
and he will recover." They did as instructed, pounding the earthworms, and he revived.
"Records of the Spirits"
Striking Down Jealousy
Mǐn Wáng Yánhàn,
son of Zhōngyì Wáng Shěnzhī,
had a wife from Bólíng of the Cuī clan who was fierce, jealous, and cruel.
She once bound her maids with silk cords and whipped them,
only stopping when the cords turned crimson with blood.
She also used a wooden palm to slap people.
One day during the height of summer,
without a trace of cloud, a thunderclap struck,
killing her in the central courtyard.
Some said:
"Zhōngyì's sudden death
was due to Bólíng's poisoning."
"Stories of the Five States"
Attack on Zhāng Dūn
Zhāng Dūn,
during Emperor Huīzōng's reign, was demoted to Registrar of Léizhōu,
and after his death, when Emperor Qīnzōng was captured and taken north to Tánzhōu,
lightning struck among the people,
revealing vermilion writing on a man's back:
"Traitorous Minister Zhāng Dūn."
From "Nán Jìn Lù".
Léigōngmò
West of Léizhōu stands a temple to the Thunder God,
where the local people annually contribute thunder drums and thunder chariots.
If anyone consumes yellow fish and pork together,
they are immediately struck by thunder,
and all hold the deity in reverence and awe.
After every heavy thunderstorm,
many people gather dark stones from the fields, calling them Thunder God's inkstones.
When struck, they produce a clanging sound,
gleaming and smooth as lacquer.
Moreover, at sites struck by thunderbolts,
or within earth or wood, wedge-shaped objects resembling axes are found,
known as thunderbolt wedges.
When carried by children, they ward off fright and evil spirits;
when ground and ingested by pregnant women, they serve as a labor-inducing remedy,
both proving effective.
"Lingbiǎo Lù Yì"
In all legal disputes, when submitting petitions,
it is considered advantageous to write with Thunder God's ink mixed with ordinary ink.
"Tóuhuāng Zálù"
Pīlì Zhēn
West of Yùmén there is a country,
within the country there is a mountain,
on the mountain stands a shrine,
the people of the country annually produce several thousand stone anvils and deliver them to the shrine,
named thunderbolt anvils,
supplied for the thunderbolts' use.
From the spring thunder, the anvils are taken out and daily diminish until by autumn they are exhausted.
"Records of the Mysterious Middle"
Fú tà
On the Yúcì Mountain there is a bird named Tuófēi;
wearing its feathers
makes one unafraid of thunder.
"Classic of Mountains and Seas"
Eating Fish
In the Zhèngguò River there are flying fish,
and eating them makes one unafraid of thunder.
Guō Pú's eulogy says:
"Flying fish resemble pigs,
with red patterns and no feathers.
Eating them wards off weapons,
and one becomes unafraid of thunder's sound."
From the "Classic of Mountains and Seas"
Léi Xué
In Xīngzhōu there is a place called Thunder Cave,
whenever thunder sounds, water fills the cave,
and fish follow the current,
so the local people always wait for the thunder,
set nets around the trees,
and catch countless fish.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Léi Táng
In Liǔzhōu there are Thunder Mountain and Rain Cliff,
from which the East and West Thunder Waters emerge,
accumulating in the cliff called:
Thunder Pond can emit vapor,
the vapor forms thunderstorms and transformations,
when luminous phenomena appear for prayers,
using sacrificial fish, beans, and swine,
with dried meat, polished rice, glutinous rice, dark wine, and piety, then there will be a response.
"Liǔ Wén"
The sound of thunder,
the Tuṣita Heaven produces chanting melodies,
the Jambudvīpa continent produces tidal wave sounds.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Diāoléi
The deities of the Thunder Department toil by day and labor by night,
facing flogging for minor offenses and execution for major ones,
carving clouds and engraving thunder without cease,
summoning dragons and commanding crows to halt their activities.
from The Jade Pivot Classic
Identical
Hòu Hàn Huán Tán's memorial states briefly:
The common saying "thunder-like agreement,"
is carefully understood by the refined in their elegant plans. Note:
When thunder produces its sound,
all things respond in unison.
Vulgar people lack a sense of right and wrong;
when their spoken words agree, it is called "thunder-like agreement."
Féng Yǎn's "Xiǎn Zhì Fù" says:
Chaotically flowing towards power and profit,
they cling to thunder-like agreement and envy difference.
Thunder God
In Léizé there is the Thunder God,
with a dragon's head and a human body,
who produces thunder by drumming on his belly.
"Shānhǎi Jīng"
Five Thunders
The Jade Firmament Mansion governs the thirty-six heavens,
the central offices in the inner court,
the Eastern and Western Magnolia Terraces,
the mysterious lodges and marvelous pavilions,
the four offices and six departments along with various bureaus each divided into specialized sections,
all collectively administering the Five Thunders and overseeing the Three Realms.
Yùshū Jīng
Léi Gēng
When thunder startles the underworld,
on cloudy and foggy evenings it is called thunder tilling.
At dawn, one will surely find traces of plowing in the fields,
and having this is considered an auspicious sign.
"Miscellaneous Records of Exile to the Wilderness"
Léi Zàng
The villagers carved caves into the mountains,
offering various tributes to the thunder god,
hoping the thunder would enjoy them,
hence the name Léi Zàng (Thunder Treasury).
"Fānyú Zájì"
Léi Láng
When a commoner's daughter is possessed by a deity,
she is called Léilángdézǐ,
meaning "Thunder Child."
Ibid.
Jade Tiger
There was a jade tiger in the wilderness of Zīyě,
which roared like thunder in the morning.
The sage, sensing the auspicious timing, rose to prominence.
"Kuòdì Zhuàn"
Do not cover the sauce
Thunder does not cover the sauce,
as the common saying goes, it is when people's stomachs rumble.
According to the "Fengsu Tong",
during the first and last quarters of the moon,
touching the sauce will spoil it,
a taboo among the local customs.
From the "Piya".
Restrain demeanor and conduct
When thunder is about to sound,
those who do not guard their demeanor,
born of unpreparedness,
will surely meet with calamity.
The "Monthly Ordinances" state:
Children conceived during thunder and lightning will inevitably suffer from madness.
"The Mysterious Woman's Bedchamber Classic"
Explanation of Thunder
The *Shuōwén* states:
Lightning is the dazzling radiance produced by the interaction of yīn and yáng.
The *Zìzhǐ* says:
It is the sudden, flickering light of lightning.
The *Shìmíng* explains:
It means "to annihilate,"
for it appears abruptly and vanishes in an instant.
Lightning
Electricity is called thunder's light.
"Wǔjīng Tōngyì"
sunlight
The "Yueling" chapter of the Book of Rites states:
In the second month, lightning begins to appear. The commentary explains that lightning is the light of yang energy,
when yang is weak, its light is not visible.
In this month, yang energy gradually strengthens,
striking against yin energy,
thus its light becomes visible.
Yīnyáng fēn zhēng
Zēngzǐ said:
When the energies of yin and yang interact, lightning is produced.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
Yin energy lies hidden beneath the Yellow Springs,
While yang energy ascends and connects with the heavens.
When yin and yang struggle and separate, lightning occurs.
Lièquē
"Rhapsody of the Great Man":
Penetrating the inversion of Lièquē,
Jìng Fúqián said:
It is the flash of heaven.
"Book of Former Han"
"Rhapsody on Contemplating the Mysterious"
Lièquē shines brilliantly illuminating the night.
Zhāng Héng said:
It is lightning.
"Book of Later Han"
Biting and snapping Lièquē, striking and flashing brilliantly.
The commentary says:
Lièquē,
is the movement of striking thunder,
flashing brilliantly,
is the radiance of scorching lightning.
"Yuán Bāo"
The Yuezhi presented a fierce beast,
its two eyes like the intersecting light of heaven's brilliant flashes.
"Records of the Ten Continents"
Proclaiming Radiance
In an age of great peace,
electricity does not dazzle the eyes,
but merely displays its radiance.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Winding around the Dipper
Huángdì of the Yǒuxióng clan, his mother was called:
Fù Bǎo, daughter of the Yǒujiǎo clan.
She saw a great flash of lightning encircling the Northern Dipper,
with the Pivot Star illuminating the outskirts and wilderness.
Fù Bǎo was affected and became pregnant.
"Records of Emperors and Kings"
Tiānxiào
"Immortal Biographies and Forgotten Records":
Lord Mù and a jade maiden were playing pitch-pot,
and if the arrow failed to enter, heaven would chuckle for them.
Note:
"Chuckle"
means to open the mouth and laugh.
"Classic of Divine Marvels":
Lord Dōngwánggōng and a jade maiden were playing pitch-pot,
and if the arrow, when tossed, missed or failed to be caught,
heaven would laugh for them,
opening its mouth and streaming light—
which is what we now call lightning.
Summoning Thunder and Lightning
The Queen Mother of the West said:
Dōngfāng Shuò was an immortal official of Mount Tài,
sent by the Supreme Deity,
appointed by the Three Heavens to command fate.
Yet Shuò only indulged in roaming mountains and waters for amusement,
presumptuously playing with thunder and lightning,
stirring waves and raising winds,
causing flood dragons to walk on land,
mountains to collapse and seas to dry up.
The Supreme Deity thus demoted and banished him to live among mortals.
"Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn"
His eyes blazed like lightning.
Wáng Róng was intelligent and perceptive from a young age,
with a distinguished and clear spirit,
able to gaze at the sun without being dazzled.
Péi Kǎi remarked of him:
"Róng's eyes shine brightly like lightning beneath a cliff."
Book of Jìn
Pacing around the room
During the Shangyuán era,
in Táizhōu, a Dàoist priest named Wáng Yuǎnzhī excelled in the Yìjīng and was skilled at
predicting people's life, death, misfortune, and fortune.
He composed a fifteen-volume work titled Yì Zǒng.
One day, while sunning his books, a sudden thunderstorm arrived;
crimson lightning encircled the room in the dark mist,
and an old man shouted:
"Where are the books that revealed the secrets?"
"The Heavenly Emperor ordered me to summon the Liù Dīng thunder and lightning to retrieve them,"
and thus the Yì Zǒng was lost.
"Records of Lóngchéng"
Circling around the desk
Mù Zhāofú was a native of Jīnlíng.
During the Bǎodà era, he served as the prefect of Chángzhōu.
One day, while seated in the main hall,
a thunderstorm suddenly arrived,
with lightning resembling golden snakes coiling around his desk.
The clerks and soldiers all trembled and prostrated themselves,
but Mù Zhāofú showed no fear, patting the desk and scolding the storm.
The thunder and lightning immediately dispersed,
and when the desk was lifted, only an iron chain weighing a hundred jīn was found.
Mù Zhāofú still did not change his expression,
calmly ordering the chain to be stored in the treasury.
"History of the Southern Táng."
Sìfāng Electric
In the east there is lightning called Wúhòu,
in the south there is lightning called Shùnliú,
in the west there is lightning called Duòguāng,
and in the north there is lightning called Bǎishēngshù.
Wúhòu and Duòguāng strike and oppose each other,
Shùnliú and Bǎishēngshù strike and oppose each other,
thus within the gathering of empty clouds a great light is born,
called lightning.
Qǐshìjīng
Dá Dá
The thunder rumbles rumblingly,
its sound shakes;
the lightning flashes brightly,
its light glitters.
From "Yuán Bāo"
Yīnyáng gather
Yīnyáng gathering forms clouds.
"Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo"
The aura of mountains and rivers
The *Shuōwén* says:
Clouds are the vapor of mountains and rivers,
and also says they are the moist vapor of great marshes.
The *Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Zhuàn* states:
Clouds arise from mountains and spread across the sky.
Shě Yáng
The term "cloud" (yún) denotes movement (yùn),
rising upon touching stone it is called cloud,
it forms by leaving behind yang and moving with essence.
"Chūnqiū Shuōtící"
The foundation of heaven and earth
Cloud is the foundation of heaven and earth.
The Hétú Dìtōng Jì
Xí Jù
Xún Yǐ submitted a memorial to Emperor Shun stating:
The virtuous are the foundation of transformation,
clouds are the means for rain;
to obtain the virtuous yet not employ them
is like prolonged overcast skies without rain.
Book of the Later Han
Earth's Qi
Huángdì Sùwèn states:
The clear and ascending forms Heaven,
The turbid and descending forms Earth.
Earth's Qi ascends to become clouds in Heaven,
Heaven's Qi descends to become rain,
Rain originates from Earth's Qi,
Clouds originate from Heaven's Qi.
Annotation says:
When Yin congeals and ascends, it coalesces to form clouds,
When Yang disperses and descends, it flows down to become rain,
Rain is distributed through transformation from clouds,
Hence it is said clouds originate from Earth's Qi relying on Qi,
Through mutual interaction, hence it is said clouds originate from Heaven.
Friends of the wind, companions of the rain
"The Rhapsody on Clouds" says:
It rests upon the earth and roams the cosmos,
making the wind its companion and the rain its child.
Xúnzǐ
Cloudy Veil
Initially emerging as clouds,
dense clouds form veils.
Lùnhéng
Clouds and Springs Respond to Each Other
The dust of the Yellow Spring ascends to form yellow clouds,
the dust of the Blue Spring ascends to form blue clouds,
the dust of the Red Spring ascends to form red clouds,
the dust of the White Spring ascends to form white clouds,
the dust of the Dark Spring ascends to form dark clouds.
"The River Chart's Beginnings Revealed"
Analogies are used to show people

Mountain clouds resemble grass and thickets,
water clouds resemble fish scales,
drought clouds resemble smoke and fire,
rain clouds resemble water vapor.

All analogize their origins to show people.

Sòng's clouds resemble chariots,
Lǔ's clouds resemble horses,

Yuè's clouds resemble dragon heads,
Shǔ's clouds resemble granaries.
"The Art of War"
The Sun Rises in Auspicious Splendor
The Green Emperor rises with green clouds supporting the sun,
the Red Emperor rises with red clouds supporting the sun,
the Yellow Emperor rises with yellow clouds supporting the sun,
the White Emperor rises with white clouds supporting the sun.
From the "Luò Shū"
Wǔ Yún
The Rites of Zhōu states:
The Bǎozhāng official used the appearances of the five clouds to distinguish auspicious and inauspicious signs,
and the atmospheric influences indicating floods, droughts, abundance, or famine.
Commentary by Senior Official Zhèng notes that at the two solstices and two equinoxes,
observing the cloud's energy: green indicates insect plagues,
white signifies mourning,
red foretells war and famine,
black warns of floods,
and yellow predicts abundance.
Qìngyún
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Like smoke, yet not smoke,
like clouds, yet not clouds,
dense and profuse,
serene and coiling,
this is called the auspicious cloud.
The appearance of the auspicious cloud signifies joyful energy.
(The Book of Han writes it as "celebratory.")
The Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital by Dǒng Zhòngshū says:
In times of peace,
clouds appear in five colors,
and the celebratory cloud forms with three colors to become resplendent.
Jǐng Yún
Jǐngyún Sūnshì Ruìyìng Tú states:
Jǐngyún is
an omen of peace,
also called qìngyún.

Wáng Bì states:

yin is above and yang presses against it,
and when it cannot pass through, it evaporates and becomes rain.
This explanation is incorrect.
Why?
Because the two qì of yin and yang,
are born from the Yellow Springs,
intertwine and blend,
and emerge from the earth as clouds.
When the two qì are equal in strength,
they can produce rain.
If either yin qì is less and yang qì is more,
or yin qì is more and yang qì is less,
neither can produce rain.
The reason for no rain in Xiǎo Xù is
that yin qì is insufficient.
The reason for no rain in Xiǎo Guò is
that yang qì is insufficient.
In the top line of Xiǎo Xù,
when it rains and then stops,
it is because yang reaches its peak and turns into yin.
Therefore, Confucius said:
Heaven creates seasonal rain,
mountains and rivers produce clouds.
Clouds,
are not something a single qì can produce.
Take cooking as an analogy:
if there is water but no fire,
or fire but no water,
neither can produce steam.
Only when both water and fire are present can steam be generated.
Steam originates from the pot,
not formed above the steamer.
From this perspective,
clouds must form within the earth,
with yin and yang emerging together.
If yin comes first and yang follows,
it cannot even form clouds,
how could it produce rain?

Terrestrial Qi
Wind is the qi of heaven,

Wind follows the seasons in its course,
rain descends in response to the wind.

When the qi of heaven descends,
and the qi of earth ascends,
yin and yang communicate,
and all things are accomplished.

Confucius went out,
Zǐlù requested to bring rain gear,

and indeed there was no rain.

the omen is about to be fulfilled.

so respect can be maintained."

Lǐ Jìng Conducts the Rain
When Lǐ Jìng was still obscure,
he once went hunting in Líng Mountain.
As dusk fell,
he sought lodging at a large mansion.
An old woman invited him in. At midnight,
there came urgent knocking at the door.
The woman said:
"This is not the human world but the Dragon Palace.
Today we received the celestial mandate to make rain,
but both my sons are away.
Considering the distance between the two cloud routes exceeds ten thousand miles,
may I trouble you for just a moment?"
She then ordered a servant to saddle a black-maned white horse,
and had a rain-making device—a small bottle—tied to the front of the saddle.
She warned him:
"When the horse leaps and neighs,
take one drop of water from the bottle and drip it on the horse's mane.
Be careful not to use more."
Soon he was galloping through flashing clouds,
and seeing the village where he had rested, he poured twenty drops consecutively.
After returning, the old woman wept and said:
"How could you betray my trust so severely?
Each drop becomes one foot of rain on earth.

how could anyone survive?
I have already been punished,
receiving eighty strokes of the cane."

and immediately close the ward gates.
How could one ward or one market
thereby summon the Spiritual Star?
Temporarily closing and temporarily opening

Nowadays, in discussions in alleys and words on streets,
people jointly call the ward gates 'the Chancellor,'
saying they can regulate the wind and rain,

when it is about to clear up,

The Censor's Rain
Yán Zhēnqīng during the Kāiyuán era served as a supervisory censor,

Zhēnqīng arrived and immediately resolved it.

Lǐ Déyǔ
On the twenty-eighth day of the second month in the seventh year of the Tàihé era,
while I was favored to retain my official position as Grand Councilor,
confidential matters were not kept secret.
By the twenty-sixth day, the capital was already abuzz with rumors that an imperial edict would be issued the next day.
On the twenty-seventh day, it was quiet,
and everyone said the matter had been halted and would not proceed.
Emperor Wénzōng showed the chief ministers a handwritten decree to the Bureau of Military Affairs,
which read:
"Appointing a councilor is an extremely important matter. I have just consulted the calendar,
and tomorrow morning is not auspicious.
It will be issued on the twenty-eighth day instead."
There had been no rain or snow since last winter and this spring,
with heavy haze being particularly severe.
On that day, however, a sweet rain fell abundantly.
The chief of the Bureau of Military Affairs said to me:
"The palace is delighted by this.
The palace attendants are mistakenly calling the Grand Councilor by the mispronounced name Lǐ Déyǔ (meaning 'Lǐ of Virtuous Rain')."
Lǐ Déyù, "Records of Advising the Calendar in Two Reigns"
Qián Yǔ
Wáng Zhōngzhèng, the gatekeeper of Sìzhōu, said:
During the Kāichéng era,
he died and revived after twelve days.
He first saw a person in blue clothes and a red headscarf,
who extended an arm and ascended the clouds, saying:
"Heaven summons you to go,
join the left rain brigade."
In the left and right rain brigades,
there were armored cavalry from five directions each,
clustered atop the clouds,
looking down below.
Inside multi-storied buildings, deep chambers, bags, and cabinets,
even the tiniest details were visible.
What was even more extraordinary was seeing grains of rice several feet long.
There were two brigades in total,
with one brigade carrying small-necked bottles
filled with water from the human world.
The other brigade carried something resembling powdered Glauber's salt,
called "dry rain."
The rain brigades were at the front,
with wind chariots bringing up the rear.
From "Minor Records of the Táng Era."
The rain is heavy.
Dòu Lú Zhuàn was appointed chancellor during the Qiánfú era,
on the day the imperial decree was proclaimed, a great storm with thunder and rain uprooted trees.
Vice Director of the Left Wéi Chán, who was on good terms with Zhuàn, went to congratulate him,
Zhuàn mentioned the unusual thunderstorm,
Chán said:
"This corresponds to the auspicious sign of Your Excellency becoming the timely rain that brings relief."
Zhuàn laughed and said:
"But how excessive this rain is!"
When the rebel Huáng Cháo attacked the capital,
Zhuàn was killed at Zhāng Zhífāng's residence,
those with insight considered the storm an ill-omened portent.

Fake Rain Gear
When Minister Kǒng Jí was serving as a supplementary compiler,
he once returned from court,
encountered rain but had no rain gear,
so he took shelter under the eaves of someone's house.
After mealtime, the rain intensified,
and the host invited him into the main hall.
An old man came out to greet him very respectfully,
and the food and wine were also very abundant.
Jí expressed his gratitude and requested to borrow rain gear.
The old man said:
"I live in seclusion and do not involve myself in worldly affairs,
never venturing out in cold, heat, wind, or rain.
Why would I keep such things here?"
He then had someone borrow rain gear from elsewhere to offer him.
Jí withdrew and sighed:
"[He seems to] have forgotten official ambitions."
He told people:
"This is a great recluse."
From "Beimeng Suoyan"

During the Southern Táng period,
the customs duties and tax rates were particularly heavy,
causing merchants great distress.
When a severe drought occurred in the nearby suburbs one day,
while feasting at the North Garden,
Liè Zǔ said to his attending ministers:
"It rains in the outskirts,
but not in the capital city.
Why is this?
Could it be due to some injustice in the judicial or market systems that violates heaven's will?"
Shēn Jiàngāo seized the opportunity to jest and said:
"The rain is afraid of being taxed,
so it doesn't dare enter the capital."
Liè Zǔ laughed heartily,
and immediately ordered the abolition of all extra taxes.
Within two days, ample rain fell abundantly.

"Yì Fēihòu"

When Confucian scholars discuss the auspicious responses of peace,
they describe the wind as auspicious and the dew as sweet,
the wind not howling through branches,
and the rain not breaking up clods of soil.
They also claim wind every five days and rain every ten days,
which is an excessive praise.
Although wind and rain may be moderate,
they cannot precisely follow the cycle of every five or ten days.
