not something humans can create.
Earth Dragon
The Huainanzi says:
Earthen dragons bring about rain.
The commentary states:
When Tāng encountered a drought, he made earthen dragons to resemble them,
for clouds follow the dragon.
The Fayan says:
To imitate a dragon in bringing rain,
how difficult it is!
O dragon, O dragon!
Yìng Qú's "Letter to Cén Wényú" states:
Earthen dragons raise their heads at the Dark Temple,
clay figures stand like cranes in Quèlǐ.
Self-Reproach for Six Matters
After Tāng conquered Xià,
a great drought occurred,
and for five years there were no harvests.
Tāng then prayed with his own body in the Sānglín,
cutting his hair and paring his nails,
using his own body as a sacrificial offering.
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū"
records him blaming himself for six matters:
Was it because governance lacked regulation,
or because the people were made to suffer,
or because palaces were too lofty,
or because women's influence was excessive,
or because bribery was practiced,
or because slanderers flourished,
that the rain has not come to such an extreme?
The "Xúnzǐ"
says before he finished speaking,
clouds gathered from all four seas,
and rain came from a thousand lǐ away.
The "Huáinánzǐ"
states at this time,
stringed music, singing, drumming, and dancing were prohibited.
The "Shīzǐ"
records:
Tāng blamed himself during the drought,
and Heaven responded with rain.
The Great Rain Sacrifice in spring and autumn,
and Dǒng Zhòngshū's setting up of earthen dragons,
were all for a single period.
When it did not rain for a period,
they feared and performed rain sacrifices to seek yin and request blessings,
showing concern for the common people.
Tāng encountered drought for seven years,
and blamed himself for five faults.
What time does this refer to?
Did he blame himself whenever there was a drought for a period?
When the drought reached seven years,
then he blamed himself.
If we say he blamed himself whenever there was a drought for a period,
and it took seven years for Heaven to respond with rain,
how could the response be so delayed?
If we say he only blamed himself after seven years,
showing concern for the common people,
how could it be so late?
This does not match the methods of rain sacrifice,
nor satisfy the principle of caring for the people.
The records in the texts cannot be trusted.
"Lùnhéng"
Conquering Yīn
King Wǔ on the night of Guǐ Hài in the second month,
before the battle formation was completed, rain poured down.
On the day King Wǔ arrived at Mùyě,
he deployed his troops at night.
Before the deployment was finished, it rained.
The rain
was a response signifying harmony between heaven, earth, spirits, and humanity.
"Guóyǔ"
records that when King Wǔ's army entered the southern suburbs,
they sang in front and danced behind.
On the Jiǎzǐ day they advanced the troops,
and by the Yǐchǒu day it had rained.
"Tàigōng Fúfú Yīnmóu"
Campaign against Xíng
Wèi experienced a great drought,
divination for sacrificing to the mountains and rivers proved inauspicious.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Formerly when Zhōu suffered famine, it conquered Yīn and the harvest was abundant.
Now Xíng is without virtue, and the feudal lords lack a leader—
is Heaven perhaps wishing to have Wèi attack Xíng?"
They followed this advice,
and when the army was raised, rain fell.
(Zuǒzhuàn, Xī 19)
Six faults, self-reproach
In the third year of Duke Xī,
there was no rain in spring and summer.
Thereupon Duke Xī, distressed and concerned, donned dark garments and vacated his residence,
led his ministers in praying to the mountains and rivers, and with six faults blamed himself,
dismissed the influence of women petitioners,
executed thirteen persons including slanderous flatterers Guō Dū and others,
released nine persons including officials who had accepted bribes such as Zhào Zhù,
remitted defaulted corvée labor,
abolished military punishments,
eliminated harsh laws and cruel teachings,
and repealed forty-five superfluous decrees, saying:
"Now that there is a drought,
the fields bear no crops,
I should die,
but what crime have the common people committed?
I dare not trouble the people,
I beg for fate to spare the multitudes,
and am willing to bear the blame for this disaster myself."
After the prayers, he fasted at the southern suburb, and heavy rain fell.
The "Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yóu"
and the "Yì Nèizhuàn" state:
"When a ruler is extravagant,
and adorns his palaces excessively,
there will be drought and the disaster of fire.
Therefore, when Lǔ Xī encountered drought,
he reformed his governance and disciplined himself,
removed the hanging bells and drums,
and suspended construction officials.
Though uneasy,
seasonal rain fell of its own accord."
"Hòu Láng Yǐ Zhuàn"
Burning the Shaman and the Deformed
There was a great drought in Xià,
the duke wanted to burn the wūwāng (shamans and deformed persons),
Zǎng Wénzhòng said:
What can the wūwāng do?
If Heaven wished to kill them,
then it would be as if they had not been born;
if they could cause drought,
burning them would only make it worse.
The duke followed his advice.
． From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xī 21st Year
Duke Mù wanted to expose the wāng and wū to the sun,
Xiànzǐ replied by suggesting moving the market.
From Tángōng
Self-deprecation
Confucius was in Qí,
where a great drought occurred.
In spring, there was famine.
Duke Jǐng asked Confucius,
"What should be done about the drought?"
Confucius replied,
"In a bad year, one should ride inferior horses,
refrain from mobilizing labor for public works,
not repair the imperial highways,
and use silk and jade for sacrificial offerings.
Do not reduce the sacrificial animals to the lower grade,
for this is the rite by which a worthy ruler humbles himself to save the people."
From "The School Sayings of Confucius"
Exposure
The state of Qí suffered a great drought.
Duke Jǐng wanted to make sacrifices to the Spirit Mountain.
Yànzǐ said:
"The Spirit Mountain,
has rocks for its body,
and grass and trees for its hair.
If the heavens do not send rain for a long time,
its hair will be scorched and its body will grow hot.
Does it alone not desire rain?
What good would sacrificing to it do?"
The Duke then wanted to sacrifice to the River Earl.
Yànzǐ said: "The River Earl,
has water for his kingdom,
and fish and turtles for his people.
If the heavens do not send rain for a long time,
the hundred rivers will dry up,
and his kingdom and people will perish.
Who alone does not need rain?
Sacrificing to him would be of no benefit."
The Duke left his palace,
exposing himself to share the worries with the mountain spirit and River Earl.
If they were fortunate and it rained,
the Duke then went out into the wilderness,
exposing himself for three days,
and indeed the heavens sent heavy rain.
"The Spring and Autumn Annals of Yànzǐ"
After people built a shrine, it rained.
During the time of Duke Jǐng of Sòng,
there was a great drought,
and after three years of divination it was said:
"It is necessary to offer a human sacrifice for it to rain."
Duke Jǐng descended the hall, kowtowed, and said:
"All my efforts to seek rain
are for the sake of my people.
If it is now demanded that I offer a human sacrifice for it to rain,
I myself shall take that role."
Before his words were finished, the heavens poured down heavy rain,
covering an area of a thousand li square.
In the "Zhuāngzǐ," this is recorded as Duke Jǐng of Qí.
Shǔ Hóu Yǔ
The King of Qín executed the Marquis of Shǔ,
Yùn later went to welcome the coffin for burial in Xiányáng,
but heavy rain fell for three days, blocking the way,
so they buried him in Chéngdū instead.
Hence, when the people of Shǔ pray for rain,
they sacrifice to the Marquis of Shǔ, and it always rains.
"Records of the Origins of Shǔ"
Release the yin and block the yang
Dǒng Zhòngshū governed the state,
using the anomalies and disasters recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
to deduce the reasons for the disruptions in yīn and yáng.
Therefore, when seeking rain, he would suppress all yáng elements,
and release all yīn elements.
To stop rain, he did the opposite.
Yán Shígǔ commented:
This means such acts as closing the south gate,
prohibiting the lighting of fires,
and opening the north gate,
sprinkling water on people, and the like.
Sacrifice to the Star Deity
In the second year of the Yuánfēng era, during a summer drought,
Gōngsūn Qīng said:
"During Huángdì's time, when fēng sacrifices were performed, there was a drought;
after three years of dry sacrifices, the emperor issued an edict,
asking 'Does the drought indicate dry sacrifices?'
He then ordered the whole country to worship the Spiritual Star.
"Former Records of Sacrifices"
When Zhào Yáo served as Lángzhōng magistrate,
the western region suffered from drought.
Yáo led his officials to fast and pray at the Spiritual Star Pond,
attributing the blame to himself and accepting responsibility,
kowtowing until he bled,
and heavy rain fell in response.
"Biographies of the Elderly in Yì Province"
The Injustice of the Filial Daughter-in-Law
In the Eastern Sea there was a Filial Daughter-in-law,
who was widowed young and had no children,
yet she cared for her mother-in-law for over ten years with great diligence.
The mother-in-law, fearing she was a burden preventing her from remarrying, hanged herself to death,
and the mother-in-law's daughter accused the daughter-in-law of killing her mother.
The officials arrested and interrogated her, and the Filial Daughter-in-law falsely confessed under duress, completing the case.
Yú Gōng of the superior prefecture argued to clarify her innocence,
but the Grand Administrator would not listen,
and ultimately sentenced the Filial Daughter-in-law to death.
The commandery then suffered a severe drought for three years.
Later, a new Grand Administrator arrived,
and divination was performed to determine the cause.
Yú Gōng attributed it to the former Grand Administrator's wrongful execution of the Filial Daughter-in-law,
whereupon the Grand Administrator personally offered sacrifices at the Filial Daughter-in-law's grave,
and erected a stele at her tomb.
Heaven immediately sent heavy rain, and the year's harvest was abundant.
From the "Book of Hàn"
and the "Book of Later Hàn": Yīn Dān, following Mèng Cháng's advice, offered sacrifices to the widow of Shàngyú.
The "Biographies of Exemplary Women" of the Jìn dynasty records that during Liú Yào's time, Hūyán Mó handled a case involving a woman from Shǎnxiàn County, which was similar.
Deciding a Lawsuit to Bring Forth Rain
In the thirteenth year of the Yǒngpíng era,
King Yīng of Chǔ plotted a rebellion, and over a thousand people were implicated and imprisoned.
For three years the case remained unresolved,
with more than a hundred people dying from torture and harsh confinement.
Heaven responded with calamitous drought, leaving a thousand miles of barren land.
Yuán Ān was appointed as the Grand Administrator of the Chǔ Commandery,
and he immediately took the reins and set off.
Upon arrival,
he adjudicated the legal case,
personally recording each person's testimony.
Those who were not the chief conspirators,
but had been implicated by their leaders,
were promptly processed and released.
Within ten days, he saved the lives of a thousand people.
At that time, sweet rain poured down abundantly,
and the year saw a great harvest.
From "Traditions of Former Worthies of Rǔnán" and "Book of the Later Hàn".
Cease the Corvée Labor
In the third year of the Yǒngpíng era, during a summer drought, the construction of the Northern Palace was greatly expanded.
Zhōnglí Yì removed his official cap and submitted a memorial. The Emperor responded with an edict stating:
"Recently, Heaven has sent down drought,
yet dense clouds have gathered multiple times.
We have distributed prayers and observed the winds and clouds.
In the north, we prayed at the Míngtáng;
in the south, we performed the Rain Dance at the Wūyú altar.
Now, We also command the Minister of Works to halt construction of various palaces
and reduce non-essential expenses,
hoping thereby to avert calamity and reproach."
The edict further expressed gratitude to the dukes, ministers, and all officials.
Thereupon, timely heavy rain fell.
(From the Biography of Zhōnglí Yì)
Dismiss the Commandant
Gāo Huò of Rǔnán was skilled in astronomy.
When Bào Yù served as Governor of Rǔnán,
the commandery suffered a severe drought.
Yù personally went to ask how to bring about rain,
and Huò said, "Quickly dismiss the three supervising secretaries.
Your Excellency should personally go north to the post station thirty lǐ away,
and rain can be brought about."
Yù followed this advice and indeed obtained heavy rain.
From "Xiè's Records"
Burying the guest's remains
Zhōu Chàng was benevolent and tolerant by nature.
While serving as Governor of Hénán,
a summer drought persisted despite prolonged prayers for rain without response.
He thus gathered and buried
over ten thousand corpses of those who had died away from home near Luòchéng.
Rain promptly fell in timely abundance,
resulting in a year of plentiful harvests.
From "A Letter of Thanks":
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng expressed concern that if the Inspector were not dismissed,
the fault would lie with the Governor of Rǔnán for leaving corpses unburied;
this would not implicate the Governor of Hénán.
Heaping firewood to burn oneself
Liàng Fǔ, styled Hànrú,
was a native of Xīndū in Guǎnghàn.
He served as an official in the commandery.
At that time, there was a great summer drought,
so he went out to pray to the mountains and rivers, saying:
"As a key official of the commandery,
I have failed to offer loyal advice,
recommend the worthy and dismiss the wicked,
harmonize yin and yang,
leading to the current separation between heaven and earth,
the withering of all things,
and the people having no one to turn to with their grievances.
The fault lies entirely with me, Fǔ.
Now the governor has reflected on his own faults and exposed himself in the courtyard,
sending me, Fǔ, to seek atonement and pray for blessings for the people.
I now dare to make this vow:
If by noon there is no rain,
I beg to offer my body to atone for my failures."
He then piled up firewood
and prepared to burn himself.
When it approached noon,
mountain mists began to rise,
and heavy thunder and rain came,
drenching the entire commandery.
Later generations praised his utmost sincerity.
"In Search of the Supernatural"
Lǐ Yǒng's "Ode to the Scorching Sun" describes how dried water and earth create disasters,
while vows made by noon bring answered prayers.
"Luxuriant Gems of the Spring and Autumn Annals":
When water dries and earth cracks, there is great drought.
Praying to the Famous Mountains
In the fifth year of the Jiànchū era, an edict stated:
Last year, rainfall was untimely,
and now drought persists, scorching like fire.
Let
the officials of two-thousand-dàn rank
adjudicate wrongful cases and record minor offenses,
praying to the Five Peaks, Four Rivers, and famous mountains capable of gathering clouds and bringing rain,
hoping to receive the response of widespread rain across the land within a single morning.
The Book of the Later Hàn
records Emperor Míng’s edict:
Senior officials shall each fast and pray with purity, hoping to receive blessed showers.
Promoting the Subduing of Yin and Yang
Yáng Tǒng during the Jiànchū era of the Hàn dynasty served as the magistrate of Péngchéng County.
The entire province suffered a severe drought.
Tǒng deduced the waxing and waning of yīn and yáng,
and his county received timely rain.
The Grand Administrator Zōng Zhàn ordered Tǒng to pray for rain on behalf of the commandery,
and rain promptly poured down.
(From the "Hòu Hàn Shū: Yáng Hòu Zhuàn")
Not turning back all day long.
In the first year of the Yuánhé era,
Zhèng Hóng served as Grand Commandant.
At that time there was a drought,
and all the officials of the court exposed themselves to pray for rain.
When summer's heat brought a light drizzle,
the assembled officials immediately returned to their residences.
Hóng, however, did not turn back for the entire day,
and heavy rain poured down, making the crops flourish.
From "Records of Xiè."
The fire rises and the rain falls.
Dài Fēng, styled Píngzhòng,
was appointed as the magistrate of Xīhuá.
That year, a severe drought occurred,
and prayers for rain proved futile.
He then piled up firewood and sat on it, intending to burn himself,
but as the fire ignited, heavy rain fell from afar,
earning widespread admiration.
From "Xiè Shū."
Zhù Lìng suffered extreme hardship.
Hàn Zhù Liàng, courtesy name Shíqīng,
Xiè Shū Shàopíng
During the reign of Emperor Shùn, served as the magistrate of Luòyáng.
At that time, there was a severe drought,
and the Son of Heaven prayed for rain without success.
Liàng exposed himself in the courtyard, sincerely confessing his faults and accepting blame,
from morning until noon.
Then, purple clouds gathered densely,
and sweet rain began to fall abundantly.
People sang of him, saying:
"Heaven long withheld rain,
causing the people to suffer and lose their homes.
The Son of Heaven personally intervened,
Magistrate Zhù endured special hardship.
His sincere plea moved Heaven to respond,
pouring down a heavy, drenching rain."
From Jìn Liú Yù's "Chronicles of the Elderly of Chángshā."
The magistrate's records burned themselves.
The Guìyáng Records of Former Worthies states:
Línwǔ's Zhāng Xī, styled Jìzhì,
served as magistrate of Píngyú.
At that time, there was a great drought across the land.
Xī personally prayed but received no response.
He then piled up firewood and set himself ablaze.
The registrar Chóng and minor official Zhāng Huà followed Xī in the immolation.
Once the fire blazed up,
heaven's numinous power responded and rain immediately poured down.
《Water Classic》
Donating salary to support the people
Xià Xiāng, styled Mànqīng,
was a native of Yǒngxīng.
At the age of fifteen,
when the county magistrate, Gé Jūn, went to preside over the Língxīng sacrifice,
he gathered guests for a drinking feast.
At that time, the commandery was suffering from a severe drought,
and Xiāng offered admonition, saying:
"In ancient times, when Shāng Tāng encountered drought, he reproached himself with six faults,
and rain promptly fell in response.
When King Chéng repented of his errors,
the fallen grain stood up again.
Since antiquity, the sage kings have been reverent and cautious,
reflecting on transformation when Heaven showed anomalies,
and thereby saved the people's lives.
Now we have just encountered this heavenly disaster,
and our county is particularly afflicted,
yet I have not heard of any enlightened understanding
to honor the virtues of the Shāng and Zhōu dynasties.
Instead, you alone rejoice during the sacrifice,
while the common people are withered and suffering.
If the spirits have any power,
they will surely not accept this offering.
When the common people do not have enough,
how can the ruler have sufficiency? It is fitting
to return to your duties as county magistrate
and immediately end the feast, personally donating your salary to relieve the starving people."
(Records of Kuàijī)
Shǒuyáng Shénshǐ
In the fifth year of the Xīpíng era under Emperor Líng, a great drought occurred,
yet prayers offered at renowned mountains received no response.
At that time, a recluse from Píngyáng named Sū Téng, styled Xuánchéng,
dreamt of ascending Shǒuyáng Mountain, where a divine envoy on horseback awaited on the road.
Upon waking and reflecting on it,
he reported the details of his dream ascent to the Son of Heaven.
The Three Excellencies were ordered to conduct rain-petitioning rites,
with envoys and county officials ascending the mountain to offer sacrifices at the temple.
They personally inscribed the plea:
"May you bestow upon our sagely ruler the blessing of abundant grace,
so that clouds may gather and sweet rain promptly fall."
(From Cài Yōng's "Stele Inscription for Bó Yí and Shū Qí")
Zhú Rén Zhì Yǔ
Mǎ Jūn, being greatly skillful, could carve bamboo to make a man that could speak.
At that time, there was a great drought in the world,
and people all brought wine to converse with this bamboo man about the world.
In a short while, it rained.
Building a House to Bring Rain
During the Wu period of the Three Kingdoms, Dǒng Fèng lived in Yùzhāng.
There was a severe drought at the time,
and the county magistrate Dīng Shìyàn proposed:
"I have heard that Master Dǒng possesses the Way,
surely he can bring about rain."
He then went to seek him out personally.
Dǒng Fèng said:
"Rain is easy to obtain,
but this humble Daoist's house is open to the sky—
how could it withstand the rain when it comes?"
The magistrate said:
"If you, sir, can bring about rain,
I will build you a proper house."
The next day, Dīng had a house constructed for him,
gathering earth to make mud,
and planning to fetch water from several miles away.
Dǒng Fèng said:
"There is no need for that.
This evening there will be heavy rain,
so stop."
That evening, heavy rain indeed fell,
leveling both high and low ground.
"Biographies of the Divine Immortals"
He wrote a charm in the temple.
The Lord of Wú once sat with Gě Xuán on high,
gazing at the people in the street praying for rain.
The emperor said:
"The commoners pray for rain,
but how can it be obtained?"
Xuán replied:
"It's easily obtained."
He then wrote a talisman and placed it in the village temple.
By noon, heaven and earth turned dark,
torrential rain poured into the central courtyard,
flooding the level ground to over a foot deep.
"Biography of Immortal Gě"
Sincerity moves the gods.
Shù Xī,
during the Tàikāng era, the commandery suffered a severe drought,
crops were failing,
and Xī prayed for rain on behalf of the villagers.
Within three days, three feet of rain fell,
the crowd believed he possessed mystical arts,
his sincerity moved the deities,
and they sang of him:
Master Shù communicates with the divine,
beseeched heaven for sweet rain in three days,
nourishing our millet and bringing our grain to life,
how can we repay Master Shù?
From "Wáng Yǐn's History of Jìn."
Fáng Xīn brings forth rain
The inscription on the Xiāngshān Stele in Fúlí County states:
In the fifth year of the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
an imperial decree ordered feudal lords to worship the mountains and rivers within their domains.
At that time, Xiāngshān belonged to the Pèi Kingdom,
and the magistrate Guō Qīng said:
Xiāngshān corresponds to the stars Fáng and Xīn in the heavens,
capable of summoning clouds and rain, responding promptly when prayers for rain were made during droughts.
Thus, a temple was erected, and a stone inscription was carved with the following words:
Lofty is Mount Xiāngshān,
winding and soaring high,
aligned with Fáng and Xīn,
reaching the clouds of heaven,
bringing forth clouds and spreading rain,
enriching the harvest of crops.
It was erected in the first year of the Yǒnghuī era of the Táng Dynasty.
From "Universal Geography".
The White Dragon Descends to the Shrine
During Shí Hǔ's reign, there was a severe drought.
Shí Hǔ dispatched his crown prince to the west of Línzhāng at Fǔkǒu to pray for rain,
but no rain fell for a long time.
He then ordered Fótú Chéng to go himself,
whereupon a white dragon descended at the sacrificial site,
and on that day heavy rain fell,
covering an area of several thousand lǐ.
From the Book of Jìn.
Offering Sacrifices in Gratitude
Chén Zhěn,
zì Guózhèn,
after crossing the river served as Minister of the Imperial Stud,
during a prolonged severe drought,
it finally rained in the fourth month of the fourth year.
Officials submitted a memorial,
proposing to offer thanksgiving sacrifices to the ancestral temple and mountains-and-rivers.
Emperor Zhōngzōng decreed:
"Praying at the temple is called offering thanksgiving sacrifices,
but this is not the proper language for honoring superiors.
I have doubts about this."
Zhěn believed that since prayers had been made to the mountains-and-rivers,
they should therefore give thanks for the rain.
However, offering thanksgiving sacrifices was not a major affair,
and should not be reported at the ancestral temple.
A subject should not impose demands upon the sovereign and ancestors,
nor defile sacrifices by calling them thanksgiving offerings,
as this would violate proper principles.
The emperor followed his advice.
Zāng Róngxù's History of the Jìn Dynasty
Hàn Yì Píng Yìn
In the first year of the Tàiyán era of Emperor Shìzǔ of the Northern Wèi dynasty,
from the third month there was no rain,
until the sixth month.
Officials were sent to pray to all the deities,
and after several days, clouds gathered, rain fell with thunder,
soaking the land thoroughly.
A humble woman brought a square-inch jade seal
to sell to the household of the Marquis of Lù County, Sūn.
The Sūn family obtained the seal and found it remarkable,
seeking to find the woman,
but her whereabouts were unknown.
The jade was bright and pure white,
shining from within, revealing three characters on the seal,
formed in the shapes of dragons and birds,
exquisitely intricate and marvelous, unlike human craftsmanship.
The inscription read:
"Hàn Yì Píng Kòu Tiān Shī Yuē:"
The dragon-patterned knob inscription stated:
"This is the seal of the three divine characters."
From "Běnpǐ jí Língzhēng Zhì."
Whipping the Deity's Idol
Nán'ān Wáng Yuán Zhēn served as the Governor of Xiàngzhōu.
In Yèchéng, there was a stone tiger,
which temple attendants worshipped and made offerings to.
Zhēn addressed the tiger deity statue, saying:
"If it does not rain within three days,
I will whip you as punishment."
When his prayer for rain went unanswered,
he whipped the statue one hundred times.
That same month, a carbuncle broke out on his back, and he died.
From the Wèi Shū.
Xī Kāngshēng served in Xiàngzhōu.
Due to a drought, he ordered someone to whip a portrait of the stone tiger.
He then prayed for rain at Xīmén Bào's temple,
but it was unsuccessful.
He ordered an official to cut out Bào's tongue (from the statue).
Not long after, his two sons suddenly died,
and he himself fell ill.
Shamans believed it was the vengeful spirits of the tiger and Bào.
From the Wèi Shū.
Zhāng Shuǐ Cáo
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng prayed for rain at Jiǎngshān Mountain but received no response.
A deity appeared in his dream and said:
"In Yángyì County, at Jiǔdǒu,
there is a mountain where a deity named Zhāng Shuǐcáo resides,
who can summon clouds and rain."
The emperor followed these words,
dispatching an envoy to offer sacrifices.
Rain promptly followed,
and thereafter, whenever drought struck and prayers were made, they were answered.
Temple of the Heavenly Well
Liáng Shǐxīng Wáng Xiāo served as the military governor and prefect of Jīngzhōu.
At that time, there was a severe drought.
Xiāo ordered a sacrifice to be offered at Tiānjǐng.
A huge snake, twenty feet long,
emerged and coiled around the sacrificial altar, bringing heavy rain.
The year yielded a great harvest.
(From the *History of the Southern Dynasties*)
The *Records of Jīngzhōu* state:
There was a foreigner skilled in casting spells on dragons.
When he arrived at Tiānjǐng,
there was said to be a huge snake.
Líng Zé
In the third year of the Bǎodìng era of the Later Zhōu dynasty, extensive construction of palaces was undertaken.
A severe drought occurred in spring and summer.
Lǐ Jìmíng submitted a memorial stating:
Chéng Tāng encountered a drought and confessed to six faults himself,
King Xuān excessively exhausted the jade discs and bi.
Now, in the crucial months for agriculture,
the seasonal rain is still delayed.
All under heaven harbor a thirst and yearning—could it be
that perhaps our actions are immoderate,
violating the seasonal commands,
or our measures are misapplied,
thus inviting this drought?
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, the thirty-first year of Duke Zhuang, there was no rain in winter;
the "Treatise on the Five Elements" considers it due to building three terraces in one year that year,
indicating extravagance and lack of concern for the people.
In the twenty-first year of Duke Xī, a severe drought occurred in summer;
the "Treatise on the Five Elements" attributes it to constructing the south gate at that time, exhausting the people with corvée labor.
In the fifth year of Emperor Huì of Hàn, a severe drought occurred in summer;
the "Treatise on the Five Elements" holds that it was preceded by conscripting 146,000 people to build the city of Cháng'ān.
In the third year of the Yuánshòu era of Emperor Wǔ, a severe drought occurred in summer;
the "Treatise on the Five Elements" considers it because that year, former officials from across the realm were sent to dig the Kūnmíng Lake.
Thus, construction projects that mobilize people and initiate corvée labor are invariably met with celestial response.
If we reflect on the warnings in the classics,
heaven's reprimand can be rectified for the better.
Now, if we cease labor and reduce corvée to answer heaven's admonition,
perhaps timely rains will descend,
and abundant grains will flourish,
then a bountiful year can be hoped for,
and the people's voluntary support will not be late.
"Biography in the History of the Northern Dynasties."
Sacrifice to Mount Huà
Dá Xī Wǔ served as the governor of Tóngzhōu.
At that time, there was a drought.
Wǔ went to offer sacrifices at the Huàshān Temple to the mountain deity.
The mountain was lofty and steep, with few traces of human passage.
Wǔ was over sixty years old.
He climbed up by grasping vines.
There, he knelt and prayed,
expressing the sincere pleas of the common people.
As it grew late and he could not return,
he slept on the mountain, using grass as a makeshift bed.
He dreamed that a person in white clothes came to him,
took Wǔ's hand, and said:
"Your arduous efforts are deeply admirable."
Wǔ then awoke with a start.
He became even more reverent and solemn.
By morning, timely rain fell,
soaking the near and far regions.
Emperor Gāozǔ heard of this,
and sent an imperial edict to commend Wǔ, saying:
"Moved by your utmost sincerity,
the sweet rain has responded accordingly."
He bestowed upon him one hundred bolts of assorted silk.
From the "Zhōu Shū"
Praying to Báizhào
Yú Yì, during the second year of the Jiàndé era, served as the Area Commander of Ānzhōu.
At that time, a severe drought occurred,
causing the Yǔn River to cease flowing.
According to old customs, whenever there was an extreme drought,
prayers were offered at Báizhào Mountain to beseech rain.
The emperor had previously banned all group sacrifices,
and the mountain temple had been dismantled.
Yì dispatched his Registrar to offer sacrifices there,
and on that very day, heavy rain fell,
leading to a fruitful harvest that year.
The common people, moved by gratitude, gathered together,
singing and dancing in praise of him.
(From *History of the Northern Dynasties*)
Dǎo Mù Xiān
Lǔ Bān was a Dūnhuáng native,
whose exact era is unknown,
his skill rivaled nature's creation,
once crafting a wooden kite.
His father rode it to Wú,
where the Wú people deemed it demonic,
and killed him.
Bān resented the Wú people for killing his father,
so south of Sùzhōu's city wall he made a wooden immortal,
raising its hand to point southeast,
causing Wú lands to suffer a great drought for three years.
Divination revealed:
it was Bān's doing.
Thereupon, they offered thousands in valuables to apologize,
Bān broke off one of its hands,
and that month heavy rain fell in Wú.
In the early Táng dynasty, craftsmen still prayed to this wooden immortal.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The rain prohibition is extremely strict.
Shén Xuánzhào was lecturing on scriptures at Mount Sōng,
when three old men came to listen.
Upon inquiry, they turned out to be dragons.
Xuánzhào said:
"There has been a drought now,
could you bring timely sweet rain?"
The three old men replied:
"Summoning clouds and sending rain is indeed a trivial matter,
but the prohibition against rain is extremely strict.
Executing punishment without receiving orders is no light offense.
If the elder seeks help from Layman Sūn,
then rain can be brought immediately." Xuánzhào sought assistance from Sīmiǎo,
and indeed within one day and one night, a thousand li were thoroughly soaked.
"Biographies of Immortal Encounters"
Ballad of the Envoy Tián
Tián Rénhuì, in the second year of the Yǒnghuī era, served as the prefect of Píng Prefecture,
encouraging education and promoting agriculture, which was praised as benevolent governance.
He was later transferred to be the prefect of Yǐng Prefecture,
during a time of drought.
Rénhuì exposed himself to the sun to pray, and eventually obtained welcome rain,
leading to a bumper harvest that year.
The common people sang:
"Our parents gave us the fields,
but the prefect's sincere devotion moved heaven to hear.
Rain falls on the fields, clouds emerge from the mountains, granaries
are filled, and ritual righteousness is upheld.
We only wish you would always remain, never fearing poverty."
From the Old Book of Táng.
The Jade Dragon,
obtained by Emperor Táng Tàizōng in the Jìnyáng Palace,
was only a few inches wide yet warm, smooth, and exquisitely crafted,
unlike anything of the mortal world.
The emperor passed it down as an auspicious state treasure.
Empress Wǔ later bestowed it upon Emperor Xuánzōng,
and upon his ascension, whenever the capital faced drought, prayers with it invariably brought heavy rain.
Upon close inspection, it seemed to stir with scales and mane unfurling.
During a great drought in the three metropolitan regions one month,
the emperor prayed again, but after ten days, there was no response.
He then ordered it secretly cast into the Lóngchí pond in the Southern Palace,
whereupon clouds and mist suddenly gathered, followed by wind and rain.
"Records of the Divine and Strange: Separate Annals of Emperor Míng Huáng"
White Sandalwood Dragon
Emperor Xuánzōng once ordered the occultist Luó Gōngyuǎn and Bùkōng to pray for rain together,
comparing their skills as equals.
The emperor inquired about it,
and Bùkōng said:
"Your subject yesterday burned a white sandalwood incense dragon."
The emperor ordered his attendants to scoop water from the courtyard and smell it,
and indeed there was the fragrance of sandalwood.
Whenever praying for rain, he used no other method
but simply set up several embroidered seats,
hand-tossed a spinning wooden deity several inches tall,
recited incantations and threw it,
whereupon it would stand upright on the seat.
When waiting for the wooden deity's mouth corners and teeth to emerge,
that was the sign that rain would arrive.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Mirror Dragon
Sēng Yīxíng,
during the Kāiyuán era there was a drought,
Emperor Xuánzōng ordered prayers for rain.
Yīxíng said:
"We must obtain a vessel,
with a dragon-shaped decoration on it,
only then can rain be summoned."
The emperor ordered a complete search through the inner treasury,
but all were said to be unsuitable.
Several days later he pointed to an ancient mirror with a coiled dragon on its knob,
and exclaimed joyfully:
"Here is a true dragon!"
He then brought it into the ritual area,
and in one night rain fell.
Same as above.
Summoning Dragons to Bring Rain
Emperor Xuánzōng once visited the Eastern Capital,
when a great drought occurred.
At that time, there was an Indian monk named Wúwèi, also known as the Tripiṭaka Master, skilled in summoning dragons and bringing forth clouds.
The emperor sent Gāo Lìshì to summon him to request rain.
Wúwèi said:
"This drought is fated to happen now,
summoning dragons would only harm living beings and should not be done."
The emperor insisted,
so Wúwèi filled a bowl with water and stirred it with a knife,
chanting incantations in a foreign tongue.
Soon, a dragon the size of a finger appeared in the bowl's water.
He chanted again,
and white vapor rose from the bowl,
like a roll of plain silk.
Shortly after, strong winds and thunder arose,
and by the time Lìshì reached the south of the Tiānjīn Bridge, wind and rain had already arrived.
Many large trees along the streets were uprooted,
and when Lìshì returned to report, his clothes were completely drenched.
"Old Stories of the Liǔ Family"
Drawing Dragons to Bring Rain
During the Kaiyuán era, a great drought occurred.
The emperor built a hall by the new pond,
summoning Féng Shàozhèng to paint two dragons on each of the four walls.
On the western wall was a white dragon,
coiling as if about to soar.
Wind and clouds emerged with each stroke of the brush,
and the scales on the wall grew hot.
White vapor rose from the eaves into the pond,
where waves surged violently.
Suddenly, a white dragon ascended riding the clouds,
and a great storm erupted.
(From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Mínghuáng")
Sacrifice to Jiè Tuī
Wáng Wéi's "Stele of the Virtuous Governance of Duke Zhāng of Jīngzhào" states:
When the Duke governed Bīn,
there was a great drought for years.
The commandant sacrificed to Jiè Tuī,
and although they danced gracefully repeatedly, the divine response was not as expected.
The Duke ordered bundled herbs to be used for fire and trees to be cut down,
then set up firewood, poured wine, and prayed, saying:
"One who has merit among people
is worshipped as a bright deity;
one without virtue who receives offerings,
disaster will also befall.
Since the time of Jiàng,
people have truly sacrificed to you,
yet the deity has not responded—
how then shall people look up to you?
If it rains by noon,
then we shall set up egret feathers and hold this red hair
(in reverence); otherwise, the fire will spread,
blazing to the sky and scorching the earth,
your divine robes will turn to ashes,
and your grand temple will become overgrown with grass.
Consider this well."
Before his words ended, clouds gathered;
before he rose from his bow, rain poured down,
covering the entire region without extending to other commandants.
"Collection of the Right Assistant Director"
Withdraw the Earth Dragon
Mǎ Lín was appointed as the marching camp military commissioner during the early years of Emperor Dàizong's Yǒngtài era,
when a severe drought occurred.
The villages made earthen dragons,
gathering shamans to pray. Mǎ Lín said:
"The drought is caused by poor governance."
He immediately ordered their removal,
and it rained the next day.
That year, there was a great harvest.
"From his main biography."
Shamans and Wizards Dancing Together
Lí Gàn in the eighth year of the Dàlì era was reinstated as the Capital Governor,
during a severe drought.
Gàn constructed an earthen dragon and personally danced opposite shamans and wizards,
but after a full month there was no response.
He then prayed at the Confucius Temple,
where the Emperor sighed and said:
"Qiū has been praying for a long time."
He ordered the earthen dragon destroyed,
and the Emperor reduced his meals and practiced frugality, after which continuous rain fell.
(New Book of Táng)
Self-blame
Wú Gōng Xìnlíng,
during the Zhēnyuán era served as magistrate of Wàngjiāng County,
implemented benevolent governance,
and during a drought composed a prayer for rain.
It stated:
If personal desires are pursued within the county,
or corrupt governance is imposed upon the people,
this is the crime of the magistrate,
for which the gods may punish him;
how could such blame be transferred to others to harm the harvest?
After his death in office,
the people requested his burial within the county borders,
erected a shrine in his honor,
and during the Chóngníng era of the Sòng dynasty it was officially designated as the Língshī Temple.
"Sūzhōu Gazetteer"
No bitterness, no sorrow
Duàn Wénchāng,
during the Tàihé era of Emperor Wénzōng, governed Jīngzhōu. When there was a drought,
he would pray for relief and it would surely rain;
when there was prolonged rain,
if he went out on an excursion, it would surely clear up.
The people thus said of him:
"In drought, we do not suffer—pray and rain comes;
in rain, we do not worry—when the lord goes out, it clears."
"Original Biography, New Book of Táng"
Throw the witch into the water.
During the Huìchāng era, Dí Wéiqiān served as the magistrate of Jìnyáng.
The region suffered from severe drought,
so prayers were offered at the Jìn Temple,
but there was no response whatsoever.
At that time, there was a female shaman from Bīngzhōu named Guō Tiānshī, skilled in talismanic arts from a young age,
who moved freely within the palace.
Dí earnestly requested her to pray for rain,
but when the deadline passed, there was no sign of rain,
and she even insulted Dí for not understanding the ways of heaven.
The next day, Wéiqiān accused her of being a deceitful fraud,
ordered his attendants to whip her in front of the deity,
and threw her into the pond.
He then immediately set up an altar to burn incense,
and released the officials who had been detained—just as everyone was in fear,
sand and stones began to flow and melt,
when suddenly a patch of clouds as large as a carriage canopy appeared,
first covering the spot where Wéiqiān stood,
then gathering with mists from all directions, accompanied by several claps of thunder,
and a heavy, sweet rain poured down.
The regional commander reported the incident,
and an imperial edict praised the extraordinary event, awarding him five hundred thousand coins.
Wéiqiān was a descendant of Dí Rénjié.
From "Jù Tán Lù".
Hēilóng Qiū
When Niú Sēngrú governed Xiāngyáng,
there was a prolonged drought.
A recluse who could tame dragons
was asked by the duke to bring rain.
The recluse said:
"There are no dragons in the Jiāng-Hàn region,
except for a black dragon in a single deep pool.
It is difficult to control,
and forcibly driving it will surely cause disaster."
The duke insisted on the command,
and indeed heavy rain came,
but it washed away ten thousand households.
"Shàngshū Gùshí"
I offer my servants and horses.
Gūzāng Lǐ Zhònglǚ, at the end of the Xiántōng era, was appointed as the magistrate of Lǔshān in Rǔzhōu.
He governed with clarity and proficiency, and officials did not dare deceive him.
During a drought, he requested prayers for rain,
but all appeals to various deities went unanswered.
Zhònglǚ then purified himself and personally prayed at the Yáo Temple on Lǔshān, twenty lǐ from the county seat,
offering his black horse and his attendant Zhāng Hàn as sacrifices.
After the sacrifice, as they were about to descend the mountain,
clouds and fog suddenly rose, and heavy rain fell across the plains and marshes.
Both the servant and the horse suddenly perished.
Thereupon, Zhònglǚ performed another sacrifice and painted images of the servant and horse on the eastern wall.
"Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú"
Snake Doctor
Wáng Yànwēi was stationed in Biàn,
and there was a summer drought.
Lǐ passed through Biàn,
and during a banquet,
Wáng brought up the matter of the drought.
Lǐ, being drunk, said:
"Wanting rain is very easy.
You can seek four snake doctors,
two stone jars,
fill each jar with water,
float two snake doctors on it,
seal them tightly with wooden lids and mud, and place them separately in bustling areas.
In front and behind the jars, set up mats and burn incense,
select more than ten children under ten years old,
have them hold small green bamboos and take turns striking the jars day and night,
without any pause."
Wáng followed his words and tried it,
and within a day and two nights, heavy rain poured down.
According to an old saying, dragons and snake masters are relatives by marriage.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The dragon draws in the inkstone's water.
A monk was expounding the scriptures at a mountain temple,
and there was always an old man who came to listen.
When asked his name, he said:
"I am a dragon from the pond at the foot of the mountain.
Fortunately, the drought this year has given me leisure to come here and listen to the Dharma."
The monk asked:
"Can you relieve the drought?"
He replied:
"The Lord of Heaven has sealed the rivers and lakes, and their water cannot be used arbitrarily."
The monk said:
"Can the water in this inkstone be used?"
Thereupon, he drew water from the inkstone and went straight away.
That evening, a great thunderstorm arose,
and by dawn,
the rain was all black water.
From "Mùfǔ Yànwén"
The heavy rain comes from heaven.
Zhāng Shìbó prayed for rain at Yì Shān,
when suddenly he heard a voice from the sky saying:
"Heavy rain comes from Heaven,
light rain comes from the mountain."
From "Hǎilù Suìshì".
Pú Xiāo Praying for Rain
During the reign of Emperor Xīzōng,
there was a summer drought.
An edict was issued to the Grand Capital Governor,
ordering the use of ritual vessels, water, incense burners, cattails, wormwood, and crimson banners
to be placed at the gates of wards and markets,
intending to summon rain through traditional methods.
Luó Yǐn submitted a memorial stating:
"Your Majesty employs cattails and wormwood as supplications—
is it because they possess spiritual power over mountains and rivers?
Mountains and rivers receive sacrifices and hold territories,
yet they still cannot exert effort for Your Majesty.
How then could those cattails and wormwood
be sufficient to move Heaven?
Heaven possesses rain and blessings
just as Your Majesty holds gracious favor.
If rain and blessings can be obtained through indirect means,
then Your Majesty's gracious favor could likewise be obtained indirectly.
I request the revocation of the edict issued on the Guǐsì day."
From "Wén Cuì"
Whipping the Dragon
During the Five Dynasties period, Lǐ Yuànyì of the Later Zhōu served as magistrate of Běihǎi County in Qīngzhōu.
When clay dragons failed to bring rain despite prayers,
Magistrate Lǐ had the dragons flogged as punishment,
and sufficient rain fell that very day.
From "History of the Later Zhōu"
Lóng Rùn
Lǐ Yù, while still in his own state, personally composed a prayer for rain, stating:
"Yet the auspicious sign of the dragon's moisture remains absent."
"Qīng Yì Lù"
The Lizard Prays for Rain
During the Xīníng era, the capital experienced a prolonged drought.
Following ancient regulations, they ordered neighborhoods to store water in jars,
insert willow branches and release lizards.
Children chanted:
"Lizard, lizard,
bring forth clouds and exhale mist,
pour down heavy rain,
and we'll set you free."
At that time, lizards couldn't be fully obtained,
so geckos were often used as substitutes.
Once put in water, they would immediately die.
The children then changed their chant:
"Injustice and suffering, injustice and suffering!
I am but a gecko.
With such dim-witted methods,
how could sweet rain be obtained?"
From "Miscellaneous Records of a Weary Traveler"
É Yā Jiànyì
In the yǐmǎo year of the Shàoxīng era of the Sòng Dynasty, prayers for rain were offered due to a drought.
The Remonstrance Official Zhào Pèi submitted a memorial stating:
Traditionally, during prayers, the prohibition of slaughter has only applied to pigs and sheep.
From now on, I request that geese and ducks also be prohibited.
At that time, Hú Zhìtáng was serving in the two departments,
and upon seeing this, he laughed and said:
This can be called the 'Goose and Duck Remonstrance Official.'
I have heard that among the enemy, there is a 'Dragon and Tiger General,'
Your Majesty should match him with the 'Goose and Duck Remonstrance Official.'
Divine Dragon Pool
North of Jiàng there is Yángshí Mountain where the Divine Dragon Pond is located,
and during the time of Huángdì, Yúnyáng Xiānshēng was sent to raise dragons here.
It was a place where successive emperors raised dragons through the ages,
and whenever the state suffered from untimely floods or droughts,
they would offer sacrifices at the pond to pray for rain.
"Dùnjiǎ Kāishān Tú"
The Wooden Fish
Dǒng Zhòngshū prayed for rain in autumn using a wooden fish.
"Huáinánzǐ"
Fāngshì Lóng
The envoy Gān Zōng's report on the Western Regions states:
Taoist masters capable of magical incantations
would pace the Yu steps and blow breath while facing springs,
whereupon dragons would surface,
measuring over ten zhǎng in length.
Upon further blowing,
the dragons would shrink to just a few cùn,
allowing them to be picked up and placed in pots.
Some kept four or five dragons, raising them with little water.
Hearing of places suffering drought, they would carry the dragons there to sell,
with one dragon valued at dozens of jīn of gold.
They would open the pots to release a dragon into a pond,
again pacing the Yu steps and blowing toward it,
causing it to grow to over ten zhǎng.
In moments, clouds and rain would gather from all directions.
From "Bàopǔzǐ"
Měnggǔ Dǎo Yǔ
The Mongols who pray for rain are not like alchemists;
they merely soak a few stones in a basin of clean water.
The larger ones are about the size of chicken eggs, while the smaller ones vary in size.
Then, silently reciting secret incantations,
they rinse and play with the stones.
After doing this for a long time, rain often falls.
The stones are called zhǎdá,
which are produced in the bellies of running animals,
with those from dogs, cattle, and horses being the most effective.
From "Chuògēng Lù" by Yáng Yǔ's "Shānjū Xīnyǔ".
Fēngzǐ
The Erya says:
The maple is rustling.
Sǔn Yán's commentary notes:
The maple grows by the river,
with parasitic plants three to four feet high,
covered in hair,
also called "maple seeds."
During droughts, smearing them with mud brings rain.
Records from court and countryside state that in the mountains east and south of the river, there are many maple tree spirits.
They grow at the base of maple trees, resembling human forms,
three to four feet tall.
During night thunderstorms, they grow as tall as the tree,
but shrink back to their original size upon seeing a person.
Someone once covered one with a bamboo hat,
and the next day, the hat was found hanging on the tree.
Locals, wishing for rain during droughts,
tie its head with bamboo and wedge it, and rain follows.
People have tried this method and found it extremely effective.
Tiger Bone
When the southern mountains suffered a long drought, they would tie a tiger's skull with a long rope,
and cast it into a dragon's deep pool.
Once in the water, it would immediately become uncontrollable,
and soon clouds would rise from the pool, rain would follow and fall until sufficient, then it was taken out.
Dragons and tigers are adversaries,
even dried bones can stir up such a response.
"Liú Bīnkè Jiāhuà Shàngshū Gùshí"
Throw the Dog
At the foot of Qiánshān in Shūzhōu, there are nine wells, which are actually nine spring eyes.
During droughts, killing a dog and throwing it into one of them
will surely cause heavy rain to fall,
and the dog will also flow out.
From "Liú Bīnkè Jiāhuà".
Whipping the Yin Stone
In Hěnshān County, there is a solitary mountain, steep and towering.
To its northwest lies a stone cave,
walking alone about a hundred paces inside,
there are two large stones.
The distance between their entrances is approximately ten feet,
commonly known as one being the Yang Stone and the other the Yin Stone.
During disasters of flood or drought, whipping the Yang Stone brings rain,
while whipping the Yin Stone clears the weather.
From Shèng Hóngzhī's "Records of Jīngzhōu"
Mud and Stone Ox
To the southeast of the mountains in Yùlín Commandery there is a pond,
beside which stands a stone ox,
which people worship.
In times of drought, the common people would kill an ox to pray for rain,
mixing the ox’s blood with mud to smear on the stone ox’s back.
Once the ritual was completed, heavy rain would pour from the sky,
washing away all the mud from the ox’s back, and then it would clear.
From the "Guǎngzhōu Jì".
Burning Yáshān
East of Tàiyuán Commandery stands Yá Mountain,
where locals often burn the earthen hills during droughts to pray for rain.
Folklore says the deity of Yá Mountain married the daughter of the River Earl,
so whenever the River Earl sees fire, he must send rain to rescue her,
which is why abundant water plants now grow on the mountain.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Lifting the Recumbent Stone
In Dōngxiāng Village of Yǒngfēng County, Jīngzhōu, there is a recumbent stone measuring one zhang, nine chi, and six cun.
Its form resembles a human,
with a bluish-yellow surface and raised patterns that appear as if carved.
When the region suffers from drought, people lift it together with their hands;
a small lift brings light rain,
a big lift brings heavy rain.
It is said that this stone suddenly appeared here.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Yǔmǔ Shān
East of Xiāng there is Yǔmǔ Shān,
on the mountain there is a sacrificial altar,
whenever prayers are made, rain never fails to descend, hence it is named so.
"Jīngzhōu Jì"
Wēn Tíngyún's description of rain says: Copper Lady still pours, Stone Grandma is just diligent.
Yǔ Lài
In Láiyáng County, there was a rain-inducing rapid.
When the county suffered from drought,
the local people would jointly block it,
and sweet rain would fall everywhere.
If only one township blocked it alone,
the rain would also fall partially,
responding according to the direction,
its reliability was like carved tallies.
"Records of Jīngzhōu"
Luó Xiāo Stone Nipple
Wáng Fú's "Record of Ānchéng" states:
From the marsh waters of Luóxiāo Mountain in Píngxiāng, Yíchūn,
stone milk flows forth alongside,
during droughts, officials pray to it,
then throw large logs three or four feet long into the well to bring rain,
when water surges and fills the well, the logs float up and the rain stops,
for this is the dwelling of hidden dragons,
residing in yin with yang essence connecting above, thus striking it must elicit mystical response,
as described in the "Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ" about rain answering the beat of drums.
Shén Shí
The Records of Jiāozhōu states:
Three lǐ from Jiǔzhēn Commandery lies Zhēn Mountain,
on which there is a shrine for the sacred stone.
When there is severe drought,
the governor personally goes to pour water on the stone,
and rain immediately falls.
The rain stops.
The *Shuōwén* says:
Jì means the rain stops,
Qī means the rain clears,
Kuò describes the appearance when the rain stops and the clouds disperse.
Sacrificing at the Gate
The Book of Rites states:
Yú and Yìng are sacrifices for flood and drought.
The Meaning of the Three Rites explains:
Yú is a sacrifice to pray for rain,
Yìng is a sacrifice to stop rain,
and each Yìng is performed at the city gate.
Playing the Flute to Stop the Rain
During the reign of King Mùwáng of Zhōu, it rained continuously for three months across the land.
King Mùwáng then played his flute,
and the rain subsequently ceased.
In response to the mandate of the Wèi dynasty,
In the first year of Yánkāng, heavy rain persisted for over fifty days,
and it cleared up only when the state of Wèi possessed the realm,
which was a response to Wèi receiving the imperial mandate.
"Wèi's Brief Records: Treatise on the Five Elements"
Sū Jùn perished.
In the fourth year of Xiánhé, it rained continuously for over fifty days,
and only cleared up after Sū Jùn's demise.
"Records of Auspicious Signs from the Mid-Jìn Revival"
Dreaming of an Old Man with White Hair
Wén Qián, styled Zhòngrú,
served as the Commandery Merit Officer.
At that time, continuous rain had halted the people's livelihoods,
and the Grand Administrator, troubled and distressed, summoned Qián, the Household Registrar.
Qián received the instruction and observed purification rituals.
After three days and nights at the altar, he dreamed of an old white-haired man who said:

Cuī Jié was a descendant of Xuánhuī,
serving as Governor of Hénán.
In the county was a great merchant Wáng Kějiǔ who traded goods across rivers and lakes,
during the rebellion of Páng Xūn,
he lost all his wealth and could not return home.
His wife visited fortune-teller Yáng Gānfū to inquire about his fate.
Gānfū, known for his divination skills but secretly attracted to the wife's beauty,
and coveting her wealth, performed the divination then feigned shock saying:
"Your husband is unlikely to return."
He secretly bribed a matchmaker with a hundred taels of gold to persuade her to remarry him.
The wife then married Gānfū, who thus became wealthy.
Years later when Xúzhōu was pacified,
Kějiǔ, in dire poverty,
begged for food and clothing as he returned to his hometown to see his wife,
but Gānfū flew into a rage, insulted and drove him away.
The wife appealed to the authorities, but Gānfū heavily bribed them,
so Kějiǔ was instead found guilty,
and upon appealing again was convicted of false accusation.
Kějiǔ, filled with resentment and sighing, eventually lost his eyesight.
When Cuī Jié took office,
Kějiǔ presented his grievance,
and Jié, uncovering the truth,
immediately ordered officials to arrest Gānfū along with the previous prison officials and imprison them,
exposing all bribery and corruption, and executed them in one day,
returning the wife's property to Kějiǔ.
At that time, there was continuous rain,
but after the judgment, the sky cleared,
and the capital's people talked among themselves, singing and dancing in the streets.

"Annals of Wú and Yuè"
Soaked shoes
Wú intended to attack Qí,
and the king issued an order:
"Anyone who dares to remonstrate shall die."
Crown Prince Yǒu knew that Wǔ Zǐxū was loyal but not employed,
while Grand Steward Pǐ was crafty and monopolized power.
He wished to speak frankly,
but feared incurring blame,
so he used indirect remonstration to provoke the king.
At dawn, carrying pellets and a slingshot, he came from the rear garden,
with his clothes disheveled and shoes soaked.
The king, finding it strange, asked him:
"Why are your clothes disheveled and shoes soaked, and your body in such a state?"
Crown Prince Yǒu replied:
"I was just wandering in the rear garden,
and hearing the sound of an autumn cicada, I went to observe it.
The autumn cicada climbs a high tree,
drinks clear dew,
sways with the wind,
chirping long and mournfully,
thinking itself secure,
unaware that a mantis, leaping across branches, clinging to twigs, stretching its waist and raising its claws, is targeting it.
The mantis, concentrating its mind and advancing,
is intent on gaining an advantage,
unaware that a yellow sparrow, filling the green woods, hovering in the shade of branches, stealthily approaches, wanting to peck the mantis.
The yellow sparrow only knows to watch for the tasty mantis,
unaware that I, holding a slingshot, aiming carefully, stumbling, launched a pellet that struck its back.
Now, I was solely focused on the yellow sparrow,
unaware of the empty pit beside me, suddenly falling into the pit,
trapped in a deep well,
hence my disheveled clothes and soaked shoes,
nearly becoming a laughingstock for Your Majesty."
The king said:
"Under heaven, there is no folly greater than this,
only coveting the immediate gain without seeing the subsequent disaster."
The crown prince said:
"Under heaven, there is folly even worse than this."

King Wǔ was attacking Zhòu's capital Luòyì,

accumulating over one zhàng deep.

five great officers riding five chariots followed by two horsemen halted outside the gate,
wishing to pay respects to King Wǔ,
and King Wǔ was about to refuse them audience.
Tàigōng said:
"It cannot be.
The snow is over one zhàng deep,
yet the chariots and horsemen leave no tracks;
I fear they may be sages."
The king sent Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ to address the five great officers, saying:
"Our guests honor us with their presence,
and we failed to inquire first;
we are just now preparing the ceremonial robes."
Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ had someone bring out a vessel of porridge,
offering it to the five chariots and two horsemen, saying:
"The great officers inside are currently facing the Son of Heaven,
and as it is cold, we offer hot porridge to ward off the chill.
We do not know the order of seniority; from whom should we begin?"
The two horsemen said:
"First serve the Lord of the South Sea,
then Hé Bó, Fēng Bó,
and Yǔ Shī."
After the porridge was finished,
the messenger reported everything to Shàngfǔ.
Shàngfǔ informed King Wǔ, saying:
"The guests may be received."
King Wǔ said:
"Do these various gods each have names?"
Shī Shàngfǔ said:
"The South Sea God is named Zhùróng,
the North Sea God is named Xuánmíng,
the East Sea God is named Gōumáng,
the West Sea God is named Rùshōu,
and Hé Bó is named Féng Xiū."
"I request that the usher
summon each by their respective names."
King Wǔ then stood in the hall,
the usher below the hall,
and outside the gate, Zhùróng was ushered in.
The five gods were all startled,
looking at each other and sighing.
Zhùróng bowed to King Wǔ,
and the king said:
"In such overcast weather, you have come from afar;
what instruction do you bring?"
The god said:
"You, King, attack Yīn and establish Zhōu;
we have respectfully come to receive commands,
and we wish to order Fēng Bó and Yǔ Shī each to fulfill their duties."
King Wǔ said:
"Throughout the seasons and years, I will not neglect the rites."

Yáo Shú, the Vice Director of the Left of Wénchāng, replied:
"The Book of Fàn Shèngzhī states:
'Snow is the essence of the five grains,
and if seeds are mixed with its liquid, the year's grains will be greatly abundant.'
Moreover, during the fifth year of the Dàmíng era of Emperor Wǔ of the Sòng Dynasty, snow fell on New Year's Day and was considered an auspicious omen."
The Emperor said:
"I rule over the myriad people,
with my heart set on the well-being of the common folk.
If the harvest is plentiful year after year, that itself is a great blessing.
What use would there be even if I obtained a qílín or a phoenix?"

Swearing an Oath to the Deity in the Snow

Wáng Jùn led Bīngzhōu troops westward to suppress rebellious tribes,
advancing swiftly by taking shortcuts and doubling the daily march.
One night in the mountains, they suddenly encountered fierce wind and snow.
Wáng Jùn, fearing he would miss the deadline, looked up to heaven and vowed:
"If I, Jùn, serve my sovereign disloyally,
or fail to punish the guilty,
may the bright spirits strike me down - this I deserve.
But what crime have my soldiers committed to suffer such hardship?

and Heaven understands clearly,
may the snow cease and winds turn to aid our military mission."
When he finished speaking, the winds shifted and the snow stopped.

The concentrated essence of Yáng
The Elder Dai's Records states that Master Zēng said:
When the concentrated qi of yang manifests, it becomes hail;
when the concentrated qi of yin manifests, it becomes sleet;
sleet and hail are transformations of the same qi.
When the abundant qi of yang
is in rainwater, it becomes warm and turns into rain;
if yin qi presses upon it and they cannot merge, it then transforms into hail.
When the abundant qi of yin is in rainwater, it congeals and stagnates, becoming snow;
if yang qi presses upon it and they cannot merge, it disperses and descends,
forming sleet due to the water.
Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals and Gǔliáng Commentary state:
Hail
is the symbol of yin coercing yang, while sleet is the sign of yang coercing yin.

Hail Protection
In the spring, during the king's first month, heavy rain and hail fell.
Jì Wǔzǐ asked Shēn Fēng, saying:
"Can hail be prevented?"
He replied:
"When a sage is above, there is no hail;
even if there is, it does not become a disaster.
In ancient times, when the sun was in the northern constellation, ice was stored; when in the western constellation,
it was taken out at dawn.
Its storage was thorough,
and its use was widespread.
Thus, in winter there was no unseasonable warmth,
in summer no hidden cold,
in spring no bitter winds,
in autumn no continuous rain.
Thunder emerged without causing shock,
and there were no calamitous frost or hail.
Now, the ice from rivers and ponds is stored but discarded and not used,
winds do not disperse but kill,
thunder does not release but shocks.
Hail becoming a calamity—
who can prevent it?"

while Cuī Hàng and Dòulú Zhuàn were appointed as chancellors on the same day.
During the proclamation of their appointments,
the hall was filled with mist on all sides.
When the officials lined up in the administrative hall to offer congratulations, hailstones as large as chicken eggs fell.

The following year, the capital fell,
and both chancellors met with disaster.
From "Jùtán Lù".
Gāoděng Sì Lóu
Yáng Xíng claimed that during the early Tiānyòu era, while escaping summer heat at a Buddhist temple in Gǔchéng,
a hailstorm was raging fiercely when
he suddenly heard a thunderous roar shaking the ground.
Rushing to look outside the gate, he saw a hailstone as tall as the temple tower,
penetrating over ten feet into the earth.
It took a full month for the hailstone to melt away.
Records of the Supernatural
The lizard spits
Liú Jūzhōng reached the summit of Mount Sōngshān,
where there were hundreds of large lizards,
each three to four chǐ long.
People fed them with food,
stroking their bodies,
which were moist and smooth like grease.
One day they gathered around a water basin,
each taking water,
and upon swallowing it immediately spat out hailstones.
These soon solidified into pellets like bullets, accumulating beside them,
and in a moment hailstones piled up all over the ground.
Suddenly, with a clap of thunder,
the pellets all vanished.
The next day, people came and reported that there had been a heavy hailstorm the previous day,
and thus it was realized that it was the work of the lizards.
"Yíjiān Zhì"
no different from carving
During the Xīníng era, Hézhōu experienced a hailstorm,
with the largest hailstones as big as chicken eggs,
and the smallest resembling lotus seeds.
Some were shaped like human heads, complete with ears, eyes, mouths, and noses,
as if meticulously carved.
The following year, the imperial army pacified Hézhōu.
Hard Rain
In early May of the seventeenth year of the Shàoxīng era,
Lín'ān experienced heavy hail.
The roof tiles of the National University were all shattered,
and the academic officials reported to the imperial court for repairs,
but could not refer to the hail as "hard rain."
The "Xuān Qú Lù"
records a village where many people engaged in wrongdoing.
One night, a traveler heard a deity passing by, saying:
"Dispatch hard rain for execution."
The next day, hail fell, severely damaging the crops.
Trees blossom again,
summer brings hail.
《Yǒuyáng Zázǔ》
In the eastern quarter of Cháidū there is a Cháidū,
in the state of Qí there is a mountain,
on the mountain there is a spring,
like a well, unfathomably deep.
In spring and summer, hail emerges from the well,
often destroying the five grains,
people often block it with firewood,
if not blocked with firewood, it emerges,
hence it is called Cháidū.

Flowing Copper

There is a giant born in the northern frontier,

In Hedong Puban, Xiàng Màndū was devoted to the Dao,

His family asked about his experiences,

Rainbow
The Book of Songs says:
"A rainbow appears in the east."
The Erya states that a rainbow is called a "yu rainbow,"
which is a rainbow.
Annotation:
It is commonly referred to as "beauty" in Jiangdong,
and called "yu" in the Monthly Ordinances.
In the third month of spring, rainbows begin to appear.

When rainbows appear in pairs,
the one with vibrant colors is the male,
called "hóng."
The dimmer one is the female, called "ní,"
which is the energy of the union of yin and yang.

Tiāngōng,

Guànniú Shān
The Spring and Autumn Annals: Wén Yào Gōu states:
"A white rainbow pierced through Niúshān.
Guǎn Zhòng remonstrated, saying:
'Do not approach the consorts' palace,
lest you lose power.'
The Marquis of Qǐ grew greatly fearful,
departed,
removed his faction of beauties and established worthy ministers instead,
ordering the queen to go out and face Niúshān in worship,
listening to all four sides to appease the spirits."
Sòng Jūn annotates:

represents the ruler's position;

signifies yin energy.

'Facing in worship' means offering sacrifices to atone for faults."
The Hòu Hàn Lǐ Shì Jiā Shū records Lǐ Hé saying:

Huà Yù
After Confucius had completed the revision of the Spring and Autumn Annals and composed the Classic of Filial Piety,
he fasted and bowed in reverence toward the Northern Dipper star,
announcing their completion to Heaven.
Thereupon, a crimson vapor resembling a rainbow descended from above and transformed into a yellow jade,

White rainbow adorned with jade pendants
"Heavenly Questions" from the "Songs of Chu":
The white rainbow, adorned with clouds,
Why does it appear in this hall?
How did it obtain that fine medicine,
Yet could not firmly conceal it?

Cuī Wénzǐ studied immortality under Wángzǐ Qiáo.
Wángzǐ Qiáo transformed into a white rainbow,
Holding medicine to give to him.
Wénzǐ, startled and alarmed, raised a spear to strike the rainbow,
Hitting it, causing the medicine to fall.
Bending down to look, it was the corpse of Wángzǐ Qiáo.
He placed it in the room, covering it with a worn basket.
In a short while, it transformed into a great bird.
Opening the basket to look,
It fluttered its wings, cried out, and flew away.
Penetrating the Sun
The Strategies of the Warring States says:
Táng Jū said to the King of Qín:
When Niè Zhèng assassinated Hán Guī,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.

After Jīng Kē departed, the Crown Prince saw a rainbow piercing the sun without breaking through,

he said:
Now I understand.
The Book of Hàn, Biography of Zōu Yáng, says:
Jīng Kē admired Crown Prince Dān of Yān's righteousness,

and welcome the King of Yān to the throne.

An auspicious sign for women.
In the first year of the Héguāng era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
a rainbow appeared in front of the imperial throne hall during daytime,
its colors being cyan and red.
The Emperor summoned Cài Yōng to inquire about it.
He replied:
"The rainbow,
is an auspicious sign for young women.
"From Zhāng Fán's Records of the Hàn Dynasty"
Heaven cast a rainbow.
In the first year of the Guānghé era,
a black object fell into the eastern courtyard of the Wēnmíng Hall in the Northern Palace,
black like a carriage canopy.
It rose up vigorously, its body displaying five colors,
and had a head.
Its body was over ten zhǎng long,
and its shape and appearance resembled a dragon.
The Emperor asked Cài Yōng,
who replied:
"This is what is called a rainbow cast down by Heaven.
Since feet and a tail are not seen, it cannot be called a dragon."
"Records of the Five Elements" from the Book of the Later Hàn
Circling the boat forebodes disaster.
The Records of Wú states:
Zhūgě Kè attacked Xīnchéng,
set out for Dōngxīng,
and a white rainbow appeared over his ship.
Upon returning, he paid respects at Jiǎnglíng,
and the white rainbow again encircled his army.

"Why has the rainbow come here?"
He was indeed killed by Sūn Jùn.
A broken rainbow enters the trees
Therefore, on the old palace of King Wúzhū of Yuè, there was a large cedar tree,
in whose hollow ten or more people could sit.
Xià Shìlóng of Yuè, a nobleman who did not serve in office,
often went to the old palace.
As the rain cleared and dusk approached,
a broken rainbow drank from the palace pond,
gradually shrinking and transforming into a man,
who, wearing clothes of mixed yellow, red, and purple, entered the tree.
After a long time, he did not come out,
Shìlóng found it strange,
so he called over a dozen young neighbors to go and look,
and they saw the man being coiled around by a large red snake.
Everyone was afraid and dared not approach,
but the young men threw tiles and stones from a distance,
hearing an extremely strange sound from within the tree,
like a woman crying.
Soon, clouds and mist made it impossible to see,
and they heard a faint sound like distant thunder.
Suddenly, a colorful dragon and a red crane flew away.
By dawn, when Shìlóng went to look,
he saw inside the tree a purple snake skin and a five-colored dragon skin.
As he intended to take them back,
fire erupted within the tree,
and the tree was completely burned to ashes.
This occurred in the seventh month of the third year of the Yǒng'ān era of Emperor Jǐng of Wú.
"The Later Records of Dōng'ōu."
Interacting with Others
Chén Jì, a man from Bāqiū in Lúlíng, served as a local official,
while his wife Qín stayed at home.
One day, a man,
tall, handsome, and wearing a dazzling crimson and green floral robe, came
and followed her.
Later, they often met by a mountain stream,
sleeping together.
Unaware, they connected as if by a supernatural bond.
This continued for years,
and villagers noticed a rainbow appearing wherever she went.
When Qín went to the water's edge,
the man drew water with a golden bottle,
and after they drank together, she became pregnant and gave birth to a child,
who was plump like a normal person. When Jì returned home,
Qín, afraid he would see the child,
hid the baby in a jar.
The man gave her the golden bottle,
instructing her to cover the child with it.
He said, "The child is too young to take with me now,
and there's no need to make clothes for him,
as I will clothe him myself."
He then gave her a crimson pouch to wrap the child in,
so she could take him out occasionally to nurse him.
At that time, amid wind, rain, and darkness,
neighbors saw a rainbow descend into their courtyard,
and shortly after, the man took the child away, also amidst wind, rain, and darkness.
People saw two rainbows emerge from their home,
and years later, the child returned to visit his mother.
Later, when Qín went to the fields and saw two rainbows by the stream,
she was frightened,
but soon the man appeared and said:
"It's me,
do not fear."
After that, he never appeared again.
From "Shényì Zhuàn Sōushén Jì".
Mèng Hóng
Lǐ Tè's eldest son Dàng and youngest son Xióng,
initially Lǐ Tè's wife Luó shì dreamed of two rainbows rising from the gate to heaven,
one rainbow broke in the middle and thereafter she gave birth to Dàng.
Later, Luó shì while drawing water suddenly fell into a trance,
and again dreamed of a large snake coiling around her body, subsequently becoming pregnant,
and after fourteen months gave birth to Xióng. Luó shì
often said, "If one of my two sons dies first,
the survivor will surely achieve great nobility."
Later, Xióng indeed became king of Shǔ.
"Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms"
The heavens have their divergences
In the first year of Línjiā under Liú Cōng, a red rainbow stretched across the sky from east to west,
with a fork extending southward.
The Grand Historian Kāng Xiàng said:
"The rainbow spanning east to west signifies Xǔ and Luò,

The southern-reaching fork
indicates that the Lǐ clan will continue to dominate Bā and Shǔ,
while Sīmǎ Róng will ultimately hold
the entirety of Wú.
Is this an omen that the empire will be divided into three parts?"

Covering the sky

Going Out at Night
The Records of Emperor Ān of Jìn states:
On a night in the seventh month of the second year of the Yìxī era,
a rainbow appeared in the west,
shrouding the moon and spitting gold.
Xuē Yuàn of Jìnlíng, during the early Yìxī era, had a rainbow drink from his cauldron,

Drink congee
Liú Yìqìng was in Guǎnglíng,
and he fell ill.
A white rainbow spanned the city, and a wild deer entered his residence,
which he found very ominous, so he petitioned to return.
In the "Book of Sòng",
it is recorded that Yìqìng, lying ill in Guǎnglíng and eating congee,
suddenly saw a white rainbow enter his room,
and it approached to drink his congee.

Huànǚ
In the summer, the sixth month of the second year of the Zhengguang era of Emperor Ming of the Later Wei,
a rainbow descended in the Shouyang Mountains and drank from a stream.
A woodcutter named Yáng Wàn saw it at the foot of the ridge,
and after a long while, it transformed into a girl of about sixteen or seventeen.
Finding this strange,
he questioned her, but she did not speak.
So he reported it to the garrison commander Yǔwén Xiǎn at Pujin,
who took her to inform Emperor Ming.
Summoned to the palace, she was received in the Weiyang Palace.
The emperor looked at her,
saw her exquisite beauty,
and asked her.
She said, "I am a heavenly maiden,
temporarily descended to the mortal world."
The emperor tried to force himself upon her, but her expression turned stern.
He then ordered his attendants to seize her,
but her voice rang like bells and chimes,
and she transformed into a rainbow and ascended to the heavens.

Passing through the Eastern Palace Gate
Sui Dynasty Crown Prince Yǒng, knowing he was about to be deposed,
was filled with anxiety and fear, unable to devise any strategy,
so he consulted the diviner Wáng Fǔxián.
Fǔxián said:
"A white rainbow piercing the Eastern Palace gate,
and the planet Venus encroaching upon the moon—
these are omens of the Crown Prince's deposition."

Angel
Wéi Gāo, while governing Shǔ, once feasted with guests in the western pavilion of the commandery.
A sudden storm cleared after a short while,
and unexpectedly, a rainbow descended from the sky,
directly entering the courtyard.
It lowered its head over the banquet, sucking up all the food and drink,
its colors like a rosy cloud,
its head resembling that of a donkey.
It looked around in all directions for a long time before finally leaving.
Wéi Gāo, frightened, ended the feast, saying:
"I have heard that rainbows are an ominous, baleful energy;
now it has halted our feast—how strange indeed!"
Dòu Lú Shǔ said:
"The rainbow is a messenger of Heaven;
if it descends upon evil, it portends calamity,
but if it descends upon righteousness, it signifies good fortune.
You, sir, are a righteous man—I dare to congratulate you on this auspicious sign."
More than ten days later, an imperial edict arrived appointing him as Zhōngshū Lìng.
"Records from the Chamber of Manifestation" and "Records of Chéngdū"
Entering the Residence
In the third month of the second year of the Yuánhé era,
a rainbow entered the residence of General Zhāng Zǐliáng in Rùnzhōu,
first dipping into the water jar,
then completely entering the well to drink.
In the ninth month of that year, Lǐ Qǐ rebelled,
ordering Zǐliáng to capture Xuānshè,
but Zǐliáng turned his troops to besiege the city,
leading to Qǐ's capture. Zǐliáng
was appointed as the Imperial Guard and later served as a regional military governor.
"Collection of Auspicious and Ominous Signs Verified"
Nílóng
Hóu Hóngshí was a man from Púbǎn.
When he was just thirteen or fourteen years old,
he once slept under the eaves.
As heavy rain was about to fall,
a rainbow appeared from the river to drink water,
and soon it passed through Hóngshí's mouth.
His mother saw this but dared not startle him.
After a long while, the rainbow vanished from the sky into Hóngshí's mouth
and did not emerge again.
When he awoke,
his mother asked if he had dreamed anything.
He replied:
"I just dreamed of entering the river to drink water,
and returned full and satisfied."
His mother silently rejoiced,
knowing he was destined for greatness.
Months later, a Shu monk visited to read his physiognomy,
telling his mother:
"This is a dragon in disguise.
Only by leaving his hometown and serving near rivers or seas will he achieve prominence."
Hóngshí later became a military commander.
In the third year of Tongguang, he followed the Crown Prince Xìngshèng to conquer Shu and was appointed Prefect of Méizhōu,
governing Kuízhōu with authority.
He later moved from Jiāngníng to the Qián Prefecture headquarters,
with both posts and two military commands located near great rivers.

Entering the Hall
In the eighth month of the ninth year of the Qiánhēng era of Liú Yǎn of the Southern Hàn,
a white rainbow entered his Sānqīng Hall.
Yǎn was quite worried and fearful,
and those outside were shocked and afraid.
It happened that the court scholar Wáng Hóng, wishing to please Yǎn,
took the white rainbow to be a white dragon and presented a rhapsody celebrating its appearance to the emperor.
Yǎn was greatly pleased,
and thus changed the era name to Báilóng and altered his personal name to Yǎn.

The four seasons and four directions each have their own period of time,
never missing their appointed times,
