Four Prohibitions
The enlightened king has four prohibitions:
In spring, no killing or attacking,
no excavating large mounds,
felling great trees,
leveling high mountains,
spreading large fires,
executing high officials,
or collecting grain taxes and money.
In summer, no damming waterways to reach famous rivers or blocking great valleys,
undertaking earthworks,
or shooting birds and beasts.
In autumn, no pardoning faults, releasing criminals, or delaying punishments.
In winter, no granting titles, awarding honors, or distributing salaries that harm the storage of the five grains.
Thus, if spring prohibitions are not enforced, the five grains will not ripen;
if summer prohibitions are not enforced, plants and trees will not flourish;
if autumn prohibitions are not enforced, wickedness and evil will not be overcome;
if winter prohibitions are not enforced, the earth's energy will not be stored.
If all four are violated, yin and yang will be imbalanced, and wind and rain will not come in season.
"Guǎnzǐ"
Arriving at the forbidden area

and cold and heat will lose their proper order.
In such cases, the harvest will be poor and the five grains will not ripen;
the sage ruler, when issuing decrees, must carefully consider the four seasons,
this is the utmost prohibition.

National Prohibitions

autumn brings maturity and then ends life,
winter receives and stores.
If spring is severe and does not produce, it is because the king's virtue is not thorough.
If summer is cold and does not foster growth, it is because the ministers do not follow the ruler's commands.

Decree of Occurrence
In the Beginning of Spring season, the first five days,
the east wind thaws the ice.
The next five days,
hibernating insects begin to stir.
The last five days,
fish swim up to the ice.
Next comes the Rain Water solar term.
The first five days, otters offer fish,
the next five days, wild geese arrive,
and the last five days, grass and trees sprout.
Next comes Mid-Spring,
the Awakening of Insects season,
the first five days, small peach trees bloom,
the next five days, orioles sing,
and the last five days, eagles transform into doves.
Next comes the Spring Equinox solar term,
the first five days, swallows arrive,
the next five days, thunder begins to sound,
and peonies flourish. The last five days, lightning first appears.
Next comes Late Spring,
on the day of Clear and Bright,
the first five days,
paulownia trees begin to bloom,
the next five days, field mice transform into quails,
and tree peonies bloom.
The last five days,
rainbows first appear.
Next comes the Grain Rain solar term.
The first five days, duckweed begins to grow,
the next five days, cooing doves preen their feathers,
and the last five days, hoopoes descend on mulberry trees.
All these six solar terms,
eighteen pentads,
are periods when spring's yang energy spreads and fosters growth.
Thus, those who nurture life must carefully follow the timing of heaven.

If it rains on New Year's Day, spring will be dry,

If it rains on the second day,
people will eat two liters.

"If the year is to be sweet,

if the year is to be bitter,
the bitter herb that appears first is pepperweed;
if the year is to be rainy,

The Earthen Ox
The Monthly Ordinance prescribes the presentation of an earthen ox,
to indicate the earliness or lateness of agricultural work.
It is said that south of the capital city, an earthen ox is erected,
indicating that if the Beginning of Spring falls on the full moon of the twelfth month,
the ox-herder should stand in front to show that farming should begin early.
If the Beginning of Spring falls on the last day of the twelfth month or the first day of the first month,
then the ox-herder should stand in the middle to show that farming should begin at the usual time.
If the Beginning of Spring falls on the full moon of the first month,
the ox-herder should stand behind to show that farming should begin late.
This is a major state policy to ensure agricultural timeliness,
thus the sages urgently attend to nourishing the people,
striving to complete the spring cultivation.
Nowadays in all provinces and commanderies under heaven,
on the day of the Beginning of Spring, an earthen ox is made,
adorned with colorful decorations,
then whipped with colored sticks,
and subsequently smashed,
with everyone taking a piece of the earth to pray for a bountiful harvest.
Is this not contrary to the original meaning?

What are the three subtleties?
When the yang energy begins to spread,
all things in the yellow springs move subtly without yet being manifest.
In the month of November,
yang energy starts to nurture roots beneath the yellow springs,
and all things are red,

honoring red.
In the month of December,

The Great Commentary of the Book of Documents states:
Xia took the first month of spring as the correct beginning,
Shang took the last month of winter as the correct beginning,
Zhou took the middle month of winter as the correct beginning.
Xia used November as the correct beginning,
honoring black and taking dawn as the start of the month.
Shang used December as the correct beginning, honoring white,
and took cockcrow as the start of the month.
Zhou used November as the correct beginning,
honoring red,
and took midnight as the start of the month.
They did not use the second month or later as the correct beginning
because all things are not yet aligned, and there is no suitable system to govern them,
so it must be in the months of the three subtleties.

Treasure the essence
Yáo reigned for seventy years,
when young phoenixes gathered every year,
qílín roamed the marshes,
and owls fled to remote deserts.
The Zhīzhī Kingdom offered the Chóngmíng bird, also called Chóngjīng.
It was said to have double pupils in each eye,
resembled a chicken in appearance,
and was similar to a phoenix.
It sometimes shed its feathers and flew with bare wings,
capable of fighting off fierce beasts like tigers and wolves,
preventing disasters and evil from causing harm.
It was fed with jade nectar,
sometimes coming several times a year,
other times not appearing for several years.
The people always cleaned their doors, hoping for the Chóngmíng's arrival.
When it did not come,
they carved wood or cast metal into its likeness,
placing it by their doors,
which naturally repelled evil spirits and malevolent beings.
Today, on the first day of the year, people carve wood, cast metal, or paint chickens on windows,
which are vestiges of the Chóngjīng.

Dreaming of Zhōng Kuí
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng held a military review at Líshān during the Kāiyuán era.

stealing people's things as if in play.

turning joy into sorrow."
The emperor grew angry
and was about to call for his guards
when suddenly he saw a large ghost
wearing a tattered hat,
dressed in a blue robe,
girded with a horn belt,
and shod in court boots.
He went straight to seize the small ghost,
first gouging out its eyes,
then splitting it open and devouring it.

five pungent ingredients refine the body.
Annotation:
The five pungents,
are used to stimulate the qi of the five organs,
namely garlic, wild garlic, chives, yúntái, and coriander.
Zhuāngzǐ says:
In the first month, drink wine and eat scallions,
to unblock the five organs.
"Shí Yī Xīn Jìng" says:
Consume the five pungents to ward off pestilential qi.
Cultivating the Form
Zhōu Chù's "Fēngtǔ Jì" states:
On New Year's Day, one should swallow a raw egg,
calling it "refining the body."
Gě Hóng's "Liàn Huà" chapter says:
In the first month, swallow seven eggs and seven red beans each,
to ward off pestilent vapors.
Zhāng Zhòngjǐng's prescription states:
There are malignant vapors in some years,
which, if they strike a person, cause sudden death;
take twenty-seven soybeans,
an egg, white sesame, and swallow them with wine.
"Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì" records:
When the Liáng dynasty ruled the land,
they abstained from eating pungent foods,
and from then on, the people of Jīng did not eat eggs,
following this regular practice.
Presenting pepper and cypress wine
Dǒng Xūn states:
At the beginning of the year, one should drink spiced wine,
as pepper is fragrant and also serves as medicine,
hence on this day, pepper flowers are offered to elders.
Cuī Shí's "Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes" says:
On New Year's Day, pepper and cypress wine is presented;
pepper is the essence of the Jade Balance star,
and consuming it makes the body light and able to resist aging.
Cypress is an immortal's medicine.
Chéng Gōngzǐ'ān's "Inscription on Pepper Blossoms" says:
It begins at the year's start,
used to rectify the New Year's Day;
its flavor is truly precious,
dispelling all ailments.
Take Peach Soup
The Record of the Year and Seasons in Jīngchǔ states:
On New Year's Day, one should drink peach soup.
The Canon of Arts says:
The peach is the essence of the Five Elements,
suppressing evil influences
and controlling all demons.
Five Woods Decoction
The "Miscellaneous Cultivation Texts" states:
On the first day of the first month,
take five kinds of wood to boil into a decoction for bathing,
which will keep one's beard and hair black until old age.
Note:
Taoists call:
Qīngmùxiāng (costus root) as Wǔmùxiāng (five woods incense),
also saying:
the five woods,
Taoists often use these for bathing,
this is its meaning.
Jiāoyátáng
On New Year's Day, people eat sticky tooth candy,
which symbolizes firmness and stability.
Records of the Seasons of Jīngchǔ
Breaking Seven Pines
Dǒng Xūn answered the question:
At the beginning of the year, break off pine branches,
seven for men and two for women, to make medicinal drinks.
Resolving the Eight Winds
Wèi divination observes the eight winds on the first day of the first month to make judgments.
If the wind comes from the south,
there will be a great drought in the southwest,
a minor drought in the west.
There will be military conflict in the northwest,
beans will ripen in the north,
an average harvest in the northeast indicates an excellent year,
great floods in the east,
epidemics in the southeast.
When the year is unfavorable, the eight winds
often oppose each other,
with the stronger prevailing over the weaker,
the enduring overcoming the transient, and the swift surpassing the slow.
"Hàn Tiānwén Zhì"
Immortal Tree
The "Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn" states:
On New Year's Day, peach boards are made and placed on doors,
called divine wood,
resembling the mountain peach trees of Yùlǜ,
which all ghosts fear.
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" states:
In the Dùshuò Mountain of the Eastern Sea,
there is a large peach tree coiled for three thousand miles,
its low branches facing northeast are called the ghost gate,
where myriad ghosts enter and exit.
There are two deities,
one named Shéntú,
the other named Yùlěi,
who oversee and lead the ghosts that harm people,
capturing them with reed ropes to feed tigers.
Thus, the Yellow Emperor modeled and imitated this,
after driving away evil,
he set up peach figures on the doors,
depicting Shéntú and Yùlěi holding reed ropes to ward off malevolent ghosts,
and painted tigers on the doors to devour ghosts.
The "Fēngsú Tōng" states:
In ancient times during the era of the Yellow Emperor, there were two brothers, Shéntú and Yùlǜ,
endowed with the ability to capture ghosts across the land.
The illustration says:
On the Táodū Mountain, there is a large peach tree,
coiled for three thousand miles,
on which stands a golden rooster,
that crows when the sun shines upon it.
Below are two deities,
one named Shén,
the other named Yù,
both holding reed ropes to watch for ominous ghosts,
and killing them upon capture.
The "Hòu Hàn" commentary:
Peach figures,
the term "figure" (gěng) means
renewal.
At the year's end and beginning,
it receives great blessings.
The tiger, a yang creature,
the leader of all beasts,
is capable of striking and devouring malevolent spirits.
The "Dōngdū Fù" says:
Dùshuò creates the figures,
guarded by Yùlǜ.
Shéntú assists,
both holding reed ropes.
They inspect every corner with their eyes,
capturing any remaining ghosts.
The capital is secure and pure,
with no evil left unchecked.
Túsū
"Suìhuá Jì" records:
Lìtúsū was the name of a thatched hut,
where someone once lived in ancient times.
Every New Year's Eve, he would give the neighborhood a medicinal prescription,
instructing them to soak it in a bag placed in a well.
On New Year's Day, they would fetch the water and place it in wine vessels,
then the whole family would drink it to avoid epidemic diseases.
Nowadays, people have the prescription but do not know its name,
simply calling it Túsū.
"Sìshí Zuǎnyào" states:
Túsū
was the name of Sūn Sīmiǎo's hut,
some say "tú" means slaughtering,
and "sū" means decay.
Drinking starts from small sips.
The "Monthly Ordinances for the Four Classes of People" states:
On New Year's Day, when offering wine,
the order should start from the youngest.
Begin with the youngest.
Jìn Hǎixī once asked Dǒng Xūn:
Why is it that common people drink on New Year's Day,
starting with the youngest?
Dǒng Xūn replied:
It is said that the young gain a year first,
so wine is offered to congratulate them.
The old lose a year,
hence they drink later.
In the Táng dynasty, Liú Mèngdé and Bái Lètiān exchanged poems while drinking on New Year's Day.
Liú wrote: "You and I share the same birth year,
yet I yield the first cup of New Year's wine."
Bái responded: "You and I share the same birth year—who should drink the New Year's wine first?"
Bái also wrote in "Drinking by Decree During the New Year's Holiday":
"I cannot decline the New Year's wine when offered first,
for you have pushed me to be the young one."
Gù Kuàng wrote:
"Unaware that old age arrives with spring,
together we come,
yet grieve—how many companions remain by my side?
In solitude, I shy from the bright mirror,
holding the tú sū wine, I yield to the youth."
Péi Yízhí wrote:
"Knowing my years are few compared to others,
I take the tú sū wine first, not yielding to spring.
If I pass a few years and meet this day again,
I shall still lament, envying others."
Chéng Wéngàn wrote:
"Under the stars, I first raise the cup to wish for Yáo's longevity,
startled in the mirror by the frost on my temples.
Best to steal a laugh before the lamp,
for tú sū wine should not be tasted first."
Fāng Gàn wrote:
"Drinking tú sū wine determines age,
all at the table laugh at my graying hair."
Disliking inauspiciousness
At dawn on New Year's Day,
people dress formally at home,
set off firecrackers in the courtyard and post paintings,
place eggs or carve five-colored earth above their doors,
to ward off misfortunes.
Yì Tōng Guà Yàn
Ode to the Pine and Cypress
From "Records of Customs":
On New Year's Day, people of Chǔ present odes to pine and cypress,
while Zhōu Yǔxìn composed an inscription on cypress leaves.
With the inscription arrives,
followed by the ode to pepper blossoms.
The beginning of the year
Wáng Xīzhī's "Monthly Etiquette" states:
As days pass and months come,
the new year's beginning arrives,
Tàicù announces the dawn,
faint sunlight starts to spread,
nothing is unsuitable,
nourishing spirit and cultivating simplicity.
Dividing groups to divine the year's epidemics
In Xīyù Níngyuǎn, every New Year's Day, the king and chieftains would divide into two teams,
each team selecting one person to don armor and fight,
while the crowd pelted them with tiles and stones.
If someone died, it was used to foretell the fortune of the year,
interpreting good or bad omens. Bàirì Xīnluó
had a custom of worshipping the sun and moon gods on New Year's Day.
"Book of Táng"
Yúnkāi Festival
In Yuèzhōu, from New Year's Day when neighbors
celebrate with feasts and drinking,
until the twelfth day when it concludes,
this day is called the Cloud-Clearing Festival.
"Yuèyáng Local Customs Record"
The Beginning of Spring
Emperor Zhuān established the first month of early spring as the beginning of the year,
at that time, the new moon of the first month
coincided with the Beginning of Spring, and the five planets converged in the celestial realm at the constellation Yíngshì.
Ice began to melt,
dormant insects started to emerge,
roosters crowed three times,
Heaven was said to create the seasons,
Earth was said to bring prosperity,
humankind was said to produce music,
and birds, beasts, and all things responded in harmony,
thus the sage Emperor Zhuān became the patriarch of the calendar.
From the "Treatise on Harmonics and the Calendar" of the Jìn dynasty, discussing Dǒng Bā's proposal of the Wèi.
Xuánjī
On the first auspicious day of the first month, he received the throne from the Cultured Ancestor,
and observed the revolving jade sphere to harmonize the seven administrative affairs.
What is the revolving sphere?
The commentary says:
"Revolving" means to return,
"sphere" means subtlety,
minuteness.
Its changes are subtle yet what it moves
is great, hence it is called the revolving sphere.
Therefore, the revolving sphere refers to the North Pole,
"received" refers to Shùn,
the "auspicious day" is the first day.
"Great Commentary on the Book of Documents"
Nine Fermentations
Under the Hàn system,
the ancestral temple used nine fermentations for the Eighth Month Zhòu libation,
with the emperor attending the sacrifice using the Tàiláo offering.
The wine was started on the first day of the first month,
and completed in the eighth month,
named Zhòu,
also called nine fermentations,
and also known as pure Zhòu.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Jiǔbīn Yuè
On New Year's Day,
the Son of Heaven proceeded to the Hall of Yang Virtue,
where the music of the Nine Honored Guests was performed.
A sharīra came from the east,
frolicking in the courtyard,
then entered the hall and transformed into a flatfish by splashing water before the hall,
leaping and rinsing in the water.
It then transformed into a yellow dragon amidst mist,
eighty zhang tall,
emerging from the water to play in the courtyard.
Two large silk ropes were tied at both ends,
with several zhang between them,
and two female dancers performed opposite each other while walking on the ropes.
They passed each other without their shoulders tilting,
and also stepped and twirled, bending their bodies to hide within a dipper.
Bells and chime stones sounded together,
and after the music ended, a fish-dragon sprawling performance was presented,
with yellow flutes playing three rounds.
"Han Official Duties"
The seventh day marks the formation of man.
Dǒng Xūn, a court counselor of the Jìn Dynasty, wrote in his *Answers on Rituals and Customs*:
The first day of the first month is for chickens,
the second day for pigs,
the third day for sheep,
the fourth day for dogs,
the fifth day for cattle,
the sixth day for horses,
and the seventh day for humans.
On New Year's Day, a chicken is painted on the door,
and on the seventh day, a human figure is pasted on the bed curtain.
Nowadays, on the first day, chickens are not killed,
on the second day, dogs are not killed,
on the third day, sheep are not killed,
on the fourth day, pigs are not killed,
on the fifth day, cattle are not killed,
on the sixth day, horses are not killed,
and on the seventh day, punishments are not carried out.
On these days, from early morning to the front of the door,
people call out to cattle, sheep, and various livestock,
urging them to come,
then place millet and beans mixed with ashes and scatter them inside the residence,
saying it is to attract cattle and horses.
According to another account:
When heaven and earth first opened,
on the first day,
chickens were created,
and on the seventh day, humans were made.
*Imperial Readings*
Ribbon-cutting
The Record of the Seasons of Jīngchǔ states:
The seventh day of the first month is Human Day,
when seven kinds of vegetables are used to make a soup,
colored silk is cut into human figures,
or gold foil is carved and pasted on screens,
and they are also worn in the hair.
Dǒng Xūn inquired about customs and said:
When people enter the new year,
their appearance should be renewed, changing from the old.
Zhì Ānrén
Wèi Dōngpíng Wáng Xī ascended Ānmín Mountain in Shòuzhāng County on the seventh day of the month,
excavating the mountaintop to create a meeting and viewing place,
and carved an inscription on the cliff,
the text of which still remains.
The inscription reads:
"On the seventh day of the first month,
this day is for people,
I drive my fine steeds,
ascending that Ānrén."
From Guō Yuánshēng's "Records of Military Expeditions"
Making Huāshèng
Jiǎ Chōng's wife Lady Lǐ's "Classic of Admonitions" states:
On Renri people make huāshèng ornaments to gift each other,
depicting the complete victory patterns from auspicious diagrams,
also resembling the Queen Mother of the West wearing her shèng headdress.
Lǐ Shāngyǐn's poem reads:
"Carving gold to make shèng ornaments continues the customs of Chǔ,
cutting colored silk to fashion human figures originates from Jìn traditions."
Ascending the West of Shàn
Jìn Lǐ Chōng ascended Shànxī Temple on the seventh day of the first month,
his poem reads:
I command my carriage to climb the western hills,
and rest my eyes gazing upon the plains and fields.
Ascending the Heights
In the Jin Dynasty, Huán Wēn's staff officer Zhāng Wàng also wrote a poem titled "Climbing Heights" on the seventh day of the first lunar month.
Plum Blossom Makeup
The Book of Sòng records:
On Renrì, Princess Shòuyáng, daughter of Emperor Wǔ, was napping beneath the eaves of Hánzhāng Hall when
a plum blossom drifted onto her forehead,
forming a five-petaled pattern.
The blossom would not brush away,
so the empress preserved it,
wondering how long it would last.
After three days, it washed off completely.
The palace ladies, marveling at this wonder,
vied to imitate it—
this is the origin of the "plum blossom makeup" still known today.
The Records of Jīnlíng
Dēng Yúnlóng
Emperor Xiàojìng of Wèi ascended the Yúnlóng Gate on the Day of Man.
Cuī Zhān and his father Cuī Míng both attended the banquet and composed poems.
The edict asked Xíng Shào and others:
"How does this poem by Zhān compare?"
His father Xián said:
"Míng is broad and elegant, displaying splendor.
Zhān's tone is fresh and clear,
both are leaders among poets."
When the banquet concluded, everyone praised them:
"Today's banquet
was entirely for Cuī Zhān and his father."
"Northern History"
Asked about precedents
The Emperor of Wèi held a banquet for all officials,
asking why the day was called Human Day,
but none could explain the reason.
Wèi Shōu replied:
According to Dǒng Xūn, a court gentleman of Jìn:
the first day of the first month is for chickens
and so on
and so forth
the seventh day is for humans.
At that time, Xíng Shào was also present,
and felt quite ashamed as well.
From "History of the Northern Dynasties"
"Tán Sǒu" records:
Gāozǔ of Northern Qí,
on the seventh day ascended a height,
feasting his ministers including Wèi Shōu.
and so on
and so forth
The superior person prevails.
Liú Zhēn's wife, Chén Shì, presented a ritual protocol stating:
On the seventh day of the first month, superiors prevail over inferiors.
Homesick Poem
Xuē Dàohéng was on a diplomatic mission to Chén,
and composed a poem for Human Day that said:
"Only seven days have passed since spring began,
Yet I've been away from home for two full years."
Southerners mocked him, saying:
"What kind of talk is this?
Who said this northerner understands poetry?"
But when he continued:
"My return comes after wild geese head north,
Though homesickness arose before flowers bloomed,"
they then rejoiced and said:
"Indeed, a famous scholar is never unworthy of his reputation."
From "Anecdotes from Suí and Táng Dynasties"
Court Audience
Duke Zhèng once went on a journey,
and on the seventh day of the first lunar month, he had an audience with Tàizōng.
Tàizōng consoled him, saying:
"Your arrival today
can indeed be called the Human Day."

Jiānbǐng
The Ministry of Provisions had festival food materials,
referring to the jiānbǐng eaten on the seventh day of the first month.
"Tang Liu Dian"
Qīng Huī Gé
On the seventh day of the first lunar month in the third year of the Jǐnglóng era of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
the emperor visited the Qīng Huī Pavilion,
climbed high and encountered snow,
whereupon he bestowed golden colored rénshèng and ordered the academicians to compose poems.
On this day, there was great joy.
Zōng Chǔkè's poem reads:
Graceful is the divine pavilion,
Unevenly set amongst the Milky Way.
The ninefold forbidden center opens,
The seventh night of early spring returns.
The Tài Yè Pond takes heaven as its water,
Mount Pénglái uses snow for its mountains.
Today, the trees of the Shànglín Garden,
Nowhere are they not fit to climb.
Liú Xiàn's poem:
The wind seeks out songs to carry aloft,
Snow swirls around the dancing lines.
Zhào Yànzhāo's poem:
In the courtyard, a thousand flowers bloom,
On the míng steps, seven leaves are new.
Lǐ Qiáo's poem:
The three yang energies particularly prevail on this festival,
The seventh day is the most divine hour.
Spreading blessings, we pass the fragrant wine,
Ascending high, we adorn with colorful figures.
Another heptasyllabic poem:
A thousand cups of imperial wine grace the feast,
Six-petaled blossoms swirl chaotically around the branches.
Right here, immortals face the jade garden,
Why trouble to trace the path to the Jasper Pool?
"Records of the Jǐnglóng Literary Institute"
Dàmíng Diàn
In the fourth year of the Jǐnglóng era, in the seventh month,
a banquet was held at the Dàmíng Hall,
where colorful silk human-shaped adornments were bestowed upon princes and nobles and those of lower ranks,
and polo playing was also observed.
Lǐ Qiáo's poem composed by imperial command:
"The iron phoenix once soared, shaking off auspicious snow;
The bronze crow turned delicately, entering the propitious wind."
Mǎ Huáisù's poem:
"For the three yang seasons awaiting the festival, gold forms the adornments;
With a hundred blessings extending good fortune, jade serves as the cup."
Lǐ Qiáo's poem:
"The cassia emits a half-wheel, welcoming this night;
The míng grass unfolds seven leaves, responding to this morning."
Sū Tǐng's poem:
"The seven-leaved immortal míng bears the moon's glow;
A thousand jade-like willows brush through the mist as they open."
"In the early years, there was competition to post the Yìchūn adornments;
For long life, the longevity cup is floated first in offering."
Cuī Rìyòng's poem:
"The mossy hues of the Qǔjiāng appear like liquid before ice;
The plum blossoms in the Shàngyuàn are delicate amidst the snow."
Wéi Yuándàn's poem:
"As the verdant spring commences, humans create the day;
The ornate adornments are first completed, the eyes fashioning the human form."
Wǔ Píngyī's polo poem:
"On the festive occasion, we roam and revel once more,
Dividing our steeds to play with the colorful ball."
"Galloping back and forth through the Shàngyuàn,
Pacing and winding around the connecting moats."
"Shadows vanish into the red dust,
Light follows the reddish sweat flowing."
"As the appreciation concludes, the clear scene turns to dusk,
Singing and dancing cease when the joyous time ends."

Treading on the Riverbed
The people of Kuízhōu revere Zhūgě Wǔhóu,
and on Renrì the entire city goes out to the Bāzhèn Shoal,
which is called "treading the shoal."
Women gather small stones that can be strung and thread them with colorful strings,
attaching them to hairpins,
as an auspicious sign for the year.
The prefect hosts a banquet on the shoal.
"Tújīng"
The Story of Xiū Yóu's Divination
In Jiading, Shǔ, there is a deep pool on Jīndēng Mountain.
Every year on Renri, the commandery governor performs the oil divination ritual there,
which involves sprinkling oil on the water surface
and observing the patterns to predict the year's harvest or famine.
Praying for Silkworms
They have Lèshān,
where on the seventh day of the first month, the townspeople play music and feast for entertainment,
praying for sericulture affairs.
"Dàngqú Affairs"
Weather Divination Based on Cloudiness
Dōngfāng Shuò's Divination Text states:
The eight days following the New Year,
the first day is for chickens,
and so on,
and so forth,
the seventh day is for
humans, the eighth day is for grains. If the day is clear, it signifies the prosperity of the corresponding creature; if overcast, it foretells disaster.
The Bestowed Flower Was Taken Away
On the eighth day of the first month, the Beginning of Spring was established,
the palace distributed colored flowers to grant to the close ministers.
Wǔ Píngyī composed a poem in response to the imperial order:
The imperial carriage with blue banners descends from the emperor's terrace,
From the eastern suburbs and imperial gardens, we gaze upon spring's arrival.
The orioles have yet to understand their songs among the woods,
But red blossoms already begin to bloom within the palace halls.
In painted pavilions, the gentle wind first transforms the willows,
By silver ponds, the winding waters half-conceal the moss.
Joyfully encountering the emperor's brilliant writings that illuminate the melodies of Sháo,
We further hasten the rosy-hued cups, fearing the swift passage of time.
That day, Emperor Zhōngzōng personally wrote an edict commenting:
"Although Píngyī's years are the fewest,
his writing is remarkably alert and fresh.
Delighting in the red blossoms' early blooming,
and marveling that the orioles have not yet sung.
Circling back to recite and savor,
both admiration and sighing fill my heart.
Now I further grant him one branch of flower to highlight his excellence.
The flowers granted to the academicians were all ordered to be inserted in their hair,
later, those granted to Píngyī were crossed and inserted on both sides,
whereupon he danced and bowed in gratitude.
At that time, Cuī Rìyòng, taking advantage of the merry drinking,
wanted to seize the flower granted to Píngyī.
The emperor, seeing this from behind the curtain,
said to Píngyī:
"Why does Rìyòng want to take your flower?"
Píngyī knelt and replied:
"Reading ten thousand volumes follows Rìyòng,
full of empty boasts, he is granted one branch of flower,
but learning from Píngyī, he would never obtain it in his lifetime."
The emperor and attending ministers laughed heartily,
and thus further granted him a cup of wine,
earning admiration and praise at the time.
"Records of the Jǐnglóng Literary Institute"
Shàngyuán
The fifteenth day of the first month is the Shangyuan Festival.
Báitiē
Offer congee and sacrifice at the gate
The Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn states:
On the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, prepare rich congee to sacrifice to the doors.
The Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì states:
Nowadays, the local custom is to offer sacrifices to the doors on the full moon day,
first inserting willow branches into the doors,
following the direction the willow branches point,
and then using wine, dried meat, food, and bean congee with chopsticks inserted to make the sacrifice.
Sacrifice to Tàiyī
The Han dynasty worshiped the Great One,
from dusk until dawn.

Nowadays, people tour and view lanterns on the night of the first full moon in the first month,
which is a legacy of this practice.
Yǔyáng Càn Zhuā
Mǐ Héng was demoted by Emperor Wǔ of Wèi to the position of a drum official.
On the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, he was ordered to perform a drumming test.
Mǐ Héng raised his drumstick and played the "Yǔyáng Càn Zhuā" melody deeply,
which resonated with the clarity of metal and stone.
All those present were moved to change their expressions.
Kǒng Róng said:
Mǐ Héng's crime is like that of Xū Mí,
yet he could not inspire the dream of an enlightened king.
"Shì Shuō"
Sacrifice to the Silkworm Goddess
One night, Zhāng Chéng of Wú County got up
and suddenly saw a woman standing on his house.
She raised her hand from the southern corner, beckoning to Chéng,
who immediately approached her.
The woman said:
"This place is your family's silkworm room,
and I am the local deity here.
Next year on the fifteenth day of the first month, you should make white congee and float fat on top to offer to me.
I will surely make your silkworm harvest a hundredfold."
Having said this, she left
and completely vanished.
Chéng made the fatty congee as instructed,
and from then on, he gained a great abundance of silkworms.
This is the origin of making white fatty congee on the fifteenth day of the first month.
"Qí Xié Jì"
Another version says that on the fifteenth day of the first month, a deity descended upon the Chén family's residence,
claiming to be the Silkworm Goddess.
Climbing High
On the fifteenth day of the first month, there is a gathering for ascending heights.
"Shí Hǔ's Records of Yèzhōng"
Zhào Yuánzhòu
Emperor Wén of Suí once ascended a height with his close ministers on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month.
At that time, Yuán Zhòu was not present,
so the emperor immediately ordered him to be summoned urgently.
When Zhòu saw the emperor, he was told:
"You, sir, ascending the height with outsiders,
is not as good as joining me."

From "The Book of Suí"
Jiaodi Opera
During the Suí dynasty, the capital's residents
would engage in wrestling games every fifteenth day of the first month,
competing to outdo one another,
to the point of squandering wealth and resources.
Liǔ Yù submitted a memorial stating:
In recent times,
the capital and outer prefectures have filled streets and alleys on the full moon night of the first month,
gathering for revelry with drums clamoring to the heavens,
torches illuminating the ground,
performers and acrobats displaying bizarre forms and strange shapes,
viewed by all, both inside and outside,
without any restraint,
tall stands spanning the roads,
broad canopies reaching the clouds,
people in gorgeous attire and exquisite makeup,
carriages and horses causing congestion,
food and wine spread out abundantly,
music strings and pipes flourishing in gatherings,
exhausting assets and bankrupting families,
all competing for this moment,
gradually becoming a custom,
truly harming the people,
I request an edict to be issued throughout the land,
prohibiting it immediately.
The emperor approved his memorial.
(End)
Selling half a portrait
The wife of Chén Tàizǐ Shèrén Xú Déyán,
who was the younger sister of the later sovereign Shūbǎo,
was enfeoffed as Princess Lèchāng.
Her talent and beauty were unparalleled.
At that time, the political situation in Chén was in turmoil,
and Déyán knew they could not be preserved together.
He said to his wife:
"With your talent and appearance,
if the state falls, you will surely enter the household of a powerful noble,
and we will be forever separated.
If our bond of affection is not yet broken,
and we still hope to meet again,
we should have a token of faith."
Thereupon, he broke a mirror in two,
each keeping half,
and made a pact, saying:
"In the future, you must sell this on the fifteenth day of the first month in the capital market,
and I will be there;
on that day I will come to seek you."
When Chén fell,
his wife indeed entered the household of Duke Yuè Yáng Sù,
where she received exceptional favor and affection.
Déyán wandered through hardships and toil,
barely managing to reach the capital.
So, on the fifteenth day of the first month, he went to the market to search,
and there was an old servant selling half a mirror,
pricing it very high,
which made people laugh at him.
Déyán went straight to his residence,
provided a meal and explained the reason,
then produced his half of the mirror to match it.
He then inscribed a poem:
"The mirror and its owner have both departed;
the mirror returns, but not its owner.
No longer is there the shadow of Cháng'é,
only the empty radiance of the bright moon remains."
Upon reading the poem, Madame Chén wept and refused to eat.
When Sù learned of this, he was deeply moved and his expression changed.
He immediately summoned Déyán and returned his wife to him,
and additionally bestowed generous gifts upon them.
Those who heard of it were all deeply moved and sighed.
He then drank with Déyán and Madame Chén,
and asked Madame Chén to compose a poem:
"What kind of day is today,
facing the new official and the old official?
I dare neither to laugh nor to cry,
truly realizing how difficult it is to be human."
Thereupon, she returned to Jiāngnán with Déyán,
and they lived together until old age.
From "Běnshì Shī"
Jīnwú Enforce Night Curfew
In the capital city of the Western Capital, the streets had patrol officers,
who called out day and night to enforce the curfew.
Only on the night of the fifteenth day of the first lunar month,
were the patrol officers allowed to relax the curfew,
for one day before and after the event.
From Wéi Shù's "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Gentlemen and Ladies Roaming at Night
During the Tang Dynasty, on the night of the fifteenth of the first lunar month,
people were permitted to roam for three consecutive nights.
Temples, streets, and alleys were brightly lit as if it were daytime,
with festive scaffolds towering over a hundred feet high.
After the Shénlóng era, the decorations became even more elaborate,
and gentlemen and ladies all roamed at night without exception,
carriages and horses clogged the roads,
some people's feet did not touch the ground,
floating along for dozens of steps.
"Yōng Luò Líng Yì Xiǎo Lù"
Traveling incognito through the city
On the Lantern Festival night in the fourth year of the Jǐnglóng era,
Emperor Zhōngzōng and Empress Wéi, in plain clothes, passed through the market,
wandering and gazing freely.
They then visited the residence of Xiāo Zhìzhōng, the Secretariat Director's younger brother.
That night,
they released several thousand palace maids to view the lanterns,
leading many to escape and disappear.
On the Dīngmǎo night, they again went incognito to see the lanterns,
visiting the residence of Wéi Ānshí and Princess Chángníng's younger brother.
The "Book of Táng"
records Wéi Ānshí as a Palace Attendant.
Emperor Zhōngzōng and Empress Wéi visited his residence on the full moon night of the first month,
bestowing lavish gifts.
The Emperor
notes this single event yet finds discrepancies between the annals and biographies.
Imperial Carriage Wheels
On the fifteenth day of the first month in the second year of the Xiāntiān era of Emperor Ruìzōng,
on the sixteenth and seventeenth nights, a lantern wheel was erected outside the Ānfú Gate in the capital,
standing twenty zhang high,
clad in brocade and damask,
adorned with gold and silver,
lit with fifty thousand lamps,
appearing from afar like a blossoming tree.
Thousands of palace maidens,
dressed in silk gauze and damask,
trailing embroidered finery,
glittering with pearls and jade,
scented with fragrant powder,
each floral headdress,
each scarf costing up to ten thousand coins.
The attire for a single courtesan could amount to three hundred strings of cash.
Over a thousand young maidens and women from Cháng'ān and Wànnián were selected for their clothing and hairpins.
Even their maidservants were similarly adorned,
and for three days and nights, they sang and danced beneath the lantern wheel,
reaching the pinnacle of joy,
an event unprecedented in history.
(Records from the Court and the Commonality)
Yù Yánxǐ
Emperor Ruìzōng was fond of music,
and would listen to it until he forgot his weariness.
Emperor Xuánzōng was also skilled in music and temperament.
On the night of the first full moon in the first month of the second year of the Xiāntián era,
the foreign monk Pótuó requested that the city gates be opened at night to light thousands of lamps.
Emperor Ruìzōng attended the Yánxǐ Gate to enjoy the music.
This lasted for four days in total.
Yán Tǐngzhī submitted a memorial stating:
"Who is it that disturbs the night with drumming,
continuing until dawn under the pretext of guarding against emergencies?
This was originally a good practice for maintaining order.
Now, Your Majesty does not deeply consider caution and lightly disregards the principles of action and rest,
relaxing the prohibitions of the heavily guarded gates.
If cunning individuals take advantage—should there be galloping horses and speeding carriages,
spreading rumors and startling cries,
even the slightest disturbance to Your Majesty's attention would burden the imperial heart.
I believe this is not permissible."
(From the Old Book of Táng biography)
Release palace maidens for song and dance
In the early Xīntiān era,
the emperor ascended the Ānfú Gate to view the lanterns.
The Court of Imperial Sacrifices performed songs and music,
palace maidens emerged to sing and dance,
and court officials skilled in literature composed walking songs,
their melodies soaring into the clouds.
From the Tang dynasty capital's "Annual Events Record"
Lǐ Mō Tōuqǔ
Emperor Míng Huáng visited the Shàngyáng Palace,
where a new tune was composed overnight.
On the evening of the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, he went out incognito,
when he suddenly heard the same new tune played on a flute from a tavern.
Greatly astonished,
he secretly had the flutist arrested
and interrogated.
The man claimed that on that night, while admiring the moon on the Tiānjīn Bridge,
he heard the tune being performed in the palace.
Enchanted by the melody, he notated it by scratching the notes with a melon rind.
This was Lǐ Mó, a youth of Cháng'ān.
As Yuán Zhěn wrote in his "Song of the Liánchāng Palace":
"Lǐ Mó, flute pressed to palace walls,"
"stole notes of the newly composed tune."
Note to "Song of the Liánchāng Palace"
Constructing the Lantern Tower
The emperor, while in the eastern capital on the night of the first full moon,
moved his retinue to the Shàngyáng Palace,
where he grandly displayed lanterns and lit bonfires in the courtyard.
From the inner palace to the main hall's courtyard,
candles were arranged everywhere,
stretching continuously without interruption.
At that time, there was a skilled artisan named Máo Shùn from Fāngdū,
who ingeniously constructed a lantern tower of twenty sections using silk and colored fabrics,
reaching a height of one hundred and fifty feet.
Pearls, jade, gold, and silver were suspended from it,
and when a gentle breeze arose,
they chimed melodiously in harmony.
The lanterns were shaped like dragons, phoenixes, tigers, and leopards.
"Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng Huáng"
Making Noodle Cocoons
During the Lantern Festival in the capital, people make dough cocoons,
inscribing official titles on them,
to divine the rise or fall of one's official rank.
Some wager banquets as playful amusement.
"Records of the Tianbao Era"
and "Miscellaneous Records of the Seasons" state:
Dough cocoons are filled with meat or vegetarian stuffing—
essentially thick-skinned steamed buns.
Admonition Against Travel
The Emperor was at the Huaqing Palace on Líshān,
and it happened to be the Lantern Festival night when he wished to go out for an excursion.
Chén Xuánlǐ memorialized, saying:
"The open fields outside the palace require preparations;
if you insist on touring at night,
I hope you will return to the city gates."
The Emperor could not override him.
"New Book of the South"
Roaming in Guǎnglíng
On the evening of the Lantern Festival in the eighteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Emperor Xuánzōng said to Master Yè Fǎshàn:
"The grandeur of all regions
is displayed this evening.
Where is the most magnificent?"
He replied:
"None in the world surpasses Guǎnglíng."
The Emperor asked:
"By what means can I see it?"
The master said: "Your Majesty can go immediately."
Suddenly a rainbow bridge appeared before the hall,
with plank pavilions suspended in air and railings,
as if painted by a master artist. When the bridge was completed,
he warned not to look back.
Thereupon the Emperor stepped onto it,
with Tàizhēn, Gāo Lìshì, and several dozen musicians following.
With each step rising higher,
they reached straight into the clouds,
and in moments arrived at a temple in Guǎnglíng.
Viewing the lavish display,
the brilliance of lantern lights,
illuminating the temple grounds where elegantly dressed men and women
all looked up and exclaimed:
"Immortals have appeared in the five-colored clouds!"
As the Emperor took large strides,
the master said:
"I request Your Majesty command the musicians to play 'The Song of Rainbow and Feather Garments' once,
so it may be verified later."
Several decades later,
Guǎnglíng reported:
"On the fifteenth of the first month during the second watch,
immortals riding colored clouds came from the west,
descended upon Xiàogǎn Temple,
towering several dozen zhang high,
and played 'The Song of Rainbow and Feather Garments' once,
before finally departing westward."
On the morning of the Yuánzhāo ritual ceremony, auspicious clouds appeared where your humble servant was practicing,
and celestial music was performed.
The Emperor was greatly pleased upon reading the memorial,
and finally believed Master Yè had not deceived him.
"Records of the Mysterious and Strange"
The Emperor and Master Yè often traveled to Xīliáng Prefecture.
"Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng"
Hundred-Branched Lamp Tree
Lady Hánguó set up a hundred-branch lantern tree,
eighty feet high,
erected it on a high mountain,
lit it on the Lantern Festival night,
visible from a hundred miles away,
its brilliance outshone the moonlight.
"Tales of the Tianbao Era"
A thousand torches encircling
Yáng Guózhōng's sons and younger brothers,
every year on the Lantern Festival night,
would each have a thousand torch-like red candles surrounding them.
The Emperor
Wǔ Zhái's Night Excursion
On the Lantern Festival in the tenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
the five households of the Yáng family went on a night excursion.
They then contended with the entourage of Princess Guǎngníng for the gate of the West Market.
A servant of the Yáng family mistakenly struck the princess's clothing with his whip,
causing the princess to fall from her horse.
Her consort, Chéng Chāngyì, helped the princess up,
and was consequently struck several times.
The princess tearfully reported the incident to the emperor.
The emperor ordered the execution of one of the Yáng family's servants,
suspended Chéng Chāngyì from his official post,
and forbade him from attending court audiences.
Thereafter, the Yáng family became increasingly arrogant,
entering and exiting the palace gates without being questioned.
Officials in the capital regarded them with disdain,
hence the popular saying of the time:
"A son may not be enfeoffed as a marquis,
but a daughter becomes the emperor's consort.
Behold, it is the daughter who brings honor to the family."
"The Unofficial Biography of Tàizhēn"
Lighting lanterns and playing music
Empress Xiāo, the wife of Emperor Mùzōng,
was honored as Grand Empress Dowager
after Emperor Wénzōng ascended the throne.
On the night of the first full moon in the third year of the Kāichéng era,
lanterns were displayed and celestial music performed in the Xiántài Hall,
where the three palace dowagers gathered to offer toasts and celebrate,
following the rituals of a family gathering.
All imperial princes, princesses, consorts, and relatives attended the banquet.
"Old Book of Táng"
Wandering in Hèlín
Zhào Wèinán Gǔ once had his home in Western Zhè,
where he had a beautiful concubine of whom he was deeply enamored.
When he went to take the imperial examinations,
because his mother prevented it,
he did not take her along.
During the Lantern Festival, while visiting Hèlín Temple,
the military governor of Western Zhè caught sight of her,
and she became his.
The following year,
Gǔ passed the examinations,
and so composed a quatrain to admonish him:
"Lonely before the hall, the sun sets once more;
from the sunny terrace, you've become clouds that don't return.
In the past, I heard of Shāchìlì;
today, the green-browed maiden belongs to the envoy."
The military governor of Western Zhè felt uneasy,
and sent a messenger to return her to Gǔ.
Gǔ was just then leaving the pass,
and stopped at Héngshuǐ Station on the way,
where he saw a procession of sedan chairs and horses, quite grand.
By chance, he inquired of the attendants, who replied:
"The minister of Western Zhè has sent us to escort the newly passed examination candidate Zhào's lady to the capital."
The concubine in the sedan chair also recognized Gǔ.
Gǔ dismounted and lifted the curtain to look at her.
She embraced Gǔ, wept bitterly, and died.
She was then buried on the south bank of Héngshuǐ.
From "Records of Selected Sayings."
Gāomíng Shìjiè
Chén Xī was dismissed from the position of Vice Minister of Revenue,
and went to visit his elder sister in Gūsū.
It happened to be the Lantern Festival night when he went to see the lanterns.
With chariots and horses clamoring and surging,
his eyes were dazzled and his spirit intoxicated.
He sighed and said:
"Having traversed frost and ice, sailed through misty waters,
suddenly beholding this brilliant world,
I feel my spirit and clarity instantly restored to their former state."
From "Qīng Yì Lù"
Lantern Festival at the Fifth Watch
In the fifth year of Qiándé, an imperial edict stated:
"The court is free from troubles,
and all within the realm is peaceful.
Moreover, the harvests have been abundant year after year,
so it is fitting for officials and commoners to indulge in celebration.
On the Shangyuán Festival, two additional nights—the seventeenth and eighteenth—shall be added."
The Sòngcháo Lèiyào records:
"The capital celebrated the Shangyuán lantern festival for three nights.
After the Qián family surrendered their territory and offered money to purchase two extra nights,
the current addition of the seventeenth and eighteenth nights for lantern displays is due to the Qián family."
From the Jiāng Línjǐ Zájì.
Yuánxiāo Pò Zéi
Dí Qīng was appointed as the pacification commissioner of Guǎngxī,
while Nóng Zhìgāo was guarding the Kūnlún Pass.
When Dí Qīng arrived at Bīnzhōu,
it happened to be the Lantern Festival with grand lantern displays.
On the first night, he feasted with his officers,
and on the second night, he hosted a banquet for the military officials.
At the first watch, Dí Qīng claimed illness and rose to leave,
instructing Sūn Yuánguī to temporarily preside over the banquet.
He repeatedly sent people to attend to the guests,
so that by dawn, none dared to leave.
Suddenly, a swift report arrived:
that night at the third watch,
Dí Qīng had already captured the Kūnlún Pass.
From "Bǐ Tán"
The long lamp writes the night
Cài Jūnshǒu governed Fúzhōu,
and on the Lantern Festival, he ordered each household to light seven lanterns.
Chén Liè crafted a large lantern,
over ten feet long,
inscribed with the words:
For a wealthy family, one lantern is but a grain from a vast granary;
For a poor family, one lantern brings father and son to face each other in tears.
Do you know, elegant Governor,
or do you not,
that you still lament the lack of exquisite tunes in the music and songs?
When Jūnshǒu saw it,
he turned his carriage around and canceled the lantern order.
From "Cháomín Kèhuà."
Welcoming Zǐgū
On the evening of the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, Zǐgū is welcomed for divination.
Liú Jìngshū's "Garden of Marvels" states:
Zǐgū was originally a concubine in a household,
envied by the principal wife,
and died of grief on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month.
Therefore, later people made her effigy in the toilet area,
welcoming her with the divination chant: "Zǐxū is not here."
It is said this refers to her husband
Cáo Fū having departed,
and "her mother-in-law
and sister-in-law may come out." Píngchāng Mèng shì once welcomed her on this day,
and she pierced through the roof to leave.
Since then, old clothes are placed in the toilet,
likely for this reason.
"Comprehensive Readings" states:
She was the daughter of Emperor Kù,
who said before dying,
"I have always loved music,
so on the fifteenth of the first month, you may welcome me with proper attire."
Another account appears in the "Miscellaneous Five Elements Manual":
The toilet deity is named Hòudì.
"Garden of Marvels" records:
When Táo Kǎn went to the toilet,
he encountered someone claiming to be Hòudì,
wearing a single-layer garment and a flat-topped headpiece, who told him:
"Do not speak for three years,
and you will achieve unimaginable nobility."
This suggests Hòudì's spirit spoke through Zǐgū.
Custom holds:
The toilet must be kept clean
to successfully invite Zǐgū.
"Records of Seasonal Festivals in Jing-Chu"
and "Garden of Marvels" note:
People welcome Zǐgū in the toilet on the fifteenth day,
or by the pigsty.
When the holder feels a heavy weight,
it signifies the deity's arrival.
Offering wine and fruit, her face appears radiant with color;
she jumps restlessly, capable of predicting various matters and future silkworm harvests.
She is also skilled at guessing hooks,
leaping joyfully for favorable outcomes,
or lying face up for unfavorable ones.
Píngchāng Mèng shì consistently doubted this,
but when he personally tried to hold her,
she leaped through the roof and vanished,
never to be found again.
Another version says:
On New Year's Day, it is customary
to invite the spirit of Qī Gū,
as Lady Qī of the Hàn dynasty died in a toilet,
so invokers must summon her there.
The Táng dynasty Zǐgū spirit
was from Láiyáng,
named Hé Mèi, courtesy name Qìqīng.
She was literate from childhood,
eloquent and intelligent. During the Gǒng era's third year,
Lǐ Jǐng, governor of Shòuyáng, took her as a concubine,
but his wife killed her in the toilet
on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month.
She later manifested spiritually.
"Records of Manifest Marvels"
Playing polo
In Huáinán, during the three nights of the Lantern Festival, lanterns were arranged outside every household.
They ordered strong women from the market to strike balls with painted sticks,
to the extent of pulling hair and injuring skin,
and it only stopped when heads were broken and blood flowed.
From "Travel Records of Yān and Wú"
The śarīra emits light.
On the fifteenth day of the first month in Magadha,
monks and lay people gather like clouds to behold the Buddha,
the śarīra emits light,
and flowers rain down.
"Records of the Western Regions"
Sānguān Cháotiān
The Orthodox Unity "Essentials of Cultivating Perfection" states:
On the Shangyuan Festival,
the Three Officials of Heaven, Earth, and Water ascend to heaven,
and it is the ascension day of Perfected Person Zhāng Língyuán
and Perfected Person Zhāng Yuánjīng.
The Ten Celestial Officials of Shangyuan, divine immortal troops and cavalry,
along with lofty sages, high perfected ones, and wondrous practice perfected ones, descend together to the human world
to examine and determine sins and blessings.
Midpoint of the Quail Fire constellation
An ancient poem says:
At that time, the sun and moon were facing each other in the Quail Fire,
The Quail Fire means the full moon of the first month.
The Chronicles of Imperial Relatives Passing Oranges
On the Lantern Festival night, when ascending the towers,
it was customary for the noble relatives to present yellow tangerines to each other,
which was called "passing the tangerines."
Borrowing the Lantern Festival in Advance
In the fifth year of the Xuānhé era,
the capital city was ordered to display lanterns on artificial hills from the first day of the twelfth lunar month,
until the night of the fifteenth day of the first lunar month of the following year,
which was called the pre-celebration of the Lantern Festival.
When Emperor Huīzōng went out to watch them at sunrise,
there was a playful lyric whose final lines said:
But our emperor,
did not wait for the Lantern Festival scenery to arrive,
fearing that the weather of the following month might not be guaranteed.
"Accounts of the Xuānhé Era"
In the third year of the Chúnyòu era,
the capital prefect Zhào Jiézhāi provided bamboo,
requesting an early twelve-day Lantern Festival display.
On the fourteenth day, all lanes, streets, bridges, and roads were lined with bamboo for lantern hanging arrangements.
Officials submitted memorials quoting this lyric,
with the last two lines being:
The following year on the fifth day of the fifth month,
came the omen of the Jīn invasion,
and on the fifteenth day in the morning, they were all dismantled.
"Records of a Clear Night"
Mǎshàng Yuè
During the Shénlóng era,
in the capital on the Lantern Festival, there was a grand celebration with elaborate lantern displays.
The night curfew was lifted,
and nobles, relatives, as well as commoners and merchants all roamed at night.
Carriages and horses crowded the streets,
making it impossible for people to pay attention to the mansions of princes and lords.
Music was played on horseback to boast and compete,
and scholars composed poems to record the event.
Only Sū Wèidào, Guō Lìzhēn, and Cuī Yè wrote the most outstanding verses.
Guō Lìzhēn's poem:
"Nine avenues connect with lantern shadows,
a thousand gates are bathed in moonlight.
The entire city rides out on precious steeds,
fragrant carriages turn on all roads.
Revelry only fears the dawn,
circling around without thought of home.
When clear pipes begin to play,
plum blossoms fall everywhere."
Other poems are not recorded here.
"Táng Xīn Yǔ"
Hàomó Rì
On the sixteenth day of the first lunar month,
ancients called it the Day of Wastage.
In Zhāng Yuè's "Poem on Drinking on the Wastage Day":
The wastage tradition continues this day,
unrestrained paths remain unspoken.
So long as one does not become intoxicated,
it instead becomes joyful non-action.
It also says:
The past month diminishes this morning,
spreading the time of wastage.
Still engaging in no affairs,
getting drunk together with common folk.
This day is called the Wastage Day,
where officials merely refrain from opening granaries.
"Miscellaneous Notes from the Straw Hut"
Tí Yuè
. The Gongyang Commentary on the "Mentioned Month":
Six egrets retreated,
flying past the capital of Sòng,
what is meant by "mentioned month" is merely.
Reaching this month,
it is the last day of the month.
Hé Xiù's annotation:
"Mentioned month,"
means border,
is the language of the people of Lǔ,
refers to the near end of this month.
gathering for a feast
"Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì":
From New Year's Day until the last day of the month,
people everywhere prepare feasts with wine,
men and women dine and drink, either boating or enjoying banquets by the waterside.
Note:
Every month has its first quarter, full moon, last quarter, and new moon days,
but as it is the beginning of the year in the first month,
customs of the time esteem these days as festivals.
Dù È
From New Year's Day until the end of the month, people all prepare feasts and food,
crossing waters where men and women thoroughly wash their skirts and offer wine libations,
placing them by the riverbanks as a means to ward off calamities.
Nowadays, people only go to the riverside at the month's end,
to perform cleansing rituals, and some women still wash their skirts.
"Yùzhú Bǎodiǎn"
Sending Off the Poor Ghost
Gāoyáng Shì's son was thin and frugal, fond of wearing tattered clothes and eating simple food,
and died in a lane on the last day of the first lunar month.
Later generations would make porridge and discard worn-out clothes,
and on that day offer sacrifices in the lane,
calling it "sending off the poor ghost."
From "Records of the Seasons"
Rowing a boat
On the last day of the first lunar month in Northern Qí,
the Zhōngshū Shèrén presented a memorial for a purification ceremony and boating excursion.
The emperor then rode in the imperial carriage,
with drums and winds playing, to the traveling palace,
ascended the imperial throne,
and mounted a palanquin.
He boarded the boat with the princes and dukes,
and wine was served.
Those not participating in the boating
sat in temporary tents.
"Suí Lǐ Zhì"
Wèi Shōu's "Poem in Response to the Edict for Boating":
Tender and delicate, the spring branches sway,
New birds call as we boat away.
Suddenly, the oars' song winds afar,
Lotus-gatherers' tunes glance back with care.
The wise admires the moon's fragrant light,
Feasting words make dusk slip from sight.
Roaming comforts people's hearts,
His radiance guides the state's forward parts.
From dusk to dawn
If it coincides with the midnight of the first day, then the morning of the last day of the month
is like the evening of the first day.
Hence, the moon is often seen.
"Treatise on Calendars"
The last day of the month, rich congee
The Catering Department had provisions for festival meals.
Annotation:
On the last day of the month, rich congee.
"Six Codes"
Poem on Kunming Pond
On the last day of the first lunar month, Emperor Zhōngzōng visited Kūnmíng Lake and composed a poem.
Over a hundred courtiers responded with regulated verses.
A colorful tower was erected in front of the tented palace,
and Zhāoróng was ordered to select one poem to be set as a new imperial song.
The attending officials all gathered below the tower,
as papers descended like flying flakes.
Each identified and kept their own.
After they withdrew,
only the poems by Shěn and Sòng remained undecided.
After a while, another paper fluttered down,
and they rushed to take and read it,
finding it was Shěn's poem.
When they heard the critique:
"Both poems are equally skilled in craft,
but Shěn's concluding couplet reads:
'This petty minister, a decaying stump,
Shames to see talents of Yùzhāng timber.'
His poetic energy is exhausted.
Sòng's poem says:
'Fear not the bright moon's end—
Night pearls will naturally come.'
It still soars with vigor."
Shěn then conceded,
not daring to contend further.

causing the elderly and young to suffer unbearably,
and many died each year.
After Zhōu Jǔ arrived in the province, he wrote a eulogy and placed it in Jiè Zǐtuī's temple,
stating that extinguishing fires in the harsh winter harmed people's lives,
which was not the intention of a virtuous man,
and used this to enlighten the ignorant people to resume eating warm food,
whereupon the public's confusion gradually dissipated,
and the custom was largely reformed.
A note explains:
The Dragon Star is in the position of wood,
appearing in the east in spring,
with the Heart constellation representing great fire,
and the fear of excessive fire led to the fire prohibition.
It is popularly said that Zǐtuī was burned on this day, hence the fire prohibition.
Extinguish the Fire

Emperor Wǔ of Wèi issued the Decree on Clear Punishments, stating: I have heard that in Tàiyuán, Shàngdǎng, Xīhé, and Yànmén, for one hundred and five days after the winter solstice, all fires are extinguished and cold food is consumed, claiming it is for Jiè Zǐtuī. Moreover, these are extremely cold northern regions.

The elderly, young, and weak will suffer unbearable hardships. The decree mandates that no one shall observe the cold food practice. Violators will result in the head of the household being sentenced to six months of penal servitude, the responsible official to one hundred days, and the magistrate to forfeiture of one month’s salary.
Hail Anomaly
During Shí Lè's reign, hailstones fell starting from the Western River border mountains,
extending over a thousand miles through Tàiyuán, Lèpíng, Wǔxiāng, Zhàojùn, Guǎngpíng, and Jùlù.
Shí Lè consulted Xú Guāng about this,
and Xú Guāng said:
"Last year, the Cold Food Festival was banned.
Jiè Zǐtuī is a deity of the emperor's homeland,
revered throughout the ages.
Some believe it is inappropriate to abolish this practice.
Even if we cannot enforce it uniformly across the realm, the area around Jiè Mountain was enfeoffed by Duke Wén of Jìn,
so the local people should be permitted to observe it."
Shí Lè ordered a formal deliberation,
and the officials proposed that since Zǐtuī had been honored for generations,
the Cold Food Festival should be universally restored.
Wéi Xiǎo remarked:
"According to the Spring and Autumn Annals, improper storage of ice
causes yin and yang energies to erupt as hail.
Before Zǐtuī's time, what caused hailstorms then?
Zǐtuī was a virtuous man;
how could he bring such violent harm?
It is appropriate to honor him in the area between Mián and Jiè,
but applying this universally is unreasonable."
Shí Lè followed his advice.

Seeking Marriage
Lú Chōng saw a river deer and shot it with an arrow,
then followed it without realizing how far he had gone.
Suddenly, he saw a black gate resembling a government office.
He asked the gatekeeper, who replied:
"This is the residence of Vice Director Cuī."
He entered and met the Vice Director,
who said to Chōng:
"Your esteemed father has arranged a marriage with my young daughter, hence we have invited you here."
After three days, the wedding was completed,
and they sent Chōng home in a carriage.
His mother asked him about it,
and he recounted everything in detail.
Four years after parting from Cuī,
on the third day of the third month, Chōng was playing by the water.
In the distance, he spotted a calf-drawn carriage by the water's edge.
Chōng went and opened the carriage door,
where he saw Cuī's daughter and their son together inside.
Their affection remained as before.
She handed the child over to him,
and Chōng also received a gold ingot before they parted again.

Praying for a Bountiful Harvest
The March Winding Water Banquet,
is a purification sacrifice.
Han rituals involved washing on the eastern flowing water,

During the Jin dynasty, officials and commoners alike performed purification rites by the Luo River.

Examining purification and winding water,
their meanings are inconsistent.
Traditionally, it is said that yang energy spreads freely,

gathered by the Guxian note.
The si day signifies blessing,
meaning to pray for great blessings.

on this month and day, women avoid staying home,
instead going to the eastern flowing water
to pray, exorcise, and cleanse themselves,
with washing called the purification shrine,
and floating cups along divided streams formed winding water.

Qǔjiāng Capsized Boat
Lǐ Shāoyún,
son-in-law of Lú Ruòxū,
was frivolous and indulged heavily in drinking.
One night, his wife dreamed of capturing Shāoyún and over ten others,
mixed with courtesans,
bound by a long rope,
and driven away in a line.
Startled awake, she recounted the dream,
and Shāoyún’s own dream coincided with it.
Thus, greatly frightened and disgusted, he abstained from meat
and upheld Buddhist scriptures for three years.
Later, as the dream increasingly seemed unfulfilled,
Shāoyún resumed his heavy drinking as before.
The following year on the Shangsi Festival, with Lǐ Méng, Péi Shìnán, Liáng Bāo, and over ten others,
they boated on the Qu River,
extensively selecting famous courtesans of Cháng'ān,
indulging lavishly in singing and dancing.
As the wine flowed freely,
the boat capsized,
and all drowned.

"Sāntǒng Lì"
The Six Climates
At the Beginning of Summer solar term,
the first five days mole crickets chirp,
the next five days earthworms emerge,
the last five days red arrow plants grow.
At the Lesser Fullness solar period,
the first five days hollyhocks bloom,
the next five days delicate grasses wither,
the last five days wheat harvest arrives.
At the Grain in Ear solar term of mid-summer,
the first five days praying mantises are born,
the next five days shrikes begin to call,
the last five days mockingbirds become silent.
At the Summer Solstice solar period,
the first five days deer antlers shed,
the next five days cicadas begin to sing,
the last five days pinellia grows,
trees store their glory.
At the Lesser Heat solar term of late summer,
the first five days warm winds arrive,
the next five days crickets dwell in walls,
the last five days young eagles learn to fly.
At the Great Heat solar period,
the first five days rotten grass transforms into fireflies,
the next five days earth is moist in sultry heat,
the last five days heavy rains occur frequently.
All these six periods with eighteen pentads,
are when summer energy promotes lush growth,
thus those who nurture life must respectfully follow the timing of heaven.

King Zhòu once hunted in the western lands in the sixth month,

The people remonstrated, saying:

Cease Fishing

and creatures hibernating in the earth emerged,
the water officials would then examine the large nets and fish traps,
catch renowned fish,
and gather river creatures,
to offer them in the ancestral temple,
distributing them among the people of the state,
to help disseminate the vital energy.
On mountains, they did not cut down sprouting trees,
in marshes, they did not harvest young reeds,
fish eggs and fry were prohibited from being caught,
fawns were allowed to grow,
birds were permitted to nurture their fledglings and eggs,

From the "Jìn Shū"
Double Fur
Sāng Jí of Qinghé Bèiqiū,
whose strength could lift a tripod,
was cruel and lacking in kindness.
In the sweltering heat of June, he wore double fur and layered mats,
having over ten people fan him.
If he did not feel cool,
he would behead the fan bearers.
He was a prominent family member of Bìngzhōu.
Tián Lán and Bó Shèng
executed him on the plains.
Men and women celebrated, running through the streets, singing:
"How shameful for a slave to become a general,
in June wearing layered mats and draped in fox
and leopard
fur.
He knew not heat or cold, yet severed heads,
the hero Tián Lán sought revenge,
at midnight beheading him to answer Bìngzhōu."
Yuèfǔ Guǎngtí, same as in the Zhào Shū.
Writing on a skirt
Yáng Xīn at the age of twelve followed his father Yáng Bùyí, who served as the magistrate of Wúchéng.
Wáng Xiànzhī, the governor of Wúxìng, was fond of him.
Xīn once wore a new silk skirt on a summer day,
and while he was napping, Xiànzhī entered the county office and saw him.
He wrote several lines of calligraphy on the skirt before leaving.
From "The Book of Sòng."
The clouds and atmosphere condensed into brilliant colors.
Emperor Gaozu of the Northern Wei was conducting ceremonies at the Square Marsh,
and at dawn, the officials came to inquire about his well-being.
Emperor Gaozu said:
"Yesterday at the Square Marsh, it was exceptionally grand.
The summer heat was met with dense shade from the sky's clouds,
so the participants managed to avoid any discomfort."
Prince Xiān of Xianyang said:
"Your Majesty's virtue moves Heaven and Earth,
hence the clouds and atmosphere condensed into brilliant colors.
Even if the Rain Master were to sprinkle and sweep,
and the Wind Earl were to clear the dust,
how could they surpass this?"
Emperor Gaozu said:
"Between the Yi and Luo rivers, north and south,
this is where the cosmic energies of yin and yang mingle,
and where wind and rain
naturally converge and respond;
it is not something my meager virtue alone could bring about."

The emperor then ordered a small horse,

The Ice Beast Presented to Duke Wáng
Yáng Guózhōng's sons and younger brothers used flattery and ingratiation to befriend court officials.
Every summer, they would take solid ice,
have craftsmen carve it into shapes of phoenixes and beasts,

and present them to princes, dukes, and high ministers.

Hán Yù qiàn jīn

Guìfēi měi zhì xià yuè,

Yíngliáng Cǎo
In Lǐ Fǔguó's home,

Although appearing dried up,
it never withers or falls.
When hung between windows during intense heat,

Lóngpí Shàn
Wáng Yuánbǎo,
a great magnate in the capital.
He owned a leather fan at home,
exquisitely crafted and very precious.
Every summer month when hosting banquets,
he would place this fan in front of the seats,
sprinkling fresh water on it,
whereupon a cool breeze would suddenly arise.
During the wine feast,
guests would appear chilly,
so he would order it removed.
Emperor Míng Huáng once sent a palace envoy to fetch and examine it,
but Wáng, fond of it, did not hand it over, saying:

"Kāiyuán Yíshì"
Bīngsī Yīn
Kāng Lǎozǐ,
originally the son of a wealthy family in Cháng'ān.
After his livelihood was completely depleted,
he encountered an old woman holding an old brocade mattress for sale,
and he acquired it for five hundred coins.
Soon, a Persian man saw it,
and said:
"This is woven from the silk of ice silkworms;
if placed on a seat in the summer,
the entire room will become cool and refreshing.
I will pay ten million for it immediately."
from "Miscellaneous Records of the Music Bureau"
Dragon's Beard Whisk
Yuán Zài had a purple dragon-whisker duster,
its color like overripe mulberries,
with a handle carved from crystal.
When placed in the hall,
mosquitoes and midges dared not enter at night.
When waved, it produced a sound,
startling all chickens and dogs into fleeing.
"Du Yang Compilation"
Lǐ Shǎoshī
Zōngmǐn
was skilled at drinking.
When feasting with guests and subordinates,
in the summer months by the water,
he would use lotus leaves as cups,
fill them to the brim and tie them securely,
bring them close to the mouth,
then pierce them with chopsticks.
If not finished, he would drink again,
after the feast someone remarked,
that yesterday's drinking was very joyful.
The master said:
"Speaking of joy today is clear,
but as for the lack of joy the previous day,
regardless of likes or dislikes,
none should be mentioned."
"Records of Conversations"
White Dragon Skin
Lǐ Déyù once invited his colleagues and court officials to a banquet on a summer day,
when they were all suffering from the oppressive heat of the blazing sun.
They all felt the misery of the sweltering weather.
After being ushered into a small study and seated,
as the wine was opened, the intense heat
completely dissipated, replaced by a refreshing and cool breeze,
as if they had stepped into late autumn.
The banquet lasted until dusk,
and when they stepped outside, the fiery clouds and scorching sun
were blazing and burning fiercely.
An inquisitive person sought out a close confidant to ask about it,
and was told that on that day, a golden basin was filled with water,
in which a white dragon skin was soaked and placed at the edge of the seating area.
As for the dragon skin,
it was obtained from the sea by a monk from Silla.
"Jù Tán Lù"
Ode to the Lycium and Chrysanthemum
Lù Guīméng styled himself Tiānsuízǐ,
often consuming wolfberries and chrysanthemums.
By the fifth month of summer,
their branches and leaves grew old and tough,
their flavor bitter and astringent,
yet he continued eating them without cease.
Thus he composed "The Wolfberry and Chrysanthemum Rhapsody"
to console himself, saying:
"The wolfberries are not yet thorny, the chrysanthemums not yet withered—
what can they do to me?"
Linked Verses
In summer, Emperor Wénzōng composed a linked verse with his academicians,
saying:
"All suffer from the sweltering heat,
But I cherish the long summer days."
Gōngquán continued:
"The fragrant breeze drifts from the south,
Cooling the palace halls with gentle air."
Though five academicians presented their verses, the emperor solely recited Gōngquán's two lines,
commanding him to inscribe them on the wall.
The characters, five inches square,
made the emperor gaze and sigh:
"Even if Zhōng Yáo and Wáng Xīzhī were reborn,
They could not surpass this."
From "Records of Tang Poetry"
Chéngshuǐ Bó
Princess Tóngchāng one day convened a grand gathering of the Wéi clan at the Jade Hall in Guǎnghuà Ward.
All the delicacies were arrayed,
and as the summer heat grew intense,
the princess ordered someone to fetch Chéngbīng silk, dip it in water,
and hang it in the southern corridor for a long while.
All the guests felt cool,
as if wrapped in silk floss. The Chéngbīng silk measured eight or nine feet long,
resembling cloth but finer,
translucent and thin enough to reflect light.
It contained ambergris within,
thus capable of dispelling summer toxins.
From "The Du Yang Chronicles."
Heaven-created Rankings
Lù Yǐ repeatedly advanced to the position of Hanlin Academician,
initially when Yǐ passed the imperial examination, he had just moved,
fortunately the results were announced in June,
up to this point, every time during the intense summer heat,
other academicians would jokingly say:
"Heaven made the list."
to mock Yǐ for advancing at an inopportune time.
Composing Summer Assignments
In Cháng'ān, the scholars who failed the imperial examinations
would not leave after June,
which was called "passing the summer."
They often borrowed clean temples and monastery courtyards to write essays,
known as "summer assignments."
There was a saying:
"When the pagoda tree flowers turn yellow,
the scholars become busy."
From "New Book of the South."
Roaming by Washing Flowers Stream
The custom in Chéngdū
is that every year on the nineteenth day of the fourth month,
scholars and women go boating on the Hundred Flowers Pond of the Huànhuā Creek,
and the prefect also comes to the pond,
setting up wine for a grand gathering,
arranging water performances and crossings,
returning only after exhausting their joy,
which is said to be a tradition from the story of Lady Jìguó of the Táng dynasty.
Lady Jìguó's surname was Rèn,
a girl from a humble family in Hànshàng, whose mother, Madame Rèn, once prayed at a temple,
dreaming that a deity gave her a large pearl,
and upon waking, she was pregnant.
The following year, on the nineteenth day of the fourth month, she gave birth.
As the girl grew older, she followed the teachings of Shíshì,
with great reverence.
A monk passed by her home,
covered in sores and scabies,
his clothes filthy and tattered,
and those who saw him felt disgusted,
but the girl alone respected and served him.
One day, the monk brought his clothes with him,
asking the girl to wash them,
and she gladly scrubbed them.
Each time she rinsed the clothes by the creek,
lotus flowers would appear at her touch.
The villagers were astonished and sought him out,
but the monk had already disappeared.
Thus, they marked the spot,
establishing the Hundred Flowers Pond Gathering.
During the Táng dynasty, Nìng governed Xīchuān,
and while traveling incognito among the people,
he saw the girl and was delighted by her,
visited her home,
and took her as his concubine.
After Nìng's wife died,
she became his official wife,
and she was successively enfeoffed up to the rank of Jì.
Once she became noble,
on each of her birthdays, she would come to set up wine at her home,
moor boats on the river,
and visit the place where she had washed clothes,
lingering there all day.
Later, this became a regular practice,
and on the nineteenth day of the fourth month in Chéngdū,
it is called the Huànhuā Áotóu,
with feasts held at Cānglàng Pavilion in Dù Zǐměi's Thatched Cottage,
the entire city turns out,
with brocades and embroideries lining the streets,
starting from the New Year banquets,
the outings continue until this day,
making it the most splendid of all times.
The people of Shǔ say:
"Even white-haired elders
have never seen the creek flowers on a rainy day."
From "Lǎoxué'ān Bǐjì."
Shark Silk
At the end of the Qiánfú era,

He once carried out a military mission to Bóhǎi,

Later, when Later Táng Míngzōng held a suburban sacrifice,
a fellow villager of Jiànzhāng was in charge of the treasures in the eastern hall,

It was stored in a box,
rolled up as thin as a chopstick,
and tied with three red threads.
It was said that in the summer heat,
unfolding it could make the entire room feel cool.

"Imperial Reader"
Chìzhāng
. The Rites of Zhōu: Grand Minister of Rites states:
With a green guī tablet, rituals are performed for the eastern direction;
with a red zhāng tablet, rituals are performed for the southern direction.
The rituals for the east correspond to the beginning of spring,
referring to the Emperor of Azure Essence,
with Tàihào and Gōumáng receiving offerings.
The rituals for the south correspond to the beginning of summer,
referring to the Emperor of Red Essence,
with Yándì and Zhùróng receiving offerings.
The guī is pointed,
symbolizing the initial growth of spring things;
half a guī is called a zhāng,
symbolizing the half-death of summer things.
The Commentary explains:
It symbolizes the half-death of all things,
as in summer, shepherd's purse and wheat die,
which is what is meant by half-death.
Virtue flourishes in fire.
The Grand Historian, three days before the beginning of summer,

"On such-and-such a day, summer begins,
the flourishing virtue resides in fire,
