On the day of the beginning of summer,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, and high officials
to welcome summer in the southern suburb.

Xuánbīng Wán
Someone asked about the method to avoid heat,
and the reply was:
"On the day of the Beginning of Summer,
either take the Xuánbīng Pills,
or take the Fēishuāng Powder,
along with the charms of the sixth heavenly stem and the tenth earthly branch,

Yòu Bózi

Fó Jié
The Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhāo of Zhōu,
from his mother's right side,
and at the age of nineteen, on the eighth day of the fourth month at midnight, he left the city,
went to the Snowy Mountains to pursue enlightenment,
spent six years in contemplation without eating,
and also on the eighth day of the fourth month, he attained Buddhahood.
"Suìhuá Jìlì"
Bathing the Buddha
The people of Jīngchǔ hold vegetarian feasts at various temples on the eighth day of the fourth month,
bathing the Buddha with five-colored fragrant water,
and jointly celebrate the Dragon Flower Assembly.
The "Records of the Year and Seasons" states:
On the eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha is bathed,
using dūliángxiāng for blue water,
yùjīnxiāng for red water,
qiūlóngxiāng for white water,
fùzǐxiāng for yellow water,
and ānxīxiāng for black water,
to pour over the Buddha's head.
The "Biographies of Eminent Monks" records:
Chan Master Dàhuì, while bathing the Buddha, addressed the assembly saying:
"Today is precisely the eighth of the fourth month,
when Suddhodana's palace gave birth to Siddhartha;
nine dragons spurt water from beyond the heavens,
seven lotuses rise from the earth to support his feet."
The "Comprehensive Records of the Buddha's Legacy"
Bǎi Jīn Chèn Zhāi
Prince Zǐluán of the Sòng dynasty established a fasting ceremony to bathe the Buddha statue,
while Zhāng Róng alone contributed a hundred gold coins.
Pouring a Statue for His Mother
Liú Jìngxuān on the eighth day of the fourth month saw people bathing the Buddha statue,
then took off the golden mirror from his head,
and used it to bathe the statue for his mother,
whereupon he wept uncontrollably from grief.
Huán Xù sighed with admiration,
and said to his father, Liú Láozhī:
"This son of yours is already a filial son to the family,
and will surely be a loyal minister to the state."
Book of Sòng
Bathing the Buddha
On the eighth day of the fourth month, Yàoshān
saw Zūn Bùnà washing a Buddha statue
and said:
"You only wash this one,
can you wash that one?"
Zūn replied:
"Please bring that one here."
Yàoshān then silently returned to
his quarters. Chán Master Mìyìn commented:
"Yàoshān stirred waves without wind,
but when pressed by Zūn Bùnà,
he was left speechless in a moment of sharp confrontation."
From "The Recorded Sayings of Mìyìn"
Commencement of Summer Retreat
In the seasonal customs of Jīngchǔ,
it is recorded:
On the fifteenth day of the fourth month,
monks and nuns throughout the land gather at Chán temples to take up residence,
known as jiéxià (summer retreat),
also called jiézhì (commencement of restraint).
For summer is the season of growth,
and traveling outdoors might harm plants and insects,
hence the ninety-day retreat. The Zōngguī of Chán Monasteries states:
When Zhùróng presides over the season,
and Yándì governs the direction,
it is the time for the Dharma King’s prohibition of wandering,
and for disciples to protect life.
By the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
the monks and nuns residing at Chán temples
all disperse,
known as jiěxià (end of summer retreat),
also called jiězhì (lifting of restraint).
The Zōngguī of Chán Monasteries says:
As the golden breeze gently blows,
and jade-like dew abundantly falls,
it is the time of the Awakened Lord’s lifting of restraint,
marking the completion of the Dharma year.
The Tripiṭaka states:
Sitting under trees from the fifteenth day of the fourth month
until the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
monks and nuns sitting on grass count as one year,
termed the Dharma year in Chán discourse records.
Yīng Sǔn Chú
In Cháng'ān after the fourth month,
from the main kitchen to all government office kitchens,
they were collectively called the cherry bamboo shoot kitchens.
The abundance of official feasts differed from ordinary days.

The Celestial Festival
falls on the fifth day of the fifth month at noon, known as the Mid-Celestial Festival.

Dì Là
The fifth day of the fifth month is the Earth La Festival,
when the Five Emperors review and determine the official ranks and titles of the living,
the flourishing and decline of flesh and blood,
nourishing all things externally,
and extending lifespan internally,

On this day, one may confess sins and make requests,

Bathe in orchid-scented water and wash with fragrant flowers,

Storing Medicine
In this month of the Xià Xiǎozhèng, medicines are stored to eliminate toxic vapors.

vermilion cords and five-colored seals

Fēngsú Tōng records:
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
tying five-colored silk threads to the arms
wards off weapons and ghosts,

life-prolonging threads,
weapon-warding silks,
five-colored threads,
five-colored silk,

On the fifth day of the fifth month, gathering five-colored silks
wards off weapons.
I asked Master Fú,
and he replied:
Using blue, red, white, and black to represent the four directions,
with yellow in the center,
it is called a folded ornament,
which is worn square on the chest,
displayed to women

Wheat stalks are hung on the door,

Zòngzi
On the Double Fifth in midsummer,
ducks are cooked and zòngzi are prepared.
Duān
means "first,"
referring to the fifth day of the fifth month.
Customarily, the fifth day and the summer solstice are both highly regarded.
One day before the festival,
glutinous rice is wrapped in wild rice leaves,
and boiled until cooked with chestnuts, dates, and lye water.
On the festival day, it is eaten.
A fat turtle is boiled
until extremely tender,
its bones removed and seasoned with salt and fermented beans.
Mixed with garlic and polygonum, it is called "pickled turtle with glutinous rice,"
also known as zòng,
or jiǎoshǔ (horn-shaped millet).
This likely symbolizes the state of yin and yang still wrapped and undivided.
The turtle's shell protects the flesh inside,
representing the form of yang within and yin without,
chosen to honor the season.
"Records of Local Conditions"
Treading on a Hundred Grasses
The four classes of people all tread upon the hundred herbs,
and nowadays people also have the game of contending with the hundred herbs.
The Record of the Year and Seasons in Jing-Chu states:
orderly and unimpeded
On the Dragon Boat Festival,
there are also items like woven silk ribbons and other miscellaneous objects,
which are given as gifts to one another.
The "Xiaojing Yuanshenqi" states:
In mid-summer, silkworm cocoons emerge,
women dye and refine silk,
all engaging in their tasks.
The "Yuzhu Baodian" says:
This festival involves extensive preparations,
a tradition that has long been upheld.
There are also patterns of the sun, moon, stars,
and shapes of birds and beasts,
adorned with embroidered texts and golden threads,
pasted and painted as tributes.
As the respected poem says:
Wrapped around the arms are paired ribbons,
which are the "dá" mentioned here.
The Talisman to Ward Off Weapons
Someone asked about the method to ward off the five weapons,
and the Bàopǔzǐ says:
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
make a red spirit talisman and place it in front of the heart.
The Suìshí Jì states:
This is what is now known as the hairpin talisman.
Bestowing Owl Soup
The Han dynasty ordered commanderies and feudal states to present owls,
on the fifth day of the fifth month,
owl soup was bestowed upon all officials,
because it was a detested bird, hence they ate it.
"Annotations to the Book of Music"
Floating the Calamus Wine
On the Dragon Boat Festival, calamus
—whether shredded or powdered—
is steeped in wine.
Records of the Year and Seasons
Dragon Boat Race
On the fifth day of the fifth month, dragon boat races are held,
a custom originating from the day Qū Yuán threw himself into the Mìluó River.
Grieving over the place of his death,
people commanded boats to rescue him.
The boats were chosen for their lightness and speed,
called "flying wild ducks,"
also known as "water chariots,"
and "water horses."
Provincial generals and scholars all gathered by the water to watch.
"Records of the Seasons"
notes the custom of holding dragon boat races on the fifth day of the fifth month,
popular from Xiāngzhōu southward.
It is traditionally said that
when Qū Yuán first sank into the river,
his fellow villagers raced in boats to search for him,
urgently competing to be first,
thus originating this tradition.
"Anecdotes from the Suí and Táng Dynasties"
Sacrifice to Qū Yuán
On the fifth day of the fifth month, Qū Yuán threw himself into the Mìluó River and died.
The people of Chǔ mourned him,
and every year on this day, they would store rice in bamboo tubes
and cast them into the water as offerings to him.
During the Jiànwǔ era of the Hàn Dynasty,
Ōu Huí of Chángshā one day
suddenly saw a man who claimed to be Sānlǘ Dàfū (Qū Yuán),
who said to Huí:
"I have heard that you intend to make offerings to me, which is very kind,
but the offerings sent over the years
have all been stolen by flood dragons.
If you wish to bestow favors now,
you can stuff them with chinaberry leaves,
and bind them with five-colored silk threads.
These two things are what flood dragons fear."
Huí followed his advice.
Today, on the fifth day of the fifth month, people make zòngzi,
and also attach five-colored silk threads and chinaberry leaves,
all of which are customs passed down from the Mìluó River.
From "Xù Qíxié Jì".
Gave birth to a son
Tián Wén of Qí was the son of Tián Yīng's concubine,
born on the fifth day of the fifth month. Yīng
ordered the infant not to be raised.
Later, the mother secretly raised Wén.
When he grew up among his brothers,
Yīng became angry upon seeing Wén, who asked:
"Why did you not want to raise a child born in the fifth month?"
Why is that?"
Yīng replied:
"A child born in the fifth month,
when grown, will be as tall as the door, which is inauspicious."
Wén said to his father:
"Does human life receive its mandate from Heaven,
or from the door?"
Yīng fell silent. Wén continued:
"If it is mandated by Heaven,
what is there to worry about?
If it is mandated by the door,
then simply raise the height of the door.
Who could then reach it?"
Yīng said:
"Enough, my son."
Later, Wén succeeded him and became Lord Mèngcháng.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Wáng Fèng was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
His father, following a common saying,
wanted not to raise him.
His uncle said:
"In the past, Tián Wén was born on this day,
and later became Lord Mèngcháng,
whose mother was called the Great Lady of Xuē by the Lord.
Judging by ancient events,
it is not inauspicious."
Thus, he was raised.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Hú Guǎng originally had the surname Huáng.
Born on the fifth day of the fifth month,
his parents despised him, hid him, and abandoned him in the river inside a gourd.
A resident by the shore took him in and raised him.
When he grew up and gained great fame,
his birth parents wanted to reclaim him.
Guǎng believed that turning his back on his birth parents would harm righteousness,
while turning his back on his adoptive parents would be ungrateful.
With nowhere to belong,
as he had been entrusted to the gourd for life,
he took the surname Hú,
and the name Guǎng.
Later, he rose to high office seven times,
and was known as the Master of the Mean.
"Novels of Yīn Yún"
Later, Guǎng did not observe mourning for his birth parents,
saying:
"My birth parents thought I was already dead."
The world considered this a profound criticism.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Jì Mài was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
His mother abandoned him,
but the wife of villager Jì Chún raised him.
At age six, his birth parents said:
"You are our son."
Mài wept,
and gave all his earnings to his mother.
"Biographies of Filial Sons"
Wáng Zhèn'è,
grandson of Wáng Měng,
was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
His family, following a common superstition,
wanted to give him away to a distant relative.
Měng saw him and found him extraordinary,
saying:
"This is no ordinary child.
In the past, Lord Mèngcháng was born on this day and became Chancellor of Qí.
This child will also bring prosperity to our family."
Thus, he was named Zhèn'è.
"Book of Sòng"
Prince Zhuò of Nányáng,
born at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month,
was violent and unrestrained.
Later, he was accused of rebellion by Hán Chángluán's confidant and executed.
After more than four hundred days during his encoffining,
his complexion and hair remained as if alive.
It is commonly said:
those born on the fifth day of the fifth month,
their brains do not decay.
"Book of Northern Qí"
Cuī Xìnmíng was born at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month.
There was a rare type of sparrow,
with a very small head and body,
adorned in five colors,
perched on a tree,
flapping its wings and chirping in unison,
its voice clear and bright.
When Suí's Grand Astrologer Shǐ Liáng was sent to Qīngzhōu,
he encountered it and divined:
"The fifth month corresponds to fire,
fire to Lí,
Lí to literary brilliance,
and the sun at its zenith,
signifies the peak of literary splendor.
Moreover, the sparrow has five colors,
flutters its wings, and sings:
this child will surely have dazzling literary talent,
and his fame will spread throughout the world."
As the sparrow was small in form,
his official rank would likely not be high.
When he grew up, he was knowledgeable and had a retentive memory,
able to write essays effortlessly.
Gāo Xiàojī, a fellow villager,
had the insight to recognize talent,
and often told people:
"Cuī Xìnmíng is richly endowed with talent and learning,
though his fame leads the age,
it is a pity his position does not match."
"Old Book of Táng"
During the reign of Emperor Sùzōng of Táng,
Zhāng Jiā,
courtesy name Bódá,
was born on the fifth day of the fifth month,
and was named Wǔláng.
In his youth, he admired Confucian teachings,
and prided himself on integrity and righteousness.
At fifteen, he traveled to Cháng'ān,
and became friends with Lǐ Mì, courtesy name Chángyuán.
When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
he went to the capital to submit a memorial,
was appointed as a参军,
and contributed to suppressing the rebels,
becoming the magistrate of Yúnjū,
where he implemented benevolent governance.
He died at twenty-three,
and the local people built a shrine to honor him,
which became renowned for its spiritual responses.
Lǐ Mì sent a eulogy to mourn him.
"Shǎnxī Chronicles"
Emperor Huīzōng of Sòng was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
Due to common superstitions,
he changed it to the tenth day of the tenth month,
calling it the Tiāníng Festival.
"Miscellaneous Records of Guǐxìng"
Jīn's Transport Commissioner Tián Tèxiù,
courtesy name Yànshí,
was from Yì County.
He became a Jìnshì in the nineteenth year of the Dàdìng era.
His residence was named Bànshí Lane,
he was the fifth in his family,
born on the fifth day of the fifth month,
with the childhood name Wǔ'ér,
at twenty-five, he took the provincial, prefectural, ministerial, and palace exams,
achieving fifth place in all four.
At fifty-five, he died on the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
"Miscellaneous Records from Diligent Study"
Sacrifice to Chén
Chén Lín served as the governor of Cāngwú Commandery,
governing with sincere trustworthiness,
and guiding people with filial piety and fraternal duty.
After Chén Lín was summoned away,
the commandery erected a shrine to him at the eastern city gate on the fifth day of the fifth month,
instructing young children to dress in clean attire and perform dances.
(from Xiè Chéng's Book)
Against the Waves
The woman Cáo É,
a native of Shàngyú in Kuàijī,
had a father skilled in playing stringed instruments and singing,
who served as a shaman.
In the second year of Emperor Ān of the Hàn dynasty, on the fifth day of the fifth month,
he drowned in the county's river while rowing against the waves to welcome the Wave God,
and his body could not be found.
É, at the age of fourteen,
then wept along the riverbank day and night without ceasing her cries,
and after seven days, she threw herself into the river and died.
"Kuàijī Diǎn Lù"
Avoid building houses and exposing mats and straw mats.
The Customs and Manners states:
Building a house in this month causes one's head to go bald.
It also says:
One must not sun-dry bed mats and mats.
The Garden of Marvels says:
Yǚ Shí of Xīnyě,
once sun-dried a mat on the fifth day of the fifth month,
when suddenly he saw a small child dead on the mat,
and in a moment it disappeared.
Afterward, Yǚ Shí's son died.
Hence, it has been passed down as a taboo.
five-colored thread
In Bìngzhōu, it is customary to believe that Jièzǐtuī was burned to death on the fifth day of the fifth month.
People consider this day taboo,
so they do not prepare or eat meals,
but this is incorrect.
In the northern regions on the fifth day of the fifth month,
people themselves make food and drinks to offer to the gods,
and create five-colored threads,
exchanging five-colored new plates as gifts,
not for the sake of Jièzǐtuī.
From "Records of Yèzhōng."
Bathing together
Xí Zàochǐ wrote in "A Letter to Attendant Chǔ":
"I recall the old days with you,
and our bathing and frolicking together on the fifth day of the fifth month in Jiāngzhōu.
As I trace back to our former promises,
your jade-like demeanor seems vaguely present,
yet my heart is truly sorrowful."
Diagram of the Five Periods
During the Northern Dynasties, women
would present the Diagram of the Five Periods in May,
decorating canopies with flowers of the five seasons.
On that day,
they would also present long-life threads
and pliant cords,
all twisted into human figures to be worn.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The Court of Imperial Sacrifices Borrowed Skirts and Jackets
In the early Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
Sūn Fújiā presented a remonstrance with three matters, saying:
"Variety shows and informal music,
are originally not proper sounds,
this is called decadent customs,
which must be reformed.
Recently, the officials of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices
borrowed women's skirts and jackets from the common people,
more than five hundred sets in total,
to serve as costumes for informal performers."
He further stated:
"They planned to perform plays at the Xuánwǔ Gate on the fifth day of the fifth month,
this is not something to be taken as an example for descendants."
From the Old History of the Táng Dynasty
Flying White Script
On the fifth day of the fifth month in the eighteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Emperor Tàizōng wrote in flying white script,
creating characters such as "luan," "phoenix," "butterfly," and "dragon."
The brushwork was astonishingly exquisite.
He said to Minister over the Masses Zhǎngsūn Wújì and Minister of Personnel Yáng Shīdào:
"According to the old custom of the fifth day,
it is necessary to exchange clothing and playthings for congratulations.
Now, I bestow upon each of you two flying white fans,
hoping they may stir clear breezes
to enhance your virtuous qualities."
(from "Táng Huì Yào")
Shooting at Zòngzi and Powdered Rice Balls
In the Kaiyuan era of the palace,
on the Dragon Boat Festival, they made flour balls and zongzi,
stored them in a golden plate, and crafted small bows,
exquisite and charming,
using arrows to shoot the flour balls on the plate,
those who hit them could eat them.
Because the flour balls were slippery and hard to shoot,
this game was highly popular in the capital.
"Records of the Tianbao Era"
On the Dragon Boat Festival, they made water balls,
also called white balls,
sometimes mixed in five colors,
shaped like humans, animals, flowers, and fruits,
the finest ones were called dripping powder balls,
sometimes added with musk,
and there were also dry balls not put in water.
"Annals of the Seasons"
Cut off Xiè Língyùn's beard
Jìn's Xiè Língyùn had a beautiful beard.
Before his execution,
he donated it to be the beard of the Vimalakīrti statue at the Zhīhuán Temple in Nánhǎi.
During the reign of Táng's Emperor Zhōngzōng,
Princess Ānlè engaged in a hundred-herb competition on the fifth day,
wishing to expand her collection.
She ordered it to be fetched by post horse,
but feared others might obtain it.
Thus, she cut off and discarded the rest.
"Suí Táng Jiāhuà"
Bestow stalactite
On the Dragon Boat Festival,
Emperor Xuánzōng bestowed stalactite upon his ministers.
Sòng Jǐng, having received the gift,
ordered a physician to refine it.
The physician requested to take it home for refinement,
but Sòng Jǐng's family members admonished him, saying:
"This stalactite is rare and precious,
unmatched by others.
If entrusted to him to take home,
we fear it may be deceitfully swapped."
Sòng Jǐng cautioned them:
"You conceal your own intentions,
yet suspect others' hearts?
Relying on trust to show sincerity,
we still fear it may not be enough;
if we specifically harbor suspicions and blame,
how could we possibly achieve [trust]?"
"Táng Xīn Yǔ"
Yàn Wǔchéng
In the middle of the Kāiyuán era, on the fifth day of the fifth month,
a banquet was held at Wǔchéng Hall,
where court officials were bestowed with ceremonial garments,
and specifically, purple robes with golden fish pendants
were granted to Lǐ Yuánhóng and Xiāo Sōng,
an honor unmatched by any other officials.
"Basic Biography"
Embracing a young girl
Empress Zhāng, the deposed empress of Emperor Sùzōng,
on the day of the Dragon Boat Festival,
the emperor summoned the hermit Lǐ Táng for an audience.
The emperor was holding his young daughter in his arms at the time,
and he said to Táng:
"I am thinking of her,
do not find it strange."
Táng replied:
"The Grand Emperor (Tàishàng Huáng) must also be thinking of Your Majesty today."
The emperor shed tears,
but being controlled internally by the empress,
he ultimately did not dare to visit the Western Palace.
"Biography of the Empress"
Dragon's Birthday
On the thirteenth day of the fifth month,
known as the dragon's birthday,
planted bamboo grows especially lush.
"Yuezhou Local Records"
Sī Zhì
Tánzǐ said:
"Shàohào shì used birds as officials,
and the Bózhào shì
was the one in charge of the solstices."
Note: Bózhào
is the butcherbird.
It sings at the summer solstice
and stops at the winter solstice.
"Zuǒzhuàn, Seventh Year of Duke Zhāo"
Zhèngqì
Departing from the southern direction,
at the summer solstice at noon,
red qi emerges directly,
this is the proper qi of Lí.
If the qi emerges on the right,
all things will half perish;
if the qi emerges on the left,
barren land will stretch for a thousand miles.
"Yì Tōng Guà Yàn"
Jǐngfēng
The summer solstice departs by five days,
the auspicious wind takes effect,
now the ruler should bestow ranks,
honoring the virtuous and enfeoffing the meritorious.
Jīng Fáng's "Divinations on the Yì"
Three Meanings
The Summer Solstice falls in the fifth month because
the term "solstice" carries three meanings:
first, it signifies the zenith of yang energy,
second, it marks the initial emergence of yin energy,
and third, it indicates the sun's northernmost path.
Hence, it is called "solstice."
from "Interpretations of the Three Ritual Classics"
The Three Lights are at their peak.
The "Zhōu Bì" states:
At the winter solstice, the Three Lights are faint,
At the summer solstice, the Three Lights are at their peak.
The "Fàn Zǐ"
Zhū Suǒ Lián Hūn
In the mid-summer month,
all things are at their peak,
the day of summer solstice arrives,
when yin energy begins to sprout,
fearing things may not flourish.
The ritual uses red cords to connect garlic and onions,
peachwood seals inscribed with characters,
to display on doors and gates,
replacing decorations with what was esteemed.
"History of the Later Hàn Dynasty"
The eight winds arise
Wèi Xiàng memorialized saying:
"The transformations of heaven and earth
must follow yin and yang.
The division of yin and yang
is marked by the sun as its guideline.
When the sun reaches winter and summer solstices,
the sequence of the eight winds is established,
the nature of all things is formed,
each having its constant duty,
and none may interfere with another.
The Book of Hàn"
Stop the traveler
Lǔ Gōng's "Memorial" states:
In the Yì, the fifth month,
Gòu governs affairs.
The "Classic" says:
"The ruler thereby issues commands to proclaim to the four directions."
This means the ruler on the summer solstice day,
issues commands to halt travelers in the four directions,
in order to assist the rising yīn.
If even travelers should be stopped,
how much more so arresting, summoning, interrogating, and torturing,
depriving them of their season.
"Book of the Later Hàn"
Cease warfare and beat the drums
At the summer solstice, yīn qì begins to rise,
deer shed their antlers,
so weapons are laid aside and drums silenced,
seeking to calm the spirit,
wishing for tranquility and not attending to affairs,
for a period of five days.
"Dú Duàn"
Sacrifice to the Great Ancestor
When the summer solstice arrives and the wheat ripens,
the Son of Heaven offers sacrifices to the great ancestors,
using wheat as the main offering,
for wheat is the first among the grains.
Guanzi
No congratulations.
At the summer solstice, yin energy begins,
the way of the ruler declines,
therefore no congratulations are offered.
From Dú Duàn
Five Colors Ward Off Weapons
On the Summer Solstice, one wears five-colored talismans to ward off weapons,
inscribed with the words:
"Wandering Light and fierce demons,
those who know their names will not suffer from warm diseases,
the five colors ward off the five weapons."
from "Fēngsú Tōng"
Dredging the Well
On the summer solstice, dredging wells and changing water,
on the winter solstice, drilling wood for fire and changing the fire source,
can eliminate warm diseases.
"Sequel to the Book of Rites and Ceremonies"
The Minister of Rites uses the summer solstice to invoke the earth deities and all spirits
dark
to avert the state's calamities and famines,
and the people's mourning rites.
"Rites of Zhōu"
Heaven and earth unite, called day.
The Daoists consider the sixteenth day of the fifth month as the day when Heaven and Earth unite,
and husbands and wives should sleep separately.
Those who violate this will inevitably die prematurely,
hence it is regarded as a taboo in the world.
Fènlóng Jié
In Chízhōu, it is customary to regard the 29th and 30th of May as the Fēnlóng Festival.
If it rains, there is often a great flood.
People in Mǐn take the summer solstice as Fēnlóng,
and each has its own regional practice.
The "Tújīng"
Yǔ Shēng's Birthday
In Shǔshíquán there is a temple to Yǔ,
traditionally said to have been born on the sixth day of the sixth month.
"Annotations to the Spring and Autumn Annals of Wú and Yuè"
Tiānkuàng Festival
On the sixth day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Xiángfú era,
the heavenly texts descended again with an imperial decree,
designating this month as the Tiānkuàng Festival.
From "Sòng Huìyào"
Summer Heat Day
The sixth day of the sixth month is the day for escaping the summer heat.
The "Classic of the Way"
states that on this day, the Lord of the Northern Dipper Mansion is born.
"Dreams and Records"
Jīn Cáng
The Calendar Taboos explains:
What is
the 'Fu' period?
It is the day when the Metal qi lies hidden.
The four seasons alternate,
each giving rise to the next.
At the start of spring, Wood replaces Water,
for Water gives birth to Wood.
At the start of summer, Fire replaces Wood,
for Wood gives birth to Fire.
At the start of winter, Water replaces Metal,
for Metal gives birth to Water.
But when it comes to the start of autumn,
when Metal is to replace Fire,
Metal fears Fire,
so when the Geng day arrives, it must lie hidden (Fu).
Geng
represents Metal.
Sānfú
From the summer solstice onward,
the third Gēng day marks the beginning of the first fu period,
and the fourth Gēng day marks the middle fu period.
After the beginning of autumn, the first Gēng day
marks the final fu period,
collectively known as the three fu periods.
Cáo Zhí referred to them as the three ten-day periods.
"Yīnyáng Shū"
First established the sacrificial rites for the Fu Festival
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
In the second year of Duke Dé of Qín, the first "Fú" was established,
using dogs to ward off venomous creatures.
The Chronological Tables say:
The "Fú" was first instituted,
sacrifices were made to the soil god,
and dogs were dismembered at the four gates of the city.
The Annotation on Suburban Sacrifices of the Hàn dynasty:
Mèng Kāng said:
The "Fú" day is in the sixth month,
it did not exist during the Zhōu period,
and only came into being at this time.
Shī Gǔ said:
"Fú" means
that the yin energy is about to press upon the fading yang,
but has not yet risen,
so it remains hidden and latent,
hence the name "Fú day."
Select an appropriate day for the summer retreat
The "Fēngsú Tōng" states:
In Hànzhōng and Bāshǔ,
they themselves choose the Fú days.
Common saying has it:
The land there is warm and humid,
plants and trees sprout early,
and wither late, the climate being different.
The central states treated the Yí and Dí peoples like livestock,
therefore allowing them to choose their own Fú days.
According to the "Hàn Shū":
Emperor Gāozǔ divided the forces of the four commanderies,
employed the strategies of Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng,
reconquered the Three Qín,
and swept across the realm.
Indeed, the gentleman relies on fundamentals.
Merits were assessed and fiefs granted,
bestowing gold and silk,
with repeated honors and special favor,
allowing them to choose their own Fú days,
different from common custom.
Sacrifice to Huáng Shí
Zhāng Zǐfáng,
initially encountered the old man on the bridge in Xiàpī,
who gave him the Tàigōng's military treatise.
Thirteen years later, while accompanying Emperor Gāozǔ past Jìběi,
he indeed saw a yellow stone at the foot of Gǔchéng Mountain,
retrieved it, enshrined it as a treasure, and as the Marquis of Liú,
upon his death, was buried together with the yellow stone.
Every time during the Fú and Là sacrifices when visiting the grave,
he would worship the yellow stone.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Cutting Flesh
Dōngfāng Shuò was a court gentleman.
On the day of the summer sacrifice, an imperial edict granted
meat to the attending officials from the Office of Provisions.
The office assistant did not arrive until late in the day.
Shuò alone drew his sword and cut a piece of meat,
saying to his fellow officials:
"On the day of the summer sacrifice, one should return home early,
so I beg to receive the gift."
He then put the meat in his robe and left.
The Office of Provisions reported this.
Shuò entered the court,
and the Emperor said:
"Yesterday when the meat was granted, you did not wait for the decree,
but cut the meat with your sword and left.
Why?"
Shuò removed his official cap and apologized.
The Emperor said:
"Sir, rise,
and censure yourself."
Shuò bowed twice and said:
"Shuò, oh Shuò!
Receiving a gift without waiting for the decree—
how disrespectful!
Drawing a sword to cut meat—
how bold!
Cutting not too much—
how frugal!
Taking it home to give to my wife—
how benevolent!"
The Emperor laughed and said:
"I asked you, sir, to censure yourself,
but instead you praised yourself."
He then granted Shuò an additional shi of wine
and a hundred catties of meat,
to take home and give to his wife.
History of the Hàn Dynasty
Avoiding Ambushes
The Book of Rites and Ceremonials states:
On the third day of the sixth month, which is the Fu Day,
in the past, Jiǎ Yì was in the southern region of Xiāng,
on the third gēng day of the sixth month,
when a peng bird arrived,
due to the southern region's toxic and harmful climate,
which assists the sun in scorching all things,
it thus harms people,
and therefore one should avoid it.
winter and summer sacrifices
Yǎng Yùn wrote in his letter to Sūn Huìzōng:
Farming families toil hard,
during the seasonal Fú and Là festivals,
they cook mutton and roast lamb,
and drink a measure of wine to reward themselves.
Pān Ānrén's "Ode to a Leisurely Life" states:
"Raising sheep and selling wine,
to cover the expenses of the Fú and Là festivals."
The "Book of Etiquette" says:
During the Fú days in the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
there were gatherings with wine and food.
The day is spent in seclusion.
In the sixth year of Emperor Hé's Yǒngyuán era, an initial decree was issued,
ordering the closure of offices throughout the Fú day.
A note from the Hàn Guān Jiù Yí states:
On the Fú day,
malignant spirits roam about,
hence offices were closed for the entire day,

Capture the traitors
Sūn Bǎo served as the Governor of the Capital,
and on the day of the Beginning of Autumn, he appointed his former subordinate Hóu Wén as the Eastern District Inspector.
When Hóu Wén entered to see him,
Sūn Bǎo instructed him, saying:
"Today, hawks and falcons begin to strike;
we should follow the heavenly energy to capture the treacherous and wicked,
thereby executing the severe frost's punishment.
Is there such a person in your district?"
Hóu Wén raised his head and replied:
"If there were no such person, I would not dare to accept the position in vain."
Sūn Bǎo asked:
"Who is it?"
Hóu Wén said:
"Dù Zhìjì of Bàlíng."
Sūn Bǎo then asked:
"Who is next?"
Hóu Wén responded:
"When wolves block the road,
one should not bother asking about foxes."

Plotting to seize
Shēntú Jiàn and others conspired with the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Wěi Xiāo,
to launch a joint attack during the Chūlóu festival on the day marking the Beginning of Autumn.
Gēngshǐ,
Liú Néngqīng reported this,
and Jiàn was captured and executed.

Tiānhàn white vapor
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
that night they would sweep and clean the courtyard,
set out mats and low tables in the open air,
arrange wine, dried meat, and seasonal fruits,
and scatter fragrant powder while addressing the Herdboy and Weaver Girl stars, saying:
"These two stellar deities shall meet," and those keeping vigil at night,
all harboring private wishes,
some say:
they see movement in the Milky Way,
a shifting pure white aura,
glowing with five colors.
Taking this as an omen,
those who witness it should bow and make a wish,
begging for wealth or longevity,
or for a child if childless.
Only one wish may be made,
multiple requests are not allowed.
It takes three years to be granted,
and there are quite a few who speak of it,
those who receive its blessings.

Praying for Dexterity
On Qīxì,
women thread silk strands,
threading a seven-holed needle,
or using needles made of gold, silver, or brass,
presenting melons and fruits in the courtyard,
to request skill. If there is a spider's web on the melons,
it is considered auspicious.

riding a white crane
Wáng Zǐqiáo,
seeing Huàn Liáng, said:
"Tell my family,
on the seventh day of the seventh month,
to wait for me at the summit of Gōushì Mountain."
His family awaited him,
and when the day came,
he indeed rode a white crane at the mountain summit,
visible yet unreachable,
nodded in farewell to the people of the time,
and departed.
Wáng Zǐqiáo
was Crown Prince Jìn of King Líng of Zhōu.

In a moment,
a Vermilion Bird alighted on the furnace and said:
"Āngōng, Āngōng,
your smelting has connected with Heaven.

you will be welcomed by a crimson dragon."
When the time came,
Āngōng rode the crimson dragon and departed toward the southeast.

Empress Dòu's Divine Light
Empress Dòu had a bald head since childhood,
and was not valued by her family members.
On the day of the Qīxī Festival,
while everyone went to see the Weaving Maid star,
she alone was not permitted to go out.
Then a divine light illuminated the room,
which became an auspicious sign of her future as empress.

Yīlán Hall
Emperor Jǐng dreamed that Emperor Gāozǔ said to him:
"The beauty Wáng will give birth to a son,
who should be named Zhì (Pig)."
In the year Yǐyǒu,
on the morning of the seventh day of the seventh month, Emperor Wǔ was born in Yīlán Hall.
"Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn"
Emperor Jǐng dreamed of a red pig,
descending from the clouds to the Chóngfāng Pavilion,
The emperor awoke and sat in the pavilion,
and indeed saw red mist like a forest covering the doors,
so he renamed the pavilion Yīlán Hall.

Jiǔhuá Lamp
In the fourth month of the first year of the Yuánfēng era, on the day Wùchén,
the Emperor was leisurely residing in the Chénghuá Hall,
with Dōngfāng Shuò and Dǒng Zhòngshū at his side,
when suddenly they saw a maiden in blue attire who said:
"I am the Jade Maiden of the Yong Palace,
Wáng Zǐdēng."
The Queen Mother sent me to inform the Emperor:
'On the seventh day of the seventh month, the Queen Mother will briefly visit.'"
On that day, the Emperor cleaned and prepared the palace chambers,
burned incense of a hundred harmonies,
hung curtains of cloud-patterned brocade,
lit lamps of ninefold radiance,
arranged dates from the Jade Gate,
and poured wine made from grapes,
awaiting the arrival of her cloud-borne carriage.
Suddenly, from the southwest, what appeared to be white clouds arose,
billowing forth directly toward them,
and in a moment, they reached the palace.
The Queen Mother rode in a purple cloud chariot,
drawn by a nine-colored dappled dragon,
and supported by two attending maidens, she ascended to the hall.
On her head, she wore a Tàihuá-style chignon,
adorned with the Tàizhēn Morning Tassels Crown,
and stepped in black jade phoenix-patterned shoes.
Gazing upon her,
she appeared to be around thirty years of age.
She set out a celestial feast herself,
with delicacies extraordinarily rare and exquisite.

A flock of bluebirds gathers before the palace
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
while the Emperor was fasting in the main hall of Chenghua Palace,
a blue bird suddenly flew from the west and alighted before the hall.
The Emperor asked Dōngfāng Shuò about it,
and Shuò replied:
"This means the Queen Mother of the West wishes to come."
After a short while,
the Queen Mother arrived,
attended by two blue birds resembling crows at her side.

The Weaver Girl Marries the Herdboy
In the Later Hàn Dynasty, Chéng Wǔdīng of Guìyáng,
who possessed immortal arts and often stayed in the mortal world,
said to his younger brother:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month, the Weaver Girl crosses the river,
all immortals return to their palaces,
I have already been summoned and cannot delay,
I bid you farewell."
The younger brother asked why the Weaver Girl was crossing the river,
and when his elder brother would return.
He replied:
"The Weaver Girl is briefly visiting the Herdboy,
I will return after three thousand years."
The next day,
Chéng Wǔdīng had disappeared,
and people to this day say:
"The Weaver Girl married the Herdboy."
From "Xù Qíxié Jì"
"Huáinánzǐ" states:
Magpies filled the river to help the Weaver Girl cross.
"Fēngsú Jì" records:
On the seventh night of the seventh month, the Weaver Girl crosses the river,
using magpies to form a bridge.
Thus an ancient poem says:
After the incense silently extinguishes,
magpies scatter, leaving the crossing bridge empty.
Liáng poet Fàn Yún wrote:
Not refusing the bitter toil of Jīngwèi,
yet the river cannot be filled.
Yǔ Jiānyú's poem:
I send word to the magpies of Diāolíng to fill the river,
you cannot yet fly across as described in Ěryǎ Yìshè.
On the seventh day of autumn, magpies' heads are inexplicably bald,
tradition says on this day the Herdboy and Weaver Girl meet east of the Milky Way,
employing magpies to form a bridge for crossing,
hence all their feathers fall out.
Auspicious day
During the Wei period, someone asked Dǒng Xūn:
"The seventh day of the seventh month is considered an auspicious day,
yet the food and drink customs differ from ancient times.
Why is this?"
Xūn replied:
"In the seventh month, the millet ripens,
and the seventh day is considered a yang number,
so cooked millet was regarded as a delicacy.
Nowadays on this day, only soup noodles are prepared,
and cooked millet is no longer served.
From 'Fēngtǔ Jì'"
Exposing the calf-nose trousers
Ruǎn Xián,
courtesy name Zhòngróng,
was the nephew of Ruǎn Jí.
Previous generations of the Ruǎn family were all Confucian scholars,
and their households were amply wealthy.
Only Xián throughout his life esteemed Daoism,
abandoned worldly affairs, indulged in wine, and remained impoverished as before.
Customarily, on the seventh day of the seventh month, it was customary to air clothes in the sun.
In the courtyard of the Ruǎn family, it was resplendent,
with nothing but fine silks and brocades.
At that time, Xián, still wearing his hair in two tufts as a child,
then erected a tall pole and hung a large cloth,
exposing his calf-nose underpants in the courtyard,
saying:
"Unable to escape convention,
I merely follow along in this manner."

Sunbathing the Books in One's Belly
Hǎo Lóng on the seventh day of the seventh month,
saw his neighbors airing and drying their clothes and belongings,
so Lóng lay on his back,
exposing his abdomen in the courtyard, saying:
"I am airing the books in my belly."
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World."
Waiting for the Weaver Girl to cross,
Emperor Hòufèi Liú Yù of the Song dynasty,
on the seventh day of the seventh month went out incognito,
taking the Dew-collecting Carriage to the Green Garden Nunnery,
and in the evening arrived at the New Peace Temple,
where he stole a dog from the monk Tán Dù,
cooked it, and drank wine.
That night, he ordered Yáng Yùfū to wait for the Weaver Girl to cross,
and report back to him.
Afterward, he and his consorts performed the needle-piercing ritual,
became heavily intoxicated,
and lay down in a felt tent in the eastern corner of the Benevolent Longevity Hall.
Yùfū, seeing that Yù was drunk and unconscious,
entered with Yáng Wànnián,
took the Qianniu dagger, and killed him.

Ascending Shùn Shān
In the seventh month, on the seventh day, Wèi Púshè ascended Shùn Mountain while overseeing a replacement assignment,
pacing back and forth and gazing into the distance.
He said to his Registrar Cuī:
"I have traveled through many places,
but when it comes to mountains, rivers, fertile land,
strategic locations with natural defenses,
and famous prefectures under heaven,
none can surpass this one.
I only wonder how Dōngyáng compares."
Cuī replied:
"Qīng has ancient fame,
Qí possesses an old reputation - these two places
have similar landscapes and strategic positions.
From what I have heard in discussions,
they cannot surpass this one."
The Duke then called for a writing brush,
wishing to compose a poem at that moment.
During the transition between old and new administrations,
the office supplies were incomplete,
and no brush could be found.
So he used a Wǔbó staff to write on the north wall of the hall,
composing a poem that said:
Fulfilling duties without virtuous governance,
The return journey blocked by mountains and rivers.
Recalling the days of command and canopy,
I offer thanks to this mountain slope.

Song of Pacing the Void
Lǐ Xíngyán during the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
served as a Jǐshìzhōng,
was skilled at singing the "Steps of the Void" chant.
On the seventh day of the seventh month, the emperor held a banquet at the Liǎngyí Hall,
and commanded him to perform.
Xíngyán knelt for a long time before the emperor,
produced the tones and lyrics of a Sāndòng Taoist priest,
and sang several pieces.
His appearance was majestic and his voice resonant,
earning frequent praise and admiration from the emperor.
(From "Records of Events")
Whispered Words at the Palace of Eternal Life
Emperor Xuánzōng and Consort Yáng were escaping the summer heat at the Líshān Palace,
on the seventh day of the seventh month, the evening when the Cowherd and Weaver Maid meet,
at midnight, the consort alone attended the emperor.
Leaning shoulder to shoulder intimately,
they pledged their heartfelt vows to each other,
wishing to be husband and wife for all lifetimes.
Hence, the "Song of Everlasting Regret" says:
On the seventh day of the seventh month in the Hall of Eternal Life,
at midnight when no one was around, in whispered words,
in heaven, we wish to be lovebirds flying wing to wing,
on earth, we wish to be twin branches on a tree.

Divining Skill with Spider Silk
The Emperor and his noble consort,
every year on the seventh night of the seventh month,
would feast and revel in the Huáqīng Palace,
where the palace maids,
arranged melons, flowers, and wine,
setting the delicacies out in the courtyard,
to seek blessings from the stars of the Cowherd and Weaver Girl.
They also caught spiders and confined them in small boxes,
until dawn,
when they opened them to examine the density of the spiderwebs,
using this as an omen for gaining skill:
dense webs indicated abundant skill,
while sparse ones suggested little,
a practice emulated by the common folk.

Qǐqiǎo Lóu
The palace maidens wove a tower from brocade,
a hall one hundred feet high,
capable of holding several dozen people atop it.
They arranged melons and fruits,
wine and roasted meats,
and set out seating to worship the two stars, the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl.
The consorts and concubines each used nine-eyed needles
and five-colored threads
to thread them toward the moon;
those who succeeded were considered to have obtained skill.
They played melodies of the Qīngshāng music,
feasting and celebrating until dawn,
a practice emulated by scholars and commoners alike.
In
the customs of the Qín people at night,
they displayed embroideries and set out drinks.
They adorned the courtyard with tree blossoms, banners, and incense,
calling it the Palace of Begging for Skill,
especially popular in the women's quarters.
"The Tale of Everlasting Regret"
Zhēnrú obtained five treasures.
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a woman surnamed Lǐ who became a nun,
named Zhēnrú.
On the seventh day of the seventh month in the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era,
she suddenly saw a five-colored cloud descend to the ground,
and within a pouch were five objects,
which were precious jades.
In the first year of the Sùzōng era,
Zhēnrú was summoned by a deity to a transformed city,
where she saw the Celestial Emperor bestow upon her eight treasures,
ordering her to present them to the court.
Zhēnrú then combined them with the previous ones,
and offered all the objects.

Aerial Carriage Canopy
Guō Zǐyí was serving in the army in the desert,
when he went to the capital to expedite military provisions and returned to Yínzhōu.
At night, he saw his attendants
all looking up at a red light in the sky,
where a carriage with embroidered curtains
carried a beautiful woman sitting on a couch,
her feet dangling as she descended from the heavens.
Zǐyí bowed and prayed, saying:
"Today is the seventh day of the seventh month,
surely the Weaving Maid has descended.
I wish for longevity, wealth, and honor."
The woman smiled and said:
"Great wealth and honor shall also bring long life."
After speaking,
she gradually ascended to the sky,
still gazing directly at Zǐyí for a long time before disappearing.
Later, Zǐyí achieved great merit, wealth, and prominence,
his prestige shining brilliantly.
In the early Dàlì era,
while stationed in Hézhōng,
he fell seriously ill,
causing worry and fear among the three armies.
Zǐyí told the imperial physician and his advisor Wáng Yánchāng, among others:
"I know this illness of mine,
it has not yet reached the point of decline and death."
He then recounted the event,
and everyone congratulated him.
He later passed away at over ninety years of age.
"Collection of Encounters with Immortals"
Qiáo Lín
On the seventh day of the seventh month in the first year of the Xīngyuán era,
the false official Qiáo Lín was beheaded.
As he was about to face execution,
he wrote:
"Lín was born on the seventh day of the seventh month,
and shall also die on this day.
Is this not fate?"
From "Supplementary Records of the National History".
Golden Needle
During the reign of Emperor Sùzōng of the Táng Dynasty,
Zhèng served as the governor of Rùn Prefecture.
His elder brother Kǎn's wife, Madame Zhāng, had a daughter
who was sixteen years old,
named Cǎiniáng.
On the night of the Qīxī Festival, she set up an incense altar
and prayed to the Weaving Maid.
That night,
she dreamt of a cloud-borne carriage with feathered canopies
covering the sky as it halted.
The Weaving Maid addressed Cǎiniáng, saying:
"What blessing do you seek from me, the Weaving Maid?"
She replied:
"I wish only for cleverness."
Thereupon, the Weaving Maid gave her a golden needle over an inch long,
attached it to a piece of paper,
and placed it in her skirt sash.
She instructed her not to speak for three days,
promising she would become exceptionally skillful
and would not be reborn as a man.
After two days, she told her mother,
who looked and found only blank paper.
Yet the needle's mark remained.
Madame Zhāng had several daughters who all died young.
When pregnant with a girl, she fell ill and remained silent,
feeling resentful,
she intended to take medicine to abort the fetus.
As the medicine was brought to Cǎiniáng,
she exclaimed in surprise:
"If I am destined to become a man,
it is the child my mother carries."
Her mother, finding this strange, refrained.
Soon after, Cǎiniáng passed away, and within a month,
she gave birth to a boy.
When Madame Zhāng wept,
the infant girl cried;
when she stopped, the crying ceased.
When the child learned to speak,
he often played with items
that were Cǎiniáng's in her previous life.
Thus, he was named Shūzǐ.
When he grew up,
he attained the position of a high-ranking official.
From "Guìyuàn Cóngtán"

excelled at needlework.

Suddenly, she saw a shooting star fall onto her feast mat.
The next day, a golden shuttle appeared on the melon.

The Heavenly Gate opens
The Miscellaneous Records of Yì states:
There was a girl who was still young at the time.
On the Qīxī Festival, she saw her family go out to the hall to watch for the opening of the heavenly gate,
but she alone stayed in her room and did not go out, saying:
If it is fated that I should see it,
even in a dark room, I ought to see it clearly.
Late at night,
she suddenly saw the heavenly gate open above,
with clouds glowing brilliantly,
and she prayed for wealth.
When she grew up and married, she became rich,
accumulating a fortune of millions.
There was a merchant
who bought a hundred bolts of silk from her,
but after he left, his boat capsized and the goods sank,
and all the merchandise was lost.
By chance, the girl opened the back room
and saw the silk inside,
only damp.
Later, when the merchant returned, the girl said to him:
"The silk has returned."
He verified it and believed.

floating them on water as a game,

Zhōngyuán Festival
The Daoist Canon states:
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, during the Zhongyuán Festival,
the Earth Official investigates and selects all people,
distinguishing good from evil.
On this day, a grand offering is made at the Jade Capital Mountain,
using rare and exquisite banners, canopies, and precious objects from the world as offerings,
along with fine food and drink presented to the multitude.
Daoist priests on this day recite the Laozi,
while sages from all directions chant spiritual texts.
The Essentials of the Zhengyi Tradition states:
Divine beings from the Nine Earths, immortals of famous mountains and grotto heavens,
along with their troops, descend to the human world,
to examine and determine sins and blessings.
It further states:
The Earth Official of the Seven Qi,
in charge of the hundred offices,
ascends to the celestial court,
to present the records of human sins and blessings.
The Yàn Shū Lèi Yào states:
At the time when the Earth Official reviews the registers,
it is the season when the White Emperor reigns.
Ullambana
Mùlián's mother was reborn among the hungry ghosts,
the Buddha instructed him to prepare an Ullambana basin,
on the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
using a hundred flavors and five fruits,
to place them in the basin,
making offerings to the virtuous ones of the ten directions,
after which his mother could eat.
Mùlián addressed the Buddha, saying that all disciples who are filial
should accordingly present the Ullambana basin as an offering,
the Buddha greatly praised this for future generations,
because of this, it became widely adorned,
even to the point of carving wood,
splitting bamboo and coating with wax,
cutting colorful silks,
imitating the shapes of flowers and leaves,
reaching the height of exquisite craftsmanship.

The Silver Bridge Ascends to the Moon Palace
During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang Dynasty, on the Mid-Autumn Festival night,
Luó Gōngyuǎn accompanied Emperor Xuánzōng admiring the moon in the palace.
Luó Gōngyuǎn addressed the emperor:
"Would Your Majesty like to go to the moon to see it?"
He then took his staff and threw it into the air,
where it transformed into a great bridge,
silver in color.
He invited Emperor Xuánzōng to ascend it with him, and after walking several dozen li,
they encountered dazzling brilliance,
and an invasive chill.
They then arrived at a grand city gate.
Luó Gōngyuǎn said:
"This is the Moon Palace."
They saw several hundred fairy maidens, all dressed in plain white flowing robes,
dancing in a vast courtyard.
Emperor Xuánzōng asked:
"What melody is this?"
The reply came:
"It is the 'Melody of the Rainbow and Feather Garments'."
Emperor Xuánzōng secretly memorized the tune,
and then they returned.
Looking back at the bridge,
they saw it disappear step by step as they walked.
The next morning, he summoned the court musicians
and had them compose the "Melody of the Rainbow and Feather Garments" based on what he remembered.
(From "Unofficial Histories of the Tang," also found in the Moon section.)

Xiè's rhapsody and Bào's poetry:

Wǔyí Ensemble Music
The deity of Mount Wǔyí is called Lord Wǔyí.
In the second year of Qín Shǐ Huáng's reign,
one day he told the villagers:
"You shall gather at the mountain summit on the fifteenth day of the eighth month."
On that day, all the villagers assembled,
and saw a curtained pavilion and colorful tents set up with a precious throne,
adorned with red clouds and purple mist.
The cushions and utensils were exquisite,
arranged so that men and women sat separately.
They drank wine and ate delicacies,
and shortly after, music began to play.
They could only see the musical instruments,
but not the musicians.
As the wine was served, they were urged to eat,
and the flavors were all sweet and delicious,
though the wine was somewhat light in taste.
After the immortals had departed,
everyone was overjoyed,
having feasted together with the divine lord.
Thus, they named the place Tóngtíng (Same Pavilion).

Wén Xiāo Meets Cǎi Luán
At Mount Xīshān in Zhōnglíng, there was a Yóuwéi Temple.
Every Mid-Autumn Festival,
carriages and horses bustled noisily,
for ten lǐ it was like a marketplace.
Many prominent figures summoned famous beauties skilled in singing;
at night, they stood interspersed with men,
holding arms and stamping in unison while singing.
Only those quick-witted in repartee could win.
Later, a scholar named Wén Xiāo went to watch
and saw a maiden of exceptional charm.
Her lyrics said:
"If you can accompany me to ascend the immortal altar,
you shall have Wén Xiāo riding a colorful phoenix.
With embroidered robes and a celestial tent of my own,
the jade terrace fears not frost and snow's cold."
The scholar, suspecting she was an immortal, stood rooted and would not leave.
The maiden also gazed back at him.
After the song ended,
she alone took a candle and walked through a path of large pines.
As it nearly ended, she climbed the mountain, grasping rocks and braving dangers to ascend.
The scholar followed her trail, and the maiden said:
"Could it be Wén Xiāo?"
They led each other to a level area at the summit.
Later, suddenly wind and rain tore the curtains asunder,
and in a moment,
a celestial youth appeared holding a heavenly decree, saying:
"Wú Cǎiluán, for leaking celestial secrets out of personal desire,
is banished to be a mortal's wife."
After twelve years, the maiden then descended the mountain with the scholar and returned to Zhōnglíng.

and sets in the Yǒu direction,
dividing the heavens with balanced yīn and yáng energies.
Daylight spans fifty marks,
night spans fifty marks,
the two energies are equally divided between one day and one night,

Dropped Hat
Mèng Jiā served as General of the Westward Expedition,
and was a staff officer under Huán Wēn, who held him in high regard.
On the ninth day of the ninth month, while Huán Wēn was visiting Lóngshān,
all staff and officials gathered.
At that time, the attending officers were all wearing military uniforms.
A gust of wind came and blew,
causing Mèng Jiā's hat to fall off.
Mèng Jiā did not notice it.
Huán Wēn instructed his attendants and guests not to mention it,
in order to observe his reaction.
After a long while, Mèng Jiā went to the restroom.
Huán Wēn ordered someone to retrieve the hat and return it to him.
At the time, Sūn Shèng was present.
Huán Wēn handed him paper and a brush, ordering him to mock the incident in writing.
He placed it at Mèng Jiā's seat.
When Mèng Jiā returned and saw it, he laughed,
requested paper to write a reply, and without pausing for thought,
he composed a text,
which was exceptionally elegant.

Wáng Bó was passing through Zhōnglíng when,

Lín Wèi Tíng
On the Double Ninth Festival in the ninth month of the third year of the Jǐnglóng era,
Emperor Zhōngzōng visited the Línwèi Pavilion,
climbed high and composed poems,
with all the academicians joining in harmony.
The imperial preface stated:
The cornelian cherry chambers exude fragrance,
chrysanthemum stamens contain aroma,
like Táo Qián filling his hands,
already floating with the joy of nine-brewed wine,
and Bì Zhuó holding crabs,
one must exhaust a lifetime's delight.
Each person was assigned a four-rhyme theme,
all composing five-character poems,
and whoever finished last,
would be penalized by drinking a full cup.
The emperor, receiving the character "autumn," wrote:
The ninth day truly rides autumn,
three cups' inspiration already complete.
Floating osmanthus greets the full cup,
blowing petals toward the floating wine.
Chángfáng's cornelian cherries ripen early,
Péngzé's chrysanthemums first gathered.
Why need the desert sands,
to freely linger here?
Wéi Ānshí, receiving the character "branch," wrote:
Golden winds waft chrysanthemum stamens,
jade dew drips from cornelian cherry branches.
Sū Guī, receiving the character "light," wrote:
Deep favor answered with shallow effort,
soberly drunk serving morning light.
Lǐ Qiáo, receiving the character "joy," wrote:
Noble season at late triple autumn,
Double Ninth ninth day joy.
Xiāo Zhìzhōng, receiving the character "surplus," wrote:
Favor extreme, cornelian cherry chambers everywhere,
grace deep, chrysanthemum libation surplus.
Zhào Yànbó, receiving the character "flower," wrote:
Hairpins hang red cornelian cherry stamens,
cups rinse purple chrysanthemum flowers.
Yáng Lián, receiving the character "pavilion," wrote:
Distant sun gazes upon Qín's outskirts,
Double Ninth seated at Bà Pavilion.
Cén Xī, receiving the character "shore," wrote:
Thus enjoying the view of Qín's outskirts,
climbing high overlooking Bà's shore.
Lú Cángyòng, receiving the character "open," wrote:
Cornelian cherries bloom from pendants,
chrysanthemums open by the wine's edge.
Lǐ Xián, receiving the character "straight," wrote:
Yellow chrysanthemums float near wine,
green pines stand straight against frost.
Shěn Quánqī, receiving the character "long," wrote:
Yearly Double Ninth celebrations,
sun and moon serve heaven long.
Dòu Xījiè, receiving the character "bright," wrote:
Ninth dawn accompanying imperial meals,
ten thousand years serving brightness.
Xuē Jì, receiving the character "calendar":
Wish to accompany nine-ninth days,
long serve thousand-thousand calendars.
Lǐ Yì, receiving the character "rich":
Holding boxes, cornelian cherry fragrance widespread,
raising cups, chrysanthemum scent rich.
Mǎ Huáisù, receiving the character "wine":
Orchids spread leaves for mats,
chrysanthemums use scent to float wine.
Yú Jīngyě, receiving the character "goblet":
Cassia feasts display jade stands,
chrysanthemum wine overflows fragrant goblets.
Lú Huáishèn, receiving the character "return," wrote:
Cranes seem to hear lutes arrive,
people suspect feasting at Hào return.
At this banquet, Wéi Ānshí
and Sū Guī's poems
were completed first, while Yú Jīngyě
and Lú Huáishèn finished last and were penalized with wine.

Inscribed on the Eastern Pavilion

After Chǔ's son Lìng Hú Táo succeeded him,
he showed Lǐ Yìshān no particular favor.
On the Double Ninth Festival,
Yìshān went to Táo's office

"We once drank together with the old master,
While white chrysanthemums bloomed freely in the frosty sky.
Ten years have passed with no word from the underworld,
But on this ninth day, thoughts arise before the wine cup.
Don't imitate the Han officials planting alfalfa,
Rather join the Chǔ poet singing of riverside smartweed.
Your honor now holds high office with barriers erected,
No longer may I glimpse the eastern pavilion."
Táo then closed this hall,
and never used it again in his lifetime.

The Crane Forest Blooms
In Rùnzhōu, the azaleas of Hèlín Temple grew over ten feet tall.
Every late spring when the flowers bloomed in profusion,

strolling together beneath the trees.
It was commonly believed they were flower goddesses.
When Zhōu Bǎo governed Zhèxī,

"The flowers of Hèlín Temple
are uniquely spectacular in the world.
I've often heard you can make flowers bloom out of season.
Now that the Double Ninth Festival is approaching,
could you make them bloom for this occasion?"
So two days before the festival,
Qīqī stayed overnight at Hèlín Temple.
At midnight, a woman came and said to Qīqī:
"I have been commanded by the highest heaven
to oversee these flowers below.
Now I shall open them together with you, Daoist."
The next morning when they rose,
the temple monks were suddenly surprised to find
the flower buds gradually splitting open.
By the ninth day,
they were blooming as luxuriantly as in spring.
When this was reported,
Bǎo and all the city's scholars and commoners were astonished,
and they came to admire the flowers just as in springtime.

The Six Climatic Influences
At the beginning of the Winter Solstice period,
on the first five days,
water begins to freeze.
In the next five days,
the earth begins to harden.
In the following five days,
pheasants enter large waters and transform into clams.
Next comes the Lesser Snow solar term,
on the first five days rainbows hide and disappear.
In the next five days,
the celestial qi ascends upward,
while the terrestrial qi descends downward.
In the following five days,
blockage occurs and winter is fully formed.
Next comes the mid-winter Great Snow period,
on the first five days,
ice grows thicker,
the earth begins to split,
and shrikes cease singing.
In the next five days,
tigers begin to mate.
In the following five days,
rue begins to grow,
and iris shoots emerge.
Next comes the Winter Solstice solar term,
on the first five days,
earthworms curl up.
In the next five days elk antlers shed,
in the following five days spring waters begin to flow.
Next comes late winter,
the Lesser Cold period.
On the first five days,
wild geese head north.
In the next five days,
birds of prey become fierce and swift.
In the following five days,
the depths of marshes freeze solid.
All these six qi,
eighteen periods in total,
represent winter's proper command of storing and nourishing,
therefore those who cultivate life
must carefully follow the timing of heaven.

matters of extravagance and frugality

"Every New Year's Eve,
he would set up incense mountains in the courtyards before the halls,
using dozens of cartloads of aloeswood roots—
each mountain burning several carts of aloeswood
soaked with shell-based incense—
flames rising several zhàng high,
fragrance detectable for dozens of lǐ.

In the chambers, no oil lamps were lit;
instead, one hundred and twenty precious pearls were hung,
their illumination
rivaling daylight.

and in the halls, what is burned is oil—

verbally criticizing the extravagance,
yet inwardly impressed by the splendor."

Sound tube
The "Yuè Lìng" chapter states:
Lǜ,
is a standard,
the pitch pipes of sound.
The ancient sages,
based on the distinctions of yīn and yáng,
examined the clarity and turbidity of wind sounds,
which could not be recorded in writing or transmitted orally.
Thus, they began to cast metal to make bells,
to govern the sounds of the twelve months,
and then to imitate the ascending and descending qì.
As bells were difficult to distinguish,
they cut bamboo into tubes,
calling them lǜ.
Lǜ are
the standard measures for clarity and turbidity.
The clarity and turbidity of sounds
are regulated by determining their length.
born of the five notes
Sounds have clear and turbid distinctions,
thus they are harmonized by the gōng and shāng notes;
forms have long and short variations,
thus they are measured by the zhàng
and chǐ; vessels have large and small capacities,
thus they are standardized by the hú
and dǒu; substances have light and heavy weights,
thus they are balanced by the jūn
and shí. Therefore, the Yú Shū states:
"Thus, the pitch-pipes, measurements, and weights were unified."
Hence, the musical pitches and notes
originate from this principle.
"Sòng Zhì"
Observing the Qi
The five tones are born from yīn and yáng,
divided into twelve pitches,
which further generate sixty,
all used to record the energy of the Dipper,
and reflect the categories of things.
Heaven manifests through shadows,
Earth manifests through resonance,
which is the pitch.
When yīn and yáng harmonize, shadows appear;
when pitch energy responds, ashes disperse.
Thus, the Son of Heaven routinely on the winter and summer solstices presides in the front hall,
assembling masters of the eight abilities,
arranging the eight tones to listen to music,
balancing sundial measurements and awaiting bell pitches,
weighing earth ashes to align with yīn and yáng.
At winter solstice, when yáng energy responds, music harmonizes,
shadows are clear and reach their longest extreme,
Huángzhōng connects with earth ashes,
light and balanced, tilting upward;
at summer solstice, yīn energy
responds, then music harmonizes,
shadows are turbid and reach their shortest extreme,
Ruíbīn connects with earth ashes heavy,
and balanced, tilting downward.
Advancing or retreating within the sequence,
over five days,
the eight abilities each report their observations to the Grand Historian for sealing,
if the manifestation aligns, there is harmony;
otherwise, divination is used.
The method for observing energy:
build a triple-walled room with doors closed,
seal cracks thoroughly,
spread orange silk densely inside,
set up wooden stands in the room,
one for each pitch,
low inside and high outside,
following their directional positions,
place the pitches atop them,
press reed ashes
against their inner ends,
and observe according to the calendar.
When energy arrives, ashes disperse;
those moved by the energy
have ashes scattered;
if moved by people or wind,
the ashes gather.
In the hall, observation
uses twelve jade pitches;
only at the two solstices is the Spiritual Terrace used,
with sixty bamboo pitches,
observing the sun as per its calendar. "Hòu Hàn Zhì"
The six pitch standards generate one another.
Emperor Yuán was versed in music theory himself.
The court official Jīng Fáng understood the five tones
and the principles of the six pitch standards.
Thus, he had Wěi Xuánchéng and others test Jīng Fáng with various questions.
Jīng Fáng replied that he had learned from Jiāo Yánshòu the method of generating the sixty tones,
whereby the upper generates the lower,
all by a ratio of three to two,
and the lower generates the upper, all by a ratio of three to four.
The yang generates the yin below,
and the yin generates the yang above,
ending with Zhōnglǚ,
thus completing the twelve pitch standards.
Zhōnglǚ generates Zhíshǐ above,
Zhíshǐ generates Qùmiè below,
as upper and lower generate each other,
ending with Nánshì,
thus completing the sixty tones.
The transformation of the twelve pitch standards
into sixty
is akin to the transformation of the eight trigrams
into sixty-four.

Establishing laws using millet grains
The initial quest for tones was based on pitch pipes,
and the creation of pitch pipes relied on millet grains.
Starting from the width of a single millet grain,
they accumulated to form units of length like the fēn and cùn,
while the length of a millet grain was accumulated to form
the yuè and hé.
The weight of a single millet grain,
accumulated, formed the zhū.
These were the foundations for creating the pitch pipes.
Thus, the method for determining length
was recorded in the standards of measurement.
The method for determining volume
was recorded in the standards of capacity.
The method for determining weight
was recorded in the standards of scales and weights.

The edict commands the undertaking of affairs.
In ancient times, when the sage kings created the calendrical system,
they observed the movements of celestial bodies and laws,
watched the operation of cosmic mechanisms,
traced the successive transit of stars,
and comprehended the variations in gnomon shadow lengths.
Thereupon they constructed instruments to standardize measurements,
erected gnomons to conduct surveys,
used water clocks to verify calculations,
and deployed arithmetic to pursue precision,
so that the beginning of the year aligned above,
and the lunar phases synchronized below,
with cold and heat following in proper sequence,
and the four seasons never erring.

Without the vital energy
The Book records that a full cycle comprises three hundred and sixty-six days,
and by intercalating months, the four seasons are fixed to complete the year.
Thus, all official duties are properly regulated,
and numerous achievements flourish.
For this reason, the Son of Heaven
must appoint officials in charge of the calendar,
and feudal lords must have their own calendar officers,
who practice their profession generation after generation
to examine and refine their methods.
Speaking in whole numbers,
it is said there are truly six days,
with five and a quarter days,
the sun moves one degree per day,
while the moon moves thirteen degrees and nineteen parts daily.
Due to the irregularity in degrees,
the calendar officials must gather and account for these variations in speed,
to verify the complexities of new and full moons,
and thereby establish intercalary months.
An intercalary month lacks a mid-season solar term, and the Big Dipper slants,
pointing between two celestial markers,
which distinguishes it from other months.
Accumulating these adjustments harmonizes the four seasons and eight nodes,
ensuring no deviation, thus completing the year.
Its precision is utmost.
Grasping its subtleties
to align with the heavenly way,
affairs proceed orderly without contradiction.
However, the movements of yīn and yáng
deviate with each motion,
and these deviations accumulate endlessly,
leading to discrepancies with the calendar.
Therefore, Confucius and Qiūmíng
often wrote about new moons and intercalations,
aiming to correct errors,
thereby elucidating calendrical calculations.

Celestial Degrees
Qíbó said:
Heaven uses six times six as its rhythm,
Earth uses nine times nine to regulate convergence,
in order to determine the degrees of Heaven and the numbers of Qì.
The celestial degrees
are what regulate the movements of the sun and moon.
The Qì numbers
are what record the functions of transformation and generation.
Heaven is Yáng,
Earth is Yīn,
the sun is Yáng,
the moon is Yīn,
their movements have divisions and records,
their cycles follow paths and principles,
the sun moves one degree per day,
the moon moves thirteen degrees,
with some remainder.
Thus, in the large and small months of three hundred sixty-five days,
a year is completed by accumulating Qì,
with the remainder forming intercalary months.
Establish the beginning at the start,
show the correct alignment in the middle,
calculate the remainder at the end,
and the celestial degrees are fully accounted for.
The annotation states:

Zhōng means the middle of the month.
Tuī means to calculate the remaining position,
meaning to set the first Qì at the day of the initial solar term,
to show the Dipper's position at the middle of the month,
and to allocate the intercalary remainder after the full moon,
so before the intercalary month,
the Qì does not reach the month; after the intercalary month,
the month does not reach the Qì.
Therefore, in the regular month system,
the beginning is established and the middle is set for intercalation;
in the intercalary month's record,
there is no beginning and no middle.
Even if the calendar includes them,
they belong to other solar terms.
Thus, the calendar does not mention the intercalary month's climate,
nor which solar term is intercalary,
nor which month's middle is intercalary.
The meaning of calculating the end can be clearly understood.
Hence it is said: establish the beginning at the start,
show the correct alignment in the middle,
calculate the remainder at the end.
From this, calculating the days forms the intercalary month,
thus enabling the celestial degrees to be fully accounted for.

"Treatise on Harmonics and the Calendar":
The twenty-eight lunar mansions are divided into twelve stations.
Jìn Zhuó's commentary on the "Treatise on Astronomy" states:
When the Year Star is in the four midpoints,
it traverses three mansions per year;
when the Year Star is in the four beginnings and four seasons,
it traverses two mansions per year.
Two times eight makes sixteen,
three times four makes twelve, thus covering the twenty-eight mansions,
completing a circuit of the heavens in twelve years—this is the Year Star's annual
movement through one station.
The later "Treatise on Harmonics and the Calendar"
states: The sun moves one degree per day,

and one quarter of a degree,

which is called a year.

Avoidance of Taboos
The qi differs;

enabling yīn and yáng to achieve their work externally.
During the three months of summer,
when the myriad things flourish and grow,
the yīn qi avoids them and hides below,

Yáng is responsible for generating the myriad things;

Virtue and Punishment
The constancy of the Way of Heaven,
lies in the alternation of yīn and yáng.
Yáng represents the virtue of Heaven.
Yīn represents the punishment of Heaven.
The Way of Heaven
relies on yáng and not on yīn.
The Way of the King
relies on virtue and not on punishment,
in accordance with Heaven.
The "Fán Lù"
states: Yáng operates through compliance,
while yīn operates through opposition.
Opposition that turns to compliance,
and compliance that turns to opposition,
is the nature of yīn.
Therefore, Heaven employs yīn as expediency,
and yáng as constancy.
When yáng emerges, there is rain;
when yīn emerges, there is north.
Constancy is used in prosperity,
expediency is used in decline.
From this, it is evident that Heaven manifests constancy and conceals expediency,
placing virtue before punishment.
Hence it is said:
Yáng is the virtue of Heaven,
yīn is the punishment of Heaven.
The qì of yáng is warm,
while the qì of yīn is cold.
The qì of yáng gives life,
while the qì of yīn takes away.
The qì of yáng is benevolent,
while the qì of yīn is harsh.
The qì of yáng is generous,
while the qì of yīn is urgent.
The qì of yáng loves,
while the qì of yīn hates.
The qì of yáng gives life,
while the qì of yīn brings death.
Therefore, yáng always occupies the position of substance,
and operates in fullness.
Yīn always occupies the position of emptiness,
and operates in decline.
Heaven favors benevolence,
drawing near to the transformation of aversion and harshness,
while distancing itself from great virtue,
and the intention of minor punishment.
It prioritizes constancy over expediency,
valuing yáng and devaluing yīn.
place
The movement of yīn and yáng each lasts six months,
with the same measure in distance and proximity,
yet their positions differ.
The movement of yīn:
in spring it resides in the east,
in autumn it resides in the west,
in summer it resides to the right of the void,
in winter it resides to the left of the void,
in summer it resides below the void,
in winter it resides above the void,
this is the constant position of yīn.
The movement of yáng:
in spring it resides above,
in winter it resides below,
this is the constant position of yáng.
Yīn shifts four times throughout the year,
while yáng remains constant,
this is truly not favoring yáng and neglecting yīn,
but rather valuing virtue and distancing punishment.

Concealing its service,
therefore,

When yin emerges,
it enters emptiness with emptiness.
Heaven employs yang,
not yin,
favoring virtue over punishment,

Governing yīn and yáng
Empress Wǔ issued an edict inquiring about the way to harmonize the primordial energy.
Chén Zǐ'áng replied:
"The primordial energy is the beginning of heaven and earth,
the ancestor of all things,
and the great foundation of royal governance.
Nothing in heaven and earth is greater than yīn and yáng,
nothing among all things is more intelligent than humans,
and nothing in royal governance takes precedence over pacifying the people.
Therefore, when the people are pacified, yīn and yáng are harmonized;
when yīn and yáng are harmonized, heaven and earth are balanced;
when heaven and earth are balanced, the primordial energy is rectified.
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor united virtue,
Yǒuyú gathered the seasons,
Yáo had the thoroughfare chamber, and Xià had the ancestral hall—
all these were means to harmonize the primordial energy
and regulate yīn and yáng.
At the end of the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
Jié and Zhòu were foolish and tyrannical,
causing yīn and yáng to act contrary,
and heaven and earth to be enraged."

water,

wood,

From the "Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals"
Celestial Order
Heaven possesses the Five Phases,
Wood being the beginning of the Five Phases,
Water being the end of the Five Phases,
and Earth being the center of the Five Phases.
This is the natural sequence of their order.
Wood generates Fire,
Fire generates Earth,
Earth generates Metal,
Metal generates Water,
Water generates Wood,
this represents their father-son relationship.
Wood resides on the left,
Metal resides on the right,
Fire resides in front,
Water resides behind,
Earth resides in the center,
this is the father-son sequence,
arranged through mutual reception.
Therefore,
Wood receives from Water and Fire receives from Wood,
Earth receives from Fire,
Metal receives from Earth,
Water receives from Metal.
All that give,
are the fathers,
and all that receive,
are the sons.
Constantly through the father to employ the son,
is the Way of Heaven.
Thus,
when Wood has grown, Fire nourishes it,
when Metal has perished, Wood stores it,
Fire delights in Wood and nourishes it with Yang,
Water overcomes Metal and mourns it with the Yin of Earth's affairs,
Heaven exhausts its loyalty,
therefore the Five Phases,
are the conduct of filial sons and loyal ministers.

It is said:

It is said:
Focus on the mother overcoming the child.
It is said:
Control the child overcoming the mother is called:
distress.

The scholar
