Zhāng Héng, styled Píngzǐ,
constructed a seismoscope,
made of refined bronze,
with a diameter of eight cùn,
its lid raised and rounded,
resembling a wine jar.
Adorned with seal script,
and patterns of mountains, turtles, birds, and beasts,
inside was a central pillar,
with eight channels extending sideways.
Outside the mechanism were eight dragons,
each holding a bronze ball in its mouth,
below them were toads,
with open mouths ready to catch the balls,
the intricate mechanism,
all concealed within the base,
covered seamlessly without gaps.
If an earthquake occurred,
the base would shake,
triggering the dragon mechanism to release a ball,
which the toad would catch.
The sound would resonate loudly,
alerting observers,
even if only one dragon’s mechanism activated,
while the other seven remained still,
by examining the direction,
the location of the earthquake could be determined,
proven accurate as if by divine power.
In all recorded texts,
nothing like it had existed before.
Once, when one dragon’s mechanism activated,
yet no earthquake was felt locally,
scholars in the capital initially doubted its lack of evidence.

Your subject Xiàng
In the first year of the Yǒnghuī era,

Emperor Gāozōng turned to his attending officials and said:
"My governance and teachings are not clear,
causing the land of Jìnzhōu
to shake repeatedly."
Attendant Zhāng Xíngchéng said:
"Heaven is yang,
earth is yin;
yang represents the sovereign,
yin represents the ministers.
The sovereign should initiate movement,
while ministers should maintain tranquility.
Now Jìnzhōu experiences earthquakes
that continue unabated for over ten days -
I fear this indicates women's improper influence in affairs
and ministers' secret plots.
Moreover, Jìnzhōu was Your Majesty's original fief,
so these repeated earthquakes particularly manifest this response.
I humbly urge deep reflection and long-term consideration
to prevent these sprouts from growing."
The emperor deeply agreed with him.

Why do the benevolent delight in mountains?
Mountains are what all things look up to,
where plants and trees grow,
where myriad beings stand,
where birds gather,
where beasts rest,
where treasures are nurtured,
and where rare beings dwell.
They tirelessly nurture all creatures,
providing endlessly for all directions.
They release clouds and guide winds,
soaring between heaven and earth.
Through them heaven and earth are perfected,
and nations are pacified.
They resemble benevolent scholars with lofty ideals.
This is why the benevolent
delight in mountains.

Through them all things are perfected,
and the common people are nourished.

Mount Pánjiā,

Throughout the world, there are famous mountains,
five thousand three hundred seventy,
that produce iron.
Three thousand six hundred nine,

gold lies below.
Where lodestone is found above,

Mount Tài,

Mount Huò,
the Southern Peak.
Mount Huà,
the Western Peak.
Mount Cháng,

Mount Sōnggāo,

They broadly distribute clouds and rain,

What the eyes have witnessed

Having delighted in obtaining such a marvelous view,
if the mountains and waters possess a spirit,

Kōngtóng Shān
Huángdì was established as the Son of Heaven,

Hearing that Guǎngchéngzǐ was atop Mount Kōngtóng,
he went to visit him,
inquiring about the essence of the ultimate Way.
"Zhuāngzǐ"
In Línrǔ County of Rǔzhōu,
to the west of Guǎngchéng Slope,
there is a small mountain called Kōngtóng,
which is the place where Huángdì sought the Way,
and where Guǎngchéngzǐ lived in seclusion.
At its peak, there is a cave opening like an earthen bowl.
When heavy wind and rain are about to come,
a white dog emerges from the cave to the fields,
and the locals take this as an omen, also naming the mountain
Jade Dog Peak.
The elders say:
During the three springs and nine autumns,
when the sky is clear and beautiful,
white mist inevitably rises from the peak.
In a short while, powdered battlements and blue bricks stretch for several miles,
with pavilions and halls interwoven,
and flowers and trees radiantly splendid.
Within a few breaths, the mist gradually disperses,
and it is no longer visible.
Common folks, unaware that it is an abode of immortals,
mistakenly believe it to be Guǎngchéngzǐ’s illusory city,
which is merely a vulgar tale.

The north bears the Dipper and Pole Star as Kōngtóng,

Qīngchéng
Huángdì broke through mountains and opened paths,
traveled extensively across the Five Sacred Mountains,
designating Qīngchéng Mountain as the Elder of the Five Sacred Mountains,
making it the superior authority over the mountains and rivers,
and the ancestral rank of true immortals.
Within a month,
all the sacred mountains paid homage twice,
with springs flowing at the six periods of the day,
replacing the sundial and water clock.
It is also called Chìchéng,
Qīngchéng Capital,
and Tiānguó Mountain,
and is recognized as the Fifth Great Grotto-Heaven,
the Heaven of the Precious Immortals' Nine Chambers.
It lies northwest of the commandery,
south of the Mín Mountains,
where numerous peaks are veiled and reflected,
interconnected with one another.
It is the dwelling place of divine immortals,
with many auspicious and extraordinary phenomena.
According to the "Yù Guì Jīng,"
over ten li north of Qīngchéng Temple,
there is a solitary platform towering high,
uniquely elegant above the clouds,
named Xuānyuán Platform.
Looking down from it, the myriad mountains appear like ant hills,
and trees that require multiple embraces seem as small as shepherd's purse.
This platform cannot be inhabited
by those who have not attained immortality.
The "Shān Jì" records
that the Mín Mountains form continuous peaks and ridges,
stretching unbroken for a thousand li,
with Qīngchéng as its foremost peak.
It was formerly known as Qīngchéng Peak,
and later called Dàmiàn Mountain.
The mountain has seventy-two small caves,
corresponding to the seventy-two pentads of the year,
and eight great caves,
aligned with the eight solar terms and the celestial granary.
The peaks stand majestically,
numbering thirty-six in total.

the place where Jiǎn Kēng refined elixirs according to Lièxiān Zhuàn.

Luófú
Luófú is
a general designation.
Luó refers to
Luó Mountain.
Fú refers to
Fú Mountain.
These two mountains merged into one entity,
hence called Luófú.
On the summit of Luó Mountain grows cassia,
known as the cassia of Běnyú,
and there is also a mirror-like Heavenly Pond,
with a circumference of about five lǐ,
its waters responding to the ocean tides,
called the Divine Lake.
As for Fú Mountain,
it was originally a peak of Pénglái.
During the time of Yáo,
a great flood swept it across the sea,
and it is said to have attached to the cliffs of Luó Mountain.
To this day, the flora on Fú Mountain differs,
all being species from the sea.
There are also seven mǔ of level fields,
unaffected by flood or drought,
where the crops are extraordinary.
Yuán Bó of Chénjùn
and Xú Lǚdào of Dōngguǎn
both stated:
"Pénglái has three islands,
and this is one of them."
The peaks rise elegantly over more than four hundred lǐ,
with ridges and summits casting shadows upon each other,
thirty-two prominent peaks emerge,
their tops piercing the layered heavens,
while below lie deep, secluded caves,
extending sideways for several tens of lǐ.
Flying clouds crown the mountain's summit,
also called the Gathering Clouds Peak,
where purple mists often linger.
Climbing it at midnight,
one can witness the sunrise,
and it is referred to in Zhēn Gào as the Layered City.
The Shān Jì records
a cave named Zhūmíng, the Heaven of Shining Truth.
The Máo Jūn Nèi Zhuàn states
Zhūmíng is the Yang Palace,
and Yàozhēn the Yin Chamber.
In Xiè Língyùn's rhapsody,
it is said that five hundred Perfected Ones often gather and roam in the cave.
In the 26th year of the Kāiyuán era,
an imperial decree ordered the establishment of a ceremony at Huāshǒu Terrace.
Early in the Tiānbǎo era,
an edict commanded the Daoist priest Shēn Tàizhī to sacrifice to the mountain,
seeking to find the Zhūmíng Cave.
At that time, the local official Rèn Zhīxuān,
leading elders, discovered a cave,
using vines to lower a basket of stone vessels,
and sent a person down about over five zhàng,
who returned saying that looking down, it appeared bottomless,
with sun, moon, stars, and constellations
all visible at first,
and white clouds
that soon scattered into five colors.
The Luófú Yì Jì records this.
Mount Wūxián
Now, Wūxián was one
who truly used great arts to serve as Emperor Yáo's healer,
honored as a high noble in life,
and revered as an exalted spirit after death.
Could it be that he was enfeoffed with this mountain, and thus it was named after him?
Ah, the famous mountain of Wūxián—
it rises in solitary grandeur, lofty and steep;
it complements Huà and Huò in supporting the realm,
and brings numinous moisture for a hundred miles around.
From "Guō Pú's Rhapsody"
Jiǔyí
In the south, there are the Cāngwú Hills,
the Cāngwú Abyss,
within which lies the Jiǔyí Mountain.
It is where Shùn was buried,
located within the boundaries of Línglíng in Chángshā.
From the "Classic of Mountains and Seas":
The Jiǔyí Mountain spreads its foundation,
in the wilderness of Cāngwú,
its peaks stand out beautifully among several commanderies,
with layered cliffs rising nine times,
each guiding a floating ridge over the valleys,
bearing rugged, distinct ridges sharing the same imposing presence,
causing travelers to doubt.
Hence, it is called Jiǔyí (Nine Doubts).
From the "Water Classic":
Peaks connect with ridges,
competing in elegance and height,
embracing clouds and rolling mists,
dividing the sky and blocking the sun.
From the "Jīngzhōu Records":
Lǔ Miàodiǎn entered Jiǔyí for over ten years,
when a deity spoke to her, saying:
This mountain is governed by the great Shùn,
the supreme authority of heaven and earth,
the ancestral master of the nine provinces.
In ancient times, there were lofty Daoist masters
who built three resting platforms at the mountain's base,
providing shelter from wind and rain,
and a dwelling for cultivating truth through form and mind.
From the "Records of Assembled Transcendents":
The nine peaks
are named: first, Xiāosháo;
second, Nǚměi;
third, Shíchéng;
fourth, Éhuáng;
fifth, Zhūmíng;
sixth, Guìlín;
seventh, Huágài;
eighth, Bālín;
ninth, Shílóu;
encircling an area of over a hundred lǐ.
From the "Illustrated Records":
Jūnshān
Mount Dòngtíng,
the two daughters of the Emperor dwell there.
"Classic of Mountains and Seas"
Mount Jūn,
is Mount Dòngtíng,
the two daughters of the Emperor dwell there,
called:
the Lady of the Xiāng.
The Emperor's daughter sent Jīngwèi,
to the Queen Mother to fetch the jade seal of the Western Mountains,
to seal the Northern Mountains of the Eastern Sea.
"Records of Broad Knowledge"
The Lady of the Xiāng,
is the daughter of Emperor Yáo.
Qín Shǐ Huáng sailed the river to Mount Xiāng,
encountered heavy rain and asked the Erudite Scholar,
"What deity is the Lord of Xiāng?"
The Erudite Scholar said:
"I have heard they are the two daughters of Yáo,
consorts of Shùn.
They died and were buried here."
"Jade Slip of the River Chart"
The First Emperor wished to enter Xiāng,
to view Mount Héng but encountered wind and waves,
was nearly drowned and wrecked but reached this mountain and was spared,
thus named it Mount Jūn.
"Records of Xiāng Province"
Where the Lord of Xiāng roamed,
therefore called Mount Jūn.
If one prays to the spirit,
then it is favorable for crossing.
"Maps and Records of Jīng Province"
There is a passage on Mount Jūn,
that connects subterraneously with Mount Bāo in Wú,
on it are several pecks of fine wine,
one who drinks it will not die.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn fasted for seven days,
sent several tens of men and women to Mount Jūn,
obtained the fine wine,
wished to drink it,
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"If I recognize this wine, please let me inspect it."
Thereupon drank it all in one go,
the Emperor wanted to kill him.
Shuò then said:
"If you kill Shuò and I die,
this proves it ineffective,
since it is effective,
even if killed, I will not die."
So he was pardoned.
"Records of Broad Knowledge"
Lóng Zhǒng
Yǔ was born at Shíniǔ,
emerged from Lóngzhǒng,
the source of the river being the Mín Mountains.
There is a temple of Yǔ on Tiánxǔ Mountain,
the temple covering eighty mǔ of level ground,
and on every new and full moon the pond spontaneously drains,
followed by water sufficient for a thousand households,
left behind by Yǔ.
"Record of Qīngchéng"
Wǎnwěi
South of Kuàijī Mountain,
there is Wǎnwěi Mountain.
On its summit lies a rock shaped like a bamboo basket,
commonly called the Stone Cabinet.
Its cliffs stand tall enough to scrape the clouds,
presenting the peril of crossing by suspension.
Those who ascend must pile ladders
before they can reach it.
Kǒng Língfú's "Record of Kuàijī Mountain"
states: Yǔ consulted
the "Yellow Emperor's Central Classic" and saw the sages' record, which said:
"To the southeast of Jiǔyí Mountain,
there is a mountain called Tiānzhù,
also known as Wǎnwěi,
supported by patterned jade,
and covered with a massive rock.
Its texts are on golden slips,
with characters of green jade,
bound with silver.
Yǔ then traveled east to Héng Mountain,
sacrificed a white horse as an offering,
and encountered a man in crimson embroidered robes,
who called himself the Envoy of Xuányí Cāngshuǐ.
He said to Yǔ:
'If you wish to obtain my texts on slips
and learn the methods of channeling water,
fast and purify yourself at the Yellow Emperor's mountain.'"
Yǔ then fasted and ascended the Stone Basket Mountain,
where he indeed obtained the texts.
Thus, he understood the sources of the four great rivers
and the courses of all streams.
He cut through Lóngmén and connected Yīquē,
then traveled across the world.
He ordered Bó Yì to record it all,
naming it the "Classic of Mountains and Seas."
"The Annals of Wú and Yuè"
records: Yǔ opened Wǎnwěi Mountain and obtained a red jade tablet as bright as the sun
and a green one like the moon, each measuring one foot two inches.
"The Chart of Opening Mountains"
Bāo Shān
Yǔ was controlling the floodwaters when he reached Mount Mùdé,
where he saw a divine being.
The being said to Yǔ:
"Toiling your body,
exhausting your mind,
to control the floodwaters—
is this not wearisome?"
Yǔ recognized him as a divine being,
bowed twice and requested instruction,
whereupon the divine being said:
"I possess the Five Talismans of the Numinous Treasure,
which can command flood dragons and water leopards.
If you can transmit them,
your task will be completed in no time."
He then gave them to Yǔ and admonished him:
"When your work is done, you may conceal them in the numinous mountains."
After Yǔ succeeded, he hid them in a cave on Mount Bāo in Dòngtíng.
During the time of King HéLǘ of Wú,
an old man named Lóngwēi obtained the talismans and presented them.
The King of Wú showed them to his ministers,
but none could recognize them.
He then ordered a messenger to take the talismans
and inquire of Confucius, saying:
"While the King of Wú was at leisure,
a red crow brought this text in its beak
to the king's presence.
None can decipher its script,
so he has sent me from afar to inquire."
Confucius replied:
"Long ago, when Yǔ was controlling the waters at Mount Mùdé,
he encountered a divine being who gave him the Five Talismans of the Numinous Treasure.
Later, they were hidden on Mount Bāo in Dòngtíng.
What Your Majesty has obtained—
could it not be these?
As for the matter of the red crow,
I have no detailed knowledge of it."
The messenger returned and reported this,
and HéLǘ revered it.
Prior to these events,
there was a children's rhyme in Jiāngzuǒ that said:
"Yǔ controlled the floodwaters and obtained the five talismans,
hiding them in the lake of Mount Bāo in Dòngtíng.
The old man Lóngwēi stole Yǔ's book;
he who obtains the five texts will lose his state and home."
Soon after, Wú indeed perished.
As seen in the Zhēnzhèng Lùn from the WúYuè Chūnqiū and YuèJuéShū.
King HéLǘ of Wú,
while traveling to Mount Bāo,
met a man who claimed his surname was Shān,
and his given name Yǐnjū.
HéLǘ questioned him,
whereupon he entered Dòngtíng
and retrieved a scroll of plain text to present to HéLǘ.
Its meaning was unrecognizable,
so he sent a messenger to inquire of Confucius,
who said:
"I have heard a children's rhyme that goes:
'The King of Wú travels to view the shaking lake;
Lóngwēi the old man, Shān Yǐnjū,
enters the numinous ruins of northern Mount Bāo,
then goes into Dòngtíng to steal Yǔ's book.
The great text of the Heavenly Emperor cannot be unrolled.
This text is to be passed down until the hundred and sixth era begins;
if forcibly taken, it will cause the loss of state and home.'"
From the Língbǎo Yàolüè.
Dǐzhù
In ancient times, Yǔ controlled the great flood,
where mountains and hills blocked the water,
he cut through them,
thus breaking the mountains to open the river's path,
the river water divided its flow,
encircling the mountain as it passed,
the mountain appeared in the water like a pillar,
hence it was called Dǐzhù (Steady Pillar).
After three channels were cut through,
the water flowed in divided streams,
pointing to their shape to name them,
it was also called Sānmén (Three Gates).
From the "Shuǐ Jīng"
Huìjī
Yǔ arrived at Dàyuè,
ascended Miáo Mountain to hold a grand assembly,
evaluating ranks and virtue,
enfeoffing the meritorious,
and thus renamed Miáo Mountain as Kuàijī.
He fell ill and died, and was buried there.
"Yuè Tradition"
The mountain of Kuàijī,
was the ancient Fáng Mountain,
also called Máo Mountain,
and also known as Dòng Mountain.
"Yuè Jué" states:
Dòng means to guard,
likely referring to the guardian mountain of Yángzhōu as mentioned in the Zhōu Lǐ.
The mountain is square in shape,
abundant with gold and jade on its summit,
and rich in beautiful stones below.
At the foot of the mountain lies Yǔ's temple,
which houses a statue of the Holy Maiden.
"Lǐ Yuè Wěi" records:
When Yǔ controlled floods and droughts,
heaven bestowed a divine maiden,
and the Holy Maiden is her likeness.
On the mountain is Yǔ's tomb;
in the past, when the Great Yǔ assumed the throne,
he conducted an eastern inspection tour in the tenth year,
and passed away at Kuàijī,
where he was subsequently buried.
Birds came to tend the grave,
uprooting weeds in spring,
and pecking away debris in autumn.
Therefore, the local officials
prohibited the people from harming these birds arbitrarily,
with no pardon for offenders.
East of the mountain lies a chasm,
a mile from the temple,
so deep its bottom cannot be seen,
called Yǔ's Well.
It is said:
"Many eastern travelers explore its caverns."
"Shuǐ Jīng"
The mountain contains the Yángmíng Cave, also named Jí Xuán, the heaven of the Great Origin.
"Báiyù Shàng Jīng"
Mount Lú
Mount Lú emerges from the capital of the Son of Heaven,
also called the Son of Heaven's Barrier.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas
records its ancient name as the Three Barrier Mountains of the Son of Heaven.
The Collection of Dongxuan
calls it the Southern Barrier Mountain in antiquity.
The Records of Commanderies and States
states that during King Wǔ of Zhōu's time,
Master Fāng Fǔ and Lǐ Lǎo rode a white donkey into the mountain to refine elixirs,
achieved the Way and ascended as immortals,
leaving only their hut behind.
Hence it was named Mount Lú.
The Records of Jiǔwēi
notes that Mount Fǔ
is actually Mount Lú.
The Ancient and Modern Records of Yùzhāng
relates that during the transition from the Shāng to Zhōu dynasties,
Master Kuāng Sú received the Way from an immortal and roamed this mountain together,
so people of the time called his dwelling the immortal's hut,
thus naming it Mount Kuānglú.
Huìshī's Mountain Records
say that Kuāng,
styled Zǐxiào,
lived during King Wǔ of Zhōu's era.
Born with divine intelligence,
he dwelled in a hut on this mountain,
later transformed into an immortal,
leaving his empty hut still standing.
The world called him Lord Lú,
so the mountain was named Mount Lú.
Zhōu Jǐngshì's Mountain Records
record that King Wěiliè sent a carriage to welcome Kuāng,
who then continuously ascended as an immortal,
with only his hut remaining.
Thus, the mountain was named Mount Jìnglú.
The locals called it Mount Kuāng after the master's surname,
also known as Kuāngfù.
Xiè Hào's Stele of the Guǎngfú Temple
states that Kuāng,
styled Jūnxiào,
had a father, the Prince of Dōngyě,
who together with the magistrate of Xúnyáng, Wú Ruì,
assisted the Hàn in pacifying the realm but perished.
The Hàn enfeoffed Sú in Xúnyáng,
calling it Yuèlú.
The lord and his six brothers,
all fond of Daoist arts,
then settled their essence on the mountains of Dòngtíng,
hence the world called it Mount Lú.
When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn toured south,
he enfeoffed Sú as the Duke of Dàmíng.
The Old Records of Yùzhāng
and the Biography of Cáo Zhù in the Records of Broad Knowledge note:
The mountain spirit claimed the surname Xú,
was enfeoffed on Mount Lú.
Later, when Wú Měng passed by the mountain,
the spirit greeted him.
Měng said:
"You, lord, have ruled this mountain
for nearly six hundred years;
your mandate has expired,
it is not fitting to remain long."
Not according to
the Water Classic,
Mount Lú is the mountain of Péngzé.
Though not counted among the Five Sacred Mountains,
its lofty and towering peaks
truly make it a renowned mountain of extreme height.
Wáng Biāozhī's Rhapsody Preface
says south of Xúnyáng Commandery lies Mount Lú,
the guardian mountain of the Jiǔjiāng region.
It overlooks the marsh of Pénglí,
bordering a flat and open plain.
Sūn Fàng's Rhapsody
describes the mountain as square in shape,
circuit over four hundred lǐ,
with layered, majestic cliffs,
ten thousand rèn high, embracing numinousness,
and harboring various immortals.
Traces
in the Mountain Atlas
show its lofty peaks reaching extreme heights,
blocking the light of the stars,
with deep, clear ravines,
accumulating purity a hundred rèn deep.
Barriers of repeated perils
make it inaccessible to human travelers;
its secluded and harmonious depths
often contain mist and store ethereal energy.
Truly it can be called a divine realm,
a garden for the perfected ones.
Zhàn Fāngshēng's Preface to the Poem on Immortals
states Mount Lú
is the famous peak of Jiāngyáng,
its grand form
backs the Mín River,
faces Pénglí,
with deep roots spanning
hundreds of lǐ,
and ranges of steep barriers.
It pierces the clouds and sun above,
overlooking the flows of rivers and lakes below.
Fú Tāo's Preface to Mountain Travels
says Mount Lú
embodies the virtue of the southern land.
Though its forests and rocks vary in form,
they share the hues of clouds and mist.
Looking east to Hóngjǐng,
one recognizes the site where silk was trailed.
Gazing west at the Stone Bridge,
one sees treasures that can be gathered.
Liáng Yuándì's Stele Preface
describes its clear and bright mountains and rivers,
pure and vast winds and marshes,
refreshing air and harmonious seasons,
fertile land and content people.
Noble recluses
echo in the caves and cliffs.
Worthy ones, like hidden dragons and phoenixes,
forget to return once they go.
Qín Shǐhuáng, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
and the Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān
all ascended its cliffs,
gazing upon the Jiǔjiāng and overlooking Zhōng Péng.
The Water Classic
calls Mount Lú a famed mountain, a celestial realm for chanting the true.
The Inner Biography of Master Máo
says south of Mount Lú,
there is the high cliff of Shàngxiāo Stone,
soaring distantly to connect with the heavens.
In the thirty-sixth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
he marveled at the mountain's remoteness,
thus recording it as Shàngxiāo.
South of Shàngxiāo,
Great Yǔ carved stones,
marking their dimensions and distances,
and the name "carved stone" remains to this day.
The Water Classic
says the peak rises seven thousand rèn above the plain,
with ancient traces stating:
this was where Xià Yǔ, during his flood control,
moored his boat,
drilling holes in the rock
to tie the cables.
He polished the cliff into a stele,
with all text in ancient seal script,
faintly visible.
Jade Hall Anecdotes
note southeast lies Incense Burner Peak,
a solitary peak uniquely elegant,
emerging with wandering mists enveloping it.
Above, vapors rise like incense smoke;
white clouds reflect outside,
making it strikingly distinct from other peaks.
Before rain,
water vapor surges below like carriage covers,
emanating from the Dragon Well.
Huì Yuǎn's Mountain Records
say southwest is Stone Gate Mountain,
with a faint gate shape between two cliffs,
hence the name.
A waterfall cascades down,
with red and green hues interweaving brilliantly.
Xiè Língyùn's Records of Famous Mountains Traveled
notes a pond atop Mount Lú,
with three stones in it;
when geese frost falls, they fly.
North of the mountain are the Five Old Men Peaks,
the most precipitous of Mount Lú,
stretching across the azure sky,
with jagged, piled rocks,
looming over Pénglí.
Their shape resembles the five old men before Yúxiāng County in Hézhōng,
hence the name.
The Records of Xúnyáng
mention Lǐ Tàibái's study lies below the peaks.
Sāngōng
Sēng Jǐng,
a native of Xiāngxiāng in Héngyáng.
During the Yǒngmíng era, he dreamed of the deity of Lúshān,
who said:
"Lúshān stands as a great peak,
soaring steeply to the heavens.
Here, three palaces rise like walls,
looming thousands of ren high yet appearing to bend,
where true immortals dwell."
He also dreamed of accepting an invitation and journeying to the summit of Xiānglú Peak's Stone Gate,
where he saw silver towers and golden pavilions,
cinnabar springs and jade trees,
rare sights in the world.
Later, he shook his monk's staff and ascended the peak,
finding it exactly as seen in his dream.
"Yú Xī's Account of Master Jǐng's Conduct, from the Guang Hong Ming Collection"
Qúnyù
The Son of Heaven journeyed north and returned eastward,
arriving at the Qúnyù Mountains.
Level and without peril,
the four chariot tracks aligned as if measured by a string,
this was what the former kings called the Repository of Bamboo Slips,
sparse in plants and trees, devoid of birds and beasts.
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven took three chariot-loads of jade,
jade vessels and ceremonial objects,
loading ten thousand pieces of jade.
The Son of Heaven rested at the Qúnyù Mountains,
then ordered Marquis Xíng to find jade workers.
"The Biography of King Mù of Zhōu"
Spring Mountains
King Mù ascended the northern peak of Chūnshān,
gazing upon the four wildernesses,
calling it Chūnshān.
This is the highest mountain under heaven,
what former kings called Xuánpǔ,
where hundreds of beasts gather,
and flying birds congregate.
Here dwell red leopards,
white tigers,
crows,
and blue eagles,
hunting dogs and sheep,
feeding on boars and deer.
King Mù surveyed from Chūnshān's heights,
then inscribed his traces upon Xuánpǔ,
to instruct later generations.
"The Biography of King Mù"
Shānhǎi Zhù calls it Zhōngshān.
Yǎnshān
On the jiazi day, the Son of Heaven was a guest of the Queen Mother of the West.
He then took a white jade scepter and a black jade disc,
to meet the Queen Mother of the West.
The Queen Mother of the West bowed twice and accepted them.
On the yichou day, the Son of Heaven feasted,
the Queen Mother of the West above the Jasper Lake.
The Queen Mother of the West sang a ballad for the Son of Heaven, saying:
"White clouds are in the celestial mountains,
emerging from the paths, the journey is long through mountains and rivers.
If you, my lord, do not die,
may you still be able to return."
The Son of Heaven replied to her, saying:
"I shall return to the eastern lands,
bring harmony and order to the various Xia states,
so that the myriad people are equal and balanced.
I will look forward to seeing you again.
Wait until three years have passed,
I shall return to your wilderness."
The Son of Heaven then drove his chariot and ascended Mount Yǎn.
He recorded his traces on the stones of Mount Yǎn,
and planted a locust tree at the brow,
naming it "The Mountain of the Queen Mother of the West."
"The Biography of King Mu of Zhōu"
Annotation:
This is Mount Yǎnzī.
"The Great Tradition of Yǔ" says:
The waters of Juānpán flow from Mount Yǎnzī.
"Lí Sāo" states:
Gaze upon Yǎnzī but do not press forward.
Mount Tàiháng and Mount Wūwū
The two mountains measured seven hundred li square,
and were ten thousand ren high.
The Foolish Old Man of the North Mountain,
who was nearly ninety years old,
dwelt facing the mountains.
He was troubled by the mountains blocking the north,
and the circuitous routes for coming and going,
so he planned to level them.
The Wise Old Man of the River Bend tried to stop him but couldn't.
The god who held snakes,
hearing of this, feared he would not cease,
reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor, moved by his sincerity,
ordered the two sons of Kuā'é
to carry the two mountains away:
one was placed east of Shuò,
the other south of Yōng.
From then on,
south of Jì and north of Hàn,
there were no more mountain barriers.
“Liezi”
The Son of Heaven commanded a chariot drawn by eight steeds,
a team of red thoroughbreds,
with Zàofǔ as the driver,
traveling southward in flight,
cutting straight through the Dí road,
ascending the Tàiháng,
crossing the river southward,
galloping a thousand li,
and finally entering the ancestral Zhōu.
“The Biography of King Mù”
Zhōnghuáng Bó said:
“I hold the prowess of Tàiháng in my left hand,
and with my right grasp the carved tiger, only the elephant remains,
to test it against my heart.
Those with strength then wish to be oxen,
desiring to test themselves against the elephant;
now you few consider it righteous.
How then shall we test it?”
Poverty is the ape of Tàiháng,
neglect and lowliness the carved tiger of righteousness.
And it is said:
encountering it is enough for a test.
“Shizi”
The essence of Tàiháng's attached road.
Charts and weft texts descended as images,
King Wǔ, having overcome Yīn, wished
to build a palace on the mountain of the Five Elements.
Now Tàiháng Mountain,
the Duke of Zhōu said:
“It cannot be.”
For the mountain of the Five Elements
is a place of solid barriers and perilous obstacles.
“Huáinánzǐ”
Wángwū was originally the Héyáng Mountain in Jìzhōu.
Ancient and modern place names,
the mountain's shape
resembles a wall.
“Bówù Jì”
Wángwū Mountain,
is called the Small Existence, Clear and Void Grotto-Heaven.
Tàiháng, the folded mountain, serves as its佐命 (assisting mandate),
Zhōngtiáo, the ancient bell, acts as its辅翼 (supporting wings).
Of the thirty-six grottoes,
Small Existence is the foremost among the grottoes;
of the forty-nine mountains,
Wángwū is the highest among the significant mountains;
truly it is the spiritual land of immortality,
the grotto realm of the Perfected.
“Xiān Jīng”
Wángwū Mountain,
is a separate heaven for immortals,
what is called the Solar Terrace.
Those who first attain the Way,
all go to the Solar Terrace,
which is the palace of clarity and void.
The Lady of the Southern Peak said:
“Tomorrow I shall go to the Clear and Void Palace of Wángwū.”
“Zhēn Gào”
Tiānmù
Lǎo Zǐ said he wished to cross south,
to avoid the flood disaster.
Tiānmù Hǎilíng Mountain is considered the foremost.
"Universal Geography" records:
Tiānmù Mountain has extremely lofty peaks,
on which there is a very beautiful spring,
to the southeast there is a waterfall,
pouring down over several acres.
"Wúxīng Records" states:
Tiānmù has two peaks,
each peak top has a pond,
left and right facing each other like Heaven's left and right eyes.
"Yuánhé Geographical Records":
Guō Pú of the Jìn dynasty wrote in his "Qiántáng Tiānmù Mountain Poem":
Before Tiānmù Mountain stretch two long breasts,
dragon flies and phoenix dances reaching Qiántáng.
At Hǎimén a point, the Xùn peak rises,
within five hundred years emperors will emerge.
When Emperor Gāozōng restored the dynasty and founded the state,
Tiānmù was the sovereign mountain.
By the Jiǎxū year of Emperor Dùzōng, the mountain collapsed,
the capital city was in turmoil,
and there were proposals to move the imperial seat.
Not long after,
the Sòng dynasty's cauldron was thus moved.
Someone composed a poem saying:
Before Tiānmù Mountain, water gnaws at the rocks,
the heart of heaven and veins of earth reveal hidden crisis.
Western Zhōu grows cold, the goblet moves with the moon,
not necessarily was the move to Qí said in vain.
"Ancient Hángzhōu Miscellany":
In the past, someone climbed the north of Tiānmù Mountain,
encountered rain and saw clouds and mist at the mountain's waist,
the thunder sounded like an infant's cry.
"Leisure Readings from the Retreat Studio":
Tiānmù Mountain has thirty-six caves,
every autumn there must be one month of wind, rain, and darkness,
local custom says:
this is the mountain god meeting with the river god.
"Illustrated Classics":
Though there are many mountains,
none compare to Tiānmù in greatness,
its height,
is thirty-nine thousand chǐ in total.
Looking up at the great void—
sun and moon appear low.
Standing on the absolute summit—
heaven and earth feel narrow.
"Táng Háng Capital Rhapsody"
Yuán Tiān
È Yì's servant,
Yǔ Yīn Yì's grandson,
and È Shì's son,
three scholars conspired together.
They brought people before the Creator,
ascending together to the peak of Yuántiān.
Yuántiān,
its height reveals four constellations.
Sīmǎ Biāo said:
"Yuántiān is a mountain's name."
Zhuāngzǐ
Yán Yánnián's poem:
"Yuántiān high in the northern constellations."
Shālù
In autumn, the eighth month, on Xīnmǎo day, Shālù collapsed.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn, fourteenth year:
A historian of Jìn divined about it and said:
"Yin forms a mound for yang,
Earth and Fire act upon each other,
Hence there was the collapse of Shālù.
After six hundred and forty-five years,
There should be a sage woman rising in Qítián, should there not?"
The Hàn Yuánhòu Zhuàn.
Kǒngzǐshān
One hundred lǐ east of Huángzhōu is Kǒngzǐ Mountain,
traditionally said to be where Confucius traveled to Chǔ,
and once climbed this mountain.
Atop it is a sitting stone,
untouched by plants and trees,
and an inkstone rock.
Whenever it rains,
ink appears to soak out from it.
Twenty lǐ north of the city is Xiǎoqí Mountain,
on which lies a "flown-in" stone,
and below it stands a stone pillar.
When pushed, it can rotate without falling.
From "Shānchuān Jìyì" (Records of Extraordinary Mountains and Rivers)
Shàn Shān
Hélǘ went out and entered, roaming and resting,
in autumn and winter he governed from within the city,
in spring and summer he governed from outside the city,
administering the Gūsū Tower.
He ate morning meal at Qiūshān,
and roamed by day at Sū Tower.
He shot arrows at Ōubēi,
and galloped at Yóu Tower.
He enjoyed pleasures at Shíchéng,
and coursed hounds at Chángzhōu.
"Annals of Wú and Yuè"
Yè Quán
Traveling west along the river to pay homage at Quánshān,
also known as Yǐnquánshān,
the mountain contains a stone chamber,
which was the retreat of Zǐxià.
According to the Suí Geographical Records,
at Quánshān, it is customary to pray for rain or clear weather depending on the season;
supplications made here receive responses,
hence the mountain derives its name.
The mountain features perilous rocky cliffs and treacherous terrain,
with sheer walls naturally fortified like heaven's ramparts,
adorned with layered pines decorating the crags,
and rows of cypress trees offering elegant views.
The Water Classic
Hǔqiū
Tiger Hill was originally named Sea Surging Mountain.
Wáng Pò's inscription
states that when Hé Lǘ died,
he was buried northwest of the state,
and it was named Tiger Hill.
They dug through earth to create waterways,
and piled up soil to form a hill.
Laborers were summoned from five capitals,
with one hundred thousand people working together on the project.
Elephants were brought from a thousand miles away
to carry soil for the tomb mound and pool,
which was surrounded by water over ten feet deep.
The outer coffin had three layers,
and liquid mercury was poured to form a pool,
with the pool spanning sixty paces wide.
Golden ducks and geese were crafted from gold, pearls, and jade,
along with Biǎnzhū swords
and three thousand Yúcháng swords placed therein.
Three days after the burial,
a metallic essence rose upward,
transforming into a white tiger guarding the tomb,
hence the name Tiger Hill.
"Records of the States of Wú and Yuè"
Tiger Hill's peaks soar above steep cliffs and deep ravines,
with dense forests and thick bamboo groves,
making it a model of hills and valleys east of the Yangtze River.
Chǔ Yuān, Governor of Wúxīng,
once traveled to report on his duties
and passed through the territory of Wú.
He lingered for several days
but felt his visits were insufficient.
He sighed and said, "What is praised today
often exceeds reality.
But viewing Tiger Hill now,
it surpasses what I had heard."
"Wáng Sēngqián's Records of the Wú Region"
A magnificently beautiful famous mountain,
a scenic wonderland of Great Wú.
"Gù Yětǔ's Preface to the Mountain"
Among the three rivers and five lakes,
and the vast beauty of Dòngtíng,
the most outstanding and exquisite
is truly the divine mound of Tiger Hill.
Shěn Jiǒng's "Reply to Zhāng Zhǒng's Letter"
Wú Shān
On Wúshān in Hángzhōu,
the people of Wú, pitying Wǔ Zǐxū for dying in remonstrance, erected a shrine for him,
which was also named Xūshān.
To its left lies the great river,
to its right overlooks West Lake,
making it a scenic highlight of the entire prefecture.
According to the "Records of Commanderies and States,"
when the Jīn ruler Liàng was about to invade the south,
he secretly hid painters among his envoys,
ordering them to sketch the lakes and mountains of Lín'ān.
Upon returning, he had them made into a screen with his own portrait,
depicting him galloping his horse atop the summit of Wúshān,
and inscribed a poem on it:
it contained the line, "Halting my steed on Wúshān's foremost peak."
"Historical Records"
Guài Shān
The King of Yuè intended to build city walls,
Fàn Lǐ then observed celestial phenomena,
modeling them after the Purple Palace.
They constructed a small city,
and once the city was completed, a strange mountain spontaneously arose,
east of Lángyá,
in the sea of Wǔ.
It arrived overnight,
startling the common people,
hence it was named Guàishān (Strange Mountain).
"Annals of Wú and Yuè"
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic" states:
it flew here and settled,
crushing and killing several hundred households.
It is also said:
King Wújiāng of Yuè,
being attacked by Chǔ,
departed from Lángyá and stopped.
People from Dōngwǔ followed and settled at the mountain's base,
and from afar, looking at this mountain,
its shape resembled a turtle,
so it also gained the name Guīshān (Turtle Mountain).
Yuè erected a spiritual terrace on the mountain,
and also built a three-story tower,
to observe clouds and phenomena;
the rivers and land were bright and beautiful,
making it a scenic spot as well.
Thus Wáng Yìshǎo said:
traveling along the Shānyīn road,
is like walking in a mirror.
"Waterways Classic"
Sān Shén Shān
Qí Wēi, Xuān, and Yān Zhāo
sent people to sea to seek Pénglái,
Fāngzhàng,
and Yíngzhōu.
These three divine mountains,
according to legend, are in the Bó Sea.
They are not far from people,
but when trouble is about to arrive,
the ships are blown away by the wind,
though there have been those who reached them,
where all the immortals and the elixir of immortality reside.
All the creatures and animals there are entirely white,
and the palaces are made of gold and silver.
Before reaching them,
they appear like clouds from a distance.
Upon arrival,
the three divine mountains instead lie beneath the water.
When approaching them,
the wind always blows one away,
so ultimately, no one can reach them.
It is said.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
To the east of the Bó Sea, there is a great abyss,
within which are five mountains:
Dàiyù,
Yuánqiáo,
Fānghú,
Yíngzhōu,
and Pénglái.
Their towers and pavilions are all of gold and jade.
The inhabitants are all of immortal and sage descent.
The roots of the five mountains are unanchored,
constantly rising and falling with the tides,
unable to remain stable.
The immortals and sages complained to the Emperor,
who, angered, exiled them to the western extreme,
commanding Yù
and Yùqiáng to dispatch fifteen giant sea turtles
to lift their heads and support them,
so the five mountains finally stood firm.
"Questions of Tāng"
Xú Fú and others from Qí submitted a memorial saying:
"In the sea, there are three divine mountains,
named Pénglái,
Fāngzhàng,
and Yíngzhōu,
where immortals dwell.
We request to fast and purify ourselves,
and with young boys and girls, seek them out."
Thereupon, Xú Fú was dispatched,
mobilizing several thousand young boys and girls,
to go to sea in search of the immortals.
"Qín Annals"
Dōngfāng Shuò's inscription on the precious urn says:
"Precious clouds arise from the dew altar,
auspicious winds stir in the moon pavilion,
viewing the three hú as if a foot in size,
gazing upon the eight hóng as if a sash.
The three hú
are the three mountains in the sea.
One is called Fānghú,
which is Fāngzhàng.
The second is called Liánhú,
which is Pénglái.
The third is called Yínghú,
which is Yíngzhōu.
These three mountains are shaped like urn vessels.
The eight hóng
refer to the eight directions,
hóng meaning vast.
Ascending the moon pavilion to gaze upon the four seas,
the three mountains appear like gathered rice or a winding sash.
"Records of Gleanings"
Pénglái is also known as Fángqiū,
and alternatively as Yúnlái.
Fāngzhàng is also called Luánzhì.
Yíngzhōu is also known as Húnzhōu,
and alternatively as Huánzhōu.
Yuánqiáo is also called Huánqiū.
Above
Sānfēng
East of King Yān's Immortal Terrace stand three peaks,
extremely lofty and precipitous.
Soaring clouds crown their summits,
while high-lying mists flank the ridges.
Gorges and ravines plunge deep,
shrouded in converging haze and fog.
The Records of the Elderly states this was where King Zhāo of Yān sought immortality.
The Classic of Waterways
Yù Sì
To the left of Qūtán lies the Yùsì Mountain,
where Qū Píng was exiled and dwelt upon this mountain,
and composed the "Nine Songs" here.
According to the "Zhēnliè Xiāngzhōng Jì":
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, fond of immortality, at Yùsì Mountain,
set up a Zhēnxiān Altar on its summit,
with a grand elixir furnace.
Taoist priests prayed day and night,
and Heaven, moved by their sincerity,
descended a white jade case to place upon the altar.
Emperor Wǔ dispatched an envoy to retrieve it,
but upon reaching the altar's side,
a fierce whirlwind arose,
sweeping the jade case away.
Hence, it became known as Yùsì Mountain.
From the "Yùsì Shān Lù"
Wūshān
The Great Wūshān is not only unmatched in the Three Gorges,
but also rivals the peaks of Mín and É,
and stands shoulder to shoulder with Héng and Yí.
Its surrounding mountains,
all reaching the azure clouds,
can only be distinguished by their heights near the heavens.
Stretching one hundred and sixty lǐ from end to end,
it is called the Wū Gorge,
named after the mountain.
The "Shuǐ Jīng" records:
When King Xiāng of Chǔ and Sòng Yù were traveling in the wilderness of Yúnmèng,
they saw a mist over the Morning Cloud Pavilion,
which changed endlessly in an instant.
The king asked:
"What kind of mist is this?"
Sòng Yù replied:
"Long ago, the former king traveled to Gāotáng,
and, weary, took a nap by day.
He dreamed of a woman who said:
'I am the youngest daughter of the Heavenly Emperor,
named Yáo Jī.
I died before I could marry,
and was enshrined on the terrace of Wūshān.
My essence transformed into a plant,
which is the sacred lingzhī mushroom.
I am the so-called maiden of Wūshān,
the lady of Gāotáng. Hearing of your arrival,
I wish to share my bed with you.'
The king then lay with her, and as she departed,
she said: 'I dwell on the sunny side of Wūshān,
amid the heights and ridges.
At dawn, I am the morning clouds;
at dusk, the passing rain.
Morning after morning, dusk after dusk,
I am beneath the Sun Terrace.'
At dawn, when he looked,
it was indeed as she had said.
He built a pavilion for her there,
named Morning Clouds."
The "Collection of Sòng Yù"
lists the twelve peaks as:
Dawn Glow Peak,
Jade Screen Peak,
Morning Cloud Peak,
Pine-Clad Peak,
Immortals' Gathering Peak,
Cranes' Assembly Peak,
Pure Altar Peak,
Ascending Peak,
Rising Clouds Peak,
Soaring Phoenix Peak,
Dragon Ascent Peak,
Sacred Spring Peak.
Wǔdān
A man from Wǔdū transformed into a woman,
with exceptionally beautiful features,
likely a mountain spirit.
The King of Shǔ took her as his consort,
but she passed away shortly after.
Grieving for her,
the king sent Wǔ Dīng to Wǔdū
to carry earth and build a tomb for the consort,
covering several acres of land,
and standing seven zhàng high,
named Wǔdān.
A stone mirror was crafted
to mark her grave,
and the stone is commonly known today as Shísǔn.
"Records of the Kings of Shǔ & Chronicles of Huáyáng"
Wú Shān
The sacred mountain of Yōngzhōu is called Wúyuè.
The "Zhōulǐ"
and the Guóyǔ refer to it as Western Wú,
in ancient texts it is considered Qiān Mountain,
and when Qín established its capital at Xiányáng, it was regarded as the Western Peak.
The "Hàn Geographical Records"
also name it Wúyuè,
while Mǎ Róng wrote it as Kāi Mountain
in his commentaries.
Mount Wú has three peaks,
rising elegantly as if lifted by rosy clouds,
with precipitous cliffs that seem to collapse into the clouds,
yet when viewed from the mountaintop, they appear to support each other,
always giving a sense of impending fall.
The "Shuǐjīng"
Qín Wàng
Kuàijī Qínwàng Shān:
It is the most outstanding among all peaks,
visible upon entering the region.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
Qín Shǐhuáng ascended it to gaze upon the South Sea,
from the flat land to the mountain's summit spanning seven ridges,
the path solitary, perilous, steep, and extremely treacherous.
It is recorded:
one must cling to vines and grasp creepers,
only then can one ascend the mountain.
There are no tall trees on the summit,
likely due to the exposed terrain and frequent winds.
South of the mountain lies Jiāoxiàn,
within the xiàn is a large city,
the old capital of King Wúyú of Yuè.
Above
Sìmíng
Sì Míng is famously called Dān Shān,
the heaven of Chì Shuǐ,
on which there are four cave openings,
channeling the light of the sun, moon, and stars,
hence the name Sì Míng.
During the Qín dynasty, when mountains were driven and seas blocked,
ghosts and spirits were forced into labor,
fleeing into the Sì Míng caves and never emerging,
thus it was named Guǐ Cáng Shān.
Its summit features five extremely high peaks,
shaped like lotus flowers.
Liáng Cháng
Qín Shǐhuáng ascended the northern ridge of Jūqǔ and sighed, saying:
"The joy of imperial tours
surpasses not that of mountains and seas.
From now on,
Liángcháng shall be the constant practice."
His assembled ministers joined in offering congratulations and exclaimed:
"Liángcháng shall indeed be constant!"
Thereupon, he renamed the northern ridge of Jūróng as Mount Liángcháng.
"Records of Jīnlíng"
Dà Hé
In Jūyōng County there are Great Wing
and Little Wing Mountains,
whose lofty peaks pierce the clouds,
whose layered ridges cleave the mist,
twin hills sharing splendor,
competitively rising above all other peaks.
A county man named Wáng Cìzhòng showed unusual ambition from youth,
and upon reaching capping age,
transformed Cāngjié's ancient script into the modern clerical script.
During Qín Shǐhuáng's reign, official duties were numerous and complex;
because the script modified by Cìzhòng
simplified essential matters,
the emperor found it remarkable and summoned him.
Thrice summoned, he consistently refused to come.
Cìzhòng walked in truth and embraced the Way,
exhausting the beauties of numerology.
The First Emperor grew angry at his disrespect
and ordered him sent in a caged cart.
As Cìzhòng journeyed,
he suddenly transformed into a great bird and flew out of the cart,
soaring away,
dropping two wings upon these mountains.
Hence the peaks bear the names Great and Little Wing.
"Commentary on the Water Classic"
Cìzhòng concealed his arts,
hid his arts from the First Emperor of Qín,
dropped
twin wings
and soared to heaven.
"Yáng Gù's Rhapsody on the Northern Capital"
The Mountain-Dispelling Bell
In the Yíchūn area, at Zhōng Mountain,
there is a gorge several dozen lǐ long,
its waters being the Yíchūn River.
Winding, clear, and deep beyond measure,
once a fisherman, while angling, caught a golden lock,
pulled it up several hundred feet, and retrieved a bell,
shaped like a duó.
As the fisherman lifted it,
a sound like thunder roared through the sky,
darkening the day and obscuring the mountains and rivers,
shaking Zhōng Mountain,
causing one side to collapse over five hundred zhàng,
and the fishermen all sank with their boats into the water.
The collapsed part of the mountain appears as if sliced smooth,
remaining so to this day.
Some who know of it say:
This is the very duó that Qín Shǐ Huáng used to drive the mountains.
"Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Jùshén Shān
In Móuzhōu there is Jùshén Mountain,
located five lǐ east of the prefecture.
When the First Emperor attempted to quarry stones to build a bridge,
this mountain resisted and would not yield,
hence it was named accordingly.
Four lǐ south of the mountain,
there is a yellow silver mine.
From "Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks"
Bāsù
The Bāsù Mountain is located east of Wǔyì County in Dōngyáng.
The "Record of Mountains and Rivers" states:
At the end of the Qín dynasty, eight scholars came to live in seclusion
here, hence the name.
Wǔ Lǐng
To the north, the Qín dynasty undertook the construction of the Great Wall,
while to the south, it established garrisons at the Five Ridges.
The Book of Hàn
records that the Five Ridges begin with Dàyǔ Ridge,
followed by Ānlínhè,
Guìyáng,
and Jiēyáng.
The Guǎngzhōu Records
state that Dàyǔ Ridge,
also known as Sài Ridge,
is called Sàishàng as well.
In the fourth year of the Yuándǐng era of Emperor Wǔ,
Lǚ Jiā, the chancellor of Nányuè, killed the Hàn general Hán Qiānqiū,
and placed the sealed credentials of the Hàn envoy at Sàishàng,
which refers to this ridge.
The Nánkāng Records say:
When the Hàn troops attacked, Lǚ Jiā's forces collapsed,
and there was
a supervising commander surnamed Yǔ
who fortified this ridge; due to his surname Yǔ, it was thus called Dàyǔ Ridge.
Additionally, because it abounds with plum trees that bloom early,
it is also known as Méi Ridge.
The Hǎilù
records ancient sayings:
The Five Ridges
are what Heaven and Earth used to separate the inner and outer realms,
stretching continuously to the sea.
Gazing upon the nine ridges from afar, they appear vast and remote,
no longer mere paths through rugged terrain,
truly a dark and desolate frontier land.
The Water Classic
Máoshān
Mount Jūqū,
known in the Qin dynasty as the Heaven of Huáyáng,
was inhabited by the Three Lords Máo,
hence the name derived from them.
Outer Jīnshān was named after its altar,
while during the Zhou dynasty, its marshland source
was called the Cave of Jūqū.
Due to the mountain's winding and twisting shape,
later generations named it Mount Jūqū.
Within the mountain lies the land of Jīnlíng,
covering forty-seven to forty-eight qǐng,
which is the lung of the earth in Jīntán.
Those who dwell in this land are destined to transcend the mortal world.
"The Inner Biography of Lord Máo"
records that the cave heaven of Jūqū connects east to Línwū,
north to Dàizōng,
west to Éméi,
and south to Luófú.
"The Declarations of the Perfected"
states that Mount Jūqū is deep and winding,
capable of containing within,
thus it was called the Hamlet of Jūróng.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Fāngshān
Northwest of Húshú there is Fāngshān,
whose summit is perfectly square,
with a pond on its top.
The Yǔdìzhì records:
"The mountain's shape is square like a seal,
hence it is called Fāngshān,
also known as Tiānyìn Shān."
The Dānyáng Jì states:
"During the reign of Qín Shǐhuáng,
those who observed celestial omens reported:
'East of the river, there is an imperial aura.'
The emperor therefore traveled east to suppress it,
and further excavated Jīnlíng to sever its energy.
The current stone ridge at Fāngshān
marks the very place that was cut through."
The Yǔdìzhì records.
Yǒuyáng
Mount Xiǎoyǒu,
within its stone cavern lies a collection of a thousand scrolls,
traditionally said to have been left behind by people of the Qin dynasty who studied here.
Hence, Prince Xiāngdōng of Liáng remarked:
"It is here that one seeks the lost classics of Yǒuyáng."
Records of Jīngzhōu
The Zhōngnán
and Jīng Mountains,
are the perilous peaks of the nine provinces in central China.
The Zuǒzhuàn states:
Zhōngnán is also called Zhōngnán,
meaning it lies at the center of the heavens
and south of the capital.
The Guānzhōng Jì records:
Tàiyī is located in the Lí Mountains,
the most elegant of the western hills.
It is also named the Dìfèi Mountain,
capable of avoiding floods.
The Sānqín Jì notes:
Even the Mèngmén and Zhōnglóng Mountains
could not hold it back.
Annotation:
Zhōnglóng
refers to Zhōngnán.
Huáinánzǐ states:
In Wǔgōng County of Fúfēng,
there is Mount Tàiyī,
known in ancient texts as Zhōngnán.
The Hàn Geography Treatise records:
During the Qin era, the Four Haos
together entered Shāngluò to hide in the Dìfèi Mountains,
awaiting the stabilization of the realm.
When the Qin fell, Emperor Gāo of Han heard of them and summoned them,
but they did not come.
They deeply concealed themselves in the Zhōngnán Mountains,
unwilling to bend their principles.
The Gāoshì Zhuàn recounts:
When Lú Cángyòng first lived in seclusion,
he possessed a steadfast and perilous integrity,
traveling between the Shàoshì
and Zhōngnán Mountains.
He was called the "imperial carriage hermit" by contemporaries.
Later, upon joining the court, he wavered and became deceitful,
serving only the powerful.
When the Daoist priest Sīmǎ Zǐwēi returned to Tiāntāi Mountain,
officials bid him farewell, and Cángyòng,
pointing to Zhōngnán Mountain, said:
"There are excellent spots here;
why go to Tiāntāi?"
Zǐwēi replied:
"From my perspective,
this is merely a shortcut to officialdom."
Cángyòng showed a ashamed expression.
The Old Táng History records:
According to the "Ode to the Western Capital":
Zhōngnán and Tàiyī have lofty caves,
and Cuī Zú's "Ode to the Western Campaign"
faces Zhōngnán with its back to Yúnyáng,
spanning the plains and connecting to Pánzhǒng.
Jiǔzōng, Mièniè, and Tàiyī
are towering, while Zhōngnán
and Tàiyī are not the same mountain.
The Yuánhé Zhì states:
Zhōngnán is the general name for the southern mountains,
and Tàiyī is a specific name for one peak.
The Five Classics Essentials notes:
According to records:
the Four Haos first hid in Dìfèi
and later concealed themselves in Zhōngnán.
Thus, Dìfèi
and Zhōngnán
are also not the same mountain.
Celestial Steps
At the foot of Tiānjiē Mountain in Jiānglè County,
there is Bǎohuá Cave,
which is the place where Chìsōngzǐ gathered herbs.
Inside the cave are stone swallows,
stone bats,
a stone chamber,
stone pillars,
along with a stone mortar,
and a stone well.
It is commonly said:
this well
connects southward to the stream in Shāxiàn,
and there is also a milky spring dripping from above.
People who drink it
and climb to the mountain peak
feel as if ascending to the azure heavens,
hence the name Tiānjiē (Heavenly Stairs).
"Jiàn'ān Jì"
Solitary Cloud, Twin Peaks
South of Xìngyuán, there is a road leading to Bāzhōu,
with deep ravines and steep cliffs.
Clutching vines and groping over rocks,
it takes three days to reach the mountain summit.
Then one ascends Cuòdà Ridge,
which is a relatively flat area.
Its highest peak is called Gūyún Liǎngjiǎo,
and a local proverb says:
"Gūyún Liǎngjiǎo is a hand's breadth from heaven."
There stands the temple of Huáixīn Hóu.
Long ago, when Hán Xìn fled,
Xiāo Hé caught up with him at this mountain.
Wáng Rényù wrote a poem that says:
"Lone clouds cannot conceal strategies of rise and fall,
Two peaks once hung between decisions to leave or stay."
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Mount Bāgōng
At Shòuchūn's Bāgōng Mountain,
the mountain had no trees,
only layered mounds.
On the mountain stood the temple of Huáinán King Liú Ān,
who humbled himself to receive scholars,
ardently loved Confucian learning,
and supported several dozen practitioners of esoteric arts,
all of whom were outstanding talents.
They possessed many secret methods of immortality
and the Way of the Vast Treasure.
Suddenly, eight elders appeared,
all with white beards and eyebrows,
seeking an audience at the gate.
The gatekeeper said:
"Our king seeks eternal life;
since you gentlemen lack the art of halting decay,
I dare not announce you."
The eight elders all transformed into youths,
and the king greatly revered them.
The eight scholars could refine gold and transmute elixirs,
passing through barriers unimpeded.
They then ascended the mountain with Ān,
buried gold in the earth,
and ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Remaining medicine in the vessels,
when licked by chickens and dogs, enabled them to ascend too.
The place from which they ascended
had hoof and footprints sunk into the stones.
Thus the mountain was named after the Eight Elders.
During the Jìn dynasty, Xiè Xuán,
defending against Fú Jiān in the north,
prayed at Bāgōng Mountain.
When deploying troops at the Féi River,
Fú Jiān looked up at the mountain's plants,
all appearing as human figures—
not because the Eight Elders' spirits aided him,
but rather an omen of the Fú clan's impending downfall.
"Water Classic"
Hán Shān
In Qíjùn's Hánshān,
there is a bird with feet,
blue beak,
reddish-yellow,
white wings,
and crimson forehead,
named the Queen Mother's Messenger.
Long ago, when Emperor Wǔ of Hàn ascended this mountain, he obtained a jade box,
five inches long.
As the emperor descended the mountain, the jade box suddenly transformed into a white bird and flew away.
It is traditionally said that on the mountain there is the Queen Mother's medicine box,
constantly guarded by this bird.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Tiāntái
Mount Tiāntāi is
the divine splendor among mountains.
When crossing the sea, there are Fāngzhàng
and Pénglái;
when ascending the land, there are Sìmíng
and Tiāntāi,
all places where mysterious sages roamed,
and where transcendent immortals made their abodes.
"Sūn Chuò's Rhapsody Preface"
In the fifth year of the Yǒngpíng era of Emperor Míng,
Liú Chén
and Ruǎn Zhào from Shàn County
together entered Mount Tiāntāi.
Crossing the mountain, they came upon a great stream;
by the stream were two maidens,
of exquisite beauty beyond compare.
They stayed for half a year before longing for home and seeking to return.
Once they emerged,
their relatives and old friends had scattered and perished,
the villages and houses had changed,
and none recognized them.
Upon inquiry, they met their seventh-generation descendants.
"Yōumíng Lù"
Mount Tiāntāi corresponds to the celestial Tái star,
transcendent and elegantly prominent.
The mountain has eight layers,
appearing as a single sail,
standing eighteen thousand zhàng high,
with a circumference of eight hundred lǐ.
"Línhǎi Jīng"
Mount Tiāntāi
is not far from heaven.
The path follows the Zhūxī stream,
whose waters are perilous, clear, and cold.
Ahead lies a stone bridge,
with a path less than a chǐ wide,
stretching thousands of zhàng long.
Below, it overlooks a bottomless chasm.
Only by forgetting oneself
can one then cross successfully.
Climbing the rocky cliffs and grasping the vines of creepers,
one reaches level ground
and sees Mount Tiāntāi, lush and magnificently arrayed,
with twin peaks piercing the azure sky.
Above are jade towers and gem pavilions,
heavenly halls and emerald groves,
complete with sweet springs and immortal marvels.
The Jin dynasty hermit Bái Dàoyóu once passed through,
obtaining sweet springs, purple fungus, and divine music.
"Qǐméng Jì Zhù"
Mount Chìchéng
is the southern gate of Tiāntāi.
Mount Pùbù
is the southwestern peak of Tiāntāi,
where water cascades from the southern cliffs,
appearing like a draped cloth when viewed.
"Tiāntāi Shān Tú"
The soil of Mount Chìchéng is entirely red;
its layered cliffs and peaks
resemble rosy clouds.
A hanging stream of ten rèn
is called the waterfall,
its flying flow scattering spray,
never drying up in winter or summer.
The mountain valleys and sheer gorges
are precipitous and bottomless,
with tall pines and creeping vines
shrouding them in deep shade.
Within lies the void peak of Tiāntāi,
and immortal chambers with jade terraces.
"Kuàijī Jì"
Mount Chìchéng is also known as the Burnt Mountain.
"Míngshān Lüèjì"
This mountain was formerly called the remnant land of five counties,
the five counties being Yúyáo,
Yín,
Gōu,
Zhāng,
Shàn,
and Shǐníng.
"Kuàijī Jì"
Crossing the Zhūxī stream and advancing directly,
descending through five boundaries in swift journey.
Sūn's Rhapsody:
Mount Tiāntāi has the Bāguì Ridge.
"Dìlǐ Jì"
Mount Báishí,
appearing like snow when viewed,
has a lake on the mountain.
Legend says:
it is where golden geese gather,
and where the eight cinnamon trees are planted.
"Línhǎi Jì"
The eight cinnamon trees stand tall, defying the frost.
"Rhapsody"
Mount Tiāntāi,
blocked by Mount Chìchéng on its path,
and its routes stirred by the waterfall's torrents,
has rocks perilous with moss,
and abysses of unfathomable depth.
"Yì Yuàn"
Yānrán
Dòu Xiàn battled the Chányú at Mount Jīluò,
thoroughly defeating them,
and then ascended Mount Yānrán,
where he carved a stone to record his achievement.
Bān Gù composed an inscription that said:
"We sealed the divine mound,
and erected a lofty monument."
(Book of the Later Hàn)
Zhùshān
Liáng Jì extensively opened up gardens and parks,
excavated earth to build hills,
with ten li and nine slopes,
imitating the Two Xiáo Mountains,
deep forests and steep ravines,
as if naturally formed,
rare birds and tame beasts,
flying and running within them.
"History of the Later Hàn"
Qí Shān
North of the Hàn River, mountains connect continuously,
with elegant peaks standing in rivalry like a row of competitors.
Qí Mountain lies west of Bōzhǒng,
and on the mountain, there is a fortress,
extremely rugged and secure.
In the past, when Zhūgě Liàng attacked Qí Mountain,
it was this very fortress.
The Kāishān Tú states:
Southwest of Hànyáng lies Qí Mountain,
with winding streams and paths,
towering peaks and perilous cliffs,
a famous rugged terrain within the Nine Provinces,
a spectacular steepness under heaven.
《Shuǐ Jīng》
Zhōngshān
Ten li northeast of Jiànkāng lies Zhōngshān,
formerly known as Jīnshān.
In the late Hàn dynasty, the commandant of Jīnlíng,
Jiǎng Zǐwén, died in battle fighting bandits.
His spirit manifested on the mountain,
leading to the establishment of a shrine for Marquis Jiǎng.
Hence it was called Jiǎngshān.
Zhūgě Liàng regarded Zhōngshān as a coiling dragon,
which is Jiǎngshān.
In Xú Yuán's "Explanatory Questions Summary,"
the capital had continuous ridges both north and south,
but Jiǎngshān stood uniquely lofty and steep,
its shape resembling a true dragon,
serving as the guardian mountain of Yángdū.
Sūn Quán was buried south of the mountain,
and it was named after the mountain,
called Sūnlíng.
The "Records of Dānyáng"
state that Jiǎngshān is referred to as Zhōngshān in the "Geographical Maps."
Before Emperor Yuán crossed the river,
those who observed celestial signs said:
Purple clouds appeared over Jiǎngshān,
often seen in the morning.
From Yǔ Chǎn's "Annotation to the Rhapsody of Yángdū,"
Jiǎngshān
was formerly named Jīnlíngshān.
Thus, the name Jīnlíng was established.
The "Geographical Records"
note that during Qín Shǐhuáng's time,
observers of signs reported:
Jīnlíng had an imperial aura,
so gold, jade, and various treasures were buried at Zhōngshān,
and the land was severed,
renaming it Mòlíng.
The "Records of Jīnlíng"
mention that the great emperor's ancestor had the taboo name Zhōng, so it was renamed Jiǎngshān.
The "Records of Wú"
and Xiāo Shìyūn,
in annotating Lǐ Bái's "Song of Jīnlíng," state:
The great emperor built a temple for Zǐwén,
and Zǐwén's ancestor had the taboo name Zhōng,
leading to the change to Jiǎngshān.
The "Unified Records" also say this is incorrect.
Shíchéng
The mountains of Stone City stretch for thousands of li in overlapping ridges,
as if inviting travelers to explore.
It is believed that Stone City of Wú
is comparable to Jiǔyí of Chǔ.
A fortress stands atop the mountain,
hence the name derived from it.
In the sixteenth year of the Jiàn'ān era of the Hàn dynasty,
Sūn Quán of Wú renovated it,
renaming it Stone City.
Its location is west of the present-day Qīngliáng Temple.
According to the "Jiāngchéng Geographical Records,"
Zhūgě Liàng once said to the Great Emperor of Wú:
Mòlíng's terrain,
with Zhōngshān coiling like a dragon
and Stone City crouching like a tiger,
is truly fit for an imperial capital.
Jǐngyáng
In the first year of the Huángchū era,
Emperor Wén increasingly exalted the palace halls,
adorning the towers and pavilions with carvings,
fetching white quartz, purple quartz, and large stones of five colors from the mountains of Tàiháng and Gǔchéng,
he erected Jǐngyáng Mountain in the Fānglín Garden with trees,
pines, bamboos, and various plants,
and captured birds and beasts to fill its grounds.
At that time, numerous labor services flourished,
the emperor personally dug the earth,
leading the three highest ministers and all officials,
so that none below failed to exert their strength.
(From Sūn Shèng's "Wèi Chūnqiū")
Běi Máng
Emperor Míng intended to level Běimáng,
ordering a terrace to be built upon it,
from which one could see Mèngjīn.
Xīn Pí said:
"The nature of heaven and earth
is to have heights and depths.
Now to reverse this
is contrary to its principle,
and moreover involves wasteful expense.
The people cannot bear the labor of service,
and if the nine rivers should overflow,
with floodwaters causing harm,
and all the hills and mounds are leveled,
how shall we defend against it?"
The emperor then stopped.
Records of Wèi
Běimáng Mountain is the tail of Lǒng Mountain,
also called Píngféng Mountain,
also called Jiá Mountain.
Records of Commanderies and States
The northern mountains form continuous ridges,
stretching over four hundred lǐ,
truly the eastern Luò area of past and present,
the land of Jiǔyuán.
Records of Luòyáng
To the south it faces the Luò River,
to the north it rests against Máng Mountain,
relying on heights for its dwelling,
and using dense woods for shade.
Yìng Qú's Letter to Chéng Wénxìn
When Sū Sháo died,
he appeared in form to Sū Jié,
requesting reburial, saying:
"My nature loves the capital Luò,
whenever I come and go,
gazing at Máng Mountain, how joyful!
It is a foundation for ten thousand generations.
To the north it backs on Mèngjīn,
the vast and mighty river,
to the south it looks toward the heavenly capital,
with its magnificent prosperity."
Wáng Yǐn's History of Jìn
Tàibái
Jí Mào and Sū Zé encountered turmoil,
so they secluded themselves south of Fúfēng,
in the Tàibái Mountains, amusing themselves with classical texts.
The Wèi Lüè records:
"The height of the Tàibái Mountains is unknown,
but common saying goes:
'Wǔgōng's Tàibái
stands three hundred [miles] from heaven;
when troops march at its base,
they must not beat drums or blow horns,
for if they do, fierce winds and torrential rains will arrive together.'"
The Sān Qín Jì
Sōng Liáng
In Wǔlíng Commandery, the Sōngliáng Mountain peak stood solitary and lofty,
with sheer cliffs stretching thousands of fathoms,
appearing elegantly slender when viewed from afar,
resembling an incense burner.
In the sixth year of the Yǒng'ān era,
the mountain cavern suddenly split open,
revealing a dark, luminous passage like a gate.
It stood three hundred zhang high,
and two hundred zhang wide.
On each corner of the gate grew a bamboo,
hanging upside down and sweeping downward,
called the "Heavenly Broom."
Sūn Xiù considered this an auspicious sign and divided Wǔlíng,
establishing the Tiānmén Commandery.
According to the "Shuǐjīng Jīngzhōu Records,"
Emperor Wén of Suí renamed it the Shímén Mountain.
Kūnshān
Two hundred li northeast of Hǎiyán County lies the Long Valley,
where Lù Xùn and Lù Kǎi once resided.
Twenty li to the east is Kūn Mountain, where their fathers and ancestors were buried.
According to the "Wúdì Jì" by Lù Dàozhān,
the Lù family's ancestors were interred here,
and Shìhéng and his brothers were born in this place.
People at the time compared it to jade emerging from Kūnlún Mountain,
hence in Shìhéng's poem dedicated to his cousin, the Chariot and Cavalry General,
it is referred to as "the serene shade of Kūn Mountain."
From "Yǔdì Guǎng Jì."
Mount Xiànshān
Yáng Hù once with his aide Zōu Zhàn,
together climbed Mount Xiàn,
and shed tears saying:
"Since the universe came into being,
this mountain has existed.
Throughout the ages, many virtuous and outstanding men have climbed here to gaze into the distance,
like you and me,
yet all have vanished into obscurity.
Thinking of this brings me sorrow.
After my death,
my soul shall still ascend this mountain."
Zhàn replied:
"Your virtue crowns the four seas,
your wisdom matches the ancient sages,
your fine reputation and noble character
will be passed down along with this mountain.
As for someone like me,
I shall indeed be as you said."
From "Xiāngyáng Records of the Elderly"
Chén Bēi
Dù Yù was fond of leaving a name for posterity,
often saying that high banks become valleys,
and deep valleys become hills.
He had two stone tablets engraved,
recording his meritorious achievements:
one was sunk beneath Wàn Shān,
and the other erected on Xiàn Shān.
He said:
"Who knows if these places will not become hills and valleys hereafter?"
The History of the Jìn Dynasty
Many people of the time had the sinking of the tablet at the summit of Xiàn Shān,
which was often mentioned by Tang dynasty worthies.
According to The History of the Jìn Dynasty,
it states
and so forth,
the sinking of the tablet at the summit of Xiàn Shān is incorrect;
it should be the sinking of the tablet at Wàn Shān.
The New Book of the Southern Regions
Wǔtái
Mount Wǔtái has five majestic peaks,
hence the name "Five Terraces."
In the third year of the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn dynasty,
over five hundred families from Yànmén Commandery sought refuge in these mountains to escape turmoil,
witnessing mountain dwellers leading the way,
and thus never returned.
They settled peacefully in the wild cliffs,
with few travelers catching sight of them.
Even when villagers went to search for them,
none could locate their whereabouts.
Thus, common folk regarded it as a capital of immortals.
On the central terrace mountain,
the summit spans three lǐ square,
with a spring to the northwest,
whose waters do not flow,
called Tàihuá Spring.
As the layered beauty of Mount Wǔtái is described in Taoist texts,
it is named the Purple Residence where immortals dwell.
The northern terrace mountain,
perpetually covered in ice and snow winter and summer, is uninhabitable,
being the place where Mañjuśrī often subdues venomous dragons.
Nowadays, it hosts many Buddhist temples,
with monks and devout followers from all directions frequently visiting to pay homage.
"Commentary on the Water Classic"
refers to it as Mount Qīngliáng.
"Records of the Yuanhe Era"
states that between Yún and Dài lies a spiritual mountain.
Facing the Vulture Peak of India,
they stand in majestic opposition.
The eastern peak features the Líyuè Fire Orb,
the western peak holds the Lìnóng Jade Chamber,
the southern peak boasts the Dòngguāng Pearl Tree,
the northern peak nurtures the Yùjiàn Jade Fungus,
while the central peak contains self-illuminating gold
and circular glowing jade.
"Extensive Records of the Taiping Era"
Tàihé
Wǔdāng Shān is also called Tàihé Shān,
also known as Shēn Shān.
The mountain's form is exceptionally beautiful,
and it is also called Xiānshì.
During the Xiánhé era of the Jìn dynasty,
Xiè Yǔn of Lìyáng,
abandoned his position as magistrate of Luóyì,
and went into seclusion in this mountain,
hence it is also called Xièluó Shān.
The "Shuǐ Jīng"
describes the Wǔdāng Shān area,
as being four to five hundred lǐ in circumference.
At its center is a peak named Sì Shēn,
the ridge over twenty lǐ high.
Viewed from afar, its beauty is peerless,
towering beyond the cloud layer.
Only on clear, bright days can one see the peak;
within a month, it is visible fewer than four or five times.
Light mists cover its summit,
white clouds encircle its front.
In the morning, they invariably move west,
by evening, return east.
It has thus been called the Court-Paying Mountain,
likely because all other mountains seem to bow in homage to it.
The "Shān Jì"
states: Wǔdāng Shān,
with its lofty and precipitous heights,
resembles the Incense Burner Peak of Lúshān,
soaring steeply to the extreme,
emerging from the clouds and mist into the sky.
Those studying the Dào often number in the hundreds,
succeeding one another without end.
If anyone on this mountain
has wavering commitment in their studies,
they are immediately chased away by wild beasts.
The "Nán Yōngzhōu Jì"
Yìnzhǔ
The Yìnzhǔ Mountain receives the water from the Fú River above,
from the islet upward to the county,
it is entirely rocky shallows and treacherous paths,
making it impassable for boats.
Downstream, the waterway is free of dangers,
hence travelers gather here.
When Jìn's Wáng Húzhī served as the governor of Wúxīng,
he reached the islet and sighed:
"Not only does it cleanse one's heart and refresh the spirit,
but it also makes the sun and moon seem clearer and brighter."
It is recorded that:
the rock patterns on the islet resemble seals,
thus it was named accordingly.
From "Records of Wúxīng."
Dōngshān
Wáng Yòujūn said to Liú Yǐn:
"We should all recommend Ānshí."
Liú Yǐn replied:
"If Ānshí establishes his aspirations at Eastern Mountain,
then we should join the world in recommending him."
Shì Shuō
When Xiè Gōng was at Eastern Mountain,
court appointments were repeatedly issued but he remained unmoved.
Later, when he took office as Huán Xuānwǔ's military advisor,
and was about to depart from Xīntíng,
all the court officials came out
to gaze after and see off Gāo Líng.
At that time, he was the imperial censor,
and also went to bid farewell earlier.
After drinking some wine,
he leaned as if drunk
and joked:
"You repeatedly defied the court's orders,
reclining high at Eastern Mountain.
Everyone often said among themselves,
'If Ānshí refuses to come out,
what will become of the common people?'
Now it's the common people
—what will become of you?"
Xiè smiled but did not answer.
Above
is Eastern Yǒng'ān,
Western Yǒng'ān,
which was Ānshí's Eastern Mountain.
Lín Yào Tú Jì
Whenever Ānshí went sightseeing,
he always had female entertainers accompany him.
Now at the mountain's summit,
there remain traces of Xiè Gōng's horse-training path,
White Cloud,
and Bright Moon pavilions.
Dì Zhì
Later, at Jiànkāng's Tǔshān, he constructed estates
to emulate Eastern Mountain.
Liù Cháo Shì Jì
Aiding Victory
Xǔ Xún, whose courtesy name was Xuándù,
enjoyed traveling through mountains and rivers, and his physique was well-suited for climbing and wading.
People of the time said:
"Xǔ not only possesses a noble spirit for scenic beauty,
but truly has the physical means to reach it."
from A New Account of the Tales of the World
Buying a Mountain
Zhī Dàolín asked someone to purchase Mount Yìn from Shēn Gōng,
to which Shēn Gōng replied:
"I have never heard of Cháo Fǔ or Xǔ Yóu buying a mountain to live in seclusion."
Records of the Grand Historian
Upon hearing Shēn Gōng's words, Dùn
felt ashamed and that was all.
Biographies of Eminent Monks
Vying in Beauty
Gù Kǎizhī returned from Kuàijī,
and when people asked him about the beauty of its mountains and rivers,
he said:
"Thousands of peaks vie in beauty,
myriad valleys contend in flowing,
with lush plants and trees covering them,
as if clouds were rising and glowing mists flourishing."
From "Shì Shuō"
Reflecting and Radiating
The region of Kuàijī is especially renowned for its many famous mountains and waters,
with towering and steep peaks and ridges,
exhaling and inhaling clouds and mist,
where pines, junipers, maples, and cypresses
raise their trunks and erect their branches,
and the pools and ravings are mirror-clear,
with pure streams pouring forth.
The "Record of Kuàijī Commandery"
states that Wáng Zǐjìng said:
"Traveling along the road in Shānyīn,
the mountains and rivers reflect and radiate off one another,
leaving one with no leisure to attend to all,
especially in the autumn and winter seasons, when it is overwhelmingly moving."
The "Shì Shuō"
Gathering Medicinal Herbs
Xǔ Mài's childhood name was Ā Yìng,
who went up the mountain to gather herbs
and did not return for months.
It was often said that Yìng loved mountains and forests,
like fish getting water.
"Zhēn Gào"
Tiānmǔ
Mount Tiānmǔ connects with Mount Kuòcāng,
on the stone cliffs are inscriptions,
the characters in tadpole script,
too high to decipher.
In spring, woodcutters
hear the cacophony of flutes, drums, and reed pipes.
During the Yuánjiā era,
famous painters were dispatched to depict its form on round fans,
referring to this very mountain.
"Records of Commanderies and States"
At dusk, I lodge in Shànzhōng;
at dawn, I climb the peaks of Tiānmǔ.
"Xiè Língyùn's Poem to Huìlián"
Among southeastern landscapes,
Yuè ranks first,
Shàn forms the face,
while Wòzhōu and Tiānmǔ are the eyebrows and eyes.
"Record of Wòzhōu Chan Monastery"
Climbing and ascending
Xiè Língyùn, when exploring mountains and ascending ridges,
would invariably seek out secluded and lofty places,
even if cliffs and peaks rose in a thousand layers,
he would spare no effort to reach them all.
For climbing, he often wore wooden clogs,
removing the front teeth when going uphill,
and the rear teeth when descending.
The Book of Sòng
Divine Realm
Shèngshān encircles the mountains,
facing the river, the pine-covered ridges are lush and dense,
connecting with the Tūshān peaks of Shǐtāníng County.
Among them, cascading streams cradle mist, springs and creeks meander,
fog drifts over fields, fragrant breezes caress the ridges, inviting prolonged admiration.
Thus, Wáng Yuánlín called it a divine realm.
Details are recorded
in Xiè Kānglè's "Record of Dwelling in the Mountains."
"The Water Classic"
mentions Tiāntāi to the east,
Tóngbǎi and Fāngshí,
Tàipíng and Èrjiǔ,
Sìmíng and Wǔ'ào,
Sānjīng, all documenting divine wonders in ancient texts,
verifying responses through auspicious spirits.
Linked ridges accumulate into hidden, undulating ranges,
while raised peaks stand tall in clustered majesty.
"Rhapsody on Dwelling in the Mountains"
Guān Jǐngyáng
Emperor Xiàowén once visited Huálín Garden,
and thereby observed the former Jǐngyáng Mountain.
Zuò said,
"A mountain is virtuous when it stands tranquil,
water is wise when it flows;
I wish Your Majesty to cultivate this."
The emperor said,
"Wèi Míng's undertaking failed with the past,
why should I follow in its wake?"
Zuò said,
"A lofty mountain is revered."
The emperor said,
"Is this not the essence of a noble path?"
"Běi Shǐ"
Shān Yún
Táo Hóngjǐng loved forests and springs by nature.
Qí Gāozǔ asked him,
"What is there in the mountains?"
Hóngjǐng replied with a poem:
"What is there in the mountains?
On the ridges there are many white clouds,
They can only delight myself,
But cannot be picked to send to you."
Gāozǔ appreciated it.
"Tán Sǒu"
The Qí dynasty had no Gāozǔ,
It is suspected to be Liáng Wǔdì.
Xiùshān
In Chízhōu, Mount Xiùshān
has beautiful peaks and ridges,
towering into the clouds.
After Crown Prince Zhāomíng passed away, his spirit
attached itself to a resident of Mount Xiùshān,
saying:
"I loved this place in the past,
and now the Emperor has bestowed it upon me.
The people built a shrine for him in the mountain recess."
From "The Illustrated Classic"
Qìng Shān
During the reign of Wǔ Zétiān,
in Lùtái Township southeast of Xīnfēng County,
due to violent storms with hail and thunder,
a mountain surged forth two hundred chi high,
with a pond three qing in circumference.
In the pond appeared forms of dragons and phoenixes,
and anomalies of grain and wheat.
Wǔ Zétiān considered this an auspicious sign,
naming it Qìngshān (Celebration Mountain).
