Yù Wénjùn, a native of Jīngzhōu, went to the palace and submitted a memorial stating:
"I have heard that when the qi of heaven is disharmonious, cold and heat become disjointed;
when the qi of humans is disharmonious, warts and excrescences grow;
when the qi of earth is disharmonious, mounds and hillocks emerge.
Now Your Majesty, as a female ruler, occupies the masculine position,
reversing the firm and the yielding,
thus the earth's qi is blocked and obstructed,
and the mountain transformation becomes a disaster.
Your Majesty considers it a celebration mountain,
but your subject does not see it as a cause for celebration."
Wǔ Zétiān was enraged,
and exiled him to Lingnan.
"Old Tang Records"
Giveishi Wèi Shūlín said:
"The earth producing a bony mound—
what is there to celebrate?"
Someone reported this to the emperor,
and he was sentenced to death.
"Record of the Routes Between the Two Capitals"
The mountain moves.
In Yǒngchāng, Zhōnghuá Prefecture,
on the great mountain south of the Chìshuǐ River,
suddenly, during the day, the wind grew dark with a sound,
faintly like thunder, and in a moment,
it gradually moved east several hundred paces.
It pressed upon the Chìshuǐ River, crushing over thirty households of the Zhāng village residents.
The mountain was over two hundred zhang high,
the water was thirty zhang deep,
yet the grass and trees on the slope remained as they were.
From the "Táng Records."
Jīntíng Shān
On Tóngbǎi Mountain in Shèng County,
there is the Jīntíng Cave,
which Taoist texts regard as the twenty-seventh cave heaven.
Below it lies
the Cinnabar Pool and Red Water.
In the sixth year of the Táng dynasty's Tiānbǎo era,
it was renamed Cinnabar Pool Mountain.
Yàn Shū's Classified Essentials states:
"Yuè has the Jīntíng of Tóngbǎi,
a blessed land for nurturing truth."
Fǔ Táng
Tàihé Xiānshēng Wáng Mín,
was one who had attained the Way.
He often roamed the famous mountains and the Five Peaks,
and Emperor Xuánzōng greatly respected and trusted him.
Lǐ Xiázhōu, a Daoist of the Southern Peak,
fearing that Mín might cling to worldly pleasures,
urged Mín to leave,
so Mín requested to perform joint alchemy at Láoshān in Gāomì,
which Emperor Xuánzōng permitted.
Consequently, Láoshān was renamed Fǔtángshān,
and Mín was allowed to reside there.
Records of Anecdotes
Jiǔhuá
The Record of Jiǔhuà Mountain states:
The peaks and ridges have extraordinary shapes,
their number being nine,
hence called Nine Offspring.
Lǐ Bái, seeing the nine peaks resembling lotus blossoms,
renamed it Jiǔhuá.
Liú Yǔxī said:
"Jiǔhuà Mountain is truly a unique wonder of heaven and earth."
Lùhún
Yuán Déxiù served as the magistrate of Lǔshān County.
When his term ended, he traveled south to Lùhún,
where he saw the beautiful landscape stretching into the distance,
and felt a desire to remain there permanently.
He then settled in the Lúshān mountains,
living contentedly and joyfully,
detaching himself from worldly affairs.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Jìgān
Yuán Jié during the Tiānbǎo era took Zhōng Xíng as his teacher,
and I first lived in the Shěnyú Mountains,
calling myself Yuánzǐ when fleeing from calamity,
entering the Yīgān Mountains.
I called myself Yīgānzǐ,
or sometimes Làngshì (Wandering Scholar).
Fishermen called me Áosǒu (Old Fisherman),
drinking companions called me Mànsǒu (Unrestrained Old Man),
and when I became an official, they called me Mànláng (Unrestrained Gentleman).
"Supplement to the National History"
The Ninth Day
Qín Xì,
courtesy name Gōngxù.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era, he sojourned in Quánzhōu,
where in Nán'ān stood Mount Jiǔrì,
with over a hundred large pine trees.
The "Zhāngsú Chronicle" records:
They were planted during the Eastern Jìn dynasty,
and Qín Xì built a hut atop them,
while Jiāng Gōngfǔ,
demoted to biéjià, visited him.
Qín Xì would spend entire days there, unable to leave,
and constructed a dwelling nearby,
forgetting the hardships of his exile until his death.
The people of Nán'ān remembered him fondly,
erecting a small pavilion in his honor,
and named the mountain "Peak of the Noble Scholar."
From the "Táng History."
Purchase Mountain Money
When Yú Dí was governing
Xiāngyáng,
the hermit Fú Zǎi
sent a letter requesting to purchase a mountain,
for one million coins.
The Duke then gave it to him,
and additionally provided paper, ink, clothing, and other items.
"Yúnxī Yǒuyì"
Mountain Building
In the final years of Emperor Yìzōng's reign,
laborers in Cháng'ān
quarried stones from the imperial gardens
to construct perilously steep hills,
winding and twisting as if naturally formed.
They were also ordered to transplant vegetation from the Zhōngnán Mountains,
releasing mountain birds and wild beasts
to roam freely among them,
and built dwellings resembling commoners' homes.
The emperor frequented these places with his concubines,
prompting nobles and officials to compete in imitating such constructions.
Within half a year,
exotic flowers and rare grasses spontaneously overgrew the palaces.
Those with foresight interpreted this as an omen of ruin.
Later, when Huáng Cháo entered the capital,
he burned everything nearly completely,
reducing all to rubble.
(Records of Extraordinary Events)
Jǐn Wéi
Wáng Róng was fond of heterodox teachings,
and stayed with the Daoist priest Wáng Ruònà,
traveling to the Western Hills and ascending to the Queen Mother Temple.
He had women hold brocaded silk ropes to pull and support him upward,
forgetting to return for over a month.
"History of the Five Dynasties"
Yìjǐn Shān
Lín'ān Shíjìng Shān,
on its eastern peak there is a round stone path,
two chi and seven cun in diameter,
shining like a mirror.
When King Qián Liú of Wúyuè was still a commoner,
he once looked into this mirror,
where it rose and trembled,
reflecting his appearance and attire as if crowned like a king.
"Huányǔ Jì"
Later, Emperor Táng Zhāozōng renamed the camp where Liú resided,
calling it Yìjǐn Camp,
and further elevated Yìjǐn Camp to Yìjǐn City,
renaming Shíjìng Shān to Yìjǐn Shān,
and Dàguān Shān to Gōngchén Shān.
When Liú visited Jǐnchéng for a banquet,
he covered the forests of the elders
with brocade banners,
naming the large tree he played under as a child "General Yìjǐn."
"Wǔdài Shǐ"
Jīnshān
Jīnshān was originally named Fúyù,
meaning it came from the peaks of Yùjīng,
floating to this place.
The "Dàozàng Jīng"
describes this mountain encircled by the great river,
whenever winds and waves rise on all sides,
it appears as if about to float away,
hence it was called Fúyù Shān in the Southern Dynasties.
During the Táng dynasty, a monk named Péi Tóutuó
opened up the mountain here and discovered gold,
thus it was renamed Jīnshān.
From Zhōu Bìdà's "Miscellaneous Records"
Màijī
North of the mountain spans the clear Wèi River,
stretching south toward Liǎngdāng.
Halfway up, a massive rock rises abruptly,
towering hundreds of thousands of fathoms high.
Viewed from afar, it appears rounded like a stack of wheat in folk tradition,
hence the name.
Amidst the clouds halfway up its verdant slope,
within the steep cliffs,
Buddhas are carved into the stone,
with ten thousand niches and a thousand chambers.
Though crafted by human effort,
their artistry seems almost supernatural.
The relics of the divine nun are separately enshrined,
placed in a casket beneath the eastern pavilion.
In an adjacent chamber,
an account by Yǔ Xìn is engraved on the cliff.
An ancient record states:
Six states collaborated in its construction,
piling firewood from the flat ground
up to the cliff's summit.
From above, they carved the niches, chambers, and Buddha images,
dismantling the woodpile gradually upon completion to descend.
Thereafter, ladders and scaffolds were erected perilously for ascent.
On its peak, countless rooms and structures
cling to the void, defying gravity.
Those climbing dare not look back.
Nearing the absolute summit,
stands the Hall of Ten Thousand Bodhisattvas,
hewn entirely from stone.
Above this chamber lies another niche,
called the Paradise,
accessed by a solitary ladder suspended in midair.
Climbing upward,
fewer than one in ten thousand dare ascend here.
Gazing down from this point upon the mountain ranges,
they appear mere molehills.
In the year Xīnwèi of the late Táng dynasty, Wáng Rényù
alone managed to climb it,
inscribing a poem on the western cliff of the celestial camp:
It reads:
"Treading the suspended ladder of ten thousand ren,
My form casually merges with the white clouds.
Below the eaves, the mountains seem small;
In the hall, the sun and moon hang low."
And so on.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Dǒushān
In Xìngyuán there is Dǒu Mountain,
viewed from the plain,
it rises steeply from within,
precipitous on all sides,
its summit shaped like the base of a dipper,
hence its name. Vines, pines, and junipers
create a scene of secluded wonder.
Upon it lies the site where Táng Gōngfǎng
drank the immortal wine of Lǐ Bābǎi,
and his entire household ascended with their residence.
The foundation of their home, three mǔ in area,
sank into a pit,
this being because they rose together with the land.
Wáng Rényù, in the year Xīnsì,
served as military commissioner judge,
and once inscribed a poem on a wooden plaque at the temple.
Old accounts say a cave in Dǒu Mountain
extends two thousand lǐ westward,
connecting to Dàmiàn Mountain in Qīngchéng,
and also links with the well at Yángòng Temple.
In the year Guǐwèi, Wáng Rényù entered Shǔ
and visited Yángòng Temple,
where he saw the poetic plaque from Dǒu Mountain.
When questioned,
none knew how it had come there,
and all marveled at it.
Wǎn Gōng
When Lǐ Jiāmíng accompanied Emperor Yuánzong on the relocation to the southern capital,
they had already lost fourteen prefectures north of the river.
As boats mostly traveled along the southern shore reaching Zhàotún,
the emperor ceased music and set down his wine cup,
gazing north toward Wǎngōng Mountain.
He said to Jiāmíng:
"What strikingly green and steep peaks—
I wonder what they are called?"
Jiāmíng responded immediately:
"The dragon boat glides lightly with brocade sails in the wind,
just as Your Majesty tours gazing into the distant sky.
Turning to see Wǎngōng Mountain's verdant hue,
its slanting shadow fails to reach the birthday wine cup."
Emperor Yuánzong felt ashamed at this,
and passed by with bowed head.
From "History of Southern Táng"
Wǎn Mountain is located in Qián Mountain,
connected to Tiānzhù Peak.
This mountain features three peaks standing like a tripod,
with layered ridges and repeated ranges,
blocking clouds and scraping the sun,
making ascent impassable.
From "Hàn Treatise on Geography"
Shānwáng has a past connection
In Nánhàn's Sháozhōu,
there was a monk named Rú Mǐn,
who knew future events and left many extraordinary traces.
Initially, he had an ascetic as his attendant,
calling him Suǒyóu.
One day, while following him up a mountain ridge,
he sent him back ahead,
ordering him to descend and look back,
where he saw Rú Mǐn entering the ground.
The ascetic hid in the grass,
waiting for a long time,
then came out to greet and ask:
"Master, where have you been?"
He replied:
"I have an old acquaintance with the Mountain King,
who invited me for a conversation,
and I returned at this time.
Sometimes the deceased would emerge from a burrowed hole in the ground."
He sternly warned him:
"Suǒyóu,
do not speak of this outside,
divulging my private affairs."
From the "Biographies of Eminent Monks."
Tiānzhōng
Sòng Liú Chǎng stated:
Yùzhōu is the center of heaven and earth,
and Rǔnán is in turn the center of Yùzhōu.
Therefore, three lǐ north of Rǔníng,
there is a mountain named Tiānzhōng,
also called Tiāntái.
It is said that since ancient times, for measuring shadows and setting up sundials,
no place has been more accurate than this.
Yàndàng
The "Western Regions Record" states:
The fifth venerable one,
the great arhat Nóujùnà,
continued to reside in the southern coastal region of China,
at Yàndàng Mountain, also known as Dragon Waterfall and Wild Goose Peaks,
which was the transformed capital of our Buddha's disciple Nóujùnà.
When Nóujùnà reached the mountain and beheld the waterfall,
he then passed away in meditation.
The Tang dynasty poet Guànxiū wrote:
"Through Yàndàng's paths, the clouds stretch vast;
At Dragon Waterfall seated in feast, the rain falls thick."
During the reign of Emperor Tàizōng of the Sòng dynasty, the monk Quánliǎo from Yǒngjiā
traveled to Jīngzhōu,
and reached Mount Yùquán,
where he encountered a deity from India.
The monk said to him:
"There is a Nóujùluó in Jiā,
whose sites of practice are numerous and suitable;
you should go and visit,
to complete his work."
Liǎo asked where it was,
and the deity replied:
"The land is named after flowers,
the mountain is named after birds.
Within lies the Dragon Waterfall where one sits in meditation;
it is the dwelling place of the venerable one."
Liǎo searched extensively among the mountains,
traveling until he reached the seaside,
where he saw the landscape clear and profound.
He asked the name of the village and was told it was Fúróng (Lotus).
He asked the name of the mountain and was told it was Yàndàng (Wild Goose Peaks).
Liǎo was greatly enlightened,
and thus settled in the mountain, building a hermitage at the key convergence of the landscape,
named Fúróng Hermitage,
which is the present-day Néngrén Temple.
The terms "Great Fúróng"
and "Small Fúróng"
refer to the mountain names in the western outer valley of Yàndàng Mountain.
The "Mountain Records"
state that the "dàng" (marsh) is at the mountain's summit,
where reeds and rushes abound.
Every late autumn, wild geese gather here,
hence the name. The place is perilous and remote,
with very few visitors.
At the foot of the mountain, there are eastern and western valleys.
The eastern valley has Scissors Peak,
with a notably grand and wondrous waterfall spring;
the Dragon Waterfall lies above it.
The western valley has Long Cloud Peak,
east of Saddle Rock.
Flags Unfurled Stone,
Sky-Screening Pillar,
Jade Maiden, and Writing Brush,
all these peaks are strangely steep and towering straight,
reaching halfway to the sky without a speck of soil.
To the north, the highest and largest,
spans over a dozen stones,
with stone textures like surging waves,
named Level Rosy Clouds Barrier.
Língyán Temple stands amidst these jagged peaks;
gazing westward from here alone,
one's heart and eyes are struck with awe,
the pure air pierces to the bone,
as if not of this mortal world,
making one linger and hesitate, unwilling to leave.
Looking back at peaks like West Lake's Feilai,
they seem mundane and devoid of lingering charm.
In a cave west of Level Rosy Clouds Barrier,
there is a stone from which water drips,
trickling from two openings;
it is named Elephant Trunk Spring.
Kuòcāng
The Preface to the "Map of the Five Sacred Mountains" states:
Kuòcāng Shān
is the assistant ruler of the Eastern Sacred Mountain.
Annotations in the "Secret Instructions for Ascending to Perfection" and the "Records of Wú" note:
Ascending Kuòlù Shān,
one overlooks thunderstorms below.
Tíhú Shān
Tíhú Shān has two peaks,
towering to the heavens.
High cliffs pierce the clouds,
with steep rocks offering no steps.
Even the nimblest climbers lose their agility,
and flying squirrels exhaust their light skills.
Only when the peaks stand firm beneath the eternal sky,
crowned by layered clouds,
can one distinguish their superiority.
Hence the names Great and Little Tíhú.
"Water Classic"
Bǎi Tī
East of the Hé River lies the Fénshuǐ River,
south stands the Yándào Mountain,
to its west are stone cliffs a thousand fathoms high,
to its east the Pánxī Gorge towers ten thousand ren,
square ridges coil with clouds,
fantastic peaks rise like rosy dawn,
solitary markers emerge elegantly,
enveloping the summits of massed mountains.
Jade-green pines shade the peaks,
clear springs cascade over the crest.
Guō Jǐngchún remarked:
"What the world calls 'mandarin duck nectar',
emerges above while flowing hidden below.
Its summit is flat and square,
bearing fine medicinal herbs."
Shénnóng's Materia Medica states:
this land produces species like gùhuó, nǚshū, tóngyún, and zǐwǎn,
thus black-robed thinkers of mystery,
and deerskin-clad seekers of unity,
journey here through the ages.
The path emerges from northern cliffs,
mostly perilously steep,
travelers all grasp vines to scale summits,
seek kudzu to descend depths.
To the east one climbs via connected trees
and descends by hundred-ladder steps,
traces of tethered chains on cliff-sides
remain visible to this day,
hence it's also called Bǎitī Mountain.
Above,
Fènghuáng Shān
At the foot of Fènghuáng Mountain in Hángzhōu,
overlooking the great river and directly facing the sea gate,
it appears as if a phoenix is about to take flight.
There is a rock resembling a slice of cloud,
standing tens of feet high,
with a hole at its peak.
I named it Yuèyán (Moon Rock),
for only during the Mid-Autumn Festival's full moon
does the moonlight pass straight through the hole.
On the fourteenth and sixteenth days,
it misses the hole,
and on other months, it is even more oblique.
Jīshū Yán
North of the Jīshí River there are layered mountains,
which are very sacred and beautiful.
Upon the mountain peaks,
stand rocks hundreds of feet high,
tall and upright,
competing in posture and vying for height.
From afar they appear like clustered pillars reaching the clouds;
below them, layered cliffs rise steeply,
with sheer banks offering no steps.
Among the overhanging cliffs are many stone chambers,
within which there seem to be accumulated scrolls.
Yet scholars of the world rarely reach this place,
so it is called the Jīshū Yán (Accumulated Books Cliff).
Within the cliff's halls,
divine beings are often seen coming and going.
These are men in swan-feather garments,
practitioners who refine their essence and ingest special foods.
Common people, unaware they are immortals,
call them spirits and ghosts.
The Qiāng people refer to ghosts as:
"Tángshù," hence it is also named Tángshù Shān.
Pointing to the densely clustered dwellings,
they call them the Tángshù Caves.
Those who cherish the Way and revere the mysterious,
men with plain caps and shaven heads,
also go there to reside.
《Water Classic》
Qīngshān
West of Línjǔ County,
lies the source of the Qīng Stream from the Green Mountains.
Following the stream up its course,
one finds it strikingly deep and steep.
Shèng Hóngzhī noted:
"Dense waters grow alongside,
intertwining high in the air,
like precarious towers leaning over peaks,
ever seeming on the verge of collapse.
Breezes and springs echo through the green woods below,
while rocky streams resound above the white clouds.
Travelers often feel their eyes cannot take in all the beauty,
nor their hearts fully appreciate it.
Thus, forest dwellers settle here for refuge,
and cloud-wanderers make it their spiritual home."
Many Daoist retreats are built beside these springs.
Lóngmén
Southeast of Běi Xúzhōu,
there is a stone gate,
commonly known as Lóngmén.
Its upper part is closed while the lower opens up,
with the opening standing sixty feet high,
where flying ice traverses through.
To the south, it rides the cliffs with cascading torrents,
pouring down over seventy feet,
the roaring sound
is remarkably fierce and mighty,
striking rocks to form deep pools,
with unfathomable depths,
white waves churning fiercely,
billows surging against the surrounding land,
startling the spirits of those who gaze upon it,
and terrifying the souls of those who approach.
Above,
Zhū Tí
It is Mount Zhūtí,
with winding sheep-gut paths over eighty li long,
where one sometimes climbs by holding onto trees,
or pulls oneself up with ropes.
Those ascending along these paths feel as if they are scaling the heavens,
hence Yuán Xiūmíng's "Records of Bāshǔ" states:
"Lofty peaks rise precipitously,
rocks lie piled in rugged heaps,
twisting and turning on steep inclines,
overlooking sheer ravines below.
Travelers cling to the edges,
pulling themselves along with ropes.
The people of the Three Shǔ regions,
and the various comm
anderies of Nánzhōng,
consider this the most perilous place." The Floating Mountain in Shǐxīng County of Qǔjiāng,
has Mount Fúyuè,
where stepping on one spot of the mountain causes a hundred paces
to sway as if on water,
hence it is named Mount Fúyuè (Floating Mountain).
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Gāo Liáng Shān
At the southern end of Gāoliáng Mountain in Nánpǔ Commandery,
it stretches eastward across the river, with its head at Jiàngé in the west,
spanning several thousand li from east to west.
The ridge is long and steep, its peaks towering majestically over Shǔ's markets,
appearing like a long cloud hanging from the sky.
Traveling for a day,
one reaches its summit.
Looking down, all mountains vanish as if they were a plain.
As described in the "Inscription on Jiàngé":
Majestic is Liáng Mountain,
piled with lofty rocks.
This precisely recounts it.
"Records of the River's Origin"
Shí Zhōng Shān
In Nánkāng Prefecture's Dūchāng County, there stands the Stone Bell Mountain,
which rests its west against Pénglí Lake,
with connecting peaks and layered ridges,
standing steep as if cut by a blade.
Its south, west, and north sides are all embraced by water,
unchanging through the four seasons,
where white waves pound the mountain,
producing sounds like a bell,
hence its name.
Lǐ Bó's "Record of Distinguishing the Mountain Bell" states:
"The 'Water Classic' says:
At the mouth of Pénglí Lake lies Stone Bell Mountain.
Lì Yuán noted:
'It overlooks a deep pool below,
where gentle winds stir waves,
water and rocks strike each other,
resounding like a great bell,
thus earning its name.'
I explored East Lake,
climbing cliffs and traversing caves,
and rested at the southern corner,
where I suddenly encountered twin rocks leaning by the pool's edge,
their reflections submerged in the waves.
Inquiring along the waterfront,
I was told it is called Stone Bell.
There is a distinction between copper and iron.
Striking and listening to them,
the southern one sounds deep and muffled,
the northern one clear and resonant,
their strikes echo and rise,
the lingering tones slowly fade.
If not for the marsh nourishing the mountain,
the mountain containing its essence,
uniting energy and solidifying substance,
manifesting as supreme spirit,
how else could such wondrous stones be produced?
Thus, I realized the mountain has long been named after the stones.
If we follow Shànzhǎng's argument,
then every peak along the flowing waters
could be labeled with this name.
I hereby correct the previous error,
leaving it for future generations.
"Records of the Universe"
Mǎdāng
Mǎdāng Mountain stands eighty zhang high,
with a circumference of four li,
located north of the ancient Péngzé County.
The mountain lies horizontally along the great river,
resembling the shape of a horse.
When winds swirl and strike fiercely,
waves surge and boil,
causing boats traveling upstream and downstream
to harbor much anxiety and fear.
At the mountain's edge stands the Mǎdāng Mountain Temple,
dedicated to its worship.
According to the "Jiǔjiāng Records,"
Táng dynasty poet Wáng Bò, hindered by contrary winds, moored his boat beneath it
and encountered an old man who aided him with favorable winds,
enabling him to reach Hóngdū in one night to compose the "Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Téng." Lù Lǔwàng’s inscription states:
Of the perils under heaven,
among mountains, it is Tàiháng;
among waters, it is Lǚliáng.
Combining these two perils into one,
I have also heard of Mǎdāng.
One Mountain with Four Names
"Records of the Grand Historian: Account of the Xiongnu":
The Swift Cavalry General attacked the Xiongnu,
passing through Jūyán to assault Qílián Mountain.
Annotation:
"Old Accounts of Xīhé" states:
A Xiongnu song says:
"We lost our Qílián Mountain,
causing our six domestic animals to cease multiplying."
Qílián is another name for Tiānshān,
also called Báishān.
Annotation to "Account of Huò Qùbìng":
Xiǎo Yán said:
The Xiongnu call heaven Qílián.
"Annals of Emperor Míng":
Defeated Báishān,
captured prisoners at Púlèi.
Annotation by Zhāng Huái on the sea states:
Xīhé
"Old Accounts" says:
Báishān has snow in both winter and summer,
hence called Báishān by the Xiongnu.
They call it Tiānshān; passing this place,
all dismount and pay respects.
Also, Dòu Gù defeated King Hūyǎn at Tiānshān.
Annotation:
Tiānshān,
is Qílián Mountain,
also known as Xuěshān.
Now called Zhéluóhàn Mountain,
located north of Yīzhōu; Qí is pronounced shí.
Língjiù Shān
In the Western Regions, Qíshéjué is rendered in Chinese as:
Língjiù Shān (Vulture Peak).
The Great Treatise states:
Qíshé means stone vulture, and Jué means head,
so the mountain is named Língjiù because its summit resembles a vulture.
The Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra says:
Various holy beings and immortals
dwell there because of it.
The Records of the Western Regions states:
It is both inhabited by vultures
and resembles a high platform,
hence it is called Vulture Peak,
also known as Vulture Terrace.
Master Yìng explains:
According to the Sanskrit original, there is no meaning of "spiritual,"
but this bird is considered spiritual
for knowing human life and death,
thus it is called Língjiù (Spiritual Vulture).
Póshā states the mountain has three peaks,
like upturned chicken feet,
resembling the tracks of a wolf,
and is also named Wolf Tracks.
It is also called Pǔxián Shān,
Báishàn Shān,
Xiānrén Shān,
and Fùzhòng Shān.
The Translation of Terms
states that Dharma Master Wú said:
In the foreign language, the country is Rājagṛha,
and there is Língjiù Shān,
called Qíshéjué Shān in the foreign tongue.
The mountain is of blue stone,
resembling a vulture bird.
King Aśoka had people carve the stone,
artificially adding two wings and two feet,
and sculpting its body.
It still exists today, looking like a vulture from afar,
hence the name Língjiù Shān.
The Water Classic
records Língjiù Shān in Qūjiāng, Shǐxīng,
originally named Hǔjùn Shān,
also called Hǔshì Shān,
due to the prevalence of fierce tigers.
During the Yìxī era of the Jìn dynasty,
the monk Shì Sēnglǜ built a dwelling in the rocky cliffs,
and the fierce tigers retreated far away,
which was attributed to Sēnglǜ's benevolence,
leading to its renaming as Língjiù Shān.
Above
is Língjiù Shān in Jīngmén Prefecture,
with a cave called Lóng Dòng (Dragon Cave),
five lǐ deep,
and a very high stone platform.
In spring, the sound of water resembles bells, drums, pipes, and flutes,
causing listeners to forget their weariness.
During the Xīníng era of the Sòng dynasty, the mountain spring overflowed,
and lacquered vessels and carts flowed out,
inscribed with the characters "Jiāzhōu,"
indicating the spring connects with Shǔ.
The Gazetteer
Xūmí
The "Records of the Western Regions" states:
Sūmílú, in Tang language, means Exquisite Height.
It was formerly called Xūmí.
The "Garden of the Dharma" states:
Within the trichiliocosm,
the four continents take Sūmí,
Lú Mountain as the center.
According to the root sutra, it states:
This mountain is made of four treasures,
composed together in the great ocean,
resting upon the golden wheel,
where the sun and moon
orbit and where the various heavens
sojourn and dwell. Seven mountains
and seven seas encircle it, standing firm,
arranged around on all four sides,
each having one color:
east is gold,
south is lapis lazuli,
west is silver,
north is crystal.
According to their directions,
the water shares the mountain's color.
The Abhidharma Kośa
states that Exquisite Height is formed from seven treasures,
hence it is called "exquisite" for emerging from the seven metals,
and "height" for the mountain.
Iron Enclosure
The center of the four continents is Mount Sumeru,
outside the mountain there are eight other mountains,
beyond them lies the salt sea,
vast and boundless,
beyond the sea there is a mountain,

Four sides

Ascending to Immortality
Wáng Qiáo, son of King Ling of Zhou,
was the crown prince Jin.
He loved playing the sheng.
While roaming the shores of the Yi and Luo Rivers, producing phoenix cries,
he invited the Daoist priest Fú Qiū Gōng,

After several days, he departed.
His family obtained the shoes he left behind.
The place is also called Fǔfù Duī (Father's Mound),
where a shrine to Zǐ Jìn stands atop the mound.

Sōng Cén
Péi Yǎn,
courtesy name Wénshū,
surrendered from Liáng to Wèi
and was appointed Gentleman Cavalier Attendant.
Yǎn wished to decline the court appointment
and requested to retire in Sōnggāo Mountain.

nurturing renowned herbs,
where cultivation of life and healing of illnesses

so I may companion with shadows among wind and clouds,

dwell where white clouds originate,
and consume mushrooms in clear valleys.

Bǎo Shénxiàng
During the time of Wèi Tàiwǔ,
there was a treasured divine statue in the Tàishì of Sōngyáng,
several inches tall.
Suddenly during the Xiàowén Tàihé era,
someone with leprosy took refuge in this temple,
and saw Tàiwǔ preparing to create a deity.

who has permitted the relocation of the capital to Luòyáng,
and it is to last four hundred years.

Visiting a Recluse
Tián Yóuyán,
initially known for his Confucian scholarship,
repeatedly declined official summons.
He lived in seclusion on Mount Sōng with his mother.
During the Diàolù era,
Emperor Gāozōng visited Mount Sōng,
and sought out his dwelling.
Yóuyán came out to pay homage,
whereupon an edict appointed him Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Xuē Yuánchāo was sent to inquire after his mother,
