The Mountain God Transplants a Tree
During the Yǒngchún era,
at the Xiánjū Temple on Mount Sōng,
the monk Yuánguī resided in Péngwù of Mount Lú.
One day, a majestic man arrived with his retinue to pay homage,
saying:
"I am the mountain god of this peak,
and I request to receive the proper precepts."
Yuánguī responded:
"Without self and without you,
who is there to receive precepts?"
The god said:
"My supernatural powers are second only to the Buddha's."
Yuánguī asked:
"Can you command the Eastern Heaven to journey westward with the seven luminaries?
Can you overpower the earth deities, melt the five sacred mountains, and congeal the four seas?"
The god replied:
"I cannot."
Yuánguī said:
"The eastern cliff of the temple,
barren and treeless,
while the northern ridge has trees but lacks protective screening—
can you transplant the northern trees to the eastern ridge?"
The god answered:
"I have heard your command,
please do not be alarmed, Master."
That night, violent winds roared and thunder crashed,
shaking all things unrestfully,
but by dawn, calm and clear weather returned,
revealing that all the pines and cypresses from the northern cliff had been transplanted,
now standing densely aligned on the eastern ridge.
(From the "Sòng Gāosēng Zhuàn")
Shén Yuè
In the first year of the Zhengshèng era of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
preparations were made for ceremonies at Mount Sōng,
first sending envoys to offer sacrifices.
An edict was issued designating Sōnggāo as the Divine Peak,
and honoring its deity as the King of the Center of Heaven.
His consort was honored as the Divine Consort. By the second year of the Wànsuì era, in the twelfth month on the day Jiǎshēn,
the empress personally performed the rites of ascent and fēng sacrifice,
changing the era name to Wànsuì Dēngfēng.
On the day Dīnghài, she performed the chán sacrifice at Mount Shǎoshì.
In the third year, on the day Xīnsì of the second month,
the King of the Center of Heaven was elevated to Emperor of the Center of Heaven,
and the Divine Consort to Empress of the Center of Heaven.
"Old Records and New Annals"
Ten Scenes
Lú Hǒng,
also known as Hàorán.
He was erudite and skilled in calligraphy,
living in seclusion on Sōngshān.
Early in the Kāiyuán era, he declined an official summons,
and personally illustrated ten scenes with prefaces and verses.
Lǐ Cānxuán commented:
The Ten Records of a Reclusive Dwelling
include the Thatched Cottage as a place for self-cultivation and nurturing virtue.
The Canopy Pavilion serves for hosting guests,
and the practice of rites.
The Mysterious Grotto Chamber is for discussing the Way,
the origin of all wonders.
The Verdant Court provides a resting place for leisure,
embodying the essence of the valley spirit.
The Immortal's Stairway deepens emotions,
offering the comfort of lofty detachment.
The Cleansing Rock purifies the mind,
symbolizing self-purification.
The Brocade Cascade washes away ambitions,
renewing virtue daily.
The Golden Blue Pool rectifies form,
reflecting clarity like a mirror.
The Inverted Shadow Terrace is bustling,
with the joy of a spring terrace.
The Misty Pillow Courtyard is vast and distant,
inspiring the allure of immortal mountains.
The number ten represents the completion of heaven and earth,
and the records document it,
collectively titled "Reclusive Dwelling."
The heart of the Way is subtle,
and secluded appreciation varies,
making this a remarkable work of reclusion,
unheard of in past or present.
Thus, it is fully presented
for the enjoyment of discerning gentlemen.
Sì Míng
On Mount Sōngshān,
there is the Jade Maiden's Cloth-Pounding Stone,
sparkling and lustrous,
its depth unfathomable to people.
The locals at the mountain's foot say:
"On the eve of the Beginning of Autumn,
pounding sounds are often heard at midnight."
Northwest of the mountain stands a peak,
named the Wàngdū Peak.
It is said that when the weather is clear and warm,
one can see Luòyáng from there,
faintly resembling the shape of a carriage canopy.
Another peak to the northeast of the mountain,
is called the Jīmíng Peak."
They say:
"At the start of the fifth watch,
the sunrise becomes visible."
At the mountain's summit lies the Zhōngtiān Pond.
During the Kāiyuán era, the hermit Lú Hóng,
wherever there were extraordinary scenic spots,
had inscriptions carved,
with the most exquisite being
these four inscriptions."
From "Records of the Extraordinary"
Lú Sōngshān
Lú Hóng lived in Mount Sōngshān,
granted reclusive attire and official position.
He built a thatched cottage,
went into the mountains to widely pursue learning,
where Lú gathered five hundred disciples.
The "Old Book of Táng"
records Lú Hóng under two names,
matching the inscription on the stele of Zhōngyuè's Liú Zhēnrén in the New History,
which omitted one character,
with unknown justification,
thus the old history should be considered correct.
"Shílín Cǎotáng Tú Xù"
Hidden
Lǐ Bó,
courtesy name Jùnzhī,
lived in seclusion on Mount Sōngshān,
devoting himself to reading and literary pursuits.
During the early Yuánhé era,
he was summoned to court as a Left Omissioner despite being a recluse.
According to the Old Book of Táng,
Deputy Governor Dù Jiān of Hénán sent an official with an imperial edict and gifts to the mountain,
urging him repeatedly, but Lǐ Bó declined the appointment.
Hán Yù wrote him a letter stating:
"Scholars at court crane their necks gazing eastward,
as if competing to be the first to see a propitious star or phoenix for joy.
We hope you will don official attire,
gracefully board the carriage to come,
and apply your accumulated wisdom
to mend the deficiencies of our magnificent virtue."
Lǐ Bó appreciated his words,
and thus left seclusion for the Eastern Capital.
Title
On the twenty-sixth day of the third month in the fourth year of the Yuánhé era,
I, along with Court Gentleman for Editorial Service Fán Zōngshī and Recluse Lú Tóng,
traveled from Luòzhōng to Shǎoshì Mountain,
to pay a visit to Recluse Lǐ Bó.
Fán stayed at Yùchuān,
fell ill,
and returned.
The next day, with Lú and Lǐ,
we went east from Shǎoshì to stay overnight at the central peak of Tàishì Mountain,
at the stone chamber below the Fēngshàn Terrace.
Then, from Lóngchuān Temple,
we fished at the Dragon Pool and encountered thunder.
The following day, we viewed Qǐmǔ Stone,
and entered Tiānfēng Temple.
On the third day of the intercalary fourth month, Hán Yù inscribed this.
("Yúnlù Mànchāo" does not record this.)
At Empress Wǔ's Fēngshàn site, there is a stone inscription stating:
Those who visit the Dragon Pool
should not laugh or speak disrespectfully to the Dragon God;
if the dragon becomes angry, there will be the terror of thunder.
("Collection of Ancient Inscriptions")
Sī Zhēntiān
The Central Peak Mountain Cave,
named the Heaven of the Supreme Deity's True Governance,
was where Xuānyuán, as the Yellow Emperor, administered the Central Peak,
presiding over virtue and distributing essence,
with Huáng-Lǎo residing there.
Above, there are the immortal Bodhi trees,
and the chambers where jade maidens weave brocade,
with stone marrow and jade rings,
jade figures and golden statues,
below, it corresponds to the essence of the Willow Mansion,
and stabilizes the division of the land of Zhōu.
"Collection of Cave Abysses"
Jupiter
Jiànglóu and Xuánxiāo,
bearing the Eastern Sea,
their deities preside over Dàizōng,
where the Year Star resides.
"Records of the Tang"
Shān Zūn
Tàishān,
the most revered of mountains,
also called Dàizōng.
Dài
means "beginning".
Zōng
means "chief".
It is where all things begin,
where yīn and yáng alternate,
thus it stands as chief of the Five Sacred Mountains.
Kings receiving the Mandate
always performed the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices here.
From "Fēngsú Tōng"
Reaching for the sky
Mount Tài's height,
reaches the sky and pierces the clouds,
yet from a hundred lǐ away, one cannot discern its mound.
Lùn Héng
Change of Reign
The reason why the Eastern Peak is called Dài
is because of the meaning of succession and replacement.
When spring takes charge,
it eliminates the old and generates the new.
This is the way all things renew themselves and replace each other,
hence it is named Dài.
"Sān Lǐ Yì Zōng"
Tiānsūn
Mount Tài,
also known as the Celestial Grandson.
It is said to be the grandson of the Heavenly Emperor.
It governs the summoning of human souls,
and as the east is where all things begin to form,
it thus knows the length of human life.
From "Bówùzhì"
Fēng Shàn
When a king receives the Mandate of Heaven, he must perform the Feng and Shan sacrifices.
Feng means
to increase height.
Shan means
to broaden and deepen.
Both involve carving inscriptions on stone to record achievements,
thereby holding oneself accountable.
Heaven regards height as noble,
Earth regards depth as virtuous.
Therefore, by increasing Mount Tài's height,
one demonstrates reverence to Heaven through the Feng sacrifice;
at the base of Liángfǔ Mountain,
one repays Earth.
In the Báihǔ Tōng,
it states: "Feng at Mount Tài
announces great peace and elevates harmonious energy to Heaven.
Offering soil constitutes Feng,
meaning to carry earth,
and building an altar at Mount Tài for sacrifice."
In Xiàng Wēi's Hànshū Zhù,
it is said: "The East
is where all things begin.
Mountains
are the abodes of spiritual energy.
Thus, to seek the origin of things,
one must go to their beginning;
to access their essence,
one must go to their dwelling.
Elevating the altar grounds
is called Feng.
Proclaiming the rise of a new dynasty
is called Shan.
Therefore, Feng and Shan
are the grand ceremonies
by which a king inaugurates his governance."
Yuán Hóng's Hàn Jì
Shénfǔ
Mount Tài has abundant glossy ganoderma and jade stones,
with a grotto-heaven beneath,
spanning three thousand lǐ in circumference,
serving as the abode of spirits and deities.
from "Records of Blessed Lands"
The Heavenly Gate
winds up with twisting paths,
altogether over fifty bends,
passing the Small Heavenly Gate,
and the Great Heavenly Gate.
Looking up at the Heavenly Gate,
it resembles viewing a skylight from a cave.
From the base to the ancient fēngshàn site,
it spans forty lǐ in total.
The western cliff at the mountaintop is the Immortal's Stone Gate,
while the eastern cliff is called Jièqiū.
The Yellow River lies over two hundred lǐ from Mount Tài,
yet from the temple site, it appears as narrow as a ribbon,
as if at the mountain's base.
"Record of Mount Tài"
Rìguān
Southeast Cliff,
named Rìguān.
Rìguān means
when the rooster first crows,
one sees the sun just beginning to rise,
stretching about three zhàng long.
Further southeast,
is named Qínguān.
Qínguān means
one can see Cháng'ān from there.
Wúguān means
one can see Kuàijī from there.
Zhōuguān means
one can see Qí from there.
To the west there is a stone chamber altar,
south of which lies a jade plate,
in the middle stands the Jade Tortoise Mountain.
To the south flank is a divine spring,
drinking its water is extremely clear, sweet, and beneficial to people.
"Records of Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices"
Shénfáng
Within Mount Tài Shān,
there is a divine chamber with ornate pavilions.
"Records of Emperors and Kings"
"Shīzǐ"
Changing the surname to confer a fiefdom
When a new surname assumed the throne and performed the royal rites,
they would enfeoff Mount Tài,
and hold the shàn ceremony at Liángfǔ.
There were seventy-two generations,
with visible traces and boundaries,
and over 1,800 stone inscriptions were carved.
The "Zhuāngzǐ"
records that in ancient times, seventy-two families
enfeoffed Mount Tài and held the shàn ceremony at Liángfǔ,
but what Guǎn Zhòng recorded
amounted to only twelve.
The "Guǎnzǐ"
Jiè Qiū
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Petition on Imperial Feng and Shan Sacrifices" states:
When the Zhou dynasty fish leaped and fell onto the boat,
they offered it in sacrifice by burning.
If such a trivial occurrence could serve as an omen,
then to ascend the great mountain for the Feng sacrifice
would it not be shameful?
"History of the Hàn Dynasty"
Zhēngsì
The Zuo Zhuan:
The Earl of Zhèng requested to discontinue the sacrifices at Mount Tài and instead sacrifice to the Duke of Zhōu,
exchanging the territory of Fēng at Mount Tài for the fields of Xǔ.
Annotation:
Zhèng had assisted in the sacrifices at Mount Tài,
with Tángmù's fief located in Fēng.
The Annals of Duke Yǐn
Gazing at Wú
Yán Yuān and Kǒngzǐ together ascended Mount Tài in Lǔ,
Kǒngzǐ gazed southeast toward the outside of Chāng Gate in Wú,
where there was a tethered white horse,
and pointing it out to Yán Yuān,
said:
"Do you see the Chāng Gate of Wú?"
Yán Yuān replied:
"I see it."
Kǒngzǐ asked:
"What is outside the gate?"
He answered:
"There appears to be something resembling a tied-up white silk ribbon."
Kǒngzǐ covered his eyes and stopped him.
Thereupon they descended together,
but after descending Yán Yuān's hair turned white and his teeth fell out,
and consequently he fell ill and died.
From Lùn Héng
Wǔ Dàfū
Qín Shǐ Huáng gazed upon the mountains and rivers in worship,
then ascended Mount Tài,
when a sudden storm of wind and rain arrived,
so he enfeoffed the tree there as the Fifth Rank Grandee.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
The First Emperor rested beneath a pine tree,
and thus enfeoffed it as the Fifth Rank Grandee.
"Han Official Ceremonials"
Little Heavenly Gate,
where the Fifth Rank Grandee Pine from the Qín dynasty still exists.
"Records of Mount Tài"
Yù Cè
In ancient times, during the Feng and Shan sacrifices at Mount Tài,
according to old accounts from Liángfǔ,
there was a golden casket and jade tallies atop Dài Zōng,
capable of revealing a person's lifespan.
It is known that Emperor Wǔ of Hàn drew a tally bearing the number eighteen,
so he reversed it to read as eighty.
Subsequently, he indeed lived to the age of eighty.
From "Fēngsú Tōng".
Immortal's Lǘ
The Book of Hàn states:
Emperor Wǔ performed the fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài and the chán sacrifice at Shílǘ.
Yìng Shào's commentary says:
Shílǘ is located at the foot of Mount Tài,
and southern locals speak of it as the gate of immortals.
Qǐ Yún
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn performed the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
and white clouds arose from the Fēng altar.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Seeking immortality
Emperor Wǔ sought to attain immortality,
and was advised by those skilled in occult arts:
"The Yellow Emperor achieved immortality only after performing the fēng and shàn sacrifices,"
whereupon he desired to conduct these sacrifices.
The fēng and shàn sacrifices were not regularly performed,
so people of the time knew little about them.
"Records of the Later Han"
Mù Jiǎ
One li and more east of Tiānmén,
one finds Mùjiǎ.
Mùjiǎ was
a deity from the time of Emperor Wǔ.
Above
Divine Pillow
At the foot of Tàishān Mountain,
there was an old man whose name was lost.
When Emperor Wǔ was on an inspection tour,
he saw the old man hoeing by the roadside,
with a white light shining from his head several zhàng high.
"Xiān Zhuàn"
Jìqiū Jūn
Tài Shān dàoshì Jì Qiū Jūn,
during Emperor Wǔ's reign, was rewarded for his Daoist arts,
later when the emperor toured east.
Tài Shān's Jì Qiū Jūn came holding a qin to pay respects to Emperor Wǔ,
saying:
"Your Majesty must not ascend,
for you will surely injure your foot."
The emperor insisted on ascending,
and after going up several li,
the toes of his left and right feet indeed broke,
so he stopped.
"Lièxiān Zhuàn"
Golden couches and jade tables
Mǎ Míng,
a native of Línzī in the state of Qí.
Originally surnamed Hé,
courtesy name Jūnxián,
he served as a county official.
While capturing bandits, he was injured,
nearly dying at the time.
After a long while,
he suddenly saw a woman on the road,
who took a pill from a tube behind her elbow,
as small as a bean,
and gave it to Míng to take.
It immediately healed his wound and stopped the bleeding,
so he followed the goddess to Mount Dài.
In the chamber, steep cliffs rose above and below,
hidden deep over a thousand zhàng above the ground,
with golden beds and jade tables inside,
a place unreachable by human footsteps.
Above,
Clouds form into palace towers.
Emperor Guāngwǔ performed the fēng ceremony at the Shānjū Pavilion,
with officials spread across the fields,
and for several days cloud formations on the mountain took the shape of palace towers,
which all the officials witnessed.
On the evening of the twenty-first day during the animal sacrifice,
a white mist one zhang wide appeared,
stretching far to the southeast,
growing particularly dense at times.
The sky was clear and harmonious, an auspicious sign without clouds,
so it was deemed an omen corresponding to Mount Tài,
with the sun serving as the response.
When the ceremony concluded,
the emperor bowed twice,
and all officials shouted "Long live the emperor!"
Their voices shook the mountains and valleys,
while a mist connected to the heavens,
making the mountain peaks invisible from a distance,
and those on the peaks were unaware they were within the mist.
"Records of the Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices"
To Address a Letter to the Heavenly Emperor
Línzī Cài Zhī,
once went to Mount Tài,
where at the foot of the mountain he saw an official
with very grand ceremonial guards,
who said to him:
"Clerk, deliver a letter for me to my grandson."
The clerk asked:
"Who is your grandson?"
He replied:
"I am the God of Mount Tài,
and my grandson is the Heavenly Emperor."
The clerk, astonished, went out the gate,
mounted a horse and arrived in a short while,
suddenly reaching the Heavenly Emperor's seat in the Tàiwēi Palace.
After Zhī delivered the letter,
the Emperor ordered him to sit and bestowed wine and food upon him,
then comforted and questioned him.
"Liè Yì Zhuàn"
To Write a Letter to the River God
"In Search of the Supernatural":
Hùmŭ Bān of the Later Hàn dynasty once reached the side of Mount Tài,
where he was summoned by the Lord of Mount Tài's Mansion,
who ordered him to deliver a letter to his son-in-law, the River Earl.
The Lord said:
"When you reach the middle of the river,
knock on the boat and call for the blue-clad attendant,
and there will naturally be someone to take the letter."
Indeed, he succeeded in delivering it,
and then delivered a return letter from the River Earl to the Lord of the Mansion.
"Records of Shǔ" states:
King Bān
was the brother-in-law of Kuāng.
Shí Jīn
The recluse Zhāng Zhōng,
lived in seclusion on Mount Tài,
dwelling among cliffs and drinking from valleys,
cultivated the methods of nurturing life,
hewed stone to make cauldrons,
which the people of Mount Tài still emulate today.
"Records of the Former Qín"
Prefect
Emperor Gāozǔ was about to perform the Fēngshàn ceremony at Mount Tài,
but there had been continuous rain for a long time,
so the emperor grew doubtful.
He sent Liú Rénguì to ask Lǐ Bō, a Huàshān Taoist priest,
to petition the Jade Capital Heavenly Emperor.
Bō said:
"We must ask the Prefect of Mount Tài."
Thereupon he summoned him for a long while,
and the Prefect arrived,
paying his respects very reverently.
Bō said:
"The Táng emperor wishes to perform the Fēngshàn ceremony—what do you think?"
He replied:
"He should perform it sixty years later,
and then once more after that."
Bō bowed to him and he left,
at which time Rénguì was standing by Bō's side.
He noticed the Prefect repeatedly glancing at him.
Bō called him back and said:
"This is the Táng prime minister who doesn't recognize you, Prefect,
so please don't take offense."
After the Prefect left,
Bō said to Rénguì:
"The Prefect was somewhat displeased that you, Prime Minister, didn't bow to him,
so he ordered his attendants
to record your name—
that's why I called him back to settle the matter."
Rénguì was terrified and sweating for a long time,
but Bō said:
"The matter has been settled,
so don't worry.
After that, the emperor did perform the Fēngshàn ceremony."
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
Bō was the father of Lǐ Chúnfēng.
The Empress served as the secondary officiant.
Emperor Gāozōng of Táng ascended Fèngshān Mountain to perform the fēng sacrifice,
offering prayers to the earthly deity at Shèshǒu.
The emperor served as the secondary sacrificer,
while Consort Yān of the Yuè Kingdom acted as the final sacrificer.
Some officials secretly laughed at the edict.
According to "Records of Fēng Sacrifices,"
the sacrificial altar was named the Dancing Crane Terrace,
the Jieqiū Altar was called the Longevity Terrace,
and the descending ritual altar was designated as the Auspicious Cloud Terrace,
to commemorate the auspicious signs witnessed at that time.
From the "Old Book of Táng."
Tiānqí Wáng
In the winter of the thirteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Emperor Xuánzōng ascended Mount Tài to perform the fēng sacrifice.
On the evening of the ascent and sacrifice,
the air was dense and gloomy,
with fierce, swift winds.
Emperor Xuánzōng stepped out of the fasting palace,
standing exposed to plead.
By dawn, it cleared,
and the banners hung still.
After the ceremony concluded,
upon reaching the foot of the mountain,
the sun appeared haloed,
radiant with five colors,
and thousands of officials offered congratulations.
That day, a great amnesty was declared,
attributing it to the sacred mountain's clear response,
and the deity of Mount Tài was enfeoffed as the King of Tiānqí.
From "Yuánhé Jùn Guó Zhì"
Lái Sūdùn
Emperor Xuánzōng was conducting the eastern fēng sacrifice,
when the imperial carriage arrived at the Láisū Station west of Mount Tài.
A great wind arose from the northeast,
tearing apart tents and snapping pillars from noon until evening,
frightening everyone.
Zhāng Yuè declared:
"This must be the sea god coming to welcome us."
The emperor
Sān Gōng
The cave of Dàizōng is named Three Palaces, the heaven of emptiness.
"Inner Biography of Máo Jūn"
Mount Tài,
named Péng Xuán,
the heaven of empty peaks,
is where Tàihào serves as the Green Emperor,
governing the Eastern Peak,
presiding over the birth of all things,
examining deceased souls,
and is the abode of ghosts and deities.
It is the mountain where emperors throughout history reported achievements and performed fēng and shàn sacrifices,
corresponding above to the essence of Kuí and Lóu constellations,
and stabilizing below the celestial division of the Lǔ region.
"Collection of Cave Abysses"
Ghost Commander
Dōngyuè Tàishān Jūn,
commands a host of five thousand nine hundred deities,
primarily governing life and death,
and is the chief commander of all ghosts.
He is the one revered in blood sacrifices and temple worship.
The ghost shrines worshipped by common folk,
the spirits of essence,
and the deceased all return to Tàishān to undergo judgment for their sins.
Golden Rooster
The Zhou Changes' Divination Categories says:
Mount Tài loses its golden rooster.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
The golden rooster
is the essence of Mount Tài.
There are no venomous insects.
Mount Tài is the highest among all the mountains along the route,
with towering peaks rising majestically,
overlooking numerous hills.
Its mists, clouds, plants, and trees flourish abundantly,
creating a mystical realm of divine wonders,
hence there are no venomous insects or fierce beasts.
"Records of Campaigns"
Fènggāo
is the location of Mount Tài, the Eastern Peak,
straddling the boundary between Yíng and Bó counties.
When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn performed the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
he designated this county to supply the rituals for Mount Tài,
hence it was called
Fènggāo. Thirty lǐ away,
lies the tomb of the Yánlíng child.
From Qiū Yuānzhī's "Records of Qí"
Jiāoyáo
If the paths of the sun and moon do not span a thousand miles,
They cannot illuminate the six directions and shine upon the eight poles;
If Mount Tài is not lofty and towering,
It cannot gather dense clouds and disperse rising vapors.
"The Guest's Difficulty"
Jǐn Fù
Yáng Qiáo said:
"Like dust clinging to Mount Tài,
or dew gathering in the vast sea.
Though it brings no real benefit,
my sincere feelings still dare not remain silent.
From Xiè Chéng's Book"
Selling Medicine
Cuī Wénzǐ was a native of Tàishān,
who was fond of the arts of Huáng-Lǎo.
He lived in seclusion at the foot of the mountain,
making yellow pills and selling medicine.
Those afflicted with epidemic diseases,
upon drinking his medicine, would recover immediately.
From "Biographies of Exemplary Immortals"
Liángfǔ
Mount Tài is on the left ridge,
the father is on the right ridge,
the father knows life,
Liángfǔ knows death,
the king fēngs Mount Tài,
and shàn Liángfǔ.
"Kāishān Tú"
Tàibái
Descending Wing Quail sinks,
to bear the Western Sea,
its spirit presides over Huàshān,
where Tàibái holds position.
Huà Shān
The Western Peak Huàshān,
where the lesser yin holds sway,
and all things bloom with splendor,
hence it is called Huàshān.
In the "Báihǔ Tōng",
it is said the mountain bears a pond,
where thousand-petaled lotuses grow,
and consuming them leads to ascension, thus it is named Huàshān.
From the "Huàshān Jì".
Èr Huá
"Rhapsody on the Western Capital":
Adorned with the two Huà mountains.
"Classic of Mountains and Seas":
The Tàihuà Mountain,
is steep and square.
Its height is five thousand ren,
its breadth spans a thousand li.
The Xiǎohuà Mountain,
on its southern side has much jade of túfú.
Annotation:
That is Shàohuà.
God created
Huà Shān faces Shǒuyáng Shān across the river in Hédōng,
with the Huáng Hé flowing between the two mountains.
An ancient saying states:
This was originally one mountain blocking the river,
causing the river water to bend as it passed.
The river deity Jù Líng,
used his hands to split open the mountain above,
and stepped with his feet to separate it below,
dividing it into two parts in the middle,
to allow the river to flow through.
Today, on the peak, the shape of fingers and palm remains,
and at the foot of Shǒuyáng Shān, footprints are also preserved.
The "Annotations to the Rhapsody on the Western Capital"
mention a being named Jù Líng Hú,
who fully attained the Way of the Divine Origin,
and could create mountains and rivers, bringing forth rivers.
The "Chart of Opening Mountains"
describes the river spirit as vigorous and leaping,
palming Huà and treading on Xiāng.
Yáng Xióng's "Rhapsody on Hédōng"
states: South of Hù County in Yōngzhōu,
there is Jìtóu Shān,
which was originally a boatman,
who moored his boat at its summit,
hence the name.
In the past, when Tàiyǐ had not yet separated the mountains and seas,
Tàiháng and Wángwū,
along with the Báilù River water,
halted in this region,
called the mountain and sea.
When the great being Jù Líng, Qín Gǒnghǎi,
was troubled by the vastness of the water,
he propped up Tàihuà with his left palm,
and stepped on Zhōngtiáo with his right foot,
causing Tàiyǐ to split apart,
the river flowed through and the land emerged,
and the mountains thus became high and prominent.
As stated in "Zhāng Huá's Rhapsody":
Jù Líng, with immense strength,
raised his palm high and stepped far,
to make the river bend flow.
"The Pearl Forest of the Dharma Garden"
Sìhé
The "Record of Huàshān" states:
Huàshān has high cliffs surrounding it on four sides,
with layered ridges rising elegantly.
On its summit, there is a stone pond,
and to the north, a stone drum.
The elders pass down a tale:
There was once someone who heard it sound.
Èr Cén
Huàshān has two peaks,
soaring straight up thousands of ren,
from the base, the smaller peaks rise in elegant layers,
extending all the way to the ridge,
as if carved by a knife.
"Records of Campaigns"
Sānfēng
On the mountain stand three peaks,
soaring straight into the clear sky,
offering views of what are called the Lotus and Maonǚ junipers.
"Mountain Records"
Èr Quán
Atop Mount Huàshān, about seven lǐ high,
there are two sacred springs,
one named Púchí,
the other Tàishàngquán.
Above
courtyard
Huàshān Middle Road,
named Tiānjǐng.
It barely allows a person to pass,
winding and turning steeply upward,
reaching a height of over six zhàng.
On the mountain, there is a trickle of fine water,
that flows into the well without wetting people,
and emerging from the well to gaze at the sky and view the moon,
is like looking through a window from inside a room.
"Commentary on the Water Classic"
Liánhuā Fēng
Above are three peaks,
reaching up to connect with the three lights,
within which lie twenty-eight stone pools.
They correspond to the twenty-eight constellations,
with green pines and verdant bamboos,
clustering on the high ridges,
white clouds and emerald mists,
circling the secluded hills,
embracing hidden gold and jade,
storing winds and thunder,
serving as the detached palace of the Great Emperor,
and indeed the dwelling place of immortals.
It is also called Tàishàng Shān.
"Records of the Zhāowén Hall"
Dūnwù
Huàshān,
in ancient texts known as Dūnwù Shān.
"Shuǐ Jīng Zhù"
Jade Maiden
On Huàshān, there is the Bright Star Jade Maiden,
who holds jade nectar; if one obtains and drinks it,
they immediately attain the path to immortality,
but the path is perilous and inaccessible.
"Shī Hán Shénwù"
states: The Bright Star Jade Maiden
dwells on Huàshān,
drinks jade nectar,
and ascends to heaven in broad daylight.
On the mountain peak, there is a stone turtle,
covering several acres in area,
and thirty feet high.
By its side, there is a ladder,
with steps visible from afar.
In front of the Jade Maiden Temple,
there are five stone mortars,
known as the Jade Maiden's Hair-Washing Basins.
The water within is emerald green and crystal clear,
not overflowing even in rain,
nor diminishing during drought.
Inside the temple, there is a horse of the Jade Maiden.
"Jí Xiān Lù"
records: This horse is extraordinarily divine,
its neighing is heard at night,
and hermits on the peak often see it.
"Shān Zhì"
Cypress Arrow
King Zhāo of Qín ordered craftsmen to erect hooked ladders and ascend Huà Mountain,
where they used pine and cypress heartwood to make a board,
with arrows eight chǐ long,
and game pieces eight cùn long,
inscribing upon it:
"King Zhāo once played a game here with the heavenly gods."
Hánzǐ
The Lost Jade Disc
In the thirty-sixth year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
a traveler named Zhèng came from east of the Hángu Pass and reached Huàyīn,
where he saw a plain carriage with white horses
descending from the mountain.
Knowing it was no ordinary being,
he stopped and waited for it.
It then arrived and handed a jade disc to the traveler Zhèng,
saying:
"Deliver this for me to the Lord of Hàochí.
Next year, the First Dragon will die."
Records of the Grand Historian
Máo Nǚ
Máo Nǚ was
in the Huàyīn Mountains,
where mountain travelers and hunters
have seen her through generations.
Her body covered in hair, she claimed
to be a palace maid of Qín Shǐ Huáng.
"Biographies of Exemplary Immortals"
Stone couch
Xiū Yánggōng was a man of Wèi,
who lived on Huàyīn Mountain.
In a stone chamber there was a hanging rock,
upon which he would lie on his couch to sleep,
until the rock became completely worn and sunken.
He ate very little,
occasionally taking some huángjīng to eat.
Later, he sought an audience with Emperor Jǐng using the Dào.
The Emperor asked him:
"What abilities do you possess, sir?"
Xiū Yánggōng did not reply,
but instead turned into stone.
Inscribed on his back were the words:
"Xiū Yánggōng thanks the Son of Heaven."
Later, the stone sheep was placed at the Tōnglíng Terrace,
but the sheep disappeared again, and no one knew where it had gone.
Jílíng Gōng
At the foot of Huàshān, there is the Jílíng Palace.
Emperor Wǔ intended to gather immortals,
thus naming the hall the Gate of Preserving Immortals,
and the Tower of Gazing at Immortals.
From the "Preface to Huán Tán's Rhapsody on Immortals,"
a divine horse emerged from Huàshān.
The emperor ordered it to be stabled within the palace,
but the horse did not stay long.
He sent people to search for it,
and they found it beneath a stone niche in this mountain valley.
Hence, it was named the Valley of the Hidden Horse,
and the Niche of the Hidden Horse.
In the northeastern stream,
the horse's hoofprints are still preserved on the rocks.
From the "Mountain Records."
Driving a deer
Wèi Shūqīng often rode clouds and drove a white deer,
appeared before Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
who intended to make him a minister,
but Shūqīng left without speaking.
The emperor regretted it,
found his son Dùshì,
and ordered him to pursue his father.
Dùshì ascended Mount Huà,
where he saw his father playing a board game with several people on a rock,
and Shūqīng instructed Dùshì to return.
"Biographies of the Immortals"
Riding a Dragon
Hū Zǐxiān was
a fortune-teller at the Hànyáng Pass during the Hàn Dynasty.
He lived over a hundred years.
Before departing, he called to the old woman from the wine shop,
urgently saying, "Prepare quickly, and I shall go with you."
That night, immortals arrived,
holding two straw dogs.
They called to Zǐxiān,
who took one and gave it to the old woman.
Once she received it, they mounted them together,
and the mounts turned out to be dragons.
They ascended Huàyīn Mountain,
where he often shouted loudly,
declaring, "Zǐxiān and the wine mother are here."
(From "Biographies of the Immortals")
Jīnyè
Mǎ Míngshēng studied under Master Ānqī,
receiving the formula for the Golden Elixir Divine Pill,
then entered Huàyīn Mountain,
where he compounded the Golden Elixir but chose not to ascend to heaven,
consuming only half the dose to become an earthly immortal.
End.
Jade Slip
Shí Jìlóng sent someone to gather herbs,
and they descended Huàshān to obtain a jade slip.
"Records of the Former Yān"
Catching lice
Wáng Měng lived in seclusion on Huàshān,
when Huán Wēn entered the pass,
Měng wore coarse clothing and visited him,
discussing contemporary affairs at their first meeting,
picking lice while speaking,
as if no one else was around.
End
Yúntái Fēng
Northeast of the mountain lies Yúntái Peak,
where two peaks stand lofty and steep,
precipitous on all sides,
capped by radiant clouds above,
and connecting to the earth's veins below.
Towering in solitary splendor,
it features a Cloud Terrace,
with a cave beneath.
In the past, someone entered this cave
and emerged east of the mountain, claiming:
"I passed beneath the Yellow River,
hearing the sound of flowing water overhead."
During Emperor Wǔ of the Northern Zhōu dynasty,
a Taoist named Jiāo Dàoguǎng
lived alone on this peak,
abstaining from grains and consuming mist.
Three azure birds often foretold future events to him.
Emperor Wǔ personally visited the mountain retreat,
approaching the terrace to inquire about the Way.
Consequently, Yúntái Temple was established at the valley entrance.
Later, his disciples Hóng Xiān and others
witnessed Dàoguǎng riding a creature resembling a qilin,
departing never to return.
To the southeast lies Shéntǔ Cliff,
where through Dàoguǎng's profound meditation,
when he wished to construct buildings,
divine soil emerged from the stone,
replenishing itself when depleted,
a phenomenon that persists to this day.
Within the cliff wall resides an immortal oil vessel,
whenever Dàoguǎng performed ceremonies,
heaven would send oil into it.
But since Dàoguǎng
rode away on the qilin,
this oil has never reappeared.
"Mountain Records"
Sùlíng Palace
Mǎ Zhōu was
an immortal official of the Sùlíng Palace on Huàshān.
When the Táng dynasty was about to receive the Mandate of Heaven, the Supreme Elder commanded him
to descend and assist the nation, but he became addicted to wine,
sinking into the worldly dust for over twenty years.
Yuán Tiāngāng read his physiognomy and predicted his impending death,
instructing him to follow an old man riding an ox inside,
saying:
"The old man looked back and saw him."
He told him:
"You were originally an immortal official of the Sùlíng Palace,
now the Immortal King of Tàihuà has sent someone to summon you."
He was then led into the palace gates,
arriving before a curtain where someone declared and reprimanded him,
then sent him to another courtyard.
Looking at the gate inside,
he saw his name inscribed there.
Suddenly five figures dressed in five-directional colors
stood before him saying:
"We are the deities of your five vital organs.
You have indulged excessively in wine and wandered aimlessly,
defiling and dishonoring your body,
so we have long departed from you."
They told him to close his eyes to return to the divine chamber.
When Mǎ Zhōu closed his eyes for a moment,
he suddenly felt his mind clear and enlightened,
remembering events from over twenty years prior
as if they had happened just ten days ago.
During the Zhēnguàn era, he repeatedly held high offices,
until one day a group of immortals descended to his chamber saying:
"Your merit in assisting the state is accomplished,
it is time to withdraw.
The Great Unity summons you,
you may no longer remain."
The next day,
he passed away without illness.
"Supplementary Records of Immortal Biographies"
Zhù Mèng
Péi Jì was initially poor,
with no means to establish himself.
He often walked to the capital on foot,
passing by the Huàyuè Temple to offer sacrifices and pray:
"In such poverty and hardship,
I dare to cultivate sincerity in my visit,
if the deity has spiritual power,
please observe my fate and fortune.
If wealth and honor are within reach,
may you bestow an auspicious dream."
After bowing twice, he left.
That night, he dreamed of a white-haired elder who said to him:
"After you reach thirty years of age,
you will then achieve your ambitions,
ultimately attaining the highest position among officials."
(Old Book of Táng)
The deity proclaimed
Lǐ Jìng was initially distressed by poverty and low status,
and once passed by the Huàshān Temple,
where he poured out his grievances to the deity,
even asking to be informed of his future official rank.
His words and expression were resolute and stern,
astonishing the onlookers.
He stood for a long while before leaving,
and after walking about a hundred steps out of the temple gate,
he heard a loud voice from behind saying:
"Farewell, Vice Director Lǐ."
Turning to look,
he saw no one behind him.
In the end, he rose to the highest ministerial position.
"Supplement to the National History"
Xiào Huá
Minister of Agriculture Zhào Lǚwēn,
for Princess Ānlè's estate,
constructed piled stones resembling Mount Huà,
with slanting bridges and paths,
winding pools with nine turns,
channeling water through stone conduits.
"History of the Táng Dynasty"
Jīn Tiānwáng
Emperor Xuánzōng was born in the year Yǐyǒu,
taking Mount Huà as his fate-determining sacred site.
In the seventh month of the second year of the Xiāntiān era, he ascended the throne,
and on the Guǐchǒu day of the eighth month,
he enfeoffed the deity of Mount Huà as the Golden Heavenly King.
"Old Records"
The mountain deity came forth to greet
the imperial carriage, which halted at the foot of Huàyīn Mountain.
The mountain deity appeared several miles ahead to welcome them,
so the emperor summoned the various shamans to inquire about the deity's well-being.
Only the old shaman Ā Mǎpó reported:
"He is by the roadside,
dressed in vermilion and purple robes, awaiting Your Majesty."
The emperor looked back and laughed at this.
When the emperor reached the temple,
he saw the deity clad in armor,
prostrating under a large cypress tree in the southeast of the courtyard.
He again summoned Ā Mǎpó to question her,
and her response matched what had been seen before.
The emperor then showed increased reverence.
He personally composed and inscribed a stele text,
to honor the deity exceptionally.
The stele was over fifty feet tall,
more than ten feet wide,
and four feet thick,
unmatched by any other stele in the world.
From "Records of Trustworthy Accounts":
It says, Mount Tàihuà stands in the central plains,
occupying the western flank at the rightful position of the seven celestial palaces,
embracing the Táolín Pass to the left,
and yielding fields of blue jade to the right.
It is surely the lower capital of Shǎohào,
and the separate lodge of Rùshōu.
Emperor Xuān traveled here
to assemble the multitude of deities;
Emperor Yú offered burnt sacrifices here
to observe the various lords.
Below, there are alchemists and true humans,
golden tripods and stone chambers;
above, there are the Bright Star and Jade Maiden,
with immortal herbs and jade pools.
From "Literary Essence"
Wèngdù Fēng
At Huàyuè's Yúntái Temple,
there was a mountain rising abruptly on the central plateau,
shaped like half a jar,
named Jàr-Belly Peak.
The emperor admired the view from above,
praising its lofty isolation,
and wished to carve the characters "Kāiyuán" on the belly of the peak.
They were to be filled with white stone,
making them visible from over a hundred lǐ away.
An admonishing official submitted a memorial,
and the plan was halted.
From "Records of Credible Accounts."
Raw Gold
Lǐ Shìzhī once contended for power with Lǐ Línfǔ and was at odds with him.
Línfǔ, being treacherous and fond of flattery,
said to Shìzhī:
"Mount Huà produces gold,
mining it could enrich the state.
It's just that the Emperor is unaware of it."
Shìzhī, being straightforward by nature,
believed his words.
Another day, he casually mentioned it to the Emperor.
The Emperor, pleased, asked Línfǔ about it.
He replied:
"I have known about this for a long time.
However, Mount Huà is Your Majesty's destiny,
the abode of imperial aura,
and should not be excavated or disturbed.
That is why I did not dare to report it."
The Emperor thought Línfǔ cared for him,
and regarded Shìzhī with disdain for not being close.
"Book of Táng"
On the seventh day, submit the accounts.
Lǐ Shí from Zhào Commandery,
during the Kāiyuán era,
visited the Huà Mountain Temple,
passing by the Three Ladies' Courtyard,
when he suddenly saw goddesses,
all appearing as living humans,
who invited him into a precious tent.
There they repeatedly shared intimacy with him.
At parting, they told Lǐ Shí:
"Every year from the seventh to the twelfth day of the seventh month,
the Mountain God must report to Heaven.
At that time,
do not decline when we come to welcome you.
Our meeting today
also coincides with this period,
hence we could fully enjoy ourselves."
From then on for seven years,
he met with them each year.
When he asked about his official career, they said:
"You should pass the imperial examinations,
but end up only as a minor county magistrate."
Everything happened as they predicted.
"Guǎng Yì Jì"
A Letter to Běihǎi
In the early years of the Kāiyuán era,
a Sānwèi officer was returning from the capital to Qīngzhōu.
When he reached the front of the Huàyuè Temple,
he saw a woman with a sorrowful and haggard appearance who said:
"I am no longer among the living.
I am the third daughter-in-law of the Huàyuè deity.
My husband is extremely cruel,
and his home is in Běihǎi.
For three years, I have had no letters.
Hearing that you are returning from afar,
I wish to trouble you with a letter.
At the second tree by the seaside pool,
just knock on it,
and someone will respond."
After speaking, she bid farewell and left.
When he reached Běihǎi,
he delivered the letter as instructed.
After reading the letter, the recipient was furious,
and then issued orders to march west to attack Huàshān.
He commanded his attendants to fetch two bolts of silk
and gave them to the messenger, the Sānwèi officer.
Later, when he arrived at Huáyīn,
he encountered the same woman again,
who bowed in gratitude.
She said:
"Sānláng is angry with you
for delivering the letter and leading troops
to harm you at Tóngguān.
You should return to the capital immediately.
Soon, the imperial procession will journey east,
and ghosts and spirits fear the drum carriage.
If you ride in the drum carriage,
you will have nothing to worry about."
A few days later,
Emperor Xuánzōng traveled to Luòyáng,
and the Sānwèi officer followed the drum carriage out of the pass.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
Ascending Mount Huàshān
Hán Wéngōng ascended to the peak of Huàshān,
gazing upon its extreme seclusion and peril,
his heart palpitating and vision blurring,
unable to descend,
he cried out frantically and wept,
sent a letter to his family,
bade farewell to the magistrate of Huàyīn,
and only after numerous attempts was he able to come down.
"Supplement to the National History"
Ascending Lotus Peak
Wáng Xuánzhòng wished to ascend Lotus Peak,
and arranged with a temple monk that upon reaching the summit,
he would light smoke as a signal.
The next day, he carried fire and climbed up.
The monk waited for several days,
and indeed smoke rose.
Wáng Xuánzhòng stayed for twenty days,
then descended again.
The monk asked him about it, and he said:
"On the peak, there is a pond,
where lotus flowers bloomed beautifully and delightfully,
and within it, a broken iron boat remains.
"San Shui Xiao Lu"
Paying Respects at the Mountain
Among the Dōngyí people was one who knew mountains.
He traveled to worship at all Five Sacred Mountains,
bowing once at each before withdrawing,
except when he reached Wàngguān Huàshān.
Starting from the western gate of the pass, he worshipped with ritual,
then gazed upward from the mountain's base for seven days,
before sighing in amazement and departing.
He declared that the flourishing of culture and refinement in the capital
originated from this place.
"Yǔlín"
Interrogating Yuè Líng
Lè Kūn,
formerly named Chōng Lěi,
failed the imperial examinations repeatedly.
In the twelfth year of the Yuánhé era, he gave up the exams and headed east,
arriving at Huàyīn where he prayed at the mountain temple at night,
seeking divination on whether to advance or retreat.
At midnight, he suddenly dreamed of a person in blue attire,
who checked the register and reported:
"Next year there is a Lè Kūn,
whose name is already in the underworld records,
but Lè Chōng is not found."
Chōng then changed his name to Kūn,
and the following year, as foretold, after the spring examinations,
he passed by the mountain temple to give thanks,
and again prayed for an official position.
In a dream, the temple registrar
stated he would only serve four terms as a prefect,
and he indeed ended his life in Yǐngzhōu."
(Yúnxī Yǒuyì)
In the second year of the Shangyuan era,
Mount Huà was renamed
as
Mount Tài.
In the first year of the Bǎoyìng era, its former name was restored.
"Treatise on Geography"
Tàijí Zǒng Xiān
Huàshān is known as the Celestial Domain of the Supreme Immortals,
where Shǎohào, as the White Emperor, governs the Western Peak,
aligning above with the essence of the constellations Jǐng and Guǐ,
and stabilizing below the territorial division of the Qín region.
"Records of the Grotto-Heavens"
Yíng Huò
The constellation Starry Dipper and Quail's Tail,
bearing the Southern Sea,
has its deity presiding over Mount Héng,
where Mars takes its position.
Bǎodòng
Mount Héng of the Southern Peak,
the divine terrace of Zhūlíng,
the precious cavern of Tàixū,
receives the obscure constellations above,
weighing virtue and balancing things,
hence named Héng (Balancing) Mountain.
Below it occupies the palace of Fire,
governing the position in the fiery region,
thus called the Red Emperor of the Southern Peak.
He lodges on its ridges,
while Zhùróng dwells on its southern face,
majestic and awe-inspiring in divine power,
casting towering shadows,
thus making it an abode for spirits,
a dwelling place for immortals.
"Records of the Southern Peak"
Its constellation lies at Zhěn and Yì,
its measure corresponds to the celestial balance,
hence named Héng Mountain.
The mountain possesses brocade stones,
brilliantly forming patterns.
"Records of Xiāngzhōng"
Gǒulǒu
Mount Héng is commonly known as Gǒulǒu.
According to the "Annotations on the Classic of Mountains and Seas"
and the "Records of Central Xiāng":
There is a jade tablet on Mount Gǒulǒu.
Yǔ studied its inscriptions
to control the floods,
and thus the Yǔ Stele exists.
As Hán Yù's poem says:
On the peak of Mount Gǒulǒu stands the divine Yǔ Stele,
Its characters blue, the stone crimson, in wondrous form.
with Qián Huò as deputy
The Southern Mountain ranges eight hundred li in circumference,
with Huíyàn as its head,
and Lùyuè as its foot.
The "Records of the Southern Mountain"
state: Mount Héng
has one peak so exceedingly high
that geese cannot fly over it.
When spring arrives, they turn back northward,
hence the name Huíyàn (Returning Goose).
Some say the peak's shape resembles a goose turning back,
thus the name.
The "Geographical Records"
cite Dù Xúnhè's poem:
"By nightfall, monkeys cry atop Yuèlù Peak;
Geese, knowing spring's call, bid Héngyáng farewell."
Wǔfēng
Mount Héngshān soars loftily over nine thousand zhang high,
with a hierarchy of peaks,
featuring seventy-two peaks, caves, streams, ravines, springs, and rocks of scenic beauty,
interwoven throughout.
Additionally, there are several dozen caves,
fifteen cliffs,
thirty-eight springs,
twenty-five streams,
nine ponds,
nine deep pools,
six sources,
eight grottoes,
nine wells,
three perforations,
and three leaks.
The most notable among these
are the seventy-two peaks.
The five largest are
Fúróng,
Zǐgài,
Shílǐn,
Tiānzhù,
and Zhùróng,
with Zhùróng being the highest.
"Chángshā Zhì"
Sānfēng
Mount Héng has three peaks.
One is called Zǐgài Peak,
where the sky is clear and bright,
and a pair of white cranes soar and circle above it.
One peak is named Shíqūn,
beneath which lies a stone chamber,
from within which the sound of chanting is often heard.
One peak is called Fúróng Peak,
the most towering and majestic of all.
Unless the weather is clear and rain has just ceased,
it cannot be seen in the early morning.
On the peak, a flying spring is visible,
its stream like a bolt of silk,
reflecting against the green woods,
and plunging straight down to the foot of the mountain.
Jiǔ Xiàng
Mount Héngshān and Jiǔyí,
both have temples of Shùn.
From afar, Mount Héngshān appears like layered clouds;
along the Xiāng River for a thousand lǐ,
it is seen nine times facing and nine times with its back turned,
until it is no longer visible.
"Records of the Xiāng Region"
Shí Qūn
Liú Línzhī loved to roam the mountains and marshes,
gathering herbs until he ventured deep into Héngshān, forgetting to return.
He came across a stream,
with two stone granaries south of the water,
one open and one closed.
The water was too deep to cross,
and as he tried to turn back, he lost his way.
He met a woodcutter and asked for directions,
barely managing to return home.
Some said that within the granaries
were all immortal elixirs and medicinal recipes.
Línzhī wished to search for them again,
but he never again found the location.
From the "Jìn Shū".
Holding the brush
Xiāngdōng Yáo Zǔ,
toward the end of the Tàiyuán era, served as a commandery clerk.
While passing by Héngshān, he gazed at the cliffs below,
where several young men
were all holding brushes and writing.
Zǔ thought they were fellow travelers resting,
so he made a detour to approach them.
Before he could get within a hundred paces or so,
the young men together suddenly soared up and flew away.
From *Yì Yuàn*
Resting Carriage
In the decade of Gūxiǎn,
I first reached Héngyuè,
so I borrowed a light carriage,
and drove swiftly through the night.
I rested the carriage on white stones,
bathed my reflection by the water's edge,
gazed up at the emerald peaks,
distant against the horizon,
my body soaring into the vast clarity,
alone communing with the rosy clouds.
"Huán Xuán's Preface Poem on Mountain Travel"
Holding a Book
Initially, there was one who gathered herbs on Mount Héng,
and saw an old man
with four or five youths,
sitting opposite each other holding books.
The "Jīngzhōu Records"
He built a house
Zǒng Bǐng sought out famous mountains,
traveling west to Jīng and Wū,
and south ascending Héngyuè.
Thus he built a house on Mount Héng,
wishing to embrace Shàng Píng's aspiration.
"Book of Sòng"
A Stranger Bestows a Technique
Shēn Tàizhī, styled Yuánzhī,
abandoned worldly life to cultivate the Way.
He once ascended the Southern Peak (Nányuè),
where he encountered an extraordinary man who taught him the art of the Golden Elixir and Fire Dragon,
enabling him to ride the void in spiritual journeys,
his appearances and disappearances, comings and goings, being unfathomable.
In the early Tiānbǎo era,
he was ordered by imperial decree to offer sacrifices at Luófú Mountain,
and there he sought out and found the Zhūmíng Cave.
On the way, he met another extraordinary man,
who informed him that at Jiǔyí Mountain,
there was formerly a set of celestial music,
which over the years had transformed into five wild boars.
The local people captured them,
and they then transformed into five ancient vessels.
Tàizhī traveled back and forth,
and also managed to find them.
When he struck them,
their tones harmonized in musical accord.
He told his disciples:
"This must surely be an omen.
Twenty years from now, there will be a corresponding event."
And indeed, when Ān Lùshān revealed his rebellious intentions,
his appearance was plump like a pig,
commonly called a 'pig-dragon.'
He had once stolen the Líyuán music troupe
and made them perform at the Níngbì Pond,
which was then said to be the fulfillment of the prophecy."
(From "Immortal Biographies")
I wish to live in seclusion.
Cuī Yuán and
Lǐ Fǔguó, because Lǐ Mì was trusted and favored by Emperor Sùzōng,
were jealous of him.
Fearing disaster,
Lǐ Mì wished to retreat to Héng Shān.
An imperial edict granted him the salary of a third-rank official,
bestowed upon him the attire of a recluse,
and built a residence for him.
"Táng Chuán"
records that Lǐ Mì studied at Héng Yuè Temple,
startled by Lǎn Cán,
who said:
"This is no ordinary man."
In the middle of the night, Lǐ Mì secretly went to pay his respects.
Lǎn Cán invited him to sit,
lit a fire and brought out taro,
offering it to Lǐ Mì to eat,
saying:
"Be careful not to speak too much,
and you shall attain the position of prime minister for ten years."
Lǐ Mì bowed and withdrew,
later assuming the position of prime minister.
In the month of his death, the palace envoy Lín Yuǎn,
encountered Lǐ Mì at an inn in Lán Guān,
riding alone in ordinary attire,
saying he was temporarily going to Héng Shān.
They spoke of the old days through three reigns,
parting sorrowfully after a long while.
When Lín Yuǎn reached Cháng'ān,
he then heard of Lǐ Mì's death.
"Yè Hóu Jiā Zhuàn"
Visiting the Mountain Temple
During the Dàlì era, Dù Fǔ
left Qútáng,
went down to Jiānglíng,
sailed up the Yuán and Xiāng rivers,
to ascend Héng Shān,
and consequently lodged at the Lěiyáng Yuè Temple.
From the "Táng Shū"
Immortal Mountain
Lǐ Bái bids farewell to Lord Lín traveling to Mount Héngyuè,
the immortal mountain south of the river,
with the refreshing air of Huánghè,
then ascends the peaks of Zhùróng,
gazing upon the misty fires of Chángshā.
As the foremost peak
among the Five Great Mountains in central China,
Mount Héng is the most remote.
Among the southern mountains,
those towering high and grand
number in the hundreds,
yet only Héng stands as the foremost.
Being the most remote yet uniquely paramount,
its deity must be divine.
Master Liào, a native of Chēnzhōu, studied at Mount Héng.
