and wished to approach it.
Shàojūn said:
"This stone is toxic,
it may be gazed upon but not approached."
"Records of Forgotten Tales"
Jiéshí
The "Treatise on Geography" states:
The Great Jiéshí Mountain lies to the right,
in Běipíng's Lí City,
southwest of the county, Emperor Wǔ once climbed it,
to gaze upon the vast sea,
and had an inscription carved on the stone here.
Now by the sea, there is a stone,
like a passageway extending for several tens of lǐ,
at the mountain's summit,
there is a large stone shaped like a pillar,
often seen rising from the vast sea,
when the tide rises high,
and when the tidal waves recede,
it remains unmoving and unsubmerged,
its depth unknown,
the world names it the Pillar of the Heavenly Bridge.
Wéi Zhāo also identified this as the Jiéshí.
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Fossil
In Línhè Féngchéng County,
five li east there is an old county temple.
Legend says when Huáinán King Liú Ān of Hàn was executed,
his son fled and arrived here,
then suddenly turned into a stone figure overnight,
standing right at the county gate.
The common people found it strange and went to see it,
but those who approached too closely
all developed sores and festering on their hands and feet.
"Records of Jīngzhōu"
Shílì
During the Yuánfèng era of Emperor Zhāo,
south of Láiwú Mountain in Tàishān,
a large stone stood upright by itself,
supported by three stones as feet.
Where the stone stood,
thousands of white birds gathered nearby.
Suī Mèng believed that stones belong to the yin category below,
representing the common people, while Mount Tài
is the sacred peak of Dàizōng where kings
announce changes of dynasty and campaigns.
He predicted there would be a commoner becoming the Son of Heaven.
Suī Mèng was consequently executed.
"Records of the Five Elements"
During Emperor Āi's reign, in Wúyán,
soil from Wēi Mountain rose by itself,
covering the grass like galloping.
It was reported again that mountain stones turned and stood upright.
King Dōngpíng Yún and his queen,
Yè, went to the stone themselves,
sacrificed to and venerated the stone,
imitating the standing stone at Hù Mountain,
binding double grass and offering sacrifices together.
Those who understood disasters and anomalies,
such as Gāo Shàng, said:
"The standing stone is an omen of Emperor Xuān's rise.
Xīfū Gōng reported it,
the king committed suicide, and Queen Yè was executed in the market."
"Basic Biography"
Zhī Jī
In Chéngdū,
the Weaving-lady Stone at the Divination Market,
was obtained by a seafarer from the Milky Way,
and the Weaving Maiden instructed him to inquire of Yán Jūnpíng about it.
The Grand Commandant, the Duke of Dūnhuáng, being fond of curiosities,
ordered a piece to be carved off,
intending to make it into a utensil.
During the carving process,
the craftsman suddenly suffered a dizzy spell,
and it fell onto the stone.
Those beside it, the Three Dukes,
recognized its spiritual nature,
and thus it was halted.
It has now become jade.
"Records of Spiritual Manifestations"
also mentions the heavens.
Swallowing a Literary Stone
Wǔlù Chōngzōng
studied under Mí Chéngzǐ.
Mí Chéngzǐ once encountered a person
who gave him a patterned stone resembling an egg.
Chéngzǐ swallowed it
and subsequently became exceptionally intelligent.
Later, when Chéngzǐ fell ill,
he vomited out this stone
and gave it to Chōngzōng.
After swallowing it, he too became renowned for his scholarship.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Xiàozǐ Shí
Kuí Xiàng Shūtōng,
was a native of Qiándào.
He was extremely filial to his mother.
Whenever she desired water from the main current of the river,
Xiàng would draw it in both winter and summer.
One day, a transverse rock appeared in the main current,
enabling Shūtōng to draw water from it.
The rock in the river
was named the Filial Son Rock.
"Records of Shǔ"
states that Xiàng was recommended as Xiàolián during Emperor Āi's reign,
and served as a court gentleman under Emperor Píng.
"Chronicles of Huáyáng"
Shāo Shí
Yǔ Xǔ served as the governor of Wǔdū.
About thirty lǐ east of Xiàbiàn,
there was a spring in a gorge,
where water flowed over large rocks,
blocking the watercourse,
causing overflow every spring and summer.
By autumn,
it damaged crops and flooded settlements.
Yǔ Xǔ then had people burn the rocks,
pouring water on them,
causing the rocks to crack.
They then chiseled away the rocks,
eliminating the flood hazard.
"Continuation of Histories"
Lǐ Xì,
courtesy name Bó Dū,
served as governor of Wǔdū.
The road through the western gorge of the commandery,
was dangerously steep and obstructed,
with walkways along cliffs,
sheer cliffs on both sides,
and unfathomable streams below,
frequently causing overturning and falling hazards.
He ordered the canal officials and others,
following the regular labor service route,
to burn and break through,
carving through the towering heights,
reducing high areas to lower ones,
making it passable even at night.
The people sang of his virtuous kindness,
and carved a stone to praise him.
"Collection of Metal and Stone Inscriptions"
Battle Formations
Upstream from Mǐanyáng City,
fifteen lǐ on the Hàn River,
stands the fortress guarded by Zhūgě Wǔhóu,
located south of the Hàn River,
backed by mountains and facing the water gate.
Stones were piled up to suppress the water,
yet they deteriorated,
their alignment with the water,
when washed away, would always return to their original state.
From the "Liángchuān Jì".
Grindstone
Wèi Wén was hosting a banquet for various literary scholars in the Eastern Palace,
and had Lady Zhēn come out to pay respects.
Liú Zhēn looked up at her,
prompting Wǔ Dì to punish him in anger,
ordering him to be exiled for labor at the rear palace.
The Emperor went to the Shangfang workshop,
to inspect,
and saw Zhēn sitting grinding stones without moving.
Tài Zǔ asked what nature the stone possessed.
Zhēn replied:
"The stone comes from Jīng Mountain,
at the peak of a sheer cliff.
Within it contains the treasure of Biàn Hé,
yet polishing it cannot make it more lustrous,
nor carving it add to its patterns."
Wǔ Dì said:
"Its reputation is indeed not in vain."
"Records of Literary Scholars"
Quartz
Emperor Ming enhanced the grandeur of the palace,
carving and adorning its towers and pavilions,
quarried quartz from the Taihang Mountains,
gathered patterned stones from Gǔchéng,
raised Jǐngyáng Hill in the Fānglín Garden,
and built the Zhāoyáng Hall north of the Tàijí Palace.
"Records of Wei"
Now constructing the Luòyáng Palace,
selecting white stones,
workers drill mountains in search of rare rocks,
carve stone to seek mica,
the toils of labor
surpass none other than this.
"Memorials of Wei Ministers"
Entwined Branches
At the foot of Mount Tài, there are interlocking patterned stones,
standing twelve zhàng high,
resembling cypress trees in appearance.
Their patterns are brilliantly displayed,
as if carved by human hands.
From bottom to top,
they join together yet split in the middle,
with a width of six chǐ,
appearing like real trees when viewed from afar.
The elders say:
"During the end of the Qín dynasty,
the two stones stood over a hundred steps apart,
overgrown with weeds and obscured,
with no paths leading to them.
By the beginning of Emperor Míng's reign,
they gradually seemed to draw closer, resembling paired watchtowers.
As earth and stone belong to the yīn category,
and Wèi corresponds to the virtue of Earth,
this serves as a spiritual omen.
Records of Omissions"
Crusade Against Cáo Cāo
In the third year of the Qinglong era of Emperor Míng of Wei,
at the entrance of the Great Willow Valley in Dīchí County, Zhāngyè Commandery,
at night,
torrential waves surged and overflowed,
their sound like thunder.
By dawn, a blue stone stood in the water,
with white veins forming patterns resembling horses, cattle, and other shapes.
Its inscription read:
"Great Campaign Against Cáo."
The emperor, detesting its rebellious implication,
ordered it to be chiseled away as a countermeasure,
filling the space with blue stone.
Overnight, the area was filled with white stone.
By the early Jìn dynasty,
the inscription became even clearer,
and the patterns all gleamed translucent like jade.
(Records of the Hàn and Jìn Dynasties)
Patterned stone is an auspicious sign.
In Féngchéng County there was Mount Qín.
When Sūn Quán presumptuously assumed the imperial title,
one night this mountain suddenly produced a sound like thunder,
causing a cave to open.
The space within measured about six or seven lǐ,
and the stones inside bore colorful patterns.
There were also stone pillars,
stone drums,
and stone pellets.
The commandery reported this to Sūn Quán,
who considered it an auspicious sign.
"Records of Jīngzhōu"
Patterns formed characters.
In Póyáng's Lìyáng County,
there was a stone mountain facing the water,
one hundred zhang high.
At about thirty zhang,
there were holes arranged in rows,
the insides of the holes were reddish-yellow,
different from the main body,
commonly known as the stone seal.
It was also said:
When the stone seal opens,
the world will be at peace.
Below was a shrine,
where the shamans claimed the stone seal deity had three lords.
At that time, the magistrate of Lìyáng reported that the stone seal had opened,
and Sūn Hào sent an envoy to offer a grand sacrifice at Lì Mountain.
The shaman said,
the three lords of the stone seal proclaimed,
the world was about to be at peace.
The envoy built a tall ladder,
climbed up to see the seal inscription,
and fraudulently wrote twenty characters in red on the stone,
saying:
"Chǔ's nine provinces are islets,
Wú's nine provinces are the capital,
the land of Yángzhōu,
produces the Son of Heaven,
four generations reign,
peace begins."
Returning, he reported to Sūn Hào,
who was greatly pleased.
He said:
"Shall Wú become the capital and islets of the nine provinces?
From the Great Emperor to me, four generations have passed,
the lord of peace,
if not me, then who?"
He again sent an envoy,
to bestow seals and ribbons, appointing the three lords as kings.
"Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn"
Shí Shù
In the first year of the Tiānxǐ era,
Wǔ Yào, an official of Línhǎi Commandery,
obtained a stone tree by the seashore,
over two chǐ in height,
with purple branches and stems,
twisting and bending gracefully,
radiant with brilliance.
As recorded in the Classic of Mountains and Seas:
it belonged to the category of the Jade King's trees.
Records of the Sòng Dynasty
Yùlín Stone
Lù Jì of Sūn Quán's era,
was initially appointed as the governor of Yùlín.
Upon completing his term and returning,
he carried no treasures, making the boat too light to cross the sea.
He used a massive stone to weigh it down,
and upon reaching Gūsū, he placed it there.
His disciples named it the "Yùlín Stone."
As recorded in "Chronicles."
Shízǐ
Jiè Xiàng,
courtesy name Yuánzé,
was from Kuàijī.
He entered the mountains seeking immortals,
and saw in a valley some stones,
all purple in color,
as large as chicken eggs.
Xiàng picked up two of them,
then saw a beautiful woman,
clad in five-colored garments.
Xiàng kowtowed and begged her for immortality.
The woman said:
"Quickly return the objects you took
to their original place."
Xiàng returned the stones,
and the woman taught him a formula for huándān.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn".
Stone Marrow
Jī Kāng met a man from Hándān named Wáng Liè,
who claimed to be over one hundred years old.
They entered the Tàiháng Mountains together,
where they obtained a stony marrow resembling malt sugar.
Wáng Liè immediately consumed half of it himself,
giving the remaining half to Jī Kāng,
but it all solidified into stone.
In a chamber, they saw a scroll of plain silk with writing,
yet when Jī Kāng reached for it, it vanished with a breath.
According to Zāng Róngxù's History of the Jìn Dynasty,
the realm of immortals opens once every five hundred years,
from which the stony marrow emerges.
Those who obtain and consume it
will enjoy a lifespan as enduring as the heavens.
As recorded in The Classic of Immortals.
Míng Shí
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
on the bank of Línpíng in Wú Commandery,
a stone drum emerged from a collapse.
When struck, it produced no sound.
They consulted Zhāng Huà about it,
and Huà said:
"Fetch catalpa wood from Shǔ,
carve it into the shape of a fish,
and strike it—then it will resonate."
They followed his advice and struck it,
and the sound could be heard for tens of lǐ.
From "Yì Yuàn":
In the first year of the Yǒngkāng era,
the commandery of Xiāngyáng presented a resonant stone,
resembling jade in appearance and green in color.
When struck, its sound could be heard for seven or eight lǐ.
Now, in Yǒngzhèng Village of Quánlíng County in Línglíng,
there are two resonant stones.
One is shaped like a common drum,
hence it is named the Stone Drum.
From "Shān Hǎi Zhù".
Ránshí
In Yùzhāng there is a stone,
yellowish-white in color with coarse texture.
When water is poured on it, it becomes hot,
and placing a tripod pot on it for cooking
provides sufficient heat.
When it cools, water is poured on it again. Léi Huàn
asked Zhāng Huà about it,
and Huà said:
"It is a burning stone."
From The Records of Extraordinary Things.
Shrine Stone
Chén Zǒng was promoted to Palace Censor,
and was dispatched to Zhōngnán Mountain to pray for rain.
Zǒng first cleared away the small stone shrines,
preserving only one large stone site to offer prayers.
His prayer text said:
Oh, lofty great stone,
assisting the sacred mountain in ordering principles,
containing moisture and releasing nourishment,
bestow kindness upon our four seas.
From Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū
The writing is like bamboo leaves.
North of the Grand Temple gate in Jiāngdōng,
there were stone markings resembling bamboo leaves,
discovered during the renovation of the temple in the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of the Liú Sòng dynasty,
which Lù Chéng believed to be the fertility ritual stone from Emperor Wǔ's filial piety period of the Jìn dynasty.
"Tōngdiǎn"
Shí Lái
During the Yǒngníng era of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
there was a large stone in the lake of Húshú County,
two hundred paces from the islet,
that floated ashore.
The common people watched in astonishment,
and someone said:
"The stone's coming next year
will bring Shí Bīng into Yángzhōu."
from "Records of Dānyáng"
White spots form constellations
In the first year of the Yǒngjiā era, Zhāng Guǐ
went to Gūzāng to present the mysterious stone,
which had white spots resembling stars,
forming the twenty-eight constellations.
"Records of the Former Liáng"
The Stone Box
In Yùzhāng County,
in the eastern countryside of Lǚ Village,
there is a stone box in the mountains,
which no one could open through the ages.
Wú Měng then obtained it,
and upon opening it, found many stone slips with ancient characters.
None of his disciples could understand them,
and Wú Měng did not explain.
When dozens of disciples joined forces to lift it,
the lid remained as immovable as a mountain.
Yet Wú Měng lifted it effortlessly,
as if it weighed nothing.
On the southern mountain of the county, there is a stone
standing upright in the water,
steep and towering thousands of feet high,
inaccessible even to monkeys.
Wú Měng then ascended it by riding a wooden clapper,
ordering two disciples to follow him,
and suddenly it felt like a level path.
"Biography of Wú Měng"
Shí shēng rì yuè
Initially, in the village where he resided at Yuánqiū,
stones in the ground bore images of the sun and moon,
and the likeness of horses bridled with iron.
At that time, the elders and physiognomists all said:
"This barbarian has a remarkable appearance,
great ambitions,
and his end cannot be measured."
The townspeople treated him generously.
"Biography of Shí Lè"
Cǎishí
Shí Jìlóng built a bridge across the river,
and at Yúnchāng Ford, stones were gathered for the central piers.
Regardless of their size,
the stones were used as they flowed with the current.
Over five million laborers worked on it,
but it was not completed by Jìlóng.
He sent an envoy to offer sacrifices,
sinking a jade disc into the river.
Soon after,
the sunken disc floated onto a sandbar,
an earthquake caused waves to surge upward,
and the towers and halls at the ford collapsed,
crushing more than a hundred people to death.
"Records of Extraordinary Events"
To Sharpen the Teeth
Sūn Zǐjīng said to Wáng Wǔzǐ:
"One should pillow on the stream and rinse mouth with the stone jade mortar,
but stones cannot be rinsed with,
nor can streams be pillowed on."
Sūn replied:
"Pillowing on the stream is to wash one's ears,
rinsing with stones is to sharpen one's teeth."
The Book of Jìn
floating on the water
During the time of Hèlián Bóbó,
there was a blue stone,
as large as a horse's head,
floating on the water,
moving upstream.
Travelers saw it and presented it to the court,
and all the ministers congratulated him,
believing that stones are sinking objects,
so one floating on water symbolized spontaneous emergence,
and its upstream movement toward Jīng and Wú
was an omen of their submission to the court.
Bóbó was greatly pleased.
"Records of the Former Zhào"
Drunken Stone
Táo Yuānmíng resided in Lìlǐ,
where there was a large rock.
Yuānmíng once lay drunk upon it,
and it was named the Drunken Rock.
From "Records of Mount Lú"
Zhào Xiáng
In the seventh year of the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty, in the fifth month,
there was a flood in Wǔlíng,
and Shàndé Mountain collapsed.
Two stones, taller than ten feet,
resembling human figures,
were intricately carved with exquisite craftsmanship,
embodying ancient styles and designs.
An oracle declared:
"A Son of Heaven will emerge from Wǔlíng,
and it will happen in the eighth month.
Xiàowǔ was born then,
later ennobled as the King of Wǔlíng,
and eventually ascended to the imperial throne."
From "Qià Wénjì"
Jǐnshí
Jǐnshā Village nestles against mountains and valleys,
where clear waves reflect purely,
and splendid stones unfold their patterns.
Wú Xǐ, a champion, heard of it and visited.
Rowing his boat to wander and float,
he forgot to return for ten full days,
sighing:
"Famous mountains and beautiful stones
truly deserve their praise,
making one lose the desire for wealthy gates."
From "Records of Xīn'ān"
Wearing a talisman
In the fifth year of the reign of Emperor Wèi Míng,
Zhāngyè Commandery reported in a memorial:
At the Great Willow Valley Mountain in Dīchí County,
a large stone with a blue background and white patterns
formed written characters in between,
recording the taboo names of the state's ancestors,
and displaying the signs of the Mandate of Heaven and the succession of dynasties.
The emperor then dispatched an envoy to draw and copy the text.
The assembled officials memorialized, saying:
This is the highest spirit
bestowing the Mandate upon the state,
an omen of its endless duration.
"Record of Spiritual Signs"
Bā Fēng Hēi Shí
During the Tàihé era,
the Tàihé Hall was built east of the Píngchéng Hall,
below the steps stood a stone stele,
which was also one of the Luòyáng Eight Winds,
the black stone of the valley.
"The Water Classic"
Bleeding
After Yùqín's death,
before the tomb gate there were stone figures and lions,
Zǐxián, being poor and humble,
sold them to the Fàn family to obtain an ox for plowing.
The ox died,
the Fàn family then beat him,
causing wounds that all bled.
"Dūnhuáng Shílù"
Líng Shí
In the seventh year of the Yǒngmíng era,
Zhū Líng, the Chief Secretary,
was surveying the Zhèjiāng River,
when he obtained ten spiritual stones.
When lifted, they rose,
floating in water three chǐ deep.
The Emperor Shìzǔ personally cast them into the Tiānyuān Pond,
and had them carved into Buddha images as a test.
"Records of the Southern Qí"
Yuèwáng Shí
Yú Yuàn served as the governor of Jìnpíng,
where by the seaside stood the Yuèwáng Stone,
often shrouded in mist and clouds.
Legend has it that
only a thoroughly honest governor
could behold it. Yú Yuàn journeyed there
and gazed upon it clearly, unobscured.
From the Qí Shū
Zǐshí
In the early years of the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng dynasty,
an edict was issued to the Gōngchē Office,
ordering the placement of a box beside the slander-post and the lung-stone,
where those with dragon-snake talents hung in suspense,
the highly gifted harbored sighs,
and the powerful oppressed the humble.
If anyone wished to present their case,
they could submit it to the lung-stone.
In the fifth year, an edict stated:
At dawn, I dwell in fasting,
concerned only with punishments,
following the three punishments and five hearings,
carrying these thoughts while resting or rising.
Thus, I display the lung-stone in the capital,
and add officials to the streets for handling edict-related cases.
"Basic Annals"
Dào Gōngshí
Dào Gài resided near the Huái River studio,
where in front of the mountain pond stood a remarkable rugged stone,
measuring sixteen feet in length.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng jokingly wagered with him for it,
along with a copy of the Book of Rites,
and Dào Gài lost both.
The emperor summoned and had it moved to the Huálín Garden.
On the day the stone was relocated in front of the banquet hall,
the entire capital city turned out,
all gazing upon what was called "Dào's Stone Lord."
(History of the Southern Dynasties)
The Book of Liáng does not include the character for "rugged."
Shí Gě
Jiǎng Gé, from the position of Kuàijī Assistant,
was appointed as the Minister of Personnel.
As he was about to return, gifts were presented to him,
but he accepted none of them.
According to the old practice, a boat was prepared for him,
which he also did not accept.
He only rode in the single boat provided by the court.
The boat's hold was unevenly tilted,
making it impossible to rest comfortably.
Someone said to Gé:
"The boat is already unsteady,
and crossing the river is very risky.
You should move the heavy objects
to balance the lighter side of the hold."
Since Gé had no possessions,
he went to the Xīlíng shore,
gathered over ten stones,
and used them to weigh it down.
From the Book of Liáng.
Sān Hóu
In the rear hall of Xú Líng,
stood the Inscription on the Beauty Mountain,
which read:
"Peaks form the Five Ladies,
stones mark the Three Marquises."
from "Hǎi Lù"
Third Rank
In front of Tóngtài Temple in Táichéng, there are four stones,
each over ten feet tall,
which are the Third Rank Stones of the Chén dynasty.
Yáng Shùxíng
Emperor Xuān of Zhōu pacified Yǒngzhōu during the Dàdìng era,
where he obtained a white stone.
In the second year,
it was cut into two sections,
revealing inside the form of a poplar tree,
with yellow roots and purple leaves.
From "Guǎng Wǔxíng Jì"
Biànyù
Sui Dynasty's Xiàngzhōu Governor,
Nèiyáng Gōng Xuē Zhòu,
the foundation stones of his residence hall,
suddenly turned into jade. Zhòu
considered this an auspicious omen,
and held a vegetarian feast to celebrate it.
Shì Língyù remarked:
"This is merely glass.
You should be cautious about it,
guard against it,
and can avert misfortune through blessings."
Zhòu did not follow his advice.
Later,
when Yáng Liàng started a rebellion,
the circumstances were connected,
so he was exiled to the border regions,
and it was too late for regrets.
"Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks"
Diàotái Stone
In the second month of the seventh year of the Dàyè era,
when the fishing terrace was first being constructed,
there were many stone transporters.
The soldiers operating the boats were exhausted,
worn out by the labor,
and their sighs and laments
could be heard along the roads.
At that time, the stone transporters
brought their boats to the eastern bank of the river,
quarried stones from the mountain,
and piled them up to form the foundation of the fishing terrace.
Suddenly, more than ten large stones, each as big as an ox,
flew down from the mountain top,
went straight into the boats,
as if placed there by human hands,
without damaging the boats.
From "Dàyè Shíyí"
Qīngshí Dānshū
Táng Qí Wáng Lǐ Yuánjí,
at the Jìnyáng Palace obtained a green stone,
resembling the shape of a turtle,
with four characters in vermilion script,
which read:
"Lǐ Yuān Wàn Jí."
Yuánjí sent an envoy to present it,
the characters were translucent and clear,
vividly like a turtle's shape,
all who saw it found it extraordinary.
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"Soak and polish it with water,
to verify it."
The characters became even more distinct,
whereupon both inside and outside the court all offered congratulations.
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"Heaven's clear mandate,
bestowing ten thousand auspicious signs,
it is fitting to sacrifice to the stone turtle with a shǎoláo offering and pour a libation to send it off."
"Guǎngdé Shényì Jì"
Zhēn Shí
Emperor Tàizōng ascended the throne in the eighth month of the ninth year of the Wǔdé era,
on the ninth month, Rénxū day,
Línzhōu presented an auspicious stone,
with faintly raised characters forming the text:
"The Sage Lord So-and-so, greatly auspicious,
descendants for five thousand years."
The base was plain white, the characters black,
combining seal script and clerical script.
From the "Cèfǔ Yuánguī"
Azure base with white veins
In the seventeenth year of the Zhēnguàn era, in the eighth month,
at Hóngchí Valley in Chāngsōng County, Liáng Prefecture,
there was a stone with a blue base and white patterns forming characters.
Emperor Tàizōng dispatched an envoy to offer sacrifices to it, saying:
Heaven has a destined mandate,
manifesting auspicious signs on this steadfast stone.
The characters are clear and bright,
the succession of reigns shall be eternal.
"Treatise on the Five Elements"
Míng Shí
In the fourth year of the Xiǎnqìng era,
a fisherman caught a green stone in his net in the river,
four feet long and nine inches wide,
its surface smooth and glossy,
unlike ordinary stones.
When hung and struck,
it produced a clear, melodious sound.
Travelers who heard it
all stopped in their tracks.
Governor Téngwáng submitted a report and presented it to the Ruìfǔ (Hall of Auspicious Signs).
"Records of Yùzhāng":
A fisherman netted a stone,
which made a loud sound when struck,
audible for dozens of miles.
Dàowáng served as governor of Hóngzhōu,
broke it open and found a pair of swords.
Looking at their inscriptions,
one bore the characters "Xǔ Jīngyáng,"
the other "Wànrèn."
Thus emerged the master Wànrèn.
"Accounts from Court and Country":
"History of the Táng":
Dàowáng Lǐ Yuánqìng
never governed Hóngzhōu—
this was likely a confusion with Lǐ Yuányīng's affairs.
Pánshí
Xuē Yuánchāo,
was the grandson of Xuē Dàohéng.
When he was transferred to the Secretariat as a Drafter,
there was a flat stone in the department
that Dàohéng, when he was Vice Minister,
used to lean on while drafting edicts.
Every time Yuánchāo saw it,
he would shed tears.
History of the Táng Dynasty
Fake Stone
Táng Tóngtài, a native of Yǒng'ān County in Yōngzhōu,
obtained an auspicious stone from the Luò River,
on which purple veins formed a pattern of text,
saying:
"The Holy Mother governs the court,
eternally prospering the imperial enterprise."
He presented it,
and was appointed to the fifth rank,
with Guǒyì establishing Yǒngchāng County.
It turned out that characters were carved into the stone,
and filled with powdered purple stone mixed with medicine.
Later, in Wénshuǐ County of Bìngzhōu,
a stone was similarly found in a valley,
bearing the characters "Wǔxīng,"
so Wénshuǐ was renamed Wǔxīng County.
From then on, such stones were frequently fabricated,
until the Empress discovered the deception,
and ceased to adopt them,
thus ending the practice.
From "Supplement to the National History":
Lǐ Qiáo's congratulatory memorial stated:
"People say Tóngtài matches the county name Yǒng'ān in surname,
and the national title aligns with the mystical signs of the land,
corresponding with the stone's inscription."
In the "Yīnghuá," Prince Wèi Wǔ Chéngsì
forged the text of an auspicious stone.
As stated in the "Old Táng History."
Stone Trees Intertwined
In the middle of the Yǒngchāng era,
Mèng Shēn, the Sima of Táizhōu, reported that
under the sea off Línhǎi,
Féng Yì had obtained three stone trees with interlocking branches,
all made of white stone.
From the "Records of Widely Heard Matters."
The Auspicious Stone
Fán Wénjìn presented an auspicious stone,
which Empress Wǔ displayed publicly at the imperial court,
showing it to all officials.
Féng Yuán boldly admonished, saying:
"Fraudulent falsehoods should not be shown to the assembled ministers."
The empress, enraged, exiled him to serve as prefect of Lǒng Prefecture.
From the "History of Táng"
A Loyal Heart
During the Tiānshòu era, someone found several red spots on a white stone in the Luòshuǐ River,
and went to the imperial court to present it.
When the ministers questioned him,
he replied:
"This stone has a loyal heart,
that is why I came to present it."
Lǐ Zhāodé rebuked him, saying:
"If this stone has a loyal heart,
does that mean all the other stones in the Luòshuǐ River
are rebels?"
Everyone present laughed.
The Emperor
Zhù Shí
Emperor Zhōngzōng, deposed by Empress Tiānhòu and exiled to Fánglíng,
looked up to the sky and sighed,
making a silent vow in his heart.
He then threw a stone into the air,
saying:
"If I am to regain the throne,
may this stone not fall."
The stone was caught and hung on a tree branch,
and it remains there to this day.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Huà Miàn
During the Xuánzōng era,
Wáng Chuí reported from Wǔwēi Commandery,
at Tiānbǎo Mountain in Jiāruì Township, Fānhé County,
covering an area of five to six lǐ in circumference,
stones had transformed into flour.
In nearby villages,
and various tribal areas,
from the first month of this year onward,
people had been gathering it to eat,
finding it sweet, delicious, and beneficial.
Sūn Tì's memorial stated:
"How can ordinary wheat compare,
what falling grain could rival this?"
As recorded in the Yù Yīng Huá, in the eighth month of the fourth year of the Tàihé era,
Liǔ Gōngchuò, military governor of Tàiyuán, reported that in the valleys of Yún, Yù, and Dài prefectures, stones had turned into flour,
and people gathered it to eat.
(From the Táng Huì Yāo)
to trip over a stone
During the Kaiyuan era, Lǐ Sìyè campaigned against Bólǜ,
clearing a path through the Cōnglǐng mountains.
A massive boulder blocked the narrow pass,
which he kicked with his foot until it fell
into the deep valley. Observers noted
that this was due to the power of his utmost sincerity.
"History of the Táng Dynasty"
Luòxīng Shí
In the Imperial Library, there is a fallen star stone,
cranes painted by Xuē Jì,
phoenixes painted by Hè Zhīzhāng and Láng Yúlìng,
collectively known as the Four Masterpieces.
"New Book of the South"
The auspicious tally
was discovered at the ancient Hángǔ Pass in Hóngnóng toward the end of the Kāiyuán era,
a white stone bearing an auspicious tally,
with red markings,
clearly forming the character "sāng" (mulberry).
Those knowledgeable interpreted it, saying:
"The character 'sāng' signifies the number forty-eight."
This was taken as an indication of the emperor's destined reign,
and indeed, the year he took refuge in Shǔ was the forty-eighth of his reign.
Upon its discovery,
songs spread throughout the land at the time,
leading to the era name being changed to Tiānbǎo.
From "Records of Signs from the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo Eras"
Iron Plowshare
Lǐ Qíwù in the Tiānbǎo era,
initially served as the Prefect of Shǎnzhōu,
opened up the perilous Dǐzhù,
amidst the solid rocks obtained,
an ancient iron plowshare,
bearing the characters Pínglù,
thus changed Héběi County to Pínglù County.
Submitted to the emperor.
Shí Yú
In the fourth year of the Kāibǎo era,
Qiánnán reported,
saying there were stone fish in the river's center.
It was seen with an ancient inscription stating:
"In the second month of the first year of the Guǎngdé era,
when the great river's waters receded,
the stone fish appeared,
and the local people traditionally consider this an omen of abundant harvests."
The "Lúlíng Record of Extraordinary Things"
states: In Fúzhōu,
upstream from Jiàn Lake,
there are stone carvings of twin fish,
each with thirty-six scales,
one holding a daylily in its mouth,
the other holding a lotus flower,
and when the fish appear,
the year will be abundant.
From the "Record of Extraordinary Mountains and Rivers"
Treading on Stone
Shì Míngzàn lived on Nányuè Mountain.
One day, the regional inspector was offering sacrifices at the mountain,
and the road repairs were extremely strict.
Suddenly, in the middle of the night, there was wind and thunder,
and a peak collapsed.
The stone steps along the mountain path
were blocked by a huge rock.
They used many people and oxen to push and pull it,
but their strength was exhausted and the rock became even more firmly stuck.
Míngzàn said:
"Let me try to remove it."
He then stepped on the rock and it moved,
suddenly turning and rolling down.
The sound was like rumbling thunder.
The governor revered him as a divine being."
"The Biographies of Eminent Tang Monks"
Língshí
Púgù Huái'ēn,
having rebelled and fled to the Huíhé,
his family was confiscated,
and entered the rear palace.
In the fourth year of the Dàlì era, his daughter was enfeoffed as Princess Chónghuī,
and sent to marry the khan.
Passing through Fénzhōu,
she pressed her palm against the stone wall,
leaving a handprint.
Today in Língshí there exists the Princess Chónghuī Handprint Stele.
"Guǎngchuān Shūbá"
Falling Stone
Lǐ Shīhuì and his brother obtained a piece of fallen star stone from a patch-robed monk.
The monk said:
"While traveling early on the Shǔ road,
I saw a star fall in front of me.
I then dug it up and obtained a piece.
The stone resembled a broken chime stone,
with carvings on its end
depicting the head of a Suānní,
also like a chime stone.
There was a hole for threading a cord,
still smooth.
Could it be that celestial musical instruments were destroyed and fell,
and this stone was passed down to Lǐ Jífǔ's residence in Ānyì?
《Shàngshū Gùshí》
Carrying Stones
Yán Zhēnqīng in his later years once carried stones with him while traveling,
polished and stored them,
writing wherever he went when events occurred,
leaving behind the stones he had engraved.
The stone moves.
In the first year of the Bǎolì era,
on a mountain in Zīyáng County of Zīzhōu,
there was a large rock
that suddenly roared and leaped,
descended the mountain and crossed a stream,
then went back up a slope
for about a hundred paces.
While the rock was moving,
it was seen by people hoeing crops.
Each holding their hoes,
they chased it to where it stopped.
The rock was twenty feet high.
Stone Thrower
In the early years of the Tàihé era,
Lǐ Tóngjié, the military governor of Cāngjǐng, rebelled against the sovereign.
Lǐ Zhīxìng led troops to suppress him.
Tóngjié sent an eloquent man to climb the city wall and insult Zhīxìng.
One soldier said:
"We can use a catapult
to strike off his head."
They then prepared and launched the catapult,
and one stone hit him squarely in the head.
His head burst and fell with the stone.
The army cheered and shouted,
while those on the city wall were thrown into panic.
Zhīxìng rewarded the soldier with a thousand pieces of gold.
(From "Dú Yì Jì")
Mǎoshí
Attendant-in-ordinary Cuī Yuánliàng,
while strolling leisurely in Luòzhōng,
picked up a stone from the riverbank.
It was as large as a hen's egg,
black and glossy, quite lovely.
After carrying it for about a li,
it suddenly cracked open,
and a bird as large as a wren flew out.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The Abandoned Stone
Bái Jūyì resided in Lǚdào Lane in the Eastern Capital,
where he dredged ponds and planted trees,
constructed the Stone Tower at Xiāngshān,
and excavated the Eight-Bend Rapids.
The New Book of Táng records:
Yáng Zhēn of Hóngnóng
once obtained a bluish stone,
three spans long,
smooth enough to sit or lie upon.
The Old Book of Táng states:
In the ninth year of the Tàihé era,
a mountain dweller gifted me a massive stone,
which I transported to Lǚdào Lane.
At the time, it was the height of summer heat,
and I would sit or recline upon it,
growing fond of it and inscribing these words:
"Its substance congeals like white clouds,
its veins crack like azure mist."
From the Chángqìng Collection.
Tiānzhú
Bái Lètiān was dismissed from Hángzhōu,
obtained from Tiānzhú
a stone and a Huátíng,
two cranes.
From Sūzhōu he obtained Tàihú stones,
five bending-waist
water chestnuts, all placed by the pond at his residence.
"Old Book of Táng"
Digging up stones reveals inscriptions.
The Sweet Dew incident failed,
Wáng Fán and his entire household, young and old, all died.
Earlier, when Wáng Fán was repairing the city wall in Zhèxī,
during the moat construction,
someone dug up a square stone,
on which were twelve characters:
"The mountain has stone,
the stone has jade,
the jade has flaw,
the flaw means cessation."
Wáng Fán looked at it but didn't understand its meaning,
an elderly man from Jīngkǒu explained it, saying:
"This stone is not an auspicious omen for the Minister."
The Minister's grandfather was named Yín,
Yín gave birth to Chǔ,
this is 'the mountain has stone'.
Chǔ gave birth to the Minister,
this is 'the stone has jade'.
The Minister's son,
named Xiáxiū,
xiū means termination.
How could this be considered auspicious?
The omen indeed resulted in the extermination of his clan.
Old History
Jiā Shí
Niú Sēngrú at the beginning of the Kāichéng era,
remained in the Eastern Capital,
built a mansion in Luòyáng's Guīrén Ward,
gathered many fine stones and beautiful trees,
and entertained with guests.
"History of the Táng Dynasty"
Taihú Shí
Qízhāng Gōng had a passion for rocks,
and his subordinates stationed by rivers and lakes
would present him with rare and marvelous specimens.
He arranged them in the eastern mansion and southern villa,
and during his leisure hours,
he kept company with the rocks.
Rocks have their clans and gatherings,
with those from Lake Tai being the finest,
followed by those from Luófú and Tiānzhú.
They varied greatly in size,
divided into four grades,
classified as A, B, C, and D,
each with upper, middle, and lower ranks,
all inscribed on the back of the stones.
It was said:
"The Niú family rock,
upper of grade A,
middle of grade C,
lower of grade B,
a single peak towering hundreds of ren,
a thousand miles captured in one glance.
This is what brings contentment to the Duke."
From the "Chángqìng Collection"
Insect Borer
A senior official dispatched an officer
to purchase Taihu Lake stones from Western Zhèjiāng,
and the officer submitted a report stating:
"The aforementioned stones are worm-eaten,
and unfit for purchase."
From "Miscellaneous Accounts of the Lú Family"
Lǐ Xīng Shí
Zànhuáng Gōng's Píngquán Estate had the Lǐ Xīng Shí,
which was ten feet wide,
over a foot long,
with natural grain patterns
forming the Big Dipper,
resembling a lion.
The stone stood two to three feet high,
with countless holes and cavities
interconnected throughout,
its appearance exactly like a lion,
complete with head, tail, nose, and eyes.
"Jiǎ Shì Tán Lù"
Píng Shí
Lǐ Déyù's Píngquán Manor,
thirty lǐ from Luòchéng,
with its flowers, trees, terraces, and pavilions,
resembles a celestial mansion,
before the empty balustrade,
a winding stream is channeled through carved waterways,
imitating the Bā Gorges and Dòngtíng Lake,
with twelve peaks and nine tributaries,
stretching to the sea gate,
depicting scenes of rivers and mountains.
Along the bamboo-lined paths,
there are flat stones that, when rubbed by hand,
faintly reveal patterns of clouds and mist,
and forms of dragons, phoenixes, grasses, and trees.
"Jù Tán Lù"
Sobering Stone
Lǐ Déyù at his Píngquán Villa,
collected rare trees and peculiar stones from across the land,
for the enjoyment of his garden and pond.
There was a Sobering Stone,
which Déyù especially treasured and cherished,
and upon getting drunk, he would sit astride it.
"Táng Yú Lù"
In Hénán's Chángchūn Hall,
to the south stood a Póluó Pavilion,
where green stones were stored.
It is traditionally said to be Lǐ Déyù's Sobering Stone,
noted for its water-like patterns and natural forest appearance,
now called the Póluó Stone.
"Hénán Jì"
Déyù's "Record of the Píngquán Mountain Residence" states:
"Whoever sells Píngquán,
is not my descendant;
whoever gives away a single tree or stone from Píngquán to others,
is not a worthy offspring."
"Huìchāng Yīpǐn Jí"
During the reign of Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng,
when Zhāng Quányì served as the military governor of four towns,
a eunuch supervisor once obtained the Sobering Stone from Píngquán.
Déyù's grandson Yángǔ entrusted Quányì to seek its return,
but the eunuch supervisor angrily said:
"Since the rebellion of Huáng Cháo,
no gardens or residences in Luòyáng have been preserved intact,
how could it be just one stone from Píngquán?"
Quányì, having once been among Huáng Cháo's rebels, took this as a personal insult,
became enraged,
and had the eunuch flogged to death by imperial decree.
"Wǔdài Shǐ"
The Píngquán Sobering Stone,
was previously taken by the Yùqīng Zhāoyìng Palace.
After the palace was destroyed by fire,
Emperor Rénzōng divided the land,
granting it to the six princes of Pú, Lù, Tán, Yuè, Hán, and Jì.
The son of Prince Jì, Dānyáng Commandery Prince Shǒujié,
received the garden land,
and upon excavating the soil, discovered finely crafted stones,
amounting to nearly ten thousand pieces in total,
many of extraordinary shapes and appearances.
The Sobering Stone was among them,
with an inscription carved in a winding pattern reading:
"Prince Hán embraces the pure light,
in the leisurely courtyard, the view is serene and elegant,
solitary amidst heaven and earth,
naturally standing alone."
In the second month of the year Guǐmǎo of Chángqìng,
inscribed by Jǐng Shèng."
During the Shàoshèng era, it was transported back to the imperial palace,
and placed in the Xuānhé Hall.
"Zhāng Yòuchéng Zhēng Dànyán Jí"
Píngquán Stone
Lǐ Déyù's Píngquán Manor
gathered all the world's rare and extraordinary treasures,
leaving none uncollected.
From Rìguān and Zhènzé,
Wūlíng and Luófú,
to Guìshuǐ's steep rapids
and Lúfù's Lòután stones—all were present there.
The wondrous stones of Táilǐng and Bāgōng,
the cliffs of Wū Gorge,
and the waters of Lángláng Terrace
were arranged along the clear canals,
while stones bearing immortal footprints
and deer tracks
were displayed before the Buddhist couch.
These included: Tàishān stones (sent by a Yǎnzhōu official), Luófú stones (gifted by the Pānyú commander), Lòután stones (presented by a visitor from Lǔ), and fishing stones (obtained from a friend).
The Yīpǐn Collection
also contains a poem about the deer-resembling stone at Sīpíngquán.
Feldspar
When Yú Jìyǒu was the prefect of Lìzhōu,
there was a temple by the river,
where fishermen often gathered in front of it.
One fisherman cast his net,
and when he lifted it, he felt it was heavy.
He tore the net to check
and found a stone the size of a fist.
He then asked the temple monks to place it in the Buddha hall.
The stone then grew without stopping,
and after a year, it weighed forty catties.
Commissioner Zhāng,
witnessed this personally when he entered Shǔ.
"Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Sōngfēng Shí
In the early years of the Huìchāng era,
the Fúyú Kingdom presented a Pine Breeze Stone,
measuring ten feet square,
as translucent as jade.
Within it was a tree pattern resembling an ancient pine,
spreading like a canopy with a rustling sound.
And cool breezes arose from within it.
By the height of summer,
the emperor ordered it placed inside the palace hall,
where gradually an autumn-like chill would whisper forth,
and then he commanded it be removed.
"The Miscellaneous Records of Dūyáng"
Pine Petrified into Stone
During the Dàzhōng era, Mǎ Zìrán
at the Tiānbǎo Temple east of Yǒngkāng County,
where there was an ancient withered pine tree.
Xiāng pointed at it and said:
"This pine has existed for over three thousand years,
and will soon turn into stone."
Afterward,
the pine indeed transformed into stone.
Suddenly, a great storm with thunder shook,
causing the stone to topple and break into several sections.
Yáng Fā, demoted from his post as military governor of Guǎngzhōu to prefect of Wù Prefecture,
who had a fondness for the unusual,
then moved two sections to his commandery office,
and two sections to the Lóngxīng Temple,
in the Jiǔ Sōng Courtyard,
each standing six or seven chǐ tall,
with a diameter of over three chǐ,
the stone retaining the bark texture and scaly wrinkles of the pine,
which remain to this day.
From "Continued Biographies of Immortals"
Lù Guīméng's preface to "Two Legacy Poems":
East of Yuè, Dōngyáng has many famous mountains,
and the land of Yǒngkāng lies connected among them,
abundant with ancient pines,
which often transform into stone,
with coiled roots and large branches,
their grain and texture clearly defined,
connoisseurs quarry them and place them among people,
as remarkable sights to behold.
Tàishān's Yáng Zhènwén obtained a piece for a pillow base,
Zhàojùn's Lǐ Zhōngxiù obtained one for a zither stand,
both being of this stone.
They gifted them to me,
and moved by the wonder of these two legacies,
I composed poems to express gratitude.
From "Sōnglíng Collection"
Obtained a Golden Hairpin
Xiàhóu Zī served as the mountain tomb commissioner for Emperor Xuānzong,
and while excavating the imperial burial chamber for Zhēnlíng,
they dug to a depth of one zhang,
finding within solid rock half of a broken gold hairpin.
It was as long as a palm and more,
still embedded in the stone.
The workers then pried it out and presented it to Zī,
who, considering the proximity to the imperial tomb
and the unusual nature of the matter,
chose to conceal it and did not report it.
"An Unofficial History of the Táng"
The stele suddenly rang out on its own.
At the Huàyuè Jīn Tiānwáng Temple,
there was a stele inscribed by Emperor Xuánzōng.
In the early Guǎngmíng era,
the stone suddenly began to sound on its own,
its faint echo audible for several miles,
and it continued for ten days before settling.
The following year, when the Cháo rebels attacked the capital, the temple
was also set ablaze by the bandits' fire,
destroying its gate tower.

Zhū Zì
Táng Qiánzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Zhé,
was building a residence in Píngkāng Lǐ,
when his family members dug up a stone from the ground,
on which was written in vermilion ink:
"Building here is inauspicious."
The family wiped it,
but the characters became even clearer.
They then presented it to Zhé,
whose family suspected someone had lazily used vermilion paint.
He personally ground the vermilion,
which had penetrated deep like the stone's veins.
Zhé was greatly disturbed by this,
and that very month he passed away.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
There is no Tángshí.
In the second year of Qianning,
Luò Quánguàn and
Lǐ Jìpéng rebelled against the emperor.
The emperor took refuge in Shāchéng Town.
He intended to enter the southern mountain valley
to fortify himself there.

he detested it,
so he relocated to Shímén
and stationed himself at the Buddhist palace.

Shuò Shí
During the Tiānfù era, in the Hóngzhōng period,
a meteorite fell at the foot of Yuèwáng Mountain,
in front of Zhāoxiān Temple.
It was seven to eight chǐ long,
over three zhàng in circumference,
and green as jade.
Military Governor Liú Wēi

Within seven days it shrank slightly,
to three chǐ in length.
After several days,
the stone measured just over a chǐ.
Now it is only seven to eight cùn.
It remains in the temple.

ǒu shí dé yī xiǎo shí,
qīng hēi píngzhèng,

Fallen Stone
Xú Shàoláng, the Director of Education,
in his youth was traveling on Tiāntāi Mountain.
He rested under the shade of a large tree.
A stone plate on the cliff was about to fall through the air
and spoke, saying:
"There is someone below."
The stone then creaked, caught on the tree, and turned around,
before finally falling and shaking the ground with a thunderous crash.

Extraordinary Stone
Shǔ Wéngǔ once visited the Secretariat Drafter Liú Guāngzuò,
where there was a Daoist priest named Liú Yún,
who produced a white stone,
round like a chicken egg.
On its surface were patterns,
faintly emerging like a painting.
