their eyebrows, eyes, hair,
hats, shoes, robes, and capes
were all finely detailed and complete.
He said:
"I obtained this from a stone cave in Má Gǔ Valley."
There was also another guest, Shěn Mò,
who likewise produced a stone,
one and a half inches wide,
two and a half inches long,
on which a coiled dragon was faintly visible,
with scales and shells,
claws and nails,
all fully and meticulously rendered.
He said:
"I obtained this from the mountains of Wūxiá Gorge."
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà"
Buddha's Seat
King Wǔsù Qián Liú,
from childhood often gathered with village children to play beneath the shade of trees upon a stone,
pointing at that tree and stone, said:
"When I attain noble rank and rewards, I shall cover them,
establishing a monastery for meritorious officials,
thus using this stone as a Buddha's throne."
from "The Supplementary History of Wúyuè"
The crushed stones were like powder.
Tán Zǐxiāo, a monk of Lúshān,
by a pavilion on the stream's bank,
was troubled by a large rock lying across the path,
which workmen could not level.
Zǐxiāo went to see it,
and said:
"This is indeed easy."
Thereupon, he formed hand seals with his fingers,
spat water upon it,
and ordered them to strike the rock,
which crumbled like dust at the touch.
From "History of Southern Táng"
Living Stone
At Hǎilíng's Dōngtái Shèngguǒ Monastery,
there is an ancient well curb.
It is said to have been made during the Bǎodà era of the Southern Táng,
and originally had rope grooves about an inch deep,
but now they have grown back together,
and the inscribed text has also worn away beyond recognition,
leading to speculation that it is living stone.
From the "Yànxī Records":
Lǐ Yángbīng's three stelae at Jìnyún
were carved with the most delicate and slender seal script,
and it is said in the world that these three stelae are all alive,
gradually growing over the years,
so that the carved areas have nearly closed up,
hence their slenderness.
From the "Collection of Ancient Inscriptions"
Golden Silkworm
Right Thousand Oxen Military Officer Wáng Wénbǐng, a native of Dānyáng,
was skilled in stone carving for generations.
His grandfather once served as the Lianxi of Western Zhè,
when Péi Jù was collecting steles beneath the piled stones,
he found a naturally round stone,
shaped like a ball,
as if polished and carved,
layered like shells enveloping each other.
Carving it to the very core,
it was as large as a fist,
and upon breaking it open,
inside was a silkworm-like grub,
writhing and able to move,
which no one could identify,
so it was discarded for several years.
During the rebellion in Western Zhè, Wáng fled to Xiàshǔ,
and one night, gathering with fellow villagers,
they spoke of the tale of the qīngfú returning money.
Someone among them remarked:
"If one seeks wealth,
nothing compares to obtaining a golden silkworm from a stone and raising it,
for treasures will come of their own accord."
When asked about its appearance,
it was the grub from the stone.
"Records of the Supernatural"
Lóngjīng Shí
Dīng Wèi had a miniature mountain,
only a few inches tall.
Lush green and hollowed out,
he often placed a basin of water in midsummer
and set the small mountain inside it.
One day,
when Zhāng Yàn had guests, one of them scooped water to sprinkle on it.
Soon, clouds and mist emerged from its crevices,
with a light like lightning.
Looking closely,
a small, winding dragon,
thin as a thread, hung in the mist. After a while,
it scattered and coiled,
and no one knew where it went.
The astonished guests said to him:
"How extraordinary! This is a dragon-essence stone.
Dragons mate upon the sea,
and their essence flows into the stone."
From "Records of Leisurely Dwelling in the Southern Villa"
Appearing in a Dream
In Jīnlíng there were three large ancient stones.
When Wú Zhòngshù served as prefect,
he dreamed at night of three examination candidates pleading for mercy,
who said:
"If you do not grant protection,
tomorrow we shall become ashes."
The prefect found this very strange.
The next morning he questioned all his subordinates,
but none could explain its meaning.
Later, while reviewing official documents,
he saw a report from the Military and Horse Department,
requesting permission to burn the three unsightly stones into lime
for construction use.
The prefect then understood,
and ordered the temple monks to protect them.
During the Yuányòu era,
when Máo Jiàn served as transport commissioner,
he wanted to move them to his official residence.
They dug extremely deep,
but the stone roots remained unbroken,
making movement impossible, so they abandoned the effort.
(From "Yáng Gōng's Notes")
Língbì Shí
During the Zhèng hé era, the Gèn Mài garden was constructed,
with exotic flowers and rare stones
brought from the southeast,
indescribable in form.
Suddenly, Língbì County
presented a massive rock as tribute,
over twenty chǐ high.
Its circumference matched its height,
transported by boat to the capital,
destroying the water gate tower
to enter with a thousand laborers,
yet unable to move it.
Someone reported to the emperor,
saying:
"This is a divine object."
It should be honored as extraordinary.
The Yùlíng Emperor personally brushed
his imperial calligraphy: "Auspicious clouds in myriad forms,"
and additionally hung a golden belt upon it.
Thereupon it became movable,
and within half a moment reached the imperial garden.
From "Huī Chén Lù"
Pángù
Hóu Xuān presented a rock from Gèn Yuè,
forty zhang high,
named Shényùn Zhāogōng.
When Zhū Miǎn returned from Píngjiāng Prefecture,
he built a massive ship,
loaded a large stone from Tài Lake,
and transported it to the capital with a thousand men pulling it forward.
Miǎn was rewarded and granted a ceremonial banner,
while the stone was enfeoffed as Marquis Pángù.
"Huáibō Yǎ Zhì"
Huge rocks follow the current
In the third year of the Jiànyán era,
a giant rock in Dǐngzhōu,
floated down with the great flood,
bearing the inscription:
"In the effortless Great Way,
heaven knows human sentiments;
in the effortless profound darkness,
spirits see human forms;
words of the heart and thoughts of the mind,
ghosts hear human voices;
when transgressions overflow,
earth collects human souls."
From the History of the Sòng Dynasty
Wèi Shí
At court, Lǐ Fēn was known for his eccentric tastes,
and possessed a peculiar stone.
It was about two feet tall,
exquisitely patterned and delightful,
often placed in the courtyard by the railing.
Every day just before the hour of wèi (1–3 PM),
vapor would emerge from its crevices,
appearing like mist or smoke; by observing this phenomenon,
the timing was never off even once.
Thus, it was named the "Wèi Stone."
From *Continued Ink Guest Waving the Rhinoceros*
Shí Zhōng Yú
Dù Wǎn,
courtesy name Jì,
was the grandson of Dù Yǎn.
He once obtained a round green stone from the Yellow River in Lánzhōu,
as large as a persimmon,
which he used as a paperweight.
After resting overnight alongside bamboo slips,
they would become moist, so he later stored it in a container.
After some time, water would seep out,
until one day it suddenly fell to the ground,
breaking into three or four pieces,
revealing a small fish inside,
only about an inch long,
that jumped briefly before dying immediately.
"Yúnlín Shípǔ"
Like a painting
On the Tiānjīn Bridge in Biànjīng of the Sòng Dynasty,
there was a large piece of extraordinary stone,
bearing a natural map of China and foreign lands.
The mountains were verdant and the waters emerald,
the rivers yellow and the roads white,
vivid and splendid as a painting.
"Miscellaneous Records of Guǐxīn"
The Stone of the Chaste Woman
There is a stone of the chaste woman on the path.
It is said that in the past, there was a chaste woman
whose husband died without leaving a son.
She served her mother-in-law with great filial piety.
Her mother-in-law pressured her to remarry,
but she ultimately refused to comply.
After her mother-in-law passed away,
she herself died.
In the house where she lived,
a large stone emerged.
Later generations admired her chastity
and named the stone the Stone of the Chaste Woman.
"Records of the Universe"
Huànǚ
Yángxìng County minor clerk Wú Kān,
once saw a five-colored floating stone in a stream,
so he took it and placed it by his bed,
and by night it transformed into a young woman.
"Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds"
Fire-Water Stone
On Yānzī Mountain, there is a stone,
red and white in color.
When two such stones are struck together,
they produce moisture,
and if struck repeatedly,
once the moisture is exhausted, fire emerges.
All the mountain stones are like this,
flames rising several zhang high,
lasting all day without extinguishing.
A great black wind
emerges from the flowing sands,
enveloping it before it dies out,
and the stones return to their original state. It is said:
The act of stirring fire
triggers illnesses that last for years,
therefore one dare not approach it lightly.
"Commentary on the Water Classic"
Dìtái Stone
On the Xiūyǔ Mountain,
there is a stone on its summit.
It is named
the Chess Pieces of Dìtái.
It has five colors and patterns,
its shape resembling a quail's egg.
The stone of Dìtái
is used to pray to the hundred deities,
and wearing it prevents bewitchment.
"Classic of Mountains and Seas"
Harmonizing Metals and Stones
Someone obtained a bluish stone,
as large as a brick.
Each had a nose pierced with an iron chain,
tens of zhang long,
forming an endless loop.
A maritime merchant saw it,
and traded several tens of thousands for it, saying:
This is a gold-gathering stone;
when suspended in the sea,
and pulled up after a night,
it bears gold on it.
From "Mùfǔ Yànxián Lù"
Lóngjū Shí
Someone once owned a stone,
for which a Qiāng person offered one hundred thousand to purchase it.
The owner sold it and inquired about its peculiarity,
whereupon the foreigner instructed him to fetch a basin of water,
place the stone inside it,
and look—a horse appeared within the stone,
appearing as if it were flying and moving.
The owner asked about its use,
to which he replied:
"This is a Lóngjū Stone.
Soak it in water,
and give the water to a horse to drink,
then the horse will give birth to a Lóngjū,
an invaluable treasure."
"Běi Chuāng Zhì Guǒ"
Xiāoshí
Niter comes from the country of Wūchǎng,
capable of dissolving metals and stones into water.
Taking it enables one to attain longevity,
yet the place where this stone is found
has extremely foul and putrid air,
so foul that birds cannot fly over it.
If a person passes by alone after taking it,
all the parasites in their body will dissolve into water,
thus achieving longevity.
Those shaped like goose quills
are the best. The immortal's prescription says:
This is the Mysterious Pearl of the Emperor.
Qǐzǐ Shí
There is a Begging-for-Son Stone along the way,
two stones flank the Qīngyī River,
standing opposite each other like a couple facing one another.
According to ancient legend,
the eastern stone follows the western stone,
begging to bring home a child.
Thus, the "Customs" records:
if a person has no son,
prayers here will be answered.
"Universal Geography"
Xiāng Shí
Biàn Shān is at the foot of Hú Shān,
where there is priceless incense.
An old woman picked up a patterned stone,
lustrous and delightful to handle.
By chance, it fell into the fire,
and a remarkable fragrance spread far and wide.
She kept it as a treasure,
and whenever she threw it into the fire,
the extraordinary fragrance arose as before.
Hot Stone
Xīnběi Shì is the old foundation of Jǐngguān,
where there is a huge rock as large as a column base.
People from Jǐng sometimes sit on it,
or step on it,
and soon it becomes as hot as if burned by fire,
causing them to fall ill in response to the heat,
often leading to fatal heart conditions.
Some say:
if a fire is gathered to burn it,
this rock roars,
and then the Qútáng Mountain roars as well,
causing the water to boil.
This is an ancient legend passed down.
Also, in the mountains of Jìnyuán County, Shǔzhōu,
there are two large stones in a pavilion,
each about two feet in diameter,
protruding from the ground.
When seventy or eighty people sit on them,
some experience heart pain, often with no cure.
Additionally, there are the fallen star stones,
where sitting on the eastern one brings spiritual effects,
while the western one appears no different from ordinary stones in color,
both tinged with shades of blue and white.
From "Lù Yì Zhù".
Xiǎng Shí
On the Gǒulǒu Peak of Nányuè,
there is a sounding stone.
When called, it responds,
as if conversing with a person, yet its meaning remains incomprehensible.
In Nánhé County of Nánzhōu,
thirty lǐ to the southeast,
lies the sounding stone of Dānxī.
It stands thirty-five feet high,
and twenty feet wide.
Shaped like a crouching beast,
it answers when people call,
and echoes laughter in return.
Solitary in its existence,
it is also known as the Lone Stone.
From "Records of Widely Heard Matters"
Diamond
Beyond the borders, diamonds are produced.
The stone is hard and resembles gold,
possessing a brilliant luster,
and can be used to carve jade. Additionally,
the people of the land wear them, saying:
they ward off evil influences.
"Commentary on the Classic of Mountains and Seas"
Huàméi Shí
Eyebrow stone is found in Wǔchāng,
produced from Fán Lake,
and can be used as a substitute for seven-fragrance pills.
"Suǒ Suì Lù"
Líng Shuǐshí
Língshuǐshí is produced in the valleys of Chángshān,
When this stone is ground into powder and placed in water,
It can turn into ice during the summer months.
Bùhuī shí
In Ānfú County, at Chánglǐng Mountain,
there is a black stone.
It can be used to kindle fire,
thus called the unburnable stone.
"Records of the Universe"
Zhì Shí
In the waters of Wèizhōu, there is a creature,
quite resembling a fish in its cry,
sometimes called "zhì".
When local people see the zhì,
they often strike it with clubs or blades,
or hit it with hard objects,
and it often transforms into stone,
with a bluish-black, warm, and smooth stone color.
It is suitable for sharpening purposes.
The zhì stone is only a foot or so in length,
valued at several tens of thousands,
and any weapon sharpened with it
gleams with a blue light and does not rust.
"Shí Pǔ"
Léi Móshí
In Línhè Commandery, there is a bluish stone,
on which there are marks of sharpening knives and axes.
In spring and summer, it is bright and clean,
while in autumn and winter, it becomes overgrown and filthy.
It is said to be the stone where thunder sharpens its tools.
From "Records of Jīngzhōu"
Stone Swallows
In Línglíng, there are stone swallows that,
when encountering wind and rain, fly about as if alive.
When the wind and rain cease,
they revert to being stones.
"Records of Xiāngzhōu"
Xiè Hóng said that while studying at a mountain temple in his hometown,
he saw something resembling swallows on a high cliff.
He then marked the stones with his brush.
When the stones were exposed to the scorching sun,
suddenly a heavy rain passed by,
and the marked ones often fell to the ground.
This is likely due to the alternation of heat and cold causing them to fall together,
not because they could fly.
"Miscellaneous Records of a Weary Traveler"
There are stone slabs with lumpy formations shaped like swallows,
called swallow nests.
"Stone Catalog"
Píng Shí
The Shípíng stone comes from the White Crane Mountain in Línglíng,
the place where Qū Chǔjìng ascended to immortality.
During the Rénwǔ year of the Shàoxīng era,
a member of the imperial clan residing in the county
one day moored his boat at the foot of the mountain,
and found a stone in the water,
its radiance dazzling and extraordinary,
its patterns resembling towering, elegant peaks,
as if naturally formed.
From then on, stoneworkers quarried it in increasing numbers,
with scenes of mist, clouds, snow, and moonlight,
and images of surging waves, dragons, and phoenixes,
faintly visible.
The larger pieces could be four to five feet square,
and even the most skilled painters
could not match their exquisite beauty.
"Línglíng Chronicles"
Yú Shí
In Héngyáng Xiāngxiāng County,
there is a Shíyú Mountain.
Below it are many dark stones,
whose color is black and texture resembles mica.
When split open one layer,
there immediately appears a fish shape,
with scales, fins, head and tail,
as if carved and painted,
several inches long,
the fish form completely present.
When burned, it takes the form of fish oil,
hence it is named accordingly.
"Records of Nányuè"
states: in Lǒngxī region,
by digging the ground where fish and dragons dwell,
stones are obtained by breaking them open,
no different from those produced in Xiāngxiāng.
"Stone Catalog"
records Dù Fǔ's verse: "As water recedes, fish and dragons appear; at night mountains stand empty, birds and rats autumn."
Soft Stone
Nánxióng County produces soft stone,
which can be used to make pots and cauldrons.
"Records of the Universe"
Shí Guǒ
North of Yǐnshān in Guìzhōu, Guǎngxī,
there is a stone chamber,
a stone platform,
and also stone fruits
shaped like lychees,
walnuts,
and chestnuts or dates.
People gather them
and sometimes give them as gifts arranged on plates.
Sháo Shí
At Qǔjiāng there is a stone a hundred zhang high,
five li in circumference,
with two rocks standing opposite each other,
one li apart.
They are roughly equal in size,
resembling a pair of watchtowers.
They are named Sháoshí,
and to the south lies Língshí,
also called Táoshí.
It is thirty zhang high,
with a circumference of five hundred zhang.
The Old Records state:
"The stone originally belonged to Wǔchéng County in Guìyáng,
but due to a sudden thunderstorm one night,
it unexpectedly moved here.
People who came to see it marveled, saying:
'The stone has fled here,'
hence it was named Táoshí (the Fleeing Stone)."
Because of its spiritual nature,
and its miraculous relocation, it is also called Língshí (the Spiritual Stone).
Its prominent part faces the river, standing like a cliff,
with mottled colors as if painted.
Water and stones create startling rapids,
their echoes reverberating endlessly.
Merchant boats linger here,
listening and admiring without cease.
The Water Classic
Yùnǚ Fáng
On Lóngpán Mountain there is a stone,
forty zhang in length,
five zhang in height,
which has a door and a door-leaf,
as if closed by someone.
Ancient tradition identifies it as the Jade Maiden's Chamber.
from Yìzhōu Jì
Nǚguān Shí
In Nánlíng County there is a Nǚguān Mountain.
Local legend says:
Long ago there was a woman
whose husband held office in Shǔ.
He repeatedly delayed his return date.
Worried and longing, she was deeply grieved.
She climbed this mountain to gaze into the distance,
and thereupon turned into stone,
taking on human form.
The dog accompanying her also turned to stone,
and today only the dog's form remains.
"Records of the Land"
Wàngfū Shí
On the northern mountain of Wǔdāng,
there stands the Gazing-at-Husband Stone,
shaped like a person standing.
Legend says: In the past, there was a faithful woman
whose husband joined the army
and went far away to serve the country in crisis.
Carrying their young child, she bid him farewell on this mountain,
stood gazing until she turned into stone.
(Shì Shuō)
Dūyóu
At the boundary between the
Yídū and Jiànpíng Commanderies,
there are five or six peaks
rising unevenly in succession.
Upon them stand leaning rocks resembling two figures,
appearing as if rolling up their sleeves facing each other.
Local tradition holds that the two commanderies’
Chief Officials contested the border here.
“Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds”
Yán shí
Mount Wénshān has salt stones,
which yield salt when boiled.
"Records of Huáyáng"
Forty-three lǐ into the Tāngkǒu entrance there are stones,
boiled to serve as salt stones.
The larger ones are like a shēng measure,
the smaller ones like a fist.
When boiled, the water dries up and salt forms.
"Jìn Division Geographic Records"
To bear the stone
At the mouth of the Mǐshuǐ River in Zhùyáng,
there is a stone beneath,
protruding over a foot above ground to an unfathomable depth,
with a circumference of about three feet.
Its color is extremely azure,
its surface polished and bright like a mirror,
capable of reflecting people.
It is traditionally believed to be a fallen star.
West of the county, a solitary rock stands out prominently,
overlooking a deep pool below.
At times, people see the root of this stone,
resembling bamboo and yellow in color.
Those who see it often meet with misfortune.
Together, they call it the Chéngshòu Stone.
"Supplementary Records of the Prefectural Maps"
Lěng Shí
On Mǎlǐng Bridge,
there are many vipers whose venom kills people.
There is a cold stone that can counteract it;
when its powder is applied to the wound, the person revives.
"Records of Commanderies and States"
Yùshí
guàn,
a water bird.
When incubating eggs,
it frequently enters water,
and if the eggs get cold they won't hatch.
Yùshí is used to surround the eggs,
helping maintain warmth.
Therefore, practitioners of esoteric arts consider the yùshí from stork nests to be genuine.
"Bówù Zhì"
Shí Zhū
Qīnglíng County,
there is a Stone Pig Ridge in the long valley,
with thousands of stone pigs, both mothers and piglets.
The elders pass down the story,
that the Yí people once herded here,
but one morning they turned into stone,
and to this day the Yí people dare not go there to herd.
"Water Classic"
Shílǐn
Shílǐn resembles a granary,
capable of holding a thousand hu inside.
When its opening gapes, the year is lean;
when closed, the harvest is abundant.
Línchuān Jì
Stone Mirror
On the eastern side of Stone Mirror Mountain, a round stone hangs from the cliff,
bright and clear enough to reflect people,
revealing even the finest details.
"Records of Xunyang"
By the shore of Gongting Lake,
it is said there were several stones,
round in shape like mirrors,
so bright they could reflect people.
They were called stone mirrors.
Later, someone passed by and burned one with fire,
and now it no longer shines,
causing that person's eyes to go blind.
"Records of the Hidden and Visible"
In Hezhou's Fu River, there is a stone standing in the water,
perfectly round like the moon,
emerging when the water level drops,
about three zhang high,
commonly known as the stone mirror.
"Records of Extraordinary Mountains and Rivers"
At Zhongxing Cliff in Lingling,
there is a stone mirror.
Liú Yuàn's preface states:
When moistened with water,
its light becomes brilliant,
the winding of rivers and mountains,
the flourishing and withering of plants,
all are clearly reflected without escape.
Pántuó Shí
In the Eastern Sea of Míngzhōu's Chāngguó,
on Pǔtuójiā Mountain,
there is a flat-topped rock.
Its broad surface can accommodate over a hundred people standing,
overlooking the great sea below,
precisely where the sun rises over Fúsāng.
As the torch dragon prepares to harness the celestial light,
a radiant display of five colors
suddenly bursts forth in dazzling splendor.
A full orb emerges,
its magnitude beyond description.
"Old Records of Sìmíng"
Zhī Dǐng
East of Chénzhōu there are three mountains,
standing like a tripod's legs pointing straight up,
each several dozen zhang high.
An ancient saying goes:
Kuāfù raced with the sun,
and here he cooked his meal.
These three mountains
are the stones Kuāfù used to prop up his tripod.
"Records of Affairs in and out of Court"
Nǚwā Shí
The mountain rocks of Guīměi Mountain,
are brilliantly red as if painted with vermilion,
towering elegantly and scraping the sky,
are named Nǚwā Stone by the locals.
After heavy rain and wind, when the sky clears and the air calms,
the sound of strings and pipes can be heard.
"Records of Nánkāng"
Mirror Polishing Stone
It is popularly said of Mirror Lake that
Xuānyuánshì cast a mirror by the lake,
and today there remains Xuānyuán's mirror-polishing stone,
which is always clean with no creeping weeds growing on it.
"Records of Strange Things"
Map of the Nine Provinces
Lǔ Bān carved the stone into Yǔ's Map of the Nine Provinces,
which is now located at Shíbǎo Mountain in Luòchéng.
Above
Shí wept.
During Jié's time,
Mount Tài's rocks moved and wept,
early Confucian scholars said this occurred as Jié approached his downfall,
with Mount Tài weeping for three days.
Now when looking at Mount Tài's rocks from afar,
they appear like weeping people,
which likely confirms this account.
King Wǔ of Zhōu told the Duke of Zhōu:
"Jié acted without virtue,
causing the mountain rocks to move and weep."
Shí Yāyá
A hundred li south of the capital Biàn,
there was a stone figure in front of Duke Zhōu's tomb that could cause hauntings.
If people encountered it,
it would call itself Stone Bailiff Lǔ Xiàoshū.
"Dòng Wēi Zhì"
Moon Mirror
During the reign of King Líng of Zhōu,
a foreign land offered a stone mirror as tribute.
This stone was white as the moon,
reflecting one's face like snow,
and was called the Moon Mirror.
"Records of Omitted Affairs"
Stone Turtle
By the seashore there is a large stone turtle,
commonly said to be
the work of Lǔ Bān.
In summer it enters the sea,
and in winter returns to rest upon the mountain.
Lù Jī's poem says:
"The stone turtle often longs for the sea,
how could I forget my homeland?"
From "Records of Strange Things"
King Yuèwáng Shí
By the riverside in Xìng'ān County lies a flat stone,
upon which there is a stone comb
and a pair of stone shoes,
each set.
Folklore says:
When the King of Yuè crossed the stream,
he took off his shoes and dropped his comb here.
"Records of Jīngzhōu"
Zhào Shí
West of Fāngzhàng Mountain there is a mirror stone.
From ten lǐ away,
it reflects images of people and objects as clearly as a mirror.
Even broken fragments of the stone can reflect people.
The stone measures exactly one zhàng square,
yet weighs only one liǎng.
King Yān Zhāo
pounded this stone into mud,
plastered the Nìngxiá Platform with this mud,
and often roamed and dwelled at this platform with the Queen Mother of the West.
"Records of Omissions"
Just sitting
At Huìjī's Qínwàng Mountain,
there is a stone inscribed by the First Emperor,
in front of which lies a stone several zhang wide.
It is said to be the stone where the First Emperor sat.
On both sides, there are eight square seating areas.
These are said to be the stones where the Chancellor and others sat,
hence the name "Chancellor Stones" persists to this day.
From "Records of Geography"
Erecting a Stone
Off the coast of the state of Láizǐ there is a stone figure,
fifteen feet tall,
and ten arm-spans in girth.
It is said that the First Emperor of Qín once dispatched this stone figure to pursue Mount Láo, but failing to reach it, it remained standing there.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ".
Gold Transforms into Stone
In the first year of the reign of Qín Èrshì, gold rained down in the palace, and within moments it all turned into stone.
"Shù Yì Jì"
Painting Stones
Dǒng Yǎn often lay in the Yánqīng Chamber,
using painted stone as his bed,
with patterns like brocade.
The stone was very light in substance,
originating from the Zhìzhī Kingdom.
"Records of Omissions"
Stone Man
Emperor Guāngwǔ arrived south of Zhàozhōu at night,
got lost and heard human speech,
asked but received no response,
saw two figures standing nearby,
angrily drew his sword and beheaded one of them,
hurried over for a closer look,
only to find it was a stone statue.
"Unofficial History: Zhàozhōu Records"
Shí Xiàng
East of Hénán Prefecture stands an elephant village,
where legend tells of a Western monk in the Hàn Dynasty who brought scriptures on an elephant's back to Luòyáng.
The elephant turned to stone,
and the stone elephant remains there today.
From "Shānchuān Jìyì"
Stone Bed
North of Jiāo's Mountain, several mountains away,
there is the tomb of Lǔ Gōng, the Han Dynasty Colonel-Director of Retainers,
in front of which stands a stone shrine.
The four walls of the stone temple are all made of bluish stone with raised carvings,
since the beginning of written records,
of loyal ministers,
filial sons,
chaste women,
and images of Confucius and his seventy-two disciples.
Beside each image is a stone inscription recording it, with clear and distinct writing.
There was also a stone bed eight feet long,
polished to a bright and gleaming finish,
that produced a sound when struck, audible from far and near.
At the time, the Grand Commandant's Attendant Officer, Fù Zhēnzhī,
and the Consultant General, Zhōu Ān,
broke the stone bed,
each taking a piece away.
They were sued by the descendants of the Lǔ family,
and both men were dismissed from their posts.
"Dài Yánzhī's Record of a Western Campaign"
Yǔ Shí
In the final years of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi,
multicolored stones rained down in Yèzhōng.
"Records of Strange Events"
Shí Yáng
In Jīngkǒu there is a stone resembling a sheep,
called the wolf stone.
Zhūgě Liàng once sat upon it,
discussing with Sūn Quán how to resist Cáo Cāo.
According to the Records,
the wolf stone has a cross-shaped fracture mark,
which was made when Liú Bèi and Sūn Quán privately performed divination.
The Romance
describes Sūn and Liú getting drunk while hunting together and each occupying a stone sheep,
later giving the name Stone Sheep Lane to the place.
As recorded in the Geographical Records.
Stone Statue
In the first year of Yǒngxī of Xiàowǔ of Wèi,
at Píngděng Temple a five-tiered pagoda was constructed.
In the second year, the work in earth and wood was completed.
The emperor led all the officials to hold an assembly of ten thousand monks.
On that day, outside the temple gate, there was a stone statue
that moved by itself and lowered its head,
then raised it again, continuing all day long before it stopped.
The emperor, amazed at its strangeness,
the Palace Secretary Biàn Língjǐng said,
"The stone moves the community,
this has existed since ancient times,
what does Your Majesty find strange about it?"
The emperor then returned to the palace.
In mid-July, the emperor fled to Cháng'ān.
In October, he moved the capital to Yè.
"Luòyáng Jiālán Jì"
Shénzhēng
South of Wǔ'ān County stands Gǔ Shān,
on which there are two drum-shaped stones,
facing each other from north and south.
Legend says when these drums sound, war will arise.
In the final years of Northern Qí,
these drums often resonated,
and Qí was annexed by Zhōu.
During the final years of Suí Wéndì's reign,
the drums sounded again spontaneously,
audible for hundreds of lǐ,
and Táng replaced Suí to rise.
Hence it is also called Shén Zhēng.
From "Shān Chuān Jì Yì Jīn Hú Bēi Jì":
North of Tiānshuǐ, south of Běijì County,
lies Zhū Yǔ Shān,
where the mountain has a stone drum depicted in the Kāi Shān Tú,
referred to as Tiān Gǔ Shān.
When disasters arise across the nine provinces, it sounds,
always with a consistent response.
It also states:
Shí Gǔ Shān has a stone drum,
corresponding in the stars to Hé Gǔ,
when the star moves, the stone drum sounds.
If the stone drum sounds, the land of Qín will face calamity.
A shallow sound brings disaster to all things,
while a deep sound brings calamity upon the ruler.
From "Shuǐ Jīng":
Féng Shān is located thirty lǐ south of Guǎnggù, with a shrine,
alongside a stone drum.
When the Qí region is about to fall into chaos,
stone figures strike the stone drum,
audible for tens of lǐ.
From "Shù Zhēng Jì".
Biànyù
At the end of the Kāihuáng era,
Emperor Gāozǔ buried two small stones in the ground within the palace,
to mark the location for placing the bed.
Before long, they transformed into jade,
Liú Xiàng remarked:
"Jade is
the ultimate symbol of nobility.
It signifies the humble turning into the noble."
By the end of the Dàyè era, when rebels rose,
they all usurped imperial titles.
Suí Shū
Casting the Talisman
Yè Fǎshàn chose to dwell at Mǎoyǒu Mountain,
his gate being close to the mountain,
where a giant rock blocked the path.
Each time he returned, he had to detour
to avoid it. The master cast a talisman,
and in a moment, it flew away.
The path then became level and smooth,
leaving everyone astonished by the marvel.
"Immortal Biographies Supplement"
Bestowing the Stone Eagle
Yáng Hóngyù was a man from Héshuò.
One day, while traveling in the suburbs,
a messenger from the north came riding swiftly.
He asked, "Are you not Yáng Yù?"
"The Northern Peak bestows upon you a gift,"
"kneel and receive it."
The messenger reached into his bosom and retrieved an object,
wrapped as if in silk.
Yù returned home, lit incense,
and upon opening it, found two stone eagles—
one male and one female.
The one with the left wing covering the right
was the male.
The one with the right wing covering the left
was the female.
Later, he had a son and a daughter.
The son was named Tíngzhāng,
who served as a Feilong official in the Zhōu dynasty.
The daughter became the consort of Emperor Tàizǔ of Zhōu.
From "Jìnshēn Cuǒshuō."
Repelling Bookworms
Xióng Shānyě enjoyed visiting unusual objects,
There were stone turtles,
stone peaches,
stone dates and the like.
He once dreamed of a man who claimed his surname was Shí (Stone),
and later obtained a stone figure,
over a foot tall,
with fully formed eyebrows and eyes.
Later generations have stone swallows,
stone crabs and similar things,
while pine trees also transform into stone.
Lǒngzhōu has fish stone seeds,
which when placed among books can repel moths.
"Secret Pavilion Casual Conversations"
Shí Tuó
Five days' journey north of the country,
there is another mountain.
On the mountain, there is a stone camel,
from which polluted water drips down.
If gold, silver, or other vessels
are used to catch it, they all leak.
Even holding it in one's palm causes leaking,
only a gourd can catch it without leaking.
Some who handle it develop a foul body odor,
and their skin and hair change.
"Records of Widely Heard Matters"
Shí Zhù
Jié bǐ tā guó,
a dependency of Central India.
There is a stone pillar seventy feet high,
glossy in color and luminous.
When one observes its surface,
according to one's sins or merits,
all are seen reflected in it.
Above
Washing Block
Dǎoyī Shān,
also known as Líng Shān,
is located in Lángláng Shān.
To the south lies an extremely perilous cliff,
where there is a square stone.
In ancient times, a divine maiden
pounded clothes here,
and the stone became luminous and lustrous.
It is called the Jade Maiden's Clothes-Pounding Stone.
"Shù Yì Jì"
Hǎi Shí
Jiǎ Chéngshì's cousin followed his advice;
when he was young, he once destroyed a bird's nest
and found a black stone,
smooth and lovely like a sparrow's egg.
Later, he accidentally placed it in a vinegar container,
when suddenly he felt the stone move.
Looking closely, he saw it had four feet;
as he lifted it with a thread,
the feet retracted accordingly.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Huáyuè Palm
Huà Yuè's palm rock is cinnabar purple,
exactly like human flesh in color.
Whenever the sun shines directly on it,
it becomes completely visible;
and as dusk falls, it gradually fades and disappears.
Woodcutters say the Immortal's Palm
is atop an isolated peak,
where numerous ravines converge.
Viewed from afar, the rock's reddish hue
happens to resemble a palm.
"Jiǎ Shì Xián Tán"
Shí Jiǔ Zǐ Mǔ
The Shí Jiǔ Zǐ Mǔ,
seated seven feet high,
is located in the Jīnzhōu Temple,
with nine children all attached to the stone body.
Legend says:
it arrived floating across the sea,
and when scholars and commoners pray and offer sacrifices,
seeking children is often efficacious.
"Jiāozhōu Records"
Yúngēn
Poets often refer to stones as "cloud roots,"
as clouds are born when they touch the stones.
Emperor Xiaowu of Song wrote in his poem "Climbing Leshan":
"Gathered smoke disturbs the wind caves,
Accumulated water drowns the cloud roots."
Emperor Xuanwu of Northern Wei issued an edict to Péi Càn:
"Dwelling by the cloud roots in simplicity,
Nourishing on ganoderma in clear valleys."
Bái Jūyì wrote in his "Tianzhu Stone Poem":
"Below, sweeping across the cloud roots."
Dù Fǔ's poem reads:
"Piercing water, suddenly reaching cloud roots."
Qián Qǐ wrote:
"Strange stones with shallow cloud roots."
Jiǎ Dǎo described:
"Unmovable cloud roots."
Sloping
The Erya says:
A slope is
a hillside.
Guō Pú notes:
Sloping and uneven,
it is not level.
Chángsōng
The Son of Heaven returned south,
ascending the slope of Chángsōng,
and climbed eastward up the three paths.
"The Biography of King Mù of Zhōu"
Nine Bends
The Luo River flows eastward,
its course winding for ten li through nine bends,
with nine slopes along its twists.
The "Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
records King Mu of Zhou ascending the Nine Slopes during his western expedition.
Guo Pu noted:
It is likely present-day Xīn'ān County,
where ten li contain nine slopes.
The "Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital" states:
Blocked by the Nine Slopes to the west,
and the eastern gate at the whirls.
Huányuán
Luán Yíng passed through Zhōu,
and the king sent an officer to escort him out through Huányuán.
"Zuǒzhuàn"
Zhāng Yí said:
"Block the pass of Huányuán."
"Strategies of Qín"
Its slope has twelve winding paths,
so when one is about to leave, they turn back again, hence the saying.
"Records"
Diānlíng
In Tàiyáng County,
over ten lǐ northeast of Fù Yán,
there is Diānlíng Slope.
It is the place mentioned in the *Zuǒzhuàn* as "entering from Diānlíng."
There are east-west ravines,
with a road built in the valley,
called Líng Bridge.
North of Yú City, facing a long slope about twenty lǐ away,
it is called Yú Slope.
Dài Yánzhī said:
"From top to bottom,
seven mountains overlap."
The *Strategies of the Warring States* says:
"In the past, a fine horse pulled a salt cart,
going up Yú Slope slowly,
struggled under the yoke and could not advance,
which was its place of hardship."
The *Water Classic*
states that Zhēnlíng is north of Wú City,
now called Wú.
Slope
The *Ancient and Modern Place Names*
records Liú Yuèshí's letter to Lú Chén saying:
"In the past, a fine horse leaned against the shaft at Wú Slope,
neighing long to Bó Lè,
whether understood or not."
Goat's Gut
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was ascending the steep slope of Yángcháng,
and all his ministers were pushing the carriage.
Only Zōng Huì leaned on his halberd and walked along singing.
Jiǎnzǐ asked,
"If a minister insults his lord,
what should his punishment be?"
Zōng Huì replied,
"His crime deserves death.
But have you, my lord, also heard of
a lord who insults his ministers?
Then the wise will not offer counsel,
the eloquent will not contend,
and will not the state then be in peril?"
Jiǎnzǐ said,
"Well said," and treated Zōng Huì as his honored guest.
From "Xīn Xù"
Gāo Yòu commented:
The mountain Yángcháng
winds and twists like sheep's intestines;
it is the barrier of Tàiháng and Mèngmén.
Wèi Wǔ, suffering the bitter cold, traveled Yángcháng Slope,
where the winding path broke the wheels of his carriage.
Nine bends
Wáng Yáng, while serving as the Governor of Yìzhōu, came to the steep and winding slope of Áng Cuàn,
and sighed, saying:
"How can I risk the body inherited from my ancestors
by traversing such danger?"
He then resigned from his post due to illness.
Later, when Wáng Zūn became the Regional Inspector,
he reached this slope and asked his subordinate:
"Isn't this the path that Wáng Yáng feared?"
He then shouted at his driver to urge the carriage forward, declaring:
"Wáng Yáng was a filial son,
Wáng Zūn is a loyal minister."
Hàn Shū
Huáng Mǎ
Sūn Dēng, as Yáng Jùn pressed urgently to welcome him,
spoke with him but received no reply.
Yáng Jùn bestowed a cloth robe upon Sūn Dēng,
who borrowed a knife to cut it and discarded it in the doorway,
shouting loudly:
"Stab and slash."
He eventually fell ill and died.
Later, people saw him at Huángmǎ Bǎn.
From "Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū":
North of Chénggāo, there is Huángmǎ Bǎn,
where Sūn Dēng departed,
and Yáng Jùn wrote a letter
to his old acquaintance in Luòyáng.
From "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù":
Pān Ní's "Ode to the Evil Path" states:
If the slope is named Yánggēng,
the eight special ones form Chénggāo's Huángmǎ.
Bātè Bǎn
The eastern slope of Hángǔ,
is called Bātè Slope.
From the "Treatise on Geography."
Revolving Gate
The river flows east past Chénggāo,
west of Xuánmén Slope,
north of present-day Chénggāo,
one of the four great slopes.
Ascending this slope,
and climbing eastward to Chénggāo,
the city where Cáo Dàgū's "Eastern Expedition Rhapsody"
gazes upon the converging flows of the Yellow and Luò Rivers,
and beholds the Xuánmén of Chénggāo.
Yìfù Slope
Lǚ Róng was
the wife of Xǔ Shēng from Wújùn.
Shēng was killed by bandits,
and Róng firmly preserved her chastity.
When Huángjīn bandit Chén Bǎo attempted to violate her,
Róng maintained her virtue and refused,
so Bǎo killed Róng.
That day,
fierce winds and torrential rain arose,
with thunder, lightning, and darkness.
Bǎo became terrified and kowtowed,
apologized by burying her, then left.
The prefect heard of Róng's noble conduct,
sent his registrar to offer sacrifices to her,
and contributed money to help the county build a tomb for her
north of the ruins in the outer district of Jiāxīng,
naming it Righteous Woman Slope.
From "Later Biographies of Exemplary Women"
Chìxū Slope
Bān Biāo's "Ode to the Northern Expedition":
Ascending the long slope of Chìxū to enter.
Yìqú's "Old City Commentary":
Chìxū Slope is in Běidì Commandery.
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic":
Chìxū River flows out of Chìxū Valley,
Flowing southwest into Luó River Slope,
Named after the river.
"Selections of Refined Literature"
Lǒngbǎn
Zhāng Héng's "Poem of Four Sorrows":
My beloved dwells in Hànyáng,
But Lǒng's slopes stretch far when I'd pursue.
Yìng Shào notes:
In Tiānshuǐ there lies a great slope,
Named Lǒng Slope.
The "Wénxuǎn"
describes Lǒngxī Pass with its nine winding slopes,
Unmeasured in height by miles,
Where ascent takes seven days to cross,
The summit spacious enough for a hundred homes,
The base hosting hundreds of thousands of households,
And atop it flows clear water.
A folk song of the region sings:
On Lǒng's peak, the flowing stream,
Its murmur soft and mournful.
Gazing afar toward Qínchuān,
Heart and liver break with grief.
A thousand miles from Cháng'ān,
Qínchuān appears but a ribbon.
Those from Guānzhōng ascending Lǒng,
Looking back upon their homeland,
Sing with sorrowful longing,
And some perish from despair.
From "Records of the Three Qín."
Bái Sīmǎ
During the Chuígōng era,
an imperial edict ordered the construction of a large statue at Báisīmǎ Slope,
which incurred enormous expenses,
amounting to tens of thousands. Sū Xiàng,
citing harm to agriculture, submitted a memorial,
urgently admonishing Wǔ Zétiān, who accepted his advice.
The Old Book of Táng records:
Hóu Sīzhǐ served as Left Censorate Attendant,
and once interrogated Vice Censor-in-Chief Wèi Yuánzhōng in prison, saying:
"Quickly confess to Báisīmǎ,
or else face Mèng Qīng."
Báisīmǎ refers to
a slope in Luòyáng,
named Báisīmǎ Slope.
Mèng Qīng,
a general surnamed Mèng and named Qīng,
was the one who clubbed Lángyá Prince Lǐ Chōng to death.
Hóu Sīzhǐ, originally a servant of Gāo Yuánlǐ,
often used these phrases to intimidate prisoners.
Hóu Sīzhǐ's speech was unrefined,
prompting contemporaries to mimic it,
using it as material for jokes.
From the Old Book of Táng: Biographies of Cruel Officials.
Steep Slope
During the Jiǔshì era, Empress Wǔ Zétiān visited Sānyáng Palace,
staying from summer through autumn,
without returning to the capital promptly.
Zhāng Yuè submitted a memorial stating:
"The palace is one hundred sixty lǐ from Luòyáng,
separated by the Yī River,
and the steepness of the È Slope."
The Old Book
and the New Book record:
The Empress escaped the summer heat at Sānyáng Palace.
Chánglè Pǎn
Zhāng Jùn was appointed as the Pacification Commissioner,
and he led his cavalry to depart from the capital.
Emperor Zhāozōng saw him off from the Ānxǐ Tower,
where Zhāng Jùn, flushed with wine, tearfully addressed the emperor.
Yáng Fùgōng was displeased upon hearing this.
The eunuch commanders and palace attendants held a farewell banquet for him at Chánglè Slope,
where Fùgōng offered wine to Zhāng Jùn.
Zhāng Jùn declined,
and Fùgōng teased him, saying:
"Your Excellency does not accept Fùgōng's goodwill,
are you putting on airs?"
Zhāng Jùn laughed and replied:
"Only after the rebels are pacified will we see who has the face."
Fùgōng bore a grudge against him for this.
"Old Book of Tang"
Yùlún Pō
The source of the Wènjiāng River,
emerges beneath the Jade Wheel Slope.
Records of Yìzhōu
The cow kowtows.
The Way has an ox kowtowing,
a slope horse slapping its cheeks on the slope.
"Huáyáng Zhì"
Thirty-Six Caverns
Within the great heavens,
there are thirty-six caves in the profound abyss.
Among the eight seas,
Kūnlún,
Pénglái,
Fāngzhàng,
Yíngzhōu,
Cāngbō,
Báishān,
Bātíng,
the divine mountains,
each mountain has a cave palace,
not counted among the thirty-six heavenly caves.
The cave of Luófēng Mountain,
with a circumference of fifteen thousand lǐ,
is named the Northern Emperor.
The heavens of life and death,
are all governed by the god of death,
the palaces of the five emperors,
are the offices for examining transgressions.
Governed by ghosts and deities,
there are also twenty-eight mountain caves,
the hidden palaces of heaven,
or where earthly officials reside,
unable to record the names of all the caves and mountains one by one,
the remaining six cave heavens,
the hidden palace mountains,
are all inhabited by barbarians and strange races,
not governed by ghosts,
the great Rong tribes of birds and beasts,
the naked and barbarian kinds.
The world of the Xiōngnú,
the virtuous mountains of the northern Rong,
and the Gōulǒu of Nányuè are such.
Within the cave palace of Jūqǔ Mountain,
there were originally immortals,
a person named Guō Sìcháo,
managed the palace and also oversaw the three offices,
leading the morning watch at Luófēng,
Sìcháo was from Yān.
Four brothers attained the Way,
Sìcháo was the eldest.
Qīngliáng Dòng
North of Jīnyāng Mountain in Jùyě,
there is a stone cave,
named Qīngliáng.
It is over ten zhang deep,
with stone carvings inside,
forming four small pavilions.
Outside the pavilions lies a hall,
with steps three chi high,
and two doors outside the hall.
Beyond the doors are two large pavilions,
connected by a stone path thirty zhang long
and sixteen chi wide.
It is traditionally said to be the summer retreat palace of Qín Shǐ Huáng.
"Geographical Records"
Zhūgě Dòng
South of Qiánzhōng Commandery,
a stone cliff stands tall,
beside which lies a cave several zhàng deep.
Legend has it that when Zhūgě Liàng campaigned against the Jiǔxī Man,
he once passed by and stayed overnight in this cave,
setting up a bed
and hanging a handful of millet to feed his horse.
These later turned into a stone bed
and stone millet,
which remain to this day.
Above
Bǎoxiān Cave
In the tenth month, on the gēngshēn day of the ninth year of the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Xuánzong,
he visited Huáyīn in Qīng Prefecture,
where Wáng Yuányì, a hermit from Mount Tàibái, reported
that the Mysterious Sovereign and Primal Emperor had descended into the Bǎoxiān Cave.
(Basic Annals)
The Jade Spring Cave
At the Yùquán Temple in Jīngzhōu,
near the various mountains by Qīngxī,
jade springs are often found in mountain caves,
with many interconnected stalactite grottoes.
There are white bats as large as crows,
and after a thousand years,
their bodies become as white as snow.
It is said they achieve longevity by drinking the stalactite water.
"Bái Collection"
Yīyú Cave
Yuán Jié wrote about himself, saying:
When the military conflicts arose across the land,
he fled the chaos and entered the Yīyú Cave,
calling himself Yīyúzi.
From the "Táng Shū"
Dàyǐn Dòng
Wéi Xiàqīng in his late years was about to retire and return home,
and named his residence Dàyǐn Dòng.
"History of the Tang Dynasty"
White Deer Grotto
During the Zhēnyuán era,
a man from Luòyáng named Lǐ Bó, along with his elder brother Shè,
lived together in seclusion studying,
in a cave beneath Wǔlǎo Peak of Lúshān,
raising a white deer for their amusement,
later naming the cave after it.
In the Bǎolì era,
Bó served as the governor of Jiāngzhōu,
and built terraces and pavilions at the cave,
diverting water to flow through and planting flowers there.
"The County Gazetteer"
Jīnshā Dòng
Mount Líshān has the Golden Sand Cave and Jade Stamen Peak.
"The Unofficial Biography of Consort Yáng"
Hánhuī Cave
Xuē Jǐnghuì served as the prefect of Dàozhōu,
where he discovered a remarkable site in the suburbs.
There stood a stone arch soaring like a grand hall,
leading him to name the place Hánhuī Cave.
From the Collection of Yǔxī
Nánshān Rǔdòng
Someone traveled to the Rǔ Cave of the Southern Mountain,
which extended several miles deep.
Stalactites dripped and coalesced into shapes resembling flying immortals,
with dozens already formed in the cave.
Their features appeared as if carved from jade,
with exquisitely crafted clothing and forms.
At one spot, dripping reached above the waist level.
The person cupped their hands to catch and rinse with it.
A year later, returning for another visit,
they saw the dripped image they had caught had fully formed.
The stalactites no longer dripped there,
but precisely where their hands had caught the droplets,
a two-inch gap remained unfinished in the clothing.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Lóngdòng
Táng Shìmín of the State of Lǔ,
courtesy name Túchāng,
was originally a native of Línglíng.
He served as a yáxiào in the commandery,
and during the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng of the Táng dynasty, when banditry arose,
Shìmín organized local militia,
protecting the local community. Liú Jiànfēng
appointed him as Prefect of Yǒngzhōu.
In the early Guānghuà era,
Mǎ Yīn attacked him, but he refused to surrender
and died. Afterwards, some heard the sounds of bells and drums,
and he was even seen several times during the day.
Once, a piece of wood flowed out from a cave,
stopped at a rocky thornbush,
and people on the bank sent it back to the midstream.
By the next morning, it had returned again,
and this happened repeatedly.
Coincidentally, during a drought, prayers were offered and rain fell,
so they took the wood, carved it into an image, and enshrined it.
The Mǎ family of Húnán
bestowed upon it the title of Temple of the Prince of Línglíng.
"Old Records"
Shénnóng Xué
In Xiàpíng County there are layered mountains,
which are the Liè Mountains.
At the foot of the mountains there is a cave,
and according to the elders' tradition, this is the place where Shénnóng was born.
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Yǔ Xué
The Book of Hàn, Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān states:
He ascended Kuàijī to explore Yǔ Xué,
and there was also Yǔ Jǐng.
Yáng Dū Fù states:
The cave connects to Cāngwú, Wāng states:
A person from Línglíng said,
entering from Yǔ Xué,
one emerges at Cāngwú.
"Records of Kuàijī"
Fleeing to the Vermilion Nest
For three generations, the Yuè people
had killed their monarchs.
Zǐ Sōu, troubled by this,
fled to a cinnabar cave.
With the Yuè people left without a ruler,
they followed him to the cave.
Prince Sōu refused to come out,
so the people smoked him out with mugwort,
and bore him away in a jade carriage.
"Zhuangzi"
Dānxué
Bà Guǎfù Qīng,
her ancestors obtained a cinnabar mine,
and monopolized its profits.
"Records of the Grand Historian: Biographies of Moneymakers"
The Five Clans Emerge from the Cave
The Bāmán had five clans,
all originating from Wǔlù,
residing at Luòzhōnglí Mountain.
This mountain had red and black caves,
the sons of the Bā clan
were born in the red cave,
while the sons of the four other clans
were all born in the black cave.
They had no chieftain,
and all served ghosts and deities.
They then jointly threw swords into a stone cave,
vowing that whoever could hit the target
would be honored as their chieftain.
Wù Xiàng, son of the Bā clan,
alone succeeded in hitting it.
All marveled,
and thus they established him as Lǐnjūn.
From the "Book of the Later Hàn."
Mǎ Xué
In Zhōnglú County there is Mǎxué Mountain,
beside which lies an underground passage.
During the Hàn Dynasty, several
white horses often emerged from it,
all small in form resembling Zhēnchí horses,
hence it was named Horse Cave.
"Jīngzhōu Tújì"
records: thirty lǐ north of Xīlíng is a stone cave,
named Horse Passage.
There once was a white horse
that emerged from the cave and ate people.
When chased, it entered the cave
and secretly emerged in Hànzhōng.
When people of Hànzhōng lost horses,
they would often appear from this cave,
though the distance between them is several thousand lǐ.
"Yídū Jì"
Terrestrial Veins
In Tàihú Lake there is Bāo Mountain,
beneath which lies the Dòngtíng Cave,
winding underground,
connecting to all places,
known as the earth's veins.
"Fēngtǔ Jì"
South of Wú Kingdom,
in the Jùqū Marsh lies Bāo Mountain,
housing the Dòngtíng treasure chamber,
descending underground and traveling covertly,
reaching Lángyá and Dōngwǔ.
"Xuánzhōng Jì"
Dòngtíng Mountain has three caves,
all with clear springs flowing out,
only the northwestern cave,
one must stoop to enter Wú,
the Great Emperor sent people over thirty lǐ,
and friends said they heard wave sounds above,
there are large bats,
like birds that can kill people,
lighting a fire in the high parts of the cave,
the firelight does not illuminate,
the cave has goose-quill stalactites,
one can enter when icy cold,
but not in spring or summer.
"Lóudì Jì"
Dòngtíng Mountain has a cave with five entrances,
east connecting to Línwū,
west reaching Éméi,
south linking Luófú,
north joining Dàiyuè,
east has a stone tower,
below the tower are two stones,
striking them produces a clear, far-reaching sound,
what is called the divine bell,
a green youth riding a single whirlwind flying wheel chariot arrived here,
his traces remain.
Above is the Celestial Emperor's Altar Mountain,
the mountain has a golden ox cave,
during Sūn Quán's time in Wú,
he ordered people to dig for gold,
the gold turned into an ox and ran up the mountain,
its tracks remain.
Hence it is named the Golden Ox Cave.
"Shù Yì Jì"
In Zhènzé Lake lies Dòngtíng Mountain,
with a cave over a hundred chǐ deep,
Yǎng Gōng accidentally fell into the cave,
reaching beneath a dragon palace,
where green mud glows day and night,
eating the green mud when hungry,
it tastes like jīngmǐ rice.
He remembered the way back,
and managed to get out,
the matter was reported to Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
the emperor asked Jié Gōng,
who said:
"This cave has four branches,
one connecting to the west bank of Dòngtíng Lake,
one to the north bank of Qīngyī Pú on the Shǔ road,
one to the large stream between Luófú's two mountains,
and one to the east of Kūsāng Island."
"Liáng Sì Gōng Jì"
In Tàihú Lake,
there is also Fūjiāo Mountain,
beneath which lies a great cavern celestial palace,
secretly connecting to the Five Sacred Mountains.
"Wúdì Jì"
secretly communicating
In Xúnzhōu there is a dragon cave,
which secretly connects to the sea,
and lies beside Dòngtíng.
The "Ode to the Capital of Wú" says:
"Gazing upon Lóngchuān and girding the wilderness refers to this."
"Records of Commanderies and States"
Dragon's Lair
At Jiānglíng's Lóngxué Zhōu (Dragon's Lair Isle),
there exists a Jiàbù landing.
When Emperor Wén of Sòng's carriage procession
departed from Jiānglíng and reached this spot,
a black dragon leaped forth,
bearing the vessel upon which the emperor rode.
Those nearby turned pale with fright,
but the emperor said to Chief Secretary Wáng Tánshǒu:
"This is how Xià Yǔ received the Mandate of Heaven.
By what virtue am I worthy of this?"
Hence originates the name "Dragon's Lair."
From "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù"
Fēng Xué
On Wǔtái Shān there is a wind cave.
If people make even slight noise,
or throw objects to strike it,
immediately a great wind arises with roaring force,
lifting roofs and uprooting trees,
inevitably causing harm to creatures.
During the early Bǎolì era,
Yān person Lǐ Qiú fell into the cave,
where he saw two Daoist priests playing chess inside the cavern,
who gave him a cup of water,
and had someone lead him out.
The guide said:
"This mountain is the Daoist Zǐfǔ Grotto,
the cave has three gates and one path,
one path leads west to Kūnlún,
emerging beneath this cliff,
one direction leads to the wind cave,
which is the main gate of the grotto.
All are guarded by dragons and snakes,
here is the path of the northern cliff,
you can return to your original place, Qiú."
He returned as instructed.
"Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Dà Huò
There is a cave in the Xiāng River named Dàhuò,
its connection to other places unknown.
Every spring and summer when the river rises, hundreds of paces away,
water rushes into the cave,
with a sound like thunder.
During the Kāibǎo era,
a diver descended into the water,
and upon looking,
saw only sunken timber from past years,
scattered crisscross within,
along with two clams as large as cart wheels.
"Records of Famous Sites"
Tiānzhōng Jì Volume Eight
Written document
The word for water means
to extend.
Through the transformation of yīn, it moistens and soaks,
flowing and spreading, moving stealthily.
Thus, in forming the character,
two individuals intersect with one,
and what emerges from the center is water.
One represents the beginning of numbers,
the two individuals symbolize male and female,
indicating the interaction of yīn and yáng with things,
initiated by the one.
Yuánmìng Bāo
Journey to the North
It is the standard,
the movement of the north,
symbolizing all waters flowing together,
within which lies the subtle energy of yang.
Xú Yuǎn states:
"Multiple bends form water,
the softest can overcome the hard,
hence it unifies its interior."
Shuōwén
Bāo Tiān
Water is
the encompassing veil of heaven and earth,
the origin of the five elements.
It is that from which all things arise,
the fluid essence of primordial qi.
(Yuánmìng Bāo)
The earth is borne
The heavens are outside the earth,
water is outside the heavens,
and water floats the heavens and bears the earth.
The "Yellow Emperor's Book"
states that the most abundant thing under heaven
is water.
It floats the heavens and bears the earth,
reaching all heights and depths,
and moistening all things.
The "Records of the Mysterious Middle"
Tàiyī Zhōngjīng
Residing the vital energy of the three yangs within the water's pivot,
its concentrated essence is named Tàiyī.
Tàiyī is the true yang,
water contains the inner essence of Tàiyī,
thus it can moisten all things,
and flow beneath the earth.
"Zǐhuá Zǐ"
Moistening and Flowing Downward
The Book of Documents describes water as moistening and descending.
Kǎn represents water,
positioned in the northern direction,
which ultimately stores all things.
When governance follows the seasons,
yin and yang are harmonized,
and beginnings and endings complement each other.
All twelve months receive their proper energy,
then water maintains its nature,
this is called moistening and descending.
If governance opposes the seasons,
mountain waters burst forth violently,
all rivers overflow,
destroying villages and drowning residents,
and excessive rain damages crops,
this is water failing to moisten and descend.
Hàn Shū
Establish Heaven and Earth
That which establishes heaven and earth,
is water.
Now water
is the foundation of heaven and earth.
It exhales the primordial breath,
emanates the sun and moon,
and guides the stars and constellations—
all arise from water.
Beyond the Nine Provinces, all is water.
I once was in Kuàijī,
looking up at the Southern Mountains,
and saw clouds like a waterfall,
spanning several dozen zhàng,
their sound rumbling and crashing.
In a moment, at the foot of the mountain,
the residents were struck with terror,
as a great flood arrived.
From "Discourses on Principles of Things"
Origin of Things
Earth is
the fundamental origin of all things,
the root and garden of all living beings.
Beauty,
ugliness,
worthiness,
unworthiness,
folly,
and brilliance are born from it.
Water is
the blood and vital energy of the earth,
flowing through it like sinews and vessels.
Thus it is said that water embodies qualities.
Water is soft and yielding,
clear and good,
much like human benevolence.
Though it appears black, it is said to be essence.
Its measure cannot be fixed,
yet when ladled to the brim, it levels itself.
It flows ceaselessly,
stopping only when perfectly level—
this is righteousness.
All things move toward heights,
but water alone descends to low places—
this is humility.
Humility is
the abode of the Way and the vessel of kings.
And water makes this its dwelling place.
" Guǎnzǐ"
The Standard of Things
Water is
the standard of all things,
the essence of all living beings,
the substance of right and wrong, gain and loss.
Thus, there is nothing it does not fill,
nothing it does not dwell in.
It gathers in heaven and earth,
and is stored within all things.
It is produced from metal and stone,
and collects in all living beings,
therefore it is called the divine water.
Wǔ Shuǐ
Waters vary in size,
and in distance;
those that originate from mountains
and flow into the sea
are called main rivers.
Waters that branch off from other waters
and enter large bodies of water or the sea
are called tributaries.
Mountain gullies
that sometimes have water
and sometimes are dry
are called valley streams.
Waters that emerge from other sources
and flow through channels into large bodies or the sea
are named rivers.
Water that emerges from the ground but does not flow
is called deep water.
These five types of water
can be utilized for their benefits,
which is acceptable.
To control them by force
is also possible.
But if not managed sustainably,
danger will arise.
Zhìdé
Among all things under heaven,
none is softer and weaker than water.
Yet it is so vast that it cannot be exhausted,
so deep that it cannot be measured,
extending infinitely to the utmost,
reaching distantly to the boundless.
Its increase and decrease,
are immeasurable.
Rising to heaven, it becomes rain and dew;
descending to earth, it moistens and nourishes all things.
It gives birth without forcing,
and all affairs are accomplished through it.
It embraces all living beings without partiality,
its moisture reaches even the tiniest insects,
yet it seeks no reward or wealth.
It enriches the world without depletion,
its virtue benefits the people without cost,
its flow cannot be exhausted,
its subtlety cannot be grasped.
Strike it—it leaves no wound,
stab it—it is not injured,
chop it—it does not break,
burn it—it does not catch fire,
soft and fluid, it flows and drifts,
intertwining in complex patterns,
yet it cannot be dispersed.
Its sharpness pierces metal and stone,
its strength sustains the world,
it moves in the realm of the formless,
and soars above all things.
It winds through valleys and rivers,
and surges across the vast wilderness.
Whether in surplus or shortage,
it lets the world take or give freely,
receiving and bestowing upon all things without preference,
thus it is without selfishness,
and without partiality.
Flowing and surging,
it merges with heaven and earth in vast continuity,
without leaning left or right,
coiling and intertwining,
it endures with all things from beginning to end,
this is called the ultimate virtue.
The reason water is able to achieve
this ultimate virtue in the world
is because of its softness, fluidity, and smoothness.
"Huáinánzǐ"
Alternative Names
An inhabitable place in water is called a zhōu,
also called a tán.
A small zhōu is called a zhǔ,
a small zhǔ is called a zhǐ,
also called a small zhǐ,
called a chí,
again a small zhǐ.
Called a qì.
All water edges are called chuí,
called yá,
called pàn,
called gān,
called zì,
called bīn,
a flat upper and lower yá is called chún,
also called dī,
double yá is called àn,
the land above the àn is called hǔ,
a curved yá is called ào,
also called wēi.
Where water and plants meet is called méi,
adding soil by the water's edge.
Where people stop is called shì,
a water bend is called ruì,
north of water is called yáng,
south of water is called yīn,
water emerging between mountain rocks is called lín.
Mountains flanking water is called jiàn,
water flowing into a river is called xī,
water flowing into a xī is called gǔ,
water passing through a gǔ is called hè.
Rocks blocking water is called liáng,
building earth to hold back water is called táng,
also called dī, also called fáng.
A large fáng is called fén.
Where water gathers is called zé,
a wide zé is called yǎn,
a curved zé is called gāo,
a barrier is called bēi,
a zé without water but with plants and trees,
is called sǒu.
Water flowing freely is called chuān,
the origin of water is called yuán,
yuán is called quán,
a quán emerging straight up is called jiàn,
a quán emerging sideways is called guǐ quán,
where quán emerge from the same place,
but return to different places is called féi,
different quán emerging but flowing together is called fèn.
Deep water is called tán,
swift water is called liú,
over sand and stones is called lài,
also called tuān,
called tān,
called qì shuǐ,
a separate flow is called pài,
a small opening in large water,
connecting separately is called pǔ,
wind blowing water to surge is called bō,
also called làng,
large bō is called tāo,
small bō is called lún,
calm bō is called lán,
straight bō is called jìng,
water arriving morning and evening is called cháo,
wind moving over water creating patterns is called lián,
water patterns like brocade are called yī,
walking through water is called shè,
going upstream against the current is called sù huí,
going downstream with the current is called sù yóu,
also called yán liú,
crossing the current to the other side is called luàn,
wading through water with clothes on is called lì,
from below the knee is called jiē,
from above the knee is called shè,
a place to cross water is called jīn,
also called jì, moving underwater is called yǒng.
From "Ěryǎ," "Shìmíng," "Shuōwén."
The highest good
The highest good is like water,
Water benefits all things without contention,
It dwells in places that people disdain,
Therefore it is close to the Way.
—Lǎozǐ
The noble person observes
Confucius observed the east-flowing water,
Zǐgòng asked:
"When a noble person sees great water, they must observe it,
Why is this?"
Confucius said:
"Water gives to all living things,
yet acts without striving, resembling virtue,
it flows to low places,
following its course in every bend, resembling righteousness,
vast and unceasing, resembling the Way,
it rushes into valleys ten thousand ren deep,
unafraid, resembling courage,
in measurement it remains level, resembling law,
full yet needing no leveler, resembling justice,
soft yet penetrating everywhere, resembling discernment,
entering and emerging purified, resembling goodness,
issuing from its source always eastward, resembling purpose,
therefore when a noble person sees great water, they must observe it."
Xúnqīngzǐ
Confucius said:
"Water is something
the noble person compares to virtue."
It gives universally without partiality,
resembling virtue.
Where it reaches, life grows,
resembling benevolence.
Shallow places flow freely,
deep places remain unfathomable,
resembling wisdom.
It receives impurities without protest,
resembling tolerance.
Turbid when entering,
pure when emerging,
resembling transformation through goodness.
"Shuō Yuàn"
The wise find joy in water.
What is it about the wise?
They take delight in water.
It is said that water,
flows according to principle,
leaving no small gap, resembling the wise.
It moves downward,
resembling the courteous.
It treads depths without hesitation,
resembling the courageous.
Blocked, it becomes clear,
resembling those who know fate.
It traverses dangers to reach afar,
yet ultimately remains unharmed,
resembling the virtuous.
Through it, heaven and earth are formed,
and all things come to life.
States and families find peace,
all affairs are balanced,
and all beings are rectified.
This is why the wise take delight in water.
"Han Shi Wai Zhuan"
Gain it, and one lives;
lose it, and one dies.
It resembles the virtuous,
profound and deep, unfathomable,
resembling the sage.
"Shuo Yuan"
Standard Objects
Water is the standard,
and the level is the measure of things.
In the "Guǎngyǎ,"
without water, there is no means to level the vast expanse of ten thousand miles;
without water, there is no way to connect distant paths and bear heavy loads.
From the "Shàngshū Dàzhuàn."
Four Virtues
Gù Yízǐ and Zǐhuá were strolling by the Eastern Pond.
Zǐhuá said:
"Water possesses four virtues:
It bathes all living beings,
Its blessings flow through ten thousand generations—
This is benevolence.
It lifts the pure and sweeps away the turbid,
Washing off filth and impurities—
This is righteousness.
Soft yet difficult to violate,
Weak yet difficult to overcome—
This is courage.
It guides rivers and clears waterways,
Transforming fullness into humility—
This is wisdom."
The Gùzǐ
Huī zhǐ
In ancient times,
the four pillars were broken,
the nine provinces split apart,
and the waters overflowed endlessly.
Then Nǚwā piled up reeds and ashes
to stop the flooding waters.
"Huáinánzǐ"
Shuǐ Ruì
Gònggōng shì received the water auspice,
all officials and leaders took water as their designation,
Méngshuǐ is the auspicious water.
When the ruler rides on earth and becomes king,
his governance is peaceful,
then Méngshuǐ emerges from the mountains.
