Soil and earth
The deluge rose to the heavens,
Gǔn stole the Swelling Earth from the Emperor,
to block the floodwaters.
Classic of Mountains and Seas
Shén Fèn
Yǔ regulated the waters and land, making it a single realm,
where there was no wind, rain, fog, or dew,
and no birds or beasts were born.
There was a mountain named Húlǐng,
whose summit had an opening like a circular ring,
called the Zīxué.
Water gushed forth from it,
named the Shénfèn,
whose fragrance surpassed pepper and orchids,
and whose flavor surpassed rich wine.
From "Lièzǐ"
Familiarity breeds contempt
Zhèng Zǐchǎn said to Zǐ Tàishū:
"Only the virtuous
can use leniency to make the people submit.
Next to this, nothing is better than severity. Fire is fierce;
people see it and fear it,
therefore few die in it.
Water is weak,
people take liberties and play with it,
thus many die in it.
Therefore leniency is difficult."
Zuǒ Zhuàn
Cleansing
Duke Jǐng asked Yànzǐ, saying:
"Integrity and longevity,
how are they practiced?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"They are practiced like water.
How beautiful is clear water!
When turbid, it never fails to settle;
When clear, it never fails to cleanse.
Therefore it endures."
Yànzǐ's Spring and Autumn Annals
Discriminating the Taste of Water
Bái Gōng asked Confucius, saying:
"Can one speak secretly with others?"
Confucius did not respond.
Bái Gōng said:
"If one throws a stone into water,
what then?"
Confucius said:
"The skilled swimmers of Wú can retrieve it."
He said:
"If one pours water into water, how then?"
Confucius said:
"When the Zī and Shéng rivers merge, Yìyá
can taste and know them apart."
Bái Gōng said:
"So indeed one cannot speak secretly with others."
Lièzǐ
Perfume
The former palace of Wú had a Perfume Stream,
commonly said to be the bathing place of Xī Shī.
People called it the Rouge and Powder Pond.
The palace ladies of the King of Wú washed their makeup in this stream,
and its source remains fragrant to this day.
An ancient verse says:
How can I obtain the Perfume Spring,
to wash the dust from my lord's clothes?
There is also Perfume Water in Bīngzhōu,
whose water is fragrant and pure,
and bathing in it cures illnesses.
"Records of Strange Things"
Mòshuǐ
The Mòshuǐ River from Mount Méngshān to Nán'ān is obstructed by Hùn Cliff,
where the mountain torrents rush swiftly,
thus endangering boats and ships, a problem throughout the ages.
The governor of Shǔ Commandery, Lǐ Bīng, dispatched troops to chisel and level Hùn Cliff.
The river god raged in fury,
so Lǐ Bīng took up his blade and entered the water,
battling the deity.
He thus subdued Hùn Cliff,
clearing the proper waterway.
The opened passage is the very one Lǐ Bīng cut through.
"Water Classic"
Shuǐfǔ
At the confluence of the Hàn and Miǎn rivers,
there is a stone inscription on the bank that reads:
"Thirty-one lǐ down to the Water Mansion,
it is said that Lǐ Sī carved this stone here."
The Shù Yì Jì records
there are eighteen Water Mansions under heaven.
Divine Water
Master Fù Jú ascended Wú Mountain,
and said to the people below:
"I wish to return to Pénglái Mountain,
and will bestow divine water upon you all."
Suddenly, water appeared on the cliff top,
white in color,
flowing down from between the rocks.
Drinking it often cured many illnesses.
"Biographies of Immortals"
Restoring Water
In Shǔ there was a river with a backflow,
where the river deity had often drowned people.
Wén Wēng, as the governor, made offerings to it,
but when the deity did not finish the wine offered,
he drew his sword and struck it,
and thereafter it ceased to cause harm.
From the "Commentary on the Waterways Classic".
Zhú Wáng Shuǐ
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
a Bamboo King rose by the Tuǎnshuǐ River.
There was a woman washing clothes by the riverside,
when a large bamboo of three joints floated to her feet.
She pushed it away, but it would not leave.
Hearing a sound from within,
she split it open
and found a baby boy inside.
He later became leader of the Yípú clan,
taking Bamboo as his surname.
The damaged bamboo left in the wild grew into a forest—
this is the Bamboo Grove where the king’s temple stands.
Once, the king stopped with his followers atop a large rock
and ordered soup to be made.
His attendants said there was no water.
The king struck the rock with his sword,
and water gushed forth—
this is the present-day Bamboo King Water.
End
Chopping the Stone Man
The "Records of the Jade Box" states:
Liú Zǐguāng of the Former Hàn dynasty was traveling westward across mountains,
and grew thirsty with no water to be found.
Zǐguāng saw a stone figure on the southern side of the mountain,
and asked it:
"Where can water be found?"
The stone figure did not reply.
He then drew his sword and struck the stone figure,
and in a moment,
water gushed forth from the mountain.
"The Chronicles of Unique Phenomena"
Júshuǐ
In Nányáng there is Chrysanthemum Water,
whose source is surrounded entirely by fragrant chrysanthemums.
The water is extremely sweet and aromatic,
and there are thirty households living there
who no longer dig wells,
but drink this water directly.
Their longest-lived reach one hundred twenty or one hundred thirty,
while medium longevity is over one hundred years.
Seventy-year-olds
are still considered to have died prematurely.
Hàn Dynasty Minister of Works Wáng Chàng
and Grand Tutor Yuán Kuí,
while serving as magistrates of Nányáng,
had over thirty dàn of this water delivered monthly to the county,
using it for all drinking, cooking, and bathing.
Grand Commandant Hú Guǎng’s
father suffered from wind-emaciation disorder,
but consistently
drew and drank this water from Nányáng,
and this illness was then cured.
These chrysanthemums have short petals and large [flowers],
and eating them is sweet and delicious,
different from other chrysanthemums.
Hú Guǎng also collected their seeds
and planted them in the capital,
so they became widespread everywhere.
"Jīngzhōu Records"
Fighting over water and cutting fingers
Yáng'ān County Magistrate Zhào Guī and Lǎnglíng Prefecture Governor Huáng Méng disputed over water rights,
Guī cut his finger and swore an oath:
"Follow where the blood flows into Yáng'ān's territory."
Méng became enraged and killed Guī,
Minor official Wáng Shuò then stabbed and killed Méng,
Lǎnglíng's officials subsequently killed Shuò,
The people built a sacrificial altar for Shuò on Jīng Mountain,
Whenever there was drought, they would go there to pray.
"Traditions of Former Worthies of Rǔnán"
Drinking Water
Zhū Cāng,
courtesy name Yúnqīng,
was a native of Shífāng.
He studied under Zhāng Níng of Shǔjùn Commandery,
sustaining himself on beans and water while reciting classics.
His fellow students pitied his poverty,
offering him rice and meat which he consistently declined.
Records of the Lands South of Mount Huá
Drinking water and becoming pregnant
In the late Hàn dynasty, the Línglíng governor Shǐ Mǎn
had a daughter
who admired a clerk under his administration.
She had her maid fetch the leftover water from his hand-washing and drank it,
then became pregnant,
and eventually gave birth to a child.
When the child could walk,
the governor held the boy
and had him seek out his father.
The boy crawled
straight into the clerk's arms.
When the clerk pushed him away,
the boy fell to the ground and turned into water.
Upon fully recalling the earlier events,
the governor married his daughter to the clerk.
From Sōu Shén Jì
Prohibition of Water
Zuǒ Cí and Zhào Míng, among others,
used their vital energy to control water,
causing it to flow backward,
and could control water for ten or twenty feet;
when they placed it in the courtyard exposed to the open air,
it remained extremely cold but did not freeze.
From "Bàopǔzǐ"
Dàjīn Yuánjīng
During the time of Zhūgě Kǒngmíng,
there was a man named Pú Yuán
whose sword-making skill equaled Ōu Yě
and Fēng Hú.
He often forged swords and blades for Kǒngmíng,
claiming that only the River Shuǐ had the crisp and vigorous quality,
which was a natural division of its territory,
the primordial essence of great metal.
The Hàn Shuǐ was dull and weak,
and neither it nor the Fú Shuǐ were suitable for quenching blades.
If someone mixed Fú Shuǐ with River Shuǐ,
he could immediately discern it.
"The Biography of Pú Yuán"
Water Veins
In the eighth year of Sūn Quán's Chìwū era,
he dispatched Commandant Chén Xūn for water transport,
who broke open a stele midway in Jùróng,
unearthing
a black
object
without head or tail,
shaped like a ship of several hundred hú capacity,
hundreds of zhǎng in length,
writhing sluggishly.
After a short while,
it entirely melted into liquid,
which people at the time could not identify.
Thereafter,
a spring source was obtained, and some said
it was an underground stream. Whenever severe drought occurred,
all other watercourses dried up,
yet this massive flow alone remained.
"Yì Yuàn"
Selling Water
Wáng Měng attacked Yè,
Mùróng Píng resisted Měng,
but constantly sold water,
and the soldiers collectively planned to rebel,
thus Měng was able to defeat them.
"Chē Yǐng Qín Shū"
Earth Mirror
During Fú Jiān's time,
there was a watery reflection in Cháng'ān,
which appeared like water from a distance,
but looking at the ground revealed people,
and it ceased by Fú Jiān's later years.
In the winter of the 25th year of Emperor Wén of Sòng's Yuánjiā era,
south of Qīngzhōu city,
a watery reflection was seen in the ground from afar,
called the earth mirror.
On the rénzǐ day of the second month in the second year of Táng's Shénlóng era,
seven lǐ east of Luòyáng city,
the ground appeared watery,
with trees, carriages, and horses clearly visible,
the reflection gradually moved toward the capital,
and disappeared after over a month.
On Cháng'ān streets,
watery reflections were often seen,
at the end of the Dàlì era in Shùnlù County of Shēnzhōu,
there was a watery reflection seven or eight chǐ long,
from afar, people and horses coming and going were visible,
as if in water,
but upon approaching, no water was seen.
Nǚ Shuǐ
At the foot of Niúshān in Línzī,
there flows the Nǚshuǐ River.
A proverb among the people of Qí states:
"When the world is well-governed, the Nǚshuǐ flows;
when the world is in chaos, the Nǚshuǐ runs dry."
During the time of Mùróng Chāo,
the river remained completely dry for an entire year,
but when Emperor Wǔ of Sòng launched his northern campaign,
torrential waters suddenly surged forth.
According to the Shùzhēng Jì:
In the sixth year of the Jiànpíng era of Yān,
the river abruptly dried up,
which Xuánmíng took as an ill omen,
and he gradually fell ill and died.
In the fourth year of the Tàishàng era of Yān,
the Nǚshuǐ dried up once more,
and Chāo likewise viewed it as a bad portent;
soon after, the Yān dynasty fell.
From the Shuǐ Jīng
Ràng Shuǐ
Fàn Bǎinián
was a man of Hànzhōng.
He once had an audience with Emperor Míng of the Sòng dynasty,
during which the conversation touched upon the Spring of Greed in Guǎngzhōu.
The Emperor then asked Bǎinián:
"Is there such a spring in your province as well?"
He did not answer directly,
but said:
"In my province, there are only the Civil River and the Martial District,
the Spring of Integrity and the River of Modesty."
The Emperor asked further:
"Where is your residence located?"
He replied:
"I dwell between Integrity and Modesty."
The Emperor praised his responses.
From History of the Southern Dynasties
Digging the City Wall and Encountering Water
When Shěn Yōuzhī's rebellion arose,
Qí Wǔdì occupied the Pénkǒu Fortress,
where digging a moat yielded a large coin
inscribed with the words:
"Peace for a Hundred Years."
At that time,
the fortress suffered from water shortage,
so they sought to channel water inside.
Upon first digging within the walls,
they encountered hidden springs gushing forth—
nine locations in total, providing inexhaustible supply.
The Emperor
The sand pool does not leak.
Within Jīngzhōu City there was a sandy pool,
which often leaked water.
When Xiāo Yǐngzhòu served as Chief Clerk,
the water ceased to leak,
but after Yǐngzhòu's death,
it dried up again.
From the Book of Southern Qí
Water of Eight Merits
During the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng dynasty, there was a foreign monk named Tán
who resided in retreat at Jiǎngshān.
The mountain lacked water,
when an old man with thick eyebrows said to him:
"I am the mountain dragon,
knowing that you, Master, thirst for drink,
it is no trouble to provide it."
Suddenly,
a pool bubbled forth.
Later, another Western monk arrived and said:
"Originally there were eight pools in the Western Regions,
one has been lost,
it seems that one emptied to fill this one."
The spring's qualities are: first, clear;
second, cool;
third, fragrant;
fourth, soft;
fifth, sweet;
sixth, pure;
seventh, never drying up;
eighth, curing illnesses.
Hence it was named the Eight Merit Waters.
Since the Liáng dynasty,
it has been supplied to the imperial court,
said that drinking it can cure diseases.
The "Fángyú Shènglǎn"
lists: first, sweet;
second, cool;
third, soft;
fourth, light;
fifth, clear and pure;
sixth, odorless;
seventh, does not harm the throat when drunk;
eighth, does not injure the stomach after drinking.
The "Shùnzhèng Lǐlùn"
Xiūrén Shuǐ
In Shàozhōu's Qūjiāng County, the Xiūrén River,
flows southwest into the Lián River,
where there is a Sānfēng Pavilion,
and the Wǔdù River.
Fàn Yún of the Qí dynasty, as governor of Shǐxīng,
came to the Xiūrén River,
scooped up water and drank it.
He composed a poem that said:
How rustling are the three maples,
How meandering are the five crossings,
Just drink from the Xiūrén River,
Do not draw from the treacherous stream.
"Shàozhōu Illustrated Gazetteer"
I saw the water god
During the Northern Qí dynasty, Lú Yuánmíng was dispatched as an envoy to Liáng.
His wife accompanied him by carriage to the riverbank.
Suddenly, they noticed an extraordinary fragrance emanating from the water.
Turning around, they saw a water deity emerging from the waves.
The oxen were startled and bolted,
dragging the carriage into the river.
His wife drowned,
while his young nephew Shízhù,
who was riding in the same carriage,
managed to escape by jumping out.
(From "History of the Northern Dynasties")
A cup of water to bid farewell
Zhào Guǐ served as the Assistant Inspector of Qízhōu,
and when he went to the capital for his performance review,
the local elders saw him off, each wiping their tears and saying, "Assistant Inspector,
during your tenure, you never accepted even water or fire from the common people,
so we dare not offer you a pot of wine as a farewell gift.
Your integrity is as pure as water—
please allow us to offer a cup of water in farewell."
Guǐ accepted it and drank.
Book of Suí
Parrot Water
In July of the first year of the Wǔdé era,
the water in the Yīngwǔ Valley of Xīnfēng became clear.
It is traditionally said that when this water clears, the world is at peace.
At the beginning of the Kāihuáng era, it briefly cleared,
then became turbid again,
and by this time it had cleared once more.
From the "Book of Táng".
Tuó Shuǐ
Tuò Shuǐ is the Lǔ Shuǐ.
It enters the city from the northwest,
and the common people rely on it,
calling it the Lìrén Qú.
This is correct.
The Shǎn Xiàn Tújīng
records that in the first year of the Wǔdé era,
Zhǎngsūn Cāo, a Jīnbù Lángzhōng of the Shǎndōng Circuit Branch Department,
diverted water from east of the commandery into the city again,
to replace well-drawing,
and the common people relied on it,
both this and the earlier canal benefiting the people.
The "Táng Shǐ"
Water entered the emperor's bedchamber.
Emperor Gāozōng was at the Wànnián Palace when
a flash flood suddenly arrived.
At night, it breached the Xuánwǔ Gate,
and the palace guards all fled in panic.
Xuē Rénguì said:
"At a critical moment for the Son of Heaven,
how can one fear death?"
He then climbed the gate and shouted loudly
to alert those inside the palace.
The emperor hurried out
and ascended to higher ground.
Shortly after,
water flooded the emperor's bedchamber.
The emperor said:
"Thanks to you, I was saved—
now I know what a loyal minister is."
From the "History of the Táng Dynasty"
Dān Shuǐ
North of Huáizhōu flows the Dān River,
whose source is in the Chángpíng Mountains.
Legend has it that
when Qín slaughtered Zhào's soldiers,
the water turned crimson,
hence it was given this name.
While the Emperor was in Tàiyuán,
upon learning this history,
he issued an edict to rename it the Huái River.
"Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn"
Set up seats
Kǒng Ruòsī often said to people:
"To serve as far as Palace Attendant
is enough."
When he was promoted to the position of Treasury Director,
he placed a stone still water vessel by his seat,
to show his intention of knowing when to stop.
Old Book of Táng
Dripping Water
Within the territory of Ānxī, there is the Qiánjiàn Mountain.
At the foot of the mountain, there is a monastery.
The water there drips and trickles,
forming delightful sounds.
The local people annually gather these sounds
to compose melodies.
Hence, it is called Yépósèjī.
During the Kāiyuán era, it was used as the name of a jiégǔ tune.
Musicians found the technique of controlling the rhythm most challenging,
so they would approach the monastery near the dripping water.

Block the water flow
Lǐ Jìngyí's residence was in Luòyáng,
in Yùcái Ward,
where the earth god was most efficacious.
His servant Zhāng Xíngzhōu served it and received responses.
Before the great flood arrived,
he dreamed it requested food and drink in advance.
When the day came,
it led its kind to block the floodwaters,
and the residence was not washed away.
"New Book of the South"
Shuǐ Yuè
Yuánzǐ in the mountains particularly cherished what was called water music.
Water music was the cascading waterfall of Náncéng,
gurgling and murmuring,
pleasing to hear,
especially soothing to the ears.
"Yuán Cìshān's Record of Water Music"
Pénglái is separated by the Ruòshuǐ.
Xiè Zìrán heard that Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn resided at Yùxiāo Peak,
so she went there to visit him,
and later bid farewell to Chéngzhēn.
Carrying a mat, she cast it into the sea,
floating upon the waves,
and was carried by a ship from Xīnluó.
Soon she reached a mountain,
and wandered alone to a place
where a Daoist priest, wearing a floral crown and rainbow mantle,
was approached by Zìrán paying respects.
The priest asked where she intended to go.
Zìrán replied, "To Pénglái to seek a master."
The priest laughed and said, "Pénglái is separated by the Ruòshuǐ,
which lies
three hundred
thousand miles away.
It cannot be crossed by boat,
and none but a flying immortal can reach it.
Chéngzhēn's name is recorded at Dāntái,
and he resides at Chìchéng—
he is a fine master indeed."
From "Continued Biographies of Immortals":
The "Account of the Western Regions" states that the state of Wūyì was over fifteen thousand miles from Cháng'ān,
and traveling west for about a hundred days would bring one there.
The state of Tiáozhī bordered the Western Sea.
Elders passed down tales of the Ruòshuǐ and the Queen Mother of the West.
The "Account of the Eastern Barbarians" also says:
Several thousand miles beyond the Great Wall,
there is also the Ruòshuǐ,
though none have seen it.
The "Huáinánzǐ" states:
The Ruòshuǐ originates from Qióngshí,
and Qióngshí
is present-day Xījùn,
Jùn Rǎn,

From "Annotations to the Classic of Mountains and Seas":
The Ruòshuǐ at Kūnlún
cannot float even a goose feather.
From "Records of the Mysterious Middle":
The Ruòshuǐ is north of Fūyú,
unable to bear feathers.
From "Extensive Records":
During the Hàn Emperor Wǔ's reign,
the Yuèzhī state sent an envoy to present incense, saying:
"We rode in a felt-covered carriage to cross the Ruòshuǐ."
From "The Abyss and the Staff":
A steed's strength can traverse the flying sands,
enduring the distant journey,
toiling along the rugged paths.
From "Records of the Ten Continents":
Nánlǎn Shuǐ
During the reign of Emperor Dàizōng, Lǐ Jìqīng was appointed as the governor of Húzhōu and arrived at Wéiyáng.
He encountered Lù Hóngjiàn at the Yángzǐ Courier Station, who was about to have a meal.
Lǐ said:
"I have heard of your expertise in distinguishing tea, Master Lù,
and the water from Nánlíng in Yángzǐ is exceptionally fine.
Today, these two marvels meet once in a thousand years."
He ordered a cautious soldier
to go deep into Nánlíng
and had Lù prepare his tea utensils to wait.
Soon, the water arrived.
Lù scooped and stirred the water, saying:
"It is from the river, indeed,
but not from Nánlíng;
it seems to be from near the bank."
The messenger said:
"I rowed the boat deep into the river, with hundreds of witnesses;
how dare I deceive you?"
Lù said nothing.
Later, when the water was poured into a basin up to half full,
Lù abruptly stopped it,
stirred it again with the scoop,
and said:
"From this point onward, it is from Nánlíng."
The messenger, startled, rushed to confess:
"I brought it from Nánlíng, but upon reaching the shore,
the boat rocked and more than half spilled.
Fearing it was too little, I added water from the bank.
Your discernment, Master,
is truly divine.
How could I dare to hide it?"
From "Wēn Tíngyún's Record of Tea Picking"
Water Play
Zhāng Zhìhé, while intoxicated, performed water play,
spread a mat on the water,
sat alone drinking and toasting,
whistled and chanted on his mat,
moving back and forth slowly or quickly,
as if rowing a boat.
"Continued Biographies of the Immortals"
Holy Water
Biànsòng Observer Líng Hú Chǔ reported,
that holy water emerged in Bózhōu, and those who drank it would recover from illness.
Péi Dù judged:
Superstitions arise from people,
water does not create itself.
He ordered it to be blocked up.
《Book of Táng》
In the second year of the Bǎolì era,
Bózhōu reported the emergence of holy water,
and those who drank it were cured of diseases.
Lǐ Déyù memorialized:
I have investigated and heard that this water
was originally due to cunning monks deceiving people to beg for money.
In the past few months,
people from Jiāngnán have crowded the roads,
with every twenty or thirty households hiring one person to fetch water.
When preparing to fetch it,
the sick would abstain from meat and blood, and after drinking it,
they would also eat vegetarian for two weeks,
while critically ill people waited for it to cure their diseases.
The water cost three strings of cash per dou,
and those fetching it would add other water to it,
selling it to people along the way.
The elderly and sick who drank it
often became critically ill.
Recently, counting the people from Liǎngzhè and Fújiàn crossing the river,
there were thirty to fifty daily.
I have already increased arrests at the Suànshān crossing,
If we do not cut off its root,
I fear it will ultimately not benefit the common people.
In the past, during the Wú period, there was holy water,
and in Sòng and Qí there was holy fire,
all matters of superstition and deceit condemned by the ancients.
I beg to order the local Observer Líng Hú Chǔ
to quickly have it filled in,
to stop the source of superstition.
This was approved.
《Old Táng》
Those profiting from the holy water deceived each other,
Déyù, while in Zhèxī,
ordered a cauldron set up in the main market gathering people,
took the water,
and had five catties of pork boiled in it.
Saying:
If it is holy water,
the meat should remain unchanged.
In a short while,
the meat was thoroughly cooked and soft,
from then on, people's minds gradually settled,
and the deceivers were soon exposed.
《Historical Records》
Distinguishing Waters
When Lǐ Déyù was serving in the court,
a close acquaintance was sent on a mission to Jīngkǒu.
Lǐ said:
"Upon your return,
fetch a jug of cold water from the Yángzǐ River at the foot of Jīnshān Mountain."
The person set sail,
but forgot about it day after day while indulging in drink.
Only when the boat reached the foot of Shíchéng
did he remember.
He then drew a bottle of water from the river.
Returning to the capital, he presented it.
After drinking it,
Lǐ sighed in surprise,
and said with great astonishment:
"The taste of the water from the region south of the Yángzǐ River has changed from previous years.
This water closely resembles that from the foot of Shíchéng in Jiànyè."
The person apologized for his mistake,
not daring to conceal the truth.
"Tales from the Central Court"
Water Relay
Lǐ Déyù, while serving in the Central Secretariat, enjoyed drinking the spring water from Huìshān Temple in Chángzhōu.
He established a relay transport system from Pílíng to the capital, called the "water relay."
A monk came to visit him,
and Déyù asked:
"What brings you to see me, Minister?"
The monk replied:
"To inform the Minister that the water veins of Chángzhōu extend here.
There is a well in the capital
connected to the same water vein as Huìshān Temple's spring."
Lǐ laughed heartily:
"How absurd!"
The monk said:
Déyù asked:
"In which ward and alley is the well located?"
The monk answered:
"It is behind the permanent storage of Hàotiān Temple."
Lǐ then took one jar of Huìshān water,
one jar from Hàotiān Temple,
mixed them with eight other bottles,
secretly marking the origins of all ten bottles,
and sent the monk to distinguish them.
The monk sipped and tasted,
identified the Huìshān Temple and Hàotiān waters,
and found the remaining eight to be of the same taste.
Déyù was greatly amazed.
He immediately discontinued the water relay,
sparing people the labor,
and quelled the idle discussions.
The water turns into fragrant wine.
When Emperor Xuān was still a feudal lord,
he often accompanied the imperial carriage.
Having fallen from his horse into the snow and suffering greatly from the cold,
he asked a patrolling guard for water due to thirst.
He said:
"I am Prince Guāng."
When the guard presented water and he raised the cup,
it all transformed into fragrant wine.
"Jade Spring Master"
The Lord provides water for use
Mr. Qìzhēn Lǐ Yìfàn lived at Xuányuán Temple on Mount Běimáng.
At the end of the Xiántōng era, a certain Mr. Lǐ visited his place,
and they became exceptionally intimate.
Suddenly one evening, he said to Mr. Qìzhēn:
"I am about to depart from this world.
I have received orders from the Underworld Ministry,
to be in charge of supplying the daily water used by the households of a city.
Now that my monthly term has ended,
I will die three days later.
I came to bid you farewell first."
He then said, "In the human world, water usage should not exceed three to five shēng per day per person.
If one exceeds this limit,
it will result in a reduction of blessings and a deduction from one's allotted lifespan.
You must be very cautious about this."
When the predicted time arrived, he indeed passed away.
From "Records of the Strange."
Jellyfish
Wáng Xuánzhī encountered a Taoist priest at night,
and followed him to the bottom of the West River.
Under the moonlight, no mud, sand, or water was visible,
as the path opened before them on its own.
Beside them was a creature,
resembling both a dragon and a snake, ten zhang in length.
The Taoist priest said, "This is a jellyfish,
and those who see it will attain longevity."
Wángshì Shénxiān Zhuàn by Dù Guāngtíng
Yōng Guān
During the Xīníng era, when Wáng Ānshí was in charge of the state,
someone was appointed as magistrate of Xūyí County in Sìzhōu.
He personally requested to change his name to Yōng Guān.
When asked strangely about the reason,
he said:
"A deity informed me thus in a dream."
Later, while returning from the city to his county post,
as he was crossing a floating bridge,
he drowned in the Huái River.
The incident was reported to the imperial court.
Wáng Ānshí said:
"I had suspected this person had no reason to change his name,
and upon consulting the Classic of Mountains and Seas,
I learned it was the name of a water official.
Thus I feared he would meet a watery fate,
and now it has indeed come true."
Later, some county officials dreamed of Yōng Guān with a magnificent retinue,
coming and going along the Huái River banks,
leading them to suspect he had become a water official after death.
From "Records of the Chariot of Divination"
Gòng Shuǐ
Throughout the land, tributes and taxes were levied,
but only Cháng'ān County offered earth and Wànnián County offered water.
From "New Book of the South"
Heavy water
All things contain water,
and water originates from the land.
Thus, east of the Yangtze River is suitable for producing silk gauze and paper,
due to the water's clarity.
The people of Shǔ weave brocade,
and upon its initial completion, they must wash it in the river water,
after which the patterns and colors become radiant.
The people of Zhèng and Xíng brew wine,
and the water near the city is heavier,
so the weight per unit volume is several times that of the distant suburbs.
"Supplement to the National History"
Huì Shuǐ
The Records of Chénliú states:
The Huàn River emerges to the south of Xiāngyì,
while the Suī River flows past its north.
Tradition says that between the Suī and Huàn,
patterns and colors are produced,
hence the embroidered silks and fine linens,
adorned with suns, moons, and brilliant creatures.
These are used for ceremonial robes in ancestral temples.
The Records of the Strange says:
The two rivers, Suī and Huàn,
have waves like the five colors.
Because they bear patterns, they are called the Embroidered Waters.
When Chén Lín served Cáo Hóng,
he wrote in a letter to Wèi Wén:
Those who wander by the Suī and Huàn
learn the splendor of ornate embroidery.
Jǐn Shuǐ
West of the Chéngdū Road,
was the former Brocade Official's residence.
When brocade from the Jǐn River was washed in this river, it became exceptionally vibrant;
washing it in other waters did not yield the same result,
hence it was named Brocade Lane City.
"Records of the Lands South of Mount Huá"
The Xiāng River
The Xiāng River originates from Yángshuò.
It is extremely clear,
with a depth of five to six zhàng,
so limpid that the bottom is visible,
distinctly revealing pebbles like gambling chips,
white sand like frost and snow,
and crimson banks like morning clouds.
From "Luó Hán's Record of the Xiāng River"
The Chángshā Chronicles state:
Traveling a thousand lǐ along the Xiāng, one hears fishermen's chants,
harmonizing in midstream,
their voices lingering and distant, pleasing to the ear.
This is what is called crossing the clear Xiāng,
lighting Chǔ bamboo,
with one sound of the creaking oar,
mountains and rivers come alive with color.
How could this be the realm of ordinary fishermen?
Xiàoshuǐ
Pān Ānrén's "Rhapsody on a Westward Journey,"
bathed in the Xiàoshuǐ and cleansed his hat strings,
praising the virtuous name that lies here.
Zìlín states:
Xiàoshuǐ is in Hénán Commandery.
Zǐshuǐ
In Wǔdū there is mud in Zǐshuǐ,
its color is purple and sticky,
tribute is used to seal imperial documents.
Hence imperial edicts have the beauty of purple mud.
"Records of Lǒngyòu"
Yì Shuǐ
Yìyáng County is in Chángshā Commandery.
The boundary river lies to its south.
Looking east from the county seat,
one occasionally sees Chángshā.
City walls and people on horseback
can be clearly distinguished in form and color.
Sometimes when gazing at noon for a while,
they gradually scatter and vanish.
The county is still three hundred lǐ from Chángshā.
Crossing over multiple mountains logically prevents such manifestation.
Perhaps it is the mountain peaks
vividly revealing their true appearance—
is this what has been transmitted?
"Records of the Extraordinary"
Míng Shuǐ
At Gāo'ān's Míngshuǐ, emerald streams cascade and fly,
in the empty valley echoes resound; atop the peak stands a stone,
tens of feet high—when struck with an object,
its sound resembles a drum,
hence it was named after this.
"Huáyáng Shílù"
Qiongjiang Water
In Fudai Mountain, Yanting, Guanghan,
there is Feilong Spring.
It gushes downward.
Flowing south into Zitong River.
The water is clear and cool,
its taste sweet and delightful,
often regarded as Qiongjiang Water.
"Records of the Universe"
Liùshí Shuǐ
In Shǔ, Qīngchéng has Yánqìng Palace,
to the west of which stands Chángdào Temple.
To its south lies Liùshí Shuǐ,
where water is sprinkled six times a day in place of a water clock.
It sprinkles during the yang periods,
yet ceases during the yin periods, regardless of day or night.
It is named Liùshí Shuǐ precisely because water is sprinkled six times daily.
"Fāngyú Jì"
Dīngdōng Shuǐ
West of Géguī Huà Palace,
beneath a massive rock,
lies Dīngdōng Shuǐ.
It emerges from the cliff's belly,
dripping into a hollow stone cavity.
It does not increase with heavy rain,
nor deplete during prolonged drought.
If someone defiles it,
it immediately dries up.
"Seven Tablets, One Hundred Twenty-Two"
Fěn Shuǐ
In Bà County there is a clear water spring,
where the Bà people use this water to make powder.
It then becomes glossy, bright, fresh, and fragrant,
and is offered as tribute powder to the capital.
Hence it is named Powder Water,
so the world calls it the Falling Forest Powder of Jiāngzhōu.
"Records of Huáyáng"
states the Powder Water in Zhùyáng County originates from Fánglíng.

it is exceptionally fresh and clean compared to other waters.
"Records of Jīngzhōu"
notes it is the place where Lady Xiāo Hé soaked powder.
"Records of Nán Yōngzhōu"
Jiàng Shuǐ
The Jiàng River flows from Mount Jiàng,
east to Hánquán,
where it surges and raises waves.
It turns north and pours into the county's streams,
rushing through ravines for about eleven zhàng.
The green cliffs appear as if dotted with dark ink,
and the white rapids resemble unrolled silk.
The sight is an extremely marvelous spectacle.
The "Water Classic"
states that the Huì River originates in Hédōng,
east of Jiàng County at the intersection of Huì and the high eastern mountains.
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" records:
Duke Jǐng of Jìn planned to leave the old Jiàng
and wished to reside in Xúnxiá.
Wei Xiànzǐ said:
"It would be better to go to Xīntián, where the Fén and Huì rivers
can carry away impurities."
Thus, they settled in Xīntián.
It was also called Jiàng,
likely because it was located north of the Jiàng and Huì rivers.
Qiānqiū Shuǐ
In Guìyáng Chēn County, there is Wànsuì Mountain,
where a stone chamber stands.
Inside the chamber, stalactites hang.
The mountain is covered with Língshòu trees,
and at its foot flows the Qiānqiū Stream.
Along the stream dwell residents,
in a village named Wànsuì.
Above,
Yuán Shuǐ
In Chēn County's southern Xiāngbēi Village,
there is a round body of water,
approximately two hundred paces in diameter.
One side is warm,
the other side cold.
The cold area is extremely clear and green;
where shallow, stones are visible,
where deep, it appears bottomless.
The warm area has white and turbid water.
Since darkness and purity differ in coolness and warmth,
its name is Chú Spring.
It resembles the Bàn Hot Spring of Jiāngshèng.
When water is abundant, it flows into Huáng Creek;
when water diminishes, the stream path ceases its flow.
Lǒng Shuǐ
West of Liángzōu City flows the Lóng Shuǐ.
It is said that a filial daughter-in-law of Qí so sincerely moved the deities,
that a spring gushed forth inside her house.
She secretly covered it with a woven bamboo basket,
thus sparing the labor of drawing water with jars.
Her family grew suspicious.
Waiting until she went out, they searched her room,
and attempted to lift this basket.
Thereupon, the spring surged forth, flooding the dwelling.
Hence, it was named Lóng Shuǐ (Basket Water).
From "Xù Shùzhēng Jì".
Shímén Shuǐ
North of Lùshān Mountain,
there is the Shímén River.
The river flows from the ridge,
where at its peak stand two towering rocks,
so lofty they resemble a gate.
Hence, it is called Shímén (Stone Gate).
The water courses between these twin rocks,
cascading as a flying waterfall for nearly three hundred paces,
spreading out below over a dozen paces.
Gazing upward, it seems to touch the sky,
as if a flying silk ribbon is trailing across the heavens.
Below lies a broad rock where dozens can sit,
and Champion General Liú Jìngxuān often ascended here.
From the "Water Classic"
Báishuǐ
Báishuǐ is located south of Huánglóng,
which is the waterfall.
The water emerges from the mountain and cascades down three to four hundred zhang.
The flying torrent appears above the treetops,
looking like a suspended white silk.
Where it pours down, there are all huge wells of immeasurable depth,
and the water flows down into the river abyss.
"Record of Lúshān"
Plain Water
In Zhōnglú County's tributary waters,
there is a creature resembling a three- or four-year-old child,
with scales like a pangolin,
impenetrable to arrows.
During the seventh and eighth months,
it often basks on gravel banks,
its knees resembling those of a tiger,
its paws and claws usually submerged in water,
revealing only its knees to people.
Unaware children
who attempt to capture and play with it
are immediately killed
by it.
Some say:
if someone captures one alive,
and plucks its nose or ears,
it can be controlled to a small extent,
and is called a water tiger.
"Records of Xiāng and Miǎn"
Yī Shuǐ
The Classic of the Upper Reaches of the Yī River records:
In the two counties of Xīnchéng and Lùhún, regardless of age or gender,
all the people fell ill.
Goiters, commonly said to be caused by the local water and soil,
made the Yī River water undrinkable.
From "Records of a Journey West"
Ghost Bullet
During the Han Dynasty, in Bùwéi County of Yǒngchāng Commandery, there was a forbidden river,
whose waters contained poisonous vapors.
Only in the eleventh and twelfth months was it somewhat safe to cross.
From the first month to the tenth month, passing through it
invariably harmed people.
Within the vapors were malevolent entities,
invisible in form.
When they stirred, there was a sound,
as if something were being thrown to strike within,
hitting trees would break them,
striking people would cause harm.
Locals called them "ghost bullets."
Thus, criminals from the commandery were exiled to this forbidden area for punishment,
and none survived more than ten days.
"Sōu Shén Jì"
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ" states:
"Ghost bullets fling pellets to shatter and destroy,
while fiery wells blaze with radiant light."
Annotation from "Shì Shuō":
Not found in current editions.
Lúshuǐ
The Lújīn River flows east past the north of Bùwéi County,
with high mountains on both banks.
Lú Peak stands out as the most magnificent,
soaring alone over three thousand zhàng high.
Along the river’s banks are paths for horses and pedestrians.
Though barely passable, they are plagued by miasma.
Traversing them in the third or fourth month inevitably leads to death.
Even outside these months, it causes nausea and vomiting.
After the fifth month,
travelers may pass without harm.
Hence, Zhūgě Liàng stated in his memorial,
"I crossed the Lú in the fifth month,
eating only every other day.
It is not that I do not value my own life,
but because the royal enterprise cannot be confined to Shǔ alone."
The "Water Classic" notes
that the two peaks of the Lú River harbor a lethal aura.
In the summer months, passage was traditionally avoided.
Thus, Lord Wǔ found crossing in summer arduous.
The "Records of Yìzhōu" mention
that the present-day ferry on the Kūnmíng route still bears traces of Lord Wǔ’s path.
According to the "Geographical Records,"
the waters are turbulent and filled with jagged rocks.
Locals use boats made of oxhide
to cross the river.
The "Records of Ten Circuits" adds...
Fànyīn Shuǐ
South of Lízhōu city there is the Fànyīn Spring,
which gushed forth when the Tang Dynasty monk Sānzàng chanted Sanskrit hymns here,
hence the name.
Its color resembles rice-washing water.
Its taste is sweet.
During the Zhènghé era of the Sòng Dynasty,
Governor Yǔwén passed by, drank from it, and said:
"An excellent spring!"
He renamed it Cànyù Spring.
Several dozen paces south of the spring,
there are two massive rocks.
One is called the Kasaya Rock,
displaying five intermingled colors.
The other is called the Sūtra-Drying Rock,
both being relics of Sānzàng.
"Geographical Records"
Waters of Longing
A hundred li east of Fūzhōu there is a river,
named the River of Longing.
On its bank stands a courier station,
also called the Station of Longing.
Líng Hú Tǐng inscribed a poem on the wall:
Who named this river the River of Longing?
When frontier wagons and horses pass endlessly by?
Only because since ancient times, the tears of soldiers
Have sprinkled the empty valley, forming waves and ripples.
From "Classified Anecdotes of the Sòng Dynasty"
Guó Shuǐ
The waterways of Qí are turbulent and winding,
so its people are greedy, crude, and fond of bravery.
The waters of Chǔ are gentle and clear,
so its people are frivolous, resolute, and treacherous.
The waters of Yuè are turbid, heavy, and stagnant,
so its people are foolish, irritable, and filthy.
The waters of Qín are murky, sediment-laden, and sluggish,
clogged and impure,
so its people are greedy and cruel,
deceitful and fond of litigation.
The waters of Qí and Jìn are dry, drought-prone, and meandering,
clogged and impure,
so its people are flattering, sycophantic, and deceitful,
cunning, artful, and fond of profit.
The waters of Yān gather low and are weak,
stagnant and impure,
so its people are foolish, simple, and fond of integrity,
frivolous, hasty, and prone to death.
The waters of Sòng are light, strong, and clear,
so its people are straightforward and good.
Therefore, when a sage transforms the world,
the key lies in governing water in the world.
The pivot is in water.
Guǎnzǐ
Where water flows
Where the water is light, there are many bald and goitrous people;
where the water is heavy, there are many swollen and lame people;
where the water is sweet, there are many fine and beautiful people;
where the water is pungent, there are many carbuncled and stunted people;
where the water is bitter, there are many hunchbacked and crippled people.
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū"
Square and round,
Generally, water that is square
and bends
contains jade;
that which is round and bends
contains pearls.
Clear water holds gold,
and dragon abysses contain jade essence.
"Shīzǐ"
The Six Waters
What are the six waters?
Answer:
The Héshuǐ, Chìshuǐ, Liáoshuǐ, Hēishuǐ, Jiāngshuǐ, and Huáishuǐ.
Huáinánzǐ
Clear and Turbid
Clear water sounds faint,
turbid water sounds loud.
Rapid water makes people feel light,
slow water makes people feel heavy.
Above
Shuǐ Yí
White waters are suitable for jade,
black waters for whetstones,
blue waters for jade discs,
red waters for cinnabar,
yellow waters for gold,
clear waters for turtles,
the turbid Fén River is suitable for hemp,
the harmonious Jì River for wheat,
the weak and muddy Hé River for beans,
the light and swift Luò River for millet,
the powerful Wèi River for broomcorn millet,
the heavy and tranquil Hàn River for bamboo,
the fertile and benevolent Jiāng River for rice,
people of level land are intelligent and suited to the five grains.
Huáinánzǐ
The Divine Spring of the Emperor
The River originates from Kūnlún.
Northeast of it,
lies the Chìshuǐ.
To its southeast,
the Yángshuǐ and Hēishuǐ emerge from the northwest.
These four waters,
divine springs of the Emperor,
harmonize all medicines and nourish all things.
From "Shānhǎi Huáinán"
Dìtái Jiāngshuǐ
Mount Gāoqián,
upon which there is water,
extremely cold and clear,
is the beverage of Dìtái.
"Classic of Mountains and Seas"
Cold and Hot Waters
In a remote corner of the Great Wilderness stands a mountain that remains unjoined,
named Bùzhōu.
There exist the Cold and Hot Waters.
Above
Líng Líng
On Mount Kōngsāng,
there is a beast called Línglíng.
It looks like an ox with tiger stripes,
its call sounds like its own name,
and when it appears, great floods occur under heaven.
On Mount Yǎn there is a beast named Héyǔ,
and when it appears, great floods occur under heaven.
On Mount Áo'àn there is a beast called Fūzhū,
which resembles a deer but has four horns,
and when it appears, the city experiences great floods.
Mánmán
On Mount Chóngwú there is a bird,
with one wing and one eye,
that can only fly when they pair up,
its name is Mánmán.
When it appears, there will be great floods in the world.
On Mount Yù there is a bird resembling a pheasant and red in color,
named Shèngyù,
whose appearance causes great floods in its state.
Xuánzhōu Shuǐ
Xuánzhōu is in the Northern Sea,
one hundred thousand lǐ from the southern shore.
On it grows glossy ganoderma in the dark ravine,
the ravine's water is like honey,
and drinking it leads to longevity.
"Yúlóng Hétú"
Sweet Water
Sweet Water is eighty li from Yūyuān,
where there is a sweet stream.
Its taste is like honey.
Dōngfāng Shuò traveled to this water,
obtained several hú of it,
and presented it to the Emperor.
He poured the water into a well,
and the well water remained perpetually sweet,
while bathing in its coldness made the skin soft and smooth.
"Records of the Hidden Realms"
Xī Táng
In the West Sea islands, there is a substance like grease, black in color,
that corrodes other objects.
When contained in vessels, it leaks through them all,
except for ox horns, which can store it.
In the South Sea, it is used as bait
for wild elephants.
Apply a small amount on tree leaves,
and when an elephant brushes against it,
it will linger and not leave.
The Kūnlún slaves also apply it on their bodies,
then ride the elephants back,
as if they were domesticated animals.
From the "Lù Shǐ"
Treacherous and cowardly
In the Brāhmaṇa countries there is a Pàntú,
where a timid stream emerges from the mountains,
and in a stone mortar stands a stone statue guarding it.
The water has seven colors,
sometimes cold, sometimes hot,
capable of dissolving plants, trees, metals, and iron.
If a human hand probes into it, it immediately rots,
so they use a camel skull to transfer it into a gourd.
"New Book of Táng"
Bà Shuǐ
In Tíngzhōu, when the Bà River water is held in vessels of gold, silver, or iron,
it all leaks through.
Only a gourd leaf does not leak.
"Records of Diverse Matters":
North of the Jūyí Kingdom's mountains, there is a stone camel's urine,
which drips down like syrup.
When held in vessels of gold, silver, copper, iron, wood, or tile, it all leaks through;
even catching it in the palm penetrates,
only a gourd dipper does not leak and can be drunk.
It causes the corpse hairs on a person's body to fall out completely,
and one becomes an immortal, 20,000 lǐ from Dūnhuáng.
"Garden of Marvels":
The stone camel urinates in that country,
with a Brahmin guarding and watching over it.
"Records of the Western Regions":
See also "stone."
Clear Green
At Cāngzhōu beneath the Jiǔshì Mountain flows a clear green water,
its spring spanning one hundred paces wide,
also called the Flowing Green Canal.
Even if metals and stones are thrown into it,
they never sink to the bottom.
Thus the local people make boats and barges from earthenware and iron.
"Records of the Strange from the Dūyáng Biān."
Shízhī
South of Yánshòu County in Jiǔquán,
there is a mountain spring emerging from rocks,
gushing forth like a pouring vessel.
The ground forms ditches,
and its water contains a fatty substance resembling boiled meat,
flowing continuously like uncoagulated grease.
When ignited, it burns extremely brightly,
but is inedible.
The locals call it "stone lacquer."
The Bówù Jì records:
There is moss resembling fatty meat,
which burns with intense brightness. On the water floats a black grease,
collected using grass,
used to coat leather wine bags and grease cart axles.
Emperor Wǔ of the Zhōu dynasty,
when the Turks besieged Jiǔquán, obtained this grease to light fires,
burning their siege equipment.
It burns even brighter when meeting water,
enabling Jiǔquán to survive relying on this.
The Yuánhé Zhì records:
The Xiongnu called it "stone grease water,"
with greasy substance floating on the surface like lacquer,
collected for greasing carts and lighting lamps with extreme brightness.
The Yǒuyáng Zázǔ records:
Fūyán grease,
which is Yán'ān petroleum.
It originates along water margins,
mixed with sand, stones, and spring water,
seeping out sluggishly.
Locals collect it using pheasant tail feathers,
then gather it into earthen jars.
It closely resembles pure lacquer.
When burned, it produces smoke like hemp,
considered superior to pine resin for making ink.
The Bǐtán Zázhì records:
Hēixī
In the southern wilds there is a Black Stream,
within Zhāngzhōu's borders lies the Black Foot Creek,
where those who wade through it find their feet turning ink-black.
For dozens of miles, the water is undrinkable,
as drinking it causes miasmic illness.
Travelers all carry their own water with them.
When Méi Gōngyí fell into it,
he submerged completely, and all his chronic ailments were cured.
"Brush Talks"
Piāo Piāo Water
The Qìnshuǐ flows south past the Yīshì Pass,
then further south joins the Biāobiāo River.
This river originates from the vast Jùjùn Mountain to the northeast.
Cascading from heights, it dashes against rocks with roaring echoes,
hence people named it for its sound.
"Classic of Rivers"
Luòjì
The water reaches Péng Hú and gradually becomes lower,
near Liúqiú it is called luòjì.
Jì means
water flowing downward without returning.
Whenever fishing boats from the western coast reach Péng Hú and encounter a hurricane,
drifting into luòjì,
fewer than one or two in a hundred return.
"Yuán Shǐ"
Yánghóu
The Lúnyǔ Zhāi Fǔ Xiàng states:
Yánghóu is the rivers and seas.
Sòng Jūn notes:
Yánghóu governs the rivers and seas.
The text suggests that regarding Yánghóu as the wave deity
likely originates from this.
Similar to how Zhùróng and Gōumáng
are considered sea deities.
． In the "Jiǔ Zhāng Āi Yǐng," it is said:
Riding over the overflowing waves of Yánghóu,
suddenly soaring and wandering aimlessly.
Approaching.
Wáng Yì explains:
Yánghóu,
the deity of great waves.
In the Hán Cè, when boarding a boat,
if the boat leaks and is not plugged,
the boat will sink.
Plugging the leak but underestimating the waves of Yánghóu,
the boat will capsize.
Annotation:
Bówùzhì:
The Marquis of Jìnyáng Kingdom drowned,
thus becoming the deity of the great sea.
Huáinánzǐ states:
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
crossing at Mèngjīn,
the waves of Yánghóu
surged and struck against him.
Gāo Yòu explains:
Yánghóu,
the Marquis of Língyáng Kingdom.
His kingdom was near water,
and he drowned in it.
His spirit could create great waves,
causing harm,
referred to as the waves of Yánghóu.
Yìng Shào says:
Yánghóu,
an ancient feudal lord,
who, guilty, threw himself into the river,
his spirit became great waves.
These are likely fabrications.
"Jiǎng Fù":
Yánghóu hides his form in the great waves,
and also says:
Yánghóu rises towering from the shore,
"Hǎi Fù":
Not floating on Yánghóu.
Tiān Wú
In the Classic of Mountains and Seas, the deity of Cháoyáng Valley is called Tiān Wú,
who is known as the Earl of Water.
In "Rhapsody on the Sea":
Tiān Wú appears faintly at first glance,
and in "Rhapsody on the Qin":
Tiān Wú leaps and dances in the deep abyss.
Féng Yí
The Classic of Mountains and Seas states:
The abyss of the central pole is three hundred ren deep,
where only Bīng Yí resides.
Bīng Yí has a human face and rides a dragon.
The Biography of Emperor Mu says:
The Son of Heaven journeyed west and reached Mount Yángyū,
where Hé Bó Wú Yí dwelled, also known as Bīng Yí,
and Wú Yí is Féng Yí.
Huainanzi also writes it as Féng Chí.
In the "Explaining Ghosts" chapter of Bàopǔzǐ, it is said:
Féng Yí drowned while crossing the river on the seventh day of the eighth month,
and the Heavenly Emperor appointed him as Hé Bó.
The Qīnglíng Biography states:
Féng Yí
was a man from Dīshǒu in Tóngxiāng, Huáyīn.
He ingested eight minerals and became an immortal of water,
thus becoming Hé Bó.
The Lóngyú Hétú says:
Hé Bó's given name is Gōngzǐ,
and his wife's surname is Féng, given name Yí.
The Kuòdìtú states:
Féng Yí often rides a cloud chariot,
driving two dragons.
Liù Láng
Wéi Pǔ encountered a ghostly guest Guī Yuánquán, who said:
The early attendant Féng Liùláng was in Hézhōng.
Pǔ asked who Liùláng was,
Guī replied that Féng Liùláng's name was Yí,
the beloved son of Xuānyuán Tiānzǐ, the River God.
Pǔ said:
How did Féng get the rank of six?
He replied that Féng was a water official,
and water's completed number is six.
"Records of Hédōng"
Qìng Jì
In marshes that have not dried up for hundreds of years, where valleys do not shift and waters do not cease,
Qìngjì is born.
As for Qìngjì,
its form resembles a human,
standing four inches tall.
It wears yellow robes,
dons a yellow crown,
carries a yellow canopy,
rides a small horse,
and delights in swift galloping.
Call it by its name,
and it can travel a thousand miles away and return within a single day.
This is the essence of the undried marsh.
As for the essence of the undried river,
it is born from the wēiwēi creature.
It has one head and two bodies,
its shape resembling a snake,
measuring eight feet in length.
Call it by its name,
and it can catch fish and turtles.
This is the essence of the undried river's water.
From "Guǎnzǐ."
Xiǎorén Jǐng
In the fourth year of Wáng Mǎng's establishment of the state,
in Chíyáng there appeared small human figures.
They were over a foot tall,
some riding in carriages,
some walking on foot,
handling various objects,
each of different sizes, and they claimed to stop after three days.
However, these figures in Chíyáng
might have been Qìngjì.
"Sōu Shén Jì"
Illustrated Classic of Watercraft
Emperor Suí Yángdì specially commissioned academician Dù Bǎo to compile the "Illustrated Water Ornaments Classic" in fifteen volumes, newly completed.
On the third day of the third month, he assembled his ministers at the Qūshuǐ,
to view the water ornaments.
There was a divine turtle carrying the Eight Trigrams emerging from the river,
presenting them to Fúxī.
A yellow dragon emerged from the river bearing a chart,
a turtle holding a tally emerged from the Luò River,
a large weever fish carrying a register chart emerged from the Cuìguī waters,
to bestow upon Huángdì.
Huángdì fasted at Xuánhù,
a phoenix descended upon the Luò River,
a red-shelled divine turtle holding writing emerged from the Luò and gave it to Cāngjié.
Yáo and Shùn floated on the river in a boat,
a phoenix carried a chart,
a red dragon bore a diagram,
emerging from the river to present to Yáo.
A dragon-horse carrying inscribed armor emerged from the river and gave it to Shùn,
Yáo and Shùn traveled on the river,
encountering five old men who came to announce the emperor's reign.
Yáo met the four masters south of the Fén River.
Shùn fished at Léizé,
made pottery by the riverbank,
a yellow dragon carrying a chart of yellow script and the imperial seal,
emerged from the river and gave it to Shùn,
Shùn harmonized with the hundred artisans in song,
fish leaped in the water.
A white-faced tall figure with a fish body,
presented the river chart to Yǔ,
danced and entered the river.
Yǔ regulated the waters,
Yìnglóng used its tail to draw on the ground,
guiding where the waters should be channeled,
cut through the Dragon Gate to dredge the river.
Yǔ crossed the Yangtze,
a yellow dragon carried his boat,
the Xuányí and Cāngshuǐ emissaries gave Yǔ the "Classic of Mountains and Seas."
He met two goddesses above Shénquán,
Emperor Tiānyǐ viewed the Luò,
twin yellow fish leaped,
transforming into a black jade belt with red patterns.
Jiāngyuán stepped into a giant's footprint by the river,
abandoned Hòujì on the cold ice,
birds covered him with their wings.
King Wén sat at Língzhǎo,
fish leaped abundantly,
Prince Fā crossed the river,
a white fish with red patterns leaped into the king's boat,
King Wǔ crossed at Mèngjīn,
wielding a yellow battle-axe to command the waves of Yánghóu.
The Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng,
performed Shùn's rituals,
music and glory covered the river.
King Mù of Zhōu played universal music at Xuánchí,
hunted at Zǎojīn,
captured a black raccoon dog and a white fox,
toasted the Queen Mother of the West at Yáochí,
crossed the Nine Rivers,
with giant turtles and crocodiles forming a bridge.
The state of Túxiū presented King Zhāo with a green phoenix and red crane,
drank at Yùxī.
Prince Jìn played the shēng at the Yī River,
a phoenix descended,
Qín Shǐhuáng entered the sea,
saw the sea god,
Hàn Gāozǔ hid in the marshes of Mángdàng Mountains,
with purple clouds above.
Emperor Wǔ sailed a tower ship on the Fén River,
toured Kūnmíng Pond,
removed the hook from a giant fish and swam in the Luò,
the water deity offered bright pearls and dragon marrow.
Emperor Huán of Hàn traveled on the river,
encountered a green ox emerging from the river,
Cáo Mān bathed in the Qiáo River,
struck a water dragon,
Emperor Wén of Wèi raised an army,
reached the river but did not cross,
Dù Yù completed the construction of a river bridge,
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn attended the gathering,
raised a toast to Dù Yù,
five horses floated across the river,
one transformed into a dragon,
an immortal drank from the sweet spring water.
A golden figure rode a golden boat,
a dark turtle with blue patterns holding writing emerged from the Luò,
a green dragon bearing writing emerged from the river,
both presented to the Duke of Zhōu.
Lǚ Wàng fished at Pánxī and obtained a jade huáng,
fished at Biànxī and caught a large carp,
found military tallies inside its belly.
Duke Huán of Qí inquired about Yúgōng Valley.
The King of Chǔ crossed the river and obtained a duckweed fruit.
King Zhāo of Qín feasted at the river bend,
a golden figure presented a water-heart sword to him.
The Great Emperor of Wú looked toward Gě Xuán from the fishing platform,
Liú Bèi rode his horse across Tánxī.
Dāntái Zǐyǔ crossed the river,
two dragons flanked his boat,
Zīqiū Xīn battled the water deity,
Zhōu Chǔ beheaded a dragon.
Qū Yuán encountered a fisherman,
Biàn Suí threw himself into the Yǐng River.
Xǔ Yóu washed his ears,
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ met the ferryman's daughter,
Confucius met the maiden of Āgǔ.
Qiū Hú's wife drowned herself,
Kǒng Yú released a turtle.
Zhuāngzǐ and Huìzǐ observed fish,
Zhèng Hóng had the wind return on the woodcutter's path,
Zhào Bǐng crossed the river under a canopy,
the Yánggǔ maiden bathed the sun,
Qū Yuán drowned in the Mìluó River,
Jùlíng split the mountain,
a giant whale swallowed a boat,
and such scenes totaled seventy-two tableaus,
all carved from wood.
Some rode in boats,
some on mountains,
some on flat islets,
some on large rocks,
some in palaces.
The wooden figures were about two feet tall,
clothed in silk,
adorned with gold and jade,
along with various birds, beasts, and fish,
all able to move as if alive,
following the meandering waterway.
Interspersed among them were courtesan boats,
alternating with the water ornaments.
The courtesan boats and water ornaments were also exquisitely carved and decorated,
circling the winding pond,
all operated by hydraulic mechanisms,
their wondrous and strange movements beyond expectation,
all created by Huáng Gǔn.
"Great Enterprise Reminiscences"
The transformation of blood heralds an auspicious omen.
Fǔ Gōngshí occupied Jiāngdōng and rebelled,
so the court ordered Héjiān Wáng Lǐ Xiàogōng to attack him.
Lǐ Xiàogōng advanced from Jīngzhōu towards Jiǔjiāng,
and just as he was about to depart,
he held a banquet with his generals.
When water was fetched, it suddenly turned into blood.
All those present turned pale with fright,
but Lǐ Xiàogōng remained composed and unperturbed.
He slowly explained to them, saying:
"Misfortune and blessing have no gates;
they are summoned only by men themselves.
I reflect upon myself and find I have done no wrong to anyone.
Why, gentlemen, are you so deeply worried?
Fǔ Gōngshí's evil deeds have accumulated and his misfortunes are full.
Now, in accordance with the court's strategy, we are launching a punitive expedition against him.
The blood in this bowl
is an omen that Fǔ Gōngshí will be beheaded.
Thereupon, he drank it all and ended the banquet.
People at the time admired his insight and composure, as well as his ability to reassure the crowd.
"Old Book of Táng"
Ominous portent
West of Xíngyáng Commandery's city wall lay Yǒngfú Lake.
It was filled by channeling water from the Zhèng River.
In ordinary times, its banks were planted all around with flowers and trees,
and it served as the place where the Grand Administrator hosted farewell feasts for departing officials.
To the southwest, on the low-lying land, grew many tall bamboos and lofty trees,
which formed the estate of the late tutor of Xú Prefecture, the Regular Attendant Cuī Yànzēng.
During the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty, when Páng Xūn rebelled,
Yànzēng was captured by the rebels.
For three days, the lake's water turned red like clotted blood,
and before long, news of his death arrived.

Nature is pure

Clouded wisdom cannot guide with correctness,
and turbulent water cannot reflect stillness.

Wěilǘ
Zhuāngzǐ said:
When the autumn floods arrived, all the rivers poured into the Yellow River,
filling the spaces between the islets and banks,
making it impossible to distinguish oxen from horses.
The River Earl was overjoyed with himself,
believing that all the beauty under heaven was gathered in himself.
Following the current eastward, he reached the North Sea.
Looking eastward,
he could not see the water's end.
Then he began to turn his face around,
and, gazing out over the ocean, he sighed to Ruò.
The North Sea Ruò said:
A frog in a well cannot be spoken to about the sea—
it is confined to its hollow.
A summer insect cannot be spoken to about ice—
it is bound to its season.
he is shackled by his doctrines.
Under heaven, no water is greater than that of the sea.
All rivers flow into it,
yet one never knows when it will cease and yet it never fills.
The Wěilǘ drains it, yet one never knows when,
but it never empties, be it spring or autumn.
It does not change with floods or droughts.
One does not know how much greater this is than the flow of the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers—
it cannot be measured.
When we calculate the position of the four seas within heaven and earth,
is it not like a pimple on a large swamp?
When we calculate the position of the Middle Kingdom within the sea,
is it not like a tiny grain in a great granary?
Sīmǎ comments:
Wěilǘ
is what drains the sea water outward.
Wěi (tail) is below all rivers,
hence it is called wěi.
Lǘ (gate)
means to gather;
it is where water gathers together,
hence it is called lǘ.

Wò Jiāo

Wò Jiāo

The Buddhist Canon says:
There is a rock in the great sea,
named Jiāo.
All streams pour into it, reaching the rock,
and all are exhausted,
which is why the seawater does not increase.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
The sea has an end and nothing beyond;
the treasure can shrink what is poured into it.
Thus, there is no increase or decrease,
and when the water surges forth from the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King at its appointed times,
the tides never miss their season.

The Joy of the Eastern Sea
The turtle of the Eastern Sea said to the turtle in the shallow well,

yet this is not enough to convey its vastness;

nor advance or retreat with the abundance or scarcity of water—
this is the joy of the Eastern Sea."

Qí Jǐng Gōng was traveling on the sea and enjoying it,

Crossing the Sea
Qín Shǐ Huáng constructed the Sun-Viewing Bridge,
intending to cross the sea.
Some say it was not built by humans.
The sea god drove stones and erected pillars for him.
Qín Shǐ Huáng, grateful for this favor,
then paid respects to the god,
requesting to meet him.
The god said:
"My form is ugly; do not attempt to depict my shape.
I shall meet with the Emperor."
Qín Shǐ Huáng then entered the sea via the stone bridge for forty li,
and met with the god.
A skilled person among his attendants secretly traced the god's form with his foot.
The god angrily said:
"The Emperor has broken the agreement; leave quickly."
As Qín Shǐ Huáng turned his horse, the front hooves had just landed,
when the rear section collapsed immediately after.
He barely managed to reach the shore.
Today, from Mount Xiányáng eastward to the sea route, there are standing stones,
often visible in pairs resembling bridge stones.
There are also two pillar stones that sometimes appear and sometimes submerge,
markers left by Qín Shǐ Huáng.

Sea Ice
Mùróng Huàng intended to cross the sea to attack his brother Rén,

The ministers considered the sea route dangerous and obstructed,
advising that they should take the land route.

Qīnghǎi
West of Yǔnwú County lies the Bēihé Qiāng Sea,
known as Qinghai.
Lǐ Dàliàng campaigned against the Tǔyùhún,
serving as Hedong Circuit Campaign Commander.
He and Lǐ Jìng jointly advanced via the northern route,
crossing Qinghai to observe the source of the Yellow River.
"Records of the Thirteen Provinces"
Gate of Hell
During the Zhēnguàn era, the court dispatched Gāo Biǎorén, the governor of Xīnzhōu,
bearing credentials as an envoy to the state of Wō.
In the midst of the great sea,
Biǎorén sailed for several months before arriving,
claiming that the route passed through the gates of hell,
where the atmosphere above was thick and gloomy,
and the sounds of screaming and hammering could be heard,
making it utterly terrifying.
From "Táng Huì Yào"
The Lost Boat
Liú Rénguǐ was disliked by Lǐ Yìfǔ,
and was sent out as the governor of Qīngzhōu.
At that time, the campaign against Bǎijì was underway,
and Liú Rénguǐ was responsible for transporting grain by sea.
Before it was feasible to set sail, Lǐ Yìfǔ pressured him to depart,
but they encountered a storm and lost the ships,
resulting in the drowning of many laborers.
The emperor ordered the censor Yuán Yìshì to investigate the matter,
and he submitted a full report of the case.
Lǐ Yìfǔ said to the emperor:
"If Liú Rénguǐ is not executed,
there will be no way to appease the people."
The court official Yuán Zhíxīn remarked:
"The sudden storm at sea was beyond human control."
Thereupon, the emperor ordered Liú Rénguǐ to be stripped of his official rank but allowed to remain as a commoner,
joining the army to redeem himself.
"Comprehensive Mirror"
Crossing the sea
When Empress Wǔ Zétiān carried out her revolution, she sent Lù Yuánfāng to pacify the region beyond the southern mountains.
As he was about to cross the sea,
the wind and waves were extremely fierce,
and the boatmen dared not set sail.
Lù Yuánfāng said:
"I have received my orders selflessly,
how could the gods harm me?"
He immediately ordered them to cross,
and soon the wind and waves indeed subsided.
(Old Book of Táng)
King Fēng
In the first month of the tenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
the East Sea was designated as the Vast Virtue King,
the South Sea as the Vast Profit King,
the West Sea as the Vast Moistening King,
and the North Sea as the Vast Marsh King.
Ministers and supervisors were separately dispatched to the sacred mountains and rivers,
to perform ceremonies and confer titles
on the seventeenth day of the third month at the same appointed time.
From the Tōngdiǎn
Not taking a small boat
Guī Chóngjìng served as an envoy to bestow the official title on the king of Xīnluó.
When they reached the middle of the sea,
the waves surged rapidly,
causing the ship to break and leak.
Everyone was terrified,
and the sailors suggested using a small boat to carry him.
Guī Chóngjìng said:
"There are dozens to hundreds of people on this ship.
How could I bear to cross alone?"
Shortly after, the wind calmed.
"Tán Bīn Lù"
Chisel the Sea
North of Jiāozhǐ, there was a water route extending to the South Sea,
where many boats capsized.
Gāo Pián went to inspect the area
and discovered submerged, barely visible horizontal rocks.
He then submitted a memorial proposing to dredge the rocks to facilitate navigation to the South Sea.
His memorial roughly stated:
"People wield sharp oars, yet rocks block the crossing;
once boarding a departing boat,
they prepare for a journey to the netherworld."
At that time, an imperial edict approved the plan.
Workers were recruited with generous rewards and eventually cleared the rocks,
a benefit the people rely on to this day.
Some say:
Pián used magic to harness thunder and lightning for the excavation.
(From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán")
Encountering an Immortal
At the end of the Qiánfú era, Zhāng Jiànzhāng served as the military commander of Yōuzhōu.
As a staff officer, he once carried out a military order to Bóhǎi,
but encountered stormy waves and had to anchor his boat.
Suddenly, a woman in blue appeared in a small boat,
and said to Jiànzhāng:
"By the command of the Great Immortal, I invite you, sir."
Jiànzhāng responded and followed her,
arriving at a large island.
There he saw towering towers and pavilions where a female immortal resided,
attended by a grand entourage.
The utensils and food were all common flavors from Jiànzhāng's hometown.
After the meal, he prepared to take his leave.
The female immortal said to Jiànzhāng:
"You do not deceive in dark rooms,
truly what is called a gentleman.
Fearing you would suffer from the stormy waves,
I shall have this blue-clad woman guide you back and forth."
When he returned, the wind and waves were calm,
and he had nothing to fear on his journeys.
He then presented the mermaid silk given by the water immortal as ordered,
and those fond of remarkable events wrote a biography for him.
Hǎiyǎn
In Běihǎi County, five-zhu coins were unearthed while digging the ground,
and they could not be exhausted no matter how many were taken.
Among them, a stone was found,
with an inscription stating that this was a sea eye,
which had been suppressed with coins.
The crowd, afraid, covered it up again.
"Táng Jīnhuázǐ"
Suǒ Shān
On Lìshān Mountain in Qíjùn there is an ancient iron chain,
as thick as a man's arm,
coiled around its peak.
Twice encircling it.
Legend says it was originally a mountain in the sea,
whose mountain deity was fond of moving.
Therefore, the sea deity chained it down,
and when the chain snapped, it flew here.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Gāntáng Gǎng
In Fújiàn Circuit, at the coastal area of Huángqí Bank,
the rugged and steep horizontal rocks
often posed a danger to boats and ships.
Mǐn King Wáng Shěnzhī contemplated taking measures to address this,
but was daunted by the labor required.
During the Qiánníng era,
he dreamed of a golden-armored deity,
who claimed to be King Wú'ān.
This was none other than Wǔ Zǐxū.
He promised to assist in the excavation.
Upon waking, the king ordered his administrator Liú Shānfǔ to personally go and offer sacrifices.
As soon as the third offering was completed,
various sea spirits and monsters all appeared before Liú Shānfǔ.
Taking advantage of the high vantage point to observe the wind,
a thunderstorm suddenly arose, revealing a creature that was neither fish nor dragon, with a yellow mane
and a red body, possibly hundreds of feet long.
It leaped and attacked fiercely,
and after three days, the wind and thunder ceased, and the sky cleared.
By then, a new harbor had been opened,
greatly facilitating travelers.
At the time, this was recorded and reported to the court,
which bestowed upon it the name Gāntáng Harbor.
"Jīnxī Xián Tán"
also referred to this place as the Path of Heavenly Might.
"Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Do not fear.
Duàn Xīyáo was sent as an envoy to Wúyuè,
at that time,
the Jiāng-Huái route was impassable,
all those dispatched to Wúyuè
had to travel by sea,
often facing the peril of storms.
While crossing the sea, Xīyáo encountered a great storm,
and his attendants were all terrified.
Xīyáo said:
"In my whole life, I have never deceived you all,
trust in me and you need not fear."
Soon after, the storm subsided.
"History of the Five Dynasties"
Mirage
The Book of Hàn states:
By the sea there is shèn vapor forming towers and terraces;
in the seas of Dēngzhōu, clouds and mist sometimes appear,
resembling palaces, terraces, and pavilions,
with figures, carriages, and horses clearly visible,
which is called a sea market.
When Ōu Yángxiū was dispatched to Héshuò,
he passed through Gāotáng County,
and at night, ghosts and spirits passed through the air,
the sounds of people and horses being distinguishable.
The elders said:
twenty years ago they passed by during the day,
and figures could also be vaguely seen,
which was called a sea market.
From "Brush Talks"
The Sea God Relocates
Ōuyáng Shǎoshī said,
while serving as the Military Commissioner of Héběi,
one winter he was inspecting the region and arrived at a roadside pavilion between Cāngzhōu and Jǐngzhōu.
At midnight, he heard the sounds of chariots, banners, and troops,
which lasted almost until dawn.
He asked the people lodging there,
who said it was the sea god relocating,
an event that occurs once every five to seven years.
"Records of Retiring from Court at Spring Brightness"
Sea People
When Lǐ Zhòngyóu, the Court Advisor, was serving as the magistrate of Tóng'ān County,
there were people who sailed overseas for trade.
They returned only after a year abroad,
claiming to have been blown by a great wind to an island.
Under the bright moonlight, they saw over ten figures emerging from the sea arm-in-arm,
ascending the island while laughing and chatting.
Their speech was incomprehensible,
though their physical appearance was no different from humans',
except they were completely naked.
When the sailors sounded gongs and drums to frighten them,
they simply linked arms again and laughed heartily,
before returning to the sea and departing.
People living near the island said these were called "sea people,"
whose dwellings lay beneath the island.
"Sequel to The Ink Garden Anecdotes"
Ocean
Sòng Yáng Kāngguó and Qián Xié were envoys to Goryeo, with Fēng Jì serving as Yáng's secretary in charge of documents and memorials. It was said that
the Eastern Sea is a treasury of the Dragon Palace.
The atmosphere is like thick fog,
and even without wind, there are huge waves.
People lie in wooden boxes,
and though tossed about, their bodies do not sway.
They vomit all their food,
leaving only a little liquid.
In front of the boat, a giant turtle as large as a house appears,
with eyes like giant candles,
shining brightly on the sand.
The sailors use this as an omen;
if seen, there is no danger.
"Sūn Gōng Tán Pǔ"
Sānhǎi
The monk Jiànzhēn, whose secular surname was Chúnyú,
was a native of Guǎnglíng.
When Japanese monks Róngruì and others came east to seek the Dharma,
Jiànzhēn agreed to go and thus purchased a boat to carry sutras and monastic rules there.
Soon they drifted into the Sea of Snakes, then entered the Sea of Fish,
and again entered the Sea of Birds.
After emerging, they moored at an island
where the pond was deep and clear,
and people drank its sweet water.
They subsequently reached Japan.
From "Biographies of Eminent Monks"
Hǎijǐng
In Huàtíng City there was an object,
resembling a water bucket but without a bottom.
It was not made of metal, stone, bamboo, or wood,
and for a long time no one knew its name
or its use.
One day, an old merchant from a sea vessel saw it and was overjoyed,
stroking and admiring it, then inquiring about its price.
The owner casually asked for five hundred strings of coins.
The merchant immediately paid three hundred for it,
and the owner then asked the merchant about it. The merchant said, "This is a supreme treasure.
It is called a 'sea well.'
When sailing the seas, one must always carry fresh water,
but now, simply by filling a large container with seawater
and placing this well in it to draw water,
it all becomes sweet spring water."
From "Miscellaneous Records of Guǐxīn"
Sea Louse
All seafaring vessels must have large planks protecting their exterior,
otherwise the ship's hull will inevitably be eroded by shipworms.

Muddy oil
The southern seas' various countries have naphtha,
nowadays the shallow barbarian ships that go to sea all store it.
When shallow barbarian ships encounter each other on the sea,
they assess each other's strength and then fight, which is called ship engagement.
In all ship engagements, four men stand on the steering platform,
placing naphtha in small bottles.
They seal the mouths with betel nut bark,
ignite fire on the betel nut bark,
and throw it from above—when naphtha lands on the deck,
it causes people to immediately fall.
Moreover, fire combined with naphtha spreads everywhere without extinguishing,
and if water is poured on it, it burns even more fiercely.
The only things that can control it
are dry mud and stove ashes.
The reason official military ships cannot approach shallow barbarian vessels nowadays
is precisely because they fear this substance.
Ship engagement is akin to speaking of state engagement;
without this, one lacks the foremost combat equipment.
Yīn Huǒ
The fish and clams born in the sea,
when placed in a shady place, emit light.
Initially seeing them, one might consider them strange,
but the locals often deduce their nature.
It is because they are born in the salty sea water,
where, when the water meets overcast darkness,
the waves resemble flames filling the ocean.
Striking them with an object causes sparks to scatter like stars,
but they are no longer visible when there is moonlight.
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" says:
"Hidden flames glow faintly,"
could this be referring to it?
"Strange Things of Lingnan Record."

Its dragons, fish, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, sand, stones, plants, and trees
are all purple without exception.

Mount Wúgāo,
looking south to Yòuhǎi,
Yòuhǎi,

Xiè Chéng's Book records:
To the southwest of Dàqín in the Zhang Sea,
one may travel some seven or eight hundred lǐ to reach the Coral Islands,

Azure Sea
Fú Sāng is located within the azure sea,
where the palace of the Great Emperor stands,
governed by Tài Zhēn Dōng Wáng Gōng.
Beyond the Eastern Sea,
there is a separate circular sea encircling Péng Lái Mountain,

referred to as the Míng Sea.
Without wind, it surges with waves a hundred zhang high,

"Records of the Ten Continents"
Where there is water, it forms the sea.
Lǐ Jífǔ states:
In Héběi, any body of water is called a "hé" (river),
while in Sàiběi, any body of water is called a "hǎi" (sea).
Nine Waters Converge
Mount Jiǔyí,
has nine peaks.
Each peak has a river,
nine rivers in total,
which divide and flow below to pour into the six directions,
cycling endlessly,
and ascending back here.
They irrigate the Milky Way,
hence the nine rivers originate from this mountain.
Flowing up and down, they circulate throughout the four seas.
The nine rivers are:
first, Yínhuā River;
second, Fùshū River;
third, Cháo River;
fourth, Xǔ River;
fifth, Guī River;
sixth, Shā River;
seventh, Jīnhuā River;
eighth, Yǒng'ān River;
ninth, Jìn River.

Hǎilǎo

Jīntái

Jīnyín Chéng

one arrives at the Silver City,

"The Sūtra of the Great Vow"
Three Virtues
The sea possesses three virtues:
first, it is deep and vast without boundaries;
second, it is pure and does not accept impurities;
third, it stores and accumulates immeasurable treasures.
The virtues of a Bodhisattva are akin to those of the sea.
Five Virtues of the Sea
The sea possesses five virtues:
First, it remains clear and pure, not accepting corpses;
Second, it abundantly produces marvelous treasures;
Third, when great dragons pour down rain as plentiful as cart axles,
it receives without overflowing;
Fourth, wind and moonlight cannot exhaust it;
Fifth, its depths are unfathomable.
"Records of the Sea"
The Eight Virtues
The sea has eight characteristics:
First, it gradually deepens;
Second, its tides do not exceed their limits;
Third, it does not retain dead bodies;
Fourth, all rivers flow into it;
Fifth, it has no different names;
Sixth, all streams return to it;
Yet it neither increases nor decreases;
Seventh, it produces treasures like pearls;
Eighth, large beings dwell within it;
And all share the same salty taste. These are the eight.

Non-action
