"Eulogy on the New Dynasty"
Sailing the Seas
When Xiè Ān was lingering on Dōngshān,
he, along with men like Sūn Xìnggōng,
went boating on the sea.
Suddenly, the wind rose and the waves swelled.
Sūn, Wǎng, and the others all turned pale in panic and at once called out
to turn back.
The Grand Tutor's expression remained cheerful and calm;
he chanted and whistled, saying nothing.
The boatman, seeing that his lordship looked serene and pleased, still kept going without stopping.
When the wind grew fiercer and the waves more violent,
the others all clamored and stirred, unable to remain seated.
His lordship then said calmly, "In that case, shall we not go back?"
The company immediately responded to his words and turned back.

Tides
The Gāolì Tújīng states:
The ebb and flow of tides
are the utmost faithfulness of heaven and earth.
The Shānhǎi Jīng states:
It is the measure of the sea monster's entry and exit.
The Buddhist scriptures state:
It is caused by the transformations of the divine dragon.

It follows the waxing and waning of the moon.
Lú Zhào's
Hǎicháo Fù states:

and strikes it to form the tides.
Bàopǔzǐ states:

The Dòngzhēn Jīng states:

Fēng Yǎn states:

Riding the Tide
It is named Zhejiang for its meandering course,
flowing northeast from the Shezhou border past Jieshi Mountain.
Further northeast, it merges with the sea's tidal waves.
Twice daily, day and night, the tides arrive regularly.
They are smallest on the 10th and 25th of the lunar month,
and largest on the 3rd and 18th.
During small tides, the water gradually rises,
not exceeding a few feet,
while large tides surge to heights of several zhang.
Every year on the 18th of the eighth lunar month,
across hundreds of miles,
men and women gather to watch
as boatmen and fishermen ride the waves,
an activity called "tidal boating."
From the Yuanhe Gazetteer
Zǐxū stirs the waves
King Wú bestowed upon Zǐxū
the sword named Zhǔlòu.
After his death, they took his corpse,
placed it in a leather sack,
and cast it into the river.
Zǐxū then rode the waves with the current, appearing with the tides,
eroding and collapsing the riverbanks.
(From *The Annals of Wú and Yuè*)
King Yuè executed Wén Zhǒng,
burying him on the western hill of the state.
A year after the burial,
Wǔ Zǐxū came from the sea, pierced the mountain's flank, and took Zhǒng away,
floating together with him on the sea.
Thus, the vanguard tide,
the surging waves,
are Zǐxū.
The following heavy waters,
are Minister Zhǒng.
Zhǐ Tāo
Fūchāi killed Wǔ Zǐxū,
boiling him in a cauldron.
He then threw his body into the river in a leather sack.
Zǐxū, filled with resentment, drove the waters to form raging tides,
drowning people.
Nowadays, along the great rivers of Kuàijī and Dāntú,
Qiántáng,
and the Zhè River, temples to Zǐxū have been erected,
seeking to appease his embittered heart,
and calm his fierce tides.
"Lùn Héng"
records sightings of Zǐxū riding a plain carriage with white horses,
amid the tidal surges.
Hence, temples were built to worship him.
"Lù Yì Jì"
notes that on the banks of the Féi River within Lúzhōu city,
there is also a temple to Zǐxū.
Every morning and evening at high tide,
the waters of the Féi River also surge violently,
rising to a height of one chi and spreading over ten zhang before the temple.
After a meal's time, it calms down; local tradition says
it corresponds with the tidal bore of Qiántáng.

Drum Fury
Lù Yuánfǔ's "Preface to the Inscription on Mount Xū" states:
The gift of the sword Zhūlòu,
ultimately reached his own body.
His corpse was placed in a leather sack and cast into the water,
where his pent-up indignation and wrath stirred the waves, matching their fury.
He became a deity,
and his spirit arrives twice daily to this day.
Sea gulls flock and fly, with the wave god Yánghóu attending on both sides,
raging in Wú,
seething in Yuè,
and surging in Chǔ,
before receding.
Thus, in mid-autumn,
on the first day
and the fifteenth day, the people of Hángzhōu welcome him with flags and drums,
accompanied by reed pipes and flutes,
while crowds from a hundred cities gather to witness the great display of his mighty power.

Cast upon the river,
he commands the waves himself,
arriving twice daily, reminiscent of the lament in "Embracing the Sand."
He washes the south and north,
and churns the east and west.
Though not an officially recognized sacrifice,
his reverence rivals that of the river deities.

"Gāosēng Zhuàn"
Shooting the Tide
In the fourth year of the Liáng Kaīpíng era,
King Qián Wǔsù began constructing a seawall,
located outside the Hòucháo Tōngjiāng Gate.
As the river tides surged day and night,
the earthen banks could not be stabilized with plank reinforcements.
He then ordered hundreds of crossbows to shoot at the tidal bore,
and also built a shrine on Zǐxū Hill, composing a poem for the occasion.
The poem was sealed and placed at the river mouth.
Subsequently, the tidal bore shifted northwest,
enabling the transport of massive stones,
which were placed in bamboo cages with large pillars as reinforcements.
The foundation of the wall was thus secured.
The deep moats, layered trenches, broad avenues, and wide roads
were also constructed as a result.
"Wúyuè Bèishǐ"
Local legend holds that where the arrows shot by the King of Wúyuè landed,
iron pillars were erected.
Hence the name Tiěchuáng Pǔ (Iron Pillar Bank).
"Lín'ān Zhì"
After King Qián shot the tidal bore
and it receded,
he had iron arrows cast in its shape.
Large as pestles, they were placed in roadside pavilions.
Beside the Arrow Pavilion,
one iron arrow was buried with seven chǐ still exposed above ground,
symbolizing suppression of the tides.
"Qiántáng Yíshì"
Distinguishing Waves
Historical records state that King of Wú killed Wǔ Zǐxū,
and threw his body into the river—this is true.
But claims that his hatred drove the waters to form tidal waves
are false.
When Qū Yuán, filled with resentment, threw himself into the Xiāng River,
the Xiāng River did not produce tidal waves.
When Shēntú Dí drowned himself in the Yellow River,
the Yellow River did not produce tidal waves.
Just as the earth has numerous rivers,
so humans have blood vessels.
Blood flows and circulates,
rising and falling in motion,
following its own rhythm;
the hundred rivers are the same.
Their ebb and flow,
like human breathing,
involves the exhalation and inhalation of energy.
In *Lùn Héng*,
common people claim tidal waves are created by Wǔ Zǐxū—this is absurd.
Wǔ Zǐxū had only just died,
yet since the separation of heaven and earth,
tidal waves have already existed.
*Bàopǔzǐ*
Tàcháo
The morning tide ebbs,
the evening tide flows,
and the waters merge,
which is called the overlapping tide.
The "Record of Pānyú"
states in Liǔ Yǔxī's preface on the overlapping tide:
In the summer, the fifth month of the tenth year of Yuánhé,
a great wind drove the tide,
causing the South Sea to overflow.
Southerners call it the overlapping tide,
occurring roughly once every three years.
Qiónghǎi Cháo
The Qióngguǎn Records state:
The tides of Jiāngzhè and Qīnlián
all have fixed periods.
The tides of the Qiónghǎi flow east for half a month,
and west for half a month;
the size of the tides
follows the long and short stars,
and is not related to the waxing and waning of the moon.
"Universal Records"
Sòng Nǚ Cháo

where in ancient times the King of Wú bade farewell to his daughter.

flowing backwards for seventy lǐ,
earning the name "King of Wú's Farewell Tide."

In Guìlín Prefecture, the Holy Water Cave's tide rises at midnight,

Yǐn Gōng Cháo
The Tiáo River flows in Yúháng,
with reeds blooming abundantly on both banks,

skilled in divination,
possessing extraordinary arts.
A local family named Wáng had a daughter of exceptional beauty,
whom Gōng Yǐn sought but failed to win.
He commanded the waters to surge and flood their residence,
and to this day,

"The Illustrated Classic"
The mountain cave is pitch dark.

When entering the sea, divers must tie a rope to their bodies,
held by people on the shore.
If a monster or tide comes, the rope will surely move,
and the shore people pull it to help them ascend.
They also say that when the tide rises, the mountain caves on the seafloor become dark with thunderous roars,
and the water surges upward violently.
By the time they reach the shore, the tide has already entered the river inlets.

Interaction and Transformation of Qi
The tide arrives twice daily,
during the months of Mǎo and Yǒu, which mark the transition between yīn and yáng,
the energy intensifies through this interaction,
thus the tide is uniquely greater than in other months.
After the new and full moons, when yīn and yáng transform,
the energy strengthens through this change,
hence the tide is exceptionally larger than on other days.
"Lín'ān Zhì"

The dragon bore the boat.
Yǔ traveled south to inspect the region and crossed the Jiāng River,

Yǔ looked up and sighed, saying:

and strive with all my strength to nourish the people.

death is decreed by fate.

deep

Origin

"Yóu,
why are you so elaborately dressed?

Wèngkǒu
Yègōng Zhūliáng asked about music,
Wáng Fù said:
What kind of person is the Jìn Grand Master Zhào Wénzǐ?
The reply was:
He loves learning and accepts admonishment.
Yègōng said:
I suspect that's not the full story.
The reply was:
To love learning is wisdom,
to accept admonishment is benevolence.

its source being as narrow as a jar's mouth,
yet by the time it reaches the state of Chǔ, it spans ten lǐ in width,
for no other reason

Yǐn Jiāng
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ asked Zǐgòng:
What kind of person is Confucius?
Zǐgòng replied:
I am unable to comprehend him.
Jiǎnzǐ was displeased,
saying:
You served Confucius for several decades,
completed your studies and then left him,
yet you say you don't comprehend him -
why is this?
Zǐgòng said:
I am like a thirsty person drinking from the Yangtze River and sea,
knowing only when I am satisfied;
Confucius is like the Yangtze and sea -
how could I possibly comprehend him?
Jiǎnzǐ said:
Excellent indeed
are Zǐgòng's words.

Jiāngshàng Zhàngrén
Wǔ Yuán went to Wú,
passing through Jīng until he reached the river,
intending to cross.
He saw an old man spearing a small boat just about to fish,
and so asked him for help.
The old man ferried him across,
and after crossing the river, when asked his name and clan, he refused to tell.
Wǔ Yuán untied his sword and gave it to the old man,
saying:
"This is a sword worth a thousand pieces of gold.
I wish to offer it to you, old man."
The old man refused to accept it,
saying:
"The law of the state of Jīng states that whoever captures Wǔ Yuán will be enfeoffed as a 'Zhí Guī' noble,
given a salary of ten thousand dàn,
and a thousand yì of gold.
Previously, when Zǐxū passed by,
I still did not seize him.
Now, why would I take your thousand-gold sword?"
After Wǔ Yuán crossed over to Wú,
he sent people to search for the old man along the river,
but could not find him.
Whenever he ate, he would always make offerings to him,
praying:

Turning spears midstream

Yàolí pretended to have offended the King of Wú and fled to Wèi, where he met Prince Qìngjì and said: "Allow me to accompany you to seize back your state." Prince Qìngjì replied: "Excellent." So he crossed the river with Yàolí. Midstream, Yàolí drew his sword to stab Qìngjì, but Qìngjì grabbed him and threw him into the river. When he floated up, Qìngjì seized and threw him again, repeating this three times. Finally, he said: "You are a champion of the realm. I grant you the chance to complete your fame." Thus Yàolí was spared and returned to Wú.
Jiàntái manifested integrity.

King Zhāo of Chǔ went on an excursion, leaving his wife Zhēn Jiāng on the Jiàn Terrace. When the river rose greatly, he sent a messenger to fetch her but forgot to give him the tally. The lady said: "The king made an agreement with the palace women that summons must be accompanied by the tally. Now the messenger has no tally, so I dare not go." Thereupon the messenger went to fetch the tally, but the terrace collapsed, and the lady drowned and died.

Falling Sword
A man of Chǔ was crossing a river,
when his sword fell from the boat into the water.
He hastily cut a mark on the boat, saying:
"This is where my sword fell."
When the boat stopped,
he entered the water to search for it from the place he had marked.
The boat had moved on,
but the sword had not.
Is it not foolish to search for a sword in this manner?
Another man was passing by the river,
when he saw someone about to throw an infant into the river.
The infant was crying,
and the man asked the reason.
The reply was:
"This child's father is a good swimmer."
Though the father is a good swimmer,
how can the child necessarily be a good swimmer?
From "The Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi"
River God's Battle
King Zhāo of Qín appointed Lǐ Bīng as governor of Shǔ,
who opened two rivers in Chéngdū, irrigating ten thousand qǐng of farmland.
A deity demanded two young maidens annually as wives,
so Bīng offered his own daughter to marry the deity.
He went straight to the temple and urged the deity to drink,
but the wine cup kept rippling unnaturally.
Bīng sternly reprimanded the deity,
who suddenly vanished.
After a long while, two bulls were seen fighting on the riverbank.
Standing nearby, Lǐ Bīng
returned sweating and told his officials:
"I fought intensely
and need your help.
The bull facing south with the white mark on its waist—
that is my ribbon.
Have the registrar stab the one facing north."
The river deity was thus slain,
and the people of Shǔ admired his courageous resolve.
All robust children were consequently named "Bīng's child."

Govern lawsuits to make the waters clear.

Drinking from the Jiāng River
Jiǎng Shī of Guǎnghàn,
whose wife was née Páng,
served her mother-in-law with utmost filial piety.
The mother-in-law enjoyed drinking water from the Jiāng River,
which was seven lǐ from their home.
The wife often fetched water upstream at cockcrow,
but once encountered wind and snow and failed to obtain water.
Jiǎng Shī reproached and dismissed her.
The wife went to a neighbor's home to spin and weave for provision,
and through the neighbor's mother sent supplies to her mother-in-law.
Upon hearing this, Jiǎng Shī pursued her and brought her back home.
Suddenly, a spring gushed forth beside the house,
with a taste like that of the Jiāng River.
"Biographies of Exemplary Women" from the Chronicles of Huáyáng.
Heaven divides north and south
Emperor Wén of Wèi arrived at Guǎnglíng,
reviewing his troops by the river,
with the intention to cross it.
Sūn Quán set up strict defenses and held firm,
and as it was extremely cold at the time,
the boats were frozen and could not enter the river.
The Emperor saw the turbulent waves surging,
and sighed, "Alas!
It is truly Heaven that divides north and south,"
and thereupon returned.

Mèngmén
In ancient times, before the Lóngmén Gorge was opened,
before the Lǚliáng Mountains were breached,
the river emerged at Mèngmén,
overflowing greatly,
and flowing backward without hills or fertile plains,
submerging all plateaus and high grounds,
it was called the Great Flood.
Yǔ then dredged the rivers and breached the channels,
creating barriers at Pénglǐ Lake,
thus saving eighteen hundred states in the eastern lands.
From "The Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi."
Dǐzhù
In ancient times, Yǔ controlled the floods and mountains,
cutting through where water was blocked,
thus breaking mountains to open the river's path,
causing the river to divide its flow,
encircling the mountain as it passed,
the mountain appearing in the water like a pillar,
hence it was called Dǐzhù (Pillar).
After three channels were cut through,
the water flow divided like spread fingers,
and it was also named Sānmén (Three Gates).
To its east, the Qiānxiáo River flows into the Yellow River,
with banks flanking the mountains,
towering peaks rising steeply,
ranges layered in elegance,
ridges piled high to the sky.
According to Zhèng Xuán's geographical records,
the Yellow River flows east through Dǐzhù,
striking obstructing currents—what is now called Dǐzhù.
This is likely the obstructed flow,
and Dǐzhù should be in Xīhé,
though details are unclear.
From Xīhé, there should be no mountains blocking it,
from Dǐzhù down to Wǔhù,
a distance of one hundred twenty lǐ,
the river thrusts rocks upward,
their force connecting to the high land,
likely cut by Yǔ to open the river,
suspected to be this obstructed flow.
Though the mountain was split, it still poses obstacles,
with rapids striking rocks,
waves swirling furiously like clouds,
containing nineteen treacherous shoals in total.
The current is swift and urgent,
comparable to the Three Gorges in force,
damaging boats and ships,
a peril since ancient times.
From "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù":
In the middle reaches of the Yellow River lies Dǐzhù Mountain,
also named Sānmén Mountain,
as in the "Yǔ Gòng":
Directing the river from Jīshí,
reaching Dǐzhù.
This rock resembles a pillar,
hence the name; the mountain has three gates,
cut by Yǔ to open the river,
the southern called Guǐmén (Ghost Gate),
the central Shénmén (Divine Gate),
the northern Rénmén (Human Gate),
impassable for boats,
only Rénmén allowing raft passage.
From "Shǎnzhōu Zhì"
Lóngmén
Yǔ excavated the Dragon Gate,
opened up the Yīquē Gorge, diverted rivers, opened the Mín Mountains, and channeled the Four Great Rivers.
The Yuán Shén Qì
notes:
He excavated the Dragon Gate to connect the Yellow River,
cut through the Mín Mountains to open the Yangtze River,
channeled the Huái River at Tóngbó,
and guided the Jì River at Wángwū,
hence the term "channeling the Four Great Rivers."
When the Yellow River passes through the Dragon Gate,
its current rushes like a bamboo arrow,
so swift that even a team of four horses cannot catch up.
The Shènzǐ
states: The Yellow River ford is also called the Dragon Gate.
Yǔ cut through the mountains to create this gateway,
about one lǐ wide,
with the Yellow River flowing through the center.
The two banks are impassable for carts and horses.
Every year in late spring,
yellow carp swim upstream against the current,
and those that succeed transform into dragons.

Hé Jīng
Yǔ was managing the floodwaters,
and while observing the river,
he saw a white-faced, long-bodied creature with a fish's form emerge and say:

then presented Yǔ with the River Chart before returning to the depths.

King Wǔ attacked Zhòu and crossed at Mèngjīn,
the waves of Yáng Hóu surged against the current and struck,

who dares oppose my will?"

The Son of Heaven campaigned westward,
traveling swiftly until he reached Mount Yángyū,
the domain of Hé Bó Wúyí,

Hé Zōng Bó Yāo welcomed the Son of Heaven at Mount Yānrán.

The Son of Heaven campaigned westward,
hunted at Shèn Swamp,

Shěn Bì
Duke Wén of Qín welcomed Chóng'ěr,
and when they reached the Yellow River,
Zǐ Fàn presented the prince with a jade disc,
saying:
"I have followed Your Highness, traveling by carriage throughout the realm,
and my faults have been many.
If even I am aware of them, how much more must you be?
Unable to bear the thought of facing death for them,
I beg to take my leave here."
The prince replied:
"If I do not share the same heart with my uncle,
may I be as this jade disc sunk in the river as pledge."
Guóyǔ
Shǐjì:

Shuōyuàn:
May the clear waters be my witness.

Shěn Yù
Wángzǐ Cháo usurped the throne,
and battled with King Jìng,
so he altered the precious jade of Zhōu,
sinking it into the river to pray for blessings.
Two days later,
a ferryman retrieved it from the riverbank.
King Jìng's minister,
Yīn Bùnìng, invaded south with troops from Wēn
and intended to sell it,
but it transformed into stone for King Jìng.
When the position was secured, the one who obtained the jade presented it,
and it reverted to being jade.
"Zuǒzhuàn Shuǐjīng Zhù"
Roaming the River
Fàn Xiànzǐ was traveling on the river,
with all his ministers present.
The ruler said:
"Do you know the descendants of the Luán family?"
None of the ministers replied.
The boatman Qīng Juān laid down his oar and responded:
"Why does my lord ask about the descendants of the Luán family?"
The ruler said:
"Those who caused our Luán family to perish were the elders,
and before they died, the younger ones had grown strong."
Qīng Juān said:
"If you govern the state of Jìn well,
winning the support of ministers internally,
and not losing the common people externally,
even if there are descendants of the Luán family,
what can they do to you?
But if you do not govern the state of Jìn well,
failing to win the support of ministers internally and losing the common people externally,
then everyone in this boat will be descendants of the Luán family."
The ruler said: "Well said."
From "Shīzǐ"
No sacrifice is offered.
Hán Hèzǐ was crossing the river,
when the ferryman told him:
"Those who pass this way,
none fail to make offerings for ease of passage.
Will you, sir, not do so?"
Hán Hèzǐ replied:
"The Son of Heaven sacrifices to the gods within the four seas,
the feudal lords sacrifice within their domains,
high officials sacrifice to their ancestors,
and commoners sacrifice to their parents.
As for me, Hè,
I am not qualified to make offerings to the River Earl."
The ferryman, plying his oar, found water entering the boat and it began to drift.
The ferryman said:
"Earlier,
this servant had already warned you,
but you, sir, did not heed this servant's words.
Now water is entering the boat and it drifts severely—
should we prepare our belongings and swim downstream?"
Hánzǐ said:
"I will not change my principles because others dislike me,
nor alter my righteous words because I face death."
Before he finished speaking, the boat suddenly moved forward smoothly.
《Shuō Yuàn》
Shěn Hé
Lord Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào drowned Luán Jiǎo in the river, saying:
"I once favored music and women,
and Luán Jiǎo provided them.
I once favored palaces, towers, and pavilions,
and Luán Jiǎo built them.
I once prized fine horses and skilled drivers,
and Luán Jiǎo procured them.
Now for six years I have sought worthy scholars,
yet Luán Jiǎo has never recommended a single one.
This is encouraging my faults and obstructing excellence."
"The Annals of Lǚ"
Blocked River
Mount Liáng collapsed,
blocking the river,
so it did not flow for three days.
The ruler of Jìn summoned Bó Zūn,
and Bó Zūn encountered a cart driver.
He got off his carriage and asked him,
"What should be done about this?"
The cart driver said:
"Heaven has mountains;
Heaven causes them to collapse.
Heaven has rivers;
Heaven blocks them.
What can even summoning Bó Zūn accomplish?
If the ruler personally dons plain white mourning garments
and leads his ministers to weep,
then afterward make offerings,
the river will flow again."
When Bó Zūn arrived,
the ruler asked him,
and Bó Zūn followed the driver's words, after which the river flowed.
When Confucius heard of this, he said:
"Bó Zūn,
did he not claim credit?
He appropriated another's good idea."
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn
(In the Zuǒ Zhuàn, he is called Bó Zōng.)
causing calamity
King Zhāo of Chǔ fell ill,
and divination indicated:
the River God was causing the affliction.
The ministers requested to offer sacrifices in the suburbs.
The king said: "The Three Dynasties mandated sacrifices
should not exceed one's own rivers—the Jiāng, Hàn, Suī, and Zhāng are Chǔ's proper rivers.
The Yellow River is not one for which I could have incurred offense."
Thus he did not perform the sacrifice.
Confucius said:
"King Zhāo understood the great principle.
It is fitting that he did not lose his state."
Zuǒzhuàn
Crying Purity
Fèi Zǐyáng said to Zǐsī:
"I think the Zhōu dynasty is about to perish,
and I cannot stop my tears."
Zǐsī replied:
"Indeed,
for one person to worry about the world's lack of order
is like worrying that the river is muddy and crying for it to be clear.
The 'Shīzǐ'
says that to worry about the chaos under heaven with our limited lifespan
is like worrying that the river will dry up and crying to add to it.
The 'Wénzǐ'"
Carrying a Stone
Shēntú Dí, not a general of his time,
threw himself into the river.
Cuī Jiā stopped him, saying:
"A sage is
the parent of the people.
Now, for the sake of getting your feet wet,
you would not save a drowning person—
is this acceptable?"
Shēntú Dí replied:
"In the past, Jié killed Guān Lóngfēng,
and Zhòu killed Bǐgān, leading to their downfall;
the state of Wú killed Wǔ Zǐxū,
and Chén killed Xiè Yě, leading to its destruction.
It is not that these states lacked sages,
but that their wisdom was not heeded."
Thereupon, he carried a stone and sank into the river.

Thus, Shēntú Dí drowned in the Yōng River,

losing his life while clutching the stone.

Falling into the water
When the Prime Minister of Liáng died,
Huìzǐ intended to go to Liáng.
While crossing the river, he suddenly fell into the water.
The boatman rescued him.
The boatman said:
"Where are you heading in such a hurry?"
He replied:
"Liáng has no prime minister,
I wish to go and become its prime minister."
The boatman said:
"You became helpless while aboard a boat;
without me, you would have died.
How can you become the Prime Minister of Liáng?"
Huìzǐ said:
"In managing boats and oars, I am not as skilled as you.
But when it comes to bringing stability to the state and preserving the altars of soil and grain,
compared to me,
you are as ignorant as a puppy that has not yet opened its eyes."

Jade Tablet
King Zhèng of Qín cast white jade discs into the river,

Filling the River
During the reign of Emperor Wén of the Hàn,
the Yellow River breached its banks,
and Suānzǎo's Jīndī collapsed.
In the Yuánguāng era, Emperor Wǔ breached the Hùzǐ,
whereupon the Son of Heaven approached the river and submerged a white horse and jade discs,
ordering all officials from generals downward to carry firewood to fill the river,
using bamboo from Qí Garden to construct barriers.
When the effort proved unsuccessful,
he composed a song saying:
When Hùzǐ breaches, what can be done?
Vast and boundless, villages are exhausted by the river.
The emperor asks Hé Gōng, why so unkind?
Ceaseless flooding brings sorrow to our people.
Nièsāng floats, Huái and Sì overflow,
Long without return, the water's restraint slackens.
The river surges, churning and rushing,
Northward crossing twists, swift currents hinder.
Lifting long reeds, submerging fine jade,
Hé Gōng consents, but firewood falls short.
Thereupon, Hùzǐ was finally blocked,
and a palace named Xuānfáng was built upon it.

Fish Dance

where he issued an edict stating:

the weather is clear and tranquil,
divine fish dance in the river,
and at the Wànsuì Palace, sacred sparrows gather in flight."

Dīfáng
In the fifth year of the Jiànshǐ era, the Yellow River burst its banks,
flooding Dōngjùn,
and four prefectures of Yǎnzhōu and Yùzhōu.
The Han historians, consulting charts and prognostications, determined that someone capable of continuing Yǔ's achievements
would be found in Zīyáng of Qiánkē.
They sought and found Wáng Yánshì,
summoned and appointed him as a River Dike Attendant.
He managed the river using bamboo cages,
four zhàng long and nine wéi in circumference, bound together,
small boats carrying small stones,
and in thirty-six days of management,
the dikes were completed.
The emperor praised him,
and changed the era name to Hépíng.
From "Records of Huáyáng"
Breaches and Flooding
During the reign of Emperor Āi,
Lǐ Xún advised Wáng Gēn, saying:
"Recently, there have been errors with mountains collapsing and the earth shaking,
and the river not following its proper course.
I request to summon Hán Fàng.
In 'Fàng's Understanding of Water',
the clerks Zhōu Chǎng and Wáng Wàng can be consulted on this matter.
He further submitted a memorial stating:
'Among the Five Elements, water is fundamental,
its stars are Xuánwǔ and Wùnǚ,
which mark the order of heaven and earth,
and the source of all beginnings and endings.
Water serves as the standard of balance,
and the Kingly Way is just and upright.
When cultivated and enlightened, all rivers are regulated,
and their networks flow freely;
but when partiality and factionalism lose their guiding principles, they surge and overflow, leading to disaster.
The 'Book of Documents' says:
'Water is called moistening,'
and the lower yin moves while the humble do not lose their way.
When the world follows the Way, the River gives forth the Diagram,
and the Luo produces the Writing.
Therefore, breaches and overflows of the Yellow and Luo Rivers are the most significant events.
'Records of the Hàn Dynasty'"
Lú Dī
Wáng Zūn of Zhuōjùn, having moved from the post of Governor of Yìzhōu to Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn,
encountered a great overflow of the Yellow River,
which flooded Hùzi,
completely breaching the entire embankment.
Zūn personally led the officials and commoners,
cast in a white horse as a sacrifice,
and prayed to the river god Hé Bó.
Holding a jade tablet in his own hands,
he offered to sacrifice himself at the embankment,
dwelling in a hut atop it.
Though the officials and commoners all fled,
Zūn stood firm without moving,
and the floodwaters halted just at his feet.
Both the court and the public admired his courageous integrity.

to benefit nine li

Hé Qīng
In the ninth year of the Yánxī era of Emperor Huàn, in Jìyīn and Dōngjùn,
the Yellow River at Píngyuán in Jǐběi ran clear,
and Lí Kuǐ submitted a memorial stating:
The Spring and Autumn Annals' records contain no instance of the river clearing,
yet now it has occurred.
The Yì Qián Záo Dù states:
When Heaven is about to bestow auspicious signs,
the Yellow River clears first.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn says:
When the Yellow River clears,
the world will be at peace.
Now Heaven sends down ominous signs,
the earth spews forth portents,
and the people suffer plagues—
these three occur simultaneously,
yet the river has cleared.
The river represents the feudal lords,
and clarity is an omen of brightness;
could it be that the feudal lords alone have designs on the capital?
The following year, the emperor passed away,
and the Marquis of Xièdú was summoned to succeed the Hàn line,
becoming Emperor Líng.
The Continued Hàn History
records the river clearing once every thousand years.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn
states the Yellow River clears once every thousand years,
a great auspice of the sage.
The Shí Yí Jì
says when the Yellow River clears, a sage is born.

Against the Current
Liáng Jì monopolized governance,
heaven manifested anomalies,
the river water flowed backward,

Water,

when stagnant and flowing backward,

Long and leisurely

Dài Yánzhī's "Records of a Western Expedition" states:
Shǎnchéng County to the south leans against the mountains and plains,
to the north it faces the Yellow River,
with hanging waters over a hundred ren high,
those approaching it are all filled with awe and caution.
To the northwest, the river water surges up,

when the Jìn army was about to arrive,

gurgling with sound,

according to the great river Hong is a massive watercourse,

the rushing currents and long river with huge waves,

the reason this water gathers into waves,

Shěn Bì
During the Jiànwǔ era of the Hàn dynasty, a pontoon bridge was built at the ford,
using stones for the central piers.
However, stones of any size would immediately be washed away by the current,
requiring immense labor and resources,
yet the project remained unfinished for a year.
Shí Hǔ personally inspected the site,
and had the artisans cast a jade disc into the river as an offering.
The next day, the disc was found washed up on a sandbar,
its waves lapping against the shore.
Thereupon, he executed the chief craftsman and departed.
Above.
Ode to the River's Clarity
During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
both the Yellow River and the Jì River ran clear,
which was considered an auspicious omen at the time.
Bào Zhào composed a "Eulogy for the Clear River" with the preface stating:
When the year's celestial position aligns with the northwest and the moon traverses the Green Path,
the long Yellow River and mighty Jì River,
though from different sources, become equally clear,
their pure waves filling countless valleys,
their clean ripples stretching a thousand miles.
From "Biography of Yìqìng in the Book of Sòng"
the eulogy reads:
Clear sources from the Kunlun Mountains,
mirror-like flows from the Onion Mountains,
springs and rocks settle sediment,
water palaces become pure and smooth.
Tsunami Order
After Èrzhū Róng's death,
his nephew Èrzhū Zhào led light troops, doubling their speed to launch a surprise attack on the capital.
Previously, someone by the river dreamed of a deity saying:
"The Èrzhū family wants to cross the river,
and will use you as the ferry wave officer.
You shall shrink the water veins for them."
Over a month later, the dreamer died.
When Zhào arrived,
a passerby claimed to know where the water was shallow,
marking the way by inserting grass stalks along the route.
Suddenly, he disappeared without a trace.
Zhào then whipped his horse and waded across.
That day, a violent storm raged fiercely,
yellow dust blotted the sky,
cavalry knocked on the palace gates,
and the guards only then realized the danger,
fleeing in disarray.
Emperor Zhuāng stepped out of Yúnlóng Gate,
where he was captured by Zhào's cavalry.
"History of the Northern Dynasties"
Sacrifice to Hé Bó
In Later Wèi, Gāo Áng served as the Grand Governor of the Southwestern Circuit.
He went directly to Shāngluò to make an offering to the River Earl,
saying:
"The River Earl is a deity of the waters,
Gāo Áocáo is a tiger on land.
As I pass by your domain,
I therefore make this libation to you."
(Book of Northern History)
Líng Yuán
In the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
the River was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lingyuán.
The Tōngdiǎn
prayer text states:
O Spirit, you ascend to the Milky Way,
illuminating and revealing charts and writings,
dividing and guiding the nine branches,
moistening the land for a thousand miles around,
as the pure autumn marks the season,
we follow the established rites.
We offer this sacrifice.
Vast and magnificent
At the beginning of Emperor Dàizōng's reign,
the Tǔbō invaded Biàn Bridge.
When the emperor traveled to Shǎn, there was often purple qi like a canopy,
welcoming his horse's head.
Upon returning to Tóng Pass, he sighed and said:
"The river waters surge vast,
escorting me eastward."
When the emperor reached Shǎn,
he gazed upon the iron oxen,
and suddenly said to his attendants:
"When I was fifteen or sixteen,
there was a nun in the palace called Gōngdé Shān,
who repeatedly patted my back and said:
'When disaster strikes the world,
you will return upon encountering an ox.'
Now I have seen the ox,
so I shall return."
From "Dūyáng Zábiān"
Hé Dú's In-Laws
Guó Fényáng guarded Pú,
intending to build a floating bridge,
but the swift current destroyed the foundation.
He offered wine and promised to give his young daughter in marriage to the river god,
that evening the water receded,
wood stood on the foundation and thus formed a bridge,
but his young daughter soon died and was enshrined in the temple,
people therefore built a shrine for him,
calling him the River God's Father-in-Law.
"Qián Zhuàn Zǐ"
Dredge and guide
Xuē Píng began to harness the river,
which overflowed east of Páozi,
flooding within merely two li of Huá City before being controlled.
Investigating the old course, he found it emerged southwest of Líyáng,
so he ordered his assistant Péi Hóngtài to request permission from Tián Hóngzhèng, military governor of Wèibó,
who granted it.
He then registered the farmland that would be affected,
exchanging it for other land,
dredged twenty to thirty li,
to divert the water in a winding course,
reclaiming seven hundred qǐng of riverside land south of the river,
from then on, the people of Huá were free from disaster.
"History of the Táng Dynasty"
Shěn Zhào
Lǐ Yànzuǒ was in Cāngjǐng,
when in the ninth year of the Tàihé era, an edict summoned the Fúyáng troops to cross the Huáng Hé.
It was then winter, the twelfth month,
and they reached Jǐnán Commandery.
They were ordered to break the ice to advance the boats,
but the ice struck the boats, causing them to capsize,
and the edict was lost.
Yànzuǒ was alarmed and fearful,
ordering that if the edict was not retrieved from the river, all would be put to death.
The officials were terrified,
and together requested that he offer prayers to the river,
hoping that by showing reverence and making offerings, it could be recovered.
Yànzuǒ then ordered the preparation of ceremonial wine and prayers,
sending words to interrogate the river.

The Wèi garrison at Shòuyáng gradually relocated,

"The Holy Mother oversees the people,
eternally prospering the imperial enterprise."
Táng Guótài of Yōngzhōu then memorialized that it had been obtained from the Luò River,
which greatly pleased Wǔ Zétiān.
She named the stone the Precious Diagram,
and in the seventh month, renamed the Precious Diagram as:
"The Heaven-conferred Sacred Diagram."
The Luò River was renamed Yǒngchāng,
its deity was enfeoffed as Marquis of Manifest Holiness,
fishing was prohibited,
and sacrifices were made equal to those for the Four Great Rivers at its source,
named the Sacred Diagram Spring.
Yǒngchāng County was established beside the spring.
In the twelfth month, Wǔ Zétiān personally worshipped at the Luò River,
receiving the Heaven-conferred Sacred Diagram.
An altar was built north of the Luò River,
to the left of the central bridge, where the crown prince,
all attending from within and without,
civil and military officials, and chieftains of barbarian tribes stood according to their positions,
with rare birds and extraordinary beasts arrayed before the altar.
After the ceremony, she returned to the palace.
Elders erected a stele in front of the worship altar at the Luò River,
titled "Commemoration of the Heaven-conferred Sacred Diagram."
In the fifth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Left Rectifier of Omissions Lǚ Lǚbīng petitioned for its destruction.
"Old Records and Annals"
Constructing defenses
Lǐ Shìzhī served as Governor of Hénán.
Emperor Xuánzōng was troubled that the Gǔ and Luò Rivers flooded annually, depleting corvée labor.
He ordered Shìzhī,
using treasury funds to construct three great embankments called:
Shàngyáng Jīcuì,
Yuèbēi Zìshì.
From then on, the waters ceased to cause disasters.
"Book of Táng"
The five colors
The virtue of the emperor flourished in response to the Luo River,
first warm for nine days,
then cold for five days,
transforming into five colors of mysterious yellow.

Yùshí
At the bottom of the Luòshuǐ there is yùshí,
therefore there is no ice on the surface.
"Shù Zhēng Jì"
Fúfēi,
the daughter of Fúxīshì,
drowned in the Luò River and became a deity.

Bā Liú
The eight streams also originate from famous mountains,
the Wèi River from Niǎoshǔ Mountain,
the Hàn River from Bōzhǒng Mountain,
the Luò River from Xióng'ěr Mountain,
the Jīng River from Shǎoshì Mountain,

Sān Chuān Bā Shuǐ
The Jīng, Wèi, and Luò Rivers are the three major rivers of Guānzhōng,
the Jīng, Wèi, Bà, and Chǎn,
the Láo, Jué, Fēng, and Hào,
are the eight rivers of Guānzhōng.
"Records of Guānzhōng"
states that during the Qín and Hàn dynasties when the capital was at Xījīng, the Bà, Chǎn, Fēng, and Láo rivers
were not listed among the great rivers, nor were the Jīng and Wèi,
but because they were near Xiányáng, they all received sacrifices comparable to those of great rivers.
"Book of Hàn"
records an edict from the ninth year of the Tiānbǎo era which said:
"The five materials are all utilized, especially manifesting the supreme spirits,
the eight rivers flow separately, truly praised for their beneficial uses.
The capital's rich soil,
the royal domain of Qín's territory,
where the Bà and Chǎn connect with the Jīng and Wèi,
and the Láo and Jué converge with the Fēng and Hào,
storing and releasing clouds and rain,
nourishing and cultivating crops,
it is appropriate to order the preparation of rituals for offering sacrifices,
ensuring the presentation of pure and clean offerings."

hú,

Tàihú
In Lake Tài there are the large and small Lěi mountains,
also called the Three Mountains Lake,
and also known as Lake Dòngtíng.

Its head is at Wúxī,
its feet tread at Sōngjiāng,
bearing Wúchéng on its back,
embracing Tàiwú at its chest, towering and lofty,

The large and small Lěi mountains,

Wǔhú
The Rites of Zhōu:
Yángzhōu's irrigation source is the Five Lakes.
An irrigation source is
that which is relied upon for irrigation.
The Five Lakes are also called Jùqū,
and because they have five distributaries, they are called the Five Lakes.
They are also called Zhènzé,
and also Lìzé.
Zhàng Bó's Wú Lù:
The Five Lakes
are another name for Tài Hú.
Because it extends five hundred lǐ in circumference,
covering thirty-six thousand qǐng,
it is therefore named the Five Lakes.
Yú Fān said:
Tài Hú has five channels.
Lù Guīméng said:
Tài Hú receives the energy of the Xiánchí above,

Donating the Pearl
Shùn discarded gold on the Zhǎnyán Mountains,
cast away pearls and jades into the springs of the Five Lakes,
to block the paths of depravity and excess.
"New Discourses by Lù Jiǎ"
Shùn then ordered Yǔ to dredge the Three Rivers and Five Lakes.
"Huáinánzǐ"
Opening Lakes
The kings of the Xià people dredged the Five Lakes.
Guǎnzǐ
Yǔ regulated the world,
making the Jiāng and Hàn rivers in the south,
and the Huái and Rǔ rivers flow eastward,
pouring into the Five Lakes.
Mòzǐ
Yǔ connected the Three Rivers and Five Lakes,
cut through the Yīquē gap and channeled the waters,
directing them overland to the Eastern Sea,
utilizing the power of water.
Lǚlǎn
In Yǔ's time, the world suffered great floods,

dredged the river to guide it through nine branches,
cut through the Jiāng to open nine routes,
opened the Five Lakes and stabilized the Eastern Sea.
Huáinán

Yǔ cut through the Jiāng to connect with the nine tributaries,
channeled the Five Lakes and stabilized the Eastern Sea.

The state of Sānmiáo,

Annals of Jīngzhōu
A small boat
Wǔ Zǐxū remonstrated with the King of Wú:
"Is it not Yuè that contends with us for the benefits of the Five Lakes?"
After Yuè was destroyed,
Fàn Lǐ of Wú then took a small boat and roamed the Five Lakes.
"Guóyǔ"
When Gōu Jiàn destroyed Wú,
he said to Fàn Lǐ:
"I shall share the state with you and we shall possess it together."
Lǐ replied:
"The ruler carries out commands, the minister follows his will."
He then took a small boat and floated away on the sea,
never to return.

Liàndú
King Wú toured Five Lakes,
passing through Liàn Ditch and said:
This water is as pure and white as silk,
reflecting the sky in its embrace,
hence named Liàn Ditch.
From "Sēng Wénjiàn's Record of Dòngtíng"
Wǔzhǔ
The "Strategies of the Warring States" states:
Qín fought with Jīng,
greatly defeated it,
and captured Dòngtíng and Wǔzhǔ.
The "Records of the Grand Historian" states:
Qín rode the current down the Hàn River,
arriving at Wǔzhǔ in four days.
Péi Yǐn's annotation:
Wǔzhǔ is in Dòngtíng Lake.
The city fell
Yóuquán County,
was Chángshuǐ County during the Qín dynasty.
During the reign of Qín Shǐ Huáng, a children's rhyme said:
"When the city gate bears blood,
the city will sink and become a lake."
An old woman heard this,
and worried, she went to spy on the city gate every morning.
The gate guards wanted to bind her,
but the woman explained her reason.
After the woman left, the gate guards killed a dog
and smeared its blood on the gate.
When the woman went again,
she saw the blood,
fled, and dared not look back.
Suddenly, a great flood rose, nearly submerging the county.
The registrar ordered a clerk to report to the magistrate,
who said:
"Why have I suddenly become a fish?"
The clerk replied:
"Your Honor has also become a fish."
Thus, it sank and became a lake.
From Shén Yì Zhuàn.
Huáinánzǐ states:
"The capital of Lìyáng
turned into a lake in one night."
Annotation:
Lìyáng,
a state name in Huáinán,
once had an old woman who often practiced benevolence and righteousness.
Two scholars passed by
and told her:
"This state will sink and become a lake.
When you see blood on the threshold of the eastern city gate,
flee to the mountains,
and do not look back."
From then on, the woman repeatedly went to inspect the gate.
The gate officer asked her,
and the woman answered truthfully.
In the evening, the gate officer killed a chicken and smeared its blood on the gate.
The next morning, the woman went early, saw the blood, and fled to the mountains.
The state sank and became a lake.
Longmù
Lóngmù Lake,
the King of Qín traveled east to survey the terrain and said:
There is an imperial aura here,
so he ordered convicts in red garments to dig through the long ridge in the lake,
cutting it open,
and subsequently renamed it Dāntú,
now the water flows north into the river.
"Records of Jīngkǒu"
in Rùnzhōu, there is a lake called Lóngmù Lake by the dam,
Jīngkǒu produces fine wine,
and its people are skilled in warfare,
thus Huán Wēn said:
Jīngkǒu has barren land and impoverished people,
with nothing to be attached to,
only the wine is drinkable,
and the soldiers are usable.
"Records of the Commanderies and States"
Raw wild rice stems
Gu Āng of Kuàijī lost his father in his youth,
and served his mother with utmost filial piety.
His mother was fond of eating wild rice stems,
so he often led his children to personally gather them and bring them home.
He channeled water, dug streams, and cultivated the rice himself to provide for her,
often having a surplus in storage.
His home was also near Lake Tài,
where wild rice later grew naturally in the lake,
with no other weeds remaining,
and insects did not dare approach the area.
Thus, he was able to use it for sustenance.
The commandery and county authorities honored his household.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Jìnghú
In the fifth year of the Yǒnghé era of Emperor Shùn of the Hàn dynasty,
Mǎ Zhēn, the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī, established Mirror Lake.
He built a dike between the two counties of Kuàijī and Shānyīn to store water,
which was over ten feet high,
and the fields were also over ten feet higher than the sea.
When water was scarce, the lake was drained to irrigate the fields;
when there was excess water, it was released from the lake to drain the fields.
The moderate water flowed into the sea,
ensuring there were no years of famine.
The dike and embankment stretched 310 lǐ in circumference,
irrigating 90 qǐng of fields.
At the beginning of its construction, many tombs and houses were flooded,
and over a thousand people filed complaints against Mǎ Zhēn with the authorities.
Consequently, he was executed in the marketplace.
When the authorities dispatched envoys to investigate, they found no one,
and upon checking the records, all were names of people who had already died.
"Records of Kuàijī"
The Southern Lake of Shānyīn winds around the suburbs,
with clear waters and verdant scenery,
and the cliffs reflect each other brilliantly,
as if painted in a picture.
"Geographical Records"
The lake opens
Before Wú fell,
in Línpíng Lake of Wújùn,
it suddenly opened by itself one day.
Stones were found by the lake,
inside a stone box was a small green stone,
carved with the characters for "Emperor."
It was traditionally said that when Línpíng Lake is blocked,
the world is in chaos; when it opens,
then there is peace under heaven.
The people of Wú considered it a favorable omen.
Soon after, Wú perished,
and later Emperor Yuán of Jìn rose in Jiāngzuǒ.
The "Book of Sòng" records
that during Huán Xuán's rebellion,
the lake water turned red,
glowing like cinnabar.
The "Record of Qiántáng"
Great Peace
Chén Xùn studied astronomy in his youth.
During Sūn Hào's reign,
when the Qiántáng Lake opened,
some claimed it meant peace would reign under heaven,
and the green-canopied carriage would enter Luòyáng.
Hào asked Xùn about this,
to which he replied:
"Your subject can observe celestial signs,
but cannot interpret the opening or closing of lakes."
After withdrawing, he told his friend:
"The green-canopied carriage entering Luòyáng
will involve carrying coffins and holding jade in the mouth—
this is not an auspicious sign."
(Book of Jìn)
Bāqiū Lake
As the military governor of Jīngzhōu,
he was cherished by the people of the Jiāng and Hàn regions,
who honored him as Father Dù.
Previously, the only water route was via the Miǎn and Hàn Rivers to reach Jiānglíng,
with no passage for over a thousand lǐ,
and Lake Bāqiū,
the confluence of the Yuán and Xiāng Rivers,
formed a natural barrier with its surrounding mountains and rivers,
making it a stronghold relied upon by the Jīngmán tribes.
Dù Yù then opened the Yángkǒu passage,
diverted the Xià River,
reaching as far as Bālíng,
creating a drainage system spanning over a thousand lǐ,
which connected the perils of the Chángjiāng externally to the waterways of Líng and Guì.
The southern people sang of him:
"No rebellions in later times, thanks to Elder Dù,
who recognizes wisdom's fame and valor's deeds?"
From the "Book of Jìn":
East of Huáróng County lies the Yúnmèng Marsh,
also known as Lake Bāqiū,
the great marsh of Jīngzhōu.
From Liú Chéngzhī's "Records of Jīngzhōu."
Qū'ē
Xiè Wàn passed by the Qū'ā Rear Lake,
and asked his attendants, "What body of water is this?"
They replied:
"It is Qū'ā Lake."
Xiè said:
"It naturally gathers and pools deeply,
collecting and storing without flowing away."
"Shì Shuō"
records that Qū'ā was originally named Yúnyáng.
Qín Shǐhuáng, because the area had royal aura,
had Běikēng Mountain excavated to break its potency,
cut its straight path to make it winding,
hence the name Qū'ā (Crooked Slope).
During the Wú period, it was restored to Yúnyáng,
but is now again named Qū'ā.
"Tàikāng Dìjì"
notes that Dāntú has Gāolí Mountain.
Legend says a woman from the former Gāolí kingdom came here,
and the East Sea deity arrived by boat with wine to court her.
The woman refused,
whereupon the sea deity overturned the boat, spilling the wine,
which flowed into Qū'ā Lake.
Thus, Qū'ā wine is renowned for its excellence.
"Yǔdì Zhì" states:
Qū'ā produces famous wines,
all said to be brewed from the Rear Lake's water,
hence its mellow and strong character.
Now, examining the lake water, it is fed by streams from Dāntú, Gāolí, Fùchuán Mountain, and Mǎlín Creek, with water that is clear
and tastes sweet.
"Huányǔ Jì"
Throw into the lake
Chǔ Gōng was traveling on Qǔ'ē Lake,
when a sudden fierce wind arose on the rear lake,
causing the boat to capsize.
Chǔ Gōng, already drunk,
then said:
"None of the people on this boat have done anything to incur Heaven's wrath,
except that Sūn and you, sir, have much worldly dust;
this should suffice to appease Heaven's desires."
He then wanted to seize Sūn and throw him into the water.
Sūn, terrified,
had no plan,
and could only shout loudly:
"Jìyě, have regard for me!"
From "Yǔ Lín".
The "Imperial Readings" notes separately:
"Chǔ Gōng"
refers to Chǔ Yànhuí.
"Jìyě"
is Yànhuí's courtesy name.
According to the "History of the Jin":
Chǔ Póu's courtesy name was Jìyě.
The "History of the Southern Qi":
Chǔ Yuān's courtesy name was Yànhuí,
separated by one hundred and twenty to thirty years.
Yet to take Póu's courtesy name as Yuān's courtesy name,
what is the reason for this?
Lìtáng
Wǔchāng's South Lake connects to Jiāngxià,
where the water dries up in winter,
and at that time nothing was produced there.
Grand Commandant Táo built a dike to hold back the water,
making it constantly full without drying up.
He then brought fish and water chestnuts from Lángyá Commandery across the lake,
and placed them in the lake.
The water chestnuts became very sweet and delicious,
different from others,
so the crucian carp produced there grew to three chǐ in length.
"Records of Wǔchāng"
also calls it Five Zhàng Lake.
"Gazetteer"
Seeking the Lake
The Governor of Kuàijī, Mèng Yǐ, served the Buddha with utmost devotion,
but was looked down upon by Xiè Língyùn.
East of the city wall lay the Huízhǒng Lake,
and Língyùn requested to drain it for farmland.
Emperor Tàizǔ ordered the local authorities to inspect the matter.
This lake was close to the city walls,
a source of aquatic resources,
and the common people cherished it.
Yǐ firmly refused to grant it.
Since Língyùn could not obtain Huízhǒng,
he then sought the Pīhuáng Lake in Shǐníng as farmland from Yǐ,
who again adamantly refused.
Língyùn claimed that Yǐ was not acting for the people's benefit,
but merely feared that draining the lake would harm many lives,
and spoke slanderously to damage his reputation.
Thus, he and Yǐ became bitter enemies.
"Book of Sòng"
Qīnglín Hú
Emperor Míng of Sòng dispatched Shěn Yōuzhī on a western campaign,
Zǐ Xún attacked the stockade at Qīngshān,
where he saw a youth of exceptional beauty,
who said:
"By the end of the decade, this campaign shall be pacified here."
Why did he suddenly vanish?
Hence it was called Qīnglín Lake.
The lake contains crucian carp,
eating them is rich and delicious,
providing refuge from cold and heat.
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Gāoshā Hú
Gāoshā Lake lies on Méihuí Islet,
its emerald expanse smooth and gleaming,
stretching wide over water and land,
where water caltrops and lotuses flourish in abundance,
and fish and fowl multiply in plenty.
South of the lake, the woods and fields are clear and open,
fit for dwelling and reliance,
thus the recluse scholar Zōng Bǐng once made his home here.
To the north, a small stream
flows from the lake to the river,
known as Zēngkǒu.
From "Jīngnán Records"
Huángdūn Lake
In Huángdūn Lake of Shè County there was a clam,
which often fought with the clam of Lǚ Lake.
Chéng Língxiǎn was brave and skilled in archery.
He dreamed that the clam transformed into a human and told him:
"I am being oppressed by the clam of Lǚ Lake,
if you can help me, I will surely repay you generously.
The one tied with a white silk ribbon is me."
The next day, Língxiǎn drew his bow and assisted it,
hitting the opposing clam directly,
which then disappeared without a trace.
Later people named that place Clam Beach.
At that time, a Daoist priest came to Língxiǎn's mother begging for food,
and after eating said:
"I've troubled you, mother, to provide food,
now I should find you a good burial site."
He had the mother follow him up the mountain,
and marked the spot with a white stone, saying:
"Burying here can bring sudden wealth and nobility."
Língxiǎn therefore moved his father's grave to that location.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
Língxiǎn led over ten thousand troops from his commandery and hometown to defend Xīn'ān,
and subsequently followed Emperor Wǔ of Chén,
achieving remarkable military successes.
When Emperor Wǔ of Chén received the abdication from Liáng,
Língxiǎn, as a meritorious official who assisted the founding,
together with Zhōu Wényù and Hóu Āndū, were called the Three Heroes.
"The Illustrated Classic"
also calls it Flood Dragon Lake.
"The Excellent Views of the Realm"
Xīyuàn Wǔ Hú
Emperor Yáng of Sui established sixteen gardens in the Western Park,
and excavated five lakes,
each lake covering forty square lǐ,
the eastern one called Cuìguāng Lake,
the western one Jīnguāng Lake,
the northern one Jiéshuǐ Lake,
the southern one Yíngyáng Lake,
and the central one Guǎngmíng Lake.
In the lakes, earth and stones were piled to form hills,
upon which palaces and halls were constructed,
winding and encircling,
all shimmering with crystalline blue,
reaching the pinnacle of worldly splendor.
"Record of the Labyrinth"
Shàn Chuān
Hè Zhīzhāng fell ill in the early Tiānbǎo era,
dreamed of visiting the imperial palace,
and awoke after several days.
He then requested to become a Taoist priest and return to his hometown,
which was approved by imperial decree.
He converted his residence into the Qiānqiū Temple and resided there,
further requesting several qǐng of Zhōugōng Lake to establish a pond for releasing living creatures.
An imperial decree granted him a winding section of Jìnghú and Shànchuān.
From the "Book of Táng"
Dānyáng Lake
Lǐ Bái once roamed Dānyáng Lake,
deeply enamored with its scenery.
He then set sail with wine, indulging freely in his comings and goings,
and composed a poem that reads:
"The lake merges with the primal ether,
its winds and waves vast and hard to still.
From beyond the sky, merchants return;
amid the clouds, a lone sail rises."
Records of Jīnlíng
Lángguān Hú
My old friend, the Minister Zhang Wei, was on a mission to Xiàkǒu.
The Governor of Miǎnzhōu, Dù, and the Magistrate of Hànyáng, Wáng,
hosted a banquet by the South Lake of the river city.
That night, the moonlight on the water was like silk,
its clear radiance almost tangible.
Zhang Wei felt particularly exhilarated.
Gazing around in transcendence,
he turned to me and said:
"Throughout history, many virtuous and eminent figures
have visited this lake, yet it has been neglected,
its fine scenery left obscure and unknown.
Could you, Master, bestow upon it an elegant name?"
I then raised my cup, toasted the water, and named it:
"Lángguān Lake."
Just as the Zhèng Garden has its Púshè Marsh.
From "The Collected Works of Lǐ Bái."
Gāntáng Lake
South of Xúnyáng in Jiāngzhōu lies the Gāntáng Lake.
In the second year of the Chángqìng era, Governor Lǐ Bó constructed sluice gates to regulate water storage and discharge.
"Records of the Táng Dynasty"
to water the horse
After Emperor Zhuāngzōng of the Later Táng destroyed the Later Liáng and Chǔ,
Mǎ Yīn sent his son Mǎ Xīfàn to the capital to present tribute,
and submitted the seal of commander-in-chief conferred by the Liáng court.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng inquired about the breadth of Lake Dòngtíng,
to which Mǎ Xīfàn replied:
"If Your Majesty's carriage were to tour the south, it would only be sufficient for watering horses."
Emperor Zhuāngzōng praised him for this.
From the Historical Records of the Five Dynasties.
Hòu Hú
North of Jīnlíng there is a lake,
several dozen lǐ in circumference.
The Mùfǔ and Jīlóng mountains encircle its west like a bell,
while the various peaks of Jiǎngshān rise steeply to its left.
Famous mountains and great rivers are set off against each other as if in a painting,
and many historical sites from the Six Dynasties period are located here.
Each year, the profits from water caltrops, lotus roots, and fishing nets
amount to no less than several tens of hundreds of thousands.
One day, while the various senior court officials were waiting for the morning audience at court,
the conversation turned to matters of forests and springs.
Among those present, Féng Mì mentioned Emperor Xuánzōng bestowing three hundred lǐ of Mirror Lake upon Hè Zhīzhāng,
truly considering it a grand affair.
He then said:
"I dare not hope for such a thing,
but if I were granted the Rear Lake, it would satisfy my lifelong desires."
Xú Xuàn replied in a gentle voice:
"Our sovereign esteems the worthy and humbles himself before scholars,
always acting as if he falls short.
Why would he begrudge a single Rear Lake?
What is lacking is another Hè Zhīzhāng."
Féng showed a greatly ashamed expression.
"Nán Táng Jìn Shì"
The Rear Lake is also called Xuánwǔ Lake,
Jiǎnglíng Lake,
Mòlíng Lake,
and Liàn Lake.
"Jīnlíng Zhì"
In the first year of the Bǎodǐng era of Sūn Hào of Wú,
a canal was dug north of the city,
channeling water from the Rear Lake,
which wound around the palace halls,
employing the utmost in craftsmanship.
In the third year of the Dàxīng era of Emperor Yuán of Jìn, the northern lake's long embankment was built,
to block the waters from the northern mountains,
extending east from Fùzhōu Mountain
to Xuānwǔ City in the west.
"Jiànkāng Shílù"
The lake was originally Mulberry Marsh; Emperor Yuán developed it into this lake,
and the Sòng dynasty used it to train naval forces.
Xú Yuán Shí Wèn
In the twenty-third year of the Yuánjiā era of Sòng, the northern dike of Xuánwǔ Lake was constructed north of Lèyóu Garden.
"Jì"
The emperor wished to erect the three divine mountains—Fāngzhàng, Pénglái, and Yíngzhōu—in the lake,
but Hé Shàngzhī firmly remonstrated, so the plan was abandoned.
"Běn Zhuàn"
In the twenty-fifth year of the Yuánjiā era, a black dragon appeared twice in Xuánwǔ Lake.

In the seventh year of the Dàshí era of Emperor Míng,
a grand naval review was held at Xuánwǔ.

Additionally, a large conduit was made beside the lake,
channeling water into the Tiānyuān Pond of Huálín Garden,
leading the various channels within the palace past the Tàijí Hall to the east,
and through the eastern and western side gates to fill the ponds south of the city.
Thus, the water in the various channels within the palace grounds constantly meandered without ceasing.
"Yǔdì Zhì"
Viewing Zhōngshān from the north is like viewing Lú Mountain from Gōngtíng Lake.
Emperor Wǔ of Qí drilled his naval forces here,
naming it Kūnmíng Pond.
Hence, Shěn Yuē's poem "Responding to Instruction at Zhōngshān" says:
"Gazing south at the Chǔxū Lodge,
looking west toward Kūnmíng Pond."
This refers to that very place.

"Yùlǎn" states:
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era, a dragon appeared in the lake,

There are three divine mountains in the lake.
The "Shìjì" mistakenly followed this account.
Dòngtíng Hú
South of Bālíng lies Qīngcǎo Lake,
encircling a hundred li,
where the sun and moon rise and set within it.
South of the lake is Qīngcǎo Mountain,
hence it is named after it.
Qīngcǎo Lake is also called Dòngtíng Lake,
and Dòngtíng is also known as Tài Lake.
The "Jīngzhōu Records"
state that on the western shore of Dòngtíng Lake, there are sandbars and mounds rising high,
specifically within the lake below Qīngcǎo Temple, there is this sandbar,
with the southern part named Qīngcǎo and the northern part named Dòngtíng,
referred to as the twin lakes.
The "Nánqiān Lù"
records that the Xiāng River flows north to Yuèyáng,
reaching the Shǔ River in Xià,
after flooding, the Shǔ River's rising momentum,
blocks the waves of the Xiāng River,
forcing them to retreat,
overflowing to form Dòngtíng Lake,
spanning several hundred li in width,
with Jūn Mountain seemingly floating in the water.
When autumn waters recede into the valleys,
this mountain returns to land,
leaving only the Xiāng River flowing through.
There was a chief bailiff surnamed Cài,
who playfully composed a poem.
He recited it to the monk Qíjǐ, saying:
How pitiful is Dòngtíng Lake,
just in time for deep winter to disappear.
Because it no longer formed a lake,
all the monks laughed at him.
The "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
notes that in autumn and summer, the waters of the western part of Dòngtíng Lake swell,
merging with Dòngtíng, but when they dry up,
only red sand is visible.
Old records say:
Dòngtíng connects to Qīngcǎo in the south,
stretching to Chìshā in the west,
spanning seven to eight hundred li, it is also called the Three Lakes.
The "Geographical Records"
state that the Lǐ River flows east and meets Chìshā Lake,
with the lake waters connecting to the river in the north and flowing south into the Lǐ,
known as the Breach.
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù"
Gōngtíng Lake
The temple deity of Gōngtíng Lake is extremely efficacious,
travelers passing through all pray to it,
as it can split the winds on the lake, allowing sails to go north and south.
"Jīngzhōu Records"
During the Later Hàn Dynasty, the temple on Lúshān Mountain had a deity
who would speak and drink with people from behind a curtain,
and by tossing a cup, could make Gōngtíng Lake split winds for ships,
so travelers raising their sails would meet.
When Luán Bā was appointed as the governor of Yùzhāng, within ten days of his arrival,
the temple deity ceased to make sounds.
"Biographies of the Immortals"
In the center of Pénglí Lake lies the great Gū Mountain,
according to "Records of Commanderies and States," Pénglí Lake
has a circumference of four hundred and fifty lǐ,
with a rock tens of zhàng high,
where the Great Yǔ carved inscriptions to record his achievements.
There are also begging birds that follow the boats,
and boatmen toss rice balls to feed them,
not missing a single grain, whether high or low.
"Jiǔjiāng Records"
Turning the helm to ride the tributary waters,
raising the oars to chase the split winds.
Poem by Liú Shān
Splitting the wind into two,
cleaving the current into pairs.

West Lake
West Lake in Hángzhōu originates from Wǔlín Spring,
with beautiful mountains and rivers,
and splendid scenery.
Since the Táng dynasty, it has been a renowned scenic spot for tourism in the southeast.
Records state:
In the second year of the Chángqìng era, Bái Jūyì served as the prefect of Hángzhōu,
and began constructing a dike to protect Qiántáng Lake,
storing and releasing its water to irrigate thousands of hectares of farmland.
Biography notes:
Releasing water for irrigation,
every inch of reduction could water fifteen hectares,
ensuring no years of famine.
Bái's "Record of West Lake"
states that when Bái Jūyì was prefect,
West Lake irrigated over a thousand hectares of farmland.
Later, the Qián family stationed a thousand soldiers to dredge the lake,
working day and night to clear it.
Dōngpō's description:
In spring, the lake resembles a painted scroll,
with chaotic peaks encircling the calm water.
Pines line the mountains like layers of emerald,
the moon dots the waves like a single pearl.
Early rice sprouts like green毯 threads,
new cattails unfold like a blue silk sash.
Unable to leave Hángzhōu behind,
half the reason to linger is this lake.
Bái's poem:
When Sūn Hé governed Qiántáng,
Liǔ Qīngqīng composed the poem "Gazing at the Tide" for him,
which included the lines: "fragrant osmanthus in late autumn,
lotus blooms spanning ten miles."
This poem spread to the Jīn ruler,
who, upon hearing it,
was stirred to plan a campaign to cross the river.
He sent painters secretly to Lín'ān,
to depict West Lake,
and displayed it on a soft screen,
adding his own image
on horseback atop Wú Mountain's peak,
inscribing it with:
"Why not unite all under one rule?
Could Jiāngnán remain a separate land?
Leading a million troops to West Lake,
I'll halt my steed on Wú Mountain's highest peak."
Xiè Chùhòu's poem remarks:
Who sang the ballad of Hángzhōu,
with ten-mile lotuses and autumn osmanthus?
Who knew these senseless plants
would stir the eternal sorrow of the Long River?
During the Shàoxīng and Chúnxī eras, the ruler and ministers indulged in pleasure,
obsessed with the lake and hills,
forgetting the tears of Xīntíng.
Thus, critics likened West Lake to a femme fatale,
comparing it to Xī Shī's role in destroying Wú.
Zhāng Zhìdào's poem laments:
Lotus and osmanthus bring endless grief,
recalling past glory by the river's bounds.
From Tiānmù Mountain, the lone phoenix rests,
as tides recede, six dragons depart.
Jiǎ Chōng's errors left no remedy for the world,
while Yǔ Xìn mourned the times with his verse.
Boast not of this supreme view to the Central Plains—
through ages, Xī Shī remains the eternal regret.
Tài Hú
East of Lake Tàihú,
during the Wú period, five hundred soldiers were stationed there.
When about to breach the dam,
they first offered wine and meat to pray to the gods,
vowing that the water would dry up.
That night, someone dreamed of a person saying the pond water would quickly drain,
and if they saw a giant-scaled fish,
they must not kill it.
There was also a bronze cauldron that should not be uncovered. The next day, they went to breach the dam,
and the water swiftly vanished.
They found a white fish of unusual shape,
but the greedy commoners,
cut it open and cleaned it,
only to see the previous day's sacrificial offerings filling its intestines.
Soon after, they retrieved the cauldron
and attempted to draw water again,
causing a sudden surge
that drowned all five hundred men at once.
Only the supervising officer survived,
and he recounted the entire incident.
To this day, the lake is still called "Five Hundred Marsh."
From "Yì Yuàn"
Yànquè Hú
Crown Prince Zhāomíng had a lapis lazuli bowl and a purple jade cup,
both bestowed upon him by Emperor Wǔ.
After his passing,
they were decreed to be placed in the imperial coffin,
but during a later reburial when the tomb was opened,
a eunuch smuggled them into a large vessel,
whereupon tens of thousands of swallows and sparrows attacked him,
leading to his capture by the authorities.
Thus, the two treasures were recovered,
and the Emperor, astonished upon hearing this,
decreed they be given to the Crown Prince's grandson.
During the resealing of the tomb,
tens of thousands of swallows and sparrows again brought earth to mound it higher,
and beside the tomb now lies a lake,
later named Yànquè Lake by people.
From "The Garden of Profound Mysteries"
Bàntāng Lake
In Jùróng County, there is Bàn Tāng Lake at Wú Dú Pond,
where half the lake water is cold and half is hot.
The hot part can boil chickens,
yet whenever fish swim into it, they die instantly.
"Yǒu Yáng"
Huāshù Lake
In Cíxī there is Huāshù Lake,
which was constructed by the people under the encouragement of Táng dynasty governor Rèn Yǎn.
Within it was a small villa,
where spring flowers were bright and lovely,
hence it was named accordingly.
"Illustrated Classics"
High ground in the water
In ancient times, when Yáo encountered a great flood,
people dwelled on high grounds amidst the waters,
hence it was called the Nine Provinces.
The Book of Songs says:
"On the isle in the river,"
but writing it as "洲" is incorrect.
According to the Shuōwén.
A continent formed from silt
The Fāngyán states:
A place in the water where one can dwell is called a zhōu (islet),

In the "Shànglín Fù," it is written:

Cānglàng Zhōu
Forty lǐ northwest of Wǔdāng County in the river lies Cānglàng Zhōu.
The Tribute of Yǔ states that the Hàn River flows east to form Cānglàng Zhōu,

Quèzhōu
Quèzhōu is located north of the county,
as recorded in the Zuǒzhuàn:
In the fifth year of Duke Zhāo,
Chǔ led the feudal lords to attack Wú,
and Wú defeated them at Què'àn.
According to research:
Quètóu and Quèwěi are eighty lǐ apart.

It is Wú territory,
with Quèwěi Zhǔ southeast of Shū County in Lújiāng.

notes that present-day Jūcháo is south of the river,

Parrot Islet
Yīngwǔ Zhōu is north of the county.
According to the Book of the Later Han:
When Huáng Zǔ served as Governor of Jiāngxià,
Huáng Zǔ's eldest son Shè hosted a grand gathering of guests,
and someone presented a parrot on this islet,
hence it was named after it.
Records of Jiāngxià
Cài Zhōu
Cài Mào of the Later Hàn dynasty, styled Déguī,
was a native of Xiāngyáng,
whose home was on Cài Island.
His residence was exceptionally fine,
with all four walls constructed of blue stone and corner joints,
and he possessed several hundred maidservants and concubines,
along with forty or fifty separate estates.
During the late Hàn period, the Cài family was at its peak of prosperity.
By the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
the household remained wealthy,
and the clan was very powerful,
uniting for mutual protection on the island.
However, they were defeated by the grass-bandit Zhāng Rú,
and the entire lineage was wiped out.
From "Xiāngyáng Qíjiù":
Chángshuǐ Colonel Cài Mào resided there,
hence the name Cài Island.
To the west of the island's large bank lies Huí Lake,
which holds water covering several dozen acres,
stretching several lǐ in length,
and narrowing to less than a hundred paces in width.
The water is always emerald green.
Yáng Yí lived in Upper Huí,
and Yáng Yóng lived in Lower Huí,
both opposite Cài Island.
From "Shuǐ Jīng"
Yúliángzhōu
In the Miǎn River there is Yúliáng Islet,
where Páng Dégōng resided.
Shìyuán lived on the north bank of the Hàn River,
south of the White Sands,
hence the place was called White Sands Bend.
Sīmǎ Décao's home was on the south side of the islet,
facing each other across the way,
their friendship naturally connected,
boating and wading through waters,
all spontaneously relaxed and pleasant.
Why wait to turn the rudder from a thousand miles away,
to offer deep feelings through constant longing?
Dǎnzhōu
Sūn Quán dispatched Wèi Wēn and Zhūgě Zhí with ten thousand armored troops to sail across the sea in search of Yízhōu and Dǎnzhōu, which were located in the ocean.
Elders passed down tales that Qín Shǐ Huángdì had sent the alchemist Xú Fú with several thousand young boys and girls into the sea,
to seek the mythical Pénglái Mountain and the elixir of immortality.
They settled on these islands and never returned,
generations succeeding one another,
until there were tens of thousands of households.
The people from there occasionally came to Kuàijī to trade cloth,
while residents of the eastern counties of Kuàijī, when sailing at sea,
also sometimes encountered storms and drifted to Dǎnzhōu.
The place was extremely remote,
making it ultimately unreachable,
so they only managed to bring back several thousand people from Yízhōu.

Fànzhōu
In Lóngyáng County, on Fànzhōu, Lǐ Héng, the governor of Dānyáng, planted sweet orange trees on it.

"In my home region, there are a thousand 'wooden slaves,'
which will not fail to provide you with clothing and food,
yielding a thousand bolts of silk annually."

Lièzhōu
The Geographical Records states:
Jiāngníng's Lièzhōu,
was formerly a Wú ferry crossing.
Within it were small waterways suitable for mooring boats,
and merchants often stopped there to avoid strong winds,
hence it was named accordingly.
Wáng Jùn moored here when attacking Wú,
and it was also the place where Jiǎnwén, while serving as chancellor, met Huán Xuán.
It was also called Lìzhōu,

Luógōngzhōu
Over a hundred paces west of Shixing City stands the Qixia Tower,
built by the Prince of Linchuan as a retreat for escaping the summer heat.
When Luo Junzhang resided there, it was named Luogong Isle.
Below the tower on the isle, fruit trees and bamboos cast interlaced shadows,
with tall poplars reflecting alongside,
and lofty parasol trees standing erect ahead.
Though situated within the city walls,
its charm rivals that of mountains and valleys.
"Records of Shixing"
Jiāzǐzhōu
The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Thirty States says:
In the second year of the Xianhe era of the Jin dynasty,
Wēn Qiáo and Táo Kǎn raised a righteous army,
to attack Sū Jùn,
leading forty thousand troops,
heading straight for Stone City.
Kǎn moored at Jiazi Isle,
where boats could anchor in summer,
but the water became shallow and dried up in winter.
Since the beginning of the Yongchang era,
the isle suddenly collapsed and sank for several li one morning,
following its shape to form nine bends in all,
which travelers relied on,
making the east and west sides appear vast and boundless.
Records of Dānyáng
Not even a hundred years old
West of Zhījiāng County extends to Shàngmíng in the east and Jiāngjīn,
within which lie ninety-nine islets.
A Chǔ proverb says:
"If the islets number not a full hundred,
then a true king shall not arise."
Huán Xuán, harboring ambitions to seize the throne,
artificially divided one islet into two,
forcing the count to a hundred in his usurpation.
Yet within a short time, he was slain and his clan exterminated.
Upon his downfall,
the added islet also vanished.
Later, when Emperor Wén of Sòng was still a prince,
a new islet suddenly emerged.
Indeed, he ascended the throne south of the Yangtze,
but this islet submerged again during the turmoil of the Crown Prince's revolt.
From "Jīngzhōu Records"
There is a shore in the water.
Yīn Zhòngcān was strolling by the riverside,
when he saw a floating coffin, which he retrieved and buried.
Within ten days, the ditch in front of his gate suddenly rose to form a bank.
That evening, someone visited Zhòngcān,
claiming to be Xú Bóxuán,
and said, "I am grateful for your kindness,
but have no way to repay it."
Zhòngcān then asked,
"What omen is the bank in front of my gate?"
The reply was:
"When there is a bank in water,
it is called a 'zhōu' (island),
and you will become a governor (zhōu)."
With these words, the visitor vanished.
Later, Zhòngcān indeed became the governor of Jīngzhōu.
From the Book of Jìn
Before the gate, an islet grows.
Zhāng Xìngshì lived by the Mian River,
from Xiāngyáng down to the great river for two thousand lǐ,
where there had never been any islets before.
When Xìngshì was first born,
an islet suddenly appeared one morning in the water before his gate,
growing gradually year by year.
By the time Xìngshì became a regional governor,
the islet had expanded to over ten qǐng.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Shìqiáo Shēngzhōu
During the Tàishǐ era of the Sòng dynasty, a small islet suddenly emerged at the market bridge in Yìzhōu.
The Dàoshi Shào Shuò saw it and said:
"A noble king will come to govern this province."
After the fall of Sòng, Wáng Shèngxǐ came to administer this province.
At the beginning of the Qí dynasty's Yǒngmíng era, military generals were no longer appointed to Yìzhōu.
They began appointing Prince Shǐxīng, Jiàn, as Governor of Yìzhōu,
supervising military affairs in both Yìzhōu and Níngzhōu,
with an additional military band.
Shèngxǐ's reversed pronunciation forms "Shǐxīng",
thus verifying Shào Shuò's prophecy.
End.

the place where Emperor Wǔ of the Liáng Dynasty released captive animals,
Later, when Lǐ Xié of the Northern Wèi came as an envoy,
Emperor Wǔ asked him:
"Does your country also release captive animals?"
Lǐ Xié replied:
"We neither capture nor release them."
The Emperor was greatly ashamed.

During Gǎo Jìchōng's time,
Lǐ Jǐngwēi said that according to old traditions, there were ninety-nine islets in various places of Jiānglíng,
and when they reached one hundred, a true king would arise.

Zhūyá Zhōu
Zhūyá is located in the great sea,
from afar Zhūyá Island appears as large as a mat,
sailing for one day and one night reaches the island,

its diameter is seven to eight hundred lǐ,
it can accommodate one hundred thousand households,
