"Wáng Yǐn Jìnshū"
Yùzhōu
In the northeastern sea, there is a large island called Yùzhōu,
which is the Yù Mountain in the sea mentioned in the Classic of Mountains and Seas.
It is said that this mountain moved here from Cāngwú,
and that southern plants still grow on the mountain.
Thus, Cuī Jìguī, in his account,
initially described Yùzhōu as the former Cāngwú Mountain,
and felt both delighted and puzzled by it.
Hearing that there was an immortal's stone chamber on it,
he went to see it,
where he found a Daoist living alone,
serenely silent, neither speaking nor laughing,
and realized he could not match him.
Water Classic
Ten Continents

Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, having heard Queen Mother of the West speak of the ten continents—Zǔzhōu, Yíngzhōu, Xuánzhōu, Yánzhōu, Chángzhōu, Yuánzhōu, Liúzhōu, Shēngzhōu, Fènglínzhōu, and Jùkūzhōu—located within the vast seas of the eight directions,
these ten continents,
are places rarely trodden by human footprints,
and knowing they were not ordinary worldly beings,
thus summoned her to a secluded chamber to personally inquire about the locations of the ten continents,
and recorded the names of all things there based on ancient writings.
"Records of the Ten Continents"
Gullies and Valleys
Sòng Jūn said:
A valley without water is called a gǔ,
one with water is called a xī.
The Qiánxī,
east of Wúchéng County, flows southeast into Lake Tàihú,
where it is called Fēngzhǔ.
Arrow bamboo grows densely along both banks of the stream.
The Hòuxī is located north of the market at Yúbùtíng.
Shěn Chōng, the Jin Dynasty Chariot and Horse General, resided by the Qiánxī,
and the Music Bureau includes the "Qiánxī Song,"
which was composed by Shěn Chōng.
Its lyrics read:
At dawn, before day fully breaks,
a hundred birds cry in haste.
Later, the young Emperor of the Song Dynasty continued with seven songs,
one of which says:
Worried, I step out the door,
and meet you, my love, at the Qiánxī crossing.
Do not be like flowing water,
drawing the new and abandoning the old.
From "Records of the World."
Wǔyúnxī
This is where Ōu Yězǐ cast swords,
below which lies a solitary deep and green pool,
with a lone rock towering above it.
Above the pool stands a large oak tree,
where Kè'ér and his younger brother Huìlián composed poetry and crafted verses,
carving them on the tree.
Táng official,
Vice Minister Xú Hào, visited and remarked:
"Zēngzǐ would not dwell near a lane named 'Victorious Mother,'
how could I roam Ruòyé Stream?"
Thus, he renamed it Wǔyún Stream.
From the "Records of Commanderies and States."
Rèngōng Xī
In Shè County there is Fǎng Village.
Local tradition says that when Rén Fǎng was governor of Xīn'ān,
he came here during a spring tour and fell in love with its cloudy stream,
following its source to seek seclusion,
remaining for days without returning.
The common people thus named the stream Fǎng Stream.
The village by the stream was called Fǎng Village.
Near the village there was a mountain close by,
so whenever stones fell from this mountain, it boded ill for the county magistrate of Běiyě County,
but after the county was abolished, these occurrences also ceased.
In the tenth year of the Dàzhōng era, Governor Lú Fān renamed them:
Lord Rén's Village,
Lord Rén's Stream.

Hǎoxī
Ten li east of Chùzhōu there is the Evil Stream,
with many water monsters.
During the reign of Emperor Xuānzōng, the prefect Duàn Chéngshì implemented benevolent governance,
causing the water monsters to disappear.
The people called it the Good Stream.

Wēn Liáng Èr Xī
Shānyīn Xiàn xī sìshí lǐ yǒu èr xī,
dōng xī guǎng yī zhàng jiǔ chǐ,

Bǎiguǎn Xī
Bǎiguǎn Creek, with a circumference of over a zhang,
has extremely turbulent waters,
surging like the sound of oil frying over a fierce fire.
From Pei's "Records of Guǎngzhōu"
Wǔ Xī
The Wūxī River originates from Wūshān,
flowing southeast into the Yuán River.
Hence, a song was composed:
"Deep, and deeper still is Wūxī,
where flying birds cannot cross,
and roaming beasts dare not approach."
From "Shàn Gē Lù"
Kāngwáng Gǔ
Mount Lú has a Kāngwáng Valley,
where in the past, Qín Shǐhuáng unified the six states,
and King Kāng of Chǔ hid here to evade capture, hence the name.
Inside, there is a Water Curtain Cave,
as Sòng dynasty's Wáng Yǔchēng briefly noted in his preface:
Kāngwáng Valley is the finest under heaven,
with a water curtain 350 zhàng high,
estimated to take nearly a month's journey to traverse.
Its flavor remains unspoiled,
when tea is brewed with it,
it appears like scattered clouds and snow,
vastly different from well or spring water.
Lù Yǔ left an inscription:
"It pours from thousand-ren cliffs,
and travels with the Jiǔjiāng boats."
The Comprehensive Gazetteer
records a fortress atop Kāngwáng Valley called Zhāo Fortress,
where whenever rain approaches, drumbeats, horns, flutes, and reed pipes are heard from the mountain,
the sound gradually reaching the fortress as wind, rain, and darkness converge,
a regular omen for the entire village.
Legend says this was the fortress of King Kāng of the Zhōu dynasty,
who loved the extraordinary and unusual,
touring famous mountains
and journeying far to reach this fortress.
He often obtained ancient artifacts, large tripods, crossbows,
gold and jade,
and the like,
indicating it was no ordinary person's dwelling.
Thus, the mountain bears King Kāng's name,
and the fortress is called Zhāo,
suggesting this tale may have evidence.
Records of Strange Events
(According to King Kāng of Chǔ during the reign of King Líng of Zhōu, the First Emperor captured was actually Fù Chú; this record contains a major error.)
Jīngǔ
Zǐzé is located thirty lǐ northwest of the royal city,
close to Jīngǔ.
According to the Yǔdìzhì,
Zǐzé is Jīngǔ,
where the Jīnshuǐ River originates,
hence it is called Jīngǔ.
The villa of Jìn dynasty's Shí Jìlún (Shí Chóng) was situated there.
The Jùnguózhì records,
"I have a separate residence within the boundaries of Hénán County,
in the Jīngǔ Ravine, with varying elevations, clear springs, and lush forests.
All kinds of fruits, bamboos, cypresses, medicinal herbs, and the like are fully available.
There are also water-powered trip-hammers, fish ponds, and earthen caves—everything to delight the eyes
and gladden the heart is provided."
At that time, Wáng Xǔ, the Army Advisor to the General of the West, was about to return to Cháng'ān,
and I, along with many worthy companions, escorted him to the ravine.
We feasted and toured day and night,
frequently changing our seating,
sometimes ascending heights to look down,
other times sitting in rows by the water's edge.
Lutes, zithers, reed pipes, and zhus were all carried together in the carts,
playing along the way.
When we stopped, they were ordered to play alternately with the military band.
Then, each composed a poem to express our innermost feelings.
Those unable to do so were penalized with three dǒu of wine.
Moved by the brevity of life
and fearing the uncertainty of its end,
I fully listed the titles, names, and ages of those present at the time.
I also wrote the poems afterward.
May later enthusiasts peruse them!
There were thirty people in total.
Shí Chóng's "Jīngǔ Poem Preface"
Xiè Gōng remarked that among those at Jīngǔ, Sū Shào was the most outstanding.
Shào was the brother-in-law of Shí Chóng,
and the son of Sū Yú, grandson of Sū Zé.
From the Shìshuō.
Dàgǔ
Five miles east of Gǒng County lies the Great Valley,
as Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital" states:
Mèngjīn extends behind it,
the Great Valley opens before it.
Prince Sī of Chén's "Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luò River" says:
passing through the Great Valley.
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on Living in Idleness" states:
the pears of Lord Zhāng's Great Valley,
all refer to this place.
The "Record of the Ten Circuits"
Yōu Qī Gǔ
Wéi Sìlì built a separate residence at Parrot Valley on Lí Mountain,
where the Emperor paid a visit and commanded
his attending officials to compose poems and create a preface.
The leading piece praised and favored him,
so consequently, Wéi Sìlì was enfeoffed as the Duke of Carefree,
and the place was bestowed with the names Clear Void Plain and Secluded Dwelling Valley.
"Records of the Hanlin Academy"
Lángjūn Gǔ
Wáng Guī accompanied his father to Hézhōng,
residing in Zhōngtiáo Mountain,
returning home to the prefecture once on the first and fifteenth days of each lunar month to pay respects,
earning the local name Lángjūn Gǔ (Valley of the Young Gentleman).
"History of the Táng Dynasty"
Wáng Guān Gǔ
Sīkōng Tú resided in Zhōngtiáo Mountain's Wáng Guān Gǔ,
at a time when bandits ravaged everywhere they passed,
yet they alone did not enter Wáng Guān Gǔ.
The
Jiǔjīn
Yǔ traveled east to the land where trees are entwined,
where the sun rises over the nine fords and the wilds of Qīngqiāng,
the villages of Bird Valley and Green Hill,
south to the surging waters,
floating by the mountains of Nine Suns,
west to the people who drink dew and inhale qi,
the mountains where gold accumulates,
north to the remoteness of the Summer Sea,
and atop Mount Héng,
the mountains of accumulated waters and stones,
never showing slackness or neglect.
"Lǚ's Annals"
Sānjīn
Gōu Jiàn entered Wú, and the King of Wú pardoned him, allowing his return to his own state.
Fàn Lǐ held the reins, arriving at the banks of the Sān Jīn,
where he looked up to the sky and let out a long sigh.
Tears streamed down, soaking his lapels, as he said:
Alas!
To endure such hardship and peril,
who would have thought I would live to cross this ford again?
"Annals of Wú and Yuè"
Dòu Jīn
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn traveled incognito to Bǎigǔ,
where he was humiliated at the Dòu family's gate,
yet was moved by the wife's insightful gift of provisions.
After returning to the jade steps of his palace,
he richly rewarded them.
He granted them control of the river crossing to operate the ferry—now known as Dòu Ford.
Thus, Pān Yuè wrote in "Rhapsody on a Journey West":
"The reward to the woman was already excessive,
how much more mistaken was the office given to her husband."
From the "Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Jūnzǐ Jīn
Between Yúnzhōng and Dìngxiāng there was a ford called Jūnzǐ.
When Emperor Huán of Hàn traveled west to Yúzhōng in the thirteenth year of his reign,
he journeyed eastward through the Dài region.
A wealthy merchant from Luòyáng, carrying gold and valuables, followed behind the emperor's procession.
One night, he lost his way
and went to seek help from the ferry chief, saying:
"Zǐfēng, escort him."
While crossing the river, the merchant suddenly died.
The ferry chief buried him.
Later, the merchant's son came searching for his father's remains.
When the grave was opened and the body exhumed,
the buried valuables were completely intact, not a single item missing.
The son offered all the gold to the ferry chief,
but the ferry chief refused to accept it.
When the matter was reported to the emperor, he declared:
"This is a true gentleman."
Thus, the ford was named Jūnzǐ Ford.
From the "Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Báimǎ Jīn
In the old Dōngjùn, at the Shénmǎ Tíng in Báimǎ County, there was a Shénmǎ Temple,
about twenty lǐ from the Báimǎ Crossing,
and approximately fifty lǐ southeast of the old Báimǎ County city,
which is the Báimǎ Mountain mentioned in the Kāishān Tú.
On the mountain, herds of white horses often roamed; when they neighed sorrowfully, the river would burst its banks,
and when they galloped, the mountain would collapse.
Above,
the river passes south of Líyáng County as the Báimǎ Crossing,
which Shí Lè named the Língchāng Crossing.

Qīng Wān
Qīngwān lies seven li southeast of the county seat.
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty, Governor Liáng Wénqiān assumed office
and drew water solely from this bay for his personal use to uphold purity.
Later generations, cherishing his virtue, named it Qīngwān (Clear Bay).
From "Records of Póyáng."
Bǎijiā Wān
Xú Wēn once returned from Yíngluán
and arrived at Bǎijiā Wān,
when a violent storm arose.
The boatmen looked at each other, their faces pale with fear.
Xú Wēn then stripped off his upper garment and tied his son Jǐng with a silk band,
turning his head to say to his concubines and attendants:
"I am a good swimmer.
If I drown,
I won't have time to save you.
Please protect this child."
As soon as he finished speaking, the wind and waves gradually subsided.
"Jiǔ Guó Zhì"
Báibì Wān
The Yuán River flows east past Lín,
west of Yuán County lies the Bright Moon Pool,
and White Wall Bay.
The bay is shaped like a half-moon,
with a clear, mirror-like pond,
where the sounds of wind echo emptily above,
and the gurgling of springs never ceases below.
Travelers all grasp their oars and play joyfully,
lingering with fond delight along the Yuán River.
Further east, it passes by the Three Stone Gullies,
standing evenly like a tripod’s legs,
elegant as if carved by nature,
beside which lush bamboo sways gracefully, truly delightful to behold.
Commentary on the Waterways Classic
Sānyuán Wān
The Sānyuán Pavilion in Yuèchéng County is one hundred and twenty lǐ from the commandery seat,
where the stream water is as clear as a mirror.
In the past, someone once caught a dead catfish here,
with fins as large as five or six arm spans around,
and a single fin alone could yield several tens of hú of pickled fish.
This bay can accommodate anything,
so there was a man with a great capacity for eating
who often compared himself,
saying his belly was like the Sānyuán Bay,
capable of holding anything.
Records of the Yǒngjiā Commandery
Nánpǔ
Nánpǔ is located three lǐ south of Jiāngxià County,
as stated in "Lí Sāo":
"Bidding farewell to the beauty at Nánpǔ."
Its source originates from Jīngshǒu Mountain and flows into the great river,
drying up in spring and winter while flooding in autumn and summer.
Merchants and travelers all moor their boats at this shore,
and because it lies south of the city walls, it is called Nánpǔ.
"Jiāngxià Jì" records:
"Seeing you off at Nánpǔ—
how sorrowful it is!"
From "Bié Fù."
Waterside
In Shàngyú County, there is a stone camel step by the water's edge, which is called a "bù,"
Guābù is located in Wúzhōng,
where people of Wú sold melons along the riverbank,
hence it was named after this.
In the river, there are Yúbù and Guībù,
and in Xiāngzhōng, there is Língfēi Bù.
According to records, in the regions of Wú and Chǔ, "pǔ" is referred to as "bù,"
likely due to a dialectal corruption.
"Shù Yì Jì"
Quicksand
The quicksand lies beyond the Yùmén Pass,
stretching two thousand lǐ from north to south,
and several hundred lǐ from east to west.
It has three sections known as the Three Ridges.
According to the "Guǎngzhì"
Shā Chéng
Cáo Cāo was campaigning against Mǎ Chāo,
separated by the Wèi River.
Lóu Zǐbó advised him:
"Now that the weather is cold, you can build a city with sand,
and by pouring water on it, it can be completed overnight."
From the "Biography of Cáo Mán"
Shācháng
In Wúfùchūn County, a river sandbar emerged,
and Wǔ Liè, as a commandery official, was heading to the prefectural office.
The villagers held a farewell banquet for him,
gathering on the sandbar.
The elders said:
"This sandbar is narrow and long—
you will later become the Grand Administrator of Chángshā."
It indeed came true, and thus it was named Sūnzhōu.
"Wú Lù Dìlǐ Zhì"
Shāmǐ
In Yuánzhōu there is a river,
where during spring, white sand resembling rice grains appears upstream,
stretching over ninety lǐ along both banks, called "rice sand."
If one bank is fully covered with this rice-like sand,
it indicates a bountiful harvest in that region.
Recorded in the Wáng Fú Jì.
Sand Mound
In Xīnchāng River there is a sand mound,
located fifty lǐ northeast of the county,
its shape resembling an overturned boat,
exceptionally clean and distinct.
Each year when the harvest is abundant, the sand accumulates as before;
if the sand shifts toward the bank,
that year will bring poor harvest.
Since ancient times, this has been passed down as a constant omen.
"Records of Póyáng"
Yùnǚ Shā
In Gōushì there is the Eight Winds Stream,
whose waters flow south to join the Three Crossings Water's bank.
There is sand, fine and moist, suitable for bathing,
which was often presented to the rear palace during the Suí dynasty,
mixed with fragrant herbs,
to serve as bean meal substitute,
named:
Jade Maiden Sand.
"Records of the Universe"
Shāmíng
When the weather is clear in Shāzhōu, the sand sings,
audible within the city walls.
It is also said that when people travel to the Sand Mountains, if they have few companions or have never been there before,
they become fearful,
and dare not proceed.
The sand sometimes collapses beneath one's feet,
but by the next day, it returns to the mountain on its own.
"Records of Old Héxī Affairs"
Míngshāshān is also known as Shénshāshān,
its peaks formed by accumulated sand,
steeper and more precarious than rocky mountains,
surrounded by sand ridges on all sides,
with backs as sharp as blades.
When people climb it, it sings,
collapsing under their feet,
yet after a night of wind, it restores itself to its original state.
"Yuánhé Annals"
There is a spring called Shājǐng,
enduring through ancient and modern times,
never filled by the sand,
with exceptionally sweet and clear water.
Shājiǎo Shān
West of the river stands Shājiǎo Mountain,
its peaks perilous and precipitous,
steeper than stone mountains.
Its sand grains are coarse,
yellow in color, resembling dried rice.
On the sunny side of the mountain lies a spring called Shājǐng,
enduring through ages past and present,
yet never buried by the sand.
Those wishing to ascend the peak must first descend into the cave,
where immediately the sound of drums and horns arises,
vibrating through one's feet.
"Records of Sān Qín"
Different Names
The beginning of water is called the source,
the source is called a spring,
one that emerges straight upward is called a threshold spring,
a spring that flows down from above is called a lower spring,
one that gushes out is called a gushing spring,
one that emerges from the side is called a side spring,
when springs emerge from the same place and return to the same place,
but differ, they are called abundant springs,
when different sources flow together, they are called converging springs.
"Erya Shizhu"
Lǐquán
Sweet Spring water is the essence,
its taste sweet like sweet wine,
it emerges when the ruler follows principles.
"Records of Auspicious Signs"
Shénnóng cultivated virtue and created the plow,
and the earth responded with Sweet Spring.
"Lǐ Hán Wén Jiā"
During Huángdì's time, Sweet Spring was used as a drink.
"Xú Zhěng's Calendar Correction"
Sweet means sweet,
named after sweet wine,
Yáo revered virtue without slackening,
Sweet Spring emerged,
Wén Mìng possessed abundant virtue,
with talented officials in government,
Sweet Spring emerged from the mountains.
"Shangshu Zhonghou"
During the prosperity of Chéng and Kāng,
Sweet Spring gushed forth.
"Chunqiu Mingli Xu"
"Yǔ's Basic Annals" states the Yellow River emerges from Kūnlún,
on which there are Sweet Spring and Jasper Lake.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
East of Mount Tài there is Sweet Spring,
its form like a well,
its substance is stone,
those wishing to draw water to drink must purify their hearts and kneel to scoop it,
then the spring flows like a stream,
the amount sufficient for use,
but if disrespectful, the spring retracts,
truly an extraordinary manifestation of the divine.
"Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Law"
Tàigōng Quán
Thirty li north of Jí County is Tàigōng Spring,
above which stands the Temple of Tàigōng.
Beside the temple, tall groves and elegant trees
compete in luxuriance, said to be the former residence of Tàigōng.
Northwest of the city, stones clamp the water,
where rapids fly swiftly and urgently.
People also call it Pán Creek,
claiming Tàigōng often fished here.
Tàigōng avoided the chaos of King Zhòu,
hiding from the market and court life,
retreating to fish in the waters.
Why must it be the banks of the Wèi River?
If it pleases the spirit, any winding shore will do.
The name Pán Creek
thus holds no impropriety.
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Dào Quán
Confucius arrived at Shèngmǔ County,
and though it was evening, he did not lodge there;
he passed by Dào Quán,
and though he was thirsty, he did not drink from it,
because he detested the names.
From "Shīzǐ":
The water named Dào Quán, Zhòngní did not drink;
the village named Shèngmǔ, Zēngzǐ adjusted his collar in respect.
From "Lúnyǔ Zhuǎnkǎo Chèn":
Dào Quán is located in Sìshuǐ County,
its source emerges from the northern side of Gāojìng Mountain.
From "Yuánhé Zhì":
Hot Spring
The hot springs of Líshān were traditionally said to be accessible only after offering sacrifices of three types of livestock,
capable of curing diseases and eliminating ailments.
Folklore recounts that Qín Shǐhuáng, while traveling with a goddess, offended her will,
whereupon the goddess spat on him, causing sores to appear.
Terrified, Qín Shǐhuáng apologized to the goddess,
who then released hot springs to wash away the affliction,
a tale later generations regarded as verification.
Records of the Three Qín
state that wherever a water source contains sulfur,
the spring will be warm,
some say warmed by divine beings,
and it primarily heals human illnesses.
Records of Broad Matters
note that the hot springs of Líshān were initially developed by Qín Shǐhuáng, who laid stones and erected structures,
and by the time of Hàn Wǔdì, they were further renovated.
Tales of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn Dynasty
Drawing Sword Spring
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn entered Péngchéng,
where he was once besieged by the forces of Chǔ in Xúzhōu.
The Hàn troops suffered from thirst and exhaustion,
so the emperor thrust his sword into the ground.
Upon drawing it out, a spring gushed forth,
and to this day, its waters never overflow,
nor dry up in drought.
Local people call it the Dragon's Pool.
Wǔ Quán
The Five Springs Water in Lánzhōu is at the foot of Gāolán Mountain,
with five spring eyes,
where waterfalls cascade down,
creating a gurgling sound pleasant to the ear.
Multiple streams converge into a creek,
providing extensive irrigation,
and it is commonly said that Huò Qùbìng struck the ground with his whip to bring them forth.
According to the "Records."
Jiǔquán
Fúlùchéng was built by Xiè Ài,
below which there is a golden spring with a taste like wine,
hence the name Jiǔquán (Wine Spring).
"Xīhé Jiùshì"
During the reign of Emperor Xuān of Hàn, a spring was opened whose water tasted like wine,
therefore it was used to name the county.
"Fāngyú Jì"
The golden spring emerges from several openings,
clear and bottomless.
"Yúnyáng Gōng Jì"
Someone drank from this spring water,
and saw a golden light shining from the mountain onto the water,
went and obtained gold, hence the name.
"Yōngzhōu Jì"
Tān Quán
Wú Yǐnzhī, styled Chǔmò,
was upright and of unsullied virtue.
Huán Xuán, wishing to remedy the ills of Lǐngnán,
appointed Yǐnzhī as Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
Twenty lǐ before reaching the province,
at a place named Shímén,
there was a spring called the Greedy Spring,
of which it was said that those who drank from it would be filled with insatiable desires.
When Yǐnzhī arrived there,
he said to his relatives:
"If one does not see what excites desire,
the mind remains undisturbed.
To cross a cliff and lose one's purity—
I understand this now."
Thereupon he went to the spring, scooped up some water and drank it,
then composed a poem:
"The ancients said of this water that a single sip makes one covet a thousand pieces of gold.
But if Bóyí and Shūqí were to drink it,
they would never change their hearts."
And when he was in the province,
his unsullied virtue became even stronger.
Jìn Shū
The waters of Shímén
are commonly said to pass through Dàyǔ, where pure and foul energies
separate; drinking from Shímén changes the nature of black and white.
This is the place where Wú Yǐnzhī scooped and drank.
Nányuè Zhì
When Yǐnzhī left his post,
he saw that his wife had a catty of aloeswood in her chest,
so he threw it into the waters at Shímén.
Later generations called it the Aloeswood Bank,
also known as the Casting Incense Bank.
Huányǔ Jì
The Héngliú Stream's water is very scant,
yet it never dries up in winter or summer.
Commonly regarded as the Greedy Spring,
those who drink from it become greedy for wealth and bribes,
similar to the greedy flow at Shímén in Guǎngzhōu.
If one is honest and upright as a two-thousand-bushel official,
one does not drink from it.
In the past, Yǐnzhī scooped it without declining;
how could it have muddled his true nature?
Rather, he detested its reputation.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù
Cōngmíng Quán
At the foot of Luòxīng Mountain in Xúnyáng County, there is the Five Pine Bridge.
In the past, Master Huìyuǎn and Yīn Zhòngkān once sat by the stream here discussing the Book of Changes,
when a spring gushed forth beneath the trees,
named the Spring of Intelligence.
According to the "Universal Geography,"
in Yǒngxīn there is also a Spring of Intelligence,
where water surges from the mountain.
Throughout history, scholars who drank from it often achieved success,
and the locals call it the Spring of Intelligence.
Xiàogǎn
Wáng Péng,
a native of Xūyí,
lost his mother in his youth.
In the early Yuánjiā era, his father also passed away.
His family was poor and he had little strength,
so when preparing for the burial, the villagers helped make bricks.
The bricks required water,
but during the drought, they dug a well several dozen zhàng deep
and found no water.
One day, a spring suddenly emerged in front of the brick kiln,
which they used until the task was completed, after which it dried up again.
The helpers marveled at this.
During the Yuánjiā era, their village was renamed Tōnglíng Village.
From Shěn Yuē's "History of the Sòng Dynasty"
Ān Jīncáng, a native of Cháng'ān,
served as Tàicháng Chéng.
When his mother first passed away,
he temporarily buried her north of the Dū'nán Quèkǒu
and built a hut beside the grave.
He personally constructed a stone tomb and stone pagoda,
working ceaselessly day and night.
Originally, there was no water on the plain,
but suddenly a spring gushed forth on its own.
From the "Táng History"
Tàijí Spring
In the seventh year of Dàmíng during the reign of Xiàowǔ of the Sòng dynasty,
an edict of pardon was issued stating:
"Reflecting upon the scattered springs of Tàijí,
to bless beyond measure.
The Zhì
by Hán Wénjiā states:
The spirits of the emperor's observatory,
grant blessings to all things from the boundless source,
summon the pure springs of Tàijí,
to nurture the roots of agriculture.
In the subsequent Lède Zhì annotation one,
the elixir includes the springs of the Tàijí well.
Yǒuyáng Zázǔ."
Mad Spring
Yuán Càn of the Sòng Dynasty once said to his associates:
There was once a kingdom,
in which a spring was called "Mad Spring",
and all who drank from it went mad.
Only the king, who drew water from a well he had dug,
remained unaffected.
Since all the people were mad,
they instead considered the king's sanity as madness.
So they gathered and plotted to seize the king,
to cure his madness,
employing every means like moxibustion, acupuncture, and medicine.
Unable to endure the suffering,
the king went to the spring to fetch water and drank it.
After drinking, he too became mad.
Then, from the ruler to the subjects, all were equally mad,
and the people were overjoyed.
Since I am not mad, it is hard to stand alone;
I too wish to try drinking from this spring.
(From the "Biography in the History of the Southern Dynasties")
Liáng Quán
In Lánzhōu's Dídào County, there was a spring called Liángquán.
Long ago, a man named Liáng Huī, a general of the Later Zhōu,
was besieged by the Qiāng tribes at Báishí Mountain.
With no water available,
Huī thrust his whip into the ground,
offered a green sheep in prayer to the mountain deity, and a spring gushed forth,
while elm trees grew into a forest.
From the "Records of Commanderies and States."
Jade Nectar
Lú Jì,
in the early Suí dynasty, was appointed as the governor of Wèi Prefecture,
where he implemented very benevolent governance.
Niǎoshǔ Mountain was commonly called Gāowǔ Ridge,
below which the Wèi River originates.
The mountain had sheer cliffs a thousand fathoms high,
and had always lacked water,
causing the various Qiāng tribes to suffer from it.
Where Lú Jì's horse hoof trod,
a spring suddenly gushed forth,
and a white bird soared down to rest in front of the government office.
The people then composed a folk song, saying:
"We possess Dānyáng,
where jade nectar flows from the mountain.
It relieves our people, both Hàn and tribal,
as the divine bird comes to hover."
Thus, the common people named the spring "Jade Nectar."
"Suí Shū"
Drawing Water for Drinking
Féng Lì, during the reign of Táng Tàizōng, was appointed governor of Nánhǎi.
Previous governors had mostly been greedy and corrupt,
causing distress among the indigenous peoples,
who repeatedly rebelled.
Féng Lì did not engage in profit-seeking ventures,
taking only what was necessary for food and clothing.
Once, he came to the Greed Spring and sighed, saying:
"This is the spring from which Wú Yǐnzhī drank.
What harm is there in drinking one cup?
I shall draw from it for my meals,"
and after drinking his fill, he departed.
From "Táng Xīn Yǔ."
Hot Spring
In the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
the hot spring was renamed Huáqīng Palace.
According to the "Geographical Records,"
the emperor expanded the hot spring at Huáqīng Palace,
with a grand and magnificent design.
Ān Lùshān, in Fànyáng, crafted fish, dragons,
wild ducks, and geese from white jade stones, offering them along with stone bridges and stone lotus flowers.
The carving was exquisitely skillful,
almost as if not made by human hands.
The emperor was greatly pleased
and ordered them to be displayed in the hot spring,
with the stone bridge spanning across it
and the lotus flowers just emerging from the water's edge.
When the emperor visited Huáqīng Palace
and arrived at the site,
he undressed to enter,
but the fish, dragons, ducks, and geese
all seemed to flare their scales and raise their wings,
as if about to fly and move.
The emperor was extremely startled
and ordered them removed.
However, the lotus flowers remain to this day.
He also once built several dozen long hot spring chambers in the palace,
with winding walls enclosing them,
adorned with patterned stones as silver.
Pleasure boats and white fragrant water boats were placed inside,
with oars and paddles all decorated with pearls and jade.
Moreover, in the hot spring, he piled lutes, zithers, and eaglewood to form mountains,
resembling the mythical islands of Yíngzhōu and Fāngzhàng.
From the "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng."
Shèng Yìng Quán
Yáng Cháoshèng served as the military governor of Bīnníng during the Zhèngyuán era,
and requested to fortify Fāngqú, Hédào, and Mùbō to block the Tǔbō route.
When the troops were stationed at Fāngqú,
there was no water,
and the soldiers grew restless.
Suddenly, a green snake descended from a height,
and following its trail, water began to flow.
Cháoshèng ordered the construction of a protective embankment around it,
which then formed a still pool.
The soldiers drank from it and recorded the event in a drawing.
When the emperor heard of it, he issued an edict to establish a shrine there,
naming the spring "Shèng Yìng."
From the "Two Books of Táng."
Spraying Jade
In Shòu'ān County, there was the Spouting Jade Spring,
where the stone streams were among the most spectacular landscapes of mountains and waters.
During the Zhēnyuán era, Lǐ Bīnkè served as the county magistrate,
who cleared away the thickets and opened up paths and tunnels,
so people began to hear about it and marvel.
In the Tàihé era, Cuī Méng from Bólíng served as the registrar,
who erected markers along the roadside,
so people then visited and toured the place.
"Records and Accounts"
Bànyuè Quán
Lǐ Shēn inscribed a poem at Tiānyī Temple on Fǎhuá Mountain,
the poem said: "The hall surges with the whole body,
the pond beneath the pagoda opens to the Half-Moon Spring."
This spring was hidden beneath the rocks,
so even when the moon was full, only half of it could be seen in the pond,
making it the most exquisite spot.
In the early Shàoxīng era,
the foolish bald monk Fǎ Cōng excavated the rock above it,
renaming it the Full Moon Pond Spring,
which was truly regrettable.
"Xī Xī Cóng Yǔ"
Under the stone cliff at Cíxiàng Temple in Déqīng, Wúxīng, there is a Half-Moon Spring.
During the Xiánhé era of the Jìn dynasty, the monk Tán Zhuō built a hermitage there,
carving a crevice in the rock shaped like a half-moon,
and discovered a cool, sweet spring,
naming it the Spiritual Spring.
Later generations renamed it Half-Moon based on its shape,
and built a pavilion over it.
"Xī Wú Jì"
Gānquán
In Zézhōu Gāopíng there is Gānshuǐ,
also called Gānquán.
In the first year of the Zhēnyuán era,
Magistrate Míng Jì channeled it into the city,
naming it Gānquán.
There is Shěngyuān Valley, originally Slaughter Valley,
which Emperor Xuánzōng visited when traveling to Lùzhōu,
and renamed Fēngzhōu upon passing through.
Three hundred lǐ north of West Shòuxiáng Fort lies Pìtí Quán.
"Geographical Records"
Shàngshàn Quán
In Fǎngzhōu's central prefecture, the city walls had no water supply.
Seven li to the northeast was the Shàngshàn Spring.
In the second year of the Kāichéng era, Governor Zhāng Yí channeled the water into the city,
to alleviate the burden of drawing water from afar.
In the fourth year,
Governor Cuī Pián further enhanced the project,
and the people benefited from it.
Later, in remembrance, they established a shrine for him.
Above.
Míngyuè Quán
Below the Piāomiǎo Peak of Mount Dòngtíng in Wú, there is a spring,
which in the fourth year of the Tiānyòu era of the Táng dynasty, Governor Cáo Guī named Míngyuè.
"Sūzhì"
Jīnshā Quán
Jīnshā Spring is at Gùzhǔ Mountain,
where an emerald spring gushes forth with sand,
sparkling like golden stars.
Táng Dynasty scholar Máo Wénxí recorded this;
during the Táng Dynasty, tribute water used two silver bottles.
When brewing tea with this spring's water,
the flavor is exceptionally fine,
unmatched by any other spring.
In ancient times, people would send it from afar,
using bottles to store the water,
and placing small stones from the spring's edge inside to preserve it,
so it would not spoil over time.
"Records of West Wú"
states: at Zhuómù Ridge in Chángchéng County, Húzhōu,
Jīnshā Spring was the site for annual tea production.
Normally, there was no water;
only when the governors of Hú and Cháng prefectures
arrived at the border and made offerings to the spring with sacrifices,
would it flow clear and abundant that evening.
After imperial tea production concluded, the water would gradually diminish;
once the governor finished production, it would dry up completely.
If the governor delayed returning beyond schedule, storms and thunder would manifest as warnings,
and sometimes fierce beasts, venomous snakes, or water spirits would appear.
"Supplementary Accounts by Zhāng Jūnfáng"
Qí Quán
Wáng Huī, a general of Western Shǔ, served as the Prefect of Jízhōu.
The city lacked springs,
and when Qí troops besieged it, cutting off its water supply,
the inhabitants suffered extreme thirst.
Lord Wáng prayed to the deities at midnight,
and in his dream, an old man appeared and said:
"Beneath the prefectural prison lies a divine spring."
Startled awake,
Wáng waited until dawn,
then urgently ordered shovels and baskets,
digging at the indicated spot.
A spring gushed forth,
saving many lives.
The Qí troops, assuming the city had no water,
planned to wait for its fall.
Lord Wáng commanded water to be drawn from the spring and
displayed it atop the city walls,
whereupon the invaders withdrew.
That same day, the miraculous spring dried up.
"Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Pray
Sòng Sīlǐ,
served as registrar of Xiāo County.
During a severe drought,
wells and ponds dried up.
His mother, frail and ill, could only drink comfortably from spring water.
Sīlǐ, anxious and fearful, prayed earnestly.
A spring emerged in the courtyard,
its water sweet,
never running short even in cold weather.
The county's people marveled at this.
"Biographies of Filial Friends of the Táng Dynasty"
Waterfall Spring
Sīkōng Tú's former retreat was at Sānfēng,
but at the end of the Tiānyòu era he moved to dwell in Zhōngtiáo Mountain.
Wángguān Valley extends over ten-plus lǐ in circumference,
its beauty of springs and rocks being the finest of all.
On the northern cliff of the mountain, there is a waterfall that flows into the valley,
irrigating several dozen mǔ of farmland.
To this day, his descendants still preserve it
as Sīkōng's estate.
"New Book of the South"
Jade Nectar
On Yíngzhōu there is a jade stone,
towering a thousand fathoms high,
from which a spring flows like wine,
sweet in flavor,
named the Jade Nectar Spring.
Drinking several shēng of it makes one drunk,
and enables people to live long lives.
"Records of the Ten Continents"
Bā Quán
Língchí Mountain is located in Wēngyuán County above,
with eight springs called Gushing Spring,
Sweet Spring,
Warm Spring,
Thunder Spring,
Dragon Spring,
Jade Spring,
and Héng Spring.
"Shuǐ Héng Jì"
Róng Quán
The Book of Hàn:
Song of the Red Wild Goose:
The elephant carries jade,
White gathers in the west,
Feeds on sweet dew,
Drinks from the glorious spring.
Note: Glorious spring
means the spring has splendor.
Báiquán
The spring's color is white,
it naturally emerges from mountains and marshes,
when ritual systems are properly established, the white spring from the blessed valley appears,
drinking it enables people to attain longevity.
"Ruì Yìng Tú"
Yùquán
Kūnlún and Pénglái are on it,
birds and beasts drinking from Yùquán all attain longevity without death.
"Bàopǔ"
Tài Xuán Quán
Mount Héng has the Tàixuán Spring,
with nineteen kinds of divine herbs;
consuming them enables one to transcend the mortal world.
"The Map of the Five Sacred Mountains"
Chìquán Yīngquán
On Yuánqiū Mountain there is a Scarlet Spring;
drinking from it prevents aging.
The Divine Palace has a Heroic Spring;
drinking from it makes one sleep for three hundred years,
then awaken unaware of death.
"Kuòdìtú"
The Divine Springs of the Emperor
The Four Waters of Kūnlún,
these are the Divine Springs of the Emperor,
used to blend all medicines,
and to moisten the myriad things.
"Huáinánzǐ"
Kǒngzǐ Quán
Three hundred paces northeast of the city lies the Confucius Spring,
whose waters are sweet and fragrant,
surpassing even the nectar of emperors.
"Records of Jingzhou"
Lóngquán
In Shānxī there was the Lóngquán Monastery,
when the Venerable Fǎshī Yuǎn first sent disciples to select a site,
they rested here and grew thirsty,
whereupon the Fǎshī dug the ground with his staff,
and a spring immediately emerged.
During a drought,
the Fǎshī ordered the disciples to recite the Sūtra of the Ocean Dragon Kings,
whereupon a creature resembling a snake emerged from the spring,
soared into the sky with horns,
and shortly after, rain fell.
From Zhōu Jǐngshì's "Record of Lúshān"
Língquán
In Hédōng, Mount Huòtài has a mountain temple that is very sacred,
where birds and sparrows do not roost in its forests,
and fierce tigers often guard its courtyard.
There is also a spiritual spring used for sacrificial ceremonies;
when drums are beaten, the spring flows, but when the sound ceases,
the water dries up.
In Yīnshān County, Xiāngdōng, there is Mount Hòután,
on which stands a spiritual altar.
In front of the altar is a stone well several feet deep,
usually dry and without water,
but when prayers are offered, sweet spring water gushes forth,
and stops once the prayers are concluded.
This is a similar case.
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Tāngquán
Zhāng Bó's Wú Lù states:
In Jiāngshèng County of Dānyáng, there is a Tāng Mountain,
from beneath which hot springs emerge,
totaling six locations in all,
with a hot spring stream winding around its east and west,
constantly warm in both winter and summer,
birds and fish that enter it immediately rot,
yet boiling beans or grains in it all day fails to cook them,
while plants and trees washed in it become even more vibrant and lush,
the former hot spring establishments are now abandoned.
"Huányǔ Jì"
Shū Gū Spring
Forty li south of Línchéng County stands Gài Mountain,
and after climbing about a hundred steps, one reaches Shūgū Spring.
Long ago, a girl from the Shū family was gathering firewood with her father
when she sat down by the spring.
She became unable to move despite efforts to pull her,
so her father returned home to inform the family.
Upon his return, all he saw was the clear spring and the girl
as her mother said:
"My daughter always loved music."
Then, as strings were played and songs sung, the spring water surged,
and through her tears, a pair of red carp appeared.
Now, when music and play occur here, the spring gushes forth.
From "Records of Xuānchéng."
Jīnxiàn Quán
In Qízhōu city's west there is a Golden Thread Spring,
so clear one can see to the bottom.
At the center of the pond, running north to south, is a golden thread,
slightly raised above the water's surface.
If oil is dripped onto it, the thread's pattern returns;
if disturbed with a stick, the thread disappears,
only reappearing once the water calms.
It is also invisible on overcast days.
"Xiāngshān Yě Lù"
Dùnǚ Quán
In Tàiyuán's Guǎngyáng there is a Jealous Maiden Spring,
which initially emerges as large as a carriage wheel,
with clear, emerald-green water.
Beside it stands a shrine,
and the local people observe that
when women wear ornate dresses and heavy makeup, it inevitably stirs up rain and hail,
hence it is called the Jealous Maiden.
According to an old legend passed down through generations, there is a spirit in this spring resembling a softshell turtle,
which hides by day and roams by night; when the spirit emerges from the water, it surges forth with the spring.
From "Yuánhézhì"
Tidal Spring
At the foot of Jīlóng Mountain, there are dozens of spots in the stream
where stones are piled up as if by human effort,
and the water is always over a foot deep.
Morning and evening, a spring gushes forth,
like the tide,
with unfailing regularity.
Looking ahead, it appears even larger,
earning the name "Tide Spring,"
constantly bubbling like boiling water.
From "Xúnyáng Records"
intertwining like a coiling dragon
In Yúnjiē County there was a spring,
whose water swirled in the eye of the spring like a coiled dragon.
If someone disturbed and broke the swirl, it would immediately reform into a dragon shape.
All livestock approaching to drink would fearfully avoid it and run away,
so it was called the Dragon Spring.
"Commentary on the Water Classic"
Irrigating Fields
In Chēnzhōu, there are fields below the hot springs,
which rely on them for irrigation.
Often, seeds are sown in the twelfth month and by the third month of the following year,
new grain is already harvested.
"Xiānggǎn Zhì"
Female and Male
In Liángshān County stands Duōxǐ Mountain,
where there are two springs, one male and one female.
One is called the Bathing Elixir Well,
in spring and summer the left one is full while the right one dries up,
and in autumn and winter the right one is full while the left one dries up.
Shèngquán
In Wǔyáng of Shǔ there is a sacred spring,
its water is emerald green.
Those suffering from sores often recover after washing in it,
silver turns golden upon being thrown in,
and pregnant women miscarry after drinking it.
Common people consider it a sacred spring.
"Records of the Universe"
Tián Gōngquán
On Huáyáng Léipíng Mountain there is Tiángōng Spring,
also known as Liǔqiān Spring, or alternatively Liǔgǔ Spring.
Drinking its water eliminates the three worms in the abdomen.
Its taste is the same as that of Yǐn Spring.
It is said to be the flowing essence of jade sand.
When used for washing clothes, no ash is needed,
which is considered its peculiarity.
In ancient times, there was a man named Tián Shū who lived on Léipíng Mountain,
and later attained the Way.
The spring was named after him.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Shíquán
In Qiáo Commandery there was a merit official, Qiū.
During the Tiāntǒng era,
the Prefect of Jǐnán, Lái, was appointed to govern Qiáo Commandery.
At that time, the merit official, Cuī Shù of Qīnghé,
was a young man of virtuous character.
It was then the spring and summer seasons with prolonged drought,
and over a thousand people came to bid farewell.
When they reached this Qiū,
the crowd was extremely thirsty and longed for water,
as the price of a shēng had reached ten thousand coins.
Prefect Lái showed signs of longing for water,
but Shù alone spotted a blue-black bird on the Qiū, now flying, now perching.
Finding it strange, he approached the spot.
The bird flew up, revealing a stone about five or six cùn square.
Using his whip to move it aside,
a clear spring gushed forth.
They then collected the water in a silver vase,
but once the vase was full, the water immediately ceased.
Only Prefect Lái and Shù were able to quench their thirst with it.
Commentators believed this was due to the influence of their great virtue,
and people of the time found it remarkable, hence this account.
End.
Lùquán
Hán Xìn was about to attack Zhào when he heard that Chén Yú had not adopted Lǐ Zuǒchē's strategy,
and led his troops out of Jǐngxíng Pass.
His army worried about the lack of wells,
so he divined and obtained the Méng hexagram, knowing there was a spring beneath the mountain.
Hán Xìn dispatched a Hu general, Zhōu, to search for it,
where they saw two white deer pawing the ground, from which a spring gushed forth.
Later generations built the Húwáng Shrine to the left of the spring to honor them.
"Jīn Zhōu Yì Jì"
Shénquán
In Dūnhuáng, there is the Xuánquán Spring,
also known as the Shénquán Spring.
It originates from a dragon,
carved into the mountainside.
The Yìwùzhì of Liángzhōu records:
When Hàn Dynasty General Lǐ Guǎnglì attacked Dàyuān,
on his return,
his troops were thirsty and exhausted.
Lǐ Guǎnglì then drew his sword and struck the mountain,
causing a spring to gush forth.
The entire army relied on it to survive,
and today, a solemn shrine stands there,
visited annually by the local governor.
From the Huányǔjì.
Hóng Quán
Xiè Língyùn's "Rhapsody on Dwelling in the Mountains":
Cinnabar drifts in the crimson spring.
Also inscribed on Huázǐ Ridge:
Bronze peaks reflect in the emerald stream,
Stone steps cascade with crimson springs.
The Jade Maiden Casts Herself into the Spring
In Huìzé of Xīnyáng County, there is a hot spring.
In winter, before one is several miles away,
from afar, one can see white steam floating and rising like smoke,
reflecting brilliantly above and below,
appearing like patterned carvings.
There are also shapes resembling wheels and double shafts of a carriage.
It is traditionally said that in the past, a jade maiden rode a carriage and cast herself into this spring.
Nowadays, people occasionally see a maiden,
with a graceful and radiant appearance,
coming and going in an instant.
"Records of Jīngzhōu"
Fēi Quán
At the foot of Jūjiàng Mountain in Yídào County, there were three springs.
It was said that originally there were no springs here,
and the residents all suffered from the long distance to fetch water.
Many water carriers sold water to them.
There was a woman
who was poor and alone, dressed in rags,
with nothing to trade.
There was a beggar,
coarsely dressed and ugly in appearance,
covered all over with sores.
None of the villagers who saw him did not find him filthy and repulsive.
Only the woman alone took pity on him,
sharing her food to feed him.
After the beggar finished eating, he said:
"I am moved by your kindness,
and wish to repay you.
What do you need?"
The woman replied:
"What kindness is there to repay?
Moreover, what I need now is something you cannot obtain."
He then asked what she needed.
The woman said:
"I only wish there were water at the foot of this mountain that could be drawn."
The beggar then took a dagger from his waist and stabbed three places at the foot of the mountain.
Immediately, gushing springs emerged.
He then bid farewell and left,
suddenly disappearing.
Above.
Dé Rùn Quán
In the second year of the Yōngxī era, on the guǐyǒu day of the fifth month,
Fèngxiáng Prefecture reported that at the Duke of Zhōu Temple in Qíshān County, a spring suddenly gushed forth.
The elders passed down that it flows in times of peace,
and dries up in times of chaos.
During the Ān-Shǐ Rebellion of the Táng dynasty,
the spring dried up and did not flow again until the Dàzhōng era,
when it was named the Dé Rùn Spring.
After that, it dried up once more,
but now it suddenly surged forth, clear, sweet, and pure, remarkably different from the ordinary,
so a depiction was made and presented.
Yàn Shū composed a eulogy, saying:
"Hidden or revealed according to the times,
the divine sign is profoundly manifest."
From "Yù Hǎi"
Shénquán
At the foot of Jǐnxiù Peak of Lúshān, there was a divine spring.
During the Shàoxīng era of the Sòng dynasty, Huángfǔ Lǚ lived in seclusion on this mountain,
and Emperor Gāozōng named his dwelling Qīngxū Hermitage.
When Emperor Guāngzōng was still the crown prince, he asked Lǚ what he lacked,
to which Lǚ replied:
"Only that the water is somewhat distant."
Guāngzōng then wrote the two characters "Divine Spring,"
which Lǚ brought back and placed beside the hermitage.
As they dug a small well,
just as they began to use baskets and spades, the spring emerged,
hence the name.
From the "Jiǔjiāng Records."
Untie
A well,
is clear,
being a source of pure spring water.
The Explanation of Names
states that a well
means connectivity,
as it is universally utilized by all things.
The Commentary on the Book of Changes
explains that the well symbolizes constancy in meaning and doctrine,
with purity as its essence.
The Zìlín
describes the well as deep.
The Guǎngyǎ
defines the well
as a model,
and a regulation,
indicating it establishes norms for residents,
enabling them to regulate their consumption of food and drink without exhaustion.
The General Customs
Digging a Well
Huángdì first dug a well.
The "Zhōu Shū"
states that Bó Yì made wells.
The "Shì Běn"
records that in ancient times, when Cāng Jié created writing, grain fell from the sky like rain,
and ghosts wept at night.
When Bó Yì dug wells, dragons ascended to the dark clouds,
and spirits dwelled on Kūnlún Mountain.
The "Huáinánzǐ"
Jiǔ Jǐng
In Suíjùn's Chóngshān there is a cave,
which elders traditionally claim to be where Shénnóng was born.
Within the ground are nine wells,
and it is said that after Shénnóng was born, the nine wells spontaneously formed.
It is also said that drawing water from one well causes the water in all the others to stir.
Therefore, the site was designated as the Shénnóng Shrine,
where annual sacrifices are regularly performed.
"Jīngzhōu Jì"
Lǎozi Well
South of Xiāngyì County lies Lài Township,
the former hometown of Lǎozi.
There is a temple dedicated to Lǎozi,
within which are nine wells.
Those who observe purification rituals and enter to worship
will find the water's temperature and clarity change according to their thoughts.
Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds
Yù Yáng
Duke Āi of Lǔ had a well dug,
and after three months no spring was found,
but a jade sheep was obtained.
Duke Āi was very frightened.
Confucius said:
"I have heard that the essence of water becomes jade,
and the essence of earth becomes sheep.
This sheep's liver is actually earth."
The duke had someone kill the sheep,
and its liver was indeed earth.
"Han Shi Wai Zhuan"
Jì Huánzǐ had a well dug and obtained something like an earthen jar,
inside which there was a sheep.
He sent someone to ask Zhòngní about it,
saying:
"I dug a well and obtained a dog—
why is that?"
The reply was:
"According to what I have heard,
it is a sheep.
I have heard that the monsters of wood and stone are called Kuí Wǎngliǎng,
the monsters of water are called Lóng Wǎng,
and the monster resembling earth is called Fényáng."
"Guóyǔ"
Holding the Jar
Zǐgòng passed by the south of the Hàn River,
where he saw an old man working on his garden plots.
The man dug a tunnel to reach the well,
carried a jar in his arms to draw water for irrigation.
Zǐgòng said:
There is a tool here,
heavy in the back and light in the front,
which draws water as if pumping,
called a shadoof.
It can irrigate a hundred plots in a day,
using little effort but achieving great results.
Don’t you wish to use it?
The gardener replied:
Where there are mechanical devices, there must be mechanical minds.
If a mechanical mind resides in one’s chest,
then the Way will find no place to dwell.
"Zhuangzi"
Winning the people's support
The Sòng family named Dīng had no well,
so they often had one person fetch water from outside.
When they dug their own well,
he happily told others:
"I gained one person by digging the well."
Those who spread the story reported it to the ruler of Sòng,
who summoned and questioned him about the reason.
He replied that he gained the service of one person,
not that he found a person in the well.
From "Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals"
The Ill-fated Well
At Bǎnzhǔ Ford,
south of the ford on the plain there is a Well of Peril.
Elders say when the Han founder was defeated by Chu and fled,
he fled to this well,
and when the pursuing army arrived they saw two turtledoves emerge from the well,
thus he escaped peril,
hence the name Well of Peril.
Records of a Western Campaign
says he was spared because of a spiderweb above it.
Treatise on Commanderies and States
Inscription of Guàn Yīng
Pénchéng was built by Guàn Yīng.
During the Jiàn'ān era, Sūn Quán passed by this city and personally marked a well site.
He ordered people to dig it and indeed found an ancient well,
with a stone inscription that read:
"Opened by Yǐngyīn Hóu in the sixth year of the Hàn dynasty.
It was divined:
This well shall be blocked after three hundred years,
and within a century after being blocked, it shall be reopened by one destined to respond to the Mandate of Heaven."
When Sūn Quán saw the inscription,
he was delighted, considering it an auspicious sign for himself.
At that time, everyone regarded it as extraordinary.
The well was very deep,
and whenever the great river had wind and waves, this well would also stir.
The locals called it the "Wave Well."
From "Xúnyáng Jì."
Buying the Fù Well
To the east of the Southern Temple in Xiāngzhōu,
at Jiǎ Yì's residence, there was a well with water that narrowed at the top and widened below,
its deep shape resembling a pot,
which was the well dug by Jiǎ Yì himself.
According to the "Jīngzhōu Records,"
Jiǎ Yì had a well
that was round above and square below.
The "Universal Geography" records this.
The well is exhausted.
Zhū Bó served as the Grand Censor,
with over a hundred official residences in his compound,
yet all the well water dried up.
The elders found it strange,
and he was indeed later dismissed from his post.
Book of Hàn
Throwing the Linchpin
Chén Zūn was fond of wine.
Whenever he drank with guests,
he would take the linchpins of their carriages and throw them into the well,
so that even if they had urgent matters, they ultimately could not leave.
The Emperor
Tōngxiān Jǐng
In Yìzhōu, Yán Zhēnguàn had a well connected to immortals.
It was said that this well was connected to the well at Jūn Píng's residence in Miánzhú, Guǎnghàn.
Someone found three copper coins while cleaning the well, each about two inches in diameter.
As a result, they felt uneasy and disoriented.
After throwing the coins back into the well, they immediately recovered.
Some say these were divination coins used by Jūn Píng.
Well Overflow
During Emperor Yuán's reign, a ballad said:
"Well water overflows, extinguishing hearth smoke,
Flooding the Jade Hall, flowing to the Golden Gate."
By Emperor Chéng's time, the northern palace's wellsprings overflowed,
Which was an omen of Wáng Mǎng's rise to power.
From the "History of the Hàn Dynasty"
Worshipping the Well
When Gěng Gōng attacked the
Xiongnu, he chose Shūlè City because there was a stream beside it that could be fortified.
In May,
he led his troops to occupy it.
In July, the Xiongnu came again to attack Gěng Gōng.
Gěng Gōng recruited several thousand vanguard troops and charged straight at them,
causing the enemy cavalry to scatter and flee.
The Xiongnu then blocked the stream below the city,
so Gěng Gōng dug a well fifteen zhàng deep inside the city but found no water.
The officers and soldiers were thirsty and exhausted,
squeezing juice from horse dung to drink.
Gěng Gōng looked up and sighed, saying:
"I have heard that in the past, General Èrshī drew his sword and stabbed a mountain,
and a spring gushed forth.
Now, with the virtue and divine power of the Hàn,
how could it be exhausted?"
He then straightened his clothes and bowed twice toward the well,
praying for his officers and soldiers.
After a short while, water rushed out,
and everyone shouted, "Long live!"
Gěng Gōng personally drew water with a bucket,
then ordered the soldiers not to drink yet,
but first mix mud to plaster the city walls,
and display it openly.
The enemy, taken by surprise,
thought it was divine power,
and thus withdrew.
From History of the Later Hàn
The water was named Xuán Quán (Hanging Spring),
which would flow abundantly when many spirit carriages and horses arrived,
and flow sparingly when few came.
From Records of the Yuánhé Era
Lǐ Sìyè served as the commander of Shūlè Garrison.
The old well of Hàn's Gěng Gōng had long been dry,
but after prayers, the spring flowed again.
From History of the Táng
Water the Ox
At Chúnyú Gōng's door there was a well,
and the village children would compete to water their cattle there.
Gōng disliked this,
so he often fetched water vessels to draw water and fill them.
From "Dōngguān Hànjì".
Setting up vessels
In the village where Guǎn Níng resided, there was a well from which people drew water.
Sometimes men and women mingled in disorder,
and at other times, conflicts and disputes arose over the well.
Guǎn Níng was troubled by this,
so he purchased many vessels and placed them separately by the well,
drawing water in advance to await their use,
without letting others know it was his doing.
When the villagers came and found the vessels, they were surprised,
and upon inquiring, learned it was Guǎn Níng's action?
Thereupon, they reproached themselves,
and no longer fought or brought lawsuits.
"Biographies of Noble Scholars"
The well contains cinnabar.
In Línyuán County, there was the Liào family,
who enjoyed longevity for generations.
Later, when their descendants moved away,
they often suffered premature deaths.
When others lived in their former residence,
they again attained longevity for generations.
It was then realized that this was due to the residence itself,
though the reason was unknown.
Suspicion fell on the well water, which was unusually red,
so they excavated around the well
and found dozens of hú of cinnabar buried by ancient people.
A few feet away,
the cinnabar juice seeped into the well through the spring water,
which explained why drinking the water led to longevity.

Ornate Balustrades
In front of Emperor Míng's Nine Dragons Hall were jade wells with ornate railings,
where toads received water spat out by divine dragons.

Lǜzhū Well
In Báizhōu, at the foot of Shuāngjiǎo Mountain, there is a Lǜzhū Well.
In the past, a woman of the Liáng family possessed remarkable beauty,
and Shí Jìlún, serving as the investigating commissioner of Jiāozhǐ,
purchased her with thirty hú of pearls.
The old well at the Liáng family's residence remains to this day.
Elders pass down the tale:
those who draw and drink from this water
will inevitably bear daughters of great beauty.
However, perceptive individuals in the village,
believing that such beauty brought no benefit to the times,
proceeded to fill the well with massive stones.
Thereafter, although daughters were occasionally born with dignified features,
they often suffered from incomplete facial orifices or limbs.
How strange indeed.
Within the prefecture flows a stream,
originating from Shuāngjiǎo Mountain,
which merges near Róngzhōu to form the Lǜzhū River—
much like how Guīzhōu boasts a Zhāojūn Village,
named after the birthplace of the renowned beauty.
(From "Língbiǎo Lù Yì")
Qījìng Jǐng
During the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty,
Xǔ Xùn, the magistrate of Jīngyáng, once refined elixirs at Huánglóng Mountain in Àichéng.
There was a flood dragon spirit dwelling in the abyss,
which frequently caused great floods,
intending to wash away the elixir chamber.
Xǔ Xùn captured it and nailed it to the stone cliff.
Upon returning to the commandery, at Hǎihūn,
there was a giant snake occupying the mountain as its lair,
spewing breath to form clouds.
Xǔ Xùn executed it,
employing the method of the Big Dipper's seven stars,
each time capturing and placing one in a tranquil well to suppress it.
The eulogy says:
The earthly domain of Hǎihūn,
the prefecture of Dāngyáng and Nánchāng,
upon the grounds of Lóng'ān,
encircling the ancient city ridge of Ài County.
The land connects to the snake's lair,
encroaching upon and blocking rivers,
occupying its soil,
guarding against the people's calamity.
To this day, tranquil wells are established,
bringing eternal auspiciousness.
"Geographical Records"
Let's drink
Ruǎn Zhān once traveled with a group in sweltering heat,
becoming extremely thirsty.
There was a well at the inn,
and everyone rushed toward it.
Only Ruǎn Zhān hung back,
waiting until all the others had finished drinking before he calmly approached.
Such was his humility and lack of competitiveness.
From the History of the Jin Dynasty
Sān Lóng
Xiè Huì, styled Xuānshí,
had an ancient well on the road south of his residence.
In the second year of the Yuánjiā era, a drawer of water suddenly saw three dragons very clearly,
and passersby went to look,
all marveling in astonishment.

only then realizing it was bricks molded in relief to form dragon shapes.

Boiling Well
In the second year of the Shēngpíng era,
north of the boiling well at the temple of Jìzǐ of Yánlíng, a metallic sound was suddenly heard,
arousing suspicion of something unusual.
Digging three feet deep, they discovered a boiling well,
gushing forth like waves.
The ground resonated again,
so they dug once more,
uncovering another well,
similarly surging and boiling.
From the well, they retrieved a wooden slip,
one foot long and two fen wide,
with raised characters inscribed, reading:
"Zhāng Líng, the Daoist of Lúshān, pays his respects again."
The slip was large, hard, and white, with characters
colored yellow.

Brocade Emerges
During the Southern Qí Dynasty, brocade emerged from the Son of Heaven Well east of Jīngzhōu City.

and it ceased only after a full month.

Buying Water
Liáng Héyuǎn served as the prefect of Wǔchāng.

so he often paid people for cool well water.
If someone refused payment, he would return the water along with the money.

Yùjǐng
Prince of Héjiān Chén placed a jade well with a golden jar,
using a rope woven from five-colored gold threads.

Wáng Hóng made a well adorned with precious inlays.

Zhù Jǐng
The Records of the Three States says:
The Eastern Wèi appointed Píng Jiàn as the governor of Huái Prefecture.
Jiàn then opened a road and built a city at the old Zhǐ to defend against the Western army.
Soon, Yáng Fán, the Cavalry General of the Western Wèi, along with Zhǎngsūn Qìngmíng, led troops to campaign eastward.
At that time, the newly built city had little grain and lacked water,
and the people were greatly frightened.
Inside, there was an earthen well,
which dried up as soon as water was drawn.
Jiàn then straightened his attire, bowed to the well, and prayed.
Soon, a spring gushed forth,
supplying the entire city sufficiently.
They raised the water to show Fán,
and Fán retreated without achieving any success.
The History of the Northern Dynasties also records this.
Zhèng Gǎn
Fáng Bào, styled Zhònggàn,
was appointed as the Governor of Lèlíng.
He cultivated customs and education, earning praise for his exemplary governance.
The commandery bordered the sea, and the water tasted mostly salty and bitter.
Fáng Bào ordered the digging of a well,
which then yielded sweet spring water.
People near and far believed it was the result of his transformative governance.
After Fáng Bào left his post and returned home,
the well's water turned salty again.
From "The History of the Northern Dynasties"
Got the boat
At the foot of Wūshān Mountain, there was no water.
At the end of the Wèi dynasty, someone dug a well five zhàng deep and found a stone case.
Inside the case was a turtle,
as large as a horse's hoof.
Five piles of charcoal were placed beside the case.
Digging another three zhàng, they encountered bedrock.
Below it, water surged torrentially.
They then chiseled through the rock to access the water,
which flowed northward rapidly.
Suddenly, a boat appeared,
striking the rocks.
The craftsmen peered into the boat
and found a fir plank.
On the plank, carved characters read:
"On the tenth day of the eighth month, the second year of Chìwū era of Wú,
the boat of Wǔchāng's Wáng Zǐyì."
Jǐngyáng Well,
at the end of the Chén dynasty, the last emperor along with Zhāng Lìhuá and Kǒng Guìpín threw themselves into it to evade Suí troops,
an old account states:
the railing has a stone vein,
when wiped with silk,
it leaves a rouge stain,
also called the Rouge Well,
also known as the Well of Disgrace.
Located at Fǎhuá Temple.
Shèng Jǐng
To the left of Guǎnghuì Temple in Chángxīng, Wúxīng, there are five wells,
dug by a local named Chén during the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn Dynasty.

Hán Gōng Jǐng

Ten zhang

Hán Huǎng served as the governor of Rùnzhōu.

Dig a well

was appointed as the military governor of Jīngnán in the early Zhēnyuán era.

covering a total of two hundred lǐ,
had over ten inns and villages along the way.

End.
The well runs dry.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
at the home of Wáng Dí, a military officer in Jīngzhōu,
the well suddenly boiled over,
and after ten days it dried up completely, revealing the bottom.

two brothers became blind,

Jǐng Dà

westward,
southward,

Shèng Ruì
Emperor Mùzōng was conducting ceremonies at the southern suburbs,
and was about to pay homage at the Tàiqīng Palace.
Zhèng Jiǎn, the registrar of Cháng'ān County, was standing in attendance in the western corridor of the imperial courtyard,
when he saw an old man dressed in white who said:
"Beneath this spot lies a well,
and it happens to be right where the Yellow Emperor passes.
You must quickly fill it in;
otherwise, the consequences will be unpredictable."
Frightened, Jiǎn ordered it to be repaired.
The ground there had already sunk several feet,
and upon excavation,
they discovered it was indeed an ancient well. In the midst of his astonishment,
the old man had already vanished.
Liú Hóngguī, the Commissioner of Merits and Protectorate General of the Army, reported this to the emperor.
After the emperor completed the morning offerings at the palace,
he halted his horse at the palace gate while proceeding to the southern suburbs.
The chief ministers and attending officials offered their congratulations,
whereupon the emperor ordered Wéi Chǔhòu, an academician of the Hànlín Academy, to compose a record.
He also instructed Liǔ Gōngquán, the court diarist,
to inscribe it above the filled well,
titled:
"Record of Sacred Auspices and Responses."
Additionally, Zhèng Jiǎn was bestowed with crimson official robes.

Falling into a well
Bái Lètiān's mother fell into a well while viewing flowers,

leading to his demotion over poems about admiring flowers and the new well.

This man will struggle to get water to drink his whole life.

The cock's crow

Yu Mu

dig a well eighty feet deep
Niú Cúnjié was left behind in Fūzhōu,
later Liú Zhījùn rebelled and fled to Lǐ Màozhēn,
Zhū Yǒuguī ascended the throne,
Zhū Yǒuqiān rebelled and pledged allegiance to Jìn, connecting with Fèngxiáng in the west,

Tóngzhōu had salty water and no wells,
Zhījùn rebelled against Liáng,
believing Tāng could not hold the city and fled,
thus Yǒuqiān and Qí troops jointly besieged it for a long time,
intending to exhaust them with thirst,

Xiāng Jǐng

Sīmìng

"Huányǔ Jì"
Èrsè Jǐng
In Lúlíng City there was a well,

the water was half blue and half yellow.

The auspicious sign of Lúlíng
only preserves the name of two colors.
Míng Yì Jǐng
South of the Míngyì Tower lies the Míngyì Well,
which in summer has cool water,
sweet enough to drink with rice.
There are three types of fans: luóshàn, língshàn, and yǔshàn.
The bathhouse above is for bathing kings, nobles, and high officials,
the middle level for gentlemen,
and the lower level for common people.
During the dog days of summer, when the heat is scorching and intense,

worrying before they reach it,
but delighting once they arrive.

Curing Illness
During the Sòng dynasty,
a man named Qiū Càiyuán from Qiū village dug a well and obtained a stone,
inscribed with the words:

Silver Bed
An ancient dance song says:
"Huáinán King proclaims his own majesty,
A hundred-foot tower connects with the heavens,
In the rear garden a well is dug with a silver railing,

Xǔ Yànzhōu stated that during the Jiāyòu era, a fisherman netted a stone from the riverbank,
Carving a poem that reads:

Jǐnghán,
Refers to the wooden railing around a well,
The character is also written as 韓,
Its shape being square or octagonal,
Also called yínchuáng,
All denoting the well railing.
The Well Enigma
Bào Zhào's well riddle says:
One eight four eight, a spring flowing upward,
For combined it becomes five eight,
Five eight is forty,
Forty forms the character for "well,"
One version records:
Two eight three eight, Qián Zhāodù.
His poem "Eating a Pear" says:

The Well Deity
Hence, the essence of the well is named Guān, appearing like a beautiful woman,
fond of playing the flute,
and calling it by its name will make it leave.

Digging a Well
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Shìpíng,
in his middle years, both he and his wife became blind.
They sought various remedies but could not be cured.
One day, a scholar dug a well for them,
and upon obtaining fresh water to wash their eyes, they recovered as before.
Thus, he left this method to be passed on to save others,
to alleviate suffering and increase hidden virtue.
The essentials are:
In years of Zǐ and Wǔ, the fifth month on days Xū and Yǒu,
the eleventh month on days Mǎo and Chén are auspicious; in years of Chǒu and Wèi,
the sixth month on days Xū and Hài,
the twelfth month on days Chén and Sì;
in years of Yín and Shēn,
the seventh month on days Hài and Zǐ,
the first month on days Sì and Wǔ;
in years of Mǎo and Yǒu,
the eighth month on days Zǐ and Chǒu,
the second month on days Wǔ and Wèi;
in years of Chén and Xū,
the ninth month on days Shēn and Wèi,
the third month on days Yín and Chǒu;
in years of Sì and Hài,
the tenth month on days Shēn and Yǒu,
the fourth month on days Yín and Mǎo.
Choose the corresponding direction,
and the year, month, day, and hour will be a blessed site.
Dredging the well and drawing water will surely yield good results.
Shìpíng bowed twice and received the instructions,
then ascended to heaven and departed.
The scholar was the official of the Great White Star (Venus).

Six Wells

Hángzhōu used to store water from ponds and lakes,
but the land was hot and often plagued by malaria and dysentery,

Bái Jūyì,
while serving as the prefect of Hángzhōu, dredged Lǐ Bì's Six Wells again, and the people relied on them for water.

Stagnant water is called a chí.

A zhǎo,
is a chí.

Sūnzǐ had the saying about a "metal wall and a boiling moat,"

to rear fish and turtles.
A round one is called a chí,
a winding one is called a zhǎo.
Open the pond

This is the place of the Zhōu Son of Heaven's Bìyōng.

Xuánchí

Yáochí

Lánchí

Hàochí

someone holding a jade disc intercepted his envoy and said:

Kunming Pond,
was excavated in the third year of the Yuanshou era of Emperor Wu of Han.
Initially, the Han sought to reach Shendu,
but the route was blocked by the Kunming tribes.
The Kunming region had Dian Pond, three hundred li in circumference,
named Dian River.
The Han planned to attack Kunming,
to open the route to Shendu, using exiled conscripts,
they cleared brambles in Shanglin Park,
and modeled Kunming Pond after Dian River to practice naval warfare.

In Kunming Pond, jade and stone were carved into fish,
whenever thunder and rain came,
the fish would often roar,
with fins and tails all moving,
in the Han dynasty, they were sacrificed to pray for rain,
and it was often effective.

In Kunming Pond, there were spear boats,
and tower ships,
each numbering in the hundreds,
the tower ships had erected turrets,
the spear boats were equipped with spears and halberds,

Tiānquán Pool

Later, the emperor and palace entertainers rode a dragon boat,

Tiānchí
Fényáng has a Celestial Pond,
located on Yan Capital Mountain, encircling eight li.
During sunny droughts, it does not dry up,
and during cloudy rains, it does not overflow.
The elders say that someone once rode a cart,

Later, Emperor Xiàowén of Northern Wei released seven gold-threaded fish with pearls

Later, at Sāngqián Plain, fish with gold threading were found,

Again, they used a gold-tipped arrow to shoot a large fish here,

The mountain is located northeast of Jìnglè County in Lánzhōu,

Qílián Chí
In the Xiùróng region, there are three pools,
located high upon the mountains,

known in Wei language as the Heavenly Pools.
Ěrzhū Xīnxīng,

During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign, Investigating Censor Wáng Shǒushèn avoided the judicial office,

During the Shénlóng era, Princess Ānlè, relying on imperial favor,

The princess grew angry,
and using her own family wealth, had another pond dug,

Qǔjiāng Chí
The Qǔjiāng Pond was originally the Yǐzhōu of the Qín Dynasty; during the Kāiyuán era, it was dredged and excavated,
becoming a scenic spot.
To its south stood the Zǐyún Tower
and the Fúróng Garden,
while to its west were the Xìng Garden
and the Cí'ēn Temple.
Flowers and plants encircled the area,
with misty waters bright and beautiful.
The capital's residents visited for leisure,
most bustling during the Zhōnghé
and Shàngsì festivals.
Colorful tents and green canopies lined the embankments,
with sleek carriages and sturdy horses crowded wheel to wheel.
On the Shàngsì Festival, the emperor bestowed feasts
upon officials and the Jīngzhào Prefecture,
grandly setting out banquets.
The two counties of Cháng'ān and Wànnián competed in magnificence,
sparing no effort in displaying brocades, embroideries, and rare treasures.
All officials gathered at the mountain pavilion,
granted music from the Tàicháng Office and the Jiàofāng Conservatory.
Several decorated boats were prepared on the pond,
reserved only for the chancellor, three envoys, officials of the northern departments, and Hànlín Academy scholars to board.
Each year, it stirred the imperial capital as a grand spectacle.
In summer, the wild rice and reeds grew lush and green,
with willow shades enveloping on all sides,
emerald waves and red lotuses,
serenely delightful.
Enthusiasts admired the fragrant season and enjoyed the clear scenery,
riding together with wine cups in hand,
in an endless stream.

Qiánlú Pō
During the Jiànzhāo era of Emperor Yuán,
Shào Xìnchén served as the Grand Administrator of Nányáng,
constructing the Qiánlú Embankment sixty li south of Rǎng County,
building a stone levee,

Hóngxì
In Rǔnán there was formerly the great Hóngxì reservoir,
which the commandery considered a source of prosperity. During Emperor Chéng's time,
east of the pass there were several floods as reservoirs overflowed causing damage.
Zhái Fāngjìn
served as chancellor
and together with the Imperial Secretary Kǒng Guāng dispatched clerks to investigate,
deeming it should be breached,
draining the reservoir waters.
The land became fertile and excellent,
saved costs on embankment maintenance,
and eliminated water-related worries.
Thus they memorialized to abolish it.
After the Zhái clan was destroyed, the villagers turned against him,
speaking ill of Fāngjìn,
claiming he sought the fine fields below the reservoir but couldn't obtain them, so he memorialized to abolish it.
It's said that during Wáng Mǎng's time there was constant drought,
and the commandery retrospectively resented him.
A children's rhyme about Fāngjìn went:
"Who ruined the reservoir? Zhái the gentleman!"
"We ate millet, now we eat beans."
"Our soup is taro roots, will it reverse?"
"When the reservoir is restored, who will do it?"
The singers were two yellow swans.
《Hànshū》
During the Jiànwǔ era,
Governor Dèng Chén wished to restore it to its former function.
Hearing that Xǔ Yáng understood water courses, he summoned him for discussion.
Yáng said:
"Formerly Emperor Chéng followed Fāngjìn's advice,
but soon dreamed of ascending to heaven,
where the Heavenly Emperor angrily said:
'Why did you destroy my
Zhuólóng Deep?' After this the people lost its benefits,
often suffering famine and hardship.
If you, wise governor, now revive
this abandoned work, there will be signs.
I sincerely wish to devote myself to this task, even to death."
Chén was greatly pleased,
and appointed Yáng as Chief Water Officer,
entrusting him with the project.
Yáng then constructed embankments over 400 lǐ following the terrain's elevation,
which took several years to complete.

After the reservoir was completed, people
slandered Yáng, saying he embezzled funds.
Chén imprisoned Yáng.
The cell door opened by itself, and his shackles came off.
Chén released him. When he emerged,

guiding him forward—a testament to his pure virtue's influence.

A lake of ten thousand acres
Guō Tài entered Rǔnán,
befriending Huáng Shūdù,
arriving at Nánzhōu,
he first visited Yuán Fènggāo but left without staying overnight,
then stayed with Shūdù for several days.
Someone asked Tài about this,
Tài replied:
"Yuán Fènggāo's capacity
can be compared to an overflowing stream -
though clear, it is easily exhausted.
Shūdù's capacity,
however, is like a vast lake of ten thousand qǐng -
when you try to clarify it, it doesn't become clearer;
when you try to muddy it, it doesn't become turbid;
it cannot be measured."

Měibēi originates from the valleys of the Zhōngnán Mountains,

Marsh
Sǒu means abundance.
It contains plants, trees, fish, and turtles, which serve to abundantly nourish the ruler and the common people.
The tradition says:
Where water and plants intermingle is called a marsh,
and a marsh
means that it moistens and nourishes all things
to enrich the people's livelihood.
The "Fēngsú Tōng"
states: A large marsh is called a sǒu.
The "Zhōulǐ Zhífāng Zhù"

Nine Marshes
What are the nine marshes?
Jùqū of Yuè,
Yúnmèng of Chǔ,
Yánghuá of Qín,
Dàlù of Jìn,
Pǔtián of Liáng,
Mèngzhū of Sòng,
Hǎiyú of Qí,
Jùlù of Zhào,
Dàzhāo of Yān.
The "Lǚlǎn"
and Huáinán mention Yángyū of Qín,
Zhāoyú of Yān,
while the "Ěryǎ" lists ten marshes.
Lǔ had Dàyě,

Yān had Zhāoyú,

The nine marshes,
in Qīngzhōu are called Wàngzhū,
in Yōngzhōu are called Xiánpú,
in Yōuzhōu are called Xīyǎng,
in Jìzhōu are called Yángyū.
Prosper and multiply
Bó Yǔ reflected on the former improper measures and modeled after natural phenomena,
taking heaven and earth as standards to regulate all living beings.
Gòng’s descendant,
assisted by the Four Peaks,
leveled the high and low, dredged rivers and cleared blockages,
accumulated water to enrich resources,
built embankments around the nine marshes,
cultivated and multiplied the nine wetlands,
tamed and crossed the nine plains,
settled in the nine sheltered lands,
connecting and opening up the four seas.
Thus, heaven had no hidden darkness,
earth no scattered yang energy,
water no stagnant vapor,
fire no calamitous flames,
spirits no erratic wanderings,
people no excessive desires,
seasons no reversed order,
and creatures no harm to life.

Pǔtián
In Zhōngmóu County lies the Pǔtián Marsh,
which shares its northern waters with Yángwǔ.
