The marsh lies west of Zhōngmóu County,
bounded west by the Great Wall,
extending east to Guāndù,
and girded north by canal waters.
Spanning approximately forty lǐ east-west
and twenty lǐ north-south,
it contains sandy ridges
and twenty-four interconnected ponds across its expanse,
where channels flow directly,
and deep pools link continuously,
each bearing distinct names.
There are Dàjiàn and Xiǎojiàn,
Dàhuī and Xiǎohuī,
Yìlǔ, Liànqiū,
Dàbáiyáng and Xiǎobáiyáng,
Sǎnrùyúzhōng,
Yángjuàn, Dàgǔ and Xiǎogǔ,
Lóngzé, Chàngbà,
Dà'āi and Xiǎo'āi, Dàcháng and Xiǎocháng,
Dàsuō and Xiǎosuō,
Bóqiū, Dàgài, Niúmián, among others.
When the pond waters swell, they flow north into canals;
when overflowing, they spread southward.
Thus, the Bamboo Annals record:
"In King Huìchéng of Liáng's tenth year, river waters entered Pǔtián,
and a great ditch was dug to channel the Pǔ waters."

To the west, there is a mound,

Beside the mound are three stone caves,

The water level fluctuates,

The local residents recognize the signs of leakage
and preemptively block the cave openings with curved wooden barriers,
resulting in an abundance of fish and turtles of various species.
From here, a continuous ridge extends northwest for about forty lǐ,
and at the western end lies the source of the Sì River.

Storing Ice and Distributing Ice
Shēn Fēng said:
In ancient times, when the sun was in the northern constellation, ice was stored; when it moved to the western constellation,
it was taken out at dawn.
As for storing the ice,
it was collected from deep mountains and remote valleys where solid shade and freezing cold prevailed,
thus it was gathered there.
When it was taken out,
it was used for the salaries and positions of the court, for hosting guests, funerals, and sacrifices.
When storing it,
a black bull and millet were offered to the deity of cold. When taking it out,
peach-wood bows and thorn arrows were used to ward off disasters. In both storing and retrieving it,
those entitled to eat meat and receive salaries were all allotted ice.
High-ranking officials and their wives used ice for washing the deceased,
sacrifices were made to the cold when storing it,
and a lamb was offered when opening the storage.
The ruler began using it first,
and when the Fire Star appeared, the distribution was completed.
From titled officials and their wives
down to the elderly and infirm, none failed to receive ice.
Mountain dwellers collected it,
county officials transported it,
cart drivers delivered it,
and servants stored it.
Ice hardens with the wind,
and is brought out with the wind.
Its storage
is thorough, and its use
is widespread. The final section of the "Seventh Month"
illustrates the principles of storing ice.

Emperor Guāngwǔ, fleeing from the troops of Wáng Láng, arrived at the Hūtuó River from Hándān.

and it was indeed so.
Wáng Bà, concerned that reporting the truth would alarm the troops,

He immediately reported:

The troops were overjoyed,

They scolded until they reached the river, where the flowing ice had congealed enough to walk on.
The horses were about to freeze stiff,
so they used bags filled with sand to spread on the ice and crossed.
Before the crossing was complete, several carts fell through the ice.
Emperor Guāngwǔ said to his officials:
"Wáng Bà used expedient means to accomplish the task,
this must be a heavenly blessing."

Selling Ice

In the past, a man from Kuài engaged in trade,

When a customer unaffected by the heat was about to buy it,
the man from Kuài thought he had caught the right moment
and sought to demand several times the profit.
The customer became angry and left,
and soon the ice also melted away.

and not repeat the mistake of the man from Kuài.

Therefore, we say we know there is the Way of Heaven."

Bó Jī replied:

if her governess is not present,

Zuǒ

South leaning
The people of Lǔ set fire to a marshy area,
and with a north wind, the flames spread southward,
threatening to burn the capital.
Duke Āi grew fearful,
and personally led the crowd to urge them to fight the fire.
However, his attendants were all off chasing wild animals,
so the fire was not extinguished.
He then summoned Zhòngní for advice.
Zhòngní said:
"Those chasing animals find it enjoyable and face no punishment,
while those fighting the fire find it toilsome and receive no reward.
This is why the fire remains unextinguished."
Duke Āi said, "Well said."
Zhòngní continued:
"The situation is urgent, and there's no time for rewards;
if all fire-fighters were rewarded,
the state's resources would be insufficient to compensate everyone.
I suggest instead implementing punishments."
Duke Āi said, "Well said."
Thereupon, Zhòngní issued an order:
"Those who do not fight the fire will be treated as guilty of desertion;
those chasing animals will be treated as guilty of trespassing."
Before the order had even been fully disseminated, the fire was already extinguished.

Dreaming of Fire
When Zhì Bó was defeated and about to flee,

Moving the Firewood
Chún Yú Kūn went to a neighbor's house,
and saw that their chimney was straight,
with firewood piled up beside it.
He told them:
"A straight chimney will cause a fire,
you should bend the chimney and move the firewood away."
The neighbor didn't listen,
and later their house indeed burned down.
The neighbors put out the fire together,
then cooked lamb and prepared wine to thank those who helped extinguish the fire,
but they refused to invite Kūn to know about it.
A scholar mocked them, saying:

This laments how people value the trivial while neglecting the fundamental.

Beg for Fire
A guest said to Kuǎi Tōng:
"You know that Liáng Shíjūn
and Dōngguō Xiānshēng are worthy men.
Why not recommend them to Chancellor Cáo?"
Kuǎi Tōng replied:
"Very well.
In my village, there was a housewife who was on good terms with an elderly woman in the neighborhood.
One night, the housewife lost some meat,
and her mother-in-law suspected her of stealing it.
Furious, she drove her out.
The next morning, as the housewife was leaving, she passed by the elderly woman she was close to,
told her what had happened, and bade her farewell.
The elderly woman said:
'Go slowly on your way.
I will make your family come after you right away.'
She then tied up some hemp and went to the house that had lost the meat to ask for fire, saying:
'Last night, my dogs got hold of some meat
and fought over it until they killed each other.
I need fire to deal with them.'
The family that had lost the meat immediately rushed out to call back their daughter-in-law.
Thus, the elderly woman was not a skilled rhetorician,
nor was tying hemp to ask for fire a direct way to bring back the housewife.
Yet things can resonate with each other,
and circumstances can align.
I can go ask for fire from Chancellor Cáo."

there is a bird resembling a crane,

The preface to the "Classic of Mountains and Seas" records ancient facts.
The essence of fire is called Bìfāng,

Wáng Shào, based on the ancient principle of drilling wood to change fire,

continuously without extinguishing.

I propose to gather five types of wood in the five seasons to change the fire,
requiring minimal effort
yet offering substantial benefits."

Huáng
The sovereign is like Heaven,
which does not speak,
yet the four seasons proceed,
and all things are born.
The Three Sovereigns ruled with folded hands,
acting through non-action and setting forth no words,
yet the people did not disobey.
Their virtue and way were profound and tranquil,
resembling the August Heaven,
thus they were called Huáng (sovereign).
Huáng means centrality,
radiance,
and vastness.
Embracing vastness and treading the mean,
opening the yin and spreading the net,
above they conformed to the supreme standard,
their influence was bright and luminous,
pointing to Heaven and drawing on Earth,
their spiritual transformations silently penetrated,
their resplendent glory and abundant beauty were immeasurable.

Huáng means ruler,
beauty,

is praised as beautiful and great,

Huáng means resplendent,
the Way manifestly clear and bright.

Emperor
The title "Dì" is a heavenly designation,
whose virtue matches heaven and earth,
not privatizing the public position,
thus called "Dì".
The Son of Heaven,
succeeds heaven in governing all things,
corrects the calendar and unifies the realm,
each finds its proper place,
fathering heaven and mothering earth,
nourishing living people,

The Great Sovereign,
is the pinnacle of ruling people.

with clear and discerning laws,
rewarding in spring and summer,

the emperor,

states the emperor,
is one name of heaven,
hence named "Dì".

indicating heaven is vast and without intent,

Fair and far-reaching,
handling affairs with careful deliberation, thus called "Dì",
the five emperors' way is the same as this,
also capable of thorough examination,
hence taking this name.
The "Shū Zhèngyì"
The Way is deficient
The royal way was deficient,
so the emperors arose.
The "Luò Shū"
Emperor
The title of emperor is the most supreme designation,
where "huáng" (皇) signifies brilliance,
indicating a magnificent and virtuous radiance
that illuminates everything.
"Dì" (帝) means discerning,
referring to the ability to practice the Way of Heaven,
and serving Heaven with careful deliberation,
hence the title "huángdì" (皇帝).
In the Dú Duàn,
"huáng" denotes greatness,
describing its splendid and magnificent beauty;
"dì" symbolizes virtue mirroring Heaven and Earth,
meaning the capacity to enact the Way of Heaven,
with actions carried out through thorough consideration,
and regarding Heaven as father and Earth as mother to rule over all under heaven.
From the Hàn Guān Yí.
Wáng
The ancient creators of writing,
drew three strokes connected through the center,
calling it 'wáng'—three strokes.
These represent Heaven, Earth, and Humanity,
connecting through the center signifies unifying their principles,
integrating the essences of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.
Who but a king could embody this?
Thus, a king must emulate Heaven,
covering and nurturing all things with great benevolence,
both transforming and giving them life,
and fostering them to maturity.
Dǒng Zǐ
A king is one towards whom [people] go,
where the divine directs its focus,
and humans return with joy.
Yuán Mìng Bāo
The Way is great,
Heaven is great,
Earth is great,
and the king is also great.
Within the realm, there are four greatnesses,
and the king occupies one among them.
Lǎo Zǐ
Lǐ Yángbīng said:
In the character for 'king,' the middle stroke is closer to the top,
symbolizing the king's alignment with Heaven's meaning.
The king is supremely revered,
a distinct title among the four designations,
referred to within the royal domain.
The king possesses all under Heaven,
hence called 'wáng.'
Dú Duàn

Dìwáng
The term "Dì" (Emperor) signifies
the one whom all under heaven turn to,
and "Wáng" (King) signifies the one towards whom all under heaven proceed.
If all under heaven neither turn to nor proceed towards a ruler,
they cannot be called an Emperor or King.
Therefore, an Emperor or King cannot achieve success without gaining the people,
and even with the people, if they lose the Way, they cannot maintain their rule.
《Wénzǐ》
states: "Emperor and King are titles,
and titles are the symbols of merit,
used to display merit and illuminate virtue,
and to issue commands to subordinates.
One whose virtue aligns with heaven and earth is called an Emperor,
while one who embodies benevolence and righteousness is called a King,
distinguishing between superior and inferior."
《Lǐjì Shìfǎ》says:
"One whose virtue mirrors heaven and earth is called an Emperor,
and one born of benevolence and righteousness
is called a King. The title 'Emperor' is a heavenly designation,
while 'King' is a term associated with the Five Phases."
《Báihǔ Tōng》
explains: "The title 'Emperor' is a heavenly designation,
and 'King' is a human one. Heaven has the Five Emperors to establish names,
while humanity has the Three Kings to set standards."
《Shàngshū Wěi》
The Son of Heaven
The Son of Heaven is the definitive title for the supreme sovereign.
Responding to the spirits and receiving the mandate,
he is regarded as the child of Heaven,
hence called the Son of Heaven.
From the "Dìwáng Shìjì":
Those whose virtue matches heaven and earth are called Huángdì,
and those blessed and adopted by Heaven are titled the Son of Heaven,
thus, a sage king is called the Son of Heaven upon birth.
From the "Fánlù":
All Sons of Heaven are the essence of the Five Emperors,
each with their ordained sequence and rotation,
their rise is inevitably marked by divine signs and records,
supported by various deities,
enabling them to establish foundations and achieve success.
From the "Chūnqiū Yǎnkǒng Tú":
The dignity of the Son of Heaven
lies in his spirit being connected with heaven and earth,
his vitality containing the essence of the Five Emperors,
loved by Heaven,
and adopted as its child.
From the "Chūnqiū Bǎoqián Tú":
In the earliest times,
when the masses first emerged,
there was no hierarchy,
and they naturally followed the order of Heaven without intervention.
Rulers had not yet been established,
but later, conflicts arose,
with some oppressing others,
and encroachments continued unchecked,
causing great harm to the people.
Thus, Heaven mandated a sage to govern them,
ensuring they did not lose their nature,
so all under heaven benefited,
and none were untouched by his virtue,
unanimously honoring and supporting him,
calling him the Son of Heaven.
From the "Qiánfū Lùn":
Heaven and earth give birth to all things,
but humans nurture them to completion;
one who can nurture what Heaven produces without disrupting it is called the Son of Heaven.
The actions of the Son of Heaven
are aimed at preserving the integrity of Heaven.
From the "Lǚshì Chūnqiū":
When the Son of Heaven receives feudal lords in court,
he refers to himself as the child of Heaven and earth,
hence called the Son of Heaven.
From the "Dúduàn":
In ancient times, sacred mothers conceived children through divine inspiration from Heaven,
thus they were called Sons of Heaven.
From the "Shuōwén":
Sages who receive the mandate are all born of Heaven,
hence called Sons of Heaven.
From the "Chénggōng Bā Gōngyáng Zhù".
Lord
The ruler of the world is Heaven,
the successor to Heaven is the sovereign,
and what defines the sovereign is his mandate.
For a minister to usurp his sovereign's mandate and wield it
is to fail as a minister.
For a sovereign to lose his mandate
is to fail as a sovereign.
"Gǔliáng Zhuàn"
The sovereign (jūn) is the multitude (qún),
the one to whom the hearts of the multitude below return.
"Báihǔ Tōng"
The way of the sovereign is the ability to form communities.
"Xúnzǐ"
The one who dispenses rewards and punishments is called the sovereign.
"Zuǒzhuàn Commentary"
The sovereign (jūn) is the multitude (qún),
he who assembles all the people under Heaven,
and removes their harms,
is called the sovereign king.
To go (wǎng) means
all under Heaven go to him,
he who is good at nurturing the living,
thus people honor him;
he who is good at governing people,
thus people are content with him;
he who is good at elevating people,
thus people are close to him;
he who is good at embellishing people,
thus people delight in him.
When these four virtues are complete, all under Heaven go to him;
when even one of these four virtues is lacking, all under Heaven depart from him.
Going to him is called kingship (wáng),
departing from him is called ruin (wáng).
Thus it is said: when the Way exists, the state exists;
when the Way perishes, the state perishes.
"Hánshī Wàizhuàn"
"Shuōwén":
Sovereign (jūn),
means honor,
from "govern" (yǐn) and "mouth" (kǒu) to issue commands.
Xú Yuè says: the sovereign (jūn)
is the governor (yǐn),
the rectifier,
a general term for the leader of the people.
Duke Dào of Jìn said:
The reason ministers seek a sovereign is to have one who issues commands,
in writing, "mouth" (kǒu) and "govern" (yǐn) form "sovereign" (jūn).
Qí Yī
The establishment of emperors and kings in ancient times
was not to indulge their desires;
sages ascending the throne
was not for their own comfort and pleasure.
For the people under heaven,
the strong oppressed the weak,
the many abused the few,
the cunning deceived the simple,
the brave encroached upon the timid,
and moreover, those possessing wisdom and cunning did not teach others,
those accumulating wealth did not share it,
therefore the Son of Heaven was established to unify them.
Wénzǐ
established as the ruler of the world
In ancient times, the establishment of the Son of Heaven was esteemed,
not for the benefit of one person,
but because:
if there were no single authority in the world,
rites would have no means to be communicated,
and communicating principles is for the sake of the world.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven was established for the world,
not the world established for the Son of Heaven.
A ruler of a state is established for the state,
not the state established for the ruler.
From "Shènzǐ"
The ruler's role as a sovereign
Confucius said:
Shāng, do you understand why a ruler is a ruler?
Zǐxià said:
If fish lose water, they die;
but if water loses fish, it remains water.
Confucius said:
Shāng understands it.
"Shīzǐ"
All the wisdom and foresight in the world
The ruler sees through the eyes of the world,
listens through the ears of the world,
deliberates with the wisdom of the world,
and strives with the strength of the world.
Thus, decrees can be thoroughly implemented,
and the sentiments of ministers can reach the ruler.
All officials are harmoniously aligned,
and ministers gather like spokes around a hub.
Joy is not expressed through rewards,
nor anger through punishments.
Therefore, authority is established and not abandoned,
clarity and intelligence shine without being obscured,
laws and decrees are clear but not harsh,
perception and understanding are comprehensive and not dimmed.
The realities of good and bad,
are daily presented without opposition.
Huáinánzǐ
Bright as the sun and moon
The ruler's residence is,
like the brightness of the sun and moon,
shared by all under heaven,
gazing at with sidelong glances,
listening with inclined ears,
stretching necks and rising on tiptoes to look.
Therefore, without tranquility and indifference, one cannot manifest virtue;
without peace and stillness, one cannot reach far;
without broad-mindedness, one cannot embrace all;
without kindness and generosity, one cannot win over the masses;
without fairness and justice, one cannot make judgments.
The sovereign
Kindness nurtures like spring
The ruler who governs men occupies the southern-facing position,
wielding the power of life and death.
His authority is like autumn frost,
his benevolence like spring nourishment.
What desire could go unfulfilled?
What transformation could fail to follow?
A true ruler
should take rivers and seas as his belly,
mountains and forests as his face,
ensuring that observers cannot discern what the rivers and seas conceal,
nor what the mountains and forests contain.
From "Tángzǐ"
Presenting and Recommending with Appropriate Words
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven could dress himself with his own hands,
yet the steward would arrange his attire;
he could walk with his own feet,
yet the usher would guide his steps;
he could speak for himself,
yet the herald would announce his words,
so there were no improper words or breaches of etiquette.
The method of a ruler
is to abide by non-action and practice wordless teaching,
remaining serene and unmoving,
maintaining unity without wavering, following the natural course and entrusting affairs to subordinates,
demanding completion without toil.
Thus, the mind knows the rules while mentors instruct and guide,
the mouth can speak while diplomats articulate words,
the feet can walk while attendants lead the way,
the ears can hear while upright officials offer counsel.
Hence, deliberations involve no miscalculations,
plans encounter no errors,
words become literary compositions,
and actions serve as models for the world.
Huáinánzǐ
Obscure the Bright and Conceal the Audible
The ancient kings wore ceremonial caps with hanging beads in front to obscure their vision,
and filled their ears with yellow silk to muffle their hearing.
The Son of Heaven had an outer screen to shield himself,
thus those honored were kept at a distance while those appointed were kept close,
and those governed were many while those retained were few.
The
Son of Heaven sits within nine layers of walls,
with trees blocking his gate,
beads to veil his sight,
earplugs to conceal sounds,
and carriage bells to restrain his speed.
"The Writings of Sūzǐ"
Power and Influence
Power is the ruler's chariot,
and ministers are the ruler's team of horses.
If one's body leaves the safety of the chariot,
and one's hands lose the hearts of the horses,
yet can avoid peril,
such a thing has never existed from ancient times to the present.
Huáinánzǐ
The movement is without accumulation.
The Way of Heaven operates without accumulation, thus all things are accomplished;
the Way of Emperors operates without accumulation,
thus the world submits;
the Way of Sages operates without accumulation,
thus all within the seas obey.
Understanding Heaven and comprehending the Sages,
the six directions and four seasons in the virtue of emperors and kings
are their spontaneous actions.
Emptiness, stillness, tranquility, and simplicity,
solitude and non-action
are the root of all things.
With these, one dwells in the virtue of emperors, kings, and sons of Heaven.
"Zhuangzi - The Way of Heaven"
The virtue of the sovereign
The virtue of emperors and kings takes the world as its foundation,
with the Way and its virtue as the guiding principle,
and non-action as the constant practice.
Through non-action,
they govern the world with ease and to spare;
through action,
they are governed by the world and find it insufficient.
"Zhuāngzǐ"
Non-action
The ancient rulers of the world,
though their knowledge encompassed heaven and earth, did not rely on their own thoughts;
though their eloquence adorned all things, they did not speak for themselves;
though their abilities surpassed all within the seas, they did not act for themselves.
Heaven does not produce, yet all things transform;
earth does not grow, yet all things are nurtured;
the emperor does nothing, yet the world achieves merit.
Thus it is said: nothing is more divine than heaven,
nothing is richer than earth,
nothing is greater than the emperor.
Therefore, it is said that the virtue of the emperor matches heaven and earth.
Riding upon heaven and earth,
galloping through all things,
this is the way to employ the masses of people.
Above
Guānghuà
In ancient times, the sage kings
looked upward to take images from heaven,
looked downward to take measurements from earth,
and in between took models from humanity,
harmonizing the energies of yin and yang,
and balancing the nodes of the four seasons.
They examined the suitability of hills, plains, waters, marshes, fertile and poor soils, high and low lands,
to establish affairs and generate wealth,
eliminating the troubles of hunger and cold,
and warding off the calamities of disease and illness.
From within human affairs they received the means to institute rites and music,
and practiced the way of humaneness and righteousness to govern human relationships.
They classified the natures of metal, wood,
water, fire,
and earth,
to establish the affection between father and son and form the family.
They listened to the five notes, clear and turbid,
and the numbers of mutual generation among the six pitch-standards,
to establish the righteousness between ruler and minister and form the state.
They examined the sequence of the four seasons' first, middle, and last months,
to establish the order between elder and younger and form officialdom.
They divided the land into provinces,
and partitioned the states to govern them,
establishing the Great Academy to teach in them.
These are the guiding principles of governance.
When the Way is obtained, they are implemented;
when the Way is lost, they are abandoned.
《Wénzǐ》
According to the object and the person
The ruler does not leave his chamber yet understands all under heaven because
he comprehends things through other things,
and knows people through other people.
Thus, when efforts are accumulated for an undertaking,
there is nothing that cannot be overcome;
when the wisdom of the multitude is employed for a task,
there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
A group of a thousand people will not lack provisions,
and a multitude of ten thousand will not waste their efforts.
The sovereign
Like rivers and seas
In ancient times, those skilled at being rulers followed the example of rivers and seas;
rivers and seas act without action, thereby achieving their vast capacity,
and by staying low, they achieve their breadth.
Thus they can endure long,
serving as the valleys and gorges for all under heaven.
Their virtue then becomes sufficient;
by acting without action, they can receive all streams;
by not seeking, they can obtain;
by not traveling, they can reach.
Therefore, they take all under heaven without exertion;
by not esteeming themselves, they become rich;
by not displaying themselves, they become illustrious;
by not boasting, they endure long.
Residing in a place of not possessing, they become kings of all under heaven;
by not contending, none can contend with them;
ultimately, by not striving for greatness, they can achieve their greatness.
Wénzǐ
Power and Influence
The state is the most valuable instrument in the world,
and the ruler
holds the most advantageous position in the world.
If he upholds them with the Way, there will be great security
and great honor,
a source of accumulated excellence.
If he does not uphold them with the Way, there will be great danger
and great burden.
It would be better to be without them than to have them without security.
When they are lost,
he cannot even hope to become a commoner.
"Xúnzǐ"
The prosperity of the state
The ruler is the exalted one of the state,
the father is the exalted one of the family.
With one exalted, there is order;
with two, chaos.
From above
Guiding Benefits
Ruì Liàngfū remonstrated with King Lì, saying:
A ruler of men
should guide benefits and distribute them among high and low,
so that spirits, people, and all things may each attain their proper place.
Yet daily he remains cautious and fearful of incurring resentment.
If a commoner monopolizes benefits, he is called a robber.
If the king acts thus,
his support will be scant.
"Discourses of Zhou"
Orthodoxy and Heterodoxy
Lǐ Gé said:
"A ruler is one
who shepherds the people and corrects their wrongdoings.
If the ruler indulges personal crookedness and neglects the people's affairs,
the people will all harbor wickedness,
with no means to examine it,
then wrongdoings will multiply greatly.
What use will he be then?"
From "Lǔyǔ"
Illuminate virtue and block impropriety
Zāng Āibó said:
"A ruler of men,
should manifest virtue and suppress transgression to illuminate all,
yet officials still fear they may fail in this,
therefore he manifests illustrious virtue to show his descendants,
so officials become vigilant and apprehensive,
and dare not disregard discipline.
Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Huán, Year 2"
The Way of the Sovereign
Duke Píng of Jìn asked Shī Kuàng, saying:
"What is the way of a ruler?"
He replied:
"The way of a ruler
is to be clear and tranquil, acting through non-action,
devoting oneself to universal love,
and hastening to appoint the worthy.
Broaden your sight and hearing to observe all directions,
do not be obstinately mired in popular customs,
nor bound and fettered by those around you.
Be expansive and far-seeing,
stand alone, lofty and outstanding.
Repeatedly examine and assess achievements to oversee your ministers.
This is the conduct of a ruler."
Duke Píng said, "Excellent."
From "Shuō Yuàn"
The affairs of the ruler
King Xuān of Qí said to Yǐn Wén:
What should a ruler's affairs be like?
Yǐn Wén replied:
A ruler's affairs should be non-interventionist and able to tolerate subordinates,
for with few affairs people find it easy to follow, and with simple laws they find it easy to comply,
so the people do not incur punishment due to governance,
the great Way tolerates the multitude,
great virtue tolerates subordinates,
the sage does little yet the world is well-governed,
King Xuān said: Excellent.
Administrator
When the state of Wèi expelled Duke Xiàn,
Duke Dào of Jìn said to Shī Kuàng:
"The people of Wèi have driven out their ruler,
is this not excessive?"
He replied:
"Perhaps it is actually their ruler who was excessive.
Heaven gives birth to the people and establishes rulers for them,
to shepherd and govern them,
not letting them lose their nature.
A good ruler will reward the good and remove the people's troubles,
loving the people as his own children,
sheltering them like heaven, containing them like earth.
The people serve their ruler,
loving him as their parents,
looking up to him as to the sun and moon,
revering him as a deity,
fearing him as thunder.
Now the ruler is the host of the spirits,
and the people look to him.
Heaven's love for the people is profound indeed;
how could it allow one man to act recklessly over the people,
indulging his excesses and abandoning the nature of heaven and earth?
This certainly cannot be.
If he oppresses the people's nature,
neglects the sacrifices to the spirits,
leaves the common people in despair,
and the altars of soil and grain without a host,
then what use is he?
If they do not remove him, what else should they do?"
The Duke said, "Well spoken."
From "Xīn Xù"
Three Fears
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The enlightened king has three fears:
first, being in a high position yet fearing he might not hear of his faults;
second, achieving his ambitions yet fearing arrogance;
third, hearing the ultimate Way of the world yet fearing he cannot practice it.
These three fears
are the concerns of an enlightened ruler."
Hánshī Wàizhuàn
Four Arts
There are four methods to govern the world:
the first is loyalty and love,
the second is selflessness,
the third is employing the worthy,
the fourth is measurement and judgment.
Facilitating wealth and ensuring sufficiency,
employing the worthy yields many achievements without selfishness,
it is the source of all wisdom,
loyalty and love,
are the conduct of rulers and fathers.
"Shīzǐ"
Xiāngōng
In ancient times, when the former sage kings governed the world,
they always prioritized impartiality.
Impartiality brings peace to the world.
Let us observe those in high positions:
many have aspired to rule the world,
and those who attained it did so through impartiality,
while those who lost it did so due to partiality.
The establishment of any ruler
arises from impartiality.
Thus, the Hóng Fàn states:
"Be without bias, without factions."
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū"
Yú Cè
Power is the ruler's carriage; authority is
the ruler's whip; ministers are
the ruler's horses; the people are
the ruler's wheels. When power is consolidated, the carriage is stable;
when authority is established, the whip is effective;
when ministers are obedient, the horses are fine;
when the people are harmonious, the wheels are smooth.
If a state loses these,
there will inevitably be the disaster of overturned carriages, runaway horses,
broken wheels, and ruined loads—
how can it avoid peril?
《Dèng Xīzǐ》
takes the throne as the carriage,
power as the horses,
commands as the reins,
and punishments as the whip.
If Yáo or Shùn drove it, the world would be well-governed;
if Jié or Zhòu drove it, the world would fall into chaos—
thus, the difference between the worthy and the unworthy is vast.
《Hán Fēizǐ》
The state is the ruler's carriage;
power is the ruler's horses.
If one does not employ power to prohibit and punish,
but instead indulges favored ministers and insists on excessive benevolence,
competing with the world for the people's allegiance,
this is like not riding in the ruler's carriage,
not utilizing the advantage of the horses,
and abandoning the carriage to walk on foot.
The Five Blockages
A ruler faces five types of obstruction:
ministers who isolate their ruler are obstructing ministers,
those who control wealth and profits are obstructing ministers,
those who presume to issue commands are obstructing ministers,
those who appropriate the practice of righteousness are obstructing ministers,
those who cultivate personal followings are obstructing ministers.
Isolating the ruler causes the ruler to lose his position,
ministers controlling wealth and profits causes the ruler to lose beneficence,
ministers presuming to issue commands causes the ruler to lose control,
ministers appropriating righteousness causes the ruler to lose reputation,
ministers cultivating followings causes the ruler to lose supporters.
These are matters the ruler alone should control,
not what ministers should be allowed to manipulate.
Three Paths
The sage's methods for governing are three:
first is benefit,
second is authority,
third is reputation.
Benefit is what wins the people's support,
authority is what enforces orders,
reputation is what superiors and subordinates share in common.
Apart from these three,
though there may be other measures, they are not urgent.
The ruler
Two Handles
The means by which an enlightened ruler guides and controls his ministers
are but two handles.
These two handles
are punishment and favor.
Killing and execution are called punishment;
commendation and reward are called favor.
When an enlightened ruler bestows rewards,
they are as warm as timely rain,
and the people benefit from their moisture;
when he carries out punishments,
they are as fearsome as thunderclaps,
which even the divine and sage cannot evade.
Thus, the enlightened ruler grants no careless rewards
and pardons no punishments.
If rewards are given carelessly, then meritorious ministers will neglect their duties;
if punishments are pardoned, then wicked people will easily commit wrongs.
Therefore, if one is truly meritorious, even if distant or lowly, he must be rewarded;
if one is truly at fault, even if close or beloved, he must be executed.
If the close and beloved are executed when at fault,
then the distant and lowly will not be negligent,
and the close and beloved will not become arrogant.
Personal observation
If a ruler personally oversees all officials,
then his days will be insufficient and his strength inadequate.
Moreover, if the ruler uses his eyes, those below will embellish appearances;
if the ruler uses his ears, those below will embellish sounds;
if the ruler uses his thoughts, those below will multiply words.
The former kings considered these three methods insufficient,
therefore they abandoned their personal abilities and relied on laws and methods,
carefully administering rewards and punishments.
This was the essential principle the former kings upheld,
hence laws were concise yet not infringed upon,
and they alone governed all within the Four Seas.
The clever and intelligent could not employ their deceit,
the treacherous and impulsive could not practice their flattery,
and the wicked and corrupt had nothing to rely on.
Even those a thousand miles away
dared not alter their reports;
those in positions close to the ruler
dared not conceal the good or disguise the bad.
All officials at court directly served the ruler,
none daring to overstep their boundaries.
Thus, governance seemed effortless yet was said to be abundant,
all because the ruler employed his power to make it so.
The ruler
To achieve merit and establish fame
The enlightened ruler achieves merit and fame through four factors:
first, opportune timing;
second, popular support;
third, ability and skill;
fourth, position and power.
Thus, with opportune timing, one thrives without striving;
with popular support, one is encouraged without urging;
relying on ability, one acts swiftly without haste;
with position and power, fame is achieved without promotion.
Like water flowing,
like a boat floating,
they uphold the natural way,
enacting inexhaustible decrees.
Hence, they are called enlightened rulers.
End
The steps are hurried.
The Three Sovereigns paced, the Five Emperors trotted,
the Three Kings galloped,
the Five Hegemons raced.
Some were called Emperors,
and when addressing Heaven, they called themselves the Son of Heaven,
making clear their duty to serve Heaven through their rank.
When addressing their subjects, they called themselves Sovereigns or Emperors,
making clear their authority to command the officials.
"The Unspoken Destiny of the Classic of Filial Piety"
Yīng Huá Gēn Hé
The emperor obtains its essence,
the king obtains its core,
the hegemon obtains its appendages.
Heart
Thus, if the Way of the Emperors is not practiced, one cannot become a true king;
if the Way of True Kings is not practiced, one cannot become a hegemon;
if the Way of Hegemons is not practiced, one cannot even preserve oneself.
"Lǐ Dǒu Wēi Yí"
Rén Dé
The emperor does not prioritize righteousness but relies on the Way and its power,
the king does not prioritize strength but esteems humaneness and righteousness,
and the hegemon does not prioritize rectitude but esteems military force.
"Lúnyǔ Zhāi Fǔ Xiàng"
Míng Yī
He who embodies unity is a Sovereign;
he who investigates the Way is an Emperor;
he who comprehends virtue is a King;
he who achieves plans and triumphs in war is a Hegemon.
"Guǎnzǐ"
Centered
A ruler who humbles himself in ritual and honors the worthy becomes a true king,
one who emphasizes laws and loves the people becomes a hegemon,
while one who is fond of profit and frequently deceitful faces peril.
To be close to all four directions, nothing is better than the center;
therefore, a true king must reside at the heart of the world.
"Xúnzǐ"
Establishing Righteousness
He who governs a state with righteousness established becomes a true king;
with trustworthiness established, he becomes a hegemon;
with schemes and machinations established, he perishes.
These three are what an enlightened king carefully chooses among.
"Xúnzǐ"
Pure, one becomes a true king;
mixed, one becomes a hegemon;
possessing neither, one perishes.
Above
Embodiment of Tàiyī
The emperor embodies the Great One,
the king models himself on yin and yang,
the hegemon follows the four seasons,
the ruler employs the six pitch standards.
Those who uphold the Great One
encompass heaven and earth,
control mountains and rivers,
contain and emit yin and yang,
extend and pull the four seasons,
regulate the eight extremities,
order the six directions,
shelter, dew, illuminate, and guide,
universally spreading without partiality.
Flying and crawling creatures
all look up to their virtue and live.
Yin and yang receive the harmony of heaven and earth,
form bodies of myriad differences,
contain qi and transform things,
to complete all categories.
Waxing and waning, coiling and stretching,
they sink into the immeasurable;
ending and beginning, empty and full,
they revolve without origin.
Following the four seasons means
spring for growth, summer for development,
autumn for harvest, winter for storage,
taking and giving with moderation,
exiting and entering with timing,
opening and closing, expanding and contracting,
without losing their sequence.
Joy, anger, firmness, and flexibility do not depart from their principle.
Using the six pitch standards gives life
and death,
reward and punishment,
giving and taking away.
Without this, there is no way.
Therefore, be careful with scales and standards,
examine lightness and heaviness,
sufficient to govern within their borders.
Huáinánzǐ
Those who embody the Great One
understand the conditions of heaven and earth,
penetrate the principles of the Way and virtue,
their intelligence shines like the sun and moon,
their spirit connects with all things,
their movement and stillness harmonize with yin and yang,
their joy and anger accord with the four seasons.
Sheltering and dewing, all follow the Way, pervasive and impartial;
flying and crawling creatures all rely on their virtue to live.
Their virtuous influence flows beyond the borders,
their fame is transmitted to later ages.
Modeling on yin and yang means receiving the harmony of heaven and earth,
virtue matching heaven and earth,
participating in brightness, shining alongside the sun and moon,
spirit equaling the numinousness of ghosts and gods.
Wearing the round, treading the square,
embracing the mark, resting on the line,
internally able to order the self,
externally winning people's hearts.
Issuing commands,
the world follows like the wind.
Following the four seasons means spring for growth, summer for development,
autumn for harvest, winter for storage,
taking and giving with moderation,
exiting and entering with measure,
joy, anger, firmness, flexibility,
not departing from their principle,
soft but not brittle,
firm but not breaking.
Huáinán zuò guì
Broad but not unrestrained,
stern but not perverse,
leisurely and compliant to nurture all kinds,
their virtue embraces the foolish and tolerates the unworthy,
without any private affection.
Using the six pitch standards means punishing disorder and prohibiting violence,
promoting the worthy and abolishing the unworthy,
correcting the crooked to make them straight,
removing danger to achieve peace,
straightening the bent to make them upright.
Understanding the way of giving and withholding, opening and blocking,
they seize the time and follow the situation to serve and employ people's hearts.
If the emperor does not embody yin and yang, he is encroached upon;
if the king does not model on the four seasons, he is diminished;
if the hegemon does not use the six pitch standards, he is disgraced;
if the ruler loses the standards, he is abandoned.
Therefore, if the small practices the great,
they become constrained and alienated;
if the great practices the small,
they become narrow and intolerable.
Wénzǐ
Governance by the Way and transformation through virtue
In ancient times, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors were spoken of first, followed by the Three Kings and Five Hegemons,
all of whom were the foremost rulers of the world.
Thus, it is said that the Three Sovereigns governed through the Way,
the Five Emperors transformed through virtue,
the Three Kings acted with benevolence and righteousness,
and the Five Hegemons employed strategy and wisdom.
The explanation states: having no decrees or punishments is called being a Sovereign;
having decrees but no punishments is called being an Emperor;
rewarding the good, punishing the evil, and having feudal lords pay court is called being a King;
raising armies, forming alliances, and correcting the age with trust and righteousness is called being a Hegemon.
"King" means "to go to,"
indicating that their grace and favor are abundant and far-reaching,
so the world turns to them.
The Kingly Way is pure and unadulterated,
its virtue is like that,
while the Hegemonic Way is mixed and impure,
its achievements are like this,
yet both possess the world and rule over the myriad people,
handing down their legacy to their descendants.
In essence, they are the same.
If aiming for kingship fails,
one can still achieve hegemony.
From Huán Tán's Xīn Lùn.
Advantages and Disadvantages of Steps
The Book of Changes states that Heaven brings spring before autumn,
the earth produces growth before decay,
the sun and moon provide light before darkness,
thus the king models himself upon this,
also implementing education before punishment.
The Three Sovereigns used knotted cords,
the Five Emperors employed symbolic images,
the Three Kings imposed corporal punishments,
the Five Hegemons practiced cunning strategies,

who rule over Jambudvīpa.
The third are the Copper-wheel Kings, who govern two continents.
The fourth are the Silver-wheel Kings, who transform three continents.
The fifth are the Gold-wheel Kings, who rule over all four continents.

Far and ancient was Huángdì Xuānyuán,
Responding to Heaven, bearing divine power.
Qiān Xiù's "Ode to Huángdì"
Dé Guàn
Huángdì's virtue crowned him as emperor.
"Chūnqiū Hé Chéng Tú"
Harmonizing the sun and moon
Huángdì governed the world with the assistance of Lì Mù and Tàishān Jī.
In the Huáinánzǐ,
he harmonized the movements of the sun and moon,
regulated the energies of yīn and yáng,
moderated the measures of the four seasons,
corrected the calculations of pitch standards and calendars,
distinguished men from women and clarified the roles of superiors and subordinates,
ensuring the strong did not oppress the weak,
the many did not bully the few,
so the people preserved their lives without premature death,
the harvests ripened annually without calamity,
officials were upright and impartial,
the upper and lower classes were harmonious without resentment,
laws and decrees were clear and not obscure,
assistants were just and not sycophantic,
farmers yielded field boundaries,
no one picked up lost items on the road,
merchants did not inflate prices in the market.
Thus, at this time,
the sun, moon, and stars did not stray from their courses,
winds and rains came in season,
the five grains flourished abundantly,
phoenixes soared in the courtyards,
and qílins roamed the suburbs.
In the Wénzǐ,
green dragons drew carriages,
flying steeds were stabled in their stalls,
and countries as far as the northern Dān Ěr
all presented their tribute and taxes.
Huáinánzǐ
Orchid Mat
Huángdì had the hundred officials and assembled ministers,
those receiving virtuous teachings first arranged jade tablets on the orchid mat,
lit sinking-elm incense above them,
pounded assorted treasures into powder,
using sinking-elm resin,
mixed it into paste to smear on the ground,
distinguishing positions of nobility and baseness, Chinese and foreign.
"Supplemented Lost Records from the Fengshan Chronicles"
Wáng Róng's memorial states:
Heaven shifted and clouds stirred,
carving the Feng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
unifying the Five Emperors and surpassing the Three Sovereigns,
gathering seventy assemblies with three torches on orchid mats,
hearing the auspicious sound of ten thousand years,
is this not magnificent?
"Book of Southern Qí"
on all sides
Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
"The ancient Huángdì had four faces,
is this true?"
Confucius replied:
"Huángdì selected four men who suited him,
and set them to govern the four directions.
Without consulting each other they were intimate,
without making arrangements they achieved success.
They achieved great success,
this is what is meant by 'four faces'."
The Shīzǐ
and the Lǚshì Chūnqiū state:
"Huángdì established four faces."
Three hundred years
Zǎi Wǒ asked Confucius, saying:
In the past, I heard from Róng Yī that:
Huángdì lived for three hundred years.
May I ask, was Huángdì a human?
Or was he not human?
How could he have lived for three hundred years?
The Master said:
During his life, the people benefited from his advantages for
one hundred years;
after his death, the people revered his spirit for one hundred years;
after his passing, the people followed his teachings for one hundred years.
Therefore, it is said he lived for three hundred years.
From "The Book of Rites by Dai the Elder"
Nine Conducts
Huángdì established four historians to manage maps and records,
appointing practitioners of the nine virtues to govern all states.
The nine virtues were filial piety, kindness, cultural integrity, loyalty, respect, courage, righteousness, observing heaven and earth,
and worshipping all spirits,
thus creating ministers of the nine virtues.
"Shí Yí Jì"
He entrusted Fēng and Lì
and appointed Fēnghòu, Lìmù, Chángxiān, and Dàhóng to govern the people.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Huángdì dreamed of a great wind blowing,
sweeping away all the dust and grime from the world,
and also dreamed of a man holding a thousand-jun crossbow,
driving tens of thousands of sheep.
Awakening with a sigh, the Emperor said:
"Wind represents the one who issues commands and governs,
while the removal of grime signifies that the land will have a ruler.
Could there be someone named Fēnghòu (Wind Ruler) in the world?"
"As for the thousand-jun crossbow,
it symbolizes extraordinary strength,
and driving tens of thousands of sheep
represents the ability to shepherd the people toward goodness.
Could there be someone named Lìmù (Strength Shepherd) in the world?"
Thereupon, following these two interpretations, he sought them out,
finding Fēnghòu by the seashore,
and appointing him as chancellor;
he found Lìmù in the great marsh,
and promoted him as general.
"Chronicles of Emperors and Kings"
Huángdì studied under Fēnghòu,
who was well-versed in the ways of Fúxī,
thus he elaborated on the principles of yin and yang.
"Spring and Autumn Annals: Inner Affairs"
Huángdì observed the celestial bodies above to trace their paths,
and discerned fortune and misfortune below,
systematizing the calendar and numerology,
after which the movements of heaven became regular,
all achieved through Fēnghòu's efforts.
"Biography of Hòu Zhǎnghéng"
Huángdì obtained Lìmù and thus became one of the Five Emperors,
just as Dà Yǔ earlier obtained Gāo
and Yáo, becoming ancestors of the Three Sovereigns.
"Biography of Qián Cháocuò"
The reason Huángdì could rule the world effortlessly
was because he entrusted Fēng and Lì;
the reason Emperor Yáo could gloriously possess the world
was because he entrusted Jì and Xiè.
"Old Book of Tang: Biography of Lú Huáishèn"
Táo Tiānxià
Huángdì asked Bógāo, saying:
I wish to mold the world into a single family,
is there a way to do this?
Bógāo replied:
Please cut down the sedge and plant it anew,
I shall carefully evade its fangs,
then the world can be molded into a single family.
Guǎnzǐ
Unite with the spirits and gods
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor assembled spirits and deities atop Mount Tài,
riding an elephant-drawn chariot with six蛟龍 dragons,
Bìfāng birds harnessed alongside,
Chīyóu positioned at the front,
the Wind God swept the path ahead,
the Rain Master sprinkled the road,
tigers and wolves leading the way,
spirits and deities following behind,
flying snakes prostrate on the ground,
phoenixes hovering above,
gathering all spirits and deities in grand assembly,
to create the "Clear Horn" music.
From "Hánfēizǐ: Ten Faults"
Establishing Laws
When the Yellow Emperor governed the world,
his people came without being summoned,
and went without being urged.
They accomplished tasks without being directed,
and ceased without being forbidden.
Thus, under the Yellow Emperor's governance,
he established laws without altering them,
enabling the people to abide peacefully by these laws.
"Guanzi: On Relying on Law"
Ask about the Way
Huángdì heard that Guǎngchéngzǐ was upon Mount Kōngtóng,
so he went to see him and said:
"I have heard that you, my master, have attained the ultimate Way.
I venture to ask about the essence of the ultimate Way.
I wish to take the essence of Heaven and Earth to assist the five grains,
in order to nourish the people.
I also wish to govern yīn and yáng to fulfill the lives of all beings.
How should this be done?
How can one govern the body so that it may endure long?"
Guǎngchéngzǐ started up abruptly and said:
"The essence of the ultimate Way
is deep and obscure;
the pinnacle of the ultimate Way
is dim and silent.
Zhuāngzǐ
Roaming the Celestial Thoroughfare
Huángdì traveled the celestial thoroughfare,
playing the drums of the heavenly music,
raising the banners of the sun and moon,
riding a chariot of carved clouds,
driving a six-winged dragon,
with Péng Zǔ leading the way,
and Sōng Qiáo flanking the wheels.
The light and shadows flowed by unseen,
the long winds chased but could not catch up.
Setting out from the Purple Palace,
he circled the six directions before a single morning passed.
"Sūn Zǐzǐ"
He went to Kūnyú.
Huángdì was about to journey to the hills of Kūnyú,
when midway he encountered Róngchéngzǐ,
riding under a canopy of kingfisher-feather splendor,
bearing banners adorned with the sun and moon,
steering a pair of birds with purple dragons as outriders.
Huángdì commanded Fāngmíng to clear the way,
and said to Róngchéngzǐ:
"I intend to angle for fish in a single gully,
and perch upon a single hill."
From "Fúzǐ"
Lóng Xiāng
In the early days of Huángdì,
he cultivated his nature and nurtured the people,
disliking warfare and conquest.
Yet the four emperors, each identified by the color of their respective regions,
joined forces to plot against him.
Border towns were alarmed daily,
and armor was never removed.
Huángdì sighed and said:
"When the ruler is endangered above,
the people cannot live in peace below.
If a lord loses his state,
his ministers will remarry elsewhere.
Is the root of this ailment
not the nurturing of bandits?
Now, positioned above the common people,
with four brigands opposing me,
repeatedly shaking my army,
I shall thus establish camps to eliminate the four emperors.
Had Huángdì not risen like a dragon and transformed like a tiger, but instead followed the common path,
his people would have been wedded to the four emperors."
"Jiǎng Zǐ Wàn Jī Lùn"
Huáng Líng
"Rhapsody on Contemplating the Mysterious":
The Yellow Spirit arrived and sought fate,
Searching for the Way of Heaven, where would it lead? Annotation:
The Yellow Spirit refers to the Yellow Emperor,
"arrived" means reached,
"sought" means consulted,
"searching" means seeking,
"where" indicates direction,
"would it lead" expresses inquiry about the path.
Huáng Yán
Huángdì and Yándì thus employed water and fire.
Gònggōng shì indeed subsequently initiated rebellion,
the Five Emperors certainly struggled against each other,
successively rising and falling, with the victors assuming power.
"Lǚlǎn Dàng Bīng"
Now warfare
is the means to prohibit violence and punish rebellion.
Yándì caused fire disasters,
therefore Huángdì captured him;

"Huáinánzǐ"
Hereditary succession
Gàn Bǎo's "Discussion on Dynastic Change" from the Jin Dynasty states:
Hóng and Huáng passed down through generations to unify the people,
Huángdì abdicated internally,
embodying civil virtue.
"Annals of Jin"
"Zuǒ Zhuàn: Shǐ Kè" says:
In the past, Emperor Hóng had an unworthy son Jiǎ Kuí.
Dù Yù states:
Emperor Hóng is Huángdì,
According to "Shānhǎi Jīng":
Dì Jùn gave birth to Dì Hóng,
Dì Hóng gave birth to Báimín.
Gàn mentions generations passing down, thus Jiǎ and Dù seem mistaken in the Táng,
Féng Xíngguī's commentary on "Yùzǐ":
says Xuānyuánshì Shào Diǎn,
second son's father called Dì Hóngshì,
Lùshì,
claims Dì Hóng was Huángdì's son,

The Three Cardinal Guides
Emperor Yándì divided the year into eight periods to initiate agriculture,
and Emperor Huángdì established the three fundamental bonds to elucidate writing and covenants.
"Jìn Treatises on Pitch and Calendar"
Method of Preparation
The impoverished sage spirits, endowed with virtue, nurtured the sprouts of morality,
as primordial energy opened up the Great Beginning,
this was how the Heavenly Sovereign Shì responded to Heaven.
Relying on the earth and illuminating divine spirits,
he harnessed six wings to soar upward,
traversing the nine provinces to descend and aid below,
this was how the Human Sovereign Shì complied with humanity.
Creating written records and teaching hunting and fishing,
he harmonized the five planets to regulate the four seasons,
ascended the nine heavens to categorize all things,
this was how the Ox-Tamer Sovereign Shì established human laws.
Devoted to sowing and cultivation, encompassing adaptation,
he tasted herbs to save the multitudes,
gathered goods to interact with all under heaven,
this was how the Farming Sovereign Shì promoted human welfare.
Shaking the Kui drum and bearing the dragon banner,
Heaven had the Mysterious Maiden bestow talismans,
the Emperor had the Yellow Spirit descend with the Dipper,
this was how Xuānyuán Shì eliminated human calamities.
《Cuī Róng's Inscription for the Qǐ Mother Temple》
Seize the opportunity
When the time is right to establish teachings,
a great sage is bound to emerge,
to lead the way.
Fúxī Shì cultivated talents and illuminated culture,
ruling over people and serving Heaven;
Shénnóng followed this,
initiating imperial rule while embodying the ultimate Way.
Xuānyuán Shì devised divination and appointed officials,
regulating directions and aligning with cosmic order;
Zhuānxū upheld this,
initiating imperial governance while emulating profound virtue.
"Cháng Zhòngrú's Stele of the Temple of King Wenxuan"
Speechless
The Three Sovereigns governed without words, yet their influence spread across the four seas,
thus no credit was claimed in the world.
The Emperors embodied the ways of Heaven and Earth,
issuing decrees and commands,
bringing peace to the world,
with rulers and ministers deferring credit to one another,
their transformative influence pervading the four seas,
while the common people remained unaware of how this came to be.
The Seven Military Classics
Five Emperors
Huángdì, Shàohào, Zhuānxū, Dìkù, Tángyáo, Yúshùn are considered the Five Emperors.
Though there are six individuals, they are referred to as the Five Emperors
because they all correspond to the Five Emperor Star seats.
According to Kǎng Chéng,
Huángdì, Zhuānxū, Dìkù, Tángyáo, Yúshùn are the Five Emperors.
The Records of the Grand Historian
lists Shàohào, Zhuānxū, Gāoxīn, Tángyáo, and Yúshùn as the Five Emperors.
Kǒng Ānguó
Kǎng Chéng regarded Nǚwā as a sovereign,
and Xuānyuán as an emperor.
Since Xuānyuán's virtue was not inferior to Nǚwā's,
why was he not titled sovereign,
but instead relegated to emperor,
making a total of six individuals?
Sīmǎ Qiān omitted Shàohào from the recent era while including Huángdì from antiquity,
which is quite negligent.
Only Ānguó's account is considered definitive.
From the Jiānmíng Shū
Sacred
The Five Emperors were divine and sagely,
and none of their ministers could match them,
so they personally attended to affairs in the Hall of Laws,
in the Hall of Enlightenment,
their actions aligned with Heaven above and conformed to Earth below,
and they attained harmony among humans,
thus all living beings were covered,
and all rooted creatures were supported,
illuminated with light without partiality or bias,
their virtue reached up to the flying birds,
and down to the aquatic creatures, plants, and all products,
all were bathed in their grace,
then yin and yang were harmonized,
the four seasons were regulated,
the sun and moon shone, wind and rain came timely, and sweet dew descended,
the five grains ripened, and calamities vanished,
thieves perished, and the people were free from illness and epidemics,
the River produced the Diagram, the Luo produced the Writing,
divine dragons arrived,
phoenixes soared,
virtue and grace filled the world,
and numinous light spread throughout the four seas.
This is called matching Heaven and Earth,
the great achievement of governing the state.
From the "Biography of Cháo Cuò" in the Book of Hàn.
The Transformation of the Dào
In the era of the Five Emperors, the Way and transformation were pure and complete.
The Gǔliáng Commentary notes
Zhū Xuān
The River Chart says:
The White Emperor Zhū Xuān.
Sòng Jūn says:
It refers to Shǎohào.
In Wáng Yuáncháng's "Essay on Selecting Scholars," the five regulations were established under Zhū Xuān,
so the common people were without error.
Shǎohào
Qióngsāngshì, surname Yíng,
ruled by virtue of metal,
hence titled Jīntiānshì,
also called Zōngshī.
Following the ways of Tàihào,
thus known as Shàohào.
"Gǔ Shǐ Kǎo"
records Shàohào as ruling the west,
also named Jīntiānshì.
Also called Jīnqióngshì,
when five phoenixes of directional colors gathered at the imperial court,
thus titled Fèngniǎoshì.
"Shí Yí Jì"
Diligently serving the people
In ancient times, Jīntiān was diligent in the people's affairs,
appointing the Spring Bailiff to summon for plowing and sowing,
the Summer Bailiff for weeding and hoeing,
the Autumn Bailiff for harvesting and gathering,
and the Winter Bailiff for storing and preserving.
"Jìn Treatise on Food and Money"
Presenting Fur Garments
Shǎohào's capital was at Qūfù,
where the Jiàndī hairy people presented their feathered fur garments,
and the Qúshōu people, submitting to Yǔ's virtue,
presented their precious fur garments,
with fur displaying five colors.
"Tián Qiúzǐ"
When the king upholds the five elements and teaches the people to plant cypress trees,
in due time the Qúshōu come to present fur garments;
when virtue flourishes and one is not ashamed of coarse clothing,
then the four barbarian tribes present their white fur garments.
"Sūnshì Ruìtú"
Severing the Connection between Heaven and Earth
Chǔ Guàn Yìfù said:
When Shǎohào was in decline,
the Jiǔlí disrupted virtue,
humans and spirits intermingled chaotically,
making it impossible to distinguish things.
(The Hànshū writes it as "fàng")
Every household acted as shamans and scribes,
sacrifices were performed without restraint,
defiling the pure offerings so the spirits would not accept them,
while misfortunes and disasters repeatedly descended without cease.
Zhuanxū inherited this situation,
then appointed the Southern Director Zhòng to oversee heaven and manage the spirits,
and the Fire Director Lí to oversee earth and govern the people,
restoring the old norms without
mutual infringement and defilement.
This is called "cutting off the connection between heaven and earth."
(From the Chǔyǔ and earlier Jiāosìzhì)
Paying homage to the spirits
Zhuānxū's reign was marked by extraordinary auspicious signs,
and all blessings converged without exception.
Those who did not follow the official calendar
crossed mountains and sailed seas to arrive.
The Emperor then paid respects to the spirits of the four directions,
with feudal lords holding jade tablets to ceremoniously receive the numerous officials,
each arranged in proper order.
Those who embraced civil virtue were bestowed with bells and chimes,
while those who upheld martial virtue were granted shields and spears.
"Shí Yí"
The Way of Causality
In ancient times, Emperor Zhuānxū,
at the age of fifteen assisted the Yellow Emperor,
and at twenty governed the world.
In his governance of the world,
he followed the ways of the Yellow Emperor and implemented them,
studied the principles of the Yellow Emperor and consistently upheld them.
From "Yùzǐ"
Day by day with increasing caution
Zhuānxū said:
No merit is greater than abandoning evil to do good,
and no crime is greater than abandoning good to do evil.
Therefore, it is not that I merely praise goodness,
but that goodness follows goodness;
nor is it that I merely condemn evil,
but that evil follows evil.
I become more cautious with each passing day,
and that is all.
Jiǎ Tàifù Xīnshū
Model Heaven and Earth
A gentleman inquired about the Twelve Almanacs, and Lord Wénxìn said:
I have studied how Huángdì instructed Zhuānxū.
There is the great circle above,
and the great square below—
can you emulate them?
To be a parent to the people,
I have heard that in the orderly ages of antiquity,
they modeled themselves on heaven and earth.
All twelve almanacs
record order and chaos, survival and demise.
(The Annals of Lǚ)
Inscribed Vessels
In the first year of the Tiānhé era, an imperial edict stated:
In ancient times, when the King of Zhōu received the Mandate,
he inquired about the temple of Zhuānxū,
where there was a vessel warning against excess,
and the hall bore inscriptions on restoring rites.
From the "History of the Later Zhōu Dynasty"
Emperor Kù
In the past, Emperor Kù assisted the emperor at the age of fifteen,
and governed the world at thirty.
In governing the world,
he followed the ways of the Yellow Emperor and elucidated them,
studied the ways of Emperor Zhuānxū and practiced them.
"Yùzǐ"
Xìnrén
Emperor Kù said:
No virtue is higher than universal love for people,
and no governance is higher than universal benefit for people.
Therefore nothing is greater in governance than trustworthiness,
nothing is greater in rule than benevolence.
I am simply cautious about these matters.
from "New Writings of Grand Tutor Jiǎ"
On the Three Luminaries
Zhuānxū's minister bore the weight of office,
his title was Gāoxīn,
his duty was divine and numinous,
his virtue was reverent and solemn,
he welcomed and escorted the sun and moon,
following the laws of heaven,
able to order the three luminaries to secure the people.
《Qiánfū Lùn》
Dài Gàn
Emperor Kù had double teeth, a superior method,
the sun participated in upholding measures to complete the calendar, thereby ordering yin and yang.
"The River Chart's Square Emergence"
Emperor Kù wore a shield on his head,
this was called clarity and brightness,
issuing nodes and shifting measures,
resembling the constellation Zhāoyáo.
"The Unwrought Destiny"
Dàodé
Emperor Kù possessed the world and was called Gāoxīn,
Gāoxīn means
great integrity in virtue and morality,
Kù means ultimate,
indicating his ability to implement and exhaust the ultimate Way.
In the Báihǔ Tōng,
Kù means to examine,
and to perfect,
meaning he examined and clarified laws and institutions with pure excellence,
like the fragrance of fine wine.
From the Fēngsú Tōng.
Huáng Táng
Since ancient times, Huángdì and Tángyáo governed myriad states,
harmonizing east and west,
and demarcating north and south.
The "Former Narrative"
states the Hàn dynasty's foundation was elevated from Fúxī,
and its institutions broader than Huángdì and Tángyáo.
From Bān Gù's "Admonitions for Guests"
the five-rank system began with Huángdì and Tángyáo.
Lù Jī's "Discourse on the Five Ranks"
notes the Zhōu dynasty, learning from Xià and Yīn's longevity,
followed Huángdì and Tángyáo's parallel establishment.
Táng dynasty Lǐ Bǎiyào's "On Feudalism"
Jí Yáo
During the reigns of Jí Yáo,
the finest treasures of Hùnwú lay below,
their principles not unique to that era alone.
Mountains remained untouched yet barren,
marshes unspoiled yet provided ample sustenance.
"Extravagance and Waste" from Guǎnzǐ
Táo Táng
Yáo first lived in Táng and later moved to Táo Qiū,
hence he was called the Táo Táng clan.
In the "Yuán Hé Jùn Xiàn Zhì"
it is recorded that he examined the heavenly principles above,
descended to receive the dragon's support,
and his brilliance is manifested in the canonical texts,
making his virtue preeminent and unparalleled.
In "Wǔ Chén Zuò Chuò"
none is more revered than Táo Táng.
From "Bān Gù Bīn Xì"
Clear Laws
In ancient times, when Yáo governed the world,
it was like clay in the potter's hands,
subject only to the potter's actions;
it was like metal in the furnace,
freely molded by the smith to cast his people.
He drew them near or pushed them away,
enabled them to achieve or restrained them from acting.
Thus, Yáo's governance
was simply about perfecting clear laws and prohibitions.
"Guǎnzǐ: Rèn Fǎ"
Roaming at Fén River
Yáo governed the people under heaven,
and brought order to the administration within the four seas.
He went to see the four masters on Mount Miǎogūyè,
north of the Fén River,
and became oblivious of his empire in the remote distance.
"Zhuāngzǐ: Free and Easy Wandering"
The four masters: Wángní, Nièquē, Bèiyī, and Xǔyóu.
Annotation:
Embracing the primordial is greatness,
gazing longingly toward the slopes of Gūyè.
"Preface to the Winding River Poems"
I once heard of the excursion at the Fén River,
now I see the bridles beyond the dusty world.
Xiè Língyùn's "Poem of Běigù"
Déyuǎn
Emperor Yáo said:
"I set my heart on the ancient past,
as recorded in Shuō Yuàn (Garden of Discourses),
and focused my will on the destitute people.
I grieve that the myriad families suffer from crimes,
and worry that the multitude of living beings do not thrive.
Therefore, if even one person is hungry, I say, 'This is because I have made him hungry.'
If even one person is cold, I say, 'This is because I have made him cold.'
If even one person commits a crime, I say, 'This is because I have led him into it.'
Benevolence is practiced and righteousness is established,
virtue is broad and transformation is widespread.
Hence, without rewards, the people are encouraged;
without punishments, the people are well-governed.
First show forgiveness and then act,
thus the sound of virtue reaches far."
From Jiǎ Tàifù's Xīn Shū (New Writings); Shuō Yuàn records the same words from Héjiān Xiànwáng.
Punishments Laid Aside
When Emperor Yáo governed the world,
he executed one person and punished two, yet the world was well-governed.
Hence it is said:
"Awe is stern yet not applied,
punishments exist yet remain unused."
This saying refers to this.
From "Xúnzǐ: Debating Military Affairs"
Zǐgòng said:
The tradition states:
When Yáo and Shùn ruled as kings,
not a single person was punished yet the world was well-governed,
for their teachings were sincere and their influence profound.
From "The Great Commentary to the Book of Documents"
Frugal Virtue
A ruler who possesses the world
may have nine-tiered jade towers, yet Yáo lived in a thatched hut;
may wear nine patterns of embroidered robes, yet Yáo wore coarse cloth;
may host three markets within the palace, yet Yáo dwelled like a quail;
may enjoy hundreds of delicacies, yet Yáo ate coarse rice and vegetable porridge;
may ride green dragons and qílín, yet Yáo traveled in plain carriages with simple horses.
"Shīzǐ"
The reason people desire to be sovereign
is to indulge their senses and enjoy physical comforts.
Now high towers and multi-storied pavilions
are what people admire,
yet Yáo used unhewn rafters,
and plain lintels without carving.
Rare and exotic treasures
are what people find beautiful,
yet Yáo ate coarse millet
and soup of wild herbs.
Embroidered silks and white fox furs
are what people covet,
yet Yáo covered his form with plain cloth,
and warded off cold with deerskin.
He did not enrich life's comforts
but increased the burden of responsibility.
Therefore he handed the world over to Shùn,
as if relieved of a heavy load—
not merely out of modesty,
but truly because he had no alternative.
"Huáinánzǐ·Jīngshén Xùn"
When Yáo possessed the world,
it was not out of greed for the wealth of millions or to enjoy the sovereign's position,
but because the people struggled by force,
the strong bullied the weak,
the many oppressed the few.
Thus Yáo personally practiced frugality
and demonstrated benevolent mutual love,
thereby harmonizing them.
Therefore, his thatched roof was untrimmed,
his wooden beams unplaned,
his great carriage unadorned,
his rush mat unhemmed,
his broth unseasoned,
his millet food unrefined.
He traveled on inspections to spread teaching,
laboring diligently for the world,
journeying across the Five Sacred Mountains.
Was it that his provisions were insufficient for pleasure?
He took the world as his charge
without seeking personal gain.
As he aged and his vigor declined,
he handed the world to Shùn,
like walking backward to shed worn sandals.
"Shàng Zhǔ Shù"
When Emperor Yáo ruled the world,
he did not wear gold, silver, pearls, or jade;
he did not dress in brocade, embroidery, or fine silk;
he did not look at strange or exotic objects;
he did not treasure curios or rare vessels;
he did not listen to licentious music;
he did not whitewash his palace walls or rooms;
he did not carve or decorate his beams, pillars, or columns;
he did not trim his thatched roof;
he did not replace his coarse clothes and straw shoes until they were worn out;
he did not eat rich or heavy foods;
he did not change his warm rice and soup even if slightly sour or stale.
He did not, for private reasons,
delay the farming seasons.
He restrained his heart and moderated his desires,
engaging in effortless action.
His personal upkeep was very meager,
his taxes and levies very light.
Thus, the myriad people were prosperous and happy, without hunger or cold,
and the common people revered their ruler like the sun and moon,
and cherished him like parents.
"Liù Tāo"
When Yáo ruled the world,
he had an untrimmed thatched roof,
unhewn wooden beams,
ate coarse millet,
and soup of wild herbs,
wore deerskin in winter,
and hemp cloth in summer.
Even the gatekeeper's clothing and sustenance
were no worse than this.
"Hánfēizǐ"
Yáo, possessing the world, ate from earthen bowls,
drank from earthen vessels.
His territory reached Jiāozhǐ in the south,
Yōudū in the north,
and where the sun and moon rise and set in the east and west—
all submitted willingly.
Previously,
Yànzǐ asked Zǐhuá,
saying:
"I have heard that sages value frugality,
that Yáo did not consider earthen steps crude,
and that Yǒuyúshì was wary of painted decorations.
Is this recorded in tradition?"
Zǐhuá replied:
"In the past, Yáo resided in the Qúshì Palace,
draped in robes with folded hems,
profound as a dwelling of spirits.
Gathering the five jade tokens, he received the feudal lords;
those coming to court with sashes and shoes
were like stars surrounding the North Star,
and Yáo accepted this as natural.
Shùn strolled in his pillared corridor,
clad in fine robes, playing the five-stringed zither,
with the sun and moon painted on his banner,
adorned with twelve brilliant patterns
of black, white, azure, and yellow.
When he went out, there were carriage bells;
when he moved, there were jade pendants;
his steps matched the rhythm of court music,
and Shùn too accepted this as natural.
Thus, Yáo and Shùn possessed such complete provisions—
how could there be so-called 'earthen steps three feet high',
or 'untrimmed thatched roof'?
How could there be 'painted decorations for self-warning'?
These are the beliefs of pedantic scholars,
and the deceptions of vulgar customs,
praised by rustics,
but not transmitted in reliable records." "Zǐhuázǐ"

In the time of Yáo,

Above

Yǔ was Minister of Works,

In guiding the myriad people,
those who lived by water fished; those who lived in the mountains
gathered timber; those who lived in valleys
herded; those who lived on plains
farmed. The land was suited to its tasks,
the tasks suited to their tools,
the tools suited to their use,

In marshes, nets were woven;
on hillsides, fields were plowed.
They could exchange what they had for what they lacked,
and what they were skilled at for what they were unskilled at.

the round ones roll to the marshes,
the square ones stay on high ground,

Huá Fēng's Blessing
Yáo was touring at Huá,

"Ah,
a sage! Let me bless the sage:
may the sage live long!"
Yáo replied:
"I decline."
"May the sage be wealthy,"
Yáo said:
"I decline."
"May the sage have many sons."
Yáo said:
"I decline." The border official said:
"Long life, wealth, and many sons
are what all people desire.

Yáo answered:

wealth means many troubles,
long life means many humiliations.
These three things do not nourish virtue.

but now I see you are but a gentleman.

and eats like a fledgling;
he moves like a bird
and leaves no trace.
When the world has the Way,
he joins all things in prosperity;
when the world is without the Way,
he cultivates virtue and retires into leisure.
After a thousand years, weary of the world,
he departs and ascends to become an immortal,
Kāngqú Yáo
Yáo ruled the world for fifty years,
but did not know whether the world was well-governed or not?
Was it well-governed or not?
Did he know if the millions of people were willing to support him?
Or were they unwilling to support him?
He turned to ask his attendants,
but his attendants did not know.
He asked the outer court officials,
but the outer court officials did not know.
He asked the common people in the countryside,
but the common people in the countryside did not know.

where he heard children singing a folk rhyme:
"Establish us, the multitude of people,
all follow your supreme standard.
Without knowledge or awareness,
we follow the rules of the sovereign."
Delighted, he asked:
"Who taught you these words?"
The children replied:
"We heard them from a senior official."
He asked the senior official,
who said:
"It is an ancient poem."
Yáo returned to the palace and summoned Shùn,
then abdicated and handed over the world to him.

punishments multiply from this.

When a sage king occupies the highest position, there are no military conflicts in the world,

When a sage king is above, he ensures the people use their time and resources with moderation.

Ten Perish
After the First Emperor had unified the empire,
he became exceedingly extravagant and wasteful.
There were magicians: the Korean visitor Hóu Shēng,
and the Qi visitor Lú Shēng, who plotted together to flee.
The First Emperor was greatly enraged,
and buried alive over four hundred and sixty lawbreakers.
Lú Shēng escaped, but Hóu Shēng was later captured.
The First Emperor summoned him, intending to reprimand and then have him torn apart by chariots.
Hóu Shēng said:
"Your servant has heard that one who knows death is bound to be brave.
Will Your Majesty deign to listen to one word from your servant?"
The First Emperor said:
"What do you wish to say?"
"Speak."
Hóu Shēng said:
"Your Majesty is extravagant, licentious, and dissolute.
Those below are mute and those above deaf; thus we left like Dān Zhū,
who was arrogant, cruel, and fond of unrestrained wandering,
and consequently did not ascend to the throne.
Now Your Majesty's excesses
surpass Dān Zhū ten thousandfold and King Zhòu a thousandfold.
I fear that Your Majesty faces ten causes for downfall,
without even one for preservation."
The First Emperor remained silent for a long time.
Then he said:
"Why did you not speak earlier?"
Hóu Shēng said:
"Your Majesty's mind was soaring on azure clouds,
floating amidst displays of literary embellishments,
considering yourself wise and strong,
insulting the Five Emperors above,
trampling the Three Kings below,
abandoning simplicity for trivial skills.
The signs of Your Majesty's downfall have been visible for a long time.
We feared that speaking would be of no benefit,
and would only bring death upon ourselves.
Therefore we fled.
Now that I am certain to die,
I present this to Your Majesty,
hoping to make you aware of it yourself."
The First Emperor said:
"Can I change?"
Hóu Shēng said:
"The form is already set.
Your Majesty's assistants are also unfit.
I fear that even change cannot ensure survival."
The First Emperor sighed and released him.

Nest Staff
Lǎo Zǐ said:
In the way of ordinary people,
the heart should be small,
the will should be great,
wisdom should be round,
and conduct should be square.
By a small heart is meant
to consider troubles before they arise,
to guard against calamities and be cautious in small matters,
not daring to indulge one's desires;
by a great will is meant
to embrace all states,
to unify diverse customs and judgments of right and wrong,
gathering them like spokes converging at the hub;
by round wisdom is meant
having no beginning or end,
flowing in all directions,
like an abyssal spring that never runs dry;
by square conduct is meant
standing upright without bending,
pure and untainted,
not changing principles in poverty,
nor indulging ambitions in success.
Thus, a small heart guards against the subtle,
a great will encompasses all,
round wisdom knows everything,
and square conduct refrains from certain actions.
Later,
Sūn Sīmiǎo told Lú Zhàolín:
"Be bold in will but small in heart,
round in wisdom but square in conduct.
The Book of Songs says:
'As if standing on the edge of an abyss,
as if treading on thin ice.'
This refers to a small heart.
'Valiant warriors,
bulwarks of the lords.'
This refers to a bold will.
'Not swayed by profit,
not shamed by righteousness.'
This is square conduct.
'Seize the opportunity and act,
without waiting all day.'
This is round wisdom."
