belonging to the wood phase in the five elements,
hence its structure resembles branches and trunks,
as all things take wood as their framework.
From *Shìmíng*
Wáng Zǐ Cháo sent an envoy,
who informed the feudal lords, saying:
In the sixth year of King Dìng's reign,
the Qín people reported an omen,
stating that Zhōu would have a bearded king,
who would also be capable of fulfilling his duties.
When it came to King Líng,
he was born with a beard,
and the king was exceptionally divine and sagacious,
committing no wrongs against the feudal lords.
"Zuǒ Zhuàn"
The liver corresponds to benevolence among the five organs.
Why does the liver correspond to benevolence?
The liver
is the essence of wood.
Benevolence favors life; the east,
which is yang,
is where all things begin to grow.
Thus, the liver resembles wood in color,
being green and having branches and leaves,
with the eyes serving as its external manifestation.
"Yuè Dòng Shēng Yí"
King Wǔ of Zhōu attacked King Zhòu,
who fought and died,
and his body was abandoned outside the Jade Gate.
The observing people all stepped forward to kick it,
trampling his belly,
stomping his kidneys,
crushing his lungs,
and treading on his liver.
King Wǔ of Zhōu then sent people to set up a curtain and guard it,
but the people lifted the curtain and entered,
and those who struck it with stones still did not stop.

Swallowing Jade Essence
The father of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn was named Liú Zhíjiā.
Zhíjiā's mother dreamed of a red bird resembling a dragon,
which frolicked with her before she gave birth to Zhíjiā.
His mother was named Hánshǐ,
and she became known as Empress Zhāolíng.
Empress Zhāolíng was wandering by Luò Pond
when a jade chicken appeared holding a red pearl in its beak,
inscribed with the words "Jade Essence."
It was said that whoever swallowed it would become king.
Empress Zhāolíng took and swallowed it.
Later, while resting on the bank of a great marsh,
she dreamed of encountering a deity.
At that moment, thunder, lightning, and darkness prevailed,
and her husband, the Grand Duke, looked on
and saw a dragon above her.
She then became pregnant and gave birth to Jì,
who became Emperor Gāozǔ.
(Sòng Records)
Duke Yì of Wèi had a minister named Hóng Yǎn who was involved in a matter.
He had the Dí people attack Wèi,
killing Duke Yì,
and they completely ate his flesh,
only sparing his liver.
When Hóng Yǎn arrived,
he reported his mission to the liver,
crying out to heaven and weeping,
until his grief was exhausted, then said:
"Your servant requests to become the outer coffin."
Thereupon he committed suicide,
first cutting open his own abdomen,
and placed Duke Yì's liver inside it.
Duke Huán of Qí heard of this,
and reestablished Wèi at Chǔqiū.
"The Annals of Lü"

"Tears flow down like reeds and orchids,

The gallbladder,
is the organ connected to the liver.
In the "Shuōwén",
the gallbladder

and the liver

governing benevolence and compassion,
hence it is used for decision-making,
thus the benevolent possess courage,

how do we know they function as interconnected organs?
The liver
is the essence of wood,

Yuè King Gōu Jiàn, upon returning to his country, tormented his body and anguished his thoughts.

and whether sitting or lying down, he would look up at the gall,

With a sorrowful heart and bitter resolve,
he hung the gall by the door,

he possessed the lands of four provinces,
with a force of over a hundred thousand soldiers.

but Lord Cáo remarked:

fierce in appearance yet timid at heart.

and his provisions abundant,

intending to reinforce him with two thousand soldiers.
Yù refused,
saying:

and considers himself invincible.

he will certainly not attack."
Tàizǔ followed his advice,
and indeed Yuán did not come.

Emperor Guāngwǔ's father, Liú Qīn, initially served as the magistrate of Jìyáng.
There was an imperial traveling palace of Emperor Wǔ, usually kept sealed.
When the emperor was about to be born,
Qīn found the magistrate's residence damp and low-lying,
so he opened the rear hall of the palace to reside in.
On the night of the jiǎzǐ day in the twelfth month of the first year of the Jiànpíng era, when the emperor was born,
a red light illuminated the room,
bright as daylight throughout.
Qīn found it extraordinary,
and had the diviner Wáng Cháng perform a divination.
Cháng dismissed the attendants and said:
"This is a fortunate matter that cannot be spoken of."
That year, auspicious grain grew with one stalk bearing nine ears,
unusually large compared to ordinary grain.
The county experienced a great harvest,
so they named the emperor "Xiù" (meaning "outstanding").
That year, phoenixes came to gather at the old palace in Jìyáng,
and all depicted the auspicious sign of the phoenixes.

Emperor Guāngwǔ's birth was accompanied by a red light filling the room,

The Marvel of Divine Light
Zhào Yún, styled Zǐlóng,
when the First Sovereign entered Yìzhōu,
Yún remained guarding the camp.
Lord Cáo contended for the land of Hànzhōng,
transporting tens of millions of bags of rice to the northern foothills.
Huáng Zhōng believed it could be seized,
and Yún’s troops followed Zhōng to take the rice.
When they did not return past the deadline,
Yún led several dozen cavalry to ride out and observe Zhōng’s situation.
They encountered Lord Cáo’s troops advancing in full force,
and were attacked by the vanguard.
Yún charged forward to break through their formation,
fighting while retreating.
Lord Cáo’s army, having scattered, regrouped again.
Yún, trapped among the enemy, fought his way back to camp,
then had the gates opened wide,
lowered the flags and silenced the drums.
Lord Cáo’s army suspected Yún had set an ambush,
and withdrew.
Yún thundered the drums, shaking the heavens,
and had crossbowmen shoot at Lord Cáo’s army from the rear.
Lord Cáo’s troops panicked, trampling each other in chaos,
and many drowned in the Hàn River.
The next morning, the First Sovereign personally came to Yún’s camp,
surveyed the previous day’s battlefield, and said:
“Zǐlóng is all courage, from head to toe!”
The army honored Yún as the General of Tiger’s Might.
From the Bié Zhuàn.

and cannot generate each other.

During the reign of Emperor Yuán, Yì Fèng submitted a confidential memorial stating:
"The five natures do not harm each other,
the six emotions alternately rise and fall.
Observe nature through the calendar,
observe emotions through pitch-pipes."
The Book of Hàn records
Yì's theory of the five natures:
The liver's nature is calm,
practicing benevolence,
governed by jiǎ and jǐ;
the heart's nature is restless,
restlessness practices propriety,
governed by bǐng and xīn;
the spleen's nature is forceful,
forcefulness practices faithfulness,
governed by wù and guǐ;
the lungs' nature is firm,
firmness practices righteousness,
governed by yǐ and gēng;
the kidneys' nature is wise,
wisdom practices respect,
governed by dīng and rén.
In the late years of Emperor Chéng's reign, he became quite fond of esoteric arts.
Gǔ Yǒng advised the emperor, saying:
"There are those in the world who claim to be immortals,
who take elixirs of immortality,
and practice the arts of transforming colors and the five storehouses -
all are deceitful people using heterodox ways to delude worldly rulers."
The Book of Hàn
records Lǐ Qí's commentary:
"They meditate on having five colors within their bodies,
and five storehouses in their abdomen.
If the spirit's five colors are preserved, one does not die;
if the five storehouses are preserved, one does not hunger."
The emperor
Auspicious clouds appeared.
The human body universally contains Three Corpses and Nine Worms.
When a person is born,
their form is all entrusted within the parents' womb,
nourished by the essence of the five grains.
Thus, within the human abdomen, there are corpse worms entirely,
which pose a great harm,
often on the night of the Gēngshēn day ascending to report to the Heavenly Emperor,
recording the person's faults and transgressions,
cutting off the register of human life,
wishing to cause rapid death,
so the soul ascends to the azure heavens,
and the earthly soul enters the Yellow Springs,
leaving only the corpse worms to roam alone upon the earth,
called ghosts.
Sometimes during the four seasons and eight festivals,
if the sacrifices of the three types of livestock
are not pure, they will cause harm to people,
bringing heart pain and obstinate illnesses,
cutting short human life.
The Upper Corpse is named Péng Jù,
fond of treasures;
the Middle Corpse is named Péng Zhì,
fond of the five flavors;
the Lower Corpse is named Péng Jiǎo,
fond of sensual desires.
The Three Corpses as entities
constantly reside in the human spleen.
The Upper Corpse Péng Jù is also called Blue-Clothed,
the Middle Corpse Péng Zhì is called White-Clothed,
the Lower Corpse Péng Jiǎo is called Red-Mouth,
these Three Corpses appear like small children,
or resemble the shape of a horse,
all having beard and hair,
with hair three to four inches long.
Once a person dies, they emerge to become ghosts,
resembling the person's appearance during life,
with clothing of the same length,
so when relatives see them,
they think it is the deceased returning home,
but it is truly not the spirit of the deceased.
"The Classic of King Zhōngshān's Coffin"
states: If desires arise, the Three Corpses arise;
if desires are extinguished, the Three Corpses are extinguished.
Those who swiftly achieve the Way by removing the Corpses
first externally restrain sounds, sights, fame, and profit,
internally pacify joy and anger.
If one is negligent, unrestrained, and disrespectful,
transgressing in sleep and rest,
greedy in eating and drinking,
the Corpses will then transform in a thousand ways, ten thousand changes,
following desires and returning,
causing the person's worldly afflictions to deepen daily and increasing foolishness,
leading to early demise. The method to control them
is that every time the Gēngshēn day arrives,
to stay awake day and night guarding it,
preventing them from appealing to the Heavenly Emperor.
When the faults fill five hundred entries,
the person is certain to die.
After guarding three Gēngshēn days,
the Three Corpses tremble and are shaken;
after seven Gēngshēn days, the Three Corpses are permanently severed,
boiled to death in the Tàixuán cauldron's boiling water.
Only then is the essence-spirit stabilized and pacified,
the five viscera tranquil and harmonious,
no longer causing disturbances.
"The Yuánshǐ Register of the Supreme Clarity"
states: The Upper Corpse is also called Qīng Gū,
one version writes Qīng Shí;
the Middle Corpse is also called Bái Gū,
one version writes Bái Shí;
the Lower Corpse is also called Xuè Shī,
one version writes Xuè Gū.
"The Jade Coffin Classic"
states: The Three Péng are the surnames of the Three Corpses,
constantly residing within the human body,
watching for human faults,
wishing to cause people to die.
Each on the Gēngshēn day, they list human offenses item by item,
and report them to the Upper Heaven.
Scholars learning immortality,
if they do not remove the Three Corpses,
have no means to attain the Way,
only suffering to no avail.

Shāng Tāng originated from the mysterious bird's mandate,

the sun at the Duānwǔ festival,

named 'Competing in Celebration',
the emperor repays the field deities,
illuminating the mysterious heavens above,
radiantly revealing the great sage,
manifesting imperial transformation below,
establishing customs for endless generations."
The emperor responded with a handwritten edict:
"All established festivals
either follow celestial transitions,
or commemorate human affairs.

offering an auspicious name,
creating precedent from my reign,

I approve your request,
to be promulgated to the relevant authorities."

Where battles were fought and deaths occurred,
the blood of men and horses, accumulating over the years, transforms into phosphorescence.
This phosphorescence attaches to the ground and vegetation like dew,
barely visible.
If a passerby happens to touch it,
it adheres to the body and emits light.
When brushed off, it scatters into countless fragments,
intensifying with faint crackling sounds,
like frying beans.
Only by remaining still for a long time does it extinguish.
Afterward, the person feels dazed as if having lost their soul,
recovering only after a full day.

Zhuāngzǐ went to Chǔ and saw an empty skull, bleached and yet retaining its shape.
He poked it with his horse whip,
and then asked it, saying:
"Did you, sir, due to greed for life,
lose principle and come to this?
Or did you have the misfortune of a state's destruction,
and suffer execution by axe and thus come to this?
Or was it that you had improper conduct,
felt ashamed to leave your parents, wife, and children in disgrace, and thus came to this?
Or did you suffer the distress of cold and hunger and thus come to this?
Or was it simply that your years
had reached their limit and thus you came to this?"
Having finished speaking, he took the skull and, using it as a pillow, lay down to sleep.
At midnight, the skull appeared to him in a dream and said:
"The way you talk makes you sound like a sophist.
All that you have spoken of are the burdens of the living.
In death, there are none of these.
Would you like to hear about death?"
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Yes."
The skull said:
"In death, there is no ruler above,
no subjects below,
and also no affairs of the four seasons.
Freely, we take heaven and earth as our spring and autumn.
Even a king facing south on his throne
cannot surpass this."
Zhuāngzǐ did not believe it,
and said:
"If I were to have the Director of Fate restore your life,
return your form to you with bones, flesh, skin, and muscles,
and give you back your parents, wife, children, neighbors, and acquaintances,
would you want that?"
The skull frowned deeply, with a worried expression, and said:
"How could I abandon the happiness of a king facing south and return to the toils of the human world?"

Scattered Flames
In the fifth year of the Yǒngjiā era, Gāo Róng served as patrol commander of the Gāopíng garrison.
At that time, the rebel Cáo Yí brought chaos and turmoil,
and the people all fortified themselves in strongholds.
A fire broke out in the mountains,
with flying embers and intense flames
reaching over a hundred zhàng high.
Blazes flickered atop the trees at dusk,
their roar shaking the mountain valleys,
and the sounds of men, horses, and armor were heard.
Thinking the Yí rebels were approaching,
all were terrified and rushed out in full armor to confront them.
Leading cavalry to the mountain's base,
they found no one there,
but only saw scattered flames sprinkling down,
burning the soldiers' robes, armor, and the manes of their horses.
Thus, the troops
fled back. At dawn,
they returned to inspect the mountains,
finding no trace of the fire,
only a hundred skulls
scattered across the mountains.

What is meant by hún and pò?
Hún is like something fluttering,
moving without rest,
the qì of Lesser Yang,
thus ceaselessly active externally.
Pò is like something pressing,
attached to the person,
this being the qì of Lesser Yin,
resembling metal and stone that adhere to a person without shifting.
Hún means "to weed,"
using emotion to remove impurities,
while pò means "to press,"
acting to regulate the inner essence and spirit.
What is meant by this?
Jīng (essence) means tranquility,
the qì of Greater Yin that sustains transformation,
resembling water's transformation that awaits gestation to produce life.
Shén (spirit) is the elusive qì of Greater Yin,
entering and exiting without gaps.
《White Tiger Discourse》
states: Pò means white;
hún means weeding.
White signifies clarity and understanding,
while weeding signifies movement.
The body has substance and takes clarity,
white being named for qì,
only through exhalation and inhalation is it obtained,
and weeding movement constitutes its meaning.
《Explanation of the Classic of Filial Piety》
Pò asked Hún, saying:
"How does the Dào take form?"
Hún replied:
"It takes formlessness as its form."
Pò said:
"Does formlessness have shape?"
Hún said:
"Formlessness has no pò."
Pò said:
"Then how can formlessness be perceived?"
Hún said:
"I merely encounter it directly,
looking at it reveals no form,
listening to it yields no sound,
we call it the obscure and dark.
The obscure and dark
serves to describe the Dào but is not the Dào itself."
Pò said:
"What then is this speaking about?
I shall return to my origin."
Pò turned back to look at Hún,
but suddenly Hún was nowhere to be seen,
turning inward to exist by itself,
Pò too sank into formlessness.

Huángdì said:

"When pathogenic factors invade the interior from the exterior without a fixed location,
they spread indiscriminately to the zang organs,
failing to settle in a definite place,
traveling together with the nutritive and defensive qi and causing the ethereal and corporeal souls to float restlessly,
making people unable to sleep peacefully and prone to dreaming.
When qi spreads to the fu organs, there is excess externally,
and deficiency internally;
when qi spreads to the zang organs, there is excess internally,
and deficiency externally."
Huángdì asked:
"Are there physical manifestations of excess and deficiency?"
Qíbó answered:
"When yin qi is abundant, one dreams of wading through great waters and feeling fear;
when yang qi is abundant, one dreams of great fires and burning heat;
when both yin and yang are abundant, one dreams of fighting and killing.
When upper energy is abundant, one dreams of flying;
when lower energy is abundant, one dreams of falling;
when very hungry, one dreams of taking;
when very full, one dreams of giving.
When liver qi is abundant, one dreams of anger;
when lung qi is abundant, one dreams of fear and terror,
weeping and floating;
when heart qi is abundant, one dreams of laughing happily and feeling afraid;
when spleen qi is abundant, one dreams of singing and joy,
but the body feels heavy and unable to lift;
when kidney qi is abundant, one dreams of the waist and spine separating and not connecting.
For all these twelve types of excess,
when they arrive, drain them,
and the reversal qi will immediately cease.
When pathogenic qi lodges in the heart, one dreams of hills and mountains with smoke and fire;
when it lodges in the lungs, one dreams of floating,
and seeing strange metal objects;
when it lodges in the liver, one dreams of mountain forests and trees;
when it lodges in the spleen, one dreams of hills and large marshes,
ruined houses, wind and rain;
when it lodges in the kidneys, one dreams of facing deep abysses,
submerging and dwelling in water;
when it lodges in the bladder, one dreams of wandering about;
when it lodges in the stomach, one dreams of eating and drinking;
when it lodges in the large intestine, one dreams of open fields;
when it lodges in the small intestine, one dreams of crowded towns and busy crossroads;
when it lodges in the gallbladder, one dreams of fighting, litigation, and self-mutilation;
when it lodges in the genitals, one dreams of sexual intercourse;
when it lodges in the neck, one dreams of being beheaded;
when it lodges in the shins, one dreams of walking but unable to advance,
and dwelling in deep underground cellars;
when it lodges in the thighs and arms, one dreams of ceremonial bowing and rising;
when it lodges in the bladder and intestines, one dreams of urination and defecation.
For all these fifteen types of deficiency,
when they arrive, supplement them,
and they will immediately cease."

whose borders are unknown,

Birth
Dreams can be direct or symbolic,
stem from essence or thought,
relate to persons or feelings,
correspond to seasons or reverse,
reflect illnesses or temperaments.
In ancient times, when King Wǔ's consort Yì Jiāng was pregnant with Shū of Yú,
she dreamed the Emperor told her:
"I command your son Yǔ to possess Táng,"
and when he was born, the character "Yǔ" was written on his palm,
so he was named accordingly.
When King Chéng destroyed Táng,
he enfeoffed Shū of Yú there,
this is called a directly fulfilled dream.
The Book of Songs says:
"Bears and grisly bears
Are auspicious signs for sons;
Vipers and snakes
Are auspicious signs for daughters.
Many fishes
Truly mean a fruitful year.
Banners and standards
Mean households flourishing."
This is called a symbolic dream.
Confucius, born in troubled times,
daily contemplated the virtue of the Duke of Zhōu,
and dreamed of him at night,
this is called a dream of sincere essence.
When people think of something, they dream of its arrival;
when worried, they dream of the matter,
this is called a dream of memory and thought.
If a noble person appears in a dream,
it is considered auspicious;
if a commoner appears, it is ominous;
if a gentleman appears, it brings honor;
if a petty person appears, it brings disgrace,
this is called a dream relating to social status.
Duke Wén of Jìn, before the battle of Chéngpú, dreamed the King of Chǔ was upon him sucking his brains,
which was a terrible omen,
yet he achieved great victory in the battle,
this is called an extremely reversed dream.
Dreams on rainy days
make people weary and confused.
Dreams on dry, sunny days
make people disordered and scattered.
Dreams in severe cold
make people resentful and sorrowful.
Dreams on windy days
make people feel floating and soaring.
This is called a dream influenced by climatic energy.
Spring dreams concern growth,
summer dreams are lofty and bright,
autumn and winter dreams involve ripening and storing,
this is called a seasonally responsive dream.
Yin illnesses bring dreams of cold,
yang illnesses bring dreams of heat,
internal illnesses bring chaotic dreams,
external illnesses bring dreams of dispersal,
dreams of various illnesses
may be scattered or gathered,
this is called a dream of pathological energy.
People's emotions and preferences differ:
some consider certain dreams auspicious,
others consider them inauspicious,
each should examine themselves,
and follow what they usually experience,
this is called a dream of temperament.
Thus, prior discrepancies
are called essential manifestations;
having daytime thoughts
and dreaming of them at night,
alternately auspicious, good, or evil,
if not believed, is called thought;
noble and base, wise and foolish,
male and female, old and young, are called persons;
wind, rain, cold, and heat are called influences;
the waxing and waning of the five phases are called seasons;
the extreme of yin brings auspiciousness,
the extreme of yang brings inauspiciousness,
this is called reversal; observing one's ailments
and examining one's dreams
is called illness;
the essence of the heart and its preferences,
verified in events,
is called temperament.
All these ten aspects
constitute the general principles of dream interpretation,
yet those who determine auspiciousness and inauspiciousness
often misclassify them.
Is it because human wakefulness is yang,
human sleep is yin,
and the functions of yin and yang are opposite?

images;

what the heart thinks of,

"The Book of Dreams"
Yáo reigned for seventy years,
and was about to abdicate the throne to Shùn,
so he purified himself and built an altar platform at the Hé and Luò rivers,
leading Shùn and others up Shǒu Mountain.
On the river isle, five elders were roaming about,
who were the essences of the five stars.
They said to each other:
"The River Chart is about to emerge,
a dragon holds a jade case in its mouth,
with inscribed boards bearing mandates,
sealed with golden clay,
and wrapped in jade covers.
The one who knows us
is the double-pupiled Huáng Yáo."
They saw the five elders soar up like shooting stars,
entering the constellation Mǎo.
The "Sòngshū Bǐ Kǎochèn"
also records this under the astral section.
Rén Yànshēng's Empress Xuāndé
mentions the five elders roaming the river,
and shooting stars entering Mǎo.
Lǐ Hàn's commentary states:
"Yáo saw five elders by the river;
one elder said, 'The River Chart will come to announce the emperor's timeline';
another said, 'The River Chart urges the turtle to reveal the emperor's plans';
another said, 'Mountains, rivers, fish, and turtles receive the sage's grace';
another said, 'The River Chart urges the dragon to hold the jade cord.'
After singing,
the five elders flew into the sky,
entering Mǎo.
It is unknown which classic records this;
Suìshì quotes it."
There are four methods by which people interpret dreams:
first, the perfuming of ignorance;
second, the wandering of past consciousness;
third, the predominance of the four elements;
fourth, the foretoken of good and evil.

That country had no leaders,

they knew not the joy of life,

The emperor awoke with serene contentment,

and dreamed what you have heard.
Now I understand the supreme Way cannot be sought through ordinary feelings,

I have attained it."
After another twenty-eight years,
the world was greatly well-governed,
almost like the country of the Huáxū clan.

A man of the Zhōu clan, named Yǐn, was managing a large estate.
His servants, who were driven to labor, toiled from dawn till dusk without rest.
There was an old servant whose strength was exhausted, yet he was made to work even harder.
By day, he groaned and sighed as he went about his tasks,
and by night, he fell into a heavy, exhausted sleep.
His mind was scattered and confused,
and night after night he dreamed of being the ruler of a state,
seated above the people,
overseeing all the affairs of the kingdom.
He wandered through palaces and towers,
indulging in whatever he desired,
and his joy was beyond compare.
But when he awoke, he returned to his labor.
When someone tried to console him for his toil,
the old servant said:
"A human life spans a hundred years,
divided equally between day and night.
By day, I am a slave,
and though it is bitter, indeed,
by night, I become a ruler,
and my joy is beyond compare.
What is there to complain about?"
Yǐn, for his part, was preoccupied with worldly affairs,
constantly anxious about his family's wealth,
and both his mind and body were weary.
At night, he too fell into an exhausted sleep,
and night after night he dreamed of being a servant,
running about and performing all kinds of labor,
leaving nothing undone.
He was scolded, beaten, and caned,
suffering every form of abuse.
In his sleep, he muttered, groaned, and cried out,
until dawn brought relief.
Yǐn found this distressing,
and so he went to consult a friend.
The friend said:
"Your status is sufficient to bring you honor,
and your wealth is more than enough.
You surpass others by far.
That you dream at night of being a servant
is the natural alternation of toil and ease—
the constant rule of fate.
If you wish to have both ease in waking and ease in dreams,
how could that be possible?"
When Yǐn heard these words,
he relaxed the demands on his servants
and reduced his own anxieties.
His afflictions then diminished somewhat.

"Those who reverence prevails over negligence shall prosper,
those who negligence prevails over reverence shall perish;
those who righteousness prevails over desire shall succeed,
those who desire prevails over righteousness shall meet misfortune.
In all matters, without strength there is no integrity,
without reverence there is no correctness.
The corrupt shall be destroyed,
the reverent shall last ten thousand generations.
What is gained through benevolence,
and maintained through benevolence,
shall last a hundred generations.
What is gained without benevolence,
but maintained through benevolence,
shall last ten generations.
What is gained without benevolence,
and maintained without benevolence,
shall not last even a single generation."

Duke Jǐng fell ill,

and dreamed at night of fighting with two suns but failing to win.

yang.

The dream interpreter entered and addressed the duke,

but Yànzǐ said:

so it was effective.

Confucius was stranded between Chén and Cài,
with no vegetable soup to ladle,
and for seven days tasted no grain, sleeping by day.
Yán Huí sought and obtained some rice to cook.
When it was nearly done,
Confucius saw Yán Huí snatch some from the pot and eat it.
Soon after, the food was ready, and Yán Huí presented it to Confucius to eat.
Confucius pretended not to have seen.
Confucius rose and said:
"Just now I dreamed of my late father; I should first offer pure food before eating."
Yán Huí replied:
"That would not do. Just now, soot fell into the pot,
and discarding the food would be inauspicious."
So I snatched and ate it.
Confucius sighed and said:
"What we trust are our eyes,
yet even eyes cannot be trusted;
what we rely on is our heart,
yet even the heart is not fully reliable.
Disciples, remember this:
understanding others is truly not easy."

had Zēng Zǐ hold the Hé

Confucius fasted and purified himself,
bowed toward the North Star,
and reported completion to Heaven,
saying:
"The Classic of Filial Piety in four volumes,
the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and the Hé and Luò documents totaling eighty-one volumes,
are reverently prepared."
Heaven then surged with dense energy,
white fog rose,
brushing the ground,
a crimson rainbow descended from above and transformed into yellow jade,
two feet long,
with carved characters on it,
Confucius knelt to receive it and read:
"Precious writing appears,
Liú Jì grasps it,
Mǎo Jīn Dāo,
north of Zhěn constellation,
characters Hé Zǐ,
the world submits."
Records of Sòng
Confucius dreamed between three locust trees of crimson whirlwinds rising in Fēng and Pèi markets,
called Yān Yuān.
Zǐ Xià went to observe,
saw a crimson snake transform into yellow gold,
with writing on it saying:
"Mǎo Jīn Dāo."
Later Gāozǔ rose from Fēng and Pèi.
Master of the Golden Tower
During Duke Āi's time, hunting westward,
a firewood gatherer caught a qilin,
struck and injured its left leg,
and was about to show it to Confucius.
Confucius saw it,
bowed and wept,
embraced the qilin and said:
"Why have you come!
Why have you come!"
He turned his sleeve to wipe his face,
looked up at the person,
who had dragon brows and sun horns,
the Master attended to the qilin's mouth,
momentarily it vomited three scrolls of diagrams.
One said Chì Fú Liú Jì would rise as king,
two said Zhōu would perish,
the Master would soon die,
three said Hàn would be established,
and he would create the Classic of Filial Piety.
The Master returned,
told Zǐ Xià:
"A new ruler will rise,
this person is like the one who obtained the qilin."
Qín Cāo
King Chǔ was traveling with Sòng Yù in the wilderness of Yúnmèng,
and was about to have Sòng Yù compose a rhapsody on the events of Gāotáng.
Looking at the hall of morning clouds, they saw ethereal mist above it,
soaring straight upward,
suddenly changing its appearance,
in a mere instant,
transforming endlessly.
The king asked Sòng Yù:
"What vapor is this?"
He replied:
"Long ago, the former king was traveling at Gāotáng,
and, weary, napped during the day.
He dreamed of a woman, hazy like a cloud,
radiant like a star,
about to approach but not yet arrived,
as if floating, as if pausing.
Looking at her carefully,
she had the form of Xī Shī.
The king, pleased, inquired of her.
'I am the youngest daughter of the Red Emperor,'
named Yáo Jī.
I died before I could marry,
and was enshrined on the terrace of Wūshān.
My essence and soul cling to the grass,
truly becoming stemmed mushrooms.
If one admires and consumes them, one will meet in dreams.
I am the so-called maiden of Wūshān,
the lady of Gāotáng.
Hearing that you are traveling at Gāotáng,
I wish to offer my pillow and mat.'"
The king thus favored her.
From "Xiāngyáng Records of the Elderly"
The aura of the Son of Heaven
Emperor Wén once dreamed of wanting to ascend to heaven but could not,
when a yellow-turbaned man pushed him up to heaven.
Turning back, he noticed the man's garment had a hole at the back of the waistband.
Upon waking, he went to the Jiàn Terrace,
and secretly searched for the yellow-turbaned man based on his dream.
He saw Dèng Tōng, whose garment had a hole at the back,
exactly as seen in the dream.
Summoning him, he asked for his name,
which was Dèng Tōng.
"Dèng" resembles "ascending,"
which greatly pleased Emperor Wén.
He honored and favored him increasingly each day.
"Book of Hàn"
Those who observed the celestial phenomena said:
There is an imperial aura in the Shāndōng region,
so Qín Shǐ Huáng journeyed eastward,
intending to suppress it.
Records of the Hàn Dynasty
state that Gāozǔ, suspecting himself,
fled and hid,
concealing himself among the rocks and marshes of the Mángdàng Mountains.
When Lǚ Hòu and others searched for him,
they often found him.
Gāozǔ found this strange
and asked Lǚ Hòu about it.
She replied:
"Above the place where Jì resides, there is often an aura of clouds,
so by following it, I can always find Jì."
Gāozǔ was inwardly pleased.
When the young men of Pèi heard of this,
many desired to join him.
Historical Records of the Hàn Dynasty
Bào Pǔ Zǐ states:
"Bān's history says:
Lǚ shì could discern Gāozǔ's location by observing the clouds.
Could it be that Heaven opened only Lǚ shì's eyes while blinding everyone else's?"
Dǒng Zhòngshū dreamed of a flood dragon entering his embrace,
and thus composed the words of "Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals."
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Tiānshòu
Xiàngrú was about to present a rhapsody,
but did not know what to write.
He dreamed of an old man in yellow clothes who told him:
"You can write the Rhapsody on the Great Man."
Thereupon he composed the Rhapsody on the Great Man,
which described matters of immortals and presented it,
receiving four bolts of brocade as a reward.
The emperor
Wéi Xuánchéng became Chancellor,
and proposed that the shrine and garden of Empress Dowager Xiàowén should be maintained according to the rites,
and not be renovated,
which the Emperor approved.
Over a year later, the Emperor fell ill and took to his bed,
dreaming that his ancestors reproached him for abolishing the temples in the commanderies and kingdoms.
His younger brother, Prince Xiào of Chǔ, also had a similar dream.
The Emperor summoned Kuāng Héng for consultation,
intending to discuss the restoration of the temples.
Kuāng Héng strongly advised against it.
Later, as the Emperor's illness persisted for years,
he eventually restored all the abolished shrines and temple gardens,
and resumed the sacrificial rites as before.
The Emperor
When the matron Liú was pregnant with Gāozǔ,
she dreamt of encountering a deity.
There was thunder, lightning, and darkness,
with the strange phenomenon of a dragon and serpent.
When he grew up, he possessed much spiritual power,
differing from the masses.
Thus, Wáng Wǔ was moved by this and tore up the contract,
while Lǚ Gōng, upon seeing his appearance, offered his daughter.
The Qín emperor traveled east to suppress his aura,
and Empress Lǚ, by observing the clouds, knew his whereabouts.
At the beginning of his mandate, a white serpent was severed,
and upon entering the pass in the west, the five planets converged.
Hence, Huáiyīn and Liú Hóu declared it heaven-bestowed,
not achieved by human effort.
The "Treatise on the Mandate of Kings" is all seen in the Records of the Grand Historian.
When the Jī clan was by the waterside,
the yuèzhuó cried at Qí Mountain.
When the Liú surname was in Zhōngyáng,
a flood dragon descended upon Fēng Marsh.

Zhū Guāng
Yáng Zǐyún during Emperor Chéng's reign accompanied the emperor to the Gānquán Palace,
where he was summoned to compose a rhapsody.
Zǐyún composed it,
but suddenly collapsed from exhaustion and lay down,
dreaming that his five internal organs had fallen out onto the ground.
He used his hands to gather and put them back inside.
When he awoke,
he suffered from a deficiency of vital energy and illness,
and died within a year.
From Huán Tán's "New Discussions"
Magnificent was Gāozǔ,
who first received Heaven's mandate,
though his traces were hidden in Zhōngxiāng,
his fame soared to the imperial records.
Auspicious clouds responded with radiance,
the imperial throne was bestowed through the virtue of Wood,
crimson clouds gathered by day,
while the white spirit wept at night.
The essence of Metal thus declined,
and the Red Emperor's glory flourished.
"Eulogy for the Meritorious Officials"
From his rise in Pèi Marsh, the divine mother cried out by night,
to manifest the omen of the Red Emperor.
"On the Mandate of Kings"
All the generals urged Emperor Guāngwǔ to ascend the throne,
so he summoned Féng Yì,
and the emperor said:
"Last night I dreamed of riding a red dragon up to heaven,
and upon waking I felt my heart pounding with excitement."
Féng Yì then stepped down from his mat, bowed, and congratulated him, saying:
"This is the Mandate of Heaven manifesting through your spirit."
Féng Yì then joined the other generals in formally deciding to honor him with the imperial title.
From "Dōngguān Hànjì"
Portents and Responses
When Cài Mào was first in Guǎnghàn,
he dreamt of sitting in the Tàijí Hall,
where there was a three-ear grain plant.
Cài Mào jumped to take it,
obtaining the middle ear,
but then immediately lost it.
He asked Guō Hè about it,
and Guō Hè rose from his mat to congratulate him, saying:
"The great hall
is a symbol of the imperial palace and government.
Having grain at the pinnacle
represents the highest emolument for a minister.
Taking the middle ear
means the position of the Central Bureau.
In writing, 'grain' (禾) lost becomes 'rank' (秩).
Although it is said to be lost,
this is actually how you gain official rank."
Within a month, Cài Mào was summoned for office,
and he then appointed Guō Hè as his assistant.
From the Book of the Later Hàn
Zhōu Pán, styled Jiānbó,
gathered his students at the New Year's assembly,
lecturing and discussing throughout the day.
He then instructed his two sons, saying:
"Recently I dreamed of my late teacher, Dōnglǐ Xiānshēng, discoursing with me in the innermost chamber of the dark hall."
Afterward, he heaved a long sigh,
"Could this mean my life is nearing its end?"
On the full moon day of that same month,
he passed away suddenly without any illness.
End
It is said that Gāozǔ's rise was due to five attributes:
first, he was a descendant of Emperor Yáo;
second, his appearance was extraordinary;
third, his divine prowess had auspicious signs;
fourth, he was tolerant, wise, benevolent, and forgiving;
fifth, he knew people well and appointed them adeptly.
Zhèng Xuán dreamed that Confucius told him:
"Arise, arise! This year's year is in Chén,
next year's year is in Sì."
After waking up,
he matched it with prophecies,
and knew his life was due to end.
Soon after, he fell ill and died.
In the
Northern Qí dynasty, Liú Zhòu, though highly talented, never found opportunity.
His biography comments on Xuán, saying:
"Chén represents the dragon,
Sì represents the snake,
when years reach dragon and snake, the worthy lament."
Dà Héng
There was a man named Zhōu Qiánzé who was poor but devoted to the Way.
One night, after toiling in the fields, he and his wife lay down exhausted.
He dreamed that the Lord of Heaven passed by and took pity on them,
ordering that something be given to them.
The Director of Fate consulted the register and said:
"This man's fate is poverty,
and his limit cannot exceed this.
Only Zhāng Chēzi is due to be granted ten million coins,
but Chēzi has not yet been born.
May we lend them to him?"
The Lord of Heaven said:
"Good."
At dawn, he awoke and told his wife.
Thereupon, the couple worked diligently together,
managing their livelihood day and night,
and everything they did earned them assets reaching ten million coins.
Earlier, there was a woman named Zhāng Jī who often went to Zhōu Qiánzé's home to hire herself out for work and had a clandestine union.
When she was full-term and about to give birth,
she was sent outside to deliver her child under a cart shed.
The master went to see her,
pitying her loneliness and hardship,
prepared porridge for her to eat,
and asked what she would name her child.
Jī said, "Since he was born under a cart,
and I dreamed that Heaven told me to name him Chēzi."
Qiánzé then realized and said:
"I once dreamed of borrowing money from Heaven,
and was told that it was Zhāng Chēzi's money lent to me.
It must be this child,
and the wealth should be returned to him."
From then on, their silver and coins dwindled,
and when Chēzi grew up,
he became wealthier than the Zhōu family.
"In Search of the Supernatural"
When Emperor Wén was still the King of Dài,
the Chancellor and Grand Commandant together eliminated the various Lǚ clans,
and sent someone to welcome him.
The Emperor consulted the Empress Dowager for a plan,
hesitating and unsettled.
They performed a divination,
and the omen obtained was "Great Horizontal," interpreted as:
"Great Horizontal on Gēngyín,
I shall become the Heavenly King.
Like Xià Qǐ bringing glory,
the Emperor calls himself 'the solitary one'—
I am already a king,
so what other king could I be?"
The diviner explained that the so-called Heavenly King
means the Son of Heaven.
Hàn Shū
After Jiǎng Wǎn was recommended for promotion,
he dreamed at night of an ox head at his door,
gushing with blood profusely,
and felt very disturbed by it.
He summoned Zhào Zhí, the dream interpreter, to ask about it.
Zhí said:
"Seeing blood signifies that matters will become clear.
The ox's horns and nose
form the character '公' (lord),
indicating your position is destined to reach that of a duke—
a most auspicious omen."
(Records of Shu)
White-robed Son of Heaven
When Dèng Ài was about to launch a campaign against Shǔ,
he dreamed of being on a mountain with flowing water.
He consulted Diǎn Lǔ Army Protector Yuán Shào about it,
and Shào said:
"According to the Yìjīng hexagram,
'Water on the Mountain' represents Jiǎn (Obstruction).
The judgment for Jiǎn says: 'Jiǎn is favorable in the southwest,
unfavorable in the northeast.
Confucius explained: 'Favorable in the southwest'
means going there will bring achievement;
'unfavorable in the northeast'
means the path there leads to exhaustion.
You will certainly conquer Shǔ,
but perhaps you will not return.'"
Ài appeared disappointed and unhappy.
Records of Wèi
In the second year of the Yuánfèng era of Emperor Zhāo,
a large rock on Mount Tài stood up by itself,
and in the Shanglin Park, a willow tree,
withered and stiff, rose on its own,
growing branches and leaves.
Insects nibbled on its leaves, forming characters that read:
"Gōngsūn Bìngyǐ stands,
and the royal altar of Chénliú Xiāngyì suddenly moved to Cháng'ān."
Dr. Suī Mèng interpreted this, saying:
"The rock, a yin entity, and Mount Tài Dàizōng are sites for imperial abdication and succession.
There will be a deposed former family,
with the surname Gōngsūn,
and the personal name Bìngyǐ,
who will rise from commoner status to become the Son of Heaven."
At that time, Emperor Zhāo was young,
and Huò Guāng was assisting in governance.
He executed Mèng for his ominous words.
After Emperor Zhāo passed away,
Huò Guāng deposed the Prince of Chāngyì and enthroned Emperor Xuān,
the great-grandson of Emperor Wǔ,
whose original name was Bìng,
and who had lived as a commoner for three generations in the populace,
just as Mèng had predicted."
From the "Book of Hàn."
Someone once asked Zhōu Xuān:
"Last night I dreamed of a straw dog,
what is the omen?"
Xuān replied:
"You will obtain fine food."
Shortly after, when going out,
he indeed encountered a lavish meal.
Later he asked Xuān again:
"Last night I again dreamed of a straw dog,
what does it mean?"
Xuān said:
"You are about to fall from a carriage and break your leg,
you should be cautious."
Soon it happened exactly as Xuān predicted.
Later he asked Xuān again:
"Last night I once more dreamed of a straw dog,
what does it mean?"
Xuān said:
"Your house is about to catch fire,
you should guard it well."
Soon a fire broke out.
He said to Xuān:
"I didn't actually have any of these three dreams,
I was just testing you,
so why were all your predictions accurate?"
Xuān replied:
"This was the spirits moving you to speak,
so it was no different from real dreams."
He asked Xuān again:
"Three dreams of straw dogs but with different interpretations,
why is that?"
Xuān said:
"Straw dogs
are objects for sacrificial rituals,
so your first dream meant you would get food and drink;
after the sacrifice is completed,
the straw dog is run over by carts,
so your second dream meant falling from a carriage and breaking your leg;
after the straw dog is crushed by carts,
it must later be carried away as firewood,
so your last dream worried about fire."
End
Pheasants Gathering
During the reign of Duke Wén of Qín,
a hunter from Chéncāng captured a beast resembling a pig,
not knowing its name,
and led it to present as tribute.
He encountered two youths,
who said, "This is called Wèi."
The Sòng Zhì records:
"It often feeds on the brains of the dead underground.
Just as they intended to kill it,
striking its head,
Wèi also spoke:
'The two youths are named Chén Bǎo.
Whoever obtains the male will become king,
whoever obtains the female will become hegemon.'"
The hunter from Chéncāng then chased the two youths,
who transformed into a hen pheasant,
ascended the northern slope of Chéncāng and turned to stone.
The Qín state established a shrine for them.
From Liè Yì Zhuàn and Jìn Tàiyuán Dìzhì:
"The male flew to Nányáng,
and later Emperor Guāngwǔ arose from Nányáng."
From Sōu Shén Jì.
The Sòng Zhì states:
"Duke Mù obtained it,
and by Duke Wén's time a shrine was established.
Considering Wén as Mù's distant ancestor
is a grave error."
Yú Fān annotated the Classic of Changes,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"My commandery's official Chén Táo dreamed that I met a Daoist priest,
who let down his hair and wore deerskin clothing and coarse cloth.
He burned three of the six lines of the Classic of Changes and gave them to me to drink.
I begged to swallow all of them,
but the Daoist priest said the Way of Changes lies with Heaven,
and three lines are sufficient.
How could it be that I, by receiving this mandate, should understand the classics!"
Separate Biography
White Water True Man
In Wúxīng, Qián Chéng, during Sūn Quán's time, once lay down for a nap by day.
After a long while, unaware, several liters of foam flowed from both corners of his mouth.
His mother, frightened, called out to him, saying:
"Just now I saw an old man feeding you roasted tendons,
and I regret that you were called before finishing them."
Chéng was originally frail and thin,
but after this incident, he became known for his strength,
and rose to the position of Wúnán Supervisor.
"Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds"
Táo Fǎtōng dreamed
that someone gave him three donkey loads of tendons.
He ate one load,
and his mother woke him with a call, similar to the previous story.
"Records of Strength Contests"
During the reign of Emperor Āi, Xià Hèliáng submitted a memorial stating,
"The Hàn dynasty's calendrical fortune has declined midway,
and it is time to receive the Mandate again." Therefore,
the era name was changed to Tàichū Yuánnián,
and the emperor was titled "Chén Shèng Liú Tàipíng Huángdì",
to suppress the ominous signs.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he harbored hatred and aversion toward the Liú clan.
Since the coin inscription contained the characters "金刀" (jīn dāo),
he changed it to "huòquán" (currency),
while some interpreted the characters "huòquán" as "Báishuǐ Zhēnrén" (White Water True Man).
Later, the diviner Sū Bó'ā, sent as an envoy by Wáng Mǎng,
traveled to Nányáng and gazed from afar,
seeing the walls of Chūnlíng.
He exclaimed:
"How splendid the aura is!
So luxuriant and verdant!"
When (the uprising) first began,
(Liú Xiù) returned to Chūnlíng and looked into the distance south of his residence,
where a blazing light,
reaching up to the sky for a moment,
then disappeared as it had first appeared.
Taoists such as Xīmén Jūnhuì and Lǐ Shǒu also claimed that Liú Xiù would become the Son of Heaven.
From "The Later Chronicles"
Wú Xuǎncáo Lìngshǐ,
Chángshā Liú Zhuó fell ill,
dreaming that someone gave him a white Yuè single-layer robe and said:

when it gets sweaty, burn it with fire,

"Liè Yì Zhuàn"
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was suspicious and jealous,

Signs and Portents

The rise of the Ancestral Emperor had four auspicious signs:
first, he possessed the legitimate lineage of sovereigns;
second, his appearance bore many extraordinary marks;
third, he was cultured in body and skilled in martial arts;
fourth, he upheld trustworthiness and cherished scholars.
As for its prophetic omens,
at his birth, a divine light illuminated the inner chamber,
and auspicious grains flourished in the fields of his hometown.
When he gazed upon his old residence,
there was the marvel of fiery light;
when he crossed the Hūtuó River,
there was the response of the river converging.
Xīmén Jūnhuì foreknew his taboo name,
Qiáng Huá presented the prophetic signs,
and from a thousand miles away, they were verified.
Liú Xīn changed his name and met his demise,

Thus, Wáng Zūn declared it was bestowed by heaven,
not by human effort.
The discussions on the Mandate of Kings by Zhuàn Gàn
are all recorded in the later texts.
During Emperor Huì's reign, Lù Jī was campaigning for Prince Chángshā Yì,
when Hé Dōng Prince Guǒ dreamed at night of a black curtain encircling his chariot,
and Lù Jī could not break through to escape.
The next morning he was killed.
"Book of Jìn"
Bountiful Harvests of Grain
I recall when Wèi Jiè, as a child with his hair in tufts, asked Minister Yuè about dreams,
and Yuè said:
"They are thoughts."
Wèi asked:
"When body and spirit are not connected, and one dreams,
how can that be thought?"
Yuè replied:
"There must be a cause.
One never dreams of riding a carriage into a mouse hole,
or of pounding and eating an iron pestle,
precisely because there is neither thought nor cause for such things."
Wèi pondered the cause for days without finding an answer,
until he fell ill.
Hearing of this, Yuè had his carriage prepared to go and analyze it for him,
whereupon Wèi's condition slightly improved.
Yuè sighed and said:
"This child surely will never suffer from incurable diseases in his heart."

Zhāng,
being a water name.

there were indeed omens.
Yet the imperial standard was not established,

"Jìn Dynasty Annals Commentary"
The Response of the Perfected One
Yáng Xióng served as the magistrate of Chūnyáng,
raised troops to resist Wáng Dūn,
and when the city fell, he was captured by Dūn.
On the day Xióng was first seized,
he dreamed at night of riding in a carriage with meat hanging beside it.

"Meat surely has sinews and strength,
and a carriage beside the character for 'jin'

From the Book of Jìn.
Initially, when Qín Shǐhuáng made his eastern tour and crossed the river,
those who observed the auras said:
"Five hundred years later,
there will be an aura of the Son of Heaven emerging from Wú in the region east of the river,
and the land of Jīnlíng possesses the potential for a king.

he claimed it corresponded to this prophecy.

and upon examining the chronological calculations,

"Records of Jìn"
When Fú Jiān was about to lead his army south,
he dreamed of sunflowers growing on the city wall and said:
"Tomorrow I will ask my wife about this."
His wife said:
"If you dispatch the army on a distant campaign,
it will be difficult to achieve victory as a commander."
Fú Jiān also dreamed that the land tilted to the southeast,

to which she replied:
"The region south of the Yangtze cannot be pacified.

this is surely an omen of defeat."
Fú Jiān did not heed her advice,
and ultimately suffered defeat.
(From Yì Yuàn)
