When Fú Jiān sent Mùróng Chuì on his mission,
his attendant Quán Yì advised against it but was not heeded.
Thereupon, Yì secretly dispatched strong men at night,
to ambush and attack him along the main road.
That night, Chuì dreamed of walking on a road that came to a dead end,
and looking back, he saw Confucius’ tomb beside him.
The tomb had eight openings, and he awoke feeling troubled by this.
He summoned a dream interpreter,
who analyzed it, saying:
"A road coming to an end means the path is blocked,
and you cannot proceed.
Confucius’ personal name is Qiū,
and combining 'eight' with 'Qiū'
forms the character for 'soldier.'
There must be an ambush on the road;
you must be extremely cautious."
Thus, Chuì took an alternate route and advanced,
and Yì’s ambush failed to capture him.
"Continuation of the Jìnyáng Autumn Annals"
Before Wú perished,
in Línpíng Lake of Wú Commandery,
one day the lakeside spontaneously opened,
revealing a stone casket,
inside which was a small green stone,
carved with the characters for "Emperor."
It was traditionally said that when Línpíng Lake was blocked, the world would be in chaos;
when it opened, the world would be at peace,
and the people of Wú considered this an auspicious omen.
Soon after, Wú was destroyed,
and later Emperor Yuán rose in Jiāngdōng.
After Wú's demise,
purple clouds were often seen on Jiǎng Mountain by numerologists,
who also said that Jiāngdōng still had imperial aura.
According to the "Records of Sòng,"
when Emperor Yuán crossed the river,
observers of celestial signs remarked:
"The purple aura of Jiǎng Mountain is often seen at dawn."
From Yǔ Chǎn's "Rhapsody on Yángdū."
Wáng Dǎo dreamed that someone offered a million coins to buy his eldest son Chángyù,
who was delighted.
Dǎo found this very ominous,
and secretly made all preparations for prayers.
Later, when building a house,
they unexpectedly dug up a cellar full of coins,
which amounted to hundreds of millions upon calculation.
Greatly displeased, he stored them all away and sealed them,
but soon after, Chángyù passed away.
"Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds"
In his final years, Liú Yào dreamed of three men with golden faces and vermilion lips,
who paced hesitantly facing east,
then retreated without speaking.
Yào bowed and stepped where they had trodden.
The Grand Historian Rèn Yì said:
"Three represents the ultimate phase of cyclical destiny,
facing east signifies Zhèn, the beginning order of kingship,
now turning to Duì indicates the decline of all things.
Vermilion lips,
yet silence means affairs are concluded,
hesitant pacing with bows and deference,
shows the path of relinquishment,
your bowing to them
signifies submission to others,
treading in their footsteps means caution against venturing out,
yet fierce armies will surely rise greatly."
Three years later, Yào was captured by Shí Lè.
"Records of the Former Zhào"
The catalpa tree grows even more luxuriantly.
Jiǎn Wén saw a prophecy saying:
"The destiny of the Jìn clan is exhausted,
Chāngmíng and Xiàowǔ are yet to be born."
Empress Dowager Lǐ dreamed a divine figure telling her:
"You will bear a son and name him Chāngmíng,
when he is born, the east will begin to dawn,
hence his name."
Later, Jiǎn Wén realized this,
and wept.
"Book of Jìn"
Inside the Sōngyáng Gate stood a large catalpa tree,
measuring forty-five arm-spans in circumference,
with the entire tree having withered and died.
During the Yǒngjiā era, one morning,
it suddenly grew lush and flourishing again.
In the Tàixīng era,
Emperor Yuán indeed succeeded to the great enterprise.
"Records of Yùzhāng"
Decayed trees flourish luxuriantly in Yùzhāng.
"Yǔ Zhòngchū's Rhapsody on the Capital of Yáng"
The withered catalpa displayed splendor in the ancestral city,
as Emperor Xuān's ancestor served as governor of Yùzhāng,
hence called the ancestral city.
Guō Pú's "Rhapsody on the Southern Suburbs"
Wáng Yì served as governor of Póyáng,
where a withered camphor tree revived,
Wáng Dūn memorialized urging Zhōngzōng to ascend the throne, saying:
"The white beast arrives in response to auspicious signs,
the long-withered camphor tree grows lush again."
Zāng Rǒng's "History of Jìn"
Táo Kǎn served as the governor of Guǎngzhōu,
and he dreamed that someone gave him armor as a Simā.
His senior official Chén Xié interpreted this, believing that Simā represented the imperial surname,
and armor was a defensive weapon,
indicating that His Excellency would be promoted.
In the second year of the Tàixīng era,
Táo Kǎn was indeed appointed as General Who Pacifies the South.
From Wáng Yǐn's "Book of Jìn."
A sparrow alights on a rooster's back
During the era of Huán Wēn, Xiè Ānshí
constantly feared for his safety,
and one night dreamed of riding in Huán's carriage for ten miles,
stopping when he saw a white chicken,
unable to proceed further.
No one could interpret this dream.
After Huán Wēn's death,
he indeed succeeded him as chancellor,
serving for sixteen years before falling ill.
Xiè Ān then realized:
"The sixteen miles
represent sixteen years,
and seeing the chicken stop means
this current year falls under the sign of Yǒu (the Rooster).
My illness will likely prove fatal."
A few days later, he passed away.
(From "Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds")
When Zhōngzōng was the chancellor,
a chick had sparrows flying to perch on its back.
They were driven away but returned,
and this happened repeatedly.
A diviner said:
"The chicken
represents the west; the west
corresponds to metal and fire. The sparrows transformed and came to join it,
which is an omen of the king ascending the throne."
It was also said:
"During Yuándì's reign, three sparrows together mounted a rooster,
all three entered Āndōng,
and the diviner in the hall believed it signified advancing three ranks to become the Son of Heaven."
From "Records of the Forest of Caves"
A maidservant of the Zhōu family in Chénliú, named Yǔ, entered the mountains to gather firewood.
Suddenly she dreamed of a woman who said:
"I have a thorn in my eye,
and I trouble you to pull it out for me.
I shall richly reward you."
The maidservant then saw a decayed coffin with a skull,
and grass growing in its eye socket.
She accordingly pulled out the grass,
and immediately found a pair of gold rings at that very spot.
"Shù Yì Jì"
Azure vapor emerges from the shrine
Someone asked Yīn Hào:
"Why is it that one dreams of a coffin when about to take office,
and dreams of dung when about to obtain wealth?"
Yīn Hào replied:
"Official positions are inherently putrid,
so one dreams of corpses when about to get an appointment;
money is essentially dirt,
thus one dreams of filth when about to acquire money."
Contemporary people considered this a famous saying.
From History of the Jìn Dynasty:
Suǒ Chōng initially dreamed of two coffins falling from the sky.
Suǒ Dǎn told Chōng:
"Coffins symbolize
official positions.
A noble from the capital will recommend you,
and the two coffins mean
frequent promotions."
Soon after, Minister Wáng Róng wrote to the governor,
urging him to recommend Chōng for the post of governor.
First, Chōng was appointed as a merit official and then recommended as a xiàolián.
From Biographies of the Jìn Dynasty.
In the first year of the Xiánníng era of Emperor Wǔ,
a great wind blew on the Imperial Shrine,
breaking the trees.
A blue vapor emerged from the shrine,
and diviners interpreted it as an indication of the aura of the Son of Heaven in Dōngguǎn.
At that time, Wǔwáng Zhòu of Lángyá was enfeoffed in Dōngguǎn,
and Zhòu
was the grandfather of Emperor Yuán.
Earlier, when Emperor Wǔ attacked Wú,
Wǔwáng Zhòu of Lángyá led troops out through Túzhōng,
while Wáng Hún pressed toward Lìyáng,
and Wáng Jùn had already advanced along the nearby route.
Sūn Hào intended to surrender,
and sent the imperial seal and ribbons,
bypassing the two nearby generals and delivering them afar to Zhòu,
which puzzled all who understood the situation.
"Records of Sòng"
In the early years of the Xiánhé era, Xú Jīng traveled afar.
He dreamed of sleeping with his wife and her becoming pregnant.
The following year when he returned,
his wife indeed gave birth,
which later matched his dream.
"Yōu Míng Lù"
The drooping willow suddenly sprouts.
Swallowing Earth
Liú Jìngxuān, who was well-versed in astronomy,
knew that the Jìn dynasty would be restored.
In Qí, he dreamed of swallowing a pellet of earth,
and in the dream, he asked a diviner,
who replied:
"This means you will swallow the land of your homeland."
After waking up,
he joyfully said:
"A pellet
represents Huán,
and Huán means to swallow.
I shall return to my native land."
Within ten days, Huán Xuán was defeated,
and he was able to return.
"Records of Emperor Ān of Jìn"
When Kāngníng first became Prince of Wú,
in the sixth year of the Xiánhé era of Emperor Chéng, in the fifth month,
in Qū'ē, a willow tree that had fallen for six years,
suddenly stood up and revived this month.
In the ninth year, on the jiǎxū day of the fifth month,
at Wú Xióng's home, a dead elm tree,
on that day, due to wind and rain, stood up and revived,
sharing the same omen as the broken willow reviving in the Hàn dynasty's Shànglín Park.
Although he had been re-enfeoffed as Prince of Lángyá at that time,
he still received Wú Commandery as his fief,
which signified the Emperor's surpassing of the legitimate heir,
an omen of enjoying the state.
Qū'ē was originally also Wú territory,
the omen appearing at Wú Xióng's residence in Wú town,
all were the will of Heaven.
"Records of Jìn"
Liú Mùzhī once dreamed that he and Emperor Gāozǔ were sailing together on the sea,
when suddenly they encountered a great wind.
In fear, he looked down beneath the boat,
and saw two white dragons flanking the vessel.
Afterward, they arrived at a mountain,
with peaks towering and elegant,
and forests dense and lush.
He felt very pleased by it.
When Emperor Gāozǔ captured the capital,
he asked Hé Wújì:
"We urgently need a chief clerk for the administration.
How can we find one?"
Wújì replied:
"None surpass Liú Dàomín."
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"I know him as well."
He immediately sent a messenger to summon him.
"Book of Sòng"
Stiff and shivering, life arises
When Xiàowǔ Dì was four years old,
during the third year of Āi Dì's Xìngníng era in the fifth month,
a gānglì tree at the home of Xiūmíng in Xīchāng County, Lúlíng,
suddenly sprang to life on this day.
When he ascended to the throne and inherited the rule,
those with insight secretly said:
"The auspicious sign of Xiūmíng in Xīchāng
indeed corresponds to the Emperor's given name."
This is the same omen as that of Hàn Xuāndì.
Above
Liú Mùzhī often crossed the Yangtze River,
and one night dreamed of joining two boats into a large vessel,
topped with a magnificent canopy,
adorned with splendid decorations.
At daybreak,
an old woman asked him:
"Did you have an auspicious dream last night?"
Mùzhī then recounted it in detail.
The old woman said:
"You will surely rise to the position of chief minister."
After speaking, she vanished.
Later, he indeed rose to the office of Minister of Works,
and Governor of Dānyáng due to his paramount achievements.
From "Yì Yuàn"
Cuī Hào for thirty-nine days and nights did not cease,
focusing his mind on studying texts,
forgetting sleep and food,
to the extent that he dreamed of debating with ghosts,
and thus obtained the essential methods of the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
beginning to understand that among the ancients there were both false and true,
with many speaking falsely,
and few being genuine.
"Basic Biography"
The deity spoke of the jade disc.
Initially, Cuī Hào plotted to harm Lǐ Shùn,
the foundation for disaster had already been laid.
Hào dreamed that he was holding a torch to burn Shùn,
fire broke out in the bedchamber and Shùn died.
Hào stood with his family watching it together,
suddenly Shùn's younger brother and son rushed out wailing, saying:
"These people are our murderers!"
They struck him with spears,
and Hào fell into the river.
He woke up disturbed by the dream,
and told it to his resident guest Féng Jǐngrén.
Jǐngrén said:
"This is truly ominous,
not merely an empty matter.
To burn someone with fire
is the extreme of cruelty,
it creates steps to chaos and portends disaster,
you have indeed brought this upon yourself."
The Book of Documents says:
"When evil spreads,
like fire raging across the plains,
one cannot approach it,
can it still be extinguished?
Moreover, those who initiate evil will ultimately meet calamity,
those who accumulate wickedness will have no surplus blessings.
The steps to disaster have been formed,
you should consider this carefully."
Hào said:
"I am thinking about it but cannot reform."
In the eleventh year of the Zhēnjūn era, his clan was exterminated.
During the reign of Emperor Ān of Jìn, the monk Fǎ Chēng of Jìzhōu was dying,
and told his disciple Pǔ Yán:
"The god of Sōngshān informed me that in Jiāngdōng there is General Liú,
a descendant of the Hàn dynasty,
who is destined to receive the Mandate of Heaven.
I have thirty-two jade discs and one cake of imperial gold for him—
this represents the divined number of generations for the Liú family."
Yán informed his fellow student Fǎ Yì,
and in the thirteenth year of the Yìxī era, Fǎ Yì found thirty-two jade discs beneath the stone altar of the Sōngshān temple.
The number thirty-two
means two times sixteen.
The Sòng dynasty held the empire,
with eight emperors in succession,
enjoying a reign of sixty years.
"Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì"
The village tree flourishes luxuriantly
When Yuèpíng King Pī passed away and the diviner Dǒng Dàoxiù died,
Gāo Yǔn then composed the "Discourse on Divination," stating:
"In the past, at the end of Míngyuán's reign, the White Tower was erected,
reaching a height of over twenty zhàng.
Yuèpíng King once dreamed of ascending it,
gazing out in all four directions and seeing nothing.
The king consulted a diviner,
and Dǒng Dàoxiù, after performing the divination, declared it highly auspicious.
The king remained silent but showed a pleased expression.
Later, when the incident occurred,
the king died of worry, and Dàoxiù was executed in the market.
If Dàoxiù had interpreted the six lines and responded to the king, saying:
'The Yìjīng states that the dragon at the zenith has regrets,'
for reaching the extreme height is called 'zenith,'
high and without people,
it is not a favorable state.
If he had spoken thus, he would have brought peace to the king above
and safeguarded himself below.
Fortune and prosperity would then have arrived—
how could disaster have ensued?
But now, abandoning the root to follow the branch,
the arrival of calamity and blame—
is it not fitting?"
Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn established the imperial altar in Nányáng during the Hàn dynasty,
but by the end of the dynasty its tree died.
When Liú Xuándé possessed Shǔ, it responded and flourished,
until the final years of the Jìn dynasty,
when the old roots first sprouted again,
reaching full growth by the early reign of Emperor Wǔ of Sòng.
"Records of the Southern History"
The young emperor grew increasingly violent and cruel by the day,
yet Shěn Qìngzhī still remonstrated with him outspokenly.
The emperor sent Qìngzhī's cousin Shěn Yōuzhī to deliver poison and force him to commit suicide,
at which time he was eighty years old.
At the beginning of that year,
Qìngzhī dreamed that someone gave him two bolts of silk,
saying, "This silk is just enough to span."
Upon waking, he told others:
"This old man will not escape death this year.
Two bolts make eighty chi,
just enough to span,
with nothing left over."
Book of Sòng
Xú Xiànzhī, courtesy name Zōngwén,
once had a person approach him during his youth, saying:
"I am your ancestor."
Xiànzhī bowed to this person,
who continued:
"You possess noble features but will face a great calamity.
You should bury twenty-eight coins at the four corners of your residence
to avoid this disaster.
After this passes, you may reach the highest ministerial position."
Later, Xiànzhī followed his family to a county,
where they resided within the county town.
Once when he was temporarily away, bandits attacked and destroyed the town from behind,
leaving no survivors among the townspeople.
Even chickens and dogs were completely wiped out,
yet Xiànzhī, being outside, alone survived unharmed.
"History of the Southern Dynasties"
Drunk and Lying on an Alien Form
Emperor Liú Yù of the Sòng dynasty was fond of drinking from a young age during his birthday celebrations.
Returning from the capital,
he rested at an inn,
where the elderly innkeeper said:
"There is wine inside the room;
you may enter and take it yourself."
The emperor entered the room,
drank beside the jar,
then lay down drunk on the ground.
At that time, Minister Wáng Mì had a disciple living in Dāntú,
who was also returning home and stopped at this inn.
The elderly innkeeper said:
"Young Master Liú is inside the room;
you may enter and drink with him."
This disciple entered the room,
came out in shock,
and said to the innkeeper:
"How could there be such a strange creature inside the room?"
The innkeeper hurried in,
and saw that the emperor had already awakened.
The innkeeper secretly asked what he had seen earlier,
to which the disciple replied:
he saw a creature with five colors,
like a flood dragon,
not Young Master Liú.
The disciple returned,
and reported this to Wáng Mì,
who warned him not to speak of it,
and instead formed a close bond with him.
From "Records of the Sòng Dynasty"
The emperor appeared impoverished,
having once owed Diāo Kuí thirty thousand coins for community funds,
and had no means to repay them for a long time,
so he was seized by Kuí.
Wáng Mì secretly repaid the debt with his own money,
freeing him as a result.
From "Annals of the Southern History"
Xú Xiàosì, courtesy name Shǐchāng,
once napped beneath the northern wall at the headquarters,
dreaming of two boys urgently saying, "Move, sir, your bed!"
Startled, Xiàosì awoke,
and the wall made a noise;
after he walked a few steps, the wall collapsed, crushing the bed.
"Tán Sǒu"
Lóng Zhāng
Qí Yídūwáng Kēng was seven years old when he left the inner palace,
with Táo Hóngjǐng serving as his tutor.
For eight or nine years, they were very close.
Later, Kēng was killed,
while Hóngjǐng was living in seclusion in the mountains.
He dreamed that Kēng came to him, sorrowfully bidding farewell,
saying:
"I have now passed away without guilt,
and in three years, I will be reborn into a certain family."
Hóngjǐng inquired about it,
but matters of the underworld are often secret and not revealed.
Upon waking,
he immediately sent someone to the capital to investigate,
and indeed, it matched the dream.
Hóngjǐng therefore wrote the Record of Dreams.
"Record of Dreams"
When Emperor Xiàowén reached Běimáng,
he then visited Hóngchí,
and ordered Rènchéng Wáng Chéng to accompany him on the dragon boat.
The emperor said:
"Last night, I dreamed of an old man,
his hair white,
properly dressed in official attire,
standing and bowing on the left side of the road.
I was puzzled and asked him,
and he identified himself as Jìn Shìzhōng Jī Shào,
saying he was here to welcome me,
his spirit appeared humble and fearful,
as if he had a request."
Chéng replied:
"During the chaos of the Jìn era,
Jī Shào protected his lord with his life and perished,
Zēng also was a loyal minister of Jìn.
Bǐ Gān faced Zhòu's tyranny,
loyally admonishing and was executed,
he can be called a virtuous scholar of the Yīn dynasty.
Both died in service to their kings,
and their tombs are near the path.
However, after Your Majesty moved to Yīn Luò,
passing through Chánxū to pay respects to Bǐ Gān,
and going to Luòyáng but neglecting Jī Shào,
this could have invoked the dream due to seeking favor."
The emperor said:
"How could I have such virtue to inspire noble spirits?
However, I truly wish to honor the virtuous of the past,
to praise loyalty and valor.
Bǐ Gān and Jī Shào were both truly steadfast of ancient times,
but I gave more emphasis to Bǐ Gān,
and was neglectful of Jī Shào,
causing personal regret.
This dream then arose,
perhaps as Rènchéng has said."
Thereupon, he sought their burial places,
and sent an envoy to mourn and offer sacrifices.
"Book of Wei"
Emperor Wǔ once traveled to Bamboo Grove Temple in Jīngkǒu,
and lay alone in front of the lecture hall.
Above him appeared a five-colored dragon pattern,
which the monks saw
and were so astonished they reported it to the emperor.
The emperor alone rejoiced, saying:
"The venerable monk does not speak idly."
In his movements and rest,
two small dragons were sometimes seen attached to his wings.
While gathering firewood or fishing in the mountains and marshes,
his companions occasionally witnessed them too.
When he became noble,
the dragon forms grew larger.
He also once passed through Xiàpī as a guest at an inn,
where he met a Buddhist monk
who said to him:
"The region south of the Yangtze will fall into chaos,
and you will be the one to bring it peace."
The emperor
Jí Shìzhān, styled Liángróng,
was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Xīyáng and Wǔchāng,
where he governed with integrity and frugality,
leaving no private savings in his household.
Earlier, Shìzhān had dreamed of obtaining a pile of deer hides,
and upon counting them,
found there were eleven pieces.
Upon waking, he joyfully exclaimed:
"The deer (lù)
symbolizes official emolument (lù),
shall I receive eleven such emoluments?"
From the start of his official career,
he had already held nine posts,
and upon being assigned these two commanderies,
he felt foreboding,
refusing treatment when he fell ill,
and died in his commandery in the seventh year of the Pǔtōng era.
(From History of the Southern Dynasties)
Riding a Dragon to Chase the Sun
In the eleventh year of the Tiānjiàn era, Fù Zhāo served as the Internal Historian of Ānchéng.
Since the Sòng dynasty, Ānchéng had experienced military turmoil, and the commandery office was known as ominous.
When Zhāo assumed office in the commandery,
a person within the commandery dreamed at night of soldiers and horses with abundant armor,
and heard someone say, "We should avoid the virtuous man."
The troops together soared into the void and vanished.
The dreamer awoke in alarm,
and soon a swift wind and heavy rain
suddenly arrived.
Several rooms collapsed entirely,
exactly where the dreamer had seen the army and horses trampling.
From then on, the commandery office became peaceful,
all attributing it to Zhāo's integrity and uprightness.
From the Book of Liáng.
Emperor Gāo of Qí, at the age of seventeen,
once dreamed of riding a blue dragon into the heavens,
heading west in pursuit of the sun.
Additionally, Sūn Fèngbó also dreamed that the emperor sent a dragon to ascend to the sky,
but from below, he tried to grasp the dragon's leg and failed to reach it.
Upon waking, he recounted the dream,
and consequently said to him:
"Yǎnzhōu shall greatly shelter the people,
yet you, my younger brother, will not partake in it."
"Nán Jì"
Xiàhóu Guài, styled Yuántíng,
was the son of Dàoqiān.
He had a fondness for wine,
and did not grieve during mourning periods,
never ceasing to consume strong liquor and rich delicacies.
Spending heavily on buying drinks and food,
he nearly exhausted the fields and gardens left by his father,
and still owed several thousand bolts of silk in debts,
often lacking even grain to eat,
so that his younger siblings suffered from hunger and cold.
Initially, Dàoqiān, knowing Guài’s fondness for wine,
did not wish to pass on the fiefdom to him.
Before Guài’s death, he suddenly dreamed that General Zhēnglǔ Fáng Shìbǎo came to his home,
sat in the hall with his father,
and spoke secretly after dismissing others.
Guài felt alarmed and fearful,
saying to people:
"Shìbǎo holds an official position;
in a moment, he will surely strike me."
Soon, someone arrived saying the official summoned the young master,
and he followed the summons immediately.
He was ordered to be caned two hundred times by attendants,
unable to endure the severe pain,
he screamed loudly for a long time before waking,
drenched in sweat that soaked through his bedding.
By dawn, the former capital prefect Zhào Zhuó visited him,
and seeing his clothes wet with sweat,
said to Guài:
"You must have drunk heavily last night,
to be drenched like this."
Guài then recounted his dream in detail.
Over ten days earlier,
the Secretariat Director Zhèng Dàozhāo had died suddenly from illness.
Hearing this, Guài said to Zhuó:
"How constant is human life?
One should only indulge in drinking."
Thereafter, he drank to excess even more recklessly.
Two days after the dream, he lost the ability to speak,
and only regained speech after acupuncture, but remained weak.
Soon, he died from chest distress.
Those who washed his body observed
numerous marks from caning
with blue and red bruises faintly raised,
approximately from two hundred strikes.
(From *History of the Northern Dynasties*)
Tiān Shíjiǔ Zǐ
Military Adviser Cuī Língyùn dreamed that Heaven spoke to him:
"Xiāo Dàochéng is my nineteenth son,
I already commanded last year that he be granted the position of Son of Heaven."
Examining the sequence of those receiving the Mandate since the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
the Emperor was indeed the nineteenth.
In the fourth year of the Yuánhuī era,
when the Emperor was General of the Army returning from the southern suburbs,
the diviner Chén Ānbǎo observed a yellow-purple aura emanating from the Grand Ancestor connecting to the heavens.
Ānbǎo said to his relative Wáng Hóngfàn:
"In my youth, I never saw a person's body possess such an aura."
Records
Cáo Wǔ, styled Shìwēi,
served as the Governor of Yōngzhōu,
amassed seventy million coins in cash,
was frugal and stingy by nature,
and never gave gifts to anyone.
While in Xiāngyáng, he alone provided supplies to Liáng Wǔ,
saying to him:
"You are destined for great nobility,
though I may not live to see it.
I now entrust my young son to you."
He often secretly sent money, goods, and fine horses.
At that time, the Emperor, being frequently in military campaigns, often faced shortages,
so he would go to Wǔ to exchange or borrow,
and was never refused,
accumulating up to one hundred and seventy thousand coins.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he forgot this kindness.
In the second year of the Tiānjiàn era,
the Emperor suddenly dreamed of walking along a ridge between fields,
with deep, bottomless water on both sides.
In the dream, he was very frightened,
when suddenly he saw Wǔ coming to carry him on his back.
Emperor Wǔ thus managed to cross over,
and Wǔ said:
"You are now the ruler of the realm,
yet you have forgotten me
and the words of my entrustment.
My son suffers from hunger and cold, without clothing.
The one hundred and seventy thousand coins you once exchanged—please return them for him to purchase a house."
The Emperor awoke
and immediately sent a secretary to return the money to him,
for him to use to buy a house.
His sons, Shìchéng and Shìzōng, both received promotions,
and within two or three years, they successively served as governors of major commanderies.
(From *History of the Southern Dynasties*)
Nine Bestowments
When Emperor Zhuang was still a prince,
Yuán Shùn dreamed of a mass of black clouds coming straight from the northwest,
colliding with the southeast,
shattering both the sun and moon,
and obscuring all the stars,
plunging heaven and earth into complete darkness.
Soon the clouds dispersed and the fog lifted,
and a sun emerged from the southwestern corner,
extremely bright and clear,
called the Sun of the Prince of Chánglè.
Then he saw Emperor Zhuang entering through the Chānghé Gate and ascending the Tàijí Hall,
with three hundred people shouting "Long live,"
all officials dressed in court attire,
paying homage to the emperor.
Only Shùn gathered at the Book Collection Bureau,
under the locust tree in the western corridor,
removed his clothes and hat and lay down.
After waking,
he told Yuán Huīyè:
"Last night I dreamed about myself,
and it was particularly inauspicious."
He explained the dream, saying:
"Black clouds,
being malevolent energy,
are the color of the north.
Eventually, there will surely be northern enemies causing chaos in the capital,
harming the two palaces,
and destroying the officials.
Why the sun?
It symbolizes the ruler.
The moon symbolizes the empress.
The numerous stars
symbolize the officials.
Based on this,
is the capital destined for calamity?
In the past, Liú Yào destroyed the Jìn dynasty and built a Skull Platform.
As for future events,
could it not be like this?
However,
Prince Péngchéng Xié had virtue and favor throughout the land,
and now I dream of his son becoming the Son of Heaven.
Accumulated virtue must be rewarded;
this is inevitable.
I only regret that his reign will not last long.
The reason for this
is that it emerged from the southwest,
changing time for years,
lasting no more than three years.
I only regret I will not live to see it.
Why did I dream of lying under a locust tree?
The character for locust (槐) has 'wood' beside 'ghost',
and being with a ghost while also removing my crown
—does this not signify death?"
However, after death, he would receive the posthumous title of one of the Three Excellencies,
all as in his dream.
(From Běi Shǐ)
Yáng Yuánshèn was profound and thoughtful,
skilled in interpreting dreams.
During the Xiàochāng era, Prince Guǎnglíng Yuān Yuān was newly appointed as General of the Chariots and Cavalry
and led a hundred thousand troops to suppress Gě Róng.
One night, he dreamed of wearing imperial robes and standing leaning against a locust tree,
thinking it an auspicious sign.
He asked Yuánshèn about it,
who said:
"It is an omen of the Three Excellencies."
Yuān was very pleased.
Yuánshèn withdrew and told others:
"Guǎnglíng will die.
The character for locust (槐) is 'wood' beside 'ghost';
after death, he will attain the Three Excellencies."
Guǎnglíng was indeed killed by Gě Róng,
and was posthumously honored as Minister of Works,
exactly as predicted.
(From A Record of Buddhist Monasteries of Luòyàng)
This matter is recorded in Yǒuyáng Zázǔ,
and Tàipíng Guǎngjì cites it under the category of dreams.
According to Wèi Shū, Liú Shēn of Guǎngyáng, styled Zhīyuǎn,
was killed by Gě Róng,
not Prince Guǎnglíng.
His son, Zhàn, styled Shìyuān,
inherited the title and was appointed Grand Commandant.
At that time, the Wèi capital had been in Luòyàng for a long time,
and it was certainly not the case that a son would use his father's personal name as his style name.
It is suspected that this is the matter of Zǐhé being misattributed,
an error in the recorded account.
Duàn Chéngshì loved the unusual and neglected the official histories,
and even mistook Gě Róng for Ěrzhū,
which is even more erroneous.
Emperor Tàizǔ of Qí, while digging a moat in Huáiyīn Lǐ City, unearthed nine ancient tin objects,
beneath which were seal script inscriptions,
which Xún Bóyù and others were all unable to recognize.
At that time, Jì Sēngzhēn alone remarked:
"Why bother identifying such ancient relics?
There being nine pieces of tin
signifies the omen of the Nine Bestowals."
The Emperor was pleased and rewarded him.
(From "Tán Sǒu")
Ěrzhū Róng campaigned against Gě Róng,
and as they were about to engage in battle,
he dreamed at night of a person demanding a thousand-ox blade from Gě Róng,
who initially refused to give it.
This person declared himself to be Emperor Dàowǔ,
whereupon Gě Róng presented the blade.
The person held it in hand and bestowed it upon him.
Róng awoke and rejoiced,
confident of his inevitable victory.
(from History of the Northern Dynasties)
Heaven bestows the royal seal
Ěrzhū Shìlóng once took a nap during the day,
when his wife Xī shì suddenly saw a man carrying Shìlóng's head away.
Startled, Xī shì approached to look, yet Shìlóng was sleeping as usual.
After he woke up,
he said to his wife:
"Just now I dreamed that someone cut off my head and carried it away."
He felt extremely uneasy,
and not long after, he was executed.

On the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month in the third year of the Shēngmíng era,
Yǐn Qiān of Xíngyáng Commandery saw a stone fall from the sky at the southeastern corner of Mount Sōng,
which split open upon hitting the ground.
Inside was a jade seal,
three inches square,
with the inscription:
"Those born under Wù and Dīng walk with the Way,
Solemnly entering the wilds to answer Heaven's mandate,
Sweeping clean Héluò and purifying the Wèi capital."
It also said:
"The emperor shall rise."
Qiān presented the seal to Yōng Province,
submitting it to Inspector Xiāo Chìfǔ,
who offered it up.
(Records of the Southern History)
Shěn Yuē at the end of the Qí dynasty suggested deposing the Qí Emperor Hé,
later fell ill and dreamt of Emperor Hé,
who cut off his tongue with a sword,
summoned a shaman to examine him,
the shaman's words matched the dream,
then called for a Taoist priest to present a red petition to Heaven,
claiming that the matter of abdication and succession,
was not initiated by himself,
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng was greatly angered,
several imperial envoys were sent to reprimand him,
Shěn Yuē, in fear, subsequently died.
"Book of Liáng"
Lì Fàn, styled Shìzé,
was from Zhuō County in Fànyáng.
Fàn once dreamed at night that his pubic hair brushed against his ankles.
Some days later, he recounted this dream,
and at that time, a dream interpreter from Qí said:
"The historian says you will become a prominent figure in Qí,
and you will be appointed to govern Eastern Qín,
spreading virtue across the coastal and mountainous regions.
You are destined to govern the entire Qí region,
and receive double emoluments in Yíngqiū."
Fàn laughed and responded:
"If I become a high official,
this dream will surely be verified."
Indeed, as predicted,
he became the Governor of Qīngzhōu.
"Book of Later Wèi"
A Strange Dream
Yáng Xiūzhī was about to take office in Luòyáng when
he dreamed at night of walking east to west on the postal road north of the Yellow River.
South of the road stood a burial mound,
extremely tall and large.
Xiūzhī climbed to the top of the mound on foot,
where he saw a bronze pillar,
its base shaped like a lotus flower.
Xiūzhī ascended a pillar base from the northwest,
grasped a pillar with his hand,
and the pillar then turned to the right.
Xiūzhī chanted:
"If the pillar turns three times,
I shall reach the rank of Sāngōng."
The pillar then turned three times and stopped.
Xiūzhī soon awoke,
and the location seemed to be southeast of Yèchéng.
After achieving honor and nobility,
the residence where he lived
was indeed in that very place.
From "History of the Northern Dynasties"
Emperor Wǔ's given name was Yuàn,
courtesy name Xuānyuǎn,
childhood name Lóng'ér,
born at the Qīngxī residence in Jiànkāng.
That night, Empress Chén Xiào and Empress Liú Zhāo both dreamed of a dragon perched on the roof,
hence his childhood name.
"The Southern Qí Annals"
At age thirteen, he dreamed his entire body grew hair,
extending down to his feet.
He also dreamed someone pointed at the ground he was stepping on and called it King Wén of Zhōu's fields,
and dreamed of flying through the void,
and dreamed of wearing a peacock feather garment.
Yǔ Wēn interpreted: "The peacock symbolizes noble rank."
He also dreamed of the Void Sovereign descending from heaven to the front of the Qīngxī residence's study,
its two wings spanning over ten zhang,
with purple cloud energy beneath.
While in Xiāngyáng,
he dreamed of wearing mulberry bark shoes while ascending the Tàijí Hall steps.
Yǔ Wēn interpreted: "Shoes signify destiny aligned with wood."
While in Yǐngzhōu,
he dreamed of a person descending from heaven in flight,
who came and painted on his upper garment with a brush in his hair,
then departed without speaking from both sides.
Yǔ Wēn explained:
"The painting
represents mountain dragons and splendid pheasants."
"The Records"
Residence Cloud Qi
During the Dàtóng era, Grand Physician Lìng Zhū Dān once served in the imperial palace.
Unexpectedly, he dreamed of a dog and a sheep each occupying the throne.
Upon waking, he told others:
"Dogs and sheep are not auspicious creatures.
Now that they occupy the throne,
will there be a rebellion?"
Soon after, the emperor was forced to flee,
and Jǐng ascended the main hall.
(History of the Southern Dynasties)
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng was born with an extraordinary radiance,
his appearance was remarkably distinctive,
with a sun-like forehead and dragon-like countenance,
prominent cheekbones resembling a tiger's,
an eight-shaped pattern on his tongue,
and a shimmering light around his neck.
His body cast no shadow in sunlight,
and he had fused bones in both thighs,
with a raised ridge on his neck.
There was a mark on his right hand that read:
"Emperor Wǔ as a child."
In his youth, he could tread on air,
and as he grew, his residence was often
filled with an aura like mist.
Those who encountered him
would immediately feel a sense of awe.
Initially serving as a military guard,
Wáng Jiǎn, upon meeting him once,
held him in high esteem,
saying to Hé Xiàn:
"This young gentleman Xiāo will become a palace attendant before thirty;
beyond that, his nobility will be beyond description."
Wáng Róng, known for his exceptional judgment,
especially revered and regarded the Emperor as extraordinary,
telling his confidants:
"To rule the world,
it must be this man."
While passing through Niúzhǔ,
he encountered a storm and moored at Lóngdú,
where an old man said to the Emperor:
"Your gait is like a dragon's and your stride a tiger's,
your physiognomy is indescribable;
the world is descending into chaos,
will it be you who brings peace?"
When asked his name,
he suddenly vanished.
(Records of the Southern Dynasties)
Initially, the Crown Prince dreamed that Hóu Jǐng became Qín Shǐ Huáng,
and the diviner said:
"This man again wishes to burn books."
When Hóu Jǐng entered, the Crown Prince's collection was burned,
and the books and records of the Eastern Palace were completely destroyed,
thus fulfilling the dream.
"Records of the Three Kingdoms"
In the third year of Dàbǎo, Chén Bàxiān campaigned against Hóu Jǐng,
advancing to station at Dàléi.
A soldier named Dù Líng dreamed of the god of Léichí Pond, Zhōu Hé,
who called himself the Great General Who Conquers,
riding in a vermilion boat,
displaying armor and weapons,
and announced he was descending to subdue Hóu Jǐng.
After a short while, he returned,
saying he had already killed Jǐng.
"Book of Chén"
Liù Lóng Shǒu Zhù
Initially, Emperor Gāo of Qí dreamed of ascending the palace hall wearing clogs.
Looking back, he saw two emperors, Wǔ and Míng, with another person behind them holding a spread-out map of heaven and earth, but he did not recognize him.
He asked,
and the person replied:
"I am after the obedient son."
When Cuī Huìjǐng's forces pressed close,
Chángshā Xuānwǔ Prince Yì came to aid,
reaching Yuè City.
He dreamed of riding a horse that flew halfway to the sky and then fell,
while the horse the emperor was riding transformed into a red dragon,
soaring alone into the void.
At that time, within the court, there was a guard who served as a shaman,
who often saw six dragons in the Tàijí Hall, each guarding a pillar.
Suddenly, two of them disappeared,
and later they were seen at Xuānwǔ's residence.
At that time, Xuānwǔ was in Yìzhōu,
so the shaman went to Shǔ to serve him.
When Xuānwǔ was in Yè,
this shaman returned to the capital,
and then saw the six dragons
all in the emperor's sleeping chamber.
He then left Yè for Yōng.
On the way, he fell ill and was near death,
and said to his companions:
"Xiāo, the Governor of Yōngzhōu, will surely become the Son of Heaven."
He recounted the previous events to them in detail.
The emperor
Liǔ Xiá, styled Zǐshēng,
was particularly esteemed and regarded as exceptional by his paternal uncle Qìng Yuǎn,
who said to Xiá:
"I once had the chance to serve my elder uncle,
and the Grand Commandant once told me:
'I dreamed last night that you ascended a tower,
a tower exceedingly lofty and splendid,
and I gave you my seat.
Your future official career will surely be illustrious,
but I regret I shall not live to see it.'
Just now I happened to take a nap,
and again dreamed that I gave you that very seat from before.
Your official rank will likely equal mine,
so you must especially strive diligently,
to correspond with this auspicious omen.'"
Book of Zhōu
The character "Wén" of King Wén
Shěn Jiǒng, the former Imperial Censor of Jiānglíng under the fallen Liáng dynasty, was relocated to Cháng'ān,
where Tàizǔ conferred upon him the title of Commandant Equal in Honor to the Three Ministers.
He was treated with great courtesy,
but Shěn Jiǒng feared that Tàizǔ admired his literary talent,
so he consistently kept his gate closed and avoided social interactions,
refraining from any social engagements.
Whenever he composed literary works,
he would immediately destroy them,
not allowing them to circulate.
Once, while walking alone past the Hàn Emperor Wǔ's Tōngtiān Tower,
he composed a memorial to present,
expressing his longing to return home.
After submitting the memorial,
that night he dreamed of a palace precinct,
heavily guarded and strict.
Shěn Jiǒng then pleaded his case,
and heard someone say, "It is not that we are unwilling,
but how many days can we allow you to return?
If you can pass through the barrier within a month,
I fear it may no longer be up to me."
He awoke, finding it strange,
and at the time thought it was a delusion.
Over ten days later, an order was issued for his release and return,
so he, along with Wáng Kè and others, managed to return east.
From "Records of the Three Kingdoms".
On the day Emperor Wǔ first received the abdication,
that night a court attendant,
Shǐ Pǔ from Kuàijī who was staying overnight at the palace, dreamed of someone descending from heaven.
Clad in vermilion robes and a military cap,
with dozens of attendants following,
he arrived in front of the Tàijí Hall facing north,
holding a golden plaque
with characters inscribed on it.
Shǐ Pǔ looked closely at it:
the text read:
"The Chén clan shall have five rulers for thirty-four years."
Then the figure ascended into the sky and vanished.
The next day, the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Kǒng Zōngfàn sighed:
"My service is finished.
Should we worry for our descendants?"
From Emperor Wǔ onward, including the deposed emperor, there were indeed five rulers.
From the beginning of the Yǒngdìng era to the end of the Zhēnmíng era,
exactly thirty-four years passed.
The Book of Chén
Emperor Wén of Suí had a dragon-like countenance,
with five ridges on his forehead converging at the crown,
his radiance shining outward,
and the character "king" inscribed on his palm.
Emperor Wén of Zhōu, upon seeing him, sighed and said:
"This child's bearing and bone structure
do not resemble those of an ordinary mortal."
The city gate of Dìngzhōu had long been closed and impassable.
During the reign of Wénxuān of Qí, someone petitioned to open it
to facilitate travel,
but Wénxuān did not permit it,
saying:

When the Emperor was appointed Regional Commander,
he arrived and opened it,
causing universal astonishment.

Emperor Wén was the governor of Wúxīng,
Hán Zǐgāo diligently attended to him,
always understanding his intentions,
the emperor greatly favored and loved him,
never letting him leave his side.
The emperor once dreamed of riding a horse up a mountain path,
in danger of falling,
Zǐgāo pushed and supported him to ascend.

Scholar Shěn Jūndào dreamed of a tall man in front of the hall,
wearing vermilion robes and a military cap,
his head protruding above the railing,
who shook his sleeves angrily and said:
"How dare you accept these treacherous Xiāos and mislead people!"
When the Later Sovereign heard this, he became suspicious of the two Xiāos,
and thus dispersed their followers to distant places.
"Records of the Southern History"
At the northern end of the Western Capital's court hall stood a large locust tree.
During the Sui Dynasty, it was said to be at the entrance of Tángxīng Village.
When the capital was moved to Cháng'ān City,
the Director of the Palace Buildings, Gāo Jiǒng, often sat under this tree to oversee affairs.
Later, when the tree was replanted,
it grew crooked,
and they intended to remove it.
The Emperor said:
"Gāo Jiǒng sat under this tree;
there is no need to cut it down."
To this day, one hundred and thirty years into the Xiāntiān era,
the tree still stands,
its branches and leaves lush and towering,
its roots sprawling and robust,
unlike any other tree.
Chéngtiān Gate directly faces the entrance of Tángxīng Village,
where the Táng family now resides.
(From "Records of Court and Commoners")
In the early Wǔdé era, a loud voice from Dàxíng Mountain proclaimed:
"The Táng state shall prosper for ten thousand years."

The aura of the Son of Heaven
Emperor Wén of Suí dreamed of floodwaters submerging the city,
which he considered an ill omen,
so he moved the capital to Dàxīng.
A diviner interpreted that "floodwaters" referred to the name of Táng Gāozǔ.
From "Anecdotes from Suí and Táng Dynasties"
Cherishing Books
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era,
after the pacification of the Eastern Capital,
over eight thousand volumes of new books from the Bǎo Chú of the Guānwén Hall were to be transported to the capital.
Shàngguān Wèi dreamed of Emperor Yáng rebuking him loudly:
"Why are you taking my books to the capital?"
At that time, Sòng Zūnguì, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, was overseeing the transportation and arrangements from the Eastern Capital.
He then loaded the books onto large ships in Shǎnzhōu,
intending to transport them to the capital.
However, the ships encountered a storm on the river and capsized,
with not a single volume remaining.
Shàngguān Wèi again dreamed of the emperor, who said joyfully:
"I have retrieved my books."
During his lifetime,
the emperor cherished books and historical records.
Although they accumulated like mountains,
not a single character was permitted to be taken out.
After his demise,
his spirit still clung to this cherished possession with reluctance.
It is noted that the new books of the Bǎo Chú
were all the secret books from the Dàyè era.
"Great Undertakings: Omitted Records"
At the end of the Suì dynasty, those who observed celestial phenomena said:
"At Lóngmén there is the aura of the Son of Heaven,
which extends continuously to Tàiyuán and is extremely strong."
Therefore, Emperor Yáng established a detached palace,
and frequently traveled to Fényáng to suppress it.
Later, Gāozǔ raised his righteous army in Fényáng,
and subsequently possessed the empire.
From "Xián Dìng Lù"
Grandma
Zhào Wénruò, in the early years of the Kāihuáng era, fell ill and died,
After seven days, he revived,
Saying that among the various sins in the underworld, killing living beings was extremely severe,
He then ceased eating meat.
Later, due to official business, he arrived at a relay station,
Suddenly dreaming of a woman in black clothing pleading for mercy,
He inquired of the station attendant:
"What food is available?"
The reply was that a plump and tender sheep was prepared,
Upon questioning further:
"It is a black female sheep."
Wénruò said:
"I do not eat meat."
So he ransomed it and set it free.
"Records of Retribution"
During the Dayè era, a man once dreamed that a phoenix alighted on his hand,
and he deeply considered it auspicious.
He went to consult Xiāo Jí for interpretation,
and Jí said:
"This is an extremely inauspicious dream."
The dreamer resented this,
thinking it was baseless talk.
Over ten days later, the dreamer's mother died.
He sent a close relative to ask Jí the reason,
and Jí explained: "A phoenix will not perch except on a parasol tree,
nor eat except bamboo seeds.
The reason it landed on your hand
is that your hand resembles the shapes of parasol and bamboo.
The Book of Rites states:
'The mourning staff for a mother is made of bamboo,
while for a father, it is made of parasol wood.'
Thus, I knew there must be profound sorrow."
From "Records of the Dayè Era Omissions"
and "Collection of Extraordinary Tales": Yángpíng's Sòng Jǐn similarly interpreted a dream for the Sūn family regarding seeking an official position.
Emperor Suí Yángdì and Shén Yáo were both maternal relatives of the Dúgū family.
Later, during a banquet hosted by the emperor,
Suí Yángdì teased Shén Yáo in front of the crowd.
Shén Yáo had a wrinkled forehead and face,
so the emperor called him "Grandma Face."
Shén Yáo felt angry and resentful,
and returned home dejected.
He told Empress Dòu about it,
and she joyfully exclaimed:
"You are enfeoffed in Táng,
and 'Grandma' signifies the head of the hall.
The word 'hall'
refers to Táng."
Shén Yáo was delighted,
and privately celebrated with the various princes of Qín and Qí.
From "The Records of Zhītián."
Empress Wǔ asked Shíquán Gōng Wáng Fāngqìng, saying:
"Last night I dreamed of losing at double sixes;
what does this mean?"
He replied:
"It likely signifies there is no heir in the palace,
suggesting the spirits may be alarmed,
warning Your Majesty,
thus I express the people's loyalty to the Táng dynasty."
The Empress was greatly enlightened,
recalled the Prince of Lúlíng to restore his position as crown prince,
appointed Shíquán Gōng as palace minister,
to assist and support him.
Lǐ Pó's "Great Táng Anecdotal Compilation"
The "New Táng History" states Dí Rénjié and Fāngqìng said the same thing.
The voice in the air said it was the Son of Heaven.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng served under the Suí dynasty as the Junior Supervisor of the Palace Interior.
At that time, the Provisioning Attendant Guō Hóngdào, who was skilled in physiognomy,
said to Gāozǔ:
"Your Honor has a concealed rhinoceros horn on the forehead,
extending down to the eyebrows—
this is not the appearance of a subject."
Gāozǔ took Hóngdào's silver basin and placed it on the ground,
drew his bow and shot at it,
saying:
"If your words prove true,
I should hit it with one shot."
After releasing the arrow,
it struck the basin as the bowstring sounded.
Hóngdào said:
"I hope when Your Honor's matter is verified,
you will reward me with a golden basin."
Gāozǔ was greatly pleased.
Later, when he was the Tàiyuán Garrison Commander guarding Bīngzhōu,
Wǔ Shìjié once walked alone in the street at dawn
and heard a voice from the sky saying:
"The Duke of Táng is the Son of Heaven."
Following the sound, he saw no one.
He then reported this to Gāozǔ
and also presented military texts,
which pleased Gāozǔ.
That night, Shìjié dreamed of Gāozǔ riding a dragon into the sky.
In the morning, he reported the dream,
and Gāozǔ was greatly pleased.
Thereafter, Shìjié was allowed access to the private quarters
and was entrusted with confidential matters.
Later, when Gāozǔ raised troops in Tàiyuán
and stationed at Línfén,
about twenty-plus lǐ from Jiàngjùn,
a purple cloud appeared in the shape of a canopy and pavilions,
directly above Gāozǔ.
The Secretariat Director Cuī Shí and the Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs Lú Cángyòng were part of the Tàipíng faction,
and both were exiled to Lǐngnán,
traveling together.
Cuī Shí said to Lú Cángyòng:
"My younger brother has received imperial favor,
so perhaps there is hope for leniency."
Thus, they delayed and did not hurry,
proceeding as far as Jīngzhōu,
where Cuī Shí dreamed of looking in a mirror in a lecture hall, saying:
"A mirror symbolizes clarity,
I will surely be understood by the sovereign."
He told this to the dream interpreter Zhāng Yóu,
who replied:
"The lecture hall
is a place for receiving teachings;
the mirror,
in terms of writing, stands for 'immediately seeing metal (gold)',
which is not an auspicious sign."
That very day, the pursuing envoy arrived,
and Cuī Shí was strangled in the relay station.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Zhāng Yóu said to Lú:
"Sitting down to listen to teachings
means it comes from above.
The character for mirror has the metal radical,
signifying 'end',
could it end today?"
From the Records of Collected Events.
Gù Cóng served as a supplementary official,
and once committed a crime that led to his imprisonment in the imperial prison,
facing execution.
One night, Gù Cóng sat in sorrow and dozed off,
suddenly dreaming of his mother's lower body.
He grew even more fearful, his anxiety showing on his face.
His colleagues asked him about it,
and he told them the dream,
believing it to be extremely ominous.
At that time, someone skilled in interpretation congratulated him, saying:
"You will likely be spared."
When asked how he knew,
he replied:
"Your mother's lower body represents your path to life;
to see the path to life again
is as auspicious as can be.
That is why I congratulate you."
The next day,
the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, Sū Jì, reported an error in the sentencing,
and Gù Cóng was ultimately spared.
He later rose to the position of chancellor.
"Guǎng Yì Jì"
Stone Imprint of Boots
Zhāng Zhuó, styled Wénchéng,
once dreamed of a large purple bird with colorful patterns,
which flew down and lingered in the courtyard.
He reported this to his grandfather,
who said it was an auspicious sign.
In the past, Cài Héng stated there were five types of phoenixes:
the crimson one with patterns is the fèng,
the blue one is the luán,
the yellow one is the yuānchú,
the white one is the hónghú,
and the purple one is the yuèzhuó.
This bird serves as an assistant to the phoenix,
indicating you will become an imperial aide.
Thus, he was given this name.
When Zhuó first took the imperial examination,
he dreamed at Huáizhōu of auspicious clouds covering him.
That year, during his policy response,
the examination official Qián Wèidào ranked him first in the empire.
Earlier, while serving under Prince Qí,
he dreamed at night of wearing scarlet and riding a donkey.
In his sleep, he wondered:
"I wear green robes and ride a horse—
why would I wear scarlet and ride a donkey?"
That year, he passed the examination
and was appointed Hónglú Assistant Minister,
directly receiving the fifth rank without the usual evaluation—
this was the fulfillment of his dream.
(From "Qiān Zǎi")
In the sixth year of Wǔdé,
the chariot and cavalry general Liú Shāntāo submitted a memorial stating,
that when Gāozǔ was still in obscurity,
he frequently traveled to a manor in the outskirts of Luò,
and once stepped on two stones,
where boot prints appeared in the stones,
and they remain to this day.
Gāozǔ ordered them to be chiseled,
but after digging more than two cun deep,
the prints became even clearer,
so he stopped.
His name is recorded in the prophetic registers.
Jǐshìzhōng Chén Ānpíng's son, having reached the age for official selection,
was lying down with his fellow villager Lǐ Xiānyào,
when he dreamed at night of raising silkworms in the eleventh month.
Xiānyào interpreted the dream, saying:
"Raising silkworms in the eleventh month
means winter silk (dōngsī),
so you will surely be sent to the Eastern Bureau (dōngsī)."
A few days later, he was indeed sent to the Ministry of Personnel.
End
Xǔ Shìxù,
a native of Bìngzhōu,
seeing that the Suì dynasty was about to fall,
said to Gāozǔ:
"The Way of Heaven supports virtue,
human affairs favor the capable.
If one fails to act at the critical moment,
one will surely regret it later.
Now the Suì government has lost its order,
the world is in turmoil,
your surname corresponds to the prophetic charts,
your name answers to the folk songs."
Old Book of Táng
Dòu Kàng had been intimate with Gāozǔ since youth,
and when Yáng Xuángǎn rebelled,
while Gāozǔ commanded troops in Lǒngyòu,
Kàng said to Gāozǔ,
stating:
"Xuángǎn is but the one who starts the hunt,
the Lǐ family is named in the prophetic charts - this opportunity should be seized,
it is indeed heaven's revelation."
Gāozǔ replied:
"Do not initiate disaster,
how reckless your words are."
Emperor Xuánzōng dreamed of falling into a well,
where a soldier wearing crimson trousers
carried him out on his back.
The next day, he ordered a search,
and in the garden, they found a gatekeeper wearing crimson trousers.
He was brought for an audience,
and the emperor asked, "What did you dream last night?"
The man replied, "I carried the sun out of a well on my back,
ascended to heaven, and saw its form."
This matched the emperor's dream.
The emperor then asked, "Do you wish for an official post?"
He answered, "I do not understand how to be an official.
My family is poor."
So the emperor bestowed five hundred thousand coins upon him.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Signs of an Emperor
Shǐ Cháoyì and Luò Yuè plotted to assassinate Sīmíng.
That night, Sīmíng awoke startled from a dream,
sat up on his bed in melancholy and said:
"I just dreamed of a herd of deer crossing the water from the sandy shore,
the deer died and the water dried up."
After speaking, he went to the toilet.
The court entertainers said to each other:
"Deer
symbolize fortune;
water
symbolizes life.
His fortune and life are both exhausted."
Yuè ordered men to seize him,
and he was strangled at Liǔquán Station.
(Old Book of Tang)
Lǐ Fǔguó acted arbitrarily without regard for his sovereign,
and Dàizōng gradually grew to detest him.
Once while sleeping,
he dreamed of ascending a tower,
where he saw Gāo Lìshì leading several hundred iron-clad cavalry to stab Fǔguó with halberds,
causing blood to spill all over the ground.
They sang and cheered before and after, comparing themselves as they departed.
The emperor sent an attendant to ask the reason,
to which Lìshì replied:
"It is by Emperor Míng Huáng's command."
The emperor awoke
but did not speak of it immediately.
Later, when Fǔguó was killed by bandits,
the emperor found it strange,
and only then did he recount his dream to those around him.
From "Dū Yáng Biān"
Emperor Gāozǔ was about to raise his righteous army,
marching west to enter Cháng'ān,
when he dreamed one night that he suddenly died,
fell beneath the bed,
and was eaten by a swarm of maggots.
Upon waking,
he felt deeply disturbed by it,
so he went to Zen Master Zhì Mǎn and secretly recounted the dream.
Mǎn immediately congratulated him, saying:
"You will obtain the empire."
The Emperor was greatly startled,
and said to Mǎn:
"What do you mean?"
Mǎn said:
"A subject dare not directly point to the Son of Heaven,
so 'dying by the steps' means perishing,
and 'falling from the bed' means descending.
Maggots signify attachment and drawing near,
and being eaten by a swarm of maggots
is an image of the multitude drawing near and attaching themselves to the Supreme Sovereign.
It is very auspicious."
He also said:
"When I was a novice monk,
I was skilled in the 'Book of Changes',
and now I dare to divine for you."
When the hexagram was completed,
he said:
"You obtained Qián,
'The dragon flies in the heavens',
which is also an omen of an emperor."
When the Emperor reached Huòyì,
he again dreamed of countless armored horses,
filling the sky as they flew.
The Emperor asked what they were,
and the troops replied:
"These are the spirits within your body.
Without them,
how could you awe and control the empire?"
Having spoken,
they all flew into the Emperor's body.
The Emperor awoke,
summoned Tàizōng and told him,
adding:
"My cause will succeed."
Tàizōng bowed before him,
repeatedly shouting 'Long live the Emperor' four times,
and the Emperor was again greatly pleased.
Later, when he ascended the throne,
he ordered the restoration and expansion of the temple,
bestowing upon it the name Xīngyì Temple,
and granted it all the property and estates of his former residence in Tàiyuán,
to be permanently endowed.
Today, within the temple, one can still see the Hall of Dream Interpretation and the statue of the Master.
"Record of Marvels in Luòyáng"
Fú Tàijiē
Lǐ Xūzhōng, styled Chángróng,
was most profound in the art of the Five Elements.
When he fell ill,
he said to his friends Wèi Zhōngháng and Hán Yù:
"I dreamed of a great mountain splitting open,
and red-yellow substance like gold flowing out."
Someone said this was what is called the Great Return,
and now three years have passed.
After Xūzhōng died,
Yù recalled and interpreted his dream, saying:
"The mountain corresponds to the Gen trigram,
the splitting and flowing of red-yellow substance
is the image of a malignant ulcer,
while the Great Return
means the great return to the origin
—it had already foretold this."
(From the Epitaph for the Late Lǐ)
Wéi Wēn, courtesy name Hóngyù,
in the fifth month of the fifth year of the Huìchāng era, developed a boil on his head.
He summoned his son-in-law Zhāng Fùlǔ
to entrust him with final arrangements,
to which Fùlǔ replied:
"Last year, you had two boils on your head,
and now there is only one, still minor.
Why do you speak so gravely?"
Wéi Wēn said:
"When I was twenty-nine and serving as a proofreader,
I dreamed of two yellow-clad messengers arriving with a summons to pursue me.
As we reached the Chǎn River about to cross,
one who came after said:
'His grave mound requires ten thousand days to complete,
and it is not yet finished.'
Thus, we did not cross, and I awoke.
Now ten thousand days have passed,
how could I escape it?"
From the Collected Works of Fánchuān.
In the fifth month, on the day Jiǎzǐ, of the second year of Xīníng,
Emperor Gāozǔ ascended the throne.
The stem was called Jiǎ,
the branch was called Zǐ.
The stem and branch generated each other,
forming the character Lǐ.
Although on Zǐ and Mǎo days no celebrations were held,
this was taken as a warning,
which is why the ministers submitted to the Tàijiē.
Respectfully, from the "Memorial on Gāozǔ's Founding of the Táng."
Naming
Tàixué bóshì Zhèng Huángǔ married the daughter of Minister of Justice Liú,
and after the betrothal rites,
he later stayed overnight in Zhāoyìng County with the Daoist priest Kòu Zhāng.
That night, he dreamed of riding in a carriage across three small bridges,
arriving at a house behind a temple,
where he proceeded to marry.
The host's surname was Fáng.
Startled awake,
he recounted the details to Kòu Zhāng,
and recorded the event with pen and paper.
Kòu Zhāng said:
"Having just married, it's natural to have such a dream;
it's nothing to be surprised about."
Liú's daughter soon passed away.
Several years later,
he remarried a woman named Lǐ in Dōngluò at Zhāochéng Temple.
On the day of the wedding feast at the borrowed residence, it happened to be at the three bridges,
and the host's surname was Hán.
At that time, Fáng Zhíwēn was the Deputy Governor of Dōngluò,
who was his wife's maternal uncle,
and the banquet arrangements and such
were all overseen by Fáng.
"Yì Shǐ"
In "Táng Shī Jì Shì," the Liú family is recorded as the Liǔ family.
When Gāozǔ was governing Qízhōu,
Tàizōng was four years old at the time.
A scholar who claimed to be skilled in physiognomy
paid a visit to Gāozǔ and said:
"You, sir, are a noble man,
and you will have a noble son."
Upon seeing Tàizōng, he said:
"With the bearing of a dragon and phoenix,
and the appearance of heaven and the sun,
by the age of twenty,
he will surely save the world and bring peace to the people."
Gāozǔ, fearing his words would be leaked,
intended to kill him,
but the scholar suddenly disappeared.
Thus, drawing from the meaning of "saving the world and bringing peace to the people,"
he used it as a name.
The "Old Book of Tang" and "Chéngdìng Record" state that Tàizōng was three days old at the time.
When Tàizōng was the Prince of Qín,
Gāozǔ composed a poem that said:
"Holy virtue aligns with the heavenly emperor,
five constellations appear as a string of pearls.
A gentle breeze caresses Shìmín,
all above and below rejoice together in celebration."
When the Emperor's residence west of the palace was first completed,
Gāozǔ presented a jade seal,
and when it reached the Emperor's place, the officials remarked to one another:
"The poem and the jade seal
are surely auspicious signs for the state of Qín."
"Cèfǔ Yuánguī"
Dù Mù once sought the position of junior ceremonial officer from the prime minister,
but was unsuccessful;
he then requested the post of junior autumn official,
again without success.
He once dreamed someone told him:
"Farewell to spring before reaching autumn,
the foot of Kun and the head of Jie."
Later, he indeed became vice director of the ministry of justice.
"Shangshu Gushi"
Dù Mù held low positions,
often feeling unhappy.
Approaching fifty, he fell ill,
writing his own epitaph and funeral oration.
He also dreamed someone informed him:
"After you change your name to Bì,
within a month a servant will come from home to report."
Saying the rice was nearly cooked when the steamer cracked.
Dù Mù said these were all ominous signs.
Soon he dreamed again of writing on paper:
"Bright and white the colt,
in that empty valley."
Waking, he sighed and said:
"This is the white horse passing a crack;
I was born under Jué and Zhǐ,
and will return to Jué,
becoming the eighth house -
this is my great misfortune.
From lake governor I was promoted to court official,
wood returning to Jué is enough."
That year he died from illness.
"Old Book of Tang"
Duàn Chéngshì once recounted what he heard from a physician:
When yin energy dominates in the visceral qi, one dreams frequently;
when yang energy is vigorous, one dreams little,
and even those dreams are not remembered.
The blind have no dreams,
which shows that dreaming is a matter of habit.
Duàn Chéngshì's cousin Lú Yǒuzé dreamed of watching drumbeats,
and upon waking,
found his younger brother playfully knocking on the door like衙门 drums.
Another brother-in-law, Péi Yuánsú, said that among his cousins was one fond of a neighboring girl,
who dreamed a courtesan gave him two cherries;
after eating them,
upon waking,
he found the pits fallen beside his pillow.
Lǐ Xuàn, in his "Lǐ Zǐzhèng Biàn",
states that in the most refined dreams,
one's dream-self becomes visible,
as when Liú Yōuqiú saw his wife
through his dream-self,
showing dreams cannot be interpreted by a single rule.
Foolish people dream little—
not only the sagely hear of this,
even stable hands and servants rarely dream in a hundred nights.
"Yǒuyáng"
The dragon drinks from the pond.
Zhèng Chāngtú passed the imperial examination,
and was residing in Cháng'ān,
when one night after cooling off in the courtyard,
he dreamed of being assaulted by someone,
dragged out through the Chūnmíng Gate,
and only managed to break free at the stone bridge where the main roads converged,
losing one of his purple silk shoes in the process.
He rushed back to his residence and woke up,
feeling extremely exhausted.
He told his brothers about it,
and indeed one shoe was missing by his bed.
At dawn, he sent someone to search for it on the stone bridge, where it was found.
"Records of Hearing Marvels"
Before Tàizōng launched his righteous campaign,
he often drank and lay drunk at Liú Wénjìng's home.
Wénjìng, sitting upstairs,
saw a white dragon descend into the large pond south of the residence to drink from it,
causing numerous big fish to leap onto the bank,
numbering in the hundreds.
After a long while, it vanished.
The household servants all witnessed it,
and were extremely astonished.
When Tàizōng awoke,
he said to Wénjìng:
"While drunk, I was very thirsty,
and dreamed of entering your pond to drink water—
it was incredibly clear, cool, and refreshing."
Wénjìng looked at his body,
and it was still wet.
"Yù Jiǎn"
Zǐyún pertains to Heaven.
When Liú Réngōng of Liáng was in humble circumstances, he once dreamed of a Buddhist banner flying out from his fingers.
A diviner said:
"When you are forty-nine years old, you will certainly attain the high honor of commanding banners and canopies."
Later events matched this prediction,
and he indeed became the military governor of Yōu Province.
"Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Three Dreams
Duàn Sīpíng was born with extraordinary omens,
and the Meng ruler Yáng Gānzhēn, suspicious of him,
sent men to hunt and capture him.
Sīpíng fled into hiding,
and in hunger plucked a wild peach.
Splitting it open, he found characters written on the pit's skin:
"Qīng Xī."
Sīpíng analyzed them, saying:
"Qīng means the twelfth month,
Xī means the twenty-first day.
Now that the Yáng clan's rule is in chaos,
should I rise in rebellion on that day?"
Thereupon, he borrowed troops and led his forces to Hé Wěi.
That evening, Sīpíng dreamed someone cut off his head,
then dreamed a jade vase lost its handles,
and dreamed a mirror broke.
Fearing, he dared not advance his troops.
His strategist Dǒng Jiāluó said:
"All three dreams are auspicious signs.
You are a dàfū (high official),
and removing the head from 'fū' makes 'tiān',
a sign of the Son of Heaven;
a jade vase losing its handles becomes 'wáng',
a sign of kingship;
in a mirror there is a reflection,
as a person has enemies;
the mirror breaking means no reflection,
no reflection means no enemies.
All three dreams are auspicious signs."
Sīpíng then resolved,
and the next morning,
led his troops across the river,
drove out the Yáng clan and took the Meng kingdom,
then changed the state's name to Dàlǐ,
in the second year of the Later Jìn dynasty's Tiānfú era.
From "Zhēn Jì"
When Gāozǔ raised the
righteous army,
above Tàizōng's dwelling there was purple cloud,
which soon transformed into five colors,
taking the shape of a flying dragon.
In the eighth year of Wǔdé,
he was appointed as Zhōngshū Lìng.
Once at night by Jiāyóu Gate, he saw a divine being,
tens of feet tall,
dressed in plain white clothes and hat,
who called out to Tàizōng saying:
"I shall make you the Son of Heaven."
Tàizōng bowed twice in reverence,
and suddenly the being vanished.
In the Hóngyì Palace where he resided, there was a large pond,
from which auspicious energy often arose,
billowing hundreds of feet high.
Tàizōng alone found this extraordinary in his heart.
By the ninth year,
this energy grew even more intense,
reaching up to the heavens.
In the sixth month, he resolved the internal crisis,
and was established as Crown Prince.
There was also a fāngshì named Qiáo Fúrén, skilled in predicting fate,
who saw that Jiànchéng and Yuánjí both had contentious intentions.
He thus said to those close to him:
"Qínwáng corresponds to the celestial mandate,
and is destined to be the paramount ruler.
These two are merely to be swept aside.
Xīyǐn and Hǎilíng have yet to act."
The Grand Astrologer reported:
"When Venus enters the Southern Dipper,
Qínwáng will obtain the empire.
His momentum cannot be withstood;
if not for the favor of the August Heaven,
how could this be achieved?"
Cèfǔ
King Zhōu Wángchǔnè,
dreamed of a person holding a giant mirror reflecting the sky,
with constellations shining brightly filling it.
He carved its belly and absorbed it,
thus mastering the study of celestial bodies and astrology.
"Tán Yuàn"
The snail's trail forms the heavens.
Avoiding the Meteor
Wú È Shuài Wáng Yú, when young and a minor officer,
joined the army besieging Rùnzhōu.
One night, he dreamed a Daoist priest warned him:
"Tomorrow a meteor will fall to the ground.
If you can avoid it, you will rise to general and minister."
The next day, as the troops stormed the city,
arrows and stones rained down from the walls.
Yú leaned against a palisade, sword in hand, directing the battle,
when suddenly a huge rock struck the very wood he leaned on.
Half his armor was crushed to pieces,
yet Yú remained unharmed.
He sighed and said:
"So this was the meteor."
From then on, he believed in his destiny.
"Records of the Spirits"
While attacking Rùnzhōu, Yú was shot by a giant crossbow,
the bolt piercing his right ear
and exiting through the left,
then hitting another soldier beside him,
who died instantly. Yet Yú stood firm.
He was helped back to camp, lay ill for over a hundred days, then recovered,
and his hearing remained sharp into old age,
with no scar or injury.
"History of Southern Táng"
When Rùizōng was first born in the Hánliáng Hall,
Empress Wǔ Zétiān had a Buddhist statue built within the hall,
which was made of jade.
As he grew older,
he was idly observing beside it
when the jade statue suddenly spoke:
"You will later become the Son of Heaven."
In the Cèfǔ Yuánguī,
it is recorded that when he was Prince of Jì,
snail trails on his bedroom wall formed the character for "heaven,"
which frightened him;
he wiped them away,
but after several days they reappeared as before.
After he ascended the throne,
he carved jade and cast gold into snail shapes,
placing them separately before Buddhist and Daoist statues.
From the Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
Unharmed After Falling from a Building
Xú Wēn once dreamed of over ten yellow dragons in the water;
Wēn caught one dragon and woke up.
The next day, he obtained Lǐ Biàn.
When
Lǐ Biàn was in the government,
he was once unhappy for a day.
His wife asked him about it,
and Lǐ Biàn said:
"I had an inauspicious dream last night,
and I'm worried because of it."
His wife said:
"Dreams have no inherent good or bad fortune;
it depends on how people interpret them."
Lǐ Biàn then went out to attend to official matters,
and soon saw Zhōu Zōng in the courtyard below.
He then said to him:
"Last night I dreamed of passing through Shùn Tiān Gate,
and then suddenly fell to the ground.
What does this mean?"
Zhōu Zōng bowed and congratulated him, saying:
"This means Your Excellency should send someone to be enthroned."
Lǐ Biàn was greatly pleased,
led Zhōu Zōng into the inner chamber,
and drank with him at the same table as his wife.
"Stories of the Five States"
Xuánzōng was only three years old when
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Chǔ.
At that time, Wǔ Zétiān was in a high tower,
holding him to look into the distance,
when he accidentally fell to the ground.
The attendants cried out in alarm,
rushing down to support and gather around him.
The emperor remained calm and showed no signs of injury,
which Wǔ Zétiān found very remarkable.
Administrator Zhāng fell ill,
dreamed of being pregnant,
and found it very disturbing.
Guǒ Guāngféng said:
"This will pass when you encounter a Rénshēn day.
What does this mean?"
He replied:
"Being pregnant
means gestation,
indicating great fortune is present.
Your abdomen symbolizes this."
Later events unfolded as he said.
From "Bǎoguāng Lù"
Zǐyún is above
Lú Jiàng, styled Jìnqīng,
was suffering from malaria and near death,
when one night he dreamed of a woman in white singing "Bodhisattva Barbarian,"
who urged Jiàng to drink wine from a goblet,
and then said to him:
"Your illness will be cured if you eat sugarcane."
The next morning he sought out sugarcane and ate it,
and indeed his illness subsided.
A few nights later, he again dreamed of the same beautiful woman in white, who said:
"I am Gěng Yùzhēn,
and we shall meet again in prosperity at Gùzǐ Slope."
Jiàng awoke,
and pondered the meaning of Gùzǐ Slope.
Later, he went to Jīnlíng and became the military governor of Xuānzhōu,
after the fall of the Táng dynasty, he submitted to the Liáng,
but was implicated in the case of Gǒng Shènyí and sentenced to death.
At the execution, a woman in white was beheaded together with him,
her appearance exactly like the one in his dream.
When he asked about the place of execution,
it turned out to be Gùzǐ Slope.
The woman's surname was Gěng, her given name Yùzhēn;
after her husband died,
she had an affair with her stepson,
and for this capital crime,
she was executed alongside Jiàng.
From "Records of the Southern Táng"
As the state of Jīnlíng was about to fall,
Xú Kǎi was afflicted with illness.
He suddenly dreamed of a giant holding a large iron sieve.
The giant took him and his brother Xú Xuàn,
along with Xú Yóu,
and placed them together into the sieve.
When sieved, Xú Kǎi and Xú Yóu both fell to the ground, while Xú Xuàn alone did not.
Soon after, both Xú Kǎi and Xú Yóu died of illness.
Emperor Xuánzōng concurrently served as the Military Governor of Lùzhōu.
Within the prefecture's borders, a yellow dragon ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
He once went hunting,
and purple clouds appeared above him,
later observed and confirmed by his followers.
Throughout this period, auspicious signs
amounted to nineteen occurrences in total.
Outside his residence was a pond,
which overflowed across more than a qǐng of land,
diviners interpreting it as an aura of the dragon.
In the fourth month of the fourth year,
Emperor Zhōngzōng visited his estate,
and while touring the pond,
a decorated pleasure boat was fashioned,
with a giant elephant made to tread on it.
The Old Book of Táng records:
"The hidden dragon transforms the sea,"
and the pond also manifested blessings.
The Cèwén states:
When the Later Sovereign first usurped the throne,
he once dreamed of a sheep ascending the imperial bed in the Wǔdé Hall,
which he regarded with great apprehension.
By the time Jinlíng fell,
the Rectifier of Omissions Yáng Zhīràng was the first to take charge of the prefectural affairs.
The principle of prosperity and decline—
is this not its clear evidence?
From "Recent Events of the Southern Táng"
Chìlóng jù àn
Xuánzōng visited Lùzhōu,
on the seventeenth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Jǐnglóng era,
while dozing off in the main hall,
Sòng Dàbiàn and thirty others from the Báihè Temple saw a red dragon coiled around the desk.
Pān Yàn's "Rhapsody Fourteen"
When the emperor was still obscure,
he once went to Luòyáng,
and had Cuī Rìzhī prepare a meal.
Before it was fully cooked,
the future emperor Minghuáng fell asleep in the front courtyard,
where a trellis of wisteria flowers had just bloomed.
Rìzhī saw a huge snake eating the wisteria flowers,
which soon disappeared.
When the emperor awoke,
he said:
"I was very hungry in my dream,
and ate wisteria flowers that were extremely delicious."
Rìzhī then realized this was an omen of the emperor's future sage enlightenment.
"Unofficial History"
Shǔ Zōngzhèng Shǎoqīng Mèng Déchóng,
son of Yānwáng Yíyè,
daily relied on his noble lineage,
behaving recklessly, arrogantly, and wildly.
Once, while offering incense at the Grand Ancestral Temple,
he brought a courtesan along.
One night, he dreamed of an old man reproaching him,
who then took a brush from the desk, scolded him to open his hand,
and wrote ninety strokes before he awoke.
The next day, while speaking with guests about this matter,
he said himself:
"The old man reproaching me is because he values me;
writing ninety strokes grants me
a lifespan reaching ninety years."
Among the guests, Fēng Lián teased him, saying:
"Ninety strokes actually form the cursive character for 'death';
could it not be an ominous sign?"
Within ten days, he indeed passed away.
"Yěrén Xiánhuà"
Yēlǜ Yǐxīn's mother was pregnant when,
one night she dreamed of wrestling with a ram,
pulling off its horns and tail.
After waking, she sought a divination.
A fortune-teller said:
"This is an auspicious sign.
A ram without horns and tail forms the character for 'king'.

Yī believed that among the officials, only Zhì was worthy of entrusting his reputation,
so he went daily to his gate, seeking Zhì and forcing his way in.
Zhì was still lying in bed and had not risen,
when Yī went straight up to the hall, approached him, and said:
"I have long resided in Xīzhōu,
holding your high virtue in esteem for ages.
Yet now that I finally meet you, it is so abrupt—
how fated is this?"
Thereupon, he raised his voice and wept, startling Zhì in the hall.
Zhì invited him to speak,
found him extraordinarily remarkable,
and then, together with Yuán Féng, praised and recommended him,
making his name renowned throughout the capital.
