The surname is
what one is born with.
In ancient times, sages
were born when their mothers were inspired by Heaven,
hence they were called Sons of Heaven.
Thus, the character for surname (姓) follows the radical for woman (女),
as woman
gives birth,
and also carries the phonetic element "shēng" (生).
From *Shuōwén Jiězì*.
Why do people have surnames?
To honor affection,
strengthen kinship,
distinguish from beasts,
and regulate marriage.
Thus, lineages are recorded and categories distinguished,
so that the living may love one another,
the deceased may be mourned,
and those with the same surname may not marry—
all to emphasize human relationships.
The term "surname" (xìng)
means "birth."
It signifies that humans receive the qi of heaven to be born,
as the Shī Jīng says, "Heaven gave birth to the multitude of people,"
and the Shàng Shū states, "He harmoniously distinguished the hundred surnames."
Why are there a hundred surnames?
Because ancient sages determined surnames by blowing pitch-pipes,
to record their clans,
embodying the five constants and giving rise to righteousness.
There are five tones:
gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ;
they blend and mix,
five times five making twenty-five,
which further generate the four seasons.
With diverse qi and distinct sounds all present,
thus there are a hundred surnames.
Why are there clan names (shì)?
To honor virtue and merit while devaluing mere skill or force,
some take their office as the clan name,
others their occupation,
so that upon hearing the clan name, one may understand—
this encourages people to do good.
Some use their grandfather's style name.
What is a style name (zì)?
It distinguishes the descendants of feudal lords,
to revive fallen states and continue extinguished lineages.
The son of a king is called "Prince,"
the grandson of a king "Royal Grandson,"
the son of a feudal lord "Duke's Son,"
the grandson of a feudal lord "Duke's Grandson,"
and the great-grandson takes his grandfather's style name as the clan name.
Thus, the Chūn Qiū mentions Prince Xiá, the Lún Yǔ
speaks of Royal Grandson Jiǎ, and there are also Duke's Son of Wèi, Duke's Grandson of Jīng,
while Lǔ has the clans of Chōng, Mèng, Shū, and Jì,
Chǔ has Zhāo, Qū, and Jǐng,
Qí has Gāo, Guó, Cuī, and Lú—
all to identify their descendants.
The son of a king is also called "Prince,"
when brothers are established and enfeoffed.
Some say the grandson of a king is also called "Royal Grandson."
Regarding punishment and virtue, it is said:
Yáo commanded to honor Jì and Qì,
granting them the surname Jī; Gāo Yáo
oversaw punishments but was not honored with a surname,
indicating heaven favors virtue over punishment.
Yǔ's surname was Sì,

was born from a coix seed.
The Yīn dynasty's surname was Zǐ,
as their ancestor was born from a swallow's egg.
The same surname Jī
originated from an ancestor born by stepping in a giant's footprint.

Yì Xià
In ancient times, the sage kings observed the phenomena in the cosmos,
examined measures through divine insight,
explored the rise and fall of fate and calendars,
and assessed the virtues and achievements of various lords.
They bestowed surnames and designated clans,
thereby highlighting the records of virtue and merit.
It is said that the clans with full official roles numbered in the hundreds,
while the descendants of kings and nobles spanned a thousand generations.
Those capable of fulfilling their official duties
were granted surnames accordingly,
which were referred to as the "hundred surnames."
Surnames had comprehensive ranks,
and in relation to the king, they were called the "thousand ranks."
In the past, Yáo bestowed the surname to Qì,
and the son bestowed the surname to Qì (abandoned),
Jī was granted to Yǔ with the surname,
the Sì clan was called Yǒu Xià,
Bó Yí became the Jiāng clan,
known as Yǒu Lǚ, extending down to the Three Dynasties.
Officials with hereditary merits
then had official clans,
and the same applied to fiefs.
In later ages, as they declined and became obscure,
they adopted these as surnames,
which could not be changed.
Thus, some passed down their original surnames,
some used clan names or posthumous titles,
some derived from ranks,
and some from aspirations.
As for the eras of the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns,
these were what are called designations.
Wén, Wǔ, Zhāo, Jǐng,
Chéng, Xuān, Dài, Bó,
these are what are called posthumous titles.
Qí, Lǔ, Jīng, Chǔ,
Qín, Jìn, Yān, Zhào,
these are what are called states.
Wáng shì, Hóu shì,
Wáng sūn, Gōng sūn,
these are what are called ranks.
Sīmǎ, Sītú,
Zhōngháng, Xiàjūn,
these are what are called offices.
Bó yǒu, Mèng sūn zǐ,
Fú shū zǐ,
these are what are called courtesy names.
Wū shì, Jiàng shì, Táo shì,
these are what are called occupations.
Dōngmén, Xīmén, Nángōng, Dōngguō, Běiguō,
these are what are called residences.
Sān Wū, Wǔ Lù, Qīng Niú, Bái Mǎ,
these are what are called aspirations.
All such surnames and clans
originate from affiliations and are too numerous to record in full.

Empress Wáng of Emperor Yuán,

Her grandfather Wēngrú,
moved from Dōngpínglíng to Yuánchéng.

the Jìn historian divined it as yáng,
indicating the mutual conquest of yáng's male earth and fire,
thus 645 years after Shālù's collapse,
should a sage woman arise from the Tián clan?
Now Wēngrú's residence is precisely at that location,
with the sun and moon aligning.
East of Yuánchéng's outer walls lie the ruins of Wǔlù,
which is the Shālù area.
Eighty years later, a noble woman shall rise to prominence in the realm."
Wēngrú begat Jìn,
Jìn's wife Lǐ Shì was pregnant,

Whenever she was betrothed,

The white swallow carries stones in its beak.
Mǎ Yuán, courtesy name Wényuān,
his ancestor Zhào Shē was a general of Zhào,

so his descendants took this as their surname.
The Hòu Hàn Shū

Annotation
When Empress Yuán was at home,
there was once a white swallow carrying a white stone,
as large as a finger, that fell
into her spinning basket.
She picked it up,
and the stone split into two by itself.
Inside, there was an inscription that read:
"Heaven and Earth's mother, the Empress, shall unite them."
It then rejoined and closed up,
and she treasured it as a precious record.
Later, when she became Empress,
she often placed it together with the imperial seal in a box,
calling it the Heaven-bestowed Seal.

Emperor Píng ascended the throne,

The Grand Empress Dowager, mother of Emperor Chéng, held court and governed.
Wáng Mǎng wanted to marry his daughter to the emperor

Wáng Mǎng devised a deceptive memorial stating,
"The emperor has been on the throne for three years,
yet the Chángqiū Palace has not been established in the inner court,
and the ranks of consorts are not filled."
He had others submit a memorial saying
his daughter had been nurtured in virtue and transformation,
possessing a graceful and beautiful appearance,
and was fit to continue the heavenly succession,
to perform sacrifices,
and receive the imperial decree.
They reported to the ancestral temple,
and conducted various divinations,
all of which said:
"The omens encountered the flourishing phase of metal and water,
the hexagrams showed parents in their proper positions,
this is what is called the prognostication of health and strength,
a sign of encountering good fortune."
She was promptly welcomed into the Wèiyāng Palace
and established as empress.
Over a year later,
Emperor Píng passed away,
and the infant Rúzǐ Yīng was enthroned,
with the empress honored as Grand Empress Dowager.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
the Grand Empress Dowager became the Grand Duchess of Āndìng.
The Grand Empress Dowager was then eighteen years old,
and was resolute in character,
with moral integrity.
Since the Liú family was deposed,
she often claimed illness and did not attend court.
Wáng Mǎng, feeling respectful yet troubled and sorrowful,
wanted to remarry her,
so he changed her title to Huánghuáng Shìzhǔ.
He ordered the General Who Establishes the State, Chéngxīn Gōng Sūn Jiàn's eldest son, adorned and accompanied by a physician, to visit her under the pretext of inquiring about her illness.
The Grand Empress Dowager was greatly angered,
whipped the attendants beside her, and consequently fell ill, refusing to rise.
Wáng Mǎng then did not press further.
When Hàn troops executed Wáng Mǎng,
and set the Wèiyāng Palace ablaze,
the Grand Empress Dowager said:
"How can I face the Hàn house?"
She threw herself into the fire and died.

The Emperor had four favored Noble Ladies,

He intended to use lots to let the spirits determine the selection.
Hú Guǎng and others submitted a memorial saying:
"The decree to establish an Empress
is a major affair.
If you wish to rely on lots,
to resolve doubts through spiritual means,
depending on divination with stalks,
it may not necessarily match worthiness or encounter the right person,
and the selection would still not be based on virtue.
For innate wisdom manifests naturally,
and one who matches heaven must have extraordinary signs.
It is appropriate to consider women from good families,
select and seek those with virtue.
If virtue is equal, consider age;
if age is equal, consider appearance.
Consult the classical texts,
and decide with your sage judgment."

Marquis of Chéngshì Liáng Shāng,

should be matched with heavenly blessings,
and rightly positioned as the Empress.

and thus in the Shòu'ān Hall, he established the Noble Lady as Empress.

Composing a Poem to Express My Feelings
Zhū Yē Chìxīn,
it is said his ancestors were from the frontier regions,
mostly making a living by riding and hunting.
Thirty Hu tribesmen
saw numerous flying birds in the great mountains,
gathering in a valley.
The Hu people approached them,
and saw a child of about two years old,
being fed with fruits carried by the birds.
The Hu people found this extraordinary,
so they took him in and raised him collectively.
When he grew up and sought a surname,
the group said, "We all raised him to adulthood,"
thus giving him the surname Zhū Yē,
meaning "all together."
The form Zhū Yē is a corruption.

Xiàowǔ's Consort Yīn Shū was the daughter of Nánjùn King Liú Yìxuān. After Yìxuān's defeat, the Emperor secretly took her in, and she became the most favored in the rear palace, assuming the false surname Yīn. When she died, the Emperor often longed to see her, so he had a sliding coffin made, pulling back the lid to view the corpse whenever he wished. After many days, her form and complexion remained unchanged. She was posthumously honored as Guìfēi.

The Emperor, endlessly pained by his love, was distraught in spirit and established a separate temple for her in the capital. At that time, there was a shaman who could see ghosts and told the Emperor that the Guìfēi could be summoned. The Emperor was overjoyed and ordered her to be called forth. After a short while, she indeed appeared within the curtains, looking as she did in life. The Emperor wanted to speak with her, but she remained silent and unresponsive. As he reached to hold her hand, she suddenly vanished.
The Emperor was especially choked with regret, and thus composed an "Ode to Lady Lǐ" to express his feelings.
(End)
After the burial,
he frequently went with his ministers to Yīn's tomb,
and said to Liú Déyuàn:
"If you weep for the Guìfēi,
and it is mournful,
I will grant you a generous reward."
Déyuàn immediately wailed in grief,
beating his chest and stamping his feet,
with tears and snivel streaming down.
The Emperor was very pleased,
and appointed him as Governor of Yùzhōu.
He also ordered the physician Yáng Zhì to weep for Lady Yīn,
and Zhì also sobbed mournfully.
Another day, someone asked Zhì:
"How did you manage to produce such ready tears?"
Zhì had recently lost his beloved concubine,
and replied:
"That day, I was actually weeping for my deceased concubine."

Chéng Ruì was unprincipled in his youth,
and while drunk, he killed someone.
He fled and became a Buddhist monk,
later joining the Cai bandits and becoming their leader.
He was adopted and changed his name to Guō Yǔ,
and during Emperor Zhāozōng's reign, he served as the military governor of Jīngnán.
The "Book of Táng"
records that his assistant official Zhèng Zhǔn submitted a petition requesting to revert to his original surname,
stating: "My name is not for dominating Yuè,
nor do I emulate Táo Zhū by sailing a boat.
My resolve is to serve Qín,
and upon leaving the state, I adopted the name of Zhāng Lù.
Chéng is my original surname,
while Guō is an assumed one.
To avoid the guilt of violating the law,
I dare to request the restoration of my lineage, following the precedent of the Minister of Justice's separate clan and enfeoffment.
I am truly ashamed before the feudal lords."
This petition was highly regarded by the imperial court.
The "Supplementary History of the Five Dynasties"
records that Fàn Yǔchēng, a native of Jiǔlǒng,

I mistakenly bore the name of Zhāng Lù.

Why must a person who expresses feelings have a name?
It is because expressing feelings serves to record and honor one's service to others.
The Analects say:
"If names are not correct, speech will not be in accord."
Why is a name given at three months?
Heaven's way follows seasonal periods,
and things undergo their changes.
When a human reaches three months of age,
the sun warms them and they can already smile and laugh,
able to interact and respond with others.
Therefore, they are named when they first show awareness.
Thus the Lǐ Fú Zhuàn states:
"When a child is three months old, the father names it."
Naming in the ancestral temple
refers to the father's own temple,
showing that the child should become master of the ancestral line.
Another theory says naming occurs in the private chamber.
A name is
a designation for the young and humble,
so it is done simply in the private chamber.
Why did the Shāng dynasty name children by days?
The Shāng were straightforward, so they directly used birth days to name children.
The Shū Jīng mentions Tàijiǎ and Emperor Wǔdīng.
Could ministers and commoners also use jiǎ-yǐ birth days to name children?
This was not exclusive.
According to the Shū Jīng, among Shāng ministers there were Wū
and Xián, and also Zǔjǐ.
How do we know feudal lords did not imitate kings
in naming children by birth day?
Because Tàiwáng was named Dǎnfǔ,

these were Shāng feudal lords
who did not use zǐ-chǒu as names.
Why? Because jiǎ-yǐ are stems,
zǐ-chǒu are
branches.
Stems are the foundation,
the essence, hence jiǎ-yǐ were used for names.
Names may be compound or single.

sometimes listening to their cries and using pitch-pipes to determine the name,
sometimes basing it on events or resembling their form,
hence compound or single.
Basing on events—Hòujì is an example.
He was abandoned, hence named Qì ("abandoned").
Resembling form—
Confucius' head resembled
the Níqiū mountain in Lǔ state,

Sometimes the name suggests the style (zì)—
hearing the name, one knows the style;
hearing the style, one knows the name.
Like name Cì, style Zǐgòng;
name Lǐ, style Bóyú.

Why do people have courtesy names?

Casting Metal
According to the customs of the Northern Wei Dynasty,
when establishing an empress,
she was required to personally cast a golden statue,
with success considered auspicious;
failure meant she could not be installed.
If a consort gave birth to a son designated as heir,
the second in line,
the mother was invariably ordered to commit suicide.
Dàowǔ's consort Liú shì failed to cast the golden statue,
while Mùróng shì succeeded,
and thus was installed as empress.
Liú shì gave birth to Míngyuán,
and at the end of Dàowǔ's reign, she died in accordance with the old law.
"Book of Wei"
A ruler towards his ministers,
a teacher towards his disciples,
may call them by their given names.
As for colleagues in office towards one another,
clansmen towards their brothers,
fellow students towards friends,
they may use their courtesy names but not address them directly by their given names.
Therefore, the Gongyang Commentary states that "a name is not as good as a courtesy name,"
not meaning that a person's given name is less honorable than their courtesy name,
but rather that being addressed by one's courtesy name implies being treated with respect,
while being called by one's given name implies being treated with lesser regard.
In ancient times, when noble individuals named their children,
they necessarily chose auspicious and virtuous terms based on sincerity and righteousness,
thereby making the name auspicious;
they did not use official titles,
thereby distinguishing the name;
they did not use livestock or currency,
thereby valuing the name;
they did not use concealed ailments,
thereby making the name manifest;
they announced it widely to both family and outsiders,
thereby publicizing the name;
they wrote it down and stored it,
thereby treasuring the name;
those of lower status avoided using it,
thereby honoring the name;
upon capping, a courtesy name was bestowed,
thereby revering the name.
The name is established through ritual,
the courtesy name is based on the given name,
the given name is the foundation,
the courtesy name is the extension.
Being the foundation, it is honored;
being the extension, it is of lesser regard;
honored, therefore its rituals are detailed;
of lesser regard, therefore its rituals are simplified.
Moreover, women do not have given names,
hence they are considered inferior to men.
Rustic people do not have given names,
hence they are considered inferior to scholars.
The given name is what one uses to be honored,
and what those who honor one use to address one;
the courtesy name is what one uses to interact with those of lower status,
and what those of lower status use to address one.
There has never been a case where using it for those of higher status results in lesser regard,
or using it for those of lower status results in honor.

Shī Fú remarked:

righteousness gives rise to ritual,
ritual forms the basis of governance,
and governance rectifies the people.
Thus when governance is accomplished, the people obey;
if altered, it breeds disorder.
A harmonious match is called 'consort',
a discordant match is called 'enemy'—
such were the designations in antiquity.
Now the ruler names his crown prince 'Enemy',
and his younger brother 'Complete Army',
this begins to portend disorder.
Will the elder brother perhaps be replaced?"

organizing them into ten volumes,
titled "Nǚ Zé",
and wrote the preface herself.
She also authored a critique refuting Empress Mǎ of Hàn Míngdé,
believing she failed to restrain her maternal relatives,

In youth, I imitated the Songs of Chu
Sūn Xiū decreed:
"People have names
to distinguish one another,
and when grown up are given courtesy names,
out of reverence for their personal names.
The rites dictate that naming children should make names difficult to offend yet easy
to avoid; at fifty, one is called by their seniority titles like Bó or Zhòng.
In ancient times, some had single-character names,
but now people compete to create fine personal names and fine courtesy names,
further making them match each other,
yet their conduct does not correspond—
this is like Gǔ Zì Bó Míng.
I have often mocked this.
I now create personal and courtesy names for my four sons:
the crown prince is named Wān
with the courtesy name Qiú
Qì
the second son is named Gōng
with the courtesy name Lì
Xián
the third son is named Mǎng
with the courtesy name Wēn
Jǔ
and the fourth son is named Bāo
with the courtesy name Yǒng
(擁). These are entirely unlike those used in the world,
so I copied old texts and combined them to create these.
Of the eight styles of writing,
additions and subtractions arise according to circumstances.
Now, in crafting these personal and courtesy names,
they are not matched to each other,
and the courtesy names consist of only one character,
Tàizōng's Virtuous Consort Xú, named Huì,
could speak at five months old,
recited the *Analects* and *Máo Odes* at four,
and excelled at composing essays by eight.
Her father Xiàodé tested her by imitating the *Songs of Chǔ*,
writing "One cannot linger long in the mountains,"
with exceptionally elegant and beautiful diction.
From then on, she extensively studied classics and histories,
never letting books leave her hand.
Emperor Tàizōng, hearing of this,
took her as a Talented Lady.
Her literary compositions
were written swiftly with a brush,
adorned with ornate and rich language.
The Emperor
Chén Wǔ
was a Hú person,
raised by the magistrate of Línshuǐ, Lord Chén.
Lord Chén found him extraordinary,
and proposed to change his original courtesy name.
Wǔ knelt respectfully and said to him:
"There is a local saying about the capital pavilion rat,
which often hears the words of elders.
Now that my courtesy name is to be changed,
I do have a personal wish.
I have heard that Sīmǎ Xiàngrú admired the conduct of Lìn Xiàngrú,
so he took the courtesy name Xiàngrú.
Previously in my hometown,
I long heard the tales of the elders,
praising the Hàn envoy Sū Wǔ,
who upheld loyalty and maintained his resolve,
refusing to submit to the Chányú,
and was exiled to the northern deserts,
holding his imperial tally while herding sheep,
entrusting his heart to the autumn wild geese,
and placing his sincerity upon the passing clouds.
I look up to such lofty mountains with admiration,
and in my heart, I secretly yearn to emulate him."
The Chén family praised his aspiration,
and thus named him Wǔ.
They also wished to give him the courtesy name Zhòng,
to indicate his origin as a Hú person.
However, since Shì Lè and Shì Hǔ prohibited the term 'Hú' and called them 'countrymen',
they instead gave him the courtesy name Guówǔ.

was well-versed in classics and history,

The Minister of Works Gāo Zhào,
being the uncle of Xuānwǔ Emperor,

it is to continue the ancestral temple,
and mother the world,
so one should choose from renowned families of propriety and righteousness, those gentle and virtuous,
to meet the expectations of the realm,

In a village, there was a man who named his eldest son Dào (meaning "robber"),
and his second son Ōu (meaning "beat").
Dào went out to weed in the fields, carrying his clothes.
His mother called out to him, "Dào!"
The officials, upon hearing this, seized him.
His mother then called out "Ōu!"
Ōu tried to explain to the officials but was in a hurry and couldn't articulate clearly,
only managing to say "Ōu, Ōu."
The officials then beat him,
and Dào nearly died from the beating.

ordering Shàngguān Wǎn'ér to sit beneath the hem of the bed curtain,

Zhāoróng, named Wǎn'ér,
was the granddaughter of Xītái Shìláng Yí,
her father Tíngzhī died with Yí.
During Empress Wǔ's time,
her mother Zhèng was pregnant,
dreamed of a giant giving her a large steelyard, saying:
"Hold this to weigh the world."
More than a month after Zhāoróng's birth,
her mother jokingly said:
"Could the weigher be you?"
She immediately responded with a gurgling sound.
Later, she internally handled confidential governance,
fulfilling her dream,
it is said that since the Tōngtiān era,
she internally managed imperial edicts.
When Zhōngzōng ascended the throne,
she was promoted to Zhāoróng,
the emperor invited famous scholars,
bestowed banquets and composed poems,
Wǎn'ér often composed for the emperor, empress, and the two princesses Chángníng and Ānlè,
multiple pieces were created simultaneously,
and the beauty became increasingly novel,
she also ranked the court officials.
Because of the gold cups bestowed for compositions,
the court uniformly followed this trend,
the literary compositions of that time,
were mostly flowery and ornate,
yet all had merit to behold,
which was due to Zhāoróng's influence.
After the downfall of Empress Wěi,
she was executed at the palace gate.

瓜子
贺知章秘书监有高名，
告老归吴中，
上嘉重之，
每别优异焉。
知章将行，
涕泣辞上，
上曰：
“何所欲？”
知章曰：
“臣有男，
未有定名，
幸陛下赐之，
归为乡里荣。”
上曰：
“为道之要，
莫若信孚者，
信也，
履信思乎顺，
卿子必信顺之人也，
宜名之曰孚。”
知章再拜而受命，
知章久而谓人曰：
“上何谑我耶？
吴人孚乃瓜下为子，
岂非呼我为瓜子耶？”
《传信记》
Emperor Xuánzōng's Empress Wáng,
initially advanced through her beauty,
and when the emperor ascended the throne,
within a few years, his favor waned daily,
the empress grew anxious and fearful, unable to find peace,
yet she treated her subordinates with kindness,
fortunately avoiding slander,
which together endangered her.
Suddenly one day, she tearfully pleaded with the emperor:
"Sānláng, do you not remember Ā Zhōng taking off his new purple half-sleeve garment,
to exchange for a dou of flour,
to make birthday noodles for Sānláng?
How can you bear not to recall those past times?"
Upon hearing this,
the emperor grew sorrowful and changed his expression.

Ā Zhōng,
was the name the empress used to refer to her own father.
Dù Xiànghóngjiàn's father was named Péngjǔ,
father and son having names resembling those of brothers.
The father once dreamed of going somewhere,
where he saw a large stele said to be the Ministers' Stele,
with the names of those already appointed filled in gold,
and those yet to be appointed inscribed plainly.
Dù asked:
"Is there a son of the Dù family?"
The reply came:
"Yes,
look for yourself."
He remembered that under the surname was a radical resembling a bird with a trailing stroke,
but forgot the character was actually Péngjǔ,
and was told:
"If you do not become minister,
your descendants for generations will bear names with bird radicals and trailing strokes."
Péngjǔ begot Hóngjiàn,
thus even names are predetermined,
let alone official rank and lifespan?

Niángzǐ
In the early Kaiyuan era,
Consort Wǔ Huìfēi enjoyed exceptional favor and attention,
leading to the deposition of the Empress.
After Consort Huìfēi passed away,
the Emperor mourned and lamented for a long time.
Despite having thousands in the rear palace,
none pleased him.
(Old Book of Tang)
The Emperor felt disconsolate and unhappy,
so he sent Gāo Lìshì to secretly search outside the palace,
where he found the daughter of Yáng Xuǎnyǎn at the Shou Mansion,
already of hair-pinning age.
She was ordained as a Taoist nun,
with the religious name Tàizhēn.
She had been betrothed by imperial decree to the son of Wéi Zhàoxùn,
and married into the Shou Mansion.
Tàizhēn had lustrous hair and fine skin,
slender yet well-proportioned,
with graceful and virtuous demeanor,
radiant and brilliant,
her every movement illuminating those around her.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and at the Phoenix Garden, he enfeoffed her as Guìfēi (Highest-ranking Imperial Consort).
On the day of her audience,
the "Rainbow and Feather Garments" music was performed to welcome her.
On the night they pledged their love,
he bestowed upon her gold hairpins and inlaid jewelry,
using them to solidify their union.
The Emperor also personally took a purple polished gold step-shaker, crafted from Líshuǐ's treasury gold,
went to her dressing chamber,
and with his own hands placed it in her hair,
saying to the palace attendants:
"Having obtained the Guìfēi,
it is as if I have acquired a supreme treasure."
He then composed a tune called "Débǎo Zǐ" (Obtaining the Treasure),
and from then on, no other consorts in the six palaces received his favor.
In the palace, she was called "Niángzǐ" (Lady),
and the honors she received were in fact equal to those of an Empress.

The Southern Hàn's Liú Yǎn was initially named Yán,
and later changed to Zhì.

and the era name was changed to White Dragon at the Sānqīng Hall,
followed by another name change to Yǎn,

Wāng Táifú was a heavy drinker and skilled in writing,
which Lièzǔ appreciated,
but Sòng Qíqiū envied his superior talent,
repeatedly slandering him,
causing Táifú to feel resentful.

Zēngzǐ was in Bì,
where there was a man with the same name and clan as Zēngzǐ who killed someone.
Someone told Zēngzǐ's mother:
"Zēng Shēn has killed a man."
Zēngzǐ's mother said:
"My son would not kill anyone."
She continued weaving calmly.
After a while,
someone again said:
"Zēng Shēn has killed a man."
His mother still continued weaving calmly.
Shortly after, another person came and told her:
"Zēng Shēn has killed a man."
His mother became frightened,
threw down her shuttle, climbed over the wall, and fled.
Now, with Zēng Shēn's virtue
and his mother's trust in him,
when three people cast doubt,
even a loving mother could not maintain her faith.

Plum Blossom Spirit
Consort Méi's surname was Jiāng,

and the emperor, indulging her preference,

When the emperor competed with her in tea tasting,
he jested to the princes:
"This is the essence of plum.
She plays the white jade flute,
performs the Startled Swan Dance,
illuminating the entire gathering.
Now she has surpassed me in tea competition too."
Later, when Consort Yáng entered service,
Consort Méi was moved to the eastern palace of Shàngyáng.
The emperor met with her several times at the Huā'è Tower.
When foreign envoys arrived,
he ordered a peck of pearls sealed
and secretly bestowed upon the consort.
She declined to accept them,
instead handing a poem to the envoy, saying:
"Present this before His Majesty."
It read:
"Willow-leaf eyebrows long left unadorned,
faded makeup stained with tears on crimson silk.
Since arriving at Chángmén, I've ceased my toilette -
why comfort loneliness with pearls?"
When the emperor read the poem,
he grew melancholy and displeased,
ordering the Music Bureau to set it to a new melody,
titled "A Peck of Pearls."
This was the origin of the song's name.

He saw her and was pleased with her,

"I have a husband,
who went away to serve as an official and has not returned.

She gathered leaves without looking back,
Hú, ashamed, withdrew and returned home,
asked his family where his wife was,
they said she had gone to gather mulberry leaves in the suburbs and had not returned.
When she returned,
she was the woman he had just propositioned.
Husband and wife were both ashamed,
the wife threw herself into the Yí River and died.
The present Qiū Hú is not the Qiū Hú of the past."

Chángqiū
In the third year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han Dynasty,
the officials submitted a memorial to establish the Chángqiū Palace.
Annotation:
This is the palace where the empress resides.
"Cháng" means
long-lasting.
"Qiū" refers to
the beginning of the maturation of all things.
Hence, it was named accordingly.
When requesting the establishment of an empress,
they did not dare to speak directly,
so they referred to it by the palace name.
The "Annals"
state that the Qiū Palace was also hastily built,
with the view in front being obstructed.
The "Book of Southern Qí"
records that the virtuous empress died early,
leaving the Chángqiū position vacant.
The "Book of Liáng"
mentions that when the Qín official position was to be implemented,
Emperor Jǐng renamed it Grand Chángqiū.
Yìng Shào said:
"The empress
is a high-ranking official."
Shī Gǔ explained:
"Qiū signifies
the time of harvest.
Cháng means
a long-lasting duty."
Therefore, it was used as the official title for the empress.

According to analysis,

"Zhāo

Sháo

There originally existed the character "佋" for the ancestral temple sequence,

Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's childhood name was Āliàn,
so his descendants all referred to "liàn" as "juàn".
Thus, they called smelting objects as "melting juàn objects",
fearing it distorted the meaning.
Some who avoided the name "Yún"
called "fēnyún" (chaotic) as "fēnyān".
Those avoiding the name "Tóng"
referred to the wútóng tree as the "white iron tree",
making it seem like a jest.
From "Family Instructions of the Yán Clan"
The term "wáng shìzǐ" (crown prince)
refers solely to the second in command to the king.
The crown prince of the Son of Heaven
inherits the world.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn
asks why he is named shìzǐ?
It means wishing him to continue the lineage generation after generation without interruption.
The Hán Shī Nèi Zhuàn
states in the Spring and Autumn Annals:
"The crown prince met at Shǒuzhǐ.
Jìn had Crown Prince Shēnshēng,
Zhèng had Crown Prince Huá,
Qí had Crown Prince Guāng,
thus under the Zhōu system, the titles crown prince
and heir were not fixed either.
Under the Hàn system,
the Son of Heaven was called Emperor,
his legitimate heir was called Crown Prince,
the legitimate heirs of feudal kings were called shìzǐ,
and later generations all followed this practice."

Emperor Tàizōng was named Shìmín,
so characters like Dié, Yè, and Qì had the Shì component removed and replaced with Yún;

Shì and Yún are similar in shape,

thus, all were changed to Yún:

The establishment of a crown prince by the ruler is
to prevent usurpation and assassination,
and to suppress the chaos caused by ministers and sons.
If the ruler passes away and the principal wife has no son,
and there is a posthumous child, one must wait for its birth before establishing it,
why? To honor the principal line and emphasize legitimacy.
The selection of a son is based on nobility, not age,
to block favoritism and resentment.
Thus, the Spring and Autumn Annals' Gongyang Commentary states:
"Establish the heir by age, not by virtue;
establish the son by nobility, not by age."

In the thirteenth year of the Tàiyuán era, Kǒng Ānguó was summoned to serve as Palace Attendant,
and he submitted a memorial stating that Wáng Yú's name violated his personal name taboo,
making it inappropriate for them to jointly sign documents.
He requested to be relieved of his duties.
The relevant officials deliberated and concluded:
"While it is natural to feel startled upon hearing a name that violates a personal taboo,
previous edicts have clarified ritual protocols,
stating that the ruler has no personal taboos,
while high officials observe public taboos but not personal ones.
When Wáng Yòu's name violated his father's taboo,
he was permitted to transfer to another office,
but this was an exceptional act of grace beyond standard regulations.
The court's rituals are comprehensive,
with all officials fulfilling their duties,
their positions and titles clearly designated,
and their actions frequently interconnected.
If everyone could avoid others based on personal taboos,
it would lead to constant changes in assignments,
with officials shifting posts and moving without end."

Duke Āi asked:
"What is meant by a sage?"
Confucius replied:
"What is called a sage
harmonizes virtue with heaven and earth,
adapts without fixed methods,
exhausts the beginnings and ends of all things,
aligns with the natural state of all beings,
spreads the great Way and thus completes their inherent nature,
shines like the sun and moon,
transforms with divine efficacy,
the common people do not recognize his virtue,
observers cannot discern his boundaries,
this is what is called a sage."

"The so-called sage
is one whose knowledge penetrates the Great Way,
responds to changes without exhaustion,
and can fathom the nature of all things.
Therefore, his affairs are great and match heaven and earth,
correspond with the sun and moon,
mingle with clouds and rain,
encompass all things in their essence,

the common people are calmly unaware of his goodness,
such a one may be called a sage."

Rising and Sinking with the Dào
The sage nurtures his spirit,
harmonizes and softens his vital energy,
levels and calms his form,
and with the Dào rises and sinks, bends and lifts.
When tranquil, he lets it go;
when pressed, he employs it.

in employing it, it is like releasing a trigger.

and the changes of all affairs all meet their response.

neither sending nor welcoming,
responding without storing.

Duke Líng of Wèi was sitting with his wife one night,
when they heard the rumble of a carriage,
which stopped upon reaching the palace gate,
and then resumed after passing the gate.
The Duke asked his wife,
"Do you know who this might be?"
His wife replied,
"It must be Jù Bóyù."
The Duke said,
"How do you know?"
"I have heard that according to ritual, one should dismount at the duke's gate
and salute the carriage horses to show respect.
A loyal minister or a filial son does not uphold his principles only in the light,
nor does he abandon his conduct in the dark.
Now, Bóyù is a virtuous senior official of Wèi,
benevolent and wise,
respectful in serving his superiors.
Such a man would never neglect ritual due to darkness or obscurity.
That is how I know."
The Duke sent someone to check,
and it was indeed Bóyù.
He turned back and teased her, saying,
"It wasn't him."
His wife presented a cup of wine and bowed twice,
offering congratulations. The Duke said,
"Why are you congratulating me?"
His wife replied,
"At first, I thought Wèi had only Bóyù,
but now there is another who matches him.
This means you have two virtuous ministers.
A state with many virtuous ministers
is blessed indeed.
That is why I congratulate you."
The Duke exclaimed in surprise,
"Excellent!"
He then told his wife the truth.

The essence and excellence among plants is called "yīng" (brilliance),
the extraordinary among beasts is called "xióng" (might),
thus when referring to people's civil and martial qualities across generations,
these terms are adopted.
Therefore, intelligence and outstanding talent are called "yīng",
while courage and strength surpassing others are called "xióng".
"Yīng" relies on wisdom for planning,
beginning with clear insight,
awaiting "xióng"'s courage to act upon opportunities;
"xióng" uses strength to command the masses,
and bravery to overcome difficulties,
relying on "yīng"'s wisdom to achieve success.
Only then can each fulfill their strengths.
Wisdom capable of planning from the start and clarity
to perceive opportunities, coupled with courage to decide,
then one can be called "yīng",
as exemplified by Zhāng Liáng.
With extraordinary physical strength,
courage to take action,
and sufficient wisdom to judge matters,
one can be called "xióng",
as exemplified by Hán Xìn.
Thus, "yīng" can serve as chancellor,
"xióng" can serve as general.
If one person embodies both "yīng" and "xióng",
they can rule the world,
as exemplified by Gāozǔ and Xiàng Yǔ.
However, the element of "yīng" should outweigh that of "xióng",
and "yīng" cannot be lacking.

There are five grades of worthies:
those who are diligent and careful in household affairs,
and obedient and fraternal within their kinship groups,
are the gentry of the village;
those who are vigorous and intelligent,
and proficient in civil affairs without fault,
are the gentry of the county court;
those who are sincere and steadfast in conduct,
incorruptible, fair, and just,
and serve superiors while managing subordinates,
are the gentry of the commandery;
those who are well-versed in the classics,
of high reputation and conduct,
capable in administration,
broad-minded, harmonious, and firm in principle,
are the gentry fit for high ministerial positions;
those of exceptional talent,
standing out from the masses,
skilled in grand strategies,
and capable of achieving great deeds for the age,
are the gentry of the empire.

One who surpasses ten thousand in wisdom is called yīng,

one who surpasses a hundred is called háo,
one who surpasses ten is called jié.
One who understands the way of heaven,
observes the principles of earth,
comprehends human feelings,
whose greatness is sufficient to embrace the multitude,
whose virtue is sufficient to win over distant lands,
whose trustworthiness is sufficient to unify differences,
and whose wisdom is sufficient to recognize change—
such a person is the yīng among men.
One whose virtue is sufficient to educate and transform,
whose conduct is sufficient to uphold righteousness,
whose benevolence is sufficient to gain the multitude,
and whose clarity is sufficient to illuminate those below—
such a person is the jùn among men.
One whose conduct is sufficient to serve as a model,
whose wisdom is sufficient to resolve doubts,
whose integrity is sufficient to distribute wealth,
whose trustworthiness is sufficient to keep agreements,
whose actions can be emulated,
and whose words can be followed—
such a person is the háo among men.
One who holds to duty without neglect,
dwells in righteousness without partiality,
faces difficulty without seeking escape,
and encounters gain without wrongful acquisition—
such a person is the jié among men.

Zhōng Huángzǐ said: Heaven has five directions,
earth has five phases,
sounds have five notes,
things have five flavors,
colors have five patterns,
humans have five ranks,
thus between heaven and earth there are twenty-five types of people.
The upper five include the divine person, the true person, the dao person, the perfect person, and the sage;
the next five include the virtuous person, the worthy person, the wise person, the good person, and the eloquent person;
the middle five include the impartial person, the loyal person, the trustworthy person, the righteous person, and the courteous person;
the next five include the scholar, the artisan, the forester, the farmer, and the fisherman;
the lower five include the common person, the slave, the foolish person, the flesh-bound person, and the petty person;
the upper five compared to the lower five,
are like humans compared to oxen and horses.
The sage
sees with the eyes,
hears with the ears,
speaks with the mouth,
walks with the feet;
the true person
sees clearly without looking,
hears keenly without listening,
follows without walking,
is just without speaking.
Thus, what the sage uses to move the world,
the true person has never engaged in;
what the worthy person uses to rectify the customs of the age,
the sage has never observed.

Emulating the cosmic embrace of heaven and earth,
Radiating brilliance to illuminate subtle truths—
With writings luminous and style refined,
Perceiving the unique to attain spiritual insight,
Is the sage.
Endowed with lofty purity,
Upholding stern principles to transcend vulgarity,
Holding spiritual wisdom while appearing foolish,
Never repeating errors or flattering blindly,
Is the worthy.
Dwelling in silent non-action,
Treading the straight path with unwavering fairness,
Is the Daoist.
Exhausting rites for the living and deceased,
Preserving body and hair to manifest clarity,
Is the filial.
Extending compassion to all beings,
Constantly forgiving others as oneself,
Is the benevolent.
Devoting life to serve the state,
Enduring perils with unshaken integrity,
Is the loyal.
Discerning subtle principles hard to grasp,
Foreseeing hidden outcomes of the future,
Is the perceptive.
Assessing order and chaos to adapt,
Judging advance and retreat to preserve self,
Is the wise.
Accepting fortune and adversity alike,
Following destiny without obstruction,
Is the enlightened.
Never distorting an inch for a yard,
Never stooping to disgrace for survival,
Is the noble.
Acting with measured composure,
Always clear and deliberate without regret,
Is the dignified.
Embracing icy purity,
Unstained by power or profit,
Is the incorruptible.
Steadfast through heat and cold,
Unwavering even in mortal danger,
Is the righteous.
Keeping one’s word through long trials,
Unchanged despite aging years,
Is the trustworthy.
Wielding sharp prose to establish views,
With elegant diction clear and fitting,
Is the literary.
Rousing valor in fierce ranks,
Wielding arms to quell turmoil,
Is the martial.
Mastering ancient classics’ depths,
Exhausting prior wisdom to probe truth,
Is the Confucian.
Focusing mind on essential truths,
Cherishing every moment for virtue,
Is the self-improving.
Knowing hoarding brings great loss,
Facing wealth as if discarding it,
Is the frugal.
Unchanged by gain or loss,
Unaltered by temptations,
Is the steadfast.
Relieving distress forgetting fatigue,
Bearing others’ woes as his own,
Is the devoted.
Guarding purity to the end,
Never yielding to evade hardship,
Is the principled.
Soaring with eloquent brilliance,
Speaking concisely to resolve stagnation,
Is the articulate.
Humbly crediting others’ merits,
Growing more reverent in high station,
Is the modest.
Honoring kinship among clans,
Always upright in fulfilling duty,
Is the compliant.
Decisive in critical moments,
Impartial wielding the law,
Is the capable.
Distinguishing truth from falsehood,
Resolving doubts with fairness,

Tracking celestial cycles’ shifts,
Deducing rise and fall’s patterns,
Is the strategist.
Charging blades without fear of death,
Confronting beasts in wild valleys,
Is the brave.
Commanding awe to discipline masses,
Upholding laws without exception,
Is the stern.
Devising tools for practical use,
Mastering arts and melodies alike,
Is the artistic.
Defying tyrants undaunted,
Unbroken under dire threats,
Is the shrewd.
Untiring dawn to dusk,
Toiling through steep hardships,
Is the diligent.
Calm amid slander and hate,
Fearless before terrors,
Is the resolute.
Unaltered by fame or praise,
Steadfast through trials,
Is the composed.
Acting when duty calls,
Unswayed by others’ doubts,
Is the decisive.
Moving within moral bounds,
Never gambling on luck,
Is the cautious.
Reverent in ritual observance,
Impeccable to kin and stranger,
Is the virtuous.
Treading the simple path desireless,
Unchanged by shifting times,
Is the质朴.

Lacking none to tread the good path,

Neglecting parents’ nurture,
Harming self by abandoning Dao,
Is the perverse.
Cloaking evil for false glory,
Seeking gain at life’s expense,
Is the treacherous.
Deviating from righteousness’ path,
Endangering others for safety,
Is the malevolent.
Insatiable in contention,
Persecuting the just and honest,
Is the wicked.
Transgressing norms with cruelty,
Delighting in slaughter callously,
Is the brutal.
Spreading falsehoods to corrupt,
Framing slanders against loyalty,
Is the slanderous.
Sweet words masking deceit,
Foul deeds feigning purity,
Is the sycophant.
Ignoring right and wrong,
Raging to dominate,
Is the violent.
Feigning virtue for trust,
Harboring venom without kinship,
Is the cunning.
Flattering to please superiors,
Abetting errors for favor,
Is the obsequious.
Words heedless of consistency,
Promising lightly without substance,
Is the hollow.
Betraying duty for profit,
Abandoning shame for gain,
Is the greedy.
Entranced by beauty,
Adorning excess with vile thoughts,
Is the lustful.
Doubting accomplished facts,
Erring in plans with regret,
Is the obtuse.
Scorning classics for pride,
Refusing guidance from betters,
Is the detrimental.
Knowing good but failing,
Acting much without success,
Is the inept.
Neglecting virtue’s cultivation,
Fawning on power for advantage,
Is the corrupt.
Seeking shortcuts for speed,
Bribing to seize opportunities,
Is the depraved.
Arrogant and rude,
Bullying those superior,
Is the brutish.
Confessing falsely under pressure,
Trembling without cause,
Is the timid.
Arguing trivialities in crowds,
Speaking freely to the wrong ears,
Is the shallow.
Ignoring what’s feasible,
Yearning but never achieving,
Is the stubborn.
Persisting in known errors,
Worsening despite good counsel,
Is the deluded.
Lacking compassion’s heart,
Cutting ties lightly with kin,
Is the callous.
Resenting others’ excellence,
Rejoicing in others’ misfortunes,

Hoarding wealth, scorching duty,
Ignoring the needy’s plight,
Is the stingy.
Risking all for luck,
Unrepentant after ruin,
Is the foolish.
Petty-minded and biased,
Seeking only profit,
Is the petty.
Chasing beasts with hounds,
Obsessed with games endlessly,
Is the infatuated.
Forgetting ranks and norms,
Indulging in lavish display,
Is the extravagant.
Drowning in sensual pleasures,
Neglecting human rites,

Uninterested in self-cultivation,
Slacking in household duties,
Is the lazy.
Lacking dignified restraint,
Acting rashly without thought,
Is the frivolous.
Dazed by virtue’s path,
Agitated by wealth’s talk,
Is the base.
Relying on shallow flaws,
Blind to choices’ worth,

Despising the worthy,

Confusing right and wrong,

Hesitating on virtue’s path,

Mocked in every action,

Serving tyrants like slaves,

Abandoning poor old friends,
Scorning others with arrogance,

Discarding restraint for desires,
Roaming far without duty,

Lacking loyal sincerity,

Agreeing face-to-face,
Slandering after parting,

Stubborn in tyranny,

"Bàopǔ Xíng Pǐn"
Huòwáng Lǐ Yuánguǐ,
was a son of Gāozǔ.
Tàizōng once asked his ministers:
"Which of my younger brothers and sons is virtuous?"
Wèi Zhēng replied:
"Your servant is ignorant and dull-witted,
and does not fully know their capabilities.
Only the Prince of Wú has spoken with me several times,
and I have never failed to be impressed."
The Emperor said:
"Whom from previous dynasties would you compare him to?"
Zhēng said:
"In classical learning and refined elegance,
he is like the Prince of Dōngpíng of the Hàn dynasty."
Later, while in Xúzhōu,
he only formed a commoner's friendship with the recluse Liú Xuánpíng.
Someone asked Xuánpíng about the Prince's strengths,
Xuánpíng replied:
"He has none."
The questioner, finding this strange, asked again,
Xuánpíng said:
"People have shortcomings,
which is how their strengths become apparent.
As for Huòwáng,
there is nothing he lacks,
how could I possibly praise him?"
(from the Old Book of Táng)
Zhū Dǐ
Confucius said:
"There are five types of people:
the mediocre person,
the scholar,
the gentleman,
the worthy person,
and the sage.
By examining these five types,
the way of governance is fully understood."
Duke Āi asked:
"May I ask about them?"
Confucius said:
"The so-called mediocre person
has no principle of caution about endings in mind,
utters no instructive words from mouth,
does not choose the worthy to entrust himself to,
does not exert effort to establish his own views,
is confused about important matters while not knowing what to attend to,
follows things as they flow,
not knowing what to hold firm -
this is the mediocre person.
One whose mind has stability,
whose plans have consistency,
though unable to fully grasp the foundation of the Way and methods,
must have guidelines to follow;
though unable to possess all the beauty of hundred virtues,
must have principles to abide by;
therefore knowledge need not be extensive,
but must be examined in what is known;
words need not be many,
but must be examined in what is said;
actions need not be numerous,
but must be examined in their origins;
when wisdom already knows,
words already express it,
actions already follow it,
then it is as if one's nature and physical form cannot be changed;
wealth and honor cannot add to it,
poverty and low status cannot diminish it -
this is the scholar.
One whose words are loyal and trustworthy without resentment in heart,
who possesses benevolence and righteousness without boasting in appearance,
whose thoughts are penetrating and clear without being dictatorial in speech,
steadfast in action and faithful to the Way,
striving tirelessly without cease,
serenely as if
one could surpass but ultimately cannot reach -
this is the gentleman."
Family Sayings
One whose conduct follows rules without harming the root,
whose words can be models for the world without harming oneself,
who possesses the wealth of the world without resentment,
who distributes wealth throughout the world without suffering poverty,
such a one may be called a worthy person.
One whose knowledge penetrates the Great Way,
who responds to changes without exhaustion,
who discerns the nature of all things -
the Great Way
is that by which changes occur and all things are accomplished;
the nature
is that by which things are ordered without choice or rejection;
therefore his affairs greatly distinguish heaven and earth,
are as clear and perceptive as the sun and moon,
gather all things like wind and rain,
profound and sincere,
his affairs cannot be followed,
as if succeeding heaven,
his affairs cannot be recognized,
the common people shallowly do not recognize,
his neighbors being like this,
such a one may be called the great sage.

Guanzi
Princess
When the Son of Heaven marries off his daughter to a feudal lord,
he must have a feudal lord of the same surname preside over the ceremony.
When a feudal lord marries off his daughter to a senior official,
he must have a senior official of the same surname preside over the ceremony.
"Gōngyáng Zhuāng Yuán"
The Son of Heaven does not personally preside over the marriage,
hence it is called gōngzhǔ (princess).
The various kings personally preside over the marriage themselves,
therefore their daughters are called wēngzhǔ.
Wēng means
father,
indicating that the father presides over the marriage.
It is also called wángzhǔ,
meaning the king personally presides over the marriage.
"Hànshū Zhù"
Liú Bān said:
"The term gōngzhǔ (princess)
originally came from Qin customs,
where boys were called gōngzǐ,
and girls were called gōngzhǔ.
In ancient times, the wives of senior officials were called zhǔ,
so gōng was paired with it.
If it means someone of the same surname presides over it,
then it is called gōngzhǔ.
When marrying off daughters in ancient times,
it should be like in Zhou where senior officials presided over it,
so why wasn't it called fūzhǔ?
However, calling it wángzhǔ
is like saying wángzǐ (prince).
Calling it wēngzhǔ
derives from gōng.
"Chūxué Jì" states:
By the middle period of the Zhou dynasty,
the daughters of the Son of Heaven began to be called gōngzhǔ,
and the Qin dynasty followed this practice.
Could it be because of what is stated in the "Gōngyáng Zhuàn"?
The source of this is not clearly known."
There are three ways of loyalty,
there is the highest loyalty,
there is the secondary loyalty,
and there is the lower loyalty.
To cover the ruler with the Way and transform him,
this is called the highest loyalty;
to harmonize the ruler with virtue and assist him,
this is called the secondary loyalty;
to remonstrate against wrong with what is right and incur resentment,
this is called the lower loyalty.
Like the Duke of Zhōu towards King Chéng,
this can be called the highest loyalty.
Like Guǎn Zhòng towards Duke Huán,
this can be called the secondary loyalty.
Like Wǔ Zǐxū towards Fūchāi,
this can be called the lower loyalty.
"Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn"
Marrying a princess was not an ancient practice.
Lowering one's posture and humbling one's body,
rising early and retiring late,
unceasingly recommending the virtuous,
frequently citing the virtuous deeds of ancient times,
to encourage the ruler's will,
hoping to be of benefit,
so as to secure the state, the altars of soil and grain, and the ancestral temple—
those who act in this manner
are loyal ministers.
From "Shuō Yuàn"
The system of marrying princesses is not ancient.
When he sent down his two daughters,
it was the canon of Táng Yáo;
marrying off the younger sister brought great fortune,
as per the instruction of Dì Yǐ;
the royal princess married into Qí,
following the rites of the Zhōu dynasty.
For the yin to override the yang,
defies heaven by taking a wife,
and elevates the wife above the husband, going against human relations.
To defy heaven is inauspicious,
to go against human relations is unrighteous.

to obey orders that harm the ruler is called flattery,
to disobey orders that benefit the ruler is called loyalty,
to disobey orders that harm the ruler is called rebellion."
A loyal minister:
Wèi's Zhōu Xū assassinated Duke Huán,

When Zhōu Xū went to Chén,

Female Rebellion
The Han dynasty had marquises marry the emperor's daughters,
while the feudal lords had their subjects marry the princesses of the principalities.
This made men serve women,
and husbands yield to wives,
reversing the positions of yīn and yáng.
Hence, many scholars became disorderly.
From the "Biography of Wáng Jí" in the Book of Hàn

breaking his neck.

hurried to the scene,
and encountered him at the gate.

Píngyáng
Duke Yì of Wèi had a minister named Hóng Yǎn,
who was sent on a mission.
The Dí people attacked Wèi,
and its people said:
"The one to whom our lord gives position and emolument is the crane,
the ones he honors and enriches are the palace attendants.
Let our lord send the palace attendants and the cranes to fight;
how can we fight?"
Thereupon they scattered and fled.
The Dí people arrived,
caught up with Duke Yì at Róngzé and killed him,
ate all his flesh,
but only left his liver.
Hóng Yǎn arrived,
reported his mission to the liver,
then cried out to heaven and wept,
and after fully expressing his grief, said:
"Your servant requests to become the outer coffin."
Thereupon he committed suicide,
first cutting open his own abdomen,
and placed Duke Yì's liver inside.
Duke Huán heard of this and said:
"I considered Wèi to be lost,
thinking it was without principle.
But now that it has such a minister,
I cannot fail to preserve it."
He reestablished Wèi at Chǔqiū.
Hóng Yǎn can be called loyal indeed,
sacrificing his life and abandoning his body to follow his lord.
Not only did he follow his lord,
but he also caused Wèi's ancestral temple to be reestablished,
with sacrifices never ceasing.
He can be said to have achieved merit.

Yùquǎng forced his remonstrance upon the King of Chǔ,
but the King would not listen.
Yùquǎng then approached him with weapons,
and the King, in fear, complied.
Yùquǎng said:

no crime could be greater than this."

Emperor Wǔ's Empress Wèi, styled Zǐfū,
was a singer for Princess Píngyáng.
The emperor performed the purification rite at Bàshàng,
and on his return visited Princess Píngyáng,
where he saw the beauties she had gathered.
After drinking,
the singers were presented to the emperor,
and he was particularly pleased with Zǐfū alone.
The emperor rose to change clothes,
and Zǐfū, attending him in the dressing room, won his favor.
Returning to his seat, he was very joyful,
and bestowed a thousand catties of gold upon Princess Píngyáng.
The princess then presented Zǐfū to be sent into the palace.
As Zǐfū mounted the carriage,
the princess patted her on the back and said:
"Go now,
eat well and strive hard.

"Former Biography"
Duke Xiàn sent Xún Xì to tutor Xī Qí.
The Duke, being ill, summoned him and said:
"This young and helpless orphan,
I am entrusting to your care, Minister.
What will you do about it?"
Xún Xì bowed his head to the ground and replied:
"I will exert all the strength of my limbs,
and add to it loyalty and steadfastness.
If I succeed, it will be due to your spirit's blessing;
if I do not succeed, I will follow it with death."
The Duke said:
"What do you mean by loyalty and steadfastness?"
He replied:
"What benefits the ducal house,
I will do everything I know to be done—
that is loyalty;
sending off the deceased and serving the living,
without suspicion on either side—
that is steadfastness."

Ascending to Immortality and Leaving Behind the Shoes
Duke Huì of Jìn died,
Duke Huái took the throne,
and ordered that no one should follow the exiled man beyond the set time.
If the time limit was exceeded and they did not return,
there would be no pardon.
Hú Tū's sons, Máo and Yǎn, were following Chóng Ěr in Qín,
and he did not summon them back.
In winter,
Duke Huái arrested Hú Tū, saying:
"If your sons return, you will be spared."
He replied:
"When a son is able to serve,
his father teaches him loyalty—
this is an ancient institution.
Once his name is recorded and he has pledged his service,
to be disloyal is a crime.
Now my sons
have their names registered under Chóng Ěr,
for many years already.
If I were to summon them back now,
I would be teaching them disloyalty.
If a father teaches disloyalty,
how can one serve a ruler?"

had no concubines wearing silk,
no horses eating grain.

have served two rulers,
yet your concubines don't wear silk, your horses don't eat grain -
people will think you are stingy and not bringing glory to the state."
Wénzǐ said: "I would like that too,
but I observe our people -
there are still many whose fathers and brothers eat coarse food and wear poor clothing.

yet I have beautiful concubines and horses -
would that not be unbefitting for one who governs others?
Moreover, I have heard that virtue's glory makes a state splendid,
not that concubines and horses do."

wore nothing beyond cloth of seven shēng,
his horses were fed nothing better than weeds.
Wénzǐ heard of this and said:
"One who can reform after error
is superior among the people."

Duke Wén attacked Zhèng on the pretext of their observing his physical characteristics,
The people of Zhèng offered famous treasures to seek peace with the Duke,
but he refused, saying:
"Give me Shū Zhǎn."
The Zhèng minister Shū Zhǎn
requested to go,
but the Earl of Zhèng refused.
Shū Zhǎn firmly insisted, saying:
"One minister can save the common people and stabilize the state—
why should Your Lordship cherish me?"
The people of Zhèng then gave Shū Zhǎn to the people of Jìn.
The people of Jìn were about to kill him,
when Shū Zhǎn said:
"I wish to exhaust my words before dying—
this is truly my wish."
The Duke listened to his words.
Shū Zhǎn said:
"Heaven brought disaster upon Zhèng,
causing us to improperly observe your physical characteristics,
abandoning ritual and turning against relatives.
I said it should not be done.
The Jìn prince is wise and brilliant,
his attendants all have the talent of ministers.
If he restores his state and achieves his ambition among the feudal lords,
there will be no pardon for this disaster.
Now disaster has arrived.
To honor the wise and overcome calamity—
this is wisdom;
to sacrifice oneself to redeem the state—
this is loyalty."
He then approached the boiling cauldron and grasped its ears,
shouting loudly: "From now on,
those who serve their lord with wisdom and loyalty
will share my fate."
The Duke then ordered that he not be killed,
but instead treated him with great courtesy and sent him back.

Zhōngháng Bó, having conquered Gǔ,
brought Gǔzǐ Yuǎnzhī back,
ordering the people of Gǔ to each return to their places,
with none but officials to follow.
A minister of Gǔzǐ said:
"Sùshā Lí, along with his wife and children,
was seized by the army officers."
He explained:
"I serve my lord,
not the land.
We are called lord and minister,
how can we be called land and ministers?
Now that my lord is actually relocated,
what reliance do I have on Gǔ?"
Mùzǐ summoned him, saying:
"Gǔ has a lord now,
if you stay and serve this lord,
I will secure your salary and rank."
He replied:
"I pledged my allegiance to the Dí's Gǔ,
not to the Jìn's Gǔ.
I have heard that
once allegiance is pledged as a minister,
there should be no second thoughts,
and to pledge allegiance and then die by the record
is the ancient law.
If the lord has a glorious name,
the minister should not betray his pledge.
How dare I seek personal gain to trouble the Minister of Justice and disrupt the old laws?
What if unforeseen events occur?"
Mùzǐ sighed and said to his attendants:
"What virtue must I cultivate to have such a minister?"
So he let him go.
After the tribute was presented,
he spoke to Duke Qǐng,
granting Gǔzǐ land south of the Yellow River,
and appointed Sùshā Lí to assist him.

swarms of bandits rose up like hornets.
Princess Yìyáng fled from Luòyáng to the south of the Luò River,
with over two thousand soldiers
remaining to guard the area without leaving,
in order to protect the capital.
