Liú Yào admired her unwavering integrity,
had her buried,
and erected a shrine for Princess Yìyáng.
The people pitied her,
built a temple for her,
which is now known as the Shrine of Yìyáng.
The emperor
noted that the "Book of Jìn" does not record the events of these three princesses at all.
Could it be that Rén Fǎng alone had access to a separate history of Jìn?
In the Battle of An,
Hán Jué of Jìn pursued the Marquis of Qí.
Féng Chǒufù exchanged positions with the duke,
making the duke descend,
as if to fetch water from Huá Spring.
Zhèng Zhōufù drove the auxiliary chariot,
with Wǎn Pèi as the right guard.
The Marquis of Qí thus escaped.
Hán Jué presented Chǒufù,
and Xì Xiànzǐ was about to execute him.
He cried out:
"From now on, there will be none who bear hardship in place of their lord.
Here is one such man,
will he be executed?"
Xìzǐ said:
"It is no light matter for a man to face death to save his lord.
It would be inauspicious for me to execute him."
He pardoned him to encourage those who serve their lords,
and thus spared him.
The Marquis of Qí, having escaped,
sought Chǒufù three times entering and exiting the fray.
(Chéng 2)
In the past, Wú and Chǔ fought at Bǎi,
as the armies clashed and soldiers engaged,
Mò Áo Dàxīn patted his charioteer's hand,
turned and sighed deeply, saying:
"Alas,
my friend,
the day Chǔ State forgets this is coming.
I shall plunge deep into the Wú army,
strike down one man,
grab another,
to share this with Dàxīn—
might the state then be secure?"
Thus to sever the neck and burst the belly,
close the eyes once and never see eternity again,
unknowing of any gain,
yet grieving for the state—
such was Mò Áo Dàxīn.
"Strategies of the Warring States"
Kept male favorites
In the past, Wú and Chǔ battled at Bǎi,
and after three engagements, [the Wú army] entered Yǐng.
Our lord personally fled, leaving all the common people scattered and displaced.
Fénmào Bósū said:
"If I don armor and take up sharp weapons,
and go to face a strong enemy to die,
that would merely be like one soldier.
It is better to flee to the feudal lords."
Thereupon, carrying provisions, he traveled in secret,
climbed up Zhēng Mountain,
crossed deep ravines,
until his soles were pierced and his knees exposed,
and after seven days reached the court of the King of Qín.
He stood like a bird, unmoving,
moaning by day and weeping by night.
For seven days he could not get his message through,
with not a drop of water or broth entering his mouth, he was exhausted,
and fell into a faint, unconscious.
The King of Qín, hearing of this, ran to him,
his cap and sash not even properly fastened,
supporting his head with his left hand,
and moistening his mouth with his right.
Then Bósū revived.
Thereupon, Qín sent out troops to rescue Chǔ,
repelled the Wú army, and restored Chǔ.
Thus, one who toiled his body,
and distressed his thoughts, worrying for the altars of soil and grain,
was Fénmào Bósū.
When
the Wú army had already retreated,
and King Zhāo was restored to the state,
he began the rewards with Shēn Bāoxū.
Bāoxū said:
"To assist the ruler and bring peace to the state
is not for one's own sake;
to rescue from crisis and eliminate harm
is not for fame.
If, after achieving merit, one accepts a reward,
that is selling one's courage.
Since the ruler is already settled,
what more is there to seek?"
Thereupon he fled from the reward,
and for his whole life did not appear before the ruler.
It is said:
"Master Shēn's acceptance of the mission to go to Qín
was loyal;
for seven days and seven nights, without ceasing his voice,
was profound.
Not accepting the reward
was unyielding.
However, rewards are the means to encourage goodness;
declining rewards is also not the constant rule."
Xīnxù
The Princess of Sòng Shānyīn,
daughter of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
was married to Hé Jí.
During the time of Jǐnghé,
her indulgence became excessive.
She said to the emperor,
"Though I, standing here below,
differ in gender,
both our forms were entrusted by the late emperor.
Your Majesty has countless numbers in the six palaces,
yet I have only one consort,
how could matters be so unequal and unfair to this extent?"
The emperor then appointed male companions for the princess,
thirty people in attendance.
Whenever the emperor went out with his court ministers,
they always accompanied the imperial carriage.
The princess, because Chǔ Yuān of the Bureau of Personnel was handsome,
requested the emperor to have him attend her,
to which the emperor agreed.
"Sòng Jì":
The emperor summoned Yàn Huí to the west upper pavilion,
where he stayed for ten days.
At night, the princess approached him,
subjecting him to persistent coercion.
Yàn Huí stood his ground
from evening till dawn,
without changing his resolve.
The princess said,
"Sir, with such a beard like a lance,
how do you lack the spirit of a man?"
Yàn Huí replied,
"Though I am not clever,
how dare I be the first to sow the seeds of discord?"
"Chǔ Zhuàn":
Yàn Huí ultimately refused to comply, living together with Jí,
for just over a month.
From then on, their friendship only deepened.
"Jí Zhuàn":
The personal name of Shānyīn was Chǔ Yù.
Heavenly Marriage
In the state of Chǔ, there was a scholar named Shēn Míng,
who stayed at home to care for his father,
and his filial piety was renowned throughout Chǔ.
The king wished to appoint him as prime minister,
but Shēn Míng declined and would not accept.
His father said:
"The king wishes to make you prime minister,
why do you not accept?"
Shēn Míng replied:
"To abandon being a filial son to my father and become a loyal minister to the king—
how can this be?"
His father said:
"If you receive a salary from the state,
and establish righteousness at court,
I will be happy and free from worry.
I want you to become prime minister."
Shēn Míng said:
"Very well."
Thereupon he entered the court,
and the king of Chǔ appointed him prime minister.
After three years in office,
Bái Gōng rebelled,
killing Simǎ Zǐqī.
Shēn Míng prepared to go and die in the conflict,
but his father stopped him, saying:
"To abandon your father and die—
is that acceptable?"
Shēn Míng said:
"I have heard that those who serve give their persons to the ruler,
and their salaries to their parents.
Now that I have left you to serve the ruler,
should I not die in his crisis?"
So he took his leave and went,
leading troops to surround Bái Gōng.
Bái Gōng said to Shí Qǐ:
"This Shēn Míng
is a brave warrior of the world.
Now he has surrounded me with troops;
what should I do?"
Shí Qǐ said:
"Shēn Míng
is a filial son of the world.
Go and seize his father with troops;
when Shēn Míng hears of it,
he will certainly come."
After discussing it with him,
Bái Gōng said:
"Good."
Then he went and captured his father,
holding him with troops,
and announced to Shēn Míng:
"If you join me,
I will share the state of Chǔ with you;
if you do not join me,
your father will die."
Shēn Míng responded with tears:
"Formerly I was a filial son to my father,
now I am a loyal minister to my ruler.
I have heard that
he who eats another's food should die for his affairs,
and he who receives a salary should exhaust his abilities.
Now I can no longer be a filial son to my father,
but must be a loyal minister to my ruler.
How can I preserve both?"
Seizing a drumstick, he beat the drum,
and thereupon killed Bái Gōng,
but his father also died.
The king rewarded him with a hundred catties of gold,
but Shēn Míng said:
"To eat the ruler's food
and avoid the ruler's calamities
is not loyalty.
To stabilize the ruler's state
but cause one's own father's death
is not filial piety.
These reputations cannot both stand,
these actions cannot both be complete.
To live on like this,
what face have I to stand under heaven?"
Thereupon he committed suicide.
From "Shuō Yuàn"
Cuī Zhù killed Duke Zhuāng,
Shēn Kuǎi was serving as a fisherman,
and upon retreating said to his steward:
"You can escape with my family,
I am going to die."
His steward said:
"To escape from this
would violate your principle."
So he died together with him.
From the 25th year of Duke Xiāng
When Cuī Zhù assassinated Duke Zhuāng,
Shēn Kuǎi was fishing at sea,
and was about to enter and die for it.
His charioteer stopped him, saying:
"The lord's lack of virtue is known throughout the land,
it is not right to die for him."
Shēn Kuǎi said:
"How can I accept the salary of a disorderly lord
and handle the affairs of a well-governed state?"
Shēn Kuǎi arrived at the gate and said:
"Please inform Cuī Zhù that I wish to enter and mourn."
Zhù ordered that he not be admitted,
Shēn Kuǎi said:
"Do you doubt me?
I will give you my arm."
Then he cut off his left arm and gave it to the gatekeeper,
who showed it to Cuī Zhù.
Zhù arrayed eight rows of guards,
and ordered him to enter.
Shēn Kuǎi threw down his sword, cried out to heaven, and fought,
killing seven rows of guards,
but before reaching Cuī Zǐ,
he died in the eighth row.
From the "Xīn Xù"
In the Song dynasty, all the rulers
were intensely jealous,
with Emperor Míngdì often feeling envious.
Jiāng Yù was supposed to marry the daughter of Xiàowǔ,
but the emperor had someone draft a memorial for Yù
to decline the marriage, saying:
"I respectfully received the imperial decree,
once bestowing the marriage with Línhǎi Princess,
yet our humble doors
were never fit for heavenly unions.
When I carefully consider my humble self,
I am filled with anxiety and fear.
Though the noble family is glorious,
it brings no fortune to me.
Since the time of the Jìn dynasty,
those marrying royal princesses,
though often from illustrious lineages,
repeatedly had great talents,
but they were as subdued as Wáng Dūn,
as humbling as Huán Wēn.
Zhēnzhǎng feigned foolishness to avoid calamity,
Zǐjìng endured suffering to defy the decree,
Wáng Yǎn lacked Zhòngdū’s fortitude,
yet was exposed to downfall.
Hé Yǔ, lacking the grace of a dragon artisan,
cast himself into a deep well.
Xiè Zhuāng nearly became like an old fool,
Yīn Chōng almost didn't escape from border troubles.
Wáng Zǎo, though tough and harsh,
was fairly learned,
but through laughter and jest,
became a wronged ghost.
Zhǔ Ài, in distress,
suffered an untimely death,
harming both reason and justice,
is hard to fully convey.
Therefore, facing this unsuitable prospect,
I reveal my sincere feelings,
not only expressing my own
wish for complete well-being,
but also fervently representing the collective
concerns and fears of the whole clan.”
The emperor circulated this memorial among the rulers,
warning them of its implications,
even using it for derision.
"Nán Shǐ: Wáng Dàn Zhuàn"
treacherous and cruel
When Cuī Zhù assassinated Duke Zhuāng,
there was one Chén Bùzhàn who, upon hearing of his lord's peril,
set out to rush to his aid.
By the time he left, he had dropped his spoon during the meal,
and upon boarding the carriage, he lost the handrail.
The driver said:
"If you are this timid,
will going there be of any use?"
Bùzhàn replied:
"To die for one's lord is righteousness,
while lacking courage is a personal matter.
One should not let personal matters harm public duty."
So he proceeded,
but upon hearing the sounds of battle,
he died of terror.
People said:
Bùzhàn may be said to have possessed the courage of a benevolent person.
Emperor Wǔ and Yīn Ruì were old acquaintances,
so he married his daughter Princess Yǒngxīng to Yīn Ruì's son Jūn.
Since the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
princesses had often been arrogant, promiscuous, and immoral,
and Princess Yǒngxīng added treachery and cruelty to these traits.
Jūn was short and small in stature,
which made him despised by the princess.
Whenever he was summoned to her chambers,
she would first cover the walls with the characters for "Yīn Ruì,"
causing Jūn to weep and leave.
The princess then ordered her maids to bind him and bring him back,
but Jūn could not endure it.
In anger, he reported this to the emperor,
who struck him with a rhinoceros horn rúyì,
shattering it instantly on his back.
Yet the princess still harbored hatred for Jūn.
*History of the Southern Dynasties*
The Marquis of Qí asked Yànzǐ,
"How does a loyal minister serve his ruler?"
Yànzǐ replied,
"When there is calamity, he does not die for it;
when the ruler flees, he does not see him off."
The ruler said,
"If I grant him land to enfeoff him,
and bestow titles to honor him,
yet when I face calamity he doesn't die for me,
when I flee he doesn't see me off—
can this be called loyalty?"
Yànzǐ replied,
"If his words are heeded,
the ruler will face no calamity throughout his life—
how then would the minister die for him?
If his counsel is followed,
the ruler will never flee—
how then would the minister see him off?
But if his words are not heeded,
and he dies when calamity strikes,
that is a meaningless death;
if his remonstrance is ignored,
and he sees off the fleeing ruler,
that is hypocritical conduct.
Thus, a loyal minister is one who can impart good counsel to his ruler,
not one who shares calamity with him."
From "Shuō Yuàn"
called Xiàguān
Chén Héng assassinated his ruler,
and sent six warriors to seize Zǐyuān Qī.
Zǐyuān Qī said:
"Do you wish to have me join you,
because you consider me wise?
For a minister to assassinate his ruler
is not wise.
Because you consider me benevolent?
To turn against one's ruler for profit
is not benevolent.
Because you consider me courageous?
To seize me with weapons,
and for me to join you out of fear,
is not courageous.
If I lack these three qualities,
what use would I be to you?
If I possess these three qualities,
I would never follow you anyway."
So they released him.
From "Xīnxù"
King Zhāo of Yān sent Yuè Yì to attack Qí.
King Mǐn fled.
When Yān first entered Qí,
they heard that
a man named
Wáng Chù from
Gài
was virtuous.
They sent someone to tell Chù:
"Many in Qí praise your righteousness.
We appoint you as general,
enfeoffing you with ten thousand households."
Chù firmly declined the Yān people.
The Yān people said:
"If you do not heed us,
we will lead the three armies to slaughter Gài."
Wáng Chù said:
"A loyal minister does not serve two rulers;
a chaste woman does not marry two husbands.
The King of Qí did not heed my advice,
so I withdrew to plow in the fields.
Now that the state is destroyed,
I cannot preserve it.
If you coerce me with arms now,
to become your general would be aiding a tyrant in his cruelty.
Rather than living without righteousness,
it is better to die."
Thereupon, he hung his body from a tree branch,
thrusting himself to break his neck and die.
The exiled ministers of Qí heard this and said:
"Wáng Chù was a commoner,
yet his righteousness kept him from betraying Qí.
How much more should those
in office,
living on official salaries?"
They then gathered in Jǔ,
sought out the various princes,
and established King Xiāng.
Yùzhāng returned to Wèi Míngdì,
who appointed Zǒng as Grand Commandant,
enfeoffed him as Prince of Dānyáng,
and he also married the emperor's daughter, Princess Shòuyáng.
The princess, styled Jǔlí,
was beautiful in appearance,
and Zǒng respected her greatly.
When speaking with the princess,
he often referred to himself as "your humble official."
When the capital fell,
Zǒng abandoned the province and fled north.
At that time, Ěrzhū Shìlóng held exclusive power,
and he sent for the princess to be brought to Luòyáng.
Shìlóng tried to force himself on her,
but the princess cursed him, saying:
"How dare you, a rebel, insult the daughter of the Celestial King?"
Enraged, Shìlóng then had her strangled to death.
(Records of the Buddhist Monasteries)
During the reign of Emperor Jǐng, the seven states of Jīng and Chǔ and King Xiào of Qí were suspicious,
while the two states of Jiāoxī and Jìběi besieged Qí.
Qí sent Grand Master Lù Zhòng to the Son of Heaven, who returned and reported:
"Hold firm."
By the time he arrived, the two states had surrounded Qí with multiple layers,
making it impossible to enter.
The two states made a pact with Grand Master Lù Zhòng, saying:
"If you return,
say that Hàn has been defeated."
The Grand Master agreed to this.
When he reached the city walls and saw the King of Qí, he said:
"Hàn has dispatched a million troops,
ordering Grand Commandant Zhōu Yàfū to crush Jīng and Chǔ,
and is now leading troops to rescue Qí.
Qí must hold firm."
The two states executed him.
"Miscellaneous Records of Hàn"
Niángzǐ Jūn
The Xiōngnú sought peace through marriage alliance,
and all the ministers deliberated before the emperor.
Scholar Dí Shān said:
"A marriage alliance is advantageous."
The emperor asked Zhāng Tāng,
and Tāng replied:
"This is the ignorant view of a foolish scholar."
Dí Shān retorted:
"I may be foolishly loyal,
but the Imperial Censor Zhāng Tāng is deceptively loyal."
Hàn Shū
Emperor Gāozǔ's daughter Princess Píngyáng married into the Chái family,
raised righteous troops at Sīzhú Garden,
which were called the Lady's Army,
and she was the wife of Chái Shào.
"New Book of the South"
Guāngwǔ served as the Grand Marshal,
appointing Wáng Bà as the assistant official in charge of achievements,
and ordered the clerks to cross the northern bank of the Yellow River.
Several dozen guests followed,
but gradually departed.
The superior said to Bà:
"Those from Yǐngchuān who followed me have all left,
yet you alone remain.
Only now do I truly understand that a strong wind reveals strong grass."
"Records of the Eastern Hàn"
Yǔ Dēngzǐ Zhòngyuǎn served as a palace guardian for Emperor Sòng Míng.
During the reign of the Deposed Emperor's Jǐnghé era,
Emperor Míng was suspicious and guarded,
and none of his old acquaintances or guests visited him anymore.
Only Zhòngyuǎn continued to pay his respects unfailingly.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne, he said:
"You can indeed be called strong grass in a strong wind."
"History of the South"
Emperor Tàizōng said:
"After the sixth year of Wǔdé,
there were discussions about the dethronement and establishment of the Supreme Emperor.
At that time, I was not accepted by my brothers;
there was truly fear of being unappreciated despite great merits.
Xiāo Yǔ could not be swayed by large profits,
nor could he be intimidated by punishment;
he is truly a minister of the state."
He then bestowed a poem, saying:
"A strong wind reveals strong grass;
chaos reveals loyal ministers."
"Old Tang History"
Lǐ Jiàng discussed ancient and modern times,
concerning matters like eunuchs commanding armies.
Xuānzōng was angered,
and Jiàng apologized.
The emperor’s expression changed as he said:
"You have informed me of what others find difficult to say;
a strong wind reveals strong grass,
and you truly embody this."
"Original Records"
Demolishing the Wall
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ,
born to Empress Wǔ,
was deeply loved by the empress,
surpassing all her sisters.
Xuē Shào was chosen to marry her,
and Wànnián County was used as the wedding venue.
The gate was too narrow for the pheasant-feathered carriage to pass through,
so the officials demolished the wall to allow entry.
Torches were lined up all the way from the Xīng'ān Gate,
causing the trees along the road to wither.
At that time, minister Liú Yīzhī wrote a poem:
"Dreaming of catalpa trees illuminating the green steps, lush peach blossoms
fill the purple palace." Yuán Wànqǐng wrote:
"Separated in spring, the imperial descendant
descends in autumn." Rèn Fènggǔ wrote:
"The imperial son ascends the green steps,
the royal princess descends from the purple palace."
Guō Zhèngyī wrote:
"The cassia palace first dons the crown,
the orchid chamber early raises the hairpin,"
all expressing the meaning of accepting a consort and royal marriage.
"Records of the Literary Institute"
Radiant Beauty
Bào Yǒng, styled Jūncháng,
arrived at Baling in Jīngzhào,
passing by Gēngshǐ's tomb.
He directed his carriage into the path,
intending to alight,
but his attendant advised against it.
Bào Yǒng said:
"Having served him personally as my sovereign,
how could I bear to pass by his tomb in a carriage?
Even if I incur blame from the Director of Retainers, I will not avoid it."
Thereupon, he descended from the carriage and wept,
expressing his full grief before proceeding.
When he went west to Yòufúfēng,
he sacrificed an ox at Xún Jiàn's tomb.
The Emperor heard of this
and asked his ministers:
"What do you think of an envoy who acts thus?"
At that time, Grand Master of Palace Counsel Zhāng Kān replied:
"Benevolence is the foundation of all conduct,
and loyalty is the essence of ritual and righteousness.
Benevolence does not abandon the old,
nor does loyalty forget the sovereign.
These are the highest forms of conduct."
The Emperor was pleased with this.
From "Dōngguān Hànjì"
Bào Yù, styled Wényuān,
was appointed Colonel-Director of Retainers.
The edict ordered Bào Yù to go to the Imperial Secretariat,
to seal and issue a proclamation on the surrender of the Hú people.
The Emperor sent a junior eunuch to ask Bào Yù
why he appeared puzzled and did not respond,
to which he replied:
"Your servant has heard that according to precedent,
high officials do not include their surname in documents,
and furthermore, when the Minister over the Masses issues an open proclamation,
I found it strange that the Colonel-Director of Retainers was ordered to issue a document with his surname included."
The Emperor responded:
"I wished to let the empire know the son of a loyal minister."
He was again appointed Colonel-Director of Retainers.
The Emperor
Princess Ānlè,
the youngest daughter of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
married off to Wǔ Chóngxùn,
her radiant beauty captivated the entire realm.
The New Book of Tang
associated her with the Wéi clan's scorching power that could burn one's hand,
fearing spread across the roads,
when Wàn Huí saw her carriage and horsemen,
he repeatedly spat and said:
"The stench of blood,
the stench of blood,
do not approach it."
Not long after, they were annihilated.
The New Account of the South
to observe and worship
When Master Fú Tóng retreated with the army to cover the rear and resist the enemy,
his soldiers were completely wiped out.
A Wu general urged Tóng to surrender,
but Tóng cursed him, saying:
"You Wu dogs,
how could there be a Han general who surrenders?"
He then died in battle.
His son, Fú Qiān, later became the Area Commander of Guānzhōng.
During the Jǐngyào era, he sacrificed his life when faced with peril.
Commentators praised the father and son for their generations of loyalty and righteousness.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn decreed:
"The Shu general Fú Qiān previously at Guān Fortress,
personally resisted the imperial troops,
facing death without regard,
and his father Tóng also died fighting for Liú Bèi.
Goodness in the world is one and the same,
how can it be differentiated by this side or that?"
"Annotations to the Records of Shu"
Yì Xióng,
a native of Liúyáng in Chángshā,
served as magistrate of Chōnglíng.
Upon hearing that Wáng Dūn had launched a rebellion,
and that Prince Chéng of Qiáo had issued a proclamation,
Yì Xióng swiftly circulated the proclamation far and wide,
enumerating Wáng Dūn's crimes.
Soon the imperial forces suffered defeat,
enabling Wáng Dūn to unleash his violence.
He apprehended Yì Xióng at Gūshú,
presenting the proclamation to him.
Yì Xióng declared:
"It is true.
I regret that my position was lowly and my strength weak,
unable to save the nation from calamity.
How could I cling to life?
If I am executed today,
I shall become a loyal ghost.
That is my wish."
From "Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū".
Wáng Dūn was daunted by his righteous words,
and released him.
Everyone congratulated him,
but Yì Xióng laughed and said:
"Last night I dreamed of riding in a carriage with meat hanging beside it.
Now meat must have chopsticks,
and 'chopsticks'
means 'ax'.
A carriage beside an ax—
am I to be executed?"
Soon after, Wáng Dūn sent someone to kill him.
Witnesses at the time
were all filled with sorrow and regret.
From "Jìn Shū".
Xiāo Sōng's son Héng married the Princess of Yǒngchāng,
and when Sōng's wife, Madame Hè, came to pay respects at the ceremony,
Emperor Xuánzōng called her "dear in-law,"
with very grand etiquette.
(Old Book of Táng)
Zhāng Yī was a native of
Wújùn.
When the Emperor Gōng was the Prince of Lángyá,
he appointed Yī as his Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace.
After the emperor ascended the throne,
Liú Yù, considering Yī a former subordinate of the emperor
and one long trusted by him,
sealed a jar of poisoned wine and gave it to Yī,
secretly ordering him to poison the emperor.
Yī sighed and said:
"To kill one's sovereign in order to seek survival—
how could I bear to live on in the world?
It is better to die."
He drank the poison himself and died.
(From the History of the Jìn Dynasty)
Watching a Performance
Zhèng Hǎo married Emperor Xuānzong's daughter, Princess Wànshòu.
The emperor decreed that the princess must observe wifely duties,
all in accordance with commoner laws.
If she violated his warning,
there would surely be disasters like those of Tàipíng and Ānlè.
When Hǎo's younger brother Yǐ fell critically ill,
the emperor sent an envoy to inquire about him.
Upon returning, the emperor asked where the princess was.
The reply was:
"At the Cí'ēn Temple watching a performance."
Furious, the emperor sighed and said:
"No wonder scholar-official families are unwilling to marry into our house—
there is good reason for it."
He immediately summoned the princess to the palace,
rebuking her:
"How could you not visit your ailing brother-in-law,
but instead go watch a performance?"
He sent her back to the Zhèng family.
From then on, the imperial relatives
all diligently observed rituals and laws,
like the esteemed clans of Dōngshān.
(From the Comprehensive Mirror)
Breaking chopsticks
Yú Jiǎnmén,
a man of Dài,
was sent by Emperor Tàizōng as an emissary to persuade Féng Bá.
Upon reaching Hé Lóng,
he stayed outside the city and refused to enter,
sending a message to Féng Bá:
"The Great Wèi Emperor has issued an edict;
Lord Féng must come out to receive it,
before I dare enter."
Féng Bá sent men to force him,
compelling him to appear.
Féng Bá did not bow,
and had men press down on his head.
Yú Jiǎnmén said:
"If Lord Féng bows to receive the edict,
I will naturally pay respects as a guest to a host.
Why must you force me so harshly?"
In his exchanges with Féng Bá,
his voice and expression were stern,
yet he never yielded or bent.
Later, Féng Bá detained Yú Jiǎnmén,
who, amidst the crowd,
turned his back to Féng Bá,
exposing the rear of his trousers to shame him.
After being imprisoned,
he kept only the clothes on his person,
which wore out almost completely,
with lice covering his body.
Féng Bá sent him garments,
but Yú Jiǎnmén refused to accept them.
The people of Hé Lóng heard and sighed:
"Even ancient martyrs
could not surpass him."
After twenty-four years,
Féng Wéntōng submitted a petition declaring himself a subject,
and only then was Yú Jiǎnmén sent back.
He was appointed as a治书侍御史 (Palace Secretary).
Emperor Shìzǔ issued an edict stating:
"Yú Jiǎnmén, on his mission to Hé Lóng,
faced the tyranny of a madman,
yet his courage and will were strong and fierce,
never compromising his integrity.
Even the ancient Sū Wǔ—
how could he surpass this?"
He was bestowed a thousand sheep,
a thousand bolts of silk,
promoted to Senior Grand Master,
his deeds recorded in the ancestral temple,
proclaimed throughout the land,
so all would hear of them.
(Book of Wèi)
Emperor Xuānzōng selected Yú Cóng to marry Princess Yǒngfú,
but the matter was abruptly suspended.
The chancellor requested the imperial decree,
and the emperor said:
"This girl recently, while dining with me,
broke her spoon and chopsticks in my presence.
With such a temperament,
I fear she is unfit to be a scholar's wife."
He then permitted Yú Cóng to marry Princess Guǎngdé instead.
From "Records of the Eastern Pavilion"

Eating a thousand plates
Chén Bàxiān plotted to usurp the throne,
and ordered the Palace Secretariat Attendant Liú Shīzhī to lead Shěn Kè with troops into the palace,
to escort the Emperor Jìng of Liáng to another palace.
Kè pushed open the door and entered to see Bàxiān,
knocked his head on the ground and apologized, saying:
"I, Kè, have served the Xiāo family all along,
and cannot bear to witness this event today.
I am prepared to die instead,
but will absolutely not obey the command."
Bàxiān praised his loyalty,
and did not press him further,
instead replacing him with the leader of the army, Wáng Sēngzhì.
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign, Xǔ Qīnjì battled the Khitan at Chóngzhōu,
was defeated and captured.
The enemy general besieged Āndōng,
ordering Qīnjì to persuade the remaining cities that had not surrendered.
Peí Xuánguī, the Protector-General of Āndōng, was in the city.
Qīnjì told him:
"The reckless rebels face heaven's calamity,
and will perish by dawn.
You must only strengthen your troops and guard carefully,
to preserve your loyalty and integrity."
The enemy killed him.
His younger brother Qīnmíng was Governor of Liángzhōu,
defeated in battle and captured by the Turks.
When taken to Língzhōu,
he was ordered to persuade the city to surrender early.
Qīnmíng instead shouted loudly:
"There are no food or drinks in the enemy camp."
"In the city there are fine
sauces - I beg for two shēng,
millet - I beg for two shēng,
ink - I beg for one ingot."
At that time,
the enemy camp was surrounded by muddy rivers on all sides,
with only one road for access.
Qīnmíng requested these items to hint to the city,
hoping they would select troops and deploy generals,
awaiting a night assault.
But no one in the city understood his meaning.
Soon he was killed.
The brothers died in the same year serving the royal cause,
and commentators praised them.
(Old Book of Táng)
Chéngdéjūn jiédùshǐ Wáng Yuándí,
since assuming control of the fiefdom,
has notably reformed his father's ways,
with tributes forming an unbroken line along the roads.
Emperor Wénzōng decreed his marriage to Princess Shòu'ān.
"New History: Daughter of Jiàng King Wù"
Yuándí sent his aunt Duàn to the court to present betrothal gifts,
Duàn presented two thousand platters of food,
along with imperial garments, warhorses, the princess's dowry, and private eunuchs and female attendants,
her retinue was as numerous as clouds,
earning honor from both court and public.
"Old Tang History"
Hé Bì Shì Lèi mistakenly interprets "thousand platters" as presenting food on ivory trays,
greatly misleading readers.
Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng summoned former officials of Shǔ to compose poems about the Shǔ ruler's surrender to the great Táng.
Wáng Xié and others satirized his decadence,
but only Vice Censor-in-Chief Niú Xījì said:
"The Táng sovereign renews the sun and moon;
the Shǔ king cannot preserve his former mountains and rivers."
Emperor Míngzōng remarked:
"Xījì does not forget his lord and kin—
this is loyalty and filial piety."
He awarded him one hundred bolts of colored silk.
(Yìyuàn Cíhuáng)
Fěn Hóu
In the Song dynasty, the title of Commandant-Escort was referred to as the "Powdered Marquis,"
as recorded in the letter by Wén Jífǔ,
where Xíng Shù mentioned that Hán Jiāyàn, the brother-in-law of the emperor,
had an elder brother named Zhōngyàn, who was called the "Powdered Brother."
From "The Biography of Liú Zhì."
At the end of the Yìngshùn era, the Later Táng Shǎodì lost his throne,
and crossed the Yellow River from Luòyáng with several hundred cavalry intending to flee to Yè.
At that time, Jìn Gāozǔ had been reassigned to govern Chángshān,
and was also traveling from his commandery to the capital.
They met by chance east of Huòjiā at night,
and proceeded to enter a courier station in Wèi Commandery together.
That very night,
Shǎodì set up an ambush with armed soldiers,
planning to conspire with his attendants to harm Jìn Gāozǔ.
Under the pretense of a private conversation,
they sat beside the pavilion's eaves,
while Jìn Gāozǔ secretly sent his guard Shí Gǎn to stand behind him with a hammer concealed in his sleeve.
The ambushers suddenly arose,
causing panic and commotion among those present.
Shí Gǎn, known for his courage and strength,
protected Jìn Gāozǔ by ushering him into a room,
blocking the door with a large timber,
and single-handedly withstanding the assault.
He soon perished in the conflict.
From "History of the Five Dynasties"
When Emperor Shìzōng of the Later Zhōu attacked the Southern Táng and reached the Huái River,
the Huái army suffered a major defeat,
with various generals either fleeing or surrendering.
Liú Rénshān defended Shòuzhōu
and alone held firm, making it impossible to capture.
"Mǎ's History of the Southern Táng"
records that his youngest son, Chóngjiàn, took a small boat across the Huái River at night,
planning to alleviate his family's crisis,
but was captured by an army officer.
Rénshān ordered him to be cut in two at the waist.
The supervising army commissioner, Palace Commissioner of the Wéndé Hall, Zhōu Tínggòu, wept at the central gate,
and also rushed to seek help from Rénshān's wife, Madame Xuē.
Madame Xuē said:
"Chóngjiàn is my young son,
and it is truly unbearable for me,
but if I spare him from death,
then the Liú family will become a disloyal house."
She urged that he be executed,
and only then held the funeral.
Those who heard of this all shed tears.
"Lù's History"
records that the following year, Emperor Shìzōng came again to attack,
and Rénshān was ill and near death.
His deputy Sūn Yǔ and others forged a letter from Rénshān surrendering the city.
The emperor ordered Rénshān to be carried before his tent,
sighed with admiration for a long time,
and then sent him back into the city to recuperate.
Emperor Shìzōng issued an edict stating:
"Liú Rénshān was utterly loyal to his duty,
maintained his integrity without fail,
among the famous ministers of former dynasties,
few can compare.
In my southern campaign, obtaining you was a great gain."
He then appointed him as Grand Commandant and concurrently Head of the Secretariat.
"Mǎ's History"
records that Rénshān did not rise,
but pointed to his mouth and died.
At that time, the sky was overcast,
and yellow sand fell like rain.
He was fifty-eight years old.
"The Unofficial History of Jiāngnán"
records that all the people of the city wept,
and deputy generals and soldiers who killed themselves to follow him in death numbered over twenty.
Emperor Shìzōng sent an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices,
posthumously enfeoffing him as Commandery Prince.
His wife refused to eat,
and died five days later as well.
"Lù's History"
records that Emperor Yuánzōng of the Southern Táng heard of Rénshān's death,
wept bitterly for him,
and posthumously awarded him the title of Grand Tutor.
He burned the official document, saying:
"If your soul has consciousness,
witness the favor of Zhōu.
Accept my command."
That night, he dreamed of Rénshān bowing below the steps,
as if accepting the appointment.
The old seat of Shòuzhōu was in Shòuchūn.
Emperor Shìzōng, because it was difficult to capture,
moved the city below,
renamed the army, saying:
"I name it 'Loyal and Upright' to honor
Rénshān's integrity."
Mǎ's "History of the Five Dynasties"
records that Rénshān, to this day, is continuously honored with temple offerings in Shòuchūn.

with Attendant-in-ordinary Wáng Chóngzhì as deputy.
When Shèng reached Biànjīng,
he said to Chóngzhì:

He then memorialized to Emperor Shìzōng,

"Our generals have besieged Jīng Province,
yet long failed to capture it;
if you can induce its surrender,

When Shèng reached the city walls,
he saw Liú Rénshàn from afar and called out:

The Later Ruler of Southern Tang passed away,
and Emperor Tàizōng ordered his court officials to compose an epitaph.
At that time, someone vying for fame with Xú Xuàn
wished to harm him,
so he claimed that no one knew the deeds of the King of Wú better than Xú Xuàn.
Emperor Tàizōng thus ordered Xuàn to write it.
Xuàn immediately requested an audience and tearfully said:
"I formerly served Lǐ Yù.
If Your Majesty permits me to uphold the duty of loyalty to my former lord,
I dare not accept the decree."
Emperor Tàizōng allowed Xuàn to compose the epitaph,
which only stated that the allotted fate had ended,
and the Mandate of Heaven had found its rightful place.
It included phrases such as "the eastern neighbor caused disaster,"
"the Southern Winnowing Basket fanned suspicions,"
"casting aside the shuttle led to the confusion of a loving mother,"
"there was no old woman's tale of begging for fire,"
"first troubling the army at the ramparts,"
"finally delaying the meeting at Túshān."
Emperor Tàizōng read it and sighed in admiration.
He also obtained the elegy for the King of Wú that Xuàn had composed,
and often praised Xuàn's loyalty and righteousness to his ministers.
The elegy read:
"Green pines on the Luòyáng road,
wild grasses in the Jiànkāng palace."
"Eastern neighbor" refers to Qián Chù.
From "Sòngcháo Lèiyuàn"
Capital Cities
In governing the world and administering the state,
one must attend to the root before the branches;
nothing is more important in attending to the root than filial piety.
If the ruler is filial, his reputation will be illustrious and honored below,
and the world will submit and listen with praise;
if ministers are filial, they will serve their lord with loyalty,
hold office with integrity,
and face death in times of peril;
if the common people are filial, they will farm diligently, defend resolutely, fight steadfastly, and not retreat in defeat.
Filial piety
is the fundamental duty of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors and the guiding principle of all affairs.
To hold one method and have all virtues arrive,
all evils depart,
and the world follow—
this is only filial piety.
Lǚlǎn
A capital is
where the sovereign resides,
a place where people gather and assemble.
A town is like a gathering,
a term for assembly.
In the *Shiming*,
it is said that any settlement with ancestral temples and tablets of former rulers is called a capital,
while those without are called towns;
towns are referred to as "built,"
and capitals as "walled."
From *Zuo Zhuan*, the 28th year of Duke Zhuang.
Jīngshī
The filial piety of the Son of Heaven is called "accomplishment,"
meaning that it signifies completion.
When the virtue of the Son of Heaven covers all under heaven,
and his grace extends to all things,
bringing fulfillment from beginning to end,
then his parents attain peace,
hence it is called "accomplishment."
The filial piety of feudal lords is called "adherence to standards,"
where "standards"
refer to laws.
When feudal lords reside in their states,
able to uphold the laws and standards of the Son of Heaven,
avoiding peril and excess,
then their parents attain peace,
hence it is called "adherence to standards."
The filial piety of high ministers and officials is called "reputation,"
meaning it signifies fame.
When the words and deeds of high ministers and officials are widely known,
free from ill repute,
and their fame reaches far and near,
then their parents attain peace,
hence it is called "reputation."
The filial piety of scholars is called "thorough understanding,"
where "thorough understanding" implies the meaning of clarity and careful examination for scholars,
who, upon first ascending to court, bid farewell to their parents and enter official service,
able to scrutinize the rites of serving a father to serve a ruler,
then their parents attain peace,
hence it is called "thorough understanding."
The filial piety of common people is called "nurturing,"
where "nurturing"
carries the meaning of containing and cultivating.
Common people harbor emotions and embrace simplicity,
personally plowing and laboring diligently,
to nurture their virtue,
then their parents attain peace,
hence it is called "nurturing."
"Yuán Shén Qì" is seen in the "Old Tang Records."
The primordial energy is in chaos,
yet filial piety resides within it.
When the Son of Heaven practices filial piety,
heavenly dragons bear diagrams,
earthly tortoises present writings,
calamities and disasters vanish,
and auspicious clouds roam freely;
when common people practice filial piety, the marshes and forests flourish,
floating treasures unfold,
marvelous grasses bloom,
and divine fish emerge from the waters.
"Yuán Shén Qì"
What is the capital?
It is the residence of the Son of Heaven.
What does "jīng" mean?
It means great.
What does "shī" mean?
It means multitude.
The residence of the Son of Heaven must be described with terms denoting multitude and greatness.
Gōngyáng Commentary, Duke Huán Year 9
The territory spans a thousand li,
the city walls measure a thousand zhì,
with palaces, residences, and government offices,
built on a grand scale and system,
the four directions each bring tribute according to their duties,
leaving nothing unprepared or unprovided,
the reason it must possess its own land
is that governance begins from what is near.

the four barbarian tribes live in peace.
The ultimate in filial piety and fraternal duty
reaches the divine spirits.
When parents are ill, one expresses his anxiety,

The capital is the designation for a city of a thousand lǐ.
Modeled after the diameter of the sun and moon being a thousand lǐ,
the "Royal Regulations" state:
"The Son of Heaven's domain is a thousand lǐ square."
Some say:
"In the Xià dynasty it was called Xiàyì,
in the Yīn dynasty it was called Shāngyì,
and in the Zhōu dynasty it was called Jīngshī."
The "Shàngshū" says:
"Leading the oppression of Xiàyì refers to Jié,
in Shāngyì refers to the Yīn."
The "Báihǔtōng"
and "Ěryǎ"
state that a mound of extreme height and greatness is called jīng,
meaning it cannot be formed by human strength,
but is of the nature of heaven and earth,
spontaneous.
The "Zuǒzhuàn" says:
None can match its height.
The "Guóyǔ" says:
Zhào Wénzǐ and Shū Xiàng traveled to Jiǔjīng,
now Jīngzhào,
the capital's meaning is derived from this.
The "Fēngsútōng"
The way the ancient kings governed the world was such that,
because they loved their own parents,
they dared not despise others;
because they respected their own parents,
they dared not be disrespectful to others.
When love and reverence are fully expressed in serving one's parents,
their radiance extends to the common people,
and reaches throughout the four seas.
This is the filial piety of the Son of Heaven.
Zēngzǐ said:
"The body,
is the legacy of one's parents.
To act with this legacy of one's parents,
how dare one not be reverent?
To be undisciplined in daily life is unfilial;
to be disloyal in serving one's ruler is unfilial;
to be disrespectful in holding office is unfilial;
to be untrustworthy with friends is unfilial;
to be cowardly in battle is unfilial.
If these five practices are not fulfilled,
disaster will befall one's parents.
How dare one not be reverent?"
The Shěn Shū states:
"Among the three hundred punishments,
none is heavier than that for unfilial conduct."

"Imperial Readings of the Historical Records"
Unify the four directions
Zēngzǐ said:
"That which, once gone, can never be returned
are one's parents;
that which, when reached, cannot be surpassed is the limit.
Therefore, though a filial son wishes to provide for them, his parents may not wait;
though a tree wishes to grow straight, time may not wait.
Hence, to sacrifice an ox at the tomb
is not as good as offering a chicken or a pig while the parents are still alive.
Thus, when I once served as an official in Qí,
my salary was no more than a pound of grain,
yet I was still joyful and happy—
not because I considered it abundant,
but because I delighted in being able to support my parents.
After they had passed away,
I traveled south to Chǔ,
where I obtained a high position.
The hall was nine ren high,
the rafters three arm-spans thick,
and the carriages numbered a hundred,
yet I still faced north and wept—
not because I felt demeaned,
but because I grieved that I could no longer support my parents.
Therefore, if the family is poor and the parents are old,
one should not be selective about the office one takes.
He who later trusts in his ambition
and neglects his parents
is not filial."
(Hánshī Wàizhuàn)
When a king receives the Mandate to initiate a new era,
he must establish the state and set the capital in the central land,
thereby harmonizing the forces of Heaven and Earth,
grounding in the balance of yīn and yáng,
equally governing the four directions,
and extending control over all states.

The "Odes of Wáng" in the Book of Songs states, "In the garden there is tuī,"

The Hán School of the Odes and the Sān Cāng both say it refers to yìmǔ (motherwort),

Construction of the Royal City
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn injured his foot while descending the hall,
and though he recovered after several months, he did not go out,
still wearing a worried expression.
His disciples asked him about it,
saying:
"Master, you injured your foot while descending the hall,
and though you recovered after several months, you have not gone out,
still wearing a worried expression.
May we ask the reason for this?"
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn replied:
"Excellent is your question.
I heard from Zēngzǐ,
who heard from Zhòngní,
that parents give us life whole,
and we should return to them whole,
without harming our bodies,
without damaging our forms,
which can be called filial piety.
A gentleman in his actions
should not forget this even for a single step.
I forgot the way of filial piety,
hence my worry.
Therefore it is said: The body is not one's private possession,
but the physical legacy of one's strict parents."
"Lǚ Xiàoxíng"
Yáng Fàn, courtesy name Wénduān,
was a person from Qí.
During the turmoil between Qí and Sòng,
his mother was among the bandits,
he gathered mulberries and hid them underground,
taking them out at night to offer to his mother.
This happened not just once.
Suddenly, from the ground, he obtained ten hú of rice,
on which were written the words: "Ten hú of rice,
bestowed upon the filial son."
Yáng Fàn used this to support his mother.
"Fēngsú Tōng"
In ancient times, when the former kings founded their capitals,
they surveyed all the hidden corners,
leaving no land unplanned.
They measured the shadows with the gnomon,
ensuring neither shortening nor excess,
gathering where wind and rain converge,
and only then established the royal city.
"Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital"
Jì Mài was a man from Lújiāng,
originally surnamed Shū,
born on the fifth day of the fifth month,
his mother abandoned him.
Zhào shì, wife of villager Jì Chún, raised him,
at age six,
his birth parents occasionally came to visit,
saying:
"You are my child."
Mài tearfully told Zhào,
who then explained the whole story,
by age ten,
he divided his earnings from labor equally between both mothers,
Chún died without sons,
Mài observed three years of mourning in coarse hemp,
when his birth parents subsequently died,
he again observed three years of mourning with heart-grief,
Zhào wanted to bring wine and rice to the in-laws' family,
encountered drunkards who beat her unconscious,
suddenly a dog came tugging at Mài's clothes,
this happened three times,
Mài felt alarmed,
ran to the in-laws' family,
met the drunkards just then drinking in the grass,
Mài killed both drunkards with his carrying pole,
Zhào recovered safely,
he surrendered to the county magistrate who pardoned him,
then vowed never to marry.
Later while Mài was sleeping,
suddenly a woman appeared saying she was surnamed Wèi,
had suddenly died yesterday,
the Heavenly God pitied him for having no wife,
so sent her to repay him.
Mài described her appearance,
mother and son went outside the Wèi residence,
indeed found a funeral as described,
the funeral ox-cart refused to move,
Zhào explained everything to the host,
the host opened the coffin,
the woman showed signs of breathing,
by evening could speak,
and recounted everything,
exactly as Zhào had said,
so they became husband and wife,
when Zhào died Mài repeatedly revived from fainting,
at fifty Mài fell seriously ill near death,
dreamed of a deity saying:
"Your filial conduct is supreme,
your lifespan shall extend to a hundred years."
Indeed he died at ninety-seven.

In the early years of the Tàihé era, he was appointed as the governor of Jiàngjùn.

His thighs and feet,

Zhào Jùn, courtesy name Zǐqí,

One night upon returning to his village estate,

Jùn, seeing his father's late return,

His father was too drunk to be carried on his back.
It was midwinter, and the cold was severe.
Jùn removed his own clothes to cover him.
The mountains of Yuèyáng had many fierce beasts.
A leopard looked at them,
but turned aside and left the path for them.
After his father's death, he was buried at Yíngqiū.

His mother returned east,

and provided grain while exempting his family from taxes.
When Jùn was to bury his mother,

The contract had already been settled,

But Qīng vowed with unwavering resolve.
Later, both his parents-in-law committed suicide,
and their daughter accused Qīng of murdering them.
The county magistrate tortured him,
leading to a false confession.
In the seventh month, Qīng was executed in the marketplace.
Before his death, Qīng said to the execution supervisor:
"I beg to set up a tall pole with a white banner.
If I killed my parents-in-law,
my blood will sink into the ground;

my blood will ascend to the sky."

"Luòyáng is vulnerable on all sides,
making it unsuitable for a military stronghold.
Guānzhōng, however, has Yáo and Hán to the left,
Lǒng and Shǔ to the right,
with fertile plains stretching a thousand miles.
To the south, it enjoys the riches of Bā and Shǔ,
and to the north, the advantages of the Hú and Wǎn regions.
It is protected on three sides,
requiring defense only on one front,
from which to control the feudal lords to the east.
This is what is called 'a thousand miles of impregnable walls,'
the land of abundant natural resources."
Shǐ
Huáng Xiàn, courtesy name Shūdù,
was a native of Shènyáng in Rǔnán.
Dài Liáng of the same commandery, though highly talented and arrogant,
would always straighten his countenance upon seeing Xiàn,
and upon returning home would feel lost as if having misplaced something.
His mother asked him:
"Have you been visiting that ox doctor's son again?"
He replied:
"When I do not see Shūdù,
I do not consider myself inferior,
but having met the man,
I find him ahead when I look forward,
and suddenly behind when I turn back,
truly difficult to fathom."
One hundred twenty
Huáng Xiàn did not boast of his reputation to deceive the times,
nor did he resist conventions to feign eccentricity.
Those who peered at his gate dared not tread his courtyard,
and those who observed his flow could not fathom its depth.
Commentators all said, "Yánzǐ has been reborn in the Hàn Dynasty!"
Yet his ancestors came from humble origins,
his father was a cattle veterinarian,
and he received no formal education in youth.
Nevertheless, he later emerged outstandingly brilliant—
truly one may say he was heaven-endowed.
(Records of Former Worthies of Rǔnán)
No records of Huáng Xiàn's discourses and principles have been transmitted,
yet when scholar-officials encountered him,
none failed to be profoundly impressed,
casting aside their flaws and pettiness,
aspiring to perfect the Way,
his nature so complete that it defied description.
Fàn Xuánpíng considered Xiàn unassuming,
his compliance profound as the abyss,
the depth of his Way beyond measure,
his purity beyond discussion,
had he studied under Confucius,
he would have nearly attained perfection.
Later Records
Qín,
a country of strategic terrain,
embraces the river and is shielded by mountains,
stretching across a thousand lǐ,
with a million halberd-bearing soldiers,
Qín holds a position where two can hold off a hundred.
Its geographical advantages are convenient,
allowing it to deploy troops against the feudal lords,
as if pouring water from a high roof's eaves.
"Qián Jì"
Huáng Xiàn moved in accordance with rules,
and spoke with virtuous words.
"Biographies of Ancient Worthies Within the Seas"
Lù Hǎi
With the rise of the Hàn dynasty, they moved away from the lands of the Three Hé,
settled west of the Bà and Chǎn rivers,
and established their capital south of the Jīng and Wèi rivers.
This is what is called the land of the terrestrial sea under heaven,
the place from which Qín subjugated the Western Róng
and annexed the regions east of the mountains.
"Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò"
The foundation of moral transformation,
Cháng'ān,
the capital of the Son of Heaven,
personally receives the sagely influence,
yet its customs are no different from those of distant regions.
Those who come from the commanderies and kingdoms
have no model to follow,
and some, upon seeing extravagance and waste, imitate it.
This is the foundation of moral transformation,
the pivotal mechanism of customs,
and what should be rectified first.
"Biography of Kuāng Héng"
Dài Liáng, styled Shūluán,
possessed extraordinary talent,
his outstanding reputation spread far and wide,
the young cherished him,
the elder admired him,
from the gentry in his hometown,
down to the common people,
none dared to have households with disputes.
"Biographies of Earlier Worthies Within the Seas"
Defending Against External Threats
Xú Rúzǐ never left his home when summoned for official appointments,
yet he would travel thousands of miles to attend funerals.
When the esteemed gentleman Huáng of Jiāngxià passed away,
he went to attend the burial.
Being poor and having no means to support himself,
he carried a mirror-polishing kit with him.
Whenever he reached a place,
he would hire himself out to polish mirrors for payment,
and only then could he continue his journey.
Upon arriving,
he set up an offering,
wept, and then returned.
When Chén Zhòngjǔ served as the governor of Yùzhāng,
he would come when summoned
and accept what was given to him,
but he did not serve in office,
thus preserving his integrity.
Later,
when Guō Línzōng was mourning his mother,
Xú Zhì went to offer condolences.
He placed a bundle of fresh grass in front of the mourning hut and left.
The crowd was puzzled,
not knowing the reason.
Guō Línzōng said:
"This must be Xú Rúzǐ, the noble scholar of the southern provinces.
Does the Book of Songs not say:
'A bundle of fresh grass,
the man is like jade'?
I lack the virtue to deserve this."
The Later History
records this grandly in its annals,
but it mistakenly claims that Xú Zhì placed the fresh grass before Huáng Qióng's tomb,
greatly misleading its readers.
When Xú Zhì passed away,
the eminent scholars across the land discussed his pure character and lofty aspirations,
comparing him to Bóyí and Shūqí,
or associating him with Xǔ Yóu.
Xiàhóu Yùzhāng, admiring his renowned virtue,
erected a pavilion by Zhì's tomb,
first naming it the Pavilion of Longing for the Worthy.
From "Bié Zhuàn"
The grandeur of the Great Hàn,
relied on the abundance of Yōngzhōu,
mastering the art of defending against external threats and governing internally.
Yōngzhōu was the land where emperors nurtured their enterprises,
and hegemonists expanded their achievements,
a battleground where warriors contended in hardships.
With perilous passes and bridges,
it formed many strategic points.
A single soldier raising a stone,
could halt a thousand men in stagnation.
Initiated as one of the twelve provinces,
it was deemed fertile and rich.
This was indeed the deep preserve of emperors and kings,
and a sharp tool for safeguarding the state.
From Dù Dǔ's "Rhapsody on the Capital" of the Later Hàn Dynasty.
Shàngdū
In the eastern state, people respected Cài Yōng without mentioning his name,
all calling him Lord Cài.
In Yǎnzhōu and Chénliú, they painted his portrait and praised him, saying:
"His literary talent equals that of the Three Ministers of State,
his filial piety matches that of Zēng Shēn and Mǐn Sǔn."
From "Biography of Bó Jiē":
When Wáng Yǔn wanted to kill Cài Yōng,
Grand Commandant Mǎ Rìdī rushed to tell Wáng Yǔn:
"Bó Jiē is a rare talent of our generation,
who knows much about Hàn affairs.
He should continue writing the later history,
to create a great canon for our era.
Moreover, his loyalty and filial piety are well-known,
yet he faces charges without proper cause.
Wouldn't executing him disappoint public expectations?"
Wáng Yǔn did not listen.
Mǎ Rìdī withdrew and told others:
"I fear Lord Wáng will not last long.
Virtuous people are the nation's foundation,
cultural creations are the nation's institutions.
To destroy the foundation and abandon the institutions -
how can this last long?"
Thus Cài Yōng died at court.
All officials and scholars shed tears without exception.
Zhèng Xuán of Běihǎi heard this and sighed:
"Who will now rectify
the affairs of the Hàn dynasty?"
Throughout Yǎnzhōu and Chénliú, people painted his portrait and praised him.
From "History of the Later Hàn"
While Zhèng Xuán was in Xúzhōu,
Kǒng Wénrǎng, then Governor of Běihǎi,
wished him to return to the commandery,
and urged him earnestly and sincerely,
sending messengers one after another.
Upon his return,
Róng instructed his subordinates:
"In ancient times, the Zhōu people revered their teacher,
calling him Shàngfù.
Now, we may all address him as Lord Zhèng,
and must not use his personal name."
When Yuán Shào met him,
Xuán sighed and said:
"I originally thought Lord Zhèng was a renowned scholar of the eastern provinces,
but now I see he is a venerable elder of the realm.
For a commoner to achieve eminence in the world,
how could this be without reason!"
From "Yīn Yún's Xiǎoshuō"
At the beginning of the Hàn's establishment,
they actually moved westward,
making it our capital.
"The Rhapsody on the Western Capital"
Shào Yán recruited Běihǎi's Zhèng Xuán but did not treat him with due respect,
Zhào Róng, hearing of this, said:
"A virtuous man is
the hope of a gentleman;
not respecting the virtuous
is to lose the hope of a gentleman."
From "Jiǔzhōu Chūnqiū"
Imperial Domain
The Western Capital of Hàn was located in Yōngzhōu,
actually called Cháng'ān.
Its flowers and fruits,
were the most fertile among the Nine Provinces;
its defensive barriers,
were the most secure region between Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, it extended across the six directions,
three times became an imperial capital,
with Zhōu rising like a dragon,
and Qín gazing like a tiger.
A guest said to Hé Jìn:
"Kǒng Wènróng was an outstanding hero of his time,
compared to other beings,
he was like the North Star among all stars,
or millet and grain among all crops—
all under heaven turned their eyes toward him."
Family Biography
Chén Shí, styled Zhònggōng,
served as the Chief of Tàiqiū.
Upon his death,
Hé Jìn dispatched envoys to offer condolences and sacrifices,
while scholars and officials of the Confucian tradition discussed his virtues and achievements,
posthumously honoring him as Wénfàn.
His sons, Chén Jì and Chén Chén, shared his virtues and conduct,
with father and sons all renowned for their lofty reputations,
earning the contemporary title "Three Excellencies."
Whenever the ministerial offices issued summonses,
they were often honored with simultaneous appointments,
with ceremonial gifts like lambs and geese arriving in flocks,
and all the hundred cities of Yùzhōu depicted images of the Three Excellencies.
"Posthumous Account and Stele Inscription from the Later Documents."
Strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches
Kǒng Wénjǔ possessed lofty aspirations and genuine feelings,
which were sufficient to stir righteous indignation and provoke ambitious hearts.
How could any arbitrary compromise have allowed his life to be extinguished?
With awe-inspiring dignity,
and pristine purity,
he may be compared in quality to jade from Kūnshān and autumn frost.
From the *History of the Later Hàn*
In the realm of the talented and distinguished,
where officialdom flourishes,
strengthening the trunk and weakening the branches,
exalting the capital to oversee all nations.
The
several prefectures within the capital region,
truly form the foundation of the state,
with limited land and dense population,
where reserves are not abundant,
they particularly deserve preferential treatment and compassion,
to allow them rest and recuperation,
for strengthening the root and weakening the branches,
has always been a common practice since ancient times.
． "Old Book of Tang: Biography of Gāo Jìfǔ"
Tiānyì
Mǐ Shēng, styled Zhòngshū,
his father was of low status,
hence Zhāng Bóyīng wrote to Lǐ Yòucái:
"Mǐ Zhòngshū possesses lofty virtue and fine reputation,
a talent destined for the age,
not what the minor Mǐ clan ought to have,
nor what the barren land of Xīnfēng ought to produce."
From "Records of the Three Capital Regions"
The Han dynasty initially established its capital on the banks of the Wei River,
where the Qin territory extended northward,
in what was actually Xiányáng,
a vast and fertile plain,
with land of the highest quality,
truly a profound and divine region of the earth.
When Emperor Gāozǔ planned the capital,
his intentions also considered the deities,
making it fitting to designate as the celestial capital.
"Rhapsody on the Western Capital"
The rebellious Hú Liú Yào,
rampaged through the western capital,
daring to act like wild dogs and sheep,
trampling upon the celestial capital.
Liú Kūn's "Memorial Urging the Emperor to Ascend the Throne"
Thus I dare to seek,
your celestial capital, O Shāng.
"Book of Documents"
Xǔ Shào, courtesy name Zǐjiāng,
was the younger brother of Xǔ Chǔ.
He stood firm as a mountain and was profound as a deep pool,
his conduct conforming to rules and models.
Xiè Zǐwēi of Shàolíng, a man of great talent and foresight,
upon seeing Shào at ten years old,
sighed and said:
"This is a truly rare and great man of the age."
The Biographies of Former Worthies Within the Seas
records that when Shào was young,
Zǐwēi already said:
"This worthy shall one day hold the keys of Rǔnán."
Separate Biography
The Land of Abundance
Wáng Jī recommended Guǎn Níng, saying:
"He embodies the harmony of the two cosmic forces,
possessing the pure excellence of the nine virtues.
His inner brilliance and simple nature,
are pure as ice and deep as clear abyss.
During the middle and peaceful period,
when the imperial governance slackened and faltered,
he avoided the troubles of the times,
riding a raft to cross the sea.
He sojourned in Liáodōng for over thirty years.
At the beginning of the Qian hexagram,
he concealed his brilliance and hid his light,
passing through dangers and treading perilous paths,
yet never changing his integrity.
Like the sound of gold and the color of jade,
his virtues grew more evident with time.
His moral conduct is truly exceptional,
unmatched throughout the land."
Records of Wèi
Níng's appearance was very respectful,
his speech very humble.
Observing his conduct,
he seemed remote and unattainable when approached,
yet amiable, very gentle and warm.
At his passing,
whether people in the world knew him or not,
all who heard of it sighed in regret.
Fùzǐ's Commentary
Chúnyú Dìng advised Prince Módùn of Nányáng, saying:
"Guānzhōng is
a land blessed by heaven,
a place for hegemon-kings.
Now, if we return because we cannot pacify and govern it,
it will damage our prestige."
From Jìn Biography Seven
How majestic is Kǒngmíng,
With foundations vast and far-reaching,
From the start, a dragon's essence,
His noble resolve grew ever firmer.
Had he not been destined for the age,
Who could have swept away the mists and gloom?
Shedding common garb in the central groves,
He flourished as the pillar of his time.
"Yuán Hóng's Eulogy"
The Pivot of the World
How outstanding is my lord,
Alone endowed with heavenly brilliance,
Is it the blessing of the gods,
Or the essence of humanity?
Divine beings respond to opportunity,
Great vessels have no fixed form,
Flowing unimpeded through fullness,
Supreme virtue is not constant.
In ancient times, Diǎn and Yāo,
Had fame but left no traces.
How can they compare to our kind,
With excellent strategies and marvelous plans?
Since Zāng Wénzhòng passed away,
He was praised for his words.
Yet he still cannot compare to you,
Whose words and deeds are both exemplary.
Yí Wú had flaws reversed,
Yuè Yì did not meet his end,
How can they compare to you?
Wise and profound, maintaining humility,
Receiving trust at life's end,
Surpassing Xǔ Yóu in yielding merit,
Shouldering responsibility to govern affairs,
The people's words do not spread idly,
Punishments as balanced as in Zhèng,
Education as fine as in Lǔ,
The people of Shǔ know shame,
Hé and Wèi rivers rest peacefully,
If not Gāo Yáo then Yī Yǐn,
Rather than those Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Yīng,
How could mere sage declarations,
Evoke such heartfelt repeated sighs?
"Shǔ Jì Lǐ Xìng's Writing"
The imperial edict stated:
"You shall establish extraordinary achievements for Jì Hàn,
Matching the great merits of Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Gōng."
"Records"
Péng Yàng wrote to Zhūgě Liàng:
"You are the Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng of our age,
Should well counsel our lord in affairs,
To accomplish his great plans, as heaven illuminates and earth discerns,
What more need be said?"
Above
Kǒngmíng embodied the virtues of both civil and military arts,
using civil means to bring peace within,
and military might to subdue enemies.
In his military campaigns,
no one would pick up lost items on the road,
not even a hair was harmed.
His noble principles were grand and far-reaching.
When achievements were made, he would yield credit to his subordinates;
when faults occurred below, he would take the blame upon himself.
Upon seeing goodness, he would strive to emulate it;
when receiving admonition, he would correct his ways.
Thus, his reputation and influence shook both near and far,
nearly placing him on par with Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng,
how could he merely be ranked alongside Yuè Yì?
Zhāng Fǔ's "Comparison of Yuè Yì and Zhūgě Liàng's Superiority"
Qín is the pivot of the world,
eight parts gather talents and worthies.
Yuán Shū's "White Horse Poem"
Fàn Zǐ said when meeting the King of Qín:
"Now Hán and Wèi,
are the pivots of the world."
"Strategies of the Warring States"
The Profound Mystery of the Divine
Sīmǎ Yì wrote to Zhūgě Liàng, saying:
"Huáng Gōnghéng is a forthright gentleman;
he constantly praises you in his conversations,
never ceasing to speak of you."
Records of Shǔ
The land of Yōngzhōu,
anciently called the Storehouse of Heaven,
controls Lǒng and Shǔ to the right,
and holds the strategic passes of Xiáo and Hán to the left.
In front, it has the natural barriers of Zhōngnán and Tàihuà Mountains,
while behind, it is secured by the clear Wèi and muddy Huáng Rivers.
As a profound abode of spirits,
it has been the capital of monarchs,
a state suited for military exploits,
unlike any other in the Central Plains.
The Qín and Hàn dynasties relied on it,
and ultimately achieved imperial dominion.
Recently, mad rebels
stirred chaos throughout the nine regions,
causing the lands north and south of the Yellow River to collapse and split,
all submitting to the rebel command.
Yet the late emperor, with the forces of Shuòfāng,
drove Qìngxù to flee and perish.
Your Majesty, using the armies of the western territories,
brought about the execution of Cháoyì.
Was this merely due to Heaven's favor of the righteous,
or was it also the result of the strategic terrain?
. From "The Old Book of Táng: Biography of Guō Zǐyí"
The renowned scholar
Wǔhóu and Sīmǎ Xuānwáng were at the banks of the Wèi River,
about to engage in battle.
Xuānwáng arrived in military attire to oversee the affairs,
and sent someone to secretly observe Wǔhóu.
He was riding in a plain carriage wearing a coarse silk headscarf,
holding a white feather fan,
directing the three armies,
which advanced and halted according to his commands.
Upon hearing this, Xuānwáng sighed and said:
"He can truly be called a renowned scholar."
From "Yǔ Lín"
The Foundation of the Imperial Enterprise
Huán Wēn campaigned against Shǔ,
where he still saw Wǔhóu,
at that time a minor official was over a hundred years old.
Huán Wēn asked about Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng,
"Who today can compare with him?"
His intention was somewhat self-praising.
The reply was:
"When Lord Gě was alive,
we did not find him extraordinary,
but since Lord Gě passed away,
we have seen no one to compare with him."
"Miscellaneous Records"
The present Guānzhōng,
is the land of the ancient royal domain spanning a thousand lǐ.
As the foundation of the royal enterprise,
it lies precisely here.
The Qín dynasty once utilized it
to overpower the feudal lords,
and the Hàn dynasty relied upon it
to pacify the four seas.
This was due to relying on the strategic advantage of its mountains and rivers,
and dwelling on its fertile farmlands.
When weak, one can internally safeguard this region,
which constitutes half of the empire,
thereby nurturing strength while awaiting the opportune moment.
When strong, one can externally control the eastern Xià,
holding the greatest part of the realm,
thereby accumulating authority and manifesting virtue.
Lù Xuāngōng's "Memorial on Matters in Guānzhōng"
Zhūgě Liàng was truly an extraordinary figure of his time,
governing the state with clear distinctions,
commanding the army with established methods,
accumulating achievements and promoting enterprises,
handling affairs with perfect timing,
entering without leaving a weapon behind,
and exiting with surplus provisions,
knowing that Shǔ was fundamentally wealthy yet precarious,
thus he maintained caution to stabilize it.
From "Fùzǐ"
Reside in strength to control the weak
Fù Xùn possessed the discernment to know people,
in Fángzhōu he regarded Páng Tǒng as half a hero,
later when Tǒng attached himself to Liú Bèi,
he was treated as second only to Zhūgě Liàng,
just as Fù Xùn had said.
"Yīn Yún's Xiǎoshuō"
The establishment of a state
relies on a strong foundation and weaker branches,
thus ensuring its stability.
(Zuo Shifu's words)
The royal domain is
the foundation of the four regions.
The capital city is
in turn the foundation of the royal domain.
The situation should be such that the capital is like the torso,
the royal domain like the arms,
and the four regions like the fingers.
This is how to maintain central control while governing the periphery,
the great authority of the Son of Heaven.
Emperor Tàizōng established the garrison militia system,
distributing them under imperial guard command.
There were altogether over eight hundred garrisons,
with nearly five hundred located in Guānzhōng.
The rest of the empire could not rival Guānzhōng,
making clear the intention of maintaining central control while governing the periphery.
Zhòngfù
Sūn Cè, on his deathbed,
entrusted his younger brother Sūn Quán to Zhāng Zhāo's care,
saying to Zháo:
"If Zhòngmóu proves incapable of handling state affairs,
you may take his place yourself.
Even if we ultimately fail to achieve victory,
you can still retreat westward at a measured pace,
with nothing to worry about."
From "Wú Lì"
In Wú, Zhāo was called Zhòngfù,
showing that he was truly an outstanding statesman of his time.
It is regrettable that he wasn't endowed with resources like Mount Sōng,
but was instead planted in Kuàijī.
From "Diǎn Lüè"
Now only records about Zhāoliè and stories of Wǔhóu are preserved.
Zhāng Zhāo and Zhāng Hóng both participated in Sūn Cè's strategic planning.
When Lǚ Bù seized Xúzhōu and declared himself its governor,
he did not wish to let Hóng serve under Cè.
He pursued and recommended Hóng as a Màocái (outstanding scholar),
issuing an official document to transfer and dispatch Hóng.
Hóng inwardly detested Bù,
feeling ashamed to yield to him.
Cè also deeply valued and cherished Hóng,
wishing to have him assist himself.
He replied with a written response and did not send Hóng away,
saying:
"The sea produces bright pearls,
which are treasured wherever they are found.
Although Chǔ had talents,
Jìn actually employed them.
An outstanding and noble gentleman
is valued wherever he travels.
Why must it be his native province!"
Records of Wú
Nèishǐ
Initially, Sūn Quán among his ministers
often addressed them by their courtesy names,
only addressing Zhāng Zhāo as Lord Zhāng,
and Zhāng Hóng said:
"This is why the Eastern region holds these two men in high esteem."
from "Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn"
The Qin capital was the Nèishǐ.
From the former "Treatise on Geography"
Shī Gǔ notes:
"The capital,
is the area within the royal domain where the Son of Heaven resides.
When Qin unified the world,
it established commanderies and counties,
and the area under the capital's jurisdiction
was specifically designated as Nèishǐ,
meaning it was inside,
to distinguish it from the various commandery governors."
A family treasure shown to others.
Sūn Cè appointed Yú Fān as a merit official,
treating him with the courtesy of a friend,
and personally visited Fān's residence.
Records
Cè wrote to Fān, saying:
"Today's affairs
should be shared with you;
do not think Sūn Cè treats you as a mere commandery official."
Chronicles of Jiangbiao
Cè campaigned against the Shānyuè; Fān excelled in using a spear,
requesting to be in the vanguard,
and on level ground urged Cè to ride a horse.
Cè said:
"You have no horse;
what is to be done?"
He replied:
"Fān can travel on foot,
covering three hundred lǐ in a day.
Since the campaigns began,
no officer or soldier has matched Fān.
If my lord tests his steed,
Fān can stride steadily to keep pace."
Records of Wu
Cè said:
"You are widely learned and well-informed.
I previously wished to send you to Xǔ to meet court officials,
to refute the talkers of the Central Plains,
but you were unwilling to go.
I then sent Zǐgāng,
fearing Zǐgāng could not silence those fellows' tongues."
Fān replied:
"Fān is my lord's family treasure; if shown to others,
they might keep it,
thus depriving my lord of a fine assistant.
That is why I did not go before."
Cè laughed and said:
"Indeed."
Chronicles of Jiangbiao
Disdaining power and avoiding hardship
Yú Fān heard that Lord Cáo was summoning him and said, "A bandit
wants to use his ill-gotten wealth to taint a good family?"
He then refused the offer.
The Wú Shū records:
Fān wrote a letter to Kǒng Róng,
and showed him his annotations on the Yì Jīng.
Róng replied in a letter:
"Having heard of Yánlíng's principles,
I am delighted to observe your study of the Yì,
and now know that the excellence of the southeast
is not merely the bamboo arrows of Kuàijī."
Zhāng Hóng also wrote to Róng, saying:
"Yú Zhòngxiáng was previously somewhat slandered by critics,
but with a precious gem as his substance,
polishing only makes him shine brighter—
it cannot diminish him."
The Records
Yì Fèng submitted a memorial to Emperor Yuán at the beginning of his reign, saying:
"The Way of Heaven is constant,
while the Way of Kings is not constant.
Being not constant
is the means to respond to the constant.
I wish Your Majesty would move the capital to Chéngzhōu,
with Chénggāo on the left as a stronghold,
Miǎnchí on the right as a barrier,
facing Sōnggāo in front,
and bordered by the great river behind,
establishing Yíngyáng,
supporting Hédōng,
creating a pass spanning a thousand li from north to south,
and entering the area of Áocāng covering eight or nine hundred square li,
sufficient for self-contentment.
To the east, it would suppress the power of the feudal lords,
and to the west, it would distance the troubles of the Qiāng and Hú.
If Your Majesty practices non-action,
residing in the manner of Chéngzhōu,
and embodying the virtue of Pán Gēng,
then after ten thousand years,
you will long be honored as Gāozōng."
"Qián Hàn"
Eastern Capital
Zhāng Wēn was sent as an envoy to Shǔ,
Zhūgě Liàng met him and sighed, saying:
"From among the wild grasses and reeds of Jiāngdōng emerges such a remarkable talent."
from "Records of Jīnlíng"
Duke Shào surveyed the site for the capital,
divined and chose Luòyì,
Duke of Zhōu laid the foundation,
the measuring cord was straight,
facing the Luò River with the Yellow River at its back,
the Yī River on the left and the Chán River on the right,
blocked by the Jiǔ'ā Mountains to the west,
the eastern gate winding around,
the Tàishì Mountain serving as a guardian,
marked by the Xióng'ěr Mountains,
the Dǐzhù Rocks directing the flow,
guarded by the Dàpí Mountain.
"Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital"
Expanding the old Zhōu, they built Luòyì,
towering and majestic,
radiant and grand,
illuminating the Hàn capital among all states,
uniting the eight directions as its pinnacle.
Moreover, secluded and bordering the Western Róng,
with perilous barriers on all sides,
relying on its defenses—
how could it compare to dwelling in the center?
The central plains are level and open,
connecting to all regions,
converging like spokes at the Qín Ridge,
with the Jiǔzōng Mountains and the Jīng and Wèi Rivers—
how do they compare to the Four Rivers and Five Peaks, the realm of the Hé-Tú and Luò-Shū, girded by rivers and facing the Luò?
"Rhapsody on the Eastern Qí"
Luò Tǒng's memorial stated:
"Zhāng Wēn possesses the substance of broad refinement,
the virtue of outstanding excellence,
the brilliance of literary composition,
and the clarity of discourse and debate.
He towers above the multitude,
shining brightly upon the age—
no one in the world can match him.
Thus, those devoted to power envy his favor,
those contending for fame resent his talent,
those who dwell in mystery criticize his discussions,
and those with flaws avoid his critiques."

Bǐng Yuán, knowing that the world was about to fall into chaos,
took refuge in Liáodōng,

he returned to his hometown by night,
and only after several days did Dù realize it.
When officials wanted to pursue him,

"Lord Bǐng is what they call a white crane in the clouds—

Thus, he was spared from peril.
After returning to his homeland,
Yuán then lectured on rites and music,
recited poetry and classics,
with several hundred disciples,

At that time, Zhèng Xuán, renowned for his vast erudition, annotated classical texts,
so refined and scholarly men gathered around him.
Yuán, too, with his lofty purity,
nurtured a serene and detached will,
spoke without careless words,
acted without reckless deeds,
thus attracting heroic and outstanding men to him.
At that time, the clear discourse within the realm held:
"In Qīngzhōu, there are the teachings of Bǐng and Zhèng."

After Yáng departed,
Guō saw him off,

How magnificent is Xiányáng,

Wèi Jiè, whose courtesy name was Shūbǎo,
often believed that when others fell short,

when faced with unintended offenses,

Dǒng Zhuó proposed moving the capital to Cháng'ān,

"In the past, the Duke of Zhōu built Luòyì
to bring peace to the Jī clan,
Emperor Guāngwǔ divined
the eastern capital to prosper the Hàn.
What Heaven has initiated,
what the spirits have settled,
once the great enterprise is established,
how can one recklessly move it,
to disappoint the hopes of all within the Four Seas?"
In the History of the Later Hàn,
Dǒng Zhuó said to Chén Jì:
"The Three Adjuncts are level and open,
secure and solid on all sides,
with fertile and rich land,
known as the Land's Sea.

what do you think?"
Chén Jì replied:
"When the world follows the Way,
defense lies with the Four Barbarians.
We should cultivate virtuous governance to win over the unsubmissive.
If you wish to move the imperial carriage for self-preservation,
you will face the danger of piled eggs,
the peril of towering heights."

Deep roots and a solid foundation
Governor Liú remarked that on clear breezy nights with a bright moon,
he would always think of Xuándù.
In *A New Account of the Tales of the World*,
Attendant Xǔ once visited Jiǎnwén.
That night, the wind was calm and the moon bright,
so they sat together in a winding chamber, conversing and expressing their heartfelt feelings through poetry,
which happened to be Xǔ's forte.
His words and sentiments were pure and graceful,
surpassing his usual self.
Although Jiǎnwén had always appreciated him, he was especially moved by this encounter and sighed in admiration,
unconsciously drawing closer to share in the meaning,
talking with gestures until nearly dawn.
Then he said:
"Xuándù's talent and sentiment
are indeed not easily found in many others."
