Xǔ Xuándù stayed in the capital for a month,
and Liú Yǐn visited him every single day.
He then sighed and said:
"If you don't leave for a while longer,
I'll become the frivolous capital governor."
Xún Yù said:
"In the past, Gāozǔ secured Guānzhōng,
and Guāngwǔ occupied Hénèi.
Both deeply rooted and solidified their foundations,
thereby controlling the world.
Advancing, they were sufficient to overcome enemies;
retreating, they were sufficient to firmly defend.
Therefore, although they encountered difficulties and defeats,

Xiè Hùn and his nephew Xiè Língyùn enjoyed equal fame.

Soaring Aloft to the Clouds
Qí Héngyáng Wáng Jūn conducted himself with purity and integrity,
and never spoke of current affairs.
Zhāng Róng of Wújùn was aloof and detached from worldly conventions;
even when facing princes and nobles,

"Héngyáng Wáng soars aloft with an aura reaching the clouds;

are all the more worthy of admiration.

History of the Southern Dynasties
Zhāng Xù, whose courtesy name was Sīmàn,
was renowned from a young age,

Yuán Càn remarked to Emperor Míng of the Liú Sòng dynasty:
"Zhāng Xù possesses the lingering ethos of the Zhèngshǐ era."
Wáng Jiǎn once said:

In the third year of the Yǒngmíng era,

"Xù honors me with his position,

Xù's speech and demeanor are so refined and captivating

and even after spending a whole day with him,
none can fathom his depths."

Cuī Sēngyuān replied to his cousin Huìjǐng in a letter, saying:

Four Frontiers
In Peiguo, there were Liú Huán,
and his younger brother Liú Jìn,
both outstanding scholars of their time.
Huán was known as the Confucius west of Hangu Pass,
thoroughly versed in the Six Classics,
patient and skillful in teaching,
devotedly upholding Confucian conduct.
Jìn possessed a resolve as stern as autumn frost,
a heart as pure as Kunlun jade,
standing tall and upright,
yet remaining engaged in worldly affairs.
Both cultivated virtue in humble circumstances,
and their reputations spread across heaven and earth,
yet Huán was only appointed as a Gentleman of the Palace,

fulfilling King Wǔ's intention,
while the Yīn people moved five times,
accomplishing the enterprise of King Tāng's successors."
Luòyì has been a capital since ancient times,
within the royal domain,
where heaven and earth converge,
and yīn and yáng harmonize,
controlled by three rivers,
fortified by four passes,
with water and land routes facilitating tribute and taxes equally.
Thus Emperor Hàn Gāozǔ said:
"I have traveled widely across the realm,
yet only upon seeing Luòyáng,
the desolate ruins of Chéngzhōu,

immediately establishing officials and dividing duties,
to serve as the ultimate standard for the people."

Vice Director Sū Wēi replied:
"It was not that people in antiquity were unaware,
but rather they were waiting for Your Majesty."
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
for the location rested against the northern foothills,

none could compare to this.

Topographical advantage is not as good as being within the passes.
Wáng Sù, courtesy name Gōngyì,
was a descendant of Wáng Dǎo.
In the seventeenth year of the Tàihé era, he fled to Wèi.
When Emperor Gāozǔ heard of Sù's arrival,
he received him with open-mindedness,
summoned him for an audience to inquire about his circumstances.
Sù's speech was elegant in tone,
fluent in argument and courteous,
and Emperor Gāozǔ admired and accepted him.
They drew their mats closer as the sunlight shifted,
unaware of the weariness from long sitting.
Later, he was appointed as the provincial governor of Yùzhōu,
and soon summoned to the court.
Emperor Gāozǔ wrote a personal edict saying:
"Not seeing you, noble man,
my heart feels as if intoxicated,
one day seems like three years,
how weary am I?
I have adorned a residence in Huálín,
prepared the mat to await you,
on which day will you depart from your ancestral home?
Hence, I issue this decree again."

Hé Diǎn once praised Lù Huìxiǎo's mind as being like a clear mirror,

all became bright and clear.

also having a frosty aura,
which was considered a truthful record at the time.

my eastern and western residences,

therefore praising the fertile land of the celestial storehouse,

girding the rich soil of the royal city,
spreading green palaces on the river isles,

not establish the state among the three rivers,

Tián Bā, a debater of Qí, debated at Cúqiū,

slandered the Five Emperors,
condemned the Three Sovereigns,
criticized the Five Hegemons,
distinguished hardness from whiteness and united similarities with differences,

There was a man named Xú Jié,
whose disciple he was.
Lǔ Lián said to Xú Jié:
"I wish to challenge Master Tián and stop him;
he will certainly debate no more.
May I?"
Xú Jié spoke to Bā, saying:
"Though my disciple is but twelve years old,
he is a thousand-lǐ colt.
I wish for him to debate before you instead.
May he?"
Tián Bā said:
"He may."
Lǔ Lián, having gained audience, said:
"Now the Chǔ army is at Nányáng,
Zhào attacks Gāotáng,
the Yān people, a hundred thousand strong, are at Liáo.
The state's destruction is imminent.
What will you do, sir?"
Tián Bā said:
"There is nothing to be done."
Lǔ Lián said:
"If in danger you cannot secure safety,
in peril you cannot ensure survival,
then there is no worth in a learned scholar.
Now I shall disband the army at Nányáng,
withdraw the troops from Gāotáng.
What is valued in debate and discourse—
this is what it means.
As for your words, sir,
they are like the cry of an owl:
all men detest them.
I wish you would debate no more."
Tián Bā said:
"I humbly accept your instruction."
The next day, he saw Xú Jié and said:
"Your colt is a flying hare or a swift niǎo,
how could he be merely a thousand-lǐ steed?"
Thereupon, Tián Bā sealed his lips and changed his profession,
and never debated again for the rest of his life.

"According to the principles of residential design,

Línzōng fell silent and had no reply,

not casually receiving scholars.
When guests arrived from outside,
unless they were renowned figures of the time or came from families with longstanding ties,
none could gain an audience.
Kǒng Róng, then over ten years old,
wished to observe his character,
so he went to Lǐ Yīng's gate,
and said to the gatekeeper:
"I am a descendant of a family with longstanding ties to Lord Lǐ."
The gatekeeper reported this,
and Lǐ Yīng invited Kǒng Róng in, asking:
"Did your esteemed grandfather once share an old bond of gratitude with me?"
Kǒng Róng replied:
"Indeed.
My ancestor Confucius and your ancestor Lǎo Jūn shared virtues and principles, acting as teachers and friends to each other,
thus I and you, sir, are families with ties spanning generations."
All present sighed in admiration.
They unanimously said:
"An extraordinary child!"
Lǐ Yīng seated him and asked:
"Do you wish to eat?"
Kǒng Róng said:
"I should eat."
Lǐ Yīng said:
"Let me teach you the etiquette of a guest:
one should decline, not necessarily thank the host."
Kǒng Róng replied:
"Not so.
Let me teach you the etiquette of a host:
simply set out the food,
without needing to ask the guest."
Lǐ Yīng, ashamed, then sighed and said:
"I am about to die,
and will not see you achieve wealth and honor."
Kǒng Róng said:
"You, sir, are far from death."
Lǐ Yīng asked why,
and he answered:
"When a bird is about to die,
its song is sorrowful.
When a person is about to die,
their words are kind.
Just now, your words lacked kindness,
therefore I know you are not dying."
Lǐ Yīng found him remarkable.
At that time, the official Chén Wěi arrived later,
and those seated told Wěi about it.
Wěi said:
"A person who is clever in childhood
may not necessarily be extraordinary when grown."
Kǒng Róng said:
"I imagine you, sir, in childhood,
must have been clever."
Wěi was greatly embarrassed,
and the entire company laughed heartily.
From "Hòu Hàn Shū," "Shì Shuō Xīn Yǔ," "Yǔ Lín."
Emperor Wén of Suì disliked the old capital's layout for being cramped and small,
with many ghostly apparitions in the palace.
One night, he discussed with Gāo Jiǒng and Sū Wēi and decided to move the capital.
The next morning, Yǔ Jìcái memorialized:
"Looking up at celestial phenomena,
and examining charts and records below,
the tortoise shell augury confirms it—
a capital move is inevitable.
Moreover, since the Hàn dynasty built this city,
nearly eight hundred years have passed.
The water has turned brackish,
hardly suitable for people.
I hope to align with the will of heaven and humanity,
and plan for relocation."
The emperor was astonished,
and said to Jiǒng and others:
"How divine this is!
From now on,
I truly believe in the Way of Heaven."
(From his biography)
In the second year of the Kāihuáng era,
they moved to the new city,
located southeast of the old Hàn capital in Wànnián County,
facing due south to the Zǐwǔ Valley of the Zhōngnán Mountains,
resting against Lóngshǒu to the north.
The current court hall
was originally Yángxīng Village,
and the large tree at the village gate still stands today.
(From the Records of the Two Capitals)
Cuī Yǎn, styled Jìguī,
when Yuánfāng of Qīnghé was Inspector of Jìzhōu,
recommended Xiùcai,
Yǎn was nine years old at the time,
and was selected.
Yuánfāng said:
"It is not that you are not of noble lineage,
but you are too young for this selection."
Yǎn replied:
"In ancient times, Xiàng Tuó at seven was teacher to Confucius,
and now I regret that I am already older."
Yuánfāng asked:
"How closely related are you to Cuī Zhù?"
Yǎn answered:
"About as closely as you are to Chén Héng."
Yú Fān, styled Zhòngxiáng,
was a native of Yúyáo in Kuàijī.
In his youth, he was fond of learning
and possessed lofty spirit.
At the age of twelve,
a visitor came to see his elder brother but did not call on Fān.
Fān pursued him and sent a letter saying:
"I have heard that amber does not attract rotten straw,
and a magnet does not attract bent needles.
To pass by without stopping,
is it not appropriate?"
The visitor, upon receiving the letter, thought him extraordinary,
and from then on, he became well-regarded.
"Wú Shū"
Xiāng-Dèng
Zhāng Dūnzǐ Chún,
along with Zhāng Yǎn and Zhū Huánzǐ Yì,
all being young lads,
went to visit the General of Agile Cavalry Zhū Jù.
Jù, having heard of the three youths' literary talents,
wished to test them.
He announced:
"This old rustic has long heard of you,
and his thirst to meet you is great.
Now, the swift steed is prized for its speed,
and the hawk and falcon for their nimble swiftness.
Each of you shall compose a rhapsody on one object for me,
and only then may you take your seats."
Yǎn then composed one on a dog, saying:
"In guarding, it has presence;
in the hunt, it makes captures.
Hán Lú and Sòng Què,
their names are recorded in the annals."
Chún composed one on a mat, saying:
"The mat is laid in winter,
the bamboo mat spread in summer.
With bows and deference one sits,
fitting for a gentleman."
Yì composed one on a crossbow, saying:
"Timber from the Southern Peak,
copper from Mount Zhōng.
It responds to the moment and strikes the target,
capturing the falcon on the high wall."
The three youths each composed based on what their eyes fell upon,
and only after all had finished did they sit.
Jù was greatly pleased.
(From "The Biographies of Literary Men")
In the early Qiánníng era,
Zhū Pǔ submitted a memorial discussing relocating the capital,
saying:
"The ancient kings
did not permanently reside in one place,
but observed the rise and fall of heaven and earth,
governing affairs according to the times.
Guānzhōng,
the capital of the Suí dynasty,
we indeed inherited.
During the Guǎngmíng era, great bandits
captured and destroyed the capital,
and the systems of Gāozǔ and Tàizōng were completely lost.
Now Xiāng-Dèng is a strategically located territory,
a fertile and expansive region.
Since ancient times, rulers who restored dynasties
left what was already declining,
and moved from decline to where kingship had not yet been established to establish it.
Now Nányáng's Guāngwǔ
rose from there though he was not yet king.
Jiāngnán has thin soil and shallow waters,
and people's hearts are restless, frivolous, and cunning -
it cannot be the capital.
Héběi has thick soil and deep waters,
and people's hearts are stubborn, obstinate, and fierce -
it cannot be the capital.
Only Xiāng-Dèng is truly the Central Plains,
where people's hearts are simple and good,
close to Qín by a short distance,
and with Shàngluò as its boundary,
eternally free from the worry of barbarian invasion -
this is the optimal choice for establishing the capital."
The Book of Táng
records that Tāng Sītuì, due to the Jin people's peace negotiations,
wanted to abandon Táng, Dèng, Hǎi, and Sì.
An imperial edict stated that Táng and Dèng were not strategically important
and could be disregarded.
Yú Yǔnwén memorialized that Dèng served as the protective barrier for Xiāng-Hàn,
and Nányáng in turn served as Dèng Prefecture's protective barrier,
being an ancient strategically located state.
Lù Yún, courtesy name Shìlóng,
was the fifth son of Lù Kàng.
At the age of six, he could already compose poetry,
and his contemporaries considered him the equal of Xiàng Tuó and Yáng Wū.
At eighteen,
he was appointed Registrar by Inspector Zhōu Jùn,
who often sighed and said:
"Lù Shìlóng
is the Yán Yuān of our time."
From the "Bié Zhuàn"
The general situation
Critics say:
"Luòyáng,
a place contested on all sides,
is already unsuitable.
Púbǎn,
the ancient state of Emperor Yú Shùn,
is protected by mountains and rivers.
Jiānglíng,
has also once served as a capital,
controlling Wú and Shǔ,
and guiding distant retreats from the Dí tribes.
Are these not fit for residence?"
The reply states:
"Púbǎn,
has barren soil and poor people,
its exhaustion is worse than Luòyì.
Jiānglíng,
was never a strategic point,
as the Liáng ruler lost his state within a few years.
To govern all states,
one especially relies on strategic advantage,
Qínchuān is the most fertile land under heaven,
Guānzhōng is the most powerful territory within the seas,
if one resides there, the influence is great and authority far-reaching,
if one abandons it, the influence is small and authority limited,
I fear people's hearts will waver because of this,
not merely leading to danger and chaos."
Tōngdiǎn, chapter 174
Hè Xún, styled Yǎnxiān,
was a native of Shānyīn in Kuàijī.
He was the son of the Wú official Hè Jùn, who served as Secretary of the Central Secretariat.
His conduct and aspirations were lofty and transcendent,
and even as a child he stood out from his peers.
In his speech, actions, advances, and withdrawals,
he always adhered to ritual and deference.
At the beginning of the Jiànwǔ era, he was appointed Secretary of the Central Secretariat.
Emperor Yuán issued an edict stating:
"Hè Xún's words and actions are guided by ritual,
making him the hope of our times
and a model for society."
The Book of Jìn
records: "Hè Xún of Kuàijī
possessed clear insight and far-reaching understanding,
and his words and actions were guided by ritual.
He was not merely the finest of the southeast,
but truly an outstanding talent of the entire realm."

Jīngzhào,
the ultimate height is called Jīng.
Jīng,
means great.
Ten billion is called Zhào,
intending the imperial capital to be prosperous and abundant.
Left support and right assistance,
protecting and upholding to inherit the legacy.
Zhāngyè first opened,
extending like spreading arms to shelter.

the ultimate height is called Jīng,

Crown Prince Mǐnhuái was exceptionally intelligent from a young age,
and Emperor Wǔ doted on him greatly.
When he was six or seven years old, a fire broke out in the palace one night,
and Emperor Wǔ climbed a tower to observe it.
The crown prince tugged at the hem of his robe,
urging him to step into the shadows.
The emperor asked him the reason,
to which the crown prince replied:
"In the haste and confusion of the night,
we must guard against unexpected dangers.
It is unwise to stand near the light of the fire,
lest it reveal the emperor's presence."
Imperial Carriage

was accomplished in all manner of ingenious arts.

and even composed the inscription himself before carving it.
The prose was elegant and the craftsmanship exquisite,
leaving all his contemporaries in awe.

Wáng Xuàn,
the eldest son of Wáng Yù,
whose childhood name was Tóngwū,
and courtesy name Chángsù,

At the age of five or six,

His maternal grandfather Hé Shàngzhī once found him extraordinary.

how can it be mocked?

Píng's father did not understand why,
so Zhèn (from Cāngwú) said:

At that time, Píng was just a few years old,

Xiè Fěi, courtesy name Jìngchōng,
was intelligent and discerning from a young age.
His father, Zhuāng, esteemed this
and often kept him by his side.
At the age of ten, he could compose essays.
One day, while Zhuāng was traveling to Mount Huá and composing poetry,
he asked Fěi to write a piece.
Fěi took up the brush and completed it immediately.
Wáng Jǐngwén of Lángyá remarked to Zhuāng,
"Your virtuous son truly deserves to be called a prodigy,
and he will certainly achieve great success in the future."
Zhuāng patted Fěi on the back and said,
"Truly, he is worth a thousand gold to our family."
During the reign of Emperor Sòng Xiàowǔ, when Gūshú sent a decree to Zhuāng,
he took Fěi to accompany the entourage.
An edict was issued for him to compose an eulogy for the Dòngjǐng Well,
which was presented during the assembly.
The emperor remarked,
"Though young, he is indeed a great talent."

Lù Qióng, courtesy name Bóyù,

Qíong carried himself with alert brilliance and dignified bearing,

At eleven, he mourned his father's passing,

His paternal grandfather Xiāng sighed in admiration:

Xú Miǎn, courtesy name Xiūrén,

Jiǎ Jiāyǐn, at the age of seven, was summoned for an audience as a child prodigy.
Lǐ Jì teased him in the court hall, saying:

Jiāyǐn replied:

why do you say it's a pine?"
Jiāyǐn said:

how could it not be 'pine' (松)?"
Chángsūn Wújì then asked:

Chángsūn said:

Lǐ said:

they were all praised as outstanding young talents.
A family friend Dù Yìjiǎn often praised them, saying:
"These are the Three Pearl Trees of the Wáng family."
Old Book of Tang
Wáng Bó's ancestor Wén Zhōngzǐ saw Bó playing with a brush,
and ordered him to compose a piece titled "The Grand Duke Meeting King Wén",
with the eulogy reading:
"Jī Chāng cherished virtue,
Lǚ Wàng concealed his brilliance.
Though the city walls were near,
the wind and clouds were still distant. The fishing boat leaned against the rocks,
the fishing shore stretched across the sands.
The path was secluded and the mountains remote,
the stream deep and the banks slanting.
The leopard's strategy warded off evil,
the dragon's seal repelled malignance.
Though the encounter was imminent,
he still awaited the comfort carriage.
The sovereign grasped his hand,
how free and unrestrained!"
Zhītián Records
Both Old Book of Tang and Wén Zhōngzǐ record
that he died in the first year of the Yìníng era of Sui,
Yáng Jiǒng's preface to Wáng Bó's collected works states: "Chén Qún received Tàiqiū's instruction,
but his time did not match it,"
indicating Bó never met his grandfather.
Dīng Yònghuì's claim that Wén Zhōng ordered him to compose the eulogy
is mistaken.
Both the preface and Old Book of Tang state he was twenty-eight years old,
thus he was born in the twenty-second year of the Zhēnguàn era.
The New Book says twenty-nine,
which is also incorrect.
Famous Capital
Sū Guī initially did not recognize Sū Tǐng's talent,
often making him work alongside servants and laborers.
One day, a guest visited Guī,
waiting in the main hall.
Tǐng, while sweeping with a broom as he hurried across the courtyard,
dropped some written documents.
The guest picked them up to look,
and they turned out to be poems about a Kunlun slave,
with the verses reading:
"Ten sticks of ink on the fingers,
two spoons on the ears."
The guest found this remarkable.
After a while, Guī came out
and lingered with the guest.
During their cheerful conversation,
the guest recited the poems and described the appearance,
asking Guī who it was,
wondering if it might be a child from his own clan.
Guī explained the whole situation,
and the guest expressed surprise and congratulations,
urging Guī to treat him with respect and nurture him,
confident he would become a distinguished son of the Sū family.
Guī then began to show him more affection.
When someone presented a rabbit hanging in the corridor,
Guī summoned Tǐng and asked him to compose a poem about it.
He immediately responded with:
"The rabbit lies dead and limp,
soon to be hung on a bamboo pole.
If you try to reflect it with a bright mirror,
it looks no different than when seen in the moon."
Guī was greatly astonished.
(From "Records of Messages from the Kaiyuan Era")
Yān's Zhuōjì,
Zhào's Hándān,
Wèi's Wēnzhǐ,
Hán's Xíngyáng,
Qí's Línzī,
Chǔ's Wǎnqiū,
Zhèng's Yángdí,
the Èrzhōu's Sānchuān,
were the wealthiest within the Four Seas,
all renowned capitals of the realm,
situated at the crossroads of the five feudal lords,
spanning the main thoroughfares.

Sū Tǐng at the age of five,
when Péi Tán visited his father,
Tǐng was reciting Yǔ Xìn's "Ode to the Withered Tree."
To avoid the taboo character Tán,
he altered the rhyme, saying:
"In years past, willows were transplanted,
lingering by the Han's southern shade.
Now I behold their swaying fall,
mournful by the river's edge.
If trees can be thus,
how can humans bear it?"
Tán marveled at this,
knowing he would surely dominate literature in the future.
"Guǎng Rénwù Zhì"
Sū Tǐng had just learned to speak when
a Capital Governor passed by Guī,
and after he left,
Guī ordered Tǐng to compose a poem about the character "Yǐn" (尹).
So he said:
"Though chǒu has feet,
jiǎ is not a complete body.
Seeing you without a mouth,
I know yī is missing a person."
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Ming"
Centered
Lord, with divine intelligence and outstanding talent,
was naturally born with knowledge.
At the age of five, he began to focus on literature,
often reciting and chanting whether sitting or lying down,
never pausing even briefly.
By the time he was eight or nine years old,
he seemed as if he had already achieved great mastery.
He could read and recite a thousand words at a single glance,
as if he had long been familiar with them.
At seventeen, he studied at the Imperial Academy,
and achieved the highest grade in the policy response examination.
Hán Xiū, "Preface to the Collected Works of Sǔ Tǐng"
To be close to all four directions,
there is no better place than the center.
Therefore, the ruler must reside at the center of the world,
as dictated by ritual.

Sòng Jǐng,
a native of Guǎngpíng,
could compose literary works at the age of seven.
He memorized the "Rhapsody on the Owl" in a single reading,
and at eight or nine years old, he once dreamed of a great bird carrying a document in its beak.
It spat it into his mouth, and he swallowed it,
then rode the bird soaring straight upward.
Suddenly, he awoke with a start,
still feeling as if it were lodged in his chest.
From then on, his literary talent grew increasingly profound,
and his spiritual clarity became even more refined.
From Yán Zhēnqīng's "Composed Spirit Way Stele."
To Secure Repose
In ancient times, the Duke of Zhōu served the Zhōu dynasty, and the four seas were in a state of great order,
securing repose in the capital.

Foundation
When Emperor Xuánzōng was performing the fēngshàn ceremony at Mount Tài,
Liú Yàn was only eight years old.
He presented a eulogy at the imperial camp,
and the emperor, amazed by his youth,
ordered Zhāng Yuè to test him.
Zhāng Yuè said:
"He is an auspicious sign for the state."
He was immediately appointed as a proofreader for the crown prince,
with nobles vying to invite him from all directions.
He was called a child prodigy,
and his fame spread far and wide for a time.
He was brought into the palace,
where he sat on Consort Yáng's lap,
and she personally drew his eyebrows and tied his hair in a child's bun.
The palace maidens showered him with flowers and fruits.
Emperor Xuánzōng was at the Qínzhèng Tower,
where a grand music performance was held,
with hundreds of performers arrayed.
At that time, in the Imperial Music Bureau, there was a woman named Wáng Dàniáng,
who was skilled at balancing a hundred-foot pole,
on which a wooden structure shaped like a mountain was placed,
resembling the mythical islands of Yíngzhōu and Fāngzhàng.
She had children holding crimson banners moving in and out of it,
singing and dancing without pause.
At that time, Liú Yàn, a child prodigy, served as a proofreader in the Imperial Library,
ten years old,
with an unattractive appearance but extraordinary intelligence.
Emperor Xuánzōng summoned him beneath the curtain in the tower,
and Consort Yáng placed him on her lap,
applying powder and makeup, and giving him a scarf and comb.
Emperor Xuánzōng asked Liú Yàn:
"As a proofreader, how many characters have you corrected?"
Liú Yàn replied:
"All characters under heaven are correct,
only the character 'péng' (friend) remains uncorrected."
The Consort then ordered him to compose a poem about Wáng Dàniáng's pole balancing.
Liú Yàn responded immediately:
"Before the tower, a hundred acts compete in novelty,
but only the long pole is divinely skillful.
Who would think silk-robed ladies could display such strength,
yet still find it light and add more people."
Emperor Xuánzōng, the Consort, and the palace ladies laughed joyfully for a long time,
their voices heard outside,
so he bestowed upon him an ivory tablet and a yellow embroidered robe.
(From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Mínghuáng")
The capital is
the foundation of all Xià.
In the "Mín Láo" annotation of the Shījīng,
the capital uses the various Xià as its protective barrier.
In the "Tiáo Zhī Huá" annotation,
the capital,
being the root of the various Xià,
is where governance is observed and the cunning and powerful overstep regulations.
In the "Liú Fén zhuàn,"
the fourth year of Duke Xiāng of Zuǒ,
Wèi Jiàng admonished the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"The various Huá will certainly rebel,
note: the various Huá refer to the central states."
The Shī Zhèngyì states:
"It is the same as the various Xià."
Above,
the capital is
the parent of the feudal lords.
From the "Miǎn Shuǐ" commentary of the Shījīng.
The Beginning of Wáng Huà
Lǐ Mì, styled Chángyuán,
had the childhood name Shùnshēng,
and his hair reached his eyebrows.
From a young age, he was intelligent and quick-witted;
he could recite anything after just one reading,
and at six or seven years old, he learned to compose essays.
In the sixteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Emperor Xuánzōng hosted a grand feast at the tower,
setting up a high seat below the tower at night,
and summoned a debate among the three teachings.
Mì's cousin Yuán Chù, aged nine,
secretly asked his aunt to prepare Confucian robes for him,
ascended the high seat at night,
and his eloquent arguments swarmed like bees,
leaving all debaters defeated.
Emperor Xuánzōng, amazed by him,
summoned him into the tower to ask his name.
Upon learning he was the grandson of Bànqiān,
the emperor remarked, "No wonder he is like this,"
and then asked,
"Are there any other children like you outside?"
Chù replied,
"My maternal cousin Shùn, aged seven,
can compose poetry
with great agility."
The emperor ordered a eunuch to summon him urgently.
At the time, the emperor was playing chess with Zhāng Yuè,
and the eunuch carried Mì in.
Chù and Liú Yàn were both by the emperor's side.
The emperor then commanded Yuè to test Mì's poetry skills,
immediately instructing him to compose a poem on "square, round, movement, and stillness."
Mì said,
"I wish to hear the description."
Yuè responded,
"Square like the chessboard,
round like the chess pieces.
Movement as the chess comes to life,
stillness as the chess lies dead."
Yuè, considering his youth,
instructed him further,
"You may only respond;
do not fabricate it."
He then emphasized the word "chess."
Mì said,
"It is very easy to improvise."
Emperor Xuánzōng laughed and said,
"His spirit is far greater than his body."
Mì then spoke,
"Square as in practicing righteousness,
round as in employing wisdom.
Movement as in displaying talent,
stillness as in fulfilling intentions."
Yuè thus congratulated,
"This is an auspicious sign of our sage era."
Emperor Xuánzōng was greatly pleased,
held him in his arms,
stroked his head,
ordered fruits and sweets to be fed to him,
and bestowed upon him clothing and several dozen bolts of colored silk.
He also instructed his family,
"He is still young;
I fear an official post may harm him,
so I cannot grant him one yet.
Take good care of him,
for he is a vessel of the state."
Two years later, he composed a long song titled "The Ballad of Wandering," which said:
"Heaven covers me,
earth carries me;
heaven and earth gave me life with purpose.
If not so,
I would abstain from grains and ascend to heaven,
or if not that,
I would roam the imperial capital with jade pendants chiming.
If I cannot be noble nor depart in vain,
I shall be a dignified man,
a man, oh, a man—
my lifelong aspirations are my true plan.
I ask you to behold the achievements of a hundred years,
then board a small boat to drift on the Five Lakes."
Those who copied the poem upon its completion all praised it.
From "The Unofficial Biography of the Marquis of Yè."
Yán Tǐngzhī treated his wife coldly but doted on his son Wǔ,
who was eight years old.
Wǔ asked his mother,
"Father always favors Xuányīng
(Tǐngzhī's concubine)
and has never comforted or visited you.
How did it come to this?"
His mother replied,
"Your father dislikes my plain appearance.
After just a few nights together I conceived you,
and he abandoned me since then."
His mother sobbed bitterly,
and Wǔ grew indignant.
Waiting until his father went out
and Xuányīng was asleep,
Wǔ took a small iron hammer and smashed her head.
When Tǐngzhī returned, he was shocked
to find her already dead.
The servants said,
"The young master was playing with a hammer and caused this."
Tǐngzhī called Wǔ and asked,
"Why did you play so recklessly?"
Wǔ replied,
"How can a court official favor his concubine
while humiliating his son's mother?
So I had to strike and kill her—
this was no game."
His father said,
"Truly a son of Yán Tǐngzhī."
Dù Yù served as Governor of Hénán,
believing the capital was where the king's influence began,
spreading from near to far,
in all his policies and discussions,
he always emphasized the greater principles.
《Book of Jìn》
Yáng Wǎn, courtesy name Gōngquán,
was born intelligent,
at the age of four while among a crowd,
his sharp perception surpassed others,
once at a nighttime family banquet,
guests pointed to an object in the room,
calling it out using the four tones,
before any guest could speak,
Wǎn immediately pointed at the iron lamp stand and said:
"Lamp base handle bent."
All were astonished by him.
(from the Old Book of Tang)
The offices of all officials
Emperor Wén issued an edict to the capital,
the offices of all officials,
to which all within the four seas turn.
"Suí Jì"
Lǐ Déyù was brilliant and talented from a young age.
Emperor Xiànzōng admired him,
seating him on his lap.
His father Jí Fǔ often boasted of his intelligence and eloquence to his colleagues.
Wǔ Yuánhéng summoned him and asked,
"What books do you, young man, like to read?"
He wished to gauge his ambition,
but Déyù did not respond.
The next day, Yuánhéng informed Jí Fǔ of this,
jokingly saying,
"Sir, you are truly quite foolish."
Jí Fǔ returned home and reproached him.
Déyù replied,
"Wǔ Gōng holds the position of an imperial advisor,
yet he does not inquire about governing the state or balancing yin and yang,
but instead asks what books I like to read.
This is the role of the Ministry of Rites and the State Academy,
therefore his question was improper,
which is why I did not respond."
Jí Fǔ reported this back to Yuánhéng,
who was greatly embarrassed, and thus Lǐ Déyù's reputation greatly increased.
"Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
The gathering of the robed and capped
Zhāng Jiǔlíng said:
"The capital is where the officials and scholars gather,
where personal fame arises,
where one can leisurely adapt and connect,
succeeding without hard work—
this shows that great advantage lies within [the capital],
not outside it."
From his "Biography"
Quán Déyú at three years old could distinguish the four tones,
at four years old could compose poetry,
devoted his thoughts to classical studies,
and mastered them comprehensively.
In the early Yuánhé era, he was appointed Minister and Grand Councilor,
elegant and refined in demeanor,
naturally admirable,
and during the Zhèngyuán and Yuánhé periods, he was regarded as a model for officials.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Cháo Zōng
Gāo Yǐng, styled Gōngchǔ,
mastered the Spring and Autumn Annals at nine years old,
and was capable of composing literary works.
His son Dìng was exceptionally clever and alert beyond his peers from a young age.
At the age of seven, while reading the "Oath of Táng" in the Book of Documents,
he asked Yǐng:
"How can a minister attack a ruler?"
Yǐng replied:
"In response to heaven and compliance with the people,
it is not an unjust way.
Why call it an attack?"
Dìng responded:
"Those who obey orders are rewarded before the ancestral temple,
while those who disobey are executed before the altar of the land.
Is this compliance with the people?"
His father could not answer.
His childhood name was Dǒng Èr,
and because of his youthful wisdom,
people often referred to him by this name.
During the reign of Emperor Xuánzōng,
when grain prices in the capital were high, Péi Yàoqīng remarked:
"The imperial enterprise of the state,
is fundamentally rooted in the capital,
where all nations come to pay homage,
a place unchanging through the ages."
Old Book of Táng
The great foundation of the state lies in the capital,
but the Qín region is narrow and vulnerable to famine from floods and droughts.
New Book of Táng
Yáng Shōu, courtesy name Cángzhī,
was orphaned at age seven,
yet observed mourning rites like an adult.
His mother, Lady Zhǎngsūn, who was literate,
personally instructed him.
By thirteen, he had mastered the meanings of all classics,
excelling at composing poems on the Thousand Character Classic,
and people of Wú called him a child prodigy.
Once, his elder brother Yáng Fā playfully bade him compose a poem on frogs,
and he immediately said:
"By the rabbit's side, sharing jade trees,
beneath the dragon, bronze instruments leap.
We shall join in the same music,
never asking of official or private."
Again ordered to compose on the brush,
he rhymed with the character "drill" and said:
"Though not an object from the pouch,
what hardness cannot it drill?
One day handling affairs of state,
it shall surely crown the three tips."
Whenever there was fine weather and beautiful scenery,
people of Wú would visit to see the child prodigy,
requesting poems and rhapsodies.
The crowd pressed so hard they broke his fence,
and Shōu mocked:
"You're fortunate to lack weak horns,
why must you breach my fence?
If you wish to enter the hall,
you should find the door yourselves."
The world originally
Lǐ Gānshǐ,
a native of Hénán.
Yáng Láo possessed exceptional moral conduct,
and Gānshǐ wrote a letter recommending him to the governor, saying:
"Láo could compose poetry as soon as he was weaned.
Among the children in Luòyáng who were stronger than Láo,
none surpassed him in talent."
According to history, Yáng Láo of Hóngnóng was orphaned at a young age.
When he was six years old, returning from school,
he mistakenly entered someone's house,
which turned out to be his father's friend.
Two elders were playing chess,
and upon seeing young Yáng,
they teased him:
"Can you compose a poem about this chessboard for us?"
Yáng immediately recited a poem:
"The chess pieces form shapes beneath the cloudy sky,
like the moon seen through a twenty-four-inch window."
The elders were amazed and patted his head,
giving him pears and chestnuts, saying:
"You will surely achieve literary fame in the future."
At eighteen, on his first attempt,
he passed the imperial examination.
"Zhītián Lù"
Cuī Xuàn,
the son of Cuī Yuánlüè,
when he was a child,
accompanied his father to visit Hán Huàng.
Huàng saw him and took a liking to him,
Yuánlüè said:
"This child has made considerable progress in poetry recently."
Huàng then pointed to a hawk on a perch and ordered him to compose a poem about it,
so he was given paper and a brush,
without the slightest hesitation in thought,
then he presented it, saying:
"A heart and courage from the edge of the sky, a body perched on the frame,
Wishing to soar high, yet without a reason to start.
Eventually, it will fly away into the vast blue sky,
I wonder who will be the one to untie its tether."
Huàng found him even more remarkable,
and sighed, saying:
"This child can be said to have a future of ten thousand miles ahead."
"Nán Chǔ Xīn Wén"
Lǐ Shèng said:
"Cháng'ān,
where the ancestral temples are located,
is the foundation of the empire.
If everyone holds the reins
who will restore the capital?"
Old Book of Tang:
"The capital is the foundation of the empire."
New Book of Tang.
Bái Jūyì wrote in a letter to Yuán Zhěn:
"When I was just six or seven months old,
my wet nurse held and played with me beneath a screen with calligraphy.
Someone pointed to the character for 'no' and showed it to me.
Though I could not yet speak,
my mind had already silently recognized it.
Later, when people asked about these two characters,
even after dozens of tests, I never pointed incorrectly.
Thus my predestined affinity from past lives
was already manifest in written characters.
By age five or six, I began learning to compose poetry,
and by nine, I was thoroughly familiar with tones and rhymes."
From the "Chángqìng Collection"
Within the Four Seas
Huánnèi zhūhóu Yǐn Gēngshǐ yuē:
"Tiānzǐ yǐ qiānlǐ wéi huán."
《Gǔliáng》
Wéi Wēn, courtesy name Hóngyù,
was the son of Wéi Shòu.
At the age of seven, he could recite one volume of the Book of Songs daily,
and at eleven, he passed the imperial examination in two classics,
excelling in the literary and judgment tests.
He was appointed as a proofreader in the Imperial Library.
At that time, Shòu had retired to the countryside.
Upon hearing of Wēn's success in the examination,
he exclaimed in surprise:
"To achieve a high rank in judgment,
surpassing all other scholars,
was it not due to currying favor with the powerful?"
He then ordered a mat to be laid in the courtyard,
and personally set two judgment tests for him.
Wēn completed them effortlessly with his brush,
to which Shòu joyfully said:
"This is indeed well-deserved!"
(Old Book of Tang)
Zhāng Tóng lived in Luòyáng,
and Jùn Ruò obtained an ancient tripod inscription,
which read:
"The first year of the Huángchū era of Wèi, second month of spring."
Tóng considered this strange,
and his son Cè, aged thirteen,
explained:
"In the twenty-fifth year of the Jiàn'ān era of Hàn, Duke Cáo passed away,
the era name was changed to Yánkāng,
and in the tenth month of that year Cáo Pī received the abdication,
changing the era name again to Huángchū's first year,
so there was no second month inscription,
how could this be an error?"
Tóng was greatly astonished by this.
"History of the Five Dynasties"

Wáng Yuánzhī, a member of the Hanlin Academy, could compose poetry by the age of five.

the deputy informed the prefect about him,
who then summoned him to recite a quatrain:

Sānhé
Huáng Tíngjiān at the age of five had already memorized the Five Classics,
one day he asked his teacher:
"People speak of the Six Classics,
why do I read only five?"
The teacher said:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals is not worth reading."
Tíngjiān said:
"Since it is called a classic,
how can it not be read?"
In ten days he completed memorizing it,
without missing a single character.
His father Huáng Shù, delighted by his quick comprehension,
wanted him to study for the child prodigy imperial examination.
Tíngjiān secretly heard of this,
then laughed and said:
"What kind of accomplishment is that?"
Shù particularly cherished and valued him.
At that time, a fellow villager was departing for the imperial examinations,
Shù led his colleagues to host a farewell banquet,
all composed poems to see him off.
Someone asked Tíngjiān to also compose a poem,
which he completed in a moment,
containing these lines:
"When you arrive before the Jade Emperor's incense table,
if asked about the former Huáng Tíngjiān,
say he was banished to the mortal world and now eight years have passed."
Recorded in "Clear Talks from the Dao Mountain"
and "Seeing you return before the enlightened ruler" etc.
from "Poetry Talks from the Western Clarity"
Yǐngzhōu Biéjià Huáng Yǒng, styled Sòngyǒng,
at the age of three,
could recite any text after seeing it just once.
In the second year of the Daguan era, he took the child prodigy examination,
and was summoned to the imperial court for an audience.
Emperor Huīzōng selected the line "like the longevity of the southern mountains" from the Book of Songs for him to recite,
and Yǒng responded immediately,
saying: "Neither diminished nor collapsed."
The emperor then questioned him about the word "collapsed,"
to which he replied:
"The poet's words
do not recognize taboos;
how dare I repeat them?"
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and led him to have an audience in turn,
where the empress and consorts vied to give him coins and fruits.
The following year,
he was granted the "Master of the Five Classics" degree.

In the past, the Táng people had their capital in Hédōng,
the Yīn people in Hénèi,
and the Zhōu people in Hénán.
These three Hé regions stood at the center of the world like the legs of a tripod,
where the sovereigns made their capitals,
and their states endured for hundreds or thousands of years.
"Records of the Grand Historian: Biographies of Moneymakers"
Zhōu was at the central pivot,
the division of the three Hé regions,
where wind and rain arose,
a land of four strategic barriers.

During the reign of Gāozōng, a young cadet named Liú Gū, aged five,
excelled in horseback riding and archery,
and was appointed as a captain.
Zhū Hǔchén,
a native of Fúliáng,
was skilled in forming battle arrays and archery on foot,

and was appointed as a trusted officer,
summoned for an audience and gifted a gold belt.

from Qúzhōu,

mastered the phonetic changes in the four tones,

Yàn Shū was first ranked in Fǔzhōu,
Hé Zhèngchén was famous in Línjiāng,
both raised as prodigious children.

Sān Chuān
Zhāng Yí said:
"Those who contend for fame do so at court,
those who contend for profit do so in the marketplace,
now the Three Rivers region,

everything he experienced or encountered,
he could memorize without fail.

Upon his return,
the Grand Administrator questioned him thoroughly.
Fèng orally recounted the names, crimes, and circumstances of the imprisoned,

Yìng Fèng in his youth served as an accounting clerk,
with Xǔ Xùn as his assistant.
They both went to the capital together,
setting out from their hometown.
On the road, they rested by day and lodged at night.
Xǔ Xùn secretly recorded the names of all the officials, soldiers, and servants they encountered,
intending to test Yìng Fèng.
Upon returning to the commandery, he showed the list to Yìng Fèng,
who remarked, "When we previously ate in Yǐngchuān at Lúnshì,
the captain of the capital post station, Hú Nú, named Lù, served us drinks.
Why is he not on the list?"
Everyone present was astonished.

Yìng Fèng, at the age of twenty,
once visited Yuán Hè, the Chancellor of Péngchéng.
Hè was away on a trip at the time,
with a carriage craftsman working behind closed doors inside.
The craftsman opened the door halfway, showing half his face to look at Fèng,
who then left immediately.
Decades later, Fèng encountered the carriage craftsman on the road
and recognized him, calling out to him.

so Dǔ borrowed the text and memorized it by recitation.
When his provisions ran out, he bid farewell to return home.
Diǎn asked:

why are you leaving?"
Dǔ replied:
"I have already memorized it."
Hearing this, Diǎn sighed and said:
"Alas, Yǎn Dǔ,
even if Duānmù could infer two things from hearing one,
it would not suffice as a comparison.

you would be ranked among the seventy disciples in Zhūsì,
vying with Zǐyóu and Zǐxià for a match."

Mí Héng, courtesy name Zhèngpíng,
when Huáng Shè served as Governor of Zhānglíng,
Mí Héng accompanied him,
where they saw a stele composed by Cài Bójiē.
Zhèngpíng glanced at it once,
admired it and said it was excellent.
Later, each returned to Zhānglíng,
and he regretted not having had a scribe copy it.
Zhèngpíng said:
"Although I saw it only once,
I remember all the words,
except that in the fourth line, the stone was worn away,
and two characters were unclear."
So he took up a brush and wrote it out,
with virtually no omissions,
only the two characters missing.

he ascended the hall and beheld its depths;
whatever his eyes saw once,
he could recite aloud;
whatever his ears heard in passing,
he did not forget
in his heart.
His nature
was in harmony with the Way,
his thoughts as if divinely inspired.
Compared to Sāng Hóngyáng's hidden calculations
and Zhāng Ānshì's silent memorization,
using Héng as a standard,
this is truly not surprising."

A zhōu (administrative division),
is a division of land.
Each division cultivates its own territory to sustain life.
In *Shuōwén*,
a zhōu
is interpreted as a place of reliance,
where commanderies and states depend and look up to.
In *Shìmíng*,
the term zhōu implies distinction,
uniting similar elements while separating differences,
thus defining its boundaries.
In *Chūnqiū Shuōtící*,
the Rites of Zhōu define five dǎng (communities) as one zhōu.
A zhōu,
as a division,
has a chief appointed to ensure mutual support and sufficiency.

Huángdì received the Mandate,

divided the land and distributed the Nine Provinces,
establishing twelve states.

states that before Shénnóng, there were names such as the Great Nine Provinces, Zhùzhōu, Yíngzhōu, and Shénzhōu,
but since Huángdì,
virtue did not reach far,
so only within Shénzhōu,
it was divided into the Nine Provinces.

Xíng Shào, courtesy name Zǐcái,
could compose essays at the age of ten,
was intelligent with a strong memory,
reciting over ten thousand words daily.
Once during a prolonged rain, he read the Book of Han in five days,
almost covering it entirely.
Later, after tiring of drinking and jesting, he broadly sought knowledge,
reading classics, histories, and multiple texts simultaneously,
memorizing at a single glance,
with nothing forgotten.
His writings were elegant and beautiful,
both rich in content and swiftly produced.
Before reaching twenty,
his fame stirred the scholar-officials.
Once, he lodged and drank at the residence of Wáng Xīn of Běihǎi with Yáng Gù of Yòuběipíng, Péi Bómào of Hédōng, his cousin Xíng Fú, and Lù Dàohuī of Hénán,
composing poems together,
amounting to several dozen pieces,
all left with the host's servant.
The next morning, the servant departed,
and everyone failed to retrieve the poems.
Xíng Shào recited them all from memory,
even when some doubted their authorship.
When the servant returned with the originals,
not a single character was amiss.
They compared him to Wáng Càn.

He returned them after about ten days.
Cháng Jǐng doubted that he could have read them,
so he tested him on each volume,

Yáng Yīn, courtesy name Zūnyǎn,
was exceptionally intelligent with a prodigious memory,
never forgetting a face even after a single glimpse.
Whenever he summoned someone,
he would sometimes address them by surname only,
or by given name only.
Occasionally, when someone made a mistake,
later there was a candidate named Yú Mànhàn
who claimed he was too lowly
to be remembered alone.
Yáng Yīn said:
"Previously, when you rode a tailless donkey on Yuánzǐsī Lane,
you passed by me without dismounting,
using a square winnowing fan to cover your face—
how could I not recognize you?"
Mànhàn was astonished and convinced,
and people remarked:
"A name confirms one's nature,
and Mànhàn indeed lived up to his name."

The waters and springs of the Nine Provinces
each differ in hardness and softness.
In Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu, the Jué and Yǔ tones gather,
broad and unhurried,
human voices are slow,
their springs are salty and sour.
In Jīngzhōu and Yángzhōu, the Jué and Zhǐ tones meet,
the qi drifts lightly, human voices are urgent,
their springs are sour and bitter.
In Liángzhōu, the Shāng and Zhǐ tones connect,
firm and brave, swift,
human voices are strained,
their springs are bitter and pungent.
In Yǎnzhōu and Yùzhōu, the Gōng and Zhǐ tones combine,
tranquil and thoughtful,
human voices are upright,
their springs are sweet and bitter.
In Yōngzhōu and Jìzhōu, the Shāng and Yǔ tones join,
upright, swift, and intense,
human voices are firm,
their springs are pungent and salty.

In the early years of the Kāiyuán era,
Cháng Jìngzhōng of Lùzhōu, who had passed the imperial examination in the Mingjīng category at fifteen,
mastered the Five Classics thoroughly within a few years.
He submitted a petition recommending himself,
claiming he could memorize a thousand characters in one reading,
and ten thousand in ten readings.
When asked if he had tested this himself, he replied he had not.
Duke Yān then produced a book,
unlike any seen in the mortal world,
and told him to recite it after ten readings.
Jìngzhōng sat upright and read it,
marking the ground with each reading.
After seven readings, he stood and said:
"I have already memorized it."
Duke Yān said:
"You should complete ten readings."
Jìngzhōng replied:
"If it were ten readings, I would need ten to memorize it;
now that I have it in seven,
why must I reach ten?"
As Duke Yān held the text and read,
before he could finish, Jìngzhōng had recited it entirely,
without missing a single character.
All who witnessed this were filled with admiration.

Taking up the brush and writing from memory in reverse order,
Wèi Fènggǔ was appointed as the captain of Yōngqiū.
Once during a Double Ninth Festival official banquet,
a guest drafted a five-hundred-word preface.
Fènggǔ remarked that this was an old text,
and taking up his brush, he wrote it out from memory in reverse order.
The one who had drafted the preface was silently dismayed,
while all those seated clapped their hands.
Fènggǔ smiled leisurely and said:
"I just happened to recall it from memory,

Another day, he brought a stable inventory,
and had it shown to Fènggǔ,
who, after one look, recited over a thousand words from memory.
Tǐng stood up in surprise and said:
"Having served as an official for nearly forty years,
I have never seen anything like this."

A guest came to see the Duke of Zhōu, who met him at the gate,
and asked:
"What do you have to say to Dàn?"
The guest replied:
"If outside, speak of outside matters;
if inside, speak of inside matters.
Shall I enter or not?"
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"Please enter."
The guest said:
"If standing, speak of righteousness;
if sitting, speak of benevolence.
Shall I sit or not?"
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"Please sit."
The guest said:
"If speaking quickly, the words become indistinct;
if speaking slowly, they cannot be heard.
Shall I speak or not?"
The Duke of Zhōu nodded in agreement,
and Dàn was enlightened.
The next day, he raised an army and punished Guǎn and Cài.
Thus the guest was skilled at conveying meaning without words,
and the Duke of Zhōu was skilled at understanding unspoken words.
One could say the Duke of Zhōu was capable of comprehending subtle messages,
for when a gentleman advises others, he does so subtly,
and when he rescues people from urgency, he does so effectively.

Shuò said:

Shèrén exclaimed:
"I knew Shuò couldn't guess it!"
Shuò replied:
"Fresh meat is called 'kuài',
dried meat is 'pú',
on a tree it's a parasite,
under a pot it's 'jù shù'."
The emperor ordered the entertainer supervisor to flog Shèrén,
who couldn't bear the pain and cried out loudly.
Shuò laughed at him, saying:
"Hey, mouth without hair,
voice crying 'áo áo',
rear rising higher."
Shèrén angrily said:
"Shuò dares to slander an official of the Son of Heaven;
he deserves public execution."
The emperor asked Shuò why he insulted him,
and Shuò replied:
"I didn't dare slander him,
I was just making a riddle."
The emperor asked:
"What's the riddle?"
Shuò explained:
"'Mouth without hair' is a dog hole,
'voice crying áo áo' is a bird feeding its young,
'rear rising higher' is a crane pecking downward."
Shèrén, unconvinced,
then said:
"I wish to ask Shuò another riddle;
if he doesn't know it, he should be flogged,
and if he makes up nonsense, it's just frivolous talk."
He said:
"Lìng hú jǔ,
lǎo bǎi tú,
yī yōu yà,
yí hōu yá—
what do these mean?"
Shuò answered:
"'Lìng' means command,
it's an order.
'Hú' is a vessel,
used for holding things.
'Jǔ' means teeth,
that are uneven.
'Lǎo' refers to the aged,
whom people respect.
'Bǎi' is a cypress tree,
the court of ghosts.
'Yī yōu yà' signifies words,
that are undecided.
'Yí hōu yá' describes two dogs,
in a fight."
Whatever Shèrén asked,
Shuò responded immediately,
his clever retorts sharp and endless,
leaving no one able to corner him.
All present were greatly astonished,
and the emperor appointed Shuò as a regular attendant,
thus gaining his favor and trust.

Naming
The term "jùn" (commandery) derives from "jūn" (ruler),
replacing the titles of dukes and marquises,
as "jūn" signifies the supreme authority.
The commandery governor holds exclusive power,
enhancing the ceremonial reverence between ruler and subject.
In the character for "jùn" today,
"jūn" (ruler) is on the left,
and "yì" (settlement) is on the right,
with the ruler as the head,
and the settlement supporting the people.
Thus, it takes its name from "jūn",
and is called "jùn".

Some commanderies were named after former states,
such as Chén, Lǔ, Qí, and Wú;
some after old cities,
like Chángshā and Dānyáng;
some after mountain slopes,
such as Tàishān and Shānyáng;
some after rivers and plains,
like Xīhé and Hédōng;
some after local features,
Jīnchéng
where gold was found beneath the city wall; Jiǔquán
where spring water tasted like wine;
Yùzhāng
where camphor trees grew in courtyards;
and Yànmén
where wild geese nurtured their young.
Some were named after imperial decrees,
such as when Yǔ convened feudal lords for grand planning
at Mount Dōngyě,
naming the region after the accounting of states,
hence Kuàijī.
The Hàn Guān Yí
records that Dūnhuáng and Jiǔquán
were so named because their waters were sweet like wine,
hence the names.
Zhāngyè means "extending the empire's arm"
to intimidate the Qiāng and Dí tribes.
Yìng Shào's Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì
further states that when the Son of Heaven established states,
capital names either combined elements
or derived from mountains and forests.
Thus Yùzhāng was named after trees in the capital,
and Suānzǎo after thorn trees in the region.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù
In the thirteenth year of Yuanli,
Pei Du attacked Wu Yuanji,
when the people of Feng were dredging a moat, they discovered a stone inscription,
and presented it with the text saying:
"A bamboo pole at the bottom of a well,
the bamboo's color is deep green,
the chicken is not yet fat,
the wine is not yet mature,
the young men blocking the carriage must shrink back."
Pei Du ordered his staff to interpret its meaning,
one soldier congratulated saying:
"Wu Yuanji will be captured.
'A bamboo pole at the bottom of a well,
the bamboo's color is deep green' means
that Wu Shaocheng rose from being a common soldier in the ranks,
and eventually commanded a hundred thousand troops,
becoming a regional commander,
and this illustrates his glory.
'The chicken is not yet fat' means
it has no meat,
for removing the meat (肉) from 'fat' (肥) leaves the character 己.
'The wine is not yet mature' means it has no water,
for removing the water (氵) from 'wine' (酒) leaves the character 酉.
'The young men blocking the carriage' refers to the armed soldiers,
and 'must shrink back' means they should retreat and defend their position.
Reasoning from this,
then the jǐyǒu day will be the day of victory."
Pei Du was amazed by his interpretation,
that winter Li Su captured Wu Yuanji alive,
and it was indeed on the jǐyǒu day,
whereupon Pei Du promoted the soldier to deputy general.
"Records of the Xuan Shi"
During the Tàihé era, there was a man named Liǔ Guāng,
who once traveled south and traversed a mountain path.
As dusk fell, he mistakenly entered a mountain hermitage,
below which was a spring,
its water tasting like sweet wine.
Liǔ Guāng drank from it and became intoxicated,
then lay down on a couch.
By dawn,
he saw carved characters on the stone wall,
so he copied them and placed them in his sleeve.
They read:
"When Wǔ resides in mǎo,
Yáo reigns for eight seasons,
I abandon my resting place,
I leave my screen.
Profoundly deep,
loftily high,
none recognize me.
From now onward, over a hundred sacrifices later,
blazing its light,
harmonious its beginning,
from the east comes a rabbit with small head and dark tail,
traversing my path,
arriving at my abode,
drinking from my spring to drunkenness,
ascending my couch to slumber,
carved upon my wall,
profound in its meaning,
who can decipher it?
It is Dōngpíng's son."
Liǔ Guāng read it and found it strange,
then walked out along the path several dozen paces,
turned back to look, but the chamber had completely vanished from sight.
Liǔ Guāng investigated but found nothing.
A certain Chāng Shēng examined it and explained:
"These are the words of one who attained the Way.
Now, at the beginning of the Táng dynasty when the reign title was established,
the second year of Wǔdé was the year jǐmǎo,
so 'Wǔ in mǎo'
refers to the second year of Wǔdé.
'Yáo the king' denotes Gāozǔ, who was called Shén Yáo.
'Eight seasons' also means two years.
'Abandoning the resting place, leaving the screen'
indicates the time of departure was the second year of Wǔdé.
'Profoundly deep,'
'none recognize me'
means he concealed himself unknown to others.
'From now onward, over two hundred sacrifices later'
refers to your arrival being two hundred years apart.
'Blazing its light'
signifies the year being dīngwèi,
for 'blaze' is fire,
occupying the south's bǐng-dīng position.
'Harmonious its beginning'
denotes the current emperor's first year of Tàihé.
'From the east comes a rabbit with small head and dark tail'
narrates your name.
East corresponds to jiǎ-yǐ wood,
rabbit signifies mǎo,
mǎo attached to wood forms the character Liǔ,
small head and dark tail forms the character Guāng.
'Traversing my path, coming'
and 'my abode' mean your arrival,
'drinking from my spring to drunkenness,'
'ascending my couch to slumber'
describe your stay,
'carved upon my wall,'
'profound in its meaning,'
'who can decipher it?'
'Dōngpíng's son'
implies the meaning is profound and only I can interpret it,
Dōngpíng being my district,
thus it is verified."

In the fourth year of the Tàihé era, Liú Zūngǔ served as military governor of Dōngchuān,
borrowing over a thousand people to compile books.
Suddenly one day, a great flood surged,
soaking all the books thoroughly.
Liú ordered them to be dried in the sun,
and among them was found one scroll of the "Zhōuyì Zhèngyì",
at the end of which was inscribed:
"On the eleventh day of the third month in the second year of the Shàngyuán era,
while studying the Zhōuyì, I composed this Zhèngyì,
and from then on, the era name changed.
Ten minus three equals one person,
eight thousand mouths shall encounter a great flood causing drowning,
thus allowing them to be spread out and sun-dried.
Héngyáng Daoist Lǐ Déchū."
Liú read the inscription and marveled at its strangeness,
summoning his aides to show them.
A document officer pondered and understood it, saying:
"From Shàngyuán to Tàihé is exactly thirteen years,
and the changed era name 'one person eight thousand mouths'
refers to the characters for Tàihé.
Thus, nothing in the world can escape the ultimate fate
that has long been predetermined."

Grand Guardian Xiàng Hú was stationed in Huáihǎi,
and one day, his secretary Bān Méng, along with fellow officials, was strolling along the western corridor of Dàmíng Temple,
when they suddenly noticed an inscription on the front wall:
"One person, grand and dignified,
two luminaries shining doubly bright,
a spring deep, one foot and one inch,
remove the dot beside ice,
two persons joined together,
not missing a single side,
three beams and four pillars,
blazing flames burning,
add double hooks, two suns complete."
The assembled guests and staff gazed at it,
but none could decipher it,
except Secretary Bān alone, who said:
"'One person'—isn't that the character for 'big'?
'Two luminaries' are the sun and moon,
isn't that the character for 'bright'?
'One foot and one inch' means 'inch' and 'earth',
isn't that the character for 'temple'?
'Remove the dot beside ice' removes the water radical,
'two persons joined together' forms the character for 'heaven',
'not missing a single side' is the character for 'below',
'three beams and four pillars, blazing flames burning' is the character for 'none',
'add double hooks, two suns complete' is the character for 'compare',
thus it reads: 'The water of Dàmíng Temple is unparalleled under heaven.'"
Everyone suddenly understood and exclaimed:
"The wonder of the yellow silk—
how no different is this wisdom!"

At the bell tower of Tàiqīng Temple on Mount Běimáng in Luòjīng,
during the Xiāntōng era of the Táng dynasty, it suddenly collapsed.
There was one roof beam
that was hollow inside.
Taoist priest Lǐ Wēiyì broke it open and found inside
a black lacquered board
with inlaid gold characters that read:
"Mountains and waters—who is without words?
In the first year, encountering Fú, it shall be rebuilt."
The Taoist priest presented it in Luòzhōng,
but none of the officials could understand it.
Later, when Lǐ Fú was relieved of his post as military governor of Xīchuān
and returned to Luò, he saw this cryptic text.
After pondering it repeatedly,
he then used his remaining salary
to single-handedly restore it.
After the temple was completed,
someone asked him the reason.
Fú replied:
"'Mountains and waters—who is without words?'
refers to the current emperor's personal name.
Xiāntōng was named Cuī.
'In the first year, encountering Fú'
means that Fú took up his post at the beginning of the new era,
received his salary, and returned.
If Fú did not repair it,
then who else would?"

At the end of the Qiánfú era, a visitor came to Qīnglóng Temple.
The temple monks did not show him courtesy.
The visitor angrily wrote on the gate before leaving,
the verses saying:
"The shrine dragon has gone to the Eastern Sea,
The sun hides as the west slopes.
Jìngwén is no longer here,
Crushed stones enter flowing sand."
The monks could not decipher the meaning.
A novice monk said:
"'Shrine dragon gone' forms the character hé (合),
'Sun hiding' contains the character sì (寺),
'Jìngwén absent' makes the character gǒu (苟),
'Stones entering sand' creates the character zú (卒).
These are disrespectful words,
insulting us."
The monks suddenly understood,
but when they pursued the former visitor, he had vanished without trace.
After the visitor departed,
it was revealed the novice was Wénhào, an attendant official from Emperor Yì's court.

A county with over ten thousand households is governed by a magistrate,
equivalent to a viscountcy.
One with a thousand households is governed by a chief, equivalent to a barony.
Nowadays, people refer to counties as "a hundred *lǐ*,"
since viscountcies and baronies originally measured a hundred *lǐ* square.
Hence, it is said that today's hundred-*lǐ* area
was the domain of feudal lords in ancient times.

"Your servant has heard of a mountain spirit named Yú'ér,
a foot tall yet fully formed in features.
When a hegemon's lord ascends the mountain,
the spirit appears and runs,
swiftly before the horse to show the way,
rolling up the sleeve indicates water ahead,
rolling up the right sleeve means to cross from the right side."
Upon reaching the stream of Bēi'ěr,

the depth will reach one's cap;
if crossing from the right,
the depth will only reach the knees;
thus crossing from the right is greatly feasible."

Guǎn Zhòng replied:

Duke Huán rode on his horse,

hedgehogs eat jùn birds,
yì birds eat leopards,
leopards eat bó beasts,
bó beasts eat tigers.

"Yes."

"I have heard that

one who deceives himself twice will suffer disgrace,

certainly not due to your virtue and righteousness, my lord.

Duke Jǐng raised an army to attack Sòng,
and as his troops passed by Tài Shān,
he dreamed of two men standing in anger,
their fury was intense.
The duke awoke in fear,
opened his door and summoned a dream interpreter.
The duke said:
"Tonight I dreamed of two men standing in anger,
I could not understand what they said,
their fury was intense,
yet I still remember their appearance,
and recognize their voices."
The dream interpreter said:
"The army passed Tài Shān without performing the proper rites,
so the mountain god is angry.
I request you quickly summon priests to offer sacrifices at Tài Shān."
The duke said:
"Agreed."
The next day, Yànzǐ came to court, and the duke told him
what the dream interpreter had said.
The duke said:
"The dream interpreter said that because the army passed Tài Shān without performing rites,
the mountain god is angry,
so I am sending someone to summon priests to offer sacrifices."
Yànzǐ bowed and after a moment,
replied:
"The dream interpreter is mistaken,
these are not the spirits of Tài Shān,
but rather Sòng's ancestors Tāng and Yī Yǐn."
The duke doubted this, thinking they were mountain spirits,
Yànzǐ said:
"If you doubt this,
then I beg to describe Tāng and Yī Yǐn's appearances.
Tāng had fair skin, a long face with a beard, broad above and pointed below,
he stood erect and spoke in a loud voice."
The duke said:
"Yes, that's right."
"Yī Yǐn was dark and short,
with disheveled hair and a beard, broad above and pointed below,
he stooped and spoke in a low voice."
The duke said:
"Yes, that's right,
what should we do now?"
Yànzǐ said:
"Now Tāng, Tài Jiǎ,
Wǔ Dīng, Zǔ Yǐ,
were all sage rulers of the world,
they should not be without descendants,
and now only Sòng remains,
yet you attack it,
so Tāng and Yī Yǐn are angry.
I request you disband the army to make peace with Sòng."
Duke Jǐng did not follow this advice,
and proceeded to attack Sòng.
Yànzǐ said:
"To attack an innocent state,
angering the bright spirits,
not changing your course,
pressing forward with the army despite these clear warnings,
this is beyond my understanding.
If the army indeed advances,
it will surely meet with disaster.
When the army advanced two encampments,
the drums were destroyed and the general died."
The duke then took leave of Yànzǐ,
disbanded the army and did not ultimately attack Sòng.

Emperor Wǔ of Hàn was traveling to Gānquán Slope when,
on the imperial road, there was an insect
coiled and covering the ground,
red like raw liver,
with head, eyes, mouth, nose, ears, and teeth all complete.
The vanguard scouts
galloped back to report it.
The Emperor sent someone to examine it,
but no one knew what it was.
At that time, Dōngfāng Shuò was in the auxiliary carriage,
and the Emperor ordered him to go and see it.
He returned and replied:
"This insect is called 'How Strange!'"
The Emperor said:
"What does that mean?"
He replied:
"Qín Shǐhuáng detained the innocent
and secretly killed the guiltless.
The masses were full of sorrow and resentment,
all raising their heads to sigh:
'How strange!
How strange!
It is born from pent-up anger.'
This place must be the site of a former Qín prison."
An edict was issued to the chancellor Gōngsūn Hóng to check the maps,
and it indeed was a Qín prison.
The Emperor said:
"Good,
but how should we get rid of it?"
Shuò said:
"All accumulated sorrows can be dissolved with wine.
Pouring wine on it should make it vanish."
Thereupon, they had someone fetch the insect and place it in wine,
and in a short while, it disintegrated.
The Emperor laughed and said:
"Dōngfāng truly is a master."
After bestowing a hundred bolts of silk,
wine was carried in the auxiliary carriage for this reason.
"Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò"
Emperor Wǔ traveled east to Hángǔ Pass,
where a creature blocked the road,
several zhàng long,
shaped like an ox,
with green eyes that gleamed brightly,
its four feet sunk into the earth,
moving but not shifting.
The officials were terrified,
so Dōngfāng Shuò requested to pour wine on it,
and after several tens of hú, it vanished.
The Emperor asked the reason,
and he said:
"This is born from accumulated sorrow and worry.
This must be the site of a Qín prison,
or else a gathering place for convict laborers.
Wine makes one forget sorrow,
so it can dissolve it."
The Emperor said:
"A man of broad learning
has reached such a level!"

During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the bell in the front hall of Wèiyāng Palace rang without cause,
continuing for three days and three nights without ceasing.
The emperor summoned the court astrologer Wáng Shuò for consultation,
and Shuò expressed concern that it might indicate military energy.
When asked again, Dōngfāng Shuò
replied:
"I have heard that copper is the child of the mountains,
and the mountains are the mother of copper.
Speaking in terms of yīn and yáng energies and their categories,
mother and child influence each other.
I fear there may be a mountain collapse,
hence the bell rang first.
As the Yì Jīng says:
'The calling crane is in the shade,
its young answers it,
this is the perfection of essence.'
The response should occur within five days."
After three days,
the governor of Nánjùn Commandery submitted a report stating
that a mountain had collapsed,
extending over twenty lǐ.

Xīnfēng
Jīngzhào Xīnfēng,
called Líyì in Qín,
was established in the seventh year of Gāozǔ's reign.
"Hànshū·Dìlǐzhì"
records that the Grand Supreme Emperor was unhappy in Guānzhōng,
longing for his hometown.
Gāozǔ relocated people from Fēng and Pèi,
where they sold wine and cooked cakes,
and merchants established it as Xīnfēng.
"Sānfǔ Jiùshì"
states that after Gāozǔ built Xīnfēng,
he also moved the old shrines,
with streets, alleys, and buildings
matching the original in every detail.
Men and women, old and young,
walking hand in hand at the crossroads,
each recognized their own homes.
Even dogs, sheep, chickens, and ducks released on the main roads
competed to find their own households.
This was the work of the craftsman Hú Kuān,
and the relocated people were pleased with its resemblance and grateful for it.

and also mentioned what it should eat.
It turned out as Shuò had said.
When asked how he knew,
he replied it came from the "Classic of Mountains and Seas."

saying, "This is the Bìfāng bird mentioned in the 'Classic of Mountains and Seas.'"
Upon verification,

During the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn, when the monk Zhuó Fǎlán came to Luòyáng,

"Hàn Jì"
Emperor Wǔ was feasting with his close ministers in the Wèiyāng Hall,
when suddenly he heard voices.
After a long while, an old man appeared on the beam,
eight or nine inches tall,
descending along a pillar.
He set down his staff and bowed his head,
remaining silent without speaking.
He looked up at the roof,
then bent down to point at the emperor's feet,
and suddenly vanished.
The emperor was astonished and alarmed,
so he summoned Dōngfāng Shuò and told him.
Shuò said:
"His name is Zǎolián,
the essence of water and trees.
In summer, he nests in secluded forests,
in winter, he hides in deep rivers.
Your Majesty has recently been constructing palaces,
cutting down his dwelling,
so he came to plead.
Looking up at the roof and the hall,
the hall is named Wèiyāng,
he is pleading that Your Majesty is encroaching on his dwelling, Wèiyāng.
Bending to point at Your Majesty's feet means 'enough,'
hoping that Your Majesty's palaces are sufficient as they are,
and no more should be built."
The emperor was moved and halted the construction.
Later, the emperor visited the Hùzǐ River,
and heard the sound of string music and singing from the riverbed.
Soon, the old man from the beam and several young people appeared,
all eight or nine inches tall,
with one person over a foot tall,
emerging over the waves.
Some carried musical instruments.
The emperor was eating at the time,
and invited them to sit in front of the table.
The emperor asked:
"I heard music from the riverbed,
was it you?
Could you play some music?"
"We brought instruments for this purpose,
how dare we not play?"
The tallest one then played the strings and sang,
his voice no different in volume from a human's,
clear and resonant, echoing through the beams.
Two others played pipes and kept rhythm,
harmonizing perfectly with the tune.
The emperor, delighted, raised his wine cup,
and urged the old man and others to dance.
They bowed and accepted the toast,
each drinking several sheng without getting drunk.
They presented the emperor with a purple conch,
inside which was a substance resembling ox fat.
The emperor asked:
"I am ignorant,
unable to recognize this object.
Dōngfāng Shēng knows about such things,
could you give him something rare and precious?"
The old man turned and gave an order,
to fetch the treasure from the cave.
One person accepted the command,
descended into the depths of the river,
and returned in an instant,
with a large pearl,
several inches in diameter,
radiant and unparalleled in the world.
The emperor admired it greatly,
then the old man and others suddenly vanished.
The emperor asked Shuò what was inside the purple conch shell.
Shuò said:
"It is the marrow of a flood dragon, used on the face,
it makes one's complexion beautiful,
and if a woman is pregnant,
it ensures an easy childbirth."
It happened that a consort in the rear palace had a difficult labor,
they tried it,
and it had miraculous effects.
The emperor applied the fat to his face, and it became fair and smooth.
He also asked:
"Why is this pearl called the Cave Pearl?"
Shuò said:
"There is a cave at the bottom of the river,
hundreds of zhang deep,
inside are red clams,
the clams produce pearls,
hence the name."
The emperor deeply marveled at these events,
and also bestowed five hundred thousand coins upon Shuò,
placing the pearl in the inner treasury.

both men and women had hairpins."
Sù said:
"Mourning attire refers to men being uncovered and women having disheveled hair.
Men wear caps and women wear hairpins.
From this, men should not have hairpins."
Fāng said:
"This specifically refers to mourning situations.
At the beginning of mourning,
when men are uncovered, women have disheveled hair.
When men wear caps, women have hairpins.
It indicates a change over time,
differing in the practices for men and women regarding covering and hair arrangement.
Furthermore, the cap is more respected,
thus replacing the hairpin;
it is simply a matter of expression,
not that men have no hairpins.
Moreover, the 'Lǐnèizé' states that a son serving his parents
combines his hair and ties it with a hairpin before dawn.
From this, it is clear
that men had hairpins."

saying:

Six Grades
The counties of the Great Táng were divided into six grades: red, metropolitan, prosperous, strategic, upper, and lower.
The capital's administered area was designated as a red county,
while the adjacent counties of the capital were metropolitan counties.
The rest were graded
based on the size of the population and the quality of the land.
"Records of Commanderies and States"
During the Kāiyuán era, the prefectures near the capital were designated as the Four Supports,
namely Tóng, Huà, Qí, and Pú.
The others were classified as the Six Powers, Ten Prestigious, Ten Strategic, and the upper, middle, and lower grades.
The Six Powers were
Zhèng, Shǎn, Biàn, Jiàng, Huái, and Wèi.
The Ten Prestigious were
Sòng, Bó, Wèi, Xǔ, Rǔ, Jìn, Luò, Guó, Wèi, and Xiàng.
Initially, there were ten strategic prefectures,
but later, many more were included as strategic.

During the Zhēnguàn era, a Brahmin monk claimed to possess a Buddha's tooth,
which could damage any hard object it touched.
As a result, men and women flocked to see it,
gathering like a market crowd.
Fù Yì happened to be bedridden due to illness
but upon hearing this, he told his son:
"This cannot be a Buddha's tooth.
I have heard that diamond is the hardest substance
and nothing can withstand it,
except for antelope horn, which can break it.
You should go and test it."
The monk had stored it with extreme care,
sealed tightly for a long time.
Only after much effort was it brought out.
When struck with the horn, it shattered immediately upon contact.
The spectators then dispersed,
and this method is still used today by those who work with pearls and jade.

so he went to the residence of the Palace Attendant Hǎo Chǔjùn to inquire.
Chǔjùn said:

He then submitted a memorial himself, stating:
To obtain fat mutton without grease,

Kill them one after another in front of the flock.

After the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
the division of territories by emperors and kings was inconsistent,
and the establishment of prefectures and commanderies
varied in records.
What is recorded in this local chronicle
can certainly be verified and understood.
The summary of arts and literature covers the Nine Provinces,
while "Primer for Beginners" only describes the Ten Circuits.
Subsequent compilations
each followed their respective dynasties,
some mentioned but not in detail,
others chaotic and lacking system,
truly presenting difficulties for recording local history.
Now consulting old texts,
a brief outline is preserved
for reference purposes.
Mèng Shēn was a native of Píngchāng.
His father Yuè was well-versed in the classics,
and having passed the imperial examination, was appointed as an academic official.
Shēn was bright and perceptive from a young age,
erudite and exceptionally talented,
with no one to rival him.
When Liú Yīzhī, the Vice Minister of the Phoenix Pavilion, was bedridden due to illness,
Shēn visited him and said:
"I've brought a meal, with cheese stored in a golden bowl."
Shēn looked at it in surprise and said:
"This is medicinal gold, not the kind mined from rocks."
Yīzhī replied:
"It was bestowed by the emperor;
it surely cannot be counterfeit gold."
Shēn said:
"Medicinal gold,
is used in immortal recipes,
it is not fake."
Yīzhī asked:
"How do you know this?"
Shēn replied:
"When medicinal gold is burned,
five-colored vapor rises from it."
Upon burning it, it indeed happened as described.
Yīzhī reported this to Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
who, considering him a close minister,
should not have been investigating unorthodox techniques,
demoted him to the position of Sima of Táizhōu.
A city wall

It is also called a breast wall,
referring to its low and small stature,
compared to the city wall,
like a woman to a man.
In the *Shìmíng*,
a battlement
is the breast wall on the city.

a parapet
is a battlement,

hence called a white battlement.

In the early Yuánhé era, Péi Zhòu governed Jīngzhōu.
He had the ground dug to a depth of six feet,
unearthing a stone,
whose structure and watchtowers
all resembled those of Jīngzhōu City.
Its hollow interior measured six feet eight inches in diameter,
exquisitely crafted.
He ordered it moved to the outskirts.
That spring, there was excessive rain,
continuing unabated through the fourth month,
with floods rising uncontrollably,
and people feared they would become fish.
It happened that Ōu Xiàn, dwelling in Chǔshān,
was urgently consulted.
He replied that the situation was critical,
and carving stone would be too slow,
so he instructed them to mold a model of Jiānglíng City from clay,
with an interior width of six feet eight inches,
and not the slightest discrepancy in its towers, battlements, gates, or thresholds.
They were to bury it six feet deep, eighty paces outside the south gate,
and the rain would stop.
Only then did Zhòu marvel in astonishment
and follow the methods of the ancients.
After burying it and offering sacrifices,
by evening, the mound had risen again.
Xiàn was a Dàoshi from Luòyáng,
learned and widely knowledgeable.

with the saddle torn and the reins broken.
