it still pulled back on the reins and stood its ground.
Xuàn sent a letter to inquire about the matter,
and Monk Zàn Níng replied:

which neither water nor fire can destroy.

Xuàn dug down over ten feet into the earth,
and indeed discovered the bone of a massive beast.
Its upper leg bone was about five feet long,
and from the knee down, it measured three feet.

But when steeped in fermented grains, it quickly rotted away.

To steal another's property is still called theft;
how much more is it so to claim the merit of Heaven's act as one's own?
It is difficult to be with them."
His mother said to him,
"Why should you not also ask for some reward?
With this you may die;—for whom should you wait?"
He replied,
"If I were to imitate them and do what is wrong,
my crime would be greater than theirs.
Moreover, I have uttered words of complaint;
I will not eat of his emoluments."
His mother said,
"But let the ruler know your story;—what do you say to that?"
He replied,
"Words are the ornament of the person.
When the person is about to withdraw into concealment,
where is the use of adorning it?
To do so would be to seek to be conspicuous."
His mother said,
"Can you carry out your resolution?

Zhèng attacked Chén,
entered it,
and sent Zǐchǎn to present the spoils of war to Jìn.
The people of Jìn said:
"Why did you invade a small state?"
He replied:
"By the command of the former kings,
wherever there is guilt,
each should receive its punishment.
Moreover, in the past, the Son of Heaven had a territory of a thousand square lǐ,
and the feudal states each had a hundred square lǐ,
from which it decreased in order—
such was the system of Zhōu.
Now the great states mostly have territories of several thousand square lǐ;
if they did not invade the small,
how could they have reached this?"
The people of Jìn said:
"His words are reasonable."
In the Family Sayings,
Zhòngní said:
"There is a saying:
Words are to complete one's will,
and literary elegance is to complete one's words.
If one does not speak, who will know his will?
If words lack literary elegance, they will not travel far.
When Jìn was the hegemon and Zhèng entered Chén,
without elegant rhetoric, they would not have succeeded.
Be cautious with your words!"

Confucius went to Zhōu,
and asked Lǎozi about the rites.
Lǎozi said:
"What you speak of,
the man and his bones have already decayed;
only his words remain."
Modern editions lack these three sentences.
As Confucius took his leave,

saying:
"I have heard that the wealthy and noble see people off with gifts,
while the benevolent see people off with words.
I am not wealthy or noble,
but presuming the title of a benevolent man, I send you off with these words:
'Those who are intelligent and deeply perceptive yet close to death,
are fond of criticizing others' faults.
Those who are broadly learned and eloquent yet endanger themselves,
are those who expose others' evils.
As a son,
do not hold too much of yourself;
as a minister,
do not hold too much of yourself.'"

Yuán Cìyáng's wife

After the wedding carriage arrival ceremony concluded,
Wěi asked:
"The way of being a wife
lies solely in chastity and obedience.
Why then do you have dozens of carriages, servants, and maids,
and decorations of embroidered silks, dark yellows, and pearls?"
The lady replied:
"A woman has the principle of three obediences.
At home, I was bound by my parents' affection,
who endlessly desired my richness and beauty,
so I dared not disobey their command.
Now if you wish to emulate Bào Zidū's style,
and refuse the gifts from the wife's family,
this is indeed a pure and lofty extraordinary conduct.
I also wish to observe your aspiration,
and return all I have to fulfill your nobility,
wouldn't this be appropriate?"
Wěi asked again:
"For a younger brother to be recommended before his elder brother
is still considered vulgar,
and not done by noble scholars.
Your elder sister remains unmarried, yet you, the new bride, have married first.
What is your hurry?"
She replied:
"My elder sister has the style of Sòng Bójī,
and the conduct of Liáng Gāo.
Her moral integrity reaches the blue clouds,
her chastity and integrity shine brighter than the white sun.
My father follows Yáo's matching with Shùn,
and Confucius marrying his daughter to Gōngyě Cháng's principle.
The world lacks such worthies,
hence the hesitation.
I am simple and untalented,
and can marry whomever I encounter."
Wěi fell silent,
and regretfully, those listening outside said:
"Make an effort, sir,
how can you be trapped by a woman?"

Wú Zhào Zī,
whose courtesy name was Bódù,
was sent as an envoy to Wèi.
Wèi's ruler Cáo Pī mocked Zī, saying:
"Does the King of Wú have much learning?"
Zī replied:
"The King of Wú commands ten thousand ships upon the river,
leads a million armored troops,
appoints the worthy and employs the capable,
and focuses his mind on statecraft and strategy.
Though he has spare time,
he broadly studies the classics, commentaries, and historical records,
drawing from extraordinary sources,
not merely imitating scholars
who merely seek out elegant phrases and sentences."
Pī said:
"Can Wú be conquered?"
He responded:
"Large states have armies for conquest,
small states have solid defenses."
Pī said:
"Does Wú pose difficulties for Wèi?"
He replied:
"With a million armored troops,
and the Yangtze and Hàn rivers as our moats,
what difficulties could there be?"
Pī said:
"How many men like yourself does Wú have?"
He replied:
"Those of exceptional intelligence and talent number eighty to ninety,
but those like your servant
are as numerous as cartloads and bushels,
too many to count."

Hào, as the ruler of a state,
holds the power of life and death.
When criminals fall into the law and are punished to set an example,
what is there to criticize?
Those punished by Yáo,
could not help but feel resentment;
those rewarded by Jié,
could not help but feel admiration—
this is human nature."
They asked further:
"It is said that the Marquis of Guīmìng,
being an evil man,
would gouge out the eyes of those who glared sideways or looked at him rebelliously—
is this true?"
Lǐ Rén said:
"This also did not happen;
it is a falsehood spread by rumor."
The Book of Rites states:
"When looking at the Son of Heaven, look below the collar;
at feudal lords, below the chin;
at high officials, at the level of the girdle;
at scholars, on a level plane,
allowing the eyes to wander within five steps.
Looking at a scholar above the girdle is arrogant,
below the girdle is worrisome,
to the side is improper.
In observing with ritual propriety,
the height and direction must be carefully considered—
how much more so with a ruler?
If one looks at a ruler directly in the face,
this is what ritual calls arrogance.
Arrogance leads to lack of propriety,
lack of propriety leads to disloyalty,
disloyalty leads to crime,
and crime leads to unpredictable dangers.
Even if such punishments existed,
what fault would there be?"
Annotation to the Records of Wú
Lù Xùn heard of Chē Jùn's fine reputation,
and requested to meet him.
He said to him:
"I have long admired your elegant demeanor,
but why do you remain coiled like a dragon and perched like a phoenix,
unwilling to condescend to visit me?"
Jùn replied:
"I truly recognize you as a noble lord,
who emulates the Duke of Zhōu's broad acceptance,
and matches Confucius' skill in guidance.
However, a lizard cannot borrow thick clouds to ascend,
nor can a quail ride fierce winds to soar.
Therefore, I had no means to approach you."
At that time, most guests present were from Wú,
and they looked at each other, saying:
"Even from the barbarian commandery of Wǔlíng
comes such an extraordinary man!"
Jùn said:
"Through Wú Tàibó's cultivation of proper attire and ceremonies,
he transformed the custom of disheveled hair and tattooed bodies.
Now above, we have an outstanding sage ruler,
and below, wise assistants are born.
How could this be considered ordinary?"
Xùn sighed and said:
"Our state is indeed flourishing,
to have such a man."

but now the city walls are red,
why is that?

all the soil from Lóngshǒu Mountain was excavated to build the city walls,
and the same was done for all the city gates and towers.

From "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
The ancient city of Cháng'ān,
was the former capital of the Han Dynasty.
In the seventh year of Emperor Gaozu, the palace city of Cháng'ān was built,
and the court moved here from Yuèyáng,
originally a detached palace of the Qin Dynasty.
When Cháng'ān was first established,
it was rather small and narrow,
but Emperor Hui expanded it further,
with a circumference of sixty-five li.
The southern part of the city was shaped like the Southern Dipper,
while the northern part resembled the Northern Dipper,
which is why people still refer to the old Han capital as the Dipper City.
According to the "Sānfǔ Huángtú,"
Cháng'ān had three gates on each side,
twelve gates in total on all four sides,
each leading to broad thoroughfares,
forming a grid pattern,
with roads level and straight,
wide enough for twelve carriages to travel side by side.
The gates were reinforced with metal piles,
surrounded by woods,
allowing passage on both sides,
serving as paths for travelers,
with distinctions for ascending and descending.
The "Sānfǔ Jué Lù"
describes the city's layout,
with three gates on each side,
smooth and level roads,
twelve parallel tracks,
and intersecting streets.
The "Rhapsody on the Western Capital"
mentions "opening three broad roads,"
and "establishing twelve thoroughfare gates."
The "Rhapsody on the Western Metropolis"
When Emperor Wǔ of Jìn first ascended the throne,
he drew a lot and obtained "one."
As the number of generations of a ruler's reign
was tied to this figure,
the Emperor was displeased,
and the officials turned pale,
with none able to speak.
The Palace Attendant Péi Kǎi stepped forward and said:
"I have heard that Heaven, by obtaining oneness, becomes clear;
Earth, by obtaining oneness, becomes tranquil;
and feudal lords and kings, by obtaining oneness, become the standard of the world."
The Emperor was pleased,
and the officials sighed in admiration.

Cài Hóng went to Luòyáng,
where people from Luòyáng asked him:
"With the new government office just established,
and all the lords issuing summons,
seeking outstanding talents from obscure places,
gathering worthy sages from mountain caves—
you, sir, are a scholar from Jīngchǔ,
a remnant of a fallen state.
What exceptional talent do you possess to respond to this summons?"
Cài Hóng replied:
"The pearl that shines at night
does not necessarily come from the Mèngjīn River;
the jade disc that fills the palm
need not be mined from the Kūnlún Mountains.
The Great Yǔ was born among the Eastern Barbarians,
King Wén among the Western Qiāng.
Where saints and sages emerge
must not always be the same place.
When King Wǔ of old overthrew Zhòu,
he moved the stubborn people to Luòyì—
could it be that you gentlemen are their descendants?"

was built by the King of Wú, Liú Bì.
Wáng Yì's "Guǎnglíng Jùn Tújīng"
records the city's circumference as fourteen and a half lǐ.
The "Annotations to the Later Chronicles"
extravagantly followed Qín laws,
and exceeded Zhōu decrees.
They carved out towering walls,
and dug deep moats.
The earnestness of rammed-earth construction for the battlements,
and the diligence in building watchtowers and beacon towers.
Their height rivaled the Five Sacred Mountains,
their breadth spanned three ancient mounds.
Precipitous like a severed bank,
soaring as if long clouds.
They used magnetite to repel assaults,
and applied red clay to create flying patterns.
Observing the robust fortification of the foundations and gates,
it seemed one ruler would reign for ten thousand years.

and upon returning,

with a profound and elegant demeanor;

The Shàngzhúlín Qī Xián Lùn and Yǔlín record this as being said by Wáng Jì.
Someone said to Huà Tán:

is like the difference between nine oxen and one hair -
can this really be true?"
Huà Tán replied:
"In ancient times, Xǔ Yóu and Cháo Fù declined the honor of being emperor,
while market vendors fight over the profit of half a coin.
How is the difference between these any different from
nine oxen and a hair?"
Those who heard this praised his answer.

Wèi Jiè was renowned from a young age for his profound reasoning,
excelling in the "Book of Changes" and "Laozi",
but he suffered from chronic illness himself,
and initially did not casually engage in discussions with outsiders.
A friend of the time sighed, saying:
"When Wèi Jūn does not speak, his words are bound to penetrate the truth."
Lángyá's Wáng Píngzǐ Chéng,
with his lofty spirit unmatched by others,
stood aloof from the world in solitary pride,
yet whenever he heard Jiè's discourses,
especially when it came to the comprehension of principles,
at the crucial points of subtlety,
he would invariably be overwhelmed in his seat,
having heard it three times in total,
he was overwhelmed three times for it,
so people of the time said:

Wáng Dūn served as the Grand General,
stationed in Yùzhāng.
Jiè, fleeing the turmoil, came from Luòyáng,
to seek refuge with Dūn.
Arriving in Wǔchāng,
he met with Dūn.
Dūn engaged in conversation with him throughout the day,
for two nights.
Dūn turned to his subordinate Xiè Kūn and said:
"In the past, Wáng Fǔsì
uttered golden tones in the central court;
this man now again resonates with jade in the region south of the Yangtze.
The thread of subtle words,
broken, is now continued.
I had not realized that in this unworthy age,
I would once more hear the sounds of the Zhèngshǐ era.
If Ā Píng were here,
he would surely be overwhelmed again.
Above

Zhāng Tiānxī was the Cishi of Liángzhōu,
asserting command over the western region.

he was made a Shìzhōng.

he arrived in the capital,
where he was esteemed by Xiàowǔ.
Each time he engaged in discussions,
they would last the entire day.
Some harbored envy,
and while seated, they asked Zhāng:

the owl's leather is sonorous,

Jìn Zhū Xù guarded Xiāngyáng,
Fú Jiān dispatched troops to attack it.
Xù's mother personally ascended the city wall to inspect its defenses,
and predicted that the northwest corner would be the first to be breached.
She then led over a hundred maidservants and the women of the city to build a slanted wall over twenty zhàng long at that corner.
When the enemy attacked the northwest corner, it indeed collapsed,
but the defenders held the new wall.

After arriving,
Tiānxī observed that his demeanor was pure and composed,
his speech flowed effortlessly,
he elaborated on past and present affairs,
mastering every detail without omission,

Relocating the City
The city of Wúxīng Commandery,
was known as Xiàgū City during the Qín dynasty,
and also as the old city of King Xiàng.
Guō Pú of the Jìn dynasty intended to relocate the commandery to Dōngqiān,
and his daughter was also skilled in geography.
She advised Guō Pú not to proceed with the relocation,
suggesting that modifying the existing site
would eliminate concerns about future damage and decay.
Guō Pú followed her advice.
Initially, when Guō Pú planned to move the city to Dōngqiān,
every time markers were set up, birds would carry them away.
Coinciding with his daughter's counsel again,
he ultimately decided on the current location.
His daughter was honored as the "Young Lady of the Relocated City,"
and she is worshipped alongside Guō Pú in his temple.
Zhèng Jiàn, the Sòng dynasty prefect, wrote the "Record of Minister Guō Pú."

courtesy name Yànbó,

son of the magistrate of Línrǔ, Xù.

and when Hóng was appointed as the governor of Dōngyáng from the position of an official,

ascending the wall to observe the enemy,
awaiting the exhausted with ease,

ceasing constant preparedness,

The emperor responded with a gracious edict.
"Basic Biography"
Emperor Xiàowǔ once bestowed a treasured sword upon Xiè Zhuāng,
who then gave the sword to Lǔ Shuǎng, Governor of Yùzhōu.
Later, Lǔ Shuǎng rebelled against the emperor.
During a banquet, the emperor asked about the sword's whereabouts.
The reply was:
"In the past, I gave it to Lǔ Shuǎng,
secretly considering it as Your Majesty's gift of Dùyóu."
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and at that time, it was seen as a wise remark.
"Běishǐ Volume Ten"
Shěn Yōuzhī attacked Yèchéng,
one night encountering wind and waves,
causing grain ships to sink.
The Granary Officer Cáo Cānjūn Cuī Língfèng's daughter had previously married Liǔ Shìlóng's son.
Yōuzhī sternly said to him:
"At present military provisions are critically important,
yet you show no concern for this matter,
still maintaining marriage ties with the city at night?"
Língfèng replied:
"As Yuè Guǎng once said,
how could I trade five sons for one daughter?"
Yōuzhī was pleased and his anger dissipated.
From History of the Southern Qí.
Chéng Jīng
Péi Zhāomíng served in various commanderies with integrity and diligence.
He often said to people:
"What need is there in life to amass wealth?
Beyond one's own person,
what more is truly necessary?
If descendants lack talent,
what I gather, they will squander;
if they can stand on their own,
then it is better to leave them a classic."
Thus, he never engaged in acquiring property throughout his life.
*History of the Southern Dynasties*
Liǔ Shìlóng was by nature pure and honest,
devoting himself solely to the study of ancient texts.
Zhāng Xù asked him:
"Observing your actions,
it seems you intend to bequeath a reputation of integrity to your descendants."
Liǔ replied:
"Beyond one's own person,
what more is truly necessary?
If descendants lack talent,
wealth will become a source of contention;
if they are talented,
it is better to leave them a classic."
The Emperor
Xú Miǎn, though holding a high position,
did not engage in acquiring property.
When his disciples or old friends occasionally advised him casually,
Miǎn would reply:
"Others bequeath wealth to their descendants,
I bequeath them integrity.
If descendants are talented,
they will acquire carriages and riches themselves;
if they lack talent,
wealth will ultimately end up in others' hands."
*Book of Liáng*
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng attacked Yèchéng.
At night,
hundreds of hairy figures climbed over the battlements of Yèchéng weeping,
then threw themselves into Huánghújī.
They were likely the essence of the city,
and by dawn the city surrendered.
"History of the Southern Dynasties"
Liù Bì
Liú Huáizhēn served as General of Chariots and Cavalry for Prince Zǐshàng of Yùzhāng.
He left his post due to his mother's passing,
and after the mourning period ended,
he visited King Yìgōng of Jiāngxià.
Yìgōng said:
"It has been years since we parted,
how could you not have aged?"
He replied:
"Your grace's kindness remains unrepaid,
how dare I grow old?"
Yìgōng praised his response.
From the Book of Southern Qí
Emperor Gāo of Qí had a former subordinate named Dōngguǎn Zhú Jǐngxiù,
who was once imprisoned in the workshop due to a fault.
The Emperor said to Bó Yù:
"Have you visited Jǐngxiù lately?"
He replied:
"I have visited him several times."
He went and reproached him, saying:
"If you allow me to reform myself,
I will surely swallow a knife to scrape my intestines,
and drink lime to cleanse my stomach."
The Emperor approved of his reply,
and immediately released him,
and he eventually became a loyal and trustworthy gentleman.
From the History of the Southern Dynasties.
The Liùbì Prefecture,
in the fifth year of the Tàipíng Zhēnjūn era of the Wèi dynasty, campaigned against the Hú at Liùbì,
which is this city.
Commonly, because the city had six walls,
it was thus named accordingly.
"Records of the Commanderies and States"
Emperor Wǔ of Qí once consulted with his court ministers,
and after drinking, he asked the assembled officials:
"What posthumous title will I receive after my time?"
None of the officials dared to answer,
until Wǎng Jiǎn signaled to Yǔ Gǎozhī, who calmly replied:
"Your Majesty's longevity equals the Southern Mountains,
your brilliance rivals the sun and moon.
A thousand years from now,
how could your subjects presume to make such estimations?"
Contemporary scholars greatly admired his eloquent response.
Gǎozhī often served as chief receptionist
when receiving Wei dynasty envoys.
On one occasion, an envoy asked Gǎozhī:
"Why do common households everywhere post 'for sale' signs on their gates?"
Gǎozhī replied:
"Since the imperial court intends to cleanse Luòyáng,
and recover the divine realm,
every household is selling their properties in preparation."
The Wei envoy sniffed disapprovingly but offered no retort.
Yùbì
in Jiàngzhōu Jìshān County,
was established as Jīngzhōu during the Later Zhōu dynasty,
featuring the Yùbì Fortress,
which Wáng Sīzhèng of the Later Zhōu built as a strategic stronghold.
Qí Shénwǔ attacked it twice,
but failed to capture it after sieges.
Wéi Xiàokuān succeeded Sīzhèng in defending Yùbì,
and when Gāo Huān assaulted it,
both his strategies and forces were exhausted.
"Zhōu Shū, Biographies II"
Liùhé
Qí Wáng Jiǎn served as the Minister of Personnel.
At that time, there was a guest surnamed Tán,
who visited Jiǎn seeking an official position.
Jiǎn said:
"Lord Huán of Qí destroyed the Tán state,
how could there be you?"
The guest replied:
"The son of Tán fled to Jǔ,
hence there is your servant."
Jiǎn appreciated his skillful reference,
and he eventually obtained the position.
The Emperor once visited the Lèyóu Garden,
feasting with all the ministers,
and when music was played, the Emperor said:
"You enjoy music—
who shares this with me?"
Jiǎn responded:
"Bathing in the customs of Táng,
affairs extend to every household;
since being in Qí,
I have not known the taste of meat."
The Emperor praised him.
"Tán Sǒu" "Nán Shǐ"
Suí Hé Chóu constructed a mobile palace and a six-directional city for Emperor Yáng,
who was confronting rebels in Liáodōng.
The work was carried out overnight,
with the city wall extending eight lǐ in circumference,
and the combined height of the wall and parapet reaching a thousand rèn.
Soldiers in armor were stationed atop it,
flags were raised ceremoniously,
watchtowers were erected at the four corners,
each side featured a tower,
with three gates beneath each tower.
By dawn, it was completed.
When the Gāolì people saw it,
they deemed it a feat of divine power.
"Original Biography"
Zhōu Yǒng's speech was eloquent and elegant,
his words flowed endlessly,
with tones and colors emerging,
forming sentences as he spoke.
When conversing with guests and friends,
his diction and rhythm were like a stream.
Whenever he met Zhāng Róng,
they would engage in profound discussions that lingered,
unresolved for days on end.
He was pure and poor, with few desires,
eating only simple vegetarian meals daily,
despite having a wife and children,
he lived alone in a mountain cottage.
General Wèi Wáng Jiǎn asked Yǒng:
"What do you eat in the mountains?"
Yǒng replied:
"Red rice and white salt,
green mallows and purple vines."
Prince Wénhuì asked Yǒng:
"What flavors do your vegetable dishes have?"
Yǒng answered:
"Early leeks in early spring,
late cabbages at autumn's end."
Accepting surrender
Qí Jìnglíngwáng Zǐliáng often gathered many guests,
Fàn Zhěn was among them.
Zǐliáng devoutly believed in Buddhism,
while Zhěn strongly asserted there were no Buddhas.
Zǐliáng asked him:
"If you do not believe in cause and effect,
how then do you account for wealth and honor, poverty and lowliness?"
Zhěn replied:
"Human life is like a tree,
its blossoms bloom together,
and fall with the wind.
Some brush against curtains and fall onto the matted seats,
while others hit the fence walls and drop into the filthy latrines.
Those falling on the matted seats—
that is Your Highness;
those dropping into the latrines—
that is your humble official.
Though honor and lowliness indeed follow different paths,
where, pray tell, is cause and effect?"
In the third year of the Jǐngyún era,
Zhāng Rényuàn, the military governor of Shuòfāng, built three Shòuxiáng Fortresses north of the Yellow River,
cutting off the path for the northern tribes to invade southward.
The three fortresses were completed within sixty days.
"Basic Biography"
Lǚ Wēn's inscription reads: Gazing down at the Yīn Mountains,
looking up at the revolving heavens.
With one man standing on the battlements,
a vista of ten thousand lǐ lies open.
Rényuàn was enfeoffed as the Duke of Hán,
the official decree praised his might.
He carved a crescent moon upon the celestial pathway,
and sliced through long clouds across the earth's veins.
Ruǎn Xiàoxù once received a joint summons with Fàn Yuányǎn of Wú Commandery but did not respond.
Yuán Jùn of Chén Commandery said to him:
"In the past, when heaven and earth were closed,
worthy men went into hiding.
Now the path of the world has been cleared,
yet you still cherish the life of a recluse?"
The retired scholar replied:
"In former times, though the virtue of Zhōu flourished,
Bó Yí and Shū Qí did not spurn the ferns they ate;
when the Hàn dynasty was at its peak,
the Four Haos did not leave their mountain forests.
The practice of benevolence depends on oneself—
what has it to do with the affairs of the world?"
Fèngtiān
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng attacked Qí,
Yuán Áng remained unyielding,
and was later appointed by Liáng as Minister of Revenue.
The Emperor said to him:
"Emperor Míng of Qí employed you as a 'black-haired Minister',
while I employ you as a 'white-haired Minister'."
Yuán Áng replied with much shame:
"Your servant has lived forty-seven years to this day;
the first forty years were my own,
the following seven were nurtured by Your Majesty.
It is not too late to serve as Minister."
The Emperor remarked:
"Indeed, a scholar does not gain reputation without cause."
The Book of Liáng.
In the first year of the Jiànzhōng era, in the fifth month,
the city of Fèngtiān was built.
In the fourth year, in the tenth month,
the emperor took refuge in Fèngtiān.
Earlier, the occultist Sāng Dàomào had petitioned for the construction of the city,
claiming that Fèngtiān was a place fit for a ruler.
Only then was this proven true.
"The Book of Táng"
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng raised his army,
Liǔ Tán responded from Hànzhōng in support.
As the Emperor was stationed in Xiāngyáng,
Tán held a farewell ceremony,
and the Emperor untied a jade ring from his own garment and presented it to him.
At the New Year's assembly in the second year of the Tiānjiǎn era,
the Emperor asked him:
"Is the jade ring you wear the one I gave you at Xīntíng?"
Tán replied:
"Since it carries an auspicious response from the divine heart,
I have respectfully worn it without ever tiring of it."
The Emperor then urged him to drink.
On another occasion, the Emperor said to him:
"Xú Yuányú defied orders in Lǐngnán,
yet the Book of Zhōu states that fathers, sons, and brothers should not be punished for each other's crimes.
I have pardoned his sons—
what do you think?"
Tán replied:
"Punishment does not extend to descendants,
while rewards may continue through generations;
this is now evident in Your Majesty's sagely court."
His words were considered wise at the time.
End
Jiāngxià
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng first had a tiger enter the outer city walls,
he was displeased,
and questioned his ministers about it.
None of the ministers responded,
until Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yíng, who was at the imperial banquet,
gathered his tablet and replied:
"In ancient times, when stones were struck
and stones were tapped,
all the beasts came to dance.
Your Majesty, having received the mandate and ruling the realm,
tigers and elephants come to pay homage."
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and all were impressed by this.
Liáng Shìzhōng Zhōu Shě set up an altar at the foot of Zhōngshān.
Emperor Wǔ asked how the altar was,
to which he replied:
"The wind does not rustle the branches,
the clouds do not gather even a tiny bit,
deer-skin caps and yellow cloaks,
there are many white petitions,
scarlet-robed officials rarely come,
hence it is named the Silent Altar."
from "Records of Jīnlíng"
Niú Sēngrú was appointed as the prefect of Èzhōu.
The climate and soil of Jiāngxià City were loose and poor,
making it difficult to erect walls.
Every year, additional planks were used for construction,
and levies were imposed on vegetable gardens to cover the costs,
allowing officials to exploit the situation for corruption.
This malpractice persisted for years.
Upon arrival, Niú Sēngrú calculated the expenses of the laborious plank construction,
which amounted to over a hundred thousand annually.
He then levied bricks instead,
using them to cover the cost of the plank construction.
Within five years, all the walls were repaired with bricks,
and the long-standing malpractice was permanently eradicated.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Sānchéng
Zhēn Shēn of Wèi sent Lǐ Dàogù as an envoy,
and the Qí emperor held a banquet for him.
Shēn raised his cup at the imperial feast to urge Dàogù to drink,
but Dàogù declined,
saying:
"In the court, there is no private etiquette,
so I cannot accept your urging."
Shēn calmly replied:
"As the Book of Songs says, 'The rain falls on our public fields,
and then reaches our private lands.'"
All present were impressed,
and Dàogù then accepted the wine.
Book of Liáng
Hé Jìngróng was selecting officials one day,
when a visitor came to see him,
whose surname was Jí.
Hé Jìngróng asked him:
"How closely are you related to Bǐng Jí?"
The visitor replied:
"Just as closely as you are to Xiāo Hé."
Lǐ Déyù was appointed as the military governor of Huá Prefecture,
then transferred to Jiànnán Xīchuān,
where he built the Fort of Upholding Righteousness,
to control the strategic barriers of Dàdù and Qīngxī Pass,
constructed the Fort of Resisting Insult,
to secure the pincer formation at Róngjīng,
and erected the Fort of Pacifying Distant Lands,
to block the Tǔbō forces from the Western Mountains.
(New Book of Táng)
Dà Xuán
In the first month of the third year of Dàtóng era,
the Vermilion Bird Gate was destroyed by fire.
Emperor Gāozǔ said to his ministers:
"This gate's construction was humble and narrow;
I had just begun planning to rebuild it,
when it was struck by heavenly fire."
They all looked at each other without response.
Only Hé Jìngróng said:
"This is what is called 'Your Majesty acts before Heaven, and Heaven does not contradict.'"
It was considered a famous reply at the time.
From "Liáng Shū"
The Wei envoy Lǐ Xié was on a diplomatic mission to Liang,
and upon reaching Stone City,
Emperor Wǔ dispatched his reception official Fàn Xū to host him.
Xū said:
"The royal aura of Jinling was foretold in earlier times;
the yellow banners and purple canopies,
originally emerged from the southeast,
to rule over all nations,
thus rightly belong here."
Xié replied:
"How could the imperial mandate
compare in glory with the Central Plains?
The purple canopies and yellow banners
ultimately entered Luoyang—
is this not self-inflicted harm?
Such glib talk
is merely jesting banter,
hardly worth mentioning!"
Gāo Pián was transferred to Jiànnán Xīchuān,
governing as military commissioner in Chéngdū City.
That year, Gāo Pián replaced it with brick and tile,
the parapets and battlements were complete and new,
he leveled all the hills and mounds
that abutted the city,
to facilitate farming and sericulture. When the project was completed,
he consulted the oracle and obtained the hexagram Dà Xù.
Pián said:
"Xù means
to nurture.
Aided by strength and steadfastness,
its brilliance is renewed daily—
what fortune could be greater?
The text suggests removing the lower and preserving the upper,
so it was named Dà Xuán City."
End.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng personally asked Lǐ Xié:
"Among the personages of the Wèi court,
how many are there who possess the four categories of virtuous conduct?"
Xié replied:
"The multitude of scholars is like a forest,
I cannot provide a complete account."
Emperor Wǔ said:
"King Wǔ had ten able ministers,
although Wèi has an abundance of talented individuals,
how could it immediately be as you say?"
Xié said:
"I humbly submit that when Zhōu refers to ten men,
it fundamentally cites those who assisted the Mandate,
as for 'the many officers, majestic and reverent',
this is truly from the odes of King Wén.
The talents in our imperial court's corridors and temples,
are sufficient to compete with the people of Zhōu."
． From "The Biography of Lǐ Píng in the Wèi Shū"
Presenting the Map
The king sent Chén Zhāng to fortify Qúzhōu,
and upon completion of the work, he presented a map.
The king noticed the dense camphor trees by the western gate,
and said to his attendants:
"If these trees are not included in the city plan,
they will never truly be mine."
Later, Zhāng indeed rebelled.
From "Bèi Shǐ"
Wèi Lǐ Qiān and Cuī Shào arrived at Tóngtài Temple,
where the host Wáng Kè, attendant Hè Jì, and three monks greeted them,
leading them into the pagoda.
Beside them stood someone holding a writing tablet and brush.
A monk said to Qiān:
"This is the Corpse Head,
solely responsible for recording people's sins."
Qiān replied:
"He is the Dǒng Hú of the monks."
They then entered another hall,
where before the Buddha stood a bronze bowl,
with a lamp burning inside it.
Shào remarked:
"One might say the sun and moon have risen,
yet the torchfire does not cease."
From "Yǒuyáng"
Qīng Jiàn
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng once leisurely said to Xiāo Zǐxiǎn:
"I am compiling the Comprehensive History,
once this book is completed,
all other histories can be discarded."
Zǐxiǎn replied:
"When Confucius praised the Way of the Changes,
he dismissed the Eight Investigations;
when expounding on regional geography,
he eliminated the Nine Mounds.
Your sage compilation coincides with this,
and is repeated today."
This was considered an exemplary reply at the time.
Book of Liáng
During Emperor Zhēnzōng's reign, Chǒng Shìhéng governed Yánzhōu,
and built Qīngjiàn City.
Initially, they suffered from a lack of water,
so they dug 150 feet into the ground until reaching rock, chiseled through the stone, and obtained a spring.
Once the city was completed,
it was bestowed the name Qīngjiàn City.
Shāmén Chònggōng once paid a visit to Emperor Wǔ of Liáng and asked him:
"I have heard there are four tones outside,
which ones are correct?"
Chònggōng immediately replied:
"The spire of Tiānbǎo Temple."
After leaving,
he encountered Liú Chuò,
who considered this answer skillful.
Chuò then said:
"How does it compare to saying 'May the Son of Heaven have ten thousand blessings'?"
From "Tán Sǒu"
Ghostly Work
Vice Minister Wèi Guàn was governing Guǎngzhōu when
a corner of the inner city wall suddenly collapsed,
revealing an ancient brick inscribed with four large characters:
"Entrusted to Ghostly Work,"
which formed the character Wèi (魏).
Moved by this inscription,
he extensively rebuilt and renewed the wall.
Soon after his departure,
the Nóng rebels attacked Guǎngzhōu.
The outer walls crumbled at first assault,
yet the inner city remained firm,
saving countless lives.
After the rebellion was quelled,
recognizing his foresight and preparations,
he was promoted to Reminding Counselor,
and reappointed to govern Wǔyáng.
Due to his wall-building achievement,
he long awaited unrewarded recognition,
expressing in a reflective poem:
"Though favored with imperial audience at dragon-headed steps,
Merit for battlements remains unacknowledged."
When Duke Wén Yànbó presented the poem,
he was appointed Academician of the Lóngtú Pavilion,
and appointed prefect of Yīngtiān Prefecture.
"Talks on Poetry Past and Present"
Chéng Jùn,
courtesy name Línjū,
studied under Liú Bǐng.
He was naturally intelligent and eager to learn,
later serving as a Zhùzuò Láng.
The Xiànwén Emperor frequently consulted him for discussions on the meanings of the Yì and Lǎo classics,
and also inquired about his age.
He replied:
"I am sixty-one."
The emperor said:
"In the past, Tàigōng was old
when he met Wén Wáng,
now you meet me,
isn't it rather early?"
Jùn said:
"Although I cannot compare to Lü Wàng in talent,
Your Majesty surpasses Xībó in honor.
I hope Heaven grants me more years
to fully demonstrate the effectiveness of the Liù Tāo."
Records of the Northern Wei Dynasty
People are the Great Wall
Xú Jūnqiàn,
courtesy name Huáijiǎn,
was eloquent in speech.
The Prince of Xiāngdōng once led his troops on an expedition,
and someone brought along a woman as a companion.
The Prince remarked:
"My talent falls short of Lǐ Líng's,
who failed to execute the women first;
I am no Sūn Wǔ,
yet I end up driving women into battle."
Jūnqiàn immediately responded:
"Even the mighty warrior Xiàng Jí
had his beloved Yú Xī;
and Jì Xìn, who achieved success,
also relied on a woman's aid."
From History of the Southern Dynasties, Book 5
Shì Bǎohǎi returned to Shǔ,
where Wǔlíng Wáng Jì of the Liáng dynasty governed the region of Jǐngluò,
and held him in great esteem and affection.
Whenever he stayed overnight,
by dawn when the prince was about to wash his hands,
as the sun's rays first emerged,
the prince said:
"The sunlight paints the white wall, reminiscent of the city;
the wind stirs the temple bells, reminding me we're in the monastery.
This morning, the carriage canopy comes to welcome me,
and the horse neighs once more."
Bǎohǎi replied:
"From afar, I see the canopy move,
delighted by thoughts of battle formations;
suddenly hearing the horse's neigh,
I rejoice at encountering the Dragon Tree."
They laughed together and departed.
From "The Biographies of Eminent Monks".
Emperor Wén of the Sòng Dynasty fell ill,
and Yìkāng forged an edict to arrest Tán Dàojǐ and hand him over to the Court of Judicial Review.
Dàojǐ drank a hú of wine,
removed his headscarf and threw it to the ground, saying:
"You have destroyed your own Great Wall!"
When the Wèi people heard of this,
they all said that Dàojǐ was already dead,
and men like the Wú people were no longer to be feared.
Later, when the Wèi army reached Guābù,
Emperor Wén climbed the Shítóu City wall to look out,
wearing a very worried expression.
He sighed and said:
"If Dàojǐ were still here,
how could it have come to this?"
(From History of the Southern Dynasties)
Liáng Xiàoyuán repeatedly sent envoys to Shǔ,
summoning Liú Fán's authority and influence.
Wáng Jì knew he could not be used for his own purposes,
so he bestowed generous gifts and sent him off.
At parting, Jì also took off his own waist knife and presented it to Fán,
saying:
"I hope when you see this object, you will think of me."
Fán replied:
"How dare I not uphold your authority,
and eradicate the treacherous villains."
"History of the Northern Dynasties"
Jīnchéng
Táng Yǒng, styled Dàolì,
was a man of Jìnyáng,
possessing the talent to govern the age.
Emperor Wénxuān of Qí once ascended Tóngfó Temple,
gazed upon Bīngzhōu City,
and said:
"What manner of city is this?"
Someone replied:
"This is a city of metal and a moat of boiling water,
a land of abundant stores."
The Emperor said:
"I say Táng Yǒng is the city of metal,
this is not the city of metal."
From the Book of Northern Qí:
"When dogs do not bark in alarm,
it is called a metal city;
constantly avoiding peril,
it is called being without insult."
From the Garden of Stories:
Jiǎ Yì said:
"When superiors establish integrity, shame, propriety, and righteousness to treat their ministers,
thus transformation is accomplished and customs are settled.
Ministers who are like fathers and elder brothers
truly die for the ancestral temple.
Ministers of laws and regulations
truly die for the altars of soil and grain.
Ministers who assist and support
truly die for their ruler.
Ministers who guard prisons and defend against enemies
truly die for the city walls and borders.
Therefore it is said that the sage possesses a metal city,
this thing and this intent."
The commentary states:
"It means the sage cultivates this integrity to command his subordinates,
then all people cherish virtue and exert their strength,
united in heart for the state,
secure and firm, unable to be destroyed,
appearing like a metal city."
From the Book of Hàn:
"Build a metal city of ten thousand zhi,
gaping moats surrounding it to form an abyss."
From the Rhapsody on the Western Capital.
Wèi Kǎi resigned from the position of Chief Clerk,
and remained in obscurity for years.
Later, he met Yáng Yīn on the road,
and subtly stated his case.
Yáng Yīn replied:
"The issuance of edicts to appoint officials
all comes from the Emperor's decree;
it is not something the Ministry of Personnel handles entirely,
so you need not trouble yourself to plead with me."
Wèi Kǎi immediately responded:
"Although the rain falls from heaven,
it ultimately depends on the clouds rising from the four sacred mountains.
How can you claim not to know?"
Yáng Yīn said delightedly:
"This statement is extremely concise and to the point,
and requires no further elaboration."
A few days later,
Wèi Kǎi was appointed as Governor of Huò Prefecture.
From The Book of Northern Qí
Shíchéng
Emperor Xuān of Chén once perused trivial documents,
pointed at Xiāo Yǐn's signature and said:
"The stroke of this character flips upward,
flipping like a bird about to take flight."
Yǐn humbly replied:
"This is only because Your Majesty has lent it feathers."
The Emperor further said to Yǐn:
"Whenever I am filled with anger and you appear,
my rage immediately dissipates.
Why is this?"
Yǐn responded:
"This is because Your Majesty does not transfer your anger to your servant.
How could I claim credit for this grace?"
《Book of Chén》
Shénnóng's teachings state:
Even with a stone wall ten ren high,
a moat a hundred paces wide,
and a million armored troops, without grain,
one cannot hold it.
"Treatise on Food and Money"
Lǐ Xiàozhēn,
courtesy name Yuáncāo,
was studious and skilled in composing writings.
He served in the Qí dynasty,
and along with his younger brother Xiàojī, he once met with the Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel Lù Áng.
Áng teased them, saying:
"Your younger brother is named Xiàojī (Filial Foundation),
so you, the elder brother, must be his replacement."
Xiàozhēn replied:
"Although I am unworthy,
I wish to attach myself to Zǐzāng."
Áng shook his hand and said:
"A scholar indeed does not have a reputation in vain;
you, my worthy one, are sure to achieve great success."
Later, Xiàozhēn was promoted to Prefect of Méng Province,
where the officials and people were content under his governance,
and from then on he no longer devoted attention to literary pursuits.
When asked the reason for this,
he sighed with emotion and said:
"Fifty years of age,
has passed by in a flash;
white hair hangs at my temples,
my physical strength has already declined;
both my ambition for officialdom and passion for literature
have vanished all at once—
how lamentable!"
(Book of Suí)
The character "Yà"
Wúluó City was constructed in the shape of the character "Yà",
built in the sixth year of King Jìng of Zhōu, the year Dīnghài.
It stretched twelve lǐ from north to south,
and nine lǐ from east to west.
Within the city flowed a great river,
with three horizontal and four straight waterways,
Sūzhōu was renowned,
a land of ten prospects,
all six major and eight gates were accessible,
connecting both water and land in the commandery and its outskirts,
with over three hundred lanes.

Sui Crown Prince Yǒng's

why was he born in an unsuitable place?"
Líng replied:

People at the time considered this a clever response.

Crescent Moon
Suí Dynasty official Xiè Dàohéng once visited Zhōngshān Kāishàn Temple,
and said to a young monk:

The monk replied:

to subdue the four demons;
the Bodhisattva lowers her gaze
to show compassion to the six realms of existence."
Dàohéng was taken aback and could not respond.

thus far surpassing him."
Tàizōng appointed him to serve in the Historiography Institute.

citing examples and analogies,
weighing the past and present,
highlighting essentials while omitting trivialities,
combining elegance with logical precision

Listening to him was captivating,

Brocade Weaving
Zhèng Yuánshú was well-versed in literature and the arts.
When the Turks attacked Tàiyuán,
Yuánshú, holding his official insignia, went to confront them,
but the enemy blamed the Central Kingdom for being untrustworthy.
Yuánshú refuted their accusations with words without yielding,
and then said to Jiélì:
"Now, if you plunder wealth and resources,
seize people,
they all go to your tribes.
How would it compare to lowering your banners and making peace,
so that gold, jade, and valuable goods
would all belong to the Khagan?"
If the Khagan agrees to the terms as spoken,
why would I spare bestowing metal and stone upon you?
From the "Kǒng Tiē".
Someone reported that Féng Āng had rebelled,
and Emperor Tàizōng ordered Lán Mó to mobilize armored troops from Jiānghuái to prepare an expedition against him.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
"A true king's army should not be mobilized for barbarians.
Victory over them brings no martial glory,
while defeat would be humiliating.
The evidence of Āng's rebellion is unclear;
he should be won over with virtue.
Āng, being fearful,
will certainly come of his own accord."
The emperor then dispatched the Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Wéi Shū to persuade Āng,
and Āng sent his son Zhì Dài to serve at court.
The emperor said:
"Zhēng's single remark was worth more than a hundred thousand troops."

Empress Wǔ Zétiān appointed Wǔ Chéngsì as Left Minister,
and Lǐ Zhāodé memorialized:
"I do not understand why Your Majesty
has entrusted such important authority to Chéngsì."
Wǔ Zétiān replied:
"He is my nephew, so I have entrusted him with a position of trust."
Zhāodé said:
"The closeness between an aunt and her nephew—
how does it compare to that between father and son,
or between mother and child?"
Wǔ Zétiān said:
"It is not as close."
Zhāodé said:
"Even between father and son or mother and child, there are instances of coercion and usurpation.
How much less can one rely on the relationship with a nephew?
If he were to seize the opportunity to ascend the throne,
would Your Majesty's position be secure?
Moreover, Your Majesty is the sovereign ruler.
What blessings has Your Majesty's aunt received
that you should entrust such authority to your nephew?
This will lead to the loss of your power!"
Wǔ Zétiān was startled and said:
"I had not considered this."
That very day, she dismissed Chéngsì from his governmental duties.

Xiàkǒu
Lacking substantial savings despite integrity,
Luǒ Tǎn from Luòyáng,
styled Bǎohéng,
while serving as the captain of Hénán,
with Dù Huángshang as the prefect,
summoned Tǎn to stand below the hall,
saying:
"A certain family's son associates with wicked people,
has depleted his family fortune—why not investigate it?"
Tǎn replied:
"Generally, those who hold office with integrity,
even as high officials, do not amass great wealth.
Those capable of accumulating riches
must have exploited their subordinates to achieve it.
If their descendants manage to preserve it,
it would mean Heaven enriches unjust families.
Better to let their injustice run its course,
so wealth returns to the people."
Huángshang was astonished by his words,
and from then on treated him with increased respect.

Liú Xùn,

Valuing Righteousness
When it comes to righteousness, does the wise person consider it noble?
Or righteousness?
It is said:
"Righteousness,
this is why Yáo gave the empire to Shùn."
Is it said to be wealth?
Or righteousness?
It is said:
"Righteousness,
this is why Zǐ Hǎn considered refusing jade as precious."
It is said:
Life?
Or righteousness?
It is said:
"Righteousness,
thus Wù Guāng threw himself into the water and perished."

Fóxī rebelled with Zhōngmóu,
placed a cauldron in the courtyard,
and addressed the officials:
"Those who support me
shall receive fiefs;
those who do not support me
shall have their officials boiled."
All complied until it came to Tián Jī.
Tián Jī
said:
"I would rather die righteously than avoid punishment by axe and halberd,
prefer poverty with principle over high position and carriage,
to live without righteousness,
or to gain wealth through lack of benevolence
is worse than being boiled."
He lifted his robe and approached the cauldron,
whereupon Fóxī removed his own shoes and spared him.
When the Zhào clan heard of the rebellion,
they attacked and captured the city;
learning that Tián Jī had refused to join,
they sought to reward him.
Tián Jī said:
"This cannot be.
For one man to be elevated while ten thousand bow their heads
is what the wise do not do.
To reward one man and shame ten thousand
is what the righteous do not accept.
If I accept this reward,
I would make the scholars of Zhōngmóu
bear the shame of unrighteousness."
He declined the reward and moved away, saying:
"To use one's conduct to lord over others
is unjust,
so I shall leave."
He then went to Chǔ.

Háo
Bái Gōng Shèng was about to assassinate King Huì of Chǔ,
the king fled,
the Lìng Yǐn and Sīmǎ both died,
Bái Gōng Shèng drew his sword and handed it to Qū Lú, saying:
"If you side with me,
I will spare you;
if you do not side with me,
I will surely kill you."
Qū Lú replied:
"You killed my uncle and now seek my support,
is that acceptable?
I have heard that a man who understands fate
remains unmoved by profit,
unafraid in the face of death.

one should live when it is time to live,
and die when it is time to die—
this is called the ritual of a subject.
Thus, understanding the Mandate of Heaven above
and the Way of the subject below,
how can one be coerced?
Why do you not reconsider this?"
Bái Gōng Shèng then sheathed his sword.

After Bái Gōng Shèng had killed the Prime Minister and the Minister of War,
he wished to enthrone Prince Lǘ as king.
Prince Lǘ refused,
and when threatened with a blade,
he said:
"If you, a descendant of the royal house, would assist in governing the state of Chǔ,
rectify the royal court,

that is my wish.

why do you not accept it?"

that would be unrighteous;
if I yielded under the threat of a blade and abandoned righteousness,
that would be cowardly.
Though you tempt me with profit
and intimidate me with weapons,

Bái Gōng tried to force him,
but he would not yield,
so he killed him.

Palace
The "Shì Míng" states:
"A palace,
is lofty.
It refers to a building visible above the walls.
Lofty,
means elevated and grand."
Guō Pú explained:
"A palace,
means that which surrounds."
The "Records" says:
"It is appropriate for a ruler to build a palace as a dwelling."
The "Ěr Yǎ" states:
"A room is called a chamber,
and a chamber is called a palace.
The 'Shī Jīng' says:
'Built the Chǔ palace,'
and also:
'Enter this chamber to dwell'—these are examples."
The "Fēng Sú Tōng" states:
"A palace
and a chamber are the same.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
the esteemed have used it as a common designation,
while those of lower status avoid using it."
The "Lǚ Lǎn Shèn Dà" states:
"When King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he pacified Jīzǐ's palace."
The "Lǐ Jì" states:
"From appointed scholars upward,
fathers and sons all have separate palaces."
It also says:
"A scholar may have a palace of one mǔ,
a chamber with walls all around."
It further states:
"When Jì Fūzǐ entered the palace,
he did not dare to weep."
Thus, both scholars and commoners had the designation of palace.
It is said that a man from Qí was driving an empty cart,
when a man from Lǔ carrying a cauldron
placed his cauldron in the cart.
They traveled three hundred miles,
and upon parting, the man took his cauldron without asking,
nor did he express thanks.
Later, the cart owner was imprisoned
and sentenced to death.
The cauldron owner went directly to him,
tunneling through the wall to rescue him,
but before breaking through,
he said:
"How extreme!"
The cart owner angrily refused to come out,
making the cauldron owner ashamed,
and willing to die together.
The next day, the jailer reported the incident to the ruler of Qí,
who, moved by their righteousness, pardoned them.

was a man of Liáng.

he often associated with Bù.
Later, Bù was abducted and sold,
becoming a slave in Yān,
where he avenged his master's family.

the Hàn attacked Yān,

before he returned,
the Hàn summoned Péng Yuè,
accused him of plotting rebellion,

His head was displayed in Luòyáng,
with an edict that anyone who viewed it
would be arrested immediately.
When Bù returned,
he reported his mission before Péng Yuè's head,
set up a shrine, and wept for him.
The officials arrested him and reported it.
The Emperor summoned Bù and berated him,
ordering him to be boiled alive,
but Bù, having justified Yuè's cause,
asked to be boiled,
whereupon the Emperor pardoned him,
and appointed him as Commandant.
From "Records of the Hàn."
Chén Yì,
courtesy name Chūnqīng,
was a native of Shū County in Lújiāng.
While traveling to Lánxiāng,
he saw a horse by the roadside,
beside which lay a sick man,
who called out:
"I am Duke Wèi of Cháng'ān,
having heard that Lújiāng is a pleasant land,
I came to visit,
but now I am too ill to continue.
If possible, I beg for your help."
Yì helped him back,
caring for him daily until his condition worsened,
when the man said:
"I have ten gold ingots,
and twenty bolts of plain silk.
After I die, sell them for my burial,
and give the remainder to my host as thanks."
After his death,
Yì sold the silk to buy a coffin,
arranging the burial with shrouds and garments,
but placed the gold beneath the coffin,
and rode the horse when going out.
Later, his elder brother Chánggōng saw Yì riding the horse,
and reported him to the authorities for arrest.
Yì explained the whole story,
and the gold was found under the coffin.
Chánggōng kowtowed in apology,
and threw the ten gold ingots into Yì's doorway.
Yì sent them to Cháng'ān,
returning them to the family.
Yì later became the captain of Lǔyáng,
and was known as the Golden Captain of Lǔyáng.
． "Biography of Fàn Yàn's Hidden Virtue from The Seven Worthies of Lújiāng"
In ancient times, people did not yet know how to build houses,
so they dwelled near hills,
residing in low, damp places,
which harmed the people. Therefore,
the sages established the methods for constructing houses:
the height should be sufficient to avoid dampness,
the interior adequate to ward off wind and cold,
the roof strong enough to withstand frost and snow,
and the walls high enough to separate men and women.
Thus, it was for the convenience of life,
not for the pursuit of pleasure.
Nowadays, when building houses,
they heavily tax the common people,
ruthlessly seizing their wealth,
to create elaborate and winding structures,
adorned with carvings in blue and yellow,
so the state becomes impoverished and the people have no one to appeal to.
From "Mòzǐ"

Pínglíng Yún Chǎng studied under Wú Zhāng,
and often enjoyed pointing out others' faults,
considering them frivolous,
which everyone agreed with.
Later, Wú Zhāng was executed by Wáng Mǎng,
and no one dared to collect and bury his body,
his disciples all changed their names
to follow other teachers.
At that time, Chǎng was an official in the Ministry of Personnel,
yet he alone claimed to be Wú Zhāng's disciple,
collected and buried his corpse,
revealing how the upright and honest are not tolerated by the mediocre.
The people of Pínglíng erected a stele for him beside Wú Zhāng's tomb during his lifetime,
located on the southern ridge of Lóngshǒu Mountain.

"Chǎng,

Lián Fàn was a disciple,
and served under Doctor Xuē Hàn.
When Xuē Hàn was implicated in the affair of King of Chu,
executed for assisting him,
none of his followers dared to visit him except Lián Fàn,
who alone went to attend to his remains.
This was reported to the authorities,
and the Emperor Xiǎnzhōng was enraged.
He summoned Lián Fàn,
demanding,
"Xuē Hàn conspired with the King of Chu,
causing upheaval in the realm.
As an aide of the public office, you do not align with the court,
instead tending to criminals.
Why?"
Lián Fàn knelt and said,
"I am foolish and ignorant,
believing that Xuē Hàn and others were already executed,
I could not help my sense of duty to my teacher;
I deserve ten thousand deaths for my crime."
The emperor's anger gradually eased,
and he asked Lián Fàn,
"Are you a descendant of Lián Pō?
Are you related to General Bāo or Grand Marshal Dān?"
Lián Fàn replied,
"Bāo,
was my great-grandfather;
Dān,
was my grandfather."
The emperor said,
"No wonder you have such courage!"
And thus pardoned him.
From this, his renown spread.

Kàn Chǎng,
courtesy name Zǐzhāng,
was from Píngyù.
He served as an assistant official in the commandery.
When Grand Administrator Dìwǔ Cháng was summoned to the capital,
just before his departure,
he hastily left 1.3 million coins of his salary with Chǎng for safekeeping.
Chǎng buried the money in his hall.
Then troubled times came suddenly,
and travel routes were cut off.
Chǎng grew old, hungry, and emaciated.
His wife said:
"The money entrusted by Grand Administrator Dìwǔ
could be taken for our sustenance,
and repaid later."
Chǎng replied:
"Though I am poor and old,
how could I presume to use my former superior's wealth?
When the roads reopen, I will deliver it despite hunger and cold -
what harm is there?"
Meanwhile, Dìwǔ Cháng's entire household suffered from plague,
and his wife and children all died.
As Cháng lay critically ill,
he had only an orphaned grandson
aged nine years.
Cháng told him:
"I left 300,000 coins with my former assistant official Kàn Chǎng of Píngyù."
Then he breathed his last.
Later, when the grandson grew up,
he traveled on foot to Rǔnán,
inquiring after Chǎng.
Chǎng met him,
and they shared both sorrow and joy.
Before the young man's departure,
Chǎng dug up 1.3 million coins.
The orphaned grandson said:
"My late grandfather, in his final moments,
mentioned only 300,000 coins.
Now there are 1.3 million -
I dare not accept this."
Chǎng replied:
"The Grand Administrator was gravely ill and short of breath,
so he misspoke."
The grandson then had no more doubts.
(From "Biographies of Former Worthies of Rǔnán")

Yáng Biāo,
courtesy name Wénxiān,
during the Jiàn'ān period, seeing that the Hàn dynasty's mandate was about to end,
claimed to have cramped feet,
and ceased walking.
After ten years had passed,
when Cáo Pī accepted the abdication,
he wished to appoint Yáng Biāo as Grand Commandant,
first sending an official to convey his intention.
Yáng Biāo declined, saying:
"I, Biāo, served as one of the Three Excellencies of Hàn,
yet encountered a time of turmoil and collapse,
unable to contribute any remedy or benefit.
Now in old age and afflicted by illness,
how could I assist a newly established court?"
Thus he firmly declined.

Èr Gōng
Zhī Xí,
courtesy name Yuánshēng,
was a native of Jīngzhào.
During the Zhōngpíng era, he served in the commandery,
was recruited by the ducal office,
achieved top ranking in the examinations,
and became close friends with Kǒng Róng, the Minister of Stewards.
When Cáo Cāo served as Minister of Works,
his power and influence grew daily,
yet Róng, out of old sentiments,
wrote letters in an arrogant manner.
Xí often reproached Róng,
urging him to change his conduct,
but Róng did not comply.
When Róng was executed,
none of the officials in Xǔ who had previously been close to him
dared to collect and mourn his body,
but Xí alone went to stroke the corpse and wept over it:
"Wénjǔ,
you have left me to die;
with whom shall I speak now?"
He lamented endlessly.
Tàizǔ heard of this,
arrested Xí,
and intended to punish him,
but soon pardoned him due to the righteousness of his actions.
During the Huángchū era,
an edict sought to employ him,
but due to his old age,
and in recognition of his loyalty to old friendships,
which demonstrated the integrity of Luán Bù,
he was bestowed the title of Palace Gentleman.
"Wèi Lüè"
Cáo Cāo led his army to attack Yuán Tán at Nánpí.
Wáng Xiū was transporting provisions in Lè'ān at the time.
Hearing of Yuán Tán's crisis,
he took the troops under his command and several dozen officials to aid Yuán Tán.
Upon reaching Gāomì,
he learned of Yuán Tán's death.
Dismounting his horse, he wailed,
"Without my lord, where shall I return?"
He then went to see Cáo Cāo,
begging to collect and bury Yuán Tán's body.
Cáo Cāo wanted to test Wáng Xiū's resolve,
so he remained silent and unresponsive.
Wáng Xiū repeated,
"I have received great kindness from the Yuán family.
If I am allowed to bury Yuán Tán's body,
I will then accept execution,
with no regrets."
Cáo Cāo admired his righteousness,
and granted his request.
Records of the Three Kingdoms
After Lord Cáo had executed
Yuán Tán, he displayed his severed head with the order:
"Anyone who dares to mourn him
will be executed along with their wife and children."
Thereupon, Wáng Shūzhì and Tián Zǐtài said to each other:
"We received appointments while he lived,
yet do not mourn him in death—
this is unjust.
If we fear death and abandon righteousness,
how can we stand in this world?"
They then went to the severed head and mourned it,
their grief moving the entire army.
The military judge reported to carry out the execution,
but Cáo Cāo said:
"They are righteous men."
And pardoned them.

Sīmǎ Zhāo assassinated the Wei ruler,
Máo arrested Wáng Jīng,
executed him,
and his former subordinate Xiàng Xióng wept for him,
moving the entire market with his grief.
Zhōng Huì had Xiàng Xióng arrested and reburied him.
Zhāo heard of this,
summoned him and reprimanded him, saying:
"When Wáng Jīng died before,
you wept for him at the eastern market,
and I did not question it.
Now Zhōng Huì personally committed treason,
and yet you again took it upon yourself to rebury him.
If I continue to tolerate this,
how will the royal law be upheld?"
Xiàng Xióng said:
"Once the royal punishment has been carried out,
the law has been satisfied.
I, moved by righteousness, reburied him—
this does not violate moral teachings.
Why must you force me to betray the dead and defy the living to establish myself in this world?
If Your Highness holds a grudge,
leaving his bones abandoned in the wilderness,
a hundred years from now, you will be laughed at by slaves—
can such a thing be concealed by benevolence and worthiness?"
Zhāo was pleased, feasted and conversed with him, then sent him away.
"Chronicles of Han and Jin"
After Zhūgě Kè's death,
Zāng Jūn of Línhuái submitted a memorial requesting permission to bury him, saying:
"In the past, Xiàng Jí received the charity of burial,
and Hán Xìn obtained the grace of interment;
this was because Hàn Gāo displayed a reputation of divine enlightenment.
Luán Bù presumptuously ordered Péng Yuè's burial;
I privately resent this,
for not first requesting the sovereign's approval,
but arbitrarily acting to indulge personal feelings.
That he escaped execution
was indeed fortunate."

Jì Zhān, courtesy name Shìyuǎn.
When Wǔ Gǔ, the governor of Lìyáng from the Pei Kingdom, was dying,
he worried his family would not be established,
so he wrote a letter entrusting them to Jì.
Zhān welcomed them all,
provided housing,

In his youth, he was close with the brothers Lù Jī,
and after the entire Lù family was executed,

caring for Jī's daughter,
arranging her marriage.

Long night
Shí Lè said to his Right Chief Clerk Zhāng Bīn:
"Yè is the old capital of Wèi,
I plan to construct it,
who would be suitable to take charge?"
Bīn replied:
"Zhào Péng, the former Eastern Lài governor of Jìn, is loyal, upright, sincere and diligent.
If you appoint him to Yè,
he will certainly fulfill your divine plan."
Shí Lè then summoned and appointed him as Governor of Wèi Commandery.
When Péng arrived,
he tearfully declined, saying:
"Your servant once served the Jìn court,
and enjoyed its emoluments.
Moreover, to receive honor and favor from one,
then serve another house—
this is something my will cannot do.
Not only is this your foolish servant's scrupulous resolve,
but I fear it would also be something you would disapprove of.
I would rather die
than dare accept this command.
If you would grant me my remaining years,
and fulfill this humble wish of your servant,
it would be a great act of generosity on your part."
Thereupon, he was given a comfortable carriage with a team of four horses,
and provided for with a minister's salary.
"Records of the Later Zhào"
During the reign of Jié of Xià,
he built the Palace of Eternal Night,
located in a deep valley,
where men and women mingled promiscuously.
For thirty days he did not emerge to attend to state affairs,
after which a great wind blew sands
that filled this palace valley in a single night.
"Records of Diverse Matters"
Gǒng Yǐng
was a native of Suìníng.
In his youth, he was fond of learning.
Máo Qú, the Inspector of Yì Province, recruited him as an Education Officer,
and he served under Qú.
When Qú was killed by Qiáo Zòng,
all the subordinate officials fled.
Yǐng wailed in grief,
and hastened to attend the funeral and pay his respects according to ritual.
Later, Zòng held a banquet,
inviting Yǐng,
but he did not come.
Eventually, he arrived,
and as music began to play,
Yǐng shed tears and stood up,
saying:
"Having served a lord in the north,
I failed to die with him in his demise.
How can I bear to hear music played,
and follow the path of rebellion and disorder?"
Zòng's general Qiáo Dàofú dragged him out,
intending to behead him.
Dàofú's mother was Yǐng's aunt,
and she rushed out barefoot to save him,
so he was spared.
After Zòng usurped the throne,
he summoned Yǐng with full ceremonial honors,
but again Yǐng did not come.
So Zòng arrested Yǐng and threw him into prison,
threatening him with weapons,
yet Yǐng's resolve grew firmer,
and he never wavered or changed,
until Shǔ was pacified,
ultimately without yielding his integrity.
In the twenty-fourth year of the Yuánjiā era,
the Inspector Lù Zhēng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Like Wáng Chù's defiance of the Yān army,
and Zhōu Kē's cursing of the King of Chǔ,
compared to Yǐng,
none could surpass him.
Truly, he is a loyal and brave man of our time,
a remnant of the heroic spirit of antiquity."
The Book of Sòng
Xú Guǎng,
courtesy name Yěrén.
When Huán Xuán initially usurped the throne,
and Emperor Ān was forced to leave the palace,
Guǎng stood in the ranks weeping bitterly,
his grief moving all those around him.
When Emperor Wǔ accepted the abdication,
and Emperor Gōng yielded the throne,
Guǎng was again overcome with sorrow,
tears and snivel streaming down his face.
Xiè Huì saw this
and said to him:
"Surely, Lord Xú, this is somewhat excessive."
Guǎng wiped his tears and replied:
"My position is different from yours.
You are a founding minister of the Sòng court,
while I am a remnant elder of the Jìn house.
Matters of sorrow and joy
naturally differ in their time."
He then sighed even more deeply.
Pleading his advanced age and declining health,
he begged to return to his native place.
He had a fondness for reading,
and even in old age never tired of it.
Leaning Palace
In the fifth year of Dàmíng, Sūn Jí conscripted a group of men.
His younger brother Sà was supposed to report for duty,
but failed to arrive by the appointed time.
Jí went to the prefecture himself to explain that as the head of the household,
he had ordered his brother not to go,
and thus the fault lay with him.
He requested to take Sà's place,
but Sà also declined,
insisting on taking responsibility himself.
Prefect Zhāng Dài doubted their sincerity,
so he placed Jí and Sà in separate locations,
and reported saying:
"They agree to substitute for each other,
and their expressions are both content,
willingly facing death. "
Jí's wife, Xǔ Shì, also sent a message to admonish her husband, saying:
"You are the head of the family,
how can you place the blame on the young man?
When the master of the family was passing,
he entrusted the young man to your care.
Now, he remains unmarried,
the family's affairs are unsettled.
You have already lost two sons,
what else is there to regret?"
Dài submitted a report based on the events,
and Emperor Xiào Wǔ issued a special decree pardoning the crime.
"History of the Song Dynasty."
King Zhòu built the Leaning Palace,
constructed halls of jade and terraces of jasper,
adorned them with beautiful jade,
which took seven years to complete.
It spanned ten lǐ in breadth,
and reached a thousand zhàng in height.
There were one hundred large palaces,
and seventy-three smaller palace sites,
with nine markets within the palace grounds.
"Records of the Emperors and Kings"
Lù Chāozhī,
a man of Wú,
was esteemed by Prince Zǐ Mào of Jìn'ān for his purity, tranquility, and refinement.
When Zǐ Mào raised an army,
and after his defeat,
Yú Línzhī urged Lù Chāozhī to flee.
He replied:
"All men must die;
this is nothing to fear.
If I were to flee,
not only would I betray Prince Jìn'ān's favor,
but I would also fear being laughed at by Tián Héng's retainers."
Xuán Miǎo and others, moved by his righteousness,
intended to detain him and bring him back to the capital,
and Lù Chāozhī sat upright awaiting his fate.
A student of Lù Chāozhī, surnamed Zhōu,
believed that killing Lù Chāozhī would bring a reward,
so he waited until Lù Chāozhī was seated,
and beheaded him from behind.
His head fell, yet his body remained upright.
Xuán Miǎo praised his integrity,
and gave him a lavish burial.
Zhōu also helped carry the coffin,
but before it left the doorway,
the coffin fell,
directly crushing his head,
and he died instantly.
Those who heard of this all believed it to be the work of heavenly justice.
From *The History of the Southern Dynasties*
Hāo Gōng
During the Zhōu dynasty, virtuous influence was harmonious and pervasive,
so mugwort grew abundantly and was used as palace pillars,
hence the name "Mugwort Palace."
The Great Dai Records state:
"When Zhōu's virtue flourished,
plants and trees grew luxuriantly,
mugwort could be used for building palaces,
thus named the Mugwort Hall.
After gaining the entire realm,
they subsequently established their capital at Hào."
The Bamboo Annals
and The Annals of Lü Buwei state:
"The Zhōu dynasty's Bright Hall had thatched roofs and mugwort pillars,
with earthen steps of three levels,
to demonstrate frugality,
referring precisely to this matter."
An annotation notes:
"Thatch can be used for roofing,
but mugwort cannot bear the load of pillars.
Although this is said to exemplify frugality,
it is actually something unheard of and mistaken."
Emperor Míng fell gravely ill,
and Prince Nánkāng Lián was ordered to commit suicide at his residence.
Bì guarded the corpse,
weeping and wailing day and night,
his grief moving passersby.
At that time, all the princes were being executed along with their old associates,
and none dared to look on,
except for Bì, Zǐ Jùn the Prince of Héngyáng, and Yán Zhí the court lecturer,
who each arranged the funeral affairs,
earning contemporary praise for their integrity.
Bì, styled Shìqīng,
was a native of Jìyáng.
In Wú Jūn's "Spring and Autumn of Qí",
his clansman Bì, who served as Attendant Officer in Yǎnzhōu,
was the son of the Imperial Gatekeeper Yù,
and shared the same name as Bì,
so people called the former Filial Bì,
to distinguish them.

Huàrén
In the final years of the Shénguī era of the Wèi dynasty,
Qīnghé King Yuán Yè, serving as Grand Commandant, appointed Yáng Gù as his Assistant Officer.
After Yáng Gù was implicated and killed due to Yè's victimization,
Yuán Yì took control of the government,
causing shock and fear throughout the court and the populace.
Yè's sons, disciples, and officials all feared disaster,
hiding and avoiding public appearances.
Those who had been deeply favored by Yè
felt increasingly insecure.
Yáng Gù, having once been appointed by Yè,
went alone to the place of mourning to express his grief fully,
weeping bitterly for a long time,
before returning.
Vice Director Yóu Zhào heard of this and sighed,
"Even Luán Bù and Wáng Xiū could not surpass this.
Is he not a true gentleman?
Such a man."
(From the Original Biography)
During King Mù of Zhōu's reign, a magician from the westernmost lands came to visit and traveled with the king.
The king then grasped the magician's sleeve,
soared upward,
and stopped at mid-heaven.
They reached the magician's palace,
which was constructed of gold and silver,
adorned with pearls and jade,
rising above the clouds and rain.
The king considered it a treasure, believing it to be the Pure Capital and Purple Tenuity,
with heavenly music widespread,
the dwelling place of emperors and kings.
From "Lièzǐ"
Prince Liáng Wáng Lín raised a righteous army for Liáng,
but was killed by Wú Míngchè,
his head was sent to Jiànkāng,
and hung in the marketplace.
Lín's former subordinate Zhū Yáng sent a letter to Chén's Vice Director Xú Líng,
requesting Lín's head,
saying:
"I consider that when Diǎnwǔ was about to perish,
Xú Guàng became the surviving elder of the Jìn house;
when Dāngtú had already declined,
Mǎ Fú was called a loyal minister of the Wèi court.
The late Liáng Duke Jiànníng, Lín,
lightly gave his person to die for his lord,
pledging his life to the state.
He only harbored the resolve of Bāo Xū,
yet ultimately met the fate of Cháng Hóng's blue blood.
So that his body lies in the nine springs,
his head travels a thousand miles,
body and head in separate places,
with no divination for his burial mound.
I, Yáng, early on served in a minor post,
participating in the lower seats,
receiving the spittle and grasp of Lord Xuē,
and bearing the recognition and treatment of Duke Wèi.
Therefore, I wet my sleeves with tears,
grieving for a recognizable face,
my intestines writhing and head aching,
aching for a face as if still alive.
I humbly consider the sage's grace broad and deep,
a clear edict has been issued,
pardoning the weeping of Wáng Jīng,
allowing the burial of Tián Héng.
Though I, Yáng, am lowly as straw,
I too have a heart.
Lín once governed Shòuyáng,
and traveled in the region south of the Yangtze;
I wish to return him to that territory,
and restore his eternal rest.
So that once the lonely grave is built,
perhaps swallows will fly carrying earth;
a grand stele erected,
may there always be those who shed tears.
Recently, old acquaintances like Wáng Wǎn and others have already submitted memorials,
relying on the court's deliberation,
but their petitions were not granted.
In the past, when Lián Gōng passed away,
his tomb was built by the Féi River;
when Shūsūn departed,
catalpas were planted by the Sháobēi.
From this it is said,
there are indeed precedents.
Do not let it be that under the walls of Shòuchūn,
only the man who reported Gé is remembered;
on the island of Cāngzhōu,
there alone is the mourner of Tián.
I risk death to present my plea,
awaiting punishment.
"Líng praised his integrity and resolve,
and also Wú Míngchè repeatedly dreamed of Lín requesting his head;
together they memorialized to the Chén sovereign and it was permitted."
(From History of the Southern Dynasties)
Chǔ Palace
Xú Líng,
courtesy name Xiàomù,
was by nature pure and frugal,
never seeking personal gain, sharing his salary and emoluments with his relatives.
During the Dàjiàn era,
he received the revenue from the Jiànchāng district,
and when the households of the district delivered rice to the waterside,
any of Xú Líng's relatives who were impoverished
he allowed to take it,
so it was exhausted within a few days,
and his own family soon faced destitution.
His subordinates found this strange and asked him the reason.
Xú Líng replied:
"I have carts, oxen, and clothing that I can sell;
do other families have anything they can sell?"
(Book of Chén)
Sīmǎ Gǎo,
courtesy name Wénshēng.
During the Chéngshèng era,

you still cherish the sentiment of seeing off the departed."

Wáng Yuánguī,

was by nature filial,
and served his mother with great diligence,
never leaving her side from morning till night.
During the Liáng dynasty, a flash flood struck Shānyīn County,
sweeping away residential dwellings.
Yuánguī possessed only one small boat.
In haste, he helped his mother, younger sister, and orphaned nephew into the boat,
then took up the oars himself and rowed away,
leaving his own three children
stranded atop a tree.
When the floodwaters receded,
they were found safe and sound.
People of the time all praised his utmost virtuous conduct.

As Jiànxù was about to take up his post,

He thus said to Jiànxù:
"Hesitate for a while,
and we shall share wealth and honor together."
Jiànxù, considering himself a minister of the Zhōu dynasty,
showed righteous indignation on his countenance,
and said:
"Your Excellency's intention
is not something I wish to hear."
Emperor Gāozǔ was displeased,
and Jiànxù then departed.
At the beginning of the Kāihuáng era, he came to court,
and the Emperor said to him:

Jiànxù bowed his head to the ground and replied:
"My position is not like that of Xú Guǎng,
but my sentiment resembles that of Yáng Biāo."
The Emperor laughed and said:
"Although I do not fully understand literary allusions,
I know that your words are disrespectful."

Wáng Yìfāng,
a native of Liánshuǐ, Sìzhōu.
He was orphaned and poor in his youth,
served his mother with great diligence,
was well-versed in the Five Classics,
yet upright and aloof, walking his own path.
Initially, he passed the imperial examination in the míngjīng category,
and thus went to the capital.
On the way, he met a man traveling on foot,
who said his father was the magistrate of Yǐngshàng,
and upon hearing that his father was critically ill,
he was rushing day and night to get there.
The traveler could not proceed,
and had no plan to resolve the situation.
Yìfāng dismounted from his horse,
gave it to him,
and left without revealing his name.
Later, he became a proofreader for the Crown Prince,
but not long after,
he was implicated for associating with Zhāng Liàng, the Minister of Justice,
and was demoted to assistant magistrate of Jí'ān, Dānzhōu.
In the twenty-third year of the Zhēnguàn era,
he was reassigned as assistant magistrate of Huánshuǐ.
At that time, Zhāng Liàng's nephew Zhāng Jiǎo was exiled to Dānzhōu,
came to rely on Yìfāng but passed away,
entrusting his wife and children to him on his deathbed,
and requesting that his body be returned to his hometown.
Yìfāng and Jiǎo's wife made a vow to the sea god,
had a servant carry the coffin,
instructed Jiǎo's wife to hold her infant child,
and ride on Yìfāng's horse,
while he himself walked alongside them on foot to return.
First, they went to Yuánwǔ to bury Jiǎo,
and reported the funeral to Zhāng Liàng.
Then, he escorted Jiǎo's wife and children back to their home,
and proceeded to Huánshuǐ.

Guō Yuánzhèn at sixteen entered the National University,
with Xuē Jì and Zhào Yànzhāo as friends.
At that time, a family letter arrived,
sending four hundred thousand coins for his examination provisions.
Suddenly, someone in mourning clothes knocked at the door,
saying:
"Five generations remain unburied,
each in different places.
Now I wish to move them simultaneously for burial,
but lack the financial means.
Hearing that your family letter has arrived,
could you possibly assist me?"
Guō immediately ordered a cart,
loaded all the money at once and sent it away,
keeping nothing back,
without even asking the person's name.
He was deeply ridiculed for this by Xuē and Zhào.
Yuánzhèn calmly replied:
"Helping them with such an important matter—
what is there to ridicule?"
That year, his provisions ran out,
and he ultimately did not complete the examinations.
