Lǐ Yuē was the son of the Duke of Qiān, who served as Vice Director of the Ministry of War.
His insight and character were pure and broad-minded,
far surpassing worldly norms.
Once, while traveling by river,
he sailed alongside a merchant from the Western Regions.
The merchant fell gravely ill,
and invited Lǐ Yuē to meet,
entrusting his two daughters to him—
both of exceptional beauty—
and also bequeathing him a pearl.
Lǐ Yuē assented to everything.
After the merchant died,
his wealth, amounting to tens of thousands,
was fully documented and handed over to the authorities,
while Lǐ Yuē sought suitable marriages for the two daughters.
When initially encoffining the merchant,
Lǐ Yuē had personally placed a luminous pearl in the mouth,
unknown to anyone.
Later, when the deceased merchant’s relatives came to claim the assets,
Lǐ Yuē petitioned the authorities,
requesting an exhumation for inspection.
The luminous pearl was indeed found inside.
Such were his discreet acts of integrity.

When Yáng Píng was found guilty of an offense,
he was demoted to the position of wèi in Línhè,
and none of his friends or relatives dared to see him off.
Only Xú Huì accompanied him to Lántián,
where he bid farewell to Yáng Píng.
The former chancellor Quán Déyù, who had the deepest friendship with Yáng Píng,
learned of Xú Huì's actions,
and thus said to Xú Huì:
"Today, seeing off Línhè (Yáng Píng),
is indeed an act of great kindness,
but might it not bring you trouble?"
Xú Huì replied:
"I, Huì, received Yáng Gōng's care and favor since my days as a commoner.
Now that he is being exiled,
how could I bear to remain silent?
If, in the future,
you, Excellency, were slandered by treacherous villains,
and fell out of favor, being sent away,
how could I lightly bid you farewell?"
Quán Déyù praised his sincerity and earnestness,
and spoke highly of him.
Within a few days at court,
the Vice Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Yíjiǎn requested to appoint him as a監察 (investigating censor).
Xú Huì said to Lǐ Yíjiǎn:

how did you come to trust me,
and thus reward and promote me?"
Lǐ Yíjiǎn replied:
"I heard that you saw off Yáng Línhè (Yáng Píng),
regardless of the risk involved;
how could you be willing to betray the state?"
From then on, he became well-known.

daring not to be less than in the household of Duke Qízhāng!"
Déyù did not take offense,
and Zhòngyǐng always felt grateful for Déyù's recognition.

using the salary to support the southern residence.

he was quite displeased.

what use would that be today?"
Grand Marshal Lǐ had long been condemned,
his family was destitute,
and the ancestral sacrifices had ceased.
I often feel sincere and increasing pain and sorrow.

Lǚ Yǎn served as the military commissioner's judge of Cāngzhōu.
When Liú Shǒuguāng captured Cāngzhōu,
Lǚ Yǎn was apprehended,
and his clan was executed, including his son.
Lǚ Qí, at fifteen years of age,
was about to be killed,
when a man named Zhào Yù,
a righteous scholar from Yōujì,
who had long been a guest of Lǚ Yǎn,
seeing Qí in peril,
deceived the executioners by saying:
"This youth is my own brother,
I beg you not to harm him unjustly."
He then took him away.
Qí had a foot ailment,
so Yù carried him on his back as they traveled,
covering several hundred lǐ,
changing their names,
and begging for food along the way,
thus escaping the disaster.
Qí often felt that Yù had saved him from calamity,
and wished to repay him generously.
When Yù fell ill,
Qí personally attended to him,
providing him with medicine and care.
After Yù's death,
Qí arranged his funeral on behalf of the family.
Yù's son later said:
"Since I, Wéndù, was orphaned,
and was young, Qí instructed me with great dedication,
until I reached adulthood,
passed the imperial examination,
and soon advanced in my official career,
all due to Qí's efforts."
Contemporary commentators held that without Yù's righteousness, the Lǚ family line could not have been preserved,
and without Qí's benevolence, the Zhào orphan could not have been nurtured;
only these two gentlemen embodied benevolence and righteousness,
becoming a celebrated tale among the scholars of Yān and Zhào.

During the Jiànzhōng Jìngguó era,
Sū Shì returned north from Dānzhōu,
and chose to reside in Yángxiàn.
A local scholar named Shào Mínzhān studied under Sū Shì,
and purchased a house for him,
costing five hundred strings of coins.
Sū Shì exhausted his savings to barely afford it,
and selected an auspicious day to move in.
After settling in,
he took a moonlit stroll with Shào one night,
and happened upon a village,
where they heard a woman weeping bitterly.
Sū Shì lingered to listen,
then pushed the door open with Shào and entered,
asking the old woman why she was so grief-stricken.
The woman replied:
"I have a home
that has been passed down for a hundred years.
My unworthy son
sold it to someone,
and today I must move out.
To suddenly bid farewell to this century-old residence
is why I weep."
Sū Shì was also moved to sorrow,
and asked where her former home was located—
it turned out to be the very house he had acquired.
He repeatedly comforted her,
saying:
"Do not grieve so deeply, madam.
I shall return this residence to you."
He immediately had the property deed brought forth and burned it in her presence.
Summoning her son,
he instructed him to bring his mother back to the old home the next day,
without demanding repayment.
Sū Shì then returned to Pílíng,
never purchasing another house,
but borrowing the Sūn family's residence at Gùtáng Bridge for temporary lodging.
That year in July,
Sū Shì passed away in the borrowed dwelling.

A Beauty
Yán Shūzǐ was alone in his house,
and the widow next door was also alone in her house.
At night,
a violent storm arrived,
and her house collapsed.
The woman hurried over,
and Yán Shūzǐ let her in,
having her hold a candle.
By daybreak the candle had burned out,
so he tore down part of his roof to continue providing light.
He considered himself not cautious enough in avoiding suspicion.
As for those who are cautious,
they are like the man from Lǔ.
There was a man from Lǔ who was alone in his house,
and the widow next door was also alone in her house.
At night,
a violent storm arrived,
and the widow's house collapsed.
She hurried over to seek shelter.
The man from Lǔ closed his door
and did not let her in.
The widow spoke to him through the window:
"How unkind
to not let me in!"
The man from Lǔ replied:
"I have heard that men and women under sixty should not stay together.
Now you are young,
and I am also young,
therefore I dare not let you in."
The woman said:
"Why aren't you like Liǔxià Huì,
who warmed a woman who couldn't get through the gate,
yet no one in the state accused him of impropriety?"
The man from Lǔ said:
"Liǔxià Huì could do that,
but I certainly cannot.
I will use what I cannot do
to learn from what Liǔxià Huì could do."
When Confucius heard this,
he said:
"Excellent!
Those who wish to learn from Liǔxià Huì
have never been like this man.
He aims for perfection without imitation -
can this be called wisdom?"

Emperor Guāngwǔ once asked Sòng Hóng about scholars of broad learning,
and Hóng recommended Huán Tán of the Pei State,
a man of talent and extensive knowledge,
nearly comparable to Yáng Xióng and the father and son Liú Xiàng.
Thereupon, he summoned Tán
and appointed him as a court gentleman for consultation and a palace attendant.
Whenever the emperor held banquets,
he would order Tán to play the zither,
favoring its elaborate melodies.
Hóng, upon hearing this, was displeased
and regretted having recommended him.
Waiting until Tán had left the palace,
he sat in his official residence in full court attire
and sent an officer to summon him.
When Tán arrived, Hóng did not offer him a seat
but reproached him, saying:
"The reason I recommended you
was to have you assist the state with virtue and morality,
yet now you repeatedly present decadent music,
disrupting the elegant and classical hymns.
This is not the conduct of a loyal and upright man.
Can you reform yourself,
or shall I have you impeached according to the law?"
Tán kowtowed and apologized,
and only after a long while was he dismissed.
Later, at a grand assembly of officials,
the emperor ordered Tán to play the zither.
When Tán saw Hóng,
he lost his composure,
and the emperor, surprised, inquired about it.
Hóng then rose from his seat,
removed his official cap, and apologized, saying:
"The reason I recommended Huán Tán
was in the hope that he would guide Your Majesty with loyalty and integrity,
yet he has caused the court to indulge in decadent music.
This is my fault."
The emperor changed his expression and apologized,
ordering Hóng to resume his attire.
Thereafter, he no longer ordered Tán to serve as a palace attendant.

The Epang Palace measured three li from east to west,

where wine was served from carriages

Xiāo Hé constructed the Wèi Yāng Palace.

saying to Hé:
"The world is in turmoil,
after years of hardship,
the outcome is still uncertain.
Why then construct such a lavish palace?"
Hé replied:
"Since the world is not yet at peace,
it is opportune to complete the palace.

without splendor, there is no majesty.

The Emperor was pleased,
and thus moved the capital from Lì Yáng.

would prostrate themselves upon glimpsing his dust.
Yet Càn merely greeted Zhǎo with a simple bow.
His family members especially reproached him for this,
to which Càn replied:
"How could I lower myself to the level of common customs?"
The emperor
Tiānliáng
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng raised an army,
and all the provinces and commanderies surrendered upon hearing the news,
yet Yuán Áng alone defended his territory against them.
The Emperor wrote to him personally, saying:
"Exhausting one's strength for a foolish ruler
does not suffice to be called loyalty;
having one's family slaughtered and exterminated
is not what is meant by filial piety.
If both loyalty and filial piety are lost,
what then will you rely on?"
Yuán Áng replied:
"Even for a single meal, a small favor given,
one would still repay with one's life;
how much more so when one has eaten another's provisions,
should one suddenly forget it in a single day?
Not only would public opinion not permit it,
but I also fear that you, illustrious sir, would despise me."
(From History of the Southern Dynasties)
Tiānliáng Palace,
its beams reaching to the sky,
speaks of the palace's height.
Above
Qí's Imperial Censor Zhōngchéng Yán Jiànyuǎn,
when Liáng Wǔdì received the abdication, Jiànyuǎn,
refused to eat and in anger died after several days.
Wǔdì heard of this,
and said:
"I merely responded to Heaven and followed the people's will,
what concern was it of the empire's scholar-officials,
that Yán Jiànyuǎn would go to such an extent."
"Xù Shì Shuō"
Zhāomíng was strolling with renowned scholars in the rear pond of Xuánpǔ Garden when
Fānyú Guǐ enthusiastically suggested that female musicians should perform there.
Zhāomíng did not respond,
but instead directly recited Zuǒ Sī's "Summoning the Recluse" poem:
"Why must we have strings and bamboo?
Mountains and waters possess pure music."
Guǐ felt ashamed and desisted.
From "The Book of Liáng"
Jílíng Palace
At Huáyīn, there is the Jílíng Palace,
located at the foot of Mount Huá.
It was constructed by Emperor Wǔ
with the intention to gather and honor immortals,
such as Wáng Qiáo and Chì Sōngzǐ.
Thus, the hall was named
to preserve the traces of immortals,
with the gate facing south called the Wàngxiān Gate.
"Huán Tán's Immortal Fu"
records that Emperor Wǔ toured and inspected the Five Great Mountains,
with ample sacrifices and offerings,
leading to the establishment of the palace.
It is called Jílíng Palace beneath it.
"Record of the Western Mountain"
mentions Jílíng Palace,
Jíxiān Palace,
Cúnxiān Hall,
Cúnshén Hall,
Wàngxiān Terrace,
Wàngxiān Temple,
all within the boundaries of Huáyīn County,
all named after Emperor Wǔ's palaces and temples.
"Huángtú"
refers to an inscription on the Hàn "Western Mountain Huáshān Temple Stele," which briefly states:
Filial Emperor Wǔ performed the rites of fēng and shàn,
touring and inspecting the Five Great Mountains,
and established a palace beneath them.
This palace was called Jílíng,
the palace hall called Cúnxiān,
and the hall gate called Wàngxiān Gate.
"Collected Records of Ancient Stones" notes:
"Only this stele of Jílíng is seen."
According to
geographical records, Huáyīn has Jílíng Palace,
established by Emperor Wǔ.
"Commentary on the Water Classic" states:
"The Fū River,
flows north past Jílíng Palace."
Thus, its mention is not limited to this stele alone.
The so-called Cúnxiān Hall
and Wàngxiān Gate
are not recorded in other books.
"Record of Metal and Stone"
confirms that
both Jílíng and Cúnxiān
are mentioned in the records,
yet the interpretations of the two gentlemen are as follows.
Xú Miǎn served as the Minister of Personnel.
Once he gathered with his disciples for an evening gathering.
A guest named Yú Hǎo requested the position of Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
Xú Miǎn sternly replied:
"Tonight we may only discuss the breeze and the moonlight,
not public affairs."
People of the time admired his impartiality.
Yù Yù,
styled Chéngxīng,
was upright by nature.
During Emperor Míng's reign, he served as General of the Martial Guards.
At that time, Yuán Yì, the Commander of the Imperial Guard, held power,
and all officials paid their respects to him,
but Yù alone gave a long bow without kneeling.
Soon he was appointed General Who Pacifies the West,
Governor of Liáng Province in the Eastern Region.
The scarlet dye of Liáng Province was the finest in the empire.
Yì sent him two thousand bolts of white silk,
ordering Yù to dye them,
but Yù refused and did not comply.
(Book of Wèi)
Gazing at the Immortals
In the third year of Yuánfēng, construction began on the Wàngxiān Palace.
"Records of the Cave of Truth"
Xiāo Yǐn,
courtesy name Shēngxiū,
while serving as magistrate of Jiànkāng,
received numerous requests from Palace Attendant Wú Jìn and eunuchs Lǐ Shàndù and Cài Tuō'ér,
all of which Xiāo Yǐn refused.
His nephew Xiāo Mì, then serving as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
admonished him:
"The influence of Lǐ and Cài
is feared by all in office.
You should make some considerations for yourself."
Xiāo Yǐn replied:
"In establishing my conduct,
I have my own principles from beginning to end.
How could I change my behavior for Lǐ and Cài?
At worst, I would only be dismissed from my post."
Wú Jìn ultimately fabricated an anonymous accusatory letter,
which Lǐ and Cài corroborated,
leading to Xiāo Yǐn's dismissal from office.
Book of Chén
Bùgāo
Yuán Xiàn,
styled Dézhāng,
was the grandson of Jūnzhèng and son of Áng.
During the Dàtóng era,
when examination candidates submitted policy responses,
many practiced bribery.
His retainer Cén Wénháo requested to prepare gifts,
but Jūnzhèng said:
"How could I use money to buy an official rank for my son?"
The examination officials resented him for this,
yet soon he achieved high honors in the examinations.
As a nobleman's son, he married Emperor Jiǎnwén's daughter, Princess Nánshā.
When Emperor Wǔ of Chén served as chancellor,
he appointed Xiàn as Minister of Revenue in the Secretariat.
At his first audience,
he merely bowed with hands clasped instead of prostrating,
whereupon the Imperial Secretary Wáng Mài said to Xiàn:
"Why do you deliberately oppose custom
by not bowing to the Recorder Duke?"
Xiàn replied:
"According to principle, I should not bow."
The Commandant of the Guards Zhào Zhīlǐ remarked:
"Yuán's demeanor is composed and proper,
truly possessing the style of Chén and Rǔ."
In the third year of Dàjiàn,
he was promoted to Imperial Censor.
At that time, Prince Shūyīng of Yùzhāng disregarded laws and regulations,
forcibly seizing people's horses.
Xiàn impeached Shūyīng based on the facts, leading to his dismissal,
from then on, both court and commoners held him in awe.
Once, while attending a banquet at Chéngxiāng Pavilion,
after the guests had departed,
Emperor Xuān detained Xiàn,
and with the Commandant of the Guards Fán Jùn, moved their mats to the mountain pavilion,
conversing and feasting all day.
The Emperor said to Jùn:
"The Yuán family indeed produces remarkable men."
When the Later Sovereign considered deposing the Crown Prince,
knowing that Xiàn would remonstrate,
he responded:
"Yuán Dézhāng is truly an upright and outspoken minister."
That very day, he was appointed Chief Minister of the Secretariat.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng,
when Suí troops invaded,
the Suí general Hèruò Bì advanced and set fire to the northern side gate of the palace city,
the guards all fled in disarray,
and court officials hid themselves,
only Xiàn remained by the sovereign's side.
The Later Sovereign said to him:
"I have always treated you no less than others,
today seeing you here,
truly, only in cold winter do we see the pine and cypress last.
This is not only due to my lack of virtue,
but also because the way of the gentry in Jiāngdōng is exhausted."
When they reached Cháng'ān,
Emperor Wén of Suí, admiring his noble conduct,
issued an edict praising him as the foremost of Jiāngbiǎo.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Lù Yóumíng studied under Zhōu Hóngzhèng,
excelling in discoursing on profound principles.
When Wáng Shìchōng usurped the imperial title,
he enfeoffed his son as the Prince of Hàn,
appointing Dé Míng as his tutor,
and went to his home
to perform the ceremony of presenting the teacher's gift.
Dé Míng felt ashamed of this,
so he took the mirabilite powder,
and lay down beneath the eastern wall.
When Wáng's son entered
and knelt by the bed,
Dé Míng pretended to have dysentery,
ultimately not speaking with him,
and subsequently moved due to illness to Chénggāo.
Later, when he entered the service of Táng Tàizōng,
he was appointed as an academician of the College of Literary Studies,
had Yán Lìběn paint his portrait,
and Chǔ Liàng composed a eulogy for him, saying:
"Classical scholarship is esteemed,
profound teachings can be followed,
diligent study is not far off,
the accomplished Confucian is here."
"Táng Xīn Yǔ"
In the capital region, there was the Bùgāo Palace.
"Records of the Capital"
Gazing into the Distance
Wéi Ānshí served as the Grand Secretary,
and was deeply resented by Zhāng Yìzhī, Wǔ Sānsī, and others.
Once, during a banquet held in the inner palace,
Yìzhī brought several Shu merchants, including Sòng Bàzǐ, to gamble in front of everyone.
Ānshí knelt and memorialized,
"Lowly merchants like those from Shu are unfit to attend this banquet."
He then turned to the attendants,
ordering them to drive the merchants out.
All those present turned pale with shock,
but Empress Wǔ Zétiān, recognizing the integrity of Ānshí's words,
consoled and encouraged him warmly.
At the time, Lù Yuánfāng, the Vice Minister of the Secretariat, was among the guests.
After retiring, he told others,
"This is a true chancellor,
far beyond what the rest of us can achieve."
Old Book of Tang
In Cháng'ān, there was the Wàngyuǎn Palace.
The emperor
Zhāng Yìzhī and Zhāng Chāngzōng once commissioned painters to depict the images of eighteen individuals including Wǔ Sānsī, Lǐ Qiáo, and Sū Wèidào,
naming it the "Portraits of Noble Scholars".
They frequently invited Zhū Jìngzé to participate in the affair,
but he firmly declined and would not comply,
such was his noble integrity and adherence to principle.
The Emperor
Drinking from a Cup and Stomach Ache
Wáng Máozhòng was favored by Emperor Xuánzōng,
and all officials attached themselves to him.
One day, when Máozhòng was marrying off his daughter,
the Emperor asked:
"What do you need?"
Máozhòng kowtowed,
and replied:
"Your subject has everything prepared,
but has not yet secured guests."
The Emperor said:
"Couldn't you invite the likes of Zhāng Yuè and Yuán Qiànyào?"
He replied:
"They are already secured."
The Emperor said:
"I know there is one person you cannot get,
it must be Sòng Jǐng."
He replied:
"It is exactly as Your Majesty says."
The Emperor laughed and said:
"I will summon the guests for you tomorrow."
The next day,
the Emperor said to the ministers:
"My servant Máozhòng has a wedding,
you all should go with the high officials to his residence."
Afterwards,
by noon the guests dared not lift their chopsticks,
waiting for Sòng Jǐng for a long time,
until he finally arrived.
He first took wine and bowed westward to give thanks,
drank not a full cup,
then abruptly claimed stomach ache and left.
"Continued Tales of the World"
At that time, Máozhòng's favor was unmatched,
whenever he attended banquets,
he was rewarded and sat with various princes and Jiǎng Jiǎo before the imperial tent,
sharing connected couches.
If Emperor Xuánzōng sometimes did not see him,
he would feel quietly as if something was missing;
when he saw him,
they would enjoy themselves all night,
sometimes until late in the day.
His wife was already entitled Lady of Guó State,
and his bestowed wife Lǐ Shì,
was also made a State Lady,
whenever they entered the court for audience,
both ladies received gifts together.
"Old Book of Tang"
Yánglíng
The Son of Heaven is solemn and serene,
purifying his heart in the jade tower,
storing his essence and seeking to express it,
searching for a companion to join him,
aligning with the palace of the yang spirit,
gathering in the garden where rituals honor the gods,
ascending the hall where praises are offered to the earth deity.
Yáng Xióng's "Rhapsody on Gānquán"
When Sòng Jǐng served as the military governor of Guǎng Prefecture,
Emperor Xuánzōng missed him,
and dispatched the palace eunuch Yáng Sīxù to ride post-haste to summon him back.
After Sòng Jǐng set out on the journey,
he ultimately did not exchange a single word with Yáng Sīxù.
Yáng Sīxù, being a favored general in the palace,
complained to Emperor Xuánzōng.
The emperor sighed for a long while,
and appointed Sòng Jǐng as Minister of Justice.
"Táng Yǔ Lín"
Shénguāng
Wèi Yuánzhōng's son Wèi Shēng married the daughter of Xíngyáng's Zhèng Yuǎn.
Wèi Shēng conspired with Crown Prince Jiemin to kill Wǔ Sānsī,
depose Empress Wěi,
but they failed,
and he was killed by rebel soldiers.
Wèi Yuánzhōng was implicated and imprisoned.
Zhèng Yuǎn then went to Wèi Yuánzhōng to demand a divorce document.
The day he obtained the divorce document,
he remarried his daughter the next day.
Palace Censor Má Chà was indignant about this,
and drafted a memorial impeaching Zhèng Yuǎn, stating:
"Zhèng Yuǎn accepted five million coins,
exchanging his daughter for an official position.
Once married to the state minister's family,
father and son enjoyed great prominence.
But as soon as Wèi Yuánzhōng was imprisoned,
he immediately sought private divorce.
The day he obtained the document,
he remarried her the next day.
If he claimed the marriage was mismatched,
it shouldn't have been contracted initially.
Since the union was happily established,
they should share the same grave in principle.
Before the husband's funeral concluded,
a new son-in-law was already arranged.
No evidence of entrusting death or orphans,
nor risking life in danger.
This is what we call polluting social ranks,
disgracing the scholarly class.
Confucian principles should come first,
requiring disciplinary reform.
I request judgment according to law,
with lifelong prohibition from office."
Zhèng Yuǎn was subsequently dismissed,
and both court and public praised Má Chà's impartiality.
From "Táng Xīn Yǔ"
Princess Āndìng first married Wáng Tóngjiǎo,
later married Wéi Zhuó,
and then married Cuī Shēn.
Cuī Shēn died first,
and when the princess passed away,
Wáng Tóngjiǎo's son Wáng Yóu, who was a royal son-in-law,
requested to bury her together with his father,
and an imperial edict specially permitted it.
The supervising secretary Xiàhóu Kuò objected, saying:
"When the princess first entered marriage,
the parasol tree was half dead;
by the time she remarried,
both lute and zither were gone.
Thus, during her lifetime,
she had already severed ties with her former husband,
and upon her death,
she should be buried according to the rites with her later husband.
Now if we follow Wáng Yóu's request,
and instead bury her with her former marriage,
I fear that if the soul is aware,
Wáng Tóngjiǎo would not accept her in the netherworld;
if the dead could rise,
Cuī Shēn would surely protest to the highest heavens.
The state has established regulations,
and matters should not overstep them.
I, though unworthy, have been entrusted with the duty of objection and correction,
dare not neglect my responsibility!
I request to refer this to the礼仪 officials for a definitive ruling."
The court all admired his stance.
The emperor
Entering the Western Garden,
visiting Shénguāng,
treading the Huì fields,
stepping upon the Lán Terrace.
"Rhapsody on the Imperial Hunt"
Zhāng Yàn notes:
"Shénguāng,
is the name of a palace."
Sū Guī,
styled Chāngróng,
served successively as the prefectural governor of Lǎng and Shè.
At that time, Lái Jùnchén was demoted to a military advisor in the prefecture,
and people feared he would be reinstated.
Many sent letters to Guī,
but Guī rebuked the messengers, saying:
"I am the governor of this prefecture;
my rank and duties are clearly defined.
How could I excessively accommodate a petty man?"
Thus, he did not send the letters. Before Jùnchén arrived, he recalled this
and resented Guī for it,
leading to Guī's repeated assignments to remote posts,
preventing him from returning to the capital for a long time.
(From the *New Book of Tang*)
Zhuólóng
In the ninth year of the Yánxī era under Emperor Huàn,
he performed rites to Huáng-Lǎo at the Zhuólóng Palace.
The Annals record
that he performed rites to Lǎozǐ at the Zhuólóng Palace,
using music reserved for suburban sacrifices to Heaven.
The Continued Hàn Records state:
"He adorned the Fānglín Garden and renovated the Zhuólóng Palace,
setting up a huágài canopy to perform rites to the Buddha and Lǎozǐ.
Was this not what is called 'leaving matters to the spirits'?"
The Discussion remarks
Lǐ Jífǔ,
styled Hóngxiàn,
in the nineteenth year of the Zhēnyuán era became Prefect of Ráo Prefecture.
Previously, the prefectural city had lost four prefects in succession,
so the official residence had been abandoned for seven years.
After the Duke took office,
he ordered the locks opened, cleared away the thorns, and resided there.
The prefectural officials firmly insisted there were hauntings,
but the Duke said:
"Spirits favor the upright;
maintain integrity and spirits will withdraw.
Evil cannot overcome virtue;
lose virtue and evil arises.
Residing here depends on the person."
"Táng Yǔ Lín"
When Lǐ Jífǔ served as chancellor,
there was a dining table in the Hall of State Affairs.
It was believed among the officials that moving it would lead to the dismissal of the chancellor,
so it had remained untouched for fifty years.
Lǐ Jífǔ said:
"This is a place where we gather daily to discuss governance.
How can we allow a decaying object to remain filthy and uncleared?
Such superstitious beliefs
are not worth heeding.
If I am to be dismissed for this,
I would gladly accept it."
He ordered the table removed and burned,
and beneath it, fourteen baskets of accumulated dirt were shoveled away.
Commentators praised his uprightness.
From "Records of Anecdotes"
Chéngguāng
Péi Dù did not believe in occult arts,
nor did he favor consuming elixirs.
He often told others:
"Chicken, pork, fish, and garlic—
when encountered, I eat them;
whether one dies of illness or old age,
when the time comes, it simply happens."
From "Records of Conversations"
Emperor Shun appointed Zhǒng Gǎo to supervise the Crown Prince at the Chengguang Palace.
"Biography"
Cuī Xián,
styled Chóngyì,
was a man of unwavering integrity and moral uprightness,
highly esteemed by his contemporaries.
When Péi Dù returned from Xìngyuán for an audience with the emperor,
Lǐ Féngjí, unwilling
to see Dù re-enter the Zhōngshū Province,
instigated the Capital Governor Liú Qīchǔ—
a member of Féngjí's faction—
along with over ten others to slander Dù.
Meanwhile, court officials who vacillated between both sides
daily crowded Dù's gate.
One day, as Dù hosted guests with wine,
Qīchǔ pretended to seek Dù's favor,
bending close to Péi's ear to whisper.
Xián, disgusted by this affectation,
raised his goblet and rebuked Dù, saying:
"The Chancellor should not permit a subordinate official to whisper in your ear."
Dù laughed and drank the penalty wine,
leaving Qīchǔ ill at ease.
He hurriedly departed,
while all the seated guests admired Xián's boldness.
(Old Book of Táng)
The Great Beginning was bright and clear,
Wú had the Tàichū Palace,
which measured three hundred zhàng square,
constructed by Sūn Quán.
The Zhāomíng Palace,
measuring five hundred zhàng square,
was built by Sūn Hào.
The "Tàikāng Geographical Records"
notes that the Wúzhì, to avoid the Jìn taboo, changed the name to Xiǎnmíng.
In Cháng'ān,
there was a competition for epitaphs,
as if in a marketplace.
When a high official passed away,
his doorway became as bustling as a market,
to the point of clamorous disputes,
not initiated by the bereaved family.
When Péi Jūn's son requested an inscription from Wéi Guànzhī,
he offered ten thousand bolts of silk.
Wéi refused, saying:
"I would rather starve to death
than compose one carelessly."
(Guó Shǐ Bǔ)
Hán Yù in his dealings with others,
remained unchanged whether in glory or decline,
and when observing the powerful and wealthy,
he treated them as servants,
staring blankly without regard.
Emperor Mùzōng appointed Hán Yù as the Capital Governor,
and the six armies dared not break the law,
whispering among themselves:
"This is the one who even wanted to burn the Buddha's bone,
how could we offend him?"
Continued Accounts of World Tales
Free and Unfettered
Lǐ Shīzhōng,
styled Chéngzhī,
when he was still a child,
pleaded his father Lǐ Wěi's merits at court,
but received no response for a long time.
He personally went to the water-clock office and presented his petition to Duke Wèi of Hán,
who said:
"If you truly study,
you will naturally obtain an official rank through examinations,
there's no need to repeatedly seek rewards."
Chéngzhī replied:
"My father's achievements and faults remain unresolved,
I deeply fear he may pass away before me,
leaving me unable to face him in the afterlife,
thus I endure the pain of speaking for myself.
If I sought office,
with my modest literacy,
achieving second place in the imperial examination would not be difficult."
Duke Wèi had placed second in the examination under Wáng Yáochén's cohort,
hence Chéngzhī's remark.
The Duke was startled upon hearing this,
and some say although Duke Wèi's virtue commanded universal respect,
he never reconciled with Chéngzhī throughout his life.
After Chéngzhī passed the examination,
his official rank gradually rose,
and his reputation for integrity grew stronger.
Later, when Wáng Ānshí served as prime minister under Emperor Shénzōng,
advocating the "Three Things Not to Fear,"
Chéngzhī strongly denounced him.
Upon the death of Vice Censor-in-chief Lǚ Xiànkě,
Chéngzhī mourned him with a poem,
containing the lines:
"When villains advance, the worthy must retreat,
Loyal ministers die for the nation's woes.
What purpose does my life ultimately serve?
I wish to journey to the netherworld."
Wáng Ānshí's faction member Lǚ Huìqíng grew even more resentful of him,
and Chéngzhī never attained high office throughout his life.
From Shàoshì Wénjiàn Lù
Mùróng Xī constructed the Palace of Carefree Ease.
From "Gāo Lǚ's Records of Yān."
Wáng Ānshí first participated in major governance,
one day while reading Yàn Yuánxiàn's short lyrics,
Wáng Ānshí said:
"How can a prime minister possibly write lyrics?"
Wáng Ānguó replied:
"He was merely occasionally pleased with himself and wrote them,
but his achievements were by no means limited to this."
Lǚ Huìqīng, who held an academic post,
was also present,
and abruptly said:
"Governing must begin with banishing licentious music,
how much more so should one avoid composing it oneself!"
Píngfǔ said with a stern expression:
"Banishing licentious music
is not as important as keeping away flatterers."
Lǚ was greatly ashamed.
"Miscellaneous Records from the Eastern Pavilion"
Jiǔhuá
In Yè County, the Bronze Sparrow Terrace,
to the north, Shí Hǔ built a palace,
arranged in three-by-three positions,
called Jiǔhuá.
The palace beams—
Shěn Yuē's poem reads:
"Shining upon the Sparrow Terrace,
wandering in the shade of Jiǔhuá."
"The Illustrated Classic"
Emperor Shénzōng once praised Zhāng Āndào's merits to Zhāng Dūn,
asking if Dūn knew him.
Dūn later informed Lǚ Huìqíng of this,
and the next day, Huìqíng happened to enter the court alongside Āndào.
He relayed the emperor's words to Āndào,
adding:
"You are about to receive a major appointment."
Āndào wrinkled his nose and did not respond.
That evening, while Āndào was sitting with a guest,
Dūn arrived at his gate with attendants, requesting an audience.
Āndào had someone decline on his behalf, saying:
"We have never been acquainted,
so I dare not accept your visit."
Dūn left in shame and embarrassment.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ hosted a banquet for his ministers.
As dusk fell and they were deep in their cups, the lamps and candles went out.
Someone tugged at the robe of a beautiful woman.
The woman seized the opportunity to snap the tassel of his hat,
then informed the king, urging him to bring a light quickly
to identify the one with the broken tassel.
The king said:
"I provided wine for my subjects,
causing them to become drunk and lose propriety.
How can I shame a gentleman to uphold a woman's honor?"
He then ordered all over a hundred ministers to break off their hat tassels before lighting the lamps,
and the feast concluded with utmost joy.
Three years later,
when Chǔ battled with Jìn,
one minister consistently fought at the forefront,
engaging in five clashes with five vigorous charges,
leading the repulse of the enemy
and ultimately securing victory.
King Zhuāng, surprised, inquired of him,
to which he replied:
"I am the one whose tassel was broken that night."
From "Shuō Yuàn"
Ten Palaces
Zhāng Ānshì,
courtesy name Zǐrú,
served as Commandant of the Palace Gentlemen.
A gentleman once got drunk,
and urinated in the palace hall.
The officer in charge reported it to enforce the law,
but Ānshì said:
"How do we know he didn't accidentally spill his drink?
How can we convict someone for a minor fault!"
Another gentleman had illicit relations with a palace maid,
and the maid's brother reported it.
Ānshì said:
"The slave is making false accusations out of anger,
slandering an educated official."
It was remarked that:
"He would often conceal others' faults like this,
always acting in this manner."
From History of the Former Han Dynasty
The Ten Palaces are located within the Chángfù Garden five li north of Jiāngdū County,
nestled against the forest and beside the stream,
spanning the heights across the hill,
arranged according to the terrain,
all established by Emperor Suí Yángdì.
They are named Guīyàn Palace, Huíliú Palace, Jiǔlǐ Palace, Sōnglín Palace, Fēnglín Palace, Dàléi Palace, Xiǎoléi Palace, Chūncǎo Palace, Jiǔhuá Palace, and Guāngfén Palace,
these are called the Ten Palaces.
"Shídào Zhì Shòuchūn Tújīng"
Bǐng Jí,
courtesy name Shǎoqīng,
served as chancellor during Emperor Xuān's reign,
towards his subordinate officials and clerks,
always concealed their faults and highlighted their merits.
His carriage driver was fond of wine and frequently neglected his duties,
once while accompanying Bǐng Jí on an outing,
he got drunk and vomited on the chancellor's carriage.
The chief clerk of the West Bureau reported this and wanted to dismiss him,
but Bǐng Jí said:
"To lose a capable man over drunken indulgence,
where else could this person find acceptance?
The West Bureau should endure this,
it's merely soiling the chancellor's carriage mat."
Thus he was not dismissed.

Hé Wǔ,
courtesy name Jūngōng.
Dài Shèng, Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng,
who was known in the classics as Xiǎo Dài,
governed with many unlawful practices. Previous regional inspectors,
considering him a great Confucian scholar, tolerated him.
When Hé Wǔ became Regional Inspector,
he toured his jurisdiction and reviewed prisoners,
making recommendations to the commandery.
Dài Shèng said:
"What does this junior know,
daring to disrupt others' governance!"
He made no decisions on any cases.
Hé Wǔ sent his assistants to investigate and uncover his crimes.
Dài Shèng,
fearing punishment, resigned voluntarily.
Later, as an Erudite,
he slandered Hé Wǔ at court.
Hé Wǔ heard of this
but never exposed his misconduct.
When Dài Shèng's son and his followers became bandits,
they were captured
and imprisoned in Lújiāng.
Dài Shèng believed his son would surely be executed.
Hé Wǔ judged the case impartially,
and the son ultimately avoided death.
From then on,
Dài Shèng felt ashamed and became respectful.

The Great Ming Palace in the upper capital,
originally named the Eternal Peace Palace,
was renamed the Great Ming Palace in the ninth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
to serve as a summer retreat for the Retired Emperor,
with all officials contributing funds for its construction.
Emperor Gāozōng, displeased with the dampness of the Western Palace,
commenced major renovations in the second year of the Lóngshuò era,
renaming it the Penglai Palace,
and changed it to the Hanyuan Palace in the first year of the Xiánhēng era.
"Treatise on Geography"
The Great Ming Palace,
was constructed under the supervision of Vice Minister of Agriculture Liáng Xiàorén by order of Emperor Gāozōng.
It stood on high ground to the north,
with clear views to the south,
on every bright and sunny day,
offering a view of the Zhōngnán Mountains to the south,
the capital city visible as if in the palm of one's hand,
with its wards, markets, and streets,
appearing as if viewed from within a railing when looking down.
"Chronicles of Cháng'ān"
Celestial phenomena shine brightly,
the emperor's seat is triple-supported.
The Great Táng established its position,
observing above and examining below.
The central chamber stands upright,
with traveling palaces to the south.
To the north rises the Hanyuan Palace,
its appearance majestic and profound.
In summary,
like the longevity of mountains,
it is called Penglai.
Like the rising sun,
it is called Great Ming.
Lǐ Huá's "Rhapsody on the Hanyuan Hall"
Wú Hàn,
courtesy name Zǐxiǎn,
was resolute and strong by nature.
Whenever he followed campaigns,
when other generals saw the battle formations turning unfavorable,
many would panic and lose their composure.
Wú Hàn remained calm and unperturbed,
focusing only on maintaining weapons and equipment,
and inspiring officers and soldiers.
The Emperor once sent someone to observe what the Grand Marshal was doing,
and the messenger returned reporting he was preparing tools for attack and defense.
The Emperor then sighed and said:
"Wú Gōng somewhat meets expectations,
standing firm as if against an enemy state."
From the Book of the Later Hàn.
Tàihé
When Zhuō Mào was an official in the chancellor's office,
he once went out.
Someone claimed his horse was theirs,
and Mào asked how long they had lost the horse.
The person replied,
"Over a month now."
Mào said,
"But I have raised this horse for several years."
Nevertheless, he untied the horse and gave it to them,
saying,
"If it turns out not to be the one you lost,
please return it to me at the chancellor's office."
He then pulled the carriage on foot and left.
Later, the horse's owner found their own horse,
felt ashamed, and went to see Mào,
kowtowing to apologize.
"Records of the Eastern Pavilion"
In the Tàihé Valley south of Cháng'ān County stood Tàihé Palace,
established in the eighth year of the Wǔdé era.
In the twenty-first year of the Zhēnguàn era, ministers proposed renovating the derelict Tàihé Palace,
suitable for escaping summer heat.
An imperial decree ordered Yán Lìběn, the Grand Artisan, to dismantle the residence of Shùnyáng Prince,
using its timber and tiles for construction.
The palace enveloped the mountain to form a garden,
and was renamed Cuìwēi Palace.
"Geographical Records Compendium"
Yùhuá
Liú Kuān once encountered a man
who had lost his ox and came to Kuān's carriage to claim it as his own.
Kuān said nothing,
but descended from the carriage and walked home.
After a short while,
the man who had claimed the ox found his own ox,
and returned Kuān's ox to him,
apologizing, saying:
"I am ashamed to have wronged you, elder."
Kuān replied:
"Things may look alike,
and mistakes can happen.
I am grateful that you took the trouble to return it,
why should you apologize?"
From the Book of the Later Hàn
Guō Línzōng often stayed awake,
and one night he ordered congee to be made.
Wèi Dégōng prepared and presented it to him.
Línzōng took one sip,
then threw the cup to the ground,
and angrily scolded him, saying:
"The congee lacks seasoning—
how can it be eaten?"
Despite being scolded in this manner,
Dégōng showed no change in expression.
(Bié Zhuàn)
In the twenty-first year of the Zhēnguàn era, the Yùhuá Palace was built at the Fènghuáng Pavilion in Yíjūn County.
Old Records
They dredged the moats and smoothed the embankments,
constructing the edifice against the cliff,
with earth devoid of ornate patterns,
and wood uncarved and unadorned.
They replaced the knockers with thorny gates,
and transformed the elegant windows into jar-like openings.
Edict
Concubine Xú Xián submitted a memorial admonishing:
"The foundation of governance
lies in valuing non-action.
The labors of construction
cannot be pursued simultaneously.
The northern gate was just built,
and the southern Cuìwēi was being developed,
hardly past a season
when Yùhuá's creation began.
Although it follows the mountains and utilizes the waters,
it is not without the toil of erecting structures;
reducing and reducing again,
it still incurs considerable cost and labor.
Ultimately, using thatch to demonstrate frugality,
yet still incurring the burden of timber and stone.
Even if workers are hired,
employing people unavoidably brings the drawback of disturbance.
Thus, a ruler with the Way
brings ease to others through his own ease;
a ruler without the Way
pleasures his own body through amusement."
Old Biography
In the first month of the twenty-first year,
trees at Yùhuá Palace grew with interlocking branches,
joining across the ravine.
Essential Records
Kǒng Róng, Governor of Qīng Province,
was attacked by Yuán Tán.
From spring to summer,
only a few hundred soldiers remained.
Arrows fell like rain,
spears and halberds clashed within,
yet Kǒng Róng leaned on his desk reading,
calmly talking and laughing as usual.
From the *History of the Later Hàn*.
Chángchūn
Sīmǎ Huī possessed the ability to discern human character and talent.
When people of the time came to ask Huī about individuals,
he initially would not distinguish between their superior and inferior qualities,
but would always say they were excellent.
His wife admonished him, saying:
"When people bring their doubts to you,
you ought to analyze and discuss them,
yet you uniformly declare everyone excellent -
is this really what people consult you for?"
Huī replied:
"What you have said
is also excellent."
When Liú Biǎo's son Cóng went to visit Huī,
he sent someone to ask if he was in.
It happened that Huī was weeding his garden himself,
and Cóng's attendants asked:
"Is Lord Sīmǎ in?"
Huī replied:
"I am he."
Cóng's attendants, seeing his plain appearance,
cursed him, saying:
"You wretched laborer!
The young master wishes to see Lord Sīmǎ -
what kind of field slave are you to claim being him?"
Huī returned home,
put on his headcloth and came out to meet Cóng.
The attendants recognized Huī as the same old man from before,
and feared they would be reported to Cóng.
Cóng rose and kowtowed to apologize,
whereupon Huī said to him:
"You really shouldn't have done this,
I am quite ashamed of it,
and this matter of my weeding the garden - only you know about it."
From the Bié Zhuàn.
In the thirteenth year of the Daye era,
Emperor Gāozǔ raised his righteous army,
stationing at the Chángchūn Palace.
The Record
describes the detached palace beyond the river,
truly a unique beauty within the realm.
Soaring towers rise elegantly layered,
encircled by long walls with tiered foundations.
"Cháng" signifies the omen of benevolence and longevity,
"chūn" represents the place where life germinates.
Rhapsody on Chángchūn Palace
Fèi Yī,
courtesy name Wénwěi.
When the Wèi army was stationed at Xīngshì,
he was granted imperial authority to lead troops to resist them.
The Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Lái Mǐn came to bid Fèi Yī farewell,
requesting to play a game of wéiqí together.
At that time, urgent military dispatches were rapidly exchanged,
soldiers and horses were clad in armor,
and preparations for departure were complete.
Yet Fèi Yī and Lái Mǐn focused intently on their game,
showing no sign of weariness or impatience.
Lái Mǐn said:
"I was merely testing you a moment ago!
You are truly a capable man,
one who will surely defeat the enemy."
When Fèi Yī arrived at the front,
the enemy forces retreated.
"Records of the Shǔ Kingdom"
Jiǔ Chéng
In the early summer of the sixth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
the emperor retreated to the Jiǔchéng Palace to escape the heat,
which was the Rénshòu Palace of the Suí dynasty.
Crowning the mountain with halls,
spanning ravines to create ponds,
bridging waters with pillars,
and parting cliffs to erect towers,
lofty pavilions were built all around,
with long corridors extending in all directions,
surpassing even the Gānquán Palace of the Hàn dynasty.
On the sixteenth day, the emperor and the empress
toured the terraces and observatories,
strolling leisurely along the western wall,
and looking down at the ground,
they noticed a slight dampness.
Using a staff to probe,
they guided a spring to flow,
which then gushed forth.
They contained it with a stone balustrade
and channeled it into a canal.
Its clarity was like a mirror,
and its taste as sweet as sweet wine.
From "Wèi Zhēng's Inscription":
Encompassing the universe,
summoning the eight deities,
scaling the heavens and reaching the zenith,
examining ancient ruins on the Wèn River,
and consulting old texts in Yānzhōng.
The sun spirit opened the summer retreat palace,
and auspicious blessings built the cooling hall.
Dragons face the eaves,
iron phoenixes connect the roof ridges.
From Wáng Bó's Eulogy:
Mǎ Zhōu submitted a memorial stating:
"The edict commands a visit to Jiǔchéng Palace in February,
but I humbly consider that the Grand Emperor is advanced in age,
and Your Majesty should attend to his meals morning and evening,
and care for his daily needs.
The palace to be visited
is over three hundred lǐ from the capital.
With the imperial carriage setting out
and strict protocols lasting for days,
it cannot be reached quickly.
If the Grand Emperor feels longing
and wishes to see Your Majesty immediately,
how could he do so?
Moreover, this journey
is intended for escaping the heat,
yet the Grand Emperor remains in the heat,
while Your Majesty seeks coolness alone.
This does not align with the way of providing warmth and coolness.
I am deeply uneasy about this.
However, since the edict has been issued
and plans are already made,
I hope you will announce a swift return date
to clear everyone's doubts."
From the Old Biography.
Yùzhāng Tàishǒu Gù Shào was the son of Gù Yōng.
Shào died while serving in the commandery.
Yōng was hosting a grand gathering of his subordinates, playing weiqi,
when a messenger arrived from outside.
Yet there was no letter from his son.
Although his expression remained unchanged,
in his heart, he understood the reason.
He dug his nails into his palm,
and blood flowed, soaking his mat.
After the guests had dispersed,
he finally sighed and said:
"I have not attained the lofty virtue of Yánlíng,
how could I bear the reproach of losing my sight?"
Thereupon, he released his emotions and dispersed his grief,
and his countenance returned to its normal composure.
From "Shuō Yuàn".
Shàngyáng
Wáng Yífǔ once entrusted a clansman with a matter,
but after some time it still hadn't been done.
Meeting at a drinking feast,
he then said to him:
"I recently entrusted you with that honorable matter,
how could you not have done it?"
The clansman flew into a rage,
and immediately lifted a food tray and threw it in his face.
Yífǔ said nothing at all,
and after washing up,
took Chancellor Wáng's arm,
and rode off together with him.
In the carriage, looking in a mirror,
he said to the Chancellor:
"Look at my eyes,
they gaze out over the ox's back."
Shìshuō
During Emperor Gāozǔ's reign, the initial construction of palaces such as Pénglái, Shàngyáng, and Hébì began,
gradually depleting the treasury.
Zhāng Wénguàn thereupon presented a remonstrance, saying:
"Human labor must not be spared consideration,
and the common people must not be left uncared for.
Nurturing them in ease leads to wealth and health,
while driving them to toil breeds resentment and rebellion.
Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdì,
who extensively campaigned against the four barbarian tribes,
and built numerous palaces,
caused the state to crumble like tiles shattering,
reducing the population by half.
Your servant has heard that order should be established before chaos arises,
and the state secured before danger emerges.
People do not constantl
cherish, but cherish those who are benevolent.
Your servant wishes to gradually pacify and comfort them,
so as not to let resentment grow."
"Old Biography"
The Shàngyáng Palace was located in the eastern part of the Dōngyuàn Garden, southwest of the imperial city,
facing the Luò River to the south,
and bordered by the Gǔ River to the west.
It was constructed during the Shàngyuán era by Wéi Jī, who served as commissioner,
featuring long corridors lining the banks in an unbroken sequence.
While digging the ground, a bronze vessel was unearthed,
resembling a basin but shallower,
with a raised design of two carp inside,
and between the fish were four seal-script characters,
which read:
"Eternal Blessings to Descendants,"
contemporaries considering it an omen of the Lǐ family's revival.
Emperor Gāozōng often resided in this palace in his later years,
conducting state affairs there.
"Records of the Eastern Capital"
The Shàngyáng detached palace,
adorned with vibrant colors and myriad forms,
touching the clouds at dawn and connecting with the sunset glow,
stood majestic and magnificent,
spreading like wings from the Tàihé Hall with towering views,
flanking the guest stars and opening onto spacious verandas.
Lǐ Yǔ's "Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital"
Cloud-like eaves layered, supporting the celestial canopy,
dew-laden covers cleansing the sun.
Jiǎ Dēng's "Rhapsody on the Shàngyáng Palace"
Wáng Yífǔ and Péi Jǐngshēng had different aspirations and preferences.
Jǐngshēng disliked this,
and wanted to win him over,
but ultimately could not change his mind,
so he intentionally visited Wáng,
ranting and cursing vehemently,
demanding that Wáng respond to him,
hoping to share the blame,
yet Wáng did not show any change in expression,
and calmly said:
"The white-eyed boy is acting up again."
Zǐ Guì
Yīn Jīngzhōu had an acquaintance
who wrote rhapsodies in the style of Shù Xī's playful compositions.
Yīn considered him very talented
and said to Wáng Gōng:
"I've just seen some new writings that are quite remarkable."
He then took them out from a handkerchief case.
Wáng read them,
while Yīn couldn't contain his laughter.
After Wáng finished reading,
he neither laughed nor commented on their quality,
but simply pressed them down with his ruyi scepter.
Yīn was left disappointed and dejected.

Zōng Què,
courtesy name Yuángàn,
was unrestrained and fond of martial arts in his youth,
and was not praised by his fellow villagers.
During the Xiàojiàn era,
he was promoted to the position of Governor of Yùzhōu,
overseeing military affairs of five provinces.
Previously,
his fellow villager Yǔ Yè's family was very wealthy,
and would serve lavish feasts to entertain guests.
However, when Què arrived,
they served him pickled vegetables and millet rice,
saying to the guests:
"Commander Zōng
is accustomed to eating coarse food."
Què ate his fill and left.
Later,
Yè became Què's Chief Clerk,
administering Liáng Commandery,
yet Què treated him very generously,
holding no grudge over the previous incident.
Book of Sòng
In the fourth year of the Yìfèng era,
the Zǐguì Palace was built west of Miǎnchí County.
That year,
the Emperor entered Luòyáng,
and moved his residence to the Northern Shaded Hall in Luòyáng,
where the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Liú Rénguǐ,
said to the Attendant Censor Dí Rénjié:
"In ancient times, ponds, terraces, and pavilions
were all located within deep palaces and fortified walls,
not wishing outsiders to see them,
for fear of hurting the common people's hearts.
Wéi Hóngjī's construction,
with its lined banks and long corridors,
stands outside the city walls,
where all envoys come to pay homage,
and none fail to see it.
Is this the way to make one's ruler like Yáo and Shùn?"
Hóngjī, hearing this, said:
"When the world follows the Dào,
all officials fulfill their duties.
Ministers who assist the ruler consider matters of remonstrance,
while officials in charge of storehouses simply follow decrees and guard their posts.
I dare not overstep my bounds."
The Jiān Fǔ records
that in the second year of the Tiàolù era it was renamed the Summer Retreat Palace,
and in the first year of the Yǒngchún era it was renamed the Fāngguì Palace.
The Treatise on Geography
in the New Book attaches Hóngjī's matter to the Shàngyáng Palace.
Liú Xū,
courtesy name Yàndù,
came from an extremely impoverished family,
often eating only every other day.
During the harsh winter months,
he sometimes lacked felt blankets and cotton padding,
yet Xū remained perfectly composed,
with others never sensing his hunger or cold.
From youth to adulthood,
he never showed signs of joy or anger.
Whenever in situations where competition was possible,
he would prevail precisely by not competing;
if anyone tried to domineer over him,
they would invariably retreat in shameful admiration.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Sānyáng
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng was giving a lecture at Tóngtài Temple,
with tens of thousands of people in attendance.
Suddenly, the tame elephant presented by Nányuè broke loose,
causing the crowd to flee in panic.
Only Zāng Dùn and Péi Zhīlǐ remained steadfast and unmoving,
for which the Emperor greatly praised them.
From "Continued Accounts of Worldly Tales"
Wǔ Sānsī, seeing that Empress Zétiān was weary of residing in the deep palace,
and wishing to accompany Zhāng Yìzhī and Zhāng Chāngzōng in galloping about,
to enhance his own power,
requested the construction of Sānyáng Palace on Mount Sōnggāo
and Xīngtài Palace on Mount Wànshòu,
inviting Zétiān to visit annually.
The labor conscription was extremely heavy,
causing resentment among the common people.
"Old Biography"
In the first year of the Jiǔshì era,
Zétiān stayed at Sānyáng Palace,
from summer through autumn,
delaying her return to the capital.
Zhāng Yuè submitted a memorial advising:
"Sānyáng Palace is 160 li from Luò City,
separated by the Yī River,
with steep cliffs and slopes.
After summer turns to autumn,
floodwaters accumulate,
roads deteriorate and mountains are perilous,
blocking transport.
How can one abandon the ancestral temples above,
and settle in a remote mountain valley?
This is like holding a spear upside down,
showing others the handle -
I privately believe Your Majesty should not do this."
"Yuè's Biography"
The original account was clear,
but the New Book uses obscure language.
It says the Empress avoided heat at Sānyáng Palace,
thus knowing thunder had no time,
covering ears alone was insufficient,
mocking its awkward phrasing.
As for "avoiding heat at Sānyáng",
it's already unidiomatic,
and Kǒng Tiě further states she built a heat-avoidance palace,
which is even more mistaken.
Huáqīng
Liáng Ānchéng Wáng Xiù,
was benevolent and tolerant by nature,
never showing joy or anger on his face.
Once an attendant killed his pet swan by throwing stones at it,
and the fasting master requested to punish the attendant's crime.
Xiù said:
"How could I harm a person over a bird?"
While in the capital,
he attended to official business daily.
Once when a cook mistakenly served food
and then removed it after spilling,
he mounted his carriage and went through the entire court session,
without eating,
yet never reproached the cook for it.
From "The Book of Liáng"
Wēn Zǐshēng,
courtesy name Péngjǔ.
When Emperor Zhuang killed Ěrzhū Róng,
Zǐshēng participated in the plot.
The pardon edict at that time
was composed by Zǐshēng.
When Róng entered the court,
he encountered Zǐshēng holding the edict,
and asked what document it was.
Zǐshēng, without changing his expression, said:
"It's an imperial order." Róng did not look at it.
(From History of the Northern Dynasties)
In the 18th year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Yán Lìdé was ordered to build the Hot Springs Palace,
and Tàizōng personally visited and composed a stele inscription.
In the 3rd year of the Xiánhēng era, it was named the Hot Springs Palace.
Records of the Ten Circuits
states that when Fáng Guǎn served as a Jǐshìzhōng in the 5th year of the Tiānbǎo era,
Emperor Xuánzōng had wandering ambitions,
frequently touring and visiting the extensive hot springs.
To establish the Huáqīng Palace, various government offices and residential quarters were arranged around the palace.
Because Guǎn possessed resourcefulness and strategic planning skills,
he was ordered to oversee the development of Lí Mountain,
clearing cliffs and removing thickets,
to create a place for the emperor's excursions and sightseeing.
Official Biography
records that Consort Yáng, every October when the emperor visited the Huáqīng Palace,
the carriages and cavalry of the five residences all followed,
each family forming its own procession,
each procession in a single color.
Soon the processions of the five families merged,
blazing like myriad flowers filling valleys,
forming brocades and embroideries.
Dropped hairpins and lost slippers,
pearls and jade beads,
lay scattered along the road,
with fragrance detectable for tens of lǐ.

Gazing at Spring
When Cuī Kāng was serving as the magistrate of Wújí County,
Zhēn Chēn held the position of chief clerk.
Once, during a dispute over official matters,
Cuī Kāng struck Zhēn Chēn with his fist,
causing him to fall from his seat.
Zhēn Chēn, out of respect for Cuī Kāng's status as the county magistrate,
merely laughed and did not pursue the matter.
"Book of Wèi"
Within the Western Capital's forbidden garden stood the Wangchun Palace,
perched atop a high plateau,
bordering the Bà and Chǎn rivers to the east.
The current emperor once ascended its northern pavilion,
composing the "Ode to the Spring Terrace,"
to which hundreds of court officials submitted matching verses.
The "Records of the Western Capital"
record a memorial by Yáo Nánzhōng during Emperor Daizong's reign:
"A monarch must occupy elevated brilliance
to illuminate the hidden depths,
which is why the late emperor built Wangchun upon Dragon's Head plateau."
"Official Biography"
To the left of the Green Gate,
layered valleys rose steep and rugged.
It stood uniquely prominent above the imperial park,
solemnly connected by covered pathways with clear vistas.
The verdant hues of the Southern Mountains filled the foreground,
while the pristine glow of the Wèi River flowed below.
Lǐ Jǐngxùn's rhapsody
Yuán Wényáo,
styled as Déyuǎn.
When he first moved from Luòyáng to Yè,
he possessed only over ten qǐng of land,
and his family was poor,
relying on it for clothing and food.
Towards the end of the Wèi dynasty,
members of the imperial clan were persecuted,
and someone falsely claimed and encroached upon his land,
but Wényáo immediately gave it to him.
After Wényáo became prominent,
this person was still alive,
and fled with his family to avoid retribution.
Wényáo was greatly surprised,
pursued and comforted him,
and returned the land to him.
The man felt ashamed and refused to accept it,
both parties yielded to each other,
so the land became unused fields.
"Book of Northern Qí"
Cuī Xiān,
courtesy name Jìlún,
was fond of recommending talented individuals.
He stated that Xíng Shào should be closely trusted and valued,
yet during discussions,
Shào ended up slandering Xiān.
Wén Xiāng was displeased,
and said to Xiān:
"You praised Zǐcái's strengths,
yet Zǐcái solely speaks of your shortcomings;
this is a foolish person."
Xiān replied:
"Zǐcái speaks of my shortcomings,
and I speak of Zǐcái's strengths;
both are based on facts,
not foolishness."
《History of the Northern Dynasties》
Fish and Water Plants
After Shùnzōng became the crown prince,
he attended a banquet at the Yúzǎo Palace,
where decorated boats were displayed for water performances,
and palace maids sang rowing songs.
Amidst the music from various instruments,
Dézōng was exceedingly pleased.
He turned to the crown prince and said:
"How about today?"
The crown prince recited a verse:
"Indulge in pleasure but not to excess,"
as his reply.
"Annals of Shùnzōng"
On the Rénchén day of the eighth month in the fifteenth year of Yuánhé,
(the emperor) visited the Yúzǎo Palace,
dispatched two thousand soldiers from the Divine Strategy Army to dredge the Yúzǎo Pond,
and on the Xīnchǒu day of the ninth month, held a grand music performance at the Yúzǎo Palace to watch boat races.

"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Wéi Fù,
courtesy name Jìngyuǎn,
had aspirations for a simple and unadorned life,
indifferent to fame and wealth.
The residence where he lived
was nestled among woods and springs.
Fù would face them while playing the qin and reading,
serenely enjoying his own leisure.
People of the time called him a lay Buddhist.
There were even those who admired his idle simplicity,
sometimes bringing wine to follow him.
Fù would also share in the joy with them,
engaging in conversation without tiring.
His son Wéi Guàn served as the governor of Suízhōu
but died due to illness,
and Xiàokuān's son Wéi Zǒng also fell in battle in Bīngzhōu.
Within a single day,
the tragic news arrived together.
The family members faced each other in grief and sorrow,
yet Fù's expression remained composed as ever.
He said to them:
"Life and death are fate,
coming and going are ordinary matters—
why should they be cause for sorrow?"
He then took up the qin and played it as usual.

Yùqīng
Niú Hóng's younger brother Bì,
who was fond of alcohol and prone to drunken violence,
once shot and killed the ox pulling Hóng's carriage while intoxicated.
When Hóng returned,
arriving home,
his wife came to greet him and said:
"Your younger brother shot and killed the ox."
Hóng heard this,
showed no surprise or questioning,
and simply replied:
"Make dried meat."
After sitting down,
his wife spoke again:
"Your younger brother suddenly shot and killed the ox,
this is truly an extraordinary matter."
Hóng said:
"I already know."
His expression remained composed,
and he continued reading without interruption.
Book of Sui
Táng Lín,
was frugal and had few desires,
he did not build grand residences,
his clothing and utensils were simple and plain,
and he was lenient in dealing with others.
Once, when he intended to attend a funeral,
he ordered his servant to go home and fetch a white gown.
The servant mistakenly brought another garment,
and, fearing reprimand, dared not present it.
Táng Lín, noticing this,
summoned him and said:
"Today my energy is adverse,
it is not suitable for mourning,
so the fetching of the white gown can be stopped for now."
Another time, he had someone prepare medicine, but it was improperly made;
secretly aware of the reason,
he said to them:
"In darkness, it is not fitting to take medicine,
it should be discarded immediately."
He never publicly exposed their faults,
such was his tolerance and forgiveness.

Péi Xíngjiǎn once ordered a physician to prepare medicine,
requesting rhinoceros horn and musk,
but the messenger mistakenly lost them,
and fled in fear and panic.
Another time, an imperial decree gifted him a horse and a new saddle,
but the clerk galloped it recklessly,
causing the horse to fall and the saddle to break,
so the clerk also fled.
Péi Xíngjiǎn sent someone close to summon them back,
and said to them:
"Do you think I look down on you?
These were merely mistakes."
He treated them as before.
When he first pacified the Dūyǒu
and captured abundant treasures from Zhēfú,
the tribal chieftains and generals wished to see them,
so Péi Xíngjiǎn hosted a banquet,
displaying them for all to see.
There was an agate plate,
over two feet wide,
with exceptionally rare patterns.
The military officer Wáng Xiūliè, holding the plate,
hurried up the steps,
but tripped on his clothes,
stumbled and fell,
and the plate shattered.
Wáng Xiūliè was terrified,
kowtowing until his head bled.
Péi Xíngjiǎn smiled and said to him:
"It was not intentional,
why go to such extremes?"
He showed no change in expression.

Liúlí
Lú Chéngqìng, during the early Zǒngzhāng era, was evaluating internal and external officials.
There was one official in charge of grain transport,
who lost rice due to a storm.
Lú evaluated him, saying:
"Supervisor of transport lost grain,
evaluation: medium to low."
The man maintained his composure as usual,
and withdrew without a single word.
Lú, valuing his magnanimity,
amended the assessment, saying:
"Beyond one's control,
evaluation: medium to medium."
He showed neither joy
nor words of shame.
Lú changed it again, saying:
"Unaltered by favor or disgrace,
evaluation: medium to high."

Lóu Shīdé
was simple, loyal, and profoundly sincere,
with no personal biases in his heart.
When Dí Rénjié became chancellor,
Shīdé had secretly recommended him.
After they served together as colleagues,
Rénjié rather looked down on Shīdé
and repeatedly maneuvered him out to external posts.
Shīdé knew of this
yet bore no resentment.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān became aware of the situation
and asked Rénjié:
"Is Shīdé virtuous?"
He replied:
"As a general, he is cautious and steadfast;
as for virtue, I do not know."
She asked further:
"Does Shīdé know people well?"
He answered:
"I have served alongside him,
but never heard of him knowing people well."
Wǔ Zétiān then said:
"My appointment of you
was due to Shīdé's recommendation.
This can indeed be called knowing people well."
Thereupon, she ordered her attendants to fetch a case,
from which she took about ten memorials of recommendation and gave them to Rénjié.
Rénjié was greatly ashamed,
and after withdrawing, sighed:
"Lóu gōng's great virtue embraced me;
I was tolerated by him,
yet never perceived the extent of it.
I am far from matching him!"

got drunk and lay down on the road.
Yáng Chéng wondered what had happened,
and went with his brother to find him.
The servant had not yet sobered up,
so they carried him back on their shoulders.

Fáng Wénliè

and was never angry.
He served as Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel.

so he sent a maidservant to buy rice.
She took the opportunity to run away,
and only returned after three or four days.
Wénliè calmly asked her:
"The whole family has no food,
where have you been?"
In the end, he did not beat her.

Traveling Palaces
From Xiāngguó to Yè was two hundred lǐ,
every forty lǐ along the way a palace was erected,
each palace housed one lady,
with several dozen maids in attendance,
and eunuchs standing guard through the night.

Guī Dēng was broad-minded and tolerant.

The horse kicked,
and the servant became angry,
breaking the horse's leg.
Guī Dēng knew about it but did not reprimand him.
In his later years, he became quite fond of consuming elixirs.
Someone presented him with mineral-based medicine,
claiming to have already tried it himself.
Guī Dēng took it without suspicion.
The medicine's toxicity nearly killed him.
Only then did he inquire,
and the person admitted he had not actually tried it.
Others were furious on his behalf,
but Guī Dēng looked at the man

He always admired Lù Xiàngxiān's character,

Fényáng
In the sixteenth year of the Dayè era,
I returned to Luòyáng from Jiāngdū.
By imperial decree, the Fényáng Palace was built north of Fénzhōu by the Fén River,
at the source of the Fén River from Guǎncén Mountain.

when washing by the river,
a chilling cool breeze would arise,
as if it were the eighth or ninth month. The area receives much rain,

then suddenly clear,
with neither rain nor sunshine lasting the entire day.
Although the mountains stand thousands of ren high,
residents on the ridges need only dig two or three feet deep

was devoted to the study of calligraphy,

valuing only his brushes, inkstones, and paintings,

Huá,
means disorder.
Jī,
means sameness.
This refers to a person who is eloquent and quick-witted,
who can make the wrong seem right,
and the right seem wrong,
thus confusing distinctions and similarities.
The "Chǔ Cí" states:
"Be slick and smooth,
slippery like grease,
like soft leather."
Cuī Hào said:
"Huá
is pronounced as gǔ;
Jī
is a wine vessel.
It tips and pours out wine,
unceasing all day long.
This metaphor describes someone who speaks with eloquence,
with endless words,
like the continuous pouring of wine from a gǔjī vessel."
Thus, Yáng Xióng's "Ode to Wine" says:
"The leather bag gǔjī,
with a belly as large as a pot.
It holds wine all day,
and people rely on it for buying wine."
Additionally, Yáo Chá said:
"Gǔjī
is like jesting.
Huá
is read as in the common pronunciation;
Jī
refers to schemes.
It describes speech that is witty and smooth,
with clever ideas emerging rapidly,
hence it is called gǔjī."

In the eighth year of King Wēi of Qí,
Chǔ raised a large army to attack Qí.
The King of Qí sent Chún Yú Kūn to Zhào to request reinforcements,
providing him with one hundred jīn of gold,
and ten teams of chariots and horses.
Chún Yú Kūn looked up to the sky and laughed heartily,
causing the tassels of his hat to shake.
The King asked:
"Do you find it too little, sir?"
Kūn replied:
"How dare I?"
The King said:
"Then why are you laughing?"
Kūn said:
"Earlier, as I was coming from the east,
I saw a man praying for a good harvest by the roadside.
He held one pig's trotter,
and one bowl of wine,
and prayed:
'May the highlands fill baskets,
the lowlands fill carts,
the five grains flourish and ripen,
and abundance fill my home.'
I saw that what he offered was meager,
yet what he desired was extravagant,
so I laughed at him."
Thereupon, King Wēi increased the gifts to gold, jade, chariots, and horses before sending him to Zhào.
When Chǔ heard of this,
they withdrew their troops overnight.

The Emperor
Dōngfāng Shuò's reputation exceeded his actual merits because
he was versatile and knowledgeable in many fields,
not specializing in a single discipline.
He responded with humor like an entertainer,
appeared endlessly resourceful like a wise man,
offered upright remonstrance like a straightforward official,
yet concealed his virtue like a recluse.
He did not emulate Bó Yí and Shū Qí,
but rather endorsed Liǔxià Huì,
admonishing his son with the principle of accommodating to circumstances:
"The Shǒuyáng Mountain path is clumsy,
while serving at court is skillful.
Eat your fill and walk steadily,
exchange farming for official service,
dwell in seclusion while amusing yourself with the world,
adapt to the times to avoid misfortune."
Was he not the master of wit and humor?

Master

Zhāng Yì served as the Chief Clerk of the Administrative Office,
and traveled north to consult Zhūgě Liàng on official matters.
Hundreds of people came to see him off,
filling the road with carriages.
Upon his return, Zhāng Yì wrote to a close friend, saying:
"Recently, while traveling,
I received guests day and night,
without a moment of peace.
People respect the Chief Clerk of the Chancellor,
and I, the man Zhāng Jūnsì, am merely attached to that title,
so exhausted I could die."
His witty and sharp remarks
were often of this kind.
Before the Shang and Zhou dynasties,
their names were not recorded.
The "Ding Fen" chapter of the Book of Lord Shāng states:

The "Biography of Jīng Kē" in Records of the Grand Historian records:

Shǔ envoy Zhāng Fèng was on a mission to Wú,
and before Sūn Quán he listed the name of Shàngshū Kàn Zé to mock him.
Zé was unable to reply to Xuē.
Zōng Xià, while serving wine,
took the opportunity to propose a toast, saying:
"What is Shǔ?
With a quǎn (dog) it becomes dú (solitary),
without the quǎn it is shǔ,
horizontal eyes and a bent body,
a chóng (insect) enters its belly."
Fèng said:
"Shouldn't we also list your state of Wú?"
Zōng immediately responded:
"Without a kǒu (mouth) it is tiān (heaven),
with a kǒu it is wú,
the sovereign overlooking all states, the capital of the Son of Heaven."
At this, the entire company burst into laughter.

Palace Steps
Zhūgě Kè was conversing with Nányáng's Hán Wénhuǎng,
and mistakenly called him by his father's given name.
Huǎng questioned him, saying:
"Before a man's son, to call his father by his given name -
is this according to propriety?"
Kè laughed and replied:
"When one threads a needle toward the sky and fails to see it,
it's not that one is distant from heaven's intent, but that there is a reason for it."
Sūn Quán had the Crown Prince mock Kè, saying:
"Zhūgě Yuánxùn should eat one dàn of horse dung."
Kè replied:
"Your subject may jest,
and the gentleman may jest."
His father replied:
"Clearly the Crown Prince does not dare."
The Emperor said:
"You may."
Kè said:
"I beg the Crown Prince to eat three hundred chicken eggs."
The Emperor asked Kè:
"Someone tells you to eat horse dung,
and you tell someone to eat chicken eggs -
why is this?"
Kè replied:
"They come from the same source."
The Lord of Wú laughed heartily.

Zhōng Yù served as a court official,

While seated at a banquet hosted by Sīmǎ Shī,

Then, turning to Xuánbó and Yuánxià, he said:

sociable yet not partisan."

In grand halls, there are elevated steps (bì),
while regular halls have stairs but no elevated steps.
The left side has a tiered section (cè), the left side is level,
the level part is paved with patterned bricks laid in sequence,
and the tiered section forms the steps of the elevated stairway.
In the ceremony of the Nine Bestowals,
one ascends by the "presented steps" (nàbì),
meaning to receive these steps for ascent.
The main hall of the palace is the "Road Chamber" (lùqǐn).
Regarding seating arrangements in halls,
proximity to the honored position is considered superior,
if there is no designated honored position, then for east-facing seats,
the north side is superior,
for south-facing seats, the west side is superior,
for west-facing seats, the south side is superior,
and for north-facing seats, the east side is superior.
In the hall,
only the Son of Heaven occupies a raised platform (bed),
all others kneel on mats before it.
For the mat-setting ceremony,
the Son of Heaven's hall
measures nine mats from east to west,
and seven mats from north to south.
According to Zhì Yú's "Essential Annotations for Resolving Doubts,"
the Son of Heaven's hall is nine chi high,
with nine steps on the stairs,
each consisting of nine levels.

Xún Mínghè and Lù Shìlóng had not met before,
when they both attended a gathering at Zhāng Màoxiān's home.
Zhāng asked them to converse,
as both were highly talented,
and urged them not to use common expressions.
Lù raised his hand and said:
"I am Lù Shìlóng from among the clouds."
Xún replied:
"I am Xún Mínghè from beneath the sun."
Lù then said:
"Since the clouds have parted to reveal the white pheasant,
why not string your bow
and set your arrows?"
Xún responded:
"I thought it was a majestic cloud-dragon,
but it turns out to be a mountain deer or wild elk.
With a weak beast and a strong crossbow,
I therefore delayed my shot."
Zhāng then clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
Lù Jī visited Wáng Wǔzǐ,
who had a hundred jars of sheep's milk cheese.
Pointing to it, Wǔzǐ said:
"What delicacy from your Eastern Wú can rival this?"
Lù replied:
"We have water shield soup from Qiānlǐ Lake -
it just needs no fermented beans added!"
While Lù Jī was seated,
Pān Ānrén arrived,
and Lù immediately rose to leave.
Ānrén remarked:
"When the pure wind arrives,
the dust flies up."
Lù responded immediately:
"When flocks of common birds gather,
the phoenix soars away."

Xiè Yòuyú said to Zhōu Hóu:
"You resemble the village shrine tree.
Gazing at it from afar,
it soars majestically, brushing against the azure sky;
but approaching to examine it closely,
its roots are where packs of foxes take shelter,
merely gathering filth below."
He replied:
"Though its branches brush the azure sky,
I do not consider this height remarkable;
though packs of foxes cause chaos beneath it,
I do not consider this defilement;
the foulness of gathered filth
is what you yourself preserve—
how can this be worth boasting about!"

your courage surpasses the ancients."

"I've been scheming for thousands of districts and still can't obtain them,
yet you scheme to become a Buddha—
isn't that grand indeed?"

Covering the entire meal.

Lùo Yǒu of the Jìn dynasty came from a poor family,
and sought an official position from Huán Wēn.
Although Huán Wēn treated him with respect for his talent and learning,
he considered Lùo Yǒu to be unrestrained and eccentric,
unsuited for governing the people,
so he made a promise but did not employ him.
When a colleague in the same office obtained a governorship,
Huán Wēn held a farewell banquet,
and Lùo Yǒu was also invited.
He arrived particularly late,
so Huán Wēn asked him the reason.
He replied:
"Yesterday, I received your instruction and left my home,
but on the way, I encountered a ghost who mocked me, saying:
'I only see you sending others off to their posts,
so why don't I see anyone sending you off to a post?'
I was first frightened and then ashamed,
unconsciously causing this delay and slowness, for which I am guilty."
Huán Wēn laughed at his wit but also felt a sense of shame on his behalf,
and later appointed him as the Grand Administrator of Xiāngyáng.

Xiè Gōng initially cherished the ambition of retiring to the Eastern Mountains,
but later, stern imperial decrees repeatedly reached him,
leaving him no alternative
until he finally took up the position of Minister of War under Huán Gōng.
At that time, someone presented Huán Gōng with medicinal herbs,
among which was "yuǎnzhì" (Polygala tenuifolia).
Huán Gōng picked it up and asked Xiè:
"This herb is also called 'xiǎocǎo' (little grass).
How can one thing have two names?"
Xiè did not immediately reply.
At that moment, Hǎo Lóng was present,
and he promptly answered:
"This is very easy to explain—
when it remains hidden, it is called 'yuǎnzhì' (far-reaching ambition),
but when it emerges, it becomes 'xiǎocǎo' (insignificant grass)."
Xiè wore a deeply ashamed expression.
Huán Gōng looked at Xiè and said with a laugh:
"Administrator Hǎo's remark here is not bad at all,
and it captures the essence perfectly."
