where the courtyard within the ministry was painted vermilion with cinnabar,
hence it was called the Vermilion Steps.
The Imperial Secretary knelt below them to report affairs,
and the Gentleman of the Yellow Gate saluted and received the memorial to handle the matters.
"Records of Han Officials"
Shì Bǎohǎi once while expounding the sutra,
held a brass incense burner.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng said:
"Although the Dharma master has severed stinginess and greed,
you still won't hold an incense burner unless it's made of brass."
Bǎohǎi responded immediately:
"Your Majesty occupies the imperial throne,
yet you won't wear a cap without the imperial insignia hairpin."
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and all present marveled in admiration.
From "The Biographies of Eminent Monks"
Liáng Zhōushě,
learned in both secular and Buddhist classics,
and also eloquent,
said to the monk Fǎyún:
"Confucius would not drink water from the Spring of Thieves,
so why does the Dharma Master handle a brass incense burner?"
He replied:
"Since the donor can wear a ceremonial banner,
why should this humble monk not hold brass?"
From "Tán Sǒu"
Jīnhuá
Bān Bó studied the Book of Songs under Shī Dān in his youth.
Grand General Wáng Fèng recommended that Bān Bó was suitable to encourage learning,
summoned him to the Yànnì Hall for an audience,
and appointed him as a Regular Palace Attendant.
At that time, the emperor was devoted to learning,
Zhèng Kuānzhōng and Zhāng Yǔ entered the Jīnhuá Hall daily to lecture on the Book of Documents and the Analects,
and an imperial decree ordered Bān Bó to study with them.
After several years, the scholarly activities at Jīnhuá Hall ceased.
From "Biographical Sketches"
Prefect Liú and Huán Xuán attended a lecture on the Book of Rites together,
Huán remarked:
"Whenever a point touches the heart,
it feels as if the gate of profound mystery is just a foot away."
Liú responded:
"This has not yet reached the ultimate truth."
This has since become known as "the talk of Jīnhuá Hall."
From A New Account of the Tales of the World
Qí Púshè Dōnghǎi Xú Xiàosì repaired Gāozuò Temple,
and often rested there.
Fǎyún also managed Xiāo Temple,
each visiting these two temples day and night,
adjacent yet not visiting each other,
Xiàosì once said to Fǎyún:
"You, Master, often sit on the high seat,
yet do not visit Gāozuò Temple."
He replied:
"Since you, Patron, serve the Xiāo family,
why not come to Xiāo Temple?"
"Tán Sǒu"
Eight Regions
During Emperor Wǔ's reign,
the rear palace had eight sections including Zhāoyáng, Fēixiáng, Zēngchéng, Héhuān, Lánlín, Pīxiāng, Fènghuáng, and Yuānyāng Halls,
later adding Ānchù, Chángníng, Bǔruò, Jiāofēng, Fāyuè, and Huìcǎo Halls to make fourteen positions.
"The Yellow Diagrams"
When Dào Gài was serving as the Minister of Personnel,
Hé Jìngróng participated in the selection process,
and whenever there were matters not approved,
Gài would oppose and argue with him. Jìngróng remarked to others:
"Dào Gài still carries a lingering foul odor,
yet he tries to act like a nobleman."
Originally,
Gài's grandfather, Dào Yànzhī, initially made a living by carrying nightsoil,
hence this was used by contemporaries to mock him.
*History of the Southern Dynasties*
Dào Qià once asked Liú Xiàochuò:
"I very much wish to buy the land east of my house to expand my residence,
but the owner is making it difficult,
what should I do?"
Chuò replied:
"Simply cart more nightsoil and pile it beside his property,
to make him suffer."
Qià became angry,
and ultimately used an incident to harm him,
impeaching and pressuring him.
Jìzhōu Chief Clerk Lǐ Zhù often hosted gatherings,
where all court officials assembled.
Yōuzhōu Chief Clerk Lù Rénhuì did not attend,
and Zhù deeply resented this.
Zhōu Yànyuān remarked:
"Can a net missing one mesh
ever catch birds?"
Zhù was blind in one eye,
while Lù was nicknamed Horned Owl.
Later Cuī Biāo said to Yànyuān:
"My calligraphy is poor—
I cannot make the character 'Biāo' look good."
Yànyuān responded:
"You may as well drag the stroke long like a person's leg,
or let it sweep diagonally like a bison's tail."
From "Tán Sǒu"
Zhāo Yáng
Xú Líng,
courtesy name Xiàomù,
was the son of Xú Chī.
In the second year of the Tàiqīng era, he was sent as an envoy to Wèi,
where the Wèi people hosted him at a guesthouse with a banquet.
The day was extremely hot,
and the chief host, Wèi Shōu, teased Xú Líng, saying:
"Today's heat
must be because of Chief Attendant Xú's arrival."
Xú Líng immediately replied:
"In the past, Wáng Sù came here
and established rituals and ceremonies for Wèi;
now that I have come on this mission,
I have made you aware of the cold and heat again."
Wèi Shōu was greatly ashamed.
(From *History of the Southern Dynasties*)
Emperor Chéng's Empress Zhào resided in the Zhāoyáng Palace.
According to the "Huángtú,"
later, her favor waned slightly,
and her brother Jié was favored as a Zhāoyí,
residing in the Zhāoyáng Palace.
The courtyard was vermilion red, and the hall above was lacquered.
The steps were all clad in bronze,
covered with gold,
paved with white jade steps.
The walls were adorned here and there with golden sconces,
containing Lántián jade,
embellished with bright pearls and kingfisher feathers,
such luxury had never been in the back palace before.
According to the "Qiánzhuàn,"
Zhāoyáng Palace was uniquely splendid,
flourishing during Emperor Xiàochéng’s time.
The beams of the house were not visible,
and the walls did not reveal their shape.
"Xīdū Fù"
Líng Bō
Liáng Lù Yànzǐ was sent as an envoy to Wèi,
and Wèi dispatched Lǐ Xié to greet him at the outskirts.
Passing by the Cháogē city,
Yànzǐ said:
"The remnants of the Yīn people should indeed be here."
Xié responded:
"After the Yǒngjiā southward crossing,
they all ended up south of the river."
From "Tán Sǒu"
South of Gānquán Palace lies Kūnmíng Pond,
within which stands the Língbō Hall,
all constructed with cassia wood as its pillars,
so that the wind carries fragrance as it passes.
"Records of the Capital"
Lú Sīdào once stood under the sun while hosting guests,
when the Imperial Secretary Lǐ Délín said to him:
"Why not move to the shade of the tree?"
Sīdào replied:
"Hot it may be,
but I cannot stand beneath the forest."
From "Yǒuyáng"
In the Northern Qí dynasty, Lú Sīdào was dispatched as an envoy to Chén,
where a banquet was held with linked verse poetry.
Those who started first mocked the northerners, saying:
"Elms grow to feed the hungry men,
While lush grass fattens the donkeys."
This referred to northerners eating elms
and the absence of donkeys in Wú region,
hence these lines.
Lú Sīdào immediately continued:
"From one pot, each takes his share of rice,
In the same pan, different fish they fry."
This meant southerners lacked righteousness,
sharing a stove but eating separate meals.
The people of Wú felt ashamed.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Yángmíng
Yán Zūn, styled Zǐlíng,
in the fifth year of the Jiànwǔ era, was summoned by imperial decree,
a banquet was set in the Yángmíng Hall,
he was commanded to attend the feast,
and stayed overnight at dusk,
that night a guest star intruded upon the celestial region of the Son of Heaven.
"Records of Kuàijī Classics"
Déyáng
The Emperor Míng desired to construct the Northern Palace,
and the Supervisor of Affairs Zhōnglí Yì submitted a memorial to advise against it.
He was then sent to serve as the Chancellor of Lǔ.
Later, the Déyáng Hall was constructed.
Once the hall was completed, the officials gathered for a grand assembly.
The Emperor said to the dukes and ministers,
"If the Minister Zhōnglí were here,
this hall would not have been completed."
From the "Records of the Eastern Observations of the Hàn"
On the first day of the first month,
the Son of Heaven visited the Déyáng Hall and ascended the steps,
where dukes, ministers, generals, and all officials joined to offer their greetings,
and the Man, Mò, Hú, and Qiāng paid tribute.
The accounting officers of the various commanderies,
all ascended to receive orders at the courtyard torch.
Members of the imperial clan, the Lius, gathered together.
From Cài Zhì's "Hàn Rites"
Yǎnshī, forty-three lǐ from the palace,
overlooked the five-tiered Ziǎo tower.
Above it was Déyáng,
seamlessly aligned with the heavenly motions.
From the "Memorandum on the Luòyáng Palace"
By the time of Xiǎnzōng,
having newly ennobled Dé,
they built Déyáng,
opening the special gates of the south entrance,
and established the grand gates of the main entrance.
Inside, it contained the Hándé Zhāngtái,
Tianlu Arch of Illumination,
Wēnchì Hall welcoming spring,
Shòuān for everlasting peace,
the flying pavilions traversed by spirits,
which none could delineate.
From the "Rhapsody of the Eastern Capital"
The grand sky bears its symbols,
demonstrating them for the emperors.
Beside the Purple Wei,
spirits were born and radiated light.
Great Hàn embodied the celestial order,
manifesting it with Déyáng.
Lofty and grand in beauty,
encompassing all directions.
Internally receiving tributes,
externally providing for the distant wilds.
From Lǐ Yóu's "Inscription on the Déyáng Hall"
Déyáng Hall, in its expanse, can accommodate ten thousand people,
channeling the Luò River beneath the hall.
From the "Hàn Officials' Roles and Positions"
Suí envoy Lú Sīdào was dispatched to Chén,
where the Chén ruler teased Sīdào using a quote from Guānshìyīn Sūtra:
"What merchant is this, bearing such precious treasures?"
Sīdào immediately responded with another quote from Guānshìyīn Sūtra:
"Suddenly encountering violent winds,
I drifted and fell into the land of rākṣasa demons."
The Chén ruler was greatly ashamed.
"Qǐ Yán Lù"
Jiǔlóng
Suí Dynasty's Xuē Dàohéng served as an envoy to the Southern Dynasties,
where a southern monk was exceptionally eloquent and quick-witted.
Xuē Dàohéng went to the temple to pay respects.
Upon reaching the door of the Buddha hall,
the monk loudly recited from the Lotus Sutra, saying:
"The Kumbhāṇḍa demons
are now outside the door."
Xuē Dàohéng immediately responded using the Lotus Sutra in reply:
"The Piśāca demons
are actually inside it."
The monks felt ashamed and were convinced.
End
In the third year of the Qinglong era of Emperor Míng,
a fire broke out in the Chónghuá Hall of Luòyáng.
On the Dīngsì day, the emperor returned to the Luòyáng Palace,
ordering the officials to rebuild the Chónghuá Hall,
and renamed it the Jiǔlóng Hall.
According to the Records of Wèi,
when the emperor rebuilt the Chónghuá Hall,
nine dragons appeared in the commanderies and kingdoms,
hence it was renamed the Jiǔlóng Hall.
From the Biography of Gāotáng Lóng.
Suí Dynasty's Héjiān Commandery's Liú Zhuō and his cousin Liú Xuàn were both Confucian scholars,
who once committed a crime and were imprisoned together.
The county officials did not know they were great scholars,
and put cangues on both of them.
Liú Zhuō said:
"Sitting in the cangue all day, yet not seeing home."
Liú Xuàn said:
"Carrying the cangue and sitting all day,
yet not seeing my wife."
Tàijí
Suī Jīngzhào Dù Gōngzhān,
the nephew of Wèiwèi Táiqīng,
once invited Yáng Jiè to his home.
As they drank to their heart's content,
they engaged in banter and jest.
Gōngzhān remarked:
"Since you bear the surname Yáng,
Yáng Huǒ truly insulted Confucius."
Jiè retorted:
"Since you bear the surname Dù,
Dù Bó once shot King Xuān."
Diànnéi Jiāngjūn Lǒngxī Niú Zǐchōng,
whose wit was praised by colleagues,
once said to Jiè:
"Your sheep (Yáng) has jiè (a ritual object),
I fear it cannot serve in the kitchen."
Jiè replied:
"Since your ox (Niú) is subdued,
it is just right for slaughter."
Seeing Jiè eat pickled mustard greens, he added:
"Your name is Jiè,
how can you still eat jiè cài (mustard greens)?"
Jiè responded:
"Since you bear the surname Niú (ox),
how can you not abstain from beef?"
There was Tàicāng Lìng Zhāng Cè,
who debated Jiè at Yúnlóng Gate,
and finding himself outreasoned,
said to Jiè:
"You originally lack virtue and measure,
yet unexpectedly share the name Shūbǎo."
Jiè raised his voice and declared:
"You are no hero,
how dare you connect your taboo name with Bófú."
Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ Lánlíng Xiāo Xǔ, sharp-witted and eloquent,
once said to Jiè:
"Exiling Gònggōng to Yōuzhōu,
Yìběi is hardly a land of joy."
Jiè replied:
"Banishing Huāndōu to Chóngshān,
Jiāngnán is no paradise either."
"Tán Sǒu"
Hóu Bǎi was quick-witted and eloquent,
and Yáng Sù maintained a friendly relationship with him.
Sù was from Guānzhōng,
while Bǎi was from Shāndōng.
Sù once deliberately posed a difficult question to him,
hoping he would have no reply.
Now, the local dialect of Guānzhōng
pronounces "water" as "bà,"
while Shāndōng dialect also says "qìng jiāng qù" for "take it away" as "qiè diāo."
Sù once teased Bǎi, saying:
"Shāndōng is indeed rich in benevolence and righteousness,
borrowing one but getting two."
Bǎi asked:
"How so, getting two?"
Sù replied:
"Someone asked to borrow a bow from another,
and said:
'Qiè diāo qù' (take the knife away).
Isn't that borrowing one but getting two?"
Bǎi responded immediately:
"The people of Guānzhōng are also very clever,
asking one but knowing two."
Sù said:
"How do you know that?"
Bǎi replied:
"Someone asked recently,
'With all the rain lately,
has the Wèi River risen?'"
The answer was:
"Bà zhǎng (the tyrant grows)—isn't that asking one but knowing two?"
Sù admired his quick wit and eloquence.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù" (Records of Sparking Laughter)
Emperor Míng of Wèi modeled the Supreme Ultimate in the Southern Palace of Luòyáng,
erecting the Supreme Ultimate Hall on the former site of the Hàn dynasty's Chóngdé Hall.
According to the "Commentary on the Waterways Classic",
the Wèi possessed halls such as the Supreme Ultimate, Nine Dragons, Lotus, Nine Splendors, and Inherited Light.
The "Register of Luòyáng Palaces"
records that the Supreme Ultimate Hall
was the royal resting hall under the Zhōu system.
During the Qín and Hàn dynasties it was called the Front Hall,
now termed Supreme Ultimate.
The designation Front Hall in the Luò Palace
originated from the Wèi.
It is noted,
based on "Records of the Grand Historian":
the Qín Emperor renamed palaces as temples,
modeling them after the Supreme Ultimate.
The Wèi designated the main hall as Supreme Ultimate,
adopting this concept but adding 'Supreme',
similar to how the Hàn's Xià Gate was renamed Grand Xià by the Wèi.
During the Xiánkāng era, the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Yǔ Chǎn proposed changing 'Grand' to 'Supreme',
which was erroneous.
Shān Qiānzhī's "Record of Dānyáng"
Hóu Bái held a sinecure post,
subordinate to Yáng Sù,
who admired his talent for witty conversation.
Every time it was his turn for duty,
he was ordered to entertain with jokes and banter,
sometimes from morning till night before he could return.
Just as he left the ministry gate,
he encountered Sù's son, Yáng Xuǎngǎn,
who said:
"Scholar Hóu, could you tell Xuǎngǎn a good story?"
Hóu Bái, detained and unable to refuse,
then said:
"A tiger went into the wilderness seeking meat,
and saw a hedgehog lying on its back.
Mistaking it for a piece of meat,
he tried to pick it up,
but suddenly the hedgehog curled around his nose.
Startled, he fled,
not daring to rest.
He ran until deep in the mountains,
exhausted,
and unknowingly fell into a deep sleep.
The hedgehog then released his nose and left.
The tiger suddenly awoke, overjoyed,
and walked to an oak tree.
Looking down, he saw an acorn
and, turning sideways, said to it:
'I encountered your esteemed father this morning;
I beg you, young sir, to please make way.'"
Bǎizǐ
"Ode on the Hall of Blessings":
Then comes the Hundred Sons,
where the rear palace resides,
Annotation:
"Wěi Dàn's 'Ode on the Hall of Blessings' states:
'Praising the era of the Hundred Sons,
dwelling in the auspicious decree of excellence',
the Máo Poetry Commentary says:
'Tàisì had ten sons,
thus the concubines were appropriate'.
The Hall of Hundred Sons is named,
likely derived from this."
Selections of Refined Literature
Péi Xuánběn was fond of jesting.
While serving as Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue,
Chief Minister Fáng Xuánlíng was gravely ill at the time.
When ministry officials were about to visit him,
Péi Xuánběn jokingly remarked:
"If the Chief Minister's illness were mild,
we should inquire after him;
but since it's already severe,
what's the point of asking?"
Someone leaked his words.
Later when he followed the others to visit,
Fáng Xuánlíng said with a laugh:
"Since Vice Director Péi has come,
Xuánlíng won't die."
From "Táng Xīn Yǔ"
Wéi Qìngběn's daughter was selected to be an imperial consort,
and he went to the Ming Hall to express gratitude.
Now, Wéi Qìngběn's ears were naturally curled beforehand,
so many court officials called him "Juǎn'ěr" (Curled Ears).
At that time, the Magistrate of Cháng'ān, Dù Sōngshòu, saw him and congratulated him, saying:
"I always knew your daughter would become a consort."
Qìngběn asked:
"How did you know?"
Sōngshòu then touched his own ears and curled them, saying:
"Juǎn'ěr (Curled Ears)
signifies the virtue of a queen or consort."
From "Amusing Anecdotes from Communal Living"
Shénlóng
The Vice Minister of Personnel Lǐ Ānqī,
grandson of Suí's Internal Secretary Dé Lín,
son of the Duke Ānpíng Lǐ Bǎiyào,
was by nature quick-witted.
Once, a candidate who had failed the selection
complained, saying:
"I am ashamed to go back the way I came."
Ānqī asked:
"Which pass did you come through?"
He replied:
"I came through the Pújīn Pass."
Ānqī said:
"Then take the Tóng Pass road back."
The candidate said:
"I am ashamed to face my wife and children."
Ānqī said:
"Your good wife already knows you well,
she surely won't laugh at you."
Another time, a candidate was being assessed for appointment,
Ānqī looked at his examination paper and said:
"Your calligraphy is somewhat weak."
The candidate replied:
"Yesterday I fell from a horse and injured my foot."
Ānqī said:
"How does an injured foot prevent you from writing well?"
Then reading the paper aloud, he said:
"Looking at this paper now,
it's not just your foot that's injured,
you must have internal injuries as well."
The man left in shame.
From "Qiān Zǎi"
The same incident is recorded in Huìchāng's "Jiě Yí" regarding Lǐ Jiǒngxiù.
In the Tàichū Palace stood the Shénlóng Hall,
located three lǐ from the county seat,
as Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú" states:
"Raise high the splendid hall of the divine dragon,
adorned with ornate railings in jagged array."
Records of Jiànkāng Palaces
Chìwū
Chìwū Hall,
located five lǐ northeast of the county,
followed the architectural system of Wú's Zhāomíng Palace,
corresponding to the constellations above,
as described in the "Rhapsody on the Wú Capital":
"Towering like the lofty Línhǎi peaks,
adorned with Chìwū's radiant splendor."
Above
Cuī Xínggōng and Jìng Bō were teasing each other,
Bō was wearing a palm wood dagger,
Xínggōng asked Bō:
"What kind of wood is this?"
Bō replied:
"It's palm wood."
Xínggōng said:
"I only asked about the dagger,
not about the person wearing it."
"Records of Making People Laugh"
Minister of Revenue Lǐ Xùn was stern and severe by nature,
and did not enjoy jesting or laughter.
At that time, Zhōu Yuàn was in charge of the salt and iron monopoly in Jiāngxī,
and was about to visit Lǐ in his capacity as acting governor. Lǐ warned his staff members,
"Mr. Zhōu is fond of banter and jokes,
I hope you all can be somewhat solemn when receiving him."
When Yuàn arrived,
Lǐ exchanged only a few polite remarks about the weather with him during banquets,
and did not speak further with him.
Thus Zhōu had no opportunity to display his humor.
One day, when hosting a banquet for relatives and guests,
Yuàn was also present.
A young man who was the son of an old friend of Lǐ's came seeking assistance,
having fallen into poverty and idleness.
Lǐ asked him extensively about various family estates
and valuable books and paintings,
to which the young man replied that all had been sold.
Lǐ reproached him,
"Young master, though you haven't yet obtained an official post,
and your family is poor enough to sell property,
how could you go so far as to dispose of books and ancient paintings?"
After lamenting for a while,
he asked again,
"There was one copy of the Book of Documents handwritten by Yú Shì'nán,
is that still around?"
The young man, ashamed and fearful,
dared not admit he had sold it,
and said,
"I only pawned it temporarily for money."
Suddenly Yuàn interjected,
"This Book of Documents has encountered great difficulty."
Lǐ had forgotten his previous resolve to avoid Yuàn's humor,
and asked,
"What difficulty has the Book of Documents encountered?"
Yuàn replied,
"It already suffered being pawned by Yáo and Shùn,
and now it's pawned again by this young man."
Lǐ's face broke into a broad smile despite his previous anger.
Records of Conversations
Qiānguāng
Zhāng Jùn dominated Héxī,
and built the Qiānguāng Hall in Gūzāng,
painting it in five colors,
adorned with gold and jade,
exhausting all precious craftsmanship.
On each of the four sides, a hall was erected:
the eastern one called Yìchūn Qīng Hall,
the southern one called Zhūyáng Chì Hall,
the western one called Zhèngxíng Bái Hall,
the northern one called Xuánwǔ Hēi Hall,
each matching the color of its direction,
and he resided in each according to the season.
"Jìn Shū"
Lù Chángyuán, by virtue of his senior virtue, served as the marching commander of the Xuānwǔ Army,
while Hán Yù was the patrol officer.
They both worked in the same commissioner's headquarters,
and some ridiculed the wide gap in their ages.
Zhōu Yuàn remarked:
"Both the tiger and the rat are among the twelve zodiac animals;
what is there to be surprised about?"
Within ten days, this story spread throughout Cháng'ān.
From "Supplement to the National History"
Qīngshǔ
Lǐ Chéng was in Xiàkǒu,
when one day a passing traveler came to bid farewell.
Chancellor Lǐ urged him to stay a couple more days,
but the traveler said:
"I have already set out,
and my boat is waiting at Hànkǒu."
Lǐ Chéng replied:
"Just trust me and stay,
that Hànkǒu is not to be trusted."
The traveler chuckled behind his hand and withdrew.
On another occasion, Chéng was drinking with his cousin, Chancellor Liú Shí,
when Shí mistakenly picked up the dice,
and the referee penalized him with a large cup of wine.
Shí said:
"What penalty is this?"
Chéng replied:
"When you were busy making a commotion earlier,
you took away his official seal,
so how can you refuse this?"
This was because taverns called "double four" the "official seal," mocking Shí.
In the winter of the ninth year of Tàihé,
due to Lǐ Xùn's rebellion,
he was hastily appointed to office.
From "Jiāhuà":
Chéng also once asked Shí:
"Have you ever taken stalactite powder?"
Shí replied:
"I've taken it recently,
and feel it gives me great strength."
Chéng said:
"I haven't gotten any strength from you at all."
This mocked Shí for having accomplished nothing urgent or difficult while in the ministerial office.
From "Yǔlín Shànxuè Jí"
Emperor Lièzōng built the Clear Summer Palace,
those with insight said "Clear Summer,"
in reverse pronunciation sounds like "Chǔ's voice,"
to name a palace with a sorrowful sound,
is not auspicious.
Soon Emperor Lièzōng passed away,
Huán Xuán proclaimed himself King of Chǔ.
"Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū"
Tàijí
Liú Xuánzuǒ governed Biàn.
Once, due to anger from a dispute,
he intended to execute the military officer Zhái Xínggōng.
Everyone inside and outside lamented this,
yet no one dared to plead for him.
The recluse Zhèng Shè, skilled in humor,
quietly went to see Xuánzuǒ.
He remained silent throughout,
but as he was about to take his leave,
he said:
"I heard Zhái Xínggōng is to be executed.
I beg to have his body handed over for a look."
Xuánzuǒ, puzzled, asked him why.
He replied:
"I've heard that the faces of the wrongly executed—
I've never seen one in my life,
so I wanted to borrow a look."
Xuánzuǒ gradually understood,
and thus spared him.
From "The Collection of Good Humor"
In the third year of the Xiàowǔ Emperor's Tàiyuán era,
Xiè Ān, the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, constructed the new palace's Great Ultimate Hall.
It was short one beam,
when a plum wood log drifted to the foot of Stone Fortress City.
They therefore took and used it,
painted plum blossoms on the beam,
to signify the auspicious omen,
and consequently named it the Beam Hall.
It lasted through the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
and later was where Liáng Wǔdì resided.
"Jīnlíng Historical Sites"
When the Xiàowǔ Emperor built the Great Ultimate Hall,
Guō Pú divined and said:
"In two hundred and ten years,
this hall will be destroyed by a slave."
Later, Liáng Wǔdì demolished it,
having renounced the throne to become a slave.
"Records of the Jìn Restoration"
Guō Pú
was killed by Wáng Dūn during the Míngdì era,
already over fifty years prior,
is an error.
Yú Dí heard that Wéi Gāo presented "Music in Praise of Saints",
so he also composed "Obedient Saint Music" to present,
and at every banquet he would have it performed.
When the music was about halfway through,
all the dancers in the rows would kneel down,
while one person danced alone in the center.
His aide Wéi Shòu laughed and said:
"Why exhaust the troops for a solo dance?"
This was mocking Dí for being a tyrannical military governor of Xiāngzhōu,
where people called him the "Xiāng-style military governor".
"Supplement to the National History"
Yùzhú
Luó Yǐn and Gù Yún together visited Huáinán's Gāo Pián.
Yún was by nature refined and esteemed,
while Yǐn had an arrogant and disdainful temperament.
Lord Gāo retained Yún but distanced Yǐn,
so Yǐn intended to return to Wǔlíng.
He drank with the guest staff,
and they bid him farewell at Yún Pavilion.
At the time, it was the height of summer,
and a bluebottle fly entered the seating area.
Gāo ordered it to be driven away with a fan,
and thus teased Yǐn, saying:
"The bluebottle fly, fanned,
is fanned away from the seat."
Yǐn noticed a White Zé diagram nailed to the door,
and immediately responded:
"The White Zé, nailed,
is nailed to the door."
This was meant to mock Yún.
"Jiàn Jiè Lù"
and "Jùn Gé Xián Tán"
attribute this to Kòu Bào and Xiè Guàn.
Sòng Yǒngchū's residence,
was solely referred to as the Western Palace,
until Xiàowǔ constructed new palaces like Zhèngguāng, Yùzhú, and Zǐjí.
They had intricately carved railings and decorated columns,
and pearl windows and mesh doors.
"Nán Shǐ"
Wáng Jiàn was in Xǔxià,
and had once been punished by penal servitude for an offense,
but without any cane marks.
When he came to rule Shǔ,
he obtained Mǎ Juān as an aide.
Juān was fond of slandering and exposing others,
so Jiàn feared being ridiculed by him.
Thus, he took an opportunity to ask:
"I've privately heard outside discussions
that I once suffered penal servitude;
is this true?"
Juān replied:
"It is true."
Relying on the absence of cane marks,
Jiàn then bared his back in front of everyone to show Juān, saying:
"Please take a look, sir—
could one who has been caned have skin like this?"
Juān knew he was being deceitful,
so he patted his back and sighed:
"How extraordinary!
Where did you get such excellent ointment back then?"
The guests and aides all turned pale with shock,
but Juān remained composed.
"Supplement to the History of the Five Dynasties"
Yù Shòu
Qí Dōng Hūn went on an excursion,
burning down the Xuán Yí and Yào Líng palaces,
then extensively constructed Fāng Lè and Xiān Huá palaces,
and additionally built three separate palaces—Shén Xiān, Yǒng Shòu, and Yù Shòu—for Pān Shū Fēi,
all decorated with gold and jade from the market,
among which the Yù Shòu Palace featured a flying immortal tent,
embroidered with silk on all four sides,
and every window was painted with immortals.
"History of the Southern Dynasties"
Monk Guànxiū was witty and sharp,
Dù Guāngtíng wanted to blunt his edge,
and every time they met,
he would watch for his actions to tease him.
One day, while riding through the main street,
Guànxiū's horse suddenly dropped dung,
and Guāngtíng immediately called out:
"Great Master, Great Master,
your prayer beads have fallen to the ground."
Guànxiū replied:
"Those are not prayer beads,
but rather the great elixir of immortality!"
Zhāngzhù
The Left Street Buddhist Registrar Huìjiāng and Master of Ceremonies Chéng Zǐxiāo
were both quick-witted
and often ridiculed each other.
Jiāng, being rather plump,
once bared himself during the summer heat.
Xiāo suddenly saw him and said:
"The Buddhist Registrar has pipa legs."
Jiāng retorted:
"The Master has a bìlì head."
They then saw several camels,
and Xiāo pointed at a large one, saying:
"This one must be a ascetic."
Jiāng said:
"These creatures multiply in a certain order;
this one is the senior,
not an ascetic."
From "Records of the Unusual"
When Hóu Jǐng was pacified initially,
the fire burned down the Tàijí Hall,
Liáng Yuándì proposed to rebuild it,
but one pillar was missing.
By the second year of Chén Yǒngdìng's reign,
a large camphor tree, eighteen arm-spans in girth,
forty-five feet long,
drifted and moored at the rear isle of the Táo family.
Supervising army officer Zōu Zǐdù reported it,
and an imperial decree ordered Shěn Zhòng, the Head of the Central Secretariat, and Cài Tuó, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, to construct the Tàijí Hall.
"Book of Chén"
In the past, during the Jìn dynasty, when repairing the hall, there was a shortage of apricot wood,
a plum beam auspiciously arrived,
decorated with painted flowers.
From then until now,
another divine object was obtained,
namely the camphor tree,
and a certain pillar in the hall is exactly that one.
"Inscription on the Tàijí Hall"
Lú Zhì,
courtesy name Zǐzhēng,
had a playful and joking nature,
served as Secretary to Zhuāngzōng.
When the imperial physician Chén Xuán was appointed as the Erudite of Medical Studies in Tàiyuán Prefecture,
the relevant department requested a draft,
and Zhì immediately composed it.
The final line read:
"Having obtained the talent of Hòupò,
it is fitting to oversee the duty of Cōngróng."
Zhuāngzōng reviewed it,
and for a long time was unable to stop laughing.
From "Jì Yì".
In Húnán, Mǎ Xīshēng heard that Liáng's Zhū Wēn was fond of eating chicken,
so he had fifty chickens slaughtered for a meal.
While in mourning for his father, King Wǔmù,
on the eve of the funeral procession,
he devoured several plates of chicken stew.
The Vice Minister of Personnel, Pān Qǐ, mocked him, saying:
"In the past, Ruǎn Jí ate steamed pork while in mourning;
what era lacks its worthy men?"
The Unicorn's Hoof
Zǒng Lìn was a renowned figure in the southern region of Jiānglíng.
After the pacification, he entered the pass with Wáng Bāo and others.
During the early reign of Emperor Míng, he worked with Bāo and others in the Línzhǐ Hall to compile and revise various books,
and was frequently honored with banquets and gifts.
The "Book of Zhōu"
records that Emperor Wǔ opened the Línzhǐ Hall,
gathering scholars,
among whom Xiāo Dàyuán participated.
Above.
Lǐ Màozhēn's son Cóng Yǎn served as the military governor of Fèngxiáng.
On his birthday,
the emissary from Qínfèng, who was in charge of rituals,
was ugly and had a thick beard.
The emissary from Wèibó was a youth as beautiful as a lovely woman.
The Wèibó emissary joked:
"Today is my misfortune,
to be seated next to the King of Water Plants."
The Qínfèng emissary retorted:
"Madam, do not speak too much,"
and all those seated around laughed.
"Supplementary Records of the History of the Five Dynasties"
Tiānróng Academician Xú Zhòngyǎ,
possessed outstanding talent,
with a penchant for humor and wit.
Zhōu Xíngféng had long heard of his reputation,
and summoned him to serve as Military Commissioner's Judge.
Initially, when Wáng Kuí raised his army,
he understood that official positions could vary in importance,
and, seeking to win over the masses,
anyone who could answer the call to enlist
was appointed as Minister of Works or Grand Guardian to entice them.
From then on, in the villages and markets of Wǔlíng,
countless arrogant and domineering individuals styled themselves as Ministers of Works or Grand Guardians.
"Sānchǔ New Records"
On Xíngféng's birthday,
various regions each sent envoys to offer congratulations.
Xíngféng wore a proud expression,
and said to Zhòngyǎ:
"Are the four neighbors also afraid of me?"
Zhòngyǎ replied:
"Within the borders under Your Excellency's command,
the heavens are filled with great harmony,
and the earth is covered with Ministers of Works—
how could the four neighbors not be afraid?"
"Continued Accounts of the World"
Observing the Customs
During the Tàidìng era,
the Western Róng invaded the border,
and the imperial army suffered defeat.
A chancellor of the state retired due to old age,
and his colleagues gathered at his residence to congratulate him.
As they drank merrily,
he boasted, saying:
"I am but a mountain dweller,
who encountered the right time and gained the ruler's favor.
Now I retire at home,
at a time when there is not a single trouble in the world—
I can truly be called a fortunate man of peace."
Shí Zhōnglì remarked:
"There is only that band of thieves in Shǎnxī who haven't been caught yet."
The entire room burst into laughter.
From "Xiāngshān Yě Lù"
Emperor Yáng of Suí made an imperial tour to the north,
Yǔwén Kǎi built an observatory mobile palace,
which could accommodate several hundred imperial guards,
constructed in detachable sections,
with wheels and axles installed below for movement,
swiftly shifting as if by divine power.
The Róng and Dí tribes witnessed it,
and none were not astonished.
"Basic Biography"
When Wáng Jīnggōng was chancellor,
he extensively promoted water conservancy projects across the land.
At that time, someone even proposed draining Lake Tài,
claiming it could yield tens of thousands of qǐng of fertile farmland.
Everyone laughed at the idea.
Jīnggōng happened to mention it while conversing with guests,
with Liú Gòngfù present at the time.
Gòngfù immediately responded,
"This is easy to accomplish."
Jīnggōng asked,
"How so?"
Gòngfù replied,
"Simply dig another Lake Tài nearby
to hold the water, and it's done."
Jīnggōng laughed heartily.
"Records of the Bright Way"
"Miscellaneous Records by the Eastern Window" notes that Lake Tài is written as Mount Liáng Marsh.
Zhōnghuá
Liú Gòngfù and Wáng Jièfǔ were the closest of old friends.
Jièfǔ once playfully dissected Gòngfù's name, saying:
"Liú Bān isn't worth a single coin."
This referred to his name.
Gòngfù then dissected Jièfǔ's name in return:
"Lose the 'woman' and it becomes 'to delay',
Without the 'roof' it's truly 'jealous',
Below, 'cross' confuses with 'true',
Above, the top mistakenly becomes 'ruler'."
Jièfǔ was greatly embarrassed,
and held a grudge in his heart.
From "Wáng Zhí's Silent Records"
In April of the ninth year of the Wǔdé era,
sweet dew descended upon the paulownia wood in the Zhōnghuá Hall,
glistening like ice and snow,
and it was shown to the assembled ministers.
The "Huìyào" records:
In the early years of the Yǒnghuī era,
Emperor Gāozōng summoned his chief ministers to the Hóngwén Pavilion,
and the academicians were seated in the Zhōnghuá Hall.
He asked what cultivation leads to kingship,
and what conduct leads to hegemony.
Líng Hú Défēn replied:
"Kingship relies on virtue,
while hegemony relies on punishment."
From the "Old Biography."
Dānxiāo
Wáng Jièfǔ argued that Yángzǐ's leaping from the tower was a historian's error,
and the writing of "Jù Qín Měi Xīn" was also a later fabrication against Zǐyún.
One day, when discussing this with Dōngpō,
Dōngpō said:
"Shì also doubts one thing."
Jīnggōng asked:
"What do you doubt?"
Dōngpō replied:
"I wonder if there really was a Zǐyún in the Western Hàn dynasty?"
Those who heard this all laughed heartily.
"Běi Chuāng Zhì Guǒ"
Dōngpō called on Lǚ Wēizhòng,
who was taking a nap and only came out after a long time.
In the reception room,
there was a basin of calamus with a green-haired turtle.
Dōngpō pointed and said:
"This is easy to obtain,
but one with six eyes would be hard to find."
Wēizhòng asked:
"Where does a six-eyed turtle come from?"
Dōngpō replied:
"During the Tongguang era of Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng,
the kingdom of Linyì once presented a six-eyed turtle.
At that time, Jìng Xīnmó was at court,
and offered a rhyme saying:
'Don't make noise,
listen to this turtle's rhyme:
with six eyes, one sleep
equals three sleeps for others.'"
