Tàizōng feasted his ministers at the Dānxiāo Hall,
commanding Duke Wèi to play a game of wéiqí,
and bestowed upon him a horse from the Imperial Stables,
along with a gold-adorned saddle, bridle, and bit.
"Records of Duke Wèi's Admonitions"
Fēishuāng
In the seventh month of the twentieth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
an imperial banquet was held for officials of the fifth rank and above at the Fēishuāng Hall,
with string and wind instruments playing in succession,
the assembled ministers offered toasts,
and silk brocades were bestowed as gifts.
The hall was located north of the Xuánwǔ Gate,
taking advantage of the high and open terrain,
with layered pavilions rising three stories,
channeling water for cleanliness,
and a clear pond to wash away the summer heat.
"Veritable Records"
Jiāhé Fāng Qiānlǐ,
one day met and became acquainted with Zhāng Gēngshēng.
Qiānlǐ then composed a jesting rhyme saying:
"The ancient one was Liú Gēngshēng,
the present one is Zhāng Gēngshēng,
holding in hand a volume of the 'Diamond Sutra',
I ask whether you are born from womb, egg, moisture, or metamorphosis."
Gēngshēng said to Fāng:
"The ancient one was Mǎ Qiānlǐ,
the present one is Fāng Qiānlǐ,
holding in hand a volume of the 'Treatise on Criminal Law',
I ask whether you are exiled five thousand lǐ, one thousand lǐ, or three thousand lǐ."
"Wěiháng Jì Tán"
Zhāng Yì,
a native of Yánpíng,
entered the National University and became a dormitory prefect.
He was short in stature yet strictly enforced rigid etiquette among the students.
Lín Shūgōng from Putian, also a frivolous scholar,
composed a poem and rhapsody based on his name,
mocking him. The rhapsody read:
"His figure is short and small,
lacking six feet of Cáo Jiāo's height.
His belly is hollow and empty,
devoid of a single drop of Liú Yì's ink."
The poem read:
"Split the character 'Yì' into two parts,
let the wind slant the ten horizontal strokes.
On top, there is no trace of refinement,
yet before others, he forces out some presence."
Those who heard it were convulsed with laughter.
"Qídōng Yěyǔ"
Two Forms
In the sixteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era, the Emperor said to his attending ministers:
"While reading the biography of Liú Cōng,
I learned that Empress Liú was about to build the Luányí Hall.
Chén Yuándá remonstrated with me
about procuring timber from Lántián
to construct a separate hall,
modeled after the Liǎngyí Hall,
and even planned to build a multi-story pavilion.
But recalling Liú Cōng's story, I stopped the project."
Old Book of Táng
records: When Emperor Zhōngzōng held a banquet in the Liǎngyí Hall,
he ordered barbarian performers to sing and play the shēng.
Wǔ Píngyī submitted a memorial remonstrating:
"The Liǎngyí Chéngqìng Hall
is where Your Majesty holds court and hears legal cases.
When feasting with all the ministers,
it is improper to allow entertainers' vulgar familiarity."
The Emperor
Yè Héng was dismissed from his position as chancellor,
and returned to his hometown in Jīnhuá,
often inviting commoners to drink with him daily.
One day, feeling unwell,
he suddenly became melancholy and asked his guests:
"I am about to die,
but my regret is not knowing whether it is pleasant after death."
A scholar named Jīn replied:
"It is very pleasant."
Yè looked at him in surprise and asked:
"How do you know?"
He said:
"If death were unpleasant,
the dead would all escape and return;
yet once dead, none come back,
so I know it must be pleasant."
All present laughed.
The following year, the chancellor indeed passed away.
As recorded by Wáng Guānzhī in Chéng Shǐ.
Yáochí
According to the old system, contributing three thousand hu of grain to a border commandery
earned one the position of assistant instructor in their home prefecture.
A certain Wáng from Qíshān obtained an official post through grain contribution,
and purchased a fine horse at a high price,
yet remained unsatisfied,
often regretting it.
Once, while riding through the market,
healer Lǐ praised the horse highly for its robustness.
When asked about its price,
Wáng, surprised, inquired further,
to which Lǐ said:
"It can carry three thousand dan of grain,
isn't that robust enough?"
From "Wěiháng Jìtán"
Shī Dàomín was tattooed by Sūn Wēimǐn,
and later regained his freedom,
then borrowed a small-character soldier's sedan chair to go out,
Zēng Zǐgù saw it and said:
"What a fine footnote sedan chair."
from Zhìlín
Emperor Tàizōng once visited the Yáochí Palace,
and turning to his attending officials, asked:
"How long has it been since the Western Barbarians made contact?"
from "Wèi Zhèng Gōng's Record of Remonstrances"
Lovesickness
On the Pole's End
A scholar from Jízhōu went to the provincial examination,
writing on his signboard first "Ōuyáng Bólè, Top Candidate from Lúlíng."
Someone mocked him, saying:
"A guest has come from afar from Jízhōu,
His name is written on the carrying pole's end.
Though we know you are Ōuyáng's descendant,
After all, we've never known Xiū."
"Yíjiān Zhīzhì"
The Beginning of the Wind
Wú Jǐshì's daughter was intelligent and skilled in poetry.
She later married Chén Zǐcháo of Huáyáng,
a renowned scholar,
who in his later years became infatuated with a concubine,
and because of this contracted a wind-induced illness.
One day when relatives came to visit,
Wú was present with the concubine,
and pointing at the concubine, she said:
"This is the beginning of the wind."
Afterward, among the scholar-officials in the southwest, whenever someone became infatuated,
they all used "the beginning of the wind" as a byword.
From "Huìmǔ Shíyīng Jí Juànyǒng Lù"
In the sixteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era, Zhēnzhū Kèhán of the Xuēyántuó sent an envoy,
with his nephew Shílì Shè presenting betrothal gifts and offering a feast.
The Emperor hosted at the Xiāngsī Hall,
feasting all his officials grandly,
and arranged performances from ten music divisions.
"Comprehensive Mirror"
"Tianzhong Ji, Volume Twenty-Six"
Zǐwēi
In the seventh month of the twenty-first year of the Zhēnguàn era,
the Emperor went on an excursion,
and ordered Fengyù Wáng Xiàojī to construct thirteen bays of the Zǐwēi Hall inside the Xiǎndào Gate,
with patterned bricks and layered foundations,
tall, spacious, and grand.
The Emperor was very pleased upon seeing it.
"Veritable Records"
Qīng (clear),
means qīng (blue-green),
being far removed from turbidity,
its impure color is like blue-green.
Lián (incorruptible),
means to restrain,
to restrain and examine oneself.
From *Shì Míng*
Zǐchén
A man of Sòng obtained a piece of jade and presented it to Zǐ Hǎn,
but Zǐ Hǎn declined to accept it.
The presenter said:
"I showed it to a jade craftsman,
who confirmed it as a treasure;
therefore I dared to offer it."
Zǐ Hǎn replied:
"I regard non-greed as my treasure,
while you regard jade as treasure.
If you were to give it to me,
we would both lose our treasures;
it would be better
for each to keep their own treasure."
The man bowed his head to the ground and explained:
"A commoner carrying such a precious jade
dare not travel through the countryside;
I present this to beg for my life."
(Xiāng 15)
When the Qìng clan perished,
Yànzǐ was offered the fief of Bèidiàn,
with its sixty border towns,
but he declined to accept it.
Zǐ Wěi said:
"Wealth is what all men desire,
why do you alone not desire it?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"The Qìng clan's cities were sufficient to satisfy their desires,
and thus they perished.
My own cities are not sufficient to satisfy my desires.
If I were to add Bèidiàn to them,
then they would become sufficient to satisfy my desires.
Once desires are satisfied,
ruin would not be far off.
If I were exiled abroad,
I would not even be able to govern a single one of my cities.
I do not accept Bèidiàn
not because I detest wealth,
but because I fear losing wealth.
Moreover, wealth is like cloth and silk which have a fixed width;
rules and measures are established for them
to prevent any deviation.
Since the people are born with strong desires for material benefits,
we must therefore use virtue to regulate them,
so that there is no excess or negligence—this is called 'regulated benefit.'
When benefits are excessive, it leads to ruin.
I dare not be greedy for more;
this is what is meant by 'regulation.'"
He was then offered sixty towns from the northern suburbs,
and he accepted them.
When offered a fief by Zǐ Yǎ,
he declined the larger portion and accepted only a small part.
When offered a fief by Zǐ Wěi,
he accepted it but soon returned most of it.
(From the 28th year of Duke Xiāng)

In the third year of the Lóngshuò era, in the fourth month, the imperial guard was moved to the Pénglái Palace, and for the first time, the emperor held court in the Zǐchén Hall to attend to state affairs,
with all officials offering congratulations.
From the "Essential Documents"
Lìndé
Duke Jǐng presented Xián Zhāng with fifty carts of fish.
Zhāng returned home,
with fish carts blocking the road.
Patting his charioteer's hand,
he said:
"In the past, Yànzǐ declined rewards to correct his ruler,
thus faults and errors were not concealed;
now all the ministers flatter and toady to seek profit.
If I accept these fish,
this would contradict Yànzǐ's principles,
and comply with the desires of flatterers."
He firmly declined the fish and did not accept them.
The gentleman says:
"Xián Zhāng's integrity
is the legacy of Yànzǐ's conduct."
Yànzǐ Chūnqiū
Wú Yánlíng Jìzǐ was traveling in Qí,
when he saw some lost gold,
and called to a herdsman to pick it up.
The herdsman said:
"You dwell on high,
yet look down low;
your appearance is that of a gentleman,
but your words are uncouth.
I have a lord but do not act as his subject,
have friends but do not act as their companion;
in the heat of summer I wear furs—
do you suspect me of taking the gold?"
Yánlíngzǐ realized he was a worthy man,
and asked to know his surname and given name.
The herdsman said:
"You are but a man who judges by outward appearance—
why should I trouble to tell you my name!"
With that, he departed.
Yánlíng Jìzǐ stood gazing after him,
and did not cease until he was out of sight.
From the Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn.
Emperor Míng Huáng was by nature harmonious and amiable,
and even slanderous talk could not shake him.
At that time, thousands of wagtails gathered at the Lìndé Hall,
perching and soaring on the courtyard trees for a full day.
Wèi Guāngchéng composed a eulogy,
considering it an auspicious sign of the Son of Heaven's fraternal affection,
and the emperor was pleased,
also composing a eulogy himself.
"Biography of Nìng Wáng Xiàn"
To the southwest of Jīnluán Hall was the Cháng'ān Hall,
north of Cháng'ān Hall was the Xiānjū Hall,
and northwest of Xiānjū Hall was the Lìndé Hall.
This hall had three sides,
hence it was named the Three Halls.
Dàfú Hall was north of the Three Halls,
and Shícuì Hall was southeast of Dàfú Hall.
"Records of the Two Capitals"
Zēngzǐ established integrity,
refusing to drink from the Robber Spring,
which is what is called cultivating one's will.
Huáinánzi · Sayings on the Mountain
Jīnluán
Zǐlù asked Confucius, saying:
"When a benevolent person or an incorruptible scholar
faces poverty, would they change their principles?"
The Master said:
"If they changed their principles, how could they be called incorruptible and benevolent?"
Family Sayings
During the Tiānbǎo era, Lǐ Bái was recommended by Hè Zhīzhāng to Emperor Xuánzōng.
He was summoned to the Jīnluán Hall,
where they discussed contemporary affairs.
Lǐ Bái presented a eulogy,
was granted a meal,
and the emperor personally seasoned the soup for him.
"Basic Biography"
North of the Zǐchén Hall in the Dàmíng Palace was the Pénglái Hall,
while west of the Lóngshǒu Mountain ridge rising from the flat ground stood the hall named Jīnluán Hall,
with the adjacent slope called Jīnluán Slope.
"Records of the Two Capitals"
The hall derived its name from the Jīnluán Slope,
and it was connected to the Hànlín Academy.
"Institutions of the Five Dynasties"
The Emperor once summoned the financial officials from various commanderies,
inquiring about their local customs and the competence of past and present governors and magistrates.
The financial clerk from Shǔ Commandery, Fǎn Xiǎn, stepped forward and said:
"When Zhāng Kān, the Governor of Yùyáng, was previously in Shǔ,
his benevolence brought kindness to the people,
and his authority was capable of punishing the wicked.
After Gōngsūn Shù was defeated,
treasures piled up like mountains, and the wealth he handled
was enough to enrich ten generations.
Yet on the day Zhāng Kān left his post,
he rode in a carriage with a broken shaft,
with only a cloth-covered bag."
Upon hearing this, the Emperor sighed with admiration.
From "Dōngguān Hànjì"
Hányuán
Dàmíng Gōng,
in the third year of the Lóngshuò era, was moved to Pénglái Gōng,
and a new Hányuán Diàn was built.
《Huì Yào》
states: Hányuán
was the imperial hall for grand court assemblies.
《Wǔxíng Zhì》
records that on the left and right of Hányuán Diàn stood the Qīfèng and Xiángluán pavilions,
with a dragon-tail staircase extending in front of the pavilions.
The distance from the hall's gate to the southern gate was five lǐ,
and during the New Year's court assembly,
those who came to pay homage
gazed up at the jade throne
as if it were amidst the clouds and heavens.
Minister of Works Sòng Hóng once received his salary in grain,
and ordered his students to sell it at the time.
The students did not sell because the price was low,
which angered Hóng.
He then sold all the grain at a low price,
refusing to compete for profit.
The emperor
Yáng Zhèn,
courtesy name Bóqǐ,
was a person from Hóngnóng.
He was impartial and incorruptible by nature,
and did not accept private gifts.
He often had his children and grandchildren eat plain vegetables and walk on foot.
Some old friends and elders wanted him to start building family assets,
but Yáng Zhèn refused,
saying:
"To let later generations call me a pure and honest official,
and to leave this reputation to my children and grandchildren—
isn't that a rich legacy?"
When he served as the Governor of Dōnglái,
while passing through Chāngyì on his journey,
the county magistrate Wáng Mì,
who was a former Excellent Talent recommended by him,
came at night carrying ten catties of gold to present to Yáng Zhèn.
Yáng Zhèn said:
"Your old friend understands you,
but you do not understand your old friend.
Why is this?"
Wáng Mì said:
"There is no one who knows at night."
Yáng Zhèn said:
"Heaven knows,
the gods know,
how can you say no one knows?"
In the
Fànshū it is recorded as: Heaven knows,
the gods know,
you know,
and I know.
Jiǔlóng
Mǎ Xīfàn built the Nine Dragon Hall,
with eight dragons coiling around the pillars,
declaring himself to be the ninth dragon.
"History of the Five Dynasties"
Zhōnglí Yì served as a Secretary.
The Governor of Jiaozhi, Zhāng Huī,
was corrupt in his official duties,
amassing illicit wealth exceeding a thousand gold pieces,
with pearls, jewels, and rare treasures amounting to several stone measures.
The records of the confiscated assets were submitted to the Minister of Agriculture,
and an imperial decree ordered all the pearls to be bestowed upon the various Secretaries.
All of them bowed and accepted,
but Yì alone cast the pearls and jewels to the ground,
refusing to bow and accept them.
Emperor Ming asked why he had cast the pearls aside,
to which he replied:
"I have heard that Confucius endured thirst
rather than drink water from the Spring of Thieves;
Zēng Zǐ turned his carriage around
and would not enter the lane named 'Surpassing Mother,'
detesting their names.
Now, Your Majesty is bestowing pearls obtained through corruption upon loyal ministers,
which is why I did not bow to accept them."
From the "Bié Zhuàn."
Tàihé
Lián Fàn at age fifteen,
went to Shǔ to retrieve his grandmother's remains,
and upon reaching Jiāméng,
the boat capsized and he nearly drowned.
Governor Zhāng Mù offered him several boxes of cloth from his official salary,
but Fàn said:
"Stone is born hard,
orchid is born fragrant—
these are fundamentally incompatible,
I cannot bear to accept this."
Thus he did not accept it.
"Records of the Eastern Pavilion"
Within the Yùqīng Palace are the Liáoyáng Hall and the Tàihé Hall.
The "Dēng Zhēn Yǐn Jué"
Huáng Xiàng,
courtesy name Wénzhāng,
was of an honest and upright character.
While walking on the road one day,
he found a bag of gold beads,
worth over two million coins.
He sought out its owner
and returned it.
From Xiè Chéng's Hòu Hàn Shū
Fàn Dān,
courtesy name Shǐyún,
was from Wàihuáng.
He went west to Guānzhōng to study.
He served as the magistrate of Láiwú,
but left office,
and then told fortunes in the market for a living,
while his wife spun and wove to support themselves.
When summoned to serve in the official bureau,
he had no carriage to ride,
so he carried his own bag and followed on foot.
He once sent his son to buy wheat,
and obtained five hú.
A fellow villager gave him an additional hú,
and instructed the son, saying:
"Don't let your father know."
When the son returned home,
he didn't dare not to tell.
Fàn Dān immediately ordered to send all six hú back,
saying the wheat had already been mixed,
so the villager didn't dare to accept.
Fàn Dān's disciple Kǎi saw that his fence was incomplete,
and loaded firewood to repair it,
just as Fàn Dān happened to be away.
When he returned, he was angry,
and ordered his son to pull out the firewood and return it.
The local people sang about him:
"In Fàn Shǐyún's rice steamer dust collects,
in Fàn Láiwú's cauldron fish swim."
Knowing himself to be impatient by nature,
whenever he served as an official,
he always wore a leather belt.
From "Yuán Shānsōng's Later Book":
When Fàn Dān's elder sister was ill, he went to visit her,
and his sister prepared food.
Fàn Dān, because he considered his brother-in-law to be lacking in virtue,
left two hundred coins at the door upon leaving.
His sister sent someone to chase after him and return the money,
but he gave it back,
and Fàn Dān had no choice but to accept it.
The grass-cutting servants in the neighborhood angrily said to each other:
"They say you are pure and lofty,
but how could someone like Fàn Shǐyún say he didn't steal from us?"
Fàn Dān heard this and said:
"My humble integrity is judged by the mouths of servant boys,
I must not be remiss."
So he threw away the money and left.
From "Xiè Chéng's Later Book":
See also the entry on sisters.
Tiānzhōng Jì Volume Thirteen
Building
Yǐngchuān's Huáng Zǐlián,
every time he watered his horse,
would throw coins into the water.
Fēngsú Tōng
records that Ānlīng's virtuous Xiàng Zhòngshān,
when watering his horse in the Wèi River,
would give three coins daily
as compensation.
Sānfǔ Jué Lù
Luòyáng Lìng Dǒng Xuān died,
an imperial edict ordered an inspection of his household,
finding only a single worn-out carriage,
and one horse.
The Emperor said:
"Dǒng Xuān's integrity,
I only came to know upon his death."
"Chronicles of the Elderly from Chénliú"
Narrow and elongated with curves is called a lóu.
"Ěryǎ"
Lóu,
means a multi-storied building,
a thatched watchtower in marshes guarding the grass.
"Shuōwén"
Lóu,
has doors, windows, and various openings,
appearing layered and intricate.
"Shìmíng"
Xú Wěi's slave was prone to rebellion,
and an acquaintance wanted to purchase him for Wěi.
Wěi said:
"It cannot be done.
If the slave goes,
he will surely flee again.
How could I accept payment for him in vain at a cheap price?"
Such was his righteous integrity.
Records of the Elderly of Chángshā
twelve
Fánguài have said,
in the time of Huángdì there were five walled cities and twelve towers,
to await the divine beings at Zhíqī,
named Yíngnián.
"Fēngshàn Shū"
Kūnlún Mountain has accumulated gold,
forming the Heavenly Rampart City,
upon which are placed five golden platforms,
and twelve jade towers.
"Shízhōu Jì"
Chéng Jiān,
courtesy name Móufǔ,
was a native of Wǔyīn in Nányáng.
He was benevolent, filial, and incorrupt,
living in poverty without means.
He polished mirrors to support himself
and did not accept others' alms.
When several old women were washing clothes together
and took turns calling each other to eat,
if someone did not eat,
they would say to each other:
"You are not Chéng Móufǔ,
why do you not eat others' food?"
From the Diǎn Lüè.
Hú Zhì served as the governor of Bèi Province,
and upon his death,
his household had no surplus wealth,
only bestowed garments and a book chest remained.
Records of Wèi
Wēi,
courtesy name Bóhǔ,
was resolute and pure from a young age,
held various high offices,
Emperor Wǔ granted him an audience,
admiring his father's integrity,
and thus said to Wēi:
"How does your integrity compare to your father's?"
Wēi replied:
"Your subject falls short."
The Emperor said:
"In what way do you fall short?"
He responded:
"My father's integrity feared being known by others,
while my integrity fears not being known by others,
this is why I fall far short!"
Chronicles of Jìnyáng
Kūnlún
The magistrate of Gé, Yuán Yì, was corrupt in his governance,
and bribed the imperial court to build a false reputation.
He once sent Shān Tāo a hundred catties of silk,
but Shān Tāo, not wishing to differ from the crowd,
accepted it,
then ordered it hung from a beam.
Later, when Yì's deeds were exposed,
and officials arrived to investigate all the implicated officials,
Tāo retrieved the silk from the beam,
where it had gathered years of dust,
with the seal still intact as before.
"Discourses on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove"
Jǐnán rén Gōngyù Dài presented a diagram of the Bright Hall from the time of the Yellow Emperor,
in the center of which was a hall,
connected by a covered corridor with a tower above,
entering from the southwest,
named Kūnlún.
"Treatise on Sacrifices"
Fàn Xuān,
courtesy name Zǐxuān,
at the age of eight,
was pure in conduct and frugal by nature.
Hán Yùzhāng
Bó
presented him with a hundred bolts of silk,
which he did not accept.
When reduced to fifty bolts,
he still did not accept.
In this way, it was halved repeatedly
until it reached just one bolt,
and still he refused.
Later, Hán rode in the same carriage with Fàn,
and inside the carriage, he tore off two zhang of silk and gave it to Fàn,
saying:
"How can one let his wife have no trousers to wear?"
Fàn laughed and accepted it.
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World."
Flying Wings
Fàn Lǐ built the Flying Wings Tower for Gōu Jiàn,
modeling it after the Heavenly Gate with two coiling dragons,
and winding around the ridgepole to resemble dragon horns.
"Annals of Wú and Yuè"
Nine Pillars
Emperor Zhōngzōng decreed:
"Tàicháng Hè Xún is as pure as ice and jade,
his conduct sets an example for common customs.
I once visited his residence,
where his house, rooms, and daily utensils
were only sufficient for his personal needs."
He bestowed upon him a bed, mattress, and two hundred thousand coins.
From "Xú Guǎng's Records of Jìn"
Fàn Lóng served as Grand Commandant,
and often made recommendations.
Those who obtained desirable official posts would send him gold within the palace chambers.
Fàn Lóng counted and reproached them with these words,
to which the person replied:
"I did not know,
and would not dare to disclose it to my parents or brothers."
Fàn Lóng said:
"The spirits already know of it,
how could it be acceptable?"
Thereupon he severed ties with them.
"Cuī Hóng's Records of the Former Zhào"
The Lǎozǐ Temple has the Huángtiān Tower,
the Nine-Pillared Tower,
and the Niàn Tower,
all painted with immortals and ethereal clouds.
"The Làixiāng Records"
Wáng Dūn confiscated Zhōu Yǐ's household,
finding in the bamboo trunks old wadding,
five jars of poisoned wine,
and several hu of rice.
Those in office admired his integrity.
"Dèng Càn's Records of Jìn"
Yú Shì
The Yú family,
wealthy people of Liáng,
ascended a high tower,
overlooking the main road,
struck the tower and laughed,
while a knight-errant was passing by.
A flying kite happened to fall,
and its rotten rat hit him.
The knight-errant said:
"The Yú family has long enjoyed wealth and pleasure;
I did not trespass against them,
yet they insult me in this manner.
This leaves me no way to establish my reputation in the world."
Thereupon, he led his followers to exterminate their household.
From "Explaining Omens" of the *Lièzǐ*
Returning the Gift
Zhái Tāng,
courtesy name Dàoyuān,
was a native of Xúnyáng
and known for his sincere conduct and integrity.
Gān Bǎo, the Governor of Shǐ'ān, who was a close family friend of Zhái Tāng,
sent a boat with provisions to him,
instructing the officer,
"Lord Zhái is incorruptible.
If he declines the gift and sends a written refusal,
simply leave the boat and return."
As Zhái Tāng had no one to send it back,
he instead traded the goods for silk fabrics,
and had them returned to Gān Bǎo.
Gān Bǎo had originally intended to bestow a favor upon Zhái Tāng,
but instead caused him trouble,
making Gān Bǎo feel even more ashamed and sigh in admiration.
"Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū"
Kǒng Yǐ,
courtesy name Sīyuǎn,
did not value affectation or ornamentation.
His clothing and utensils were coarse and worn,
yet he never changed them.
At that time, Gù Yǐzhī of Wú Commandery also admired frugality and simplicity,
wearing fur garments and using vessels all of the humblest quality.
In the Liú Sòng dynasty, when speaking of purity and restraint,
these two men were praised.
Kǒng Yǐ's younger brother Dàocún,
along with their cousin Huī, extensively managed property and business.
When the two younger brothers requested leave to return east,
Kǒng Yǐ went to the islet to welcome them.
They had more than ten boats of heavy baggage,
all filled with items like silk floss, silk fabric, paper, and mats.
Upon seeing this,
Kǒng Yǐ feigned delight and said to them:
"I have been impoverished lately,
so obtaining these is most timely."
He then ordered the goods to be placed on the bank.
Soon after, with a stern expression, he said to Dàocún and the others:
"You shamefully occupy the ranks of scholars;
how could you sink to returning east as merchants?"
He commanded his attendants to fetch fire and burn it all,
departing only after everything was reduced to ashes.
(Book of Sòng)
Lìqiáo
Xú Wúguǐ appeared before Wǔhóu and said:
"Your lordship must certainly not deploy troops like cranes in formation between the ornate watchtowers,
nor station foot soldiers and chariots in the palace of the altar of grain."
Annotation:
"Lìqiáo,
means a watchtower for battle,
referring to something magnificent and towering."
Zhuangzi
When Chén Shèng attacked Chén,
the defending minister fought with him at the gate tower.
Yán Shīgǔ commented:
"A tower is also called qiáo,
hence a beautiful tower is called lìqiáo."
Book of Han
Zhào Chōngguó built defensive walls and wooden watchtowers.
Yán Shīgǔ commented:
"Qiáo here is the same as qiáo (watchtower)."
Basic Biography
Primer for Beginners:
The state of Wèi had ornate watchtowers,
which probably refers to the same matter in Zhuangzi.
Báitiě however states that Wèiwǔ had a lìqiáo tower,
leading to errors in Hé Bì, Shì Lèi, and Rhyme Dictionary which all followed this mistake.
Basic Biography
Yán Yánzhī's "Court Admonitions" states:
"Purity is
the proper path for humans."
Jǐnghán
Péi Zhāomíng,
during the Yuánhuī era of the Sòng dynasty, was appointed as the Deputy Governor of Chángshā Commandery.
Upon his dismissal, Inspector Wáng Yùnzhī said to him:
"You are of pure poverty and surely lack resources for the return journey.
If there are any gentlemen in Xiāngzhōng who require an official appointment,
I would not be sparing."
Zhāomíng replied:
"This humble official serves as a commandery assistant,
yet cannot bring glory to the superior prefecture.
How could I burden your pure reputation with matters of official appointments?"
During the Yǒngmíng era of the Qí dynasty, he served as the Internal Historian of Shǐ'ān.
When he returned,
he was extremely impoverished.
Emperor Shìzǔ said:
"When Zhāomíng left his commandery post,
and returned,
he had no residence.
I have not read extensively,
and do not know who among the ancients could be compared to him."
"History of the Southern Dynasties"
Zhēn Bīn was a man of integrity and profession,
praised by his local community for his goodness.
He once took a bundle of ramie to the treasury of the Chángshā Temple in the provincial capital to pawn for money.
Later, when he redeemed the ramie,
he found within the bundle
five taels of gold,
wrapped in a handkerchief.
Bīn obtained it and returned it to the temple treasury.
The monk exclaimed in surprise:
"Someone recently pawned this gold for money,
but due to urgent matters, they failed to retrieve it and lost it.
How could you, benefactor, return it?"
He then offered half of the gold as a reward,
but after more than ten attempts to persuade him,
Bīn firmly refused to accept it.
He then said:
"Would someone who wears a sheepskin in May while carrying firewood
be one to pick up lost gold?"
He ultimately returned the gold.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, while still a commoner, heard of this.
When he ascended the throne,
he appointed Marquis Xīchāng, Zǎo, as the governor of Yìzhōu,
and then made Bīn the military registrar and administrator in the prefecture,
concurrently serving as the magistrate of Pí County.
As he was about to depart,
along with four other colleagues,
the emperor admonished them to be honest and cautious.
When it came to Bīn, he alone was told:
"You once had the virtue of returning gold,
so I need not reiterate these words to you."
From then on, his reputation for virtue grew even more prominent.
End
Emperor Wǔ built the Shénmíng Tower and Jǐnghán Tower,
which were five hundred zhàng high,
with elevated passageways connecting them.
Yán Shígǔ commented:
"The Jǐnghán Tower
was constructed by piling up timber to form a tall structure,
resembling the shape of a well frame.
The term jǐnghán
refers to the wooden railing around a well."
The "Treatise on Sacrifices" records
climbing the Jǐnghán Tower before reaching halfway,
one's eyes grow dizzy and mind becomes confused.
The "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states
the Shénmíng Tower rises majestically alone,
while the Jǐnghán Tower stacks up to a hundred stories.
The "Rhapsody on the Western Metropolis"
Fàn Xiù in every office he held,
was always renowned for his integrity and honesty.
When serving as the magistrate of Chángchéng,
he had a boxwood storage case for official headwear,
which he used for several decades,
and never replaced despite experiencing wealth and honor.
While in Jìnlíng, a pair of ivory tubes were made for him,
yet he still considered them extravagant.
Book of Liáng
Chì Lóu
Gōngsūn Shù built a ten-story red tower.
"Dōngguān Hànjì"
Yuán Yùxiū,
courtesy name Shūdé,
was incorruptible and cautious while in office,
serving as a Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel for ten years,
yet never accepted even a dou of wine as a gift.
Xíng Shào, the Minister of Personnel, had long been on friendly terms with Yùxiū,
and during conversations and banter in the ministry,
often called Yùxiū the "Incorruptible Secretary."
In the early years of the Tàiníng era,
Yùxiū, as a Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, was sent on an inspection tour,
passing through Yǎnzhōu,
where Xíng Shào was then the Regional Inspector.
After their parting,
Xíng sent white silk as a token of goodwill,
but Yùxiū declined to accept it,
writing to Shào:
"Today, our encounter
differs from ordinary conduct;
I hope to keep this intention
and avoid bringing severe reproach upon myself."
Shào also cheerfully accepted the refusal with understanding,
replying in a letter:
"The gift I offered that day
was given without much thought;
I respectfully accept your stance,
and I hold no grievance.
You, my brother, were once the 'Incorruptible Secretary,'
and now you have become the 'Incorruptible Minister'!"
From The Book of Northern Qí.
Ascending the Tower
Xīn Shù,
courtesy name Huáizhé,
during the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Wénxuān,
when the governor of Suīzhōu and all the commandery administrators under his jurisdiction were sentenced to death,
their hundred household slaves and all their property were bestowed upon Xīn Shù,
but after declining three times without being permitted,
he then sent them to the relevant authorities,
and did not report it again.
Xíng Shào heard of this,
and sent Xīn Shù a letter saying:
"As Zhōnglí Yì once said:
'Confucius endured thirst rather than drink from the Spring of Thieves',
thus casting pearls upon the ground.
Your action today,
can be said to echo across generations."
End
Péngchéng Wáng Yōu was recalled from Cāngzhōu, and the local elders,
bringing food together, said:
"Your Highness has only drunk the water of this village,
but has not eaten the people's food;
we humbly offer this simple meal."
He took a bite of the food.
《History of the Northern Dynasties》
Huáng Chāng was the commandery governor,
the Péng family of Shǎn County built a tall house overlooking the road,
when Chāng was touring the county, the Péng family's wife would always ascend the high building to watch,
so Chāng had her killed.
History of the Later Hàn
Falling Star
Péi Xiá was upright and incorruptible.
His cousin Péi Shènfèng,
along with Péi Bófèng and Péi Shìyàn, who were then serving as chancellors,
said to him through their aides:
"In pursuing an official career, one must consider both status and reputation.
But you live in such extreme austerity and hardship—
what do you actually aim to achieve?"
Xiá replied:
"Integrity is the foundation of governance,
and frugality is the basis of personal conduct.
I am fortunate, despite my mediocrity, to have received exceptional favor.
Thus, my poverty is not something I take pride in.
My aspiration lies in self-cultivation,
fearing to bring disgrace upon my ancestors.
Yet instead, I am mocked and scorned.
What more is there to say?"
Bófèng and the others felt ashamed and withdrew.
"Later Zhou Dynasty, Twenty-Seventh Scroll"
Péi Wénjǔ,
courtesy name Dàoyù,
served as the Governor of Yìzhōu.
The land of Shǔ was fertile and rich,
with merchants making profits a hundredfold,
and some advised Wénjǔ to seek such gains.
Wénjǔ replied to them:
"What is truly valuable
is nothing more than peace of mind.
With peace of mind, the Way flourishes—
this does not refer to material goods.
Thus, I refrain from such pursuits,
not because I despise wealth."
Duke Qí, Yǔwén Xiàn, pitied his poverty,
and often wished to provide him with support,
but Wénjǔ always remained humble,
declining much and accepting little.
From the "Book of Zhōu"
In the first year of the Jiāhé era of Wú, a three-story tower was built on Luòxīng Mountain in the Guìlín Garden,
named Luòxīng Tower.
"Records of Jīnlíng Geography"
counted military supplies in the Guìlín Garden,
and feasted troops at Luòxīng Tower.
"Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú"
Wú had Báiquè Tower.
"Annals of Wú"
A hundred feet
Kòu Jùn,
courtesy name Zǔjùn,
was by nature incorruptible and tolerant,
never setting his heart on wealth or profit.
His family once sold goods to someone
and gained a bolt of silk as profit.
Jùn later learned of this
and said:
"One must not rest even briefly under the shade of a poisonous tree,
nor mistakenly drink from the waters of a stolen spring.
To gain wealth but lose integrity—
this is something I cannot accept."
He then sought out the buyer
and returned the silk.
In the northwest corner of Luòyáng city there is a fortified inner wall,
and in the northeast corner stands a tower,
one hundred chǐ high,
which was built by Emperor Wén of Wèi.
"Luòyáng Miscellaneous Records"
After Marshal Yīn was deposed,
he resentfully said of Jiǎnwén:
"The superior man climbs the hundred-chǐ tower,
taking the ladder away with him upon ascending."
"Shì Shuō"
Sòng Shìliáng served as the governor of Héqīng.
When his replacement arrived, the entire city turned out to bid him farewell.
An old man named Dīng Jīngāng
stepped forward tearfully and expressed his gratitude, saying:
"I am ninety years old
and have witnessed thirty-five administrations.
Your governance is not only virtuous but also thoroughly incorruptible.
Now that we are losing a worthy man,
how can the people carry on?"
Everyone clung to the shafts of his carriage, weeping.
(From History of the Northern Dynasties, Volume 14)
Ascending the Tower
Zhào,
during Suíwén's time served as Deputy Inspector of Qízhōu.
At that time, there was a famine,
and mulberries from a neighbor's tree fell into his residence.
He sent someone to gather them all
and return them to their owner.
He admonished his sons, saying:
"I do not do this to seek fame;
my intention is that anything not produced by my own loom,
I do not wish to take from others.
You should take this as a warning."
Later, he was summoned to the court,
and the local elders seeing him off
each wiped their tears, saying:
"While the Deputy Inspector held office,
he never accepted even water or fire from the common people,
so we dare not offer you wine as farewell.
Your integrity is as pure as water—
please allow us to offer a cup of water."
They presented it as a farewell gift,
and he accepted and drank it.
"Shàng Wǔshíbā"
At the city tower of Dāngyáng County,
Wáng Zhòngxuān ascended it and composed a rhapsody.
The "Jīngzhōu Records"
state that seventy lǐ southeast of Dāngyáng lies the tomb of King Zhāo of Chǔ,
visible upon ascending the tower,
referred to as Zhāoqiū.
The "Jīngzhōu Illustrated Records"
Féng Lǚqiān,
was appointed as the deputy of Héběi.
A local named Zhāng Huáidào served as the deputy of Jiāngyáng,
who was an old acquaintance of Qiān,
gifted him a mirror.
Qiān gathered his colleagues and subordinates,
showing it around and said:
"This was given by Lord Zhāng,
I have an old friendship with him,
but I serve in office and uphold integrity with my salary—
how could I privately accept gifts?"
He then declared solemnly:
"Clear water reveals the bottom,
a bright mirror reflects the heart;
my service as an official must aspire to this purity."
He wrote a reply to the messenger,
and returned it.
From the "Book of Táng".
Dù Xiǎn passed the imperial examination in the Mingjīng category,
and was appointed as a military advisor in Wùzhōu.
When his term of service was completed and he was about to return home,
the local officials presented him with over ten thousand sheets of paper as a gift,
but Dù Xiǎn only accepted one hundred sheets,
returning all the rest.
At that time, colleagues who were bidding him farewell
witnessed this and exclaimed in admiration:
"In the past, there was an honest official who accepted just one large coin -
how is this any different?"
He was later promoted to investigating censor,
and traveled to the Western frontier to handle official matters.
The tribal people offered him gold as a gift,
but Dù Xiǎn firmly declined to accept it.
His attendants said:
"You have traveled far to this remote region,
you should not offend the tribal people's goodwill."
Dù Xiǎn had no choice but to accept it,
but he buried it under his tent,
and after he departed,
once he had crossed the border,
he sent an official document instructing them to retrieve it.
The tribal people were greatly astonished,
and chased after him across the desert,
but were unable to catch up and gave up.
The emperor
Fènghuáng
The Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs Lǐ Yì
was known for his incorruptible virtue.
His younger sister
was the wife of Liú Yàn.
While Liú Yàn held significant power,
he once visited Yì,
and was invited into his bedchamber.
Noticing that the door curtain was very worn,
Yàn secretly had its dimensions measured,
had one woven from bamboo,
and did not add any decorative trim,
intending to gift it to Yì.
Three times he carried it to Yì's gate,
but dared not speak of it and left each time.
"Supplement to History"
In Luòyáng there were Fènghuáng Tower, Zǒngzhāng Pavilion, and Yífèng Tower.
From the pavilion one could widely view and observe them.
To the south there was also a separate Xiángfèng Tower,
and there were also Qìngyún Tower and Sìxīng Tower.
"Jìn Palace Pavilion Names"
Lù Chángyuán served as the prefect of Rǔzhōu,
being straightforward and lacking authority,
yet maintaining integrity and self-discipline.
Later, when leaving the prefecture,
he was sent off with two carriages,
and he sighed, saying:
"When Wǔzǔ left Wèizhōu,
he had only one carriage,
with half of it filled with books and documents,
falling far short of my ancestors."
From "The Official Biography"
Looking out in all directions,
Shí Hǔ built a tower in front of the Tàijí Hall,
forty zhang high,
adorned with pearl curtains,
from which hung jade pendants of five colors.
When the wind blew, they chimed melodiously,
creating a harmonious and elegant sound.
During the height of summer,
he would ascend the high tower to gaze at the four extremities,
playing music of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments,
continuing day and night.
At the beginning of early spring,
he would grind assorted treasures and rare fragrances into powder,
ordering hundreds of people to scatter it from the tower,
calling it "fragrant dust."
"Records of Omissions"
Yǔ Gōng
Mǎ Kàng served as a court reader.
When Lǐ Bàozhēn died,
Kàng was sent as an envoy to offer condolences,
and silk was presented to him as a gift,
but he did not accept it.
When it was sent to the capital again,
Kàng submitted a memorial firmly refusing it.
At that time, the position of Lǐquán County magistrate was vacant,
and the chief ministers were selecting a candidate of high quality.
Emperor Dézōng said:
"The former envoy to Zélù who refused the gift,
that man is incorruptible,
and can be employed."
Thus, the position was given to Kàng.
Yǔ Liàng was in Wǔchāng,
when his assistants Yīn Hào and others, taking advantage of the fine autumn night scenery, climbed a high tower together.
Suddenly, without their noticing, Yǔ Liàng arrived,
and the crowd was about to avoid him,
but he said:
"With this old man here,
the mood for enjoyment is not shallow."
He then sat down to chat and recite poetry,
and to this day it is called the Tower of Lord Yǔ.
"Jiǔjiāng Records"
Among the famous sights that rival heaven and earth,
there are those like the Téngwáng Pavilion in Yùzhāng,
the Yǔ Tower in Jiǔjiāng, the Xiāoshǔ Tower in Wúxīng, and the Diézhàng in Xuānchéng.
Beyond these, there are no more than two or three others.
"Preface to Téng Zōngliàng's Poem Presented to Fàn Xīwén"
See also the Moon Gate.
Dù Yòu,
during the Dàlì era,
received a legacy of one hundred taels of gold left by an ancient person.
Thirty years later,
while serving as the Huái military governor,
his son came to join him.
Dù Yòu took the gold and returned it,
with the seal and wrapping intact as before.
"Records of Anecdotes"
Xiāo Fǎng
was known for his pure reputation and frugal virtue,
highly esteemed by his contemporaries.
He once commanded troops in Pānyú,
earning praise for his integrity, as symbolized by drinking from a pure spring and discarding incense.
The "Unofficial History of the Tang"
records that Fǎng,
courtesy name Sīdào,
was just and incorruptible by nature.
While serving as the military governor of Lǐngnán,
though Nánhǎi was wealthy,
beyond his monthly salary of rare treasures,
he allowed nothing else to enter his household.
When a family member fell ill,
the physician prescribed black plums for the medicine,
and attendants took some from the official kitchen.
Upon learning of this, Fǎng ordered them returned,
urging that they be bought from the market instead.
Nánhǎi produced abundant paper,
and Fǎng instructed his children to copy and repair missing texts.
His son Lǐn remarked:
"It is indeed fitting to mend the missing family books,
and truly appropriate to restore them,
but from here to the capital,
the journey spans ten thousand miles by land and water,
so they cannot be carried openly.
They must be placed in boxes.
If others see additional baggage,
they may assume it contains valuables,
inviting suspicion like the ancient slander of Job's tears,
which serves as a profound warning."
Fǎng replied:
"I had not considered that."

Entering Hàn
In the eighth year of the Yìxī era,
he erected a tall tower within the eastern city of Shítóu,
which rose layer upon layer into the heavens,
connecting the battlements with the accumulated waters,
and named it the Rùhàn Tower.
"Jìn Shū"
Lǐ Shàngyǐn,
was transferred to the position of Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
and concurrently served as the Military Commissioner of the Five Prefectures.
When he left his post,
someone intended to present him with gold as a farewell gift,
but Shàngyǐn firmly declined, saying:
"It is my inherent nature,
which cannot be changed—
not merely out of caution against the 'Four Awarenesses'."
In the end, he did not accept it.
The Emperor
Lǐ Shīgǔ was domineering and arrogant,
but he feared Dù Huángshang was the chancellor,
so he dared not be discourteous.
He then ordered a capable official to send several thousand strings of coins,
along with a felt-covered carriage,
which was also worth nearly a thousand strings.
The messenger did not dare to deliver them immediately,
so he waited at the residence gate for several days.
A simple green carriage came out of the residence,
followed by two maids,
both dressed in worn-out blue clothes.
He asked,
"Who is this?"
The reply was,
"The chancellor's wife."
The messenger hurried back,
and reported to Shīgǔ.
Shīgǔ then abandoned his plan,
and never dared to breach etiquette for the rest of his life.

Wànsuì
There is Huánghè Mountain within the county boundaries.
During the Jìn dynasty, Wáng Gōng, as the provincial governor,
renovated the southwestern part,
naming the tower "Wànsuì,"
and the northwestern one "Fúróng Tower,"
which remain to this day.
"Records of Jīngkǒu"
Folklore says this tower once flew toward the river's outer reaches,
and was only stabilized after being tethered with iron chains.
"Geographical Records"
Additionally, a white mist like smoke is sometimes seen above the tower,
which foretells the death of the provincial governor,
or at least his demotion to a lower post,
a phenomenon people still regard as a regular omen.
"Records of Yángtóu Mountain"
Tíng Tíng
Mǐn Jiǎ Yù,
served as the magistrate of Xiānyóu.
A local guest presented him with fruit,
but he declined it.
The guest said:
"This fruit is freshly harvested from my home,
and not many people know about it yet."
Jiǎ Yù asked:
"Do you have younger brothers?"
The guest replied:
"I have two younger brothers,
and several children."
Jiǎ Yù said:
"The ancients feared the 'four knowings',
but now your elder brother would know,
your younger brothers would know,
your children would know,
and those who brought it would know—
this doubles what the ancients feared!"
The guest left in shame.
From "Jiǔ Guó Zhì"
The Pǔyáng River flows northeast from Mào Mountain past Tàikāng Lake,
where Chējì General Xiè Xuán's country estate was located.
To the right it borders the Long River,
to the left it leans against continuous mountains,
with flat ridges stretching far,
and clear lakes mirroring distant views.
A tower was built at the river bend,
whose sides were all planted with paulownia and catalpa trees,
towering lush and delightful.
Local residents called it the Paulownia Pavilion Tower.
The tower faces the river on two sides,
fully capturing the pleasure of ascending for a view.
Reed gatherers and fishermen
drift about filling the scene.
《Commentary on the Waterways Classic》
Zhào Guāngféng,
served as Grand Councilor during the Five Dynasties period.
At that time, the Jurchens entrusted a box of gold to his household.
Amidst the chaos of war,
for over twenty years it remained unclaimed,
whereupon he ordered Governor of Henan Zhāng Quányì to memorialize the throne to distribute it among the palaces.
Observing his incorruptible integrity in this manner,
all regarded Guāngféng as the standard-bearer of orthodox teachings.
"History of the Five Dynasties"
Wēn Liǎn, an official of Yōuzhōu,
was a native of Yān,
renowned for his Confucian scholarship,
and had been friends with Féng Dào since childhood.
Amid the turmoil of war,
someone was selling a lacquered lamp stand in the market,
which Liǎn mistook for iron,
so he paid the asked price and purchased it.
After several days,
when his household used it to hold an oil lamp,
and wiped it clean,
they realized it was silver.
Everyone who saw it, young and old,
was overjoyed.
Only Liǎn sighed with concern and said:
"How can we treasure
something obtained unjustly?"
He then sought out the seller to return it.
The seller initially refused to accept it back.
Liǎn insisted on returning it,
so the seller bowed in gratitude, accepted it, and left.
Later, it was sold for forty to fifty thousand coins,
and the seller offered half the proceeds to thank Liǎn,
but Liǎn firmly declined.
The money was then donated to a Buddhist temple,
to adorn the Buddha statue,
hoping to pray for Liǎn's longevity.
At that time, everyone praised him for possessing the conduct of a benevolent person.
"Liú Shì's Records of Hearsay"
Jǐng Yáng
In the 22nd year of the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty, the Guǎnghuá Lín Garden was renovated,
and Jǐngyáng Mountain was constructed.
The Jǐngyáng Tower was first built.
In the first year of Dàmíng of Xiàowǔ,
a purple cloud emerged from Jǐngyáng Tower,
resembling smoke,
swirling and lingering for a long time.
An edict was issued to rename it as Zǐyún Tower.
"Yúdìzhì"
Zhòng Tíngyù served as tutor to the Prince of Jiā of Shǔ,
and although his sons were well-versed in the classics,
he often suffered from hunger and cold.
Even when visiting the prince's household,
he was not treated with much respect.
During a severe cold spell,
the prince sent an old brazier to the academy.
While Tíngyù sat alone sighing,
he poked the ashes with a fire poker,
and suddenly discovered a pair of golden fire tongs in the ashes.
He immediately sought an audience with the prince.
The prince suspected he had some other request,
but reluctantly granted the audience.
Tíngyù then produced the golden tongs
and recounted how he had found them.
The prince said:
"Our family lost these ten years ago.
You, sir, having found them,
returned them to show us—
truly possessing the virtue of the ancients."
He then bestowed generous gifts upon him,
and ultimately treated him as an honored guest,
showing him great respect
and recommending him for the position of Records Consultant in Chóngzhōu.
From "Yùxī Biānshì"
Qú Yuàn did not alter his integrity due to dim circumstances,
Yán Huí did not change his demeanor despite bathing at night.
Gōu Jiàn was confined in a stone chamber,
yet the rites between ruler and subject were not abandoned;
Jì Quē tilled the fields in the wilderness,
but the respect between husband and wife remained undiminished.
These all exemplify caution in the subtle and hidden,
dwelling with goodness as their pillow.
"The Master Liú"
Qīxiá
In the state of Lǔ there was a respectful scholar,
named Jī Fàn,
who was seventy years old,
yet his respectfulness increased even more.
In winter he walked in the shade,
in summer he walked in the sun,
in the marketplace he dared not fail to walk with deference,
when walking he always followed others,
when sitting he maintained a proper posture,
even during a single meal,
he would rise three times without feeling ashamed,
and when he saw people wearing coarse clothing, he would bow to them.
The ruler of Lǔ asked him:
"Master Jī, you are quite advanced in years,
can you not relax your respectful demeanor?"
Jī Fàn replied:
"A nobleman loves respectfulness,
to establish his reputation,
a common man learns respectfulness,
to avoid punishment.
Sitting before my lord,
is it not secure?
Yet there can still be missteps.
The food at a meal,
is it not delicious?
Yet one can still choke.
Now someone like me is what is called fortunate,
but I certainly cannot be assured of my fate.
When swans and wild geese fly soaring to the sky,
is it not high?
Yet arrows with strings can still reach them.
Tigers and leopards are fierce,
yet people still eat their flesh,
and use their skins as mats;
those who praise others are few,
those who criticize others are many,
being seventy years old,
I constantly fear that the executioner's axe might fall upon me,
why should I relax my respectful demeanor?"

Beacon fire
Táng Xī Gōng appeared before King Zhāo and said:
"Suppose there is a white jade wine vessel without a bottom,
and an earthenware wine vessel that has a bottom.
If you were thirsty, which would you use to drink?"
The king replied:
"The earthenware vessel."
Táng Xī Gōng said:
"The white jade vessel is beautiful, yet you would not use it to drink,
because it has no bottom, is that not so?"
The king said:
"Indeed."
Táng Xī Gōng said:
"For a ruler to leak and divulge the words of his ministers,
is just like a jade vessel without a bottom."
Every time Táng Xī Gōng had an audience and left,
King Zhāo would invariably sleep alone,
fearing that he might talk in his sleep and reveal secrets to his wives and concubines.

and commanded his court officials to compose poems.
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu's poem met with imperial approval,
so the emperor said to Yǐngzhòu:

From "The Basic Biography."

In the first year of the Lóngchāng era of the Qí dynasty, Shěn Yuē, serving as the Minister of Personnel, was appointed as the Prefect of Dōngyáng.
He inscribed the "Eight Odes" poems on the Yuánchàng Tower,
which were hailed as unparalleled masterpieces at the time.
Later generations thus renamed Yuánchàng as the "Eight Odes Tower."
According to the "Jīnhuá Records,"
Cuī Hào wrote a poem about the Hidden Marquis's Eight Odes Tower:

Built a tower to gaze upon Yuèzhōng."

Huò Guāng,
courtesy name Zǐmèng,
served as Commandant of the Imperial Carriages.
When going out, he attended to the imperial carriage;
when inside, he served by the emperor's side.
For over twenty years, he moved through the forbidden palace gates,
always cautious and careful,
never making a mistake.
Whenever he passed through the palace hall gates,
he would stop and advance at fixed spots.
The palace attendants secretly observed him,
and found his movements never deviated by even an inch.
Such was his inherently upright nature.

served closely by the emperor's side,
never once looking directly at him,

he dared not approach them;
when the emperor wished to bring his daughter into the harem,

The emperor
Kǒng Guāng,
courtesy name Zǐxià,
was meticulous and cautious,
never having made a mistake.
On days off returning home to rest,
when chatting leisurely with his brothers, wife, and children,
he never spoke of court or government affairs.
Someone once asked Guāng:
"In the warm chamber of the palace,
what kinds of trees are planted there?"
Guāng remained silent without responding,
instead answering with other topics.
Such was his discretion against disclosure.
The sovereign
Hán Zhāohóu, when plotting with Tángxī Gōng,
would sleep alone throughout the night,
fearing he might reveal secrets through sleep-talking to his wives and concubines.
Kǒng Guāng not answering about the trees in the warm chamber
was due to fear that speaking might lead to disclosure among his attendants.
"The Master Liú"

he still refrained from speaking;
when questioned about the horses before his carriage,

Looking North
I once attended upon the late emperor,
when there were three senior officials,
all present.
As we were about to take our leave and depart,
the emperor said:
"To be an official, one must be upright,
cautious,
and diligent in self-cultivation.
With these three, what worry is there about not governing well?"
We all received the edict.
The emperor turned to us and said:
"If forced to abandon one,
which of these three should go first?"
One replied:
"Uprightness is surely the foundation."
He asked me again,
and I replied:
"The ways of uprightness and caution
complement each other to achieve success.
If forced to choose,
caution is the most important."
The emperor said:
"Your words have captured it.
Can you name someone in recent times who exemplifies caution?"
I then mentioned the former Grand Commandant Xún Jǐngqiàn,
Minister Dǒng Zhòngdá,
and Deputy Minister Wáng Gōngzhòng.
The emperor said:
"These individuals,
gentle and respectful day and night,
diligent in their duties,
each indeed practiced caution.
However, the most cautious person in the world,
is it not Ruǎn Sìzōng?
Whenever I spoke with him,
he discussed profound and distant matters,
yet never commented on current affairs,
nor judged people's character.
Can this be called the utmost caution?"
"Family Admonitions of Jì Kāng"
In the tenth year of Dàtóng, he visited Lánlíng,
and composed a poem about returning to his old hometown.
On the jǐyǒu day, he visited Jīngkǒu,

Initially, west of the capital, there was a separate ridge extending into the river,

facing water on three sides,
called Běigù.
Cài Mó built a tower on it
to store military supplies.
Later it collapsed,
with only a small pavilion remaining on top,
with very narrow ascending and descending paths.

he descended from his carriage and proceeded on foot.

and installed railings alongside.
The next day, the emperor visited,
and was able to pass through in a small carriage.
The emperor was pleased,
gazing into the distance for a long time,
and decreed:
"This ridge is insufficient
and must be firmly guarded.
However, Jīngkǒu is truly magnificent,
so it was renamed Běigù (Northward Gaze)."

was a native of Yǒngxīng.

swept and cleaned the courtyard,

Qīng Dé

constantly striving to improve himself without respite,
and often said to others:

so how much more should ordinary people value every minute?
How can one indulge in idle wandering and drunken revelry?

and to die without leaving a reputation for posterity—

although he held the highest positions of general and minister,

Duke Huán of Qí assembled the feudal lords, but the envoy from Wèi arrived late.
The Duke held court and consulted with Guǎn Zhòng about attacking Wèi.
After court adjourned, he entered his chambers,
where his consort from Wèi, Lady Wèi, saw him approaching.
She descended the hall and bowed twice,
pleading for the ruler of Wèi's offense.
The Duke said:
"I have no grievance with Wèi,
why do you plead for them?"
She replied:
"When I saw you enter,
your steps were lofty and your spirit forceful,
showing intention to attack a state.
When you saw me, your expression changed,
so it must be Wèi you plan to attack."
The next day at court,
the Duke bowed to Guǎn Zhòng and invited him forward.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Has Your Majesty abandoned the plan against Wèi?"
The Duke said:
"How did you know, Father Zhòng?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Your bow at court was reverent,
your speech was measured,
and when you saw me, you showed a ashamed expression,
thus I knew."
The Duke said:
"Excellent.
Father Zhòng manages external affairs,
my lady manages internal matters,
now I know I shall never be laughed at by the feudal lords."
What Duke Huán had concealed went unspoken,
yet Guǎn Zhòng discerned it through demeanor and tone,
while his lady detected it through gait and spirit.
Though Duke Huán spoke nothing,
it was as illuminating as a torch in dark night.
"Lǚ's Subtle Admonitions"
The Lǔ nobleman Suǒshì was about to perform a sacrifice,
but lost the sacrificial animal.
When Confucius heard of this,
he said:
"Nobleman Suǒshì will surely perish within three years."
A year later, he perished.
A disciple asked:
"Previously, when Nobleman Suǒshì lost his sacrificial animal,
you, Master, said:
'He will surely perish within three years,'
yet now he perished after just one year.
How did you, Master, know he would perish?"
Confucius replied:
"The word 'sacrifice' (jì) relates to 'searching' (suǒ),
and 'searching' means 'exhausting oneself',
which is how a filial son exhausts himself in devotion to his parents.
If one loses the sacrificial animal when it's time to offer sacrifice,
then there must be many other things he has lost as well.
This is how I knew he would perish."

Initially, a man from Yǐngchuān named Huà Hóng followed the Former Ruler into Shu,
was granted the surname Wáng,
and named Zōngkǎn.
At this time, he constructed a red tower,
and people from the city flocked to see it,
saying they were "viewing the painted red tower."
The Former Ruler considered this an omen corresponding to Huà Hóng,
and thus had him executed.
"Records of Ancient and Modern Chéngdū"
Tortoiseshell
Xí Sīmí visited Tián Chéngzǐ,
who ascended a terrace with him to survey the view on all four sides.
Three directions were unobstructed,
but looking south, the trees at Xí's home blocked the view.
Tián Chéngzǐ, however, said nothing.
Upon returning home,
Xí ordered the trees to be cut down.
After a few axe cuts had been made,
he stopped the work.
His steward asked:
"Why change your mind so quickly?"
Xí replied:
"There is an ancient saying:
'To know the fish in the deep is unlucky.'
Tián Chéngzǐ is about to undertake great actions,
and if I reveal my ability to perceive subtle hints in such major affairs,
I will surely be in danger.
Not cutting the trees is no crime,
but knowing what others do not speak of—
that is a grave offense."
Thus, the trees were not cut down.
From "Hán Shuō Lín"
Zhì Bó wanted to attack Wèi,
so he pretended that his crown prince Yán was a fugitive,
and sent him to flee to Wèi.
Nán Wénzǐ said:
"Crown Prince Yán is his lord's son,
and is deeply loved;
though he has committed no great crime, he is sent away as a fugitive—
there must be a reason for this."
However, to refuse a fugitive would bring misfortune,
so he sent an official to meet him with the warning:
"If the carriages exceed five in number,
be careful not to let them enter."
Upon hearing this, Zhì Bó abandoned his plan.
"Shuō Yuàn"
Emperor Wén of Western Wèi demolished the Eastern Palace,
constructed various courtyards for imperial concubines,
and erected the Tortoiseshell Tower.

King Zhāo of Qín sent his receptionist Wáng Jǐ to Wèi,
who took Fàn Jū back to Qín in his carriage.
When they reached Húguān,
they saw the carriage and horsemen of the Marquis of Ráng heading east through the counties and towns.
Fàn Jū said:
"I have heard that the Marquis of Ráng monopolizes power in Qín,
and dislikes admitting guest advisers from other states.
I fear he will humiliate me,
so I would rather hide in the carriage for now."
After a short while,
the Marquis of Ráng indeed arrived,
greeted Wáng Jǐ,
and stood by his carriage to talk,
saying to Wáng Jǐ:
"I hope you haven't brought any guest advisers from other states with you?
They are of no benefit,
only disrupt people's states."
Wáng Jǐ replied:
"I wouldn't dare."
Then they parted.
Fàn Jū said:
"I have heard that the Marquis of Ráng is a wise man,
but he is slow to notice things.
Just now he suspected there was someone in the carriage,
but forgot to search it."
Thereupon Fàn Jū got out of the carriage,
and fled,
saying:
"He will certainly regret this."
After they had traveled over ten lǐ,
the Marquis indeed sent horsemen back to search the carriage.
Finding no guest adviser,
they gave up.
Wáng Jǐ then entered Xiányáng with Fàn Jū,
who later replaced the Marquis of Ráng as Chancellor.
(Records of the Grand Historian)
Scattering Flowers
In Táng, Chéngdū had the Scattering Blossoms Tower,
and Hédōng had the Fragrant Breeze Tower.
Chén Píng served King Xiàng,
fearing execution,
he fled alone on foot carrying a sword.
Crossing the river,
the boatman saw he was a handsome man
traveling alone,
suspected he was a fleeing general,
and thought he must have precious objects, gold, and jade at his waist.
Watching him,
he intended to kill Chén Píng.
Chén Píng grew fearful,
so he took off his clothes and worked naked to help paddle the boat.
The boatman then knew he had nothing,
and stopped.
Chén Píng thus reached Xīuwǔ
and surrendered to Hàn.
From "Qián Hàn."
Chén Xián served as a Secretary.
During Emperor Píng's reign,
when Wáng Mǎng was regent,
he altered many Hàn institutions,
which Chén Xián inwardly disapproved of.
When Wáng Mǎng used the Lǚ Kuān incident to execute those who opposed him,
such as Hé Wǔ, Bào Xuān, and others,
Chén Xián sighed and said:
"The Yì Jīng says of the noble person,
'Upon seeing the subtle signs, one acts,
without waiting for the day to end.'
I must take my leave!"
He immediately requested retirement,
and resigned from his post.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he summoned Chén Xián to appoint him as Grand Master for Bandit Control,
but Chén Xián declined due to illness and refused the appointment.
At that time, his three sons—Cān, Fēng, and Qīn—were all in office,
so he ordered them all to resign their positions.
Father and sons together returned to their hometown,
shut their doors, and never went out again.
End
Piercing the Clouds
The Northern Qí had the Pīyún Tower,
and the Suí had the Chéngyún Tower.
Wèi Huán,
courtesy name Zhòngyīng,
was repeatedly summoned for office during Emperor Huán's reign.
His fellow villagers urged him to accept,
but Wèi Huán replied:
"Seeking official position and advancement
is meant to fulfill one's aspirations.
Yet now the palace has thousands of concubines—
can they be reduced?
The stables hold ten thousand horses—
can their numbers be decreased?
All those in power are influential nobles—
can they be removed?"
The villagers all answered:
"They cannot."
Wèi Huán then sighed deeply and said:
"If I were to go forth in life only to return in death,
what good would that bring any of you?"
Thereupon he lived in seclusion and never took office.
From History of the Later Hàn
Bathing the Sun
Guō Tài,
courtesy name Línzōng,
was a native of Jièxiū in Tàiyuán.
He traveled to Luòyáng,
and his reputation shook the capital.
Minister over the Masses Huáng Qióng summoned him,
and Minister of Ceremonies Zhào Diǎn recommended him as a man of virtue,
but when some urged Línzōng to pursue an official career,
he replied:
"By night I observe the celestial phenomena,
by day I examine human affairs.
What Heaven intends to ruin
cannot be supported."
Thus he declined all offers.
Although Línzōng was skilled in evaluating character,
he refrained from harsh criticism and extreme judgments,
so when eunuchs monopolized power, they could not harm him.
When the Partisan Proscriptions began,
many renowned scholars fell victim,
but only Línzōng and Yuán Hóng of Rǔnán escaped unscathed.
The Upper Sun Palace had the Beautiful Spring Terrace and the Sun-Bathing Tower.
Wéi Shù's "Miscellaneous Records of the Two Capitals"
Shēntú Pán,
courtesy name Zǐlóng,
was twice recommended for the "Outstanding Talent" selection but declined to serve.
Previously, itinerant scholars in the capital such as Fàn Pāng from Rǔnán and others had criticized court politics,
and everyone from high-ranking officials downward humbled themselves to defer to them.
Imperial students vied to emulate their style,
believing that literary scholarship was about to flourish
and reclusive scholars would be reinstated.
Only Pán sighed and said:
"In the past during the Warring States period,
reclusive scholars made unrestrained criticisms,
and the kings of various states
even went so far as to hold broomsticks and clear the way for them,
yet ultimately this led to the calamity of burying Confucian scholars alive and burning books.
What we see now is just like that."
Thereupon he disappeared between Liáng and Dàng counties,
building a dwelling among trees,
making himself like a common laborer.
After residing there for two years,
Fàn Pāng and others indeed fell victim to the Partisan Prohibitions,
while Pán alone escaped suspicion and criticism.
Xǔ Shào was a native of Píngyú in Rǔnán.
He initially served as the Commandery Merit Officer,
and later was recruited by Minister of Works Yáng Biāo,
who recommended him as Upright and Sincere,
but he did not accept either position.
Someone urged Shào to take office,
to which he replied:
"Now the way of petty men is ascendant,
and the royal house is about to fall into chaos.
I wish to take refuge in the Huái-Hǎi region,
to preserve the lives of my elders and children."
Thereupon he went south to Guǎnglíng.
The Governor of Xúzhōu, Táo Qiān, treated him with great courtesy.
Shào felt uneasy about this,
and told his followers:
"Táo Gōngzǔ outwardly courts reputation,
but inwardly lacks true integrity.
Although he treats me generously,
his attitude is bound to change,
so it would be better to leave him."
Thus he went to Qū'ē and sought out Liú Yáo, Governor of Yángzhōu.
Afterwards, Táo Qiān indeed arrested various resident scholars.
End

must be this man."

will begin with you, my lord."

Morning Sun
Fán Zhòu incited the various barbarian tribes to rebel,
Pān Jùn requested five thousand troops to capture Zhòu.
Sūn Quán said:
"Why do you underestimate him?"
Jùn replied:
"Zhòu is from an old Nányáng family,
quite capable of glib talk,
but actually lacks true debating talent.
The reason I know this is
Zhòu once prepared a feast for his fellow townspeople,
but by noon,
the food still wasn't ready,
and he had to get up more than ten times himself.
This is like judging a dwarf by one limb - it reveals his true capability."
Quán laughed heartily,
and immediately sent Jùn on his mission,
who indeed suppressed the rebellion.
From "Records of Wú"

From the "Yù Hǎi"
Sūn Dēng,
courtesy name Gōnghé,
was followed by Jī Kāng for three years of study.
When asked about his aspirations,
he never replied.
Yet his profound insights were truly marvelous.
Jī Kāng often sighed in admiration.
Before parting,
he said:
"Will you truly not speak, sir?"
Sūn Dēng then replied:
"Do you understand fire?
It is born with light,
yet does not use its light -
its true value lies in how the light is used;
humans are born with talent,
yet should not use their talent -
its true value lies in how the talent is employed.
Thus using light depends on obtaining fuel,
thereby preserving its brilliance;
using talent depends on understanding circumstances,
thereby preserving one's life.
Now you have much talent but little discernment -
difficult indeed to avoid trouble in this world!
Do not seek too much."
Jī Kāng failed to heed this advice.
When the Lǚ Ān incident occurred,
he wrote a poem in prison blaming himself:
"Once I shamed Xiàhuì,
now I shame Sūn Dēng."
From "Biographies of Literary Men"

Wéi Zhōng,
courtesy name Zǐjié.
When Péi Wěi served as Minister,
he repeatedly recommended him to Zhāng Huá,
who summoned him to office,
but Wéi Zhōng declined on grounds of illness and did not take up the post.
When people asked his reason,
Wéi Zhōng said:
"I am but a humble scholar living in a thatched hut,
with no desire for officialdom from the start.
Moreover, Màoxiān (Zhāng Huá) is showy without substance,
while Péi Wěi is insatiably greedy.
They abandon classical rites to attach themselves to the usurping empress -
such behavior,
how could it be fitting for a true gentleman?
Péi once intended to entrust me with responsibilities,
but I often fear that when great waves shake mountains,
even the ripples might sweep one away -
how much more so when facing the maelstrom and peering into the boiling abyss!"
Book of Jìn
In the Northern Qí Dynasty, there were the Wànsuì Tower and the Qiānqiū Tower.
Zhāng Hàn,
courtesy name Jìyīng,
was a man of Wú Commandery.
He served as Senior Clerk of the East Bureau under Grand Marshal Qí Wáng Jiǒng.
At the time when Jiǒng
held power, Hàn
said to his townsman Gù Róng:
"The world is in turmoil,
disasters and chaos have not ceased.
Those who have fame throughout the land
find it truly difficult to retire.
I am originally a man of the mountains and forests,
who long lost hope for this age.
I cherish goodness,
using clarity to guard against what lies ahead,
and wisdom to consider what follows."
Róng grasped his hand
and said sorrowfully:
"I too shall gather ferns on South Mountain with you,
and drink from the Three Rivers."
Hàn then noticed the autumn wind rising,
and longed for the wild rice stems, water shield soup, and perch mince of his homeland in Wú.
He said:
"What matters in life is to follow one's heart's desire.
How can I remain an official bound thousands of miles away,
just to seek fame and rank?"
Thereupon he ordered his carriage and returned home.
He wrote the "Ode to the First Hill,"
and soon after,
Jiǒng was defeated.
People therefore said he knew the moment.
End

After Wáng Dūn's death,
Wáng Yìng wanted to seek refuge with Shìrú,
who was the governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Wáng Hán wanted to seek refuge with Wáng Shū,
who was the governor of Jīngzhōu.
Hán said to Yìng:
"How was Dūn's usual relationship with the governor of Jiāngzhōu,
that you want to go to him?"
Yìng replied:
"This is precisely why we should go there.
When others were powerful and prosperous,
the governor of Jiāngzhōu dared to oppose them,
which is not something an ordinary person would do.
When he sees us in decline and distress,
he will certainly feel compassion.
The governor of Jīngzhōu sticks to conventions,
how could he act beyond expectations?"
Hán did not listen,
so they went together to Shū.
Shū indeed drowned Hán and his son in the river.
When Wáng Bīn heard that Yìng was coming,
he secretly prepared a boat to wait for him,
but Yìng ultimately couldn't come,
which Bīn deeply regretted.

but then reported it and betrayed the prime minister,

yet he could not enter any of the three capitals.

During Emperor Sòng Míngdì's deposition and enthronement,
Wáng Sīyuǎn said to his cousin Wáng Yàn:
"You received Emperor Wǔ's deep favor,
yet now you support such actions.
He may temporarily need you for his schemes,
but how will you establish yourself afterward?
If you take your own life now,
you can still preserve our family's standing,
and maintain your reputation for posterity."
Wáng Yàn replied:
"I'm busy eating porridge,
and have no time for such matters."
Later, when appointed Cavalry General,
he gathered the younger clansmen,
and said to Sīyuǎn and his elder brother Sīzhēng:
"At the end of the Lóngchāng era,
Āróng advised me to commit suicide.
Had I followed his advice,
would I have reached this position today?"
Sīyuǎn immediately responded:
"Following Āróng's insight,
it's still not too late."
Since Wáng Yàn couldn't modestly withdraw,
holding a prominent court position,
he often made arbitrary decisions,
appointing his proteges
to all important posts inside and outside court.
Though the emperor appeared gracious outwardly,
he secretly grew suspicious and alienated.
Sīyuǎn told him:
"The situation is changing slightly,
do you notice, brother?
Most people are clumsy in planning for themselves,
yet clever in scheming against others."
Wáng Yàn remained silent without reply.
After Sīyuǎn withdrew,
Wáng Yàn finally sighed:
"Now everyone is urging others to kill themselves."
Ten days later,
Wáng Yàn met his downfall.

and when he fell ill,

Fáng Qiáo,
courtesy name Xuánlíng,
was exceptionally bright and clever from a young age.

at a time when the empire was at peace,
and everyone discussing state affairs believed the dynasty's reign would last long.
Xuánlíng then dismissed the attendants

Xuē Kègòu served as Director of the Ministry of Revenue.
His nephew,
Shào, was the son of Princess Yángchéng.
He was to marry Princess Tàipíng. As Shào was about to wed,
his elder brother Yǐ, concerned about the princess's powerful favor,
was deeply worried and consulted Kègòu.
Kègòu said:
"For an emperor's nephew to marry a princess,
has always been customary.
If one acts with respect and compliance,
what is there to fear?
However, having an arrogant wife in the household,
is detested by virtuous men,
hence despised.
As the proverb goes:
'To marry a princess as a wife,
is like buying a government office on level ground—
In ancient times, Princess Píngyáng and Princess Gài brought ruin through their monstrous deeds,
while in recent times, Princess Xīnchéng and Princess Jìn'ān serve as warnings for our era.
I heard that Princess Xīnchéng died of illness,
yet her husband suffered humiliation and punishment,
and Princess Jìn'ān's scandalous acts,
were reported to the emperor, who issued an edict,
investigating the matter.
Lǐ Sīzhēn, Judicial Officer of Biànzhōu,
Dúgū Yuánkāng of the Right Imperial Guard, and others,
were all exiled simultaneously for their lewd conduct,
with eleven persons sentenced to caning.
When the curtains are thus revealed,
unless one is naturally virtuous enough to match a gentleman,
seeking to avoid trouble is difficult indeed.'"
Although Yǐ was greatly afraid,
he ultimately did not dare to speak out.
(From the Cèfǔ)

Yáo Yuánchóng and Zhāng Yuè both served as chief ministers,
and harbored considerable suspicion and obstruction towards each other,
repeatedly infringing upon each other over matters,
with Zhāng bearing a deep grudge.
When Yáo fell ill,
he admonished his sons, saying:
"Chancellor Zhāng and I are not in harmony,
the rift between us is very deep,
yet he has long been fond of luxury,
especially enjoying fine clothing and curios.
After my death,
since we once served together,
he will come to pay his respects to you.
Display prominently all my lifetime possessions,
including fine garments, precious belts,
and valuable artifacts arranged before the curtain.
If he pays them no attention,
quickly settle the family affairs,
for our entire clan will be doomed.
Once you see that we have no worries,
then record all the curios and items,
and present them to Lord Zhāng,
also requesting him to write the epitaph for the tombstone.
Once you obtain his text,
immediately transcribe it for submission,
and prepare the stone slab in advance,
then have it carved right away.
Chancellor Zhāng is slower than I in reacting to matters;
a few days later,
he is bound to regret it.
If he tries to retrieve the epitaph under the pretext of revising it,
lead the envoy to see that it has already been carved,
and inform him that it has been reported to the emperor.
That will be the end of it."
After Yáo passed away,
Zhāng indeed came,
and glanced at the curios and garments three or four times.
Yáo's sons all followed their father's instructions.
Within a few days, the text was completed,
with a detailed and comprehensive narrative,
considered a masterpiece of the time.
It read in part:
"Eight pillars support the heavens,
occupying the lofty and bright positions;
the four seasons complete the year,
preserving the nurturing power of nature."
A few days later,
Zhāng indeed sent an envoy to retrieve the text,
claiming that the wording was not thorough enough,
and wishing to make further deletions and revisions.
Yáo's sons then led the envoy
to see the stele and informed him that it had been presented to the emperor.
The envoy returned to report,
and Zhāng, beating his chest in regret, said:
"Even dead, Yáo Chóng could outwit the living Zhāng Yuè.
Only today do I realize
that my talent falls short of his."

When Gāo Pián was governing Shǔ,

Facing the commandery on a mountaintop stood Kāiyuán Temple.
At dusk, the monks were worshipping the Buddha,

He ordered the military officers to capture and shackle them all and bring them before him.

saying to them:

took up arms, and called themselves the 'Greatly Shaven.'

harassing and coercing the regional commander, which indeed fulfilled his words.

One night, an old man in yellow clothes,

ascended the pavilion and entered.
Seeing Xiàng sitting alone in the dark reciting texts,

illuminating Xiàng.
He spoke of times before creation,
and Xiàng received texts on the Five Phases and Great Plan.
Fearing he would forget the extensive discourse,
he tore his robe and sash to record the words.
At dawn, the man departed.
Xiàng asked his name,
and he replied:
"I am the essence of the Great Unity, sent by the Celestial Emperor upon hearing of the son of the Golden Mao.
Seeing a learned scholar below, I came to observe."
He then produced bamboo slips from his bosom,
containing texts on astronomy and geography,
and said, "I shall briefly impart them to you."
When Xiàng's son Xīn learned these arts from his father,

notes that Emperor Āi commanded Zǐ Xīn to continue his father's work,

totaling 33,090 volumes.
