There was a man from the lakes and seas named

"Chén Yuánlóng,
a man of the lakes and seas,
has not abandoned his heroic spirit."
Bèi inquired:

is there some particular matter?"
Sì replied:
"Once, while fleeing turmoil, I passed through Xiàpī
and met Yuánlóng.
Yuánlóng showed no host's courtesy,
did not speak with me for a long time,
but climbed onto the large bed to sleep,
leaving his guest to sleep on the lower bed."
Bèi said:
"You, Sir, bear the name of a national scholar,
yet you seek fields and inquire about houses,
your words containing nothing worth adopting—
this is what Yuánlóng despises.
Why should he speak with you?
If it were someone like me,
I would wish to sleep on a tower amidst a hundred fires,
leaving you to sleep on the ground—
why merely distinguish between upper and lower beds?"
Biǎo laughed heartily.

Wēi Bó,
is the lush pine in winter's cold,
the escaping light in the dark night;
Lù Shìhéng and Shìlóng,
are the soaring of the swan geese,
the suspended drum awaiting the mallet.
All these gentlemen:
take their mighty brushes as plows and hoes,
their paper slips as fertile fields,
their profound silence as sowing and reaping,
their righteous principles as abundant harvests,
their discussions as blossoms,
their loyalty and forgiveness as treasures.
They compose writings as brocade and embroidery,
store the Five Classics as silk and cloth,
seat humility as mats and cushions,
spread righteousness and deference as curtains and screens,
practice benevolence and righteousness as their dwelling,
cultivate the Way and virtue as their spacious mansion."

Sù was terrified,

The next day, Sù was summoned repeatedly,

Sù later asked Lún:
"How did you know this would happen?"
Lún replied:
"The emperor is frugal by nature;
though initially angry,
he readily listens to the empress.
Women delight in beauty alone;
since the empress was pleased,
the emperor's mind would surely change—
that is how I knew."
Sù sighed and said:
"The talent for divining others' thoughts
is beyond my reach."
Sù, then a high-ranking meritorious official,
showed deference to almost no one,

"Young master Féng,
will surely occupy this seat of mine in time."

would always examine them for signs of fortune and prosperity,
and only then dispatch them.
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"Those with ill-fated lives are not worthy to share in achieving merit and fame."
Gentlemen consider this a wise saying.
"Dìng Mìng Lù"
When the Mǎ clan dominated Húnán,
in their final years, the Tiāncè Pavilion was burned by heavenly fire at Lǎngzhōu Temple.
That night, people heard shouts in the sky,
saying "Make way for the Tiāncè Pavilion!"
The clouds churned as if ten thousand people
were carrying heavy loads,
and it lasted for days before reaching Tánzhōu in full force.
From "The Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Sòng Dynasty"
Shēngyuán
In the nineteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
the examination official Yuánwàiláng Wáng Shīdàn oversaw the imperial examinations.
He failed candidates Zhāng Chānglíng and Wáng Gōngjǐn in the policy essay,
whereupon Emperor Tàizōng sighed and said:
"Both men possess literary talent."
Wáng replied:
"Their character is frivolous,
and their writing excessively ornate.
They will never become accomplished scholars.
The reason I did not recommend them
is for fear they might corrupt Your Majesty's refined standards."
The Emperor considered this a wise remark,
and later events proved him right.
End
In the ninth year of the Kāiyuán era,
the southwest corner of the Wǎguān Temple's pavilion in Jiāngníng County had long been tilting,
but it righted itself by the wind,
and during the Shùnyì era of Wú, the temple was renamed Shēngyuán Temple,
and the pavilion became Shēngyuán Pavilion.
According to Gǒng Yǐng's "Chart of Successive Reigns,"
Kāng Rénjié, recommended by Chén Déchéng, arrived in Jīnlíng,
where he attended a gathering of officials during their旬沐 (xún mù, a day off every ten days) banquet at Shēngyuán Pavilion.
Rénjié joined the feast,
and composed a poem harmonizing with the theme of ascending the pavilion,
which included the lines: "When clouds scatter, one gazes afar a thousand miles;
As the sun slants, it casts shade over half the city."
All present were greatly astonished.
From the "History of Southern Táng,"
it is recorded that Shēngyuán Pavilion was built with the mountain as its foundation,
reaching a height of about ten zhàng,
with its shadow stretching calmly halfway across the river.
Later, during the Bǎozhōng era, when the imperial army recaptured the area,
the families of scholar-officials, along with wealthy merchants and powerful elites,
sought refuge in the pavilion with their beautiful women and young wives,
numbering nearly several thousand people.
The Yuè troops set fire to it,
and the cries of those inside shook the heavens,
reducing it to ashes in a single day.
From the "Records of Jīnlíng."
Xú Jìngyè,
at the age of over ten years old,
was fond of shooting arrows.
Duke Yīng often said:
"This boy's physiognomy is unfavorable,
he will bring ruin to our clan.
When he shoots, arrows overflow the target,
when he rides, he vanishes like the wind,
even veteran cavalry cannot catch up."
Once Duke Yīng was hunting,
he ordered Jìngyè to drive game into the forest,
then took advantage of the wind to set a fire,
intending to kill him.
Knowing there was no escape,
Jìngyè slaughtered his horse,
and hid inside its belly.
After the fire passed,
he stood up covered in blood,
which greatly amazed Duke Yīng."
From "Yǒuyáng":
During Emperor Gāozōng's reign,
barbarian tribes gathered as bandits,
and military campaigns against them repeatedly failed,
so Xú Jìngyè was appointed as provincial governor.
The prefecture sent troops to welcome him at the outskirts,
but Jìngyè dismissed them all to return,
proceeding alone to his office.
When the bandits heard the new governor had arrived,
they prepared their defenses and waited.
Jìngyè asked nothing about them,
and only after handling other matters
did he finally say:
"Where are the bandits?"
The reply came:
"On the southern bank."
He then went with just one or two assistants,
to the astonishment of all observers.
The bandits initially held weapons and watched cautiously,
but when they saw nothing in the boats,
they instead closed their camp and hid.
Jìngyè went straight into their camp,
and announced:
"The state knows you have suffered under corrupt officials,
and that you have no other wickedness.
You may all return to your fields,
those who remain later will be considered bandits."
He only summoned their leaders,
reproached them for not surrendering sooner,
had each beaten several dozen strokes and sent them away,
whereupon the region became perfectly orderly.
When his grandfather Duke Yīng heard of this,
he admired his courage and strategy,
saying:
"I cannot judge this,
but the one who will destroy our family
must be this boy!"
From "Accounts of Extraordinary Events in National History"
Tiānyòu Performs Merits
Dí Rénjié had a broad knowledge of the classics and histories,
and was moderately skilled in literary composition.
His admonitions and earnest remonstrance
reflected the style of the ancients;
his eradication of illicit shrines
demonstrated the integrity of a principled scholar.
His mind was upright and honest,
untainted even when stained;
his courage was firm and resolute,
discerning and decisive.
In his later years, he developed a penchant for wealth,
akin to Hé Qiáo and his ilk.
From "Qiān Zǎi"
Lǐ Bái possessed the wisdom of discernment.
While staying in Bīngzhōu,
he recognized Guō Zǐyí, the Prince of Fényáng, among the ranks of common soldiers.
He helped him escape punishment and commended him highly.
Later, when the Hànlín Academician (Lǐ Bái) was implicated in the affair of Prince Yǒng,
and the Prince of Fényáng had achieved great military success,
he requested to redeem the Hànlín Academician with his own official rank and title.
The emperor granted this request,
thus sparing him from execution.
From "Preface by Yuè Shǐ"
Prime Minister Liǔ Cǎn memorialized that the Western Capital formerly had the Lingyan Pavilion,
which depicted the founding heroes of the dynasty.
Now that the capital has moved to the Eastern Capital,
such a structure has yet to be erected.
The Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Four Garrisons, Prince of Liáng, has achievements surpassing antiquity,
so it is requested that a separate pavilion be built near the Lingyan Pavilion
to portray the Prince of Liáng and honor his virtuous deeds.
An imperial edict stated:
"The state of Wèi rewarded the merits of Péngyáng
by constructing a separate hall to record achievements;
the state of Qí honored the accomplishments at the Sìshuǐ River
by erecting the Tower of Admirable Virtue.
To establish a new model
in accordance with ancient precedents,
the relevant officials shall select an auspicious site within the imperial city
to build a separate Lingyan Pavilion for portraiture,
and it shall be bestowed the name 'Pavilion of Heaven-Bestowed Merits.'"
History of the Five Dynasties
Lǐ Huá,
styled Xiáshū,
respected Yuán Déxiù as an elder brother and befriended Xiāo Yǐngshì and Liú Xùn, composing "The Treatise on Three Worthies,"
saying:
"Yuán's aspirations and conduct
should use the Way to order the world;
Liú's aspirations and conduct
should use the Six Classics to harmonize people's hearts;
Xiāo's aspirations and conduct
should use antiquity to reform the present age.
When they approach the Master's gate,
they are among those who have attained understanding.
Yuán occupies the position of a teacher and guardian;
observing his appearance,
one sees his benevolence.
Liú wears the robes of a high official,
residing in the role of a guest and friend,
discussing the roots of order and chaos,
the subtle and evident aspects of human relations,
penetrating the primordial essence,
and only then does one see his profundity.
Xiāo is like tempered steel,
unbending and unyielding;
at times of rise and fall, advance and retreat,
in moments of life and death,
only then does one see his great integrity.
Adopting his balanced actions,
one can take him as a teacher.
Mǎotǐng's father served as an assistant magistrate in Jǔ,
and offended Zhāng Wéiyī of Qīnghé,
who at the time assisted the investigating commissioner in pressing the charge.
When Mǎotǐng first passed the imperial examination,
he traveled from Luò to Jǔ,
intercepted the commissioner's carriage on the road,
and pleaded with sorrowful words.
Wéiyī shed tears,
releasing him that very day,
and said:
'Assistant Magistrate Xiāo has produced a worthy son,
whose talent benefits the world's customs and teachings.
If I incur offense for this,
I have no regrets!'
In this manner,
can it not be called filial piety?"
Grand Marshal Fáng Guǎn, whenever he saw Lǔshān, would sigh all day long,
saying to me:
"Seeing Zǐzhī's countenance
makes one's heart for fame and profit vanish entirely."
Director of the Imperial Academy Sū Yuánmíng often said to the famous scholars of the time:
"If I unfortunately live in a decadent age,
what I am not ashamed of
is knowing Yuán Zǐzhī."
When Liú was in the capital,
he once fell seriously ill;
Fáng visited him frequently.
Fúfēng, hearing of this,
could not sleep the entire night,
and said to his attendants:
"If Bǐngqīng does not recover,
there will be no more divine principle."
Minister Liú Yàn,
whenever he had profound insights,
would invariably visit and converse with him for several days,
forgetting to return,
and upon leaving would sigh:
"Hearing
Liú Gōng's
pure discourse,
I see the principles of sovereigns and kings."
Yǐn Yín of Chénjùn, renowned for judging character,
upon seeing Xùn, exclaimed:
"He is the Huáng Shūdù of today!
Unfortunately, Yuán was dismissed from Lǔshān
and died in Lùhún;
Liú, avoiding turmoil, passed away in Ānkāng;
Xiāo, returning to bury his ancestors,
died in Rǔnán.
These three worthies did not attain high positions,
nor enjoy long lives,
yet they lived in compliance and acceptance—
this is the attainment of the worthy.
Not receiving their teachings
is the ailment of living people."
《Tángshū Yīnghuá》
Riding the Wind and Gazing Afar
The Cloud Terrace has fourteen high pavilions,
and the Wind-Riding Viewing Pavilion has twelve rooms.
"Records of Luòyáng"
Hè Zhīzhāng was
the maternal cousin of Lù Xiàngxiān,
and Lù was particularly close friends with Zhīzhāng.
He once said to others:
"Brother Hè's discourse
and demeanor truly make him a man of grace and culture.
Even when separated from my own younger relatives,
I do not miss them,
but if a single day passes without seeing Brother Hè,
I feel vulgar and narrow-minded."
(Old Book of Tang)
During the Zhēnyuán era,
the brothers of the Yáng and Mù families,
in character and spirit,
were evenly matched.
Some said of the Yáng brothers,
their guests were all alike;
of the Mù brothers,
their guests were all distinct.
Thus their superiority was judged.
The Mù family had four brothers:
Zàn, Zhì, Yún, and Shǎng.
Contemporaries called Zàn, common yet principled, "fermented milk";
Zhì, refined and benevolent, "butter";
Yún, "ghee";
Shǎng, "dried milk curd."
(from "Supplementary Records of the National History")
Facing the Waves
The Purple Tenuity Palace has the Linbo Pavilion and the Changhe Pavilion.
"Records of the Eastern Capital"
Liú Fén was well-versed in Confucian teachings.
Once while reading Wénzhōngzǐ,
he indignantly remarked:
"It's not that he lacks talent,
but to compare his works to those of the ancient sages—
isn't that going too far?"
A guest asked:
"How does Wénzhōngzǐ compare to the Six Classics?"
Fén replied:
"If we judge person by person,
Wénzhōngzǐ compared to the Six Classics
is like a servant compared to their master."
Thus the world came to regard Wénzhōngzǐ as the servant of the Six Classics.
From "Nánbù"
Flying Pavilion
Hán Xīzǎi was sent as an envoy to the Later Zhōu,
and upon his return,
Emperor Yuánzōng inquired extensively about the generals and ministers of Zhōu.
Xīzǎi said:
"The Palace Commander Zhào's gaze and demeanor are extraordinary,
truly unfathomable."

A thousand rows of guard huts stand,
the patrol paths crisscross like silk threads.
The imperial carriage routes are laid out,
with orchid-scented steps and soaring towers.
From Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital"
How towering the Chang Gate appears,
with flying pavilions spanning the flowing waves.
From Lù Jī's "Yuefu Poem"
Flying pavilions adorned with crimson ribbons.
Above,
When Dí Qīng was a junior officer, he committed an offense,
and was due to be executed,
but Yōng pardoned him.
"History of the Song Dynasty: Yōng's Biography"
Bǐngyìláng Yuè Fēi violated the law,
and was due to be punished.
Zōng Zé, upon seeing him, recognized his exceptional talent,
saying:
"This is a general's material."
At that time, the Jin forces attacked Sìshuǐ,
so Zé entrusted Yuè with five hundred cavalry,
ordering him to achieve merit to redeem his offense.
Yuè Fēi soundly defeated the Jin army and returned.

A gé is

states that a small inner door is called a gé.

Emperor Gāo of Hàn knew that Wúwáng Bì would cause chaos in the southeast,
Xǔ Shào recognized Cáo Cāo as a treacherous minister in turbulent times,
Kǒng Xún and Qíwáng Yōu foresaw that Liú Yuān would inevitably bring disorder,
Wáng Yǎn discerned that Shí Lè would become a calamity for the realm,
Pān Tāo knew that Shù Wáng Dūn would act as a rebel beyond the river,

Annotation:
Yán Shīgǔ stated:
The pavilion,
is a small gate.
Opened facing east,
to avoid the main gate,

"Biography of Gōngsūn Hóng"
When Gōngsūn Hóng arrived,
the Chancellor opened the eastern pavilion to receive worthy men,
consulting with them on court audiences and memorials,
thereby discussing state advantages,
the Emperor ordered Zhù and others to debate with senior officials inside and outside court,
corresponding with principled writings.
"Biography of Yán Zhù"
Xuē Xuān said to Zhū Yún:
"Remaining in my eastern pavilion,
you may observe extraordinary scholars from all regions."
"Biography of Zhū Yún"
Zǐ Chǎn went out in the morning,
passing by the alley of the coffin maker,
he heard a woman wailing,
and he held her husband's hand while listening.
After a while,
he sent an official to seize and interrogate her,
and it turned out she had strangled her husband with her own hands.
Another day,
his carriage driver asked him:
"How did you know, Master?"
Zǐ Chǎn replied:
"Her voice was fearful.
Generally, when people are with their beloved ones,
they worry when they first fall ill,
fear when approaching death,
and grieve after they have died.
Now she was wailing for her already dead husband,
yet instead of grief, there was fear—
that is how I knew there was foul play."
"Hánzǐ"
Hán Huǎng's case in Rùnzhōu was similar.
"Yǒuyáng" quotes "Lùn Héng"
Huáng Gé
Huáng Bà served as the Inspector of Yángzhōu,
and once intended to conduct an inspection.
He selected an elderly, honest official to send on the mission,
instructing him to be thorough and meticulous.
The official, upon departure, dared not lodge at postal stations,
but ate by the roadside,
where a crow snatched his meat.
A commoner who wished to speak at the government office
happened to see this and reported it to Huáng Bà,
recounting the incident to him.
Later, when the official returned to report to Huáng Bà,
Huáng Bà met him,
greeted and consoled him,
saying:
"You’ve had a hard time,
eating by the roadside,
only to have a crow steal your meat."
The official was greatly astonished,
believing Huáng Bà knew all about his activities in detail,
and dared not conceal even the slightest detail in his responses.
For widowers, widows, orphans, and the childless who died with no means for a burial,
the local officials would report to Huáng Bà in writing,
and he would make appropriate arrangements for each case.
Pointing out that a large tree at a certain place could be used for a coffin,
or piglets at a certain station could serve as sacrifices for the officials,
everything turned out just as he said.
His insight and intelligence were such that
both officials and commoners could not fathom the source of his knowledge,
and all praised him as divine.
"Qián Hàn"
In Yǐngchuān, there was a wealthy household,
where brothers lived together,
and both of their wives became pregnant within a few months.
The elder brother's wife suffered a miscarriage,
so she concealed it.
When the time of delivery came for both,
they went to the wet nurse's house.
The younger brother's wife gave birth to a boy,
which the elder brother's wife stole at night.
They disputed over the child for three years,
and the local authorities could not resolve the case.
Chéngxiàng Huáng Bà came out and sat before the hall,
ordering a soldier to hold the child,
and had the two women stand ten steps away each.
He sternly said to them:
"Go and take the child yourselves."
The elder brother's wife grabbed the child urgently,
and the child cried loudly.
The younger brother's wife, fearing the child would be harmed,
thus let go and stopped,
appearing deeply sorrowful.
The elder brother's wife was very pleased.
Huáng Bà said:
"This is the younger brother's son."
After questioning, she confessed.
From "Fēngsú Tōng".
The Grand Commandant had a Yellow Chamber Registrar,
who recorded various affairs of the ministry.
The "Reading of Records"
states that the Three Excellencies had yellow chambers,
but there was no such meaning prior to this.
"The Book of Rites: Scholars' Leather Kneepads":
are the same as the Son of Heaven's,
while those of dukes, marquises, and high officials differ.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary:
says that scholars are humble and thus the same as the ruler,
without suspicion.
Now, vermilion gates wide open
are the proper color facing the sun.
Since the Three Excellencies and the Son of Heaven are close in ritual rank,
their chambers are yellow to show humility,
an old system of the Hàn.
The "Records of Sòng"
describes the system of the Three Excellencies,
opening the yellow chamber for conducting affairs,
and installing owl-tail ornaments.
In the Northern Qí, the Three Excellencies' offices
had three gates with the middle gate
being the yellow chamber, equipped with an inner screen,
and the Yellow Chamber Registrar was in charge of the decorum under the chamber.
The "Comprehensive Institutions"
records Zhāng Chāo's letter to Lord Chén:
"The appointment to the Yellow Chamber will take place soon."
In Pei Commandery, a household possessed assets exceeding two hundred thousand,
with a son only a few years old,
who had lost his mother.
There was a daughter who was unvirtuous.
When the father fell ill,
he summoned his clansmen to draft a will,
ordering that all property be given to the daughter,
but leaving only a sword
with the instruction that when the son reached fifteen, it should be given to him.
Later, when the daughter did not give it to the son,
he brought a lawsuit to the grand administrator.
Minister of Works Hé Wǔ reviewed the will
and said to his subordinate officials:
"The daughter is domineering by nature,
and her husband is also greedy and despicable.
The father feared harm would come to his son,
so he temporarily gave everything to the daughter,
but in reality, it was only entrusted to her.
As for the sword,
it symbolizes decisive judgment.
Setting the age at fifteen
indicates he estimated his son’s intelligence and capability would be sufficient to be independent by then,
and he could appeal to the authorities
to seek justice.
His foresight and deep consideration were such
that all the property was taken from the daughter and returned to the son."
Hàn Shū
Provincial Cabinet
During the Hàn Dynasty, a man from Línhuái took a bolt of silk to the market to sell it.
On the way, he encountered rain,
and used the silk to cover himself.
Another man arrived later,
seeking shelter from the rain,
and was given one end of the silk to share.
When the rain stopped and they were to part ways,
they ended up arguing with each other,
each claiming the silk was his own.
They went to the prefecture to state their cases.
Chéngxiàng Xuē Xuān ordered the silk to be cut,
giving each man half,
and sent a mounted officer to listen to their reactions.
The latter man accepted it without guilt,
even stepping forward to gather his share,
while the true owner cried injustice.
Xuē Xuān, now convinced,
summoned and reprimanded the impostor,
who then confessed fully.
From "Fēngsú Tōng".
Yáng Cì was appointed Grand Commandant,
and in the first year of the Zhōngpíng era, he was summoned to a council meeting,
where he went to the imperial chambers to offer blunt admonitions.
"Later Biography"
Golden Light
Zhāng Jǔ served as the magistrate of Jùzhāng County.
A wife had murdered her husband,
then set fire to their house,
falsely claiming he died in the blaze.
The husband's relatives grew suspicious,
and reported the wife to the authorities.
The wife resisted and refused to confess,
so Zhāng Jǔ had two pigs brought forth—
one dead and one alive—
piled up firewood and burned them.
The dead one's mouth contained no ashes,
whereupon he examined the husband's mouth and found no ashes.
The wife then confessed to the crime.
From "Yì Shū"

In Luòyáng Palace, there were the Golden Light Pavilion, Qīngyáng Pavilion, Chéngxiū Pavilion, Vermilion Brightness Pavilion, Peaceful Joy Pavilion, White Storage Pavilion, Xiǎnrén Pavilion, Chóngmíng Pavilion, Zhāngdé Pavilion, Flying Cloud Pavilion, Peaceful World Pavilion, and Cháng'ān Pavilion.
In Cháng'ān, there were the Dōngmíng Pavilion, Western Splendor Pavilion, and Purple Portal Pavilion.
"Record of Jìn Dynasty Palace Pavilions"
Fú Róng was in Jīngzhōu,
when an old woman encountered a robber on the road.
The woman cried out loudly against the thief.
A passerby chased the robber for the woman,
and once the robber was captured,
he falsely accused the passerby of being the thief.
As dusk was approaching,
neither the woman nor the people on the street could tell who was right,
so they sent both men to Fú Róng.
Upon seeing them, Fú Róng smiled and said:
"This is easy to figure out.
Let the two men run together,
and whoever exits the Fèngyáng Gate first is not the thief."
After they returned,
Fú Róng sternly said to the one who came out later:
"You are truly the robber,
why did you falsely accuse someone?"
"Jìn Zǎijì"
Chuán Yǎn,
courtesy name Jìguī,
served as the magistrate of Shānyīn when Emperor Gāo of Qí was regent.
Because legal cases in Shānyīn were numerous and piled up,
he was reappointed as magistrate of Shānyīn.
An old woman selling needles and an old woman selling sugar disputed over a ball of silk,
and came to Yǎn.
Yǎn hung the silk ball on a pillar,
whipped it,
and secretly observed that there were iron filings,
so he penalized the sugar seller.
Also, two old farmers disputed over a chicken.
Yǎn asked each what they fed the chicken,
one said millet,
the other said beans.
He then cut open the chicken and found millet,
and punished the one who said beans.
Within the county, he was praised as divine and wise,
and no one dared to steal.

Cuī Guāngchéng arrived at the Eastern and Western Upper Pavilions by foot-drawn carriage.

The Northern Qí had a Western Upper Pavilion.

To the left of Xuānzhèng Hall is called the Eastern Upper Pavilion,

"Six Statutes"
Lǐ Huì was transferred to serve as the Governor of Yōngzhōu,
excelling in contemplation and observation.
At that time, there were two men—one carrying salt and the other carrying firewood—
who set down their heavy burdens together to rest under the shade of a tree.
As the two men were about to depart,
they argued over a sheepskin,
each claiming it was the mat they had used to cushion their backs.
Lǐ Huì sent the disputing parties out
and turned to his chief clerk, saying:
"Can we determine the owner of this sheepskin?"
The subordinates thought he was joking,
and none offered a response.
Lǐ Huì then ordered someone to place the sheepskin on a mat,
struck it with a stick,
and observed a small amount of salt residue.
He declared:
"We have uncovered the truth."
He had the disputing parties look at it,
whereupon the firewood carrier admitted his guilt.
(Book of Wèi)
Prince Péngchéng Yóu,
courtesy name Zìshēn,
served as Governor of Dìng Prefecture.
At that time, someone had a black ox stolen,
which had white hair on its back.
Chief Clerk Wéi Dàojiàn said to Attendant Official Wèi Dàoshèng:
"When our lord was in Cāng Prefecture,
he captured wrongdoers as if divine;
if he catches this thief,
he will truly be godlike."
Yóu then forged an official requisition,
purchased ox hides,
paying double the market price.
He had the ox owner identify them,
thus capturing the thief.
Jiàn and others sighed in admiration.
There was also an old woman surnamed Wáng,
who lived alone cultivating three mǔ of vegetables,
repeatedly stolen from.
Yóu then sent someone secretly,
writing characters on vegetable leaves,
the next day checking leaves with writing in the market,
and caught the thief.
After this, there were no thieves within his jurisdiction,
and his governance became the foremost of his time.
"Book of Qí"
Zhū Huá
Yǔ Zhòngwén,
styled Cìwǔ,
served as the governor of Āngù.
There were two families, Rén and Dù,
each of which had lost an ox.
Later, one ox was found,
and both families claimed it.
The provincial authorities could not settle the dispute for a long time.
Hán Bójùn, the senior official of Yìzhōu, said:
"Yǔ Zhòngwén was clever and perceptive in his youth;
he can be entrusted to resolve this."
Zhòngwén said:
"This is easy to solve."
He then ordered the two families to drive their herds of oxen away,
and released the disputed ox.
The ox went straight toward the Rén family's herd.
He then had someone slightly injure the ox.
The Rén family sighed in distress,
while the Dù family remained indifferent.
Zhòngwén then reprimanded and interrogated the Dù family,
who admitted their guilt and left.

Suī Yáo Chá was appointed as the Secretary of the Imperial Library and received an imperial edict to serve as a senior advisor in the Zhūhuá Pavilion.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
Left Assistant Lǐ Xínglián's
younger brother Xíngquán
had a son named Zhōng from a former wife,
who committed incest with his stepmother,
then secretly took her into hiding.
They claimed an imperial edict summoned them to the palace.
Xínglián, unaware of the truth,

An imperial order mandated strict investigation,

lying in the street.
When Cháng'ān County interrogated her,

"Someone falsely proclaimed an edict summoning me,
a purple-robed man detained me for several nights,
I don't know his name,
then strangled me and abandoned me in the street."
Zhōng grew fearful,
secretly consulted a diviner,
aroused suspicions of patrol officers,
and was arrested and delivered to the county.
County Captain Wáng Jǐng took him into a room,
but interrogation yielded no confession.
Jǐng first had a man hide under the desk mat to eavesdrop,
sent another running to report and summon superiors,
then locked the door and left.
Mother and son said to each other:
"We must not confess."
Along with other confidential remarks.
When Jǐng returned and opened the door,
the man under the desk arose.
Mother and son were greatly startled,
and both fully confessed and were executed.

When Lǐ Déyù was stationed in Zhèyòu,
the abbot of Gānlù Temple
reported that the temple's property handed over during the transition
had been embezzled by the previous abbot,
specifically a certain amount of temple gold.
He cited evidence from several predecessors,
all of whom had conducted handovers,
with clearly documented records of receipt.
All testimonies pointed to the new abbot concealing and using the gold.
Moreover, it was stated:
When initially taking office,
the weight of the gold received was clearly recorded,
but on the day of handover,
the gold was nowhere to be found.
The case was fully investigated and concluded,
with the crime confessed and evident.
However, the whereabouts of the misused gold remained unknown.
Some speculated that the monk, unrestrained by monastic discipline,
had squandered it,
leaving him with no justification to plead,
resigned to face death.
During a moment of reflection,
Lǐ Déyù suspected the case was unresolved,
and pondered it carefully.
The monk then confessed the truth, saying:
"Those residing in the temple
enjoy holding authority.
Successive abbots
over the years
have falsified documents about the gold's weight,
but in reality, there is no gold.
The community, seeing me isolated
and not mingling with their clique,
sought to exploit this to oust me."
He wept bitterly, overwhelmed by injustice.
Lǐ Déyù, moved with compassion, said:
"This is not difficult to resolve."
After a moment of contemplation, he declared:
"I have the solution."
He immediately summoned several sedan chairs,
ordered the implicated monks to confront the matter,
and had them all seated in the sedan chairs.
Once the curtains were drawn,
he directed that the doors be closed to prevent them from seeing each other,
then commanded yellow clay be brought,
instructing each to mold the shape of the gold passed down through successive handovers as evidence.
Since the monks had never seen the actual form of the gold,
none could successfully mold it.
Enraged,
Lǐ Déyù ordered the investigation of the previous abbots,
who all confessed one by one.
Thus, the falsely accused
was cleared and vindicated.
From "Guìyuàn Cóngtán"

Xǔ Zōngyì governed Jiànzhōu.
A citizen had suffered a robbery,
and under the lamplight recognized the violent intruder.
At dawn, he reported to the patrol,
and the thief could not withstand the torture,
so he confessed his crime,
was imprisoned, and sent to the prefecture.
Zōngyì conducted a review,
where the imprisoned thief and the victim had conflicting statements.
Zōngyì promptly ordered both households to bring their silk reeling machines,
and each to present the material used as the core when winding the silk fabric.
One claimed it was an apricot kernel,
the other a tile fragment.
He then instructed them to unwind the silk thread,
revealing the apricot kernel,
which matched the prisoner's account.
He also used silk to weigh the machine,
measuring its weight and size,
confirming it was originally from the prisoner's household.
Thus, the one who had falsely accused was convicted,
along with the patrol officer.

Que stands on both sides of the gate,

The "Guangzhi"

In ancient times, two observation towers were erected in front of every gate,
serving as markers for the palace entrance.
Their tops were habitable,
and ascending them allowed one to gaze into the distance,
hence the name "observation tower."
When officials approached for court,

Their surfaces were painted with clouds, immortals,

King Xiàng glared and shouted at him,
causing Lóufán to dare not look him in the eye,
nor release his arrow,
so he fled,
returned to the fortress,
and dared not come out again.
The "Annals"
and the biography of Xìn convey the meaning of sudden, fierce intimidation.
Jì Zūn served as General Who Conquers the Caitiffs,
leading troops south to attack the barbarian bandits of Hóngnóng, Yànxīn, and Bóhuá.
During the battle,
a crossbow arrow entered his mouth,
pierced through and emerged from his raised sleeve,
and as he covered his mouth, blood flowed into his sleeve.
When the troops saw Jì Zūn wounded,
they retreated.
Jì Zūn rebuked his officers and soldiers,
whereupon they advanced to fight,
each one striking down ten enemies,
and utterly defeated them.
From "Dōngguān Hànjì"
The Sūn family had no watchtowers,
and the great Jìn's southern capital also had no time to erect them,
so the gate watchtowers were abandoned.
Zàng Róngxù's "Book of Jìn"
records that during the Dàxīng era, discussants all said the two tall and sturdy watchtowers at the tomb of Hàn's Minister over the Masses, Xǔ Yù of Yìxīng,
could be relocated for use,
but Wáng Màohóng was unwilling.
Later, while riding in the imperial carriage out of Xuānyáng Gate,
he looked south at the two peaks of Niútóu Mountain,
and immediately said, "These are the heavenly watchtowers,
why trouble to alter them?"
The emperor followed his advice.
Now, when exiting Xuānyáng and gazing at this mountain,
it truly resembles watchtowers.
"Records of Dānyáng"
In the sixth year of the Jiàn'ān era,
Liú Biǎo attacked Xī'è.
The magistrate of Xī'è, Dù Zǐxù, led the men and women of the county to guard the city walls.
At that time, the Nányáng official Bó Xiàozhǎng was also in the city.
Hearing the sounds of the attack,
he was terrified,
entered his room and closed the door,
pulling the quilt over his head.
After half a day of fighting,
he gradually dared to show his face.
The next day,
he stood by the wall and listened.
On the second day,
he went out to ask for news.
By the fourth or fifth day,
he was even carrying a shield to personally observe,
and said to Dù Zǐxù:
"Courage can be cultivated."
From the *Jiǔzhōu Chūnqiū*
Bówàng
On the banks of the Shàngmíng River in Jīngzhōu, there were often flood dragons,
and many who fetched water from the valley did not survive the year.
During the Shēngpíng era,
Dèng Xiá of Chénjùn,
courtesy name Yìngyuǎn,
was inherently brave and strong.
Enraged, he entered the water,
found the flood dragon,
and immediately raised his fist,
dragging it ashore,
intending to hack it to death.
His mother said to him:
"The flood dragon is a divine creature;
you should not kill it.
Now you can chant and feed it,
so it will no longer cause harm."
Xiá chanted and released it.
From then until now,
this calamity has completely ceased.
From "Yì Yuàn"
See also flood dragons.
In the seventh year of Xiàowǔ Tàimíng, at Bówàng Liángshān,
twin towers were erected.
"Sòng Shū"
Stone Tower
Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Cài Yì,
possessed great courage,
and his voice was like the roar of thunder.
Once, two thieves entered his room,
Yì slapped the bed and gave a shout,
and the thieves both fell dead.
Yīn Hào entrusted him with the vanguard of the army.
"Jìn Zhuàn"
In the seventh year of the Tiānjiàn era, on the Wùxū day of the first month, divine dragon and benevolent beast towers were constructed outside the Duānmén and Grand Marshal Gates.
"Liáng Records"
The edict stated:
"In the past, when the Sūn clan moved south under the blue canopy,
they had no time to spare,
and thus failed to build the two observation towers,
leaving no place to display the laws.
Now our rites are flourishing and transformation widespread,
with public works simplified and duties light,
so we may construct symbolic towers,
to manifest the ancient statutes."
Thereupon craftsmen were selected and work measured,
stone was carved to make the towers,
reaching the ultimate in magnificence and splendor,
surpassing all ancient and modern works,
with marvelous birds and exotic plumes,
all completely prepared.
Liú Pán's "Liáng Chronicles"
When the towers were completed,
court officials inscribed them,
at that time Lù Chuí, styled Zuǒgōng,
composed a particularly excellent text,
admired and respected by the literati class.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
he burned the ancestral temples,
city walls, government offices and administrative buildings,
leaving virtually nothing remaining.
Soon after, when Gāolì and other states came to pay tribute,
seeing this devastation,
they wept beneath the towers.
"Accounts of the Six Dynasties"
Lù Chuí's preface stated:
"The institution of symbolic towers
has distant origins.
The Spring and Autumn Annals established teachings of ancient statutes through the rites,
handing down texts for promulgating laws,
the Dài Records reveal words about imperial tours,
the Zhōu history records dreams of erecting towers,
the northern wilderness's bright moon,
the western extremes' flowing essence,
the seas and mountains' yellow gold,
the Hétíng purple shells, blue dragon and black turtle designs,
the bronze sparrow and iron phoenix craftsmanship,
some for hearing cases and reviewing grievances,
some for spreading transformation and displaying laws,
some for properly marking the royal residence,
some for glorifying the imperial capital.
It also says the Jìn borrowed the heavenly towers at Niútóu,
the Sòng entrusted distant plans to Bówàng,
which deceived the eyes and ears,
but did not supplement the statutes.
Therefore we appointed officials to examine right and wrong,
selected scholars of clear judgment,
displayed jade tablets and set up standards,
observed the stars and measured the earth,
hastened to show respect,
observed and understood the ritual objects,
gazed upon the twin stone tablets' appearance,
the people recognized the hundredfold classics.
The inscription says: spreading teachings becomes manifest,
as the ten-day cycle begins to shine,
colors follow the circle above,
forms model the square below,
facing four gatherings ahead,
turning back to nine chambers behind,
north connecting two tracks,
south converging five directions.
"Selections"
Emperor Wǔ greatly appreciated poetry and rhapsodies,
those presenting literary works at the southern tower
continuously received imperial commands,
to compose new tower inscriptions with Lù Chuí.
"Yuán Jùn Biography"
Yáng Dàyǎn,
grandson of Wǔdū Dí Nándāng,
was brave and daring from a young age,
able to leap and run as if flying.
When Emperor Gāozǔ campaigned south,
Lǐ Chōng was in charge of selecting officers for the expedition.
Dàyǎn applied to join,
but Chōng refused him.
Dàyǎn said:
"Sir Minister, if you do not recognize my ability,
let me demonstrate by running with a three-zhang long reed tied to my hair."
He then tied the reed to his topknot and ran,
the reed straight as an arrow,
so fast that even galloping horses couldn't catch up.
All who witnessed this were amazed.
Chōng exclaimed:
"In a thousand years, there has never been such an extraordinary talent!"
He then appointed Dàyǎn as an army commander.
From "Tán Sǒu":
In all battles he fought, he was the most outstanding military leader.
Dàyǎn's wife, Madame Pān, was skilled in archery.
When she visited the army,
and Dàyǎn went out
for battles, campaigns, or hunts,
Madame Pān would also don military attire, ride alongside him with bridle to bridle.
Returning to camp,
they would sit together under the tent,
chatting and laughing freely with the officers.
Dàyǎn would point to her and tell everyone,
saying:
"This is General Pān."
In the Huái and Sì river regions, when children cried,
people would frighten them by saying:
"Yáng Dàyǎn is coming,"
and the crying would immediately stop.
From "Hòu Wèi"
Shí Jīn
Yáng Kǎn,
courtesy name Zǔxīn,
possessed extraordinary physical strength.
The bow he used was as heavy as twenty dàn,
while on horseback he used a six-dàn bow.
Once at the Yáo Temple in Yǎnzhōu, he kicked against a wall,
ascending vertically up to five xún,
and left seven footprints horizontally.
There were several stone lions on the Sì Bridge,
each eight chǐ tall
and ten wéi in girth.
Kǎn lifted them and struck them together,
smashing them all to pieces.
In the third year of the Dàtōng era, he arrived at Jiànyè.
He initially served under the Wèi dynasty,
holding the position of Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat,
and became renowned for his strength.
The Wèi Emperor once said to him:
"The court officials call you a tiger,
but are you truly a tiger or just a sheep in tiger's skin?"
He then asked him to imitate a tiger.
Kǎn crouched down and pressed his hand
into the palace floor, sinking his fingers deep into it.
The Wèi Emperor, impressed by his strength,
bestowed upon him a pearl-encrusted sword.
(From History of the Southern Dynasties, Chapter 53)
In the southeast, there is a stone well,
which is a hundred zhang square.
Above it stand two stone towers,
on the southeast side of which is a carved bear,
and a plaque is attached to the towers,
inscribed with the words:
"The Earth's Door is to the northwest,
where in the wilderness stand two golden towers,
a hundred zhang high,
golden towers with silver plates,
fifty zhang in circumference,
the two towers are a hundred zhang apart,
above them is a bright moon pearl,
three zhang in diameter,
its light illuminates a thousand li,
inside there is a golden staircase,
entering the two towers from the northwest,
the place is named the Gate of Heaven."
(Shényì Jīng) See also the Gate of Heaven.
Emperor Xiàowén of Wèi, Hóng,
was skilled in archery from a young age,
possessing great strength.
At just over ten years old, he was able to shatter sheep shoulder blades with his fingers.
When shooting at birds and beasts,
none escaped his aim; they fell wherever he reached.
"The Běi Shǐ Jì"
Emperor Xiàowén of the Eastern Wèi, Shànjiàn, was fond of literature and had a graceful appearance,
able to hold a stone lion and leap over walls,
never missing a shot with his bow.
Up
Flowing Essence
Mount Kūnlún has three peaks,
one facing directly east has Yōngchéng,
where golden terraces and jade towers shine brilliantly,
and there is the Flowing Essence Gate,
which is governed by the Queen Mother of the West.
"Records of the Ten Continents"
On the ninth layer of Mount Kūnlún,
the mountain shape gradually narrows,
below are fields of magical mushrooms and orchids,
each spanning hundreds of acres,
where groups of immortals cultivate and tend them.
Beside them stand one or two jade platforms,
each a thousand paces wide,
all with foundations made of five-colored jade,
the lowest layer has the Flowing Essence Gate,
rising straight up forty zhang,
to the east are the Gates of Wind, Cloud, and Rain Masters.
"Records of Omissions"
Shénwǔ raised troops in Fànyáng,
Lú Cáo was renowned for his bravery and strength under Ěrzhū's occupation of Jì.
Cáo stood nine chǐ tall,
with a rugged and imposing face,
his arm hair bristling like boar bristles, possessing strength
enough to uproot trees.
Once while lying ill,
he could still extend his leg to lift two Rúrú tribesmen.
When bandits invaded Fànyáng,
Cáo ascended the city wall,
shot an arrow three hundred paces,
then threw his bow outside the walls—
none of the marauders could draw it.
At that time,
there was a monk named Tánzàn known as divine in strength.
Only Cáo could wrestle with him,
and Tánzàn would prevail upon hearing Cáo's shouts.
(From History of the Northern Dynasties, Chapter 19)
Gold
Péng Lè's valor was unmatched.
At that time, Shénwǔ led Lè and over a hundred thousand troops to battle Yǔwén Hù at Shāyuàn.
At that moment, Lè, having drunk wine and riding on his drunkenness, charged deep into enemy lines.
He was stabbed,
his liver and intestines spilled out.
When they could not fully stuff them back in,
he cut off the protruding parts and returned to battle.
Hù's troops were then defeated,
with over thirty thousand corpses piled upon one another.
"Dú Yì Zhì"
Lè was stabbed,
his intestines spilled out.
When they could not fully stuff them back in,
he cut them off and resumed fighting.
His body suffered multiple wounds,
the army's momentum was thus thwarted,
and they returned in defeat.
Shénwǔ often recounted this afterward,
using it as a warning.
"Běi Shǐ"
Quán Wǔ was resolute and vigorous from a young age,
possessing extraordinary courage and strength,
capable of mounting a horse in heavy armor.
He once dove headfirst into a well,
before reaching the water,
he leaped back out again,
such was his swiftness and agility.
The Emperor
Pénglái, Fāngzhàng, and Yíngzhōu,
these three mountains are in the sea,
where all the immortals' elixirs of immortality are found,
with palaces made of gold and silver.
Hànshū
Yú Jùluó was eight feet tall,
possessed extraordinary physical strength,
had a powerful and majestic voice,
which could be heard several hundred paces away.
The Emperor
Purple Shell
With fish-scale roofs and dragon halls,
Purple shell watchtowers and pearl palaces.
"Songs of Chu"
Wáng Yì said:
This means the dwelling of the River God has watchtowers made of shells.
Magnificent Palaces
Ròu Fēi Xiān
Shěn Guāng,
courtesy name Zǒngchí,
was agile and nimble from a young age,
excelling at equestrian performances,
and was considered the best in the world.
When Chándìng Temple was first built,
its flagpole stood over ten zhang high,
and the rope happened to break beyond human reach,
Shěn Guāng said to the monks:
"I will fasten the rope for you."
The monks were astonished and delighted.
Shěn Guāng then took a pole in his mouth and climbed up,
reaching the dragon head at the top,
tied the rope,
released both his hands and feet,
and leaped down through the air,
landing on his palms and walking backward over ten steps.
The onlookers were both amazed and delighted,
and all marveled at his feat.
People of the time called him Ròu Fēi Xiān (Flesh-Flying Immortal).
Later, he answered the call to serve under Emperor Yáng,
attacking Liáodōng,
using assault ladders to strike the city walls.
The pole was fifteen zhang long,
and Shěn Guāng climbed to its top,
engaging the enemy on the city walls,
fighting at close quarters,
and killing or wounding over ten people.
The enemy concentrated their attacks and he fell,
but before hitting the ground,
he happened to catch a hanging rope on the pole,
grasped it, and climbed back up.
The Emperor saw this, admired his bravery, and found it extraordinary,
sent a messenger to speak with him,
and was greatly pleased.
He often kept Shěn Guāng by his side until the Jiāngdū disaster,
when Shěn Guāng, along with Mài Mèngcái and Qián Jié, secretly plotted against Yǔwén Huàjí to avenge the Emperor, but the plan was exposed.
In a hurried and fierce attack,
the enemy forces were routed.
Sīmǎ Dékǎn dispatched cavalry with crossbows to flank and shoot him.
Shěn Guāng wore no armor,
and thus was killed.
Hundreds of his subordinates fought to the death,
with not a single one surrendering.
When brave men heard of this,
none failed to shed tears for them.
Book of Suí
Cuī Hóngdù,
possessed extraordinary physical strength,
with a tall and imposing stature.
He once ascended to the upper floor of a tower with Yǔwén Hù's son Xùn,
which was four or five zhang above the ground.
Looking down from above,
Xùn said:
"This is terrifying."
Hóngdù replied:
"What is there to fear about this?"
Suddenly, he leaped down,
landing on the ground without any injury.
Xùn, amazed by his agility and strength,
found it truly remarkable.
"Shàng Shū"
The resplendent towers that reach the celestial splendor,
The vermilion halls that crown the mountain's grandeur.
"Rhapsody on the Western Capital"
Chóng Quē
Chái Shào's younger brother possessed remarkable physical strength,
light-footed and swift,
leaping upward,
erect as if flying,
covering over ten paces before stopping.
He once wore leather boots and ran up a brick city wall,
reaching the parapet,
without using his hands for support,
and also stepped up a Buddhist temple pillar with his feet,
reaching the eaves,
gripping the rafters to climb further,
traversing hundred-foot towers and pavilions,
completely unobstructed.
Tàizōng found him extraordinary,
saying:
"This man cannot remain in the capital."
He was appointed to an outlying post.
Contemporaries called him the Wall Dragon.
"Qiān Zǎi"
Sòng Lìngwén was
a man of extraordinary strength.
At Chándìng Temple, there was an ox that gored people,
and no one dared approach it,
so they built a pen to confine it.
Lìngwén inquired and learned the reason,
then stripped off his clothes and entered.
The ox raised its horns and charged forward,
but Lìngwén seized both horns and slammed it down,
causing it to collapse instantly,
with its neck bones all broken, and it died.
He also used five fingers to grip the pestle's tip,
writing a forty-character poem on the wall.
At the Imperial Academy, he lifted a lecture hall pillar with one hand,
and pressed a fellow student's clothes under the pillar,
only removing it when a heavy banquet was set.
Lìngwén had three sons:
the eldest, Zhīwèn, was skilled in literature;
the second, Zhīxùn, excelled in calligraphy;
the youngest, Zhītì, possessed great courage.
Later, Zhītì was demoted to Zhūyuān,
and when bandits attacked Huánzhōu,
he was appointed as commander
to lead the counterattack.
He recruited eight strong men,
and Zhītì, standing eight feet tall,
clad in heavy armor,
charged forward shouting:
"Move, and you die!"
Though the bandits numbered seven hundred,
they were all subdued at once,
and utterly defeated.
The emperor
Grand houses and spacious halls,
Lofty towers stretch for a hundred miles.
Xú Gàn's Seven Parables
Zhū Quē
Péng Bótōng was
a man from Héjiān.
He was eight feet tall.
Once, he stood on the edge of the lecture hall steps,
took a pair of shoes and held them under his arm,
then had a strong man pull them from behind.
The shoe soles snapped in half,
yet Bótōng's feet never moved.
When an ox-cart was moving forward,
Bótōng pulled the cart backward by its tail,
reversing it several dozen steps,
then wrenched the cart shafts sideways,
sinking them two feet deep into the ground,
splitting them lengthwise and crosswise.
Once while traveling on the Guābù River,
a strong wind filled the sail,
but Bótōng grabbed the stern cable
and pulled, preventing the boat from advancing.
Indeed,
Bótōng's physical strength was unparalleled.
He once tested his strength in Cháng'ān against the strong men Wèi Hóng, Sòng Lìngwén, and Féng Shīběn.
Bótōng lay firmly on his bed,
challenging the three to take his pillow from him.
The three men exerted their utmost strength,
until their feet were nearly broken,
yet the pillow didn't move.
Spectators climbed over the host's courtyard walls,
causing the buildings to collapse,
and his fame shook the capital.
Once while drinking with guests,
as dusk fell,
he alone carried two couches down the steps,
bringing them to the moonlight in the courtyard,
with wine and food dishes -
not a single thing spilled.
"Records of the Censorate"
Hǎo Pín, the commander of Línjīng Fort, was brave and peerless,
his reputation shook the enemy court.
He served on the frontier for thirty years,
and in every battle where he captured barbarian prisoners,
he would disembowel them and return their corpses,
making the barbarians fear him like a deity.
The Tibetan ruler issued an order to his people:
"Whoever captures Hǎo Pín alive,
will be rewarded with gold equal to his body weight."
Among the Tibetans, when children cried,
they would invoke Pín's name to frighten them.
(From the Old Book of Tang)
Lofty walls connect along ridges and peaks,
adjoining the vermilion cliff,
which stands as a pair.
Rhapsody on the Hall of Numinous Brilliance of Lǔ
Five li northwest of Dàhuī Village in Jìxī County, there was a man named Wāng Jié.
His mother, while avoiding malaria under the Vajra statue at Lùtián Temple west of the village,
took a nap,
and through a spiritual encounter, gave birth to Jié.
Jié possessed divine strength.
He went to Cháng'ān,
and upon arriving at the Dōng Wèi Bridge,
there was a stone lion beside the bridge,
weighing a thousand jīn.
Jié pointed at it and told the people,
saying:
"I can lift this and throw it."
The crowd did not believe him,
so Jié lifted the lion and threw it over ten feet away.
The crowd was astonished,
and later, several dozen people could not move it.
They then bribed Jié to request his help,
and Jié lifted it again and returned it to its original place.
Soon after, he was recommended to join the Imperial Guard,
and was appointed as a general in the Shéncè Army.
Once, in the emperor's presence,
he bent down and carried a stone roller on his back,
placed a square timber two zhàng long on the roller,
and on top of that, set a platform,
on which sat a troupe of musicians from Qiūcí,
who played a piece to its end before descending,
yet Jié showed no sign of strain from the weight.
Emperor Dézōng highly favored and cherished him,
repeatedly bestowing rewards.
Even the strength to uproot mountains or pull oxen
could not surpass his.
(From the "Shèzhōu Tújīng")
Qīng Què
Flowing clouds veil the azure sky,
the bright moon shines upon the crimson palace.
Yán Yánnián's poem "At the Eastern Palace"
The chess player Yáng Hé,
had a massive build.
During the Xiántōng era,
he traveled to the region south of the Yangtze River,
playing chess in a temple.
A monk said:
"I've heard the army officer has great physical strength,
and can wrestle.
I wish to watch by leaning on the railing."
Hé simply took off his loose robe,
and kicked up
the stone used for pounding cloth in the courtyard; with another kick, he caught it with his hand, threw it high, and caught it again as if playing kickball."
From "Records of Wrestling"
Hé,
also written as Tīng.
Yīquē
During the Xiántōng era,
in the Capital's Left Army, there was a man named Zhāng Jìhóng,
who was brave and exceptionally strong.
Once, passing through Shèngyè Ward,
he encountered a deep, overflowing muddy area.
A villager came along driving a donkey loaded with firewood,
blocking the path entirely.
Jìhóng became angry with him,
so he grabbed the donkey by its four legs
and threw it several steps across the water channel.
All who witnessed this were astonished.
Later, while serving in Xiāngzhōu,
he moored at Shěn Mountain at dusk.
An old woman at the inn said to her son:
"The wicked one has returned."
Thereafter, she sighed sorrowfully,
and all appeared fearful.
Jìhóng asked the old woman,
and she explained that her daughter-in-law was disobedient
and so strong and brave that no one could oppose her.
Jìhóng laughed and said:
"I will rid you of her."
At dusk,
the woman returned carrying firewood.
In the backyard, there was a large rock.
Jìhóng sat on it
and summoned her to reprimand her.
The woman said to Jìhóng:
"On such and such a day,
in such a matter, was it really my fault?"
Each time she mentioned an incident,
she placed her hand on Jìhóng's rock
and drew lines with her middle finger, leaving marks as she moved her hand,
which were several inches deep.
Jìhóng broke into a cold sweat, terrified,
and admitted that her reasoning was correct.
He closed the door and pretended to sleep,
waiting for dawn to depart.
Upon his return,
he inquired about her,
and the daughter-in-law had already gone elsewhere.
From "Jùtán Lù".
In ancient times, Great Yu dredged waterways to facilitate the flow of water,
with two mountains facing each other,
appearing like a gate when viewed from afar.
The Yī River passes between them flowing northward,
hence it is called Yīquē (the Yī Gate).
It is the Quēsài mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
where in the 26th year of Duke Zhāo,
Zhào Yǎng sent Nǚ Kuān to guard Quēsài.
Lù Jī stated that Luòyáng had four gates,
and this was one of them.
Both the eastern cliff and western ridge bear carved inscriptions,
with elevated eaves and constructed pavilions on the western side of the peak,
where springs from the sacred cliffs below flow eastward into the Yī River.
Fù Yì's "Rhapsody on the Luò Capital" says:
"Using Lóngmén to spread enlightenment,
opening Yīquē to broaden understanding."
The "Water Classic"
Yáo Jié'ěr,
who served as the Chief Attendant of the Southern Táng chancellor,
possessed extraordinary physical strength.
Later, he became a monk at Kāiyuán Temple on Lú Mountain,
and soon after became a Chan practitioner.
When provoked by his courage and strength,
he would flare up,
intending to strike the monk,
but restrained himself upon reflection.
Still, in front of the monk who invited him to preach,
he would uproot giant trees,
split their intertwined trunks,
and strip off their bark,
repeating this with several trees before stopping.
The monk fled and hid.
Shénquè
Wǔ Xíngdé initially made a living by gathering firewood,
possessing a heroic spirit and robust strength.
He could carry an entire valley's worth of firewood
on his back alone,
earning him the nickname "Wǔ Yīgǔ" (武一谷) among the villagers.
"Supplement to the History of the Five Dynasties"
When Emperor Gāozǔ of the Hàn dynasty went out hunting,
Wǔ Xíngdé was just entering the city to sell firewood.
Noticing his imposing stature
and the fact that the firewood he carried could not be lifted by several attendants,
the emperor admired his strength,
retained him in his retinue,
and he later rose to the rank of military governor.
"Tán Yuàn"
In Nánkāng County, there is Guīyì Mountain,
located seven hundred lǐ from the county seat.
At its foot lies a stone fortress,
several zhàng high,
appearing lofty and precipitous from afar,
with its divine towers soaring into the sky.
Thus, the elders refer to it as the "Divine Towers."
From Dèng Démíng's "Records of Nánkāng."
Qìdān Yēlǜ Déguāng sòng Gāozǔ zhì Lùzhōu,
lín jué,
zhǐ Liú Zhīyuǎn yuē:
"Cǐ dū jūn shèn cāolà,
wú dàgù wù qì zhī."
Shàng
shìsú wèi yǒngměng wéi cāolà.
Guì Pú
Lú Yǐng,
was studious and talented,
with extraordinary physical strength.
Xú Xuàn married Yǐng's sister,
and once received an order from the Later Ruler to compose an essay,
but could not complete it for several days,

Yǐng said:
"I am willing to try to write it."
He then played with a hundred-jun stone ball to test his strength,
after a short while,
drank a cup of wine,
and resumed playing as before,
repeating this several times.
Xuàn, watching him, said:
"He is not my kind of scholar,
what could he possibly accomplish?"
Nevertheless, he decided to test him.
Yǐng said:
"It is already finished."
He then dictated it to a scribe who wrote it down.
Xuàn was greatly astonished,
and subsequently presented Yǐng's essay.
The Later Ruler said to Xuàn:
"The style is vigorous and powerful,
it does not seem to be your work."
Xuàn truthfully replied,
and Yǐng thus became famous.

Twin Towers
There is superior courage,
there is middling courage,
and there is inferior courage.
In the world, there are those who dare to stand upright in their person;
when the former kings had the Way, they dared to practice their intentions.
Above, they do not follow the rulers of chaotic times;
below, they do not conform to the people of chaotic times.
Where benevolence resides,
there is no poverty;
where benevolence is absent,
there is no wealth or honor.
If the world knows them,
they desire to share hardships and joys with the world;
if the world does not know them,
they stand loftily and independently between heaven and earth without fear—
this is superior courage.
Ritually respectful and modest in intent,
they greatly value faithfulness and lightly regard material goods;
they dare to promote and exalt the worthy,
and dare to pull down and depose the unworthy—
this is middling courage.
Lightly regarding their own person and heavily valuing goods,
calmly facing disaster and widely seeking excuses to avoid blame,
not caring about the truth of right and wrong,
with the sole intention of surpassing others—
this is inferior courage.
"Xúnzǐ: On the Evil of Human Nature"
There is the courage of dogs and pigs,
the courage of merchants and thieves,
the courage of petty persons,
and the courage of scholar-gentlemen.
To fight over food and drink,
to be without integrity and shame,
to know neither right nor wrong,
to not avoid death or injury,
to not fear the strength of the multitude,
and to be greedily focused solely on the sight of food and drink—
this is the courage of dogs and pigs.
To act for profit,
to fight over goods and wealth,
to have no polite refusals or deference,
to be resolute and bold in action,
to be fiercely greedy and profit-seeking,
and to be greedily focused solely on the sight of profit—
this is the courage of merchants and thieves.
To take death lightly and be violent—
this is the courage of petty persons.
Where righteousness lies,
not to be swayed by power,
not to consider one's own profit,
even if the whole country is given to him,
he does not change his view,
to value life yet uphold righteousness without yielding—
this is the courage of scholar-gentlemen.

Gōngyí Bó was renowned among the feudal lords for his strength.
Tángxī Gōng spoke of him to King Xuān of Zhōu,
and the king prepared gifts to invite him.
When Gōngyí Bó arrived,
he appeared to be a timid and weak man.
King Xuān, perplexed and doubtful,
asked:
"How does your strength
compare to that of Gōngyí Bó?"
He replied:
"My strength can break the leg of a spring locust
and pierce the wing of an autumn cicada."
The king, changing countenance, said:
"As for my strength,
I can tear apart the hide of a rhinoceros,
drag nine oxen by their tails,
yet still regret its weakness. You break the leg of a spring locust
and pierce the wing of an autumn cicada,
but are famed throughout the land for your strength.
Why is this?"
Gōngyí Bó sighed deeply, stepped back from his mat, and said:
"Excellent indeed
is Your Majesty's question!
I dare to answer truthfully.
My teacher was one Shāngqiū Zǐ,
whose strength was unmatched in the world,
yet even his close relatives did not know of it,
because he never had occasion to use his strength."

Xī Kāngshēng,

Shì Fǎtōng,
joined the monastic order at a young age,
was extremely frail and weak,
and was looked down upon by his peers.
He daily wept before an image of Guānyīn, seeking guidance and inspiration.
After more than a year,
he dreamed that someone gave him three donkeys carrying tendons,
Fǎtōng began to eat one donkey as a meal,
and woke up startled.
From then on, his physical strength became mighty and brave,
secretly lifting large logs and stones,
without considering them heavy.
In the temple, there was a monk named Kān,
who was the strongest in physical strength,
Fǎtōng secretly took his kasaya and placed it under a pillar,
Kān at first did not see it,
and thought it was done by ghosts or spirits.
Fǎtōng laughed and lifted the beam to retrieve it,
Kān was greatly astonished.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Sui heard of this and held him in high regard.
There was a tribute from the Western Regions, one person said:
"There is a very strong man at the north gate,
we tried wrestling and no one could beat him."
The Emperor felt rather ashamed,
and ordered Fǎtōng to be summoned for a wrestling match.
Fǎtōng said:
"If I must know his strength,
just by grasping hands I will know."
So he called that man over.
Fǎtōng let him grab and hold,
that man exerted all his effort to grab and hold,
but Fǎtōng paid it no mind.
When it was Fǎtōng's turn,
he later grabbed and held both of his hands,
squeezing them tightly at once,
blood spurted out,
that man immediately curled up and lay on the ground,
begging for his life,
Fǎtōng then released him,
and thus he was greatly subdued,
the entire court celebrated.
Those in the capital who displayed strength heard of this and visited him,
Fǎtōng would crush beans and wheat by grasping them,
and could pull oxcarts backward,
the strong men of the time called him the Heavenly Strongman.
Next,
Shì Mínggōng resided at Huìshàn Temple in Zhèngzhōu, his strength was like that of a god, unstoppable.
He once disputed over land with Chāohuà Temple,
they gathered over a hundred ruffians to seize the autumn crops of Huìshàn.
Everyone was worried and distressed.
Mínggōng said:
"Do not worry."
He went alone to Chāohuà,
removed their large bell,
blocked its holes,
put six shēng of dried rice inside,
added water to make it edible,
held the bottom with one hand,
and ate with the other hand.
In a short while, he finished it all,
then took a large stone that would require thirty men to move,
Mínggōng alone lifted it like a small clod of earth,
and threw it far to the ground.
When the people of Chāohuà saw this,
they fled in fear all at once.
Another time, while traveling in the mountains, a tiger and a boar were fighting, the boar was gradually losing, Mínggōng
said to the tiger:
"Let it go."
The tiger refused,
so he grabbed its head with one hand,
and its tail with the other,
and threw it into a deep valley.
At Huìshàn, there was a visiting novice monk,
who spoke with a Wú dialect,

with dried bamboo as thick as an arm,
he broke it with two fingers and burned it.
Mínggōng at the time found it strange and surprising,
and also tried to break it with his fingers but could not.
After the novice left,

When the novice came to retrieve his robe,
he could not get it,
saw it under the pillar,
wanted to take it but could not,

and lifted the pillar to retrieve the robe for him.

records that Gāo Biāo, recommended for filial piety and integrity, became a court gentleman,

notes that Yáng Qiú petitioned to abolish the Hóngdū Academy of Literature,

to quell the criticism of the realm."

states that the Eastern Lodge of the Later Hàn
was a repository for books
and also a place for writing,
where literary scholars of the time
were sent to collate texts therein,
hence the role of proofreading officials existed.
"The Táng Hundred Officials Records"
notes that all books and records of the Eastern Capital of Hàn were in the Eastern Lodge,
and many renowned Confucian scholars were appointed to serve there,
compiling the national history,
referred to as the Eastern Lodge writings.

White Tiger
In the eleventh month, on the Rénxū day of the fourth year of the Jiànchū era,

an imperial edict was issued ordering the Grand Master of Ceremonies, generals, court gentlemen, erudites, gentlemen of the palace, and various scholars and Confucians to assemble at the White Tiger Hall,
to discuss the similarities and differences in the Five Classics,
with the Commandant of the Palace Guard Wèi Yīng posing questions according to imperial decree, and the Palace Attendant Chúnyú Gōng submitting memorials,
while the Emperor personally attended to make final decisions,
following the precedents set by Emperor Xuān’s Gānlù Pavilion and Shíqú Pavilion conferences,
resulting in the compilation of the "White Tiger Discussions and Memorials."

Líng Xiāo
When Crown Prince Xuān was departing,
Shí Jìlóng ascended the Lingxiao Observatory in his rear palace to watch him,
and said with a laugh:
"If my family's fathers and sons are like this,
unless the heavens collapse and the earth splits open,
what worries should we have?
We need only embrace our fine sons and grandsons,
and daily enjoy our pleasures."
(Jìn Zǎijì)
During the time of Xiànzōng,
the Rong and Jié rebels caused chaos in China.
An edict was issued to the southern Liáng,
raising three thousand soldiers,
ordering them to proceed to the capital.
When about to depart,
the troops rebelled,
expelling their commander,
and thus gathered together in defiance for over a year.
Xiànzōng was deeply troubled by this.
The Jīngzhào Yǐn, Wēn Zào, requested permission to go with his cavalry.
Upon reaching their territory,
the Liáng people saw him,
stopped him, a mere scholar,
and all congratulated him for there would be no trouble.
Upon his arrival,
he merely announced the edict for peace,
asking no questions.
However, those commanders of Liáng who had committed offenses,
did not set down their weapons,
nor did Wēn warn them.
Another day,
music was arranged in the playing field,
the entire army gathered,
and they were ordered to dine beneath the long corridor.
In front of the sitting banquet,
two long ropes were set up along the steps, to the north and south.
The soldiers were ordered to hang their swords and knives on the ropes before them,
and as they began the meal and wine arrived,
at the sound of a shout,
both ends of the ropes were pulled simultaneously,
raising the swords and knives over three zhàng from the ground.
The soldiers panicked,
unable to employ their bravery,
then the doors were shut and they were executed.
From then on, the southern Liáng people dared not rebel again for generations.
"Wáng Shì's Records of Things Seen and Heard"
Bīn Xiá
Zhāng Jùn's territory gradually stabilized,

Xiè Shí, the Yellow Gate Attendant Gentleman,

Yáoshùn Hall
The hall of a true king,
Mòzǐ describes the halls of Yáo and Shùn
as being three feet high,
which the Confucianists considered lowly.
Assuming this was the case,
in a hall three feet high,
if the calendrical plant grew beneath the steps,
one would need to approach the hall to observe it
in order to know the number of pods.
Now, rising to look at the pods below the hall—
how does this compare to hanging a calendar on the screen behind the throne,
where a glance would immediately reveal it?

Qīng Huī
Xiàowén returned to Luòyáng from the southern campaign,
and received the nobles and attendants in the Qīnghuī Hall.
The emperor said:
"Since this hall was completed,
we have not yet conducted the rituals of feasting and merriment with the nobles.
Today, I wish to ascend everywhere without reservation,
and to enter the depths without hesitation,
thereby spreading culture,
and cleansing the pond of troubles."
Next, in the Níngxián Hall,
the emperor said:
"This hall embodies the meaning of peaceful dwelling,
one must not indulge in luxury and forget frugality,
become complacent and forget danger.
Therefore, behind the hall is the thatched cottage."
He said to Lǐ Chōng:
"This eastern area is called Bùyuán Wǔ,
the western area is called Yóukǎi Wǔ.
Though there is no Yáo or Shùn in this seat,
you must not feel ashamed before Yuánkǎi!"
Chōng replied,
"I have encountered a ruler like Tāng Yáo,
and dare not refuse the praise of Yuánkǎi."
Gāozǔ said,
"As the light fades,
I, being of the same lineage, have the duty to honor our ancestors.
When you all depart,
how can you not silently acknowledge their virtues?"
He then ordered Huángménláng Cuī Guāngyè, Guō Yǎ, Xíng Luán, Cuī Lín, and others to compose poems expressing their aspirations.
When the officials excused themselves,
Gāozǔ said,
"During the night, we honor the ancestral lineage,
you may return,
I will join the princes and relatives
to complete this night of drinking."

also records an edict summoning the sons of the four temples,

In the

Miáocí
To the south of Nàilín stands a stone stele,
erected by Emperor Míng of the Wèi dynasty.
It is inscribed as the "Miáocí Stele",
and Emperor Gāozǔ built the Miáocí Hall north of the stele.
During the Yǒng'ān era,
when Emperor Zhuāng practiced mounted archery in the Huálín Garden,
all officials came to read the stele
and suspected the character "miáo" was an error.
Lǐ Tóngguǐ, Erudite of the National University, said:
"Emperor Míng of Wèi, a man of outstanding talent,
is acclaimed by the world as one of the Three Ancestors,
with Gōnggàn and others as his assistants.
However, without knowing the original intent,
one cannot claim it to be an error."
Yáng Xuànzhī, then serving as a Court Gentleman,
requested to explain it immediately, saying:
"Because it was thatched with hào grass,
it was called miáocí.
How could this be an error?"
All present praised this,
believing he had grasped its true meaning.
From "Luòyáng Qiélán Jì".
The "Shuǐ Jīng" states:
"In front of the Máocí Hall of Emperor Wén of Wèi, there is a Máocí Stele,
erected during the Huángchū era."
Note:
Xuànzhī was a man of Wèi
who personally explained the meaning of miáocí.
Dàoyuán's claim that it was erected during Huángchū
is incorrect.
The "Yù Hǎi" followed this,
recording it between the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
which is also an error.
Yí Xián
In the sixth year of the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng dynasty, on the yǐhài day of the ninth month,
the Yuèwǔ Hall was renamed Déyáng Hall,
and the Tīngsòng Hall was renamed Yíxián Hall.
As recorded in the Annals.
Waterside Pavilion
Qí Wén Xiāng built mountain ponds east of Yè,
and the dazzled populace frequented them for sightseeing.
Xiào Yú then constructed a water hall and dragon boats at his residence,
planting banners and halberds on the boats.
He frequently gathered his younger brothers,
holding banquets and archery for amusement.
When Wǔ Chéng visited his residence,
he was delighted at the sight,
thus greatly promoting the development of imperial garden entertainments.
Thereupon, nobles and commoners alike admired such opulence,
and construction flourished everywhere.
(From "The Northern Qí")
Moving the Hall

"The Duke built Xī Hall,
where flowing water connects in all directions.
Shallow areas have cattails and lotuses,
deep areas have reeds and rushes.
The Duke hosts guests with feasts,
the drums resound impressively.

guests and officers are drunk and full.

on the banks gather birds.

chopping and polishing
Zhào Wénzǐ was building a house,

Zhāng Lǎo saw it in the evening,
and said:

hewing its rafters and polishing them,

for officials, the ends are prepared.

following their rank is ritual propriety.
Now you, being noble, forget appropriateness;
being wealthy, forget ritual propriety;

High and Dry
Initially, Duke Jǐng wanted to change Yànzǐ's residence,
saying:
"Your residence is near the market,
damp, cramped, noisy, and dusty,
unfit to live in;
please allow me to move you to a higher and drier place."
Yànzǐ declined, saying:
"Your servant's ancestors dwelt here,
and I am unworthy to succeed them;
to me, this is already extravagant.

I can obtain what I need morning and night—this is the common man's advantage.

Later, when Yànzǐ went to Jìn, the Duke
had his residence altered,
and it was completed by the time he returned.
After expressing gratitude, he had it demolished
and restored the neighbors' houses to their original state,
then made the residents return.
He also cited a proverb:
"It is not the house that should be divined about,
but the neighbors.
My ancestors divined about the neighbors first.
To go against the divination is inauspicious;
a nobleman does not court such misfortune,
nor does a commoner act against propriety.
Not courting misfortune
is an ancient rule.
How dare I violate it?"
In the end, he restored his old residence.

Dōng Yì
Duke Āi asked Confucius, saying:
"I have heard that expanding one's residence eastward is inauspicious.
Is this truly so?"
Confucius replied:
"There are five types of inauspiciousness,
and expanding eastward is not among them.
To harm others to benefit oneself
is inauspicious for the individual;
to neglect the elderly and favor only the young
is inauspicious for the family;
to choose the unworthy over the virtuous for office
is inauspicious for the state;
when the elderly do not teach,
and the young do not learn,
it is inauspicious for customs;
when sages remain hidden,
and fools seize power,
it is inauspicious for the world.
There are five types of inauspiciousness,
and expanding eastward is not among them."
*Family Sayings*
Westward Expansion
Duke Āi wished to expand his residence westward,
but the court historian opposed it,
believing that expanding westward would bring misfortune.
Duke Āi's countenance changed and he grew angry;
his attendants repeatedly advised him, but he would not listen.
So he asked his tutor Zǎi Zhé Jū, saying:
"I wish to expand my residence, but the historian considers it inauspicious.
What is your opinion?"
Zǎi Zhé Jū replied:
"There are three inauspicious things in the world,
and expanding a residence westward is not among them."
Duke Āi was greatly pleased and delighted.
After a moment, he asked again:
"What are the three inauspicious things?"
The reply was:
"Not practicing ritual and righteousness
is the first inauspicious thing.
Having insatiable desires
is the second inauspicious thing;
not heeding strong remonstrance
is the third inauspicious thing."
Duke Āi fell silent and reflected deeply,
then with indignation turned inward,
and thus did not expand his residence westward.
