Observing the Aura
West of Chángliújiě were the residences of Liáng Cáoyítóng Jǐngzōng, Liǔ Yítóng Qìngyuǎn, and Wéi Yítóng Ruì,
all adjacent to the western gate of the outer city wall.
When Wéi Ruì was young,
a man from Nányáng named Cài Láng, skilled in reading auras,
predicted that Ruì's residence would produce one of the Three Excellencies,
and the provincial governor would achieve unparalleled nobility.
At that time, Ruì's home had ten thatched huts,
while Láng's residence was south of the city,
entirely tiled-roofed.
He asked to exchange homes with Ruì,
but Ruì hesitated and refused.
Ruì's two elder brothers, Wéi Chǎn and Wéi Zuǎn, held official posts
and enjoyed higher status and reputation than Ruì.
The locals believed these brothers would attain high ministerial positions.
Later, Chǎn and Zuǎn died successively,
while Ruì rose to prominence under imperial favor,
fulfilling the residence's prophecy.
When Emperor Jiǎnwén summoned him with an official missive,
Ruì arrived and wandered [the grounds],
remarking: "The prediction about this residence's aura
has indeed proven true."
From "Xiāng Miǎn Jì"
Inn
Xú Miǎn's Admonition to His Son says:
"My residence at Qīngmíng Gate,
with the Xuānwǔ Temple built on its west side,
is no longer perfectly square,
so I consider it merely a temporary lodging.
Why would it need to be magnificent?
I often wonder at contemporaries
who call it my house.
From ancient times to the present,
the wealthy and noble have followed one after another,
but when they suddenly die,
whose house will it certainly become?"
Liáng Shū
Shared Lodgings
Yáng Gù, styled Jìng'ān,
in the late years of Emperor Shìzōng of the Northern Wèi, when Commandant Wáng Xiǎn had completed building his mansion,
he gathered his subordinates for a feast.
Flushed with wine, he asked Yáng Gù:
"How is this mansion?"
Yáng Gù replied:
"Yàn Yīng's humble abode,
is still praised to this day.
While grand houses invite disaster,
as recorded in the Zhōu Yì.
This is but a temporary lodging;
only virtue can bring fulfillment to one's wishes.
May you strive for it, sir."
Wáng Xiǎn fell silent.
From the Běi Shǐ
Tall and strong
Wáng Chūn, courtesy name Yuánshòu,
was the son of Ruì.
He constructed a grand hall at his residence,
extremely lofty and imposing.
People at the time suddenly remarked:
"This is the residence of the Prince of Tàiyuán,
how could it be Wáng Chūn of Tàiyuán?"
Previously, while serving as the governor of his commandery,
he was commonly known as Wáng of Tàiyuán.
Soon after, Ěrzhū Róng occupied Chūn's
residence, and Róng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Tàiyuán.
From "The Biographies of Favored Officials in the Book of Wèi"
Guǎng Yíng
Liǔ Màn,
while Yǔwén Hù was in power, he extensively built mansions and residences.
He once summoned Màn to his residence to consult on governmental affairs.
Màn looked up at the hall,
and slowly sighed, saying:
"Indulging in wine and music,
erecting lofty buildings with carved walls—
if even one of these is present,
none escape downfall."
Hù was displeased,
but those with insight considered it wise counsel.
(History of the Northern Dynasties)
Haunted House
In Cháng'ān's Dàixián Ward,
there stood the residence of Suí Dynasty General-in-Chief Shǐ Wànsuì.
The house was initially haunted by supernatural phenomena,
where occupants would invariably die.
Wànsuì, disbelieving the tales,
decided to reside there himself.
One night, he encountered a figure dressed in majestic attire,
who approached Wànsuì.
When Wànsuì inquired about his origin,
the figure replied:
"I am Fán Kuāi, a Hàn Dynasty general.
My tomb lies near your restroom,
and I constantly suffer from the filth and foulness.
If you would kindly relocate it elsewhere,
I shall richly repay you."
Wànsuì agreed,
then questioned why living people had been killed.
The spirit answered:
"They died of their own fear,
not by my hand."
After unearthing the coffin and remains,
Wànsuì had them reburied.
The spirit returned another night to express gratitude, saying:
"You shall become a general,
and I will surely aid you."
Later, when Wànsuì served as a Suí general,
he often felt ghostly assistance against enemies,
achieving great victories in every battle.
From "Records of the Two Capitals."
Pleasant
Dōngjīng Yírén Ward,
half of which was originally the residence of Suí Dynasty Prince Qí Yáng Huì,
Emperor Yáng's beloved son.
Initially intending to take the entire ward for the residence,
the Emperor asked Yǔwén Kǎi:
"What is the name of this ward?"
Kǎi replied the ward was called Yírén (Suitable for People),
The Emperor said:
"Since it's named Suitable for People,
how can there be no people?
Let half be used for the Prince's residence."
End
Kūn Liǔ
In the eastern corner of Yánshòu Ward,
was the residence of the imperial son-in-law Péi Xùn.
By the end of Gāozǔ's reign, Péi Xíngjiǎn lived there.
Before Xíngjiǎn's time,
those who dwelt there invariably died.
After Xíngjiǎn chose to reside there,
a mad monk burst in,
completely shaved the large willow tree in the courtyard,
from which a pig ran out,
went straight into the northern neighbor's house,
and within a few days, they all died suddenly.
Thereafter, this residence became peaceful.

Declining the Mansion

During the Wǔdé era, the former residence of Suí Yángdì when he was a vassal king was bestowed to Xiāo Yǔ, the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, who made its western part into a garden.
Later, Yǔ's son Ruì married Princess Xiāngchéng,
and an imperial edict ordered the construction of a separate residence for the princess.
The princess declined, arguing that it would be improper for mother-in-law and daughter-in-law to live apart, contrary to ritual.
She thus firmly insisted on her request,
and the garden land was then used for the princess's residence.
She also declined the princess's ceremonial halberds,
not wishing to have a separate gate,
so they were instead placed together at the gate of Yǔ's courtyard.
From "Records of Cháng'ān"
Cease to be useful
Wèi Zhēng,
a high-ranking official of the court,
lived in a humble and crude house.
Tàizōng wished to build a residence for him,
but he modestly declined the offer.
When Zhēng fell ill and was bedridden,
Tàizōng was planning to construct a small hall,
so he halted the project and used the materials
to build a main hall for Zhēng instead,
which was completed in just five days.
During the Kāiyuán era, this hall still stood,
but due to the family's carelessness,
it was accidentally set ablaze and burned down.
His descendants mourned for three days,
and court officials all came to offer condolences.
"Records of Fēng's Observations"
Later, his descendant Wèi Mó served as chancellor under Emperor Xuānzōng
and resided in the old family estate.
"Chronicles of Cháng'ān"
Avoiding a Bad Reputation
In the southwest corner of the Mingjiào Fāng neighborhood near Lóngxīng Temple,
stood the residence of Kāifǔ Sòng Jǐng.
To the east of the southern gate,
was the home of Guózǐ Sīyè Cuī Róng.
When Sòng Jǐng constructed his residence,
he aligned all structures directly east-west facing each other,
avoiding any diagonal or curved layouts,
to steer clear of unfavorable reputations.
Cuī Róng, having received an imperial decree to compose a eulogy,
applied such intense concentration and effort
that upon returning from duty and passing his gate on horseback,
he unexpectedly completed the text but passed away immediately after.
"Records of the Two Capitals"
Bǎi Liáng
Zǒng Chǔkè built a newly completed residence,
all made of fragrant cedar for the beams,
using aloeswood mixed with red powder to plaster the walls,
which, when opened, emitted a flourishing fragrance,
polished patterned stones were used for the steps,
paved all the way to the ground,
whenever a guest wearing boots arrived,
they would stumble and fall upon walking,
Zǒng Chǔkè was arrested by Prince Tuī of Chāng and found to have embezzled over ten thousand strings of cash,
he and his brothers were exiled,
Princess Tàipíng went to see his residence,
and sighed, saying:
"Looking at his living and sitting places,
we have lived in vain."
After a year of wandering and near death,
he was recalled to serve as Vice Minister of the Phoenix Pavilion,
during the Jǐnglóng era, he became Zhongshu Ling,
when the Wěi clan fell,
he was executed.
"Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Chónglì
After the reign of Wǔ Zétiān,
the mansions of princes, marquises, and imperial consorts in the capital
grew increasingly magnificent and luxurious day by day.
By the Tiānbǎo era,
Censor-in-Chief Wáng Hóng was convicted and ordered to commit suicide.
When officials inventoried his mansion in the Tàipíng ward,
they could not complete the task even after several days.
Within the estate stood a self-raining pavilion,
where water cascaded from the eaves in all directions.
Staying there during summer,
one felt the crisp coolness of late autumn.
There was also a well railing adorned with precious gems,
whose value was beyond estimation,
and other objects of comparable worth.
"Féng Shì's Account of Observations"
Residential Qi
Fútú Hóng and Zhāng Yuè had a residence in the southeast of Yǒnglè, the first of its kind,
where a resident of the alley warned them:
"The northwest corner of this house is the king's land,
be careful not to dig earth there."
After a month,
Hóng arrived and examined it closely,
saying to Lord Yān (Zhāng Yuè):
"The aura of this residence has suddenly become extremely desolate;
I fear someone must have dug earth at the northwest corner."
Lord Yān and Hóng went together to the northwest corner of the residence,
and indeed found several pits where earth had been dug,
each over a zhàng deep.
Hóng was greatly alarmed and said:
"A disaster!
Your lordship will enjoy wealth and honor alone,
but after twenty years,
none of your sons will live out their natural lifespans."
Lord Yān, terrified, asked:
"Can we fill them in?"
Hóng replied:
"Foreign soil has no vitality;
it does not connect with the earth's veins.
Even if we fill the pits now,
it is like a person with sores and wounds;
even if we patch them with other flesh,
it will ultimately be of no benefit."
Lord Yān's sons, Zhāng Jūn and Zhāng Jì,
were both appointed by Ān Lùshān,
and after the recovery of the capital, Jūn was ordered to commit suicide,
while Jì was exiled for life.
(From "Chángshì Yán Zhǐ")
Seizing the Residence
The elder sister of the Noble Consort, the Lady of Guó, enjoyed favor that overwhelmed the age for a time.
She once built a mansion,
and the magnificence of its beams and structure
was unmatched in the world.
The site was originally the old residence of Wéi Sìlì.
At noon, the sons of the Wéi family were resting in the hall and side rooms
when suddenly they saw a woman,
dressed in a yellow draped gown,
descend from a palanquin,
with several tens of maidservants in attendance.
She spoke and laughed with composure
and said to the sons of the Wéi family:
"I have heard this residence is for sale;
what is the price?"
The Wéi family members descended the steps and replied:
"This is our ancestors' old dwelling;
we cannot bear to part with it."
Before the words were finished,
hundreds of workmen
ascended the two wings of the house
and began digging up its tiles and timbers.
The sons of the Wéi family, unable to stop them,
then led their household servants, carrying their lutes and books,
and abandoned them in the main road, sighing to themselves:
"Incapable and without merit,
we are seized by the powerful;
is the warning of the ancients to be witnessed today?"
They were given over ten mǔ of vacant land by the Wéi family,
but gained nothing else.
"Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng"
Supremely Sublime
In the southwest corner of Chóngrén Ward,
stood the residence of Princess Chángníng.
Having received imperial favor and prosperity,
it was further adorned with carvings and decorations,
featuring vermilion towers and elegant pavilions
that were considered the finest of the time.
There was also a separate courtyard with hills and ponds,
where valleys provided shade and seclusion,
appearing as if formed by nature.
Emperor Zhōngzōng and Empress Wéi visited here frequently,
often lingering for entire days,
composing poetry and holding drinking feasts.
Shàngguān Zhǎoróng wielded the brush,
inscribing the poems on the pillars of the pavilion.
After the Wéi clan's downfall,
the princess accompanied her husband to a provincial post.
Initially planning to sell the timber and stones,
valued at twenty million coins,
the ingenious hills and ponds were beyond valuation.
It was then petitioned to become a Daoist temple,
where poets and renowned scholars flocked to visit and admire.
From "Records of the Two Capitals"
Yù zhǎn
The monk Hóng said:
The southeast of Yǒngníng Ward in Cháng'ān is the golden cup land,
and west of Ānyì Ward is the jade cup land.
Later, Yǒngníng became the land of Grand Tutor Wáng È,
Ānyì became the land of Mǎ Suì, Duke of Běipíng,
and later both Wáng and Mǎ's properties were confiscated by the government.
Wáng's residence was repeatedly bestowed upon others,
including Hán Lìnghóng, Shǐ Xiànchéng, Lǐ Zàiyì, and others,
which is what is meant by the golden cup breaking and being completed.
Mǎ Suì's residence became the Garden of Sincere Offering,
which is what is meant by the jade cup breaking and remaining incomplete.
From "Records of Anecdotes":
Regarding Lǐ Jífǔ's residence,
Master Hóng said its topography was a jade cup,
and Niú Sēngrú's residence was a golden cup,
stating that once a jade cup breaks, it cannot be restored to wholeness,
while a golden cup, even if severely damaged, can be repaired.
Niú Sēngrú's residence was in Xīnchāng Ward,
originally the residence of Kāng, the Minister of Works during the Tiānbǎo era,
who himself discerned the topography,
believing that the land would produce a chancellor.
Whenever a chancellor was appointed,
he would crane his neck to watch,
and the residence eventually came into Niú Sēngrú's possession.
Lǐ Jífǔ's residence, by the time of Lǐ Déyù's demotion,
had seen his family extinguished.
From "Miscellaneous Accounts of the Lú Family":
Wànhuāgǔ quotes "Records of Anecdotes" as mistakenly attributing this to monk Yīxíng,
and also states that Sāng Dàomào was known as the appraiser of the residences of Cháng'ān's nobility,
giving them names like golden cup and jade cup.
Wood Demon
In the seventh month of the fourteenth year of the Dàlì era,
the residences of Yuán Zǎi, Mǎ Lín, and Liú Zhōngyì were demolished.
Since the Tiānbǎo era,
the halls and chambers in the capital had already been extremely grand and magnificent,
yet residential mansions had not excessively exceeded regulations.
However, the temple of Duke Wèiguó Lǐ Jìng had already been taken over by the favorite concubine Yáng shì.
After the two rebels Ān and Shǐ,
high-ranking officials and veteran generals
competed in constructing magnificent buildings,
without any limits,
only stopping when their resources were exhausted.
People called it the "wooden demon."
Among them, Mǎ Lín's hall was particularly extravagant,
costing two hundred thousand strings of cash,
with his other rooms being similarly expensive.
When Mǎ Lín died in the army,
his coffin was returned to the capital,
and both scholars and commoners wished to view it.
They borrowed names from former subordinates to present their name cards,
with hundreds of people gathering for the condolence visit.
Therefore, an order was issued to dismantle and demolish it,
and from then on, all towers and pavilions in the capital that exceeded regulations were destroyed.
"Dézōng Veritable Records":
During Sùzōng's reign, the mansions in the capital
were repeatedly damaged and destroyed.
When Dàizōng ascended the throne,
chief ministers and powerful court officials competed in building residences,
causing considerable trouble and harm.
Commentators considered it the "demon of construction,"
and before long,
they all changed owners.
"Féng Shì's Record of Hearsay and Observations"
Construction
In Guō Zǐyí's residence, across its various courtyards,
carriages and horses came and went,
with servants and guests passing through the main gate,
yet none acquainted with one another.
The poet Liáng Huáng once composed a verse:
"From the high hall, one gazes afar;
in the vast estate, carriages freely roam."
This saying aptly describes it.
Once, as Marshal Guō was about to depart,
he saw the wall builders and said to them:
"Build this wall well,
ensure it stands firm."
A builder set down his hammer and replied:
"Over the decades,
the walls of eminent officials in the capital,
all were built by me.
I've only seen people come and go,
but the walls remain to this day."
Hearing this, Marshal Guō was deeply moved with sorrow,
and thus went to report the matter to the emperor,
firmly requesting retirement due to old age.
From "Fēngshì Jiànwén Lù"
Selling Property
Xiāo Fù, courtesy name Lǚchū,
served as the Crown Prince's Attendant.
During the Guangdé era, successive years of poor harvests
caused grain prices to soar.
His family being poor, he intended to sell his secondary estate at Zhāoyìng.
At that time, the chancellor Wáng Jìn,
hearing of the beauty of its woods and springs,
desired it in his heart,
and sent his younger brother Wáng Hóng to entice him, saying:
"With your talent,
you certainly deserve to hold a high position.
If you offer the estate to my elder brother,
you will be appointed to an important post."
Fù replied:
"I am selling the old estate due to my family's poverty,
intending to use the proceeds to aid my widowed mother and young children.
Were I to exchange it for a prestigious position for myself,
while leaving my family to suffer cold and hunger,
that would not be the intention of a humble man."
Jìn resented him for this,
and had Fù dismissed from office.
Fù remained in obscurity for several years,
yet faced it with composure. From the Old Book of Táng.
Frugal Virtue
Hán Huàng was by nature frugal and upheld integrity,
his residence was humble and crude,
barely able to shelter him from wind and rain.
His younger brother Hán Yǒng once added corridors and rooms to their hometown house,
but when Huàng returned from the Jiangnán region,
he immediately ordered them to be demolished,
saying:
"Our late father dwelt here,
and we uphold his legacy,
constantly fearing to lose what we possess.
If it collapses, we should merely repair it—
how dare we alter or rebuild it and thereby harm the virtue of frugality?"
(Old Book of Táng)
The Path of Conduct
Bái Lètiān acquired Yáng Píng's residence,
with its bamboo, trees, pond, and pavilions,
possessing the charm of forested springs,
thus composing "The Poolside Essay" which states:
"Within the capital's environs,
the finest landscapes with earth and timber lie in the southeast,
and the finest spot in the southeast is Lǚdào Lane.
This residence has a pond,
where boats can float upon the water.
Whenever Lètiān entertained guests,
he would surround the boat with hundreds of oil bags,
sinking them into the water,
following the boat's movement.
When one item was depleted, those on either side would fetch another,
storing feasts and platters beneath the water's surface."
From "Sòng Jǐngwén's Chicken Feet" and "Records of Exhaustive Years"
Not catering to the powerful and noble
Yáng Sǔn resided at Xīnchāng Lane,
his home adjacent to the estate of Lù Yán.
At the time, Yán was serving as chancellor
and wished to acquire Sǔn's stable to expand his own residence.
More than ten family members of Sǔn who held official posts deliberated, saying:
"The rise and fall of our family
depends on the favor or displeasure of the powerful—we cannot refuse."
Sǔn responded:
"Every inch of this land is the legacy of our ancestors;
it does not belong to us.
How can we yield it to a powerful minister?
Poverty and success are matters of fate."
In the end, he did not concede.
From the Old Book of Táng
The dwelling was somber and oppressive.
Yáng Xíngmì once ascended the city wall in Chǔzhōu,
and saw Wáng Màozhāng's residential estate,
saying:
"The empire is not yet pacified,
yet Màozhāng lives in such lavish comfort,
would he be willing to sacrifice himself for me?"
Màozhāng immediately had it demolished and reduced.
The emperor
The residence weeps.
Gù Quánwǔ searched extensively for fine nanmu wood in Yuèzhōng to build a residence,
which was very grand and imposing.
Upon completion of the work,
the beams and pillars all seeped water,
the doors and windows were soaked and damp,
so he ultimately could not move in.
He died without ever occupying this house,
and people called it "the weeping residence."
From "Bǎoguāng Lù"
encroach and occupy
Yáng Bīn served in Shǔ to a high official position,
followed Wáng Yǎn upon his return,
and later in the Later Táng dynasty retired due to old age,
returning to Cháng'ān.
His former residences were mostly encroached upon by neighbors,
and his children intended to go to the authorities to complain about the matter.
Bīn wrote on the back of the petition:
"The neighbors encroach on me, I yield to them;
after all, one must think back to the time when I had nothing.
Try ascending the foundation of the Hányuán Palace and gaze upon the autumn wind—
the withered grass is luxuriantly overgrown."
His children dared not speak of it again.
From "Tán Yuàn"
Magnificent
Mèng Zhīxiáng arrived in Shǔ,
at that time Prince Wèi Jìjí had just eliminated Wáng Yǎn's regime,
and was quartered in the official residence.
Zhīxiáng therefore took up lodging in the mansion of Xú Yáncóng—Yáncóng was Yǎn's maternal uncle.
Yǎn had once visited his mansion,
admired its splendor,
and playfully wrote the character "Mèng" on the wall to tease him,
for in Shǔ, "Mèng" was considered incompetent.
Yáncóng had it covered with red gauze.
Upon seeing it, Zhīxiáng laughed and said:
"This reckless and arrogant tyrant
actually foresaw that I would succeed him,
knowing I would reside here!"
From "Shǔ Táowù"
Three Prohibitions
During the reign of Emperor Shénzōng of the Sòng Dynasty,
Prime Minister Chén Shēngzhī built a mansion in Rùnzhōu,
which was extremely magnificent,
stretching for hundreds of paces.
When the mansion was completed,
Chén Shēngzhī was already severely ill,
and only managed to ride in a sedan chair to ascend the west tower once.
People called it the "Three Cannots":
cannot live in it,
cannot sell it,
cannot repair it.
"Bǐ Tán"
Two beams
During the reign of Emperor Lǐzōng,
Prime Minister Cuī Yǔzhī returned to Shǔ,
and built a magnificent mansion.
A wealthy merchant surnamed Lǐ in the neighborhood followed suit,
using the same craftsmen and design as Cuī's residence.
When construction was completed,
Cuī went to see it,
and upon returning summoned the craftsman to ask:
"The house you built for him is fine,
but it lacks two beams."
The craftsman replied:
"This exactly follows the design of Your Excellency's residence."
Cuī said:
"One beam represents lack of careful consideration,
the other beam represents lack of thoughtful deliberation."
This became material for jokes at the time.
From "Yíjiān Xùzhì"
Four Matters
Lù Qióngzhī, Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates,
was the brother of the Empress Dowager
and the grandson of Qìngzhī.
He lived next to Wáng Sēngdá,
and dressed in formal attire to pay a visit to Sēngdá.
Sēngdá refused to speak with him,
saying:
"In the past, among my disciples, there was a prominent Lù Qìngzhī,
what relation is he to you?"
Subsequently, Sēngdá burned the bed where Qióngzhī had been sitting.
The Empress Dowager was furious
and tearfully complained to Emperor Xiàowǔ.
The Emperor said:
"Qióngzhī is young,
and had no reason to visit Wáng Sēngdá.
Being insulted was only fitting."
End
When a person has a residence,
the eastern chamber invites worthiness,
the southern window draws in light,
the northern casement beckons the wind,
and the western lattice reflects the moon.
The master sits properly in the central room,
gathering the benefits of these four aspects.
Xiāo Chēn's refutation of the Treatise on the Annihilation of the Soul
Residence should be suitable
Any residence with the east lower and the west higher,
brings wealth, nobility, and heroic prowess.
If the front is high and the back low,
it completely lacks access or means.
When the back is high and the front low,
there will be plenty of cattle and horses.
All residential land should be level and even,
called Liáng land,
with the back high and the front low,
called Jìn land,
living in either is auspicious;
if the south is high and the north low,
called Lǔ soil,
living there brings wealth and nobility,
and will produce virtuous people;
if the front is high and the back low,
called Chǔ soil,
living there is inauspicious,
if all four sides are high and the center low,
called Wèi soil,
living there leads to initial wealth followed by poverty.
"The Classic of Dwellings"
A Home Has No Inherent Good or Bad Fortune
If a mansion fit for the Three Excellencies is built,
and a foolish man is appointed to live in it,
it is certain that he will not become one of the Three Excellencies.
Now, the impossibility of seeking longevity or premature death
is even greater than that of seeking nobility or baseness.
Thus, to select a palace meant to last a hundred years and hope for the longevity of a child who dies young,
or to dwell in an isolated place in order to hasten the premature death of one like Péng Zǔ,
is surely hopeless.
It follows, then, that there truly is no such mansion
—this is the natural course of life and destiny,
which cannot be sought.
Jī Kāng discusses
Stop and gather
A pavilion (tíng),
is for stopping (tíng),
a place where people gather and stop.
From the "Shìmíng"
Watching from the Outpost
The Spring and Autumn Annals and Discourses of the States mention watch stations,
which are what we now call pavilions,
places where the people find stability.
Pavilions have towers,
derived from the character for high with omission,
and pronounced with the dīng sound.
The Han dynasty followed the Qin,
generally establishing one pavilion every ten lǐ.
A pavilion
means to detain.
In current language, there is the phrase "pavilion awaiting cover,"
referring to a lodging where travelers eat and stay.
A pavilion also signifies fairness;
when the people have disputes,
officials detain them to handle the matter,
ensuring justice is not lost.
Fēngsú Tōng
Wànsuì
In the first year of the Yuánfēng era, Emperor Wǔ visited Gōushì,
ascended Tàishì Mountain,
and heard the mountain shout "Long live" three times,
so he erected the Longevity Pavilion.
Records of the Hàn Dynasty
states: east of Qǔchéng and Qíchéng lies the Longevity River,

Cài temporarily got up,

Chǔ Gōng, having been promoted from magistrate of Zhāng'ān to recorder and army consultant of the Grand Commandant,

so not many people recognized him.
When Chǔ Gōng traveled east,
he rode on a merchant ship,
and several former subordinates escorted him to stay at the Qiántáng post station.
At that time, Shěn Chōng of Wúxīng was the county magistrate,
and happened to be seeing off guests across the Zhè River.
As the guests left the station,
the station officer drove Chǔ Gōng to move under the ox shed.
When the tide came in,
Magistrate Shěn rose
and anxiously asked, "Who is that in the ox shed?"
The officer replied:
"Yesterday a coarse fellow came to lodge at the station,
and because there were noble guests,
we temporarily moved him."
The magistrate, flushed with wine,
then called out to the coarse fellow from a distance,
asking if he wanted to eat some cakes,
what his surname was,
and if he could converse with him.
Chǔ thereupon raised his hand and replied:
"I am Chǔ Jìyě from Hénán.
Far and wide, I have long known of your esteemed name."
The magistrate was then greatly alarmed,
not daring to move Chǔ Gōng,
so he prepared a name card under the ox shed to visit Chǔ Gōng,
further had animals slaughtered to prepare a feast,
set it before Chǔ Gōng,
and flogged the station officer,
wishing to atone for his shame.
Chǔ Gōng drank and feasted with him,
his words and expression unchanged,
appearing as if unaware of the incident.
The magistrate escorted Chǔ Gōng to the boundary.

Rest, rest
Sīkōng Tú originally resided in Guān Valley on Mount Zhōngtiáo,
where he had ancestral farmland,
so he withdrew into seclusion and never left,
building pavilions, observatories, and simple dwellings.
He displayed portraits of all the exemplary scholars and literary figures of the Tang dynasty's flourishing period,
naming the pavilion "Xiūxiū" (Restful Rest),
and composed an essay to express his intent,
saying: "Xiū means 'beautiful.'
Having ceased [from official life], one attains beauty.
Considering my capabilities,
first, I deserve to retire because I advanced by flattering the powerful;
second, I deserve to retire because I am old and hard of hearing;
third, I deserve to retire because I am, on the contrary, immature in some ways,
lazy in others,
and generally obstinate.
These three traits render me unfit for the times,
thus I further deserve to retire."
Consequently, he styled himself "The Lay Buddhist Who Endures Humiliation."

Folding
During the reign of Emperor Lǐzōng of the Sòng dynasty, the imperial gardens gradually fell into disrepair.
While hosting a banquet by the lotus pond,
they had to set up canopies and screens under the scorching sun.
Dǒng Sòngchén silently understood the emperor's intention,
and within days, a pavilion was completed beside the pond.
At the next banquet,
the emperor was greatly pleased.
Not long after,
during winter while admiring plum blossoms in the garden,
another pavilion appeared.
The emperor appeared displeased,
and instructed Sòngchén, saying:
"Previously, when you built the lotus pavilion,
I didn't make an issue of it.
But now there's this again—
within half a year,
you've burdened the people and mobilized the masses like this."
Sòngchén replied:
"This plum pavilion is actually the previous lotus pavilion."
The emperor asked how this could be,
to which he responded:
"This is a collapsible and foldable pavilion."
The emperor praised him even more.

Xiūwén

In the ninth year, it was renamed to the Hóngwén Institute.
In the first year of the Shénlóng era, it was renamed to the Zhāowén Institute
to avoid the name of Emperor Xiàojìng.
"Records of Officials"
Literature
In the fourth year of Taizong's reign, he pacified the Eastern Xia,
and with peace throughout the land,
he devoted himself wholeheartedly to classical texts,
establishing a Literary Institute at the Prince of Qin's residence,
widely recruiting scholars of literature,
appointing eighteen individuals including his subordinate Dù Rúhuì as academicians.
"Old Biographies of Confucian Scholars"
The emperor, noting that Prince Wèi Lǐ Tài was fond of scholars
and skilled in writing,
decreed the establishment of a Literary Institute at his residence,
allowing him to personally recruit academicians.

Chóngxián
In the thirteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era, the Chóngxián Academy was established.
In the second year of the Shàngyuán era, to avoid the crown prince's name,
it was renamed the Chóngwén Academy.
"Treatise on Officials"
Lǐ Shàn served as a direct academician of the Chóngxián Academy.

Guǎngwén
Emperor Xuánzōng admired Zhèng Chù's talent,
and wanting to place him nearby without assigning specific duties,
established the Guǎngwén College instead,
appointing Chù as an Erudite.
Upon receiving the appointment,
Chù did not know where the Guǎngwén administrative office was located,
so he complained to the Chancellor,
who said:
"The Emperor has expanded the National University,
establishing the Guǎngwén College to accommodate worthy scholars.
Future generations will say the Guǎngwén Erudite began with you—
is this not splendid!"
Chù then assumed the post,
with rank and salary equivalent to the Grand Academy.
After some time,
rain damaged the building's corridors and rooms,
and the authorities did not repair them,
so he had to lodge in the National University quarters.
From then on, the college fell into disuse.
From his Official Biography.
In the eighth month of the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
Qíwú Qián was promoted to Guǎngwén Erudite.
From the Jíxián Annotated Records.
Empty Lodge
Jìnglíng's clerk Liú Fěng sought lodging in an empty hall one night,
when three maidens arrived,
singing:
"Bright moon and clear breeze,
this fine night we gather;
the starry river easily turns,
joy and mirth do not last.
Green goblets and jade ladles,
we pour wine for you;
if the maiden does not drink,
when shall we find delight?"
Suddenly a person in yellow appeared and said:
"King Pótí summons,
maidens, come quickly."
The maidens all rose and departed,
and by dawn several jade hairpins were found.
"Records of the Mysterious and Strange"
Solitary Lodge
Táo Gǔ was sent as an envoy to the Southern Táng,
and wrote twelve characters on the wall of the official residence,
saying:
"A dog from Xīchuān,
the eyes of commoners,
a horse's bundled offspring,
meals from the imperial kitchen."
Sòng Qíqiū explained:
These twelve characters contain four words,
meaning 'sleeping alone in a solitary lodge.'
From "Yú Wénhǔ's Preface"

Jade Terrace
Jié built a jade tower,
exhausting the wealth of the common people.
Yī Yǐn remonstrated with him,

Xīn Xù
Xiàowǔ was very close and respectful to Wáng Guó and Wáng Yǎ.
Yǎ recommended Wáng Xún to the emperor,
and the emperor wanted to see him.
Once at night, he was facing Guóbǎo and Yǎ,
the emperor was slightly tipsy.
He ordered Wáng Xún to be summoned.
As Xún was about to arrive,
the sound of the messenger's announcement could be heard.
Guóbǎo knew that his talent was inferior to Xún's,
and feared losing the emperor's favor.
He thus said:
"Wáng Xún is a famous person at present;
Your Majesty should not meet him while tipsy.
It would be better to issue a separate decree to summon him."
The emperor agreed with his words,
considering them loyal,
and thus did not meet Xún.

Lùtái
Zhòu built the Lùtái,
which took seven years to complete.
It measured three lǐ in circumference,
stood a thousand chǐ high,
and overlooked the clouds and rain.
The Xīnxù
and the Zhúshū Jìnián record:
King Wǔ personally captured Emperor Shòu at the Nándān Terrace,
thus dividing the brilliance of heaven.
The Nándān Terrace
is likely an alternative name for the Lùtái.

and the Duke of Zhōu Dàn built the Spirit Tower.

The Huáinánzǐ
records that King Wén of Zhōu constructed the Spirit Tower,
extending to ponds and marshes,
and his benevolence reached even decaying bones.
The New Prefaces

leading to the advancement of worthy individuals.

The Son of Heaven traveled to the Héjì rivers,
where Lord Shèng presented a maiden,

The Bìyù Terrace in Púzhōu,
was constructed by King Mù of Zhōu for his beloved consort Shèng Jī,

Yítái
King Jǐng of Zhōu built the Luòyáng Chǐ Terrace,
as stated in the *Analects*:
"Chǐ means 'to sever the feet,'
signifying separation and parting."
The *Shuōwén* explains:
During the time of King Mù of Zhōngtiān,
a magician came from the westernmost countries.
Because the king's palace was humble and crude, unfit for dwelling,
the king then had it rebuilt for him.
The construction work of earth and timber,
the colors of red ochre and whitewash,
left no craftsmanship unattempted.
The five treasuries were emptied before the tower was finally completed.
It stood a thousand ren high,
overlooking the peak of Zhōngnán,
and was named the Tower of Zhōngtiān.
"Lièzǐ"
Fèngtái
Xiāo Shǐ had a splendid appearance and imposing stature,
with an exceptionally transcendent demeanor,
excelling at playing the flute,
producing sounds like those of the phoenix.
Duke Mù of Qín had a daughter named Nòng Yù,
who admired him,
so the duke gave her to him in marriage.
He taught Nòng Yù daily to mimic the phoenix's call,
and after several years,
her flute playing resembled the phoenix's song.
Phoenixes came to perch on their house,
and the duke built a Phoenix Tower for them.
The couple resided atop it,
neither drinking nor eating,
and did not descend for several years.
One day, Nòng Yù mounted a phoenix,
and Xiāo Shǐ rode a dragon,
ascending to the heavens and departing.
Qín erected the Shrine of the Phoenix Maiden for them,
where the sound of the flute could occasionally be heard.
"Supplementary Records of the Biographies of Immortals"
Sī Yān
Duke Wén of Jìn burned a forest to seek Jiè Zhītuī,
when a white crow circled the smoke cawing,
and at times alighted beside Jiè Zhītuī,
the fire could not burn him,
so the people of Jìn praised it,
erecting a high tower named the Tower of Longing for Smoke.
"Records of Omissions"
Nine Layers
Duke Líng of Jìn built a nine-story tower,
costing billions in expenses,
and said to his attendants:
"Anyone who dares to remonstrate will be executed."
Xún Xì heard of this,
submitted a request for an audience,
and Duke Líng met him with a crossbow drawn and arrows in hand,
saying:
"Do you intend to remonstrate?"
Xún Xì replied:
"I dare not remonstrate.
I can stack twelve game pieces and place nine eggs on top of them."
The duke said:
"Show me how you do it."
Xún Xì then composed his expression,
steadied his resolve,
placed the game pieces below,
and added nine eggs on top of them.
The attendants held their breath in fear,
Duke Líng crouched low,
barely able to breathe,
and exclaimed:
"How perilous!
How perilous!"
Xún Xì said:
"This is not perilous;
there is something even more dangerous than this."
The duke said:
"I wish to see that."
Xún Xì said:
"The nine-story tower,
unfinished after three years,
prevents men from farming,
women from weaving,
empties the state's treasury,
invites criticism from neighboring states,
who may raise armies against us,
leading to the destruction of the state.
What future do you hope for then?"
Duke Líng said:
"This is my fault."
He then ceased the project,
and dismantled the nine-story tower.
From *Shuō Yuàn*
To shoot a person
Duke Líng of Jìn was unprincipled,
he heavily taxed the people to decorate his walls,
and shot pellets from a terrace to watch people dodge them.
(Zuǒzhuàn, Xuāngōng 2nd year)
Táng Cì was unjustly demoted and banished,
languishing for a long time in a barbarous wilderness.
His lonely heart was oppressed and gloomy.
Hence, he gathered accounts of loyal and virtuous men of old who suffered exile.
Even though they faced death,
the rulers remained unenlightened.
He composed three writings titled "Biàn Bàng Luè."
When presented to Dézōng,
he became even more enraged,
saying to those around him:
"Táng Cì openly compares me to the muddleheaded rulers of antiquity."
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he summoned him back,
eventually appointing him to the position of Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Xiànzōng, while reviewing the books,
found the three works submitted by Cì in the inner palace.
He appreciated them,
and said to the scholar Shěn Chuánshī:
"The writings on discerning slander submitted by Táng Cì
should be regularly studied by rulers.
I suspect the compilation is not complete.
I order Chuánshī to expand them into ten volumes,
titled 'Yuán Hé Biàn Bàng Luè.'
Its preface states: 'When the ruler's virtue is evident,
how can slander arise?'
"Xù Shì Shuō"
Gazing at Mother
South of the Wěi River stands Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng's Terrace for Gazing at His Mother.
Lady Jiāng disliked the duke for being born feet-first,
and she lived together with Duàn.
Duàn showed no brotherly respect,
and Lady Jiāng failed to instruct him.
Duke Zhuāng confined his mother in Chéngyǐng,
vowing:
"Not until the Yellow Springs (death)
shall we meet again."
Thus he built this terrace to gaze toward his mother,
expressing the longing in his heart.
Moved by Kǎoshū's words,
he rejoiced in the poem of the great tunnel,
where maternal kindness flowed more freely,
and constant filial piety was restored.
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
tiered terrace
King Zhuāng of Chǔ built a multi-tiered tower,
extending stones for a thousand layers,
stretching earthworks over a hundred miles.
Laborers had provisions for three months reversed (confiscated),
seventy-two ministers who remonstrated
all died.
There was one Zhū Yùjǐ
who left Chǔ territory for a hundred miles,
abandoned his plowing and went to see King Zhuāng.
King Zhuāng said to him:
"Zhū Yùjǐ, you have come.
Do you intend to remonstrate?"
Zhū Yùjǐ said:
"Your Majesty has the application of righteousness,
the practice of laws.
Moreover, I have heard
earth that bears water becomes level,
wood that bears the marking line becomes straight,
the ruler who accepts remonstrance
becomes a sage king.
Building a multi-tiered tower,
extending stones for a thousand layers,
stretching earthworks over a hundred miles—
the blood from people's crimes and faults
fills the thoroughfares,
yet I have not dared to remonstrate;
how would I dare to remonstrate now?"
Thereupon he detailed how emperors and feudal lords who did not honor the worthy and accept remonstrance
met personal death and state destruction.
Then he hurried out.
The King of Chǔ quickly pursued him, saying:
"Jǐ, sir, return!
I will certainly follow your advice."
He then dismantled the multi-tiered tower that very day and relieved the people.
The people of Chǔ sang about it:
"Firewood ah, brushwood ah,
without Zhū Yùjǐ.
There would be no descendants ah!
Brushwood ah, firewood ah,
without Zhū Yùjǐ,
there would be no people ah!"
Qiáng Tái
Prime Minister Zǐpèi invited King Chǔ to a banquet,
and King Zhuāng consented.
Zǐpèi bowed respectfully,
stood facing north beneath the palace hall, and said:
"Previously, Your Majesty agreed to attend,
but now you have not come as promised.
Could it be that I have committed some offense?"
King Zhuāng replied:
"I heard that you have prepared this at Qiángtái.
Now Qiángtái
looks south toward Liàoshān,
overlooking Fānghuáng,
with the river on its left and the Huái on its right—
a place so delightful one could forget death.
But as a person of shallow virtue like myself,
I am not fit to indulge in such pleasures,
fearing I might linger and be unable to return."

Kūnzhāo
In the twenty-third year of King Líng of Zhōu,
he erected the Kūnzhāo Tower,
also named Xuānzhāo,
gathering rare woods from across the land,
where divine artisans filtered water,
refining it into mud.
The tower stood a hundred zhàng high,
ascended to observe the hues of clouds.

Chí Dǐ
Wáng Yīngwǔ,
was originally the maidservant of Princess Dōngyáng.
Initially, the princess had a servant named Chén Tiānxīng,
whom Yīngwǔ raised as a son,
and engaged in illicit relations with him.
Both Yīngwǔ and Tiānxīng were involved in the wicked witchcraft affair of Xiāo.
The princess passed away.
Xiāo, fearing words would leak,
married Yīngwǔ to Shǐxìng Prince Jùn's assistant Shěn Huáiyuǎn as a concubine.
Later, the affair was exposed,
causing shock and dismay to the Emperor,
leading to the arrest of Yīngwǔ's household.
Letters from Xiāo and Jùn were found,
containing words of curses and witchcraft.
Xiāo's rebellion ended in failure,
and his wife, the Yīn family, was sentenced to death by the Minister of Justice.
At the execution, she said to the prison official Jiāng Kè:
"Your family members destroy each other,
why condemn the innocent people of the world?"
Kè replied:
"To accept the empress's position without guilt?"
The Yīn family said:
"It was only temporary,
Yīngwǔ was to be the empress."
Huáiyuǎn was penalized for accepting Yīngwǔ,
and Emperor Xiàowǔ exiled him to Guǎngzhōu.
His brother Huáiwén was thus demoted to Managing Censor.
"Nán Shǐ, Biography of Xiāo Huáiwén." Yīngwǔ, as the peacock flower blooms,
before the mirror, the eyebrow shape anew.
Taught somewhat to have the beauty of Hóng'ér,
yet not betrothed to Southern Court Shěn the courtier.
"Comparing to Hóng'ér Poem."
Jìn Píng Gōng sent Shū Xiàng on a diplomatic mission to Wú,
where the Wú people cleaned their boats to welcome him,
with five men on the left,
and five hundred on the right. Among them were those wearing embroidered robes with leopard fur,
and those in brocade garments with fox fur.
Shū Xiàng returned and reported this to Píng Gōng,
who said:
"Is Wú about to perish?
Why show respect through boats?
Why not show respect to the people?"
Shū Xiàng replied:
"You, my lord, are building the Chídǐ Terrace,
which can deploy a thousand troops above,
and display bells and drums below.
If the feudal lords hear of this,
they will also ask why show respect through a terrace,
why not show respect to the people.
The objects of respect simply differ."
Thereupon, Píng Gōng halted the construction of the terrace.
From "Shuō Yuàn"

Jìn Pínggōng hosted a banquet at Shìhuì Tower.

Zhānghuá
King Líng of Chǔ built the Zhānghuá Terrace,
and ascended it with his ministers.
The king said:
"The terrace is beautiful."
Wǔ Jǔ replied:
"I have heard that a ruler considers being honored with virtue as beauty,
bringing peace to the people as joy,
heeding counsel as wisdom,
and achieving far-reaching governance as clarity.
I have never heard that towering structures of earth and wood,
intricate carvings of insects and patterns,
the clear tones of metal and stone,
or the mournful sounds of strings and bamboo
are considered beauty.
Former King Zhuāng made the Páo
(Wúyuè records it as Bào)
Terrace, whose height did not exceed what was necessary for observation,
whose size did not exceed what could accommodate ritual vessels,
whose timber did not interfere with defense preparations,
whose construction did not burden the government offices,
whose labor did not disrupt the people's seasonal work,
and whose administration did not alter court routines.
Now you have built this terrace for seven years,
causing resentment among the people,
exhausting financial resources,
ruining the year's harvest,
plaguing the common people,
arousing indignation among the feudal lords,
and drawing criticism from ministers and officials.
How can this be what former kings praised,
or what constitutes beauty for a ruler?"
King Líng immediately removed the earthworks and decorations,
and ceased visiting the terrace.
(from "Discourses of Chǔ" and "Annals of Wú and Yuè")
In the past, King Líng failed to act as a proper ruler,
and his ministers' admonitions did not reach him.
He then built the terrace at Zhānghuá,
exhausting the state of Chǔ,
and his people could not endure the calamities of hunger and toil,
leading the three armies to rebel at Gānxī.
(from "Discourses of Wú")
Biàn Ràng's rhapsody says:
"King Líng traveled in the Yúnmèng marshes,
rested on the Jīng Terrace,
with the Huái River waters before him,
the waves of Dòngtíng to his left,
the depths of Pénglǐ to his right,
and the slopes of Wū Mountain to the south,
then proceeded to build the Zhānghuá Terrace."
(from "History of the Later Hàn")
The viscount of Chǔ completed the Zhānghuá Terrace,
and wished to celebrate its completion with the feudal lords.
(from "Zuǒzhuàn", Zhāo 7)
Sān Xiū
The King of Dí sent an envoy to the State of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ boasted to the envoy about the Zhānghuā Tower,
which was extremely high,
requiring three rests to reach the top.
The King of Chǔ asked,
"Does the State of Dí have such a tower?"
The envoy replied,
"No.
Dí is a humble state,
and we would disdain such a tower.
When the King of Dí built his own palace,
the hall was only three chǐ high,
with three layers of earthen steps,
thatched roofs left untrimmed,
and rough-hewn rafters unplaned.
Moreover, the King of Dí still believed that building it caused great hardship for the workers,
and living in it would bring excessive ease to the residents.
Thus, the State of Dí would disdain such a tower."
The King of Chǔ felt ashamed.
From "New Discourses of Master Jiǎ."
Qiánxī
King Líng of Chǔ built the Gànxī Tower,
a tower five hundred ren high,
intending to ascend and peer into celestial patterns through the floating clouds.
From Lù Jiǎ's "New Discourses"
hinders agriculture
Sòng Huáng Guófù was building a terrace for Duke Píng,
which interfered with farming.
Zǐ Hǎn requested to wait until the farming
work was completed.
The builders sang:
"The pale-skinned one from Zémén,
truly started our labor.
The dark-skinned one from the city,
truly comforts our hearts."
Hearing this, Zǐ Hǎn took a whip
and struck those who were not diligent, saying:
"We common people
all have houses to avoid dryness, dampness, cold, and heat.
Now our lord is building a terrace,
and if we don't complete it quickly,
how can we serve as laborers?"
The commentary praises Zǐ Hǎn for sharing the criticism.
"Zuǒzhuàn", 17th year of Duke Xiāng.
Chónghuá
Long ago, Duke Líng of Wèi was seated in the Chónghuá Tower,
attended by hundreds of servants,
with luminous pearls shining like the sun,
and silk garments flowing with the wind.
Zhòng Shū Yù admonished him, saying:
"In the past, Jié acted like this and perished,
and Zhòu did the same and was destroyed.
Now our borders are being invaded,
the feudal lords are sending troops against us,
our territory is diminishing daily,
and the common people are turning away.
Your Majesty's inner harem
is perhaps too extravagant!"
The Duke descended from his mat, bowed twice, and said:
"I have been at fault."
Without your words,
the state would have nearly collapsed.
Thereupon, he dismissed several hundred palace women who had not been promoted,
and the common people were greatly pleased.
Zǐ Gòng, hearing of this, said:
"This is what is called being able to accept admonition."
Wáng Sūnzǐ's "New Writings"
Cháng Lái
Duke Jǐng was building the Chánglái Terrace,
Yànzǐ sat in attendance,
after three rounds of drinking,
Yànzǐ rose to dance and said:
"The year is already drawing to a close,
yet the grain remains unharvested,
how fleeting it is,
what can be done?
The weather has already turned cold,
yet the labor service is not halted,
how distressing it is,
what can be done?"
After dancing three times, his tears fell and soaked his lapel,
Duke Jǐng felt ashamed,
and because of this, he halted the Chánglái labor service.
From "Yànzǐ"
Lù Qǐn
Duke Jǐng of Qí built the tower of the Lùqǐn Palace,
and when it was completed, he did not ascend it.
Bó Chángqiān said:
"The construction of the tower was urgent,
and now that it is finished,
why does Your Lordship not ascend it?"
The Duke replied:
"Indeed.
Previously, when the owl hooted with its cry,
there was nothing it did not portend,
and I detest it exceedingly.
This is why I do not ascend it."
Bó Chángqiān said:
"I request to perform an exorcism to drive it away."
The Duke asked:
"What preparations are needed?"
He replied:
"Build a new chamber and place white mao grass inside it."
The Duke had the chamber built,
and when it was completed, white mao grass was placed there.
Bó Chángqiān said:
"Proceed with the ritual."
The next day,
he asked the Duke:
"Did you hear the owl's cry last night?"
The Duke said:
"It hooted once and was heard no more."
He sent someone to check,
and the owl was at the steps,
with wings spread, lying dead on the ground.
《Shuō Yuàn》
Bǎi Qǐn
Duke Jǐng and Yànzǐ were traveling at Shǎo Hǎi,
ascended the Bǎiqǐn Terrace and looked back at their state,
saying:
"How beautiful!
Vast and magnificent,
grand and majestic,
who in later generations will possess this?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Would it be Tián Chéngshì?"
The duke shed tears and said:
"Is this not sorrowful!
I possess the state,
yet Tián Chéngshì holds it.
What should be done about this now?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Why should you worry, my lord?
If you wish to take it back,
then draw near to the worthy and keep the unworthy at a distance,
bring order to its chaos,
relax its punishments,
relieve the poor and comfort the orphaned and widowed,
practice kindness and provide for the needy,
the people will turn to you,
and even if there were ten Tián
Chéngshì, what could they do to you?"
Hánfēizǐ
During the reign of Emperor Xiàomíng, he read "The Biography of Sū Wǔ,"
and saw an official title called:
"Yízhōngjiān"
and asked the various officials about it,
but they did not know.

Chuántái
The Marquis of Qí arrived,
and from the hunt, Yànzǐ attended him at Chuántái.
As they drank wine merrily,
the lord said:
"If from ancient times there were no death,
how would this joy be?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"If from ancient times there were no death,
then this would be the joy of the ancients;
how would you, my lord, obtain it?
Formerly, Shuāngjiūshì first dwelt in this land,
Jìcè succeeded them,
Yǒuféng Bólíng succeeded them,
Púgūshì succeeded them,

Líng Yáng
Chén Huìhóu greatly fortified the city,

Before it was completed, a legal violation occurred,

When the Master arrived in Chén,

and together they ascended the tower to view it.
The Master said:
"How magnificent this tower is!

none have succeeded in such a feat without executing anyone."
The Marquis of Chén silently withdrew,
and promptly secretly pardoned the arrested officials.
Later, when he saw the Master,

The reply was:
"When King Wén rose to power,
six provinces submitted to him.
The masses from these six provinces
each came with the devotion of sons.
Thus, for this modest tower,
it was completed

Why would there be any executions?
Only a ruler
who regards the few as few
can accomplish great achievements with the many."

The King of Yuè obtained a pair of divine trees,

failure of the five grains to ripen,
heaven sending down disasters upon them,
the people left destitute and the state transformed,
leading to their destruction and demise.
If you accept these, Great King,
you will surely be slain by the King of Yuè."
The King of Wú did not listen,

It took three years to gather the materials,
and five years to complete,

King Xiāng of Wèi intended to build the Mid-Heaven Tower,

"Anyone who dares to remonstrate shall die."
Xǔ Wǎn entered carrying a shovel on his back and said:
"I have heard that Your Majesty intends to build the Mid-Heaven Tower,
and I wish to contribute some effort."
The King asked:
"What effort can you contribute?"
Wǎn replied:
"Although I have no strength,
I can discuss the tower."
The King said:
"How so?"
He responded:
"I have heard that heaven and earth are fifteen thousand lǐ apart,
now if Your Majesty takes half of that,
you should build a tower seven thousand five hundred lǐ high.
Since the height is like this,
its foundation must be eight thousand lǐ square.
All of Your Majesty's territory
is insufficient for the tower's foundation.
In ancient times, Yáo and Shùn established feudal lords
with territories five thousand lǐ square.
If Your Majesty must build this tower,
first you must use troops to attack the feudal lords,
but even possessing all their lands would still be insufficient.
Then you must attack the four barbarian tribes to obtain eight thousand lǐ square,
which would be sufficient for the tower's foundation.
The accumulation of timber,
the multitude of laborers,
the storage of granaries,
would amount to tens of thousands of billions.
Beyond the eight thousand lǐ area,
you must allocate farmland
sufficient to supply Your Majesty's tower.
Only when all preparations for the tower are complete,
can construction begin."
The King of Wèi fell silent with no response,
and abandoned the plan to build the tower.
