if connected to the Platform Terrace, it would be close,
but if connected to the west of the city, it would not be possible,
thus it is known that the Platform Terrace was not within the city.
Prince Liáng enjoyed outings there with the likes of Zōu, Méi, and Xiàngrú,
making it a grand event of the time.
When Xiè composed his "Snow Rhapsody,"
he also mentioned Prince Liáng's displeasure,
while wandering in the Rabbit Garden,
now the singing halls have fallen into ruins,
the musical pipes buried and silent,
lonely tombs stand ruggedly,
no longer possessing the splendor of former days.
The "Water Classic"
preserves the lingering echoes of the Platform Terrace.
The "Discourse on the Biography of Língyùn in the Sòng Shū"
and the annotations by Jìn and Rú in the "Hàn Shū" seen in the "Water Classic,"
are nearly entirely deleted in current editions,
hence they are fully recorded here.
The Comprehensive Gazetteer states:
Xiè Huìlián composed his snow rhapsody here,
thus it is also named the Snow Terrace.
However, Xiè resided in Jiāngzuǒ,
and his rhapsody borrowed from Xiàngrú's style,
how could it be said that he composed the snow rhapsody here?
The General Gazetteer follows this,
both are mistaken.
Chuī Tái
The Customs of Chénliú records:
In the county there is a Cāngjié [site],
on the city wall of Shī Kuàng there is a platform for immortals to play music,
which King Liáng of Wèi built into a music platform.
The city walls have been destroyed,
leaving only traces of the former site.
The platform was about one hundred paces square,
as mentioned in Ruǎn Sìzōng's "Poems of My Cares":
"Setting out from the Wèi capital,
I gaze south toward the music platform.
The sound of flute and pipe still lingers,
but where is King Liáng of Wèi now?"
During the turmoil of the Jìn dynasty,
refugees settled here,
leveling the original foundation,
which then formed two layers.
The upper foundation remains about forty to fifty paces square,
over ten feet high.
It is commonly called the Refugee Platform,
and also known as Pó Platform City.
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic
notes that later the Fán family lived nearby,
so it was also named Fán Platform.
Records of Commanderies and States, The Nine Regions Record
Lǐ Tái
Constructed by Liáng Xiàowáng within the Tù Garden,
its winding path resembles a conch shell,
hence the name.
In the "Records of Military Expeditions,"
Sīmǎ Biāo's "Treatise on Commanderies and States" states:
"In Suīyáng County, there is the Lú Gate Pavilion;
within the city stands a high terrace,
exceptionally elegant and spacious,
majestically solitary,
towering uniquely above all,
called the Conch Terrace,
also known as the Ascending Terrace.
In its heyday of the past,
it indeed rivaled the clouds and mist in height."
The "Sequel to Records of Military Expeditions" says:
the winding path resembles a conch,
thus it is called the Conch Terrace—
this is incorrect;
it is what the Quēzi refers to as the Tiger Enclosure Terrace.
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Bǎi Liáng
In the second year of Yuándǐng, spring,
the Bǎiliáng Terrace was constructed.
"Annals of Emperor Wǔ"
Emperor Wǔ cast bronze pillars for Bǎiliáng.
"Treatise on Sacrifices"
The beams were made of fragrant cypress,
whose scent could be smelled for dozens of lǐ.
"Old Affairs of the Three Capital Regions"
The Bǎiliáng Terrace was built to house the Divine Lord.
"Stories of Emperor Wǔ"
The Emperor once hosted a banquet upon it,
commanding all officials of two thousand dàn rank who could compose seven-character poems
to take the seats of honor.
"Ancient Literary Garden of the Three Capital Regions"
Tōng Tiān
In the second year of Yuánfēng, the Gānquán Tōngtiān Platform was constructed.
Yán Shīgǔ notes:
"Tōngtiān" means this platform is so high it reaches the heavens.
"Stories of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn" records:
The Tōngtiān Platform was built at Gānquán,
rising over a hundred zhàng above ground,
with clouds and rain seen entirely below it,
three hundred lǐ from Cháng'ān,
from which the Cháng'ān city walls were visible.
During Emperor Wǔ's reign, when sacrificing to Tàiyǐ,
he would ascend the Tōngtiān Platform to dance,
with three hundred eight-year-old girls
arranged for ceremonial worship,
to summon immortals.
Regarding the sacrifice to Tàiyǐ, it is said:
People were sent up the Tōngtiān Platform to await heavenly deities,
and when deities descended to the sacrificial site,
appearing like large shooting stars,
beacon fires were lit toward the Bamboo Palace,
where worship was conducted. Above stood a dew-collecting plate,
held by a bronze immortal's hand raising a jade cup,
to catch dew from beyond the clouds.
During the Yuánfèng period,
the platform's beams and rafters spontaneously collapsed,
transforming into dragons and phoenixes
that flew away with the wind and rain.
It was also called the Deity-Awaiting Platform,
or the Immortal-Viewing Platform,
for awaiting divine beings and watching for immortals.
"Records of the Capital"
describes flanking Tōngtiān Platforms
over thirty zhàng high,
where celestial deities were awaited during heaven-worship ceremonies.
"Records of Guānzhōng"
Divine Spirit
Your Majesty considers the city too small,
planning to build Jiànzhāng Palace,
with Fèngquè Tower on the left,
Shénmíng Terrace on the right,
boasting thousands of gates and myriad doors.
"Fǎng Shuò's Biography"
Shénmíng Terrace,
built by Emperor Wǔ,
was a place for worshipping immortals.
Above stood a dew-receiving plate,
with a bronze immortal figure,
stretching its palm to hold a bronze plate and jade cup,
to collect dew from beyond the clouds,
mixing the dew with jade powder to consume,
seeking the path to immortality.
"Temple Records"
When Emperor Wǔ first built Shénmíng Terrace,
they dug thirty zhàng into the ground,
finding a spring,
with yellow water,
beside which people dwelled,
without sunlight or moonlight,
using fire for illumination day and night,
among them were people,
eating earth and drinking water,
wearing reddish-brown cloth garments,
the Hàn people asked:
"How long have you been here?"
They replied:
"The Shāng king was tyrannical,
sending countless people a thousand zhàng underground,
to seek blue-hard soil for making tiles,
building jade palaces and golden halls,
workers were all lowered into the ground by ropes,
carrying vessels to fetch soil,
many were crushed and died,
only two of us remain now."
The Hàn people asked how they alone survived,
they replied:
"We use jade as clothing,
gold as rings,
our bodies possess gold and jade,
thus our vital energy remains unextinguished."
The Hàn people asked:
"Do you wish to emerge and become human again?"
They replied:
"Eating earth and drinking from springs,
keeping company with ants and insects,
how could we still hope to see the sun and moon?"
They were then brought out,
but died after three days,
their flesh and bones turning to ashes,
only their hearts remained, the size of pellets,
hard as stone,
when struck with objects,
they were merely dried blood.
"Records of the Hidden"
Shénmíng Terrace,
fifty zhàng high,
had nine chambers above,
often housing a hundred Nine Heaven Daoist priests.
"Hàn Palace Records"
Shénmíng Terrace had nine platforms,
now called Jiǔzǐ Terrace.
"Yellow Charts"
Watching the Wind
In the second year of Tàichū,
the Sweet Springs Observatory was built,
where a pearl was discovered on the platform.
When gazed upon, it resembled a shining moon,
hence it was named the Moon-Illuminating Pearl.
From "Records of the Hidden and Mysterious."
Téng Guāng
In the second year of the Jiànyuán era,
the Emperor erected the Téng Guāng Tower,
to gaze upon the four directions,
where there were often flying lights like stars,
gathering upon the tower.
It was also called the Jīngxīng Tower,
where practitioners of esoteric arts gathered to discuss matters of immortality.
The Emperor
Summoning Immortals
Emperor Wǔ built the Terrace for Summoning Immortals
north of the Míngtíng Palace.
The Míngtíng Palace
is another name for Gānquán.
On the terrace, they struck the green jade bell,
hung the xuánlí chime stone,
played the shuāngdí bamboo flute,
and sang the song "Clouds Follow the Sun,"
yet those listening below the terrace
could not hear the sound of the pipes and songs.
Ascending to Immortality
Mount Sōng is the Central Sacred Mountain,
its eastern part is called Tàishì,
its western part is called Shǎoshì,
seventeen lǐ apart from each other,
Sōnggāo being the general name.
Emperor Wǔ built the Ascending Immortals Terrace,
located beneath Shǎoshì Peak.
Dài Yánzhī's "Records of a Western Expedition"
Seeking the Truth
On Mount Sōnggāo there is a Jade Maiden Terrace,
said to be where Emperor Wǔ saw three immortal jade maidens,
hence the terrace was named after them.
"Mountain Records"
The emperor ascended the Terrace of Seeking Truth,
and fasted until the night of the seventh day of the seventh month,
when in the southwestern sky something like a white cloud arose,
and in a moment the Queen Mother arrived.
"Inner Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn"
The emperor ascended the Terrace of Extending Numinous Power,
devoutly fasting and preserving the Way,
while affairs of the four directions
were temporarily entrusted to the prime minister.
On the seventh day of the seventh month, the Queen Mother arrived.
"Extensive Records" quoting the "Inner Biography"
Spiritual Connection
Lady Gōu Yì accompanied the emperor to Gānquán and died there.
After her body was encoffined,
the fragrance from her corpse could be smelled for over ten lǐ.
She was buried at Yúnyáng.
The emperor grieved deeply,
suspecting she was no ordinary person.
He thus erected a Spirit-Communication Terrace at Gānquán Palace.
A blue bird came and perched on the terrace, flying back and forth.
By the time of Emperor Xuān's reign,
the bird no longer came.
Wáng Bāo's "Records of Yúnyáng"
Gazing with Gratitude
Emperor Wǔ realized that the Crown Prince Lì
had been unjustly killed,
so he built the Palace of the Longing Son,
and erected the Terrace of Gazing with Longing for the Return,
which became known throughout the land,
and all who heard of it grieved.
From the "Plans of the Han Capital" in the Book of Hàn.
Guì Tái
In the first year of the Yuánshǐ era of Emperor Zhāo,
a forest pond was excavated,
spanning a thousand paces wide.
To the south of the pond, Cassia Terrace was erected,
overlooking the distant east.
Water from the Tàiyè Pool was channeled in,
and at times, aquatic festivities were commanded for amusement,
prolonging the joyous days.
Boats were crafted from patterned catalpa wood,
with magnolia wood used for rudders.
Carved flying swallows and soaring waterfowl
adorned the prows of the vessels,
gently swaying with the wind.
As the sunset glow faded, one forgot to return,
and the Shāng Terrace was built atop the pond.
"Records of Omitted Legends: Huángtú"
Take shelter from the wind
The Emperor often on leisurely autumn days,
would frolic with Fēi Yàn at the Taiye Pond,
using sand pear wood for boats,
valuing their ability not to sink or float.
Whenever a clear breeze arose,
Fēi Yàn nearly followed the wind into the water,
so the Emperor tied her skirt with a green silk ribbon.
She often lamented,
"I am humble and lowly,
how dare I presume to have my skirt tied with a ribbon?"
To this day at Taiye Pond,
there remains a Wind-Sheltering Terrace,
which is where Fēi Yàn's skirt was tied.
Records of Omissions
Moon Shadow
The Hàn Palace had the Moonlit Terrace, Cloud Radiance Hall, Nine Splendors Hall, Ringing Bells Hall, Open Lapel Pavilion, and Riverside Observatory,
which were not recorded in official registers,
all being places where splendor and grace resided.
Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital
Resembling a White Tiger
Emperor Chéng visited the residence of Wáng Gēn,
where he saw a man-made hill and a terrace in the garden,
resembling the White Tiger Hall.
The emperor was enraged by this,
and reprimanded Chējì General Wáng Yīn.
"The Relatives of the Empress"
Wēnmíng
At Wēn Míng Tái in Míngzhōu,
Emperor Shìzǔ of the Later Hàn,
lay resting in this hall by day
when Gěng Yǎn entered, approached his couch, and urged him to ascend the throne.
From the "Treatise on Commanderies and States"
At the Yúntái,
Zhōu Dǎng was presented by Guāngwǔ,
but he bowed without saluting.
Fàn Shēng reported critically,
saying:
"I wish to sit beneath the Yúntái
to evaluate and deliberate national strategies."
From the "Records of Recluse Men,"
at the beginning of Yǒngpíng,
Mǎ Yuán's daughter was made Empress.
Xiǎnzōng depicted the renowned ministers and generals of Jiànwǔ on the Yúntái.
Because of the influence of the Pepper Chamber,
only Yuán was not included.
Dōngpíng Wáng Cāng observed the portraits,
and said to the Emperor:
"Why is the image of the Fúbō General not painted?"
The Emperor laughed and did not reply.
From the "Main Records,"
in the second year of Zhōngpíng, on the day jǐyǒu in the second month,
there was a disaster at the Nángōng Yúntái.
As for the Yúntái,
it was constructed by the Zhōu family.
Books and technical works,
rare treasures and strange valuables
were all stored there.
From the "Treatise on the Five Elements."
Jǐngshēng
South of the Miǎn River stands a tiered tower,
named Jǐngshēng Tower,
which was built by Liú Biǎo when he governed Xiāngyáng.
It is said that Liú Biǎo frequently roamed here,
often resting at this spot.
He had a fondness for falcons,
and once ascended this tower to sing the "Song of the Wild Falcon."
Its melody and rhythm resembled Mèng Dá's "Shàngdǔ Chant."
From the "Water Classic"
Reading
In Huáyáng there is a Reading Terrace,
built by Zhūgě Kǒngmíng when he served as chancellor of Shǔ.
He erected this terrace to gather scholars,
and also to receive virtuous men from all regions,
thus it was named the Reading Terrace.
"Records of the Known World"
Summer Retreat
At Zhūgě Liàng's former residence in Lóngzhōng, there was an old well.
Now it is dry and waterless.
Shèng Hóngzhī recorded:
"The well is five zhàng deep,
and five chǐ wide.
In front of the hall are three rooms.
The foundation mound is extremely high,
said to be Kǒngmíng's summer retreat platform.
The residence faces water to the west of the mountain,
where Kǒngmíng once ascended,
played the qin while singing 'Liáng Fù Yín',
hence naming this place Lè Shān (Music Mountain).
Previously, the Dǒng family lived in this residence,
but they declined and perished,
so later people dared not dwell there again.
During the Jiànwǔ era of the Qí dynasty, someone repaired the well
and found a stone pillow,
one chǐ two cùn high,
and nine cùn long,
which was presented to Prince Jìn'ān.
Xí Zàochǐ
also composed a residence inscription.
"Nán Yōngzhōu Jì"
Sāntái
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi established three towers northwest of Yèchéng,
the central one named the Bronze Sparrow Tower,
the southern one called the Golden Tiger Tower,
and this one named the Ice Well Tower.
Lù Huì's "Records of Yèzhōng"
states that all three towers were built on the city's foundation,
towering majestically,
as high as mountains.
In the fifteenth year of the Jiàn'ān era,
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi initiated their construction,
with the central one known as the Bronze Tower,
standing ten zhàng high,
and containing over a hundred rooms.
Upon the tower's completion,
he ordered his sons to ascend it,
and had them compose rhapsodies.
Prince Sī of Chén wrote his piece swiftly,
earning admiration at the time.
This was also where Emperor Wǔ of Wèi awaited Fèngcháng Wáng Shūzhì.
To the south was the Golden Sparrow Tower,
eight zhàng high, with 109 rooms.
To the north stood the Ice Well Tower,
also eight zhàng high,
with 140 rooms.
Above it was an ice chamber,
containing several wells,
each fifteen zhàng deep,
storing ice and graphite.
Graphite could be used for writing,
and when burned, it was hard to consume entirely,
also known as coal.
There were also grain cellars and salt cellars,
prepared for emergencies,
and today, stone inscriptions still remain above the cellars.
Zuǒ Sī's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wèi" says:
"The three towers stand in a row, lofty and majestic."
"The Water Classic"
records: In the ninth year of the Tiānbǎo era of Wénxuān,
300,000 laborers were conscripted,
to construct the three towers in Yè,
expanding and heightening the old structures,
erecting grand palaces,
and gardens for leisure,
until the three towers were completed.
The Bronze Sparrow was renamed Golden Phoenix,
the Golden Tiger became Sacred Response,
and the Ice Well was called Exalted Light.
In November, he ascended the three towers,
presided at the Qiánxiàng Hall,
held court and feasted with his ministers,
and ordered them to compose poems.
"Book of Northern Qí"
Líng Yún
In the second year of the Huángchū era of Emperor Wén,
the Língyún Tower was constructed.
According to the Records of Wèi,
the Língyún Tower
had exquisitely crafted pavilions and viewing structures.
First, the weight of all the timber was carefully balanced,
and only then was the construction carried out,
so that not even the slightest imbalance occurred.
Although the tower stood tall and steep,
it often swayed with the wind,
yet it never faced the risk of collapsing.
When Emperor Míng of Wèi ascended the tower,
he feared its precarious state,
and had it reinforced with additional large timbers.
As a result, the tower collapsed,
and commentators attributed this to the imbalance of weight distribution.
According to A New Account of the Tales of the World,
the Língyún Tower
was 23 zhàng high,
and from its top, one could see Mèngjīn.
Yáng Lóngxiāng's Records of Luòyáng
states that the Língyún Tower was located at the Míngguāng Hall,
standing 8 zhàng tall to the west,
with a brick-paved pathway built step by step,
leading to the top for elevated and distant views,
offering a comprehensive panorama of Luòyì,
and to the south, one could gaze upon Shǎoshì Mountain,
the pinnacle of mountain beauty.
According to the Record of a Journey of Campaign,
in the first year of the Jǐngchū era of Emperor Míng,
magnificent creatures such as yellow dragons and phoenixes were cast,
to adorn the Jīnyōng Fortress, Língyún Tower, and Língxiāo Tower.
Numerous labor projects were vigorously launched,
involving tens of thousands of workers.
From high-ranking officials and nobles down
to students,
all exerted their efforts.
The emperor even personally dug soil to set an example for them,
prompting Gāotáng Lóng to submit a memorial with stern admonitions.
From his biography.
Candlestick
Emperor Wén constructed an earthen platform,
with a foundation forty zhang high,
arranged candles placed beneath the platform,
named it the Candle Platform,
viewed from afar like stars falling to the earth,
to house the beautiful woman Xuē Língyún there.
"Records of Omissions"
Diàotái
Sūn Quán was at the fishing terrace in Wǔchāng,
drinking heavily until quite drunk.
He ordered water to be splashed on his ministers,
saying:
"Today we shall drink to our hearts' content, and only when
we fall from this terrace shall we stop."
Zhāng Zhāo said:
"In the past, King Zhòu built hills of dregs and ponds of wine,
drinking through the long night.
At that time, he too considered it pleasure,
not recognizing it as evil."
Sūn Quán fell silent with a look of shame,
and thus ended the drinking.
Records of Wú
The ruler of Wú regarded Lady Pān as a goddess,
and whenever he roamed the Zhāoxuān Terrace with her,
he felt supremely content.
Once, while strolling with her on the fishing terrace,
they caught a large fish.
The ruler was overjoyed,
but Lady Pān said:
"I have heard of weeping over fish in ancient times,
but now there is joy.
Where there is joy, sorrow must follow,
and I take this as a grave warning."
The ruler of Wú then ended the banquet.
Lady Pān was indeed later rejected and banished,
and the foundation of the fishing terrace remains to this day.
Records of Omissions
Viewing Horses
North of the Yèzhāng River stood Zhào Yuèmǎtái,
its foundation five zhang high,
with viewing pavilions arranged atop it.
Shí Hǔ would frequently conduct military drills below it,
ascending the pavilions to observe them.
Hǔ himself would shoot whistling arrows from the platform,
using them as signals for the chariots and cavalry to advance or retreat.
"Water Classic"
Fāng Chén
Shí Hǔ built a tower in front of the Tàijí Hall,
forty zhàng high.
During the height of summer,
he would ascend the high tower to gaze at the four corners of the world,
with music of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo playing,
continuing day and night.
At that time, there was a severe spring drought,
so he ground assorted treasures and rare incense into powder,
ordering several hundred people to scatter it from the tower,
calling it "fragrant dust."
On the terrace stood a bronze dragon,
its belly capable of holding several hundred hú of wine.
He had foreigners pour wine from the tower in crowds,
and when the wind blew, it looked like dew from a distance,
naming it the "Sticky Rain Terrace,"
used to sprinkle the dust.
The sounds of laughter and amusement from the tower shook the air.
"Records of Omissions"
Líng Jūn
Liáng's Zhāng Mào built the Língjūn Platform,
with a circumference of over eighty sections,
and a foundation nine ren high.
A man from Wǔlíng named Yán Zēng knocked on the gate at night,
calling out:
"Duke Wǔ sent me."
He said:
"Why do you toil the common people to build this platform?"
Gūzāng's magistrate Xīn Yán considered Yán Zēng's words delusional and false,
and requested to have him executed.
Zhāng Mào said:
"I do believe I have overworked the people,
but Yán Zēng invoked the command of my late father,
how can this be called delusion?"
The Grand Prefecture's Registrar Mǎ Fáng said:
"Now that the world's troubles have not yet been pacified,
we should only promote and uphold the Way,
and simplicity, and should not impose corvée labor,
or extravagantly adorn towers and pavilions.
In recent years,
we have gradually come to realize that various affairs
are daily becoming more extravagant than before.
Every undertaking
lightly violates proper standards,
and is truly not what the gentlemen and ladies expect from an enlightened ruler."
Duke Mào said:
"I have been at fault."
He ordered the construction work to cease.
"Jìn Shū"
Soaring to the sky
Hèlián Bóbó erected a soaring terrace on the southern mountain, intending to ascend it to gaze upon Cháng'ān.
"Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms"
Commissioner of Education
Fàn Lín served as the governor of Yùzhāng,
establishing extensive schools,
attracting over a thousand people from near and far,
providing all expenses,
entirely from his personal salary,
and also selecting youths from the four prominent clans of the commandery,
all to serve as students,
instructing them in reciting the Five Classics,
constructing an academic platform,
with increasingly broad impact.
"Basic Biography"
Prajñā
Yáo Xīng gathered over five thousand Buddhist monks,
among whom fifty were great practitioners,
and built a pagoda in Yǒngguì Lane,
erecting a Prajñā Platform.
In the center, they constructed Mount Sumeru,
with towering cliffs and steep walls on all sides,
featuring rare birds and exotic beasts,
exquisite plants and trees,
along with immortals and Buddha statues—
all things unheard of by people,
who considered them extraordinary.
(Chronicles of Cháng'ān)
Língzhī
North of the path inside the Qiānqiū Gate lies the West Roaming Garden,
within which stands the Soaring Cloud Terrace,
built by Emperor Wén of the Wei dynasty.
On the terrace is an octagonal well,
and north of the well, Emperor Gāozǔ constructed the Cool Breeze Pavilion.
Ascending it to gaze afar,
one's view extends to the Luò River.
To the east lies the Lingzhī Fishing Terrace,
constructed with layered timber,
projecting over the lake,
twenty zhàng above the ground.
Wind whispers through its windows,
and clouds seem to rise from its beams.
A stone-carved whale,
bearing the fishing terrace on its back,
appears as if it surged from the earth
or descended from the sky.
The fishing terrace is surrounded by four halls on each side,
all connected by elevated walkways leading to the Lingzhī Terrace.
During the hottest summer months,
the emperor resides at the Lingzhī Terrace to escape the heat.
"A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luòyáng"
Jìng Lún
Northeast of the Celestial Master altar of the Wèi state formerly stood the Quiet Wheel Palace,
built in the fourth year of the Shénjiā era of Wèi,
which could also be considered akin to the Bǎiliáng Palace.
Its terrace was lofty and vast, rising beyond the clouds,
intended to extend upward to welcome celestial guests
and cut off the clamorous dust below.
"Water Classic"
Yǔhuā
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, Dharma Master Yúnguāng once lectured on scriptures at this platform,
where he moved the heavens to send down a rain of flowers as offerings,
and celestial kitchens presented food.
Yáng Wúwéi wrote a poem that reads:
"Empty scriptures came to the Land of Zhèn,
Kānglè pursued profound clarity.
Sūtra leaves translated in deep mountains,
Mandarava flowers flew at midnight.
Fragrance pure, though penetrating bamboo baskets,
Petal scatter, never clinging to robes.
The old White Lotus Society ages,
Venerable Yuǎngōng should gaze for return."
From "Records of the Six Dynasties"
Lè Shàn
Behind the high study is a hall,
west of the hall are five archery ranges,
south of the archery ranges lies a large pond,
upon the pond stands a terrace,
named the Terrace of Delighting in Goodness.
"Records of Southern Yōngzhōu"
The Jade Maiden
Lǐ Guǐ, courtesy name Chǔbié,
was a native of Gūzāng in Wǔwēi.
At the end of the Dàyè era, he proclaimed himself the Prince of Great Liáng of Héxī,
later arrogating the imperial title,
and refused to accept office under the Táng.
At that time, a foreign shaman deluded him, saying:
"The Supreme Deity once sent a jade maiden,
descending from heaven."
Thereupon he dispatched troops to build a terrace,
to await the jade maiden,
incurring great waste and expense,
causing the common people to suffer.
When he was defeated,
he sighed, saying:
"The people's hearts have left me;
has Heaven forsaken me?"
Taking his wife and children up to the Jade Maiden Terrace,
he set out wine to bid farewell,

Yìng Shào noted:
"Golden Gate"
refers to the Golden Horse Gate.
The Biography of Yáng Xióng
records an edict to disband the Yellow Gate,
and the imperial carriage's dogs and horses.
Yán Shīgǔ explained:
"Yellow Gate"
refers to the inner offices.
The Annals of Emperor Yuán
state: "The Golden Horse Gate
is also called the Yellow Gate."
Jade Sea
Bì Mén
The Book of Hàn states:
South of the Jiànzhāng Palace stood the Jade Hall,
with a three-tiered gate of jade discs,
the terrace rising thirty zhàng high,
the inner hall of the Jade Hall having twelve gates,
its steps and platforms all made of jade,
a bronze phoenix cast,
standing five chǐ tall,
adorned with gold,
perched atop the roof,
with rotating pivots below,
facing the wind as if soaring,
the rafter ends thinly coated with disc jade,
hence called the Gate of Jade Discs.
The Yellow Diagrams
Qīng Suǒ
The Gentleman of the Yellow Gate belongs to the Yellow Gate,
who are ordered to enter at dusk through the Blue-Locked Gate,
and pay respects, hence called the Evening Gentleman.
"Old Rituals of the Hàn"
states the Blue-Locked Gate is in the Southern Palace.
"Records of Palaces and Pavilions"
notes Wáng Gēn was arrogant and extravagant,
usurping the red steps and blue-locked patterns reserved for the emperor.
Mèng Kāng explained:
"Painting the door edges blue,
with carvings in between, is an imperial standard."
Rú Chún said:
"The lintel grids are double-layered,
like the overlapping collar of a garment,
painted blue, called blue-locked,
which is the emperor's gate design."
Shī Gǔ noted:
The blue-locked pattern
is carved as interlocking chains,
with designs painted blue.
"Biography of the Empress Yuán"
describes carved rafters and engraved brackets,
blue-locked patterns and red pillars.
"Rhapsody on the Wú Capital"
notes Wèi Guàn annotated blue-locked
as blue carvings on door edges.
"Later Treatise on Officials Commentary"
records Dǒng Bā saying:
The forbidden gate is called the Yellow Portal,
managed by palace attendants,
hence titled Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
Ascending
to office at the blue-locked portal,
gazing distantly at the Phoenix Pool.
"Fàn Yún's Poem"
Léi Mén
Wáng Zūn served as the Chancellor of Dōngpíng,
where the prince, due to his close kinship, acted arrogantly and disregarded laws and regulations.
When Wáng Zūn arrived at the court,
the prince sat in front and recited the poem "Xiàng Shǔ",
to which Wáng Zūn said:
"Do not beat a cloth drum before the Thunder Gate."
From "The Main Biography".
Kāiyáng
When the Kāiyáng Gate was first completed, it had no name.
One evening, a pillar appeared on its tower.
Lángyé's Kāiyáng County reported that a pillar from the southern city gate had flown away.
Emperor Guāngwǔ sent someone to identify it and sighed with regret.
They then firmly bound it in place,
carved a record of the year and month,
and thus named it accordingly.
"Yìng Shào's Hàn Official Records"
Hé Tāng Zhònggōng once served as a gatekeeper.
When the emperor returned incognito at night,
Tāng closed the gate and did not admit him.
The court praised him for this.
"Water Classic and Xiè Chéng's Book"
The Kāiyáng Gate
was originally called the Jiànyáng Gate.
"Jìn Palace Pavilion Names"
Shàngdōng
The Gǔ River flows east past the stone bridge below the Jiànchūn Gate,
which is the Shàngdōng Gate.
As Ruǎn Jìzōng described in his "Poems from the Heart":
"At dawn I leave the Shàngdōng Gate,
Gazing afar at the foothills of Shǒuyáng.
Through the winding nine-curved gate,
I wander, wondering where to go."
In the "Commentary on the Waterways Classic",
Zhì Yùn served as the guard of the Shàngdōng Gate.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ once returned late at night,
he ordered the gate to be opened for his entry,
but Yùn refused him admission.
The emperor commanded to be recognized through the gate's crevice,
to which Yùn replied:
"The torchlight is too distant and unclear."
He thus adamantly kept the gate shut,
earning even greater respect from the emperor.
According to the "Records of the Eastern Pavilion",
Jiān Xín attacked Luòyáng,
while a subordinate general of Zhū Wěi rebelled,
secretly arranging with Xín to open the Shàngdōng Gate at dawn.
From "His Main Biography".
Shàng Xī
The Chānghé Gate,
which was the Upper West Gate of the Han Dynasty.
The "Han Official Ceremonies" states:
The Upper West Gate,
the reason it was not entirely white
was because the Han Dynasty faced adversity in the Wù year,
so it was carved and painted in vermilion.
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Zhuólóng
In the second year of the Jiànchū era,
the officials petitioned to enfeoff the maternal uncles according to the old statutes,
to which the Empress Dowager decreed:
"Previously, when I passed by above the Zhuólóng Gate,
I saw the carriages of my maternal family flowing like water and their horses like dragons.
I did not reprimand or anger them,
but only cut off their annual allowances,
hoping they would silently reflect and feel ashamed in their hearts."
From Yuán Hóng's "Records of the Hàn Dynasty"
Yúnlóng
In the seventeenth year of the Yǒngpíng era, Bān Gù along with Jiǎ Kuí, Fù Yì, Dù Jǔ, Zhǎn Lóng, and Xī Méng were summoned to the Cloud Dragon Gate,
where the junior eunuch Zhào Xuān presented the "Basic Annals of Qín Shǐ Huáng",
and asked us:
"In the historian Sīmǎ Qiān's evaluative comments,
could there possibly be anything incorrect?"
Diǎn Yǐn
Jīn Shāng
Yáng Cì, in the first year of the Guānghé era, was led into the Jīn Shāng Gate,
and asked about auspicious and ominous signs.
Annotation:
To the west of the Tàijí Hall is the Jīn Shāng Gate.
The Later Biography
opens the special gate at the southern end,
and establishes the majestic main gate.
It displays benevolence and kindness at Chóngxián,
and upholds righteous reputation at Jīn Shāng.
It soars like a cloud dragon on the spring road,
and stations the divine tiger in the autumn quarter.
The Eastern Capital Rhapsody
has the Azure Dragon in the east,
and the White Tiger in the west.
The Book of Hàn
Hóngdū
Emperor Líng summoned scholars who could compose literary pieces, rhapsodies, and letters, as well as those skilled in calligraphy and bird-script seal carving,
to await appointments at the Hóngdū Gate.
"Biographies of the Palace Attendants"
Tōngdé
Zhèng Kāngchéng,
a native of Gāomì in Běihǎi,
was deeply respected by the state chancellor Kǒng Róng,
who instructed the magistrate of Gāomì
to establish a special district for Kāngchéng,
saying:
"The state of Qí established scholar districts,
and Yuè had an army of gentlemen—
both were expressions of honoring the worthy."
He further stated that "gōng" (lord)
is the proper title for benevolence and righteousness,
not limited to the three senior ministers.
Now, Zhèng Gōng's district may have its roads widened
to allow the passage of tall carriages,
and be named the Gate of Communicating Virtue.
"From the Original Biography"
Chāngmén
According to the old Tang system, scholars were not allowed to be recognized with the title of Chéng for themselves.
They would respond to consultations,
participate in meetings with a lower rank,
according to their official ranks.
In the first year of the Xiànzōng Emperor's Yǒngzhēn era,
Zhèng Yīn was first appointed as Chéngzhǐ,
with a position above other scholars,
residing in the first pavilion on the east side.
The "Chéngzhǐ Yuànjì" records that during internal banquets, they sat next to the prime minister,
occupying a seat above the Yīpǐn rank.
According to the "Hànlínzhì," later the Míngzōng Emperor of the Later Tang decreed that when scholars entered the academy,
they should be arranged according to seniority,
only Chéngzhǐ is appointed based on the emperor's will,
regardless of official rank or seniority,
and positioned above the scholars.
In November of that year,
an edict appointed new Hànlín scholars.
Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn, having entered the imperial courtyard early,
had long held the position of historiographer,
previously served in the court of authority,
and steadily advanced to deputy minister.
Now, having been promoted to the inner court,
it is fitting to declare a separate class,
arranging their standings,
appropriate to follow Cuī Shuì.
"Wǔdài Zhíguānzhì."
Sūn Jiān's mother gave birth to Jiān.
She dreamed that her intestines came out and circled the Chāng Gate of Wú.
She told a neighboring woman,
who said:
"How do you know it is not an auspicious sign?
Chāng Gate,
is a gate of Wú's city wall.
During the Xiàngpíng era of Xiàn Dì's reign,
there was a rumor in Wú:
'A golden chariot,
with speckles like spotted deer,
opens the Chāng Gate,
and brings out the Son of Heaven.' "
— Sòng Fúruìzhì
Qiānqiū
A stream flows south from the Qiūqiū Gate, passing beneath the Shénhǔ Gate,
facing east toward the Yúnlóng Gate.
Above the railings of both waterways,
are arrayed carvings of dragons, clouds, phoenixes, and tigers.
When illuminated by the Great Qí's radiance,
and at the first light of dawn when they appear,
or when the setting sun casts slanting rays,
the frost-like patterns gleam with emerald hues,
dazzling the eyes with their iridescent splendor.
Further south, the stream turns eastward,
passing by the Chānghé Gate.
Emperor Míng of the Southern Wèi, emulating the Supreme Ultimate,
erected the Tàijí Hall in the southern palace of Luòyáng,
transforming the Zhì Gate into the Chānghé Gate at the former site of the Hàn Dynasty's Chóngdé Hall.
Outside the Chānghé Gate, giant watchtowers were erected on both sides,
to correspond with the celestial constellations.
"Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Chéngmíng
In early December of the first year of the Huángchū era,
the Luòyáng Palace was constructed,
and on the Wùwǔ day, the emperor visited Luòyáng.
Annotation:
According to various records, the emperor resided in the Northern Palace,
holding court with his officials in the Jiànshǐ Hall,
with its gate named Chéngmíng.
As reflected in Prince Sī of Chén's poem: "I visited the emperor at the Chéngmíng Lodge."
From the "Annotations to the Records of the Three Kingdoms,"
the Chéngmíng Gate
was the gate for the harem's comings and goings.
I often wondered about "visiting the emperor at the Chéngmíng Lodge,"
and asked Lord Zhāng, who said:
Emperor Míng built the Jiànshǐ Hall,
and court assemblies all passed through the Chéngmíng Gate.
From Lù Jī's "Record of Luòyáng."
Frontier Gate
Zhāng Zhāo remonstrated with Sūn Quán,
but he did not comply,
so Zhāng Zhāo claimed illness and did not attend court.
Sūn Quán resented him for this,
and had earth piled up against his gate.
Zhāng Zhāo then also piled up earth from inside to seal it.
Later, Sūn Quán passed by his gate while going out and called to Zhāng Zhāo,
but Zhāng Zhāo declined, saying his illness was severe.
Sūn Quán set fire to his gate,
intending to frighten him,
but Zhāng Zhāo instead closed his door more tightly.
Sūn Quán had his men extinguish the fire and wait at the gate.
After a long while,
Zhāng Zhāo's sons together helped him rise,
and Sūn Quán carried him back to the palace in his carriage.
"Records of Wú"
Inscribed on the Gate
Lú Dān of Guǎngzhōu served as a junior official in the province and possessed immortal arts.
The provincial governor Bù Zhì despised him,
reported his case,
and intended to execute him.
Later, Lú Dān inscribed the word "execution" on his gate,
stating that though the state with execution gates still exists,
in the year Wúshè, should one wish to know,
this writing would return to Lú Dān.
The governor ordered it scraped off,
but the characters regrew as they were scraped away.
(Records of Commanderies and States)
Returning to Simplicity
Jī Hán was studious and skilled in composing essays.
His home was at Bóqiū in Gǒng County,
and he styled himself Master Bóqiū.
His gate was named the Gate of Returning to Thickness,
and his chamber was called the Chamber of Careful Endings.
(From the Biography of Jìn)
The vermilion gates
Qū Yǔn,
a native of Jīnchéng,
whose family and the Yóu clan had been powerful families for generations.
In the western provinces, there was a saying about them:
"The Qū and the Yóu,
their sheep and cattle are beyond count,
their southern mansions are vermilion chambers,
they do not gaze upon blue towers."
I acted privately.
During Emperor Yuán's reign, the Commandant of Justice Zhāng Kǎi lived in the Small Market area,
where he privately built a main gate for the neighborhood,
closing it early and opening it late.
The common people were troubled by this,
and when their appeals to the prefectural government went unaddressed,
they proceeded to beat the Drum of Appeal at the palace.
Still, their case was not adjudicated.
Upon hearing that Minister of Works Hè was traveling,
they went as a group to Pògǎng to petition Hè collectively.
They complained to Hè, saying:
"We are but common laborers,
and the officials in charge of rites pay no heed to our plight."
The people kowtowed and said:
"If Your Excellency also fails to redress this matter,
we will have nowhere else to turn."
Hè did not respond immediately,
but instructed them to go see Commandant of Justice Zhāng first,
assuring them he would take up the matter.
When Zhāng heard of this, he immediately had the gate demolished,
and personally went to Fāngshān to welcome Hè.
When Hè emerged, he declined the gesture, saying:
"This matter did not necessarily require my intervention,
but out of friendship with your family,
I felt compelled to take pity on the people."
Zhāng was ashamed,
and apologized, saying:
"I, your humble servant, was at fault in this matter,
and had I known earlier, I would have dismantled it long ago."
From A New Account of the Tales of the World.
Báimén
In the final years of Emperor Sòng Míngdì, there were many taboos.
The Yíyáng Gate was called the White Gate,
and the emperor considered it inauspicious and avoided mentioning it.
Once, the Assistant Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs, Jiāng Mì, mistakenly referred to it,
causing the emperor to change his expression and say:
"Whiten your own family's gate."
"Basic Annals"
Dàxià
To the north of Luòyáng, there are two gates.
The one on the western end is called Dàxià Mén,
known as Xià Mén in the Hàn Dynasty,
and Dàxià Mén in the Wèi and Jìn Dynasties.
A three-story tower was once built here,
rising two hundred feet above the ground.
The gate towers of Luòyáng are all two stories high,
standing one hundred feet above the ground,
but only the ridgepole of Dàxià Mén reaches the clouds.
"A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luòyáng"
Zhū Bái
Emperor Yuán of Liáng ordered Hú Sēngyòu to reinforce Wáng Sēngbiàn.
As he was about to depart,
he tearfully told his son:
"You may open the red and white gates.
If I do not triumph, I will die.
If auspicious, I shall return through the red gate;
if inauspicious, through the white gate."
Emperor Yuán, upon hearing this, admired his resolve.
Advancing to the Chìshā Pavilion,
he met with Lù Fǎhé's arrival,
and together they dealt a major defeat to Hóu Jǐng's forces,
capturing the army of Rèn Yuē,
and sending Yuē to Jiānglíng.
(From *The History of the Southern Dynasties*)
Lùmén
In the third year of the Jiàndé era of Emperor Wǔ, on the Rénxū day of the first month,
he held court for his officials at the Lù Gate.
The "Zhōu Shū" records
that Shěn Zhòng lectured on the "Analects" at the Lù Gate Hall.
The "Yù Hǎi"
Long Sealed
When Gāozǔ first became the Governor of Dìngzhōu,
the west gate of Dìngzhōu city had long been sealed and unused.
During the reign of Emperor Wénxuān of Qí,
someone requested to open it
to facilitate travel,
but the emperor refused,
saying:
"A sage shall come to open it."
When Gāozǔ arrived and opened it,
all were astonished.
Book of Suí
County gate
The gate of Wànnián County,
was built by Yǔwén Kǎi.
At the end of Emperor Gāozōng's reign,
when Princess Tàipíng was married,
the county office was used as the wedding residence.
As the county gate was too narrow,
it was intended to be demolished.
Emperor Gāozōng decreed:
"It was built by Yǔwén Kǎi,
and should not be dismantled for other purposes.
Thus the gate was preserved."
From Wéi Shù's "Records of the Western Capital"
Chūnmíng
In the fifth month of the seventeenth year of the Kāiyuán era, on the day Dīngmǎo,
attendants and officials below feasted at the garden pond of Nìngwáng Lǐ Xiàn outside the Chūnmíng Gate,
while the Emperor watched from the Huā'è Tower and invited them,
ordering the returning cavalry to sit, drink, and dance in turn,
with graded rewards bestowed accordingly.
"Veritable Records"
Wáng Yá's poem:
"Do not say the two capitals are not a distant parting,
Outside the Chūnmíng Gate lies the world's edge."
Guāng Fàn
The princess received the investiture,
with the investiture table and temporary quarters set up outside the Guangfàn Gate and the Chánglè Gate.
The Tōngdiǎn records
Hán Yù's letter to the prime minister,
submitted while kneeling outside the Guangfàn Gate.
Door pivots
The noble relatives feared their households would be inauspicious,
and gathered all auspicious names,
feared their gates would not be sturdy,
and made iron pivots for them.
Ultimately, the reason for their downfall
was not due to suffering from taboos,
nor because their door pivots rotted when new,
but constantly suffering from hoarding wealth and acting arrogantly and presumptuously,
oppressing the common people and losing the people's hearts.
"Qiánfū Lùn"
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, the princes and marquises
had deep halls and multiple staircases,
with golden pivots and white steps.
"Fùzǐ"
Mr. Lǔ Zhònglián met Lord Mèngcháng at the gate of Xìng Hall,
and Lord Mèngcháng said:
"I have heard that you, sir, possess the art of leverage and strategy;
may I hear about it?"
Lián replied:
"The art of leverage and strategy
is like a door bolt:
if lifting it is convenient,
then one finger can hold the center
and raise it; but if it is inconvenient,
then even two hands cannot move the bolt.
It is not that the weight has increased,
nor that the two hands have become weaker.
What determines the outcome
is not the act of lifting itself,
but the feasibility of lifting;
only when it can be lifted does one apply leverage—this is what is called the art of leverage and strategy.
From 'The Book of Lǔ Liánzǐ':
The Qian hexagram of Great Accumulation signifies metal,
pillars of iron and bolts secure to guard against disaster;
the nobleman dwells therein,
peaceful and free from worry and doubt.
From 'Forest of Changes'
House
A large house is called a wǔ.
Wǔ
means to cover.
To cover
means to shelter.
People in Bìng and Jì call it yǎ.
Yǎ
means correct,
referring to the house being correct and large.
In the "Shì Míng",
a house
means warmth,
as its interior is warm and cozy.
Above,
the guest hall is called yǎ.
From the "Tōng Sú Wén".
Yīn Wū
The system of the ruler's main hall is the Yin chamber,
also known as the Xia chamber,
while ministers and high officials have the Xia chamber,
with the northern half partitioned as the main room,
and the southern half as the hall's main room and purification chamber.
Cuī Kǎi's "Rules for Mourning Attire"
Yellow Canopy
The yellow canopy was not Yáo's heart.
Selected Texts
When Xiàng Yǔ besieged Hàn at Xíngyáng,
Jì Xìn deceived the Chǔ army,
riding in the royal carriage with a yellow canopy,
and with the left banner said:
"The King of Hàn surrenders to Chǔ,"
thus enabling the King of Hàn to escape.
Hàn Shū
The Son of Heaven's carriage used yellow silk for the canopy lining.
Annotation
Xuē Fàng passed the imperial examinations,
by nature he was upright and of few words.
Emperor Xiànzōng sought virtuous scholars for the Crown Prince's education in poetry and classics,
to assist in teaching the classics,
and selected him to serve as the tutor to the Crown Prince.
When Emperor Mùzōng ascended the throne,
during the time when he had not yet taken control of the government,
Fàng was often at his side, privately offering advice on crucial matters.
Emperor Mùzōng often said to Fàng:
"I newly inherit the grand treasure,
fearing I may not succeed in bearing it.
You, sir, should become the chancellor,
to assist where I fall short."
Fàng bowed his head and said:
"I am truly shallow in talent,
yet being able to serve under the imperial canopy,
it is not enough to rashly assume the high office of chancellor."
He was naturally virtuous and capable,
his words without embellishment,
all of his actions were of this kind.
Emperor Mùzōng deeply appreciated his sincerity,
and thus summoned him to an audience at the Sīzhèng Hall,
bestowing upon him robes of gold and purple.
"Old Táng"
Thatched Cottage
The Duke of Zhōu, while occupying the esteemed position of Prime Minister,
still humbled himself before scholars from humble dwellings,
receiving one hundred and seventy individuals daily.
In the "Family Sayings,"
Xiāo Wàngzhī remarked to Huò Guāng:
"I fear this does not resemble the Duke of Zhōu assisting King Chéng,
personally practicing the etiquette of spitting out food and grasping hands,
to win the hearts of those in humble dwellings."
The "Original Biography"
explains that "humble dwellings" refer to houses with plain roofs,
thatched with cogon grass.
Annotation
Golden House
Emperor Wǔ was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jiāodōng at the age of four.
The Elder Princess often held him on her lap,
and asked him:
"Do you want a wife, child?"
The Elder Princess pointed to over a hundred attendants on her left and right,
but he said he didn't want any of them.
Then she pointed to her own daughter and asked:
"Is Ājiāo nice?"
He replied with a laugh:
"Yes,
if I could have Ājiāo as my wife,
I would store her in a golden house."
The Elder Princess was greatly pleased,
and persistently entreated the Emperor,
so they were married.
"Stories of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn"
Shénwū
Above was erected a divine hall of nine bays,
cast with bronze pillars,
gilded with gold,
large and five arm-spans around,
with red kingfisher feathers forming the steps and rafters,
carved in gold and tortoiseshell into dragons, tigers, birds, and beasts,
thinly overlaid upon them,
the rafter ends all shaped as dragon heads holding bells in their mouths,
with tassels suspended from them,
cast bronze tiles,
using red and white litharge as mortar,
mixed with pepper juice,
overlaid thinly with fire-polished mirrors,
fans and screens all made of white glass,
their light shining through brilliantly,
curtains of white pearls,
weighed down with tortoiseshell,
beds of ivory,
then with glass beads, jade, bright moons, and night-shining pearls,
intermingled with rare treasures from across the land to form the A-canopy,
and next the B-canopy,
the A for housing the deities,
the B for the emperor's own use,
the front courtyard planted with king trees,
coral for branches,
green jade for leaves,
some blue, some red,
all made of pearls and jade.
The seeds were all hollow inside,
like small bells clinking,
sounding from the roof ridge,
crafted golden phoenixes soaring aloft,
as if flying with tassels in their mouths,
over ten zhang long,
with mica windows and coral windows,
even the Kunlun Mystic Garden could not surpass this.
"Stories from the Inner Biography of Emperor Wu of Han"
Fèng Zuò
Zhōnglí Yì served as the magistrate of Tángyì County.
Upon arrival, there was no official residence.
Yì then used his salary to build one.
The people contributed pillars and eagerly assisted in the construction.
It was completed within ten days.
Upon finishing, he made a vow to the local deities on behalf of the people:
"The one who initiated this project is the magistrate.
If any misfortune arises,
may the magistrate bear the consequences."
The people were greatly pleased.
From "Dōngguān Hànjì".
Build a house
Shì Yí, styled Zǐyǔ,
did not manage any property in his personal life,
and when building a house,
it was just enough to accommodate his needs.
His neighbor constructed a large mansion,
and when Sūn Quán went out and saw the newly built house,
his attendants said:
"That is Shì Yí's home."
Sūn Quán replied:
"Shì Zǐyǔ is frugal;
this surely cannot be his."
He sent someone to verify in person,
and it indeed turned out to be the neighbor's house.
"Records of Wú"
Three rooms
Sītú Cài was in Luòyáng,
where he saw Lù Jī and his brother living in three rooms of an official's residence,
with Shìlóng residing in the eastern one,
and Shìhéng in the western one.
Shìlóng was gentle and amiable in character,
while Shìhéng was over seven chǐ tall,
his voice resonant like a bell,
and his words often impassioned and fervent.
From "Shì Shuō"
Carved Pillars
Hóngnóng Wáng Cuì, as a noble prince, married the princess,
his residence was magnificent,
with a portrait of Zhuāng Zhōu in the chamber,
gathering many court officials,
and ordering Jī Hán to compose a eulogy for it.
Jī Hán took up the brush to write a preface,
without pausing for corrections,
which read:
"Imperial son-in-law Wáng Hóngyuǎn,
with splendid ponds and lavish houses,
widely invites worthy talents,
portraying the true man
in a hall with carved rafters,
placing the recluse in a hall of ambition.
Alas,
the noble traces of the master,
why confine them to dwelling in mountain caves while alive,
and entrust them to ornate pillars in death?
Placed in an inappropriate setting,
there is disgrace even after death."
Wáng Cuì showed a ashamed expression.
"Jìn Biography"
Thatched hut
Huán Wēn appointed Luó Hán as his assistant military commander,
but because the government office was noisy and disruptive,
unsuitable for a tranquil dwelling,
he built a thatched hut on a small islet in the western city pond.
Bamboos and fruit trees shaded the courtyard,
he cut wood to make a bed,
wove reeds into a mat,

plank house
In Qínzhōu, it is customary to value physical strength,

Since the roof shelters human forms

why should they be harmed by the year or month?
If one must select dates for these,
then similarly for outfitting carts and crafting boats,
one should also choose days.

Pánlóng

In the studio, five-colored clouds often swirled,
resembling coiled dragons;
above the roof, purple clouds constantly rose,

Those watching from afar
were all astonished by the sight.

Bend the chimney
Chúnyú Kūn went to a neighbor's house,
saw that their chimney flue was straight,
with firewood piled beside it,
and said to them:
"This straightness invites fire;
you should make the flue bent and move the firewood away."
The neighbor did not listen.
Later, as expected, their house burned down.
The neighbor put out the fire with help,
then cooked a lamb and prepared wine to thank those who helped fight the fire,
but refused to invite Kūn to know.
A scholar mocked this, saying:
"Bending the flue and moving firewood brings no great favor,
while the scorched and battered become honored guests."
This laments how they devalued the root and prized the branch.
Huán Tán's "New Treatise"

Sacrifice to the Kitchen God
During Emperor Wǔ's reign,
Lǐ Shàojūn was presented to the emperor through his methods of sacrificial altars, cave stoves, grain diets, and longevity techniques,
claiming that sacrificial altars could summon supernatural beings,
and with these beings, cinnabar could be transformed into gold,
once the gold was produced,
using it for food and drink vessels would prolong life,
and with prolonged life, the immortals of Pénglái in the sea could be seen,
and by performing the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices, one could achieve immortality,
as Huángdì had done.

Nourishing Life
In the first year of the Yuánfèng era of Emperor Zhāo,
a pig from the Yān King Liú Dàn's palace's inner lane came out of the pigsty,

the foundation of livelihood and nourishment.

The wind blows
Lǐ Nánmíng was skilled in wind divination,
and his daughter also understood the family's art.
She became the wife of a man from Yóuquán County.
One morning when she entered the kitchen,
a sudden violent wind arose.
The woman immediately went to the main hall to ask her mother-in-law for permission to return home,
bidding farewell to her parents.
Her mother-in-law would not allow it,
so she knelt and wept, saying:
"Our family has passed down this art through generations.
When a sudden gust of wind arises
and blows through the stove pipe and well,
this misfortune falls upon the woman in charge of the kitchen.
I am about to die,
and the prediction should record my death date."
She was then permitted to return home,
and she fell ill and died exactly as predicted.

The Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Zhōng appointed

set up a sacrificial stove in his dwelling,

A chicken entered
When Biàn Bóyù was serving as the governor of Dōngyáng Commandery,

A chicken entered from a distance through the opening,
and after a long while, it went in through the chimney.

and it crowed and pecked as usual.

The Kitchen God
Huángdì created the kitchen stove,

Huáinánzǐ
The Kitchen God returns to heaven on the last day of the lunar month,
to report human transgressions.
Wàn Bì Shù
The Kitchen God's name is Kuí,
appearing like a beautiful woman.
Also said to be surnamed Zhāng, named Dān,
courtesy name Zǐguō,
his wife's courtesy name Qīngjì,
with six daughters,
all named Cházhì.
They always on the last day of the lunar month,
ascend to heaven to report human offenses,
major offenses result in loss of a jì,
a jì being three hundred days;
minor offenses result in loss of a suàn,
a suàn being one hundred days.
Thus serving as the Heavenly Emperor's supervising envoy,
and below as earth spirits.
On the jǐchǒu day at sunrise,
ascending to heaven during the mǎo hour and descending before noon to perform duties.
Making offerings on this day brings blessings.

Subordinate deities include the Heavenly Emperor's Tender Grandson, Heavenly Emperor's Great Officer, Heavenly Emperor's Commandant, Heavenly Emperor's Elder Brother, Boy on the Whetstone, Purple Lord of the Chimney, Lord of Great Harmony, Lady of the Jade Pond, etc.
Another account says the Kitchen God's name is Rǎngzǐ.

Dream
During the reign of Duke Líng of Wèi, Mí Zixiá enjoyed great favor,
and monopolized power in Wèi. A dwarf who gained an audience with the duke said:
"My dream has come true."
The duke asked:
"What dream?"
He replied:
"I dreamed of a stove, and now I see you."
The duke angrily said:
"I have heard that those who see their ruler dream of the sun,
why did you dream of a stove?"
He said:
"The sun illuminates the whole world,
and no single thing can block it;
a ruler illuminates his entire state,
and no single person can monopolize him.
Therefore, those who are to see their ruler dream of the sun.
But if one person warms himself at the stove,
then others cannot see its fire.
Now perhaps there is someone who is warming himself at your stove,
so even if I dreamed of a stove,
isn't that appropriate?"

Confused

Toilet

Hédōng Shuò Mànqīng entered the mountains to learn the ways of immortals,

In the past, Huáinán Wáng Liú Ān ascended to heaven,

Nightmare

Without wearing a hat

crossing the sea and encountering a storm,

Guǎn Níng thought he had no transgressions,

Passing the furnace
Liú Jìhé had a fondness for fragrance,
and whenever he went to the restroom,
he would pass by the incense burner on his return.
His aide Zhāng Tǎn remarked:
"People say you act like a commoner,
and indeed it's true."
Jìhé replied:
"When Lord Xún visited someone's home and sat for three days,
the fragrance lingered without fading.
How do I compare?
If Lord Xún disliked it,
then I love it."
Tǎn said:
"In ancient times there was a beautiful woman
who suffered and held her heart while frowning,
and all who saw her thought her lovely.
Her ugly neighbor imitated her,
but all who saw her fled.
Do you wish to make me flee as well?"
Jìhé laughed heartily,
and through this came to understand Tǎn.

Wéi Chéngqìng,
styled Yánxiū,
passed the imperial examination for advanced scholars (jìnshì) at a young age.
His beautiful literary style was unrivaled at his time.
He was repeatedly promoted to the position of Palace Secretary of Debate.
The Crown Prince Xián was in charge of state affairs,
avoiding indulgence in music and women.
Chéngqìng submitted a memorial advising him, saying:
"Your Highness stands like a mountain and is deep like a pool,
with virtues of gold and jade.
The hundred officials look up to your brilliance,
and the people hear the sound like recurring thunder.
In living, apparel, and possessions, you must adhere to thrift,
and avoid excessive hunting and pleasure,
to be able to enjoy enduring happiness and fortune,
and long preserve prosperity and righteousness."
He also composed the "Exhortation to Good Conduct" to present to the Crown Prince,
who rewarded him generously.

and was reassigned as the Tutor to the Crown Prince.

Female Servants
In Shí Chóng's toilet, there were always over ten maidservants standing in attendance,
all dressed in beautiful garments and adorned with elegant ornaments.
They had prepared items such as shell powder and eaglewood juice,
leaving nothing unprepared.
Moreover, they provided new clothes for guests to change into,
causing many visitors to feel too embarrassed
to use the toilet.
When Wáng Dūn went there,
he removed his old clothes,
put on the new ones,
with an expression of pride and composure.
The maidservants said to one another:
"This guest is surely capable of becoming a rebel."
From "Shì Shuō".
The Brocade Pouch
Jìn Tàiwèi Liú Shí visited Shí Chóng,
and when he went to the toilet, he saw crimson silk curtains,
a large bed with beautiful cushions and mats,
and two maids holding brocade incense pouches.
Shí immediately turned and hurried away,
then said to Chóng:
"I mistakenly entered your private chamber just now."
Chóng replied:
"That was the toilet."
Shí said:
"A poor scholar like me has never experienced anything like this."
He then went to another toilet.

Xiàguǒ
When Wáng Dūn first went to pay respects to Princess Wǔyáng,
he entered the restroom and saw a lacquered box filled with dried dates,
which were originally meant to block the nose.
Wáng thought that fruits were also served in the restroom,
so he ate them all.
After returning,
a maid held out a golden basin filled with water,
and a glass bowl containing bath beans.

thinking it was dried rice.

To set up a libation ceremony
Guō Pú had always been on friendly terms with Huán Yí.
Whenever Yí visited him,
if he happened to find Pú with his wife,
he would enter directly.
Pú said:
"You may come straight in
in other places,
but you must not seek me out in the toilet.
If you do, both host and guest will suffer calamity."
Later, Yí went to see Pú while drunk,
and happened to find him in the toilet.
He peered through a crack and saw
Pú naked with his hair loose,
holding a knife in his mouth and performing a libation.

he beat his chest in great alarm and said:

During Emperor Wén's reign, Shěn Qìngzhī

The Lavatory Ghost
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Jìnshì Lǐ Chì from Wú commandery traveled to Mǐn with Zhào Mǐnzhī.
They lodged at a post station's pavilion,
when at midnight a woman suddenly entered the courtyard.
Lǐ Chì immediately rose, descended the steps, and bowed in greeting.
After a long while,
he went up to the hall, took paper and brush, and wrote a letter to his family,
saying:
"I, so-and-so, have been chosen by Lady Guō
to be her son-in-law."
The woman then slapped his scarf and strangled him with it.
Zhào Mǐnzhī ran out shouting loudly,
whereupon the woman arranged her scarf and fled.
When they looked at his letter,
Lǐ Chì had done as if in a dream.
The next day they traveled together again by daylight,
but Lǐ Chì went missing once more.
Zhào Mǐnzhī hurried after him,
and found Lǐ Chì sitting in the latrine,
who said angrily:
"I was just about to perform the ceremonial thanks,
when you startled me."
After ten days they reached Mǐn,
where colleagues who were old friends of Lǐ Chì held a banquet.
During the feast, Lǐ Chì disappeared again.
Zhào Mǐnzhī urgently searched for him in the latrine,
and found Lǐ Chì lying stiff on the ground,
having died from breath stoppage.

squatting on the toilet
Wáng Shēng once walked to a house's fence,
where he saw a creature with both hands gripping the latrine,
deep-set eyes, a tiger's nose, and a pig's body,

See the form

Sacrificial Report
In Táizhōu, there was a commoner named Wáng,
who often worshipped the toilet deity.
One day, when he went to the place,
he saw a woman dressed in yellow who said:
"I am the toilet deity.
Have you ever heard the words of ants?"
The commoner replied:
"No, I haven't."
Then she took a small box from her bosom,
dipped her finger in a little ointment,
like lip rouge, and applied it under his right ear,
admonishing him:
"If you see ants,
tilt your ear and listen carefully,
and you will surely gain something."
The next morning, the commoner saw a swarm of ants bustling under the pillar base.
When he listened, he indeed heard them
talking about moving their nest to a warmer place.
A nearby ant asked why,
and they replied that there was treasure below,
which was very cold,
making it uncomfortable to live there.
The commoner waited until the ants had all left,
searched the spot,
and obtained ten ingots of silver.

Wūtóu
Common people call the toilet "wūtóu",
as it is said that people in Bìngzhōu all dig earth to build rooms,
and the toilet is located above the living quarters.
Another account states that Emperor Wénxuān of the Northern Qí dynasty was angry with his Wèi Commandery assistant Cuī Shūbǎo,
and poured toilet water over his head.
Later generations either ate there or avoided it,
and elders could not directly say "hùn" (toilet),
so they indirectly referred to it as "pouring over the head".

Villa
Shí Chòng delighted in unrestrained freedom,
sincerely loving forests and marshes,
so he retreated contentedly to his estate in Héyáng,
where his residence was designed
with a long embankment behind it,
and a clear canal in front,
nearly ten thousand cypress trees,
flowing water encircling the house,
with viewing pavilions, towers, ponds, and pools,
and many birds and fish raised there.
"Longing for Home"
Tǔshān
Xiè Ān built villas and pavilions on Tǔshān,
with abundant forests and bamboo,
often taking his inner and outer nephews on outings,
gathering for feasts,
and repeatedly spending hundreds of gold coins.
"Basic Biography"
Betting on the Villa
When Fú Jiān invaded,
Xiè Ān and Xiè Xuán hosted a banquet for relatives and friends at the villa on Tǔshān.
As they were about to part, Xiè Xuán challenged Xiè Ān to a game of Go, betting the villa.
Xiè Ān's Go skills were usually inferior to Xiè Xuán's,
but that day Xiè Xuán felt apprehensive,
and thus lost.
Xiè Ān said to his nephew Yáng Tán:
"I give the villa to you."
In the Song Dynasty, it belonged to Tán Dào,
named Tánchéng,
referred to as Chéngzǐ Shù on maps.
Wēn Tíngyún of the Tang Dynasty wrote in his "Poem of Xiè Gōng's Villa":
"South of the Vermilion Sparrow Bridge, fragrant paths wind,
Connecting to the spring greenery of Master Xiè's eastern villa."
By imperial decree, I take
Wáng Qiān had an old estate at Zhōngshān,
covering over eighty qǐng,
which he cultivated together with various relatives and old friends.
He often said to people:
"I am not as fortunate as Zhèng Gōngyè, who owned four hundred qǐng of farmland,
yet often lacked sufficient food;
I feel ashamed by this comparison."
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng built the Great Temple of Reverence west of Zhōngshān,
the part of Qiān's estate adjacent to the temple
was originally the farmland granted to Wáng Dǎo.
The emperor sent a secretary to deliver an edict demanding the land,
to which Qiān replied:
"This land is not for sale;
if it is taken by imperial decree, I dare not protest."
The emperor grew angry,
then referred the matter to the market to assess the land's value,
and reimbursed him at the forced price.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Yuánzhuāng
Yuán Bànqiān's estate is located in Jiāodàichuān,
resting against the White Deer Plain to the north,
with lotus ponds and bamboo pathways,
rose trellises and crabapple trees,
a cave meeting scenic hall,
flower terraces and herb gardens,
millstones for grinding hemp and rice.
A local proverb says:
"Heaven above,
Yuán's estate below."
Records of Cháng'ān
Wǎng Chuān
Wáng Wéi acquired Sòng Zhīwèn's Lántián villa,
located at Wǎngkǒu,
where the Wǎng River encircled the residence,
with additional bamboo islets and flower banks,
he and his friend Péi Dí boated along the river,
playing the qin and composing poetry,
chanting and singing all day long,
collecting the poems about his rural life,
titled the Collection of Wǎngchuān.
Old Book of Táng
My villa lies in the Wǎngchuān valley,

with scenic spots including Mèngchéng'ào, Huázǐgāng, Wénxìngguǎn, Jīnzhúlǐng, Lùzhài, Mùlánzhài, Zhūyúpàn, Gōng Huái Bǎi, Línhú Tíng, Nán Zhái, Qīhú Liǔlàng, Luánjiā Lài, Jīnxiè Quán, Báishí Tān, Běi Tuó, Zhúlǐ Guǎn, Xīnyí Wù, Qīyuán, etc.,
where Péi Dí and I leisurely composed quatrains.
Collection of Wǎngchuān
After his mother passed away,
he petitioned to convert his Wǎngchuān estate into a temple.
New Book of Táng
South of the city
Zhāng Shǒuguī was implicated in bribing a eunuch,
Niú Xiāntóng offended Lǐ Línfǔ,
who had long harbored jealousy,
Xiāo Sōng thus stated:
"Sōng once gifted Xiāntóng a villa south of the city,
and was demoted as a result."
The New Book of Tang
records Xiāo Sōng requesting retirement to a forest garden,
where he cultivated herbs and practiced alchemy for personal contentment.
The Old Book of Tang
Zhāoyìng
Xiāo Fù, courtesy name Lǚchū,
was the grandson of Xiāo Sōng.
He served as a palace gate official.
During the Guǎngdé era, a famine struck and his family fell into poverty,
so he planned to sell his villa at Zhāoyìng.
At that time, the chancellor Wáng Jìn, having heard of the beauty of its woods and springs,
coveted it in his heart.
He then sent his younger brother Wáng Hóng to tempt Xiāo Fù with an important official post.
Xiāo Fù replied:
"I am selling my ancestral property due to family poverty,
intending to use the proceeds to save and support my widowed mother and young children.
If I were to exchange it for a prestigious position for myself,
only to let my family members suffer from cold and hunger,
that would not be the intention of a lowly man like me."
Wáng Jìn resented him for this,
and subsequently had Xiāo Fù dismissed from his post.
From the Old Book of Táng
Jìyuán
Xiāo Fǔ, courtesy name Sīqiān,
was the great-grandson of Xiāo Sōng.
His mother, of the Wéi family, was virtuous and wise,
and managed the household strictly.
Although Fǔ served as chancellor,
he attended to his mother by her side
no differently than when he wore coarse cloth.
After retiring from office,
to avoid the bother of visits from officials and guests in Luoyang
during festivals and seasons,
he returned to his estate in Jìyuán,
roaming freely in the mountains and fields,
chanting and reciting poetry all year long.
In the second year of the Kāichéng era,
his younger brother Xiāo Chù was appointed Prefect of Chǔ Prefecture.
On the day of his farewell audience,
Emperor Wénzōng said to Chù:
"I bestow upon Fǔ an imperial edict and bolts of silk.
You shall take them to Jìyuán
and convey my sentiments to him."
Demolish
Yáng Wǎn was appointed chancellor,
and Cuī Kuān, the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
younger brother of Cuī Níng, the military governor of Jiànnán,
whose family was wealthy,
owned a villa south of the imperial city,
with ponds, halls, terraces, and pavilions
that were considered the finest of the time.
Kuān secretly had it demolished that very day.
(Old Book of Táng)
Recluse Scholar
Wēn Zào, styled Jiǎnyú,
prided himself on his moral integrity,
secluded himself on Mount Wángwū to fish,
devoting himself to a carefree life,
and people called his dwelling the "Hermitage of the Recluse."
"Old and New"
Family Villa
Péi Xiū, courtesy name Gōngměi,
was strict and upright in his conduct.
He and his brothers lived in seclusion at their family villa,
lecturing on classics by day,
writing books by night,
and never leaving their home all year round.
"Tang Dynasty"
Dù Shù
Hán Chānglí's "Nánshān Shī" states:

Annotation:
Dù Shù,
is Dùlíng,

Yùtán Zhuāng
Lǒngxī Lǐ Yòuqīng, courtesy name Chángfū,
during the Dàlì era served as Right Assistant Director while governing Chúzhōu,
with a separate estate in Chángzhōu,
Yìxīng said:
"The Jade Pool Manor is in Chúzhōu,
at that time he entrusted a letter to Dúgū Zhìzhī,
Dúgū sent back a poem saying:
'Each day I long for the jade trees,
Every letter speaks of the jade pool'
and wrote of the jade pool:
'Green jade but an empty name,
An ice vessel cannot match its virtue.
Only the heart in silent reflection,
May compare with its deep swirling colors.'
What Yòuqīng called:
'Weary in minor office, heart tired and slow,
In old mountains desolate, waters deep and swirling.'"
Wǔqiáo
Péi Dù established his residence in the Eastern Capital,
building hills and digging ponds at Jíxián Lane,
where bamboos and trees grew in lush clusters,
featuring breeze pavilions and waterside kiosks,
with ladder bridges and elevated corridors,
islands winding around each other,
embodying the finest scenery of the capital.
He also built a villa at Wǔqiáo,
with tens of thousands of flowering trees,
in the midst of which stood cool terraces and summer lodges,
named the Lǜyě Hall.
Sweet waters flowed through it,
channeled into branching streams,
reflecting and adorning both sides.
During breaks from official duties,
Péi Dù feasted all day with poets Bái Jūyì and Liú Yǔxī,
singing loudly and speaking freely,
finding joy in poetry, wine, zither, and books,
with renowned scholars of the time all following him in excursions.
From the Old Book of Tang,
Péi inscribed about the Southern Manor:
"Rustics don't recognize the Secretariat Director,
mistaking him for Táo or Xiè's household."
Bái Jūyì harmonized:
"Táo's humble hut cannot compare,
Xiè's secluded villa isn't worth aspiring to.
Why then the thirty-six peaks of Sōng Mountain,
forever following Shēn and Fǔ as their home mountains?"
From the Chángqìng Collection, mutual references to the hall
Zhāng Qíxián retired as Minister of Works and returned to Luòyáng,
acquired Péi Dù's Wǔqiáo estate,
with its splendid ponds, kiosks, pines, and bamboos,
daily drinking and composing poetry there with relatives and old friends,
his mood profoundly relaxed and content.
From the History of Song biography
Píngquán
Lǐ Déyù established his Pingquan Villa south of Yīquē in the Eastern Capital,
with clear streams and emerald bamboos,
trees and rocks of secluded wonder.
In his early years before entering officialdom,
he lectured and studied there.
After serving as a regional military governor and general,
then as a chief minister for thirty years,
he never revisited the place,
yet his inscribed poems and songs
were all engraved on stone.
The Old Book of Tang records:
When Déyù first developed Pingquan,
people from distant lands often presented him with rare objects.
One poem inscribed at Pingquan reads:
"Nobles from Lǒngyòu offered talking birds,
the Governor of Rìnán sent famed flowers."
The Jù Tán Lù notes:
Wāng Zūn's poem "Píngquán Zhuāng" says:
"Springs, flowers, and trees favor tall groves,
Mount Sōng and Shào stretch boundless before the eyes.
Distressed by the injustices of this human world,
today I find myself south of the Hǎi."
The Tángshī Jìshì
praises:
The Duke's Pingquan Estate,
spanning ten lǐ in circumference,
had over a hundred pavilions and towers constructed,
with exotic flowers and rare grasses from across the land,
precious pines and wondrous stones,
all gathered there.
Among them,
Déyù thus personally compiled the "Record of Plants at Pingquan."
Now all lies in ruins and extinction,
only the goose-wing junipers, pearl cypresses, lotus-pod jade stamens, etc.,
barely remain.
There were numerous famous varieties of strange stones,
some taken by powerful figures from Luòchéng,
only the Worship-Star Stone and Lion Stone were later moved by Academician Táo to his Liáng Garden villa.
Jiǎshì Tán Lù
Dōng Shù
When Qián Yuánliáo, Prince of Guangling of Wuyue, commanded the region of Wu,
his son, Yáqián Commander Wén Fèng, established the Southern Garden east of Jing Villa,
which he developed over thirty years,
achieving the utmost in garden and pond beauty.
Rare flowers and exotic trees,
numbering tens of thousands of renowned varieties,
by the time he witnessed them,
had all grown to arm-span girth.
He also piled earth to form hills,
which became cliffs and valleys,
and in his later years, he continued planning without cease.
Whenever he hosted feasts there,
he let guests roam as they pleased,
while Wén Fèng rode a white donkey,
draped in a crane-feather cloak,
strolling slowly along flower-lined paths,
or drifted in a boat on the pond,
moving leisurely back and forth.
Hearing guests' laughter and chatter,
he would join them to drink,
such was his passion for these pleasures.
From "The Supplementary History of Wuyue and the Records of the Nine States."
Wall
A wall that provides concealment is called a qiáng,
which is a wall or barrier.
In the Shuōwén,
a qiáng is referred to as a yōng.
In the Ěryǎ,
yōng
means a wall or barrier.
In the Guǎngyǎ,
yōng
means to contain,
as it serves to conceal and hide one's appearance.
A wall (bì)
means secluded,
as it is used to ward off wind and cold.
A qiáng
means to obstruct,
as it serves to shield and conceal oneself.
A barrier (yuán)
means to support,
as people rely on it for protection and defense.
In the Shìmíng,
a qiáng
is used to guard against unexpected events.
Bēn Yōng
The Son of Heaven has a grand wall,
while the feudal lords have a diminishing wall.
Zhèng Xuán comments:
"Grand"
means large,
indicating that the wall is straight and upright.
"Diminishing"
means to reduce.
"Wall"
also refers to the wall.
It signifies reducing its top and bottom,
so it cannot be straight and upright.

featuring five layers of halls,

Book Collection
Dù Ān, styled Bóyí,
had noble aspirations from a young age.
At thirteen, he entered school,
and was called a child prodigy.
Noble relatives in the capital admired his reputation,
and some sent him letters.
Dù Ān did not open them,
but stored them all hidden in a wall.
Later, when there were arrests and investigations of noble relatives and their guests,
Dù Ān opened the wall and brought out the letters,
their seals intact as before.
He ultimately avoided calamity,
and was highly regarded by people of the time.

Below the foundation
Shǐ Shūbīn was
a person from Chénliú.
He enjoyed great fame from a young age.
Guō Línzōng, upon meeting him, remarked to others:
"A high wall with a low foundation
will surely collapse even if it stands for a time."
Later, indeed, Shǐ Shūbīn ruined his reputation by engaging in biased and unjust arguments.

Cài Mào, styled Déguī,
was a native of Xiāngyáng,
whose home was on Cài Isle.
His residence was exceptionally fine,
with all four walls constructed of blue stone and corner joints,
and he had several hundred maids and concubines,
along with forty or fifty separate estates.
"Records of the Elderly and Ancient"
Penetrating the Wall
Lǚ Méng fell ill,
while Sūn Quán was in Jiāng'ān at the time,
he had him brought to the inner palace for treatment and care.
He wished to see his countenance repeatedly by all means,
yet feared to disturb him.
He often peered at him through a hole in the wall;
if he saw that he could eat a little, he was delighted,
otherwise, he would sigh in distress.

Lying beneath the wall
Xú Xiàosì was initially serving in the commandant's office,
when he lay down for a nap beneath the northern wall of his study.
He dreamed of two young boys urgently saying, "Move, sir, your bed!"
Startled, Xiàosì awoke and rose,
walked several steps before the wall collapsed.

Yuán Xié, during the Suí dynasty, when Gāozǔ was still the Chancellor,
was brought to his side.
Xié said to Gāozǔ:
"You have no factional support,
just like a single wall in the midst of water,
which is extremely perilous."
He urged him to strive harder.
Later, when Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
the Emperor looked at Xié and said with a laugh:
"How about that wall in the midst of water now?"
Thereupon, he bestowed a feast with great joy.

Mole cricket
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was hunting at Lóu,
when Shǐ Àn heard about it.
He waited at the gate with a hound,
and Jiǎnzǐ, upon seeing him, asked:
"What are you doing?"
He replied:
"I have obtained a hound,
and wish to test it in this hunting park."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Why didn't you inform me?"
He answered:
"When the ruler acts,
and his minister does not follow, it is disobedience.
If the lord is going to Lóu and the gamekeeper doesn't know,
how dare I trouble the officer of the day?"
Jiǎnzǐ then returned.

Yuèlín

the palace of Hóngtái,
