The current edition of "Strategies of the Warring States" reads Sānglín.
Shànglín
The Shànglín Park was originally an old park from the Qín dynasty.
The "Cháng'ān Zhì" records:
Chancellor Xiāo petitioned, saying:
"There is much vacant land in Shànglín,
I hope to allow the people to farm within the park."
The "Shǐjì" records:
Emperor Wǔ traveled incognito,
and considered the journey too long and arduous,
also causing trouble for the common people,
so he ordered Grand Master Wúqiū Shòu and Wáng, along with court attendants,
who were capable of using bamboo ropes to survey Āchéng,
to the south reaching Zhōuzhì,
to the east reaching Yíchūn,
to the west reaching the boundaries,
measuring the acreage and its market value,
and attaching it to the Southern Mountains to create the Shànglín Park.
Dōngfāng Shuò remonstrated:
"Qín built the Ēpáng Palace and the empire fell into chaos,"
then presented matters concerning the Tàijiē
and Six Signs.
The emperor then appointed him Grand Master,
and eventually established the Shànglín Park.
Therefore, Xiàngrú requested to compose a rhapsody about the emperor's hunting excursions,
featuring Mr. Wūyǒu and Lord Wúshì, and presented the "Shànglín Rhapsody."
The "Shuǐjīng Zhù" records:
The Shànglín Park spanned three hundred lǐ in breadth and length,
various animals were reared within the park,
where the Son of Heaven hunted in spring and autumn,
capturing countless birds in the park,
containing seventy detached palaces,
accommodating thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of cavalry.
The "Hàn Jiù Yí" records:
When first constructing the Shànglín Park,
ministers from distant regions
each presented over three thousand varieties of famous fruits and rare flowers,
which were planted within it,
some were given elegant names to signify their splendor.
The "Xījīng Zájì" records:
Zhāoxiáng
Zhāoxiáng Garden lies west of Gānquán Palace,
spanning a thousand lǐ in circumference,
where myriad states present rare curiosities,
all gathered within this place.
"Records of Penetrating the Obscure"
Lè Yóu
In the spring of the third year of Shénquè, the Lè Yóu Garden was established.

In the Lè Yóu Garden, rose trees grew naturally,
under the trees there was much alfalfa,
alfalfa is also called Huáifēng,
some people in the past called it Guāngfēng,
the wind among it often whistles softly,
when the sun shines on its flowers, they have a brilliant glow,

its foundation is the highest,
with wide and open views in all four directions.

Fānglín
The Pond of Zhàolóng and the Fragrant Forest Garden,
With nine valleys and eight streams.

Zhàolóng,
is the name of a pond.
Fragrant Forest,
is the name of a garden.

Guǎngchéng
Emperor Ming frequently visited the Guǎngchéng Park,
and Zhōnglí Yì considered hunting a neglect of governance.
He once stopped the imperial carriage to offer remonstrance,
regarding the indulgent pleasures of hunting excursions.
The emperor immediately returned to the palace.
(From his biography)
When Emperor Huán visited Guǎngchéng,
Chén Fān remonstrated during a military hunt, saying:
"I have heard that when a ruler engages in activities within parks and preserves,
it should only be during mid-autumn in the western suburbs, following the seasons,
for military exercises and regulated hunting,
to assist in sacrifices and strengthen filial piety.
How can it be appropriate to wave banners and display martial prowess,
indulging in the spectacle of carriages and horses?"
(From his biography)
In Xīnchéng county of Hénán,
there was a settlement called Guǎngchéng with the Guǎngchéng Park.
(From the Continued Treatises)
The Rǔ River flows east and merges with the waters of Guǎngchéng Marsh.
(From the Commentary on the Water Classic)
A thousand lǐ
Liáng Jì possessed vast mulberry groves,
His enclosed parks rivaled the imperial household's.
To the west, they reached Hóngnóng,
To the east, the boundary was Xíngyáng,
To the south, they extended to Lǔyáng,
And far north to Hé and Qí rivers.
They encompassed mountains and marshes,
Stretching to distant hills and wastelands,
Circling the enclosed domain,
Nearly a thousand lǐ in circumference.
He also established a rabbit park west of Hénán City,
Spanning several tens of lǐ.
According to the "Main Biography",
If anyone killed a rabbit from the park,
They were pursued relentlessly one after another,
Resulting in the deaths of thirteen people.
Zhāng Fán's "Records of the Hàn"
Notes that after Liáng Jì was executed, his parks were disbanded,
And given to impoverished people for their livelihood.
Bì Guī
Emperor Líng intended to construct the Bìguī Língkūn Garden,
when Yáng Cì remonstrated:
"In ancient times, when former kings established hunting parks,
they limited them to just enough for practicing the ritual of the three drives,
where gathering firewood, picking greens, and pasturing livestock
were all permitted to take place.
According to the system of the former kings,
the Hóng Pond was opened on the left,
and the Shànglín Park was created on the right,
neither extravagant nor frugal,
but perfectly conforming to ritual standards.
Now there are already five or six parks outside the city walls,
sufficient to satisfy desires and harmonize with the four seasons.
It would be appropriate to cherish the intentions of Xià Yǔ's humble palace and Tàizōng's open terrace,
so as to console the toiling common people."
The memorial was submitted,
and the Emperor considered halting the project,
but when he consulted Attendant-in-ordinary Rèn Zhī and Regular Palace Attendant Lè Sōng,
Sōng and others said:
"In the past, King Wén's park covered a hundred lǐ,
yet people considered it small;
whereas King Xuān of Qí's
fifty-
lǐ
park was deemed large by the people.
Now if you share it with the common people,
it will do no harm to governance."
The Emperor was pleased,
and thus ordered the garden to be built.

Mùróng Xī constructed the vast Lóng Téng Garden on a grand scale,
spanning over ten lǐ in area,
employing twenty thousand laborers.
He erected Jǐngyún Mountain within the garden,
with a foundation measuring five hundred bù in width,
and a peak reaching seventeen zhàng in height.
Additionally, he built the Xiāoyáo Palace and Gānlù Hall,
comprising several hundred interconnected rooms,
with viewing towers and pavilions linked together.

Nányuàn
Emperor Míng of Sòng once lent the Southern Park to Zhāng Yǒng, saying:

The Southern Park

Records of Southern Dynasties Palaces and Gardens
Fāng Lín
Fānglín Yuàn, also known as Táohuā Yuán (Peach Blossom Garden),
was originally the old residence of Emperor Gāo of the Qí dynasty,
located north of the main road along the Qínhuái River, east of the abandoned Dōngfǔ City.
Wáng Róng of the Qí dynasty composed the "Preface to the Poem of the Winding Stream":
"Carrying thoughts of the calm shore,
I gaze upon Fānglín."
This refers to this very place.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
the Qīngxī Palace from the Qí dynasty was renamed Fānglín Yuàn,
and at the beginning of the Tiānjiàn era, it was bestowed upon Nánpíng Prince Xiāo Wěi as his residence.
Wěi further expanded and constructed it,
planting more fine trees and rare fruits,
making it exquisitely ornate and beautiful.
He often roamed here with guests,
commissioning his aide Xiāo Zǐfàn to write a record of it.
Among the magnificent mansions of the Liáng dynasty's nobility,
none surpassed it.
"Liáng Records"
Fānglè
Emperor Dōng Hūn of Qí converted the Yuèwǔ Hall into the Fānglè Garden,
making it extremely extravagant and beautiful.
He planted trees during the hot summer,
but they would die by evening if planted in the morning,
and once they died, he would plant again,
yet ultimately none survived.
Thereupon, he requisitioned from households,
taking any tree he saw,
demolishing walls and houses to transplant them.
Even large trees that required an arm-span to encircle were all uprooted and moved.
The inserted leaves and lush flowers
provided only momentary amusement.
He dug up fine grasses to plant in the courtyard steps,
but under the scorching sun,
they would wither and dry up upon arrival.
People bustled back and forth,
with no end in sight.
All the mountain rocks were painted in colorful hues,
and across the pond,
a Purple Pavilion was erected,
with walls in various towers painted with images of men and women in intimate and indecent scenes.
(Records of the Southern Dynasties)
Jiànxīng
Liáng Jì shǎoyóu Jiànxīng Yuàn,
the poem reads:
"Crimson hills embrace the celestial city,
Purple springs ascend to the Shanglin Park.
Jade terraces reach a hundred feet high,
Silver trees rise a thousand fathoms tall."
Xiāngdōng
The Prince of Xiāngdōng built the Xiāngdōng Garden within the inner city,
excavating ponds and constructing hills,
stretching several hundred zhang in length,
planted with lotus marshes along the banks,
intermixed with rare trees.
Upon it stood the Tōngbō Pavilion,
built spanning across the water.
To the south was the Fúróng Hall,
to the east was the Xìyǐn Hall,
behind the hall was the Hermit’s Pavilion,
north of the pavilion was the Zhèngwǔ Hall,
in front of the hall were archery targets and horse-training grounds,
to the west was the Xiāngshè Hall,
where movable archery targets were set up,
allowing them to be shifted.
To the southeast was the Liánlǐ Hall,
behind which grew intertwined trees,
and in the early Tàiqīng era, northern intertwined trees appeared,
which were then regarded as an auspicious sign of Xiāngdōng’s ascension to the throne.
To the north were the Yìngyuè Pavilion, Xiūzhú Hall, and Línshuǐ Studio,
in front of the studio stood a high mountain,
on the mountain was a stone cave,
winding and meandering underground for over two hundred paces,
on the mountain was the Yángyún Tower,
the tower was exceptionally lofty,
visible from near and far.
To the north were the Línfēng Pavilion and Míngyuè Lodge,
as Yán Zhītuī’s poem says:
"Often accompanying the bright moon,
feasting together with the general,"
built by Hù Xīyì.
"Records of the Zhǔgōng"
Xiāndū
In the fourth year of the Wǔpíng era of the Later Lord of Qí,
large-scale construction projects were undertaken at Xiāndū,

with towers and halls rising intermittently,
reaching the pinnacle of splendor and luxury,

Xī Yuàn
In the first year of the Daye era, Emperor Sui Yang constructed the Western Garden in May,
with a circumference of three hundred li.
Within it was a sea,
over ten li in circumference, featuring mountains such as Fangzhang, Penglai, and Yingzhou,
rising more than a hundred chi above the water.
Towers, pavilions, and palaces
were scattered across the mountains,
facing and backing each other as if divinely arranged.
To the north of the sea was the Dragon Scale Canal,
winding and flowing into the sea.
Along the inner bank of the canal were sixteen courtyard gates,
all facing the canal,
each managed by a fourth-rank lady.
Halls, palaces, and towers
were extravagantly luxurious,
and when palace trees withered in autumn and winter, colored silk was cut into flowers
and leaves to adorn the branches.
When the colors faded, they were replaced with new ones,
keeping it perpetually like spring.
In the ponds, colored silk was also cut into lotuses, water chestnuts, and caltrops.
When the emperor traveled for pleasure,
the ice was removed and these decorations were laid out.
The sixteen courtyards competed to outdo each other with exquisite delicacies and elegance
to win favor,
seeking to curry imperial grace.
The emperor enjoyed moonlit nights, riding with thousands of palace maidens
to tour the Western Garden,
performing the "Clear Night Excursion" melody on horseback.

At Zaojian, the Xianren Palace was built,
gathering rare birds, exotic animals, and plants from across the land to fill the gardens.

intending to plant them in the Shangyuàn Gardens.

Selling Fruits

In the Western Regions, there was a country where an apple tree bore a fruit,

from *Jīzhíjí*
When Xiàowén was in Luò,

selecting and appointing officials.

The Book of the Later Hàn
Garden Plots
Zǐgòng traveled south to Chǔ,
returned to Jìn,
passed by the south bank of the Hàn River,
where he saw an elderly man working on his garden plots.
The man had dug a tunnel to enter the well, embracing a jar to draw water,
laboring strenuously with much effort,
yet achieving little result.
Zǐgòng said:
"There is a device here,
which can irrigate a hundred plots in one day,
using very little effort,
and achieving great results.
Wouldn't you, sir, desire it?"
The gardener looked up and said:
"What is it?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"Carve wood into a machine,
with the back heavy and the front light,
it lifts water as if drawing it up,
rapidly like pouring boiling water,
its name is the shadoof."
The gardener flushed with anger and laughed, saying:
"I have heard it said,
that where there are mechanical devices, there will be mechanical affairs;
where there are mechanical affairs, there will be a mechanical heart.
If a mechanical heart resides in the breast, then purity and simplicity
will not be complete.
If they are not complete, then the spirit becomes unsettled;
an unsettled spirit
is something the Dào cannot bear.
It is not that I do not know of it,
but I am ashamed to use it."
Zǐgòng reported this to Confucius,
and Confucius said:
"He is one who feigns cultivation of the art of Hùndùn's school."

Tethering the Horse
During the reign of Duke Mù of Lǔ, the ruler was old and the crown prince young,
a girl from Qīshì leaned against a pillar and sighed,
a neighboring woman laughed at her,
the Qīshì girl said:
"Once a guest from Jìn lodged at our house,
we tethered his horse in the garden,
the horse broke loose and ran about,
trampling our mallows,
leaving us without mallows to eat for the entire year."

Gardening

In Liángjùn Méng County,

Tùyuán
The Records of the Grand Historian states that King Xiào of Liáng built the Eastern Park,
spanning three hundred li square,

Dǒng Zhòngshū, during Xiàojǐng's time, served as a scholar.
He secluded himself in curtains to lecture and recite.

such that some never saw his face.
For three years, he did not look into the garden;
his dedication was such.

Huán Róng, styled Chūnqīng,
was diligent without tiring.

Fǎ Zhēn lived in seclusion in a great marsh,

Běimáng
Yuǎnguǎng Hàn, a wealthy man of Màolíng,
possessed treasures worth tens of thousands,
with eight to nine hundred household servants.
He built a garden at the foot of Běimáng Mountain,
stretching four li from east to west,
and five li from north to south.
Water was channeled to flow through it,
and within, rocks were piled to form mountains,
reaching over ten zhang in height,
extending continuously for several li.
He raised white parrots, purple mandarin ducks, yaks, and green rhinoceroses,
along with rare beasts and exotic birds,
gathered in abundance throughout the grounds.
Sand was heaped to create islets,
and water was agitated to form waves and tides,
where river gulls and sea swans were introduced,
breeding and nurturing their young,
spreading across the forests and ponds.
Rare trees and unusual plants
were all cultivated there.
The buildings were designed with winding paths,
interconnected multi-storied pavilions and long corridors,
so extensive that one could walk for hours without covering them all.
Later, Yuǎnguǎng Hàn was found guilty of a crime,
executed, and his property confiscated, turning the garden into an imperial park.
The birds, beasts, trees, and plants were all transplanted to the Shànglín Imperial Garden.

Emperor Wǔ of Hàn had a famous garden called Fánchuān,
also known as the Imperial Lodging Garden,
which produced fifteen chestnuts,

Famous Gardens
Wáng Zǐjìng passed through Wú from Kuàijī,
and heard that Gù Pìjiāng had a famous garden.
Not having previously known the host,
he went directly to his house.
It happened that Gù was just gathering guests and friends for a lively feast,
and after Wáng had finished touring the garden,
he pointed out its good and bad points,
acting as if no one else was around.
Gù flared up, unable to bear it, saying:
"To be arrogant toward your host
is discourteous.
To act haughtily due to your high status
is unprincipled.
Lacking these two virtues,
you are not worth mentioning, you boor."
He then drove Wáng's attendants out the gate.
Wáng remained alone in his carriage,
turning his head to look back.
After his attendants failed to arrive for some time,
he then had someone send his chopsticks outside the gate,
appearing unperturbed and disdainful.

making one feel that birds, beasts, and fish naturally draw close to humans.

planting gardens and fruit trees in the eastern city,

Free and Unfettered

with pavilions on the left and right of the hall courtyard,

Liǔ Yuánjǐng served as the Minister of Works,

Yuánjǐng said:

Xuānpǔ
Crown Prince Wénhuì of Qí was fond of Buddhism,
establishing six charity houses to support the poor,
yet his nature was rather extravagant and luxurious.
The halls and palaces within his residence were all ornately decorated,
with exquisite elegance surpassing the imperial palace.
He expanded the Xuánpǔ Garden,
making it equal in scale to the northern moat of the imperial city.
Within it, artificial hills were constructed,
along with ponds, pavilions, towers, and pagodas
of extraordinary and extreme beauty,
costing tens of millions.
He gathered numerous rare stones,
creating landscapes of marvelous perfection.
Fearing they might be seen from the imperial palace,
he planted tall bamboos along the sides
and erected high barriers outside.
He built several hundred viewing structures,
incorporating various mechanical devices.
When concealment was needed,
they could be set up instantly;
if demolition was required,
they could be dismantled immediately. During the time when Emperor Míng of Jìn was crown prince,
he established the West Pond, following Emperor Wǔ's precedent.
He requested to build a small park at Dōngtián,
which the emperor permitted,
and it became magnificently splendid beyond description.

Free from Defilement
Liú Huìfěi, whose courtesy name was Xuānwén,

and also built a garden on the northern side of the mountain,
naming it the Lígòu Garden.

Lotus Flower
Fúróng Garden was originally a detached palace of the Sui dynasty,
occupying an area of thirty qǐng,
with a circumference of seventeen lǐ.
During the Qin dynasty, it was called Yìchūn Garden,
and in the Han dynasty, it was named Lèyóu Garden.
Yǔwén Kǎi, in planning the capital city,
found the high terrain in the southeast of the outer city inconvenient,
so he left this corner as an open space,
digging out the Lotus Pond to create emptiness.
"Records of the Two Capitals"
states: Fúróng Garden is located at the southeast corner of the outer capital wall,
with lush green woods layered upon each other,
and verdant embankments stretching far and wide,
resembling the splendid scenery of the imperial city,
visited by the emperor during his travels.
"Records of the Jǐnglóng Literary Institute"
Sīzhú
The Bamboo Administration Garden is located twelve li east of Zhōuzhì County.

he then planted bamboos,
which is exactly this place.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"A thousand mǔ of bamboo along the Wèi River."
In the Hàn dynasty, it was called "the Bamboo Groves of Hù and Dù."
Hence, there was the Commandant of Bamboo Administration,
as described in the "Rhapsody on the Western Capital":

with bamboo groves and fruit orchards,

Do not establish

once saying:

before I die,
how could I have worries of hunger and cold?

though possessing rich fields and property,

Recent scholars and officials strive for expansive residences,
making them expenses for unworthy descendants' food and drink,
but I am not like this."

Market procurement

but Mǎ Yí admonished him, saying:
"Zhāng Jiǎnzhī contributed to the restoration of the Táng dynasty.
His remaining estate should be preserved for a hundred generations.
How can we let his descendants sell it?"
The prince apologized, saying:

bringing shame upon you.
Without you, how could I have heard these words?"

Suì's son, Court of the Imperial Treasury Supervisor Mǎ Chàng.

By Emperor Shùnzōng's reign it was recorded again,
that palace eunuchs frequently coerced him to hand it over,

leading to destitution until his death,
his sons having no house,
sought shelter in the Fèngchéng Garden's pavilions and halls.
Thus contemporaries regarded Chàng as a caution against amassing great wealth.

Chàng once gifted large apricots from his estate to Dòu Wénchǎng,
Wénchǎng presented them to Emperor Dézōng,
Dézōng had never seen such apricots before,
found it rather strange,

and inscribed his own garden to express his aspirations, saying:

Garden bamboo and pond lotus, do not be disheartened,

Unrestrained and free-spirited
Yán Xiè,
a descendant of Duke Lǔ,
resided in a place graced with springs, rocks, pines, and bamboos.

where Mèng Bīnyú inscribed a poem that reads:

yet procrastination delayed my visit for twenty autumns.
Today, with an open heart, my verses cannot exhaust its beauty,
as emerald mountains layer and waters flow eternally."

Lìzhī
The Western Barbarians have a lychee garden,
where the Bó tóng of the Shīyí tribe are the most virtuous,
renowned in ancient times for the wealth of the tóng people,
who largely make their living from lychees,
planting over ten thousand trees in the garden,
yielding a harvest of one hundred and fifty hú.
From the "Records of Commanderies and States."
Chestnut Garden
In Xuánhù Bay there is an area of several qǐng,
where the soil contains chestnut orchards.
The chestnuts are small and quite different, not comparable to others,
yet they are indeed the produce of Gù'ān.
However, three hundred are offered as annual tribute,
truly to supply the imperial court.
The islet in the water is Chestnut Islet,
where the trees are tall and lush,
appearing from afar like gathered clouds and accumulated mist.
Within the grove stands the Chestnut Hall,
and the archery mound is very spacious and open,
frequented by many local officials and eminent scholars.

Jìyuán
Elder Xūdáduō
addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Your disciple wishes to build a monastery to invite the Buddha to dwell in.
Only Prince Zhītuó's garden,
spanning eighty qǐng,
with lush woods suitable for residence, remains."
He addressed the prince,
and the prince jokingly said:
"Cover it entirely with gold,
and I shall give it to you."
Xūdáduō brought out gold to cover eighty qǐng,
and the monastery was completed,
comprising twelve hundred sections in total.
The "Scripture and Vinaya Marvels"
also calls it the Garden for the Solitary.
The "Diamond Sutra Commentary"
states: the Śrāvastī monastery,
six hundred lǐ to the northeast,
Viśākhā's mother built a monastery,
invited the Buddha, and lent this place,
thus it is at the Jetavana Monastery.
The large garden compound has two gates,
one facing east,
one facing north.
This garden is where Elder Xūdáduō spread gold coins to purchase the land.
The monastery stands at the center,
where the Buddha resided the longest,
preaching the Dharma to liberate people.
The paths where he walked and sites where he sat,
as well as stūpas for filial piety,
all have names.
From the "Faxian's Record"
Ānluó Garden
Ānluó is the name of a fruit tree,
its fruit resembles a peach,
some say it resembles a pear,
this tree bloomed flowers,
from the flowers was born a girl,
the people of the country marveled at this wonder,
and bestowed the garden upon her.
Since the garden belonged to the girl,
and the girl guarded it,
it was thus called the Ānluó Tree Garden.
Through the subtle influence of past virtuous deeds,
she saw the Buddha and rejoiced,
offering the garden to the Buddha,
the Buddha accepted it and made it his dwelling place.
"Interpretation of Meanings"
From the city of Kuśinagarī,
traveling east to the city of Vaiśālī,
to the north lies a large forest with a multi-storied pavilion monastery,
a dwelling place of the Buddha,
and the half-body stūpa of Ānanda,
within the city was originally the home of the Āmrapālī woman,
who built a stūpa for the Buddha,
which still remains today, three li south of the city, west of the road,
the Āmrapālī woman offered the garden as the Buddha's dwelling place.

The residences of the hundred officials are called offices.

Government office
In modern times, it is commonly referred to as the government court as the public yá,
which is the ancient public temple,
the character originally being erroneous,
with "yá" (牙) being used as "yá" (衙).

government offices
Since the Hàn Dynasty, the residences of the Three Dukes have been called fǔ,
while those of the Nine Ministers have been called sì.
The Fēngsútōng states:
"Fǔ
means 'to gather'.
The offices of dukes, ministers, governors, and prefects
are where moral principles are gathered.
Treasuries and private storehouses
are where goods and wealth are gathered.
Sì
means 'to administer'.
With courtyards having laws and regulations,
places where officials reside
are all called sì."
The Zuǒzhuàn Commentary explains
sì
as 'to succeed'.
Those who handle affairs succeed one another,
continuing within them.

Official Residence
Hé Bìng was of a pure and honest nature,
and when he served as the governor of Yǐngchuān,

Lù Kàng and Zhūgě Kè exchanged garrisons at Cháisāng,
and before leaving, both had their city walls thoroughly repaired,
fortifying the ramparts,
maintaining the houses and mulberry groves,
ensuring nothing was arbitrarily damaged.
When Kè moved into the garrison,
it appeared as good as new,
whereas the original Cháisāng garrison
assigned to Kè was rather dilapidated,
causing him deep embarrassment.

Banned and Destroyed
When Yáng Hù was overseeing Jīngzhōu,
a senior official had died in office,
and his successor disliked it,
so he extensively demolished the old government building.
Hù believed that life and death are fated,
not determined by one's residence.
He issued a written order to the military commands,
universally prohibiting such acts.

Shàn Shì
Dù Yù served as the governor of Qínzhōu.
Shí Jiàn impeached him for unauthorized renovation of the city gates,
overseeing the army of Kuàijī without authorization,
and dispatched imperial censors with a prison cart,
summoning him to the Court of Judicial Review.
Because Dù Yù was married to the emperor's daughter and was among the eight privileged ranks,
the council proposed that he be allowed to redeem his offense.
"Original Biography"
Huài Shè
Ruǎn Jí served as the governor of Dōngpíng,
riding a donkey to the commandery.
He tore down the screens and partitions of the government office,
making the inside and outside visible to each other.
His laws and decrees were clear and simple,
and he returned within ten days.
"Jìn Chuán"
He embezzled funds from the government office.
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
Xiānyú Jì of Xīhé served as the governor of Qīnghé and constructed an official residence,
which was not completed before his death.
Later, Governor Zhào Gāo estimated the cost at two million coins,
while the official Huáng Bǐng and the registrar Liú Shì claimed it was four million coins.
Thereupon, Jì appeared as a ghost,
entering the government office in broad daylight,
and confronted Gāo and Bǐng,
jointly verifying the accounts.
It was discovered that Shì and Bǐng had embezzled funds,
so Jì wrote a petition to state his case,
roughly stating:
"Gāo values wealth over integrity,
a mere rustic,
yet he sits arrogantly among his kind,
failing in careful planning and missing opportunities,
with the nature of a servant,
flattering the world to seek fame,
stealing honors and positions,
dishonoring his official post.
The Yìjīng mocks those who bear burdens unfit for them,
truly describing Gāo.
I, as a ghost, cannot remain silent,
and thus report this via the relay stations over a thousand miles,
entrusting Gāo to submit it."
Then, he traveled thirty li northwest,
where his carriage and horses vanished, never to be seen again.
Bǐng and others prostrated in terror,
so Gāo reported the incident to the court.
An imperial edict was issued,
restoring Jì's fields, property, wife, and children in Xīhé,
and arranging for a replacement,
to honor the lawsuit from the underworld.
From the "Commentary on the Waterways Classic."
Administrative Office
Wáng Dǎo was overseeing the renovation of the administrative headquarters in Yángzhōu,
and while inspecting the progress, he remarked:
"I am precisely preparing this place for Cìdào.
Hé Shǎo was highly regarded by Lord Wáng,
hence he repeatedly expressed such sighs."
from "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
A sunken pit
Héng Gōng served as Huán Shìmín's
army advisor in Dāntú.
In front of the bed in his residence was a small sunken pit,
which upon closer inspection turned out to be an ancient tomb.
Héng would always first throw sacrificial food into the pit before eating,
and this continued for a full year.
Later, while sleeping, he suddenly became aware of a person standing before his bed,
who said:
"It has been over seven hundred years since my death,
and with the extinction of my descendants,
there has been no one to conduct sacrificial offerings.
You have consistently shared your meals with me,
for which I am endlessly grateful.
According to your official records,
you are destined to become the Prefect of Níngzhōu."
Later events indeed confirmed these words.
From "Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds"
The deity resides
Xiāo Huìmíng at the beginning of the Tàishǐ era served as governor of Wúxīng,
within the commandery's borders stood Mount Biàn,
at the foot of the mountain was a temple to Xiàng Yǔ,
tradition held that Yǔ frequently resided within the commandery's boundaries to oversee affairs,
previous governors had not dared to ascend the hall,
Huìmíng said to the officials:
"Kǒng Jìgōng once governed this commandery,
and I have not heard of any disasters befalling him."
Thereupon, he ordered a grand feast with mats to be prepared,
and for several days received guests,
when he saw a man over ten feet tall,
drawing a bow and aiming an arrow at Huìmíng,
who then vanished,
after which Huìmíng developed a boil on his back,
and died within ten days.
"Anecdotes from the Southern Histories"
Abandoning the Strange
Yuè Guǎng served as Governor of Hénán,
where previously the official residence was haunted by many strange phenomena.
Former governors all dared not occupy the main quarters,
but Yuè Guǎng resided there without hesitation.
Once the outer door closed by itself,
startling all his attendants,
he alone remained composed.
Noticing a hole in the wall,
he ordered someone to dig into it,
where they found and killed a wildcat,
after which the hauntings ceased entirely.
Clamor and disturbance
Luó Hán, courtesy name Jūnzhāng,
served as the assistant inspector of the province.
Finding the official residence too noisy and disruptive,
he built a thatched hut on a small islet in the western city pond.
He cut wood for timber,
wove reeds into mats,
and lived there wearing plain clothes and eating simple vegetables,
remaining content and at ease.
Entering the Moat
Fù Zhāo, styled Màoyuǎn,
served as the Prefect of Ānchéng during the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng Dynasty.
Since the Sòng period, the commandery had been plagued by successive wars and chaos,
with government buildings considered ominous.
At dawn and dusk, humans and ghosts often encountered each other,
and few officials ended their terms auspiciously.
When Fù Zhāo arrived,
someone saw armored soldiers emerging at night, saying:
"Lord Fù is a virtuous man,
not to be violated,"
then they ascended into the void and departed.
Shortly after,
wind and rain suddenly arrived,
lifting the commandery's main hall
into the moat.
From then on, the commandery was free from calamities,
all attributing it to Fù Zhāo's integrity and uprightness.
From "History of the Southern Dynasties"
Repairing the Office Building
Cài Níng, courtesy name Zǐjū,
served as Vice Director of the Secretariat,
and was promoted to Governor of Jìnlíng.

he further ordered his attendants to maintain the Secretariat office,
saying to his guests:
"So that future occupants need not toil."

Suppress Demons
Lǐ Bó,
courtesy name Jùnzhī,
was promoted to Assistant Director of the Treasury Department.
At that time, Huángfǔ Bó was assisting in government affairs,
reducing expenditures for supporting costs.
Bó submitted a memorial:
"The village households in the source area of Wèi River are now 400,
but presently only forty;
households in Wēn village number three thousand,
but now only one thousand.
Most other counties are similar to this,
and the trouble began with taxing absconding persons,
I wish an edict to be issued to stop it.
In less than three years,
people will surely return to farming.
Agriculture is the foundation of the state,
and only when the foundation is established can peace be discussed.
He also stated:

causing many postal horses to die."
Emperor Xiànzōng read the memorial and was astonished,
immediately providing several hundred flying dragon horses to the post stations within the vicinity.
"Old Tang"
Xú Xiàokè was appointed as the Minister of Personnel in the first year of the Zhēnmíng era,
since the Jìn Dynasty,
officials of the Ministry had all brought their families to reside in the ministry compound,
which was located within the inner imperial city,
with a side gate in the lower quarters leading to a hidden path,
stretching east and west across the road,
connecting to the imperial court hall,
the first section being the Ministry of Personnel,
extending west to the elevated walkway,
over many years,
numerous ghostly phenomena occurred,
every night at dusk,
unexplained sounds and lights appeared,
sometimes a person dressed in official robes was seen emerging from a well,
only to vanish moments later,
or doors would open and close by themselves,
resulting in many deaths among residents,

Xiàokè succeeded Què,
and immediately moved in,

contemporaries unanimously attributed this to his unwavering integrity.
Repair and maintain

where his governance focused on promoting benefits and eliminating harms,
repairing government offices,
earning considerable renown.
"Old Book of Táng"
Encountering a Deity
The residence of the Xiàngzhōu Governor was long haunted.
Former governors Wáng Dàojiān, Lǐ Shǐjūn, and Zhū Xīyù
all failed to leave the prefectural city alive;
if not meeting sudden death,
they would be demoted.
During the Kāiyuán era, when Zhāng Jiāyòu first arrived at the prefecture,
supernatural disturbances immediately occurred,
causing extreme turmoil.
Yòu showed no fear
and went to investigate,
where he saw a woman who said:
"I am the daughter of the late Great General and Xiàngzhōu Governor Yùchí.
When Yáng Jiān usurped the throne previously,
I died serving the sovereign,
with my entire family massacred—
over sixty skeletons lie beneath this hall.
I wished to inform people,
but all feared death.
I beg Your Excellency to show compassion."
Yòu gave his promise.
Another day, he ceremoniously buried them behind the hall
and converted the hall into a shrine,
offering annual sacrifices thereafter.
Yòu had an eight- or nine-year-old daughter.
When family members had inquiries,
they would have her convey them,
and the deity would invariably respond.
When the deity wished to communicate,
Yòu would also have his young daughter receive the message,
making this a regular practice.
Three years later,
Jiāyòu was summoned to court as Grand Imperial Guard,
reaching Wú,
where he was honored with official regalia.
Subsequently, he achieved glorious promotions.

leading to its dilapidation.

Shì Dì
When Zhào Huìbó was Governor of Hénán,
he once purchased Yáng Yán's residence for use as an official government office.

demanding an exorbitant price for it.

In Hézhōng Prefecture there was a Green Sedge Hall,

if there were imperial edicts or external memorials,
urgent documents,

and frequent leaks of information.

Riding a relay carriage
When Mount Liáng collapsed,
the Marquis of Jìn summoned Bó Zōng by relay carriage.
Bó Zōng ordered the heavy carriage to make way,
saying:

Courier Station is located in

Yīn Qiánzhī's poem reads:
"In the depths of planning and scheming,
wielding the brush to decide victory.
The strategy unfolded in eight diagrams,

The mountains' beauty supports heroic spirit,
rivers flow into ingenious thoughts.
Calculations lead to success within grasp,

Dù Mù's poem:
"Receiving the edict at Yǒng'ān Palace,
lost in thought at Chóubǐ Station.
Mapping the world on paper,
victory or defeat known with a wet brush.
Rivers winding with wisdom,
mountains towering in support.
Just as the midnight star falls,
the Hóngdū tripod shifts.
The courier station changes with the ages,

Lǐ Yìshān's poem:

wind and clouds long guard the stockades.

In later years, passing the temple in Jǐnlǐ,

Luó Yǐn's poem:

northward campaigns and eastern expeditions all well-planned.

when fortune wanes, even heroes are not free.

two dynasties' officials resent Qiáo Zhōu.

still understanding to flow yearly by the station."

The envoy of relay posts
Péi Lín, during the Yuánhé era, warfare erupted in the Lianghe region.
Initially, Emperor Xiànzōng favored and entrusted inner court officials
to fulfill the role of envoy of relay posts.
Among them was one named Cáo Jìnwǔ,
who relied on favor to act tyrannically.
When meeting envoys from various regions, he often took advantage,
even going so far as to physically insult some.
Chancellor Lǐ Jífǔ reported and had him dismissed.
In the twelfth year, during war in Huáixī,
again an inner court official served as envoy.
Péi Lín submitted a memorial stating:
"The duties of the relay stations
are overseen at each location by dedicated officials.
Within the capital area, we have the Jīngzhào Yǐn,
and in the provinces, there are the Guānchá Shǐ,
with prefects monitoring each other in rotation.
Moreover, in the imperial court, censors also serve as envoys of relay posts
tasked to investigate deficiencies.
If palace servants
are sent to engage in affairs of relay stations,
then inside servants handle outside matters,
with distinct responsibilities.
It is crucial to block the source of official encroachments
and stop the trend of usurping positions."
Although his words were not heeded,
the emperor appreciated them.

with a relay station called Xiāngsī Pù (Longing Inn).

Wànchūn
During the Yanhe era, Jìng Zhāodào was appointed as the Investigating Censor.
Previously,
ten conscripts from Jīngzhōu, including Shū Wànfú, had stopped at Bāyáng Beach,
where they drowned.
While on a mission to Bāyú,
Zhāodào arrived at Wànchūn Station.
As he was sleeping,
he saw the ten men pleading mournfully.
He awoke from his dream,
and this recurred repeatedly.
He then summoned the station officer to inquire,
whose account matched the dream.
Zhāodào immediately hired skilled swimmers to retrieve the bodies,
prepared wine and food to offer libations,
and issued documents to nearby counties,
arranging coffins to return them to their hometowns.
When conscripts heard of this,
they were deeply moved.

West of Háozhōu there was a Gāotáng Inn,

and inscribed a poem that read:

Readers all could not help but smile.

Bāochéng
Yuán Zhěn served as the Censor,
and was dispatched to Dōngchuān.
At Bāochéng Station, he heard that Huáng Chéng of Yúxiāng had violated orders and fled.
When he was again sent to Dōngchuān,
and arrived at Bāochéng Station,
Huáng Chéng offered wine and moored the boat,
Zhěn drank with him,
and inquired extensively about the landscapes of Bāoyáng.
To the left was the city where Bāo Sì eloped,

Moved by the present and cherishing the past,
he composed a poem for Huáng, saying:
"In bygone years, we once drank heartily,
Magistrate Huáng overwhelmed by flying cups.
You fled from the mat back then,
Today you welcome me before my horse.
Winding are the paths of Qīpán,
Undulating the walls several zhàng high.
Blossoms seem like the smile of Lady Bāo,
The plank roads rest from Wǔhóu's campaigns.
One kind lies buried in secluded stones,
Only hearing a name that lasts a thousand years."

Bāochéng Station was known as the finest under heaven.

Article inspection
In the first year of the Chángqìng era, Liǔ Gōngchuò served as the Metropolitan Governor,
at a time when Héshuò had rebelled again.
The imperial court was employing troops to pursue and capture them,
and the various generals in the field camps
had their orders changed from morning to evening,
with couriers constantly passing each other on the roads.
Gōngchuò memorialized, saying:
"Since the military campaign against Yōuzhèn began,
official missions have multiplied and converged,
causing post stations to be depleted and lacking,
with many shortages of saddled horses.
Moreover, there are no restrictions on the number of attendants for imperial commissioners' journeys.
Those wearing crimson and purple robes ride twenty to thirty horses each,
while those in yellow and green ride no less than ten or five horses each.
Post station officials cannot examine their credentials,
but must provide for them immediately upon their word.
When the post station horses are exhausted,
they then seize saddled horses and official attire from travelers on the road,
causing alarm, disturbance, resentment, and lamentation among officials and commoners alike.
The uproar spreads far and wide,
and travel is nearly halted.
I humbly hope some limits can be temporarily set."
The memorial was then sent to the Secretariat,
where regulations on the number of attendants were established.
From then on, the officials no longer complained of hardship.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Guǎnchéng
In the second year of the Tàihé era, Yáng Guīhòu, the governor of Xíngyáng, was ordered to complete the new post station,
surrounded by high walls,
and built a tower over its gate.
It served to welcome travelers with the respect of cleanliness and comfort,
and to bid farewell with thoughts of ascent and departure.
With carriages speeding and hooves galloping,
urgent missions and swift dispatches,
those entering forgot their weariness,

Sān Xiāng
Liǔ Yǔxī arrived at Sānxiāng Station,
where he saw Emperor Míng Huáng's poem gazing at the Nǚjī Mountain,
and was profoundly moved, saying:
"The Kāiyuán Emperor had all things fulfilled,
Only regretting that those glorious days were too brief.
On the Sānxiāng path he gazed at the immortal mountain,
And returned to compose the 'Rainbow Skirt, Feathered Coat' melody.
His immortal heart thenceforth dwelled in the Jasper Pool,
The eight scenes of Sānxiāng following in pursuit.
Suddenly he rode a white cloud to the heavens above,
Leaving behind in this world only the 'Autumn Wind' ode."
From the "Original Collection"
During the Huìchāng era, someone inscribed at Sānxiāng:
"I originally lived east of Ruòyē Creek,
Following my husband westward through Hánguān Pass,
Residing in the Jìnchāng Lane estate.
Unfortunately, my husband has passed away,
Leaving me desolate and without support.
In the capital, spring is just beginning,
I journey eastward, mourning my solitary shadow,
Crossing the Chǎn River,
Traversing the Wèi River plains,
Leaving Zhōngnán Mountain behind,
Ascending Tàihuà Mountain,
Passing through Guóluè,
Arriving at the outskirts of Shǎn,
Bowing to the clear streams of Jiāxiáng,
Facing the verdant beauty of Nǚjī Mountain.
All the places I pass through,
Are sites where we once laughed and feasted together.
Thus I take up my brush to write these lines,
Yet unable to wash away the sorrow in my heart."
Writing is not a woman's pursuit,
Therefore my name remains hidden and unrecorded.
The poem reads:
"Once I followed my husband west through the pass,
Now he is gone and I return alone.
Xiè Niáng and Wèi Nǚ wait not for me,
Like rain and clouds, I return to my old mountain."
There were eleven matching poems,
Wáng Zhù's poem reads:
"Before Nǚjī Mountain the mist hangs low,
Where a beauty left her regrets inscribed.
Who knows where the rain and clouds have gone?
Only that nobles become enchanted at the sight."
Liǔ Gǔ's poem reads:
"Orchids' fragrance reveals jade-like grace,
By the roadside flowers smile as scenery lingers.
At the foot of Zhùluó Mountain, endless sentiments
All converge at Sānxiāng in this farewell moment."
Zhāng Qǐ's poem reads:
"Luòzhōu's scenery remains as fine as ever,
But no chance remains to see the maiden in her lotus tent.
Since the rain and clouds dispersed, news has ceased,
In this life, my eternal regret rests at Sānxiāng."
From "Yúnxī Yǒu Yì"

A guest said to Kuǎi Tōng:
"You, sir, towards Chancellor Cáo,

make the worthy prominent and advance the capable,
yet in the state of Qí, none surpass you, sir.
Since you know of Liáng Shíjūn and Dōngguō Xiānshēng,
why not recommend them to the chancellor?"
Kuǎi Tōng replied:
"Very well.
There was a woman in my village who was on good terms with the other matrons of the village.
One night, the village woman lost some meat,
and her mother-in-law thought she had stolen it,
became angry and drove her out.
As the woman was about to leave,
she passed by the matron she was friendly with,
told her what had happened and took her leave.
The village matron said:
'You go slowly,
I will now make your family pursue you.'
She then tied some hemp and asked for fire from the household that had lost the meat, saying:
'Last night, the dogs got some meat,
fought over it and killed each other;
I ask for fire to deal with it.'
The household that had lost the meat hurriedly pursued and called back their woman.
Thus, the village woman was not a skilled debater,
and tying hemp to ask for fire
was not the way to bring a woman back.
Yet things have their mutual influences,
and affairs have their appropriate methods.
I shall ask for fire from Chancellor Cáo."

During the Northern Wei dynasty, along the Yiluo region flanking the imperial road, four foreign guesthouses were established.

the second Guīdé (Returning to Virtue),

People from the Wu region who surrendered to the state were lodged at the Jīnlíng Guesthouse,

Northern foreigners who came to submit were lodged at the Yānrán Guesthouse,

Western foreigners who came to submit were lodged at the Yānzī Guesthouse,

Now the Three Rivers region and the Zhōu court
are the court and marketplace of the world,
yet Your Majesty does not contend there,
but instead contends with the Róng and Dí tribes,
which is far from achieving royal supremacy."

Seeking Survival
Lord Mèngcháng, having been expelled from Qí and then returned,
was met at the border by Tán Shízi,
who said to Lord Mèngcháng:
"You must harbor no resentment toward the officials and scholars of Qí."
Lord Mèngcháng replied:
"I do."
Tán Shízi said:
"Events have inevitable outcomes,
principles have inherent truths.
When one is wealthy and honored, people gather around;
when poor and lowly, they depart.
This is the inevitable outcome of events,
the inherent truth of principles.
Allow me to use the market as an analogy:
in the morning it is full,
by evening it is empty.
This is not because people love the market in the morning and hate it in the evening;
it is because they seek what is available,
and avoid what is gone.
I hope you will not hold resentment."
Lord Mèngcháng dared not speak of it again.
From the "Strategies of the Warring States," the story of Lǔ Liánzǐ
is similar to the account of Féng Xuān dismissing guests in the "Records of the Grand Historian."
When Lián Pō was relieved of duty at Chángpíng and returned,
in his time of lost influence,
all his former guests left.
When he was reappointed as chancellor,
the guests returned once more.
Lián Pō said:
"Guests, leave!"
A guest replied:
"Alas,
why are your views so outdated?
All under heaven interact with the ways of the market:
if you have influence, we follow you;
if you lack influence, we depart.
This is the inherent principle—
what is there to resent?"
From the "Original Biography" in the "Records of the Grand Historian."
Playing the Zhú
After Jīng Kē arrived in Yān,
he befriended a dog butcher from Yān,
and Gāo Jiànlí who was skilled at playing the zhù.
Jīng Kē was fond of drinking,
and daily drank with the dog butcher and Gāo Jiànlí in the Yān market.
When they were drunk,
Gāo Jiànlí would play the zhù,
and Jīng Kē would sing along in the market,
enjoying themselves together.
Then they would weep together,
as if no one else was around.

The Earthly Market
The First Emperor created the Earthly Market,
to conduct trade with the living and the dead,
issuing the decree:
"The living must not cheat the dead of their possessions."

Once the living enter the market gate,

and sold them at the market in Cháng'ān,

Yuàn Shì
Emperor Dōng Hūn of Qí converted the Yuèwǔ Hall into the Fānglè Garden,
and within the garden, he established shops and stores modeled after a grand market.
He would roam the market daily,
mixing various goods for sale,
and together with palace maids and eunuchs, he engaged in petty trade.
He appointed Consort Pān as the market administrator,
while he himself served as the market clerk and recorder.
Those involved in disputes were brought before Consort Pān for punishment.
He also dug canals and built dams,
personally pulling boats at the dams.
Above, he set up shops and sat to butcher meat.
At that time, the common people sang a ballad:
"The Yuèwǔ Hall,
now planted with willow trees.
The Emperor butchers meat,
Consort Pān sells wine."

Market Exchange
In the sixth year of the Daye era, various foreign tribes came to court,

whereupon the various market lanes were renovated,
shops and inns were repaired,
all made with uniform and orderly rooftops,

the people and items were splendid and prosperous,

Fēngdū
The Southern Market in Luòyáng was the Fēngdū Market of the Suí dynasty.
When its outer wall was first built,
a tomb was excavated,
without bricks or tiles.
Inside the coffin was an inscription in red on a flat surface, which read:
"The yarrow stalks foretold dwelling at court,
the tortoise shell foretold proximity to the market.
After five hundred years, the temple
shall be seen here."
Upon verifying its date,
it corresponded to the second year of the Huángchū era of the Wèi dynasty.
From "Anecdotes from the Suí and Táng Dynasties."

Wǔ Yōuxù,

He was tranquil and had few desires,

Palace Market
During the reign of Emperor Dézōng, eunuchs controlled the palace market,
stationing dozens to hundreds of people to inspect goods.
Those on the left side of the market were called "White Watchers,"
lacking imperial edicts for verification,
yet anyone claiming "palace market" authority went unquestioned.
Generally, the prices paid
did not even compensate one-tenth of the value,
and remonstrating officials submitted repeated memorials,
but the emperor refused to accept them.
The emperor
had Wú Còu, a relative from the imperial in-laws' quarter, serve as Capital Governor,
who strongly criticized these abuses.
Zhāng Jiànfēng, attending court audiences, also submitted detailed memorials,
and Emperor Dézōng somewhat praised and accepted their advice.
However, Sū Biàn, currying favor with the eunuchs,
took the opportunity to report,
arguing it benefited idle and unproductive individuals,
so the palace market system remained unchanged.
According to the Old Book of Táng,
in Emperor Dézōng's later years,
administrative power was fragmented among many factions,
and the abuses of the palace market
were criticized by remonstrating officials to no avail.
Hán Yù once submitted a memorial of several thousand words,
vehemently arguing against it,
but it was ignored,
and he was angrily demoted to Magistrate of Shānyáng in Lián Prefecture.

and after eating my fill, mount it,

People of Eastern and Western Chuān often belittled each other.

Hài Shì
Fēnníng County,
was originally the market held on the Hài day in Chángzhōu.
In the villages south of the mountains, markets are called xū,
as they are not regularly held and there are many vacant days.
In Western Shǔ, it is called gāi,
similar to how malaria recurs at intervals.
The people of Jiāngnán disliked using the term for illness,
so they stopped.
It is simply called hǎi instead.
Moreover, according to the customs of Jīng and Wú,
markets gather on the days of Yín, Shēn, Sì, and Hài,
hence the name Hài market.

Market Prohibitions
Confucius told Zhònggōng:
"There are fourteen other prohibitions:
Official robes and carriages,
are not to be sold in the market;
Jade guī, zhāng, bì, and cóng,
are not to be sold in the market;
War chariots and banners,
are not to be sold in the market;
Sacrificial animals and ritual wine,
are not to be sold in the market;
Weapons and armor,
are not to be sold in the market;
Utensils not meeting standards,
are not to be sold in the market;
Cloth and silk of improper texture,
or incorrect width and length,
are not to be sold in the market;
Colors that confuse proper hues,
are not to be sold in the market;
Embroidered brocades and jade vessels,
with extravagant carvings and decorations,
are not to be sold in the market;
Clothing and food,
are not to be sold in the market;
Fruits out of season,
are not to be sold in the market;
Timber not properly felled,
are not to be sold in the market;
Birds, beasts, fish, and turtles not properly caught,
are not to be sold in the market;
All who enforce these prohibitions,
to regulate the people,
shall not pardon offenses."

Chicken Market
In Cháng'ān, a wealthy commoner named Luó Huì made his living by collecting and removing excrement,
and the locals called him the "Chicken Pen,"
meaning that, like chickens,
he obtained something by picking through dung.
Huì had inherited this trade from his ancestors,
and his family wealth amounted to millions.
A scholar named Lù Jǐngyáng was once invited by Huì to visit his residence,
where the buildings were exceptionally splendid.
Upon entering, he washed and groomed himself,
and his garments were extremely fresh and clean.
There were screens, woolen rugs,
and all kinds of cooking utensils—nothing was lacking.
Jǐngyáng asked,
"Since you, sir, live so comfortably,
why not give up this filthy business?"
Huì replied,
"I once stopped for a year or two in between,
but then my servants died,
and my cattle and horses scattered and were lost.
After resuming the trade,
my household gradually prospered again.
It’s not that I do it willingly,
but it seems to be my destined lot."

Discarding Ashes
Under the Yīn dynasty's law, those who discarded ashes in the street were punished.
Zǐgòng considered this severe,
and asked Zhòngní about it.
Zhòngní said:
"This is the way to understand governance.
Discarding ashes in the street will inevitably soil others,
soiling others,
will inevitably make people angry,
anger will lead to fights,
and fights will inevitably cause three clans to harm each other,
this is the path to destroying three clans,
so even punishing it is acceptable.
Moreover, serious crimes
are what people detest,
while not discarding ashes is what people find easy.
Making people do what is easy and avoid what they detest,
this is the way of governance."
Another version says:
"Under Yīn law,
those who discarded ashes on public roads had their hands cut off."
Zǐgòng said:
"The crime of discarding ashes is minor,
while the punishment of hand-cutting is severe,
why were the ancients so harsh?"
The reply was:
"Not discarding ashes is easy,
losing a hand is detestable,
doing what is easy without involving what is detestable,
the ancients considered this easy,
therefore they practiced it."

The path is overgrown with weeds
King Dìng sent Duke Shàn Xiāng on a mission to Sòng,
passing through Chén,
when the morning star was visible at dawn.
The roads were overgrown and impassable,
the Minister of Works did not inspect the pathways,
and there were no trees lining the roads.
Duke Shàn returned and reported to the king:
"Unless Marquis Chén meets with great misfortune,
his state is bound to perish.
For when the Horn star appears, the rains cease;
when the Root-of-Heaven star appears, the waters dry up.
Thus the teachings of the former kings said:
'When the rains cease, clear the roads;
when the waters dry up, build the bridges.'
Therefore the Summer Ordinances state:
'In the ninth month, clear the roads;
in the tenth month, build the bridges.'
The Zhōu regulations have it thus:
'Plant trees in rows to mark the roads,
and provide food in border stations to enforce orders.'

Wǔfǔ
Jìsūn was the chancellor of Lǔ,
Zǐlù served as the magistrate of Hòu.
Lǔ mobilized the masses in May to dig a long canal,
while this project was underway,
Zǐlù used his private salary grain to prepare meals for the people,
and invited the canal workers to eat at the crossroads of Wǔfǔ.
When Confucius heard of this,
he sent Zǐgòng to overturn the rice,
smash the utensils,
and said:
"The ruler of Lǔ possesses the people,
why are you feeding them?"
Zǐlù became enraged,
rolled up his sleeves and entered to protest:
"Does the Master detest Yóu
for practicing benevolence and righteousness?"
Confucius said:
"Yóu, you are being uncouth.
You feeding them
is out of love for them.
But according to ritual,
the Son of Heaven loves all under heaven,
the feudal lords love within their domains,
the high ministers love their official positions,
and the scholars love their households.
To exceed what one should love is called encroachment.
Now the ruler possesses the people, yet you presume to love them -
this is your encroachment.
Is this not presumptuous?"
Before his words were finished, Jìsūn's messenger arrived,
rebuking him:
"Féi
mobilized the people and employs them.
The Master sends his disciples
to now feed the conscripted laborers -
does he intend to steal Féi's people?"
Confucius had his carriage prepared and left Lǔ.

I wish to dismiss the most egregious ones.

Lǐ Jiàng replied:
"This is not Your Majesty's intention.
It must be deceitful people misleading Your Majesty's heart.
Since ancient times, receiving criticism leads to prosperity,
while rejecting criticism leads to ruin.
For a minister to present advice to the throne,
is it easy?
The ruler is held in esteem like heaven,
while the ministers are humble like the earth,
with the added fear of thunderous authority.
They ponder day and night,
wishing to present ten matters,
yet soon they retract five or six.
When about to report, they hesitate again,
and reduce it by half.
So what reaches the sovereign is only about one fifth of what it was.
Why do they venture such unfathomable risks?

Even when accepting and rewarding criticism,
there is still fear that it won't reach you.

causing the righteous to be silenced,

Empress Guō of Emperor Xiànzōng.
Emperor Wǔzōng enjoyed hunting trips.
One day, he inquired of the empress about her well-being,

The empress replied:
"Of the remonstrating ministers' memorials,

The emperor bowed twice,

From then on, hunting excursions became infrequent,

Planting a Scholar Tree
Lǐ Xiàokuān served as the Governor of Yōngzhōu.
Previously, an earthen mound marker was placed every li along the roadside,
which would collapse and deteriorate after rain, requiring frequent repairs.
After Xiàokuān took office in the province,
he ordered that locust trees be planted at the sites of the mounds within his jurisdiction as replacements.
This not only eliminated the need for repairs,
but also provided shade for travelers.
Later, Emperor Wén of the Northern Zhōu dynasty noticed this and found it unusual.
Upon inquiring, he learned the reason.
He said:
"How can one province alone have this benefit?
It should be implemented throughout the realm."
Thereupon, he ordered the roads in all provinces
to be planted with one tree every li,
two trees every ten li,
and five trees every hundred li.
(From History of the Northern Dynasties)

To quarry the mountain
Lù Xiàngxiān served as the Chief Administrator of Yìzhōu.
He proposed that the Jiāqióng route was too long,
requesting to excavate south of Mínshān for a shortcut.
Conscripted laborers were mobilized for the project,
but the local inhabitants could not endure it,
with many fleeing or dying along the way,
making the expedition unprofitable.
Zuǒ Shíyí Zhāng Xuānmíng, overseeing military affairs in Yáojùn and serving as a pacification envoy,
personally inspected the route,
assessed its dangers and difficulties,
and sent a dispatch to Yìzhōu stating:
"This path has high mountains touching the clouds,
deep valleys without sunlight,
featuring precipitous cliffs and immense dangers,
barely passable by human tracks.
Those who traverse it must cling to cliffs and sidle along edges,
holding their breath to cross.
Even after a full day's arduous travel covering only about twenty lǐ,
a wooden figure would still weep,
and an iron horse could wear through its hooves."
After reading this, Lù Xiàngxiān became fearful and cautious,
immediately halting the project.
He reported following the original route,
and the people of Shǔ benefited from this.
(Táng Xīn Yǔ)
Avoid delay
During the reign of Emperor Shùn,
the Minister of Finance Liú Jù was summoned due to a reprimand related to his duties.
He went to see the Secretary,
and was hurried along with orders to quicken his steps.
Additionally, he was subjected to beating and flogging.
Zuǒ Xióng presented a memorial stating that the rank of the Nine Ministers was second only to the Three Excellencies,
placed among the high officials.
Their conduct followed the rituals of wearing jade,
and their actions adhered to exemplary decorum.
Emperor Xiàomíng was the first to institute beating as punishment,
which was not in accordance with ancient traditions.
The emperor responded by changing this practice,
and thereafter the Nine Ministers were no longer subjected to beating.

Initially, Fáng Guǎn had served as the sheriff of Féngyì.
Lù Xiàngxiān's clerk Dǎng Fēn

Guǎn also went to see him to explain the matter

Lost Path
In the second year of the Zhenyuan era, Lǐ Shèng recaptured the capital.

Cassia
Sū Qín went to the state of Chǔ,
and only after three days was he able to see the king.
After the conversation ended, he took his leave and prepared to depart.
The king said:
"I have heard of you, sir, as if hearing of an ancient worthy,
and now you have come a thousand lǐ without regard to the distance to visit me,
yet you refuse to stay.
I wish to hear your reason."
Sū Qín replied:
"In the state of Chǔ, food is more expensive than jade,
firewood is more expensive than cassia,
the ushers are as difficult to see as ghosts,
and the king is as difficult to see as Heaven.
Now you would have me eat jade and burn cassia,
and through ghosts seek an audience with Heaven."
The king said:
"Sir, please return to your lodgings,
I have received your instruction."

Seeking lodging
When the Emperor ascended the throne, he traveled incognito.
Once he reached Bǎigǔ,
and at night sought lodging at a village head's place.
The village head did not accept him,
so he stayed with an old man at an inn.
More than ten unruly youths,

The woman said to her husband:

and all the youths fled.

bestowed a thousand catties of gold upon the woman,

How many times have I gazed from a Mùlán boat,
