The seated guests were greatly astonished,
and upon inquiring,
they realized it was Yìshān.
"Gǔjīn Shīhuà"
"Línglíng Zǒngjì" was written by Lù Guīméng.
Yǔ Huì
Túshān in Zhōnglí County, Háozhōu,
is where Yǔ took his wife.
To the southwest of the mountain lie the ruins of Yǔ and Yǔhuì Village,
which was likely the place where Yǔ assembled the feudal lords.
"Yǔdìzhì"
Shí Niǔ
Yǔ, a native of Guǎngróu in Wènshān, was born in Shí Niǔ Village,
the place named Kū'ér Píng.
Yuánhé Jùnxiàn Zhì
Now the indigenous people jointly manage this land,
covering an area of a hundred lǐ,
dare not engage in animal husbandry,
if someone commits a crime and flees into this wilderness,
the pursuers dare not chase them,
fearing Yǔ's divinity,
able to hide for three years,
without being captured by others,
then they are collectively pardoned,
saying they are protected by Yǔ's divinity.
Huáyáng Guó Zhì
Lù Lǐ
In the Tài Lake of Wú, within the Dòngtíng region, southwest lies Lùlǐ Village,
where Master Jiǎolǐ resided.
"Shǐ Zhèngyì"
Zhāojūn
Wáng Zhāojūn was born in Xiázhōu,
and there is now a Zhāojūn Village.
Lǜ Zhū was born in Báizhōu,
and there is now a Lǜzhū River.
Guìfēi was born in Shǔ,
and once accidentally fell into a pond,
later generations called it the Luòfēi Pond.
"The Unofficial Biography of Consort Yáng"
Through countless valleys and hills that converge toward Jīngmén
there is still the village where the bright consort grew up.
From a poem by Dù Fǔ
Wūyè Cūn
Jìn Mùdì's empress's father Hé Zhǔn resided three lǐ south of Hǎiyán.
When the empress was about to give birth,
a flock of crows startled the village at night,
after which the crows crowed even more.
The crowd found it strange,
and by daybreak a great amnesty was declared,
which was the day Mùdì established Hé Zhǔn's daughter as empress.
"Tú Jīng"
Jǐnshā
In Jǐnshā Village of Qīngxī County, Mùzhōu, nestled against mountains and valleys,
clear waves reflect serenely,
and beautiful stones display their patterns.
Champion Wú Xǐ, hearing of this, visited the place,
rowing his boat to wander and float,
lingering for ten days without thought of return.
He sighed and said:
"Famous mountains and exquisite stones
truly deserve their praise,
making one forget the ambitions of the red-lacquered gates."
From "The Record of Mùzhōu"
Fǎng Cūn
In Shèxiàn there was Fǎng Village,
according to popular tradition, when Rèn Fǎng served as governor of Xīn'ān,
he came here during his spring tour,
and fell in love with its cloudy streams.
Following the streams to seek secluded places,
he remained for many days without returning.
The local people therefore named the stream Fǎng Stream,
and the village beside the stream Fǎng Village.
Beside the village there was a mountain,
which was close to the northern wilds county.
Whenever stones fell from the mountain, it brought misfortune,
but after the county office was abolished,
these occurrences also ceased.
In the tenth year of the Dàzhōng era,
Governor Lú Fān changed the names to Rèngōng Village and Rèngōng Stream.
"Universal Geography Record"
Huànhuā
I humbly beg for a hundred peach saplings,
To be delivered to Huànhuā Village before spring.
Dù Fǔ's Poems
record that Dù Fǔ planted bamboos and trees at Huànhuā Lane in Chéngdū,
built a cottage overlooking the river,
indulged in drinking and chanted poems freely,
mingling intimately with farmers and old villagers.
Old Book of Táng
Burying one's thoughts
Mǎ Suì plotted against Lǐ Huáiguāng,
leading troops from Tàiyuán to encamp beneath Bǎo,
inquired about the place,
and learned it was called "Mái Huái Village."
He then exclaimed with great joy:
"We will surely capture the rebel!"
From "Supplement to the National History."
Zhū Chén
In ancient Fēng County of Xúzhōu, there was a village called Zhū-Chén,
where only two clans inhabited the entire village,
generation after generation intermarrying with one another.
Bái Jūyì's poem
Ruòxià
Chángxīng Ruòxī and Jiāxī,
are both overgrown with arrow bamboo,
the southern bank is called Shàngruò,
the northern bank is called Xiàruò,
both Ruò are village names.
The villagers use the water from Xiàruò to brew wine,
its richness and excellence surpass that of Yúnyáng,
commonly known as Ruòxià wine.
"Yǔdìzhì"
Bāxiāng
The Yúfù garrison was stationed on the left bank of the river,
where there was a Bāxiāng Village.
The villagers were skilled at brewing,
hence the local saying that Bāxiāngqīng County was famous for its fine wine.
Beside the village was a stream,
in which grew abundant sacred longevity trees.
Within it lived fish,
whose heads resembled those of sheep,
with plump flesh and few bones,
tastier than other fish.
From the "Water Classic"
Pínglè
Yúfù County's eastern Hěnshān County originally belonged to Wǔlíng County.
About ten li north, there is a divine cave,
normally dry without water.
When thirsty people sincerely pray,
and request water, they always receive it.
If someone jokingly asks,
the water never emerges.
About ten li east of the county lies Pínglè Village,
where there is another stone cave emitting clear spring water.
Within it resides a hidden dragon.
Whenever a severe drought occurs,
the residents of Pínglè Village and nearby villages push grass and filth into the cave.
The dragon becomes angry,
and in a moment, water gushes out,
washing away the grass and filth,
enabling the irrigation of the surrounding fields.
Dōngtíng
Traveling five or six li downstream from Pínglè,
the northern mountain of Dōngtíng Village is very high and steep.
It is solid above and hollow below,
with the hollow crevice spanning about two zhang from east to west.
Inside, rising as high as a house, there is a stone forest,
very orderly and well-arranged.
Wild chives grow beside it,
and when people go to ask for them,
if the deity permits, the wind blows and divides them accordingly.
One must bow and offer them in return,
and cannot exceed the limit.
If one does not bow while offering,
misfortune will surely follow.
Those who go to observe it
find the path unusually level when leaving,
and upon reaching the place, naturally become reverent and solemn.
Shítáng
Northwest of Guìyáng Yángshān County there is Shítáng Village,
beside the flowing water of the village stands a camphor tree,
its trunk measuring about two zhàng in circumference,
its stump still remains.
When it was cut down,
the load was piled up yet the axe marks appeared fresh,
feathered creatures flew about,
ceaselessly hovering by its side.
Many branches scattered and drifted afar,
the villagers could not fathom where they went,
only to see one branch remaining alone,
seeking the water's edge.
Long live the emperor
In Guìyáng Chēn County there is the Qiānqiū River,
which originates from Wànsuì Mountain to the southwest.
The mountain contains a stone chamber,
within which are stalactites.
The mountain is entirely covered with Língshòu trees,
and below the stream lies the Qiānqiū River.
Along the riverbank is a settlement called Wànsuì Village,
whose waters flow downstream to merge with the Huáng River.
Xiāngbēi
In Chēn County's southern Xiāngbēi Village,
there is a round pond,
approximately two hundred paces in diameter.
One side is warm while the other is cold;
the cold area is extremely clear and green—
shallow enough to reveal stones,
deep enough to have no bottom.
The warm area has white and turbid water.
Their natures differ as black and white,
and their temperatures also vary.
It is named the Chú Spring,
similar to the Bàn Tāng Spring of Jiāngchéng.
When water is abundant, it flows into the Huáng Stream;
when depleted, it ceases its course along the path.
Broken Stone
In Xiūníng County's Xīduànshí Village,
formerly known as Wúkǒu Village,
there is a stone cliff to the southwest,
overlooking a deep stream below.
According to old records, two boats once moored here,
one making offerings and the other not.
At night, a deity moved the offering boat,
while on the northern bank stood a stone.
It fell from the sheer cliff,
shattering the non-offering boat.
At the spot where the stone fell,
a stone chamber was formed.
From "Records of Geography"
Plum Blossoms
Mount Luófú stands thirty-six hundred zhang high,
with a circumference of over three hundred li.
It has fifteen ridges,
and thirty-two peaks.
Among its most elegant peaks are Fēiyún, Yù'é, Jǐnxiù, and Dàimào.
Beside the path of Fēiyún Peak lies the Plum Blossom Village.
Records of Nányuè states,
as Sū Shì's poem says: "At the foot of Mount Luófú lies the Plum Blossom Village, where jade snow forms the bones and ice the soul."
Mùxiāng
Sixty li west of Yíchéng County is Mùxiāng Village,
the former estate of Duàn Chéngshì of the Táng Dynasty.
"Geographical Records"
Méi Huí
Below Hóngtíng Village is Méihuí Village,
which was traditionally said to be where plum and locust trees grew together forming a single tree,
hence the name.
Now the pronunciation has been corrupted,
and it is called Méihuí.
Wáng Duānxiū's "Records of Jiānglíng"
Mùkè
In Yuè there is a Mùkè Village,
in the Póyáng Mountains dwell the Mù'ān,
who were builders of the Ēpáng Palace during the Qín dynasty.
They attained immortality by consuming tree fruits,
and occasionally descend to human settlements to obtain wine.
They composed a poem that reads:
"When wine runs dry, sir, do not buy more;
When the jar tilts, I shall depart.
The city bustles with dusty clamor,
I return to mountains to sport with the bright moon."
Xú Xuàn's notation.
Old Man
In Shǔ, at Qīngchéng Mountain, there is an Elderly Village.
In its stream, there are roots of gǒuqǐ (wolfberry).
Drinking its water leads to longevity.
From the "Tú Jīng" (Illustrated Classic).
Wild Fox
The Wild Fox Spring Inn is west of Tóngguān Pass,
with the spring located south of the road.
Behind the inn, at the foot of the slope, an old legend says:
a wild fox dug and the spring gushed forth.
The innkeeper turned it into cold noodles,
which passing travelers would stop to eat.
Nowadays, among the refined dishes, there is one called Wild Fox Spring,
made with mung bean starch,
also imitating this tradition.
From "New Book of the South".
Original
A broad and level area is called yuán,
a low and damp area is called xí.
The "Ěryǎ"
and the "Chūnqiū Shuōtící" state:
"A high and level area is called Tàiyuán.
Yuán,
means 'proper'
—level and having measure.
A vast and extensive area is called dàlǔ,
which is Tàiyuán."
The "Shìmíng" says:
"Land that does not produce living things is called lǔlú."
The "Gǔliáng Zhuàn" states:
"In the Central States, it is called Tàiyuán,
among the barbarians, it is called dàlǔ."
The "Shàngshū Dàzhuàn" says:
"The eastern plain is thoroughly level,
what is large and high-level is called Tàiyuán,
what is low and level is called xí."
The "Shuǐjīng"
states that the upper level is called yuán,
the lower level is called xí.
The "Gōngyáng Zhuàn"
and the "Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì" say:
"Yuán,
means extensively level,
hence it is called píngyuán (plain)."
The "Shuǐjīng"
describes land that is broad, extensive, and level as
being named yuán.
Lǐ Xún's "Ěryǎ Zhù"
Bìyuán
Zhōu Wénzhèng was buried at Bì,
southeast of Cháng'ān there was originally a place called Bìyuán.
"Guānzhōng Jì"
Liú Xiàng said:
"King Wén, King Wǔ, and Duke Zhōu were buried at Bì."
Shī Gǔ said:
"Bìmò is forty lǐ northwest of Cháng'ān."
"Hànshū"
Shǐpíng
North of Cháng'ān City lies the Shǐpíng Plain,
spanning several hundred lǐ without mountains, rivers, or lakes.
Its inhabitants draw water from wells and dwell in nests,
with wells fifty zhàng deep.
There is the tomb of Bó Yí,
where people eat ferns,
which can be consumed regularly.
Some say Yí and Shū ate them for three years,
yet their complexions remained unchanged.
In the Hàn dynasty, it was also called the Běimáng Cliff.
"Records of the Three Qín"
Báilù
To the east of Cháng'ān lies Líshān,
to the west lies Báilùyuán (White Deer Plain),
looking north toward Yúnyáng,
one can fully see the shapes of the mountains and hills,
yet they always appear as if shrouded in clouds and mist.
"Records of Campaigns"
When King Píng of Zhōu moved the capital east,
a white deer roamed this plain,
hence it got its name,
likely an auspicious omen.
"Records of the Three Qín"
To the east of Dùlíng's Gǒujiāchuān is also called Báihǔyuán (White Tiger Plain),
on which stands Gǒujiābǎo (Dog Yoke Fort),
"Records of the Three Qín" states:
West of Líshān is Báilùyuán,
on the plain stands Gǒujiābǎo,
it is said that during Duke Xiāng's time, a large dog descended,
when bandits came, the dog would bark at them,
thus the fort remained unharmed,
so the river gained its name.
"Water Classic"
Sānzhì
Sānzhìyuán was located twenty lǐ south of Yōng County in Qízhōu,
as recorded in the "Treatise on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices":
"Duke Wén of Qín established the Fūzhì,
Duke Xiāng established the Xīzhì,
and Duke Líng established the Wúyáng Shàngzhì,
all on this plain, hence the name."
The Kuòdìzhì
quotes the Treatise on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices in the Imperial Readings:
Duke Wén established the Fūzhì,
Duke Líng established the Wúyáng Shàngzhì,
and Duke Xuān established the Mì Xiàzhì.
Since these three zhì were on this plain,
it was called Sānzhìyuán (Plain of the Three Zhì).
Jiǔyuán
The old city of Jīnglíng County was the land of Jiǔyuán during the Spring and Autumn period.
The "Guóyǔ" states:
"Zhào Wénzǐ and Shūxiàng were traveling in Jiǔyuán,
and said:
'If the dead could be revived,
whom should I follow?'
Shūxiàng said:
'Perhaps Yángzǐ?'
Wénzǐ said:
'His wisdom is not worthy of praise.'
Shūxiàng said:
'Perhaps Jiùfàn.'
Wénzǐ said:
'His benevolence is not worthy of praise.
Perhaps Suí Wǔzǐ?
He accepted remonstrance without forgetting his teacher,
thus his capital still remains.
When the Hàn dynasty rose, a mound was added below it,
hence it was called Jīnglíng.'"
The "Shuǐ Jīng"
August Heaven
The Yùjiàn River emerges north of the Hàn region,
flowing past the Huángtiān Plain,
where the western end is broad and level,
spanning over a square lǐ,
with three sides of sheer cliffs rising about a thousand rèn high.
During the Hàn dynasty, sacrifices to heaven were held here,
naming it the Huángtiān Plain.
On it stands Emperor Hàn Wǔdì's Terrace of Longing for His Son.
Above
Zhào Qí's original name was Jiā,
he was born in the Yùshǐ Tái,
hence he received the courtesy name Tái Qīng.
During the time of Emperor Xiàn, he served as the Imperial Stable Master.
When Lǐ Jué was handling the government affairs,
the Grand Tutor Mǎ Rìzhī pacified the realm,
appointing Qí as the deputy.
When Rìzhī reached Luòyáng,
he presented a separate dispatch for Qí,
to propagate the imperial edicts.
Wherever he arrived in the counties,
the common people were all delighted and said:
"Today, we once again see the envoys' carriages and horses."
In the "Later Hàn," Emperor Xiàn appointed Qí as the Imperial Stable Master,
holding the tally to pacify the realm.
The "Continued Later Hàn," "General Code," and "Imperial Review" all agree.
Lè Yóu
Emperor Xuân had lived with the Xǔ family in his youth,
and grown up in Dù County, delighting in it.
Later, he was buried in Nányuán,
and a temple was erected north of Qǔchí,
with a pavilion named Lèyóu Yuán.
"Records of Guānzhōng"
Shǎolíng
The Shǎolíng Plateau connects to Zhōngnán Mountain in the south,
and reaches Chǎnshuǐ River in the north.
It was originally known as the Hónggù Plateau during the Hàn Dynasty,
where Empress Xǔ of Emperor Xuān was buried,
hence it became commonly called Shǎolíng Plateau.
"Records of Cháng'ān"
Wǔzhàng
Zhūgě Liàng occupied the southern bank of the Wèi River,
Sīmǎ Yì said to his generals:
"If Liàng marches through Wǔgōng,
and turns eastward along the mountains,
that would show his courage.
But if he heads west to Wǔzhàngyuán,
you gentlemen need not worry."
Liàng indeed garrisoned this plain,
and faced off against Yì.
《Water Classic》
Shí Ān
Fú Jiàn attacked Zhāng Jǔ at Yíqiū,
and upon returning, ascended Shí'ān Plateau, sighing:
"How beautiful this plateau is!"
He felt a wistful longing to settle there permanently.
From Cuī Hóng's "Records of the Former Qín".
Wànshòu
Emperor Gāozǔ conducted a military hunt on the Wànshòu Plain of Huá Chí,
where a white deer appeared before the newly enthroned Emperor Gāozǔ,
who shot and captured it with his bow and arrows.
"Old Book of Táng"
Fènghuáng
Wéi Sìlì constructed his estate at Phoenix Plain and Parrot Valley on Lí Mountain,
featuring layered cliffs, cavernous gorges,
cascading streams and waterfalls.
Emperor Zhōngzōng newly visited this place,
thus bestowing upon Wéi Sìlì the title Duke of Carefree Wanderer,
naming his residence Clear Void Plain and Secluded Dwelling Valley.
In the second year of Yánguāng era of Later Hàn dynasty,
phoenixes gathered at Xīnfēng,
which was precisely this plain,
also a subsidiary ridge of Lí Mountain.
Records of Cháng'ān · Old Táng History
Hányuán
Hán Féngyì had an original poem that said:
"There is a lofty path,
Marquis Hán received the mandate,"
this refers to this origin.
Also, "Ancient and Modern Place Names" states:
"Hán Wǔzǐ received territory at Hányuán,"
where Qin and Jin also battled at this place,
capturing Dù Huí,
and where Qin captured Marquis Huì of Jin and returned with him.
"Records of Commanderies and States"
Qī Shān
Hédōng, Yánchí, Dōngwú, Jīdēng, Qīshānyuán,
each time ascending one plateau,
it would steeply rise five or six lǐ,
the plateau's soil was level and vast,
one could not discern its immense extent.
Dài Yánzhī's "Records of a Western Campaign"
Fēngliáng
To the west of Lìshān, within the river valley lies a mound called Fēngliángyuán,
located on the northern side of Kuǐshān, a blessed land of Yōngzhōu.
"Guānshàngtú"
Suburbs
Outside the city is called the suburbs,
outside the suburbs is called the pasture,
outside the pasture is called the wilderness.
From "Ěryǎ"
Xiāngchéng
Huángdì was going to see Dàwěi at Mount Jùcí,
with Fāng Míng as his charioteer and Chāng Yǔ as his companion in the carriage,
until they reached the wilderness of Xiāngchéng,
where the seven sages all lost their way,
with no one to ask for directions.
By chance, they encountered a boy herding horses,
so they asked him for the way.
"Zhuāngzǐ"
Dòngtíng
Běimén Chéng asked Huángdì, saying:
"You performed the music of Xiánchí in the wilderness of Dòngtíng.
When I first heard it, I was afraid;
then hearing it, I became weary;
finally hearing it, I became confused.
Vast and silent,
I could no longer hold on to myself."
Severed Reins
Emperor Yándì executed Chīyóu in Zhōngjì,
naming the place the Field of Severed Bridles.
"The Annals of Emperors and Kings"
Qīng Qiāng
Yǔ traveled east to the wilderness where trees were twined,
where the sun rose over nine fords,
the wilds of Qīngqiāng,
the lands of Bird Valley and Green Hill,
south to the Mountain of Nine Suns, the land of immortality,
west to the Mountain of Accumulated Gold,
where the Gònghóng people had one arm,
the land of the three-faced people,
north to the remotest shores of the Summer Sea,
the wilds of Kuāfù.
"Lǚ's Annals: Seeking the Worthy"
Mùyě
From Zhāogē southward,
reaching the extreme south at Qīngshuǐ,
the land is flat and expansive,
resting on high grounds and spanning marshes,
all part of the Mùyě Plain,
as stated in the Guózhì: Zhāogē County,
to the south lies Mùyě,
the Zhúshū Jìnián records:
"King Wǔ of Zhōu led the western feudal lords to attack Yīn,
defeating them at Mùyě,
as described in the Shījīng: 'Vast is the Mùyě Plain,
brilliant are the sandalwood chariots.'"
The Shuǐjīng
Dūnwù
Qín, since Fēizǐ received his enfeoffment,
until the year King Zhāo destroyed Zhōu, which was in the constellation Dàliáng,
moved its capital seven times in total,
all within the region of Yōngzhōu as recorded in the Tribute of Yǔ,
in the wilderness of Jīngshān, Zhōngnán, and Dūnwù,
under the division of the constellations Dōngjǐng and Yǔguǐ,
and in the lunar mansion Chúnhuǒ.
"Records of the Emperors and Kings"
Planning in the Wilderness
When Zǐchǎn conducted state affairs,
he selected capable men and employed them.
Píchén was skilled in planning,
and when he planned in the countryside, he achieved success,
but when he planned in the city, he did not.
Whenever the state of Zhèng was about to engage in matters with the feudal lords,
Zǐchǎn would then take a carriage with Píchén to go to the countryside,
having him deliberate on what was feasible or not,
and then inform Féng Jiǎnzǐ to make the final decision.
"The Rites of Zhōu"
Shào Yuán
Confucius was traveling in the wilderness of Shǎoyuán,
when he saw a woman weeping in the marsh,
her voice extremely mournful.
Confucius sent a disciple to inquire,
saying:
"Madam, why do you weep so mournfully?"
The woman replied:
"Earlier, while cutting mugwort for firewood,
I lost my mugwort hairpin,
and that is why I grieve."
The disciple said:
"To lose a mugwort hairpin while cutting mugwort for firewood—
what is there to grieve about?"
The woman replied:
"It is not the loss of the hairpin that pains me,
but rather that I cannot forget the past."
from *Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn*
Dānyě
Huán Wēn campaigned north against Yáo Xiāng at the Yīshuǐ River,
Xǔ Xùn said:
"You may not capture Xiāng but will achieve great merit."
Seeing Xiāng flee into the Tàixuán region,
Huán Wēn asked:
"What kind of place is Tàixuán?"
The reply came:
"South is the Vermilion Wilderness,
north is Tàixuán,
he will surely flee northwest."
It indeed happened as predicted.
"Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds"
Guǎngmò
Zhuāngzǐ said to Huìzǐ:
"You have a large tree,
worried about its uselessness.
Why not plant it in the land of nothingness,
the vast and barren wilderness,
wandering idly by its side doing nothing,
and roaming freely while sleeping beneath it?"
"Zhuāngzǐ: Free and Easy Wandering"
Vast wilderness
The Nameless Man said:
"I am about to join with the Creator and become a person;
when weary, I shall mount the bird of chaos and obscurity,
to fly beyond the six poles,
and wander in the land of Nothingness,
dwelling in the wilds of boundlessness."
"The Sovereign Who Responds"
Wújí
Guǎngchéngzǐ said:
"Now all living things are born from the earth,
and return to the earth.
Therefore, I shall leave you,
entering the gate of the infinite,
to wander in the realm of the limitless."
"Zàiyòu"
In the spring of the sixth year of Shǐyuán of Emperor Zhāo,
Sū Wǔ was appointed as the Director of Dependencies at Yízhōng.
In the time of Emperor Xiàomíng, according to the "Hànshū",
while reading the "Biography of Sū Wǔ",
he saw that Sū Wǔ held the title of Director at Yízhōng,
and inquired with his officials,
but none of the officials knew.
The description of Cāng Jié,
and the study of primary texts,
were thoroughly equipped with characters,
yet none could answer the question of the sacred nation.
All of these were individuals of splendid fate following orders,
often serving as officials.
With numerous texts beside them,
they could not recognize the characters;
to aspire to reach the understanding of Dǒng Zhòngshū's knowledge of Zhòngcháng,
or Liú Zǐzhèng's knowledge of Èrfù,
is indeed challenging!
In "Lùnhéng Biétōng," Fēnjì mistakenly recorded Sū Wǔ as the Director of Dependencies.
This is incorrect.
Vast and boundless
The great man is serene and free from thought,
tranquil and without anxiety,
letting his will roam freely and his steps unfold,
so as to gallop across the vast expanse.
"Tiāndì"
He travels upward to the ethereal mists,
"Dí"
and downward through the gate of the boundless wilds,
grasping the handle of the essential Way,
to wander in the limitless realm.
"Huáiyuán Dào"
Wǎng Làng
Ruòshì said:

Vast Wilderness
To the west lies the Mountain of the Queen Mother of the West,
where the Land of Plenty is located.
The people of Plenty dwell here,

They eat the eggs of phoenixes,

Sǎnguān
In the first year of the Zhōu Wújí era,
Lǎozi was crossing the pass,
when the pass official Yǐn Xǐ first instructed the gate officer, saying:
"If there is an old man coming from the east,
riding in a light blue ox-drawn cart,
do not allow him to pass through the gate."
That day, they indeed saw an old man riding in a blue ox-cart requesting to cross the pass,
and the gate officer entered to report to Yǐn Xǐ, saying:
"Yes,
the Way has now arrived.
I have seen the sage."
Immediately, he brought his official seal and went out to greet him,
performing the rites of a disciple.

Yángguān
The Wèn River flows southwest past Yángguān,
west of the old city.
In the seventeenth year of Duke Xiāng during the Spring and Autumn period:
Zāng Hé was welcomed from Yángguān here,
Yáng Hǔ occupied it,

Lùmén
Jìsūn attacked the Zāng clan,
Zāng Hé cut through the bar of the Lù Gate,
and fled to Zhū.
Jìsūn, following Mèng Jiāo's advice,
made a covenant with the Zāng clan, saying:
"Let no one be like Zāngsūn Hé,
who violated the laws of the state,
and broke through the gate by cutting its bar."
Zāngsūn heard of this and said:
"There is a capable person in the state;
who could it be but Mèng Jiāo?"
(Xiānggōng 23rd Year)
Zhāoguān
Wǔ Zǐxū, along with Crown Prince Jiàn and his son Shèng, all fled to Wú.
They traveled by night and hid by day.
When they reached Zhāoguān,
the border guards wanted to arrest them.
Zǐxū then deceitfully said:
"The reason the ruler is searching for me
is because I possess beautiful pearls.
Now I have already lost them.
I will tell you where to find them."
The border guards therefore let them go.
"Spring and Autumn Annals of Wú and Yuè"
Zǐxū, carrying a bag, passed through Zhāoguān.
He traveled by night and hid by day,
until he reached Língshuǐ.
Having no means to feed himself,
he crawled on his knees,
kowtowed and bared his upper body,
beat his belly and played the chí flute,
begging for food in the market of Wú.
He eventually revived the state of Wú,
making Hé Lǘ a hegemon.

Dū Guān
In the fourth year of King Sù of Chǔ,
Shǔ attacked Chǔ,
capturing Zīfāng,
so Chǔ built the Hànguān Pass to defend against them.
"Historical Records"
Chǔ built fortifications from Wūshān to Fāngchéng,
connecting Wū and Qiánzhōng,
and established the Hànguān Pass to resist Qín.
"Discourses on Salt and Iron"
The Jiāng River flows east from the pass, passing by Ruòguān and Hànguān.
Annotation:
Hànguān Pass,
was established by Lǐnjūn when he sailed on the Yí River.
Ruòguān borders the area of Píng Zǐguī,
where Bā and Chǔ repeatedly attacked each other in the past,
and they set up passes at strategic points for mutual defense.
"Water Classic"
In Yúfù County of Bā Commandery, there is Hànshuǐ and the Hànguān Pass.

Yānshì Sài
When the wife of the young ruler of Qín employed eunuchs to effect a change,
the multitude of worthies were displeased,
and the people, concealing themselves, were filled with resentment against their superiors.
The prince Lián, who had fled to Wèi,
hearing of this, desired to enter Qín.
He sought to do so through the ministers and the people,
and approached the pass of Zhèngsuǒ.
Yòu Zhǔ Rán, who guarded the pass, would not admit him,
saying:
"Your servant holds the principle of not serving two masters.
Let the prince depart."
Prince Lián thereupon left and entered Dí.
He then entered through Yān Dī Hán Jūn Gǎi.
When the ruler's wife heard of this,
she was greatly alarmed,
and ordered the officers to raise troops,
commanding them that there were invaders at the border.
When the troops and officers first set out,
they all said they were going to attack the invaders,
but midway, they changed their plan, saying it was not to attack invaders,
but to welcome their rightful lord.
Prince Lián then came together with the troops,
arriving at Yōng,
where they surrounded the ruler's wife.
The ruler's wife committed suicide,
and Prince Lián was established as Duke Xiàn.
He resented Yòu Zhǔ Rán and intended to punish him severely,
while feeling grateful to Jūn Gǎi and wishing to reward him richly.
Jiān Tū remonstrated, saying:
"This cannot be done.
There are many princes of Qín abroad.
If this is done, then the people of Qín will contend to bring them in,
and you will lose your position as prince.
This is not beneficial to the ruler."
Duke Xiàn considered this reasonable,
and therefore pardoned Yòu Zhǔ Rán's offense,
while bestowing upon Jūn Gǎi the rank of Guān Dàfū,
and granting twenty dàn of grain to each of the officers guarding the pass.
Duke Xiàn may be said to have been capable of employing rewards and punishments appropriately.

Four frontiers sealed
Qín is a state surrounded by natural barriers.
From "Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of Sū Qín"
The land of Qín is embraced by mountains and girdled by rivers,
secure within its fourfold ramparts.
From "Biography of Lóu Jìng"
The territory of Qín has Xiáo and Hán passes to the east,
Lǒng plateau to the west,
Shǔ and Hàn regions to the south,

protected by these four natural barriers,
forming an impregnable domain spanning a thousand lǐ.

Hángǔ
Sū Qín formed an alliance of the six states east of the mountains to jointly attack Qín,
with King Huái of Chǔ serving as the alliance leader.
They advanced to Hángǔ Pass,
where Qín dispatched troops to attack the six states,
causing their armies to retreat and withdraw.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Hángǔ Pass features towering cliffs and lofty skies,
with deep, secluded valleys,
and narrow mountain paths
where two carts cannot pass side by side.
It is renowned as a natural fortress,
hence the "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states:
"With perilous cliffs encircling firmly,
it is easily defended like a girdle."
This illustrates the saying, "Qín, possessing such a strategic advantage, could conquer the various lords."
Thus, Wáng Yuán advised Wěi Xiāo, saying:
"I request to seal off Hángǔ Pass to the east with a single pellet of mud.
Even if achieving kingship fails,
the worst outcome would suffice to establish hegemony."

Púbǎn
In the seventh year of King Xiāng of Wèi,
the King of Qín came for an audience at the Púbǎn Pass.
"The Bamboo Annals"
The rooster crows.
Mèng Chángjūn left the Qín Pass at night,
but the roosters had not yet crowed and the pass remained closed.
A low-ranking guest among his retinue
flapped his arms and imitated a rooster's crow,
whereupon all the roosters joined in chorus.
The pass was thus opened, allowing Mèng Chángjūn to escape.
(Lùnhéng Dìngxián)
When Yān Dān fled Qín,
he reached the pass by night.
The gate had not yet opened,
so Yān Dān imitated a rooster's crow,
causing all roosters to crow in response.
Thus he managed to escape and return home.
(Yān Dānzǐ)
The righteous actions of Yān Dān and Mèng Chángjūn
moved even the roosters beneath them to crow,
demonstrating how profound sincerity can evoke response,
and how unwavering genuine intent cannot be thwarted.
In ancient times, when Lǎozǐ journeyed westward,
Guān Yǐn Xǐ observed the aura here.
Thus, Zhào Zhì wrote in his letter to Jī Màoqí:
"When Old Master Lǐ entered Qín,
he sighed upon reaching the pass."
(Shuǐjīng)
White Horse
Ní Shuō,
a man of Sòng known for his skill in debate,
held that a white horse is not a horse.
When the debaters of Jìxià in Qí
rode a white horse to pass through the gate,
they were still required to pay the horse tax.
Thus, relying on empty rhetoric,
they could prevail over an entire state,
but when examined against reality and form,
they could not deceive even one person.
" Hán Fēi Zǐ "
Gōngsūn Lóng often argued,
"A white horse is not a horse."
No one could refute him,
but later, when he rode a white horse without a pass
and tried to leave through the gate,
the gatekeeper would not permit it.
This shows that empty words cannot override facts.

Hǔláo
In the seventh month of the second year of Duke Xiāng of Lǔ,
Duke Chéng of Jìn met with the feudal lords at Qìsuì City,
fortifying Hǔláo to pressure Zhèng.
The "Biography of King Mù" states:
"The Son of Heaven was shooting birds and hunting beasts in the gardens of Zhèng,
ordering the gamekeepers to sweep the woods,
when a tiger was found among the reeds.
As the Son of Heaven approached,
the warriors of the Seven Elite Guards,
Gāo Bēnróng,
captured the tiger alive and presented it.
The Son of Heaven commanded it to be tamed and kept in the Eastern Game Park,
hence it was called Hǔláo (Tiger Cage).
Thus, the name Hǔláo originated from this.
The Qín dynasty made it a pass,
and the Hàn dynasty established it as a county seat.
In the northwest corner, there is a small fortress,
with a circumference of three lǐ,
its northern side lined with watchtowers,
overlooking the river stretching far into the distance.
A solitary path ascends straight upward,
from this town, one ascends to gaze upon the clear and distant view,
where the landscape fully unfolds across rivers and plains.
Travelers arriving on their journey
are moved to profound emotion."
"Water Classic"
The matter concerns the official in charge.
Wèi Sìgōng sent an envoy as a traveler to pass through the customs market,
where the customs officials harshly troubled him.
After disputing with the customs officials,
he bribed them with gold,
and only then was he released.
Sìgōng then said to the customs officials:
"At that time, a traveler passed through,
and the gold that was given to you,
you thereupon let him go."
The customs officials were greatly frightened,
and considered Sìgōng to be perceptive and observant.

and stationed his troops at Bàshàng.

Zhōng Jūn
When Zhòng Jūn first left Jǐnán,
as he was about to pass through the frontier gate to see the Erudites,
the gate officer gave him a silk pass.
Jūn asked what it was for,
and the officer replied:
"For your return passage,
to be matched with the tally."
Jūn declared:

shall never return through this gate again."
He discarded the silk pass and departed.
Later, when Jūn became an Imperial Usher
and was sent on a mission through the commanderies and kingdoms,
he carried the imperial insignia eastward out of the gate.
The gate officer recognized him
and said:
"This envoy is the scholar who discarded the silk pass before."

Moving the Pass
The Hángǔ Pass was originally located west of Húchéng County in Hóngnóng.
In the winter of the third year of Yuándǐng,
General of Towered Ships,
Yáng Pǔ, having repeatedly achieved great merits,
was ashamed of being an outsider beyond the pass,
and submitted a petition requesting to move the pass eastward.
He offered to build the fortifications with seven hundred of his household servants,
and to cover the expenses with his personal wealth.
Emperor Wǔ, who also favored expansion,
thus relocated the pass to Xīn'ān,
three hundred lǐ away from Hóngnóng.

He was then sent back to his own state,

Jūyōng
In the second month of the fifteenth year of the Jiànwǔ era, the people of Yànmén, Dàijùn, and Shànggǔ were relocated,
establishing Chángshān Pass and Jūyōng Pass to the east.
"Wǔ Jì"
The Shīyú River flows from Jūyōng Pass in Shànggǔ,
on the eastern bank of the eastern stream are three layers of stone chambers,
their windows, doors, and panels are all made of stone,
likely the watchtowers of the ancient pass.
To the south, a deep valley is filled with stones forming the pass foundation,
with towering walls and steep cliffs,
not easily scalable with light effort,
the mountain peaks are layered and deep,
the side paths narrow and constricted,
the forest dense and perilous,
the road barely wide enough for a cart,
where morning birds and evening beasts
call coldly to each other,
and traveling officials and wandering sons hearing this
cannot help but feel sorrowful longing.

Sealing the Talisman
Guō Dān first went to Cháng'ān,
and bought a border pass from a man of Wǎn named Chén Zhào to enter Hángǔ Pass.
After entering,
he sealed the pass and gave it to someone, saying:
"Unless I ride in an envoy's carriage,
I shall not leave the pass.
Since Guō Dān entered the pass,
he did not return home for twelve years.
Later, when he was sent on a mission, he then left the pass,
ultimately not acting against his original intention."

Yùmén
Guāngwǔ closed the Yùmén Gate,
rejecting the tribute from the Western Regions.
In the "Annals,"
Bān Chāo, long residing in the distant territories,
in his old age yearned for his homeland,
he submitted a memorial saying:
"I do not dare hope to reach Jiǔquán County,

In the "Main Biography,"
traveling west from Dūnhuáng through Yùmén Gate and Yángguān, passing through Shànshàn,

the Western Regions were first connected during Emperor Xiàowǔ's time,

by Yùmén and Yángguān,
while in the west bounded by the Cōnglǐng.

Shàngdǎng
Féng Yì attacked northward at Tiānjǐng Pass,
capturing two cities in Shàngdǎng.
Note:
Tiānjǐng Pass lies at the foot of Tàiháng Mountain.
The Basic Biography
states that Hánshuǐ originates from Fù Mountain in Tàiháng,
which is another name for Wǔxíng.
Huáinánzǐ says:
"King Wǔ wanted to build a palace on Wǔxíng Mountain,
Duke Yòng said:
'Wǔxíng is steep and secure,
virtue can cover it,
tribute comes from afar,
if we act violently and disorderly, then attacking us would be difficult,
the gentleman considers this ability to maintain fullness.'"
Gāo Yòu said:
"This is present-day Tàiháng Mountain,
located northwest of Yěwáng County in Hénèi, at Shàngdǎng Pass.
The Shī says 'only treading the road of Yěwáng,
tilting the carriage cover at Shàngdǎng Pass',
referring to this mountain."
The Water Classic
records Féng Yǎn's letter to Tián Yì saying:
"Shàngdǎng has the security of four barriers,
girdled by three passes to the east,
serving as the state's western shield."
Note:
"The three passes refer to Shàngdǎng, Húkǒu, and Shíxíng."

Eight Abstentions
The Sǎnguān Barrier stretches from the Southern Mountains across the Luò River,
extending north to the Yellow River,
all being passes and fortifications.
It was built by the household servants of Yáng Pǔ.
Its walls lie west against rugged ramparts,
and resist the Huì River to the north.
In the first year of the Zhōngpíng era of Emperor Líng, Hé Jìn, Governor of Hénán, was appointed Grand General,
with troops from the five camps stationed at Dūtíng.
The Hángǔ Pass was established,
along with Guǎngchéng, Yīquē,
Tàigǔ, and Huányuán,
Xuánmén Ford being narrow,
Píng and Mèngjīn entering the pass,
with the Commandant's office in charge.
This Hángǔ Pass stands as the foremost,
included among the eight passes.
Thus, later generations collectively termed them
with the name "Eight Passes."

flowing southward, its torrents pounding against the mountains of the pass,

the Three Passes of Shǔ

The Liú clan occupied the strategic terrain of the three passes,

In Bāochéng, Hànzhōng—formerly Bāozhōng County of Hàn—stood Hàn's Yángpíng Pass,

White Horse
Mèng Dá of Shǔ surrendered,
and Wèi Wéndì appointed him as the governor of Xīnchéng,
governing Fánglíng.
There was a White Horse Mountain,
whose rocks resembled horses,
appearing strikingly lifelike from a distance.
Beside the water, it was called White Horse Pass.
Mèng Dá climbed it and sighed, saying:
"Liú Fēng and Shēn Dān,
held a thousand-mile stronghold yet lost it?"
He composed the "Shàng Dǔ Yín,"
its melody mournful and poignant,
touching people's hearts with sorrow.
Even now, it is still sung by the waterside.
