Mùlán
On the stone bank of the Hàn River stands a city called Língchéng,
encircling several lǐ in circumference,
with dozens of rows of stones piled along the left bank,
stacked continuously for tens of lǐ.
This place is known as Mùlán Sài,
and it is said:
The Wú dynasty dispatched troops here to rescue Mèng Dá.
Above
Gate of the Underworld
The Ghost Gate Pass is located thirty li south of Beiliu County,
with two rocks facing each other,
the space between them spanning thirty li,
commonly known as the Ghost Gate Pass.
It was the route taken by Han Dynasty General Fubo Mǎ Yuán when campaigning against the Linyi barbarians,
where he erected a stele,
and the stone tortoise still remains.
In the past, those heading to Jiaozhi all passed through this pass,
with the area to the south particularly rife with miasma and pestilence,
so few who went there ever returned alive.
A proverb says:
"At the Ghost Gate Pass,
out of ten who go,
nine do not return."
When Tang Dynasty Chancellor Lǐ Déyù was exiled to Yazhou,
he passed through this pass one day,
and thus composed a poem:
"Once gone, ten thousand li away,
a thousand know, a thousand won't return.
Where is Yazhou?
To cross the Ghost Gate Pass alive."
From "Records of the Universe" and "Records of Tang Poetry Events" by Yáng Yán.
When Grand Marshal Li was in Yazhou,
there was a northern pavilion in the commandery,
called the Gaze-at-the-Capital Pavilion.
Whenever the Grand Marshal climbed it,
he would always look northward with sorrow and choked emotions,
and wrote a poem:
"Alone I ascend the riverside pavilion, gazing toward the imperial capital;
even birds flying would take half a year's journey.
The green mountains too seem to fear people's return,
encircling the commandery city a hundred times, a thousand layers."
Formerly Yazhou,
is present-day Qiongzhou.
From "New Book of the South".
"West of the miasmic river, fire becomes mountains,
south of the fiery border, ghosts make a pass."
From Zhāng Jūn's poem in exile in Puzhou.
The Ghost Gate Pass in Rongzhou,
where the soil lacks iron,
uses Ying stone for cooking vessels to boil fish,
northerners call it the Five Marquises' Roaster.
Once the stone is heated by fire,
it remains warm for a long time,
which is today's talc.
From "Synopsis of the Finest Scenery".
Peach Grove
Táolín Sài is located four hundred li east of Cháng'ān.
If military forces pass through,
under favorable conditions they may pasture at Huàshān and rest beneath the trees,
but under adverse conditions the river will burst its banks and flood the area,
making it impassable for both men and horses.
"Records of Sānqín"
Yànmén
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
"The waters of Yànmén originate from Mount Yànmén,
where wild geese emerge from between its peaks,
located north of Gāoliǔ.
Gāoliǔ lies within Dài Province,
where the mountains rise in layered ridges and stacked summits,
lifting to rosy clouds and soaring heights,
their connected ranges fading into the distance,
stretching eastward beyond the Liáo frontier."
The Water Classic
Yànsài
Yànsài borders Liang Wènyáng Commandery to the north,
where wild geese pass by flapping their wings,
similar to Yànmén.
The "Jīngzhōu Jì"
records that within the boundaries of Liángbó County lies Yànsài,
and legend has it that this mountain has a large pond
where waterfowl and wild geese roost and gather,
hence the name Yànsài.
The "Liángzhōu Jì"
Chǔ Sài
Sixty li west of the commandery, traveling upstream along the river, there is a mountain on the southern bank,
named Jīngmén Shān,
and a mountain on the northern bank named Hǔyá,
the two mountains face each other,
forming the western fortress of Chǔ.
Jīngmén is joined at the top and open at the bottom,
opening through to the south of the mountain,
resembling the shape of a gate,
hence the name Jīngmén.
"Jīngzhōu Jì"
Lǔyáng
In Lǔyáng County there was the Lǔyáng Pass,
with continuous mountains on both sides piercing the sky,
and elegant trees reaching the clouds.
Therefore, Zhāng Jǐngyáng wrote in his poem:
"At dawn I climb Lǔyáng Pass,
the gorge path is steep and deep."
The "Water Classic"
A bridge,
is a beam over water.
A footbridge,
is a horizontal log over water,
used for crossing,
also called zhuó,
now referred to as lüè.
In Eastern Chǔ, a bridge is called yí.
In Shuōwén Jiězì,
stone piers are called yī.
In Ěryǎ,
stones gathered in water to form stepping stones,
are for crossing footbridges.
Annotation:
All Officials
Shàngyú County, also known as Yúbīn,
the Jìn Tàikāng Geographical Records state:
"Shùn avoided Dānzhū here,
hence the county was named after this event.
All the officials followed him,
so north of the county there is Bǎiguān Bridge.
It is also said that Yǔ met with the feudal lords for hunting,
and after the affairs were concluded, they enjoyed music together,
thus it was called Shàngyú."
The "Water Classic"
giant turtles and crocodiles
In the thirty-seventh year of King Mù of Zhōu, he attacked Chǔ,
mobilizing nine great armies,
reaching as far as the Jiǔjiāng River,
where he constructed a bridge using giant sea turtles and crocodiles.
The "Bamboo Annals"
and "Rhapsody on Regret" state:
"Just as he built a bridge using giant sea turtles and crocodiles."
It aptly cites the "Bamboo Annals" that King Wǔ of Zhōu, while attacking Zhòu,
advanced eastward to the Jiǔjiāng River.
And so on.
And so forth.
Shùn ordered Yǔ to dredge the rivers,
stabilize the mountains and cross the vast sea,
then using giant sea turtles and crocodiles as a bridge.
"Records of Omissions"
Liáng Zhā
Chǔ Lìngyǐn Dòu Qí cleared the way and built a bridge over the Zhà River,
stationing troops at Suíjià.
("Zuǒzhuàn", Duke Zhuang Year 4)
Zhà is the name of a river.
Jǔliáng
Duke Píng of Jìn stationed guards and descended to hold a meeting at Jùliáng.
"The Sixteenth Year of Duke Xiāng"
No bridge is greater than Jùliáng.
"Ěryǎ"
Jīqiáo
Crown Prince Dān of Yān was held as a hostage in Qín,
and the King of Qín treated him disrespectfully.
He then sought to return home,
so the King of Qín set up a mechanically triggered bridge,
intending to trap Dān.
When Dān crossed it,
the bridge did not trigger.
Another account says that intertwined dragons supported the carriage, and the mechanism did not activate,
but it is said that now the original location is unknown.
From the "Shuǐ Jīng"
Qīxīng
Shǔ had seven bridges,
first Chōnglǐ Bridge,
second Shì Bridge,
third Jiāng Bridge,
fourth Wànlǐ Bridge,
fifth Yílǐ Bridge,
sixth Suàn Bridge,
seventh Chángshēng Bridge.
Lǐ Bīng constructed bridges along the water,
corresponding to the seven constellations above,
thus Emperor Guāngwǔ said to Wú Hàn:
"The army should be stationed between the Seven Star Bridges."
from "Huáyáng Guózhì"
Héngqiáo
The Qin constructed a horizontal bridge,
the Han inherited the Qin system,
with a width of six zhang and three hundred eighty paces,
establishing a Director of Waterways to manage it,
and it was called the Stone Pillar Bridge.
"Old Affairs of the Three Capital Regions"
states the horizontal bridge symbolizes the Herdboy.
"The Yellow Map"
notes at the northern end of the bridge,
stones were piled in the water,
where there was formerly a statue of the deity Cǔnliú.
This deity once spoke with Lǔ Bān,
who asked him to come out.
Cǔnliú said:
"My appearance is fierce and ugly,
and you are skilled at depicting things;
I cannot show myself."
Bān then clasped his hands and spoke to him, saying:
"Show your head to see me."
Cǔnliú then revealed his head,
whereupon Bān used his foot to draw on the ground.
Cǔnliú became aware of this,
and immediately submerged back into the water.
Therefore, his image was placed in the water,
with only the back and above standing above the water.
Regarding Cǔnliú's statue,
Lord Cáo, while riding a horse, saw it and was startled,
and again ordered it to be taken down.
"Water Classic"
Wèi Qiáo
The Wèi Bridge is three lǐ north of Cháng'ān,
spanning the Wèi River as a bridge.
The First Emperor built the Wèi Bridge,
but the iron anchors were too heavy to move,
so he carved stone statues of strongmen like Mèng Bēn and made offerings to them,
whereupon the anchors could be moved.
The stone figures remain to this day.
From "Huáng Tú":
There are three Wèi Bridges,
one on the Xiányáng road northwest of the city,
called the Western Wèi Bridge;
one on the Gāolíng road to the northeast,
called the Eastern Wèi Bridge;
among them, the Wèi Tower stands north of the old city.
From "Suǒyǐn: Zhāng Shìzhī Zhuàn"
Bà Qiáo
Bàqiáo is located east of Cháng'ān,
spanning the water with a bridge.
During the Hàn Dynasty, people would see guests off to this bridge,
breaking off willow branches as farewell gifts.
During Wáng Mǎng's reign, Bàqiáo suffered a fire disaster,
and thousands of people tried to extinguish it with water but failed.
The name was then changed from Bàqiáo to Chángcúnqiáo (Long-lasting Bridge).
"Huáng Tú"
To water the horse
During the Hàn Dynasty, there was a Watering Horses Bridge at the Qīlǐ Canal.
The "Cháng'ān Map"
records that Chancellor Xiàhóu Yīng's tomb was located south of the main road east of the Watering Horses Bridge,
which people called the Horse Mound.
According to "Old Accounts of the Three Capital Regions"
Ascending to Immortality
Ten li north of Shǔ City stands the Ascending to Immortality Bridge,
a place for seeing off guests.
When Sīmǎ Xiàngrú first entered Cháng'ān,
he inscribed on its pillar:
"A true man shall not pass beneath you
unless riding a red carriage drawn by four horses."
from "Records of the States South of Mount Huà"
Bamboo Bridge
Zhūgě Liàng's memorial states:
"I dispatched Tiger Pace Supervisor Mèng Yǎn,
to occupy the east of Wǔgōng River.
Sīmǎ Yì, taking advantage of the rising Wèi River,
attacked Yǎn's camp.
I constructed a bamboo bridge,
crossed the water to shoot at them,
and once the bridge was completed, they swiftly retreated."
《Commentary on the Water Classic》
Wànlǐ
Wànlǐ Bridge is located eighty li south of Chéngdū County.
When the Shǔ envoy Fèi Yī was dispatched to Wú,
Zhūgě Liàng saw him off here.
He sighed and said:
"The journey of ten thousand li begins here."
Thus the bridge was named Wànlǐ Bridge.
From "Huáyáng Guózhì"
River Bridge
Dù Yù proposed building a bridge over the river at Fùpíngjīn,
but public opinion held that since it was the site of capitals during the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties,
and no sage or worthy had undertaken such a project,
it must be impossible to build one.
Dù Yù replied:
"In ancient times, creating boats to form a bridge is what is meant by a river bridge."
Thus, the bridge was successfully constructed,
and the emperor, accompanied by all the officials, attended its inauguration.
At the gathering, he raised his cup to toast Dù Yù, saying:
"Without you, this bridge would not stand."
Dù Yù responded:
"Without Your Majesty's wisdom,
I would not have had the opportunity to carry out this imperial project."
Everyone praised his words.
The Traveler
In Luòyáng's Qīlǐ Jiàn there is a stone bridge,
which is the Lǚrén Bridge.
In the past, Sūn Dēng did not wish to remain long in Luòyáng,
knowing that the Yáng family's prosperity would not last,
and ultimately thought of fleeing,
to disappear into the forested countryside,
concealing himself to avoid a meaningless death,
Yáng Jùn buried him east of this bridge,
and Yáng Jùn himself soon perished.
Zhū Chāoshí wrote to his elder brother that the bridge is six or seven lǐ from the Luòyáng Palace,
constructed entirely with large stones below round,
to allow water passage capable of accommodating large vessels,
its construction is uniquely shaped.
"Water Classic"
Mùlán
Zhūlán Qiáo,
originally named Dílán Qiáo,
had abundant reeds and wormwood on both sides of the bridge.
East of the bridge, Liú Jìhé raised pigs in large numbers.
The governor of Xiāngyáng said:
"This place reeks of pig manure,
so it should be renamed Zhūlán Qiáo."
Initially said in jest,
but the common people eventually adopted it as the official name.
"Xiāngyáng Qíjiù Zhuàn"
Pontoon Bridge
During the Jiànwǔ era of Zhào, a pontoon bridge was built at the river crossing,
using stones for the central piers.
Regardless of the stones' size,
they would wash away upon placement.
After expending immense labor,
the project remained unfinished for a year.
Shí Hǔ personally inspected the work,
submerging a jade disc in the river.
The next day, the disc drifted to a sandbar,
its waves lapping ashore.
He then executed the general and returned.
"Water Classic"
Zhūquè
In the second year of the Tàiníng era of Emperor Míng, on the dīngmǎo day of the sixth month, Yìng Zhān was appointed as General of the Central Army,
granted imperial authority to oversee all military affairs south of the Scarlet Sparrow Bridge.
Records of the Jìn Dynasty
During the Wú period, it was called the Southern Ford Bridge, also known as the Scarlet Sparrow Pontoon.
Wǔzhàng
Mùróng Chuí battled against Liú Láozhī at Wǔzhàngqiáo Marsh,
where he heavily defeated the chariots and cavalry.
Mùróng Dé and others led troops to press them at Wǔzhàng Bridge,
Láozhī galloped his horse and leaped across the Wǔzhàng Ravine,
meeting the rescue forces of Fú Pī just in time to escape.
Cuī Hóng's "Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen States: Later Yan Records"
Hélì
Tǔyùhún built a bridge over the river,
called Hélì,
measuring one hundred and fifty paces long,
with stone foundations piled on both banks,
section by section in succession,
using large timbers laid crosswise,
further reinforced on both sides,
spaced three zhàng apart,
and large wooden planks were laid horizontally between them,
with very ornate railings.
From Duàn Guó's Shāzhōu Jì.
Cháng Fēn
Outside the Chānghé Gate, there is the Chángfēn Bridge spanning seven li.
During the middle period of the court, due to the swift flow of the Gǔ River,
it poured down at the city's edge,
often damaging commoners' homes.
A stone bridge was erected to contain it,
so the long flow would divide and enter the Luò River.
Hence, it was named the Long Division Bridge.
Some say that when the Jìn dynasty's Héjiān King was in Cháng'ān,
he dispatched Zhāng Fāng to campaign against Chángshā,
and the king stationed his troops here.
Thus, it was also called Zhāng Fāng Bridge.
Nowadays, among the folk, there is a mispronunciation,
and it is referred to as Zhāng Fūrén Bridge.
Court officials seeing off and welcoming others
often gather at this place.
From "A Record of Buddhist Monasteries."
Bǎikǒu Bridge
Sòng Tàiyuán tàishǒu Gù Xùn's five generations lived together under one roof,
his descendants were wealthy and prosperous,
the entire household was harmonious,
the family consisted of one hundred members,
contemporaries held them in high esteem,
hence the name.
"Kūnshān Biān"
previous records mention Eastern Hàn's Gù Xùn.
Cuī Gōng
Cuī Liàng served as the Governor of Yōngzhōu.
North of the city, the Wèi River was too shallow for boats to pass,
causing difficulties and obstructions for travelers.
It happened that heavy rain fell,
and mountain torrents suddenly arrived,
floating out several hundred long logs.
Utilizing these materials,
a bridge was subsequently completed,
benefiting the local people.
To this day, it is still called Cuī Gōng Bridge.
"Book of the Later Zhōu Dynasty"
Tiānjīn
Tiānjīn Bridge is located four lǐ north of Hénán County,
first built in the first year of the Suí dynasty's Dàyè era,
using large boats as pontoons,
connected by iron chains and hooks,
with roads flanking it north and south,
and four towers facing each other,
the towers symbolizing the sun and moon as emblems of triumph.
In the fourteenth year of the Zhèngguān era,
stone workers were ordered to stack square stones for piers.
The Ěryǎ states:
between the Dǒu and Niú constellations lies the ford of the Milky Way,
hence the name was derived.
Yuánhé Zhì
Shíqiáo
The Zhàozhōu Stone Bridge is exquisitely crafted,
polished smooth and fine as if cut by a knife,
appearing like a new moon emerging from clouds,
a long rainbow drinking from the stream.
Above are balustrades,
all made of stone,
with stone lions on the balustrades.
During the Lóngshuò era,
a Goryeo spy stole three lions away.
Later, craftsmen were recruited to repair them,
but none could match the original.
By the Dàzú era of Empress Regnant Wǔ Zétiān,
Mòchuò breached Zhàozhōu's Dìngzhōu.
When the invaders sought to advance southward,
they reached the stone bridge,
where their horses knelt and refused to proceed.
They saw only a blue dragon lying on the bridge,
vigorous and furious,
so the invaders fled.
"Records of Court and Commoners"
The stone bridge over the Xiáo River in Yějùn,
is the work of Sui craftsman Lǐ Chūn.
Its construction is extraordinary,
with inscriptions by Zhāng Jiāzhèng, Liǔ Huàn, and Zhāng Yù.
"Literary Essence"
Tàiyáng
The Tàiyáng Bridge is seventy-six zhàng long,
two zhàng wide,
constructed spanning the Yellow River,
located three lǐ northeast of Xiáxiàn.
In the eleventh year of the Zhèngguān era,
Emperor Tàizōng toured the east,
and dispatched General of the Imperial Guards Qiū Xínggōng to oversee its construction.
"Yuánhé Annals"
Féixiāng
During the Shénlóng era, Wěi Jǐngjùn served as the magistrate of Féixiāng County.
The northern part of the county bordered the Zhāng River,
which flooded year after year.
The old embankments were pressed against the canal,
and though the steep banks were immediately repaired after breaches,
Jǐngjùn surveyed the terrain,
extended it a thousand paces further south,
and built up high embankments.
When the Zhāng River reached the dikes, it receded.
The northern area dried into fertile farmland,
and though bridges were erected over the canal, the long bridge was abandoned,
achieving much with little expense.
The people erected a stone to commemorate his achievements.
Several years later,
while traveling through Féixiāng as the inspector of Zhàozhōu,
the people said, "The schools, lodgings, and bridges are all visible,
all built by you."
From "The Official Biography."
Lì Shè
Initially,
east of the Luòshuǐ's Tiānjīn Bridge in the capital city,
at the southwestern corner of Lìdé Ward,
there were the Zhōng Bridge and Lìshè Bridge for passage.
During the Shàngyuán era, Sīnóng Qīng Wéi Jī moved the Zhōng Bridge to the left street of Ānzhòng Ward,
facing the Xià Gate.
The city residents found this very convenient,
so the Lìshè Bridge was abandoned,
saving tens of thousands in costs.
However, it was annually eroded by the Luòshuǐ.
Note:
Constant maintenance was required,
until Lǐ Zhāodé innovated by building stone foundations,
sharpening their fronts to divide the water's force.
From then on, there was no more washing away or damage.
"Old Book of Táng"
Héqiáo
The Pǔjīn River Bridge,
a crucial thoroughfare under heaven.
Emperor Míng of the Táng dynasty decreed the casting of eight iron oxen,
twenty-four cable-posts,
twelve connecting chains,
eight mountain-like frames,
and eight herdsmen figures in the central shoal,
standing majestically apart,
resembling the form of a rainbow,
truly an extraordinary marvel of myriad constructions.
He also ordered Zhāng Yuè, the Head of the Secretariat, to compose a eulogy for the river bridge,
which was placed atop the central shoal.
From "Records of the Extraordinary."
Heart-wrenching
East of Cháng'ān at Bàlíng there is a bridge,
where all welcomes and farewells take place,
making it a site of separation,
thus people call it the Soul-Dissolving Bridge.
"Tales of the Tianbao Era"
Breaking Willow
Táo Yōng served as magistrate of Yáng'ān,
and once saw off a guest at the Bridge of Exhausted Affection.
He asked his attendants about it,
and they replied:
"This is the limit for farewells,
hence the bridge is named 'Exhausted Affection'."
Táo took up his brush and inscribed on its pillar:
"Bridge of Breaking Willow."
From then on, farewells there always inspired his poem,
which goes:
"Since time began, only affection proves hard to exhaust,
Why then name this bridge 'Exhausted Affection'?
Henceforth let it be called 'Breaking Willow' instead,
And let each strand of parting grief hang its head."
Records of Tang Poetry
Ghost Bridge
In Fāngyú County, at the Ghost Bridge,
one night, the sound of people calling was suddenly heard,
with carts rumbling like thunder,
and by dawn, the stone bridge had completed itself,
leaving all the oxen in every household panting and unsettled.
"Records of Campaigns"
The Luòtuó Bridge in Wúxīng spans the Zhà River,
built in the early Táng dynasty,
also known as the Yíngchūn Bridge,
because it directly faces the Yíngchūn Gate.
It was traditionally said that whenever the bridge was damaged and on the verge of collapse,
at night, from afar, the sound of over a thousand people working and shouting could be heard on the bridge,
and by morning,
the parts of the bridge about to collapse were焕然一新,
all made from the mast wood of sunken ships.
Those living near the bridge,
heard and noticed nothing at all,
some say this was the work of the immortal Lǔ Bān.
A hundred flowers
Yuán Chè and Liǔ Shí, two men, drifted to a solitary island in the sea,
where they saw the Jade Pot Venerable Master and the Lady of the Southern Sea,
bowed in reverence and begged for a way to return.
The Lady said:
"There is a Hundred Flowers Bridge you may cross."
Suddenly, a long bridge appeared,
adorned with exotic flowers.
The two men stepped ashore,
and when they looked back, the bridge had vanished.
From "Chuánqí"
Throwing the Handkerchief
Cuīshēng entered the mountains and encountered an immortal maiden who became his wife,
returned home and obtained an invisibility talisman,
sneaked into the palace,
was detected by a sorcerer,
pursuit grew urgent,
Cuī fled back to the mountains,
saw his wife across a chasm,
informed her of the situation,
whereupon she threw her scarf,
which transformed into a five-colored rainbow bridge for Cuī to cross,
thus enabling him to escape the pursuers.
"Unofficial History"
Fish and turtles
The king of Gāolì had a maidservant
who claimed that an aura like an egg descended upon her,
thus she became pregnant.
Later, she gave birth to a son named Dōngmíng.
Dōngmíng was skilled in archery,
and the king, fearing he would endanger the state,
wanted to kill him.
Dōngmíng fled to the Yān River,
struck the water with his bow,
and fish and turtles surfaced to form a bridge.
After he crossed,
the fish and turtles dispersed.
"Lùn Héng"
The king of Fúyú obtained the daughter of the River God and gave birth to an egg,
from which a boy hatched,
named Zhūméng.
The ministers of Fúyú intended to kill him,
so Zhūméng fled southeast,
encountered a great river,
and said:
"I am the River God's grandson."
Thereupon, fish and turtles gathered to form a bridge,
and he crossed over.
"Suí Shū"
Tiānzhōng Jì, Volume Sixteen
Zōng
The Hànshū's commentary by Yán states:
"Zǔ means
the beginning.
The beginning
is receiving the mandate.
Zōng means
to revere,
that which has virtue can be revered.
In ancient times, there were the great zōng and the small zōng.
The great zōng
does not change for a hundred generations,
while the small zōng
changes after five generations.
Furthermore, the source from which a branch flows is called zōng."
The Yùnhuì
Three Clans
Emperor Zhāng's edict stated:
"When one person commits a crime,
punishment extends to three affiliations."
Annotation:
"That is, the three clans,
meaning the father's clan, mother's clan, and wife's clan."
The Later Records
define three clans as
parents, siblings, and wife.
Some commentators claim it refers to father's clan, mother's clan, and wife's clan,
but this is incorrect,
as evidenced by Hàn executing Yīng Bù but sparing Wú Ruì,
from which we can understand.
Bù was Ruì's son-in-law.
Hǎi Lù
the nine degrees of kindred
The Book of Documents speaks of "being affectionate to the nine kindreds."
Kǒng's commentary states:
"The kindred from the high ancestor to the great-great-grandson."
The Explanation of Texts says:
"From the high ancestor above,
down to the great-great-grandson,
these constitute the nine kindreds."
Xiàhóu, Ōuyáng, and others considered the nine kindreds to be:
four from the father's kindred,
three from the mother's kindred,
and two from the wife's kindred,
all related through different surnames with mourning obligations.
The Annotations and Subcommentaries
record Suí Jìliáng saying:
"Be affectionate to his nine kindreds to carry out his sacrificial ceremonies."
The commentary notes:

"The nine kindreds refer to the maternal grandfather, maternal grandmother, children of maternal cousins, as well as the wife's father, wife's mother, sons of paternal aunts, sons of sisters, sons of daughters,
along with one's own same lineage,
all being external relatives with mourning obligations but of different clans."
Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Huán, 6th year.
Several generations
In ancient times during the Zhōu dynasty, the Yǐn noble family for several generations did not eat separately,
with a household of thousands,
they once encountered a famine,
the sound of setting up cauldrons to cook porridge could be heard for dozens of lǐ,
while preparing to eat, thirty people fell into the cauldron,
digging to get the porridge at the bottom,
the cauldron was deep and large,
so people did not notice them.
"Records of the Extraordinary"
Yú Zú
Shū Guǎng returned to his hometown,
daily ordering his household to prepare wine and food together,
inviting his clansmen, old friends, and guests,
to enjoy themselves with them.
After residing there for over a year,
Shū Guǎng's sons and grandsons secretly spoke to an elder among his brothers,
whom Shū Guǎng loved and trusted,
the beloved ones requested to establish an estate foundation,
the elder then took advantage of a leisurely moment to speak to Shū Guǎng about it,
Shū Guǎng said:
"Am I so old and confused as to not think of my sons and grandsons?
If they are virtuous and have abundant wealth, it will diminish their ambition;
if they are foolish and have abundant wealth, it will increase their faults.
Moreover, the wealthy are envied by the multitude;
this gold is what the sage ruler bestowed to care for his old minister,
therefore I delight in sharing this bounty with the village community and clan,
to spend my remaining days thus—is that not acceptable?"
"Qián Zhuàn"
Three generations sharing wealth
Fán Zhòng, whose courtesy name was Jūnyún,
was skilled in agriculture through generations,
excelling in trade and commerce.
He was gentle and kind by nature,
and adhered to principles and discipline.
For three generations, the family shared wealth,
accumulating assets worth tens of thousands,
yet he provided relief and support to his clan,
extending kindness to his hometown and community.
When his maternal grandsons, the Hé brothers, quarreled over property,
Zhòng felt ashamed of this,
and resolved their dispute by giving them two qǐng of farmland.
From the Later Biography.
Gāo Yì
Cài Yōng, courtesy name Bójiē,
was exceptionally filial by nature.
When his mother was bedridden with illness for three years,
unless there were seasonal changes between cold and heat,
he never loosened his girdle or garments,
and for seventy days he did not sleep.
He lived together with his uncle and cousins,
and for three generations they did not divide their property.
The local community esteemed his righteousness.
From the *History of the Later Han*.
However, the Zōngmén
Xǔ Shào's clansman Xǔ Xiàng,
who was immersed in fame and profit,
attained the position of Minister over the Masses,
and the entire clan bowed and scraped to him.
His household inherited this practice and hastened to secure official posts through bribery,
yet only Xǔ Shào never passed through his gate.
"Biographies of Former Worthies"
Zhèn Zú
Gù Hé, styled Jūnxiào,
displayed noble character even in his youth.
His clan uncle, Gù Róng, held him in high esteem,
saying:
"This is the qílín of our family,
who will surely revive our declining clan."
At that time, another clansman, Gù Qiú, also had a fine reputation,
serving as the Assistant Inspector of the province.
Róng said to him:
"You may walk quickly,
but Jūnxiào will surpass you."
"Separate Biography of the Book of Jìn"
Nán Ruǎn Běi Ruǎn
Ruǎn Xián and his uncle Ruǎn Jí roamed among the bamboo groves,
with Xián and Jí living south of the road,
while the other Ruǎns lived north of the road.
The northern Ruǎns were wealthy while the southern Ruǎns were poor.
Xián was close with his nephew Ruǎn Xiū,
always finding joy in following their inclinations.
All the Ruǎns drank wine,
and when Xián gathered with his clansmen,
they no longer used cups or goblets for serving.
Instead, they filled a large basin with wine,
sat in a circle facing each other,
and drank freely in turn.
All the cousins and brothers
embraced uninhibitedness as their way of conduct.
Book of Jin
The perfection of human relationships
Initially, when Wáng Dǎo crossed the Huái River,
he had Guō Pú perform a divination.
When the hexagram was completed,
Guō Pú said:
"Auspicious,
with nothing unfavorable.
When the Huái River runs dry,
the Wáng clan shall perish."
Thereafter, his descendants flourished,
exactly as Guō Pú had said.
《Jìn Biography》
Since the heartland was in turmoil,
the Jìn dynasty situated itself east of the river,
resisting the superior state with a corner of land,
lasting three hundred years—
this surely had its foundation.
An early proverb said:
"The Wángs and the Sīmǎs
share the empire,"
indicating the prominence of the Wáng clan in human relations,
which truly began then,
until Xiūyuán.
《Hóng》
The brothers jointly shouldered the responsibility as pillars,
down to their descendants,
who maintained the elegance of culture undiminished.
The reason their official ranks never ceased
was surely not without cause.
《Discourse on the Biography of Wáng Hóng in the History of the Southern Dynasties》
By the time of Chénwáng's era,
the Huái River indeed ran dry,
and the eminent figures of old were utterly swept away.
This was an omen of rise and fall,
predestined long before.
《Discourse on the Biography of Wáng Yùzhī》
To Strengthen the Clan
Fàn Yù, styled Zhìchūn,
was a man of Lú in Jìběi.
His family for generations had been Confucian scholars,
and they always maintained harmonious relations with the entire clan.
People at that time said of his household that the children had no fixed fathers,
and clothes had no fixed owners.
From the Book of Jìn.
Běi Shè
Liǔ Gōngchuò,
styled Qǐzhī,
was appointed as the Capital Commandant of Jīngzhào.
When he was about to assume his duties,
there was a junior officer from the Divine Strategy Army
who did not yield to him while riding a horse in the street.
He was beaten to death,
and Liǔ Gōngchuò was summoned to give an explanation.
Emperor Xiànzōng, with a stern expression, questioned him about the unauthorized execution.
Liǔ Gōngchuò said:
"The Capital Commandant of Jīngzhào is in a position to set an example.
When Your Majesty initially conferred the command upon me,
you promoted him from within the army.
This officer dashed across on horseback,
which was disrespectful to both Your Majesty and the law.
It was not merely a test of my authority.
I knew that I was punishing someone for their rudeness,
not that I was punishing a Divine Strategy Army officer.
The Emperor said:
"Why did you not report it?"
Liǔ Gōngchuò replied:
"I should resolve this without reporting it.
The Emperor asked:
"Since he is already dead,
who should have reported it?"
Liǔ Gōngchuò said:
"If it occurred in the street, the local officials and the Jīnwú General should report it.
If it happened within a residential area, then the surrounding patrol officers should report it.
The Emperor then ceased questioning.
Liǔ Gōngchuò,
styled Kuān,
was also nicknamed Qǐzhī.
"Táng"
Xiè Mì, styled Hóngwēi,
was adopted by his cousin Xiè Jùn.
In the early Yìxī era, he inherited the title of Marquis of Jiànchāng County.
Hóngwēi's own family was originally poor and frugal,
while the family he was adopted into was wealthy,
yet he only accepted several thousand volumes of books and a few state officials,
refusing any involvement with the inherited wealth, salary, or official rank.
Xiè Hún, upon hearing this, was astonished and sighed in admiration,
addressing the State Minister.
He instructed Qī Kǎizhī:
"The state salary of Jiànchāng
should originally be shared with the North House,
but since the Marquis shows no interest in it,
it may now be distributed according to the usual practice."
Hóngwēi, valuing Xiè Hún's words,
then accepted a small portion.
The North House
was Hóngwēi's original family,
and Xiè Hún held them in special respect and honor,
calling Hóngwēi "Wēizǐ."
From *The History of the Southern Dynasties*
Wūyī Wanderers
Xiè Hún's demeanor was lofty and stern,
seldom accepting social interactions,
only with his clan nephews Xiè Língyùn, Xiè Zhān, and Xiè Huìyào,
did he appreciate literary meanings and gather for enjoyment,
often feasting and spending time together.
They resided in Wūyī Lane,
hence it was called the Wūyī Gatherings,
as mentioned in Xiè Hún's poem: "In the past, we roamed in Wūyī,
all closely bound by kinship."
Beyond them, even though there were other eminent figures,
none dared visit their gate despite the contemporary acclaim.
Rewards and Encouragement
Xiè Hún once, amidst a joyous banquet, composed rhyming verses
to encourage and advise Xiè Língyùn, Xiè Zhān, and others,
saying:
"Kānglè (Xiè Língyùn) possesses innate breadth and tolerance,
Truly bearing the elegance of a renowned family.
If further polished and refined,
He will be like jade carved into fine jade pendants.
Xuānmíng (Xiè Zhān) embodies profound insight,
Brilliant, profound, and sagacious.
If he can shed rigid stubbornness,
He will harmoniously align with the three realms.
Āduō (Xiè Huī) stands out with unique understanding,
In his youth, he continues a glorious lineage.
Though substance outweighs ornament, a caution against lack of refinement,
His integrity is lofty and firm.
Tōngyuǎn (Xiè Hóngwēi) cherishes clear enlightenment,
Gleaming like the fragrance of orchids.
To charge straight ahead often leads to stumbling,
Restraint helps to resolve biases and pettiness.
Wēizǐ (Xiè Yào) bases himself on humble aspirations,
His diligence stems from admiration for the virtuous.
Do not轻视 a single basket of earth as too little,
Persisting will surely reach great heights.
Strive hard, all of you,
Let elegance and refinement be revived through your efforts.
If you do not violate what you know to be right,
Beyond this, there is nothing more to caution."
Xiè Língyùn, Xiè Zhān, and others all received words of warning and exhortation,
Only Xiè Hóngwēi was solely praised and commended.
Note: Xiè Yào, Xiè Hóngwēi's elder brother, had the childhood name Āduō, and Tōngyuǎn
was Xiè Zhān's courtesy name Kèjiàn,
while Xiè Língyùn's childhood name was Kè'ér.
Sù Tuì
Xiè Zhān, courtesy name Xuānyuǎn,
also known as Dān,
with the courtesy name Tōngyuǎn,
was the second son of Xiè Huì.
He later became the Chancellor of Emperor Wǔ of the Sòng dynasty,
serving as a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
At that time, Huì held the position of Right Guard of the Sòng court,
wielding considerable power and influence.
When he returned to the capital from Péngchéng to fetch his family,
guests flocked to him.
Zhān, then at home,
was alarmed
and said to Huì:
"Our family has always upheld withdrawal as its principle.
Yet you now hold sway over both court and countryside.
Is this truly a blessing for our household?"
He then erected a fence to separate the courtyard, declaring:
"I cannot bear to witness this."
Démén
Since the Jin dynasty, the Xiè family
has passed down the way of elegance through generations.
Jǐnghéng
Dàn
and Jǐngrén
Yù
were renowned for their virtuous simplicity,
Jǐngmào
Chún
and Jǐngxiān
Shù
were celebrated for their moral integrity and righteousness,
Fāngmíng with his personal conduct standards,
Yuánhuī with his extraordinary literary talent,
each excelled in their own time,
truly deserving to be called a virtuous family.
Língyùn, with his talent and fame in Jiangnan,
stood out alone but acted recklessly without cease,
ultimately bringing about his own downfall.
Aristocratic families
Wáng Sēngqián served as the Imperial Censor, a position traditionally avoided by prominent clans,
as they had long refrained from holding office in the Censorate.
Among the Wáng clan's branch residing in Wūyī,
their official ranks had slightly declined.
When Sēngqián assumed this post,
he remarked:
"This is the seat once occupied by the gentlemen of Wūyī;
I too can give it a try."
Admonition to My Son
Wáng Sēngqián,
in the Sòng dynasty, once wrote a letter admonishing his son, saying:
"At that time, the outstanding ones in the Wáng family were like dragons and phoenixes,
while the inferior ones were still akin to tigers and leopards.
After losing the family's protection,
how could one still be judged as a dragon or tiger?
Moreover, I cannot provide you with political shelter,
so you should each strive diligently on your own."
Zhǎngzhě
Wáng Zhì, styled Cìdào,
resided in Mǎfèn Lane, Jìnzhōng Ward of Jiànkāng.
His father, Wáng Sēngqián,
maintained a family tradition of tolerance and forgiveness,
and Zhì was particularly sincere and kind.
His brothers, sons, and nephews were all honest, humble, and harmonious,
earning the Wáng family of Mǎfèn the contemporary reputation of being virtuous elders.
Qī Yè
Wáng Yún, courtesy name Yuánlǐ,
wrote in a letter to his sons discussing
the family's collected works:
Historical records praise the Cuī family of Ānpíng
and the Yìng family of Rǔnán,
both having literary talent accumulated over generations.
Therefore, Fàn Yèzōng remarked:
"The Cuī family possesses雕龙(dragon-carving) literary brilliance,
yet it spans no more than two or three generations of fathers and sons.
None have achieved seven generations
where renowned virtue shines anew,
official ranks follow in succession,
with each member producing collected works,
as seen in our family."
Shěn Yuē, the Junior Tutor, often told others:
"In my youth, I admired the writings of various schools,
and personally compiled histories of four dynasties.
Since the dawn of creation,
there has never been such flourishing continuity of official positions and literary talent as in the Wáng family.
You should gaze upon this ancestral legacy and each strive diligently."
Our humble lineage
Wáng Huì, courtesy name Lìngmíng,
was a younger cousin of Wáng Dàn from the same paternal lineage.
He was serene and composed,
did not engage in social interactions,
and never involved himself in trivial matters.
Xiè Zhān of Chénjùn Commandery, known for his eloquence and dignified demeanor,
once visited Huì with his brothers and clansmen.
As the conversation grew spirited and intense,
with discussions spanning literature and history,
Huì occasionally offered guidance,
responding with clarity and reasoned arguments.
Xiè Yuǎn, Xiè Zhān, and the others felt ashamed and withdrew.
Emperor Wǔ of the Liú Sòng dynasty, having heard of his reputation,
inquired about him from his elder cousin Wáng Dàn.
Dàn replied:
"Huì is an outstanding talent among the younger generation,
a pride of our humble clan."
Well-known
The Zhāng clan was renowned, with predecessors like Zhāng Fūyǎn and Jìng Chàng,
and successors such as Zhāng Kèróng and Juàn Jì.
From the *Book of Southern Qí*
Not associating with one's clansmen.
Hé Zhīyuán's clansman Jìngróng,
who held a powerful and prestigious position,
frequently visited and consulted him,
yet Zhīyuán never went to visit in return.
When someone asked the reason,
he said:
"In the past, the people of Chǔ gained favor with Guān Qǐ,
and all those who owned horses perished.
When virtue is shallow and responsibilities are great, failure is surely near.
I fear I would not gain benefits but instead incur disaster."
Those who understood praised him for this.
"Book of Chén"
A hundred mouths sharing the same cooking fire
In the household of Yáng Bō,
men and women numbered a hundred,
yet they wore mourning garments together and shared the same cooking fire,
with no discordant words in the courtyard.
Since the Wei dynasty, only the brothers Lú Yuān and the siblings of Bō—Chūn and Jīn—
were unmatched by any in their time.
Wei Shu
Seven Generations Living Together
In Bólíng Ānpíng, Lǐ Jǐ's family lived together for seven generations,
sharing wealth with twenty-two branches in the household,
totaling one hundred and ninety-eight members.
Young and old flourished harmoniously,
their customs and rites were widely renowned.
When it came to labor and duties,
the younger and lower-ranking members vied to contribute,
earning the admiration and sighs of the local community.
The emperor
Yìmén
Lǐ Zhīběn served his parents with utmost filial piety,
and with his younger brother Zhīyǐn, they were renowned for their harmony.
Their descendants numbered over a hundred,
and in matters of property and servants,
not the slightest dispute arose.
During the late Suí dynasty, bandits passed by their village but did not enter,
saying to one another:
"Do not violate the gate of righteousness."
Over five hundred families took refuge there at the same time,
and thus all were spared.
(Old Book of Táng)
Nine Generations Living Together
Zhāng Gōngyì maintained a nine-generation household living together,
during the Northern Qí dynasty, Prince of Dōng'ān Gāo Yǒnglè visited his residence,
to console and honor them with a commendation.
In the Suí dynasty, the Grand Emissary Shàoyáng Duke Liáng Zǐgōng also personally consoled them,
and re-commended their household.
In the early Zhēnguàn era, an imperial edict specially ordered officials to add further honors.
Emperor Gāozōng, while performing rites at Tàishān,
passed through Jīngzhōu,
and visited his residence in person,
inquiring about the principle behind their harmony.
The man requested paper and brush,
and simply wrote the character for "forbearance" over a hundred times,
causing Emperor Gāozōng to shed tears,
and bestow upon him fine silk.

Táng Tàifǔ Qīng Lǐ Xíyù xìng yánzhěng,
suǒ zài yǐ wēi sù wén,
fán huò fènglù bì sàn zhī zōngqīn,
qí yú zī duō xiě shū éryǐ,
jí cóng Yángzhōu bà zhí jīngshǐ,

Different mothers, same milk
During the Kaiyuán era,
Cuī Yǐnfǔ reported that Lǚ Yuányīng from Běihǎi in Qīngzhōu had four generations living together,
to the extent that the cattle, horses, sheep, and dogs they raised all nursed from mothers not their own,
and requested they be commended; an imperial decree granted it.
False Patronage
Lǐ Huáiyuǎn was orphaned at a young age,
when his clansmen offered him the privilege of high-ranking protection,
he firmly declined it.
Withdrawing, he sighed and said:
"Relying on others' influence,
a noble scholar does not seek borrowed shelter;
is pursuing office truly my original aspiration?"
The scholar-official's teacher
Cuī Chuí of Bólíng, who observed mourning rites for distant relatives,
maintained a shared household for three generations.
Since the Zhèngyuán era, those discussing family discipline have regarded Chuí as exemplary,
He fathered six sons,
one of whom became chancellor,
while five served as high officials:
Court Minister Cuī Bīn,
Commandant Cuī Fēng,
Secretary Cuī Yǎn,
Chief Justice Cuī Xún,
Commandant of Armed Guards Cuī Shàn,
and Left Assistant Director Cuī Yùn who participated in policy-making.
Moreover, Bīn and Yǎn presided over the imperial examinations five times,
selecting 148 candidates.
From their initial appointments to high positions, the brothers shared a residence in Guāngdé Ward.
When Emperor Xuānzōng learned of this,
he sighed in admiration:
"The Cuī Yùn household
exemplifies filial piety and fraternal duty, serving as a model for scholarly clans."
Records of Jiǎ's Conversations
Míngzú
Péi Hào, styled Sīdōng,
was a native of Hédōng.
Since the times of Jìn and Wèi,
the Péi clan had been a renowned lineage for generations.
Those residing in Yān were called the Eastern Branch,
those in Liáng the Western Branch,
and those in Hédōng the Central Branch.
Hào hailed from a distinguished family,
and his demeanor was dignified and refined.
He served as Vice Minister of Rites in the Later Táng.
"History of the Five Dynasties"
Initially, the Péi and Wáng clans flourished during the Jìn and Wèi eras,
contemporaries likened the eight Péis to the eight Wángs:
Péi Huī corresponded to Wáng Xiáng,
Péi Kǎi to Wáng Yǎn,
Péi Kāng to Wáng Suí,
Péi Chuò to Wáng Chéng,
Péi Zàn to Wáng Dūn,
Péi Xiá to Wáng Dǎo,
Péi Wěi to Wáng Róng,
and Péi Miǎo to Wáng Yuán, it is said.
"Jìn Biographies"
The Péi clan was a prominent surname,
becoming even more illustrious upon entering the Táng dynasty,
with branches dividing and clans separating,
each forming great households.
"Writings of Hán Yù"
Mào Zú
The Lǐ family of Jīnlíng first named their state with the title Táng,
King Qián Wénmù heard of this,
and said:
"The Mào family of Jīnlíng,
claiming lineage from the great Táng dynasty,
isn't that shocking?"
Shěn Tāowén replied:
"This can be illustrated with an analogy.
For instance, in a local school,
if there happens to be someone surnamed Kǒng,
people call him Confucius,
so what's so strange about it?"
The king laughed heartily,
and rewarded him with a cup of wine.
A Hundred Dogs Sharing a Single Pen
The Jiāngzhōu Chén clan, descendants of Jīng who served as a Supervising Secretary during the Yuánhé era,
had a lineage of seven hundred members.
Each day, they set up a grand banquet,
where old and young sat in order and ate together.
They kept over a hundred dogs that shared one trough for meals;
if one dog did not arrive,
the other dogs would not eat because of it.
They built a library at their villa
to host scholars from all directions,
and many students studying there relied on them.
The local community was influenced to follow their example,
lawsuits became rare,
and people near and far marveled at this.
(From "History of Southern Táng")
Four Clans
Jìn Hán Xuānzǐ Qǐ went to Chǔ to escort the bride,
with Shūxiàng as his deputy.
King Zhuāng wanted to humiliate Jìn,
when Wěi Qǐjiāng said:
"Jī Xiāng, Xíng Dài, Shū Qín, Shū Jiāo, and Zǐ Yǔ
are all from great families.
The four Yángshé clans,
are all powerful families."
Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāogōng 5th Year
Commentary:

Bó Huá,

Dōngjīng's Renowned Clans
Yáng Zhèn to Yáng Biāo,
four generations served as Grand Commandant,
their virtue and achievements continued successively,

"Later Biography"
The Yáng and Yuán clans of the Eastern Capital,
held the position of chancellor for generations,
and were famous families of the Hàn dynasty.
However, the Yuán clan's carriages, horses, and clothing were extremely extravagant and excessive,
while the Yáng clan could preserve their family traditions,
and were esteemed by the world,
surpassing the Yuán clan.

old clans
The old clans of Wú such as Gù and Lù,
often held high positions,

Zhāng's proclamation to Wú
Lù Xùn, originally named Yì,

Zōng Gǔn
Xiè Yuǎnhuī's "He Wáng Zhùzuò Bāgōngshān Shī" says:

Bǎikǒu Qiáo
During the Song dynasty, Gù Xùn, the Grand Administrator of Tàiyuán, maintained a five-generation household living together,
with descendants prosperous and flourishing,
the family harmonious and amiable,
the household comprising a hundred members,
earning the esteem of contemporaries,

Tall gate
Hóu Jǐng defected to Liáng,
requesting to marry a woman from the Wáng or Xiè families.
Emperor Wǔ replied:
"The Wáng and Xiè families' status is too high,
they are not suitable matches for you.
Seek a bride from the Zhū or Zhāng families or below."
Hóu Jǐng angrily said:
"I will eventually match the daughters of Wú men with slaves."
History of the Southern Dynasties
Shì Wàng
In the early years of Emperor Tàizōng of the Táng dynasty,
the scholars of Shāndōng prided themselves on family prestige and influence,
and even though their families had declined over generations,
they still relied on their hereditary reputation,
demanding large dowries for marriages,
so people called it "selling marriages."
Emperor Tàizōng despised this practice,
and thus ordered Gāo Shìlián and others to revise and correct family names,
compiling the "Register of Gentry Clans."
Shìlián and others classified them by rank and presented the list,
with Cuī Gàn still ranked first.
Emperor Tàizōng said:
"I have no past grievances with the Cuī, Lú, Lǐ, and Zhèng families of Shāndōng,
but as their generations have declined,
they no longer produce officials,
yet they still call themselves gentry.
It is only because of the Qí dynasty,
and based on the Liáng and Chén dynasties of Héběi,
which were remote in Jiāngnán—
though they had notable figures at the time,
they were isolated small states,
not worthy of high regard.
Today, people still value the Cuī, Lú, Wáng, and Xiè families,
but my purpose in defining clan ranks now
is to honor the officials of the current dynasty."
Thus, Cuī Gàn was placed in the third rank.
(From the New Book of Táng)
The Seven Surnames and Ten Families

Emperor Gāozōng decreed that the seven surnames and ten families—Lǒngxī Lǐ Bǎo, Tàiyuán Wáng Qióng, Xíngyáng Zhèng Wēn, Fànyáng Lú Zǐqiān, Lú Zé, Lú Fǔ, Qīnghé Cuī Zōngbó, Cuī Yuánsūn, former Yān Bólíng Cuī Yìjìn, and Zhàojùn Lǐ Kǎi—
were forbidden from intermarrying among themselves.
Previously, during the Tàihé era of the Later Wèi dynasty,
these families were recognized as the foremost of the four seas' esteemed clans, with Bǎo and others at the pinnacle.
Later, as they grew arrogant about their social status,
the "Record of Gentry Clans" consequently demoted them all.
"New Book of Táng"
On the hilltop and in the marsh bottom
The four great clans:
the Zhèng family never left Xíngyáng;
the Lú family from Gāngtóu, the Lǐ family from Zédǐ, and the Cuī family from Tǔmén
all produced top scholars in the imperial examinations.
The Wáng family of Tàiyuán was also a match for the four clans,
yet they were called the "Chiseled Silver Wang Family,"
metaphorically meaning silver in substance but gold in ornamentation.
"Supplement to the National History"
Eighth Xiāo
The Liáng clan of the Xiāo family rose in Jiāngnán,
truly having merits for the people,
and in the end committed no major wrongdoings,
yet gradually declined and lost their remaining blessings.
From their descendants starting with Xiāo Yù to Xiāo Gòu,
there were altogether eight generations of chancellors,
with renowned virtue spanning generations,
their fortunes rising and falling with the Táng dynasty.
The prosperity of this hereditary family
was unprecedented in ancient times.
"Táng Zàn"
Two Gates
Mù Níng was strict in managing his household,
and served his widowed elder sister with great respect,
once composing a family code to instruct his sons.
Previously, Hán Xiū had also disciplined his sons and nephews with extreme strictness,
and during the Zhēnyuán era, those discussing family discipline still praised the households of Hán and Mù.
Family Instructions
Liǔ Yǐng once wrote a book admonishing his descendants, saying:
"For those of noble family background,
in establishing themselves and conducting their affairs,
if even one matter fails to meet ancestral teachings,
their offense is greater than others'.
High status leads to self-conceit,
prosperous clans become objects of envy,
genuine talents and virtuous conduct,
people may not necessarily believe,
but the slightest flaw or minor fault, ten hands will point in accusation.
Therefore, the longevity of distinguished families,
does not depend on consulting tortoise shells, yarrow stalks, or astrological calculations,
but lies in their intentions and conduct.
Cuī Shānnán Guǎn of Zhāoguó Lane,
with his flourishing descendants,
was rarely matched among scholar-official families.
Minister Péng Kuān of Rénhé Lane,
with his numerous descendants,
was truly a renowned aristocratic family.
All prominent families and noble clans,
are established through ancestors' loyalty, filial piety, diligence, and frugality,
and all are destroyed by descendants' obstinacy, extravagance, and arrogance.
Establishment is as difficult as ascending to heaven,
while destruction is as easy as singeing hair.
Our family was originally renowned among scholar-officials for learning and ritual propriety,
but since the turmoil of war,
our family fortune has declined,
the heavy responsibility of maintaining the foundation
falls upon the younger generation.
Filial piety, parental kindness, brotherly love,
loyalty, trustworthiness, and sincere conduct—
these are like the vinegar and salt of daily sustenance,
can we be without them for even a single day?"
Families and clans vied for supremacy
The Táng dynasty endured for a long time as a state,
passing down through many generations, and its various officials each cultivated their family traditions,
striving to elevate their clan status,
ensuring that their talented descendants
did not let fade the virtues of their ancestors.
"Table of Chancellors' Genealogies"
Zōng Shèng
Sūn Hào asked Chancellor Lù Kǎi, saying:
"How many members of your clan are at court?"
Lù replied:
"Two chancellors and five marquises,
and more than ten generals."
Hào said:
"How prosperous!"
Lù said:
"When the ruler is wise and the ministers loyal,
that is the state's prosperity.
When the father is kind and the son filial,
that is the family's prosperity.
Now governance is decadent and the people are suffering,
we fear complete collapse and destruction,
how dare I speak of prosperity?"
"Shì Shuō"
Xún Chén
During the Zhèngshǐ era, people compared five members of the Xún family to five members of the Chén family:
Xún Shū was compared to Chén Shí,
Xún Jìng was compared to Chén Chén,
Xún Shuǎng was compared to Chén Jì,
Xún Yù was compared to Chén Qún,
and Xún Yǐ was compared to Chén Tài.
From "Shìshuō Xīnyǔ"
Nánzǔ
The Lǐ clan of Zhào Commandery descended from Wǔ'ān Jūn Lǐ Mù, a general of Zhào.
During the conflict between Chǔ and Hàn,
Guǎngwǔ Jūn Lǐ Zuǒchē was their ancestor.
Lǐ Zuǒchē's fourteenth-generation descendant Lǐ Huī, styled Zhòngxīng,
lived during the reigns of Emperors Huán and Líng of Hàn, maintaining a noble reclusion from office,
and was known as the Virtuous Gentleman.
Lǐ Huī fathered Lǐ Dìng,
styled Wényì,
who served under Wèi as the Grand Administrator of Yúyáng,
and had four sons,
all of whom served under Jìn.
Lǐ Píng, styled Bókuò,
served as Grand Administrator of Lèpíng;
Lǐ Jī, styled Zhòngkuò,
held the position of Erudite of the National University;
Lǐ Yǐn, styled Shūkuò,
and Lǐ Bǎo, styled Jìkuò,
both served as Gentleman of the Masters of Writing.
The brothers were all renowned for their Confucian integrity,
and were called the Four Kuò by contemporaries.
Lǐ Jī's son Lǐ Kǎi,
styled Xióngfāng,
served as Attendant Censor of the Palace Library,
and settled in Píngjí.
He had five sons to the south,
Lǐ Jí, Lǐ Huǎng, Lǐ Rěn, Lǐ Jìng, and Lǐ Ruì.
Lǐ Jí, styled Hùzōng,
Lǐ Huǎng, styled Zhònghuáng,
Lǐ Rěn, styled Xiùhuáng,
Lǐ Jìng, styled Shǎohuáng,
and Lǐ Ruì, styled Yòuhuáng,
were all celebrated for their fraternal devotion,
respected by their contemporaries,
and known as the Four Huáng.
Lǐ Jí served as Grand Administrator of Gāomì,
and had two sons, Lǐ Shèn and Lǐ Dūn.
Lǐ Huǎng served as Chief Clerk to the General of the Southern Pacification,
and had one son, Lǐ Yìjìng.
The Attendant Censor of the Palace Library
had four sons: Lǐ Shèng, Lǐ Mǐn, Lǐ Lóng, and Lǐ Xǐ.
Lǐ Ruì served as Grand Administrator of Gāopíng,
and had two sons, Lǐ Xù and Lǐ Chōng, in his later years.
Lǐ Shèn and Lǐ Dūn resided in Bórén,
where their descendants became quite obscure.
Lǐ Yì moved south to the old fortress,
and his lineage was called the Southern Ancestral Branch.
Lǐ Xù and his brothers lived on the east side of the lane,
while Lǐ Shèng and his brothers lived on the west side.
People pointed to their residences,
and thus used these as designations,
which likely originated from this.
From the Běi Shǐ.
Háoshèng
The Lǐ clan's lineage was powerful and prosperous,
and during the spring and autumn community festivals, they would hold grand gatherings with lavish feasts,
where everyone would become intoxicated and boisterous.
On one occasion during such a gathering,
with sumptuous dishes laid out before him, Shìqiān
first served millet,
saying to the assembled relatives:
"Confucius called millet the chief of the five grains,
and Xúnzǐ also said that one should eat millet and broomcorn millet first.
How can we disregard
what the ancients valued?"
The young and old became solemn, and no one dared to be negligent or lazy.
Afterward, they said to one another:
"Only after meeting a true gentleman
do we realize our own lack of virtue."
When Shìqiān heard this, he reproached himself, saying:
"How have I made people so awestruck and overwhelmed?"
A Family of Sages
Guō Zuò, styled Jìyòu,
was a descendant of Guō Huái of the Wèi state,
continuing his lineage.
He accompanied Emperor Gāozǔ on an imperial visit to Cháng'ān,
passing by the Wèi River Bridge,
where they came upon Guō Huái's temple.
The Emperor asked Zuò:
"Is this the ancestral legacy of your family?"
Zuò replied:
"He was my seventh-generation paternal great-uncle."
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"Former sages and later wise men
all emerge from one household."
Zuò responded:
"In the past, my ancestor, with his profound scholarship and outstanding wisdom,
served only Emperor Wén of Wèi.
Though I am unworthy and shallow,
I have encountered a brilliant sovereign,
and consider myself most fortunate."
The Emperor then ordered a grand sacrifice at Huái's temple,
and commanded Zuò to compose the sacrificial address himself. [From the "Wèi Shū," chapter 52]
Nánzhèng Běizhèng
Grand Tutor Zhèng Yīn's residence was in the south,
descended from the Southern Ancestor;
Minister Zhèng, Duke of Yí's residence was in the north,
descended from the Northern Ancestor,
contemporarily called the Southern Zhèng Minister and Northern Zhèng Minister.
The Minister's elder cousin, Duke Wénxiàn, successively served as chancellor under Emperor Dézōng,
called the Elder Zhèng Minister and Younger Zhèng Minister.
"Records of Conversations"
This originates from Huángdì
Lǐ Huì, courtesy name Jìngwén,
served as an envoy to the State of Liáng,
and during a casual conversation with a person from Liáng about prominent families,
Yuán Xiá remarked:
"None compare to my lineage, which traces back to Huángdì,
with our surname listed among the fourteen ancient clans."
Lǐ Huì retorted:
"Though your ancestry is ancient,
you might as well share a single character with Chē Qiānqiū."
Everyone present laughed.
(Book of Northern History, Volume 21)
Yuán Shū,
courtesy name Mǎirén,
could bend a bow of three hundred jin,
and was skilled in horse riding and archery.
During the reign of Xiàowén, he served as the governor of Hédōng,
where the local customs were heavily commercial,
with little activity in agriculture or sericulture.
Some people reached the age of thirty without recognizing farming tools.
Shū dismounted to encourage their instruction,
personally going to teach and demonstrate.
Within two years, families were well provided for,
and a song about him was composed:
"In Tàizhōu's Hédōng,
looms and shuttles replaced the pounding mills,
when Lord Yuán arrived,
fields and lands were first managed."
He had seven sons, the youngest being Jì Hǎi,
courtesy name Yuánquán,
who was the most renowned among his brothers,
holding the position of magistrate in Luòzhōu.
Jì Hǎi’s wife was the daughter of Sīkōng Lǐ Chōng,
and was the maternal aunt of Emperor Zhuāng as well.
Amidst the political turmoil,
when rebellion was imminent,
he first advised Jì Hǎi to take an external official position
to avoid getting embroiled.
When the difficulties of Emperor Xiàozhuāng arose,
Jì Hǎi indeed escaped due to being stationed afar.
"Běishǐ"
Jiǎ Mén
Yuán Lǎng,
a native of Cháng'ān in Yōngzhōu,
was the son of Yuán Shū, who served as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs in the Chén dynasty.
His ancestors had moved from Chénjùn to serve in the Jiāngzuǒ region,
and for generations, they were a prominent clan.
After the fall of the Chén dynasty,
they relocated to Guānzhōng.
Lǎng was diligent in his studies and skilled in writing,
and during the Chén dynasty, he began his official career as a Gentleman of the Palace Library,
highly regarded by Jiāng Zǒng, the Director of the Department of State Affairs.
After the fall of Chén, he served under the Suí dynasty as a Vice Director in the Ministry of Rites,
and during the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty, he held the position of a Palace Attendant.
His thirteenth-generation ancestor was Yuán Pāng, who served as Minister over the Masses in the Hàn dynasty,
Pāng fathered Yuán Huàn, who served as a Gentleman of the Palace and Censor-in-Chief in the Wèi dynasty,
Huàn fathered Yuán Zhǔn, who served as a Director in the Jìn dynasty,
Zhǔn fathered Yuán Chōng, who served as a General of the Right and Governor of Yùzhāng in the Eastern Jìn dynasty,
Chōng fathered Yuán Dān, who served as a Gentleman of the Masters of Writing in the Ministry of Personnel,
Dān fathered Yuán Zhì, who served as a Prefect of Lángyá,
Zhì fathered Yuán Bào, who served as Governor of Dānyáng and Senior Adjutant to the Duke of Sòng,
Bào fathered Yuán Xún, who served as Governor of Wújùn in the Sòng dynasty,
for generations, they held high reputations and important positions,
and their biographies are recorded in previous histories.
His fifth-generation granduncle was Yuán Shū, who served as Grand Commandant in the Sòng dynasty,
his great-great-grandfather Yuán Yǐ served as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and Governor of Yōngzhōu,
and his great-grandfather Yuán Chá served as Minister of Works,
all of whom died for the state in times of crisis.
His great-grandfather Yuáng Āng served as a Palace Attendant and Minister of Works with the title of Duke Mù in the Liáng dynasty, having previously served as Governor of Wúxīng under the Qí dynasty,
and when Emperor Gāozǔ of Liáng usurped the Qí throne,
he long declined court appointments.
His father Yuán Shū and his granduncle Yuán Xiàn served under the Chén dynasty,
both as Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs, and his granduncle Yuán Jìng served as President of the Chancellery.
After the fall of the Chén dynasty,
Xiàn risked danger to protect the last emperor.
Lǎng considered his family's lineage,
as the leading clan in the realm,
and though the Wáng clan of Lángyá successively held high ministerial positions,
they had supported each new dynasty's founding in successive reigns,
so he disdained to associate with them.
Lǎng's grandson Yuán Yì was also the maternal grandson of Yú Shìnán,
and during the Shéngōng era, he served as Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Once, while attending to official duties, his aide Zhāng Pèi from Qīnghé came to pay his respects,
Pèi was the son of Zhāng Wènguàn, a Palace Attendant.
Yì greeted him and said:
"What brings you here, Aide?"
Pèi replied:
"This prefecture has gained a Senior Adjutant,
Lǐ Dǎn from Lǒngxī, a top-ranking family in the realm."
Yì said:
"Aide, your words are mistaken.
A family's status must be built on generations of virtuous men,
reputation, integrity, and moral influence,
earning the respect of the elite,
before it can be praised.
This old man is an example.
People from Shāndōng prioritize marriage alliances,
seek office and profit,
act as pillars of their time,
but when faced with danger and called to sacrifice,
they are absent through the ages.
How can such be spoken of as a distinguished family?"
Pèi withdrew in shame,
and this became a topic of discussion among contemporaries.
The Old Book of Táng,
the Book of Jìn, the History of the Southern Dynasties, and the Yuán Family Biographies all state that the Yuán clan were natives of Yángxià in Chénjùn,
and notable figures are too numerous to record fully.
The New Book states that Lǎng's ancestors were from Yōngzhōu;
could this be a misreading of the old texts?
Lù Bó,
the eldest son of Sì,
was intelligent
and had the bearing of his father.
The great ancestor saw and was pleased with him,
and said to the court ministers:
"I have often praised his father's wisdom, which exceeded his stature,
and now this one surpasses his father."
He was appointed as the Prefect of Xiāngzhōu,
temporarily holding the title of Duke of Chángguǎng.
His governance was clear and just,
suppressing the strong and supporting the weak.
In the province, there were virtuous and respected elders of high reputation,
whom he treated with the courtesy of friendship.
He consulted them on political matters,
and demanded strategic plans from them.
There were ten such people,
who were collectively called
the "Ten Virtuous Ones."
As a result, he exposed corruption and brought about peace,
ensuring that every case was verified.
The common people regarded him as a divine figure,
and none dared to commit robbery or theft.
He was summoned to serve as a Cavalier Attendant,
and over a thousand commoners petitioned for Bó to remain.
Xiànwén did not approve,
saying to the ministers:
"Bó's good governance,
how could even the ancients surpass it?"
When Bó's term ended and he returned,
the officials collected cloth and silk to present to him.
Bó refused to accept any,
nor did the others take anything.
Thus, they used these materials to build a Buddhist temple,
naming it Chángguǎng Duke Temple.
Huázhòu
Liáng Hé Chāngyù served as the Minister of Personnel.
A person surnamed Mǐn came seeking an official post.
Chāngyù asked, "Whose descendant are you?"
The man replied, "A descendant of Zǐqiān."
Covering his mouth with a laugh, Chāngyù said:
"You've traced your noble lineage from afar."
From *The History of the Southern Dynasties*.
All the Dùs
Dù Zhènglún sought to establish genealogical connection with the southern Dù clan,
though their ancestral lineage was historically distant. His request for shared genealogy
was refused, leaving him resentful.
The Dù clan's residence was called Dùgù,
with legends claiming the land possessed vibrant energy,
hence generations produced distinguished officials.
After Dù Zhènglún assumed power,
he proposed digging through Dùgù to channel water for public benefit.
Once excavated,
the river flowed like blood,
ceasing only after ten days.
From then on, the southern Dù clan gradually declined.
《New Book of Tang》
the Lǐs
Lǐ Yìfǔ had already become prominent,
then claimed his lineage originated from Zhàojùn,
and arranged generational order with the various Lǐ clans,
those craving advancement often honored him as father or elder brother.
The imperial advisor Lǐ Chóngdé included him in the same genealogy,
but after being demoted,
Pǔzhōu promptly removed Yìfǔ's name,
and when Yìfǔ returned to power,
he fabricated charges against him,
forcing him to commit suicide in prison.

The Meaning of Clan Selection
Dù Zhènglún had already attained high rank and wealth,
while Lǐ Yìfǔ's official position was still low,
yet when serving together in government he would not defer to him,
the Secretariat Director Lǐ Yǒuyì,
who was a clansman of Yìfǔ,
later attached himself to Zhènglún,
and together they picked on Yìfǔ's faults and shortcomings,
Yìfǔ had someone accuse Zhènglún
and Yǒuyì of colluding,
deceiving the emperor with treacherous schemes,
Emperor Gāozōng was displeased with this,
and sent Zhènglún out to be Governor of Jīngzhōu,
exiled Yǒuyì to Fēngzhōu,
Zhènglún died in exile.
