Genealogy of Fāng Xiàng
In the Táng dynasty, there was a scholar surnamed Fāng,
who was fond of boasting about his family background.
Whenever there was a distinguished person with the surname Fāng, he would invariably claim them as a relative.
Someone once teased him, saying:
"What relation is the Fāngxiàng from Fēngyì to you?"
He promptly replied:
"He is my second cousin on my father's side."
The teaser laughed and said:
"Since you are the nephew of a Fāngxiàng,
you are only fit to scare ghosts."
Fēngyì Lane
was a place where
funerary objects
were made and sold.
The prominent clan is hailed as the foremost.
Cuī Tǐng,
a Presented Scholar in the early Zhēnyuán era, served as the Governor of Tóng Prefecture.
He had eight sons,
Guǎn, Qí, Jìn, Zǎo, Yú, Qiú, and Xiàng,
all of whom achieved high-ranking official positions,
leading contemporaries to compare them to the "Eight Dragons of the Xún Family."
During the Xiántōng and Qiánfú periods of the Cuī family,
brothers and descendants adorned with official sashes and girdles,
over twenty individuals served in central government offices and as regional governors.
Since the Dàzhōng era, this prominent clan
was regarded as first-class at the time.
The Old
History records that his great-grandmother, the elder Mrs. Zhǎngsūn,
was too old to chew.
His grandmother, Lady Táng, served her mother-in-law with filial piety,
nursing her every morning.
One day, the mother-in-law fell ill
and summoned the family to declare:
"I have no way to repay my daughter-in-law,
but I pray that all future descendants will be as filial as she."
It is said that the prosperity of the Cuī family had its foundation in this.
New Book of Táng
Falsely claiming distant ancestors
There was a former chancellor from a distant branch residing in Gūsū,
who, while amusing himself, wrote on a wall:
"So-and-so, the grand chancellor's second cousin, once visited here."
A scholar named Lǐ Zhāng, who always enjoyed witty banter,
inscribed beside it:
"Lǐ Zhāng, the thirty-seventh generation descendant of the Primordial Emperor, subsequently arrived."
From "Casual Notes"
Unwilling to speak of extermination
Xiàhóu Dǎn was articulate and quick-witted,
capable of handling matters on behalf of his clansmen.
When Xiàhóu Yì was appointed as the Interior Historian of Héngyáng,
Dǎn attended at the imperial seat during the farewell audience.
Emperor Gāozǔ asked Dǎn:
"How close or distant is Xiàhóu Yì to you?"
Dǎn replied:
"He is my younger cousin."
Emperor Gāozǔ realized that Yì was actually quite distant from Dǎn,
and said:
"You are a fellow countryman,
how can you not distinguish clan relationships?"
Dǎn responded:
"I have heard that kinship ties can easily become distant,
which is why I cannot bear to speak of clan relations."
At the time, this was considered a skillful reply.
"Book of Liáng"
Bó Hǎi
Liǔ Zòngyuán and Liú Yǔxī passed the imperial examination in the same year,
and inscribed their names on the pagoda of Cí'ēn Temple.
Tán Yuànmào held the brush to write the names,
all according to their prestigious clans.
However, no one knew Xīn Nánróng's background.
Tán Yuànmào paused his brush and said:
"Please, Senior Xīn, tell us your distinguished clan."
Xīn happened to be elsewhere at the moment,
so Liǔ said:
"He is from the East Sea."
Yuànmào asked:
"How do you know that?"
Liǔ replied:
"The East Sea is vast—
what could it not contain?"
Soon after, Xīn arrived,
and when asked about his clan,
he said "Bóhǎi,"
causing everyone to laugh heartily.
(From the Jiāhuà Lù)
The tip of a pole
A scholar from Jízhōu was heading to the provincial capital for the examinations,
with a sign in front reading "Ōuyáng Bólè, Top Candidate from Lúlíng."
Someone mocked him,
saying:
"A traveler has come from afar, from Jízhōu,
His name is displayed atop a carrying pole.
Though we know you are a descendant of Ōuyáng,
After all, we've never known Xiū."
From "Yíjiān Zhīzhì"
Originator
Zǔ,
means zuò.
Zuò,
means xiān.
In Shì Míng,
bízǔ,
refers to the earliest ancestor.
The initial birth of an animal is called bí,
the initial birth of a human is called shǒu,
in Liáng Yì, bí is referred to as zǔ,
or sometimes called bízǔ.
From Fāng Yán.
Wáng Fù
The father's deceased father is the royal father,
the father's deceased mother is the royal mother.
"Erya"
Goodness reaches all.
Qín Jǐngbó asked Shì Yǎng, saying:
"Which great officer will be the first to perish?"
He replied:
"Would it be the Luán clan?"
Luán Yǎn was excessively arrogant and cruel,
but could this spare his son Yíng?
When Luán Yǎn died,
Yíng's goodness had not yet reached others,
the benefactions of Luán Wǔ (Luán Shū) had faded away,
and Yǎn's offenses had become truly apparent - it would happen then.
In Jìn, the Luán clan was indeed destroyed.
Zuǒ Zhuàn, 14th year of Duke Xiāng
Yìng Shào said:
"Jìn great officer Luán Shū,
Shū's son Yǎn,
Yǎn's son Yíng,
Shū was virtuous but his merit covered Yǎn,
Yǎn was wicked and brought harm to Yíng.
Cáo Dàgū said:
'Heaven's mandate protects the good,
calamity for the wicked is not without distinction,
yet its way is vast and great,
even between father and son over generations,
it is still as if they are one body.'"
Kè Chāng
The Master was at leisure,
and sighed deeply.
Zǐsī bowed twice,
and asked:
"Are you concerned that your descendants may not cultivate themselves,
and thus fail to honor their ancestor?
I admire the Way of Yáo and Shùn,
but regret that I cannot attain it."
The Master said:
"How can you, a young child, understand my aspirations?"
Zǐsī replied:
"When I serve meals,
I frequently hear the Master's teachings.
If the father chops firewood,
but the son cannot carry the load,
this is called being unworthy.
Whenever I reflect on this,
I feel greatly fearful and never slacken."
The Master smiled joyfully and said:
"Indeed!
Now I have no worries.
If the generations do not abandon the family tradition,
surely it will flourish!"
The Kǒng Cóng Zǐ
Grandfather
Zhèng Dāngshí, courtesy name Zhuāng,
was young and held a low-ranking official position,
yet his close friends were all senior figures who traveled throughout the land,
renowned scholars.
《History of the Han Dynasty》
He did not call them by their names.
Shí Fèn retired in old age to his home.
When his sons and grandsons, serving as minor officials, returned to visit,
he would always receive them in court attire,
and did not call them by their names. If his sons or grandsons had faults,
he did not reprimand them directly,
but would sit aside and refuse to eat.
Then his sons would reproach one another,
bared their upper bodies to apologize for their offenses,
only then would he eat. When his grown sons and grandsons were by his side,
even during leisure moments, he would always wear his cap,
maintaining a dignified and proper demeanor.
《Book of Hàn》
Zì Sūn
Yú Xǔ,
a native of Chénguó,
his grandfather served as a prison officer in the commandery and county,
and was dedicated to leniency and forgiveness.
He often declared:
"Yú Gōng of Dōnghǎi raised the gate of his village,
and Dìng Guó eventually rose to become Chancellor.
I have adjudicated legal cases for sixty years;
even if I cannot match Yú Gōng's descendants,
how can I fail to become one of the Nine Ministers?"
Therefore, he gave Xǔ the courtesy name Shèngqīng,
and later Xǔ was promoted to Master of the Imperial Secretariat.
From the Book of the Later Hàn.
Innocent
Yáng Zhèn was of a frugal nature,
his descendants often ate plain food and walked on foot.
Some wished for him to establish estates,
but Yáng Zhèn said:
"If future generations call me an incorrupt official,
and my descendants inherit this from me,
isn't that bountiful enough?"
Emperor Líng said to Yáng Zhèn's grandson Yáng Qí:
"You are unyielding,
truly a descendant of Yáng Zhèn."
Chúnsūn
Yuán Gǔ was a man of unknown origin.
His grandfather had grown old,
and his parents found him burdensome,
intending to abandon him.
Gǔ, being fifteen years old at the time,
wept and pleaded earnestly,
but his parents would not listen.
They then made a litter to carry him away and abandon him.
Gǔ followed the litter and brought it back.
His father said to him:
"Why are you keeping this inauspicious tool?"
He replied:
"I am afraid that when you, Father, grow old, I will not be able to make another one,
so I am keeping it."
His father was deeply moved, felt ashamed and fearful,
and then brought the grandfather back home to care for him.
He restrained himself and blamed himself,
becoming truly filial instead.
Gǔ became a truly filial grandson.
"The Biographies of Filial Sons"
Jiāgōng
Hóu Bà's descendants referred to their grandfather as family elder. Pānní,
referred to his ancestor as family ancestor. Bān Gù,
in his collected writings, also mentioned family grandson.
The Family Instructions of the Yán Clan
Xīngzōng
Chén Qún, courtesy name Chángwén,
his grandfather Chén Shí,
once said to his clansmen:
"This child will surely bring prosperity to our clan."
When he grew up, he possessed discernment and judgment,
and those he befriended were all his father's associates.
"Wèi Shū"
Different from the multitude
Wèi Jiè possessed an outstanding elegance of emptiness and purity,
a spirit of clarity and superiority,
among the crowd he had the aura of an extraordinary person.
His grandfather, the Grand Guardian Wèi Guàn, saw Jiè at the age of five
and said:
"This child has a divine intelligence and keen wit,
greatly different from the masses,
I fear in my old age I may not live to see his maturity."
"Bié Zhuàn"
Hardly sage-like
Hé Zēng attended a banquet with Emperor Wǔ,
and upon returning home, he told his son Zūn:
"The state has responded to heaven's mandate,
founding an enterprise and establishing a tradition.
Yet every time I attend these banquets,
I never hear grand strategies for governing the country,
only talk about ordinary daily matters.
This is not a sign of planning for future generations.
Are our descendants in danger?
This is my worry for my grandchildren.
Your generation might still die peacefully."
Pointing at his grandchildren, he said:
"These ones will surely encounter chaos and perish."
When Zūn's son Suí died,
his elder brother Sōng wept for him, saying:
"Our grandfather was almost a sage."
From History of the Jìn Dynasty.
Stabbing Tears
Fú Shēng, whose courtesy name was Chángshēng,
was the second son of Fú Jiàn,
and was unruly from a young age.
His grandfather Fú Hóng detested him greatly.
Fú Shēng was born blind in one eye,
and when he was a child,
Fú Hóng teased him, saying:
"I've heard that a blind boy sheds only one tear,
is that true?"
Fú Shēng became angry,
drew his dagger and stabbed himself, drawing blood,
saying:
"This is also a tear."
Fú Hóng was greatly shocked,
and whipped him,
to which Fú Shēng said:
"I can endure swords and spears,
but not whips and canes."
Fú Hóng said:
"I will make you a slave."
Fú Shēng replied:
"I might not even match up to Shí Lè."
Fú Hóng, frightened, rushed barefoot to cover his mouth.
End
Jiā'ér
Zhāng Cāngwúzhèn was Zhāng Píng's grandfather,
who once said to Píng's father:
"I am not as good as you."
Píng's father didn't understand why,
so Cāngwú explained:
"You have a fine son."
At that time Píng was just a few years old,
but he clasped his hands and said:
"Grandfather, should you really use a son to tease his father?"
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Young and brilliant
Xiè Língyùn's grandfather, Xiè Yuán, was a Chariot and Horse General of the Jin Dynasty.
His father, Xiè Huàn,
was born unintelligent
and died young.
Língyùn was exceptionally bright from a young age,
which Yuán found remarkable.
He said to his relatives and friends:
"I gave birth to Huàn,
so why is Huàn's son not inferior to me?"
The strength bequeathed to posterity
Dào Gài's son Dào Jìng died young,
his grandson Dào Jìn was exceptionally intelligent from an early age,
and held the position of Gentleman in the Ministry of Personnel.
He once accompanied Emperor Wǔ of Liáng on an imperial visit to Jīngkǒu,
where they ascended the Běigù Tower to compose poetry.
Dào Jìn received the imperial command,
and immediately completed his poem, presenting it to Dào Gài with the words:
"Jìn is certainly talented;
I fear that all along, your writings have been ghostwritten by Jìn."
Thereupon, the emperor bestowed twenty bolts of silk upon him.
Later, whenever Dào Gài composed poems in response to the emperor's,
the emperor would issue a handwritten edict teasing Dào Gài, saying:
"Is this not the fruit of your descendant's labor?"
From History of the Southern Dynasties.
Opening the Register
Lǐ Qiānzhé was once appointed as the Prefect of Zhēnzhōu,
which was his home province.
Qiānzhé had over a hundred concubines,
with sixty-nine sons and daughters.
Along the Han River for over a thousand li,
his residences stood in succession.
Concubines who had borne him children were housed separately in these residences.
Qiānzhé would sound his reed whistle to announce his arrival with attendants,
moving among them,
indulging in wine and joyous feasts.
When his children and grandchildren came to pay respects,
he sometimes forgot their names
and had to consult the register to verify them.
From the Book of the Later Zhōu:
Guō Zǐyí had several dozen grandsons.
Each morning when the grandchildren came to greet him, he couldn't recognize them all,
so he simply nodded in acknowledgment.
Praying for blessings
Zhāng Yuán, styled Xiàoshǐ,
at the age of sixteen,
his grandfather had been blind for three years.
Yuán constantly grieved and wept,
studying Buddhist scriptures day and night,
and performing rituals to pray for blessings.
Later, while reading the "Medicine Buddha Sutra," he came across a passage stating that the blind could regain sight.
He then invited seven monks to light seven lamps for seven days and seven nights,
performing the Medicine Buddha ritual.
Each time he prayed, he said, "O Heavenly Teacher,
I, Yuán, am an unfilial grandson,
causing my grandfather to lose his sight.
Now, by offering the light universally to the Dharma realm,
I pray that my grandfather's eyes may see clearly again.
I seek to take on his darkness," continuing this for seven days.
That night, he dreamed of an old man treating his grandfather's eyes with a golden probe,
and in his dream, he leaped for joy,
then suddenly awoke with a start.
He immediately informed all his family members,
and three days later, his grandfather's eyes indeed regained sight.
"History of the Northern Dynasties," Volume 72
Ghostwriting
Xǔ Jìngzōng's grandson Yàn Bó,
was the son of Áng,
and quite literary.
In his later years, Jìngzōng no longer wrote,
all major ceremonial documents were composed by Yàn Bó.
He once jokingly said to Áng:
"My son is not as good as your son."
The reply was:
"His father is not as good as Áng's father."
The Book of Tang
records that Jìngzōng was excessively fond of women without restraint.
His wife Péi's maid was beautiful,
Jìngzōng favored her and made her his second wife,
giving her the false surname Yú.
Áng had long been intimate with her,
and their illicit relationship continued unabated.
Jìngzōng became angry, dismissed Lady Yú,
accused Áng of unfilial conduct,
and requested his exile beyond the southern mountains.
Later, influenced by a favored concubine's slander,
he petitioned for Yàn Bó's exile beyond the southern mountains too,
but they were later pardoned and returned.
The Old [Book of Tang]
records that because of Yuán Sīgǔ's deliberation,
proposing to grant Jìngzōng the posthumous name "Mù",
Yàn Bó, bearing a grudge, planned to ambush him on the road.
Sīgǔ said:
"I was merely avenging my late father."
Yàn Bó, ashamed, desisted.
The New [Book of Tang]
Leaning on the rock
Xuē Yuánchāo during Gāozōng's reign served as Zhōngshū Lìngrén,
in the department there was a stone slab,
where his grandfather Xuē Dàohéng, when serving as Nèishǐ Shìláng,
often leaned against while drafting imperial edicts.
Whenever Yuánchāo saw this stone,
he could not help shedding tears.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Carrying a Staff
When a disciple of Confucius came from afar,
Confucius, leaning on his staff, asked him:
"Is your grandfather well?"
Then, holding his staff with both hands and bowing,
he inquired:
"Are your parents well?"
Setting aside his staff, he asked:
"Are your brothers well?"
Walking side by side with him,
he questioned:
"Are your wife and children well?"
Thus, with a staff of six feet,
Confucius demonstrated the distinctions of nobility and humility,
clarified the principles of closeness and distance in relationships,
how much more could this be applied to positions of honor and generous emoluments?
"Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals"
Shedding the mortal form
Shùn asked Chéng, saying:
"Can the Way be possessed?"
Chéng replied:
"Your body is not your possession,
how could you possess the Way?"
Shùn said:
"If my body is not my possession,
then who possesses it?"
Chéng answered:
"It is the form entrusted by Heaven and Earth,
your life is not your possession,
it is the harmony entrusted by Heaven and Earth,
your nature and destiny are not your possessions,
they are the compliance entrusted by Heaven and Earth,
your descendants are not your possessions,
they are the metamorphosis entrusted by Heaven and Earth,
therefore when you walk, you know not where you go,
when you dwell, you know not what you hold,
when you eat, you know not the reason why,
all are but the vigorous energy of Heaven and Earth,
so how could they possibly be possessed?"
《Liezi》
deceased parents
Father is called kǎo, mother is called bǐ.
The Erya
states: "When alive, they are called father and mother; when deceased, they are called kǎo and bǐ."
The Quli
Qiáo Zǐ
Bóqín and Kāngshū went to see the Duke of Zhōu,
but were caned three times after three visits.
Kāngshū looked alarmed
and said to Bóqín:
"There is a worthy man named Shāngzǐ.
Let us go see him together."
So they went to see Shāngzǐ and asked him about it.
Shāngzǐ said:
"On the sunny side of the southern mountain, there is a tree
called the Qiáo."
The two young men went to observe it
and saw the Qiáo tree standing tall and upright.
They returned and reported to Shāngzǐ.
Shāngzǐ said:
"The Qiáo tree
represents the way of a father.
On the shady side of the southern mountain, there is a tree called the Zǐ."
The two young men went again to observe it,
and saw the Zǐ tree bending low and following along.
They returned and reported to Shāngzǐ.
Shāngzǐ said:
"The Zǐ tree
represents the way of a son."
The next day, the two young men went to see the Duke of Zhōu. They entered the gate and hurried in,
ascended the hall and knelt down.
The Duke stroked their heads,
comforted them, and gave them food, saying:
"Who taught you the proper way to see a gentleman?"
From the "Shū Dà Zhuàn"
Exhausting one's strength and thoughts
Zǐlù appeared before Confucius and said:
"Carrying heavy loads and traveling far,
I would not choose where to rest.
With a poor family and elderly parents,
I would not choose my salary when taking office.
In the past, when I,
Zǐyóu, was serving my two parents,
I often ate coarse meals of wild vegetables,
and carried rice for my parents from a hundred lǐ away.
After my parents passed away,
I traveled south to Chǔ,
with a hundred chariots following me,
accumulating ten thousand zhōng of grain,
sitting on layers of cushions,
and dining with rows of tripods.
I wish I could again eat coarse vegetables
and carry rice for my parents,
but this can no longer be done.
A dried fish on a string - how can it not rot?
My two parents passed as suddenly as light through a crack."
Confucius said:
"Zǐyóu,
in serving your parents you may be said to have exerted all your strength while they lived,
and exhausted your thoughts after their death."
Family Sayings
Revenge
Zhòngzǐ Cuī was
the son of Zhòng Yóu.
Zǐlù served in Wèi,
and went to face the crisis of Kuǎi Kuì.
A Wèi man, Gǔ Yǎn, who was guarding the gate, killed Zǐlù.
After Zǐ Cuī grew up,
he told Confucius he wanted to avenge his father.
The Master said:
"Go."
Zǐ Cuī then went.
Yǎn's son learned of this,
and said:
"The courage of a noble man
does not take advantage of another's unpreparedness.
We must meet to fight tomorrow west of the city."
On that day,
Yǎn, armed with a cattail bow and wooden halberd, fought Zǐ Cuī and died.
"Shī Juéshòu's Biographies of Filial Sons"
Caning on the Back
Zēngzǐ was weeding the melon patch,
and accidentally cut off the roots.
Zēngxī became enraged,
took a large staff and struck him on the back.
Zēngzǐ fell to the ground unconscious,
and only after a long while did he revive.
He rose cheerfully,
approached Zēngxī and said:
"Just now, Shēn offended you, father.
You used your strength to teach Shēn a lesson—
I hope you haven't hurt yourself?"
He then withdrew to his room, took up his qin and sang,
wanting Zēngxī to hear it
and know that he was physically well.
When Confucius heard of this, he was angry
and told his disciples:
"When Shēn comes, do not admit him."
Zēng Shēn believed himself to be without fault,
and sent someone to ask Confucius why.
Confucius said:
"Have you not heard?
In ancient times, Gǔsǒu had a son named Shùn.
When Shùn served his father,
if his father wanted him, he was always at his side.
But when his father sought to kill him,
he was never to be found.
For minor beatings he would await the punishment,
but for major staff strikes he would flee.
Thus Gǔsǒu never committed the crime of being an un-fatherly father,
and Shùn never failed in his profound filial piety.
Now Shēn, in serving his father, offered his body to await violence.
He did not avoid his father's lethal rage.
Had he died, he would have trapped his father in unrighteousness.
Could there be any greater unfiliality than this?
Are you not a subject of the Son of Heaven?
What is the crime of killing a subject of the Son of Heaven?"
When Zēng Shēn heard this,
he said:
"My offense is great indeed!"
Thereupon he went to Confucius and apologized for his fault.
Family Sayings
Lord Yán
Gōngxī Huá's care for his parents was,
as if he were with friends;
Zēng Shēn's care for his parents was,
as if he were serving a stern ruler or severe lord.
"Huáinánzi · Qí Sú"
Cooking a Pig
Zēngzǐ's wife was going to the market,
and their child followed her crying.
The mother said:
"Go back home,
and when I return, I will slaughter a pig for you."
Upon returning from the market,
Zēngzǐ prepared to catch and kill the pig,
but his wife stopped him, saying:
"I was only joking with the child."
Zēngzǐ replied:
"One should not joke with children!
Children lack knowledge
and learn from their parents,
following their parents' teachings.
If you make a promise to the child
but then break it,
this teaches the child to be untrustworthy.
A mother should not educate her child through deception."
So they cooked the pig.
From "Hánfēizǐ"
Textual Evidence
In the state of Chǔ there was a man named Zhígōng,
whose father stole a sheep and he reported it to the authorities.
The authorities arrested his father and were about to execute him,
Zhígōng requested to take his father's place.
When he was about to be executed,
he told the officials:
"My father stole a sheep and I reported it,
is this not trustworthy?
When my father was to be executed, I took his place,
is this not filial?
If someone both trustworthy and filial is executed,
will there be anyone in the state who is not executed?"
The king heard this and did not execute him.
Confucius heard about this and said:
"How strange
is Zhígōng's version of trustworthiness!
He used one father to gain two reputations.
Therefore Zhígōng's trustworthiness would be better if it didn't exist."
Lǚ's Annals
Breaking the Hairpin
Fàn Wénzǐ returned late from court,
and Wǔzǐ said:
"Why are you so late?"
He replied:
"There was a guest from Qín speaking in riddles at court,
and none of the high officials could respond to him,
but I understood three of them."
Fànzǐ angrily said:
"It's not that the high officials were incapable,
but that they yielded to their elders.
What does a youth like you know?
And yet you overshadowed others three times at court!
If I were not here,
Jìn would be on the verge of collapse any day now."
He struck him with his staff,
breaking his hatpin.
From "Discourses"
Sipping Broth
Yuè Yáng was a general of Wèi who attacked Zhōngshān.
His son was in Zhōngshān.
The ruler of Zhōngshān had his son boiled and sent the broth to him.
Yuè Yáng sat under the tent and drank it,
finishing a whole cup.
Marquis Wén said to Dǔshī Zàn:
"Yuè Yáng, for my sake, ate the flesh of his own son."
The reply was:
"He boiled his own son and ate him—
then who wouldn't he eat?"
Yuè Yáng captured Zhōngshān,
and Marquis Wén rewarded his achievement but doubted his heart.
Hánzǐ
Receive the teaching
Qín, by way of Hán and Wèi, attacked Qí.
King Wēi of Qí sent Zhāngzǐ to lead troops in response.
They encamped facing the Qín army,
with messengers frequently traveling back and forth.
Zhāngzǐ altered his army's insignia to blend in with the Qín forces.
Scouts reported that Zhāngzǐ had defected to Qín with the Qí army,
but King Wēi did not respond.
After a short while, scouts reported again,
saying Zhāngzǐ had surrendered the Qí troops to Qín.
King Wēi remained silent despite three such reports.
An official pleaded:
"Those who speak of Zhāngzǐ's defeat,
though different people, all say the same thing.
Why does Your Majesty not send generals to attack him?"
The king replied:
"It is clear he has not betrayed me—
why attack him?"
Soon after, news came that the Qí army had won a great victory,
and the Qín forces were utterly defeated.
The attendants asked:
"How did you know this?"
He said:
"Zhāngzǐ's mother, Qǐ, offended his father,
who killed her and buried her beneath the horse stable.
When I appointed Zhāngzǐ as general,
I encouraged him, saying:
'With your strength,
if you return with the army intact,
I will surely rebury your mother.'
He replied:
'It is not that I cannot rebury my late mother;
but my mother, Qǐ, offended my father,
and my father died without instructing me [to do so].
If I, as a son, were to rebury my mother without my father's instruction,
that would be betraying my deceased father.
Therefore, I dare not.'
As a son, he would not betray his deceased father—
how could he, as a subject, betray his living sovereign?"
"Qí Cè"
Fēn Jīn
Lù Jiǎ was sent as an envoy to Nányuè,
Zhào Tuó bestowed gifts upon Jiǎ,
the goods in the bags were worth a thousand gold,
and other gifts also amounted to a thousand gold.
During Empress Lǚ's reign, he retired due to illness and lived at home,
finding the fields of Hǎozhì fertile and suitable for settling.
He had five sons,
so he took out the goods obtained from his mission to Nányuè, sold them for a thousand gold,
and divided it among his sons,
giving each two hundred gold,
instructing them to engage in livelihood.
Lù Shēng often rode in a comfortable carriage drawn by four horses,
with ten attendants following him, singing, dancing, and playing zithers,
and a precious sword worth a hundred gold.
He said to his sons:
"I make an agreement with you: when I visit you,
you provide me with servants, horses, wine, and food,
and I will drink to my heart's content for ten days before moving to the next son's home where I will die.
I will have the precious sword, carriage, horses, and attendants;
within a year, as I come and go visiting other guests,
I will generally not visit more than two or three times.
Frequently slaughter fresh animals, do not let your daughters toil for long."
"Shǐ Hàn"
The Virtue of Father and Son
The virtue of Shí Fèn and Shí Jiàn, father and son,
without such a father,
there would be no such son;
without such a son,
there would be no such father.
From "Yángzǐ"
The body left behind
Huò Qùbìng's father, Zhòngrú,
served as a county official in the household of the Marquis of Píngyáng,
and had a secret affair with the marquis' maidservant Wèi Shào'ér,
giving birth to Qùbìng.
When Zhòngrú completed his official service and returned home,
he married a woman and had children,
with no further communication between them.
After a long time, Qùbìng became the Swift Cavalry General,
and while attacking the Xiōngnú,
passed through Hédōng,
arriving at the Píngyáng relay station.
He sent officials to fetch Zhòngrú.
Zhòngrú hurried to pay his respects,
and the general greeted him, then knelt and said:
"I did not realize earlier that I am the body left behind by you, father."
Zhòngrú prostrated himself and kowtowed, saying:
"This old minister's life has been entrusted to the general,
this is the power of Heaven."
Qùbìng then purchased much farmland, houses, and slaves for Zhòngrú before departing.
"Biography of Huò Guāng"
Admonishing One's Father
Wú Yòu's father Wú Huī served as the Grand Administrator of Nánhǎi,
and at the age of twelve, Yòu accompanied him to his official post.
Huī intended to prepare bamboo slips by scorching them to write the classics,
but Yòu admonished him, saying:
"Crossing the Five Ridges,
the region is abundant with rare treasures,
above, you may be suspected by the state,
below, you may attract the envy of powerful relatives.
If these books are completed, they would require double the carts to transport them.
In the past, Mǎ Yuán was slandered because of coix seeds,
and Wáng Yáng gained fame through his clothing bag."
Huī then desisted from the plan,
and patting his son's head, said:
"The Wú family will not lack a Jìzǐ for generations to come."
(From the Original Biography)
Extraordinary
Xuē Qín served in the commandery as an official in charge of personnel,
Chén Zhòngjǔ being fifteen years old at the time,
went on behalf of his father to deliver a letter to Qín.
Qín looked at him and observed him carefully,
and the next day paid him a visit.
Zhòngjǔ's father came out to greet Qín,
whereupon Qín said:
"You have an extraordinary son,
I have come to see him,
not for your sake."
They conversed the entire day.
(Records of Former Worthies of Rǔnán)
Nephew
There was an unfilial son,
whose family possessed ten thousand gold in assets,
yet from childhood he never obeyed his father's words.
As his father was dying, he wished to be buried on a mountain,
but feared his son would not comply,
so he conventionally instructed to bury him beneath the marsh on the rocky shore.
The unfilial son said:
"I have never followed your teachings,
but today I shall obey this one command."
Thereupon, he dispersed all the family wealth,
piling up earth around it to form an islet,
several hundred paces long,
which was finally destroyed by water during the Yuánkāng era.
This unfilial son
was a man from the Former Hàn Dynasty.
From "Bówùzhì"
Old Clam
Wéi Kāng, styled Yuánjiàng,
and his younger brother Wéi Dàn, styled Zhòngjiàng.
Kǒng Róng wrote a letter to their father saying:
"The day before yesterday Yuánjiàng came;
profound in talent, brilliant and outstanding,
elegant in demeanor, broad-minded and resolute,
truly a vessel for great achievements in the world.
Yesterday Zhòngjiàng came;
cultured, quick-witted, sincere and steadfast,
he is the pillar who will maintain the family.
I never expected twin pearls to emerge from an old clam."
In the History of the Later Han,
Emperor Shìzǔ met Wáng Guǎngzhī's son Zhēn Guó,
and recognizing his potential for great responsibility,
said to Guǎngzhī:
"You, sir, may indeed be called an old clam."
Guǎngzhī replied:
"Your subject dares not decline the compliment."
The Emperor laughed heartily.
Book of the Southern Qí
Digging a well, obtaining bronze
Páng Jiǎn of Wèijùn lost his father during the turmoil,
at that time Jiǎn was three or four years old,
his mother carried him in swaddling clothes and moved to a hut as a tenant,
where they dug a well and obtained tens of thousands of coins,
thus becoming wealthy.
They then bought an elderly servant to manage household affairs.
One day, while music was playing in the hall,
the old servant secretly said in the kitchen:
"The elderly mother in the hall
is my wife."
When asked for the reason,
the servant said:
"My wife's surname is Ài, her given name is Āhóng,
she has a black mole on the sole of her foot,
and a red birthmark under her arm."
The mother said:
"This is my husband."
Thus they became husband and wife again.
People at the time made a saying about this:
"Páng Gōng in the hut,
dug a well and obtained copper,
bought a servant and got a husband."
From "Fēngsú Tōng"
Licking the Calf
Yáng Biāo held the position of Grand Commandant,
and seeing that the Hàn dynasty's mandate was nearing its end,
he claimed his feet were cramped and could no longer walk,
accumulating ten years thus.
Later, his son Yáng Xiū was killed by Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo, upon meeting Yáng Biāo, asked:
"Why have you grown so thin?"
He replied:
"I regret lacking the foresight of Jīn Mìdī,
yet still cling to the love of an old cow licking its calf."
Cáo Cāo was moved to change his expression.
From the Book of the Later Hàn
Drive the chariot
Chén Tàiqiū visited Xún Lǎng,
and being poor and frugal, had no servants.
So he had Yuánfāng drive the carriage,
with Jìfāng following behind carrying a staff.
Chángwén, still young, was seated in the carriage.
When they arrived,
Xún had Shūcí greet them at the gate,
while Címíng served wine and the remaining six dragons served food.
Wénruò, also young, sat in front of the knees.
At that time, the Grand Astrologer reported that a true man was traveling east.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
According to the main biography, Shǔ died in the third year of the Jiànhé era of Emperor Huàn,
while Yù was born in the sixth year of the Yánxī era,
which is already thirteen years apart.
My father
The Governor of Yǐngchuān punished Chén Zhònggōng by shaving his head.
A guest asked Yuánfāng, "What kind of official is your father?"
Yuánfāng said,
"He is a wise and brilliant official.
What kind of person is your father?"
The guest said,
"He is a loyal minister and a filial son."
The guest then asked,
"How can there be a wise and brilliant official who punishes a loyal minister and filial son?"
Yuánfāng said,
"How absurd your words are!"
Therefore, he did not answer.
The guest said,
"You are merely feigning humility and cannot answer."
Yuánfāng said,
"In the past, Emperor Gāozōng exiled the filial son Xiàojǐ,
Yǐn Jífǔ exiled the filial son Bóqí,
and Dǒng Zhòngshū exiled the filial son Fúqǐ.
Only these three officials
were wise and brilliant,
and only these three sons
were loyal ministers and filial sons."
The guest felt ashamed and left.
End
Seated apart
Wú Jìzhì, styled Zǐshàng,

Melting snow with hot water
Wáng Yíng, styled Fèngguāng,
rose through the ranks to become the Governor of Yìxīng.
He replaced Xiè Chāozōng in the commandery,
and the two became hostile toward each other.
Upon returning to the capital, Chāozōng went to Yíng’s father, Wáng Mào, to request a letter,
entrusting Yíng with the matter.
One official said:
"With a single directive from you, sir,
it would be like pouring hot water on snow."
But when Yíng replied that public officials could not comply,
Chāozōng went to Mào’s place to confront him.
The guests there said to Mào:
"Hot water indeed cannot melt snow."
Mào’s face flushed crimson with deep shame.
Later, Mào went to Chāozōng’s residence,
where exquisite whitefish, fine minced fish, and roe deer offerings were prepared.
Mào asked how he had obtained such delicacies,
and Chāozōng deceitfully replied:
"They were first sent as gifts from Yìxīng."
He added in surprise:
"Could it be that you, sir, did not receive any?"
Mào grew furious,
reported the matter to the imperial court,
claiming that Yíng provided insufficient support for him.
As a result, Yíng was dismissed from his commandery post
and remained in obscurity for a long time.

Dripping to the bone
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's second son Zōng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yùzhāng.
Initially, his mother Shūyuàn Wú was in the palace of the Marquis of Dōnghūn of Qí.
When she was favored,
Emperor Wǔ was born in the seventh month.
Many in Zōng's palace doubted this.
When Zōng was fourteen years old,
he often dreamed of a plump, sturdy youth
holding his own head and facing him.
Zōng repeatedly questioned his mother,
and his mother asked about the appearance in the dream.
It resembled the Marquis of Dōnghūn.
She secretly informed him not to reveal it.
Zōng then conducted sacrifices in a temple chamber,
yet still lacked self-confidence.
Hearing the folk belief that if a living person's blood drips on a deceased's bones
and it seeps in, they are father and child,
Zōng privately opened the Marquis of Dōnghūn's tomb,
took out the bones, dripped blood to test it.
After it was verified,
he had a second son in Xīzhōu.
Over a month later, he secretly killed him,
buried the bones, and tested it again.

Seeing his father

Disobeying his father
Cuī Yì served as Vice Minister of Rites,
while his son Cuī Shí served in the Ministry of War.
Father and son simultaneously held deputy positions in the Southern Department,
something unprecedented since the Tang dynasty's establishment.
Cuī Shí later became Zhongshu Ling,
while Cuī Yì retired as Minister of Revenue.
Cuī Yì was corrupt by nature,
accepting others' requests
and frequently interfering with Cuī Shí's official matters.
Cuī Shí often refused to comply,
drawing widespread ridicule from contemporary opinion.
Old Book of Tang
records: When Cuī Shí was Vice Minister of Personnel,
he was greedy and unrestrained.
The elder brother relied on the younger's influence,
the father exploited the son's authority—
all accepted solicitations.
Their corruption was rampant.
Cuī Yì, as Director of the Imperial Academy,
accepted money from an official candidate.
Cuī Shí was unaware of this.
When the candidate failed the selection,
he protested:
"Your own father took the bribe—
why wasn't I given a post?"
Cuī Shí replied:
"Who is this relative?
I'll have him captured and flogged to death!"
The man said:
"Flogging him would bring you mourning."
Cuī Shí was greatly ashamed.
When the emperor, considering Cuī Shí's father's age,
bestowed a melon at its first ripening,
Cuī Shí gave it to his concubine
instead of his father,
drawing ridicule from court and public.
At that time, Cuī Shí, Cén Xī, and Zhèng Yīn all served in the Ministry of Personnel.
A capital ballad said:
"Cén and Yīn, clever southerners;
Cuī Shí, the minister's grandson.
When the three are compared,
none beats the Tǔgǔhún."

adept at discussing matters but flawed in making judgments.

Mutual Ridicule
Péi Xūn's appearance was short and insignificant, and his nature was especially straightforward and unguarded.
While drinking with his father Péi Yuán,
Yuán had them pass the cup around,
each person to whom it came was to describe their own condition.
Yuán passed the cup to Xūn, saying:
"Short people are full of talk,
a broken cart needs many wedges—
Péi Xūn: ten points."
Xūn drank and then returned the cup, saying:
"The bat doesn't see itself,
yet laughs at the swallow on the beam.
Eleventh Young Master: ten points—
for Yuán is the eleventh."
Yuán became angry
and caned him.

Direct Meal
In the early Zhēnyuán era, Mù Níng served as the prefect of Hézhōu.
His sons—the later Wǎnlíng Minister Zàn, Supervising Secretary Zhì, and Yuánshǎng—had not yet received official posts,
and served before Níng.
At that time, the Mù family rules were strict and severe.
Níng ordered his sons to take turns preparing meals,
and if they were slightly unsatisfactory, he would cane them.
As the sons approached their duty days,
they would invariably seek out rare delicacies to array before the dining table,
vying to innovate the flavors,
leaving no scheme untried.
Yet they never avoided the offenses of being caned and scolded.
One day, when Supervising Secretary Zhì was on duty before the tripod,
there were bear fat and dried venison, and he suddenly said:
"The fat is rich and the dried meat lean;
would blending them enhance the harmony?"
He then tried it together and said:
"It is exceptionally different from the usual fare."
So he wrapped the dried meat with the fat, modified it, and presented it to Níng,
who indeed ate his fill again.
Wǎnlíng and the younger brothers looked at Supervising Secretary Zhì with expressions full of admiration and envy,
saying:
"Not only will you avoid the cane,
but you should also receive a reward."
The Supervising Secretary was quite pleased with himself.
After Níng finished his meal,
he instructed his attendants:
"Bring the one on duty here with the cane."
Thus, the punishment was meted out as usual.
As the Supervising Secretary was about to receive the caning,
Níng hastily called him forward and said:
"With such a flavor,
why was it presented so late?"
Upon hearing this, those present laughed and spread the story.
From "Zīxiá Lù"

to whip one's father
In Shǔ there was a Grand Tutor Jiāng,
a native of Xǔtián.
In his youth he was captured by the Yellow Turbans,
losing both his parents.
There was an old stablehand named Jiǎng
who, after being whipped repeatedly,
could no longer endure the suffering due to his age,
and begged the lady of the house to let him return home.
The lady inquired about his hometown
and questioned him about his wife and children,
all of which he described in detail.
When Jiāng returned to the residence,
the lady recounted the entire matter to him.
Jiāng, suspicious and startled that it might be his father,
sent someone to question him carefully,
asking what distinctive marks were on his son's body.
The old man verified:
"My son has a black mole on the sole of his foot,
I remember nothing else."
Jiāng wept bitterly,
secretly had him escorted beyond Jiànmén Pass,
and reported to the Former Sovereign:
"My father has recently come from Guāndōng."
He then welcomed him into his home,
and father and son were reunited as before.
To atone for the fault of beating his father,
Jiāng provided alms to tens of thousands of monks,
and never again whipped his attendants for life.

Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng confined his mother, Lady Jiāng, in Chéngyǐng,
and swore to her:
"Until the Yellow Springs,
we shall not see each other."
Later he regretted it.
Yǐng Kǎoshū was the warden of Yǐng Valley,
and as a border official heard of this.
He presented a gift to the duke,
who in return gave him food.

and he replied:

who has tasted all my food,
but never the duke's broth.

The duke said:
"You have a mother to give things to,
why is it that I alone have none?"
Yǐng Kǎoshū said:
"What do you mean?"
The duke explained the reason,
and told him of his regret.
Yǐng Kǎoshū replied:
"What trouble is there in this, my lord?
If you dig the earth until you reach the springs,
and meet
in a tunnel
, who can say it is not in accordance with your oath?"
The duke followed his advice.
The duke entered and recited about the great tunnel.
Inside it,
the joy was harmonious.
Lady Jiāng came out and recited:
"Outside the tunnel,
the joy was overflowing."
Thus mother and son were reconciled as before.
The gentleman
says: Yǐng Kǎoshū was of pure filial piety,
loving his mother,
and extending it to Duke Zhuāng.
Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Yǐn 1st Year.
Mother Spinning
Gōngfù Wénbó retired from court,
and found his mother spinning.
Wénbó said:
"In a household like ours, for the mistress to still spin
fears to provoke Jìsūn's anger.
Does he think I am unable to serve my mother?"
His mother sighed and said:
"Is Lǔ about to perish?
To appoint youths to office without instructing them!
Sit, and I will tell you.
In ancient times, when sage kings settled the people,
they chose poor land to settle them,
made the people labor and employed them,
thus they long ruled the world.
When people labor, they think;
when they think, good intentions arise.
In ease, they become licentious;
when licentious, they forget goodness;
forgetting goodness, evil intentions arise.
People of fertile land are unproductive and licentious,
people of poor land all turn to righteousness through labor.
Men and women devote themselves to spinning,
transgressions then have punishments,
such was the ancient system.
Noblemen labor with their minds,
common people labor with their strength,
this was the teaching of former kings.
From high to low,
who dares be licentious in mind and idle in strength?
Now I am a widow,
and you hold a low position,
diligent morning and night in your duties,
still fearing to forget the legacy of our ancestors.
How much more if idle and lazy,
how could you avoid punishment?
I hoped you would daily cultivate yourself, saying:
'I must not abandon my ancestors,'
yet now you say why not take your ease.
Holding the king's office with this attitude,
I fear Mùbó's line will be cut off."
"Lǔyǔ"
When Wénbó died,
his wives all wept aloud,
Jìng Jiāng admonished them:
"I have heard that those who favor external affairs die for scholars,
those who favor internal affairs die for women.
Now my son died young,
I fear he is known for favoring internal affairs.
You wives who wish to continue the ancestral sacrifices,
follow the rites and be quiet,
thus you will illuminate my son."
Confucius heard of this and said:
"No maiden's wisdom equals a married woman's,
no youth's wisdom equals a husband's.
The Wén family's wife was wise indeed,
cutting through emotion and reducing rites,
wishing to show her son as having fine virtue."
"Family Sayings"
When Wénbó died,
his mother did not weep.
Jìsūn heard of this,
and said:
"Gōngfǔ Wénbó's mother
is a chaste woman.
Her son died, yet she does not weep,
there must be a reason."
He sent someone to ask her,
she replied:
"Formerly, this son of mine,
I had him serve Zhòngní.
When Zhòngní left Lǔ,
he did not see him beyond Lǔ's suburbs.
When giving gifts, he did not give family treasures.
When ill, no scholars came to visit.
When dead, no scholars shed tears.
On the day he died, ten palace women in hempen mourning followed on foot.
This shows insufficiency towards scholars but excess towards women.
Therefore I do not weep."
"Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn"
Heartache
Zhèng Zǐchǎn was devoted to serving his mother.
Once, he was ordered to go on a diplomatic mission to Jìn,
when along the way, he felt a sudden pain in his heart.
He immediately sent someone back home
to inquire about his mother's well-being.
His mother said:
"I suddenly felt unwell,
and was thinking of you,
but there is nothing else."
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Heartbeat
Zēngzǐ followed Confucius in Chǔ when his heart stirred,
so he bid farewell and returned home to ask his mother, who said:
"I missed you so much that I bit my finger."
Confucius remarked:
"Zēng Shēn's utmost sincerity
can move spirits across ten thousand miles."
From Sōushénjì
Gripping the arm
Zēng Shēn was out gathering firewood in the wilderness,
when a guest arrived at his home.
The guest was about to leave,
when his mother said:
"I wish you would stay."
Just as Zēng Shēn was arriving,
she immediately used her right hand to pinch her right arm.
Her arm hurt,
and Zēng Shēn rushed over to ask his mother:
"Why does your arm hurt?"
His mother said:
"Just now a guest came,
I pinched my arm to call you."
Lùn Héng
Cutting the Loom
When Mèngzǐ was young and reciting texts,
his mother was weaving.
Mèngzǐ suddenly stopped,
then resumed and finished.
His mother knew he had been distracted,
called him and asked:
"Why did you stop?"
He replied:
"I lost my place but found it again."
His mother took a knife and cut her weaving,
using this to warn him.
From that time onward,
Mèngzǐ never got distracted again.
When Mèngzǐ was young, the eastern neighbor killed a pig.
Mèngzǐ asked his mother:
"Why did the eastern neighbor kill a pig?"
His mother said:
"To feed you."
Then she regretted her words and said:
"When I was pregnant with this child,
I wouldn't sit if the mat wasn't straight,
I wouldn't eat if the cut wasn't proper -
this was prenatal education.
Now that he's beginning to understand, if I deceive him,
this would be teaching him dishonesty."
So she bought pork from the eastern neighbor and fed it to him,
to show she hadn't deceived him.
"Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn"
Counting the Children Behind Closed Doors
The Chu general Zǐ Fā attacked Qin,
ran out of provisions,
sent someone to request from the king,
and upon returning home, visited his mother.
His mother asked the messenger,
who replied:
"The soldiers share beans to eat,
while the general enjoys fine grains and meats morning and night."
When Zǐ Fā defeated Qin and returned,
his mother closed the door and would not let him in,
sending someone to reprimand him, saying:
"Have you not heard of Gōu Jiàn's campaign against Wu?
To send others into deadly peril,
while indulging in comfort and pleasure oneself,
even if victory is achieved,
it is not the right way.
You are not my son,
do not enter my door."
Zǐ Fā then apologized to his mother,
and only then was he admitted.
Biographies of Exemplary Women
Biting the arm
Wú Qǐ departed eastward from the outer gate of Wèi's capital,
bidding farewell to his mother,
he bit his arm and swore an oath:
"I shall not return to Wèi unless I become a high minister or chancellor."
Thereupon he served Master Zēng as a disciple,
but soon after his mother passed away,
yet Qǐ never returned home.
Master Zēng thought little of him for this,
and severed ties with Qǐ.
Leaning against the door
Wángsūn Gǔ at the age of fifteen served King Mǐn,
the king fled the capital,
(Wángsūn Gǔ) lost track of the king's whereabouts.
His mother said:
"When you go out in the morning and return late,
I lean against the door waiting for you.
When you go out at dusk and don't return,
I lean against the village gate waiting for you.
Now you serve the king,
the king has fled,
you don't know his whereabouts,
what place do you have to return to?"
Wángsūn Gǔ then entered the marketplace,
saying:
"Nào Chǐ has brought chaos to the state of Qí,
and killed the king.
Those who wish to join me in punishing him, bare your right arms!"
Four hundred people from the marketplace followed him,
and together they went to punish Nào Chǐ,
stabbing and killing him.
"Strategies of the Warring States"
Declining the Gold
Tián Jìzǐ served as the prime minister of Qí and accepted a bribe of one hundred yì of gold from a subordinate official,
which he presented to his mother.
His mother said:
"You have been prime minister for three years,
yet your official salary has never been this substantial.
Could this be the expenses of cultivating relationships with other officials?
How did you obtain this?"
He replied:
"I truly received it from a subordinate."
His mother said:
"I have heard that a gentleman cultivates himself and remains pure, not engaging in improper gains.
A minister serving his ruler
is like a son serving his father.
With integrity and impartiality,
one can thus proceed without calamity.
Now you have done the opposite and strayed from loyalty.
To be a disloyal minister
is to be an unfilial son.
Ill-gotten wealth
is not what I possess;
an unfilial son
is not my son.
Leave!"
Tián Jìzǐ felt ashamed and left,
returned the gold,
and voluntarily confessed his crime to King Xuān,
requesting to be executed.
King Xuān, upon hearing this,
greatly praised his mother's righteousness,
then pardoned Jìzǐ's crime,
and bestowed public funds upon the mother.
The gentleman would say that Jìzǐ's mother was incorruptible and transformative.
"Biographies of Exemplary Women"
knowing what to abolish
Chén Yīng was a native of Dōngyáng.
In his youth, he cultivated virtuous conduct,
and became renowned in his local community.
During the great turmoil at the end of the Qín dynasty,
the people of Dōngyáng wished to support Chén Yīng as their king.
His mother said:
"This must not be.
Since I became a bride to your family,
I have only known poverty and low status from a young age.
To suddenly attain wealth and honor would be inauspicious.
It would be better to place the troops under someone else's command.
If they succeed,
you will receive some benefit,
but if they fail,
the disaster will fall upon others."
"Shì Shuō"
Zhī Xīng
King Hàn captured Xiàng Jí,
Wáng Líng led his troops to join Hàn,
Jí took Líng's mother and placed her in the army,
when Líng's envoy arrived, she sat facing east,
Líng's mother was intended to be used to summon Líng,
Líng's mother privately sent off the envoy, saying:
"I ask you to tell Líng for this old woman,
serve King Hàn well.
King Hàn is a virtuous man,
do not, because of this old woman, hold divided loyalties,
I will send off the envoy with my death."
Then she fell on her sword and died,
King Xiàng angrily boiled Líng's mother,
ultimately, Líng followed King Hàn to stabilize the empire.
"Book of Hàn"
Húshēng Diāohú
Gu Āng from Kuàijī lost his father in his youth,
and served his mother with utmost filial piety.
His mother was fond of eating wild rice seeds,
so he often led his children to personally gather them.
Returning home, he channeled water and dug streams,
planting it himself to provide for her.
Whenever there was surplus stored,
and as his home was near Tài Lake,
wild rice later grew naturally in the lake,
with no other weeds remaining.
Insects and birds dared not approach the area,
thus enabling him to use it for her sustenance.
The commandery and county honored his household.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Diagram of Gānquán
Jīn Mìdī's mother educated her two sons,
with proper methods and discipline,
which the emperor heard of and praised.
When the mother fell ill and died,
an imperial decree ordered her portrait painted in the Gānquán Palace,
inscribed with the words:
"The Yānzhī of the Tu King."
Mìdī, who tended horses in the imperial park,
would lead his horses past it,
and upon seeing the portrait, he would bow before it, weeping.
From the "Book of Hàn"
Asked about the wrongful convictions he had overturned
When Juàn Bùyí served as the Metropolitan Governor,
he would return from his tours of the counties where he reviewed prisoners' cases,
and his mother would always ask if he had exonerated anyone,
and how many lives he had saved.
If he had exonerated many,
his mother would smile joyfully and prepare food and drink,
acting differently than usual.
If there were none released,
his mother would be angry and refuse to eat.
Therefore, when Juàn Bùyí served as an official,
he was strict but not cruel.
"Basic Biography"
Yán Yù
Yán Yánnián governed Hénán,
employing cruel punishments and favoring executions.
His paternal aunt repeatedly reproached Yánnián,
saying, "Heaven, earth, and the divine spirits
deem it unacceptable for a man to kill excessively.
I never expected in my old age to witness my robust nephew face execution.
Go away now,
return east to clean the family gravesite."
She then left and returned to her commandery.
Over a year later, he was executed in the marketplace.
The people of Dōnghǎi all esteemed his mother as wise.
Yánnián and his brothers, five in total,
all attained high official positions,
earning their mother in Dōnghǎi the nickname "Mother Yán of Ten Thousand Bushels."
From "The Main Biography."
Alternative Names
The neighbor's mother died,
but her son did not cry sorrowfully.
The son from the western house saw this,
and upon returning told his mother:
"Why do you hesitate to die quickly?
I will certainly mourn and weep for you."
Huáinánzǐ
In Jiāng-Huái region, mother is called shè.
Annotation
Jiāng-Huái
region calls mother tí,
in Shǔ, mother is called jiě.
Shuōwén
In Qí, people call mother mí.
Miscellaneous
In Wú custom, mother is called mǔ,
in Huáinán, mother is called rǎn.
Jíyùn
Kill the sacrificial ox and offer the son
During Wáng Mǎng's time, Lǚ Mǔ's son from Lángyá served as a county official.
He was wronged by the magistrate,
so he killed his mother and distributed the family wealth,
using it to purchase wine, bows, and crossbows.
Secretly, he generously treated impoverished young men,
gathering over a hundred followers.
They then attacked Hǎiqū County,
killed the magistrate,
and offered sacrifices at his mother's tomb.
Afterward, they went to sea and became pirates,
with their numbers gradually swelling to tens of thousands.
(From the Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Governance)
Quán Yì
Liáoxī Governor Zhào Bāo, styled Wēiháo,
upon assuming office sent an envoy to fetch his mother, wife, and children.
They were captured by bandits,
who used them as hostages to attack the commandery.
Bāo wept bitterly and said to his mother:
"I had intended to support you with my humble salary,
never expecting to bring disaster upon you.
In the past I was your son,
but now I am a servant of the sovereign.
Duty forbids me to prioritize personal affection."
His mother called to him from afar:
"Wēiháo,
every person has their own destiny.
How can you care for me at the cost of loyalty and righteousness?
In ancient times, Wáng Líng's mother faced the Hàn court,
and made him draw his sword to strengthen his resolve.
You must exert yourself!"
Bāo then engaged the bandits in battle,
and both his mother and wife perished.
After burying them, Bāo said:
"To evade difficulty while receiving official salary is not loyalty;
to cause one's mother's death to preserve righteousness is not filial piety."
He vomited blood and died.
From the History of the Later Hàn
Encountering Mother
Bù Yóuzhāng from Rǔnán lost his mother at a young age,
and when he became a county magistrate,
he encountered his mother in Línhuái Commandery,
at Qǔlǜ City.
His fine horse hesitated and paced,
the light carriage refused to advance.
He looked around and inquired about an ailing elderly woman,
who turned out to be his mother.
Truly, his sincere wish, long held in his heart and hidden in the depths,
was moved and manifested by a clear sign.
From the "Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
He was made to recite the Classic of Filial Piety.
Qiú Lǎn, whose courtesy name was Jìzhì,
served as the chief of Yángsuì post in the county.
He was fond of educating and transforming people.
Chén Yuán was wicked and unfilial,
and his mother went to Lǎn to speak about Yuán.
Lǎn summoned Yuán,
reproached and admonished him,
using the principles of a son's duty,
and gave him a copy of the "Classic of Filial Piety" to study and recite.
Yuán deeply repented and reformed,
going to his mother's bedside to apologize, saying:
"I was orphaned at a young age,
and was spoiled by my mother.
As the proverb says:
'An orphaned calf butts the udder,
a spoiled child curses his mother.'
I beg to reform myself from now on."
Mother and son faced each other and wept,
whereupon Yuán then cultivated filial piety,
and later became an exemplary scholar.
"Xiè Chéng's Book"
Bending for family
In his youth, Máo Yì of Lújiāng was poor,
but was renowned for his filial conduct.
Zhāng Fèng of Nányáng, admiring his reputation,
went to visit him.
Just as they had sat down, an official dispatch arrived,
appointing Yì as Acting Magistrate of Ānyáng.
Yì took the dispatch and went inside,
his joy showing in his face and voice.
Fèng was a man of high ideals,
and inwardly looked down on this,
regretting his visit.
He firmly declined to stay and left.
Later, when Yì's mother died,
he observed the mourning period according to regulations,
declined an appointment from the central government to serve as a county magistrate,
and in all his actions strictly adhered to ritual propriety.
Later, when he was recommended as a Virtuous and Excellent candidate
and a government carriage was sent to summon him,
he ultimately did not go.
Zhāng Fèng sighed and said:
"Indeed, one cannot fathom a worthy man.
His joy in those days was because he had to bend his principles for his parent's sake.
This is probably what is called 'when the family is poor and the parent old,
one does not choose one's office when taking a post.'"
"Preface to the Biographies of Liú Píng and Others"
Corrupt Official Buries Mother Alive
Yǐngchuān's Zhēn Shào flattered and attached himself to Liáng Jì, becoming the magistrate of Yè.
A fellow candidate who had offended Liáng Jì,
fled to seek refuge with Shào.
Shào pretended to take him in but secretly reported him to Liáng Jì.
Liáng Jì immediately captured and killed him.
When Shào was due to be promoted to prefectural governor,
his mother happened to pass away.
Shào temporarily buried her body in the stable,
first accepted the appointment,
and then announced the funeral.
When Shào returned to Luòyáng,
Lǐ Xiè encountered him on the road.
He ordered his soldiers to throw Shào's carriage into the ditch,
and beat him indiscriminately with whips.
He then wrote in large characters on a cloth attached to Shào's back:
"Flatters the powerful and betrays friends,
greedy for office and buries his mother."
He then submitted a full report of the incident,
and Shào was dismissed from office and barred from government service for life.
From the "History of the Later Hàn."
Your Excellency
During Emperor Huán's reign, there was a great persecution of the partisans.
Fàn Pāng went to prison.
His mother came to bid him farewell,
and Pāng said to his mother:
"Zhòngbó is filial and respectful,
and can sufficiently provide for you.
I shall follow Lóngshū Jūn to the netherworld,
so the living and the dead each have their proper place.
I only ask you, Mother, to sever the unbearable bond of affection,
and not increase your grief."
His mother replied:
"You now stand side by side in reputation with Lǐ and Dù,
what regret can there be in death?
Since you already have a good name,
and still seek long life as well—
can both be obtained together?"
Pāng knelt to receive her teaching,
bowed twice, and took his leave.
End
Chicken Offering
Máo Róng, whose courtesy name was Jìwěi,
was encountered by Guō Línzōng while traveling.
Guō requested to lodge overnight.
The next morning, Máo killed a chicken to prepare a meal.
Guō assumed it was prepared for him,
but it was instead served to Máo's mother,
while Máo himself ate plain vegetables with his guest.
Guō rose and bowed to him, saying:
"How virtuous you are!"
He then encouraged Máo to pursue studies,
and eventually Máo achieved moral excellence.
From "The Biography of Guō Línzōng"
Placing objects in a bottle
Lord Cáo ordered Lù Cuì to draft a false accusation against Kǒng Róng, stating that previously,
he had spoken recklessly with the commoner Mí Héng:
"What connection should there be
between father and son?
Considering its original intent,
it arises merely from lust.
As for the son's relation to the mother,
what is it again?
It is like placing an object in a vase—
once it comes out, they separate."
"Biography of Kǒng Róng"
Isolated
In the past, there was a man from Chángshā named Wáng,
who went to the capital during the late Hàn dynasty as an official reporter,
but then Wú and Wèi became separated,
and he remained in the northern state,
where he remarried and had a son named Chāng.
After his death, his son Chāng became the Chancellor of Dōngpíng,
and only then learned that his mother in Wú had passed away.
He became deeply attached and burdened by grief,
and could no longer attend to his official duties.
"History of the Northern Dynasties: Biography of Suí Liú Xǔ"
Sìzhēn
Qín Yīng, wife of Nánzhèng's Yáng Xiàng,
daughter of the Grand Herald Liú Jùgōng, had
four sons and two daughters.
After Xiàng's death, she educated the six children,
ensuring every action followed rules and standards.
When the eldest son Yuánzhēn returned drunk from an outing,
his mother refused to see him for ten days,
saying:
"If you behave like this while I'm still here,
how will you lead your siblings after I'm gone?"
Yuánzhēn kowtowed and apologized for his mistake.
The second son Zhòngzhēn asked his mother to host guests,
but when they arrived,
none were virtuous.
His mother angrily reprimanded him,
so Zhòngzhēn reformed his conduct,
befriending worthy individuals,
and the brothers became renowned scholars.
Tài Yīng's teachings
extended through three generations to four sons,
whose talent and official ranks surpassed their ancestors.
Thus contemporaries composed a rhyme:
"Three Míaos cease,
four Zhēns rise again."
Huáyáng Zhì
Lìng Dé
Dù Tàijī, a native of Nánzhèng,
was the wife of Zhào Xuān,
bearing seven sons and seven daughters.
Among them, Yuánguī and Zhìguī showed promise,
while the other five all possessed admirable virtues.
Her method of educating her sons was as follows:
"The nature of ordinary people
can be elevated or degraded,
depending on their self-restraint.
If indulged without restraint, they will fall into wickedness.
In ancient times, Xīmén Bào wore a leather girdle to remind himself to be patient,
while Fúzǐ Jiàn wore a taut string to urge himself to be diligent.
Thus they were able to transform their inherent tendencies
and become renowned scholars of the world."
Later, all seven sons received official appointments through recommendations and inspections, governing provinces and commanding commanderies.
The Grand Administrator of Hànzhōng
and the Magistrate of Nánzhèng often
participated in the annual final examinations with the seven sons.
When reporting on administrative affairs, they all showed due respect,
while Tàijī observed the rituals befitting a mother and grandmother.
End
Heart and mind in disarray
While the First Sovereign was at Fán,
he heard that Liú Cóng had surrendered to Lord Cáo,
so he led his followers southward.
Zhūgě Liàng and Xú Shù accompanied him, but they were pursued by Lord Cáo’s forces,
who captured Shù’s mother.
Shù then took leave of the First Sovereign and, pointing to his heart, said:
“My desire to assist you, General, in achieving the imperial enterprise
was rooted in this square inch of land [i.e., my heart].
Now that I have lost my aged mother,
my heart is in turmoil,
and I can be of no further use.
I beg to take my leave from here.”
Thereupon he went to Lord Cáo.
(Records of Shǔ)
Yuǎnzhì
Jiāng Wéi was a native of Tiānshuǐ.
After he defected to Shǔ,
he became separated from his mother.
Someone made his mother write a letter by hand, summoning Wéi to rebel,
and sent "dāngguī" (Chinese angelica) as a metaphor for his return.
Wéi replied:
"With a hundred qǐng of fine fields,
one does not care for a single mǔ.
I only have lofty ambitions,
not any intention to return."
In the end, Wéi could not avoid his fate.
Sūn Shèng's Miscellaneous Records, Sòng "Treatise on the Five Elements"
No Burden
Wáng Jīng, styled Yànwěi, was poor in his youth,
but rose to the rank of two thousand bushels.
His mother said to him:
"You were originally the son of a poor family,
yet you've attained the rank of two thousand bushels.
Isn't this enough to stop now?"
Wáng Jīng did not follow this advice and became a Minister.
He assisted Wei and was not loyal to Jin,
whereupon he wept and bid farewell to his mother, saying:
"Because I did not follow your instruction,
I have come to this day."
His mother showed no trace of sorrow,
and said to him:
"As a son, be filial;
as a minister, be loyal.
With both filial piety and loyalty,
how have you failed me?"
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Making a large quilt
Wújiāng Xià Mèngzōng in his youth traveled to study,
and lived together with his classmates.
His mother made him a twelve-panel quilt.
A neighboring mother found it strange,
and asked his mother about it.
She replied:
"My son has no exceptional virtues,
and I fear his companions may not care for him.
Therefore, I made a large quilt to accommodate poor students to sleep,
hoping he might hear the words of gentlemen."
From "Biographies of Exemplary Women"
Holding the Emblem of Authority to Serve His Mother
Jìn Rǔnán Wáng Sīmǎ Liàng's mother, Fú Tàifēi, once had a minor illness.
She performed an ablution ceremony in the Luòshuǐ River.
Liàng and his two brothers accompanied her,
all holding ceremonial banners with musicians playing.
Their splendor shook the banks of the Luòshuǐ.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn ascended the Língyún Tower,
gazed upon the scene, and said:
"Fú Tàifēi can indeed be called wealthy and noble."
(From "The Main Biography")
Carrying his mother on his back
Initially, Pān Yuè's mother admonished him with the principle of knowing when to stop,
but when he was captured by Sūn Xiù,
he bid farewell to his mother, saying he had failed her.
From Wáng Yǐn's History of the Jìn Dynasty.
tearing off his sleeve in determination
Wēn Gōng initially accepted the appointment from Minister over the Masses Liú Kūn,
who sent him to urge the advancement of the imperial cause.
His mother, Madame Cuī, firmly detained him,
but Wén Qiáo tore off his robe and departed.
Even after achieving high status and honor, his local rank was still not elevated,
and every bestowal of rank required an imperial edict.
In the *Shìshuō*,
when Emperor Yuán ascended the throne,
he appointed Wén Qiáo as a Gentleman Cavalier Attendant.
Wén Qiáo, because his mother had passed away,
was unable to reach her due to the bandits,
and went to the gate to mourn her burial.
He declined the edict, saying:
"Qiáo, because the burial has not taken place,
and court discussions also have considerable disagreements,
therefore does not accept the appointment.
Let the eight high officials deliberate,
and I will mediate their differences."
Annotation
Looking around in all directions
Fú Biǎo,
the nephew of Fú Lǎng,
resided in Ānchéng Commandery.

Shěn Yōuzhī did not punish him

Later, when she was promised return to the court,

married Línjìn the Eldest Princess, the twelfth daughter of Emperor Míng,

Lǐ Jǐngràng, courtesy name Hòuyǐ,

In their early days of poverty,
while repairing a wall, they uncovered a hoard of coins.
A young servant rushed to inform the mother, who said:

Dù Gāo had a profoundly filial nature.
His father, a minor official in Héběi, had passed away,
and his mother was not the principal wife.
After the chaos of war, her whereabouts were unknown.
It happened that his cousin Dù Jiān served as a judicial officer in Zélù,
and was once hearing a case at his private residence.
An elderly woman was presenting her defense
when she saw Dù Gāo coming and going.
She secretly said to someone:
"This young man's appearance resembles my son."
Upon questioning her,
she turned out to be Dù Gāo's mother.
From then on, he welcomed her back and attended to her.
He also went to search for his ancestors' graves,
but the elders in the town had all passed away,
and their location was unknown.
Staying at a Buddhist temple,
he wept sorrowfully day and night.
Suddenly, beneath the soot on a temple pillar,
he noticed several lines of writing.
Wiping it clean to look,
it was his father's handwriting,
saying:
"If my descendants seek my grave,
they should inquire at a certain village household."
Dù Gāo went weeping to the village,
where an old man over eighty years old
pointed out the burial mound.
Thus, he was able to retrieve the remains for proper burial.
Dù Gāo's official career reached the position of Minister of Works before retirement.

often meditating in the mountains.

a woman came seeking shelter,
with graceful and charming appearance,
wearing bright clothing.
She claimed to be a celestial woman,
sent by heaven due to Huìwéi's virtue,
to offer him comfort.

she tried to persuade him to change his mind.

with a single-minded focus,

Cuī Yuánhuī served as Vice Director of the Bureau of Provisions,
and his mother once admonished him, saying:
"In the past, I heard from my maternal cousin, Tun Tian Langzhong Xīn Yuánlǚ:
'When sons take up official posts,
if someone comes saying they are impoverished and unable to survive,
this is good news;
if we hear their assets are abundant,
their clothes and horses luxurious,
this is bad news.'
I have always valued these words,
considering them a true saying.
Recently, I've seen many among relatives and in-laws who serve as officials
bringing money and goods to their parents.
The parents only know to rejoice,
never asking where these things come from.
If they are surplus from official salaries,
that is indeed a good thing.
But if obtained improperly,
how is this different from theft?
Even without major punishment,
wouldn't one feel inner shame?
The mother who refused the gift of pickled fish
did so for this reason.
You now enjoy an official salary,
your glory and splendor are already ample.
If you cannot be loyal and honest,
how can you face heaven and tread earth?
Confucius said:
'Even if one provides three sacrificial animals daily,
it still does not constitute filial piety.'
He also said:
'Parents worry only about their children's illnesses,'
so you should especially cultivate yourself and maintain purity.
Do not forget my meaning here."
Yuánhuī followed his mother's teachings
and was praised for his integrity and diligence.

Different breath
There was a man named Shěn Xǐ who had lost his mother.
Hearing a beggar singing beneath his gate, he was moved to sorrow,
his emotions showing on his face.
He told the gatekeeper to admit the singing beggar,
then, coming to himself, he questioned her,
saying:
"What has brought you to beg?"
When he spoke with her,
he found she was his mother.
Thus, between parents and children,
and children and parents,
they are one body divided into two,
sharing the same vital energy though breathing separately,
like flowers and fruits on plants and trees,
or the roots and heartwood of a tree.
Though in different places, they are interconnected.
Their hidden feelings reach each other,
they relieve each other's pain and sickness,
and share each other's worries and thoughts.
In life, they delight in each other;
in death, they mourn for each other.
This is what is called the bond of flesh and blood.
The spirit emerges from thought and responds from the heart.
When two essences connect,
is there any need for words?"
