When King Xuān went on an excursion,
Jífǔ accompanied him.
Bó Qí composed a song to move his father,
and King Xuān, upon hearing it, said:
"Is this the lament of an exiled son?"
Jífǔ then searched for Bó Qí and, realizing the truth,
shot and killed his wife.
From "Qín Cǎo"
Yáng Shì
Chén Yuán, styled Zǐyuán,
was the crown prince of Marquis Chén.
At seven years old, he lost his mother.
His father remarried a woman of the Zhōu family,
who had a son named Zhāo.
Lady Zhōu slandered Yuán,
and the Marquis intended to kill Yuán.
Zhāo wished to die first,
but Yuán would not allow it.
Leading a white sheep, he swore an oath:
"If I am filial, let the sheep's blood flow upward for thirteen feet."
It happened just as the oath stated.
Later, Lady Zhōu slandered him again,
enraging the Marquis,
who ordered Yuán to commit suicide.
Yuán threw himself into the Liáo River,
where a large fish carried him on its back.
Yuán said,
"I am a guilty man."
The fish then departed.
Zhāo arrived later
and inquired of the fishermen,
who said Yuán had drowned himself.
Zhāo fainted for a long time,
then said,
"He was my brother."
He also threw himself into the river and died.
From Xiāo Guǎngjì's "Biographies of Filial Sons"
Sincerity Moves
Yìng Shèn, styled Zhònghuá,
served as the Chancellor of Dōngpíng.
He attended to his stepmother with utmost filial piety,
and his sincere devotion evoked a spiritual response:
a catalpa tree grew on the roof in front of the hall,
which was then transplanted to the government courtyard,
where it flourished and grew tall.
From "Dōngguān Hànjì".
Sweeping the House
Xuē Bāo was diligent in study and steadfast in conduct.
After his mother passed away,
he became known for his exceptional filial piety.
His father remarried,
and under the influence of his stepmother, ordered Xuē Bāo to leave home.
Bāo wept day and night,
unable to bring himself to depart,
until he was beaten with a stick.
Compelled by circumstances, he built a hut outside the house,
entering at dawn to sweep and clean.
His father grew angry
and drove him away again,
so he then built a hut by the village gate,
yet never ceased his morning and evening duties.
After over a year had passed,
his father and stepmother felt ashamed and allowed him to return home.
(from "Records of Former Worthies of Rǔnán")
Weaving sandals
At the age of twelve or thirteen, Zhái Fāngjìn lost his father.
He served as a minor clerk in the prefect's office,
but due to illness, he returned home.
Bidding farewell to his stepmother,
he intended to travel west to the capital to study the classics.
His mother, pitying his youth,
accompanied him to the capital,
where she wove sandals to support Fāngjìn.
After more than ten years of accumulation, he rose to the position of chancellor,
and his mother was still alive.
From the "Book of Hàn."
Remove the Ladder
Liú Biǎo's sons were named Qí and Cóng.
Initially, Biǎo favored Qí because his appearance resembled his own,
but later, after arranging for Cóng to marry the niece of his subsequent wife, Lady Cài,
he came to favor Cóng and dislike Qí.
Slanderous remarks were heard by Biǎo daily,
and as Biǎo was infatuated with his later wife,
he often believed and accepted them.
Moreover, his brother-in-law Cài Mào, his nephew, and Zhāng Yǔn all enjoyed Biǎo's favor,
and they were on good terms with Cóng,
leaving Qí feeling uneasy.
《Hòu Hàn》
Qí repeatedly sought to discuss strategies for his own safety with Zhūgě Liàng,
but Liàng consistently refused and did not offer any plans.
Qí then took Liàng on a tour of the rear garden,
and while they were drinking together upstairs,
he had the ladder removed,
and said to Liàng:
"Today, we are neither reaching the sky above
nor touching the ground below.
Words leave my mouth
and enter your ears alone.
Can you speak now?"
Liàng replied:
"Have you not heard of Shēnshēng, who was in danger while remaining inside,
and Chóng'ěr, who found safety by staying abroad?"
Qí understood the implication,
and secretly planned to leave.
《Shǔ Zhì》
The yellow sparrow enters the tent.
Wáng Xiáng, courtesy name Xiūzhēng,
was a native of Lángyá.
He was extremely filial.
His stepmother, Madame Zhū, was unkind,
causing him to lose his father's favor,
who ordered him to clean the cowshed.
Wáng Xiáng remained ever more respectful.
When his parents were ill,
he would not undress to sleep.
His mother ordered him to guard the ripening fruit,
and during wind and rain, he would embrace the trees and weep.
Once, his mother craved roasted yellow sparrows,
when suddenly dozens of yellow sparrows flew into the tent,
which he then offered to her.
"Book of Jìn"
Kòu Bīng catches a fish
Wáng Yán was nine years old when he lost his mother,
and his filial piety became well-known.
His stepmother, Madame Bǔ, treated him harshly and unfairly,
yet Yán served her with even greater respect and care.
Bǔ often gave him worn-out rushes and hemp to make clothes,
but Yán knew and said nothing.
In winter, Bǔ beat him until he bled,
then ordered him to fetch live fish.
Yán wept bitterly while breaking the ice and managed to obtain the fish for her.
Bǔ then came to a realization,
and cared for him as if he were her own son.
"Chronicles of the Thirty Kingdoms"
Dreaming of a Tiger and Escaping Danger
Héng Nóng, courtesy name Piāoqīng,
was from Dōngpíng.
He lost his father in his youth,
yet served his stepmother with utmost filial piety.
Once while lodging at another residence,
during a night of thunder and rain,
he repeatedly dreamed of a tiger biting his feet.
Nóng called his wife and they went out into the courtyard,
where he kowtowed three times.
Suddenly the house collapsed,
crushing to death over three hundred people,
yet only Héng Nóng and his wife were spared.
From "In Search of the Supernatural"
Yìzi
The Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Yuán Yí recommended Guō Dàoshì of Kuàijī for his utmost filial piety in serving his stepmother.
His family was poor when a child was born,
and he feared he could not raise it.
He said to his wife:
"By harming kindness to fulfill filial duty,
I shall have no regrets."
Thereupon he buried the child alive.
From Péi Zǐyě's "Brief Records"
Indistinguishable Brothers
Gāo Qiānzhī, styled Xiàoràng,
was renowned for his filial piety in serving his stepmother Lǐ,
who also raised him with greater care than her own children.
No one could distinguish the differences in origin among the brothers,
and commentators esteemed both of them.
"Book of Wèi"
A spring emerged.
Sòng Sīlǐ, styled Guòtíng,
was renowned for his filial piety towards his stepmother.
He served as the chief registrar of Xiāo County.
During a drought, wells and ponds dried up,
and his mother, frail and ill, could only tolerate spring water.
Sīlǐ, anxious and fearful, prayed fervently,
when suddenly a spring appeared in the courtyard,
its water sweet,
and never ran dry even in cold weather.
The county's people marveled at this,
and the county lieutenant Liǔ Huǎng engraved a stone to commemorate the miracle.
From the "Book of Táng."
For my younger brother, I drove the donkey.
Lú Cāo, styled Ānjié,
was a person from Hédōng.
He was known for his filial piety in serving his stepmother, Madame Zhāng.
Madame Zhāng had three sons of her own,
and often ordered Cāo to perform chores and cook for the three sons.
Cāo carried out the chores without considering them laborious.
Madame Zhāng taught her sons to study,
and whenever the three sons went out,
she commanded Cāo to follow the donkey to urge it along,
holding the whip and leading the rope like a servant.
The three sons once said to him:
"How does following a donkey compare to our studying?"
Cāo replied:
"It is because I do not study that I chase the donkey."
He was constantly insulted and scolded by the three sons,
and Cāo would weep,
bowing to appease them.
Later, he passed the imperial examination with honors in the Mingjīng category.
"Shǐ Xì"
Shouted "Kill!"
Although Ān Chóngróng of the Five Dynasties was a military man, he understood judicial matters.
A couple brought a lawsuit against their son for being unfilial.
Chóngróng handed a sword,
giving it to the father to kill him.
The father wept and could not bear to do it.
The wife scolded from the side,
snatched the sword from the father, and chased him away.
Upon inquiry, it was found that she was the stepmother.
Chóngróng scolded the mother and drove her out,
then had her killed later.
Brothers
Elder brother,
means huāng.
Huāng,
means great.
Therefore, people from Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu call elder brother huāng.
Younger brother,
means sequence,
born in succession.
From "Shìmíng"
Favored Younger Brother
Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng's younger brother Gōngshū Duàn resided in Jīng,
and was called the Grand Young Master of the Capital City.
Jì Zhòng remonstrated, saying:
"A city wall exceeding a hundred zhì in length
is a harm to the state.
Do not let it grow and spread.
Even creeping weeds cannot be eradicated once they spread,
how much more so for Your Lordship's favored younger brother?"
To my younger brother
Duke Mù of Sòng fell ill,
summoned Grand Marshal Kǒngfù and entrusted Duke Shāng to him,
saying:
"The former ruler passed over Yíyí and established me,
which I have not dared to forget.
If by your grace I can preserve my head until death and the former ruler asks about it,
what words shall I have to answer regarding Yíyí?
I beg you to support him,
to preside over the altars of soil and grain,
and even in death I shall have no regrets."
Kǒngfù replied:
"The ministers wish to support Féng."
The duke said:
"That will not do.
The former ruler considered me worthy,
and set me to preside over the altars of soil and grain.
If I were to abandon virtue and not yield,
this would nullify the former ruler's selection.
How can it be called worthy to display and illuminate the former ruler's excellent virtue?
Can we not strive for this, my son?
Do not
nullify the former
ruler's achievement."
He sent his son Féng to reside in Zhèng.
On the Gēngchén day of the eighth month, Duke Mù of Sòng died,
and Duke Shāng ascended the throne.
The gentleman says: Duke Xuān of Sòng may be said to have known men well.
He established Duke Mù,
and his own son enjoyed it—his command was according to righteousness.
Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Yǐn third year.
Yì Sì
After Wú Zhūfán had completed the mourning period,
he intended to establish Jì Zhá as his successor.
Jì Zhá declined, saying:
"At the death of Cáo Xuāngōng,
the feudal lords and the people of Cáo intended to establish Zǐ Zāng,
but Zǐ Zāng withdrew from it,
thus enabling another to become the ruler of Cáo.
The gentleman says he was able to maintain his integrity.
You are the rightful heir,
who would dare to oppose this?
To hold the state is not consistent with my principles.
Although I, Zhá, am without talent,
I wish to follow the example of Zǐ Zāng,
so as not to fail in maintaining my integrity."
They insisted on establishing him,
but he abandoned his home and took up farming,
so they finally left him alone.
(Xiānggōng 14th year)
Family Head
Lord Zhū resided in Táo,
where his youngest son was born.
When the youngest son reached adulthood,
Lord Zhū's middle son killed someone,
was imprisoned in Chǔ,
and Lord Zhū instructed his youngest brother to visit him.
He then packed a thousand yì of gold,
placed it in coarse containers,
loaded it onto an ox cart,
and prepared to send his youngest son.
The eldest son requested to go instead,
but Lord Zhū refused.
The eldest son said:
"In a family, the eldest son is the steward.
Now that my younger brother has committed a crime,
if you, Father, do not send me
but instead send the youngest brother,
it shows I am unworthy."
He threatened to kill himself,
and his mother pleaded on his behalf.
Lord Zhū relented.
The eldest son ultimately returned with his brother's corpse.
His mother and the townspeople all mourned deeply,
but Lord Zhū alone laughed and said:
"I always knew he would cause his brother's death.
It is not that he did not love his brother,
but that he could not bear to part with things.
He grew up with me
and experienced the hardships of making a living,
so he values wealth too much.
As for the youngest son,
he was born into wealth,
rode in solid carriages,
and chased clever hares with fine dogs—
how could he know where wealth comes from?
Thus, he easily parts with it.
The reason I originally wanted to send the youngest son
was precisely because he could abandon wealth.
But the elder son could not,
so he ended up causing his brother's death.
This is the logic of the matter,
and there is no need for grief.
Day and night, I have been expecting the arrival of his corpse."
"Yuè Family Chronicles"
Zhōu Shùmǔ
When Zǐliǔ's mother died,
Zǐshuò requested to arrange the funeral expenses,
Zǐliǔ said:
"How can I manage it?"
Shuò said:
"Please sell our stepmother."
Zǐliǔ said:
"How could that be?
To sell another's mother to bury one's own mother,
is not permissible."
After the burial,
Zǐshuò wished to use the leftover funeral funds for sacrificial vessels,
Zǐliǔ said:
"No.
I have heard that
a nobleman does not profit from mourning,
let us distribute it among our impoverished brothers."
"Tángōng"
It is for mourning.
A man from Chéng had an elder brother who died,
but he did not observe mourning for him.
Upon hearing that Zǐgāo was to become the magistrate of Chéng,
he then began to observe mourning.
The people of Chéng remarked:
"The silkworm spins, yet the crab provides the basket;
the wasp dons a cap, yet the cicada bears the tassels;
the elder brother dies, yet it is for Zǐgāo that he dons mourning."
End
Song of Cloth and Grain
Huáinán Lìwáng Cháng,
the younger son of Gāozǔ,
committed a crime,
and Emperor Wén exiled him to Shǔ,
where he died from refusing to eat,
and the people composed a song about Huáinán King,
saying:
"Even a foot of cloth can be sewn together,
even a peck of grain can be pounded,
yet two brothers,
cannot tolerate each other."
Hàn Shū
records that Huáinán returned to his state with a yellow-canopied carriage,
and with a left banner proclaimed himself the Eastern Emperor,
but was exiled to Yándào in Shǔ and died at Yōng.
Mǐn posthumously enfeoffed his four sons as marquises,
and at that time the people sang:
"Even a foot of silk is beautifully smooth,
even a liter of grain fills one up,
yet two brothers,
cannot tolerate each other."
Huáinán Xù
Twins
General Huò's wife gave birth to twins,
raising the question of who should be considered the elder brother.
Some said the firstborn should be the elder brother,
and the later-born the younger brother,
even though they were born on the same day,
it was appropriate to consider the firstborn as the elder brother.
Others argued that the one positioned above should be the elder brother,
and the one below should be the younger brother.
The one below was born first,
so the firstborn should now be considered the younger brother.
In the past, Huò Guāng heard of this and said:
"Long ago, King Zǔ Jiǎ of the Yīn dynasty had twins,
named Yín and Liáng.
Yín was born on a mǎo day,
and Liáng on a sì day,
thus Yín was considered the elder brother,
and Liáng the younger brother.
If the one positioned above were to be considered the elder brother,
Yín would then be the younger brother.
Lord Xǔ Lí Zhuāng had twin daughters,
named Jué and Mào.
The Chǔ official Táng Lè had twins,
one boy and one girl.
The boy was named Zhēn Fū,
the girl Qióng Huá.
In all these cases, the firstborn was considered the elder.
In more recent times, Zhèng Chāng, Xī Wéncháng, and Qiàn each had twin sons,
Shèng Gōng had twin daughters,
and Lǐ Lí had a son and a daughter.
All regarded the firstborn as the elder.
Thus, the Huò family also considered the firstborn as the elder brother."
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Similarity
There were brothers named Zhāng Bóxié and Zhòngxié,
whose appearances were extremely similar.
When Zhòngxié's wife had just finished applying her makeup,
she suddenly saw Bóxié
and playfully asked him:
"How does my new makeup look today?"
Bóxié responded to her:
"I am Bóxié."
The wife, embarrassed, hurried away to avoid him.
Shortly after, she saw Bóxié again,
but still thinking it was Zhòngxié,
called out to him once more:
"Earlier I made a big mistake,
mistaking Bóxié for you."
Bóxié said:
"I am indeed Bóxié."
From "Fēngsú Tōng":
Lǐ Dēng of Jìběi served as an administrative clerk.
When he fell ill and obtained leave to return home,
he felt his appearance wasn't sufficiently sickly,
so he told his twin brother:
"Since we brothers look so alike that people can't tell us apart,
you should pretend to be sick and take my place at the government office."
Later generations said this caused problems when people met after long separations.
The younger brother became very angry and said:
"You're from Jìběi and yet you want me to do this for you?"
Dòu Déxiōng
Chénliú Prefecture Governor Tàishān Wú Wénzhāng was orphaned young,
living in an age of sorrow and decline,
he was separated from his elder brother Bówǔ.
After being apart for twenty years,
they met at the Xiàpī market,
where they argued and fought.
Bówǔ beat him,
and Wénzhāng wanted to strike back,
but his heart was filled with grief,
and his hand could not lift.
He found it very strange himself.
So he threw his staff to the ground,
and all the onlookers laughed at him.
Then they inquired of each other,
and realized they were brothers.
They held each other and wept,
and the onlookers said again:
"The elder brother can beat the younger, but the younger cannot retaliate against the elder.
What we laughed at earlier
was actually righteousness."
Above
Elder brother sits facing north.
Tián Fēn was enfeoffed as Marquis Wǔ'ān and appointed Chancellor.
He summoned guests for a drinking gathering.
His elder brother, the Marquis of Gài, faced north,
while Tián Fēn himself sat facing east,
believing that as the Chancellor of Hàn,
his dignity should not be compromised for his brother's sake,
and from this, he grew increasingly arrogant.
(Book of Hàn)
Yielding Property and Yielding Gold
The woman of Guǎnghàn,
was the wife of Rǔ Dūn.
They lived in a time of great wealth,
but the brothers were orphaned early.
The sister-in-law was greedy,
and begrudged Dūn the fields, houses, and over three million slaves he had inherited.
He yielded them all to his elder brother,
keeping only a few dozen acres of garden land for himself.
There he built a hut and farmed.
While tilling the soil, he unearthed a vessel of gold.
Dūn showed it to his wife, saying:
"We originally said we were yielding what belonged to our ancestors.
But does this not also belong to them?"
Dūn replied:
"This was indeed my intention."
So they carried the gold together to his elder brother and sister-in-law.
The sister-in-law initially thought her younger brother-in-law had come in poverty,
seeking to borrow money,
and showed displeasure on her face.
But when she saw the gold, she was delighted.
The elder brother, however, was moved with compassion and awakened to understanding.
He dismissed his wife and returned the gold.
Biographies of Exemplary Women
Great talent matures late.
Mǎ Yuán, styled Wényuān,
was a native of Màolíng in Fúfēng.
His three elder brothers, Mǎ Kuàng, Mǎ Yú, and Mǎ Yuán, all possessed talent and ability,
and during Wáng Mǎng's time, each held the rank of two thousand shi.
Mǎ Yuán was orphaned at the age of twelve,
yet from a young age, he harbored great ambitions.
His elder brothers found him extraordinary,
and though he once studied the "Qí Shī,"
he felt unable to confine himself to textual minutiae.
He thus bid farewell to Mǎ Kuàng, intending to farm and herd in a border commandery.
Kuàng said to him:
"Your great talent will mature late;
a skilled craftsman does not reveal his unfinished work.
Remain simple and follow your inclinations."
It happened that Kuàng passed away,
and Yuán observed a year of mourning,
never leaving the gravesite.
He respectfully served his widowed sister-in-law,
never entering her dwelling without his cap on.
"Later Biography"
Zhū Bó, styled Shūyáng,
could recite the "Shī" and "Shū" by age twelve.
He often visited Yuán's brother Kuàng,
wearing a square-collared robe
and walking with measured steps, his speech refined and elegant.
Yuán, who had only begun to learn writing, felt inadequate upon seeing him.
Kuàng, aware of his feelings,
poured wine to comfort Yuán, saying:
"Zhū Bó is a small vessel that matures quickly;
his wisdom ends here.
In the end, he will have to learn from you—do not be intimidated."
Bó never reached two thousand shi,
though Fúfēng recommended him to trial as magistrate of Wèichéng.
By the time Yuán became a general and was enfeoffed as a marquis,
Bó's position did not exceed that of a county magistrate.
Even after Yuán attained high status,
he often treated Bó with the familiarity of old favor, yet demeaned him.
Bó, however, drew closer personally.
When Yuán encountered slander,
only Bó remained loyal to the end.
"Records of the Eastern Pavilion"
Acting righteously
Dù Lín, styled Bóshān,
was erudite and well-informed,
renowned in his time as a profound scholar.
He initially served as a commandery official.
After Wáng Mǎng's downfall,
he sojourned in Héxī with Wèi Xiāo,
who deeply respected and treated him well.
Although constrained by Xiāo, Dù Lín never compromised his integrity.
When his younger brother Chéng passed away,
Xiāo permitted Lín to return for the funeral.
However, after sending him off, Xiāo regretted his decision
and dispatched assassin Yáng Xián to intercept and kill him at Lǒngzhǐ.
Xián observed Lín personally pushing a deer-drawn cart carrying his brother's coffin
and sighed, saying:
"In the present age,
who else acts with such righteousness?
Though I am but a petty man,
how could I bear to kill a righteous gentleman?"
Thereupon, he fled and disappeared.
(From the Book of the Later Hàn)
Abdicating the Throne
Dèng Biāo, styled Zhìbó,
was a native of Nányáng.
His father, Dèng Hán,
during the restoration under Emperor Guāngwǔ,
followed the campaign and was enfeoffed as a marquis for his merits.
Biāo cultivated filial conduct from a young age,
and disciplined his will towards purity and integrity.
He, along with Zōng Wǔbó, Zhái Jìngbó, Chén Suíbó, and Zhāng Dìbó from the same commandery, shared aspirations and were equally renowned,
known as the Five Bó of Nányáng.
Biāo, being the eldest son by the principal wife, was the heir.
When Dèng Hán passed away,
he was due to inherit the title,
but he yielded the fief to his younger half-brother, Dèng Fèng.
Emperor Míng esteemed his integrity,
and issued an edict granting permission.
Fèng thus succeeded to the title,
while Biāo served in provincial and commandery offices.
(From the "Records of the Eastern Pavilion")
Brother Shòuyí
Zhèng Jūn, whose courtesy name was Yú Zhòng,
was a native of Rènchéng.
He studied the "Book of Documents",
was fond of the teachings of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi,
was indifferent to fame and free from desires,
maintained purity and tranquility by self-restraint,
and did not aspire to official positions.
His elder brother Zhòng was a wandering knight in the county,
who frequently accepted gifts and bribes.
Jūn repeatedly admonished him to stop,
but he would not listen.
So Jūn left home to work elsewhere,
and after over a year, he had earned several tens of thousands of coins.
He returned and gave them to his brother,
saying:
"Money can be regained, and one can become an official again,
but if convicted of corruption, one will be discarded for life."
His brother was moved by these words,
and subsequently became honest and upright,
earning the reputation of a clean official.
self-flagellation
Miào Róng, courtesy name Yùgōng,
was orphaned in his youth,
with four brothers who all shared property and livelihood.
When each took a wife,
the younger brothers then sought to separate,
and there were frequent words of conflict.
Róng closed his door,
struck himself, and said:
"Miào Róng,
you cultivate yourself and act cautiously,
studying the ways of the sages,
intending to rectify social customs.
How can you fail to set your own family right?"
His brothers and their wives heard this,
all bowed their heads in apology, and thereafter practiced harmonious conduct.
(Book of the Later Hàn)
Brothers Sharing a Quilt
Jiāng Gōng, styled Bó Huái,
along with his two younger brothers Bó Hǎi and Jì Jiāng, were all renowned for their filial conduct.
Their fraternal affection was naturally profound,
and they often slept together.
When each took a wife,
the brothers remained attached to each other
and could not bear to sleep apart.
Only because the continuation of the family line necessitated it
did they take turns going to their wives' chambers.
Once, Gōng went with Jì Jiāng to visit the commandery,
and at night on the road they encountered robbers
who intended to kill them.
The brothers vied to die for each other,
so the bandits released them both,
merely seizing their clothes and belongings.
After arriving at the commandery,
people saw Gōng had no clothes
and wondered, asking the reason.
Gōng evaded with other words,
never mentioning the robbers.
When the robbers heard of this, they were moved and remorseful,
and later sought an audience to apologize,
returning the stolen goods.
Gōng did not accept them
but instead consoled and sent them away.
Diet without bias
Lǐ Quán, courtesy name Yuánjī,
was a native of Píngqiū.
In his youth, he was intelligent and wise,
with aspirations and virtuous conduct.
Quán's elder brother, Quán,
born of the former wife,
was deeply unloved by the stepmother,
who provided him with clothing and food inferior to Quán's.
At the age of five,
Quán noticed his own clothes were better than his brother's,
so he took them off and refused to wear them,
insisting that his brother receive the same,
and only then would he wear them.
Thus, his mother could no longer show favoritism.
As he grew older,
Quán inwardly supported his mother,
while outwardly respecting his brother,
so the household was harmonious and peaceful,
earning praise from the clan.
"Jiāng Wēi's Records of Chénliú"
Cutting the arm and scattering the bones
Chén Yè, styled Wénlǐ,
when his elder brother perished while crossing the sea,
there were fifty to sixty people who had met the same fate,
their flesh decomposed beyond recognition.
Chén Yè, raising his eyes to the august heavens and vowing to the earth, said:

Poison placed on the date stem
Emperor Wén of Wèi was jealous of his younger brother, the Prince of Rènchéng, for his valor and robust health.
Once, while they were playing chess in Empress Dowager Biàn's chamber and eating dates,
Emperor Wén placed poison on the stems of some dates.
He then selected the safe ones for himself to eat,
but the Prince, unaware of the plot,
ate the dates indiscriminately.
After he was poisoned,
the Empress Dowager sought water to save him,
but the Emperor had previously ordered his attendants to destroy all bottles and jars.
The Empress Dowager, running barefoot to the well, had nothing to draw water with,
and the Prince died shortly after.
When the Emperor later sought to harm the Prince of Dōng'ē,
the Empress Dowager said:
"You have already killed my Rènchéng,
you shall not kill my Dōng'ē as well."

Hé Qiào served as Junior Guardian and Regular Attendant in the Imperial Secretariat,
and was extremely frugal and stingy by nature.
His younger maternal brother Hé Yù had always been obscure,
and Hé Qiào looked down upon and insulted him,
considering him worthless.
In the remaining years, to substitute for his younger brother,
during the Tàiyuán era, there was a master who came from afar,
no one knew his origin.
He said that when a person's life is due to end,
if someone willingly substitutes for them, the deceased can be revived.
But if one forces others to seek substitution,
it will not last long either.
When people heard this,
they all considered it absurd and unfounded.
Wáng Zǐyóu
and Wáng Zǐjìng
were especially close and harmonious as brothers.
When Zǐjìng fell critically ill and was near death,
Zǐyóu said to him:
"My talent is not as great as my younger brother's,
and my official position is also obstructed.
I ask to use my remaining years to substitute for my brother."
The master said:
"For the living to substitute for the deceased,
one must have surplus years in their own lifespan,
to make up for what the deceased lacks.
Now that your worthy brother's life is due to end,
Your Lordship's allotted time is also about to be exhausted.
What is there to substitute?"
Zǐyóu previously had a back ailment.
When Zǐjìng's illness became critical,
he was constantly prevented from visiting.
Upon hearing of his brother's death, he clutched his chest in grief and lamentation,
unable to utter a single sound,
and his back immediately burst open.
Considering the master's words,
they proved credible and true.

Xiè Jǐngrén loved his third brother Hán but detested Shù.
Once he prepared a banquet for Emperor Wǔ of Sòng,
hoping the emperor would order Hán to join the table, but the emperor summoned Shù instead.
Shù knew this was not Jǐngrén's original intention,
and feared the emperor's command to join.
He urgently did not follow the emperor's summons,
but Jǐngrén sent for Shù, insisting he must arrive before the meal began.
When Jǐngrén fell ill,
Shù attended to him wholeheartedly.
He tasted all decoctions, medicines, and food before serving them,
never loosening his belt,
and went without washing or combing for dozens of days.
Jǐngrén felt deeply ashamed,
and their fraternal affection thus grew profound.
After Jǐngrén passed away,
Shù wailed in mourning beyond ritual norms.
Jǐngrén was stout and robust,
and several coffins prepared did not fit.
Shù, in sorrow and anxiety, personally selected one until he found a suitable one.

saying to the court officials:
"When the Jin dynasty pacified Wu,
they rejoiced in obtaining the two Lùs;
now as I campaign against the rebels,
I too have gained the two Zhōus."
When he arrived,
the honors shown him were exceedingly generous,
unmatched by any court minister.
The emperor...
Gathering in the hall to eat together
Yáng Bō, courtesy name Yuánqìng,
came from a family of pure and profound heritage,
all devoted to righteousness and deference.
The brothers served each other like father and son.
Bō was resolute and steadfast,
while Chūn and Jīn were reverent and humble.
When speaking with others, they referred to themselves by their given names.
The brothers gathered in the main hall each morning,
facing each other all day long,
never entering the inner quarters.
If there was a delicacy,
they would not eat unless all were assembled.
In the hall, curtains often served as partitions,
creating resting places
where they would occasionally recline,
then return to converse and laugh together.
When Chūn grew old and once returned drunk from elsewhere,
Jīn supported and attended him back to his room,
then pretended to sleep outside the door,
awaiting news of his well-being.
Though Chūn and Jīn were both over sixty and had ascended to high ministerial positions,
Jīn would still regularly inquire after Chūn.
Morning and evening, sons and nephews would line up below the steps;
if Chūn did not command them to sit,
Jīn would not dare to sit.
Whenever Chūn went out nearby and had not returned by sunset,
Jīn would not eat first;
only after Chūn's return would they dine together.
When eating, Jīn would personally hand him the spoon and chopsticks,
tasting each dish first.
Only when Chūn ordered him to eat
would he then eat.
When Jīn served as Minister of Works,
and his superior summoned his subordinates,
someone asked Jīn to seek an official post for him.
Jīn replied:
"This matter must be decided by my elder brother.
Why are you asking me?"
Earlier, when Jīn was in Sìzhōu
and Chūn was at the capital residence,
whenever there were seasonal delicacies,
Jīn would insist on sending them in sequence.
If they had not yet been sent,
he would not taste them first.
Whenever Chūn received what was sent,
he would weep over it.
(Book of Wèi)
White Brow
Mǎ Zǐjié and his two brothers were all well-versed in literature and history.
When Yáng Xiūzhī governed Xīyǎn, Zǐlián, Zǐshàng, and Zǐjié, along with various court officials, each composed poems
as gifts for Xiūzhī.
These were compiled into a collection with responses,
as the poem states:
"The three Mǎs are all white-browed talents."
Book of Northern Qí
The finest choice of the time
Wēn Dàyǎ, courtesy name Yànhóng,
was extremely filial by nature,
studious from a young age,
and renowned for his talent and eloquence.
During the Sui dynasty, he served in the Eastern Palace alongside Yán Sīlǔ,
while Yànbó (Wēn Yànhóng) and Sīlǔ's younger brother Mǐnchǔ held concurrent posts in the Palace Secretariat.
Yànbó and Yóuqín, younger brother of Mǐnchǔ, managed the imperial library's collation work.
The brothers from both families were considered outstanding figures of their time.
In their youth regarding scholarly achievements,
the Yán family excelled,
but later in official positions, the Wēn family achieved greater prominence.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Sān Fèng
Xuē Yuánjìng, together with Xuē Shōu and his cousin Xuē Déyīn, enjoyed equal fame,
and were known to the world as the Three Phoenixes of Hédōng.
Xuē Shōu was called the Chánglí,
Xuē Déyīn the Yuèzhuó,
and Xuē Yuánjìng, being the youngest, was called the Yuānchú.
During the Wǔdé era, he served as a scholar in the College of Literary Studies.
Rúhuì exclaimed in admiration:
"The junior recorder cannot be approached with familiarity,
nor can he be kept at a distance."
The emperor
Two quatrains
Zhāng Zhījiǎn and his elder brothers Zhīyuán and Zhīhuì,
younger brothers Zhītài and Zhīmò, five in total, devoted themselves to studying,
all passed the imperial examinations through their mastery of classics,
and became high-ranking officials.
When Zhījiǎn went to the capital from Jīngzhōu for an audience,
Empress Wǔ Zétiān valued his talent and ability,
and also observed that his appearance was exceptional,
ordered a painter to portray him,
and presented him with the portrait, saying:
"Some may have talent but lack the appearance,
yet your brothers can be called perfect in both."
People of the time praised them.
End
Shuāng Jǔ
Zhāng Chǔjīn showed ambition and virtuous conduct from a young age,
and was known for his filial piety in serving his parents.
Initially, he and his elder brother Yuèshí were both candidates for the provincial imperial examination.
When the prefectural official was about to dismiss
Yuèshí and recommend Chǔjīn instead,
Chǔjīn declined, saying:
"In terms of seniority, Yuèshí is the elder,
while in talent, I, Chǔjīn, am not his equal.
I firmly request that we both withdraw."
At that time, Lǐ Jì served as the military governor,
and he sighed, saying:
"The purpose of selecting scholars is to seek both talent and virtue.
With such mutual deference between them,
why hesitate to recommend both?"
Thus, both were recommended and passed the examination.
End
Hédān
Liú Jùlín during the Kāiyuán era served as Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
his younger brother Zhòngqiū was an Academician of the Lìzhèng Hall,
the brothers were affectionate and caring,
a Dàoguī from Luófú prepared a medicinal elixir for Jùlín,
intending to share half with Zhòngqiū,
he ordered it be cut through the middle with a knife,
and the division was without the slightest discrepancy in weight.
"Transmitted Records"
Ancient Xún Chén
Lù Jǐngróng was the younger half-brother of Lù Xiàngxiān by a different mother.
When Xiàngxiān was caned,
Jǐngróng remonstrated but was not heeded.
He then voluntarily endured the rod himself to reduce his mother's severity,
and many people praised his fraternal devotion.
The New Book of Tang
records that Xiàngxiān's younger brothers Jǐngqiàn, Jǐngróng, Jǐngxiàn, and Jǐngyì
all enjoyed fine reputations.
When the monk Yīxíng was young, he was close friends with Xiàngxiān and his brothers,
and often remarked to others:
"All the Lù brothers possess both talent and virtue.
Even the ancient Xún and Chén families
could not surpass them."
The Old Book of Tang
notes that Xiàngxiān's original name was Jǐngchū.
Qǐzǐ
Zhōngshū Lìng Zhāng Yuē valued scholars of literary talent,
oversaw the Jíxián Academy,
Wéi Shù, Zhāng Jiǔlíng, Xǔ Jǐngxiān, Yuán Huī, Zhào Lìngxī, Sūn Tì, and Wáng Hàn often visited his residence.
Zhào Lìngxī's elder brother Dōngrì, younger brothers Hébì, Jūzhēn, Ānzhēn, and Shùnzhēn—six in total,
and Wéi Shù's younger brothers Yóu, Dá, Jiǒng, Dùn, and Xún, also six in number,
all passed the imperial examinations through literary talent.
Zhāng Yuē remarked:
"The Zhào and Wéi brothers,
are the finest timber of our time."
From "The Biography Above"
Not to introduce
While Lǐ Kuí held the position of chancellor,
his elder brother, who already had a contemporary reputation,
remained stuck in an insignificant post,
and was never recommended for promotion.
After Kuí was dismissed from office,
a few days later,
his elder brother was transferred to the position of Vice Director of the Bureau of Gates.
(Old Book of Tang)
Mèng Shén
Brother Liú Shīzhēn fell ill,
and for over ten days his condition did not improve.
Shīzhēn stayed by his side day and night without undressing,
eating only one meal a day,
and recited the "Dàodéjīng" for him. In a dream, a deity said:
"If your brother suffers from wind ailment,
soak Húwángshǐzhě in wine and take it to recover."
Shīzhēn searched for it at medicinal shops,
but no one could identify it.
Suddenly, he dreamed of his mother saying:
"Húwángshǐzhě
is qiānghuó (Notopterygium root)."
Upon waking, he sought it out,
and his brother recovered immediately.
"Shǐ Xì"
Repaying gambling debts
Xíngyáng's Zhèng Huángǔ,
was naturally filial and fraternal.
His younger brother, Qígǔ, was fond of gambling and playing games for money.
Huángǔ would allow him to use
even the treasured possessions of his wife from the family treasury,
letting him use them freely.
Qígǔ would spend them all as soon as he got them.
Every time Huángǔ went out, he would seal the keys and entrust them to the family members, saying:
"Keep these for the Twenty-ninth Young Master to pay his gambling debts,
so he won't have to borrow elsewhere with interest,
and fall into the traps of wicked people."
Touched by his intention,
the younger brother somewhat restrained himself because of it.
"Records of Conversations"
Edicts arrived in succession.
Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs Lú Wò, styled Zǐzhāng,
enjoyed such flourishing official honors
that no one in recent times could compare.
Among the four brothers,
all held prominent positions.
At the beginning of the Qiánfú era,
after the mourning period for their mother ended,
Wò was appointed from his former post as Secretariat Drafter to Surveillance Commissioner of Shǎn Prefecture,
his younger brother Zhǎo was promoted from former Magistrate of Cháng'ān to Supervising Secretary,
his younger brother Yuán was promoted from former Collator of the Jíxiàn Institute to Left Reminder,
and his younger brother Yě was elevated from Metropolitan County Sheriff to Investigating Censor.
With imperial edicts arriving in succession,
the scholar-official families regarded it as an honor.
When they departed for the outskirts of Shǎn to assume their posts,
officials from the Vice Minister in charge of the Eastern Capital down to all the court ministers in Luòchéng prepared farewell banquets,
leaving Luòchéng virtually empty.
The capital's residents watched in awe,
the crowd stretching for dozens of lǐ.
Those court guests who had brought wine and food out of the city
spread across the fields,
selecting scenic spots in all directions,
with singing and music rising from everywhere,
as ethereally enchanting as the Lǐzhōu Shangsi Festival or the Kuàijī purification ceremony.
No distinction was made between noble and commoner;
by dusk, all returned drunk.
An old white-bearded courier station officer said loudly, pointing:
"I have been tending the clean postal stations for fifty years,
but never have I witnessed such a magnificent farewell ceremony."
Wò inscribed a poem at the Jiāxiáng Courier Station.
From "Unofficial History of the Táng"
Sending a Letter
Hán Pǔ and Hán Jì both possessed literary talent.
Jì often looked down upon Pǔ,
and said to others:
"My elder brother's writing,
is like a hut with a rope-hinged door and thatched roof,
barely providing shelter from wind and rain.
As for my writing,
I am a master builder of the Five Phoenix Tower."
Pǔ secretly heard these words,
and by chance obtained some Shu paper,
so he presented a poem to Jì that read:
"Ten varieties of southern paper come from Yìzhōu,
sent anew from the head of Wǎn River.
My elder brother would find this completely useless,
so I'll help you add to your Five Phoenix Tower."
From "Tán Yuàn"
Seeking Blessings
Wáng Píngfǔ was erudite and skilled in debate,
When discussing new policies with his elder brother Jièfǔ, he often cited references,
but Jièfǔ would not listen.
When his nephew Wáng Pāng was critically ill,
Jièfǔ ordered Taoist priests to perform rituals,
lavishly displaying paper money.
Píngfǔ remarked:
"As the elder brother holds the position of chancellor,
you must set an example for future generations under heaven to follow.
Though Pāng has long been ill, prayers at the hillside have persisted—
what benefit does this bring?
Moreover, you have often used state laws to restrain corrupt officials;
now you seek blessings with paper money.
How can you be sure that the realm of the Three Pure Ones does not enforce your own laws?"
From "Old Anecdotes from Qū Xiáo"
A team
Lǐ Hànyīng and his brothers visited a courtesan's quarters together,
inscribed a poem on the wall, and then left.
A jester wrote beside it the lines of an old wild goose poem:
"Two lines—what idle writing is this?
One flock—whose fine brothers are these?"
(From "Casual Readings of the Hermit")
Horse Fight
Mùróng Huì's father Shèguī divided seven hundred households from the tribe and gave them to his eldest son born of a concubine,
Tǔyùhún distributed horses to provide for him,
When Huì succeeded to the throne, the horses of the two tribes fought,
Huì became angry and sent an envoy to reprimand Hún, saying:
"Our late father established separate domains with distinctions,
Why have you not kept far apart,
Causing the horses to fight and injure each other?"
Hún replied:
"Horses graze on water and grass,
Fighting is their natural instinct,
Why direct your anger at people?
If brothers who are closest kin quarrel,
And extend it to horses,
I should distance myself ten thousand li from you."
Thereupon he moved eight thousand li to the west,
Huì later regretted this,
Sent Yǐnàlóu to pursue Hún and apologize to him,
Then tried to drive Hún's horses back,
The horses walked east for several hundred paces,
But kept sorrowfully neighing and galloping westward,
This happened more than ten times,
He said:
"This is not human affairs,"
So they settled by the Yin Mountains facing the Yellow River,
During the Yongjia rebellion of the Jin dynasty,
They moved south to Longyou,
Huì, missing his brother, composed the Elder Brother Song,
In his year-end melancholy thoughts,
He often sang it,
Later, Mùróng Chuí, when proclaiming himself emperor, made it the main melody for the imperial carriage.
"Former Yan Records"
The Xianbei called elder brother "agàn."
"Book of Jin, Biography of Hún"
Breaking an Arrow
Tǔyùhún Āchái had twenty sons.
When he fell ill,
he ordered each son to present one arrow.
Taking one arrow, he gave it to his younger brother Mùlìyán,
commanding him to break it.
Mùlìyán broke it.
Then he took nineteen arrows and ordered him to break them.
Mùlìyán could not break them.
Āchái then instructed them, saying:
"Do you understand?
Alone, it is easily broken;
united, it is hard to destroy.
You must strive together with one heart,
only then can you protect the state and bring peace to the family."
Having spoken these words, he passed away.
Defeat Jīng
In the capital, the Tián Zhēn brothers, three in total, jointly discussed dividing their property.
Their assets were all to be divided equally,
except for one purple vetch tree in front of the hall,
which they planned to split into three pieces.
The next day, they were about to cut it down,
but the tree immediately withered and died,
looking as if it had been burned by fire.
Tián Zhēn went to see it,
was greatly shocked,
and said to his younger brothers:
"The tree originally grew from the same trunk;
upon hearing it was to be cut apart,
it withered in distress—
this shows that humans are inferior to the tree."
Overcome with sorrow,
they no longer intended to split the tree.
The tree, in response, flourished again.
The brothers, moved by this,
pooled their wealth and treasures,
and thus became a family known for filial piety.
Tián Zhēn later rose to the position of Grand Master for Splendid Happiness.
"Qí Xié Jì"
Lù Jī's poem: "Three vetches viewed as one trunk."
He drank poisoned wine and died, younger brother.
Lǐ Hóng of Rǔnán served as an aide to the Grand Commandant. His younger brother committed murder and was sentenced to death.
Hóng voluntarily impeached himself and went to the court to plead for his brother's life,
offering to drink poison and die so that his brother could be spared.
From Kǒng Róng's "Discussion on the Superiority and Inferiority of Rǔnán and Yǐngchuān."
Exchanging a son for a younger brother
The Prince of Shàngjùn, Jùn, styled Xuányīng,
was praised for his talent and skill.
When Jùn was seven or eight years old,
he followed his elder brother Mì and his nephew Yuánzhí westward into Liángzhōu.
On the road, their provisions ran out,
so Mì left Yuánzhí by the wayside,
and went begging among the common people.
By the time he returned, Jùn had been captured by bandits,
while Yuánzhí had managed to escape.
Mì then led Yuánzhí in pursuit of the bandits,
knocked his head on the ground, and pleaded sorrowfully:
"It is human nature that everyone loves their own child,
but this younger brother was not yet born
when our father passed away.
We orphans grew up together,
reaching this point today.
I beg you to take Yuánzhí in exchange for Jùn."
The bandits said to each other:
"To exchange one's own son for a younger brother
is a great act of righteousness."
Thereupon, they accepted Jùn and Mì took Yuánzhí and left.
Later, when Mì passed away,
Jùn did not let even a spoonful of water pass his lips for five days,
and though he observed mourning for one year formally,
he grieved in his heart for six years. From the "Records of the Former Zhào."
Striving to die for each other
Yuán Huàn, styled Wěicái,
was appointed Consultant to the Prince of Lúlíng.
At that time, in Jiānglíng County of Nánjùn Commandery, the wife of Xún Húzhī, younger brother of Xún Jiǎngzhī, was debauched by a novice monk from Zēngkǒu Temple.
The monk entered the Xún residence at night,
and Jiǎngzhī killed the monk.
When the case was investigated by the authorities,
Jiǎngzhī presented the family's disgraceful conduct,
feeling ashamed to file a complaint,
yet finding it unbearable to endure.
He admitted to the killing,
and Húzhī's statement was similar.
The brothers contended to take the blame and die for the crime.
Zōng Gōng, the Magistrate of Jiānglíng, reported to the province, and the Inspector of Jīng Province, Prince of Lújiāng, sought Huàn's opinion. Huàn said:
"Only in severe cold and urgent times
can one see the steadfastness of pines and bamboos;
only when confronted with grave crises
can one recognize the integrity of the loyal and solitary.
I consider that Jiǎngzhī and Húzhī, in the original intent of the killing, were not violent;
during the trial,
they displayed fraternal devotion by yielding the chance to live,
moving all who witnessed it to sorrow.
In the past, Wénjǔ avoided punishment by admitting guilt and was spared by the lenient net;
if they are subjected to severe punishment,
it would truly harm the encouragement of good deeds."
Thus, the brothers were exempted from the death penalty.
From *History of the Southern Dynasties*
Mutual respect
Fáng Jǐngxiān was composed, astute, and upright in character.
He served his elder brother with reverence and respect.
When going out, he would inform his brother, and upon returning, he would report back to him.
Morning and evening, he paid his respects and inquired after his well-being,
standing attentively for extended periods.
His brother also sat solemnly upright,
and they treated each other with the courtesy of guests.
On one occasion, his elder brother fell seriously ill,
and Jǐngxiān attended to him, administering decoctions and medicine.
He did not remove his clothes or cap,
and his appearance became haggard and worn.
None among his relatives and friends failed to pity him.
"The Book of Wèi"
I wish to be your brother
Lǐ Mì visited Wú,
and the King of Wú was broadly discussing moral principles with his ministers,
saying he would rather be a younger brother.
Lǐ Mì said:
"I would prefer to be an elder brother."
The King of Wú asked:
"Why be an elder brother?"
Lǐ Mì said:
"Because the time for providing for one's parents as an elder brother is longer."
The King of Wú and all his ministers praised this answer.
(From Huáyáng Zhì)
Tiānzhōng Jì, Scroll Seventeen
Shìfù
The father's elder brothers,
the elder ones are called shìfù,
the younger ones are called shūfù.
The "Ěryǎ"
states that the eldest son inherits the lineage,
because he continues the family line.
The "Commentary"
explains that the eldest son inherits the lineage,
being older than his father in terms of succession,
thus called shìfù.
The "Shuōwén" writes shū as 卡,
Xǔ Shèn says it derives from 'above' and 'small',
meaning the younger in seniority.
The "Exegesis"
states: Bó
means 'to grasp',
as in managing household affairs.
The father's younger brother is called Zhòng.
Zhòng
means 'middle',
indicating his middle position.
The younger brother of Zhòngfù is called Shū,
Shū
means 'young',
and the younger brother of Shūfù is called Jì.
Jì
corresponds to the tenth celestial stem,
in the order of the stems,
being the last.
The "Shìmíng"
Coarse Mourning Garments
Xiànzǐ Suǒ said:
"I have heard that,
in ancient times, there was no reduction in mourning degrees,
and both superiors and inferiors mourned according to their actual relationship.
Téng Bówén, for Mèng Hǔ,
wore the zīcuī mourning for his uncle.
For Mèng Pí,
he also wore the zīcuī mourning for his uncle."
"Tángōng"
Zì Shū
Yuǎn Àng, styled Sī and renowned for his integrity,
was often called upon at court to uphold grand principles with fervor.
The eunuch Zhào Tán, favored repeatedly, frequently harmed Àng,
causing him great distress.
Àng's nephew Zhǒng advised him, saying:
"If you publicly humiliate him,
even if he later bears you ill will,
the emperor will no longer trust him."
When appointed as the chancellor of Wú and bidding farewell before departure,
Zhǒng said to Àng:
"The king of Wú is arrogant,
and over time, the state has become rife with treachery.
Now, if you, Sī, intend to govern strictly,
he will either submit a memorial accusing you or have you assassinated with a sharp sword."
The southern regions are low-lying and damp;
if you, Sī, can drink daily
and find a way to persuade the king not to rebel,
thus you may fortunately escape harm."
Àng followed his plan,
and the king of Wú treated him generously.
"Original Biography"
Your Excellency
Shū Guǎng, styled Zhòngwēng,
served as Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent during Emperor Xuān's reign.
His elder brother's son Shòu, styled Gōngzǐ,
served as Junior Tutor.
Whenever the Heir Apparent held court audiences,
the Grand Tutor would stand in front,
while the Junior Tutor stood behind.
Father and son both serving as tutors
was considered an honor by the imperial court.
Guǎng advised Shòu about knowing when to stop,
to which Shòu kowtowed and said:
"I shall follow your esteemed suggestion."
That very day, both father and son pleaded illness to resign.
(From the Book of Hàn)
Ten Rises
Dì Wǔ Lún, styled Bó Yú,
was a native of Chánglíng in Jīngzhào.
Someone asked Lún:
"Do you have any selfishness?"
He replied:
"When my nephew was once ill,
I visited him ten times in one night,
yet returned to sleep peacefully.
When my own son was ill,
though I did not go to see him,
I could not sleep the entire night.
In such cases,
how can one say there is no selfishness?"
From the Book of Later Hàn
Quoting Lǎozǐ
Xuē Bāo, styled Mèngcháng,
had younger brothers who requested to divide the family property and live separately.
Bāo could not stop them,
so he divided the property equally.
Among the servants, he took the old and sick ones, saying:
"They have worked with me for a long time,
you wouldn't be able to use them effectively."
For fields and houses, he chose the neglected and dilapidated ones,
saying:
"I cultivated these in my youth,
and have emotional attachment to them."
For utensils and objects, he selected the worn-out and broken ones,
saying:
"These are what I've used and consumed throughout my life,
and my body and mouth feel comfortable with them."
The emperor
Living Nephew
Láng Láng's son, Zǐ Míng, during a year of famine, encountered a situation where
his elder brother was about to be eaten by starving people.
He bound himself and kowtowed,
offering to be eaten in his brother's place.
The starving people admired his righteousness in fulfilling both duties,
and spared them without eating either.
After his brother died, he took in and raised his orphaned child,
loving him no differently than his own son.
When the famine year worsened and grain was exhausted,
he could not keep both children alive,
so he let his own son starve to death
to save his brother's son.
Xǔ Jūnshū of Lín Huái also raised his elder brother's orphaned son.
In a time of sudden famine,
he let his own child go hungry
to keep his brother's son alive,
sharing the same righteousness as Zǐ Míng.
From "Lùn Héng":
Wèi Tán had an orphaned
nephew, one or two years old,
whom he often cared for and watched over himself.
During a famine, he abandoned his own daughter
to raise and save his brother's son,
and the provincial authorities praised his righteousness.
From "Dōng Guān Jì."
As intimate as a young child
Cài Yōng wrote:
"Yōng, unfortunate, lost both parents early,
past the age of thirty,
with hair graying at the temples,
my uncle treated me as if I were still a young child,
riding together in the same carriage,
eating from the same bowl."
Pulling firewood, carrying it back.
Fàn Dān served as the magistrate of Láiwú but resigned from his post,
and he made a living by fortune-telling in the market.
His wife spun and wove to support themselves.
Fàn Dān's disciple Kǎi noticed that the fence around his teacher's home was damaged,
so he loaded firewood to take to the guest for repairing the fence.
Just then, Fàn Dān happened to return from his outing,
and he became angry.
He ordered his disciple to remove the firewood
and return it with the cart.
From "Yuán Shānsōng's Records".
Afflicted by evil wind while in the sun
Tàizǔ, also named Jílì,
styled Āmán,
in his youth was fond of flying hawks and coursing hounds,
and wandered about without restraint.
His uncle repeatedly reported this to Sōng,
which troubled Cāo.
Later, encountering his uncle on the road,
he then feigned a contorted face and a wry mouth.
His uncle, astonished, asked the reason,
and Tàizǔ said:
"I was suddenly struck by a malign wind."
The uncle reported this to Sōng,
who, alarmed and surprised, summoned Cāo.
Cāo's mouth and appearance were as before,
and Sōng said:
"Your uncle said you had suffered a stroke—
are you better now?"
Cāo replied:
"I never had a stroke;
it's just that I have lost my uncle's affection,
so he deceives you."
Sōng then became doubtful,
and afterwards,
no matter what the uncle reported,
Sōng ultimately did not believe him,
and Cāo thus became even more able to indulge his will.
Injured ear
Xún Yōu, styled Gōngdá,
when seven or eight years old, was accidentally injured on the ear by his drunken uncle Xún Qú.
Yet when Xún Yōu went out to play,
he often avoided and concealed it, not wishing to let Qú see.
When Qú later learned of this,
he marveled at such early wisdom.
From the Records of Wei:
When his grandfather Xún Tán died,
a former subordinate Zhāng Tuī requested to guard Tán’s tomb.
Yōu, then thirteen,
became suspicious
and said to his uncle Qú:

Foolish Uncle
Wáng Zhàn initially possessed hidden virtues,
unknown to others,
and even his brothers and clan members considered him foolish.
His nephew Wáng Jì looked down upon him,
and when a lavish feast was spread before them,
he did not offer any to Wáng Zhàn.
Wáng Zhàn then asked for vegetables,
and ate them facing the feast.
Once, Wáng Jì visited and noticed the Book of Changes by his bedside,
asking:
"Uncle, what use do you have for this?"
Wáng Zhàn replied:
"I occasionally read it when I'm not feeling well."
Wáng Jì requested an explanation,
whereupon Wáng Zhàn analyzed its profound principles,
revealing subtle and extraordinary insights,
all of which were unheard of by Wáng Jì.
History of the Jin Dynasty
Previously, Wáng Jì had shown no respect due to a nephew,
but after hearing his words,
he couldn't help but feel awed,
becoming solemn in both heart and demeanor.
He then stayed for days and nights on end.
Although Wáng Jì was talented and sharp-witted,
he now felt inadequate by comparison,
and sighed deeply, saying:
"To have such a distinguished scholar in the family,
and not know it for thirty years,
is my fault."
Later, when he bid farewell and returned,
his father Wáng Hún asked why his short trip had taken so many days.
Wáng Jì said he had just discovered an uncle.
Wáng Hún asked for an explanation,
and Wáng Jì recounted everything with admiration.
Wáng Hún then asked:
"How does he compare to me?"
Wáng Jì replied:
"He is superior to me."
Emperor Wǔ would often tease Wáng Jì about Wáng Zhàn, asking:
"Has your foolish uncle died yet?"
Wáng Jì responded:
"My uncle is not foolish;
I praise him for his true excellence."
The Emperor asked:
"Who can he be compared to?"
Wáng Jì said:
"Below Shān Tāo
but above Wèi Shū."

the two Wèi

you should be more direct."

breast milk
Yuán Déxiù was poor in his early years when his elder brother died prematurely,
leaving behind an orphaned child.
A month later, his sister-in-law also passed away,
and there was no one to breastfeed the infant.
Déxiù wept day and night in grief,
then held the child and put his own nipple into its mouth.
After ten days, milk began to flow,
and the child thus grew up healthy.
Déxiù later served as magistrate of Lǔshān County,
where he governed with integrity,
spreading benevolence throughout the region,
and the entire commandery sang his praises.

Bamboo Chamber
Yáng Yīn, styled Zūnyǎn,
childhood nickname Qínwáng,
studied in the courtyard as a child when
plums from a tree fell to the ground.
While all the other children scrambled for them,
Yīn sat alone unmoved.
His youngest uncle Yáng Wěi happened to enter the school and witnessed this,
greatly amazed and impressed,
turned to his guests and said:
"This child's tranquility and magnanimity reflect our family's traditions."
There being lush bamboo groves within the residence,
he then had a separate room built for Yīn beside the woods,
instructing him to dwell there alone.
He often had meals served to him lavishly on bronze plates,
using this to admonish and encourage his other sons:
"If you all would only be as prudent as Zūnyǎn,
you too would naturally gain a separate chamber by the bamboo grove,
and meals of double meat portions on bronze plates."
Yáng Yù, Yīn's elder cousin and a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, particularly valued him highly,
once saying to others:
"Though this boy's milk teeth have not yet fallen out,
he is already the dragon-marked steed of our family.
After another ten years,
we shall seek his like a thousand miles away."

Carrying the Classics
Huángfǔ Mì, styled Shì'ān,
at the age of twenty,
did not enjoy learning,
wandered aimlessly without restraint,
and whenever he obtained melons or fruits, he would offer them to his aunt Rén Shì.
Rén Shì said:
"The Classic of Filial Piety states that even providing the three sacrificial animals
is still considered unfilial.
You are now over twenty years old,
your eyes do not retain teachings,
your heart does not embrace the Way,
and you have nothing to comfort me."
She then sighed and said, "In ancient times, Mèng's mother moved three times to cultivate benevolence,
and Zēng's father cooked a pig to preserve teaching.
Is it because I did not choose neighbors when settling,
or that my teaching was lacking,
that you are so exceedingly dull?"
They then wept facing each other,
and Mì became deeply moved.
He went to his villager Xí Tǎn to receive instruction in books,
diligently applying himself without slackening.
Living in poverty, he personally engaged in farming,
carrying classics while farming,
and thus comprehensively mastered the writings of classical texts and the Hundred Schools of Thought.
He styled himself Master Xuānyàn.

nor too broad.

"Too high means excessively tall,
too broad means excessively wide.

for the mourning of the aunt, the ribbon is eight inches.

Yì Gū
Lǔ Yì Gū was the father of a common man.
Qí attacked Lǔ and reached the outskirts, where from afar they saw a person carrying one child
and holding another child in their arms. When the army arrived,
they abandoned the one they were holding and picked up the one they were carrying.
As the soldiers were about to shoot them,
they stopped and asked:
"Whose child is the one you're holding?"
The reply was:
"My elder brother's child."
"Whose child is the one you abandoned?"
They said:
"My own child.
I saw the great army approaching,
and I couldn't save both,
so I abandoned my own child."
The soldiers said:
"A child is most dear to its mother's heart.
Why abandon your own child and carry your brother's child?"
The reply was:
"A child to its mother
is a private affection,
but a nephew to his aunt
is a public duty.
To turn my back on public duty for private affection
is something I cannot do."
The Qí army said:
"Even a woman in the outskirts of Lǔ maintains such moral integrity in her conduct,
how much more so the court officials?"
So they turned the army back and did not attack Lǔ.
The ruler of Lǔ heard of this,
bestowed silk upon her,
and gave her the title Yì Gū (Righteous Aunt).

The aunt's daughter
Wēn Gōng lost his wife,
and his paternal aunt Liú Shì's family was scattered due to war and chaos.
They only had one daughter who was very beautiful and intelligent.
The aunt entrusted Wēn Gōng with finding her a husband,
but he secretly intended to marry her himself.
He replied:
"A good son-in-law is hard to find,
but someone like me,
what do you think?"
The aunt said:
"In our reduced circumstances after the devastation,
I only hope for basic survival to comfort my remaining years.
How dare I expect someone as distinguished as you?"
A few days later, Wēn Gōng reported to his aunt:
"I have found a marriage match.
The family background is acceptable,
the groom is an official with reputation,
in no way inferior to me."
He then presented a jade mirror stand as betrothal gift.
The aunt was very pleased.
After the wedding ceremony,
the bride lifted her veil,
clapped her hands and laughed heartily, saying:
"I suspected it was this old fellow,
and indeed it turned out as I guessed."
The jade mirror stand was obtained by Wēn Gōng when he served as Chief Clerk to Liú Yuèshí during the northern expedition against Liú Cōng.

Marrying a One-Eyed Woman
Cuī Jùlún had an elder sister
who was intelligent and virtuous,
but suffered from blindness in one eye.
None of the relatives inside or outside the clan sought her hand in marriage.
Her family discussed marrying her to someone of lower status.
Cuī Jùlún's aunt, the wife of Lǐ Shūyìn from the state of Zhào, heard this and lamented:
"My brother was of great virtue,
yet unfortunately passed away early.
How can we let this girl stoop to serve a humble family?"
She then arranged for her son Yì to marry her.
People at the time praised her righteousness and wisdom.

Appreciated
Yuán Shū, styled Yángyuán,
was the son of Yuán Bào.
He displayed an extraordinary demeanor from a young age,
and when he was just a few years old,
his paternal uncle Yuán Zhàn said to the family,
"This is no ordinary child."
By the time he reached over ten years old,
he was admired by his maternal uncle Wáng Hóng.
He did not engage in trivial textual studies,
but extensively explored various fields with broad understanding,
and his literary talent was vigorous and splendid.

Not visiting the door
During the reign of Zhōngzōng,
Yáo Chóng memorialized, saying:
"Buddha is not external,
seek it within the heart.
Though Fó Túchéng was the most virtuous,
he was of no benefit to Jīnzhào;
though Rāshí had many skills, he couldn't save the fallen Qín;
Hé Chōng and Fú Róng both faced defeat and extinction.
Even Qí Xiāng and Liáng Wǔ could not escape disaster.
Only by cultivating a heart of compassion,
performing actions that benefit others,
allowing the people to live in peace,
does one embody the Buddha's final teachings.
He said:
"Buddha is
awareness,
located within the heart,
even if vast as myriad phenomena,
it does not extend beyond the five aggregates.
With impartial compassion,
doing good and not evil,
the path of Buddha is complete.
Why indulge in trivial tales,
confused by ordinary monks,
wasting human lives,
with no benefit to the deceased.
Moreover, the Tathāgata's universal compassion truly serves all beings,
diminishing the inadequacies of sentient beings,
to enrich those monks with excess,
certainly not.
From "Wan Nian Gui Jing Old Táng" the present-day Buddhist scriptures,
translated by Rāshí,
with Yáo Xīng guiding the original text alongside Rāshí for translation,
Yáo Xīng constructed a pagoda at Yǒngguì Lǐ,
exhausting the treasury,
extensively embellishing it,
yet his fate could not be extended,
and the state fell in succession.
Further, Qí occupied Shāndōng,
Zhōu held Guānyòu,
Zhōu abolished much of Buddhist practice,
while strengthening military power;
Qí established numerous monasteries,
relying on Buddha's power.
When battles ensued,
the Qí lineage perished,
the state no longer existed,
what monasteries could there be?
The supposed reward of cultivating virtue,
why so insignificant.
Liáng Wǔdì had tens of thousands at his command enslaved,
Hú Tàihòu led her six palaces into the way,
not only were they personally disgraced,
but their states and families were also destroyed.
Recently, the filial Hé Emperor dispatched envoys to ransom lives,
exhausting the state to build temples.
Tàipíng Princess and Wǔ Sān Sī defied propriety,
Zhāng Fūrén and others also ordained people and built temples,
their schemes filled the streets,
all were ultimately subjected to execution and family ruin,
becoming the laughingstock of the world.
The scriptures say:
"Seek longevity, receive longevity;
seek wealth and honor, receive wealth and honor.
Blades make sections break,
fire pits turn to pools.
In recent times, who gains wealth, honor, and longevity through diligence?
Such matters are easily understood while living,
yet seem without response;
after death, hard to probe,
who sees any proof?
Moreover, death is constant,
never avoided in antiquity,
what purpose do scriptures and statues serve?
The fundamental doctrine of Śākyamuni,
is a great misfortune to sentient beings,
I, having passed, must not allow this harmful doctrine.

Bribery
Péi Jí often told a story from his youth about his uncle who served as a court official.
He had an elegant reputation,
and when Jí went to his residence to meet him after court dismissal,
he sighed deeply and said:
"Who is this Cuī Zhào,
that everyone praises so highly?
He must be practicing bribery.
How can things not be in chaos like this?"
Before he finished speaking,
the gatekeeper announced:
"Cuī, the governor of Jīngzhōu, requests an audience."
The uncle angrily scolded the gatekeeper,
intending to whip him.
After a long while, he reluctantly straightened his attire to receive the guest.
Soon he urgently called for tea,
then ordered wine and food,
and later commanded a full meal be prepared.
Jí's aunt asked:
"Why were you so arrogant before but so respectful now?"
When he entered the room, he had a self-satisfied expression,
bowed to Jí and said:
"Please rest in the study."
Before Jí had descended the steps,
the uncle took out a document from his bosom—
it was a gift of a thousand bolts of official silk.

Presenting betrothal gifts
Zhèng Xú Wú Fàn's younger sister was beautiful,
Gōngsūn Chǔ had already betrothed her,
but Gōngsūn Hēi again sent someone to forcibly present betrothal gifts.
Fàn was afraid,
and informed Zǐchǎn.
Zǐchǎn said:
"This shows the state lacks governance,
it is not your fault."
He let her choose according to her wish,
and requested from both men,
asking to let the woman choose between them.
Both agreed.
Zǐxī entered in splendid attire,
laid out his gifts and left.
Zǐnán entered in military dress,
shot arrows to left and right,
leaped into his chariot and departed.
The woman watched from her room,
and said:
"Zǐxī is indeed handsome,
but Zǐnán is a real man.
Husband being husbandly and wife being wifely is what is called harmony."
She married into Zǐnán's family.

Unable to bear removing mourning garments
Zǐlù had a sister's mourning period,
which could be ended,
but he had not ended it.
Confucius said,
"Why have you not ended it?"
Zǐlù said,
"I have few brothers and cannot bear to do so."
Confucius said,
"The rites established by the former kings must not be transgressed."
So he ended it.

Zhào Xiāngzǐ ascended Xiàwū,
to observe the customs of Dài,
finding its pleasures exceedingly fine.
Upon returning,
he contemplated how to seize Dài, first befriending its ruler.
The lord of Dài was fond of women,
so he offered his elder sister to marry him,
and the lord of Dài consented.
After the sister had gone,
the means to befriend Dài
included the endless pastures of Mǎjùn, ideal for horses.
The lord of Dài presented fine horses to Xiāngzǐ,
who then invited the lord of Dài to a feast at Mǎjùn.
He first ordered dancers to conceal weapons in their feathers,
with hundreds preparing large bronze ladles in advance.
When the lord of Dài arrived and the wine flowed freely,
they overturned the ladles and struck him,
smashing his head to the ground in one blow.
The dancers took up arms and fought,
killing all his attendants.
They then used the lord of Dài's carriage to fetch his wife,
who, hearing of the events on the way,
sharpened a hairpin and stabbed herself.
Thus, the Zhào clan to this day bears the mark of the hairpin stab
mountain
and the name "overturned ladle."

Liè Zǐ
Niè Zhèng assassinated the Chancellor of Hán for Yán Zhòngzǐ,
then mutilated his own face and disemboweled himself to die,
Hán took his corpse and exposed it in the market,
offering a thousand in gold for identification,
but for a long time no one knew who he was.
Niè Zhèng's elder sister Yīng heard of this,
and sorrowfully said in her town:
"Could that be my brother?"
She then went to the market of Hán,
and the deceased was indeed Niè Zhèng,
she prostrated over the corpse weeping with extreme grief,
and said:
"This is the Niè Zhèng from Shēn Jǐng Lǐ in Zhǐ."
She then cried out to heaven three times,
and also killed herself beside Niè Zhèng.
When Jìn, Chǔ, Qí, and Wèi heard of this,
they all said it was not only Niè Zhèng who was capable,
but his sister was also a woman of fierce integrity.

Presented his younger sister
Lǐ Yuán,
a retainer of Chūnshēnjūn,
presented his sister to Chūnshēnjūn.
She was already pregnant initially,
and he made his sister say to Chūnshēnjūn:
"The King of Chǔ has no son.
After a hundred years,
his brothers will be enthroned.
You have been in power for a long time
and have often been disrespectful to the king's brothers.
If his brothers truly ascend the throne,
disaster will befall you.
Now I am with child,
and no one knows it.
If you present me to the king,
and later I give birth to a boy,
then your son will become king."
Chūnshēnjūn then spoke of this to the king,
who summoned her and favored her.
She subsequently gave birth to a boy,
who was established as the crown prince.
Later, when King Xiàoliè passed away,
Lǐ Yuán, resenting Chūnshēnjūn's favor,
assassinated him.

Touching the Sickle
Qín Péng, styled Bópíng,
served as the Grand Administrator of Sānyáng.
A citizen, Jiāng Bó, intended to marry off his widowed elder sister,
but the sister took a sickle and cut herself.
Bó rushed forward to rescue his sister,
accidentally touched the sickle, injured her, and she subsequently died.
The county officials deliberated on the law,
Péng said:
"His intention to rescue was without malice."
Thus, he imposed a lighter punishment.

Holding the book, listening to the neighbor read
When Jiǎ Kuí was five years old,
he was exceptionally intelligent beyond his peers.
His elder sister, the wife of Hán Yáo,
had married Yáo but returned to live at home due to having no heirs,
and was also praised for her virtue and wisdom.
Hearing the neighbors reciting texts,
she would hold Kuí day and night by the fence to listen.
Kuí would listen quietly without speaking,
which delighted his sister.
By the age of ten, he could recite the Six Classics from memory.
His sister said to Kuí:
"Our family is impoverished,
and no scholar has ever entered our door.
How do you know of the world's Three Fen and Five Canons, reciting them without missing a single line?"
Kuí replied:
"I recall when you held me by the fence to listen to the neighbors reading—
now I’ve retained nearly every word."

Go ahead

The Chángguǎng Bridge:
Emperor Wǔ of the Liú Sòng Dynasty's elder sister once sold silk to buy rice and was returning across the bridge,

whose surname was Li,
was named Er,
style name Bóyáng,
posthumously titled Dān,
was the historian who oversaw the archival room of Zhou.
Confucius went to Zhou,
intending to inquire about rituals from Lǎozǐ.
Lǎozǐ cultivated the Dao and virtue,
focusing on self-concealment and namelessness.
He lived in Zhou for a long time,
observed the decline of Zhou,
and thus left and reached the pass.
The official Yǐnxǐ at the pass said:
"You are going to retreat,
please write a book for me."
Thereupon, Lǎozǐ wrote the book in two sections,
expressing the meaning of Dao and virtue in over five thousand words and left,
and no one knows where he ended.
It is said Lǎozǐ lived over one hundred sixty years,
or some say over two hundred years,
due to his cultivation of Dao and nurturing longevity.
Lǎozǐ
was a recluse of worth.
Lǎozǐ's son was named Zōng,
Zōng was a general for Wei,
and was enfeoffed at Xiàyú.
Zōng's son was Zhù,
Zhù's son was Gōng,
Gōng's great-grandson was Jiǎ.
Jiǎ served Emperor Xiàowén of the Han.
And Jiǎ's son, Jiě, served as the Grand Tutor for the Prince of Jiaoxi, Wángyáng,
thus settling the family in Qi.
Lǐ Ěr practiced non-action to transform himself,
maintaining purity and tranquility to rectify himself.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Yǔ Zhuó served as the military officer of Hénán,
and had a widowed elder sister at home.
At that time, prices in Luòyáng were soaring high,
making it difficult to obtain daily sustenance.
Yǔ often set aside portions from his own meals at the official hall to send to his sister,
falsely claiming it was for his beloved young son.
His colleagues initially looked down on and laughed at him,
but later, upon learning the truth,
they were moved and praised him admiringly.

Strict Teacher
The court official Sòng Ruòzhāo,
whose father Tíngfēn had five daughters,
the eldest Ruòshēn,
next Ruòzhāo,
Ruòlún,
Ruòxiàn,
Ruòxún,
Ruòzhāo's literary talent was particularly outstanding,

take into custody
Hú Mǔ Bān, courtesy name Jìyǒu,
was one of the Eight Compassionate Officials,
and the brother-in-law of Wáng Kuāng.
Kuāng, following Yuán Shào's order,
arrested Bān and imprisoned him,
intending to execute him to boost army morale.
Bān wrote a letter to Kuāng, which roughly said:
"You have confined me in prison,
wishing to use my blood to anoint the drums—
how utterly perverse, brutal, and unprincipled this is!
What kinship do I share with Dǒng Zhuó?
How could my principles align with his wickedness?
You open the jaws of a tiger or wolf,
spewing the venom of a long serpent,
venting your anger at Zhuó upon me—
how cruel this is!
Death
is something all men dread,
yet I am ashamed to be slain by a madman.
If the dead possess consciousness,
I shall surely accuse you before the August Heaven.
Marriage alliances
are the pivot of fortune and misfortune,
and today this is made clear.
Once we were as one body,
now we are blood enemies.
My two daughters are your nieces;
after my death,
do not let them approach my corpse."
Upon reading the letter,
Kuāng embraced Bān's two sons and wept,
but Bān ultimately died in prison.
(From Xiè Chéng's Book)
Èr Xiè
Wáng Yòujūn's wife, Lady Xī, said to her two younger brothers, the Minister of Works and the Palace Attendant:
"When the Wáng family sees the two Xiè brothers,
they empty their baskets and turn out their bags (to entertain them).
But when you come, they treat you indifferently.
You need not trouble to visit them again."
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
He impeached and memorialized against
Liú Lǎnrú's younger brother,
who was appointed as the Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs,
was upright and incorrupt in his official duties,
showing no favoritism.
His brother-in-law, the Vice Censor-in-Chief Chǔ Yān, and his cousin, the Director of the Bureau of Appointments Xiào Chuò,
were involved in corrupt practices during their tenure,
so Liú Lǎnrú impeached and memorialized against them, leading to their dismissal from office.
Xiào Chuò resented him for this,
and once remarked to others:
"A dog bites passersby,
but Liú Lǎnrú bites his own family."

Zhèng Yuánlǐ was

Wèi Shōu was
Áng's brother-in-law.
Áng, holding Yuánlǐ's
several poems, showed them to Lú Sīdào, saying:
"Yuánlǐ lately
has not been good at composing poetry either."
Wèi Shōu and Sīdào said:

"The Northern Qí"
Mistakenly Killed, Dāo Yuè
Wáng Zhìxīng was in Xúzhōu,
where his laws and decrees were extremely strict.
A frontier defense officer returning from duty went to his brother-in-law's home,
and a feast was prepared there to celebrate.
He himself sharpened a knife in the kitchen,
intending to sit and cut mutton shanks.
After sharpening it, he hurriedly carried it;
his brother-in-law rushed in from the hall,
and they abruptly met in the kitchen.
The blade struck right into the brother-in-law's heart,
and he died immediately.
The authorities captured him and reported to Zhìxīng.
When questioned, he claimed it was a mistake,
with no malicious intent originally.
Zhìxīng did not believe him
and ordered his execution.
But the knife leaped out of the executioner's hand
and fell to the ground three times;
each attempt was the same.
Zhìxīng found it strange,
so he did not kill him.
(Records of Causeries)
The younger sister wears mourning attire.
When Bì Gǒu first lost his stepmother,
he had two infant sisters in swaddling clothes,
whom he personally nurtured and raised,
enabling both to reach adulthood.
Upon Bì Gǒu's death,
his two sisters wailed until nearly breathless for a long time,
and due to his nurturing kindness,
they observed the three-year mourning period.
His younger brother Xǔ also grieved to the point of physical decline,
and both were praised by contemporaries.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Èrmèi
Yuán Yàndào had two younger sisters,
one married to Yīn Yuānyuán,
the other married to Xiè Rénzǔ.
He said to Huán Xuānwǔ:
