Saving the Younger Brother
Yǔ Xī was executed and about to be killed,
the younger brother Yùtái's daughter-in-law,
who was Xuānwǔ's younger sister,
rushed in crying and said:
"Yǔ Yùtái always relied on others being three inches shorter in the feet,
could he still commit treason?"
Xuānwǔ laughed and said:
"The son-in-law is indeed anxious."
Thus Yùtái was pardoned.

Nánshān
The Southern Mountain criticizes Duke Xiāng of Qí,
whose conduct was like that of beasts and birds,
being licentious with his sister.
High and lofty is the Southern Mountain,
The male fox looks for his mate.
The Máo Shī
states that the Marquis of Qí escorting Jiāng Shì was contrary to propriety.
When a duke's daughter marries into a state of equal rank,
if she is a sister, a high minister escorts her according to propriety.
For a daughter of a former ruler, a junior minister escorts her to a large state.
Even for a duke's daughter, a high minister escorts her.
When escorting her to the Son of Heaven,
all ministers go.
The duke does not personally escort her to a small state,
then a senior great officer escorts her.
In the third year of Huán,
the duke went with Jiāng Shì to Qí.
Shēn Xū said:
"A woman has her home,
a man has his wife,
and they should not defile each other;
this is called propriety.
To change this will certainly lead to ruin."
The duke met with the Marquis of Qí at Luò,
then went with Wén Jiāng to Qí.
The Marquis of Qí had illicit relations with her,
the duke reproached her,
and she informed the Marquis. On the bǐngzǐ day, he feasted the duke,
and had the duke's son Péng Shēng assist the duke into his carriage.
The duke died in the carriage.

Shining Cauldron
Emperor Gāozǔ's elder brother Bó's wife,
when Gāozǔ was in humble circumstances and once avoiding official duties,
at that time went with friends to visit his sister-in-law,
the sister-in-law disliked her brother-in-law bringing guests to eat,
feigned that the soup was finished,
scraped the pot as the guests left,
Gāozǔ saw there was still soup in the pot,
from then on held a grudge against her,
later when he stabilized the empire, Bó's son alone was not enfeoffed,
saying:
"His mother is not a magnanimous person."
Seven years later he was enfeoffed as Juégēng Hóu.

Eating Chaff
Chén Píng's elder brother Bócháng farmed the fields,
allowing Píng to travel and study freely.
His sister-in-law resented this,
and neglected household duties.
When someone asked what Píng ate to become so plump,
he replied:
"I only eat chaff and husks."
His sister-in-law said:
"Having such a brother-in-law,
it would be better to have no elder brother."
Upon hearing this, Bócháng divorced his wife.

Zhí Bùyí served as a court gentleman.
The court officials slandered Bùyí, saying:

he excels at seducing his elder brothers' wives."
Bùyí responded:

Demand for Money
Zhèng Hóng was the magistrate of Yángxiàn County.
There was a younger brother who had used his elder brother's money,
and was reproached by his sister-in-law.
He had not yet returned it
when the sister-in-law went to Zhèng Hóng.
Zhèng Hóng repaid the money on behalf of the younger brother.
When the elder brother heard of this, he felt ashamed,
and had himself confined in prison.
He then sent someone to bring the money to repay Zhèng Hóng,
but Zhèng Hóng did not accept it.

should grow more resolute in poverty,

Gāo Fèng, styled Wéntōng,
was a native of Nányáng.
As Fèng grew old, his fame became widely known,
and the Grand Administrator repeatedly summoned and invited him.

he declared himself:

He also feigned a dispute with his widowed sister-in-law,

at the age of fourteen or fifteen,
saw that Wáng Yífǔ's wife Guō Shì was greedy
and wanted to make her maids carry dung on the road.

stating it was unacceptable.

Dàoist Monk Lín visited Xiè Ān in Dōngyáng.
Lǎng
was still wearing his hair in two tufts at the time,
having just recovered from an illness,
and his body was not yet fit for exertion.
While discussing with Monk Lín,
they ended up distressing each other.
His mother, Lady Wáng, was listening behind the wall,
and repeatedly sent messages urging him to return,
but the Grand Tutor detained him.
Lady Wáng then came out herself and said:
"Since my youth, I have encountered family misfortunes,
and all my hopes in this life
rest solely on this child."
Thereupon, she wept, embraced her son, and returned with him.
Xiè Ān told those sitting with him:
"My sister-in-law's words were deeply moving and fervent,
truly worth passing on and recounting.
It is a pity that the court officials could not witness it."
Lifting the Siege
Wáng Níngzhī's wife Xiè Dàoyùn,
when Níngzhī's younger brother Xiànzhī was once discussing with guests,
and his arguments were about to be defeated,
Dàoyùn sent a maid to tell Xiànzhī:
"I wish to help the young master break the siege."
She then set up a blue damask screen to conceal herself,
and elaborated on Xiànzhī's previous arguments,
leaving the guests unable to refute her.
History of the Jìn Dynasty
The wind blows wealth back.
In the second year of the Lóng'ān era of the Jìn dynasty,
a man from Wújùn named Zhū Míng established himself through filial piety and righteousness and became very wealthy.
He lived together with his younger brother,
but his wife said the courtyard tree was damaged and wanted to abandon the elder brother to live separately.
Míng understood his brother's intention,
so he gave all the gold, silk, and surplus grain to his younger brother,
keeping only the empty house.
Suddenly one night, a fierce wind arose abruptly,
blowing all the wealth and silk back to Míng's home.
Ashamed to face their fellow villagers,
they committed suicide.
Míng then donated his house to establish a temple,
named the Zhū Míng Temple.
"Records of Wú Region"
Respectfully Harmonious
Cài Xìngzōng established his moral character from a young age,
and was particularly meticulous in his family conduct.
He served his aunt who had returned to the clan,
attended to his widowed sister-in-law,
and raised his orphaned nephew,
earning renown in the world.
Fàn, wife of the Crown Prince's Left Guard Wáng Xī,
was an intelligent woman
with literary talent and learning.
Upon seeing a letter exchanged with Xī's younger brother Sēngdá,
she admonished him, saying:
"In the past, Grand Tutor Xiè served his sister-in-law, Lady Wáng, as a filial son would his mother;
now Cài Xìngzōng is also praised for his respect and harmony.

Book of Sòng
Requesting the Return of Funds
Liú Xiáng, styled Xiǎnwēi,
had an elder brother Liú Zhěng who previously died while serving in Guǎngzhōu.
Last year, Xiáng requested permission to retrieve the coffin,
but upon reaching Dàléi,
he argued with Zhěng's wife Mèng over the funeral expenses,
becoming enraged.
Xiáng then abandoned the coffin and returned to his post.
Xiá submitted a memorial stating:
"Xiáng, though his brother's coffin was exposed to the elements,
showed not a day's grief.
Southern gold was not obtained,
yet he caused his sister-in-law and nephew to be lightly abandoned and isolated,
while vermilion and distant matters concerned both living and dead.
His abandonment allowed violent men to plunder the bones and coffin,
passersby sighed with flowing tears,
and all understanding hearts were wounded."
From the History of the Southern Qí

Hán Língmǐn's elder brother Língzhēn died,
leaving no son.
His wife, née Zhuó, preserved her chastity and did not remarry.
Fearing her family would force her to change her resolve,
she never returned to visit them.
Língmǐn served her as his mother.

Self-sale
Wú Dázhī was a man from Yìxīng.
When his sister-in-law died without means for burial,
he sold himself as a laborer for ten men,
using the proceeds to build her tomb and coffin.
His cousin Jìngbó
and wife, during a famine year,
were abducted and sold north of the river.
Dázhī owned ten mu of farmland,
which he mortgaged to redeem them,
then shared his property and home with them.
When the commandery appointed him as registrar,
he firmly declined in favor of his elder brother.
He also yielded his inherited farmland to his clan younger brother,
but the brother likewise refused the fields,
so they were left unused.
Buying Rice
Qí Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐ Liáng served as the governor of Kuàijī,
when a man from Shānyīn named Kǒng Píng approached Zǐ Liáng,
accusing his sister-in-law of selling rice
but failing to repay the money owed.
Zǐ Liáng sighed and said:

but the righteousness in that case differed from this one."
He then bestowed rice and money to repay Píng.

Shūláng
Fàn, wife of Liú Yín, the former Minister of the West of Qí, submitted a petition to the court,
alleging that her husband's younger brother, Liú Zhěng, constantly sought to harm and seize their property,
taking away Liú Yín's son Qūn's maid Lǜcǎo and Liú Yín's second son Shīlì.
Last year in October,
when she went to Zhěng's fields,
after twelve days,
Zhěng demanded six dǒu of rice from Fàn for meals,
but before the rice could be delivered,
he suddenly appeared at her door,
cursing loudly through the screen, shaking his fist,
and barged into the room, taking the carriage curtain from behind the screen as compensation for the rice.
On the night of February 9th,
Zhěng's maid Cǎiyīn stole the carriage rail, clamps, staff, and dragon reins,
and when Fàn inquired about the missing items,
Zhěng beat her son Qūn,
then Zhěng, his mother, and six servants together came to Fàn's house,
shouting insults loudly,
and the maid Cǎiyīn raised her hand to grab Fàn's arm, demanding an investigation.
Rèn Fǎng submitted an impeachment memorial stating:
"Reason should cut off communication, yet he wildly utters vile words;
he stays awake all night and falsely imposes severe beatings."
From the "Selections"
Speaking of old age
Lú Chù's second wife Yuán Shì ascended the hall to lecture on Lǎo Zǐ's "Classic of the Way and Virtue",
while Chù's younger brother Yuánmíng listened from behind a silk curtain.
"Record of Confrontation in Yè and Luò"
Mourning Attire for a Younger Brother and Sister-in-Law
Emperor Tàizōng said to his attendants:
"Even those who share a cooking fire still have the kindness of wearing mourning garments of sīmá,
yet there are no mourning rites for a sister-in-law and brother-in-law.
It is appropriate to gather scholars to deliberate this in detail."
Attendant-in-Chief Wèi Zhēng and others deliberated:
"The Record says that a brother's son is like one's own son,
this is to draw him close and bring him near.
The absence of mourning rites for sister-in-law and brother-in-law,
is to push them away and keep them at a distance.
Moreover, there are numerous records praising service to sisters-in-law,
Zhèng Zhòngyú was deeply sincere in his kindness and courtesy,
Yán Hóngdū was utterly sincere in his emotional devotion,
Mǎ Yuán would always don his cap when seeing her,
Kǒng Jí would weep and maintain her memorial tablet,
examining the underlying principles they upheld,
were they not indeed men of foresight?"
Old Records
Consultation on matters
Wáng Guī served his widowed sister-in-law with utmost propriety,
consulting her on all household matters before taking action,
and educated and cared for his orphaned nephew
no less than he did his own son.
(New Book of Tang)
Exhausting the Purse for His Uncle
Qiū Xù, whose courtesy name was Mèngyáng,
traveled to Jīnlíng for the imperial examinations nine times in total,
failing six or seven times with blank papers submitted,
yet he disciplined himself with increasing diligence,
not considering it a disgrace.
Later, when he became impoverished and lost the will to advance,
as the autumn examinations approached,
his widowed sister-in-law asked about his departure date.
Xù informed her of his financial difficulties,
to which Liú replied:
"If it can fulfill your honorable aspirations,
even an orphan could be sold,
let alone material resources?"
Thereupon, she exhausted her entire purse to give to him.
Xù had no alternative
but to once again attempt the provincial examinations.
The following spring, during the examinations,
his rhapsody on "Virtue Bears All Things"
was ranked first.
He returned home in coarse clothing,
and his family still doubted he had not been assigned a post.
Only when the village elders and local leaders came to pay respects,
and the commandery officials altered the name of his neighborhood,
did they realize he had achieved the highest rank.
(From *The History of Southern Táng*)
The master's household affairs
Lǐ Guāngjìn's younger brother Guāngyán married first, and their mother entrusted him with household affairs.
By the time Guāngjìn married, their mother had already passed away.
His younger brother's wife registered the assets, stored them, and handed the keys to her elder sister-in-law.
Guāngjìn ordered her to return them,
saying:
"You attended to our mother-in-law and received her instructions,
so you should continue managing the household affairs without change."
They then held each other and wept, finally restoring their former relationship.
From the "History of the Tang Dynasty"

Zhàn
married the daughter of Hǎo Pǔ,

Hún,

Yǎn
and daughter

Zhōng and Hǎo were sisters-in-law,
treating each other with mutual affection and respect.

"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Paying respects to the younger brother's wife
Lǐ Tāo and his younger brother Huàn married the daughters of Minister of Rites Dòu Níngguó.
Being somewhat older in age,
on the wedding night,
when the Dòu family women came out to pay respects,
Tāo immediately bowed toward the dust before Huàn,
who exclaimed in surprise:
"Is Elder Brother mad?
How can one return a bow when a new bride pays respects to her elder brother-in-law?"
Tāo replied:
"I'm not mad,
I merely thought she was my mother-in-law."
Huàn felt both ashamed and angry.
After the Dòu family women were seated,
they bowed again to Tāo,
who then clasped hands before his chest and uttered a cryptic remark:
"Ashamed I lack Dòu Jiàn's virtue,
embarrassed to face Liáng Mountain's height,
yes, yes."
Those who heard this couldn't help roaring with laughter.
From "Supplementary Records of the History of the Five Dynasties"
Sisters-in-law
Many people call a younger brother's wife "dì",
and a younger brother's wife calls her elder brother's wife "sì".
In the eleventh year of Duke Chéng in the Zuǒzhuàn,
Mù Jiāng referred to Shēng Bó's mother as "sì",
and in the eighth year of Duke Zhāo, Shū Xiàng's sister-in-law called Shū Xiàng's wife "sì".
These are all cases of calling a husband's younger brother's wife "sì".
Jiǎ, Zhèng, and Dù all stated that the terms "dì" and "sì"
do not depend on the husband's age.
Nowadays, they are called according to the order of marriage,
or referred to as "zhóulǐ".
Explained in the "Ěryǎ Shū".
Escorting the Bride
The Marquis of Qí escorted Jiāng Shì to Huān.
According to ritual, when sending off a daughter, the father does not descend the hall, the mother does not go beyond the temple gate,
and aunts and brothers do not pass the palace gate.
The father admonished her, saying:
"Be cautious and follow the words of your father-in-law."
The mother admonished her, saying:
"Be cautious and follow the words of your mother-in-law."
The aunts reiterated, saying:
"Be cautious and follow the words of your parents."
Escorting the daughter beyond the border
is contrary to ritual.
From the Gǔliáng Zhuàn, third year of Duke Huán.
Abandon
Initially, the Sītú of Ruì in Sòng gave birth to a daughter,
who was red and hairy,
so they abandoned her at the foot of the dike.
A concubine of Gòng Jī picked her up and brought her in,
naming her Qì.
She grew up to be beautiful.
When Duke Píng entered in the evening, Gòng Jī dined with him,
and the duke saw Qì.
He gazed at her intently,
and took her as his favored concubine.
(Zuǒzhuàn, Xīgōng 26th Year)
Submitting a Petition to Ransom Father
Chún Yú Yì, the chief of the granaries of Qí, was accused of a crime punishable by penalty,
and was to be escorted west to Cháng'ān.
He had five daughters,
who followed him weeping.
Furious, Chún Yú Yì scolded them:
"I only have daughters and no sons,
so in times of crisis, there is no one to rely on."
Thereupon, his youngest daughter, Tí Yíng, accompanied her father westward to the capital.
She submitted a petition stating:
"My father served as an official,
and in Qí he was praised for his integrity and fairness.
Now he has been convicted and faces punishment.
I am willing to offer myself as a government slave,
to redeem my father from his criminal penalty."
When the petition reached the emperor,
he was moved by her devotion,
and that year, the corporal punishment laws were abolished.
(Records of the Grand Historian)
Female Prisoner
In Wúxīng's Yúbù Township, there was a Female Prisoner Mountain,
also called Female Prison Mountain.
During the Hàn dynasty, Shěn Huī found the landscape of Kētián exceptionally beautiful,
and planned to settle there.
His daughter disclosed this to her in-law's family, the Shěn Róng household,
who seized the land.
Huī resented his daughter for this,
lured her back for a home visit,
and imprisoned her in the mountain ruins north of Zhù Creek,
showing no remorse until his death.
He further decreed that for three generations thereafter, no female children should be raised.
Róng, whose courtesy name was Wēiqīng,
persuaded the formidable bandit Yǐn Liáng to surrender,
for which Emperor Guāngwǔ commended him,
and offered him the title of Marquis of Hǎihūn, which he declined.
"The Illustrated Classic"
Since Chén Jiàn's dream
Fú County Magistrate Zhào Zhǐ dispatched his subordinate Xiān Níhé,
who in the eleventh month of the first year of the Yǒngjiàn era went to Bà Commandery,
but drowned and died at Chéngrú Tān.
His son Xián searched for the body but could not find it.
His daughter Luò was twenty-five years old,
and had two children aged five.
By the second month of the second year, on the fifteenth day, the body still had not been found.
Luò then took a small boat to the place where her father had drowned,
wept in grief, and threw herself into the river to drown.
She appeared in a dream and told Xián:
"On the twenty-first day, I will emerge together with Father."
When that day arrived,
father and daughter indeed floated up together on the river in the commandery and county,
and the authorities reported this, erecting a stele for them to honor her filial sincerity.
The "Water Classic"
records her in Later Hàn as Shūxiān Xióng.
Throwing Clothes to Pray for Father
The filial daughter Cáo É
was a person from Shàngyú.
Her father Cáo Xū was a shaman,
able to beat time and sing along,
dancing to entertain the gods.
In the fifth month of the second year of the Hàn'ān era,
he went upstream against the waves to welcome the Five Lords,
but was drowned by the water,
and his body could not be found.
At that time, É was fourteen years old.
She wailed with longing for Xū,
grieving and chanting by the marsh's edge.
After seventeen days,
she threw a garment into the water,
praying that where her father's body was,
the garment would sink.
The garment drifted with the current to a place and sank,
so É followed the garment and threw herself into the river to die.
"Xiàng Yuán's Biographies of Women"
After five days, she emerged holding her father's corpse.
"The Stele"
The county magistrate Dù Shàng, moved by pity for her righteousness,
had her reburied,
and ordered his disciple Hándān Zǐlǐ to compose a stele for her.
"Kuàijī Diǎnlù"
Later texts write "welcoming and dancing," which seems to be an error.
Seeking Revenge
Shēntú Pán, styled Zǐlóng,
was from Wàihuáng.
In the same commandery, a woman named Gōushì Yù sought revenge for her father,
killing members of her husband's clan.
The officials arrested Yù and reported to the magistrate,
Liáng Pèi, who intended to sentence her to death.
Pán remonstrated with him, saying:
"Yù's integrity and righteousness are sufficient to move even the shameless descendants
and inspire those who have endured humiliation.
Pèi then submitted a judgment sentencing her to death."
Hòu Hàn shū
Sān Nǚ Zàng Fù
The governor of Shǔ Commandery, surnamed Wáng and styled Zǐyǎ,
was a native of Xī'è in Nányáng.
He had three daughters but no sons,
and the family had accumulated a fortune of a thousand gold pieces.
When their father passed away and was to be buried,
the daughters said to one another:
"Our late father gave birth to us sisters,
with no male siblings.
Now we must lay his spirit to rest in the dark dwelling,
shrouding his soul in the earth.
If he remains obscure and without descendants in the afterlife,
how can we manifest our father's virtue?"
Each contributed five million coins:
one daughter built the tomb,
while the other two each erected stone towers
to express their filial devotion.
The towers stood nearly eighteen feet high,
with columns over twenty feet in circumference.
The stone was bluish-green in color,
so polished it could serve as a mirror.
The craftsmanship was exquisite and intricately carved,
surpassing human skill in its perfection.
From the "Commentary on the Waterways Classic"
Throwing into the furnace
In Xuānchéng Commandery's Qīngyáng County, there was Méigēn Foundry and a filial daughter named Lǐ É.
É's father, a man of Wú, served as the iron official during the Great Emperor's time,
smelting to cast military weapons.
One evening, the refining metal was exhausted, but the metal did not emerge from the furnace.
At that time, Wú was newly established, and its laws were extremely strict:
anyone who wasted or damaged official property worth one hundred thousand would be sentenced to execution,
and their family's assets would be confiscated.
Yet the losses and damages caused by É's father amounted to over ten million.
É was fifteen years old
and deeply grieved by this.
Due to the intense fire, she threw herself into the furnace.
A brilliant light shot up to the heavens,
whereupon the molten metal boiled and surged,
overflowing from the furnace's mouth.
The two shoes É had been wearing floated out,
while her body transformed within the furnace.
The molten metal flowed down, blocking the furnace,
and thus formed a canal,
with springs feeding it for twenty li,
until it joined the river.
The metal recovered amounted to hundreds of millions of jin,
and the iron in the canal remains to this day.
Therefore, it became a custom in Wú that whenever copper or iron is smelted, a shrine must first be erected for É,
where offerings are made to pray for blessings.
From "Jì Wén".
Treating the guest as the host
Péi Chénggōng's wife was Wáng Róng's daughter.
Wáng Róng went to visit them one morning.
Without being announced, he went straight into Péi's quarters.
Péi got down from the south side of the bed,
while his wife got down from the north side,
and facing their guest, they performed the roles of host and hostess,
without the slightest sign of embarrassment.
Shì Shuō
Loan money
Wáng Róng's daughter married Péi Wěi,
and borrowed tens of thousands in cash.
When the daughter returned home,
Wáng Róng looked displeased.
The daughter promptly repaid the money,
and only then did he become relieved.
End
Breaking out to seek reinforcements
Xún Sōng's youngest daughter Guàn displayed extraordinary courage from a young age.
When Sōng served as governor of Xiāngchéng,
he was besieged by Dù Zēng's forces.
With weakening strength and exhausted supplies,
he wished to seek help from his former subordinate General Píngnán Shí Lǎn,
but had no way to send the message.
Guàn, then only thirteen years old,
led several dozen warriors to scale the city walls, break through the siege, and escape at night.
The bandits pursued them fiercely,
but Guàn commanded and encouraged her soldiers to fight while advancing.
They managed to enter Lǔyáng Mountain and escape danger,
then she personally approached Lǎn to request troops.
She also wrote a letter on Sōng's behalf to Zhōu Fǎng, General of the Southern Central Army, seeking assistance,
and even formed a brotherly alliance with him.
Fǎng immediately sent his son Fǔ with three thousand troops to join Shí Lǎn,
and together they rescued Sōng.
When the bandits heard the troops had arrived, they scattered and fled.
This was all due to Guàn's efforts.
Records of the States South of Mount Huà
exclaimed in admiration
Xiè Huì's daughter of the Sòng dynasty was the consort of Péngchéng King Liú Yìkāng,
intelligent, talented, and beautiful.
With disheveled hair and bare feet,
she bid farewell to Huì, saying:
"Father, a true man should die in battle,
why suffer disgrace in the city streets?"
After speaking, she cried out and fainted,
passersby shedding tears for her.
From "History of the Southern Dynasties"
Body shielding
Zhāng Jì's eldest daughter Chǔ Yuàn married into the Kǒng family of Kuàijī,
but having no son, she returned to her paternal home.
When Zhāng Jì was attacked and killed,
his daughter shielded her father with her body, taking the blade,
and died before her father.
From the Book of Liáng
A jade hairpin
Wáng Yá held the position of prime minister,
and had a daughter married into the Dòu family.
She wanted to ask for 170,000 coins to buy a jade hairpin,
but Wáng Yá said:
"It's not that I'm unwilling to spend on you,
but this is an ominous object,
and it will surely bring disaster."
A few months later,
the daughter returned from a wedding banquet,
and told Wáng:
"That jade hairpin from before is now among the hair ornaments of Vice Director Féng's wife,
who is Féng Qiú's wife."
Wáng sighed and said:
"Féng is merely a minor official,
yet his wife's hair ornament costs 170,000 coins.
How can this last long?
How can he come to a good end?"
From "New Book of the South"
Accompanied his father
In the sixth year of the Xiántōng era,
a clerk of the Cāngzhōu Salt Bureau named Zhào Lín was convicted of a crime punishable by death.
As he was about to be executed, his daughter requested to die with her father,
explaining that her mother had died when she was seven,
and she had relied on her father's illicit salt trade for official profits to sustain her livelihood.
Now that her father's crime had been exposed,
she felt it right to share his fate.
The Salt Bureau official Cuī Jù, moved by her righteousness,
reported the matter in full.
An imperial decree praised her,
and pardoned her father from death.
The daughter then wept and said:
"I was once born by my father,
and now am granted life by the officials.
I vow to shave my head and devote myself to Buddhism to repay the sovereign."
Thereupon, she drew a blade from her bosom,
immediately cut off her ear to show her sincerity,
and after her father recovered from the illness following his pardoned death sentence,
she entered the Buddhist order.
From "Wén Sǒu".
Luring the bandits to the river
Zhèng Lù's brothers included one who held office beyond the river.
One evening, while mooring his boat on a riverbank,
local bandits suddenly arrived.
Zhèng immediately laid out all his gold and silk on the shore,
allowing the bandits to take whatever they wanted.
They touched none of it,
but only said, "We just want the attendant's young lady."
His daughter was of great beauty,
and the bandits had secretly learned of this.
The family members looked at each other,
unable to respond.
The daughter cheerfully offered to go.
The bandits prepared a small boat and carried her away.
The daughter said to the bandits:
"Although you are thieves,
surely you have homes
and relatives?
However, my family belongs to the official class.
Since I am to be your wife,
how can I be treated without proper ceremony?
If we reach your home,
and I can meet your relatives,
that would suffice to establish our union."
The bandits said:
"Agreed."
She then pointed to the two maids who had accompanied her,
"Since you are known as thieves,
these maids should not remain with me.
For your consideration,
it would be better to return them to my family."
The bandits, seeing the girl's beauty and her compliance,
found nothing objectionable.
They immediately rowed the boat themselves and carried the two maids away.
The daughter then threw herself into the river and died.
People of the time praised her virtue.
From "Qīng Suǒ Gāo Yì"
Cānjūn
Wáng Shǔ's chancellor Zhōu Xiáng,
who initially served in the Qiōngnán administration,
was managing the affairs of the capital bureau
when Línqióng County sent in the arson suspect Huáng Chónggǔ.
Upon being imprisoned, Huáng immediately presented a poem:
"By chance I left seclusion for Línqióng;
My conduct steadfast as valley pines.
Why must your governance, clear as water-mirror,
Tether this wild crane in a deep cage?"
Zhōu read the poem and summoned Huáng for an audience.
Huáng claimed to be a provincial graduate,
around thirty years of age,
with detailed and quick responses.
Zhōu ordered Huáng's immediate release.
Days later, Huáng presented more poems.
Zhōu found Huáng remarkably talented
and invited Huáng to the academy
to accompany his nephews and students.
Huáng excelled at chess and zither,
and was skilled in calligraphy and painting.
The next day, Zhōu recommended Huáng for the acting position of Bureau Registrar.
Huáng gained renown for concise judgments,
inspiring awe and submission among clerks,
and handling documents with strict clarity.
Zhōu, impressed by Huáng's intelligence
and admiring Huáng's elegant demeanor,
after nearly a year in office,
wished to marry his daughter to Huáng.
Huáng then submitted a sealed letter of decline
with another poem:
"Since leaving emerald streams' shores,
I've dwelled in thatched hut, composing verse.
Assuming blue gown as commandery aide,
I've forever cast aside mirror and brow-paint.
My character stands tall like green pines;
My resolve rings true as white jade.
If the administration would take me as son-in-law,
I pray Heaven swiftly make me male."
Zhōu read it with astonishment
and summoned Huáng for questioning.
It was revealed Huáng was the daughter of Prefect Huáng,
orphaned young,
living only with an old nurse,
never having married.
Zhōu admired her chastity even more;
the entire commandery marveled at this.
She soon requested to resign and return
to her former seclusion in Línqióng.
None ever knew her fate thereafter.
From "Records from Yùxī."
Jīng Guān
In the crevice of the cliff in Jīngguān Gorge lies a coffin,
made of brambles.
Long ago, a man with nine sons could not bury his father after his death,
but a daughter wove brambles into a coffin.
The identity of this person is unknown,
as the saying goes:
"Nine sons failed to bury their father,
while one daughter crafted a bramble coffin."
From "Records of Ancient and Modern Times"
Tiger Crown
Empress Lü passed away,
Zhōu Bó and others completely exterminated
the various Lüs, and the King of Lángyé also came from Qí to Cháng'ān.
The high officials deliberated and wished to enthrone the King of Qí,
all saying:
"The maternal family of Sì Jūn is vicious and cruel,
like a tiger wearing a hat.
The Hàn dynasty nearly lost the empire because of the Lǚ family,
and now if we enthrone the King of Qí again,
this would be wishing to restore the Lǚ clan.
The maternal family of the King of Dài, the Bó family,
are gentlemen and honorable persons."
Hàn Jì
On Calligraphy
Yǎng Yùn's mother was
the daughter of Sīmǎ Qiān.
When Yùn first read his maternal grandfather Grand Historian's records,
he became quite skilled in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and was praised for his talent.
The Book of Han
records that after Qiān died,
his grandson Yáng Yùn propagated his work,
thus making it widely known.
Above
Resolving Resentment
Fán Zhòng, styled Jūnyún,
was the maternal grandfather of Emperor Guāngwǔ.
His wealth amounted to millions,
yet he generously benefited his clan.
When his grandsons, the Hé brothers, quarreled over property,
Zhòng felt ashamed by this,
and used two qǐng of farmland to resolve their dispute.
The county praised his virtue,
electing him as village elder.
He died at over eighty years of age.
(Book of the Later Hàn)
Wúwéi Wàijiā
Wáng Fú, styled Jiéxìn,
was a native of Línjìng in Āndìng.
In his youth, he loved learning and had lofty aspirations and integrity,
and was on friendly terms with Mǎ Róng, Dòu Zhāng, Zhāng Héng, Cuī Yuàn, and others.
The custom in Āndìng was to look down upon children of concubines,
and since Fú had no maternal relatives,
he was despised by the local people.
Appraising and Evaluating
Yǐn Yǐ and Yǔ Héng were both grandsons of General Xiè Zhènxī,
Yǐn was straightforward and intelligent from a young age,
while Yǔ often did not acknowledge this.
Once, they went together to visit Xiè Ān,
who looked closely at Yǐn and said:
"Ā Cháo truly resembles General Zhènxī."
Thereupon, Yǔ whispered softly:
"In what way exactly does he resemble him?"
Xiè Ān continued and added:
"Cháo's cheek resembles General Zhènxī's."
Yǔ then said:
"If it's just the cheek that resembles,
is that enough to make him outstanding?"
Beware of fear, for it brings affliction.
Xiāo Huìkāi,
the son of Sīhuà,
was spirited from a young age.
He initially served as a Gentleman of the Palace Library,
and his literary works were all by renowned masters.
Being young,
Huìkāi's interests and inclinations often differed from others';
he might not speak to his peers for up to three years.
His maternal grandfather, the Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments of Pei Commandery, Liú Chéng of Shào, admonished him, saying:
"You are the son of an honored and related family,
and should adapt to the customs of the times,
fostering harmony both within and without.
If you persist in your own ways,
will it not lead to minor harms and many peculiarities,
thereby incurring the troubles of the world?"
Huìkāi replied:
"It is indeed fitting for people in the world to seek harmony as if with kindness,
but I cannot help being upright and unyielding.
I am ashamed to be seen as an ordinary person.
Like an unfinished painting of a dragon,
this is why I often end up being contrary."
Book of Sòng
All seem graceful and charming
Wáng Yún was pure and diligent in study.
Shěn Yuē, upon seeing Yún, thought he resembled his maternal grandfather Yuán Càn,
and said to the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Zhāng Jì:
"Is it not only the forehead of the young gentleman Wáng that resembles Lord Yuán?
His demeanor and charm are all quite similar."
Jì replied:
"Lord Yuán would always appear stern and solemn when meeting people,
while the young gentleman Wáng invariably greets others with cheer and smiles.
Only in this one aspect they are not exactly alike."
Book of Liáng
Yáng Yuán
Lù Chuí was recognized as exceptional by his maternal grandfather Zhāng Dài in his youth,
who said to his sons:
"This is the Yáng Yuán of your family."
Self-flagellation
Huángfǔ Jì sān suì ér gū,
wèi wàizǔ Wéi Xiàokuān suǒ jū yǎng,
cháng yǔ zhū wàixiōng bóyì,
Xiàokuān dū yǐ yán xùn,
Jì tàn mìng zuǒyòu zì zhàng,
Xiàokuān wén ér duì zhī liútì,
yúshì bó shè jīngshǐ.
"Suí Shū"
Patting the back
Yáng Yúlíng had a son named Sìfù,
whose maternal grandfather Hán Huàng patted him on the back and said:
"Both your fame and rank shall surpass your father's,
this is the Yáng family's blessing."
From the "Original Biography"
Wèi Yáng
Wèi Yáng is about Duke Kāng's longing for his mother.
Duke Kāng's mother was the daughter of Duke Xiàn of Jìn.
When Duke Wén suffered the disaster caused by Lí Jī and had not yet returned,
Lady Qín passed away.
Duke Mù installed Duke Wén,
and Duke Kāng, then the crown prince,
saw Duke Wén off north of the Wèi River.
Longing for his mother whom he could no longer see,
he said, "When I see my maternal uncle, it is as if my mother were still alive."
From the "Odes of Qín"
Threw the jade disc
In the seventeenth year of Yǒngpíng,
an edict stated:
"Sīmǎ Qiān's writing was completed,
bringing fame to his family for generations.
Yet because of his personal disgrace in punishment,
he used subtle literature to satirize and criticize his era.
He is not a righteous man!
In "Bān Gù's Citation," Emperor Wèi Míng asked Wáng Sù:
"Did Sīmǎ Qiān, because of his punishment,
harbor hidden grievances in writing the "Shǐjì,"
not disparaging Emperor Xiàowǔ leading to resentment?
Wáng Sù replied:
"Sīmǎ Qiān's record-keeping
neither exaggerated the virtuous
nor concealed the wicked.
Liú Xiàng and Yáng Xióng admired his skill in narration,
claiming he had the talent of a good historian,
calling it a true record.
Emperor Hàn Wǔ heard of his "Shǐjì" narrative,
viewed the annals of Emperor Xiàojǐng and his own,
then became very angry,
had them removed and discarded.
To this day, these two annals exist in record but not in text.
Later, due to the case of Lǐ Líng,
Sīmǎ Qiān was imprisoned in the silkworm chamber.
Thus, any hidden criticism was directed at Emperor Xiàowǔ,
and not at Sīmǎ Qiān himself.
"Wèi Zhì"
Duke Wén of Qín welcomed Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn,
and when they reached the Hé River, Zǐ Fàn presented a jade disk to the prince, saying:
"I have followed you, carrying the tether and halter, on your travels throughout the world;
my offenses are many.
I myself am aware of them,
how much more so must you be?
I beg to take my leave from here."
The prince replied:
"If I do not share the same heart with my maternal uncle,
may the clear waters bear witness against me."
He then cast the jade disk into the Hé River.
(Zuǒzhuàn, Xī 24)
Sānshēng
King Wén of Chǔ attacked Shēn and passed by Dèng.
Marquis Qí of Dèng said:
"He is my nephew,
let us stop and entertain him."
Zhuīshēng, Dānshēng, and Yǎngshēng requested to kill the ruler of Chǔ,
but the Marquis of Dèng did not consent.
The three nephews said:
"The one who will destroy the state of Dèng is certainly this man.
If we do not plan early,
later, my lord, when you bite your navel, will it be time to plan then?
Planning now is the right time."
The Marquis of Dèng said:
"People will not eat my leftovers."
They replied:
"If you do not follow your three ministers,
then the altars of soil and grain will indeed not receive blood sacrifices, and from where will you, my lord, obtain leftovers?"
He did not follow their advice.
In the same year, the ruler of Chǔ attacked Dèng.
In the sixteenth year, Chǔ again attacked Dèng,
and destroyed it.
Zhuāng 6
Punishing the Maternal Uncle
Initially,
Shū Xiàng wanted to marry a daughter of Shēn Gōng Wūchén,
but his mother wanted him to marry someone from her own clan.
Shū Xiàng said:
"My father has many concubines but few sons by them,
so I take warning from my maternal uncles' situation."
Zhāo (Twenty-eighth Year)
Commentary:
This means the father had many concubines but few sons by them,
suggesting the mother's nature was not tolerant.
Revenge
Jiǎ Shū, styled Zǐhòu,
avenged his maternal uncle Sòng Yuàn,
was captured by officials in the county,
imprisoned and sentenced to death.
Guō Línzōng spoke with Shū,
shedding tears of sincere grief.
He went to the county magistrate,
and eloquently described Shū as a man who pursued righteousness in seeking vengeance.
Shū was pardoned,
but the county did not forgive him; only after the commandery submitted a petition was he ultimately exonerated.
(from Xiè Chéng's Book)
unsummoned
Fàn Pāng's nephew Xīpíng Lǐ Sòng,
a descendant of a noble clan yet rejected by his village,
the Regular Palace Attendant Táng Héng recommended Sòng to Zōng Zī, who intended to employ him as an official.
Fàn Pāng deemed him unworthy,
so he delayed and did not summon him.
Zī redirected his anger,
flogging the clerk Zhū Líng.
Líng looked up and said:
"Fàn Pāng's pure judgment
is like using a sharp blade to cut through decayed wood.
Today, I would rather be beaten to death than disobey Fàn Pāng."
Zī then stopped.
"History of the Later Han"
Chewing dates to feed
Píngqiū Chéng Mò at the age of fourteen when his father died,
embraced the corpse wailing in grief and sorrow,
his maternal uncle pitied his frail condition,
chewed date flesh to feed him,
but Mò, upon seeing the food, sobbed,
unable to swallow it.
"Cài Yōng's Memorial"
Funeral Arrangements
Jí Hóng had a reputation for brilliance from a young age,
and by age nine had mastered the Book of Documents.
When his maternal uncle Hé Miǎo died,
the family was impoverished with young children,
so Hóng personally constructed the tomb and conducted the burial.
(Records of the Three Capital Regions)
Clothing and bedding not accepted.
Huáng Xiāng, styled Wénqiáng,
at the age of twelve,
his family's livelihood was impoverished and destitute,
with insufficient clothing and food.
His maternal uncle, the Marquis of Lóngxiāng, made clothes and bedding for him,
but he did not accept them.
"Records of the Eastern Pavilion"
The physiognomy of the residence
Wèi Shū, styled Yángyuán,
was a native of Fán in Rènchéng.
Orphaned young, he was raised by his maternal family, the Níngs.
When the Níngs built a residence,
a geomancer predicted it would produce an eminent nephew.
His maternal grandmother, considering her Wèi family nephew young and intelligent,
believed he would fulfill the prophecy.
Shū said:
"I shall bring this residence to fruition for my maternal grandfather."
Later, he became a参军 (cānjūn) to the相国 (xiàngguó),
and Emperor Wén remarked:
"Wèi Shū is the hall,
the very leader among men."
From the "Jìn Biography"
corrupting morals
Wáng Yífǔ's father, Wáng Yì, served as General Who Guards the North.
An official document was about to remove him from his post.
At the time, Yífǔ was seventeen years old.
He went to see his maternal uncle by succession, Yáng Hù, to present the circumstances of the case.
His arguments were exceptionally brilliant and forceful.
However, Hù did not agree with him.
Yífǔ flicked his sleeves and stood up to leave.
Hù turned to his guests and said:
"This man is certain to achieve great fame and hold high positions in the world,
but the one who will corrupt customs and damage moral teachings
will surely be this man."
from "Jìnyáng Qiū"
Bright Illumination
Wáng Jì, courtesy name Wǔzǐ,
was the maternal uncle of Wèi Jiè.
Handsome and dashing with an elegant demeanor,
he would sigh upon seeing Jiè, saying:
"With a pearl and jade by my side,
I feel the shabbiness of my own appearance."
In A New Account of the Tales of the World,
it is recorded that Jì once traveled with Jiè
and told people:
"Yesterday I went out with my nephew,
and it was like having a bright pearl beside me,
radiantly illuminating those around."
From his Separate Biography.
Hán fàn
Xī Jiàn encountered the chaos of the Yǒngjiā period,
while in his hometown,
he was extremely impoverished and hungry.
The villagers, recognizing his reputation and virtue,
took turns providing him with food.
He often brought along his elder brother's son Xī Mài and his nephew Zhōu Yì, two young boys, to eat.
The villagers said:
"Each of us is suffering from hunger and hardship.
Because of your virtue,
we wish to help you collectively,
but we fear we cannot support all of you."
Thereupon, Xī Jiàn went alone to eat,
but would always hold rice between his cheeks,
and upon returning, spit it out to feed the two boys.
Later, they all survived and crossed the river together.
After Xī Jiàn passed away,
Zhōu Yì resigned from his position as magistrate of Shàn County and returned,
keeping vigil by Xī Jiàn's spirit bed,
observing mourning in his heart for three full years.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Grand and majestic
Liú Yǔ, styled Qìngsūn,
and his younger brother Liú Kūn, styled Yuèshí,
both served as Imperial Secretaries,
being nephews of Guō Yì.
They were renowned figures of their time,
and the capital had a saying about them:
"In Luòyáng, brilliant and outstanding,

Removing a Tumor
Zhū Língshí from a young age enjoyed martial pursuits,
being quite frivolous and unrestrained in conduct.
His maternal uncle of the Huáinán Jiǎng clan was a man of meager talent and inferior quality,
Língshí made his uncle lie down in the reception hall,
cut a one-cun square piece of paper,
and pasted it on his uncle's pillow,
then he himself would stand and throw a knife at it from a distance,
eight or nine feet away,
hitting the target a hundred times out of a hundred throws.
Although the uncle was terrified and trembling with fear,
out of fear of Língshí he ultimately dared not move.
The uncle had a large tumor on his head,
Língshí waited until his uncle was asleep,
sneaked in and cut it off,
and the uncle died immediately.

every time his parents had not yet eaten,
the wet nurse wanted Lìn to eat first,

His maternal uncle Ruǎn Xiàoxù heard of this

Executing the Nephew Despite His Innocence
During the siege of Nínglíng by Liú Chāng,

His lone nephew Zhāng Jùn was defending the northwest section,
and had never looked back,
yet Liú Chāng dragged him down and beheaded him.

the historian commented that when commanding troops to defend the city against rebels,
one relies solely on rewards and punishments.
But now he executed his nephew without cause,
causing the soldiers' loyalty to waver—
nothing could be more inauspicious than this.

Judgment of Defamation
Cuī Hù failed the imperial examination,
and was angry with his examiner Miáo Dēng,
who was actually his maternal uncle three times removed.
He then privately wrote a judgment header,
slandering his uncle by saying:
"There is a man with pigskin on his back,
when asked why he doesn't remove it,
he says it was bestowed upon him."
The judgment stated:
"When the people of Cáo bared Zhòng Ěr's back,
his fused ribs were revealed for all to see.
When Xiàng Lǐ stripped Miáo Dēng,
the pigskin came into view."
Earlier, when Dēng served as magistrate of the eastern capital region,
Xiàng Lǐ Zào, who was then the governor,
wanted to cane him,
and when his back was bared, there was a patch of hair several inches long,
hence the reference.
It also said: "In times of peace,
the fire drill becomes useless,
but during days of idleness and gluttony,
it wags and begs,"
both referring to his tail.

Not serving a female ruler
When Dí Rénjié served as chancellor,
his maternal aunt of the Lú family resided in a villa south of Wǔqiáo.
The aunt had only one son who had never visited the capital.
As a relative, Lord Liáng (Dí Rénjié) would meticulously observe ceremonial etiquette
during seasonal festivals and lunar transitions,
often taking leave during heavy snowfall periods.
Once while inquiring after Aunt Lú's well-being,
he happened to see his cousin returning with bow and arrows,
carrying pheasants and hares for meals.
After presenting the game to his mother in the northern hall,
the cousin casually greeted Lord Liáng
with rather dismissive demeanor.
Thereupon Lord Liáng addressed his aunt:
"Though I now serve as chancellor,
what pursuits bring my cousin joy?
I wish to fully support his aspirations."
The aunt replied:
"Your eminence matters not to us -
I simply don't wish my son to serve a female sovereign."
Lord Liáng withdrew in great shame.

is an external brother,

playing the qin

excelled at playing the qin.

Cuī Yànzhāo and Wáng Níng were maternal cousins,
Níng had achieved prominence early in the Dàzhōng era while Yànzhāo was still without an official post.

Father One
Jì Zhòng held exclusive power,
the Earl of Zhèng was troubled by this,
and sent his son-in-law Yōng Jiǔ to kill him.
He was about to feast him in the suburbs,
when Yōng Jī learned of it.
She said to her mother,
"Which is closer, father or husband?"
Her mother said,
"Any man can be a husband,
but there is only one father.
How can they be compared?"
So she informed Jì Zhòng, saying,
"The Yōng family is leaving his residence and plans to feast you in the suburbs.
I am suspicious of this and so inform you."
Jì Zhòng killed Yōng Jiǔ and displayed his corpse.
Duke of Zhōu's Wāng carried him out, saying,
"He consulted a woman about his plans,
no wonder he died."
Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Huán, Year 14
The Son-in-Law Who Lives with the Wife's Family
Chúnyú Kūn was
a son-in-law who lived with his wife's family in the state of Qí.
"The Biographies of Jesters" in Records of the Grand Historian
states: In Qín, when a wealthy family's son came of age, he would establish a separate household;
when a poor family's son came of age, he would marry into his wife's family.
"The Biography of Jiǎ Yì" in Book of Hàn
comments by Yán Shīgǔ:
"He is called a 'zhuìxù'
because it is inappropriate for him to reside in his wife's home,
just like a wart or tumor on the human body—
something that should not be there."
Annotations
explain that people often mockingly call such sons-in-law 'bùdài' [cloth bag],
meaning it's like being stuffed into a cloth bag
where one cannot breathe freely.
Another interpretation says:
When a family has daughters but no sons,
fearing the family line will end with them,
they are unwilling to marry their daughters out.
Instead, they bring in a son-in-law to continue the family line.
"Yī Jué Liáo"
Did not bow
After Chén Shèng was established as king,
his wife's father and brothers went to see him.
Shèng treated them as ordinary guests,
bowing with hands clasped without prostration,
showing no additional courtesy.
His father-in-law angrily said:
"Assuming a false title through rebellion and showing arrogance toward elders,
this cannot last long."
He left without taking leave.
King Chén knelt in apology,
but the father-in-law paid no attention,
making the king feel ashamed.
He asked Kǒng Fù about this,
and Zǐyú replied:
"According to ritual, marriage makes one brothers,
and the wife's parents become external uncles and aunts.
From this principle, whether to bow in prostration becomes clear.
Previously, Lord Xìnlíng of Wèi once consulted my father about this matter,
and my father said: For maternal uncles' wives,
and paternal uncles with matching kinship,
if they are older in virtue and years,
even bowing in prostration is permissible.
For those younger than oneself,
a bow with hands clasped is sufficient.
This arises from human feelings and can be practiced regularly.
Under the way of the Zhōu dynasty, even after a hundred generations,
marriages should not occur between certain families,
to honor the shared substance of former rulers."
The king said: Excellent.
From "Kǒng Cóngzǐ" chapter six
Son-in-law
Zhāng Ěr's son Zhāng Áo succeeded him as King of Zhào,
Gāozǔ's eldest daughter, Princess Lǔyuán, became the queen of King Áo of Zhào.
In the seventh year of Hàn, Gāozǔ passed through Zhào from Píngchéng,
the King of Zhào attended from morning till night, baring his arms and wearing leather armguards,
presenting food with very humble etiquette,
observing the rites of a son-in-law. Gāozǔ sat with legs spread apart,
arrogantly cursing and showing great disrespect,
treating him with contempt.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Qiàn
Sòng Jiàn originally had a weak lower back,
and the pain had persisted for four or five days.
When it rained,
the various sons-in-law of the Huáng family saw a foundation stone below the lintel at Jiàn's house,
and proceeded to play with it.
Jiàn also wanted to imitate them,
but when he tried, he couldn't lift it.
He then put it back,
and by evening, his lower back was so painful he couldn't manage,
and the ailment has not healed to this day.
"The Biography of Tǔ Cāng Gōng"
Xú Guǎng said:
"Qiàn
means son-in-law."
Married Far Away
Zhāng Yǔ would report his daily life whenever he fell ill,
and Emperor Chéng personally visited to inquire about him.
Zhāng Yǔ said:
"This old minister has four sons and one daughter.
I love my daughter more than my sons.
She was married far away to Xiāo Xián, the governor of Zhāngyè,
and I cannot overcome my personal paternal feelings,
wishing to be closer to her."
The emperor immediately transferred Xiāo Xián to be the governor of Hóngnóng.
"Basic Biography"
Pure as ice and smooth as jade
Wèi Jiè possessed a natural grace that set him apart in his time,
and his father-in-law Yuè Guǎng enjoyed a renowned reputation throughout the land.
Commentators remarked, comparing Péi Shūtōng, that the father-in-law had the purity of ice,
while the son-in-law held the promise of jade's luster.
They were deemed a match akin to the historic alliances between Qín and Jìn.
Later, as the empire fell into great turmoil,
Wèi Jiè relocated his family westward to Jiāngxià.
His wife passed away first,
and General Zhēngnán Shān Jiǎn, upon meeting him,
held him in high esteem and deep respect.
Shān Jiǎn said:
"In the past, Dài Shūluán married off his daughter solely to the virtuous,
without regard for status or wealth.
How much more so for the Wèi family, a powerful and noble lineage,
and a man of such esteemed reputation?"
Thus, he gave his daughter to him in marriage.
In the "History of Jìn" and other biographies, "jade" is written as "jade disc."
Restraint and Slander
Dài Ruòsī's younger brother Miǎo,
was the son-in-law of Huà Tán.
During his lifetime, Tán often suppressed Yuān while promoting others,
Miǎo and Ruòsī always resented this, and when they came to power,
they frequently slandered Tán before the Emperor,
thus blocking his official advancement.
Tán often felt discontent and disappointment,
and once remarked calmly to the Emperor:
"Your servant has grown old,
and will await death in the Imperial Library—
Jí Àn's words live on today."
The Emperor was displeased for a long time,
but eventually appointed him as an Additional Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
《Book of Jìn》
Trapped
Sànqí Péi Xiá married the daughter of Tàiwèi Wǎng.
Three days after the wedding,
all the sons-in-law gathered for a grand meeting,
where renowned scholars and descendants of the Wǎng and Péi families all assembled.
Guō Zǐxuán was present,
and he initiated a debate with Péi.
Zǐxuán's talent was exceptionally profound and extensive.
Initially, after several exchanges, the debate was not yet satisfying,
as Guō presented his arguments with great vigor and intensity.
Péi calmly elaborated on his previous statements,
with reasoning and implications that were remarkably subtle.
All those seated sighed in admiration and expressed delight.
Wǎng also found it extraordinary,
and said to everyone:
"Do not engage in this,
or you will be bested by my son-in-law."
From "Shì Shuō".
Late decree
Xiè Lángzhōng Wàn was the son-in-law of Wáng Lántián,
and once, wearing a white silk turban and riding in a sedan chair,
he went straight to the main hall of Yángzhōu,
where he saw Wáng and said bluntly:
"People say Your Lordship is foolish,
and indeed Your Lordship is truly foolish."
Lántián replied:
"It's not that there is no such talk,
only that I came to recognition late."
From "Shì Shuō"
punish the widowed wife
Qí Xiè Tiǎo was the son-in-law of Wáng Jìngzé.
It was said that Jìngzé's daughter often carried a dagger, intending to take revenge on Tiǎo,
so Tiǎo dared not meet her.
When he was about to be appointed to the Ministry of Personnel,
he was especially modest and self-effacing.
The Secretary Lang Fàn Zhèn mocked him, saying:
"Your talent is beyond reproach,
but it is a pity that this appointment cannot set an example for your own wife."
Tiǎo looked ashamed.
When he faced execution,
he sighed and said:
"How can the Way of Heaven be obscured?
Although I did not kill Duke Wáng,
Duke Wáng died because of me."
Bǐ Zhāng Yǔ
Cuī Guāng of Wèi, since attaining high rank,
rarely recommended anyone.
He once petitioned for his son-in-law,
Liú Jìngwēi of Péngchéng, stating:
"Jìngwēi serves as the warden of Wǔlǒng Fort in Jīngzhōu, and my daughter accompanies her husband there.
I constantly worry about bandit raids and their separation across north and south.
I beg to appoint him as Assistant Chief of Xúzhōu,
so they may temporarily gather in the capital."
Emperor Sùzōng granted this,
and contemporaries compared him to Zhāng Yǔ.
(Basic Biography)
Caning the Son-in-Law
Tián Shìzǐ Xiǎnbiāo, upon first being appointed as the Governor of Xiāngzhōu during the Suí dynasty,
focused solely on establishing authority. For those who violated prohibitions,
even if they were his closest intimates,
he
showed no leniency.
His son-in-law Dù Níng
traveled from Cháng'ān
to visit him. Shìzǐ
warned him
not to go
outside,
but Níng, having long been unable to return,
secretly ascended the north tower to ease his feelings of confinement.
When Shìzǐ learned of this,
he caned him fifty strokes.
From "The History of the Northern Dynasties."
Zhàngrén
Emperor Míng Huáng performed the fēngshàn ceremony at Mount Tài,
with Zhāng Yuè serving as the fēngshàn envoy.
Zhāng Yuè's son-in-law, Zhèng Yì, originally held a ninth-rank official position.
According to established precedent:
after the fēngshàn ceremony,
all officials from the three senior ministers downward were promoted one rank.
However, Zhèng Yì, due to Zhāng Yuè's influence, was suddenly promoted to the fifth rank,
and was also granted crimson official robes.
During a grand feast,
Emperor Xuán Zōng noticed Zhèng Yì's rapid rise in official rank
and questioned him in surprise.
Zhèng Yì had no answer to give.
Huáng Fān Chuò then said:
"This is the power of Mount Tài."
From the Yǒu Yáng Zá Zǔ
thereafter, father-in-law came to be referred to as "Mount Tài."
Sū È's Yǎn Yì
suggests it might be because Mount Tài has a peak called Zhàngrén Peak, hence the name.
From the Cóng Shū
Qīngchéng Mountain is considered the foremost of the Five Great Mountains,
thus it is also called Zhàngrén Mountain.
Nowadays, it is customary to call one's father-in-law "Lìng Yuè,"
and one's wife's uncles "Liè Yuè,"
often for this reason.
From the Qīngchéng Shān Jì
father-in-law and son-in-law
Zhāng Jì married Princess Nìngqīn,
and Emperor Xuánzōng held Jì in high regard,
even establishing a residence for him within the palace,
where he served by composing literary works.
The precious gifts he received were countless,
both he and Zhāng Jūn served in the Hànlín Academy, yet Jì boasted to Jūn about the gifts he received.
Jūn remarked:
"These are from a father-in-law to his son-in-law,
not bestowed by the Son of Heaven upon a scholar."
(From the Basic Biography)
Jì, having married the princess,
served in the Hànlín Academy,
and often flaunted his rare treasures before his colleagues.
Zhāng Shū said:
"These come from a father-in-law to his son-in-law,
not granted by the Son of Heaven to a scholar."
(From the Supplement to the National History)
Shòu Bó
Wéi Gāo was humiliated by Zhāng Yánbīn,
Cuī Yuán was treated coldly by Lǐ Yànyǔn,
both being sons-in-law of their elders,
yet later Wéi succeeded Zhāng in Xīchuān,
and Cuī saved Lǐ from capital punishment.
"New Book of the South"
Lǐ Yànyǔn
Cuī Yuán was poor and lowly in his youth,
and relied on relatives.
Lǐ Yànyǔn was then the Minister of Justice,
and treated him without much courtesy.
One night, Lǐ dreamed that he was in shackles,
and among a hundred of his peers who had become soldiers,
they were herded into a great hall where names were called,
and after passing by, the judgment was pronounced:
"According to the law."
Lǐ looked and saw a man in purple robes seated at the bench,
who was none other than Cuī.
He leaped forward and cried out in sorrow,
The man in purple robes said:
"Lǐ Yànyǔn is to be specially detained."
He woke up sweating,
and told Cuī all about it.
From then on, he treated Cuī generously,
and recommended him to Yáng Guózhōng.
Later, Cuī was appointed to oversee the capital's affairs,
and within a month, he was made chancellor.
After the capital was recaptured,
Lǐ had accepted a false official post,
and was among two hundred people, including Chén Xīliè, sentenced to execution.
Cuī, as the Secretariat Director,
during the interrogation and sentencing,
called out the names,
and after passing by, pronounced the judgment according to the law.
Lǐ cried out:
"Does the Chancellor not recall the prayer of years past?"
Cuī then realized,
and sentenced Lǐ Yànyǔn to detention,
submitting a detailed report of the matter,
requesting to redeem his crime.
It was approved, and he was exiled beyond the mountains.
How divine
was the dream of old!
"Unofficial History of the Táng"
Zhāng Yánshǎng
Zhāng Yánshǎng sought a son-in-law but found none to his satisfaction.
His wife, Miáo shì, virtuous and discerning,
specially selected the presented scholar Wéi Gāo and betrothed their daughter to him.
Gāo was by nature unrestrained and unconventional,
unbound by minor proprieties.
Yánshǎng secretly regretted the match,
so the maids and servants treated him with considerable disrespect.
Only Miáo shì treated him with increasing kindness.
Gāo thus bid farewell to travel east,
and the Zhāng family exhausted the dowry to prepare for his journey.
Yánshǎng, glad to see him leave,
offered seven loads of goods as a parting gift.
As Gāo departed,
he returned them all the next day,
keeping only the dowry items and books.
Five years later, Gāo rose to hold the commander's tally,
coinciding with Emperor Dézōng's visit to Fèngtiān,
and was appointed to Xīchuān with authority.
Replacing Yánshǎng, he changed his name to Hán Áo,
and none dared speak of it.
Upon reaching Dàhuí Station, thirty lǐ from the prefecture,
someone reported:
"The one replacing you, sir, is Wéi Gāo,
not Hán Áo."
Miáo shì said:
"It must be Wéi Láng."
Yánshǎng replied:
"There are many people in the world with the same name.
That Wéi scholar must have perished in obscurity;
how could he ascend to my position?"
The next day, it was indeed Wéi Gāo.
Yánshǎng felt ashamed and fearful,
and secretly fled through the west gate.
Gāo entered to see Miáo shì,
treating her with even greater respect than in his humble days.
He sought out those who had previously disrespected him,
and had them all beaten to death.
At that time, Guō Wéi of Sìbīn composed a poem:
"Like Confucius following Zhou and entering Qin,
which sage of old did not endure hardship?
How surprising it was then of Zhāng Yánshǎng,
not to recognize Wéi Gāo as a man of nobility."
From "Yúnxī Yǒu Yì"
When Emperor Dézōng returned to the capital,
he appointed Gāo as military governor of Fèngxiáng,
but Gāo earnestly declined and requested to be assigned to Xīchuān instead.
From "Dàojiào Língyàn Jì"
He did not observe the customary rites for a son-in-law.
Dù Huángsháng initially served as an official.
His daughter married Wéi Zhíyì,
but he was not highly regarded by Zhíyì.
When Zhíyì became prime minister,
Dù Huángsháng was appointed as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
He then suggested to Zhíyì,
"Lead all the officials
to request that the Crown Prince oversee the state."
Zhíyì quickly responded,
"You have just obtained this position,
how dare you speak of matters within the forbidden palace?"
Huángsháng indignantly replied,
"I have received favor from three reigns,
how can I be bought for a mere position?"
He immediately brushed off his sleeves and left.
Shortly after, Emperor Shùnzōng passed away,
and Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne.
Huángsháng became the prime minister,
while Zhíyì was demoted to Yázhōu.
Huángsháng ultimately protected him,
and upon his death in Língbiǎo,
he requested to return his remains
to handle the funeral affairs.
"Old Tang History"
called Yōnglǎo
Cuī Yá's wife, née Yōng,
was the daughter of a commander in Yángzhōu.
Yōng, because Cuī had a reputation for poetry,
provided a very generous dowry.
Yet Cuī showed no respect whatsoever,
merely calling his father-in-law "Old Yōng."
Yōng, grasping his sword, summoned his daughter,
and said to Cuī:
"I am a man from Héshuò,
accustomed only to archery and horsemanship.
My daughter should have married into a military family;
I merely admired the virtue of scholars.
My daughter shall not marry another.
I now order her to leave the household,
only to shave her head and become a nun."
Cuī, weeping in sorrow and regret,
parted from her in anguish, leaving a poem that said:
"The flowing stream on Longshan divides below,
Its heartbroken sobbing is too painful to hear.
Once Cháng'é entered the moon palace,
For a thousand autumns, White Cloud over Wū Gorge has been in vain."
Unrestrained
Shì'ān's son-in-law was named Huángfǔ Mì,
who in his youth was unrestrained
and solely devoted himself to gambling.
At that time, Shì'ān was serving as prime minister,
and despite repeated admonitions, Mì did not reform.
Shì'ān intended to personally report the matter to the emperor,
seeking to have him demoted and reprimanded.
Just as he began to speak,
saying, "Your subject has a son-in-law named Huángfǔ Mì,"
it happened that a border emergency arose.
With urgent news arriving,
there was no time to elaborate.
On another day, when he again intended to report in person,
he encountered the emperor's need to relieve himself.
The emperor hastily rose, pulling his sleeve, and called out from a distance,
finishing by saying:
"You have repeatedly mentioned your son-in-law Huángfǔ Mì.
Is it not that you wish him to be promoted?
He may be advanced one rank."
Shì'ān dared not explain,
so he assented and withdrew.
Mì was then promoted to Palace Attendant,
and later successively governed major prefectures,
retiring as Vice Minister of the Right,
and lived to the age of eighty-five.
Records from the Miscellaneous Notes of the Green Box
Ordered to strip off the sash
Zhāng Āndào never ate without being properly dressed.
Once during a hot summer month, he was having a meal with his son-in-law Wáng Gǒng,
and told Gǒng to remove his belt,
while he himself kept his gown and hat on as usual.
Gǒng did not dare to do so.
Zhāng said:
"From being a commoner and scholar, I have achieved my current status;
every meal is bestowed by the sovereign.
To enjoy the sovereign's bounty,
how dare I not show respect?
As for you, eating the food I provide,
even informal attire would be acceptable."
Bànzǐ

The next year, the Uighur Khagan sent his chancellor, Diédū Dudu, and over a thousand followers, along with his sister, Princess Gǔduōlù Pígā, leading fifty wives of great chieftains to welcome the bride and present betrothal gifts.
Diédū reached Zhenwu but was plundered by the Shiwei tribe,
and died in battle.
About seven hundred subordinates were all permitted to enter the court and lodged at the Honglu Hostel.
The emperor received the envoys at the Yanxi Gate.
At that time, the Khagan's letter was extremely respectful,
stating that they were all like brothers,
and now a son-in-law is half a son.
If Your Majesty is troubled by the Western Rong,
I, your son, request to eliminate them with troops.
《Book of Tang》
Child Example
The Turks sent a letter saying:
"The emperor is my wife's father, thus my elder;

brother-in-law
Two sons-in-law refer to each other as yà.
"Ěryǎ"
"The Book of Songs" says:
"Insignificant marriage connections.
Now people in Jiāngdōng call men married to sisters 'colleague sons-in-law.'"
"Commentary"
The reason two sons-in-law refer to each other as yà is,
that when one marries the elder sister,
and another marries the younger sister,
they are arranged in sequence;
also, when both come to the woman's family,
the elder sister's husband comes first,
the younger sister's husband follows,
which also creates a sequence.
"Shìmíng"
Brother-in-law
Yán Zhù during Hàn Wǔdì's reign served as Grand Master of the Palace,
was specially appointed and trusted,
once attended an informal banquet at leisure,
the Emperor asked Zhù about his life in his hometown,
Zhù replied that his family was poor,
and had been humiliated by a wealthy friend's son-in-law,
the Emperor asked what he desired in response,
he expressed his wish to become the Governor of Kuàijī,
thus he was appointed as the Governor of Kuàijī.
《Hàn Shū》
They did not pay homage.
Cài Āihóu married a woman from Chén,
Xīhóu also married one from there.
When Xī Guī was returning home and passed through Cài,
the Marquis of Cài said:
"She is my sister-in-law."
He detained her and met with her,
but did not treat her with due respect.
When Xīhóu heard of this,
he became angry,
and sent a message to King Wén of Chǔ, saying:
"Attack me,
and I will seek help from Cài, then you can attack them."
The Viscount of Chǔ followed this plan.
Zhuāng, year 11
Èr Wěi
Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn fled to the Dí tribe,
where the Dí people attacked the Qiánggāorú tribe,
capturing two of their daughters,
Shū Wěi and Jì Wěi, who were presented to the prince.
The prince took Jì Wěi as his wife,
and gave Shū Wěi in marriage
to Zhào Cuī.
(From the 22nd year of Duke Xī)
Dàqiáo Xiǎoqiáo
Zhōu Yú, styled Gōngjǐn,
served as a follower of the Central Protector Army.
Sūn Cè attacked Wǎn and captured Lord Qiáo,
whose two daughters were both of exceptional beauty.
Cè himself married the elder Qiáo,
while Yú married the younger Qiáo.
Cé casually teased Yú, saying:
"Though Lord Qiáo's two daughters have endured hardship,
having the two of us as sons-in-law should bring them joy enough."
Reciting a Rhapsody
Yǔ Dēngzhī, when Xiè Huì became the governor of Jīngzhōu,
requested to serve as his chief clerk,
while the grand administrator of Nánjùn concurrently held the position of chief clerk of the guard army.
Dēngzhī and Huì were both sons-in-law of the Cáo family,
and their reputations and status were originally equal.
Suddenly becoming his subordinate,
Dēngzhī felt very displeased.
When submitting documents at the office, he would only mention the current date,
and upon arriving, he never expressed words of gratitude.
Every time he entered for an audience,
he would fully carry boxes, bags, small tables, and mats—
if even one item was missing, he would refuse to sit.
Once, while seated with Huì, he recited the "Ode to the Western Expedition,"
saying:
"Life has its long and short fates,
positions have their smooth and blocked fortunes."
Although Huì resented this, he often tolerated him.
When Huì resisted the imperial army,
he wanted Dēngzhī to remain behind and guard,
but Dēngzhī refused.
After Huì's defeat,
Dēngzhī was dismissed from his post for not having fulfilled his duties,
placed under house arrest, and sent back home.
Hé Chéngtiān teased him, saying:
"Turning misfortune into fortune,
is not necessarily understood by all."
Dēngzhī replied:
"I almost ended up executed alongside those three scoundrels."
Chéngtiān had drafted a memorial for Huì that stated:
"When sailing east, execute these three scoundrels."
Hence, Dēngzhī was mocked for this.
From "The History of the Southern Dynasties"
match
Husband and wife,
signify a relationship of equals.
Among common scholars and people, it is called qī,
qī,
means to be equal,
as the husband is humble and not worthy of an honorable title,
thus they are spoken of as being on equal terms.
From "Shì Míng".
The Great Bonds of Human Relations
The Classic of Changes bases itself on Qián and Kūn, and the Book of Songs begins with "Guān Jū";
the Book of Documents praises the marriage of noble descent;
the Spring and Autumn Annals criticizes the failure to personally welcome the bride;
the relationship between husband and wife
is the most important principle of human relations,
and in the application of rites, only marriage is treated with utmost care.
Records of the Grand Historian
Resembling the Moon
The wife represents the Great Yin,
the minister models after the Metal position.
The "Chūnqiū Hànhánzī"
states that water and fire interact,
and yin and yang establish the symbol of husband and wife.
Above
Matching Yin and Yang,
the way of husband and wife,
corresponds with Yin and Yang,
and connects with the divine and enlightened.
If the husband is not virtuous, he cannot govern his wife;
if the wife is not virtuous, she cannot serve her husband.
If the husband does not govern his wife, dignity and propriety are abandoned;
if the wife does not serve her husband, righteousness and principle fall into ruin.
The harmony between husband and wife
should last a lifetime without separation.

married Túshān
Yǔ was thirty and still unmarried.
When he arrived at Túshān,
he feared that time was passing and he would miss the proper age for marriage,
so he declared:
"If I am to marry,
there must be a sign."
Then a nine-tailed white fox appeared before Yǔ.
Yǔ said:
"White
is the color of my garments.
The nine tails
are the emblem of kingship.
The song of Túshān says:
'Graceful white fox,
with nine tails so grand.
Establish home and family,
I come and you prosper.'"
Thus Yǔ married a woman of Túshān,
named Nǚ Jiāo.
From "The Annals of Wú and Yuè":
When Yǔ was traveling on official duties, he saw a woman of Túshān.
Before Yǔ could meet her, he had to inspect the southern regions.
The woman of Túshān then sent her maid to wait upon Yǔ at the southern side of Túshān Mountain,
and composed a song,
which went:
"Waiting for my love, oh, ah!"
From "The Annals of Lǚ".
First match
Zhèng's prince Hū went to Chén to meet his bride Guī,
on Xīnhài day he returned with Guīshì,
on Jiǎyín day they entered Zhèng,
Chén's Zhēnzǐ escorted the maiden - they first consummated marriage and then presented themselves at the ancestral temple,
