"This does not make them husband and wife,
they have deceived their ancestors,
it is contrary to ritual,
how can they produce offspring?"
Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Yǐn year 8
Not speaking
Marquis Āi of Cài, because of the affair at Shēn, praised Xī Guī to the King of Chǔ,
so the King of Chǔ went to Xī and entered under the pretense of a feast,
then destroyed Xī,
took Xī Guī back with him, and she bore Dǔ Áo,
and later King Chéng. Yet she did not speak,
the King of Chǔ asked her about it,
to which she replied:
"I, one woman, have served two husbands.
Even if I could not die,
what more is there to say?"
Zhuāng 14
Divination for Auspiciousness
When the Yì clan first divined about marrying their daughter to Jìng Zhòng,
and Jìng Zhòng took her as his wife,
the divination stated:
"Auspicious.
This is described as 'the male and female phoenixes flying together,
their harmonious cries ringing clear and melodious.
The descendants of the Guī clan
shall be nurtured among the Jiāng.
By the fifth generation, they shall flourish;
reaching the rank of chief minister.
After eight generations,
none shall match their greatness."
《Zuǒzhuàn》Duke Zhuāng, 22nd Year
My wife
The Dí people returned Jí Wěi to Jìn,
and requested her two sons.
Duke Wén married his daughter to Zhào Cuī,
who gave birth to Yuán Tóng, Píng Kuò, and Lóu Yīng.
Zhào Jī requested to welcome them back,
but Zhào Dùn and his mother Zǐ Yú declined.
Zhào Jī said:
"To forget the old upon gaining favor,
how can one command others?
They must be welcomed back."
She firmly pleaded until permission was granted for their return.
Considering Zhào Dùn talented,
she earnestly petitioned the duke,
making him the heir and placing her own three sons beneath him,
appointing Shū Wěi as the principal wife
while positioning herself below her.
*Xi* 24th year
treating each other with the respect due to a guest
Jì Jiù sent someone to lodge in Jì,
where Quē was weeding.
His wife brought him food,
and they treated each other with respect as if they were guests.
He returned with him,
and spoke to Duke Wén, saying:
"Respect is the accumulation of virtue.
One who can be respectful is sure to have virtue,
and virtue is used to govern the people.
I beg you, my lord, to employ him."
The duke appointed him as a junior army officer.
In the "Thirty-Three Discourses of the States," "accumulation" is written as "reverence."
Husband and Wife
Shēng Bó's mother was not betrothed through proper rites.
Mù Jiāng said, "I will not treat a concubine as a sister-in-law."
She gave birth to Shēng Bó and was then sent away.
She married Guǎn Yúxī of Qí, bore two children, and was widowed.
She returned to Shēng Bó.
Shēng Bó appointed his half-brother as a senior official and married off his half-sister.
Shī Xiàoshū and Xì Chōu came seeking a bride.
They sought a wife from Shēng Bó.
Shēng Bó seized Shī's wife and gave her to them.
The woman said, "Even birds and beasts do not lose their mates.
What will you do?"
He replied:
"I cannot die,
nor flee."
The woman then went.
She bore two children in the Xì family.
When the Xì family fell,
the people of Jìn returned her to Shī.
Shī welcomed her at the Yellow River,
but drowned her two children.
The woman angrily said:
"You could not protect your own wife and let her be taken away,
nor could you care for another's orphans but killed them.
How will you end?"
She then swore an oath against Shī.
The eleventh year of Chénggōng.
Refrain from blunt speech
Sūn Bó Zōng returned from court cheerfully, and
his wife said:
"You look pleased,
why is that?"
He replied:
"I spoke at court,
and all the ministers said my wisdom resembles that of Yáng Zǐ."
His wife responded:
"Yáng Zǐ was flashy without substance,
fond of speaking but lacking strategy,
that's why disaster befell him.
Why should you be pleased?"
Bó Zōng said:
"Let me invite the ministers for wine and converse with them,
you can listen and see."
She said:
"Very well."
After the drinking, his wife said:
"None of the ministers compare to you,
however, the people have long been unable to bear their superiors.
Disaster will surely reach you.
Why don't you quickly seek scholars to protect Zhōu Lí?"
They found Bì Yáng and Luán.
During the disaster of Fú Jì,
the ministers harmed Bó Zōng,
plotting to kill him.
Bì Yáng indeed escorted Zhōu Lí to Jīng.
"Jìn Yǔ"
Initially, whenever Bó Zōng went to court,
his wife would always warn him:
"Thieves hate the master,
the people detest their superiors.
You love speaking bluntly,
disaster will surely befall you."
"Chéng" fifteen
Distinguishing Surnames
The wife of Duke Táng of Qí
was the elder sister of Dōngguō Yǎn.
Dōngguō Yǎn served as a minister to Cuī Wǔzǐ.
When Duke Táng died,
Yǎn drove Wǔzǐ's carriage to offer condolences.
Wǔzǐ saw Táng Jiāng and found her beautiful,
so he ordered Yǎn to take her for him.
Yǎn said:
"Men and women should be distinguished by surname.
Now you are descended from Dīng,
and I am descended from Huán,
so it is not permissible."
Wǔzǐ consulted the milfoil stalks in divination,
obtaining the hexagram Kùn changing to Dàguò, and showed it to Chén Wénzǐ.
Wénzǐ said:
"The husband follows the wind,
the wind destroys,
so the wife should not be taken.
Moreover, the oracle says:
'Beset by stones,
resting on thistles and thorns,
entering his house,
he does not see his wife,
inauspicious.'"
Cuīzǐ said:
"What harm can a widow bring?
Her former husband has already borne it."
So he took her.
Duke Zhuāng had an affair with her,
frequently visiting the Cuī household.
Zhù had someone assassinate him.
The duke pleaded, saying:
"I, your servant, am on night watch duty,
and in matters of debauchery, I do not accept dual commands."
So they assassinated him.
《Xiāng》25th year
Zǐchǎn said to Shūxiàng:
"Distinguishing surnames between men and women
is a great principle of ritual.
Now in your inner court, there are actually four Jī women."
《Zhāo》1st year
The Inner Lord
Jìn's Hán Xū went to Qí to fetch a bride,
Qí's Chén Wúyǔ escorted the girl, presenting Shào Jiāng.
Shào Jiāng was favored by the Marquis of Jìn,
and was called Shào Qí. Shào Jiāng died,
and Duke Zhāo went to Jìn,
reaching the Yellow River,
when the Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Wénbó to decline, saying:
"She was not the principal wife,
I beg you, my lord, not to trouble yourself."
The Marquis of Qí sent Yàn Yīng to request a successor from Jìn,
saying:
"My unworthy ruler has the late ruler's daughter to fill the inner chambers,
illuminating my hopes,
but again without fortune,
she died prematurely,
If you, my lord, do not forget the friendship of the late rulers,
shining upon our humble state to pacify it,
and comfort its altars of soil and grain,
then there are still the late ruler's daughters,
and remaining aunts and sisters,
such persons. If you, my lord, do not reject our humble state and condescend,
to have them carefully selected to fill the ranks of consorts,
that is my hope."
Hán Xuānzǐ sent Shū Xiàng to reply, saying:
"My unworthy ruler cannot alone bear the affairs of his altars of soil and grain,
and has no principal wife.
If you kindly regard our humble state,
and grant an inner mistress,
not only my unworthy ruler,
but all his ministers will indeed receive your bounty.
From Táng Shū downwards,
they will truly honor and praise it."
Thus, the marriage was concluded.
Jìn's Hán Qǐ went to Qí to fetch the bride,
Gōngsūn Lěi, because Shào Jiāng had been favored,
substituted his own daughter for the duke's daughter and married the duke's daughter to another.
From "Zhāo" 2-3.
No laughter
Shū Xiàng obtained Zōng Míng.
In the past, Minister Jiǎ, who was ugly, married a beautiful wife.
For three years, she neither spoke nor smiled.
He drove her to the marshland and shot a pheasant, capturing it.
Only then did his wife begin to smile and speak.
Minister Jiǎ said:
"Talent cannot be dispensed with.
If I could not shoot,
you would never have spoken or smiled."
Twenty-eight.
Yuǎn Zhàngfū
The Wu army entered Yǐng,
and the King of Chǔ took his younger sister,
Jì Mǐ, with him as he fled.
When King Zhāo of Chǔ fled to Yún,
Zhōng Jiàn, a senior official of Chǔ, carried Jì Mǐ on his back while following the king.
When they were about to marry off Jì Mǐ,
she declined, saying:
"The reason a woman should avoid a man
is because Zhōng Jiàn has already carried me on his back."
So she was given in marriage to Zhōng Jiàn,
who was appointed as Music Minister.
The fourth year of the Dìng era
Xiào Kuàng
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ raised troops to attack Qí,
when an armored soldier named Shēn Hù laughed at Jiǎnzǐ.
"Why are you laughing?"
He replied,
"I have an old laugh.
During the mulberry season,
my neighbor, a man, went to the fields with his wife and saw a woman among the mulberry trees.
He chased after her but could not catch her.
Returning, he found his wife angry and leaving him.
I laugh at his foolishness."
Jiǎnzǐ said,
"Now I am attacking a state,
and the state is my foolishness."
He withdrew his army and returned.
《Shuō Yuàn》
Jìn Wéngōng went out to a meeting,
intending to attack Wèi.
Gōngzǐ Chú looked up at the sky and laughed.
The duke asked why he was laughing,
and he said,
"I laugh at my neighbor who was escorting his wife
to a private home when he saw a mulberry-picking woman on the road.
He was pleased and spoke with her,
but when he turned to look at his wife,
someone was also beckoning to her.
I secretly laugh at this."
The duke understood his words,
and stopped, leading the army back.
Before they arrived, someone had already attacked their northern borders.
《Liè Shuō Fú》
My son-in-law
In the past, a son of the Eastern Yí admired the rites of the Central States;
he had a daughter who became a widow,
so he arranged for her to take a private husband,
and she never married again.
Though she did not remarry,
it was not out of a sense of chastity.
Cāngwú Rǎo married a wife who was beautiful,
and he yielded her to his elder brother.
Though he yielded,
it was not a yielding in accordance with the rites.
From "Family Sayings"
The Love Pea Tree
Sòng dàfū Hán Féng married a beautiful wife,
which King Kāng seized from him.
Féng resented this,
so the king imprisoned him
and sentenced him to hard labor building the city walls.
His wife secretly sent Féng a letter with cryptic words,
saying:
"The rain falls incessantly,
the river is wide and deep,
the sun rises facing my heart."
The king asked Sū Hè about this,
who replied:
"'The rain falls incessantly' means sorrow and longing;
'the river is wide and deep'
means they cannot meet;
'the sun rises facing my heart' means she has death in mind."
Soon after, Féng committed suicide,
and his wife secretly rotted her clothes.
When the king climbed a tower with her,
she threw herself down.
Those around tried to grab her but her clothes tore in their hands.
She left a note in her belt,
saying:
"Your Majesty values my life,
but I value my death.
I wish for my bones to be buried with Féng."
The angry king refused,
ordering them buried in graves facing each other,
saying:
"If you lovers are so devoted,
let your graves join together—I won't stop it."
Overnight,
large catalpa trees grew from both graves,
within ten days becoming so large they embraced,
their trunks bending toward each other and roots intertwining below.
A pair of mandarin ducks,
always perched in the trees,
mournfully called day and night with necks entwined,
their cries moving all who heard.
The people of Sòng pitied them,
naming the trees "Longing Trees."
(From *Sōu Shén Jì*)
Hán Féng served as a minor official under King Kāng of Sòng during the Warring States period.
His wife, née Hé, was beautiful,
and the king desired her.
He arrested Féng
and built the Qīnglíng Tower.
Lady Hé wrote the "Magpie Song" to express her resolve,
then hanged herself.
"In the south mountains flies a magpie,
in the north mountains spreads a net.
The magpie flies high away—
what can the net do anyway?"
"Magpies fly in pairs,
caring not for phoenix's airs.
I am a common wife,
wanting not the Sòng king's life."
(From *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* and *Yù Tái Xīn Yǒng*)
Adopt the strong points
Chén Zhěn left Chǔ and went to Qín,
Zhāng Yí requested the King of Qín to kill him,
the king informed Zhěn,
Zhěn said:
"There was a man who had two wives;
someone flirted with the elder one,
the elder one scolded him,
he flirted with the younger one,
the younger one responded to him.
Not long after, the man with two wives died,
a guest asked the flirtatious man:
'Will you take the elder one?
Or the younger one?'
'I'll take the elder one.'
The guest said:
'The elder one scolded you,
the younger one responded to you,
why do you choose the elder one?'
He replied:
'When she was another's wife, I wanted her to respond to me;
now as my wife, I want her to scold others.'"
"Strategies of the Warring States"
There was a man who flirted with his neighbor's wives;
the elder one cursed him,
the younger one reciprocated his advances.
Later, when their husband died, he married the elder one.
Someone said, "Wasn't she the one who cursed you?"
He replied, "When she was another's, I wanted her to respond to me;
when she is mine, I want her to curse others."
"Later Biography of Féng Yǎn"
Ballad of Mòsāng
A woman from Hándān surnamed Qín named Luófū,
was the wife of a fellow townsman, Qiānchéng Wáng Rén.
Later, Wáng Rén served in the household of the King of Zhào,
who ordered Luófū to go out and gather mulberry leaves by the roadside.
The King of Zhào, ascending his terrace, saw her and was delighted,
prepared a feast and intended to take her by force.
Luófū was skilled at playing the zither,
and composed "The Roadside Mulberries" to make clear her refusal to comply.
"Annotations on Past and Present"
I am afraid
Zōu Jì was over eight feet tall,
and his appearance was handsome and elegant.
One morning, he dressed in his court robes and looked in the mirror,
asking his wife:
"Who is more handsome, me or Lord Xú of the north of the city?"
His wife replied:
"You are extremely handsome,
how could Lord Xú compare to you?"
Lord Xú of the north of the city
was the most handsome man in the State of Qí.
Zōu Jì, lacking self-confidence, asked his concubine again:
"Who is more handsome, me or Lord Xú?"
The concubine said:
"How could Lord Xú compare to you?"
The next day,
Lord Xú came,
and after carefully observing him, Zōu Jì thought he was not as handsome.
Looking in the mirror at himself, he felt even less handsome by far.
That evening, as he lay in bed thinking, he said:
"My wife finds me handsome
because she is partial to me;
my concubine finds me handsome
because she fears me."
"Strategies of Qí"
Baring Both Shoulders
It is said that in Qí there was a daughter,
whom two men sought in marriage.
The son of the eastern family was ugly but wealthy,
while the son of the western family was handsome but poor.
When asked to decide whom she wished to marry,
finding it difficult to point out directly, she was told to bare an arm to indicate her choice,
so they would know.
The daughter then bared both arms.
Her parents found it strange,
and asked the reason.
She replied:
"I wish to eat at the eastern house and rest at the western house.
This is why I bared both arms."
From "Fēngsú Tōng".
Killed his wife
Wú Qǐ was fond of using military force,
served the ruler of Lǔ,
when the Qí people attacked Lǔ,
the ruler wanted to make him a general,
but doubted him because Qǐ had married a woman from Qí,
Qǐ desired to achieve fame,
so he killed his wife to demonstrate he had no ties with Qí,
Lǔ finally appointed him as general,
he attacked Qí and thoroughly defeated them.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Decided to Marry
Zhāng Ěr once fled and wandered to Wàihuáng,
where a rich man's daughter was very beautiful.
She had married a common laborer but left her husband,
and went to stay with her father's friend.
The friend had long known Zhāng Ěr,
so he said to the girl:
"If you must seek a worthy husband,
follow Zhāng Ěr."
The girl listened,
and eventually requested to end her previous marriage to wed Zhāng Ěr.
At that time, Zhāng Ěr had escaped and was traveling,
so the girl's family generously provided for him.
Thanks to this, Zhāng Ěr attracted followers from afar,
and the friend secured him an official post in Wèi as the magistrate of Wàihuáng.
His reputation thus grew even more renowned.

Huàméi
Zhāng Chǎng, whose courtesy name was Zìgāo,
served as the Metropolitan Governor,
and painted his wife's eyebrows.
In Cháng'ān, it was said that Governor Zhāng's eyebrows were charming,
and officials reported Chǎng for this.
Emperor Xuān asked him about it,
to which he replied:
"I have heard that within the private chambers,
in the intimacy between husband and wife,
there are matters more intimate than painting eyebrows."
The emperor, valuing his ability,
did not reprimand him.

Marry a Witch
Chancellor Huáng Bà, styled Cìgōng,
formerly served as a patrol officer in Yángjiǎ.
While riding together with a skilled physiognomist,
they saw a woman.
The physiognomist said this woman was destined for wealth and nobility,
and would become the wife of a marquis.
Otherwise,
the art of physiognomy would be unreliable.
Huáng Bà inquired about her,
and found she was the daughter of a shaman from his village.
He then married her as his wife.
*Lùn Héng*
left behind a short coat
Dàizhào Jǐng Zǐchūn, who was always skilled in divination,
was imprisoned due to a legal matter.
His wife, Madame Zhū, came to the prison gate,
sent in a message about leaving a jacket.
Zǐchūn was alarmed and said:
"Madame Zhū has come to say
that with 'Zhū' meaning 'to execute,'
and the jacket being cut off from the trousers,
I am to be executed and severed."
Later, he was indeed cut in two at the waist.
From Huán Tán's "Xīn Lùn"
Sent to prison
Dīng Hán, styled Shūchūn,
was a native of Yánglíng in Jīngzhào.
Being the brother-in-law of the Hànzhōng Grand Administrator,
he was captured by Gōngsūn Shù's general, and his wife was sent to Nánzhèng Prison.
He removed his cap and went barefoot to plead his case before the edict, saying:
"The wife of the Hànzhōng Grand Administrator is now imprisoned in Nánzhèng.
Who would be able to scratch the grime off her back?
Hanging a cow's head,
but selling horse meat jerky,
acting like the robber Zhí,
yet speaking like Confucius—
if Hán were to admit guilt,
moreover, Hán has but one wife,
let him not be made to apologize for his cap and shoes."
From the "Jué Lù Zhù"
To obey orders
The wife of Bào Xuān from Bóhǎi
was a daughter of the Bǎi family,
courtesy name Shàojūn Xuān.
He studied under Shàojūn's father,
who admired his integrity in poverty,
so he gave his daughter to him in marriage,
providing a lavish dowry.
Xuān was displeased,
saying:
"Shàojūn was born wealthy and accustomed to luxury,
used to fine adornments,
while I am poor and lowly,
I dare not accept such ceremony."
Shàojūn then returned all her attendants and fine clothing,
changed into short hemp garments, and pulled the deer-hide cart home with Xuān.
After paying respects to her mother-in-law in the village,
she carried pots to fetch water,
cultivating wifely virtues.
Xuān served as Colonel-Director of Retainers,
and their son Yǒng became Governor of Lǔ Commandery during the Chūyuán era.
Yǒng's son Yù once casually asked Shàojūn:
"Does my lady still remember the days of pulling the deer-hide cart?"
She replied:
"My late mother-in-law taught:
'Remember death while living,
remember danger while in safety'—
how would I dare forget?"
(Book of the Later Hàn)
Lifting the tray to the level of the eyebrows
Liáng Hóng, styled Bóluán,
came from a poor family but upheld integrity,
and many prominent families admired his noble character,
wishing to marry their daughters to him.
However, Liáng Hóng rejected all proposals.
In the same county, the Mèng family had a daughter
who was plump, dark-skinned, and considered unattractive,
yet strong enough to lift a stone mortar.
She declined all marriage proposals
until the age of thirty.
Her parents asked her the reason,
and she replied:
"I wish to marry someone as virtuous as Liáng Bóluán."
Upon hearing this, Liáng Hóng proposed to her.
She requested plain cloth garments and hemp shoes,
along with tools for weaving baskets and spinning,
but when the wedding took place,
she initially appeared in ornate attire.
For seven days after entering his home, Liáng Hóng ignored her.
His wife then knelt by the bed and pleaded:
"I have heard of your high principles,
having rejected several women,
and I too have declined many suitors.
Now that you have chosen me,
dare I not ask for my fault?"
Liáng Hóng replied:
"I sought someone in coarse clothing
who could join me in seclusion in the deep mountains.
Yet now you wear fine silks
and apply powder and makeup.
Is this what I desired?"
His wife said:
"I did this to test your resolve.
I have my own garments for a reclusive life."
She then changed into a simple bun and plain clothes,
approaching him while working.
Liáng Hóng was overjoyed and said:
"This is truly the wife for Liáng Hóng,
one who can accompany me faithfully."
He gave her the courtesy name Déyào,
and she was named Mèng Guāng.
After they had lived together for a while,
his wife said:
"I have often heard that you wish to live in seclusion to avoid troubles.
Why are you silent now?
Could it be that you intend to lower your head and submit?"
Liáng Hóng replied:
"Very well."
They then entered the Bàlíng Mountains together,
making their living by farming and weaving.
Later, they went to Wú and stayed under the eaves of the wealthy Gāo Bótōng,
working as hired grain pounders.
Every time Liáng Hóng returned home,
his wife would prepare his meal
and dared not look up directly at him,
instead raising the tray to eyebrow level.
Gāo Bótōng observed this and found it remarkable,
saying:
"A mere laborer who can earn such respect from his wife
is no ordinary man."
He then provided them proper lodging in his home.
Talent and virtue spread their renown
Qín Jiā of Lǒngxī, styled Shìhuì,
was an outstanding scholar.
His wife,
"Xú Shù also gained renown for her talent and beauty."
During Emperor Huán's reign, Qín Jiā served as a clerk,
and traveled to Luòyáng.
Xú Shù had returned to her parental home,
where she lay napping with tears streaming down her face.
Her sister-in-law asked in surprise,
and she replied:
"I just saw Jiā telling me he fell ill and died at Jīnxiāng Post Station,
with two companions remaining there -
one guarding the funeral,
while the other brings a letter back,
which should arrive by noon."
The whole family was greatly shocked,
and when the letter arrived, the events matched her dream exactly.
Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds
The Hàn dynasty clerk Qín Jiā
and his wife Xú Shù -
their marital story is moving enough to grieve over,
and their writings are equally poignant and mournful.
Among those who composed in five-character verse, there were only a few masters,
yet two were women,
and Xú Shù's farewell poems
rank second only to "The Round Fan."
Gradings of Poetry
Qín Jiā's wife, Madame Xú,
acted in accordance with ritual propriety,
her speech followed established norms.
She disfigured herself and refused to remarry,
grieving until it impaired her health -
this exemplifies one who possessed both talent and virtue.
The Book of Later Hàn lists exemplary women yet excludes Xú Shù,
making one wonder what standard
the red-tube brush should follow in its recordings.
Generalities on History
The Qín couple's poems survive only in the Imperial Reader of Arts and Letters, with most verses omitted.
Cutting the Loom
The wife of Yuè Yángzǐ from Hénán,
Yángzǐ once found a lost piece of gold while walking on the road,
and brought it home to give to his wife.
His wife said:
"I have heard that a person of integrity does not drink from the Robber's Spring,
and an honest person does not accept food given contemptuously.
The Literary Garden
How much worse is picking up lost property for profit, thus soiling one's character?"
Yángzǐ was greatly ashamed,
so he discarded the gold in the wilderness,
and went far away to seek a teacher and study.
After one year he returned home,
his wife knelt and asked the reason,
Yángzǐ said:
"After being away for so long, I felt homesick,
there is no other reason."
His wife then took up a knife and went to the loom, saying:
"This fabric is born from the silkworm's cocoon,
and completed on the loom.
Thread by thread it accumulates,
until it reaches an inch,
accumulating inches without cease,
until it becomes yards and bolts.
Now if I cut this weaving,
then the completed work would be lost,
and the time spent would be wasted.
You, my husband, are accumulating learning,
you should daily learn what you lack to achieve virtuous character.
If you return midway through your studies,
how is it different from cutting this weaving?"
Yángzǐ was moved by her words,
returned to complete his studies,
and thus did not return for seven years.
History of the Later Hàn
Unsuccessful
Zhōu Zé, styled Zhìqīng,
was a native of Ānqiū in Běihǎi.
While serving as Grand Master of Ceremonies,
he lay ill in the fasting palace.
His wife, pitying him for his old age and sickness,
peeped in to inquire about his suffering.
Zé grew greatly enraged,
considering it a violation of the fasting prohibition,
and had her arrested and sent to the imperial prison,
while also impeaching himself to apologize to the world.
Some doubted his agitation was insincere.
Moreover, a proverb said:
"In this life, ill-fated is the wife of a Grand Master of Ceremonies;
Throughout the three hundred and sixty days of the year,
Three hundred and fifty-nine are spent in fasting;
On the one day not fasting, drunk as mud he lies,
And even when working, again he's dazed and confused."
From "Hàn Guān Yí".
Chónghé
Huáng Chāng,
a native of Yúyáo in Kuàijī,
served as the Grand Administrator of Shǔ Commandery.
Earlier, when Huáng Chāng was a clerical assistant in the province,
his wife returned to her parental home,
but encountered bandits and was captured.
She was taken to Shǔ and became someone else's wife.
When her son committed an offense,
he went to Huáng Chāng to plead his case.
Huáng Chāng suspected he didn't resemble a Shǔ native,
so he inquired about his background.
The woman replied:
"I am originally the daughter of Dài Cìgōng from Yúyáo in Kuàijī,
wife of Huáng Chāng, the provincial assistant.
I was supposed to return home,
but was seized by bandits,
and thus ended up here."
Huáng Chāng exclaimed in surprise:
"How do you recognize Huáng Chāng?"
She replied:
"Huáng Chāng has a black mole on the sole of his left foot,
and he often said he would become an official with a salary of two thousand piculs."
Huáng Chāng showed her his foot,
they embraced and wept bitterly,
then resumed their relationship as husband and wife.
Earlier, when Huáng Chāng was about to go to Shǔ Commandery,
there was a rumor that two suns appeared in the sky.

Return the clothing
It is said there was a widow who vowed not to remarry after her husband's death,
pledging to shroud his corpse with an embroidered garment
and place it in the coffin.
Three years later, the widow prepared to remarry,
with the wedding day already set.
A traveler sought lodging overnight at a household,
and at dawn the host spoke to him,
entrusting the garment that symbolized the widow’s vow
with these words:
"When you travel a thousand miles, you will encounter her;
return this garment to her."
The traveler indeed encountered the wedding procession and relayed the matter,
returning the embroidered garment.
The widow then hanged herself and died.
From "Wùlǐ Lùn"
Both Satirized
Wáng Gǒng, styled Bó Zōng,
enjoyed a high reputation throughout the land.
During the reign of Emperor Shùn, he served as Grand Commandant.
Earlier, when Xuē Qín, Governor of Shānyáng, lost his wife,
he did not weep as her coffin was being encoffined for burial.
Approaching it, he said:
"Fortunately, she did not die young;
what regret is there, then?"
Later, when Wáng Gǒng's wife passed away,
Gǒng and his sons all carried staffs and observed mourning.
Some people of the time criticized both men.
From Zhāng Fán's "Records of the Hàn"
Drowning Oneself
In Héféi there is a Xiǎolì Port,
during the Jiàn'ān era of the Hàn dynasty,
the wife of petty official Jiāo Zhòngqīng from Lújiāng, née Liú, was divorced by her mother-in-law,
and vowed not to remarry.
Her family pressured her,
so she drowned herself in the water and died.
Zhòngqīng heard of this,
and also hanged himself.
People at the time pitied them,
and later they became famous.

Courting Power
The eunuch regular attendant Táng Qú wished to marry his daughter to Fù Gōng of Rǔnán,
but Fù Míng refused to marry her,
so she was instead married to Xún Yù.
Xún Yù's father, Xún Gǔn, admired power and influence,
and urged Xún Yù to marry her,
for which they were ridiculed by critics.
According to the Diǎn Lüè,
Xún Yù's father, Xún Gǔn, feared and dreaded the eunuchs,
so he arranged for Xún Yù to marry Héng's daughter.
Because Xún Yù had shown talent and reputation from a young age,
he thus managed to avoid criticism and censure.

Choosing a Wife
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, the various Cài families were most prominent,
Cài Fěng's elder sister married Grand Commandant Zhāng Wēn,
his eldest daughter became Huáng Yànchéng's wife,
and his younger daughter became Liú Jǐngshēng's subsequent wife,
who was the elder sister of Wèi.
The "Xiāngyáng Chronicle"
records that Huáng Chéngyàn was lofty, forthright, and open-minded,
a renowned scholar south of the Miǎn River,
who said to Zhūgě Kǒngmíng:
"I hear you are selecting a wife;
I have an unattractive daughter,
with yellow hair and dark skin, but her talent is worthy of matching yours."
Kǒngmíng agreed,
and Huáng immediately sent her to him.
People of the time found this amusing and entertaining,
and the local folk made a saying about it:
"Don't imitate Kǒngmíng choosing a wife,
ending up with old Chéng's ugly daughter."

Beating one's wife
Shǔ Liú Yǎn's wife, Hú Shì, went to congratulate the Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager specifically detained Hú Shì,
only releasing her after a full month.
Hú Shì was of exceptional beauty,
so Yǎn suspected she had an affair with the Later Sovereign.
He summoned five hundred soldiers to beat Hú,
even striking her face with a shoe before abandoning and expelling her.
Hú reported everything in detail,
leading to Yǎn being imprisoned.
The officials deliberated and stated:
"Soldiers are not the ones to beat a wife,
nor is the face the place to receive a shoe."
Yǎn was ultimately executed in the marketplace,
and from then on, the wives and mothers of high officials ceased attending court celebrations.
"Records of the Three Kingdoms"
Shoulder to shoulder
During the Huánglóng era of Wú, Lù Dōngměi from Hǎiyán in Wú commandery,
had a wife, née Zhū,
who was graceful in appearance and demeanor.
Husband and wife held each other in high esteem,
never parting even for a single step,
so contemporaries called them "Shoulder-to-Shoulder Couple."
After the wife passed away,
Dōngměi refused to eat and died.
Within a year of their joint burial,
a catalpa tree grew upon their grave,
with twin trunks from a single root
that embraced and merged into one tree.
Frequently, a pair of wild geese would roost upon it.
When Sūn Quán heard of this,
he sighed in admiration and named their village "Shoulder-to-Shoulder"
and their tomb "Twin Catalpas."
Later, their son Lù Hóng and his wife, née Zhāng, also deeply loved each other,
so the people of Wú called them "The Little Shoulder-to-Shoulder Couple."
"Records of Sān Wú" "Accounts of Marvels"
without blasphemy
Gù Tì,
a clansman of Gù Yōng,
treated his wife with respect,
often entering at night and leaving at dawn,
rarely showing his face.
Once when he was gravely ill,
his wife came out to visit him,
Tì ordered his attendants to help him up,
put on his cap and outer garment,
rose to respond and urged his wife to return,
such was his genuine purity and avoidance of impropriety.

Repair and maintenance
In the Jìn dynasty, Hé Zēng's household rules were strict and proper.
Upon reaching the age of fifty or above,
he would always straighten his attire and cap upon seeing his wife,
sitting facing south while his wife sat facing north.
They would toast each other with wine,
but this occurred no more than two or three times a year.
He passed away at the age of eighty.

Lúzhàng
Liú Shí, styled Zǐgòng,
held high positions and enjoyed great prestige,
yet always esteemed frugality and simplicity.
Although he lived in glory and favor,
he resided without a mansion.
Even as ritual teachings declined, he conducted himself with integrity.
Upon his wife's death, he observed the mourning hut and staff rites,
abstaining from marital relations throughout the mourning period.
Frivolous people mocked him,
but Shí paid no heed.
From the Book of Jìn.
Fit to be a lady
Shān Tāo, when he was still a commoner and his family was poor,
said to his wife, née Hán:
"Endure the hunger and cold,
for I will later become one of the Three Excellencies.
I just don't know if you will eventually be worthy of being a lady?"
Using His Body to Warm Her
Xún Fèngqiàn and his wife were deeply devoted to each other.
One winter his wife fell ill with a fever,
so he went out into the central courtyard to chill himself,
then returned to press his body against hers to cool her.
After his wife died,
Fèngqiàn himself also passed away not long after.
Because of this, he was criticized by his contemporaries.
Fèngqiàn had said:
"A woman's virtue is not worthy of praise;
it should be her beauty that matters most."
Minister Péi heard of this
and said:
"This was merely a whim,
not the words of a truly virtuous man.
I hope later generations will not be misled by these words."
My dear
Wáng Ānfēng's wife often called him "Qīng",
Ānfēng said:
"For a wife to call her husband 'Qīng' is disrespectful according to etiquette,
do not do it again."
His wife said:
"I'm intimate with you, I love you,
therefore I call you 'Qīng',
if I don't call you 'Qīng',
then who else will call you 'Qīng'?"
So he always allowed her to do so.
Jí Zhù
In the second year of Xiánkāng, Lǐ Fán's elder sister was first married to Chén Shēn of Nánpíng Commandery as his wife,
bore four sons but encountered bandits,
pleaded with the bandits to spare her mother-in-law's life,
the bandits abducted and took the sister away,
Shēn then married Yán Shì,
who bore three sons,
Fán later obtained news of his sister,
went to bring her back to Shēn,
Shēn registered having two wives in the records,
and when Lǐ died,
Shēn was uncertain about mourning attire,
so he presented the matter to the office of General-in-Chief Conquering the West Yǔ Liàng for deliberation,
at the time opinions often differed,
Marshal Wáng Qiānqī deliberated:
"According to ritual there should not be two principal wives,
thus Duke Huì's primary consort was Mèngzǐ,
when Mèngzǐ died,
Shēngzǐ succeeded as consort,
even feudal lords were thus,
how much more commoners?"
Shēn could not plan ahead to avoid calamity,
thus losing his wife,
she did not violate the seven grounds for divorce to be repudiated by Shēn,
initially not repudiated,
finally welcomed back,
cared for her mother-in-law in the home,
her sons being the primary heirs,
registered in the official records,
then Shēn's wife was Shēn's wife,
the wife was Huī's mother,
Huī wearing mourning attire is without doubt.
Shēn had an elderly mother,
who could not be left uncared for,
the wife had no date of return,
taking a concubine would have been permissible,
though Lǐ was lost,
the bandits might still be alive,
hoping Shēn's efforts to seek her were incomplete,
yet he hastily married a wife,
truly Shēn's shortcoming,
however, a rustic fellow does not comprehend ritual propriety,
examining historical records yields no perfect solution.
Xiào Shūshū's wife was violated by Xì Chōu yet not abandoned,
because it was not her fault,
Shēn having two wives,
was not intentionally breaking the law,
Lǐ, though a rustic woman, could plead to spare her mother-in-law's life in danger,
in peril not forgetting devotion,
could be called a filial daughter-in-law.
Those deliberating want her in captivity,
to fully maintain bitter chastity,
preferring death to remarriage,
this expects ordinary people to all be like Sòng Bójī.
Though Shēn should not have married,
considering Yán as wife,
the wife being the successor,
was originally not the principal wife,
though called not principal, the duty lies in constancy,
how can Shēn's improper two wives make her enter two households?
If she can yield,
then there is the principle of Zhào Jī,
if saying she cannot,
the authorities should have regulations,
first principal then successor,
has existed since ancient times.
Liàng followed Qiānqī's deliberation to decide.

Hào Liáng
Sǔn Guǐ, styled Wéndù,
was respectful, filial, pure, and frugal,
and his learning and understanding were grounded in reason and righteousness.
At that time, Yú Xǐ of Kuàijī was living in seclusion by the sea,
embodying the lofty demeanor of a recluse from the world.
Guǐ admired his virtue,
and married the daughter of Xǐ's younger brother Yù.
Xǐ admonished his niece to abandon extravagance and uphold simplicity,
sharing the same aspirations as Guǐ.
People of the time referred to them as the couple Liáng Hóng and Mèng Guāng.

Shooting a Woman
Guō Mò's brother-in-law Lù Jiā from the same commandery took several dan of government rice to feed his sister,
Mò considered this a violation of regulations,
and was about to execute Jiā,
Jiā fled in fear to Shí Lè,
whereupon Mò personally shot and killed his wife,
to demonstrate his impartiality.

To value family
Sòng Dōng Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
Zhāng Dǎng's wife Huángfǔ shì was captured,
bestowed upon a palace eunuch as a maidservant.
Huángfǔ then feigned madness, unable to wash or groom herself.
Later, Dǎng became Sòng's Jìzhōu Zhǎngshǐ,
and through goods worth over a thousand bolts of silk, sought to redeem her.
Wén Chéng found it strange that he offered so much wealth,
and when summoning her for an audience,
Huángfǔ was nearly sixty years old.
Wén Chéng said:
"Southerners have peculiar preferences and value the bonds of family deeply.
What use could this old woman possibly serve,
that he would go to such expense?"
Huángfǔ shì returned,
Dǎng ordered his concubines to welcome her at the border.
She passed away a few years later,
and a decade after that, Dǎng entered Wèi.

Silkworm Chamber
Biàn Bīn, styled Shìwèi,
was fond of drinking from a gourd ladle,
using a spoon made of peach kernel skin as his dish,
he wore a silk cap that remained unchanged for nearly a decade,
used a large gourd as a fire basket,
and possessed numerous peculiar objects,
he referred to himself as Biàn Tiánjū,
while his wife was known as Fù Cánshì.
From the *Book of Southern Qí*
Drinking Together
Shěn Wénjì served as the governor of Wúxīng,
Wénjì could drink up to five dǒu of wine,
while his wife, née Wáng—daughter of Wáng Xī—could also drink up to three dǒu.
Wénjì and his wife would drink opposite each other all day long, yet he never neglected his official duties.
The Emperor
Respect for His Wife
Liǔ Tán, courtesy name Wéntōng,
was the son of Shìlóng.
His temperament was broad and tolerant,
and his family members never saw him show extreme joy or anger. He greatly respected
his wife, who was quite formidable and intimidating.
He had a fondness for music
and kept skilled and beautiful female performers,
yet he hardly dared to look at them directly.
The Minister of Works, Zhāng Jì, was on intimate terms with Tán and was respected by Tán's wife.
Whenever Jì visited Tán,
he would first inquire after the lady of the house.
Whenever Tán wished to see the performers,
he would always have Jì request a performance.
His wife would sit behind a curtain,
and only then would the performers come out,
allowing Tán to gaze at them freely.

Féng Zhuó of Bóhǎi married a woman from Péngchéng of the Liú clan,
After just one night of marriage,
Zhuó took up an official post in the capital.
Later, he was executed for certain offenses.

she suddenly dreamed and knew that Zhuó had died.
She wept mournfully without ceasing,
and then, filled with grief and lament, she passed away.
People of the time compared her to the wife of Qín Jiā.
Gāo Yǔn, moved by her noble integrity,
composed eight poems in her praise.

A capable woman is half the husband.

shared a deep and affectionate bond with him,
unable to bear even brief separation.
Whenever Zé accompanied the imperial carriage,
his wife would not sleep alone
—such was her resolute and devoted nature.
Contemporaries regarded her as a woman of vigor, equal to half her husband.

A dog barks.
Xíng Shào, courtesy name Zǐcái,
was quite distant from his wife,
never spending the night inside her chambers.
He once claimed that during the day he entered the inner quarters,
only to be barked at by a dog,
and after telling this story, he clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
From "The Northern Qí History"
Entrusted Dream
Lǐ Shù was born a eunuch,
his wife was the daughter of Yuán Luó.
After Shù's death, his elder brother Yuè had his wife accompany her to sleep and stay,
for five years in total.
Later, Yuán Shì remarried Zhào Qǐ.
She once dreamed that Shù said to her:
"I have meager blessings,
and have been reborn as a daughter in the Liú family.
Tomorrow morning, I will be born into that household,
which is very poor,
and I fear they cannot raise me.
Given our past marital affection,
I have come to see you,
to tell you that you should go and take me. The Liú family is located in Qīdì Block, south of the cross street, entering east into a poor alley."
Yuán Shì did not respond,
and Shù said:
"You seem to fear Zhào Qǐ's opinion,
I will speak to him myself."
Thereupon, Qǐ also dreamed of this.
Qǐ woke and asked his wife,
and her account matched.
So he took money and silk and personally went to seek out the Liú family,
and as in the dream, obtained the girl to raise.
When she grew up, they married her off.

Hometown
Wáng Biāo was defeated,
and said to his wife, calling her by the affectionate name Xiānglǐ:
"I cannot bear to let Xiānglǐ fall into the hands of others,
so I must first kill Xiānglǐ,
and then face death myself."
Yáng offered her neck to the blade,
without the slightest hesitation or fear.
From the History of the Southern Dynasties,
Shěn Xiūwén's poem "The Liǔ Family Daughter of Shānyīn" says:

how could she be fit to be my wife?"
Remembering the Cake Maker
Níngwáng Lǐ Xiàn was noble and prosperous,
with dozens of favored singing girls,
all of exceptional talent and beauty.
To the left of his residence lived a pancake seller,
whose wife was slender, fair, and radiant.
The prince, captivated at first sight,
lavished gifts upon her husband,
took her into his care and cherished her.
After more than a year had passed,
he asked her:
"Do you still remember the pancake seller?"
She remained silent, offering no reply.
The prince summoned the pancake seller to let her see him.
His wife gazed intently,
tears streaming down both cheeks,
as if overwhelmed with emotion.
At that time, over ten guests were seated in the prince's hall,
all renowned scholars of the era,
and none were not moved with sorrow.
The prince commanded them to compose poems.
Wáng Yòuchéng Wéi's poem was completed first:
"Do not cling to present favor,
but remember past kindness.
Seeing flowers fills the eyes with tears;
she would not speak with the King of Chǔ."
became even closer
Táng Liǔ Zǐshēng's wife, Madame Zhèng, passed away without any illness.
Before her death, she told Zǐshēng:
"I will not leave your side,
and in eighteen years, I will be your relative again."
Later, when Zǐshēng was nearly seventy years old,
he remarried Madame Cuī,
who often recalled events from her previous life,
and after giving birth to a son, she passed away.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Bǔ Huì hòu qǐng
When Qíwáng Lǐ Màozhēn dominated Qín and Lǒng,
Jīngzhōu secretary Xuē Chāngxù was pedantic and eccentric by nature.
His temperament was innate,
and even when meeting his wife,
he always observed formal etiquette.
He would first order a maidservant to relay messages,
going back and forth several times until permission was granted,
then he would carry a candle to her chamber.
They would engage in lofty, abstract discussions,
take tea and fruits, and then withdraw.
If he wished to enter the bedchamber,
the same etiquette applied.
He once said:
"Considering the importance of continuing the family line,
whenever I wish to seek a favorable encounter,
I must await her consent before proceeding."
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Hékuí is in the room.
Lǐ Dàirén was by nature pedantic and slow-moving.
He married a woman from the Yán family,
who was very young.
He lived in a separate room from her,
and they had a private agreement:
"We shall meet only when the mood strikes."
One evening, he suddenly heard a knock at the door.
A young servant reported,
"The lady of the household wishes to see you, sir."
Dàirén hurriedly fetched the Almanac of Hundred Taboos,
looked at it under the lamp,
and exclaimed in great alarm:
"Tonight, the River Chief is in the chamber;
it is not suitable to engage in such activities."
He sent a message to the lady, thanking her for coming.
Lady Yán, ashamed and angry, left.
(From "Surviving Stories of Jīng and Hú")
Wáng Wànqīngchún
A man saw his neighbor's husband and wife living in harmony.
When the husband returned home from outside,
he saw his wife blowing on the fire,
and so he presented her with a poem, saying:
"Her vermilion lips move as she blows the fire,
Her jade-white wrists slant as she adds more fuel.
Gazing from afar at her face within the smoke,
She greatly resembles a flower in the dew."
His own wife waited for her husband to return,
and told him:
"I often see that neighbor's husband and wife are extremely affectionate.
Just now, the husband saw his wife blowing on the fire and composed a poem praising her.
Couldn't you learn to do the same?"
The husband said:
"What did that poem say?"
The wife then recited it.
The husband said:
"You should blow on the fire, and I'll compose a different one for you."
The wife also imitated blowing on the fire,
and the husband then composed a poem, saying:
"Her blue lips move as she blows the fire,
Her black wrists slant as she adds more fuel.
Gazing from afar at her face within the smoke,
She exactly resembles a demon hag."
"Forest of Laughter"
Parted and reunited
Xú Xiàokè was the son of Xú Líng's younger brother.
He was extremely filial by nature.
After his father's passing,
he initially could not bear the grief of mourning.
His birth mother, Chén Shì, fully devoted herself to caring for him.
At the end of the Liáng dynasty, Hóu Jǐng's rebellion brought chaos,
and Xiàokè could no longer provide even congee for his mother's sustenance.
His wife, Zāng Shì from Dōngguǎn,
who was the daughter of General Zāndùn,
was very beautiful.
Xiàokè then said to her:
"With such severe famine now,
and our means of support lacking,
I wish to marry you to a man of means,
hoping that both of us may be saved through you.
What do you think?"
Zāng Shì did not agree.
At that time, there was a man named Kǒng Jǐngxíng, a general under Hóu Jǐng,
who often had many followers.
He forced her to marry him and took her away.
Zāng Shì left in tears.
The grain and silk she received
were all given to her mother.
Xiàokè also shaved his head and became a Buddhist monk,
changing his name to Fǎzhěng,
and supplemented his livelihood by begging for food.
Zāng Shì also deeply remembered their past affection,
and often secretly sent him provisions,
so he did not suffer from want.
Later, when Kǒng Jǐngxíng died in battle,
Zāng Shì waited for Xiàokè on the road,
and after several days, she finally saw him.
She said to Xiàokè:
"What happened in the past
was not because I betrayed you.
Now that I am free,
I should return to care for you."
Xiàokè remained silent without replying.
Thereupon, he returned to secular life,
and they became husband and wife again.
From *The History of the Southern Dynasties*
Separated and reunited
Lǐ Déwǔ's wife, Madame Péi, styled Shūyīng,
had been married to Déwǔ for one year
when Déwǔ was implicated in his uncle Jīncái's case and exiled to Lǐngbiǎo.
Péi's father, Péi Jǔ, petitioned for Déwǔ's divorce,
and Emperor Yáng granted it.
As Déwǔ was about to part with Péi,
he said to her:
"Our marital bliss has just begun,
yet we must part.
I am heading far into miasmic lands,
fearing I may never return.
Your father has petitioned to keep you,
intending for you to remarry.
Here we part forever."
Péi wept and replied:
"A wife serves her husband,
with no rite of remarriage.
The husband
is like heaven—
how can I betray him?
I will remain faithful unto death,
with no other intention."
She then took a knife to cut off her ear in pledge,
but her guardians stopped her.
For over ten years, she had no contact with Déwǔ.
Péi Jǔ tried to change her resolve,
and when Liǔ Zhí sought to marry her,
he agreed.
As the wedding date approached,
she cut off her hair with scissors,
wept bitterly, and refused to eat.
Péi Jǔ could not sway her,
so he relented.
Déwǔ had married Èrzhū Shì in Lǐngbiǎo,
but when he was pardoned and returned,
reaching Xiāngzhōu, he heard of Péi's fidelity and divorced his later wife.
He reunited with Péi,
and they had three sons and four daughters.
During the Zhēnguàn era, Déwǔ died as magistrate of Lùchéng,
and Péi passed away over a year later.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Tiānzhōng Jì Volume Eighteen
Huái'ān
When Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn encountered calamity,
he fled to Qí.
Duke Huán of Qí gave him a wife,
along with twenty teams of horses.
The prince grew content with this life,
but his followers deemed it unacceptable.
As they planned their departure beneath mulberry trees, a silkworm maid overhead overheard them,
and reported it to Jiāngshì.
Jiāngshì had the maid killed and said to the prince:
"You have ambitions to travel the four directions;
I have killed the one who overheard this."
The prince replied:
"I have no such intentions."
Jiāngshì said:
"Go! Attachment to comfort and peace will truly ruin your reputation. You must not stay."
Jiāngshì then conspired with Zǐfàn,
made the prince drunk, and sent him away.
When sober, the prince pursued Zǐfàn with a spear.
Zuǒzhuàn, 23rd year of Duke Xī
Weaving Sandals
King Zhuāng of Chǔ dispatched an envoy,
who brought a hundred catties of gold to invite Mr. Northern Outskirts.
The gentleman said:
"I have a wife who manages the household,
I wish to consult with her."
He then said to his wife:
"Chǔ wants to make me its chancellor.
If I become chancellor today, I'll have carriages and horsemen arrayed in rows,
with a feast of delicacies spread before me.
What do you think?"
His wife said:
"You make your living by weaving sandals,
eating porridge and wearing coarse shoes,
yet why do you have no anxieties or fears?
It's because you don't contend with the world.
Now if you have carriages and horsemen arrayed in rows,
the comfort they provide is no more than enough to accommodate your knees;
with a feast of delicacies spread before you,
what pleases your palate is but one portion of meat.
To trade the comfort of enough space for your knees
and the taste of one portion of meat
for the worries of the state of Chǔ—
how could that be acceptable?"
Thereupon he did not accept the invitation,
and left with his wife.
Throwing the Dustpan
Lǎo Láizǐ fled the world,
farming on the sunny side of Méng Mountain.
The King of Chǔ arrived at his gate in a carriage,
saying:
"I, the orphan guarding the state,
wish to see you, sir."
Lǎo Láizǐ replied:
"Very well."
His wife said:
"I have heard that
those who can be fed with wine and meat
can be followed with whips and clubs;
those who can be given official positions and salaries
can be followed with axes and execution blades.
Now if you, sir, eat others' wine and meat,
accept others' official positions and salaries,
you will be controlled by others.
Can you avoid calamity?
I cannot be controlled by others."
She threw down her basket of vegetables and left.
Lǎo Láizǐ said, "Come back, I will reconsider for you,"
but she continued walking without looking back,
reaching south of the river before stopping.
Biographies of Exemplary Women
Weeping for Wealth
Táo Dāzǐ governed Táo for three years,
yet his reputation did not flourish.
His family wealth tripled,
but his wife alone held their child and wept.
Her mother-in-law angrily said:
"How inauspicious this is!"
The wife replied:
"My husband has little ability but holds a high office,
this is what is called inviting disaster;
he has no achievements yet his household prospers,
this is what is called accumulating calamity.
I have heard that on South Mountain there is a black leopard,
that during seven days of misty rain does not come down to feed.
Why does it not eat?
It wishes to moisten its fur and develop its patterned coat,
therefore it hides to avoid harm.
Dogs and pigs do not choose their food to fatten themselves,
and thus await death.
Now my husband does not cultivate virtue, yet our household grows increasingly wealthy—
this is an omen of ruin and downfall."
A year later, Dāzǐ was indeed executed for embezzlement.
Biographies of Exemplary Women
The Song of the Yellow Crane
Lǔ Táo Yīng was
the daughter of Táo Míng.
She was widowed young,
and raised her young orphan without strong brothers,
spinning and weaving to make a living.
Some people in Lǔ, hearing of her righteousness,
wished to seek her hand.
Yīng heard of this,
fearing she could not avoid it,
then composed the Song of the Yellow Swan,
to make clear she would not remarry into another household.
The people of Lǔ heard it,
and thus did not dare to seek her again.
End
Halt!
Wáng Zhāng, styled Zhòngqīng,
lived alone with his wife.
When he fell ill and had no quilt, he lay under a cowhide,
bidding farewell to his wife with tears.
His wife scolded him angrily, saying:
"Zhòngqīng, you are noble and honorable—
who in the court surpasses you?
Now, in illness and distress,
you fail to rouse your spirits,
but instead weep—how pitiful!"
Later, Wáng Zhāng became an official in the capital.
When he intended to submit a memorial criticizing the emperor's uncle Wáng Fèng,
his wife stopped him, saying:
"One should know contentment.
Have you forgotten the time you wept under the cowhide?"
Wáng Zhāng replied:
"This is not something a woman can understand."
The memorial was then submitted,
and indeed, he was imprisoned by the Commandant of Justice and died.
《Book of Hàn》
Revenge
Guī Lǎn and Dài Yuán, who were close associates of Biān Hóng and others, had repeatedly been oppressed by Sūn Yì,
and they often contemplated rebellion.
At that time, all the county magistrates and officials gathered to meet Yì,
and since Yì's wife, Xú Shì, was quite skilled in divination,
Yì went in and said to Xú:
"Tomorrow, I intend to host a banquet for the senior officials;
could you try divining for it?"
Xú replied:
"The omen is not favorable;
it should be postponed to another day."
Yì, thinking that the senior officials had long sought an occasion and should be sent off quickly,
then invited a large number of guests.
When Yì went out to see off the guests,
Hóng followed from behind and hacked him to death,
then fled into the mountains.
Xú Shì offered a reward for his pursuit and capture,
and Lǎn and Yuán shifted the blame by killing Hóng.
All the generals knew that Lǎn and Yuán were behind it but lacked the strength to challenge them.
Lǎn moved into the military headquarters,
took all of Yì's concubines and attendants,
and wanted to take Xú as well.
Fearing that resistance would lead to harm,
she deceived him, saying:
"I beg to wait until the last day of the month to perform the sacrificial rites and remove mourning garments, as the month is nearly over."
Lǎn agreed to wait until after the sacrifice.
Xú secretly sent her trusted confidants to convey her intentions to Yì's close former generals, Sūn Gāo and Fù Yīng, among others.
Gāo and Yīng wept and accepted the task.
They then secretly summoned over twenty of Yì's former attendants,
and together they swore an oath and conspired.
On the last day of the month, the sacrifice was set up,
and Xú Shì wept mournfully,
after which she removed her mourning clothes, perfumed herself, and bathed.
She then set up curtains in another room,
speaking and laughing joyfully,
showing no sign of sorrow.
Everyone, young and old, felt distressed
and found her behavior strange.
Lǎn secretly spied on her
and no longer harbored suspicions.
Xú called Gāo, Yīng, and the maids to position themselves inside the door,
and sent someone to report to Lǎn that she had removed the inauspicious garments and was ready for auspiciousness,
awaiting his command.
Lǎn, filled with anticipation, entered,
and Xú came out to bow to Lǎn.
Just as she finished one bow,
Xú shouted, "You two, rise now!"
Gāo and Yīng both rushed out,
and together they killed Lǎn.
The others immediately went outside and killed Yuán.
The lady then returned,
dressed in mourning attire, and offered the heads of Lǎn and Yuán in sacrifice at Yì's tomb.
The entire army was shocked and awed,
considering it a miraculous feat.
When the ruler of Wú arrived later,
he exterminated the entire clans of Lǎn and Yuán's remaining followers.
(From "Wú Lì")
Having no son, she sought to leave.
The wife of Pèi Gōngsūn Qùbìng
was the daughter of Dài Yuánshì from the same commandery.
After being married for a long time without bearing a child,
she said to her husband:
"I am untalented,
yet had the honor to serve you with towel and comb,
but after all these years I have produced no heir.
According to ritual, there are seven grounds for divorce,
I beg to accept my dismissal."
Her husband did not consent,
so she spoke again:
"No blessing is greater than flourishing prosperity,
no misfortune greater than cutting off the lineage.
If you cannot bear to send me away,
you should take more wives."
Her husband again refused.
After her husband died and the mourning period ended,
her parents wanted to remarry her,
whereupon the woman took a knife and cut off her nose.
The commandery honored her household with a public表彰.
Biographies of Exemplary Women
Female Teacher
Lǐ Xiū, wife of Zhào Sōng,
was a daughter of the Zhāng family.
Her mother-in-law was cruel and wicked, without virtue,
and treated her improperly,
yet Xiū never showed anger.
When she visited her parents,
they asked about it,
but she only took the blame and did not speak of it.
Eventually, her mother-in-law was moved to realization,
and became more caring towards her.
The villagers admonished one another, saying:
"Shouldn't a wife be like the wife of Zhào Bógāo?
She made a wicked mother-in-law change her ways—
truly, she can be called a model for wives."
Later, when her mother-in-law fell ill, her daughter came to visit,
but the mother-in-law refused her, saying:
"I surely deserve to die at the hands of such a virtuous wife."
Later, when bandits invaded,
and Sōng died,
she smeared her face with blue pigment,
disheveled her hair, and hid a knife,
pretending to be ill,
so the bandits did not molest her.
She raised her orphaned daughter,
and lived by the principles of her father and uncle for the rest of her life.
From "Huáyáng Guózhì"
Far-sighted consideration
Lǐ Héng, styled Shūpíng,
was a native of Xiāngyáng.
Xí Zhú married his daughter Xí Yīngxí to him.
During the Wú period, while serving as the Grand Administrator of Dānyáng under Sūn Xiū, who had been relocated to Dānyáng,
Héng repeatedly used the law to cut him off,
and Yīngxí often remonstrated, saying:
"To oppress the noble while being lowly,
and to estrange the close while being distant,
is the way to invite disaster."
Héng did not listen.
When Sūn Liàng was deposed,
Héng entered through the gate,
and Yīngxí met him and asked:
"Why do you have a fearful expression?
Has the Prince of Lángyá been enthroned?"
Héng replied:
"Yes.
I did not heed your words,
and it has come to this."
He then gathered his household retainers, intending to flee to Wèi,
but Yīngxí firmly remonstrated, saying:
"You cannot do this.
You were originally a commoner.
The late emperor promoted you excessively,
and you have repeatedly acted disrespectfully without considering the long-term consequences.
Now, you further suspect and resent, seeking to escape and rebel to save your life.
If you go north like this,
what face will you have to see the people of the Central Plains?"
Héng asked:
"What plan do you suggest?"
Yīngxí said:
"The Prince of Lángyá has always been fond of goodness and admired reputation.
Now that he has just ascended the throne and wishes to establish himself in the world,
it is clear that he will not kill you over personal grievances.
If you are still uncertain,
you can imprison yourself and go to the court, presenting your case.
By openly seeking judgment for your offenses like this,
you will instead be treated leniently,
not merely spared."
Héng followed her advice,
and indeed, an edict was issued, stating:
"Lǐ Héng, Grand Administrator of Dānyáng,
due to past grievances,
has voluntarily submitted himself to the authorities.
Shooting through a hook and cutting a sleeve,
in a ruler, is loyalty.
Send Héng back to his commandery,
and do not let him doubt himself."
He was additionally appointed General of Weīyuǎn,
and granted a ceremonial halberd.
Whenever Héng wanted to manage household affairs,
Yīngxí would not allow it,
and Héng often quoted the Grand Historian,
saying that a thousand orange trees in Jiānglíng
would make one's family as prosperous as a noble,
but Yīngxí said:
"People should worry about lacking virtue and righteousness,
not about not being wealthy.
If one can remain humble despite being noble, that is good.
What is the use of this?"
(From "Xiāngyáng Records of the Elderly")
Yìgū
Lù Jì had a daughter born in Yùlín,
named Yùshēng,
who was married to Zhāng Wēn's younger brother, Bái.
Yáo Xìn's collection contains a memorial praising her, stating:
"I have heard that the governance of Táng and Yú promoted the virtuous and educated,
honoring morality and elevating the exceptional,
which the Three Sovereigns prioritized.
Thus, loyal ministers and martyrs
gained renown in the state court,
while virtuous women and chaste maidens
had their deeds recorded in their hometowns.
This was to propagate and uphold transformative achievements,
broadly cultivating pure customs,
so that those with noble nature
would be renowned in both light and darkness,
and those possessing exemplary qualities
would bring honor to both men and women.
Hence, Wáng Zhú established the integrity of winter pines, and the King of Qí honored his village;
the Righteous Aunt demonstrated extraordinary conduct, and the Marquis of Lǔ elevated her gate.
I humbly observe that the daughter of the late Yùlín Governor Lù Jì, Yùshēng,
practiced chaste and steadfast conduct from youth,
and established an unshakable resolve in childhood.
At just thirteen years of age,
she married Zhāng Bái of the same commandery.
After three months of serving in the ancestral temple,
before completing the rites of matrimony,
Bái encountered family misfortune
and died in a distant commandery.
Yùshēng upheld her integrity with unwavering voice,
her righteousness visible in her expression.
Though nobles and officials came proposing,
she vowed and refused them all.
She supported Bái's sisters through perilous circumstances,
enduring fire and water,
her will embracing frost and snow.
Her righteous heart was firm as metal and stone,
her sincerity piercing through to the divine.
She conducted funeral rites with propriety,
and the gentry of the land admired her example.
I have heard that virtue is manifested through action,
and action is honored with rank.
Without such recognition,
the encouragement of goodness lacks rigor.
Thus, when a scholar is eulogized,
the people of Lǔ remember his courage;
when the woman of Qǐ is recorded,
the people of Qí mourn her weeping.
I beg the Sacred Court
to honor Yùshēng with the title 'Righteous Aunt,'
to encourage the integrity of young widows,
so the imperial customs may flourish harmoniously,
and men and women may renew their perspectives."
Annotations to the Records of Wú
Illustrations, Paintings, Eulogies, and Odes
Zhāng Wēn's three sisters all had virtuous conduct,
because of Zhāng Wēn's affair,
those who were already married
all had their marriages annulled.
Among them, the youngest sister was first married to Gù Chéng,
but the authorities arranged for her to marry the Dīng family,
with the wedding date set,
so she drank poison and died.
The Wú court praised and admired her,
and the local people painted her portrait and composed eulogies for her.
The "Wénshì Zhuàn"
records the aspirations of two women,
but does not include this,
likely due to limited knowledge.
The "Tōngzhì" is brief,
and does not highlight this,
perhaps because it did not see Péi's annotations?
The "Jìn Shū":
Wáng Hún's wife, whose surname was Zhōng, had the courtesy name Yǎn,
gave birth to Jì, making Hún
say it was enough to comfort people's hearts.
Yǎn laughed and said:
If I had been matched with the参军,
my younger brother Lún
would have produced offspring, not just this.
How could this be a woman's words?
The "Wángshì Pǔ" says Hún's wife was the daughter of Zhōng Yǎn, yet also says her courtesy name was Yǎn,
are the father and child to have the same name?
The "Tōngzhì" follows this,
unable to make corrections,
yet criticizes Zǐcháng for entirely using old texts?
Spent all his money
Mèng Chǎng plotted with Liú Yù to eliminate Huán Xuán,
Chǎng's wife Zhōu shì possessed substantial wealth,
Chǎng said to her:
"Liú Mài slandered me before Lord Huán,
causing my lifelong ruin,
I am determined to become a rebel,
you should fortunately sever ties early and escape,
so I may welcome you back when we gain wealth and honor,
if you haven't escaped by then."
Zhōu shì replied:
"Your parents are still living,
and you wish to undertake this extraordinary scheme,
how could a wife dissuade you?
If the endeavor fails,
I shall serve your family in the government offices,
resolved never to return."
Chǎng remained sorrowful for a long time before rising,
Zhōu shì followed Chǎng,
sitting said:
"Observing your actions,
this isn't a matter requiring consultation with a woman,
you merely desire financial resources."
Thereupon pointing to the daughter in her arms showed him saying:
"If even she could be sold,
I would not hesitate."
Then poured all her assets to supply him.
Chǎng's younger brother Yǐ's wife,
was Zhōu shì's maternal cousin,
Zhōu shì deceived her saying:
"Last night I had an inauspicious dream,
all crimson items in the household should be gathered,
to perform apotropaic rites."
The cousin believed and gave them to her,
whereupon they were all used for soldiers' robes.
"Biographies of Exemplary Women of Jin"
Holy Mother
Lady Xiǎn was from Gāoliáng,
her family had for generations been chieftains of Nányuè,
with a tribe of over a hundred thousand people.
From a young age, she was virtuous and wise,
and while still in her parents' home, she was able to pacify and govern the tribal masses,
subduing the various Yuè peoples.
Féng Bǎo, the Grand Administrator of Gāoliáng, heard of her aspirations and conduct,
and took her as his wife.
She often participated with her husband Bǎo in deciding legal disputes,
and governmental orders were carried out systematically.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
the Commander-in-Chief Xiāo Bó conscripted troops for reinforcement,
and sent Inspector Lǐ Qiānshì to summon Bǎo.
Bǎo intended to go,
but Lady Xiǎn suspected he would rebel,
and stopped him.
He indeed later rebelled.
After Bǎo's death,
the region south of the mountains fell into great turmoil,
but Lady Xiǎn pacified and united it,
and the Hundred Yuè peoples lived in peace.
Her son Féng Pú was still young, and due to Lady Xiǎn's merits, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xìndū.
An imperial edict appointed Lady Xiǎn as Grand Lady of Gāoliáng Commandery,
bestowing upon her an embroidered carriage cover, oiled cordage, and a team of four horses,
a comfortable carriage with musical escort,
banners, streamers, and insignia,
with ceremonial honors equivalent to those of an Inspector.
After Pú's death,
the Hundred Yuè peoples hailed Lady Xiǎn as the Holy Mother.
When Wáng Zhòngxuān rebelled,
Lady Xiǎn led troops and defeated him,
personally donning armor and riding a horse to inspect and pacify the various provinces.
The region south of the mountains was completely pacified,
and she was enfeoffed as Lady of Qiáo.
The military headquarters established the office of Chief Clerk,
provided with official seals,
authorizing her to act according to circumstances.
The Empress Dowager bestowed upon her a set of head ornaments and ceremonial banquet attire.
At that time, Zhào Nè, the Commander of Pān Province, was corrupt and cruel,
causing many Lí and Liáo people to flee or rebel.
Lady Xiǎn submitted a sealed memorial discussing this,
and an imperial decree ordered Lady Xiǎn to summon and appease them.
Lady Xiǎn personally carried the imperial edict,
calling herself an envoy,
traveled through more than ten provinces,
proclaiming the emperor's benevolent intentions,
and wherever she passed, the people submitted.
Emperor Wén bestowed upon Lady Xiǎn the district of Línzhèn as her fief for personal upkeep,
and upon her death, she was posthumously honored as Chéngjìng.
Remote momentum
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān, the Grand Coachman Lái Jùnchén was extremely powerful,
and court officials viewed him with fear and sidelong glances.
The Director of the Imperial Forest Hóu Mǐn served him assiduously,
but his wife, Madame Dǒng, advised him against it,
saying:
"Jùnchén is a traitor to the state,
his power will not last long.
Once his affairs collapse,
his faction will be the first to suffer.
You should respect him but keep your distance."
Mǐn gradually withdrew his service,
which angered Jùnchén,
who had him demoted to Magistrate of Wǔlóng County in Fúzhōu.
Mǐn wanted to resign and return home,
but Madame Dǒng said:
"Go quickly, do not seek to stay."
They then traveled to the province,
where Mǐn presented his name card to the provincial general.
He mistakenly wrote on a single sheet of paper,
and when the provincial general unrolled it to look,
there was writing at the end,
so he became very angry and said:
"If you cannot even write your name properly,
how can you serve as a county magistrate?"
He did not allow Mǐn to take up his post.
Mǐn was endlessly worried and depressed,
but Madame Dǒng said:
"Just stay, do not seek to leave."
After staying for fifty days,
bandits from Zhōngzhōu broke through,
killed the former magistrate of Wǔlóng,
and plundered and killed the entire household.
Mǐn was spared because he had not taken up his post.
Later, Jùnchén was executed,
and his faction was exiled to Lǐngnán,
and Mǐn was again spared.
"Records of Affairs from the Court and the Country"
Tying Up Her Hair
In the Táng dynasty, during the reign of Emperor Dézōng, Jiǎ Zhíyán's father leaked confidential palace matters.
The emperor, enraged, bestowed poisoned wine.
Zhíyán pleaded with the eunuch envoy,
requesting to personally hold the vessel and serve it to his father.
The eunuch envoy agreed.
Zhíyán then took the cup and drank it himself,
immediately collapsing as if dead.
The wine seeped out from between his left foot,
and he revived.
A full report was submitted,
leading to his father's exile to Nánhǎi.
Later, upon an imperial pardon, they returned to Dōngpíng.
Renowned for his integrity and forthrightness,
he was appointed as a Reminding Advisor.
Zhíyán's wife, Madame Dǒng, also displayed remarkable fidelity.
When Zhíyán followed his father into exile,
he said to Madame Dǒng, "Life and death are uncertain;
we may never meet again.
I urge you to remarry."
Dǒng entered her chamber, tied her hair with a rope,
and had Zhíyán seal it with ink.
The seal inscription read:
"Only you can undo this;
it shall never be opened until death."
Twenty-two years later, they reunited,
the old seal mark still vivid. When she washed it with oil,
her hair all fell out.
"Records of Unique Wonders"
Her hair fell into the rice-washing basin,
and she remained a bald woman.
"Records of Destined Fate"
Cursing at the Bandits
Lady Fèng Xún of Bóhǎi,
courtesy name Jǐngwén,
was the granddaughter of Fèng Áo.
She excelled at cursive and clerical script calligraphy,
and was skilled in literary composition.
Her relatives regarded her as a virtuous lady.
In the wùzǐ year of the Xiántōng era, she married Bǎo Huì, a proofreader in the Imperial Library. During the Guǎngmíng era,
in the winter of the gēngzǐ year,
when baleful stars crossed the path of the sun,
and the imperial carriage fled to distant regions,
the capital's populace scattered in great disorder.
The proofreader, from his residence in Yǒngníng Ward,
secretly moved with his wife to the pond pavilion of the Xiāo family in Lánlíng Ward,
thinking the rebels would not enter again.
But by the next day, a horde of villains had gathered like mist,
and the proofreader was captured.
The rebel captors wanted to take her away with them,
but the lady straightened her robes, flung her sleeves, and cursed them loudly.
Enraged, the bandits killed her.
The proofreader escaped and returned,
where a maidservant met him at the gate, saying:
"The lady has already passed away."
The proofreader beat his chest and wailed in profound grief,
shedding tears upon the lady's face,
and said:
"Jǐngwén, we shall meet soon."
Then, with a long cry, he collapsed dead on the ground.
Three maidservants, witnessing both their master and mistress deceased,
joined hands and threw themselves into a deep well, dying together.
From "Minor Records from Sānshuǐ"
This old servant is no match.
Wénchāng Zuǒ Chéng Lú Xiàn's second daughter was first married into the Zhèng family,
but her husband died early,
and she vowed not to remarry.
She was dignified and beautiful in appearance,
with a very noble character.
Her elder sister's husband, Yǔlín General Lǐ Sīchōng,
after his wife passed away,
petitioned to continue the family ties by marriage,
and her brothers agreed to it,
but did not dare to inform her.
Sīchōng chose an auspicious day and prepared the ceremonies,
with lavish betrothal gifts,
and went to the Lú residence to finalize the marriage.
She shut the door and scolded him, saying:
"Old slave, I am not your match!"
Then she climbed over the wall to a relative's home and cut off her hair.
Sīchōng reported this to the court,
and the imperial decree respected her resolve, not forcing her to change her mind.
Later, she became a nun,
and was very diligent in her practice.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Both the Old and New Books of Táng record her as Cuī Huì's wife.
Lìng Dé
Xuē Yuánguì,
the paternal uncle of Xuē Bō,
his wife was the younger sister of Jǐnán Lín Yáng, the governor of Dānyáng,
possessed maternal dignity and virtuous conduct,
was extensively versed in the Five Classics,
excelled in literary composition,
and the essays she wrote
were often recited and studied by contemporaries.
After Xuē Yuánguì passed away,
his sons Yǎnfǔ, Yánguó, Yǎnwěi, Yǎnyún, and Bō's elder brother Jù, all were orphaned at a young age,
and were all tutored and guided by Lady Lín in their childhood,
eventually achieving renown in literature and learning.
During the twenty years between the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras,
Yǎnfǔ, Jù, and five others all passed the imperial examinations as jìnshì,
successively earning academic honors,
bringing glory to their family and lineage.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Teaching the Husband to Guard the City
At the end of the Jiànzhōng era, Lǐ Xīliè captured Biàn,
planning to attack Chén Prefecture.
Lǐ Kǎn was the magistrate of Xiàngchéng County.
Lǐ Xīliè dispatched troops to conquer various counties.
Kǎn, considering the city small and the bandits strong, wanted to flee.
His wife, Madame Yáng, said:
"When the enemy arrives, we should defend.
If our strength is insufficient, then we die here.
If we flee, who will defend?
I request offering heavy rewards to recruit daring warriors—this may still save us."
Kǎn then summoned the officials and people, saying:
"As magistrate, I am merely a transient official who will leave when my term ends,
unlike you officials and people whose ancestral graves are in this land.
Let us defend unto death together.
How can we bear to lose our integrity and serve the bandits?"
The crowd wept and pledged allegiance.
Kǎn led them to man the city walls.
His wife personally cooked to feed the masses.
They sent a message to the bandits:
"The elders of Xiàngchéng uphold righteousness and will not surrender.
The bandits should leave quickly.
To persist will only bring you loss, with no benefit."
The bandits laughed loudly.
Kǎn was hit by a stray arrow,
and returned to his residence.
His wife reproached him:
"If you are not there,
who will remain steadfast?
To die outside
is still better than dying in bed."
Kǎn hurriedly returned to the walls.
It happened that the bandit general was struck by a stray arrow and died,
so they withdrew.
The county was thus preserved intact.
An imperial decree promoted Kǎn to magistrate of Tàipíng.
From the "Táng History"
Zì Mài Jì Xíng
Zhōu Dí's wife, née Mǒu,
was skilled in trade,
traveling to and from Guǎnglíng.
At that time, Bì Shīduó's rebellion occurred,
and people were seizing and selling each other for food.
Dí was starving and on the verge of death.
His wife said:
"Now if we wish to return,
we cannot both survive.
Your parents are alive,
so we cannot die together.
I wish to be sold to aid your journey."
Dí could not bear this,
but his wife insisted and went with him to the market,
where she was sold for several thousand coins, which she gave to Dí.
When they reached the city gate, the guards questioned them, suspecting deceit,
and went with Dí to the market to investigate.
There they saw his wife's head already placed on the beam.
Dí wrapped her remaining body and returned to bury it.

Severed Arm
Wáng Níng's wife, Madame Lǐ,
whose family was from between Qīngzhōu and Qízhōu,
served as the Registrar of Guó Prefecture.
He died in office due to illness,
and his family was always poor.
Their only son was still young.
Madame Lǐ took her son
and carried his remains back home.
Passing east through Kāifēng,
she stopped at an inn.
The innkeeper, seeing a woman traveling alone with a child, grew suspicious
and refused to let her stay.
Madame Lǐ, noticing it was already dark, was unwilling to leave.
The innkeeper grabbed her by the arm and pulled her out.
Madame Lǐ looked up to the sky and wailed loudly, saying:
"I am a woman.
If I cannot preserve my chastity, how can this hand be held by a man?
I cannot let one hand defile my whole body."
She then took an axe and cut off her own arm.
Passersby who saw this gathered around and sighed,
some clicking their tongues in sympathy,
others shedding tears.
The Magistrate of Kāifēng heard of this,
reported the incident to the court officials,
and had medicine bestowed to dress her wound,
generously compensated Madame Lǐ, and flogged the innkeeper.
Alas!
Scholars who do not cherish their own integrity and endure shame to cling to life—
upon hearing of Madame Lǐ's integrity,
should feel some shame.
Preface to the Biographies of Féng Dào and Others in the *History of the Five Dynasties*.
