Lǐ Zōng
The wife of Huángfǔ Guī from Āndì was a woman whose maiden name is unknown.
After Guī lost his first wife,
he remarried her.
She was skilled in composing literature
and capable of cursive script calligraphy.
She often drafted letters and documents for Guī,
and people marveled at her exquisite work.
When Guī passed away,
his wife was still young and beautiful.
Later, when Dǒng Zhuó became Chancellor,
he courted her with a hundred carriages of dowry gifts,
twenty horses,
and servants, money, and silks filling the road.
The wife, dressed in plain clothes, went to Zhuó's gate,
knelt to plead her case,
and her words of refusal were deeply sorrowful.
Zhuó ordered his attendants and guards to draw their swords and surround her, saying:
"My authority and teachings are meant to sway all under heaven—
how could they fail to move one woman?"
Knowing she could not escape,
she stood up and cursed Zhuó:
"You, a descendant of Qiāng barbarians,
have you not done enough harm to the world?
My ancestors were virtuous for generations,
and the Huángfǔ family, with their civil and military talents,
were loyal ministers of Hàn.
Were you not once a petty official under their command?
How dare you act improperly toward your lord's wife?"
Zhuó then had his carriage driven into the courtyard,
where he ordered her head to be tied to it and whipped relentlessly.
The wife said to those wielding the whips:
"Why not strike harder?
Grant me the mercy of a quick death."
Thus, she died beneath the carriage.
Later, people painted her portrait,
hailing her as the "Model of Propriety."

Presenting a goose as a ceremonial gift
Zhèng Mào's wife, Cáo Shì,
was from Xuē in the state of Lǔ.
Mào had previously married Sūn Shì,
who died early,
so he married Cáo as his second wife.
She served her parents-in-law with great filial piety,
personally engaging in spinning and weaving to provide for the family,
and among her husband's younger siblings and sisters,
she fulfilled all proper etiquette,
winning everyone's affection.
When Mào became Minister of Works,
and their son Mò and others achieved high positions at court,
contemporaries praised their honor and wealth.
Yet Cáo deeply feared excessive prosperity,
and whenever Mò was promoted, she would worry,
showing it in her expression and tone.
She ate simple meals without multiple dishes,
wore laundered clothes,
and whatever salaries Mào and others received,
Cáo would distribute among relatives and in-laws,
ensuring all were provided for,
leaving no surplus wealth at home.
Initially, Sūn Shì was buried in Líyáng,
and when Mào passed away,
some argued that the long-interred burial would be difficult to move,
suggesting not to combine the burials.
Cáo said:
"Sūn Shì was the principal wife,
so it is proper to bury her together.
How can we leave her solitary soul with no place to rely?"
Thus, she arranged full funeral processions to welcome the remains,
prepared burial garments and quilts,
personally attended the memorial rites,
and performed the ceremonial rituals.
Those who heard of this could not help but sigh in admiration,
considering that even beneath Zhào Jī,
Shū Wěi was not worthy of praise.
(From "Biographies of Exemplary Women of Jìn")

From a young age, she was studious, clear in speech,
and had high aspirations and integrity.
She first married Fúfēng's Mǎ Yuánzhèng,

she became Gǎo's second wife.

she remained silent for three years,

and held out in the tower on the western hill of the city.
Emperor Wén of Chén dispatched Zhāng Zhāodá to capture him and also to seize his wife and bring her back.
Knowing escape was impossible,
Wáng Biāo called to his wife to bid her farewell, saying:
"Life and death part us from this moment on."
They then killed Wáng Biāo.
Zhāng Zhāodá advanced with his troops to meet Wáng Biāo's wife,
bowed and announced he was following Emperor Wén of Chén's order to welcome her as the head of the household.
Yáng then turned her weeping into laughter,
appearing pleased and willing.
She requested Zhāng Zhāodá to bury Wáng Biāo.
After the funeral and burial were completed,
as Yáng was returning, she passed by Wáng Biāo's residence
and said to Zhāng Zhāodá:

Having endured hardship for so long,
I ask to briefly stop at the residence to adorn myself."
Zhāng Zhāodá permitted it.
Upon entering the house, Yáng used a knife to cut her hair and disfigure her face,
wailing in extreme grief until she fainted.
She vowed never to remarry.
When Emperor Wén of Chén heard of this,
he sighed incessantly in admiration,
and subsequently allowed her to become a nun.
Later, when soldiers of Emperor Wǔ of Chén came to take her,
Yáng threw herself into a well to end her life.
At the time, it was cold in the north; they pulled her out near death and built a fire to warm her,
and after being warmed, she revived.
Getting up, she threw herself into the fire.
Lady Yáng was from Tiānshuǐ,
the daughter of the Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Yáng Jiǎo.
She was beautiful
and had previously been the wife of Péi Rénlín from Hédōng.
Due to the turmoil, she was taken by Wáng Biāo.

Guó Zhē
Dòu Huáizhēn, courtesy name Cóngyī,
avoided Empress Wěi's personal name and was addressed by his courtesy name.
During the New Year's Eve banquet held by Emperor Zhōngzōng,
a close minister said to him:
"I heard you lost your wife.
Would you like to remarry now?"
Huáizhēn meekly agreed.
Soon, palace fans screened off the area,
and someone dressed in pheasant-feather ceremonial robes emerged—
it turned out to be Empress Wěi's wet nurse, Wáng, known as the Lady of Jǔ State,
originally a barbarian slave girl.
Huáizhēn accepted her without objection.
People commonly called a wet nurse's husband "Āzhē".
Whenever Huáizhēn attended court or submitted petitions,
he would sign himself as "the Empress's Āzhē".
Some people referred to him as "the State's Āzhē",
yet he remained unashamed, proudly acting as the Empress's son-in-law.
When Empress Wěi and Emperor Ruìzōng built temples for the two princesses, Jīnxiān and Yùzhēn,
Huáizhēn personally supervised the construction,
urgently overseeing the repairs.
A contemporary saying went: "First he became the State's Āzhē,
then the Chief of the Princesses' Estates"—
meaning he served the princesses like a local official.

Killed the maidservant
A certain official named Zhōu from Héngyáng, whose given name is lost,
was a native of Shǔchuān.
After his wife died, he remarried,
also to a woman from Shǔchuān.
The second wife brought along three daughters, all grown up,
whom Zhōu raised as his own.
The second wife was vicious and jealous.
Zhōu had previously kept several maidservants,
two of whom became pregnant.
The wife found other pretexts
to whip them daily without fail.
As both maids were pregnant,
they often received the blows on their backs, arms, or legs,
but she deliberately used the rod to strike their abdomens,
intending to harm the fetuses.
Eventually, both maids died from miscarriages caused by the whipping.
After killing the two maids,
her three daughters later married in succession.
They temporarily resided in Héngyáng and did not return.
Within five years, all three daughters died in childbirth.
Each time a daughter died,
the wife would offer meals to monks and repent of her wrongdoings,
commissioning sutra readings for the two maids who had died from the whipping and miscarriages,
and performing the Liáng Wǔ Confessional Rites herself.
Yet all three daughters died in childbirth.
Before dying, each would cry out in agony for days,
writhing in pain until their end.
The wife wept incessantly, consumed by worry and distress, and fell ill.
A little over a year after her daughters' deaths, she too died.
Alas,
as the saying goes:
"The net of Heaven is vast,
wide-meshed but letting nothing through."
How clearly evident is the retribution in Buddhist scriptures!
Thus,
may jealous and cruel women
hearing this be filled with greater fear,
and may it serve as a warning
beneficial to societal morals.
From "Old Stories of Luòyáng Officials."

The King of Wèi presented a beautiful woman to the King of Chǔ,

Zhèng Bāo knew that the king was pleased with the new woman,
so she showed great affection for her,
selecting clothes and amusements according to her preferences,
and choosing chambers and furnishings to her liking.
She loved her more than the king did. The king said:
"What women use to serve their husbands is their beauty,
and jealousy is their nature.
Now Zhèng Bāo knows that I am pleased with the new woman,
and she loves her more than I do.
This is how a filial child serves their parents,
and a loyal minister serves their ruler."
Zhèng Bāo knew that the king thought she was not jealous,
so she said to the new woman:
"The king loves your beauty,
however,
he dislikes your nose.
When you see the king, you must cover your nose."
When the new woman saw the king, she covered her nose.
The king asked Zhèng Bāo:
"Why does the new woman cover her nose when she sees me?"
Zhèng Bāo replied:
"I know the reason."
The king said:
"Even if it's unpleasant, you must tell me."
Zhèng Bāo said:
"It seems she dislikes the smell of Your Majesty."
The king said:
"How insolent!"
He ordered her nose cut off,
not allowing defiance of his command.

Strangled and Hung from the Beam
The daughter of Sīlì Féng Fāng was a beauty of the land.
She fled the turmoil to Yángzhōu,
where Yuán Shù, upon ascending the city wall, saw her and was delighted,
and thus took her as a consort.
He doted on her greatly,
and the other women resented her favor.
They told her:
"The general, a noble man, values resolve and integrity.
If you constantly weep and show sorrow,
you will surely long be respected and esteemed."
Lady Féng took this to be true,
and thereafter, whenever she saw Shù, she would shed tears.
Shù, thinking she had deep feelings,
pitted her even more.
The other women then took advantage of this to strangle her and hang her from a beam in the privy.
Shù truly believed she had died from unmet aspirations,
and so gave her a lavish funeral and burial.

playing with the child in her arms.

Nine Bestowments
Chancellor Wáng Dǎo's wife, Lady Cáo, was extremely jealous by nature.
She forbade the chancellor from having any concubines or attendants,
and even his personal servants were subjected to her scrutiny.
Whenever there were beautiful women,
she would reproach and blame them,
which Chancellor Wáng could no longer endure.
So he secretly established a separate residence,
where numerous concubines were arranged,
and children stood in rows.
Later, on the day of the New Year's assembly, Lady Cáo was watching from the Green Sparse Tower
when she suddenly saw two or three young children riding sheep.
They were all handsome and adorable,
and from afar, Lady Cáo felt great affection for them.
She said to her maid,
"Go out and ask whose children these are."
The servant, unable to bear the deception, replied, "They are the fourth and fifth young masters, among others."
Upon hearing this, Lady Cáo was shocked and enraged,
unable to contain herself.
She ordered her carriage and, with over twenty eunuchs and maids holding kitchen knives, went out personally to search and confront them.
Chancellor Wáng also hastily ordered his carriage and sped out of the gate,
still worried that the oxen were too slow.
He used his left hand to grip the carriage railing
and his right hand to hold a duster, using its handle to help the driver whip the oxen.
In a frantic rush,
he barely managed to arrive first.
Minister Cài Mò, upon hearing of this, laughed
and deliberately went to see Chancellor Wáng, saying to him:
"The court intends to bestow upon you the Nine Bestowals;
are you aware of this?"
Wáng thought it was true
and began to modestly decline the honor.
Cài said:
"I haven't heard of other things,
only of a short-shafted oxcart
and a long-handled duster."
Wáng was greatly ashamed.
Later, he disparaged Cài, saying:
"In the past, I associated with Ānqī and Qiānlǐ
at gatherings by the Luò River,
and I never heard of any Cài Chōng's son in the world."
"Anecdotes of Jealousy from A New Account of the Tales of the World"
I, too, find her pitiable.

Transformed into a Sheep
In the capital, there was a scholar whose wife was extremely jealous and suspicious of her husband.
For minor matters, she would curse him,
and for major ones, she would certainly beat him.
She often tied a long rope to her husband's foot,
and whenever she called for him, she would pull the rope.
The scholar consequently conspired with an old sorceress.
Taking advantage of his wife's sleep,
he went to the toilet and tied the rope to a goat.
The scholar then climbed over the wall to escape.
When the wife woke up and pulled the rope, the goat came instead.
She was greatly shocked and bewildered,
summoned the sorceress to inquire,
and the sorceress said:
"Madam, due to your accumulation of wickedness,
your ancestors are blaming you,
so your husband has turned into a goat.
If you can repent and reform,
then we can pray for him."
The wife then wailed in sorrow,
embraced the goat and wept bitterly,
blaming herself and vowing to change.
The sorceress then ordered a seven-day fast,
with the whole family, young and old, avoiding the main room,
to offer sacrifices to the ghosts and gods while the sorceress prayed.
The goat returned to its original form,
and the voice gradually came back.
The wife saw her husband and cried,
asking, "After so many days as a goat,
wasn't it very hard?"
The husband said:
"I still remember eating grass that wasn't tasty,
and having a stomachache."
The wife became even more sorrowful.
Later, when she became jealous again,
the husband crouched on the ground and bleated like a goat.
The wife, startled, rose barefoot,
called upon her ancestors to vow,
that she would not dare to do so again.
From then on, she was no longer jealous.
"The Record of Jealousy"
Madwoman
During the Tàiyuán era, there was a man named Xún,
whose wife, née Yǔ, was extremely jealous.
When Xún once stayed out overnight,
she killed their two sons.
She built their house without a study,
only having a main hall without a back wall,
so that from the main room,
one could clearly see outside.
Generally, men without beards were not allowed to enter the gate.
If a messenger delivering letters came close to Xún's hand,
he would be severely beaten without exception.
If a guest shared a bed with Xún,
both guest and host would suffer.
A young man from the neighborhood rushed straight in to visit Xún,
sitting knee-to-knee with him.
Immediately, loud cursing was heard,
and she searched for a knife or staff.
Xún said to the guest:
"My mad wife's behavior,
as you have heard—
if you don't leave, it will surely ruin your affairs."
The guest said:
"I'm not afraid of this."
He then reached forward and grabbed Xún's hand.
The wife immediately took a staff and charged straight at the guest.
The guest was very strong and had a short staff hidden in his clothes,
so he fought with the old woman.
The old woman, lacking strength, fell to the ground immediately.
The guest beat her nearly to death.
Xún fled in rebellion, not daring to return.
The wife secretly sent someone to find Xún, saying:
"I happened to encounter a madman;
it wasn't your fault.
You can come back now."
Only then did Xún dare to come out.
When the wife's brother came to visit Xún,
he was lying on a square bed, and the wife didn't know it was him.
She came to grab her brother's head, dragging him to the ground intending to kill him.
Only then did she realize it was her brother.
She fled in shame into the inner quarters.
The brother, claiming their father's order, gave her several hundred strokes with a staff,
yet she showed no repentance.
It is said above
that according to common tales, Chē Wǔzǐ's wife was very jealous.

and hung a crimson skirt on the screen.
His wife drew a knife, went straight to the bed, and pulled back the covers,
only to find it was her brother.
Ashamed, she withdrew.

Línjì had a Jealous Woman's Ford,
legend says during the Tàishǐ era of Jìn,
Liú Bóyù's wife, Duchess Duàn, styled Míngguāng,
was of a jealous disposition.
Bóyù once recited the "Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luò River" before his wife and said to her:

now I have become one."
Bóyù thereafter never crossed water again in his life.
Women crossing this ford would all dishevel their garments and ruin their makeup,
only then daring to cross.
Otherwise, storms would suddenly arise.
Ugly women, even crossing without adornment,
would not incur the goddess's jealousy.
If a woman crossed the river without wind or waves,
it was taken as proof of her ugliness, unable to attract the water goddess.
Ugly women dreaded this,
and none failed to mar their appearance to avoid mockery.
Hence, the people of Qí had a saying:
"To seek a fair wife,
stand at the ford's mouth;
by the water's edge, women's
beauty or ugliness reveals itself."

Hatred and jealousy
Emperor Míng of the Liú Sòng dynasty detested women's jealousy.
Róng Yànyuǎn was favored for his skill in chess,
but his wife, in a fit of jealousy, injured his face.
The Emperor said:
"Shall I handle this for you?"
Yànyuǎn replied without thinking:
"I defer to Your Majesty's decree."
That evening, poison was bestowed, and his wife was killed.
Liú Xiū's wife, Wáng Shì, was also jealous.
The Emperor heard of this,
bestowed a concubine upon Xiū,
ordered Wáng to be caned twenty times,
commanded that a small shop be opened behind Xiū's residence,
and made Wáng personally sell brooms and soap pods to humiliate her.

but have four differences.
Jìngtōng had a jealous wife,
to the extent that he personally performed household chores;
I have a shrewish spouse,
and my family life is full of hardships—
these are the three similarities.
Jìngtōng had a son named Zhòngwén,
who achieved official rank and established his reputation;
my misfortune resembles that of Bó Dào,

Cutting off fingers and tongues
In the late Northern Wei Dynasty, Guǎ Chāng's wife, Liǔ Shì of Sōngyáng, was extremely jealous.
She had a maid named Jīn Jīng whom Chāng ordered to comb his hair while he was bathing.
Liǔ Shì cut off both of her fingers.
Soon after, Liǔ was stung by a fox, causing both of her fingers to fall off.
There was another maid named Yù Lián,
who could sing well.
Chāng admired her and praised her talent.
Liǔ Shì then cut off her tongue.
Later, Liǔ Shì developed festering sores on her tongue.
In desperation, she went to Chán Master Chóu to confess and repent.
The Chán master already knew beforehand
and said to Liǔ Shì:
"Madam, due to your jealousy,
you first cut off the maid's fingers and have already lost your own fingers.
Then you cut off another maid's tongue.
Now you are about to lose your own tongue as well.
If you repent sincerely,
you may be spared."
Liǔ Shì prostrated and begged for mercy for seven days.
The Chán master ordered her to open her mouth and chanted a spell over her.
Two snakes,
over a foot long,
emerged from her mouth.
He urgently chanted the spell,
and they fell to the ground.
Her tongue then healed completely.
From then on, she was no longer jealous.
Bestow wine
In the early Tang dynasty,
Rén Guī, the Minister of War,
was granted palace maids of exceptional beauty by imperial decree.
His wife was jealous,
and burned the hair of two maids until they were completely bald.
Emperor Tàizōng heard of this,
and ordered a eunuch to bring a golden vessel of poisoned wine to bestow upon her,
saying:
"Drinking this will cause immediate death.
Rén Guī holds the third rank,
and is entitled to keep concubines.
If you are not jealous, you need not drink it;
if you are jealous, then drink it."
Lady Liǔ bowed upon receiving the decree,
and said:
"I and Rén Guī have been husband and wife since youth,
both coming from humble origins.
We supported each other,
and thus achieved honored office.
Now that Rén Guī keeps many favored women,
I would truly rather die."
Thereupon she drank it all,
but it was not actually poison.
After she awoke from sleep,
the Emperor said to Rén Guī:
"With such a temperament,
even I must fear her."
He then issued an edict regarding the two maids,
ordering them to be housed in a separate residence.

Three Things to Fear
During the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng, the Censor-in-Chief Péi Tán revered Buddhism.
His wife was fierce and jealous,
and Péi Tán feared her as if she were a stern sovereign.
He once said there were three reasons to fear one's wife:
In her youthful beauty,
she appears like a living bodhisattva—
who wouldn't fear a living bodhisattva?
When surrounded by children,
she resembles the Nine-Children Demon Mother—
who wouldn't fear the Nine-Children Demon Mother?
And at fifty or sixty,
with light makeup applied,
appearing bluish or dark,
she looks like a Jūpánchá demon—
who wouldn't fear a Jūpánchá demon?
At that time, Empress Wéi somewhat inherited Empress Wǔ Zétiān's mannerisms,
and Emperor Zhōngzōng gradually grew afraid of her.
During a palace banquet, performers sang the "Huíbō Song" with lyrics that said:
"Huíbō at this moment—fearful of wives!
It's perfectly fine outwardly,
but inside, none surpass Péi Tán, yet even he doesn't exceed Old Man Lǐ."
Empress Wéi appeared pleased and self-satisfied,
and rewarded them with bolts of silk.

Child's Play
When Cuī Xuàn was in Huáinán,
he once had musicians teach his household servants various plays. One day the musicians reported their accomplishment,
and requested a trial performance.
Xuàn ordered them to perform in the hall below,
and sat watching with his wife Lǐ Shì.
The servants, knowing of Lǐ Shì's jealousy,
dressed several servants in women's clothing, calling them wife and concubines, arranging them to the side.
One servant then held a tablet and tightened his belt,
bustling about with constant assent between them,
setting out music and ordering wine,
with jokes and conversation inevitably directed at someone.
Lǐ Shì had not yet realized it.
After a while, the play became more intense,
completely resembling Lǐ Shì's usual behavior.
Although Lǐ Shì began to understand slightly,
she thought it was just coincidental in the play,
privately believing they wouldn't dare,
and so continued watching.
The servants aimed to make her realize,
and intensified the performance.
Lǐ indeed became angry and scolded them:
"How dare you slaves be so impudent?
When have I ever been like this?"
A servant pointed at her and shouted:
"Hah! You red-eyed one,
now acting with white eyes to deny it!"
Xuàn laughed heartily,
nearly collapsing with laughter.

Bestowed silver and colored silks
Minister of War Dù Yè served in the Privy Council,
possessing strategic adaptability,
fully seizing opportunities,
with military provisions and civilian registers
all held firmly in his grasp.
His wife, Madame Zhāng, was exceptionally jealous and fierce,
completely forbidding maids and concubines in the household.
Dù Yè feared her as if serving a strict parent.
Emperor Lièzǔ once commanded Empress Yuán to summon Madame Zhāng to the inner court and admonish her:

he is entitled to keep concubines.

Madame Zhāng wiped her tears and replied:

who encountered this sacred reign

yet he is already prematurely aged and often ill.

and may impede his performance of duties."

he greatly praised her,
rewarding her with a silver basin and colored silks.

serving maidservants

serving the three maids with the respect due to parents-in-law.

committed suicide
There are cases of women's jealousy that are exceptionally severe.
Forty years ago, the wife of Fàn Sìchéng, the Deputy Director of the Wine Office in Fǔzhōu, was beautiful but extremely jealous.
Fàn, both fond and fearful of her,
was never able to participate in the banquets with courtesans that his colleagues held during their leisure time.
One evening, when it was Fàn's turn to be on duty overnight,
an incident arose requiring the reporting of overnight brewing,
so Fàn led his clerks and soldiers straight to the scene for a search and arrest at dawn.
One of his colleagues, Lǐ Gòngfèng, who was well aware of Fàn's wife's jealousy,
playfully took a courtesan's shoe and secretly placed it in Fàn's bedding.
Shortly after, the duty clerk brought the quilt and mattress back home.
When the wife unfolded the quilt and found the shoe,
her expression turned despondent.
She questioned where it came from,
but the clerk said he did not know.
Thereupon, she wept with resentment,
and after a long while, beating her chest, she cried out:
"Heavens, how could this be?"
She then entered her room, closed the door, and went to bed.
Soon after, Fàn returned,
and when he pushed the door open and entered, he found she had hanged herself.

Blade
There was an assistant prefect in Húnán,
whose wife had given birth to a son already one year old,
and the couple cherished him dearly.
One day, when the prefect was away,
he instructed the assistant to act in his stead.
It happened that a neighboring prefect was visiting,
so a banquet was held with courtesans summoned.
Among them was one elegant and clever, standing by the assistant’s side.
He turned to chat with her,
and even playfully offered her wine.
Just as their laughter and conversation were at their peak,
suddenly a bailiff brought two plates of raw meat and placed them before the host and guest.
The assistant, startled, asked the reason,
only to learn it was his son’s flesh.
It turned out the wife, enraged by her husband’s conversation with the courtesan,
had personally killed their son,
cut his flesh, and presented it.
Her cruelty reached such an extreme.
End.
Seven Grounds for Divorce
Kǒngzǐ said there are five types of women one should not marry:
those from rebellious families,
those from disorderly families,
those whose families have had criminals,
those with severe illnesses,
those who have lost their fathers,
and the eldest daughters.
There are seven grounds for divorcing a wife and three exceptions,
The seven grounds are:
disobedience to parents,
failure to bear children,
adultery and lewdness,
jealousy,
severe illness,
gossip and quarrelsome nature,
and theft.
The three exceptions are:
when she has no family to return to,
when she has observed the three-year mourning period with her husband,
and when the husband was poor before marriage but became wealthy afterward.
All these were established by the sage to regulate relationships between men and women,
and to emphasize the importance of the beginning of marriage.

thus the Kǒng family was said to have three generations of divorce.

Taking Dates and Dismissing the Wife
Wáng Jí, in his youth while pursuing studies in Cháng'ān,

Xiè Chéng's "Hòu Hàn Shū"
The mother-in-law detested her and sent her back home.
Yīng Shùn, styled Huá Zhòng,
was a native of Nándùn, Rǔnán,
and served Emperor Gāozǔ.
His wife was originally the former wife of Dèng Yuányì of Rǔnán.
Yuányì's father, Bó Kǎo, was a shàngshū púyè.
When Yuányì returned to his hometown,
his wife remained to serve her mother-in-law with great diligence.
However, the mother-in-law detested her,
confined her in an empty room,
restricted her food and drink,
and she grew increasingly emaciated and distressed day by day.
Yet the wife never uttered a word of complaint.
Later, Bó Kǎo found it strange and inquired about it.
At that time, Yuányì's son Lǎng was a few years old
and said his mother was not ill,
but only suffering from hunger.
Bó Kǎo shed tears and said:
"Who would have thought that her own mother-in-law would cause such misfortune and hardship?"
He sent her back to her family to remarry and become Huá Zhòng's wife.
Zhòng served as jiàngzuò dàjiàng.
Once, his wife rode out in a court carriage,
and Yuányì watched her from the roadside.
He said to others:
"This is my former wife.
She committed no fault,
but my family treated her extremely harshly.
She was originally noble in character."
Their son Lǎng was then a láng official.
When his mother sent him letters, he never replied,
and when she sent him clothes, he burned them.
His mother did not take it to heart
and wished to see him.
She went to the Lǐ family's hall, where he was related by marriage,
and had someone summon Lǎng under another pretext.
Lǎng arrived and saw his mother,
bowed twice and wept,
then stood up and left his mother.
She chased after him and said:
"I nearly died,
abandoned by your family.
What crime did I commit
to be treated like this?"
After this, they severed ties completely.

ordering her to gather it up.

Tài Gōng said:

spilled water is certainly hard to retrieve."
The woman then died of resentment,
and today there is the tomb of Mother Mǎ.

he sent a letter to his ministers saying:
"I have let you all down,
the situation is already beyond remedy,
like spilled water that cannot be retrieved."

once sold firewood,
walking while reciting books,

Later, Mǎichén walked alone singing on the road,

The Burning of Books
Wáng Huān, courtesy name Jūnhòu,
was a man of Lèlíng.
He was content with poverty and cherished the Way,
not managing any property or business.
He often begged for food while reciting the Shījīng,
and although his household lacked even a peck of stored grain,
he remained cheerful and content.
His wife was troubled by this,
and at one point burned his books, hoping he would change and she could remarry.
Huān laughed and said to her:
"Have you not heard of the wife of Zhū Mǎichén?"
Those who heard of this often laughed at him,
but Huān held even more firmly to his aspirations,
and eventually became a widely learned scholar.
From the Jìn Shū
Search for a Book
Yán Zhēnqīng served as the prefect of Fǔzhōu.
A local man named Yáng Zhìjiān was devoted to learning but lived in poverty.
His wife, due to insufficient financial support,
demanded a divorce document to end their marriage.
Yáng Zhìjiān sent her off with a poem that read:
"In earlier years, I aspired to follow a master early,
But today, my temples are streaked with gray.
I know my落魄 state comes from seeking success too late,
And I willingly accept that abandoning myself was delayed.
You may freely adorn your new hair with golden hairpins,
And let the phoenix mirror guide you to paint another's eyebrows.
From now on, we are but fellow travelers on the road,
Meeting again only when descending the mountain."
His wife took the poem to Yán Zhēnqīng, seeking permission to remarry.
Yán Zhēnqīng ruled on the case, stating:
"Yáng Zhìjiān has long embraced Confucian teachings,
and holds some renown for his poetry.
His foolish wife, seeing he had not yet achieved success,
thus developed thoughts of leaving.
Like Wáng Huān, whose granary was empty,
how could he respect the yellow scrolls?
As the wife of old man Zhū was bound to leave,
could she have waited to see brocade robes?
She did not emulate the wife of Jì Quē,
who supported her husband's noble endeavors,
but instead imitated the wife of Zhū Mǎichén,
lightly abandoning a good man.
She has disgraced the village,
and damaged moral customs.
Without punishment,
who will curb such frivolous arrogance?
The wife shall receive twenty lashes,
and is then free to remarry.
Yáng Zhìjiān, the scholar, shall be provided with grain and silk,
and additionally appointed to the army.
When this was heard from afar,
all were pleased and convinced.
From then on, no woman in Jiāngzuǒ dared to abandon her husband.
From "Conversations from Yúnxī"
Gift of Pearls
King Fūchāi of Wú had a young daughter named Zǐyù,
who was both talented and beautiful.
A youth named Hán Chòng wished to marry her,
but the king would not permit it,
so Zǐyù died of suppressed grief.
When Chòng returned from his studies and learned of this,
he was moved by her devotion and brought silk and coins to mourn at her tomb.
Zǐyù's spirit emerged from the grave,
and upon seeing Chòng, she wept.
Together they returned to the tomb.
After three days and nights, she presented him with a pearl one inch in diameter and a white jade pot,
then stretched her neck and sang:
"In the southern mountains there is a bird,
in the northern mountains nets are spread.
My heart wishes to follow you,
but slanderous words are many.
Grief has solidified into illness,
ending my life in the yellow earth.
My fate was not fortunate,
what can my soul do?
My clan's elder is called the phoenix;
one day she loses her mate,
for three years she grieves.
Though there are many other birds,
she will not form a pair.
Thus I show my humble form,
meeting you in your splendor.
Though bodies are far, hearts are near—
how could I ever forget you, even for a moment?"
In Sōushén Jì, she is recorded as Zǐyù.
Fùmǎ
Xīndào Dù of Lǒngxī was traveling for study,
and when he reached five li west of Yōngzhōu City to the north,
he saw a large mansion,
with a maidservant at the gate.
Xīn Dù asked at the gate for a meal,
and the maidservant went in to inform the young lady of Qín.
The young lady ordered him to be brought in,
and Dù hurried into the chamber.
The young lady of Qín was sitting on the western couch,
and after Dù gave his name and exchanged greetings,
he was told to sit on the eastern couch.
A meal was then served,
and after eating,
the young lady said to Dù:
"I am the daughter of the King of Qínguān,
betrothed to the State of Cáo,
but unfortunately, I died before marrying.
It has been twenty-three years since my death,
and I have lived alone in this mansion.
Now that you have come,
I wish to become husband and wife with you."
After three days and nights,
suddenly the young lady said herself:
"You are a living person, and I am a ghost.
Though we share a predestined bond,
this meeting can only last three nights;
we cannot stay together long,
or disaster will strike.
Yet in these few nights,
we have not fully expressed our affection.
Since we are about to part,
how can I give you a token of my faith?"
She ordered a box behind the bed to be opened,
took out a golden pillow,
and gave it to Dù as a keepsake.
Then they parted in tears,
and she sent the maidservant to see him out the gate.
Before he had gone more than a few steps,
the mansion was no longer visible,
and there was only a grave mound.
Dù fled in panic at that moment,
but seeing the golden pillow still in his embrace,
he found it unchanged.
He then went to the State of Qín,
and tried to sell the pillow in the market.
It happened that the Qín princess was touring by carriage,
and she personally saw Dù selling the golden pillow.
Suspicious, she demanded to see it,
and asked Dù where he had obtained it.
Dù told her everything.
When the princess heard this, she wept uncontrollably,
though she still had doubts.
So she sent people to open the grave,
and upon examining the coffin,
found all the original burial items intact,
except for the golden pillow.
When they opened the shroud to look,
the signs of intimacy were still fresh.
Only then did the Qín princess believe it,
and she sighed, saying:
"My daughter has been dead for a great many years,
yet after twenty-three years she could still interact with a living person.
This is truly my son-in-law."
She then enfeoffed Xīndào Dù as Commandant-Escort,
bestowing upon him gold, silk, carriages, and horses,
and ordered him to return to his homeland.
From this time on,
people later referred to sons-in-law as 'fùmǎ',
and today, the imperial son-in-law is also called 'fùmǎ'."
From "In Search of the Supernatural"
Gēngshēng
During the reign of Qín Shǐhuáng, there was a man named Wáng Dàopíng,
a native of Cháng'ān.
In his youth, he and the daughter of fellow villager Táng Shūxié,
whose childhood name was Fù Yù,
both of outstanding beauty,
pledged to become husband and wife.
Soon after, Wáng Dàopíng was conscripted for military campaigns,
and became trapped in the southern regions,
unable to return for nine years.
Her parents, seeing their daughter grown,
arranged her betrothal to Liú Xiáng as his wife.
The girl, bound by her solemn vow to Dàopíng,
refused to change her commitment.
Under parental coercion,
she was compelled to marry Liú Xiáng.
After three years,
she became despondent and joyless,
constantly yearning for Dàopíng,
growing resentful,
and deeply depressed until she died.
Three years after her death,
Dàopíng returned home
and inquired among the villagers about the girl's whereabouts.
The villagers replied:
"This girl's heart belonged to you,
but she was forced by her parents
to marry Liú Xiáng,
and now she has passed away."
Píng asked where her grave was,
and the villagers led him to the tomb.
Overcome with grief, he wept and sobbed,
calling her name three times,
circling the tomb in unbearable sorrow.
Then Píng prayed:
"You and I made vows to heaven and earth,
pledging to be together for life.
Who could have foreseen official duties entangling me,
leading to our separation?
Your parents and Liú Xiáng thwarted our original intent,
and now death parts us forever.
If your spirit has divine power,
let me see your face once more;
if there is no such divinity,
then we part here forever." After speaking,
he wept again, lingering in sorrow,
when the girl's spirit emerged from the tomb,
asking Píng where he had come from.
After a long separation,
she said, "I originally pledged to be your wife for life,
but forced by my father,
I was betrothed to Liú Xiáng.
Three years passed,
and missing you day and night made me ill,
my pent-up resentment leading to death,
separating us by the dark path.
Yet remembering our former vow,
I cannot forget to seek reunion and comfort.
My body remains unharmed,
and I can live again;
we can still be husband and wife.
Quickly open the grave,
break the coffin, and let me out—I am truly alive."
He then opened the tomb and felt her,
and the girl indeed revived.
She dressed and followed Dàopíng home.
Her husband Liú Xiáng, hearing of this, was astonished
and appealed to the local authorities to examine the law,
but no statute covered the case.
So, they recorded the details and reported to the king,
who ruled that she should be returned to Wáng Dàopíng as his wife.
They lived to be 120 years old,
truly a case where sincere devotion moved heaven and earth,
eliciting such a response.
From "Sōu Shén Jì"
During the Yuánkāng era, a woman in Liángguó was betrothed,
having already received the betrothal gifts,
but soon her fiancé was stationed in Cháng'ān,
and did not return for years.
Her family remarried her to another,
but she was unwilling to go.
Her parents forced her,
and she had no choice but to leave,
soon falling ill and dying.
Later, her fiancé returned,
asking where the woman was,
and her family told him everything.
He went straight to her grave,
overwhelmed with grief,
and opened the tomb and coffin,
whereupon she revived.
He took her back with him.
When her later husband learned of this,
he went to the authorities to dispute it,
but the local office could not decide.
The Secretary Lang Wáng Dǎo proposed:
"This is an extraordinary event,
not to be judged by ordinary principles;
she should be returned to her former fiancé."
The court followed his proposal.

Japanese soldiers
Lú Chōng was
a man from Fànyáng.
Thirty lǐ west of his home lay the tomb of Cuī Shàofǔ.
One day before the winter solstice, Chōng went hunting west of his home,
saw a river deer,
raised his bow and shot it, hitting it immediately.
The deer fell but rose again,
and Chōng pursued it unconsciously
until suddenly he saw a village gate resembling a government office.
Inside the gate, under a bell, someone announced his arrival.
Chōng asked, "What office is this?"
The reply came, "It is Shàofǔ's office."
Chōng said, "My clothes are shabby; how can I meet a noble person?"
Immediately, someone brought a bundle of new clothes to welcome him.
Chōng put them on, and they fit perfectly.
He then went in to see Shàofǔ,
exchanged names,
and after several rounds of wine and roasted meat,
Cuī said, "I recently received a letter from your honored father,
requesting marriage to my young daughter for you,
hence I have invited you here."
He then showed the letter to Chōng.
Though Chōng was young when his father died,
he had seen his father's handwriting
and sighed, unable to speak.
Cuī then ordered the inner quarters to prepare the young lady and had Chōng go to the eastern corridor.
When Chōng arrived, the woman had already alighted from the carriage,
and they stood at the head of the mat to bow together.
After three days, he returned to see Cuī,
who said, "You may go back now.
My daughter shows signs of pregnancy;
if a son is born, he will be returned to you,
if a daughter, she will stay and be raised by us."
He ordered the outer quarters to prepare a carriage to send the guest off.
Cuī saw him to the gate,
held his hand, and shed tears—
the feeling of parting was no different from that among the living.
He also gave him a set of clothes
and a pair of bedding.
Chōng then boarded the carriage,
which departed like a flash of lightning.
In a moment, he reached home.
His family saw him,
and amid joy and sorrow, they questioned him.
They realized that Cuī was a deceased person and that Chōng had entered his tomb,
and they regretted it deeply.
Four years later,
on the third day of the third month, while playing by the water,
he suddenly saw an ox-drawn carriage now floating, now sinking.
Once it reached the shore,
Chōng went to open the rear door and saw the Cuī maiden with a three-year-old boy inside.
Chōng was overjoyed to see them
and tried to take her hand,
but she raised her hand, pointing to the carriage behind, saying:
"The Prefect wishes to see you," meaning Shàofǔ.
Chōng went to greet him,
and the woman returned the boy to him.
Chōng also gave her gold as a farewell gift and presented a poem:
"Resplendent is the spirit mushroom's essence,
How radiant and lush its beauty.
In Huàyīn, it shone in its time,
A wondrous marvel, displaying divine wonder.
Holding blossoms, not yet in full bloom,
In midsummer, it withered by frost.
Its glory long extinguished in darkness,
Its path in the world forever barren.
Unaware of the workings of yīn and yáng,
A sage suddenly came in grace.
Brief the meeting, swift the parting,
All guided by spirits and gods.
What can I give to my beloved?
Gold to comfort the child.
Love and grace end here in farewell,
Severance wounds the liver and spleen."
Chōng took the child and the poem,
and suddenly the two carriages vanished.
He brought the child back, and all present
thought it a ghostly illusion and spat from afar,
but the form remained unchanged.
They asked the child, "Who is your father?"
The child went straight into Chōng's arms.
At first, everyone was suspicious and repulsed,
but upon reading the poem,
they sighed in awe at the mysterious connection between life and death.
Chōng went to the market to sell the gold,
setting a high price
and not wishing to sell quickly,
hoping for someone who understood.
Suddenly, an old maidservant asked Chōng how he obtained it,
then reported to her master,
who was the girl's aunt.
She sent someone to look and confirmed it was true,
saying to Chōng:
"My elder sister's daughter was Cuī Shàofǔ's daughter,
who died before marrying.
Her family grieved for her
and buried gold hairpins in her coffin.
Now, seeing you, it seems very similar.
May I hear the whole story?"
Chōng recounted the events,
and she went to his home to welcome the child.
The child had the Cuī family's features
and also resembled Chōng.
The aunt said:
"My niece gave birth at the end of the third month."
The father said:
"This spring is warm and mild,
may he rest strong."
Thus, he was named Wēnxiū,
for Wēnxiū signifies a ghost marriage,
as the omen had foretold.
The child later became a man of talent,
serving as a governor in several commanderies,
all with notable achievements.
His descendant, Zhí,
became a Minister of the Hàn dynasty.
Zhí's son, Yù, served as Minister of Works under the Wèi dynasty.
Their official honors have been passed down to this day.
From "Records of the Strange."
Classmate
Liáng Shānbó and Zhù Yīngtái were both people of the Eastern Jìn Dynasty.
Liáng's family was from Kuàijī,
Zhù's family was from Shàngyú.
They once studied together,
Zhù returned home first,
Later, Liáng passed through Shàngyú,
and went to visit Zhù,
only then did he realize she was a woman.
After returning home, he informed his parents,
wishing to marry her,
but she was already betrothed to the son of the Mǎ family.
Liáng was disconsolate as if having lost something.
Three years later, Liáng, serving as the magistrate of Yín, fell ill and died,
leaving instructions to be buried at the foot of Qīngdào Mountain.
The following year, Zhù was to marry into the Mǎ family,
Passing by that place,
violent winds and waves arose,
preventing the boat from advancing.
Zhù then went to Liáng's grave,
wailing in unrestrained grief,
Suddenly, the ground split open,
Zhù threw herself in and died there.
The Mǎ family reported the incident to the court,
and Chancellor Xiè Ān requested she be honored as a Righteous Woman.
During the reign of Emperor Hé, Liáng manifested his spiritual presence again,
serving the state with merit,
and was posthumously honored as Righteous and Loyal.
The authorities built a temple for him in Yín.
It is said that in the Wú region, there are flower butterflies,
transformed from citrus tree borers,
which women and children call Liáng Shānbó and Zhù Yīngtái.
(From the "Níngbō Gazetteer")
Shénnǚ Zhǒng
During the reign of Emperor Shàodì of Sòng, a scholar from Nánxú traveled from Huàshān to Yúnyáng.
He saw a young woman at an inn,
and fell for her without cause,
which led to a lovesickness.
His mother asked the reason,
and he told her everything.
The mother went to find the woman,
and explained the situation fully.
The woman, moved by his feelings,
then untied her apron,
and told the mother to secretly place it under his mat,
saying that lying on it would cure him.
After a few days, he indeed recovered.
Suddenly lifting the mat, he saw the apron,
grasped it and wept until he nearly lost his breath,
saying to his mother:
"When I am buried, pass by Huàshān."
His mother followed his wish.
As they reached the north side of the woman's door,
the ox stopped and refused to go on.
While they waited a moment,
the woman finished dressing and bathing, then came out singing:
"At Huàshān's edge, since you have died for me,
for whom should I live alone?
If you have pity on me,
let the coffin open for me."
As soon as she finished speaking,
the coffin opened,
and the woman slipped into it.
They were then buried together,
and called the tomb of the Divine Maiden.
From "Cān Chá Zǐ"
Heavy Labor
During the Kaiyuan era, the daughter of Zhèngzhōu's Sima Zhāng Guǒ in Yìzhōu passed away,
and was temporarily buried beneath the pavilion.
When Liú Yǐ came to replace him,
his son often stayed in the pavilion.
One evening, a beautiful woman came,
and their affection grew deep.
After several months,
she suddenly said to Liú:
"I am the former Sima Zhāng's daughter,
buried in this pavilion.
It is my fate to live again,
and three days after our union,
you can open my burial place and take me away."
Liú opened it as scheduled,
and by dawn she had revived,
gradually able to speak.
After sitting up for several days,
her father came to the pavilion and saw her there.
Learning the reason,
he sighed and said:
"This is a profound connection from the netherworld,
why hide it?"
He then sent word to Guǒ to propose marriage.
The parents were surprised and delighted,
and the wedding proceeded as planned.
The happy couple later had several children.
"Guǎng Yì Jì"
Demonic Conception
It is said that Zhèng Tián was conceived from a ghostly womb.
After his mother passed away, she reunited with his father, Zhèng Yà, and gave birth to Tián.
Initially, Yà had not yet achieved success,
and he traveled to various places,
leaving his wife and a maidservant near the Taoist nunnery at a mountain temple.
When he returned, his wife had already died.
He inquired with the maidservant,
who said:
"The lady was about to give birth,
lying down,
when in the evening, a voice from the air spoke:
'You must leave the temple grounds,
do not defile my pure realm,
or I will kill you.'"
The wife prayed:
"I am but a woman,
with nowhere to go if I leave.
I beg the holy one to have mercy."
By the fifth watch,
after the pregnancy, she died inside the temple.
The Taoist community buried her in the wild fields outside the wall.
Yà brought money and wine to offer sacrifices.
That night, he dreamed of his wife saying:
"My life was not yet over;
I was destined to bear you a noble son.
Unfortunately, I defiled the Taoist temple,
and the deity killed me.
Ten li south from here, there is a Buddhist monastery,
where only one monk resides,
around fifty years old.
He is an extraordinary man.
You should go and seek his help.
The monk will likely refuse,
but if you plead earnestly and repeatedly,
I may be able to serve you again."
Upon waking,
he did not believe it,
but the next night, he dreamed again,
with the same words as before.
Yà then hurried to the monastery,
and indeed saw the monk.
At first, the monk greeted him warmly,
but when Yà explained,
he paid no attention, saying:
"I am just an ordinary man,
who happened to become a monk.
How could I intervene in matters of the underworld?"
Yà pleaded again,
and the monk angrily drove him away with his staff.
Yà endured the humiliation,
stayed for days without leaving,
and did not sleep at night.
The monk then agreed:
"Since your resolve is so firm,
wait while I investigate."
He sat in meditation,
and after midnight, rose and told Yà:
"The matter is settled.
At dawn, return first,
and I will send her to you."
That evening, Yà returned to the temple.
In the third watch, he heard voices outside the door,
and his wife was brought to him.
She said her body had already decayed,
and this was her soul.
He should take good care of her,
and with these words, she left.
Their life together was as it had been in the past,
except she avoided bright places.
After two or three years,
she gave birth to Tián.
A few more years later,
the wife bid farewell,
saying her allotted time was up,
and she must depart.
They parted in tears,
and soon, she disappeared without a trace.
"Stories from the Central Court"
Entering the Mourning Hall to Wail for the Resurrected
Cuī Hù failed the imperial examination,
and during the Qingming Festival, he wandered alone south of the capital,
where he came across a village dwelling.
Flowers and trees grew in profusion.
He knocked on the door for a long time,
and a young woman asked through a crack in the door.
He replied,
"I am wandering alone in search of spring,
and thirst for wine, seeking a drink."
The woman opened the door and offered him a bowl of water.
She then stood alone leaning against a small peach branch, gazing at him with deep affection.
Cuī bid farewell and escorted her to the door,
where she seemed overwhelmed with emotion before going inside.
Afterward, he never returned.
The following year during Qingming,
he went directly to find her.
The courtyard appeared unchanged,
but the door was bolted shut.
So he wrote a poem on the left door panel, saying:
"On this day last year within this door,
a face and peach blossoms mirrored each other's blush.
The face is gone, I know not where;
the peach blossoms still smile in the spring breeze."
A few days later, he went back
and heard crying inside.
When he inquired,
an old man said,
"Are you not Cuī Hù?
Since last year, my daughter has been dazed as if she had lost something.
When she saw the words on the left door panel,
she fell ill and died."
Cuī asked to enter and mourn her.
She lay as if alive on the bed.
Cuī lifted her head, rested it on his lap, and said,
"Hù is here,
Hù is here."
Soon, she opened her eyes,
and after half a day, she revived.
The old man was overjoyed
and gave his daughter to him in marriage.

Yún Yīng
Péi Háng encountered Lady Yúnqiào,
who gave him a poem saying:
"One drink of jade nectar awakens a hundred emotions,
When dark frost is pounded away, Yún Yīng appears.
Blue Bridge itself is an immortal's grotto,
Why must one toil to reach the Jade Capital?"
Later, while passing Blue Bridge thirsty,
he came upon a cottage where an old woman lived.
He bowed and asked for a drink,
The woman had Yún Yīng bring a bowl of nectar for him.
She was a beautiful maiden,
Péi Háng wished to marry Yún Yīng,
The old woman said:
"If you can obtain a jade pestle and mortar, I shall give her to you."
Later, Péi Háng acquired the pestle and mortar to pound medicine,
Only then could he marry her,
Thus attaining immortality.

Cǎiluán
Wén Xiāo arrived at Mount Zhonglíng's western hills, where there stood the immortal ascension site of Immortal Lord Xǔ.
Each year during the midsummer festival,
young men and women would gather densely like comb teeth.
Scholar Wén caught sight of a maiden singing:
"If you can accompany me to climb the celestial altar,
you ought to ride colorful luan birds with Wén Xiāo.
I possess embroidered robes and celestial canopies,
where jade terraces fear not frost and snow's chill."
After singing, she took a candle and climbed the mountain, feeling her way along the stones.
The scholar secretly followed her footsteps.
The maiden turned and said:
"Are you not Wén Xiāo?"
She led him to the precipitous summit,
where guards stood in strict formation.
Later came a celestial judgment stating:
Wú Cǎiluán, for leaking heavenly secrets due to private desire,
is condemned to be a mortal's wife for twelve years,
after which she shall enter Yuèwáng Mountain.

To Accompany Wine
Lú and Lǐ, two scholars, secluded themselves on Tàibái Mountain,
practicing breath control and meditation.
Lǐ, unwilling to endure poverty,
wandered aimlessly along rivers and lakes.
Later in Yángzhōu, he encountered Lú,
who, now addressed as Second Uncle, came to greet him on horseback.
A vermilion gate swung open obliquely,
with hundreds of maidservants in attendance.
One young woman assisted with the wine,
skilled in playing the konghou,
her appearance exceedingly beautiful.
Above her was a line of vermilion characters:
"Distinguishing river trees amid the clouds,
recognizing the returning boat at the horizon's edge."
After the banquet, he said:
"Would you be willing to form a marriage bond?"
That year, Lù Chángyuán of Biànzhōu married his daughter to him,
who closely resembled Lú's uncle's skilled konghou player.
Lǐ recounted the past events in detail,
and the woman said:

From Lú Zhào's "Lost History"
Zhēnzhēn
Jìnshì Zhào Yán obtained a painted screen from an artist,
depicting a woman of extraordinary beauty. Yán
said to the artist:
"There is no such person in this world.
How can I make her come to life?
I wish to take her as my wife."
The artist replied:
"This is a divine painting.
She also has a name, Zhēnzhēn.
Call her name for a hundred days,
ceaselessly day and night,
and she will eventually answer.
Once she responds, pour the wine mixed with colored ashes from a hundred families over her,
and she will surely come to life."
Yán followed these instructions,
calling her name for a hundred days,
without stopping day or night,
until she finally answered:
"Yes."
He quickly poured the wine with colored ashes from a hundred families over her, and she came to life.
She walked, spoke, and laughed,
eating and drinking as normal,
saying:
"Thank you for summoning me.
I wish to serve you as your wife."
A year later, she bore a son.
When the child was two years old,
a friend said:
"This is a demon.
She will surely bring you calamity.
I have a divine sword that can slay her."
That evening, he gave Yán the sword.
As soon as the sword entered Yán's room,
Zhēnzhēn wept and said:
"I am an earth immortal from Nányuè.
Somehow, someone painted my likeness,
and you called my name.
Since I did not refuse your wish,
but now you doubt me,
I cannot stay."
Having spoken,
she took her son and returned to the painted screen,
vomiting out the wine with colored ashes from a hundred families she had drunk.
Looking at the screen,
they saw only an additional child painted on it.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Pine Window" and "Records of Hearing Marvels"
did not remarry

nor as capable as Jífǔ in the middle.
How can I be sure to avoid wrongdoing?"

Zēng Shēn lost his wife,

Declining on Grounds of Illness
Chén Huà, styled Yuányào,

Huà firmly declined on grounds of illness,

having lost his wife early,

his carriage and attire were consistently plain,

Living alone in a single room

Recommending Water Caltrops
Sīmǎ Zǐqī wished to make his concubine his principal wife,
and consulted the court historian Yǐ Xiàng, saying:
"I have a concubine who is virtuous and I wish to have her wear the hairpin [of a principal wife],
would this be permissible?"
Yǐ Xiàng replied:
"Zǐ Xī was fond of water caltrops,
yet at the root there were sheep offerings but no caltrop offerings.
The gentleman said:
'To deviate yet follow the way of the gentleman's conduct,
is to desire that way.'
You, sir, are fundamentally able to deviate,
like Ruò'áo's wish to use this way to remove caltrop offerings.

would this be permissible?"
Zǐqī then desisted.

Grand Rites
The mother of Gōngzǐ Jīng was a favorite and was about to be made the principal wife,
so the Duke had the minister of rites, Xìn Xià, present the ceremonial procedures.
He replied:
"There is no such ceremony."
The Duke angrily said:
"You are the minister of rites.
Establishing a principal wife is a major ceremony of the state.
Why do you say there is no such ceremony?"
He replied:
"Dukes Zhōu and Wǔ married from Xuē,
Duke Xiàohuì married from Shāng,
and from Duke Huán downward, all married from Qí.
This is the proper ceremony.
As for making a concubine the principal wife,
there is indeed no such ceremony."
The Duke eventually established her,
and made Jīng the crown prince,
so the people of the state began to resent him.

Fán Tōngdé
In the Later Hàn Dynasty, Líng Xuán's concubine Fán Tōngdé could recount the stories of the sisters Zhào Fēiyàn and her sibling,
and later wrote "The Unofficial Biography of Fēiyàn."
Líng Xuán, a contemporary of Bān Gù, was renowned for his literary talent.
Xuán said to Tōngdé:
"These individuals have all turned to dust and vanished.
In their prime, they were exhausted,
their spirits restless and wandering,
their desires and cravings quieted—
did they know they would ultimately return to desolate fields and wild grasses?"
Tōngdé covered her sleeves and gazed at the candle's shadow,
holding her hair bun with her hand,
and wept sorrowfully, tears streaming down.

Ā Wù
Zhōng Yáo and Xún Yōu were close friends.

he should be entrusted with the later affairs."
Lord Zhōng Yáo then teased Yōu, saying:

Xún indeed died before Yáo,
who managed his household affairs,
married off his concubine Āwù,
ensuring she was well settled.
Lǜ Zhū
In the past, there was a woman of the Liáng family who possessed great beauty.
Shí Jìlún, serving as an inspector of Jiāozhǐ,
purchased her with three hú of pearls,
and she was none other than Lǜ Zhū.
She excelled at playing the flute.
Sūn Xiù sent someone to demand her,
and Shí Chóng replied:
"Lǜ Zhū is my beloved concubine,
she cannot be given away."
Sūn Xiù ultimately had Shí Chóng executed and came for Lǜ Zhū.

Shí Jìlún had a beloved maid named Xiángfēng,

Resentful, Xiángfēng composed a poem:
"Who does not admire the beauty of spring blossoms,
yet ultimately grieves when they fall in autumn.

Luòxiù
When Zhōu Jùn was serving as the General Pacifying the East, he went hunting
and encountered a heavy rainstorm.
He passed by the Lǐ family of Rǔnán,
a wealthy household where the men were absent.
There was a daughter named Luòxiù
who heard that an important person was outside.
She and a maidservant slaughtered pigs and sheep inside the house,
preparing food and drink for several dozen people.
The tasks were meticulously handled without any sound of people being heard.
Secretly observing,
he saw only one woman whose appearance was extraordinary.
Jùn then requested to take her as a concubine.
Her father and brothers did not consent,
but Luòxiù said:
"Our family lineage is in decline;
why begrudge one daughter?
If we form a marriage alliance with a noble clan,
it may bring great benefits in the future."
Her father and brothers complied with her.
She subsequently gave birth to Bó Rén and his brothers.
Luòxiù told Bó Rén and the others:
"The reason I lowered my status to become a concubine in your family
was for the sake of our family's standing.
If you do not treat my family as kin,
I would not cherish my remaining years."
Bó Rén and the others all obeyed her command.
From then on, the Lǐ family
received proper recognition and treatment.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Sòng Huī
Sòng Yī was a disciple of Shí Chóng's courtesan Lǜ Zhū,
possessing exceptional beauty,
and skilled in playing the flute.
She was in the service of Emperor Míng of Jìn,
who fell critically ill.
The ministers advised
that Sòng Yī be dismissed.
At that time, all the court worthies were present,
and the Emperor said:
"Which of you gentlemen wishes to have her?"
The assembly remained silent,
until Ruǎn Yǎojí, then Minister of Personnel,
said:
"I beg she be granted to me."
The Emperor immediately gave her to him.
After Yī's death,
she was buried on the southern hill of Jīnchéng,
facing the gate of Lángyá Commandery.
Yuán Shānsōng was the governor of Lángyá,
and whenever drunk, he would ride in his carriage to Yī's grave,
singing the "Song of the Hard Road."
A common tale says
Sòng Yī was once a concubine of General Wáng,
and later belonged to General Xiè of the Western Regions.
Xiè asked Yī:
"How do I compare to Wáng?"
She replied:
"Wáng, compared to you, my lord,
is but a wealthy rustic."
The Annotations to Shì Shuō
state that Sòng Yī's details are unclear.

Shí Hǔ's Empress Zhèng, named Yīngtáo,

The Book of Zhào states that Shí Hǔ betrothed Lady Cuī as his wife,

Opening the chamber to drive away the concubine
Wáng Chùdùn was praised by his contemporaries as a man of noble character.
He had once been unrestrained and indulgent in sensual pleasures,
to the point that his health deteriorated.
His attendants admonished him about this,
and Chùdùn said:
"I hadn't realized it was like this.
If that's the case, it's easily remedied."
Thereupon he opened the rear chambers,
drove out several dozen maids and concubines,
and allowed them to go wherever they pleased.
People of the time marveled at this.
Táoyè,
the concubine of Wáng Zǐjìng,
was deeply cherished by him,
who composed songs for her.
One of them reads:
"Peach leaves reflect the flowers' red,
graceful even without a breeze."
Another says:
"Peach leaf after peach leaf,
the peach tree connects to the peach root."

Féng Yuèhuá
When Sòng Shěn Yōuzhī was the governor of Jīngzhōu,
there was a herd of horses in the stable,
which would leap and neigh in fright every night.
Yōuzhī ordered someone to keep watch by the trough,
where they saw a white pony with a rope tied around its belly,
leaping and darting as if flying,
too swift to be caught.
They checked the stable, which was still locked,
yet it dashed into the inner chamber.
Upon questioning the household,
they learned that only his beloved concubine Féng Yuèhuá had a jade horse on her arm,
threaded with a green cord,
which she always placed under her pillow when sleeping.
At night, it would sometimes disappear,
but by morning, it was back in place.
Examining its hooves,
they indeed found traces of mud.
Yōuzhī later vanished, and no one knew where he went.
"Tales of the Zhǔ Palace"
Yào Huá
Ruǎn Diànfū of Lújiāng, Hé Huī had a singing girl named Zhāng Yàohuá,
who was beautiful and greatly favored.
When Hé Huī was about to depart to take up his post as Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
he invited Ruǎn Diànfū to a drinking party.
During the musical entertainment, Ruǎn saw Lady Zhāng and was captivated by her,
repeatedly asking Huī:
"Huī can be obtained,
but this person cannot be obtained."
Ruǎn Diànfū flicked his sleeves and walked out the door, saying:

to impeach Huī on public affairs.

Xú Yuèhuá
After Gāoyáng Prince Yōng passed away,
all his singing girls were ordered to become nuns,
though some married.
The beauty Xú Yuèhuá excelled at playing the konghou,
and could perform the "Míngfēi's Journey Beyond the Frontier" melody.
Those who heard her singing were all deeply moved.
During the Yǒng'ān era, she became the concubine of General Wèi Yuán Shìkāng,
residing near the Qīngyáng Gate.
When Xú played the konghou and sang,
her mournful voice pierced the clouds.
Passersby listening soon formed a crowd like a market.
Xú often told Shìkāng:
"The prince had two beautiful consorts—
one named Xiūróng,
the other Yànzī.
Both had delicate eyebrows and pearly teeth,
with flawless looks that could topple a city.
Xiūróng could also sing the 'Green Water' song,
while Yànzī excelled at the 'Fire Phoenix' dance.
They were both adored in the inner chambers,
their favor surpassing all other consorts."
Hearing this,
Yuán Shìkāng often had Xú play the "Green Water" and "Fire Phoenix" melodies.
(Records of the Monasteries of Luòyáng)
Cháoyún
Prince Chén of Héjiān had three hundred singing girls,
all of them beauties of the land.
Among them was a maid named Zhāoyún,
who excelled at playing the chí flute,
and was favored for her songs of "Round Fan" and "Mound Melodies."
When Chén served as governor of Qín Province,
the various Qiāng tribes rebelled externally,
and repeated campaigns failed to subdue them.
Chén ordered Zhāoyún to disguise herself as a poor old woman,
begging while playing the chí flute.
When the Qiāng people heard it,
they were all moved to tears,
and said to one another in turn:
"Why abandon our ancestral graves and wells to become bandits in the mountains and valleys?"
They immediately surrendered in succession.
The people of Qín said:
"Swift horses and sturdy men,
are no match for an old woman playing the chí flute."
Spring breeze
In Luòyáng's Shànggāo Lǐ was the residence of Champion General Guō Wényuǎn,
with halls and gardens
matching those of a feudal lord.
At that time, Lǒngxī's Lǐ Yuánqiān delighted in double-entendre speech,
and often passed by Wényuǎn's residence.
Passing by and seeing its magnificent gate and pillars,
he then said:
"Whose residence is this, so exceedingly fine?"
The maid Chūnfēng came out and said:
"It is the home of Champion General Guō."
Yuánqiān said:
"A lowly maid, yet skilled in double-entendre."
Chūnfēng replied:

Yuánqiān was impressed by the maid's ability,

Zǐguāng
Yuán Zhàn's fame and status gradually increased,
he indulged in sensual pleasures,
initially gifting the maid Zǐguāng to the court official Sòng Yóudào,

Yù'ér
