whose beauty and talents were unmatched at the time.
Zhīzhī doted on her
and remained unmarried for her sake.
Wǔ Yánsì, upon hearing of her, sought to see her once.
The pressure was irresistible,
and once he saw her, he detained her,
with no intention of returning her.
Zhīzhī, heartbroken and enraged, fell ill.
He then composed a poem on silk,
bribed the gatekeeper heavily to deliver it to Yǎoniáng.
Yǎoniáng, upon receiving the poem, wept bitterly,
tied the three stanzas to her skirt,
and threw herself into a well to her death.
When Yánsì saw the poem,
he had cruel officials falsely accuse and frame Zhīzhī,
destroying his family.
Zhīzhī's poem reads:
"In the Shí family's Golden Valley, new songs arise,
Ten hu of bright pearls bought a graceful beauty.
In the past, you pitied and pledged yourself to me,
Now your song and dance win others' favor.
Your family's towers were never hard to scale,
Gladly lending your songs and dances for others to admire.
Wealth and power defy reason,
Arrogance and influence encroach unjustly.
Parting from you, I cannot bear it,
In vain, I hide my sleeves, mourning my fading beauty.
A century's separation atop the high tower,
In one moment, my youthful beauty is spent for you."
As recorded in "Běnshì Shī" and similarly in the "Old Book of Táng."
Lǐ Déyù's "Treatise on Auspicious Signs" states,
Bāo Sì and Lí Jī were both national demons who brought calamity,
while Lǜ Zhū and Yǎoniáng
were domestic demons
who brought disaster to the Qiáo and Shí families.
"Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi" records Yǎoniáng as Bìyù.
Xiān'é
The censor supervising Qīnghé, Zhāng Jí, had a maidservant named Xiān'é who could sing and dance and was literate.
He often took Xiān'é along as an attendant when on official missions.
Someone who secretly learned of this was about to expose him,
but Zhāng Jí repeatedly knelt and bowed in supplication,
and ultimately managed to avoid exposure.
"Records of the Censorate"
Shí Chōng had a concubine named Xiān'éniáng,
whose reputation was second only to Lǜzhū.
"Tales of the Mysterious and Strange"
Piánzhū
Yáng Guózhōng was originally the son of Zhāng Yìzhī.
At that time, Yìzhī was favored by Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
receiving incomparable grace and favor.
Every time he returned from court,
the Empress Dowager ordered him to reside in a tower with the ladder removed.
Fearing he would have no heir,
Yìzhī's mother secretly had a maidservant, Piánzhū, privately sleep with him in the tower.
She later became pregnant and gave birth to Guózhōng.
Piánzhū then married Yáng, Guózhōng's father,
and their son took the surname Yáng.
Since he shared the same surname as Consort Yáng,
they formed a clan affiliation.
"Unofficial Biography of Consort Yáng"
Sù'é
Wǔ Sānsī's courtesan Sù'é possessed extraordinary beauty,
Dí Liánggōng requested her to come out,
but she suddenly disappeared.
From the inner hall came the fragrance of orchids and musk,
and when he leaned close to listen,
it was Sù'é speaking:
"I am a flower-and-moon spirit,
sent by the Emperor to entertain you with conversation and laughter.
But Lord Dí is a righteous man of his time,
I dare not appear before you."
Míngzhū,
a maidservant of Yáng Shènjīn,
was of great beauty.
She gave burial herbs and blood-stained artifacts to the practitioner Shǐ Jìngsī,
and later became the Eighth Aunt.
Through connections, she gained an audience with the emperor,
but the emperor detested her sorcery,
so Shènjīn was consequently executed.
"Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Ming"
The maidservant Chūncǎo was sold by Tàizhēn's sister Liǔ shì to serve in the palace.
"Tang Chronicles"
Yíng Yíng
Dáxī Yíngyíng was
the concubine of a nobleman during the Tiānbǎo era,
her beauty unparalleled at the time.
It happened that the nobleman fell ill,
and the son of a fellow official serving as Qiānniú went missing.
The search for him was urgent,
and Emperor Míng Huáng heard of it.
He ordered a thorough search of the capital,
leaving no stone unturned,
but no trace of him was found.
The emperor then asked where he had last been seen,
and his father mentioned the nobleman’s illness,
saying he had gone to inquire after him.
The emperor ordered a search of the nobleman’s residence,
where Yíngyíng said to the Qiānniú:
"Now it’s impossible to hide any longer,
but coming out won’t do much harm."
The Qiānniú feared punishment,
so Yíngyíng advised him:
"Just don’t say you were here.
If the emperor asks where you were,
only describe the people and things you saw as such,
the curtains and canopies as such,
the food you ate as such,
and say you had no choice—
then you’ll surely be safe."
After he emerged,
Emperor Míng Huáng was furious
and questioned him.
He replied as Yíngyíng had instructed,
and the emperor laughed without further inquiry.
A few days later, when Lady Guóguó entered the palace,
Emperor Míng Huáng teased her, saying:
"Why have you been hiding a young man for so long?"
Lady Guóguó only laughed in response.
"The Tale of Yíngyíng"
Péi Liùláng
Gēshū Hàn had a beloved concubine named Péi Liùláng,
whose beauty and grace were unparalleled in her generation,
and she excelled in singing and dancing.
"Records of Communing with the Hidden"
Yùxiāo
Wéi Gāo, the military governor of the two Shu circuits during the Táng dynasty, traveled to Jiāngxià in his youth,
staying at the residence of Prefect Jiāng.
A young girl of the Jiāng family said:
"Jīng Bǎo has a young maidservant named Yùxiāo,
only ten years old."
She was often ordered to attend to Brother Wéi,
and Yùxiāo diligently served him.
Two years later, Prefect Jiāng went to the capital to seek an official post,
so Wéi took up residence at the Shàngtóutuó Temple.
Jīng Bǎo would frequently send Yùxiāo to serve and attend to him.
As Yùxiāo grew older,
feelings developed between them.
When Wéi later returned home to visit his family,
he made a promise with Yùxiāo: he would return for her in five years at the earliest,
or seven years at the latest.
He left her a jade ring
and a poem as keepsakes.
When five years passed without his return,
Yùxiāo quietly prayed at the Parrot Islet.
Another year went by, until the spring of the eighth year,
when Yùxiāo sighed and said:
"Young Master Wéi has been gone for seven years;
he is not coming back."
Thereupon, she stopped eating and died.
The Jiāng family, moved by her fidelity,
placed the jade ring on her middle finger before burying her.
Later, when Wéi governed Shǔ,
he encountered Jīng Bǎo, who was imprisoned for some offense.
Wéi secured his release,
and asked about Yùxiāo's whereabouts.
Jiāng replied that because the general had failed to return by the promised time,
she had starved herself to death.
He then recited the poem Wéi had left for her with the jade ring:
"The yellow sparrow brought it springs ago;
Parting, I left it for the fair one.
No letters came from the Long River;
To send my longing, dreams entered Qín."
Hearing this, Wéi was filled with even greater sorrow and lament.
He sponsored the copying of sūtras and the creation of Buddhist statues to repay his longstanding feelings,
yet his longing thoughts
had no way of reuniting them.
At that time, there was a recluse named Zǔ
who possessed the arts of Shào Wēng,
capable of making the deceased appear.
He instructed the governor to observe a fast for seven days.
On a clear night, Yùxiāo indeed appeared.
She expressed her gratitude, saying:
"Thanks to the general's merit in having sūtras copied and statues made,
I will be reborn in ten days.
Thirteen years from now, I will again be your maidservant,
to repay your great kindness."
Before leaving, she smiled faintly and said:
"Husband, your fickleness forced life and death to part us."
Later, Wéi governed Shǔ due to his achievements in Lǒngyòu,
and his administration continued without interruption.
He was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng.
The people of Lúshuǐ submitted willingly.
On the occasion of his birthday celebration,
all the regional commanders presented rare treasures as gifts.
Only Lú Bāzuò of Dōngchuān sent a singing girl,
not yet sixteen years old,
who was also named Yùxiāo.
Looking at her, she was truly the Yùxiāo of the Jiāng family,
with a flesh ring faintly visible on her middle finger,
no different from the jade ring left at parting.
Wéi sighed and said:
"Now I understand the distinction between life and death,
the cycle of going and coming.
Yùxiāo's words
have indeed been verified."
From "Yúnxī Yǒu Yì"
Wáng Yǎn had a palace lady named Lǐ Yùxiāo.
From "Shǔ Shǐ Táowù"
Xiùnú Qīqī
Duke Li Qián Mǐn had a natural aversion to mundane sounds,
except for his two favorite courtesans named Xiùnú and Qīqī, both of whom were intelligent,
skilled in playing the qin and zither as well as singing.
He often had them perform,
and personally composed qin scores.
"Records of Conversations"
Xuē Yáoyīng
Yuán Zǎi's favored concubine Xuē Yáoyīng
was well-versed in poetry and literature,
excelling in singing and dancing.
With immortal grace and royal elegance,
her skin was fragrant and her body light,
surpassing even Xuánbō, Yáoguāng,
Fēiyàn, and Lǜzhū.
Yáoyīng's mother Zhào Juān,
originally a beloved concubine of Prince Qí,
later left to become the wife of the Xuē family,
giving birth to Yáoyīng and perfuming her since infancy with fragrant sachets,
hence her naturally fragrant skin.
When Zǎi took her as his concubine,
he housed her in a golden silk canopy,
with dust-repelling bedding.
The bedding came from the state of Gōulí,
said to be made from the fur of dust-repelling beasts,
its color deep and vibrant,
unparalleled in sheen and softness.
She wore garments of dragon-mist silk,
each weighing no more than one or two liǎng,
grasped fully within a single handful.
As Yáoyīng's body was too light to bear heavy clothing,
Zǎi sought such attire from foreign lands.
Only Jiǎ Zhì and Yáng Gōngnán, being close friends of Zǎi,
often had the chance to witness her singing and dancing.
Jiǎ Zhì thus composed a poem for her:
"Fear not the weight of the gossamer robe,
Smiling, your peach-blossom face blooms.
Compared to Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
In vain he built the Wind-Avoiding Terrace."
Gōngnán also wrote a long poem praising her beauty,
roughly stating:
"A heavenly maiden with snowy face and serene brows,
Phoenix flute and simurgh wings, ready to take flight.
Jade hairpins and emerald steps, untouched by dust,
A Chǔ waist like willow, overwhelmed by spring's grace."
Yáoyīng was skilled in charming allure,
and Zǎi was bewitched by her,
neglecting his official duties.
After Zǎi's death,
Yáoyīng became the wife of a commoner.
"Records of Dù Yáng"
Tiny
Wáng Jìn served as chancellor,
and built Bǎoyìng Temple for his concubine,
unparalleled in its grandeur and beauty.
Today, the temple's statues of Brahma and celestial maidens
are all portraits of the courtesan Xiǎoxiǎo and others from Duke Qí's household, painted by Hán Gàn.
Southern region's Yǒuyáng Temple pagoda
Shàngqīng
Dòu Cān's favored maidservant was named Shàngqīng,
Dòu Cān was found guilty and entered the imperial palace service.
"Yì Wén Jí"
Rèn Shì huī bīng
During the Dàlì era, Cuī Níng replaced Dù Hóngjiàn as the military governor of Xīchuān.
When Cuī Níng went to the imperial court,
he left his younger brother Kuān to guard Chéngdū.
Yáng Zǐlín of Lúzhōu seized the opportunity to lead several thousand elite cavalry in a surprise attack on Chéngdū,
occupying and defending the city.
Kuān fought repeatedly but was exhausted,
while Zǐlín's prestige grew significantly.
Cuī Níng's concubine Rèn Shì, who was imposing and resolute,
then contributed one hundred thousand in family wealth to recruit brave warriors.
Within two days, she gathered a thousand men,
organized them into units with officers,
personally commanded the troops,
and advanced to pressure Zǐlín.
Fearing that the city's food supplies would run out,
Zǐlín abandoned the city and his forces collapsed.
Zǐlín, who had long practiced sorcery,
that evening summoned heavy rain,
led his cinnabar to the courtyard,
and ascended it to escape.
From Old Book of Táng, chapter 67.
Chǔ Bīn
The commandant of Nánzhèng County, Lǐ Yún, sought to take a concubine in Cháng'ān,
named Chǔbīn.
"Records of Heard Marvels"
Pearl
During the Bǎolì era, there was Lǐ Yuàn,
the son of Grand Marshal Lǐ Shèng.
Early on, he entered officialdom through hereditary privilege for military merits,
serving successively in regional posts.
His nature was extremely extravagant and he kept many concubines.
In his later years, he obtained a maidservant
who was exceptional among beauties,
so he named her Zhēnzhū (Pearl),
intending to suggest that even Jì Lún's Lǜzhū did not surpass her.
When Lǐ Yuàn grew old,
Zhēnzhū's fame increased,
so he consulted with relatives and friends, saying:
"An ordinary man is guiltless,
but possessing a treasure becomes his crime.
I am now old,
and keep a woman as a jewel at home,
never having reported her to the emperor.
I fear this is improper for a subject.
If I could find a skilled writer,
like Dēngtúzǐ capable of describing her beauty,
hoping to present a memorial to offer her,
I would die without regret."
His relative then sought a memorial from Hàn Gōng,
but Hàn Gōng declined, saying he couldn't write well.
He then informed Yú Qīng,
who wanted to handle it himself,
saying:
"I must see her once,
to imprint her appearance in my eyes,
then I can compose the text."
Lǐ Yuàn agreed.
When Yú Qīng saw this maiden,
he was dazzled and beside himself,
realizing he could never obtain her,
so he spoke to Niú Sēngrú.
Niú Sēngrú then held state power,
and said:
"What does Lǐ Yuàn want?
I can get it for him,
why must it be reported to the emperor?"
Yú Qīng said:
"Lǐ Yuàn's mind is already made up.
If you, Minister, directly take her,
I fear it may not go as wished.
If we scheme to obtain her,
we will surely succeed."
He then recommended Hàn Gōng as an envoy,
saying:
"This man wields a three-inch tongue,
able to change people's hearts."
Niú Sēngrú agreed.
Hàn Gōng went to see Lǐ Yuàn, saying:
"I've privately heard the Minister of Works wishes to offer a courtesan,
is this true?"
Lǐ Yuàn said:
"Yes."
Hàn Gōng said:
"I worry for the Minister of Works."
Lǐ Yuàn asked in surprise:
"Why would I be in danger?"
Hàn Gōng said:
"The current emperor is in his prime,
with thousands of beauties like Xīzǐ in the rear palace.
If the Minister of Works now throws Zhēnzhū among them,
how is it different from tossing one grain into a great granary?
If Zhēnzhū gains favor,
and the emperor's sacred intention turns to her,
her influence would overwhelm the six palaces.
She would surely blame the Minister of Works for long keeping her beloved
and not presenting her for years—a fault.
Thinking it over yesterday,
I became worried for the Minister of Works."
Lǐ Yuàn suddenly said:
"What should I do?"
Hàn Gōng said:
"Generally, exceptional beauties
inevitably bring disaster to people.
Whether Zhēnzhū is presented or not,
I fear she will ultimately bring calamity to the Minister of Works.
However, outside I've learned the Minister of Works has long intended to present this courtesan.
If you suddenly stop,
people will surely say the Minister of Works is too infatuated to let go.
Considering for the Minister of Works,
it would be better to give her to someone else."
Lǐ Yuàn said:
"Who can I give her to?"
Hàn Gōng said:
"Chancellor Niú has long sought a great beauty.
Now the Minister of Works merely seeks a major governorship,
hoping to influence the emperor's mind.
Why not give her to Chancellor Niú?
Chancellor Niú gets the courtesan,
the Minister of Works gets the governorship,
wouldn't that be suitable?"
Lǐ Yuàn was very pleased,
and gave Zhēnzhū to Niú Sēngrú.
Hàn Gōng then became a close companion,
using Zhēnzhū as a means of pleasure.
Although dukes and ministers waited for audiences from all quarters,
some urgently wished to see her but never could,
so the capital nicknamed Yú Qīng "the minister's broker,"
originating from this.
"Niú Yáng Rìlì"
Huángfǔ Sōng, Niú Qí,
nephew of Lord Zhāng,
resented that his uncle didn't recommend him,
and wrote a slanderous poem:
"Entering Zhēnzhū's chamber at night,
roaming the tortoiseshell palace by morning."
Zhēnzhū was the name of his uncle's concubine.
"Zhíyán"
Zhēnzhū was taken when he governed Xiāngyáng,
possessing extraordinary beauty,
her singing and dancing grace
were then called peerless.
"Zhēnzhū Xùlù"
Lord Qízhāng took a courtesan named:
"Zhēnzhū had extraordinary beauty."
When Lú Zhào visited Qízhāng,
the latter valued his literary talent,
and invited him into the inner chamber.
It happened that Zhēnzhū was washing her hair,
just holding her hair knot with her hands,
inserting hairpins between her two temples.
The Chancellor said:
"Why not compose a verse?"
Lú Zhào said:
"Knowing the pities your jade wrists,
thus with slender hands adjusting the golden hairpins."
"Yínchuāng Xùlù"
Jiàngtáo Liǔzhī
Hán Tuìzhī had two concubines,
one named Jiàngtáo,
the other Liǔzhī.
When Tuìzhī was sent to Shāndōng,
he wrote a poem:
"The east wind stirs as I leave Cháng'ān,
mid-spring yet the border town is unusually cold.
I see no garden flowers or lane willows,
only the round moon above my horse's head."
Later, Liǔzhī escaped by climbing over the garden wall,
and there was a poem:
"Since parting, the willow by the steps,
tossed by spring wind, seems ready to fly away.
Yet the peach and plum in the small garden remain,
their buds unopened, awaiting your return."
From "Yǔlín"
Guān Xìxì
Lè Tiān had "Matching the Swallow Tower Poems,"
the preface of which states:
"The late Minister Zhāng of Xúzhōu also had a beloved courtesan named Pàn Pàn,
skilled in singing and dancing,
elegant and full of graceful charm.
When I, as a collator, was traveling between the Huái and Sì rivers,
Minister Zhāng hosted a banquet for me.
As the wine flowed freely, he brought out Pàn Pàn to add to the joy,
so I composed a poem for her, ending with the lines:
'The charming drunk cannot be surpassed,
like the wind gently swaying a peony blossom.
We parted after that one joyful encounter,
and I never heard of her again'—
that was twelve years ago.
Yesterday, Vice-Director Zhāng Zhòngsù (styled Huìzhī) of the Bureau of Honors visited me
and recited three poems titled 'Swallow Tower Poems,'
the words of which were exceedingly tender and beautiful.
When I inquired about their origin,
he said they were composed by Pàn Pàn.
Huìzhī serves
in the Wǔníng Army and has known Pàn Pàn's story for many years.
He said that after Minister Zhāng passed away,
there was an old residence of the Zhāng family in Péngchéng,
within which stood a small tower named Swallow Tower.
Pàn Pàn, cherishing her past love, refused to marry
and lived in that tower for over ten years,
remaining there to this day.
Pàn Pàn's poems read:
'The fading lamp in the tower accompanies the dawn frost;
the solitary sleeper rises from the shared bed.
How much longing fills a single night?
Even the ends of the earth are not too far.'
Another:
'Pines and cypresses at Běimáng are veiled in sorrowful mist;
the dweller of Swallow Tower is lost in quiet thoughts.
Since burying the sword and footsteps, the songs and dust have scattered;
the red sleeves' fragrance faded for ten long years.'
And another:
'Just as I saw the wild geese return from Yuèyáng,
I witness the dark swallows approaching the shrine.
Jade zithers and flutes hold no interest for me;
let spiderwebs and dust gather as they may.'
I admired her new compositions
and thus matched them with:
'Bright moonlight fills the window, frost covers the screen;
the quilt is cold, the lamp dim, I tidy the bed.
In Swallow Tower on a chilly moonlit night,
autumn seems to lengthen for one alone.
Silk gowns and jeweled belts fade like mist;
how many times I've tried to rise, only to weep silently.
Since ceasing to dance the Rainbow Skirt melody,
they've lain folded in an empty chest for twelve years.'
Another:
'This spring, a traveler returned from Luòyáng,
and went to pay respects at the late Minister's tomb.
He said the white poplars could serve as pillars now;
how could the fair one not turn to dust?'
I also gave her a quatrain:
'Gold was spared to purchase moth-eyebrowed beauties;
four or five branches of flowers were carefully chosen.
Teaching them song and dance exhausted heart and strength;
yet when I departed this world, none followed.'
Later, Zhòngsù showed my poems to Pàn Pàn.
She read them repeatedly
and wept, saying:
'Since my lord's passing,
it's not that I couldn't have died,
but I feared that in a hundred years, people might think my lord valued beauty so much
that he had a concubine follow him in death,
thus tarnishing his pure reputation.
That is why I have clung to life.'
She then composed a poem matching Bái Jūyì's:
'Alone I guard the empty tower, restraining sorrowful brows;
my form resembles a peony branch after spring.
The courtier does not grasp my profound intent,
surprised I haven't followed to the netherworld.'
After receiving the poem,
Pàn Pàn was deeply despondent for ten days,
refused food, and passed away,
only murmuring:
'Children do not recognize what soars to the heavens;
they vainly smear snow-white brushes with mud.'"
From the Collection of the Chángqìng Era,
the Swallow Tower in Xúzhōu stands behind the prefectural residence,
built by Táng military commissioner Zhāng Jiànfēng for his maid Pàn Pàn.
Chén Yànshēng once left a poem:
"The fields where the Minister lies deserted, hares and foxes roam;
the maid still dwells in the tower west of the water.
Cool breezes on the jade mat, too lazy to lean on the pillow;
bright moonlight through beaded curtains, unwilling to draw them up.
Waking from cold dreams to the vastness of the sea;
new sorrows chanted, purple orchids signal autumn.
Lè Tiān's talent, like spring's deep rain,
ended the fading flowers in a single night."
During the Song dynasty, the keju examination for ministerial positions was only passed by one person, Fù Bì.
In the time of Xiàozōng,
only one person, Lǐ Hòu from Méishān, passed the revived keju examination.
His courtesy name was Zhòngxìn,
and he worked on the historical records of the South and North dynasties.
"Kùnxué Jìwén"
Fán Sù and Xiǎo Mán
Bái Jūyì had two concubines;
Fán Sù was skilled in singing,
while Xiǎo Mán excelled in dancing.
He once wrote a poem:
"Cherry-like are Fán Sù's lips,
willow-like is Xiǎo Mán's slender waist."
When the two concubines grew older,
he wrote another poem:
"A tree in spring breeze with countless branches,
more tender than gold and softer than silk."
Later, when both concubines left him,
he composed these lines:
"Sickness keeps Bái Jūyì company,
while spring departs with Fán Sù all at once."
From "Talks on Poetry Past and Present"
Spring Grass
The Collected Works of Liú Yǔxī contains a poem dedicated to Little Fán that reads:
"A flowery-faced maiden of thirteen or fourteen,
In spring, graceful and charming when facing others.
I must buy and name her Spring Grass,
Accompanying me everywhere with every step."
Additionally, a note in a poem from Tongzhou written to Bái Jūyì states:
"Spring Grass is your dancing courtesan."
The Ornamented Zither
Lǐ Shāngyǐn wrote the poem "Jǐn Sè,"
but no one understood its meaning.
Some said it referred to a maid named Jǐnsè in Líng Hú Chǔ's household.
In the "Gòngfù Shīhuà,"
the sound of the ornate zither
evokes feelings of sorrow, resentment, clarity, and harmony.
In the past, Líng Hú Chǔ's attendant could play these four lines,
and the four lines in the poem
describe these four melodies.
Zhāng Zǐhòu once doubted this poem,
but Magistrate Zhào deeply explained it in this way.
Xǔ Yǐ's "Shīhuà"
Chén Zhēnzhēn
Tàicháng Bóshì Zhèng Huángǔ resided in the Eastern Capital,
living in the same lane as General Liǔ.
When Huángǔ was about to be transferred to the Western Capital,
Liǔ hosted a lavish banquet to bid him farewell,
bringing out all his household entertainers.
They sang and offered wine, passing cups around.
Among them was the third concubine, whose beauty was enchanting and peerless.
Zhèng secretly gazed at her,
feeling deeply enamored.
Liǔ said to Zhèng:
"This is Shěn Zhēnzhēn,
originally from a respectable family,
quite fond of literature.
Please compose a poem to pledge your affection,
and once you receive your official appointment,
I will send her as a congratulatory gift."
Huángǔ composed a poem:
"From the inner chamber emerges an immortal,
her clear voice rivals pipes and strings.
Her lyrics surpass the 'White Ramie' melody,
her songs rise like the 'White Clouds' verse.
Though not yet bearing Péi Xiù,
why not seek Zhèng Xuán?
Unable to bear the Jīngǔ waters,
she passes before the falling tower."
Liǔ read the poem with great delight,
bade Zhēnzhēn to bow in gratitude.
Huángǔ reached the capital,
and was soon appointed Magistrate of Yīquē,
but fell gravely ill.
He sent an urgent letter to Liǔ,
who immediately dispatched Zhēnzhēn to the capital.
Welcoming Zhèng, she asked to meet him.
Zhēnzhēn adorned herself and paid respects.
Huángǔ rose and approached,
suddenly grasping Zhēnzhēn's hand,
heaved a long sigh and passed away.
"Collection of Beautiful Passions"
Liǔ Shùnyīng
Yú Mèiniáng was a talented woman,
married into the Zhōu family.
After her husband's death, she maintained her chastity and purity.
Lù Xīshēng, then serving as a senior official,
hearing of her beauty and skill in calligraphy,
with unparalleled wit and intelligence,
sent a persuasive matchmaker to woo her.
Mèiniáng said:
"If Vice-Director Lù truly wishes me to serve as his wife,
he must vow not to take concubines or female servants;
only then may I become the Lù family's bride."
Xīshēng agreed.
After two years of marriage,
they composed poems together,
exchanging verses in harmony.
Mèiniáng could also prepare five-colored minced fish,
with exquisite skill beyond compare.
Unexpectedly, Xīshēng acquired the famous courtesan Liǔ Shùnyīng.
Mèiniáng resented this,
instructing her to enter the household and live together.
Xīshēng believed it sincere.
Once living together,
there was no apparent issue.
Waiting until Xīshēng was away,
she summoned Shùnyīng,
locked her in a room and killed her with a blade,
dismembered her body,
placed it in two large boxes,
labeled them:
"Sending goods to the country villa."
The gatekeeper found it suspicious,
reported it to the Capital Prefecture prison.
Mèiniáng was then executed by extreme penalty.
Dù Qiūniáng
When Lǐ Qí rebelled, he had a concubine named Dù Qiūniáng,
who was confiscated into the palace and later released.
Dù Mù, moved by her story, wrote a poem that includes:
"Pepper walls hung with silk banners,
Mirror cases coiled with jade dragons.
The moon rises over the white jade gate,
Shadows of cassia drift unevenly.
Golden steps heavy with jade dew,
Leisurely playing the purple flute.
Swallow matchmakers won the imperial son,
The lady personally held and nurtured him.
Tiger-eyed pearls adorned the swaddling cloth,
Golden plates and rhinoceros horns secured the curtain."
from "Supplementary Records of the National History"
Qínkè,
Liǔ Yíchéng's beloved concubine,
excelled at playing the qín and sè.
When Yíchéng retired due to old age and Qínkè left,
she married Gù Kuàng,
who composed a song for her.
"Lìqíng Jí"
Què Yào
was a maidservant of Observation Commissioner Lǐ Gēng, named Què Yào.
She possessed beauty and grace,
and was skilled in speech.
Lǐ had four sons,
the eldest named Yánxǐ,
the next Yánfàn, Yánzuò, and Yányòu,
known as the First, Second, Third, and Fifth Young Masters,
all of whom desired to seduce her but could not succeed.
Once on a clear and bright night,
the First Young Master encountered her amidst the cherry blossom shadows,
and seized her, seeking intimacy.
Què Yào took a mat and gave it to him,
deceiving him, saying:
"Wait in the southeast corner of the hall."
Then she met the Second Young Master,
and teased him, saying:
"Wait in the northeast corner of the hall."
Then she met the Third Young Master,
and bound him with words, saying:
"Wait in the southwest corner of the hall."
Then she met the Fifth Young Master, who held her hand and would not let go, saying:
"Wait in the northwest corner of the hall."
All four young masters took the mats she gave them,
and each hurried to a corner,
though puzzled in their hearts, they dared not speak out.
Soon after, Què Yào lit a torch and flung open the door,
shining it upon them, saying:
"You paupers,
how dare you seek a place to sleep here!"
The four sons each dropped what they carried,
covered their faces, and fled,
and from then on, they dared not show disrespect.
"Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú"
Fēi Yān
Lín Huái's Wǔ Gōngyè during the Xiántōng era served as the Registrar of Merit in Hénán Prefecture.
His beloved concubine, named Fēiyān,
had a delicate and beautiful appearance,
as if unable to bear the weight of silk garments.
She excelled at Qín music,
was fond of literary composition,
and Gōngyè doted on her greatly.
Their neighbor, a young man of the Zhào family named Xiàng,
was handsome and cultured,
having just reached the age of twenty.
One day, through a crack in the southern wall, he caught sight of Fēiyān,
and was utterly captivated,
losing all appetite and sleep.
He then richly bribed Gōngyè's gatekeeper,
confessing his feelings to him.
The gatekeeper's wife relayed everything to Fēiyān,
who only smiled with a fixed gaze and did not reply.
The old woman gatekeeper fully informed Xiàng,
who became wildly excited and agitated,
not knowing how to contain himself.
He then took Xuē Tāo stationery and inscribed a quatrain:
"At first sight of a city-toppling beauty,
My mortal heart is left to its own doubts.
Not following Xiāo Shǐ away,
I intend to learn from Ā Lán's example."
Sealing what he had written,
he begged the gatekeeper woman to deliver it to Fēiyān.
After reading it, Fēiyān sighed for a long time,
and said to the woman:
"I too have glimpsed young master Zhào's exceptional talent and appearance.
In this life, I have meager fortune,
and cannot be matched with him.
It is because I despise Wǔ's crude and violent nature,
that he is not a suitable match."
She then replied with a poem written on golden phoenix stationery:
"My dark brows sorrowful, beyond my control,
Only because hidden regrets lie in new verses.
Your heart should resemble the zither's plaintive heart,
To whom shall I confide these silent spring sorrows?"
She sealed it and gave it to the gatekeeper woman,
instructing her to deliver it to Xiàng.
Xiàng opened the letter and recited it repeatedly,
clapping his hands joyfully and saying:
"My affair is settled!"
Later, when Gōngyè was on duty,
they consummated their deep affection.
This continued for about a year,
until they were reported by a maidservant.
Gōngyè had her flogged to death.

Sù'é
Wéi Xúnměi passed the imperial examination during the Kāichéng era,
and was appointed to a position under Dèng Dūcóng.
He brought his beloved Sù'é along with him.
Luó Shàowēi, hearing of her beauty,
sought her,
and Xúnměi dared not refuse,
so he presented her to him.
Sù'é's surname was Cuī,
a daughter of a respectable family from Dàliáng,
skilled in witty conversation and writing.
With tears, she composed a poem:
"I remain secluded in my quiet chamber while you travel the forked road;
My heart and your regrets cling to each other.
If my soul chances to meet the witch's companion,
I will still return with the morning clouds and evening rain."
Xúnměi did not accept the situation,
and crossed the river by night, lodging in a temple.
Sighing deeply and unable to sleep, he said:
"Where is there someone who can right this injustice?"
A temple attendant asked about the injustice,
and Xúnměi told him everything.
The attendant vanished abruptly,
and by the third watch, suddenly threw down a leather bag—
it contained Sù'é, who had arrived.
At dawn, when they inquired at the temple,
they were told the attendant had been striking the temple bell there,
toiling diligently for over thirty years,
but had already disappeared without a trace.
Xúnměi then fled to another place.
"Idle Talks Under the Lamp"
Dispelling Sorrow
Pān Kàng and his younger brother Pān Qiào together served as the key administrators for Shǔ King Wáng Jiàn,
and were called the Great Pivot and the Lesser Pivot.
Kàng was infatuated with his beautiful concubine Xièchóu,
and consequently developed an illness due to emotional distress.
Xièchóu's surname was Zhào,
and her mother dreamed of swallowing a crabapple flower bud before giving birth to her.
She possessed remarkable beauty fit for a kingdom,
excelled at creating new melodies and was skilled at composing short poems.
When Jiàn visited Kàng's residence,
he saw her and said:
"There is no one like this in my palace."
He intended to take her for himself,
but Kàng said:
"She is but a lowly person in your servant's household,
I dare not offer her to Your Majesty,"
though in truth he was being stingy about giving her up.
His younger brother Qiào said:
"Shouldn't we take warning from the disaster of Lǜ Zhū?"
Kàng replied:
"Life's value lies in following one's heart's desires,
how can one fear death and feel discontent in one's own heart?"
From "Unofficial History: Táojī"
To catch the phoenix
Dù Dàzhōng rose from the ranks to become a general,
and was ruthless in his dealings with others.
Westerners called him Dù Dàchóng (the "Big Bug"),
and even if his wife made a mistake,
he would publicly cane her.
He had a beloved concubine, talented and beautiful,
who composed all of Dàzhōng's memorials and documents.
One day, while Dàzhōng was napping,
the concubine noticed fine paper and a brush on the desk,
and wrote a poem to the tune of "Immortal at River Lin,"
which contained the line "a colorful phoenix follows a crow."
When Dàzhōng awoke and read it,
he said, "The crow will now strike the phoenix,"
and slapped her face,
breaking her neck and killing her.
From "Jīnshì Táng Shǒulù"
Lotus
Chéntáo, a recluse of the Southern Táng dynasty, lived in seclusion on the Western Hills,
maintaining a pure and upright conduct.
At that time, Yán Zhuàn, the governor of Yùzhāng, sought to disturb him,
and sent his concubine Liánhuā to visit him frequently.
Chéntáo paid her no attention at all,
so the concubine composed a poem, pleading to depart:
"Lotus is my name, my cheeks are jade fair,
I am sent by the Minister with utmost care.
If in this world you dream not of Wū Gorge's delight,
In vain I descend from the balcony, cloud and rain in vain unite."
Chéntáo replied:
"Lately my poetic thoughts are clear as water,
With age, my romantic passions thin as cloud I falter.
I've found the gate to ascend the heavens high,
In brocade quilts, I shame Zhūo Wénjūn with a sigh."
From "Collection of Beautiful Romances"
Later generations mistakenly attributed this story to Chén Túnán.
Zhào Yángtái
Dòu Tāo, courtesy name Liánbō,
had a wife, Madame Sū, named Huì,
courtesy name Ruòlán,
the third daughter of Wǔgōng Dàozhì, the magistrate of Chénliú.
She married at sixteen.
Tāo served as the governor of Qínzhōu under Fú Jiān,
but was demoted and exiled to Dūnhuáng for offending the emperor.
Later, he was appointed General of Annan and stationed in Xiāngyáng
to defend against the Jìn.
Initially, Tāo had a favored concubine named Zhào Yángtái,
whose singing and dancing skills were unparalleled,
so Tāo kept her in a separate residence.
When Madame Sū learned of this,
she severely beat and humiliated her,
causing Tāo deep resentment.
Yángtái, in turn, constantly spied on Madame Sū's faults and slandered her,
further angering Tāo.
At that time, Madame Sū was twenty-one.
When Tāo was about to garrison Xiāngyáng,
Madame Sū, in her anger,
refused to accompany him.
Thus, Tāo took Yángtái with him to his post,
cutting off all communication with Madame Sū.
Filled with regret and self-pity,
Madame Sū wove a reversible brocade with five interwoven colors,
measuring eight inches square,
containing over 840 characters.
Read vertically, horizontally, or in reverse, it formed coherent passages,
with not a single stroke missing.
It was named the Xuánjī Diagram.
However, readers could not fully decipher it,
so Madame Sū laughed and said to others:
"Winding and turning,
it naturally composes literary pieces.
Unless one is my beloved,
none can comprehend it."
She then sent a servant to deliver it to Xiāngyáng.
When Tāo examined the brocade's text,
he was moved by its exquisite beauty,
and sent Yángtái back to Guānzhōng.
He then prepared carriages, attendants, and lavish ceremonies to welcome Madame Sū back to Hànnán,
where their affection grew even stronger.
The "Chronicle of Empress Wǔ of Táng"
differs slightly from the "Book of Jìn."
In Imitation of the Four Sorrows
Lǐ Féngjí had a stubborn, suspicious, and jealous nature,
fond of endangering others.
Liú Yǔxī possessed a singing girl of exceptional beauty,
and Lǐ, in a single day, secretly plotted,
arranging a meeting to seize her.
Liú, bewildered and sighing in distress, returned home,
knowing there was nothing he could do.
Thus, filled with indignation, he composed four stanzas,
modeled after the "Four Sorrows," as follows:
"The jade hairpin rejoined, yet both are without fate,
Like a fish in the deep pool and a crane in the sky.
The content purple phoenix ceases dancing before the mirror,
The eloquent blue bird stops carrying letters.
The golden basin overturned, the water cannot be retrieved,
The jade tuning peg long discarded, the string remains unstrung.
If passing by the foot of Míwú Mountain,
From afar, shed crimson tears upon the desolate spring.
The phoenix, leaving its old companion, where shall it perch?
The phoenix finding a new nest is already content.
The rouge still lingers, fragrance faint and diffuse,
The azure clouds just severed, messages silent and deep.
Fully aware of the defilement, like jade cast into mud,
Yet still striving to earn gold for fleeting smiles.
From now on, the person on the mountain is like stone,
In the form of a husband, deeply marked by tear stains.
Everywhere I once roamed, I search again,
Though a living separation, it feels like death itself.
Before the Tower of Fleeting Smiles, the flowers have aged,
Under the window where eyebrows were painted, the moon remains waning.
Clouds hide the Wu Gorge, voice and appearance cut off,
The road blocked by the Star Bridge, passage difficult.
Do not say that when the poem is done, no tears fall,
Even if the Eastern Sea were poured out, it would surely dry up.
The three mountains unseen, the sea deep and still,
How could there be any immortal traces left to seek?
When the blue bird departed, the cloud path was severed,
Cháng'é returned, the Moon Palace deep and remote.
Through the gauze window, I reminisce of spring's memories,
Who pities the solitary chant in the night by the book-lit lamp?
I imagine the mirror in the sky come nightfall,
Should only reflect the hearts of us two."
From "Běnshì Shī"
and "Yuèxià Xiántán," it is considered to be about Huáng Sǔn's wife,
taken by Péi for Lǚ Yòngzhī, and thus composed.
The last stanza is missing.
Sǔn later encountered an old man,
who transformed into the bracket of Yòngzhī's roof,
and commanded from above to return Péi to Sǔn.
The Returned Concubine from Xiāngyáng
Scholar Cuī Jiāo,
residing in Hànshàng,
was well-versed in literature and arts but impoverished in material wealth.
Before long,
he became involved with his aunt's maid,
often following in Ruǎn Xián's footsteps.
The maid was graceful and beautiful,
highly skilled in music,
the finest in Hánnán.
Initially poor,
he sold the maid to the military governor,
who adored her,
comparing her to Wú Shuāng.
Wú Shuāng,
the beloved concubine of Xuē Tàibǎo,
is still admired in paintings today.
The governor paid four hundred thousand coins,
cherishing her deeply.
Cuī Jiāo missed her incessantly,
so he boldly approached the governor's residence,
hoping to see her once.
On the Cold Food Festival, the maid went to tend a grave
and encountered Cuī Jiāo under the willow shade.
From her horse, she wept continuously,
vowing eternal love like mountains and rivers.
Cuī Jiāo composed a poem for her:
"Princes and nobles chase after dust,
Lǜ Zhū sheds tears upon her silk gown.
Once entering the noble's gate, deep as the sea,
from then on, Xiāo Láng becomes a stranger."
Someone envious of Cuī Jiāo wrote the poem on a seat.
The governor saw it
and summoned Cuī Jiāo.
His attendants were perplexed,
and Cuī Jiāo feared he had nowhere to hide.
When he met the governor,
the latter grasped his hand and said:
"'Once entering the noble's gate, deep as the sea,
from then on, Xiāo Láng becomes a stranger'—
this is your work, sir.
Four hundred thousand is trivial;
why not show me the poem earlier?"
He then ordered the maid to return with Cuī Jiāo,
along with curtains, boxes, and mirrors,
all enhanced and adorned,
enriching Cuī Jiāo modestly.
Earlier, a guest from Línglíng
mentioned Róng Yù,
whose banquet featured a skilled singer.
Duke Xiāngyáng promptly summoned her.
Governor Róng dared not refuse,
and she arrived a month later.
When ordered to sing, she performed Governor Róng's poem:
"Adorned with jewels and fragrant, in a jade-green skirt,
made up, she weeps, about to depart like a cloud.
Earnestly win Lord Xiāng's favor,
do not dream of the governor at the sunny terrace."
The duke said:
"A man who cannot achieve merit and fame
to be praised by later generations
should not seize another's beloved for his own pleasure."
From this, it is clear
one should retreat to a place of solitude.
He gave her ample silk for the journey
and wrote an apologetic letter to the governor of Línglíng.
In the past, Wáng Dūn dismissed his female musicians to unite his troops,
and Yáng Sù returned Xú Déyán's wife, showing no greed for wealth
or吝 for beauty.
These deeds became elegant tales among contemporaries.
Is Duke Xiāngyáng not a truly exceptional hero?
From "Yúnxī Yǒu Yì."
Gāolì Pō Jiāng
Líng Yùjū, a scholar whose name is forgotten,
had a beautiful concubine who was very poor.
He sought official positions between Jiāo and Guǎng regions,
traveling and spending tens of thousands,
preparing five years' worth of provisions.
He warned his concubine, saying:
"If I do not return within five years,
you are free to remarry."
After the scholar left, five years passed without his return,
so the concubine was taken in by the former provincial governor,
residing at the foot of Gāolì Slope.
When the scholar returned the following year,
his concubine was already gone from her original place.
After searching and learning her whereabouts,
he composed a poem seeking a matchmaker,
sending it to her with these verses:
"Dark clouds descend silently from the Sun Terrace,
entangling with King Xiāng, never to return.
Five years gone, only tears remain in vain,
a heart tightly knotted, never to loosen.
Fine ivy naturally clings to fragrant trees,
spilled water never thinks of returning to its cup.
How melancholy, this dwelling at Gāolì Slope's base,
spring light no longer descends the mountain."
When the provincial governor saw the poem,
he provided one hundred thousand coins and travel supplies,
then sent her back to the scholar.
"Miscellaneous Stories of the Lú Family"
New Sound
Zhāng Gǔ served under Liú Cóngjiàn,
who took a woman from Hándān named Lǐ Yán's daughter as his concubine,
called Xīnshēng.
When Cóngjiàn secretly plotted to coerce Xīnshēng,
he advised Gǔ, saying:
"Initially, the Son of Heaven appointed Cóngjiàn as military governor not because
he had any merit in battlefield victories or city conquests,
but simply because his father brought the twelve provinces of Qí back to the Son of Heaven,
and in the transition, they couldn't depose his heir yet.
Since taking control of Zélù,
I haven't heard of him sending even a single thread or hoof as tribute to the Son of Heaven.
His followers are all untrustworthy,
and during the Zhāngwǔ era, several military districts collapsed,
where even men of great talent and capability couldn't maintain stability,
let alone Cóngjiàn, who was elevated from among children by the Son of Heaven's grace.
If he doesn't follow the law,
he should rightly meet his end through unlawful means.
You should leave with your clan and go west,
a true man shouldn't cling to the gratitude for a single meal,
and let his flesh and blood become food for fierce soldiers."
After speaking, he wept sadly.
Gǔ remained undecided for three months,
fearing that his words would be leaked.
Later, disaster indeed befell him.
"New Book of Tang: Biography of Liú Wù"
Graceful and upright
Lújiāng King Lǐ Yuǎn's favored concubine Tíngtíng,
originally the wife of a merchant,
possessed extraordinary beauty.
Yuǎn killed her father and took her in,
but after Yuǎn's downfall she entered the palace
and again served Emperor Wén.
"Records of Tíngtíng"
Attitude Attitude
Lì Shè arrived in Yángzhōu,
visited all the temples,
and encountered a woman
who bowed weeping, calling herself Sòng Xióng.
This Sòng Xióng
was formerly the beloved concubine of Liú Yuánwài from Wúxīng.
Liú Quánbó it was.
Liú and Lǐ had a friendship from years past,
so he composed a poem for her:
"I long recall when Cloud Immortal was young,
with lotus blossoms adorning her dark hair.
Then I awoke startled from the Gaotang dream,
only now does Sòng Yù know of this."
He also wrote:
"At the night banquet of the envoy in Héngyáng,
the flower branch that understands speech was before my eyes.
Since the bright moon sank in the western sea,
twenty years have passed without seeing Cháng'é."
Lǐ sighed and said:
"Not seeing the proud head now disheveled,
Sòng Xióng is truly fortunate for life,
yet joy and regret leave me wordless before an old friend!"
From "Records of Friends from Yúnxī"
Hóngluán
Fàn Yuánshí,
the son of Wēn Zǔyǔ,
was an extraordinary man,
who was harmed by his favored concubine Hóngluán,
and died of typhoid fever.
From "Talks from the Iron Fence Mountain"
Poplar Blossoms
Dōngpō had concubines named Zhāoyún and Liúhuā.
Zhāoyún died beyond the southern mountains,
only Liúhuā remained.
Therefore his poems often mention her.
Observe how all the frivolous blossoms fade away,
yet she accompanies you in secluded solitude—
this reveals his sentiment.
from "Continuation of Anecdotes from the Elderly"
Cuìqiào
Cuìqiào was an attendant of Hóng Nèihàn,
her surname was Fū,
she was skilled at painting,
and inscribed her works herself:
"Playful brushwork by Cuìqiào."
Her calligraphy was graceful and charming,
Chéng Dàchāng wrote a poem praising it:
"Playfully depicting wind-blown branches,
once again gracing the Jade Hall."
Orioles and swallows
Qiántáng's Fàn Shíláng had two daughters who both became concubines of a wealthy man named Lù from Yúnjiān.
The elder was named Yīngyīng,
who enjoyed favor but died early.
The younger was named Yànyàn,
who was among the other concubines.
When Lù fell ill and became impoverished,
he sold his residence and moved into a hut near the graves.
The other concubines scattered,
but Yànyàn alone could not bear to leave.
She supported him by begging for over ten years.
After Lù died,
she sold herself to pay for his burial.
Alas,
Yù Ràng cherished Zhì Bó's memory,
repaying the kindness of a state scholar with the devotion of a state scholar.
How could Yànyàn not be more virtuous than Yù Ràng!
"Suíyǐn Màn Lù"
Tiántián Qiánqián
Tiántián and Qiánqián,
were two concubines of Xīn Qìjí,
both named according to their surnames,
and both skilled in calligraphy.
They often drafted correspondence on behalf of Xīn Qìjí.
"Shǐ Shǐ Huì Yào"
Zāng huò
In the "Records of the Grand Historian" of the Former Han Dynasty, zāng huò refers to male and female slaves.
Yìng Shào said:
"According to the 'Fāngyán', between Jīng, Huái, Hǎi, and Dài regions,
calling a male slave 'zāng',
calling a female slave 'huò'."
Also, the "Zuǒzhuàn" states:
"Huò,
in the northern suburbs of Yān,
any common man who marries a female slave is called zāng,
any woman who marries a male slave is called huò."
Zhāng Yī said:
The son of one who marries a female slave is called zāng,
the daughter of one who marries a male slave is called huò.
The "Fēngsú Tōng" states:
In ancient systems, there were originally no slaves,
but those who committed crimes or were originally zāng,
were confiscated as government slaves due to zāng crime,
while huò were fugitives,
captured to become slaves.
Jì Gāng
Duke Wén of Jìn and his wife, Lady Yíng, arrived,
from Wángchéng the Earl of Qín sent three thousand men to Yá,
who served as household stewards.

Fetters and Shackles
Initially, Jìn Hóu's young attendant Tóu Xū was the keeper of the treasury.
When he departed, he stole
the treasury and fled.
Upon his return, he sought an audience,
but the duke excused himself, claiming he was washing his hair.
Tóu Xū said to the attendant:
"When washing the hair, the heart is overturned;
when the heart is overturned, plans become reversed.
No wonder I cannot gain an audience.
Those who follow are servants bound by duties,
while those who remain guard the altars of soil and grain.
Why must those who stay be blamed?
If a ruler of a state holds a grudge against a common man,
then many will become fearful."
The attendant reported this,
and the duke immediately granted him an audience.

Tóng Qiè
Lǚ Bùwéi had ten thousand household servants,
Shī Gǔ notes:
"A general term for female servants and concubines,
the Shuōwén explains:
'A guilty man is called nú (slave),
a male slave is called tóng,
a female is called qiè (concubine).'"
Jiānnú
Huò Guāng favored and doted on his superintendent slave,
Féng Zǐdū often discussed affairs with him.
"Historical Biography"
household servant
Wèi Qīng's father, Zhèng Jì, served as a county official in the household of Píngyáng Hóu Cáo Shòu.
Shòu married Emperor Wǔ's elder sister, Princess Yángxìn.
Jì had an affair with Wèi Ǎo, a servant in the princess's household, and gave birth to Qīng.
In his youth, Qīng returned to his father,
who made him herd sheep.
The sons of his father's legal wife treated him as a slave,
not regarding him as a brother.
Once, when Qīng went to Gānquán,
a convict with an iron collar in the residence read his physiognomy
and said:
"You are a noble person,
destined to become a marquis."
Qīng laughed and said:
"As a child born to a slave,
if I can avoid whipping and scolding, it is enough.
How could I attain the status of a marquis?"
Shǐ Hàn
The Crafty Slave
In Qí, it was customary to despise slaves and captives,
yet only Diāo Jiàn favored them,
valuing their cunning and shrewdness.
What others feared in slaves,
Diāo Jiàn alone recruited,
enabling him to ultimately gain their service.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Cāngtóu
Bào Xuān wrote in his letter to Emperor Āi:
"Slaves follow guests to serve wine,
and both Huò's retainers and the servants of the state use this to amass wealth,
which is not the will of Heaven."
Mèng Kāng said:
"In the Hàn dynasty, slaves were called 'blue-heads',
not pure black,
to distinguish them from commoners."
Qián Zhuàn
Zhū Tū Xī Yǒng
During Wáng Mǎng's reign, the Xiōngnú invaded and raided,
so he extensively recruited prisoners from across the land,
calling the enslaved men "Zhūtūxīyǒng."
《Book of Hàn》
personal retainer
Wáng Mǎng said, "The Qín dynasty established markets for slaves,
treating them on the same register as oxen and horses.
Now I change the term 'slaves' to 'private dependents,'
and forbid their buying and selling."
Virtuous Conduct
Lǐ Shàn, styled Cìsūn,
was originally a servant of Lǐ Yuán.
During the Jiànwǔ era, a plague struck Yuán's household, causing successive deaths,
leaving only the orphaned child Xù, who had just been born.
After several decades, the servants plotted to kill Xù and divide the property,
but Shàn, distressed and unable to prevent it,
carried Xù on his back and fled to the Xiàqiū region.
He personally cared for and raised him,
even providing milk from his own body as sustenance,
enduring hardships and discomforts,
though Xù was still an infant,
Shàn served him as if he were an elder lord.
In every matter, he knelt respectfully to seek permission before acting,
and the local community was deeply moved by his devotion.
When Xù reached the age of ten,
they returned to their hometown and ancestral estate in the county,
reporting the servants' crimes to the local officials,
who arrested and executed them all.
Zhōnglí Yì submitted a memorial detailing the circumstances,
and Emperor Shìzǔ issued an edict appointing both Shàn and Xù
as Attendants to the Heir Apparent.
Later, Shàn became the Governor of Rìnán.
While passing by Yuán's tomb,
he personally weeded and swept the path,
prepared the offerings and conducted the sacrificial rites himself,
bidding farewell with tears before departing.
(From the Book of the Later Hàn)
Dì Yú
The Grand Minister of Works, Duke Chéng of Chén, Sūn Zhìjié, had a young servant named Dì Yú,
who was seventeen years old,
intelligent and clever by nature,
with a dignified and proper appearance,
and skilled in writing and drafting documents.
Zhìjié served as an official in the Household Department,
and ordered Dì Yú to return home to fetch funds and supplies.
Taking advantage of the carriage and horses, he fled and disappeared,
arriving in Dānyáng.
There, he claimed his surname was Wáng and his given name Bīn,
with the courtesy name Wéngāo,
and subsequently remained there as an official in various departments.
When Zhìjié was appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu,
the commandery selected scions of distinguished families for official posts, but all were inferior to Bīn,
so he was appointed.
Bīn requested that those around them withdraw,
then kowtowed, weeping with tears and snivel, saying:
"Bīn is none other than Dì Yú, your servant."
Bīn later became the Grand Administrator of Cāngwú.
(From "Fēngsú Tōng")
Seeking audience
Mèng Tuó of Pínglíng exhausted his family wealth to bribe Zhāng Ràng's supervising servant,
the servant, feeling ashamed, asked what he desired,
Mèng Tuó said:
"I want you."
When Cáo Bà was paying respects, guests seeking to see Zhāng Ràng
often had several hundred carriages,
yet for many days they couldn't gain access,
Mèng Tuó arrived later,
the various servants welcomed him with bows,
directly leading his carriage alone inside,
the crowd thought Mèng Tuó was on good terms with Zhāng Ràng,
they competed in bribing Mèng Tuó with goods,
thus Mèng Tuó was able to use these bribes for Zhāng Ràng.
"Records of Decisions in the Three Adjuncts"
entering and leaving his wife's quarters
Liáng Jì loved his overseer Qín Gōng,
who was promoted to the post of Grand Granary Prefect,
enabling him to enter his wife's quarters.
Whenever they met, he would dismiss the attendants to discuss matters,
and through this, they became intimate.
He enjoyed favor both inside and outside the household,
with even regional inspectors and officials of two thousand piculs paying him respects.
A wealthy man from Fufeng named Shìsūn Fèn
was asked by Liáng Jì for a loan of fifty million coins.
Fèn gave him thirty million instead,
which greatly angered Liáng Jì.
He then reported to the commandery and county authorities,
falsely accusing Fèn's mother of being a treasury maid
who had stolen ten hu of white pearls
and a thousand jin of purple refined gold,
leading to her arrest and interrogation.
Fèn and his brother died in prison,
and all their property was confiscated.
From "Bié Zhuàn"
Gǔ Lì
Gǔ Lì was originally an attendant in Sūn Quán's retinue,
and because of his carefulness and integrity, he became a trusted supervisor.
Records of Wú
See also the biography of Mǎ.
Longevity
Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Bì Guǐ sent the former Hàn Dynasty's Cross-Liao General Fàn Míngyǒu's Xiānbēi slave,
who was two hundred and fifty years old,
yet spoke and ate like an ordinary person.
Shì Yǔ
records that at the end of the Hàn Dynasty, when Fàn Míngyǒu's tomb was excavated,
the slave was still alive.
Míngyǒu was the son-in-law of Huò Guāng,
and he recounted matters of the Huò family,
including the events of the dethronement and installation of emperors,
which largely corresponded with the Hàn Shū.
This slave often wandered among the common people,
with no fixed dwelling,
and his current whereabouts are unknown.
Bówù Zhì
Scholarly Demeanor
Xióng Qiào once served as Shí Chóng's servant, yet his nature was honest and upright,
possessing the demeanor of a scholar.
The court official Pān Yuè saw him and expressed admiration,
urging Shí Chóng to free him.
Thus, he returned to his hometown.
"Biography of Yuǎn from the Book of Jìn"
Literacy
I was reading the "Book of Han: Biography of the Xiongnu,"
and came across the characters "chēnglí gūtú" which I did not recognize.
A Hu slave holding a candle looked at them,
and I asked him about it.
He said:
"Chēnglí
means 'heaven';
gūtú,
means 'son'.
This indicates that the Xiongnu title Chányú
is equivalent to the Han people having the Son of Heaven."
I suddenly had a clear realization.
"Xuānyàn Chūnqiū"
Húnú
Zǔ Tì had an ugly slave named Wáng Ān,
whom he treated very generously.
When he was in Yōngqiū,
he told him:
"Shí Lè is of your kind,
I will not keep you alone."
Then he gave him ample funds and sent him away,
and he became a general under Lè during the persecution of the Zǔ family.
Ān often took his followers to observe in the market,
secretly took Tì's illegitimate son,
Dào Chóng, and hid him by making him a Buddhist monk,
at that time he was ten years old.
When the Shí family fell,
he later returned.
"Jìn Shū"
Minister of Works Xī
Jiàn
had a northern servant in his household,
who was knowledgeable in literature,
and thoughtful in every matter.
Wáng Yòujūn praised him to Prefect Liú
Tán,
who asked how he compared to Fānghuí
Yīn?
Wáng said:
"This is merely a servant with some aspirations,
how can he compare to Fānghuí?"
Liú replied:
"If he is not as good as Fānghuí,
then he is just an ordinary servant after all."
"Shì Shuō"
Hǎishān Shǐzhě
Táo Kǎn had over a thousand household servants,
and he often obtained a foreign slave,
who did not like to speak,
and often sat silently.
One day, Táo Kǎn went out to the suburbs,
and the slave followed, holding a whip.
A foreign monk saw him and, startled, paid respects, saying:
"This is the envoy of the sea and mountains,"
and then shed tears.
Táo Kǎn found it strange,
and by night, the slave had disappeared from his place.
Boosting
Táo Kǎn served as the magistrate of Péngzé,
and did not let his family burden him.
He sent a laborer to his son with a letter saying:
"Your daily expenses
are difficult to provide for yourself.
I am now sending this laborer to help you with the toil of gathering firewood and drawing water.
He is also someone's son, so treat him well."
fled well
Zhāng Cún was skilled in acupuncture.
He had a servant prone to running away.
When putting him up for the night, Cún would insert needles into the servant's feet,
and when he needed to use him, he would remove the needles.
From the "Dūnhuáng Shílù".
Diǎn Qín
In the Northern Qí dynasty, Wáng Yuánjǐng served as Minister of State.
Although his nature was scholarly and deliberate, he was quick-witted in every matter.
He had a servant named Diǎn Qín (典琴, "Pawn Lute"),
who once, upon rising one morning, was ordered to fetch food,
referred to as "ending the fast."
The servant said:
"You, sir, do not observe fasting,
so why do you always say 'ending the fast'?"
Wáng Yuánjǐng slowly replied to the servant:
"If I do not fast,
I cannot speak of ending the fast.
You are named Diǎn Qín (Pawn Lute),
but where is there a lute to pawn?"
"Records of Amusing Tales"
Admiring the Lord's Profound Mystery
Xiāo Yǐngshì was exceptionally harsh and cruel.
He had a servant named Dù Liàng who served him for over ten years.
Every time Yǐngshì caned him, it would be over a hundred strokes.
Dù Liàng could not endure the suffering.
Some people urged him to find another master,
but the servant said:
"It's not that I cannot serve elsewhere,
the reason I stay is solely because I admire his erudition and profound knowledge."
Lǐ Rǒng, "Dú Yì Zhì"
Dāng Qiān
The Minister of the Imperial Stud, Zhào Zòng, was the son-in-law of Guō Zǐyí.
He was imprisoned due to his servant Dāng Qiān exposing his secret affairs.
Dāng Qiān was detained within the palace.
The Attendant Official Zhāng Yì submitted a memorial stating:
"Emperor Tàizōng once said to his attendants:
Recently, there have been cases of servants accusing their masters,
which is extremely detrimental to the law.
This must be specifically prohibited and stopped.
Henceforth, any servant who accuses their master
shall all be ordered to be executed.
Recently, the Magistrate of Cháng'ān, Lǐ Jì, was implicated due to a servant;
the Magistrate of Wànnián, Huò Yàn, was implicated due to a servant.
Such acts of defiance and disrespect
often lead to false accusations.
Now Zhào Zòng has been imprisoned,
and the servant is held in custody.
This concerns the fundamental principles
and runs counter to moral education."
The Emperor deeply accepted his advice.
Zhào Zòng was then demoted,
and Dāng Qiān was beaten to death.
Zhāng Yì then ordered the summoning of several hundred servants from Guō Zǐyí's household,
and showed them the dead servant.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Memorial Submitted in Place of a Deceased Official
Wáng Jì's family had two slaves who accused Jì of exchanging his father's legacy,
De Meijin's tribute items,
detaining the slaves in the armory,
and sending an imperial envoy to the Eastern Capital to seize Jì's family property.
Péi Dù presented a memorial, saying:
"After Wáng È's death,
his family has already contributed a lot in tribute,
and now, because of the slaves' accusation,
they are being investigated for their family matters.
I fear that if the generals across the country hear of this,
they will surely have concerns regarding their own families."
The Xiànzōng emperor the same day ordered the returned slaves to be sent back,
and handed them over to the Jīngzhàofǔ for execution.

Wáng Yì
When Wǔ Huángmén died,
Péi Jìngōng was assassinated by bandits,
and his subordinate Wáng Yì blocked the blade and died.
Dù personally wrote a eulogy for him,
that year two-thirds of the imperial examination candidates composed biographies of Wáng Yì.
"Southern Chronicles"
The Fishing Lad
Emperor Sùzōng once bestowed upon the reclusive scholar Xuánzhēnzǐ, Zhāng Zhìhé, a male and a female servant each.
Xuánzhēnzǐ paired them as husband and wife,
naming them the Fishing Lad and the Firewood Maiden.
When people asked the reason,
he replied:
"The Fishing Lad is to hold the fishing rod and gather the lines,
rowing the boat among the reeds;
the Firewood Maiden is to gather orchids for fuel and cassia for firewood,
brewing tea amidst the bamboo grove."
Yínlù
Yán Xiàn's family servant was named Yín Lù,
who later served Lǔ Gōng his entire life.
"Supplement to the National History"
Fāng Jiè
During a famine year in Yángchéng,
he kept to himself and did not visit his neighbors,
grinding elm seeds to make porridge,
yet he never ceased his discussions and teachings.
A servant named Dū'ér, moved by his virtue,
also became upright and self-disciplined.
Some, pitying his hunger,
offered him food,
but he would not accept it.
Later, when they brought him several cups of bran and grain husks,
he then accepted them.
Huángqín
Gāo Gù was born into a humble family and was sold by his family,
later becoming Hún Jiān's child servant,
styled Huáng Qín,
and was intelligent and clever by nature.
The Banished Immortal
Quán Tóngxiū's friend hired a servant,
who fell ill and became impoverished.
He stripped off his dirty clothes and ordered him to prepare wine and food,
saying:
"I will meet with the village elders to beg for travel funds."
The servant said:
"This is certainly not enough to prepare,
but I will manage it."
He then cut mulberry branches and spat to transform them into beef,
then drew several bottles of water, and in a moment,
it became fine wine.
Moreover, he said, "I am indeed an extraordinary person."
From "Yǒuyáng"
Lǐ Hóngzhāng
Lú Sùjūn's grandson Zhēnjiǎn possessed his grandfather's demeanor,
and in the early years of the Guānghuà era, he passed the imperial examinations at the temporary imperial seat in Huàzhōu.
By the time the great rebels invaded the capital twenty years later,
the officials were all impoverished.
Sù had just passed the examinations
when a man named Lǐ Hóng came to visit him,
offering to work as a laborer.
Hóng used his meager resources,
and in his spare time, he often provided financial support to Sù instead.
Beyond this, he never concerned himself with his own needs.
Sù had an old estate in Nányáng,
and he often sent Hóng to collect the rent.
Hóng always returned on time,
traveling thousands of miles without ever embezzling a single coin.
After Sù passed the examinations,
Hóng continued to serve diligently as before.
Once the spring affairs were concluded,
Hóng took his leave.
《The Gleaned Records》
Wǔ Gōnggàn
Wǔ Gōng Gàn often served Kuǎi Xīyì for over ten years,
being exceptionally diligent and capable.
By the time Xīyì passed the imperial examination,
Gàn excused himself due to his parents being alive,
begging to return home to care for them.
Though the lord firmly urged him to stay, he would not remain.
The lord, already impressed by his loyalty and filial piety,
saw him off with a poem,
roughly saying: "On perilous mountains, I never left my horse;
after sobering from wine,
I always see it before my bed."
Colleagues pooled silk as a farewell gift,
and all composed matching poems in response.
Jīngzhào
Gāo Áng, courtesy name Áo Cáo,
joined Hóu Jǐng and others in attacking Dúgū Xìn at Jīnyōng.
Áng sent his slave Jīngzhào to spy on the western army; Jīngzhào delayed,
and a maidservant forcibly took Áng's waist sword to proceed.
Áng seized and killed her.
Jīngzhào said:
"Thrice have I saved you in great peril,
how can you bear to have me killed over a minor matter?"
That night, Áng dreamed that Jīngzhào was smearing him with blood.
After waking in anger, he ordered Jīngzhào's shins broken.
At that time, Liú Táobàng was in Bóhǎi,
and also dreamed of Jīngzhào saying his plea was justified,
"I will deliver you to the enemy."
Táobàng knew Áng would surely die,
and rushed to him.
Áng underestimated the enemy,
erecting banners and canopies to intimidate their formation.
The western forces attacked with full might,
and his entire army was wiped out.
Áng fled east on a light horse toward Héyáng City,
but before crossing, pursuers arrived. Hiding under a bridge,
the pursuers saw his attendant slave holding a golden belt,
and asked where Áng was.
The slave pointed him out,
and the pursuers killed him.
Prior to this,
Áng had dreamed of being killed by this slave,
and told Lú Wǔ he would kill him,
but Wǔ advised against it, so he refrained.
Indeed, he met his fate.
(From *History of the Northern Dynasties*)
Xī
The "Rites of Zhōu" states: "Three hundred Xī slaves," with the annotation explaining they are now government-owned female servants.
Gūbù Zǐqīng saw Wúxù and said:
"This is truly a general."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"His mother was a lowly Dí maid,
how can he be noble?"
Zǐqīng said:
"Heaven's bestowed,
though lowly, must become noble."

Turn the meat over
Liú Kuān once had a guest,
and sent his servant to buy wine.
After a long delay, the servant returned very drunk.
Liú Kuān scolded him, saying:
"You beast."
He then sent someone to check on the servant,
suspecting he might commit suicide.
His wife wanted to test Liú Kuān's patience,
so she ordered a maid to wait until he was dressed for court.
When he was fully attired,
she had the maid serve meat soup and spill it on his court robes.
The maid hurriedly cleaned it up,
but Liú Kuān's expression remained unchanged.
He then calmly said:
"The soup has scalded your hand."
From "Dōngguān Hànjì"
Reading
Zhèng Xuán's household servants were all literate.
Once, Xuán was dissatisfied with a maidservant's performance,
and was about to whip her.
As she was trying to explain herself,
Xuán became angry and had her dragged into the mud.
Shortly after, he sent another maidservant to ask:
"Why are you in the mud?"
She replied:
"I went to plead my case,
but encountered his anger."
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Zhái Sù
Huìjī's Dí Sùyǒu,
a daughter of the Dí family,
was betrothed but not yet married.
It happened that bandits tried to assault her,
threatening with blades:
"If you do not comply, you will die now."
Sù said:
"You may kill me but cannot,
dishonor this humble maid's name."
Qīngqīng begged to take Sù's place,
so the bandits killed Sù.
Later when attempting to assault Qīngqīng, she said:
"Earlier I wished to replace Sù,
fearing she would be shamed and harmed.
Now that Sù is dead,
why should I live?"
The bandits killed her too.
Huángfǔ Mì's "Later Biographies of Exemplary Women"
Marrying Off a Maidservant
Zhào Míngfǔ, named Rénměi,
was from Tiānshuǐ.
He was transferred and appointed as magistrate of Pú County.
Being well-versed in the Three Destinies,
he knew his own official salary and lifespan limits.
One day, a fortune-teller came to visit him,
and their conversation aligned.
Zhào had an unmarried daughter,
for whom he had not yet selected a husband.
Meanwhile, he first sought a maidservant for his daughter.
One day, he ordered her to sweep the courtyard,
when she suddenly burst into tears.
Zhào asked why,
and the girl said:
"My surname is Wáng,
my father's name is Délín,
who once served as magistrate of this county.
I was born in this county,
but after losing both parents,
I was abducted and sold here."
Zhào, deeply moved, said to his wife:
"I no longer worry about our daughter's marriage."
He then selected a worthy local scholar and diverted his daughter's dowry
to marry her (the maidservant) first.
Suddenly one day, a skilled physiognomist passed by
and visited the magistrate again.
Upon seeing him, he was greatly astonished and said:
"Yesterday when I observed your countenance,
your fate appeared near its end.
But today when I look at you,
your fortune, official salary, and lifespan are beyond measure."
When asked about any extraordinary deeds or redressing of injustices,
Zhào said:
"I have no other notable governance achievements."
He then recounted the story of marrying off the maidservant.
The physiognomist congratulated the magistrate, saying:
"This alone constitutes hidden merit affecting your official salary and lifespan.
How could this be measured?"
From "In Search of the Supernatural"
Now various texts only record the story of Zhōnglí Jǐn from the Southern Táng.

had an illness,

Serve the meal
Péi Xiù at age eighteen had a fine reputation,
but his mother was a maidservant and his legal mother was jealous,
still making Péi Xiù's mother perform servile tasks.

each time Péi Xiù served food,
all the guests stood up and bowed to him.

Fù Sū
Qián Bǎo's father had a favored concubine,
and Bǎo's mother was extremely jealous.
When burying Bǎo's father, she pushed her into the tomb,
After ten years, when his mother passed away,
they opened the grave,
and found the maid lying on the coffin.
Upon closer inspection, she was still warm,
gradually showing signs of breathing.
They carried her back home, and by the end of the day she revived, speaking of Bǎo's father.
He often provided her with food and drink,
and they shared the same bed, their affection as if in life.
She would tell of the family's fortunes and misfortunes,
and upon verification, all proved true.
After recovering for several years, she eventually passed away.
Bǎo thus wrote "In Search of the Supernatural",
stating in it that it was inspired by this experience.

Lǜcǎo Cǎiyīn,

Gathering Orchids
Cài Zūn was in Línhǎi,
when a commoner named Yáng Yuánsūn had his maidservant Cǎilán serve as collateral with his neighbor Huáng Quán under an agreement,
that if she bore a child, it would repay the cost of nursing.

Respectful Heart
Wáng Yì could not tell beans from wheat,
and was considered by his contemporaries to be a remnant of the Yīn dynasty,
a pitiable outcast.
No one was willing to marry him,
so he had a maid, Gōng Xīn, serve him,

Yùsù
Secretariat Drafter Guō Zhèngyī, upon capturing P'yŏngyang, obtained a Koguryŏ maid,
named Yùsù,
who was extremely beautiful and charming.

and only Yùsù could prepare it for him.
Yùsù poisoned it,
and it was only after a long while that he realized something was wrong and searched for the maid, but she was gone.

Longing for Love

who was young and beautiful.

Ribbon-cutting
Yán Zhēnqīng was sent on a mission,
Lǐ Xīliè said to Liǔ Chángshì's paternal uncle:
"I know I will certainly not return from this journey.
I have a young maidservant named Jiǎncǎi with double buns,
who serves me quite well.

Lánsūn
In Péngchéng, Liú Yuánpǔ's daughter was about to be married,
and he sought maidservants to accompany her.

one of whom, named Lánsūn, had exceptional beauty,

Young maidservant
Minister Liǔ Zhòngyǐng had a maidservant
who, having fallen out of favor, was sold in Chéngdū.
Magistrate Gài Jùyuán desired her,
and brought her to his household.
One day, a silk merchant passed beneath the window along the main road.
As Magistrate Gài was selecting and examining silk rolls from the bundle, negotiating the transaction,
the maidservant suddenly cried out and collapsed,
as if stricken by a stroke.
Gài ordered her to be carried out.
The next day, having recovered, she said:
"Though I am but a lowly person,
I once served as a fine maidservant in the Liǔ household.
I would rather die
than serve a silk-peddling broker!"
(From *Beimeng Suoyan*)
Climbing Fig
Wǔ Yìhuáng achieved unparalleled success with his triple honors in his generation,
but later became infatuated with his maid servant Bìlì,
and mistreated his lawful wife Lú Shì.
Although Lǐ Shēn, being of the same examination year, defended him,
public opinion would not tolerate it,
ultimately leading to his exile.
The top candidate in the palace examination,
the top candidate in the decree examination—these together with the top candidate in the selective examination are called the triple honors.
"New Book of the South"
Lǜ Qiáo
Yú Xuánjī, styled Yòuwēi, a female Taoist priest at the Xiányí Temple in the Western Capital,
possessed exceptional beauty
and was fond of reading and composing writings.
Her elegant verses on romantic scenes and leisurely enjoyments
were often circulated among the literati.
She had a young maidservant
named Lǜ Qiào, who was also intelligent and attractive.
Suspecting that Lǜ Qiào had an affair with a frequent visitor, Yú Xuánjī
had her flogged to death.
From "Sānshuǐ"
Xiǎo Bì
Liú Jīzhōng's maid Xiǎo Bì suddenly began speaking in the voice of his same-year graduate Dù Shěnggōng.

Qīng Hóng
Huàzhōu Liǔ Cānjūn's wife, Madame Cuī, had a maidservant named Qīng Hóng.

for a price of one hundred and fifty thousand.

Luánfèng
Sīmǎ Tú resided in Zhōngtiáo Mountain at Wángguān Valley,
wearing plain clothes and carrying a dove-headed staff.
When going out, he was always accompanied by a maidservant named Luánfèng,
During village sacrificial ceremonies for rain prayers each year,
Tú would invariably attend them,
sitting together with the village elders,
