"Continued Accounts of the World"
Chūnyàn
Shǔ King Mèng Chǎng had a palace maid named Chūn Yàn whose surname was Lǐ.
They walked together in the same carriage,
and sat together on the same mat.
In his final years, he was killed,
and they were buried together in a joint tomb.
On their grave grew a tree with unusual flowers,
whose tops resembled mandarin ducks with necks entwined.
People did not know their name,
but simply called them the "Mandarin Duck Tree."
At that time, there was a song that went:
"We wish to be the mandarin duck trees on the grave,
flying together as a pair and returning together as a pair."
"Hǎiwù Yìmíng Jì" (Record of Marvelous Things and Their Names)
Jīnfèng
Wáng Lín's wife died early,
and his second wife Jīn shì, though virtuous, was not favored.
He took a fancy to the maid Jīnfèng,
whose surname was Chén,
and Wáng Lín doted on her,
eventually establishing her as his queen.
Initially, Wáng Lín had a favored attendant named Guī Shǒumíng, who won favor through his looks,
and was called Guī Láng.
Later, when Wáng Lín suffered from a wind ailment,
Chén shì committed adultery with Guī Láng, and the director of the Hundred Artisans Institute, Lǐ Kěyīn, also connected with Chén shì through Guī Láng.
Wáng Lín ordered the brocade workers to make a Nine Dragon Canopy,
and the people of the state sang:
"Who would say the Nine Dragon Canopy
holds only one Guī Láng?"
From the History of the Five Dynasties.
Spring Swallow
Wáng Lín's maid Chūn Yàn was beautiful,
his son Jì Péng had an illicit affair with her,
while Lín was already ill,
Jì Péng sought Chūn Yàn through Chén Shì's intercession,
and Lín reluctantly gave her to him.
The emperor
Chūnyīng
Wáng Yányì often indulged in heavy drinking like an ox.
One night, thoroughly drunk,
he ordered his chancellor Lǐ Zhǔn to be executed in the market,
but Zhǔn was also heavily intoxicated,
lying in the marketplace,
only calling for his maid Chūnyīng.
The executioner dared not carry out the killing,
so he placed Zhǔn elsewhere.
The next day during court audience,
the king summoned Zhǔn,
and his attendants recounted the previous night's order.
Yányì had no recollection of it at all,
so he urgently recalled Zhǔn and restored him to his position.
"Stories of the Five States"
Tiānzhōng Jì Volume Nineteen
Shī Zuǒ
One whose wisdom is like a gushing spring,
and whose conduct can serve as a model,
is a teacher of others;
one whose wisdom can serve as a whetstone,
and whose conduct can serve as support,
is a friend of others.
The superior ruler employs teachers as his aides,
the middling ruler employs friends as his aides.
"Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn"
He then became a disciple
When a child is born,
if it is not protected from water and fire,
it is the mother's fault.
When the child grows to the age of tying hair and becomes a youth,
if it is not sent to a teacher,
it is the father's fault.
When attending a teacher for learning,
if the mind and will lack proper direction,
and comprehension is not achieved, it is one's own fault.
If the mind and will are comprehended but reputation is not heard of,
it is the friends' fault.
From "Gǔliáng Zhuàn," nineteenth year of Duke Zhāo
The Four Arts
There are four methods of being a teacher, but extensive learning is not among them.
Being dignified and inspiring awe can make one a teacher.
Being elderly and trustworthy can make one a teacher.
Reciting and explaining without transgressing or violating can make one a teacher.
Understanding subtleties and discussing them can make one a teacher.
Thus, when water is deep, it forms eddies; when trees shed leaves, they fertilize their roots.
When students are successful, they think of their teacher.
"Xúnzǐ"
Follow the law
If a person has neither teacher nor model and yet is knowledgeable, he will surely become a thief;
if brave, he will surely become a bandit;
if capable, he will surely cause chaos;
if perceptive, he will surely become strange;
if eloquent, he will surely become absurd.
If a person has both teacher and model and is knowledgeable, he will quickly become accomplished;
if brave, he will quickly become authoritative;
if capable, he will quickly achieve success;
if perceptive, he will quickly grasp everything;
if eloquent, he will quickly make his point.
Therefore, having a teacher and model
is the greatest treasure for a person,
while lacking a teacher and model
is the greatest calamity for a person.
Seeking a Master
Gānjiàng, Mòyé,
Jùquē, Pìlǘ,
these were all fine swords of antiquity,
yet without grinding they could not be sharp,
and without human strength they could not cut.
Huáliú, Qíjì,
Xiānlí, Lǜ'ěr,
these were all fine horses of antiquity,
yet in front they must have the restraint of bit and bridle,
behind the threat of whip and crop,
and be driven by someone like Zàofǔ,
only then could they cover a thousand lǐ in a day.
Although a person may have a fine nature and a discerning mind,
they must seek out a worthy teacher to serve,
and choose worthy friends to befriend.
Revere the Teacher
Sages are born from diligent learning;
there has never been one who could become an outstanding scholar or renowned person
without diligent learning.
Diligent learning lies in respecting teachers;
when teachers are respected, their words are believed,
and their doctrines are discussed.
Therefore, those who go to teach others without being sought cannot transform them;
those who summon teachers cannot be transformed;
those who hold themselves in low esteem do not listen;
those who belittle teachers do not listen.
If a teacher employs methods that neither transform nor are heeded,
and yet forcefully instructs others, desiring the Way to be practiced
and oneself to be honored, is it not far-fetched?
If a learner is in a situation where they cannot be transformed or do not listen,
and yet act on their own, wishing for fame to be prominent and themselves to be secure,
it is like carrying rot and desiring fragrance;
it is like entering water and disliking wetness.
"Lǚ's Annals: Exhortation to Learning"
The accomplished teacher
When a master achieves excellence in teaching,
he enables his disciples to feel at ease and find joy,
to rest and wander freely,
while maintaining reverence and solemnity.
If these six qualities are attained through learning,
then the paths of depravity and deviation are blocked,
and the methods of principle and righteousness prevail.
If these six qualities are not attained through learning,
then the ruler cannot command his ministers,
the father cannot command his sons,
and the master cannot command his disciples.
(From "On the Faults of Disciples")
called Shī
In the learning of a noble person,
when explaining principles, one must cite the teacher to discuss the Way,
and when following instructions, one must exert full effort to illuminate them.
Not exerting full effort in following instructions is called betrayal,
and not citing the teacher when explaining principles is called rebellion.
A worthy ruler does not admit rebellious individuals into the court,
and a noble person does not befriend them.
"On Honoring Teachers"
Model
To devote oneself to learning is not as good as to devote oneself to seeking a teacher,
for a teacher is the model for others.
If the model is not a model,
and the example is not an example,
there are not a few such cases.
In a single market, differing opinions abound;
in a single volume of books, differing theories are numerous.
A single market must establish its standard,
and a single volume of books must establish its teacher.
From "Yángzǐ."
The Sage Teacher
What Heaven and Earth value is humanity,
what the sages esteem is righteousness,
what virtue and righteousness accomplish is wisdom,
and what the wise seek is learning and inquiry.
Even the most sagacious,
are not born with knowledge;
even the most talented,
are not born with ability.
Thus, records say: Huángdì took Fēng Hòu as his teacher,
Zhuānxū took Lǎo Péng as his teacher,
Dì Kù took Zhùróng as his teacher,
Yáo took Wù Chéng as his teacher,
Shùn took Jì Hòu as his teacher,
Yǔ took Mò Rú as his teacher,
Tāng took Yī Yǐn as his teacher,
King Wén and King Wǔ took Jiāng Shàng as their teacher,
the Duke of Zhōu took Zú Xiù as his teacher,
and Confucius took Lǎo Dān as his teacher.
If these words are to be believed,
then one cannot but follow a teacher.
These eleven rulers,
all were supreme sages,
yet still they pursued learning and inquiry,
so their wisdom became vast,
and their virtue became great.
How much more so for ordinary people?
《Qiánfū Lùn》
Duke Āi asked Zǐ Xià:

Zǐ Xià replied:
"I have heard that Huángdì studied with Dà Fén,
Zhuānxū studied with Lù Tú,

Yáo studied with Wù Chéngzǐ Fù,

King Wǔ studied with Tài Gōng,
the Duke of Zhōu studied with Guó Shū,
and Zhòngní studied with Lǎo Dān.
These twelve sages,
had they not encountered these teachers, could not have made their achievements manifest under Heaven,
nor could their names have been transmitted to later generations."

Yáo's teacher was called Xǔ Yóu,

amidst the great turmoil across the land,

In the past, Yī Yǐn of the Yīn dynasty,
Tài Gōng of the Zhōu dynasty,
and Bǎilǐ Xī of the Qín dynasty,
though all possessed natural talent,
nevertheless reached the age of over seventy before rising to become teachers of kings and lords.
Huán Tán's "New Discourses"
King Wén's Teacher
King Wén served as the Earl of the West,
Yù Xióng served as King Wén's teacher,
having rendered meritorious service to King Wén,
but died early.
By the time King Wǔ conquered the Yīn dynasty,
he had not been enfeoffed.
King Chéng selected descendants of those who had labored diligently,
enfeoffing his great-grandson Xióng Yì as the Viscount of Chǔ.
Records of the Grand Historian
Chancellor Wèi memorialized about Huò Guāng, saying:
King Wén met Master Yù when he was over ninety years old.
King Wén said:
"Alas,
you are old!"
Master Yù replied:
"If my lord orders me to capture tigers or chase fawns,
then I am indeed old.
But if you have me sit and strategize on state affairs,
I am still young in years."
King Wén approved of this,
and thus made him his teacher.

Pouring Wine
Sǎn Yíshēng, Hóng Yāo, and Nángōng Kuò—these three men studied under Tàigōng.
When Tàigōng recognized their worth as virtuous individuals,
he poured wine and sliced dried meat,
pledging friendship with them.
"Shangshu Dazhuan"
The Royal Army
Duke Huán of Qí took Guǎn Yíwú as his teacher,
Duke Wén of Jìn took Jiùfàn and Suí Kuài as his teachers,
Duke Mù of Qín took Bǎilǐ Xī and Gōngsūn Zhī as his teachers,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ took Sūnshū Áo and Shěn Shēnwū as his teachers,

King Gōujiàn of Yuè took Fàn Lǐ and Dàfū Zhǒng as his teachers.
"Lǚ Zūnshī"
Empty in going, full in returning
Cháng Jì asked Zhòngní, saying:
"Wáng Tái is a man who has lost his feet,
yet the number of his disciples is half as many again as yours in Lǔ.
When he stands, he does not instruct;
when he sits, he does not discourse.
They go to him empty
and return full.
Is there indeed such a thing as wordless instruction,
and a formless way of bringing the mind to completion?
What sort of man is he?"
Zhòngní said:
"This gentleman is a sage.
I have merely been tardy in going to him.
I will make him my teacher—
how much more should those who are not equal to me!
"The Sign of Virtue Complete"
Knocking at the door
It is said that Táng Yī Ruò knocked at Confucius's door and said:
"Is Qiū in?
Is Qiū in?"
Zǐgòng responded to him:
"The nobleman honors the worthy and accommodates the multitude,
praises the good and pities the incompetent,
shows affection to both inner and outer circles,
what he himself does not desire,
he does not impose on others.
Why do you speak my teacher's name directly?"
Táng Yī Ruò said:
"Why do you, young man, speak so sharply?"
Zǐgòng said:
"A large cart without tight binding cannot bear its load,
lutes and zithers without tight strings cannot produce their music.
Your words are sharp, therefore I respond sharply."
Táng Yī Ruò said:
"I initially thought you had the strength of a swan,
but now I see you're just flapping your wings."
Zǐgòng said:
"If not for the swan's strength,
how could it lift its wings?"
Han Shi Wai Zhuan
Three times full, three times empty
Shǎozhèng Mǎo was in Lǔ alongside Confucius,
Confucius's school thrice filled and thrice emptied,
only Yán Yuān did not leave,
Yán Yuān alone recognized Confucius's sageliness.
Lùnhéng
The Great Broker
Duàngān Mù was a great broker of Jìn,
and became the teacher of Lord Wén.
Huáinánzǐ:
Zǐzhāng was from a humble family of Lǔ,
Yánzhuō Jù was a great robber of Liángfù,
both studied under Confucius.
Duàngān Mù was a great broker of the state of Jìn,
studied under Zǐxià.
Gāo Hé and Xiànzǐ Shí were violent men of the state of Qí,
pointed at by their villages,
studied under Mòzǐ.
Suǒlú Cān was a great trickster of the east,
studied under Qíngǔlí.
These six men were people deserving punishment, execution, death, or disgrace,
yet now they not only escaped punishment, execution, death, and disgrace,
but also became famous scholars and eminent men of the world, living out their full lifespans,
with kings, dukes, and great men according them ritual respect.
This they attained through learning.
Lǚ Zūn Shī
Awaiting orders respectfully
Chéng Huí studied under Zǐlù for three years and remained
reverent and respectful without cease.
Zǐlù asked him the reason for this,
to which Huí replied:
"I have heard that
a traveler is like a bird—
above, it fears hawks and kites;
below, it fears nets and snares.
Among people, those who do good are few while those who speak ill are many.
If one does not die,
how can one know that calamity and punishment will not befall?
Having lived for seventy years,
I constantly fear failing in my conduct and integrity.
Therefore, I remain reverent while awaiting Heaven's decree."
Zǐlù bowed deeply and said:
"A true gentleman indeed."
From "Shuō Yuàn"
Jìrán
Jìrán was a man from Púshàng in Càishì,
whose ancestor was a prince of the State of Jìn.
His surname was Xīn, and his courtesy name was Wéndāng.
He traveled south to the State of Yuè and became a follower of Fàn Lǐ,
whom he served as a teacher.
From "The Subtle Discourses of Tàishǐgōng Sùshēng."
Riding the Wind
Lièzǐ took Lǎo Shěnzǐ as his teacher
and Bó Gāozǐ as his friend.
Having mastered the Way of these two men,
he rode the wind and returned.
"Lièzǐ · Huángdì"
Commentary:
Lièzǐ
was a divine man.
Living in the Southern Outer Wall
Zǐ Lièzǐ, having studied under Master Húqiū,
and befriended Bó Hūn Màorén,
then lived in the southern outer wall.
Those who followed him there were numerous daily, yet never reached the full count.
"Lièzǐ: Zhòngní"
east of
Dīng Kuān, styled Zǐxiāng,
was a native of Liáng.
Initially, Xiàng Shēng of Liáng studied the Book of Changes under Tián Hé,
at which time Kuān served as an attendant to Xiàng Shēng.
He studied the Book of Changes with exceptional acuity and diligence,
surpassing Xiàng Shēng in talent,
and subsequently became a disciple of Hé.
After completing his studies, Hé commended Kuān,
who then returned east.
Hé remarked to his disciples:
"The Book of Changes has now gone east."
Hàn Shū
Different Treatment
Zhāng Yǔ, styled Zǐwén,
was naturally versed in music,
and privately led a luxurious and dissolute life.
Residing in a grand mansion,
he would play string and wind instruments in the rear hall.
Among Zhāng Yǔ's accomplished disciples, the most prominent were
Huáiyáng's Péng Xuān, who rose to become Minister of Works,
and Pèi Commandery's Dài Chóng, who became Chief Steward, one of the Nine Ministers.
Péng Xuān was a respectful and frugal man who adhered to rules and regulations,
while Dài Chóng was amiable and shrewd.
Though the two men had different dispositions,
Zhāng Yǔ felt affection and closeness toward Dài Chóng,
but treated Péng Xuān with respect while keeping him at a distance.
Whenever Dài Chóng visited Zhāng Yǔ,
he would often urge the teacher to set out wine and music,
to enjoy himself with his disciples.
Zhāng Yǔ would then bring Dài Chóng into the rear hall to eat and drink,
with women in attendance,
and musicians playing string and wind instruments.
The music was resplendent and joyous to the extreme,
continuing until late at night before ending.
However, when Péng Xuān came,
Zhāng Yǔ would receive him in a side room to discuss classical texts,
and by day's end would offer him no more than a single meat dish when presenting food,
facing each other with a cup of wine.
Péng Xuān never had the chance to enter the rear hall.
When both men learned of this,
they understood it was what each deserved.
The emperor
Mastering the Confucian classics
Xiàhóu Shèng, styled Chánggōng, later,
first studied the "Book of Documents" and the "Great Plan" with its Five Agents theories of calamities and anomalies under Shǐ Chāng,
then served Jiǎn Qīng,
and also studied with the Ōuyáng school,
becoming thoroughly proficient in his learning,
for he did not confine his inquiries to a single teacher.
Whenever Shèng gave lectures,
he would often say to his students:
"Scholars suffer from not understanding the classics and their arts;
if one truly understands the classics and their arts,
attaining high office is as easy as bending down to pick up mustard seeds from the ground.
If one studies the classics without understanding them,
it would be better to return to farming."
The emperor
Guidance
Xiǎnzōng appointed Zhāng Pú to educate the Crown Prince,
fully observing the proper protocols for guidance.
When Zhāng Dì ascended the throne,
he honored Zhāng Pú by appointing him to the Eastern Commandery.
In the second year of Yuánhé, there was an eastern inspection tour,
and the emperor visited the Eastern Commandery.
He gathered Zhāng Pú, his disciples, and the commandery clerks in the courtyard,
where the emperor first observed the ceremony due to a disciple,
having Zhāng Pú deliver a reading of the "Shàngshū".
Afterwards, they conducted the rites appropriate to ruler and minister,
with special rewards and honors bestowed.
"Dōngguān Hànjì"
Urban residences
Zhāng Bà, styled Bó Ráo,
was known as Zhāng Zēngzǐ in his youth,
later extensively studied the Five Classics,
and Sūn Lín and others admired him,
each purchasing residences nearby to study under his son Zhāng Kǎi.
From the *History of the Later Han*.
Forgetting Age Differences
Zhū Mù, whose courtesy name was Gōngshū,
was devoted to learning and intensely focused.
His father often considered him naively single-minded.
In the same commandery, Zhào Kāng (courtesy name Shūshèng) lived in seclusion at Wǔdāng Mountain,
purifying himself and not taking office,
but teaching through classical texts and commentaries.
At that time, Zhū Mù was fifty years old,
yet he presented a letter declaring himself a disciple.
When Zhào Kāng passed away, Zhū Mù mourned him as a teacher,
showing such respect for virtue and reverence for the Way
that he was admired by his contemporaries.
Mocking the Teacher
Biān Sháo, styled Xiàoxiān,
was a native of Jùnyí in Chénliú.
He was renowned for his literary talent,
and taught several hundred students.
Biān Sháo was eloquent in debate.
Once, while napping during the day,
his disciples privately mocked him, saying:
"Biān Xiàoxiān, with his bulging belly, is too lazy to read,
and only wants to sleep."
Biān Sháo overheard this in secret,
and immediately retorted:
"Biān is my surname,
Xiào is my style,
a bulging belly—
a repository of the Five Classics;
only wanting to sleep—
pondering the classics' affairs;
in dreams, I communicate with the Duke of Zhōu,
in stillness, I share thoughts with Confucius.
If a teacher can be mocked,
from which classic is this recorded?"
The mocker was greatly ashamed.
Serving porridge
Guō Tài once stayed at Chénguó Wénxué and saw a young boy,
Wèi Zhāo, styled Dé Gōng,
knowing he had exceptional aspirations,
approached his room to provide cleaning services.
Línzōng (Guō Tài) once fell ill,
and at night ordered Zhāo to make porridge.
When the porridge was ready and presented to Tài,
he took one sip, angrily scolded him, saying:
"Making porridge for an elder without showing due respect,
making it sandy and inedible."
He threw the cup on the ground.
Zhāo made the porridge again and presented it to Tài,
and was scolded repeatedly like this three times.
Yet Zhāo's demeanor remained unchanged,
his expression particularly calm.
Línzōng said:
"At first, I saw your face,
but now I see your heart."
Thereupon, he befriended him,
and Zhāo eventually became an outstanding scholar.
"Bié Zhuàn"
Crimson Canopy
Mǎ Róng, courtesy name Jìcháng,
was a native of Màolíng in Fúfēng.
He was eloquent in speech,
and handsome in appearance with outstanding talent.
Initially, Zhì Xún of Jīngzhào, who taught Confucian classics,
lived in seclusion in the Nánshān mountains,
and did not accept official appointments,
yet his reputation was highly esteemed west of Hánguān Pass.
Róng followed him to study,
mastering the classics extensively.
Xún admired Róng's talent,
and gave him his daughter in marriage.
Róng, with his lofty talent and broad knowledge,
was recognized as a thoroughly learned Confucian scholar of his time.
He educated and nurtured numerous students,
often numbering in the thousands.
Lú Zhí from Zhuōjùn
and Zhèng Xuán from Běihǎi were among his disciples.
He was skilled in playing the qín,
and fond of playing the flute.
Living a carefree life and following his nature,
he was not constrained by conventional Confucian norms.
His residence, utensils, and clothing often featured extravagant decorations.
He frequently sat in a high hall behind a crimson silk curtain,
teaching students in the front,
while female musicians were arranged behind him.
Disciples passed on knowledge sequentially,
and few ever entered his inner chambers.
From the "Book of the Later Hàn"
Shìjiǎng
Lú Zhí, styled Zǐgàn,
was a native of Zhuō in Zhuō Commandery.
He stood eight feet two inches tall,
with a voice like a bell.
In his youth, he and Zhèng Xuán both studied under Mǎ Róng.
He was able to master both ancient and contemporary scholarship,
preferring to delve into the essence rather than adhere rigidly to textual commentaries.
Mǎ Róng, being from an influential consort clan,
often had rows of female entertainers singing and dancing before him.
Yet throughout the years Lú Zhí attended his lectures,
he never once glanced sideways at them.
Mǎ Róng therefore held him in high esteem.
After completing his studies, Lú Zhí took his leave and returned home,
shutting his doors to teach privately.
Dào Dōng
Zhèng Xuán, courtesy name Kāngchéng,
was a native of Gāomì in Běihǎi.
He attended the Imperial Academy for studies,
but finding no one in Shāndōng adequate to consult,
he journeyed west through the pass,
and through the recommendation of Lú Zhí from Zhuō Commandery, became a disciple of Mǎ Róng of Fúfēng.
Mǎ Róng had over four hundred disciples,
with only about fifty who had advanced to inner hall access.
Mǎ Róng, being arrogant and noble by nature,
kept Zhèng Xuán at his gate for three years without an audience.
He then had his senior disciples instruct Xuán instead.
Xuán studied day and night,
never slacking in his efforts.
When Mǎ Róng gathered his disciples to examine charts and apocrypha,
he heard of Xuán's skill in calculation,
and summoned him for an audience upstairs.
Xuán took the opportunity to inquire about various doubtful points,
and after finishing his questions, took his leave to return home.
Mǎ Róng sighed and told his disciples:
"Now that Student Zhèng is departing,
my teachings will go east."
From "Biography"
Mǎ Jìcháng was renowned as an eminent scholar,
Xuán went to study under him,
comparing similarities and differences.
Jìcháng later became contemptuous in treating scholars,
Xuán could not gain audience,
so he built a study nearby.
After gaining access through introduction,
at that time Lú Zǐgàn from Zhuō Commandery was the leading disciple,
Jìcháng posed seven difficult problems without explaining them,
Xuán solved five,
Zǐgàn solved three,
Jìcháng told Zǐgàn:
"Both you and I are not his equal."
When Jìcháng bid farewell,
he held Xuán's hand and said:
"The great Way goes east,
strive hard, my friend."
From "Biographies of Noble Scholars"
Zhèng Xuán studied under Róng for three years without meeting him,
receiving instruction only through senior disciples.
Once, calculations for the armillary sphere didn't match,
and none of the disciples could solve it.
Someone mentioned Xuán's ability,
so Róng summoned him to calculate,
which he resolved in one attempt,
amazing and convincing everyone.
When Xuán completed his studies and prepared to leave,
Róng subsequently lamented
that ritual and music were moving east,
fearing Xuán would overshadow his fame and growing jealous.
Xuán also suspected pursuit,
so he sat beneath a bridge,
resting his clogs on the water.
Róng indeed performed divination to pursue him,
telling his attendants:
"Xuán is under earth,
on water while resting on wood -
this means he must be dead."
Thus he stopped pursuing Xuán,
who ultimately escaped.
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Teacher's Model
Bǐng Yuán, styled Gēnjǔ,
wished to travel afar for study,
and visited Sūn Sōng in Ānqiū.
Sūn Sōng declined, saying:
"In your hometown, there is Master Zhèng.
Do you know of him?"
Bǐng Yuán replied:
"Yes."
Sūn Sōng said:
"Master Zhèng's learning spans ancient and modern times,
with broad knowledge and strong memory,
probing the profound and reaching the distant.
He is truly a model teacher for scholars.
Yet you abandon him,
and tread thousands of miles in sandals.
This is what is called treating Zhèng as the neighbor Dōngjiā Qiū.
You seem unaware, yet say you know - why?"
Bǐng Yuán said:
"Each person has their own aspirations,
with different goals and plans.
Thus some climb mountains to gather jade,
while others enter the sea to collect pearls.
Can we say those who climb mountains don't know the sea's depth,
or those who enter the sea don't know the mountains' height?
You say I treat Zhèng as the eastern neighbor,
while Qiū considers me the western neighbor -
how foolish!"
Sūn Sōng then apologized.
From "Bié Zhuàn"
Shè Shī
When the First Sovereign Liú Bèi wanted to send Zhōu Bùyí to study with Liú Bā,
Bā said:
"When I traveled north of Jīng Province in the past,
I dabbled in the learning of memorizing and reciting from my teacher's school,
which is not worth recording my name for.
It is like the Winnowing Basket in the southern sky,
empty and of no use.
For you to send a letter wishing your worthy nephew to break the splendor of the phoenix
and wander in the realm of sparrows and swallows—
how could this enlighten him?"
(The Chronicles of the Worthies of Línglíng)
Requesting words
When the Duke of Gāoguìxiāng of Wèi visited the Imperial Academy,
he sought to honor ancient institutions,
and thus appointed Wáng Xiáng as the Elder of Three Virtues and Palace Attendant,
while Zhèng Xiǎotóng served as the Elder of Five Duties. Wáng Xiáng faced south with his desk and staff,
assuming the role of a teacher,
while the Emperor faced north to seek his counsel.
"Records of Wèi and Biographies of Jìn"
The exemplar of human relations
The Grand Tutor, the Prince of Dōnghǎi Sīmǎ Yuè, was stationed in Xǔchāng,
and appointed Wáng Ānqī as his Record Officer and Army Consultant.
He held him in high esteem and deep understanding,
saying to his eldest son, Sīmǎ Pí:
"The benefits gained from learning are shallow,
while those embodied through personal experience are profound.
Being well-versed in rituals and norms
is not as good as observing exemplary conduct;
reciting the words left by predecessors
is not as good as personally receiving their teachings.
Officer Wáng is a model of human relations,
you should take him as your teacher."
Another version says:
"The three officers Wáng, Zhào, and Dèng,
are models of human relations,
you should take them as your teachers."
This refers to Ānqī (Wáng Chéng), Dèng Bódào (Dèng Yǒu), and Zhào Mù.
From "Shì Shuō"
Xuānwén
Fú Jiān visited the Imperial Academy,
inquiring of the erudites about classical texts.
The erudite Lú Kǔn replied:
"The Commentary on the Rites of Zhou lacks a master to teach it.
Wéi Chěng's mother, née Sòng, inherited her father's scholarship,
and possesses the pronunciation and meaning of the Rites of Zhou.
Were it not for this mother, there would be no one to instruct later generations."
Thereupon, a lecture hall and study were established at Madame Sòng's home,
with one hundred and thirty students,
receiving instruction separated by a crimson silk curtain.
She was bestowed the noble title Lady Xuānwén,
and granted ten maidservants.
From Péi Jǐngrén's "Records of the Former Qín"
In three
Yáo Hóng was the crown prince,
studying the classics under the court academician Chúnyú Qí.
When Qí fell ill and stayed at home,
Hóng believed that a teacher serves as a model for others,
transmits the teachings of ancient sages,
and embodies the principle of triple respect,
which must be held in high regard.
He personally visited to inquire after his illness
and knelt in reverence beside the bed.
From Cuī Hóng's "Records of the Later Qín."
Dōng Guō
When Emperor Gaozu of the Sòng Dynasty ascended the throne,
he summoned Zhōu Xùzhī with ceremonial honors,
bestowing generous gifts upon him,
and established an academy outside the eastern city walls,
gathering students there.
The imperial carriage descended in royal visit,
and the emperor met with all the students.
"History of the Sòng Dynasty"
records an imperial decree summoning the recluse scholar Zhōu Jì to Dōnglíng,
where he founded a school with provisions supplied,
instructing over a hundred disciples.
Wáng Zhìshēn's "Annals of the Sòng Dynasty"
The teacher fled.
Yángpíng Prince Zǐ Yuán Qīn, courtesy name Sīruò,
had a very dark complexion,
and was nicknamed "Black-Faced Minister" by his contemporaries.
Qīn once entrusted Gāo Sēngshòu of Qīngzhōu to find a tutor for his son.
Shortly after the tutor arrived, he fled.
Qīn reproached Sēngshòu for this,
but Sēngshòu, being crude and humorous by nature,
retorted to Qīn:
"An ordinary person can survive only seven days without food before dying.
Yet after just five days,
he fled to seek sustenance elsewhere—
this truly reflects certain shortcomings."
Qīn was greatly ashamed,
and thereafter treated his guests more generously.
(Wèi Shū)
Qīng Xī
Liú Huán's figure was delicate and small,
yet his Confucian scholarship was unmatched in his time.
Scholars and noble youths in the capital all rose from their seats to receive his teachings,
and his contemporaries esteemed him as a great Confucian master,
comparing him to ancient figures like Cáo and Zhèng.
Whenever he went out, only one disciple followed him carrying a folding chair.
He resided at Tánqiáo,
in several tiled-roof houses,
all of which had leaking roofs.
His students held him in such reverence and admiration
that they dared not address him directly, instead calling him "Qīngxī."
Prince Zǐliáng of Jìnglíng personally went to pay him a visit.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Requesting instruction
Lǐ Mì, styled Yǒnghé,
was a native of Zhuōjùn.
From a young age, he was fond of learning,
mastered all the classics thoroughly,
and extensively studied the works of various scholars.
Initially, he studied under Elementary School Scholar Kǒng Fán,
but several years later, Fán returned to seek knowledge from Mì.
Fellow students remarked about this:
"Indigo is perfected from blue,
yet blue yields to indigo;
why should a teacher always remain superior?"
He passed the imperial examination and died at thirty-two.
That year,
Kǒng Fán and others, scholars of the Four Gates Elementary School, submitted a memorial stating:
"Lǐ Mì of Zhàojùn was known as a child prodigy in his youth,
and at eighteen, he came to study under Scholar Kǒng Fán.
From beginning to end, he grasped the essentials,
explored the origins and threads of arguments,
and all who taught him delighted in his words."
Thus, he gathered various classics,
broadly comparing similarities and differences,
and analogizing the cases from the three commentaries,
naming his work "Forest of the Spring and Autumn Annals" in twelve volumes.
For Fán and others, he analyzed and judged,
uncovering nearly a hundred subtle points,
resolving stagnations without letting them persist,
and highlighting every minute detail.
He achieved fluency without complacency,
correcting errors where they occurred,
never speaking carelessly against the classics,
nor embellishing words contrary to reason.
His rhetoric was upright and forthright,
captivating audiences until they forgot their fatigue.
He often said, "A man with ten thousand volumes of books
has no need for a hundred cities to rule."
Thereafter, he withdrew from public life,
closed his doors and ceased social interactions,
sold property to acquire books,
and personally edited them,
amassing over four thousand volumes without duplicates.
He continued to organize expert works,
searching for and comparing honest opinions,
working through the night in deep winter,
and staying up all night in the heat of summer.
Even compared to Dǒng Zhòngshū, who never glanced at his garden,
Jūnbó, who shut his doors,
Gāoshì, who neglected washing,
or Zhāngshēng, who forgot to eat,
measured against this man,
they were not enough to serve as metaphors.
Former Governor of Hénán, Zhēn Chēn, said to his son:
"In the past, Zhèng Xuán and Lú Zhí traveled thousands of miles to study under Mǎ Róng in Fúfēng;
now, your enlightened teacher is very near.
Why not go and study?"
He also built a dwelling against the cliffs,
carving rooms into the precipice,
intending to instruct the young scholars,
and propagate the ancient classics,
hoping to revive the teachings of Xīhé
and restore the ethos of Běihǎi.
But before his efforts could bear fruit,
he suddenly fell ill and passed away.
The state mourned the loss of a brilliant mind,
and scholars felt the sorrow of a broken pillar.
Moreover, Fán and others, whether admiring from afar
or learning directly from him,
how could they remain silent about the duty between teacher and student?"
The matter was reported, and an edict declared:
"He may be likened distantly to Huìkāng
and closely to Xuányàn."
He was posthumously honored as Chaste and Serene Recluse,
his household was recognized,
to commend his noble integrity.
A messenger was sent with a decree,
designating his gate as the Lane of Culture and Virtue,
and as an example of filial piety and righteousness.
From "The Book of Wèi."
Undress
Jiǎ Sībó and his younger brother Sītóng studied under Yīn Fèng of Běihǎi as their teacher,
but ultimately lacked the means to compensate him.
Fèng then seized their clothing and belongings as collateral,
prompting people of the time to say:
"Yīn shēng reads books,
not out of foolish ignorance,
but to make twin phoenixes strip people of their garments."
When Sībó later sent a hundred bolts of fine silk to Fèng upon taking office,
and prepared carriages and horses to welcome him,
Fèng felt ashamed and did not go,
earning the admiration of contemporaries.
(From History of the Northern Dynasties)
Yǐng Zhì
Huáyīn Xú Zūnmíng, styled Zǐpàn,
lectured away from home for over twenty years,
and was revered throughout the land,
yet he was quite fond of amassing wealth.
Together with Liú Xiànzhī and Zhāng Wúguì, they gathered disciples to teach in Héběi,
demanding silk and grain as tuition,
and retaining clothing and belongings as security,
calling it "shadow collateral,"
which tarnished the integrity of a Confucian scholar.
Previously,
Zūnmíng saw Zhèng Xuán's preface to the Analects mentioning "books written on eight-inch bamboo slips,"
but misread it as "eighty lineages,"
and forced a far-fetched interpretation accordingly.
Such was the extent of his eccentricity.

Southern School
Hé Shàngzhī, styled Yàndé,
served as Governor of Dānyáng during the Yuánjiā era,
established a residence outside the southern outer wall,
founded a school and gathered students.
Xú Xiù from Dōnghǎi, Hé Tánhuáng from Lújiāng, Xún Zǐhuá from Yǐngchuān, Sūn Zōngchāng from Tàiyuán, Wáng Yánxiù, and Kǒng Huìxuān from Lǔjùn, all admiring his teachings, came to study,
which was called the Southern School.
Wáng Qiú once remarked:
"Shàngzhī carries on the legacy of Xīhé's tradition unfalteringly."
Shàngzhī in turn said:
"Qiú preserves the ethos of the Zhèngshǐ era."
The Emperor
As strict as a father
Cháng Shuǎng, styled Shìmíng,
during the Wǔchéng era of the Northern Wèi Dynasty, taught over seven hundred disciples,
establishing disciplinary rules that included clear systems of encouragement and punishment,
his students serving him as if he were a strict father.
Yuán Zàn, the Left Deputy Director of the Imperial Secretariat; Sīmǎ Zhēn'ān, Governor of Píngyuán; and Chéng Língdòu, a Court Writer, were all taught by Shuǎng,
and those who achieved renown like Cuī Hào and Gāo Yǔn
both praised Shuǎng's strict teaching methods,
noting his skillful encouragement,
with Yǔn remarking:
"Wén Wēng achieved through gentleness what the master accomplished through firmness in establishing his teachings,
though their methods differed, their success in shaping individuals was the same."
(From the History of the Northern Dynasties)
Dreaming of spitting
Zhèng Zhuó, courtesy name Màozhāo,
was intelligent and quick-witted from a young age,
devoting himself to Confucian studies.
In his youth, he studied under Huáng Kǎn,
and once dreamed of meeting Kǎn on the road.
Kǎn said to him:
"Open your mouth, young Zhèng."
He then spat into Zhuó's mouth,
and from then on, Zhuó's understanding of philosophical principles greatly advanced.
(Book of Southern History)
Questions from Younger Scholars
Liú Xuàn was intelligent and erudite,
his fame second only to Liù Zhuó,
thus they were called the Two Liús,
renowned Confucian scholars of the realm.
Later scholars came with questions,
and those who traveled great distances to study under them were countless.
Commentators believed that in several hundred years,
no erudite and learned scholar
could surpass them.
However, he was narrow-minded,
and stingy with money,
not accepting tuition gifts,
nor ever providing instruction.
Because of this, contemporaries looked down upon him.
History of the Northern Dynasties
At fifteen, I set my heart on learning.
Jiǎ Yí said, "The Master became a teacher at fifteen;
Chénliú Wáng Xiàoyì was an arrogant elder of advanced understanding,
yet in his old age he faced north as a pupil—
was it because of age?
Wénzhōngzǐ"
The Imperial Tutor
Zhāng Hòuyì was in Bīngzhōu,
where Tàizōng received instruction in the "Zuǒzhuàn" commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Later, he was summoned to the court and granted a banquet.
When speaking of the past,
Tàizōng leisurely said to him:
"How does your disciple compare today?"
Hòuyì replied:
"In the past, Confucius led three thousand disciples,
yet none of his accomplished followers attained the rank of a viscount or baron.
But I have assisted just one person who became the Son of Heaven,
so by this measure, my achievement surpasses that of the ancient sage."
Tàizōng was greatly pleased.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Same Teacher
Yuán Bànqiān, named Yúqìng,
in his youth, together with Hé Yǎnxiān from Qízhōu, both studied under Wáng Yìfāng as disciples.
Yìfāng esteemed and valued them highly,
and once said to him:
"Once every five hundred years, a sage appears,
and you, sir, are that one."
Thus, he changed his name to Bànfāng.
When Yìfāng passed away,
Bànqiān and Yǎnxiān both observed the mourning rituals in full,
and only after completing them did they depart.
"Shén Yì Lù"
Foreign barbarians wish to learn
Xiāo Yǐngshì, courtesy name Màotǐng,
was exceptionally intelligent and alert beyond compare,
even foreign nations knew his name.
When the Silla envoy came to the court,
he stated that the people of his country wished to have Master Xiāo as their teacher.
Such was the extent of his fame, which stirred both China and foreign lands.
According to the Old Book of Tang,
when the Japanese envoy came to the court,
he also expressed that the people of his country wished to have Master Xiāo as their teacher.
However, Zhang Jiàn, the Secretariat Drafter, and others advised against it, and the matter was dropped.
The New Book of Tang records this.
The Party's Crime
Yáng Chéng, styled Kàngzōng,
lived in seclusion in the Zhōngtiáo Mountains.
People near and far admired his virtuous conduct,
and many studied under him.
There was one Xuē Yuē who had studied under Chéng,
a man of reckless and irritable nature,
who offended by his speech on affairs,
and was banished to Liánzhōu.
Having no fixed abode as a guest,
the imperial censors tracked him down to Chéng's home.
Chéng seated the censors at the gate,
drank with Yuē in farewell,
and weeping, saw him off beyond the suburbs.
Emperor Dézōng heard of this,
and considering Chéng an accomplice of the criminal,
sent him out as prefect of Dàozhōu.
Over 270 Imperial College students including Lǔ Jiāo and Jì Cháng went to the palace gates to plead for his retention,
but after several days, officials blocked and stopped them,
so their memorial could not be presented.
(Old Book of Tang)
Liǔ Zōngyuán, hearing of this,
wrote to Hé Fān and others saying:
"In the past, when Lǐ Yīng and Jī Kāng were Imperial College students,
they merely looked up to the palace gates to present their pleas.
I had thought such things could not be seen again for thousands of years,
yet now they appear in our day.
Critics say that Lord Yáng went too far in accepting the corrupt,
and failed in the way of a teacher.
But even among Confucius' followers were the reckless and uncompromising,
and Nánguō received criticism;
Zēng Shēn had seventy-two disciples,
yet encountered trouble with Fù Chú;
Mèng Kē lodged in Qí,
and among his followers was one who stole sandals.
If even those sages and worthies could not avoid such things,
what can be done?
To reject people—
at the doors of Yú and Biǎn,
the sick are not turned away;
by the side of the marking line,
warped timber is not rejected;
in the seat of the teacher and Confucian scholar,
the unorthodox scholar is not refused."
(New Book of Tang)
For mourning attire
Zhèng Chù studied under Yáng Chéng,
but after more than a month of discussing the Guófēng section of the Classic of Poetry,
Chù could not engage in a single exchange of arguments.
Consequently, he hanged himself from a beam.
Chéng wept and said:
"Though I did not kill him,
Chù died because of me."
He observed the sīmá mourning ritual for him.
From the Nánbù Xīnshū.
Rectify oneself
Nánguō Huìzǐ asked Zǐgòng, saying:
"Why is the gate of your master so mixed?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"The gentleman rectifies himself and waits,
those who wish to come are not kept at a distance,
those who wish to leave are not detained,
moreover, at the gate of a good physician there are many sick people,
by the side of the straightening tool there are many crooked pieces of wood,
therefore it is mixed."
"Xúnzǐ - Fǎ Xíng"
Taking Leave of the Master
Xú Kuàng, styled Wényàn,
was well-read in the Five Classics,
and particularly proficient in the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals.
At that time, the great Confucian scholar Shěn Zhòng was lecturing at the Imperial Academy,
with an audience often exceeding a thousand people.
Wényuǎn went to question him,
but left after just a few days.
Someone asked:
"Why did you leave so quickly?"
He replied:
"Observing what he says,
it's all from books,
which I have already memorized beforehand.
As for the profound and subtle realms,
he seems not to have reached them."
Someone reported his words to Zhòng,
who summoned him for over ten rounds of discussion,
and Zhòng greatly admired and was convinced by him.
Wéndá was upright, honest, and sincere,
embodying the demeanor of a Confucian scholar.
Dòu Wēi, Yáng Xuángǎn, and Lǐ Mì all studied under him.
During the Kāihuáng era, he was promoted to Erudite of the Imperial Academy,
and later, Prince Yuè Dòng appointed him as Chancellor of the National Academy.
At that time, Luòyáng was suffering from famine,
and Wényuǎn went outside the city to gather firewood,
where he was captured by Lǐ Mì's army.
Mì had Wényuǎn sit facing south,
prepared the etiquette of a disciple,
and faced north to receive his teachings.
Wényuǎn said:
"I was fortunate in the past to have imparted the way of the ancient kings to you, General.
Now that you, General, wield authority over all things,
and your might extends across the four seas,
you still humble yourself to uphold the principle of honoring the teacher.
This is a virtue of you, General,
and my good fortune.
Since I have received such great respect,
how could I not speak my mind?
But I am unsure of your intentions, General.
If you aim to be like Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng, restoring what is broken and supporting what is falling,
even in my old age, I would gladly exert my efforts.
But if you act like Wáng Mǎng and Dǒng Zhuó, taking advantage of crises and dangers,
then I am too aged,
and incapable of assisting."
Mì kowtowed and said:
"I respectfully heed your command."
Soon, Wáng Shìchōng seized autocratic power,
and Mì again sought advice from Wényuǎn,
who replied:
"Wáng Shìchōng is also a former student,
and I know him quite well.
This man is cruel and ruthless,
and his intentions are narrow and shortsighted.
Since he has seized this opportunity,
he surely has treacherous plans.
Your previous strategy, General, is no longer feasible;
you must defeat Wáng Shìchōng before you can pay homage to the court."
Mì said:
"I once thought you, sir, were a Confucian scholar,
unlearned in military affairs,
but now in planning grand strategies,
you show remarkable insight and strategy."
When Mì was defeated,
Wényuǎn returned to the Eastern Capital,
where Wáng Shìchōng provided him with provisions,
yet Wényuǎn showed him utmost respect,
bowing first whenever they met.
Someone asked:
"I heard you sat upright when meeting Lǐ Mì but show respect to Lord Wáng.
Why is that?"
He replied:
"Lǐ Mì is a noble man,
who can accept the bows of men like Lì Shēng;
Wáng Shìchōng is a petty man,
capable of killing those who follow ancient principles.
One must act according to the circumstances,
is that not right!"
(From the Old Book of Táng)

The old translation says "disciple" while the new one says "the taught,"
Nánshān stated:

Héfāng
Yuán Shào, styled Běnchū,
his great-grandfather Ān,
served as the Minister of Works under the Hàn dynasty.
From Ān onwards,
for four generations they held positions among the Three Excellencies,
thus their influence encompassed the realm.
"Wèi Zhì" records that Ān served as Minister of Works during the reign of Emperor Zhāng,
and begot Jīng, the Governor of Shǔ Commandery.
Jīng's younger brother Chǎng was Minister of Works.
Jīng's son Yáng was Grand Minister over the Masses.
Yáng's son Féng,
and Féng's younger brother Wěi both became dukes.
"Huá Jiāo Shū" states that Féng's illegitimate son Shào,
was adopted by his uncle Chéng.
"Yuán Shān Sōng Shū" mentions that Féng had a son named Shù.
"Hòu Shū" recounts that Táo Qiān recommended Xiānzhǔ as Governor of Yù Province.
Xiānzhǔ said:
"Yuán Gōnglù spans four generations, five dukes,
he is revered within the realm,
and the province may be conferred upon him."
Kǒng Róng said to Xiānzhǔ:
"He is but dried bones in a tomb,
what is there to consider!?"
Sīmǎ Biāo's book states: Ān was relocated early in Emperor Huán's reign,
and the Grand Minister had three sons,
Féng, Chéng, Wěi.
Féng, styled Zhōu,
served as Minister of Works during Emperor Líng's time.
Wěi, styled Cì,
initially served as Minister of Works under Emperor Xiàn.
This seems to be an error.
Confucius said to Duke Āi:
"There are scholars who share the same aspirations and direction,
pursue the Way with the same methods,
delight in standing together,
do not weary of deferring to one another,
when long parted and hearing rumors, they do not believe them,
they advance when in agreement on what is right,
and withdraw when in disagreement,
such is the way they form friendships."

From the "Kǒng Cóng Zǐ"
Zuǒ Rú and his friend Dù Bó both served King Xuān of Zhōu.
King Xuān intended to execute Dù Bó,
though Dù Bó was not guilty of any crime.
Zuǒ Rú pleaded with the king on his behalf,
repeating his entreaties nine times, but the king would not grant his request.
The king said,
"To side with your lord and differ from your friend—
this is what you should do."
Zuǒ Rú replied,
"Your servant has heard that if the way of the lord is followed and the friend opposed, one should comply;
the lord may execute the friend.
If the way of the friend is followed and the lord opposed, one should lead;
the friend may defy the lord."
The king angrily said,
"Change your words and you shall live;
do not change your words and you shall die."
Zuǒ Rú replied,
"Your servant has heard that the noble men of antiquity did not pervert righteousness to follow others to death,
nor did they change their words to seek life.
Therefore, your servant can make clear the king's fault and die for it.
Dù Bó was innocent;
the king executed Dù Bó,
and Zuǒ Rú died for him."
《Shuō Yuàn》
Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shūyá
Guǎn Yíwú and Bào Shūyá were two men who maintained a deeply intimate friendship.
Guǎn Zhòng once sighed and said:
"When I was young and impoverished,
I once engaged in trade with Bào Shū and divided the profits,
taking more for myself.
Bào Shū did not consider me greedy,
for he knew I was poor.
I once planned affairs for Bào Shū that ended in great hardship,
yet Bào Shū did not consider me foolish,
for he knew that circumstances are sometimes favorable and sometimes not.
I served three times in office and was three times dismissed by the ruler,
yet Bào Shū did not consider me incompetent,
for he knew I had not encountered the right time.
I fought three battles and fled three times,
yet Bào Shū did not consider me cowardly,
for he knew I had an elderly mother.
When Prince Jiǔ was defeated, Zhào Hū died for him,
while I endured the disgrace of imprisonment,
yet Bào Shū did not consider me shameless,
for he knew I felt no shame over minor principles but was ashamed that my reputation had not become known throughout the world.
Those who gave me life are my parents,
but the one who truly knows me is Master Bào."
This is why the world praises Guǎn and Bào as exemplary friends.
From "Liè Lì Mìng":
Long ago, when Bào Shū fell ill,
Guǎn Zhòng refrained from eating and drinking on his account.
Nìng Qì expressed concern about this,
to which Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Those who gave me life are my parents,
but the one who truly knows me is Bào Shū.
A scholar dies for one who knows his worth,
just as a horse becomes excellent for one who understands it.
If Master Bào dies, no one in the world will know me.
What need have I for food and drink?
Even if I were to die for him,
what harm would there be in that?"
From "Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn":
When Bào Shū died,
Guǎn Zhòng lifted the hem of his upper garment and wept for him,
tears falling like rain.
His attendants asked:
"He was not your father or son.
Is there an explanation for this?"
Guǎnzǐ replied:
"This is not something you gentlemen would understand.
I once traveled with Master Bào as peddlers in Nányáng,
where I suffered three humiliations in the marketplace.
Master Bào did not consider me cowardly,
for he knew I desired to achieve something significant.
Master Bào once joined me in advising a ruler three times, but our counsel was not heeded.
Master Bào did not consider me incompetent,
for he knew I had not encountered an enlightened ruler.
Master Bào once shared wealth and divided goods with me,
and three times I took the larger portion for myself.
Master Bào did not consider me greedy,
for he knew I lacked sufficient resources.
Those who gave me life are my parents,
but the one who truly knows me is Master Bào.
A scholar dies for one who knows his worth,
so how could I not mourn for him?"
From "Shuō Yuàn"
Observing Friends
In Jīng there was a man skilled in physiognomy,
whose predictions never failed,
and his fame spread throughout the state.
King Zhuāng summoned and questioned him,
to which he replied:
"I am not able to judge men's fortunes,
but I can observe their friends.
Observing a common man,
if his friends are all filial, brotherly, pure, and cautious,
fearing the law in this manner,
his family will surely prosper daily,
and his person will surely become more honored daily—
this is what is called an auspicious man.
Observing one who serves his ruler,
if his friends are all sincere, trustworthy, and virtuous,
loving goodness in this manner,
his service to the ruler will improve daily,
and his official rank will advance daily—
this is what is called an auspicious minister.
Observing a sovereign,
if his court ministers are mostly worthy,
his attendants mostly loyal,
and when the ruler errs, they all contend and remonstrate together,
in such a case the state will become more secure daily,
the ruler more respected daily,
and the world more submissive daily—
this is what is called an auspicious ruler.
I am not able to judge men's fortunes,
but I can observe their friends."
King Zhuāng approved of this,
and thereupon urgently gathered scholars,
working day and night without respite,
until he finally became hegemon over the world.

Meeting as if the carriage canopies were tilted together
When Confucius went to Tán,
he encountered Master Chéng on the road.
They drew their carriage canopies together and conversed,
finding great mutual affinity throughout the day.
Confucius turned to Zǐlù and said:
"Fetch a bundle of silk to present to the gentleman."
Zǐlù responded disdainfully:
"I have heard it said,
when scholars meet without proper introduction,
or a maiden weds without matchmaker,
a gentleman does not engage in such irregular courtesies."
After a while he again turned to tell Zǐlù,
but Zǐlù repeated his initial response.
Confucius said:
"Yóu, does the Book of Songs not say:
'There is a beautiful person,
with clear eyes and lovely brows,
whom I encounter by chance,
exactly matching my desire'?
Now Master Chéng is a worthy scholar of the world,
if we do not present gifts now, we may never meet again.
Young man, carry this out."

Water and Sweet Wine
Kǒngzǐ asked Zǐ Sānghū, saying:
"My close relationships have become increasingly distant,
my disciples and friends increasingly scattered.
Why is this?"
Zǐ Sānghū replied:
"Lín Huí said: The friendship of gentlemen is as insipid as water,
while the friendship of petty men is as sweet as rich wine.
Gentlemen remain close through insipidity,
petty men remain attached through sweetness.
Those who come together without cause,
will separate without cause."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I respectfully heed your instruction."
He walked slowly,
strolling leisurely on his return,
abandoned learning and discarded books,
with no disciples bowing before him,
yet their affection grew even stronger.

leaving to socialize
Zǐlù asked Confucius, saying:
"There are people who support their parents yet are not called filial;
why is this?"
Confucius said:
"Let me tell you,
although one might have the strength of a champion wrestler, one cannot lift oneself up;
this is not due to lack of strength,
but because it is impossible by the very nature of things.
If one fails to cultivate personal conduct,
it is the fault of oneself;
if one's conduct is cultivated but one's reputation is not prominent,
it is the fault of one's friends;
if one's conduct is cultivated, one's reputation will naturally be established.
Therefore, the noble person at home cultivates sincere conduct,
and abroad associates with the worthy.
How can one be said to lack a reputation for filial piety?"

Sì Yǒu
King Wén of Zhōu had those who drew close, those who flocked to him, those who preceded and followed, and those who repelled insults—
these were called the four neighbors, through whom he avoided the calamity at Yǒulǐ.
Yìzǐ asked:
"Does the Master also have four neighbors?"
Confucius said:
"I have four friends.
Since I obtained Huí,
my disciples have become more intimate—
is this not drawing close?
Since I obtained Cì,
scholars from distant regions arrive daily—
is this not flocking to me?
Since I obtained Shī,
there is light ahead,
and splendor behind—
is this not preceding and following?
Since I obtained Yóu,
evil words do not reach my gate—
is this not repelling insults?"

increasing day by day
Confucius said:
"After my death, Shāng will daily progress,
while Cì will daily regress."
Zēngzǐ asked:
"What does this mean?"
The Master replied:
"Shāng enjoys associating with those more virtuous than himself,
while Cì enjoys speaking with those inferior to himself.
If you don't know the son,
look at his father; if you don't know the man,
look at his friends; if you don't know the ruler,
look at his envoys; if you don't know the land,
look at its vegetation.
Therefore it is said:
Dwelling with good people
is like entering a room full of orchids:
after a long time, you no longer notice their fragrance,
for you have become one with it.
Dwelling with bad people is like entering a fish market:
after a long time, you no longer notice the stench,
for you have become one with it too.
What is stored in cinnabar becomes red;
what is stored in lacquer becomes black.
Thus the gentleman must be cautious about those with whom he associates."

Living in seclusion
When Zǐxià was in mourning,
having lost his son and thereby his eyesight,
Zēngzǐ went to condole with him, saying:
"I have heard it said that
when a friend loses his eyesight, one should weep for him."
Zēngzǐ wept,
and Zǐxià also wept, saying:
"Heaven!
I am without fault!"
Zēngzǐ angrily replied:
"Shāng, how can you say you are without fault?
You and I served our Master between the Zhū and Sì rivers,
then you retired and grew old on the banks of the Western River,
causing the people of the Western River to compare you to our Master
—this is your first fault;
when you lost your parents,
you gave the people nothing noteworthy to hear of
—this is your second fault;
when you lost your son,
you lost your eyesight
—this is your third fault.
And yet you say, 'How am I at fault?'"
Then Zǐxià threw down his staff, bowed, and said:
"I was wrong,
I was wrong!
I have left the group and lived in seclusion,
and it has indeed been too long."

A Friend Until Death
Yáng Jiǎo'āi and Zuǒ Bótáo were sworn friends willing to die for each other.
They wished to seek official positions in the State of Chǔ,
but the journey was hindered by remote mountains,
where they encountered rain and snow, halting their progress.
With no means to counter hunger and cold,
they realized they could not both survive.
Bótáo said to Jiǎo'āi:
"Heaven does not favor us,
and we are stranded in the deep mountains in dire poverty.
If resources are combined for one person, he may survive to become an official.
If both die,
our bones will remain uncollected.
Searching my conscience, I know I am not as capable as you.
My survival would likely be of little use,
while wasting your talents.
I am content to remain within this tree."
Jiǎo'āi heeded his words,
and Bótáo entered the tree and died.
Jiǎo'āi, obtaining his clothing and provisions, proceeded to Chǔ.
King Píng of Chǔ admired Jiǎo'āi's virtue
and praised Bótáo's righteousness,
burying them with the rites of high nobility.
Jiǎo'āi dreamed of Bótáo saying:
"Thanks to your kindness, I received a grand burial,
but I am troubled by the proximity of General Jīng's tomb,
who seeks to enslave me.
I cannot obey him.
We have fought repeatedly without victory,
and on the fifteenth of this month, a great battle will occur.
With your help, I can win;
otherwise, I will be defeated."
On the appointed day, Jiǎo'āi arrayed troops and horses at the tomb,
erected three wooden figures,
and committed suicide to join Bótáo.
The nobleman said: "Upholding righteousness can set an example for the world."

former connections severed, later ties cut off
In the state of Wú there was a gentleman who said:
"Zhāng Xūbǐ and Tán Fūwú were first friends but later severed ties."
When Zhāng Xūbǐ was imprisoned and about to die for a crime,
Tán Fūwú gathered followers and rescued him.
Only after they reached the road did he realize it was Tán Fūwú,
so he stopped walking and declined, saying:
"Our principles differ from yours,
which is why we were first friends but later severed ties.
I have heard that a gentleman does not change his conduct because of danger,
yet now if I follow you,
this would mean acting recklessly in safety,
but changing my conduct in danger.
Rather than living because of you,
I would prefer to return to imprisonment and die."
Hé Lǘ heard of this,
and ordered officials to release him,
but Zhāng Xūbǐ said:
"My principles differ from Tán Fūwú's,
so I cannot accept his rescue.
Now if the officials release me because of this,
it would mean I was spared due to Tán Fūwú's intervention,
how could I accept that?"
He then dashed against a wall and died.
When Tán Fūwú heard of it, he said:
"I rescued him but he didn't accept my help - this shows I'm not clever;
I acted without understanding - this was foolish.
Lack of cleverness makes one unfit to interact with gentlemen;
foolishness makes one unfit to serve a ruler.
My actions were empty;
people would despise me for living through my efforts,
and I would be ashamed to stand in the world because of this."
He then cut his throat and died.
The gentleman comments:
"Tán Fūwú failed in his treatment of a gentleman,
and Zhāng Xūbǐ cannot be considered successful either.
They may be called resolute and brave,
but cannot be said to have attained proper integrity."
