if you succeed, you will be worthy to divide the lands of rulers."
Sū Qín descended and persuaded Guǐgǔ Xiānshēng,
causing tears to soak his lapel.
Zhāng Yí was not as skilled as Sū Qín,
who became chancellor of Zhào and concurrently chancellor of the six states.
Zhāng Yí was poor and lowly,
so he went to seek refuge with Sū Qín,
who seated him in the lower hall,
fed him with servants' food,
and repeatedly provoked and angered him,
intending to make him become chancellor of Qín.
Enraged, Yí then went west to enter Qín,
while Sū Qín had people generously provide for him along the way.
When Yí realized this, he said:
"This was within his strategy,
which I did not perceive;
this is where I fall short of Lord Sū."
From "Lùn Héng: Dá Nìng"
Raising hands in salute
Zǐgāo traveled to Zhào and stayed with Píngyuán Jūn,
among the guests there was one named Zōu Wénjié,
who was on friendly terms with Zǐgāo.
When Zǐgāo was about to return to Lǔ,
after bidding farewell to his old friends,
Wénjié accompanied him for three nights.
At parting, Wénjié shed tears streaming down his cheeks,
but Zǐgāo merely raised his hands in salute.
They parted and went their separate ways.
His disciple asked:
"You, sir, were on good terms with those two gentlemen.
They had feelings of attachment,
uncertain when they might meet again,
and wept in sorrow.
Yet you, sir, raised your voice and saluted loftily,
is this not contrary to the principle of cherishing kinship?"
Zǐgāo replied:
"At first I thought these two were true men,
but now I know they are like women.
In life, one should have aspirations for all directions;
how can we be like deer and pigs,
always gathering together?"
His disciple said:
"Then were these two wrong to weep?"
He answered:
"These two
are good men,
with compassionate hearts,
but they surely lack decisiveness."
His disciple asked:
"Is weeping then entirely without merit?"
Zǐgāo said:
"There are two kinds:
the greatly treacherous weep to gain trust,
while women and cowardly men weep to show affection."
《Kǒngcóngzǐ》
Zhāng Chén
Zhāng Ěr was a man of Dàliáng,
Chén Yú was also a man of Dàliáng.
Yú was fond of Confucian teachings,
and in his youth served Ěr as a father,
forming with him a friendship of sworn loyalty.
Later, due to the affair of Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Shì, discord arose between them.
Ěr subsequently joined Hán Xìn in defeating Zhào,
and at Jǐngxíng, beheaded Yú on the banks of the Chí River.
Records of the Han Dynasty
When Ěr and Yú first lived in humble circumstances,
they were willing to die for each other,
how could they have hesitated?
But when they came to hold power and contend for authority,
they ultimately destroyed one another.
How sincere was their former admiration and mutual trust,
yet how violent their later betrayal!
Friendships based on power and profit
were scorned by the ancients;
this indeed refers to such cases.
Commentary
Coarse grain and cloth quilts
Gōngsūn Hóng rose from humble origins to become chancellor,
and his old acquaintance Gāo Hè followed him.
Hóng served him unpolished millet for meals
and covered him with a cloth quilt.
Hè complained, saying:
"Why use an old friend's wealth to provide unpolished millet
and cloth quilts? I have my own."
Hóng was greatly ashamed. Hè told others:
"Gōngsūn Hóng wears sable and cicada insignia underneath,
but coarse hemp clothing outside;
he has five tripods of food in his inner kitchen,
yet serves a single dish for outer meals.
How can this be shown to the world?"
Thereupon the court suspected him of affectation.
Hóng sighed and said:
"I would rather meet a wicked guest
than encounter an old acquaintance."
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Dusting off the dust
I have heard that rank and emolument are not valued for their own sake but for the rites they entail,
and that companionship among kindred spirits is not bound by distance or proximity.
Thus, though Master Dōngmén dwelt in a humble thatched hut,
Lord Wèi honored him with a retinue of a hundred horsemen in a single day.
Though Lǚ Wàng never shared a mat with King Wén,
he was once offered the rule of the entire realm.
Why must great men, in their mutual understanding, wait to play with dust in childhood
or grow up together with hair hanging down,
counting the days of reclining and bowing to each other?
"A Letter from Dōngfāng Shuò to Gōngsūn Hóng"
Wáng Gòng
Wáng Jí, styled Zǐyáng,
was friends with Gòng Yǔ from a young age.
When Yáng became the Inspector of Yìzhōu,
Gòng Yǔ heard of it,
dusted off his hat in anticipation,
and Yáng subsequently recommended and praised Yǔ.
The world said, "When Wáng Yáng is in office,
Gòng Yǔ dusts off his hat,"
meaning their choices and rejections were the same.
From the "Book of Hàn," seen in the "Imperial Readings," differs from the current edition.
Xiāo Hé and Zhāng Liáng
Xiāo Yù
was the son of Xiāo Wàng,
and in his youth, he was friends with Chén Xián and Zhū Bó,
becoming renowned in their time.
In the past, there were Wáng Yáng and Gòng Yǔ,
hence the saying in Cháng'ān:
"Xiāo and Zhū present the seals,
Wáng and Gòng dust their hats,"
meaning they recommended each other for advancement.
Initially, Yù and Chén Xián were both famous as high officials and scholars,
but later Yù and Bó had a falling out,
and their friendship did not last,
so the world considered true friendship difficult.
The emperor...
Cáo Yì
Chén Zūn, styled Mènggōng,
was orphaned at a young age,
and together with Zhāng Sǒng, styled Bósōng, served as clerks in the capital's administration.
Sǒng was erudite and perceptive,
maintaining integrity and frugality,
while Zūn was unrestrained and unconventional.
Although their conduct differed,
they remained close friends.
The emperor
Hastening Home for a Funeral
Wáng Dān had a fellow student who lost a parent,
whose home was in Zhōngshān.
He informed Dān of his intention to go and offer condolences,
and was preparing to travel with companions.
Dān became angry and beat him,
ordering him to send silk instead for sacrificial offerings.
When asked the reason,
Dān said:
"The difficulties of friendship
are not easily spoken of.
The world praises Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shūyá,
then next Wáng Jí and Gòng Yǔ.
Zhǎng Ěr and Chén Yú ended in tragedy,
Xiāo Wàngzhī and Zhū Yún parted in discord.
Thus I know those who preserve it whole are few."
People of the time admired his words.
Hòu Hàn Shū
By imperial decree, I submit
Emperor Sùzōng began to restore ancient rites,
and during his inspection tour of the sacred mountains,
Cuī Yīn presented his "Ode to the Western Tour."
The emperor admired it,
and said to his attendant-in-ordinary Dòu Xiàn:
"Do you know Cuī Yīn?"
He replied:
"Bān Gù has mentioned him to me several times,
but I have not yet met him."
The emperor said:
"Your fondness for Bān Gù while neglecting Cuī Yīn
is like Lord Yè's love for dragons.
You may try to meet Yīn."
Yīn waited for an audience,
met Xiàn,
who rushed out to greet him with a smile,
and said:
"I have received an imperial decree to befriend you;
how can you slight me?"
Thereupon, he bowed and invited him in.
The emperor
Qìng Lián
Lián Fàn, styled Shūdù,
was a native of Dùlíng in Jīngzhào.
He served up to the position of Governor of Shǔ Commandery.
Throughout his life, he had high aspirations,
with a bold and fiery spirit,
and was fond of relieving others' emergencies.
The world admired his devotion to righteousness.
He formed a life-and-death friendship with Qìng Hóng of Luòyáng,
who was also generous and principled.
Qìng Hóng rose to be Governor of both Lángyá and Kuàijī Commanderies,
leaving remarkable achievements wherever he served.
People of the time praised them, saying:
"In the past, there were Guǎn and Bào;
now, there are Qìng and Lián."
Chén Léi
Yíchūn Chén Zhòng in his youth befriended Póyáng Léi Yì.
Grand Administrator Zhāng Yún recommended Zhòng for the Filial and Incorrupt selection,
but Zhòng yielded the position to Yì,
submitting over ten memorials in succession.
Grand Administrator Yún did not heed his pleas.
Later, when Yì was selected as an Outstanding Talent,
he yielded the position to Chén Zhòng.
The Inspector did not accept this,
so Yì feigned madness, loosened his hair,
and fled to avoid the appointment.
The local people thus said of them:
"Even glue and lacquer, which deem themselves strong, cannot compare to Léi
and Chén." The Three Excellencies' offices simultaneously recruited both men.
From "The Biography of Chén and Léi"
Táotáo
Yǐn Mǐn and Bān Biāo were close friends,
whenever they conversed together,
they often fasted until late dusk,
from daybreak until deep night through to dawn,
Biāo said:
"Engaging in long conversations,
is considered strange by ordinary people,
yet after Zhòng Zǐqī died, Bó Yá broke his qín,
why not delight in joyful harmony!"
Records of the Eastern Pavilion
Yǐn and Bān delighted in harmony throughout the long night.
Discourse on the Termination of Friendships
Slowly and gently
Fàn Shì, styled Jùqīng,
was a native of Jīnxiāng in Shānyáng.
In his youth, he studied at the Imperial Academy,
where he became friends with Zhāng Shào of Rǔnán.
Shào, styled Yuánbó,
both men informed their hometowns of their departure.
Shì said to Yuánbó:
"In two years, I shall return,
and will visit to pay respects to your esteemed parents and see your children."
They then set a date together.
When the day arrived, Shì indeed came,
ascended the hall to bow to Yuánbó's mother,
drank joyfully together before parting.
Later, Yuánbó fell gravely ill,
with fellow townsmen Zhì Jūnzhāng and Shāng Zǐzhēng tending to him day and night.
They said:
"Yuánbó said on his deathbed, 'My regret is not seeing my sworn friend before death.'"
Soon he passed away.
Shì dreamed of Yuánbó wearing a black crown with dangling tassels, calling:
"I have died,
and will be buried on such-and-such day.
Can you make it in time?"
Shì awoke grieving, sighing with tears streaming down.
He rushed to attend the funeral,
dressed in mourning attire for a friend,
and on the burial day,
hurried there.
Before arriving, the funeral procession had already set out.
When the coffin was lowered into the grave, it refused to move forward.
His mother patted it, saying:
"Could Yuánbó be waiting for someone?"
The coffin halted for some time.
Then a plain carriage and white horse approached, weeping heard.
The mother said:
"It must be Jùqīng."
Upon arrival,
he knocked on the coffin, saying:
"Farewell, Yuánbó.
Life and death are different paths,
we part forever here."
A thousand mourners gathered,
all wiping tears.
Shì then took the funeral cords and pulled the coffin,
whereupon it moved forward.
He stayed by the graveside,
tending the tomb and planting trees before leaving.
History of the Later Han
"Fàn and Zhāng's sincere friendship beneath the springs."
On Severing Friendships
Breaking off relations
Zhū Mù, styled Gōngshū,
wrote a letter severing ties with Liú Bózōng, stating:
"In the past, when I served as the magistrate of Fēng,
were you not in mourning for your mother?
Yet you personally removed your mourning garments
and came to the Fēng office.
When I became the Attendant Secretary Censor,
you personally came to the government bureau.
Now you hold the position of a two-thousand-bushel official,
while I am beneath as a court gentleman.
Instead, you now rely on an accounting clerk to arrange an audience with me.
Are you nothing more than an assistant or commandant?
Am I merely one of your subordinates?
Do you think I seek honor and favor through such an audience?"
Alas!
How shallow Liú Bózōng is in the ways of benevolence and righteousness!
From the History of the Later Hàn.
Breach of contract
Liáng Hóng initially made a pact with his friend Xiāo of the capital,
vowing not to serve as a subordinate minister.
When his friend became a commandery official,
Liáng Hóng then wrote a letter reproaching him before departing.
Records of the Eastern Pavilion
Bān Cǎo
Zhāng Shēng, styled Yǎnzhēn,
had great ambitions.
He lamented:
"Human life in this world
is as fleeting as a white steed passing a crack;
how can one bend principles to flatter worldly customs?"
While serving as magistrate of Wàihuáng, he encountered the Partisan Prohibitions and was removed from office.
Meeting a friend on the road, they sat on grass and spoke:
"Now eunuchs hold exclusive power at court."
Thereupon they faced each other and wept. An old man passing by said:
"Alas,
why do you two gentlemen weep so sorrowfully?
If the dragon does not conceal its scales,
nor the phoenix hide its wings,
once caught in the net of the age,
what will weeping avail?"
The two wished to speak with him,
but he paid no heed and withdrew.
Shēng ultimately was imprisoned due to the Partisan Prohibitions and died.
Hòu Hàn Shū
Discard the short and adopt the long
Lǐ Xiè, styled Dé Gōng,
in his associations always overlooked shortcomings and valued strengths,
delighting in helping others achieve their merits.
At that time, although Xún Shuǎng and Jiǎ Biāo of Yǐngchuān were both renowned, they could not get along with each other.
Xiè befriended both men,
maintaining impartial affection without favoritism,
and was praised by his contemporaries for his uprightness.
Chǔ Jiù
Wú Yòu herded pigs in the Chángyuán marshes,
reciting classics as he walked.
Gōngshā Mù from Běihǎi, while studying at the Imperial Academy, faced financial difficulties,
so he changed his clothes to become a laborer
and worked with Wú Yòu pounding grain.
Wú Yòu spoke with him,
was greatly astonished,
and thus they formed a friendship amid the mortar and pestle.
"Records of the Eastern Pavilion"
Yì Dài
Xún Jùbó traveled afar to visit his sick friend,
when it happened that the Hu invaders attacked the commandery.
His friend said to Jùbó,
"I am as good as dead now.
You should leave."
Jùbó replied,
"I came all this way to see you,
and yet you tell me to leave—
to abandon righteousness in order to survive—
is this something Xún Jùbó would do?"
When the invaders arrived,
they said to Jùbó,
"The main army has come,
and the entire commandery has emptied out.
What kind of man are you that you dare to remain here alone?"
Jùbó answered,
"My friend is ill,
and I cannot bear to abandon him.
I would rather give my own life in place of my friend's."
The invaders said to one another,
"We are unrighteous men, yet we have entered a righteous state."
Thereupon they withdrew their troops and turned back,
and the entire commandery was preserved.
From A New Account of Tales of the World.
Guǎn Níng and Huà Xīn
Huà Xīn, Běihǎi Bǐng Yuán, and Guǎn Níng all pursued studies together,
the three were close friends,
contemporaries dubbed the trio "One Dragon,"
with Huà Xīn as the dragon's head,
Bǐng Yuán as the dragon's belly,
and Guǎn Níng as the dragon's tail.
From "Wèi Lüè":
Guǎn Níng and Huà Xīn once shared a mat while studying,
when a carriage with official insignia passed by the gate,
Níng continued reading as before,
but Xīn set aside his book and went out to look.
Níng then cut the mat to separate their seating,
saying:
"You are not my friend."
From "Shì Shuō"
Extraordinary
Sūn Chǔ's "Qiān Zhāo Stele Inscription" says:
"Initially, you and Liú Bèi grew up together north of the Yellow River,
heroes sharing the same spirit,
forming a friendship of life and death,
with ambitions to stem the surging waves and block the current,
spreading wings to soar across the skies.
Soon after, you pledged allegiance to Tàizǔ Bèi,
thus establishing a tripartite balance with Shǔ Hàn,
your associations were extraordinary,
arousing the envy of the times,
each day you drank alone,
paying respects between Jì and Mèng."
End
Fù Píng
Zhāng Liǎo had a rift with his protector Wǔ Zhōu.
Liǎo went to see Wēn Huī to request Hú Zhì,
but Zhì declined on grounds of illness.
Liǎo came out and said to Zhì:
"I placed my trust in you,
why do you betray me so?"
Zhì replied:
"In the friendships of the ancients,
taking much was known not to be greed,
fleeing in defeat was known not to be cowardice,
hearing rumors they did not believe them,
thus they could endure.
Wǔ Bónán is himself an elegant scholar,
in the past you praised him,
never ceasing to speak of him,
now because of a petty grievance,
a rift has formed between you.
How much more so with someone of my meager talents,
could such friendship possibly endure?
Therefore I am unwilling."
Liǎo was moved by his words,
and made peace with Zhōu again.
Records of Wei
Separated
Zhāng Yì, styled Jūnsì,
was a native of Chéngdū in Shǔ Commandery.
In his youth, he befriended Yáng Gōng of Qiánwéi,
who died early.
Yáng Gōng's orphaned child was only a few years old,
so Zhāng Yì took him into his own household,
serving Yáng Gōng's mother as if she were his own,
and when the child grew up, arranged his marriage, purchased a residence, and established his livelihood,
enabling him to found his own family.
(Records of Shu)
Stone friendship
Zhūgě Liàng wrote to Zhāng Yì saying:
"I consider myself and you to have the friendship of ancient stone,
the way of stone friendship
is to recommend even enemies for mutual benefit,
and to cut one's own flesh to demonstrate loyalty,
without expecting thanks."
Above
Jīnlán
Zhāng Wēn, styled Huìshù,
possessed outstanding talent and imposing stature.
He was thus summoned for an audience with all due ceremony,
and his speech was elegant and refined.
The Emperor, deeply impressed, drew closer on his mat,
appointed him as a Gentleman of the Palace,
and sent him as an envoy to Shǔ, where he formed a bond of deep friendship with Zhūgě Liàng.
"Records of Wú"
Qiáo Zhá
When Zhōu Yú was stationed at Jūcháo,
he passed by Lǔ Sù to request supplies and grain.
Sù pointed to a granary of rice and gave it to Zhōu Yú,
who then further realized his extraordinary character.
Thereupon they formed a close bond, establishing a friendship like that of Jì Zhá and Gōngsūn Qiáo.
"Basic Biography"
The Jìnyáng Qiū states:
Lù Kàng and Yáng Hù
also upheld the friendship of Qiáo and Zhá.
Awaiting food from a thousand miles away
Zhuó Shù, styled Gōngháng,
was a native of Shàngyú.
When making appointments with others,
even if encountering violent storms and torrential rains,
there was never a time he failed to arrive.
He once took leave of Grand Tutor Zhūgě Kè in Jiànyè,
who asked when he would return.
Shù replied:
"On such-and-such date I shall personally pay my respects again."
When that day arrived,
Kè paused his meal waiting for Shù's arrival.
At that time, all the assembled guests thought that with Kuàijī and Jiànyè being over a thousand lǐ apart,
separated by rivers and lakes,
how could he possibly arrive as scheduled?
Moments later, Shù arrived,
astonishing everyone present.
From Yú Yù's "Kuàijī Diǎn Lù"
Sharing a Pillow
Wǔ Pānzhāng had handsome features and elegant demeanor from a young age,
and people of the time vied to admire him.
King Wáng Zhòngxiān of the State of Chǔ heard of his renowned beauty,
so he came seeking friendship,
and wished to study together.
At their first meeting, they fell in love,
their affection resembling that of husband and wife.
They then shared the same quilt and pillow in intimacy,
until they eventually died together, and their families mourned them.
They were thus buried in a tomb on Luófú Mountain,
where suddenly a tree grew.
Its branches, twigs, and leaves
all embraced each other without exception.
People of the time found it extraordinary,
and named it the "Shared Pillow Tree."
(From "Extensive Records")
Thousand-mile journey by carriage
Jī Kāng had always been friends with Xún Yù,
and whenever he missed him, he would drive a thousand li to visit.
Once, when Xún Yù came and found Jī Kāng not at home,
his elder brother Jī Xī came out to greet him.
Xún Yù did not enter,
but instead wrote the character "鳳" (phoenix) on the door before leaving.
Jī Xī did not understand Jī Kāng's intentions,
and even said, "鳳 is just an ordinary bird."
"Yǔ Lín"
Bamboo Grove
Ruǎn Jí from Chénliú, Jī Kāng from Qiáoguó, and Shān Tāo from Hénèi,
these three were all of similar age.
Jī Kāng was slightly younger,
and those who joined this fellowship were
Liú Líng from Pèiguó, Ruǎn Xián from Chénliú, Xiàng Xiù from Hénèi, and Wáng Róng from Lángyá—seven men in total.
They often gathered beneath a bamboo grove,
indulging freely in hearty drinking,
hence the world called them the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove.
In the Shì Shuō,
Wáng Róng served as Minister of Works,
dressed in official robes,
riding in a light carriage,
and passed by the tavern of Old Man Huáng.
He alighted and, looking back, said to the guest in the following carriage:
"In the past, I drank heartily here at this tavern with Jī Kāng and Ruǎn Jí.
The excursions in the bamboo grove
I also took part in, though at the end.
Since Jī Kāng met an untimely death
and Master Ruǎn passed away,
I have been bound by the constraints of the times.
Looking at this place today,
though it is near, it feels as distant as mountains and rivers."
Forgetting words
Shān Tāo had a natural affinity for Zhuangzi and Laozi,
often concealing himself and maintaining a low profile.
He was on good terms with Jī Kāng and Lǚ Ān,
and later met Ruǎn Jí.
Together they roamed the Bamboo Grove,
forming a tacit understanding beyond words.
When Jī Kāng was later implicated in an affair and faced execution,
he said to his son Jī Shào:
"As long as Jùyuán is alive,
you will not be alone."
(From the Biography of the Jin Dynasty)
Spiritual communion
Chénliú Ruǎn Jí and Qiáoguó Jī Kāng both possessed outstanding talent and profound insight,
few in their youth could match their rapport,
Shān Tāo initially did not know them,
but once he encountered them,
they immediately became spiritual companions.
Yuán Hóng's "Biography of Shān Tāo"
Recognizing and Judging Each Other as Friends
Shān Tāo and Jī Kāng and Ruǎn Jí met once,
and they bonded as closely as metal and orchid.
Shān's wife, Madame Hán, noticed that her husband's relationship with these two men was different from ordinary friendships,
so she asked Shān Tāo about it.
He replied,
"In my lifetime, the only ones I can consider as friends are these two gentlemen."
His wife said,
"Even the wife of Fù Jī personally observed Hú Yǎn and Zhào Shuài;
I wish to observe them too.
May I?"
Another day, when the two men came,
the wife urged Shān Tāo to have them stay overnight.
She prepared wine and meat,
and at night, she bored through the wall to watch them,
forgetting to return until dawn.
Shān Tāo came in and asked,
"What do you think of these two men?"
His wife replied,
"Your talent and grace are far inferior to theirs;
you should be friends with them based on your judgment and insight."
Shān Tāo said,
"They, too, often consider my judgment superior."
Drinking at the market, looking up and weeping
Long ago, Xíng Gāo and Lǚ Ān drank together in the marketplace,
looked up to the sky and wept.
The two men were not grieving over a funeral,
but lamenting how late they had come to know each other.
This is why the gentleman diligently receives the worthy
and eagerly cultivates friendships,
wishing thereby to establish his reputation.
From "Zōu Zǐ"
Intimate Friendship
Gù Mèngzhù once offered wine to Zhōu Bórén,
but Bórén declined it.
Gù then turned to offer it to a pillar, saying to it:
"How can you presume yourself to be a pillar and ridgepole?"
Zhōu, hearing this, was pleased,
and they thus became bosom friends.
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World."
Looking forward to meeting
Yǔ Yì, styled Zhìgōng,
at that time Jīngzhào Dù Yì and Chénjùn Shāng Hào both had talent and fame that led the age,
but Yì did not value them,
and often said to people:
"These people should be tied up and placed on a high shelf,
wait until the world is at peace,
and then discuss what positions they should hold."
He only maintained a close friendship with Huán Wēn,
and from their childhood hair-tufted years, they had already pledged mutual commitment for life.
"Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū"
Competitive spirit
Duke Huán was equally renowned as Marquis Yīn from a young age,
and often harbored a competitive spirit.
Duke Huán asked Marquis Yīn:
"How do you compare to me?"
Marquis Yīn replied:
"I have been dealing with myself for a long time,
I would rather be myself."
Shì Shuō
After Marquis Yīn was deposed,
Duke Huán said to everyone:
"When we were young and played riding bamboo horses together,
whenever I discarded mine, he would always pick it up,
so naturally he is beneath me."
End
The words are often imbued with allegorical meaning.
Sūn Xīnggōng composed an elegy for Duke Yǔ, stating:
"Alas, you and I shared the same refinement and destiny,
measuring our affections and entrusting our sentiments,
I regarded you as my teacher.
The friendship between noble men,
is mutual and selfless.
With an open heart, you embraced what was right,
and spoke sincerely to admonish against wrongs.
Though I am indeed not clever,
I revere and uphold your teachings as if they were the strings and leather admonitions.
Forever I shall treasure your words,
reciting them with my mouth while my heart grieves."
After completing it, he showed it to Yǔ Dào'ēn,
who, upon seeing it, sighed deeply and returned it, saying:
"My late father and you, sir, were never as close as this."
Míngqì
After Zhī Dàolín lost Fǎ Dù,
his spirit crumbled and fell away,
his demeanor began to decline,
and he often said to others:
"In ancient times, Carpenter Shī discarded his axe after the man of Yǐng died,
and Yá Bóyá broke his strings when Zhōng Zǐqī was gone.
Reflecting on myself and looking outward,
I find this is truly no empty saying.
Now that my silent confidant has departed,
my words find no one to appreciate them,
and my heart is bound with pent-up sorrows—
I fear I shall perish."
Indeed, a year later, Zhī passed away.
Same source as above.
Beyond the Mundane World
Xǔ Mài, styled Shūxuán,
entered the Western Hills of Lín'ān,
changed his name to Xuán and styled Yuǎnyóu.
Wáng Xīzhī visited him,
and would often spend entire days forgetting to return,
forming a transcendental friendship beyond worldly affairs.
Book of Jìn
proudly making friends
Kǒng Chúnzhī lived in seclusion at Shàn Mountain,
where he once met Fǎ Chóng of the Yè sect at Three Mountains.
They opened their hearts and found deep affinity,
considering it a friendship of true mutual understanding.
(Sòng Jì)
Clouds and rosy glow intermingle.
Xiè Dàn, courtesy name Jǐnghéng,
was the grandson of Xiè Ān,
unrestrained and relying on his spirit,
he did not seek worldly affairs,
and with Fàn Yǒu of Shùnyáng, he formed a friendship as lofty as clouds and rosy glow.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Abnormal intercourse
Xiè Shù, courtesy name Jǐngxiān,
had aspirations and virtuous conduct from a young age,
served in office with integrity and frugality,
Yīn Jǐngrén and Liú Zhàn both formed an extraordinary friendship with him,
possessed elegant demeanor,
and was adept in manners.
Zhàn often remarked to others:
"I never tire of seeing Xiè Dào'ér."
Dào'ér
was Shù's childhood name.
． "Book of Song: Biography of Xiè Jǐngrén"
A gentleman's friendship
Kǒng Zhìguī, styled Dézhāng,
was a man of Kuàijī.
He established his reputation early,
and the renowned scholars of his time—Lù Huìxiǎo, Xiè Zhāngróng, Hé Diǎn, and Shěn Yuān—formed a friendship of gentlemen with him.
The Book of Qì
Offering Allegiance
At the beginning of the Song Dynasty under Emperor Xiàowǔ, Emperor Gāo of Qí was an assistant,
while Liú Huáizhēn served as a direct officer.
They encountered each other in the past.
Emperor Gāo took charge of governance,
appointing his son Huǎng to replace him as the Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Some doubted that Huáizhēn would not accept the replacement.
Emperor Gāo said:
"When I was a commoner,
Huáizhēn had already offered his allegiance.
How much more so now,
would he change in any way?"
"Nán Shǐ"
Aspirations of the Heart
Xiàng Liǔ, courtesy name Xuánjì,
was Zhēn's younger brother.
He was learned and talented,
and his conduct was proper and elegant.
Grand Commandant Yuán Shū, Minister of Works Xú Zhànzhī, and Inspector of Dōngyáng Prefecture Yán Jùn were all his good friends.
When Yán Jùn became prominent,
Xiàng Liǔ still relied on their longstanding relationship,
without offering precedence.
Fàn Qú of Shùnyáng advised Xiàng Liǔ, saying,
"Names and ranks have different rites and meanings,
how can you act with the same intention as before?"
Xiàng Liǔ replied,
"I have had a long-standing heart-to-heart with Shìxùn,
how can I deal with him suddenly based on power and profit?"
When Xiàng Liǔ was involved in matters concerning Nánkāng Commandery and Shè Yìxuān's failure,
he was imprisoned in Jiànkāng,
and repeatedly requested Yán Jùn in secret to save him.
Emperor Xiàowǔ often spoke with Yán Jùn about Xiàng Liǔ's affairs,
yet did not help him.
Consequently, Xiàng Liǔ faced the law.
shàng
Treating each other as equals
Tán Chāo, courtesy name Gāozǔ,
was spirited from a young age.
He initially served as the Registrar of the Western Bureau in Southern Xú Province,
and treated Xiāo Huìkāi, the Assistant Inspector, as an equal.
Huìkāi, considering his own status superior,
gradually began to look down upon him.
However, Chāo remained carefree and unrestrained in his actions,
never deferring to him based on rank.
Widening his eyes, he said to Huìkāi:
"What noble lineage do you and I possess?
We are merely maternal relatives from when the state was humble and obscure.
How can we presume to look down on others because of an official title?"
Huìkāi was pleased by this,
and they became sworn friends from then on.
(From Qí Chūnqiū)
Conscripted and Dragged
Sūn Bóyì of Tàiyuán, though his family was poor,
often read by the light of snow,
freeing his spirit beyond worldly concerns,
and dwelling with aspirations among hills and valleys. He formed a deep, inseparable friendship with Governor Wáng Lìngjūn and General Fàn Liàngyún.
After Wáng and Fàn had served in two successive courts,
they wished to offer him an official post,
but Bóyì said:
"A human life of a hundred years is like a candle in the wind.
One should instead gladden the spirit and nurture one's nature,
expressing feelings through lute and wine.
How can I rush about toiling like this?
What Jī Kāng could not endure,
I too am unable to bear."
"Tán Sǒu"
Undressing, she kept herself apart
Liú Jìn and his friend Kǒng Chè from Kuàijī took a boat east together,
when they encountered a woman on the embankment.
Chè gazed after her and said:
"Beautiful and radiant."
Jìn responded:
"How could these be words befitting a gentleman?
You are no friend of mine."
Thereupon he removed his outer garment to separate himself.
Another account says:
While traveling east by boat with his friend Kǒng Chè,
Chè lingered watching a woman on the shore,
whereupon Jìn raised a mat to partition himself,
and would no longer sit together with him.
Recruit talents from afar
Liú Xū, styled Yǎndù,
formed a bond of deep friendship with Ruǎn Xiàoxù of Chénliú and Lǐ Shēn,
building a dwelling beside Zhōngfù Mountain,
where they jointly studied the inner meanings,
delving into profound classics.
The "Liáng Diǎn" records:
Ruǎn Xiàoxù, being erudite and reclusive,
did not associate with contemporary society,
constantly residing on a single deer-bed,
surrounded by planted bamboos and trees,
living and sleeping among them,
so that when people visited him,
they never actually saw him.
Xū paid one visit,
and Xiàoxù immediately regarded him as a spiritual friend.
Xū's cousin Liú Xiāo also practiced lofty conduct,
and the three of them daily accompanied each other in the old capital,
being called the Three Recluses.
From youth to adulthood,
Xū never showed expressions of joy or anger.
Whenever in situations where competition was possible,
he would win by not competing,
and if anyone tried to overpower him,
they would invariably retreat in shame and admiration,
thus public opinion unanimously esteemed him.
"Nán Shǐ"
Posthumous Writings
Liú Shànmíng in his youth was close friends with Cuī Zǔsī.
When Zǔsī was appointed to Qīng and Jì provinces,
Shànmíng sent him a letter saying:
"Our past excursions together
now seem so distant.
Sometimes we strolled hand in hand through spring woods,
sometimes leaned on staffs by autumn streams,
chasing the clear breeze through treetops,
pursuing the bright moon over garden walls.
How is it that our old friends have nearly all departed?
You now sound the flute in your native land,
wear embroidered robes in your hometown.
The sorrows of Sòng's final turmoil have been relieved,
yet the suffering of Hèshuò still needs rescue.
Send eloquent travelers as guides,
travel light and set forth,
to restore your ancestral lands.
Now Sìshàng returns to its ways,
Jìxià revives its customs.
To whom would you defer this task?
I merely express what's in my heart,
and respectfully offer this humble gift."
From History of the Southern Qí
When he heard of Zǔsī's death, he wept bitterly and fell ill, eventually dying.
From History of the Southern Dynasties
Set up the sacrifice
Péi Bóróng was esteemed for his refined demeanor from a young age.
In his later years, he indulged excessively in heavy drinking without restraint,
to the extent that it harmed his health.
A few days before his passing,
he suddenly declared:
"I have received a secret letter,
and I am about to be arrested."
He then fled westward with his wife in a carriage to escape,
but later, while pointing at the walls,
he claimed officials were chasing him.
His wife then realized he was ill.
After his death, he was buried in the family garden.
Friends such as Cháng Jǐng, Lǐ Hún, Wáng Yuánjǐng, Lú Yuánmíng, Wèi Jìjǐng, Lǐ Qiān, and about ten others gathered by his grave to set out wine and offer sacrifices,
weeping and mourning sorrowfully.
With each drink, they poured a libation,
saying:
"May the soul of Secretary Péi, if aware,
know of our presence here."
They each composed a poem,
and Lǐ Qiān, considering Wèi Shōu also a friend of Péi,
sent the poems to Shōu for review.
Shōu was in Jìnyáng at the time,
and he collaborated on a piece eulogizing Bóróng,
which included the lines:
"Facing the wind, I think of Xuándù;
over wine, I recall Gōngróng."
As Bóróng was known for his arrogant and disrespectful nature,
contemporaries felt Shōu's poem aptly captured the truth of his character.
(The Book of Wèi)
Dreaming of Parting
Lú Yuánmíng's friend Wáng Yóu resided in Yǐngchuān when
he suddenly dreamed that Yóu brought wine to bid him farewell,
composing a poem as a gift.
By daybreak, he recalled two lines of the poem:
"From this day onward, once departed,
I shall no longer roam the bustling streets and markets."
Yuánmíng sighed and said:
"Yóu's nature disdained worldly affairs,
yet he dwelled among mortals.
Now this dream occurs,
and the poem is thus—
there must be some unusual reason."
Three days later,
he indeed heard that Yóu had been killed by rebel soldiers.
Investigating the date of his death,
it turned out to be the very night of the dream.
From History of the Northern Dynasties
To dispel vexation
Kòu Jùn, styled Zǔjùn,
had high aspirations and virtuous conduct,
was deeply committed to benevolence and righteousness.
In his youth, he was recognized by the Minister over the Masses Cuī Guāng,
who instructed his son Lì to befriend Jùn.
Whenever Jùn visited Guāng,
they would engage in refined conversation all day long.
The Vice Minister of Rites Lú Biàn, considering Jùn's outstanding scholarship and conduct,
treated him with the courtesy due a teacher and friend.
In his leisure time, he would often call on Jùn,
conversing joyfully throughout the day.
He constantly told people:
"Not seeing Lord Xī'ān leaves me vexed and troubled,
yet I cannot deny he is a man of profound learning."
Such was the respect and esteem he received.
From the Book of Zhōu
Unyielding
Wéi Zhèng, styled Jìngzhí,
was the son of Ruì.
Initially, he was close friends with Dōnghǎi's Wáng Rúrú.
When Wáng Rúrú became the Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
and participated in the selection of officials,
all his guests, friends, and old acquaintances fawned on him,
only Zhèng remained indifferent.
After Wáng Rúrú was dismissed and removed from office,
Zhèng, however, upheld his genuine friendship,
even more than in the past.
Commentators praised him for this.
The Book of Liáng
Dissipation
Wéi Xuán, whose courtesy name was Jìngyuǎn,
had a disposition inclined towards simplicity and ease,
and was genuinely fond of reputation and righteousness.
With an open mind, he skillfully guided others,
and even if a farmer or a shepherd had a single commendable quality,
he would receive and draw them close.
He particularly formed carefree friendships with his clansman Wěi Chǔxuán and Liáng Kuàng of Āndìng.
Zhōu Shū
Change of Clothing
Zhāng Guǐ, styled Yuánguǐ,
was fond of learning from a young age,
with a broad-minded and enlightened disposition.
He initially served in Luòyáng,
but his family was poor.
He formed an inseparable friendship with Lè'ān Sūn Shùrén,
often exchanging clothes to go out,
and was praised for this.
Deceitful Alliance
Zhōu Fū, styled Zhòngyuǎn,
during the Liang dynasty formed a deep bond with his fellow townsman Zhōu Dí.
After the fall of Liang, Fū was the first to join Chén,
and was promoted to the rank of General Who Pacifies the West,
ordered to return and garrison Yùzhāng.
Dí, considering that Fū had originally been beneath him,
yet now surpassed him in prominence and status,
felt deeply resentful,
and thus raised troops in rebellion.
He sent his younger brother Fāngxīng to attack Fū,
but Fū soundly defeated him.
Later, Dí again attacked Dōngxīng,
and Fū followed Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn to campaign against him.
Arriving at Dìngchuān County,
he faced Dí,
who deceived Fū, saying:
"In the past, I and my brother joined forces with one heart,
sharing kinship, not as strangers,
how could I plan to harm you?
Now I wish to admit my guilt and return to court,
and through my brother, lay bare my innermost thoughts,
risking myself before the court to jointly establish an oath."
Fū agreed to it,
but just as he ascended the altar, he was killed by Dí.
An imperial edict stated:
"Fū received the edict for a distant campaign,
lingering beyond the time and violating military law,
embracing treachery and deceit with an open heart,
thus bringing about his demise."
The historian comments:
"In the past, Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú regarded themselves as closest kin,
and Zhōu Fū and Zhōu Dí also swore to be as intimate as relatives,
yet soon turned blades to kill and destroy each other.
Such cruelty makes them strangers like Hú and Yuè!
Enmity and strife arise from power and profit,
how despicable it is!"
Book of Chén
Wholehearted Commitment to Friendship
Lǐ Mì, styled Xuánsuì,
was the son of Suí's Púshān Duke Lǐ Kuān,
and inherited his father's title during the Kāihuáng era.
Just reaching the age of twenty,
the Minister over the Masses Yáng Sù, upon meeting him, found him extraordinary,
and said to his son Yáng Xuǎngǎn:
"Lǐ Mì's wisdom and strategies are inexhaustible,
beyond your capabilities,
you should befriend him."
Xuǎngǎn then wholeheartedly treated him with respect,
forming a bond of sworn friendship.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Financial Support
Liú Hēità was a man from Zhāngnán in Bèizhōu.
He had been friends with Dòu Jiàndé since youth.
His family was poor and unable to support itself,
so Jiàndé often provided for him.
Hēità would use up whatever was given without suspicion,
and Jiàndé never questioned him about it either.
Forgetful of years
Kǒng Shào'ān was a man from Shānyīn in Yuèzhōu,
the son of Chén's Minister of Personnel Huàn.
In his youth, he and his elder brother Shàoxīn were both renowned for their literary talent,
and at thirteen, when Chén fell, he entered Suí.
At that time, the poet Sūn Wànshòu and Shào'ān formed a deep,
ageless friendship,
and contemporaries referred to them as Sūn-Kǒng.
Shào'ān served as Investigating Censor in the late Dàyè era.
To humble oneself and yield
Cén Wénběn considered himself a scholar by origin,
and always maintained humility and modesty.
Towards old acquaintances throughout his life,
even if they were lowly and humble, he invariably treated them with equal respect.
The emperor
treated people, even if they were transient and lowly, with uniform courtesy.
"New Book of Tang"
Not changing the old ways
Although Liú Rénguǐ held a high official position, he was not arrogant,
and whenever he met old acquaintances from his impoverished and humble days,
he maintained the same humble demeanor as when he wore commoner's clothing.
Enduring
Wèi Yuántóng and Péi Yán formed a friendship,
which could be maintained from beginning to end,
thus they were called enduring friends.
"Book of Táng"
Beyond the Mundane World
Lù Yúqìng was on excellent terms with Zhào Zhēngù, Lú Cángyòng, Chén Zǐ'áng, Dù Shěnyán, Sòng Zhīwèn, Bì Gòu, Guō Xíwēi, Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn, and Shì Huái,
who were collectively known as the Ten Friends Beyond the Mundane World.
The Emperor
The Four Literary Friends
Dù Shěnyán in his youth, together with Lǐ Qiáo, Cuī Róng, and Sū Wèidào, formed the Four Literary Friends,
known to the world as Cuī, Lǐ, Sū, and Dù.
Young friend
Lǐ Mì, courtesy name Chángyuán,
knew how to write compositions by age seven.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng particularly praised and cherished him,
often taking him into his private quarters.
Jiǔlíng was on good terms with Yán Tǐngzhī
and Xiāo Tǐng.
Tǐngzhī detested flattery and sycophancy,
and advised Jiǔlíng to break off relations with Xiāo.
Suddenly Jiǔlíng pondered alone and said:
"Yán is too stern and rigid,
yet Xiāo is soft and pleasing, quite delightful."
Just as he ordered his attendants to summon Xiāo,
Mì was nearby
and promptly said:
"You rose from common cloth,
and reached the position of chancellor through upright conduct,
how can you favor the soft and pleasing?"
Jiǔlíng, startled, changed his expression and thanked him,
then called him his young friend.
(New Book of Tang)
from beginning to end
Zhāng Jiǔlíng formed a close friendship with Yán Tǐngzhī, Yuán Rénzōng, Liáng Shēngqīng, and Lú Yí,
all of whom possessed talent and capability.
Their bond remained unwavering from beginning to end,
earning high praise from contemporaries.
Old Book of Tang
Beyond the Mundane
Initially, when Lǐ Mì was exiled to Jiāngnán,
he formed friendships beyond the mundane with Liǔ Hún and Gù Kuàng,
composing poetry at their leisure.
Gù Kuàng,
a native of Jīngzhōu,
had a humorous and witty disposition.
Even with nobles and dignitaries who associated with him,
he would inevitably jest and mock them.
When Liǔ Hún assisted in governance, he recruited Gù Kuàng as a Collator,
and later, with Lǐ Mì succeeding him in office,
Gù Kuàng believed he had grasped key positions of power,
and expected to attain high office.
After a long time, he was only promoted to Editorial Director,
leaving Gù Kuàng discontented.
He sought to return to Wú.
After Lǐ Mì passed away,
Gù Kuàng did not mourn but uttered jesting remarks,
for which he was impeached by the Censorate,
and demoted to Registrar of Ráozhōu.
The emperor...
A promise made
Xī Chún, styled Gāoqīng,
was esteemed for his literary talent,
and maintained close friendships with Yán Zhēnqīng, Xiāo Yǐngshì, and Lǐ Huá.
His son, Shìměi, showed a passion for learning and a remarkable memory from a young age,
often engaging in discussions of classics and commentaries with Yán and Xiāo,
responding as fluently as a flowing stream.
Later, they remarked to each other:
"In the future, we ought to associate between the two Xīs."
Shìměi excelled in building relationships with others,
demonstrating openness and generosity in keeping promises,
earning widespread acclaim at the time.
not changing one's integrity
Zhào Yè was filial and fraternal, sincere and steadfast.
In friendship, even through hardships and dangers, he did not change his integrity.
In his youth, he was like-minded and friendly with Yīn Yín, Yán Zhēnqīng, Liǔ Fāng, Lù Jù, Xiāo Yǐngshì, Lǐ Huá, and Shào Zhěn.
Thus, during the Tiānbǎo era, it was said:
"Yīn, Yán, Liǔ, Lù, Xiāo, Lǐ, Shào, and Zhào,
for they valued righteous conduct and upheld the way of friendship."
From the Old Book of Tang,
Yè
was the father of Zōngrú.
Lying side by side in quiet conversation
Lǐ Yuē was the son of the Duke of Qiān who served as the Vice Director of the Ministry of War.
His understanding and bearing were pure and expansive,
far transcending the worldly norm.
He held office together with Zhāng Shěn, the Vice Director of the Bureau of Receptions,
and Wéi Kuàng, the Recluse Scholar who lived east of the wall,
having withdrawn from the world without marrying
or managing a livelihood.
Lǐ Yuē alone was deeply attached to Zhāng Shěn.
They would lie on connected beds and converse quietly,
remaining awake until dawn,
with no one else knowing of it.
He presented Zhāng with a poem that read:
"I have matters in my heart,
not to be told to Wéi the Third.
On an autumn night in Luòyáng city,
the bright moon shines upon Zhāng the Eighth."
from "Shàngshū Gùshí"
Social Interactions
Yáng Píng showed an indomitable spirit from a young age,
and maintained a loving bond with his younger brother Yáng Nínglíng,
both earning contemporary renown.
He valued social connections,
upheld promises,
and formed friendships with Mù Zhì, Xǔ Mèngróng, Lǐ Yōng, and Wáng Zhòngshū,
thus contemporaries referred to them as the friends Yáng, Mù, Xǔ, and Lǐ,
with Zhòngshū joining later out of admiration.
Old Book of Tang
Sì Kuí
Cuī Zào, styled Xuánzǎi,
together with Hán Huì, Lú Dōngměi, and Zhāng Zhèngzé formed a group of four,
all residing in Shàngyuán,
who delighted in discussing strategies for statecraft,
and often considered themselves capable of assisting a king,
thus being dubbed the "Four Kuí" by their contemporaries.
Divine Communication
Lù Píng of Wújùn, who from youth had high aspirations and conduct,
found delight in landscapes,
during the Zhēnyuán era traveled to Yǒngjiā,
but fell ill and died.
Píng had long been friends with Shěn Cháng of Wúxīng.
Cháng dreamed of Píng, whose countenance was haggard, saying:
"I journeyed to Yǒngjiā,
where severe illness brought me to my end.
You are one who knows me well,
I wish to entrust you with my family affairs."
Cháng grieved.
They then reminisced about past joys and feasted in conversation,
after a long while discussing literature,
and speaking of metaphysical matters,
Píng then said to Cháng:
"I present you the poem 'Floating Clouds',
to convey my feelings."
The poem read:
"Emptiness upon emptiness, void upon void,
in the blink of an eye between heaven and earth.
Temporarily formed is this image,
nor am I my own body."
After chanting sorrowfully several times,
before leaving he said:
"My funeral boat has already set sail,
and will arrive tomorrow at noon."
He clasped hands and departed. When Cháng awoke,
the memory remained exceptionally clear,
so he wrote it down.
Exactly as foretold, Píng's funeral boat arrived,
Cháng comforted the orphan and wept bitterly,
providing double the customary funeral assistance.
The poet Yáng Dān composed a record of this,
fully displayed in the "Divine Communication Inscription":
"Born sincere, our noble lord,
graceful, refined, and cultured,
departed never to rise again,
his voice entrusted to floating clouds."
From "Records of the Hidden and Mysterious"
Lín Quán
Wéi Wēn, courtesy name Hóngyù,
was the son of Wéi Shòu.
He had a straightforward disposition and few friends,
and most people kept their distance from him.
He was only close to the Regular Attendant Sū Yòu,
courtesy name Yòuzhī, a man of Lánlíng,
who was erudite and fond of antiquity,
tranquil and content with retirement.
He excelled at playing the qin and composing poetry,
roaming with his heart among forests and valleys,
whistling and chanting all day long.
Many famous scholars and eminent figures associated with him,
and the Supervising Secretary Wéi Wēn held him in especially high regard,
forming with him a friendship of woodland and spring.
(Old Book)
Eight Friends
Liú Pì initially passed the examination,
and went to the diviner Hú Lúshēng to cast a hexagram to determine his official prospects.
Lùshēng was blind in both eyes.
Once the hexagram was cast,
he told Liú Pì,
"In twenty years from now,
your fortunes lie in the southwest,
but you will not end well."
Pì left a white silk gift with him.
After taking office,
he followed Wéi Gāo to Xīchuān,
rising to the positions of Imperial Censor and Military Marshal.
After twenty years,
Wéi fell ill,
and ordered Pì to enter court and report,
requesting the extension of Dōngchuān’s territories,
similar to the system in the early Kāiyuán era.
The edict was not approved.
Pì then donned plain clothes, mounted a single horse, and again visited Hú Lúshēng for a divination.
Lùshēng sorted and formed the hexagram,
saying to Pì,
"Twenty years ago,
I once divined for a person,
resulting in the hexagram 'Following the Unforeseen.'
Now obtaining the same hexagram,
could it be the same distinguished man as before?"
Pì, upon hearing this,
consented with deference.
Lùshēng said,
"If it is indeed you,
disaster is imminent."
Pì did not believe him,
so he returned to Shǔ,
and indeed rebelled.
Emperor Xiànzōng captured and executed him.
"Yuán Huà Jì"
Wú Gǒng, Wú Xū, Wú Sōng, Pí Guāngyè, Lín Shēng, Luó Yǐn, Hé Xiāo, and Hán Bì dwelled in the Eight Seats Mountains of Chángchéng in Wúxīng,
and were known at the time as the Eight Friends.
and interact
Shùn farmed at Lìshān and befriended Yì,
made pottery by the river and befriended Yǔ.
"Lǔ Liánzǐ"
Drinking fine wine
In Wú there was a Chéng Pǔ,
who, relying on his seniority, repeatedly insulted and bullied Zhōu Yú.
Yú humbled himself and treated others with tolerance,
never contending with him.
Later, Pǔ came to respect and admire him of his own accord, growing close and holding him in high esteem,
and then said to others:
"Associating with Lord Zhōu Gōngjǐn is like drinking fine, mellow wine;
one becomes intoxicated without realizing it."
(Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn)
Obtained a wife
In Liáodōng, Mǎ Zhòngshū and Wáng Zhìdū knew each other very well and were deeply connected.
Zhòngshū passed away first.
Suddenly, he appeared to Dū and said:
"Unfortunately, I died first,
but my heart constantly misses you.
Thinking that you have no wife,
I should help you find one."
He then set a date with him.
On that day, a great wind arose,
and it grew dark toward dusk.
Indeed, a woman appeared in the bedroom.
Dū asked her about her background,
and she said:
"I am from Hénán,
my father is the governor of Qīnghé.
I was about to be married,
but I don't know how I ended up here?"
Dū explained the reason to her,
and they became husband and wife.
They went to visit her family,
who were overjoyed, believing it was a match made by heaven.
They then had a son together,
who later became the governor of Nánjùn.
From "Yōu Míng Lù".
Slander and vilification

Social interactions

Rite of Establishing Friendship
The Yuè custom is straightforward and sincere in nature.
When affection grows and a bond is formed, they remove the headscarf from their heads,
untie the five-foot knife at their waist, and give it to the other,
kneeling in mutual respect as husband and wife.
At the initial establishment of the bond, there is a ritual:
the custom is always performed under a large tree in the mountains,
where they build an altar with mounded earth,
and offer sacrifices of one white dog, one red rooster, and three chicken eggs,
called "the five beneath the tree: rooster and dog."
The altar ground is feared and no one dares to violate it.

if we meet in the future, step down and bow;
though I walk on foot and you ride a horse,

Five exchanges and three provocations
Interests in friendship share a common origin,
yet their branches and streams diverge.
To compare and outline them, there are roughly five methods:
first, friendship based on power;
second, friendship based on bribery;
third, friendship based on rhetoric;
fourth, friendship born of desperation;
fifth, friendship measured by utility.
Because of these five types of friendship,
three conflicts arise:
the corruption of virtue and annihilation of righteousness,
making one akin to beasts—
this is the first conflict;
difficult to solidify and easily broken,
gathering disputes and litigation—
this is the second conflict;
reputation sinking into greed,
shamed by the upright and principled—
this is the third conflict.
The ancients knew these three conflicts as obstructions,
and feared the swift blame brought by the five friendships.
Thus, Wáng Dān disciplined his son with the cane,
and Zhū Mù spoke boldly to demonstrate severance.
How profound it is,
how profound!

Turn a cold shoulder
A man's integrity is revealed in adversity.
Nowadays, when people live peacefully in their neighborhoods,
they admire each other and share feasts,
engage in games and social interactions,
force smiles and flatter to win favor,
shake hands as if baring their hearts,
swear by heaven and earth with tears,
vowing never to betray each other in life or death—
all seeming utterly sincere.
Yet once faced with the slightest gain or loss,
as trivial as a single hair,
they turn hostile as if they never knew you;
they won't lift a finger to save you from a trap,
but instead push you further down,
and even add stones to crush you.
Such behavior is everywhere.
This is what even beasts and barbarians would shrink from doing,
yet these people regard it as a clever strategy.

Drifting and Submerging
Chén Zūn and Zhāng Sǒng were both dismissed from their posts,
returning to Cháng'ān as marquises,
Sǒng lived in poverty with no guests,
only occasionally did curious people visit him,
to pose questions and resolve doubts,
discussing the Way and classical texts.

with carriages and horses crowding his gate,
wine and meat flowing continuously.
Zūn often said to Sǒng:

torment your body with restrictions,
daring not to make missteps,
while I follow my whims freely,
floating and sinking in worldly affairs.
Though my official rank and achievements don't surpass yours, I find unique joy -
isn't this superior?"
Sǒng replied:
"Each person has their nature,
deciding their own strengths and weaknesses.
You couldn't become me if you tried,
nor could I imitate you without failure.
Nevertheless,
those who learn from me find it easier to maintain,
while those who imitate you find it harder to sustain,
such is my constant principle."

Dé Cáo went straight into his room,

Without distinguishing between host and guest
Chén Dēng, courtesy name Yuánlóng,
was renowned for his authority in Guǎnglíng.
Xǔ Fàn and Liú Bèi were both seated with Liú Biǎo,
when Biǎo and Bèi discussed eminent figures of the realm.
Fàn remarked:
"Chén Yuánlóng is a man of lakes and seas,
yet his unbridled arrogance remains unchecked."
Bèi responded:
"Do you truly believe your valor warrants such criticism?
When I formerly passed by Xiàpī and visited Yuánlóng,
he showed no distinction between host and guest,
and refrained from conversing with me for a long time.
He himself ascended to the grand couch to recline,
leaving his guest to sleep beneath the bed."
Bèi continued:
"You bear the reputation of a state scholar,
from whom one would expect aspirations to save the world.
Yet you busied yourself with acquiring fields and inquiring about houses,
your words devoid of worthwhile counsel.
This is what Yuánlóng despises,
why should he have conversed with you?
It is as if I wished to lie atop a hundred-foot tower,
while you recline on level ground—
merely the difference between upper and lower beds!"
Biǎo laughed heartily.
(Wèi Zhì)
The Guest Speaker
Jiǎn Yǒng, styled Xiànhé,
was acquainted with the Former Sovereign from youth,
following and accompanying him.
When the Former Sovereign went to Jīngzhōu,

He was often an envoy,
traveling on diplomatic missions.
Yǒng was by nature straightforward, proud, and unconventional.

When among those below Zhūgě Liàng,

resting his head and lying down to speak,

when Zhūgě Liàng set out to station in Hànzhōng,
Yì served as the Chief Clerk of the Administrative Office,

Hundreds came to see him off,
filling the road with carriages.

Sūn Cè was in Wú,

discussing how the realm was not yet at peace,
and that it was necessary to use military force to pacify it.
Jì, being young, was seated at the far end,
but from a distance, he raised his voice and said:
"In the past, Guǎn Yíwú served as minister of Qí,
and Duke Huán assembled the feudal lords nine times,
unifying and rectifying the world,
without the use of chariots of war.
Confucius said:
'When distant subjects are unsubmissive, cultivate one's civil virtue to attract them.'

but only emphasize military achievements.
Even as a youth, I secretly find this unsettling."
Zhāo and the others were astonished by him.

Grand Gathering
Zhūgě Róng was the son of Jǐn,
whenever he hosted grand gatherings for guests, he would ask each in turn,
to speak of their talents,
then he would bring mats closer and seats together,
matching opponents based on their abilities,
some would play board games,
some would engage in gambling games, pitch-pot, or archery,

Peeking at the Guest Through the Window
Hànzhōng Yángzǐ Jù's wife, styled Dàyīng,
was renowned for her noble reputation.
Once, when she invited guests,
her mother prepared a lavish feast
and observed the guests through the window.
Afterward, she admonished her daughter, saying:
"I see that none of your friends are as virtuous as you are;
this is a path to self-diminishment."
Over a year later, when she again entertained guests,
they were all esteemed elders and outstanding scholars.
Her mother watched them and joyfully said:
"Now I have no worries."

Living simply and plainly
Lù Nà was appointed as the governor of Wúxīng.
Before arriving at the commandery,
he first went to Gūshú
to bid farewell to Huán Wēn.
Thereupon, he asked Huán Wēn,
"How much wine can you drink when you get drunk,
and how much meat can you eat?"
Huán Wēn replied,
"In recent years, I get drunk after just three shēng of wine,
and I eat no more than ten slices of white meat.
What about you?"
Lù Nà said,
"I am not a drinker by nature,
and can only manage two shēng,
and as for meat, it is not even worth mentioning."
Later, when he found Huán Wēn free,
he said to him,
"I have a small gift outside.
As I am about to govern a distant commandery,
I wish to share a drink with you to express my humble feelings."
Huán Wēn gladly accepted.
At the time, Wáng Tǎnzhī and Diāo Yí were present.
When the gift was presented, there was only one dǒu of wine
and one plate of venison.
The guests were astonished,
but Lù Nà calmly said,
"Your Excellency recently mentioned drinking three shēng of wine,
and I can only manage two shēng.
Now, I have prepared one dǒu to allow for extra servings."
Huán Wēn and the guests all admired his simplicity and sincerity,
so he ordered the kitchen to prepare a fine feast,
and they drank joyfully until the party ended.
Return to visit

The Emperor Xiàowǔ held him in high regard,

At the time of Wáng Xún's son's marriage,

Yáng Xīn once visited the commander Xiè Hùn,

accustomed to eating coarse food
Zōng Què during the Xiàojiàn era was promoted to Governor of Yùzhōu,

Previously,
his fellow villager Yǔ Yè,

Coercing one's mother
Cuī Dàogù served as a military advisor to the princes of the Song dynasty,
and was dispatched to Qingzhou,
to recruit personnel from the rank of Chief Clerk and below.
The princes visited Cuī Dàogù's elder brothers,
pressuring his mother,
forcing her to personally serve wine and roasted meat before the guests.
Cuī Dàogù stood up in shock,
and said to others:
"Our household lacks servants,
so my elderly mother must labor herself,
toiling to serve the guests."
Everyone realized this was orchestrated by his brothers,
and bowed to his mother.
His mother said to Cuī Dàogù:
"I am of low status and unworthy to receive bows from your noble guests,
you should return their bows instead."
All the gentlemen admired Cuī Dàogù and his mother, but looked down upon his brothers.

Wúxīng's Wú Guī possessed considerable talent and learning,

fond of traveling

with no surplus wealth in his household.

welcoming and engaging them tirelessly.

Sailing on the River
Sūn Yǎng, styled Dé Liǎn,
was open-minded and composed,
distributing his wealth and possessions among relatives and friends.
His personal residence, however, was rather extravagant and luxurious,
with courtyards and waterways meticulously constructed,
achieving the utmost charm of forests and springs.
Guests filled his gates,
and carriages with canopies never ceased arriving.
When he was appointed to govern Yǐngzhōu,
he joined over ten boats to form a large vessel,
erecting a pavilion and pond in the center,
and planting lotuses and water caltrops.
Whenever there was a fine day and beautiful scenery,
he would gather his guests and staff together,
floating on the Yangtze River while setting out wine,
creating a remarkable sight of the time.
(From *The History of the Southern Dynasties*)
dared not take their seats
Emperor Míng of Sòng passed away,
Cài Xīngzōng was summoned back to the capital.
At that time, General of the Right Army Wáng Dàolóng held a key position in the state administration,
wielding significant power for a time.
He shuffled in his shoes to the front of Xīngzōng,
not daring to take a seat,
and only left after a long while,
ultimately never inviting him to sit.
In the early Yuánjiā era, the Palace Secretary Dī Dāng visited the Crown Prince's Supervisor,

being favored by the emperor,
was told by His Majesty:

you must first be granted a seat by Wáng Qiú to be considered qualified.

is of no benefit.
