you may claim it is by imperial decree to take a seat."
Upon arrival, Qiú raised his fan and said:
"You may not do so."
Hóng returned,
reported the matter as it happened,
and the Emperor said:
"There is nothing even I can do about this."
End
Háoyǒu
Wáng Yuánbǎo, Yáng Chóngyì, and Guō Wànjīn, wealthy commoners of Cháng'ān, were among the nation's most prominent magnates.
Each of them made it a practice to host and support numerous scholars from all directions,
vying to provide for their needs.
Many renowned officials of the court
often emerged from their patronage.
During each imperial examination, literary scholars would gather at their residences,
leading contemporaries to regard them as patrons of the elite.
(From "Supplemental Records of the Tiānbǎo Era")
Composing poetry
Lǐ Shìzhī while serving as chancellor,
would invite guests to banter and compose poems after each court session,
never avoiding Lǐ Línfǔ's harm.
He once wrote a poem:
"Vermilion gates never closed long,
relatives and friends freely visit.
Approaching half a hundred years of age,
if not happy now, then when?"
After being removed from chancellorship he wrote another poem:
"Avoiding power, removed from chancellor's post,
enjoying sage's life while holding wine cup.
May I ask the guests before my door,
how many have come today?"
When he died from unjust accusations,
contemporaries considered him wronged.
Arrayed Delicacies
Emperor Dézōng unexpectedly appointed Wú Còu as the Capital Governor,
and immediately ordered him to assume office. Còu hurriedly gathered all the guests at his residence,
where a banquet had already been arranged.
Someone asked:
"How was this done so quickly?"
An official replied:
"We maintain two daily ceremonial feasts,
prepared by simply lifting the cauldrons and pots to serve,
so a banquet for three to five hundred people
can always be arranged instantly."
《Supplement to the National History》
Forced to bring
Lǐ Fān, styled Shūhàn,
was appointed as a secretary lang.
Wáng Shào, who held power, invited Fān,
promising immediate employment upon meeting,
but Fān ultimately did not accept.
Wáng Zhòngshū, Wéi Chéngjì, Lǚ Dòng, and their peers served as lang officials,
forming a clique that was prominent and influential.
They gathered daily to sing and drink,
and, admiring Fān's reputation, insisted on his joining their gatherings.
Fān reluctantly attended once,
but Zhòngshū and the others enjoyed spreading rumors and engaging in frivolous banter.
Later, when they summoned Fān again, he firmly refused to go,
saying:
"After spending a day with Zhòngshū and his group,
I still don't understand what they were talking about!"
Eventually, they met with failure.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Penalty Wine Cup
Lǐ Féngjí, while in power, feared that Péi Dù might return to the position of chancellor.
He ordered the Capital Governor Liú Qīchǔ and over ten others to exert all efforts to suppress and reject him.
Even Péi Dù's own guests and followers began to consider leaving him.
One day, Péi Dù hosted a banquet to entertain his guests.
Liú Qīchǔ, with feigned humility, tried to explain himself
and whispered into Péi Dù's ear.
Cuī Xián, disgusted by his hypocrisy,
raised his cup and reproached Péi Dù, saying:
"How can the Chancellor allow a subordinate official to whisper fawningly in your ear?
I propose a penalty cup for you."
Péi Dù smiled, accepted it, and drank.
Liú Qīchǔ felt uneasy,
hurriedly left his seat,
and everyone present admired Cuī Xián's boldness.
(From the New Book of Tang)
Qíkè
Cuī Hónglǐ passed through Xuānwǔ,
and joined Liú Xuánzuǒ on a hunt.
Flushed with drink, Xuánzuǒ turned to him and said:
"Does young Cuī alone not know this pleasure?"
Hónglǐ laughed and replied:
"I have always enjoyed martial pursuits,
allow me to share in your enjoyment."
Xuánzuǒ, with a hawk on his arm, galloped alongside Hónglǐ,
controlling the pace with ease.
The whole army exclaimed in surprise:
"Where did this guest come from?"
Xuánzuǒ greatly desired to keep him,
but Hónglǐ firmly declined.
A Guest at Midnight
Guō? was a close friend of the Chancellor and Commandant Yú, sharing a study desk.
When Guō? held a key position,
and managed financial affairs,
he failed to avoid suspicion and gladly became a midnight visitor.
During the Xiántōng era, along with Shěn Yúnxiáng and others, ten individuals in total all associated with powerful eunuchs,
and were called the Ten Philosophers of Fānglín,
as the Fānglín Gate was their entry point.
"Records of the Selected"
When Wáng Mǎng served as Zǎihéng,
Zhēn Fēng would enter morning and evening to discuss plans,
leading people of the time to say:
"Midnight visitor,
Zhēn Chángbó."
"Book of the Later Hàn"
Tiny
The song of Qiántáng Sū Xiǎoxiǎo says:
"I ride in an oil-painted carriage,
My lover rides a dappled horse.
Where shall we pledge our hearts together?
Under the pines and cypresses at Xīlíng."
The Ancient Music Bureau
records that Sū Xiǎoxiǎo,
a famous courtesan of Qiántáng,
lived during the Southern Qí dynasty.
Xīlíng lies west of the Qiántáng River,
hence the song's reference to "under the pines and cypresses at Xīlíng."
The Extensive Topics on Music Bureau
notes that before the magistrate's office in Jiāxīng County lies the tomb of the Jìn dynasty courtesan Sū Xiǎoxiǎo of Qiántáng.
Records of Wú Region
Xiàowǔ Lǐ Tàihòu,
was originally of humble and lowly origin.
Initially, Jiǎnwén Dì was made the Prince of Huìjī,
having three sons who all died in infancy.
Afterward, his consorts were barren for nearly ten years,
thus he ordered a skilled physiognomist to examine all the palace women.
At that time, the Empress was in the weaving house,
tall in stature and dark in complexion,
such that the palace women all called her Kūnlún.
When she arrived,
the physiognomist was startled and said,
"This is the person,
yet she has a tiger misfortune!"
The Emperor summoned her to attend him.
The Empress often dreamed of two dragons resting on her knees,
the sun and moon entering her embrace,
and she gave birth to Xiàowǔ.
When the Prince of Huìjī, Dàozǐ, ascended to a high position,
he acknowledged the accuracy of the physiognomist,
but was perplexed by the prediction of tiger harm,
as such a birth was unprecedented.
He ordered a tiger to be painted,
and played at striking the tiger with his hands,
then began to suffer from swelling and pain in his hand,
and thus succumbed to the illness and passed away.
"Yōumínglù" "The Book of Jìn"
Zhēnniáng,
a famed singing and dancing courtesan from Wú,
was buried in front of the Wǔqiū Temple after her death,
fulfilling the wishes of the youth of Wúzhōng.
Her grave was lush with flowers and plants.
"Preface to Lǐ Gōngchuí's Poem"
People of the time compared her to Sū Xiǎoxiǎo;
travelers, moved by her splendor,
competed to inscribe poems on the trees by her tomb.
Tán Yǒng, a scholar from Wúmén, wrote:
"Below Hǔqiū Hill, graves mound upon mound,
the desolate pines and cypresses all evoke sorrow.
Why do people in this world so favor beauty?
On Zhēnniáng's tomb alone, poems are inscribed."
"Yúnxī Yǒu Yí"
Spring grass at Zhēnniáng's grave is emerald green,
while Xīnnú's hair turns white as autumn frost.
Among them, only Yáng Qióng remains,
fit to accompany Xiè Gōng on Dōngshān.
"Collection of Chángqìng"
Yǒngxīn
During the Kāiyuán era, there was a daughter of the Yǐn family in Yǒngxīn County, Lúlíng.
It is said she was a descendant of General Yǔn's cleansing,
possessing beautiful features,
and a clever, kind nature.
Without relying on a nursemaid, she excelled in singing with remarkable skill.
On the Double Ninth Festival, she climbed Wén Peak on South Mountain with a group of girls,
and sang a song for her peers,
its sound carrying for dozens of miles.
Thus, the local elders said of the Yǐn family's song,
it resounded throughout Cháng'ān.
At that time, the regional inspector arrived in the county on an inspection tour and summoned her for an audience,
whereupon she was sent to the palace and enfeoffed as a singing court performer.
Her vocal talent was unparalleled in the world,
so musicians across the land, even princes and nobles, collectively called her Yǐn Yǒngxīn after her county's name.
Later, during the grand banquet at the Yuán Assembly in Hánguāng Hall,
all the commoners of Cháng'ān and chieftains of the barbarian tribes were allowed to enter and view the imperial palace.
At the time, the feast was in full swing,
but the noisy commotion of the day disturbed the emperor's mood.
Gāo Lìshì then pushed Yǒngxīn forward,
and with just one note of her song,
the entire crowd fell silent.
Thereupon, the emperor's heart was greatly eased,
and the event continued until evening.
The place where she first sang still exists today,
known as Jade Maiden Peak,
and a temple was erected there to worship her.
From "Jiāngnán Yěshǐ".
After the rebellion of Yúyáng,
Yǒngxīn was taken in by a scholar.
Later, when the scholar passed away,
she went to the capital with her mother,
presumably falling into a life of hardship.
Upon her death,
she said to her mother:
"Mother, your money tree has fallen."
"Yuèfǔ Zálù" states that this was Xǔ Hézǐ.
Yǒngxīn Liǔ Qīngniáng
Among the nation's musicians, women such as Yǒngxīn Fù, Yùshǐ Niáng, and Liǔqīng Niáng were all exceptionally skilled of their time.
There is a poem dedicated to Yùshǐ Niáng that reads:
"In all the land, none can sing like Yùshǐ Niáng,
Before blossoms, under the moon, she serves the sovereign.
Deep within the ninefold palace, unseen by any,
She alone passes new melodies to Shùn Láng."
"Collected Works from the Forest of Flowers"
The palace courtesan Yǒngxīn was an excellent singer,
The Emperor said:
A single song from this person is truly worth a thousand pieces of gold.
"Surviving Anecdotes of the Kāiyuán Era"
Jiāo Chénrú
Mùzhōu Cìshǐ Liǔ Qíwù was handsome and talented in his youth,
his family was wealthy,
and he traveled to the capital for an official assignment.
There was a famous courtesan named Jiāochénrú,
who was beautiful and skilled in the arts,
sought after by scholars.
The Governor of Mùzhōu visited her and was captivated,
Jiāochénrú said:
"If you can line twenty miles with brocade tents,
I will serve you for life."
She had said this lightly, thinking it impossible,
but the next day,
he brought the exact amount of brocade tents as promised,
Jiāochénrú was astonished and admired his extraordinary gesture,
and eventually joined the Liǔ household,
performing the duties of a servant or concubine,
and was respected by relatives.
When Emperor Xuánzōng was still among the people,
he had often heard of Jiāochénrú's fame,
and upon learning of her, summoned her to the palace.
She tearfully claimed chronic illness and old age,
and the emperor, knowing she could not be forced,
allowed her to return home.
From "Yīnhuà Lù" and "Jìwén"; Tán Qiánzhuànzǐ wrote it as Chén Jiāo
rú.
Xuē Qióngqióng
Xuē Qióngqióng was the foremost zither player in the Kāiyuán era palace.
On the Qingming Festival, the emperor ordered the palace courtesans to go spring outing.
The wild scholar Cuī Huáibǎo secretly caught sight of Qióngqióng.
At night, in the Inner Music Bureau,
Yáng Gāo covertly waited for him.
Gāo instructed Cuī to compose a short lyric before he could see Xuē.
Cuī composed the lyric, which said:
"In this life I have no other wish,
but to be a zither in the music.
To be close to the fair one's slender hands,
singing delicate tunes upon her gauzy skirt.
Even death would be an honor."
Gāo offered Huáibǎo Xūnji wine, saying:
"This is made from the evergreen herb,
also called the thousand-year herb.
It can turn white hair black,
and lead to the way of longevity."
Cuī later became the Sīlù official in Hénán.
When Qióngqióng was playing the zither and was interrogated by officials,
she was taken to the capital.
Emperor Míng Huáng then bestowed her upon him.
From "Collection of Beautiful Romances"
Chǔ Liánxiāng
The renowned courtesan Chǔ Liánxiāng of the capital,
a peerless beauty of the nation,
was constantly visited by scions of noble families vying for her attention.
Whenever Liánxiāng went out,
admirers would follow her like bees and butterflies,
drawn by her fragrance.
"Anecdotes from the Tiānbǎo Era"
Liú Guóróng
The famous courtesan Liú Guóróng of Cháng'ān,
possessed captivating beauty
and could compose poetry.
She shared a deep affection with the scholar Guō Zhāoshù,
and no one else dared to covet her.
Later, Guō Zhāoshù assumed an official post as the registrar of Tiāncháng County,
and thus had to part with Guóróng.
At dawn the next day, he set off for his post.
When he reached Xiányáng,
Guóróng sent a maidservant galloping on a small horse to deliver a brief letter, which read:
"Our joyous intimacy was at its peak,
yet I resent the crowing of the rooster for severing our love;
our affection has not yet fully blossomed,
and I lament the horse's hooves for their heartlessness.
You have burdened my heart and made me lose my appetite;
let us reunite in two years to fulfill our harmonious union."
The young men of Cháng'ān often recited these lines.
A Flower
During the Tiānbǎo era, the Prefect of Chángzhōu, Lord Xíngyáng's son, went to take the imperial examinations,
and became intimate with the Cháng'ān courtesan Lǐ Wáwa.
Later, she was enfeoffed as the Lady of Qiānguó.
The lady's former name was Yīzhīhuā (One Branch of Flower).
Yuán Zhěn, in his poem "One Hundred Rhymes Presented to Bái Jūyì in Response,"
wrote:
"We inscribe our names with brush and ink,
while time passes as we listen to tales."
The annotation states:
"Whenever Bái Jūyì and I traveled together,
we often inscribed our names on the walls of houses.
According to Gù Fùběn's account,
the story of Yīzhīhuā was told from the hour of yín to the hour of sì."
(from Yìwénjí)
Xuē Xiàoshū
Xuē Tāo was originally a daughter of a good family from Cháng'ān.
Her father, Xūn, died while serving as an official in Shǔ.
Her widowed mother raised Tāo.
Upon reaching maturity, she became known for her poetry.
She was also skilled at applying makeup and adorning her eyebrows,
unlike women from scholarly families.
Guests would secretly dine and converse with her.
At that time, Wéi Gāo, the Central Order, was governing Shǔ.
He summoned her to serve wine and compose poetry.
Many officials and scholars
changed their view of her because of this.
After a year,
the Central Order proposed to petition for her to be appointed as a Proofreader.
The Protector General said:
"It is not permissible."
Thus, it was halted.
Tāo came and went from the military headquarters,
from Wéi Gāo to Lǐ Déyù,
serving under a total of eleven military governors,
all of whom appreciated her for her poetry.
Among those who exchanged poems with Tāo
were Yuán Zhěn, Bái Jūyì, Niú Sēngrú, Líng Hú Chǔ, Péi Dù, Yán Shòu, Zhāng Jí, Dù Mù, Liú Yǔxī, Wú Wǔlíng, and Zhāng Hù,
all renowned scholars.
Records mention twenty individuals in total,
who eagerly engaged in poetic exchanges with her.
Tāo resided by the Hundred Flowers Pond,
personally crafting small, deep-red stationery,
cutting it for writing and composing poems,
which she presented to worthy and outstanding men.
It was then called Xuē Tāo Stationery.
In her later years, she lived at Bìjī Lane,
where she built a Poetry Tower,
and reposed upon it.
Later, Duàn Wénchāng again governed Chéngdū.
In the Tàihé era,
Tāo passed away at the age of seventy-three.
Wénchāng composed her epitaph.
"Shǔ Jiān Pǔ"
When Yuán Zhěn first received the position of Investigating Censor,
he was sent on a mission to Western Shǔ,
and learned of Xuē Tāo's existence,
but found it difficult to meet her.
Minister Yán, knowing his intention,
often sent Xuē to visit him.
After Zhěn ascended to the Hànlín Academy,
Xuē Tāo returned to her residence at Huànhuā,
where the people of Huànhuā made multicolored stationery.
Thereupon, Tāo created a new design,
producing small sheets of pine-patterned paper,
often used for inscribing poems.
She then sent over a hundred sheets to Lord Yuán.
Yuán, on the pine-patterned paper, sent her a poem in return, which read:
"The Brocade River, sleek and lovely, Mín and É peaks fair,
Conjure forth Wén Jūn and Xuē Tāo.
Her words cleverly steal the parrot's tongue,
Her essays share the phoenix's feather.
Numerous literary guests mostly lay down their brushes,
Every duke and marquis dreams of the knife.
After parting, longing for each other across misty waters,
The calamus flowers bloom beneath five-layered clouds high."
Xuē once enjoyed planting calamus,
hence this line.
"Mù Shù Xián Tán"
People of Shǔ all called camp courtesans Female Proofreaders,
thus Hú Zēng had a poem presented to Xuē Tāo, saying:
"By Wànlǐ Bridge dwells Proofreader Xuē,
Under the loquat blossoms, behind closed doors she lives.
How many talented ladies with painted eyebrows are known?
None can lead the spring breeze as she does."
Tāo was again favored by the military governor,
but due to an incident, she incurred blame,
and he, angered, distanced her.
She composed the "Ten Partings" poems and presented them,
the first saying:
"The dog parted from its master,
The brush parted from the hand,
The horse parted from its stable,
The parrot parted from its cage,
The mandarin duck parted from its nest,
The pearl parted from the palm,
The fish parted from the pond,
The hawk parted from its master,
The bamboo parted from the pavilion,
The mirror parted from its stand."
Thereupon, he was pleased with her again.
"Jiàn Jiè Lù"
Tāo was eloquent, witty, and knowledgeable in poetry.
A Lízhōu Prefect composed a Thousand Character Classic,
requiring the inclusion of fish, birds, and animals.
He then said:
"Yǒuyú Táotáng."
Tāo said:
"Zuǒshí Āhéng."
The man claimed her phrase lacked fish or birds and demanded a penalty.
Xuē said:
"In the character Héng,
there is the small character for fish.
Your phrase 'Yǒuyú Táotáng,'
contains not a single fish."
The seated guests laughed heartily.
"Táng Yǔ Lín"
Gāo Pián governed Chéngdū,
and ordered the wine attendant Xuē Tāo to compose a one-character riddle,
saying:
"It must depict the form of a character,
and also rhyme."
He said:
"Kǒu resembles a measure without a beam."
Tāo said:
"Chuān resembles three rafters."
He said:
"Why is one crooked?"
Tāo said:
"Your Excellency, as the Military Governor of Western Shǔ,
still uses a measure without a beam.
As for a poor wine attendant having three rafters,
with one of them crooked,
what is so strange about that?"
"Jì Yì Lù"
Tāo's courtesy name was Hóngdù,
originally a daughter of a good family from Cháng'ān.
Her father, Zhèng, resided in Shǔ due to his official post.
At eight or nine years old, Tāo understood phonology and meter.
One day, her father sat in a pavilion and, pointing to a well-side plane tree, said to her:
"In the courtyard, an ancient paulownia,
Its towering trunk reaches into the clouds."
He bade Tāo continue it,
and she responded immediately:
"Its branches welcome birds from north and south,
Its leaves see off the coming and going winds."
Her father became somber for a long while.
After her father died, her mother lived in widowhood.
Wéi Gāo governed Shǔ,
summoned her to serve wine and compose poetry,
and entered her into the music registry.
In her declining years, Tāo lived in seclusion at Huànhuā Brook,
dressed in Daoist nun attire,
and had five hundred poems.
"Jùn Gé Yǎ Tán"
Note: Pián began his tenure as Military Governor of Western Shǔ in the Qiánfú era,
which was over forty years after the Tàihé era.
It is suspected that "Jì Yì" contains errors in its account.
Regarding her appointment as Proofreader, some attribute it to Wéi Gāo,
others to Minister Yán,
while Cháo shì attributes it to Wǔ Yuánhéng.
For one person, records vary so greatly;
how can later generations determine the truth?
The "Ten Partings" poems are also attributed to Xuē's writing in "Zhí Yán."
The matter of presenting them to Yuán Zhěn.
Mirror Lake Spring Scenery
When Yuán Zhěn was inspecting Eastern Zhèjiāng,
a woman named Liú Cǎichūn came from the Huáidiàn region.
Yuán composed a poem for her containing the lines:
"Even more heart-wrenching and distressing
is selecting lyrics to sing the 'Song of Gazing for Her Husband'."
He also wrote while drunk at Dōngwǔ:
"Procrastinating and not yet returning
is not for longing of the perch fish."
Lú Jiǎnqiú jested:
"Although the Chancellor isn't staying for the perch fish,
he's staying for the charming spring scenery of Mirror Lake."
This referred to Cǎichūn.
From "Records of Táng Poetry Events"
Ā Ruǎn
When Bái Jūyì passed the imperial examination, he presented a quatrain to the courtesan Ā Ruǎn of Cháng'ān:
"A single fresh bloom of red lotus on green waters,
All other flowers and grasses pale in comparison."
Yuán Jí
records that in the late Zhēnyuán era, courtesan Ā Ruǎn gave birth to a daughter,
and asked Bái Jūyì to give her a childhood name.
Bái Jūyì said:
"This child is very fair-skinned,
you may name her Jiǎojiǎo."
A scholar once visited them,
and wondered why she was called Jiǎojiǎo.
Only after some time did he realize Bái Jūyì's jest,
which stemmed from her unclear lineage,
referencing the ancient poem that says "bright, bright shines the weaver girl."
From "Shàn Wèi Jí"
Gāo Línglóng
During the Chángqìng era, Bái Jūyì served as the Governor of Hángzhōu.
The official courtesans Gāo Línglóng and Xiè Hǎohǎo were skilled in conversation,
excelling in singing and dancing.
Later, when Yuán Zhěn governed Kuàijī,
he participated in their poetic exchanges over drinks,
often sending poems back and forth in bamboo tubes.
"Táng Yǔ Lín"
Cuī Huī
Cuī Huī was a courtesan from Pǔ,
when Péi Jìngzhōng of the same commandery, serving in the Xìngyuán administration, was sent as an envoy to Liáng,
she became infatuated at first sight,
and they stayed together for months.
When Jìngzhōng prepared to return,
Huī could not accompany him,
and her sorrow became unbearable.
Several months later,
Jìngzhōng's close friend Bái Zhītuì from the Dōngchuān administration arrived in Pǔ.
There was a Qiū Xià skilled in portrait painting,
so Zhītuì conveyed Huī's request,
and indeed obtained a masterpiece from Xià.
Holding the portrait, Huī told Zhītuì:
"Please thank Jìngzhōng for me.
Once Cuī Huī no longer resembles the lady in this painting,
I shall die for you, my lord."
The next day she went mad,
and from then on her illness progressed,
until she died, no longer looking as she did when painted.
"Collection of Beautiful Romances"
Good good
Dù Mù's "Poem for Zhāng Hǎohǎo" states:
"While I was serving as an aide to the late Minister of Personnel Shěn in the Jiangxi administration,
Hǎohǎo was thirteen years old,
and had joined the entertainment registry due to her exceptional singing.
Later, she moved to Xuānchéng when the Minister was transferred there,
and was subsequently taken in by Shěn the Archivist.
When I saw her in the eastern part of Luòyáng,
I was moved by memories and saddened at heart,
so I composed this poem to present to her."
"Records of Poetic Origins"
Zhuózhuó,
a courtesan of Jǐnchéng,
excelled at dancing the Zhèzhī
and singing the Shuǐdiào melodies.
At a banquet in the ministerial residence, she sat with a man from Hédōng,
their spirits connected through exchanged glances,
feeling as if they had long been acquainted.
From then on, they never met again.
Zhuózhuó wrapped her crimson tears in a soft silk handkerchief and secretly sent it to the man from Hédōng.
From "The Collection of Beautiful Passions"
Love love
Ài'ài, surnamed Yáng,
was a courtesan's daughter from Qiántáng.
On the Qīxī Festival, while boating on West Lake to gather lotus fragrance,
she was flirted with by a young man from Jīnlíng named Zhāng Dá.
They eloped together secretly,
and lived in the capital for over two years.
Later, she was captured and taken away by her father.
Afterwards, some rumors claimed Dá had already died.
Ài'ài, overwhelmed by longing, passed away.
Her young maid said:
"Jǐn'ér brought out her old embroidered silk shoes,
which remained fragrant and looked as if newly made."
End.
Dōng Dōng
Dòu Gǒng excelled at composing quatrains,
and once wrote "Mourning the Courtesan Dōngdōng" while serving in the army:
"Her fragrant beauty could not withstand the wind,
Before mid-spring, her rouge already fell.
Only the bell on the side-wheeled carriage,
Echoes in my ear, calling 'Dōngdōng'."
From "Collection of Lyrical Expressions"
Duānduān
Cuī Yá and Zhāng Hù were equally famous.
Whenever they wrote poems at brothels,
if they praised one, carriages and horses would crowd her door;
if they disparaged one, cups and plates would be in disarray.
They mocked Lǐ Duān, saying:
"At dusk, silent, unaware of walking,
Her nose like a smoking brazier, ears like cooking vessels.
She loves to comb her temples with an ivory comb,
On the Kunlun peak, the moon begins to rise."
Lǐ Duān then went to see the two men,
and pleaded again, saying:
"Duānduān wishes to serve the third and sixth young masters,
I beg for your compassion."
So they composed another poem for her:
"Having found a fine horse saddled with embroidered reins,
Go to Shanhe Ward to fetch Duānduān.
Recently in Yangzhou, all have become salt,
But one walking white peony remains."
Thereupon, guests competed to visit her door,
and someone said:
"Lady of the Lǐ family,
just emerged from the ink pond,
then ascended the snowy peak,
How is it that in one day,
black and white are uneven?"
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì"
Turning and turning
Yān commander Liú Réngōng sent his aide Mǎ Yù on a mission to Wáng Róng in Zhènzhōu.
Secretary Hán Dìngcí received him at the official guesthouse,
where there was a singing girl named Zhuǎnzhuǎn,
who was Hán's favorite.
Whenever they feasted,
Yù frequently glanced at her.
Hán said:
"In the past, Duke Wén of Jìn gave Jì Wěi to Zhào Cuī,
and Sūn Bófú bestowed Xiǎo Qiáo upon Zhōu Yǔ,
for renowned beauties may be presented to famous men.
I only fear this courtesan is unworthy of your esteemed attention.
I wish you would compose a verse for her,
so I may offer her to you."
Yù immediately took up the brush,
and without pause in his writing,
composed the "Rhapsody on Zhuǎnzhuǎn,"
which was exceptionally elegant.
All admired its clever excellence,
and it spread far and wide.
From "Beimeng Suoyan"
The rhapsody begins:
"The splendid banquet now begins,
elegant music is performed.
Silk curtains roll up like mist,
brocade mats bloom like flowers.
A distinguished guest from the western garden
summons a beauty from the southern land.
Her enchanting appearance displayed,
her jade-like countenance could topple cities;
her ethereal steps moving,
her silken skirts stirring dust as she treads."
Yù carried it back with him.
Liú Chóngyuǎn's "Ermu Ji" begins the same as "Beimeng"
Shū Xiān
In Cháng'ān there was a courtesan named Cáo Wénjī,
who was exceptionally skilled in calligraphy,
considered the finest in Guānzhōng,
and was known at the time as the Book Immortal.
A certain Rèn Shēng composed a poem for her:
"The Book Immortal who tends the library before the Jade Emperor's hall,
once her heart is touched by mortal dust, descends from the ninth heaven.
Do not wonder at the rich fragrance steeped into her bones—
her cloud-like robes have been caressed by the imperial incense smoke."
From "Collection of Beautiful Romances"
Xú Yuèyīng
Jiānghuái courtesan Xú Yuèyīng's farewell poem reads:
"How sorrowful that all things in this world defy our will,
Two set out together, yet only one returns.
I deeply loathe the waters by Píngwàng Bridge,
How can they bear to reflect mandarin ducks flying apart."
In Jīnlíng, a young master Xú favored an official courtesan,
Who died and was cremated.
Yuèyīng attended the funeral and said to Xú:
"This lady was charming all her life,
In death she should not be without flame."
This is known as witty banter.
From "Běimèng Suǒ Yán"
Hóng'ér
Luó'ér possessed a rich and abundant literary talent,
and was equally renowned as his clansman Lú Yǐnyè,
during the Xiantong and Qianfu eras, they were collectively known as the "Three Luós."
After the chaos of the Gengzi year in Guangming,
he went to serve Lǐ Xiàogōng in Fūzhōu.
Among the registered entertainers was one named Hóng'ér,
who excelled in music and voice,
and was often favored by the deputy commander.
On one occasion, when the deputy commander was hosting a guest from a neighboring region, Qiú,
he requested Hóng'ér to sing and presented her with silk gifts.
Lǐ Xiàogōng, aware of the deputy commander's affection for her,
did not allow her to accept them.
Qiú, enraged, rose abruptly with a flick of his sleeve and questioned the decision,
then personally killed Hóng'ér with his blade.
Later, reflecting on the incident,
he composed a hundred quatrains,
titled "Poems for Hóng'ér,"
which became widely popular at the time.
"Records of Conversations"
Ruìqīng
While Ōuyáng Bīn was in Húnán,
the Mǎ family did not employ him,
so he became destitute.
There was a street singer named Ruìqīng
who admired his talent and invited him to her home.
One day, when the convoy to Western Shǔ was about to depart,
Ruìqīng used her family wealth to support Bīn,
who followed the convoy officials to Shǔ.
There he presented the "Ode to the Lone Carp Facing Heaven,"
which greatly pleased the ruler of Shǔ.
He was promoted to a high and important position,
and later rose to the offices of Left Chancellor of the Department of State Affairs and Military Commissioner of Jīngzhōu.
"Supplementary Records of the History of the Five Dynasties"
Hán Xiāng
Hán Xiāng was a courtesan of Nánxú,
renowned for her beauty and talents,
who became involved with the son of General Yè.
She closed her doors to other guests,
intending to spend her life with him.
General Yè, angered by this,
submitted a petition to the authorities,
who assembled the official troops at the archery range.
She was married off to an old soldier among them.
Hán Xiāng went with him willingly,
and said:
"Husband and wife must observe the rites."
She bought a sheep, procured wine, and summoned relatives and friends to complete the ceremony.
When the guests arrived,
after three rounds of wine,
Hán Xiāng brought out the gold and silk she had brought with her,
distributing them according to rank,
then went to change clothes and did not return for a long time—
she had slit her own throat.
Alas,
one may tread upon a sharp blade,
but not submit to what is unjust.
When Oūyáng Xiū wrote his Miscellaneous Biographies,
he recorded the deeds of officials who served the Five Dynasties.
Though Hán Xiāng was not included in those biographies,
her integrity is also worthy of esteem.
Suíyǐn Màn Lù
Xiǎo Dōng
Xiǎo Dōng was a courtesan from Chángshā,
who won favor with the Mǎ family due to her poetic talent.
After the state was incorporated into a commandery,
she lived in poverty in the capital's alleys, completely unknown to others.
When speaking of events in the Chángshā palace,
she would always gaze southward and weep before continuing.
"Continued Record of Maids' Pet Names"
Lǐ Yànniáng
In the third year of the Guǎngzhèng era during the Later Shǔ under Mèng Chǎng, at the Lantern Festival viewing on the open-air platform,
the courtesan Lǐ Yànniáng, who was dancing, possessed great beauty.
She was summoned into the palace,
and her family was granted one hundred thousand coins.
From the "Unofficial History of Shǔ".
Jiàng Zhēn
In the Five Dynasties period, Chǔ's Mǎ Xīfàn loved the prostitute Xú Jiàngzhēn in his youth.
When he succeeded to the throne,
he gave her the title Lady of the Western Hall.
"Records of the Ten Kingdoms"
Taking a courtesan along
When Zhào Biàn served as magistrate of Qīngchéng,
he took a wandering entertainer-courtesan home with him.
When the county captain pursued and retrieved her, he was greatly pained and angered,
and further because he quarreled with his wife,
from this his resolve wavered.
"Unofficial History of the Kǒng Family"
When Qīngxiàn governed Shǔ,
daily there was a courtesan who wore apricot blossoms,
Qīngxiàn was fond of her,
and playfully said to her:
"The apricot blossom on your chignon is truly fortunate."
The courtesan responded immediately:
"Could the plum on the branch lack a matchmaker?"
As evening approached, he ordered her to be on duty overnight,
the old soldier was sent to summon her,
but by the second watch she had not arrived,
so he again sent someone to hasten her,
then immediately ordered to stop them,
the old soldier suddenly emerged from behind the curtain,
the lord was surprised and asked him,
the soldier said:
"I reckoned that Your Excellency would not last more than one double-hour,
this thought would then cease,
although I received the order,
I actually never went."
Huìmǔ's "Collection of Gathered Blossoms"
Lǐ Shīshī
Lǐ Shīshī was a famous courtesan in the capital,
favored by Emperor Huizong of Sòng while privately involved with Zhōu Bāngyàn,
their intimacy grew deep.
One day, as they were feasting intimately, it was reported
that the emperor had suddenly arrived.
Zhōu, in panic, hid under the bed.
The emperor, while seated, brought out fresh tangerines to eat,
prompting Zhōu to secretly compose a melody
celebrating the incident.
Later, when Shīshī sang it,
the emperor learned of it and was enraged,
sending Zhōu to a provincial post.
Shīshī went to bid him farewell,
and upon returning,
her melancholy remained unresolved,
tears still glistening in her eyes.
The emperor happened to arrive
and inquired about it.
Lǐ dared not conceal the truth,
confessing everything in detail.
Later, Zhōu was reinstated to his official position.
Xiè Tiānxiāng
In Jùyě there was a Lóngfāng Pavilion,
where the local people held harvest sacrifices.
One day the village elders planned to erect a stone tablet inside it,
and invited scholar Wáng Wéihàn to inscribe the characters "Lóngfāng Pavilion".
Wéihàn was delayed and hadn't arrived yet,
when a courtesan named Xiè Tiānxiāng asked:
"Since the sacrificial ceremony is already concluded,
why are we lingering here instead of drinking?"
The crowd replied:
"We're waiting for Wéihàn to inscribe the stone."
Xiè then used her sleeve
to write the two characters "Lóngfāng",
just as Wéihàn arrived.
He completed it by writing the character "pavilion",
and the elders had it carved into the stone.
Wáng and Xiè subsequently became husband and wife.
Later Wáng teasingly wrote a poem to Xiè:
"Once you danced with willowy waist in pleasure quarters,
where passersby wouldn't dare break a single branch."
Tiānxiāng replied:
"Now entrusted to the painter's hand,
it stands unshaken even by raging winds."
Later Wéihàn passed the imperial examination,
and grew old together with Tiānxiāng.
From the Gazetteer
Yán Ruǐ
Yán Ruǐ, a courtesan from Tiāntāi with the courtesy name Yòufāng,
was unparalleled in beauty and talent at the time.
Occasionally, she composed poetry with fresh expressions,
winning the admiration of Táng Yǔzhèng.
Later, Zhū Huì'ān arrived in Tái on an official inspection
and sought to fabricate charges against Táng Yǔzhèng.
He accused Táng of having improper relations with Ruǐ,
leading to her imprisonment for over a month.
Despite enduring torture, Ruǐ never implicated Táng,
even when officials tried to coax her with kind words.
Her resolve only grew firmer,
and she remained confined in prison,
suffering near-fatal torment.
Yet, her reputation soared even higher,
reaching the ears of the emperor.
Not long after,
Zhū was reassigned, and Yuè Lín Shāngqīng took over as judicial commissioner.
During a New Year's celebration,
moved by her haggard and ill state,
he finally asked her to compose a poem to plead her case.
That very day, he ordered her release to become a commoner,
and soon after, a relative of the imperial clan took her as a concubine,
where she lived out the rest of her life.
(From "Qí Cè Yě Yě")
Xīxī
Mǎ Guāngmíng served as the military commissioner of Gāoyóu,
when the garrison commander Róng Quán led his troops in rebellion,
occupying the city and allowing his soldiers to plunder.
While feasting with his accomplice Wáng Ān and others,
a courtesan named Máo Xīxī refused to attend and serve them.
Quán severely reprimanded her,
to which Xīxī responded:
"Although I am a lowly courtesan,
I have never served traitorous officials."
Quán then executed her,
and Fāng Yuè of Qiūyá wrote "The Tale of the Righteous Courtesan."
The Unofficial History of Three Reigns
reports that the matter was brought to the court's attention,
and she was posthumously honored as the Valiant and Heroic Lady.
Pán Tíngjiān wrote a poem:
"Máo Xīxī, the stunning beauty of Huáihǎi,
a peerless heroine among women.
If only she had a dagger like the Qin maiden,
or could emulate the loyalty of Gǎo Qīng.
Her jade-like bones and flower-like face now lie beneath the city walls,
her pure spirit and snowy soul are immortalized in history.
Countless throughout the ages wear golden belts,
yet spend their lives in feasts and song."
Records of Casual Seclusion
Táng Ān'ān
On the Lantern Festival during the Guǐchǒu year of Lǐzōng's reign, the emperor summoned courtesans into the palace.
Among them was one named Táng Ān'ān, whose singing and beauty were unparalleled.
The emperor grew fond of and favored her.
Vice Minister Móu Zǐcái remonstrated, saying:
"These are all the likes of Dǒng Sòngchén,
corrupting Your Majesty's virtuous conduct."
The "History of Sòng" does not record Táng's name.
Tiānzhōng Jì Volume Twenty
Beautiful and dazzling
Sòng Gōngzǐ Bào treated the people of the state with courtesy,
and Bào was handsome and strikingly attractive.
Lady Xiāng wished to have an affair with him but could not,
so she assisted him in distributing alms.
"Zuǒ Wén" sixteenth year
Handsome Appearance
During the reign of King Xiāng of Chǔ, Sòng Yù was on leave and returning home.
Táng Lè slandered him to the king,
The king said to Yù:
"Your body is handsome,
and your words are full of subtle expressions,
isn't that frivolous?"
Yù replied:
"My handsome body
was bestowed by my parents,
and my subtle expressions
were learned from the sages."
From Sòng Yù's "Ode to the Wind"
Fine jade
Zhāng Zǐfáng's wisdom,
led one to expect a man of imposing and extraordinary stature,
but upon seeing his portrait,
his appearance was like that of a beautiful woman.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Guānyù
Chén Píng was poor in his youth,
growing into a tall man with handsome features.
The wealthy Zhāng Fù alone saw greatness in Píng and said:
"How could one so handsome
as Chén Píng remain long in poverty?
I shall give him my daughter in marriage."
Later, Duke of Pèi appointed Píng as deputy general,
and someone slandered Píng, saying:
"Though Píng is a handsome man,
he is merely like ornamental jade on a cap,
with little substance within."
"Original Biography"
Like a gourd
The Duke of Pei passed through Yángwǔ while conquering territories,
and Zhāng Cāng joined his campaign as a guest advisor to attack Nányáng.
Zhāng Cāng was sentenced to execution,
but when he removed his garments and prostrated himself over the execution block,
his body appeared tall, large, plump, and pale like a gourd,
Wáng Líng, who was present at the time, marveled at his striking appearance as a handsome scholar,
and thus persuaded the Duke of Pei to pardon him and spare his life.
Records of the Hàn Dynasty
extremely beautiful
When Gōngsūn Hóng submitted his policy response, there were over a hundred candidates,
the Minister of Ceremonies reported that Hóng's ranking was among the lowest in the policy responses,
but the Son of Heaven elevated Hóng's response to first place,
summoned him for an audience, and found his appearance very handsome,
appointed him as an Erudite,
and assigned him to await orders at the Golden Horse Gate.
The Emperor
very beautiful
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's carriage and horsemen were dignified and graceful,
leisurely and elegant, very handsome.
The Emperor
Beautiful
Dǒng Yǎn initially made a living by selling pearls with his mother.
At the age of thirteen, he followed his mother to the residence of Princess Guàntáo.
Those around her remarked on his handsome appearance,
and the princess summoned him, saying:
"I shall raise you for your mother."
Thus, she kept him in her household,
teaching him writing, arithmetic, archery, and charioteering.
At the age of eighteen, he was capped,
and he served within the inner chambers.
Gentle and kind, he was beloved by others.
Due to the princess's influence, the nobility associated with him,
and his reputation spread throughout the city,
where he was known as Lord Dǒng.
Beautiful
Dǒng Xián, styled Shèngqīng,
served as a Gentleman of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
During the reign of Emperor Āi, he held the position of a Gentleman Attendant.
Once, while waiting in attendance below the palace hall,
he was a man of striking beauty.
Emperor Āi caught sight of him and was captivated by his appearance,
appointing him as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
The emperor's favor and affection for him grew daily.
When going out, Dǒng Xián would share the imperial carriage;
when inside, he attended closely by the emperor's side.
He often slept and rose with the emperor.
Once, while napping during the day, he lay partially on the emperor's sleeve.
When the emperor wished to rise,
Dǒng Xián had not yet awakened.
Unwilling to disturb Dǒng Xián,
the emperor cut off his sleeve and then arose.
Such was the depth of their affection.
to cut off from others
Wáng Shěn was over eight chǐ tall,
with a massive physique,
and exceptionally imposing features that surpassed ordinary men.
When the Chányú came to court,
he looked up at Wáng Shěn and hesitated,
then retreated before the Son of Heaven.
The Emperor, hearing of this, sighed and said:
"This is truly the Prime Minister of Hàn."
Like Jade
Lù Hòng, styled Zǐchūn,
was the son of Chàng from Wú County,
belonging to a prominent clan for generations,
sincere in conduct and fond of learning,
intelligent and possessing fine virtues.
He was intended to marry Princess Níngpíng,
but declined on grounds of illness and did not accept.
During the Jiànwǔ era, he served as Imperial Secretary.
Hòng's appearance was as flawless as jade,
and he enjoyed wearing Yuè cloth unlined garments.
Emperor Wǔ, ascending the tower, saw him and admired his greatness,
sighing and saying:
"The south indeed has many beautiful people."
From then on, he often ordered the Kuàijī Commandery to present Yuè cloth.
Xiè Chéng's "Hànshū Wúdì Jì"
Like a painting
Mǎ Yuán was seven chi five cun tall,
with a complexion, hair, and skin,
and eyebrows, eyes, and facial features as if painted.
"Records of the Eastern Pavilion"
Magnificent and beautiful
Chén Qiáo served as a minister,
with a majestic and handsome appearance.
He frequently submitted advice on state affairs,
and Emperor Huán admired his talent and looks,
ordering him to marry a princess.
Chén Qiáo firmly declined but was not heeded,
so he sealed his lips and fasted for seven days until he died.
Xiè Chéng's "Book of the Later Hàn"
His appearance differed from ordinary people.
Cài Yōng, courtesy name Bójiē,
said to his cousin Gǔ:
"Dǒng Zhuó's nature is rigid and difficult to assist,
I plan to flee east of the mountains and wait,
what do you think?"
Gǔ said:
"Your appearance differs from ordinary people,
every time you go out, onlookers crowd around,
trying to hide yourself this way,
wouldn't it be difficult?"
So he stopped.
End
Pollination
Hé Píngshū possessed a handsome appearance,
with an extremely fair complexion.
Emperor Míng of Wèi suspected he wore powder,
so during the height of summer, he was given hot soup and cakes.
After eating, he sweated profusely,
and wiped his face with his red garment.
His complexion became even more radiant.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Yàn was naturally fond of his own appearance and demeanor,
never letting go of powder and silk,
and while walking, he would gaze at his own shadow.
"Weilüe"
Leaning against Jade
Contemporaries described Xiàhóu Tàichū as radiant, like the sun and moon entering one's embrace.
Emperor Míng had his empress's younger brother Máo Zēng sit together with Xiàhóu Xuán,
and people of the time said it was like reeds leaning against a jade tree.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Dejected
Lǐ Ānguó's decline was like a jade mountain about to crumble.
"Collapse Above"
Lǐ Fēng, styled Ānguó,
was skilled at evaluating people,
and attracted attention throughout the land.
When Emperor Míng obtained defectors from Wú,
he asked them what renowned scholars from the Central Plains were known in Jiāngdōng.
They answered with Ānguó's name.
At that time, Lǐ Fēng served as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
and had changed his name to Xuān.
The Emperor asked where Ānguó was,
and the attending ministers and high officials immediately identified him as Lǐ Fēng.
The Emperor said, "So Fēng's reputation has even reached Wú and Yuè?"
"The Unofficial History of Wèi"
Dragon's grace and phoenix's bearing
Jī Kāng stood seven feet eight inches tall,
with magnificent features and complexion.
His frame was like unadorned earth and wood,
yet without embellishment or polish, he possessed the grace of a dragon and the bearing of a phoenix,
a natural quality of heaven,
so that even amidst a crowd,
he knew himself to be an extraordinary vessel.
The "Bié Zhuàn"
records observers sighing in admiration:
"So lofty and dignified,
so refreshingly clear and elevated."
Some said:
"Solemn as beneath a pine tree,
with a lofty wind gently blowing."
Shān Tāo remarked:
"Jī Shūyè's character
is towering like a lone pine standing independently;
when drunk,
he totters like a jade mountain about to collapse."
The "Shì Shuō"
records someone telling Wáng Róng:
"Jī Yánzǔ stands out conspicuously like a wild crane among chickens."
He replied:
"You haven't seen his father yet."
Wúshuāng
Shí Bāo, styled Zhòngróng,
was a native of Nánpí in Bóhǎi.
He was refined, broad-minded, and intelligent,
with a majestic and handsome appearance.
He did not bother with minor formalities,
so people of the time said of him:
"Shí Zhòngróng, peerless in elegance."
Book of Jìn
Throwing Fruits
Pān Yuè possessed exquisite features and
an elegant demeanor.
In his youth, carrying a slingshot, he roamed the roads of Luòyáng,
where women who encountered him would invariably join hands to encircle him.
"Shì Shuō"
records that Ānrén (Pān Yuè) was exceedingly handsome,
and whenever he went out, elderly women would fill his carriage with thrown fruit.
"Yǔ Lín"
Lián Bì
Pān Ānrén and Xiàhóu Zhàn both had handsome appearances,
enjoyed walking together,
and were called "paired jades" by contemporaries.
Yuè and Zhàn shared a deep bond,
hence they delighted in traveling together.
"Shì Shuō"
The Jade Man
Péi Kǎi, styled Shūzé,
served as Vice Minister of Personnel. His demeanor was lofty and transcendent,
his appearance handsome and spirited,
he extensively studied numerous texts,
and was particularly skilled in philosophical reasoning,
earning him the contemporary nickname "Jade Man."
"Book of Jin"
Minister Péi possessed outstanding looks and bearing,
whether wearing ceremonial caps, coarse clothing, or with disheveled hair, he always appeared refined,
leading people of his time to regard him as a jade man.
Those who saw him remarked:
"Seeing Péi Shūzé is like walking on a jade mountain,
his radiance illuminates those around him."
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
A being beyond worldly affairs
Wáng Yǎn's appearance was uniquely striking,
bright and elegant like a deity.
"Records of Famous Scholars"
In his youth, he once visited Shān Tāo,
who sighed in admiration for a long while.
After Wáng Yǎn left, Shān Tāo gazed after him and said:
"What kind of old woman gave birth to such a splendid child!"
"Book of Jin"
Yǐfǔ's features were dignified and handsome,
and he excelled in discussing metaphysics,
often holding a white jade-handled
duster that seemed indistinguishable from his hand.
Wáng Róng remarked:
"The Grand Commandant's divine demeanor is lofty and transcendent,
like jade trees in a gemmed forest,
naturally existing beyond the worldly dust."
Lord Wáng described the Grand Commandant as majestically pure and towering,
like a cliff standing a thousand ren high.
Wáng Dūn praised the Grand Commandant:
"Among crowds of people,
he resembles pearls and jade amidst tiles and stones."
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Shí Lè, upon seeing Yǐfǔ, said to his Chief Clerk Kǒng Cháng:
"I have traveled extensively under heaven,
yet never have I seen such a man.
Should we spare his life or not?"
Cháng replied:
"As one of the Jin's Three Excellencies, he will not serve us."
Shí Lè said:
"Even so,
we must not harm him with a blade."
That night, he had him killed by pushing a wall over him.
"Tales of the Eight Princes"
A Beauty as Exquisite as Jade
Wèi Jiè stood out among the crowd,
truly possessing the aura of an extraordinary person.
As a young child, he rode a white goat-drawn carriage through the streets of Luòyáng,
and everyone exclaimed:
"Whose jade-like person is this?"
Thus, his family, community, and district hailed him as the "Jade Person."
From Bié Zhuàn:
Chancellor Wǎng, upon seeing Wèi the Palace Guard,
remarked, "He appears so frail,
that even with constant care and nourishment,
he seems unable to bear the weight of fine silk."
From Shì Shuō:
Wáng Chéng, Wáng Xuán, and Wáng Jì all enjoyed great fame,
yet all ranked below Wèi Jiè.
It was said in the world:
"The three sons of the Wáng family
are no match for the one child of the Wèi family."
From Jìn Shū:
When Wèi Jiè traveled from Yùzhāng to the lower capital,
people had long heard of his reputation,
and spectators crowded like a wall.
Wèi had long suffered from a frail constitution,
his body unable to endure the strain,
and he fell ill and died.
People of the time said he was "gazed to death"—Wèi Jiè.
From Shì Shuō.
A person among immortals
Wáng Yòujūn, upon seeing Dù Hóngzhì, sighed and said:
"His face is like congealed lard,
his eyes like lacquer dots,
this is a man among immortals."
When people of the time praised the appearance of Wáng Chǎngshǐ,
Lord Cài said:
"I regret that you gentlemen have not seen Dù Hóngzhì."
In
the Yonghe era, Liú Tán and Xiè Shàng discussed together,
and some court officials said:
"Dù Yì possesses pure elegance and noble demeanor,
being the outstanding talent among later generations,
roughly comparable to Wèi Jiè."
Shàng said:
"How can they be compared?
There is room for several people between them, Tán."
He also said:
"Dù Yì has physical purity,
while Shūbǎo has spiritual purity,"
Huán Yí also said this.
"Records of Famous Gentlemen South of the Yangtze" and "Book of Jin"
A dazzling array of pearls and jades
Someone visited Minister Wáng,
and encountered General Ānfēng and the Chancellor present.
Going to another room, he saw Jìyìn and Píngzǐ.
Upon returning, he told others:
"Today's visit,
wherever I looked, I saw brilliant pearls and jades."
Shì Shuō
No longer resembling ordinary people.
Wáng Méng, courtesy name Shìzǔ,
possessed a handsome appearance.
Every time he looked in the mirror, he would say:
"How did Wáng Wénkāi manage to produce such a fine son?"
He was also extremely fond of hats.
Believing himself to be handsome,
he once entered a hat shop,
where the old woman selling hats gave him a new hat.
"Yǔlín"
Lín Dào remarked that Wáng Chángshǐ, when drinking, would display such elegance,
how magnificent he was,
with such graceful bearing. When Chángshǐ served as Zhōngshū Láng,
he went to Wáng Jìnghé's residence.
At that time, snow had accumulated,
and Chángshǐ alighted from his carriage outside the gate,
walking into the Ministry of Personnel.
Dressed in official robes,
Jìnghé looked at him from afar and sighed:
"This is no longer like a mortal man."
"Shì Shuō"
Character and Integrity
Huán Wēn was forthright and had an imposing demeanor,
with a very majestic appearance.
His face bore seven moles,
and in his youth, he was close friends with Liú Tán from the State of Pei.
Liú Tán once praised him, saying:
"Wēn's sideburns are like reversed hedgehog quills,
his skin and eyebrows
and eyes
resemble the ridges of purple stone;
he is truly a man of the same caliber as Sūn Zhòngmóu and Sīmǎ Xuānwáng."
"Jìn Shū Shì Shuō"
Initially, Huán Wēn believed that his imposing presence and charismatic aura
made him a peer of Xuāndì and Liú Kūn.
When someone compared him to Wáng Dūn,
he felt quite displeased.
Later, when he returned from an expedition,
he encountered a skilled elderly maidservant in the north.
Upon inquiring,
he learned she was a singing girl who had served Liú Kūn.
As soon as she saw Huán Wēn, she silently wept.
Huán Wēn asked her the reason,
and she replied:
"Your Excellency greatly resembles Minister of Works Liú Kūn."
Greatly pleased, he went outside,
adjusted his attire and cap,
and called the maidservant again to ask;
she said his face was quite similar but regrettably thinner,
his eyes were quite similar but regrettably smaller,
his beard was quite similar but regrettably redder,
his stature was quite similar but regrettably shorter,
and his voice was quite similar but regrettably more effeminate.
Huán Wēn then removed his cap and loosened his belt,
sank into a daze and slept,
and remained displeased for several days.
"Jìn Shū"
Yù Jǔ
Liú Wàn'ān, also known as Dàozhēn's nephew,
was described by Yǔ Cóng as "radiant like a jade being elevated,"
and also said, "visible among a thousand people,
visible among a hundred people."
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Roaming Clouds
People of the time described Wáng Xīzhī as floating like roaming clouds,
and soaring like a startled dragon.
Morning glow
In the Western Seas era, whenever the officials gathered at court, the hall was still dim;
only when the Prince of Kuàijī arrived did he radiate like the rising morning clouds.
Appearance and Spirit
Xún Xiàn, courtesy name Lìngzé,
followed his father Xún Sōng to Shítóu at age seven,
where Sū Jùn admired his graceful demeanor,
often seating him on his lap.
At fifteen, when a royal marriage was proposed for him,
he fled to the Yánsī in Chángshā,
but was pursued and compelled to return,
eventually marrying Princess Xúnyáng.
His aura was heroic and refined,
with bright eyes and brows that conveyed depth in every glance.
"Appearance and Bearing"
deemed him exemplary.
"Family Biography"
Fresh and Lush Spring Moon Willow, Zhāng
Wáng Gōng was handsome in appearance,
and many people adored him.
Some described him as "fresh and graceful like a willow in the spring moon."
Once, he wore a crane-feather cloak and walked through the snow.
Mèng Chǎng caught sight of him
and sighed,
"This is truly a man among immortals."
History of the Jin Dynasty
Dé Gě Wúhèn
Chényōng Chén Zhōng's daughter, named Fēng,
had a neighbor, Gě Bó, who was handsome.
Fēng and several village girls gathered to wind silk and play,
saying to each other:
"If we could get a husband like Gě Bó,
we would have no regrets."
"Yì Yuàn"
Two jade-like figures
Xiè Huì of the Sòng dynasty possessed elegant demeanor,
excelling in conversation and laughter,
with distinct eyebrows and eyes,
and hair as black as lacquer.
He dabbled in literary meanings,
being erudite and well-versed in many fields.
Contemporaries compared him to Yáng Gāozǔ, though slightly inferior,
which Huì, upon hearing, still regarded as a regret.
At that time, Xiè Hùn's elegance was unmatched in Jiāngzuǒ,
and he once stood with Huì before Emperor Wǔ.
The emperor gazed at them and said:
"In one moment, two jade-like men appear."
(From *History of the Southern Dynasties*, Volume 9)
Shuāngzhū
Mèng Yǐ, courtesy name Yǎnchóng,
was from Ānqiū, Píngchāng.
He was the younger brother of General of the Guards Mèng Chǎng.
Both Chǎng and Yǐ possessed elegant demeanors,
earning them the contemporary nickname "Twin Pearls."
The Emperor
His drinking and eating manners were admirable.
Wáng Yù, styled Jǐngwén,
was cherished by his paternal uncle Wáng Qiú from childhood for his intelligence.
His elegant demeanor was highly praised by his contemporaries.
When Yuán Càn saw him,
he sighed and said:
"Jǐngwén is not only refined and cultured,
but even his drinking and eating manners
are also quite admirable."
There was a guest who had seen Xiè Hùn in his youth,
and replied:
"When Jǐngwén is compared to Uncle Xiè,
then Xiè appears rustic."
Yuán Càn was melancholy for a long while and said:
"I regret not having seen this man with my own eyes."
Book of Sòng
Lántián shēng yù
Xiè Zhuāng, courtesy name Xīyì,
could compose essays at seven years old.
When he grew up, he was handsome with elegant demeanor,
Emperor Wén of the Sòng dynasty saw him and considered him extraordinary,
saying to the Imperial Secretary Attendant Yīn Jǐngrén and General Liú Zhàn:
"Is it empty talk that blue fields produce jade?"
The emperor
Jīngchǔ Xiānrén
Gǒng Qí, whose courtesy name was Gàidào,
was a native of Hànshòu.
His demeanor was dignified and elegant,
and his appearance was admirable.
When the Court Secretariat official Fàn Shù saw him,
he sighed and said:
"This is an immortal from the Jing-Chu region."
Wind instrument
Yǔ Gǎozhī's demeanor was harmonious and gentle,
He was skilled in elocution,
Emperor Shìzǔ ordered him to face the enemy envoy while serving as Palace Attendant,
The emperor often admired the beauty of his demeanor and bearing,
Wáng Jiǎn, who was present, said:
"Gǎozhī, illuminated by the cicada-patterned official cap,
Gains even more grace and elegance."
From *The Book of Southern Qí*
Two pairs
Emperor Xiàowǔ of the Sòng selected four attendants.
Among them, based on their demeanor and appearance,
Wáng Yù and Xiè Zhuāng were paired as one duo,
while Wán Tāo and Hé Yǎn formed another pair.
They were frequently assigned concurrent and substitute roles.
The emperor approved.
Fāng Hé
Chǔ Yànyí possessed handsome features,
elegant demeanor,
with every bow, rise, advance, or retreat
exuding refined grace.
At court assemblies,
all officials and envoys from distant countries would crane their necks and follow him with their gaze.
Emperor Míng once sighed in admiration:
"If Chǔ Yànhuí can maintain such measured steps and unhurried gait,
he is truly fit to be a chancellor."
Contemporaries compared him to Hé Píngshū.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Fāng Jī
Fú Mànróng, styled Gōngyí,
Emperor Míng of the Liú Sòng dynasty was fond of the "Classic of Changes,"
and gathered his ministers in the Qīngshǔ Hall to expound upon the imperial decree.
Mànróng, styled Gōngyí,
held the classic with an elegant demeanor,
and the emperor often compared him to Jī Shūyè.
At night, he ordered the painter Lù Tànwēi to paint a portrait of Shūyè to bestow upon him.
"Biographies of Confucian Scholars of the Liáng Dynasty"
Wèi Dù zài mù
Hé Jiǒng, styled Shìguāng,
had fair skin and handsome features.
His elder cousin Hé Qiúdiǎn often praised him, saying:
"Shūbǎo was clear in spirit,
Hóngzhì was clear in complexion;
now looking at this young man,
I see again Wèi Dù in his time."
From "Biographies of Filial Conduct"
Public Expectation
Chǔ Xiàng, courtesy name Jǐngzhèng,
was the grandson of Chǔ Yuān and father of Chǔ Xiáng.
He served as Palace Attendant,
with dignified and handsome demeanor,
his eyebrows and eyes appearing delicately painted.
Whenever he stood in court formation,
he became the focus of everyone's gaze.
After his passing,
his maternal cousin Xiè Biǎo composed his epitaph:
"Surpassing Huá in broad governance,
putting Zǐsōng to shame in magnanimity.
Wine returns beneath the moonlight,
breeze freshens over the zither."
Readers considered it a fitting portrayal of the man.
End
The spirit is immensely vigorous
Cuī Lì, styled Chángrú,
had a majestic and handsome appearance,
excelled in demeanor and conduct,
and was dignified and awe-inspiring like a deity.
The foremost of later generations
Cuī Zhān, courtesy name Yàntōng,
was fair-skinned and handsome in demeanor,
with a dignified and imposing presence.
Lǐ Shénjùn, the Palace Attendant, was widely admired for his refined character,
yet in his later years, he had no son.
Upon seeing Cuī Zhān, he sighed and remarked to Xíng Shào:
"Yesterday, I saw Cuī Líng’s son,
and he stands as the foremost among the younger generation.
I have no one like him."
Yáng Yīn appointed him as a Vice Director of the Central Secretariat, saying:
"In the past, Péi Zàn of the Jin dynasty served as a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
with a lofty and transcendent spirit.
Whenever he passed through the palace gates,
the guards would straighten up with respect.
Cuī Zhān, in his magnificence,
is surely no less worthy than Péi Zàn."
Two Heavenly Men
Cuī Zǐyuē was over eight feet tall,
with a strikingly handsome and extraordinary demeanor.
He secretly observed Liáng's envoy Liú Xiàoyí,
startling the eyes of the guests and attendants who saw him.
During the Wǔdìng era, he went to Jìnyáng with his nephew Zǐzhān,
staying at a Buddhist temple.
Every time they stood for a long time after court,
Zǐyuē would lean against a table facing him,
both possessing magnificent appearances and presence,
standing in solemn and harmonious contrast.
The monks secretly watched them,
believing them to be two celestial beings.
"History of the Northern Dynasties"
Face like a lotus
Zhāng Yìzhī had fair skin and handsome features,
and together with his younger brother Chāngzōng, both served in the palace.
They both applied powder and rouge, wearing embroidered silk garments,
and both enjoyed the favor akin to that of Pìyáng.
Wǔ Chéngsì and others called Yìzhī the Fifth Lord,
and Chāngzōng the Sixth Lord.
Yáng Zàisī flattered them, saying:
"People say the Sixth Lord's face resembles a lotus,
but Zàisī believes the lotus resembles the Sixth Lord,
not that the Sixth Lord resembles the lotus."
(Old Book of Táng)
Elegant and poised
Emperor Xuánzōng held an early court audience,
all officials hastened to their positions,
the emperor noticed that Zhāng Jiǔlíng's demeanor was elegant and dignified,
standing out among the crowd,
and said to his attendants:
"Whenever I see Zhāng Jiǔlíng,
my spirits are instantly uplifted."
From "Yǔ Lín"
The imperial court's ceremonial regalia
Lǐ Kuí possessed an elegant demeanor and appearance,
excelled in responding to imperial inquiries,
and Emperor Sùzōng admired and praised him,
once saying to Kuí:
"Your family status, personal qualities, and literary works are all unmatched in our time,
truly making you a paragon of the court."
Thus contemporaries called him the "Triple Excellence."
According to the Old Book of Tang,
when Lú Qǐ sent Lǐ Kuí on a mission to Tibet,
upon arrival,
the Tibetan chieftain asked:
"Are you the renowned Lǐ Kuí, called the foremost man of the Tang court?"
Kuí replied:
"That is not so.
How would the foremost man of Tang be willing to come here?
Fearing detention,
I deceived him with this answer."
When Kuí retired from office,
Grand Minister of Education Dù, who had left his Huaihai post,
met him in Luòyáng,
and mentioned the talk of him being foremost in everything.
Kuí responded:
"If speaking of family background,
I did inherit something,
that is true,
and regarding official positions and opportunities,
but now my body is worn and haggard,
soon to depart this world where all becomes void,
what 'foremost' can there be?"
From Yulin.
Jade-crowned
Cuī Dàn's demeanor was elegant and lofty,
contemporaries called him "the jade-crowned Zǐyuǎn,"
his literary talent was pure and exquisite,
his bearing refined and handsome.
All admired his character,
regarding him as the pear placed at the banquet table—
a treasure upon the mat.
(From Biography of Cuī Guǎn of the Tang Dynasty)
Living Bodhisattva
Xuē Tiáo and Jì Zǎn were candidates who passed the imperial examination in the same year.
Tiáo had a handsome appearance,
and people called him a living Bodhisattva.
Zǎn was talented and forthright,
and people called him a sword.
Tiáo was tolerant and forgiving, while Zǎn was suspicious and jealous.
Commentators believed that the nicknames given by contemporaries matched their temperaments.
When Liú Yuánzhāng left Jiāngxià and returned to the court,
he maintained an elegant demeanor.
One day, Tiáo paid him a visit,
and Yuánzhāng hurried out to welcome him,
admiring his refined charm.
He repeatedly urged Tiáo to stay even as he was leaving.
After Tiáo had departed,
Yuánzhāng said to his attendants:
"It’s as if one cannot find
a single
flaw in him."
Tiáo served as a Hanlin Academician,
and Consort Guō admired his looks.
She said to Emperor Yìzōng:
"How about choosing Xuē Tiáo as a son-in-law?"
(From "Yǔlín")
Lù Yán
Lù Shìzhōng Yán's beauty of appearance and demeanor
was renowned throughout the land.
During his tenure in Chéngdū,
he delegated governance to his clerk Biān,
devoting his days to alchemy and elixirs,
accompanied by feasts along the Jiāng-Huái region.
The young men and women of the capital cherished the memory of his fruit-tossing charm,
surpassing even Wèi Jiè and Pān Yuè.
He excelled in styling his headscarf,
and the people of Shǔ would imitate it upon sight.
Later, he trimmed the ends of his gauze scarf
to distinguish himself from the crowd.
When commoners dressed flamboyantly and adorned themselves excessively,
people would mock them, saying:
"Are you not Lù Shìzhōng?"
Once, arriving at a pork market,
he saw a butcher preparing pork and remarked:
"This pig's features are so regular,
even Lù Shìzhōng cannot compare."
Using such a comparison
was truly laughable.
Duānměi
Shěnxún shìláng qīngcuì duānměi,
shénxiān zhōng rén yě,
chú shānběi jiémáo,
jīngshī xián zhòng zhī,
sòng Cáo Táng 《yóuxiān shī》 yún:
"Yù zhào xīn chú Shěn shìláng,
biàn fēn máotǔ lǐng dōngfāng.
Bùzhī jīnyè yóu héchù,
shìcóng jiē qí bái fènghuáng."
Jí fēngzī kě zhī yě.
《Běi Mèng》
Guānyīn of the Water and Moon
Minister Jiǎng Níng was also a figure of distinction.
Whenever he visited the homes of court officials,
people considered it an auspicious sign,
calling him the "Water-Moon Guānyīn."
In the late Táng dynasty,
among the court officials there were those who were figures of distinction,
and they were known at the time as the "Jade Shoots Group."
Wáng Jièchǐ
Zhào Féng served in the Táng and Liáng dynasties,
passing away during the Tiānchéng era.
His literary talent and virtuous conduct,
along with his elegant demeanor and outstanding appearance,
earned him the nickname "Jade Ruler."
Twice he ascended to high court positions,
and four times he retired to a rustic garden life.
The official gentry held him in high esteem.
"Northern Dreams"
Handsome man
Duke Xiàn of Jìn wished to attack Yú but feared the presence of Gōng Zhīqí.
Xún Xī said:
"The Book of Zhōu states that a handsome man can undermine the old."
So he sent them a handsome man,
instructing him to slander Gōng Zhīqí.
Gōng Zhīqí remonstrated but was not heeded, so he fled.
Thereupon they attacked Yú,
and captured it.
"Strategies of Qín"
Sharing the Peach
Mí Zǐxiá was favored by Duke Líng of Wèi.
According to the laws of Wèi, anyone who secretly drove the ruler's carriage would suffer the punishment of foot amputation.
When Mí Zǐxiá's mother fell ill,
someone went at night to inform Mí Zǐxiá,
who then falsely took the ruler's carriage and drove out.
The Duke heard of this and praised him, saying:
"How filial!
For his mother's sake,
he forgot the crime punishable by foot amputation."
Another day, while strolling with the Duke in an orchard,
he ate a peach and found it sweet but did not finish it,
instead offering half to the Duke.
The Duke said:
"How he loves me!
He forgot his own taste
to offer it to me."
Later, when Mí Zǐxiá's looks faded and favor waned,
and he offended the Duke,
the Duke said:
"This man once falsely took my carriage to drive,
and once fed me with a half-eaten peach."
From "Hánzǐ"
Lord Ānlíng
Chán
gained favor with King Gòng of Chǔ due to his handsome and robust appearance.
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"Those who bond through wealth
will see their friendship end when the wealth is exhausted;
those who bond through appearance
will see love fade when beauty withers.
Thus, a favored beauty does not outlast the mat,
a favored minister does not outlast the carriage.
I hope you will request to follow him in death,
sacrificing your life as a burial companion."
"Chǔ Cè Shuō Yuàn"
A favored woman does not outlast the mat,
a favored man does not outlast the carriage.
"Zhēn Gào"
The Former Fish
The King of Wèi and Lord Lóng Yáng were fishing together from a boat,
when Lord Lóng Yáng caught over ten fish and began to weep.
He explained that just as he would discard his earlier catches upon hooking a bigger fish,
so might the king abandon him upon finding new beauties.
Note: He was a favored minister of Wèi.
From "Strategies of the Warring States."
Chángsūn Zuǒfǔ wrote in "Ancient Palace Lament":
"How could one feel ashamed of what is distant,
when the pond crane abandons what lies ahead?"
See "Weeping over the Boat Fish" in Wǔlíng,
and "Chángxìn Palace" says, once sorrow begins,
how many times has the day fan wept for former fish?
These all use it in the context of palace ladies,
which seems mistaken.
Male beauty
As the saying goes, "Diligent farming is not as good as encountering a good year,"
"Being skilled in officialdom is not as good as meeting the right opportunity,"
which are certainly not empty words.
It is not only women who use their beauty to charm and serve,
but eunuchs also have such cases.
In the past, many gained favor through their looks.
The "Biographies of Sycophants" in the Records of the Grand Historian
records those with gentle and delicate charm,
implying it is not solely a female virtue,
for there are also male beauties.
As stated in the "Appraisal" of the Book of Han.
Male Favorites
Since the Xianning and Taikang eras, male favoritism has flourished greatly,
even surpassing that for women,
with scholars and officials all esteeming it,
and the whole world imitating the practice.
Some even led to couples separating and breaking apart,
giving rise to numerous grievances and loneliness.
"Records of the Jin Dynasty"
Exclusive Favor
When Fú Jiān first conquered Yān,
Mùróng Chōng's elder sister, Princess Qīnghé, was fourteen years old,
possessing extraordinary beauty.
Jiān took her as a consort,
and she became the most favored in the harem.
Chōng was twelve years old,
and also had the allure of a Lóng Yáng.
Jiān also favored him intimately.
The siblings enjoyed exclusive favor,
and no other palace attendants could gain access.
A song circulated in Cháng'ān:
"One female and one male,
flying in pairs into the Purple Palace."
Everyone feared this would lead to chaos.
Wáng Měng sternly advised against it,
so Jiān sent Chōng away.
Later, Chōng advanced and besieged Cháng'ān.
Jiān sent him a brocade robe, saying:
"I have shown you great kindness and favor.
Why have you suddenly turned against me in a single day?"
From the "Records of the States."
Xí Lěi
Shěn Yuē's "Essay of Repentance" states:
"Recalling my youth,
when vitality was at its peak,
entangled by habitual burdens,
matters were hard to resolve;
at Qí River's upper palace,
truly there were not many.
Sharing peaches and severing sleeves,
were also enough to be called numerous.
This truly bores through life and death like a prison,
not easily cleansed or extracted."
Guǎng Hóng Míng Jí
Separate couch
Xiāo Sháo, courtesy name Démào,
was loved by Yǔ Xìn since childhood,
who cherished him deeply.
They shared an intimate relationship,
with all clothing and sustenance provided by Xìn.
When guests arrived, Sháo would relay messages for Xìn.
After drinking, Sháo became Governor of Yǐng Province,
while Xìn traveled west to Jiānglíng.
Passing through Jiāngxià,
Sháo received Xìn quite coldly.
Seated beneath a blue oiled tent, he summoned Xìn to a banquet,
placing him on a separate couch
with a self-important expression.
Xìn, growing somewhat intolerable,
took advantage of drunkenness to stride directly onto Sháo's couch,
trampling over the food and dishes,
then gazed straight at Sháo's face and declared:
"Your official appearance today
greatly differs from recent days."
With the hall filled with guests at that moment,
Sháo felt profoundly ashamed.
(From History of the Southern Dynasties)
Ān Mèi
Wáng Yìfāng impeached Lǐ Yìfǔ,
the memorial stated:
Yìfǔ cultivates gentleness to build trust,
taking flattery as his core disposition.
He formerly served Mǎ Zhōu,
sharing a peach to gain favor;
later befriended Liú Jì,
cutting a sleeve to receive grace.
They became his wings,
thus he ascended to prominence.
From "Wéncuì"
Wá Yuán
A beautiful woman is called yuán.
The "Máo Shī Zhù"
states that wá, tuǒ, tiǎo, and yàn
all mean beautiful.
Between Jīngchǔ, Héng, and Huái, she is called wá;
beyond Nánchǔ, she is called tuǒ;
between Sòng, Wèi, Jìn, and Zhèng, she is called yàn;
between Chén, Chǔ, Zhōu, and Nán, she is called tiǎo.
Thus, Wú had the Guǎnwá Palace,
and Sū Qín spoke of zhēn é.
Between Sū Qín and Jìn, a beautiful appearance is called é,
or sometimes jiāo;
between Zhào, Wèi, Yān, and Dài, she is called shū;
west of the pass, in the old capitals of Qín and Jìn, she is called yán.
A beautiful form is tiǎo,
a beautiful color is yàn,
and a beautiful heart is yǎo.
Yì and yè refer to appearance;
west of the pass, all beautiful appearances are called yì,
or sometimes yè.
In Sòng and Wèi, it is yè;
between Chén, Chǔ, Rǔ, and Yǐng, it is called yì.
The "Fāngyán"
states that a lovely appearance is called miáo,
a beautiful shape is tuǒ,
and a charming appearance is wān.
In Nánchǔ, beauty is called wá;
plump bones and soft weakness are wǒ;
graceful cheeks and exquisite beauty are xián;
enchanting looks are yuē.
Fú Qián's "Tōngsú"
states that jīng
means beautiful.
The Shī says:
"The woman is jīng."
In Qín and Jìn, beauty is called xíng é;
beyond Wú and Chǔ, beauty is called tuǒ.
The "Shuōwén"
Yǒuréng
In ancient times, the Yǒuréng clan had a daughter with dark hair and great beauty,
whose radiance could reflect like a mirror.
She was called Xuánqī, the Music Master,
and Hòu Kuí took her as his wife.
They gave birth to Bó Fēng,
who truly had the heart of a pig,
insatiably greedy and avaricious,
furious and unrestrained.
He was called the Great Pig,
and Yǒuqióng Hòu Yì destroyed him,
causing Kuí to have no descendants to offer sacrifices.
(Zhāo 28)
Chāng Róng
During the Yīn dynasty, there was a celestial maiden named Chāngróng,
who could see bones through windows.
"Records of the Emperors and Kings"
Jade Maiden
King Zhòu imprisoned King Wén in Yǒulǐ,
Sàn Yíshēng accepted the command and set out.
On Wǎnhuáitiáotú Mountain, there were three jade maidens,
Yíshēng obtained them,
and through Fèi Zhòng, presented them to Zhòu,
thus securing King Wén's release.
From "The Six Secret Teachings"
Chìwū
The people of Chìwū presented two women to the Son of Heaven,
Nǚ Cōng and Nǚ Liè became his favored consorts,
for the land of the Chìwū clan was that of beautiful women.
"The Biography of King Mù of Zhōu"
third for Càn
King Gōng was traveling along the Jīng River,
when Mì Kānggōng, who accompanied him, had three maidens elope to him.
His mother said:
"You must present them to the king.
For three beasts form a pack,
three men form a crowd,
and three maidens form a 'càn'.
Now 'càn' means something beautiful.
For the crowd to bestow such beauty upon you,
what virtue do you possess to deserve it?
Even the king would be unworthy,
let alone a minor lord like you?"
Kānggōng did not offer them,
and within a year King Gōng exterminated Mì.
Guóyǔ
Gazing After
Sòng Huáfù Dū saw Kǒng Fù's wife on the road,
his eyes followed her as she passed and he said:
"Beautiful and radiant."
He then attacked the Kǒng family,
killed Kǒng Fù and took his wife.
The duke was angry and Dū became fearful,
so he assassinated Duke Shāng.
The gentleman considered that Dū had a mind without regard for his ruler and afterwards proceeded to evil deeds.
Huán 2
Lí Jī
Lí Jī was a woman of national beauty.

Duke Xiàn of Jìn attacked the Lí,
the Rong people were defeated,
and Lí Jī was captured and brought back,
she gained favor,
and was established as the primary wife.
Shǐ Sū informed the senior officials, saying:
"Where there is a male military force, there must be a female one;
if one is captivated by her beauty, one will surely grant her affection,
following her wicked heart will inevitably lead to ruin,
and the state will fall into deep turmoil,
the turmoil will surely arise from the female military force."
The gentleman said:
"He knew the root of the difficulty."

Máo Qiáng and Lí Jī,
were considered beautiful by people,
but when fish saw them, they dove deep into the water,

Lí Jī,
was the daughter of the border guard of Ài.

In the past, Duke Mù of Qín and Duke Xiàn of Jìn jointly attacked the state of Lí Rong,
obtaining one beautiful woman and two jade rings,
Qín took the rings and Jìn took the woman,
who was the daughter of the border guard from the Ài territory of the Lí Rong state.
