Three youthful transformations
Duke Líng of Chén, along with Kǒng Níng and Yí Xíngfù, had illicit relations with Xià Jī.
They all wore her intimate garments beneath their court robes and jested in the court.
Xiè Yě remonstrated, saying:
"When dukes and ministers openly engage in debauchery,
the people will have no model to follow,
and moreover, it brings ill repute.
My lord, you should put a stop to this."
The duke informed the two men,
and the two men then killed Xiè Yě.
Ninth year of Duke Xuān
Duke Líng, Kǒng Níng, and Yí Xíngfù were drinking at the Xià residence.
The duke said to Xíngfù:
"Does Zhēng Shū resemble you?"
Xíngfù replied:
"He also resembles you, my lord."
Zhēng Shū was deeply offended by this.
As the duke was leaving from his stable,
Zhēng Shū shot and killed him with an arrow.
The two men fled to Chǔ.
Eleventh year of Duke Xuān
When Chǔ was punishing the Xià clan of Chén,
King Zhuāng wished to take Xià Jī for himself.
Shēn Gōng Wū Chén said:
"This cannot be done.
You summoned the feudal lords to punish crime,
yet now you would take Xià Jī out of desire for her beauty.
Desiring beauty leads to debauchery,
and debauchery brings severe punishment.
My lord, you should consider this carefully."
The king then desisted.
Zǐ Fǎn wanted to take her,
but Wū Chén said:
"This is an inauspicious woman.
She caused the death of Zǐ Mán,
killed Yù Shū,
murdered Duke Líng,
slaughtered Xià Nán,
drove out Kǒng Níng and Yí Xíngfù,
and brought about the downfall of the state of Chén.
How could there be anyone more inauspicious than this?
There are many beautiful women in the world,
why must it be this one?"
Zǐ Fǎn then desisted.
The king gave her to Lián Yīn Xiāng Lǎo.
When Xiāng Lǎo died,
his son Hēi Yāo had an illicit relationship with her.
Wū Chén then took Xià Jī and fled,
eventually reaching Jìn.
Second year of Duke Chéng
Zǐ Fǎn bore a grudge against him,
and later, together with Zǐ Zhòng, killed Wū Chén's family.
Seventh year of Duke Chéng
Xià Jī possessed inner arts and techniques,
growing youthful again in old age.
Three times she became a queen,
seven times a high-ranking consort,
and nine times a widow.
In the early Spring and Autumn period, there was a proverb in Jìn and Chǔ:
"When Xià Jī attained the Way,
her chicken-like skin underwent three youthful transformations."
Yǔwén Shìjí, Record of the Dressing Table
Shū Xiǎng wished to marry a daughter of Shēn Gōng Wūchén
and Xià Jī.
His mother said:
"Zǐ Líng's wife caused the death of three husbands,
one ruler, one son, and the ruin of one state and two ministers.
Should this not serve as a warning?
I have heard that extreme beauty
must bring extreme evil.
She is the daughter of Duke Mù of Zhèng's young concubine Yáo Zǐ,
and sister of Zǐ Hè.
Zǐ Hè died early without heirs,
and Heaven concentrated beauty
in her, which is bound to bring great ruin.
Moreover, the downfall of the three dynasties,
and the dethronement of the lords of Gòng,
were all due to such women.
Why would you want this?
For possessing a femme fatale can utterly change a man;
unless one is virtuous and righteous,
disaster is inevitable."
Shū Xiǎng, frightened, dared not take her,
but Duke Píng forced him to marry her.
She gave birth to Bó Shí,
who, with a wolf's heart and wild ambitions,
ultimately destroyed the Yángshé clan.

Xīshī
The King of Yuè, knowing the King of Wú was licentious and fond of beauty,
had his minister Wén Zhǒng dispatch a physiognomist throughout the state.
They found a girl gathering firewood on Zhùluó Mountain named Xī Shī,
and another named Zhèng Dàn. They adorned them with silk gauze,
taught them graceful carriage and gait,
drilled them in an earthen-walled town,
and had them practice in the capital's lanes.
After three years of training, they were proficient and presented to Wú,
sent by the chancellor Fàn Lǐ to offer them.
"Wú Yuè"
Yuè plotted to destroy Wú,
and had two beautiful women,
one named Yíguāng,
the second named Xiūmíng.
These were the alternative names
for Xī Shī and Zhèng Dàn.
They were presented to Wú,
where Wú housed them in pepper-scented chambers,
threading pearls into silk for curtains and drapes,
lowered at dawn to shade the light,
rolled up at dusk to await the moon.
The two sat side by side by the window,
arranging mirrors and applying makeup within the pearl drapes.
Any who secretly glimpsed them were invariably stirred in heart and soul,
calling them divine beings.
They would sigh and gaze upon them,
like a pair of phoenixes in light mist,
or lotuses swaying on still waters.
The King of Wú, bewitched and infatuated,
grew negligent of state affairs.
When Yuè's troops entered the state,
he fled, clutching the two women, as recorded in Shuō Yuàn.
The Yuè soldiers, entering in disarray, saw the two women beneath a tree.
All declared them goddesses,
gazing from afar, not daring to approach.

Xī Shī,
a beautiful woman of Yuè,
required anyone wishing to see her to first pay one coin.

With fine cheeks and gleaming teeth,
a lovely form and excellent bone structure,

her natural fragrance and disposition were pleasing—
this was Xī Shī, Yángwén.

Xī Shī was drowned for her beauty.
"Mòzǐ"
South of Jiāxīng County stands the Daughter Pavilion.

On the journey, Xī Shī and Fàn Lǐ secretly became intimate for three years
before reaching Wú.
They then had a son.
Arriving at this pavilion,
their son, one year old, could speak,
hence it was named Daughter Pavilion.
"Yuè Jué Shū" states that after Xī Shī caused the fall of Wú,
she returned to Fàn Lǐ,
and they drifted away on the Five Lakes.

a woman of extraordinary beauty in the state.

Lǘ Jū
Fú Jiān once went to Yè,
to hunt in the Western Mountains.
After more than ten days,
he enjoyed it so much that he forgot to return.
The entertainer Wáng Luò stopped his horse and remonstrated, saying:
"I have heard that the son of a wealthy family does not sit under the hall beams;
a ruler of ten thousand chariots does not tread in danger.
Thus, when Emperor Wén sped in his chariot,
Duke Yuán stopped his reins;
when Xiàowǔ was fond of hunting,
Xiāng Rú offered advice.
You are the father and mother of the common people below,
the one upon whom the masses depend,
how can you wander in hunting,
tarnishing your sacred virtue?
If calamity arises suddenly,
and changes occur unexpectedly,
what of the ancestral temple!
What of the Empress Dowager!"
Jiān said,
"It is my fault.
From then on, he did not hunt again.

In the second year of King Zhāo of Yān's reign,
the state of Guǎngyán sent two skilled dancers as tribute,
one named Xuán Juān,
the other Tí Mó.
Both possessed jade-like complexions and smooth skin,
bodies light as air with fragrant breath,
graceful and slender,
unmatched since antiquity.

or go for years without hunger.
King Zhāo housed them in brocade curtains and splendid tents,

Lush and Blooming
King Wǔlíng of Zhào was touring Dàlíng,
when he dreamed of a maiden playing the qín.
Later, she played the sè
and sang a poem, saying:
"The radiant beauty—her face like the glory of the indigo plant,
O fate, O fate,
you never favored me, Yíng."
Another day, while the king was drinking and merry,
he repeatedly spoke of his dream,
describing her appearance.
Wú Guǎng heard of this
and, through the queen, presented his daughter Wá Yíng,
also known as Méng Yáo.

Zhāo Yún
King Xiāng of Chǔ was touring Yúnmèng
when he saw cloud-like vapor above the Morning Cloud Pavilion.
Sòng Yù said, "Long ago, the former king
lingered
on a tour of Gāotáng and, feeling weary, napped by day.
He dreamt of a woman, hazy as a cloud,
bright as a star,
about to approach but not yet arrived,
now floating, now leaning.
She replied,
'I am the youngest daughter of the Red Emperor, named Yáo
Yáo
Jī.
I died before I could be wed
and was buried on the sunny side of Wū Mountain.
My essence became a plant,
the sacred mushroom,
known as the Maiden of Wū Mountain,
the Lady of Gāotáng.'"
The king then favored her.
As she departed, she bade farewell,
"I dwell on the sunny side of Wū Mountain,
at the ridge of the high hill.
At dawn I am the drifting cloud,
at dusk the passing rain.
Morning after morning, dusk after dusk,
beneath the Sunny Terrace."
At dawn the king looked,
and indeed it was as she had said.
Thus he built a temple for her,
named Morning Cloud.
(from Xiāngyáng Records of the Elderly)
Dōngjiā
Dēngtúzǐ accused Sòng Yù of being lustful before the King of Chǔ,
to which Sòng Yù replied:
"The fairest beauty in the world is none other than the maiden from the eastern house in my neighborhood.
Were she an inch taller, she would be too tall;
were she an inch shorter, she would be too short.
With powder applied, she would appear too pale;
with rouge added, she would appear too red.
Her eyebrows resemble kingfisher feathers,
her skin is like white snow,
her waist is as slender as a bound silk ribbon,
her teeth are like arranged shells,
and with a captivating smile,
she enchants the entire city of Yángchéng,
and bewilders all of Xiàcài."

Zhāng Yí went to Chǔ,
and had an audience with the King of Chǔ, saying:
"Those women of Zhèng and Zhōu,
with faces powdered white and eyebrows painted black,
standing at the crossroads and alleyways,
those who do not know them and see them would think them goddesses."
The king said:
"Chǔ is a remote and uncultured state,
I have never seen women of the central states so beautiful."
Thereupon he provided Zhāng Yí with pearls and jade.
When Queen Nán and Zhèng Xiù heard this, they were greatly alarmed,
and sent someone to say to Zhāng Yí:
"We hear you are going to Jìn,
here are ten catties of gold,
please use it for fodder expenses in Zhǎngzǐ,
we beg you to speak to the king about it."
The king summoned Queen Nán and Zhèng Xiù and spoke with them.
Zhāng Yí bowed twice and said:
"Yí deserves death for his crime,
Yí has traveled throughout the world,
yet has never seen anyone so beautiful as these two,
for Yí to say he could obtain beautiful women would be to deceive Your Majesty."
The king said:
"I have always believed there is no one in the world who can match these two."

Rhinoceros Horn Reclining Moon
Yīn Jī and Jiāng Jī vied to become queen,
Sīmǎ Xǐ supported Yīn Jī,
and thus said to the King of Zhào:
"I have heard that Zhào is renowned in the world for its music,
and is the birthplace of beautiful women.
But now, arriving at your borders and entering your capital,
in terms of appearance and complexion,
there are truly no beauties.
As for those who love beauty,
I have never seen anyone like Yīn Jī from the mountains.
Those who do not know her often mistake her for a goddess.
As for her eyebrows and eyes,
the proportions of her nose and forehead,
and the shape of her jaw resembling a reclining moon,
these are features of an emperor's queen,
not merely a feudal lord's consort."
The King of Zhào was greatly pleased,
and desired to request her.
Sīmǎ Xǐ returned and said to the Lord of Zhōngshān:
"The King of Zhào is not a virtuous ruler,
and now wishes to request Yīn Jī.
Your Majesty should establish her as queen,
to cut off the King of Zhào's intentions."
The Lord of Zhōngshān then established her as queen.

Zhōng Xiàng
Lǐ Yuán was an official under Chūnshēn Jūn, the chancellor of King Kǎoliè of Chǔ.
Yuán's younger sister, Nǚ Huán, said to Yuán:
"I hear the king is old and has no heir.
You could introduce me to Chūnshēn Jūn.
I wish to make use of Chūnshēn Jūn.
If I can meet Chūnshēn Jūn,
I will directly get to see the king."
Yuán said:
"Chūnshēn Jūn is a noble man,
a minister of a thousand lǐ,
how dare I presume to speak?"
Nǚ Huán said:
"If he does not see me,
you request an audience with Chūnshēn Jūn,
and have an attendant report a guest from afar,
asking to return home to receive them.
He will surely ask you,
'What kind of guest from afar is at your home?'
Then the guest from afar should reply:
'Yuán has a younger sister.
The chancellor of Lǔ heard of her,
and sent an envoy to seek her hand.'
Yuán's attendant will inform Yuán.
He will surely inquire further.
'What abilities does your younger sister have?'
Reply that she is skilled in drumming,
has studied texts and mastered one classic.
Thus, he will certainly see me."
Yuán said:
"Agreed."
The next day, he took leave from Chūnshēn Jūn,
saying an attendant had a guest from afar,
and requested to return home to receive them.
Chūnshēn Jūn indeed asked:
"What kind of guest from afar is at your home?"
He replied:
"Yuán has a younger sister.
The chancellor of Lǔ heard of her,
and sent an envoy to seek her hand."
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
"What abilities does she have?"
He replied:
"She is skilled in drumming,
has studied texts and mastered one classic."
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
"May I see her?
Tomorrow, have her wait at the Lí Pavilion."
Yuán said:
"Agreed."
After returning home,
he told Nǚ Huán:
"I took leave from Chūnshēn Jūn,
and he allowed you to wait at the Lí Pavilion tomorrow evening."
Nǚ Huán said:
"Yuán should first prepare to receive him."
When Chūnshēn Jūn arrived at Yuán's residence,
he sent a rider to summon Nǚ Huán.
By dusk,
Nǚ Huán arrived.
They drank liberally,
and Nǚ Huán played the qín.
Before the melody ended, Chūnshēn Jūn was greatly pleased,
and stayed the night."
The next day, Nǚ Huán said to Chūnshēn Jūn:
"I hear the king is old and has no heir,
and has entrusted the state to you.
If you indulge in debauchery and neglect affairs of state,
should the king hear of it,
you would fail the king above,
and cause me to fall below,
failing your wife.
What is to be done?
Do not let this be spoken of.
Summon and admonish them."
Chūnshēn Jūn informed his officials,
and none spoke of the wanton woman.
All said, 'Agreed.'"
Before a month had passed since their affair began,
Nǚ Huán said to Chūnshēn Jūn:
"I hear the king is old and has no heir.
Now I have been with child by you for a month.
Present me to the king.
If I am fortunate to bear a son,
you will become the king's father,
so why remain a minister?"
After pondering it for five days, he presented her,
saying there was a beautiful woman in the state,
suitable as a match,
who could continue the lineage.
King Liè said:
"Agreed."
He then summoned her.
King Liè was pleased and took her.
In ten months, she gave birth to a son,
who became King Yōu.

Portrait
The King of Qí built a nine-tiered tower,
and offered a reward of money to anyone in the state who could paint.
Jìng Jūn, a destitute soldier who often suffered from hunger and cold,
had a beautiful wife.
Jìng Jūn, skilled in painting and greedy for the reward,
left home to paint the tower.
After a long time, he missed his wife,
so he painted her portrait
and smiled joyfully at it.
Someone nearby saw this and reported it to the king.
The king then set out wine and feasted with Jìng Jūn,
saying to him:
"None of the women presented in the state are beautiful.
I offer a million coins for your wife—
is that acceptable?
If not, I will kill you."
Jìng Jūn, terrified, agreed.
From "Shuō Yuàn".
Someone asked:
"When Chén Píng
devised a plan to lift the siege of Pingcheng for the emperor,
the details were kept secret and not transmitted.
Do you know of it?"
The reply was:
"At Pingcheng, he had painters create portraits of beautiful women,
and secretly sent someone to present them to the Yānzhī,
saying that the Han had exceptionally lovely women
whose beauty was unmatched in the world,
and that the emperor, currently in distress,
had already dispatched messengers to fetch them
to offer to the Chányú.
If the Chanyu saw these women, he would surely adore them greatly,
and his affection for them would cause the Yanzhi to be increasingly neglected.
It would be better, before they arrive,
to allow the Han forces to escape,
so they would not bring the women after all."
The Yanzhi, being a woman prone to jealousy,
feared that the Han women's beauty would steal her favor,
and thus said to the Chanyu:
"The Han Son of Heaven also possesses divine protection,
and is destined to hold this land,
it cannot be taken from him."
Thereupon, they opened a gap in the siege,
enabling them to break out by this cunning stratagem,
which was kept secret and not transmitted.
From Huán Tán's "New Discourses" and "Yìyīn of the Book of Han".
A golden house to store
Princess Piáo had a daughter,
and wished to arrange a marriage with the Crown Prince.
When the princess returned to the palace,
Emperor Wǔ was just a few years old.
The princess took him on her lap and asked:

She pointed to over a hundred attendants around them,
but he said he didn't want any of them.

"Is Ājiāo good?"
He replied with a laugh:

If I can have Ājiāo as my wife,
I would house her in a golden room."
The princess was greatly pleased,
and so she entreated the Emperor,
and thus the marriage was arranged.

Lamenting one's own inferiority
Lady Yǐn and Lady Xíng were both favored concurrently by Emperor Wǔ,
who decreed they should not meet each other.
Lady Yǐn personally requested of Emperor Wǔ
to see Lady Xíng,
and the emperor consented.
He then ordered another lady to dress up and,
with several tens of attendants,
pose as Lady Xíng approaching.
Lady Yǐn came forward to see her and said:
"This is not Lady Xíng herself."
The emperor asked:

and come forward alone.

Unparalleled in the world
Lǐ Yánnián had an innate understanding of music,
excelled at singing and dancing,
and while serving Emperor Wǔ, he rose to dance and sang:

peerless and standing alone,

Lìjuān
Emperor Wǔ's favored palace maid was named Lìjuān,
who was fourteen years old,
with jade-like skin so soft
that her breath was more fragrant than orchids.
She did not wish for clothing or sashes to brush against her,
fearing it would leave marks on her body.
Whenever she sang,
Lǐ Yánnián would harmonize with her in the Chángshēng Hall,
performing the "Song of the Whirling Wind."
The flowers in the courtyard would all flutter and fall.
They placed Lìjuān behind the translucent curtain of her bed,
fearing that dust and grime might soil her body.
The emperor often tied the sleeves of Lìjuān's robe with his own belt,
enclosing her within layers of curtains,
afraid she might drift away with the wind.
Lìjuān wore an amber pendant,
concealed within the folds of her garment,
so that no one would know of it.
She then claimed that her joints produced music on their own,
and people regarded it as a supernatural marvel.
"Records of the Obscure"
Zhào Fēiyàn
Emperor Shìzǔ Yáng Nífúyì Píxuān recorded that
he drummed the Fén River and sacrificed to the Earth Queen,
ascended Gānquán to worship the Vast Heaven,
with the Minister of Ceremonies presenting rituals,
it was called the Grand Procession with a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry,
placing his favored consort Zhào Fēiyàn within the leopard-tail section among the auxiliary carriages.
"Records of Carriages and Attire of the Jìn Dynasty"
Yān and Zhào
He built the Mingguang Palace,
selecting two thousand beauties from Yān and Zhào to fill it,
generally taking those aged fifteen and above, twenty and below.
At the age of thirty, they were married off.
From all the palace beauties, two hundred were selected to regularly accompany him on tours of the commanderies and kingdoms,
riding in the rear carriages.
Sixteen of them shared the imperial carriage with him,
the number always kept full.
They were all naturally beautiful,
without the use of powder to whiten or ink to darken their features.
Those serving in the wardrobe chambers were treated the same way.
"Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn"
Jade Maiden
Emperor Wǔ had a jade maiden descend in the Gānquán Palace,
who often amused herself by playing wéiqí with the emperor.
The maiden was graceful and dignified in appearance.
The emperor secretly admired her and then forced himself upon her,
whereupon the jade maiden spat on the emperor's face and departed.
Consequently, he suffered from sores for a year.
Thus, the Hàn Shū records that he retreated to the Gānquán Palace to escape the heat,
which was during this period.
"Yōu Míng Lù"
Her face is like a lotus blossom
Zhuō Wénjūn was exceedingly beautiful,
her eyebrows resembled distant mountains,
her face often appeared like a lotus flower,
her skin was soft and smooth as cream,
widowed at seventeen,
she was unconventional and romantic by nature,
thus admiring Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's talent, she transgressed propriety with him.
Xiàngrú had long suffered from diabetes,
and upon returning to Chéngdū,
enamored with Wénjūn's beauty,
he consequently suffered a relapse of his chronic illness.
He then composed "Rhapsody on a Beautiful Woman,"
intending to satirize himself but ultimately unable to reform,
and eventually died from this illness.
Wénjūn wrote a funeral eulogy that circulated in the world.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Zhāo Jūn
Emperor Yuán had many palace ladies,
so he ordered painters to portray them,
so that when he wished to summon one, he could consult the portraits.
Those of average looks all bribed the painters,
but Wáng Míngjūn was exceedingly beautiful in appearance,
and disdained to seek favor through such means,
so the painter deliberately marred her likeness.
Later, the Xiōngnú came to seek peace,
and requested a beautiful woman from the Hàn emperor.
The emperor sent Míngjūn to fulfill this request.
"Shì Shuō"
When she was summoned to depart and appeared before the emperor,
her beauty was found to be the finest in the rear palace,
she was skilled in conversation,
and her demeanor was graceful and refined.
The emperor regretted his decision,
but her name was already registered for the mission,
and the emperor valued keeping faith with foreign states,
so he did not make any change.
People then thoroughly investigated the matter,
and all the painters were executed in the marketplace.
"Xī Jīng Zá Jì"
Wén Yǐng said:
"Zhāojūn was originally a woman from Zǐguī county in Shǔ commandery."
Qín Cāo says:
"Zhāojūn
was the daughter of Wáng Rǎng of Qí state,
aged seventeen,
her appearance was noble and beautiful,
and she was known throughout the state for her virtue.
When suitors sought her hand,
Wáng Rǎng refused them all,
and instead presented her to Emperor Yuán."
Shí Jìlún said:
"The character Zhāo violated Emperor Wén's name taboo,
so it was changed to Míng."
"Shì Shuō Zhù"
Qián Xiāoniáng's poem about Zhāojūn says:
"Had the Hàn court earlier trusted painting,
And heavily rewarded the Luòyáng masters with riches,
A thousand gold would have bought her cloud-like hair,
A million coins would have depicted her moth-eyebrows."
"Sōng Chuāng Zá Lù"
Fēi Yàn Hé Dé
Féng Wànjīn excelled at singing,
and served the Prince of Jiāngdū,
whose granddaughter married Zhào Màn of Jiāngdū.
Wànjīn was also [involved],
so Màn had an affair with the princess.
Màn suffered from an illness preventing intimacy with women,
yet the princess became pregnant.
Fearing exposure, she feigned illness,
giving birth to twin daughters,
whom she entrusted to Wànjīn.
The elder was named Yízhǔ,
the younger Hédé,
and they took the surname Zhào.
Yízhǔ was intelligent and quick-witted,
her family possessed the medical techniques of Péngzǔ,
and she excelled at subtle breath control.
As she grew, she became slender and delicate,
her movements graceful and light,
earning her the nickname "Flying Swallow."
The Emperor, enamored, said of her:
"Plentiful yet not excessive,
soft as if boneless,
modest and reserved in demeanor,
both distant and intimate,
a woman of propriety and righteousness."
Hédé possessed a beautiful appearance and form,
her skin so smooth it repelled water after bathing,
and she was skilled in music and speech,
her voice light and soothing to hear.
Newly washed and anointed with nine-fold chénshuǐ incense,
she styled her curled hair as the "New Rise" chignon,
painted her delicate eyebrows as "Distant Mountains" azure,
and applied light rouge in the "Languid" makeup style,
drawing sighs of admiration from all around.
Lady Nào, behind the Emperor, spat and said:
"This is a flood of calamity,
sure to extinguish the fire [of the Hàn]."
Presented to the Emperor, he was greatly pleased,
finding her body so soft it seemed to melt into his,
calling it the "Land of Tenderness,"
and said to Fán Yì:
"I shall grow old in this land,
unable to emulate Emperor Wǔ's quest for the Land of White Clouds."
"The Unofficial Biography of Flying Swallow"
The body was free from distress and hardship.
Fēiyàn was initially poor,
sharing a quilt with her sister Hédé.
They once had an affair with a neighbor who was an archer in the Yǔlín guard,
standing in the night dew and snow,
holding their breath and regulating their energy,
their bodies showing no shivering or goosebumps.
The archer thought they were immortals.
The emperor
Saliva Blossom
Fēiyàn and her sister Jiéyú were sitting,
when the Empress accidentally spat on her sleeve.
Hédé said:
"Sister's spittle has dyed your dark blue sleeve,
just like flowers on a stone.
Even if the Imperial Workshop were to make it,
it might not achieve such splendor as this garment."
Thus it was named the Stone-Flower Wide Sleeve.
The Emperor
Body Fragrance
Empress Zhào bathed in five-scent seven-fragrance soup,
squatting on a sandalwood seat permeated with fragrance,
burning a hundred-scent incense to invoke deities,
while Lady Jiéyú bathed in bean-scented soup,
and applied dew-blossom hundred-flower powder.
The Emperor once privately told Fán Yì:
"Although the Empress has extraordinary fragrance,
it cannot compare to Lady Jiéyú's natural body fragrance."
End
Zhāo Yáng
Zhào Fēiyàn became empress,
her younger sister was in the Zhāoyáng Hall,
and sent Zhào Fēiyàn a letter saying:
"On this auspicious day,
when my honored sister is graced with the grand appointment,
I respectfully present thirty-five burial garments,
to express my leaping heart."
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
After the empress was established,
her favor waned while her sister enjoyed exclusive favor as a Bright Lady,
residing in the Zhāoyáng Lodge.
"Book of Hàn"
Seductive demeanor
Liáng Jì's wife Sūn Shòu was beautiful in appearance and skilled in seductive charms,
she would fashion sorrowful eyebrows and weeping makeup,
adorn herself with the "fallen horse" hairstyle,
walk with a bending waist and puckered mouth,
and display teeth when laughing to appear captivating and alluring.
"Book of the Later Hàn"
Pushing a Deer Cart Himself
Zhào Xǐ and his friend Hán Zhòngbó wished to enter Wǔguān Pass.
Zhòngbó, considering his wife beautiful,
feared that she might attract violent men and bring harm upon them,
so he intended to abandon her.
Xǐ reproached him angrily,
so Zhòngbó smeared mud on his wife's face,
placed her on a deer cart,
and pushed it himself.
Whenever they encountered bandits, he would plead for mercy on her behalf,
and thus she managed to escape danger.
"Dōngguān Hànjì"
Huì ér yǒu sè
Empress Zhēn of Wèi was kind and beautiful,
first married to Yuán Xī as his wife,
and greatly favored.
When Lord Cáo sacked Yè,
he ordered her to be quickly summoned.
His attendants reported that the General of the Five Offices had already taken her away.
Lord Cáo said:
"This year's defeat of the enemy was precisely for her."
*Shì Shuō*
During the Jiàn'ān era,
Yuán Shào arranged for his middle son Xī to marry the daughter of Zhēn Huì.
After Shào's death, Xī departed,
stationed in Yōuzhōu,
while Zhēn remained to serve her mother-in-law.
When Yè City fell,
the General of the Five Offices entered and went to Shào's residence.
*Wèi Lüè*
He saw a woman with disheveled hair and a dirty face,
weeping as she stood beside Shào's wife, Liú.
Later, Emperor Wén inquired and learned she was Xī's wife,
then ordered her to tidy her hair and wipe her face with his sleeve.
Her beauty was peerless.
After he left,
Liú said to Zhēn:
"You need not die anymore."
Thus, he took her as his own and favored her greatly.
*Shì Yǔ*
When the General of the Five Offices took Xī's wife,
Kǒng Róng wrote to Lord Cáo, saying:
"King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and gave Dájǐ to the Duke of Zhōu."
Tàizǔ, thinking Róng was erudite,
truly believed it was recorded in historical texts.
Later, he saw Róng and asked him about it,
to which he replied:
"Judging the past by the present,
I imagined it was so."
*Wèi Shì Chūnqiū*
Gǎn Zhēn
It is recorded that King Dōng'ē of Wèi, in the late Hàn dynasty, sought the daughter of Zhēn Yì,
but failed to obtain her.
When Tàizǔ returned,
he granted her to the General of the Household for All Purposes, Cáo Pī, which left Cáo Zhí deeply discontented.
He thought of her day and night,
neglecting both sleep and food.
During the Huángchū era, when he attended court,
the Emperor showed Zhí the jade-inlaid golden belt pillow of Empress Zhēn.
Upon seeing it, Zhí could not hold back his tears.
By then, she had already been slandered to death by Empress Guō.
The Emperor soon realized his regret,
and thus ordered the Crown Prince to host a banquet for Zhí.
He then bestowed the pillow upon Zhí.
As Zhí returned and passed Huányuán,
resting by the Luò River,
he thought of Empress Zhēn.
Suddenly, a woman appeared and said:
"I originally entrusted my heart to you, my lord,
but my wish was unfulfilled.
This pillow was given to me before my marriage to the General of the Household for All Purposes,
and now I give it to you.
Let it serve as a pillow on the mat,
where joy and emotion intertwine—
how could ordinary words express it?
Empress Guō stuffed chaff into my mouth,
and now, with disheveled hair, I am ashamed to let you see my form again."
With these words, she vanished without a trace.
She sent someone to present pearls to the King,
and he responded with a jade pendant.
Overwhelmed with sorrow and joy,
he composed the "Rhapsody on Feeling for Zhēn."
Later, when Emperor Míng read it,
he renamed it "Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luò River."
Obtaining a concubine leads to killing one's child
In the spring, the first month of the second year of the Jiàn'ān era,
Cáo Cāo launched a campaign against Zhāng Xiù.
Xiù surrendered,
but his younger brother Jì's wife was a woman of extraordinary beauty.
Cáo Cāo took her as his concubine,
which caused Xiù to rebel.
He launched a surprise attack on Cáo Cāo's seven armies,
inflicting a major defeat,
and killing two of Cáo Cāo's sons.
From Yuán Hóng's Later Records:
According to the Records of the States, Xiù was a nephew of the Jì clan.
Zhēn Shén
Emperor Wén of Wèi had a beloved beauty whose surname was Xuē and given name Yúnyún,
a native of Chángshān.
Yún was seventeen years old,
with unparalleled beauty in the world.
At that time, Emperor Wén selected girls from good families to enter the palace,
Língyún bid farewell to her parents,
sighing sorrowfully for days on end,
her tears falling and soaking her clothes.
When the time came to board the carriage and set off on the journey,
she used a jade spittoon to catch her tears.
The spittoon gradually turned red, and by the time she reached the capital,
the tears inside the spittoon had congealed to resemble the color of blood.
The Emperor changed Língyún's name to Yèlái,
who was exceptionally skilled in needlework.
Even when inside deep curtains and layered tents,
she did not need lamps or candles,
and would finish cutting and sewing immediately.
If it was not sewn by Yèlái,
the Emperor would not wear it.
In the palace, she was called the Goddess of Needles.
"Records of Omissions"
Four Wonders
Emperor Wén's palace ladies who were most beloved included Mò Qióngshù, Xuē Yèlái, Tián Shàngyī, and Duàn Qiǎoxiào, the four of them,
staying by his side day and night.
Qióngshù created the "cicada side-locks" hairstyle,
ethereal and delicate like a cicada's wings,
hence the name cicada side-locks.
Qiǎoxiào was the first to use brocade clothing and silk shoes,
applying purple powder to her face.
Shàngyī was skilled in singing and dancing,
while Yèlái excelled at making clothing.
For a time, they were unmatched in excellence.
"Notes on the Past and Present"
Jiàngshù
Today's most exquisite dance is none more skillful than that of Jiàng Shù,
and the purest song none more stirring than that of Sòng Là.
From "Emperor Wén's Letter to Fán Qīn"
Goddess
The father of Lady Pān, consort of the Wú sovereign, was punished for breaking the law,
and Lady Pān was sent to the weaving workshop.
Her appearance and demeanor had few equals,
making her a peerless beauty in Jiāngdōng.
Among the over hundred women confined with her,
they regarded Lady Pān as a goddess,
respecting her yet keeping their distance.
The authorities reported this to the Wú sovereign,
who ordered a portrait of her likeness to be made.
Lady Pān, distressed and sorrowful, refused to eat,
becoming emaciated and altered in form.
The artisan painted her and presented the portrait,
which the Wú sovereign saw and delighted in.
Holding an amber ruyi scepter, he stroked it and sighed,
exclaiming:
"This is indeed a goddess!
Even her sorrowful countenance can captivate people,
how much more when she is joyful?"
He then ordered an ornate carriage to go to the weaving workshop
and brought her into the rear palace.
Indeed, with her beauty, she gained favor.
Four Consorts
Sūn Liàng crafted a glass screen,
extremely thin and crystal clear.
He would often unfurl it beneath the moonlight on clear nights,
and was usually accompanied by his four beloved consorts,
each a peerless beauty surpassing ancient times:
the first named Zhāo Shū,
the second Lì Jū,
the third Jié Huá,
and the fourth Luò Zhēn.
Carving an Image
Sūn Hào took Zhāng Bù's daughter as a beauty and favored her greatly.
Hào asked her:
"Where is your father now?"
She replied:
"The rebels killed him."
Hào flew into a rage,
had her beaten to death with clubs,
but later missed her appearance,
so he ordered skilled craftsmen to carve a wooden statue in her likeness,
which he always kept by his seat.
He asked his attendants if Bù had any other daughters,
and they replied:
"Bù's eldest daughter was married to Féng Chún, son of the former Commandant of the Guards Féng Cháo."
Hào immediately seized Chún's wife and brought her into the palace,
where she received great favor,
and was appointed Left Lady.
He feasted with her day and night in the bedchamber,
neglecting court affairs.
When the Lady died,
Hào grieved and longed for her,
burying her in the palace gardens,
constructing a large tomb,
and ordering craftsmen to carve cypress into wooden figures placed inside the tomb,
to serve as guards.
"Records of the Lands Beyond the River"
Heartbroken
Xún Càn often held that women's talent and intellect were not worth discussing,
and that beauty should be the primary consideration.
The daughter of Cavalry General Cáo Hóng was beautiful,
so Càn married her.
Her appearance, attire, and bed curtains were exceptionally exquisite,
and they enjoyed intimate affection alone.
After several years, his wife fell ill and passed away.
Before her burial, Chuán Gǔ went to console Càn.
Càn did not weep but was deeply grieved in spirit.
Gǔ asked him:
"A woman possessing both talent and beauty
is hard to find for marriage.
If one overlooks talent and values only beauty,
it is not so rare to encounter.
Why then do you grieve so profoundly?"
Càn replied:
"A beautiful woman is hard to come by again.
Although the deceased may not have had an extraordinary, city-toppling beauty,
she was still not easily met with.
My heartache and mourning are beyond control."
A little over a year later, he too passed away.
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World."
Guāng Lì
Hán Shòu possessed handsome features and elegant demeanor,
Jiǎ Chōng appointed him as an assistant.
Whenever Chōng held gatherings,
his daughter, observing Shòu through the green lattice, admired him.
She constantly cherished thoughts of him,
radiant, beautiful, and exceptionally charming,
graceful and peerlessly lovely.
Upon hearing of this, Shòu felt his heart stirred,
and thus secretly requested a maidservant to convey messages.
When he went to stay overnight,
Shòu, being remarkably agile,
leapt over the wall to enter,
unnoticed by anyone in the household.
From then on, Chōng noticed his daughter diligently adorning herself,
her cheerful demeanor different from usual.
Later, when meeting with various officials,
he noticed Shòu had a rare fragrance about him,
which was a tribute from foreign lands.
Once applied, it would not fade for months.
Chōng recalled that only he and Chén Qiān had received this incense from Emperor Wǔ,
and no other family possessed it.
He suspected an affair between Shòu and his daughter,
yet the walls were thick and secure,
the gates tightly guarded.
How could this have happened?
So he pretended there had been a thief,
ordering someone to inspect the walls.
The person returned and reported:
"Everything else is normal,
except for what looks like footprints in the northeast corner,
though the wall is too high for anyone to climb over."
Chōng then interrogated the maidservants attending his daughter,
who confessed the truth.
Chōng kept it secret
and married his daughter to Shòu.
"Bié Chuán"
states that the one involved with Hán Shòu was actually Chén Qiān's daughter,
who was then married to Shòu.
Before the wedding, the daughter passed away,
so Shòu married a Jiǎ,
hence the widespread belief it was Chōng's daughter.
"Comments on Various Jin Figures" notes:
"Shòu, styled Dé Zhēn,
upheld family traditions,
was by nature loyal and honest—
how could such events have occurred?
No other texts mention this,
only appearing in 'Shì Shuō',
so it cannot be considered reliable."
Annotation
states: Qiān's younger brother and his son Xìng
quarreled bitterly,
leading to accusations of Qiān's daughter's immoral conduct.
Qiān petitioned to exile his brother,
for which he was criticized by society.
"Jìn Shū"
Zhāng Dān Chén Zhū
Xià Tǒng followed his father in offering sacrifices to their ancestors,
welcoming two female shamans, Zhāng Dān and Chén Zhū,
both possessing exceptional beauty,
dressed in magnificent attire,
skilled in singing and dancing,
and also capable of making themselves invisible,
swallowing knives and spitting fire.
Tǒng broke through the fence and ran away,
returning to reprimand everyone, saying:
"In the past, when promiscuous customs arose,
Duke Wén of Wèi grieved over them,
lamenting the ominous aura of the rainbow,
which even gentlemen dared not point at upon seeing.
When Jì Huán accepted the women of Qí,
Zhòngní turned his carriage and retreated;
when Zǐlù saw Xià Nán,
he was filled with indignation and rage.
I have always regretted not being able to smash Shū Xiàng's head,
or gouge out Huá Fù's eyes.
How could you gentlemen welcome such monstrous beings?
Engaging in revelry with them at night,
indulging in unrestrained passions,
giving free rein to extravagant and licentious behavior,
disrupting the proper relations between men and women,
and destroying chaste and noble integrity—
why is this?"
Thereupon, he concealed himself on the bed,
lay down with his hair disheveled,
and spoke no more.
End.
Liù Liú
Liú Cōng sent the Grand Herald,
Lǐ Hóng to appoint Liú Yīn's two daughters as Left and Right Noble Consorts;
the elder named Yīng, styled Lìfāng,
the younger named É, styled Lìhuá,
and also took Liú Yīn's four granddaughters as Noble Ladies.
He said to Lǐ Hóng:
"These women are all of peerless beauty,
their feminine virtues unmatched in our time,
and moreover, the Grand Guardian to me,
is truly different from others."
Lǐ Hóng replied:
"The Grand Guardian's lineage traces back to the Zhou dynasty,
and is indeed separate from the imperial ancestry."
Liú Cōng was greatly enlightened,
and awarded Lǐ Hóng sixty catties of gold,

Èr Jìn
Liú Cōng visited the residence of the Central Protector Jìn Zhǔn,
and took his two daughters as his Left and Right Noble Consorts.
The elder was named Yuèguāng,
the younger Yuèhuá,
both possessing beauty that could overthrow cities.
A few months later, he appointed Yuèguāng as Empress.
Jìn Zhǔn's daughter engaged in lewd and immoral conduct,
which Chén Yuándá reported to the emperor.
Liú Cōng deposed Lady Jìn,
who, filled with shame and resentment, committed suicide.
(From the "Annals")
Gate Xuē
When Zhāng Tiānxī was critically ill,
his two concubines, Mén and Xuē, both possessed beauty that could captivate a country.
Zhāng Tiānxī said to them:
"After I die,
how could you two become wives to others?"
They both replied, "If you, our lord, should pass away,
we beg to follow you in death,
vowing before you to have no other intentions."
The two women committed suicide,
but then Zhāng Tiānxī recovered from his illness.
He mourned the two concubines,
and buried them with the rites due to a wife.
"Continued Records of the Emperors"
Chén Wǎn
At the end of the Yuánxīng era of Jìn, there was a girl from Wèi Commandery named Chén Wǎn,
whose home was in Zhāpǔ.
At sixteen years old,
during a year of famine and plague,
her parents died one after another.
She only had one elder brother who supported himself by hiring out for work.
The girl was exceptionally beautiful in appearance,
and when the scholars and commoners in the neighborhood saw her poverty and vulnerability,
they vied with each other in offering money and silk to solicit her.
Yet the girl firmly maintained her chaste integrity,
never consenting to any.
Later, when the rebellion of Lú Xún occurred,
the rebel troops intended to assault and coerce her,
but the girl sternly refused to yield,
and was consequently killed.
From Zǔ Chōngzhī's "Shù Yì Jì"
Transformation and growth
Xíng Luán, while in Hànzhōng, seized commoners to make them slaves.
Lú Yǎng had a grudge against Luán,
so he plotted with Yuán Huī,
ordering Cuī Liàng to impeach him.
Luán, fearing the consequences,
then gave Huī over twenty people, including Huàshēng, the daughter of Páng Jǐngmín, the governor of Bāxī, whom he had obtained in Hànzhōng.
Huàshēng and several others were women of extraordinary beauty.
Huī was greatly pleased,
and thus turned against Yǎng, speaking on Luán's behalf to Shìzōng.
As a result, Luán was not punished.
Book of Wèi, Chapter 53
Beautiful Woman Stone
Liáng Shílíngbǎo, originally from Yúyáo,
resided in Wǔkāng.
He had a daughter of beautiful appearance.
Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng of the Northern Qí took her as a consort.
After Yáoguāng's defeat,
she entered the palace of Dōnghūn.
When the Jiànkāng city was pacified,
she was selected by Emperor Wǔ,
and gave birth to Emperor Yuán.
She became a Xīuróng (a palace lady title),
was granted the surname Ruǎn,
and her father was appointed as Cháoqǐng.
People of the time thus named the stream where they lived Ruǎngōng Xī (Duke Ruǎn's Stream),
in which there was a large blue stone,
called Měirén Shí (Beauty Stone).

Shining with dazzling brilliance
Empress Chén's noble consort, named Lìhuá,
had hair seven feet long,
raven-black like lacquer,
its sheen could reflect like a mirror,
exceptionally intelligent and wise,
possessing a divine brilliance,
her movements were graceful and composed,
her countenance dignified and beautiful,

Flower Goddess
Cháng'ān presented to the court a carriage maiden named Yuán Bǎo'ér, aged fifteen,
with a slender and delicate waist,
a naive disposition and many charming mannerisms.
The emperor doted on her with exceptional favor.

Beautiful Scenery
One day, the emperor was about to board the wind vessel leaning against the palace,
resting his hand on the shoulder of the palace maid Wú Jiàngxiān,

and did not treat her as one of the ordinary crowd.
He cherished her for a very long time,
without moving from the spot.
Jiàngxiān was skilled at applying makeup,
with long, delicate eyebrows.
The emperor could not contain his admiration,
so the palace maids all vied to imitate her long eyebrows.
The emperor often leaned against the curtain gazing at Jiàngxiān,
lingering for a long time without leaving.
He turned to the inner attendant and said:
"The ancients said that beauty could be eaten,
and someone like Jiàngxiān truly can cure hunger."
At that time, Yuè River presented glowing silk,

with no other consorts included.
Since the palace maids arrived in Guǎnglíng,
they were all assigned to prepare the Moon View traveling palace,
so Jiàngxiān could not personally attend in the sleeping quarters.
A lieutenant returning from an official mission in Guāzhōu
presented a container of paired-joy fruits.
The emperor ordered a young eunuch to take a pair and gallop on horseback to bestow them upon Jiàngxiān.
However, the horse shook violently, causing the fruits to come apart.
Jiàngxiān bowed in gratitude for the gift,
then attached a small note on red paper and presented it, saying:
"The courier delivers twin fruits,
showing the deep affection of the sovereign.
But how could he know, since leaving the imperial city,
my heart no longer holds paired joy?"
The emperor read the note and was displeased,
turning to the eunuch to ask:
"Why does Jiàngxiān speak of departure,
and harbor such deep resentment?"
The eunuch explained the reason,
and the emperor said:
"Jiàngxiān is not only pleasing in appearance,
but her poetry is profoundly heartfelt—
she is indeed a female Sīmǎ Xiàngrú.
How does she fall short of Zuǒ Guìpín?"

enfeoffed as Lady of Hánguó,

each receiving a monthly allowance of one hundred thousand coins,
for cosmetics expenses.
However, the Lady of Guóguó did not apply makeup,
flaunting her natural beauty,
often appearing barefaced before the emperor.
At that time, Dù Fǔ wrote a poem:
"The Lady of Guóguó receives the sovereign's favor,
at dawn she rides her horse into the palace gates.
Yet she dislikes cosmetics staining her complexion,
lightly brushing her brows to face the supreme ruler."

Elegant and graceful
Hán Hóng served as the military governor of Biàn,
and he resented Lǐ Guāngyán's fierce combat efforts.
Secretly plotting to undermine him,
he searched throughout the great city of Dàliáng to find a beautiful woman,
taught her the arts of singing, dancing, and playing string and wind instruments,
along with the skill of liùbó gambling,
adorned her with pearls, jade, gold, and precious stones,
and provided her with clothing and accessories costing millions in total.
He ordered a messenger to deliver her to Guāngyán,
hoping that upon seeing her, he would be captivated and neglect military affairs.
The next morning, Guāngyán held a grand feast for his troops,
summoned the messenger to enter,
and the courtesan arrived—elegant, graceful, and refined,
almost as if not of this world.
The entire army stared in astonishment.
Guāngyán then said to the messenger:
"His Excellency pities me for being long separated from my family,
and has generously given me this beautiful courtesan.
I am truly grateful for his kindness,
but now my soldiers all leave their wives and children behind
to tread upon sharp blades in battle.
How could I, Guāngyán, alone indulge in the pleasure of lust?"
With this, he wept and sobbed,
generously rewarded the messenger,
and had him take the courtesan back from the banquet.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Fēi Luán Qīng Fèng
In the second year of the Bǎolì era, the Kingdom of Eastern Zhègōng presented two dancing girls,
one named Fēiluán,
the other Qīngfèng.
They had slender eyebrows and jet-black hair,
with an orchid-like fragrance that radiated warmth.
In winter, they wore no padded clothes,
and in summer, their bodies never sweated.
The emperor carved a jade lotus platform for the two girls to sing and dance upon.
Whenever their songs arose, they sounded like the calls of luán and fèng birds,
and when observed in the courtyard,
their dance postures were enchanting and graceful,
unlike anything found in the mortal world.
After each performance,
the emperor ordered the palace maids to conceal them in a golden chamber with precious curtains,
fearing they might be harmed by wind and sun.
Hence, a saying spread in the palace:
"Fragrance layers deep in the precious tent,
a pair of red lotuses."

A peerless beauty
Bì Chéng received exceptional favor from Emperor Xuānzōng,
who intended to appoint him as chancellor.
However, he was envied by Líng Hú Táo,
who repeatedly transferred him to regional posts.
These were all Táo's tactics to delay his appointment as chancellor.
Chéng sought ways to win Táo over,
and acquired a woman of unparalleled beauty in the northern region,
one whose beauty was unmatched by any other.
Adorning her lavishly with pearls and jade,
he specially sent her as a gift to Táo.
At first sight, Táo's heart was stirred,
but he told his son:
"Such a captivating woman is bound to bring harm.
Bì of Tàiyuán and I share no bond,
yet now he uses this as bait—
this will surely lead to the ruin of my entire clan."
He immediately returned her after one look,
instructing his envoy not to bring her back to the relay station to await Chéng's intentions.
Chéng then wrote a heartfelt, blood-sealed letter pleading with Táo,
but Táo still refused to accept her.
Chéng then ordered his subordinate to sell her to Lǐ Xuánbó, a physician in the eastern district.
Xuánbó, being intimately acquainted with her,
purchased her for 700,000 coins and brought her home.
He then had her reside in the main hall and treated her with respect,
while Xuánbó himself performed menial tasks to serve her.
After over a month, he had completely won her affection,
and then presented her to the emperor.
The emperor was utterly captivated upon seeing her,
and she became the most favored in the entire inner palace.
Xuánbó prepared elixirs by roasting and controlling fire,
presenting them to gain favor and power.
The emperor then developed abscesses and fell ill,
which was Xuánbó's crime.
When Emperor Yìzōng ascended the throne,
Xuánbó, along with the hermit Wáng Yuè and the Daoist priest Lú Xiānzhī, were all executed in the market.

Chóu Mí
In the state of Chén, there was an ugly man
named Dūnqià Chóumí.
He had a high forehead and broad face,
with a complexion like dark crimson,
his eyes drooping down to his nose,
and long arms but short legs.
The Marquis of Chén saw him and was greatly pleased,
employing him externally to govern his state
and internally to manage his personal affairs.
When the state of Chǔ assembled the feudal lords for a meeting,
the Marquis of Chén was ill and unable to attend,
so he sent Dūnqià Chóumí to offer apologies on his behalf.
The King of Chǔ, curious about his name, summoned him first.
The envoy's appearance was repulsive,
and his name suggested an ugly form.
The King of Chǔ angrily assembled his ministers and declared:
"If the Marquis of Chén did not know this man was unfit to be an envoy,
that shows his ignorance;
if he knew and still sent him,
that is an insult.
Both insulting and unwise—
we have no choice but to attack."
He raised an army and invaded Chén,
and within three months, Chén was destroyed.
Thus, ugliness sufficient to startle people
and words sufficient to ruin a state—
yet the Marquis of Chén found this man satisfactory and regarded none above him,
so even unto destruction, his friendship did not wane.

Zǐgāo had an audience with the King of Qí,

"Who is suitable to be the governor of Línzī?"

The king said:
"Mù's appearance is ugly,
and the people will not respect him."
He replied:
"Respect is based on virtue,
and what I recommend
is his talent.
Has Your Majesty heard of Yànzǐ and Zhào Wénzǐ?
Yànzǐ was no taller than three chǐ,
with an unpleasant face,
yet everyone in the state of Qí revered him.
Zhào Wénzǐ's body seemed too weak to bear clothing,
his words seemed too faint to leave his mouth;
not only was his physique unimpressive,
his speech was also hesitant,
yet when he governed the state of Jìn,
Jìn enjoyed peace and
the feudal lords respected and submitted—all because of his virtue.
Comparing Mù's physical form to these two men,
he is still fully worthy of being a good minister.
I once saw a butcher in the market of Línzī
who was eight chǐ tall,
with a beard like a halberd,
and a ruddy complexion,
yet no one in the market, man or woman, respected him—
because he lacked virtue."

and was restored by us,

What was lost by us,
yet restored by others,

The King of Qí sent his daughter with a generous dowry, wishing to marry her to Butcher Tǔ, who butchered cattle.

His friend said:

His friend asked:

upturned nose
Qí Zhōnglí Chūn was
an unattractive woman from Wúyán in the state of Qí.
Her appearance was exceptionally ugly beyond compare,
with a white-haired head and deep-set eyes,
long fingers and large joints,
an upturned nose and a protruding Adam's apple,
a thick neck and sparse hair,
a bent waist and a protruding chest,
and skin as dark as lacquer.
By the age of thirty, she had found no place to belong,
and her attempts to marry herself off were unsuccessful.
Thereupon, she brushed off her short coarse garment
and personally sought an audience with King Xuān.
King Xuān was feasting at the Jiàntái Terrace at the time,
and when his attendants heard of her,
they covered their mouths and laughed heartily, saying:
"This is the most brazen-faced woman in the world."
King Xuān summoned her for an audience,
and with wide eyes and clenched teeth,
she spoke of four perils facing the state.
King Xuān sighed deeply
and took her as his queen.

Zhāng's expression eased as he asked:

Zhāng laughed heartily and they reconciled as before.
After Zhāng established his family,

Duke Jǐng of Qí attacked Sòng,

who angrily said:

Yànzǐ identified them as Tāng, the minister of Sòng, and Yī Yǐn,
describing their appearances:
Tāng was fair-skinned with abundant hair,
Yī Yǐn was dark and short.
These matched the figures in the dream.
Duke Jǐng proceeded with the campaign, disregarding the warning,
the army drums were destroyed,

Seven Inches
Duke Huán of Qí hunted and captured a singing crane,

wearing a robe of white jade,
girded with a sword and holding a knife,
cursing angrily with glaring eyes.
Later, he also obtained a broken tooth,
three chǐ square and round,
and asked his assembled ministers:
"Does the world have such things and such small people?"
Chén Zhāng replied:
"In the past, Hú Chōng of Qín crossed the sea in one leap,
and battled with Qí and Lǔ,
breaking and injuring his flat teeth.

being three cùn and three fēn tall."

there is Lǐ Zǐ'áng, seven cùn tall,

One morning, he was swallowed by a sea crane,
and dwelling in the crane's belly,
did not die for three hundred years.

Mission to Chǔ
Yànzǐ was sent as an envoy to Chǔ.
Because Yànzǐ was short,
the people of Chǔ made a small gate beside the main gate to receive Yànzǐ.
Yànzǐ did not enter,
saying:
"Those sent to a dog country enter through a dog gate.
Now your servant is sent to Chǔ,
so I should not enter through this gate."
The usher then changed the route and led him through the main gate to see the King of Chǔ.
The King said:
"Does Qí have no men?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Línzī has three hundred neighborhoods where spreading sleeves creates shade,
waving sweat creates rain,
and people stand shoulder to shoulder and follow heel to heel.
How can you say we have no men?"
The King said:
"Then why have you been sent as envoy?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Qí appoints envoys
each according to their mission.
The worthy are sent
to worthy kings,
the unworthy are sent
to unworthy kings.
Yīng (referring to himself) is the most unworthy,
so I was sent directly to Chǔ."
From "Yànzǐ"
Tiny

Short in Stature

saying to him:

but with the seven-foot sword at my waist, I intend to behead the ill-mannered king."

Jùlíng
A short man was sent from Dōngjùn,
seven inches tall,
fully dressed in official attire.
The Emperor suspected he was a mountain spirit,
and often had him walk on his desk.
He summoned Dōngfāng Shuò to inquire.
Shuò arrived and called out to the short man:
"Jùlíng, why have you suddenly rebelled and come here?
Has the Queen Mother returned yet?"
The short man did not respond,
but instead said to the Emperor:
"The Queen Mother sent me
to inform Your Majesty of the method to seek the Way,
which lies solely in purity and tranquility,
and not in agitation and disturbance."
After five years, he would meet with the Emperor again, but when he finished speaking, he was never seen again.

Shěn Yuē asked Liú Yǎo:
"Hé Chéngtiān compiled extraordinary accounts,
broadly collecting written records,
which include matters of Zhāng Zhòngshī and the Long-Necked King.

Yǎo replied:
"Zhāng Zhòngshī's height of one chi and two cun
only appears in 'Discourses Weighed in the Balance';
the long-necked one refers to King Píqiān,
as recorded in the 'Account of South of Fúnán' from the Jiàn'ān era of the Sòng dynasty:

Yuē then consulted both texts,
and found them exactly as Yǎo had said.

Xiǎo lì

Yǒu Xī, the short man

a merchant from Daqin named Qín Lùn arrived at Jiāozhǐ.
The governor of Jiāozhǐ, Wú Miǎo, sent him to Sun Quán.
Sun Quán asked him about local customs and traditions,
and he provided detailed responses.
At the time, Zhūgě Kè was campaigning in Dānyáng,
and captured short-statured people from Yǒu and Shè. When Qín Lùn saw them, he said:

Sun Quán assigned ten men and ten women,

very short

and Yǔn, styled Shūzhēn,
both suffered from frailty and illness since childhood,
and were very short in stature.
Yet they were exceptionally intelligent and quick-witted.
Emperor Wǔdì heard of them and wished to meet them,
but Shāntāo dared not refuse directly.
He consulted Yǔn about it,
and Yǔn, considering himself frail and unimpressive, was unwilling to go.
Shāntāo believed Yǔn surpassed him in judgment,
so he submitted a memorial stating:

and should avoid social engagements.

Commentators found this remarkable.

Qīnghé Wáng Yuè, having heard of Yè's reputation,
summoned him to serve as Legal Advisor.
Upon seeing Yè's short stature and plain appearance,
he laughed without speaking.
But after observing Yè's handling of legal judgments,
he then said to Yè:
"Your clarity in decision-making
truly demonstrates that one's capabilities can surpass their physical form."

Three short

Short and Bald
Ruǎn Fú was witty and fond of wine.
He was short in stature and bald.
Emperor Wén of the Zhōu dynasty particularly favored and esteemed him.
The emperor often placed ten jars of wine in a room,
each jar holding one hú,
and covered them all with hats, intending to play a trick on Ruǎn Fú.
As soon as Ruǎn Fú entered the room and saw them,
he exclaimed in pleasant surprise:
"My brothers,
how very impolite of you
to enter the royal palace and sit opposite the emperor!
You should return home early."
Thereupon, he took the wine and left.
Emperor Wén of the Zhōu dynasty was both taken aback and amused, bursting into laughter.
Short Person
Táng Chángsūn Yuántóng was sharp and eloquent from a young age.
During the Zhēnguàn era, he once attended a banquet hosted by several nobles,
and no one could match him in debate.
Princess Gāomì then remarked:
"Our Duàn family also has talented young men."
She immediately sent for Duàn Kè
and had him face off against Xuántóng.
Although Duàn Kè was somewhat articulate,
he was exceptionally short in stature.
As soon as he was summoned and entered through the door,
Xuántóng immediately said:
"It's already getting dark."
The princess and others were greatly surprised and asked:
"It's only mealtime—
why do you say it's dark?"
Xuántóng then pointed at Duàn Kè:
"If it weren't getting dark,
how could a short man be moving among us?"
Everyone burst into laughter,
while Kè's face turned deep red,
and he had no reply.
(From "Qǐyán Lù")
Merit and Virtue
Dòu Xiǎo was short in stature,
with large, bulging eyes,
while Yuè Yànwěi was tall with prominent teeth.
Yànwěi first teased him, saying:
"You must have accumulated great merit."
Those nearby were puzzled,
and asked Yànwěi:
"Since he's already short,
and his flesh so diligently cultivated,
doesn't that indeed indicate great merit?"
Dòu immediately retorted:
"You yourself possess great merit,
why ask me about the reason?"
Dòu continued:
"Musician Yuè has grown tall since childhood."
When asked about the meaning of growing tall,
Dòu said:
"With such height,
and a mouth like a high cliff,
isn't that growing tall?"
Everyone burst into laughter.

Receiving a Guest
King Zhuāng of Chǔ besieged Sòng,
and Zǐ Fǎn climbed the rampart to spy on the Sòng city.
He saw Huá Yuán and said:
"How is your state faring?"
Huá Yuán replied:
"We exchange children to eat them,
and split bones to use as firewood."
Zǐ Fǎn said:
"I have heard that those besieging a state muzzle their horses when feeding them,
and present the fat ones to guests.
Why are you being so truthful with me?"
Huá Yuán replied:
"I have heard that when a gentleman sees others' suffering, he shows compassion;
when a petty man sees others' suffering, he takes pleasure in it.
I perceive you to be a gentleman,
and therefore I have told you the truth."

speaking of victory

Zǐgòng said:
"Why are you fat?"
Zǐ Qiān replied:
"When I go out and see beautiful carriages and horses, I desire them;
when I hear the words of the ancient kings, I also desire them.
These two minds battle each other.
Now the words of the ancient kings have prevailed,
therefore I am fat."

Yì Shèng
Zǐxià met Zéngzǐ,
Zéngzǐ said:
"Why have you grown so plump?"
He replied:
"Because I have won a battle, hence the plumpness."
Zéngzǐ said:
"What do you mean?"
Zǐxià said:
"When I stay home, I see the righteousness of former kings and honor it;
when I go out, I see the pleasures of wealth and honor and also desire them.
These two contended within my breast,
with neither winning nor losing,
so I grew thin.
Now the righteousness of former kings has prevailed,
hence I've grown plump."

wearing fat
In the fifth year of the Huángchū era, Wú Zhì came to the capital for an audience.
An edict ordered generals of the upper army and those with the title of special advance and below to gather at Wú Zhì's residence.
The imperial kitchen provided supplies, and when the wine was flowing freely,
Wú Zhì wanted to maximize the enjoyment.
At that time, General of the Upper Army Cáo Zhēn was by nature fat,
while Central Army Commander Zhū Shuò was by nature thin.
Wú Zhì summoned entertainers to perform a routine about fat and thin.
Cáo Zhēn, bearing his noble status, felt ashamed to be made a joke of,
and angrily said to Wú Zhì:

Cáo Hóng and Wáng Zhōng said:

Wú Zhì pressed his hand on his sword and said:
"Cáo Zǐdān, you are nothing but meat on a butcher's block.
Wú Zhì could swallow you without his throat moving,
chew you without his teeth shaking.

The Emperor
His belly hung down past his knees.
Zhāng Shǒuguī was the military governor of Yōuzhōu,
when Ān Lùshān was caught stealing sheep.
Shǒuguī had him stripped and seated, intending to beat him to death.
Lùshān shouted loudly:
"Does the Grand Master not wish to subdue the two barbarian tribes?
Why kill Lùshān?"
Shǒuguī, seeing that he was fat and fair-skinned,
admired his bold words and released him,
ordering him to capture spies together with his fellow villager Shǐ Sīmíng.
They were always successful in their missions,
so he was promoted to deputy general.
Disliking his fatness,
and because Shǒuguī's authority was always formidable,
he feared to eat his fill.
Renowned for his valor,
he was eventually adopted as a son.
In his later years, he grew even fatter and stronger,
his belly hanging down past his knees,
weighing three hundred and thirty jin.
Whenever he walked, he had to lift his body with his shoulders left and right
just to move a step.
When performing the Whirling Barbarian Dance before Emperor Xuánzōng,
he was swift as a wind-blown horse.
Lùshān's belly was huge;
each time he dressed and belted,
three or four people assisted him.
Two would lift his belly,
while Zhū'ér supported it with his head,
only then could they manage the skirt, trousers, and waistband.
Emperor Xuánzōng doted on Lùshān,
granting him hot spring baths at Huáqīng Palace,
and always permitted Zhū'ér and others to help him undress and dress.
Yet in the end, the one who eviscerated him was Zhū'ér.
From the Old Book of Táng.

appointed me to govern the official affairs of Dānfù.

hence the emaciation."

Five Zàng Organs
To deduce the Mandate of Heaven,
one must base it on human nature.
Humans have five zàng organs and six fǔ organs.
What are the five zàng organs?
Jīng is stored in the kidneys,
shén is stored in the heart,
hún is stored in the liver,
pò is stored in the lungs,
and zhì is stored in the spleen.
What are the six fǔ organs?
The throat is the organ that measures intake,
the stomach is called the organ of the five grains,
the large intestine is the organ of transport,
the small intestine is the organ that receives and completes,
the gallbladder is the organ that accumulates essence,

To lose one's head is easier than to change one's cap
Suppose there is a person here who cuts off his head to exchange for a crown,
and kills himself to exchange for clothing.
The world would certainly consider it absurd.
Why is that?
A crown is meant to adorn the head,
and clothing is meant to adorn the body.
Now if one kills what is to be adorned in order to obtain what adorns it,
then one does not understand the purpose of these things.
The world's pursuit of profit is like this—
they also do not understand what they are doing.

Wound Surface
When Emperor Āi first ascended the throne,
the Erudite Shēn Xián criticized the Court Gentleman Xüe Xuān for failing to support his family,
observing mourning rites,
and being neglectful toward his own flesh and blood.
He argued that Xuān should not retain his marquis title
or remain in the court ministries.
Xuān's son, Xuàng, served as a Gentleman of the Right.
After repeatedly hearing these criticisms,
he bribed a retainer named Yáng Míng
to disfigure Xián's face,
preventing him from holding office.
When the position of Director of the Capital became vacant and Xuàng
feared Xián would be appointed,
he ordered Míng to ambush and assault Xián outside the palace gate,
severing his nose and lips, inflicting eight wounds on his body.
The case was handed to the authorities, and Xuàng's death sentence was reduced by one degree.
Xuān was implicated and dismissed, becoming a commoner.

Jìn, realizing the truth was uncovered,
knocked his head on the ground in submission.

In the wilderness of all directions, there is a stone drum,

its sound like thunder.
"Shén Yì Jīng" states that in the eastern city, near the ancestral mountain, there is a stone drum,
which sounds when an invasion is imminent,
thus serving as an early warning system.
"Qí Dì Jì" records that at Mount Féng there is a shrine along with a stone,
with the stone person standing side by side,
when the world is in turmoil,
the stone person will beat the drum,
heard for dozens of miles.
In Guō Yuánzhì's "Shù Zhēng Jì," it is noted that below the eastern stone drum of Mount Fú, there are two stone drums,
beating them produces a clear resonant sound,
known as the divine bell.
"Luó Fú Shān Jì" describes that on Mount Dòngtíng, there is a palace,
and to the east of the five gates, there is a stone tower,
beneath the tower are two stone drums, when struck,
they produce a clear resonant sound,
which is what the world refers to as the divine bell,
Jìn Xiàowǔ's "Musical Composition" states:
"When the divine bell rings once,
the nine realms will converge.
According to "Jùn Guó Zhì", in Jì County, there is a heavenly drum,
the mountain has a stone like a drum,
when the River Drum star shakes, the stone drum sounds,
and when it sounds, calamity befalls the Qin.
In "Yǒu Yáng Zá Zǔ," it is noted that south of Wǎn'ān County in Cízhōu, there is Drum Mountain,
on which there are two stones like drums,

At the end of the Northern Qí,
this drum once sounded, and Qí was annexed by Zhōu.
At the end of the reign of Emperor Wén of Suí,
the drum again sounded itself,
its resonance traveling hundreds of miles,
and the Táng rose in place of Suí,
thus it was called the divine bell.

Three Absences on the Face
Lǐ Kuān served as a regular attendant,
and had a subordinate named Lú who was skilled in physiognomy.
Someone asked, "How about Lord Lǐ?"
He replied:
"Based on what is absent from his face, there are three things:

From "Jīnhuázǐ"
Can endure cold
Why is the human face alone able to withstand cold?
It is said that the head
is the convergence point of all yang meridians.
All yin meridians reach the neck and turn back without ascending,
only the yang meridians ascend to the head,
therefore the face can endure cold.
"Sùwèn"
states: All yang energies converge at the face.
The twelve regular meridians and three hundred sixty-five collaterals,
their blood and qi all ascend to the face and enter the orifices.
The essential yang qi ascends to the eyes and becomes vision,
its divergent qi goes to the ears and becomes hearing,
its ancestral qi emerges at the nose and becomes smell,
its turbid qi comes from the stomach,
goes to the lips and tongue and becomes taste.
The fluids from this qi
all steam upward to the face, and the skin is thick,
the flesh is firm,
therefore even when the weather is extremely cold,
it cannot overcome it.

Frowning with worry
During the Yuánjiā era,
the women of the capital adopted frowning eyebrows and tearful makeup,
walked with a swaying waist,
and gave decayed-tooth smiles.
The so-called frowning eyebrows
were thin and curved;
the tearful makeup
involved lightly wiping below the eyes as if from crying;
the fallen-horse bun
was tilted to one side;
the swaying-waist walk
meant the feet did not move directly under the body;
the decayed-tooth smile
resembled the expression of a toothache,
lacking genuine joy.
This began with the household of General-in-Chief Liáng Jì,
and the capital eagerly followed,
with all of China imitating it.
Heaven's warning was as if saying:
"Troops will come to arrest the women,
who will worry and frown,
weeping before the officers and soldiers,
dragged and bent at the waist and spine,
their hair buns askew,
and though they force smiles,
there will be no life in them."

Scorched Eyebrows
Wáng Chéng in Jīngzhōu,

Shū sternly said to the attendants:

Chéng angrily said:

and burn his eyebrows.

and thus Xīn was spared.
Later, Shū served Wáng Dūn,
and admonished Dūn.
Dūn said:

Prescription for Eye Pain
Fàn Nìng, whose courtesy name was Wǔzǐ,
once suffered from eye pain
and went to Zhāng Zhàn seeking a prescription.
Zhāng thereupon teased him, saying:
"The ancient prescription was first obtained by Sòng Yánglǐzǐ in his youth,
who passed it to Lǔ Dōngmén Bó.
Lǔ Dōngmén Bó then passed it to Zuǒ Qiūmíng,
and thus it was transmitted through generations.
By the time it reached Hàn's Dù Zǐxià, Zhèng Kāngchéng, and Wèi's Nántáng Lóng,
as well as Jìn's Zuǒ Tàichōng,
all these worthies had eye ailments.
They obtained this prescription which states: reduce reading,
first, diminish contemplation and worry;
second, focus on inner vision;
third, simplify outward gazing;
fourth, rise late in the morning;
fifth, sleep early at night.
These six ingredients are simmered with divine fire,
filtered through breath,
and stored within the chest.
After seven days, then contain them within the heart,
cultivating this for a period.
In the near term, you can count your own eyelashes and see distant views;
persisting with it further,
taking it continuously without cease,
you will see clearly through walls,
not only improving eyesight,
but also prolonging life."

Turtle Breathing
Lǐ Qiáo had shown exceptional talent since childhood.
He visited Yuán Tiāngāng,

"You, sir, possess a pure and refined spirit, but your lifespan may not be long."
His mother grew worried,
so Yuán Tiāngāng requested to stay with him in the study,

Yuán slept soundly upon lying down,
while Lǐ alone remained awake.
It was not until the fifth watch that he suddenly fell asleep.
Yuán happened to wake up,
observed that Lǐ Qiáo showed no signs of breathing,
and checked with his hand,
finding no breath under his nose.
Initially greatly alarmed and puzzled,
after a long while, he detected his breathing rhythm,
which was actually coming from his ears.
Patting him, Yuán informed him:
"I've found it."
He then rose and congratulated his mother, saying:
"I had checked several times without success,
but now I have finally seen it.
Your son is destined for great nobility and longevity;
this is 'turtle breathing,'
indicating high status and long life but not wealth."
Later events indeed turned out as he predicted.

"If one's learning is not refined,
and one's understanding of the Way is not profound,
generally listening is meant to attain wisdom,
to accomplish conduct,
and to achieve merit and fame.
Without refinement there is no clarity,
without depth there is no penetration.
Therefore, the highest learning listens with the spirit,
the middle learning listens with the heart,
the lower learning listens with the ears.
Those who listen with ears learn only at the skin level,
those who listen with heart learn at the muscle level,
those who listen with spirit learn at the bone marrow level.
Thus, if listening is not profound,
then understanding will not be clear.
If understanding is not clear, then one cannot exhaust its essence.
If one cannot exhaust its essence, then one's practice will not be accomplished."

Duke Huán of Qí invited his ministers to prepare wine,

and Duke Huán raised his cup to toast him.

is this in accordance with ritual?"

when speech errs, one's life is discarded.

why not quickly bring troops here'
He then deliberately dropped this letter in the courtyard of the Zhōu ruler and hastily departed.
The Zhōu court believed Cháng Hóng was betraying Zhōu,
so they executed Cháng Hóng and put him to death.

he had visited Cháng Hóng in Zhōu multiple times,

I will depose the Liú clan and establish the Shàn clan. The Liú clan requested this.'
The ruler said:
"This is Cháng Hóng's doing.
So they executed him.

Duke Huán of Zhèng intended to attack Kuài,
so he first inquired about Kuài's wise, discerning, resolute, and courageous scholars.
He recorded their names,
selected Kuài's capable ministers to befriend,
and wrote official titles and ranks for them.
He then set up an altar outside the city gate and buried the list,
sprinkling it with the blood of a boar
as if making a covenant.
The ruler of Kuài, suspecting an internal rebellion,
executed all his capable ministers.
Duke Huán seized the opportunity to attack,
and thus conquered Kuài.
The wife of the King of Qí died,
and there were seven favored young women,
all close to Xuē Gōng,
who wanted to know which one the king wished to establish.
So he presented seven earrings,
making one of them especially beautiful.
The next day, observing where the beautiful earring was,
he advised the king to establish that woman as his wife.
"Strategies of Qí"
Zhāng Chǒu was a hostage in Yān,
and the King of Yān wanted to kill him.
As he was fleeing and about to cross the border,
the border official captured Chǒu.
Chǒu said:
"The reason the King of Yān is about to kill me
is that someone said I have a precious pearl,
and the king wants to obtain it.
Now I have already lost it,
but the King of Yān does not believe me.
Now if you take me to him,
I will say that you seized my pearl and swallowed it,
and the King of Yān will certainly kill you,
cutting open your belly and your intestines.
For a ruler who desires something,
one cannot appeal with profit.
I am about to die,
and your intestines will also be cut into pieces."
The border official became frightened
and released him.
"Yàn Cè" - Hán Zǐ, Wú Zǐxū's affairs are similar.
Someone presented an elixir of immortality to the King of Chǔ,
and the court usher carried it in.
A palace guard asked:
"Is this edible?"
The usher replied:
"Yes."
So the guard snatched it and ate it.
The king, enraged, sent someone to kill the guard.
The guard had someone plead with the king, saying:
"I asked the usher,
and he said it was edible,
so I ate it.
Thus, I am not guilty—
the fault lies with the usher.
Moreover, the visitor presented an immortality elixir,
I consumed it,
yet the king has me killed—
this makes it a death potion.
If the king kills an innocent subject,
it will only prove that someone has deceived the king."
The king then refrained from killing him.
"Chǔ Cè"
When Zhòng Rǔzhī Yuán Àng often cited grand principles with fervor and indignation,
the eunuch Zhào Tán, being frequently favored,
often harmed Àng,
which troubled Àng.
His elder brother's son Zhǒng served as a regular attendant rider,
and advised Àng, saying:
"If you publicly humiliate him,
even if he later bears malice toward you,
the emperor will no longer believe him."
Thereupon, when the emperor was going to court at the Eastern Palace,
with Zhào Tán riding as an outrider,
Àng prostrated himself before the carriage and said:
"I have heard that those who share the six-foot carriage with the Son of Heaven
are all heroes and outstanding figures of the realm.
Although Hàn may lack men now,
why should Your Majesty alone share the carriage with one who has survived the knife and saw!"
Thereupon the emperor laughed,
ordered Zhào Tán to dismount,
and Tán, weeping, descended from the carriage.
《Book of Hàn》
Lǚ Bù went to see Yuán Shào,
Shào was troubled by Bù,
and wanted to kill him.
He dispatched thirty-six soldiers clad in armor to receive Bù,
ordering them to lie down by the tent.
Bù learned of this,
so he played the zither inside the tent,
and while the soldiers were lying down,
Bù slipped out of the tent and left,
without the soldiers noticing.
"Records of the Heroes"
At that time, there was a Daoist priest
who was quite skilled at curing illnesses
and had come from the Central Plains.
He deceived people,
claiming, "I am several hundred years old."
Xuán knew he was lying.
Later, at a gathering of many guests,
Xuán said to a close associate:
"Would you like to know this gentleman's true age?"
The associate replied:
"Excellent."
Suddenly, someone descended from the sky,
and all present fixed their gaze on him.
After a long while, he landed on the ground,
wearing red robes and an advanced scholar's cap.
He approached the Daoist priest
and said:
"The Heavenly Emperor commands me to ask how old you truly are,
that you dare deceive the common people."
The Daoist priest was greatly terrified,
dismounted from his seat and knelt down,
replying:
"I have committed an offense;
my true age is seventy-three."
Xuán then clapped his hands and laughed heartily,
and suddenly the red-robed figure vanished.
The Daoist priest was deeply ashamed,
and subsequently no one knew where he had gone.
From "Biographies of the Divine Immortals."
Using a horsewhip to brush past, Emperor Yuán of Jìn's uncle,
Dōng'ān Wáng Sīmǎ Yóu was killed by Chéngdū Wáng Sīmǎ Yǐng,
fearing that disaster would reach him,
plotted to flee.
That night the moon was bright,
the imperial guards were very strict,
and he could not get away.
After a while,
a sudden storm darkened the sky,
the patrolling guards dispersed,
the Emperor seized the opportunity to escape,
arriving at Héyáng he was stopped by the ferry officer,
his follower Zǒng Diǎn arrived later,
and brushed him with a horsewhip,
saying:

but you are also being detained?"
Then he laughed heartily,
and because of this he was released.
