Wēn Qiáo knew that Wáng Dūn could no longer be persuaded,
so he secretly plotted to eliminate him.
First, he diligently managed the affairs of Wáng Dūn's office day and night and catered to his desires. Qián Fèng was trusted by Dūn.
Qiáo said to others:
"Qián Shìyí is full of wisdom and spirit."
Qiáo had long been known for his ability to judge character,
and Fèng, hearing this, was pleased,
forming a friendly relationship with Qiáo.
When the position of Governor of Dānyáng became vacant,
Qiáo advised Dūn:
"The Capital Governor oversees critical communications and should be
someone skilled in both civil and military affairs.
You should personally select the right talent."
Dūn agreed,
and asked Qiáo:
"Who would be suitable?"
Qiáo replied:
"I believe Qián Fèng could be appointed,
but the decision rests with you."
Dūn thought for a long time,
finding no one better than Qiáo himself,
so Qiáo immediately declined,
but Dūn did not accept.
He submitted a recommendation to appoint Qiáo as Governor of Dānyáng.
Qiáo still feared that Qián Fèng might devise treacherous schemes,
so when Dūn held a farewell banquet for Qiáo,
Qiáo said:
"Leaving your presence,
my heart is filled with reluctance.
I wish to personally serve the wine,
to express my feelings at this parting."
When serving wine to Fèng,
before Fèng could drink,
Qiáo feigned drunkenness,
striking with his hand,
causing Fèng's headpiece to fall off, and said angrily:
"Who is Qián Fèng?
When Wēn Tàizhēn serves wine,
how dare he not drink?"
Fèng was displeased,
but Dūn thought Qiáo was drunk,
and reconciled them both.
The next day, Fèng said:
"Qiáo is very close to the imperial court,
and may not be trustworthy.
He might harbor intentions of betrayal;
we should reconsider."
Dūn replied:
"Tàizhēn was drunk yesterday,
and merely a bit harsh.
How can we use that to slander him?"
Thus, Fèng's scheme did not succeed,
and Qiáo was able to return to the capital.

Wáng Yǔnzhī was at the age of wearing his hair in two knots,
when Dūn knew him well
and said he resembled himself, so
he would sleep together with him.
Once, after drinking at night, Yǔnzhī excused himself, saying:
"I'm drunk and will sleep first."
When Dūn was plotting rebellion with Qián Fèng,
Yǔnzhī overheard everything.
Fearing Dūn might suspect him,
he vomited profusely where he slept.
Dūn indeed came with a light to check,
saw him sleeping amid the vomit,
and no longer suspected him.
Wáng Wéndù's younger brother Āzhì
was exceedingly wicked,
and when he came of age, no one would marry him.
Sūn Xìnggōng had a daughter,
who was also eccentric and difficult,
with no prospect of marriage.
He therefore visited Wéndù,
requesting to meet Āzhì.
After the meeting,
he feigned approval, saying:
"He is certainly acceptable,
far from what people say about him.
How could he remain unmarried until now?
I have a daughter,
who is not bad,
but as a poor scholar, I shouldn't scheme with you."
He intended for Āzhì to marry her.
Wéndù delightedly informed Lántián:
"Xìnggōng came unexpectedly,
wishing to marry his daughter to Āzhì."
Lántián was pleasantly surprised. After the marriage,
the daughter's obstinacy and insolence exceeded expectations.
Only then did Āzhì realize Xìnggōng's deceit.

Qí Wáng Jìngzé was the magistrate of Jìyáng County.
A group of bandits had fled into the mountains,
becoming a scourge to the people.
Jìngzé sent someone to convey a message to the bandit leader,
urging him to surrender,
promising to plead his case.
In the temple below the city walls,
the deity was known to be fierce and severe,
and the people trusted in it.
Jìngzé invoked the deity to swear an oath,
vowing not to betray him.
Once the bandit leader emerged,
Jìngzé hosted a wine banquet for him in the temple,
and had him seized and bound during the gathering,
saying:
"I prayed to the deity that if I broke my oath,
I would offer ten oxen in return.
Now, to avoid violating the oath,
I must immediately slaughter ten oxen to appease the deity."
He then executed all the bandits.
The people were pleased by this.
From "History of the Southern Dynasties"
Fàn Yún,
in the early Jiànyuán era of Qí,
when Prince Zǐliáng of Jìnglíng served as the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī,
Yún held the position of Registrar.
The prince was initially unaware of his abilities,
but later, on a scheduled day to ascend Qínwàng Mountain,
he then summoned Yún.
Yún knew that on the mountain there was a stone inscription by Qín Shǐhuáng,
with a text structured in three-line stanzas,
yet most people read it as two-line verses,
thus failing to grasp the rhyme,
and moreover, it was written entirely in large seal script,
which most could not decipher.
So he studied the "Records of the Grand Historian" overnight until he could recite it fluently.
The next day, upon ascending the mountain,
Zǐliáng ordered his guests and subordinates to read it,
but all were baffled and unable to recognize it.
Finally, he asked Yún,
who replied:
"This humble official has previously studied the 'Records of the Grand Historian',
and encountered this stone inscription text.
He then stepped forward and read it fluently.
Zǐliáng was greatly pleased,
and regarded him as a distinguished guest,
from then on, Yún enjoyed the highest favor in the princely administration.
In the third year of Yǒng'ān,
the rebel Ěrhzhū Zhào imprisoned Emperor Zhuāng in a monastery.
At that time, Prince Wáng of Tàiyuán was extremely arrogant due to his high achievements,
and acted with unrestrained opinions on right and wrong.
The emperor was afraid,
and said to his attendants:
"I would rather die as a noble prince,
than live as an emperor like Emperor Xiàn of Hàn.
He then sought advice from Prince Huī of Chéngyáng.
Huī said:
"Use the birth of the crown prince as a pretext;
Róng will surely come to court.
Then use this opportunity to destroy him.
Emperor Zhuāng said:
"The empress is pregnant for ten months;
now it is only nine months, is that feasible?
Huī said:
"There are women who give birth earlier,
and others later;
it is not strange.
The emperor accepted his plan,
and thus announced the birth of the crown prince.
He sent Huī specially to the residence of Prince Wáng of Tàiyuán,
telling him:
"The crown prince has been born;
Róng was playing games with Prince Tiānmù of Shàngdǎng.
Huī removed Róng's hat,
and danced joyfully in circles.
Huī was naturally magnanimous,
and did not show his emotions on his face,
running and shouting joyfully inside and outside the palace.
Róng believed it,
and entered the court together with Mù.
When Emperor Zhuāng heard of Róng's arrival,
he unconsciously turned pale.
The Palace Attendant for Internal Affairs, Wēn Zǐshēng, said:
"Your Majesty, your expression has changed.
The emperor repeatedly requested wine to drink,
and then proceeded with his affairs.
Once Róng and Mù were executed,
Huī was appointed Grand Preceptor and Sīmǎ.

Ěrzhū Zhào entered Luòyáng and captured Emperor Zhuāng,

In the second year of the Jiànmíng era,
Prince Chángguǎng traveled from Jìnyáng to the capital.
Upon reaching the outer walls,
Shìlóng, considering Prince Chángguǎng's distant lineage,
his governance unknown,
forced him to abdicate in favor of Prince Guǎnglíng,

During the Zhèngguāng era,
he served as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
witnessing Yuán Yì's hold on power,
with governance falling to favored associates,
so he feigned muteness and ceased speaking,
withdrawing from worldly affairs.
In the Yǒng'ān era,
he fled to the mountains of Shàngluò,
where the provincial inspector Quán Qǐ captured and sent him back.
Emperor Zhuāng suspected Guǎnglíng of deceit,
sending men at night to steal his clothes,
then drawing swords to kill him,
but Guǎnglíng opened his mouth, pointing to his tongue,
and ultimately did not speak.
Emperor Zhuāng believed his affliction genuine,
ordering him to return to his residence.
Guǎnglíng often stayed at Lónghuá Temple.
By this time,
Shìlóng plotted to depose and install a ruler,
fearing he truly could not speak,
so he had the prince's confidant convey his intent,
with added coercion,
to which the prince replied:
"Does Heaven speak?
"Weì Jì" Thus he ascended the throne as emperor,
changing the era name to Pǔtài.
Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Xíng Zǐcái drafted a pardon,
detailing Emperor Zhuāng's unjust killing of the Prince of Tàiyuán.
Prince Guǎnglíng said:
"Yǒng'ān personally eliminated a powerful minister,
not due to lack of virtue,
but because Heaven had not yet wearied of chaos,
encountering the tragedy of Chéng Jì.

stating, "I will compose it myself,"
and wrote directly:

am favored by destiny's push,
wishing to share with the multitude,

The decree of pardon,
follows the constant form.

Scholars across the land hailed him as a sage ruler.

Ěrzhū Chǎng,
called Qiánluó,
was a nephew of Ěrzhū Róng.
His father, Yànbó,
was among the Ěrzhū clan members entirely executed after Qí Shénwǔ's victory at Hánlíng.
As a child, Chǎng followed his mother and was raised in the palace.
By the age of twelve,
he escaped through a hole in the wall,
reaching the main street,
where he saw a group of children playing.
Chǎng removed his ornate silk and gold-adorned clothing,
exchanged garments, and fled.
Pursuing horsemen soon arrived,
initially not recognizing Chǎng,
so they seized the child in the silk clothes.
Only after thorough questioning did they realize it was not him,
and as it was already dusk,
he thus managed to escape.
(Book of Suì)
Qí Wén Xiāng suspected Wén Xuān was feigning foolishness,
fearing he might cause future trouble,
and planned to secretly eliminate him.
He consulted Cuī Xiān about this,
to which Cuī Xiān replied:
"I once stood in the same official procession as the second son,
and tested him by tapping his back with my hand tablet.
He showed no anger,
but instead exchanged his rhinoceros-horn hand tablet for my bamboo one,
wiping it clean and admiring it playfully.
From this, I knew he was truly foolish,
and not worth worrying about."
Later, when the emperor had Cuī Xiān imprisoned,
he reproached him for the past incident of striking his back.
Cuī Xiān recounted the words he had spoken to Wén Xiāng,
highlighting his own merit to redeem himself from death.
The emperor realized and said:
"That I avoided disaster
was due to Cuī Xiān's effort."
He released him and rewarded him.

Yǔwén Tài and Hóu Jǐng engaged in a joint battle,
when Tài's horse was hit by a stray arrow,
it panicked and bolted,
losing its way.
Tài fell to the ground,
and the Eastern Wei troops caught up to him,
his attendants all scattered.
Lǐ Mù dismounted and struck Tài with his whip,
shouting at him:

where is your master?
Why are you left here alone?
The pursuers grew suspicious,
so he gave his horse to Tài,

Yuán Zhěn, skilled in horsemanship and archery, served as the governor of Nányù Prefecture.
The Tàihúshān barbarians frequently raided and plundered,
and previous governors had merely exercised loose control over them.
Zhěn then devised a plan and summoned over thirty chieftains of the Xīncài and Xiāngchéng barbarians.
He arrayed his troops in full military attire west of the prefecture and prepared a banquet,
inviting them to observe an archery display.
First, he dispatched over twenty of his skilled archers,
and Zhěn himself shot several arrows,
all hitting their mark.
He then ordered his attendants to shoot in turn.
A prisoner condemned to death was brought forth,
dressed in military uniform,
and included in the archery lineup.
When ordered to shoot and failing to hit the target,
Zhěn immediately reprimanded and executed him.
The barbarian chieftains looked at each other, their legs trembling with fear.
He had also prearranged for his attendants to fetch ten death-row prisoners,
dressed them in barbarian clothing,
and claimed they were raiders.
Zhěn then sat solemnly,
pretending to gaze up at the sky,
and as a slight breeze stirred,
he said to the barbarians:
"The wind carries a hint of violence,
as if raiders have crossed the border,
no more than ten of them,
likely around fifty lǐ southwest of here."
He immediately ordered cavalry to pursue and capture them,
and sure enough, they returned with ten bound captives.
Zhěn declared to the barbarians:
"Your people commit such banditry—
do they not deserve death?"
The barbarians all kowtowed and said:
"They deserve ten thousand deaths."
Zhěn promptly executed them
and then sent the barbarians back.
The barbarians were deeply impressed,
and from then on, there were no more raids or plundering in the region.
Book of Wèi
Zhāng Yuè was banished to Yuèzhōu,
often feeling depressed and unhappy.
At that time, the chief ministers, due to Zhāng Yuè's wit, eloquence, and talent,
mutually excluded and rejected him.
Sǔ Tǐng was then highly employed,
and Zhāng Yuè had a good relationship with Guī, so he
composed the "Ode to the Five Gentlemen," sealed the poem in a letter, and sent it to Sǔ Tǐng,
instructing his messenger:
"Wait until the anniversary of his father's death,
and deliver it near dusk.
The messenger, approaching dusk, found mourners
arriving in large numbers, many of whom were old colleagues of Zhāng Yuè's late father."
Sǔ Tǐng read the poem,
sobbed and shed tears.
The next day,
he spoke earnestly to the emperor on Zhāng Yuè's behalf:
"Loyal and upright, outspoken and honest,
he is looked up to by the people
and should not be left stranded in a remote region."
The emperor then issued an imperial edict to console and inquire after him.
Soon after, Zhāng Yuè was transferred to the position of Chief Clerk of Jīngzhōu,
whereupon Lù Xiàngxiān, Wéi Sìlì, Zhāng Tíngguī, and Jiǎ Zēng were all demoted or exiled.
After many years, they were eventually reassessed and reinstated,
and Sǔ Tǐng, as a close friend of his father,
served him with great respect.
From "Records of Tang Poetry," the poem says:
"Desolate is the prime minister's residence,
its lingering blessings lie in Xuánchéng."
During the reign of Xiànzōng,
the Róng and Jié tribes caused turmoil in the Huá region.
An edict was issued to the Southern Liáng,
to raise three thousand armored soldiers,
ordering them to proceed to the capital.
As they were about to depart,
the soldiers rebelled,
driving away their commander.
They then gathered together to resist orders for over a year.
Xiànzōng considered this a grave problem.
Wēn Zào, the magistrate of Jīngzhào, requested to go with cavalry.
Upon reaching the region,
when the people of Liáng saw him,
stopping only a Confucian scholar,
they all congratulated each other that there was no threat.
When he arrived,
he merely announced the edict to reassure them,
asking nothing further.
However, the commanders of Liáng, those with transgressions,
did not part with their arms,
and Wēn did not admonish them.
On another day,
at the ball field, music was arranged,
and the entire army gathered,
being ordered to eat under the long veranda.
In front of the banquet seats,
along the steps, two long ropes were set up in the north and south rows,
ordering the soldiers to hang their swords and sabers on the ropes in front of them.
When the wine reached them,
there was a loud yell,
and from both ends the ropes were simultaneously lifted with force,
so the swords and sabers were raised over three zhang above the ground.
The soldiers were in great chaos,
unable to exert their bravery,
and then the doors were closed, and they were executed.
From then on, the people of Southern Liáng did not dare to rebel for generations.
"Wáng Shì Jiàn Wén"
The State Temple in Biànzhōu reported that the Buddha was sweating,
so Military Governor Liú Yuánzuǒ immediately took his carriage and personally brought gold and silk as offerings.
By noon,
his wife had also arrived.
The next day, they set up another alms-giving venue.
From then on, officials, officers, and merchants rushed about on the roads,
fearing only that they might not contribute their goods in time.
Consequently, he ordered officials to keep record books
to register the donations received.
After ten days, the temple was closed,
with the announcement:
"The Buddha's sweat has stopped."
They obtained an enormous sum of money,
which was used to cover military expenses.
from "Supplement to the National History"
Wáng È served as the military governor of Huáinán.
Once, while hearing a case, someone left an anonymous letter before him.
His attendants picked it up and handed it to Wáng È,
who tucked it into his boot.
There were already other documents in his boot, so he mixed it among them.
When the clerk later inquired about the letter,
Wáng È retrieved a different document and burned it.
People thought he had burned the anonymous letter.
After returning to review the matter,
he later used a minor unrelated incident to connect and detain the person accused in the letter for thorough investigation,
thereby deceiving his subordinates.
The clerks regarded him as divinely perceptive.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
When Líng Hú Chǔ was appointed to govern Yǎnzhōu,
the region was suffering from a drought,
and the price of rice was very high.
He sent an official to the government office,
inquiring about the current rice price,
and how many granaries the prefecture had.
After receiving the answers,
he counted on his fingers and murmured to himself:
"The previous price was such-and-such,
if each of the four granaries releases a certain amount of rice,
and sets the price at a specific level,
selling it would allow us to provide relief."
Those nearby overheard him,
and the news spread throughout the entire prefecture.
Wealthy people competed to release their stored goods,
causing prices to stabilize,
and people felt relieved, anticipating a good harvest.
From "The Zhītián Records"
Zhāng Jùn, during the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng of the Táng Dynasty,
personally commanded the six imperial guard armies,
and went to attack Tàiyuán,
but ended up losing control of the troops,
leading to the capture of his deputy commander, Vice Minister Sūn Kuí.
Soon, he planned to withdraw the army,
and the route passed through Píngyáng.
The local governor, surnamed Zhāng,
was a senior officer under Marshal Wáng Kē of Pú.
Wáng Kē was treacherous and unpredictable,
and Zhāng Jùn further worried that as the army passed through,
they might fall into his cunning trap.
Thus, Zhāng Jùn advanced several stages ahead,
and stayed at the official guesthouse in Píngyáng.
The six armies followed in sequence,
advancing through Yīndì Pass.
Zhāng Jùn deeply distrusted the governor of Jìn,
and when Zhāng came to welcome him outside the city,
after settling at the postal station,
Zhāng Jùn ordered Governor Zhāng to ascend the hall,
where tea, wine, and food were served,
detaining him until the lanterns were lit,
before allowing him to take his leave.
From morning until evening,
not a single word was exchanged.
Zhāng Jùn merely chewed on a small object in his mouth,
appearing from a distance as if he were engaged in conversation.
Wáng Kē was by nature highly suspicious,
and his actions were always guarded,
at that time, his spies had already secretly reported this to him.
Wáng Kē indeed grew suspicious,
summoned Zhāng and asked him:
"What did the Chancellor and you
talk about from morning until evening?"
Zhāng replied:
"We did not exchange a single word."
Wáng Kē utterly disbelieved him,
accusing him of dishonesty,
and had him executed.
The six armies then passed through safely on their return to the capital,
completely free of any worries.
Later, when Zhāng Jùn was in charge of state finances,
the various regions each sent luxurious silks and the like.
He did not accept any of them,
instead ordering a special envoy to deliver them in person, saying:
"Convey my intent:
use these to cover the expenses for military campaigns instead.
Pots, tents, cloth, troughs, and horse medicine,
as well as local products commonly available,
please prepare all of these."
Thereupon, the various feudal lords gladly complied,
so that even with an army of a hundred thousand on the move,
all necessities were fully supplied.
Zhū Wēn deeply resented him for this,
and ordered an assassin to kill him at his estate in Chángshuǐ.
"Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Lǐ Kèyòng sent someone into Wèi.
The scout reported:
"There are banners coming and going.
The Prince of Jìn said:
"Liú Xún has one scheme for each step he takes.
He ordered further investigation,
and indeed found straw dummies with banners tied to them,
carried by donkeys,
moving along the battlements.
Liú Xún's army had already left two days earlier.
"Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Lǐ Bàozhēn was stationed in Lùzhōu,
where military supplies were depleted,
and he had no plan to address it.
An elderly monk was highly trusted by the local people,
so Bàozhēn sought his help,
saying:
"By borrowing your authority,
may we relieve the army's needs?"
The monk replied:
"There is no problem."
Bàozhēn said:
"Just announce you will self-immolate on a chosen day at the parade ground,
and I will dig a tunnel connecting to my residence.
When the fire starts,
I will secretly bring you out."
The monk gladly agreed,
and thus made a public declaration.
Bàozhēn ordered firewood and oil stored at the parade ground,
then held a seven-day prayer ceremony,
with incense and lamps burning day and night,
amidst chanting of Buddhist scriptures.
Bàozhēn also led the monk into the tunnel,
to eliminate his suspicions.
The monk then ascended the platform holding an incense burner,
preaching to the crowd,
while Bàozhēn led officers and officials to bow below,
donating their salaries as alms,
piling them beside him.
Thus, men and women crowded in,
donating countless treasures over seven days.
Then they sent in the firewood pile,
poured oil and ignited flames,
struck bells and chanted Buddha's name.
Bàozhēn had secretly ordered the tunnel filled.
In a moment,
monk and firewood turned to ash.
Days later, he registered the acquired wealth into the military treasury,
found several dozen so-called relics,
and built a pagoda to store them.
"Shàngshū Gùshí" "Yùquánzǐ"
King Lǐ Décheng of the State of Wú governed Jiāngxī.
A fortune-teller claimed he could distinguish the noble from the base at a glance.
The king had several female entertainers,
dressed identically to his wife, the Duchess of Téng,
stand together in the courtyard
and asked him to identify them.
The fortune-teller bowed and approached,
saying,
"There is a yellow cloud above the duchess's head."
The entertainers instinctively looked up.
The fortune-teller declared,
"This is the duchess."
The king was pleased and sent him away.
From "Accounts of the Southern Táng".
The southern custom revered ghosts.
When Dì Wǔxiāng Qīng was campaigning against Nóng Zhìgāo,
as the great army first set out,
he prayed in Guìzhōu, saying:
"Victory or defeat has no basis for assurance.
So he took a hundred coins and held them himself,
and made a vow with the deity,
that if indeed a great victory was achieved,
then he would toss these coins,
hoping they would all land with the obverse side up.
His attendants admonished him to stop,
fearing that if things didn't go as wished,
it might demoralize the troops.
But Wǔxiāng didn't listen.
The multitude of soldiers watched with bated breath.
After a moment,
he waved his hand and suddenly cast them down,
and all hundred coins showed red.
Thereupon the entire army cheered with joy,
their voices shaking the forests and fields.
Wǔxiāng was also greatly pleased.
He turned to his attendants and ordered a hundred nails brought,
then following the coins' sparse or dense distribution,
he arranged them on the ground and nailed them firmly in place,
covered them with a blue gauze canopy,
and sealed it with his own hands,
saying:
"Wait until our triumphant return,
we shall give thanks to the deity,
and retrieve the coins.
Later, they captured Kūnlún Pass,
defeated Zhìgāo,
and pacified Yōngguǎn.
When the army returned,
he retrieved the coins as promised,
and together with his staff officers and officials examined them—
they were coins with obverse sides on both faces.
Cáo Wěi governed Wèi Province,
when someone reported that a garrison soldier had defected to the Xià Kingdom.
Wěi was playing chess with a guest at the time,
and promptly said:
"I sent him to go."
When the Xià people heard this,
they immediately beheaded the defector,
and threw his head across the border.
From History of the Sòng Dynasty
The wealthy families of the Tiānxióng army
had haystacks stretching across the fields.
They often secretly dug holes in the official embankments to create breaches.
During the Xiánpíng era,
when Zhào Chāngyán served as governor and was known for his integrity,
he became aware of this matter,
but did not investigate immediately.
One day, the embankment collapsed,
and officials reported the emergency.
Chāngyán ordered the immediate seizure of the hay accumulated by the wealthy families to use for repairing the embankment.
From then on, no one dared to secretly dig holes in the official embankments for illicit purposes.
"Yù Jiǎn"
At Ānfēng's Gǒubēi,
constructed by Sūnshū'áo,
there were north-south canals,
irrigating ten thousand qǐng of farmland.
The people, due to drought, often encroached and farmed within them,
and when rainwater overflowed, they would secretly breach the dikes,
thus losing the benefits of irrigation.
When Lǐ Ruògǔ governed Shòuchūn, he issued an order that if the dikes were breached,
no troops would be mobilized;
instead, he solely mobilized the people living near the dikes,
making them repair and rebuild,
and from then on, there were no more secret breaches.
End.
When Zhǒng Shìhéng was the magistrate of Miǎnchí County,
there was a temple beside the mountain.
Shìhéng repaired it,
but its beam was heavy,
and the crowd could not lift it.
Shìhéng then ordered the county attendants to cut their hair short like those who practice hand-to-hand combat,
and drove several pairs in front of his horse,
saying:
"I intend to go to the temple to teach hand-to-hand combat.
The entire town followed to watch.
Upon arrival,
he addressed the spectators,
saying:
"You must first move the temple beam for me,
and then watch the hand-to-hand combat.
The crowd gladly moved it down the mountain,
lifting it together,
and it was done in a short while.
His clever strategies were all of this kind.
"Sùshuǐ Jìwén"
Qín Huì one day noticed Emperor Gāozōng appeared displeased,
and memorialized:
"What matter troubles Your Majesty's thoughts?
The Emperor replied:
"We are short fifty thousand bolts of silk for the suburban sacrifices.
Qín Huì said:
"Your servant will undertake this matter for Your Majesty.
Suddenly one day,
he memorialized:
"I beg the palace to grant me four golden pots of wine,
and on a certain day summon Qín Yuē, and Generals Zhāng and Hán to discuss matters.
From morning until noon,
they were not granted audience,
but only saw palace eunuchs delivering imperial wine,
which made them increasingly perplexed,
and apprehensive.
When Qín met with Zhāng and Hán,
he did not utter a single word,
then suddenly said:
"The Emperor has bestowed wine,
let us drink a cup together.
Zhāng and Hán held the vessels,
trembling and not daring to drink.
Qín first took a spoonful of wine and drank it,
then after a moment calmly said:
"The master wishes to borrow ten million strings of cash from each of you two generals,
for the suburban sacrifices,
which will be repaid after the ceremony.
Zhāng and Hán respectfully accepted the order and reported to Emperor Gāozōng,
receiving an edict for exactly five million strings of cash.
From "Guì Ěr Jí"
At the beginning of the Jiànyán era,
the barbarian envoys came to negotiate peace,
demanding that all officials must greet them at the outskirts.
The court was pale with fear at their letter,
but Qín Huì remained unperturbed,
dispatching all ministry officials to receive them.
The envoys insisted on being seated on cushioned positions during the audience,
which was not a ritual befitting subjects.
On that day,
Huì ordered the court audience hall
to be entirely draped with purple curtains,
leaving the northerners no grounds for complaint before they withdrew.

The capital suddenly faced a shortage of cash coins,
causing considerable panic in the markets.
One day, Qín Huì summoned a barber to trim his hair,
and rewarded him with five thousand cash coins worth two coins.
He instructed:
"In a few days, an imperial decree will render these coins unusable,
so spend them early."
The barber, having personally received the directive,
then told outsiders about it.
Within three days,
cash coins suddenly flooded the capital.
This was a minor tactic to control the empire.
From "Guì Ěr Jí": While Huì held the position of chancellor,
he directed everyone with a mere gesture,
and none dared disobey.
At that time, goods in the capital were stagnant,
and the market for cash coins was wide open.
The prefect reported this,
to which Huì laughed and said:
"Easy to fix."
He immediately summoned an official from the Wénsī Yard,
who hadn't yet arrived
when催促的人络绎不绝,
rushing over.
Huì instructed him:
"I've just received an edict
to change the currency system.
Cast a sample string of coins for presentation,
and discontinue the use of current cash coins."
Setting a deadline for the next noon to complete the task,
the official assented and left,
summoning craftsmen to carry it out.
Wealthy families who heard the news
sold all their stored cash coins to buy gold and grain,
causing prices to soar,
and cash coins overflowed the market.
Later, when the sample coins were submitted to the ministry,
all fell silent without further ado.
Qín Huì's wife often entered the palace.
Empress Dowager Xiǎn Rén said:
"Recently, large zǐyú have been extremely rare.
The wife replied:
"My family has them,
and I shall present one hundred tails.
Upon returning home, she told Huì,
who blamed her for the indiscreet remark.
He consulted his resident advisor and decided to present one hundred tails of qīngyú instead.
Empress Dowager Xiǎn Rén clapped her hands and laughed, saying:
"I said this country woman was indeed simple-minded.
"Jade Dew of the Crane Forest"
Shē,
means extravagant.
Opposite of frugality is called shē,
derived from the character for 'large',
it signifies boasting or exaggerating beyond others.
From *Shuōwén*.
In the time of Jié of old,
there were thirty thousand female musicians,
who made a clamor at dawn at the Duānmén,
and their music was heard throughout the sānqú,
all clad in embroidered garments of patterned silk.
Guǎnzǐ
Lord Huán of Dān had the pillars carved and the square rafters engraved,
both of which were contrary to ritual propriety.
Yù Sūn remonstrated, saying:
"Your servant has heard that frugality
is the foundation of virtue;
while extravagance is the greatest of evils.
Our former rulers possessed this foundational virtue,
yet you, my lord, are embracing the greatest evil—
is this not improper?
Twenty-fourth Year of Duke Zhuāng
Qí Qìng Fēng came on a friendly mission,
his carriage was beautiful.
Mèng Sūn said to Shū Sūn:
"Qìng Jì's carriage,
is it not beautiful?"
Shū Sūn said:
"Bào has heard that
if fine garments are unbecoming,
one is sure to come to a bad end.
What is the use of a beautiful carriage?"
"Xiāng 27th year" Qìng Fēng came fleeing,
and presented a carriage to Jì Wǔzǐ,
its beautiful gloss could reflect one's shadow.
Zhuāng Shū saw it,
and said:
"The carriage is very glossy,
its owner must be haggard,
it is fitting that he should flee."
"28th year"
The head of a doomed household, Qí's Gāo Zǐróng, and Sòng's Minister of Education visited Earl Zhì,
with Nǚ Qí as the master of ceremonies.
When the guests departed,
Minister of War Hóu said to Earl Zhì:
"Both men will inevitably meet with misfortune.
Zǐróng is autocratic,
the Minister of Education is extravagant,
both are heads of doomed households.
Earl Zhì asked:
"How so?
He replied:
"Autocracy leads to swift downfall,
extravagance will cause his own strength to be exhausted,
autocracy means others will truly bring him down,
their downfall is imminent.
《Twenty-nine》
The Wú army is in Chén,
the ministers of Chǔ all fear Zǐxī's strategies.
Now we hear that Fūchāi,
has terraces and pavilions by the ponds,
and keeps consorts and attendants in his lodgings.
For a single day's pleasure,
whatever he desires must be achieved,
and his favorite amusements must be followed.
He gathers rare treasures,
and pursues only spectacles and pleasures.
He regards the people as enemies,
yet uses them ever more harshly.
Fūchāi has already defeated himself,
how can he defeat us?
(Xiānggōng 5th year)
King Fūchāi of Wú built the Gūsū Tower, which took three years to complete.
It wound around intricately,
stretching five li across,
with lavish decorations in wood and earth,
exhausting human labor and resources.
There were several thousand palace courtesans,
and a separate Spring Night Palace was erected,
for all-night drinking revelries.
They crafted a wine bell weighing a thousand shi,
and dug a large pond,
in which a Blue Dragon Boat was constructed.
The boat was furnished with courtesans and music,
where daily water games were held with Xīshī.
In the palace, they built the Sea Spirit Hall,
and the Wá Pavilion,
with bronze fittings and jade balustrades.
The pillars and railings of the palace
were all adorned with pearls and jade.
"Records of Strange Things"
Duānmù Shū of Wèi,
a descendant of Zǐgòng,
relied on his ancestral wealth, amassing ten thousand gold pieces without engaging in worldly affairs.
Thus, he indulged in his whims and desires,
doing whatever the common people wished to do,
and playing with whatever people desired to enjoy.
There was nothing he did not do,
and nothing he did not play with.
His walls, houses, terraces, pavilions, gardens, parks, ponds, moats, food, drink, carriages, attire,
music, and concubines rivaled those of the rulers of Qí and Chǔ.
As for what his heart desired to love,
his ears desired to hear,
his eyes desired to see,
and his mouth desired to taste,
even if they came from distant lands and remote states,
not produced within the territory of Qí,
he would invariably acquire them,
treating them as if they were within his own fences.
Guests in his courtyard numbered a hundred daily,
beneath his kitchens,
the smoke and fire never ceased;
in his halls and corridors,
music and revelry never ended.
Beyond what he needed for his own sustenance,
he first distributed to his clan;
after providing for his clan,
he next distributed to his village and neighborhood;
after meeting the needs of his village,
he then distributed the remainder throughout the state.
When he reached the age of sixty,
his vitality and strength began to decline,
he abandoned his household affairs,
and entirely dispersed his treasury stores, treasures, carriages, attire, and concubines.
Within a year, he exhausted it all,
leaving no wealth for his descendants.
By the time he fell ill,
he had no reserve of medicines or remedies;
and when he died,
there were no funds for his burial.
The people of the entire state,
who had received his benefactions,
joined together to contribute and inter him,
returning the wealth to his descendants.
Qíngǔlí heard of this,
and said:
"Duānmù Shū
is a madman,
who has disgraced his ancestors."
Duàngàn Shēng heard of it,
and said:
"Duānmù Shū is an enlightened man,
whose virtue surpasses that of his ancestors."
From "Liè Yáng Zhū."
Hán Yān was fond of shooting pellets,
often using gold ones,
losing more than ten in a single day.
The people of Cháng'ān thus had a saying:
"Suffering from hunger and cold,
chase the golden pellets."
Whenever the children in the capital heard that Yān was out shooting pellets,
they would follow him,
watching where the pellets fell,
and compete to pick them up.
Records of the Western Capital
Liáng Jì served as the Grand General,
his authority shook both the court and the regions.
All tributes and requisitions from the four directions,
as well as annual offerings,
were first delivered to the finest quality to Liáng Jì.
He then extensively built mansions and residences,
while his wife Sūn Shòu also constructed a residence facing his across the street,
exhausting the extremes of timber and earth,
competing in extravagance with each other.
Their halls and chambers all had secluded inner rooms for privacy,
with interconnected rooms and passageways.
Pillars and walls were carved and engraved,
additionally coated with bronze lacquer,
windows adorned with intricate latticework and green patterns,
depicting clouds, spirits, and immortals.
Towers and pavilions were interconnected throughout,
overlooking one another;
flying bridges and stone steps,
spanned across waterways.
Rhinoceros horns that startled chickens,
luminous jade discs that glowed at night,
filled the treasuries,
while famed steeds and dragon-like horses were stabled in the inner stables.
He and his wife rode in carriages with green canopies,
displaying feathered canopies,
adorned with gold, jade, and amber.
Whenever they toured ponds and pavilions,
or within their mansions,
they were often accompanied by entertainers and musicians,
sounding bells and drums,
playing flutes and singing boisterously along the roads,
continuing day and night.
When Emperor Huán executed Liáng Jì,
his assets were confiscated,
to replenish the state treasury,
and an edict was issued to reduce the empire's annual land tax by half.
《Hòu Hàn Shū》
Liú Yǎn,
courtesy name Wēishuò,
served as Chariot and Horse General.
His carriages, attire, and food and drink were renowned for their extravagance,
with several dozen maidservants in attendance,
all skilled in music and singing,
and all taught to recite the "Rhapsody on the Hall of Numinous Brilliance at Lǔ."
(Records of the State of Shǔ)
Gān Nìng delighted in chivalrous wandering.
When he went out,
on land he would arrange chariots and cavalry,
on water he would link light boats.
His attendants wore embroidered silks,
wherever they went they illuminated the roads.
When mooring, he often used brocade to tie the boats,
and when departing would cut it loose or discard it,
to display his extravagance.
"Records of Wú"
Shí Chóng,
whose assets amounted to hundreds of millions in gold,
had residences, carriages, and horses
that rivaled those of royalty,
and his kitchens always exhausted the delicacies of land and water.
In his rear chambers were hundreds of women,
all dressed in fine silk embroidery,
and adorned with gold and jadeite,
while the skills in music
were the finest of the era.
He built pavilions and dug ponds,
exhausting human ingenuity.
He competed in extravagance with noble relatives like Yáng Xiù and Wáng Kǎi and their ilk,
and Chóng stood at the forefront,
leaving Xiù and others often envious and ashamed,
believing they could not match him.
"Continuation of Records of Literary Works"
Shí Chóng served as the governor of Jīngzhōu,
fond of chivalrous but unruly acts,
he dispatched agents to rob distant merchants and traders,
amassing immense household wealth.
He had a separate estate in Jīnyáng of Héyáng,
where property overflowed in accumulation,
and the buildings were grand and magnificent,
vying in extravagance with the noble relative Wáng Kǎi, the uncle of Emperor Wǔ.
Kǎi used malt sugar to heat his cauldron,
while Chóng used wax in place of firewood.
Kǎi made a purple gauze
screening curtain stretching forty lǐ,
and Chóng made a brocade
screening curtain spanning fifty lǐ.
Kǎi coated his house with red stone ointment,
while Chóng plastered his with pepper.
Emperor Wǔ gave Kǎi a coral tree,
two chǐ tall,
which Kǎi showed to Shí Chóng.
Chóng shattered it with an iron ruyi scepter,
and Kǎi was displeased.
Chóng said,
"Do not regret it.
He ordered six or seven coral trees to be fetched and returned to him.
Emperor Huì knew that no wealth could outshine his.
At that time, a foreign state presented fire-washing cloth,
unmatched anywhere in the world.
The emperor had a robe made from it
and visited Chóng's home.
Fifty of Chóng's servants all wore robes of fire-washing cloth to greet him,
leaving the emperor greatly ashamed.
"Imperial Readings of the Jìn History"
Wáng Jì,
courtesy name Wǔzǐ,
was reprimanded and relocated his residence near Máng Mountain. At that time,
the population was dense and land was expensive.
Wáng Jì was fond of equestrian archery,
so he purchased land to build a racecourse,
lining the entire track perimeter with strung coins.
People of the time dubbed it
"The Golden Moat"
(from *A New Account of the Tales of the World*)
Hé Zēng,
courtesy name Yǐngkǎo,
was by nature extravagant and ostentatious,
devoted to splendor and luxury.
His curtains, carriages, and attire
were of the utmost elegance and beauty,
while the flavors of his kitchen and meals
surpassed even those of a king.
Whenever he attended court banquets,
he would not eat the food provided by the imperial kitchen;
the emperor would then order him to bring his own meals.
He would not eat steamed buns unless they split into a cross pattern on top.
Spending ten thousand coins a day on food,
he still complained there was no place to set his chopsticks.
If someone sent him a letter on small paper,
he would command his secretariat not to respond.
Liú Yì and others repeatedly impeached Hé Zēng for his boundless extravagance,
but the emperor, considering him a senior minister,
took no action whatsoever.
His son Hé Shào,
courtesy name Jìngzǔ,
was arrogant, lavish, aloof, and noble,
sharing his father's demeanor.
His clothing, furs, and playthings—new and old—accumulated in great piles;
his meals invariably exhausted the rare delicacies from all four directions,
with a day's provisions
limited to twenty thousand coins.
Contemporary opinion held that even the imperial kitchen's feasts could not surpass his.
"Book of Jìn"
Rěn Kǎi,
courtesy name Yuánbāo,
after losing his official position,
indulged in excessive drinking and pleasure-seeking,
pursuing the finest flavors to pamper himself.
Previously Hé Shào, being the son of a noble, lived extravagantly,
ensuring every meal included delicacies from all regions.
Kǎi then surpassed him,
spending ten thousand coins on a single meal,
yet still claiming there was nothing worth picking up with his chopsticks.
Luòxià had little firewood, and charcoal was as scarce as millet grains.
Yáng Xiù, being arrogant and extravagant,
pounded small charcoal pieces into powder,
mixed it with substances,
and molded it into animal shapes.
Later, Hé Shào and his followers,
gathered together and used them to warm wine with fierce flames,
whereupon the ferocious beasts all gaped their mouths toward people,
blazing brilliantly.
The various nobles vied in boasting,
all submitted and imitated it.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Jìn Dynasty"
Xú Zhànzhī,
styled Xiàoyuán,
was a noble relative and powerful magnate,
possessing vast estates.
His mansions, gardens, and ponds
were unmatched by any aristocrat.
The excellence of his musicians
was unparalleled in his time,
with over a thousand disciples,
all scions of wealthy families from Sānwú.
They were handsome in appearance,
dressed in bright and elegant attire.
Whenever they went out for excursions,
on muddy or rainy days, the streets would be filled, and they would all be transported in rear carriages.
Emperor Wén frequently disapproved of his extravagance and indulgence.
At that time, Duke Ānchéng Hé Xù,
son of Wújì,
and Duke Línrǔ Mèng Líng,
son of Xiūchǎng,
were both known for their luxury and opulence.
They vied with Zhànzhī in delicacies, utensils, attire, carriages, and horses.
The capital thus had a saying:
"Ānchéng for food,
Línrǔ for adornment,
but Zhànzhī excels in both, surpassing Hé and Mèng."
From *History of the Southern Dynasties*
Sòng Ruǎn Diànfū's
residences, gardens, and ponds
surpassed even those of the princely mansions.
He kept several dozen female entertainers
whose artistry and beauty were unparalleled at the time,
adorned with gold, jade, and brocades
that even the imperial palace could not match.
Whenever he had a garment made
or an object crafted,
it would inevitably be imitated throughout the capital.
He dug a canal within his estate
extending eastward for over ten li,
with neat embankments where he would
float light boats
while female musicians performed.
Once, the Imperial Secretary Liú Xiū visited him,
encountering Diànfū departing,
and they met midway.
Diànfū invited Xiū to return and join the feast,
immediately ordering arrangements;
within moments, every rare delicacy was fully prepared.
All the grand dishes were freshly cooked to perfection like this,
amounting to dozens of varieties.
Diànfū often prepared banquets for dozens of guests in advance.
Thus, he could manage such feasts effortlessly,
surpassing even Wáng and Shí of the Jìn dynasty.
From the Biographies of Imperial Favorites
Yǔ Hóng had a sleeping couch,
all made of cypress wood,
encircled on all four sides,
with no part differing from another,
uniformly using silver-inlaid golden floral patterns with double blessings and longevity as its legs.
According to the History of the Southern Dynasties, while serving as the Prince of Xiāngdōng,
he held the position of General of the Western Garrison,
and traveled westward to assume his duties.
He encountered an imperial edict to welcome an auspicious statue,
and the prince ordered him to escort the statue to the capital.
Yǔ Hóng led several hundred of his troops,
all clad in brocade robes,
their splendor filling the roads,
earning much admiration from onlookers.
While passing through Xiàshǒu,
Lǐ Kàng imitated his demeanor,
and when Lǐ Kàng's uncle Yuán Fǎsēng heard of it,
he caned Lǐ Kàng three hundred times.

Xú Jūnqiàn,
courtesy name Huáijiǎn,
was the son of Xiàosì's grandson Xú Gūn.
From a young age, he was intelligent and fond of learning,
particularly excelling in classical texts,
and could answer any question posed to him.
He was skilled in music and singing,
and served as the Advisory Army Officer to the Prince of Xiāngdōng.
He was quite fond of sensual pleasures,
with several dozen concubines,
all adorned with gold and jade,
draped in silk garments and ornaments,
all made of gold and silver.
He would become drunk after just a few shēng of wine,
then shut his doors,
singing joyfully all day long.
Whenever he encountered merry banter,
he would drink up to a dǒu.
Sometimes he would take entertainers on unrestrained excursions,
through the mountains and rivers of Jīngchǔ,
leaving no place untrodden,
yet his friends and companions
could never find him.
At that time, Yú Hóng of Xiāngyáng was also known for his extravagance,
leading to a rhyme in the official circles:
"Yú in the north,
Xú in the south,"
though his ornaments and luxuries were inferior to Hóng's.
During the Liáng dynasty, the sons of powerful families,
were mostly unrestrained and indulgent,
engaging in debauchery, theft, and slaughter as their occupations,
which their fathers and grandfathers could not control,
nor could the local authorities restrain them.
Their carriages, robes, oxen, and horses were called Xīfēng's camel-horses,
and Lèshān's black oxen.
Dǒng Xiān had a battle jacket woven with gold leaf,
worth seven million coins.
Xīfēng Hóu Zhèngdé and Lèshān Hóu Zhèngzé,
along with Dǒng of Cháogōu, the son of Dǒng Dāngmén,
were known by the world as the "Spoiled Heirs,"
and in the end, none of them died a natural death.
The Emperor
Xiàhóu Dàoqiān enjoyed conversation,
and banquets were his specialty.
All the rare delicacies of the capital were available to him,
west of the capital city,
he purchased land by the waterside,
and established extensive gardens and ponds,
planting rows of vegetables and fruits.
He invited outstanding scholars to visit frequently,
and kept over ten singing girls for his own entertainment,
with an annual official salary of more than three thousand bolts of silk,
dedicated solely to wine and feasts,
never managing family property.
He often recited Kǒng Róng's verse,
saying:
" 'Guests always fill the seats,
wine never empties from the cups'
Other matters are not my concern."
Those who understood admired him.
The Book of Wèi
Gāoyáng Wáng Yōng,
reached the highest rank among officials,
possessed wealth as vast as the mountains and seas,
his residences and mansions
rivaled the imperial palace.
White halls and red balustrades,
stretched elegantly and continuously,
with upturned eaves and soaring roofs,
intertwining and connecting throughout.
He had six thousand servants,
and five hundred singing girls,
whose pearls shone like the sun,
and silk garments fluttered in the wind.
Since the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
no other noble had been so extravagantly luxurious.
When he went out, horsemen cleared the road,
with ceremonial objects arranged in rows,
cymbals and drums resounding loudly,
and mournful melodies of reed pipes swirling;
when he returned, singing and dancing girls,
struck the zhù and played the shēng,
with string and wind instruments playing in succession,
continuing day and night without end.
His bamboo groves and fish ponds
matched the imperial gardens,
with lush grasses piled high,
and precious trees forming continuous shade.
Yōng indulged in fine flavors,
pampering himself lavishly.
Each day, he spent tens of thousands of coins as a limit,
with delicacies from land and sea,
spread lavishly before him.
Chénliú Hóu Lǐ Chóng remarked to others:
"Gāoyáng’s one day equals a thousand of my days."
From "Luòyáng Qiélán Jì"
During the Wei period, the imperial clan, princes, and marquises,
imperial relatives by marriage, and princesses,
monopolized the wealth of mountains and seas,
resided in the abundance of rivers and forests,
vied to build gardens and residences,
competing in extravagance.
With lofty gates and lavish rooms,
interconnected chambers and continuous dwellings,
flying pavilions that caught the wind,
and multi-storied buildings that seemed to rise into the mist,
high terraces and fragrant trees
were constructed by every household,
while flowered groves and winding ponds
were found in every garden.
None lacked peach and plum trees green in summer,
nor bamboo and cypress evergreen in winter.
Among them, Prince Chén of Héjiān
was the most opulent leader,
often competing with Prince of Gāoyáng.
He built the Wénbǎi Hall,
modeled after the Huīyīn Palace,
installing jade wells and golden jars,
with ropes made of five-colored gold threads.
The other princes admired his wealth.
Chén once said to people:
"Shí Chóng of the Jìn court,
merely a commoner,
could still wear pheasant-head fur and fox-axilla garments,
and carve designs on his firewood.
How much more should I, of the great Wei,
a scion of the imperial family, not indulge in magnificence?"
He built the Yíngfēng Pavilion in his rear garden.
On its windows and doors,
were arranged coin patterns and green琐 designs,
jade phoenixes holding bells in their beaks,
and golden dragons spitting pendants.
White pear and red plum branches extended under the eaves,
where courtesans sat upstairs picking and eating the fruits.
Chén often gathered the imperial clan to display his treasures:
over a hundred golden bottles and silver urns,
with an equal number of cups, stands, plates, and boxes.
Among the remaining wine vessels,
were crystal bowls,
agate and glass cups,
and several dozen red jade zhī cups,
their craftsmanship marvelous and exquisite,
unfound in the Central Plains,
all brought from the Western Regions.
He also displayed female musicians and famous horses,
then led the princes through his storehouses,
filled with brocades, carpets, pearls, and jades,
icy silks and misty crepes,
piled high inside.
Embroidered, dyed, oiled, and plain silks, colorful Yuè and Gé fabrics,
coins, silks, and such,
were beyond counting.
Suddenly, Chén said to Prince Róng of Zhāngwǔ:
"I do not regret that I never saw Shí Chóng,
but regret that Shí Chóng never saw me."
After the Héyīn campaign,
the Yuán clan was nearly annihilated,
and the mansions of princes and marquises
were largely converted into temples,
with monasteries lining the streets of Shòuqiū Lane.
Jīvyuán monasteries rose densely,
and precious pagodas soared high.
On the eighth day of the fourth month,
many gentry and women of the capital visited the Héjiān Temple,
admiring the splendor of its corridors and chambers.
All sighed in wonder,
believing even the Penglai fairy abode could not surpass it.
Entering its rear garden,
they saw winding waterways,
rocky steps, rugged stones, and red lotuses emerging from the pond,
green duckweed floating on the water,
flying bridges spanning pavilions,
and tall trees reaching into the clouds.
Everyone chirped in admiration.
Even the tile garden of Prince of Liáng would pale in comparison.
Cuī Jiǒng on his deathbed admonished his two sons, saying:
"Humility and frugality are the carriage of fortune,
while arrogance and extravagance are the trigger of disaster.
Those who ride the carriage of fortune
gradually attain health and prosperity;
those who tread on the trigger of disaster
suddenly meet with ruin and collapse.
How can one not be cautious?
History of the Northern Dynasties, Chapter 12
Hán Jìnmíng was fond of wine and unrestrained indulgence,
inviting guests,
the cost of a single banquet,
often amounted to ten thousand coins,
yet he still regretted being frugal and hasty.
"Northern Qí"
Sūn Yǎng,
courtesy name Dé Liǎn,
was open-minded and generous by nature.
He would distribute his wealth among relatives and friends,
though his household management was rather extravagant.
His residence was ingeniously constructed
to achieve the ultimate charm of woods and springs.
With singing boys and dancing girls,
his entertainments were unmatched in his time.
Guests filled his gates,
and carriages with canopies never ceased arriving.
When he was stationed in Yìngzhōu as a military governor,
he combined over ten boats into a large vessel,
erecting a pavilion and pond in the center,
where he planted lotuses and water caltrops.
On every fine day and beautiful scene,
he would gather guests and colleagues together,
floating on the Yangtze River while setting out wine,
creating a remarkable sight of the era.
(History of the Southern Dynasties)
Prince Qín Yáng Jùn extensively built palaces,
pushing extravagance and splendor to the extreme.
Jùn possessed ingenious ideas,
often personally wielding axes and clever tools,
adorning them with pearls and jade.
For his consort, he crafted a seven-treasure veil,
and coated the walls of his water pavilion with fragrant powder,
using jade for masonry and gold for steps.
Between the beams, pillars, lintels, and ridgepoles,
he surrounded them with bright mirrors,
interspersed with precious pearls,
achieving the pinnacle of luxurious decoration.
Frequently, with guests,
he entertained with courtesans playing strings and singing atop it.
"Book of Suì"
Emperor Suí Yángdì traveled to Guǎnglíng,
arriving at Biàn.
The emperor rode on a dragon boat,
while Consort Xiāo sailed on a phoenix vessel,
with brocade sails and colorful cables,
displaying the utmost extravagance and luxury.
In front of the boat was a stage,
above which hung a curtain that blocked the sun.
This curtain was presented by the state of Púzé,
made from the eyelashes of the mountain-bearing flood dragon, threaded with lotus roots,
and strung with small pearls.
It was woven between the eyelashes,
so even when the bright sun shone intensely,
the light could not penetrate it.
On each boat, a thousand beautiful, tall, and fair-skinned women were selected,
holding carved oars
and gilded paddles,
known as the palace footmaidens.
"Records of Suí Dynasty Relics"
Emperor Yáng toured the northern frontier,
and had a grand mobile palace with a seven-treasure canopy constructed,
capable of accommodating several hundred people.
Adorned with precious gems,
its brilliance was utterly dazzling.
He invited the Xiongnu leader Qǐmín
Kèhán to feast within it.
The Kèhán was dazed,
doubting such a thing could exist in the mortal world.
A discerning observer remarked:
"The grand mobile palace
is an ominous portent.
This is not comparable to Wáng Mǎng's light carriage;
it truly reflects the will of Heaven,
not merely human affairs."
From "Qiān Zǎi"
Péi Jǔ,
courtesy name Hóngdà.
When the emperor arrived at the Eastern Capital,
Jǔ suggested that many barbarian tribes came to pay tribute.
The emperor ordered grand performances in the capital,
summoning extraordinary skills and exotic arts from all regions,
displaying them along Duānmén Street.
Those dressed in embroidered silks,
and adorned with golden jade,
numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
He also commanded all officials and commoners, men and women, to sit in rows within the railings,
and watch freely.
All were dressed in bright and beautiful attire,
and this continued for a full month before ending.
He further ordered the shops in the three markets to set up curtains and tents,
lavishly displaying wine and food.
Officials in charge of foreign affairs were sent to lead the barbarians in trade with the people.
Wherever they went,
they were all invited to sit,
and dispersed only when drunk and full.
The barbarians sighed in admiration,
calling China the land of immortals.
Book of Sui
Xǔ Jìngzōng was extravagant and opulent.
He once built seventy flying towers,
commanding courtesans to ride horses atop them,
using this as entertainment.
From "Dú Yì Jì".
Zhāng Yìzhī made a seven-treasure canopy for his mother Ā Zāng,
gathering all kinds of gold, silver, pearls, jade, and precious objects without exception,
unprecedented since ancient times.
He laid an ivory bed,
wove a mat of rhinoceros horn,
used marmot and sable furs for the mattress,
and a felt of qióng and wén fibers.
With dragon's beard from Fénjìn
and phoenix feathers from Línhé,
he made the mat.
Ā Zāng and the Vice Minister of the Phoenix Pavilion Lǐ Jiǒngxiù, fearing his prominence
and disliking his old age,
indulged in excessive drinking without restraint,
constantly focusing on drunken stupor,
often called but unaware of leaving.
He was appointed as the Prefect of Héng Province.
When Yìzhī fell from power,
Ā Zāng was confiscated into the government,
Jiǒngxiù was implicated,
and demoted to the Chief Clerk of Héng Province.
"Qiān Zǎi"
Princess Ānlè was demoted to a rebellious commoner,
seized the farmlands of the common people,
and constructed the Dìngkūn estate spanning forty-nine li,
extending directly to the Southern Mountains.
Modeled after the Kūnmíng Pond,
she piled stones to form mountains,
resembling Mount Huà;
diverted water to create ravines,
imitating the Tiānjīn constellation.
Soaring pavilions and tiered eaves,
slanting stone steps layered,
adorned with brocade and embroidery,
decorated with vibrant colors,
gleaming with gold and silver,
and embellished with pearls and jade.
She also built a winding stream for floating cups,
crafted a stone lotus platform,
from which springs flowed at the center,
exhausting all the grandeur under heaven—
words cannot fully describe it.
After her rebellion failed,
the estate was confiscated by the Minister of Agriculture.
Daily, scholars and ladies came to tour and view,
their carriages and horses crowding the area.
By imperial decree,
any official who ventured there without permission was dismissed from their current post,
while commoners were flogged once before being released.
The emperor
During the Jǐnglóng era,
the families of imperial consorts and princesses competed in extravagance.
Imperial son-in-law Yáng Shènjiāo Wǔ,
and Chóngxùn went so far as
to sprinkle oil on the ground
for constructing a polo field.
"Guóshǐ Zuǎnyì"
Emperor Xuánzōng was about to visit the Huáqīng Palace,
and the Guìfēi's sisters vied to adorn their carriages and attire.
One carriage was decorated with gold and jadeite,
interspersed with pearls and jade,
the cost of a single carriage amounting to no less than several hundred thousand strings of cash.
Afterward,
it became too heavy for the oxen,
unable to pull it.
They then reported to the emperor, requesting to ride horses instead.
Thus, they competed to purchase famous steeds,
using gold for the bits and bridles,
and embroidered silk for the saddle cloths.
They gathered at Guózhōng's residence,
preparing to enter the palace together.
The brilliance illuminated everything,
onlookers crowded like walls,
from Guózhōng's residence to the southeastern corner of the inner city,
servants, drivers, carriages, and horses filled the area.
Whenever Guó Guófūrén entered the palace,
she often rode a dappled horse,
with a young eunuch driving it.
The dappled horse's elegance and strength,
and the eunuch's dignified handsomeness,
were both unparalleled at the time.
"Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng Huáng"
In Wànhuā Valley, Consort Yáng Guìfēi gained favor,
her brothers Yáng Xuān, Yáng Qí, Yáng Guózhōng, and the families of her aunts—five households in total—had interconnected residences,
with artisans crafting brocades, embroideries, and carving gold and jade,
numbering approximately a thousand people,
their transformations resembling celestial beings.
Whenever the emperor visited Huáqīng Palace,
the five families accompanied him,
each family forming a separate procession,
dressed in a single color,
the five processions reflecting each other,
like ten thousand flowers blooming brilliantly,
turning the valleys into brocade.
Hairpins and shoes were left behind,
with green gems, pearls, and jade ornaments,
scattered disorderly along the road,
their fragrance wafting for tens of miles.
From the "Old Book of Táng."
Wéi Zhì, the Duke of Xiāoyáo, was extravagant and unrestrained by nature.
He delighted in adorning his clothes and horses.
Attendants and young eunuchs standing by his side often numbered several dozen,
rivaling the households of princes and royal residences.
He exhaustively pursued exquisite delicacies,
selecting fertile lands to cultivate grains and wheat,
using bird feathers to pick out rice grains.
With every meal, he would inspect what the kitchen discarded,
and its value still amounted to no less than ten thousand coins.
When feasting at the homes of dukes and marquises,
even if delicacies from land and water were fully presented,
he would never once pick up his chopsticks.
He often used multicolored stationery for correspondence,
entrusting it to his maidservants to manage,
while he merely decided replies and conveyed his intentions.
"Basic Biography"
In the ninth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
the noble relatives competed in presenting meals to outdo one another.
Emperor Xuánzōng appointed the official Yáo Sīyì as the inspector
and food presentation commissioner. Thousands of dishes of land and sea delicacies were presented,
with the cost of a single dish equivalent to the wealth of ten middle-class families.
From "Continued Accounts of the World"
Wáng Yuánbǎo,
was a great magnate in the capital.
He often built his house by piling up gold and silver,
plastering the walls with red clay.
In his residence, he set up a Hall for Honoring the Worthy,
using sandalwood and aloeswood for the railings and balustrades,
paving the ground with jade-like stones,
and using brocade-patterned stones as the column bases.
Moreover, he threaded coins with copper wires,
paving them on the flower paths in the rear garden,
valuing that they would not become slippery in the mud and rain.
Guests from all directions
felt at home wherever they went,
so people at that time called it the Wáng Family's Den of Wealth.
"Supplemental Stories of the Tianbao Era"
Yuánbǎo loved to entertain guests,
and was devoted to luxury and extravagance.
His utensils, playthings, and attire surpassed those of princes and dukes,
yet scholars from all directions flocked to him and looked up to him.
He often had two dwarf boys carved at the foot of his bed in the sleeping tent,
holding a seven-treasure Boshan incense burner,
burning incense from dusk until dawn,
such was his pride and nobility.

Yuán Zài built two grand mansions in the northern and southern parts of the city,
with magnificent halls and chambers,
unsurpassed in their time.
He also erected pavilions and kiosks in the suburbs,
and wherever he went,
the tents, curtains, and various utensils
were always as if prepared in advance,
with supplies never needing replenishment.
In the fertile southern suburbs,
he owned dozens of contiguous estates,
with over a hundred maids and servants clad in silk and satin,
indulging in lawless acts,
and living in extravagant excess beyond all bounds.
Old Book of Tang
Yuán Zài's wife,
named Yùnxiù,
was the daughter of Wáng Jìn.
Initially, when Jìn governed Běijīng,
he married his daughter to Zǎi.
After years of marriage, upon meeting,
he looked down upon and neglected his relatives, considering them beggars,
and all despised and belittled him.
Zǎi then traveled to Qín,
and upon reaching the capital,
repeatedly presented proposals on current affairs.
Emperor Sùzōng promoted him to Zhōngshū and he served as chancellor under both Emperor Sùzōng and Emperor Dàizōng,
becoming incomparably noble and prosperous.
Relatives from Tàiyuán, both close and distant, all came to pay respects and congratulate him.
Yùnxiù settled them in a secluded courtyard.
Suddenly, taking advantage of the sunny weather,
she took forty blue and purple silk ribbons,
each thirty zhang long,
all adorned with luxurious silk and embroidery,
and beneath each ribbon,
arranged twenty gold and silver incense burners,
all burning rare incense.
The fragrance reached their clothing.
She then invited the relatives to stroll in the western courtyard.
Yùnxiù asked what these things were,
and the maidservant replied:
"Today, the chancellor and his wife are airing their night garments.
Lady Wáng said to the relatives:
"Who would have thought that the wife of a beggar
would still have two sets of coarse clothes to cover her body?
At this, the relatives felt ashamed and blushed,
and gradually took their leave.
From "Dū Yáng Biān."
Dù Yà as the governor of Huáinán,
held dragon boat races and lotus-gathering festivities,
with brocade cables and embroidered sails for entertainment,
costing hundreds of thousands in gold.
Yú Dí as the governor of Xiāngzhōu,
lit mountain lanterns daily,
consuming two thousand dàn of oil in a single event.
Lǐ Chāngkuí in Jīngzhōu,
extensively adorned for grand hunts,
his wife Dúgū shì also led a women's troop of two thousand,
all dressed in red and purple embroidered jackets,
and mounted on saddles and saddlecloths of brocade.
These three prefectures were thus depleted.
"Records of Anecdotes"
During the Qiánfú era,
in the Eastern Capital Luòyáng lived a young man from a noble family,
who inherited a legacy of merit and privilege,
dressed in silk and feasted on delicacies.
His meals were always cooked with charcoal,
yet they often failed to satisfy him.
A former prefect, Lǐ,
had returned from his post,
and feeling grateful for past kindness,
entrusted an intermediary named Shèng Gǎng
to select a day and gather rare delicacies,
inviting the young man.
On the appointed day,
the brothers sat in a row,
but as each dish arrived,
they barely tasted it.
The host repeatedly urged them to eat,
yet they only nibbled on fruits and light fare.
Lǐ could not fathom the reason.
The next day, he sent Shèng Gǎng to inquire,
who reported:
"All meals cooked with charcoal
require the charcoal to be pre-burned until fully ignited,
called 'refined charcoal.'
Otherwise, it retains smoky fumes.
The charcoal in your residence was unrefined,
hence the food was unpalatable."
Shèng Gǎng remarked:
"This was beyond my knowledge."
Later, when the rebel Huáng Cháo captured the city,
the Luòyáng brothers fled with Shèng Gǎng,
going without food for three days.
They trudged to a river bridge,
where Shèng Gǎng used a few coins from his pouch to buy coarse millet porridge,
and they ate together from earthen bowls.
Shèng Gǎng smiled and said to them:
"This wasn't cooked with refined charcoal—
I wonder if it's fit for you young masters to eat?"
They all bowed their heads in silence.
From "Jù Tán Lù"
Huáinán Yáng Wò during his mourning period,
indulged in heavy drinking and merrymaking day and night,
using candles as thick as ten hand-spans to play polo,
with each candle costing tens of thousands of coins.
《History》
Zhū Liáng's Zhū Jǐn had a famous horse he rode,
which he housed in a brocade tent in winter,
and protected with silk netting in summer.
"Continued Accounts of the World"
During the Later Jìn period, the Tǔyùhún chieftain Bái Chéngfú,
whose household was extremely wealthy,
used silver troughs to feed his horses.
The Emperor
Mǎ Xīfàn was by nature stubborn and self-willed,
fond of indulging in exaggeration and grandiosity.
Although he had reduced his ceremonial guard by half,
he modeled all military and state institutions after the imperial court.
He then launched massive construction projects,
building the Tiāncè Mansion,
within which he erected the Jiǔlóng Hall.
He used eaglewood to craft eight dragons,
each one hundred feet long,
facing each other while embracing the pillars,
assuming a posture as if vying to hold something up.
He himself sat among them,
claiming to be the ninth dragon.
His headscarf tails were over ten feet long,
symbolizing dragon horns.
At dawn before taking his seat,
he would have incense burned inside the dragons' bellies,
causing thick smoke to billow forth,
as if spewing from their mouths.
Since ancient times,
no feudal lord's extravagance and usurpation of rites
had ever reached such magnificence.
Shǔzhǔ Wáng Yǎn indulged in luxury and excess without restraint.
He often erected brocade screens to play ball within them,
frequently traveling to distant places,
yet outsiders remained unaware.
He burned various incenses day and night without cease.
After a long time, he grew weary of them,
and instead burned soap pods to disrupt their fragrance.
He constructed mountains from silk,
and built palaces, towers, and pavilions upon them.
If they were damaged by wind or rain,
he would replace them with new ones.
Sometimes he would enjoy drinking on the silk mountains,
remaining for ten days without descending.
He dug a canal in front connecting to the forbidden palace.
At times, he returned by boat at night,
ordering over a thousand palace maids to hold torches,
standing in reverse on the front boats,
illuminating the water's surface as bright as day.
Other times, he reveled in drinking within the forbidden palace,
with music and drums roaring fervently,
lasting until dawn,
making this a regular practice.
Guō Cóngyì governed Héshuò,
and built a grand mansion in Luòzhōng,
using fragrant cedar for its ridgepoles,
and patterned catalpa for its beams.
He adorned the pond with decorative stones,
leaving nothing incomplete.
Upon completion, the mansion cost approximately five thousand ingots of white silver.
Initially, some advised against such extravagance and excessive spending, but he did not listen.
Later, when summoned to court,
he happened to be touring the mansion by candlelight,
but died upon reaching the eastern commandery.
His family could not reside there,
and it became a subject of public ridicule.
Zhāng Jūn first replaced Kāng Huáiyīng as the military governor of Yǒngpíng,
plundering his family's wealth,
and then excavated the grounds of the former Táng palace,
unearthing gold, jade, and assets worth millions.
During the reign of Emperor Chū,
he resided in Luòyáng, amusing himself with wine, women, and music,
for over a decade,
earning the nickname "Earthly Immortal."
From "History of the Five Dynasties"
In the Southern Táng, Sūn Shèng served as Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and his family was wealthy, indulging in extravagance.
During banquets, he never used tables,
but instead ordered female entertainers to each hold a dish and stand around him in a circle,
calling it the "flesh table."
The "Surviving Accounts" notes that Yáng Guózhōng did the same.
Moreover, in winter, he would have courtesans encircle him,
calling it the "flesh screen."

Behaving in such a manner,
how can one avoid destruction?
From the "Continuation"
The people of Lǔ had a frugal and miserly custom,
and the Cáo Bǐng family was especially so.
They rose through iron smelting,
amassing wealth up to millions,
yet from fathers and brothers to sons and grandsons, they made a pact:
when bending down, they would pick things up,
when looking up, they would take things.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Pínglíng's Shìsūn Fèn had assets totaling one hundred and seventy million,
his wealth was renowned in the capital,
yet he was frugal and stingy by nature.
His nephew Duān,
appointed as Liáng Jì's assistant, was sent five bolts of silk by Fèn,
and served dried fish for meals.
Once, while staying at an inn,
he complained that the cost was too high.
The innkeeper said:
"You are so stingy with money,
do you wish to become another Shìsūn Jǐngqīng?"
"Sānfǔ Jué Tú"
In the Hàn Dynasty, there was an old man who had no children.
His family was wealthy, but he was miserly by nature.
He rose at the break of dawn,
and rested only when night fell,
managing his estate,
accumulating wealth without ever feeling satisfied,
yet he dared not use it for himself.
When someone came to him seeking help,
he would reluctantly go inside to fetch ten coins.
As he walked from the hall,
he reduced the amount with every step,
so that by the time he reached the outside,
only half remained.
He would close his eyes and hand them to the beggar,
then quickly add:
"I'm giving you all my family's wealth to support you.
Be careful not to tell others,
lest they imitate you and come asking."
Soon after, the old man died,
and his fields and assets were confiscated into the state treasury.
From "Forest of Laughs"
Wú Shěnjùn,
whose courtesy name was Shūshān,
was by nature frugal and stingy.
When Zhāng Wēn was sent on a mission to Shǔ,
he once visited Shěn.
Shěn went inside to part from him,
and after a long while came out,
saying to Wēn:
"I was just selecting a piece of cloth,
intending to give it to you as a gift,
but found none that was coarse enough.
Wēn appreciated his lack of concealment.
Another time, while passing by the shore of Lake Tài,
he had his attendant fetch some salt water,
but soon regretted taking too much,
and ordered him to return some.
Later, he also felt ashamed and said:
"This is my innate nature.
From "Forest of Laughs"
Minister Wáng Róng was both noble and wealthy,
with estates, servants, and livestock,
fertile fields, water-powered trip-hammers, and the like,
unmatched in all of Luòyáng.

Wáng Dǎo practiced frugality and thrift,

From "A New Account of the Tales of the World".
In the twelfth year of the Tàiyuán era,
a foreign monk possessed magical arts.
After arriving in the country,
there was an extremely wealthy family,
yet they were stingy by nature.
He said to the porter:
"I shall attempt to break your master's miserliness
for you."
He then went to their house,
where they had a fine horse they greatly treasured,
tethered under a pillar.
Suddenly it disappeared,
and though they searched, they could not find its whereabouts.
The next day, they saw the horse inside a five-shēng jar,
which ultimately could not be broken.
The monk then told the master,
"Prepare a feast for a hundred people to aid the impoverished,
and the horse will be freed."
The master hastily prepared it as requested,
and the horse reappeared under the pillar.
The following day, his elderly parents were in the main hall,
when suddenly they vanished again.
The whole family was terrified, not knowing their location,
until they opened a cosmetic container and unexpectedly saw the parents inside a chamber pot,
with no way to get out.
They went again to plead with the monk,
who said:
"You must prepare food for over a thousand people and provide for a hundred poor families,
then they shall be freed."
After it was done,
his parents were naturally back on their bed.
From "Records of Spectral Manifestations."
Shàngshū Lìng Fú Yǎ was a man who delighted in giving alms,

Wáng Kūn was frugal in his use of wealth and resources,

Cáo Hǔ served as General of the Right Guard,

Dèng Chà was a man from Línjū in Nánjùn. While traveling on the road by the river, he encountered a merchant
whom he had not previously known.
They sat by the roadside to eat together.
The merchant laid out an array of exceptional delicacies,
and Dèng Chà was invited to join.
Chà asked:
"You, sir, are a merchant traveling far from home,
and your circumstances are not necessarily affluent.
Why then do you suddenly indulge in such rare delicacies and fine foods?"
The merchant replied:
"In this life we live in the world,
we ultimately exist merely to feed our bodies and mouths.
Once we fall ill and die,
how could we still enjoy sweet flavors?
After all, we should not be like that Dèng Shēng from Línjū,
who never spent anything his whole life,
becoming nothing but a miser guarding his money!"
Chà did not reveal his name.
Returning home,
he slaughtered a goose to eat.

a bone got stuck in his throat,

Liáng Zhū Yì and his sons,

Gifts from all directions,

In Nányáng, there was a man who made a living with profound knowledge,

and reluctantly ordered more to be added,

Yuán Huī was by nature very jealous,

Běi Qí's Kù Dí Fúlián had a vulgar and stingy nature.
When his wife fell ill,

His household consisted of over a hundred people,

During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was an old man named Wáng from Xiàngzhōu,

with only husband and wife,
and no children.
They had accumulated nearly ten thousand hú of grain,
yet the couple was extremely frugal and stingy,
often eating stale food,
just enough to fill their stomachs,
never seeking abundance.
Their estate was particularly vast,
housing over two hundred tenant families. The old man
often made rounds through the tenants' quarters.
Suddenly, he saw one tenant eating a lavish meal from a plate,
and the old man asked about his occupation. The tenant said:
"I only sell assorted powdered incense and medicine.
The old man suspected him of being a thief,
asking, "With what means do you
enjoy such ample food and clothing?"
This person replied:
"I only have a capital of five thousand,
earning daily interest,
preserving only the principal,
not hoping for more,
thus my food and clothing are always sufficient.
The old man then had a great realization,
returned and said to his wife:
"That person, with small profits,
uses them to sustain himself;
he can be called understanding of principle.
Now, I have accumulated wealth amounting to tens of thousands,
yet eat and wear stale and worn-out things,
and have no descendants;
for whom am I saving it?
Thereupon, he opened the granaries,
widely purchased delicacies and fine goods,
and indulged in eating flavorful food.
Within a few days,
both husband and wife dreamed they were arrested by someone,
shackled and imprisoned,
whipped and beaten severely,
saying:
"These people recklessly wasted military provisions.
