Bái Jié Yuán Xiūyì served as the Governor of Qízhōu,
where he extensively engaged in bribery and corruption.
He was repeatedly promoted to the position of Minister of Personnel,
and while overseeing official appointments,
he focused solely on accepting bribes,
setting fixed prices for appointments to offices of all sizes.
At that time, there was a Grand Master for Splendid Happiness named Gāo Jū,
who had received an imperial decree to be prioritized for appointment,
as there was a vacancy in Dǎngjùn Commandery.
Gāo Jū then requested the position,
but Xiūyì had already privately promised it to someone else,
and suppressed Gāo Jū, refusing to grant it to him.
Gāo Jū spoke loudly and disrespectfully,
so Xiūyì ordered his attendants to drag him away.
In front of the crowd, Gāo Jū cried out to heaven, denouncing the bandit.
Someone asked Gāo Jū:
"In the broad daylight of the public court,
how could there be a bandit?"
Gāo Jū pointed at Xiūyì and said:
"The one sitting there,
violates the clear decree of the Son of Heaven,
granting offices to those who offer more goods.
In the capital, this is an open robbery—
isn't this a great bandit?"
Xiūyì turned pale with shock,
as Gāo Jū left, cursing as he went.

he would inevitably seek to obtain them.
Wealthy merchants and great traders all curried favor with him,
and he addressed them as his sons.
"Book of Sui"
Prince Jiāng Yuánxiáng,
was a son of Emperor Gāozǔ.
During the reign of Emperor Gāozōng,
he successively served as governor of Jīn, Fū, and Zhèng provinces.
His nature was greedy and base;
he amassed much gold and treasure,
ceaselessly pursuing profit,
and was detested by officials and commoners.
At that time, Princes Téng Yuán, Jiǎng Yùn, and Guó Fèng
were also known for their greed and tyranny.
Those appointed to their princely establishments,
considering the southern regions beyond the mountains as vile places,
composed a saying:
"Rather face Dān and Yá, shaking white hair,
than serve Wāng, Téng, Jiǎng, and Guó."
According to the Old Book of Táng, Princes Téng Yuán and Jiǎng Yùn
both failed to be honest and cautious.
Emperor Wén bestowed fifty rolls of silk each to the other princes,
but excluded these two princes,
issuing an edict:
"Uncle Téng and Brother Jiǎng,
manage their own affairs,
and need no gifts."
Instead, he gave them
ten thousand cords to use as coin strings,
leaving the two princes greatly ashamed.
Court officials all took this as a warning,
regarding acceptance of bribes as corruption.
Some served as officials their whole lives
without daring to commit such offenses.
From Collected Records
When Xiàhóu Biāozhī first arrived to assume his post as the magistrate of Xīnchāng County in Yìzhōu,
he asked the village head:
"How many eggs can you buy for one coin?"
The reply was:
"Three eggs."
Biāozhī then had ten thousand coins fetched,
ordering the purchase of thirty thousand eggs,
and told the village head:
"I don't need them immediately,
so leave them with the hens to hatch,
thus producing thirty thousand chicks.
After the chickens grow up in a few months,
sell them for me immediately,
at thirty coins per chicken,
yielding ninety thousand coins within half a year."
He also asked:
"How many bamboo shoots can you buy for one coin?"
"Five shoots for one coin,"
so he again took out ten thousand coins and handed them over,
buying fifty thousand shoots.
He told the village head:
"I don't need the shoots right now,
so cultivate them in the grove.
By autumn, when they've grown into bamboo,
sell each for ten coins, thus making five hundred thousand."
His greed and unscrupulousness
were all of this kind.
From "Qiān Zǎi"
Biànzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Zhìyīn,
ate refined and delicate food,
yet served guests unhusked millet rice.
A merchant had a mule
that could travel three hundred lǐ a day,
and had refused to sell it even for thirty thousand coins,
when a market vendor offered four thousand.
Yīn said:
"Four thousand in gold is too little;
increase it by another thousand."
He also ordered the purchase of a single-thread silk gauze bolt for three thousand coins.
Yīn asked:
"How many liǎng of silk were used?"
The reply was:
"Five liǎng."
Yīn had his servant bring five liǎng of silk,
giving an additional ten coins per liǎng,
for the value of the manual labor.
From "Qiān Zǎi"
Zhèng Yīn served as Vice Minister of Personnel,
overseeing selections with rampant corruption.
A candidate tied a hundred coins to his boot strap,
and Yīn asked:
"Why?"
The candidate replied:
"In current selections,
nothing gets done without money."
Yīn fell silent without speaking.
"Qiǎn Zǎi"
Cuī Shí served as Vice Minister of Personnel,
overseeing official appointments.
A candidate for selection cited his faults and pleaded:
"I am capable of lifting the city gate and carrying the cauldron.
Shí said:
"If you are so strong,
why not seek selection at the Ministry of War?
He replied:
"Everyone outside says: Under Vice Minister Cuī,
those with influence get appointed.
from Qiān Zǎi
Zhèng Rénkǎi was the governor of Mì Prefecture.
A young servant complained that his shoes were worn out.
Rénkǎi said:
"Should I, your elder, manage this for you?
Shortly after,
a doorman was wearing new shoes.
There was a woodpecker's nest on a tree in front of Rénkǎi's hall,
so he sent the doorman up the tree to fetch the nestlings.
The doorman took off his shoes to climb the tree.
Rénkǎi then ordered the servant to put on the shoes and leave.
The doorman was left barefoot,
and protested to Rénkǎi, saying:
"The governor is not a keeper of shoes.
From "Qiān Zǎi"
When Lǐ Shǎizhī was the governor of Hǎizhōu,
an envoy from Japan arrived in Hǎizhōu
with a total of five hundred people
carrying national tribute.
There were ten ships
with treasures worth millions.
Lǐ Shǎizhī saw this,
lodged them at the guesthouse,
provided generously for their needs,
but forbade them from going out.
In the middle of the night,
he took all their cargo and sank their ships.
At dawn,
he hinted to the lodging attendants to report:
"Last night, a great tide came,
and all the Japanese ships were washed away,
their whereabouts unknown."
He then reported the matter to the court.
An imperial edict ordered Lǐ Shǎizhī
to build ten ships
and provide five hundred skilled sailors
to escort the Japanese envoy back to their country.
Lǐ Shǎizhī prepared the ships and sailors.
Before the envoys departed,
the sailors bid farewell to Lǐ Shǎizhī.
He said:
"Japan is a distant journey,
and the sea is full of wind and waves.
How can you return?
On the way, handle matters as you see fit."
The escorts were pleased.
After several days of travel,
knowing the Japanese were unprepared,
they killed them all at night
and returned.
Lǐ Shǎizhī kept many followers,
harboring hundreds of fugitives.
They plundered wherever they went,
and if exposed, he killed them.
In the end, he did not meet his death
but was punished for his cruelty and excesses.
From "Jì Wén"
Fújiàn Yánqiányuàn official Lú Áng,
was implicated for embezzling three hundred thousand,
Jiǎn Cí investigated him,
and found at his home a golden bed and a sapphire pillow as large as a peck measure.
Emperor Zhāomǐn saw them,
and said:
"These are not even found in the palace,
revealing the kind of official Lú Áng was.
Old Book of Tang: Jiǎn Cí interrogated for months,
before he could present the findings,
summoned market vendors to appraise them,
some said the treasure was priceless,
others claimed it was fine stone, not genuine sapphire.
Supplement to the National History
Wèi Zhōngháng was exiled to Bōzhōu due to corruption discovered during his inspection in Fúzhōu,
and though amnesty was granted,
he died in an inn in Bōzhōu while returning north,
and was placed in a rice mortar pond.
In the southern regions, burial customs lack coffins or outer containers;
when the rice ripens,
they hollow out wood like a small boat to create a mortar for pounding rice,
which the locals call a rice mortar pond.
"New Book of the Southern Regions"
Xué Féngjí was in the Central Secretariat,
appointing officials while frequently accepting bribes,
trading power and selling offices,
drawing criticism from those who upheld integrity.
Lǐ Yǒngjí of Fèngxiáng first came to the capital for an audience,
and because Xué Féngjí knew Yǒngjí was the son of the former Prince of Qín, Cóng Yǎn,
whose family had a lineage of princes and nobles,
he assumed there must be rare treasures.
He sent someone to inform Yǒngjí,
promising him a prefecture,
in exchange for his late father's jade belt.
Yǒngjí excused himself, saying he did not have it,
so Xué Féngjí had someone purchase a jade belt,
worth several thousand strings of coins,
and demanded Yǒngjí pay for it.
The former Guest Bureau Commissioner Wáng Yún had been sent to Chǔ at the end of the Jìn dynasty,
and by this time had returned.
Xué Féngjí suspected Yún had received substantial bribes from the King of Chǔ,
so he sent someone to demand them,
again promising a prefecture.
Yún reluctantly handed over half of his baggage and belongings,
yet neither of them received a prefecture.
"History of the Five Dynasties"
Shēn Guì, the prefect of Méizhōu in Later Shǔ,
was cruel and oppressive in his excessive taxation.
He instructed prison officials
to force criminals to implicate wealthy citizens as accomplices,
in order to extort bribes from them,
and often pointed at the prison gate, saying:
"This is my family's money vault.
He was impeached and imprisoned,
demoted to the position of registrar in Wéizhōu,
and upon reaching Xīpǔ,
was ordered to commit suicide,
which the people celebrated.
From "Shǔ Tǎowù" and "Jiǔ Guó Zhì"
Wáng Lǔ served as the magistrate of Dāngtú,
and was quite preoccupied with amassing wealth.
It happened that the local people jointly filed a complaint to the county magistrate, accusing the registrar of accepting bribes.
Wáng Lǔ then wrote his judgment:
"Though you strike the grass,
I am already the startled snake."
This became a favorite anecdote among gossipers.
From "Recent Events of Southern Táng"
When Zhào Zàilǐ was in Sòngzhōu,
he acted unlawfully,
causing the people to suffer.
One day, when he was transferred to another post,
the people of Yǒngxīng were overjoyed
and congratulated one another, saying:
"If this man leaves,
it would be like pulling a nail from the eye.
What a relief!"
Upon hearing this,
Zhào Zàilǐ was furious and sought revenge for the "nail-pulling" insult.
He immediately submitted a memorial,
requesting to remain in Sòngzhōu for another year.
At that time, the court was indulgent,
and the decree permitted it.
Zhào Zàilǐ then ordered officials to register all households in his jurisdiction,
regardless of whether they were native or migrant,
demanding one thousand coins per year
to be paid to his household,
calling it
"Nail-Pulling Money."
He openly enforced this levy,
and those who failed to comply
were subjected to flogging,
making it even harsher than regular taxes.
That year, he collected a million coins.
From "Supplementary Records of the History of the Five Dynasties."
Wèi Wáng Xú Zhīxùn was the governor of Xuānzhōu,
imposing harsh taxes on the people,
causing them great suffering.
When he went to the imperial court for an audience,
he was granted a banquet,
during which actors performed a skit featuring a green-clad, masked foreigner
resembling a deity or ghost.
Suddenly, it appeared beside another person,
who asked:
"Who are you?"
The green-clad figure replied:
"I am the local earth god of Xuānzhōu."
The other asked:
"Why have you come here?"
The figure said:
"The governor came to the imperial court,
and scraped off the very land itself and brought it along,
so I ended up here."
The emperor burst into laughter.
From "Accounts of the Southern Táng Dynasty"
Zhāng Chóng governed Lúzhōu,
and was fond of unlawful practices,
causing suffering to both scholars and commoners.
Once he went to the imperial court for an audience,
and the people of Jiāngdū and Lúzhōu, hoping he would be transferred,
all said to each other:
"That guy will surely not return."
When Chóng came back, he levied a "that guy tax" per person.
The following year he went for another audience,
and there were strong rumors of his dismissal,
but people dared not speak openly;
when meeting on the road,
they would stroke their beards in mutual congratulation.
Upon his return, Chóng imposed a "beard-stroking tax."
Once during a banquet, an actor pretended to be dead,
and was condemned to become an aquatic creature.
A netherworld official petitioned the judge,
who ruled:
"With Jiāo Lake spanning a hundred li,
you may become an otter."
Chóng was greatly ashamed.
Wáng Shǒu'ēn, the military governor of the Western Capital and co-manager of affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery,
was by nature greedy and despicable.
He engaged in extortionate taxation,
and funeral carriages could not leave the city without paying money.
Even down to those who cleaned toilets
or beggars on the streets,
none could escape his levies and demands.
Sometimes he even allowed his subordinates to rob people of their property.
There was a wealthy family holding a wedding,
and Wáng Shǒu'ēn went with several entertainers to act as guests of honor,
returning with several ingots of silver.
"Later Han Emperor Yindi's Reign in the Comprehensive Mirror"
During the Kāibǎo era,
a certain Magistrate Zhāng of Shénquán County,
newly appointed to his post,
outwardly prided himself on integrity and honesty,
while inwardly indulged in corruption for personal gain.
Instances of this were numerous.
One day, he posted a notice at the county office stating:
"On such-and-such month and day is the magistrate's birthday,
this notice is displayed outside the gate to inform all,
so that people of various statuses shall not make any offerings."
A minor official discussed with the others:
"The magistrate explicitly mentions his birthday,
intending for us to know;
his words refusing gifts
are merely modesty."
The others said:
"Indeed."
When the day arrived,
each presented silk fabric as an offering.
They called it:
"longevity-extending garments,"
and the magistrate refused none,
only gratefully accepting them.
He then informed them again:
"On such-and-such day next month is my wife's birthday,
do not bring gifts again."
All who heard this scoffed at him,
as learned from Huáng Fèng, a jìnshì of Shénquán.
At that time, Wáng Yán satirized him with his poem "The Egret":
"In flight, it resembles a crane,
alighting, it seeks only fish."
This hit the mark most accurately.
From "Records of Hearsay"
Sòng Lǐbù Yuánwài Wáng Zǐsháo, upon completing the revision of the "Shuōwén,"
wrote a memorial presenting the book
and showed it to his colleague Páng Yuányīng,
saying:
"The 'Qián Hàn Yìwén Zhì' includes minor officials' theories,
which can also be utilized."
A scholar immediately remarked:
"Chancellor Fù once used this precedent."
When everyone asked for the reason,
he said:
"Greed leads to official corruption."
The entire company laughed at him.
"Wénchāng Zálù"
Xuē Jí did not maintain a clean and honest character,
while governing Fēnzhōu,
there were rumors of his accepting bribes,
meaning there were sounds of gathering and accepting.
"Hǎi Lù" recorded Gāo Zūn's reputation for greed and cruelty,
which the Emperor heard quite a bit about.
"Wèi Shū"
Wèi Yāng internally enforced punishments as severe as knives and saws,
and externally imposed executions as harsh as axes and blades.
Those who took steps exceeding six feet were fined,
and those who discarded ashes on the road were punished.
One day, while holding a discussion by the Wèi River,
he imprisoned over seven hundred people,
causing the Wèi River to run completely red.
The sounds of wailing and crying
shook heaven and earth.
"Xīn Xù"
Zhì Dū was transferred to become the Commandant of the Capital.
At that time, the people were simple and honest,
fearing punishment and valuing self-restraint,
yet Zhì Dū alone pioneered severe harshness.
He enforced the law without avoiding the noble and powerful,
so that the marquises and imperial clansmen,
when they saw Zhì Dū,
would look at him askance,
and they nicknamed him:
"The Gray Falcon."
"Basic Biography"
Nìng Chéng served Emperor Jǐng,
was fond of asserting his authority,
when he was a junior official,
he would always bully his superiors,
and when in a position above others,
he controlled his subordinates as harshly as tying up wet objects.
He was crafty, cruel, and arbitrary in wielding power.
"Basic Biography" Nìng Chéng resided at home,
the emperor intended to appoint him as a commandery governor.
Gōngsūn Hóng said:
"When your servant served as a minor official in Shāndōng,
Nìng Chéng was the commandant of Jǐ'nán,
his governance was like a wolf herding sheep,
Nìng Chéng should not be allowed to govern the people.
The emperor then appointed Nìng Chéng as the Pass Commandant.
Over a year later,
the pass officials taxed those from commanderies and kingdoms entering and exiting the pass,
it was said:
"Better to encounter a nursing tigress,
than to face Nìng Chéng's wrath.
"Yì Zòng's Biography"
Yì Zòng was the governor of Dìngxiāng.
Upon his arrival,
he raided the prison and found over two hundred serious criminals,
along with relatives and friends who had secretly visited them,
also numbering over two hundred.
Yì Zòng arrested and interrogated them all,
saying:
"They were helping the condemned escape."
That same day, he reported executing over four hundred people.
The entire commandery trembled with fear.
Cunning locals assisted officials in governance.
At that time, Zhào Yǔ and Zhāng Tāng served as the Nine Ministers,
yet their governance remained relatively lenient,
supporting the law in practice.
Yì Zòng governed like a hawk striking its prey.
The emperor
Yán Yánnián studied law in his youth,
served as the governor of Zhuōjùn,
where all officials trembled with fear,
and lost items were not picked up on the road.
He was later appointed governor of Hénán,
and in winter, he summoned prisoners from subordinate counties to his office for judgment,
resulting in bloodshed stretching for miles,
earning him the nickname in Hénèi
"Butcher Lord"
Zhǎng Chǎng wrote to admonish him,
to which Yánnián replied:
"When weeds flourish and crops are tainted,
they must be eradicated.
Yánnián's mother came from Dōnghǎi,
intending to celebrate the year-end sacrifice with him,
but happened to witness the execution of prisoners,
and was greatly shocked.
After the formal year-end sacrifice,
she said to Yánnián:
"The way of heaven is divine and clear,
one cannot kill alone.
I never expected to live to see my son in his prime face punishment and execution!
Farewell,
I leave you and return east,
to sweep the ancestral graves.
A year later,
Yánnián indeed met his downfall.
(From "Basic Biography") Xún Xī served as the inspector of Qīngzhōu,
appointing many assistants,
frequently replacing governors and magistrates,
and achieved merit through harshness,
increasing executions daily,
with bloodshed forming rivers,
making life unbearable for the people,
earning him the nickname
"Butcher Lord"
When his brother Xún Chún succeeded him in Qīngzhōu,
his punishments and killings were even more severe than Xī's.
The people called it
"The younger Xún is crueler than the elder Xún"
(From "Book of Jìn")
Yǐn Shǎng,
courtesy name Zǐxīn,
was appointed as the Magistrate of Cháng'ān during Emperor Chéng's reign,
oversaw the renovation of Cháng'ān prison,
excavating a pit several zhàng deep in each dimension,
lining it with bricks to form an enclosure,
covering its opening with large stones,
naming it
"Tiger's Lair"
He arrested frivolous youths and troublemakers,
charging them as accomplices who provided sustenance to gangs of bandits.
Shǎng personally inspected them,
selecting one out of every ten for sparing,
and had the rest sequentially thrown into the Tiger's Lair,
in groups of a hundred,
covered with large stones.
Every few days, he would open it to check,
finding all had died piled upon one another.
《Book of Hàn》
Lǐ Yán served as the Grand Protector,
enforcing laws with harsh severity,
prompting people to chant:
"Do not dare provoke Lǐ's scaly armor.
from "Chronicles of the Jiangbiao Region"
Yáng Dān during Emperor Yuán's reign was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Lúlíng,
being resolute and crude in his violence,
he relied on his status as a relative of the imperial family to act with extreme wantonness,
over the slightest grievance,
he would impose punishment and execution.
Suspecting that the commandery residents Jiǎn Liáng and others were bandits and thieves,
he executed over two hundred people,
including infants and children,
and additionally shaved heads and imprisoned over a hundred more.
Yǔ Liàng arrested him,
and sent him back to the capital,
where his crime warranted death,
but because Empress Yáng was his grandaunt,
he was eligible for deliberation.
Emperor Chéng issued an edict stating:
"This case is unprecedented in history,
what deliberation is there to be had?
Let the execution be carried out in the prison.
Empress Yáng entered the palace,
kowtowing to plead for his life.
Wáng Dǎo submitted a petition,
and he was pardoned but stripped of his official status.
Shortly after, he fell ill,
constantly haunted by visions of Jiǎn Liáng and others as vengeful spirits,
and died within ten days.
"Book of Jìn"
Shā Jù Fú Jié was cruel and tyrannical,
often appearing before court officials with drawn bow and bared blade.
Pincers, hammers, saws, and chisels—
all tools that could be used for killing—
were kept at his side.
Not long after ascending the throne,
from high-ranking officials down
to servants and slaves,
he killed over five hundred people.
Records of Fú Shēng's deeds are found in the "Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū."
When Guō Nún was seizing territories,
the eight young princes,
who had all followed their wet nurses to the Eastern Garden earlier,
were all thrown by Nún onto the blades,
some dismembered limb by limb,
and he drank their blood to swear an oath with the crowd.
Witnesses could not help but cover their eyes and shudder with fear.
Yet Nún remained composed and unruffled.
"Records of Liángzhōu"
Hèlián Bóbó was cruel and fond of killing,
often staying atop the city walls,
with spears and swords placed by his side.
Whenever he held a grudge or felt anger,
he would personally slaughter the person.
For ministers who dared to look at him defiantly,
those who squinted and laughed,
or those who spoke out in remonstrance,
he would cut out their tongues and execute them.
"Cuī Hóng's Records of Xià"
Zōng Yuè governed his troops with extreme severity,
often resorting to executions,
and for even the slightest offense,
he would apply military law.
At that time, Wáng Xuánmó also showed little kindness to his officers and soldiers,
prompting them to say:
"Better to serve five years as a convict,
than to encounter Wáng Xuánmó.
Wáng Xuánmó is still tolerable,
but Zōng Yuè will be the death of me.
Book of Sòng
During the Dàmíng era,
Xī Xiǎndù was often put in charge of supervising laborers,
but he was harsh and cruel without principle,
frequently resorting to beatings,
whether in the sweltering rain or bitter cold,
he did not allow any temporary rest,
the people could not endure such conditions,
and some even hanged themselves to death.
When laborers heard they were assigned to Xī Xiǎndù,
it was as if they were going to execution.
At that time, when Jiànkāng County interrogated prisoners,
they sometimes used square timbers to press on their ankles,
and a folk rhyme said:
"Better to suffer Jiànkāng's pressure on the ankle,
than to endure Xī Dù's slaps."
They also joked among themselves:
"Don't look back,
or you'll be handed over to Xī Dù."
Such was his extreme cruelty.
The former deposed emperor once remarked in jest:
"Xī Xiǎndù's harsh cruelty
has made him hated by the common people,
it's time to eliminate him."
His attendants promptly agreed.
That very day,
an imperial decree was issued to execute him,
and contemporaries compared it to Sūn Hào killing Cén Hūn.
During the time of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng, Xiāo Huìkāi was exceptionally perceptive.
On one occasion, he managed to read the names of three thousand shāmén,
and afterward, he forgot none.
He was appointed the Cìshǐ of Yìzhōu,
where he strictly enforced the law,
and the people of Shǔ called him
“The Lying Tiger”
According to the "Nán Shǐ", Dǒng Xuān served as the magistrate of Luòyáng,
where the capital residents called him
“The Lying Tiger”
According to the "Hòu Hànshū".
The Governor of Rǔyáng, Wáng Dàobiāo,
had two wooden figures made in a subordinate county,
each eight feet tall,
and erected them at the commandery gate.
Those who committed offenses
were made to punch the wooden figures.
If they could
knock them down, they were exempt from punishment;
those with insufficient strength
would injure and scrape their hands and fists.
"Yuánjiā Qǐjū Zhù"
Rǔnán Wáng Yuè enjoyed reading Buddhist scriptures,
perusing historical texts,
later abstained from marital relations,
but became more fond of male companions,
treating his consorts with contempt and anger,
even subjecting them to beatings like maidservants.
During the Xiàochāng era,
he was appointed regional inspector,
and had a large chopping block installed
at the prefecture gate,
threatening to cut off the hands of thieves,
causing wrongdoers to fear him
and temporarily cease their activities.
《Book of Wèi》
Yáng Zhǐ,
courtesy name Língyòu.
During the reign of Emperor Xuānwǔ of the Northern Wèi Dynasty,
he served as an official undaunted by powerful figures in the court.
At times when inspections were conducted,
he was often dispatched,
acting accordingly.
He admired legalist principles,
and was deeply influenced by harsh interpretations of the law.
Wherever he was,
people called him
"the Heavenly Dog Descended."
When he was appointed
to oversee a province,
he showed no benevolence or generosity,
and soldiers suffered under his severe cruelty.
(From History of the Northern Dynasties: Book of Wèi)
Duàn Yìyún was exceptionally cruel and brutal,
beyond the bounds of human reason,
especially within his household,
where his children, grandchildren, and servants
constantly bore wounds and bruises all over their bodies.
Lǐ Biāo served as Commandant of the Capital,
and was known for his severe cruelty.
Finding confessions of crimes difficult to obtain,
he crafted wooden hands,
with which he struck the chests and armpits of prisoners,
so that there were cases where people died and then revived.
He also pacified the rebellious Hu tribes in Fēnzhōu,
captured their chieftains,
and had them flogged on the face before execution.
When Lǐ Biāo fell ill,
sores often broke out all over his body,
causing him extreme agony.
History of the Northern Dynasties
Wèi Sòng Fān served as the magistrate of Héyīn County.
The county had an old, large cangue,
which people at the time called
"Mí Wěi Qīng"
When Fān took office as the county magistrate,
he was asked to burn it,
but Fān said:
"Let's place it by the southern wall for now,
awaiting the powerful families."
Later, the eunuch Yáng Xiǎojū came to the county to make a request,
behaving arrogantly and disrespectfully,
so Fān ordered the "Mí Wěi Qīng" to be brought out to intimidate him,
and from then on, his authority shook the capital.
"From the Original Biography"
Gǔ Kǎi was blind in one eye,
yet his nature was extremely severe and cruel,
and all his previous official missions were notorious for their cruelty and brutality.
People of the time called him
"the Blind Tiger"
Book of Wei
Lú Pèi,
courtesy name Zǐzhāng,
was cruel by nature,
known for his forceful adjudications.
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Northern Qí,
he oversaw imperial prisons in the capital region,
where brutality exceeded human decency.
Regardless of the case's severity,
he employed excessive torture,
and many died under large clubs or cart wheels.
In harsh winter cold,
he placed prisoners on ice and snow;
in sweltering summer heat,
he exposed them under the sun.
Those wrongfully condemned to death
numbered over a hundred.
He spied on officials' faults,
reporting them immediately upon discovery,
so court officials who saw him
all tread carefully and held their breath,
dubbing him "the investigator."
Pèi and Lǐ Shù were both whipped to death in prison.
(From History of the Northern Dynasties)
Yú Zàn,
the younger brother of Jù Luó,
was by nature cruel and brutal to his subordinates.
He ordered his attendants to roast meat,
and if it did not meet his expectations,
he would blind them by stabbing their eyes with skewers;
if warmed wine did not suit his taste,
he would immediately cut out their tongues.
"Book of Sui"
Yàn Róng,
during the reign of Emperor Wén of Suí, was appointed Commander of Yōuzhōu.
He was severe and cruel with an imposing presence,
flogging his attendants,
often reaching over a thousand lashes,
until blood filled the ground before him,
yet he ate and drank with composure.
Once while inspecting his troops,
he saw thorny bushes along the road,
suitable for making whips,
and ordered them to be gathered,
immediately testing them on people.
Someone protested having committed no fault,
to which Yàn Róng replied:
"If you commit a crime later,
you will be exempted."
Later, when the person committed a minor offense,
Yàn Róng prepared to whip him.
The person said:
"The other day when I was caned, you promised
to pardon any future crimes."
Yàn Róng said:
"If you were whipped without fault,
how much more when you have committed one?"
He flogged him as before.
From History of the Northern Dynasties
Yuán Hóngsì, during Emperor Wén's reign, served as the Governor of Yōuzhōu.
Whenever he interrogated prisoners,
he often poured vinegar into their noses,
or pierced their lower orifices with sharp stakes.
None dared conceal the truth,
and corruption and deceit were suppressed.
The Emperor
Zhào Zhòngqīng,
was of a crude and brutal nature.
During the reign of Emperor Wén, he was promoted to Area Commander of Shuòzhōu.
At that time, the cultivation of garrison fields was thriving north of the frontier,
and Zhòngqīng oversaw it in general.
For even the slightest mismanagement,
he would summon the official in charge and flog his chest and back,
or strip him and hang him upside down among brambles and thorns.
People of the time called him Yūtú.
Huò Hé sī adjudicated cases involving prisoners,
regardless of their virtue, vice, or social status,
they were invariably subjected to cangues, fetters, and shackles,
enduring extreme hardship and suffering.
Prisoners who saw him
were terrified out of their wits,
dubbing him
"the Living Rakshasa"
His wife successively gave birth to four children,
but each time she went into labor, she fainted and wished for death,
and the children born all had fleshy chains on their bodies,
with fleshy shackles binding their hands and feet,
causing them to stumble and fall to the ground.
Later, as a county magistrate, he was convicted and beaten to death.
"Extensive Records" During the Dayè era,
there was a jailer who treated prisoners with extreme cruelty,
and later fathered a son
with what appeared to be a fleshy cangue on his shoulders,
lacking a neck.
"Records of the Five Elements"
Cuī Hóngdù,
known for his severe and cruel nature,
served as the Governor of Xiāngzhōu,
causing officials and people to tremble with fear.
At that time, there was a man named Qūtū Gài,
who was also harsh and strict,
leading to a saying in Cháng'ān:
"Better drink three pecks of vinegar,
than meet Cuī Hóngdù.
Better burn three pecks of mugwort,
than encounter Qūtū Gài.
Gài's elder brother, Tōng, was a Left Guard General,
and while serving with vigor and integrity,
a saying arose:
"Better eat three pecks of onions,
than meet Qūtū Tōng.
From the Book of Suì. Tāng Déqián served as a Provincial Governor,
and established authority, leading to a saying:
"Better eat three pecks of charcoal,
than encounter Tāng Déqián.
From the Book of Táng.
During the chaos at the end of the Suí dynasty,
the mad rebel Zhū Càn rose between Xiāng and Dèng.
There was famine that year,
with one hú of rice costing ten thousand coins,
yet still unobtainable.
People resorted to cannibalism.
Zhū Càn then took infants, steamed and ate them,
commanding his soldiers:
"What food could be more delicious
than human flesh?
As long as other states have people,
what do I have to worry about?"
He immediately ordered his troops that whenever women and children were captured,
they should be cooked and distributed among the soldiers.
He also taxed various fortresses,
taking young and weak men and women to supplement military provisions.
Later, he sent an envoy requesting to surrender to Gāozǔ,
who ordered Duàn Cuì to welcome and receive him.
Duàn Cuì, while drunk, insulted Zhū Càn, saying:
"I've heard you eat people -
what does it taste like?"
Zhū Càn replied:
"If you eat someone who enjoys drinking,
it's just like eating pork marinated in wine dregs."
Enraged, Duàn Cuì cursed arrogantly:
"You mad rebel, after entering the court,
you'll be nothing but a slave.
Will you still get to eat people then?"
Fearing for his position,
Zhū Càn seized Duàn Cuì and dozens of his followers,
and fled to Wáng Shìchōng.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Dūdū of Luòzhōu, Dòu Guǐ,
a third cousin of Tàimù Empress,
was by nature rigid, stern, and fond of killing.
While serving as Deputy Director of the Yìzhōu Branch Department of State Affairs,
he executed many officers and soldiers.
Among his subordinates, regardless of rank or age,
if they failed to obey orders respectfully,
he would immediately behead them.
Every day, many officials and soldiers were whipped until they bled,
and all who witnessed it in the courtyard stood trembling with fear.
When Guǐ first entered Shǔ,
he took his nephew as a confidant.
Once, he went out at night and called for him,
but the nephew did not arrive on time, angering Guǐ,
who then beheaded him.
He often warned his household servants not to go out,
but once he sent a slave to fetch broth from the official kitchen,
and then regretted it.
He said to the slave:
"I truly sent you,
but I must behead you
to make the law clear."
He ordered his subordinate general to arrest the slave,
and executed him.
The slave protested his innocence,
and the supervising executioner hesitated, unable to decide.
Enraged, Guǐ
beheaded both of them.
Zhào Hóng'ān, a Gentleman of the Bureau of Operations in the Branch Department of State Affairs,
was a renowned scholar,
yet Guǐ would frequently flog him,
amounting to hundreds of times a year.
He also harmed Wéi Yúnqǐ, the Director of the Branch Department of State Affairs.
In the second year of the Zhēnguàn era (628 CE),
while seriously ill in Luòzhōu,
he suddenly said someone had brought him melons.
His attendants reported
that there were no melons in winter.
Guǐ said:
"A plate of fine melons,
how can you say there are none?"
Then, with a start, he looked and said:
"Not melons,
but human heads."
Guǐ said:
"They have come to demand my life in return."
He also said:
"Help me up to see."
After saying this, Director Wéi died.
"Extensive Records"
During the revolutions of the Zhōu and Táng dynasties,
the conspiracies of generals and ministers,
if not involving their fathers and brothers,
then certainly their sons and younger brothers,
often had their secrets leaked and were frequently impeached and accused.
Investigating envoys were dispatched to interrogate them,
and obtaining the truth would be rewarded with official positions.
Thus, those who specialized in informing,
and the agents of investigation,
mutually fabricated false accusations,
collectively engaging in harsh measures.
Within the newly established prisons,
and in the offices of the Luòzhōu administration,
secret tribunals were successively formed,
mutually constructing severe legal nets.
Windows were blocked and doors sealed,
with crude clubs and heavy cangues,
pursuing, capturing, and ambushing,
not just for a day or an evening.
Torchlights surrounded residences,
swords and clubs barred the gates,
suffering and torture through flogging,
no confession meant no release.
Lái Jùnchén promptly executed Yún Hóngsì,
and also personally beheaded Zhāng Chùxù, Guō Hóngbà, and Fù Lǐ Sīzhēng,
while Wáng Hóngyì similarly displayed the head of Máo Xuánsù.
Both court and populace held their breath in fear,
and on the roads, people only dared to exchange glances.
From the "Tōngdiǎn"
When Wǔ Zétiān assumed the regency,
she feared the world would not submit,
so she sought to control it through intimidation,
gradually employing cruel officials,
insisting on strict legal interpretations to handle criminal cases.
At that time, Zhōu Xìng, Lái Jùnchén, and others successively received her orders,
to investigate major cases.
Thus, a special judicial court was established inside the Lìjǐng Gate of the capital,
where Jùnchén's interrogations always yielded results,
and he was specifically appointed to conduct trials.
It was also called
"the Newly Opened Gate"
but for those who entered the Newly Opened Gate,
scarcely one in a hundred survived.
Wáng Hóngyì jestingly referred to the Lìjǐng Gate as
"the Gate of Certain End"
meaning that those who entered this gate
invariably met their end.
From "The Biography of Lái Jùnchén"
Lái Jùnchén every time he interrogated prisoners,
regardless of the severity of their crimes,
would often pour vinegar into their noses,
confine them in underground prisons,
or place them in large jars,
surrounding them with fire to roast them.
He would also cut off their food supplies,
to the extent that some had to pull out the cotton wadding from their clothes to eat.
The large cangues he made
had ten names in total: first was "Stabilize All Pulses,"
second was "Gasping for Breath,"
third was "Roaring from the Ground,"
fourth was "Confess Upon Contact,"
fifth was "Soul and Courage Lost,"
sixth was "Truth Equals Rebellion,"
seventh was "Rebellion Is Truth,"
eighth was "Even a Dead Pig Would Grieve,"
ninth was "Seeking Immediate Death,"
tenth was "Seeking Family Ruin."
He also forced them to sleep in filth and squalor,
subjecting them to all kinds of suffering and poison.
Whenever there was an imperial decree to pardon prisoners,
Lái Jùnchén would always first send jailers
to kill all those with serious crimes,
and then announce the decree.
"Records of the Past" Later, when Lái Jùnchén was about to falsely accuse the Wǔ family,
the various false kings, Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ, and Zhāng Yìzhī, among others, thus exposed his treachery.
Wǔ Zétiān repeatedly protected him,
but the various Wǔ members and the princess were fearful,
and together they slandered him,
leading to his execution in the market.
People of the country, regardless of age,
all harbored resentment,
vying to slice his flesh,
which was completely gone in an instant.
Wǔ Zétiān issued an edict saying:
"Lái Jùnchén, regarding the various kings who are the foundational branches of the clan,
was certain to bring about their destruction.
The civil and military officials of the northern and southern offices,
all were plotted against for overthrow.
It is fitting to add the punishment of exterminating his clan,
to appease the anger of the common people."
After his clan was exterminated, regardless of scholars, commoners, men, or women,
they celebrated together on the roads,
all saying:
"From now on when we lie down,
our backs can finally touch the bed;
otherwise,
we wouldn't know if we'd live to see the evening!"
"Records of the Censorate" People fought to gouge out his eyes,
pluck his liver,
mince his flesh into paste,
which was completely gone in a moment,
then trampled his bones with horses,
leaving nothing behind.
"Biographies of Tang Dynasty Cruel Officials"
Zhōu Xìng tortured and bound the criminals,
with methods like "immortal crane spreading its wings."
There were also "monkey grinding tea,"
"ghost dragging a bull," and "pulling out a stake."
At that time, people called him Ox-Head Yè Yì.
According to the Tán Bīn Lù and Qiān Zǎi, he was known as Ox-Head Ā Pó.
Zhōu Tuīshì sent Yuán Suǒlǐ,
who was nicknamed "Suǒ the Envoy" by people of the time.
When the Empress Dowager obtained informants,
she would order Yuánlǐ and others to interrogate them,
competing in prisoner interrogation methods.
Cruel techniques included using beams to lock limbs
and twisting them, called "Phoenix Drying Its Wings";
or tying objects to the waist,
pulling the cangue forward,
called "Donkey Colt Pulling the Stake";
or making prisoners kneel holding the cangue,
piling bricks on top,
called "Immortal Presenting Fruit";
or making them stand on high wood,
pulling the cangue tail backward,
called "Jade Maiden Ascending the Ladder";
or hanging them upside down with stones weighing down the head;
or pouring vinegar into the nose;
or placing an iron ring around the head,
adding wedges,
until some had cracked skulls and oozing brains.
Whenever prisoners were obtained,
they would first display the torture instruments to them,
causing all to tremble and sweat profusely,
confessing falsely upon seeing the methods.
"Qiān Zǎi Tōngjiàn"
Suǒ Yuánlǐ's cruelty intensified,
so Wǔ Zétiān had him arrested,
and he was executed shortly after.
People throughout the land said of him,
that his cruelty reached its peak,
and he was also the first to handle cases under the special prison system.
In the tenth month of the first year of the Zàichū era,
Zhōu Jǔ submitted a memorial admonishing:
"Recently, petty informers have made accusations,
and this has become commonplace.
The officials in charge of interrogations
all consider severity as an achievement,
fabricating charges to compete in ability,
boasting to each other about their brutality.
They seal ears and cover heads with cages,
apply cangues, crush ankles, and tighten fetters,
break ribs and insert bamboo splints under fingernails,
hang by the hair and fumigate the ears,
make prisoners lie near excrement and urine—
they show no regard for whether one can barely stay alive,
calling these methods
'prison torment'
or they restrict food for days on end,
conduct interrogations continuously through the night,
shake and disturb prisoners day and night,
preventing them from sleeping,
calling this
'protracted detention'
These people are neither wood nor stone,
and seeking temporary relief,
they falsely confess hoping to postpone death.
From his 'Original Biography'"
Wáng Hóngyì every summer month imprisoned captives,
necessarily in a small room piled mugwort,
and laid felt mattresses.
Those who encountered it,
would promptly lose consciousness.
If one falsely confessed and implicated others,
then they were moved to another room.
He and Jùnchén often issued official documents,
the prefectures and counties trembled with fear,
and he boasted himself, saying:
"My official documents,
are like wolf's bane and wild arrowroot.
《Old Book of Táng》
Guō Hóngbà once interrogated the Governor of Fāng Prefecture, Lǐ Sīzhēng,
subjecting him to torture and imprisonment,
until he succumbed and died.
During the Shènglì era,
he repeatedly saw Sīzhēng and deeply loathed it,
once, after court adjourned, he hurried home,
and ordered his family:
"Quickly invite monks to chant scriptures and hold a vegetarian feast.
Shortly after, he saw Sīzhēng leading dozens of riders into his courtyard,
saying:
"You wrongfully framed me,
now I have come for you, Bà.
Panicked and terrified,
he seized a knife and slit his own belly,
and in moments, it was infested with maggots and rotting.
That day,
the neighborhood also saw dozens of cavalrymen stationed at his gate,
but they vanished after a short while.
At that time, the Luòyáng Bridge was damaged,
causing hardship for travelers.
By this time, it was completed,
and from spring until Bà's death, there had been a severe drought,
then sufficient rain fell.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān once asked her ministers:
"Lately, what good things have happened outside?
Secretary Zhāng Yuányī, known for his wit,
replied:
"There are three celebrations outside: the first is the rain ending the drought,
the second is the new bridge's completion,
a benefit for ten thousand generations,
the third is Guō Bà's death,
which has brought joy to all the people.
The Empress laughed and said:
"Is Bà so despised?
Both "Old and New Books of Táng" record this somewhat briefly.
Attendant Censor Wàn Guójùn, who rose from the position of Clerk,
was cruel by nature,
and devoted himself to inflicting torture.
He memorialized to become an envoy to the six circuits,
executing and exiling people,
killing countless individuals.
Later, as he left the Censorate,
and reached the Tiānjīn Bridge,
to the south,
ghosts filled the road,
blocking his horse's path,
preventing him from advancing.
They cried out:
"We kowtow, spare us!"
He repeatedly groaned in agony,
then suddenly leaned against his saddle,
his tongue stretching several feet long,
his entire body turning blue and swollen.
Carried back to his residence,
he died by midnight.
The Censor Lǐ Sōng,
Lǐ Quán,
and Palace Attendant Wáng Xù
were known in the capital as the Three Leopards.
Lǐ Sōng was called the Red Leopard,
Lǐ Quán the White-browed Leopard,
and Wáng Xù the Black Leopard,
all of whom were cruel and ruthless.
Whenever they interrogated prisoners,
they would spread thorns for them to lie on,
sharpen bamboo sticks to pierce their fingers,
press square beams against their ankles,
and prop their knees with broken tiles.
They forced them to perform tricks like monkeys fetching fire, ascending wheat ropes, and descending through narrow barriers, making life unbearable,
so that the prisoners all begged for death.
The people of the capital would swear oaths to each other,
saying:
"If we betray our conscience and break our vows,
may we meet the Three Leopards.
Such was the extent of their venomous harm.
From "Qiān Zǎi"
Censor Lǐ Quánjiāo and others made entrapment their profession,
and were nicknamed in the Censorate
"Human-headed Rakshasas"
while Palace Attendant Wáng Xù was called
"Ghost-faced Yaksha"
The Emperor
Yùshǐ Wèi Jìng shàng yán yuē:
"Chén wén Guō Hóngbà zì cì ér chàng kuài,
Wàn Guójùn bèi zhē ér jù wáng,
Huò Xiànkě lín zhōng,
xī quán yú xiàng,
Lǐ Jìngrén jiāng sǐ,
shé zhì yú qí,
jiē zhòng guǐ mǎn tíng,
qún yāo héng dào.
Wéi zhēng jí yìng ruò xiǎng,
suí shēng bèi zài,
rén yáo bù wéi xū shuō.
"Táng Zhì"
The Left Historian Jiǎng Róng was upright and righteous.
When Xú Jìngyè rebelled in Yángzhōu,
Jiǎng Róng was falsely accused by the cruel officials Zhōu Xìng and others through fabricated charges,
and was executed,
beheaded in front of the Dūtíng Post Station in the Eastern Capital.
As Jiǎng Róng was about to be executed,
he requested an audience to present his case,
but Zhōu Xìng said:
"How can a prisoner present a case?"
Jiǎng Róng angrily rebuked him, saying:
"I am innocent and being wrongfully killed—
even in death, I will not let you go."
He was then beheaded,
and his corpse surged upward,
staggering over ten steps
before the executioner knocked it down.
It rose again to a sitting position,
and this happened three times
before it finally ceased.
Even with his head severed,
he seemed unrelenting in his anger.
Not long after, Zhōu Xìng died.
From "Qiān Zǎi"
Yáng Wùlián,
during the Xiàohé era, petitioned to open the Sānmén Gorge in Shǎnzhōu.
They cut through mountains and burned rocks,
building plank roads along the cliff sides to tow boats.
The river current was torrential,
and all boat trackers were ordered to fasten two hooks to their chests.
They all fell from the plank roads onto the rocks,
with not one in a hundred surviving.
Cries filled the path,
their sorrow shaking the valleys.
People all called Yáng Wùlián a human monster,
saying heaven had birthed this monster
to destroy and harm the common people.
The emperor
In the ninth year of the Kāiyuán era,
there was a Wáng Jūn who served as the commandant of Luòyáng.
In the eighteenth year,
there was a Yán Ānzhī who served as the assistant magistrate of Hénán.
Both were of a cruel and harsh nature.
When flogging people,
they feared they would not die.
After the caning was finished,
they would not allow them to rise.
They waited until the swelling caused delirium,
then slowly administered heavy blows again.
The victims wailed as blood flowed on the ground,
suffering unbearably as if wishing for death.
Only then did Jūn and Ānzhī's expressions show pleasure and satisfaction,
thus officials and people were terrified of them.
"Old Book of Táng": The Emperor ascended the Five Phoenix Tower,
attending a feast to watch the performances.
The crowd was so dense that the music could not be played.
The Golden Guard's shouted commands were ineffective in restraining them,
and the Emperor was troubled by this.
Gāo Lìshì memorialized that Hénán Assistant Magistrate Yán Ānzhī was handling the matter,
as Yán was feared by the people.
He requested to send him to stop it,
and the Emperor consented.
Ānzhī used his hand tablet to draw a line on the ground around the venue,
saying:
"Those who cross this shall die."
Thus for three full days,
people pointed at his line,
warning each other,
and none dared to cross it.
"Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government - Xuánzōng Chapter"
Jí Wēn's nature was severe,
and he indeed harmed others in the prosecution of Lǐ Línfǔ,
intending to initiate criminal cases,
eliminating those who did not align with him by drawing them into his sphere,
and collaborated with Luó Xīshì in fabricating charges.
At that time, the imperial prisons were called "Luó's Pliers and Jí's Nets,"
a reflection of the hatred for their harshness and severity.
(Old Book of Táng)
When Jí Wēn was investigating Yáng Shènjīn, the Attendant Censor Lú Xuàn,
was involved in the case.
Xuàn had previously served in the same bureau as Zhāng Xuān,
and their relationship had always been close.
However, to curry favor with powerful officials,
he falsely accused Xuān of conspiring with Yáng Shènjīn to interpret prophetic texts,
using them as leverage like a donkey foal,
and fabricating evidence to secure a conviction.
Later, when Xuàn was demoted to the position of Chief Clerk of Lújiāng,
he suddenly saw Xuān's vengeful spirit in the commandery,
and exclaimed:
"Why have you come, Your Honor?"
Begging for his life but unable to control his fate,
Xuàn died moments later.
The emperor...
Jìng Yǔ served as Investigating Censor during Sùzōng's reign,
and was entrusted with duties due to his harshness.
He created large cangues with a newly made "turtle" and "elm tail" device,
which would cause suffocation once worn;
he would also lay prisoners on the ground,
rolling a door bolt over their bellies,
calling this "meat dumplings";
he would dig pits in the ground,
filling them with thorns and covering them with worn mats,
placing them over the pits;
when interrogating prisoners near the pits,
they would inevitably fall in,
pierced by thousands of thorns.
When the subsequent Prince of Xuē, Zhēn, secretly plotted rebellion,
an imperial decree ordered Yǔ to interrogate him.
Yǔ summoned the accomplices and lined them up in the courtyard,
demanding the "turtle-elm" cangues to shackle them,
spreading them out for torture and interrogation,
completely surrounding them with it,
and within two nights completed the judicial case,
with Zhēn sentenced to death.
The Emperor
Jìng Yǔ and Máo Ruòxū served in the Censorate,
Ruòxū's eyebrows hung over his eyes,
and his nature was cruel.
For five or six years,
the Censorate's prisons were never empty.
There were also Péi Shēng and Bì Yào, both Censors,
all of them vicious and ruthless.
People fell victim to their punishments,
and at that time there was
the saying "Máo, Jìng, Péi, Bì"
to refer to them.
Péi and Bì were soon exiled to Qiánzhōng.
As for Yǔ,
in the first year of the Bǎoyìng era,
he was demoted to Prefect of Dàozhōu.
Soon an edict was issued for his execution.
The Emperor
When Emperor Sùzōng recaptured the two capitals,
Cuī Qì served as the Commissioner of the Three Judicial Offices.
He was harsh by nature and delighted in others' misfortunes,
being secretly cruel and lacking kindness.
He pandered to the emperor's wishes with strict legal interpretations,
memorializing that hundreds of officials who had surrendered to the rebels, such as Chén Xīliè and Dáxī Xún,
all deserved death.
Lǐ Xiàn firmly memorialized against this,
so they were instead sentenced according to six levels of punishment.
Later, Cuī Qì became the Censor-in-Chief.
In the first year of the Shàngyuán era, he fell ill,
his feet swelling for over a month and gradually worsening.
Whenever he closed his eyes, he would see Dáxī Xún,
and would only repeatedly kowtow, saying:
"The Governor has no choice."
When his attendants asked him about it,
after a long time he replied:
"Governor Dáxī is appealing his injustice and demanding it from me."
This continued for three months without stopping until he died.
"Tán Bīn Lù"
During the Jiànzhōng era,
Lǐ Xīliè attacked Biànzhōu,
before the city fell.
He drove commoners' women and baggage trains,
to fill the moats,
calling it "wet filling."
"Records and Accounts"
The people of Xiāngyáng excel at making lacquerware,
which is emulated throughout the land,
and called the Xiāngyáng style.
When Minister of Works Yú served as military governor and was exceedingly cruel,
and Zhèng Yuán, governing Hézhōng, was also cruel,
people near and far called them the Xiānglù military governors.
"Supplement to the National History"
Wáng Yuè served as the garrison commander of Zhōuzhì Town.
When soldiers committed offenses,
he ordered them to be caned and cangued,
and the cangue was only removed after a hundred days.
There were three exceptions where it could be removed before the hundred days:
if I die, it is removed;
if you die, it is removed;
if there is an imperial decree, it is removed.
As a result, not the slightest offense was committed.
Earlier, Wáng Yuè served as the magistrate of Tángchāng,
and he unjustly executed the clerk Lǐ Zhī.
After Lǐ Zhī died,
his eldest son, speaking as a spirit, said:
"Wáng Yuè is unrighteous;
he wrongfully killed my father,
and I will surely take revenge."
His voice was very fierce.
After several days,
while Wáng Yuè was sitting in the hall during the day,
he was suddenly punched in the waist.
The sound was heavy,
but when he looked around in shock, there was no one.
When evening came,
the spot where he was hit swelled up
and became painful.
On that day, Lǐ Zhī's son spoke again, saying:
"I have already struck Wáng Yuè,
hitting him right in a vital spot,
and I will soon kill him."
Wáng Yuè's condition worsened severely,
so he went to Shǔ Commandery to seek medical treatment,
but he did not recover.
The day before he died,
Lǐ Zhī ordered his family to prepare a meal for several people,
and then said:
"I and three others are going to Shǔ Commandery
to take Wáng Yuè's life;
after we finish eating, we will set out."
The next day, Wáng Yuè died,
and the swollen, festering spot on his body was exactly on his right kidney,
which was the work of Lǐ Zhī.
"Records of Hearsay"
Shǔ Lǐ Kuāngyuǎn served as the Director of the Court of the Imperial Treasury,
and was by nature harsh and cruel.
If even one day passed without carrying out punishments, he would feel miserable and unhappy.
He often heard the sounds of flogging and caning,
and would say to people:
"This is my orchestra of flesh and blood."
On his deathbed, he said:
"In my lifetime, I have killed dozens of Buddhist monks and Daoist priests,
and for this I have enjoyed a lifespan of eighty-two years."
When he was buried,
grave robbers dug up his tomb,
cut off his four limbs,
which was the retribution for his cruel punishments.
From "The Outer History of Táowù."
Liú Shū,
during the reign of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Hàn dynasty, served as the military commissioner of Yǒngxīng Army,
and his application of laws was inherently harsh and severe.
When commoners committed offenses,
he would ask them how old they were.
Upon their reply of a certain age,
he would immediately administer that number of cane strokes accordingly,
calling it the "age-corresponding cane";
each person was invariably struck with two canes simultaneously,
termed the "double-joy cane."
He also increased the land rent per mǔ for the people,
demanding thirty coins for public use,
making the populace unable to endure it.
"History of the Five Dynasties"
Qián Wéijì,
styled Yánfū.
During Emperor Rénzōng's reign, he served as the prefect of Dìngzhōu.
There was a woman who had been wronged,
whose husband was so unkind as to burn her arm with heated copper and iron.
Wéijì took the woman's newborn child and placed it in the snow,
then shackled the woman and forced her to watch.
Seeing the child die in such a cruel manner,
his harsh methods often resembled this.
"History of the Sòng Dynasty"
Hán Zhěn,
courtesy name Yùrǔ,
served as the prefect of Qínzhōu during Emperor Shénzōng's reign.
Once while returning late at night from a banquet,
his subordinate Chuán Qíng was drunk,
and mistakenly followed him into the prefectural residence,
where he encountered a concubine.
Furious,
Hán Zhěn ordered soldiers to beat him to death with iron-wrapped clubs.
Qíng's wife, holding his blood-stained clothes,
beat the grievance drum at the palace to appeal,
resulting in Hán Zhěn's dismissal from office,
and reassignment to the auxiliary staff in the southern capital.
The people of Qínzhōu said:
"Better to meet a nursing tigress,
than to encounter Yùrǔ.
Lǐ Jì,
styled Chángqīng,
served as the Transport Commissioner of Shǎnxī during Emperor Shénzōng's reign.
When the people of Qín built houses along the roadside,
he initiated a policy requiring them to pay fees for encroaching on the street,
causing disturbances and resentment throughout the circuit.
Both he and Lǐ Chá were notorious for their harshness and cruelty.
People at the time said:
"Better to encounter the Black Killer,
than to meet Jì and Chá.
Zhāng Sǒng drafted a memorial for Liú Jiā, stating:
"Upon hearing of Liú Chóng's rebellion today,
all wished to lift their robes, grasp their swords, and curse him;
those who arrived first
would slash his neck,
pierce his chest,
cut his body,
and slice his flesh;
those arriving later
wanted to tear down his gates,
topple his walls,
level his house,
and burn his vessels.
He would fall to the ground at their cries,
immediately covered with wounds.
The ancestral temple was especially severe,
speaking of him with gnashing teeth.
Why? Because he betrayed kindness and righteousness,
and knew not where true virtue lies."
《History of Wáng Mǎng》 Guō Bà was first summoned for an audience before Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
where he proclaimed his loyalty:
"During the campaign against Xú Jìngyè last year,
I wished to pull out his sinews,
eat his flesh,
drink his blood,
and suck his marrow."
Wǔ Zétiān was pleased,
and appointed him Palace Censor,
earning him the contemporary nickname
"Four-His Censor"
《Old Book of Táng》
When Hé Shìkāi's mother passed away,
those who relied on his favor all went to mourn and weep.
Wealthy merchants from Yèzhōng such as Dīng Zōu and Yán Xìng, among others, all acted as dutiful mourners,
and there was also a scholar among those weeping.
Fèng Xiàoyǎn entered to offer condolences,
and upon leaving, said to others:
"To the south of Yán Xìng,
and north of Dīng Zōu,
there was a court official wailing very mournfully,
which those who heard spread to Hé Shìkāi."
Hé Shìkāi, upon learning of this, became extremely angry.
(From History of the Northern Dynasties)
Hé Shìkāi was in power,
and many people flattered him.
There was a man named Cān,
who, when Hé Shìkāi fell ill,
was told by the doctor that he needed to take huánglóng soup.
Hé Shìkāi showed a reluctant expression,
so Cān said:
"This soup is very easy to take,
Your Highness need not doubt it.
Allow me to taste it first."
He drank it all in one go.
Hé Shìkāi was deeply moved by his gesture,
and forced himself to take the medicine.
He then broke into a sweat,
and recovered from his illness.
From "Continued Tales of the World".
Zhào Yuánkǎi served as the Grand Commander of the Jiaozhou Route Campaign,
while Hóu Jūnjí was the field marshal.
Hóu Jūnjí's horse suffered from a festering forehead sore,
and Zhào Yuánkǎi dipped his finger in the pus and sniffed it,
flattering Hóu Jūnjí.
He was impeached by the censor,
and demoted to Prefect of Kuòzhōu.
"Tán Bīn Lù"
Emperor Tàizōng once pointed at a tree and said,
"This is a fine tree."
Yǔwén Shìjí immediately followed with endless praise.
Emperor Tàizōng sternly told him:
"Wèi Zhēng once advised me to keep away from flatterers,
but I didn't realize who the flatterers were.
I've often suspected it might be you but wasn't certain—
now I see it's indeed true."
Shìjí kowtowed and apologized, saying:
"The officials at the southern administrative offices
often oppose Your Majesty in court discussions,
and you frequently cannot act as you wish.
Now that I'm fortunate to serve by your side,
if I don't show some compliance,
even as the exalted Son of Heaven,
what pleasure would you have?"
Emperor Tàizōng's anger then subsided.
From "New Accounts of the Great Táng"
Empress Wǔ fell ill,
and an edict was issued to offer sacrifices at all temples,
to pray for blessings and avert disasters.
Yán Cháoyǐn went to Shàoshì Mountain,
then serving as a Supervising Secretary,
personally composed a prayer offering himself as a substitute for the sacrifice,
bathed and prostrated himself on the sacrificial platter,
ordering monks and Taoists to carry him to the deity's altar,
with onlookers crowding like walls.
Coinciding with the Empress's recovery,
he was specially rewarded.
Left Department Director Zhāng Yuānyī painted a portrait of the human sacrifice and presented it,
at which the Empress laughed heartily,
and though she bestowed generous gifts,
she still despised his character.
"Yì Zhāi's Forest of Laughter"
Guō Hóngbà was promoted again to Right Censor-in-Chief,
when Grand Master Wèi Yuánzhōng fell ill,
his subordinates visited to inquire after his health.
Hóngbà alone entered last,
with a worried expression on his face,
requested to see his urine,
then dipped his finger to taste it,
to test the severity of the illness,
and congratulated him, saying:
"If it were sweet, the illness would not be cured,
but now it tastes bitter,
so it should soon heal,
I am overjoyed."
Yuánzhōng detested his flattery,
and exposed his words in court.
"Old Book of Tang"
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
Zhāng Jí flattered Preceptor Xuē,
holding up a yellow turban while following him,
and later knelt beside the horse to serve as his mounting block.
Censor Guō Bà once tasted Lái Jùnchén's excrement,
while Sòng Zhīwèn carried Zhāng Yìzhī's chamber pot.
All these acts were fawning servility to gain favor,
making them truly criminals against moral principles.
From "Qiān Zǎi"
Crown Prince's Junior Guardian Xuē Jì, Governor of Yōngzhōu Lǐ Jìn, Secretariat Directors Cuī Shí, Xiāo Zhìzhōng, and Cén Xī, among others, all outwardly displayed loyalty and integrity,
yet inwardly harbored flattery and sycophancy.
They hunched their shoulders, held their breath, licking ulcers and breaking limbs,
fawningly attaching themselves to Princess Tàipíng.
On the third day of the tenth month, their families were destroyed and they themselves were executed.
The Emperor
Zhào Lǚwēn served as Minister of Agriculture,
exploiting powerful clans for salary payments,
flattering those in power like licking ulcers,
fawning upon Princess Ānlè,
seizing commoners' farmlands for the princess,
constructing the Dìngkūn Pond,
claiming it would rival the Son of Heaven's Kūnmíng Pond,
expending countless millions in treasury funds.
With his purple robe slanted askew,
he personally pulled the princess's golden calf-drawn carriage.
Such were his treacherous deeds.
During the suppression of the rebellious Wéi faction,
as the Emperor ascended Chéngtiān Gate,
Lǚwēn feigned elation,
dancing and proclaiming "Long live the Emperor!"
The Emperor ordered his execution,
where blades rained down upon him,
slain alongside his son.
Each person carved a slice of his flesh,
until bones and flesh were utterly consumed.
The Emperor
Zhāng Yuè previously served as the Governor of Bìngzhōu,
flattering the Special Advanced Official Wáng Máozhòng,
and presented him with countless gold and treasures.
Later, when Máozhòng was inspecting the border,
he happened to meet Yuè at a grand banquet of the Tiānxióng Army.
As the wine flowed freely,
an imperial edict suddenly arrived,
appointing Yuè as the Minister of War,
concurrently holding the position of Vice Director of the Secretariat-Chancellery.
After Yuè bowed in gratitude,
he immediately took Máozhòng's hand and began to dance,
even sniffing the tip of his boot.
The emperor
General Gāo Lìshì enjoyed special favor from Emperor Xuánzōng,
and when his mother passed away,
the Left Golden Guard General Chéng Bóxiàn and the Shaofu Supervisor Féng Shàozhèng
went directly before Gāo Lìshì's mother's coffin, disheveled their hair, and wept,
more intensely than for their own relatives.
When this became known in court and among the people,
it provoked considerable ridicule.
The emperor
Chéng Jìngqí served as the Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
and was related by marriage to Yáo Chóng.
When Chóng once fell ill,
Jìngqí visited his residence to inquire after his health.
Facing Chóng, he wept,
having placed several live sparrows in his bosom.
He then took them out one by one,
requesting Chóng to hold them before releasing them.
He prayed, saying:
"May Your Excellency recover swiftly."
Chóng reluctantly complied.
After Jìngqí left,
Chóng detested his flattery and sycophancy.
He said to his family members:
"Where did these tears even come from?"
From then on, he no longer received or treated him.
"Records of the Censorate from the New Account of Tales of the Tang"
Dòu Huáizhēn used flattery to gain advancement,
progressing through promotions to become the Chief Clerk of Jìnzhōu,
currying favor with influential eunuchs,
and winning all of their favor.
Wéi Shùrén's wet nurse Wáng shì was originally a barbarian slave girl,
yet Huáizhēn married her,
and she was enfeoffed as the Lady of Jǔ.
It was customary to call the husband of a wet nurse "ā zhē".
Whenever Huáizhēn attended an audience,
or submitted memorials and reports,
he listed his official rank,
signing it as
"the ā zhē of the Sage-Assisting Empress"
People of the time despised him for this,
calling him
"zhē"
yet Huáizhēn was pleased with this designation.
When Wéi Shùrén fell from power,
he beheaded his wife,
and presented her head as an offering.
While serving in the Censorate and as Capital Governor, whenever he handled official matters,
if he saw someone without a beard,
he would mistakenly take them for a eunuch,
and would invariably bend over backwards to accommodate them.
There were even cases of scholars without beards
whom Huáizhēn mistakenly showed such courtesy to.
When Ruìzōng ascended the throne,
Huáizhēn reached the highest rank among officials,
yet he persisted in flattery and did not reform,
leading to his exile and demotion.
During the Guāngtiān era,
when Xuánzōng suppressed internal strife,
Huáizhēn drowned himself.
"Táng Xīn Yǔ"
During the reign of Emperor Jìngzōng,
Lǐ Féngjí held power and acted out of personal resentment.
When Páng Yán was exiled to a distant post, Wéi Ào, serving as a supervising secretary,
returned the imperial edict unopened.
At the time, people believed he had provoked the chancellor's anger
to defend a friend's injustice,
considering his benevolence profound.
When the memorial of rebuttal was issued,
it turned out to be a criticism of the exile.
Páng Yán had greatly underestimated both court and public opinion,
and everyone laughed heartily at Wéi Ào,
who was promptly promoted to vice minister of works.
"Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance"
Dù Bīngōng governed Yángzhōu,
indulging in excursions and feasts.
Emperor Xuānzong appointed Cuī Xuàn as his replacement,
and sent him off with a poem that read:
"In one region, the prison market gains revival,
Yángzhōu's constable Chuán Xīwén."
The imperial poem prompted the training of a Láisū team dance to welcome Lord Cuī.
Dù bore a grudge over this,
so when he returned to Luòyáng,
whenever he met people from Wéiyáng,
he would invariably ask:
"Is Láisū doing well?"
referring to Chuán Xī.
From "Jīnhuázǐ"
During the Dàlì era,
in Jīngzhōu, there was a man named Féng Xīlè who was skilled at flattery,
and would flatter even upon seeing a mouse hole.
He once went to Chánglín to visit the county magistrate,
and during the banquet, he said to the magistrate:
"Moved by your benevolent influence,
fierce beasts have left the territory.
When I first entered the county border yesterday,
tigers and wolves trailed one another westward."
Just then, a village official from Xiàng Village came to report
that a tiger had killed a person the previous night.
The magistrate jokingly questioned him about it.
Féng promptly replied:
"It must have just snatched a meal in passing.
Wéi Jiān's Guangyun Pond was completed,
Shǎnxiàn County Lieutenant Cuī Chéngfǔ composed the "Treasure Song Lyrics":
"White robes with missing lapels and green shirts,
brocade half-sleeves,
bared shoulders,
red silk headbands."
From the first boat, he acted as the lead singer chanting it,
with over a hundred women joining in chorus.
Continued Accounts of the World
The Secretariat's Registrar Huá Huàn had connections with the court eunuch in charge of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Liú Guāngqí.
When the chancellors' discussions differed from Guāngqí's views,
he would order Huàn to convey his intentions,
and they never failed to achieve what he desired.
Chancellors Dù Yòu and Zhèng Yīn both indulged him,
with Yòu even calling him Huá the Eighth.
The Emperor...
Cuī Yuánluè was appointed as Vice Minister of Revenue,
through imperial appointment.
At that time, a supervising official submitted a memorial pointing out that the eunuch Cuī Tánjùn currently held power and favor,
and Yuánluè served him as if he were his paternal uncle.
Yuánluè submitted a memorial to defend himself,
and the Emperor replied in an edict:
"The officials I appoint,
why should they fear others' words?
Yet in the end, you cannot escape the reputation of serving a eunuch as your father."
The Emperor
Lǐ Fǔguó's power was at its peak,
and the chancellor Lǐ Kuí,
a prominent clan from Shāndōng,
who held a high position in the court,
greeted Fǔguó with the courtesy of a junior to a senior,
calling him "Fifth Father."
The Emperor
Sū Xún,
when Zhuāngzōng was about to ascend the throne,
Zhāng Chéngyè was unwilling,
Zhuāngzōng hastily assumed the imperial title,
and no one dared to support it.
Xún came from Hézhōng,
entered the government compound,
and upon seeing the administrative office, immediately bowed,
calling it "worshipping the hall."
Upon seeing Zhuāngzōng, he shouted "Long live the Emperor,"
danced with joy, wept, and declared himself a subject.
The next day,
he presented thirty large brushes,
calling them "brushes for painting the sun."
Zhuāngzōng was greatly pleased,
while Chéngyè deeply detested him.
The emperor
Zhōng Chuán rose from being a merchant,
and particularly esteemed the scholar Zhūgě Hào.
Consequently, he selected ten of his most illustrious deeds,
composed them in a petition to present to him,
calling it
"The Petition of Ten Virtues,"
totaling five thousand characters.
Chuán was astonished and admiring,
rewarding each character with one thousand coins,
amounting to five thousand strings of cash.
From "Supplementary Records of the Five Dynasties"
During the Jiāyòu era,
there was a man named Wáng Yǒngnián,
who married a woman from the imperial clan,
and sought recommendations from Dòu Biàn and Yáng Huì,
obtaining the position of supervising the Golden Radiance Gate book repository.
Wáng Yǒngnián once hosted a banquet to entertain Biàn,
with Huì bringing his wife to sit in a private chamber.
The wife scooped wine with both hands to drink,
and Biàn and Huì called them white jade lotus cups.
When Hán Tuózhòu was in power,
on his birthday Gāo Sìsūn presented nine odes,
each ode containing the character "xī" (bestowal).
Xīn Qìjí praised his military campaigns in a lyric,
using the historical precedent of Sīmǎ Zhāo borrowing the yellow battle-axe
and becoming a non-imperial surname's true king.
History of Song
When Jiǎ Sìdào held the reins of state and reduced grain transport,
Zhū Jùn would always address his memorials reporting matters
with the phrase "ten thousand bows."
For this reason, contemporaries called him Zhū Wànbài (Zhū Ten Thousand Bows).
Jùn
was the great-grandson of Master Huì (Zhū Xī).
"Sū's Notes"
Zēngzǐ said to Zǐsī:
"In the past when I followed the Master on his inspection tours,
visiting the feudal lords,
he never failed in the rituals befitting a minister,
yet the Way of the Sage still did not prevail.
Now I observe that you have a heart that scorns the lords of the age,
is this not likely to make you unacceptable?"
Zǐsī replied:
"Times change and the world differs,
and people must adapt accordingly.
In the time of our former lord, though the Zhou institutions were decaying,
rulers and ministers maintained their proper positions,
and high and low supported each other as one body.
If one wished to implement his Way,
without upholding ritual to seek it,
he could not gain entry.
Now the feudal lords throughout the land are eager to contend by force,
competing to summon heroic men to serve as their wings.
This is an era where
gaining scholars leads to prosperity,
and losing them leads to ruin.
At this time, if I, Jí,
do not hold myself high,
others will lower me;
if I do not value myself,
others will despise me.
Shun and Yǔ achieved through abdication,
while Tāng and Wǔ resorted to arms -
this was not because they deliberately contradicted each other,
but because each responded to their own time."
The Congregated Sayings of the Kong Family
Tiánzǐfāng went to Wèi,
where the crown prince of Wèi, accompanied by a hundred chariots, welcomed him in the suburbs.
The crown prince bowed twice in greeting to Tiánzǐfāng,
but Tiánzǐfāng did not descend from his carriage.
The crown prince was displeased,
and said:
"May I ask under what circumstances one may act arrogantly toward others?
Tiánzǐfāng replied:
"I have heard that there are those who,
acting arrogantly toward others while possessing the entire realm, have perished.
There are also those who,
acting arrogantly toward others while ruling a single state, have perished.
From this perspective,
it is the poor and humble who can afford to be arrogant toward others.
For if one's aspirations are not met,
one can simply put on one's sandals and go to Qín or Chǔ—
where can one go and not find poverty and lowliness?
Thereupon, the crown prince bowed twice and then withdrew.
Tiánzǐfāng thus did not descend from his carriage.
"Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn"
Zhào Yī,
courtesy name Yuánshū,
was arrogant due to his talent,
and was rejected by his hometown.
In the first year of the Guānghé era,
he was recommended as a commandery accountant and arrived at the capital.
At that time, Minister over the Masses Yuán Féng was receiving the accounts,
and several hundred accounting officials all knelt and prostrated in the courtyard,
none daring to look up.
Only Yī made a deep bow with his hands clasped.
Féng saw this and found it unusual,
ordering his attendants to go and reprimand him,
saying:
"As a lowly commandery accountant, why do you only bow to the Three Excellencies?"
Yī replied:
"In the past, Lì Yìjī made a deep bow to the King of Hàn;
now I bow to the Three Excellencies—
why is it so strange?"
Féng then straightened his garments and descended the hall,
taking his hand and inviting him to the seat of honor.
He then asked about affairs in the western regions,
and was greatly pleased.
Turning to those seated, he said:
"This is Zhào Yuánshū of Hànyáng.
No court official surpasses him;
I beg to share my seat with him for all of you."
All those seated turned to look.
Book of the Later Hàn
On the Morning of the Tenth Month, Huáng Zǔ held a grand banquet for guests on a méngchōng warship,
where millet and meat broth were served.
Mí Héng, being young, was among the attendees.
When the millet and broth arrived,
Héng first ate his fill without regard for the other guests,
only lifting and playing with the food.
At that time, Zhāng Bóyún of Jiāngxià was also present,
and teased him, saying:
"According to the rites, 'Why do you eat like this?'
Zhèngpíng did not reply,
continuing to play with the millet as before.
Zǔ said:
"A scholar should not fail to answer him.
Héng said to Zǔ:
"A gentleman would rather hear the sound of a carriage or horse's hoofbeats.
Zǔ scolded him,
and Héng stared intently at Zǔ,
cursing:
"You dead metalworker.
Zǔ became enraged,
ordered the attendants to take him out,
and intended to cane him.
But Héng did not stop cursing,
so Zǔ ordered him to be strangled.
Huáng Shè came to rescue him,
but it was too late to do anything,
and he wept sorrowfully, saying:
"This man had extraordinary talent;
Cáo Cāo and Liú Biǎo did not kill him,
so why did you, sir, kill him?
Zǔ said:
"He cursed your father as a metalworker;
how could I not kill him?
Bié Zhuàn: The version by Fàn records it as "dead man" and mentions a certain Dào.
Zhāng Fēi once stayed at Liú Bā's place overnight,
but Bā did not speak with him,
which made Fēi extremely angry.
Zhūgě Liàng said to Bā:
"Although Zhāng Fēi is indeed a military man,
he respects and admires you.
Our lord is currently gathering both civil and military talents
to accomplish great deeds.
Although you are naturally noble and upright,
you should lower your pride a little."
Bā replied:
"A true man in this world
should associate with heroes from all corners,
how can I converse with a mere soldier?"
General Fǔ Wú Zhāng Zhāo once discussed Bā with Sūn Quán,
criticizing him for being too narrow-minded
and for rejecting Zhāng Fēi too harshly.
Quán said:
"If we make Zǐchū follow worldly conventions
and ingratiate himself with Xuándé by associating with inappropriate people,
how could he be called a noble scholar?"
"Records of Former Worthies of Línglíng"
Jiǎn Yōng,
courtesy name Xiàn Hé,
had been friends with the Former Sovereign since youth,
and followed him through his campaigns, serving as General of Manifest Virtue.
Carefree in demeanor and bearing,
he was by nature unrestrained and unconventional.
Even in the Former Sovereign's presence,
he would sit sprawled and leaning,
showing no solemn dignity,
simply indulging his comfort.
Below Zhūgě Liàng and others,
he alone occupied a couch,
resting his head on it while reclining and speaking,
yielding to no one.
"Records of Shu"
Zhòng Shìjì, being exceptionally talented and rational,
had not previously known Jī Kāng.
Zhòng invited the worthy and outstanding scholars of the time,
and together they went to visit Kāng.
Kāng was forging under a large tree,
with Xiàng Zǐqī assisting by operating the bellows.
Kāng continued to swing his hammer without pause,
acting as if no one was around,
and for a long while, not a word was exchanged.
Zhòng rose to leave,
and Kāng said:
"What did you hear that brought you here,
and what did you see that makes you leave?"
Zhòng replied:
"I heard what I heard and came,
and saw what I saw and left."
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World."
Jī Kāng and Lǚ Ān were close friends.
Whenever they longed for each other,
they would order their carriages for a thousand-mile journey.
Later, when Ān came to visit,
he found Kāng was not home.
Jī Xī came out to invite him in,
but Ān did not enter.
Instead, he wrote on the gate
the character
"phoenix"
and left.
Xī did not realize
that he was actually pleased,
thinking the character
"phoenix"
was merely
a
"bird."
Earlier, when Ān had followed Kāng or encountered him on his way, Kāng's elder brother Xī would wipe the mat to wait for him, but Ān paid him no heed,
sitting alone in his carriage.
Kāng's mother then set out wine and food,
