asking Kāng's son to converse with him,
and after joking for a long while, he left.
Such was his disregard for the noble.
From Gān Bǎo's "Jìn Jì"
Sūn Chǔ,
courtesy name Zǐjīng,
possessed extraordinary literary talent,
was forthright and unconventional,
often arrogant and domineering,
lacking reputation among his fellow villagers.
Later, he joined Shí Bāo's staff as a cavalry military advisor.
Sūn Chǔ, relying on his own talent and spirit, often belittled and disrespected Shí Bāo.
Upon first arriving, he gave a casual bow and said:
"The Son of Heaven ordered me to join your military staff,
thus creating discord.
It was then alleged that the new military advisor showed disrespect to his superior.
Since Sūn Chǔ looked down upon Shí Bāo,
it was established that showing respect should begin with Sūn Chǔ."
Book of Jin
Wáng Zǐyóu served as Cavalry Adjutant under Huán Chōng,
with disheveled hair and loose sash,
never attending to official matters.
Huán asked him:
"Which bureau are you in charge of?"
He replied:
"I don't know which bureau."
Sometimes seeing horses being led,
it seemed to be the Horse Department,
Huán asked again:
"How many horses does your office have?"
He replied:
"I don't ask about the horses,
how would I know their number?"
Huán asked again:
"How many horses have died recently?"
He replied:
"I don't even know about the living ones,
how would I know about the dead?"
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Grand Administrator Mèng Yǐ served the Buddha,
with utmost sincerity and diligence.
He was looked down upon by Xiè Língyùn,
who once said to Yǐ:
"Attaining the Way requires wisdom and karma,
you, sir, will ascend to heaven before Língyùn,
but achieve Buddhahood surely after Língyùn."
Yǐ deeply resented these words.
On another occasion, Xiè went with Wáng Hóngzhī and others to drink at Qiānqiū Pavilion,
stripped naked and shouted loudly,
which Yǐ found utterly intolerable,
so he sent a messenger to question him.
Língyùn flew into a rage and said:
"I shout naked of my own accord,
what business is it of yours, you fool?"
History of the Southern Dynasties
Xiè Chāozōng served as the Central Army Marshal for the Prince of Nánjùn.
Someone asked him:
"We've heard there's a court appointment—which office is it for?"
Chāozōng replied resentfully:
"I don't know if it's Marshal (Sīmǎ),
or Donkey Manager (Sīlǘ).
Since it's a donkey office,
it should indeed be Donkey Manager."
Because officials reported this,
he was dismissed for his resentment,
and confined for ten years.
The Emperor
Zhāng Fū, at the beginning of the Yongchū era, was promoted to the position of Secretary Lang,
and once while on duty in the department,
the Secretariat Director Fù Liàng, a respected senior with powerful authority,
heard of his dedication to learning,
and went to visit him.
Fū, lying down, did not rise immediately,
which Liàng found strange, and he left.
"History of the Song Dynasty"
Jiāngxià King Líu Yìgōng requested a learned monk from Emperor Wén,
just as Zhāng Fū was returning from leave to Jiānglíng,
and went to take his leave.
Emperor Wén ordered him to take the monk in his carriage,
saying:
"You may converse on the way.
But Fū declined the command, saying:
"Your servant's nature cannot bear company.
The Emperor was greatly displeased.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Wáng Róng was temporarily returning to his hometown,
and went to bid farewell to Wáng Qiǎn.
Qiǎn stood in that place,
lifting his sleeve without advancing.
Róng also raised his hand and called out to Qiǎn, saying:
"Chù says, 'The king should come forward.'
Qiǎn had no choice but to hurry over to him.
Róng said:
"If I, Róng, am not seen as admiring power,
and make you, sir, become one who hastens to scholars,
wouldn't that be excellent?
He often sighed, saying:
"I do not regret that I cannot see the ancients,
but regret that the ancients cannot see me.
Róng was on good terms with the Minister of Personnel Hé Jì,
and went to visit Jì,
but mistakenly went to the residence of the Minister Liú Chéng.
After getting off the carriage and entering the gate,
he said:
"This is not it.
Reaching the door and looking at Chéng,
he said again:
"This is not it.
After arriving at the mat and facing Chéng,
he said:
"None of this is right.
Then he left.
His eccentric behavior was like this.
End
Wáng Shàn,
courtesy name Míngyuǎn,
was arrogant and unconventional in character,
fond of criticizing and judging others.
He served as a military advisor to a prince's household in the Sòng dynasty.
Once, while visiting Liú Yànjié,
he directly climbed onto the couch and said:
"Your Lordship is a descendant of a duke,
and I am a son of a noble house.
Filling our cups and sitting knee to knee,
there are only us two here."
Yànjié was displeased.
From "Continued Accounts of the World"
Huángménláng Lù Qióngzhī,
the brother of the Empress Dowager,
was the grandson of Lù Qìngzhī.
He was a neighbor of Wáng Sēngdá,
and dressed splendidly to visit Sēngdá.
Sēngdá did not speak with him,
and said:
"The distinguished scholar Lù Qìngzhī, who used to be under my tutelage,
what relation is he to you?"
He then
burned the bed on which Qióngzhī was sitting.
The Empress Dowager was angry,
and tearfully complained to Empress Xiàowǔ.
The Emperor said:
"Qióngzhī is young,
and had no business visiting Wáng Sēngdá.
It is only fitting that he was insulted."
Shàng
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn prided himself on his talent and spirit,
serving as Minister of Personnel.
When he saw guests from various schools of thought,
he would not engage in conversation with them,
merely raising his fan in a slight wave,
which secretly incited resentment among the officials.
The Emperor
Biàn Yánzhī served as the magistrate of Shàngyú
and possessed an unyielding temperament.
The governor of Kuàijī, Mèng Yán, treated him with the authority of a superior,
which Biàn Yánzhī could no longer endure over time.
He removed his official headdress and threw it to the ground,
saying:
"The reason I have humbled myself
is solely for the sake of this headdress.
Now I have cast it before you.
You, relying on your family's single generation of merit,
look down upon the talented scholars of the realm.
Then he brushed his sleeves and departed.
The aforementioned Yánzhī
was the father of Biàn Bīn.
The "Continued Account of the World" records it as Bīn,
which is an error.
Zhū Yì looked down upon and was arrogant towards the court worthies,
not avoiding the noble relatives.
Some people admonished him,
to which Yì said:
"I am a scholar of humble origins,
who has encountered opportunities to reach this day.
All the nobles rely on their ancestors' bones to look down on me;
if I humble myself, the contempt will be even worse.
That is why I take the initiative.
The Emperor
Liú Xiàochuò relied on his spirit and bore his talent,
often being arrogant and dismissive.
Whenever at court gatherings,
he would have nothing to say among the assembled dukes and ministers,
but instead called to the grooms,
inquiring about matters on the roads.
The emperor
Wúxīng's Wú Guī possessed considerable talent and learning.
Shàolíng Prince Xiāo Lún engaged him as a guest,
treating him with profound respect.
When Lún was appointed regional inspector of Yǐng Province,
Guī accompanied him to Jiāngxià.
They encountered Zhāng Zuǎn, who was departing for Xiāng Province,
passing through the Yǐng region,
where Lún held a farewell banquet for him at Nánpǔ.
Zuǎn noticed Guī seated at the banquet,
and felt deeply displeased,
suddenly raising his cup to say:
"Wú Guī,
you are fortunate to accompany this banquet with this wine."
Guī soon returned home.
His son Wēngrú, seeing his father's displeasure,
inquired and learned the reason,
whereupon Wēngrú became choked with anger,
and died that very night.
Guī resented Zuǎn's causing his son's death,
grief and rage overwhelming him,
and within a few days he too passed away.
Guī's wife deeply mourned her husband and son,
and the following day she also died.
Contemporaries said Zhāng Zuǎn killed three members of the Wú family with one cup of wine.
His contemptuous arrogance was consistently of this nature.
Bào Quán served as a Gentleman Cavalier Attendant,
and once rode in a tall, enclosed carriage,
followed by several tens of parasols,
with his attire and ornaments being extremely exquisite.
On the road, he encountered the Director of the Imperial Academy, Wáng Chéng,
who suspected he was not of established nobility,
and sent someone to inquire.
Bào Quán's attendant replied:
"It is Gentleman Cavalier Attendant Bào." Chéng found it strange.
Wishing to insult him further,
he sent someone to press close to the carriage and ask:
"Gentleman Cavalier Attendant Bào,
what kind of person is he,
that he can have such extravagance?"
The young men of the capital then took this as a catchphrase,
and whenever they saw someone fond of luxury,
they would tease each other, saying:
"Gentleman Cavalier Attendant Bào, what kind of person is he,
that he can have such extravagance?"
using it as a joke.
Yǔ Zīqiáo served as Deputy Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
at a time when Emperor Yuán was Governor of Jīngzhōu.
A local man named Fàn Xìnghuà, though of humble origin, had managed to enter the official ranks,
and was selected as Registrar of the province.
Furthermore, the Crown Prince's decree had favored him,
so Emperor Yuán ordered Qiáo to allow Xìnghuà to assume his post.
When the New Year's Day arrived,
the provincial officials gathered for the ceremonial congratulations,
but Qiáo refused to take his place in the procession,
saying:
"I, Yǔ Qiáo, unworthily hold a senior position,
and cannot stand in line with a petty man like Fàn Xìnghuà."
Upon hearing this, Emperor Yuán promoted Qiáo and dismissed Xìnghuà,
who, filled with shame and humiliation,
returned home and died of resentment.
Chén Xuān was the son of Chén Qìng,
possessing outstanding literary talent,
but addicted to alcohol without restraint.
During the Tàikāng era of the Chén dynasty, Xú Líng served as Minister of Personnel,
and was meticulous in selecting officials,
so all scholars and officials admired him.
Xuān came wearing a jade hairpin in his topknot,
a red silk cloth wrapped around his head,
a robe that swept his ankles,
and boots that reached his knees.
Without announcing his rank and hometown,
he went straight up to Xú Líng's seat.
Líng didn't recognize him,
and ordered his attendants to remove him.
Xuān walked out slowly,
his demeanor composed,
showing no sign of shame.
He then wrote a letter slandering Líng,
which greatly troubled Líng.
When the Later Sovereign ascended the throne,
Xuān served as a companion for tours and banquets,
being very intimate with the sovereign yet treated with contempt.
He was once hung upside down over a canal,
with a blade held against him,
but his arrogant teasing only intensified.
Eventually the Later Sovereign could no longer tolerate him,
so he had mugwort tied into a cap,
placed on Xuān's head,
and set on fire,
which burned his hair.
Xuān wept and begged for mercy,
but was not released.
Liǔ Zhuāng falsely claimed an imperial pardon,
and had him taken out by order.
After several days,
Xuān died from shock and fear.
The sovereign
Cuī Zhān,
courtesy name Yàntōng,
was by nature aloof and arrogant,
taking pride in his talent and social standing.
Those with whom he associated
were all renowned figures of the time.
While serving in the Censorate, he always had his residence
supplied with exquisite delicacies for meals.
He would eat alone,
remaining composed in his manner.
There was a gentleman from Hédōng surnamed Péi,
who also served as a censor.
Noticing Zhān dining,
he went to visit him.
Zhān neither spoke to him
nor offered him utensils.
Péi sat and watched
until Zhān finished eating and left.
The next day, Péi brought his own chopsticks,
eating and drinking freely.
Zhān said to him:
"I never invited you to eat,
nor did I speak with you,
yet you remain unconstrained by such formalities.
In the past, Liú Yì at Jīngkǒu boldly requested roasted goose—
is this not similar?
You are truly a celebrated scholar."
From then on, he often ate with him.
(From *History of the Northern Dynasties*)
Cuī Biāo,
styled Qíshū,
was close friends from youth with Fànyáng's Lú Sīdào, sharing the same aspirations,
and always devoted himself to studying.
Relying on his talent and family status,
he boldly inscribed on his door:
"Those who have not read five thousand volumes of books
may not enter this room.
He served as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and after a diplomatic mission to Chén returned deaf,
often having no official duties,
he would get drunk for eight days at a time.
Yuè Guógōng Yáng Sù, then highly favored and powerful,
valued Biāo's family background,
and arranged for his son Xuánzòng to marry Biāo's daughter,
with very generous betrothal gifts.
At the beginning of the wedding procession,
all the high officials were seated in full attendance.
Sù sent horsemen to welcome him,
but Biāo appeared in shabby clothes and hat,
arriving riding a donkey.
Sù urged him to take the seat of honor,
but Biāo's manners were very arrogant,
and his words were disrespectful.
Sù became angry,
shook out his sleeves and stood up,
and the gathering was ultimately canceled.
Several days later,
Biāo came to apologize,
and Sù treated him as before.
He was appointed by imperial decree as Governor of Yìzhōu,
but someone said he was unsuitable, so the appointment was revoked,
and Biāo told people:
"What makes the Governor of Yìzhōu necessarily superior to moral principles?
The Emperor
Zhèng Shìyì, in his early twenties, had a great reputation,
but he often offended others with his words,
and was called frivolous and impetuous.
At that time, Cuī Xìnmíng prided himself on his family status,
and was quite arrogant and boastful,
frequently bullying others.
He often composed poems and chanted them aloud,
claiming that his literary talent was unmatched,
surpassing even Lǐ Bǎiyào.
Shìyì encountered him on the river,
and said to him:
"I have heard of the line 'The maple leaves fall, the Wú River grows cold.'"
Xìnmíng gladly showed him the remaining poems,
but Shìyì, before finishing reading them, said:
"What I see falls short of what I have heard."
He threw them into the river,
and Xìnmíng could not reply,
so he grasped his oar and left.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Wáng Jì's nature was aloof and arrogant.
Governor Cuī Xǐ requested an audience,
saying:
"How can one presume to summon Yán Jūnpíng while seated?" Dù Zhīsōng requested him to lecture on the rites, to which he replied:
"I cannot perform ceremonial bows at a governor's gate."
《New Book of Tang》
Dù Shěnyán was Dù Fǔ's grandfather. He relied on his talent and was arrogant and aloof, which made him envied by his contemporaries.
During the Qiánfēng era,
Sū Wèidào served as the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel. Shěnyán participated in the selection examination and after finishing the judgment essay, he said to others:
"Wèidào is sure to die."
When asked for the reason,
Shěnyán said:
"When he sees my judgment essay, he will surely die of shame."
He also once said to others:
"My literary works should have Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù serve as my subordinate officials,
and my calligraphy should make Wáng Xīzhī bow in submission."
Such was his boastful and exaggerated nature.
The Old Book of Tang and Continued Tales of the World record Qiánfēng as Dēngfēng,
and He's Forest of Sayings follows this error, both being mistaken.
Dù Shěnyán, along with Lǐ Qiáo, Cuī Róng, and Sū Wèidào, were known as the Four Literary Friends.
When he was about to die,
he said to Sòng Zhīwèn and Wǔ Píngyī:
"While I was alive,
I long suppressed you all.
Now that I am about to die,
I am indeed greatly relieved,
but I regret not seeing my successor.
New Book of Tang
Zhèng Rénbiǎo,
son of Zhèng Hù,
was especially praised for his brilliant and outstanding literary talent,
but he relied on his ability and looked down upon others,
so people despised him.
He considered his family background, personal qualities, and literary works all to be excellent,
and once said:
"Heavenly auspices include the five-colored clouds,
and human auspices include Zhèng Rénbiǎo.
When Liú Yè was young, he sought refuge with Zhèng Hù,
but Zhèng Rénbiǎo and his brothers ridiculed and scorned him.
By the end of the Xiántōng era,
Liú Yè had become the chancellor,
and Zhèng Rénbiǎo was eventually exiled and died in the southern wilderness.
Emperor Xuān enjoyed traveling incognito.
Wēn Tíngyún encountered him at an inn,
but Wēn did not recognize the imperial countenance.
Arrogantly, he questioned him, saying:
"Aren't you someone like a Chief Clerk or an Aide-de-Camp?
The Emperor replied:
"No.
Wēn then asked:
"Could you be something like a Sixth Rank Registrar or a Captain?
The Emperor said:
"No.
(Wēn was later) demoted to the position of Captain of Fāngchéng County.
From "Records of Hearsay from the North"
Luó Yǐn, relying on his talent, was arrogant and looked down on others.
Having failed the imperial examinations, he traveled eastward in hardship.
After the Huang Chao rebellion was pacified,
court officials discussed appointing him to an official post.
Wéi Yífàn objected, saying:
"I once shared a boat with him,
though we were not acquainted.
The boatman informed us:
'There is a court official here.'
Luó said:
"What kind of court official is he?
I can hold a writing brush between my toes and surpass several of his kind.
If he indeed passed the examinations and gained official rank,
then people like us would be nothing but chaff.
Because of this, he was not summoned after all.
End
"Records of Tianzhong, Volume Twenty-Eight"
Zhào Wénzǐ and Shū Xiàng were wandering at Jiǔjīng,
and said:
"If the dead could be revived,
whom would I follow?
Would it be Suí Wǔzǐ?
He accepted remonstrance without forgetting his teacher,
spoke of himself without losing his friends,
served his ruler without seeking promotion through connections,
and without flattery would withdraw.
Jìnyǔ
When Yànzǐ prostrated himself over Duke Zhuāng's corpse, weeping for him,
and only left after completing the rites,
was this not what is called
"seeing what is right but not acting upon it shows lack of courage"?
As for his remonstrations,
braving his lord's countenance,
this is what is called
"in office, think of being loyal to the utmost;
out of office, think of making up for faults."
If by chance Yànzǐ were still alive,
even if I were to hold the whip for him,
I would delight in it.
Records of the Grand Historian
Someone transmitted Hán Fēi's writings to Qín,
and the King of Qín saw the books "Gū Fèn" and "Wǔ Dù",
saying:
"Alas!
If I could meet this person,
and travel with him,
I would die without regret.
Lǐ Sī said:
"These are the writings of Hán Fēi.
Qín therefore urgently attacked Hán,
and the King of Hán, who had initially not employed Fēi,
when pressed by the emergency,
then sent Fēi as an envoy to Qín.
The King of Qín was pleased with him,
but did not yet trust or employ him.
Lǐ Sī and Yáo Jiǎ slandered him.

Lù Jiǎ composed twelve essays for Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
and each time he presented one,
Emperor Gāo never failed to praise it,
with his attendants exclaiming "Long live the Emperor,"
calling his book "New Discourses."
In the "History of Hàn," Hán Fēi's writings circulated in the Qín court,
and Emperor Qín Shǐhuáng sighed, saying:
"If only I could have lived at the same time as this man."
Each time a chapter of "Lù Jiǎ's New Discourses" was presented,
Emperor Gāozǔ's attendants exclaimed
"Long live the Emperor"
Now, sighing with longing for someone,
and rejoicing with cries of "Long live,"
how could these be empty gestures?
Truly, they arise from seeing their excellence,
with joyful feelings springing from within.
"Lùn Héng"
Emperor Wén recalled Jiǎ Yì,
and summoned him.
Upon arrival, he was granted an audience.
In the Xuānshì Hall, the Emperor inquired about the essence of ghosts and spirits,
until midnight,
with Emperor Wén moving forward on his mat.
After the audience concluded,
he said:
"It has been long since I last saw Master Jiǎ,
and I had thought myself superior to him,
but now I realize I am not his equal.
From the *Qián Hàn Shū*
In Shǔ, a man named Yáng Déyì served as the dog overseer for the Sovereign.
The Sovereign read "Zǐxū's Rhapsody," and admired it,
saying,
"Why was I not born in the same era as this person?
Yáng Déyì said,
"This composition is by Sīmǎ Xiāngrú, a native of my municipality.
The Sovereign was astonished,
and then summoned Xiāngrú for questioning.
Xiāngrú said,
"Indeed,
allow me to compose a rhapsody on hunting for Your Majesty.
Once the rhapsody was completed, it was presented.
Then he also presented "The Ode to Great Men,"
which greatly pleased the Emperor.
His spirit soared with aspirations as high as the clouds,
resembling a sentiment of wandering between heaven and earth.
In the "Shǐjì," it notes that Emperor Xiaowu appreciated "Zǐxū's Rhapsody,"
and thus summoned Sīmǎ Chángqīng.
Emperor Xiàochéng delighted in reading the many excellent books.
Yáng Zǐyún came in and out of hunts,
with Zǐyún accompanying him.
Thus it is said,
"To enjoy the compositions of Yáng Zǐyún,
is to find delight in holding an official position of a thousand bushels,
to have with him the books of Huán Junshan,
and to possess wealth surpassing the riches of Yīdùn.
From "Lùnhéng Yìwén."
Zhào Zī,
courtesy name Wénchǔ,
was appointed as Chancellor of Dōnghǎi during Emperor Shùn's reign.
While passing through Yíngyáng,
the magistrate of Dūnhuáng Cáo Hào,
who was a former xiàolián recommended by Zhào Zī,
greeted him along the road.
Zhào Zī did not stay,
so Cáo Hào escorted him to the pavilion.
Failing to catch up as the dust settled,
he said to his registrar:
"Lord Zhào is renowned;
now that he has crossed my jurisdiction without my receiving him,
I will surely be laughed at by the world.
He immediately abandoned his official seal and ribbon,
pursued Zhào Zī to Dōnghǎi,
paid his respects,
then resigned and returned home.
Such was the esteem in which he was held by contemporaries.
(Hòu Hàn)
Zhāng Kǎi,
courtesy name Gōngchāo,
was well-versed in the "Yán's Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals" and the "Old Text Book of Documents".
His disciples often numbered around a hundred,
and guests admired him,
so that even his father's generation of veteran Confucian scholars would visit his door together.
Carriages and horses filled the streets,
with followers having nowhere to stop,
while families of eunuchs and noble relatives
all built houses along the lanes,
to benefit from awaiting the coming and going of passersby.
Kǎi disliked this situation,
and would move to avoid it.
Scholars followed him,
and wherever he lived would become a market,
so that later south of Huàyīn Mountain there came to be a "Gōngchāo Market".
Lǐ Yīng,
styled Yuánlǐ,
was by nature aloof and proud,
and did not engage in casual social interactions.
He regarded only Xún Shū and Chén Shí of his own commandery as his teachers and friends.
Xún Shuǎng once went to visit Yīng,
and took the opportunity to serve as his carriage driver.
After returning,
he joyfully said:
"Today I finally had the chance to drive for Master Lǐ!"
Such was the admiration he received.
Moreover, Yīng often excused himself from seeing guests off or welcoming them due to illness,
receiving visitors only once every twenty days.
Only when Chén Zhònggōng came would he ride out in his carriage to greet him.
From "Yīng's Family Records": When Yīng lived in Yángchéng,
there were always four to five hundred disciples at his gate.
Whenever Yīng produced a piece of writing,
his disciples would compete for it,
never letting it fall to the ground.
Chén Zhònggōng initially sent his eldest son Yuánfāng to visit.
After Yīng finished speaking with him,
he had food sent from the kitchen.
Yuánfāng was delighted, thinking he had made a favorable impression,
and expected to be received again.
From "Shāng Yún's Minor Tales"
Guō Tài,
courtesy name Línzōng,
first arrived in the capital.
Fú Róng of Chénliú, upon seeing him, sighed and said:
"Noble and refined, extraordinary and grand, with profound insight and clear reasoning,
he acts without improper compromise,
speaks without flattery or exaggeration.
This is an exceptional scholar."
He spoke of him to Lǐ Yīng, the Governor of Hénán,
and arranged a meeting, saying:
"I have seen many scholars,
but none like Guō Línzōng.
His intelligence and understanding are thorough and bright,
noble and refined, meticulous and broad.
In today's Huáxià, few can compare to him."
They became friends and grew close.
Hán Zhuó of Chénliú had the discernment to judge people.
Fú Róng told him his own opinion, and Zhuó said:
"This is a scholar from Tàiyuán."
Another day, he again told Zhuó Guō Tài's words, and Zhuó said:
"This is a scholar for all within the Four Seas.
I must meet him."
Thereupon, he promptly met Guō Tài
and said to Fú Róng:
"This man's spirit is harmonious and balanced,
his words conform to standards,
with high talent and exquisite insight.
Rarely do we see his equal."
From the Hòu Hàn Jì
Guō Tài traveled to Luòyáng,
where he first met the Governor of Hénán, Lǐ Yīng.
Yīng was greatly impressed by him,
and they became close friends,
thus making his name renowned throughout the capital.
Later, when he returned to his hometown,
the scholars and officials
saw him off to the riverbank,
with thousands of carriages gathered.
Línzōng (Guō Tài) alone shared a boat with Lǐ Yīng to cross the river,
and the guests watching them
thought they were like celestial beings.
From the *History of the Later Hàn*.
Huáng Xiàn,
courtesy name Shūdù,
was a native of Shènyáng in Rǔnán.
Contemporary critics all said he was the reincarnation of Yánzǐ, yet he came from an obscure and humble clan;
his father was an ox doctor.
Xún Jìhé of Yǐngchuān grasped Xiàn's hand,
saying:
"You are my exemplar.
Later, when he met Yuán Fènggāo, he said:
"Your state has its own Yánzǐ;
do you know of him?
Fènggāo replied:
"You must have met my Shūdù!
From "Diǎn Lüè"
Huáng Shūdù's fellow townsmen Chén Fān and Zhōu Jǔ often said to each other:
"If a few months pass
without seeing Mr. Huáng,
then vulgar thoughts begin to sprout again in our hearts.
When Chén Fān became one of the Three Excellencies and attended court,
he sighed and said:
"If Shūdù were still alive,

Your reverence is sparing in food,
but profound in the virtue of drinking wine -
eating no more than an infant,
yet sometimes drinking like a young man.
I often fear for the well-being of your revered health,
and thinking of it in the midnight hours,

he sought someone knowledgeable in the Yì,
issuing a notice to all temples,
ordering them to select and send someone to his residence.
Shǒuliàng requested to go,
and upon arrival,
the Duke initially met him
without showing much respect.
But when they conversed,
he analyzed principles in detail,
delving into profound and subtle matters.
Whenever the Duke was about to raise a doubt,
Liǎng had already expounded on its meaning.
The Duke unconsciously moved his mat forward in respect,
ordered the Gānlù Temple to prepare accommodations,
and set up a lecture hall in his own residence,
instructing all officials and below to attend with their texts.
It took over a year to complete.
Afterward, he requested another lecture,
but halfway through,
he urgently asked to return to Gānlù.
Upon arriving,
he ordered a bath,
and after bathing,
he straightened his headscarf and adjusted his white robes.
The Duke said:
"My great limit has now arrived,
I cannot return to bid farewell."
After speaking, he passed away.
The Duke heard and was astonished,
the next day leading guests to offer sacrifices.
Coincidentally, an envoy from Nánhǎi brought exotic incense from Western countries,
which the Duke burned before the niche.
The smoke rose like a taut string,
piercing through the roof upward,
leaving onlookers sorrowful and reverent.
The Duke personally drafted a eulogy,
stating that all the official ranks and emoluments in the world,
if bestowed upon Liǎng,
he would accept them fully,
and could do so without shame.
From "Yǔlín."
Lǐ Xíyù,
fond of copying books,
said to his descendants:
"Near the capital, I have ten qǐng of bestowed land,
which, when cultivated, can provide sufficient food;
in Hénèi, there are a thousand bestowed mulberry trees,
which, when used for silkworms, can provide adequate clothing;
the books copied in Jiāngdōng,
when studied, can help you seek official positions.
After my death,
if you diligently pursue these three things,
what more could you envy in others?
Continuation of A New Account of the Tales of the World
Chéng Huī was appointed Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs at the beginning of the Zhēnyòu era,
while his wife and children remained in Cāngzhōu.
When Cāngzhōu fell,
his wife and children all perished.
Emperor Xuānzong moved the capital to Biàn,
and Chéng Huī remained in the Central Capital with the Crown Prince.
When the Yuán army arrived,
the Central Capital could not be defended,
and he took poison and died.
Though Huī was born into wealth and nobility,
he lived as frugally as a commoner at home.
He often placed portraits of Sīmǎ Guāng and Sū Shì in his study,
saying:
"I take Sīmǎ as my teacher,
and Sū as my friend."
《History of Jīn》
Zǐ Chǎn served as prime minister of Zhèng and had an elder brother named:
"Gōngsūn Cháo, who had a younger brother named Gōngsūn Mù.
Cháo was fond of wine,
while Mù was fond of women.
In Cháo's residence, thousands of vessels of wine were gathered,
with fermented grains piled up like mounds,
from a hundred paces away from his gate,
the smell of distiller's grains assaulted one's nostrils.
When he was immersed in wine,
he knew not the safety or peril of the world's ways,
the regrets or difficulties in human affairs,
the presence or absence within his household,
the closeness or distance of his nine kinship clans,
or the sorrows and joys of life and death.
Even if flood, fire, or weapons clashed before him,
he would be unaware.
Mù had several tens of adjoining rooms in his rear chambers,
all filled with selected young, delicate, and beautiful maidens.
When he was沉迷于 women,
he would screen off intimate associates,
sever social interactions,
and escape to his rear chambers, making day suffice for night,
emerging only once every three months,
yet still feeling unsatisfied.
If there was a lovely maiden in the village,
he would surely bribe to summon her,
use matchmakers to entice her,
and not stop until he obtained her."
Zǐ Chǎn considered this a sorrow,
and visited Dèng Xī to seek counsel.
Xī said:
"Why don't you enlighten them about the importance of life and destiny,
and entice them with the dignity of ritual and righteousness?"
Zǐ Chǎn employed Xī's advice,
taking an opportunity to visit
and admonish his brothers Cháo and Mù, saying:
"Life is hard to encounter,
while death comes easily.
To use this hard-to-encounter life
awaiting easily arriving death—
how can one bear to think of it?
Moreover, you boast of your ability to govern the state.
Those skilled at governing external affairs
may not necessarily bring order to things,
while their bodies suffer hardship;
those skilled at governing internal affairs
may not necessarily bring ritual to things,
yet their preferences find ease.
Do you intend to teach me with your methods?"
Zǐ Chǎn was bewildered and had no response.
From "Liè Yáng Zhū"
Zhuāng Zhōu was critically ill,
his disciples wept facing him,
to which he responded:
"If I die now,
who would be first?
If born a hundred years later,
who would be last?
Since death is unavoidable,
why cling to these fleeting moments."
From Huán Tán's New Discourses
Dài Liáng,
courtesy name Shūluán,
was unconventional in his youth.
His mother enjoyed the braying of donkeys,
and Liáng often imitated it to amuse her.
After his mother passed away,
his elder brother Bóluán resided in a mourning hut, consuming only gruel,
and never acted against ritual propriety.
Liáng alone ate meat and drank wine,
weeping only when grief overwhelmed him,
yet both brothers showed physical signs of deterioration from mourning.
Someone asked Liáng:
"Your observance of mourning,
is it according to ritual?"
Liáng replied:
"Yes.
Ritual exists to restrain excessive emotions.
If emotions are not excessive,
what is there to discuss about ritual?
When fine food brings no pleasure,
this naturally leads to physical deterioration;
if one tastes nothing in one's mouth,
eating such food is permissible."
Critics could not refute him.
Liáng's talents were both lofty and far-reaching,
yet his arguments favored the extraordinary,
often shocking conventional society.
A fellow townsman Jì Xiào asked him:
"How do you assess yourself in comparison to anyone under heaven?"
Liáng said:
"I resemble Zhòngní (Confucius),
who rose in eastern Lǔ,
and the Great Yǔ who emerged from the Western Qiāng,
striding alone across the world -
who could be my match?"
From the History of the Later Hàn
Zhèng Quán,
courtesy name Wényuān,
was a person of Chényì.
He was erudite with extraordinary aspirations,
yet addicted to alcohol by nature.
During his leisure,
he often said:
"I wish to obtain fine wine filling a boat of five hundred hú,
with seasonal delicacies placed at both ends,
drinking repeatedly until submerged in it,
and when weary, pausing to eat dishes.
Should the wine decrease by a dǒu or shēng,
replenish it immediately—
wouldn't that be delightful?
Approaching death,
he told his peers:
"Be sure to bury me beside a potter's workshop,
so that after a century,
when my body transforms into earth,
I may hopefully be taken to make a wine pot—
that would truly fulfill my heart's desire.

Ruǎn Gōng's neighbor's wife was beautiful,
and sold wine at a tavern.
Ruǎn and Wáng Ānfēng often drank wine with her.
When Ruǎn got drunk, he would sleep beside her;
her husband initially suspected him,
but after observing closely, found no ulterior motives.
From *A New Account of the Tales of the World*
Ruǎn Jí's neighbor had a daughter of talent and beauty,
who died before marrying.
Though unrelated to her
and never having met her in life,
he went to mourn, weeping with full grief before departing.
His unconventionality and lack of restraint
were all of this kind.
From Wáng Yǐn's History of the Jìn Dynasty
When the post of Commandant of Infantry fell vacant,
and there were several hundred hu of wine stored in the kitchens,
Ruǎn Jí requested to be appointed as Commandant of Infantry.
A New Account of the Tales of the World
Drinking Wine After Mother's Death Ruǎn Jí was extremely filial by nature.
When his mother was about to die,
he happened to be playing a game of Go with someone.
His opponent requested to stop,
but Ruǎn Jí insisted on finishing the game.
Afterward, he drank two liters of wine,
let out a loud cry,
and vomited several liters of blood.
When it was time for the burial,
he ate a steamed suckling pig,
drank two pecks of wine,
and then went to bid his final farewell.
He cried out that he had reached the end of his means,
let out another loud cry,
and again vomited several liters of blood.
He became emaciated and gaunt,
nearly to the point of self-destruction.
Péi Kǎi went to offer condolences,
and Ruǎn Jí, with disheveled hair and sitting sprawled out,
stared blankly while drunk.
Péi Kǎi finished his condolences and left.
《Book of Jìn》 When Ruǎn Jí was in mourning for his mother,
he sat with King Wén of Jìn and consumed wine and meat.
The Inspector Hé Zēng was also present
and said:
"Your Excellency governs the realm with filial piety,
yet Ruǎn Jí, in deep mourning,
openly drinks wine and eats meat in your presence.
He should be exiled beyond the seas,
to rectify moral customs."
King Wén replied:
"Sìzōng (Ruǎn Jí) is so grief-stricken and worn out,
yet you cannot share his sorrow.
Why speak of it? Moreover, drinking wine and eating meat when ill
is in fact in accordance with mourning rites."
Ruǎn Jí continued eating and drinking without pause,
his composure unruffled.
《A New Account of the Tales of the World》 Between the Wèi and Jìn periods, there were those who behaved with disheveled hair and arrogant disregard,
all being people who forgot life in the face of death,
yet they claimed to be practicing ritual.
Ruǎn Jí was among them.
《Gān Bǎo's Records of Jìn》
In the late Wei period, Ruǎn Jí indulged excessively in wine and led a dissolute life,
leaving his head uncovered and hair disheveled,
sitting naked with legs sprawled like a winnowing basket.
Later, young nobles such as Ruǎn Zhān, Wáng Chéng, Xiè Kūn, and Húwú Fǔzhī
all followed and emulated Ruǎn Jí,
claiming to have grasped the essence of the Great Way.
Thus they discarded their caps and headdresses,
removed their clothing,
exposing their ugliness,
resembling beasts.
The more extreme among them were called "unrestrained,"
while the lesser ones were termed "uninhibited."
From Wáng Yǐn's History of the Jin Dynasty.
Ruǎn Jí would often impulsively drive his carriage alone,
not following any set path.
When the tracks of his carriage reached their end,
he would weep bitterly and turn back.
Once he climbed Guǎngwǔ,
gazing upon the site of the Chu-Han battles,
and sighed, saying:
"There were no heroes in that time,
allowing a mere upstart to achieve fame.
Book of Jìn
Liú Líng,
courtesy name Bólún,
abandoned himself to his passions and followed his inclinations,
often holding the belief that the universe is insignificant and all things are equal.
When he met Ruǎn Jí and Jī Kāng,
they felt an immediate spiritual connection,
and hand in hand, they entered the woods.
He never concerned himself with whether he had family wealth or not,
often riding in a deer-drawn carriage,
carrying a pot of wine,
and having someone follow him with a spade on their shoulder,
saying:
"Bury me where I die.
Such was his disregard for his physical form.
Liú Líng constantly indulged in drinking and unrestrained behavior,
sometimes taking off his clothes and remaining naked in his room.
A visitor who came to see him witnessed this and criticized him,
to which Liú Líng laughed and said:
"I regard heaven and earth as my dwelling,
and the house as my trousers.
Since you gentlemen should not have entered my trousers,
why do you take offense?"
Such was the way he carried himself.

All members of the Ruǎn family were capable of drinking.
When Ruǎn Zhòngróng gathered with his clansmen,
they no longer used ordinary cups for serving wine,
but instead employed a large vat to hold the liquor.
Seated in a circle,
they faced one another and drank heartily.
On one occasion, a herd of pigs came to drink,
approaching directly the vat,
and they shared the drink with them.
Wáng Píngzǐ Chéng, Húwú Fǔzhī Yànguó, and others all considered unrestrained freedom as being enlightened,
and some even went naked.
Yuè Guǎng laughed and said:
"Within the bounds of propriety and morality, there is indeed a place for joy;
why must you go to such extremes?
Hú Mǔ Qiānzhī,
courtesy name Zǐguāng,
was less talented and learned than his father,
but surpassed him in arrogance and unrestrained behavior.
When heavily intoxicated,
he often called his father by his courtesy name,
yet Fǔzhī never minded it,
and commentators considered him insane.
Once, while Fǔzhī was drinking heartily,
Qiānzhī peered in and shouted harshly:
"Yànguó is old;
he should not act like this!
It will make my backside face the eastern wall."
Fǔzhī laughed joyfully

Book of Jìn
Hú Mǔ Yànguó arrived in Xiāngzhōu,
at that time during the dog days of summer,
Yànguó was sitting in the main hall,
fanning himself while attending to official matters.
His son Zǐguāng leisurely turned to him and said:
"Yànguó, why are you bringing this trouble upon yourself?
Guāng Yì,
courtesy name Mèngzǔ,
crossed the river to escape the turmoil of the times,
and sought refuge with Húwú Fǔzhī.
Upon his arrival,
Fǔzhī, along with Xiè Kūn, Ruǎn Fàng, Bì Zhuó, Yáng Màn, Huán Yí, and Ruǎn Fú, had been indulging in unrestrained drinking for days, with hair unbound and clothes discarded in a closed room.
Yì was about to push the door open to enter,
but the guard refused him entry.
Yì then removed his clothes and exposed his head outside the door,
peeking through a dog hole and shouting loudly.
Fǔzhī exclaimed in surprise:
"No one else would dare do this;
it must be you, my Mèngzǔ!"
He immediately called him in,
and they drank together,
day and night without rest,
earning them the contemporary nickname "The Eight Free Spirits."
(Book of Jìn)
Zhāng Jìyīng Hàn was unrestrained and unconventional,
earning the nickname "Infantry of Jiāngdōng" among his contemporaries.
Someone remarked to him:
"You may indulge in momentary pleasures,
but have you no regard for your posthumous reputation?"
He replied:
"If I must have a posthumous reputation,
I'd rather have a cup of wine right now."
From "Shì Shuō"
Minister Hè traveled to Luòyáng to assume his post,
serving as an attendant to the Grand Heir,
passing through the Chāng Gate of Wú,
and playing the qín aboard the boat.
Zhāng Jìyīng, who had not previously known him,
was first at the Jīnchāng Pavilion,

went down to the boat to approach Hè.
Through their conversation,

He asked Hè,

Hè replied,
"I am going to Luòyáng to take up my post,

Zhāng said,
"I too have business in the northern capital,

Thereupon he set out with Hè,
initially without informing his family,
who only found out after pursuing and inquiring.
Ruǎn Fú,

never allowing official duties to burden his heart.
At that time, Emperor Yuán had adopted the Legalist doctrines to save the world,
yet those of Fú's kind could not be without their ways.
Although he was not entrusted with heavy responsibilities,
Fú sat upright, whistling and chanting poetry,
enjoying his life in those years.
He once traded his golden sable tail hat for wine,
was impeached by the responsible officials,
but the emperor pardoned him.
Wáng Dǎo, Zhōu Yǐ, and court officials visited the Minister of Personnel Jì Zhān to watch a performance.

exposing his depravity,
yet showed no shame on his face.
A petition was submitted to dismiss Yǐ from office,
but an imperial decree specially pardoned him.
"Dèng Càn's Annals of Jìn"
Xiè Yì,

Huán Wēn appointed him as his Anxi Marshal,

from "Records of the Restoration"
Luó Yǒu served as an attendant in Jīngzhōu.
Huán Wēn was hosting a farewell gathering for Wáng Qià,
Yǒu entered and sat for a long time,
then took his leave to depart.
Wēn said:
"You earlier wished to consult on matters,
why are you leaving so soon?"
He replied:
"Yǒu heard that mutton is delicious,
and in my whole life I have never had the chance to eat it,
therefore I boldly sought to come forward.
There is nothing to consult about,
now I am already full,
and need not remain any longer."
He showed not the slightest sign of shame.
From "Shì Shuō"
Wáng Chén,
courtesy name Yuándá,
was by nature unrestrained and unconventional.
In his later years he became especially fond of wine,
sometimes drinking for months without sobering up,
and occasionally wandering about naked.
He would often sigh that if three days passed without drinking,
he felt his body and spirit were no longer intimate.
When his father-in-law was grieving,
Chén went to offer condolences while drunk,
and as his father-in-law wailed bitterly,
Chén entered with about ten guests, arms linked, hair disheveled, and bodies naked,
circled the mourner three times, then left.
Most of his behavior was of this kind.

Xiè Ān was fond of music and rhythm,
even during periods of mourning,
he did not abandon female entertainers and music,
so the gentry class emulated him,
and it eventually became a custom.
Wáng Tǎnzhī disapproved and earnestly admonished him.
Xiè Ān sent Wáng Tǎnzhī a letter saying:
"I know you care for me with utmost affection.
What I seek is music,
which I consider appropriate to express feelings and righteousness,
finding nothing unacceptable about it,
and merely use it to amuse myself.
If it is to follow established paths,
and uphold worldly teachings,
that is not what I intend to discuss,
nor do I care for it.
I often thought you somewhat understood my humble tastes,
have you not yet grasped the perspective of the river Hao?
Thus I know that perfect mutual understanding,
is not easily achieved with others.
Wáng Tǎnzhī replied:
"I fully appreciate your elegant intentions,
this is acting with sincerity,
and the beauty of independent pursuit,
yet I fear it may not align with the principles of great elegance and the Mean.
You, sir, established virtue and conduct in youth,
with profound and fair judgment,
coupled with your esteemed position,
living in leisurely comfort,
the consensus in discussions,
all praises you as pure and far-reaching,
but regarding this matter,
I truly have doubts.
Whether in public or private matters,
I see nothing commendable in it.
To regard this as the river Hao perspective,
wouldn't those who understand it be few indeed!
Moreover, what is precious to the world,
should be cherished by the world; what the world disapproves,
why not take the world's concerns to heart?
I hope you will fortunately reconsider.
Letters were exchanged several times,
but Xiè Ān ultimately did not comply.

From Xiè Chuò's "Sòng Shíyí Lù"
Xiè Língyùn, feeling discontented because Emperor Wén did not grant him significant responsibilities or favor,
often claimed illness and did not attend court or perform his duties.
He dug ponds and planted hedges,
cultivated dense groves of bamboo and trees,
and drove public laborers to work,

He traveled beyond the city walls,
sometimes covering one hundred sixty or seventy lǐ,

He neither submitted memorials to inform the court,

had a very substantial livelihood,
with many servants and attendants,

He excavated mountains and dredged lakes,

Exploring mountains and crossing ridges,
he always sought out perilous and steep places.
Even with cliffs and peaks layered dozens of folds,
he ascended and traversed every one without exception.
He often wore wooden clogs for climbing mountains,
removing the front teeth when ascending,
and the rear teeth when descending.
Once, he cut trees and cleared a path from the southern mountains of Shǐníng,
straight to Línhǎi,
with several hundred followers.
The governor of Línhǎi was alarmed,
thinking they were mountain bandits,
but felt at ease upon realizing it was Língyùn.
From "The Book of Sòng"

if people encountered him
without recognizing him
and inquired where the governor was,

History of the Southern Dynasties
Yuán Càn served as Governor of Dānyáng,
cherishing ethereal and distant ideals.
Although his position was eminent and responsibilities weighty,
he never burdened his mind with administrative affairs.
Strolling alone through gardens and woods,
he found solace in poetry and wine.
His home lay against the outer city wall,
where he often wandered leisurely with a staff.
When his spirit was content,
he would roam serenely, forgetting to return.
Once, while walking in cloth shoes through suburban fields of white poplars,
he encountered a scholar-official on the road
and promptly invited him to drink heartily together.
The next day, this man, believing he had gained Yuán's recognition,
came to the gate seeking advancement.
Yuán declared:
"Yesterday I drank merely for lack of companionship,
and casually invited you along."
In the end, he refused to receive him.
He once composed a five-character poem:
"Though my footsteps linger within these walls,
my heart journeys to the misty isles."
This truly captured his aspiration.
Hé Diǎn,

Cáo Jǐngzōng,
styled Zǐzhèn,
was quite fond of historical texts.
Whenever he read the "Biographies of Ráng Jū and Yuè Yì,"
he would put down the scroll and sigh, saying:

When traveling, he often wished to lift the carriage curtains,
but his attendants would remonstrate, citing his high status and prestige,
which drew public attention,
making it inappropriate to do so."
Jǐngzōng said to his close associates:
"In my former days in the countryside,
I rode swift horses like dragons,
accompanied by dozens of young riders.
We drew our bows with a thunderous sound,
and our arrows whistled like hungry hawks.
Chasing deer in the open marshes,
we shot them through the ribs repeatedly,
quenching our thirst with their blood,
and satisfying our hunger with their flesh,
which was as sweet as nectar.
I felt the wind rushing past my ears,
and fire seemed to blaze from my nostrils.
Such joy made one forget death,
unaware that old age was approaching.
Now, as a noble in Yángzhōu,
I cannot move freely.
When I try to open the carriage curtains on the road,
my subordinates immediately say it is not allowed.
Confined inside the carriage,
I feel like a newlywed bride of three days,
suffering from this depression,
which drains all my spirit."

Yán Yánzhī once accompanied Hé Yǎn in following the emperor to the southern suburbs,
when from a distance on the road he called out to Yánzhī,
saying:
"Yán Gōng Yánzhī, because of his frivolousness,
found it strange."
He replied:
"I am neither a Duke among the Three Excellencies,
nor am I a village elder,
nor am I your family's honored father,
so why do you address me as 'Gōng'?"
Yǎn felt ashamed and withdrew.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Yán Yánzhī often belittled the poetry of Tāng Huìxiū,
saying to others:
"Abbot Xiū's compositions are merely alleyway ballads!
Hé Chángyú served as an aide to Prince Línchuān Liú Yìqìng,
and once sent a letter from Jiānglíng to his clansman Hé Xù,
in which he described the order of officials in Yìqìng's provincial administration, such as Lù Zhǎn.
However, frivolous youths elaborated and spread it,
and all those people
were labeled with epithets,
each intensified with harsh and bitter phrases,
causing the text to circulate widely.
Yìqìng was greatly angered,
and demoted Hé Chángyú to the position of magistrate of Zēngchéng County.
(From the "Biography of Xiè Língyùn" in the Book of Sòng)
Minister of Education Chǔ Yànhuí was seeing off Provincial Governor of Xiāngzhōu Wáng Sēngqián,
when the elevated walkway collapsed,
and they fell into the water.
Minister of Personnel Wáng Jiǎn, startled,
jumped barefoot from his carriage.
Xiè Chāozōng clapped his hands and laughed,
jokingly saying:
"The Duke of Three Excellencies falls into the water,
the Minister of Personnel tumbles from his carriage.
Yànhuí emerges from the water,
drenched and disheveled.
Chāozōng had arrived earlier,
when Sēngqìng Háng loudly declared:
"Heaven's justice prevails,
unaccepted by heaven,
unreceived by earth,
cast to the River God,
yet the River God refuses him.
Yànhuí angrily retorted:
"The lowly scholar is disrespectful.
Chāozōng replied:
"If I cannot gain wealth by betraying Yuán and Liǔ,
how can I avoid being a poor scholar?
These sarcastic remarks,
gradually spread throughout the court and beyond.
(From History of the Southern Dynasties)
Liú Xiáng,
courtesy name Xiǎnzhēng,
was fond of literature from a young age.
His temperament was rigid and unrefined;
he spoke recklessly and acted without restraint,
showing no regard for status or hierarchy.
When Minister Chǔ Yuān entered court using his waist
fan to block the sun, Xiáng passed by his side and said:
"Behaving in such a manner,
you should be ashamed to show your face to others.
"What good does blocking with a fan do?" Yuān said:
"This poor scholar is disrespectful.
Xiáng replied:
"If you cannot kill Yuán and Liú,
how can you avoid being called a poor scholar?
During the Yǒngmíng era, he composed "Linked Pearls,"
which someone presented to the Emperor.
The Emperor ordered Rèn Xiá to memorialize that Xiáng drank excessively,
his speech was unrestrained and frivolous,
and not worthy of being recorded.
The Emperor's edict stated:
"Your position places you among the pure ranks,
and by status, you are not wronged.
Why do you recklessly let your mouth spew nonsense,
slandering court officials?
Whenever you take a seat and speak,
you invariably use criticism as your refrain.
You clamor and debate about the court,
showing no distinction between noble and humble,
letting your words run to extremes,
and blatantly exposing matters for all to hear.
I have recently seen your draft of 'Linked Pearls,'
its sentiments conveying defiance and arrogance—
this absolutely cannot be tolerated.
"Book of Qí"
During the Dàmíng era,
when the crown prince was crowned,
the emperor attended a banquet at the Eastern Palace,
and played dice games with Yán Shībó, Liǔ Yuánjǐng, Shěn Qìngzhī, and others.
Mǐnsūn urged Shībó to drink,
but Shībó refused.
Mǐnsūn then insulted him, saying:
"I cannot associate with a flatterer."
Shībó was favored by the emperor,
who often resented Mǐnsūn for belittling Shībó despite his humble background.
Enraged by this,
the emperor said:
"If Yuán Zhuó's son had not encountered me,
he would not even have obtained the position of vice director,
yet he dares to treat others with the arrogance of a poor scholar!"
He intended to kill him with his own hands
and ordered him dragged from his seat.
Mǐnsūn showed no change in expression.
Shěn and Liǔ both rose to apologize,
and after some time, he was released.
From the *History of the Southern Dynasties*.
Zhāng Chàng was entrapped,
Nāntiáo King Yì Xuān met,
Yuán Xiàowǔ held a feast at Cháoyáng,
Chàng was also present,
Hé Yǎn, intoxicated, said:
"Zhāng Chàng is indeed a remarkable talent,
joined Yì Xuān in rebellion,
also capable of being faultless, if not for talent, how could this be achieved?
Chàng then replied loudly:
"During the beginning of times,
who yellowed your pavilion?
The Emperor said:
"Why do you trouble each other?
During the time of Yuán's villainy,
Yǎn's father Shàngzhī was associated with Yuán's villainy,
when Sīkōng Yìshī arrived at Xīnlín,
the disciples all fled,
Shàngzhī and his sons washed the yellow pavilion together with their maidservants,
thus Chàng mocked them.
Zhāng Jìng'ér was appointed as Kāifǔ Yítóng,
Wáng Jìngzé teased him,
calling him Chǔ Yànhuí.
Zhāng Jìng'ér said:
"What I gained on horseback,
can never match the achievements in Huálín Pavilion."
Wáng Jìngzé felt deeply resentful.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Fàn Zhèn,
courtesy name Zǐzhēn,
did not believe in karma,
and when his work "On the Annihilation of the Soul" was published,
it caused an uproar in both court and country,
with Zǐliáng gathering monks to refute him,
yet unable to make him yield.
Tàiyuán's Wáng Yǎn then wrote a critique mocking Zhèn, saying:
"Alas!
Master Fàn does not even know where his ancestors' spirits reside.
Intending to block Zhèn's future responses.
Zhèn retorted again:
"Alas!
Master Wáng knows where his ancestors' spirits reside,
yet cannot sacrifice his life to follow them.
His sharp retorts were all of this kind.
Above
Wéi Càn,
courtesy name Chángqiàn,
served as the commander of the Right Guard,
and was quite arrogant and presumptuous in wielding his power,
which was resented by his contemporaries.
Zhū Yì of the Right Guard once sternly said to Càn at a banquet:
"How dare you put on the airs of a commander and face people like that!
Earlier, when Wěi Àn served as the Minister of the Imperial Stud,
his nephew Wéi Càn was the commander of the Left Guard.
Àn often discontentedly remarked to others:
"Wéi Càn has already fallen behind the finest horses;
does the court really know how to employ talent?
Discerning observers often gauged him by this.
Liǔ Jīn,
courtesy name Yuánjǔ,
was the son of Qìng Yuǎn.
Although lacking in elegance,
he was very strong-willed and upright.
When someone advised him to collect books,
Jīn replied:
"I often invite Daoist priests to perform rituals to expel ghosts,
why would I need these things called ghosts?"
Zhāng Zuǎn,
courtesy name Bóxù,
relied on his talent and spirit,
and deferred to no one.
Dìngxiāng Hóu Zhī lacked scholarly learning,
but had considerable literary talent,
and together with his elder brother Héngshān Hóu Gōng, both received the Crown Prince's favor and appreciation.
At that time, Zuǎn's paternal cousins Mì and Yù were both uneducated,
and their nature was ordinary and foolish.
Gōng and Zhī once attended a grand gathering at the Eastern Palace,
the Crown Prince teased Zuǎn, saying:
"Where are your esteemed cousins Mì and Yù?
Zuǎn calmly replied:
"I have Mì and Yù,
just as Your Highness has Héng and Dìng.
The Crown Prince's expression showed shame,
someone mentioned that Zuǎn's paternal cousins Yù and Bì were foolish and incompetent,
Xiāngdōng Prince was present,
and asked Zuǎn:
"How are your two cousins Yù and Bì's
skills and learning?
Zuǎn replied:
"Although my younger cousins are not numerous,
they are still more worthy than Your Highness's Héng and Dìng.
All present were astonished.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Hú Sǒu met Zhào Jùn Lǐ Cǎn, the Vice Director of the Secretariat, at the residence of Gāo Yǔn.
Cǎn was dressed in luxurious attire,
while Sǒu, being poor and elderly, wore coarse clothing.
Cǎn looked down upon him considerably.
Sǒu said to him:
"If I were to grant you this today,
and take off my upper-body trousers, pleated robe, and outer garment,
what plan would you have then?"
He was mocking him for relying only on borrowed fine clothing.
Cǎn became fearful and changed countenance.
《Book of Wèi》
Sūn Qiǎn,
courtesy name Yànjǔ,
was shallow in learning and deficient in conduct.
Xíng Shào once said to him:
"You should read more books.
Sūn replied:
"My three thousand elite cavalry
are enough to defeat your tens of thousands of weak soldiers.
Qiǎn once took jícì pills,
Lǐ Xié teased him:
"You should be self-sufficient,
why seek external help?
All present laughed.
From History of the Northern Dynasties
Bì Yìyún's family was wealthy for its time,
indulging in arrogance and extravagance,
his household was filthy and disorderly,
his reputation spread throughout the court and beyond.
While serving as a court official, he had a dispute over official matters with Left Assistant Sòng Yóudào,
and Yóudào confronted him at court,
insulting him by saying:
"The poem of the lustful fox,
after a thousand years, applies to you."
Yìyún had nothing to say in response.
Xú Zhīcái's father Xióng and grandfather Chéng Bó were both skilled in medicine,
and the family profession was passed down through generations.
Zǔ Xiàozhēng jokingly called him Shīgōng.
Xú Zhīcái said:
"Since I am your teacher,
and also your elder,
in the principle of the three relationships,
I occupy two at once.
Xú Zhīcái once teased Wèi Shōu with witty banter,
and Wèi Shōu stared at him intently, saying:
"Your face resembles that of a petty family's
Fāngxiàng's talent.
Xú Zhīcái replied:
"If that's the case, then you are my burial equipment.
From "Tán Sǒu"
Xú Zhīcái was intelligent, eloquent, and had a strong memory,
particularly fond of witty banter.
Lǐ Xié, in a large gathering,
mentioned his father's name, saying:
"Do you enjoy raw bear fat?"
Zhīcái replied:
"Just average."
Lǐ Xié then asked:
"Is what you said reasonable or not?"
Lǐ Xié hurriedly left,
avoiding him on the road,
where he met his nephew Gāo Dézhèng.
Dézhèng said:
"Uncle, why does your complexion look so displeased?"
Lǐ Xié told him the reason,
and Dézhèng went straight to the seating area,
repeatedly asking for bear fat.
Zhīcái said to those seated:
"What is this person avoiding?"
No one knew.
Zhīcái said:
"If one is unknown while alive,
there's nothing to avoid mentioning after death.
Why bother asking?"
When Táng Yōng and Bái Jiàn were highly esteemed,
people at the time said:
"In Bīngzhōu, illustrious are Táng and Bái."
Zhīcái looked down on them.
On New Year's Day,
he toasted the various officials in front of Yōng, saying:
"May you all achieve the status of Táng and Bái."
Also, because a junior clerk liked chewing brush handles,
he once held a brush to Yuán Wényáo's mouth, saying:
"Lend me your teeth."
His lack of respect was like this.
Book of Northern Qí
Wèi Shōu's uncle Wèi Jìjǐng was a man of literary talent,
had held official positions and was renowned,
and both were ahead of Shōu,
yet Shōu often treated him with contempt.
When Jìjǐng first went to Bīngzhōu,
Lǐ Shù of Dùnqiū,
son of the former Minister of Agriculture Lǐ Xié,
was known for his eloquent speech,
once said to Shōu:
"The hegemon court now has two Wèis."
Shōu replied casually:
"To compare me with my uncle
is like comparing Yéshū to you."
Yéshū was the son of the former Minister of Works, Duke of Chénliú Jì Bó,
notorious for his foolishness,
who enjoyed going to the market
and buying goods at high prices,
being mocked and played with by merchants.
Shōu suddenly compared Jìjǐng
to him;
such insolent remarks were frequent.
From "History of the Northern Dynasties"
Zǔ Xiàozhēng Tǐng rode an old horse,
yet called it a young chestnut steed.
He also had an illicit affair with the widow Wáng Shì,
often sending messages back and forth in public.
Péi Ràngzhī had been familiar with Tǐng since early times,
and once mocked him in front of a crowd, saying:
"How can you be so bizarre?
An old horse of ten years,
you still call a young chestnut steed;
an affair with a sixty-year-old you refer to as a young lady."
At that time, this spread noisily far and wide.
Liáng Yǔ Xìn first arrived in the North from the Southern Dynasties,
and many literati looked down on him.
He presented his "Fu on the Withered Tree" to the public,
after which no one dared to speak ill of him.
At that time, Wēn Zǐshēng composed the "Stele of Hanling Mountain Temple,"
which Yǔ Xìn read and copied.
A southerner asked Yǔ Xìn,
"How are the northern literati?"
Yǔ Xìn replied,
"Only the stone tablet at Hanling Mountain
is worth discussing.
Xuē Dàohéng and Lú Sīdǎo have some slight skill with the brush.
The rest are like the braying of donkeys and the barking of dogs,
merely grating on the ears."
"Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Liú Zhòu,
courtesy name Kǒngzhāo,
composed a rhapsody titled "The Universe,"
believing it to be unparalleled,
and lamented:
"Scholars toil yet achieve little."
He once presented the rhapsody to Wèi Shōu without bowing,
and Shōu angrily remarked:
"Naming the rhapsody 'The Universe' is already foolish enough,
the writing is foolish too,
compared to the universe,
your limbs are even clumsier than the writing."
Zhòu, displeased,
showed it to Xíng Zǐcái instead,
who said:
"This rhapsody of yours
is like a scabies-ridden camel kneeling—utterly lacking grace."
Zhòu often considered himself a prodigy of vast knowledge,
prone to boastful speech,
frequently stating:
"If I could have a few dozen volumes of my writings passed down to posterity,
it would be worth more than Duke Jìng of Qí's thousand chariots."
From History of the Northern Dynasties
Hé Tuǒ,
courtesy name Qīfèng,
was by nature resolute and impatient,
possessed eloquence,
and was fond of criticizing people.
Sū Wēi at the time concurrently held five positions,
and the emperor personally esteemed him.
Previously, Sū Wēi had once lived in seclusion in Wǔgōng,
and Hé Tuǒ submitted a memorial stating:
"Those currently holding official positions
do not assess their own virtue and capability,
lacking the abilities of Lǚ Wàng and Fù Yuè,
yet presuming the aura of Fù Yán and Wèi Shuǐ.
They give no thought to profound worries and heavy responsibilities,
only fearing that their concurrent appointments are insufficient."
After the memorial was submitted,
Sū Wēi deeply resented him for it.
In the second year,
when Sū Wēi was evaluating literary scholars,
Hé Tuǒ again exchanged insults and slanders with him.
Sū Wēi flared up and said:
"How could Hé Tuǒ not worry about having no academic position?"
Hé Tuǒ retorted immediately:
"Without Sū Wēi, why worry about having no official duties?"
From then on, they harbored mutual enmity.
Book of Sui
Xiāo Yǐngshì,
Lǐ Línfǔ, having heard of his reputation, wished to employ him,
so summoned him for an audience.
At that time, Xiāo Yǐngshì was residing in Guǎnglíng,
observing mourning for his mother,
and thus went to the capital in mourning hemp clothes,
directly calling on Lǐ Línfǔ at the Department of State Affairs.
Lǐ Línfǔ, who had never met him before,
suddenly saw him in mourning attire,
was greatly displeased,
and immediately ordered him driven away.
Xiāo Yǐngshì was extremely indignant,
and thus composed "The Ode to Cutting Down the Cherry Tree" to satirize Lǐ Línfǔ, saying:
"Promoting the trivial substance of the useless,
sheltered by the main branch yet self-protected.
Occupying the grove without rightful claim,
monopolizing the right-hand position in the court.
Though occasionally recommended before resting,
how can it be the true flavor of harmonious broth?
His unrestrained and disrespectful nature was all of this kind.
According to the Old Book of Tang, Xiāo Yǐngshì passed the imperial examination in the 23rd year of the Kāiyuán era,
relying on his talent and looking down on others,
with no one comparable to him,
he often carried a pot of wine himself, roaming the scenic outskirts,
once resting at an inn,
drinking and reciting poetry alone.
Suddenly, a storm arrived violently,
and an old man in purple robes led a young servant to take shelter from the rain there.
Xiāo Yǐngshì, seeing his ordinary appearance,
rather wantonly insulted him.
In a short while,
the wind calmed and the rain cleared,
carriages and horses suddenly arrived,
the old man mounted his horse and departed with attendants clearing the way.
Xiāo Yǐngshì hurriedly inquired about him,
his attendants said:
"It is Minister Wáng of the Ministry of Personnel.
Xiāo Yǐngshì had often visited his residence but never met him,
and was utterly astonished.
The next day, he prepared a long letter,
and went to his residence to apologize.
Wáng ordered him brought to sit under the eaves,
reprimanded him and said:
"What I regret is not being related to you,
so I could discipline you as a family elder.
After a moment, he said:
"You bear a reputation for literary talent,
yet are so arrogant and careless,
will you stop at just passing the examination?
Xiāo Yǐngshì ended his career as a Records Clerk of Yángzhōu.
Lǐ Xiáng,
courtesy name Shěnjǐ,
possessed talent, brilliance, courage, and spirit,
yet was unrestrained and uninhibited.
He began his career as the Sheriff of Yántíng.
While at Yántíng,
during an evaluation,
he was disparaged by the Recorded Affairs Adjutant.
Xiáng said to the Regional Inspector:
"The Recorded Affairs relies on the authority of the Correction Section,
occupying a pivotal position,
to make arbitrary judgments of praise and blame.
If I, Xiáng, were to wield the brush,
I too could craft such words."
The Regional Inspector said:
"Sir, please try to critique the Recorded Affairs' evaluation report."
He then handed him the brush.
Xiáng immediately wrote the Recorded Affairs' evaluation as follows:
"Timid in deciding major cases,
fond of quibbling over minor delays.
Conceals his own lack of clarity,
claims others are universally corrupt.
Two disputants before the steps,
only cease when their sincerity is exhausted.
Prisoners in the jail,
will not emerge without a pardon."
The whole world considered it the pinnacle of witty mockery.
"Records of the Censorate"
Hán Yù, the eighteenth, is truly too frivolous.
He said to Lǐ Chéng, the twenty-sixth:
"I have been visiting with the Prime Minister Cuī Dàqún as a fellow candidate of the same year,
and he is truly exceptionally intelligent.
Lǐ said:
"In what way is he exceptional?
Hán said:
"He has been interacting with me for over twenty years,
yet has never once discussed literature with me.
Isn't this indeed a sign of extraordinary intelligence?
When Hán Yù was first demoted,
the court official Xí Kuí wrote the official document stating:
"He passed the imperial examinations early,
and also gained some reputation."
After Xí passed away,
many of his friends said:
"Xí had no virtuous sons,
could it be that he suffered from yin-toxin typhoid fever because he ate unclean food?"
Hán Yù remarked:
"Xí Shíbā ate unclean food too late."
People asked him:
"Why do you say that?"
He replied:
"His words were improper,
probably because he resented Xí's critical statement: 'also gained some reputation'"
indeed.
From "Liú Bīnkè's Casual Conversations"
Péi Xūn's appearance was short and insignificant,
yet his nature was especially straightforward and uninhibited.
Cí'ēn Temple was connected to Qǔjiāng and various areas of the capital,
each year those who had newly passed the imperial examinations
would all have their names listed here.
Xūn often traveled with relatives and acquaintances,
and when he saw the name plaques of his father and various families,
most had already passed away,
so he remarked to others:
"These are all registers of ghosts.
From "Yù Quán"
Táng jìnshì Cáo Táng's "Yóuxiān Shī",
displayed an ethereal talent.
Yuèyáng's son Lǐ Yuǎn,
whenever he recited his poems,
longed to meet the man.
One day, Cáo went to visit him,
and Lǐ hurried out to welcome him.
Cáo's appearance was stout and imposing,
so Lǐ teased him, saying:
"Before, not having seen your distinguished demeanor,
I thought you might ride a phoenix or crane.
Now that I've met you,
I fear even a sturdy water buffalo might struggle to carry you."
People of the time heard this and laughed.
"Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Emperor Xuānzong loved singing lyrics to "Bodhisattva Barbarian,"
and Hú Chǔ borrowed Wēn Tíngyún's newly composed ones,
secretly presenting them to the emperor,
enjoining him not to divulge this,
yet he promptly told others.
Because of this, he distanced himself from him.
Wēn also had a saying:
"A general seated in the secretariat."
Mocking the chancellor for being unlearned.
"Beimeng Suoyan"
During the Dàzhōng era, Grand Commandant Lǐ Déyù was demoted three times until reaching Zhūyá.
At that time, all officials in the two drafting offices were drafting edicts,
and there was often a vulgar circulated edict that said:
"A snake uses two heads,
a fox wags nine tails,
the nose is not upright yet the body claims to be upright,
the eyes are already crooked and the heart is likewise crooked.
This was slander from his enemies.
From "New Book of the South"
Xuē Néng was a jìnshì during the Huìcháng era,
and excessively arrogant.
While serving in Xīchuān,
he often belittled Zhūgě Liàng's achievements,
writing in a poem:
"Who would approve of his battle formations?
I mock his temple's appearance.
He also said:
"Better to burn the Shǔ books unread—
Lord Wǔ cannot discipline me.
He ridiculed Lǐ Bái, saying:
"Had I been born in the Kāiyuán era,
how could the name 'Lǐ Hànlín' prevail?
And further:
"Lǐ Bái ultimately has no merit,
while Táo Qián remains unshakable.
He inscribed his own collection with:
"From what era did poetry's source lose its clarity?
Everywhere, only the croaking of frogs is heard.
During the Xiántōng era,
in Jīngzhōu there was a scholar nicknamed
"Táng Wǔjīng"
who was learned and erudite.
He often said to people:
"Unworthy descendants undergo three transformations:
The first transformation is into locusts,
meaning they sell their manors to eat;
The second transformation is into bookworms,
meaning they sell their books to eat;
The third transformation is into tigers,
meaning they sell their slaves to eat.
Such people who live off these three resources exist in every era.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Zhāng Shǔ and Dù Xúnhè were candidates in the same imperial examination year,
and once, while drunk, Zhāng Shǔ teased Dù Xúnhè, saying:
"Dù Boil is fortunate to have great honor.
Dù Xúnhè asked:
"What honor?
Zhāng Shǔ said:
"Being in the same year as Gentleman Zhāng Fiftieth—how could that not be an honor?
Dù Xúnhè retorted immediately:
"It is you who are honored; how could I possibly gain honor from this?
Zhāng Shǔ laughed and said:
"Why is that?
Dù Xúnhè replied:
"Everyone under heaven only knows of Dù Xúnhè;
who on earth knows of Gentleman Zhāng Fiftieth?
From "Records of Gleaned Talks"
Lǐ Shānfǔ failed the imperial examination during the Xiántōng era,
later wandered destitute in Héshuò,
served as an aide to Lè Yànzhēn,
and harbored much resentment toward the court's officials.
He once wrote a poem:
"I advise you not to boast of your prominence,
for gains and losses in dreams are never real."
From "New Book of the South"
During the Guāngqǐ era,
Jiǎng Bō imparted cinnabar to the virtuous and amicable Wéi Zhōnglìng.
Zhāng Gǔ,
a native of Wú,
was cultured yet not impoverished.
Someone satirized him, saying:
"Zhāng Gǔ requires only a thousand loads of silk,
while Jiǎng Bō uses but a single pellet of elixir.
From "Zhíyán"
Jiǎ Wěi of the Hàn dynasty, though his literary talent did not surpass others,
was resolute and strong in debate,
causing his peers to resent him.
They nicknamed him "Iron-mouthed Jiǎ."
When commissioned to compile the Veritable Records of Emperor Gāozǔ,
he falsely claimed that Sāng Wéihàn possessed eight thousand ingots of silver upon his death,
and presented the daily records he had written to the supervising editor Wáng Jùn,
in which he fabricated faults of Dòu Zhēngù and Sū Yǔguī,
and repeatedly slandered the early achievements of court officials.
Wáng Jùn detested this,
and said to his colleagues:
"Secretary Jiǎ has sons at home,
who also need unblemished family status.
Now the entire court has been subjected to his slanders—
how can scholars advance in their careers?"
He then spoke of this before Emperor Tàizǔ,
and Jiǎ was demoted to Military Commander of Pínglú.
From Continued Accounts of the World
The Minister of Rites Cuī Yísūn,
though over eighty, incessantly sought advancement,
lacking funds in his purse,
yet he had always been a hoarder,
with a nature fond of dealing with others,
delighting in petty gains.
After being demoted,
his two sons contended over the wealth,
failing to provide him with delicacies and medical care.
He wrote reproaching his sons, saying:
"In life, there are enlightened rulers and true officials,
in death, the celestial court and underworld exist.
Without this old and decrepit one,
would they let you off?
This became a laughingstock among the officials.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Hán Zhāo served as King of Shǔ up to the position of Minister of Rites,
Grand Scholar of the Wénsī Hall,
and had a rough grasp of literature.
As for zither, chess, calligraphy, mathematics, and archery, he dabbled in them all,
thereby receiving favor from the Later Sovereign.
A court official Lǐ Táigǔ said:
"Minister Hán's skills are like unraveling sock threads—
not a single one is long."
People of the time recorded this in "Suǒ Yán." Zhāo,
courtesy name Déhuá,
was from Cháng'ān.
Yǎn, during his northern tour, appointed him as a Scholar of the Wénsī Hall.
Lǐ Táigǔ, the judgment official left in charge of the capital, said:
"In all matters, Lord Hán is like a monk shaving his head—
not an inch is long."
"Shǔ Shǐ Táowù"
Sòng Qíqiū inscribed his own steles
and often asked Hán Xīzǎi to write them,
but Xīzǎi would stuff his nose with paper.
When someone asked him why,
he replied:
"The writing stinks and is foul."
The History of Southern Táng
Sūn Chéng,
courtesy name Wéndá,
also known as Jì,
served as chancellor alongside Féng Yányǐ under Emperor Yuánzōng.
Chéng looked down upon Yányǐ's character,
once saying:
"How can one fill a golden bowl and jade cup with dog excrement?
In the *History of Southern Tang*, Jì despised Yányǐ,
telling others:
"Jade vessels and ivory cups holding filth,
phoenix trees and imperial ponds inhabited by owls and pheasants.
He was subsequently dismissed from his post as chancellor.
From *Unofficial History of Jiangnan*
When Táng Jiè served as a censor,
he reported on Wén Yànfēng presenting a brocade lantern to Consort Zhāng.
The emperor was extremely angry,
and exiled him to Chūnzhōu.
Lǐ Chéngzhī saw him off with a poem,
which contained
"Leaving the state, my body light as a leaf;
A noble reputation, through the ages weighty as mountains.
How thick-skinned are the talented companions who roamed together;
Though not yet dead, the bones of flattering villains are already cold"
as its lines.
Later, Jiè, recommended by Wén Yànfēng,
served as an official at court,
and had nothing to say.
Chéngzhī wrote to Jiè asking for the poem he had sent,
but Jiè had nothing to reply with,
so he took the poem and returned it, saying:
"I simply do not use poems with mismatched rhymes."
This was because
"mountain"
and
"cold"
had different rhymes,
hence the remark.
From "Shào's Record of Things Heard and Seen"
When Liú Gòngfù was a Jǐshìzhōng, Academician Zhèng Hóngzhōng Mù submitted a memorial requesting retirement, which passed through the Chancellery. Liú said to his colleagues:
"Hóngzhōng is requesting to retire—
how old is he?"
Someone answered:
"Zhèng is seventy-three years old."
Liú immediately said:
"We must not grant his request."
They asked:
"Why not?"
Liú said:
"Let's keep him to accompany the eighty-four-year-old one."
At that time, Duke Lù was eighty-four and had been recalled to service again.
It is said that when Duke Lù heard this,
he was quite displeased.
From "Míngdào Zálù"
Liú Gòngfù in his later years contracted a severe illness,
his beard and dandruff fell off,
his nose bridge collapsed,
and the suffering was beyond description.
One day while drinking with Dōngpō,
he intended to exchange a couplet from ancient poets, but Sū Zǐzhān abruptly said:
"When the great wind rises, oh, the eyebrows soar high;
How can I find a brave man, oh, to guard my nose bridge."
The entire company burst into loud laughter,
while Gòngfù remained silent,
feeling only sorrow and regret.
"Shìlín Guǎngjì"
One day, Sū Shì was hosting guests when one proposed a drinking game requiring using two hexagram names to illustrate a historical anecdote.
One person said:
"Lord Mèngcháng's household had three thousand retainers,
'Great Possession' 'Fellowship with Men'."
Another said:
"Emperor Guāngwǔ's troops crossed the Hūtuó River,
'Before Completion' 'After Completion'."
A third said:
"Liú Kuān's maid spilled soup on his court robes,
'Family' 'Small Preponderance'."
Sū Shì then said:
"When Niú Sēngrú and his son committed crimes,
first behead 'Small Accumulation',
then behead 'Great Accumulation'."
This was clearly referring to Wáng Ānshí and his son.
"Collection of Spitting at the King"
When Sīmǎ Wēngōng passed away,
Chéng Zhèngshū used the "Yì Shuō" to shroud him,
resembling the shape of a sealed envelope.
Dōngpō detested its absurdity and superstition,
and thus angrily mocked,
"Is this a sealed document to be sent to King Yánluó?"
"Yù Jiǎn": Wú Yáoqīng served as Gāo Pián's administrator of Yángzhōu,
concurrently holding the position of grain procurement commissioner,
and embezzled six million strings of salt and iron monopoly funds.
When Guǎnglíng city fell,
soldiers who recognized him,
Yáoqīng tried to bribe them with food.
At night, Yáoqīng escaped in disguise,
reached Chǔzhōu,
where turmoil occurred,
and he was killed by his enemies,
his corpse abandoned in the street.
His wife used paper padding and a reed coffin to bury him,
before the burial was completed,
someone fond of mischief wrote on it,
saying:
"A sealed document,
to be delivered to the Avīci Hell.
Please remove the diagonal seal,
and present it to King Yánluó."
People at the time considered it a subject of ridicule.
"Guǎnglíng Yāo Luàn Zhì"
Liú Zhēn,
courtesy name Xuānzhì,
was of a distracted disposition,
engrossed in the study of classics,
and often forgot worldly affairs.
At that time, there was a man named Liú Nè who, like Zhēn, held the position of Yìtóng.
Zhēn lived in the southern part of the city,
while Nè resided in the eastern part.
Once, Zhēn intended to visit Nè
and asked his attendant:
"Do you know where the home of Yìtóng Liú is?"
The attendant, unaware that Zhēn meant to visit Nè,
thought Zhēn was referring to his own home and replied:
"Yes, I do."
Thereupon, he led Zhēn away,
and upon knocking on the door,
Zhēn still hadn't realized the mistake,
believing they had arrived at Nè's house.
He then leaned on his saddle and shouted loudly:
"Yìtóng Liú, please come out!"
His son came to the door to greet him,
and Zhēn, surprised, said to him:
"You've come too?"
His son replied:
