"This is your own home, sir."
At this, Zhēn looked around,
and only after a long while did he realize the error.
He then scolded his attendant, saying:
"You are utterly careless!
I wanted to visit Liú Nè!"
From The History of the Northern Dynasties
Wáng Hào,
courtesy name Jìgāo,
established his reputation and conduct in youth,
but was timid and slow by nature.
He once accompanied Wén Xuān on the northern expedition,
riding a red horse.
At dawn, the horse was covered with frost,
so he could no longer recognize it,
and claimed to have lost his horse.
The patrol officer searched but could not find it.
Soon the sun rose,
the frost on the horse's body melted away completely,
and it was tied right in front of the tent.
He then said:
"My horse is still here."
From History of the Northern Dynasties
Xī Áng and Wéi Zhì were close friends.
While discussing which chancellor of the current dynasty was the most virtueless,
Xī Áng mistakenly replied:
"Wéi Ānshí."
He then fled in panic,
and encountered Jí Wēn on the street.
Jí Wēn asked why he appeared so flustered,
to which he answered:
"I was just discussing with Minister Wéi about the most virtueless chancellor of our dynasty.
I originally intended to say Jí Xū,
but mistakenly said Wéi Ānshí instead."
After speaking,
he whipped his horse and fled again,
arriving at Chancellor Fáng's residence.
Fáng Guǎn held his hand to comfort him,
but Xī Áng mistakenly named Fáng Róng in response again.
Though Xī Áng enjoyed some reputation,
he had offended three people in a single day.
The entire court sighed in regret,
and only Wéi Zhì consequently severed ties with him.
Supplement to the National History
During the Zhēnyuán era,
the Imperial Advisor Zhèng Yúnkuí and the royal physician Wáng Yànbó were neighbors.
Once, Xiāo Fǔ sought medical treatment
and mistakenly went to Yúnkuí's residence.
Yúnkuí diagnosed him,
saying:
"Your hot wind ailment is quite severe.
Fǔ then requested a prescription.
Yúnkuí said:
"For prescriptions, I'm not as skilled as my eastern neighbor, the Attending Physician Wáng.
Only then did Fǔ realize his mistake,
and he hurried away in alarm.
At that time, people in the capital would mock those who behaved improperly by saying:
"Just a case of hot wind.
Péi Zǐyǔ served as the magistrate of Xiàpī,
Zhāng Qíng was the deputy magistrate,
both were influential figures,
and skilled in speech.
Once they debated matters for a long time,
the clerks secretly remarked to each other:
"The county officials are quite at odds—
when the senior official mentions rain,
the deputy immediately speaks of clear skies;
when the deputy mentions clear skies,
the senior official promptly speaks of rain.
They remain at odds like this all day long.
From "Fēngshì Jiànwén"
Yáng Bóbó served as a deputy magistrate in a county south of the mountains,
and his wife, Madame Lù,
was from a renowned family.
The county magistrate's wife was surnamed Wǔ.
One day, she hosted a gathering for the wives of all the officials.
After they had met,
the magistrate's wife asked the deputy magistrate's wife what her surname was.
She replied,
"Surname Lù."
Next, she asked the chief clerk's wife,
who answered,
"Surname Qī."
The magistrate's wife suddenly stormed into the inner quarters,
leaving the other wives bewildered
and wanting to leave.
Hearing this, the magistrate hurried inside
and asked his wife what was wrong.
She said,
"The deputy magistrate's wife said her surname is Lù,
and the chief clerk's wife said her surname is Qī.
Because my surname is Wǔ,
they're deliberately mocking me.
If I had asked the other officials' wives,
they would surely have said their surnames were Bā or Jiǔ!"
The magistrate laughed heartily and said,
"Everyone has their own surname;
why take it this way?"
He then had his wife come out again.
From "Féngshì Jiànwén"
Táng Dynasty Minister of Works Yú Shùn considered the musical piece titled "Xiǎng Fū Lián" (Longing for the Husband),
its name inelegant,
and intended to change it.
A guest laughed and said:
"The Southern Dynasties' ministerial residence once had auspicious lotuses,
hence the song was called 'Xiàng Fǔ Lián' (Ministerial Lotus).
It was only later that people's speech corrupted it,
so it need not be changed.
From "Supplement to the National History"
According to an old account, Dǒng Zhòngshū's tomb
required all visitors to dismount upon arrival,
hence it was called Dismount Mound,
which was later mispronounced as Shrimp Tomb Mound.
Nowadays, people in Jīngxiāng call embankments "tíliú",
while those in Jiàng call cauldrons "fù",
all being errors perpetuated by common usage.
There was a candidate for the imperial examination in the Táng dynasty surnamed Shàn,
who registered for the examination with the officials.
The official mistakenly wrote it as Dān,
and the candidate complained, saying:
"Although my clan is humble,
I do not wish my surname to be altered by others.
I beg you to correct it."
The official said:
"What difference does it make whether the character has a square opening or a pointed one?"
Shàn replied:
"If it makes no difference,
then could Tāizhōu Wú'ér County be changed to Jīngzhōu Liǎo'ér County?"
The examiner had no response.
From "The Collection of Good Jests"
In a rustic temple, there was a painting of Hòu Jì's mother stepping on a giant's footprint and giving birth to Jì, then abandoning him;
and of his precociousness in planting trees;
when he grew up, he begged for grain seeds from Shénnóng;
Shénnóng had Mǎ Huáng carry the grain seeds to bestow upon him;
thus, countless leeches were painted,
representing Mǎ Huáng.
Leeches are also known as Mǎ Huáng.
"Ěr Yǎ Yì"
Outside Chénzhōu City stands the Ètái Temple,
the place where Confucius was cut off from provisions.
Now inside there is a single character
"King Buddha"
said to be from the old plaque "King Wenxuan" marking Confucius' statue.
Due to wind and rain erosion,
only one
"King"
character remained,
and later generations forced a connection,
making it "One-Character King Buddha."
The attendant's headdress and robes still resemble those of Yán Yuān,
much like Dù Fǔ's case being transformed into the Ten Aunts,
showing that across the land,
such instances are too numerous to count.
from "Jī Lè Piān"
In Wēnzhōu there was a local earth god,
Dù Shíyí who had no husband,
and Wǔ Cuōxū Xiànggōng who had no wife.
The local people welcomed Dù Shíyí to match with Wǔ Cuōxū Xiànggōng, combining them into one temple.
When asked who Dù Shíyí was,
they said it was Dù Shíyí (the official title),
and who Wǔ Cuōxū was,
they said it was Wǔ Zǐxū.
"Xiè Shàng Fǔ Tán" In the southern region there was a spring,
from which many cinnamon leaves flowed out,
hence it was named Liúguì Spring.
Later a house was built over it,
which became the Hànzǔ Temple for worshipping him;
there was also a Xū Temple,
whose statue had its beard divided, called the five-whiskered one,
and it also had spiritual responses.
"Guó Shǐ Bǔ" In Jiānglíng, there were villagers serving the god Wǔ Zǐxū,
but mistakenly called him Wǔ Zīxū,
so they painted five gentlemen,
and all prayed to them in sacrifice, saying:
"First whisker,
second whisker up to fifth whisker.
"Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Someone came from the Central Plains,
where in the north there was a Temple of the Ox King.
A hundred oxen were depicted on the wall,
with the Ox King among them.
When asked who the Ox King was,
it turned out to be Rǎn Bóniú.
Thus, Bóniú became the Ox King.
From "Fǔ Tán"
The temple of Emperor Hàn Gāozǔ in Xiāngzhōu,
originally signified Jiāo Fǔ presenting his jade pendant by the Hàn River,
but is now dedicated to Emperor Gāozǔ,
which is an error.
"Records Passed Down"
In Hénán, on Guǎngwǔ Mountain, there is the Liúguì Spring.
Shǐ Sīmíng built a temple for Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn on its summit.
On it
In Wénzhōu there was a bridge called Yīnpíng.
In the early years of the Chúnxī era,
a certain prefect erected a large inscribed stone beneath the bridge,
stating
"The Route by Which Dèng Ài Captured Shǔ"
and passersby laughed at it.
From "Records of the Old Study"
King Qián named his residence
"the Hair-Holding Hall,"
but in the Wú dialect,
"hold"
and "hateful"
sound similar and are easily confused.
Thus, the people of Qiántáng said of the place:
"This is His Majesty's Hateful Outburst Hall.
Péng Láng Xiǎo Gū: In the Jiangnan region, there are large and small mountains,
standing majestically alone,
yet common folk transformed "gū" (solitary) into "this."
Beside the river, there is a stone jetty called Péng Jī,
which was then changed to Péng Láng Jī,
and it is said
"Péng Láng is Xiǎo Gū's husband."
The temple on Xiǎo Gū Mountain has a statue of a woman,
with an imperial plaque naming it the Shèngmǔ Temple.
At Lóngmén Mountain in Xījīng, the Yī River flows between,
with rapids and gate-like formations above,
appearing like twin towers when viewed from afar,
hence it is called
"Quē Sāi" (Tower Pass)
and at the mountain pass, there is a temple known as
"Quē Kǒu Temple" (Tower Pass Temple)
Its statue is very fierce, holding a knife and pressing on the knee while seated,
called
"Huō Kǒu Dàwáng" (Gap King)
"Guī Tián Lù"
Cáo Cāo and Kǒng Róng had long harbored mutual suspicions and animosity,
and Xì Lǜ further fabricated accusations against him,
prompting Lù Cuì to submit a false report against Róng, stating:
"Róng, while previously in Běihǎi,
witnessed the royal house in turmoil,
and gathered followers,
intending to plot rebellion,
saying, 'I am a descendant of the great sage,
yet was destroyed by the Sòng,
why must the one who possesses the world
necessarily be of the Liú family?'
Moreover, as one of the nine ministers,
Róng did not adhere to court deliberations,
wore plain headgear and traveled incognito,
rashly intruding into the palace quarters.
He also previously engaged in unrestrained and reckless talk with the commoner Mí Héng,
saying: 'What kinship is there between father and son?
Examining its fundamental intent,
it is merely the result of lust!
As for the son's relation to the mother,
what kinship is there again?
It is like placing an object in a jar—
once it leaves, separation occurs.'
Subsequently, he and Héng praised each other,
with Héng saying to Róng:
'Zhòngní lives on.'
Róng replied:
'Yán Huí is reborn.'
Such great impiety and lack of dao,
deserves the severest punishment."
The memorial was submitted,
and he was imprisoned and executed in the market.
Hòu Hàn Shū
Zhǒng Huì, as the Grand General Simǎ's
close associate,
heard of Jī Kāng's reputation and paid him a visit.
Huì was a renowned noble scion,
esteemed and favored for his talent and ability,
riding sturdy steeds and clad in light silks,
with a retinue of followers like clouds.
Kāng was sitting with his legs sprawled, forging metal,
and did not show Huì any courtesy upon his arrival.
"Weishi Chunqiu" For a long while, they exchanged not a single word,
and Zhǒng rose to leave.
Kāng said:
"What did you hear that brought you here,
and what have you seen that makes you leave?"
Zhǒng replied:
"I came having heard what I heard,
and I leave having seen what I saw."
"Shishuo" Kāng was on close terms with Lǚ Ān of Dōngpíng,
when Ān encountered legal trouble,
Kāng went to the prison to vindicate him.
Zhǒng Huì at court,
denounced Kāng, saying:
"Now the imperial way is open and bright,
all within the four seas follow like the wind,
the remote borders have no deceitful followers,
the streets and lanes harbor no dissenting voices.
Yet Kāng above does not submit to the Son of Heaven,
below does not serve the princes and nobles,
disdains his time and scorns the world,
refuses to be of use to society,
brings no benefit to the present,
and corrupts the customs.
In the past, Tàigōng executed Huá Shì,
and Confucius put Shǎozhèng Mǎo to death,
because they relied on their talent,
to disrupt the community and mislead the masses.
If Kāng is not executed,
there is no way to purify the Kingly Way."
Thereupon, Kāng was arrested and imprisoned.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng's Chief Secretary Lú Zhì and Jī's younger brother Yún had conflicting opinions,
and the Eunuch Mèng Jiǔ requested to be appointed as Magistrate of Hándān from Yǐng.
Yǐng instructed to hand it over to Yún,
who was then the Left Marshal,
and said:
"A person who has suffered punishment
should not govern the people."
Upon hearing this, Jiǔ resented Yún,
and together with Zhì, they slandered and framed him daily.
When Jī suffered a major defeat at Qīlǐ Jiàn,
Jiǔ falsely accused Jī of causing it through rebellion,
so Yǐng sent Qiān Xiù to execute Jī.
None of the soldiers failed to shed tears.
On that day, heaven and earth were shrouded in fog,
a great wind broke trees,
and a foot of snow covered the level ground.

"Bié Zhuàn": Initially, when Lù Kàng executed Bù Chǎn, his entire household of a hundred people was wiped out, which was criticized by the discerning. When Jī and Yún were harmed, their three clans were left with no survivors.
"Gān Bǎo Jìn Jì"
Xiàowǔ was very close and respectful to Wáng Guó and Wáng Yǎ.
Yǎ recommended Wáng Xún to the emperor,
and the emperor wished to see him.
Once, at night, he was conversing with Guó Bǎo and Yǎ,
and the emperor was slightly intoxicated.
He ordered to summon Xún.
As Xún was about to arrive,
he had already heard the sound of the envoy,
and Guó Bǎo, knowing his own talent was inferior to Xún,
feared that his favor would be lost.
So he said,
"Wáng Xún is a renowned figure at present;
Your Majesty should not meet him while intoxicated.
It would be better to summon him by a separate decree."
The emperor agreed with his words,
considering them loyal,
and thus did not meet Xún.
"Shìshuō"
Wáng Xù repeatedly slandered Yīn Jīngzhōu to Wáng Guóbǎo,
Yīn was troubled by this,
and sought a strategy from Wáng Dōngtíng,
who said:
"You just need to visit Wáng Xù frequently,
and each time you go, have others leave,
then discuss other matters.
In this way,
the friendship between the two Wángs will be broken.
Yīn followed this advice,
Guóbǎo saw Wáng Xù and asked:
"Lately, what have you been discussing in private with Zhòngkān?
Xù replied:
"It's just our usual interactions,
nothing else was discussed.
Guóbǎo believed Xù was hiding something from him,
and indeed their affection gradually waned,
thus the slander ceased.
Xiè Tiǎo looked down upon Jiāng Shí's character.
Shí often visited Tiǎo,
and Tiǎo once mentioned having a poem,
called for his attendants to fetch it,
but then immediately stopped them.
Shí asked the reason,
to which he replied:
"It's certainly not urgent anyway."
Shí took this as belittling himself.
Later, when Shí and his younger brother Sì, Liú Fǎng, and Liú Yàn all went together to visit Tiǎo,
Tiǎo said to Shí:
"One might say this is like the twin flows of two rivers"
using this to mock him.
Shí became increasingly unable to bear it,
until this point,
when he fabricated charges and had Tiǎo killed.
Before his death, Tiǎo said to his gate guest:
"Take this message to Lord Shěn,
since you are compiling the history of three dynasties,
you must not let this go unrecorded."
From History of the Southern Dynasties
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng questioned Xú Chī about the classics, histories, and various schools of thought,
but had not yet discussed Buddhism.
Chī debated broadly and comprehensively,
responding as swiftly as an echo.
The emperor expressed admiration and favor,
and his treatment grew increasingly generous.
Zhū Yì was displeased,
and said to a close associate:
"Old man Xú moves between the two palaces,
and is gradually coming to pressure me.
I must take early action."
He then seized an opportunity to tell the emperor:
"Chī is elderly,
and also loves springs and rocks,
wishing for a commandery."
The emperor thought Chī desired this,
so summoned him.
Chī said:
"Xīn'ān has magnificent landscapes,
where Rèn Fǎng and others have served.
You shall govern this commandery for me."
Thus he was appointed as governor of Xīn'ān.
Dàowǔ favored and treated Lǐ Shùn well,
no matter how significant or trivial the affairs of state,
he was involved in all of them,
which Cuī Hào detested.
Shùn was sent to Liángzhōu twelve times in total,
and Tàiwǔ praised his ability.
However, Měngxùn often feasted and socialized with Shùn,
and made quite a few rebellious remarks.
Fearing Shùn might leak them,
he slipped gold and treasures into Shùn's bosom,
thus Měngxùn's crimes and offenses went unreported.
Additionally, a Western Regions monk named Tánwúchàn possessed mystical arts,
and an edict was issued to summon him to Liángzhōu.
Shùn accepted bribes from Měngxùn,
allowing him to be killed.
Hào secretly reported this to the emperor,
but the emperor did not act on it.
In the fifth year of Tàiyán,
when discussing the campaign against Liángzhōu,
Shùn argued that Liángzhōu lacked water and grass,
making a distant expedition inadvisable,
while Cuī Hào firmly believed it should be undertaken.
The emperor followed Hào's advice.
Upon arriving at Gūzāng,
they found ample water and grass.
In a letter to Jǐngmù, the emperor expressed considerable dissatisfaction with Shùn.
Later, he said to Hào:
"What you said back then,
has indeed come true now.
After conquering Liángzhōu,
upon hearing that Shùn had accepted Měngxùn's gold and allowed Tánwúchàn's death,
he grew even more displeased with him.
Later, when assigning ranks and positions to the officials,
Shùn engaged in bribery,
and the grading was unfair.
Xú Jié, a man from Liángzhōu, exposed the matter,
and Hào further slandered him.
The emperor was enraged,
and executed Shùn west of the city.
Several years after Shùn's death,
his cousin Xiàobó gained Tàiwǔ's
trust and held a key position in the court.
After Hào was executed,
the emperor, still very angry,
said to Xiàobó:
"Your cousin in the past, though he harmed the state,
his words and intent were not to this extent.
It was Cuī Hào who caused your cousin's death.
From "Běishǐ": The matter of Hào framing Lǐ Shùn
is also recorded in the section on dreams.
Prince Péngchéng Tuán had rendered meritorious service to the state.
The Minister of Works Gāo Zhǎo was by nature cruel and obstinate.
His niece had entered the palace as a consort.
When Empress Shùn passed away,
the emperor intended to make her the new empress,
but Tuán firmly insisted it was improper.
Zhǎo bore a grudge against him for this,
and enlisted Wèi Yǎn and Gāo Zǔzhēn to testify that Tuán was plotting treason.
Emperor Yǒngpíng believed them,
summoned Tuán,
and hosted a banquet for him within the palace,
where he was poisoned to death. It was claimed:
"He passed away from excessive drunkenness."
Tuán's consort, Lady Lǐ,
who was the daughter of Minister of Works Lǐ Chōng,
wailed loudly, saying:
"Gāo Zhǎo has wrongfully slain a loyal and virtuous man.
If the Way of Heaven has any power,
you too shall one day suffer as I do."
Later, when Zhǎo was executed in this very chamber,
commentators recognized it as retribution.
《Book of Wèi》
Gāo Lóngzhī, trusted by Shénwǔ,
was inherently insidious and malicious.
Cuī Xiàofēn, the Commandant with Equal Honors to the Three Excellencies, had failed to form a marriage alliance with him,
and Tàipú Qīng Rèn Jí had jointly engaged in schemes,
yet they were at odds with each other.
Yuán Yàn, the Governor of Yíng Province, made requests and sought favors,
but they were not fulfilled,
so Gāo Lóngzhī fabricated charges against them,
and had them executed.
In the end, his own household was utterly destroyed.
Commentators say this was retribution.
From "The History of the Northern Dynasties."
Zhūgě Yǐng,
favored by Emperor Yáng,
came and went in the emperor's bedchamber.
Whenever the emperor held private banquets for him,
he would share mats and couches with the empress and imperial consorts.
Taking advantage of these opportunities,
he often engaged in slander and defamation.
People of the time called him "Yě Gě."
From *The Continued Tales of the World*.
Lǐ Jìng defeated the Tūjué,
captured Jiélì,
Wēn Yànbó envied his achievement,
slandering Lǐ Jìng's army as lacking discipline,
causing rare treasures from the enemy to be scattered among the chaotic troops.
Tàizōng severely reprimanded him.
Not long after,
Tàizōng said to Lǐ Jìng:
"Previously, someone slandered you,
but now I have realized the truth,
do not hold it against me.
Old Book of Táng
Emperor Tàizōng returned from Liáodōng and departed from Dìngzhōu,
falling ill on the journey.
Liú Jì and the Secretariat Director Mǎ Zhōu entered for an audience.
After Jì and Zhōu exited,
Chǔ Suíliáng inquired about the emperor's condition,
to which Jì tearfully replied:
"The imperial body suffers from swelling,
causing extreme worry and fear.
Suíliáng falsely accused him, saying:
"Jì stated, 'State affairs need not be worried about,
we should just follow the precedents of Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng by installing the young heir.'
Execute any senior official with rebellious intentions,
and stability will naturally follow.
After Emperor Tàizōng recovered from illness,
he summoned them to inquire about the matter.
Jì responded truthfully,
and cited Mǎ Zhōu to corroborate his account.
Zhōu's testimony matched Jì's,
yet Suíliáng persistently insisted on his accusation.
Thus Jì was ordered to commit suicide.
《Old Book of Táng》
Xǔ Jìngzōng, having assisted in establishing Empress Wǔ,
then plotted to frame Zhǎngsūn Wújì,
sending someone to submit a sealed memorial,
accusing Investigating Censor Lǐ Cháo of colluding with Wújì in a rebellion plot.
The emperor ordered Jìngzōng to interrogate him,
and Jìngzōng said:
"Wújì conspired with the previous court to seize the empire,
and everyone admired his wisdom;
he served as chancellor for thirty years,
and the common people feared his authority;
if he were to rally his followers and summon his accomplices,
it would surely bring deep worry to the ancestral temple.
He also cited the case of Bó Zhāo from Emperor Wén of Hàn.
The emperor listened to his argument,
and exiled Wújì to Qiánzhōu.
Jìngzōng then sent Yuán Gōngyú, the Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, to Qiánzhōu,
to re-interrogate Wújì about the rebellion charges.
Gōngyú pressured Wújì,
forcing him to hang himself.
(From his biography) Emperor Gāozōng wished to install Wǔ Zhāoyí as empress,
but Chǔ Suìliáng firmly opposed it,
yet the empress was established.
Suìliáng was demoted to Military Governor of Tánzhōu,
then transferred to Guìzhōu as Military Governor,
and Xǔ Jìngzōng and Lǐ Yìfǔ memorialized,
stating:
"The rebellious plot fabricated by Zhǎngsūn Wújì
was also incited by Suìliáng.
(From his biography) Furthermore, to curry favor with the empress,
they accused Suìliáng of secretly plotting treason,
and because Guìzhōu was a strategic military location,
Suìliáng had been appointed Governor of Guìzhōu,
actually to serve as external support,
so he was further demoted to Governor of Àizhōu.
(From Hán Yuàn's biography) Zhǎngsūn Wújì and Chǔ Suìliáng had long-standing grievances with Dàozōng, Prince of Jiāngxià,
and falsely accused him of being close to Fáng Yì'ài.
He was exiled to Yìzhōu,
and died of illness on the way.
Wújì, because Prince Wú Lǐ Kè was of close imperial relation and highly esteemed,
and admired both in and out of court,
slandered and had him killed using the Yì'ài affair,
to eliminate public hope.
Kè said:
"If the state has any divine power,
may Wújì's clan be exterminated,
and Suìliáng also slandered to death.
Liú Jì had offended Emperor Gāozōng over the intention to install Lady Wǔ,
and Wújì and Suìliáng did not comply,
leading to Wújì's exile to Qiánzhōu and suicide,
and Suìliáng's demotion to Àizhōu where he died.
The interplay of fortune and misfortune,
is recorded in detail in the "New Book of Táng."
Táng imperial clansman Wú Guó Gōng Xiàoyì had achieved merit in defeating Xú Jìngyè,
and his contemporary reputation grew even greater.
Wǔ Chéngsì deeply resented him,
and had someone falsely accuse him.
Xiàoyì himself said:
"I ran around the rabbit,
the rabbit is always in the moon,
the moon being close to heaven should have a share of heaven."
Zétiān, because Xiàoyì had often rendered service,
commuted his death penalty to exile,
and he soon died in Dānzhōu.
《Continuation of A New Account of the Tales of the World》 Choosing Guests for Feasts Empress Wǔ prohibited slaughter.
Right Supplements Omission official Zhāng Dé had a son born for three days,
and privately slaughtered a sheep,
to gather his colleagues for a feast.
Supplements Omission Dù Sù concealed a piece of meat,
and submitted a memorial accusing him.
The next day,
Empress Dowager facing the assembly said to Dé:
"I heard you had a son,
very pleased."
Dé bowed in thanks,
Empress Dowager said:
"Where did you get the meat?"
Dé kowtowed and admitted his crime,
Empress Dowager said:
"I prohibit slaughter,
but joyous and mournful occasions are not included,
however from now on when you invite guests,
you must also choose them."
She showed Sù's memorial to him,
Sù was greatly ashamed,
the entire court wished to spit in his face.
End
Yán Tǐngzhī served as the governor of Jiàngjùn.
Emperor Xuánzōng intended to promote and employ him,
but Lǐ Línfǔ harbored jealousy and envy.
He summoned Tǐngzhī's younger brother, Sǔnzhī.
Upon arriving at the gate,
he reminisced about their old friendship, saying:
"I should appoint you as an assistant minister.
He further stated:
"The emperor holds your esteemed elder brother in high regard,
so you must devise a plan.
Once he enters the capital and is received in audience,
he will surely be given an important position.
He instructed Sǔnzhī
to obtain a petition from Jiàngjùn stating:
"He is suffering from a minor ailment,
and requests to come to the capital for medical treatment.
Lǐ Línfǔ then presented the petition,
reporting to the emperor:
"Tǐngzhī is advanced in years,
and has recently been afflicted with an illness,
so he should be granted a sinecure position.
Emperor Xuánzōng sighed in astonishment for a long time,
and Lǐ Línfǔ recommended appointing him as an assistant minister of the household,
ordering him to recuperate in the eastern capital.
Lú Qǐ envied Zhāng Yì's reputation for integrity and moral uprightness,
but had no means to frame him.
As military operations were underway on the western frontier,
Lú Qǐ feigned a request to take command.
The emperor firmly deemed it inappropriate,
and instead recommended Zhāng Yì as Vice Minister of the Secretariat,
appointing him Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng and Lǒngyòu.
Ultimately, Zhāng Yì was killed by mutinous soldiers.
(Old Book of Táng)
Diànzhōng Shì Yùshǐ Zhèng Dān was close to Zhāng Yì,
and whenever Lú Qǐ took a daytime nap,
he would visit Yì.
Qǐ became aware of this,
and one day, he pretended to sleep soundly,
waiting for Dān to come as expected.
Just as Dān was speaking with Yì,
Qǐ suddenly arrived at Yì's chamber.
Dān hurriedly avoided Qǐ,
but Qǐ immediately began discussing confidential matters.
Yì said:
"Diànzhōng Shì Yùshǐ Zhèng Dān is here."
Qǐ feigned surprise and said:
"What was just discussed
is not for others to hear."
At that time, the Sānsīshǐ was investigating Dān's case with Yǐng,
and before the case was concluded, Dān was executed by memorial,
while Yǐng was demoted to Huánzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yì was soon removed from his post as chancellor,
and sent out to govern Fèngxiáng.
The emperor
Yǎng Xiá of the Shangqing Palace
was a maidservant of Dòu Cān.
After Dòu Cān was exiled to Huānzhōu,
his family assets were confiscated and she entered the palace,
later serving at Dézōng's side.
The Emperor once asked her:
"Dòu Cān's wealth
not only supported assassins,
but was also exceptionally vast,
involving corrupt gains.
Previously, an enormous amount of silverware was surrendered to the government."
Shàngqīng wept and replied:
"Dòu Cān served from Censor-in-chief to Chief Minister,
for six years in total,
with monthly income reaching hundreds of thousands.
Bestowed rewards were beyond measure.
The silverware sent from Chēnzhōu for government surrender
were all imperial gifts.
During the inventory process,
I personally witnessed in Chēnzhōu how prefectural officials, currying favor with Lù Zhì's decree,
scraped off the inscriptions of provincial governors' names and titles from the silverware,
falsely labeling them as corrupt goods.
I beg Your Majesty to investigate."
Thereupon the Emperor ordered Dòu Cān's confiscated silverware brought forth,
and examination confirmed the scraped areas exactly matched Shàngqīng's account.
This occurred in the twelfth year of the Zhēnyuán era.
Dézōng further inquired about the assassin support matter.
Shàngqīng said:
"This never actually existed,
but was entirely fabricated by Lù Zhì to frame him,
who had people spread these rumors."
Dézōng finally achieved full realization,
and grew furious,
exclaiming of Lù Zhì:
"This old petty official - I removed his green robe and granted him purple,
often even addressing him as 'Lù the Ninth'.
Just when I had appointed Dòu Cān
and found complete satisfaction,
he made me wrongly execute him.
Once power fell into his hands,
his weakness exceeded even clay."
He then issued an edict exonerating Dòu Cān.
Meanwhile, Péi Yánlíng detected Lù Zhì's waning favor,
and freely slandered him,
seizing opportunities to attack.
Lù Zhì consequently suffered condemnation without reprieve.
Later Shàngqīng received special pardon,
had her name removed from registry to become a Taoist nun,
and eventually married Jīn Zhōngyì.
Though Lù Zhì's disciples mostly achieved prominent positions,
none dared transmit this account,
thus the affair remained utterly unknown.
From Collected Accounts of the Unusual
Lǐ Shèng quelled the rebellion of Zhū Cǐ,
and Emperor Dézōng observed the recaptured city.
The victory proclamation stated:
"I have already cleansed the palace grounds,
and reverently visited the imperial tombs.
The bells and stands remain undisturbed,
the ancestral temple appears as before.
The Emperor wept uncontrollably,
and all attendants in the six palaces sobbed.
This victory proclamation was composed by Yú Gōngyì.
Commentators noted that for court victory proclamations,
without such writing,
it wouldn't be Yú Gōngyì.
Later, he incurred Lù Zhì's jealousy,
was falsely accused of improper family conduct,
granted one volume of the "Classic of Filial Piety",
and thus ended his life in hardship.
"Supplement to the National History" records that people lamented his talent,
and despised Lù Zhì for his narrow-minded impatience.
"Old Book of Tang"
Tāng Cì was unjustly demoted,
for a long time stranded in barbaric lands,
his heart filled with melancholy.
Hence, he collected stories of loyal and virtuous individuals from antiquity who suffered exile,
although they faced death,
yet the ruler remained unaware.
He composed three chapters entitled "Biàn Bàng Luè".
He presented them to Dézōng,
who read them with anger,
saying to those around him:
"Tāng Cì compares me to the foolish rulers of old."
When Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he was recalled,
and was promoted to the position of Zhōngshū Shèrén.
As Xiànzōng read through the texts,
he found the three chapters submitted by Tāng Cì in the imperial archives,
and praised them,
telling the scholar Shěn Chuánshī:
"The writings submitted by Tāng Cì on refuting slander
are something rulers should frequently review.
I suspect the collection is not complete;
order Chuánshī to expand them into ten volumes,
titled 'Yuán Hé Biàn Bàng Luè'.
Its preface states: 'The sage's virtue first clarifies,
whence can slander arise'."
"Continued Records of the Shìshuō"
Lǐ Féngjí,
styled Xūzhōu,
was innately treacherous and jealous, harming the virtuous and allying with disgruntled court officials.
He fabricated slanderous rumors
and employed countless methods to inflict harm.

Péi Dù, relying on Lǐ Shēn and Wéi Chǔhòu, resolved the situation. Féngjí allied with Wáng Shǒuchéng, who told Emperor Jìngzōng that Shēn had allegedly requested the establishment of Shēn Wáng as crown prince.
Consequently, Shēn was demoted to Duānzhōu
as a military advisor. Court officials who echoed Féngjí's views included
Zhāng Yòuxīn, Lǐ Xùzhī, Zhāng Quányú, Liú Qīchǔ, Lǐ Yú, Chéng Xīfàn, Jiāng Qià, and Lǐ Zhòngyán,
collectively known as the "Eight Passes and Sixteen Sons."
Among them, Yòuxīn and seven others held key positions,
while eight additional followers attached themselves to them.
The emperor...
Lǐ Féngjí detested Lǐ Shēn, Zhāng Yòuxīn, Lǐ Xùzhī, and Liú Qīchǔ,
acting as their falcon and hound in jointly inciting trouble.
Lǐ Shēn was demoted to Military Advisor of Duānzhōu,
and court officials submitted memorials to congratulate,
even going to the Secretariat to congratulate the chancellor.
Upon reaching the gate,
the gatekeeper stopped them,
saying:
"Vice Rectifier Zhāng is in the chancellor's residence."
Shortly after,
Zhāng Yòuxīn emerged sweating,
and saluted the assembled officials collectively, saying:
"Regarding the affair at Duānxī,
I, Yòuxīn, dare not yield credit to many;
all retreated in fear of him."
Together with Lǐ Xùzhī and others, they were known at the time as the Eight Passes and Sixteen Sons.
"Continued Accounts of the World"
Péi Dù had achievements in using the military to suppress rebels,
of which Huángfǔ Tuán harbored resentment,
and he, along with Lǐ Féngjì and Lìnghú Chǔ, combined forces to push Dù aside.
Cúi Qún, stationed at Dàyuán, had a public reputation
and was highly respected by the gentry.
He repeatedly spoke of the abuses in the current administration,
which Tuán disliked.
During discussions about honoring Emperor Xiànzōng's title,
Tuán presented a memorial stating:
"Recently, when the courtiers discussed offering a title,
Cúi Qún was reluctant
about the two characters 'Filial Virtue'
for Your Majesty."
Emperor Xiànzōng became angry and dismissed Qún,
appointing him as an envoy to Hunan for observation.
In the "Old Táng Records", when Hán Yù reached Cháozhōu, he submitted a memorial,
which moved the emperor to remorse;
he wished to reinstate him.
However, Tuán had long been wary of Yù's candor,
and therefore reported that Yù remained reckless and blunt,
suggesting that he should first be transferred internally,
and thus Yù was appointed as governor of Yuánzhōu.
In the "New Táng Records"...
Duke Huán of Qí had many favored consorts within his palace,
including seven beloved women treated as wives,
who were his aunts and sisters.
He carried women on his back while meeting with feudal lords.
Guǎn Zhòng explained to the lords:
"Our lord has a carbuncle sore on his back,
and without a woman,
the sore will not heal."
《Lùnhéng》records: Duke Huán's palace contained seven hundred women in a female market,
which the people of the state criticized.
Therefore, Guǎn Zhòng deliberately established three marital homes,
to conceal Duke Huán's faults from harming his reputation among the people.
《Zhànguócè》
Xià Jī was the mother of Chén Dàfū Zhēng Shū,
whose appearance was exquisite.
Thrice she regained youth in old age,
thrice she became a queen,
and feudal lords contended for her, none not bewitched.
Lord Líng of Chén, along with Kǒng Níng and Yí Fù, all had illicit relations with her.
Sometimes they wore her clothes,
sometimes adorned with her accessories.
They played at court, exposing their kneepads.
From "Biographies of Exemplary Women"
Queen Dowager Xuān of Qín was in love with Wèi Chǒufū.
When the Queen Dowager was gravely ill and nearing death,
she issued an order:
"For my burial,
Wèi Chǒufū must be buried alive with me.
Wèi Chǒufū was deeply troubled by this,
so Yōng Ruì pleaded on his behalf to the Queen Dowager,
saying:
"Do you believe the dead retain consciousness?"
The Queen Dowager replied:
"They do not.
Yōng Ruì then said:
"If Your Majesty's wise spirit knows that the dead lack consciousness,
why would you pointlessly bury someone you love in life with the unconscious dead?
If the dead do possess consciousness,
the late king has accumulated resentment for a long time.
Your Majesty would have no means to atone for your faults,
how could you spare attention for your affair with Wèi Chǒufū?
The Queen Dowager said:
"Well said.
She then rescinded the order.
From "Strategies of the Warring States"
Jìn Liú Bǎo,
styled Dàozhēn,
when his daughter-in-law first entered the household,
sent a maid to tidy up.
Liú teased her intensely,
but the maid firmly refused.
Liú then knelt and kowtowed,
and the maid, out of fear, complied.
The next day,
he told others:
"The hand push is indeed a divine thing,
with one gesture the maid submitted to lust."
From "Yǔ Lín"
Yán Yánzhī had a beloved concubine,
without her he could not eat his fill,
nor sleep peacefully.
The concubine, relying on his favor, once pushed Yánzhī off the bed, causing him injury,
and Yán Jùn killed her.
Yánzhī deeply mourned and regretted it,
often sitting by the spirit tablet crying:
"It was the nobleman who killed you,
not I who killed you.
While mourning on a winter day,
he suddenly saw the concubine pushing the screen to crush him,
Yánzhī, terrified, fell to the ground,
and fell ill as a result.
"History of the Southern Dynasties"
Wáng Yīngwǔ,
was a palace maid serving Dōngyáng Princess.
Initially, the princess had a servant named Chén Tiānxīng,
whom Yīngwǔ raised as her own son,
and they engaged in illicit relations.
Yīngwǔ and Tiānxīng both participated with the main criminal Shào in witchcraft practices.
The princess passed away.
Fearing that the plot would be exposed, Shào
married her to Shǐxīng Prince Jùn's assistant Shěn Huáiyuǎn as a concubine.
Later, the matter was exposed,
and the Emperor was shocked and dismayed.
He immediately seized Yīngwǔ's household,
discovering written correspondence between Shào and Jùn,
all containing incantations related to witchcraft.
After Shào's rebellion failed,
his wife, Lady Yīn, was sentenced to death at the dōngweǐ.
Before execution, she said to prison official Jiāng Kè:
"Your family destroys its own kin,
why wrongfully kill innocent people of the world?"
Kè replied,
"Is not receiving the empress title a crime?"
Lady Yīn responded,
"This was temporary power,
it was intended for Yīngwǔ to become the empress."
Huáiyuǎn was implicated for taking in Yīngwǔ,
and Xiàowǔ banished him to Guǎngzhōu.
His brother Huáiwén consequently lost his position and became an editor serving as a supervisory censor.
"Nán Shǐ Shào Huáiwén zhuàn" Yīngwǔ was as delicate as a flower in royal attire,
in front of the mirror her eyebrows styled anew in the palace.
She was gradually taught to have a beauty like Hóng'ér,
yet was not wed to Shěn, an official of the Southern Court.
"Poem Comparing to Hóng'ér"
Zhāng Guī,
courtesy name Zǔyì,
after returning to Wú lived in a mansion of great wealth,
with singing girls filling his chambers.
Some criticized him for keeping singing girls in his declining years.
Guī replied:
"I loved music since youth,
but only in old age have I come to understand it.
Of all the desires in my life,
none remain anymore,
except that I cannot give this up."
History of the Southern Dynasties
When Emperor Xiàowǔ of the Northern Wei was in Luòyáng,
among his elder sisters, three were unmarried.
One was called Princess Píngyuán,
who was a full sister of Míngyuè and Nányáng King Bǎojù;
the second was called Princess Āndé,
daughter of Qīnghé King Yì;
the third was Zhílí,
also given the title of Princess.
The emperor held an internal banquet and instructed the women to recite poetry,
and someone recited a Bào Zhào yuèfǔ song, saying:
"Nine-fold palace gates, nine inner chambers,
I wish to follow the bright moon into your embrace."
The emperor then took Míngyuè into the palace.
Zhílí hanged herself.
Yǔwén Tài ordered the Yuán clan princes to capture Míngyuè and kill her.
“Biographical Records”
Shénwǔ intended to go to Luòyáng,
Jīngzhào Wáng Áng's younger brother Zhòngjǐng abandoned his wife and children,
chasing the imperial carriage to Cháng'ān,
where he was enfeoffed as Shùnyáng Wáng.
After Zhòngjǐng lost his wife and children,
he married the former wife of Ěrzhū Fūguāng, Yěliè shì.
Originally a courtesan,
she was beautiful,
and Zhòngjǐng valued her greatly.
After several years,
his former wife Shūyuán Hé shì came secretly from Luòyáng.
Yěliè then moved to live in a separate residence.
After a long time,
she committed adultery,
the affair was exposed,
and an edict ordered Zhòngjǐng to kill her.
Zhòngjǐng's affection for her grew even stronger,
so he falsely killed a maidservant,
covered her corpse,
and conducted a grand burial as a substitute.
Later, he plotted to murder Yuán Hé,
but a slave reported it to Zhōu Wéndì,
who acted according to the report,
issuing an edict to cane Zhòngjǐng one hundred times.
Yěliè was exiled for confessing,
yet Zhòngjǐng continued to see her secretly,
and when another informant came forward,
an edict ordered him to be heavily caned one hundred times,
stripping him of all official positions and titles.
Zhòngjǐng still persisted in the affair.
Later, Zhōu Wén petitioned to restore his positions and titles,
and Yěliè and Yuán Hé then lived together.
"Běi Shǐ □"
Princess Lángyé was named Yùyí,
the illegitimate younger sister of Wèi's Gāoyáng Prince Yùbīn.
Wénxiāng encountered her on the road,
was pleased and took her in,
whereupon she received exceptional favor.
He petitioned the Wèi Emperor to enfeoff her,
and Wénxiāng said to Cuī Jìshū:
"You have always sought beauties for me,
but none match this extraordinary one I found myself.
Cuī Xiān will surely come to remonstrate directly,
but I have a way to handle him.
When Xiān came to consult on affairs,
Wénxiāng no longer showed him a pleasant countenance.
After three days,
Xiān carried a name card and dropped it before him.
Wénxiāng asked:
"What is this for?
Xiān said fearfully:
"I haven't been able to pay respects to the Princess.
Wénxiāng was greatly pleased,
took Xiān by the arm and brought him in for an audience.
Jìshū told others:
"Cuī Xiān often resented my flattery,
saying before the Great General
that my uncle deserved death.
But when he himself practiced obsequiousness,
he surpassed even me.
The Princess' full sister Jìngyí,
had previously married the Imperial Secretary Láng Cuī Kuò,
and Wénxiāng also favored her,
both being enfeoffed as Princesses.
Kuò and his son were thereby exceptionally promoted and rewarded,
most generously.
Gāo Yáng was cruel and violent.
When his noble consort Xuē shì committed a minor fault,
he immediately killed her,
dismembered her body,
and holding her thigh as a pipa,
played it,
then sighed and said:
"A beauty is hard to find again.
From "Records of Unique Wonders": Consort Xuē of Emperor Wénxuān
was originally a singing girl.
At the age of fourteen or fifteen,
she was favored by Prince Qīnghé Yuè.
Her father had her enter the palace,
where she received great favor and affection.
Her elder sister also entered the palace to serve the emperor.
When Emperor Wénxuān later learned that she had previously been involved with Yuè,
and that her father had requested the title of Minister over the Masses,
the emperor became furious,
first sawed her elder sister to death.
Consort Xuē was pregnant at the time,
and after giving birth, she too was executed.
From "History of the Northern Dynasties"
Línhè Wáng Xiāodé's younger sister, the Princess of Chánglè, was married to Xiè Xǐ of the Chén Commandery.
Xiāodé committed adultery with her,
set fire to the princess's residence,
bound a maidservant,
placed jade bracelets on her hands,
attached gold and jewels to her body,
and claimed that the princess had perished in the fire.
He then retrieved the maidservant's corpse,
burying it together with the gold and jade.
He continued his illicit relationship with the princess,
calling her Lady Liǔ,
and she bore him two sons.
As time passed,
rumors gradually spread.
(Nán Shǐ)
Bì Yìyún was cruel and brutal,
and he had an illegitimate son named Shànzhāo,
who had an illicit affair with his maidservant.
He flogged him countless times,
placed a halter on him,
tied him to a tree in the courtyard,
and fed him fodder,
until he collapsed after more than ten days.
At night,
Yìyún was killed by an assailant,
using the very dagger Shànzhāo carried.
"History of the Northern Dynasties"
During Empress Wu Zetian's reign,
Zhāng Chāngzōng gained favor,
and further recommended his elder brother Yìzhī,
who applied powder and rouge,
wore brocade garments,
both receiving the favor like Pìyáng's.
The Fengchen Prefecture was established with Yìzhī as its head,
who was ordered to select handsome young men as left and right Fengchen attendants.
Right Supplements Officer Zhū Jìngzé submitted a memorial stating:
"Your Majesty already has interior favorites like Xuē Huáiyì,
Zhāng Yìzhī, and Chāngzōng,
which should certainly suffice.
Recently it is heard that the Chief of Palace Maintenance,
Liǔ Mó, claims his son Liáng Bīn has fair skin and handsome eyebrows,
while Left Guard Chief Historian Hóu Xiáng boasts of his virility,
surpassing even Huáiyì,
and claims fitness to serve as Fengchen interior attendant.
Such impropriety and lack of decorum
overflow into court hearings."
Wu Zetian consoled him, saying:
"Without your frank words,
I would not have known this."
She awarded him one hundred bolts of colored silk.
"Old Biography of Yìzhī"
Mǐnzhǔ Wáng Xī married the daughter of Jīnwúshǐ Shàng Bǎoyīn as his Virtuous Consort,
who possessed extraordinary beauty.
Xī doted on her,
and while intoxicated,
whomever the consort wished to kill would be killed,
and whomever she wished to pardon would be pardoned.
"Shì Shuō"
When Yú Jí was still obscure, he was a guest in Xǔ Héng's household.
Yú had a private affair,
and would often leave the residence in the afternoon.
Xǔ would frequently visit but never find him home,
which troubled him,
so he wrote on a slip of bamboo:
"Night after night you roam out,
I know Lord Yú cannot be admonished."
Yú immediately responded upon his return:
"Time and again you come to disturb,
why is Master Xǔ not weary of the trouble?"
The next day, Xǔ came again and, seeing this, sighed in admiration, then recommended him to the court.
"Gēng Yú Bó Lǎn" states that Xǔ and Yú lived far apart in time,
which is likely an error.
In the twenty-seventh year of Duke Xiāng, Qí Qìng Fēng came on a diplomatic mission,
his carriage was magnificent,
Shūsūn said:
"Bào has heard it said: 'If fine garments are unbecoming,
one is bound to meet a bad end'
What is the use of a fine carriage?
When Shūsūn dined with Qìng Fēng,
the latter showed disrespect.
Shūsūn had the poem 'Xiàng Shǔ' recited for him,
but he did not understand it either.
The following year, when he came fleeing,
Shūsūn Mùzǐ entertained Qìng Fēng with a meal,
Qìng Fēng made a widespread offering,
Mùzǐ was displeased,
and had the musicians recite 'Máo Chī' for him,
but again he did not understand.
Zuǒzhuàn
Wángzǐ Jiàn was stationed at Chéngfù,
and he met Chéugōng Gān in a field.
He asked:
"What is this?"
Chénggōng Gān said:
"It's a field."
"What is a field
for?"
"It's for growing hemp."
"What is hemp for?"
He replied:
"It's for making clothes."
Chénggōng Gān then said:
"In the past, King Zhuāng attacked Chén
and stayed at the house of Yǒuxiāo.
He said to the people in the roadside house: 'Isn't the alley in poor condition?
Why hasn't the ditch been dredged?'
Even King Zhuāng knew that the alley was in poor condition
and the ditch wasn't dredged.
Now you don't know that fields are for growing hemp,
and hemp is for making clothes.
Are you not fit to rule the state?"
The prince indeed did not ascend the throne.
From "Shuō Yuàn"
When the Fàn clan perished,
a commoner obtained a bell.
He wanted to carry it away on his back,
but the bell was too large to carry.
He tried to break it with a hammer,
and the bell clanged loudly.
Fearing others would hear it and take it from him,
he hastily covered his ears.
It is understandable to dislike others hearing it,
but disliking hearing it oneself is absurd.
"Lǚ Zìzhī"
A man of Chǔ was crossing a river,
when his sword fell from the boat into the water.
He hastily marked the side of the boat, saying:
"This is where my sword fell in."
When the boat stopped,
he entered the water to search for it at the place he had marked.
But the boat had moved on,
while the sword had not.
To search for a sword in this manner
is indeed foolish, is it not?
When King Mǐn of Qí was exiled and living in Wèi, he said to Gōngwáng Dān:
"What kind of ruler am I?"
Gōngwáng Dān replied:
"Your Majesty is a worthy ruler.
I have heard that in ancient times there were those who relinquished the world without showing regret,
I have heard of their reputation,
and in Your Majesty I see the reality.
Your Majesty was known as the Eastern Emperor,
and truly governed the world.
Having left your state to live in Wèi,
your appearance remains full,
your countenance radiant,
with no sign of regret for having lost your kingdom."
The King said:
"Excellent!
Dān understands me.
Since I left my state to live in Wèi,
my waistband has increased by three sizes."
"Guò Zì Lǐ"
The human eye relies on light to see;
a blind person cannot perceive with their eyes yet claims to see.
A Róng tribesman saw someone bleaching cloth and asked:
"How is this vast whiteness made?"
When they pointed to hemp and showed it to him,
he angrily said:
"How can this tangled mess
produce such vast whiteness?"
"Understanding Perception"
Yáng Zǐyún composed the Fǎyán,
when a wealthy man from Shǔ offered ten million in cash,
wishing to be recorded in the book.
Zǐyún refused,
saying, "Wealth without benevolent and righteous conduct
is like a deer in a pen,
or an ox in a stall—
how could it be recklessly recorded?"
(Lùnhéng: Lost Histories)
During the reign of Xiào Míng, he read "The Account of Sū Wǔ",
and noticed an official title, which was:
"Yí Zhōng Jiàn"
and he asked all the officials about it,
but none of the officials knew.
"Lùn Héng"
When Hàn Dynasty Minister of the Masses Cuī Liè appointed Shàngdǎng's Bào Jiān as his assistant,
Bào Jiān was about to have an audience with him
and worried about not performing correctly,
so he asked those who had arrived earlier about the proper etiquette.
Someone who happened to answer said:
"Just follow what the master of ceremonies says."
When the audience began,
the master of ceremonies said:
"You may bow."
Bào Jiān also said:
"You may bow."
The master of ceremonies said:
"Take your position."
Bào Jiān also said:
"Take your position."
Then he put on his shoes and took his seat,
but when he was about to leave the mat,
he couldn't find his shoes.
The master of ceremonies said:
"Put them on your feet."
Bào Jiān also said:
"The shoes are on my feet."
From "Forest of Laughs"
In the Later Hàn Dynasty, there was a man named Gě Gōng,
whose courtesy name was Yuánfǔ,
and he excelled at writing memorials to the throne.
Once, someone asked Gě Gōng to draft a memorial on their behalf,
so Gě Gōng composed it for them.
That person forgot to include their own name
and instead submitted it with Gě Gōng’s name.
A saying of the time went:
"Though the memorial is skillfully written,
one should remove Gě Gōng’s name."
From Péi Róngqī's "Forest of Sayings"
A man of Wèi fell ill suddenly at night,
and ordered his disciple to drill for fire.
That evening was dark and gloomy,
and he urged him quite urgently.
The disciple said indignantly:
"You are being utterly unreasonable in blaming others.
Now it's as dark as lacquer;
why don't you hold a torch to light my way,
so that I can find the fire-drilling tools,
and then it will be easy to get them."
Kǒng Wénjǔ heard this and said:
"One should blame others with reason."
"Forest of Laughs"
Sīmǎ Wénwáng held a banquet for Liú Shàn with entertainment,
where the old Shǔ performances moved all onlookers to sorrow,
yet Shàn remained cheerful and unperturbed.
The Prince remarked to Jiǎ Chōng:
"How can a man be so devoid of feeling?
Even if Zhūgě Liàng were still alive,
he could not have long sustained his support,
let alone Jiāng Wéi!"
Chōng replied:
"Were it not so,
how could Your Highness have annexed his state?"
Another day,
the Prince asked Shàn:
"Do you ever miss Shǔ?"
Shàn answered:
"I am happy here,
and do not miss Shǔ."
Xì Zhèng, hearing of this,
sought an audience with Shàn and said:
"If the Prince asks again,
you should instead reply, 'My ancestors' graves are far in Lǒng-Shǔ,
my heart grieves for the west,
there is not a day I do not think of it.'
Then close your eyes."
When the Prince did ask again,
Shàn answered as instructed.
The Prince said:
"Why does that sound like Xì Zhèng's words?"
Shàn looked up in surprise and said:
"It is indeed as you say."
All attendants laughed.
Records of the Three Kingdoms
Máo Jiā,
was the father of Wèi Míngdì's Empress Máo.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Bópíng Township.
Máo Jiā was originally a craftsman in charge of imperial carriages and tools,
yet unexpectedly attained wealth and nobility.
Míngdì once ordered court officials to gather at his home for a banquet,
where his demeanor and actions appeared very foolish and clumsy,
and whenever he spoke,
he would refer to himself as
"this Marquis."
Contemporaries regarded this as ridiculous.
"Records of the Three Kingdoms" Hú Qìng,
courtesy name Wénliàng,
was a grandnephew of Empress Dowager Líng.
He served as Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Being obtuse and dim-witted,
whenever he spoke with others,
he would refer to himself as "the Vice Director."
People at the time compared him to Máo Jiā.
"History of the Northern Dynasties"
Chén Shòu was about to compose the Records of the Three Kingdoms,
and said to Dīng Liángzhōu:
"If I could borrow a thousand hu of rice from you,
I would write an excellent biography for your honored father."
Dīng did not give him the rice,
so Chén did not compose the biography.
Contemporary opinion therefore held Dīng Liángzhōu in lower regard for his lack of respect toward his father.
From Forest of Conversations
Rén Yùcháng when young was bright and adorable.
People at the time said even his shadow was pleasing,
but after crossing the river,
he lost his spirit.
Prime Minister Wáng invited former worthies to join him at Shítóu to welcome Rén,
treating him as in former days.
Yet at first sight, they sensed something amiss.
Once seated, he immediately asked about the drink:
"Is this chá?
Or is it míng?"
Noticing their puzzled looks,
he explained himself:
"I was merely asking whether the drink was hot or cold."
Once passing by a coffin shop,
he wept with sorrow.
Hearing this, Prime Minister Wáng remarked:
"This is a case of sentimental folly."
From Shì Shuō.
Xiè Hǔzi Jù once climbed onto the roof to smoke out rats.
Hú'ér had no way of knowing his father had done this,
and when he heard people say,
"Some foolish person did such a thing,"
he would laugh and mock it,
repeating this story on more than one occasion.
The Grand Tutor, realizing that Hú'ér was unaware of his own father's actions,
seized the opportunity during their conversation
to tell Hú'ér:
"People use this to slander the Palace Attendant,
and say that I was involved in it too."
Hú'ér became deeply ashamed and agitated,
and remained secluded in his study for a full month.
The Grand Tutor skillfully took the blame upon himself,
using this approach to enlighten Hú'ér,
which can truly be called virtuous teaching.
Ghost troops came to aid Wáng Níngzhī,
son of Wáng Xīzhī.
The Wáng family had for generations practiced the Five Pecks of Rice sect of the Zhāng family,
and Níngzhī was especially devout.
When Sūn Ēn attacked Kuàijī,
his subordinates requested preparations be made.
Níngzhī refused,
instead entering his meditation chamber to pray.
Emerging, he told his officers:
"I have already requested the ghost troops of the Great Way to assist us,
the rebels will be defeated by themselves."
Since no defenses were prepared,
he was consequently killed by Sūn Ēn.
Book of Jìn
Gù Kǎizhī,
styled Chángkāng,
once sealed the front of a cabinet containing his paintings and
entrusted it to Huán Xuán,
all of which were works he deeply cherished.
Xuán then opened the back of the cabinet,
stole the paintings,
and resealed it as before before returning it,
claiming it had never been opened.
When Kǎizhī saw the seal intact as originally placed,
but found the paintings missing,
he simply remarked that exquisite paintings communicate with the divine,
transforming and departing,
much like humans ascending to immortality,
showing not a trace of astonishment.
Gù Kǎizhī was excessively boastful and self-promoting,
so young people would compliment him as a form of mockery.
He also engaged in chanting poetry,
believing himself to have inherited the style and elegance of ancient sages.
Once someone asked him to perform the Luoyang chant,
to which he replied:
"Why should I imitate the voice of an old maid!
During the early Yìxī era, he served as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
sharing an office compound with Xiè Zhān.
He would often chant poetry under the moonlight,
and whenever Xiè Zhān praised him from a distance,
Gù Kǎizhī would become even more energetic and forget his fatigue.
When Xiè Zhān grew tired and wanted to sleep,
he would have someone replace him in offering praise,
yet Gù Kǎizhī never noticed the difference,
and continued chanting until daybreak.
Book of Jìn
During the time of Qín Fú Shēng, the planet Venus intruded upon the Eastern Well constellation.
The officials reported:
"The Eastern Well
is the division corresponding to Qín,
and Venus is a punitive star;
there will certainly be violent soldiers rising in the capital.
Fú Shēng said:
"When the star enters the Well, it must be thirsty—
what is there to be surprised about?
From the "Records"
In the fourth year of the Jiànpíng era of Mùróng Chuí of Southern Yān,
the rebel leader Wáng Shǐ gathered followers in the Láiwū Valley of Mount Tài,
proclaiming himself the Great Peace Emperor,
naming his father Wáng Jiǒng as the Grand Emperor,
his elder brother Wáng Xiū as the General Who Conquers the East,
and Wáng Tài as the General Who Conquers the West,
falsely appointing ministers and high officials,
deceiving and inciting the common people.
Mùróng Dé dispatched the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Mùróng Zhèn,
to suppress and capture him,
and he was to be executed at the horse market.
Someone asked him:
"Why did you bring about the extermination of your clan with such rebellious and false claims?
Where are your father and brothers now?"
He replied:
"The Grand Emperor is enduring hardships abroad, the General Who Conquers the East and the General Who Conquers the West
have been killed by the rebel troops,
so what solace do I have today?"
His wife, Lady Zhào, angrily said:
"It was your mouth that brought you to this,
leading to your death;
how can you still not change your ways even at the moment of execution?"
Wáng Shǐ replied:
"The Empress does not understand the Mandate of Heaven;
from ancient times to the present,
has there ever been a family that did not fall
or a state that did not perish?"
The executioner struck his mouth with the hilt of his sword,
and Wáng Shǐ said:
"I am now suffering and dying at your hands,
so be it if I die,
but I will never change my imperial title."
Mùróng Dé heard this and laughed, saying to his attendants:
"Such a deluded man,
still spouting madness even in death—
how could he not be killed?"
From "The Chronicles of the Sixteen Kingdoms."
Liú Yùn,
courtesy name Yànwén,
was the son of Dào Xīn,
a man of mediocre talent and vulgar character,
yet was particularly favored by Emperor Míng.
While serving in Xiāngzhōu and Yōngzhōu,
he had skilled painters depict his procession with guards and ceremonial regalia,
and often admired these paintings himself.
Once, he showed a painting to General Zhēngxī Cài Xìngzōng,
who teased him
by pretending not to understand the artwork.
Pointing at Liú Yùn's figure in the painting, he asked:
"Who is this person in the carriage?
Liú Yùn replied:
"That is precisely me.
Such was the extent of his foolishness.
*History of the Southern Dynasties*
Liú Yùndì Shù,
styled Yǎnsī,
was also extremely mediocre and incompetent.
When his nephew Yǔ was critically ill,
his father Yànjié and mother Xiāo wept before him,
and Shù happened to be visiting.
He immediately ordered his attendants to bring wine and meat for Yǔ to consume,
leaving everyone bewildered about his intention.
Someone asked him about it,
to which he replied:
"The Rites say: 'When one is ill, one may drink wine and eat meat.'
On another occasion, Shù had recently experienced the mourning period for a distant relative,
and someone visited him,
inquiring about his mother's well-being.
Shù said:
"She is only sorrowful and distressed.
Next, the visitor asked about his son,
to which he responded:
"It's what is called 'father and son sharing a doe.'
He apparently mistook the character for 'doe' (yōu) as meaning 'worry' (yōu).
Liú Yìqí was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yíngdào County,
being utterly uncouth and ignorant.
Prince Shǐxīng Liú Jùn once said to him:
"Lù Jī's poem states, 'Yíngdào has no ardent heart,'
why does he so bitterly criticize you, Uncle?"
Yìqí replied:
"This official never knew Lù Jī,
why is he suddenly attacking me?"
Such was his dull-witted and obtuse nature.
Prince Péngchéng Yìkāng had never studied the classics,
and treated literary scholars with great disdain.
Yuán Shū once visited Yìkāng,
who asked his age.
He replied:
"The year Dèng Zhònghuá received the ducal robes."
Yìkāng said:
"I don't know that reference."
Shū then said:
"The year Lù Jī entered Luòyáng."
Yìkāng responded:
"I don't read books,
don't use literary allusions with me."
Such was his shallowness and ignorance.
The Emperor
When Liú Yìxuān was defeated and returned to Jiānglíng,
he still had over ten thousand armored soldiers.
After Yìxuān entered the city,
he came out to the audience hall,
and met with his guests and attendants.
Zhái Língbǎo advised him to comfort the assembled guests,
saying
"Zāng Zhì disobeyed the proper directives,
leading to our defeat.
Now we shall train troops and repair armor,
to make new plans for the future;
in the past, Hàn Gāozǔ suffered a hundred defeats,
yet ultimately achieved great success."
But Yìxuān forgot Língbǎo's words,
and mistakenly said
"Xiàng Yǔ suffered a thousand defeats."
Everyone present covered their mouths and laughed.
From "Book of Sòng"
Xiè Chāozōng
was the son of Fèng,
diligent in study and gifted in literary composition,
selected to fill the post of State Regular Attendant to Prince Zǐluán of Xīn'ān.
When the prince's mother, Shūyí Yīn, passed away,
Chāozōng composed a eulogy and presented it.
The Emperor greatly admired it,
saying to Xiè Zhuāng:
"Chāozōng truly possesses Fèng's flair—I fear Língyùn has been reborn.
At the time, General Liǔ Dàolóng of the Right Guard was present at the imperial seat,
and upon leaving, he inquired of Chāozōng:
"I've heard you possess a rare treasure;
may I see it?
Chāozōng replied:
"In a house as empty as a hanging chime stone,
how could there be any rare treasure?
Dàolóng, being a military man,
unaware he had inadvertently touched upon his father's name,
said:
"Earlier, while attending the banquet,
His Majesty mentioned you have Fèng's flair.
Chāozōng immediately went barefoot back inside,
while Dàolóng thought he had gone to fetch the phoenix feathers,
and waited until dark without success,
before leaving.
(From *History of the Southern Dynasties*)
Ruǎn Diànfū once on New Year's Day coincided with the conjunction day (first day of lunar month),
the Minister of Personnel proposed postponing the imperial gathering.
Diànfū said:
"The New Year celebration gathering is the state's grand ceremony,
why not postpone the conjunction day instead?"
His disregard for ancient precedents was like this.
Zhāng Jìng'ér wanted to move Yáng Shūzǐ's Dropping Tears Monument,
and build a terrace in its place.
An official remonstrated, saying:
"This is the late Grand Tutor Yáng's legacy; it should not be moved.
Jìng'ér said:
"Who is this Grand Tutor?
I don't know him.
Zhāng Jìng'ér initially could not read,
and only after becoming a regional governor did he begin studying the *Classic of Filial Piety* and the *Analects*.
When first summoned to serve as Protector of the Army,
he secretly practiced ceremonial bows and responses alone in a secluded room,
bending and rising in the empty space,
while his concubines peeped in and laughed at him.
Upon being appointed to the Three Excellencies,
he said to his wife and sister-in-law:
"After my appointment, the official residence will open its yellow gates."
He then made drumming sounds with his mouth.
When he first received the honor of military music,
he was too embarrassed to have it performed immediately.
At the Grandmother Temple in Xīnlín, while praying to the deity for a son for his concubine,
he referred to himself as one of the Three Excellencies,
showing such vulgarity and lack of refinement.
Liáng Wǔdīng Guìpín's father Dàoqiān initially served as the governor of Lìyáng,
under the administration of Prince Lúlìng Xù.
Emperor Wǔ referred to her as a virtuous daughter.
She gave birth to another son,
and replied:
"Do not call him a pig or dog's offspring.
This became a joke among people.
When Hóu Jǐng usurped the throne,
Wáng Wěi requested the establishment of the Seven Ancestral Temples.
Hóu Jǐng asked:
"What are the Seven Ancestral Temples?"
Wáng Wěi replied:
"The Son of Heaven sacrifices to seven generations of ancestors,
hence establishing seven temples,
and I request the taboo names of seven generations,
ordering the Court of Imperial Sacrifices to prepare the sacrificial rites."
Hóu Jǐng said:
"I cannot recall my previous generations,
only my father's name was Biāo,
and he lived in Shuòzhōu,
how could he possibly have dared to be this?"
All who heard this laughed at him.
Hú Sēngyòu, during Emperor Yuán of Liáng's reign, was appointed General of the Central Army,
and amassed great wealth for himself.
He always kept the honor guard's wind and percussion instruments bestowed upon him in his study,
and amused himself by facing them.
Someone said:
"These are ceremonial symbols of status,
Your reputation is esteemed and weighty,
it is not fitting for you to act like this.
He replied:
"It is my nature to love them,
I constantly need to see them, that's all.
When he went out on excursions, he also took them along with him,
and people laughed at him.
Hú Sēngyòu had a natural love for reading books,
enjoyed compiling and writing,
yet his literary compositions were crude and unrefined,
often becoming subjects of ridicule and mockery,
while he himself believed they were truly skillful,
and grew increasingly boastful about them.
《History of the Southern Dynasties》 In Northern Qí's Bīngzhōu, there was a scholar from a prominent family,
who enjoyed writing ridiculous poems and rhapsodies,
looked down upon figures like Xíng and Wèi,
and was mocked by everyone,
who falsely praised him,
so he would surely slaughter cattle and strain wine to entertain them.
His wife was a woman of clear perception,
who wept and admonished him.
This man sighed and said:
"My talent is not tolerated even by my own wife and children,
let alone strangers.
He remained unenlightened until his death.
《Family Instructions of the Yán Clan》
Hé Lìngguì's powerful influence overshadowed the court,
his calligraphy was crude and flawed,
thus incurring the "Ten Shameful Writings."
When others paid him respectful homage,
he suddenly remarked: "Yǒnggǎn replied to someone borrowing a carriage,
concluding without proper formalities,
yet this original version circulated widely,
bringing shame upon the entire court—
this was the seventh of those shames."
From "Yǔ Yuánwēi's Discourse on Calligraphy"
In Jiāngnán there was a powerful official,
who read a corrupted edition of the commentary on "Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ",
explaining "dūn chī"
as "potato",
but he mistook it for
"mutton"
character.
Later, someone sent him mutton as a gift,
and he wrote in reply:
"Thank you for the gift of dūn chī."
The entire court was astonished and could not understand the meaning,
until much later, after careful investigation,
they finally realized what had happened.
"Family Instructions of the Yán Clan"
Yuán Shī,
courtesy name Jiànyán,
served as a Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel and concurrently oversaw the Ministry of Rites.
Later, during early summer,
he requested a rain ceremony based on the appearance of the dragon constellation.
At that time, Gāo Ānàgōng was the Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
and mistook it for a real dragon appearing,
becoming greatly delighted.
He asked where the dragon was,
saying:
"What color is it?
Shī composed himself and said:
"This refers to the first sighting of the Dragon Star,
and according to ritual, we should perform the rain ceremony at the suburban altar,
not that a real dragon has descended elsewhere.
Ānàgōng flushed with anger,
saying:
"These Han people are meddlesome,
forcing their knowledge of constellations!
The ceremony was not carried out.
After Shī left,
he secretly sighed and said:
"The great affairs of the state
lie in sacrifices and warfare;
since the rites have been abandoned,
how can it last long?
The fall of Qí is not far off.
"History of the Northern Dynasties: Biography of He" In Northern Qí, where did the dragon appear?
What color was it?
Why did the Suí biography mention constellations?
Grand General Xuē Róngzōng often claimed he could command ghosts,
and the Last Ruler believed him.
Passing by an ancient tomb,
Róngzōng asked Attendant Yuán Xínggōng whose tomb it was,
to which Xínggōng jokingly replied:
"It is Línzōng's tomb.
Róngzōng then asked who Línzōng was,
and Xínggōng said:
"Guō Yuánzhēn's father.
Róngzōng later reported to the emperor:
"Your servant previously saw Guō Línzōng emerge from the tomb,
wearing a large hat,
Jímò boots,
carrying a horsewhip,
and asking me:
'Has my Āzhēn come?
From "The Northern Qí History"
Xióng Ānshēng,
courtesy name Zhízhī,
while in Shāndōng,
traveled extensively year after year,
with followers flooding entire commanderies and counties.
Someone deceived him, saying:
"In a certain village, an ancient tomb
belongs to Xióng Guāng, a general of Hénán from the Jìn Dynasty,
seventy-two generations removed.
There was originally a stele,
but villagers buried and concealed it."
Ānshēng dug the ground searching for it,
but failed to find it,

Ānshēng led his clan,
wailing toward the tomb.

Hán Yì was a son of Chānglí,
and although he was taught with righteousness and principles,
his nature was rather dull and inferior.

and when he encountered
"golden root"

In the Táng dynasty, there was a person surnamed Fáng,
who was fond of boasting about his family background.

he would claim them as a new relative.
An acquaintance, annoyed by this habit of his,
said to him:

where exorcists' effigies are produced.

"He is my father's second elder brother."
The person laughed heartily and said:

Zhèng Jué responded:

this object is certainly not worth sparing,

Jué bowed his head and said:

Those around them drew back their heads and snickered secretly.
The next day,

demanding of the artist:

from "Miscellaneous Records"
Sòng Xiáng, while remaining in the western capital,
was appointed as the magistrate of Hénán in the same year,
and was fond of proposing convenient methods.
Considering that farmers' wheat cultivation required excessive plowing and weeding,
he changed to using long awls to pierce the ground for sowing seeds.
Testing it on one acre of land,
from morning until dusk,
they could not finish the task.
Moreover, encountering a locust plague,
he ordered the people to raise one chicken each,
saying:
"Not only will this eliminate the harm of locusts,
but it can also provide self-sustenance."
He commanded the people to present all their raised chickens,
and once the chickens were gathered,
they began fighting chaotically,
with no way to separate them.
The common people crowded noisily, blocking the roads,
all watching two chickens fight each other.
He then abandoned the policy.
《Chén Shǐ》
There was a court official, Chén Dōng, who served as the assistant prefect of Sūzhōu
and acted as the prefect. While adjudicating a case of exile punishment,
he ordered the criminal's face to be tattooed,
inscribing "Specially exiled to such-and-such prison camp."
After the tattooing was completed,
staff in the administrative office discussed among themselves:
"Whenever the term 'specially' is used,
it means the crime does not warrant this punishment
but is implemented by special decree of the imperial court.
Now this criminal deserved exile,
and furthermore, 'specially'
is not something local officials can employ."
Chén Dōng was greatly alarmed,
and immediately changed the characters "specially" to "according to regulations,"
and had the face tattooed again,
which made him quite the laughingstock.
Later, when someone recommended Chén Dōng's talent to the Two Councils,
Councilor Shí heard this and said:
"I know this man.
Isn't he the one who,
while acting as prefect of Sūzhōu, drafted documents on people's faces?"

According to the old practice of the Biàn Canal, the sluice gates were closed in the tenth month, halting boat traffic.
Wáng Jièfǔ wanted to maintain winter transport,

boats could not navigate,
and floating ice severely damaged vessels,
thus thousands of boat trackers were employed,
equipped with large pestles at the front,
to pound the floating ice.
However, many laborers died from the bitter cold.
A saying circulated in the capital:
"In the past, there was a method to grind and level the slurry water,
now we see giant pestles pounding the winter ice.

Jiāo Mǐn, the prefect of Jìnzhōu, was poorly informed and narrow-minded,

From Collected Conversations from Literary Gatherings
The five-rank system originated with Huángdì and Tángyáo,
and the commandery-county administration was created by the Qín and Hàn dynasties.
Thus, establishing offices and dividing responsibilities
served to lighten their duties;
while setting up five levels of local chiefs
aimed to broaden their governance.
"Discourse on the Five Ranks of Nobility"
The Book of Changes says:
"When Fúxī Shì ruled the world,
there were five ranks of nobility,
modeled after the five elements.
Some had three ranks,
modeled after the three luminaries.
Báihǔ Tōng
The king establishes the three dukes, nine ministers, and twenty-seven senior officials,
which are sufficient for teaching and guiding,
illuminating the obscure and hidden.
Why must he also enfeoff feudal lords?
It is the ultimate way of valuing the people.
Good and evil become comparable and easily discernible,
so he selects the worthy and enfeoffs them,
entrusting them to govern their people,
to manifest their virtue,
and fully utilize their talents.
Above, this serves to honor the Son of Heaven,
providing defensive support,
while below, it nurtures the common people like children and implements his principles,
opening the path for the worthy,
modestly refraining from monopolizing power.
Thus, he allocates territories and enfeoffs the worthy,
modeling after this principle,
emulating the worthy and valuing the people.
When a king ascends the throne,
he first enfeoffs the worthy,
showing his concern for the people's urgent needs.
Thus, dividing the land to establish borders
is not for expanding offices and establishing administrations for the feudal lords,
nor for the high ministers and grandees,
but all for the people.
Why are feudal lords enfeoffed in summer?
Because the yang energy is at its peak for nurturing, hence it is used to enfeoff feudal lords,
to fully nurture the worthy.
Establishing rulers for the people
is the ultimate expression of abundant yang virtue.
The king who receives the mandate,
achieves the beauty of great peace,
and the merits of all officials high and low,
therefore fully enfeoffs them.
Then, in the restoration and military campaigns,
those with great achievements are all enfeoffed,
in order to commend great merits.
Men of profound virtue are also enfeoffed,
to honor those with virtue. Those to be enfeoffed
must first be tested as vassals;
after three years of achievement,
they are accordingly enfeoffed with fifty li.
Generally, scholars with merit
also become vassals.
If they lose their position,
and a minister achieves merit,
he is enfeoffed with fifty li;
a high minister is enfeoffed with seventy li;
and a duke is enfeoffed with a hundred li.
Above.
The feudal lords' fiefs did not exceed one hundred li,
symbolizing how the thunder's vibration within one hundred li moistens with clouds and rain alike.
Thunder is
the yang within yin,
symbolizing the feudal lords.
The feudal lords, compared to the king, represent yin;
facing south to reward and punish is yin,
emulating thunder.
Above
There are five ranks of nobility, and the Duke (Gōng) represents selflessness,
hence the character is formed by turning away from selfishness to signify public spirit.
《Huán Jì Yào Lüè》 The Earl (Bó) is capable of spreading goodness to the masses,
sharing with the common people is called public spirit.
《Zhōu Shū》 The term "Gōng" means tribute,
as one with both talent and virtue surpassing others,
all people recommend them to the king,
who then employs them.
An analysis states:
"Gōng means upright,
denoting integrity and selflessness.
The character is composed of 'rù',
and 'sī',
where 'rù' sounds like turning away,
and 'sī' is the ancient character for selfishness,
so turning away from selfishness constitutes public spirit.
《Wéi Zhāo Biàn Shì Míng》 'Rù' implies universality,
while 'sī' signifies cunning and evil.
Hán Fēi said:
"When Cāng Jié created characters,
self-interest was denoted as private,
and turning away from it as public.
《Shuō Wén》 The term Gōng speaks of justice and selflessness.
《Bái Hǔ Tōng》 With a grand noble rank,
one who embodies selflessness as virtue
is a Duke.
《Mèngzǐ Zhèng Yì》 Establishing systems for the people is called public spirit.

One who can establish reputation and nurture life,
and acts in accordance with the Way of Heaven is called a Marquis.
When Marquises can form groups,
they are called Rulers.
The "Zhōu Shū" states: A Marquis,
is a marquis,
whose duty is to guard the borders.
The "Yuán Shén Chì" says: A Marquis,
is one who observes,
observing compliance and opposition.
The "Bái Hǔ Tōng" states: One who responds to all directions is called a Marquis.
The "Shì Fǎ" says: Scouting outside,
and ruling people with virtue,
is a Marquis.

When a noble's son reaches adulthood and is capable of governing superiors, he is called a Shì (Gentleman);
when a Shì leads the masses and acts timely, he is called a Bó (Elder).
The "Zhōu Shū" states: Bó means
to grasp,
to handle governmental affairs.

a leader,
clarity,
indicating that all establish five leaders,

Zǐ yóu zī,
zī,

zī yě;
zī zī,

zì yě,
zì,

Man,
means to bear responsibility,
