《Zhèng Yì》
The Grand Historian says: Before the Yin dynasty, it is ancient and remote.
The Zhou dynasty enfeoffed five ranks: Duke, Marquis, Earl, Viscount, and Baron.
Thus, Bóqín and Kāngshū were enfeoffed in Lǔ and Wèi,
each with a territory of four hundred lǐ,
reflecting the principle of favoring kin,
truly for their virtue;
Tàigōng in Qí,
held land equivalent to five marquises,
honoring his diligence and toil.
King Wǔ, King Chéng, and King Kāng enfeoffed about a hundred,
with fifty of the same surname,
the largest territory not exceeding a hundred lǐ,
the smallest thirty lǐ,
to assist and protect the royal house.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
The Official Roster Annotations state:
"The system of the monarch,
includes five ranks: Duke, Marquis, Earl, Viscount, and Baron,
High Ministers and Ministers,
Junior Ministers,
Senior Scholars, Middle Scholars, and Junior Scholars,
making five grades in total.
During the prosperous era of the Zhōu dynasty,
three sages established the laws,
setting up five noble ranks,
and enfeoffing eight hundred states.
To honor kinship, states were founded,
such as the Duke of Zhōu residing in Lǔ,
and Kāng Shū establishing Wèi.
To recognize virtue and talent,
Tàigōng was enfeoffed in Qí.
During the Spring and Autumn Period, Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng enfeoffed his younger brother at Jīng,
and Jì Zhòng said:
"When a capital city exceeds the prescribed scale,
it becomes a calamity for the state.
Later, they eventually attacked each other,
and great chaos erupted within the state.
Thus, excess leads to the disaster of powerful ministers,
while meagerness brings the worry of weakness.
Qín, with the strength of various states, unified the world,
believing it had risen from being a feudal lord itself.
Thereupon, it abolished the five ranks of nobility,
and established commanderies and counties,
so even close sons and younger brothers became commoners.
When its governance declined,
a single man's call made the empire fall away.
When the Hàn dynasty saw this downfall,
it recognized Qín perished due to isolation.
Thus, it greatly enfeoffed sons and brothers,
some with dozens of connected cities and vast domains,
lands spanning a thousand lǐ,
from east of the pass all becoming kingdoms,
with great strength and heavy authority,
hence also leading to the calamity of the Seven States.
"Yuánzǐ"
The "Miscellaneous Affairs of the Hàn" states: The Son of Heaven's Grand Shrine of the Land,
is made into an altar with five-colored earth.
When enfeoffing the feudal lords,
one takes the earth,
wraps it with white cogon grass,
and bestows it upon them.
Each receives the color corresponding to the direction of their fief,
to establish a shrine of the land in their state.
Therefore, it is called receiving the cogon grass and earth.
At the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
only the imperial sons enfeoffed as kings
were entitled to the cogon grass and earth.
Other ministers were regulated by the household taxes and rents they received,
did not receive the cogon grass and earth,
and did not establish shrines of the land.
The "Records of the Eastern Pavilion" states: The emperor enfeoffed meritorious officials,

with the largest fiefdoms comprising four counties,
and the rest varying in size.
Erudite Dīng Gōng and others deliberated: "Ancient emperors and kings enfeoffed feudal lords,
not exceeding a hundred li,
thus benefiting from easily establishing marquises,
taking the thunder as a model."
The emperor said: "Ancient fallen states
all perished due to lack of virtue;
I have never heard of a state perishing because meritorious officials were granted too much land."
King Wǔ, having pacified the Shang dynasty and become ruler of the realm,
enfeoffed his mentor Shàngfǔ at Yíngqiū in Qí.
As he journeyed east to take possession of his state,
he traveled slowly and lodged along the way.
The innkeeper said:
"I have heard that opportunity is hard to gain but easy to lose.
You sleep so soundly,
that you are probably not someone going to take possession of a state."
Tàigōng, hearing this,
dressed and set out by night,
arriving at his state at daybreak.
The Marquis of Lái came to attack,
contending with him for Yíngqiū.
"Records of the Grand Historian: Hereditary Houses" Tàigōng was enfeoffed in Qí,

he is probably not someone going to take possession of a state."
Tàigōng sprang up,
and as soon as he took to the road, pursuers arrived shortly after;
because he had already left the pass,

"Garden of Stories: Chapter Thirteen"
Lǚ Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed in Qí,
Zhōu Gōng Dàn was enfeoffed in Lǔ,
the two rulers were very close friends.
They said to each other:
"How to govern the state?"
Lǚ Tàigōng Wàng said:
"Respect the worthy and value achievement."
Zhōu Gōng Dàn said:
"Be close to relatives and value kindness."
Lǚ Tàigōng Wàng said:
"From now on, Lǔ will decline."
Zhōu Gōng Dàn said:
"Although Lǔ may decline,
as for the one who possesses Qí,
it will certainly not be the Lǚ family either."
Afterward, Qí grew larger day by day,
until it became a hegemon,
but in the twenty-fourth generation, Tián Chéngzǐ took possession of the state of Qí.
The Duke of Lǔ faced decline,
barely maintaining existence,
and perished in the thirty-fourth generation.
"Lǚ's Long View" When Lǔ Gōng Bó Qín first
received the enfeoffment to Lǔ,
it took three years before he reported on his governance to Zhōu Gōng.
Zhōu Gōng said:
"Why so slow?"
Bó Qín said:
"I changed their customs,
reformed their rituals,
and only after three years of mourning did I remove them,
hence the delay."
Tàigōng was also enfeoffed in Qí,
and in five months reported on his governance to Zhōu Gōng.
Zhōu Gōng said:
"Why so fast?"
He said:
"I simplified the rituals between ruler and minister,
and followed their customs."
Later, when he heard that Bó Qín was slow in reporting on his governance,
he sighed and said:
"Alas!
In later generations, Lǔ will face north and serve Qí."
"Records of the Grand Historian" The reason Qí was not as good as Lǔ
was that Tàigōng's worthiness was not equal to Bó Qín's.
Bó Qín and Tàigōng both received enfeoffments,
and each went to their states for three years.
Tàigōng came to court,
and Zhōu Gōng asked:
"How did you govern so quickly?"
He replied:
"Respecting the worthy, first the distant,
then the close and the benevolent—
this is the path of a hegemon."
Zhōu Gōng said:
"Tàigōng's influence will last for ten generations."
After five years, Bó Qín came to court,
and Zhōu Gōng asked:

He replied:
"Being close to relatives means first the internal then the external,
first benevolence then righteousness—
this is the path of a true king."
Zhōu Gōng said:
"Lǔ's governance will last for ten generations,
so Lǔ has the path of a true king
because of its benevolence and generosity;
Qí has the path of a hegemon
because of its martial governance.
The reason Qí was not as good as Lǔ
was that Tàigōng's worthiness was not equal to Bó Qín's."
"Garden of Persuasions"
Xīn Kuān appeared before Lǔ Mùgōng and said:
"From this day forward, I realize that our former lord Zhōu Gōng was not as wise as Tàigōng Wàng in choosing his fief.
In the past, Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed east of Yíngqiū's mountains,
a place of high, steep, and secure terrain.
Therefore, his territory expanded daily,
and his descendants grew increasingly prosperous.
Our former lord Zhōu Gōng was enfeoffed in Lǔ,
which lacked the natural barriers of mountains, forests, valleys, or gorges.
The feudal lords could come and go freely in all seasons,
so his territory diminished daily,
and his descendants declined in number and power.
After Xīn Kuān left, Nángōng
Kuò entered to see the Duke,
and informed Nángōng about it.
Kuò replied:
"Xīn Kuān is young and ignorant.
Has Your Majesty not heard the account of King Chéng's establishment of Chéngzhōu?
The words were as follows:
"I alone
have built my residence in Chéngzhōu;
I alone,
if virtuous, can easily be recognized,
and if unvirtuous, can easily be punished.
Hence it is said:
"The virtuous gain it,
the unvirtuous lose it,
which is the way of antiquity.
Would a worthy man truly wish his descendants to rely on the barriers of mountain forests to perpetuate unrighteousness?
How petty is Xīn Kuān!
His baseless slander
is truly lamentable.
《Lǚ Chánglì》 Xīn Lì appeared before Lǔ Mùgōng and said:
"Zhōu Gōng was not as worthy as Tàigōng.
Zhōu Gōng chose to be enfeoffed in Qūfù,
while Tàigōng chose to be enfeoffed in Yíngqiū; their ranks and lands were equal,
yet the land was not as fine as Yíngqiū's,
and the people were not as numerous as Yíngqiū's.
Not only that,
but Yíngqiū also possessed natural fortifications.
Mùgōng felt ashamed in his heart,
and could not respond.
Xīn Lì hurriedly exited,
and Nángōng Biānzǐ entered.
Mùgōng recounted Xīn Lì's words to Nángōng Biānzǐ in full.
Nángōng Biānzǐ said:
"In the past, when King Chéng divined about residing in Chéngzhōu,
he addressed the tortoise shell, saying: 'I alone possess all under heaven;
I govern and serve the hundred surnames,
how dare I not hold the central land?
Should I commit any fault,
let the four quarters attack me,
and it will not be difficult to do so.'
When Zhōu Gōng divined about residing in Qūfù,
he addressed the tortoise shell, saying: 'To build a city on the sunny side of the mountain;
if virtuous, it will flourish and prosper,
if unvirtuous, it will quickly perish.'
Jìsūn Xíngfǔ admonished his son, saying:
'I wish to build a house between the two altars of the land,
so that if among my descendants there are any who cannot serve their superiors,
they will be replaced all the more quickly.'
Thus it is said: 'If virtuous, it will flourish and prosper,
if unvirtuous, it will quickly perish.'
What need is there to choose a place for enfeoffment?
Or to show off natural fortifications?
Xīn Lì's words are those of a petty man.
《Shuō Yuàn》
Long ago, when Tàigōng Wàng and Zhōugōng Dàn received their fiefs and met,
Tàigōng

Later, Qí daily grew larger,
until it became hegemon,

Lǔ daily diminished,
and after twenty-four generations, it perished.
From this we observe,
that the sage can discern the subtle.
The Odes say:
"Only this sage
can see a hundred miles ahead."
Hánshī Wàizhuàn
King Chéng offered the Duke of Zhōu the fiefdom of Jiāoshì,
but the Duke of Zhōu declined to accept it.
Instead, he had his son Bó Qín enfeoffed in Lǔ.
Bó Qín was about to leave for his fiefdom,
when the Duke of Zhōu admonished him, saying:
"As you depart,
you must not let the state of Lǔ make you arrogant towards scholars.
I am
the son of King Wén,
the younger brother of King Wǔ,
and now the uncle of the reigning king;
moreover, I serve as regent to the Son of Heaven.
My status in the world is by no means insignificant.
Yet, I have often paused while washing my hair three times in one bathing,
and interrupted my meal three times to spit out food,
all for fear of missing talented scholars from across the land.
I have heard it said: He whose virtue is vast and who maintains it with reverence will be honored;
he whose land is broad and fertile and who governs it with frugality will find peace;
he whose rank and eminence are lofty and who upholds them with humility will be esteemed;
he whose people are numerous and army strong and who leads them with caution will be victorious;
he who is intelligent and wise and who guards it with apparent simplicity will gain more;
he whose knowledge is extensive and memory profound and who preserves it with modesty will broaden his reach.
These six principles of preservation
are all virtues of humility.
For one as noble as the Son of Heaven,
as wealthy as possessing all within the four seas,
to lack humility is to bring about his own ruin before all under heaven—
as witnessed in Jié and Zhòu.
Can one not be cautious?
Therefore, the Yì Jīng says: There is a way
that, in its greatness, can preserve the empire,
in its medium, can preserve the state,
and in its smallness, can preserve one's person—
this refers to humility.
For the way of heaven diminishes the full and benefits the humble;
the way of earth transforms the full and flows to the humble;
spirits and deities harm the full and bless the humble;
the way of man dislikes the full and favors the humble.
Thus, a garment, when completed, has a missing lapel;
a palace, when built, has a missing corner;
a house, when finished, has added imperfections:
to show that nothing is ever perfect—
such is the way of heaven.
The Yì Jīng says:
'Humility brings success;
the noble man carries it through to good fortune.'
The Shī Jīng says:
'Heaven bestows without delay; the sage's reverence daily ascends.'
Take this warning to heart!
You must not let the state of Lǔ make you arrogant towards scholars.
From Shuō Yuàn: Jìng Shèn
King Chéng appointed Bóqín as the Duke of Lǔ,
summoned him and admonished him, saying:
"Do you know the way of being a superior?
All who hold a high position must do so with reverence.
Be receptive to virtuous admonitions from subordinates,
and must open the door to frank criticism, restraining yourself and remaining calm to encourage those who remonstrate.
Do not intimidate them with authority,
nor block their words.
Broadly collect their counsel,
then select what is worthy of consideration.
For having civil virtues without martial might,
there is no way to awe subordinates;
having martial might without civil virtues,
the people will fear but not feel close;
when both civil and martial qualities are practiced,
then authority and virtue are perfected.
Once authority and virtue are perfected,
the people will feel close and submit.
Integrity will ascend to the top,
while cunning flattery will be blocked below.
Admonishers will gain advancement,
and loyalty and trustworthiness will accumulate."
Bóqín bowed twice, accepted the mandate, and took his leave.

Tāng asked Yī Yǐn, saying:
"The Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, Great Officers, and Arrayed Scholars -
how do they differ from one another?"
Yī Yǐn replied:
"The Three Dukes
are those whose knowledge penetrates the Great Way,
who respond to change without exhaustion and discern the nature of all things,
who are versed in the Way of Heaven.
Their words suffice to harmonize yin and yang,
rectify the four seasons,
and regulate wind and rain.
Such persons
are selected to be Three Dukes.
Thus the affairs of the Three Dukes constantly lie in the Way.
The Nine Ministers
are those who do not miss the four seasons,
are versed in ditches, canals, dikes, and embankments,
plant the five grains,
and are versed in terrestrial principles.
They can make passable what cannot be passed,
and can make beneficial what cannot be benefited.
Such persons
are therefore made Nine Ministers.
Thus the affairs of the Nine Ministers constantly lie in Virtue.
The Great Officers
go out and come in among the people,
taking and discarding with the multitude,
sharing benefits with the people,
versed in human affairs.
Their conduct is like applying a marking line,
not harming with words,
speaking in the world
without bringing harm to themselves.
They are versed in passes and bridges,
and fill the treasuries and storehouses.
Such persons are selected to be Great Officers.
Thus the affairs of the Great Officers constantly lie in Humaneness.
The Arrayed Scholars
know righteousness and do not lose their hearts,
achieve merit but do not monopolize the rewards,
are loyal in governance and strong in remonstrance without any deceit,
abandon selfishness and establish public spirit,
and their speech follows laws and measures.
Such persons are selected to be Arrayed Scholars.
Thus the affairs of the Arrayed Scholars constantly lie in Righteousness.
Thus when the Way, Virtue, Humaneness, and Righteousness are established,
the world is properly ordered through these four.
The enlightened king treats them as ministers yet not as ministers."
Tāng said:
"What does 'treat as ministers yet not as ministers' mean?"
Yī Yǐn replied:
"There are four types of ministers whom the ruler does not address by name: paternal uncles whom he treats as ministers but does not name,
elder brothers whom he treats as ministers but does not name,
ministers of former kings
whom he treats as ministers but does not name,
and men of great virtue
whom he treats as ministers but does not name.
This is called great harmony."

For generations pillars of the state.

Held firm against three temptations.

In the seventh year of Tàikāng's reign, on the first day of the year, a solar eclipse occurred,
whereupon the emperor issued a decree to the dukes, ministers, and high officials,
commanding each to submit sealed memorials,
inquiring where the fault lay.
Wáng Liàng, Prince of Rǔnán, along with Minister over the Masses Wèi Shū and Minister of Works Wèi Guàn, jointly memorialized regarding the responsibilities of the Three Dukes,
which correspond to Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.
When the Way of Heaven is not universal,
floods and droughts become disasters;
when human relations fall into disorder,
wickedness and corruption cannot be restrained.
Previously, within the territory of Jīng Province,
strange calamities repeatedly arose;
in the capital of Rènchéng Principality,
river waters turned crimson.
At the beginning of the Triple Dawns,
the sun was eclipsed;
after the season of Early Yang had passed,
solid ice had yet to melt.
We, your subjects, with our trivial talents,
have undeservedly held high positions,
which may be said to be like petty men riding in the carriage of gentlemen;
we ought to face public execution,
to respond to Heaven's intent.
Respectfully, we remove our caps, go barefoot, and return the seals and ribbons of office that were granted to us.
As for the disorder in the cosmic forces of yīn and yáng,
it is the result of Our failure in the Way of Heaven and misgovernment in punishments and administration.
Let them resume wearing caps and shoes, and say no more about it.

Emperor Míng entrusted his final commands to the assembled lords,
but his intentions rested largely with the Jiāng Yòu brothers.
In the early years of the Yǒngyuán era,

(From the Biography of Jiāng Yòu) Liángwǔ dispatched Zhāng Hóngcè to present a strategy to Wáng Yì, stating:
"In the past, Jìn Huì was an incompetent ruler,
leading the various princes to contend for power,
which resulted in nine internal conflicts arising,
and three external invasions occurring.
Now the Six Nobles vie for authority,
each grasping royal power,
and Shǐ'ān's ambitions are evident,
with signs of Zhào Lún's treachery already apparent.
For a cripple to ascend to heaven—

Yòu is timid and indecisive,

The tripod will break and the meal spill—

Xiāo Tǎnzhī harbors suspicion and jealousy in his heart,
his words often wounding others;

he follows others like an ox led by the nose,

Sū Wèidào held the position of chancellor for several years,
yet ultimately failed to make any significant contributions,
merely gliding smoothly among his peers,
seeking to please others and get by.
He once told people:
"When handling affairs, one should avoid making clear and decisive judgments,
for if there are mistakes,
one is bound to face blame and reprimand.
It is better to remain ambiguous and hold both sides."
Because of this, people of the time nicknamed him
"Sū the Ambiguous."
Lú Huáishèn and Zǐzhǐ Lìng Yáo Chóng jointly managed the Privy Council,

so Chóng always deferred to him in every matter.

Emperor Xuánzōng was skilled in the Bāfēn script,
and whenever he appointed generals or ministers,
he would first write their names with his own hand and place them on the desk.
Once, when the Crown Prince came to attend him,
the Emperor lifted a golden bowl to cover the names
and said to him:
"These are the names of the ministers.
Can you guess who they are?"
Emperor Sùzōng bowed and replied:
"Are they not Cuī Lín
and Lú Cóngyuàn?"
The Emperor said:
"Indeed."
He then lifted the bowl to show him
and bestowed a cup of wine upon him.
At that time, both Cuī Lín and Lú Cóngyuàn were expected to become ministers,
and Emperor Xuánzōng had considered relying on them as ministers several times,
but ultimately, because their clans were large and had many dependents,
he never appointed them.
"Old Anecdotes of the Liǔ Family"
In the third year of the Jǐnglóng era,
Sū Guī was appointed as the Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
At that time, when high-ranking ministers and officials were newly appointed to their positions,
it was customary for them to host celebratory feasts,
which were called
"shāo wěi" (burning the tail).
During an inner court banquet,
the Minister of the Palace Buildings,
Zōng Jìnqīng, remarked to Sū Guī:
"You were appointed as Vice Director, yet you did not hold a 'shāo wěi' feast.
Isn't that inappropriate?"
The Emperor remained silent,
and Sū Guī memorialized:
"Your subject has heard that the duty of a chancellor is
to oversee the harmony of yīn and yáng,
to assist in the natural order of heaven,
and to ensure the people have grain.
Now, food prices are soaring.
The common people do not have enough to eat,
and your subject has seen imperial guards
who have gone without food for three days.
Your subject is unworthy and unfit for the position,
which is why I did not dare to hold a 'shāo wěi' feast."
From "Tán Bīn Lù" (Records of a Guest's Conversations).
Lǐ Línfǔ's nature was reserved and secretive,
his mind deep and impenetrable,
concealing cruelty and tolerance for harm.
At the time, he was already bedridden with illness,
yet he still struggled to accompany the emperor to Huáqīng Palace,
and after a few days his condition worsened.
A shaman claimed that seeing the emperor would slightly improve his condition,
so the emperor wished to visit him,
but his attendants advised against it.
Instead, he ordered Lǐ Línfǔ to be brought out into the courtyard,
where the emperor ascended the Jiàngshēng Pavilion,
gazed from afar,
and waved a red handkerchief to console him.
Lǐ Línfǔ was unable to rise,
so he had someone bow on his behalf from his mat.
The next day, he passed away.
《Old Book of Tang》 When Emperor Xuánzōng fled to Shǔ,
Péi Shìyān accompanied him,
and on horseback they discussed the chief ministers of the time.
Péi Shìyān asked:
"What about Yáo Yuánzhī?"

"A man of talent and strength.
"What about Sòng Jǐng?"
He answered:
"A worthy but rigid man.
They discussed several dozen people,
and the emperor's assessments were all accurate.
Finally, Péi asked about Lǐ Línfǔ,
and the emperor said:
"He envied the worthy and jealous of the capable,
unmatched in all of history.
Péi Shìyān said:
"If that is so,
why did Your Majesty trust and employ him so deeply?"
The emperor lowered his head and remained silent.

During the Tiānbǎo era, rebels captured both capitals,
Emperor Xuánzōng fled westward,
Emperor Sùzōng ascended the throne,
Míng Huáng looked at the list of official appointments while on horseback,

Zhèn Yáng Wǎn,
courtesy name Gōngquán,
after Yuán Zǎi was executed,
Wǎn was appointed chancellor.
Wǎn had long been expected to become a high minister,
and when the edict was issued,
the court and public congratulated each other.
Wǎn was always known for his moral conduct,
upright and incorruptible by nature,
with frugal and simple carriages and attire.
Within a few months of serving at the court,
he naturally transformed people's hearts.
Cuī Kuān, Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review and younger brother of Níng, military governor of Jiànnán's four prefectures,
whose family was wealthy,
had a villa south of the imperial city,
with ponds, halls, terraces, and pavilions,
unsurpassed at the time.
Kuān secretly ordered its demolition that very day.
Guō Zǐyí, Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent, at his field headquarters in Bīnzhōu,
upon hearing of Wǎn's appointment as chancellor,
reduced the music in his gatherings by four-fifths.
Lí Gàn, Governor of the Capital, favored by the emperor,
used to have over a hundred outriders when coming and going,
but also reduced his carriage and horsemen that day,
keeping only ten riders.
Countless others followed suit, abandoning extravagance for frugality,
so effective was he in reforming customs and transforming morals.
All those Wǎn knew and befriended
were prominent figures of the time.
When visitors called on him,
they engaged in refined conversation all day,
never touching on fame or profit.
If a guest intended to discuss worldly affairs,
upon meeting Wǎn,
whose words were profound and far-reaching,
they dared not broach the topic,
retreating inwardly ashamed.
During the Dàlì era,
his virtue and reputation grew daily,
and upright scholars across the land vied to approach his gate,
some traveling thousands of li to do so,
as he upheld elegance and morality with his pure virtue.
He was compared to figures like Yáng Zhèn, Bǐng Jí, Shān Tāo, and Xiè Ān.
The Old Book of Tang's historian commented:
"Yáng Wǎn, within days of becoming chancellor,
swiftly achieved the transformation of customs and morals.
Even illustrious chancellors like the Duke of Zhōu, Duke of Shào, Yī Yǐn, Fù Yuè, Xiāo Hé, Zhāng Liáng, Fáng Xuánlíng, and Dù Rǔhuì
through the ages
had not been known for such a way.
Having read various collections,
I note that praise often exaggerates virtues,
and records of faults often overstate evils,
but in the case of Wǎn's appointment edict as chancellor,
the decree on posthumous honors,
and the edict altering his posthumous title,
the writers of the time had no cause for shame.
Lú Qǐ was appointed from his position as Vice Director of the Bureau of Evaluations in Xīnzhōu to be Prefect of Lǐzhōu,
but the Supervising Secretary Yuán Gāo, considering Lú Qǐ treacherous, flattering, and harmful to governance,
felt that his demotion did not suffice to atone for his faults,
so he halted the edict and submitted a memorial,
and as a result, Lú Qǐ was appointed Assistant Prefect of Lǐzhōu instead.
Some time later,
the Emperor said to Lǐ Miǎn:
"Everyone says Lú Qǐ is treacherous and evil,
but why is it that I do not perceive it?
Do you know the details?"
Lǐ Miǎn replied:
"The whole world knows he is treacherous and evil;
only Your Majesty does not know—
that is precisely why he is treacherous and evil."
Many people at the time praised his integrity.
The Emperor once remarked casually:
"Lú Qǐ is upright, incorruptible, and dares to speak out,
but he is poorly educated
and cannot broaden my knowledge with the ways of antiquity.
Everyone points out his treachery,
yet I do not perceive it."
Lǐ Miǎn replied:
"If Your Majesty could have perceived Lú Qǐ's wickedness,
how could the Jiànzhōng calamity have occurred?
Lǐ Kuí's peace mission to the Tibetans,
Yán Zhēnqīng's mission to Xīliè—
how many virtuous officials of old were harmed!
Moreover, Yáng Yán's crimes did not warrant death,
yet Lú Qǐ pushed him into it,
and implicated the Chancellor Guàn Bō.
Huáiguāng had rendered meritorious service,
but he was forced into rebellion.
This is deceiving Heaven itself."
The Emperor said:
"What you say is indeed true."
《Book of Táng》
Zhāng Jiāzhēn's son Yánshǎng,
Yánshǎng's son Hóngjìng,
three generations held the position of drafting imperial edicts,

Liú Yǔxī said:
"If official positions are not predetermined,
how can one speak of a true arbiter?"
During the Yǒnghuì era,
Lú Qíqīng temporarily died,
and upon reviving,
he recounted seeing his uncle Lǐ Mǒu,
who served as a judge in the underworld court.
A clerk presented a case file saying:
"Yǔwén Róng is to become chancellor."
The uncle said:
"How is Yǔwén Róng fit to be chancellor?"
The clerk replied:
"The official decree has already been issued,
specifying the number of days.
It's now up to the judge."
The uncle then adjudicated one hundred days.
Subsequently, Yǔwén Róng was appointed chancellor,
and indeed was dismissed after exactly one hundred days.
From "Jiāhuà"
Lǐ Fān,
courtesy name Shūhàn,
once resided in the Eastern Capital Luòyáng.
His wife was the daughter of Cuī Qiān, a lesser official,
and by the age of nearly thirty,
he had not yet achieved fame or office.
Often relying on the Cuī family,
he was not treated with full respect.
Suffering from a foot sore,
he wished to move his household to Yángzhōu,
feeling deeply troubled and anxious.
So he went to Zhōngqiáo to consult the fortune-teller Húlúshēng.
The fortune-teller said:
"You are under the protection of two gauze lanterns;
how could you fear this hardship?
Even greater adversities are manageable."
Lǐ asked about the gauze lanterns matter,
but the fortune-teller said no more.
Thus, he went to Yángzhōu,
residing near Cānsuǒqiáo.
Nearby lived Senior Official Gāo,
with whom he had long been on good terms.
One day, Gāo came to visit;
after leaving,
he returned in the evening,
saying:
"I came to see you this morning,
and upon returning home, I fell asleep, tired.
I dreamed of my former estate manager, who had been dead for ten years.
I asked him, 'How come you are here?'"
He replied:
"I serve as an underworld official,
assigned to attend to Lǐ Sānláng.
Knowing that you, Senior Official, associate with Sānláng,
I came here to wait upon you."
I asked:
"How is it that Sānláng has such status?"
He said:
"He is a man under the gauze lanterns."
When pressed further, he refused to elaborate,
only reporting this good news.
Lǐ laughed and thanked him.
A few years later,
when Zhāng Jiànfēng governed Yángzhōu,
he appointed Lǐ as a patrol officer.
It happened that a monk from Xīnlúo,
skilled in physiognomy,
declared that Zhāng would not become chancellor.
Zhāng then had him observe all the judges in the administrative office.
The monk said:
"None of them."
When Lǐ arrived,
the monk descended the steps to greet him,
telling Zhāng:
"The patrol officer is a man under the gauze lanterns;
even you, Commander, cannot compare."
Zhāng was greatly pleased
and inquired about the gauze lanterns matter.
The monk explained:
"The underworld administration secretly protects chancellors with gauze lanterns,
fearing they might be disturbed by malevolent forces;
other officials do not receive this."
Only then did Lǐ understand the words of Húlúshēng and Gāo.
Lǐ eventually became chancellor.

On the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month in the seventh year of the Dàhé era,
Emperor Wénzōng intended to appoint Déyù as a chancellor,
and the edict draft had already been submitted.
The emperor decreed:
"Appointing a chancellor is an extremely important matter.
I have just consulted the calendar,

From "Records of Advising and Substituting"
Whenever a chancellor was appointed,
the ceremony surpassed all court ranks,
with the prefectural offices carrying sand to pave the road,
from his private residence to the eastern street of the inner city,
named:
"The Sand Embankment.
If he was on leave due to mourning,
officials would visit to inquire about his health,
and all officials would gather at his residence.
The relevant offices would set up curtained enclosures,
arranging officials in order.
On New Year's Day and the winter solstice when guards of honor were stationed,
high officials all had jade-decorated canopies prepared,
with five to six hundred torches arranged in rows,
called the "fire city."
When the chancellor's fire was approaching,
all others would extinguish theirs to yield.
"Supplement to the National History" When Lǐ Déyù first became chancellor,
he discontinued the capital's practice of building the sand embankment,
and the imperial guards lining the two streets for morning court.
"Basic Biography" When Déyù first became chancellor,
the commissioners of the two streets requested to follow precedent,
seeking to have guards escort him each morning to court. He ruled:
"In a position observed by all,
the state's dignity is inherent;
in times without incident,
why trouble the military preparedness?
The escort should be discontinued.
"Records of Advising and Replacing"
Lǐ Déyù from Rùnzhōu at age fifty-four,
was appointed to Yángzhōu at fifty-eight,

Later rulers often entrusted state power to literary scholars.
At the beginning of the Yuanhe era,
Emperor Xiànzōng followed the precedents set by his holy ancestors,
observing those who had the qualities of a prime minister,
and kept them in the inner court.
As a result, those who put aside the brush and inkstone to wield instruments of transformation
were eight or nine out of ten.
"Collected Notes of Liú Rǔxī and Lǐ Jiàng"
Emperor Shùnzōng was unwell,
and the crown prince had not yet been established.
Wáng Shūwén arose from an unsavory background,
usurped the title of scholar,
and formed an alliance with Niú Měirén within the court.
Lǐ Zhōngyán conspired externally with treacherous factions,
gaining control of military power,
coveting the imperial throne,
causing nationwide alarm.
At this time, Zhèng Yīng served as a senior official of the inner court,
took the lead in devising major plans.
When Emperor Xiànzōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Yīng as the Chancellery Advisor and Chief Minister.
"Annals of Hànlín" When Emperor Dézōng passed away,
the illness of the Crown Prince was severe,
and Cāng urgently summoned scholars Zhèng Yīng and others to the Jīnluán Hall.
Some within the palace said:
"There is deliberation within,
and no decision has been reached on the successor.
No one responded.
Wèi Cìgōng promptly said:
"Although the Crown Prince is ill,
he holds the rightful position of heir,
and has the concerns of both the inner and outer courts,
if it is absolutely necessary,
the Prince of Guǎnglíng should be established.
If there is any deviation from this plan,
calamity and disaster will not cease.
Yīng and others followed his lead and advocated it,
and only then was the consensus reached.
"Old Táng Records"
Lǐ Jífǔ was appointed as the Grand Chancellor of the Secretariat,
and it happened that he was on duty at the same time as Péi Jì.
Péi Jì drafted the edict for Lǐ Jífǔ,
while Lǐ Jífǔ drafted the edict for Wǔ Yuánhéng.
They wrote behind lowered blinds, unaware of each other's work.
By evening,
Lǐ Jífǔ uttered sighs of regret,
but Péi Jì remained silent throughout.
After writing the final part of the edict,
they then congratulated each other,
and the utmost respect of ceremonial protocol
arose among those seated.
When dawn broke in the courtyard,
academicians escorted them to the Yíntái Gate,
while officials from the ministerial office waited outside the gate.
The grandeur of the imperial institution
had never been seen before.
"Records of the Hanlin Academy"
Shěn Chuánshī entered the Hanlin Academy as an academician.
When the position of Hanlin chief academician became vacant,
he was next in line for the appointment.
Emperor Mùzōng intended to appoint him in person,
but Shěn declined, saying:
"The academicians and the head of the academy
participate in the emperor's confidential deliberations
and rank next only to the prime minister.
I know for certain I am incapable of this.
I would rather govern a region
and nurture the people there for Your Majesty."
He then pleaded illness and left the capital.
(from The Book of Táng)
Lǐ Shēn,
courtesy name Gōngchuí,
was able to compose songs, poems, and local rhapsodies in his youth,
with his recitations widely circulated among the people.
In the early Yuánhé era,
he passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì,
and was summoned by Emperor Mùzōng to serve as a Hànlín academician.
He served alongside Lǐ Déyù and Yuán Zhěn in the imperial secretariat,
where they were collectively known as the "Three Talents,"
sharing deep mutual affection.
The Old Book of Táng notes that the three men were comparable in learning, knowledge, and literary fame,
and their relationship was notably intimate.
From the Biography of Lǐ Déyù.
Lǐ Déyù,
when Emperor Mùzōng ascended the throne,
was summoned to the Hànlín Academy to serve as an academician.
The emperor, while still crown prince,
had long heard of Jífǔ's reputation,
and after meeting Déyù,
held him in particularly high esteem within the palace, entrusting him with drafting many important edicts and documents.
That month, he was summoned for an audience at the Sīzhèng Hall,
where he was bestowed with the golden and purple robes.
(Old Book of Táng)
When Lǐ Déyù was governing Shǔ,
he told his aide Wéi Xuàn:
"The Hànlín Academy has hanging bells,
prepared for night duty alerts and emergencies,
when documents come and go,
they are rung instead of using shouts to relay messages.
During the Chángqìng era,
I served as an academician,
at that time there was military action in Héběi,
one night the bell sounded,
as if someone was pulling its rope,
I sent someone to check,
but there was no one there.
Later this often happened,
I had people wait with clubs hiding below,
yet ultimately saw nothing,
while the bell repeatedly rang and moved incessantly.
Everyone in the academy,
collectively verified its ringing.
At that time it always corresponded to battlefield news,
and the urgency matched exactly as before,
never differing,
all found it strange.
Chancellor Yuán's poem says: The spirit shakes the bell rope.
"Shēn Wénbǐng's Continuation of Hànlín Anecdotes"
Lǐ Déyù's poem describing a dream says:
"Lotus-clean Ponds of Penglai minced fish,
Ice-cold Yǐng River wine brew."
Annotation: Every newly appointed Academician,
is bestowed food all being Penglai pond fish slices.
At Summer Solstice again bestowed,
and distributed incense-burning wine,
because the wine flavor is somewhat strong,
each time mixed with water to drink,
indeed the palace's Yǐng River wine,
minced also.
From "Yīpǐn Collection" This text is Ráo's poem,
"Shì Wén Lèi Jù" however says:
"Lǐ Bái's poem,
Could the annotation of Bái's poem not have been seen in the original collection?
Or merely copied from old papers?
Hébì following this,
greatly misleads viewers.
Doorkeeper guests My later pity for literary guests,
My colleagues together outstanding talents.
Annotation: The previous court once proclaimed you all are my doorkeeper guests.
Above "Shì Wén" writes as Táng Empress Wǔ's court.
And so on Lǐ Wèigōng's Shīhuà mistaken.
Cuī Yǎn,
styled Guǎnglüè,
was majestic and handsome in appearance,
evoking admiration from all who saw him.
When Emperor Jìngzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Hanlin Academician and Lecturer,
soon advancing to the position of Zhōngshū Shèrén.
He declined, saying:
"Your Majesty appointed me as Lecturer,
yet for half a year you have not once inquired about the meaning of the classics.
I have achieved nothing to deserve such great favor."
The emperor replied with shame:
"I shall seek your instruction when I have some leisure."
From the "Old Book of Táng"
Emperor Wénzōng summoned the Minister of War Wáng Qǐ and
the Minister of Rites Xǔ Kāngzuǒ to serve as Lecturing Academicians,
with the Secretariat Drafter Liǔ Gōngquán as the Calligraphy Academician.
Whenever there were doubtful matters, he would summon the academicians to the informal hall for consultation and discussion, making this a regular practice.
They were called the Three Attendant Academicians,
receiving exceptional favor and honor.
Xióng Wàng passed the imperial examination,
possessing rudimentary literary talent,
yet constantly striving for advancement.
At that time, the Capital Prefect Liǔ Qīchǔ had rapidly risen to a prominent position through unconventional means,
extensively building factions,
with his courtyard bustling day and night,
ceaselessly crowded with visitors.
Wǎng frequented Qīchǔ's residence,
as if they were close relatives,
secretly devising schemes,
unbeknownst to others.
While Emperor Jìngzōng indulged in leisurely pastimes,
he studied poetry,
but considering the翰林學士 too esteemed
to be treated frivolously,
proposed establishing additional Eastern Court Academicians
specifically for banquets and poetic compositions,
ordering the selection of low-ranking officials qualified for the post.
Qīchǔ recommended Wàng by name,
but the plan was aborted upon Emperor Zhāomǐn's demise.
When Emperor Wénzōng ascended the throne,
Wéi Chǔhòu assumed ministerial duties,
vigorously purging treacherous factions.
After being expelled,
Qīchǔ had Wàng exiled to Zhāngzhōu as a Registration Officer.
《Old Book of Tang》
Líng Hú Táo served as the Hanlin Academician Receiver of Edicts and had an audience in the palace at night.
When the candles burned out,
the emperor had him escorted back using the imperial carriage with golden lotus-flower torches.
The officials at the Hanlin Academy saw this from a distance,
mistaking it for the arrival of the emperor.
But when Líng Hú Táo arrived,
they were all astonished.
"History of the Tang Dynasty"
Bì Xián,
a jìnshì graduate during the Tàihé era,
served as a Hànlín Academician.
Since the end of the Dàzhōng era,
the Dǎngxiàng Qiāng rebelled,
repeatedly harassing Héxī.
Emperor Yìzōng summoned academicians to discuss border affairs,
where Xián cited historical and contemporary examples to elaborate
on strategies to defeat the Qiāng.
The emperor was pleased
and said:
"I was just seeking a capable commander
to pacify Héxī.
Little did I expect to find such talents as Lián Pō and Lǐ Mù
within my own court.
Will you undertake this mission for me?"
Xián joyfully accepted the command,
and was immediately appointed Military Commissioner of Héxī and other posts.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Cuī Yífàn was promoted by Lǐ Màozhēn during the siege of Fèngxiáng,
and was reappointed as chancellor.
When Hán Wò was to draft the edict, he submitted a memorial opposing it.
Late at night, he sent it to the Hanlin Academy scholars,
and had the eunuch Mǎ Cónghào relay a message to Hán Wò:
"Do not gamble with your life, Scholar."
Hán Wò did not reply,
but bolted his door and slept.
The next day, no hemp-paper edict was announced. Lǐ Màozhēn said:
"Your Majesty appointed a chancellor,
but the scholar refused to draft the edict.
How is this different from rebellion?"
Emperor Zhāozōng replied:
"You recommended Cuī Yífàn,
and I did not refuse;
Hán Wò refused to draft the edict,
and I did not refuse him either.
What can be done when principles are clear?"
From "Secret Records of the Golden Luan Hall," Yáo Jì said:
"Had I been on duty,
I too would have chosen death."
From "The Tang History"
Hán Yínliàng,
the son of Hán Wò,
once recounted that on the day of Wò's death,
the military governor of Wēnlíng heard his family kept many chests and boxes,
securely locked and sealed,
rarely seen by others.
Suspecting they must contain rare treasures,
he sent a trusted aide to open and inspect them,
only to find burnt remnants of dragon-and-phoenix candles,
over a hundred gold-threaded red scarves,
with candle wax still fresh,
and the scarves' fragrance lingering.
An old servant tearfully said:
"When the master served as an academician,
he often drafted edicts in the Golden Luan Inner Palace,
returning late at night to the Hányuàn Hall.
Palace maids would escort him holding candle torches,
all of which the master kept.
After the turmoil in the Western Capital,
he was convicted and exiled south,
with scarcely one or two items remaining."
At Yánpíng's home, an old nun
recounted this story matching Yínliàng's account.
The nun was said to be Wò's concubine.
"Recent Events of Southern Tang" Wò fell out of favor with Zhū Quánzhōng,
and was demoted to Róngyì County.
In the second year of the Tiānyòu era,
he was recalled as an academician,
restoring his former position.
Wò dared not return to court,
but took his family
south to rely on Wáng Shěnzhī, where he died.
"Tang Biographies"

Emperor Zhāozōng summoned Hán Wò to the Academy to be tested on five literary compositions: "Rhapsody on All States Being at Peace," "Poem on Heeding Wise Counsel," "Appointment Decree for a Military Official as Military Commissioner of Dōngchuān," "Reply to the King of Fóshì Presenting Tribute," and "Endorsement on the Memorial of Three Meritorious Officials Declining Portraits."
He said:
"My talent does not surpass the crowd,
my ability is not extraordinary.
Awaiting recognition differs from jade in a casket,
mastering the classics shames me before gold in a basket.
Encountering this clear age,
bathed in the emperor's profound grace,
wearing tall hats and shaking pendants,
I already defile the ranks at the elephant gate;
licking the brush and blending ink,
I further receive summons at the golden gate.
Beating the bowl to decline praise for quick writing,
my literary composition lacks skill.
Examining myself and knowing my limits,
I regard this honor with fear."
The "Secret Records of the Golden Luan" states: In the first year of the Chángxīng era,
Hanlin Academician Liú Xù memorialized about the old practice of the Academy,
that when academicians entered the Academy,
except for those appointed as Secretarial Court Directors, all others were tested on drafting hemp-paper edicts and replies,
one barbarian document response each,
one poem and one rhapsody each,
collectively called the Test of Five Topics.
"Continued Comprehensive Statutes"
Lù Yǐ,
styled Xiángwén,
had swift and nimble literary thoughts,
initially without need for contemplation,
wielding his brush like flying,
with both literary grace and logic being satisfying.
His colleagues admired his ability,
and the emperor regarded and treated him with exceptional favor.
Once, when composing a rhapsody at the Jinluán Hall,
he was ordered to harmonize with academicians, yet Yǐ finished first.
The emperor read it and sighed with admiration, saying:
"I have heard that during the Zhēnyuán era,
there were Lù Zhì and Wú Tōngxuán brothers who could write inner court documents,
but later there was absolutely no one to succeed them.
Now that I have obtained you,
this literary tradition will not fall into decline."
(Old Book of Táng)
Lù Yǐ was appointed Academician Recipient of Edicts,
Concurrent Manager of Affairs, following the precedent of the three bureaus,
where appointments were accompanied by funds for a celebratory feast,
to host former colleagues.
The inner bureau originally had no such practice.
In the month Yǐ assumed the assistant ministership,
he sent five hundred strings of cash to the Academicians' Guangyuan,
specifically establishing a new precedent,
which brought honor to the inner bureau.
The Emperor
Lù Yǐ composed the "Model Proclamation for the Guangyuan" at the academy's platform,
stating:
"Expending resources to regulate the golden cauldron,
one can oversee the toil of drafting documents;
emerging adorned with the green canopy,
one is freed from the constraints of wielding the brush.
This is indeed the utmost devotion of a subject,
and also the glory of the Hanlin Academy.
As for observing local customs in a region,
or rewarding the three envoys with currency,
these are grand affairs.
Yet they are of secondary importance;
all are requested to contribute funds to glorify the Jade Office."
"Old Regulations of the Hanlin Academy"
Péi Tíngyù,
during the Qiánníng era served in the inner court,
was exceptionally swift in drafting documents,
earning the nickname "downstream boat".
When Liáng Zhū Wēn accepted the abdication, Péi Tíngyù became an academician.
Zhū Wēn once casually inquired about Tíngyù's whereabouts,
to which Péi Tíngyù replied:
"He was recently demoted,
and I heard he's now staying in Héngshuǐ."
The Emperor said:
"I've heard this man composes with remarkable speed."
Péi Tíngyù responded:
"When he served in the Hanlin Academy,
he was called 'downstream boat'."
The Emperor immediately retorted to Péi Tíngyù:
"Then you must be the upstream boat."
Péi Tíngyù smiled faintly,
but appeared deeply ashamed.
Commentators thus regarded Péi Tíngyù as "an upstream boat struggling against rapids".
From "Táng Zhí Yán"
Fēng Shòuqīng, while serving as the chief examiner in the Liáng dynasty, was disgraced.
His protégé Zhèng Zhìyōng received the same appointment to enter the Hànlín Academy as an academician.
Zhìyōng possessed outstanding talent,
while Shòuqīng's literary skills were clumsy and limited.
When tested with five essay topics,
he could not overcome his exhaustion and inadequacy,
thus entrusting Zhìyōng to wield the brush for him.
Contemporary critics deemed it a disgrace for a mentor to rely on his protégé.
He retired from office in the early years of the Tóngguāng era.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."

In the Tongguang era of the Later Táng, the Academician Recipient of Edicts Lú Zhì was granted the honorific "Meritorious Subject for Deliberative Assistance," and was subsequently appointed Military Commissioner of Hézhōng. Dào composed a poem saying:
"From the north came the Táng Academician drafting edicts,
Westward goes the Hàn General bearing a command staff.
Contemporaries considered it an honor.
"Continued Records of the Hànlín Academy"
Lǐ Huàn served as a Hanlin Academician,

and often ascended the hall to attend banquets. When attendants in embroidered robes gestured for him to withdraw, Huàn scolded them, after which he was granted crimson robes and seated alongside his examiner Hé Níng, both holding the position of academician.
When Hé Níng became chancellor,
Huàn, who often drafted imperial edicts, ordered the opening of Hé Níng's pavilion to take all the artifacts and books back for himself.
Such was his unrestrained nature.
When the Hanlin Academy was abolished,
he was appointed Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
then promoted to Director of the Ministry of Rites,
in charge of drafting edicts.
After the Hanlin Academy was reinstated,
he was promoted to Secretariat Drafter,
once again serving as an academician.
At that time, while serving in the Western Bureau,
he was honored by the officials.
(From "Fen Ji")
When Lǐ Jǐng ascended the throne of the Southern Táng,
Féng Yánsì showed joy on his face.
Before Jǐng had begun to attend to state affairs,
Yánsì repeatedly entered to report matters.
Jǐng, displeased, said:
"The secretary has his regular duties;
other matters are handled by respective offices.
Why trouble me unnecessarily?"
Soon after, Yánsì was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance
and concurrently served as a Hanlin Academician.
He then allied with Wèi Cén to undermine state affairs,
and together with his brother Yánlǔ, Chén Jué, and Zhā Wénhuī,
they mutually supported and promoted each other,
earning them the contemporary nickname "The Five Ghosts."
From "The History of the Nine States"
In the first year of the Jiànlóng era,
Academician Wáng Zhù was dismissed from his post due to drunken misconduct,
and Měng, having made requests,
both were demoted.
Emperor Tàizǔ said to the chancellor:
"In such a solemn place,
it should be occupied by veteran Confucian scholars."
Fàn Zhì replied:
"Dòu Yí is upright, incorruptible, and dignified,
but he has recently been transferred from the Hànlín Academy to the Duānmíng Palace."
The Emperor said:
"Within the palace, no one but this man will do.
You must convey my intention to him,
and urge him to assume the post."
"Fēn Jì Sòng Shǐ"
In the fourth year of the Chúnhuà era,
Zhāng Jì and Qián Ruòshuǐ were appointed as Hanlin Academicians.
When Jì and others assumed their posts,
the Emperor said:
"The position of Academician
is pure, intimate, and highly esteemed,
incomparable to other offices.
I have often regretted not being able to follow the old precedent
where, when Academicians assumed their posts,
an imperial banquet was bestowed,
which has long been discontinued.
I shall now order it to be held."
He also summoned the Academicians of the Privy Council
and the Drafters of Edicts to join the banquet.
Jì was broadly learned in the classics and histories,
well-versed in ancient precedents.
Whenever the Emperor produced writings,
or bestowed poems upon his close ministers,
Jì would invariably submit memorials,
citing classics and commentaries to support and amplify the imperial intent.
The Emperor thus bestowed a poem praising him,
containing the line
"The Hanlin elder, a learned minister."
Later, while serving as Vice Minister of Personnel and evaluating officials,
the Emperor, looking at him, told his close ministers:
"Zhāng Jì is richly endowed with literary talent,
and to this day still diligently studies—
he is the foremost among scholars of Jiāngdōng."
Zhāng Jì, styled Shī'àn, served the Southern Táng,
as Academician of the Qīnghuī Hall.
After entering the Sòng, he served together with Sū Yìjiǎn in the Hanlin Academy,
enjoying great favor,
though he did not get along with Sū Yìjiǎn.
The Shìwén erroneously places Zhāng Jì between Liú Huīzhī and Liǔ Gōngquán,
which is a mistake.
Emperor Tàizōng considered the establishment of the Jade Hall to have a long history,
but it had only an empty title
without a proper name.
Thus, on a piece of red silk, he wrote four characters in feibai script,
inscribing them as:
"The Crime of the Jade Hall."
He bestowed this upon Sū Yìjiǎn.
Lord Yìjiǎn respectfully carried it back to his private residence,
to honor and glorify his ancestors,
choosing an auspicious day to hang it up,
and still kept it securely locked in the Jade Hall.
From the officials of the Academy of Awaiting Orders down, all lined up in the courtyard to congratulate him.
Lord Yìjiǎn said:
"Since the Tang dynasty established the academicians,
nearly three hundred years have passed,
and only today do we realize its prestige."
That very day, an edict was issued to the chief ministers,
along with officials from the two departments,
to set up a banquet at the academy,
and each composed a long rhyming poem
to commemorate the event.
The collection of these poems was titled "Banquet Gathering in the Forbidden Grove."
From "Fen Ji"
When Emperor Tàizōng arrived,
the spring in the Shanglin Garden was warm,
with thousands of flowers and myriad blossoms,
their beauty unparalleled.
The emperor would invariably host intimate banquets for his chief ministers and meritorious veterans,
summoning academicians from both drafting institutions.
Leaning over the Dragon Pond,
they lowered golden hooks,
composing poems and celebrating throughout the day before concluding.
The emperor once remarked to his close ministers:
"Academicians truly hold positions akin to celestial beings.
The following day,
all submitted poems
were returned with imperial brush annotations and matching verses bestowed as gifts.
From "Fēn Jì"
In the Eastern Hall of the Jade Hall,
there was a fire burning on the window lattice of the chamber.
Emperor Tàizōng once visited the Jade Hall at night.
Sū Yìjiǎn was the academician,
already asleep,
he hastily rose,
and without a candle, put on his official attire.
A palace maid brought a candle through the window lattice to illuminate him,
and to this day, they do not wish to change it,
considering it a grand event of the Jade Hall.
"Brush Talks"
Sòng Bái and Jiǎ Huángzhōng were both eminent scholars of great virtue,
together in Ào Jìn.
In "Recorded Conversations," General Lǐ's poem "Painting of a Wall with Flying Crane Immortals Scene,"
depicts a giant turtle.
Inside the annotation, the walls of the office,
a pine crane is painted on the north.
Previously, on the west wall, there was a painting of the Curved Dragon Mountain in the sea.
Emperor Xiànzōng once planned to visit it,
but Jiǎ, being afraid, erased it.
Under the old system, whenever one entered the Two Councils,
they were permitted to recommend one candidate for an academic post,
and one official who had passed the examinations and served as a surveillance commissioner.
Councilor Wáng Déyòng, returning from Pŭtián,
was reappointed to head the Council,
and immediately had the right to recommend for an academic post.
Wáng said:
"With your talent having passed the imperial examinations,
the recommended candidate should meet the standards.
However, I am a military man who seldom reads,
if I were to submit a recommendation, it would be a 'shout of embarrassment'."
This was considered by contemporaries as a wise remark,
for people nowadays describe something as unreasonable or inappropriate as a "shout of embarrassment".
From "The History of the Millet"
South of Jìzhōu city there was Zhāng Ěr,
whose home was north of the Farewell Pavilion.
A Khitan envoy Línyá, serving as a Hanlin Academician on a mission to Sòng,
asked the prefect Wáng Zhòngpíng:
"I don't know from which generation Zhāng Ěr was."
Their chief envoy Yēlǜ Fáng apologized, saying:
"The Khitan's Hanlin Academician
is merely a title."
The Hanlin Academy is a place of pivotal and confidential affairs.
"Records of the Hanlin Academy": To elucidate grand strategies,
and embellish imperial decrees,
with a single document or brief edit,
can move both humans and spirits,
spreading across the four directions,
as if witnessed from ten thousand miles away.
Thus, decisions are made within,
and affairs are managed externally;
words issue from above,
and intentions are disseminated among the people.
Subtle are these writings,
upon which all regulations depend.
Moreover, the establishment of this academy is especially intimate and crucial,
adjoining the sleeping palace on the left,
and overlooking the crimson tower on the right;
hastening to the ornate gates at dawn,
and lodging under strict guard at night,
it is the epitome of secrecy.
Steeds from the imperial stables draw the carriages,
and entrances and exits are guided by internal officials.
Sumptuous and clean meals,
are provided by the grand provisioner,
while quilts, bedding, and attire,
are supplied from the central treasury,
such is the depth of favor.
Prepared to await consultation,
debating and refuting right and wrong,
managing silk documents,
and handling dispatched duties,
all gains and losses of an era,
instantly become subjects of praise or blame,
such is the weight of the responsibility.
If not cautious and principled,
and steadfast in integrity,
upright yet understanding,
entrusted with pivotal duties,
and favored by the imperial heart,
never uttering the names of warm trees,
cautious not to overlook the count of carriage horses,
those who hold this position,
is it not indeed difficult?
"Historical Accounts of the Hanlin Academy"
Since the Jiànzhōng era,
selection has been exceptionally stringent,
so one must be as discreet as Kǒng Guāng,
as erudite as Yánzhōu,
as literary as Qīngyún,
as learned as Xiàng and Xīn,
as capable as Huáng and Yán,
as upright as Shǐ Yú,
only then qualifying for a middle rank.
Scholars who aspire to emulate these six exemplars in their self-cultivation and conduct,
and further adorn themselves with pure and precious conduct,
piercing through metal and stone with their sincerity.
Even if concealing their reputation and traces,
none can escape notice.
In the Hàn dynasty, the establishment of the Shàngshū Láng began,
five men pacifying the realm,
submitting memorials and taking turns on duty,
establishing rituals and bearing fragrance,
grasping orchids and residing in brocade,
dining in the grand official's tent,
thus the present Hànlín Academy,
differs in name but shares the same essence.
Contemporary opinion holds it akin to ascending the jade purity and soaring through purple skies,
how could Pénglái and Yíngzhōu suffice as metaphors?
Wéi Chǔhòu's "Record of the Hànlín Academy Hall Wall" also refers to it as the jade office and jade hall.
"Records of the Hànlín Academy"
The old Tang system did not allow scholars to use "Chéngzhǐ" as a title,
in responding to consultations,
attending meetings,
their rank was determined by their official position.
In the first year of the Xiànzōng Yǒngzhēn era,
Zhèng Yīn was appointed as Chéngzhǐ,
taking a position above the scholars,
residing in the first pavilion to the east.
The "Chéngzhǐyuànjì" records that during the internal banquets, the seating arrangement was above the Chancellor,
seated above the first rank.

Méi Xún was a member of the Hànlín Academy.
One day, he had to draft many imperial edicts,
struggling greatly with composition,
and walked along the steps, holding his writing tablet.
Suddenly, he saw an old soldier lying in the sun,
stretching and yawning with great comfort.
Méi suddenly sighed and said:
"How delightful!"
Then he asked him slowly:
"Do you know how to read?"
The soldier replied:
"No, I don't."
Méi said:
"Even more carefree!"

《Memoir》
In the third month of the thirteenth year,
due to the submission of ceremonial procedures for the Feng and Shan sacrifices,
the Emperor ordered a banquet to be held at the Jíxiān Hall for academicians.
The Emperor composed a poetic preface,
and all officials composed poems.
The Emperor then orally decreed from his seat to rename the hall Jíxián Hall.
Those attending the banquet included
Chief Minister and Palace Attendant Yuán Qiányào, Duke Yàn,

and academicians Xú Jiān, Hè Zhīzhāng, Kāng Zǐyuán, Zhào Dōngxī, Hóu Xíngguǒ, Jìng Huìzhēn, Zhào Xuánmò, Wéi Shù, Lǐ Zǐzhāo, Lù Qùtài, Lǚ Xiàng, Xián Yì, Yèwú Zhào, Yú Qīn, Sūn Jìliáng, Féng Cháoyǐn, and others.
Fresh cherries had just been presented,
and the Emperor ordered them scattered across the banquet seats,
instructing each official to pick them up.
They drank fine, clear wine.
As the wine flowed freely,
colorful paper was brought out from behind the curtain,
and Duke Yàn was commanded to compose a poem using official rhymes.
All officials composed poems,
and colorful silks were also brought out.
Those who rolled matching dice in a board game won double prizes,
which were distributed during the banquet.
Golden cups and silver plates,
along with assorted colorful silks, were awarded in varying amounts.
The Emperor
Zhāng Yàngōng once remarked to someone:
"The title of Academician,
being an honorable designation for literary Confucians,
must be specially conferred by imperial decree;
how can one presumptuously adopt it for oneself?
At that time, Hè Zhīzhāng was promoted from Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices to Vice Minister of Rites,
while also being appointed as an Academician.
After expressing gratitude for both appointments in one day,
he visited Prime Minister Yuán, the Palace Attendant, and said:
"Your Excellency Hè has long enjoyed great renown.
Today you have simultaneously received two honors,
both adding luster to the Academician's position.
Nevertheless, between the Academician and Vice Minister, which is the more distinguished?
Zhāng Yàngōng replied:
"Since the establishment of our imperial dynasty,
the Vice Ministership has been a splendid position for distinguished officials.
Unless one has served in pure and important posts,
possessing both prestige and substantial merit,
none can hold it.
Yet ultimately it remains a regular bureaucratic position,
not what past worthies particularly admired.
As for the Academician,
one embraces the Way of ancient kings,
serving as a model for officials,
possessing the literary talent of Yáng Xióng and Bān Gù,
combined with the literary learning of Zǐyóu and Zǐxià—
only then can one assume the position.
Without shame between these two honors,
this is the superior one.
The Emperor
Zhāng Yuè served as chancellor three times over more than thirty years,
overseeing literary affairs,
and was regarded as the leading figure of Tang literature.
The Emperor often drafted texts within the palace,
ordering Yuè to review the drafts.
Yuè also skillfully utilized his own strengths,
recommending Confucian scholars to serve as attendants,
assisting the monarch in promoting royal influence.
The Emperor began establishing the Jíxián Institute halls with classical scholarship,
appointing eighteen academicians,
to restore Tàizōng's governance policies.
Scholars engaged in literary composition at that time
began revering ancient styles,
and the Emperor's fondness for literature
originated from Yuè's influence.

Emperor Zhēnzōng composed a poem,

"In recent appointments of academicians,
I have rarely bestowed poetic compositions,
so I remarked: 'Péngnián excels in literary scholarship,
having been promoted to a prestigious and intimate position,
he has grown increasingly prudent and discreet over time,
well-informed and fond of learning.
Few can match him;
in daily life, he writes over ten thousand words,
and is also meticulous in mastering rituals and ceremonies,
profoundly understanding laws and decrees.
When others seek his advice,
he responds fluently,
all with solid foundations.
I often assign him to examine classical precedents,
verify textual meanings,

Mǐnzhōng said:
"Péngnián is an all-around talent,
not merely elegant and composed in scholarly service;
as for deliberating on current affairs,
and meticulously investigating principles,
he consistently surpasses expectations.
The Emperor agreed,
and added:
"In the Bureau of Deliberation, no matter the size of affairs,
all await Péngnián's judgment before finalization;
this statement must not be omitted.
Previously, when deliberating on rituals, although various departments were consulted,
the insights all came from minor clerks,
now we take this as the standard.
《Cháng Biān》
Yáng Yì was renowned throughout the land for his literary talent,
but his temperament was rigid and unyielding, making him few friends.
Those who disliked him seized upon incidents to slander him.
While serving in the Hanlin Academy,
he was suddenly summoned for a nighttime audience in a small pavilion,
deep within the palace grounds.
After being granted tea,
the emperor engaged him in a leisurely conversation.
After a while, the emperor brought out several boxes of draft manuscripts, showing them to Dànián and saying:
"Do you recognize my handwriting?
All of these were drafted by my own hand,
never once assigned to any official."
Dànián was terrified and at a loss for words,
kowtowing repeatedly before taking his leave.
Only then did he realize he must have been slandered by someone,
and consequently feigned madness and fled to Yángzhái.
Emperor Zhēnzōng, who had a fondness for literature,
had initially treated Dànián with gracious favor and respect,
but gradually this too waned for this reason.

"Yáng Yì cannot be reasoned with;

Mǎ Huáisù served as Director of the Palace Library and concurrently as Academician of the Zhaowen Institute.
He was devoted to learning by nature,
never letting books out of his hand,
and was humble, respectful and cautious.
He was deeply respected by Emperor Xuánzōng,
and served as Imperial Reader along with Left Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Chǔ Wúliàng.
Every time they reached the palace gate,
they were ordered to enter by sedan chair.
When the Emperor resided at a separate lodge,
he would order them to ride horses from the palace or personally see them off and welcome them due to the long distance,
so as to demonstrate the etiquette between teacher and student.
