During the Jǐngyún era, Chǔ Wúliàng
was initially appointed by Emperor Xuánzōng, then the Crown Prince, as a tutor
and concurrently served as the Crown Prince's Lecturer.
He once composed "Records of Assisting Goodness" and presented it to him,
for which the Crown Prince sent a commendatory letter and rewarded him with silk.
He left his post to observe mourning for his parent,
and after the mourning period ended,
he resumed his role as Lecturer.
Due to his advanced age,
he was specially permitted to walk slowly when following the imperial procession,
and a sedan chair was made for him, with palace attendants carrying him within the inner court.
Initially, both Chǔ Wúliàng and Mǎ Huáisù served as Lecturers,
and they were treated with great favor.
After Chǔ Wúliàng and others passed away,
later, Deputy Director of the Palace Library Kāng Zǐyuán,
and Erudites of the National University Hóu Xíngguǒ, among others, entered to serve as lecturers.
Although they were repeatedly rewarded,
the courtesy and treatment they received did not match that given to Chǔ and Mǎ.
Bái Lǚzhì was widely learned in literature and history,
and once lived in seclusion in the ancient city of Dàliáng,
where his contemporaries called him Liángqiūzǐ.
During the Jǐngyún era,
he was summoned and appointed as a collator,
but soon resigned from office and returned home.
In the Kāiyuán era,
Wáng Zhìyīn submitted a memorial recommending him,
praising Lǚzhōng for his seclusion and devotion to study,
his steadfastness and austere integrity,
which reflected the virtues of the ancients,
making him worthy to replace Chǔ Wúliàng and Mǎ Huáisù as an attendant reader in the imperial library.
He was summoned to the capital,
but upon arrival,
Lǚzhōng declined on grounds of old age and illness,
claiming he was unfit for official duties.
The emperor issued an edict appointing him as a court gentleman for comprehensive duty,
yet he begged to return the imperial decree,
requesting permission to travel in the capital
before slowly returning to his hometown.
Lǚzhōng stayed for several months before departing.
During the Kāiyuán era,
Wáng Jùn led troops from Bīngzhōu,
marching westward to suppress rebellious tribes.
Traveling covertly and doubling their speed,
they hastened through the night in the mountains
when suddenly they encountered a fierce blizzard.
Fearing he would miss the deadline,
Wáng Jùn looked up to heaven and vowed:
"If I, Jùn, am disloyal in serving my sovereign,
or fail to punish the guilty,
may the bright spirits strike me down—
I alone should bear this punishment.
But why should the troops suffer hardship for no crime?
If my heart is truly loyal and fervent,
may heaven understand our difficulty,
stop the snow and turn back the wind,
to aid our military mission."
When he finished speaking,
the wind shifted and the snow ceased.
Wéi Bīn at every court gathering dared not leave his position,
it is said that once during heavy snow those standing in the courtyard,
all shook their robes and shifted their stance,
but Bīn did not move his feet.
The snow was so heavy,
it nearly reached over his boots,
yet he never lost his composure.
"The Biography of Ānshí"
During the early Tiānbǎo era,
Ān Sīshùn presented a five-colored belt,
and the emperor wondered why there had been no recent tribute of five-colored jade from the Western Regions,
so he ordered that Ānxī's various foreign tribes be held accountable.
The tribes claimed they were being obstructed and plundered by Xiǎo Bólǜ,
which enraged the emperor.
Lǐ Línfǔ supported the emperor's intention,
and ordered Wáng Tiānyùn to lead forty thousand troops on a campaign against them,
slaughtering the city's inhabitants,
and returning with two thousand captives and their pearls and gems.
A sorcerer among the Bólǜ people said:
"The general has no righteousness,
which is inauspicious,
and heaven will bring a great wind and snow."
After marching several hundred lǐ,
suddenly fierce winds arose from all directions,
snowflakes fell like wings,
the wind whipped up the small sea,
turning the water into pillars of ice,
which rose and then shattered.
After half a day,
the small sea surged and swelled,
and all forty thousand men froze to death at once.
"Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Wáng Yuánbǎo, whenever heavy snow fell,
would order his servants to sweep the snow from the lanes to make paths,
greet and welcome guests with a bow,
and host feasts and banquets as gatherings to ward off the cold.
"Tiānbǎo Yíshì"
In the early Dàlì era,
Zhōng Lù Cuī Xīzhēn was skilled in painting.
One winter morning, going out,
he saw an old man sheltering from the snow under his gate.
He invited him in,
served him a meal of barley flour,
and also offered him pine flower wine.
The old man took a pill from his bosom and placed it in the wine.
The wine immediately became fragrant and delicious.
He then gave Cuī several more pills.
When Cuī entered his house and came out again,
he saw that the old man had already left.
There was a drawing on the plain silk he used for painting,
all beyond ordinary imagination.
So he followed the footprints in the snow to the reed marsh,
where he saw several people in a boat,
with a woodcutter beside them.
Looking back, they laughed and said:
"Gě Sān is indeed pressed by this man.
Celestial Master Lǐ Jíguāng said:
"This is the third descendant of the Perfected Gě Hóng.
Xuē Fàng passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì,
being naturally sincere, modest, and of few words.
Emperor Xiànzōng sought upright individuals through studying poetry and books for the crown prince,
to assist with moral teachings,
and selected him to serve as the crown prince's reading attendant.
When Emperor Mùzōng succeeded the throne,
before he had assumed full governance,
Fàng often participated in secret discussions and decision-making issues at his side.
Emperor Mùzōng frequently said to Fàng:
"I have newly inherited the great treasure,
and fear I am inadequate to bear it,
sir, you should become chancellor,
to support what I am lacking."
Fàng bowed and said:
"I am indeed shallow and ordinary,
to have the opportunity to serve under the imperial canopy,
I am certainly not worthy to defile the great office of assisting the sovereign."
Since there were capable individuals,
his words were without exaggeration,
all being in this manner.
Emperor Mùzōng deeply appreciated his sincerity,
and thus summoned him to the Hall of Reflection,
bestowing upon him garments of gold and purple.
"Old Táng History"
Wéi Wēn,
courtesy name Hóngyù,
was the son of Wéi Shòu,
serving as a Hanlin Academician.
Previously, while Shòu was in the imperial court,
he accumulated anxieties and fears, leading to illness and retirement,
thus he admonished Wēn not to take up positions close to the emperor.
For this reason, Wēn firmly declined the appointment.
The emperor angrily said:
"Does Shòu's dying wish dictate this?
Transfer him to the position of Drafter,
initially also serving as Tutor to Crown Prince Zhuāngkè.
He visited the palace at dawn,
and at noon, he advised the crown prince:
"Your Highness is in the prime of youth,
you should rise at cockcrow and start early,
inquire after the Son of Heaven's well-being,
following the example of King Wén of old.
The crown prince was displeased,
and dismissed him from the tutorship.
When the crown prince incurred offense and was seen,
an edict was issued to admonish the officials.
Wēn said:
"Your Majesty instructed him,
not doing so earlier is not solely the crown prince's fault.
At that time, many considered his words upright.
From the "History of the Tang": Shòu
was the elder brother of Guànzhī,
and shares the same name as the Wéi Shòu mentioned in the previous entry.
Dīng Gōngzhù was appointed as the tutor to the crown prince and various princes,
and subsequently authored the "Ten Admonitions for the Crown Prince and Princes" in ten volumes,
During Emperor Mùzōng's reign, he was promoted to Vice Minister of Works,
due to his past service in the Eastern Palace.
(Old Book of Tang)
Wáng Qǐ,
courtesy name Jǔzhī.
Emperor Wénzōng admired literature and classical studies,
at that time Zhèng Tán excelled in classical meaning,
while Qǐ excelled in broad knowledge,
both were appointed to the Hànlín Academy,
to discuss classics and histories.
Qǐ was especially devoted to learning; although his official position was lofty and important,
he indulged in study without weariness,
there was no book he did not read,
and nothing escaped his eyes once seen.
When the crown prince was installed,
it was desired to have Confucian scholars teach him the classics,
so he was appointed Minister of War and concurrently Tutor to the Crown Prince,
creating for the crown prince an expanded "Chart of the Five Cycles" and literary works,
presenting elegant phrases from the examination grounds.
The emperor frequently consulted him on contemporary governance,
inscribed poems for the crown prince,
and bestowed a painted portrait with an imperial edict on his official tablet,
being honored in the side hall as the contemporary Zhòngní.
Xíng Bǐng,
courtesy name Shūmíng,
was appointed by Emperor Zhēnzōng when he first established the position of Academician Reader-in-waiting of the Hànlín Academy.
Bǐng was the first to receive this appointment and would lecture from an informal seat,
instructing on the "Zuǒzhuàn" commentary of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
He also lectured on the "Classic of Filial Piety," "Book of Rites," "Analects," "Book of Documents," "Classic of Changes," and "Book of Songs."
He elaborated based on commentaries and sub-commentaries,
often drawing connections to contemporary events,
for which Emperor Zhēnzōng highly praised and rewarded him.
(From "Records of the Eastern Capital")
Emperor Rénzōng often summoned the Hanlin Academician Reader Zhāng Xī to lecture on texts within the palace.
Xī expounded the essence of the classics thoroughly,
with comprehensive and appropriate discussions,
and the emperor praised him for a long time.
Xī was sixty-seven years old at the time,
with hair and temples already white.
The emperor said:
"You are old, yet your memory and knowledge have not declined.
Then, using feibai calligraphy,
he wrote the characters
"Erudite,"
and bestowed them upon him,
taking the opportunity to inquire about the way of governance.
Xī replied:
"Restraining desires is
the foundation of self-cultivation;
being prudent in punishments and rewards is
the foundation of orderly rule.
At that time, a noble consort was favored,
so he used this to subtly admonish the emperor.
The emperor's expression turned serious as he said:
"Your words are most excellent,
I regret having employed you so late.
"National History"
Xià Sǒng's son Xià Ānqī was appointed as an Academician Expositor-in-waiting.
Although his knowledge of the classics was not very profound,
he was promoted to this position.
At the imperial lectures day and night,
he would hurriedly review the classics and histories
in order to be prepared for the emperor's inquiries.
He grew weary of this himself,
and thus earnestly requested an external posting as a military governor of Yánzhōu.
Yǔ Liàng,
courtesy name Yuánguī.
During the Yuánxīng era's beginning,
he was appointed as a Secretary in the Central Secretariat,
concurrently holding the positions of Editorial Director and Lecturer to the Eastern Palace.
His discourses and interpretations
were widely praised and recounted,
and he, along with Wēn Qiáo, shared a close friendship with the Crown Prince since their days as commoners.
At that time, Emperor Yuán was emphasizing penal laws,
and presented the works of Hán Fēi to the Crown Prince.
Liàng remonstrated that the doctrines of Shēn Bùhài and Hán Fēi,
being harsh and detrimental to moral transformation,
were not worthy of attention.
The Crown Prince greatly accepted his advice.
From the "Book of Jìn".
Xiāo Déyán was extensively versed in the classics and histories,
particularly excelling in the "Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals,"
and fond of composing writings.
In his later years, he became even more devoted to learning,
from day until night,
with almost no rest or weariness.
Whenever he intended to open the Five Classics,
he would always fasten his belt and wash his hands,
sitting upright to face them.
His wife and children, waiting for an opportunity, asked him:
"Being like this all day long,
isn't it too laborious?
Déyán replied:
"Revering the words of the ancient sages,
how could I fear such effort?
At that time, Emperor Gāozōng was the Prince of Jìn,
and he summoned Déyán
to receive instruction in the classics and explain their content.
When the prince ascended to the crown prince's position,
Déyán continued to serve concurrently as a Lecturer-in-Waiting.
The "Old Book of Tang" records: Wéi Chǔhòu, whose learning followed the methods of a master,
styled himself Dézǎi,
was proficient in the Five Classics,
widely read in historical texts,
and possessed abundant and elegant literary thought.
Emperor Mùzōng, recognizing that his learning adhered to the master's methods,
summoned him into the Hànlín Academy,
appointing him as an Academician Lecturer-in-Waiting.
Chǔhòu, observing that the young emperor was negligent and idle,
and did not attend to governmental affairs,
and being in a position to offer admonitions,
felt he should have a means to enlighten and guide the emperor's nature,
so he selected and compiled the essential meanings and elegant words from the classics,
arranging them by category into twenty volumes,
calling it "The Authoritative Words of the Six Classics,"
and presented it.
He was rewarded with silk fabrics and silver vessels,
and additionally granted the golden seal and purple ribbon, along with the title of Vice Director of the Bureau of Honors,
and Compiler of the Historiography Institute.
Lù Suí was also appointed as an Academician Expositor-in-Waiting in the Hànlín Academy,
summoned to the Tàiyè Pavilion,
where they were ordered to separately expound on chapters such as the "Máo Poetry," "Guān Jū," "Shàng Shū," and "Hóng Fàn,"
and consulted on principles of governance.
Chǔhòu and others elaborated on the meanings of the classics to broaden the way of admonition and influence,
conversing calmly and accepting advice,
and were then dismissed after being bestowed with wine and fruits.
Zhèng Huànyú,
was the son of Qìng.
In the early years of Emperor Wénzōng's reign,
he was promoted to Hànlín Reader-in-waiting.
The emperor ordered him to compile the "Essentials of Classics and Histories in Twenty Volumes",
and when the book was completed,
the emperor was pleased with its precision and breadth,
thus using nineteen books for the "Categorized Sayings".
The emperor personally posed questions,
and Huǎn responded without hesitation,
for which he was bestowed with gold and purple.
"Old Book of Táng"
When Cuī Yǎn was appointed to the throne,
he was selected as a Lecturer-in-Waiting,
then transferred to the post of Drafter of the Central Secretariat.
Upon entering the Hall of Reflecting on Governance to express gratitude for the imperial favor,
he memorialized:
"Your Majesty appointed me as Lecturer-in-Waiting,
for over half a year,
yet you have never questioned me on the meaning of the classics.
Now I receive this transfer and promotion,
I am truly ashamed of my inadequate learning,
and feel unworthy of such great favor."
The Emperor said:
"When my administrative duties become less busy,
I shall certainly seek your instruction."
Cuī Yǎn withdrew and together with his colleague Gāo Zhòng excerpted passages from the Six Classics,
adding essential teachings,
and categorized them by subject matter,
compiling a ten-volume work titled "Essentials of the Various Classics",
hoping to make it easier for the sovereign to review.
The Emperor praised them,
and bestowed two hundred bolts of colored silk.
Gāo Yuányù was promoted from Attendant Lecturer to Palace Censor,
and Emperor Wénzōng found it difficult to find his replacement.
Yuányù submitted a memorial stating that his elder brother Shàoyì had the talent to take on the role.
Consequently, Shàoyì was appointed as Grand Master of Remonstrance,
replacing Yuányù as Attendant Lecturer Academician.
The brothers successively held confidential positions,
and contemporaries regarded this as an honor.
Wáng Qǐ entered the Hanlin Academy in the third year of the Kāichéng era,
becoming an expositor-in-waiting.
When Emperor Wénzōng encountered obscure characters or doubtful matters,
he would order a palace envoy to deliver oral inquiries,
whereupon Qǐ would prepare written responses on placards,
attaching them to the envoy for submission.
A collection of ten such responses was titled "Written Replies to Imperial Inquiries."
From the New Book of Táng
Zhèng Tán,
in the third year of the Tàihé era, served as a Hanlin Academician Expositor-in-waiting.
Tán excelled in classical studies,
being well-versed in antiquity and upholding righteousness,
and Emperor Wénzōng particularly valued him.
Lǐ Zōngmǐn and Niú Sēngrú, because Tán was on good terms with Lǐ Déyù,
disliked Tán discussing affairs within the palace,
and petitioned for him to be appointed as Minister of Works,
removing him from the position of Academician Expositor-in-waiting.
The emperor, who favored classical scholarship,
often thought of him with regret.
In the second month of the sixth year,
he was recalled to serve again as Academician Expositor-in-waiting.
In the seventh year,
when Déyù became chancellor,
the emperor once said to the chancellors at the Yányíng Hall:
"Yīn Yòu is well-versed in classical studies,
and his character is quite similar to Zhèng Tán's."
Zōngmǐn said:
"Although Tán truly possesses classical learning,
his opinions are not worth listening to."
Déyù responded:
"The words of Yīn and Zhèng,
others may not wish to hear,
but Your Majesty is eager to hear them.
Tán once detested people forming cliques,
and for this, he was disparaged by Zōngmǐn,
that is the reason."
Old Book of Tang
Lǐ Xùn,
in the eighth year of the Tàihé era, was appointed from exile to the position of assistant instructor of the Four Gates,
summoned to the inner palace,
personally granted the crimson fish insignia,
and appointed as a Hanlin academician expositor-in-waiting.
On the day he entered the palace,
a banquet was held where the Xuānfǎ music was performed,
with twenty disciples playing the Fǎqǔ music in the courtyard,
honoring him before the two departments.
Remonstrance officials Zhèng Sù, Gāo Yuányù, and others prostrated at the pavilion, urgently admonishing that Xùn
"is treacherous and wicked,
known throughout the land,
and should not be allowed to serve close to the emperor.
The emperor ultimately did not heed their advice.
Zhèng Zhù began his career by practicing medicine in Cháng'ān,
when Lǐ Sù suffered from paralysis,
Zhù treated him with notable success,
leading Wáng Shǒuchéng to marvel at his skills.
In the eighth year of the Tàihé era,
Zhù presented the "One Volume of Medicinal Formulas,"
whereupon the emperor ordered Shǒuchéng to summon him for an audience at the Yùtáng Gate,
bestowing upon him gold and purple robes.
On the evening of his audience,
a comet appeared in the eastern sky.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Hanlin Academician and Lecturer,
summoned through the Jiǔxiān Gate,
where the emperor personally granted him his certificate of appointment.
At that time, Lǐ Xùn attached himself to Zhù,
and since Zhù had already gained access to the imperial court,
the two collaborated closely,
attending the emperor daily by his side,
expounding on methods to achieve great peace,
believing that in no time,
they could usher in an era of prosperity.
With these two villains joining forces,
the emperor became increasingly captivated by their proposals.
Once they achieved their ambitions,
they settled every past favor or grievance,
repaying each down to the slightest detail.
Court officials were successively dismissed and exiled,
leaving the ranks of the court nearly empty.
After their downfall, an inventory was taken,
confiscating their family wealth,
which yielded one million bolts of silk
and other goods of comparable value.
Zhǎnshì,
an official position in Qín,
was responsible for the households of the empress and the crown prince.
Yìng Shào stated:
"Zhǎn
means to inspect,
to provide,
referring to serving the crown prince.
Dòu Yīng,
in the early years of Emperor Jǐng's reign, served as Supervisor of the Household.
The emperor's younger brother,
Prince Xiào of Liáng,
was beloved by their mother, Empress Dowager Dòu.
When Prince Xiào came to court,
they feasted together as brothers.
At that time,
the emperor had not yet established an heir apparent.
Amid the merriment of wine,
the emperor casually said:
"After a thousand autumns and ten thousand years pass,
I shall pass the throne to Prince Xiào of Liáng."
Dòu Yīng raised a cup of wine and presented it to the emperor, saying:
"The empire
belongs to Emperor Gāozǔ,
and the rule of father passing to son
is the covenant of Hàn.
How can Your Majesty pass the throne to Prince Xiào of Liáng?"
From this, the emperor came to resent Dòu Yīng.
From the Book of Hàn
In the Jìn dynasty, the positions of guardian and mentor were esteemed,
and they were not supposed to attend to trivial matters.
At the beginning of the Xiánníng era of Emperor Wǔ,
Yáng Yáo, a court gentleman of the Yellow Gate, was appointed as supervisor of the household of the heir apparent,
overseeing the duties of the Eastern Palace.
Yáng Yáo was later promoted to junior mentor.
From the "Six Codes".
Lù Yè,
zì Shìguāng,
shào yǒu yǎ wàng,
cóngxiōng Jī měi chēng zhī yuē:
"Wǒ jiā shìshì bù fá gōng yǐ.
Tàixīng yuán nián,
qiān tàizǐ zhānshì,
yǐ qīngzhēn zhùchēng.
"Jìn Shū"
Wishing to speak but failing to obtain, Yáng Xiù,
styled Zhìshū,
was a native of Tàishān.
He possessed versatile talents and strategies,
being of the same age as Shìzǔ,
and they were on good terms.
He once said to Shìzǔ:
"You will later achieve wealth and honor.
At that time, he was appointed as the Commander of the Imperial Guard and Supervisor of the Crown Prince's Household,
and when Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was repeatedly promoted to Left General, Central Protector of the Army, and Specially Advanced.
"Comments on the Various Dignitaries of Jìn"
Xiè Yǎn,
courtesy name Yuàndù,
was the youngest son of Xiè Ān,
serving as General Who Supports the State.
He was later promoted to General Who Conquers Caitiffs and Left Supervisor of the Masters of Writing, concurrently holding the position of Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
"Records of Chén Shào and Xiè": In the Hàn dynasty, the selection of virtue and rituals was stricter than at the office of Dòu Qīng;
in the Jìn dynasty, the appointment of the worthy brought glory to Xiè Yǎn.
"Edicts of the Great Táng Dynasty: Broad System"
Emperor Wǔ appointed Wáng Gōng as Governor of Dānyáng and concurrently Director of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
Wáng Gōng declined in a memorial, saying:
"Now that the crown prince has just been established as a model for all regions,
this position oversees the administration,
and the selection for such a crucial role should be exceptionally discerning,
requiring the most outstanding talent of the time.
How could someone as mediocre as I presume to hold it?"
The "Jìn Qǐjū Zhù" records: Tàiyuán's Wáng Gōng served as President of the Imperial Secretariat and concurrently Director of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
with learning and integrity surpassing others.
From the "Zhōngxīng Shū"
Biàn Kǔn served as the crown prince's tutor,
holding positions of instruction and military command,
fulfilling his duties of guidance and assistance with utmost dedication,
earning both respect and awe throughout the court.
During the restoration of the Jin dynasty, he was appointed as Palace Aide to the Heir Apparent and lecturer in the Eastern Palace,
later promoted to Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
Contemporary accounts praised Biàn Kǔn's judgments,
describing them as incisively straightforward and factually grounded,
demonstrating his loyalty in serving the sovereign.
Book of Jin
Jiāng Yí was appointed as the Right Vice Director.
The Emperor intended to have him concurrently serve as the Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
He said to Wáng Huái:
"You should find a precedent from the northern dynasties.
Huái replied:
"I shall go out and search for one.
Later, Huái met with the Emperor, who asked:
"Regarding the matter we discussed recently,
have you found a precedent yet?
Huái said:
"Xiè Yǎn served as Right Vice Director while concurrently holding the position of Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
Yǎn was the son of Lord Xiè,
and I fear that Yí might not be a suitable parallel to this case,
so the matter was ultimately not carried out.
"Common Sayings"
The Supervisor of the Household oversees discipline in the palace,
similar to the duties of the Imperial Secretary and the Censor.
In Wáng Mín's "Letter in Reply to Xú Miǎo," it is stated that addressing violations should focus on maintaining discipline in the Eastern Han.
According to the "Decree of the Hereditary Prince of Xǔ," the regulations for the Bo Wang and the broken loom,
along with the collective responsibility for upholding the legacy and the entrusted duty of maintaining discipline in Chéng Huá,
rest with the virtuous.
From Lǐ Kuān's "Decree."
Sòng Yīn Jǐngrén did not engage in literary composition yet was quick-witted with profound thoughts,
did not discuss righteousness yet deeply understood principles,
and as for state ceremonies, court regulations, old statutes, and recorded annotations,
he compiled and recorded them all.
Those with insight knew he possessed ambitions to serve his era.
During the reign of Emperor Shào of Liú Sòng,
he served as Palace Attendant alongside Wáng Huá, Wáng Tánshǒu, and Liú Zhàn—four men in total,
renowned for their forceful integrity and administrative competence,
they stood as the foremost officials of their time,
the glory of their simultaneous promotion
was unmatched in recent generations.
During the Yuánjiā era,
he was called from mourning his mother’s passing to assume the post of General of the Central Army,
but he firmly declined;
after the mourning period ended,
he was promoted to Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat and Supervisor of the Crown Prince’s Household.
Liú Zhàn succeeded him as General of the Central Army,
but later, due to slander from Liú Zhàn and others,
Yīn remained at home convalescing for five years,
and though he did not appear before the emperor,
secret correspondence flowed between them.
Dozens of letters were exchanged daily,
and later, when the emperor planned to arrest Liú Zhàn,
he summoned Yīn to the Huálín Garden,
entrusting him entirely
with the planning and execution of the punitive measures.
He succeeded Liú Yìkāng as Governor of Yángzhōu.
From *The History of the Southern Dynasties*
Kǒng Zhìguī,
styled Dézhāng,
was widely learned from a young age and enjoyed a fine reputation.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
he served as Zhōng Shùzǐ.
In the Yǒngyuán era,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
In his resignation memorial, he wrote:
"The Crown Prince soars like a rosy cloud above the azure palace,
his brilliance shines upon the Spring Palace,
he commands the finest talents from the Purple Valley,
and resonates with the melodies of Luòyáng's panpipes.
Unless one's virtue reaches the white clouds,
and one's refinement matches the bright moon,
how could one linger in the garden of fragrant orchids,
or place feathers among jade branches?
Dòu Yīng was honored among relatives in the Western Capital,
Lù Yè was known for his pure character in the Eastern Kingdom—
such men of excellence
are truly worthy of recommendation.
How then, am I,
to dare presume and overstep?"
Lù Chuí,
courtesy name Zuǒgōng,
was diligent in his studies from a young age,
excelling in literary composition.
For several years, he read day and night in this manner,
and whatever he read once, he would recite orally.
He was recommended as a Xiùcai (cultivated talent),
and Emperor Gāozǔ greatly admired Chuí's talent,
promoting him to Tàizǐ Shùzǐ (Crown Prince's Attendant),
and appointing him as Zhānshì (Supervisor of the Household).
In his memorial declining the position, he wrote:
"The Crown Prince's establishment is magnificent and weighty,
truly different from ordinary offices.
In the Southern Court and the Horse Palace,
scholars of refinement have already been selected,
such as Dòu Yīng and Xǔ Shāng.
They were chosen from among relatives by marriage,
but since then,
reputation and status have increasingly flourished,
with successive selections of talented and virtuous individuals.
How could I presume to overstep my bounds?"
Kǒng Huàn served as the Minister of Personnel.
During the reign of the Later Lord of Chén,
while in the Eastern Palace, he intended to appoint Jiāng Zǒng as the Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
He ordered the Secretary Lù Yú to convey this to Huàn.
Huàn said:

Wú Jìng served as Left Grand Master of the Palace.
When Emperor Xuánzōng journeyed east to perform the fēng sacrifice,
he frequently engaged in hunting along the way.
Wú Jìng remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty, since departing from Luòyì,
intending to announce the shàn sacrifice at Mount Tài,
you have passed through several prefectures,
yet repeatedly made hunting your primary activity.
This truly fosters negligence toward external affairs,
and is not an urgent matter for maintaining proper ritual decorum.
Moreover, the ceremonies of ascending Mount Tài to announce success
are rituals of great solemnity,
and hunting excursions
diminish imperial dignity.
Furthermore, during the Zhènguàn era,
Emperor Tàizōng of Wén, whenever touring,
would broadly select scholars well-versed in past and present affairs
to accompany him.
Whenever arriving at locations significant to the rise and fall of previous dynasties,
he would inquire into their causes,
using them as warnings and lessons.
I humbly beseech Your Majesty to follow this example.
For this cannot be mentioned in the same breath as
galloping horses through mountain valleys,
pursuing cunning beasts in dense forests,
disregarding the danger of falling from high halls,
and failing to consider the peril of driving with rotten reins.

To disrupt ancient statutes while accustomed to political expediency
contravenes the system of former kings.
The proposal for the Nine Bestowals
should not be implemented."
Book of Jin
Cài Mó served as Minister of Works,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"For the positions of the eight senior ministers,
none but the worthy should be placed in front.
Later, when selecting renowned worthies, there were constant examples like Kǒng Yú and Zhūgě Huī,
all possessing pure integrity and fine talent,
and long enjoying high reputations.
My reputation and standing differ from theirs,
with rank and attainment vastly disparate.
Now, unworthily promoted despite my insignificance, surpassing my peers,
above, I disrupt the orderly sequence of the sage court,
below, I contravene the fair judgment of the multitude of scholars.
This is not merely a warning of my own demise,
but truly brings the burden of dust accumulation to the sage governance.
"Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū" (Records of the Jin Restoration)
The Book of Documents is
the foundation of all affairs,
and what I hold accountable for accomplishment.
Yet the official salaries are meager and inadequate,
which greatly contradicts the principles of governance.
Although military and state expenditures are currently high,
I shall not spare emoluments for outstanding talents.
Let it be arranged according to the provisions for the Imperial Secretaries that the Department of State Affairs and each trusted official shall receive stipends and rewards for fifty personnel.
"Edict from the Daily Records of Emperor Kāng of Jìn"
Biàn Kǔn,
during Emperor Míng's reign served as Imperial Secretary,
together with Wáng Dǎo and others received the deathbed edict,
assisting the young ruler Emperor Chéng to ascend the throne.
When officials presented the imperial seal,
Minister over the Masses Wáng Dǎo did not arrive due to illness.
Kǔn declared solemnly at court:
"How could Lord Wáng be a minister devoted to the state?
The deceased emperor lies in state,
the successor sovereign has not yet been established,
this is certainly no time for a minister to excuse himself due to illness."
His exclusive authority and lack of reverence,
caused matters to be suppressed and not implemented,
making the entire court fear him.
From "Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū"
Xiè Shí served as the Minister of Works,
and submitted a memorial resigning from his position, stating:
"The Minister of Works
is the chief administrator of the state,
overseeing all governmental affairs,
establishing norms for royal governance,
and serving as a model for all officials.
Therefore, one must be selected based on virtue
and appointed according to ability."
Records of the Jin Dynasty Wáng Gōng once stayed at Sīmǎ Dàozǐ's residence,
when Minister of Works Xiè Shí sang a Wu song for him. Wáng Gōng remarked:
"Occupying such an important position as yours,
sitting among the ranks of prime ministers,
how can you perform these vulgar tunes?"
Shí showed a look of shame.
Forest of Conversations
When Xú Zhànzhī served as Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
Hé Shàngzhī, considering Zhànzhī was a relative of the imperial family,
held a position of great trust and importance,
wished to delegate the court administration to him.
Along with all memorials and appeals,
he absolutely did not review or handle them.
Zhànzhī also believed that the Director of the Department of State Affairs was responsible for presenting reports and managing affairs,
overseeing all matters without exception,
and if the Director's position was vacant, the Vice Director would assume overall responsibility.
Thus, he also deferred matters back to Shàngzhī,
each pushing duties onto the other.
The Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk Yuán Shū memorialized to have both dismissed from their posts,
but an imperial edict specifically ordered no action to be taken,
instead instructing Zhànzhī and Shàngzhī to jointly receive and handle memorials and appeals.
Although Shàngzhī held the title of Director,
all court affairs were actually managed by Zhànzhī.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Wáng Sēngqián served as the Minister of Personnel,
and once wrote in feibai script on the wall of the Department of State Affairs,
saying:
"Round things roll, square ones stay still—
this is the fixed nature of objects.
If you cultivate without cease, it leads to excess;
if you elevate without cease, it brings fear;
if you rush without cease, it results in coarseness;
if you expand without cease, it causes alternation.
Therefore, one should swiftly discard such tendencies.
At that time, people sighed in admiration,
comparing it to a motto placed by one's seat.
In the first year of the Xiàojiàn era of the Sòng Dynasty,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Department of State Affairs is the foundation of all officials,
the pivotal mechanism for all governmental achievements.
With assistant directors and various bureaus,
each office has its responsibilities.
Recently, however, matters regardless of importance
have all been referred to the Directors,
which is not the way to appoint the capable and accomplish tasks.
Instead, the system should be clarified to hold them accountable for results.
Tōngdiǎn
Since the Jìn Dynasty,
the eight high officials and court gentlemen largely ceased submitting memorials.
In the first year of the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng Dynasty,
an edict stated:
"Since the court rituals fell into decline,
a long time has passed,
with gentlemen's offices filled merely for quota,
showing no dedication to their duties.
They treat official documents as chaff,
valuing idleness and leisure.
They merely hold the title of attending court,
but lack the substance of handling fragrant orchids (i.e., performing actual duties).
Court gentlemen shall resume submitting memorials as in the past."
From then on, they began submitting memorials again.
Another edict ordered that when doubtful matters arose within the Shàngshū Province,
they should first be discussed at the court assembly,
before being reported to the emperor.
Tōngdiǎn
The Minister of the Department of State Affairs held the position of a key minister.
In the early Wǔdé era,
when Tàizōng was the Prince of Qín,
he once occupied it; thereafter,
no subject dared to assume it.
By the Guǎngdé era,
Guō Zǐyí's achievements and merits had become illustrious,
and he was specially appointed to it.
Out of respect for Emperor Wén's precedent,
Guō Zǐyí declined and did not dare accept.
"Comprehensive Statutes of the Six Divisions"
Emperor Xuánzōng intended to appoint Niú Xiānkè as Minister of Personnel,
Zhāng Jiǔlíng remonstrated:
"This is not permissible.
The Minister of Personnel was the ancient office of Chief Counselor,
and since the establishment of the Táng dynasty, it has mostly been held by former chancellors.
Otherwise, it should be someone who has served in various prestigious positions both in and out of court,
carefully selected from among those with virtue and reputation.
Xiānkè was originally merely a minor functionary in Héhuáng,
yet he was promoted to the ranks of respectable officials,
and placed among the regular ministers.
This is an abuse of official appointment.
"Táng Xīn Yǔ"
The Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
impeached officials below the eight high ministers for their conduct,
amidst the convergence of myriad state affairs,
this was the authority of the imperial court,
directly overseeing the celestial platform’s jurisdiction.
From "Fu Xián’s Preface in Reply to Xīn Kuàng’s Poem."
Hè Chēn,
courtesy name Guóbǎo,
served as Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and concurrently participated in ritual affairs.
Throughout his tenure,
he established protocols
for various suburban and ancestral temple ceremonies.
Whenever he had an audience with Emperor Gāozǔ,
their conversations would extend for hours,
prompting officials to remark:
"When he ascends the palace hall, he doesn't descend—
there's Hè Yǎ."
As Hè Chēn's demeanor was refined and elegant,
contemporaries thus addressed him.
Book of Liáng
Liú Lǎn,
courtesy name Xiàozhì,
served as Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was intelligent and quick-witted,
and could memorize the names of all seven hundred clerks in the Imperial Secretariat
upon a single encounter.
He upheld integrity and impartiality in office without favoritism.
His brother-in-law Chǔ Yān, the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor,
and his cousin Lìbùláng Xiàochuò
were involved in bribery and corruption while in office.
Lǎn impeached and had them both dismissed from their positions.
Xiàochuò resented him for this,
once remarking to others:
"A dog bites strangers on the road,
but Lǎn bites his own family."
Láng Mào,
courtesy name Wèizhī,
served as the Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs.
At that time, Yǔwén Kǎi, the Minister of Works,
and Yú Zhòngwén, the Great General of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent,
were competing for the silver mines in Hédōng.
Láng Mào submitted a memorial impeaching them,
stating:
"I have heard that the noble and the humble have different rites,
scholars and farmers have distinct occupations,
so that people understand their proper roles,
and families recognize integrity and shame.
Yǔwén Kǎi's position and prestige are already high,
his emoluments and rewards are generous;
yet he has not withdrawn from profit-seeking like uprooting mallows and abandoning weaving,
remaining silent and unknown in this regard,
seeking profit by associating with inferiors,
without any sense of shame.
Yú Zhòngwén, as a great general guarding the palace,
a close attendant serving by the court steps,
hearing daily of the virtues of Yú and Ruì,
should suppress and not covet trivial profits.
Knowing this yet still contending for them,
how can he set an example for the multitude and show the people
the proper way? If such matters are not corrected and governed,
it will damage administration and education."
Yǔwén Kǎi and Yú Zhòngwén were consequently convicted and punished.
(Book of Suì)
Yuán Shòu,
styled Chángshòu,
served as the Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
When the wife of General Xiāo Móhē was critically ill and near death,
he petitioned to send his son south of the Yangtze River to gather family assets.
The censors witnessed this but remained silent,
so Shòu submitted a memorial impeaching them,
stating:
"In the principles of human relationships,
the bond between husband and wife is paramount;
in the way of nurturing affection,
even crows show filial piety.
Móhē, thinking distantly of material wealth,
forgot the intimate bond of marriage.
Moreover, he ordered his son to abandon his mother in critical condition
to engage in acquisitive behavior.
With just one utterance,
he utterly violated moral teachings.
Yet Attending Censor Hán Zhēngzhī and others, who personally witnessed this,
ultimately failed to impeach or investigate.
Attending Censor Liú Běn, acting in his official capacity at the Censorate,
compromised the dignity of the office.
I, unworthily holding the position of Left Assistant Director,
cannot remain silent.
The Emperor
Liú Jì submitted a memorial stating:
"The Department of State Affairs handles myriad state affairs,
which truly form the foundation of governance.
Therefore, the eight high officials are comparable to the two assistants of Wénchāng,
and analogous to the linchpin of administration.
If they are unfit for office and improperly occupy positions, it invites criticism.
In the early Zhēnguàn period,
Left Assistant Dài Zhòu and Right Assistant Wèi Zhēng were both knowledgeable and capable,
their administration was fair and their character upright,
and they impeached and reported matters as appropriate,
without any avoidance.
When Dù Zhènglún subsequently assumed the position of Right Assistant,
he was quite similar to the junior officials,
failing to uphold the legal framework,
and both were meritorious officials and relatives.
Those in office were unfit for their positions,
with achievements and influence contending against each other.
To remedy this malady,
it is appropriate to streamline and select carefully;
with the right people, the legal framework will naturally be somewhat upheld,
and it will also correct the tendency to scramble for power,
not merely eliminate delays and stagnation.
After the memorial was submitted, Yǒng Jǐ soon appointed Jì as Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs.
The Sui dynasty's Left and Right Assistants were responsible for overseeing and rectifying the affairs of the various departments of the Imperial Secretariat.
The Tang dynasty followed the Sui system.
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era,
they were renamed Left and Right Supervisors of Discipline.
That year, the descendants of Yǔwén Huàjí petitioned for hereditary privileges from the court,
citing that the matter spanned two dynasties,
and also arguing that their family and clan were numerous with many advocates.
The authorities' handling of the case led to delays.
The Right Supervisor of Discipline, Yáng Fǎng, had not yet reviewed the case in detail,
while the petitioner claimed the reasoning was already clear,
with no further doubts or obstacles.
He aggressively pressured Yáng Fǎng,
who said:
"I have just returned from court and have not eaten;
after eating, I will examine the case in detail."
The petitioner retorted:
"You say you haven't eaten,
but do you know there are petitioners in the world who have been stranded for years?"
Yáng Fǎng immediately ordered the case file and promptly endorsed it, stating:
"The father assassinated the Sui emperor,
and the son petitions for Sui dynasty benefits;
the living should still be exiled to distant lands,
and the dead certainly should not be reinstated."
People of the time deeply admired this.
From "New Accounts of the Comprehensive Institutions."
In the fourth year of the Yífèng era,
Wéi Rényuē was appointed as the Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs and submitted a memorial saying:
"Your Majesty appoints officials;
if the selection is inappropriate,
there will be deficiencies.
Now you do not hesitate to entrust me with precious brocade to tailor,
this shows Your Majesty's deep trust in me,
and it is also the time for me to devote my life to duty,
to rectify the legal system,
leaving no affairs unattended,
making the court orderly and solemn."
Later, the Left and Right Surveillance Bureaus were established separately,
and Sīqiān was again appointed as the Head of the Right Surveillance Bureau.
From "Tōngdiǎn" and "Old Book of Táng"
Yán Zhēnqīng served as the Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
When the imperial carriage was returning
from Shǎn,
Zhēnqīng requested that the emperor first pay homage to the five imperial mausoleums and nine ancestral temples,
before returning to the palace.
Chancellor Yuán Zǎi said to Zhēnqīng:
"Although your opinion is commendable,
what can be done if it is not in line with the current situation?
Zhēnqīng angrily stepped forward and said:
"The decision to adopt or reject a proposal lies with you, sir, so what crime does the speaker commit?
What crime?
However, when it comes to court affairs,
how can they withstand being repeatedly undermined by you, sir?
Zǎi deeply resented him for this.
"Old Book of Tang"
Edict Appointing Yǔ Chéngxuān as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
In the past, our Tàizōng once said that the Directors of the Department of State Affairs are the pillars upholding all offices.
If even one matter is mishandled,
then the entire realm will suffer the consequences.
Therefore, he appointed Dài Zhòu, Wèi Zhēng, Dù Zhènglún, and Liú Jì,
to successively hold this position,
dividing them between the left and right offices,
to manage affairs and govern the people,
and they are praised to this day.
Thus, I previously appointed Cuī Róng to uphold the left pillar,
and now appoint Chéngxuān to grasp the right hub.
Chéngxuān is upright, sincere, diligent, and astute,
thoroughly versed in statutes and precedents,
and will surely be able to organize the orderly pillars for me,
and restrain the wheels of reckless action.
Sitting in the ministry, he may come and go freely,
and as a court official, he may memorialize and impeach;
together with the Censorate, he will deliberate on essential policies,
supporting and establishing the foundation of governance,
so that Dài, Wèi, Liú, and Dù do not exclusively shine in the Zhēnguàn era.
From the "Collection of Chángqìng."
Wéi Hóngjǐng served as the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
He refuted and corrected over sixty officials improperly promoted in rank by the Bureau of Appointments,
resulting in Zhèng Yīn, Dīng Gōngzhù, and Yáng Sìfù all having their salaries confiscated.
The officials became solemn and orderly,
rectifying themselves upon witnessing his authority.
When Vice Director of the Bureau of Appointments Yáng Yúqīng was repeatedly investigated,
an imperial decree ordered Wéi Hóngjǐng to deliberate in detail with the Censor.
Yáng Yúqīng privately visited his residence,
but Wéi Hóngjǐng sternly declared:
"There is an imperial decree to investigate you,
how dare you seek private audiences?"
Though Yáng Yúqīng had many allies for support,
he had initially believed he would surely be accepted,
but upon this,
he left in fear and panic.
Wéi Hóngjǐng advanced through upright conduct,
his discussions upheld justice with integrity,
relying on the moral standards of the time,
he became a renowned minister of the Chángqìng era.
《Book of Táng》 Wéi Hóngjǐng previously served as Vice Minister of Personnel,
impartially managing appointments systematically,
the powerful feared his strictness,
not daring to trouble him with private matters.
The Grand Steward governs the state,
commands all officials,
and harmonizes the four seas.
The duties of the Grand Steward of the Ministry of Heaven,
are to establish the six codes of the state,
to assist the king in governing the state.
In the Rites of Zhōu,
zhǒng means "grand";
zǎi means
"official."
In the Zhèng Catalog,
it balances the clear and the turbid,
harmonizes the firm and the soft,
and brings them into equilibrium, hence called zǎi.
According to Yú Shì,
zǎi is changed to zhǒng, and tài is used,
as different names for promotion and demotion.
When commanding all officials,
it is called the Grand Steward;
when listed among the king's duties, it is called the Grand Steward.
Zǎi means "to preside over,"
jiàn means "to establish,"
and bāng refers to the state where the king resides.
Zuǒ means
"to assist."
When the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent, he established the duties of the six codes,
to assist the king in governing the state.
Later, Empress Wǔ of Táng designated the Ministry of Personnel as the Ministry of Heaven,
the Ministry of Revenue as the Ministry of Earth,
the Ministry of Rites as the Ministry of Spring,
the Ministry of War as the Ministry of Summer,
the Ministry of Justice as the Ministry of Autumn,
and the Ministry of Works as the Ministry of Winter,
continuing the system of the six departments of the Zhōu dynasty.
According to the Tōngdiǎn,
during the Táng and Yú dynasties, officials were established
based on the principles of heaven, earth, and the four seasons,
with duties divided accordingly. Yìhé were the officials of heaven and earth,
and the Four Peaks were the officials of the four seasons.
The Xià dynasty followed the Yú system, as seen in the Gān Oath,
summoning the six ministers.
The Yīn dynasty had positions from the Grand Steward to the Minister of Justice,
which became the six officials of the Zhōu dynasty.
Mǐnzǐqiān was appointed as the steward of Fèi,
and inquired about governance in ancient times.
The Master said:
"Those who ruled the world in ancient times
relied on the six ministers to govern comprehensively.
The office of the Prime Minister accomplished the Way,
the office of the Minister of Education accomplished virtue,
the office of the Minister of Rites accomplished benevolence,
the office of the Minister of War accomplished sageliness,
the office of the Minister of Justice accomplished righteousness,
the office of the Minister of Works accomplished ritual.
With the six ministers in hand,
they were used as evenly balanced reins of benevolence,
to serve the Son of Heaven,
with the Court Historian as the left and right hands,
using the six ministers as reins,
and then joining with the Three Dukes to manage the six ministers,
harmonizing the five teachings,
standardizing the five laws,
thus wherever they guided, nothing failed to achieve their will.
Through the Way, the state was well-governed;
through virtue, the state was peaceful;
through benevolence, the state was harmonious;
through sageliness, the state was tranquil;
through ritual, the state was orderly;
through righteousness, the state was just—
this was the method of governing.
Therefore, when official departments are not properly managed,
duties are not clearly divided,
laws and governance are inconsistent,
and all affairs lose order, it is called chaos;
in chaos, the Prime Minister is disciplined.
When land is not cultivated,
goods and resources do not flourish,
the myriad people suffer hunger and cold,
education and instruction are not carried out,
customs become depraved and deviant,
and the people are scattered and displaced, it is called peril;
in peril, the Minister of Education is disciplined.
When father and son are not affectionate,
the order between elder and young is lost,
between ruler and minister, high and low,
there is alienation and divergent intentions, it is called disharmony;
in disharmony, the Minister of Rites is disciplined.
When the worthy and capable lose their official positions,
the meritorious and laboring lose their rewards and stipends,
soldiers become resentful and the military weak and ineffective, it is called inequity;
in inequity, the Minister of War is disciplined.
When punishments are violent and chaotic,
and villainy and evil are not overcome, it is called injustice;
in injustice, the Minister of Justice is disciplined.
When measures and standards are not carefully observed,
actions are undertaken without reason,
cities and borders are not maintained,
and goods and resources are misplaced, it is called poverty;
in poverty, the Minister of Works is disciplined.
Yáo commanded Xī Hé to take charge of the duties of yīn and yáng,
Xī Bó managed the heavens, that is, the office of celestial affairs,
Hòu Jì served under Yú and Xià,
respectfully instructing the people in the seasons,
honoring Jì as the celestial official.
When the Xià declined,
Bù Zhú, a descendant of Jì, lost the office,
leading to its abolition.
The Yīn dynasty used this office as the zhǒngzǎi,
the Duke of Zhōu was in Fēng,
serving as the grand steward,
and the Duke of Shào also held the position.
"Qí Zhí Yì"
The Grand Steward was one of the Six Grand Ministers in the Yīn dynasty,
and one of the Six High Officials in the Zhōu dynasty,
also called the Chief Steward.
During the reign of King Wǔ of Zhōu,
the Duke of Zhōu first held this position,
responsible for establishing the principles of governance.
Tōngdiǎn
The Six Codes of the Rites of Zhōu,
the Chief Minister assists the king in governing the realm.
Assistance means to serve as a deputy,
first is the Administrative Code to manage the official institutions,
second is the Educational Code to civilize the myriad people,
third is the Ritual Code to harmonize the myriad people,
fourth is the Political Code to equalize the myriad people,
fifth is the Penal Code to correct the myriad people,
sixth is the Service Code to sustain the myriad people.
From Zhòng Chángtǒng's "Discourses on Affairs"
Āndìng Liáng Hú excelled at the clerical script.
Initially, he served as the Minister of Personnel.
Tàizǔ requested to be appointed as the Magistrate of Luòyáng,
but Hú assigned him as the Commandant of the Northern District.
Later, Hú fled to Jīngzhōu to avoid turmoil.
After Tàizǔ pacified Jīngzhōu,
he sought out Hú.
Hú pleaded to redeem his life through his calligraphy,
so he was ordered to inscribe banners and plaques for the palace gates.
From "Shìyǔ".
In the past, when Máo Jiè served as Minister of Personnel,
no one dared to wear fine clothes or eat rich food.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi sighed and said:
"My laws are not as effective as Minister Máo's.
If I could make the Ministry of Personnel as conscientious as Máo Jiè,
changing social customs would not be difficult.
From "Collection of Memorials by Fù Xián": Jiè
was refined, upright, and impartial,
serving with purity and respect in office.
When overseeing selections,
he promoted the loyal and sincere,
rejected the flashy and false,
advanced the humble in conduct,
and restrained cronyism.
Officials who showed little merit in governing but had abundant personal wealth
were all dismissed and removed from office,
not selected for positions for a long time.
At that time, the whole country was unified in spirit,
with everyone striving to improve their conduct.
Even senior officials returning to court
had grimy faces and worn clothes,
often riding in crude carts.
Military officers entering government offices
wore court robes but walked on foot.
People emulated the purity of those who shared their meager food,
families mirrored the integrity of washing one's hat tassels in clean water,
the noble were free from the burden of base desires,
the humble ceased seeking ill-gotten gains.
Officials were clean above,
customs transformed below,
and people praise him to this day.
From "Accounts of Conduct of Former Worthies": Jiè once served as an assistant in the Eastern Bureau,
together with Cuī Yǎn overseeing selections,
and all those they recommended were pure and upright scholars.
Even those with great fame at the time,
but whose conduct lacked foundation,
ultimately could not advance in their duties.
He led others through frugality,
thus all scholars in the land took integrity as their personal motivation.
From "Records of Wèi"
Cuī Yǎn was pure, loyal, noble, and upright,
with refined insight and far-reaching vision,
promoting integrity and righteousness,
maintaining a stern demeanor at court.
In the early years of the Wei dynasty,
he was entrusted with the selection of officials,
overseeing fair and impartial judgments,
for more than ten years.
Many civil and military talents
were wisely appointed by him,
earning high regard from the court
and praise for fairness throughout the land.
"Biographies of Former Worthies"
Lú Yù served as the Minister of Personnel.
Previously, Zhūgě Dàn, Dèng Yáng, and others had gained fame,
but their reputations were mocked as having "four windows and eight thoroughfares" (implying superficiality).
The emperor despised this.
At the time, when appointing a Court Gentleman, the imperial edict stated:
"Whether we find the right person
depends entirely on Lú Yù.
In selecting officials, do not choose those with mere fame—
fame is like drawing a cake on the ground;
it cannot be eaten."
Lú Yù responded:
"Fame may not attract extraordinary talents,
but it can help us find ordinary scholars.
Ordinary scholars fear instruction and admire goodness,
and only then do they gain fame—
this should not be despised."
In evaluating people and making selections,
Lú Yù prioritized character and conduct,
and only then considered talent.
When the Court Attendant Lǐ Fēng once questioned Lú Yù about this,
Lú Yù said:
"Talent exists to do good;
thus great talent accomplishes great good,
and small talent accomplishes small good.
If someone is said to have talent but cannot do good,
then their talent is not fit for its purpose."
Lǐ Fēng and others were convinced by his words.
(Records of the Three Kingdoms: Wei)
Xuē Zǒng,
courtesy name Jìngwén,
served as Minister of Personnel Selection,
but firmly declined the position, recommending Gù Tán as one with keen insight and meticulous conduct,
thoroughly versed in principles and attuned to subtleties,
whose talent illuminated the character of others,
and whose virtue met public expectations.
He truly was not someone a humble minister like me could surpass,
so later Gù Tán succeeded Zǒng.
Records of Wú
Lǐ Sù,
courtesy name Wěigōng,
was a native of Nányáng.
From youth, he was renowned for his talent,
excelling in discourse and debate.
His judgments of praise and blame were always appropriate,
and he had a keen eye for recognizing the exceptional and recording the unusual.
He recommended and promoted those of later generations,
evaluating and appraising individuals,
with detailed and coherent reasoning.
Because of this, everyone respected him,
and Sun Quan promoted him to the position of Minister of Personnel in charge of selections, which were acclaimed for obtaining true talent.
(From the Wúshū in the Biography of Bù Zhì)
Wáng Jùnchōng and Péi Shūzé, both with their hair tied in tufts,

and was told Péi and Wáng.
When asked what they were like,
Zhòng said:
"Péi Kǎi is pure and perceptive,
Wáng Róng is concise and essential.
Twenty years from now, these two worthies will become Ministers of Personnel,

Shān Tāo served as Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
When his mother passed away,
he was already over sixty years old.
He observed mourning rites beyond customary requirements,
carrying soil to build her burial mound,
and personally planted pines and cypresses.
An imperial edict stated:
"Those with whom I jointly promote transformation

Lǐ Jiàn wéi lìbù lángzhōng,

"Guó Shǐ Bǔ"
King Wú Wáng Qián,
when the State of Wú established and moved Zǔo Sī Láng Zhōng,
oversaw selection affairs.
At that time, after the chaos of war,
official positions lost their proper maintenance,
genealogical records were scattered and lost,
registers and documents were destroyed,
and the genuine and fake were intermingled.
Qián received others with grace and courtesy,
his sitting room was always full of guests,
he treated people according to their talents,
and everyone felt they had gained his favor.
Xú Zhīgào, as chancellor of Wú, conducted selections in an orderly manner,
which was due to Qián's efforts.
For those who had lost their official documents,
and whose talents were deemed unusable,
he often provided them with support.
"Jiǔ Guó Zhì"
Liú Dǐngqīng,
served as the Director of the Bureau of Appointments in the central administration,
and concurrently as the Investigating Censor overseeing miscellaneous affairs.
Although Dǐng's nature seemed broad and easygoing,

"History of the Five Dynasties"
The Ministry of Personnel has two main offices,
the first being for minor appointments,
followed by the regulations office;
the Vice Ministers have two offices,

Traditionally, the Ministry of Personnel was referred to as the "eye of the department."
"Fēn Jì"
Péi Zūndù was promoted to Vice Director of the Bureau of Appointments,
specifically in charge of the Southern Section.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
the empire was at peace,
talents from all fields gathered at the capital,
and each year over ten thousand candidates sought official appointments through the Bureau of Appointments.
Péi Zūndù possessed keen discernment and a powerful memory,
was meticulous in examination and well-versed in documents,
thorough yet not rigid,
and was acclaimed as the foremost in administrative affairs,
thus becoming widely renowned.
Lǐ Xīyún was promoted to Vice Director of the Bureau of Appointments,
in charge of the Southern Section.
Xīyún adjudicated cases with clear reasoning,
causing corrupt officials to lose their nerve,
and was hailed as a divine judge.
"Book of Tang"
Wéi Zhì,
styled Chén Héng,
served as Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
This department was the eyes and eyebrows of the imperial administration,
and the arbiter of fate in selecting scholars.
He wielded an impartial brush to review records,
untangling intricate entanglements and complexities,
resolving them in a single glance.
(From "Epitaph" by Liú Yǔxī)
Cuī Yǎn had an elegant and imposing appearance,
with a clear spirit and dignified refinement,
so that people admired and loved him at first sight.
While serving as Vice Director of the Bureau of Appointments,
corrupt officials dared not act improperly,
and those who were isolated, poor, and without support were not left stranded.
His excellence in evaluating and appointing officials
was praised by his contemporaries.
Book of Táng
Cén Xī,
during the Cháng'ān era served as the magistrate of Guǎngwǔ,
and was renowned for his ability.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān once ordered the chancellors each to recommend candidates suitable for the position of vice-director.
The Vice Minister of the Phoenix Pavilion, Wéi Sìlì, recommended Xī,
and submitted a memorial saying:
"It is regrettable that his uncle, Cén Chángqiàn, committed treason, which implicates him."
Wǔ Zétiān said:
"If he has talent and capability,
why regret a minor implication?"
Thereupon, she appointed him as Vice-Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
and he was later promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel.
At that time, the Vice Minister of Personnel Cuī Shí, the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Zhèng Yīn, and the Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Lǐ Yǔngōng,
were jointly in charge of the selection of officials,
and all were known for accepting bribes and goods.
Xī was the most upright,
and contemporary opinion praised him.
Old Book of Táng
Jiǎ Yánzhōng,
was the father of Jiǎ Céng,
and was promoted to Vice Director of the Bureau of Appointments.
When Lǐ Jìngxuán concurrently served as Minister of Appointments,
Yánzhōng was known for his strong will.
He refused to defer to Lǐ Jìngxuán in the selection of officials,
and was demoted to Military Advisor of Shàozhōu.
Later, he offended Wǔ Yìzōng,
was imprisoned, and nearly died.
"History of the Táng Dynasty"
Liú Chóngwàng,
courtesy name Xīcóng,
was transferred to the position of Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
When Cuī Ānqián served as the Minister of Personnel,
Chóngwàng oversaw the Southern Bureau,
eliminating long-standing malpractices,
and restoring integrity to the selection department.
(Old Book of Táng)
Lǐ Jiǒngxiù served as an examination official,
overseeing the imperial examinations.
There was a candidate surnamed Cuī,
whose literary talent was not excellent.
Jiǒngxiù reviewed his paper for a long time,
then said to him:
"Young Master Cuī of Qīnghé,
your appearance is not bad,
with beard and eyebrows like halberds,
and your spirit is quite lofty.
Given your background, why must you insist on becoming a jìnshì?"
After repeatedly making him understand, he sent him away.
Those who heard this could not help but burst into laughter.
From the "History of the Táng Dynasty"
Xí Yù,
during the Kāiyuán era, successively held the position of Chief Examiner of Merit Evaluation,
overseeing the imperial examinations for two years,
widely praised for selecting talented scholars,
earning acclaim at the time.
He was promoted to Vice Minister of Personnel,
and Emperor Xuánzōng said to him:
"You previously served as Chief Examiner,
handling duties with fairness and impartiality,
hence this appointment is bestowed upon you."
He presided over the selection process for six years,
once again earning a commendable reputation.
When Zhōu Chí was assisting in governance, he appointed Wéi Ào as an Assistant Director of the Bureau of Evaluation.
When Chí first became chancellor,
he privately said to Ào:
"My talent is small, but my responsibilities are heavy;
how can I manage them?"
Ào replied:
"I am grateful for your deep trust,
and I wish only that you would not wield power—that would suffice."
Chí was taken aback,
not understanding his meaning.
Ào explained:
"Bestowing honors, rewards, punishments, and penalties—
if these are not matters you personally wish to execute,
I hope you will not act based on personal joy, anger, hatred, or affection.
Simply ensure that all officials and departments each fulfill their duties;
then you can sit composed in the court hall,
and the realm will govern itself.
Why would you need to wield power?"
Chí deeply agreed with him.
Lǐ Bó,
when Emperor Mùzōng ascended the throne,
was summoned to serve as an Examining Merit Vice-Director,
responsible for evaluating capital officials' performance,
not avoiding powerful and favored individuals,
and implemented promotions and demotions for all.
He memorialized:
"Evaluations of third-rank officials,
are first prepared as before;
for officials of the fourth rank and below,
their achievements should be reported upon completion,
with memorials retained in the palace without issuance."
Critics believed that since the chief ministers neglected their duties,
he should have submitted a memorial discussing this matter,
yet he overstepped his authority to seek unusual recognition,
which was not the complete way of serving one's sovereign.

The "Zhōu Lǐ" states:

Yìng Shào said:

Zhòngní was the Unrowned King,

From "Lúnyǔ Zhāi Fǔ Xiàng"
Emperor Líng sold official positions,
and the Commandant of Justice Cuī Liè paid five hundred strings of cash
to purchase the position of Minister over the Masses.
Liè's son Jūn,
courtesy name Kǒnghū,
was also renowned at the time.
Liè asked him:
"Now that I have become a duke,
what do people in the world say about it?"
Jūn replied:
"Father, you have long enjoyed a lofty reputation,
and no one would say you are unworthy of being a duke.
However, now that you have assumed this position,
everyone under heaven suspects it reeks of the stench of copper."
Liè raised his staff to strike him,
and Jūn fled.
Liè said:
"A son flees when his father beats him—
can this be called filial?"
Jūn said:
"When Shùn served his father,
he would endure minor beatings,
but flee from major ones,
so as not to entrap his father in unrighteousness."
Liè said:
"Do you take me for Gǔsǒu!"
From Sīmǎ Biāo's "Annals of the Nine Provinces of the Spring and Autumn Period."
When Wú Sūnxiū first ascended the throne,
the Minister of Revenue read a memorial at the court.
"Tōngdiǎn"
Dāngyáng Hóu Dù Yuánkǎi served as the Minister of Revenue,
benefiting the people internally
and aiding the frontiers externally,
preparing resources and establishing their use.
The measures that brought benefit to his era
numbered over fifty.
"History of the Jin Dynasty"
In the fifth year of Xiánníng,
an edict decreed that a single appointment would not be withdrawn,
causing both public and private sectors to become expensive,
not solely due to the timing of nature,
but rather human affairs,
as there were inadequacies in their execution.
The key figure responsible was precisely the Minister of Revenue,
thus appointing Zhāng Huà, the Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary and Director of the Secretariat, as the Minister of Revenue.
"Records of Daily Events of the Jìn Dynasty"
Initially,
the Emperor conspired with Yáng Hù to attack Wú,
but most officials considered it unfeasible,
only Huà supported the plan.
When the strategy was about to be implemented on a large scale,
Huà was appointed as the Minister of Revenue,
responsible for calculating water transport and supplies,
and finalizing the court's strategic calculations.
After Wú was conquered,
an imperial edict commended his achievements,
and he was promoted to the rank of Marquis of Guǎngwǔ County.
"Book of Jìn"
Wú Yǐnzhī served as Minister of Revenue,
using bamboo screens as partitions,
and sat without felt mats.
Later, he was promoted to Central Army Commander,
yet his purity and frugality remained unchanged.
Each month, from the salary he received,
he only kept enough for his own sustenance,
distributing the rest to aid his relatives and clan.
His family members spun and wove to support their daily needs,
often facing hardship and destitution.
Sometimes they ate only every other day,
his own clothing was worn and incomplete,
and his wife and children did not benefit from the slightest official emolument.
Dào Gài,
styled Màoguàn,
served as Minister of the Left for the Masses.
Gài was eight feet tall,
with finely featured eyebrows and eyes,
fair-skinned and possessing a handsome beard,
his demeanor was elegant,
and he excelled in responding to inquiries,
upholding integrity and self-cultivation in all his posts,
his nature being straightforward and frugal,
disliking music and feminine charms,
his residence had a simple bed,
with no concubines or attendants by his side,
as for his carriage and attire,
he did not pursue bright and华丽 clothing or hats and shoes,

sometimes even worn and patched,
yet when announced on the road,
it was merely to show adherence to court regulations.
From the *History of the Southern Dynasties*: Dào Qià served as Palace Censor,
while his elder brother Gài was Minister of the Left for the Masses.
According to old regulations, the Palace Censor was not allowed to enter the lower residence of the Minister.
Qià argued that close kinship should not be an impediment,
submitting a memorial for review and decision,
Left Assistant Minister Xiāo Zǐyún deliberated,
and permitted entry to Gài's ministry,
also because the brothers had always been deeply devoted,
unable to bear separation.
Regarding Dào Gài and Dào Qià,
the *Book of Liang* has their own biographies,
the *History of the Southern Dynasties* includes them in the biography of Dào Yànzhī,
but the *Fen Ji* mistakenly records it as Liú Gài,
while the *Shi Wen He Bi*,
follows this error.
Could it be that due to the slight peculiarity of the surname Dào,
they thus inherited the mistake?
This greatly misleads readers.
Hé Yìn served as the Minister of Revenue,
but later resigned from his official post and retired to the Yúnmén Temple on Ruòyē Mountain.
An imperial edict granted him the salary of a retired minister,
but Hé Yìn firmly declined it.
Book of Liáng
Cài Jǐnglì,
courtesy name Màoshì,
was appointed as the Minister of Revenue.
According to old customs, official appointments took place in the afternoon.
On the day of Jǐnglì's appointment,
he happened to encounter the imperial carriage heading to Xuánwǔ Lake,
where all officials present were attending a banquet.
Emperor Xuān, fearing that Jǐnglì might miss the occasion,
specifically ordered his appointment to be conducted early.
Such was the high regard in which he was held.
History of Southern Dynasties
Zhǎngsūn Píng,
courtesy name Chǔjūn,
was appointed Minister of Revenue.
Píng observed that many provinces and counties across the land suffered from floods and droughts,
leaving the common people destitute.
He memorialized to have each household contribute one shi of grain every autumn,
with gradations based on wealth and poverty,
storing it in local neighborhoods
as preparation for lean years.
This was called
"the charity granary"
From then on, the regions became prosperous,
