Book of Sui
In the third year of the Kāihuáng era, the Ministry of Revenue was renamed from Dùzhī to Mínbù.
When the state compiled the "Suíshū," it referred to it as Hùbù,
likely due to the imperial taboo.
In the early Yǒnghuī era of the Táng dynasty,
Mínbù was again renamed to Hùbù,
also because of the imperial taboo.
In the first year of the Xiǎnqìng era,
Hùbù was changed back to Dùzhī.
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era,
the title of Dùzhī Shàngshū was altered to Sīyuán Tàicháng Bó.
Initially,
the Ministry of Revenue was positioned after the Ministry of Rites.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān reorganized the official positions to correspond with heaven, earth, and the four seasons,
designating the Ministry of Revenue as the Earth Ministry,
which resulted in it being placed before the Ministry of Rites.
The "Tōngdiǎn" states:
"The state, referring to Dù Yòu's account of the Táng dynasty."
The "Tōngkǎo" followed this,
so why was it not changed?
Zhèng Shànguǒ, the upright and law-abiding Inspector of the Dàlǐ Court,
concurrently serving as Minister of Revenue,
devoted himself to integrity and upholding the law,
achieving remarkable merits.
By decree, he and Péi Jì along with ten others,
whenever presenting memorials or attending court,
were all permitted to ascend the hall,
with his cousin Yuán Shú among their number.
This was regarded as an honor at the time.
"Fēn Jì"
Wáng Jū assisted Emperor Míng Huáng in quelling internal rebellions,
and was appointed Minister of Revenue.
The emperor held Wáng Jū in particularly high regard and entrusted him with special responsibilities,
involving him in major state affairs,
and he was called the "Inner Prime Minister."
From "The Main Biography"
Bì Gòu was promoted to Minister of Revenue,
and in the fourth year of the Kāiyuán era,
he fell ill.
The emperor personally wrote a prescription and bestowed it upon him.
At that time, it was considered ominous to hold the position of Minister of Revenue,
so he was hastily reassigned as Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
in the hope that he would recover from his illness,
but he soon passed away.
(from Fēn Jì)
Wéi Yù resigned from the position of Judge of the Ministry of Revenue,
and upon returning home told his nephews:
"I have already declined the appointment as Commissioner of Population Registration.
from "Records of Elegant Conversations"
The Ministry of Rites,
was the responsibility of the Junior Minister over the Masses and the Grand Master of the Palace,
Emperor Yáng of Suí first established the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue,
the Táng Dynasty followed this,
later it was changed to the Ministry of Revenue,
in the second year of the Lóngshuò era it was changed to the Junior Regular Mountaineer of the Controller of the Origin.
"Tōngdiǎn"
Lú Chéngqìng,
the grandson of Sīdào,
was handsome in appearance and demeanor,
and possessed great talent and ability.
Tàizōng admired his keen discernment,
and repeatedly appointed him as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue.
Tàizōng once inquired about the population figures throughout successive dynasties,
and Chéngqìng recounted the data from the Xia and Shang dynasties onward,
through the Zhou and Sui dynasties,
all with reliable sources,
which earned Tàizōng's prolonged admiration and praise.
From the Old Book of Táng
In the thirteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
the Vice Ministers of Revenue Yáng Yáng and Bái Zhīshèn were implicated in mismanagement of funds,
and both were demoted to serve as prefectural governors.
The Emperor ordered the chief ministers and officials below the third rank
to carefully select someone capable of handling the Ministry of Revenue,
and many recommended Yuán Hóng.
He was about to be appointed as the Minister of Revenue,
but the current senior officials considered his qualifications insufficient,
deeming him unsuitable for such a rapid promotion.
Instead, he was promoted to Grand Master of the Palace,
and appointed as Vice Minister of Revenue.
Yuán Hóng then submitted a detailed memorial on the people's hardships and the strengths and weaknesses of current governance,
which greatly pleased the Emperor.
Consequently, he was rewarded with robes and silk.
The Emperor
Yáng Yáng served as Vice Minister of Revenue.
The emperor once summoned the chancellor and high officials to discuss the national household registers in the Yányīng Hall.
Yáng Yáng spoke with particular detail about the advantages and disadvantages,
earning the emperor's admiration and praise.
Thereupon, Yǔwén Róng proposed inspecting and registering the unregistered households and remaining individuals.
Yáng Yáng insisted it was inappropriate.
Yǔwén Róng was then in a position of power,
and the high officials remained silent and compliant.
Only Yáng Yáng raised objections,
so he was demoted to serve as Prefect of Huá Prefecture.
《Book of Táng》
Lǐ Jiàng served as the Assistant Minister of the Department of Revenue,
adjudicating affairs of the department.
During a routine audience,
Emperor Xiànzōng said:
"The northern part of the Department of Revenue has offerings presented,
yet you alone have none, why is that?"
Lǐ Jiàng replied:
"Offering the Department of Revenue's money to the inner treasury
is using resources to seek personal favors."
The emperor was astonished,
and further admired his frankness.
"Old Táng."
Niú Sēngrú was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue.
Earlier,
when Hán Hóng came to court,
due to past affairs in Xuānwǔ,
many people spread rumors,
so his son Gōngwǔ used family wealth to heavily bribe
many powerful and favored officials,
among the ranks of those who spoke,
all received his gifts.
Soon after,
both father and son died,
leaving a young orphaned grandson.
Emperor Mùzōng, fearing the property would be stolen by servants,
ordered a palace envoy to go to their home,
inspect the household ledger,
and hand it over to the family steward.
The ledger clearly recorded all bribery recipients,
but next to Niú Sēngrú's name was written in vermilion ink:
"On such-and-such date, delivered certain items to Vice Minister Niú,
not accepted,
returned and settled."
Emperor Mùzōng examined the ledger and was very pleased.
Not long after, when discussing the appointment of a chancellor,
the emperor first approved Niú Sēngrú's name.
Zhāng Píngshū,
during the Chángqìng era served as Vice Minister of Revenue,
was cunning, dangerous, and boastful,
rising through Wáng Bō's patronage,
and once in charge of finances,
often sacrificed public interest for private favorites,
many sycophants grew intimate with him,
enjoying the emperor's favor,
he moved with obsequious agility,
mixing in jest and buffoonery,
sometimes calling himself "old slave,"
utterly lacking a minister's dignity.
Once after reporting to the throne,
he descended the steps then climbed back up,
and his memorials were frivolous and flippant.
The emperor often smiled at his antics among the officials,
where he toyed with junior officers,
boisterous and unrestrained.
He proposed the Salt and Iron Commissioner be appointed by chief ministers,
hoping thereby to gain a key post himself,
and whenever palace edicts were issued,
he'd suspect they conferred honors on him,
adjusting his robes to wait,
earning later ridicule.
The emperor said: "Zhāng Píngshū,
is a talented servant of the state,
his plans can split autumn hairs,
officials fear him like summer heat,
in just over a month as treasurer,
he has tightened discipline greatly.
With military campaigns ongoing,
and supplies urgently needed,
relying on success for relief,
who but you can accomplish this?
Without wisdom, tasks cannot be completed,
without honesty, I cannot keep you close.
Alas,
beyond your duties,
should you not consider fulfilling official expectations and satisfying my heart?"
From "Báishì Chángqìng Collection"
Pān Mèngyáng,
whose father Yán was Vice Minister of Rites,
and mother was the daughter of Liú Yàn,
had many of his father's friends and maternal grandfather's guests among the high officials,
thus gaining recommendations for appointment.
Towards the end of Dézōng's reign,
Wáng Shào, favored by the emperor, repeatedly praised Mèngyáng's talent,
leading to his promotion to Vice Minister of Revenue.
At the beginning of Xiànzōng's reign,
Mèngyáng was ordered to inspect Jiāng-Huái,
and observe the governance of southeastern military commands.
At that time, Mèngyáng, arrogant due to his powerful status,
led an entourage of three to four hundred people,
and wherever he visited command headquarters,
he focused only on sightseeing and enjoyment,
drinking through the night with women,
and upon reaching the Salt and Iron Transport Bureau,
extensively accepted bribes,
merely appointing officials.
Upon his return,
he greatly disappointed public expectations,
and was demoted to Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
later reappointed as Vice Minister of Revenue.
Mèngyáng was still flamboyant and unrestrained,
unconcerned with minor details,
and his residence was extremely luxurious and imposing.
When Xiànzōng traveled incognito to Lèyóu,
he saw its grand spaciousness,
with construction still ongoing,
and asked his attendants about it,
who identified it as Mèngyáng's;
Mèngyáng, frightened, halted the construction.
He delighted in feasting,
and many court officials associated with him,
though critics were numerous at the time,
soon he suffered from paralysis and could not walk.
Xiànzōng sought efficiency in all matters,
and once dispatched an Imperial Commissioner to Jiāng-Huái,
Left Director of the Bureau of Appointments Zhèng Jìng on a mission,
who took leave,
the emperor admonished him:
"In my palace expenditures,
even one bolt of cloth is recorded in the accounts,
only in relieving the poor,
do I not calculate.
You are learned and virtuous,
now embarking on this mission to convey my orders,
you should understand my intentions,
do not follow Pān Mèngyáng's example,
who, wherever his missions took him,
only indulged in heavy drinking,
and visiting mountain temples.
Old Book of Tang: Initially, when Mèngyáng became Vice Minister,
he was not yet forty,
his mother told him:
"With your talent holding such a high position,
it worries me.
New Book of Tang
Lú Rǔbì,
the son of Jiǎn Qiú,
followed Emperor Zhāozōng in his relocation to Tàiyuán,
where Lǐ Kèyòng repeatedly recommended him for the position of Vice Minister of Revenue.
The military governorship in Tàiyuán had the Lóngquán Pavilion,
where Jiǎn Qiú had governed.
At that time, he personally wrote a poem,
which was inscribed on the western wall of the pavilion.
When Rǔbì later served as deputy commander,
during banquets held in the pavilion,
he never took the seat of a guest,
but instead faced west and bowed his head in reverence.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
The Zhou official system,
under the Minister of Education's subordinate officials,
included lower grand masters,
which was equivalent to the position of a director.
The Six Codes: During the Wei dynasty, there was a Director of the Ministry of Agriculture.
Comprehensive Institutions: The Wei dynasty established the Left and Right Ministries for the People,
later renamed the Ministry of the People and the People Section,
all corresponding to the Ministry of Revenue.
In the Wu dynasty, Zhāng Wēn served as a Gentleman of the Revenue Section.
Classified Matters
Gāo Gòu,
courtesy name Xiàojī,
was appointed as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice,
and soon transferred to the Ministry of Revenue.
At that time, Vice Minister of the Secretariat Jìn Píngdōng was disputing succession rights with his nephew Zhǎngmào,
the Department of State Affairs could not adjudicate,
court officials debated three times without resolution,
yet Gòu's judgment was both decisive and reasonable.
The Emperor considered him capable,
summoned him to the inner palace,
and commended him saying:
"I have heard that Ministers of State correspond to constellations in heaven,
observing your talent and insight,
I now know the ancient saying is indeed true.
Matters of legitimate and illegitimate succession,
are of great importance in ritual teachings,
I have read your judgment several times,
its reasoning and language are most appropriate,
beyond what I could have conceived.
He bestowed one hundred dan of rice upon him,
and from then on his reputation became known.
Book of Sui
Wéi Wéi,

extensively delving into literature and history,
passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì,
rose from Dàlǐ Chéng to successively become Hùbù Lángzhōng,

and at the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era, it was renamed Xiàn Bù (Ministry of Statutes).
From the Tōngdiǎn.
Liú Xiángdào was appointed Minister of Justice,
and whenever he reviewed major cases,
he would sigh repeatedly with sorrow,
and on the day of submitting verdicts, he would fast for two consecutive meals.
"Book of Tang"
Lǐ Shìzhī was appointed Minister of Justice.
Shìzhī was fond of entertaining guests and friends,
and could drink ten pints of wine without losing his composure.
He would host banquets at night,
handle official affairs during the day,
leaving no pending matters in his court.
The emperor
Cuī Yǐnfǔ,
who maintained purity and integrity by self-restraint,
was appointed Minister of Justice for his strong and upright character.
The Emperor intended to make him chancellor:
"You may converse with Niú Xiānkè,
do you often meet him?
He replied:
"Not yet.
The Emperor said:
"You may visit him.
Yet Yǐnfǔ never went.
Another day the Emperor inquired again,
and received the same response as before.
Thus the Emperor did not appoint him.
When his disciples asked the reason,
he answered:
"I do not despise him for his humble origin,
but his talent falls short of average men—
how could I engage in dialogue with him?
The commentary praises:
"Yán Tǐngzhī refused to meet Chancellor Lǐ Línfǔ,
Cuī Yǐnfǔ defied the decree and would not yield to Niú Xiānkè—
how truly resolute they were!
Both missed the chance to become chancellors for this,
yet each upheld their principles.
《Book of Táng》
During the Jingyuan Army Mutiny,
Guān Bò and Lú Qǐ accompanied the emperor to Fengtiān.
Later, when Lú Qǐ, Bái Zhìzhēn, and Zhào Zàn were all demoted,
Guān Bò still remained in charge of governance.
Both court and public were in an uproar,
deeming this unacceptable.
Consequently, he was removed from his post as chancellor,
and reassigned as Minister of Justice.
Senior official Wéi Lún and others wept at court,
saying:
"The chancellor failed to devise wise strategies and assist properly, leading to today's situation.
Yet he still serves as a minister to the realm—
how can order be achieved this way?
It is truly heartbreaking."
Those who heard this regarded him with respect and awe.
(Old Book of Táng: Biographies of Guān and Wéi)
Liǔ Gōngchuò served as Minister of Justice,
a native of the capital region.
There was a case where an aunt beat her niece-in-law to death,
and the prefectural court sentenced her to death in retribution.
Gōngchuò argued:
"When a superior strikes an inferior, it does not constitute a fight,
and moreover her son is still alive.
To execute a mother because of her daughter-in-law
is not conducive to moral instruction."
The sentence was ultimately reduced from death.
From the Old Book of Táng.
In the autumn ministry of the Zhōu dynasty,
the minor minister of justice held the rank of middle grand master.
The "Six Codes" state that the duties of the minor minister of justice included managing the affairs of the outer court,
in order to gather the myriad people and consult them.
"The Rites of Zhōu"
In the Táng dynasty, for major legal cases,
the court would appoint the Vice Censor-in-Chief, Vice Minister of Justice, and Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review to serve,
which was called the Grand Three Judicial Offices Commissioner.
"Táng Zhílín"
Emperor Tàizōng said to his attending officials:
"Zhāng Liàng has five hundred adopted sons.
Raising such a group,
what could he intend?
Precisely to rebel.
He ordered all officials to deliberate on his case,
most saying Liàng deserved execution.
Only the Junior Director of the Palace Administration Lǐ Dàorù said that evidence of rebellion was insufficient,
clarifying his innocence.
Tàizōng, already in great fury,
ultimately had him beheaded in the market,
and confiscated his family's property.
Over a year later,
a vacancy arose for the Vice Minister of Justice,
and he ordered those in charge to carefully select a candidate,
but after repeated submissions,
none were acceptable.
Tàizōng said:
"I have found the right person.
Previously, Lǐ Dàorù argued about Zhāng Liàng,
saying evidence of rebellion was insufficient—
this statement was correct.
Although I did not immediately accept it then,
to this day I regret it,
so he appointed Dàorù as Vice Minister of Justice.
Old Book of Táng
Xī Zhì,
courtesy name Yīnqīng,
was promoted to Vice Minister of Justice.
Péi Yánlíng, resenting that Capital Governor Lǐ Chōng had effective governance,
deliberately sought to frame and harm him,
falsely accusing Chōng of colluding with Lù Zhì,
and repeatedly sending him substantial bribes of gold and silk.
After Chōng was demoted,
Yánlíng further memorialized that Chōng had recklessly squandered a great amount of funds and grain from the Capital Prefecture,
requesting that the Audit Bureau investigate.
He intended to use Cuī Yuánhàn, Director of the Audit Bureau, to frame Chōng,
and thereby tarnish Zhì's reputation.
The emperor approved the request,
and Yuánhàn, currying favor with Yánlíng, prosecuted the prefectural clerks.
Whenever clerks appeared,
even if they had committed no offenses,
he flogged them to assert his authority.
Public opinion was in an uproar, so Zhì
personally reviewed the prefectural records,
and, having obtained the truth, submitted a complete judicial report.
Chōng was thus exonerated,
while Yuánhàn, failing to achieve his goal,
died of rage and resentment as a result.
The emperor
Wáng Bō,
courtesy name Míng,
was transferred to serve as Vice Minister of Justice.
Bō excelled in administrative techniques,
and although official documents were overwhelming,
he analyzed them as fluently as a flowing stream.
When cunning clerks practiced deceit,
none could escape exposure and failure.
At that time, the empire was fraught with troubles,
and the judicial courts' deliberations on verdicts
involved complex and numerous legal provisions.
Bō comprehensively compiled all previous regulations,
placing them at his side for reference.
Whenever detailed judgments were required urgently,
he executed them with godlike speed.
His subordinates at the time
were endlessly amazed and full of admiration.
The emperor
Liú Zhuǎn was promoted to Vice Minister of Justice,
whereupon he compiled and gathered all usable edicts and decrees,
from the Wǔdé era through the Dàzhōng era,
totaling 2,865 items,
which he categorized and analyzed,
adjusting and determining their severity,
and presented the work titled "Comprehensive Classified Legal Code of the Dàzhōng Era,"
which legal experts praised for its thoroughness.
"The Táng History"
Lǐ Línfǔ,
during the Kāiyuán era was promoted to Grand Master of Remonstrance,
at that time,
Yuán Qiányào served as Palace Attendant,
Qiányào's son Jié said:
"My father says Lǐ Línfǔ requested to become Director of the Bureau of Gates.
Qiányào replied:
"A gentleman official must have consistent conduct,
and high talent and reputation,
could Gēnu possibly be a gentleman official?
Gēnu,
was Línfǔ's childhood name.
Jiǎng Yǎn served as Vice Minister of Justice concurrently holding the position of Investigating Censor.
During Yuán Zǎi's administration,
scholars serving as prefects were not promoted,
causing Yǎn to remain stagnant in his vice minister position,
unable to be transferred.
When Cháng Gǔn succeeded as chancellor,
he learned that scholars resented Yǎn's unjust treatment,
and therefore promoted him to Deputy Chief Censor.
"New Book of Tang"
Féng Sù,
courtesy name Gǒngzhī,
served as Vice Director of the Bureau of Personnel Evaluation.
When Huái Dé was pacified,
he was appointed Director of the Bureau of Reviews.
The imperial edict stated:
"Haste leads to loss of truth,
delay causes detention injustice,
severity obstructs mercy,
leniency breeds wickedness.
Balancing these four aspects
constitutes the difficulty of upholding law.
《Tángshū Kǒng Tiē》"
Zhèng Gǔ was appointed as Director of the Bureau of Honors,
and composed a poem to congratulate himself,
with a preface stating: "
The late Minister of Xǔchāng, Xuē Néng, once served as Director of the Bureau of Honors;
years later, the late Vice Director of Jiànzhōu, Lǐ Pín, was transferred from the Censorate to assume the post.
Both were leading masters of poetry in their time,
making the Bureau of Honors
flourish remarkably then.
I sought their guidance early on and received profound mentorship;
now, though unworthy, I hold this position,
which is also a regular official rank."
《Fēn Jì》 records that Zhèng Gǔ's poetic fame peaked in the late Táng dynasty,
with his collection titled "Cloud Terrace Compilation,"
yet commoners simply refer to it as the poetry of Director Zhèng.
His poems contain many exquisite lines,
though their style isn't particularly elevated.
Méi Shèngyú also rose to the position of Director in his later years.
One day during a gathering,
Liú Yuánfǔ teased him, saying:
"Shèngyú's official career will end here."
The guests were all startled, but Yuánfǔ explained:
"In the past, there was Director Zhèng,
and now there is Director Méi."
Shèngyú was quite displeased.
Not long after,
Shèngyú fell ill and passed away.
His poetry is compiled in the "Wǎnlíng Collection,"
yet people today merely call it the poetry of Director Méi.
A casual remark turned prophetic,
and it indeed came true—how lamentable.
In the Táng dynasty, there were major judicial cases,
resolved by the Vice Director of the Ministry of Punishments, the Censor-in-chief, and officials of the Dàlǐ Temple to adjudicate doubtful matters,
which were called the minor three judicial commissioners.
"Records of Official Posts"
Wǔ Yuánhéng served as the magistrate of Huáyuán County.
At that time, in the capital region, there were garrison commanders and supervising generals
who, relying on imperial favor and pursuing achievements, often harassed officials and common people.
Yuánhéng found this distressing,
so he claimed illness and resigned from his post.
He detached himself from worldly affairs,
drifting along and indulging in banquets and poetry for a long time.
Emperor Dézōng, recognizing his talent,
summoned him and appointed him as an assistant director in the Bureau of Revenues.
Liú Nǎi,
in the twelfth year of the Dàlì era was summoned and appointed as a Vice Director of the Bureau of Gates.
In the fourteenth year, when Cuī Yòufǔ was in power,
he had always been friendly with Nǎi.
It happened that Guō Zǐyí was to be honored with the title of "Shangfu,"
and as the ceremonial investiture had long been abandoned,
it was reinstated at this time.
Yòufǔ ordered officials from both departments to draft the investiture text,
but none met the emperor's approval;
Nǎi was summoned to the cabinet to draft it,
and he completed it immediately,
with dignified and elegant wording and meaning.
Yòufǔ admired and praised it for a long time,
and subsequently promoted him to the position of Supervising Secretary.
During the reign of Dézōng,
Lú Nánshǐ was implicated in an incident,
demoted to Sima of Xìnzhōu,
where according to regulations, he was allowed one subordinate official,
with a monthly allowance of one thousand coins for paper and brushes.
Prefect Yáo Jì initially reported this as embezzlement,
and further accused Nánshǐ of purchasing lead to smelt into yellow lead oxide.
Dézōng dispatched Censor Zhèng Chǔxiàng, Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice Péi Xiè, and Court Judicial Official Chén Zhèngyí as a three-department commission,
to jointly investigate the case.
Péi Xiè alone memorialized:
"I find Yáo Jì's accusation not a major offense." The Emperor said:
"What about the lead smelting?"
Xiè replied:
"Smelting lead into elixir,
is not prohibited by statutes,
yet suddenly recording such a minor matter,
and sending a three-department commission,
may cause distant regions to hear of it,
and harbor anxiety and fear.
If I am fit for this mission,
I request to go alone."
Dézōng cheerfully said:
"Your words are correct."
Líng Hú Huàn,
during the Dàlì era was appointed Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice.
When Emperor Dézōng ascended the throne,
he intended to lavish offerings at Yuánlíng.
Huàn submitted a memorial admonishing him, which read in part:
"When I read the History of the Han Dynasty,
and came to the biography of Liú Xiàng discussing rulers,
his admonitions regarding imperial tombs,
were praised by good historians,
and remain fragrant through the ages.
The imperial reply stated:
"When I recently deliberated on the imperial tomb,
my mind was confused and mistaken.
Your knowledge is comprehensive,
your insight profound and far-reaching,
you deeply understood what was improper,
and expressed it in most sincere words.
Not only did you point out my fault,
but you also helped my person.
You saved me from gaining the reputation of being unfilial,
all through your efforts.
How dare I not follow righteousness when I hear it,
and recover what was lost,
maintaining this from beginning to end,
hoping not to fail.
Even the upright men of antiquity,
could not have done better.
Dù Mù once requested the position of Junior Ceremonialist from the ministers,
but was unsuccessful;
he then asked for the post of Junior Autumn Official,
but again was unsuccessful.
He once dreamed someone told him:
"Missing spring but not reaching autumn,
the foot of Kun and the head of Jie,"
and he later indeed obtained the position of Vice Director of the Bureau of Comparisons.
Minister of Works,
was the Minister of Winter Offices in the Zhōu dynasty.
The Yànlèiyào states that the Minister Grand Minister over the Masses was also called Winter Minister.
Báitiē
Shuāng Jiū,
was the Minister of Works.
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" states: The six stars east of Wēi,
arranged in pairs to the north are called the Minister of Works,
governing water and metal.
If they are guarded, the world worries about floods.
"Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo"
To regulate the earth below and harmonize with the way of Kun,
while aligning with the radiance of Qian above,
is called the Minister of Works.
《Explanations of Han Officials》 When ditches and canals are blocked,
and water becomes a calamity for the people,
with vast fields left uncultivated,
then the Minister of Works is held accountable.
《The Great Commentary to the Book of Documents》
Minister of Works,
in charge of earth but not mentioning earth but rather emptiness,
emptiness,
honoring the master's situation compared to the substantial.
《White Tiger Discussions》 Winter Official Minister of Works,
manages state affairs, constructing city walls and capitals,
establishing altars of land and grain and ancestral temples,
building tombs, residences, and tools,
overseeing all craftsmen.
《Huán Jì's Essentials》
Yǔ served as the Minister of Works,
leveled the nine mountains,
dredged the nine marshes,
channeled the nine rivers,
and made all regions present tribute according to their duties.
The territory spanned five thousand li,
reaching even the remote wilderness.
《Yútōng Diǎn Lüè》: The position corresponds to the office of the Black Tortoise,
with responsibilities of the Minister of Works.
In the era of Yú Shùn, Bó Yǔ
led his ranks in the Zhōu court,
and the court official Máo
resided in that region.
《Zhāng Zhuó Jí》: The Sòng state altered the title due to Duke Wǔ’s name taboo,
changing "Minister of Works" to "Minister of Walls."
The Chǔ state changed it to "Mò Áo,"
while the Qín established the Censor-in-Chief and abolished the Minister of Works.
《Qí Zhí Yì》: Yǔ was skilled in geography, water sources, and the nine regions, obtaining maps and charts,
so Yáo appointed him as Minister of Works.
《Shàngshū Xíng Dé Fàng》
Kǒngzǐ,
served as the magistrate of Zhōngdū,
and in the second year, Duke Dìng appointed him as Minister of Works.
He then distinguished the properties of the five types of soil,
and determined what was suitable to grow in each,
so that everything found its proper place.
From "The School Sayings of Confucius."
Wáng Liáng was initially the governor of Yěwáng.
Emperor Shìzǔ was deliberating on the selection of the Grand Minister of Works,
when the Red Hidden Talisman stated:
"Wáng Liáng governs Wèi and serves as the Dark Warrior Emperor,
because Yěwáng is where Wèi relocated."
Lord Wén of Wèi moved from Púyáng to Yěwáng.
The Dark Warrior,
is the name of the water deity;
the Minister of Works,
is the official in charge of water and earth.
Thus, Liáng was promoted and appointed as the Grand Minister of Works.
From Huá Qiáo's "Book of the Later Hàn".
Since the Jìn and Sáo dynasties, there has been a Minister of Works,
Chén Shěnzhòng served as Minister of Works in the Chén dynasty;
Later, the Northern Zhōu dynasty had a Grand Minister of Works in the Ministry of Winter,
whose duties involved overseeing the laws of the five materials and nine standards;
the Suí dynasty established the Minister of Works,
adopting the title from the Northern Zhōu's Ministry of Works,
while also taking on the responsibilities of the earlier Minister of Works.
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era, the Minister of Works was renamed Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Regulator,
and the Vice Minister was renamed Junior Minister of the Court of the Imperial Regulator.
Empress Wǔ later changed it back to the Ministry of Winter.
"Tōngdiǎn"
Zhǎngsūn Píng,
courtesy name Chǔjūn,
served as Minister of Works,
and was considered competent.
At that time, someone reported that Commandant Bǐng Shào had slandered the court as incompetent.
The emperor was enraged and intended to execute him,
but Píng remonstrated, saying:
"Rivers and marshes accept filth, thus forming their depth;
mountains conceal flaws, thus achieving their grandeur.
I humbly express my utmost wish,
that Your Majesty may possess the capacity of mountains and seas,
and cultivate the virtue of magnanimity.
As the vulgar saying goes: 'If not foolish nor deaf,
one cannot be the head of a great household.'
Though this saying is humble, it can illustrate a great truth.
Book of Suí
Yán Lìběn,
during the Xiǎnqìng era succeeded his elder brother Lìdé,
serving as Minister of Works,
brothers successively holding one of the eight high ministerial positions,
contemporaries considered this an honor.
In the first year of the Zǒngzhāng era,
he was appointed Right Minister with the title of Sīpíng Tàicháng Bó.
According to the Two Tang Histories: at that time Lìběn was Right Minister,
while Jiāng Kè was Left Minister.
Lìběn had no other talents or knowledge,
and was known at the time for his excellence in painting.
Kè had repeatedly served as a general,
achieving military successes beyond the frontier.
That year,
the capital suffered famine and drought,
students from the three academies Hóngwén, Chóngxián, and Sīchéng were all sent back to their native places,
prompting contemporary sayings:
"The Left Minister displays might in the deserts,
the Right Minister wins fame with painting;
students from the three academies are dispersed,
clerks from Wǔtái pass the imperial exams."
According to the Tōngdiǎn: the Right Minister's reputation rests on painting.
It says 'pass the imperial exams',
referring to those who advanced through minor posts,
which can serve as a clear warning.
According to the Xīnyǔ: contemporaries used a thousand-character text to say 'Left Minister'.
It says painting was previously associated with the Left Minister.
It mentions the ridicule about painting,
Tang matters unrelated to Yán Lìběn's painting skill,
these three texts differ so they are appended here.
Lǐ Xīyún,
styled Bèiyī,
served as Vice Minister of Works.

Guānzhōng had long relied on the Zhèng and Zū canals for irrigation, but powerful families blocked the upper reaches to install over a hundred watermills, seizing seventy percent of agricultural water. Xīyún petitioned to have them all demolished, recovering two million dan of grain revenue annually.
The people benefited from this income,
and his substantial achievements fostered expectations for him to become chancellor, which Yuán Zǎi resented.
"New Book of Táng"
Hú Zhèng,
courtesy name Qǐzhōng,
during the Tàihé era served as Commissioner of the Ministry of Works and was appointed as a marriage alliance envoy to the Uighurs.
According to old regulations, envoys had private gift-giving ceremonies,
but local officials could not afford to host them,
so wealthy families would pay bribes to the envoys to secure official positions.
Hú Zhèng advocated for frugality and reducing expenses,
to stop the rampant practice of selling offices.
The northern tribes south of the desert tried to intimidate him into submission,
demanding that the envoy must change to barbarian clothing,
and also wanting to control the route for faster travel.
Hú Zhèng firmly refused,
maintaining Tang official protocols throughout,
and returned without disgracing his mission.
He was appointed as Vice Minister of Works.
Hú Zhèng possessed extraordinary physical strength.
When Duke of Jìn Péi Dù was still obscure,
he dressed plainly and drank privately,
but was harassed by warriors.
Hú Zhèng heard about this,
burst in and sat at the head of the guests,
raised a goblet and drank three full cups,
causing all the guests to turn pale.
He then took an iron lamp stand,
stripped off its decorative branches and leaves,
bent its base together,
laid it across his knee,
and said to the guests:
"I want to set a drinking rule -
anyone who doesn't drink their cup dry,
will be struck with this!"
The crowd assented meekly.
Hú Zhèng would drink several liters at once,
then pass it to the guests,
but they couldn't finish even with cups and ladles.
When Hú Zhèng was about to strike them,
the ruffians kowtowed and begged to leave.
Hú Zhèng drove them all out,
thus people of the time praised his chivalry.
Liǔ Yù,
courtesy name Yòuwén,
served as Túntián Shìláng.
At that time, regulations stipulated that officials of the third rank and above
must display halberds at their gates.
Gāo Jiǒng, the Left Vice Director, had a son named Gāo Hóngdé who was enfeoffed as Duke of Yìng.
He submitted a petition requesting halberds,
to which Yù ruled:
"The son of the Vice Director
still shares residence [with his father],
and his father's halberds are already displayed outside the gate.
There is a principle that the honorable should supersede the humble,
and a ritual where the son should defer to the father.
How can it be permissible to have halberds set up at the outer gate
and also display them at the inner court?" The matter was ultimately not carried out,
and Jiǒng, upon hearing this, sighed in admiration.
From "Suí Shū". "Tōngdiǎn" states:
"Emperor Yáng removed the character 'shì',
and in the third year of Wǔdé, the Zhōngzǐ official was added,
hence establishing positions between Shìláng and Lángzhōng.
Capable of Composing Poetry, Péi Ràngzhī,
courtesy name Shìlǐ,
Wú Jiàntián, a Gentleman of the Inner Bureau, remarked in the ministry:
"He is capable of composing poetry.
Péi Ràngzhī was on friendly terms with Yáng Yīn,
and whenever they met, they would engage in refined conversation all day long.
Yīn often said: This man is refined, alert, and outstanding;
Péi Wénjì's legacy will not perish.
When envoys from Liáng arrived,
he was often appointed to act as the Receptionist Gentleman.
"History of the Northern Dynasties"
Shěn Fú served as Director of the Bureau of State Farms,
acting as Pacification Commissioner of Shǎnnán Circuit,
and arrived at Dèng Prefecture.
He memorialized:
"The granary supervisors of Nèixiāng County's Xíngbù and Huángjiàn warehouses, such as Dèng Wǎn,
were previously in charge of coarse rice transported from Húnán and Jiāngxī,
which was stored in the wilderness of Xīchuān County.
After disbursements,
had rotted into dust.
The Bureau of Revenue issued orders to investigate the originally responsible officials,
since the second year of the Zhēnyuán era,
from Dèng Wǎn, his sons, brothers, down to his great-grandsons,
successively spanning twenty-eight years,
nine people had died in custody.
Currently, Dèng Wǎn's grandsons and great-grandsons remain imprisoned in cangues."
An imperial edict stated:
"It is heard that under the Salt and Iron Commission and the Bureau of Revenue,
such cases are extremely numerous.
The four individuals including Dèng Wǎn had their entire assets confiscated and sold,
with three generations imprisoned,
dying of starvation in prison,
which truly damages harmonious energy.
Dèng Wǎn and the others shall all be released.
If similar cases exist in all prefectures,
imprisonment must not exceed three years.
Quickly resolve such matters and report."
It was considered that Shěn Fú possessed talent as a Pacification Commissioner.
From the Old Book of Táng.

"Yuánwàiláng": According to the Six Codes, the six ministries' primary duties were initially established during the Sui Dynasty under Emperor Yáng, but after the Táng Dynasty, no specific duties are recorded.
Zhāng Wénguàn was promoted to Vice Director of the Waterways Bureau,
at the time his elder brother Wéncóng served as Vice Minister of Revenue.
According to old regulations, brothers were not permitted to hold concurrent positions in the central administration,
so he was transferred out to serve as Magistrate of Yúnyáng County.
Old Book of Tang
The Departments of Gates, Penal Affairs, Agriculture, Forestry, and Tributary Relations within the Ministry were all leisurely and uneventful.
A contemporary saying went:

"Officials from the Department of Gates and Department of Waterways rarely visited the Ministry. In a comic performance, someone pretended to be a clerk from the Ministry of Personnel and another from the Department of Forestry. When they unexpectedly met, they fainted for a long while, saying it was due to the clash of cold and heat."
From "Nánbù"
Chén Fān submitted a memorial stating:
"In former times, when the Princess of Emperor Míng sought an official post for her son,
he refused to grant even ten million coins.
Those nearby asked the Emperor about this, and he replied:
"An official post,
is a heavenly appointment,
which should be bestowed according to virtue,
how could it be recklessly given to anyone?
Now Your Majesty compares an official post to a handful of vegetables,
your servant considers this improper.
From "Records of Former Worthies of Rǔnán"
Wáng Tǎnzhī,
a young man of the Imperial Secretariat.
At that time, Jiāng Bīn served as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
overseeing the selection of Directors of the Imperial Secretariat.
Someone informed Wáng of this, and Wáng said:
"Since crossing the river,
the position of Director of the Imperial Secretariat has only been filled by those of second rank.
Why consider me?" Upon hearing this, Jiāng stopped the selection.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
It was said that uncles and brothers were not allowed to serve together as court officials in the same department,
but this was not recorded in the official regulations nor was there any formal decree.
In the second year of the Zhènguān era,
Wéi Shūjǐn was appointed as Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice,
and in the third year, Wéi Jìwǔ was appointed as Director of the Treasury Bureau.
Emperor Tàizōng said to them:
"I know that you brothers have recently taken office in the Department of State Affairs,
so I have appointed you to these positions,
wishing to achieve the beauty of a harmonious family,
and you should not avoid a slight compromise in seniority.
After that, there were many who served together in the same department,
but recently, unless by special imperial favor in appointments,
they must recuse themselves from serving together.
From the Tōngdiǎn
The post of Imperial Secretary had, since the Later Han Dynasty,
been filled by individuals of exceptional talent.
From the Wǔdé and Zhēnguàn eras of the Táng Dynasty onward,
this position was held in particularly high regard.
The Ministry of Personnel and Ministry of War were considered front-line departments,
the most crucial and demanding.
Officials transferred from back-line departments

Hé Jìngróng served as prime minister.
His concubine's younger brother Fèi Huìmíng held the position of granary supervisor,
and one night stole official rice,
being captured by the prohibition officers and sent to the military command.
At that time, Hé Dōng Wáng Yù was the general,
and Hé Jìngróng sent a letter to seek Huìmíng's release.
Wáng Yù, having previously requested something from him without success,
therefore sealed the letter and presented it to the emperor.
The emperor was furious,
and handed the case over to the Southern Bureau for investigation.
The imperial censor Zhāng Wǎn memorialized that Hé Jìngróng had conspired for personal gain and deceived the emperor,
deserving the punishment of execution in the marketplace,
but an imperial decree specially exempted him from office.
Dào Gài said to Zhū Yì:
"The weather suddenly seems to have cleared up."
Such was the jealousy he aroused.
Zhāng Miǎn,
courtesy name Yuáncháng,
served as the Imperial Censor.
While Miǎn held this judicial position,
he enforced the law without any fear or favoritism,
and was thus known as
"resolute and upright"
Emperor Wǔ then ordered his portrait to be painted in the government offices,
to inspire those in official positions
Zhāng Wǎn,
courtesy name Xiàoqīng,
was equally renowned as his elder brother Zǎng in his youth.
He served as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Xuānchéng,
and was later promoted to Palace Censor.
Emperor Wǔ dispatched Zhāng Wǎn's younger brother,
the Imperial Secretary Xùan, to convey an edict stating:
"The nation's most pressing need
lies in upholding law with impartial justice.
The fundamental principle of appointing personnel
should not be constrained by hierarchical promotions.
During the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
both Zhōu Mǐn and Cài Kuò held this position while serving as Palace Attendants—
you should not consider this a demotion.
"At that time, the Prince of Xuānchéng's household held great prestige,
hence this particular edict was issued.
According to the old practice,
the seats of the Imperial Secretary and the Censor-in-Chief faced each other from east and west.
During the grand assembly on New Year's Day in the fourth year of the Datong era,
when Zhāng Wǎn served as Censor-in-Chief
and his elder brother Zuǎn held the position of Imperial Secretary,
as all officials took their positions,
the brothers both had outriders clearing their way
and proceeded along separate paths.
This was unprecedented before the imperial steps.
People at the time considered it an honor.
From "The Book of Liáng"
Lù Gǎo,
courtesy name Míngxiá,
served as the Palace Secretary.
He was upright and outspoken by nature,
fearing no one.
At that time, the magistrate of Shānyīn, Yú Jiān,
had embezzled millions in corruption during his tenure.
Gǎo impeached and prosecuted him.
The Secretariat Drafter Huáng Mùzhī interceded with Gǎo on Jiān's behalf,
but Gǎo did not respond.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng heard of this
and questioned Gǎo about it,
to which Gǎo replied:
"It is true.
The Emperor asked:
"Do you know Mùzhī?
Gǎo answered:
"I do not know the man.
At that moment, Mùzhī was by the Emperor's side, who pointed at him and said:
"This is he.
Gǎo said to him:
"How dare you, a petty man, entrust a criminal to the Censorate?
Mùzhī turned pale.
The General of the Central Army, Zhāng Jì, was Gǎo's maternal cousin.
Gǎo once impeached Jì for an official matter,
and Jì took the opportunity during an imperial banquet to complain to the Emperor:
"Lù Gǎo is my relative,
yet he impeached me over a trivial matter without leniency.
The Emperor said:
"Gǎo was performing his duty;
how can you hold a grudge?
While serving in the Censorate,
Gǎo was renowned for fearing no powerful adversary.
History of the Southern Dynasties
During the Later Wèi, the title of "Central Censor" was changed to "Central Guard."
In the Book of Official Surnames, Lǐ Biāo,
styled Dàogù,
served as the Central Guard,
while also holding the position of Historiographer.
Since Biāo was favored by Emperor Xiàowén
and was also of an upright and unyielding nature,
he frequently brought charges and corrections against others,
causing people both near and far to fear him,
with the powerful and wealthy holding their breath.
The Emperor once referred to him as
"Lǐ Shēng."
He casually remarked to the ministers:
"With Lǐ Shēng by my side,
it is like the Hàn having Jí Àn."
When Biāo first became the Central Guard,
he was known for being severe and harsh.
Because confessions of guilt were hard to obtain,
he would use wooden hands
to strike the sides of their ribs,
causing them to faint and then recover.
He also pacified the rebellious Hú of Fénzhōu,
captured their criminal leaders and executed them by whipping their faces to death.
When Biāo became ill,
his body developed sores everywhere,
and he suffered extreme pain.
(Běi Shǐ)
Gāo Gōngzhī,
courtesy name Dàomù,
served as the Commandant of the Palace Guards during the reign of Emperor Zhuangzong.
Externally, he upheld strict laws,
while internally, he participated in confidential state affairs.
Whenever there were matters beneficial to the state and its people,
he would invariably report them to the emperor.
He remonstrated with utmost candor,
fearing nothing.
He selected censors from among the most renowned figures of the time.
When the Minister of Works, Ěrzhū Shìlóng, held immense power at court,
and was seen indoors with improper attire,
Dàomù immediately impeached him.
The emperor’s elder sister, Princess Shòuyáng,
once violated the cleared imperial road.
The guard holding the red staff
shouted at her to stop, but she did not heed.
Dàomù ordered the guard to smash her carriage with his staff.
The princess deeply resented this,
and tearfully complained to the emperor.
The emperor said:
"Commandant Gāo is an upright and impartial man.
What he did was in the line of public duty.
How can you hold a private grudge and blame him?"
Later, when Dàomù met the emperor,
the emperor said:
"The other day, my elder sister offended you on the road,
for which I am deeply ashamed."
Dàomù removed his cap to apologize,
but the emperor said:
"It is I who should feel ashamed before you,
yet you instead apologize to me."
After Ěrzhū Róng’s death, the emperor summoned Dàomù,
entrusted him with the amnesty decree,
and ordered him to proclaim it publicly,
saying:
"Now we can truly select censors with care."
Previously, Róng and others had often tried to appoint their own associates as censors,
hence this edict.
The "Book of Wei" and "Comprehensive Institutions" mistakenly attribute this to the Northern Qi Dynasty,
which is incorrect.
The Censor-in-Chief Lì Dàoyuán,
courtesy name Shàncháng,
was known for his strict and severe reputation.
The Governor of Sizhou, the Prince of Rǔnán Yuè, was intimate with his attendants,
and Qiū Niàn often shared his bed and daily life.
When it came to selecting officials for the province,
many decisions were made through Niàn,
who hid in Yuè's residence.
Occasionally returning to his own home,
Dàoyuán arrested Niàn and sent him to prison.
Yuè petitioned Empress Dowager Líng,
requesting to spare him,
and an imperial pardon was issued.
Dàoyuán then executed him,
and consequently impeached Yuè.
(Book of Wèi)
Sòng Yóudào, Shénwǔ recommended him for the position of Commandant,
but Wénxiāng insisted on his own request,
so instead, Cuī Xiān, the Director of the Ministry of Personnel, was appointed as Commandant of the Censorate,
and Yóudào was made Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs.
Wénxiāng said to Xiān and Yóudào:
"One of you is stationed at the Southern Terrace,
the other at the Northern Bureau,
you should make the whole world tremble with awe."
When Yóudào entered the bureau,
he whipped and dismissed the powerful clerks such as Wáng Rú.
He began to follow the old regulations,
erecting a nameplate at the Department of State Affairs,
to record the times of entry and exit,
causing everyone from the Directors down to cast sidelong glances.
《History of the Northern Dynasties》
Cuī Xiān,
courtesy name Jìlún,
served as the Commandant of the Censorate.
Wén Xiāng and the nobles went out to the Eastern Hills,
encountering Xiān on the road.
The vanguard was struck by his red staff,
and Wén Xiāng turned his horse to avoid him.
When Emperor Wèi held a banquet in Huálín Garden,
he said to Shén Wǔ:
"Recently, in various places,
many officials have been corrupt and cruel.
In the court, there is one who acts with impartiality,
frankly impeaching others,
without avoiding even his own relatives.
You, Prince, may offer him a toast."
Shén Wǔ descended the steps and knelt, saying:
"Only the Commandant of the Censorate, Cuī Xiān, fits this description.
I humbly follow your clear decree,
dare to offer him wine in toast,
and beg to bestow upon him the thousand bolts of silk awarded to me from archery,
requesting they be given to him instead."
The Emperor again praised him.
During the reign of Emperor Zhuāngzōng,
Cuī Xiān,
courtesy name Yuánqīn,
was promoted to Governor of Yíng Province.
He was recorded in the "Biographies of Harsh Officials."
Lángyé Wáng Yǎn,
styled Rénwēi,
was the third son of Wǔchéng,
and concurrently served as the Imperial Censor.
According to the old system of the Wèi dynasty,
when the Imperial Censor went out, the road was cleared,
and he traveled on a separate route from the Crown Prince.
All princes and dukes would halt their carriages at a distance,
unhitch their oxen,
and lower the yoke to the ground,
waiting for the Imperial Censor to pass.
If anyone delayed or violated this,
they would be struck with red clubs.
After the capital moved to Yè,
this ritual was discontinued.
Wǔchéng, wishing to honor and favor Yǎn,
ordered the restoration of the old system.
Initially,
when Yǎn departed from the Northern Palace,
he was about to assume the role of Imperial Censor.
All officials in charge of infantry and cavalry in the capital region,
the ceremonial guards of the Imperial Censor and the Minister of Education,
were fully prepared.
At that time, Yǎn held four positions concurrently.
The Emperor and Empress Hú set up a tent outside the eastern gate of Huálín Garden,
separated by a blue gauze,
and watched from behind a screen.
They sent a palace attendant galloping on horseback,
urging him to enter the procession but failing to do so.
The attendant claimed to be carrying an imperial decree with red clubs,
but in response, his saddle was shattered,
his horse startled, and he fell to the ground.
The Emperor laughed heartily,
considering it well done,
and further ordered the carriage to stop and relayed messages for a long time.
Spectators crowded the entire capital.
"History of the Northern Qí"
Xú Líng,
styled Xiàomù,
served as the Palace Censor.
At that time, Prince Ānchéng Xū held the position of Minister of Works,
and as the emperor's younger brother,
his influence overwhelmed the court and the public.
His subordinate Bào Sēngrǔ exploited the prince's authority,
suppressing legal complaints,
and no high officials dared to speak out.
Upon learning of this,
Xú Líng drafted a memorial of impeachment,
leading his subordinates from the Censorate to present the case.
Emperor Shìzǔ, seeing Xú Líng's stern and solemn demeanor,
as if unassailable,
composed himself and sat upright.
Xú Líng stepped forward to read the memorial,
while Prince Ānchéng stood attending in the hall,
looking up at Emperor Shìzǔ,
sweating and turning pale.
Xú Líng ordered the palace censor to escort the prince out of the hall,
then impeached and dismissed him from his posts as Palace Attendant and Director of the Secretariat,
from then on, the court became strictly orderly.
(Book of Chén) His son, Xú Jiǎn, served as Palace Censor,
and was impartial by nature, never flattering or attaching himself to anyone.
Although the Minister over the Masses Jiǎng Zǒng was highly esteemed at the time,
he too was impeached by Xú Jiǎn.
Emperor Hòuzhǔ deeply trusted and relied on him.
Sòng Jǐng served as the Left Censorate,
when Vice Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Yìzhī and his brother Zhāng Chāngzōng grew increasingly arrogant and domineering,
with the entire court currying favor with them.
Chāngzōng privately summoned fortune-teller Lǐ Hóngtài to divine his fortune,
and the predictions involved seditious implications,
leading to an anonymous accusation.
Sòng Jǐng petitioned at court to thoroughly investigate the matter,
but Empress Wǔ Zétiān said:
"Yìzhī and others have already reported this themselves,
so they cannot be punished."
Sòng Jǐng responded:
"Though Yìzhī and others confessed after their deeds were exposed,
their offense is too grave to pardon,
moreover, conspiracy and treason
cannot be exempted by confession.
I request they be detained
at the Censorate
for interrogation to uphold national law.
Yìzhī and others have long been in service,
receiving undue favor;
I know well that speaking out will bring disaster upon me,
yet righteousness stirs in my heart,
and I would die without regret."
Empress Wǔ Zétiān was displeased,
and Grand Secretary Yáng Zàisī (cited as Yáo Shú in Imperial Readings), fearing to offend the sovereign,
hurriedly declared an edict ordering Sòng Jǐng to leave.
Sòng Jǐng said:
"The sovereign's face is right before me,
I am personally receiving the imperial words—
there is no need for a minister to presume to proclaim the royal command."
Empress Wǔ Zétiān's anger slightly subsided,
and she then had Yìzhī and others detained at the Censorate,
intending to interrogate them.
Soon, a special pardon was issued absolving them,
and Yìzhī and others were ordered to visit Sòng Jǐng to apologize.
Sòng Jǐng refused to see them,
saying:
"Official matters should be discussed publicly;
if it were a private meeting,
then the law would not be impartial."
(Old Book of Tang)
Lú Yì,
the youngest son of Huáishèn,
was equally renowned as his elder brother Huàn.
In the eleventh year of the Tiānbǎo era,
he served as Vice Censor-in-chief,
as both his father Huáishèn and brother Huàn had previously held this position.
Father and sons, all three served as Vice Censor-in-chief,
maintaining their integrity and incorruptibility without change.
Contemporaries praised them for this.
Lú Tǎn,
styled Bǎohéng,
served as the Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Péi Jūn held the position of Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
but he overstepped his position in the right row.
Tǎn requested that he step back,
but Jūn refused to comply.
Tǎn said:
"When Yáo Nánzhòng was the Vice Director,
this was the precedent."
Jūn said:
"Who is Nánzhòng?"
Tǎn replied:
"Nánzhòng was one who upheld integrity and did not associate with the powerful and favored."
Soon after, Tǎn was demoted to the position of Right Advisor to the Heir Apparent,
and people of the time blamed Jūn for it.
Lú Tǎn was promoted to the position of Imperial Censor.
Initially,
when local officials from various circuits concluded their terms and returned to the capital,
they would take funds from their respective circuits as tribute offerings.
The emperor consequently issued an edict prohibiting this practice entirely.
However, Liǔ Shèng, Military Governor of Shānnán, and Yán Jìměi, Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèxī, violated the edict by presenting tribute.
Lú Tǎn impeached Shèng and Jìměi, stating:
"They await punishment as commoners."
The emperor advised Lú Tǎn, saying:
"What these two presented
came from their personal family wealth.
I have already promised to pardon them and cannot break my word."
Lú Tǎn responded:
"The means to establish great trust
lies in the edict.
Now these two officials have disobeyed Your Majesty's decree—
how can you sacrifice great trust for minor credibility?"
The emperor said:
"Since I have accepted their offerings,
what should be done?"
Lú Tǎn replied:
"Turn them over to the relevant authorities,
to demonstrate Your Majesty's virtue."
The emperor accepted his advice.
《New Book of Tang》
Wēn Zào,
courtesy name Jiǎnyú,
served as Vice Censor-in-Chief.
His nature was rigid and narrow-minded;
when provoked, he disregarded noble status,
using his authority to bully others.
Once encountering Left Rectifier of Omissions Lǐ Yú on the street,
he grew angry at his failure to yield way,
seized his attendant,
and administered ten blows to the spine.
Left Omissioner Shū Yuánbāo and others submitted a memorial discussing this,
stating:
"According to the established precedents of our dynasty,
officials in attendance on the streets,
except for the chancellor,
have no one to avoid.
Wēn Zào scorns court rituals, bullies Your Majesty's attending officials, and acts violently without fear or restraint.
Matters may be small,
but those related to principles of order must not be neglected;
once principles of order are lost,
disorder arises from it.
Though the ranks of Omissioners and Rectifiers are low,
they are Your Majesty's attending officials;
though the Vice Censor-in-Chief is high, he is an enforcer of law.
If attending officials are bullied,
respect is not extended; if law enforcers damage
the law, how can they uphold standards?
At that time, when Secretariat Drafter Lǐ Yúzhòng encountered Zào,
Zào dragged away his lead horse.
When Drafting Edicts Official Cuī Xián encountered Zào,
Zào again seized his follower.
During the Yuánhé and Chángqìng eras,
the Vice Censor-in-Chief's procession did not exceed half a ward,
but now it extends as far as two wards,
called 'filling the streets and clearing the way.'
He merely elevates himself through arrogance,
without considering the suspicion of overstepping bounds."
An imperial edict stated:
"The duty of censors is to point out flattery and confront evil,
not to make their processions grand.
The duty of attending officials is to advise on governance,
not to compete for status on the roads.
When censors and attending officials share the same road, they may proceed in order of arrival,
and on the road, they shall simply bow and pass.
Henceforth, when announcing their presence,
the distance before and after shall not exceed three hundred paces.
Old Book of Táng
Hán Gāo served as the Censor-in-Chief.
Whenever he had matters to present,
he would invariably address the full assembly of officials in the Zǐchén Hall to make his requests,
never visiting the private chambers.
The Emperor said to him:
"When I speak with you,
if matters cannot be fully discussed here,
you may come to the Yányīng Hall,
where we can deliberate at leisure and perhaps leave no affairs unattended, my dear friend."
Someone remarked to Hán:
"Since the Qiányuán era,
all officials presenting matters have gone to the Yányīng Hall to ensure thorough discussion.
Why do you alone address the court in the outer hall before all officials?
Does this not risk compromising discretion and confidentiality?"
Hán replied:
"The Censor's role
is to uphold impartiality for all under heaven.
Wielding authority with firmness and rectifying wrongs
rests solely on acting with integrity—
why should the matters we discuss fear being known by others?
How could one seek the private chambers,
avoiding people to whisper secretly,
thereby privatizing the laws of the state?
Moreover, the establishment of the Yányīng Hall
was because Emperor Sùzōng, considering Miáo Jìnqīng advanced in years and struggling to walk,
instituted it for his convenience.
Later, when court officials gained access to the private chambers,
many used it for personal advancement, seeking favor and patronage,
aiming to exhaust their ambitions.
How can one aspire to such practices?"
From "Records and Anecdotes"
Dí Jiānmó,
a great-grandson of Rénjié,
served as the Censor-in-chief.
On the day of his gratitude audience,
Emperor Wénzōng looked at him and said:
"The Censorate,
is the disciplinary framework of the court.
If the Censorate's discipline is upright, then the court is well-governed;
if the court is upright, then the empire is well-governed.
Now, all those who enforce the law
mostly harbor a cautious, hesitant mindset,
causing official duties to remain unfulfilled.
You are a descendant of Lord Liáng,
and naturally possess family principles;
how could you share such common concerns!"
Jiānmó responded with gratitude:
"If court laws are ever found unjust,
I will certainly devote myself to impeachment and reporting."
The Old Book of Tang mistakenly attributes this statement to Wèi Mó,
which is incorrect.
Wèi Mó,
courtesy name Shēnzhī,
was the fifth-generation descendant of Wèi Zhēng,
serving as Vice Censor-in-chief.
On the day of his gratitude audience,
he was granted in person the golden purple ceremonial attire,
impeached Duāmǎ Dūwèi Dù Zhōnglì for corruption crimes,
making the imperial relatives fear him,
concurrently held the position of Vice Minister of Revenue,
overseeing the affairs of his own department.
Mó memorialized:
"The Censorate,
being the institution upholding discipline,
should not be mixed with currency officials,
I beg to resign from the Censorate position,
to focus solely on Revenue Ministry affairs."
This was approved.
Mó had a majestic appearance,
his speech was straightforward and direct,
when colleagues spoke before the emperor about other matters,
the chancellor would inevitably use tactful persuasion,
only Mó spoke honestly without fear or avoidance.
Emperor Xuānzōng often said:
"Wèi Mó truly possesses his ancestor's style,
as a descendant of a renowned senior official,
I hold him in high regard.
The emperor
The Vice Censor-in-Chief serves as the deputy to the Grand Master,
since the Grand Master holds a high rank,
the position is not permanently filled,
and the Vice Censor-in-Chief often acts as the head of the Censorate.
Now, the Vice Ministers of the Nine Courts, the Vice Directors of the Palace Library, the Directors of the National University, and the Vice Magistrates of the Capital Prefecture,
all serve as deputies in ministries and courts,
and hold the fourth rank.
Although the Vice Censor-in-Chief's official duties are significant,
their rank is not elevated,
and it is requested to be raised to the fourth junior rank.
"Collected Works of Lǐ Déyù from the Huìchāng Era"
Guī Róng, concurrently Censor-in-chief,
reported that Lú Zhōurén, the Surveillance Commissioner of Húnán, had violated an imperial decree by presenting one hundred thousand strings of surplus cash.
Róng memorialized, saying:
"All under heaven belongs to one family;
is any land not the sovereign's?
Wealth and goods from both central and regional sources
all constitute Your Majesty's treasury.
Zhōurén has presumptuously presented trivial gains,
wildly speaking of unorthodox methods,
offering wealth and goods to curry favor—
how shallowly does he regard the court!
I fear that all under heaven will emulate this,
using the name of surplus
to exploit and extort by various means,
causing the people to suffer harm.
I request that severe punishment be administered
to serve as a warning to the other provinces.
From the Grand Master down to the Censor, the five censorial offices are collectively referred to as the Five Courts of Censors.
Throughout the history of our dynasty, only three individuals have served in all five courts:
Lǐ Shàngyǐn, Zhāng Yánshǎng, and Wēn Zào.
"Shàngshū Gùshí"
According to the old practice of the Censorate,
the three departments of the Censorate, the Grand Masters of the Palace, and the Vice Censors-in-Chief were appointed by recommendation,
which required approval from the court.
When Dúgū Lǎng served as Vice Censor-in-Chief,
Cuī Miǎn and Zhèng Jūzhōng were appointed without going through the head of the Censorate,
as both were old associates of the Chancellor.
Although the imperial decree was issued,
Lǎng refused to accept them and did not dare to admit them.
Cuī Miǎn was reassigned as a Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
while Zhèng Jūzhōng was assigned to the Eastern Bureau.
The Chancellor harbored resentment against Lǎng for this.
Lǐ Jié,
originally named Wùguāng,
succeeded Sòng Jǐng as the Censor-in-Chief.
At that time, the Empress's brother-in-law, the Court Gentleman for Imperial Apparel, Zhǎngsūn Xīn,
together with his brother-in-law Yáng Xiānyù, encountered Jié in an alley,
and proceeded to assault him.
The Emperor was greatly enraged,
ordering the execution of Xīn and the others.
The Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Mǎ Huáisù argued that it was inappropriate to carry out executions during the harmonious spring month,
and repeatedly submitted memorials pleading for leniency.
Nevertheless, an imperial decree was issued,
commandering their execution,
to apologize to the officials.
(Old Book of Táng)
Jiāng Wénwèi of the Southern Táng,
in the early Bǎotài era, was promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief,
upholding the law with impartiality and integrity,
showing no favoritism or injustice.
The chancellor Féng Yánsǐ's younger brother Yánlǔ,
together with Wèi Cén and Chén Jué, secretly abused their power and authority,
and when they failed in the campaign to replace Mǐn,
an edict was issued to execute
Jué and Yánlǔ to appease the nation,
yet Yánsǐ and Cén were left unpunished.
Wénwèi, standing before the emperor, submitted a memorial of impeachment stating:
"Yesterday, our army suffered defeat,
shocking the entire realm;
to wash away the shame of the ancestral temple,
the flesh of treacherous ministers ought to be minced.
Though two offenders have been punished,
public sentiment remains unappeased;
only when all four evils are removed
will the people's anger be dispelled.
I request the enforcement of the legal code
to apologize to all directions."
Before submitting the memorial, Wénwèi
had prepared a small boat to carry his elderly mother,
awaiting demotion.
Emperor Yuánzōng indeed became angry,
demoting him to Registrar of Jiāngzhōu,
while Jué and Yánlǔ, rescued by Sòng Qíqiū's intervention,
were spared death.
Yánsǐ was temporarily dismissed,
but soon regained power.
When the edict appointing Yánsǐ was announced,
with all officials in the court,
Cháng Mèngxí loudly exclaimed:
"Though the white hemp decree is fine,
it cannot compare to Jiāng Wénwèi's memorial!"
A year later, Wénwèi was recalled and promoted.
From "Jiǔguózhì" and "Lù Yóu's History of Southern Táng": Wénwèi once served as Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Since Wáng Yìfāng of our dynasty, for hundreds of years,
there had been no such bold and stirring discourse so prominently displayed,
thus the powerful trembled in fear,
the court and commoners buzzed with excitement,
copying the impeachment text,
causing paper to become expensive.
From "Xú Qíshěng's Record": Mǎ Lìng's History of Southern Táng states:
"Wénwèi held a remonstrance position,
at a time when Sòng Qíqiū, Chén Jué, Féng Yánsǐ, and Wèi Cén
all gained favor through flattery,
causing public discontent."
Wénwèi submitted a memorial stating:
"Removing two of them
does not satisfy the people's sentiment;
only when all four offenders are eliminated
will the state's laws be clearly upheld."
It is said that later events were lost;
could this be an error?
"Jiǔguózhì" and "Lù's History" record Jūnzhāng's affairs in great detail;
here it mentions a remonstrance official,
not specifying Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and why does it say later events were lost?
At the Censorate, there was a gatekeeper
who had served there for forty years.
When announcing his presence,
he would gauge the worthiness of the Vice Censor-in-Chief
by the position of the staff he held.
If the official was worthy, he held the staff horizontally;
if unworthy, vertically.
All who served as Vice Censor-in-Chief

At the time, Fàn Fěng held the position.
One day, noticing the staff held vertically,

"Why is your staff suddenly vertical?
Is it due to some failing of mine?"
The gatekeeper replied:
"Yesterday, while hosting guests,
you repeatedly instructed the cook
four or five times on food preparation,
and admonished him just as often.
Generally, when directing subordinates,
one should assign tasks
and observe the outcome—
why such incessant nagging?
If you governed the realm this way,
would it not be exhausting?
I inwardly disapproved,
unaware the staff had turned vertical."
Fàn laughed heartily in chagrin. The next day, the staff was horizontal again.

The Imperial Censor and Deputy,

Initially,

Liáng Pí impeached Liú Fǎng, stating:

with generous emoluments already accumulated,
he should rightly guard against arrogance and remain humble,

Why then does he scheme for the profits of brewing,
compete for the smallest gains,
associate himself with drunkards,
and turn his household into a den of fugitives?
If he is not disciplined,

An imperial decree was issued not to punish him,

summoning the close ministers and attendants who were supposed to report to the Northern Army,

As a result, the sons and younger brothers of the imperial relatives were terrified,
and they all appeared before the emperor, kowtowing and pleading for mercy,
hoping to pay money to redeem their offenses.
The emperor granted their request,
ordering each to pay according to their rank,

Fàn did not dare to argue.

Lǐ Jìng served as the prefect of Qízhōu,
when someone privately accused him of plotting rebellion.
Emperor Gāozǔ ordered a censor to investigate the case,
instructing him:
"If Lǐ Jìng's rebellion proves true, you may deal with him accordingly."
The censor knew the accusation was false,
and after traveling several postal stations with the accuser,
he pretended to lose the accusation document.
Feigning panic, he flogged the accompanying clerk,
then pleaded with the accuser:
"Lǐ Jìng's rebellion is clearly evident,
and I personally received the imperial decree.
Now that I've lost the accusation document,
I beg you to save my life -
please draft another accusation." The accuser then composed a new document for the censor,
which upon examination differed from the original.
That very day the censor returned,
and reported this to Emperor Gāozǔ, who was greatly astonished.
The censor submitted a detailed memorial,
and Lǐ Jìng was not punished.
Alas, the censor's name was not recorded!

The emperor threw the draft on the ground,

The crown prince secretly ordered Xú Wénjǐng from the Eastern Palace to manufacture imperial chariots and ceremonial objects,
Wénjǐng's father Táo Rén, then serving as a palace advisor,
said to Wénjǐng:
"You will ultimately bring ruin upon our family,
I shall just sweep the graves
and await the mourning!
Thereupon he moved his household to avoid this,
Later when the crown prince died,

Táo Rén consequently did not mourn,

From History of the Southern Dynasties: Crown Prince Zhǎngmào,

The Attendant Secretaries,
for all memorials submitted by various offices,
after the Palace Attendants have reviewed and finalized them,
first read and endorse them,
to refute and correct errors or omissions.
For all imperial edicts to be promulgated,
in major matters, they extol the imperial virtue and grace,
praise and commend achievements,
then report back and request implementation;
in minor matters, they endorse and issue them directly.
For appointments of civil and military officials of the sixth rank and below,
when the responsible office submits recommendations,
they verify the depth of their experience,
assess their merits and performance rankings,
inquire into their moral conduct,
and evaluate their talents and skills;
if an official is unfit for the position,
or the appointment violates proper governance,
they report to the Palace Attendants for reconsideration.
For the copying and collation of books in the Hóngwénguǎn (Institute for the Advancement of Literature),
they also supervise and inspect the work.
For all unresolved injustices and grievances in the empire,
and cases of oppressive officials,
they must hear the appeals,
and jointly deliberate with the Censorate and the Secretarial Drafters on appropriate actions,
to redress and resolve them.
"The Six Canons"
They attend to the left and right sides of the sovereign,
divide and adjudicate matters of the department,
oversee the tasks of copying and collating in the Hóngwénguǎn,
and handle all memorials submitted by various offices.
Once the Shìzhōng has reviewed them, they correct errors and rectify violations,
and for imperial edicts or decrees that are inappropriate,
they make revisions and return them with a memorial,
which is called "returning with revisions."
At the end of the season,
they submit a record of the corrected and rectified items.
"Treatise on the Hundred Officials."
Zhāng Xíngchéng was promoted to the position of Chief of the Office of Scrutiny.
Emperor Tàizōng once addressed his court officials from the throne, saying:
"The reason I cannot indulge my personal desires,
seek pleasure in the present moment,
but instead discipline myself and endure hardships,
living in humble palaces and eating simple food,
is precisely for the sake of the common people.
As the ruler of men,
I simultaneously perform the duties of both general and minister—
does this not deprive you all of your reputations?
In the past, when Hàn Gāozǔ obtained the services of Xiāo Hé, Cáo Shēn, Hán Xìn, and Péng Yuè,
the empire was peaceful and tranquil;
when Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, and Wǔ had Jì, Qì, Yī Yǐn, and Lǚ Shàng,
the four seas were secure and orderly.
I have combined all these achievements myself.
Xíngchéng retired and submitted a memorial admonishing:
"Your Majesty's sage virtue shines brightly,
your vision is vast and far-reaching.
Although your civil and military achievements
indeed combine those of both general and minister,
why must you face the court and the multitude,
comparing and contending,
using your supreme position as the Son of Heaven,
to compete for merit with your subjects?
Emperor Tàizōng deeply accepted his advice.
(Old Book of Táng)

Lǐ Qiáo,
during Gāozōng's reign was promoted to the position of Jǐshìzhōng,
at that time the cruel official Lái Jùnchén fabricated charges against three families—Dí Rénjié, Lǐ Sìgòng, and Péi Xuānlǐ—
and submitted a request to execute them.
Empress Zé ordered Qiáo, along with the Dàlǐ Shǎoqīng Zhāng Déyù and Shì Yùshǐ Liú Xiàn, to review the case.
Although Déyù and others knew the accused were wronged,
they feared punishment,
and all complied with Jùnchén's proposal.
Qiáo said:
"How can we know they are wrongfully accused and not speak up for them?"
He then joined Déyù and others in presenting the evidence of their wrongful conviction,
thereby offending the imperial will.
He was demoted to the post of Rùnzhōu Cìshǐ,
but later was summoned back to the capital and transferred to the position of Fènggé Shèrén.
Empress Zé treated him with great respect,
and whenever the court had important writings,
she specifically ordered Qiáo to compose them.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Lú Càn
was from Fànyáng in Yōuzhōu.
In the second year of the Jǐnglóng era, he was promoted to the position of Jǐshìzhōng.
At that time, when Crown Prince Jíe Mǐn was first established, Empress Wěi,
because he was not her own son,
was deeply jealous of him,
and persuaded Emperor Zhōngzōng to issue an edict,
ordering the Crown Prince to instead take the tax revenues from the princely establishment,
to supply his annual expenses.
Lú Càn submitted a rebuttal, stating:
"The Crown Prince holds the important position of successor to the throne,
and should maintain the dignity of the heir apparent.
His annual expenses should naturally be supplied by the various government offices.
Moreover, according to the 'Zhōu Guān',
for all expenditures on goods and utensils,
accounts are settled at the end of the year,
but for items used by the King and the Crown Prince,
no accounts are settled.
This shows that the expenses of the heir apparent
are all the same as those of the King.
Now to equate him with the feudal lords and have him receive tax revenues,
how can this be called following the precedents of the past,
and establishing a model for the future!
If it is argued that the Eastern Palace has just been established,
and expenses are needed,
these should naturally be drawn broadly from the treasury,
and not permanently rely on the princely revenues."
An edict followed his advice,
and the Emperor
Lú Càn was promoted to the position of Jǐshìzhōng.
At that time, Ānlè Gōngzhǔ's husband Wǔ Chóngxùn had been killed by Jiémǐn Tàizǐ,
and he was specially posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Lǔ,
with Sīnóng Shǎoqīng Zhào Lǚwēn appointed to oversee the funeral arrangements.
Lǐ Wěn persuaded the princess to petition the emperor, requesting that, following the precedent of Yǒngtài Gōngzhǔ,
a líng (imperial mausoleum) be built for Chóngxùn.
An edict was issued granting her request.
Lú Càn submitted a rebuttal, stating:
"I have investigated the term 'líng,'
which originally belongs to emperors, kings, and crown princes.
Since the founding of the imperial family,
the tombs of princes and princesses
have never been called 'líng.'
Only Yǒngtài Gōngzhǔ received special favor for her burial,
which was an exception to the norm,
and should not be used as a precedent.
I request that we follow the established practices for princes since the Zhēnguàn era,
which would already be sufficiently generous."
A handwritten edict replied:
"Ānlè Gōngzhǔ is no different from Yǒngtài.
The principle of treating them equally
should not be changed now.
The Prince of Lǔ shall therefore have a líng constructed for him;
do not persist in your objections."
Lú Càn submitted another memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the term 'líng'
is applied to the most exalted,
and not to princes and dukes below them.
Moreover, if we consider the degree of kinship,
the Prince of Lǔ was not closer than Yōng Wáng.
Shǒulǐ, Yōng Wáng's tomb,
is still not called a 'líng,'
so the Prince of Lǔ should not receive this title because of his marriage to the princess.
Furthermore, when a ruler undertakes any action,
it is recorded in the historical records;
one must either consult past regulations
or examine precedents from previous dynasties.
Your servant has thoroughly checked the records since the Zhēnguàn era,
and no consort's tomb has ever been called a 'líng.'
Moreover, in the rites governing the relationship between ruler and subject,
mourning obligations cease with collateral relatives,
for one should not only love one's own kin,
nor only care for one's own children.
Your Majesty, out of affection for your daughter,
extends favor to her husband;
the funeral ceremonies
are already sufficiently honorable and grand.
How can we allow no distinction between superior and inferior,
or equate the ruler with his subjects?"
The emperor ultimately followed Lú Càn's advice.
End.
Wáng Wéi,
courtesy name Mójié,
served as a Jǐshìzhōng at the end of the Tiānbǎo era.
When Ān Lùshān captured both capitals,
and Emperor Xuánzōng fled the capital,
Wáng Wéi failed to accompany the imperial entourage.
He was captured by the rebels.
Ān Lùshān held a banquet for his followers at the Níngbì Palace,
where the musicians were all Líyuán disciples.
The musicians from the Jiàofāng, upon hearing this, were deeply saddened.
Secretly, Wáng Wéi composed a poem:
"Ten thousand households grieve, wild smoke rises from the fields;
When will the officials again pay homage to the Son of Heaven?
Autumn locust blossoms fall in the deserted palace;
At the edge of the Níngbì Pond, pipes and strings are played."
After the rebellion was quelled,
officials who had served the rebels were sentenced according to three grades of punishment.
Wáng Wéi's poem became known,
and Emperor Sùzōng praised him for it,
granting him a special pardon.
The supervising secretary rectified edicts,

Lǐ Yì frequently rectified Yáo Chóng's proposals,

Yuán Gāo served as a supervisory official.
