If he is appointed to a major prefecture again,

The chancellor was displeased,
and ordered another official to draft it.
When the edict was issued,
Yuán Gāo withheld it and did not promulgate it,

Emperor Xiànzōng appointed Lǚ Yuányīng, the Prefect of Tóngzhōu, again as a Palace Censor.
Initially,
when Yuányīng was removed from the position of Palace Censor to Tóngzhōu,

Yuányīng's discourse was quite impassioned and incisive,

so he can provide consultation."
The emperor was pleased and concurred with this.

Guō Chénggǔ served as a Supervising Secretary.
In the first year of the Kāichéng era (836 CE),

The Left and Right Supplements,

Whenever decrees are issued or actions taken,
if they are inconvenient for the times,

The poem says:

This meaning is taken from this.

During the Chuígǒng period, an office was established,

The rest is as above.
Lǐ Yōng,
was known in Cháng'ān from a young age.

the Inner Secretary Lǐ Qiáo and the Investigating Censor Zhāng Tíngguī both recommended Yōng for his lofty literary talent and upright conduct,

After they left,

(Old Book of Táng)
Emperor Zhōngzōng ascended the throne,
and appointed the sorcerer Zhèng Pǔsī as the Director of the Palace Library.
Lǐ Yǒng submitted a memorial admonishing:
"If Your Majesty now believes that Pǔsī possesses extraordinary arts,
capable of achieving immortality,
then the way of longevity should have long been obtained by Shàng Jiūshì,
who would have eternally possessed the empire,
and it would not be Your Majesty
who could seek it today.
If it is believed that Pǔsī can procure the elixir of immortality,
then Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdì should have long obtained it,
eternally possessing the empire,
and it would not be Your Majesty
who could seek it today.
If it is believed that Pǔsī can attain the Buddhist Dharma,
then Hàn Míngdì and Liáng Wǔdì should have long obtained it,
eternally possessing the empire,
and it would not be Your Majesty
who could seek it today.
If it is believed that Pǔsī can master the ways of ghosts,
then Mò Dí and Gān Bǎo would have each presented it to the sovereign;
and if these two kings had obtained it,
they would have eternally possessed the empire,
and it would not be Your Majesty
who could seek it today.
These matters all involve falsehood and delusion,
proven ineffective through successive dynasties.
I, in my foolishness, do not wish Your Majesty to repeat such practices in this enlightened age."

Dòu Qún lived in seclusion in Pílíng,
renowned for his moral integrity,
and authored thirty-four volumes of writings,
titled "Annotations to the Notable Officials in the Records of the Grand Historian."
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Wéi Xiàqīng, the governor of Sūzhōu, recommended him for exceptional talent in the suburban sacrifice,

Yet now Your Majesty appoints this official who was so hard to advance for twenty years as a judge official for peace missions to the Tibetans,
how easily is this done?"
Emperor Dézōng was struck by his words,
and retained him to continue serving as Censor.

Wáng Yuánzhōng,
courtesy name Zhèngméng,

Wáng Zhífāng,
during the Kāichéng era, served as Right Rectifier of Omissions.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"When Your Majesty first ascended the throne,
you ordered the Palace Entertainment Bureau and Music Bureau
to reduce their personnel entirely.
I have heard that recently this has not been strictly followed,
with musicians and their disciples receiving excessively generous rewards.
Whenever such matters occur and spread beyond the palace,
they damage Your Majesty's sagely virtue.
How can this be taken lightly?
I believe that seductive music entertains people,
its melodies are pleasing to the ear,
capable of confusing human emotions and disturbing one's nature,
causing abandonment of all duties for insufficient musical pleasure.
I humbly note that the imperial health is not yet fully recovered,
yet added to this are amusements of music and beauty,
which erode the imperial blessings.
Should this not cause concern?"
The emperor reviewed the memorial,
praised it with admiration,
bestowed one hundred bolts of silk,
and presented the memorial to his chief ministers,
ordering it to be recorded by the historiography officials.
(Cèfǔ Yuánguī)
Bái Jūyì submitted a memorial stating:
"I have been graciously appointed as Left Omissioner,
while retaining my previous position as Hanlin Academician. According to the Six Codes:
the selection criteria are extremely strict,
yet the official rank is very low.
There are reasons for this arrangement.
Generally speaking, when people hold high positions they become protective of them,
and when they enjoy noble status they become attached to it.
Protecting their positions leads them to conform silently without speaking out,
while attachment to status makes them tolerate faults without remonstrating.
This is an inevitable principle.
Therefore, the establishment of the Omissioner position
with low rank
ensures the position isn't worth protecting
and the status isn't worth clinging to.
The strict selection criteria
ensure the appointee cannot bear to betray their conscience below
nor fail the emperor's grace above.
When the position isn't worth protecting
and the grace cannot be betrayed,
then all shortcomings will be corrected,
all violations will be remonstrated,
no court affairs will escape scrutiny,
and no state benefits or harms will go unmentioned.
This was the fundamental intention behind establishing the Omissioner position in our dynasty."
Yuán Zhěn was the Eastern Censorate censor,
summoned back to the capital,
lodging at the Fūshuǐ Station.
The eunuch Liú Shìyuán arrived later,
disputing over the hall.
Shìyuán became enraged,
pushed open his door,
Zhěn fled in socks to the back of the hall.
Shìyuán pursued him,
striking Zhěn's face with a whip, injuring him.
The chief minister considered Zhěn a young junior,
bent on wielding authority,
and demoted him to the position of Military Adviser in Jiānglíng Prefecture.
Bái Jūyì, as Reminder,
submitted a memorial stating:
"I have heard that Shìyuán kicked open the station gate,
seized the general's saddle horse,
then demanded bows and arrows,

From the past until now,
such an event has never occurred.
Now the eunuch has committed a crime,
yet no punishment has been heard of,
while the censor is without fault,
but is demoted first.
When near and far hear of this,
it truly damages the imperial virtue.
I fear that from now on,
when eunuchs are sent on missions,

Bái Jūyì wrote to Yuán Zhěn saying:

one should not take too much of it.'
What kind of person am I?
I have already secretly taken much of the fame of the times,
since I have secretly taken the fame of the times,
and yet wish to secretly take the wealth and status of the times,
would the Creator be willing to grant me both?
Moreover, poets often have unfortunate fates,
like Chén Zǐ'áng and Dù Fǔ, each appointed as an advisor,

Chén Zǐ'áng was transferred to the position of Right Advisor,

At that time, there was a man from Xiàguī in Tóngzhōu named Xú Yuánqìng,

Later, when Shīyùn became a censor,

Those discussing the case considered Yuánqìng filial and resolute,

Zǐ'áng proposed that according to national law, one who kills arbitrarily
should be executed to uphold national law,

In the third year of the Tiānshòu era,
regardless of their virtue or incompetence, all candidates
were promoted and appointed.
The most outstanding were tested for positions like Vice Minister of the Phoenix Pavilion and Imperial Advisor,
while the lesser ones were tested for posts such as Vice Director, Palace Censor, Reminder, Omission Commissioner, or Editorial Director.

"Reminders fill carts in a row,

Palace Censors are like rake handles,

The Grand Master of Remonstrance is responsible for attending and assisting the sovereign,
offering admonitions and indirect exhortations.
There are five types of remonstrance: first is indirect remonstrance,
second is compliant remonstrance,
third is admonitory remonstrance,
fourth is persuasive remonstrance,
fifth is direct remonstrance.

"Jiāyǔ"
What is remonstrance? Remonstrance is
intervening,
relying on,
changing.
Right and wrong intervene,
reforming and changing one's conduct.
Humans possess the five constant virtues,
hence there are five types of remonstrance:
namely indirect remonstrance, compliant remonstrance, observing remonstrance, direct remonstrance, and bold remonstrance.
Indirect remonstrance
pertains to wisdom;
when the sprouts of calamity run deep,
observing matters before they manifest and indirectly warning—
this is the nature of wisdom.
Compliant remonstrance
pertains to benevolence;
using humble and compliant language,
not opposing the ruler's heart—
this is the nature of benevolence.
Observing remonstrance
pertains to propriety;
seeing the ruler's displeased countenance,
one temporarily withdraws with joy,
then advances again according to propriety in advancing and retreating—
this is the nature of propriety.
Direct remonstrance
pertains to trustworthiness;
pointing directly to the substance and verifying the matter—
this is the nature of trustworthiness.
Bold remonstrance
pertains to righteousness;
compassion arises from within,
directly speaking of the state's harms,
strengthening resolve and forgetting life,
not avoiding personal loss for the ruler—this is the nature of righteousness.

During the reign of Emperor Xuān,
when selecting erudites
and grand masters of remonstrance who were versed in government affairs to fill the posts of governors and chancellors of commanaderies and kingdoms,
Xiāo Wàngzhī was appointed as the governor of Píngyuán.
Wàngzhī's true intentions lay in serving at the imperial court,
and being sent far away to govern a commandery,
he felt inwardly dissatisfied.
Thus, he submitted a memorial stating:
"Your Majesty pities the common people,
fearing that virtuous influence may not be fully realized,
and has dispatched all remonstrating officials to fill local posts—
this is what is called worrying about the branches while forgetting the root.
If the court lacks ministers who dare to dispute,
then faults will go unrecognized;
if the state lacks wise scholars,
then good counsel will not be heard.
I hope Your Majesty will select those well-versed in the classics,
who review the past to understand the new,
and who comprehend subtle strategies and deliberations to serve as inner court officials,
participating in government affairs.
When the feudal lords hear of this,
they will know that the state accepts remonstrance and cares about governance,
leaving no omissions or oversights.
If such efforts are unceasing,
the way of King Chéng and King Kāng will be nearly achieved!
As for the outer commanderies being unruly—
is that truly worth worrying about?
(From the *Qián Hàn*)

Zhāng Pǔhuì,
courtesy name Hóngzhèn,
was eight chǐ tall,
with a majestic appearance,
excelling in the Three Ritual Classics,
and also well-versed in the theories of the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Hundred Schools of Thought.
Rénchéng Wáng Chéng valued his scholarship,
enhanced his reputation,

Chéng said to Pǔhuì:

When the Empress Dowager Líng's father, Minister of Education Hú Guózhēn, passed away,
he was posthumously honored as Chancellor and Supreme Tàigōng.
Pǔhuì, believing that in previous eras, the fathers of empresses had not held the title 'Supreme,' went to the palace gate,
submitting a memorial stating why this was inappropriate.
The Empress Dowager read the memorial and personally went to Guózhēn's residence,
gathering officials of the fifth rank and above to extensively discuss the matter,
sending an envoy to summon Pǔhuì,
to engage in dialogue with him.
She also ordered Attendant-in-ordinary Yuán,
and Palace Attendant-in-ordinary Jiǎ Càn to oversee and observe the merits and faults,
the Empress Dowager again dispatched Yuán Yì and Jiǎ Càn to announce the decree,
saying to Pǔhuì:
"We previously summoned you to debate with the ministers,
and after the back-and-forth concluded,
all disagreed with you.
The memorial represents Our intention to fulfill filial piety,
while your statements,
embody the way of a loyal minister.
The assembled lords have already reached a decision,
you must not stubbornly oppose Our will,
if you have further insights in the future,
do not hesitate to speak.
Pǔhuì then bowed to the decree and took his leave.
Earlier,
when Pǔhuì was summoned to receive the edict,
he rode a swift Huáliú horse with great haste,
stood waiting and was urged to depart,

Pǔhuì said to them:
"I serve in an enlightened era,
holding the office of Remonstrance Counselor.
If I do not speak what is difficult to speak,
or remonstrate what is difficult to remonstrate,
then I am merely an obsequious official neglecting my duties,
drawing a salary without merit. A person must die; if one dies in the right place,
what regret is there?
Moreover, the court is well-governed; you need not worry.
After the debate concluded,
he was consoled by the imperial decree and returned home,
relatives and friends congratulated him on his fortunate outcome.
At that time, Dù Bì of Zhōngshān sent a letter to Pǔhuì, saying:
"Illustrious Lord, profound scholar and great learned one,

uphold this public integrity,

Pǔhuì admired this letter,

In the second year of the Chuígōng era under Empress Wǔ,
a man named Yú Bǎozōng submitted a memorial requesting the installation of boxes to receive petitions from all directions.
Thus, four copper boxes were cast,
combined into one unit,
and placed in the court hall.
The eastern side, representing spring with its green color,
was for those who could report on nurturing the people
and encouraging agriculture; petitions could be deposited in the green box,
inscribed with the words
"Yán'ēn" (Extending Grace).
The southern side, representing summer with its red color,
was for those who could offer upright remonstrance on the merits and faults of current governance;
petitions could be deposited in the red box,
inscribed with the words
"Zhāojiàn" (Soliciting Admonition).
The western side, representing autumn with its white color,
was for those who could present their own grievances and injustices;
petitions could be deposited in the white box,
inscribed with the words
"Shēnyōu" (Expressing Grievances).
The northern side, representing water with its black color,
was for those with strategies and wisdom; petitions could be deposited in the black box,
inscribed with the words
"Tōngxuán" (Penetrating Mysteries).
Officials such as the Remonstrance Grand Master and Supplements and Omissions were appointed as envoys,
to manage the box affairs,
with all deposited petitions submitted by evening each day.

Yáng Chéng spoke in defense of the imperial censor Péi Yánlíng,
resulting in Lù Zhì and others being demoted or dismissed.
Emperor Dézōng was enraged,
unable to comprehend why no one at court intervened,
Yáng Chéng, upon hearing this, rose
and declared:
"As an admonishing official, I cannot allow the Son of Heaven to execute innocent people
while placing trust in treacherous ministers."
He immediately led several officials, including the remonstrance official Wáng Zhòngshū, to guard the Yányīng Gate,
submitting a memorial denouncing Péi Yánlíng's deceit and flattery,
and affirming Lù Zhì and others' innocence.
Emperor Dézōng was furious,
summoned the chancellor,
and spoke of punishing Yáng Chéng and his companions,
though after a long while, he relented.
The chancellor then discussed sending them away,
whereupon the imperial guard general Zhāng Wànfú heard that the admonishing officials were kneeling at the gate to remonstrate,
hurried to the Yányīng Gate,
and loudly congratulated them, saying:
"With upright officials in the court,
the empire is sure to be at peace."
He then bowed respectfully to Yáng Chéng, Wáng Zhòngshū, and the others, saying:
"If all admonishing officials can remonstrate like this,
how could the empire not be at peace?"
Soon after,
he repeatedly shouted, "Long live peace!"
Zhāng Wànfú was a military man,
over eighty years old at the time,
and from then on, his reputation spread throughout the land.
Lǐ Jiàng saw the Yùtáng Hall.
Emperor Xiànzōng said:
"Recently, the censors have been forming cliques,
and their reports are not truthful.
They all fall into slander.
I wish to dismiss those who are particularly guilty.
What do you think?"
Jiàng replied:
"This is not Your Majesty's intention.
Surely, deceitful people have misguided your heart.
Since ancient times, accepting remonstrance brings prosperity,
while rejecting it brings ruin.
It is not easy for ministers to offer words of advice
to the sovereign, is it?
The ruler is as exalted as the heavens,
while ministers are as lowly as the earth.
Besides, there is the threat of imperial authority.
They ponder day and night,
intending to present ten matters.
Before long, they discard five or six.
When they are about to be heard, they shrink back
and reduce them by half.
Therefore, only a few suggestions reach the ruler, diminishing any unforeseen disaster.
They do so without any personal gain!
Even with encouragement for openness,
I still fear it might not reach your ears.
Yet now you intend to rebuke them,
causing the upright officials to remain silent.
This is not beneficial for the state."
The emperor said:
"If it were not for your words,
I would not understand the benefit of remonstrance."
The ruler acknowledged.
Zhèng Tán, by virtue of his father's official rank, was appointed to the post of Reminding Official.
When Emperor Mùzōng ascended the throne,
he neglected state affairs,
Zhèng Tán and Cuī Yǎn and others addressed the emperor in court, saying:
"Your Majesty has just ascended the throne,
you should devote yourself to diligent governance,
yet within the palace you indulge in feasting and amusement,
and outside you are addicted to hunting excursions.
Now the Tǔbō are at the border,
watching our central state,
should an emergency arise,
your subjects would not know Your Majesty's whereabouts,
wouldn't that lead to failure?
The gold and silk that are expended
are indeed the people's hard-earned wealth,
how can they be lavishly bestowed upon performers who have no merit?
We hope you will practice frugality in expenditures,
and not let the officials heavily tax the common people again."
The emperor was displeased,
and turning to the chancellor Xiāo Miǎn, said:
"Who are these people?"
Xiāo Miǎn replied:
"They are remonstrance officials."
The emperor's anger subsided,
and then said:
"When I have faults,
my subordinates can fully admonish me,
this is loyalty."
Thereupon he issued an edict to Zhèng Tán, saying:
"Your words were rather blunt,
in the future when there are those who speak for me,
I will receive you at the Yányīng Hall."
At that time, memorials from the remonstrance officials had long been neglected,

the officials congratulated each other.
Empress Xiànzōng, of the Guō clan.
Emperor Wǔzōng delighted in hunting and excursions,

"Regarding the memorials of the remonstrating ministers,
it is appropriate to carefully review them and, where applicable, implement them.
If something is not applicable,
consult with the Chancellor,
and do not reject honest words,
nor accept biased words.
Make the loyal and virtuous your confidants.

The Emperor bowed twice,

The various princes will likely be trampled by the empress,
I foresee turmoil arising soon.
Táng Shū
Gūxǐan Bianzhōng Sòng Yǎn served as the Grand Changcheng.
One morning, while waiting for dawn at the Guangzhai Buddhist Temple,
he heard the sound of wind chimes from the pagoda,
and listened intently for a long time.
After the court session,
he returned to the temple quarters.
He asked the head monk:
"Venerable, the pagoda bells—
do you know their origins?"
The monk replied:
"I do not know."
Yǎn said:
"Among them is one of ancient make.
I request to ascend the pagoda,
follow the metal chains,
and try striking each to identify it,
may I?"
The monk initially refused,
but later consented.
So he struck and identified it.
The temple residents
then mentioned it often swayed without wind,
producing resonant sounds—
was it not this one?
Yǎn said:
"That's it.
It must respond
when temple bells are struck during sacrifices."
He insisted on taking it down to examine,
saying:
"This is a Gūxǐan bianzhōng.
I ask to temporarily place it alone in the monastery courtyard."
Returning,
he had court musicians and the monk assemble together.
At the appointed time,
when the temple bells were struck,
this indeed resonated,
so they purchased and obtained it.
Another time, seeing off a guest at Tonghua Gate,
he encountered the Financial Commissioner's transport convoy.
Halting his horse briefly,
he suddenly hastily bid farewell to the guest
and followed the convoy,
identifying one bell
as also a bianzhōng.
Others only noticed its exceptional craftsmanship,
unequaled by ordinary bells,
unaware of its other qualities.
When mounted for performance,
its tone and form matched the scale perfectly.
How remarkable—
this
also demonstrates recognition of subtleties in metal instruments.

Emperor Tàizōng once perused the "Three-Board Elephant Classic" authored by Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu,
but could not grasp its meaning.
Cài Yǔngōng, the Crown Prince's Assistant, had played this game in his youth,
so Emperor Tàizōng summoned and questioned him,
yet he too had forgotten and was unable to explain it.
Thereupon, Lǚ Cái was summoned for inquiry.
After studying it for one night,
Lǚ Cái was able to create diagrams and explanations,
which Yǔngōng reviewed.
Suddenly, he recalled the old method,
which exactly matched Cái's interpretation.
Thus, Lǚ Cái became renowned.
He was successively promoted to Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Previously, Wēn Yànbó had memorialized that Cái was intelligent,
capable in many areas unseen by the eye,
and unheard by the ear;
upon a single hearing or sight,
he could comprehend their subtleties,
especially excelling in music.
He requested that Cái be tested.
Emperor Tàizōng then recruited Cái,
appointing him to serve directly in the Hóngwén Hall.

Lǚ Cái served as the Grand Chang's erudite.
The emperor was troubled
that the books transmitted by the Yin-Yang masters contained many fallacies, falsehoods, and shallow, inferior content,
and the world increasingly became constrained and fearful.
He ordered Lǚ Cái, along with experienced scholars and senior teachers, to delete the redundant and erroneous,
selecting the usable parts to form fifty-three chapters,
combining them with the old forty-seven chapters,
making one hundred chapters in total,
and issued an edict to promulgate them throughout the land.
Lǚ Cái, in upholding his arguments, was Confucian yet not vulgar,
using classical principles to deduce and assess their prognosticative techniques,
which led various schools to jointly condemn and disparage him.
Moreover, the whole world deluded each other with notions of calamity and fortune,
yet in the end, none came to realize it.
Lǚ Cái's words were not very literary,
but aimed to rescue the errors of common customs,
addressing timely affairs,
making them easy to understand.

a younger brother.

brothers do not succeed one another.
Therefore, Yīn Pángēng did not follow Yáng Jiǎ,
but succeeded the previous ruler;
Hàn Guāngwǔ did not succeed Xiàochéng,
but followed Yuán Dì;

thus two temples would be abolished.

serve seven temples starting from the father's temple upward,

If brothers were accommodated,
then the ancestral temples above would be abolished,
and the Son of Heaven could not fully serve seven generations.

and during the great combined sacrifice, join in the feast with Tàizǔ.

the sacrificial order would be permanently maintained.

so Zhōngzōng was enshrined in a separate temple,

Wáng Yànwēi,

came from a family of Confucian scholars.

becoming particularly well-versed in the Three Ritual Classics,

Cuī Guīcóng,
style name Xuángào,
was appointed Grand Chief Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices in the second year of the Tàihé era.
Guīcóng excelled in ritual studies,
mastered the historical evolution of rites,
and could answer any inquiry.
During ancestral temple sacrifices in the Jìngzōng shrine,
prayer tablets referred to the emperor as "filial and fraternal."
Guīcóng argued:
"I have examined the term 'filial,'
consulted ritual texts,
and found its meaning pertains to descendants,
not properly applicable to brothers.
According to the Records of Divination for Yu Sacrifices in the Rites,
descendants use 'grieving,'
brothers use 'prayerful,'
for ancestors it is fitting to use 'reverent,'
for brothers only their names should be used.
Moreover, when Wēn Qiáo of the Eastern Jìn debated ancestral temple prayers,
he opposed using 'filial' for non-descendants,
stating collateral relatives should use 'dare to announce.'
The court then agreed
it was appropriate. Now I verify from classical rites
no brother is called 'filial';
consulting Jìn history
confirms avoiding the term for collateral relatives.
I propose for Jìngzōng's shrine sacrifices,
the words 'filial and fraternal' be removed."
Regarding the Nine Palaces Altar sacrifices,
traditionally a major rite,
Guīcóng argued:
"The Nine Palaces Deities
lack classical documentation.
Examining their charts,
they are merely constellations.
Currently,
the five planets are secondary sacrifices,
sun and moon rites are medium-level,
how can the Nine Palaces alone exceed standard rites?
I request their downgrade to medium sacrifice."
This was approved.
Guīcóng also addressed delayed court mourning
for deceased high officials,
submitting:
"Suspending court expresses grief,
a significant duty.
Lately,
mourning pauses miss the report time,
delaying ceremonies days later.
In the Zhēnguàn era,
when Rén Guī died,
officials reported during morning assembly,
Tàizōng condemned the breach;
after Cén Wénběn's death,
night patrols were canceled that evening;
when Zhāng Gōngjǐn passed,
mourning proceeded despite the day's taboo.
This shows condolence
should not be delayed.
Even with urgent state affairs,
ministers can be summoned to side halls,
avoiding main court sessions
without compromising protocol."
This was approved.

The Commandant of Justice,
an ancient official,
was to reassure the people's hearts.
All officials in charge of banditry and surveillance were called Commandants.
Commandant
means "to net,"
referring to using military and judicial means to ensnare the wicked and unlawful,
similar to how the Inspector probed and reported illegal activities.
《Wěi Zhāo's Discernment and Explanation of Terms》: The sovereign
appoints a Commandant of Justice
to adjudicate doubtful penalties,
ensuring the fairness of the office
and the trust of the subordinates.
The Commandant
reassures the people's hearts,
comforting them with reality.
The character for "Commandant" (尉) is composed of "士" (scholar/official),
with a drooping stroke above and a bent stroke below,
symbolizing the court displaying a corpse.
The "寸" (inch) component signifies
the measurement and division of legal standards,
indicating that the corpse is examined down to the inch in the court,
thus the law has its divisions,
hence the character "尉" shows the corpse and the inch.
Sòng Jūn's annotation states:
"士 (shì)
means 'affair,'
and the drooping stroke represents connection.
The corpse
signifies death,
implying that the dead cannot be without someone to bear them,
showing the world that death is inevitable.

Duke Wén of Jìn appointed Lǐ Lí as the chief judge.
He mistakenly sentenced someone to death,
confined himself at court,
and requested execution from the ruler.
The ruler said:
"Officials have high and low ranks,
punishments have light and heavy degrees.
If a subordinate official committed the crime,
it is not the fault of the chief judge."
Lǐ Lí replied:
"I hold the highest position among officials,
yet I do not yield my position to subordinates;
I receive the most generous emoluments,
yet I do not share the benefits with subordinates.
Now I have mistakenly sentenced someone to death,
and would let a subordinate bear the death penalty—
this is something unheard of.
If I do not accept Your Majesty's order,
and must consider myself guilty,
then I too am guilty."
Lǐ Lí said:
"Where law fails, punishment follows;
where punishment fails, death follows.
Your Majesty considered me capable of discerning subtleties and deciding doubtful cases,
therefore appointed me as judge.
Now I have erred in judgment,
causing the death of an innocent person—
this crime deserves death."
The ruler said:
"To abandon one's position and resign from office,
to submit to law and bring ruin to the state—
this is not what I hope for.
Quickly leave and have no worries—
this is my wish."
Lǐ Lí replied:
"When governance is disordered and the state endangered,
that is the ruler's worry;
when the army is defeated and soldiers in chaos,
that is the general's worry.
To be incompetent in serving the ruler and corrupt in governing the people,
is to enjoy emoluments without merit.
I cannot deceive myself with falsehood."
Thereupon he fell on his sword and died.
The gentleman heard of this and said:
"How loyal he was!"

An upright official upholds the law,
flexible yet unyielding,
firm yet unbreakable.
To abandon the law, defy orders, and release a lawbreaker
is to administer justice improperly,
harboring a biased heart.
How could this be my intention to seek personal gain?

I hold a high position to set an example for the officials and people.

and I cannot exempt myself from the law,

evident throughout the state.

and said:

"Wénzǐ's clansman
broke the state's laws;
the Chief Justice freed him,
but Wénzǐ refused.
He heeded the sprouts of discontent,
upright and fair.

Jì Gāo served as the chief judicial officer of Wèi,
and had a man's feet amputated.
Soon after,
when Wèi was thrown into turmoil by Kuǎikuì's rebellion,
Jì Gāo fled,
running to the outer city gate,
where the amputee was guarding the gate.
He said to Jì Gāo:
"There is a hole over there.
Jì Gāo replied:
"A gentleman does not climb over.
The man said again:
"There is a hole over there.
Jì Gāo said:
"A gentleman does not crawl through.
The man then said:
"There is a room here.
Jì Gāo then entered it.
After the pursuers gave up,
Jì Gāo was about to leave,
and said to the amputee:
"I could not undermine my lord's laws and thus personally had your feet amputated.
Now that I am in trouble,
this would be the perfect time for you to take revenge,
yet you helped me escape three times.
Why is this?
The amputee replied:
"Having my feet cut off was indeed my own crime,
there was nothing to be done about it.
Previously, when you judged me according to the laws and decrees,
you considered others before me,
wishing that I might be exempt.
I knew this when the verdict was decided and my crime determined.
When it came time to pronounce the punishment,
you looked sorrowful and unhappy.
Seeing the expression on your face,
I understood again
that you were not showing me private favor.
Heaven produced a gentleman like you,
whose way is inherently thus.
This is why I helped you escape.
When Confucius heard of this, he said:
"How excellent is he as an official!
His application of the law is consistent.
Thinking with benevolence and forgiveness builds virtue,
while adding severity and cruelty builds resentment.
To act with impartiality—
is this not Jì Gāo?

Zhāng Shìzhī served as the Commandant of Justice.
Emperor Wén once traveled,
when someone emerged from beneath the Wèi Bridge,
startling the imperial carriage's horses, and the arresting officers
brought the case to Commandant Shìzhī.
He reported the offense of violating the imperial procession,
recommending a fine as punishment.

but Shìzhī said:

is what is shared publicly with all under heaven.

if Your Majesty had executed him, it would have ended there.

the Commandant of Justice

The edict then spared the Attendant at the Yellow Gate and released Zhèng.

summoning Wényuǎn to expound on Spring and Autumn Annals topics.
Though numerous Confucians raised challenging questions like swarming bees,
he responded adaptively to each,
and none could corner him.
From Old Book of Tang
Lù Yóumíng served as a Grand Academy erudite,
and later Emperor Gāozǔ personally attended the sacrifice to Confucius.
At that time, Xú Wényuǎn lectured on the "Classic of Filial Piety,"
the Buddhist monk Huìchéng lectured on the "Prajñā Sūtra,"
and the Daoist priest Liú Jìnxǐ lectured on the "Laozi."
Démíng challenged these three individuals,
each according to their own school's tenets,
and established arguments point by point.
The audience was all subdued by him,
and Emperor Gāozǔ praised him.
In the early Zhēnguàn era, he was appointed as a National University erudite.
End
Gǔ Nàlǜ,
during the Zhēnguàn era, was promoted to Erudite of the National University,
being profoundly knowledgeable in numerous texts,
Chǔ Suìliáng once praised him as the "Repository of the Nine Classics."
"New Book of Tang"
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era,
the title of Guózǐ Bóshì was changed to Sīchéng Xuānyè.
"Tōngdiǎn"
Hé Tóngzhī,
courtesy name Shìwēi,
served in the Qí dynasty,
initially holding the position of Assistant Instructor at the Imperial Academy.
When lecturing to the princes on mourning attire,
he would tie grass to form a mourning girdle,
and fold a hand towel to make a mourning cap.
For students who did not understand,
he would patiently guide and instruct them.
The capital praised him as a genuine Confucian scholar.
(From History of the Southern Dynasties)
Shěn Jùn,
courtesy name Shìsōng,
was diligent in his studies,
conducting self-study day and night.
When sleepy, he would tie himself with a stick to stay awake,
thus becoming well-versed in the Five Classics,
especially excelling in the Three Rituals.
While serving as assistant instructor at the Imperial Academy,
Lìbùláng Lù Chuí wrote a letter to Púyè Xú Miǎn recommending Jùn.
It said:
"All books expounded by sages and worthies
must derive their meaning from the Rites of Zhou,
thus the Rites of Zhou
is truly the foundational source of all classics.
Assistant instructor Shěn Jùn particularly excels in this book.
Recently when giving lectures, numerous Confucian scholars including Liú Yán, Shěn Hóng and Shěn Xióng
all held their classics and took lower seats,
facing north to receive instruction.
None failed to sigh in admiration,
and no one voiced any criticism.
I suggest we should immediately employ this man
to specialize in this field of study,
cycling through repeatedly,
so that the orthodox canon of the sages
may be revived after being neglected."
Miǎn followed this advice.
He memorialized to have Jùn appointed as Erudite of the Five Classics,
who lectured at the academy
to audiences often numbering in the hundreds.

Zhāng Jī,
courtesy name Zhíyán,
studied under Rǔnán's Zhōu Hóngzhèng.
Whenever he had novel insights,
he was esteemed by his seniors.
During the Tiānjiā era of the Chén dynasty,
he served as an assistant instructor at the National Academy.
At that time, Zhōu Hóngzhèng was also at the National Academy.
When Hóngzhèng posed questions on the "Zhōu Yì",
his fourth younger brother Hóngzhí was also present at the lecture.
As Jī debated with Hóngzhèng,
Hóngzhèng was cornered in the argument,
whereupon Hóngzhí sat upright and raised his voice sharply,
attempting to assist his brother in defending his position.
Jī then sternly addressed Hóngzhí:
"Today's scholarly gathering
is for debating principles and logic.
Though I understand brothers stand by each other in crisis,
you, Fourth Gentleman, should not offer assistance."
Hóngzhí responded:
"I am aiding my mentor;
why should it be impermissible?"
The entire assembly found this exchange amusing.
Hóngzhèng once remarked to others:
"Whenever I take the lectern
and see Zhāng Jī in attendance,
it makes me apprehensive."
Liú Lán studied the Zuǒshì,
reading it once every five days,
and was well-versed in all Five Classics,
also understanding yīn-yáng principles,
knowledgeable about various subjects,
thus revered by Confucian scholars,
with several thousand students over time,
many of whom achieved mastery.
However, he criticized the Gōngyáng Commentary,
and disapproved of Dǒng Zhòngshū,
for which he was ridiculed by contemporaries,
later becoming an assistant instructor at the Imperial Academy.
Once while sitting quietly reading,
someone knocked at the door,
Liú Lán had them brought in,
wearing a simple hemp cloth and single-layer garment,
the visitor sat with Liú Lán,
and said to him:
"You are naturally a learned scholar,
why do you repeatedly face slander and humiliation?
The strengths and weaknesses of philosophical principles,
ultimately lie with whom?
Yet you excessively show disrespect and oppress others!
Now I have come to summon you,
to settle this matter with you properly.
After speaking, the visitor departed,
and Liú Lán died of illness shortly after.
From Běishǐ
Quán Huì was originally a poor scholar,
without servants.
When he first took up the position of assistant instructor,
he often rode a donkey to and from his duties.
His tasks were numerous,
and he would not return until late.
Once, he went out through the eastern city gate at night,
when the night was already deep.
Huì was alone riding a donkey
when he suddenly saw two figures:
one pulling the donkey's head,
the other following behind,
seeming to assist each other.
Their movements were light and drifting,
unlike living people.
Gradually, they lost their way,
deviating from the original path.
Huì felt very strange about this,
so he recited the first volume of the *Book of Changes*.
Before he could finish it,
the two figures suddenly scattered.
Huì, unaware, fell off the donkey,
and thus became dazed and confused.
It was not until dawn that he regained consciousness,
realizing where he had fallen—
it was outside the city walls,
only a few miles from home.
Lù Yóumíng,
during the Dayè era extensively summoned scholars well-versed in classics,
and many came from all directions.
He sent Dé Míng and Lǔ Kǒng Bāo together to the Chancellery,
where they engaged in mutual debate,
with no one surpassing them,
and appointed them as National University Assistants.
From the *Old Book of Tang*
Gài Wéndá,
was a native of Xìndū in Jìzhōu.
He was widely learned in the classics and histories,
and had the demeanor of a scholar-gentleman.
Provincial Inspector Dòu Kàng once gathered many Confucian scholars,
ordering them to debate each other,
with great Confucians Liú Zhuō, Liú Guǐsī, and Kǒng Yǐngdá all present,
and Wéndá also participated.
After the debate,
his arguments surpassed all the scholars' expectations,
greatly astonishing Kàng,
who asked:
"With whom did you study, young Gài?"
Liú Zhuō replied:
"This youth is exceptionally bright,
gifted by nature,
yet he consults the less learned with his abundant knowledge,
so I am considered his leading teacher."
Kàng said:
"It can be said that ice is born of water,
yet is colder than water."
During the Wǔdé era,
he was appointed as a National University assistant instructor.
His clansman Gài Wényì was also renowned at that time for his Confucian scholarship,
and they were called "the Two Gàis."
Wényì,
a native of Sòngchéng in Bèizhōu,
served as a National University assistant instructor in the early Wǔdé era.
When he once began lecturing on the "Máo Odes"
with all the high officials gathered,
engaging in mutual debate,
Wényì elucidated the "Airs" and "Odes"
with remarkable grasp of the poets' essence.
He died during the Zhēnguàn era while serving as a National University erudite.
Gāo Zǐgòng in his youth roamed the Imperial Academy,
extensively studied the Six Classics,
and was especially proficient in the "Records of the Grand Historian",
forming inseparable friendships with Xíng Wénwěi and Zhū Jìngzé.
Having passed the imperial examination in the Classics,
he successively held the position of Editorial Director in the Palace Library,
then abandoned his official post to return home,
and for leading the local community in resisting Xú Jìngyè and his younger brother Jìngyóu's forces,
was appointed as an Assistant Instructor at the National University.
End
Mǎ Róng's "Analects" commentary states:
"The xíngrén is an official in charge of diplomatic missions.
The Correct Meaning states:
"In the 'Rites of Zhōu,' the Ministry of Justice has a Senior xíngrén
and a Junior xíngrén,
both of whom are senior officials.
They are in charge of the rituals for feudal lords' court audiences,
ancestral temple gatherings and meetings,
as well as timely visits and joint assemblies.
Thus, the xíngrén of feudal lords are the same,
hence it is said they are officials in charge of diplomatic missions,
meaning they oversee the officials responsible for such missions.
The "Commentary and Subcommentary" states: The Senior xíngrén manages the ceremonies for great guests
and the protocols for important visitors;
to foster relations with feudal lords.
In spring, audiences are held to deliberate on the affairs of the realm,
in autumn, audiences are held to rectify the achievements of the states,
in summer, gatherings are held to present the strategies of the realm,
in winter, meetings are held to harmonize the concerns of feudal lords.
Occasional assemblies are held to promulgate prohibitions across the four quarters,
grand reunions are held to implement the governance of the realm,
timely visits are held to strengthen the goodwill of feudal lords,
extensive inspections are held to eliminate the evils of the states,
inquiries are made to understand the intentions of feudal lords,
tributes are received to exchange blessings with feudal lords,
congratulations are offered to praise the joys of feudal lords,
and gifts are presented to supplement the goodwill of feudal lords.
The "Rites of Zhōu: Ministry of Justice" states: The Junior xíngrén administers the rites for guests from the states,
maintaining records to receive envoys from the four quarters.
Shū Mù went to Jìn,
holding the diplomatic mission of Zhī Wǔzǐ,
and the Marquis of Jìn hosted a banquet for him.
When the metal instruments played the three pieces of "Sì Xià,"
he did not bow.
When the musicians sang the three pieces of "Wén Wáng,"
he again did not bow.
When they sang the three pieces of "Lù Míng,"
he bowed three times.
Hán Xiànzǐ sent the messenger Zǐ Yuán to ask him,
saying:
"You, sir, have set aside the grand pieces and
repeatedly bowed for the minor ones;
what etiquette is this?
He replied:
"The three 'Xià' pieces
are what the Son of Heaven uses to entertain feudal lords;
your servant dares not presume to hear them.
'Wén Wáng,'
is music for when two rulers meet;
your servant dares not partake.
'Lù Míng,'
is what you, my lord, use to praise our humble ruler;
how dare I not bow in gratitude?
'Sì Mù,'
is what you, my lord, use to comfort your envoy;
how dare I not bow repeatedly?
'Huáng Huáng Zhě Huá,'
is where you, my lord, instruct your envoy, saying:
'You must seek counsel comprehensively.'
Your servant has heard:
"Seeking advice from the good is called zī,
consulting relatives is called xún,
inquiring about rituals is called dù,
asking about affairs is called zōu,
seeking help in difficulties is called móu.
Your servant has gained five virtues,
how dare I not bow repeatedly?
Běigōng Wénzǐ Tuó accompanied Duke Xiāng of Wèi on his visit to Chǔ,
passing through Zhèng,
where Yìn Duàn greeted and entertained them at Fěilín,
using the formalities of a diplomatic reception with welcoming words.
Wénzǐ then entered to present his credentials.
Zǐyǔ served as the protocol officer,
while Féng Jiǎnzǐ and Zǐ Dàshū welcomed the guests.
After the ceremonies concluded and they departed,
Wénzǐ remarked to the Marquis of Wèi:
"Zhèng observes proper rites,
which will bring blessings for several generations.
They will likely avoid invasions from major states!
(Xiāng 33, before Xiāng 4) The protocol officer was Gōngsūn Huī.
Yànzǐ was sent as an envoy to Wú.
The King of Wú said to his usher:
"I have heard that Yàn Yīng
is an eloquent speaker and well-versed in rituals from the northern region."
He then ordered the usher:
"When the guest is received, address me as the Son of Heaven."
The next day,
when Yànzǐ had business,
the usher announced:
"The Son of Heaven requests your audience."
Yànzǐ looked startled three times,
and said:
"I have received orders from the ruler of my humble state
to be sent as envoy to the court of the King of Wú.
Being incompetent and confused,
I have mistakenly entered the court of the Son of Heaven.
May I ask where the King of Wú might be?"
Thereupon the King of Wú said:
"Fūchāi requests your audience."
He received Yànzǐ with the rites appropriate for feudal lords.
From "Shuō Yuàn"
In the third year of the Jǐngyún era, the Ten Circuit Surveillance Commissioners were established,

in the first year of the Qiányuán era, they were changed to Surveillance and Disposal Commissioners,

Lǐ Miǎn served as the military governor of Jiāngxī,
when a local's father fell ill.
Using sorcery, they crafted a wooden puppet,
inscribed with Lǐ Miǎn's name and position,
and buried it in their field.
Someone reported this, saying:
"To ward off disaster for his father,
he is also worthy of pity.
Thus, he was spared.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Lǐ Miǎn was appointed Governor of Guǎngxī,
concurrently serving as Military Commissioner and Surveillance Commissioner of Lǐngnán.
Previously, the number of ships from the Western Regions arriving by sea
amounted to only four or five per year.
Lǐ Miǎn was honest and incorruptible,
and he never inspected the incoming ships,
so by the end of his tenure, over four thousand ships had arrived.
During his years in office,
his utensils, carriages, and attire
remained unadorned.
When he was replaced and returned to Shímén,
he halted the boat and thoroughly searched his family's stored possessions,
casting southern goods such as rhinoceros horns and ivory into the river.
The elders believed he could be regarded as a successor to figures like Sòng Jǐng, Lú Huàn, and Lǐ Cháoyǐn from previous dynasties.
Officials and clerks petitioned the imperial court,
requesting the erection of a stele,
and Emperor Dàizong granted permission.
End
Líng Hú Huán was appointed Prefect of Jízhōu.
Qí Yìng was the Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī,
and while touring his circuit, he passed through Jízhōu.
According to convention,
when a prefect first met the Surveillance Commissioner,
he was to don military attire, hasten to the courtyard, and pay his respects.
Although Yìng had once served as Chancellor,
he was a recent and rapid appointee from the younger generation,
while Huán prided himself on being senior,
believing he surpassed Yìng,
and did not wish to pay his respects in military attire.
He went in and told his wife, Wéi Shì,
who was ashamed of the idea of bowing her head and hastening to the courtyard.
She said to Huán:
"What kind of person do you consider yourself to be,
that with white hair you should hasten before a young upstart?
If you do not greet Yìng with this ritual,
even if you are dismissed and die,
I would have no regrets.
Huán said:
"Agreed.
He then paid his respects using the guest ritual.
Although Yìng did not speak of it,
he deeply resented it.
When Yìng arrived at the prefecture,
he reported that Huán had investigated the faults of the previous administration,
but upon investigation, no evidence was found,
and it was deemed inappropriate for him to oversee the circuit and govern the people,
so he was demoted to Assistant Official of Qúzhōu.
The Emperor
Qí Yìng served as the Military Governor of Jiāngxī,
often recalling his previous tenure as a chancellor,
and though dismissed without major faults,
he hoped to be reappointed.
Thus, he doubled tributes and offerings,
and crafted large gold and silver vessels to curry favor.
Previously, the tallest silver vases stood over five chǐ high,
but Lǐ Jiān, as Governor of Jiāngxī, presented one of six chǐ.
On this occasion, for the emperor's birthday and the Dragon Boat Festival,
Yìng made a vase eight chǐ tall to present.

Cháng Gǔn,
at the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era was appointed as the military commissioner of Fújiàn.
Initially,
the people of Mǐn had no knowledge of learning,
but when Gǔn arrived,
he established local schools,
had them compose literary writings,
personally gave lectures and guidance,
and treated them with equal courtesy as host and guest during observations, tours, and banquets, participating together.
From this,
the local customs were completely transformed,
and the annual tribute scholars became equal to those from Jīngzhōu.
Thereafter, the people of Mǐn offered seasonal sacrifices to Gǔn in the school temple during spring and autumn.
Wú Còu,
at the beginning of Dézōng's reign, was appointed as the surveillance commissioner of Fújiàn,
where he governed diligently and incorruptibly,
earning widespread praise.
He had a grievance with the chancellor Dòu Cān,
who repeatedly slandered him,
even claiming that Còu suffered from paralysis and had difficulty walking.
The emperor summoned him back to court,
examined his condition,
and found it untrue,
thus losing faith in Dòu Cān.
He promoted Còu to surveillance commissioner of Shǎn-Guó,
replacing Lǐ Yì.
Yì,
was a member of Dòu Cān's faction.

Cuī Xián,
styled Chóngyì,
served as the Surveillance Commissioner of Shǎn-Guó.
From morning until dusk,
he would drink heartily with guests and subordinates,
often remaining intoxicated and unawakened.
Though official documents piled up,
Cuī Xián would review them late at night,
making judgments and decisions
without the slightest error.
The clerks regarded him as a supernatural being.
Wéi Dān,
courtesy name Wénmíng,
served as the Surveillance Commissioner of Jiangnandao West.
He calculated his salary based on the number of people in his household,
surrendering the surplus to the government.
He dismissed redundant officials from eight prefectures,
confiscating their wealth.
Initially,
the people did not know how to build tiled houses,
using thatch and bamboo rafters instead,
which, after prolonged dryness, would crack and catch fire.
Wéi Dān summoned artisans to teach them pottery making,
gathered materials in a yard,
estimated the costs for pricing,
and did not seek profit.
There was an official in charge of the granary for ten years;
Wéi Dān audited the grain reserves,
finding a shortage of three thousand hu.
Wéi Dān said:
"Did the official consume it himself?
He confiscated the official's property,
obtaining all the records,
which revealed it was seized by powerful officials.
Wéi Dān summoned the officials and said:
"If you relied on authority to take from the granary,
it is a crime.
I will give you a deadline,
return it within one month.
They all kowtowed in apology,
and by the deadline, none dared to disobey.
During the Dahe era,
Péi Yì, as Surveillance Commissioner of Jiangxi,
petitioned to establish a memorial hall for Wéi Dān,
and to engrave a stone to record his achievements.
There was no response.
The emperor
Wáng Wěi,
styled Wénqīng.
During the Dàlì era,
he and Lǐ Mì both served as investigating assistants under Lù Sìgōng, the surveillance commissioner of Jiāngxī.
Mì had incurred Yuán Zài's enmity,
and Sìgōng, currying favor, intended to kill him.
Wěi intervened to rescue and explain,
narrowly averting the danger.
When Mì came to power,
he memorialized that Wěi had shown him personal kindness,
and Emperor Dézōng permitted Mì to repay it,
thus promoting Wěi to the position of Supervising Secretary.
When a vacancy arose for the surveillance commissioner of Zhèxī,
Mì nominated Wěi for the post,
but the emperor said:
"Is this the one whom I allowed you to repay a debt of gratitude?
The Supervising Secretary is a crucial post,
shouldn't you keep him here to deliberate on affairs?
Mì replied:
"The tax revenues in Zhèxī are particularly heavy,
Wěi is incorruptible and loyal,
capable of benevolently nurturing the people,
hence I requested to send him there.
The emperor approved the appointment.

During the Yuánhé era,
several officials in the ministry were drinking freely in the government offices,
discussing their lifelong preferences and fears.
Some spoke of their love for paintings and board games,
while others feared deceit and flattery.
Zhōu Yuàn, the deputy minister of the Ministry of Works, alone declared:
"I love the Xuānzhōu military governor.
And I fear tigers."
From "Records of Anecdotes"
Emperor Xuānzōng, while reading the Veritable Records of the Yuánhé Era,
came across the outstanding governance of the late surveillance commissioner of Jiāngxī, Wéi Dān,
and asked his chief ministers who Dān was.

his lasting influence and benevolent legacy

Records from the Eastern Library After some time, he was appointed surveillance commissioner of Jiāngxī.

Zhòu's younger brother, Wéi Xiù,
courtesy name Bóqǐ,
recommended Lú Xié for the imperial examinations.
Though Xié was exceedingly unrefined,

When Xié came to power,

Yuán Zhěn,
courtesy name Wēizhī,
served as the Surveillance Commissioner of Zhedong.
The mountains and waters of Kuàijī were extraordinarily beautiful,
and the staff Yuán Zhěn recruited
were all literary scholars of the time.
They would visit Mirror Lake and Qínwàng Mountain three or four times a month,
composing poems that often filled entire volumes.
The Deputy Commissioner, Dòu Gǒng, was renowned throughout the land for his poetry,

Cuī Yǎn,
styled Guǎnglüè,
served as the military governor of Shǎnzhōu during Emperor Zhāomǐn's reign.
An old malpractice involved insufficient tribute deliveries,
where officials' salaries were seized to make up the shortfall,
amounting to eight hundred thousand annually.
Yǎn replaced this with the proper funds allocated for honest governance.
After two years in office,
his administrative achievements were reported to the court.
He was transferred to serve as military governor of Èzhōu, Yuèzhōu, and Western Zhèjiāng.
Upon arrival,
he implemented lenient policies to comfort the weary populace.
When stationed at Èzhǔ,
he enforced strict laws and severe punishments,
yet never pardoned a single capital offense.
Along the rivers and lakes,
where reeds grew thickly,
he had small assault vessels built,
patrolling up and down a thousand li,
and within a month eradicated all bandits.
Throughout his three postings as inspector,
he consistently governed with clarity and simplicity, minimizing affairs,
resulting in surplus resources,
and bringing peace and stability to the people.
His son Cuī Yáo served successively as military governor of Western Zhèjiāng and È-Yuè,
while Cuī Jǐn became military governor of Húnán.
End
Lǐ Déyù served as the Military Governor of Zhèxī.
Previously, following the military rebellion of Wáng Guóqīng in Rùnzhōu,
the former governor Dòu Yìzhí had exhausted the treasury's reserves for rewards,
leading the troops to become arrogant and unruly,
and depleting all financial resources.
Lǐ Déyù practiced frugality in his personal life,
and all the revenue retained by the province
was used to support the army.
Although the provisions were not generous,
the officers and soldiers bore no resentment.
After two years,
tax revenues were restored and replenished.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
In the region between the Jiāng and Lǐng rivers,
people believed in shamans and were deluded by ghosts and monsters.
When parents or siblings contracted severe illnesses,
the entire household would abandon them and leave.
Lǐ Déyù wished to change this custom,
so he selected knowledgeable individuals from the local communities,
instructed them with words,
and restrained them with laws.
Within a few years, the corrupt practice was promptly eradicated.
Regarding the shrines and temples in the subordinate commanderies,
he consulted local records,
and preserved those dedicated to famous ministers and virtuous empresses of previous dynasties.
Within the four commanderies,
he eliminated 1,010 illicit shrines,
and also abolished 1,460 private mountain retreats,
to suppress banditry.
The people appreciated his governance,
and an imperial edict praised him.
The emperor
Emperor Jìngzōng grew increasingly dissolute and reclusive,
so ministers rarely had opportunities to present their counsel.
Lǐ Déyù, though serving as a military governor in a remote region,
remained wholeheartedly devoted to the imperial house.
Intending to offer earnest remonstrance
without employing direct criticism,
he sent an envoy to present six admonitory essays titled "Dān yǐ Zhēn,"
using "Dawn Attire and Night Robes" to satirize infrequent morning audiences,
"Proper Attire" to critique inappropriate imperial garments,
"Ceasing Tributes" to admonish against demanding rare curios,
"Accepting Admonition" to reprove the disregard of forthright advice,
"Discerning Evil" to caution against trusting petty men,
and "Guarding Against Trifles" to warn against frivolous excursions.
Although the emperor could not fully implement his recommendations,
he ordered Academician Wéi Chǔhòu to draft a gracious reply
and graciously acknowledged Lǐ Déyù's loyal intentions.
When Péi Xiū was appointed inspector of Xuānchéng,
before leaving the capital,
he happened upon the lotus flowers at Qǔjiāng in full bloom,
and went with colleagues and scholars to enjoy the view.
Starting from Cí'ēn Temple,
they each dismissed their attendants,
taking only young servants with them,
and walked to the foot of Zǐyún Tower.
There they saw several people sitting by the water's edge,
and Péi and the court officials rested nearby.
Among them was a man in yellow, half-drunk,
who was pointing and looking around with an air of arrogance,
his laughter and remarks frivolous.
Péi felt somewhat displeased,
so he bowed and asked him:
"What office do you hold, sir?"
The man replied casually:
"Well,
I dare not boast,
but I've just been appointed magistrate of Guǎngdé in Xuānzhōu."
He then asked Péi in return:
"And what position do you hold, officer?"
Péi imitated his tone and said:
"Well, I dare not boast,
but I've just been appointed observation commissioner of Xuānzhōu."
At this, the man fled in embarrassment.
The court officials clapped their hands and laughed heartily.
Within a few days,
the story spread throughout the capital.

Yánshǎng diligently led by example,
governing with simplicity and restraint,
dredging rivers and canals,

Within a few years, displaced people returned and submitted to his rule,
restoring the capital region to its former state.
An imperial edict praised and commended him for this.
End.
When Zhèng Xúnyú served as Governor of Hénán,

Officials observed that his horse's steps

Commentators considered Zhèng Xúnyú's governance of Hénán

In the fourteenth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
a spring and summer drought caused grain prices to soar,

The Emperor summoned Wú Còu,

Còu diligently pursued orderly administration,
focusing on diligence and frugality,

According to the Old Book of Táng: Emperor Dézōng demoted Gāo to Military Aide of Fǔzhōu,
issuing an edict stating:

Initially,
the officials in the prefecture, considering that Wú Còu had risen from the imperial relatives' fiefdom,
and was not well-versed in official documents,
would present all doubtful and difficult legal cases
only when Còu was about to go out,
hoping to avoid criticism of flaws.
Although Còu reviewed them hastily,
he always pointed out the deceitful aspects,
made decisions with his pen,
without the slightest error.
He did not punish the officials with flogging unless for major faults,
but summoned them for face-to-face interrogation and reprimand before releasing them,
making the officials especially cautious and diligent,

Emperor Dézōng summoned Wú Còu out of season and appointed him as the Capital Governor,
ordering him to take office immediately.
Còu hurriedly drove to gather the guests,

Someone asked:

An official replied:

simply lift the pots and pans to take them,

Xǔ Mèngróng,

The Imperial Guard officer Lǐ Yù had borrowed eighty thousand strings of cash from a wealthy man in Cháng'ān,

Mèngróng dispatched officers to arrest and shackle him,
setting a deadline for repayment,
saying:
"If you fail to meet the deadline, you will face death.
Since the Xīngyuán era,
only those Imperial Guards who had meritorious service or were favored eunuchs with special grace

Mèngróng, being upright and fearless,

Liú Qīchǔ served as the Capital Governor,
suppressing the powerful and influential,
disregarding personal risks,
regardless of the size of matters,

Thus people of the time respected him,
some praised his resourcefulness,
often comparing him to Zhào Guǎnghàn of the Western Hàn period.
When Liú Qīchǔ was Capital Governor,
his commands were strict and clear,
punishing without avoiding the powerful.
Previously, young hoodlums in the capital and butchers, wine sellers, and merchants

even those hiding in the military,

Within ten days to a month, villains and entrenched thieves in the city districts and markets

Some young men shouted:

Everyone felt as if Governor Liú were watching over them,
trembling and sweating in fear, not daring to do wrong.
Yet when speaking with his subordinates,
he never hurt their dignity or scolded them.
An official once said to his prefectural and county colleagues:

when public affairs are clear like fine weather and beautiful scenery,
feel free to enjoy outings and sightseeing,

The emperor said,

The emperor said,

The governor replied,
"If it happened in the street, then the Jīngwū General in charge of the street should report it.
If it occurred in the residential area, then the patrol officers on site should report it."
The emperor then ceased his inquiries.
Liǔ Gōngchuò,

Yuánshǎng once visited Lǐ Shí's residence and heard that Shí was sitting in the audience hall,
arguing loudly with a man.
Yuánshǎng sent someone to spy and was told:
"There is a Shence Army general presenting a case.
Yuánshǎng hurried in,
admonished Shí, saying:
"Your Excellency assists the Son of Heaven,
governing the four seas,
yet now you cannot even control one army general nearby,
allowing such disrespect—
how can you pacify the four barbarians?
He immediately rushed out and mounted his horse,
ordering his attendants to capture the general and wait at Dismounting Horse Bridge.
By the time Yuánshǎng arrived, the general had already been stripped and made to kneel.
His comrades complained to Qiú Shìliáng,

Yuánshǎng replied:

Yuánshǎng responded:

and the Chancellor is also a high minister.
If the Chancellor's man were disrespectful to the Commander,
what would be done?
Now the Commander's man was disrespectful to the Chancellor—
how could that be forgiven?
The Commander shares the state's body,
and should cherish the law for the country.
Yuánshǎng had come in prisoner's garb,
saying, "My life or death rests with the Commander."
Shìliáng, knowing the general was already dead,

Wéi Ào served as the Metropolitan Governor,

Wéi Ào responded:

The emperor went to inform the Empress Dowager,
saying:

we must simply send the money."
Once the payment was made,
the taxes were settled in an instant.

Lord Bāo Xiàosù, known for his astuteness while governing the capital,

"When you see the governor today, he will surely hand you over to me for a confession.
You just keep pleading innocence,
and I will share the punishment with you:
you will avoid the flogging,
while I will receive it."
Later, when Lord Bāo brought the prisoner for questioning and finished,
he indeed handed him over to the official for a confession.
The prisoner, as instructed, argued incessantly,

saying:
"Just take the back flogging

Lord Bāo, thinking the official was abusing his power,
rebuked him in the court
and had him flogged seventeen times,
specifically lenient on the prisoner's penalty.
He intended to curb the official's influence by punishing him instead,
unaware that he had been tricked by him,
and in the end, it went exactly as planned.
Truly, the cunning of petty men is hard to guard against!
Lord Xiàosù was stern by nature,

so people said that seeing Bāo Xǐrén smile was as rare as the Huáng Hé running clear.

Huáng Bà,
courtesy name Cìgōng,
served as the governor of Yǐngchuān.

to manifest his virtue.
Huáng Bà managed affairs down to the finest details of rice and salt.
Initially,
they seemed trivial and complicated,
yet Huáng Bà had the energy to implement them thoroughly.
When officials and commoners met him,
he would converse while carefully pondering,
inquiring about hidden matters,
to use for mutual reference.
His discernment of affairs was astute,
and all praised him as divine.
Evildoers fled to other commanderies,
and thefts and robberies decreased daily.
Huáng Bà diligently promoted education and transformation,
and only afterward applied punishments,
aiming to achieve completeness and safety.
He once said:
"In general, the way of governance is to eliminate the most extreme aspects."
Huáng Bà, being outwardly lenient yet inwardly discerning,
won the hearts of officials and people.
The population increased yearly,
and his governance was ranked first in the empire.
Over a period of eight years,
the commandery became increasingly well-governed.
At that time,
phoenixes and divine sparrows
frequently gathered in the commanderies and kingdoms,
with Yǐngchuān having particularly many.
The Son of Heaven, considering Huáng Bà's governance and conduct ultimately exemplary,
issued an edict praising him, saying:
"The governor of Yǐngchuān, Bà,
proclaims decrees to the common people,
transforming them in their villages with filial sons and younger brothers,
chaste wives and obedient women,
and descendants daily growing more numerous.
Farmers yield field boundaries,
lost items are not picked up on the roads,
the elderly, widowed, and solitary are cared for,
and the poor are supported and aided.
In the prisons, for eight years there have been no prisoners guilty of heavy crimes.
Officials and people are inclined toward transformation through education,
and the flourishing extension of this has greatly diminished resentment."
He then composed "Ode to the Five Gentlemen,"
narrating the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove.
Shān Táo and Wáng Róng were omitted due to their high status and prominence.
Of Jī Kāng he wrote:
"The luan's wings may sometimes be broken,
but its dragon-like nature—who can tame it?"
Of Ruǎn Jí he wrote:
"Past events cannot be discussed,
and at a dead end, how can one not wail?"
Of Ruǎn Xián he wrote:
"Repeatedly recommended but not entering office,
with one wave of the hand, he went out to govern."
Of Liú Líng he wrote:
"Concealing his essence, daily drowning in drink,
who knows it was not reckless feasting?"
These four lines are essentially self-referential.
The History of the Southern Dynasties refers to governing a commandery as "establishing the standard,"
using Yán Yánnián's
"with one wave of the hand, he went out to govern"
line,
unaware of its error.
Yán Yánnián meant that the "wave" in "one wave"
was like King Wu of Zhou holding a white banner in his right hand,
waving it as a signal.
Yán Yánnián's poem presented to the Governor of Shǐpíng says:
"Repeatedly recommended but not entering office,
with one wave of the hand, he went out to govern,"
referring to Shān Táo recommending Ruǎn Xián for the position of Vice Minister of Personnel,
submitting three times but Emperor Wǔ not appointing him,
after which, with one push, he was sent out,
hence this line about Shǐpíng.
Yán Yánnián, having been rejected,
used this to express his own situation.
Later, Dù Mù wrote in his "Poem on Ascending Lèyóu Plateau":
"Intending to take the standard and go to the rivers and seas,
on Lèyóu Plateau I gaze toward Zhāolíng."
Thus, it became a literary allusion.
