"I heard that Prince Péngchéng served as Governor of Qīngzhōu,
and asked his guests who followed him to Qīngzhōu,
they said: 'The people of Qí land,
have shallow customs.
When the governor first enters the region,
they all embrace bricks and knock their heads,
to show their intention.
But when he is replaced and returns home,
they hit him with bricks'
This speaks of their shift in allegiance,
faster than turning a hand.
Thus, a rhyme in the capital said:
"No prisoners are held in the jail,
no Qīngzhōu natives in the homes,
even if family fortunes are bad,
no worry of embracing bricks in the belly.
The meaning of 'embracing bricks',
originated from this.
Records of the Buddhist Monasteries
Prince of Nán'ān Yuán Zhēn was appointed as the Governor of Xiàngzhōu,
arriving at Yè in May,
where a violent storm and heavy rain occurred daily,
resulting in dozens of deaths from freezing,
and in the same month, he died from a carbuncle on his back.
Later, Sūn Xī was assigned to Xiàngzhōu,
assuming office in July,
on a day of fierce wind and cold rain,
which caused over twenty deaths from freezing,
along with dozens of donkeys and horses.
Upon learning of his grandfather's previous misfortune there,
Sūn Xī felt uneasy,
and he raised an army to challenge Yuán Yì,
but was ultimately killed.
(From *History of the Northern Dynasties*)
Fáng Bào,
courtesy name Zhōnggàn,
served as the governor of Lèlíng.
He maintained discipline and moral instruction,
and was praised for his governance.
The commandery bordered the sea,
and the water tasted mostly salty and bitter.
Fáng Bào ordered a well to be dug,
and sweet water was obtained.
People near and far attributed it to his virtuous governance.
After Fáng Bào left his post and returned,
the sweet taste of the water turned salty again.
End.
Péi Xiá,
called Sōnghé,
served as governor of Héběi Commandery.
Xiá personally practiced frugality and simplicity,
cherishing the people as his own children.
His diet consisted solely of beans, wheat, salt, and vegetables.
None among the officials and people did not hold him in affection.
A song said:
"Rich delicacies he does not eat,
corvée labor he does not take.
Péi Xiá is upright and benevolent,
a model for the world."
Xiá once went with various governors to pay respects to Zhōu Wén.
Zhōu Wén ordered Xiá to stand apart,
and said to the governors:
"Péi Xiá is pure, cautious, and devoted to public service,
unsurpassed in the land.
If any among you is like Xiá,
you may stand with him."
All remained silent,
none daring to respond.
Zhōu Wén then richly rewarded Xiá,
and both court and public were convinced.
He was called the Independent Envoy.
Kǒng Huàn,
courtesy name Xiūwén,
was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng.
Since the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
although this major commandery had experienced bandit disturbances,
it remained prosperous and wealthy.
The previous officials of two-thousand-dàn rank
often engaged in exploitation and tyranny.
Huàn maintained his integrity and self-discipline,
neither bringing his wife nor children to assume office,
but only arriving at the commandery alone by a single boat.
The salary and emoluments he received
were immediately distributed to support orphans and widows.
Within the commandery, he was acclaimed as
"Divine Lord"
Yīn Qǐ, a wealthy man from Qǔ'ē, observed that Huàn lived frugally and simply,
so he presented him with a set of clothing and a felt rug.
Huàn said:
"As the Grand Administrator, I enjoy a generous salary;
why would I be unable to afford such things?
However, since the common people are not yet fully provided for,
I cannot indulge in warmth and satiety alone.
I appreciate your kind intentions,
but please do not trouble yourself further.
Book of Chén
Liáng Yànguāng,
courtesy name Xiūzhī,
served as the Governor of Qízhōu during the early Suí dynasty,
and his administration was exceptionally benevolent.
He was later transferred to Xiàngzhōu,
where he had previously governed Qízhōu.
The customs there were quite质朴,
so he governed with tranquility,
bringing great peace to the entire region.
His performance evaluations were consistently outstanding,
ranking first in the empire.
However, when he administered Xiàngzhōu,
applying the same methods as in Qízhōu,
the mixed customs of Yèjùn,
where people were often deceitful,
led them to compose songs about him,
claiming he was incapable of governance.
The emperor inquired and reprimanded him,
ultimately resulting in his dismissal.
Over a year later,
he was appointed Governor of Zhàozhōu,
and Liáng Yànguāng addressed the emperor, saying:
"I previously served in Xiàngzhōu, failing the people,
and was called 'the capped candy,'
I thought myself dismissed forever,
with no hope of wearing official attire again,
never expecting Your Majesty's grace would restore me.
I request to return to Xiàngzhōu,
to change my approach completely,
hoping to transform its customs."
The emperor consented,
reappointing him Governor of Xiàngzhōu,
and when the local cunning elites heard Liáng Yànguāng had requested to return,
they all laughed in derision.
Upon assuming office,
he exposed hidden corruption,
with almost divine insight,
causing all the crafty to flee secretly,
and astonishing the entire region.
The Suíshū's separate record writes 'capped candy piece,'
likely a misreading of the character 'chén.'
Fán Zǐgài,
courtesy name Huá Zōng,
served as the governor of Wǔwēi,
and was renowned for his good governance.
Emperor Yáng issued an edict stating:
"Gǒng Jí promoted virtuous transformation in the past,
while Zhāng Dù bequeathed a pure legacy for the future.
Zǐgài conducts himself with integrity and purity,
and guides the people with effective methods.
Even amidst wealth, his character remains uncorrupted;
even drinking from the Spring of Greed, how could his nature be altered?"
When the imperial procession toured the west,
and upon returning,
the emperor said to him:
"People say you are incorruptible and steadfast—is this truly so?"
Zǐgài humbly replied:
"How dare I claim to be incorruptible?
I am merely cautious and dare not accept bribes."
For this, he was rewarded with over a hundred hú of delicacies.
End
Xuē Dàdǐng served as the governor of Cāngzhōu.
Within the prefecture's borders lay the Wúdì River,
which had been silted up and abandoned since the late Suí dynasty.
Dàdǐng petitioned to reopen it,
thereby facilitating the transport of fish and salt from the sea.
The common people sang a ballad in praise:
"The new river opens, boats glide with ease;
Straight to the sea, fish and salt arrive.
Where once we walked, now chariots speed;
How splendid, Lord Xuē's virtue overflows!"
Dàdǐng also noted the low-lying terrain of the prefecture,
so he dredged the Chánglú, Zhāng, and Héng rivers—three waterways in total—
to divert summer floods from the region.
Thereafter, the area no longer suffered from inundations.
Together with Jiǎ Dūnyí, governor of Yíngzhōu, and Zhèng Déběn, governor of Cáozhōu,
they all implemented benevolent governance.
In Héběi, they were celebrated as the "Tripod-Leg Governors."
(From the Old Book of Táng)
In the fourth year of the Cháng'ān era under Empress Wǔ,
Nàyán Lǐ Qiáo and Tóngpíngzhāngshì Táng Xiùjǐng memorialized:
"We observe that public opinion values court officials over local posts,
whereas all those appointed as governors
are mostly due to demotions or offenses,
which does not help purify customs
nor stabilize the myriad subjects.
We request selecting talents from the central departments and ministries,
to respectively administer major prefectures,
jointly managing governmental affairs.
We beg to resign from our close attendant positions
to lead all officials by example."
The Empress Dowager then ordered names to be recorded for selection,
and those chosen were to proceed accordingly.
Twenty officials including Fènggé Shìláng Wéi Sìlì and Yùshǐ Dàfū Yáng Zàisī were selected,
all serving as investigating commissioners while retaining their original offices.
Later, among these twenty, only two achieved commendable administrative records:
Chángzhōu Cìshǐ Xuē Guāngqiān and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Sīmǎ Zhōng.
(From the Tōngdiǎn)
In the eleventh year of the Kaiyuan era,
a drought struck Shāndōng,
and Cháo Jiǎn proposed selecting court officials to serve as regional inspectors,
to provide relief to the impoverished.
Emphasis was placed on the selection of provincial administrators,
thus appointing Huángmén Shìláng Wáng Qiū as the Inspector of Huái Prefecture,
along with several others such as Zhōngshū Shìláng Cuī Miǎn,
all of whom were assigned as inspectors to various prefectures in Shāndōng.
However, none of them achieved notable accomplishments in their posts,
except for Wáng Qiū, who governed with integrity and strictness,
earning deep respect and admiration from both the people and officials.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
Péi Yàoqīng,
courtesy name Huànzhī,
was appointed Prefect of Jìzhōu in the thirteenth year of the Kāiyuán era.
That year,
the imperial procession made an eastern tour,
and the prefecture lay on the main route,
with a long stretch of road,
yet the population was sparse and weak.
Yàoqīng personally organized matters,
establishing three bridges and ten relay stations,
allocating resources appropriately.
At that time, the imperial procession passed through
more than ten prefectures in total,
and Yàoqīng was praised as the best in managing accommodations.
Upon returning from the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
a banquet was held for the accompanying officials in Sòngzhōu.
The emperor was very pleased
and said to Zhāng Yuē:
"Previously, when I sent envoys to tour the empire,
observe customs,
and inspect the merits and faults of officials,
they failed to obtain the truth.
Now that I have performed ceremonies at Mount Tài,
the Prefect of Huáizhōu, Wáng Qiū, offered nothing beyond the required sacrificial animals,
and I know he does not curry favor;
the Prefect of Wèizhōu, Cuī Miǎn, sent envoys to set up tents
without using embroidered silk,
showing me frugality—
this reveals his governance;
the Prefect of Jìzhōu, Péi Yàoqīng, submitted a memorial of several hundred words,
stating, 'If the people are heavily burdened,
it is unworthy to report success'
I placed the document by my seat as a self-admonition,
for this shows his care for the people.
New and Old Histories
Qí Huàn,
styled Xǐxīn,
served as Governor of Biàn Province.
Hénán's Biàn was a prosperous commandery connecting the Jiāng-Huái region to the Hé-Luò area,
with vessels and carriages gathering like spokes,
and the populace vast and numerous.
Previous governors had mostly been incompetent,
only Ní Ruòshuǐ and Huàn
governed with purity and strictness, earning praises from the people and officials.
When Emperor Xuánzōng sealed Tàishān,
passing through Biàn and Sòng,
he was accompanied by tens of thousands of chariots and cavalry,
with princes, dukes, consorts, and princesses,
as well as tribal chiefs from the four barbarian regions,
and also tens of thousands of horses and camels.
Their encampment stretched over dozens of lǐ.
Huàn set up long tents and canopies,
connecting continuously to present food,
in total a thousand trays were managed,
with keys personally offered during meals.
The emperor considered him knowledgeable of rites,
was greatly pleased,
and stayed for three days, bestowing silk.
End
Quán Huái'ēn served as the governor of Sòngzhōu,
governing his subordinates with authority and clarity,
causing everyone to tread cautiously in fear.
At that time, Yáng Dé Gàn, the governor of Biànzhōu, was also known for his strictness and shared equal renown with Huái'ēn.
On this occasion, Huái'ēn passed through Biànzhōu,
and Dé Gàn escorted him out of the suburbs.
Huái'ēn noticed a newly erected post in the middle of the bridge meant to prohibit carriages from passing,
and said to Dé Gàn:
"Couldn't a simple order have sufficed?
What is the need for this?"
Dé Gàn was greatly ashamed,
and contemporary opinion deemed him inferior to Huái'ēn.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Lú Huàn served as the governor of Shǎn Prefecture,
and his reputation for strictness and resoluteness was known throughout the Guānzhōng region.
When Emperor Xuánzōng traveled to the capital,
he stopped at Shǎn City,
and immediately learned of Huàn's exceptional governance.
He personally wrote a eulogy on the hall's wall, which read:
"Bearing the weight of a fortified city,
commanding the strategic might of Shǎn's division.
Benevolent though compassionate,
his nature is truly humble and modest.
Already benefiting all things,
he dedicates himself selflessly.
This is the nation's treasure,
upholding his family's tradition."
Among the people of Shǎn Prefecture,
many engaged in excessive worship.
The local gentry and commoners would say to each other:
"There's no need to compete with deities,
nor seek shamans' prayers.
Just don't offend Lord Lú,
and fortune or misfortune will swiftly follow."
《Tiānbǎo Anecdotes》In the early Tiānbǎo era,
he served as governor of Nánhǎi.
Nánhǎi was both a land and maritime hub,
with exotic and peculiar products.
Former governors Liú Jùlín and Péng Gǎo had both been dismissed for corruption,
so Huàn was appointed to replace them.
Corrupt officials restrained their hands, and even those involved in maritime trade
dared not violate his laws,
bringing peace to distant customs.
It was said that in the forty years since the Kāiyuán era,
only three had governed Guǎngzhou with integrity:
Sòng Jǐng, Lǐ Cháoyǐn, and Lú Huàn.
《New Book of Táng》The "New History" records Péi Zhòuxiān as governor of Guǎngzhou,
while the "Old History" mentions four officials known for integrity in Guǎngzhou administration,
referring to Sòng, Zhòuxiān, Cháoyǐn, and Huàn.
Why then does this account only mention three?
Zhāng Kāi was appointed as the Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and when he reached the prefecture's border,
wind and rain darkened the sky,
making it impossible to distinguish faces.
He only heard the sound of a palace guard shouting from the air,
followed by over a dozen figures in purple robes and armor appearing in the clouds.
Zhāng Kāi asked the reason for this,
and they replied:
"We are the gods in charge of the internal and external affairs of Jīngzhōu,
and we have long admired your esteemed reputation, Governor.
Therefore, we have come together to welcome and guide you to your post."
After paying respects at the temple, he offered sacrifices in gratitude to each of them,
and he also renovated and adorned the temple's appearance.
From then on, his governance and reputation were exceptionally good.
From "Kāiyuán Yíshì"
Yán Zhēnqīng was the governor of Píngyuán.
Ān Lùshān's rebellious intentions were quite evident,
so Zhēnqīng used continuous rain as a pretext,
to repair the city walls and dredge the moats,
secretly registering able-bodied men,
and storing up provisions.
Outwardly, he gathered many scholars,
sailed boats on the pond,
drank wine and composed poems.
Some slandered him to Lùshān,
and Lùshān also secretly spied on him,
thinking a scholar was not worth worrying about.
Not long after,
Lùshān indeed rebelled,
and all of Héshuò fell,
only the defenses of Píngyuán city remained intact.
He then sent the military staff officer Lǐ Píng to gallop and report this.
When Emperor Xuánzōng first heard of Lùshān's revolt,
he sighed and said:
"Among the twenty-four prefectures of Héběi,
is there not a single loyal official?"
Upon Píng's arrival,
he was overjoyed and said to his attendants:
"I do not know Yán Zhēnqīng's appearance,
but what kind of person acts like this?"
From the "Old Book of Táng"
Xiāo Dìng,
courtesy name Méichén,
served as the Governor of Yuán Prefecture,
and successively held the positions of Governor of Xìn, Hú, Sòng, Mù, and Rùn Prefectures,
where he was renowned for his effective governance.
During the Dàlì era,
the authorities evaluated
the performance of regional governors nationwide,
and only Dìng, along with Cháng Prefecture Governor Xiāo Fù and Háo Prefecture Governor Zhāng Yì,
were ranked first in administrative conduct.
They encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
balanced tax burdens,
prompted the return of fugitives,
and restored household registrations with increased numbers,
among whom Dìng was the most outstanding.
(Old Book of Táng)
In the second year of the Qián Yuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Zuǒ Zhèn, a Senior Adviser of Good Counsel, was appointed Governor of Huáng Prefecture.
Upon assuming office,
the people of Huáng sang:
"I wished to flee my hometown,
I wished to leave my ancestral graves.
But now that Lord Zuǒ has come,
who could bear to abandon him and depart?
A year later,
they sang again:
"Our land had ghostly sorcerers,
bewitching people unbeknownst to all.
While the Son of Heaven honored and trusted them,
Lord Zuǒ could slay them.
From Collected Works of Yuán Cìshān
Xué Jué,
courtesy name Wēnrú,
served as the Prefect of Chǔzhōu and the Military Farms Commissioner of the prefecture.
Previously, the Military Farms Commissioner of the prefecture was nominally held by the Chancellor,
allowing the Prefect to report directly to the throne,
with a salary and other allowances totaling over a million coins,
hundreds of agricultural officials,
three thousand households serving as laborers,
and more than ten people being promoted to official positions favorably each year.
Xué Jué streamlined all these,
retaining only one or two out of ten,
yet the rental income still showed a surplus.
Falsely accused by the Surveillance Commissioner,
he was demoted to Prefect of Shǎnzhōu,
and later transferred to Prefect of Chénzhōu.
In the early Jiànzhōng era,
the Emperor dispatched envoys to evaluate and promote or demote officials.
Lǐ Chéng of Huáinán cited Xué Jué's simplification of cumbersome administration in Chǔzhōu,
Zhào Zàn of Shānnán highlighted his integrity and purity in Shǎnzhōu,
and Lú Hàn of Huáinán praised his strict governance,
all submitting favorable evaluation reports,
leading to his promotion in rank and the grant of purple robes.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Yáng Chéng,
courtesy name Kàngzōng,
was appointed as the Prefect of Dào Prefecture.
He governed the people as if managing his own household,
punishing those who deserved punishment,
and rewarding those who deserved reward.
He did not concern himself with official documents,
and was content with his monthly salary.
The prefecture produced dwarfs,
who were annually presented to the court.
Yáng Chéng pitied their plight,
and thus none were sent.
The emperor sent for them,
and Yáng Chéng memorialized:
"All the people in the prefecture are short;
if I were to present them,
I would not know whom to select."
From then on, the prefecture was exempted,
and the people, grateful, named their children after Yáng.
The "New History"
formerly referred to them as dwarf slaves.
Appointing the high official Wáng Zōngshù as the prefect of Jìnzhōu,
a maritime merchant was selling borneol,
demanding a price twice the usual.
Zōngshù ordered someone to bring a brocade quilt past the merchant to show it,
then signaled his attendants with his eyes,
who took away the merchant's borneol cakes.
He also ordered a broker to purchase two courtesans,
each sixteen years old,
their price being thirty-two strings of coins.
Zōngshù accepted them,
summoned an old maidservant,
and said to the broker:
"This one is already fifty years old,
worth fifty thousand coins,
so besides paying for one courtesan, there is still eighteen thousand left.
He bought a cloth mattress and quilt weighing ten catties,
then ordered to take fifteen catties of old hemp rope from a wine shop and pay with it.
The common people looked at each other and laughed,
Zōngshù said:
"Common folks are happy with a profit of five catties,
officials and people filed complaints,
rebuking the Wéizhōu household registration official.
"The Outer History of Táowù": Zōngshù reprimanded the Wéizhōu household registration assistant,
asking the clerk:
"What rank is the assistant?
What clothes does he wear?
The clerk said:
"In a lower prefecture, a judicial official only wears a green robe and holds a locust wood tablet.
Zōngshù laughed heartily,
doubled over and said:

Mèngshǔ's Left Assistant Ōuyáng Bīn,
a Héngshān native,
was learned and skilled in writing.
Wáng Jiàn appointed him Prefect of Jiāzhōu,
and he joyfully exclaimed:
"Amidst blue hills and green waters,
serving as a two-thousand-bushel official,
composing poetry and drinking wine,

From "Shǔ Táowù"
Zézhōu reported that the former regional governor,
Shǐ Yántāo, upon leaving the prefecture,

and detained Shǐ Yántāo.
After three days,
he opened the city gate at night

"Old History of the Five Dynasties"
Xiè Jié served as the prefect of Gāozhōu.
The region was plagued by tigers,
which entered the city walls at night to cause havoc,
leaving the people unable to live in peace.
One day, after bathing,
Xiè Jié visited the temple of the city god.
Raising a cup of wine before the deity, he said:
"How are the ignorant people at fault,
that they suffer from the tigers' violence?
Is it not because the prefect lacks virtuous influence?
I pray that the tigers devour only the prefect,
and spare the innocent people."
Thereupon, he dismissed his attendants
and stayed alone in the temple hall overnight.
That night, at the third watch,
a creature suddenly roared from the southeast corner of the temple,
its sound like thunder,
and only after a long while did it cease.
At dawn, when he looked,
he found several tigers all dead.
From the "Jiǔ Guó Zhì"

tall and robust with immense strength,
consuming over ten catties of meat per meal,

Previously, children in Guìzhōu would gather coins on the streets,

Tián Yuánjūn governed Chéngdū with great reputation.

Wú Yuè Xuān governed Yǒngjiā,

In the ninth year of Xiángfú,
Shào Yè governed Guǎngzhōu,
digging an inner river for boats to pass through,
so typhoons caused no harm.
Chén Shìqīng succeeded him,
petitioned for exemption,
from Guǎngnán's port salt. The people of Guǎngzhōu sang:
"Father Shào and Mother Chén,
rid us of our two hardships.
When the Qin unified the empire,

"Records of Jiaozhi and Guang"
According to ritual, the Son of Heaven has six horses,
with the outer horses on both sides;
the Three Dukes and Nine Ministers have four horses,
with the outer horse on the left.
Under the Hàn system, the Nine Ministers were of the two-thousand-shí rank,
also having the outer horse on the right;
while Grand Administrators
had only four horses.
Those who were additionally granted the rank of fully two-thousand shí
then had the outer horse on the right.
Hence, "five horses" became an elegant term for a Grand Administrator.
The "Leisure Readings of Dùnzhāi" and "Forest of Learning" state:
"When Hàn court officials were sent on missions,
one horse was added for the Grand Administrator,
hence the term 'five horses'.
In "Pān Zǐzhēn's Remarks on Poetry," when ancients used the "five horses" allusion,
they mostly employed it in contexts of travel or departure.
For example, old Dù wrote in "Farewell to the Governor of Suízhōu for the Governor of Wàngzhōu":
"Two heavens open for a lavish farewell,
five horses gleam with splendid colors.
Here the distinction between host and guest's departure is clear.
Again, in "Seeing Off Lǐ Zǐzhōu,"
"When will the five horses arrive?"
In "To Yán Wǔ,"
"The five horses once knew the narrow path,"
and in "Seeing Senior Censor Jiǎ Off to Rǔzhōu,"
"In life, five horses are esteemed."
Lǐ Bái says:
"Do not linger with the five horses.
Cén Shēn says:
"Outside the gate, no need to urge the five horses.
Róng Yù
"When will the five horses court at Wèi's gates?"
Liǔ Zōngyuán
"Five horses aid the campaign steeds,"
Bái Jūyì
"Five horses have no way into the tavern."
Modern people routinely refer to Grand Administrators residing peacefully in their offices as "five horses,"
which in principle seems inappropriate.

The falcon soars above the banners,
the bear crouches before the carriage rail,

"Jìshì Xīnshū" The governor Gāo Jìtōng,
his rank shines with the falcon banners,

The Zhou official system had the position of county magistrate,
each in charge of the governance and decrees of their county,
and administering rewards and punishments in spring and autumn.
At that time when various states conquered each other,
they often made the conquered territories into counties,
thus counties were larger and commanderies smaller.
Therefore the commentary states:
"High-ranking ministers received counties,
lower-ranking ministers received commanderies,
as administrators of county towns.
According to Tongdian: In Lu they were called Zai,
as when Confucius served as Zhongdu Zai.
In Qi they were called Dafu,
as when King Wei of Qi enfeoffed the Jimo Dafu and executed the E Dafu.
In Chu they were called Yin, like Shen Yinshu,
who defended outside the Fangcheng walls,
serving as county magistrate.
They were also called Gong, like Ye Gong and Zhu Liang Gong.
According to Cefu: Generally, counties with over ten thousand households had magistrates called Ling,
those with fewer than ten thousand households had administrators called Zhang,
in marquis states they were called Xiang,
with similar ranks and positions,
all systems established by Qin,
and inherited by Han.

"I bestow upon you the golden seal and purple robe."
After he expressed gratitude again,

"Do you know the reason for receiving the purple robe?"
He answered,
"I do not know."
The emperor then ordered the placard on the palace pillar to be shown to him.

Píntóulú Píntóulú,
was an arhat and a minister of King Udayana.
He diligently practiced asceticism,
and the king permitted him to leave home to become a monk,
attaining the fruit of arhatship.
Later, whenever the king went out of the city
and entered the monastery to pay respects,
the sycophantic ministers, seeing that Píntóulú did not rise to welcome the king,
maliciously advised the king,
so the king intended to kill him.
When Píntóulú saw the king coming and entering the gate,
he immediately descended from his seat and took seven steps to greet him.
The king angrily said:
"Venerable One, you have always been difficult to move,
why do you now leave your seat to welcome me?"
He replied:
"Previously, the king came with a good heart,
so I did not rise to welcome you;
now you come with a malicious heart,
if I do not rise to welcome you,
I will surely be killed."
The king sighed and apologized to him,
however, Píntóulú predicted that because the king had caused a monk to rise to greet him,
he would surely lose his throne after seven days,
be captured by the neighboring country's uprising army,
and imprisoned with his feet shackled for twelve years.
This is found in the "Section on Respecting Monks" of the Dharmapada in the Four Part Vinaya.

"Original Biography": Lóngshù went to Southern India,
where the people mostly believed in meritorious deeds,
and the Patriarch preached the Dharma to them.
They said to one another:
"If a person has meritorious deeds,
that is the foremost in the world.
Merely speaking of Buddha-nature,
who can actually see it?"
The Patriarch said:
"If you wish to see Buddha-nature,
you must first remove self-conceit."
Those people asked:
"How big or small is Buddha-nature?"
The Patriarch said:
"Neither big nor small,
neither broad nor narrow,
without merit or retribution,
neither dying nor being born."
Hearing the superiority of this principle,
they all turned back to their initial resolve.
The Patriarch then manifested a body of self-mastery on his seat,
like a full moon disk; all
the assembly only heard the sound of the Dharma but did not see
the Patriarch's form. Among that assembly was an elder's
son named Jiātí Pó,
who said to the crowd:
"Do you recognize this appearance?"
The crowd said:
"What our eyes have never seen,
how dare we identify?"
Tí Pó said:
"This is the Venerable One
manifesting the substance of Buddha-nature,
showing its appearance to us.
How do I know this?
It is because in the formless samadhi,
the form is like a full moon.
The meaning of Buddha-nature
is vast and empty, clear and bright."
As soon as he finished speaking, the wheel-like appearance
immediately vanished, and he returned to his original seat.
Then he spoke a verse, saying:
"My body manifests the form of a full moon,
to represent the substance of all Buddhas.
Preaching the Dharma without form,
using it to distinguish what is not sound or form."
Hearing the verse,
that assembly suddenly awakened to non-arising.

Shakyamuni Buddha was born into a Kshatriya royal family,

Kāng Sēnghuì,
his ancestors were from Kāngjū,
when the great Dharma first spread to the land of Wú,
its influence was not yet complete.
Sēnghuì wished to make the Way flourish in Jiāngzuǒ and establish temples with images,
so he took his staff and traveled east,
arriving in the tenth year of Wú's Chìwū era.
He first reached Jiànyè, built a thatched hut, set up images, and practiced the Way.
At that time, the people of Wú had just seen a Buddhist monk,
and suspected it was a deceitful anomaly.
An official reported:
"A foreigner has entered our territory,
calling himself a Buddhist monk,
his clothing is unusual,
the matter should be investigated."
Sūn Quán said:
"In the past, Emperor Míng of Hàn dreamed of a spirit called Buddha,
could what he venerates be a legacy of that tradition?"
He then summoned Sēnghuì and questioned him about whether there were any spiritual manifestations.
Sēnghuì said:
"Since Rúlái passed away, suddenly over a thousand years have elapsed,
his relic bones (śarīra) shine with divine light beyond measure.
In the past, King Aśoka erected eighty-four thousand stūpas,
the establishment of stūpas and temples is a legacy of his transformative work."
Sēnghuì then purified himself through fasting in a quiet room,
placed a copper vase on a small table, burned incense, and reverently prayed.
After twenty-one days, he indeed obtained relics.
Sūn Quán was greatly amazed and convinced,
and immediately built a stūpa for them.
As this was the first Buddhist temple,
it was named Jiànchū Temple.
Consequently, the area was named Fótuó Lǐ.
From then on, the great Dharma flourished in Jiāngzuǒ.
Sūn Hào gathered his court officials,
and welcomed Sēnghuì with a carriage.
After Sēnghuì was seated,
Hào asked him:
"What does Buddhism clarify regarding
the retribution for good and evil?"
Sēnghuì replied:
"When an enlightened ruler instructs the world with filial piety and compassion,
then red birds soar and the Old Man star appears;
when he nurtures beings with benevolent virtue,
then sweet springs bubble forth and auspicious grain sprouts.
Good deeds have their auspicious signs, and so do evil ones.
Therefore, those who do evil in secret will be punished by ghosts,
those who do evil openly will be punished by people.
The Yì Jīng speaks of accumulated goodness leading to abundant blessings,
the Shī Jīng praises seeking fortune without deviance.
Although these are adages from the Confucian classics,
they are also the clear teachings of Buddhism."
Hào said:
"If that is so,
then the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius have already explained it,
what need is there for Buddhism?"
Sēnghuì said:
"What the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius said briefly indicates the visible traces,
whereas the Buddhist teachings exhaustively cover the profound and subtle.
Therefore, those who commit evil will suffer long torment in hell,
while those who cultivate goodness will enjoy eternal bliss in the heavenly palaces.
Using this to illustrate encouragement and deterrence,
is it not of great significance?"
Sūn Chùo composed a eulogy for him, saying:
"Sēnghuì, serene and austere,
was truly a man of noble substance, his heart free from petty attachments,
his spirit rich and overflowing.
He toiled diligently through the dark night,
rousing those who were especially benighted,
soaring far beyond with transcendent aim,
lofty and outstanding, he rose high above."

and thoroughly studying the scriptures of the wisdom seal.
Outstanding and uniquely distinguished,
he attained understanding from the heavenly mind.
At twenty-five, he left home to become a monk.
Whenever he attended lectures,
he excelled at highlighting the essential tenets,
though sometimes he overlooked detailed exegesis,
for which he was occasionally looked down upon by textual conservatives.
Xiè Ān, hearing of this, praised him, saying:
"This is like Jiǔfāng Yīn judging horses,
overlooking their color to grasp their excellence and spirit.
Liú Huī, Yīn Hào, Xǔ Xún, Xī Chāo, Sūn Chuò, Yuán Yǎnbó, and others,
all leading figures of their generation,
engaged in intimate associations beyond worldly dust.
Wáng Xīzhī, observing Zhī Dùn's astounding talent and literary brilliance,
then loosened his collar and untied his belt,
lingering with him unable to cease,
and subsequently invited him to reside at Língjiā Temple,
intending to keep him close.
Wáng Méng had long prepared refined arguments,
gathering his talents and rhetoric,
and went to visit Dùn,
speaking several hundred words,
confident that Dùn could not counter him.
Dùn calmly said:
"Venerable Sir, it has been many years since we parted,
yet your discourse has not advanced in the slightest.
Méng withdrew in shame,
then sighed and said:
"Truly, he is the Wáng Bì and Hé Yǎn of the black robe.
Later, Xī Chāo wrote to his relatives and friends, stating:
"Master Lín (Zhī Dùn) has penetrated the principles of the spirit,
profoundly discerning and uniquely enlightened.
For several hundred years,
he alone has carried forward the great Dharma,
ensuring that the true principle does not perish,
he is the only one.
After Dùn's death,
Chāo composed a preface and biography for him,
Yuán Hóng wrote an inscription and eulogy,
Zhōu Tánbǎo composed a funeral elegy,
and Sūn Chuò, in his "Discussion of Worthy Daoists,"
compared seven Buddhist monks to the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove,
likening Dùn to Xiàng Zǐqī (Xiàng Xiù),
remarking:
"Both Zhī Dùn and Xiàng Xiù elegantly esteemed Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi;
though the two lived in different times,
their style and preference for the profound were the same.
Later, the lofty scholar Dài Kuí passed by Dùn's grave,
and sighed, saying:
"The sound of his virtue has not yet faded,
yet the arched trees have already grown dense.
I hope his spiritual principles endure continuously,
not perishing together with the fluctuations of fate.
Dùn had a fellow student named Fǎ Chù,
whose understanding of principles reached spiritual heights,
and who died before Dùn.
Dùn lamented:
"In the past, Craftsman Shī discarded his axe after the man of Yǐng died,
and Yá Shēng broke his strings after Zhōng Zǐ's death.
Reflecting on myself and seeking such a person,
indeed, it is not in vain.
Now that this precious connection is hidden,
whatever I say finds no appreciation,
my heart is burdened with unspoken thoughts,
I too shall perish.
In the second year of the Níngkāng era,
I journeyed to Shànshí City Mountain,
where the master's mound lies.
The high tomb is overgrown with wild brambles,
the burial mounds transformed into aged thickets.
Though the traces of his existence have not vanished,
the man himself is long gone.
Reflecting on times past,
everything I touch stirs sorrow in my heart.
("Preface to a Poem at the Grave of Master Wáng Xún")
Fótú Chéng,
whose surname was Bó,
arrived in Luòyáng in the fourth year of the Yǒngjiā period.
He aspired to propagate the great Dharma,
excelled in reciting divine incantations,
and could command spirits and entities.
By applying a mixture of sesame oil and fat to his palm,
events occurring a thousand miles away
would become clearly visible in his palm,
as if face-to-face,
and he could also enable purified individuals to see them.
Furthermore, he interpreted bell sounds to predict events,
with every prediction proving accurate.
To the left of his left breast was an orifice,
measuring four to five inches in circumference,
penetrating through to his abdomen.
At times, his intestines would emerge from it;
when he stuffed the orifice with cotton,
and wished to read at night,
he would pull out the cotton,
and the entire room would become brightly illuminated.
On fasting days, he would go to the water's edge,
draw out his intestines to wash them,
and then return them inside.
When turmoil struck the capital,
he secretly retreated to the wilderness.
Shí Lè, being formidable and prone to killing,
was introduced to him through General Guō Mò, who briefly presented him to Shí Lè.
Shí Lè held him in great reverence and trust.
When Shí Hǔ ascended the throne,
he also revered Fótú Chéng as his teacher,
honoring him as the Great Monk.
He knew the day of his own death.
According to the "Separate Biography," he died at the Yègōng Temple.
Later, a monk from Luózhōu came,
claiming to have seen Fótú Chéng heading west into the pass.
Shí Jìlóng had his tomb excavated to inspect it,
finding only a stone and no corpse.
Shí Jìlóng cursed, saying:
"The stone
represents me;
burying me and leaving,
I am about to die.
The following year, Shí Jìlóng died.
According to the "Gāosēng Zhuàn," Fótú Chéng
was a man who attained sainthood.
Light emanated from the orifice in his breast,
eliminating the need for lamp or torch illumination.
By interpreting bells and reflecting in his palm,
he sat observing the signs of success and failure.
Two rulers served him as a deity,
and all officials revered him as a Buddha.
He foretold the heir apparent's duality,
and earlier indicated the calamity of Shí Cōng.
When disaster arose and omens appeared,
he admonished Shí Hǔ that excessive punishments and harsh laws would shorten his life.
In the "Guǎng Hóngmíng Biànhuò Piān," a stele at the ancient Zhōngqiū City Temple west of Nèiqiū County in Xíngzhōu,
erected in the fifth year of Guāngchū under Later Zhào's Shí Lè,
states:
"The Great Monk Fótú Chéng Yuànzhě
was the eldest son of the minor ruler of Jìbīn in the great land of India.
His original surname was Wēn,
and the reason for this designation
was his intent to moisten and govern the state,
bestowing grace without exclusion,
hence he was named Wēn.
According to the 'Gāosēng Zhuàn,' 'Míngsēng Zhuàn,' and 'Jìn Shū Yìshù Zhuàn,'
Fótú Chéng did not have this surname.
Now it is said his surname was Wēn,
which is an alternate account.
From 'Fēngshì Wénjiàn.'"
Qíyù was
a native of India,
unrestrained by nature and indifferent to worldly conventions,
making him unfathomable to others.
During the turmoil of war in Luòyáng,
he bid farewell to return to India.
In Luòyáng, there was a monk named Zhú Fǎxíng,
an eminent disciple.
People at the time compared him to Lè Lìng,
and he thus requested of Qíyù:
"You, Venerable One, are an enlightened monk;
I hope you will leave us a teaching as an eternal admonition."
Qíyù said:
"Gather everyone together."
Once the assembly had gathered,
Qíyù ascended the high seat
and said:
"Guard your speech and restrain your body,
be mindful not to commit any evils;
cultivate all that is good—
thus you may transcend the world."
Having spoken, he fell into meditative silence.
Fǎxíng approached him again, saying:
"I hoped the Venerable One would impart something unheard of,
like the meaning of such verses.
Even an eight-year-old child can recite this;
it is not what we expect from an enlightened one."
Qíyù laughed and said:
"Though an eight-year-old may recite it, a centenarian may not practice it—
what benefit is there in mere recitation?
People all know to revere the enlightened,
but do not realize that through practice one attains enlightenment themselves.
Alas!
Though my words are few,
those who practice them benefit greatly."
Thereupon, he took his leave.
Hundreds of people each invited Qíyù to a meal,
and he agreed to go to all.
The next morning,
five hundred households each had a Qíyù present;
at first, each thought he had come exclusively to them.
Later, upon comparing notes,
they realized he had miraculously manifested in multiple places.
《Gāo》 It is said that Shì Dàoqīn went to Jìngshān,
and when questioned about the Way, he responded spontaneously,
yet his answers always reached the ultimate truth.
Liú Zhōngzhōu once requested a verse on the mind,
so Dàoqīn had him hold an incense burner and listen,
repeating multiple times: "Refrain from all evils,
practice all good deeds."
Liú said:
"Even a three-foot-tall child knows this."
Dàoqīn replied:
"A three-foot-tall child may know it,
but a hundred-year-old man may fail to practice it."
This has been regarded as a profound saying ever since.
《Yǒu Yáng》 The response of Master Wūkē of Hángzhōu to Bái Jūyì was similar.
《Shì Jiàn》
Shì Dào'ān,
surname Wèi,
from Chángshān Fúliǔ.
His intellect was divinely quick,
but his appearance was very unattractive.
When he arrived at Yè,
Fótú Chéng saw him and found him remarkable,
thus serving Chéng as his master.
Later, to avoid danger, he fled south to Xiāngyáng,
where at the time Xiāngyáng's Xí Zào Chǐ was renowned,
mastering the art of eloquence and insight.
At that time, Xiān Xiè was already acquainted with Ān,
his high reputation having long since led to exchanges of letters.
Upon hearing of Ān's arrival,
he immediately went to pay his respects.
Once seated,
he declared that the world regarded Zào Chǐ,
Ān replied:
"I am the one who is Dào'ān."
Those present considered it a renowned response.
Zào Chǐ wrote to Xiè Ān, saying:
"Having come here and met Shì Dào'ān,
it is truly superior to ordinary Daoists,
regretful that you could not witness the same day."
He often expressed his wish to converse,
Xiàowǔ sent an envoy to communicate,
and also issued an edict saying:
"Master Ān's intellect and disposition are impressive,
his elegance is remarkable,
he resides in the Dao, educating the common people,
combining exemplary achievements,
how could he merely guide the present,
but also nurture future generations."
He passed away in the tenth year of Tàiyuán,
Luóshì in the west heard of Ān's reputation,
believed him to be a sage of the East,
and always revered him from afar.
Initially,
when Ān was born, there was a skin patch about a foot wide on his left arm,
attached to his arm, it could be felt,
but it could not be removed;
people of the time referred to him as the "Print-Handed Bodhisattva."
"High"
Initially,
monks of the Wei and Jin dynasties adopted their masters' surnames,
thus each had different surnames.
Sēng Dào'ān believed that the origin of all great masters
was none other than Śākyamuni,
so he adopted "Shì" (Śākyamuni) as the surname.
Later, upon obtaining the Ekottara Āgama,
which states that when four rivers enter the sea they lose their original names,
and people from the four castes who become monks
are all called Śākyas,
since this perfectly matched the scripture,
it became the permanent practice.
Jiūmóluóshí,
which means "Child Longevity,"
had a clear and bright spirit,
standing proudly above the crowd.
He grasped opportunities with understanding,
rarely having an equal.
The various kingdoms of the Western Regions were moved and subdued by his divine brilliance,
and whenever he came to preach,
the kings would kneel for a long time beside his seat,
allowing Shí to step on them to ascend.
During the Jiànyuán era of Fú Jiān,
the Grand Astrologer reported:
"A star has appeared in the foreign regions' division,
indicating that a great virtuous and wise person will enter to assist the Middle Kingdom.
Jiān said:
"I have heard that in the Western Regions there is Jiūmóluóshí,
and in Xiāngyáng there is the śramaṇa Dào'ān,
could it not be them?
He immediately sent General Lǚ Guāng to campaign west against Qiūcí,
Guāng came with Shí,
but upon hearing that Jiān had been killed by Yáo Chāng,
he occupied Xīliáng until Yáo Xīng,
destroyed Western Lǚ.
Shí was welcomed into Cháng'ān,
treated with the rites of a National Teacher,
and revered as a deity.
When engaged in conversation face to face,
they would linger all day;
delving into subtleties and exhausting principles,
they would toil year-round without tiring.
The *Gāo* records that he once lectured on scriptures at Cǎotáng Temple,
with Xīng and court officials, great virtuous śramaṇas, over a thousand people,
solemnly observing and listening.
Luóshí suddenly descended from the high seat,
and said to Xīng:
"There are two small children climbing on my shoulders,
desiring to be hindered, needing a woman.
Xīng then summoned palace maidens to present to him,
and with one union, two sons were born.
Xīng once said to Luóshí:
"Great Master, your intelligence and transcendent understanding,
are unmatched in the world,
how can we let the Dharma seed have few heirs?
So he forced him to accept ten courtesans,
after which he no longer stayed in the monks' quarters,
but in a separate residence.
The *Jìn Shū* notes that whenever he came to preach,
he often first said of himself:
"It is like a lotus born from foul mud,
only pick the lotus flower,
do not take the foul mud.
"The *Gāo* records that when the Indian Mitrayaśas reached Gūzāng,
hearing that Shí had accepted Qín palace maidens,
sighed and said:
"Shí is like fine silk,
how can he be made to enter thorny bushes?
Shí heard that Yaśas had come,
and urged the Qín king to welcome him.
When Yaśas arrived,
the king greeted him at the suburbs,
arranged a separate fine residence for him,
providing offerings as for a king.
Yaśas accepted nothing at all.
When it was time for alms-round,
he ate only one meal a day.
The *Shàn Pípóshā Lùn* mentions he had a red beard,
and was thus called the Red-Bearded Pípóshā.
The *Shì Jiàn* records this.
During the time of Xiàowǔ,
the monk Shì Huìwéi was strict and pure in his precepts,
often meditating in the mountains.
Later, due to cold snow,
a young woman came seeking shelter,
with a gentle and charming appearance,
and bright clothing.
She claimed to be a heavenly maiden,
saying that, because the esteemed monk had virtue,
heaven had sent her to offer comfort.
Through conversation,
she sought to persuade and move his mind.
Huìwéi remained resolute and unyielding,
his mind undisturbed.
He then said to the woman:
"My heart is like dead ashes,
there is no exploit to test the leather pouch."
The woman then ascended to the clouds and departed,
looking back with a sigh:
"The sea can be exhausted,
Mount Sumeru can be overturned,
yet the esteemed monk maintains his will with determination and integrity."
"Shì Shì Tōngjiàn"
Dharma Master Dù Fǎhù's original surname was Zhī,
he extensively studied the Six Classics,
and immersed his mind in the Seven Texts.
Although worldly affairs brought criticism or praise,
he never harbored them in his heart.
He resided for generations in Dūnhuáng,
and upon his death, his teachings and influence spread widely.
People of the time all called him the Bodhisattva of Dūnhuáng.
From "Biographies of Eminent Monks"
Dàochǎng Temple's monk Juéxián,
whose demeanor and conduct were simple and unadorned,
differed from the Chinese customs,
yet his aspirations and charm were pure and far-reaching,
possessing an elegant and profound bearing.
Master Shì of the city, monk Sēngbì, wrote to the śramaṇa Bǎolín, saying:
"The Chan master of Dàochǎng Temple,
has a profound natural disposition,
much like Wáng Hé of India,
a man of refined character and grace.
Tánmó Mìduō,
meaning Dharma Excellence,
was profound and wise.
He thoroughly understood the rituals and regulations,
and was born with connected eyebrows,
thus known in the world as the Eyebrow-Joining Chán Master.
Shān Zhú Fǎyǒu,
with resolute will and strong integrity,
was well-versed in numerous classics.
He once studied the Abhidharma under Zhú Dàoqián,
and could recite it after just one night. Dàoqián remarked: "To glance at a sutra and chant it recalls the praised ancients;
if Śākyamuni were to revive in the great Jin dynasty,
he would surely choose you as one of the five hundred arhats."
Zhú Dàoqián,
courtesy name Fǎshēn,
was regarded by Jiǎnpíng as a model for both monastic and lay communities.
Zhī Dùn wrote in a letter to the monk from Goguryeo:
"The venerable Zhú Fǎshēn,
a disciple of Duke Liú of Zhōngzhōu,
embodies the Way with unwavering integrity,
synthesizing both monastic and lay teachings.
When he resided in the capital,
he upheld the Dharma net,
respected by both insiders and outsiders,
truly a master in propagating the Dharma.
Once, in Jiǎnpíng's gathering,
Liú Huī asked:
"Why does the reverend frequent vermilion gates (noble households)?"
He replied:
"You yourself see them as vermilion gates,
but to this humble monk, it is like visiting a thatched hut."
Zhú Fǎtài,
when young studied together with Dào'ān,
went to the capital and resided at the Wǎguān Temple,
Jiǎnwén deeply respected him.
Commander-in-chief Sūn Qià,
Dōngtíng Wáng Xún, Grand Tutor Xiè Ān,
all revered and respected him immensely.
After his death,
Xiàowǔ's edict stated:
"Master Tài's teachings spread in all directions,
his influence flows to future generations."
Sūn Chuò's poem states:
"Chilling winds rustle through the forest,
strings echo gracefully through the valley."
Fǎtài cultivated virtues without action.
Zhù Dàoyī studied under Tài Gong,
his thoughts penetrating the profound depths,
his literary talent rich and abundant,
his reputation spreading far and wide,
his discipline pure and strict.
Monks and nuns from all directions relied on him for guidance.
People of the time called him the Metropolitan Supervisor of the Nine Provinces.
Sūn Chuò composed for him
a eulogy:
"He gallops through debates and persuasions,
his words indeed never empty.
Only this Master Yī,
is abundantly sufficient.
Like a spring garden,
both fragrant and blooming.
How lush are the branches,
the stems and twigs spreading widely.
Tài had a disciple named Tán Yī,
who also possessed refined demeanor and conduct.
People of the time called Tán Yī 'Great Yī',
and Dàoyī 'Little Yī',
their renowned virtue succeeding one another, revered by contemporary discourse.
Sēnglǎng, the monk from India, and the recluse Zhāng Zhōng shared a deep friendship amidst the woods,
journeying together to the Jīnyú Valley of Mount Tài.
This valley was once plagued by frequent tiger attacks,
forcing people to travel in groups carrying staffs.
After Lǎng settled there,
the fierce beasts submitted and grew tame,
allowing safe passage day and night,
unhindered for both monks and laypeople.
The common people praised this endlessly with admiration,
thus honoring the noble monk
—to this day, Jīnyú Valley is still called Lǎnggōng Valley.
Shì Huìyuǎn,
from a young age loved books,
brilliant in the Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ,
his nature was broad and grand,
his insight clear and outstanding.
《Gāo》 He traveled to study in Xǔ and Luò,
at twenty-one wished to cross south to study with Fàn Xuānzǐ,
but the road was blocked and impassable,
met Shì Dào'ān and took him as his teacher,
removed his hairpin and shaved his head,
diligently sought the Buddhist canon.
Shì Tányì often provided him with lamp and candle expenses,
his recitation and discernment were profound and far-reaching,
his lofty enlightenment touched the abstruse.
Ān often sighed, saying:
"The Way flows to the Eastern Land,
will it lie with Yuǎn?
After Xiāngyáng fell,
he shook his staff and traveled south,
built a dwelling on the sacred mountain,
from age sixty never again left the mountain.
His fame spread to the desert regions of that country,
the monastic community all said that in the Han land there was a Mahāyāna śramaṇa.
Whenever they arrived,
they would burn incense and bow in reverence,
always facing east to pay respects.
《Zhāng Yě Yuǎnfǎshī Míng》
Master Yuǎn,
never saw guests beyond the Hǔxī stream.
When the Daoist Wú Xiūjìng and Táo Yuānmíng entered the mountain to visit the master,
he escorted them out, holding hands and conversing together,
unintentionally crossing the Hǔxī stream.
The three looked at each other and laughed heartily.
People later depicted this scene as "The Three Laughters of Lúshān" painting.
From Shìshì Tōngjiàn.
Master Huìyuǎn resided on Mount Lú for thirty years,
his shadow never leaving the mountain,
his footsteps never entering the mundane world.
His younger brother Huìchí also possessed lofty conduct;
the community numbered in the thousands,
with Huìchí ranked first among them.
Among the community members whose fame and deeds were particularly distinguished,
there were eighteen individuals.
Lay practitioners included Liú Yímín, Léi Cìzōng, Zhōu Xùzhī, Zōng Bǐng, Zhāng Yě, and Zhāng Quán;
monastic masters included Huìyǒng, Huìchí, and Dàojìng;
from Jìbīn were the Venerables Buddhabhadra and Bátuóluó;
others such as Huìruì, Tánshùn, Táncháng, Dàobǐng, and Tánshēn,
typically left home in childhood,
cultivating together in the Pure Land Society.
Later came Zhú Dàoshēng and the Venerable Jìbīn Buddhayàoshè,
who entered the mountain in the eighteenth year of the Yìxī era,
by which time the Jīng Society had existed for twenty-six or twenty-seven years.
They were still included in the Biographies of the Eighteen Worthies that endure to this day,
their pure breeze still refreshing people.
Furthermore, Táo Yuānmíng left because the mountain lacked wine,
Xiè Língyùn was barred from joining the society due to an impure mind,
and Lù Xiūjìng once sought instruction from Master Yuǎn;
today, twenty-one individuals are traditionally recorded.
Among Yuǎn's disciples in virtue and conduct were also Dàozǔ, Sēngqiān, and Dàoliú,
all of them talented, righteous, and outstanding.
Huì Chí,
the younger brother of Master Yuǎn,
was six chǐ tall,
with a distinguished and spirited demeanor.
He served Dào'ān,
studied all the scriptures extensively,
mastered the Five Collections with ease,
and accompanied Yuǎn to reside on Mount Lú. Among their disciples, all were outstanding, with a following of three thousand,
and Huì Chí was regarded as the foremost.
Wáng Xún wrote in a letter to Fàn Nìng:
"Who is superior, Master Yuǎn or Master Chí?"
Fàn replied in his letter:
"Truly, they are worthy elder and younger brothers."
At that time, monks all admired and respected him from afar,
and those who entered Huì Chí's hall
were said to have ascended the Dragon Gate.
In the third year of the Zhènghé era of the Sòng dynasty,
Jiāzhōu reported that beside the road in its jurisdiction stood a great ancient tree,
which had been broken by the wind.
Inside was a monk,
in meditation, his beard and hair,
covering his body, his fingernails coiled around him.
Emperor Huīzōng ordered him carried by sedan chair to the capital,
and commanded the Western Regions' Master of the Tripitaka,
to awaken him from samādhi with a golden chime.
Then he asked from which era he came,
the monk said:
"I am the disciple of Master Huìyuǎn of Dōnglín,
named Jíchí. While traveling,
I entered samādhi inside a tree at Éméi.
Is Master Yuǎn well?"
The Master replied:
"Master Yuǎn was from the Jìn dynasty,
and passed away seven hundred years ago."
Chí spoke no more,
the Master asked:
"Since you have come here,
what do you intend to do?"
Chí said:
"I shall re-enter samādhi in Chénliú County."
The Emperor composed three gāthās,
ordering his portrait painted and distributed.
The gāthās said:
"For seven hundred years this ancient awl,
who in samādhi knows the news?
Better to return west with a single shoe,
why trouble wood for skin in life and death.
The sentient body is not insentient,
each and every one is in samādhi.
Understanding Bodhi is originally without tree,
no need to toil asking Lú Néng."
From "Transmission of the Lamp"
Monk Sēngzhào,
a native of Jīngzhào,
excelled in the study of the Mahayana sutras,
and was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka,
with profound and subtle talent and thought,
and skilled in discourse.
He responded to opportunities and blunted sharp arguments,
never leaving any unresolved.
Later, when Kumārajīva arrived at Gūzāng,
Zhào traveled from afar to follow him,
and was greatly admired.
Zhào composed the "Treatise on the Prajñā of Non-Knowing,"
totaling over two thousand words.
He presented it to Kumārajīva,
who read it and praised it highly,
saying to Zhào:
"The exposition is impeccable,
and your writing deserves mutual respect."
At that time, the recluse of Lúshān, Liú Yímín, saw this treatise by Zhào,
and sighed, saying:
"Who would have thought that among the robed clergy,
there would be another Píngshū."
He then presented it to Master Yuǎn,
who stroked his desk and exclaimed:
"This is unprecedented."
They then studied and savored it together,
engaging in further exchanges.
《Six》In the twenty-first year of the Tàihé era of the Wei dynasty, an edict stated:
"Master Kumārajīva can be said to have a spirit emerging from the five talents,
and a will entering the four practices."
Shì Sēngruì,
humble and inwardly sharp,
his learning competed with the times,
mastering the five gates of meditation,
and excelling in entering the six states of tranquility.
Yáo Sōng regarded him as the pine and cypress of Yèwèi,
but when Yáo Xīng met him, he observed Ruì's elegant demeanor,
refined and profound in speech.
Xīng was greatly pleased,
and later said to Sōng:
"He is a paragon for all under heaven,
why limit him to the pine and cypress of Yèwèi?
Shì Huìlóng,
devoted his mind to the Buddhist teachings,
mastered numerous scriptures,
and his thoughts penetrated beyond mere words,
excelling in pure discourse.
Wherever earlier scholars had encountered obstructions,
he illuminated and expanded upon them,
making everything clear and comprehensible.
Rǔnán Zhōu Yóng observed him,
saying:
"Lóng gōng is serene and unadorned,
like pines and bamboos beneath the frost."
Shì Fǎdù
traveled to study in the northern regions,
mastering all the scriptures.
At that time, there was a monk named Fǎzhào Róng whose conduct was pure and ascetic,
his reputation equal to Fǎdù's,
but his learning surpassed him.
Thus, contemporaries called them
the Two Sages of the Northern Mountain.
Qiúnà Bámó,
whose name means "Armor of Merit."
In the first month of the eighth year of the Yuánjiā era,
he arrived at Jiànyè.
Emperor Wén summoned him for an audience,
greeting him with earnest inquiries,
and then said:
"I, your disciple, have often wished to uphold fasting
and refrain from killing, but constrained by serving others with my person,
I have been unable to follow this aspiration.
Since you, Dharma Master, have come from afar, traversing ten thousand li to convert this country,
what teachings will you impart to me?"
Bámó replied:
"The Way lies in the heart, not in outward actions;
the Dharma is realized by oneself, not by others.
Moreover, the practices of an emperor and a commoner differ.
A commoner is of lowly status and humble name,
his words and commands lack authority;
if he does not practice austerities personally,
what use would it be?
An emperor regards the four seas as his home,
and the myriad people as his children.
Uttering one kind word brings joy to men and women;
implementing one benevolent policy harmonizes humans and spirits.
If punishments do not violate Heaven's mandate,
and corvée labor does not exhaust the people's strength,
then wind and rain will come in due season,
cold and heat will follow their cycles,
the hundred grains will flourish abundantly,
and mulberries and hemp will grow lush.
In this way, upholding fasting is also great,
and refraining from killing is also vast.
Must one then miss half a day's meal
or spare the life of one bird
to be considered broadly compassionate?"
The emperor then patted his armrest
and sighed, saying:
"Common people are deluded by distant principles,
while monks are stuck in proximate teachings.
Those deluded by distant principles
say the ultimate Way is empty talk;
those stuck in proximate teachings
cling rigidly to texts and chapters.
As for the words of the Dharma Master,
they truly enlighten and illuminate,
allowing one to speak of the connection between Heaven and humanity."
He then ordered Bámó to reside at the Qíhuán Temple,
providing him with generous support.
《Gāo》 In the sixth year of the Jiàndé era of Emperor Wǔ of the Northern Zhōu dynasty,
the monk Dàolín submitted a memorial requesting to hold Dharma services.
The emperor said:
"You claim karma does not contradict principle,
that all have the potential to enter sagehood;
nature is not beyond karma,
and the Way connects with the ordinary.
This shows the Way is omnipresent.
Encompassing both ordinary and sage, thus the teaching has no distinction between Confucius and Śākyamuni.
Vainly exalting such words,
forms penetrate both monastic and lay life,
yet you merely add the adornment of shaving.
Thus it is known that the emperor is none other than the Tathāgata,
so the sixteen-foot golden statue should cease;
princes and dukes are Bodhisattvas,
making Mañjuśrī unnecessary.
The elderly can serve as senior monks,
without needing Piṇḍola.
Benevolence and kindness truly embody dāna-pāramitā,
why borrow from renouncing the kingdom?
Harmony and peace are the foremost pure monks,
why trouble with the posadha ceremony?
Integrity and diligence complete the precepts,
why must one receive ordination?
Frugality and simplicity truly signify few desires,
no need for dhūta practices;
vegetarian eating is excellent fasting,
why trouble with grain abstinence?
Releasing life wonderfully equals selflessness,
what need to explain emptiness?
Forgetting merit fully surpasses the Mahāyāna,
why seek prajñā?
Civil and military are precisely the two wisdoms,
without contemplating emptiness and existence;
expedient means ultimately achieve skill,
why await supernatural transformations?
Promotion in office truly is prediction of Buddhahood,
no less than attaining the fruit;
ranks and emoluments together gain heaven,
why await the upper realms?
Punishments and executions manifest hell,
without pointing to niraya;
treating the people as one's children can be called great compassion,
taking the four seas as home is identical to the Dharma realm.
Governing with principle is no different from salvation,
bringing peace and happiness to the people is surely relieving suffering.
Eliminating the cruel and harmful is subduing demons,
ruling the world truly constitutes attaining the Way.
Vast and boundless, how different from the Pure Land?
Orderly and majestic, how inferior to Kapilavastu?
You hold heterodox views and wrongly generate one-sided attachments,
in terms of actual affairs, where is it not the Way?"
《Guǎng Hóng Míng》
Dào Shēng of the Zhú family,
possessed profound and extraordinary intellect,
with speech as pure as pearls and jade.
He traveled to Cháng'ān,
studying under Master Shī,
later returning to the capital and residing at Qīngyuán Temple,
becoming a leading Dharma master of his time.
Emperor Wén of the Sòng dynasty personally attended a gathering with the assembly, sitting on floor mats,
and food was served after a long while,
making everyone suspect it was already evening.
The Emperor said:
"It should be just midday."
Dào Shēng responded:
"The bright sun adorns the sky,
and the Son of Heaven says it is just midday,
how could it not be midday?"
Thereupon, he took his bowl and began to eat.
The entire assembly followed suit,
if not admiring his pivotal insight,
he attained the essence of the five greatnesses.
Fàn Tài and Yán Yánzhī both respected his moral conduct,
and sought his guidance on the Dharma.
Initially, Dào Shēng studied alongside Master Ruì, Huì Yán, and Huì Guān, and they were equally renowned.
Hence, people of the time said:
"Shēng and Ruì emanate natural authenticity,
Yán and Guān's wisdom flows from the depths,
Huì Yì advances with vigor,
while Kòu Yuān remains silent and reserved."
Wáng Wēi compared Dào Shēng to Guō Línzōng,
and thus composed a biography for him,
to honor his enduring virtues.
In recent times, there was also Shì Huìshēng,
who likewise resided at Lóngguāng Temple,
adhering to a vegetarian diet and excelling in numerous scriptures,
and skilled in both cursive and clerical script.
Contemporaries, noting their succession at the same temple,
referred to them as the Great and Little Shēng.
The "Gāo" records: Beside the Thousand-Man Seat at Hǔqiū,
there are stones that nod.
The "Shí Dào Sì Fān Zhì" states:
"Shēng Gōng expounded the Dao here,
but none believed him,
so he gathered stones as disciples,
and when he discussed the ultimate truth with them,
the stones all nodded."

Shì Dàowēn entered Mount Lú,
studying under Master Yuǎn.
Later he went to Cháng'ān,

During the Yuánjiā era he returned,

Fū replied:

Shào personally went to visit him,

I would appoint you as my Assistant Inspector."
Dàowēn responded:
"The donor is using shackles to tempt people."

Shì Xuángāo,

The monk Huìlín once wrote "On Equal Goodness",

Faith and obedience should stand equally with compassion.
Emperor Wén saw the treatise and admired it,

he consequently participated in important state affairs,

Guests gathered around him like spokes to a hub,

Seven or eight banquet tables,
were always filled with guests for Lín.
He wore high clogs,

In the Western Qín, there was the kingdom of Gāochāng,
where Master Huì Sōng comprehensively understood the Hīnayāna teachings,
and was acclaimed in his time as the Confucius of the Abhidharma.
The monk Huìshǐ, also known as Tánshǐ, initially studied under Kumārajīva,
and was widely revered by people in the Three Capital Regions.
When Emperor Wǔ of Liú Sòng destroyed the Later Qín,
he left his son Yì
to guard Cháng'ān,
but they were pursued and defeated by Hèlián Qūgài of the Xià.
Both clergy and laypeople were massacred and buried in pits,
yet Huìshǐ remained unharmed by the blades.
Furious, Qūgài
summoned Huìshǐ before him
and struck him with his own sword.
Still unable to harm him,
he then rejoiced and apologized in Tǒngwàn.
Huìshǐ later arrived in the capital,
where he provided extensive guidance.
According to the "Wèi Shí Lǎo Zhì": When Emperor Tàiwǔ suppressed Buddhism,
no monks remained within the territory.
Suddenly, Huìshǐ appeared at the palace gate with his staff,
and an official reported:
"A Daoist with feet whiter than his face
has entered through the gate."
Tāo ordered him executed according to military law, but repeated attempts failed to injure him,
so they hurriedly reported this to Tāo.
Enraged,
Tāo personally struck him with his own sword,
yet his body showed no injury,
except for a mark where the sword landed,
like a cloth thread.
At that time, tigers were kept in cages in the northern garden,
and Tāo ordered Huìshǐ to be fed to them,
but the tigers all crouched hidden,
daring not approach.
When tested with a Heavenly Master near the cage, the tigers roared immediately,
greatly astonishing Tàishǐ,
who invited Huìshǐ to the hall, bowed repeatedly,
apologized and granted permission,
restoring the teachings.
From practicing meditation until his death,
it is said that for over fifty years,
he never lay down to sleep.
Sometimes when walking,
even through mud and dust,
his feet remained unstained,
growing even whiter and brighter,
earning him the name "White-Footed Ascetic."
From "Zhì Gāo Shì Tōng."
The monk Róngjué Tánmó,
was most skilled in the practice of meditation,
expounded the Nirvana Sutra and the Avataṃsaka Sutra,
with a following of a thousand disciples.
The Indian monk Bodhi, upon seeing him, paid him respects,
and all hailed him as a Bodhisattva.
Liúzhī, who elucidated Buddhist doctrines,
was renowned in the Western Regions,
and was hailed by various foreign peoples as an Arhat.
He was versed in the Wei language and clerical script,
expounded the Daśabhūmika Sūtra,
the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, and twenty-three other sutras and treatises.
Even the transcription of golden words in stone chambers
or the transmission of the true teaching in thatched halls could not surpass this.
When Liúzhī read Tánmó's "Chapters on the Meaning of the Great Vehicle,"
he would snap his fingers in admiration each time,
exclaiming how profound it was,
and then transcribe it into foreign script,
spreading it to the Western Regions.
Monks often bowed reverently toward the east,
hailing Tánmó as the Sage of the East.
Records of the Buddhist Monasteries
Sēng Mín, a native of Sùsānqiānliáng,
was a descendant of the Great Emperor of Wú.
His spirit was profoundly insightful,
standing out uniquely among the masses,
his nature was exceptionally illuminating and thorough,
and his words were always canonical and precise.
Upon arriving in Jīnlíng, Wáng Zhòngbǎo of Lángyá, Zhāng Sīguāng of Wú, and Xiè Tiǎo,
who were the most learned of their time,
pure and genuine in their uniqueness,
all sought friendship with him,
offering gifts of white silk belts.
During the Tiānjiàn era,
he traveled to the capital,
where he received exceptionally high regard and treatment.
Zhāng Chōng, the governor of Wú Commandery, and Xiè Lǎn, the governor of Wúxīng,
submitted petitions to invite him,
and an imperial edict was issued for his dispatch.
Boats from the two commaderies filled his gate to welcome and await him,
while scholars from the capital gathered like clouds and mist following him,
and along the way, no local official failed to greet him at the outskirts.
Cài Zūn, the governor of Jìnlíng, came out to wait at the gate to welcome him,
and sighed, saying:
"In the past, Confucius was the uncrowned king in Zhōu,
and now Lord Mín is the uncrowned king in Liáng."

The monk Bǎo Gōng, who foresaw the three periods of time,
was ugly in appearance,
but astute in mind.
Past and future,
he foresaw the three periods of time.
His words seemed like prophecies that could not be understood,
only after events occurred were they verified as true.
Empress Dowager Hú heard of him,
and asked him about worldly affairs.
Bǎo Gōng said:
"Hold millet and call to the chickens 'zhū zhū'."
At that time, no one could understand it.
After the first year of the Jiànyì era,
when she was killed by Ěrzhū Róng,
his words were finally verified.
At that time, there was also a man from Luòyáng named Zhào Fǎhé who asked whether he would receive an official rank sooner or later.
Bǎo Gōng said:
"Large bamboo arrows need no feathers,
hastily build the east wing house."
At the time, no one understood his meaning.
After more than ten days,
Fǎhé's father passed away.
The large bamboo referred to the mourning staff, the east wing house
was the mourning hut where he composed the Twelve Terrestrial Branches song.
In the end, it was just as he had said.

Emperor Wǔ of Liáng deeply revered and served him,

The emperor was pleased,

Shì Dàochāo's surname was Lù.
In his youth, he was known for diligence and sincerity,

and got along very joyfully with Shídé and Hánshānzǐ.
Fēnggàn went out wandering,
just as Lǘ Qiū Yìn was appointed governor of Táizhōu.
Guóqīng said:
"Master Fēng sprinkled pure water,
and in a moment it dispelled the affliction,
asked where he came from,
he said Tiāntāi Guóqīng."
Said:
"Are there any virtuous ones there?"
Said:
"Seeing them, one does not recognize them;
recognizing them, one does not see them.
If you wish to see them,
you must not grasp at forms.
Hánshān is Mañjuśrī,
hiding his traces at Guóqīng;
Shídé is Samantabhadra,
appearing like a poor fellow,
and seeming mad,
working in the temple storehouse courtyard,
tending the fire in the kitchen."
After speaking, he took his leave.
When Lǘ Qiū took office and entered the temple,
he saw the two in the kitchen and bowed to them,
to the astonishment of the temple monks.
The two said:
"Fēnggàn talks too much."
Then arm in arm they went out,
and never returned to the temple.
Lǘ Qiū went again to Hányán to pay respects and inquire,
but they shrank into the crevices of the rocky cave,
so he ordered the monk Dàoqiào to search for their remaining writings,
and only from the forests and village house walls were over three hundred pieces copied.
There is
"What is there at the courtyard's edge,
white clouds embracing secluded rocks"
among the lines,
clearly of elegant style.
Now below the cliff stands a stone pavilion,
and the pavilion is named 'Secluded Rocks.'
When Shídé was at the temple during the monks' Posadha,
he drove an ox to the front of the hall,
clapped his hands and laughed heartily,
then the Vinaya master scolded him:
"Madman."
Shídé said:
"I am not herding oxen,
these are mostly the temple's administrative monks."
He called out each by their deceased monks' Dharma names,
and each ox responded and passed by.
The whole assembly was stunned,
feeling the Bodhisattvas' manifested traces.
At the time of liberation,
Dàoqiào compiled Hánshān's verses on the land deity hall wall,
and found Shídé's gāthās attached to Hánshān's collection.

Lǐ replied:

Cháng said:

Lǐ bowed his head speechless,
then pondered again and sighed in admiration.

Alas, beneath the great fire,

a land of warfare,

Formerly, King Huì of Liáng once said to Mèng Kē:
"How to benefit my state?"
This shows that the transformation through ritual deference
was clearly no match for the heart that loves profit.
Moreover, Liáng is a thousand miles from Lǔ,
yet even nearby paths differ,
how much more so a hundred and eight thousand miles?
King of Liáng and Mèngzǐ were men of the same era,
yet their hearts differed;
how much more so the venerable Śākyamuni?
That Mèngzǐ belonged to an era when culture was not yet lost,
yet could not promote the Way of the Unadorned King.
Now the venerable lives in an age far removed from the sage,
yet ultimately can practice the teaching of the Dharma King.
If not for the inner purity of the three karmas,
and outer clarity from the six dusts,
transforming others through utterly impartial conduct,
who could receive such transformation
with an utterly impartial heart?
Táo further narrated:
"Since the spiritual mountain was buried,

only the venerable

With a meal of hemp and wheat,

During the Dàmíng era of the Song Dynasty, Huáng Xiūyí and the Princess of Nánchāng deeply revered the Three Jewels,

Thereupon the Dharma Master spoke to her,

This was the Dharma Master's humble request,
hoping the donor would not abandon him.
She immediately replied:
"The Dharma Master is a man,
and moreover propagates the scriptural teachings,
he should naturally dwell in superior realms.
I am but a woman,
how could I surpass the Dharma Master?
He responded:
"It is not so,
although I am a man,
I cannot practice diligently and uphold precepts
as well as you.
By this time her condition had worsened,
gradually becoming critical,
yet after some time she moved again
and said:
"I went to Tuṣita Heaven and saw Maitreya and all the bodhisattvas,
all golden in color.
In her hand was a pure crystal vase,
about three feet tall or more.
Maitreya then emitted radiant light,
illuminating her body.
In Tuṣita Heaven she saw no food or drink,
yet was naturally full,
therefore she no longer needed human food.
She only smelled human food as putrid,
hence refused to eat.
There in heaven she obtained ambrosial cakes,
intending to bring them back for Dharma Master Lìng.
But Dharma Master Lìng had human karmic retribution,
how could he eat heavenly food?
She was not permitted to take it.
After this her condition further deteriorated,
and she spoke no more of other matters.
She only said:
"There are thirty-two youths,

The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra elucidates three types of karmic retribution.

where an enlightened king's filial piety and compassion,

and the longevity star to appear.

where although good or evil causes are committed in this life,

Bimbisāra transferred his retribution to the Four Heavenly Kings,
and Udayana changed his rebirth in the Six Desire Heavens.

These three types of retribution are all called fixed karma.

had each mark the land with an object,
and whoever succeeded would dwell there.

Zhìgōng said:

Soon the crane flew ahead,
and as it was about to land at the foothills,
suddenly the sound of a flying staff was heard in the air.
Zhìgōng's staff thus stood at the foothills,
while the crane, startled, landed elsewhere.

and upon waking, he discussed the matter with Liáng Wǔ's court officials Wáng Róng, Xiè Tiǎo, and Shěn Yuē.
The prince subsequently compiled the twenty-chapter "Jìnglíng Collection",
including one chapter on confession.
Later, when Liáng Wǔ ascended the throne,
he sought to repent for the sins of the six senses,
and took the confession chapter
to summon Master Zhēnguàn Huìshì,
who then expanded the text
by incorporating various scriptures.
Thus in the second volume, the text on generating the bodhicitta states:
"Huìshì,
not merely as an ordinary being lightly expressing his aspirations,
but truly out of thirst for the Mahāyāna and craving for the Buddha-dharma."
Relying on various scriptures
and drawing analogies from worldly matters,
it was not actually composed for Empress Xī,
yet the current preface
uncertain of its origin,
differs from the original account.
Recent new printed editions from the southern regions
have removed the two characters "Huìshì",
likely due to ignorance of the original context.

Gāopíng's Xī Jiābīn, holding incense, prayed:

Calculating the years of its rise and fall,

Truly knowing the imprinted hand,
the sage's veneration and establishment,
the majestic bearing that stirs and manifests,

The auspicious statue of Yùhuáyīn Iron Mine:
When Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu suppressed Buddhism,

Going to search for it at dawn,
he found a recumbent stone resembling a statue.
He then excavated around it,
discovering it was an iron ore deposit,
impossible to damage.
The statue stood three zhàng tall.
In the valley was a pedestal.
Together with villagers, they tried to lift it,
when suddenly it slid down and moved forward,
the pedestal hole standing prominently erect.
They reported the circumstances to the throne.
At that time, Emperor Xuān of Běi Zhōu had ascended and changed the era name to Dàxiàng.

At Xiāngzhōu's Xiàn Mountain Huáyán Temple,

thus surviving.
Whenever ominous signs appeared,

When Suíwén Emperor was about to pass away,

Now the thin peeling that appears,

In the fourth month of the final year of Zhēnguàn era,
nasal mucus continuously flowed without stopping,

An old woman from Dǐ was weeding mulberry trees
and picked up a bronze statue of Guānyīn.
She made a niche in the wall and placed it there,
intending to make offerings to it.
The old woman had a son
who was then serving in the army at Pānfèng.
She prayed to it day and night,
hoping for his safety.
During a battle,
her son fell in the grass.
He heard three consecutive sword strikes on his back,
sounding like hits on a bronze object.
After the battle, he got up to check
and found himself completely unharmed.
That same day, his mother saw the bronze statue fallen on the ground
with three sword marks on its back.
She was puzzled about the reason.
Only when her son returned and recounted the incident
did she realize it was divine assistance.

Wénxuān gazed and bowed with utmost reverence,

New Biography.
Chancellor Péi Xiū was deeply devoted to Buddhism,
excelling in both Chán and monastic discipline,
studying under Guīfēng Chán Master Mì,

Master Mì annotated the Contemplation of the Dharmadhātu,

There are five common slanders against Buddhism:
first, considering matters beyond this world and miraculous transformations as deceptive falsehoods;
second, viewing the lack of immediate retribution for good and evil as fraudulent deceit;
third, regarding the conduct of monks and nuns as often impure and wicked;
fourth, denouncing the waste of treasures and reduction of taxes and labor as detrimental to the state;
fifth, questioning how, even if karma exists,
the toils of today's person A
could benefit the future person B,
since they are different individuals.
