According to the legend of Śākyamuni's birth among the barbarians,
he was born from Maya's side through a surgical incision.
His mother died shortly after, akin to the behavior of owls and jackals,
and as he grew older, disputes over succession arose,
leaving him unsettled internally.
He betrayed his father and defied his ruler,
his rebellious acts growing increasingly severe.
Devadatta threw stones and troubled Nanda,
drawing his bow to instigate change.
Constantly practicing self-starvation to emaciate his body,
how could he possibly aid all beings across the ninety-six paths?
Among these paths, his was the most greedy,
catering to the lustful and foolish masses,
who revered and believed in him excessively, even as Virūḍhaka
slaughtered the Śākyas; Gautama
merely watched from the roadside.
In life, he did not preserve kinship with his own relatives;
once they perished and grew distant,
how could he save them?
Thus, he failed to practice loyalty and filial piety.
If Maṇi could illuminate yet deliberately condoned lust and killing,
then his claim of compassion was deceitful.
If he only possessed illumination but offered no salvation,
then his great enlightenment was of no benefit to living beings,
yet the world remained unaware.

In the Northern Qí Dynasty, Liú Zhòu submitted a memorial stating:

If each has one miscarriage every six months like this,

Examining this, Buddha is indeed a demon that causes epidemics and miscarriages.

Xiāo Xiān was born on the fifth day of the fifth month in the seventeenth year of King Xuān of Zhōu.
Towards the end of King Xuān's reign,
historical records became scattered and disordered.
Xiāo Xiān, being literate,
wrote an account of events to supplement what the official histories had missed.
People regarded him as a historian,
though he actually had no official name.
Wandering aimlessly, he traveled to Qín,
excelling at playing the xiāo flute.
He could attract peacocks and white cranes to the courtyard with his music.
Duke Mù had a daughter,
named Nòng Yù,
who was skilled at playing the shēng mouth organ,
but had no one to harmonize with her.
They sought someone who could play the shēng,
to match her with Mèng Míng.
The historian recommended Xiāo Xiān, who was summoned for an audience.
The Marquis of Qín inquired,
and the historian said:
"He is skilled with the xiāo."
The Duke said:
"My daughter enjoys the shēng,
but you play the xiāo.
How is it that the historian's recommendation does not suit my wish?"
The daughter, standing behind the screen door,
called out:
"Let him try playing it.
With one note, a clear breeze arose;
with a second, colorful clouds gathered;
with a third, a phoenix came."
The daughter said:
"He shall be my husband,
I wish to marry him."
The historian said:
"Let the lady also play the shēng,
and play it three times."
As the historian had suggested,
Mèng Míng then acted as matchmaker,
with Jiǎn Shū as the guest of honor.
《Xiān Jiàn》 The Duke gave Nòng Yù to him in marriage,
and he taught Nòng Yù to mimic the phoenix.
After more than a decade of practice,
her xiāo playing resembled the phoenix's cry.
Phoenixes came to rest on their house,
and the Duke built a Phoenix Tower for the couple.
They lived atop it,
neither drinking nor eating.
In less than a dozen years,
one day, the beautiful Nòng Yù rode a phoenix,
while Xiāo Shǐ rode a dragon,
and they ascended to heaven.
Qín built a Shrine for the Phoenix Maiden in their honor,
where the sound of the xiāo could occasionally be heard.
《Xiān Zhuàn Shí Yí》
Lǎozǐ,

named Ěr,
styled Bóyáng,
posthumously called Dān,
was the historian of the Zhōu dynasty's archive room.
Confucius went to Zhōu,
intending to inquire about rites from Lǎozǐ.
Lǎozǐ cultivated the Dao and virtue,
his learning focused on self-concealment and anonymity as a pursuit.
He lived in Zhōu for a long time,
saw the decline of Zhōu,
and then left for the frontier.
The guardian of the pass, Yǐn Xǐ, said:
"You are going to hide,
please write a book for me."
So Lǎozǐ then wrote a book in two sections,
expressing the meaning of Dao and virtue in over five thousand words,
and departed,
with no one knowing his end.
It is said Lǎozǐ lived over one hundred and sixty years,
or over two hundred years,
because he cultivated the Dao and nurtured longevity.
Lǎozǐ
was a recluse gentleman.
Lǎozǐ's son was named Zōng,
Zōng served as a general in Wèi,
and was enfeoffed in Jiǎyú.
Zōng's son was Zhù,
Zhù's son was Gōng,
Gōng's great-grandson was Jiǎ.
Jiǎ served the Hàn Emperor Xiàowén.
Jiǎ's son, Xiè, became the grand tutor of the King of Jiāoxī, Áng,
and thus settled in Qí.
Lǐ Ěr practiced non-action and self-transformation,
maintaining purity and tranquility.

In Hédōng Púbǎn, there was a man named Xiàng Màndū,
who entered the mountains with his son,

and Màn said:
"After three years of intense meditation in the mountains,
an immortal came to welcome me,
and we rode together on a dragon ascending to heaven.
When we reached the heavens,
we first passed through the Purple Mansion,
with golden beds and jade tables,
shining and brilliant,
truly a noble place.
The immortal gave me a cup of flowing rosy clouds to drink,
and I no longer felt hunger or thirst.
Suddenly, I thought of home,
and when I went before the Heavenly Emperor to pay respects,
I breached etiquette and was reprimanded,
sent back,
told to cultivate and accumulate virtue further,
only then might I have another chance later.
In the past, when Huáinán King Liú Ān ascended to heaven and saw the Supreme Deity,
he sat cross-legged and boasted,
calling himself 'the solitary one',
and was thus demoted to guard the kitchen for three years.
How could I compare?
Therefore, in Hédōng, Màndū was called the Reprimanded Immortal.
The Bàopǔzǐ and Lùnhéng state: The immortals will take me to live beside the moon in heaven,
where it is very cold.
As for books on immortals
and Daoist sayings,
one account claims that Fu Shuè
ascended to become the star at the comet's tail;
the Year Star descended to become Dōngfāng Shuò;
though Huáinánzǐ Ān was executed in Huainan,
it was said he attained the Way and ascended lightly;
though Lady Gōu Yí died in Yúnyáng,
it was said her corpse vanished and coffin lay empty;
how utterly
fabricated these claims are!
Moreover, the world vainly believes tales of immortals.
What are these so-called immortals?
Are they perhaps akin to monkeys and apes?
When ordinary people attain the Way,
do they transform into immortals?
Pheasants enter the sea and become clams,
swallows enter the sea and become giant clams.
When they flutter their wings
and spread their feathers unevenly,
they still retain their own consciousness.
Yet suddenly throwing themselves into the sea,
their spirit transforms and body changes,
they then keep company with turtles and softshell turtles—
how could they still remember the joy of soaring through woods and nesting under eaves?
When Niú Āi fell ill and turned into a tiger,
he encountered his elder brother and devoured him.
What value is there in such transformations?
Yet people heed commoners' claims,
accepting empty fabrications
and believing bewildering tales.
They honor them lavishly to recruit those who won't serve,
squander fortunes to fulfill vain pursuits,
bestow royal titles to glorify them,
and clear leisure halls to house them.
Year after year passes,
yet ultimately no proof emerges.
Some die at Shāqiū,
some perish at Wǔzuò;
though eventually executed
with their clans exterminated,
such chaos amply makes them the laughingstock of the world!
Now lifespan's length
and bone structure's strength
vary among individuals.
Those who nurture well see it through,
the toiled and troubled reach halfway,
the wasteful and excessive die young—
does this not refer to exactly that?

and great harmony is their friend.
Three hundred major precepts are upheld to prevent unforeseen calamities,
while two thousand dignified observances are practiced to cultivate natural blessings.
"Master Lù's Teachings"
There are five types of Daoist priests: first, the Celestial Pure Daoist priest,
such as Gāo Xuán Huángrén and his kind;
second, the Immortal Daoist priest,
exemplified by Dù Chōng and Yǐn Guǐ;
third, the Mountain-dwelling Daoist priest,
comparable to Xǔ Yóu and Cháo Fù;
fourth, the Renunciant Daoist priest,
matched by Sòng Lún and Péng Chén;
fifth, the Lay Daoist priest,
akin to Huáng Qióng and Jiǎn Kēng and their peers.
"The Three Caverns Daoist Code"
Taoists are classified into upper, middle, and lower grades,
with those deeply versed in the Tao called the highest seat.
The "Lǎo Zǐ Lì Dé Jīng" in vermilion characters and phoenix script,
illuminates the pavilion with radiant light,
seated amidst the profound and yellow,
ordering celestial purity.
The "Dòng Zhēn Yǐn Xuán Jīng"
All who follow the Three Luminosities are called Disciples of the Three Luminosities;
having guided three individuals across,
and having received transmission from teachers and companions, they may be called Masters of the Three Luminosities Method.
"The Supreme Eightfold Pure Scripture"
Zhāng Líng,
courtesy name Fǔhàn,
was a native of Fēng County in the Pèi Kingdom.
Originally a great Confucian scholar,
he later studied the Way of Longevity,
obtained the Jiǔdǐng Elixir Classic,
and hearing that Shǔ contained many famous mountains,
entered Mínggǔ Mountain,
where he authored twenty volumes of Daoist texts before ascending to immortality.
The "Declarations of the Perfected" states: Celestial Master Zhāng Líng of the Way,
secluded himself on Lónghǔ Mountain,
cultivated the practice of silent audience for the Three Primes,
and acquired the art of the Yellow Emperor's Dragon-Tiger Inner Elixir.
Upon completing the elixir and consuming it,
he could divide his form and disperse,
while Celestial Master Jǐng entered Sōnggāo Mountain from Póyáng,
gaining the arts of invisibility and controlling fate.
The "Records of the Assembled Immortals" notes: Líng studied the Way at Hèmíng Mountain in Shǔ,
at a time when humans and ghosts in Shǔ were indistinguishable,
and disasters and diseases arose in competition.
Moved by the descent of the Most High Lord Lǎo to impart the Correct Unity Covenant with Powers Method,
he separated humans from ghosts,
and established twenty-four parishes.
To this day, the people benefit from this,
and the Altar for Subduing Ghosts remains visible.
The "Correct Unity Scripture" recounts: Líng tested his disciples seven times,
and together with Zhào Shēng and Wáng Cháng, the three ascended to heaven in broad daylight,
their many disciples gazing upward for a long time,
until they vanished into the clouds.
The "Biographies of Divine Immortals" says: Two Jade Maidens bearing the Shangqing True Talismans
led Líng and his wife, Madame Yōng, to Yúntái Peak,
where they ascended to heaven in daylight.
The "Mirror of Immortals" records: Líng bestowed the secret registers, the Demon-Slaying Sword, the Jade Register, and the Jade Seal upon his son Héng,
and ascended with Madame Yōng.
Considering the varied accounts about Dàolíng,
so numerous and conflicting like this,
it is clear that they deceive the world and confuse,
the masses chasing wind and capturing shadows—
Gǔ Yǒng's assertion is indeed credible.
The Book of Hàn states:
"Zhāng Líng,
whose son Héng was the Tied Master,
and Héng's son Lǔ succeeded them,
their master titles being called the Three Masters.
The wives of these three men were called Ladies,
and all were said to have ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
The Laughing at the Dào Treatise: Zhāng Zhènnán, on the northern stone altar in the Northern Cave,
burned incense and paid respects,
then remained prostrate without rising,
and thus was liberated at night.
The next morning, he appeared as if alive.
This altar still exists today.
Declarations of the Perfected: Héng transmitted the methods of the Perfected to the Tied Master,
and together with his wife, Madame Lú, attained the Dào at Yángpíng Mountain,
flying up to heaven in broad daylight.
Mirror of Immortals: Cáo campaigned westward against Lǔ,
who drew a river on the ground with his hand tablet,
preventing the troops from crossing.
When the envoy arrived at the shore with naval forces,
Lǔ again covered the river with his hand tablet,
causing high peaks to emerge from the water,
so the troops could not advance.
Lord Cáo sent an envoy to seal him but failed,
and later, Xiū Jiàn ascended to heaven riding a dragon in broad daylight.
In the state of Pèi, Zhāng Líng studied the Way at Hèmíng Mountain in Shǔ,
traveling and composing Daoist texts,
calling himself Tàiqīng Xuānyuán,
to deceive the common people.
Those who came to study under him
were initially called "ghost soldiers,"
and those who received the Way used gold and silk as offerings,
being titled "libationers."
Each led their own followers,
with the leaders of larger groups called "district heads."
Their required tribute was limited to five dou of rice,
hence the world called them "rice bandits."
After Dàolíng died,
his son Héng continued his Way,
and when Héng died,
Lǔ carried it on.
Lǔ's mother was beautiful
and practiced ghostly arts, frequenting the home of Yìzhōu's governor Liú Yān.
Yān appointed Lǔ as Commandant of Righteousness Supervision,
stationed in Hànzhōng.
When Yān died,
his son Zhāng succeeded him,
and considering Lǔ arrogant and disobedient,
he killed all of Lǔ's mother and family.
Lǔ then occupied Hànzhōng, using ghostly arts to convert the people,
calling himself "Grand Master and Army Commander,"
similar to Zhāng Jué,
and dominated Bā and Hàn for nearly thirty years.
When Cáo Cāo campaigned against Lǔ,
Lǔ fled to Bāzhōng,
while his younger brother Wèi fortified the mountain base,
and Yángpíng City to resist him.
At night, thousands of wild elk suddenly overran Wèi's camp,
greatly startling and frightening Wèi,
who thought it was a large army,
and, finding himself ambushed, surrendered to Yán Pǔ,
who persuaded Lǔ to surrender to Lord Cáo.
Someone suggested going west to join
Liú Bèi, but Lǔ angrily said:
"I would rather be a slave to Lord Cáo
than a guest of honor under Liú Bèi."
Thus, he pledged allegiance to Lord Cáo,
who appointed him General Who Guards the South.
From "Huáyáng Zhì, Shǔ Wèi Zhì, Shìyǔ, Pòxiélùn"
Zhāng Líng took refuge from malaria in the Qiū Shrine,
where he acquired the art of cursing ghosts,
and thus mastered the method of commanding ghosts.
At the end of the Xīpíng era,
he was swallowed by a python,
and his son Héng rushed out to search for the corpse,
fearing nothing.
Burdened by the criticism of public opinion,
he devised a temporary strategy,
using traces of transformation by the pure spirit.
He tied a crane's leg with raw tether and placed it atop a stone cliff,
and when the plan was fully prepared,
he set a date to carry it out.
By the first year of the Guānghé era,
he sent an envoy to announce:
"On the seventh day of the first month, the Celestial Master ascended to the Mysterious Capital."
The common people and mountain tribes gathered like ants outside the threshold.
The administrator of Yúntái and others bowed and kowtowed twice, saying:
"We humbly hear that the sacred carriage has reached the Mysterious Capital,
and we, your subjects, must bid farewell to the shade and receive the corpse dust."
Just as they were enjoying the offerings in the deep darkness, Héng entered,
and after a long time emerged,
falsely declaring:
"I am returning at dawn's splendor,
and you should each return to your posts,
purify your hearts, maintain conduct, and remember the Master and the Way."
Héng then secretly untied the tethered crane and soared straight into the void.
The foolish common people and tribes all claimed he had ascended to immortality,
but deceiving the dying and profiting from the living, he defied heaven and earth,
with no transgression greater than this.
(From Lǐ Yīng's "Shǔ Jì," Xuánguāng's "Discourse on Discerning Deception," seen in Liáng's "Collection for the Elucidation of Doctrine")
During the reign of Emperor Shùn of the Later Hàn dynasty,
a man from Pèi named Zhāng Líng traveled to the land of Shǔ as a visitor.
He heard an ancient tradition passed down:
"In the past, Hàn Gāozǔ responded to the twenty-four climatic periods,
sacrificed to the twenty-four mountains,
and thus became king over all under heaven.
Líng, without considering his own virtue,
then devised this scheme:
he slaughtered oxen and performed sacrifices at twenty-four sites,
erected earthen altars,
and covered them with thatched huts,
calling them the twenty-four parishes.
The establishment of parish centers
began from this.
Twenty-three of these were located in Shǔ,
while one belonging to Yǐn Xǐ was in Xiányáng.
Thereupon, he deceived and enticed ignorant people, gathering a band of villains,
collecting grain as taxes and plotting to create disorder.
At that time, the rebellion was suppressed and did not erupt,
but when it reached his grandson Zhāng Lǔ, the calamity finally arose,
starting from Hànzhōng.
《Mínggài Juéduì Chuán Yì Shì》 At that time, they falsely claimed divine words,
saying "Yellow Turbans shall rule,"
so Lǔ coordinated with Zhāng Jué to assemble followers,
all wearing yellow turbans and donning Daoist robes,
numbering hundreds of thousands.
They occupied Hànzhōng themselves,
for nearly thirty years,
until they were defeated by Lord Cáo,
and the Yellow Turbans were finally eradicated.
《Pòxiélùn》 Zhāng Líng abandoned his wife.
Historical records like the Biographies and the Records of the Three Kingdoms written not long after Líng's time
document these deceptions of the three Zhāngs through direct accounts,
which should not be considered false.
Yet Daoist texts rely on fabricated tales for circulation,
failing to realize the truth,
how lamentable!
During the Later Wei dynasty,
the Mount Sōng shān Daoist Kòu Qiānzhī claimed to have encountered the Supreme Elderly Lord,
who said:
"Since Zhāng Líng passed away,
there has been no one to inherit the teachings.
I hereby bestow upon you the position of Celestial Master,
and grant you the twenty chapters of 'Cloud-Midst Sound Register Precepts',
collectively titled 'Simultaneous Advancement'.
You should propagate my new precepts,
purify and rectify Daoism,
eliminate the false practices of the Three Zhāngs,
the grain tax and monetary levies,
and the arts of male-female union through qi."
The Great Dao, being pure and void, how could such things exist?
The "Shí Lǎo Zhì" states: Daoist arts consider ascending to immortality as divine,
thus deceiving people to seek immediate gains.
In the past, Xú Fú deceived and established a separate state in Yídān,
Wénchéng and Wǔlì practiced sorcery and falsehoods during the Hàn dynasty,
the Three Zhāngs deluded people in Western Liáng,
Sūn Ēn caused disturbances in Eastern Yuè—
such great pests have been denounced since ancient times.
From the "Discourse on Discerning Deception"
Xì Chuàn's Qiè Jiǎn could abstain from grains,
consuming poria cocos;
Gān Líng's Gān Shǐ was renowned for excelling in breath control,
appearing youthful in old age;
Lú Jiāng's Zuǒ Cí mastered the arts of nourishment and guidance.
All served as military officials.
Initially,
when Qiè Jiǎn arrived at a place,
the price of poria cocos would suddenly increase severalfold.
Court Gentleman for Consultation Ānpíng's Lǐ Zhāng learned his grain abstinence technique,
ate poria cocos,
and drank cold water,
but the cold water caused diarrhea,
nearly costing him his life.
Later, when Gān Shǐ came,
everyone without exception craned their necks like owls and glanced back like wolves,
practicing inhalation and exhalation.
Army Sacrificial Wine Hóngnóng's Dǒng Fēn overdid it in his practice,
causing his breath to block and not circulate,
and only after a long time did he revive.
When Zuǒ Cí arrived,
people again vied to learn his nourishment and guidance techniques,
even to the extent that the eunuch Yán Jùn went to receive instruction.
How could eunuchs truly have any use for such arts!
People's pursuit of fame and trends
could indeed reach such extremes.
"Diǎn Lùn"
There are alchemists in the world,
all of whom our king has summoned.
From Gānlíng came Gān Shǐ,
from Lújiāng came Zuǒ Cí,
and from Yángchéng came Xī Jiǎn.
Shǐ could perform breath control and guiding exercises,
Cí understood the arts of the bedchamber,
and Jiǎn excelled at abstaining from grains,
all claiming to be three hundred years old.
The reason they were gathered in the state of Wèi
was truly out of fear that such people
would collude with deceitful schemes to deceive the masses,
practicing sorcery and wickedness to mislead others.
Thus they were assembled and restricted—
how could it be that one wished to see immortals on Yíngzhōu,
seek Ānqī by the distant seas,
abandon the golden carriage for a cloud chariot,
or discard the patterned steed in favor of a flying dragon?
As for Gān Shǐ,
he appeared youthful despite his old age,
and all other practitioners revered him.
Yet Shǐ spoke sparingly,
though in truth he occasionally uttered strange words.
I once privately inquired about his practices.
Shǐ said his original teacher was surnamed Hán,
courtesy name Shìyǎ,
and that he once made gold with his teacher in the South Sea,
casting tens of thousands of catties into the ocean.
He also spoke of taking a pair of carps,
applying medicine to one of them,
and casting it into boiling oil,
where the carp would flap its tail and puff its gills,
swimming and diving
as if in deep waters.
The one without medicine would be cooked
and ready to eat.
I asked:
"Could this be tested?"
He replied:
"This medicine is over ten thousand miles away from here,
and unless I go myself, it cannot be obtained."
Had Shǐ encountered Qín Shǐhuáng or Hàn Wǔdì, he would have become another Xú Fú or Luán Dà.
Although Jié and Zhòu lived in different eras,
how similarly false and wicked are the deceitful men across generations!
"Discourse on Distinguishing the Way"
Zhāng Zhí encountered the Daoist priest Jiāng Xuánbiàn,
who imparted to him the art of commanding the Six Ding spirits,
saying:
"Technique and the Way must be practiced together.
Without technique,
the Way cannot be attained by oneself;
without the Way,
technique cannot be prolonged.
If one obtains technique but not the Way,
it is like wishing to travel ten thousand miles
without walking a single step.
Although techniques may manifest in countless hidden ways,
they cannot remove the record of death.
Therefore, one must settle the mind in the wondrous realm,
focus thoughts on the cinnabar blossom,
perform meritorious deeds to aid the external self,
refine the soul to preserve the internal self,
unifying internal and external into one,
only then can one approach the Way,
and achieve longevity.
"Immortal Biographies Supplement"
Lǐ Hè, a Taoist priest from Pílíng,
was by nature narrow-minded and impatient,
fond of bullying and humiliating others.
Suddenly, a poor scholar came to Hè begging for food,
but Hè did not give him any,
instead scolding and reprimanding him.
After a few days,
someone came riding a white horse,
and Hè received him with courtesy, saying:
"Do you remember me somewhat?
Looking at his appearance,
it was the poor scholar from before,
who said to Hè:
"Do you know of Hánshānzǐ?
Hè replied:
"I do.
He said:
"That is I.
I initially thought you could be taught,
but now you cannot.
The way of cultivating life
involves eliminating cravings, removing desires, conserving spirit, and embracing harmony, so as to be free from burdens.
Restraining one's heart within,
examining one's body without,
so as to be without faults.
Putting others before oneself,
knowing softness and maintaining humility,
so as to secure one's person.
Attributing goodness to others,
and taking blame upon oneself,
so as to accumulate virtue.
Merit does not lie in greatness,
but in establishing it without negligence;
faults do not lie in greatness,
but in removing them without repetition.
This is how to accumulate merit.
Only then will inner conduct be fulfilled and outer elixir arrive,
allowing one to hope for the Way in its faint resemblance.
Your three poisons have not been cut off,
adorned with an official's cap and hairpin,
you may be called a tiger or leopard's skin,
but with the substance of a dog or pig.
He went out the door, mounted his horse, and left,
never to be seen again.
End
The esoteric arts of Daoism,
are turbid and impure,
such as knocking teeth as the celestial drum,
swallowing saliva as sweet spring water,
using horse dung as sacred firewood,
and regarding rats as magic mushrooms.
Relying on these to seek the Way,
how can one attain it?
"Discourse on Discerning Delusions" calls women vermilion gates,
and men jade pillars,
with mouth saliva termed jade fluid.
"Treatise on Refuting Heterodoxy" states: fire immortals of heterodox paths are named Jítóupó,
while water immortals of heterodox paths are named Yíshūluó.
Since the teachings of Huáng-Lǎo degenerated and appearances also changed,
they became neither Daoist nor laypeople,
commonly called "castrated ones" skilled in curses and abuse,
anciently named "ghost attendants,"
in their salvation from suffering.
They would loosen their hair, tie it around their necks with ropes, and bind themselves,
smear cow dung on their bodies, and whip each other,
in their religious discipline.
If they lost their talismanic registers, they would hold the hand tablet upside-down in their mouths and sweep the ground against the wind,
carry a hundred bundles of willow branches to chop and bear themselves,
for stealing memorial petitions.
They would crawl through ash prisons carrying water bubbles on their backs,
where punishments were particularly severe,
similar to slave laws,
submitting to accusations and penalties,
comparable to livestock.
"Biàn Zhèng"
Lóuguàn is
the site established by Guān Lìng Yǐnxǐ, a senior official of King Kāng of the Zhōu dynasty.
Because he built a thatched tower there,
it was named accordingly.
When King Mù of the Zhōu traveled west,
and Duke Wén of Qín hunted in the east,
they both diverted their carriages and turned their wheels
to personally revere the Dàoist teachings.
Emperor Qín Shǐhuáng built a temple south of the tower,
Emperor Hàn Wǔdì established a palace north of the observatory,
and from the Jìn and Sòng dynasties to the present, memorial tablets have been presented,
which still exist.
"The Lóuguàn Stele"
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the people of Yùsì Mountain sensed its divine wonders,
and whenever drought or locust plagues occurred,
their prayers were always answered.
They thus said to one another:
"We should build a temple
to manifest these miraculous traces."
When constructing the hall,
they lacked one central beam.
The villagers sought exceptional timber,
but after dozens of days, found none.
Suddenly one night,
thunder roared and winds raged,
clearing only at dawn.
A white jade beam descended from heaven,
perfectly matching the required dimensions.
Firmly placed atop the hall,
its radiance dazzled the eyes.
Hence it was named the Jade Beam Temple.
By the time of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi,
he sent envoys to retrieve it.
Approaching the mountain gate,
still miles from the temple,
at midday,
thunderclaps violently resounded.
The ridgepole transformed into a white dragon,
parting the mist and soaring away,
disappearing beneath the eastern mountain of the temple,
having flown off with the jade beam.
Thereafter, none could approach the site,
as all were repelled by fierce beasts and venomous snakes.
"Record of Yùsì Mountain"
At the Jade Bureau Temple in Chéngdū,
it is traditionally said that in the early years of the Yǒngshòu era,
Lǎojūn and Zhāng Dàolíng arrived here,
where a jade couch with curved legs emerged from the ground.
Lǎojūn ascended and sat upon it, expounding the "Scriptures of the Northern and Southern Dippers" to Dàolíng.
After they departed,
the seat sank into the earth,
forming a cave as a result.
Hence, it was named the Jade Bureau.
From "Péng Chéng's Records"
Buddhist monks are called "dàorén,"
while Yángpíng is referred to as the place of Daoist priests.
In the "Sēng Shùn's Three Refutations Treatise," there are twenty-four administrative districts,
among which the Yángpíng district is the largest.
Nowadays, when Daoist priests submit memorials and employ talismans for exorcism,
they all refer to Yángpíng,
emphasizing its origin.
The Shangqing tradition is considered the Cavern of Mystery,
the Língbǎo tradition the Cavern of Truth,
and the Three Sovereigns tradition the Cavern of Spirit,
hence the name Three Sovereigns.
According to the "Records of Shǔ," Zhāng Shǒuguī had a laborer about to depart,
who claimed to be an exiled immortal from the Yángpíng Cavern.
Shǒuguī asked,
"How does the size of the cavern mansions
compare to the cities and palaces of the human world?"
The laborer replied,
"There are twenty-four transformations,
each with a great cavern,
some spanning a thousand li, five hundred li, or three hundred li.
Within them, there are sun and moon flying essences,
known as the roots of hidden dawn.
They shine down into the caverns,
no different from the world above,
and within reside immortal kings, immortal officials, ministers, and assistants,
similar to the bureaucratic offices of the human world.
Those who have attained the Dao,
as well as individuals who have accumulated merits and ascended to immortality or returned to life,
all dwell there,
forming a populace.
During the three major festivals each year,
various celestial beings descend to tour the cavern heavens,
observing the good and evil deeds, human affairs, life and death,
rise and fall, floods and droughts, wind and rain,
all of which are preordained within the caverns.
Dragon deity temples and shrines,
as well as blood sacrifice offices,
are all governed by the cavern mansions.
Beyond the twenty-four transformations,
places like Qīngchéng, Éméi,
Yìdēng Címǔ,
Fányáng Bōzhǒng,
also have caverns,
not counted among the ten great cavern heavens
or the thirty-six minor cavern heavens.
Tàiqīng Palace in Zhēnyuán County, Bózhōu,
is the birthplace where Lǎojūn descended.
The nine wells and three altars all remain.
During the Xiántōng era,
when Páng Xūn occupied Xúzhōu and intended to seize the palace for a military camp,
black qi emerged from the nine wells,
darkening the entire valley and causing Páng Xūn's followers
to lose their way and trample each other.
In the Guǎngmíng era,
when the general of Huáng Cháo wanted to burn down the palace,
black fog also spread across the valley,
causing them to lose their path.
Prefect Pān Chóu reported:
"Since the great rebels invaded the capital,
and after the multitude of villains were exterminated,
various rebels,
eighteen times in total, attempted to attack Tàiqīng Palace.
Sometimes they lost their way,
sometimes dragon deities manifested themselves,
ultimately thwarting their evil plans.
The palace remains peaceful and secure,
so it is requested to relocate Zhēnyuán County to be established near the palace.
"Records of Daoist Miracles"
Jīng means
a path,
a constant norm,
like a path that reaches everywhere,
and can be constantly used.
Shìmíng
The works composed by sages are called classics,
while the writings authored by worthies are called commentaries.
Explanations of records and instructions are termed glosses,
and annotations on chapters and sentences are referred to as notes.
The "Bówùzhì Shūchāo" states: the writings of the worthy are called records, chapters and sentences, explanations, discourses, and readings.
"Yùlǎn"
The method of the Five Classics,
operates through heaven and earth,
verified by diagrams and images,
substantiated by the Three Sovereigns,
and applied throughout the four seas.
"Chūnqiū Yǎn Kǒng Tú"
The three ultimate constant teachings,
their writings speak of the classics.
The classics are
the supreme Way of eternal endurance,
the great teachings that cannot be altered.
The Book of Changes unfolds the Ten Wings,
the Book of Documents marks the seven perspectives,
the Book of Songs arranges the four beginnings,
the Rites rectify the five classics,
the Spring and Autumn Annals set five examples.
Their meanings fully express human nature and emotions,
their language is crafted with literary principles.
They may be described as Mount Tài's rain reaching everywhere,
the river's moisture extending a thousand miles.
The eulogy says:
"They refine the nature and spirit,
the profound treasury of literature.
How deep and brilliant they are,
the ancestor of all words."
Wénxīn Diāolóng
The canonical classics are the abyss of the Way and arts,
while various texts are the flowing streams that deepen them.
They are like the auspicious stars assisting the three luminaries,
or the dense undergrowth complementing the lofty peaks.
From Bàopǔzǐ
The Odes and Hymns of the Book of Songs,
the Canons and Counsels of the Book of Documents,
their substance and refinement are perfectly matched.
They seem close when appreciated,
yet distant when explored,
vast as the deep treasury of literary splendor.
Master Fu's Writings
The Five Classics are the principles of the sea,
the four seas;
the classical commentaries are,
the four great rivers;
the various masters are,
the Jīng and Wèi Rivers.
As for the hundreds of streams, ditches, and channels,
if they can connect the energies of yīn and yáng,
and reach the flow of springs and water,
returning to the four seas as their destination,
they are all beneficial.
From "Yáng Quán's Discourses on the Principles of Things"
The Five Classics are the treasury,
various arts are the kitchen.
"Collection of Gāo Biāo"
The Six Classics are the kitchen,
and the Hundred Schools are diverse delicacies.
From "Chuán Gàn's Letter to Master Sū Wén"
For reclusive scholars, the Three Primordial Texts are like gold and jade,
the Five Canonical Texts are like zithers and zheng lutes, lecture halls are like bells and drums,
and the Hundred Schools of Thought are like reed pipes.
From *Bàopǔzǐ*
The first is called Liánshān,
the second is called Guīcáng,
and the third is called Zhōuyì.
Liánshān consists of eighty thousand words,
Guīcáng four thousand three hundred words.
The Old Text Shàngshū originally had forty-five scrolls,
divided into eighteen chapters.
The Old Text Lǐjì had fifty-six scrolls.
The Old Text Lúnyǔ had eleven scrolls.
The Old Text Xiàojīng, one scroll with twenty chapters,
contained one thousand eight hundred seventy-two characters,
with over four hundred characters differing from the current version.
It is indeed a forest of excellent discourses,
an ocean of literary meaning.
Huán Tán's Xīnlùn
To establish sovereign and subject,
set distinctions of noble and base,
block incipient tendencies,
and prevent what has not yet sprouted,
nothing surpasses the Rites;
to lament the kingly way,
grieve over the governance of the age,
nothing surpasses the Poetry;
to guide yīn and yáng,
reveal remorse and regret,
nothing surpasses the Changes;
to clarify good and evil,
know what is abolished and what prospers,
utter words and commands,
nothing surpasses the Spring and Autumn Annals;

In ancient times, kings

thereby cautioning speech and conduct, and illuminating laws and models.
When the Zhōu dynasty declined,
documents and records became fragmented and incomplete.
Zhòngní (Confucius) sought to preserve the legacy of former sages.
Because Lǔ was the state of Duke Zhōu,
with complete rituals, literature, and implements,
and historiographers followed established methods,
he thus examined its historical records with Zuǒ Qiūmíng,
basing them on actual events,
adhering to human principles,
using successes to establish merits,
and failures to determine punishments,
borrowing the sun and moon to fix the calendar,
and relying on court visits to rectify rituals and music.
There were praises, taboos, and criticisms,
and the powerful ministers and rulers of the time,
with their authority and power,
had their facts all recorded in the commentary,
so the text was concealed and not publicized,
in order to avoid the troubles of the time.
By the end of that era,
oral traditions became prevalent,

Later, because of the Lǐ Líng incident,

Bān Biāo continued to compile earlier histories and critique their merits and faults,

Sīmǎ Qiān gathered classics and collected traditions,

with much that was sparse and sketchy,
not as good as the originals,
striving to take broad knowledge and extensive recording as achievement,
his discussions shallow and not profound.
In his treatment of scholarly learning,
he exalted Huáng-Lǎo and belittled the Five Classics;
in his accounts of wealthy merchants,
he slighted benevolence and righteousness and shamed the poor;
in his narratives of wandering knights,
he demeaned steadfast integrity and valued vulgar achievements.
These are his great flaws that harmed the Way,
the reason he met with the calamity of extreme punishment.
The Hòu Hàn's appraisal states: "Sīmǎ Qiān's judgments of right and wrong greatly diverged from the sages.

in describing wealthy merchants, he exalted profit-seeking and shamed the lowly and poor.
These were his blind spots."
Alas!
With Sīmǎ Qiān's vast knowledge and wide learning, he could not use wisdom to preserve himself;
having suffered extreme punishment, he gritted his teeth and wrote with fervent indignation—

Only the truly refined,
both enlightened and wise, can protect their persons.
How difficult it is!

Alas,

Now, examining Cáo Cāo's establishment of his royal enterprise:

Liú Bèi, by contrast, belonged to the Hàn imperial lineage,

How could there be any turning away from Cáo to favor Liú,

It stems from his father's humiliation of being shaved as punishment,

Máo Xiūzhī's position,

his writings,

Xiūzhī considered

Shitong
Minister of Rites Zhèng Wéizhōng once asked Liú Zǐxuán:
"Throughout history, there have been many literary scholars but few talented historians.
Why is this?"
He replied:
"A talented historian must possess three strengths.
Since there are no such people in the world,
talented historians are rare.
These three strengths are talent, learning, and judgment.
If one has learning but no talent,
it is like having a hundred acres of fertile land
and baskets full of gold,
yet letting a fool manage them—
he will never succeed in accumulating wealth.
If one has talent but no learning,
it is like aspiring to the skills of master craftsmen,
being as ingenious as Gōngshū Bān,
but having neither the finest wood nor the proper tools at home—
he will ultimately fail to complete his grand building.
Moreover, one must uphold integrity,
recording both good and evil without bias,
so that arrogant rulers and treacherous ministers may know fear.
This is like adding wings to a tiger—
perfection beyond improvement,
making one invincible in all endeavors.
If one lacks these qualities,
they should not presumptuously hold the office of historian.
Since ancient times,
those who could meet these criteria
have been exceedingly rare."
Contemporaries considered this insightful.

The Emperor
The so-called good historians of antiquity,
illuminated the principles underlying all things,
and their ways were suited to the uses of the world.
Their wisdom was sufficient to penetrate difficulties,
and to know virtue;
their literary talent was sufficient to express difficulties,
and to manifest feelings.
The works of the various masters
are books that enter the Way and manifest their aspirations.
The highest achievement is to establish virtue,
the next is to establish words.
From the pre-Qin era onward,
they were not far removed from the sages,
thus they could transcend their age with lofty discourse,
opening their own windows and doors.
After the two Han dynasties,
their style and momentum declined and weakened,
making it difficult to clarify on a broad path,
and most tended to rely on and adopt from others.
This is the gradual change between distant and recent times.
Alas!
Though their persons were at odds with their times,
their aspirations together with the Way were expressed.
They set their hearts on the ancient past above,
and conveyed their feelings to a thousand years below.
Even metal and stone may decay,
but how could their voices vanish!

Wáng Chōng's nature was tranquil and indifferent,
not coveting wealth and honor.
He immersed himself in reading ancient texts,
and delighted in hearing unconventional views.
He enjoyed befriending refined scholars,
but did not casually associate with vulgar talents.
Distressed that forged books and common writings were often untruthful,
he therefore composed the book "Lùn Héng".
Lùn Héng means
the balance of discourse.
In speech, he aimed at clarity,
in writing, he aimed at transparency.
Plans for averting danger are dismissed in the alleys,

"The Annals of Lü Buwei" and "Huáinánzǐ" were displayed at the city gates,

The writings of these two masters are not without flaws,

Those who observe and read them

Some mock Chōng for his repeated failure in officialdom and mere engagement in writing,

Those who succeed are not necessarily wise,
those who struggle are not necessarily foolish,
those who encounter opportunity gain,
those who do not, lose.
Thus, with fate granting thick salaries and good fortune,
mediocre people attain honor and prominence;
with fate granting thin salaries and misfortune,
exceptional talents fall into destitution.
If one must judge ability and virtue by chance success,
then those who rule cities and enjoy fiefs
would be more virtuous than Confucius and Mòzǐ.
If one is noble in status but base in reputation,

Enjoying a salary of a thousand zhōng,

But if one has high virtue and a pure name,
low office and meager salary,
it is not a fault of ability,

A scholar would wish to share a hut with Yuán Xiàn,

What the noble scholar values

Though his body decays with grass and trees,

To be successful in life but lacking in wisdom,
holding high office but possessing little virtue,
for them it is honor,
for me it is a burden.
Chance success and flattery,
high status and physical ease,

vanish with all things,
their names not lasting a generation,
their writings not leaving a single scroll,
though their granaries overflow with office gains,
their cultural virtue is not rich,

Virtue vast and profound,
wisdom overflowing and abundant,
writing pouring down like gathering rain,
speech gushing forth like a spring;
rich in talent and abundant in knowledge,
noble in conduct and lofty in ambition,
his person stands out in his generation,
his name transmitted for a thousand years,
this is what I call extraordinary.

Both are bound by their natural limits,
unlike literature, which is boundless and eternal.
Therefore, ancient authors
devoted themselves to writing,
expressing their thoughts in books and compositions.
Without relying on the words of skilled historians,
nor depending on the influence of rapid advancement,
their fame naturally endures through the ages.
From "Diǎnlùn"
The universe is vast and remote,
human affairs are complex and diverse;
to stand out among the masses,
one relies solely on wisdom and strategy.
Time passes swiftly,
the human spirit does not linger;
to make one's reputation endure and achievements shine,
one must create works.
Humans resemble heaven and earth in form,
endowed with the nature of the Five Constants;
their eyes and ears are likened to the sun and moon,
their voice and breath compared to wind and thunder.
They surpass all things,
truly possessing spiritual essence.
Though their physical form is as fragile as grass and trees,
their fame can outlast metal and stone.
Therefore, a noble person in this world
cultivates virtue and establishes words,
is it out of a love for argument?
It is out of necessity!
Carving Dragons
The manifestation and clarification of literary compositions
serve to manifest the images of the higher and lower realms,
clarify the order of human relationships,
exhaust principles and fulfill nature,
thereby investigating what is appropriate for all things.
"Discourse on the Origins and Branches of Literary Compositions"
To satirize and beautify customs and morals,

is called Fēng.
To gather and select events and objects,
displaying elegance and arranging form,
is called Fù.
To elucidate governance,
solemnly discussing merits and faults,
is called Yǎ.
To depict great virtue,
praising and encouraging meritorious deeds,
is called Sòng.
To harbor deep sorrow and indignation,

To be moved by events and objects,

is called Cí.
To evaluate tasks and compare achievements,
examining facts to establish names,
is called Míng.
To cite the past to criticize the present,
admonishing on merits and faults,
is called Zhēn.
With undulating rhythm,
modulating and prolonging words,
is called Gē.
Without drums or bells,
singing alone is called Yáo.
With measured steps and galloping pace,
elegantly forming a composition,
is called Xíng.
To rank in order of precedence,
narrating and inferring,
is called Yǐn.
With sounds hard to compare,
high and low, short and long,
is called Qǔ.
With sighs and lamentations,
sorrowful and deep contemplation,
is called Yín.
Chanting of emotions and nature,
combining to express aspirations,
is called Shī.
The words of emperors and kings,
issuing laws to govern people,
are called Zhì.
Words of silk and thread,
like the sun and moon shining down,
are called Zhào.
Zhì and Zhào are the same,
Zhào is also Zhì.
Expressing constancy to establish eternal laws,
is called Diǎn.
Presenting strategies to form excellent plans,
is called Mó.
is called Xùn.
Addressing someone to inform them,

Addressing the masses to declare,
is called Shì.
Appointing officials with mandates,

Issued from above,
is called Jiào.
Implemented below,
is called Lìng.
Timely warnings,
are Chì.
Explaining through words,
is Xuān.
Consulting and praising,
is Zàn.
Elevating and honoring,
is Cè.
Discussing relationships and analyzing them,
is Lùn.
Assessing appropriateness and deliberating,
is Yì.
Distinguishing doubts and clarifying them,
is Biàn.
Correcting right and wrong and making it clear,

Jì,
records events;
Jì,

Zuǎn,

Cè,

Zhuàn,

Xù,

letters unsealed,

With blues, yellows, and embroidered patterns,

These are the different names of literary forms.
From "Shānhú Gōu Shīhuà": The seven states addressing the king,

The Qin dynasty first established rules,
changing Shū to Zòu.
The Han dynasty set rituals,
with four categories: first Zhāng,

third Biǎo,

Zhāng for thanking grace,
Zòu for impeachment,
Biǎo for stating feelings,

From "Wénxīn Diāolóng."
The Five Classics
model heaven and earth,
emulate spirits and deities,
correlate with the order of things,
establish human principles,
penetrate the profound realm of human nature,
and exhaust the marrow of literary expression.
Thus, for discourses, arguments, rhetoric, and prefaces,
the Yìjīng presides at their head;
for edicts, policies, memorials, and petitions,
the Shūjīng initiates their source;
for rhapsodies, eulogies, songs, and praises,
the Shījīng establishes their foundation;
for inscriptions, elegies, admonitions, and prayers,
the Lǐjǐ governs their commencement;
for annals, biographies, inscriptions, and proclamations,
the Chūnqiū serves as their root;
together they reach the highest to set standards,
and extend to the farthest to open territories,
so that the hundred schools leap and soar,
yet ultimately remain within their sphere.
Moreover, literary writings
originally stem from the Five Classics.
Edicts, commands, policies, and proclamations
are born from the Shūjīng;
prefaces, narratives, discussions, and deliberations
are born from the Yìjīng;
songs, chants, rhapsodies, and eulogies
are born from the Shījīng;
sacrificial rites, mourning, and elegies
are born from the Lǐjǐ;
letters, petitions, admonitions, and inscriptions
are born from the Chūnqiū.
The statutes and regulations of the court,
the oaths and declarations of the army,
spreading and manifesting benevolence and righteousness,
expounding and illuminating merit and virtue,
governing the people and establishing the state,
are applied through many avenues.
As for cultivating one's nature and spirit,
gracefully offering remonstrance,
and savoring its flavors,
it is also a joyful endeavor.
Yǎnshì Jiāxùn
Zhèng Zǐchǎn presented spoils of war to Jìn,
but Shì Zhuāngbó was unable to interrogate him.
Zhòngní said:
"There is a saying:
Words are to fully express intent,
and literary refinement is to perfect words.
Without speaking, who would know one's intent?
But if words lack refinement,
they will not travel far.
When Jìn acted as hegemon and Zhèng invaded Chén,
it could not have been achieved without elegant rhetoric.
Be cautious with your words!"

and fine words are not adorned.

yúfán cannot be made into vessels;
if words are not adorned,

from the Discourses on Salt and Iron

From "Lù Jǐng's Canonical Sayings"
Writing takes qi as its foundation. In writing, qi is paramount.
The purity and turbidity of qi have their own substance,
and cannot be forced by strength.
It is like music:
although the melody may be uniform,
and the rhythm follows the same measure,
when it comes to the flow of qi, it is not uniform.
Skill and clumsiness are innate,
so even if one's father or elder brother possesses them,
they cannot be passed on to younger siblings.
From "Diǎnlùn"
People are skilled at recognizing their own strengths,
but since literature is not of a single style,
few can master them all.
Therefore, each person values their own strengths
and belittles others' shortcomings.
As the common saying goes:
"A worn-out broom in one's own home
is worth a thousand gold coins."
This is the harm of failing to see oneself clearly.
Ordinary people esteem what is distant and despise what is near,
following reputation rather than substance,
and also suffer from being blind to their own faults,
considering themselves worthy.
Now literature,
is fundamentally the same but differs in its branches.
For memorials and proposals should be elegant,
letters and discourses should be reasoned,
inscriptions and eulogies should value truth,
while poetry and rhapsodies should be beautiful.
These four categories differ,
so those skilled in them are specialized,
and only the comprehensively talented can master all styles.
Huán Tán observed that writers each have their own preferences;
some favor flashiness without knowing how to verify substance,
while others admire prolixity without seeing the need for conciseness.
Chén Sī also stated:
"Authors of our time
either delight in elaborate expressions and broad references,
making their meanings profound and obscure;
or they prefer to dissect words and debate minutiae,
splitting hairs and analyzing trifles.
Their learned habits differ,
their pursuits vary,
thus their expressive momentum diverges.
Liú Zhēn remarked:
"The substance and momentum in writing indeed have strength and weakness;
to have the language exhausted while momentum remains abundant
is a talent found in but one person in all under heaven,
truly unattainable.
What Gōnggàn discussed
also considerably involves vital energy.
Yet when writing employs momentum,
this momentum possesses both firm and gentle aspects;
it need not always be vigorous language with passionate intensity
to be deemed momentum.
Furthermore, Lù Yún himself acknowledged:
"In the past when discussing writing,
I prioritized diction over emotional content,
valuing momentum while disregarding elegance and polish.
But after attending Zhāng Gōng's discourse on writing,
I came to revere his teachings.
Indeed, emotional content should precede diction,
and momentum truly requires refinement—
this shows how one who was first misguided can later follow the good path.
《The Literary Mind》
An article should take reasoning as its heart and kidneys,
tone and style as its sinews and bones,
the meaning of events as its skin,
and elegance as its cap and crown.
In our present age, what is passed down
tends to pursue the trivial and abandon the fundamental,
mostly being flashy and ornate.
When rhetoric competes with reasoning,
rhetoric prevails and reasoning is suppressed;
when events contend with talent,
events become excessive and talent is diminished.
The unrestrained drift aimlessly and forget to return,
while the overly meticulous patch things up yet remain insufficient.
Since the customs of the time are like this,
how can one alone go against them?
One must only strive to avoid excess and extremity.

Tracing the root of what they have accumulated,
the style of their compositions,
highlights their inspired moments,
arousing and guiding their innate spirit,
causing people to boast of their achievements,
thus neglecting moral integrity,
and acting rashly in pursuit of advancement.
In today's literary scholars,
this flaw is even more pronounced.
With one satisfactory matter,
or one elegant and clever phrase,
their spirits soar to the highest heavens,
their ambitions tower over a thousand years,
they chant and admire their own work,
unaware that others exist beside them.
Moreover, the harm from grains of sand
is more cruel than that of spears and halberds;
the calamity of satire
spreads faster than wind and dust.
It is deeply advisable to guard against such concerns

End.
The pheasant displays brilliant colors,
yet soars no more than a hundred paces,
for its flesh is abundant but its strength is heavy;
the eagle and hawk lack bright hues,
but fly high up to the sky,
for their bones are strong and their spirit fierce.
The talent and strength of literary writing
are much like this.
If there is wind and bone but a lack of ornament,
then falcons gather in the literary grove;
if there is ornament but a lack of wind and bone,
then pheasants flee through the garden of letters.
Only when both are polished and gleaming can the phoenix soar—
this is truly the crying phoenix of literary writing.

like ox heads on horse's thighs,

It's only that having form is the norm,
and one should indeed ensure it always possesses form.
A true scholar ought to revise the Book of Songs and Book of Documents,
and establish rites and music—
why must one follow conventions and live under another's roof!
Moreover, the literature of the middle ages
lacked the transformation of the Way's essence,
borrowing inch by inch,
and patching up old things.
As for my own writing,
how is its form any different?

and the arrangement of events is unbridled,
neither by field paths nor lanes,
neither by roads nor routes.
Yet it conveys sounds and stirs elegance,
resonating with rhythm and startling with rhyme.
Perhaps it hasn't reached the ultimate,
but it has already reached its own limit.
I have no teacher, no friends,
no fixed literary rules or phrases,
but rather possess a solitary spirit and unique transcendence!
On his deathbed, he again admonished his son, saying:

the sea exalts supreme goodness.
"The Southern Qí"
Jiāng Yān, courtesy name Wéntōng,
was renowned for his literary talent in his youth,
but his creativity declined in his later years.
It is said that when he served as the governor of Xuānchéng,
upon returning from his post, he moored his boat at the shore of Chánlíng Temple.
One night, he dreamed of a man
who claimed to be Zhāng Jǐngyáng,
saying to him:
"I once lent you a bolt of brocade,
and now it is time to return it."
Jiāng Yān took out a few feet of it from his bosom and gave it to him.
The man was greatly angered and said:
"How could you have cut it all up?"
He then turned and saw Qiū Chí,
and said to him:
"I have these remaining few feet,
which are of no use to me now,
so I bequeath them to you."
From then on, Jiāng Yān's literary works faltered.
On another occasion, he stayed overnight at Yě Pavilion,
and dreamed of a man who claimed to be Guō Pú,
saying to Jiāng Yān:
"I left a brush with you many years ago,
and now it is time to return it."
Jiāng Yān then searched his bosom and found a five-colored brush, which he handed over.
After that, his poetry completely lacked beautiful lines,
and people of the time said his talent had been exhausted.
The *History of the Southern Dynasties* records that Jiāng Yān dreamed of a deity giving him a five-colored brush,
and those in the know said it was the deity of the five viscera.
The *Gàn Zǎizi*
Rèn Fǎng, courtesy name Yǎnshēng,
Wáng Jiǎn would always read his writings,
repeatedly and with great admiration,
believing no one at the time could match him.
He said:
"Since Chuán Jìyǒu, I have finally encountered another like Rèn Fǎng.
If this were Confucius' school,
he would surely ascend to the inner chamber."
He then asked Rèn Fǎng to compose an essay,
and upon reading it,
exclaimed:
"This perfectly captures what I had in mind!"
He then brought out his own writings,
asking Rèn Fǎng to proofread them,
and Rèn Fǎng revised several characters.
Wáng Jiǎn patted his desk and sighed:
"Who in later generations will know it was you who polished my work!"
At that time, Lángyá's Wáng Róng was exceptionally talented,
and considered himself unmatched in his era,
but upon reading Rèn Fǎng's writings,
he became disheartened by the comparison.
Shěn Yuē, the leading literary figure of his generation,
held him in high esteem.
History of the Southern Dynasties
The Three Eases: Marquis Yǐn Shěn Yuē stated:
"Writing should follow the three easinesses: easy to understand the subject matter,
first;
easy to recognize the characters,
second;
easy to read aloud,
third.
Xíng Zǐcái often said:
"Marquis Shěn's writings,
employ allusions without making readers aware of them,
as if they were words from the heart.
He deeply admired him for this.
Zǔ Xiàozhēng also once told me:
"Shěn's poem line 'the cliff shelters the stone marrow as it leans'
does this seem like using allusions?
Xíng Zǐcái and Wèi Shōu both had great reputations,
serving as standards for the contemporary customs,
and were regarded as masters.
Xíng admired and respected Shěn Yuē but looked down on Rén Fǎng,
while Wèi adored Rén Fǎng and disparaged Shěn Yuē,
often during conversations and banquets,
their words and expressions reflected this.
In Yèxià, opinions were divided,
each having their own factions.
Zǔ Xiàozhēng once said to me:
"The right and wrong regarding Rén and Shěn
actually reflect the superiority or inferiority of Xíng and Wèi.
" Yánshì Jiāxùn: Marquis Yǐn deliberated over the Two Nán,
analyzed and presented the three variations,
gave expression to the suppressed feelings of Yuān and Yún,
and revived the elegant style of Bō and Lù.
He made the musical pitches harmonious,
and the tones well-coordinated,
not only did Zǐjiàn dominate the Jiàn'ān period,
but Kè'ér also excelled as a leader in Jiāngzuǒ.

In the late Yǒngmíng era, literary compositions flourished greatly,
with Shěnyuē from Wúxīng, Xiè Tiǎo from Chénjùn, and Wáng Róng from Lángyá
mutually promoting each other based on shared temperament and interests,
while Zhōu Yóng from Rǔnán excelled in recognizing tones and rhymes.
Shěnyuē and others all applied the shāng mode in their writings,
using the level, rising, departing, and entering tones as the four tones,
and formulated rhymes based on this,
which could not be increased or decreased,
and was popularly known as
"the Yǒngmíng style"
"Biography of Lù Jué from the Southern Qí"
Wú Jūn's literary style was pure and elevated, possessing an antique air,
which enthusiasts all admired and emulated,
calling it the Wú Jūn style.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Xú Chī, styled Shìxiù,
served as study attendant to Prince Jìn'ān, Xiāo Gāng.
When the prince entered the court as crown prince,
Chī was transferred to the post of household steward with additional duties.
Chī's literary style being distinctive,
all officials in the Crown Prince's establishment studied it,
and the term "Palace Style"
originated from this.
When presenting writings and poetic compositions to Emperor Jiǎnwén,
he could complete them immediately upon taking up the brush,
yet they suffered from excessive frivolity and ornate beauty,
being called the "Official Style" at that time.
From "Liáng Annals"
Yǔ Xìn, courtesy name Zǐshān,
his father Yǔ Jiānwú served as the Palace Attendant of the Crown Prince,
in charge of records.
Xú Chī from Dōnghǎi held the position of Commander of the Right Guard,
and Xú Chī's son Xú Líng, along with Yǔ Xìn, both served as Academicians for Copying and Compilation.
Fathers and sons served in the Eastern Palace,
coming and going through the forbidden gates,
their favor and ceremonial treatment were unmatched in grandeur.
Since their literary works were both ornate and beautiful,
they were thus dubbed by the world
"the Xú-Yǔ Style"
indeed.
At that time, later scholars vied to emulate them,
and whenever they produced a piece of writing,
it was invariably circulated and recited throughout the capital.
When Yǔ Xìn was sent as an envoy to the Eastern Wèi,
his literary compositions and diplomatic rhetoric
were highly praised by the people of Yèxià.
From "History of the Northern Dynasties"
Xú Líng was a literary master of his generation,
his writing significantly transformed traditional styles,
with intricate composition and refined structure,
often imbued with novel ideas.
Whenever a piece was published,
enthusiasts would already be transcribing and reciting it,
spreading it throughout the Northern Zhōu and Northern Qí.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Liú Xiàochuò's literary grace,
was esteemed by later scholars,
and his writings were highly valued in his time.
Every piece he composed,
would spread widely by evening if finished in the morning,
with enthusiasts all reciting and transcribing them.
His works circulated as far as the north,
where no pavilion, garden pillar, or wall was left uninscribed with them.

The Liang dynasty's regular attendant Xú Líng was on a diplomatic mission to Qí.
At that time, Wèi Shōu was a literary talent, the finest of the Northern Dynasties.
He compiled his own collection of writings and presented it to Xú Líng,
instructing him to spread it in Jiāngzuǒ.
Xú Líng, however, sank it into the river upon crossing the Jiāng.
His attendants inquired about the reason,
to which Xú Líng replied:
"I am helping Duke Wèi conceal his clumsiness."
From "Suí Táng Jiāhuà Guócháo Zhuànjì"
When Yǔ Xìn from the Southern Dynasty first arrived,
northern literati often looked down on him.
He presented them with his "Ode to the Withered Tree,"
after which none dared speak disparagingly.
At that time, Wēn Zǐshēng had composed the stele inscription for Hanling Mountain Temple,
which Xìn read and copied.
Southerners asked Xìn:
"How do the northern literati compare?"
Xìn replied:
"Only the stone tablet at Hanling Mountain is worth discussing.
Xuē Dàohéng and Lú Sīdào show some skill with the brush.
As for the rest, their works are like the braying of donkeys and barking of dogs—
merely clamor grating on the ears."
From "Qiān Zǎi"
Wēn Zǐshēng, courtesy name Péngjǔ,
was widely read in the Hundred Schools of Thought,
and his writing was elegant and graceful.
The Liang envoy Zhāng Gāo copied his literary works,
which were transmitted beyond the Yangtze River.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng praised him, saying:
"Cáo Zhí and Lù Jī have been reborn in the northern lands—
how I regret that our own literary talents
are limited in number and fortune!"
When Fù Biāo, the governor of Yángxià, was sent as an envoy to Tǔyùhún,
he saw several volumes of books belonging to their ruler,
which turned out to be the writings of Zǐshēng.
Jìyīn Prince Huīyè once remarked:
"Among the literati of Jiāngzuǒ,
the Sòng dynasty had Yán Yánzhī and Xiè Língyùn,
the Liáng dynasty had Shěn Yuē and Rén Fǎng—
Zǐshēng is capable of surpassing Yán and overshadowing Xiè,
while encompassing Rén and outshining Shěn."
Yáng Zūnyǎn, in his "On Literary Virtue,"
considered him refined and virtuous by nature.
The Book of Wèi
Wèi Shōu always belittled Xíng Shào's writing,
and Xíng Shào once said:
"The literary style of Rěn Fǎng from Jiangnan was originally loose,
Wèi Shōu not only imitated it,
but also largely plagiarized it.
When Wèi Shōu heard this,
he retorted:
"Xíng Shào often steals from Shěn Yuē's collection himself,
how dare he accuse me of stealing Rěn Fǎng's words?
According to Records of the Three Kingdoms, when Wèi Shōu mentioned Shěn Yuē's collection disparagingly,
Xú Zhīcái angrily said:
"When you read Shěn's writings,
you can't understand half of them,
how can you discuss their merits and faults?
He said to Wèi Shōu:
"I have nothing to discuss with you.
Wèi Shōu left,
avoiding him.

Zǔ Yíng was esteemed for his literary talent,
and once remarked to others:
"Writing must originate from one's own loom,
forming a unique style and character;
how can one share the same livelihood with others?"
This was meant to satirize those in the world who delight in plagiarizing others' writings for their own use.
The History of the Northern Dynasties
Lǐ È, styled Shìhuī,
was skilled in literary composition.
During the reign of Emperor Wén,
as the contemporary literary style tended towards frivolity,
drifting aimlessly without return,
he submitted a memorial stating:
"Since the three ancestors of the Wèi dynasty,
successively prized literary embellishment,
in the Qí and Liáng courts south of the Yangtze,
these flaws became even more severe.
Abandoning principles while preserving eccentricities,
pursuing emptiness and chasing trivialities,
page after page and volume upon volume,
contain nothing beyond descriptions of moonlight and dew,
piling up on desks and filling boxes,
consist only of depictions of wind and clouds.
Discarding the root to pursue the branch,
this trend has spread throughout the cultured realm,
with mutual imitation and transmission,
growing increasingly prevalent over time.
The Emperor
Suí Dù Zhèngcáng composed texts with remarkable speed,
as if they were prepared in advance.
He once had several people hold paper and brushes simultaneously,
each assigned a topic to write on,
while Zhèngcáng dictated orally and all compositions were completed,
each possessing literary coherence,
which astonished contemporaries.
He also authored twenty volumes on literary forms and styles,
discussing the principles of writing,
highly systematic in organization.
Later generations treasured and practiced them,
many using these works to secure official positions,
widely circulating in society,
earning him the contemporary nickname "Literary Master."
Even in distant regions like Gāolì (Korea),
they were jointly studied and transmitted.
It was called "The Dù Family's New Book."
(From History of the Northern Dynasties)
Chǔ Suìliáng composed the elegiac address for Tàizōng's funeral.
While returning on horseback from the court,
he mistakenly entered his own home without realizing it.
"Records of the National Court"
Yáng Jiǒng,
a native of Huáyīn in Huázhōu,
was in his youth grouped with Wáng Bó from Jīngzhōu, Lú Zhàolín from Fànyáng, and Luò Bīnwáng from Dōngyáng,
all renowned throughout the land for their literary talents,
and collectively referred to as
"Wáng, Yáng, Lú, Luò"
also known as the
"Four Elites"
Upon hearing this,
Yáng Jiǒng remarked to others:
"I feel ashamed to be placed before Lú,
but humiliated to be ranked after Wáng.
Contemporary critics agreed with his assessment.
Later, Cuī Róng, Lǐ Qiáo, and Zhāng Yuè all held the Four Elites' writings in high esteem.
Cuī Róng commented:
"Wáng Bó's essays are grand and transcendent,
displaying traces of unparalleled elegance,
far beyond what ordinary writers can achieve;
Yáng Jiǒng and Lú Zhàolín, however, can aspire to reach his level,
thus Yáng Jiǒng's words ring true.
Zhāng Yuè told others:
"Yáng Jiǒng's literary thoughts flow like a cascading river pouring water,
inexhaustible when drawn upon;
he surpasses Lú in skill,
and is no less than Wáng.
His shame at being ranked after Wáng is indeed justified,
while his modesty about preceding Lú is commendable.
From the "Old Book of Táng"
Wáng Bó, whenever composing a stele inscription or eulogy,
would first grind several sheng of ink.
Then, pulling the quilt over his face, he would lie down to sleep.
Suddenly rising, he would take up the brush and write it out,
initially without making any corrections.
People of the time called this
"the draft in the belly"
From "Tán Sǒu"
Yáng Jiǒng was fond of using ancient figures' names in his writing,
such as Zhāng Píngzǐ's strategic discussions,
and Lù Shìhéng's poetic compositions.
Pān Ānrén would surely find it crude,
and Zhòng Chángtǒng was hardly qualified to understand it.
This style was mockingly called the "Register of Ghosts."
From "Qiān Zǎi"
Luò Bīnwáng was fond of using numerical pairs,
such as "the Qin region's strategic passes number one hundred and two,"
"the Han dynasty's detached palaces amount to thirty-six."
People of his time nicknamed him
"Doctor of Calculation"
Wáng Jù during the Chángshòu era served as a Secretary in the Phoenix Pavilion,
when the five princes including Shòuchūn were assigned their fiefdoms,
and were to receive their patents of appointment on the same day.
The officials in charge drafted the ceremonial procedures,
but forgot to include the text of the patents.
By the time all the officials were assembled in their positions,
they realized the ritual was incomplete.
The ministers looked at each other in dismay,
but Jù immediately summoned five scribes and ordered each to take up a brush,
as he dictated the text for them to write separately,
and in no time all the documents were completed with elegant wording and profound reasoning,
earning everyone's admiration and praise.
(From the Old Book of Táng)
The literature of the Tang dynasty,
roughly speaking, underwent three transformations.
Emperor Gāozǔ and Emperor Tàizōng followed the lingering style of the Southern Dynasties,
crafting ornate phrases and painted sentences,
matching rhythms and balancing tones,
thus Wáng Bó and Yáng Jiǒng dominated this era.
Emperor Xuánzōng favored classical scholarship,
and the court officials gradually grew weary of excessive embellishment,
upholding elegance while rejecting superficiality,
causing the literary spirit to become more vigorous and profound,
with Yàn Gōng and Xǔ Gōng leading the school.
During the Dàlì and Zhēngyuán periods,
talented writers emerged in great numbers,
delving into the true essence of the Way,
immersing themselves in the depths of sagely wisdom,
whereupon Hán Yù initiated the movement,
followed by Liǔ Zōngyuán, Lǐ Áo, and Huángfǔ Shí,
who repudiated the Hundred Schools of Thought,
imposing strict rules and structures,
surpassing the literature of the Jìn and Wèi dynasties,
and even challenging that of the Hàn and Zhōu,
elevating Tang literature to the standard of a royal model,
reaching its zenith.
As for literary attendants and ceremonial compositions, there were Lǐ Qiáo, Sòng Zhīwèn, Shěn Quánqī, and Wáng Wéi;
for policy essays, there were Cháng Gǔn, Yáng Yuán, Lù Zhì, Quán Déyǔ, Wáng Zhòngshū, and Lǐ Déyù;
for poetry, there were Dù Fǔ, Lǐ Bái, Yuán Zhěn, Bái Jūyì, and Liú Yǔxī;
for the eccentric and unconventional, there were Lǐ Hè, Dù Mù, and Lǐ Shāngyǐn.
All of them stood out with their unique strengths as the foremost of their time,
truly worthy of admiration.
From the "History of the Tang Dynasty"
Zhāng Zhuó, whenever he took the imperial examinations,
always achieved the highest rank,
participated in four selection judgments,
and his policy essays were considered the best in the evaluation office.
Yuán Bànqiān said to people:
"Master Zhāng's writings are like bronze coins,
selected ten thousand times, they hit ten thousand times,
never heard of them being rejected.
Contemporary scholars esteemed him,
regarding him as
"the Bronze Coin Academician."
At that time, he was renowned throughout the land,
regardless of whether they were virtuous or not,
everyone memorized and recited his writings.
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
the court emissary Mǎ Xiāntóng was captured by Mòchuò,
Mòchuò said to Xiāntóng:
"Is Zhāng Wénchéng still around?
He replied:
"He was recently demoted from the position of Censor.
Mòchuò said:
"Your state has such a person but does not employ him,
the Han people are incapable.
States like Silla, Japan, and other eastern barbarian tribes,
particularly valued his writings,
every time they sent envoys to the court,
they would repeatedly offer gold and shells to purchase his works,
such was the far-reaching spread of his talent and fame.
Xú Yànbó often sought novelty in his writing,
referring to the Phoenix Pavilion as the Swallow Pavilion,
the Dragon Gate as the Hornless Dragon's Abode,
the Golden Valley as the Shining Stream,
the Jade Mountain as the Jasper Peak,
straw dogs as floral dogs,
bamboo horses as slender-steed carriages,
the moon rabbit as the spirit rabbit,
and the wind ox as the blazing calf.
Later writers imitated this style,
calling it
"the obscure style"
from "Records of Anecdotes"
Fù Jiāmó and Wú Shàowēi were close friends,
holding office together.
Previously,
when literary scholars composed stele inscriptions and eulogies,
they all followed the style of Xú and Yǔ,
resulting in a gradual decline in vigor and diction.
When Jiāmó and Shàowēi composed their writings,
they both took the classics as their foundation,
earning the admiration of contemporaries,
and causing a complete transformation in literary style,
which became known as the Fù-Wú Style.
(from the Old Book of Tang, Biographies of Literary Figures)
Cuī Róng composed the elegiac address for Empress Wǔ Zétiān on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture.
He exhausted his mind excessively in the process,
and upon leaving duty on horseback,
he passed his own gate without realizing it.
Once the text was completed, he passed away.
Contemporaries regarded it as a piece without equal in two hundred years.
"Records of the Two Capitals and National Chronicles"
Lǐ Yǒng early excelled in literary fame,
especially skilled in composing stele inscriptions and eulogies.
Although demoted and serving outside the capital,
officials from the central court and Buddhist and Daoist temples throughout the empire
often offered gold and silk,
seeking his writings.
The works he produced over time,
amounted to several hundred pieces,
and the gifts he received
reached enormous sums.
Contemporary opinion held that since ancient times, no one who sold literary works for wealth
had achieved as much as Yǒng.
His works "Account of Conduct for Duke Hán," "Stele of Releasing Life in Hóngzhōu," and "Critique of Wéi Jùyuán's Posthumous Title Discussion"
were highly esteemed by literary scholars.
Old Book of Táng
Lǐ Huá's literary style was elegant and beautiful,
though lacking in heroic spirit;
Xiāo Yǐngshì's rhetoric was sharp and brilliant,
and Huá believed his own works surpassed it.
Suspecting Yǐngshì's words were exaggerated,
he then composed "An Elegy for an Ancient Battleground,"
stained it to appear like an antique,
and placed it in the Buddhist scriptures cabinet.
Huá and Yǐngshì discovered it while reading Buddhist texts,
Huá asked him:
"How is this piece?"
Yǐngshì replied:
"Acceptable."
Huá said:
"Among contemporary writers,
who could match this?"
Yǐngshì responded:
"With slightly more refined thought,
you could reach this level."
Huá was astonished.
Huá wrote essays arguing that turtle shell divination could be abolished,
which scholars found reasonable.
Lǐ Hàn was renowned as a jìnshì.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he resided in Yángdí.
His writing was meticulous,
and his thought process was laborious.
He once requested music from Huángfǔ Céng, the magistrate of Yángdí,
playing music whenever he felt mentally parched,
and composing when his spirit was inspired.
He authored a two-volume biography of Zhāng Xún, Yáo Yǐn, and others.
Scholars and friends praised him.

and said to Bái:
"Are your heart, liver, and five viscera all made of brocade?

From "The Original Collection"
When Lǐ Shèng defeated Zhū Cǐ,
Emperor Dézōng read the victory proclamation on the recapture of the city,
which stated:
"I have already cleansed the palace grounds,
and reverently paid homage at the imperial tombs.
The bell stands remain undisturbed,
the ancestral temple appears as before.
The Emperor was moved to tears and choked with emotion,
while all the attendants and palace ladies wept softly.
Commentators noted that in our dynasty's history,
no victory report or proclamation
had ever matched this one.

Later, Yú Gōngyì became disliked by Lù Zhì,

etc.

but the city walls have become ruins,
the palaces and temples suddenly collapsed,
the bell stands stand empty.

"The remote regions of Qīng and Dài
submitted at mere summons,
while Jìběi and Hénán
could be settled by circulating proclamations.
Yú Gōngyì evidently drew inspiration from these.

Literary works are often composed
during travels or in rustic obscurity.
Preface to the Collected Poems of Hán Jīngtán

literary style declined and substance was lost,

Opening and closing with wondrous astonishment,
driving waves and shaking clouds,

After the Yuánhé era, literary scholars,
studied the unconventional from Hán Yù,
and the obscure from Fán Zōngshī.
For ballad-style poetry, they learned from Zhāng Jí.
In poetic lines, they studied the vehement and unrestrained from Mèng Jiāo,
the simple and direct from Bái Jūyì,
and the decadent and ornate from Yuán Zhěn,
all collectively named
"the Yuánhé style."
Generally, the style of the Tiānbǎo era favored partisanship,

"Supplement to the National History"
At the beginning of the Tang Dynasty, the Literary Institute was established,
and Emperor Gāozōng honored the talented scholars.
Yú Shìnán and Xǔ Jìngzōng excelled in reputation earlier,
while Sū Wèidào and Lǐ Jiǎo gained fame later.
Their refined writings
were all compiled into collections.
However, those who adhered to antiquity tended to be overly obscure,
while those who pursued ornate style sometimes became unorthodox.
The narrow-minded were confined by prosodic rules,
and the unrestrained drifted into vulgar melodies.
If one were to regulate the rhythm and standards,
and evaluate both ancient and modern works,
so that both worthy and unworthy would appreciate the writings,
none achieved such prominence as Yuán Zhěn and Bái Jūyì.
In the past, during the Jiàn'ān era, the talented scholars
first established dominance with Cáo Zhí and Liú Zhēn;
during the Yǒngmíng era, the masters of ci poetry
initially yielded achievement to Shěn Yuē and Xiè Tiǎo.
As for the Yuánhé era's leadership,
it was solely held by Wēizhī (Yuán Zhěn) and Lètiān (Bái Jūyì).
"Old Discussion on the Biographies of Yuán and Bái"
Bái Jūyì and Lǐ Déyù were at odds,
and whenever Bái sent him literary works,

never opening them.
When Liú Sānfù once requested to read them,
he replied:
"Seeing his writing would unsettle my mind!

with Liú Sānfù serving on his staff.

not speed."

during the Chángqìng era, Yuán Jì was sent as an envoy to the Kingdom of Xīnlúo,
where he observed the local people
copying and reciting Dìng's compositions, the "Black Water Stele" and "Record of Painting Cranes";
