From "Miscellaneous Records of the Jade Box": Emperor Wén of Wèi and his brother Prince Sī of Chén (Cáo Zhī) were out together
when they saw two bulls fighting between walls,
and one bull fell into a well and died.
The emperor ordered Cáo Zhī to compose a poem
without mentioning "bull,"
without mentioning "fight,"
without mentioning "well,"
without mentioning "death,"
and to complete it in forty words within a hundred paces,
or face punishment if he failed.
Cáo Zhī instantly composed it,
saying:
"Two pieces of meat walk side by side,
bearing horizontal bones on their heads.
Arriving at a perilous spot,
they rise abruptly and clash.
Two foes cannot both win;
one piece of meat lies in an earthen cave.
Not due to lack of strength,
but pent-up fury finds no release."
Before even finishing the paces,
he also composed a "Self-Lament Poem" in thirty words,
saying:
"Boil beans to make a soup,
filter fermented beans to extract the juice.
The beanstalk burns beneath the pot,
while beans in the pot weep.
Born from the same root,
why torment each other so urgently!"
Such was his quick wit.
From "Authentic Accounts of the Secretary's Garden"
Poems of Bái Mǎ Wáng Cáo Biāo of the Wèi,
Poems of Wèi literary scholar Xú Gàn.
Bái Mǎ exchanged poems with Chén Sī,
Wěi Cháng and Gōng Gàn corresponded back and forth;
though it is said
"striking a bell with a reed,"
they still achieved elegance and refinement.
Shī Pǐn
Zhāng Huà's poetry,
originates from Wǎng Càn.
Its style is ornate and flowery,
with allegorical themes that are not extraordinary,
skillful in the use of language,
and strives for refinement and elegance.
Although renowned in past eras,
discerning scholars still regret its abundance of romantic sentiments,
and scarcity of heroic spirit.
The poetry of Pān Yuè
originates from Zhòngxuān.
The "Hànlín" praises it as gracefully soaring like a bird with feathers,
or like clothing made of fine silk and crepe.
Yet it is shallower than Lù Jī's works.
Xiè Hùn remarked:
"Pān's poetry is resplendent like unfurled brocade,
with excellence everywhere;
Lù's writing is like sifting sand to find gold,
often revealing treasures.
Róng states that Yìshòu favors brilliance and elegance,
thus considering Pān superior.
The "Hànlín" offers a profound critique,
therefore deeming Lù more profound.
I often say:
"Lù's talent is like the sea,
Pān's talent is like the river.
Elegiac verses are,
some say, songs from ancient funeral processions,
others claim they originated from Tián Héng's followers,
all expressing the living's grief and sorrow for the departed.
Lù Jī often wrote them as laments from the deceased's perspective,
which neither follows poetic conventions,
nor aligns with the original purpose of such compositions.
The Family Instructions of the Yán Clan
Guō Jǐngchún's poem says:
"No tree in the forest is still,
no river ceases its flow."
Ruǎn Fú remarked:
"Profoundly lofty and desolate,
it is truly beyond words.
Whenever I read these lines,
I feel my spirit transcending physical form."
Shì Shuō
Xiàhóu Zhàn completed his "Zhōu Poems,"
and showed them to Pān Ānrén.
Ānrén said:
"These are not merely gentle and elegant,
but also distinctly reveal the nature of filial piety and fraternal duty.
Because of this, Pān consequently composed his "Family Tradition Poems."
If You Offend Me, I Will Publish Your Poem When Huán Wēn was young, he was good friends with Yīn Hào.
Hào once wrote a short poem and showed it to Wēn.
Wēn said:
"You'd better be careful not to offend me,
or I will show your poem to others."
From "Shěn Yuē's Unofficial History"
Xǔ Xún possessed outstanding talent,
excelling in literary composition.
Since masters such as Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, Wáng Bāo, and Yáng Xióng,
the world had esteemed fù and sòng poetry,
all modeled after the forms of the Shījīng and Chǔcí,
while also synthesizing the teachings of the Hundred Schools.
By the Jiàn'ān period,
poetry flourished greatly.
Towards the end of the Western Dynasty,
though poets like Pān and Lù sometimes emphasized substance over style,
their fundamental principles remained unchanged.
During the Zhèngshǐ era,
Wáng Bì and Hé Yán favored profound discussions of Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ,
which subsequently became highly valued.
After the court crossed the Yangtze River,
Buddhist philosophy grew particularly influential,
so Guō Pǔ's five-character verse began blending Daoist concepts with rhyme.
Xǔ Xún and Tàiyuán's Sūn Chuò
mutually inherited and promoted this trend,
further incorporating the language of the Three Ages (Buddhist past, present, future),
until the classical Shījīng-Chǔcí style was completely transformed.
Xǔ Xún and Sūn Chuò became leading literary figures of their time,
and thereafter all writers followed their style.
By the Yìxī era,
Xiè Hùn initiated reforms.
From "Continued Annals of Jìnyáng Autumn"
Huán Xuán was composing a poem,
when his thoughts wouldn't come he had military music played,
and soon his thoughts came.
He wrote: "The crying crane echoes over the long ridge,"
and exclaimed:
"Military music indeed brings forth one's thoughts.
from "Common Sayings"
Shǔ Lǐ Shòu established the Imperial Repository in Chéngdū,
indulging in extravagance,
causing the common people to yearn for rebellion.
His minister Gǒng Zhuàng composed seven poems,
attributing them to Yīng Qú,
to satirize Shòu.
Shòu responded, saying:
"Upon reading the poems, I understand their intent.
If they were written by a contemporary,
they would be the words of a wise and virtuous person.
But if they were written by an ancient,
they are merely the usual talk of a dead ghost."
From "Wèi Shū Zǎijì Èrshíyī"
During the transition to the Liu-Song period,
was there truly no poetry!
In the Yixi era,
Xiè Yìshòu and Yīn Zhòngwén were considered the pinnacle of ornate elegance,
yet Yīn could not compete.
"The Grades of the Poets"
Yán Yánzhī and Xiè Língyùn from Chénjùn
both gained fame for their literary talents,
yet their writing speeds differed greatly.
Emperor Wén once ordered each to compose yuèfǔ poems following established models.
Yán Yánzhī completed his immediately upon receiving the command,
while Xiè Língyùn took much longer to finish.
Yán Yánzhī once asked Bào Zhào to compare his poetry with Xiè Língyùn's,
to which Bào replied:
"Xiè's five-character poems are like newly bloomed lotuses,
naturally beautiful;
your poetry resembles brocades and embroideries,
also dazzling with ornate decoration."
Yán Yánzhī often disparaged Tāng Huìxiū's poetry,
telling others:
"Huìxiū's compositions
are merely alleyway ballads.
They will likely mislead future generations."
Contemporary critics held that
since Pān Yuè and Lù Jī,
no literary figures could match
Yán Yánzhī and Xiè Língyùn.
West of the Yangtze River they spoke of Pān and Lù,
while east of the river they spoke of Yán and Xiè.
"Xiè's poetry resembles lotuses emerging from water,
while Yán's is like inlaid colors and carved gold."
Yán took lifelong offense at this comment.
《Gradings of the Poets》
Whenever Xiè Língyùn composed a poem that reached the capital,
people of all social statuses would compete to transcribe it.
Within a single night,
scholars and commoners alike throughout the realm would admire it far and wide,
stirring the entire capital with admiration.
"History of the Song Dynasty" Qí Wǔlíng Wáng Huá wrote short verses,
studying poetry under Xiè Língyùn's style.
Emperor Tàizǔ of Chén commented:
"Kānglè's unrestrained compositional style
lacks clear structure from beginning to end.
Ānrén and Shìhéng are truly worthy of emulation,
while Yán Yánzhī should be considered secondary.
"Sixteen Records of Southern Qí"
Xiè Huìlián's talent and thoughts were rich and swift,
but it is regrettable that this orchid and jade withered early,
so his long reins were never given free rein.
His works "Autumn Reflections" and "Pounding Clothes",
even if Língyùn were to think sharply again,
how could they be surpassed?
He long excelled at composing beautiful songs and ballads,
ranking first among poets.
"The Grading of Poets": Kānglè every time he faced Huìlián,
immediately obtained fine phrases.
Later, at the Western Hall in Yǒngjiā,
he thought about poetry all day without success.
Between waking and sleeping, he suddenly saw Huìlián,
and then completed
"Spring grass grows by the pond,
garden willows transform the singing birds."
Therefore, he often said:
"These lines had divine assistance,
they are not my words.
"Family Records"
During the Yuánjiā era,
there was Xiè Língyùn, whose talent was lofty and poetic expression abundant,
so richly ornate it was hard to follow his traces.
He indeed surpassed Liú and Guō,
and overshadowed Pān and Zuǒ.
Thus we know that Chén Sī was the hero of the Jiàn'ān period,
with Gōnggàn and Zhòngxuān as his supports.
Lù Jī was the flower of the Tàikāng era,
with Ānrén and Jǐngyáng as his supports.
Xiè Kè was the champion of the Yuánjiā period,
with Yán Yánnián as his support.
These all are the crowning achievements of five-character poetry,
literary compositions that commanded their age.
"Shī Pǐn"
Xiè Zhuāng was eloquent. Once, Emperor Xiàowǔ of Song asked Yán Yánzhī,
"How is Xiè Xīyì's 'Rhapsody on the Moon'?"
Yán replied,
"Beautiful it is,
but Zhuāng first knew of being a thousand miles apart,
yet sharing the same moon."
The emperor summoned Zhuāng
and told him Yán's reply.
Zhuāng responded immediately,
"When Yán composed 'Qiūhú's Poem,' he first knew that in life there are long partings and that in death there is no return."
The emperor clapped his hands and laughed, saying,
"People enjoy bantering,
but none fail to meet their match!"
Bào Zhào, styled Míngyuǎn,
excelled in crafting poetry that depicted forms and described objects;
he captured Jǐngyáng's eccentricity,
embodied Màoxiān's delicate grace,
surpassed Xiè Hùn in structural vigor,
and outpaced Yánnián in swift momentum.
He synthesized the strengths of these four masters to achieve unique excellence,
standing alone across two eras.
Alas, his talent was brilliant but his status humble,
thus he was obscured in his own time.
However, his emphasis on skillful verisimilitude,
unflinching from perilous unconventionality,
somewhat compromised the refined elegance of his tone.
Therefore, those who champion risky and common styles
often associate themselves with Bào Zhào.
《The Gradings of Poets》
Xiè Tiǎo, courtesy name Xuánhuī, wrote poetry
that originated from Xiè Hùn,
slightly flawed in its meticulousness,
somewhat lacking in coherence.
Within a single poem,
there are both gems and stones,
yet the extraordinary stanzas and elegant lines
are often strikingly powerful,
enough to make Shūyuán (Xiè Hùn) lose his footing,
and Míngyuǎn (Bào Zhào) change countenance.
He excelled at initiating poetic beginnings,
but often stumbled in the concluding sections,
which indicates sharp ideas but limited talent.
Nevertheless, he was greatly admired by later scholars.
Tiǎo frequently discussed poetry with me,
with deeper emotion and cadence than his writings.
Regarding Tiǎo's expertise in five-character poetry,
Shěn Yuē once remarked:
"For two hundred years,
there has been no poetry like this.
The History of the Southern Dynasties records that Emperor Jiǎn of Liáng highly valued Tiǎo's poetry, saying:
"If I don't read Xiè Tiǎo's poetry for three days,
I feel my mouth becomes foul.
In Talks and Anecdotes, it's noted that Liú Xiàochuò, who had great fame at the time,
yielded to no one,
yet admired only Xiè Tiǎo.
He often kept Xiè's poems on his desk,
constantly reciting and savoring them whether active or still.
Emperor Jiǎnwén loved Táo Yuānmíng's writings,
and did exactly the same.
Family Instructions
Xiāo Wényǎn was from Lánlíng,
Qiū Lìngkǎi was from Wúxīng,
Jiāng Hóng was from Jìyáng.
Qí Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng once held a nighttime gathering to compose poems,
stipulating four rhymes within the time a candle burned one inch.
Wényǎn said:
"If we must burn one inch of candle
to complete a four-rhyme poem,
what difficulty is there?"
Thereupon he joined Qiū and Jiāng in striking a bronze bowl to set the rhythm,
and when the sound faded, the poems were completed,
all worthy of appreciation.
(From the "Biography of Wáng Sēngrú" in History of the Southern Dynasties)
Wáng Jí's poem "Entering Ruòyē Creek" states:
"The cicadas' chirping makes the woods seem more tranquil,
The birds' singing makes the mountains appear even more secluded."
In Jiāngnán, it was considered uniquely superb beyond the words themselves,
with no one expressing different opinions.
Jiǎn Wén would chant it,
unable to forget it.
Xiào Yuán would recite and savor it,
believing it could not be matched again,
so much so that in his "Records of Cherishing the Past,"
he included it in Wáng Jí's biography.
Lú Xún of Fànyáng, a talented scholar of Yèxià,
however, said these lines did not form proper expression,
questioning what skill they demonstrated,
and Wèi Shōu agreed.
"Family Instructions"
Qí Xiāo Què, styled Rénzǔ,
once composed a poem on an autumn night,
of which two lines read:
"Lotus flowers fall with the dew,
Willow trees sparse under the moon.
Xíng Zǐcái remarked:
"Xiāo Rénzǔ's literary work
can be described as exquisitely crafted lines emerging occasionally.
In the past, Pān and Lù were contemporaries,
yet did not follow the style of the Jiàn'ān period;
Yán and Xiè shared similar voices,
thus transforming the essence of the Tàiyuán era.
From the Hàn to the Jìn dynasties,
emotional appreciation remained discordant.
Between Héběi and Jiāngnán,
creative concepts and compositions naturally differed.
Yán Huángmén stated:
"I admire its leisurely elegance,
vividly appearing before my eyes.
However, figures like Lú Sīdào
were never fond of it.
Different tastes like Jī and Bì constellations,
are naturally justified.
"Records of the Three Kingdoms"
Zhāng Shuài, styled Shìjiǎn,
often set a daily quota of composing one poem.
A man named Yú Nè saw them and disparaged them,
so Shuài promptly burned them all,
then composed new poems to show him,
claiming they were by Shěn Yuē.
Nè then praised every single word, finding not a single flaw.
Shuài said:
"These are my works."
Nè felt ashamed and withdrew.
From *History of the Southern Dynasties*
In the Later Wei Dynasty, Prince Péngchéng, Xié,
accompanied the emperor on a visit to Shàngdǎng.
There was a large pine tree,
and the emperor, while walking, composed a poem,
saying:
"You may compose a poem,
and bring it to me when I reach my destination."
At that time, Xié was over ten paces away from the emperor,
but he reached the emperor's location and presented it.
The poem read:
"I ask the pine, through how many winters it has endured,
how the mountains and rivers compare to the past,
the wind and clouds remain as in ancient times."
"Original Biography"
In Northern Qí's Bīngzhōu, there was a scholar-official from a prominent family,
who enjoyed composing ridiculous poems and rhapsodies,
and looked down upon eminent figures like Xíng and Wèi.
Everyone mocked him,
yet falsely praised his works,
and he would invariably slaughter an ox, brew wine, and invite them to feast.
His wife was a woman of clear discernment,
and she tearfully admonished him.
The man sighed and said:
"My talent is not even tolerated by my own wife,
let alone by strangers.
He remained unaware of the truth until his death.
From "Family Instructions."
Lǐ Délín served as the Director of the Palace Secretariat,
and together with Yáng Sù, they jointly held power in the Suí administration.
Yáng Sù, being a meritorious official, was extravagant and opulent,
with a rear chamber housing a thousand women.
Lǐ Délín's son, Bǎiyào, entered his residence at night,
and secretly had an affair with Yáng Sù's favored concubine.
The next morning, both were seized in the courtyard,
and were about to be executed.
Bǎiyào was not yet twenty years old,
with a handsome and distinguished demeanor.
Yáng Sù felt regretful for him,
and said:
"I have heard that you are skilled at composing poetry,
you may write a poem to narrate your own story.
If it meets my satisfaction,
I will spare you from death.
He was given paper and a brush,
and he completed it immediately.
Yáng Sù read it with delight,
and promptly gave the concubine to him along with a dowry of several hundred thousand.
"Records of the State Dynasty."
Emperor Yáng was skilled at composing essays,
yet he did not wish anyone to surpass him.
Sīlì Xuē Dàohéng thus offended him,
and was later executed for a subsequent incident,
with the emperor saying:
"Can you still write 'On the empty beam fall mud from swallows' nests'
now?
When Emperor Yáng composed "The Swallow's Song",
all literary scholars wrote matching verses.
Only Zhùzuòláng Wáng Zhòu refrained from writing,
which the emperor always resented.
Wáng Zhòu was ultimately executed for this,
with the emperor reciting his striking line:
"'Courtyard grass, untended, grows green as it pleases'
can you still produce such phrases?
"Records of the State Dynasty: Anecdotes from Suí and Táng"
Lú Huángmén said:
"Chén Shíyí stemmed the decadent tide,
causing a unified transformation in the substance and style of writing throughout the land.
Even now, the lingering influence of the Chén and Liáng palace style persists,
but through your great reforms,
it has been utterly swept away.
Ancient and modern literary collections are blocked and cannot circulate,
yet your writings alone spread across the four directions,
truly possessing strength that rivals the Creator!
From "Lǐ Yángbīng's Preface"
After Zhāng Yuè was demoted to Yuèzhōu,
his poetry became sorrowful and plaintive,
which people said was aided by the rivers and mountains.
The tradition of song poetry
has long been in decline.
It largely perished during the Southern Dynasties,
and was corrupted by Chén Shūbǎo.
Yet those who practice it today,
if unable to seek antiquity in the Jiàn'ān period,
turn to Jiāngzuǒ;
if unable to seek beauty in Jiāngzuǒ,
they turn to the Southern Dynasties.
Those who excessively indulge in ornate language to the point of sickness
are indeed the sinners of the Southern Dynasties.
In our Táng dynasty, one who has mastered this art,
whose words transcend heaven and earth,
whose thoughts surpass ghosts and deities,
reading them transports the spirit across the eight extremes,
contemplating them fills the heart with the four seas,
magnificent and unrestrained,
truly speaking no earthly language—
is Lǐ Tàibái.
From Pí Rìxiū's Literary Granary: Lǐ Yángbīng said,
"Tàibái's works often contain celestial verses,
most of his words carry satirical undertones.
Since the time of the Odes and Elegies,
he has galloped past Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù,
whipped Yáng Xióng and Sīmǎ Xiàngrú,
standing alone for a thousand years—
only this master alone.
Dù Zǐměi's poetry,
ascends to the heights of the "Airs of the States" and "Elegies",
and encompasses the styles of Shěn Quánqī and Sòng Zhīwèn.
Its diction surpasses that of Sū Wǔ and Lǐ Líng,
its vigor overwhelms that of Cáo Cāo and Liú Zhēn,
overshadowing the solitary elegance of Yán Yánzhī and Xiè Língyùn,
while blending the vibrant beauty of Xú Líng and Yǔ Xìn,
fully capturing the stylistic momentum of the ancients.
"Collection of Yuán Zhěn"
During the final years of the Tiānbǎo era,
Liú Xīyí, Wáng Chānglíng, Zǔ Yǒng, Zhāng Ruòxū, Mèng Hàorán, Cháng Jiàn, Lǐ Bái, and Dù Fǔ,
though they had gained renown,
all wandered in exile without meeting opportunity,
which was due to their reliance on talent and frivolous eccentricity.
The "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng" states: Poets often face hardship;
for instance, Chén Zǐ'áng and Dù Fǔ each received the post of a Reminder,
yet encountered obstruction and adversity until death;
Lǐ Bái and Mèng Hàorán did not attain even a minor official appointment,
living in poverty and distress their entire lives.
In recent times, Mèng Jiāo at sixty
finally became an Assistant Director of Music,
while Zhāng Jí at fifty
had not advanced beyond a Grand Supplicator.
Wáng Wéi was devoted to Buddhism,
hence his courtesy name Mójié.
His disposition was lofty and far-reaching,
and he acquired Sòng Zhīwèn's
"Lándscape of the Wangchuan Estate,
surpassing even today's Qīngliáng Temple"
indeed.
Wéi was renowned for his poetry,
yet he often appropriated others' lines.
For instance,
"Walking to where the water ends,
sitting to watch when clouds arise"
is a poem from the Anthology of Literary Excellence;
"Vast watery fields fly with egrets white,
shady summer woods warble with orioles gold"
is a poem by Lǐ Jiāyòu.
Supplement to the National History
Unrestrained songs and lengthy verses,
boldly surge with vigor and force,
often piercing the heart of heaven,
emerging from the ribs of the moon,
startling with unexpected expressions,
unattainable by ordinary means.
"Preface to the Collected Works of Huángfǔ Shí and Gù Kuàng"
Lǐ Duān was skilled in poetry.
During the Dàlì era, he
exchanged poetic compositions with Hán Hóng, Qián Qǐ, Lú Lún, and others,
gaining fame throughout the capital,
and was known as
one of the "Ten Talents of the Dàlì Era"
Guō Shàngfù's youngest son, Guō Ài, married Shēngpíng Princess, daughter of Emperor Dàizōng,
who was virtuous, intelligent, and talented,
and particularly fond of poets.
Thus, Lǐ Duān and the other ten talents often gathered at Guō Ài's residence.
At each banquet where poetry was composed,
the princess would watch from behind a curtain,
and for the most exquisite poems,
she would reward the poet with a hundred rolls of silk.
On one occasion, when Guō Ài was appointed to a new official position,
he gathered the ten talents and announced:
"The first to complete a poem will be rewarded."
Lǐ Duān was the first to present a striking couplet,
which read:
"Like Xún Lìng perfuming, he favors the young;
Like Hé Láng powdering, he knows no sorrow."
The princess immediately rewarded him with a hundred rolls of silk.
Qián Qǐ remarked:
"Academician Lǐ is indeed talented,
but this piece was prepared in advance.
I wish to compose a verse to challenge him,
using my surname 'Qián' as the rhyme."
Lǐ Duān promptly tore a sheet of paper and presented his poem:
"The square pond mirrors grass lush and green;
The new moon hangs like a hook, not yet full.
A new golden bit trains the horse to pace;
An old copper mine grants coins to mold."
Guō Ài exclaimed:
"This is truly masterful!"
Only then did Qián Qǐ and the others acknowledge Lǐ Duān's superiority.
Old Book of Tang: At Tang gatherings, poetry was always composed,
with one poet recognized as the standout.
At this event,
Lǐ Duān was the standout;
at the farewell for Chancellor Wáng Jìn's assignment to Yōushuò,
Hán Hóng was the standout;
at the farewell for Chancellor Liú Yàn's inspection of Jiānghuái,
Qián Qǐ was the standout.
Supplement to the National History:
Lǐ Yì was skilled in composing poetry and songs,
and was equally famous as his clansman Lǐ Hè.
Every time he wrote a piece,
musicians from the Imperial Music Bureau would bribe to obtain it,
singing them as tribute lyrics.
His works "Song of the Soldier" and "Early Journey"
were all turned into painted screens by enthusiasts.
The lines "Before Huí Lè beacon, sand resembles snow,
Outside Shòu Xiáng City, the moon is like frost"
were regarded by the whole country
as song lyrics.
(Old Book of Tang)
Bái Jūyì composed over a hundred yuefu and poems,
criticizing current affairs through allegory,
which spread to the imperial court.
The emperor saw them and was pleased,
summoning him to serve as a Hanlin Academician.
Yuán Zhěn wrote in the "Collection Preface":
"Merchants from Jīlín
eagerly sought to purchase them;
even the prime minister of their own country
would exchange one piece of gold for each poem.
As for counterfeits,
the prime minister could always identify them."
"Official Biography" Lǐ Kān once said:
"Since the Yuánhé era,
there have been poems by Yuán and Bái
that are delicate and wanton,
corrupting many
who are not dignified scholars or refined gentlemen.
Circulated among the common people,
inscribed on screens and walls,
fathers and daughters, mothers and sons
orally teach them to each other.
These licentious and vulgar words,
like winter's cold or summer's heat,
penetrate people's flesh and bones,
impossible to remove.
I hold no official position,
so I cannot use the law to control this."
"Dù Mù's Record of Lǐ Zhì" Some say that whenever Lètiān composed a poem,
he would have an old woman interpret it,
asking:
"Do you understand?"
If the woman said:
"I understand,"
then
he would record it;
if she didn't understand,
he would not practice it further.
Hence the flaw by the late Táng dynasty
was descending into vulgarity.
"Inkman Waving a Rhinoceros"
When Duke Pei was in charge of the Eastern Capital Luòyáng,
during a night banquet when the revelry was at its peak,
he called for poetic lines,
and Yuán Zhěn and Bái Jūyì wore expressions of confidence.
At that time, the duke composed the opening couplet,
then it came to Rǔshì's turn,
who said:
"In old times, Lántíng lacked beauty and grace,
but now, Jīngǔ boasts a man of lofty virtue."
Bái Jūyì, knowing he could not surpass it,
immediately tore the paper and said:
"With pipes and songs roaring like a boiling cauldron,
do not engage in such cold and detached pursuits."
Yuán Zhěn remarked, looking on:
"What Lètiān said is how one truly preserves their reputation."
From "Records of the Táng Dynasty"
During the Chángqìng era,
Yuán Zhěn, Liú Yǔxí, and Wéi Chǔkè gathered at Bái Jūyì's residence,
discussing the rise and fall of the Southern Dynasties,
and each composed a "Poem of Reminiscence at Jīnlíng".
Liǔ Yǔxí raised a cup,
drank it down,
and immediately completed his poem:
"Wáng Jùn's tower ships sailed down from Yìzhōu,

Thus, its spirit surpasses the ancients,

Its astonishing beauty and unparalleled elegance

Its influence on poets

Cāng Jié, a historian of the Yellow Emperor,
observed the tracks and footprints of birds and beasts,
and recognized that patterns could be distinguished and differentiated,
thus initially creating written records.
They were based on categorizing and pictographic forms,
hence called wén (patterns).
Later, with the addition of phonetic elements,
they were called zì (characters),
and zì
means multiplying and gradually increasing.
When recorded on bamboo slips and silk, it is called shū (writing),
and shū
means likeness.
Up to the eras of the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns,

In the Zhōu Lǐ, children enter elementary school at age eight,
where the Bǎoshì teaches the sons of the state,
first using the six scripts.
The first is called indicative: indicative characters
are recognized upon sight,
and understood upon examination,
such as "shàng" (up) and "xià" (down).
The second is called pictographic: pictographic characters
depict the object,
following its form with curves and bends,
such as "rì" (sun) and "yuè" (moon).
The third is called phonetic: phonetic characters
use a radical for meaning
and a component for sound,
such as "Jiāng" and "Hé" (rivers).
The fourth is called associative: associative characters
combine elements to convey meaning,
revealing the intended concept,
such as "wǔ" (military) and "xìn" (trust).
The fifth is called derivative: derivative characters
share the same radical
and mutually convey meaning,
such as "kǎo" (to test) and "lǎo" (old).
The sixth is called borrowing: borrowing characters
use existing graphs
for homophonous words,
such as "lìng" (command) and "zhǎng" (elder).

During the interregnum of the fallen Xin Dynasty,

At that time, there were six scripts: first, the ancient script,
which was the script from the texts in the wall of Confucius’s residence;
when Prince Gōng of Lǔ demolished Confucius’s house,
he obtained the *Classic of History*, *Spring and Autumn Annals*, *Analects*, and *Classic of Filial Piety*.
Second, the peculiar script,
which was a variant of the ancient script;
third, the seal script,
namely the small seal script,
created by Chéng Miǎo of Xiàdù under the order of Qín Shǐ Huáng;
fourth, the auxiliary script,
which was the clerical script of the Qín dynasty;
fifth, the seal-script style,
used for engraving seals;
sixth, the bird-and-insect script,
used for writing on banners and tallies.

promising to finish in three days.

and saw the two Daoists carrying a small bag,
closing the door behind them,
with nothing else visible.

the inscriptions were complete,

From heaven and earth, mountains and rivers, he grasped the constants of square and round, flowing and standing;

and sit at the central pillar of the court hall.
Outstanding scholars and filial candidates would each respond in writing according to their ranks.
Those with missing or erroneous characters
would be called to stand up behind their mats;
those with sloppy or poor handwriting
would be made to drink one shēng of ink;
those with reckless or illogical writing
would have their mats taken away and their ceremonial daggers removed.
From the "Tōng Diǎn".
Dù Zhèngxuán was recommended as a xiùcai,
and achieved top scores in the policy examination.
Yáng Sù angrily said:
"Even if Duke of Zhōu and Confucius were reborn,
they still wouldn't qualify as xiùcai.
How dare you recklessly recommend this person?"
He then threw the examination paper to the ground,
ordering him to compose five pieces imitating Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on the Imperial Park".
After reading them several times,
Yáng Sù was greatly astonished and said:
"Truly an excellent xiùcai!"
According to History of the Northern Dynasties: During the Suí dynasty, the xiùcai recommendation was highly valued,
with fewer than ten selected nationwide,
yet Dù Zhènglún's family alone produced three xiùcai.
The Palace Censor Lǐ È,
due to improper selection of talents,
submitted a memorial stating:
"Since the three ancestors of the Wei dynasty,
they increasingly valued literary embellishment,
neglecting the great principles of governing the people,
and favoring the minor skill of ornate writing.
The subordinates followed their superiors,
as shadows follow forms and echoes follow sounds,
competing in superficial elegance,
which then became a prevailing custom.
In the Jiangzuo region, during the Qi and Liang dynasties,
this malpractice became even more severe.
Regardless of status or wisdom,
all were solely devoted to chanting verses,
thus abandoning fundamental principles while preserving trivial differences,
pursuing emptiness and minutiae,
vying for the novelty of a single rhyme,
competing over the cleverness of a single character.
Page after page and volume upon volume,
contained nothing beyond descriptions of moonlight and dew;
piles of documents filling cases and chests,
were merely about the appearance of wind and clouds.
Contemporary customs esteemed this practice,
the court based official selections on these criteria,
once the path to emolument and profit was opened,
the affection and admiration for it grew even stronger.
Thus, ignorant children in villages and young nobles alike,
before even learning the basics of writing,
were already composing five-character poems,
discarding the root while chasing the branches,
this trend spread throughout the region,
mutually imitating and honoring predecessors,
making superficiality and fragmentation increasingly prevalent."

Zhāng Cóngshī's ancestor Sǔnzhī,

Each year in midwinter,

After the farewell feast, they would go with the accounting officials,
those who were recommended without studying at government schools

Empress Wǔ found that many selections by the Ministry of Personnel were dishonest,

As recorded in "Zhāng Yuē":
"During the Yǒngchāng era,
Empress Wǔ tested virtuous and upright scholars.
She decreed that Lǐ Jǐngchén, the Minister of Personnel, conceal names for reevaluation,

Cuī Miǎn was selected for his virtue and talent,

Empress Wǔ ordered the officials to reexamine him,

In the first year of the Yongchāng era of Empress Wǔ Zétiān, in the second month,
imperial examination candidates were tested in front of the Luòchéng Palace Hall,
inaugurating the palace examination system.
Today's candidates for office,
deviate from the true facts,
as local opinions are determined by the pens of petty men,
and virtuous conduct lacks the appraisal of elders.
Brothers compete noisily in the prefectural offices,
pleading for favor, unable to surpass the act of bowing low.
Sometimes, as soon as the imperial decree is issued,
they are sent to be examined and searched,
hurrying through the gates of government offices,
entering and leaving the residences of princes and dukes.
They present petitions and submit poems,
only hoping for the favor of a cough or spit;
from head to foot, they rub and bow,
wishing to bear the grace of being lifted up.
Hence, it is commonly said of these candidates,
that they are all called "seekers of recommendation."
"Seeking" is a term for self-pursuit,
not a word for being known by others.
Observe their actions and measure their talents,
then their character can be seen herein.
《Old Book of Tang》
When the pagoda trees turn yellow in Cháng'ān, the examination candidates,
after the sixth month,
those who failed do not leave the capital,
which is called "passing the summer."
Many borrow quiet neighborhoods, temple courtyards, and vacant houses to reside in,
composing new essays,
which is called "summer assignments."
There are also groups of ten or five pooling money for wine and meals,
seeking topics from knowledgeable senior officials,
which is called "private trials."
After the seventh month,
they submit their new assignments,
and are selected for recommendation from various prefectures and districts.
People say of them:
"When pagoda flowers yellow,
candidates are busy."
In the "Southern Records," Wēng Chéngzàn has a poem that says:
"In the rain, adorned, gazing at the yellow,
luring cicada songs to escort the setting sun.
I recall those years following the accounting officer,
my horse's hooves busy for you all day long."
When candidates entered the imperial examination,

they would feign illness,
submitting a request to withdraw for recuperation,
stating:
"This petition: I suddenly suffer from heart pain,
and request to leave the examination hall to rest.
Respectfully submitted as stated.
The same procedure applied for sudden illnesses.

From "Records of Anecdotes"
Under the Táng system: on examination day for candidates,
when evening fell,
they were permitted to burn three candles.
Wéi Yīyí, after finishing his exam paper by candlelight,
composed a poem saying:
"Loose robes and broad sashes covered in dust,
alone I ascend the main hall to submit my papers and return.
When will my humble lane hear auspicious news?
On what day shall I return past the bramble fence again?
As three candles burn out, the bell first sounds;
the elixir refined nine times in the cauldron remains unopened.
The waning moon gradually sinks low, candidates bustling about—
who knows which among us possesses the talent of a banished immortal?"
He also wrote:
"Ten white lotus blossoms illuminate the corridor brightly,
a scene of peace with elegant odes resounding.
Just as the third candle finishes burning out,
the scenic beauty of the examination hall cannot be captured in painting."
According to an old account, it is also said: on examination day for candidates,
when it was already late,
the chief examiner Quán Déyǔ jested from behind the curtain:
"Three candles extinguished—
burning away the candidates' hearts."
A candidate promptly replied:
"An eight-rhyme fu completed—
startling the vice-minister's courage."
Thus, the "Biography of Dòu Zhènggù in the National History" records:

night examinations were limited to two candles;

Zhènggù, finding short compositions difficult to complete,

During the Guǎngshùn era of the Later Zhōu, Dòu Yí

In the ninth year of the Dàzhōng era,

From "Nánbù Xīnshū"
Since the Shenlong era,

In the twenty-fourth year of the Kāiyuán era,

transferred the responsibility for imperial examinations to the Ministry of Rites,
placing it under the supervision of vice ministers.
The selection of scholars by the Ministry of Rites began from this time.
When relatives or acquaintances of vice ministers took the examinations, they were transferred to the examining officials,
which was called "biétóu" (separate examinations).
In the seventh year of the Zhēnyuán era,
Dù Huángshang oversaw the imperial examinations.
Hearing of Yǐn Shū's widespread reputation at the time,
he visited him in plain clothes,
inquiring about notable scholars in the examination hall.
Shū responded hesitantly.
Huángshang then fully disclosed:
"I am this year's chief examiner,
having received the appointment long ago,
but have only identified one candidate,
while being unable to fully know the others.
I venture to make this request."
Shū straightened up respectfully and replied:
"Since you have condescended to ask,
how dare I conceal anything?"
He immediately mentioned that among the younger generation was Cuī Yuánlüè,
and among the impoverished scholars were Lín Zǎo and Línghú Chǔ, among several others.
Huángshang was greatly pleased.
That year, Shū achieved top honors in the examinations,
which tested with the composition "Rhapsody on the Pearl Returning to Hépu."
While drafting his rhapsody,
Lín Zǎo leaned on his desk and dozed off,
vaguely dreaming that someone told him:
"Your rhapsody is excellent,
but regrettably it fails to describe the meaning of the pearl's departure and return."
Awakening and examining his draft,
he then added four lines,
and that year he passed the examination.
When expressing gratitude,
Huángshang said to him:
"Only you, Master Lín, described the meaning of the pearl's departure and return,
as if divinely assisted."
From "Biographies of Mǐnchuān Notables": When the pearl departed,
the mountains lost their color,
mists grew dim and obscure;
the sea lost its light,
leaving vast empty waters.
When the pearl returned,
the rivers became enchanting,
with auspicious breezes gently blowing;
the earth grew moist,
and living things flourished vibrantly.

Hán Xīzǎi first presided over the imperial examinations,
and everyone considered it a major topic.
That evening, Xīzǎi himself composed five poems,

found them all commendable.
He later authored over fifty chapters of "Admonitions,"
which few of his contemporaries could match.
He guided and encouraged younger scholars,
earning the nickname "Master Hán."
By nature, he enjoyed jesting and banter;

why does it reek so of mugwort!"

During the Huáinán examination presided over by examiner Zhāng Bì,
the jìnshì candidates were tested on the topic "Heavenly Rooster Plays with Gentle Breeze."
Bì had merely taken the line from an anthology of poetry as the theme,
without investigating it thoroughly.
A jìnshì candidate addressed the examiner, saying:
"According to the Ěryǎ,
hàn refers to the heavenly rooster.
Hàn
also refers to the heavenly rooster.
There are two kinds of heavenly roosters,
I wonder which one is correct?"
Bì was greatly startled,
and could not reply.
He urgently fetched the Ěryǎ,
and checked the "Explanation of Insects" section, which stated
"hàn,
heavenly rooster,
a small insect,
with a black body and red head,
also called shājī,
or chūjī."
The "Explanation of Birds" section stated
"hàn,
heavenly rooster,
with red feathers."
The Yì Zhōu Shū says:
"The patterned hàn resembles a colorful rooster."
During King Chéng's reign,

Chén Péngnián during the Dàzhōng Xiángfú era served as associate examiner for the imperial examinations,

enraged, he entered Chén's residence,
finding that Péngnián had not yet returned,
he came upon a yellow imperial edict on the desk,
and wrote on its back:
"Péngnián's head is utterly befuddled,
with eyes like cinnabar and hair like thistledown,
by error I was fortunate to be included among the three characters,
yet absurdly remain one of the four men.
Using his power to deceive the enlightened ruler,
casting aside kinship to betray utmost fairness,
thousands of poor scholars shed tears together,
but these words have no way to reach Yáo's ears."
Péngnián was furious,
carrying the edict he presented a memorial to the throne,
the Emperor saw it and was displeased,
yet pardoned his crime.

Initially suspecting it was an attendant,

Wáng Rényù presided over the imperial examinations,

One day,

Zhìyōng possessed outstanding talent,

During the Five Dynasties period,
Wáng Rényù served as the chief examiner for the imperial examinations.
Prime Minister Wáng Pǔ achieved the top rank as zhuàngyuán,
at the age of twenty-six.
Six years later,
he became the chancellor for Emperor Shìzōng of the Later Zhōu dynasty,
and still managed to serve in our dynasty before retiring from his position as Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
at the mere age of forty-two.
When Pǔ first assumed the role of chancellor,
Rényù was still retired and in good health.
He once wrote a poem to congratulate Pǔ, which read:
"In the literary arena, you captured the flag in one battle,
then adjusted the golden cauldron to assist in governing with non-action.
The imperial edict descended swiftly—how boundless the favor!
Upon first hearing the news, even the elderly felt joy.
Few predecessors have left such achievements to be recorded,
on the sandy causeway, your horse lingered as you returned.
Only when standing in court ranks could we meet from afar,
yet intimacy pales compared to before honors were bestowed."
While Pǔ held office,
he would visit Rényù every rest day,
spending the entire day at ease.
This reflects how, since the Táng dynasty,
the bond between examiners and their successful candidates has been particularly strong.

During the Yuányòu era,
Sū Dōngpō oversaw the imperial examinations,

As the examination hall was about to be locked,
Dōngpō sealed a letter
and instructed it to be delivered to Fāngshū.
It happened that Fāngshū was out,
and his servant received the letter, placing it on the table.
After a short while,
Zhāng Zǐhòu's two sons, Zhāng Chí and Zhāng Shòu, arrived,
took the letter and secretly read it,
finding it to be an essay titled "On Yáng Xióng Being Superior to Liú Xiàng."
The two Zhāng brothers were overjoyed,
and they took it away with them.
When Fāngshū returned,
he could not find the letter,
realized it had been stolen by the two Zhāngs,
and felt deeply regretful but dared not speak of it.
Later, this topic indeed appeared in the exam,
and both Zhāng brothers imitated Dōngpō's writing,
leaving Fāngshū almost unable to write.
When the results were announced,
Dōngpō expected the top scorer to be Fāngshū,
but it turned out to be Zhāng Yuán.
The tenth-place essay closely resembled the top one in style,
and it was by Zhāng Chí.
Dōngpō was dismayed.
Among the top twenty papers,
one stood out as particularly remarkable,
and Dōngpō said to his colleagues:
"This must be Lǐ Fāngshū."
Upon checking,
it was actually Gě Mǐnxiū.
At the time, Huáng Shān was also involved in grading the papers,

"Congratulations,
Your Excellency has discovered a talent.
This is a student
who studied under me when I served as magistrate in Tàihé."
However, Fāngshū ultimately failed the examination.
After Dōngpō left the examination hall,

and sighed with great regret.

"All my life I’ve spoken of ancient battlefields,
yet in the moment, my eyes were dazzled by five colors.
I am ashamed for not stepping forward; you laugh heartily—
our actions and fates are decreed by heaven; what blame is there?"
This is the poem.
His mother lamented:
"With Scholar Sū overseeing the exams,
and you failing to achieve fame,
what hope remains?"
She died of depression.

That evening,
I dreamed of a young woman who told me:
'Sir, for your provincial examination,
in the opening section of the first session,
you can use three ancient characters to pass the examination.
I beg you not to forget
to let my decaying bones be buried in the earth.'

When scholars first achieve honorable advancement or receive new appointments,
their colleagues and friends come to congratulate them,
and they must lavishly prepare wine, feasts, and music to celebrate joyously,
which is called "shāo wěi" (burning the tail).
One explanation says that when a tiger transforms into a human,
only its tail remains unchanged,
and it must be burned off
before it can become fully human.
Therefore, when one first receives an official appointment,
it is like a tiger becoming human:
the tail is still there,
and only after the body has fully transformed
is it burned,
hence the term "shāo wěi."
Another explanation says that a newly entered sheep is unruly
and does not integrate with the flock,
but if its tail is burned with fire, it becomes settled.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
Emperor Tàizōng once asked Zhū Zǐshē
about the matter of the sheep.
The "Xīzhāi Huàjì" also says that when a fish leaps over the dragon gate
and transforms into a dragon,
it must have its tail burned by thunder to complete the transformation.

a true beauty,
whom many sons of officials sought but could not win.
At that time, Dòu Fán was over sixty years old
and was planning to remarry.
His elder brother, a remonstrance official,
was influential
and could help others pass the examinations.
Yǔwén Hóng married his daughter to Dòu Fán,
and Dòu Fán spoke on his behalf to Yuán Bǐ,
indeed achieving success.
Chancellor Wéi Gōngshuō, a relative of his,
greatly despised this.
Later, when the residence of Minister Dù in Huátái caught fire,
nearly burning the newly placed coffin,
the family members said:
"A mouse dragged fire into the warehouse with its tail,
causing the blaze to spread."
The governor of Jīngzhào said to Yǔwén:
"When a fish is about to turn into a dragon,
thunder burns its tail.
Recently, even mice have had their tails burned."
He used this to mock him.

Chancellor Chéng laughed heartily:

Péng Kàng and Zhàn Bēn were both from Yíchūn, Yuánzhōu.
Kàng's wife was also Bēn's maternal aunt,
Kàng passed the imperial examination and became a jìnshì,
while Bēn remained a minor county official.
The wife's family held a celebration banquet,
attended by officials and renowned scholars.
Kàng occupied the seat of honor,
receiving everyone's admiration,
when Bēn arrived,
he was ordered to eat in the back room,
yet Bēn showed no resentment.
His wife angrily reproached him:
"If a man cannot motivate himself,
and suffers such humiliation,
how can he still show his face?"
Bēn was moved by her words,
and devoted himself to studying.
Within a few years,
he passed the examination in one attempt.
Kàng had often belittled him!
At that moment, Kàng was riding a donkey,
roaming freely in the outskirts,
when suddenly a servant rushed to report:
"Láng Zhàn Bēn has passed the examination."
Kàng cried out in shock and fell off.
Hence the people of Yuánzhōu joked:
"When Zhàn Bēn passed the exam,
Péng Kàng fell from his donkey."
Today west of Yuánchuān there is a Falling Donkey Bridge,
which marks the very spot.
From "Yíchūn Records of Hearsay"
When Lǐ Shēn governed Yángzhōu,
Zhāng Xiàobiāo composed a poem titled "Spring Snow":
"Six-petaled blossoms fly and drift everywhere,
Adhering to the cold branches, brushing the steps with care.
By vermilion gates, by dusk, scarce a foot deep,
All the army's joyous spirit melts away in sleep."
After passing the imperial examination,
he later sent a message to Shēn:
"Success in exams surpasses ten official posts by far,
Gilded saddle adorned, I leave Cháng'ān's bar.
My horse's head nears Yángzhōu's city wall,
To tell the world to wash their eyes and heed my call."
Shēn responded with a quatrain to admonish him:
"Only false gold requires gilding to shine,
If it were true gold, no coating would be thine.
A decade in Cháng'ān to gain one success,
Why empty pride on an empty stomach express?"
From "Records of Poetry Talks of the Complete Tang Dynasty"
Yǔ Jiānwú passed the imperial examination in the tenth year of the Yuánhé era,
and later crossed the Yángzǐ River,
composing a poem that said:
"I recall the year I was to be recommended,
holding sorrow by this river's side.
Fish and dragons flickered back and forth,
white waves higher than the sky.
Today I tread on green grass,
returning to pass this way again.
The river god also knows worldly feelings,
granting me favorable winds and weather.
Records in Tángshī Jìshì and Yúnzhāi Guǎnglù state:
"Féng Jīng, when crossing the river, inscribed a poem with the same last two lines.
Cuī Yǎn was administering the imperial examinations,
when Wú Wǔlíng from the Eastern Capital said to him:
"You are currently seeking exceptional talents for the Son of Heaven,
I dare to offer something that may be beneficial.
Thereupon he produced a document from his sleeve.
When Cuī Yǎn read it,
it turned out to be Dù Mù's "Rhapsody on the Epang Palace",
and all the seated guests were astonished.
Wú Wǔlíng said:
"Dù Mù is currently taking the examinations,
I request that he be placed in the first position.
Cuī Yǎn thanked him, saying he had already found the right candidate.
When it came to the fifth position,
and Cuī Yǎn had not yet responded,
Wú Wǔlíng suddenly said angrily:
"If not,
you should return the rhapsody to me.
Cuī Yǎn said:
"As you instruct.
Dù Mù indeed achieved an exceptional rank.
"Records of Selected Sayings" Zhèng Yìfū was proud of his contemporary reputation,
when the National University recommended him as the fifth-ranked candidate,
he felt very discontent.
In his acknowledgment to the chief examiner he wrote:
"In terms of achievements like Lǐ Guǎng's,
I consider myself peerless;
in literary talent like Dù Mù's,
I only obtained fifth place.
He also wrote:
"The thoroughbred steed has grown old,
willing to let mediocre horses precede it;
the giant sea turtle cannot display its power,
because of the stubborn rock above it.
"Brush Talks"
Wǔ Yìhuáng in the prefectural examination was selected as the top candidate,
in the imperial examination he became the top graduate,
and in the special subject examination he became the top candidate by imperial decree,
so at that time people called him
"Wǔ's Three Tops"
"Forest of Conversations from Táng" Cuī Yuánhàn in his later years took examinations,
and in all cases achieved first success: top candidate in the capital prefecture examination,
top graduate from the Ministry of Rites,
top candidate by imperial decree in the special subject examination,
and top candidate by imperial decree in the special palace examination third class.
"New Book of Southern Affairs" Zhāng Yòuxīn was called by his contemporaries
"Zhāng Three Tops"
"Same as Record of the Collected Conversations" Péi Cìyuán in the policy essay and special subject examinations,
on the same day had imperial decrees issued and was made top candidate in both,
which his contemporaries considered an honor.
"New Book of Southern Affairs"
Táng Wáng Bō passed the imperial examination at the age of fifty,
and his fellow candidate Chén Tōngfāng was the youngest among them.
Chén playfully patted Wáng on the back
and said,
"Old Wáng, old Wáng,
I present you with this degree."
Meaning that as the day grew late and the road ahead was long,
it was as if he were granting him an official position.
Wáng Bō replied,
"I intend to take the three-part examination."
Chén Tōngfāng said,
"Once is already excessive,
how could there be a second time?"
Wáng harbored resentment,
and when he became chancellor,
Chén ultimately suffered hardship under him and died.
From "Mǐn Chuān Míngshì Zhuàn"
During the Guǎngmíng era,
before Fèngxiáng deputy envoy Zhèng Chāngtú passed the imperial examinations,
a servant from his relative's household was traveling through the capital Luòyáng
when near the Gǔshuǐ Inn,
he encountered two messengers in yellow robes coming from the west.
They said:
"We two are this year's messengers delivering the examination results.
We have come from Tàishān to the place of Jīntiān,
to finalize the rankings list.
It's fortunate we met you.
The servant then requested to secretly look at the list.
The messengers said:
"This year's top graduate's surname
has the radical '䃭',
and his given name has two characters -
the second character contains the word '口' (mouth).
The last-ranked person's surname
also contains this '䃭' radical,
his given name has two characters,
and the second character also contains '口'.
Remember this, remember this.
They then took their leave.
Zhèng's relative found the matter quite extraordinary.
That year, Chāngtú indeed became the top graduate,
while the last on the list was Zōu Xīhuí -
their names and character strokes matched exactly.
"Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Xǔ Mèngróng passed the jìnshì examination,
and also passed the xuèjiū examination,
earning the contemporary nickname
"a silk robe covered with a straw raincoat"
From "Zhìyán": Cài Jīng passed the jìnshì examination and also the xuèjiū examination,
leading people to say
"good at passing examinations,
but disliked the titles obtained"
with
"adding a straw raincoat over brocade"
as the mocking phrase.
From "Tángshī Jìshì"
Lǐ Ǎi, when first sitting for the imperial examinations, was diligent, quick-witted, and exceptionally outstanding,
so people called him
"the hawk with bound wings"
He passed the examination in the second year of the Xiantong era
according to the Miscellaneous Anecdotes of the Lú Family.
Zhèng Chuán himself recounted that while preparing for the imperial examination,
he once dreamed of viewing the list of successful candidates,
on which he only saw
"phoenix"
written in large characters.
In the winter of the first year of the Dàzhōng era,
he sought an appointment in Fèngxiáng,
and happened to see the local examination papers,
where the first character was "phoenix".
When he went to the eastern capital to take the examination on Gōushān,
composing a poem upon hearing the moonlight melody of Prince Jìn's flute,
all the poems composed by others nearby contained the character "phoenix".
The following year,
he indeed passed the examination.
From "Records of Conversations".
Féng Sù's three sons Táo, Tāo, and Tú,
brothers successively passed the imperial examinations as jìnshì over consecutive years,
and successively passed the hóngcí examination year after year.
Such flourishing in one period,
was unmatched in their generation.
At the beginning of the Tàihé era,
among those who passed as jìnshì from the Féng family,
there were ten throughout the land,
with eight being brothers, uncles, and nephews from their household.
"Records of Historical Facts"
Zhāng Huán and his six brothers
all passed the imperial examinations.
"Tán Bīn Lù"
Later, there were Eastern and Western Squads,
the Eastern called the Western
"the Vast and Clueless Squad"
meaning they had no skills.
From "Miscellaneous Stories of the Lú Family".
In the second year of the Chúnhuà era,
Sūn Hànhé was recommended as a Presented Scholar,
from Kāifēng to the Department of State Affairs,
he ranked first in both the departmental and palace examinations.
In the fifth year of the Xiánpíng era,
Wáng Yīgōng from Qīngzhōu ranked first in both the departmental and palace examinations.
In the second year of the Qìnglì era,
Yáng Shěnxián Zhì, and in the first year of the Huángyòu era, Féng Jīng.
During the Yuánfēng era,
Liáng Tì from Wènshàng dreamed one night of presenting matters at the imperial court,
where he saw a placard displayed before the emperor's throne,
adorned with large golden characters
"Huáng Cháng"
written on it.
Believing this to be an auspicious omen,
he consequently changed his name to Huáng Cháng.
The following year,
when the imperial examination results were announced at court,
Huáng Cháng from Nánjiàn was ranked first.
"Shuǐ Yàn Tán" Liǔ Dàozhě,
a native of Quánzhōu,
received essential teachings from an extraordinary monk,
enabling him to predict future events.
Someone asked him:
"What will be the surname of this year's top scholar?"
He replied:
"Not black, not white,
nor red, nor green."
The questioner pressed further:
"Can you also tell his name?"
Thereupon, he lifted the hem of his garment to show people.
Several days later,
the news of success arrived,
revealing it was indeed Huáng Cháng.
"Dùn Zhāi Xián Lǎn"
During the Zhèng hé era,
Zhāng Gāng was selected through the Three Halls system.
Emperor Huīzong presided at the Chóngzhèng Hall,
granting him the jìnshì degree,
and turning to the examination officials
Zhāng Kègōng and others, said:
"People say that in the ancestors' time there were triple champions,
but now Gāng is a quadruple champion—
how is this so?
Kègōng and others replied:
"Gāng ranked first in the prefectural examination,
then first in the public examination for the Inner Hall,
first in the evaluation for the Upper Hall,
qualified for promotion,
and was placed in the upper grade—
all as the top candidate in the Upper Hall.
Thus the capital speaks of him as a quintuple champion.
The Emperor said:
"This truly shows we have obtained an exceptional talent.
Previously we only spoke of triple champions.
Now Zhāng Gāng has taken first place in five stages—
this cannot be by mere chance.
He should be specially rewarded.
He was then appointed as a Erudite of the National University.
Gāng was from Jīntán.
Later, at court,
he maintained great integrity,
becoming a renowned minister of his time.
From "Tǎnzhāi Bǐ Héng"
Zhāng Kuí, styled Rǔbì,
first passed the imperial examination in the dingwèi year of the Chúnxī era.
Earlier, in the yǐyǒu year of the Lóngxīng era, he had taken the provincial examination,
where the examiner assigned the topic:
"Level and straight, correct and upright, strong and unyielding.
Friends firm overcome Xiè,
friends gentle overcome Shēn,
Qián firm overcomes Gāo,
Míng gentle overcomes Sì,
yet he failed the Ministry of Rites examination.
He dreamed a divine being told him:
"If you encounter four 'overcomes' again,
then you will succeed.
He thought about the meaning of the classics,
but found no other four 'overcomes'!
In the dīngyǒu year of the Chúnxī era,
he took the examination again with the topic:
"Attend to the five regulators,
then all achievements will be consolidated.
Do not promote indulgence and desire among the states,
be cautious and diligent day by day,
in the ninth of ten thousand examination halls encountering Chéng Sān,
fearing stern warnings.
He said:
"Rǔbì, you may be congratulated!
Do you not remember your former dream?
Now indeed there are four 'overcomes',
so he recommended Sānwèi again as the top candidate.
"Official Travels"
In the Song dynasty, only one person rose from the Imperial Examination to become a Chancellor,
and that was Fù Bì.
During the time of Emperor Xiàozōng,
again, only one person from Měishān, Lǐ Hòu, achieved this,
known as Zhòngxìn,
famous for compiling the histories "Nánběi Shǐ" and "Shìshuō".
"Kùn Xué Jì Wén"
Zhāng Zhuò, Jiǎnzhī's grandson,
repeatedly took the imperial examinations without success.
Holding the list of successful candidates,
he placed it on his head
and said:
"This is the Sūtra of the Thousand Buddhas' Names.
History of the Táng Dynasty
Zhāng Zhuó was nicknamed
"the Bronze-Cash Scholar,"
meaning he succeeded ten thousand times out of ten thousand attempts.
At that time, there was a Dǒng Fāng who failed the imperial examinations nine times,
and was called
"the White-Wax Classicist,"
forming a contrast with Zhuó.
(from "Qiān Zǎi")
Emperor Dézōng, during the summer, traveled incognito to Xīmíng Temple,
where Sòng Jì, wearing a coarse headscarf and short trousers, was copying texts.
The emperor said:
"This humble scholar requests a bowl of tea.
Sòng Jì replied:
"The water in the cauldron is just boiling,
you may pour it yourself.
The emperor then asked:
"What occupation do you pursue?
What is your surname and rank?
Sòng Jì answered:
"My surname is Sòng, ranked fifth,
and I am sitting for the imperial examinations.
Shortly after, he heard
people addressing the emperor as "Your Majesty".
Sòng Jì rose in panic and bowed to await punishment.
The emperor said:
"Sòng Wǔ is quite straightforward.
Another version records the emperor asking:
"How would you rate the current emperor's poetry?
He replied:
"The sage's intentions are unfathomable.
The emperor said:
"Sòng Wǔ is quite straightforward.
Later, when the Ministry of Rites posted the examination results,
the emperor asked:
"Is Sòng Jì's name on the list?
The messenger returned and said:
"No.
The emperor remarked:
"Sòng Wǔ is straightforward yet again.
From "Miscellaneous Stories of the Lú Family": Sòng Jì grew old in the examination halls,
once failing a poetic composition for violating rhyme rules,
whereupon he beat his chest and said:
"Sòng Wǔ has been straightforward again!
When the Ministry of Rites later presented the ranked candidate list,
Emperor Dézōng asked:
"Is Sòng Wǔ being straightforward?
From "Supplement to the National History"
Xǔ Mèngróng and Sòng Jì were close friends when they were commoners.
When Xǔ became an examination official,
Sòng failed the imperial examination.
Xǔ invited Sòng to drink and apologize to him.
After drinking heavily, Xǔ
again boasted loudly, saying:
"This year I will select a prime minister for the country,
and the top candidate will be Yáo Sìqīng."
Several days later,
Yáo passed away.
Sòng went to see Xǔ,
and said:
"The nation has suffered a misfortune,
Minister Yáo has died."
"Miscellaneous Stories of the Lú Family"
Lú Shìzǐ failed the imperial examination,
and walked out of the capital city gate.
That day,
the wind and cold were quite severe,
so he sought lodging at an inn.
Another guest arrived later,
approached the fire and chanted:
"My skill in weaving silk brocade is still lacking,
randomly handling the loom, I mistakenly throw the shuttle.
Don't let palace brocade masters see this,
they would laugh themselves to death at such writing."
He then continued:
"Nowadays, scholars of writing are not valued,
don't boast of your writings to others."
Lú was startled,
recalling these were Bái Jūyì's poems,
so he asked the man's name.
The man replied:
"My surname is Lǐ,
my family has long been in the brocade weaving trade,
before the turmoil, we were formerly attached to the Eastern Workshop."
After the fire in the Capital Palace Brocade Workshop,
I recently tried to offer my modest skills to this profession.
Everyone says:
"Nowadays the patterns are different from before,
this cannot be called skill.
Those who try to sell their work based on literary talent,
are not valued by the world like this,
so I'm returning east."
End
In the thirteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
scholars who failed the imperial examination often wrote poems satirizing the examiners.
Only Zhāng Xiàobiāo composed the poem "Returning Swallows" and presented it to Vice Minister Yǔ Chéngxuān, saying:
"The accumulated mud in the precarious nest has already fallen,
This year I deliberately return before the spring sacrifice.
With towering pavilions offering no place to perch,
By whose house shall I fly next?"
Ōuyáng Xiè also wrote a swallow poem,
presenting it to Vice Minister Zhèng Yú:
"Gracefully flying swallows before painted halls open,
Have welcomed the new and bid farewell to the old countless times.
Always around the spring and autumn sacrifice days,
For whom do they come and for whom do they go?"
"Comments on Poetry Past and Present"
Mèng Jiāo's poem on failing the imperial examination says:
"Repeatedly cast aside and cast aside again,
my heart is wounded as if by swords and blades.
Another poem on failing again says:
"Twice I've traveled the paths of Cháng'ān,
only to see the flowers with tearful eyes.
Later, when he passed the examination,
he wrote a poem that says:
"No need to sigh over former days of hardship and distress,
today my heart is unburdened, bathed in boundless grace.
In the flush of youth, with triumphant heart and swift horse's hooves,
I see all the flowers of Cháng'ān in a single day.
Within just one day,
he has already seen all the flowers—
how rushed that is!
Success and failure in seeking office
are, after all, common matters.
Yet his spirit and bearing are so narrow,
that he reaches such a state—
how vulgar indeed!
"Surviving Histories of Táng and Sòng"
Jiǎ Dǎo's poem on failing the imperial examination says:
"Failing the exam, only an empty bag remains,
How can I dwell in the emperor's domain?
In the Apricot Garden, orioles sing,
Who revels drunk beside the flowers?
Tears fall as my homeland lies far away,
Illness comes as spring grasses grow long.
How easy is it to meet a true friend?
Alone in my boat, I bear the Three Xiangs' weight.
Lǐ Shānfǔ,
in the Xiántōng era repeatedly took the imperial examinations,
but was rejected,
later wandered to Héshuò,
serving under Lè Yànzhēn,
and held much resentment toward the court's officials.
He once wrote a poem saying:
"I advise you not to boast of your prominence,
for gains and losses in dreams are never real.
From "Nánbù"
Shěn Sōng and Luó Yǐn served together under the administration of Western Zhè,
when their lord brought out a singing girl.
Everyone praised her exceptional beauty,
declaring her to be none other than Cháng'é.
Sōng said:
"Cháng'é is quite plain—
how could she compare to our lord?"
They exclaimed in surprise:
"Does the secretary recognize Cháng'é?"
He replied:
"I, Sōng, have twice gone to the Moon Palace to pluck the cassia branch—
how could I not recognize her!"
Sōng wished to caution Yǐn,
hence these words.
From "Records of the Extraordinary": When Yǐn was in the Western Zhè administration,
Shěn Shānsōng obtained the new examination list
and showed it to Yǐn.
Yǐn inscribed at the end:
"On the loess plains the cunning hare grows fat,
arrows like shooting stars, horses like the wind.
The old general at Bàlíng has no achievements to his name,
yet still recalls returning from the night hunt long ago."
The courtesan Yún Yīng of Zhōnglíng
was known to Yǐn from before.
One day,
she teased him for still not having passed the examinations.
Yǐn retorted:
"Drunk we parted at Zhōnglíng over ten springs ago;
now I see Yún Yīng again, light as a palm.
I have not achieved fame, nor you found a husband—
perhaps neither of us measures up to others."
The Lǐ clan of Jiāngnán once sent an envoy to Yuè.
The people of Yuè asked:
"Have you seen Attendant Luó?"
The envoy replied:
"I do not know him,
nor have I heard his name."
The people of Yuè said:
"All within the Four Seas know of Luó Jiāngdōng—how can you be so ignorant?"
The envoy replied:
"Because his name is not on the golden list,
I have not heard of him."
From "Records of Events"
Shěn Bīn, styled Zǐměi,
was a native of Gāo'ān.
His poetry displayed wild genius and untrammeled spirit.
Orphaned young, he journeyed west with a vow to attempt the imperial examinations three times.
He once dreamed of wearing brocaded robes
and flying close to the moon.
Those who interpreted dreams said:
"Though your fame will spread throughout the land,
your body cannot reach the moon,
meaning you will ultimately not pass the examinations.
After qualifying in Hóngzhōu, he went to Cháng'ān,
failing twice in the examinations.
On his third attempt,
he presented a poem to Liú Xiàng that read:
"I once responded to the Great Middle Emperor's call,
Through four reigns I've faced the wind and moon, my temples growing sparse.
Why should you begrudge this single branch,
When the immortal cassia bears abundant fruit year after year?
Liú Xiàng had failed three attempts
and was poor and isolated.
When the examiner read Bīn's poem,
he passed Liú Xiàng that very year.
The Five Elders List was the omen of this.
During the Qiánfú era, when turmoil plagued the land,
Bīn traveled south through Húxiāng and Lǐngbiǎo for over twenty years,
before returning to Wúzhōng.
Crossing south of the river,
he accepted false appointment
and rose to Vice Minister of Personnel before retiring,
withdrawing to live in Gāo'ān.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Elegant Words"
Sēng Kě Lóng excelled at poetry,
and Gāo Cónghuì reviewed his scroll.
There was a line about watching a chess game that read:
"Consider every move before acting,
one misstep ruins prior achievements."
Cónghuì said to Kě Lóng:
"My teacher must have gained this poem through personal experience."
Lóng replied:
"I originally bore the surname Mùróng,
studied with Sāng Wéihàn,
and in youth carried great ambitions,
often fearing Wéihàn.
Wéihàn passed the imperial examination,
eventually becoming chancellor,
while I remained in the examination halls,
failing repeatedly over the years,
all setbacks caused by Wéihàn.
Thus I shaved my head to become a monk—
these lines truly express my feelings about past events."
Cónghuì's perceptive judgments
were often like this.
From "Tiāndìng Lù"
Shǐláng tuī shǐ gāo huàn jiǔ jǔ bù dì,
huò xuè zhī yuē:
"Yībǎi èrshí gè shǐláng,
tuī yīgè shǐkuài bù shàng.
"Zhí Yán"
Fèi Xuàn was preparing for the imperial examination,
when he dreamed of wearing brocade robes in a well.
Upon waking,
he happily said to himself:
"This means after passing the examination and wearing official robes, I will return to visit my hometown."
Someone else commented:
"This is not a good dream.
Wearing brocade in a well
signifies that your literary talent remains unrecognized."
The following spring, he indeed failed the examination.
From "Máozhāi Kèhuà"
Shí Mànqīng's "Failing the Imperial Exam: A Collection of Lines" reads:
"Throughout my life, I've gained no advantage from literary talent,
Wishing to ascend the blue sky, yet finding no means.
The sage ruler need not trouble to summon from a thousand miles away,
Why should the moon goddess begrudge a single branch of spring?
Though touched by fate under the phoenix decree,
Amidst packs of jackals and tigers, I still stand firm.
Crying until blood flows with nowhere to rest,
Who is that in red robes riding on horseback?"
From "Xī Qīng's Remarks on Poetry": Year in, year out, busy coming and going,
Sewing bridal clothes for others to wear.
Laughing heartily, face to the sky, I step out the door,
Alone, I dance a while in the spring breeze.
From "Cài Tāo's Gold and Jade Remarks on Poetry"
Liǔ Miǎn took the imperial examination,
often avoiding taboos.
He referred to "Peaceful Joy" as "Peaceful Health",
to avoid
the character "fall"
When he heard the results were posted,
he sent a servant to check;
shortly after the servant returned,
saying:
"Scholar, you have 'health-ed'."
From "Leisure Notes from the Hermitage Studio"
Shǔ rén Shí Yángxiū,
repeatedly passed the provincial examinations.
He often failed the metropolitan examinations,
so the people of Shǔ compared him to a tribute officer.
This meant:
a low-ranking officer escorting local tribute to the capital,
would return empty-handed.
When the list of successful candidates in the imperial examination was published,
after expressing gratitude,
they proceeded to the assembly hall,
where the top scholar met with his fellow graduates.
One person was invited to serve as the recorder,
while others were assigned to host the banquet, manage the wine,
and oversee the tea ceremony, such as the flower picker,
all appointed from among their cohort.
"Records of the Imperial Examination"
Chancellor Lǐ Jiàng and Liǔ Zōngyuán were fellow graduates. When someone spoke of their private friendship, Emperor Dézōng asked him:
"Do people have affection for their fellow graduates?"
Jiàng replied:
"Fellow graduates are people from all corners of the realm
who happen to pass the imperial examinations together.
Some only become acquainted after succeeding in the exams -
what affection could there be? But if they are truly talented,
even among brothers and nephews we would employ them, let alone fellow graduates?"
Records of the Táng Dynasty
Miáo Táifú, at six years old, could compose essays,
and at sixteen, he passed the imperial examination.
Zhāng Dú also excelled in poetry and prose from a young age,
passing the examination at eighteen.
They became fellow scholars and both served as aides to Shàoshi Zhèng Xūn in Xuānzhōu.
The two often inscribed poems on the east corridor of Xīmíng Temple, where someone secretly annotated them, saying:
"A pair of former scholars,
two little children."
Táifú died young at seventeen,
while Dú rose to the position of Vice Minister of Rites.
From "Records of the Selected Scholars."
Zhāng Tángqīng achieved the top rank in the imperial examination,
and during the gathering at Xīngguó Temple,
he inscribed on the wall:
"With one success, my name leads the dragon and tiger list;
in ten years, I shall reach the phoenix pool."

was born of a secondary wife, Duàn shì.

his mother Wéi shì, who was very jealous at home,

Cuī Rénjì's father Xún was skilled in archery.
While Rénjì was still in the womb, his mother fell ill,
and Xún wanted to give her medicine.
One night, his mother dreamed someone told her:
"Do not take the medicine,
for fear of harming the Púyè."
When she awoke,
she told Xún about it.
Xún suspected she was deceiving him,
and did not listen,

He saw a snake coiling on the pot,
so he overturned the medicine, and it disappeared.
Later, Rénjì indeed rose to the position of Left Púyè.

Wáng Chéngzhào,
a native of Yǎzhōu,
was the son of Shǔ King Zōng Kǎn.
His mother, Madame Cuī, dreamed of the god of Zhōugōng Mountain descending with auspicious signs,
and thus gave birth to him.
Later, a monk saw him and said:
"The mountain's energy has diminished by half,
it must have been concentrated in conceiving this child.
Later, he governed Yángzhōu as a military commissioner,
serving as Luòxíng Military Administrator.
Sòng Fàn Zhì's mother, Madame Zhāng, dreamed that someone gave her a five-colored brush, and then she gave birth to him.
Lǐ Zhì's mother, Madame Zhāng,
once dreamed of eight immortals descending from heaven,
who bestowed upon her a written talisman,
instructing her to swallow it.
Upon waking,
she still felt as if something remained in her chest,
and before long,
she gave birth to Zhì.
Wáng Yìgōng's father, whenever he saw written paper fallen and discarded,
would always pick it up,
wash it with fragrant water, and then burn it.
One evening,
he dreamed that Confucius patted him on the back and said:
"Why do you so diligently revere my written paper?
It is a pity that you are old,
and can achieve nothing more.
Another day, I shall have Zēng Shēn be reborn into your family,
to bring glory to your household.
Not long after,
a son was indeed born to him,
and he was accordingly named Zēng,
who later placed first in the imperial examinations.
"Wénchāng Huà Shū"
Yáng Dànián's grandfather Wényì
served as the magistrate of Yùshān in the Southern Táng.
Just before Dànián was about to be born,
a Daoist priest with a name card in his sleeve came to visit,
claiming to be
"Huáiyù Shānrén"
He wore a hat and coarse clothing, looking elegant and spirited,
but suddenly disappeared in an instant,
and then the lord was born.
Thirty-seven years later,
while the academician was napping in the Yùtáng,
he suddenly dreamed of the Daoist priest coming to visit,
calling himself
"Huáiyù Shānrén"
and presenting a document.
Upon reading it,
it contained thirty-seven characters.
Dànián exclaimed in surprise:
"Could this be my fate!
May I add more?"
The Daoist priest picked up a brush and made a dot,
turning it into forty-seven characters,
and indeed, that was the number of years he lived.
From "Yùhú Qīnghuà": When Dànián was first born,
his mother, Madame Zhāng, dreamed of a feathered-robed figure
who claimed to be a Wǔyí immortal taking human form.
After he was born,
he appeared as a young crane.
The whole family was shocked and frightened,
so they stored him in a container and abandoned him in the river.
His uncle said:
"I have heard that extraordinary people
are born with unusual signs,
like Jiāng Yuán abandoning her child,
or Jiǎn Dí giving birth to Qì."
He then chased to the riverbank,
opened the container to look,
and found that the crane had shed its form, revealing a complete infant.
The body still had purple down over a foot long,
which fell off after a month.

Zhāng Déxiàng,

Lǚ Gōngbì
was the second son of Duke Shēn.
Initially, when Lady of Qin was pregnant and ill,
they intended to abort the fetus,
with physician Chén Sùn boiling the medicine.
As it was about to be ready,
it was already the third watch of the night,
he sat dozing off.
Suddenly the cauldron overturned,
so he boiled it again,
and it overturned again.
He boiled it once more,
this time increasing the fire.
Being extremely exhausted,
he went to his bed,
and dreamed of a deity clad in golden armor, holding a sword, who rebuked him:
"The one in the womb
is destined to be a prime minister of this dynasty.
How dare you, a mere mortal, attempt to harm him with poison!"
Sùn woke up in fear,
and reported this to the descendants of the Chancellor.
During the Xīníng era,
Gōngbì held the position of Commissioner of Military Affairs.
From "Records of the Strange"
Shào Kāngjié's
mother, Lǐ Shì,
was treated very strictly by her mother-in-law, Zhāng Shì.
One evening,
she intended to take her own life,
but dreamed of a deity
who gave her a jade chopstick to eat a bowl of soup.

Later, she gave birth to Shào Kāngjié.

while traveling in the mountains amidst clouds and mist,

and, feeling an influence, she became pregnant.
When she was about to give birth,
magpies filled the courtyard,
which people considered an auspicious sign.
Thus, Shào Kāngjié was born.
At seven years old, while playing in the courtyard,
he saw a different sky and sunlight through an ant hole,

Hán Yì's wife, Madame Wáng,

Later, she gave birth to Zōng, Jiàng, Yì, Wéi, and Jī,

Cháo Zhīdào once said: When Vice Minister Cài Zhǔn was young,
there were always two figures
appearing before his horse's head,
or in front of his sedan chair.
They acted as forerunners,
sometimes advancing, sometimes retreating.
When he asked his attendants,
none had seen them.
Zhǔn was very frightened,
thinking they were wronged spirits,
and tried every method of exorcism,
but none could dispel them.
After a long time,
he no longer regarded it as significant.
In the fourth year of the Qìnglì era,
Jīng was born,
and one figure disappeared.
Two years later,
Biàn was born,
and then both vanished completely.
At the end of the Yuánfú era,
a children's rhyme in the capital contained
"two children in the household,
turnip spirits"
among its lines.
Most of the lyrics cannot be fully recalled,
but its final verse said:
"They encountered the Hǎizàng deity of Tánzhōu."
By the Chóngníng era,
vendors of sour stuffed buns
had another phrase about a bundle of vegetables,
all of which proved prophetic.
When Jīng was demoted and died in Chángshā early in the Jìngtáng period,
could it be that
"the Hǎizàng deity of Tánzhōu"
was also foretold here?

Lǐ Xiǎnzhōng was originally named Shìfǔ.

A monk passing by the door said:

Place a sword and arrows beside the mother,

Soon enough, Xiǎnzhōng was born,
standing on the birthing mat,

"History of the Song Dynasty"
Sòng Yíwáng Zhòng Shí was born with purple light illuminating the room;

thus obtaining an infant.
During the Jìngkāng period,
the army wanted to support and establish him as emperor,
but he wielded his sword to refuse,
enlightening his followers by saying:
"There already exists a true ruler.
His followers still had not retreated,
so he intended to fall upon his sword and die.

that if after a month the true ruler had not appeared,
then the prince should ascend to the throne.
The prince pretended to agree,
but secretly delayed the deadline.
Not long after,
Emperor Gāozōng ascended the throne at Yìngtiān,

putting him in charge of sacrifices to the Prince of Pú.

these grasses grow in pure lands.

Yáng Hù at the age of five,
asked his wet nurse to fetch a golden ring.
The wet nurse said:
"There is no such thing.
Hù then went to the eastern garden of his neighbor Lǐ's house among the mulberry trees,
and retrieved it.
The master of the house was greatly astonished and said:
"This is what my deceased son had lost.
The wet nurse explained the whole story,
and Lǐ's family was deeply grieved.
People at the time found this extraordinary,
realizing that the Lǐ's son was Yáng Hù's previous incarnation.

The Secretariat Director Wáng Mǐn,
