was acquainted with a foreign monk.
Whenever the monk beheld Wáng Mǐn's demeanor,
he greatly admired and delighted in him,
and would often say to his fellow monks:
"If in my next life,
I could become this man's son,
it would fulfill my dearest wish."
Wáng Mǐn heard this and jested with him:
"Reverend, with your talent and conduct,
you would only qualify as my younger brother."
Soon after,
the monk fell ill and died.
Over a year after his death, Ā Liàn was born.
As soon as he could speak,
he understood foreign languages.
Even regarding rare treasures from distant lands,
bronze vessels, pearls, and cowries,
things he had never seen in this life,
nor heard their names,
he could immediately name them and identify their origins.
Moreover, he naturally felt affection for all foreigners,
surpassing his regard for Han people.
Everyone said the monk had truly been his former self,
so Wáng Mǐn gave him the childhood name Ā Liàn,
which eventually became his formal name.

Emperor Wénxuān of Qí intended to kill Sēng Chóu,

and then asked him:
"What did your disciple do in a previous life?
He replied:
"You were a rākṣasa king.
That is why you still delight in killing.
He then chanted a spell over a basin of water,
instructing the emperor to look at himself,
where he saw his reflection resembling the image of a rākṣasa.

Xǔ Xún and the monk Tán Yàn jointly built a pagoda,

Fù Dàshì, named Shàn,
was a native of Wùzhōu.
During the Southern Qí Dynasty,
he descended into the family of Fù Xuāncí,
married a daughter of the Liú family,
named Miàozhì,

the robe and bowl from the Tuṣita Heaven are still present—
when will you return?"
He then instructed him to gaze at his reflection in the water,
where Dàshì saw his own halo and jeweled canopy.
Dàshì laughed.
At that time, a Dharma master, upon hearing the teaching, realized and said:

Dàshì rebuked him.
In the second year of the Tiānjiā era,
Dàshì entered nirvana while practicing the Way at Shuānglín Temple on Sōng Mountain.

During the Kaiyuan era,
Fáng Guǎn served as magistrate of Lúshì County.
When Xíng Hépú came,
Guǎn treated him with respect.
On a leisure day, they went out of the city together
and arrived at Xiàgǔ Village,
where an abandoned temple stood shaded by dense pines and bamboos.
Hépú sat beneath them
and tapped the ground with his staff,
instructing others to dig several feet down.
They unearthed a vase,
inside which were letters between Lóu Shīdé and Yǒng Gōng.
Smiling, he said to Guǎn:
"Do you somewhat recall this?"
Guǎn then felt a sudden clarity,
realizing he had been a monk in a past life—
the reincarnation of Yǒng Gōng.
Hépú thus foretold Guǎn's affairs,
and every prediction proved true throughout his life.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Ming."
When Jiànnán's military governor Wéi Gāo was just one month old,
his family summoned the local monks for a meal.
There was one foreign monk,
whose appearance was quite ugly.
After the meal,
the Wéi family ordered the wet nurse to bring out the infant,
and requested the local monks to pray for his longevity.
The foreign monk suddenly said to the infant:
"Has it been long since we parted? Are you well?"
The infant appeared to have a joyful expression,
which astonished everyone present.
The foreign monk said:
"This child is the reincarnation of Zhūgě Wǔhóu.
In previous years at Jiànmén, I formed a friendship with this person.
Now hearing he has been born into the Wéi family,
I have traveled far to come here."
Thereupon, the Wéi family named him with Wǔhóu's courtesy name.
Later, Wéi himself, starting from the position of Junior Imperial Guard, came to command the Jiànnán army,
remaining at the Shǔ frontier for eighteen years,
thus indeed fulfilling the foreign monk's words.
From "Shǎoshì Zhì"
When Lǐ Gōngchuí Shēn was young,
he studied at the Tiāngōng Buddhist Temple in Shànzhōu.
One day while napping during the day,
a black snake was resting on the ripening red plums in the room.
Just then a monk arrived,
drove it away,
and the snake entered Lǐ's bosom,
suddenly disappearing.
When he awoke,
they asked him about it,
and he replied:
"I just dreamed I was among the trees eating plums that were exceptionally delicious."
The monk found this very extraordinary.
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì"
Yuán Zī, when still obscure, resided at Wénzhōu's Qīngxī Mountain,
and through selling medicine encountered an extraordinary person who said:
"This man greatly resembles the seated meditation monk from Xīhuá in the west,
who passed away exactly forty-seven years ago by my count."
When asked his age,
Zī happened to be forty-seven years old.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Cuī Ruì served as an assistant to Lǐ Bàozhēn in Zélù,
when a Daoist priest who called himself
"Lǎo Lú"
and claimed to have served under Mr. Lǐ of Yúnjì Temple during the Suí dynasty,
could foretell past and future events.
As the region north of the Yellow River prohibited wandering visitors,
Cuī Ruì housed him at his home.
One day the priest bid farewell,
saying:
"After I die,
I shall be reborn as your son.
He then pointed to a black mole beneath his mouth,
asking to use it as an identifying mark.
When Cuī Xián was born,
he indeed had the black mole,
and his appearance and spirit were exactly those of Lǎo Lú,
so his father named him Lǎo Lú as his courtesy name.
Later he rose through official ranks to become Grand Governor and Surveillance Commissioner.
From morning till night,
he would drink heavily with guests and subordinates,
constantly intoxicated yet never fully unconscious.
Though official documents piled up,
he would review them late at night,
analyzing and making decisions
without the slightest error,
making clerks regard him as a supernatural being.
He died in the eighth year of the Tàihé era.
From "Old Book of Tang: Biographies of Literary Figures"
Minister Báizhū Zhèng Yú, due to drunkenness, fell asleep,
and his attendants saw a white pig.
"Northern Dreams"
Liú Sānfù was
recognized for his literary talent by Lǐ Déyù.
While in Zhèxī,
he was sent to various schools to seek examination opportunities.
After achieving the jinshi degree,
he held positions in the central government.
Sānfù could recall events from his three past lives,
saying: he had once been a horse,
the horse was often thirsty,
and would neigh at the sight of a courier station,
feeling heartache when its hooves were injured.
Later, when Sānfù rode horses,
on rocky terrain,
he would loosen the reins,
and remove any stones in the path.
His household did not install door thresholds,
to avoid injuring horses' hooves.
His son, Yè,
was granted the jinshi degree by imperial decree.
Rising to high office,
he submitted a memorial to clear Déyù's name.
Déyù's coffin from Zhūyá
was returned for burial in Luòzhōng,
as repayment of past kindness.
Scholar-officials praised this.
《Northern Dreams》 The family servant of Sūn Miǎn, the sheriff of Qǔwò County,
at age six,
suddenly looked at Miǎn's mother,
and said with a laugh:
"Madam, when you were a young girl,
you once raised a wild fox,
do you remember now?"
The mother recalled it.
The servant said:
"That wild fox at the time,
was none other than me.
I saw a hawk and fled,
into an ancient tomb,
but was later struck by a hunter.
Upon seeing King Yama,
the king said I was innocent and deserved a human life,
so I was born in Hǎizhōu,
as a beggar's child.
I suffered hunger and cold for twenty years before dying.
I saw the king again,
who said: 'I shall make you a servant in a noble household'
Thus I came here,
and now it has been three lifetimes.
《Records of the Vast and Strange》
Liú Lì served as the deputy magistrate of Chánggě.
His wife, Yáng shì,
suddenly one day tearfully said to Lì:
"I am fated to die on a certain day.
And entrusted their young daughter Měiměi to him,
saying:
"When Měiměi grows up in the future,
I hope you will keep her for two or three years.
That evening Yáng shì passed away.
When his term ended,
he resided in Chánggě,
already ten years had passed.
There was a certain county magistrate
who invited Lì to view flowers outside the city walls.
The magistrate asked Lì to go first,
to stay at the estate of Marshal Zhào.
After traveling two or three li,
he saw over ten women viewing flowers in an apricot garden,
Lì stopped his horse to watch them,
there was a girl about fifteen or sixteen years old,
who also approached the broken wall to peek.
Lì arrived at Marshal Zhào's residence.
Upon entering the gate,
the host took a while before coming out,
saying:
"Just now my daughter was viewing flowers with relatives,
when she suddenly suffered a violent illness,
therefore I couldn't come to welcome you properly.
Before they had settled in their seats,
a maid whispered in Zhào's ear,
Zhào rose and went inside,
where Lì heard Marshal Zhào sighing in astonishment,
then Zhào asked Lì:
"Did you serve as deputy magistrate of Chánggě in a certain year, married to Yáng shì?
Lì replied:
"Yes.
"Did you have a daughter named Měiměi,
and a servant named Qiūsǔn?
He replied:
"Yes.
Zhào again sighed in wonder.
Soon someone called Qiūsǔn into the house,
where he saw a girl
who tearfully asked him:
"Is Měiměi well?
He replied:
"She is fine.
The servant was also surprised.
Lì slowly asked Zhào:
"I don't recall having met you before,
how do you know about my circumstances?
Zhào then told him the truth:
"My daughter was just viewing flowers,
when she suddenly collapsed and died,
after reviving,
she claimed that in her previous life she was your wife.
When she peeked and saw you just now,
she unconsciously fainted.
Lì sighed sorrowfully for a long time.
Soon after,
the county magistrate also arrived,
and all the guests gathered.
Zhào explained what had happened,
everyone found it extraordinary.
Lì said:
"I am not too old this year,
and hold an official position,
I wish to renew my former marriage with the young lady.
Everyone helped bring this about,
thus they became husband and wife.
And Měiměi was three years older than her mother had been.
From "Huìchāng Jiěyí Lù"
Qián Wǔsù every night ordered an old woman to supervise the night watch.
Listening all night to the silver board lamp,
a large lizard climbed along the oil lamp and sucked it.
When it was nearly empty,
it suddenly disappeared,
but no one paid it any mind.
The next day the king said:
"Last night I dreamed of drinking sesame oil,
filling my belly until I was full,
what omen is this?"
Someone in the palace offered an explanation,
but the king merely smiled faintly.
"Recorded Traditions"
The deity Zhāng Èzi of Zǐtóng County
was at the place where the Five Strongmen pulled out the snake.
Some say it was a snake raised by a man named Zhāng from Juànzhōu,
and thus a shrine was established for it.
People called it Zhāng Èzi,
and the deity was very efficacious.
Yuányīng, the heir of Shǔ king Wáng Jiàn,
was intelligent and broadly learned,
unrivaled in horsemanship and archery.
His teeth were always exposed,
so he often covered his mouth with his sleeve,
and those around him dared not look up at him.
He had snake-like eyes and a dark complexion,
appearing fierce, vile, and obscene.
He never slept through the night,
and ultimately was executed for rebellion.
On the evening of his execution,
the temple priest of Zǐtóng
was urgently reprimanded by Èzi,
who said:
"I was not in the river,
and have just returned now.
How could the temple have become so dilapidated and filthy?"
Only then did the people of Shǔ realize that Yuányīng was the essence of the temple snake.
From "Northern Dreams"
When Jiāngnán Fēng Hào was first born,
his father suddenly dreamed of Xiè Língyùn holding a name card coming to visit,
introducing himself as the former governor of Yǒngjiā,
with a fine long beard and elegant demeanor,
his bones pure and spirit towering,
the clothes and headscarf he wore
light as mist and smoke.
He said:
"I wish to entrust myself to you as your son,
temporarily residing by Feilai Peak in western Zhèjiāng,
translating the Diamond Sutra.
Where there are parts inconsistent with the Buddha's teachings,
I hope to be born in your household to make corrections.
Be careful not to feed me meaty flavors,
at seven years old I shall leave home to become a monk,
to complete the previous sutra."
When the dream ended,
Hào was born.
His appearance resembled the one in the dream,
and his father loved him.
His childhood name was Kānglè,
when he grew into youth,
he was intelligent.
He firmly requested to leave home for monastic life,
but his father would not consent,
forcing him with meat diets.
When he reached capping age,
he was compelled to marry.
Later the succeeding ruler admired his erudition and refinement,
repeatedly employed him,
yet he was gentle, weak and indecisive,
only fond of Buddhism.
Initially when he joined the army to pacify Jiànzhōu,
he solely focused on preserving lives,
people called him
"Biān the Arhat"
When he reached Xiāngtán,
people called him
"Biān the Bodhisattva"
When he governed Tán,
administration came from multiple authorities,
completely lacking威严 and decisiveness,
the Chǔ people were disappointed,
people called him
"Biān the Monk"
"Jade Pot Pure Talk"
Gāo Lǐ,
was a yaksha spirit.
He once invited Qiū Guāngtíng, a Grand Academy erudite, to proofread books in his tower,
and Lǐ also frequently went to check on him.
One day,
Lǐ climbed up to Guāngtíng in his socks,
who was unaware of his presence,
but when he turned around,
he saw a green-faced ghost,
and cried out in alarm.
Soon he realized it was Lǐ,
who patted him and said:
"Be careful not to speak of this.
From this, it was confirmed that he was not human.
From "The Supplementary History of Wú and Yuè"
Mǎ Rényù,
a native of Xúzhōu,
was a descendant of Táng dynasty's Běipíng King Suì.
His family had served as military officers in the Wǔníng army for generations.
While Rényù's mother was pregnant with him,
she dreamed of a message announcing the return of Běipíng King,
and purple light filled the courtyard at his birth.
From "History of Southern Táng"
Pān Yòu himself said that when his mother was pregnant with him,
she dreamed of a person in ancient attire who told her:
"I am Yán Yánzhī,
and I shall be your son."
When he was born,
he did not speak until he was seven years old,
then said:
"I accidentally injured a white dragon,
and was punished by the Heavenly Emperor for it."
Thereupon he chanted a poem:
"At dawn I roamed the eastern seas,
Why so swiftly did I return by dusk?
Only because I broke the Jade Dragon's waist while riding,
Banished to the mortal world for thirty-six years."
Indeed, he died as a criminal at that very age.
"Southern Tang's Xiangshan Mountain"
Liú Hàng,
his ancestor Liú Jǐnghóng served Yáng Xíngmì as a deputy general in Jiāngxī.
There was a Péng Xū,
who claimed the governor coerced Jǐnghóng into defecting to Húnán,
but Jǐnghóng pretended to agree,
then returned to his allegiance.
Xíngmì consequently did not hold his initial actions against him.
Jǐnghóng said:
"By not following Péng Xū,
I saved over ten thousand lives,
so prosperity will surely follow."
Thus he named the mountain where he resided
"Fùlóng Shān" (Return and Prosper Mountain).
On the mountain was Niú Sēngrú's study hall,
and Hàng's mother dreamed of Lord Niú visiting before giving birth to Hàng.
Later, when Hàng went for the imperial examinations,
an old man said:
"You are originally the Jade Source Zūn Jūn of Luófú Shān."
Fàn Zǔyǔ's mother dreamed of a man clad in golden armor who came to her bedside and said:
"I am the former Hàn general Dèng Yǔ.
Zǔyǔ was born that very day,
so the gentleman was thus named.
Initially styled
"Mèng"
but after obtaining Wēn Gōng's biography praising Dèng Yǔ
for his sincere conduct and pure integrity,
he changed his style to
"Chúnfǔ"
From "Family Biography"
Zhāng Āndào was demoted from the Imperial Academy to govern Chúzhōu.
On a leisurely day, while visiting the Lángyá Temple,
he suddenly recalled his previous life.
He had once been a monk in the temple,
and had personally transcribed four volumes of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
He sent someone to climb into the rafters of the temple,
where they retrieved a sutra case.
Upon opening it and examining the brushstrokes,
the handwriting was unmistakably his.
He sighed with mixed emotions of sorrow and joy,
as past karmic obstacles melted away like ice—for Yuèquán was indeed the reincarnation of the Lángyá Mountain monk.
He then entrusted Dōngpō to transcribe this sutra,
and had it printed and distributed at Jīnshān Temple.
*Yù Jiǎn Hóu Qīng Lù*.
During the Yuánfēng era,
Dōngpō was exiled to Huángzhōu,
while Zǐyóu was also transferred to Gāo'ān.
At that time, Yún'ān resided at Dòngshān,
and once dreamed of accompanying Zǐyóu on a suburban excursion,
saying they were welcoming the Fifth Patriarch's monk Jiè.
Upon waking, he found it strange,
and at dawn told Zǐyóu about it.
Soon after, the Sìchuān monk Cōng arrived and said:
"My master dreamed of the three of us together welcoming monk Jiè,
what omen is this?"
Zǐyóu was greatly astonished and exclaimed:
"How could there be people sharing the same dream?"
They traveled over twenty lǐ with two gentlemen,
when Dōngpō arrived.
Dōngpō said:
"When I was eight or nine years old,
I often dreamed I was a monk
traveling in Shǎnxi."
He also said that while his mother was pregnant with him,
she dreamed of a monk,
thin and one-eyed,
who came seeking lodging.
Cōng exclaimed in surprise:
"Jiè
was from Shǎnxi,
had lost one eye,
and in his later years left the Fifth Patriarch,
dying after encountering dogs."
Counting back, this was about fifty years ago.
Later when Dōngpō was exiled to Yīngzhōu,
he wrote to a monk
referring to "monk Jiè"
which was another slip of memory.
From "Zhìlín"
One day, Hé Yuǎn visited the scholar Qián Jìmíng, known as the Ice Flower Hermit,
at his residence, the Misty Rain Hall.
During their conversation, they happened to recite a eulogy for Master Dōngpō (Sū Shì),
and when they reached
"Descending to Zōu Yáng after thirteen generations,
heaven made it so by chance;
though succeeding Mèng Kē after five hundred years,
I find no gap"
these lines,
the Ice Flower Hermit laughed and said:
"This was written by this old man."
Thereupon, Hé Yuǎn inquired about
the matter of
"descending to Zōu Yáng."
The Ice Flower Hermit said:
"In the early Yuányòu era,
Liú Gòngfù dreamed of arriving at
a government office,
where there were many purple-tagged scrolls of texts.
He happened to pick one scroll and unroll it to look,
which stated, 'In the Sòng dynasty, he was a certain Sū.'
Counting backward thirteen generations,
it said, 'In the Western Hàn dynasty, he was Zōu Yáng.'
This is similar to how during the Huángdì era, he was the Grand Master,
and in the Zhōu dynasty, he was the Historian at the Pillar,
all referring to the same Lǎo Dān."
Records of Things Heard in Spring
When Huáng Shāngǔ first visited the elder Qīng with Sū Dōngpō,
Qīng told Dōngpō that his previous life was as the monk Wǔzǔ Jiè,
and then said to Shāngǔ:
"Your previous life was a woman,
but I cannot elaborate further.
In the future, when you reach Fúlíng,
you will naturally encounter someone who can reveal more.
Shāngǔ thought to himself that one would only go to Fúlíng if exiled,
and hearing this left him somewhat bewildered.
Later, when he was convicted as a criminal,
he was indeed exiled to Fúlíng.
Not long after,
he dreamed of a woman who said:
"I recited the Lotus Sutra throughout my life and died with that devotion,
then was reborn as a man,
gained great wisdom,
and became a renowned figure of the time.
You, esteemed scholar,
are my previous incarnation.
The underarm odor you have suffered from in recent years
is because the coffin where I was buried has decayed,
and ants have nested in the hollows beneath both armpits,
hence this affliction.
Now, behind this residence lies my grave,
if you can open it,
and remove the ant colonies,
then the underarm odor can be eliminated.
After waking,
he indeed found the grave,
which was already ownerless.
He then had it relocated,
and the underarm odor was truly cured.
Wáng Jièfǔ was studying at Zhōngshān,
when an elder monk said:
"You are destined to become prime minister,
but you must not dwell on past grievances,
nor change the established laws of our ancestors.
Jièfǔ replied:
"I haven't even passed the imperial examination yet,
how could I have time to think about becoming prime minister,
let alone changing ancestral laws?
Is the monk joking?
The old monk said:
"I once entered deep meditation,
and saw the King of Qin entering the temple,
so I know you are the reincarnation of the King of Qin.
From "Guì Ěr Jí"
When Zhào Dǐng was first born,
his mother dreamed of a magnificent man in gold and purple entering her chamber,
with a ceremonial guide in front announcing loudly,
"The Duke of Zanhuang has arrived."
The lady awoke with a start,
as if she had seen something.
Not long after,
Dǐng was born.
Later in his official career,
his achievements and fame largely coincided with those of Dé Yù.
Dé Yù was demoted from his position in the Eastern Capital to Cháoyáng,
and Dǐng was also transferred from Sìmíng to Cháoyáng as an unassigned official.
The following year, Dé Yù was banished to Zhūyá where he died,
and Dǐng also died in Zhūyá,
both at the age of sixty-three.
"Tǎnzhāi Bǐchōng"
Wáng Wànnián,
a deputy commander-in-chief,
sent a letter to Monk Āozhōng of Mín'é Mountain.
The monk did not reply with a letter,
but only said:
"Tell the Grand Marshal to return humbly.
When the messenger arrived,
he was asked if there was a letter,
but he firmly refused to speak.
Wáng said:
"I already know,
you may speak directly.
After a long while, he finally said the monk requested the Grand Marshal to return early.
Three days later, Wáng passed away while rinsing his mouth.
Someone asked Āozhōng,
who said:
"Grand Marshal Wáng is the sixth Ten-Thousand-Year Ghost King,
hence his surname Wáng and given name Wànnián.
From "Guì Ěr Jí"
When Wáng Shípéng was about to be born,
his mother dreamed that Yán Bówēi, the teacher of his clan uncle, came to their home,
and then he was born.
Later, a monk saw Shípéng and said:
"This boy is the reincarnation of Yán Bówēi.
The "Méixī Anthology" records Shípéng's "Quatrain on the Stone Bridge":
"Before reaching the stone bridge, my spirit arrived first,
the daytime was just like in the dream.
The monk told me my name was Liú Dàozhě,
in my previous life I once inscribed the stone bridge stele.
The stone bridge refers to the entrance of the Five Hundred Arhats Cave at Tiāntāi.
"Xuěyíng Collection of Remarks"
In Jiànníng's Pǔchéng, a Daoist built a hut in the mountains to refine elixirs.
Just as he was about to succeed,
he suddenly entered deep meditation one day,
and instructed his young disciple:
"After I leave,
I may return in ten or five days;
be careful not to lightly disturb my dwelling."
A few days later,
someone suddenly knocked at the door and said:
"I know your master has been taken by the underworld;
why keep his stinking, decaying body?"
The disciple, unaware this was a demon's trick,
then lifted and burned it.
The Daoist soon returned,
circling the hut and crying out:
"Where am I?"
This went on for over a month without ceasing.
An old monk happened to hear this tale,
and sternly replied to him:
"You say you're looking for me,
but who are you?"
The voice then ceased.
At that time, his mother was pregnant,
and suddenly saw the Daoist enter her room,
whereupon she gave birth to Déxiù.
"Qídōng Yěyě"
Hú Yín's wife, Madame Wēng,
was the daughter of the Registrar of Mìzhōu.
On the night before her birth,
her grandfather, the Palace Compiler, dreamed of someone announcing a visit, saying:
"I am the Weaving Maid Star,
and I am to be born into your family."
The next day, Madame Wēng was born,
with red light filling the room.
The Palace Compiler said:
"This child is destined to be noble and long-lived."
When she grew up, she married Yín,
and was renowned for her wifely virtues.
She lived to see her great-great-grandchildren,
and was thrice enfeoffed as the Great Lady of Tàiyuán Níng Commandery.
"Inner Biography"
When Wén Tiānxiáng's mother was about to give birth,
she dreamed of a dragon descending upon their home,
and thus the lord was born.
Beside his residence was a pond,
which formed a vast expanse of water.
From the time of his birth,
the pond's water gradually became shallower.
When he grew older, he studied in the Xiùshuǐ Mountains,
and along the way, there was an inn.
One evening,
the innkeeper dreamed of a dragon shedding its claws on a stone outside the gate,
and upon opening the door at dawn,
he saw the lord had left his shoes on the stone,
and departed shortly after.
Additionally, the lord enjoyed playing chess in the water with guests,
and when the guests could not win,
he remained calm and composed all day long.
After the lord passed away,
the pond's water deepened once more.
Táng Péi Xiū was the king of Yútián.
《Běi Mèng》: The Later Lord of Nán Táng was the king of Shīzǐguó.
《Chéng Yì Jì》
Jìn attacked Qín.
The people of Jìn captured a spy from Qín,
and executed him in the marketplace of Jiàng.
Six days later, he revived,
which is probably a record of an anomaly.
Zuǒ Xuān 8
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
Guānzhōng was in great turmoil.
Someone excavated the tomb of a palace lady from the former Hàn period,
and the person was still alive.
After emerging,
she recovered and became as before.
Empress Guō of Wèi cherished and missed her,
took her into the palace,
and often kept her by her side.
When asked about matters inside the Hàn palace,
she recounted them clearly and vividly,
all in an orderly sequence.
When Empress Guō passed away,
she wept beyond the proper rites,
and subsequently died.
From "Bówùzhì": During the Wèi period, someone opened the tomb of the Zhōu king,
and found a woman who had been buried alive with the dead.
After several days, she began to breathe,
and after several months, she was able to speak.
She appeared to be about twenty years old,
and was sent to the capital.
Empress Dowager Guō loved and cared for her.
After over ten years,
when the Empress Dowager passed away,
she grieved and wept,
and after more than a year, she died.
From Gù Kǎizhī's "Qǐméng Zhù".
Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Bì Guǐ presented a Xianbei slave who had served the former Hàn Dynasty Dù Liáo General Fàn Míngyǒu,
aged three hundred and fifty years,
yet speaking and eating like an ordinary person.
The slave said:
"Huò Xiǎn
was Huò Guāng's junior wife.
Fàn Míngyǒu's wife
was the daughter of Huò Guāng's former wife.
Shìyǔ records: At the end of the Hàn Dynasty,
when Fàn Míngyǒu's tomb was excavated among the Xiongnu,
he was still alive.
Míngyǒu,
being Huò Guāng's son-in-law,
spoke of Huò Guāng's family affairs,
and regarding the events of deposing and establishing emperors,
his accounts largely align with the Hàn Shū.
This slave often wandered among the common people,
with no fixed dwelling place.
Bówùzhì records:
The Bodhi Temple was established
by people from the Western Regions.
Monks often excavated tombs to obtain bricks,
and they found a person and presented him.
At that time, Empress Dowager and Emperor Ming were in the Hualin Hall,
and they considered it an ominous anomaly.
They ordered the Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Xú Hé to ask his name,
how many years he had been dead,
and what he ate and drank.
The deceased said:
"I am surnamed Cuī, named Hán, styled Zǐhóng,
from Ānpíng in Bólíng.
My father is named Chàng, and my mother is surnamed Wèi.
Our home is in Fùcái Lane west of the city.
I died at the age of fifteen,
and now I am twenty-seven,
having been underground for twelve years.
I often felt as if lying drunk,
with nothing to eat.
Occasionally I wandered about,
and sometimes encountered food,
as if in a dream,
not very clear or distinct."
The Empress Dowager then sent the Recorder of the Chancellery Zhāng Jùn to Fùcái Lane to visit Hán's parents,
and indeed Jùn returned,
reporting fully the truth.
The Empress Dowager sent Hán back home.
His mother Wèi, holding a peach branch,
urgently ordered him to leave quickly.
Hán then left,
wandering in the capital,
often lodging under temple gates.
The Prince of Rǔnán bestowed upon him a yellow robe.
Hán had a nature of fearing the sun,
daring not to look up.
He also feared water, fire, and weapons.
He often ran on main roads,
stopping when tired,
not walking slowly.
People at the time still thought he was a ghost.
from "A Record of Buddhist Monasteries"
In the third year of the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
at the Níngguān Temple northwest of the capital, there was a monk named Fǎqìng,
who was crafting a sixteen-foot statue with a storage compartment.
Before it was completed,
he died suddenly.
At the same time, the monk Dàzhì from Bǎochāng Temple also passed away on the same day.
After three days, both revived,
saying: they saw officials,
and on the hall was someone resembling a king,
with a very large retinue.
They saw Fǎqìng in front,
when suddenly a statue arrived,
and said to the person on the hall:
"Fǎqìng has not finished making me,
why was he caused to die?"
Then they checked the records,
saying:
"Fǎqìng's food is exhausted,
but his lifespan is not yet over."
The person on the hall said:
"He may be given lotus leaves to complete his lifespan."
After these words were spoken,
suddenly everything vanished,
and Dàzhì then revived.
The crowd found it strange,
so they went to Níngguān Temple to ask Fǎqìng,
and his account matched exactly.
Fǎqìng could no longer eat regular food;
every morning he consumed six lotus leaves,
and at mealtime, eight branches.
He continued this for the rest of his life.
His fellow monks begged for alms,
to complete the statue.
"Records of the Two Capitals" In the early years of Emperor Zhāozōng,
there was a monk named Shì Níng from Fèngxiáng,
who suddenly died and then revived,
saying:
"Initially, I was taken by the underworld officials.
One judge said: 'The monk's lifespan remains,
but why is there no provision for him?'
The clerk checked,
and found only three shí of dried lotus leaves.
Thus, he was instructed to record it in the ledger.
From then on, Shì Níng, whenever he broke his fast,
only had lotus leaf soup and nothing else,
and was nicknamed
'Underworld Monk'
As for the aforementioned Fǎqìng, whenever he wished to eat,
he first softened the lotus leaves with warm water,
and only then consumed them.
"Song Biographies of Eminent Monks"
Dòu Jiàndé once excavated a tomb in Yèzhōng with no other objects,
opening the coffin to find a woman,
her complexion as if alive,
her appearance elegant and beautiful,
likely in her twenties,
her clothing and style not of recent times.
Observing her, she seemed to have breath,
so he took her back to the army to care for her.
After three days, she revived,
able to speak.
She said:
"I was a palace maid of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
who died in Yè following Empress Zhēn,
and was buried here.
I do not know what time it is now."
She recounted Empress Zhēn's persecution with clarity and detail,
and Dòu Jiàndé greatly adored her.
Later, when Dòu Jiàndé was defeated by Tàizōng,
the emperor intended to take her as a consort.
She then fully explained the events,
and declined, saying:
"I have been secluded beneath the yellow soil for three hundred years;
if not for Lord Dòu, how could I have been seen?
To die today is my fate."
Thus, she died with regret,
and the emperor was deeply saddened.
"Shén Yì Lù"
In the late years of the Sòng dynasty,
a pancake seller in Gūsū, while counting his earnings, discovered spirit money among them.
Puzzled by this,
he began noting the identity of each customer and their payment
every time he sold pancakes.
After some time,
he traced it to a woman.
He followed her to a grave,
where she vanished.
He reported it to the authorities,
who opened the tomb and found the woman lying in the coffin,
with a small child sitting beside her.
Fearing discovery by others,
she dared not emerge again,
leaving the child to starve.
A curious onlooker took the child in and raised him.
As he grew, he appeared no different from ordinary people,
but since his surname was unknown,
the villagers called him
"Guǐ Guānrén."
He was still alive in the early Yuán dynasty,
and passed away several years later.
(From "Yuán Wú Yǎn Zǐ Xíng Xián Jū Lù")
Kǎo means old or aged.
In *Shuōwén*, it means decrepit with age.
One who is old and does not die is called an immortal.
From *Shìmíng*.
Fifty is called ài.
Ài
means governance.
It signifies the ability to govern affairs decisively, cutting and weeding without hesitation.
Sixty is called qí.
Qí
means pointing,
as one no longer engages in physical labor,
but directs others to handle matters.
Seventy is called mào.
It describes hair turning white and sparse.
Eighty is called dié.
Dié
means iron,
referring to the skin darkening
to a color resembling iron.
Ninety is called táibèi,
as the skin develops patterns like those on a blowfish.
It is also called huánggǒu,
where the hair on the temples turns yellow.
Gǒu
means grime.
The skin becomes dark and haggard,
as if perpetually covered in dirt.
Another term is húgòu,
describing the neck skin sagging like a chicken's wattle.
It is also called dònglí,
with skin mottled and blackened,
resembling the color of a frozen pear.
Or referred to as ní,
where the large teeth fall out and are replaced by fine ones, like a child's teeth.
One hundred years is called qīyí.
Yí
means nurturing.
The elderly become senile and no longer discern the taste of food,
so filial children focus solely on fulfilling their duty of care.
End.
The first is longevity,
the second is wealth, etc.,
the third is health and tranquility,
the fourth is cultivation of virtue,
the fifth is a natural death.
From the "Hóng Fàn".
Yáng Zhū said:
"People cannot rest in life,
for four reasons:
first for longevity,
second for fame,
third for position,
fourth for wealth.
Having these four things,
they fear ghosts and men,
fear authority and punishment.
These are called fugitives.
Not opposing fate,
why envy longevity?
Not priding on nobility,
why envy fame?
Not seeking power,
why envy position?
Not coveting riches,
why envy wealth?
These are called compliant people.
From "Lièzǐ"
Yáng Zhū said:
"A hundred years is the utmost limit of human longevity,
but not one in a thousand
attains it.
Suppose there is one who does:
the period of infancy and decrepit old age
takes up almost half of it;
the time spent in sleep at night
and the loss during the days of waking
take up almost half of the rest;
pain and sickness,
sorrow and toil,
and loss and fear
take up almost half of what remains.
In the dozen years or so that is left,
I reckon there is not a moment
in which one can be happy
and at ease without a thought of anxiety.
What is life for?
What pleasure is there in it?"
The Robber Zhì said:
"Man's highest age is a hundred years,
a middle age eighty,
a lower age sixty.
Excluding sickness and death,
sorrow and suffering,
the time when one can open one's mouth and laugh
is only four or five days in a month."
"Zhuāng·Dào Zhi"
Huángdì said:
"For nurturing the body,
how can one achieve longevity?"
Guǎngchéngzǐ replied:
"See nothing, hear nothing,
embrace the spirit with stillness,
and the form will naturally correct itself.
Be still, be clear.
Do not toil your form,
do not agitate your essence,
then you may attain long life.
Thus I have cultivated myself for twelve hundred years,
yet my form has never decayed."
Péng Zǔ's surname was Jiān and his given name was Kēng,
He served as a minister under Yáo and was enfeoffed in Péngchéng,
served as the Keeper of the Archives in Shěn,
and as the Pillar Historian during the Zhōu dynasty,
He lived for eight hundred years,
yet still regretted not living longer.
Using high pillows and late walking sticks, spitting far, he lost forty-nine wives,
and fifty-four children.
"Xiānzhuàn Shìběn Chǔcí Zhù" Zhuāngzǐ said:
"The Dào is self-originating and self-rooted,
existing before heaven and earth,
and has existed firmly since ancient times.
Péng Zǔ obtained it, reaching up to the time of Yǒuyú,
and down to the era of the Five Hegemons.
He also said:
"Breathing in and out,
exhaling the old and inhaling the new,
imitating bears' hanging and birds' stretching,
is done solely for longevity.
These are the practices favored by those who guide energy, nurture their forms, and long-lived individuals like Péng Zǔ.
King Wén's grandfather died at the age of one hundred and twenty,
Wáng Jì died at the age of one hundred,
and King Wén died at the age of ninety-seven.
"The Six Secret Teachings"
The Garden of Stories says: Lü Wàng was seventy years old,
fishing at the Wei River's islet.
For three days and three nights,
no fish took the bait.
Wàng grew angry,
and removed his hat and clothing.
Above him was a farmer,
an extraordinary man of antiquity.
He said to Wàng:
"You should fish again,
but make your line fine,
make your bait fragrant,
gently cast it,
do not startle the fish.
Wàng did as he was told,
first catching a crucian carp,
then a carp.
Cutting open the fish's belly, he found a document,
the text of which read:
"Lü Wàng will be enfeoffed in Qí.
Wàng knew this was extraordinary.
The Shǐ commentary records Yáo Jiǎ's reply to the King of Qín:
"Tàigōng Wàng
was a husband expelled from Qí,
a failed butcher in Zhāogē,
a minister expelled by Zǐ Liáng,
and one whose services were rejected at Jíjīn.
King Wén employed him and became sovereign.
The Qín Cè: Tàigōng was ninety before achieving glory,
truly he had not met his match before.
Sòng Yù's "Nine Arguments" The "Heavenly Questions" says: Shī Wàng was in the market,
how did Chāng recognize him?
Wielding his knife and raising his voice,
why did the sovereign rejoice?
Wáng Yì said: This means Tàigōng wielded his knife in the market,
and King Wén personally went to question him.
He replied:
"Below, I butcher cattle;
above, I butcher states.
King Wén rejoiced, took him in his carriage, and returned.
The Chǔ Cì The Huáinánzǐ says: Lü Wàng made the aged strive.
Tàigōng wielded his knife and fished,
at seventy began studying books,
at ninety became King Wén's teacher.
He assisted King Wǔ in attacking Zhòu,
and King Chéng enfeoffed him in Qí.
Gāo Yòu's commentary on the "Shuō Lín Xùn" Now, King Wén was not without flatterers and close associates,
yet he loftily raised up Tàigōng from among the boatmen and employed him,
was this due to personal favor?

But Tàigōng was seventy-two,

The Garden of Stories and Hán Shī Tàigōng Wàng
was a husband expelled by an old wife,
an assistant butcher in Zhāogē,
a retainer welcoming guests at Jíjīn,
at seventy became minister to Zhōu,
at ninety was enfeoffed in Qí.
The Garden of Stories, Chapter Eight The Dùnzhāi Xiánlǎn records: Liáng Hào, at eighty-two, achieved the top rank in the imperial examinations,
his thanksgiving memorial stated:
"Eight years younger than Fú Shēng,
two years older than Tàigōng.
No source for this is seen,
yet people all say it.
That Tàigōng met King Wén at eighty,
is this perhaps an error passed down?
However, the state history and both official and unofficial records all say Hào achieved the top rank at twenty-three, not eighty-two.
Yùzǐ,
named Xióng,
was a person from Chǔ,
at the age of ninety,
he met King Wén.
The king said:
"You are old.
Yùzǐ replied:
"If you send me to hunt beasts and chase deer,
I am indeed old;
but if you have me sit and strategize on state affairs,
I am still young.
King Wén took him as his teacher.
He authored twenty-two chapters,
titled "Yùzǐ".
"Yùzǐ" is traditionally said to have been written by Yùzǐ after meeting King Wén at over ninety,
yet it records events of the Three Supervisors and Qūfù, with chapter titles and order all confused,
unintelligible due to being a fragmented text.
The "Preface" in "Historical Records: Hereditary House of Chǔ" states: During the time of King Wén of Zhōu,
a descendant of Jìlián was named Yù Xióng.
Yù Xióng served King Wén,
but died early.
King Wǔ of Chǔ, Xióng Tōng, angrily said:
"Our ancestor Yù Xióng,
was a teacher to King Wén,
yet passed away early.
King Chéng promoted our late ancestor,
granting him the land of a viscount or baron to reside in Chǔ.
Now the book mentions "in the past."
It also says in "Lǔ Zhōu Gōng": Zhōu Gōng sent Kāng Shū to be enfeoffed in Yīn.
These are all events after King Wén's time,
making it undoubtedly a forged text,
yet no one has cited this to prove it.
King Wén died at ninety-seven,
King Wǔ passed away at ninety-three.
The Duke of Zhōu,
younger brother of King Wǔ,
differed in age from his brother by no more than ten years.
After King Wǔ's demise,
the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent for seven years,
then returned governance and retired in old age,
having reached nearly a hundred years of age.
The Duke of Shào was the elder brother of the Duke of Zhōu.
By the time of King Kāng's reign,
he still served as Grand Guardian,
being over a hundred years old.
Historical records claim the Duke of Shào lived one hundred and eighty years.
Emperor Gāozōng reigned for a century,
King Mù of Zhōu also reigned for a hundred years,
and beyond their time on the throne,
they all lived to be one hundred thirty or forty years old.
《Lùnhéng》
Zuǒshǐ Yǐxiāng went to visit Zhòng Gōngzǐ Wěi,
but Gōngzǐ Wěi refused to see him.
Zuǒshǐ then criticized him,
and Jǔ Bó reported this.
Gōngzǐ Wěi angrily came out,
saying:
"Do you also think I am old and senile and abandon me,
and then criticize me!"
Zuǒshǐ said:
"It is precisely because you are old,
that I wished to see you to mutually admonish you.
If you were in your prime,
able to manage all affairs,
Yǐxiāng would be running about attending to duties in order,
in such circumstances unable to cope,
so how would I have time to see you?
In the past, Duke Wǔ of Wèi,
though ninety-five years old,
still admonished and warned in the state,
saying: 'From the ministers down to the officials and scholars,
if any are at court,
do not say I am old and senile and abandon me,
but must be reverent and respectful at court,
morning and evening mutually cautioning me;
hearing one or two words,
must recite and remember them to present to me,
to instruct and guide me.'
Thereupon he composed the Yì Admonition to warn himself.
When he passed away,
he was called the Wise and Sage Duke Wǔ.
Now you are growing old in Chǔ and wish to be at ease yourself,
if it is always like this,
Chǔ will have difficulties indeed!"
Gōngzǐ Wěi became fearful and said:
"This is the fault of old age."
Then he frequently saw Zuǒshǐ.
"Chǔyǔ"
Lǔ Shūsūn Qiáorú and Gōngsūn Guīfù's households were both extravagant.
Liú Kānggōng told King Dìng:
"When ministers are extravagant,
the state cannot bear it,
this is the path to ruin.
If they were to die early,
it might still be tolerable, but if they live long years to accumulate their poison,
they will certainly perish.
From "Zhōu Yǔ" Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Sparrows, pheasants, fish, and turtles,
none cannot transform.
Only man cannot.
Alas!
Dòu Chǒu said:
"The noble man grieves at having no worthy men,
not at having no wealth;
he grieves at his lack of good reputation,
not at his lack of long years.
From "Jìn Yǔ"
Duke Huán visited Pínglíng,
where he saw an elderly man in a household supporting himself.
The Duke asked him the reason,
and the man replied:
"I have nine sons" (the Hánzǐ records
"three"
sons),
but my family is too poor to get them wives.
I sent them out to work as hired laborers, and they have not yet returned."
Duke Huán then took five women from his outer court and gave them as wives to the sons.
(From Shuōyuàn 5) Duke Huán traveled in disguise among the common people,
and there was a man named Lùmén Jì
who was seventy years old but had no wife.
He consulted Guǎn Zhòng about this,
who then ordered that unmarried women from the palace who had not served the Duke be sent out to marry.
(From Hánzǐ 14)
Duke Huán of Qí was chasing a white deer,
and arrived at Màiqiū,
where he saw a local elder and asked:
"Old man, how old are you?
The elder replied:
"I am eighty-three years old.
The Duke said:
"How wonderful!
Such longevity!
He then drank with him.
And said:
"Why not use your longevity to offer a blessing for me?
The local elder raised his cup and bowed twice, saying:
"I wish my lord to enjoy great longevity,
to value gold and jade lightly,
and to treasure the people.
The Duke said:
"Excellent!
Virtue never stands alone,
and good words must be spoken twice.
The elder repeated his blessing:
"I wish my lord not to be ashamed of learning nor to disdain asking those below,
so that the worthy are in office,
and remonstrators are heeded.
The Duke said:
"Excellent!
Virtue never stands alone,
and good words must be spoken thrice.
The elder repeated again:
"I wish that the officials and common people do not offend my lord,
and that my lord does not offend the officials and common people.
The Duke became angry and changed his expression,
saying:
"These words
are not like the previous two blessings.
Old man, you must change them!
The elder of Màiqiū sat, bowed, and rose,
saying:
"If a son offends his father,
he can seek forgiveness through aunts or sisters,
and the father may pardon him.
If a minister offends his lord,
he can seek forgiveness through attendants,
and the lord may pardon him.
In the past, Jié offended Tāng,
and Zhòu offended King Wǔ,
these are cases where the lord offended the ministers,
and there was no one to seek forgiveness,
so they remain unforgiven to this day.
The Duke said:
"Well said!
He helped him into the carriage,
drove it himself on the return,
honored him at court,
enfeoffed him with Màiqiū,
and consulted him on governance.
"Hán Shī Xīnxù"
Duke Xiāng of Sòng fought with the Chǔ people at Hóng,
and did not capture those with gray hair.
The Duke was wounded in the thigh. Zǐyú said:
"The strong men of today
are all our enemies.
Even if they reach old age,
if captured they should be taken.
What consideration should be given to gray hair!
(The 22nd Year of Duke Xī)
Qín and Jìn besieged Zhèng.
Yì Zhīhú said to the Duke of Zhèng:
"The state is in peril.
If you send Zhú Zhīwǔ to meet with the Duke of Qín,
the army will surely withdraw.
The duke agreed.
Zhú Zhīwǔ declined, saying:
"In my prime,
I was still inferior to others;
now that I am old,
I am incapable of accomplishing anything.
The duke persuaded him.
At night, he was lowered down the city wall by rope and went out.
He met with the Duke of Qín and said:
"The strengthening of your neighbor
means the weakening of Your Lordship.
How could Jìn ever be satisfied?
To weaken Qín for the benefit of Jìn—
I ask Your Lordship to consider this.
The Duke of Qín was pleased and made a pact with Zhèng.
"The Thirtieth Year of Duke Xī"
Lady Dowager of Jìn Dào,
provided food to those who built the wall of Qǐ.
A man from Jiàng County,
who was quite elderly,
had no sons,
and went to partake of the food.
Someone doubted his age,
and had him state his age.
He said:
"I am but a humble man,
and do not know my exact years.
In the year I was born,
the first month began on jiǎzǐ,
and it has been four hundred and forty-five jiǎzǐ cycles,
with the last cycle being one-third complete today."
The officials hurried to inquire at court,
Shī Kuàng said:
"That was the year when Lǔ's Shūzhòng Huìbó met Xì Chéngzǐ at Chéngkuāng.
It has been seventy-three years."
Shǐ Zhào said:
"Hài has two heads and six bodies,
the lower two are like the body,
this is the number of days."
《Xiāng Liù》
The Marquis of Qí was hunting in Jǔ,
when Lú Pú Piè appeared,
weeping and pleading:
"My hair has grown so sparse,
what can I accomplish now?"
Zǐ Yǎ said:
"Though his hair is short, his mind is exceedingly long;
perhaps he means to make us his bed and mat."
In the ninth month,
Lú Pú Piè was banished to Northern Yān.
《Zhāo 3》
Jìn Pínggōng asked Shī Kuàng, saying:
"I am seventy years old and wish to study,
but fear it is already too late."
Shī Kuàng replied:
"Why not light a torch?"
Pínggōng thought he was mocking his lord.
Shī Kuàng said:
"Your servant has heard that studying when young
is like the morning sun's radiance;
studying in prime adulthood
is like the midday sun's brilliance;
studying when old
is like the illumination of a torch.
The illumination of a torch—
how does it compare to stumbling in the dark?"
Pínggōng said:
"Excellent indeed!"
From "Shuō Yuàn"
In the state of Lǔ there was a reverent scholar,
named Jī Fàn,
who was seventy years old,
and his reverence grew even more profound.
In winter he walked in the shade,
in summer he walked under the sun,
he dared not fail to walk in the market queue,
when walking in a group he always followed,
and when sitting he remained upright.
During a single meal,
he would rise three times without feeling ashamed,
and upon seeing someone dressed in coarse garments, he would bow in respect.
The ruler of Lǔ asked him:
"Master Jī, you are very advanced in years,
is it not possible to relax your reverence?"
Jī Fàn replied:
"A gentleman loves reverence to establish his reputation,
a commoner learns reverence to avoid punishment.
Sitting before Your Majesty,
is it not secure?
Yet there can still be missteps.
At a single meal,
is it not delightful?
Yet there can still be choking.
Now someone like me is considered fortunate,
but I truly cannot be certain of myself.
When swans soar into the sky,
is it not high?
Yet arrows with strings can still reach them.
Tigers and leopards are fierce,
yet people still eat their flesh and use their skins as mats;
those who praise others are few,
those who dislike others are many.
At seventy years of age,
I constantly fear that the executioner's axe may fall upon me—
why should I relax my reverence?"
《Shuō Yuàn》
Chéng Huí studied under Zǐlù for three years,
and Huí remained reverent without cease.
Zǐlù asked him what the reason for this was.
Huí replied:
"I have heard it said
that the traveler is like a bird:
above, it fears the falcons and hawks;
below, it fears the nets and snares.
Among men, those who do good are few,
while those who slander are many.
If one does not die,
how can one know that misfortune and punishment will not befall?
Having lived to seventy years of age,
I constantly fear failing in my conduct and integrity.
Therefore, I, Huí, remain reverent while awaiting my great destiny.
Zǐlù bowed his head to the ground and said:
"A true gentleman indeed!
Nánbó Zǐkuí asked Nǚyǔ, saying:
"You are advanced in years,
yet your complexion is like that of a child.
He replied:
"I have heard the Way.
Zhuāngzǐ
King Xuān of Qí went hunting at Shè Mountain,
where thirteen village elders came together to greet the king.
The king granted them tax-exempt land.
All the elders bowed in gratitude,
except for Lǘqiū Xiānshēng who alone did not bow.
When the king further exempted them from corvée labor,
the other elders bowed again,
yet Lǘqiū Xiānshēng still refused to bow.
The king, puzzled, asked him why.
He replied:
"I came to see Your Majesty
hoping for three things: I wish you would grant me longevity,
grant me wealth,
and grant me honor.
The king said:
"The Mandate of Heaven determines lifespan,
which is beyond my control—
I cannot grant you longevity;
though the granaries are full,
they are reserved for disasters—
I cannot make you wealthy;
high offices have no vacancies,
while minor posts are lowly—
I cannot honor you.
Lǘqiū Xiānshēng said:
"My hope is that the king would appoint good officials,
so I may gain longevity;
employ the people according to the agricultural seasons,
without burdensome corvée—
this is how I would become wealthy;
have the young respect their elders,
and elders honor the aged—
this is how I would gain honor.
If the king grants me tax-free land,
the granaries will be depleted;
if exempted from labor,
officials will have no one to command—
this is not what I desire.
The king said:
"Shall I appoint you as chancellor?"
Lǘqiū Xiānshēng replied:
"Having my three wishes fulfilled is enough for me—
why would I need to be chancellor?"
From "Shuō Yuàn"; the "Imperial Readings" version differs slightly.
Mr. Chǔqiū, at the age of seventy,
wearing a fur coat and a rope belt,
went to see Lord Mèngcháng.
Wanting to hurry forward, he could not advance.
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"Sir, you are old,
your years are advanced,
and you are very forgetful.
What could you possibly teach Wén?"
Mr. Chǔqiū replied:
"Alas!
Do you think I am old?
Alas!
Would you have me chase carriages and run after horses?
Hurl stones and leap over barriers?
Pursue deer and wrestle with leopards and tigers?
If so, I would already be dead—
what leisure would I have to be old?
Alas!
But if you would have me plan deeply and strategize far ahead,
resolve doubts and decide uncertainties,
or speak forthright words and confront the feudal lords—
then I am just in my prime,
how can I be considered old!"
Lord Mèngcháng blushed with shame,
sweating profusely down to his heels,
and said:
"Wén was wrong!
Wén was wrong!"
The Book of Songs says:
"The old man is earnest,
the young man is proud."
This means the old man wishes to offer all his counsel,
but the youth is arrogant and will not accept it.
This is why Duke Mù of Qín was defeated in battle,
and why King Zhòu of Shāng lost the empire.
Therefore, the Documents say:
"The words of the yellow-haired elders
are without fault."
The Book of Songs also says:
"Longevity is granted to be tested."
This praises the use of the elders' words to bring peace to the state.
(Hánshī Xīnxù)
Lián Pō fled to Wèi,
the King of Zhào longed to regain Lián Pō's service,
and sent an envoy to see if Pō was still fit for duty.
Pō's enemy Guō Kāi bribed the envoy heavily with gold,
ordering him to slander Pō.
When the Zhào envoy met Lián Pō,
Pō consumed a dou of rice in one meal,
ten catties of meat,
donned his armor and mounted his horse,
to demonstrate he was still capable.
The Zhào envoy returned and reported to the king:
"General Lián, though aged,
still eats heartily,
but while I sat with him,
he relieved himself three times in a short while."
The King of Zhào deemed him too old,
and thus did not summon him back.
(Basic Biography)
Zhāng Cāng was tall, large, stout, and as white as a calabash,
and served as chancellor for fifteen years before being dismissed.
After being removed from the chancellorship,
he grew old,
had no teeth in his mouth,
and drank milk,
with women serving as wet nurses.
His wives and concubines numbered in the hundreds,
and he no longer favored those who had once been pregnant.
Zhāng Cāng lived to be over a hundred years old before he died.
From Shǐjì.
During Emperor Wén's reign,
they found a musician named Dòu Gōng from Lord Wèi Wén's era,
who was one hundred and eighty years old,
with both eyes blind.
Emperor Wén found him extraordinary,
and asked:
"What practices have you followed to reach such an age?"
He replied:
"I lost my sight at the age of thirteen,
and my parents pitied me,
teaching me to play the qin,
making daily practice a regular routine.
I cannot claim any special methods,
so there is nothing I have taken or avoided.
I believe that losing sight young,
and maintaining constant ease and joy,
is what has prolonged my life.
From the Xīn Lùn"
Fú Shēng,
a native of Jìnán,
was formerly a Bóshì (Erudite) of the Qín dynasty.
During the reign of Emperor Wén, it was heard that he was able to teach the *Shàng Shū*,
and the emperor wished to summon him.
At that time, Fú Shēng was over ninety years old,
too elderly to travel,
so Cháo Cuò was sent to receive instruction from him.
*Hàn Shū*: With the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
schools were established,
and scholars of refinement were sought far and wide,
to elucidate the great principles.
Fú Shēng of Jìnán,
being over ninety years old,
had lost his original classic,
and transmitted it orally.
*Shàng Shū* Preface: Fú Shēng, being old, could not speak clearly,
and his words were incomprehensible,
so he had his daughter relay his teachings to Cuò.
The speech of the people of Qí differed greatly from that of Yǐngchuān,
and there were about two or three out of ten parts that Cuò did not understand,
so he roughly interpreted the meaning and read it as best he could.
*Wèi Hóng Gǔwén Shàng Shū Xù*
Shēngōng was from Lǔ and in his youth studied under Fúqiū Bó of Qí,
learning the Book of Songs.
When Emperor Wǔ first ascended the throne,
he sent envoys with bolts of silk and a jade disc, using a comfortable carriage with wheels padded with rushes and drawn by four horses to welcome Shēngōng,
with two disciples following in light carriages.
Upon arrival,
he had an audience with the emperor,
who asked about matters of governance and chaos.
Shēngōng, then over eighty years old, replied:
"Those who govern need not speak much,
but should focus on how diligently they put things into practice."
At that time, the emperor particularly favored literary rhetoric,
and upon hearing Shēngōng's response,
fell silent.
Book of Hàn
Yuángù,
a man from Qí,
was skilled in the Book of Songs,
and served as a scholar during Emperor Xiàojǐng's reign.
When Emperor Wǔ first ascended the throne,
he was again summoned for his virtue and intellect.
Many among the scholars envied him and
slandered him,
saying,
"Gù is old."
He was dismissed and returned home.
At that time, Gù was already over ninety years old,
yet Gōngsūn Hóng was also summoned,
and he respectfully served Gù.
Gù said:
"Gōngsūn,
strive for proper learning and speak truthfully,
do not twist scholarship to pander to the world!"
The emperor
The emperor once rode his carriage to the Lang official quarters,
where he saw an old man with white beard and hair,
his clothes worn and incomplete.
The emperor asked him:
"When did you become a Lang official?
Why are you so old?"
He replied:
"Your subject's surname is Yán, given name Sì,
from Jiāngdū.
I became a Lang official during Emperor Wén's reign."
The emperor asked:
"Why have you never been favored?"
Yán Sì said:
"Emperor Wén favored literary talents while I excelled in martial arts;
Emperor Jǐng favored older officials while I was still young;
Your Majesty favors young officials while I have grown old.
Thus I remained unrecognized through three reigns."
The emperor was moved by his words,
and appointed him as the Commandant of Kuàijī.
"Tales of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn"
Dōngfāng Shuò in the Yuánfēng era,
wandered through the marsh of Hóngméng,
when he suddenly encountered an old woman picking mulberries on the shores of the White Sea.
Soon, a yellow-robed elder pointed at the woman and said to Shuò:
"She was once my wife,
who took form from the essence of the Great White Star.
Now you too are of this essence.
I have refrained from eating and swallowed qi,
for over nine thousand years.
The pupils of my eyes
all emit a blue light,
enabling me to see hidden and obscure things.
Once every three thousand years, I return to wash my bones and marrow;
once every three thousand years, I shed my skin and replace my fur.
Since my birth, I have already washed my marrow three times,
and replaced my fur once.
Shí Jiàn served as the Commandant of the Palace Guard.
Jiàn had white hair,
yet his father, Wàn Shí Jūn, was still in good health.
Every five days, when he returned home on his day off to visit his father,
he would enter the side room,
secretly inquire of the attendants,
take his father's undergarments and chamber pot,
and personally wash them.
He would then return them to the attendants,
not daring to let Wàn Shí Jūn know about it.
This became his regular practice.
《Book of Hàn》
Liú Shàng attacked the Wǔxī barbarians in Wǔlíng,
advancing deep into their territory,
but his army was annihilated,
so Mǎ Yuán again requested to lead a campaign.
At that time he was sixty-two years old,
and the emperor, pitying his age,
did not grant permission.
Yuán personally pleaded,
"I can still don armor and mount a horse."
The emperor ordered him to demonstrate.
Yuán sat in the saddle and looked around with a spirited gaze,
to show he was fit for service.
The emperor laughed and said,
"How vigorous
is this old man!"
Thus, Yuán was dispatched.
From the Later Biography and the Dōngguān Records: "How valiant
is this old man!" The dictionary explains 㬦 as having a brave appearance.
Xiàng Lǎng,
courtesy name Jùdá,
in his youth dabbled in literature,
and was noted for his administrative abilities.
After leaving the post of Chief Clerk,

He then delved deeper into classical texts,
diligently and tirelessly.
Even after surpassing eighty years of age,

correcting errors,
and amassing volumes of writings,
which were the most abundant at that time.
He kept his door open to receive guests,
mentoring and supporting the younger generation,
discussing only ancient principles,

Chén Shòu took leave of Qiáo Zhōu, who said:

I fear that before another year passes,

It is suspected that Qiáo Zhōu knew this through some art of divination,
and spoke thus under that pretext.
From "Records of Shu".
Tián Yù served as the Inspector of Bìng Province,

Hú Zhāo,

The imperial decree is earnest,

An imperial decree granted him a cane and exempted him from court attendance.
A little over a year later, he passed away,

Liú Yì,
courtesy name Zhòngxióng,

Liáng Xiāoyìng,
served as the governor of Běi Xúzhōu.

a man from Zhōnglí named Gù Zhōngyuǎn, despite his advanced age, joined the military ranks out of a sense of duty.
Liáng Xiāoyìng noticed his remarkable condition,
and sent someone to inquire about him.
Gù Zhōngyuǎn replied:
"I am one hundred and twelve years old.
I have married seven times,
and had twelve sons,
but nearly all have passed away.
Now, only the youngest remains,
who is already sixty.
I have no grandsons or descendants,
and my family lacks support and resources,
which is why I have enlisted for service."
Liáng Xiāoyìng was greatly astonished by this,
summoned him and provided him with food,
and he ate more than an ordinary person.
Upon examination, a fleshy horn an inch long was found on his head.
Liáng Xiāoyìng then ordered him to be transported back to the capital on a following boat,
to have an audience with the emperor.
When the emperor spoke with him about past events,
many differed from common accounts.
He was promoted to the position of a cavalier attendant-in-ordinary,
granted an official salary and residence,
and had frequent audiences morning and evening.
He passed away at the age of one hundred and twenty.

His elder brother Xún Yǔ challenged him:
"The Book of Changes says: 'The sage established images to fully express ideas,

Càn replied:
"The most subtle principles
cannot be conveyed through material images.
Now you speak of establishing images to fully express ideas -
this does not communicate what lies beyond ideas.
Appending judgments to fully express words -
this does not speak of what lies beyond the appended words;
thus the meaning beyond images,
the words beyond the judgments,

yet the depletion continued as before.
Later, an old guest came from afar,
arriving at the lane entrance,
and saw several people carrying loads out from the gate.

The guest said,
"I just encountered people carrying grain out,

The brothers looked at each other,
secretly suspicious and perplexed.
Upon checking the labeled containers,
they appeared exactly as before.

and there was not even a single hú left.

were not caused by human actions.

King Xuān of Qí met Yǎn Chù and said:
"I wish for you, sir, to accompany me in my travels.
You shall dine on the finest meats,
travel by carriage when you go out,
and your wife and children shall be dressed in elegant clothes."
Yǎn Chù declined and departed, saying:
"Jade is born in the mountains,
but when carved, it is damaged.
Not that it isn't precious,
but the original simplicity is lost.
I was born in the rural wilds,
and if recommended for office, I would receive an official salary.
Not that it isn't honorable and successful,
but then my body and spirit would be incomplete.
I prefer to return home,
where eating late is as good as meat,
walking leisurely is as good as a carriage,
being without guilt is as good as nobility,
and living in purity and integrity brings me joy."
So he declined and left.
The gentleman remarks:
"Chù knew contentment.
Returning to his humble origins and recovering his simplicity,
he remained free from disgrace all his life."

tomorrow I will have teams of four horses and rows of riders, with a feast spread before me covering ten square feet.

His wife said:

finds joy within himself.
Teams of four horses and rows of riders
bring no more comfort than enough space for your knees;
a feast spread before you covering ten square feet
offers no more pleasure than a single meat dish.
Now for the comfort of knee-room and the taste of a single meat dish,
you would bear the worries of the entire state of Chǔ.
In these chaotic times, dangers abound -
I fear you would not preserve your life, sir!"
Thereupon he went out,
declined the envoy's offer,
and together they fled away,
working for others watering gardens.

pure as ice and jade,

Jùn replied:
"A gentleman acts according to his capabilities,

thus keeping regret and shame far from himself.

nor fame obtained improperly.

the way of emperors and kings has become manifest,
the capable see opportunities,
while the unworthy remove themselves -

From then on, each followed his desired path.

Yáng Xióng, in his writings discussing the scholars of his time,
praised these two men,
and his argument went:
"Someone asked: 'A gentleman fears leaving the world without his name being known;
why not grasp the opportunities among the famous ministers,
so that one may come close [to fame].'
He replied: 'A gentleman considers virtue and reputation as coming close [to the ideal].
The rulers of Liáng, Qí, Chǔ, and Zhào were not without wealth and honor,
yet how did they achieve their fame?
Zhèng Zǐzhēn of Gǔkǒu,
did not bend his will,
but farmed beneath the rocky cliffs,
and his fame shook the capital—
how could he be compared to those ministers!
How could he be compared to those ministers!
The purity of the two Gǒngs of Chǔ—
was it not indeed pristine!
Yán of Shǔ, profound and obscure,
did not engage in superficial displays,
did not pursue improper gains,
remaining long in obscurity without changing his principles—
even the jades of Suí and Hé, how could they surpass him?
Lifting him up as an example,
is this not indeed substantial!
Not coveting [the fame of] Yóu or the reclusiveness of Yí,
what desire for cunning could there be?'"
Yáng inquired about the earlier "Hànshū": In Shǔ, there was a wealthy man named Luó Chōng who asked Jūnpíng:
"Why do you not take office?"
Jūnpíng replied:
"I have nothing with which to initiate myself."
Chōng then provided Jūnpíng with carriages, horses, clothing, and provisions,
but Jūnpíng said:
"I am afflicted [by such things],
not lacking.
I have a surplus,
while you are in want;
how can one in want offer support to one with a surplus?"
Chōng said:
"I possess ten thousand in gold,
while you do not have even a dàn or shí [a small measure],
yet you claim to have a surplus—
is this not absurd?"
Jūnpíng replied:
"Not so.
I previously lodged at your home,
and when others were settled, your labors had not ceased;
day and night, you were anxious and never satisfied.
Now, I make divination my profession;
without leaving my bed, money comes to me,
and I still have hundreds left over,
with dust accumulating inches thick,
not knowing what to use it for—
is this not me having a surplus and you being in want?"
Chōng was greatly ashamed.
Jūnpíng sighed and said:
"To increase my goods is to harm my spirit;
to give me fame is to kill my body."
He ultimately did not take office.

Emperor Wǔ of Liáng initially summoned Hé Yìn to serve as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,

Gǎozhī first arrived at Hé Yìn's residence,

When Gǎozhī returned from Xiè Fěi's place,

In response to the summons,

Gǎozhī turned pale,

Lǐ Mì,
courtesy name Yǒnghé,

He repeatedly declined official appointments,

He built his dwelling nestled against cliffs,

Devoted to learning and upholding principles,

He often said:
"A true man possessing ten thousand volumes of books
has no need for ruling over a hundred cities."
Thereupon, he withdrew from society and secluded himself behind curtains,
closing his doors and refusing visitors.
He sold his property to acquire books,

Through harsh winters until dawn,

even the dedication of Dǒng Zhòngshū who never glanced at his garden,
Jūn Bó who shut his doors,
Gāo Shì who maintained purity,
or Zhāng Shēng who forgot to eat,
would not be considered extraordinary in comparison.
Yet blessings for the virtuous remained unheard,
and he died suddenly from a violent illness at thirty-two.
He was posthumously honored as the True and Serene Recluse by imperial decree.

Biǎn Què said:
"When the illness is in the texture of the skin and muscles,
hot compresses can reach it;
when in the flesh and skin,
acupuncture and stone needles can reach it;
when in the intestines and stomach,
fire potions can reach it;
when in the bone marrow,
it falls under the jurisdiction of the Director of Fate,

Now it is in the bone marrow,
therefore I make no request.
After five days,
Marquis Huán experienced body pain,
sent someone to search for Biǎn Què,

Marquis Huán then died.
Thus, when a good physician treats illness,
he attacks it at the texture of the skin and muscles,
these are all struggles at the minor stage.
The calamity or fortune of events,
also has a stage like the texture of the skin and muscles,

Hán Feizi's "Explaining the Lǎo Zǐ"
When the ancient Biǎn Què treated illnesses,
he pierced bones with a blade.
When sages rescued endangered states,
they offered loyal words that grated on the ears.
Piercing bones,
thus causes minor pain to the body,
but lasting benefits to the person.
Words grating on the ears,
thus cause slight discomfort to the heart,
but enduring fortune to the state.
Therefore, for gravely ill persons,
the benefit lies in enduring pain.
For fiercely resolute rulers,
fortune lies in heeding unpleasant advice.
Enduring pain,
thus enables Biǎn Què to fully apply his skill.
Heeding unpleasant advice,
then enables figures like Wǔ Zǐxū to preserve the methods for longevity and stability.
If ill yet unable to endure pain,
one loses Biǎn Què's skill;
if endangered yet unwilling to heed unpleasant advice,
one loses the sages' intent.
In such cases, lasting benefits will not long endure,
and achievements and fame will not long stand.

but it is mixed with other ingredients;
the primary and secondary components counteract each other,
diminishing the efficacy,

I believe this is the reason.

cannot be put into words;
creating prescriptions arbitrarily

Yú Shǎoqīng was a renowned physician from the upper reaches of the Shu region.

Grand Marshal Dǒng Zhāng had long suffered from a thirst ailment,
and sent for a physician.
The Later Shu court dispatched Yú Shǎoqīng to attend to him.
Marshal Dǒng said:
"This illness of mine,
has been treated by hundreds of famous doctors without any sign of improvement,
why is this?"
Yú Shǎoqīng replied:
"Your ailment,
is not merely a thirst for drink,
but resembles a thirst for talented men.
If you obtain many capable men,
you will recover without needing medicinal remedies."
Marshal Dǒng was greatly pleased.
At that time, Marshal Dǒng harbored ambitions to rule,
so Yú Shǎoqīng intentionally criticized him through this remark.
He further said:
"I have heard that heaven has six qi,
which descend as six excesses.
Excess gives rise to six ailments,
which attack the six bowels.
The six qi are:
yin, yang, wind, rain, darkness, and brightness,
thus the six yin follow them;
the six ailments are:
chill, fever, extremities, abdomen, confusion, and heart,
thus the six bowels correspond to them.
Therefore the spleen serves as the li palace,
the kidneys as the water organ,
excessive labor in darkness and brightness,
gives rise to hundreds of ailments.
Moreover, excessive seeing and hearing,
all cause damage.
When the mind is overburdened, it becomes disordered;
when affairs are overburdened, they change;
when opportunities are overburdened, they are lost;
when troops are overburdened, they rebel;
when the five sounds are excessive, they damage the ears;
when the five colors are excessive, they damage the eyes;
when flavors are excessive, they generate illness;
when sexual relations are excessive, they shorten lifespan.
The men of ancient times,
all guarded against these.
You, sir, today have ten thousand thoughts,
constantly face ten thousand matters,
indulge excessively in pleasures externally,
and indulge excessively with women internally,
the difficulty in curing your thirst,
surely stems from this."
After Marshal Dǒng's illness was cured,
he sent Yú Shǎoqīng back with generous gifts.

A physician must be
benevolent and loving to be entrusted,
wise and discerning to be appointed,
incorruptible and sincere to be trusted.
Thus, in ancient times when selecting physicians,
they necessarily chose those from renowned families.
Their character must be humane, tolerant, and broadly compassionate,
their wisdom capable of elucidating complexities and resolving intricacies,
able to understand the order of heaven, earth, and spirits,
able to comprehend the principles of life, fate, fortune, and misfortune,
distinguishing between deficiency and excess,
determining the patterns of adverse and favorable conditions,
assessing the severity of illnesses and injuries,
and measuring the appropriate dosage of medicines,
penetrating the subtle and reaching the profound,
overlooking no minute detail—
only such a person may be called a skilled physician.
Moreover, Daoists favor cold,
using herbs that grow in cold;
physicians favor warmth,
as blood vessels are unblocked by warmth.
If one only grasps the general principles
without understanding the detailed rationale,
unaware that firmness and softness have their respective weights,
seasonal influences vary in degree,
and progression, regression, expansion, and contraction follow rhythmic patterns,
then a renowned physician skilled in pulse diagnosis
seeks answers within the three positions of the cunkou pulse,
and thereby attains understanding.
Assessing seasonal influences to gauge warmth and cold,
correlating pulse theory with the balance of weights,
and measuring medications to achieve harmony—
this may be called a renowned physician.
There are physicians with fame who are unskilled,
and those without fame who are skilled.
When a ruler employs physicians,
they must thoroughly investigate and evaluate them.

Yán Jūnpíng practiced divination in Chéngdū City,
considering divination a lowly trade,
yet one that could benefit the masses.
When faced with queries about wicked or improper matters,
he would use yarrow stalks and tortoise shells to speak of advantages and harms.
To sons, he spoke based on filial piety;
to younger brothers, he spoke based on obedience;
to subjects, he spoke based on loyalty,
guiding each according to their duties toward goodness.
Those who followed his words
already constituted more than half.
Limiting himself to seeing a few people daily,
he earned a hundred coins sufficient for self-sustenance,
then closed his shop and lowered the curtain,
to teach the "Lǎozǐ."
Widely read and omniscient,
following the tenets of Lǎozǐ and Zhuāng Zhōu,
he authored over a hundred thousand words.
The "Hànshū" sage,
traced upward to the intent of the Dào and virtue,
measured downward the heart of heaven and earth.
Lofty and illustrious,
auspicious and virtuous,
profound and vast,
honored and esteemed to the utmost,
nothing is greater than life.
All things displayed,
strange and precious treasures,
gold, jade, pearls, and jade discs,
with deep profits and great gains,
nothing is greater than the self.
Craftsmen of calamity for the age,
artisans of chaos for the state,
cutting off benefits from heaven and earth,
harming one's own self,
nothing is greater than fame.
Life elevated and overflowing,
impoverishing the people and the state,
disturbing and muddying the spirit,
causing the heart to be full of desires,
rebelling against heaven and defying the Dào,
competing to become thieves and robbers,
the world lacking intimacy,
the age filled with weapons and armor,
nothing is greater than wealth.
Thus, gain and loss,
some harmful, some beneficial:
gaining fame and wealth,
the Dào and virtue do not reside,
divine spirits do not remain,
the great mandate is severed,
heaven cannot save.
Losing fame and wealth,
the Dào and virtue provide protection,
divine spirits offer aid,
bright and evident naturally,
richness matching heaven and earth.
Therefore, those who belittle the self and exalt fame
cannot be discussed with regarding the ultimate Dào;
those who neglect the self and prioritize the state
cannot be collaborated with in seeking benefits.

welcomed her from his private residence,

but after three evenings,
no rain fell.

"This land's calamity

and Guō abruptly demanded her horse to return to the prefectural residence.

"Mediocre petty official,

Wéiqiān replied:
"Tomorrow I will arrange to see you off.

as Guō prepared to leave,

Behind the temple was an extremely high mountain;

This shows heaven's heart still recognizes utmost sincerity,

We specially bestow the crimson绶,

Do not tarnish this renowned name,

Scholar Lǐ came to pay his respects.

Virtue and laws
are the means to govern the people,
just as bridle and reins are used to control a horse.
The ruler
is the person,
the officials
are the reins,
punishments
are the whip.
In the ruler's governance,
he merely holds the reins and whip.
A skilled driver adjusts the bridle properly,
balances the reins and whip,
equalizes the horses' strength,
and harmonizes their hearts.
Thus without uttering a sound, the horses respond to the reins;
without raising the whip, they cover a thousand miles.
If one discards the bridle and relies solely on the whip,
it is certain
that control will be lost.
Using the whip without bridle
will surely injure the horses
and wreck the carriage.
Therefore it is said: one who drives four horses holds six reins;
one who governs the world rectifies the six ministries.
Thus a skilled driver corrects himself to grasp the reins,
equalizes the horses' strength,
harmonizes their hearts,
turning and winding
as he directs them.
Thus he can undertake long journeys
and respond to urgent needs.
These are the principles by which the sage governs the world and human affairs."
From "Family Sayings of Confucius"
Wángzǐ Yúqī was competing in a thousand-mile race for the Sòng monarch.
The carriage was already harnessed,
and he inspected his hands and the patterns on the reins.
Just as they were about to set off,
he drove the horses forward,
but the wheels strained against the traces;
when he pulled them back,
the horses obscured their own tracks.
He patted them to start,
and the horses bolted out through a narrow gate.
When the horses retreated and held back,
the whip could not make them advance;
when the horses ran wild,
the reins could not steer them straight.
