Duke Dìng of Lǔ asked Yán Huí:
"Have you also heard of Dōngyě Bì's skill in driving chariots?"
He replied:
"I have heard of his skill,
however,
his horses will surely bolt.
Duke Dìng looked displeased,
and Yán Huí withdrew.
Three days later, someone came to report:
"Dōngyě Bì's horses have bolted,
with the two outer horses dragging the two inner horses back into the stable.
When the duke heard this,
he hastened to summon Yán Huí,
and asked:
"How did you know that Bì's horses would bolt?"
He replied:
"I knew it from the principles of governance.
In ancient times, Emperor Shùn was skilled in employing the people,
while Zàofǔ was skilled in employing horses.
Shùn did not exhaust the people's strength,
nor did Zàofǔ exhaust the horses' strength.
Therefore, Shùn had no fugitive people,
and Zàofǔ had no runaway horses.
Now, as for Dōngyě Bì's driving,
he mounts the chariot and takes the reins,
the bits and harness are properly adjusted,
he trots and gallops,
completing all the courtly rituals,
traverses dangers and goes long distances,
until the horses' strength is exhausted.
Yet he still incessantly demands more from the horses.
It is through this that I knew.
The duke said:
"Excellent!
It is truly as you have said.
The above is similar to the Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn, while Xúnzǐ says the question was asked to Yán Hé,

Kǒngzǐ yuē:

《Kǒngzǐ》
King Xiāng of Zhào learned charioteering from Wángzǐqī,
and soon raced against Yǔqī,
changing horses three times but falling behind three times.
King Xiāng said:
"When you taught me charioteering,
did you not fully impart the technique?
He replied:
"The technique has been fully imparted,
but in applying it, you make errors.
The essence of skilled charioteering lies in
the horses being comfortable with the chariot,
and the driver's mind harmonizing with the horses,
only then can one advance swiftly and cover long distances.
Now when you fall behind, you desire to catch up with me,
and when ahead, you fear being caught by me.
In guiding the way and contending over distance,
one is either ahead or behind,
yet your mind focused on my position,
how can you then harmonize with the horses?
This is the reason you fall behind.

Yǐn Rú was learning charioteering,
but after three years had achieved nothing.
He privately felt distressed and pained,
often lying awake thinking about it.
In the middle of the night, he dreamed of receiving the "Autumn Drive" technique from his master.
The next day, he went to pay his respects,

Huáinánzǐ
When Qiějū and Dàbǐng drove their chariots,
they removed the reins and bits,
discarded the whip and abandoned the crop,
yet the chariot needed no moving to rise of itself,
and the horses needed no driving to run on their own.
They traveled with the sun's course and moved with the moon,
stars shone as they moved mysteriously,
like lightning dashing and ghosts soaring.
Thus without beckoning gestures,
without shouts or reprimands,
they galloped as if flying,
raced as if transcending limits,
arrows treading on wind,
chasing lightning back to its source,
setting out at dawn from Fúsāng,
arriving at sunset in Luòtáng.
This demonstrates how by forgoing conventional means one can achieve their function.
Now Qiějū and Dàbǐng,
without applying reins or bits, became known throughout the world for their superb charioteering.
Fúxì and Nǚwā,
without establishing laws or regulations, left their supreme virtue to later generations.
Why is this?
Because they embodied ultimate emptiness and pure unity,
unfettered by trivial and harsh affairs.
Long ago, when Féng Yí
and Dà Bǐng drove their chariots,
they rode cloud-borne carriages,
entered rainbow mists,
wandered through fine vapors,
galloped into fathomless obscurity,
traversing vast distances and scaling great heights to reach the ultimate realms.
They charted the courses of mountains and rivers,
leapt across and soared over Kūnlún,
pushed open the gates of heaven,
and passed through the celestial portal.
Drivers of the decadent age,
even with lightweight carriages and fine steeds,
powerful whips and sharp goads,
could not compete with them for the lead.
Therefore, the great man
takes heaven as his canopy,
earth as his carriage,
the four seasons as his horses,
and yin and yang as his drivers,
riding clouds and soaring above the firmament.
He gives free rein to his will and relaxes his pace,
galloping across the great expanse.
He commands the Master of Rain to sprinkle his path,
and bids the Earl of Wind to sweep away the dust;
he uses lightning as his whip,
and thunder as his carriage wheels.
Above, he roams the wilds of layered heavens,
below, he emerges from the gate of the boundless;
his gaze sweeps across and illuminates all,
preserving completeness through his guardianship.
"Explaining the Dao"
As for horses,
when a skilled driver handles them,
they become gentle, obedient, and well-behaved,
capable of traveling long distances;
when a servant handles them,
they become sluggish, run wildly, and destroy the carriage.
The people,
are comparable to horses.
When Yáo and Shùn governed them,
the world became orderly and upright;
when Jié and Zhòu governed them,
the world fled to Lìshān.

As for driving,
when the horse's body is in harmony with the carriage,
and the driver's mind is in harmony with the horse,

advancing, retreating, and maneuvering,
all will be as desired.
Even with famous horses like Qíjì and Lù'ěr,
if Wū Huò were to drive them,
the horses would become self-willed instead,
and the person would not be in control.

*Records of the Grand Historian*
In ancient times there was Gūbù Zǐqīng,
and today in Liáng there is Táng Jǔ,
who examine people's physical form and complexion
to know their fortune or misfortune, and inauspicious or auspicious signs,
which is praised by the common people.
The ancients had no such practice,
and scholars do not speak of it.
Therefore, to judge by appearance without considering the heart,
is not as good as evaluating the heart, which is not as good as selecting the right method.
Appearance cannot overcome the heart,
and the heart cannot overcome method.
If the method is correct and the heart follows it,
then even if the appearance is ugly but the heart and method are good,
it does not prevent one from being a gentleman;
even if the appearance is handsome but the heart and method are evil,
it does not prevent one from being a petty person.
Thus, tall or short, large or small, and handsome or ugly are merely matters of appearance,
not determinants of fortune or misfortune.
For instance, Yáo was tall,
while Emperor Shùn was short;
King Wén was tall,
while the Duke of Zhōu was short;
Zhòngní was tall,
while Zǐgōng was short.
Sūnshū Áo of Chǔ,
with a bald head and a longer left side,
standing beneath the carriage rail,
enabled Chǔ to achieve hegemony;
while the Duke of Shè, Zǐgāo,
was small, short, and thin,
and seemed as if his clothes would overwhelm him when he walked.
During the rebellion of Báigōng,
he entered and secured Chǔ,
executed Báigōng,
stabilized the state of Chǔ,
as easily as turning over his hand.
Can height, size, and beauty or ugliness of appearance
really be criteria for judgment?
Moreover, the appearance of King Xúyǎn
allowed his eyes to see his own forehead;
the appearance of Zhòngní
was like wearing a fierce mask;
the appearance of the Duke of Zhōu
was like a withered stump;
the appearance of Gāoyáo
had a complexion like a peeled melon;
the appearance of Hóngyāo
had a face so hairy that no skin was visible;
the appearance of Fùyuè
was like a standing fish fin;
the appearance of Yīyǐn
had a face without beard or eyebrows;
Yǔ limped,
Tāng was lopsided,
and Yáo and Shùn had double pupils.
Should followers judge aspirations and ambitions,
comparing them to literature and learning?
Or merely differentiate between tall and short,
distinguish beautiful and ugly,
to deceive and boast of each other?

was a native of Rǔnán,
renowned in his hometown for his talent and skill,
and was nicknamed
"Ocean of Wisdom."
He particularly excelled in painting.
Though he had no ancestral tradition to follow,
he was not inferior to earlier masters.
His refined character and reputation among the elite
made those who saw his works sigh in admiration.
He was equally famous as Zhǎn Zǐqián.
He created "Illustrations of the Daoist Scriptures,"
which was praised by contemporaries.
Unless it stemmed from his innate nature,
communing with the spiritual and grasping the subtle,
entering the land of Huáxū,
and wandering with the transformed beings,
how could he have achieved this?
Shàng Qīng Sìzhēn remarked:
"Dǒng and Zhǎn are of equal rank,
Dǒng possesses Zhǎn's skill in painting chariots and horses,
but Zhǎn lacks Dǒng's talent for towers and pavilions."

I once saw one of his paintings,

It was not recorded in the "Míng Huà Lù" or historical texts,

The next day he went once more,

Wú Dàoyuán saw them,

Táng dynasty Wáng Yòuchéng Wéi resided at Lántián's Yùshān,
traveling and dwelling at Wǎngchuān.
He and his brothers topped their contemporaries in imperial examinations and literary accomplishments.
Hence it was said at the time: "The Left Minister's brush at court,
the world's Wáng Yòuchéng's poetry."
His paintings of landscapes, pines, and rocks,
though traces seemed merely alive,
possessed uniquely outstanding style.
Now at the Western Pagoda Courtyard of Jīngdū's Shífú Temple there are screen paintings,
one depicting maple trees and watchtowers,
one portraying Wǎngchuān.
Mountains and valleys densely winding,
clouds and waters dynamically flying,
conception transcending worldly dust,
marvels born from the brush tip.
He once inscribed a poem himself:
"By mistake a poet in past life,
my previous incarnation should have been a painter."
At the Eastern Courtyard of Cí'ēn Temple,

Thus at Former Vice Director Yǔ's residence,

From "Huà Duàn": Wáng Wéi once visited Yǔ Jìngtǐ's residence at Zhāoguó ward,

Wáng Wéi gazed intently and laughed,

Wáng Wéi said:

Curious people gathered musicians to verify this,

From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ"
King Níng was skilled at painting horses.
After the Kāiyuán era,
on the wall of the Huā'è Tower was the painting "Six Horses Galloping Through Dust,"

describing it as having no detail left unfinished,
with a wind-swept mane and mist-like forelock,
truly magnificent indeed.
Later, on the wall there were only five horses,
one of them missing.
It is believed that divine beings
take their transformations with them.
"Records of Lóngchéng"
Hán Gàn,
a native of Lántián.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he was summoned to serve in the imperial court.
The emperor ordered him to learn from Chén Hóng's horse paintings,
but was surprised by their differences,
so he questioned Hán Gàn about it.
Hán Gàn replied:
"I have my own teacher.
The horses in Your Majesty's inner stables
are all my teachers."
The emperor found this remarkable.
"Huà Duàn" When Hán Gàn was at leisure,
suddenly a person in red clothes and black hat arrived.
Hán Gàn asked:
"How did you get here?"
The person replied:
"I
am a messenger from the underworld.
Hearing of your skill in painting fine horses,
I wish to request one."
Hán Gàn immediately painted a horse
and burned it.
Several days later,
while going out,
someone bowed and asked him:
"Thanks to your gift of a swift steed,
I am spared the toil of traveling through mountains and rivers,
and I have something to repay you."
The next day, a friend sent him a hundred bolts of plain silk,
though he didn't know where they came from,
Hán Gàn accepted and used them.
"Dú Yì Zhì" During the early Jiànzhōng era,
someone led a horse to seek a veterinarian,
claiming the horse had a foot ailment,
offering two thousand coins for treatment.
The horse's coat color and bone structure
were unlike any the veterinarian had seen before.
He laughed and said:
"Your horse greatly resembles those painted by Hán Gàn,
as no real horse looks like this."
He then asked the horse owner to circle the market gate once,
while the veterinarian followed.
Suddenly they encountered Hán Gàn.
Hán Gàn also exclaimed in surprise:
"This is truly one of my painted horses!"
Then they realized that what he created at will
must have mysteriously matched its likeness.
He then rubbed his hands,
the horse seemed to stumble,
and injured its front leg,
which Hán Gàn found strange.
Returning home to look at his original painting of the horse,
he found a spot missing on the leg,
only then realizing his art had connected with the spiritual realm.
The money the veterinarian received
passed through several owners,
eventually becoming sunken money.
"Yǒu Yáng Zá Zǔ" Emperor Xuánzong favored large horses,
with the imperial stables housing up to four hundred thousand,
thus there were majestic large horses.
He appointed Wáng Máozhòng as overseer,

At that time, the emperor appreciated arts,
and Hán Gàn emerged,
so he was ordered to paint all the fine steeds,
including Jade Flower Dappled and Shining Night White.
When the princes of Qí and Xuē were granted estates with stables,

Hán Gàn painted them all,

After the Ān Lùshān Rebellion,

an envoy traveling to Jiangnán,

That night,
he dreamed that a deity told him to leave a horse to be helped.
After waking,
he offered his collected Hán Gàn horse painting.
Soon the wind ceased,
and he crossed.

As for Wéi Jiàn and his nephew Wéi Yǎn,

We only cite the most prominent to illustrate,

Common people, upon seeing a horse,
immediately attribute it to Cáo, Hán, or Wéi.
Upon seeing an ox,
they attribute it to Hán Huǎng or Dài Sōng.
This is quite laughable.
As the saying goes: for oxen it's Dài Sōng,
for horses it's Hán Gàn,
for cranes it's Dù Xún,

Wú Dàozǐ,
during the Kāiyuán era,
General Péi Mín was in mourning,
visited Wú Dàozǐ,
requesting him to paint several murals of deities and ghosts at the Tiāngōng Temple in the eastern capital,
to provide spiritual assistance for the deceased.
Dàozǐ replied:
"My painting brush has long been idle,
if the General is willing,
for me, tie up your garments,
perform a sword dance once,
to stir fierce inspiration,
and connect with the netherworld!"
Mín then removed his mourning clothes,
dressed as usual,
rode his horse swiftly as if flying,
spinning left and right,
waving his sword into the clouds,
reaching dozens of zhang high,
like lightning striking down.
Mín stretched out his hand holding the scabbard to catch it,
the sword pierced through the room and entered.
Thousands of spectators,
all were astonished and trembled.
Dàozǐ then took up his brush and painted on the wall,
a swift wind arose,
creating a magnificent spectacle under heaven.
In Dàozǐ's lifelong painting career,
he never achieved a more satisfying work than this.
"Jiàn Wén Zhì" The painting is in the western corridor of the temple,

During the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Míng Huáng,

Upon his return,

"I have no preliminary sketches,

He was then sent to paint them in the Dàtóng Hall;

At that time, General Lǐ Sīxùn was renowned for his landscape paintings,

Emperor Míng Huáng said:

Fényáng once displayed both paintings by his seat,

《Jiànwén Zhì》
Zhāng Nánběn painted Buddhist statues and ghost deities with great skill,
and was especially adept at painting fire.
During the Zhōnghé era, he once painted the Eight Wisdom Kings on the main hall of Jīnhuá Temple in Chéngdū.
A monk traveling on pilgrimage came to the temple,
adjusted his robes, and ascended the hall.
On the wall,
he saw the painted fire,
its flames so fierce they seemed to press upon him,
startling him so much he nearly fell.
At that time, Sūn Wèi was renowned for painting water,
and in discussions of the mastery of painting water and fire,
these two alone were highly praised.
For water approaches the nature of the Way
and responds to the divine;
without deep exploration of the principles at the tip of the brush,
it is not easy to depict them.
In the Tàipíng Temple of Chángzhōu during the Táng dynasty, there was a recluse named Xú Chǔshì Yǒunéng who painted "The Qīngjì River Flowing into the Hé,"
with a single brushstroke winding continuously,
traced from beginning to end, it stretched forty zhàng without interruption.
Standing back to view it,
billows surged like a roaring river,
dazzling the eyes.
Drawing closer to look up at it,
one felt a chilling sensation, as if splashed by a flying torrent,
and perceived a cold aura.
At that time, Lord Yáng viewed and praised it,
admiring it endlessly.
"Huà Jiàn": Sòng Qì Wénxiù of the Sòng dynasty,
excelled at painting water.
He painted "The Qīngjì River Pouring into the Hé,"
with a single brushstroke five zhàng long,
starting from the edge,
piercing through the waves.
Amidst the multitude,
it maintained order without fail,
soaring and twisting back.
"Tú Huì Bǎo Jiàn"
Zhāng Xún,
a native of Nánhǎi,
failed the imperial examinations,
and later drifted to Cháng'ān,
finding solace in painting.
Later, he went to Shǔ,
where he lodged at Zhāoqìng Temple.
For the monk Mèng Xiū,
he painted the "Scenes of Morning, Noon, and Evening" on the temple wall,

Later, the king of Wáng Shǔ wished to relocate it.
However, the painting was connected to the beams of the building,
and moving it would cause damage,
so the plan was abandoned.
Jīng Hào,
a native of Hénèi,
styled himself
"Master of the Vast Valley"
He was erudite and fond of antiquity,
specializing in landscape painting,
and achieved considerable direction.
He excelled at painting mountain peaks amid clouds,
with steep and solid features on all sides.
He authored a one-volume manual on landscape painting,
and once said to others:
"Wú Dàozǐ paints landscapes
with brushwork but without ink wash.
Xiàng Róng has ink wash but lacks brushwork.
I shall adopt the strengths of both masters
to form a style of my own.
Thus, Guān Tóng revered him as a master.
In contemporary discussions, Jīng Hào's landscapes
were considered the finest of the late Táng dynasty.
For those with brushwork but no ink wash,
the brushstrokes show traces of technique but lack naturalness;
those with ink wash but no brushwork
eliminate the marks of carving but possess abundant variation.
Biān Luán,
a native of Jīngzhào,
excelled in painting,
and was most skilled in the exquisite art of flowers, birds, and broken branches,
unprecedented in ancient times.

As if producing clear sounds,

Wáng Zǎi,

"Jade Hall Casual Conversations"
Lady Lǐ,

and particularly excelled in calligraphy and painting.
Guō Chóngtǎo obtained her when he conquered Shǔ.
As Lady Lǐ considered Chóngtǎo a military man,

One moonlit evening, sitting alone in the southern pavilion,

so she rose, took up her brush and dipped it in ink,
and traced their forms on the window paper.
The next day, looking at it,
it was full of vitality.
It is said that from then on in the human world,
people often imitated it,
thus giving rise to ink bamboo painting.
During the Lóngdé era,

Liáng Yújīng excelled at painting peonies.

his works already rivaled the real ones.
Thereafter, he pondered deeply without weariness,
and with each effort, his skill improved.
Someone presented him with a poem that said:

From the Jiàn Wén Zhì.
Liú Yànqí of the Liáng dynasty excelled at painting bamboo,

Noble families and wealthy elites
valued his connoisseurship.
His collection of renowned artworks
amounted to no less than a thousand scrolls.
Each summer during the dog days, while sunning them,
he would personally roll and unroll each one,
remaining untiring throughout the day.
He was capable of appraising them himself,
always with precision and appropriateness.
Thus, discerning people of that time all said:

indeed.
Huáng Quán,

mastering all six techniques of painting,
far surpassing his three teachers.
In the year Jiǎchén of the Guǎngzhèng era under the Later Shǔ ruler Mèng,
an envoy came from Huáinán bearing gifts.
Among the gifts were several live cranes,
and the Shǔ ruler ordered Huáng Quán to paint cranes on the walls of a side hall.
Some were alert to the dew, some pecking at moss, some preening their feathers, some arranging their wings, some calling to the sky, and some standing on one leg—
their vivid and dynamic forms
surpassed even living cranes.
Often, live cranes would stand beside the paintings.
The Shǔ ruler admired them greatly,
and thus named it
the "Hall of Six Cranes."
Before this, people in Shǔ had never seen live cranes,
and all regarded Xuē Shàobǎo's paintings of cranes as extraordinary.
After Huáng Quán painted these cranes,
noble and wealthy families vied to commission crane paintings with generous gifts.
From then on, Xuē Shàobǎo's reputation gradually declined.
A contemporary saying went:
"Huáng Quán paints cranes,
Sū Jì's value diminishes."

Additionally, a white rabbit was painted on silk,

"Painting Critiques"
In the past, Wú Dàozǐ painted Zhōng Kuí,
dressed in a blue gown,
with one foot in leather,
blind in one eye,
a waist tablet and headscarf,
his head with disheveled hair,
using his left hand to seize a ghost,
and his right hand to gouge out the ghost's eye.
The brushwork was vigorous and powerful,
truly a masterpiece of painting.
Someone obtained it
and presented it to the King of Shǔ,
who cherished it greatly,
often hanging it in his bedroom.
One day, he summoned Huáng Quán to view it.
At first sight,
Quán praised it as an unparalleled work.
The King then said to Quán:
"If this Zhōng Kuí used his thumb to gouge the eye,
it would appear even more forceful.
Try to alter it for me."
Quán then requested to take it back to his private quarters.
After several days of studying it,
he instead spread a new silk canvas and painted another Zhōng Kuí using his thumb to gouge the ghost's eye.
The next day,
he presented both Wú's original and his own version at once.
The King asked:
"I only instructed you to alter it,
why did you paint a separate one?"
Quán replied:
"In Wú Dàozǐ's painting of Zhōng Kuí,
the entire body's strength, expression, and gaze are concentrated on the second finger,
not the thumb,
so I dared not rashly change it.
Although my painting now may not match the ancients,
the full strength of the body
is focused on the thumb,
hence I dared to create a separate painting."
The King sighed in admiration,
and rewarded him with brocade, silk, and silverware to honor his discerning insight.
"Record of Observations" At the end of each winter,
academicians skilled in painting ghosts and deities
customarily presented paintings of Zhōng Kuí.
In the year Bǐngchén,
Zhōng Yì presented a Zhōng Kuí using the second finger to pluck the ghost's eye,
while Pú Shīxùn presented one using the thumb to gouge the ghost's eye.
Their Zhōng Kuí figures were similar,
differing only in the finger used.
The King asked:
"Which of these paintings is superior?"
Quán considered Shīxùn's to be better.
The King said:
"In Shīxùn's work,
the force is in the thumb;
in Zhōng Yì's,
the force is in the second finger.
The brush strength of both is comparable,
making it difficult to judge superiority."
He generously rewarded both with gold and silk.

skilled in painting Daoist and Buddhist figures.

which read:

Sū Zǐzhān painted bamboo in ink from the base,
straight up to the top in one stroke.
Mǐ Fú asked why he did not divide it section by section.
He replied:
"When bamboo grows,
does it ever grow section by section?"
His conception was clear and transcendent,
stemming from Wén Tóng Yǔkě.
He created groves of bamboo with great refinement.
Sū Zǐzhān painted withered trees,
their branches and trunks twisted and coiled,
without constraint,
and the texture of rocks rugged and hard,
also strangely peculiar,
unrestrained,
much like the pent-up melancholy in his heart.

styled

descend into the springs,

Exhaust the marvel of swimming and winding,

Moreover, there have been many throughout the ages who depicted ancient scenes in their paintings.
For instance, Zhāng Sēngyóo painted "Ministers Bidding Farewell to the Two Shū,"
yet the soldiers were shown wearing straw sandals;
Yán Lìběn painted "Zhāojūn Entering the Land of the Xiongnu,"
yet the women were depicted wearing veiled hats.
Now, straw sandals originated from regions of rivers and lakes,
and were not found in the capital;
veiled hats were created during the Suí dynasty,
and were not made in the Hàn palace.
How can critics cite these two paintings as evidence of historical facts!

Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital
In the seventh year of the Later Emperor's Yánxī era,
Wèi's Cáo Shuǎng invaded Hànzhōng. The Emperor
dispatched Fèi Yī to defend against him.
As he was about to depart,
the Grandee of the Imperial Household, Lái Mǐn, came to bid Yī farewell,
and requested to play a game of wéiqí;
at the time, urgent military dispatches were arriving incessantly,
soldiers were donning their armor,
and the carriage was fully prepared for departure,
yet Yī played against him,
showing not the slightest sign of impatience.
Mǐn said:
"I was merely testing you.
You are truly a capable man,
and will surely defeat the enemy."
When Yī arrived,
the enemy retreated.
Sūn Quán's crown prince Sūn Hé often said:
"Scholars of our time
should cultivate their skills in schools,
practicing archery and charioteering,
to serve worldly affairs,
yet they merely socialize and play board games,
thereby hindering their undertakings,
which cannot be called striving for advancement.
Later, when officials attended a banquet,
the conversation turned to board games,
considering them as obstructing affairs and wasting time,
with no practical benefit,
exhausting energy and damaging thought,
ultimately achieving nothing,
not the means to advance virtue, cultivate work, or accumulate merits.
Moreover, determined individuals cherish time and value effort,
gentlemen admire greater pursuits,
like high mountains and grand paths,
ashamed to be beneath such standards.
Human nature cannot be without amusement,
but the preference for amusement
should lie in feasting, music, literature, archery, and charioteering,
why must it be board games
to find joy!
Thereupon, he ordered eight attendants
to each write essays to correct this.
Thus, the Middle Palace Attendant Wéi Yào retired and composed a memorial,
which Sūn Hé showed to his guests.
At that time, Cài Yǐng enjoyed playing Go,
and many among those serving in office studied it,
hence this discussion.

Yīn Zhònggān was in the capital,
and once went to watch a game of Go.

while Yīn Zhònggān was inside asking Yuán about the meaning of the Classic of Changes.
Yuán responded as fluently as flowing water,

Yuán's attitude was arrogant,

was fond of playing chess.

Yǐn said:
"When the ancients encountered opportunity,
they achieved their principles through accomplishments.
If unrecognized,
they expressed their talents through words.
Compiling national histories,
all serve to dispel sorrows—
why must it be Go?

excelling at the game of Go,

Emperor Wén of the Sòng dynasty also enjoyed playing Go,

Yáng Xuánbǎo won the match,

During the Dàmíng era of the Sòng dynasty,
Lángyá's Wáng Xǐshàn
was the top-ranked player in wéiqí.
Wújùn's Chǔ Sīzhuāng and Kuàijī's Xià Chìsōng were second-ranked.
Chìsōng thought quickly,
excelling in broad strategy;
Sīzhuāng thought slowly,
but was skillful in tactical battles.
During Emperor Wén's reign of the Sòng dynasty,
when Yáng Xuánbǎo governed Kuàijī,
the emperor sent Sīzhuāng to the Eastern Palace to play against Xuánbǎo,
and they set up a game board,
then later replayed the game before the emperor.
Xiāo Dàochéng had Sīzhuāng compete against Wáng Háng in a match,
from breakfast time until dusk,
only finishing one game.
The emperor grew tired,
sent them back to their offices,
and they didn't conclude until the fifth watch.
Háng fell asleep by the board,
while Sīzhuāng stayed awake until dawn.
Some said at the time:
"The reason Sīzhuāng achieved such high ranking
was because he thought so deeply and long
that others couldn't match him.

Emperor Míng of the Sòng dynasty loved playing wéiqí,

Gǔ Bì entered to present a matter,
encountering Emperor Shìzǔ playing chess with the court official Liú Shù,
who was not paying attention to state affairs.
Gǔ Bì waited seated for a long time,
unable to get his report heard.
He then stood up,
grabbed Liú Shù by the head in front of Emperor Shìzǔ,
pulled him off the couch,
struck his ears with his hands,
and punched his back, saying:
"The court's disorder
is truly your fault!"
Emperor Shìzǔ lost composure,
put down the chess pieces and said:
"Not listening to reports
is actually my own fault.
What crime has Liú Shù committed?
Let him go!"
After Gǔ Bì finished presenting his matter, he said:
"For a minister to vent his will before the sovereign
is not without fault."
He then went to the official carriage station,
submitting a self-impeachment to request punishment.
Emperor Shìzǔ said:
"I have heard that in building an altar of the soil,
one limps while constructing it,
but dresses formally to serve it,
and the spirits grant blessings.
So what crime have you committed?"

Zhēn Chēn,
courtesy name Sībó,
was recommended as a Xiùcai.
After arriving in the capital for years,
he often wasted his days playing chess,
sometimes continuing all night long.
He often ordered his servant to hold a candle,
and if the servant dozed off,
he would severely cane him,
and this happened more than once.
Eventually, the servant, unable to bear the pain,
said to Zhēn Chēn:
"You, sir, left your parents
to serve in the capital.
If I were holding the candle for your studies,
I would not dare to complain,
but you play chess,
day and night without rest.
Is this your purpose in coming to the capital?
Yet you cane me as punishment,
isn't that unreasonable?"
Zhēn Chēn felt ashamed and reflective,
so he borrowed books from Xǔ Xiàn and Lǐ Biāo to study,
and his knowledge greatly improved.

From Yǒuyáng Zázǔ's "Yǔ Zī"
Hànlín qí player Wáng Jīxīn accompanied Emperor Míng Huáng on his westward journey,
lodging in a house by a deep stream.
There were only a woman and her daughter-in-law,
who provided only water and fire.
As soon as it grew dark,
they closed the door.
Jīxīn heard the daughter-in-law say to the woman at night:
"On such a fine evening with nothing to amuse ourselves,
shall we play a game of chess?"
There was no candle in the hall,
the woman and her daughter-in-law conversed from their respective east and west rooms.
After a while the daughter-in-law said:
"You've reached this point.
I only win by nine moves."
When dawn approached,
Jīxīn prepared gifts and made a request.
He asked them to demonstrate the game that embodied their lifelong mastery,
but before even a few dozen stones were placed,
the daughter-in-law said to the woman:
"This man can be taught,
using conventional strategies."
Thereupon she instructed him in the methods of attack and defense, killing and capturing, rescue and response, prevention and resistance.
Her explanations were very concise,
saying:
"This already makes you unbeatable among mortals."
Jīxīn expressed thanks and bid farewell,
but when he looked back, the house he had come from was gone.
"Yì Cóng Tán Jì" From then on, Jīxīn's skill
became unmatched by anyone.
Even when he laid out the remembered positions from the woman and daughter-in-law's game,
exhausting all his mental energy,
comparing their nine-move victory,
he still couldn't comprehend it.
Thus he named it "Dèng Ài's Invasion of Shǔ Formation",
which remains in chess manuals to this day,
yet no one in the world has ever been able to solve it.

In the twenty-fifth year of the Kāiyuán era,
the court appointed the Deputy Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Xíng Shú, as the envoy to offer condolences and bestow honors to Xīnluó.

the emperor said to Xíng Shú:

Huá Néng, an Attendant of the Hànlín Academy, held the highest rank in chess.

around forty years old,
who requested a match.

Huá Néng pondered meticulously for a long time.
Just as he placed a piece,
Zhāng responded immediately,

he dreamed that someone burned three volumes of a wéiqí manual and made him swallow them.
Upon waking,
he summoned a court wéiqí master to observe a game,
and every move he pointed out

often visiting the homes of high-ranking officials with wine, delicacies, chess, and gambling.

he would pretend to lose and generously compensate others.

and those obsessed with profit all associated intimately with him.

Shǔ Province's Jiǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Ān Zhòngbà was insatiably greedy for bribes.
Among the people of the province was an oil merchant,
surnamed Dèng,
who was skilled at playing chess,
and whose family was also well-off.
Zhòngbà summoned him for a match,
but only allowed him to stand while attending.
Each time he placed a piece,
he was made to retreat and stand under the northwest window.
He had to wait for Zhòngbà to calculate his move,
only then was he permitted to approach again,
so that by the end of the day, he hadn't placed even ten pieces.
Mr. Dèng, exhausted from standing and hungry,
was almost unable to endure it.
The next day, he was summoned again,
and someone hinted to Mr. Dèng, saying:
"This official is fond of bribes;
he never really intended to play chess.
Why not offer a bribe and ask to be excused?"
So he presented three ingots of medium-grade gold,
and was thus spared.

From "Dōngzhāi Yíshì"
Liao Dynasty court entertainer Luó Yīqīng,
witty and adaptable,
often offered admonitory advice through humor.
Emperor Xīngzōng was excessively intimate with his younger brother Chóngyuán,
and during a drunken banquet,
promised to pass the throne to him after his own death.
Chóngyuán was greatly pleased,
becoming arrogant and lawless.
They also played backgammon,
wagering cities with their inhabitants.
The emperor repeatedly lost,
having already paid several cities.
Chóngyuán, relying on favor like Prince Liáng Xiào's,
and possessing more faults than Zhèng Shūduàn,
found no court officials daring to speak out,
so people could only communicate their anger with their eyes on the streets.
One day during a game,
Luó Yīqīng pointed at the board and said:
"Backgammon is so foolish -
it will make you lose everything!"
Only then did the emperor realize,
and ceased gambling.
(from "History of Liao - Biographies of Court Entertainers")
Cài Jīng served as prime minister,
and his younger brother Cài Biàn held the position of chief military commissioner.
Since Cài Biàn was the son-in-law of Wáng Ānshí,
he revered his father-in-law so much that during the Confucian temple ceremony,
he offered sacrifices to Wáng Ānshí, who had been enfeoffed as Prince of Shū and given a place beside Confucius in the temple.
People arranged Confucius in the main seat,
with Yán Huí and Mèngzǐ positioned beside Wáng Ānshí.
Confucius invited Wáng Ānshí to sit,
but Wáng Ānshí bowed to Mèngzǐ, offering him the upper seat.
Mèngzǐ declined, saying:
"There are three universally recognized honors,
and noble rank is one of them.
I, Mèng Kē, have recently been granted a ducal title,
while you, sir, are honored as a true prince.
Why must you be so modest?"
Wáng Ānshí then bowed to Yán Huí,
who said:
"I, Yán Huí,
am but a commoner from a humble alley,
who achieved nothing of significance in life.
You, sir, are a Confucian scholar renowned through the ages,
and there is a great difference in our status and appearance.
Your refusal is excessive."
Thus Wáng Ānshí took the higher position.
Confucius could not remain comfortably in his seat,
and also moved to yield his place.
Wáng Ānshí became fearful and cupped his hands in salute,
saying:
"I dare not."
This back-and-forth continued without end.
Zǐ Lù came in from outside,
filled with indignation he could not contain,
hurried straight through the sacrificial hall,
and pulled Gōngyě Cháng out by the arm.
Gōngyě Cháng appeared distressed and constrained,
apologizing:
"What crime have I, Cháng, committed?"
Zǐ Lù then scolded him sternly:
"You did nothing to protect your father-in-law,
just look at how other people's sons-in-law behave!"
His intention was to satirize Cài Biàn.
At that time, there was a proposal to elevate Wáng Ānshí above Mèngzǐ,
but because of this incident, the plan was abandoned.
"Records of Yíjiān"
During the provincial examinations in the Rénxū year of the Shàoxīng era,
Qín Huì's son Xǐ, and nephews Chāngshí and Chānglíng,
were all listed as successful candidates.
Public opinion was seething with discontent,
yet no one dared to speak out openly.
By the beginning of spring in the Yǐchǒu year,
actors performing in a theater,
portraying scholars,
heading for the imperial examinations,
were speculating among themselves about who would be appointed as the chief examiner.
They pointed to certain ministers and vice-ministers as likely to hold the authority,
but a senior actor refuted them, saying:
"This year, it must be Péng Yuè."
Someone asked:
"In the imperial court,
we haven't heard of such an official."
He replied:
"He is the King of Liáng from the Hàn dynasty."
The questioner said:
"That's an ancient figure,
dead for a thousand years;
how could he come?"
The actor explained:
"Last time, it was King of Chǔ Hán Xìn, skipping one rank;
so I know it's now King Péng's turn."
Although the questioner thought it absurd,
he pressed for the meaning,
and the actor laughed, saying:
"If it weren't for Hán Xìn,
how could they have captured the three Qín regions?"
None of the audience dared to grasp the implication,
and they dispersed through the gate.
Qín Huì also did not dare to openly impose punishment.
Qín Huì, on the first day of the fourth month in the fifteenth year of the Shàoxīng era,
was granted a residence at Wàngxiān Bridge;
on the second day,
he was bestowed ten thousand taels of silver and bolts of silk,
ten million coins,
and a thousand rolls of colorful silk.
An imperial edict decreed:
"A banquet shall be held at his residence,
with performers from the Imperial Music Bureau."
All chief ministers attended.
During the banquet,
a lead performer recited a congratulatory speech,
then withdrew.
A military advisor,
stepping forward,
praised Huì's virtues and achievements,
while an actor followed him holding a lotus-leaf-shaped chair.
Witty remarks ensued,
and the guests were thoroughly entertained.
As the advisor bowed in thanks,
about to sit in the chair,
his headscarf suddenly fell off,
revealing his hair tied in a topknot,
like a soldier's headgear,
with a large ring at the back,
resembling two victory rings.
The actor pointed and asked:
"What ring is this?"
He replied:
"The Èr Shèng rings."
The actor immediately struck his head,
saying:
"You only care about sitting in the Grand Tutor's chair,
claiming silver, silk, and rewards,
so you might as well toss these rings behind your head."
The entire gathering turned pale with fear.
Huì was enraged,
and the next day ordered arrests and imprisonment,
resulting in deaths.
From then on, speech restrictions became increasingly severe.
Ruì Yè and Lìng Lǐng, among others, fell victim to the persecution,
marking the decline of the era.

Hán Píngyuán in the early Qìngyuán era,

"Chéng Shǐ"
After Empress Puchá of Emperor Zhāngzōng of Jin passed away,

The palace attendant Lǐ Shī'ér,

According to Jin dynasty customs,

One day,
Emperor Zhāngzōng hosted a banquet in the palace for entertainers,

Someone asked the emperor:
"What auspicious signs are there?"
The entertainer said:
"Haven't you heard of the phoenix's appearance?"
The person said:
"I know of it,
but haven't heard the details."
The entertainer said:
"Its flight has four directions,
each corresponding to a different omen.
If it flies upward, then wind and rain will be timely,
if it flies downward, then the five grains will be abundant,
if it flies outward, then the four nations will come to pay tribute,
if it flies inward, then official salaries will be increased."
The emperor laughed heartily and ended the banquet.
"History of Jin: Consort Biographies"

In Lín'ān, an actor dressed as a Confucian scholar,

"White Otter Marrow"
Ritual must be rooted in the Great One,
which divides to form Heaven and Earth,
revolves to become yīn and yáng,
transforms to create the four seasons,
and arranges to produce ghosts and spirits.
"Lǐyùn"
Confucius said:
"Ritual
was used by the ancient kings to follow the Way of Heaven,
and to regulate human emotions.
Therefore, those who lose it perish,
while those who obtain it survive.
The Book of Songs says:
"Even a rat has its body,
but a man without ritual;
a man without ritual,
why does he not quickly die!
Therefore,
ritual
must be rooted in Heaven,
modeled on Earth,
arranged according to spirits and deities,
and applied to mourning, sacrifice, archery, charioteering, capping, marriage, court audiences, and diplomatic visits.
Thus, the sages demonstrate it through ritual,
so the world, states, and families can be properly governed.
Rites are
the great handle of the sovereign.
They serve to distinguish what is doubtful and make clear what is subtle,
to act as a host to spiritual beings,
to examine institutions,
to distinguish benevolence and righteousness,
and thereby to govern the state and give peace to the ruler.
Hence,
Rites are
that by which intimacy and distance are determined, doubts and suspicions are resolved, similarities and differences are distinguished, and right and wrong are clarified.
Virtue, morality, benevolence, and righteousness
cannot be accomplished without rites.
Teaching, instruction, rectifying customs,
cannot be complete without rites.
Settling disputes and adjudicating lawsuits,
cannot be decided without rites.
The relationships between ruler and subject, superior and inferior, father and son, elder and younger brothers,
cannot be established without rites.
Serving as an official, studying, and serving a teacher,
cannot be intimate without rites.
Arranging court assemblies and governing the army,
assuming office and enforcing laws,
cannot be carried out with authority and dignity without rites.
Prayers, sacrifices, and offerings to gods and spirits,
cannot be sincere and solemn without rites.
Therefore, the noble person is respectful and restrained,
yielding and deferential to demonstrate rites.
"Qǔ Lǐ"
Thus, ritual and righteousness
are the great foundation of humanity.
They serve to cultivate trust and harmony, thereby strengthening the unions of human flesh
and the bonds of sinews and bones.
They are the great foundation for nourishing the living, sending off the dead, and serving the spirits and gods.
They are the great channel for comprehending the Way of Heaven and harmonizing human feelings.
Therefore, only the sages know that ritual cannot be dispensed with.
Hence, when states are ruined, families perish, and individuals are destroyed,
it is invariably because they first abandoned their ritual.
Thus, ritual in relation to humans
is like the yeast in wine:
the noble use it to become substantial,
while the petty use it to become shallow.
"Evolution of Rites"
Thus, the rites of court audience
serve to clarify the righteousness between ruler and subject.
The rites of diplomatic missions,
serve to make feudal lords respect one another.
The rites of mourning and sacrifice,
serve to manifest the gratitude of subjects and sons.
The rites of the district drinking ceremony,
serve to clarify the order between elders and juniors.
The rites of marriage,
serve to distinguish the separation between men and women.
Now, rites prevent disorder from arising,
just as dikes prevent floods from coming.
Therefore, if one considers an old dike useless and destroys it,
flood damage is certain to occur;
if one considers old rites useless and abolishes them,
disorder and calamity are certain to arise.
Thus, the transformative effect of rites is subtle;
they stop evil before it takes form,
causing people daily to move toward goodness and away from crime without realizing it themselves.
Therefore, the former kings esteemed them.

When ancient kings established rituals,

《Dìng 15》
Duke Jǐng of Qí ascended to the archery range,
while Yànzǐ prepared the rituals and waited.
The duke said:
"The rituals for selecting archers,
I am weary of them!
I wish to gather brave warriors from across the land,
and plan state affairs with them.
Yànzǐ replied:
"If a noble person lacks ritual,
they are but a commoner;
if a commoner lacks ritual,
they are but a beast.
Now ritual
is what governs the people,
just as reins
are what control a horse.
That one can govern the state without ritual—
I, Yìng, have never heard of such a thing.
Duke Jǐng said:
"Well said.
Thereupon he ordered the archery grounds be tidied and mats changed,
honoring Yànzǐ as a distinguished guest,
and inquired about ritual throughout the day.
From "Shuō Yuàn"
Yànzǐ was sent on a diplomatic mission to Lǔ.
When descending the hall steps, he quickened his pace,
and when receiving the jade token, he knelt down.
Zǐgòng found this strange
and asked Confucius about it.
Confucius inquired of Yànzǐ,
and Yànzǐ replied:
"In the ritual of ascending the hall,
the ruler takes one step,
while the minister takes two.
Now that the ruler is presenting the ceremonial token,
how dare I, a humble minister, not kneel?"
Confucius said:
"Excellent.
Within ritual, there is yet more ritual."
Hánshī Wàizhuàn
Duke Jǐng indulged in drinking until drunk,
then removed his clothes and hat, playing the qín to amuse himself.
He looked at his attendants and said:
"Do virtuous men also enjoy this?
The attendants replied:
"Virtuous men have ears and eyes like other men,
why wouldn't they enjoy it!
Duke Jǐng said:
"Harness the carriage to fetch Yànzǐ.
When Yànzǐ heard of this,
he came in full court attire.
Duke Jǐng said:
"Today I have this pleasure,
and wish to share it with you, my minister.
Yànzǐ said:
"Your words are mistaken!
In the state of Qí, anyone over five feet tall,
has the strength to overpower both me and you,
the reason they dare not is
their fear of ritual propriety.
Thus, if the Son of Heaven lacks ritual propriety,
he cannot preserve the altars of soil and grain;
if the feudal lords lack ritual propriety,
they cannot preserve their states;
if those in high position lack ritual propriety,
they cannot command their subordinates;
if those in low position lack ritual propriety,
they cannot serve their superiors;
if ministers lack ritual propriety,
they cannot govern their households;
if brothers lack ritual propriety,
they cannot live together;
if a person lacks ritual propriety,
it would be better for them to die quickly.
Duke Jǐng's face showed shame,
he left his mat and apologized, saying:
"I am unvirtuous and lack goodness,
my attendants have indulged and misled me,
leading to this state,
I request to execute my attendants,
to atone for my fault.
Yànzǐ said:
"The attendants are without fault.
If the ruler favors ritual propriety,
then those with propriety will come,
and those without will leave;
if the ruler dislikes ritual propriety,
then those without propriety will come,
and those with will leave.
What crime have the attendants committed?
Duke Jǐng said:
"Excellent!
He then changed his clothes and sat properly,
after three rounds of wine,
Yànzǐ took his leave,
and Duke Jǐng bowed in sending him off.
End
Confucius passed through Sòng,
and practiced rites with his disciples under a large tree.
Sīmǎ Huán Tuí of Sòng had the tree uprooted,
so they left for Zhèng.
From "Diǎn Lüè"
At the rise of the Hàn dynasty, amidst the chaos being reversed and order restored,
there was not a day to spare,
yet Emperor Gāozǔ still ordered Shūsūn Tōng to establish rituals and ceremonies to rectify the positions of ruler and subject.
Emperor Gāozǔ, pleased, sighed and said:
"Only today do I realize the honor of being the Son of Heaven!
He appointed Tōng as Fèngcháng,
and thus the ceremonial laws were established.
The Former Records state: Tōng, along with over a hundred disciples,
made straw markers and banners,
practicing them in the open field.
From his main biography.
During the reign of Emperor Xuān,
the Grand Master of Remonstrance Wáng Jí submitted a memorial,
expressing his wish to join with the high officials and extend invitations to Confucian scholars,
to recount the ancient rites,
clarify the institutions of the sage kings,
and guide the people of the entire generation,
elevating them to the realm of benevolence and longevity.
Hàn Shū
Cáo Bāo submitted a memorial,
fully elaborating on the fundamentals of rites and music,
and the intent behind institutional reforms.
The emperor issued an edict to Bān Gù,
inquiring about the appropriateness of revising the ritual system.
Bān Gù replied:
"It would be best to broadly summon scholars,
to deliberate on gains and losses."
The emperor said:
"As the proverb goes, 'Building a house by the roadside,
it takes three years to complete nothing'
Scholars versed in rites
are known for gathering to dispute."
The emperor ordered a eunuch to present the twelve chapters of Shūsūn Tōng's "Hàn Rituals" submitted by Bān Gù,
and instructed Cáo Bāo:
"This system is fragmented and rudimentary,
largely inconsistent with the classics.
It should be rectified according to the rites,
making it practicable."
Thereupon, Cáo Bāo compiled and arranged the systems of capping, marriage, auspicious, and inauspicious ceremonies from the Son of Heaven to commoners,
establishing them as the grand code for an era.
The emperor, finding it difficult to unify diverse opinions,
merely accepted it.
"History of the Later Hàn"
Principle is
what Heaven does.
Pattern is
what humans do.
What humans do
is called ritual.
Ritual
takes human feelings as its basis to establish refined forms,
thereby preventing disorder.
Just as dikes
are defenses against water,
so ritual
is a defense for humans.
Punishment
guards against the branches;
ritual
guards against the root.
"Dǒng Shēng Shū"
Rites are
the juncture of yin and yang,
the convergence of all affairs,
the means to honor heaven and earth, revere ghosts and spirits, and establish the order of high and low.
Báihǔ Tōng
Lǐ is
to practice,
to regulate,
with the same meaning but different names.
The five rites are:
auspicious, inauspicious, guest, military, and congratulatory.
"Wùlǐ Lùn"
Rites are
the regulations established in accordance with human emotions,
manifesting the affection of honoring fathers and cherishing kin,
and embodying the duty of respecting parents and honoring elders.
"Yuán Huái's Correct Writings"
A ruler who adapts to the times
must base himself on the rituals of former kings,
adapting to the times and circumstances,
making some reductions and additions,
regulating people's hearts,
and gradually establishing institutions.
History of the Hàn Dynasty
Zhāng Liù Xīng,
when the stars are bright,
then the king practices the five rites,
attaining the center of heaven,
Yì twenty-degree stars,
are heaven's music bureau performers.
If the stars are bright and large,
rituals and music flourish.
"Jìn Zhì"
In the way of governing people,
nothing is more urgent than ritual.
There are five classics of ritual,
and none is more important than sacrifice.
Now sacrifice
is not something that comes from external things;
it is born from within and arises from the heart.
The heart is moved and offers it through ritual.
Therefore, only the virtuous
can fully comprehend the meaning of sacrifice.
"The Summary of Sacrifice"
The Zhōu Commentary states:
"The word 'sacrifice' means to examine.
To examine means
to arrive at.
To arrive at means
human affairs.
When human affairs arrive,
then sacrifice is performed.
Sacrifice means
to present offerings,
and 'to present' means to be present.
To be present means
to be present in its proper way.
The Shàngshū Cài Commentary
Sacrifices should not be too frequent,
for frequency leads to weariness,
and weariness leads to disrespect.
Sacrifices should not be too infrequent,
for infrequency leads to neglect,
and neglect leads to forgetfulness.
The "Meaning of Sacrifices" quotes the Charge to Yue saying:
"To be profuse in sacrifices,
is at times to be irreverent.
The meaning of sacrificial rites
has two aspects: first,
"repaying merits"
second,
"honoring ancestors"
Repaying merits serves to encourage effort,
while honoring ancestors serves to revere kindness.
Lùnhéng
In ancient times, people revered sacrifices and valued deities,
sacrificing at ancestral temples
to continue providing for the deceased,
and sacrificing to heaven and earth to repay their virtue.
Yáng Quán's "Discourses on the Principles of Things"
Without proper palaces and buildings, one cannot perform sacrifices.
Sacrificing
is to offer according to the season,
to offer with reverence,
to offer with righteousness,
not to enjoy flavors.

These are performed throughout the year.

From the "Qū Lǐ"
There was a sea bird called Yuánjū.
Zāng Wénzhòng had the people of the state offer sacrifices to it.
Zhǎn Qín said:
"How far off the mark
is Zāng Sūn in governing!
Sacrificial rites
are a great institution of the state;
and institutions
are what governance accomplishes.
Therefore, we carefully establish sacrifices to serve as the state's code.
Now, to add to the code without reason
is not appropriate for governance.
The way the sage kings established sacrifices was:
those who spread laws among the people are sacrificed to,
those who died in diligent service are sacrificed to,
those who toiled to stabilize the state are sacrificed to,
those who could ward off great disasters are sacrificed to,
those who could defend against great calamities are sacrificed to.
If not these,
they are not included in the sacrificial code.
All Di, Jiāo, Zōng, Zǔ, and Bào sacrifices—
these five types
are the state's canonical sacrifices.
Added to these are the gods of Shèjì, mountains, and rivers,
all of whom have rendered meritorious service to the people.
And the former sages and virtuous people
are those who serve as models of integrity.
And the three luminaries of heaven
are what the people look up to.
And the five elements of earth
are what produce and nurture life.
And the famous mountains, rivers, and marshes throughout the nine provinces
are sources of wealth and resources.
If not these,
they are not included in the sacrificial code."
Guóyǔ
The laws of the sage kings
involve offering sacrifices to heaven, earth, the sun, moon, stars, mountains, rivers, and all things,
all of which are ancient people
who were able to regulate the qi of heaven, earth, and the five phases,
and by honoring their achievements, they became human.
Therefore, in their sacrificial rites,
they all use the rituals of human affairs,
offering the food that people eat,
not sacrificing to food, land, metal, wood, water, fire, or stone.
They also sacrifice to the Three Sovereigns, Five Emperors, Nine Sovereigns, and sixty-four clans,
all of whom were ancient rulers,
totaling eighty-one surnames.
"Han Old Rituals"
Qū Dào was fond of water caltrops.
When he fell ill,
he summoned his clan elder and instructed him,
saying:
"When offering sacrifices to me, you must use water caltrops.
At the time of the sacrifice,
the clan elder was about to present the water caltrops,
but Qū Jiàn ordered them removed.
The clan elder said:
"The master instructed this.
Zǐ Mù (Qū Jiàn) said:
"That is not correct.
The sacrificial codes state: 'For a ruler of a state, there is the offering of an ox;
for a high official, there is the presentation of a sheep;
for a scholar, there is the sacrifice of a pig or dog;
for a commoner, there is the offering of roasted fish.
One should not present rare delicacies,
nor display excessive luxuries.
The master would not let his personal desires interfere with the state's codes.
Thus they were not used.
"Chǔ Yǔ"
Zǐqī sacrificed to King Píng,
offering cattle on the altar to the king.
The king inquired of Guàn Yìfù,
saying:
"What sacrificial animals are appropriate?"
He replied:
"Sacrifices exceed regular offerings.
The Son of Heaven offers a tàiláo for regular meals,
and a grand assembly sacrifice for rituals;
feudal lords offer a single ox for regular meals,
and a tàiláo for sacrifices;
high ministers offer a shàoláo for regular meals,
and a single ox for sacrifices;
great officers offer a single animal for regular meals,
and a shàoláo for sacrifices;
scholars eat roasted fish,
and offer a single animal for sacrifices;
common people eat vegetables,
and offer fish for sacrifices.
There is order from high to low,
so the people do not become disrespectful.
The king said:
"How about their sizes?"
He replied:
"For suburban and ancestral sacrifices, they do not exceed chestnuts,
for seasonal sacrifices, they do not exceed what can be held in hand.
The king said:
"Why so small?"
He replied:
"The spirits oversee the people with clarity and intelligence,
thus they seek complete offerings,
not abundant size.
Therefore, in the sacrifices of former kings,
they used one purity, two essences, three animals, four seasons, five colors, six tones, seven affairs, eight grains, nine sacrifices, ten days, and twelve hours to reach them;
hundred surnames, thousand categories, ten thousand officials, hundred million masses,
trillion people through income and countless numbers to serve them,
illuminating virtue to make them manifest,
harmonizing sounds to make them clear,
announcing universal arrival,
then none fail to receive blessings.
The king said:
"Can sacrifices not be ceased?"
He replied:
"Sacrifices serve to manifest filial piety, give rest to the people, comfort the state, and settle the hundred surnames,
they cannot be ceased.
The Son of Heaven universally sacrifices to all spirits and categories of things,
feudal lords sacrifice to heaven and earth, three luminaries, and mountains and rivers of their lands,
high ministers and great officers sacrifice according to their rites,
scholars and common people do not exceed their ancestors.
The superior thereby teaches the people how to behave,
the inferior thereby manifest service to the superior.
The Son of Heaven personally pounds the grain for suburban sacrifices,
the queen personally spins the sacrificial garments,
from the duke down to the common people,
who would dare not be reverent, respectful and devoted to the spirits!
This is how the people maintain steadfastness,
how could we abandon it!
End
In the past, King Líng of Chǔ was arrogant and extravagant, despising his subordinates,
neglecting the worthy and focusing on ghosts,
believing in the ways of witches and invokers.
He fasted, purified himself, and made offerings fresh and clean
to sacrifice to the Supreme Deity,
and to honor the multitude of spirits.
Personally holding feather banners,
he danced before the altar.
When the people of Wú came to attack,
and his own people reported the emergency,
King Líng continued drumming and dancing as usual,
turning to respond, saying:
"I am currently sacrificing to the Supreme Deity and delighting the bright spirits;
I should receive blessings and protection.
I dare not go to the rescue."
Thereupon,
the troops of Wú arrived,
capturing his crown prince, queen, consorts, and those below them,
which was deeply lamentable.
From the Xīn Lùn of Huánzǐ
Fūchāi led his ministers out of the capital eastward,
and offered sacrifices to Zǐxū by the riverbank.
All the ministers were present.
Fūchāi then spoke, saying:
"I, the unworthy one, received the legacy of the late king's grace,
becoming the ruler of a thousand chariots.
In the past, I did not heed the words of the prime minister,
but instead employed slanderous and flattering counsel,
causing the prime minister to cast himself into the river and perish.
Since then, I have been lost and confused,
as if fog has obscured the sun,
with no one to speak to."
His tears fell, soaking his lapels,
overwhelmed by grief he could not contain,
and all the officials around him were deeply sorrowful.
The Annals of Wú and Yuè
After King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè had pacified Wú,
he offered spring sacrifices at the Three Rivers,
and autumn sacrifices at the Five Lakes.
Therefore, at that time, a shrine was established for him,
to bequeath it to later ages,
and pass it down for ten thousand generations.
Neighboring states delighted in his virtue,
and all came to learn from it.
From "Yuè Jué."
When the Lǔ official Suǒ Shì was about to offer sacrifices,
he lost the sacrificial animal.
Confucius heard of this
and said:
"Official Suǒ Shì will perish within two years."
After one year,
he indeed perished.
A disciple asked:
"Previously, when Official Suǒ Shì lost his sacrificial animal, you said: 'He will perish within two years'
Now he perished after the deadline,
how did you know this would happen?"
Confucius replied:
"Sacrifice
is how a filial son expresses his utmost devotion to his parents.
If one loses the sacrificial animal when about to offer sacrifices,
then there must be many other things he has lost.
If someone like this doesn't perish,
such a thing has never happened."

Hàn Shū
When Zhūgě Liàng first passed away,
people everywhere requested to erect a temple for him,
but the court discussion deemed it improper according to ritual protocols and did not permit it,
so the common people took to privately offering sacrifices to him on roads and paths during seasonal festivals.
Some officials suggested that it might be allowed to build a temple in Chéngdū,
but the Later Ruler did not consent.
Mào Xiǎn, Xiàng Chōng, and others jointly submitted a memorial stating:
"We have heard that the people of Zhōu cherished the virtue of Shào Bó,
and thus the pear tree was spared from being cut down;
the King of Yuè remembered the achievements of Fàn Lí,
casting a bronze statue to preserve his likeness.
How much more so for Liàng, whose virtue serves as a model far and wide,
and whose meritorious service overshadowed the latter age,
yet seasonal sacrifices are confined to private households,
with no temple or statue established,
causing the common people to offer sacrifices in alleys,
and soldiers and barbarians to worship in the wilds.
This is not the way to preserve virtue and commemorate achievements,
nor to recount and honor the past.
It would be fitting to establish one near his tomb,
in Yáng,
allowing his relatives to offer sacrifices at appropriate times."
Thereupon, the request was finally approved.
