Hàn Shù records: Yáo composed Dà Zhāng,
Shùn composed Zhāo.
Zhāo
succeeded Yáo.
Confucius said:
"Xiāo Sháo
is the surviving music of Shùn.
Warm, gentle, and harmonious,
resembling the arrival of the southern wind.
Its sound
moves things like cold, heat, wind, and rain,
as things move people,
thunder moves beasts and birds,
wind and rain move fish and dragons,
benevolence and righteousness move gentlemen,
wealth and beauty move petty persons,
thus the sage focuses on the foundation.
Yuè Dòng Shēng Yí Yú Zhuàn states:
"In the inaugural year of the imperial tour,
the four peaks and eight lords,
altars at the four corners,
sacrifices sunk in the four seas,
twelve mountains enfeoffed,
twelve provinces demarcated.
The Music Master fixed the names of music,
the inaugural sacrifice at Mount Tài,
presented the music of two lords.
The music of the Yáng Lord of the Eastern Peak,
dance Zhū Lí,
its songs comparable to Yú Yáo,
named Zhé Yáng.
The music of the Yí Lord,
dance Chāng Zāi,
its songs comparable to Dà Yáo,
named Nán Yáng.
The midsummer sacrifice at Mount Huò,
presented the music of two lords.
The music of the Xià Lord,
dance Màn Huò,
its songs comparable to Zhōng Yáo,
named Chū Lǜ.
The music of the Xī Lord,
dance Jiāng Yáng,
its songs comparable to Dà Yáo,
named Zhū Qiān.
The autumn sacrifice at Mount Huà,
presented the music of two lords.
The music of the Qiū Lord,
dance Cài Chù,
its songs comparable to Xiǎo Yáo,
named Líng Luò.
The music of the Hé Lord,
dance Xuán Hè,
its songs comparable to Zhōng Yáo,
named Guī Lái.
The sacrifice at Mount Hóng in Yōudū,
presented the music of two lords.
The music of the Dōng Lord,
dance Qí Luò,
songs called Màn Màn,
discussing all eight tones and four harmonies,
returning to honor ancestors,
using special offerings.
Tours every five years,
all lords yielding with virtue,
presenting correct music and the nine clans performing complete.
"Shàng Shū Dà Zhuàn Wèi court officials memorialized:
"Xiāo Sháo's nine performances,
witnessed in Emperor Yú's court.
Sòng Shì
Zǐ Jiājū said:
"With vermilion shields and jade axes,
they perform the Great Xia dance."
Note: The music of Xia.
The Gongyang Commentary: When Jì Zhá saw the Great Xia dance performed,
he said:
"How magnificent!
Diligent yet not claiming virtue,
who but Yǔ could have perfected this!"
The Zuozhuan: The Great Xia signifies that Yǔ was able to follow and practice the ways of the two sage-kings.
The White Tiger Discussions: The Gongyang Commentary states: In the Xia era, the people's music celebrated the succession of its three sage-kings.
Jí Zhá saw the performers of the Sháo and Huò dances,
the greatness of the sage.
Yet he still felt ashamed,
showing how difficult it is to match the virtue of a sage.
Zuǒzhuàn: Chéng Fán inquired about music.
Mòzǐ said:
"When Tāng was established as king,
his tasks were accomplished and achievements established,
he followed the music of former kings,
and also created his own music,
naming it Hù,
and further practiced the Jiǔ Sháo."
Mòzǐ Sān Biàn Piān: Tāng created the Hù music,
hearing its gōng notes,
makes people gentle, kind, and broad-minded.
The shāng notes make people upright, honest, and fond of righteousness.
The jué notes make people compassionate and loving toward benevolence.
The zhǐ notes make people joyful in nurturing and fond of giving,
the yǔ notes make people respectful and fond of propriety.
Hánshī Wàizhuàn: Tāng's music was called Dà Hù,
meaning it could protect the people in their urgent needs.
Báihǔ Tōng: Gōngyáng annotation: During the Yīn dynasty, the people's music greatly protected themselves.
□King Mù of Zhōu performed Chéngyún, Liùyíng, Jiǔsháo, and Chénlù for his enjoyment.
Annotation: Jiǔsháo,
the music of Shùn;
Chénlù,
the music of Tāng.
Lièzǐ
King Wén had the music of the Pìyōng.
The "Zhuāngzǐ" and the "Shī" say: Oh, the harmonious bells and drums,
oh, the joyful Pìyōng.
Cài Yōng's "Records" state: The elegant music of the Zhōu odes
was used in the feasts and archery ceremonies at the Pìyōng.
□King Wén composed the martial and symbolic music,
adding two strings to the qín,
called the lesser gōng and lesser shāng.
The "Centuries of Emperors and Kings" records that during King Wén's time,
the people rejoiced in his raising armies for campaigns,
hence it was called martial.
The "Yuánmìng Bāo"
A king does not create music without reason.
Music is
the harmony that fills within,
manifesting outwardly through movement.
Responding to its emergence,
he establishes rites and composes music to perfect it.
Therefore, one who creates music must trace back to the world's initial joy, making it his foundation.
In Shùn's time,
the people rejoiced in his continuation of Yáo's legacy,
hence Sháo
means "to continue."
In Yǔ's time,
the people greatly delighted in the succession of two sages,
hence Xià
means "great."
In Tāng's time,
the people greatly rejoiced in his deliverance from calamities,
hence Hù
means "to rescue."
In King Wén's time,
the people delighted in his raising armies for campaigns,
hence Wǔ
means "to attack."
These four instances
share the commonality of bringing joy to the world,
yet the origins of that joy
cannot be uniform.
King Wén's music was called "Jù Yè",
and King Wǔ's music was called "Xiàng Wǔ".
The Yuè Yuàn states: King Wǔ built upon the music of the former kings,
and also created his own music,
naming it "Xiàng Wǔ".
King Chéng, following the music of the former kings,
named it "Zōu Yú".
The Mòzǐ Sān Biàn Piān records: When King Wǔ ascended the throne,
he led the six armies to attack the Shāng.
Before the six armies arrived,
he defeated them at Mùyě with elite troops.
He then presented the captives and severed ears at the capital's temple,
and ordered the Duke of Zhōu to compose the "Dà Wǔ".
When King Chéng was established,
the people of Shāng rebelled,
and the king ordered the Duke of Zhōu to lead a punitive expedition against them.
The Shāng people used elephants to harass the Eastern Yí,
so the Duke of Zhōu led his troops to drive them out.
Reaching south of the Yangtze River,
he then composed the "Sān Xiàng",
to celebrate their virtue.
Thus, the origin of music is indeed ancient.
The Lǚlǎn states: King Wǔ composed the "Xiàng" music,
continuing King Wén's legacy to honor Heaven.
The Chūnqiū Fánlù states: The Zhōu people had the music "Dà Wǔ",
the "Sān Xiàng" and "Jí Xià",
and their ceremonial color was red.
The Huáinán records Lǐ Sī's writing:
"Sháo, Yú, Wǔ, Xiàng."
Annotation: The Yuè Qín Shēng Yí says: The Zhōu music for the time of conquest was called "Wǔ Xiàng".
Sòng Jūn stated: "Xiàng" refers to the use of shields and spears during the conquest.
The Duke of Zhōu composed the Sháo,
signifying his ability to embody the ways of the ancestors.
According to the "Records of the Hàn,"
among the music of Yú Shì,
none was more magnificent than the Sháo.
In the Zhōu dynasty,
none was more magnificent than the Sháo.
In "Emperor Wǔ's Selection of Virtuous Officials," it is recorded that the Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng in creating the Sháo music to honor heaven.
The "Chūnqiū Fánlù" states that the Duke of Zhōu sang the Yōng and chanted the Sháo,
with all regions upholding virtue.
The "Zǐhuá Zǐ" notes that the music of Zhōu was called Dàwǔ,
and the music of the Duke of Zhōu was called Zhuó.
Líng Zhōujiū replied to King Jǐng of Zhōu:
"Qín and sè favor the gōng note,
zhōng favor the yǔ note,
stone chimes favor the jué note,
gourd and bamboo instruments suit regulation,
the large do not exceed gōng,
the small do not go beyond yǔ.
Thus heavy musical instruments follow the small,
light ones follow the large.
Therefore metal favors yǔ,
stone favors jué,
earthenware and silk favor gōng,
gourd and bamboo favor zhǐ,
leather and wood produce single tones.
Pitch pipes harmonize music,
pitch standards level the tones.
Metal and stone set them in motion,
silk and bamboo carry them forward,
poetry expresses them,
songs chant them,
gourd disseminates them,
earthenware supports them,
leather and wood rhythmizes them.
When things maintain their constancy, it is called musical perfection,
what perfection gathers is called sound,
when sounds respond and support each other, it is called harmony,
when small and large do not exceed, it is called balance.
Thus,
cast in metal,
polish in stone,
string on silk and wood,
perforate in gourd and bamboo,
rhythmize with drums and carry forward,
to follow the eight winds.
Guóyǔ"
Zhōu adopted the ritual music of six dynasties,
hence possessing Yúnmén, Xiánchí, Dàsháo, Dàyú, Dàxià, and Dàwǔ.
Lǔ received the ritual music of four dynasties,
therefore did not perform Yúnmén and Xiánchí,
to show there was reduction and diminution.
Yǐng Róng's "Chūnqiū Shìlì"
Duke Píng delighted in new music,
and Shī Kuàng said:
"The ducal house is likely to decline!
Your enlightenment shows signs of decay.
Music serves to spread the influence over mountains and rivers,
and to display virtue far and wide.
It spreads virtue to expand it,
influences mountains and rivers to extend it,
affects all things to make them attentive,
cultivates poetry to chant it,
and refines rites to regulate it.
When virtue is extensive and timely regulated,
then distant regions submit and nearby ones do not rebel.
Guóyǔ"
Shī Juān
lived during the time of Duke Líng of Wèi,
capable of transcribing the music of successive dynasties,
and skilled at composing new melodies to replace ancient tunes.
Thus, he created music for the four seasons.
In spring, there were songs like "Lí Hóng," "Qù Yàn," and "Yìng Pín";
in summer, tunes such as "Míng Chén," "Jiāo Quán," "Zhī Huá," and "Liú Jīn";
in autumn, melodies like "Shāng Biāo," "Bái Yún," "Luò Yè," and "Chuī Péng";
and in winter, pieces such as "Níng Hé," "Liú Yīn," and "Chén Yún."
These sounds of the four seasons,
when performed for Duke Líng,
caused the duke to indulge his emotions and become mentally confused,
neglecting affairs of governance.
Qú Bóyù remonstrated, saying:
"Although these may enliven the spirit and rhythm,
they ultimately amount to decadent and effeminate music,
unfitting for the refined and elegant,
and not what a subordinate should present to his lord."
Duke Líng then abandoned the new music and attended to governmental duties,
so the people of Wèi praised his transformative rule.
Shī Juān regretted having strayed from the principles of elegance and颂,
failing in the way of a minister,
and thus withdrew into seclusion.
Bóyù burned his musical instruments at the crossroads of the main thoroughfares,
fearing that later generations might imitate and create such music.
His songs were lost and forgotten,
their traces distant over the generations,
with only the general meaning of their titles recorded.
From "Shí Yí Jì"
When Confucius arrived in Qí,
he encountered an infant outside the outer city gate,
carrying a pot,
walking together with him.
The infant's gaze was sharp,
his heart upright,
his conduct proper.
Confucius said to the driver:
"Hurry and drive,
hurry and drive.
Just as the Sháo music was being performed,
Confucius arrived there,
and after hearing the Sháo music, for three months he did not notice the taste of meat.
Thus, music is not only for one's own enjoyment,
but also to bring joy to others;
not only for self-correction,
but also to correct others.
From "Shuō Yuàn"
Mount Dòngtíng floats upon the waters,
beneath which are hundreds of golden halls,
where the Emperor's daughter resides.
Throughout the four seasons, the sounds of stone chimes, strings, and bamboo flutes echo to the mountain's peak.
During the reign of King Huái of Chǔ,
he composed poetry with a gathering of talents by the water's edge.
Hence it is said: the music of Xiāo and Xiāng and Dòngtíng,
those who listen to it find it hard to grow old,
and even the melodies of "Xiánchí" and "Xiāosháo" cannot compare.
At each of the four mid-season festivals,
the King would circle the mountain to feast and roam.
Each time, they drew upon the energy of the mid-season
to create musical compositions.
Only in mid-spring, when the pitch pipe matches Jiázhōng,
did they compose the poem of gentle flowing waters,
feasting on the mountain's southern side.
When mid-summer arrived with the pitch of Ruíbīn,
they created the tunes of "Hàolù" and "Qiūshuāng".
"Shí Yí Jì"
Music is what the sage employs
to move heaven and earth, communicate with spirits, pacify the myriad people, and complete the nature of all beings.
Therefore, listeners all empty themselves and elevate their spirits,
joyfully receiving its flow,
so that throughout the realm, all know the sovereign's virtue,
are clothed in his influence,
their radiance daily renewed,
transformed by the ruler to advance in goodness,
yet unaware of how this comes about.
As for the myriad things not perishing prematurely,
heaven and earth are harmonious, and auspicious responses descend.
Hence, the Book of Songs says:
"The stone chimes and pipes resound sonorously,
abundant blessings descend profusely."
History of the Han Dynasty
Shěn Yuē's "Book of Sòng" states: Qín music was called Wǔxíng, changed by Qín Shǐhuáng.
Hàn music was called Wénshǐ, changed by Gāozǔ from the Sháo dance.
Wǔdé was created by Gāozǔ,
with dancers holding shields and axes,
symbolizing that music had been implemented and martial power used to eliminate chaos.
Ānshì was originally called Fángzhōng.
Qín changed it to Shòurén,
and Xiàohuì changed it to Ānshì.
Zhāoróng was created by Gāozǔ,
originating from Wǔdé.
Lǐróng was created by Gāozǔ,
originating from Wénshǐ and Wǔxíng.
Jiāzhì was created by Shūsūn Tōng,
to welcome the spirits.
Sìshí was created by Wéndì.
Zhāodé was created by Xiàowǔdì,
and offered at the Tàizōng Temple.
Shèngdé was created by Xiàoxuāndì,
and offered at the Tàizōng Temple.
Yúnqiào and Yùmìng were both Hàn music used to worship heaven and earth.
In the early Hàn dynasty, the Bāyú assisted Hàn and achieved merit,
so this dance was created.
Wèi music was called Zhāowǔ, changed from Hàn's Bāyú.
Zhèngshì changed from Hàn's Ānshì,
and also became the hymn for offering to spirits.
Yínglíng changed from Hàn's Jiāzhì.
Wǔsòng changed from Hàn's Wǔdé.
Zhāoyè changed from Hàn's Zhāoróng.
Fèngxiáng changed from Hàn's Yúnxiáng.
Língyìng changed from Hàn's Yùmìng.
Dàsháo changed from Hàn's Wénshǐ.
Dàwǔ changed from Hàn's Wǔxíng.
Those who perform elegant music
begin with "Yáng'ē" and "Cǎilíng."
In the Huáinán, when one sings "Cǎilíng,"
and strikes up "Yáng'ē,"
rustic listeners
find them inferior to "Yánlù" and "Yángjú."
Once, a musician from Hándān composed a new tune,
attributing it to Lǐ Qí,
and everyone vied to learn it.
Later, when they realized it was not his,
they all abandoned the melody,
showing they had never truly understood music.
Note: These are names of Chǔ music.
The Chǔcí states:
"Arrange bells and set drums for new songs,
cross the river, gather water chestnuts, and strike up Yáng'ē."
Jǐnán Gōng Yáo Yōng,
whose courtesy name was Zǐhé,
was the younger brother of Yáo Xìng.
He particularly enjoyed music,
and could master the nuances of its rise and fall,
adding and modifying melodies.
His works were widely circulated among his contemporaries,
and were known as
"Jǐnán's New Tunes"
From "Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms"
In the Northern Qí dynasty, Xìndū Fāng, the Field Section Adjutant of the Divine Martial Overlord's Headquarters, known as a master of musical tones,
could use pitch pipes to observe the seasonal ethers,
and interpret the colors of the clouds.
Once while conversing with someone,
he pointed to the sky and said:
"The ether of early spring has arrived."
When people went to check the pipes,
the flying ash had already responded.
Every month's observations
proved accurate without fail.
He also made twenty-four wheel fans,
burying them in the ground
to measure the twenty-four solar terms.
When each term's ether was sensed, one fan would move automatically,
while the other fans remained still,
corresponding with the pipe ashes,
as if matching tally and contract.
"Records of Ancient and Modern Music"
During Emperor Gāozōng's reign,
Crown Prince Zhānghuái composed the Bǎoqìng Melody,
which was performed at Tàiqīng Temple.
Lǐ Sìzhēn remarked to the monk Liú Gài:
"The gōng note does not summon the shāng note,
signifying discord between ruler and minister;
the jué and zhǐ notes conflict,
indicating suspicion between father and son.
The music contains many mournful death tones.
If the state remains untroubled,
the Crown Prince will bear the blame."
Soon the Crown Prince was deposed.
Sìzhēn often said:
"The Suí court's music bureau had the Tángtáng Melody,
which foretold the Táng dynasty's renewed mandate.
Nowadays there are songs of 'slanting tángtáng'
and 'shaking tángtáng'.
'Slanting'
means improper;
'shaking'
means perilous.
The Emperor's illness worsens daily,
all affairs are decided in the inner palace,
power is delegated to others,
and recovering it won't be easy.
Though the imperial clan is numerous,
controlling external matters from within,
their strength cannot match.
The princes will likely be trampled by the Empress,
I foresee turmoil arising soon."
His predictions all proved true.
From the "Táng History"
In the first month of the Shenlong era's first year,
an ancestral ceremony was held at the Grand Ancestral Temple in the Western Capital.
As the music began, the Grand Music Director,
Péi Zhīgǔ, secretly told the Magistrate of Wànnián, Yuán Xíngchōng:
"The metal and stone instruments harmonize smoothly and gracefully,
signifying a great celebration is approaching.
Could it be for the descendants of the Táng imperial house!"
That same month,
Emperor Táng Zhōngzōng was restored to the throne,
and the state was reestablished as Táng.
During the reign of Emperor Míng Huáng,
Liángzhōu presented a new musical composition.
The emperor summoned the various princes to observe it,
and Prince Níng remarked:
"Although this composition is elaborate,
I have some observations about it.
Now, music
begins with the gōng note, disperses through the shāng, and completes itself with jué, zhǐ, and yǔ—
all inevitably rooted in and governed by gōng and shāng.
This composition, however,
has gōng notes that are detached and lacking in zhǐ,
while the shāng notes are disordered and excessively forceful.
I have heard that gōng
represents the ruler;
shāng
represents the ministers.
If gōng is not dominant,
then the ruler's authority is weakened;
if shāng is excessive,
then the ministers' actions become presumptuous.
Weakened authority leads to oppression from below,
while presumption leads to violation of superiors.
Manifested in an instant,
taking form in sounds and tones,
spread through songs and chants,
it appears in human affairs.
I fear that one day there may be the calamity of exile and upheaval."
The emperor fell silent.
Indeed, when the Ān-Shì Rebellion occurred,
it became clear how profound Prince Níng's understanding of music was.
From "Records of Signs from the Kaiyuan and Tianbao Eras."
After the Tiānbǎo era,
many lyricists expressed sentiments of exile and wandering,
and drew inspiration from rivers, lakes, and monastic temples,
while musical compositions were often named after border regions.
When these melodies reached their crescendo with complex harmonies,
they were called
"rùpò"
(breaking into the finale),
signifying a shattering intensity.
From "Táng Wǔxíng Zhì"
Sòng Shěn was skilled in music theory.
The court music had long lost the Zhǐ mode,
but Shěn restored it by studying bell temperament.
"Supplement to the National History"
Zhèng Cóngdǎng was in Biàn when,
because his elder brother Chǔhuì,
had often served as garrison commander,
and died in this commandery,
until the end of his administration and succession,
he did not perform music in the official office.
"Book of Táng"
In the early Qingtai era of the Later Táng Dynasty,
Wáng Rényù served as an aide in Liángyuàn,
under the command of Fàn Yánguāng.
In the first month of spring,
when the countryside was still cold,
he led his officials
to bid farewell to a court guest at Willow Willow Pavilion.
The music was played in the Yǔ mode,
yet the sound uniquely carried the Gōng note,
creating discord.
Wáng alone was surprised by this,
and privately said to Lǐ Jùtáng Xiàn:
"Today, there must be an event of deceit or turmoil,
for the musical tones are not harmonious;
now we perform in Yǔ,
but there is a Gōng sound.
Moreover, Yǔ corresponds to water,
and Gōng to earth;
water and earth conflict with each other—
could it be that there is no cause for worry?"
Soon after the banquet ended,
Fàn led the guests,
with hawks and hounds,
on a grand hunt north of Wángpó Inn.
He fell from a galloping horse,
and could not be saved there.
From late morning until after noon,
he lost consciousness and then revived.
"Jade Hall Casual Talk"
Wáng Rényù was naturally knowledgeable about musical tones and temperament.
In the early years of Gāozǔ's reign,
he established the ceremonial music and held a banquet for all officials at Chéngfú Hall.
When the huángzhōng note was played,
Wáng Rényù heard it
and said:
"The sound is not purely solemn, yet harmoniously resonant;
there must be conflict arising within the palace walls."
Soon after,
two military officers fought outside Shēnglóng Gate,
their clamor heard inside the palace,
and people considered him prescient.
(From the History of the Five Dynasties)
Music serves to honor the ancestral temples above,
and transform the common people below.
Records of the Grand Historian
The "Erya Shí Yuè" states:
"Gōng is called heavy,
shāng is called swift,
jué is called constant,
zhǐ is called successive,
yǔ is called willow."
Guō Pú notes: These are all alternative names for the five notes,
but their meanings are not recorded.
Liú Xīn says: Gōng means
central,
sovereign,
serving as the framework for the four other notes,
its sound is deep and weighty,
like the virtue of a sovereign,
hence it is called heavy.
Shāng means
manifest,
minister,
its sound is swift and rapid,
like the integrity of a minister, hence it is called swift.
Jué means
contact,
common people,
its sound is rounded and enduring, constant and penetrating, clear and turbid like the image of the people, hence it is called constant.
Zhǐ means
blessing,
affairs,
its sound rises and falls in continuous succession,
its tone resembles the continuity of affairs, hence it is called successive.
Yǔ means
cosmos,
things,
its sound is low and even, veiled and shimmering, rising from below to above.
The five notes combine to form harmony,
like the gathering of things,
hence it is called willow."
Xú Jīng'ān's "Book of Music"
Liú Shào's "Book of Pitch Pipes" states: When spring offices follow autumn's pitch pipes,
all plants must wither.
When autumn offices follow spring's pitch pipes,
all things must flourish.
When summer offices follow winter's pitch pipes,
rain and hail must fall.
When winter offices follow summer's pitch pipes,
thunder must sound.
Now music is of utmost importance,
for its influence is great.
Therefore it is said: Those who understand the essence of ritual and music can create them,
those who understand the form of ritual and music can transmit them.
"Fēngsú Tōng"
Hearing the gōng note,
all becomes warm, refined, and harmonious.
Wǔ Jīng Tōng Yì Hearing the shāng note,
all leads to decisiveness and resolution of affairs.
Hándān Chuò Wǔ Jīng Zhé Yí Hearing the jué note,
all evokes compassion and benevolence.
Hearing the zhǐ note,
all fosters nurturing and generosity.
Tōng Yì
There are eight types of musical instruments,
namely, the leather drum, the metal chime, the stone qin and se, the silk xiao and drum, the bamboo xun, the earth zhu and yu, the wood sheng, and the gourd instruments,
these are called the eight tones.
"The Essential Meaning of the Five Classics"
In the Rites of Zhōu, bells and chime stones are all arranged in sets and hung,
with two eights making sixteen on one frame,
which is called a set of chime stones.
One set is called a series.
The Spring and Autumn Annals states: two series of singing bells,
this is what it refers to.
They performed the music of the four barbarians,
to illuminate virtue and grace,
widely extending to the four corners.
The music of the Eastern barbarians is called Mòlí,
the music of the Southern barbarians is called Rèn,
the music of the Western barbarians is called Jìn,
the music of the Northern barbarians is called Mèi.
"General Meaning of the Five Classics"
Fúxī created the qin,
to cultivate one's character and regulate one's nature,
returning to one's innate purity.
"Qín Cāo"
Fúxī carved paulownia wood to make a qin.
Its rounded top follows the law of Heaven,
its flat base symbolizes Earth,
the eight-inch dragon pool connects the eight winds,
the four-inch phoenix pond represents the four seasons.
Cài Yōng's "Discourse on the Qin"
The qín is
the master of music.
Gentlemen often play it and never part from their person,
unlike bells and drums which are displayed in ancestral temples or hung in rows on racks.
Because its size is moderate,
and its sounds harmonious.
Its loud tones are not clamorous and unrestrained,
nor are its soft tones obscured and inaudible.
It is perfectly suited to harmonize human emotions
and inspire virtuous thoughts.
From "Fēngsú Tōng"
The qín is
that which restrains,
restraining from evil,
in order to rectify the human heart.
From the Báihǔ Tōng.
The qín is three chǐ, six cùn, and six fēn in length,
and six cùn in width.
The upper pattern is called the "chí,"
and the lower is called the "bīn."
It is wider in the front and narrower in the back,
symbolizing the distinction between noble and humble.
The top is round, and the bottom is square,
emulating heaven and earth.
The five strings represent the five elements,
with the large string as the ruler,
and the small strings as the ministers.
King Wén and King Wǔ added two strings to harmonize the bond between ruler and ministers.
"Qín Cāo" states: King Wén added one,
King Wǔ added one,
and today these two strings are called the Wén-Wǔ strings.
"Shì Zhìjiàng's Music Record" During the reign of Emperor Dézōng of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Ān Shuì,
renowned for his skill with the qín and his understanding of music.
Yáng Shōu asked about the two strings beyond the five,
inquiring what they were.
Shuì replied:
"They are said to have been added by King Wén and King Wǔ of the Zhōu dynasty."
Shōu said:
"Can you play the 'King Wén's Composition'?"
Shuì then played it with Huángzhōng as the gōng note,
using Shǎoshāng to respond to the large string.
Shōu said:
"Stop!
As you said,
Shǎoshāng
is the Wǔ string.
How could there be a Wǔ sound in the era of Wén?"
Shuì was greatly astonished.
"Táng Shū"
Fúxī created the qin,
with a width of six-tenths,

"Qín Cāo" Cài Yōng's "Qín Cāo" states: Fúxī made the qin,

"Yǎn Lián Zhū Jì" Shénnóng's sè and Fúxī's qin,

"Yuè Shū"
In ancient times, the supreme sage Fúxī Shì ruled the world.
He observed the celestial phenomena above,
surveyed the patterns of the earth below,
drew inspiration from distant objects,
and examined his own body nearby,
thus creating the Eight Trigrams for the first time,
and carving paulownia wood to make the qin.
From "The Book of the Qin."
The qín,
is for restraint,
made by Shénnóng,
with a hollowed-out bottom and refined silk strings,
originally had five strings,
to which the Zhōu dynasty added two more strings.
In the "Shuōwén," it is said that Shénnóng first made the five-stringed qín,
to encompass the notes gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, and yǔ,
and after nine generations, by the time of King Wén,
two more strings were added,
called shǎo gōng and shǎo shāng.
The "Dìwáng Shìjì" states that Shénnóng first carved a paulownia tree to make the qín,
and twisted silk into strings,
to connect with the virtue of the divine,
and harmonize with the balance of heaven and earth.
Today, the qín is four chǐ and five cùn long,
symbolizing the four seasons and the five elements.
It is also said: Shénnóng created the qín,
with seven strings sufficient to connect with all things and examine order and chaos.
In the "Huán Tán Xīnlùn," Shénnóng's qín
was three chǐ and six cùn long,
with five strings called
"gōng,"
"shāng,"
"jué,"
"zhǐ,"
and "yǔ."
King Wén added two strings,
called
"shǎo gōng"
and "shǎo shāng."
The "Guǎngyǎ" mentions that Shénnóng initially made the sè,
to return the spirit and reflect on aspirations,
and align with the heart of heaven.
The "Huáinánzǐ" also records this.
In ancient times, when Lord Zhūxiáng governed the world,
there was much wind and yang energy accumulated,
causing all things to disperse and disintegrate,
and fruits failed to ripen.
Therefore, Shì Dá created the five-stringed zither.
"Lǚshì"
The famous qín named Qīng Jué,
was the qín of Huángdì.
According to the "Compiled Essentials by Emperor Yuán of Liáng," Huángdì created the Qīng Jué,
to assemble spirits and deities atop Mount Tài.
As recorded in the "Hán Fēi Zǐ."
Yáo sent Wú Jù to make a qín,
with five strings.
The "Tōng Lǐ Zuǎn" states: "The Ecstasy of the Divine and Mortal,"
was composed by Emperor Yáo.
Yáo played the qín, moved the divine being to appear,
thus he created this composition.
Xiè Xīyì's "Discourse on the Qín"
Shùn played the five-stringed qin,
sang the poem of the Southern Breeze,
and the world was well-governed.
The poem of the Southern Breeze
is the music of growth and life,
which Shùn delighted in.
His joy harmonized with heaven and earth,
winning the hearts of all nations,
thus the world was well-governed.
"Records of Music" mentions the legacy of Chónghuá's melodies.
"Selection of Qín Fu" "The Way of the Qín" states: The melody of Shùn

he sighed with longing for his parents,

A note adds: Shùn played the five-stringed qin to transform the world,

Yáng Xióng's "Pure Essence of the Qín" records that Shùn traveled to Lìshān,
saw birds flying,
and, missing his parents, composed the "Melody of Longing for Parents."
"Ancient and Modern Records of Music."
Yǔ ascended Kuàijī,
this was done by Yǔ.
He channeled the rivers and ascended Mount Kuàijī,
from then on,
the common people descended from the hills,
the masses were peaceful and secure,
playing the qín to sigh for themselves.
"The Correct Music of the Great Zhōu"
In ancient times, when emperors performed the "Qīng Miào" hymn,
large zithers with plain strings were used in Wú and Yuè,
large zithers with vermilion strings were used in Wú and Yuè,
drums were made of leather,
and these were called bófǔ.
"Shàng Shū Dà Zhuàn"
The Song of Yuèshang,
was composed by the Duke of Zhōu.
The Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng in governance,
bringing peace to the world,
with all states harmoniously united.
Jiānghuáng paid tribute,
and Yuèshang, after passing through nine translations, came to offer gifts.
The Duke of Zhōu took up the qín and sang.
"The Music Master of the Great Zhōu"
Initially, when Mù Jiāng died,
he had them select fine catalpa wood,
intending it for his own coffin,
along with a eulogizing qin.
Zuǒ Zhuàn
The Marquis of Jìn inspected the armory,
where he saw Zhōng Yí,
and asked about his lineage.
He replied:
"I am a musician."
When given a zither,
he played a southern melody.
The lord said:
"This is a gentleman.
He speaks of his ancestors' duties,
showing he does not abandon his roots.
His music preserves his native airs,
proving he does not forget the old.
Initially, Duke Wèi had a favored concubine,
and had Shī Cáo teach her the qín.
Shī Cáo flogged her,
so the duke became angry,
and had Shī Cáo flogged three hundred times.
In the past,
Duke Líng of Wèi was about to go to Jìn.
When he reached the banks of the Pú River,
he unharnessed his carriage and let the horses graze,
setting up a lodging place to stay overnight.
At midnight,
he heard someone playing a new melody and was delighted by it.
He sent attendants to ask his retinue,
but all reported they had not heard it.
So he summoned Master Juān and told him:
"There is someone playing a new melody,
I sent attendants to ask my retinue,
but all reported they had not heard it.
It seems like the work of ghosts or spirits,
please listen and transcribe it for me."
Master Juān said:
"Yes."
Thereupon he sat quietly, playing the qin to transcribe it.
The next day, Master Juān reported:
"I have obtained it,
but have not yet practiced it,
please allow me another night to practice it."
Duke Líng said:
"Yes."
So they stayed another night.
The next day, after practicing it,
they proceeded to Jìn.
The Duke of Jìn hosted them at the Shīyí Terrace.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Duke Líng rose,
and said:
"There is a new melody,
I wish to present it for your enjoyment."
Duke Píng said:
"Excellent."
So he summoned Master Juān,
had him sit beside Master Kuàng,
and he took up the qin and played it.
Before he finished,
Master Kuàng stopped him by pressing on the strings,
saying:
"This is the music of a doomed state,
it should not be played to completion."
Duke Píng said:
"Where does this music come from?"
Master Kuàng said:
"This was composed by Master Yán,
who created decadent music for King Zhòu.
When King Wǔ attacked King Zhòu,
Master Yán fled east,
reaching the Pú River where he drowned himself.
Therefore, those who hear this music
must be by the banks of the Pú River.
The state whose ruler first hears this music
will surely decline,
it should not be played to completion."
Duke Píng said:
"What I love is music,
please let him finish playing it."
Master Juān played it to the end.
Duke Píng asked Master Kuàng:
"What is this music called?"
Master Kuàng said:
"This is what is called the Qīng Shāng."
The Duke said:
"Is the Qīng Shāng the most mournful of all?"
Master Kuàng said:
"It is not as mournful as the Qīng Zhǐ."
The Duke said:
"May I hear the Qīng Zhǐ?"
Master Kuàng said:
"No.
In ancient times, those who listened to the Qīng Zhǐ
were all rulers of virtue and righteousness.
Now my lord's virtue is shallow,
and not sufficient to hear it."
Duke Píng said:
"What I love is music,
I wish to try hearing it."
Master Kuàng had no choice,
so he took up the qin and played.
At the first playing,
sixteen black cranes
came following the road
from the south,
gathering on the ridgepole ends above the gate tower;
at the second playing they formed rows;
at the third playing,
they stretched their necks and sang,
spread their wings and danced,
their notes matching the gōng and shāng tones,
their voices heard in heaven.
Duke Píng was greatly pleased,
and all the seated guests were happy.
Duke Píng raised his cup and stood to toast Master Kuàng,
then returned to his seat and asked:
"Is no music more mournful than the Qīng Zhǐ?"
Master Kuàng said:
"It is not as mournful as the Qīng Jué."
Duke Píng said:
"May I hear the Qīng Jué?"
Master Kuàng said:
"No.
In the past, the Yellow Emperor assembled ghosts and spirits on Mount Tài,
riding an ivory carriage drawn by six蛟龍,
with the deity Bìfāng harnessing them,
Chīyóu leading in front,
the Wind Earl sweeping the way,
the Rain Master sprinkling the path,
tigers and wolves ahead,
ghosts and spirits behind,
flying snakes prostrate on the ground,
phoenixes covering above,
gathering all ghosts and spirits,
and created the Qīng Jué.
Now my lord's virtue is shallow,
and not sufficient to hear it.
If you hear it,
I fear there will be disaster."
Duke Píng said:
"I am old,
what I love is music,
I wish to hear it to completion."
Master Kuàng had no choice but to play it.
At the first playing, black clouds arose from the west;
at the second playing,
a great wind came,
followed by heavy rain,
tearing the curtains,
shattering the sacrificial vessels,
and destroying the corridor tiles.
The seated guests scattered and fled,
Duke Píng was terrified,
and crouched in the corridor room.
Jìn suffered a great drought,
with barren land for three years.
Duke Píng himself developed skin disease.
Therefore it is said: if one does not attend to governance,
but endlessly indulges in the five notes of music,
this is the way to personal ruin.
"Hánzǐ Běnguò" Master Kuàng played the qin,
communicating with the divine,
jade sheep and white magpies ascended branches and fluttered about.
"Ruìyìng Tú" When Duke Píng of Jìn spoke inappropriately,
Master Kuàng raised his qin and struck him with it,
causing him to stumble against the palace wall,
and his attendants wanted to repair it.
Duke Píng said:
"Leave it,
let this mark my fault."
Confucius said:
"It was not that Duke Píng did not feel physical pain,
but that he wanted to encourage remonstrance."
Hánzǐ heard of this,
and said:
"When ministers violate ritual and are not punished,
this is indulging fault.
This explains why Duke Píng failed to achieve hegemony."
"Huáinánzǐ Qísú" In the past,
when Master Kuàng played the music of White Snow, divine beings descended for it,
wind and rain suddenly arrived,
Duke Píng fell ill,
and Jìn suffered barren land.
"Shàng Lǎnmíng Xùn"
Confucius learned the qin from Master Xiāng.
Master Xiāng said:
"Although I hold office as a stone-chime player,
I am skilled in the qin.
You have now practiced the qin,
you may advance."
Confucius said:
"I have not yet mastered its technique."
After some time,
he said:
"You have mastered its technique,
you may advance."
Confucius said:
"I have not yet grasped its spirit."
After some time,
he said:
"You have grasped its spirit,
you may advance."
Confucius said:
"I have not yet perceived the character of its composer."
After some time,
he said: Confucius appeared deeply thoughtful,
gazing upward and looking into the distance.
He said:
"I now perceive the character of its composer.
He is dark-complexioned and tall,
with a lofty stature,
his vision encompassing all,
ruling over the four quarters.
Who but King Wén could have composed this?"
Master Xiāng rose from his mat, bowed with folded hands, and replied:
"You are a sage, my lord.
The tradition names it 'King Wén's Composition'."
Family Sayings
Confucius was playing the zither while resting indoors during the day,
when Mǐn Zǐ heard it from outside.
He told Zēng Zǐ:
"Earlier,
our Master's music
was clear, penetrating, and harmonious,
immersed in the ultimate Way.
But now,
it has changed to a somber and heavy tone.
Somberness arises from thoughts of profit and desire,
heaviness stems from greed for gain.
What could have moved our Master to be like this?
Let us go in together and ask him."
Zēng Zǐ replied:
"Agreed.
The two disciples entered
and questioned their Master.
The Master said:
"Indeed.
What you say is correct.
I had such thoughts.
Earlier I saw a cat about to catch a mouse,
and wishing for it to succeed,
I unconsciously expressed it in my music.
Do you two
wish to understand this?"
Zēng Zǐ answered:
"It was Mǐn Zǐ.
The Master said:
"He is worthy of understanding music.
The Congenital Sayings of Confucius
When Mǐn Zǐqiān had completed the three-year mourning period,
he appeared before Confucius.
Confucius gave him a zither,
and had him play it.
The melody was plaintive and sorrowful.
Confucius said:
"He is a noble man.
Though his grief is not yet exhausted,
he is able to cut it off in accordance with ritual.
The Family Sayings
When Róng Qǐqī played one tune,
Confucius was joyful for three days,
moved by the harmony.
When Zōu Jì played one melody,
King Wēi grieved all evening,
moved by the sorrow.
Moving the zithers and lutes,
expressing through sounds and tones,
they could make people feel sorrow or joy.
Yet hanging laws and setting rewards fail to transform customs and morals—
this is because sincere heart is not applied.
"Huái Zhǔ Xùn"
When Hù Bā played the qin, birds danced and fish leaped.
Zhèng Shīwén heard of this,
and abandoning his home, followed Shī Xiāng to study.
After three years, he still could not master a single piece.
Shī Xiāng said:
"You may return home now.
Shīwén set aside his qin and sighed:
"Please grant me a little more time,
to see what may come.
Not long after,
he again met with Shī Xiāng,
saying:
"I have attained it.
Thereupon, in spring he plucked the shang string to summon the nanlü mode,
and cool winds suddenly arrived,
causing plants and trees to bear fruit.
When autumn came, he plucked the jue string to excite the jiazhong mode,
and warm winds gently circulated,
causing plants and trees to bloom.
In summer, he plucked the yu string to summon the huangzhong mode,
and frost and snow fell together,
while rivers and ponds suddenly froze.
When winter arrived, he plucked the zhi string to excite the ruibin mode,
and sunlight blazed intensely,
causing solid ice to instantly melt.
As he concluded,
he commanded the gong note and gathered all four strings,
whereupon auspicious winds soared,
propitious clouds floated,
sweet dew descended,
and sweet springs gushed forth.
Shī Xiāng then pressed his hand to his heart and leaped up, saying:
"How sublime is your playing!
Even Shī Kuàng's 'Clear Horn' melody,
or Zōu Yǎn's pitch-pipe blowing,
could not surpass it.
Liezi
Bó Yá learned the qín from Master Chéng Lián.
Chéng Lián said:
"My teacher said that spring is in the ocean,
it can transform one's spirit.
So he took him to wander on Pénglái Mountain,
leaving Bó Yá there, saying:
"You stay here and practice,
I will bring your teacher to you.
He rowed his boat and left.
Bó Yá looked out,
but saw only the vast expanse of the sea,
the deep and dark mountains and forests,
and the mournful cries of birds and beasts.
He sighed and said:
"My teacher is going to transform my emotions.
So he took up his qín and sang.
When he finished,
Chéng Lián arrived.
Thus he became the most marvelous in the world,
and was called Lián the Immortal.
"Yuèfǔ Jiětí"
Bó Yá was skilled at playing the qin,
and Zhōng Zǐqī was skilled at listening.
When Bó Yá played the qin,
his thoughts were on climbing high mountains.
Zhōng Zǐqī said:
"How excellent!
Lofty and towering,
like Mount Tài.
When his thoughts were on flowing water,
Zhōng Zǐqī said:
"How excellent!
Vast and expansive,
like rivers and seas.
Whatever Bó Yá thought of,
Zhōng Zǐqī would surely grasp it.
《Liezi》 After Zhōng Zǐqī died,
Bó Yá broke his qin and severed its strings,
and never played the qin again for the rest of his life,
believing that there was no one in the world worth playing for.
《Lüshi》
Bó Yá was traveling on the northern side of Mount Tài,
when he was suddenly caught in a violent storm.
He took shelter under a cliff,
and feeling sorrowful in his heart,
he took up his qín and began to play.
At first, he played a melody resembling continuous rain,
then he created sounds like collapsing mountains.
Every time he played a piece,
Zhǒng Zǐqī would fully grasp its essence.
Bó Yá then set aside his qín and sighed, saying:
"How splendid,
how splendid!
Your listening is profound!
Your perception and imagination match my very heart.
Where could I hide my music from you?"
From "Lièzǐ"
In ancient times, when Hù Bā played the se, swimming fish emerged;

Dappled horses,

Annotation
Zhōu Shī Jīng was playing the qin,
when Wèi Wén Hóu began to dance,
and declared:
"Let no one contradict my words.
Shī Jīng took up his qin and struck at Wèi Wén Hóu but missed,
hitting and shattering the beads of his crown.
Wèi Wén Hóu said to his attendants:
"For a minister to strike his lord,
what is the crime?
The attendants replied:
"The crime warrants being boiled alive.
They dragged Shī Jīng down one level of the hall.
Shī Jīng said:
"May I speak one word before I die?
Wèi Wén Hóu said:
"You may.
Shī Jīng said:
"In ancient times, when Yáo and Shùn were rulers,
they only feared that no one would contradict their words.
When Jié and Zhòu were rulers,
they only feared that someone would contradict them.
I struck at Jié and Zhòu,
not at my lord.
Wèi Wén Hóu said:
"Release him!
This was my fault.
Hang the qin on the city gate,
to serve as my tally of warning;
do not mend the crown beads to serve as my admonition.
Same in Shuō Yuàn and Shí'èr Guó Shǐ.
Zōu Jìzǐ gained an audience with King Wēi by playing the qin,
and King Wēi, pleased, lodged him in the right chamber.
After a short while,
the king played the qin,
and Zōu Jìzǐ pushed the door open, entered, and said:
"Excellent!
This qin playing!"
The king suddenly became displeased,
put aside the qin, placed his hand on his sword, and said:
"You, sir, have seen the surface but not examined the details,
how do you know it is excellent?"
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"The thick strings, deep and warm like spring,
represent the ruler;
the thin strings, clear and distinct,
represent the minister;
the deep pressing,
and the joyful release,
represent government decrees;
harmonious in sound,
mutually beneficial in large and small,
twisting yet not harming each other,
represent the four seasons.
This is how I know it is excellent."
The king said:
"Well spoken about music."
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"Why only music?
Governing the state and pacifying the people are all within it."
The king again suddenly became displeased,
and said:
"As for discussing the principles of the five notes,
indeed, no one surpasses you, sir.
But as for governing the state and pacifying the people,
what have they to do with the strings of the qin?"
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"The thick strings, deep and warm like spring,
represent the ruler;
the thin strings, clear and distinct,
represent the minister;
the deep pressing and joyful release,
represent government decrees;
harmonious in sound,
mutually beneficial in large and small,
twisting yet not harming each other,
represent the four seasons.
That which repeats without chaos
is what brings about orderly prosperity;
that which is connected and direct
is what determines survival or demise.
Therefore it is said: when the qin's tones are in tune, all under heaven is well governed.
For governing the state and pacifying the people,
there is nothing like the five notes."
The king said:
"Excellent."
Zōu Jìzǐ had an audience for three months and then received the seal of the minister.
"Records of the Grand Historian": The thick strings
represent the ruler,
broad, harmonious, and warm;
the thin strings
represent the minister,
pure, incorruptible, and not chaotic.
"Qín Cāo"
Yìnghóu and Jiǎ Wǔzǐ were sitting together,
when they heard the sound of someone playing the qin.
Yìnghóu said:
"Why is the qin's music so sorrowful today?
Jiǎ Wǔzǐ replied:
"When the strings are taut and the tuning is low,
it naturally makes it sorrowful.
Taut strings
represent excellent material,
while low tuning
symbolizes low official rank.
To take excellent material and give it low rank,
how could it not be sorrowful?
Yìnghóu said:
"Well said.
"Shuō Yuàn"
Yōngmén Zhōu visited Lord Mèngcháng with his zither.
"Can playing the zither also make me feel sorrow?"
He replied:
"Those whom I can make feel sorrow
are those who were once noble but are now lowly,
who were wealthy in the past but are poor now,
pressed into narrow alleys,
cut off from neighbors on all sides.
Or those with outstanding talent,
holding genuine integrity,
yet encountering slander and calumny,
accumulating resentment and losing trust;
or those who formed joyful bonds and love,
only to part without enmity,
traveling to distant, isolated lands,
with no hope of reunion;
or those orphaned in youth,
without wife or children in adulthood,
living in the wild marshes as neighbors outdoors,
dwelling in dug-out hovels as homes indoors,
struggling daily,
with nowhere to turn for help.
For such people,
merely hearing the cry of flying birds,
or the autumn wind rustling branches,
brings heartache.
When I play the zither for them with long, unceasing notes,
none fail to feel anguish and shed tears.
But as for you, my lord,
you reside in grand mansions and lofty halls,
with interconnected gates and spacious rooms,
silk curtains hanging low,
cool breezes wafting in,
entertainers performing before you,
flatterers attending by your side,
singing the stirring 'Jíchǔ',
dancing like the beauties of Zhèng,
melodious sounds delighting your ears,
alluring sights captivating your eyes.
On water, you ride dragon boats,
raising feathered banners,
drumming in unfathomable depths.
In the wilds, you ascend plains,
gallop through vast parks,
shooting down high-flying birds with powerful crossbows,
pitting brave men against fierce beasts,
setting feasts for amusement,
drinking deeply, forgetting to return.
At such times,
you regard heaven and earth as less than a finger's breadth,
and even if there were a skilled zither player,
he could not move you, my lord.
Lord Mèngcháng said:

Once, Confucius was playing the se,
while Zengzi and Zigang listened by the side door.
When the melody ended,
Zengzi said:
"Alas!
Our master's se music seems to contain the ambition of a greedy wolf,
and the conduct of wickedness and depravity.
How unkind it is,
so excessively pursuing profit!"
Zigang found this reasonable,
but without responding, he entered.
The master noticed Zigang had the expression of one about to remonstrate about a fault,
and the demeanor of facing a difficulty,
so he set aside the se and waited for him.
Zigang then reported Zengzi's words.
The master said:
"Ah!
That Shen is a worthy man of the world,
and well-versed in understanding music!
Earlier,
when I was playing the se,
a mouse came out wandering,
a wildcat appeared in the room,
crept stealthily along the beam,
approached it but missed,
crouching with its back arched,
trying to catch it but failing.
I then expressed this through excessive tones on the se,
so Shen thought I was greedy, wolf-like, wicked, and depraved—
is that not fitting?
The Book of Songs says:

Zǐlù played the se,
and there was a sound of the northern borderlands.
Confucius heard it,
and said:
"Indeed,
Yóu is untalented."
Rǎn Yǒu was in attendance,
and the Master said:
"Qiú!
Come.
Why did you not tell Yóu?
The ancient kings' regulation of music
was to perform central tones,
making central rhythms,
flowing towards the south,
not returning to the north.
The south
is the region of growth and nurture;
the north
is the domain of killing and warfare.
Therefore the gentleman holds to the mean as foundation,
and focuses on life as basis.
Thus his music is gentle and centered,
symbolizing the energy of growth and nurture,
so that feelings of sorrow, affection, grief and pain
do not burden the heart,
and actions of violence, harshness, excess and recklessness
do not reside in the body.
Such being the case,
this is the air of orderly preservation,
the way of peace and joy.
But petty men are not like this -
they grasp the trivial to discuss the fundamental,
and focus on harshness as basis.
Thus their music is shrill and slight,
symbolizing the energy of killing and warfare,
so that feelings of harmony, moderation, centrality and correctness
do not burden the heart,
and actions of gentleness, dignity, respect and solemnity
do not reside in the body.
Now killing
is the air of chaos and ruin,
the way of defeat and flight.
In ancient times, Shùn performed the sounds of the southern wind,
and his rise was sudden,
to this day rulers speak of it without ceasing;
Zhòu made the sounds of the northern borderlands,
and his fall was swift,
to this day it is considered laughable.
Now Yóu,
a mere commoner,
a lowly cloth-clad man,
has neither regard for the ancient kings' regulations,
and moreover possesses the sounds of a fallen state -
how can he preserve his seven-foot body!"
Rǎn Yǒu reported this to Zǐlù,
and Zǐlù said:
"It is Yóu's fault.
A petty man cannot extricate himself and falls into this -
the Master's words are appropriate."
Thereupon he repented,
refused to eat,
and after seven days was nothing but skin and bones.
Confucius said:
"Yóu's fault has been corrected."

"Unofficial Biography"
Emperor Xuánzōng once held court,
and from time to time pressed his abdomen up and down with his fingers.
After the court session ended,
Gāo Lìshì approached and said:
"Your Majesty repeatedly pressed your abdomen with your fingers earlier,
could it be that the imperial body is slightly unwell?"
Emperor Xuánzōng replied:
"That is not the case.
Last night I dreamed of visiting the Moon Palace,
where various immortals entertained me with music from the highest purity,
resonant and clear,
almost beyond what mortals can hear.
After being deeply intoxicated for a long time,
they performed pure music together to send me back.
The melody was poignant and moving,
lingering faintly in my ears.
I have just recovered it completely using my jade flute.
During the court session,
I feared I might forget it,
so I carried the jade flute with me,
and from time to time traced the melody up and down,
not because of any discomfort."
Lìshì bowed again in congratulations and said:
"This is an extraordinary event!
I wish Your Majesty would play it for your servant."
The Emperor attempted to play it,
and the sound was ethereal and indescribable.
Lìshì again bowed and requested the name of the piece,
to which the Emperor smiled and said:
"This piece is called
'Zǐyún Huí' (Purple Clouds Return),
recorded in the music archives,
and now the Court of Imperial Sacrifices has engraved it on stone."
"Records of Messages from the Kaiyuan and Tianbao Eras"
Lǐ Mó,
during the Kāiyuán era, was the foremost flute player,
and had reason to visit Yuèzhōu.
At that time, ten local scholars who had passed the imperial examinations
jointly invited him for a boat outing on the lake.
Among the flute players present was Dúgū Wén, who sat with them,
and gradually the boat moved to the center of the lake.
Lǐ played his flute once,
and the water and trees grew eerily still,
as if spirits and ghosts had arrived.
The seated guests took turns praising him,
yet Dúgū Wén remained silent.
Lǐ resented his disrespect,
then quietly composed another melody,
even more exquisitely flawless,
but still received no admiration or astonishment.
Lǐ took out another flute, polished it, and offered it to Dúgū, saying:
"This one is quite unworthy,
only suitable for those with basic skills."
Dúgū then exchanged it and said:
"When it reaches the 'breaking' section, it will surely crack—do you mind?"
Lǐ apologized, not daring to play.
So Dúgū played, the sound soaring to the clouds,
shaking all present with awe.
Lǐ stood nervously, not daring to move.
When he reached the thirteenth repetition,
he pointed out the flaws in Lǐ's performance,
and Lǐ respectfully acknowledged, about to bow.
As he played on,
the flute indeed cracked,
and the piece was left unfinished.
Lǐ bowed again in reverence,
and all were struck with awe before dispersing.
"Unofficial History"
Emperor Míng Huáng returned from Shǔ,
residing in the Southern Palace.
Late at night, he ascended the government tower and leaned against the railing,
gazing southward at the misty moonlight filling his view.
Hóng Táo, Consort Yáng's attendant, was present there,
singing the lyrics of "Liáng Zhōu,"
which were composed by the Consort herself.
The Emperor personally played the jade flute to accompany the melody,
and when the song ended, they looked at each other, all unable to hold back their tears.
The Emperor then expanded the melody.
"The Unofficial Biography"
During the Kaiyuan era,
Lǐ Mó was skilled at playing the flute,
unrivaled in his time.
Huángfǔ Zhèng, the Governor of Yuè Prefecture, was boating on Mirror Lake on a moonlit night,
and ordered Lǐ Mó to play the flute.
Lǐ Mó performed with utmost mastery.
At that time, an old man was listening from a boat,
and as he played one note,
the lake waves shook,
and Lǐ Mó's flute split in the middle.
The old man then took out a flute from his bosom to finish the piece.
Huángfǔ Zhèng looked and
saw three dragons hovering over the boat listening.
When the old man finished the piece, he handed the flute to Lǐ Mó,
but when Lǐ Mó tried to play it, it produced no sound,
and the old man had also disappeared.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Music Bureau"
Lǐ Dān was fond of doing good deeds.
He once obtained a smoked bamboo from a village cottage,
cut it into a flute,
which was as hard as iron or stone,
and gave it to Lǐ Mó.
Mó was the finest flute player in the world.
One moonlit night while boating on the river,
he played the flute with his fellow passengers,
the sound clear and far-reaching.
Suddenly, a stranger on the bank hailed the boat and asked for a ride.
After boarding,
he requested the flute and played it,
demonstrating exceptional skill,
powerful enough to crack mountains and rocks.
Mó had never witnessed such mastery in his life.
As the melody reached its climax, the flute shattered under the player's breath and fingers,
and the stranger vanished without a trace.
The boatman, noting this, suspected he was a flood dragon.

Xǔ Yúnfēng was a musician skilled in playing the flute.
In the early Zhēnyuán era,
Wéi Yìngwù was transferred from the position of Lántái Lang to become the Governor of Hézhōu,

leaving him quite discontented.
Sailing east on a light boat,
he moored at night,
and they conversed for a long time.
Wéi Yìngwù said:
"I have a wet nurse,
whose son was named Qiānjīn.
During the Tiānbǎo era, he learned the flute from Lì Gòngfèng,
but upon mastering the art, he passed away.
I often lament this,
and the old flute he played
was a gift from Master Lǐ.
He then took out the old flute from a bag.
Yúnfēng knelt and received it,
grieving deeply as he caressed and examined it,
saying:
"It is indeed a fine flute,
but not the one my maternal grandfather played.
He then said to Wéi Yìngwù:
"Bamboo grows south of Yúnmèng,
and its quality is discerned beneath the Kē Tíng.
If it sprouts before the full moon of the seventh month this year,
and is cut before the full moon of the seventh month next year,
if harvested late,
its sound becomes dull;
if cut prematurely,
its sound becomes hollow.
Hollow bamboo is glossy outside but dry inside,
and dryness means it has not fully absorbed the vital energy.
Without full energy,
the bamboo is flawed. Truly superior music,
with one note rising and falling,
embodies nine breaths—the pinnacle of ancient music.
One piece has twelve sections,
each section twelve beats.
In today's renowned music,
such as the flowing melody of 'Falling Plum Blossoms,'
it moves wanderers at Jīngǔ Garden;
or 'Breaking Willow,' conveying emotion,
saddens garrison soldiers at Yùguān Pass.
Though these have clear and unique tones,
without the highest form of music, one cannot invoke spirits or pray for blessings.
Flawed bamboo will surely break when met with supreme music,
which is how I know this is not the flute my grandfather played.
Wéi Yìngwù said:
"I wish to trust your judgment; if the flute breaks, it's no loss.
Yúnfēng then held the flute and played it.
Before even one section was completed,
it suddenly split in the middle.
Wéi Yìngwù marveled in astonishment for a long time,
and thereafter honored Yúnfēng in the music department.
From "Gān Zé Yáo".
Merchant Lǚ Yūnqīng once moored his boat by Junshan Mountain on a mid-spring night,
called for wine and played several tunes on his flute.
Suddenly, an old man approached in a small boat
and produced three flutes from his sleeves:
the first was as large as encircling arms,
the second was of the size commonly used by ordinary people,
and the third was extremely small, like a thin brush handle.
Yūnqīng asked the old man to play one,
to which the old man replied:
"The largest one
plays the music of the heavens, which cannot be sounded;
the second one
is for playing in harmony with the immortals in their grotto-heavens;
the smallest one
is what I and my companions use for enjoyment.
I shall try to play it for you,
though I do not know if I can complete a single tune."
After speaking,
he took up the flute and blew three notes.
The wind stirred over the lake,
waves surged and swelled,
fish and dragons leaped and spouted,
with the fifth and sixth notes,
birds and beasts on Junshan Mountain cried out,
the moonlight grew dim,
and the boatmen were terrified.
The old man then stopped.

it no longer produced any sound.

Wáng Wéi was exceptionally skilled at playing the pipa,

Wáng Wéi was about to take the imperial examinations,

Prince Qí had Wáng Wéi dress in bright, new clothes,

and accompany him to the princess's residence.
He was ordered to perform a new melody,

The princess asked:

Prince Qí then recommended him, saying:

The princess smiled and said to Wáng Wéi:

Wáng Wéi rose and humbly expressed his gratitude.

Emperor Dézōng ordered him to revise music with the court musicians,

Yǎn looked at those laughing and suddenly,

"As you play the music, there is something unacceptable among you.
The emperor, startled, asked him about it.
He immediately pointed at a pipa player,
saying:
"This man has committed grave treason and cruelty, and also violated the law;

Then he pointed at a sheng player,
saying:
"This man's spirit has already wandered to the graveyard;

The emperor was then astonished,
and ordered the supervisor to secretly investigate them.
Soon after, the pipa player was accused by his peers,
who reported that six or seven years earlier his wife had hanged herself,
though the exact reason was unknown;
the emperor then ordered an interrogation, and he confessed to his crime.
The sheng player, out of worry and fear, stopped eating and died.
Afterward, the musicians dared not look Yǎn directly in the eye.

During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a premier pipa player named Kāng Kūnlún.
Due to a rain-prayer music competition between the two markets,
Kūnlún ascended a decorated tower on the main street and played a piece,
the newly composed "Green Waist" in the Yǔ mode,
believing himself to be unrivaled.
When the gallants of West Street were enjoying the music,
the East Market slightly mocked him,
and also appeared on a decorated tower.
A woman first held her instrument and said:
"I will also play this piece.
Moreover, she transposed it into the Fēngxiāng mode.
As soon as she plucked the strings, the sound was like thunder,
absolutely marvelous and divine.
Kūnlún was astonished,
and immediately bowed, asking to become her disciple.
When the woman changed clothes and came out,
it turned out to be the monk Shànběn,
whose secular surname was Duàn.
The next day,
Emperor Dézōng summoned him to the palace,
and ordered him to teach Kūnlún.
Master Duàn said:
"First, please let him play a tune,
then I will adjust it.
The master said:
"Why is your skill so mixed?
It also carries heterodox sounds.
Kūnlún exclaimed in surprise:
"Master Duàn,
you are a divine being!
When I was young and first learning the art,
I happened to receive instruction on the first-grade string tuning
from a female shaman in the neighborhood.
Afterward, I repeatedly changed teachers and learned from several masters.
Now, Master, your discernment is so profound and marvelous!
Master Duàn reported to the emperor:
"Please have Kūnlún stay away from musical instruments for over ten years,
wait until he forgets his original habits,
then he can be taught.
The emperor approved the request,
and indeed, Kūnlún later mastered all of Master Duàn's skills.

"I have taught many people!
Never before have I encountered a disciple with such innate talent."
Once, on a clear night, he carried his instrument to the Píngquán Villa by the pond and played by the water.
When he performed in the Bīn mode, sounds seemed to emerge from among the lotus leaves,
and fish leaped in response.
When he switched to another mode,
all fell silent.
Upon resuming the Bīn mode,
after a while,
an object was tossed from the pond onto the bank.
Upon inspection, it was a piece of a fāngxiǎng (metallophone),
likely because the iron resonated harmoniously with the musical tones.
Such was the marvel of his artistry.

The sun and moon radiate splendor,
dawn follows upon dawn."
The eight feudal lords all came forward,
bowed their heads and said:
"Brilliant is the high heaven,
resplendent are the stars.
The sun and moon radiate splendor,
vast is the universe with one sovereign."
The Emperor then sang again, saying:
"The sun and moon have their constant course,
the stars and constellations have their paths.
The four seasons follow their regular order,
all the people are truly sincere.
In our discussion of music,
we match the numinous power of Heaven."

Emperor Yáo ascended the throne,

Zhì imitated the sounds of mountains, forests, and valleys to sing,

The woman of Túshān ordered her handmaid to await Yǔ,

The two beautiful women of the Yǒusōng clan,

the two women composed a song,

Xià's Kǒng Jiǎ hunted at Fù Mountain in Dōngyáng,
took a commoner's child as his own,
when grown, the child was struck by an axe,
cutting off his feet,

Zhōu Zhāo Wáng personally led an expedition against Jīng and perished in Hànzhōng,

"Lǚ's Annals": The song of Túshān awaiting a person,
began the southern music;
the ballad of Yǒusōng about the flying swallow,
began the northern music;
Xià Jiǎ lamented in Dōngyáng,
the eastern music arose;
Yīn Máo longed for Xīhé,
the western music flourished.
The evolution of music and sounds,
is not uniform.
"The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons": Xià Jiǎ composed the "Song of the Broken Axe,"
thus began the eastern music;
Yīn Xīn created decadent music,
thus began the northern music;
the customs of Zhèng and Wèi favored licentiousness,
hence there were songs of Zhēn and Wěi and trysts in the mulberry groves;
the customs of Chǔ and Yuè favored bravery,
thus there were songs of charging into boiling water and treading on fire,
each singing of their preferences,
chanting of their desires.

King Zhòu imprisoned King Wén in Yǒulǐ.
Dàdiān, Hóngyāo, Sànyìshēng, Nángōng Kuò, and their companions
went to see King Wén.
King Wén, by means of his shin: turning his eyes backward
meant that Zhòu was fond of women;
patting his belly
meant that he desired rare treasures;
stamping his feet
meant that they should act swiftly.
Thereupon they traveled throughout the land,
traversed fertile territories,
obtained two beautiful women,
a great treasure from the water,
a white horse with a crimson mane,
and presented them to Zhòu,
displaying them in his central courtyard.
They said:
"These are the treasures of the Earl of the West,
to redeem his punishment."
Zhòu said:
"How generous he is to me!"
He immediately released the Earl of the West.
Zhòu said to Yìshēng:
"The one who slandered the Marquis of Qí
has a long nose and protruding ears."
Yìshēng returned
and reported the description to King Wén,
who then knew that it was Chóng Hóuhǔ who had slandered him.
When King Wén was in Yǒulǐ,
he expanded the Eight Trigrams into sixty-four hexagrams,
and composed the words of the Yùkāo.
Leaning on a rock,
entangled in thorns,
he gave vent to his indignation by composing a song, saying:
"The way of Yīn is murky,
soaked in filth and vexation.
Vermilion and purple intermingled,
without distinction.
Confused by music and women,
believing in flattering words.
The tiger in the court,
has brought me distress.
In the secluded prison,
who can speak for me?
Innocent and shackled,
who will proclaim it?
Meeting us four men,
all anxious and diligent.
Obtaining these rare treasures,
we temporarily avert great calamity.
In haste we fulfill our mission,
leaving it to posterity.
Creating these symbolic changes,
the omen lies in Chāng.
Reverently receiving the ancestral command,
Heaven does not destroy us.
Thus we shall oversee the land,
in sagely brilliance.
Punishing the violent, eliminating chaos,
executing the rebellious king."

mountains and hills rise from the earth.

Duke Āi sent envoys with gifts to Wèi to welcome the Master, but he passed away,
unable to bestow rewards.
Thus, the Master composed the "Song of the Hillocks," saying:
"I climb those hillocks,
with their winding slopes.
The way of benevolence is near,
yet seeking it feels far.
Lost and unable to return,
I bring distress upon myself.
Sighing, I turn my thoughts,
gazing upon Mount Tài.
Lush and towering its heights,
Liángfǔ winds around it.
Thorns block the path,
with no way to ascend.
Wanting to cut them, but lacking an axe,
I fret as they spread wildly.
Pondering with endless sighs,
tears fall in streams."
The Kǒng Cóng Zǐ
The King of Chǔ sent an envoy with gold and silk to invite the Master.
Zǎi Yǔ and Rǎn Yǒu said:
"The Master's Way,
will now be put into practice.
They then requested an audience,
and asked the Master:
"Tài Gōng diligently cultivated himself and endured hardships,
meeting King Wén at the age of eighty.
How does he compare to Xǔ Yóu in worthiness?
The Master said:
"Xǔ Yóu was one who perfected only himself,
while Tài Gōng benefited the whole world.
However, in this age there is no ruler like King Wén,
so even if there were a Tài Gōng,
who would recognize him?
He then sang:
"The Great Way is hidden, with ritual as foundation,
The worthy flee, awaiting the proper time,
When all under heaven are united, where would one go?
Shūsūn Shì's chariot driver said:
"Chú Shāng, while gathering firewood in the wilderness, captured a beast,
which none could recognize,
deeming it inauspicious,
and abandoned it at the crossroads of Wǔfù.
Rǎn Yǒu informed the Master, saying:
"With a deer's body and fleshy horns,
could it be a heavenly beast?"
The Master said:
"Where is it now?
I shall go and see it.
Thereupon he went,
and said to his charioteer Gāo Chái:
"According to Rǎn Yǒu's words,
must it not be a qilin?"
Arriving and looking at it,
it indeed was so.
Yán Yǎn asked, saying:
"Among flying creatures,
the phoenix is revered;
among running creatures,
the qilin is revered;
because they are hard to encounter.
May I ask, whose coming does its appearance signify now?"
He responded, saying:
"When the Son of Heaven spreads virtue,
and is about to bring about great peace,
then the qilin, phoenix, tortoise, and dragon first appear as auspicious signs.
Now the Zhou dynasty is about to perish,
and there is no true ruler under heaven,
for whom then has it come?"
Thereupon he wept and said:
"My relation to other people
is like the qilin's relation to other beasts.
The qilin has appeared only to die,
my Way has reached its end!"
Then he sang, saying:
"In the age of Táng and Yú, the qilin and phoenix roamed,
now it is not their time—what do I seek?
O qilin, o qilin, my heart is grieved.
End
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ marched south to attack Chǔ,
but the ferry official was drunk and asleep, unable to cross.
Summoning him, he intended to execute him.
The ferry official's daughter Juān, holding an oar, stepped forward
and said:
"Previously, my father heard that you, my lord, were crossing an unpredictable river to the east,
fearing the rise of wind and waves,
so he prayed to the mountain and river deities of Jiǔjiāng,
unable to resist the sorcerer's toasts,
drank cup after cup until deeply intoxicated and thus ended up in this state.
I, your humble servant, wish to exchange my lowly body for my father's life.
As Jiǎnzǐ was about to cross,
one person was short for handling the oars,
Juān offered to fill the position.
Thus, she was used for rowing and crossed with them.
Midstream, she sang the "Song of the River's Torrent," saying:
"Ascend that river and gaze west,
clear waters raise waves, vast and obscure.
Praying for blessings, drunk and unawakened,
punishment approaches, my heart trembles.
With jiāolóng's aid, the king shall return,
call for the oar, proceed without doubt.
Jiǎnzǐ was greatly pleased,
and immediately made her his wife.
"Biographies of Exemplary Women"
Xuē Tán studied singing under Qín Qīng,
but before mastering it completely,
he thought he had grasped Qīng's essence in one day,
and thus prepared to return home.
Qín Qīng then farewelled him at the suburban crossroads,
beating time and singing a mournful song,
its voice shaking the forest trees,
its echoes stopping the passing clouds.
Xuē Tán then apologized and begged to return,
and never again dared speak of leaving.
Upon returning,
Qín Qīng turned to his friend and said:
"In the past, Hán É went east to Qí,
and running out of food, passed through Yōngmén,
where she sold her songs to borrow food before leaving.
The remaining echoes circled the beams,
and did not cease for three days.
Those around thought she had not left.
Passing by an inn,
the people there insulted her,
so Hán É began to sing a long, sorrowful cry.
The entire village, old and young,
were so moved they danced with joy,
unable to control themselves.
They then gave her generous gifts and sent her off.
Thus, the people of Yōngmén to this day excel at singing and crying,
imitating Hán É's lingering voice.

*Gǔ Yuèfǔ*
The Song of the Round Fan,
refers to Wáng Mǐn, a Central Secretariat Director of the Jin dynasty,
who held a white round fan and had an affair with his sister-in-law's maid, Xiè Fāngzī.
Their affection was very deep.
When the sister-in-law excessively beat the maid,
Wáng Dōngtíng, upon hearing of it, stopped her.
Fāngzī was naturally skilled at singing,
so the sister-in-law ordered her to sing a song,
promising to pardon her.
In response, she sang:
"The white round fan, toiling and lingering,
is what my lord's eyes have seen."
Wáng Mǐn, upon hearing it, further asked her:
"Why did your song omit something?"
Fāngzī then changed it to:
"The white round fan, haggard and no longer its former appearance,
is ashamed to meet my lord."
Later generations thus sang it.
According to "Records of Ancient and Modern Music" and "Comprehensive Examination of Literature," it is said:
"The maid was naturally fond of singing,
and Wáng Mǐn liked holding a white fan,
hence the name 'round fan.'
Again, the round fan held up to hide the face,
haggard and no longer cared for,
ashamed to meet my lord."
In Píngchéng County there is Gēfù Mountain. Tradition says:
"An old man in his youth never took a wife,
but was skilled at singing songs.
When he was over eighty years old,
he fell ill and was about to die in his village.
Six or seven people carried him up to a cave.
The neighbors danced on their return,
while the village elders sang to see him off.
The sound shook the woods and marshes,
echoing so strongly it halted the passing clouds."

there was a Sūn who excelled at singing old melodies,

Emperor Míng Huáng returned from Bā Shǔ,
and one night ascended the Qínzhèng Tower.
Gazing southward, his eyes were filled with misty moonlight,
so he sang:
"The jade trees before the courtyard are already ready to be climbed,
yet the northern frontier soldiers have not yet returned."
This was originally a poem by Lú Sīdào.
After he finished singing, faint singing seemed to come from the neighborhood,
and he said to Lìshì:
"Could it be the former performers of the Lí Garden?
At dawn, find them for me."
The next day,
Lìshì summoned them from the neighborhood,
and indeed it was them.
Later, under the moonlight, he ascended the tower again,
with only Lìshì and the consort's attendant Hóng Táo by his side.
He then ordered them to sing "Liángzhōu",
which was composed by the Guìfēi herself.
The emperor personally played the jade flute,
accompanying the melody.
When the song ended, none could hold back their tears.
The emperor thus expanded the melody,
and the version of "Liángzhōu" that remains today has been further enriched.
(From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng Huáng" and "The Unofficial Biography of Tàizhēn")
The Xingqing Palace was the emperor's former princely residence in the southwest corner,
where the Hu'e Xianghui Tower was built,
and he spent time there with the various princes.
When Ān Lùshān rebelled and the news of his advance reached them, there was discussion of moving the capital.
The emperor happened to be feasting in the tower and ordered music to be played.
Someone presented the "Shuǐ Diào Gē,"
which said:
"Over mountains and rivers, tears soak my garments;
how long do wealth, honor, and glory last?
Do you not see now by the Fén River,
only the autumn geese fly year after year."
The emperor asked who wrote these lyrics,
and was told it was Lǐ Qiáo.
The emperor said:
"A true genius."
Thereupon, he did not finish the drink and left.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Ming."
During the Kaiyuan era,
a palace lady named Xǔ Zǐhé—originally a musician's daughter from Yongxin County, Jízhōu—entered the palace,
and was thus named Yongxin.
She could transform new melodies;
on autumn nights under the bright moon,
a single turn of her throat,
would carry its echo across all streets.
One day, during a grand feast at the Qínzhèng Tower,
amid the clamor of tens of thousands,
none could hear the sounds of the fish-dragon performances.
Yongxin then swept back her hair and raised her sleeves,
directly singing a lingering tune,
and the entire square fell silent as if empty;
those joyful heard it and felt their courage surge,
while the sorrowful heard it and felt their hearts break.
During the rebellion of Yúyáng,
the six palaces scattered like stars,
and Yongxin was obtained by a scholar.
Wéi Qīng, having fled to Guǎng,
on a moonlit night in Líng,
leaning on the railing, heard someone in a boat singing the "Water Melody,"
and said:
"This is Yongxin's song."
He boarded the boat to see her,
and they wept together.
Later, after the townsfolk passed away,
she fell into a life of hardship,
and on her deathbed, she said to her mother:
"Mother, your money tree,
has fallen."
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Music Bureau."
Niànnú,
possessing beauty and charm,
excelled at singing,

often holding clappers and gazing around while performing.
The emperor said to his consort:
"This woman is enchantingly beautiful,
her eyes seduce with a glance,
each time she modulates her voice in song,

he would draw out the sound,
layering it into the clouds,
like blowing on an eggplant leaf,
or lifting a floating silk thread.
Slowly rising and gently lifting,
it carried both sorrow and sobs,
whistling with poignant melancholy,
leaving listeners in poignant desolation.
It was called the mournful chant of the pines.
From the Sòng dynasty's "Biographies of Eminent Monks."
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a Dàoist priest from Mount Éméi surnamed Chén,
who traveled to the capital city.
He excelled at the art of whistling,
capable of producing melodies resembling thunder, drums, and claps of thunder.
Initially, his sounds were harmonious and smooth,
gradually becoming more dispersed and far-reaching.
In a moment, he directed them skyward like thunder,
and the tones suddenly rumbled again,
their startling noise like a thunderclap,
leaving no onlooker unawed.
From "Yǔlín"
Lǐ Áo was governing Lújiāng when,
a serious criminal was due for execution.
After consideration,
he plaintively pleaded:
"I possess a humble skill,
and wish to demonstrate it before Your Honor."
It was a long, clear whistle.
Lǐ Áo then ordered his shackles removed.
Shortly after,
the pure sound pierced through to the Milky Way.
The governor said:
"Who would have thought the style of Sūmén
could emerge from beneath a convict's garb?
Could he not share the same path as Sūn and Ruǎn?"
He immediately pardoned his crime.
From "Kǒng Tiē"
The east is called Shí,
the south is called Rèn,
the west is called Zhūlí,
the north is called Jìn.
Wine,
is that which accords with,
thus it accords with the good and evil in human nature.
One interpretation says it creates,
being the originator of fortune and misfortune.
In Shuōwén, wine
is associated with the character yǒu.
Brewed from rice and yeast,
it ferments over time to develop a fine flavor.
It is also said to mean "to tread,"
as both the capable and incapable grow forceful,
treading upon each other while awaiting to drink.
Furthermore, upon entering the mouth and being swallowed,
it makes all faces flush intensely.
From Shìmíng.
Mài niàng shǔ fán shǔ wéi jiǔ,
yáng jù yīn lì,
néng dòng,
gù yǐ mài niàng shǔ wéi jiǔ.
《Wěi》
Wine is
heaven's beautiful bounty,
used by emperors and kings to nourish the world,
for sacrificial offerings and prayer for blessings,
to support the weak and nurture the sick;
at gatherings of all rituals,
nothing can proceed without wine.
"Hàn Shí Huò Zhì" records Wáng Mǎng's edict stating:
"Salt is
the general of food;
wine is
the foremost of all medicines.
