In ancient times there was sweet fermented liquor,
during Yǔ's time Yí Dí made wine.
The Ancient Historical Investigations states: Yí Dí first made wine,
the fermented brew changed the five flavors,
Shǎokāng made broomcorn millet wine.
The Origins of Lineages records: In the past,
the emperor's daughter ordered Yí Dí to make wine, and it was excellent,
so it was presented to Yǔ.
Yǔ drank it and found it sweet,
then distanced himself from Yí Dí and abstained from fine wines,
saying:
"Later generations will surely have trouble because of wine.
Records of the Wei Strategies
Chén Gōngzǐ Wán fled to Qí,
and while drinking with the Duke,
Duke Huán was enjoying the wine,
and said:
"Let us continue by lamplight."
Wán declined, saying:
"I divined for the day,
but not for the night,
and dare not impose on a gentleman."
He added:
"Wine completes the rites,
but excess should not follow,
this is righteousness;
assisting the ruler in completing the rites,
without leading him into excess,
this is benevolence."
Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhuāng 22nd Year
Duke Huán of Qí prepared wine for his ministers,
scheduling it for midday.
Guǎn Zhòng arrived late,
and Duke Huán raised his cup to toast him.
Guǎn Zhòng discarded half of the wine,
to which Duke Huán said:
"You arrive late,
then discard the wine after drinking—
is this in accordance with ritual?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I have heard that when wine enters, the tongue comes out;
when it comes out,
one speaks improperly;
improper speech leads to the loss of one's life.
I reckoned that losing one's life
is worse than discarding wine."
Duke Huán laughed and said:
"Rise, Father Zhòng,
and take your seat."
《Shuō Yuàn》
Duke Huán of Qí got drunk while drinking,
lost his crown,
and felt so ashamed that he did not hold court for three days.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"This is not a shame that affects the state.
Why don't you wash it away through governance?"
The Duke said:
"Well said." Thereupon he opened the granaries,
gave to the poor,
and reviewed the prisons to release those with minor offenses.
After three days, the people sang in praise:
"Why doesn't the Duke lose his crown again?"
From "Hánzǐ"
King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Sòng,
with rotten meat in the kitchen,
and spoiled wine in the jars.
General Zǐ Zhòng remonstrated, saying:
"Now the meat in Your Majesty's kitchen is rotten and inedible,
the wine in the jars is spoiled and undrinkable,
yet all the soldiers in the three armies have a hungry look,
isn't it difficult to wish to defeat the enemy?"
King Zhuāng said:
"Let there be gentlemen who push forward wine,
and worthies who offer food."
Wángsūnzǐ's "New Writings"
The Jìn army attacked Guó,
and the Duke of Guó fled,
reaching a marshland,
where he said:
"I am extremely hungry and thirsty.
His charioteer offered clear wine and dried meat,
and the Duke asked the charioteer:
"Why are you flattering me?
The charioteer replied:
"I feared Your Highness would surely be exiled,
so I stored these provisions.
The Duke of Guó flushed with anger.
The charioteer then said:
"My words were mistaken;
the reason for Your Highness's exile
is that all under heaven are unworthy,
and resent Your Highness's virtue.
The Duke of Guó was pleased,
leaned on the chariot rail and laughed,
then, hungry and weary, used it as a pillow.
The charioteer placed his knee for him to lie on,
then substituted a clod of earth
in place of his knee and departed,
whereupon the Duke of Guó starved to death.
From the "Book of Jiǎ Yì"
In the Battle of Yānlíng,
the King of Chǔ summoned Zǐ Fǎn for consultation, but Gǔ Yáng Shù offered him a drink,
which he drank at Zǐ Fǎn's place.
Zǐ Fǎn became drunk and was unable to see the king.
He said:
"Heaven has defeated Chǔ,
and I cannot remain here any longer.
So he fled overnight.
(Zuǒzhuàn, Chénggōng, Part 2)
Duke Jǐng, while drinking, moved to Yànzǐ's house,
Yànzǐ stood at the gate,
and said:
"Is there no state affair?
Why does Your Grace come at an inappropriate time and dishonor me by night?"
The Duke said:
"The taste of wine,
the sweetness of spirits,
the sound of metal and stone instruments,
I wish to enjoy them with you, Master."
Yànzǐ said:
"I dare not partake."
The Duke then moved to the house of Sīmǎ Rángjū,
and Rángjū replied as Yànzǐ had.
The Duke again moved to Liángqiū Jū,
who held a qin in his left hand,
embraced a bamboo pole with his right,
and came singing as he walked.
The Duke said:
"How joyful!
Without those two gentlemen, how could the state be maintained;
without this one minister, how could I enjoy myself?"
《Yànzǐ》
Yànzǐ was drinking with Duke Jǐng,
and as dusk fell,
the duke called for torches to be prepared.
Yànzǐ declined, saying:
"The Book of Songs says: '
The cap is tilted askew.'
This speaks of losing virtue;
repeatedly dancing wildly,
speaks of losing decorum.
When drunk with wine,
and sated with virtue,
one should depart upon becoming drunk—
this shares the blessing with the guests,
and is the host's courtesy.
To remain drunk without leaving
is called damaging virtue—
a fault of both guest and host.
I divined for the day,
but not for the night."
The duke said:
"Well said."
He raised his wine cup in offering,
bowed twice, and left.
He said:
"How could I surpass him?
I entrust the state to Yànzǐ
because his household is poor yet virtuous.
I do not wish him to be extravagant,
so how much more should I consult him on governing the state?"
From "Shuō Yuàn"
Shūsūn Chuò paid a courtesy visit to Sòng,
the next day a banquet was held with music and drinking,
the Duke of Sòng had Zhāozǐ sit on his right,
they spoke and wept together,
Yuè Qí, the assistant, withdrew and told others:
"This year, both the ruler and Shūsūn will likely die,
I have heard that excessive grief in joy,
and excessive joy in grief both indicate a loss of mind.
The essence of the mind,
is called the húnpò (ethereal and corporeal souls),
if the húnpò depart from it, how can one last long?
(Zhāo, 25th year)
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè was on an excursion when
someone presented him with a jug of wine.
The king said,
"If I drink this alone, what about the three armies?"
So he poured it into the river,
ordering the three armies to drink from it,
and all reported being intoxicated.
From "Lǚshì Chūnqiū Wùlèi Xiānggǎn Zhì": In ancient times, when a fine general commanded troops,
if someone presented a single pot of unstrained wine,
he would surely pour it into the river,
meaning the officers and soldiers would drink from the flowing water in turn,
so they all shared the same taste.
From "Huáng Shígōng Jì".
Píngyuán Jūn was drinking with Zǐgāo,
and pressed Zǐgāo to drink more,
saying:
"There is an old proverb:
Yáo and Shùn drank a thousand zhōng,
Confucius a hundred gū,
Zǐlù chattered away,
yet still drank ten kè.
The sages and worthies of antiquity all could drink;
why do you, sir, decline?"
Zǐgāo replied:
"From what I have heard,
sages and worthies surpassed others in virtue and the Way;
I have not heard they did so in food and drink.
This saying originated from those fond of wine,
likely being words of encouragement and jest, not the actual truth."
《Kǒng Cóng Zǐ》
When the wine of Lǔ was weak, Hándān was besieged;
When a sage is born, great thieves arise.
Zhuangzi: King Xuān of Chǔ held court with the feudal lords,
Duke Gōng of Lǔ arrived late and his wine was weak,
King Xuān was angered,
and wished to humiliate him.
Duke Gōng would not accept the command,
and instead said:
"I am a descendant of the Duke of Zhōu,
senior among the feudal lords,
I perform the rites of the Son of Heaven,
my meritorious service lies with the Zhōu house.
For me to present wine is already a breach of ritual,
yet now you blame me for its weakness,
is this not excessive?"
Thereupon he departed without taking leave.
King Xuān was angered,
and raised troops to attack Lǔ together with Qí.
King Huì of Liáng had long wished to attack Zhào,
but feared rescue from Chǔ.
Chǔ was occupied with the affair of Lǔ,
so Liáng succeeded in besieging Hándān.
This speaks of how events are interconnected,
and is also a case of stimulus and response.
A note: When Chǔ met with the feudal lords,
both Lǔ and Zhào presented wine to the King of Chǔ.
The wine of Lǔ was weak and that of Zhào was strong.
The official in charge of wine for Chǔ requested wine from Zhào,
but Zhào did not give it.
The official was angered,
and then swapped Zhào's strong wine for Lǔ's weak wine when presenting it.
The King of Chǔ, because Zhào's wine was weak, besieged Hándān.
Xǔ Shèn's commentary on Huáinánzǐ.
Marquis Wén of Wèi was drinking with his ministers,
and appointed Gōngchéng Bùrén as the master of toasts.
He declared:
"Anyone who does not drain his cup,
shall be forced to drink a large cup as penalty."
When Marquis Wén drank but did not finish his cup,
Bùrén raised the large cup to penalize the lord.
The lord looked at him but did not respond.
An attendant said:
"Bùrén, you have already offended the lord by your transgression.
Bùrén cited the Book of Zhōu,
saying: 'When the front carriage overturns,
it serves as a warning for the following carriage.'
This speaks of peril.
Now that the lord has established the rule,
can it not be enforced?
The lord said:
"Well said."
He then raised the large cup and drank.
After finishing the drink,
he declared:
"I appoint Gōngchéng Bùrén as a distinguished guest."
From "Shuō Yuàn"
King Wēi of Qí hosted a banquet in the inner palace,
and asked Chúnyú Kūn:
"How much can you drink before getting drunk,
Sir?"
He replied:
"Your servant can get drunk after one dǒu,
or after one shí.
The king asked the reason,
and Kūn said:
"When granted wine before Your Majesty,
with law officials in front
and censors behind,
I am fearful
and get drunk after barely one dǒu.
But when shoes are scattered about,
cups and plates lie in disarray,
the hall candles are extinguished,
the host keeps me while seeing off other guests,
at such a moment,
my heart is intoxicated with joy and I can drink one shí.
Thus it is said: wine at its extreme leads to disorder,
pleasure at its extreme leads to sorrow—all things are like this.
Words cannot reach the extreme,
for at the extreme comes decline.
He thus offered indirect remonstrance.
The King of Qí said:
"Well said,"
and ceased the all-night drinking.

Shào Jī, being heavily drunk,
fell asleep and lost his fur coat.
The ruler of Sòng said:

He replied:
"Jié lost the empire through drunkenness,
and the 'Announcement to Kang' says 'Do not',
those who regularly drink,
regular drinking,
means constant drinking.
Constant drinking
causes the Son of Heaven to lose his empire,
and the common man to lose his life."

was captured by the Yān army,

but each time they were killed.

When he met the King of Yān,
the King of Yān questioned him,
to which he replied:
"A lowly person rarely sees a noble one,

He was questioned again,
and again he said:

adding:

and Yú are famous.

The King of Yān thought this reasonable,
and thus released him.
The King of Zhào returned with the menial soldier driving his carriage.

starting to make the wine at dawn,
which would mature by the eighth month,
called
"zhòu"
also known as

wine is made,
maturing by the eighth month,

during the tasting of zhòu in the eighth month,

Jì Bù served as governor of Hédōng.
During the reign of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
someone spoke of his worthiness,
so Emperor Wén summoned him intending to make him a yùshǐ.

Records of the Grand Historian
Guàn Fū,
upon Emperor Wǔ's ascension was appointed as Governor of Huáiyáng.
He entered the court as Grand Coachman,
and while drinking with Chánglè Commandant Dòu Fǔ,
a disagreement arose over trivial matters,
and Guàn Fū, drunk, struck Dòu Fǔ.
Dòu Fǔ
was the Empress Dowager's brother.
The Emperor, fearing the Empress Dowager would execute Guàn Fū,
transferred him to be Chancellor of Yān.
Guàn Fū was by nature stern and upright,
prone to drunkenness and unwilling to flatter the powerful,
yet he treated those above him
with a desire to dominate,
while those below him,
especially the poor and humble, he treated with even greater respect.
In crowded gatherings,
he recommended and promoted lower-ranking scholars, and for this, he was widely praised.
《Qián Hàn》
Hànwǔ made carefree wine,
drinking it makes one worry-free.
"Wángxiāng Miscellaneous Records"
The Han Dynasty "Record of Rites and Music: Song of the Auspicious Star" states:
"Hundred-herb fine wine spreads orchid fragrance."
Yán Shīgǔ explains: Hundred-herb,
refers to the pollen of hundreds of flowers.
Fine,
means excellent,
by mixing the pollen of hundreds of herbs into wine,
thus making it fragrant and excellent.
Jìn Zhuó states:
"Its fragrance spreads outward,
like the growth of orchids."
Méi Chéng's "Seven Stimuli" says:
"Orchid-petal wine,
poured to cleanse the mouth."
Lǐ Zhù explains:
"The wine mouth is steeped,
using orchid leaves for their fragrance."
Xiè Língyùn's poem:
"Orchid cups offered to contemporary sages,
fine wine spreads orchid fragrance.
The Record of Lóngchéng calls it the hundred-flavored fine wine of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn."
Emperor Wǔ missed Lady Lǐ,
and his personal attendants noticed his sorrowful and resentful expression.
They then offered him Hóngliáng wine,
poured into a patterned conch shell cup.
The cup came from the country of Bōqí,
and the wine from Hóngliáng County,
which belonged to the Right Fúfēng region, causing great sorrow.
The emperor abolished this county,
and southerners learned its brewing method.
Now it is said that Yúnyáng produces fine wine,
but the names have become confused.
After drinking three cups,
the emperor's expression brightened, and he felt joyful.
"Records of Omissions" - Immortal Wine of Jūnshān.
Yǔ Mù's "Account of Xiāngzhōu" states: There is fine wine on Jūnshān Mountain,
and drinking several dǒu of it grants immortality,
making one an immortal.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn heard of this,
fasted for seven days,
and sent Lú Bā with several dozen young boys and girls to seek it.
They indeed obtained the wine and presented it to the emperor.
Before he could drink it,
Dōngfāng Shuò, standing nearby, secretly drank it.
The emperor was furious,
and intended to kill him.
Shuò said:
"If the wine is effective,
killing me won't cause my death;
if it's ineffective,
what use is the wine?"
The emperor laughed and released him.
Temple monks said: In spring, the aroma of wine is often detected,
but its source cannot be found.
"Record of Yuèyáng's Local Conditions" - Taoists say there is fine wine around Jūnshān,
and drinking several hú of it grants immortality.
"Account of Central Xiāng"
Gài Kuānráo, as the Marquis of Qīngpíng'ēn in the capital,
when Xǔ Bó moved into his new residence,
the Chancellor, Imperial Secretaries, and others all went to congratulate him, but Kuānráo did not go.
Only after Xǔ Bó invited him did he finally attend.
Xǔ Bó personally poured wine and said:
"Lord Gài, you have arrived late.
Kuānráo replied:
"Do not pour too much wine for me,
for I am a wine madman.
Chancellor Marquis Wèi laughed and said:

why must it be because of wine?

From the *History of the Former Han Dynasty*
Yú Dìngguó could consume several dàn of wine without losing composure.
In winter months when handling judicial reviews,
he drank wine to become even more clear-headed.

Chén Zūn,
courtesy name Mènggōng,
was addicted to alcohol.
Whenever he held a grand drinking party,
he would close the doors as soon as the guests filled the hall,
and throw the linchpins of their carriages into the well.
Even if they had urgent matters,
they ultimately could not leave.

Emperor Chéng favored and doted on Marquis Fùpíng Zhāng Fàng and Chúnyú Chǎng,
taking them on incognito excursions outside the palace,
while they attended him within the forbidden chambers,
where banquets and drinking were arranged.
Gatherings included various palace attendants such as Zhào and Lǐ,
all filling their cups to the brim and raising them in toasts,
laughing and jesting uproariously.
Bān Bó remarked:
"Indulging excessively in wine
is why Wēizǐ had to depart with a warning;
shouting and clamoring in revelry
is what caused the 'Great Odes' to linger with lament.
Annotation:
This means the poet who composed the verses
sighed in sorrow, with tears streaming down in lingering grief.
The admonitions against debauchery in the Book of Songs and Book of Documents
all have their words directed at wine.

Once there was a man named Liú Xuánshí who bought wine from a tavern in Zhōngshān.
The tavern owner gave him Thousand-Day Wine.
After drinking it, he forgot his words,
and following the proper measure, he returned home.
Upon arriving home, he fell into a deep drunken stupor,
and did not wake up for several days.
His family, unaware of the situation, thought he had died.
They prepared a coffin and buried him.
Later, the tavern owner came,
and upon recalling that the thousand days had passed, he remembered Liú Xuánshí had come to buy wine.
He realized the drunkenness should have worn off by then.
So he went to Liú Xuánshí's home to inquire,
and was told that Liú Xuánshí had been dead for three years,
and the mourning period had already ended.
Thereupon, he went with the family to dig open the grave and look,
and Liú Xuánshí finally awoke,
rising from the coffin.
It is also commonly said that when Liú Xuánshí drank wine,
he would get drunk for a thousand days.
《博物志》: A man from Qí named Tián Nǎizhī could make Thousand-Day Wine.
Drinking more than one shēng would cause one to lie drunk for a thousand days.
An old friend, Zhào Yīng, drank beyond his capacity and left.
His family thought he had died,
and buried him.
Tián Nǎizhī calculated that after a thousand days, he should wake up.
He went to his friend's home,
broke open the coffin and brought him out,
and there was still the smell of wine on him.

political power was held by eunuchs.

and was immediately appointed Governor of Liangzhou,
exchanging it for Liangzhou.

lasting a full month without sobering.

reaching the city of Qiūcí.

(Annals) Lǐ Bái presented his "Qingping Lyrics,"
and Consort Yáng served him Western Liang grape wine in a seven-treasure glass cup.
(Biography of Consort Yang) Mèng Shēn stated:
"Grapes, regardless of the land,
when harvested and brewed into wine,
all yield excellent quality.
(Sequel to the Treatise on Curiosities)
Emperor Líng had not yet established a bureau for liquor monopoly,
and a dǒu of liquor cost a thousand coins.
Liú Biǎo had a son who was fond of drinking,
so he crafted three wine cups,
the largest called
"Bó Yǎ",
with a capacity of seven shēng;
the next called
"Zhòng Yǎ",
five shēng;

Lú Zhí could drink one shi of wine without getting drunk.
Book of the Later Han
Yuán Shào commanded troops in Jīngzhōu,
and sent an envoy to invite Zhèng Xuán to a grand gathering of guests.

yet was ushered to the seat of honor.

drank one hú of wine,
had elegant eyebrows and bright eyes,

From the "Book of the Later Hàn"
"A Letter from Kǒng Róng's Collection to Cáo Cāo" states:
"The virtue of wine has long been established.
Ancient sage kings honored deities and ancestors to harmonize spirits,
and to stabilize people and aid all states, nothing but wine sufficed.
Thus, heaven bestowed the radiance of the Wine Star,
earth displayed the prefecture of Wine Springs,
and humanity praised the virtue of fine wine.
Yáo could not have established peace without a thousand vessels;
Confucius could not have attained sagehood without a hundred goblets;
Fán Kuài resolved the crisis at Hóngmén—
without pork shoulder and wine, his fury would not have been roused;

Lǐ Zōngmǐn in the summer months approached the pond,
using a lotus leaf as his cup.
Péi Jūn held a grand banquet,
when Péi Hóngtài arrived late.
Jūn was displeased,
and Hóngtài said:
"I propose to drink from all the silver vessels here until they are empty.
Then bestow them upon me as I drink,
would that be acceptable?
Jūn agreed.
So he exhausted the small cups on the table,
moving on to the large wine vessels.
He drank them all dry,
and immediately stored the vessels.
He had a silver sea container,
with a capacity of over one dou.
Hóngtài drank it all in one go,
stepped on his sea container,
rolled it up and embraced it,
then called for his horse and left directly.
Jūn sent someone to inquire about him,
and found him sitting sprawled out,
counting the silverware he had obtained,
amounting to over two hundred liang in total.

Shēntú Chéng sat around the fire with an old man, his wife, and their maiden daughter in a thatched cottage by the roadside.
The old man brought a wine pot from outside
and said,
"You've braved the cold,
so have a cup of wine."
Chéng then bowed politely and said:
"The host should drink first."
The old man made the rounds with the wine,
and Chéng was last to drink.
The "Hédōng Jì" by Sū È states: People nowadays call the last round of wine drinking "lánwěi."
It also says: "Lán"
means greed,
referring to those seated
who haven't yet drunk and are greedy for it.
Hence the saying: Sòng Jǐngwén's poem "Shǒusuì" reads:
"Welcoming the new and seeing off the old is just like this,
so finish the last cup of wine by the lamp."
Bái Lètiān's poem says:
"Three cups of lánwěi wine,
one plate of sticky candy."
Only he changed
"lán" (婪)
to
"lán" (藍)
instead.
Some say: Lán refers to Lánshuǐ,
which is three zhàng deep,
and people of that time drew from it to make wine.
Also, "lán" should be written as "lín" (啉).
Hóu Bái's "Jiǔlǜ" states: When the wine has made a full round,
the last person to drink must down two cups in a row,
which is called "lánwěi."
The last seat is far away,
so the wine often arrives late,
hence drinking two cups in a row to console them,
using "lín" to mean greed.

Yuán Déxiù resigned from his post as magistrate of Lǔshān.
He loved the fine landscape of Lùhún,
so he settled there permanently,
building neither walls nor locks,
and kept no servants or concubines.
During years of famine,
he sometimes went without cooking.
He was fond of wine,
and cheerfully played the qin for his own amusement.
People would bring him wine and food,
and regardless of whether they were virtuous or vulgar, he would drink heartily with them.

There was a visiting monk,

The temple monks saw this,
angered by his rudeness,
snatched the bottle and smashed it against a cypress tree.
The bottle shattered into pieces,
but the wine congealed,
adhering to the tree like green jade,
unshaken when stirred.
The monk said:
"I often recite the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
and must drink a cup of this beforehand."
He then chanted clearly and melodiously.
Taking the bottle to the tree to collect it,
the wine all fell into the vessel,
suddenly flowing for him to drink,
and in a moment the vessel was empty from his hearty drinking.

Prime Minister Húlíng Gǔ Chǔ heard of his eloquence and quick wit,

from the shore take a camel.

the one coming to be carried is the crocodile,
this is called the camel carrying the crocodile."
Fēixióng responded:
"From the roof take a pigeon,
from the water take a clam.
The one carrying is the pigeon,
the one coming to join is the clam,
this is called the pigeon joining the clam."
The minister greatly marveled at him.

Privy Councillor Sūn Huìzōng,

he saw an official in crimson robes,

stomping out angrily.

where the wine had been carelessly spilled.

When Zhū Wēn first held authority over four military commands,
the King of Shǔ dispatched Pān Qī to present gifts.
Qī could drink a peck of wine,
and at every banquet,
his demeanor grew increasingly solemn.
As Wēn drank to his heart's content,
he remarked:
"Can the commander down a whole set of vessels?"
Qī replied:
"I dare not refuse."
Thereupon, all the vessels on the mat were gathered,
and wine was poured into them in turn.
Qī drank them all,
yet became even more composed and temperate.
Wēn, thinking he would surely vomit upon returning to his lodgings
and lie down exhausted,
sent someone to spy on him.
Qī, wearing a bamboo shoot sheath hat,
weighed the wine vessels he had received,
and ordered his attendants to store them.

Mǐn zhǔ Yánxī and the Hanlin Academician Zhōu Wéiyuè,

Yánxī said delightedly:

The attendants skillfully replied:

Yánxī agreed with this,
and thus he was spared.

Mǐn Wáng Yánxī,
was the son of Wáng Shěnzhī.
After ascending the throne,
he indulged in all-night drinking sessions.
He used silver-leaf cups,
which he bestowed upon his officials for drinking.
The silver leaves were delicate,
so they were nicknamed "winter melon slices,"

Once the cups were filled with wine,
they could not be set down elsewhere,
only emptied before being placed aside.
From the royal family and ministers downward,
many resisted his orders.
One evening,

became heavily intoxicated,
and ordered his chancellor Lǐ Zhǔn to be executed in the market.

so he was moved elsewhere.
The next day,
during court,
Yánxī summoned Lǐ Zhǔn.
His attendants reminded him of the previous night's order.
Yánxī had no recollection of it,
so he urgently summoned him,
and restored his position.

After Zhāng Huà had become wealthy and esteemed,

Huà drank the Nine-Brew Wine with him,

that night sleeping drunk.

he would always order his attendants
to turn him over until he awoke.
That evening, he forgot to give the order.
The attendants, as was customary, turned Lord Zhāng over,

By daybreak,

The malt was steeped in water,

When the leaves and stems are long, the infusion appears clear and white;
when the stems are short, the color turns yellowish and develops dark spots or overlapping leaves.
These are major flaws in tea:
if dark spots remain,
the color turns yellow.
If over-roasted, it retains a grassy taste;
if the oily essence is not fully removed, the liquor becomes turbid with a heavy flavor.
Exposure to smoke steals away its aroma,
over-pressing ruins its taste—

In the past, there was a monk who fell ill,

The monk said:

The old man's tea from the central peak of Méngshān

waiting for the thunder to sound,
and then picking it with joined efforts,
valuing quantity above all,
continuing until three days have passed.
If one obtains one liang from this place,
boil it in water and drink,
it can dispel chronic illnesses.
Two liang should ensure no illness before one's eyes,
three liang can solidify and transform the bones,
four liang will make one an earth immortal.
But if prepared with pure care, none will fail to be effective.
The monk thus built a dwelling at the central peak to wait.
When the time came, he obtained over one liang and consumed it.
Before finishing, his illness was cured.
Although it couldn't last forever,
through diligent seeking, he remained robust into his eighties.
His strength did not wane,

In the state of Qí, there was a man named Běiguō Sāo,
who gathered rushes,
bound reeds and bulrushes,
and wove sandals to support his mother, yet it was still insufficient.
He went in person to visit Yànzǐ,
and said:
"I wish to beg for the means to support my mother.
Yànzǐ's servant said to Yànzǐ:
"This is a worthy man of the state of Qí.
Now that he begs for the means to support his mother is right,
it shows he admires your righteousness, Master,
you must give it to him.
Yànzǐ sent someone to distribute grain from the granary and money from the treasury to give him,
but he declined the money and accepted the grain.
After some time,
Yànzǐ fell under suspicion by the ruler of Qí,
and fled the state.
Běiguōzǐ summoned his friend and told him:
"I admired Yànzǐ's righteousness,
and rightly begged from him the means to support my mother.
I have heard it said:
"When one has provided for one's parents,
one should personally withstand their calamities.
Now Yànzǐ is under suspicion,
I will use my death to clear his name.
He put on his robe and cap,
instructed his friend to carry a sword and follow with a basket,
went to the ruler's court,
and requested the usher to announce:
"Yànzǐ,
is a worthy man of the world,
if he leaves,
then Qí will surely be invaded,
I am bound to see the state invaded.
It is better to die first.
I ask to entrust my head to clear Yànzǐ's name.
Thereupon he said to his friend:
"Place my head in the basket,
and present it to entrust." Then he cut his own throat.
His friend accordingly presented it as an entrustment.
His friend said to the onlookers:
"Běiguōzǐ died for the state's sake,
I will die for Běiguōzǐ.
Then he also retreated and cut his own throat.
The ruler of Qí heard of this,
was greatly alarmed,
mounted a relay carriage and personally pursued Yànzǐ,
overtaking him at the outskirts of the state,
Yànzǐ had no choice but to return.

The cook bowed twice and pleaded:
"I have three capital offenses.
When I sharpened the knife on the whetstone,
it became as sharp as Gànjiàng's sword,
yet it cut through the meat but not the hair -
this is my first offense.
When I skewered the meat with a stick,

this is my second offense.
When I tended the blazing furnace,
the fire burned bright red and cooked the meat thoroughly,
yet the hair didn't burn -
this is my third offense.

and indeed found the culprit and had him executed.

Yáng Yì was the governor of Guāngzhōu.

The next day when they looked,

Some among the people said:
"We saw wildcats carrying them and gathering them."
According to worldly interpretation, straw sandals are the humble footwear of commoners,
symbolizing the lowly people who endure toil and humiliation.
Being worn-out represents exhaustion and hardship.
The roads,

are where the emperor's commands come and go.

about to assemble in masses and create disorder,

The next day,
this man, believing he had been recognized and favored,
went to the gate seeking an audience.

"Yesterday, I had no companion for drinking,
so I casually invited you."

The Explanation of Names says: The tablet,
is for suddenness.
When the ruler has instructions or one needs to present a report,
it is written upon it,
to guard against sudden forgetfulness.
Some say the tablet
can be used to record things.
The tablet,
the Son of Heaven uses jade to make it,
standing upright and square at its head,
signifying that he does not yield to anyone under heaven;
the feudal lords use ivory,
curved in front and straight at the back,
rounded at the head,
signifying their submission to the Son of Heaven;
the high officials use bamboo decorated with fish patterns,
the lower officials use plain bamboo, curved both in front and at the back,
signifying that they yield to all.
"The Book of Rites": The Son of Heaven holds the jade tablet,
the feudal lords hold the tea-colored tablet,
the high officials carry the tablet.

standing upright and unyielding.
"Essentials of the Five Classics": The bamboo tablet of the lower officials is decorated with ivory,
the high officials are decorated with fish whiskers.

Putting down his staff, he asked:

Taking side steps and turning around, he asked:

Liú Xiàng, in the final years of Emperor Chéng's reign, was collating texts at the Tiānlù Pavilion,
devoting himself with intense concentration and deep thought.
One night, an old man dressed in yellow clothes appeared,
holding a green staff made of Lí wood,
knocked on the door and entered to meet him.
Liú Xiàng sat alone in the darkness reciting texts,
so the old man blew on the tip of his staff, producing a flame to illuminate Liú Xiàng,
and recounted in detail events before the creation of the world.
Liú Xiàng thus received the texts of "Wǔ Xíng" and "Hóng Fàn",
fearing their content was too extensive and complex,
he tore strips from his robe and sash,
to record the words.
At dawn, the old man prepared to leave,
and when Liú Xiàng asked his name,
he replied:
"I am the essence of Tàiyǐ.
The Heavenly Emperor heard that among the descendants of Jīnmǎo there was a profoundly learned scholar,
and sent me down to observe you.
He then took out bamboo slips from his bosom,
containing texts on celestial phenomena and terrestrial maps,
saying, "I shall briefly impart these to you."
Later, when Liú Xiàng's son Liú Xīn received these teachings,
even Liú Xiàng did not realize who this man truly was.

Mí Zhú employed the methods of Táo Zhū,
growing richer by the day,
with thousands of rooms in his house and storerooms.
Mí Zhú often aided the living and pitied the dead.
Beside the stable in his home was an ancient tomb,
and at night, weeping sounds were heard.
Searching for it,
he saw a woman who lamented:
"At the end of the Hàn dynasty, I was killed by the Red Eyebrows,
my coffin was opened and I was stripped,
I beg you to bury me deeper,
and also ask for worn-out clothes to cover myself."
Mí Zhú followed her words.
After a year had passed,
he again saw the previous woman, who said:
"Your wealth and treasures can last a lifetime,
but you are destined to suffer a great calamity.
Now, with one green reed cane,
nine feet long,
I repay your kindness of clothing and burial."
Mí Zhú carried the cane and returned.
The neighbors where he lived often saw a green aura at Mí Zhú's home,
resembling the form of a dragon or snake.
Also, several blue-clad youths came,
saying:
"Mí Zhú's home is about to have a fire,
but because you were able to pity and bury dry bones,
heaven's way does not leave your virtue unrewarded,
so we have come to ward off this disaster,
ensuring that your wealth is not completely lost."
Ten days later,
a fire started from the storeroom,
burning his pearls and jades,
leaving only one-tenth remaining.
When the fire was at its peak,
ten or so blue-clad youths were seen coming to extinguish the fire,
and there was an aura like a cloud covering the flames,
which then went out.

he passed by to pray for a stable tenure,

When his term ended,
he crafted a staff to return to the temple.
He forged iron for the core,

Soon summoned to be a Regular Attendant of the Palace,

Thereupon, they took the staff to inspect it,
cut it open to see,
and all witnessed the iron core.
They then cast it into the lake,
where the staff floated on the water,

reaching Chén Mǐn's boat from afar.
Chén Mǐn's boat then capsized.

and all the timber was used for coffins and outer coffins.

"Whenever people take action,
it is either for fame or for profit."

"For those whose coffins exceed the proper measure,
their corpse shall be mutilated,
and the mourners in charge shall be punished."

and to punish the mourners brings no profit—

how is the Prime Minister at fault for not knowing?"

and my son was punished and dismissed for it.

The king said:

and additionally bestowed ten yì of gold.
The mother declined the gold and cloth,
saying:
"How could I be greedy for goods and trouble the king?
I only resent the Prime Minister's governance."
Thus she refused to accept.
The king said:
"With such wisdom in the mother,
her son cannot be foolish."

but doesn't turn to ashes.

Lóu Jìng, Marquis of Jiànxìn in the Hàn dynasty, attained the Way late in life.
He resided north of Míngyuè Mountain in Hǎozhì,
able to cultivate gold,
and the place was called Gold-Cultivating Plain.
Even now, people often find gold there.
It is said:
"As Jìng was about to die,

and I will have means to bless you.'
Then clouds and mist gathered and he departed.
In the third year of the Bǎolì era of the Táng dynasty,
County Magistrate Hán Biāo prayed for rain here,

From "Ancient Stele of Yǒngshòu County, Zhìdà Era"
"The Law of the State": When redeeming servants from the feudal lords,
all shall take gold from the treasury.
Zǐgòng redeemed them but declined to take the gold.
Confucius heard of this,
and said:
"Cì has erred in this matter.
When a sage undertakes an action,
it should be capable of transforming customs and practices,
not merely serving as personal conduct.
If accepting gold is considered improper,
then how will others afford to redeem people?
From now on,
the state of Lǔ will no longer redeem people from the feudal lords.
Between Xiāng and Zhào,
in the former Chōnglíng Báishuǐ area, many gold línzhǐ and xiāngtí gold pieces were found.
The toes are hollow with patterns on all four sides,

Locals call them persimmon gold,

Imprinted gold,

From "Xù Bówùzhì"
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
the state of Kūnmíng offered as tribute numerous golden birds,
which often spat out golden specks like millet grains.
These birds feared the cold,
so they were housed in a Cold-Warding Tower.
The palace ladies vied to use the gold spat out by the birds to adorn their hairpins and pendants,
calling it "cold-warding gold."
Hence, the palace ladies teased each other, saying:
"If you don't wear cold-warding gold,
how can you attain the sovereign's favor?"
From "Records of Omissions"
Zhāng Fèn from Wèijùn sold his house to Chéng Yīng from Líyáng.
Chéng Yīng's entire family fell ill,
so he resold it to Hé Wén from Yè.
Hé Wén, holding a large knife alone,
entered the north hall at dusk to stay overnight.
During the first watch,
a figure over ten feet tall appeared,
wearing a yellow hat and clothes,
ascended the hall and called out:
"Slender Waist,
why is there the aura of a living person here?
The reply came:
"There isn't any.
After a short while,
another wearing a tall hat and blue clothes,
and yet another wearing a tall hat and white clothes,
asked and answered similarly as before.
As dawn approached,
Hé Wén then went down to the center of the hall,
and called out in the same manner as they did.
The reply said:
"The one in yellow,
is gold,
located under the west wall of the hall.
The one in blue:
"Is coins,
five steps away from the well in front of the hall.
The one in white:
"Is silver,
under the pillar at the east corner of the wall.
"And who are you?
It said:
"I am the pestle!
Under the trough.
Hé Wén dug accordingly in order,
and obtained five hundred jin each of gold and silver,
and over ten million coins.
He then took the pestle and burned it,
and the house was thus cleansed and peaceful.
"Sōu Shén Jì"
During the Tianbǎo era,
there was a haunted house in Cháng'ān,
which no one would buy.
Sū È of Fúfēng,
being extremely poor,
learned of this,
and went to the owner to purchase it at a very low price.
In the evening, he brought a couch himself,
and slept in the main hall.
After the second watch,
he suddenly saw a red object,
shaped like a person,
without hands or feet,
transparent and glowing inside and out,
which suddenly shouted:
"Duō!
Sū È looked at it,
and it remained motionless for a long time.
It called out again:
"Rotten wood, duō!
There is something under the western wall.
A response came, asking:
"What kind of person?
It said:
"I don't know.
It added:
"Too hard and clanging.
The rotten wood said:
"Frightening, the red object has been missing for a long time.
Sū È went down into the courtyard,
and called to the rotten wood:
"Where is the one who harmed people before?
It replied:
"There is nothing else,
only the essence of gold.
People's blessings are too meager,
so it has never killed or injured anyone.
The next day, Sū È,
dug under the western wall and found a decayed cassia tree,
with a blood-red color at its heart,
as hard as stone.
Under the eastern wall, he dug up a stone,
on which were seal script characters saying:
"Thirty catties of purple gold from the Son of Heaven in summer,
bestowed upon the virtuous.
Sū È thought to himself that he was not worthy of it,
when the rotten wood suddenly spoke:
"Why not change your name to Yǒudé (Virtuous)?
Sū È said:
"Good.
The rotten wood said:
"If you, noble sir, can send me to Kūnmíng Pond,
I will no longer disturb people.
The next day, he dug up an iron urn,
obtained the purple gold,
and sent the rotten wood to Kūnmíng Pond.
"Record of the Strange"
Lǐ Shìzhī served as Left Minister,
and was at odds with Lǐ Línfǔ.
Línfǔ, being treacherous and cunning,
said to Shìzhī:
"Mount Huà produces gold,
mining it could enrich the state.
It's just that the Emperor doesn't know about it yet.
Shìzhī believed his words,
and another day mentioned it to the Emperor.
The Emperor was pleased,
and asked Línfǔ about it,
who replied:
"I've known about this for a long time.
However, Mount Huà is Your Majesty's destiny mountain,
the dwelling place of imperial energy,
I didn't dare to suggest mining it,
so I didn't dare to report it.
The Emperor thought Línfǔ cared for him,
and looked down on Shìzhī.
Shìzhī became fearful and uneasy,
and took poison to kill himself.
The commoner Zhāng Yǐ from Yíchūn Commandery was known for his family's filial piety and righteousness.
Whenever guests arrived,
he would always accommodate them.
Suddenly one evening,
a beautiful woman came to the gate seeking lodging.
The women of the household happily received her,
and late at night they retired.
One young man of the family took a liking to her,
instructed his wet nurse to house her in a separate room,
and secretly had illicit relations with her late at night.
Her body felt like ice,
which greatly startled the young man.
He ordered a candle to be lit to look at her,
and she turned out to be a silver figure,
weighing perhaps a thousand or hundred catties.
The whole family was surprised and delighted,
but fearing she might transform,
they immediately burned her with torch charcoal,
and she became genuine white silver.

Liú Yìchí took several catties of Hán Yù's gold and left,

Yù could not stop him.

During the Bǎolì era,
Wéi Sīxuán of the capital sought the art of alchemy to produce gold.
One day, a hermit named Xīn Ruì came to visit,
and Sīxuán accommodated him in his residence.
Later, Ruì developed a carbuncle,
which festered and bled profusely,
causing the entire household to loathe him.
Sīxuán once invited several alchemists to dine together,
but Ruì was not provided a meal.
Suddenly, Ruì appeared and urinated on the banquet table,
enraging the guests,
who all stood up.
Ruì then announced his departure,
walked to the courtyard,
and abruptly vanished.
Everyone was astounded,
and upon inspecting his urine,
they found it was a liquid of purple gold,
radiant with extraordinary brilliance.
Someone who understood explained:
"The hermit
is the essence of purple gold.
As for the name Xīn,
it corresponds to metal in the west, according to the heavenly stems Gēng and Xīn.
The character Ruì
combines the radical for metal with Duì (兌),
and Duì also represents the western direction in the cosmic arrangement.
(From "Accounts from the Xuānshì")
Emperor Wǔ of Táng was fond of immortal arts.
A fangshì named Zhào Guīzhēn said that raw silver was needed for flying and refining,
so an edict was issued to mine it in Lèpíng,
but nothing was obtained.
After Guīzhēn performed fasting and offerings for several days,
he wrote an imperial document and placed it in a cave.
Suddenly, an old man arrived leaning on a staff,
saying:
"Mountains and rivers conceal treasures,
which emerge only when the Way is present.
Moreover, how could a wise ruler's devotion to cultivating perfection
fail to elicit a response?
Do not let the revered master
worry any longer.
Your request shall be granted tomorrow."
After speaking, he vanished without a trace.
That evening,
a sound like thunder was heard,
the mountain mine split open,
and several zhang of molten silver gushed forth,
matching the amount needed for their use.
Refining practices in the palace were numerous,
but outsiders rarely obtained the techniques.

In Cháng'ān, there was a man surnamed Zhāng.

From "Traditions of the Elders of Yìdū."
Wěi Zhāo was
a resident of Yīn Hóng Shòu Lodge in Rǔnán,
skilled in the "Book of Changes."
On his deathbed,
he wrote on a wooden tablet and gave it to his wife,
saying:
"After my death,
there will be great hardship and poverty.
Even so,
be careful not to sell the house.
In the spring five years later,
an imperial envoy will come to stay at this lodge,
surnamed Gōng.
This man owes me gold,
so take this tablet to demand it from him."
After his death,
they indeed fell into great poverty.
Several times she considered selling the house,
but remembering her husband's words, she refrained each time.
When the appointed day arrived,
an envoy named Gōng indeed came to the lodge.
The wife then took the tablet to demand payment from the envoy.
The envoy held the tablet,
not understanding what was said,
and exclaimed:
"I have never set foot here in my life,
how could this be?"
After pondering for a long time,
he asked her:
"What was your worthy husband capable of?"
The wife replied:
"He was skilled in the 'Book of Changes' but never practiced divination for others."
The envoy said:
"That explains it."
He then ordered his attendants to fetch yarrow stalks and perform a divination.
After the hexagram was formed,
he told Wěi Zhāo's wife:
"I do not owe your worthy husband; he had his own gold.
He knew that after his death, you would face temporary poverty,
so he hid the gold to await peaceful times.
The reason he did not tell his wife and children
was to prevent the gold from being exhausted and hardship persisting endlessly.
Knowing that I am skilled in the 'Book of Changes,'
he wrote the tablet to convey his message.
There are five hundred catties of gold,

twisted and cramped, it grew upward,
its trunk measured several arm-spans in girth,
yet its height was no more than four or five feet.
Gnarled and rugged,
contracted and shriveled,
the trunk did not rely on branches,
nor branches on leaves,
resembling a coiled dragon, a limping tiger, or a bound strongman in posture.
Lù Guīméng's "In Praise of the Strange Pine"
Zhèng Xūn, in his old age,
named his residence "Hidden Cliff,"
planted seven small pine trees in his courtyard,
and styled himself "The Hermit of Seven Pines,"
so that in later times he could be paired with the "Gentleman of Five Willows."
From "New Book of the South"
Sōng Fán spoke of "two grains" and "five grains,"
but "grain" should actually refer to the needles.
Duàn Chéngshì's private residence in Xiūzhúlǐ had a main hall in front,
where two five-needle pines stood,
their trunks as large as bowls.
They bore fruit,
and the taste was no different from those of Silla.
The bark of the five-needle pine is not scaly.
At the watermill pavilion of the Tang eunuch Qiú Shìliáng,
there were two-needle pines with non-scaly bark,
and also seven-needle ones,
though it is unknown where they came from.
Commonly, they are called peacock three-needle pines.
Lǐ Déyù stated,
that the three-needle pine is distinct from the peacock pine.
He also said: To prevent a pine from growing tall,
place a stone against its vertical root below,
and it will not take a thousand years to become prostrate.
"Yǒuyáng"
Lǐ Déyù's "Ode to the Golden Pine" preface states: Southeast of Guǎnglíng,
there is the former residence of the nephew of Grand Preceptor Yán,
the site of Kǒng Běihǎi's old terrace.
One morning in spring, I roamed and gazed,
when suddenly I saw a wondrous tree,
its branches resembling tamarisk pines,
its leaves like fescue.
Drawing near to examine it,
I found emerald leaves threaded with gold,
brilliantly gleaming.
Inquiring its name,
I was told: Golden Pine.
Asking its origin,
I learned it came from Tiāntāi.
So I approached the host,
obtained one plant,
and planted it at Píngquán.
"Yīnghuá"
Zhōng Fú built a cottage by the pines,
and planted a pine tree with his own hands.
He dreamed of an official in red robes,
who said:
"When the pine's girth reaches three feet,
your son will pass the imperial examination."
Thirty years later, he finally achieved fame,
and indeed the pine's girth measured exactly three feet.
From "Records of Selected Conversations"
At Tiāntāi Zhìzhě Temple, the monk Shì Xíngmǎn resided in a room with a giant pine tree outside its threshold,
on whose horizontal branch a small parasitic tree grew.
Whenever Mǎn came out to sit,
the parasitic tree would invariably sway gently toward his side.
People at the time called this tree the "tea server making obeisance."
Some who did not believe it
would deliberately watch for it.
When Mǎn emerged,
it would flutter and sway;
when Mǎn sat down,
it would stand tall and upright,
without any further movement.
"Song Dynasty Biographies of Eminent Monks"
In Nánkāng there was a strange pine tree.
Formerly, the regional inspector often ordered painters to sketch the pine,
and it would inevitably cause several trees to wither and sicken.
Later, because a guest and a courtesan formed a circle,
drinking beneath it,
after a day the pine tree died.
From "Yǒuyáng"
In the deep mountains of Yīyáng, there is Hēisōngshān Plain,
forty lǐ high,
covered with large pine trees.
Among them, two are exceptionally large;
one is named Dàjiāngjūn (Great General),
the other Xiǎojiāngjūn (Little General).
The larger one measured three bolts of silk in circumference,
the smaller one, one bolt.
When lumberjacks gathered timber here,
they all made offerings to them.
After measuring with silk,
they created drawings and hung them on the trees.
During the Zhènghé era,
when pillars for the Bright Hall were sought,
local officials claimed there were none
meeting the standards. Later, someone reported,
saying:
"The large pine cannot be transported out,
but the small one can be taken."
The informant was then appointed an official,
while the local magistrates were all demoted.
After the tree was felled,
it too could not be transported out.
The informant soon died.
Now only Dàjiāngjūn remains standing,
while the smaller one lies abandoned in the mountains—
what a pity!
From "Táo Zhū Xīn Lù"
South of Fèngchén Bridge on Luófú Mountain,
there are seven ancient pine trees,
reaching up to the heavens where immortals often rest.
Zōu Bǎoguāng possessed magical arts,
during the Xuānhé era,
he was summoned to the Níngshén Hall,
and seven men followed him but suddenly vanished.
The emperor asked who they were,
Bǎoguāng replied:
"I dwell in the mountains,
often practicing sword arts,
these seven individuals
are the ancient pines.
The emperor found it extraordinary.
"Luófú Chronicles"
Hóng Mài, during the Shàoxīng era, studied with his brothers Huò and Zūn at the tomb hut of the Shěn family's White Mulberry Mountain estate.
That year,
two pines by the tomb
formed canopies with their intertwined branches.
Subsequently, the brothers passed the erudite literary examination,
which was considered an auspicious sign from the trees.
"Kūnlíng Records"
In the past when the Jin people attacked the Sòng Dynasty,
they felled trees from Xiāngyán Temple to build ships.
The wood grain formed a poem,
which read:
"Pines and cypresses planted when Táng flourished,
Planks became ships as Sòng fell.
Alas, Xiāngyán's millennial trees,
Casually wither in winter's chill."
This has been passed down through generations as a strange phenomenon.
"Zhèchuān County Chronicles"
The pine tree of Tiānlíng with its prostrate canopy,
the cypress of the great valley growing upside down,
all these trees match heaven in their height,
and equal the earth in their longevity.
From "Bàopǔzǐ"
At the northern cliff of Shímén,
lies the pine forest.
There are several hundred pine trees,
all so large that their trunks can be encircled by linked arms,
nearly twenty zhàng tall,
clustered together on the sheer cliff.
They face south overlooking the Shímén Stream,
and when looking up from within the stream,
they appear densely arrayed like paired duster tails,
thus named "Duster Tail Pines."
Viewed from Xúnyáng,
they are clearly visible as a gathering.
From Zhōu Jǐngshì's "Record of Lúshān"
East of the Púgǔ territory,
one thousand li to the northeast there is the Kāngyú River.
When a broken pine is thrown into it,
after three years it turns into stone,
its color blue-green,
called Kāngyú stone,
bearing pine patterns.
Ten li northwest of Mǎchéng stands a withered pine tree,
traditionally believed to be a ten-thousand-year pine.
In Luòyáng there was a fish-scale pine.
From the "Yǒuyáng Zálǔ".
On Mount Sōng there are great pine trees,
some a hundred or a thousand years old,
their essence transforms into blue oxen,
or into crouching turtles.
If one gathers and eats their fruit,
one attains long life.
"Records of Mount Sōnggāo": Thousand-year-old pine and cypress trees,
their branches and leaves do not grow at the top.
Viewed from afar, they look like reclining covers,
within them there are creatures,
such as blue oxen, blue sheep, and people,
all who consume them live ten thousand years.
"The Jade Register"
Yìzhēnguàn is located southwest of the city of Nánchāng Prefecture.
The temple has two pine trees,
five feet apart,
that merge into a single trunk,
called Righteous Pines.
From "Shānchuān Jìyì"
The water pine has leaves like those of the juniper but slender and long,
and is found in the South Sea region.
Although the land produces various fragrant woods,
this tree is not particularly aromatic,
so the local people do not use it for clothing.
People north of the mountains greatly cherish it,
yet they appreciate its fragrance far more than when it is in the south.
Plants are insentient beings,
yet they are not fragrant there but fragrant here.
Could it be that they yield to those who do not understand them and flourish among those who do?
Such is the difficulty in fully comprehending the principles of things.
In "An Account of the Plants and Trees of the Southern Regions," it is said that there is a tree that clings to it and grows by its side,
soft and pliable enough to make shoes,
called "fragrance-embracing shoes."
From "The Records of Luófú."
The tree is similar to the Chinese pine,
but its fruit is exceptionally large,
shaped like small chestnuts,
triangular,
plump, sweet, and fragrant,
a fine fruit for serving at banquets.
It originates from Línyì.
"Nánfāng Cǎowù Zhuàng"
On the summit of Mount Zhōngyuè, pine trunks stand like inserted brushes;
among them are several trees
with massive tops and slender bases,
their branches resembling withered stumps,
their bark partly peeling away,
some half-thriving.
A monk pointed and said: "These were planted upside down by the mountain deity for Chán Master Guī
when he moved celestial generals by night.
At dawn,
his ghost soldiers grew fearful
and hastily inverted them before departing."
From "Old Tales of Qǔwèi"
On the Hidden Shepherd Ridge stood an ancient pine,
its roots gnarled and wondrous in form.
Once, two brothers quarreled bitterly,
intending to bring their dispute before the authorities.
They traveled by night and rested beneath it,
and at dawn, as light revealed their faces,
they recognized each other as brothers.
Filled with remorse, they abandoned their strife and returned home,
thus naming the pine "Wooden Official."
From "The Hangzhou Chronicles"
Leaning on the lush, delicate grass,
shaded by the tall, solitary pines.
From "Tiāntāi Fù": Tall pines stand alone,
plants and trees grow thickly.
From Dù Dǔ's "Shǒuyáng Shān Fù"
Tall and erect, tall and erect, the pine on the mountain.
Liú Gōnggàn's poem: "Lush and green, the pine on the mound,"
Tall and erect, the cypress on the high mountain.
Hé Jìngzǔ: "Lush and green, the cypress on the mound."
Ancient poem.
Lush pines at the valley's floor.
Poem by Zuǒ Tàichōng
I ascend that lofty hill,
Where pines and cypresses grow thick.
From "Yin Wu" in the Book of Songs
How lofty the southern mountain's rocks!
How sturdy the pine and cypress trees!
Their top branches brush against the blue clouds,
Their trunks measure dozens of arm-spans around.
From Liú Yuèshí's "Song of Fufeng"
Pine branches are burned from top to bottom,
collecting the liquid called sōng chóu,
the green moss on the pine bark is called ài nà,
when blended with various fragrances and burned,
the smoke gathers and swirls,
appearing pure and white, delightful to behold.
"Guǎng Zhì"
The pine tree represents a ruler,
so dreaming of a pine tree
means seeing a ruler.
"Book of Dreams"
Mount Báiyú,
its heights abound with cypress trees,
and its earthen hills are rich with cypress.
"The Classic of Mountains"
Huàshān produces patterned cypress trees.
Geographical Records.
Chìsōngzǐ loved to eat cypress nuts,
and his lost teeth grew back.
Liexian Zhuan
In Hànyáng County, there is an ancient well at Bǎiquán Temple to the west.
It is traditionally said that Dà Yǔ planted a cypress on Dàbié Mountain,
and its roots twisted all the way to the bottom of the well.
The cypress roots still exist today.
Also, in front of Tàipíng Xīngguó Temple on the southern side of Dàbié Mountain, there is another ancient cypress,
commonly believed to have been planted by Yǔ during his flood control efforts.
"Shānchuān Jìyì"
In the old courtyard of Confucius in Lǔjùn, there were twenty-four cypress trees,
which had survived through the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
their trunks so large that they could barely be encircled by arms.
Two of them had previously broken and fallen,
and the local people held them in such reverence
that no one dared to harm them.
Jiāngxià King Yìgōng sent men to cut them all down,
leaving the elders sighing in regret.
"The Book of Sòng" records: Inside the gate of the Xuānwén Temple in Qūfù County, Yǎnzhōu, and to the southwest of the hall, there were trees with cypress leaves and pine trunks,
each standing fifty or sixty feet tall,
though they had long been withered.
It was said that they were planted by the Master himself.
In the third year of Yǒngjiā, they withered again.
Folklore held that millennial wood could cure heartache,
so many people secretly cut pieces from them,
causing the trunks to gradually thin.
About ten feet above the ground,
they were covered and sealed with mud,
yet this did not prevent the damage.
Some also took the wood to make official tablets,
which were purple in color and highly glossy.
During the reign of Emperor Sùzōng, the two trees still remained.
"Féngshì's Account of Observations" notes: In front of the temple of the First Sage, there were several ancient cypress trees,
also said to be over a thousand years old,
with trunks measuring ten arm-spans in circumference.
When Zī Huá served as governor of Yǎnzhōu,
the army was impoverished for provisions,
with nothing to supply as provisions for the troops,
so Huá ordered them to be felled,
cut into bamboo slips,
carved into utensils,
and used as provisions.
"Transmitted Records"
Duke Jǐng and Yànzǐ were traveling at Shǎo Hǎi,
ascended the Bǎiqǐn Platform,
and looking back at their state,
said:
"How magnificent!
So vast!
So grand!
Who in later generations will possess this?
Yànzǐ replied:
"Would it be Tián Chéngshì?
In "Hán Wài Zhuàn": Lǐ Shàojūn appeared before Emperor Wǔ,
the emperor had an ancient bronze vessel and asked Shàojūn about it,
Shàojūn said:
"This vessel was displayed at Bǎiqǐn by Duke Huán of Qí in the tenth year of his reign.
Checking its inscription,
it was indeed Duke Huán of Qí's vessel,
the entire palace was astonished.
"Shǐjì" Commentary by Shī Gǔ states: Using cypress wood to build a bedchamber atop the platform.
During the time of Qín Mùgōng,
a person from Chéncāng dug up something from the ground,
resembling a sheep but not a sheep,
resembling a pig but not a pig,
and planned to present this strange creature.
On the way, he encountered two youths,
who said to him:
"Do you know what that is?
It is called wǎng,
often dwelling underground,
feeding on the brains of the dead.
If you wish to kill it,
point a cypress branch from the southeast at it, and it will die."
The "Sòng Fúruì Zhì" states: Cypress trees are planted on graves,
and stone tigers are placed at the road's entrance.
The "Zhōulǐ" mentions the Fangxiangshi entering tombs,
to ward off the wǎng.
The wǎng
likes to eat the livers and brains of the deceased.
If households cannot manage it, they should have the Fangxiangshi stand by the tomb
to restrain and ward it off,
as the wǎng fears tigers and cypress trees.
From the "Fēngsútōng."
Bógǔ,
is the name of a valley.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn traveled incognito,
and it was here in Bógǔ that he arrogantly treated his host.
The valley has no space to turn a carriage around,
hemmed in by high plateaus,
with cypress groves casting deep shade all day long,
so dim and obscure
that sunlight is scarcely visible.
"Records of Campaigns"
South of the mountain stands the Tàishān Temple,
planted with a thousand cypress trees,
the largest being fifteen to sixteen arm-spans around.
Elders pass down that they were planted by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
The "Record of Mount Tài" states: The cypresses in the Tàishān Temple are all over twenty arm-spans around,
lining both sides of the western steps.
The Red Eyebrows once chopped one tree,
but stopped when they saw it bleed,
and the axe marks remain to this day.
"Account of a Campaign"
There is the resin of pine and cypress among medicines,
taking it can prolong life.
"Han Wu Nei Zhuan"
On Mount Bàng, there was a cypress with a hollow,
and above the hollow grew another cypress.
Long ago, Lǐ Shàowēng moved it from Làngyīn to this hollow,
planting this cypress.
It had already witnessed the Fusang tree wither three times,
and the sea waters run dry.
The emperor awoke,
and sent someone to dig around the hollow,
but they could not find its roots.
They only saw a red swallow soaring into the clouds.
The cypress was then transplanted to the Tōnglíng Tower.
From "Records of the Obscure in the Cave"
In Bàjùn there was a cypress pillar,
large enough to require ten arm spans,
over twenty zhàng in height,
which served as a tower pillar during Gōngsūn Shù's era.
At the place where it was cut,
branches unexpectedly grew without decaying.
Records of the Known World
The Daoists often make cypress leaf decoction,
regular consumption benefits people,
with ancient cypress leaves being particularly remarkable.
Now in Yìzhōu at Zhūgě Kǒngmíng's temple there are large cypress trees,
traditionally said to have been planted during the Shǔ period,
so people frequently gather them to make medicine,
their flavor being sweeter and more fragrant than ordinary cypress.
"Tú Jīng"
Yǔ Jiǎn,
courtesy name Shēng Bāo.
When someone cut down the cypress trees at his father's grave,
and no one knew who it was,
he summoned his neighbors to the grave and blamed himself,
kowtowing with tears streaming down his face,
apologizing to his ancestors.
After this, no one dared to violate it again.
From "Book of Jin": When Lǐ Chōng was mourning his father by the grave, a thief came at night to cut down cypress trees,
and Chōng personally killed him with a blade.
From "Chronicles of the Elderly of Chénliú".
Wáng Póu, courtesy name Wěiyuán,
grieved that his father did not die a natural death,
so he withdrew from the world and refused to serve in office.
He built a hut beside the tomb,
and every morning and evening he would go to the tomb,
where he would wail with grief until his voice broke.
There was a cypress tree at the tomb,
which Wáng Póu often clung to while weeping.
The tree, stained by his tears,
took on a different color from ordinary trees.
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" records: When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng paid homage at the mountain tomb,
the tears he shed
caused the pines to change color.
"Jīn Lóu Zǐ"
The Eastern Palace's Xuānpǔ Garden had a cypress wood house,
constructed in a very ancient and unadorned style.
"The Biography of Prince Yùzhāng of the Southern Qí Dynasty"
Jiāngxià Wáng Fēng, knowing that Míngdì understood power dynamics,
often felt restless and unhappy.
He composed "Ode to the Tall Cypress" to express his aspirations,
saying:
"Standing apart from the crowd, I rise in defiance,
Embracing integrity and unwavering righteousness.
Not merely fragrant in the springtime,
But flourishing even under frost.
Gales cannot break its branches,
Accumulated snow cannot alter its nature.
Though thwarted in these times,
May its enduring resilience be celebrated."
At that time, the imperial destiny was secretly shifting,
and Fēng alone harbored a determined will to restore the realm.
Later, he was killed by Míngdì.
Jiāng Yù, upon hearing of his death,
said:
"When fragrant orchids block the gate,
one has no choice but
to uproot them—such is the fate of his 'Ode to the Tall Cypress'."
From *The History of the Southern Dynasties*
Xú Bózhēn,
a native of Tàimò in Dōngyáng.
Nine li south of his residence stood a high mountain,
which Bān Gù called Jiǔyán Mountain,
the retreat of Lóngqiū Cháng of the Later Hàn dynasty.
The mountain abounded with dragon's beard cypress trees,
appearing variegated from a distance,
and was commonly known as Fùrén Cliff.
Bózhēn
moved to live by its entrance,
where a catalpa tree grew
and grew to arm-span thickness within a year.
From the Book of Southern Qí
After Hóu Jǐng captured the imperial city,
the temple trees of nobles and commoners in the capital were all destroyed,
yet only the cypress trees surrounding Empress Wénxuān's temple remained lush.
When Hóu Jǐng ordered the construction of the southern suburban road,
the false Minister of Personnel Lǚ Jìlüè advised him to cut down these trees
to build three bridges.
After felling over ten trees on the southern side,
within two nights, new shoots sprouted from the stumps,
growing several feet tall.
Though it was winter,
their verdant vitality resembled spring,
which greatly shocked the rebels,
who viewed it as ominous,
and ordered all the trees to be cut down.
Those with insight believed that
just as the withered willow's revival in the Shanglin Park
heralded Emperor Xuān of Hàn's rise,
now the temple trees' renewed greenery
must signify auspicious fortune for Shǎnxī.
《Liáng Shū Nán Shǐ》
Prince Xiāo Jì of Wǔlíng, under the reign of Liáng, took advantage of the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng to proclaim himself emperor in Shǔ.
Initially, various ominous signs appeared,
with the pillar in the inner chamber's cypress hall sprouting flowers around its joints,
the stems numbering forty-six,
delicate and charming,
resembling lotus blossoms.
Those who understood such signs remarked:
"The ominous flowers of Wáng Dūn
are not a good omen."
Later, he was indeed executed by Emperor Yuán.
From *History of the Southern Dynasties*
Cuī Hóng of Bólíng,
styled Zǐhóng,
returned to life twelve years after his death.
He feared sunlight,
daring not to look upward,
and also dreaded water, fire,
and weapons such as blades.
He often hurried along main roads,
stopping when tired,
never walking leisurely.
People of the time still considered him a ghost.
In Fèngzhōng Lane north of Luòyáng's Grand Market,
most residents sold funeral items,
including various coffins.
Hóng told them:
"Make coffins of cypress wood,
and do not use mulberry for the liners."
When asked the reason,
Hóng said:
"In the underworld,
I saw people conscripting ghost soldiers.
One ghost pleaded that his cypress coffin should exempt him,
but the officer in charge said: 'Though your coffin is cypress,
its liner is mulberry.'
Thus he was not exempted."
When the capital heard this,
cypress wood prices soared,
and people suspected that all coffin sellers were Hóng,
spreading such tales.
From "A Record of Luòyáng's Temples"
The elder sister of Wáng Zhěng from Bàchéng
married Wèi Jìngyú.
At the age of sixteen, Jìngyú died,
and her parents and parents-in-law all wanted her to remarry,
but she vowed not to consent.
She then cut off her ear and placed it in a tray as a pledge.
They then desisted.
Thereafter, she personally planted several hundred trees for her deceased husband.
Suddenly, a cypress tree in front of the tomb grew intertwined branches,
which separated once but rejoined again.
The woman then composed a poem:
"Before the tomb stands a cypress tree,
Its roots entwined, its branches unite.
If my heart can move the trees,
What marvel is Yánchéng?"
From History of the Southern Dynasties
Emperor Wǔ attacked Qí,
and Duke Yǒngchāng, Chūn, stationed his troops at Jīqīyuán.
King Xiàn of Qí secretly said to Chūn:
"For the encampment, there is no need to set up tents;
you can cut down cypress trees to make huts,
so that after the troops have left,
the enemy will still be misled.
When they were ordered to withdraw,
leading the troops back at night,
the Qí people indeed mistook the cypress huts for tents,
and only realized the mistake the next day.
"Book of the Later Zhōu Dynasty"
During the reign of Emperor Wén of Suí,
Wáng Shào submitted a memorial stating:
"At the Lǎozi shrine in Chénliú, there is a withered cypress tree.
Legend says that when Lǎozi was about to leave this world,
he declared:
'Wait until the withered cypress grows a branch pointing southeast,
then turns back to point,
and a sage will emerge.
My Way will be restored.'
By the Qí dynasty,
the withered cypress grew a branch from its base,
pointing directly southeast.
At night, three young boys were heard singing together:
'Before Lǎozi's temple stands an ancient withered tree,
its southeast branch spreads like a canopy,
the sage ruler shall depart from here.'
When Your Majesty governed Bó Prefecture,
you personally visited beneath the shrine's tree.
From then on, the cypress branches curled inward,
and its withered parts
gradually pointed northwest,
whereupon Dàoism indeed flourished.
《History of the Northern Dynasties》: In front of Lǎozi's hall in Zhēnyuán County stood a pair of cypress trees,
the one by the left steps had long been withered.
In the thirteenth year of Emperor Yáng's Great Enterprise reign period,
a new trunk suddenly sprouted from its roots,
reaching thirty-three feet tall,
with lush green branches and leaves in the Táng dynasty.
In the second year of Emperor Wǔzōng's reign,
it grew another branch,
soaring straight up five feet.
With two layers of horizontal branches,
their foliage overlapping,
it differed from ordinary trees.
《Records of Campaigns》 《Universal Geography》
When Gāozǔ was still in swaddling clothes,
his mother placed him in the shade of a cypress tree on their estate,
and went to deliver food to the fields.
By the time she returned from delivering the food,
the sun had slanted but the tree's shadow had not moved.
"Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
At Tīanfēng Temple on Sōng Shān, there stand three ancient cypress trees.
Empress Wǔ bestowed upon them the title of Fifth Rank Grand Master.
Their shade spreads over more than a hundred paces,
and they are commonly called the Great and Little Generals.
"Records of Hénán"
The cypresses at Qiánlíng differ from those elsewhere;
none of the trees lack grain patterns,
and their grains mostly form bodhisattvas, misty vapors, human figures, birds, and beasts,
with extremely distinct and remarkable appearances.
A thief who obtained one trunk a foot in diameter
could sell it for ten thousand coins.
Families in Guān and Shǎn regions often prize them,
which is fitting as their seeds are of the finest quality.
"Běncǎo"
At Mount Sōng, when Emperor Wǔ of Hàn ascended to fēng sacrifice,
a divine being hailed him with "ten thousand years."
Halfway up the peak,
lies the former site of the Sōngyáng Temple,
with a stele inscription from the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty.
East of the stele stand five ancient cypress trees,
their lush greenery swaying gracefully and delightfully.
Among them, one tree is especially large,
requiring five people joining hands to encircle its trunk.
Beneath it rests a stone,
carved with the words:
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn enfeoffed the Great General."
From "The Collection of Shàolín."
Sāng Dàomáo resided where there were two very lush cypress trees,
and said:
"When people dwell and trees flourish, one should leave;
if trees thrive, then the earth declines,
and decline causes people to fall ill.
