The Red Emperor, seeing this, was deeply grieved,
and unable to lure him back, burned the nest with fire.
The maiden then ascended to heaven,
hence it was named the Emperor's Daughter Mulberry.
Nowadays, on the fifteenth day,
people burn magpie nests,
make an ash solution,
and bathe silkworm eggs to attract silk,
imitating this event.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì".
The locust tree is
the essence of the Xu star.
"Chūnqiū Shuōtící"

The leaves of the Shǒugōng locust tree fold during the day and spread out at night. Note: The locust tree whose leaves fold together by day and spread out at night is called Shǒugōng locust. From "Ěryǎ".
When the pagoda tree begins to grow,
by late spring,
it forms rabbit-eye-like buds in five days,
mouse-ear-shaped leaves in ten days,
starts to take shape in another ten days,
and fully leafs out in twenty days.
"Huáinánzǐ"
Facing the three scholar trees stand the court officials,
where the three highest ministers take their positions.
The scholar tree,
symbolizes embrace,
meaning it embraces and attracts people.
As recorded in the "Rites of Zhou,"
Shù Huái hears cases under it.
Note: The word "huái"
means "to return,"
as in emotions being seen and returning to truth.
Yuánmìngbāo
King Wǔ asked Tài Gōng:
"The gods and spirits coming from all under heaven are very numerous,
I fear there may be those who are testing us,
how should we receive them?
Tài Gōng said:
"I request that you plant a locust tree inside the royal gate,
those who are beneficial will enter,
those who are not beneficial will be kept out.
《The Golden Casket》
Duke Jǐng of Qí had a beloved locust tree,
and ordered an official to guard it.
He decreed:
"Those who offend against the locust tree shall be punished,
those who harm it shall be put to death.
If someone with a crime offends against it,
the duke orders additional punishment."
His daughter appealed to Yànzǐ, saying:
"I have heard that a wise ruler does not harm the people for the sake of birds and beasts,
does not harm birds and beasts for the sake of plants and trees,
does not harm crops for the sake of weeds.
Now my lord is punishing my father because of a tree,
I fear neighboring states will say my lord values trees and despises people."
Yànzǐ went in and spoke of this,
the duke ordered the cessation of the locust tree guard duty,
abolished the law against harming the locust tree,
and released the prisoners who had offended against the locust tree.
From "Yànzǐ"
Dǒng Shū was about to marry into the Fàn family,
when Shū Xiàng said:
"The Fàn family is wealthy, why not give it up?
He replied:
"I want to be tied to and supported by them.
Some days later,
Dǒng Qí complained to Fàn Xiànzǐ,
saying:
"He does not respect me.
Fànzǐ seized him and tied him to the locust tree in the courtyard. As Shū Xiàng passed by,
he said:
"Won't you plead for me?
Shū Xiàng said:
"You sought to be tied, and now you are tied.
You sought support, and now you are supported.
You desired and obtained it,
what more is there to plead for?
"Jīnyǔ"
On the northern bank of Gānquán Valley stands a pagoda tree,
now called the Jade Tree.
Its roots and trunk coil and tower,
a tree of two to three hundred years.
Yáng Zhèn's "Ancient Tales of Guānfǔ" states:
"According to elders' tradition,
all consider this tree to be Yáng
It is what the "Gānquán Fù" calls "the jade trees verdant."
The Sānfǔ records: In Yúnyáng County, there were many Han dynasty detached palaces,
so in the old grounds, there grew trees resembling locust trees but with finer leaves,
which the locals called jade trees.
Yáng Zǐyún's "Gānquán Fù" says:
"Jade trees verdant"
later Zuǒ Sī considered this a false claim of rarity and wonder,
likely due to lack of detailed knowledge.
The Guóshǐ Yìzuǎn states: The jade trees
were assembled by Emperor Wǔ from various treasures,
Sī argued they were not of wood or earth,
thus missing the point.
Yán Shīshí
In the Grand Marshal's office, there was an old locust tree.
Yīn Zhòngkān faced it and sighed, saying:
"This tree is all withered and splayed,
its vitality is completely exhausted.
Book of Jìn
Initially,
the region west of the Yellow River did not grow catalpa, pagoda trees, cypress, or lacquer trees.
During Zhāng Jùn's reign,
they were brought from Qín and Lǒng to be planted,
but ultimately all died.
However, a pagoda tree grew in the northwest corner of the Jiǔquán Palace.
Lǐ Xuánshèng composed the "Pagoda Tree Rhapsody" to express his feelings,
lamenting that in this remote and backward land,
achieving merit was not the place for it.
Guǎnglíng Wáng Yuānyuān,
was first appointed as Yítóng Sānsī.
He led the northern expedition against Gě Róng.
One night, he dreamed of wearing a ceremonial robe,
standing leaning against a locust tree,
and considered it an auspicious sign.
He consulted Yáng Yuánshèn about it,
who said:
"It is an omen of the Three Excellencies."
Yuānyuān was very pleased by this.
Yuánshèn later withdrew and told others:
"Guǎnglíng will die.
The character for locust (槐),
combines tree (木) and ghost (鬼), meaning death.
Although he was destined to attain the Three Excellencies,
he was indeed killed by Ěrzhū Róng,
and posthumously honored as Grand Minister of Works,
ultimately fulfilling the prophecy.
(From "A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang")
Yǔ Jiānwú often consumed sophora seeds,
and even past seventy years of age,
he could still read fine print,
with all his hair remaining black.
During the turmoil of war,
he fled to Jiānglíng.
The Book of Liáng states: "Gather sophora seeds on the third day of the third month in the tenth month and take them
to improve complexion,
prolong life, and connect with the divine."
The Great Clarity Compendium on Herbs
Wéi Xiàokuān was the governor of Yōngzhōu.
Previously, along the roadside at every lǐ, an earthen mound marker was placed,
which would collapse after rain,
requiring frequent repairs.
When Xiàokuān assumed his post in the province,
he ordered that locust trees be planted at all marker locations within his jurisdiction,
thus eliminating the need for repairs,
while also providing shade for travelers.
When Emperor Wén later saw this,
he commanded all provinces
"to plant one tree per lǐ along the roads,
three trees every ten lǐ,
and five trees every hundred lǐ.
From the Book of the Later Zhōu Dynasty.
Gāo Yǐng,
courtesy name Zhāoxuán,
served as the Grand Supervisor of Xīndū.
He often conducted official business while sitting under a locust tree.
Later, as the trees grew disorderly and not in proper rows,
the officials requested to cut them down.
The emperor specifically ordered them to be preserved,
to serve as an example for future generations.
(Book of Suì)
Jiǎ Jiāyǐn,
at the age of seven,
was summoned for an audience as a child prodigy.
At the time, Zhǎngsūn Wújì and Minister Xú Jì were standing and talking in the court hall.
Xú teased him, saying:
"What kind of tree am I leaning against?
Jiāyǐn replied:
"A pine tree.
Xú said:
"This is a locust tree,
why do you say pine?
Jiāyǐn explained:
"With 'Duke' (公) paired with 'wood' (木),
how can it not be 'pine' (松)?
Zhǎngsūn asked again:
"What kind of tree am I leaning against?
He replied:
"A locust tree.
The duke said:
"Can't you give a clever response this time?
Jiāyǐn said:
"Why bother with a clever response,
I just take the 'ghost' (鬼) and 'wood' (木).
Xú sighed and said:
"This child has a barbarian-like face,
how can he be so intelligent?
Jiāyǐn retorted:
"A 'barbarian-head' can still become a prime minister,
why should a 'barbarian-face' hinder intelligence?
Xú had the appearance of a non-Han person.
"From 'Liú Bīnkè's Refined Conversations'"
Xiàogǎn Niǔhuí,
styled Xiàozhèng,
was extremely filial by nature.
During the Wǔchéng era of the Northern Zhōu dynasty,
when his parents passed away, he built a mourning hut beside their graves.
In front of the hut grew a hemp plant,
about ten feet tall,
with a trunk so thick it could be encircled with both hands,
its branches and leaves lush and dense,
remaining green throughout winter and summer.
Emperor Wǔ commended him.
When his son Shìxióng lost his father,
he also built a mourning hut beside the grave.
In front of the courtyard stood a pagoda tree,
initially very lush and thriving,
but after Shìxióng began his mourning observance,
the tree withered and died.
Upon completing the mourning period and returning home,
the dead tree revived and flourished again.
Emperor Gāozǔ issued an edict to commend them,
naming their residence
"Lěidé Lǐ"
From the "Suí Shū"
At Chún Yú Fēn's home,
south of the Guǎnglíng County residence stood a great ancient locust tree,
with dense branches and lush foliage.
Fēn was drinking beneath it with local nobles.
In the seventh year of the Zhēnyuán era,
he fell ill from excessive drinking.
Two friends helped him back to bed,
where he dreamed of two messengers saying:
"The King of Huái'ān Kingdom invites you.
Fēn followed the two messengers,
entering a hole in the ancient locust tree,
above which was inscribed
"Great Huái'ān Kingdom"
He entered and met the king,
who married him to his second daughter Yáo Fāng,
titled Princess Golden Branch.
There were several ladies
named Huáyáng Gū, Qīngxī Gū, Upper Immortal, and Lower Immortal,
all serving as attendants.
He was appointed governor of Nánkē County,
where Fēn remained for over twenty years.
Messengers escorted him out of the hole,
whereupon he awoke and found he had children.
The setting sun had not yet disappeared behind the western wall,
and leftover wine remained clear in the eastern window.
In the fleeting moment of his dream,
it felt as if a lifetime had passed.
He then went with guests to search for the hole beneath the locust tree,
finding a clear, bright cavity
large enough for a bed,
containing two large ants
with white wings and crimson heads,
about two inches long—
these were the King of Huái'ān.
Exploring another hole
that went straight up the southern branch,
they found it was Nánkē County.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
the Ministry of Revenue wanted to cut down the pagoda trees along the roads of both capitals for firewood,
and replace them with small trees.
First, an official order was issued.
Wèinán County Deputy Zhāng Zào submitted a memorandum stating:
"Where Duke Shào rested,
the trees were still left uncut;
how much more for the places where the late emperor once traveled,
should they be felled?"
The plan was then abandoned.
From the Old Book of Táng
During the Chángqìng era,
Governor Xiāo Yòu of Guó Prefecture reported:
Commoner Yán Fēng from Yǒngfáng Village, Húchéng County,
had five generations living together,
and a locust tree in their household
produced new branches and leaves.
In front of the Chíguó Temple in Cháng'ān stood several locust trees.
Jīn purchased one of them,
and ordered his skilled craftsman to cut it open.
When they entered inside,
the craftsman reported that the wood had nothing unusual.
Jīn sighed with deep regret,
and ordered it to be glued back together, saying:
"This is worthless!
I just wanted you to know my craftsmanship."
Then he had it split open differently.
On each piece appeared a heavenly king,
with pagodas and halberds perfectly formed.
From "Yǒuyáng"

Chancellor Lǐ Shí had a residence in Hézhōng Yǒnglè, where a single locust tree in the courtyard produced three branches. One branch extended straight past the front hall’s roof ridge, while another branch fell short. The chancellor had two brothers from the same household: Lǐ Chéng and Lǐ Shí both rose to the positions of chancellor and chief minister, while only Lǐ Fú served successively as military commissioner of seven towns, merely holding the honorary title of chancellor. This was because one branch was slightly shorter. *Yùquánzǐ*

When Pei Dù was serving as chancellor, someone sent him a burl from a pagoda tree, intending to carve it into a pillow. At the time, the court official Yǔ Wēi, renowned for his extensive knowledge, was summoned to identify it. Yǔ held and examined it for a long time before stating, "This burl comes from a female pagoda tree and is likely unsuitable for use." Pei asked, "How old are you, Official Yǔ?" Yǔ replied, "I share the same birth year as Your Excellency, both born in the jiǎchén year." Pei laughed and said, "Then you, Official, are the 'female jiǎchén'." *Miscellaneous Records of the Lú Family*

Wú Còu served as the Metropolitan Governor and concurrently as Minister of War. Previously, the street trees were sparse and damaged, so the authorities planted elms in the empty spaces. Còu remarked, "Elms do not provide shade for people," and promptly replaced them all with locust trees. When the locust trees matured, Còu had already passed away. Passersby would point at the trees and remember him fondly.
In Cháng'ān City, there was a Sūn family residence,
which they had inhabited for several generations,
with a very ancient main hall.
In front of this hall, one pillar
suddenly sprouted a pagoda tree branch.
The Sūn family initially concealed it,
not wishing others to see.
After a year had passed,
it gradually grew lush and vigorous,
until the entire pillar transformed,
damaging the roof as it thrust upward,
making concealment impossible.
Officials and commoners who came to view it
filled the streets with their carriages and horses.
Not long after,
the family attained high court positions,
holding authoritative posts.
People believed this fulfilled the omen of the three pagoda trees,
considering it quite extraordinary.
Their descendant Sūn Wěi recounted this in detail in "Casual Conversations from the Jade Hall."
Lǚ Méngzhèng was preparing for the imperial examination,
renting a room at Jiànlóng Temple,
and went to Luòyáng for official business,
locking his room before leaving.
He did not return until spring after spending the winter away.
Upon opening the door,
he saw a cluster of locust tree branches in front of his bed, two to three feet tall,
lush and thick enough to wrap one's arms around.
That year, he passed the imperial examination and became chancellor a decade later.
"Mùfǔ Yànwén Lù"
During the Xīníng era,
Wú Zhòngshù governed Chéngdū.
One day,
the large locust tree in front of the Civil Hall emitted smoke from all its branches and leaves,
bluish-white in color,
as if incense were burning,
and it did not cease until dusk,
yet the tree remained unharmed.
Yáng Sǔnzhī remarked: The "Yīnfú" states: Fire is born from wood,
and when it first emerges, it is sure to overcome;
he suspected that soldiers would stage a rebellion but fail.
A little over a month later,
it was indeed reported that garrison soldiers were plotting a revolt,
and all were captured.
From Yáng Yànlíng's "Bǐlù."
In Xīxià, there were no locust trees except for one in Xiàzhōu. If locust leaves were needed, an official document would be sent to obtain them. 《Yǒuyáng》
Bái Jūyì said:
"In Zhōngzhōu there is one lychee tree,
and one locust tree.
South of Zhōng there are no more locust trees,
north of Zhōng there are no more lychees.
From "Records and Accounts"
South of the Dūtáng hall, east of the pathway, stands an ancient locust tree,
its shade spreading wide and far.
Sometimes at night, the sound of strings and pipes is heard,
which means someone in the ministry is about to become chancellor.
Commonly known as the "Tree of Auspicious Sounds,"
from the "New Book of the Southern Regions."
In the northern corner of Jìnyáng's capital city, there was a locust tree
that within a single day
flourished and withered three times each.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Jade Box"
The Jade Balance Star scattered and became elms.
"The Pivot of the Turning Dipper"
The wúgū reaches its peak when barren,
its fruit is called yízhù.
Wúgū,
refers to the elm,
what is called wúyí.
The "Ěryǎ" states: wúyí,
also known as wúgū.
The "Běncǎo" says: wúyí found on the ground,
those with a red core are of good quality.
From "Fànzǐ Jìrán"
Liú Zǐjùn believed the empty words of alchemists,
thinking immortality could be learned.
I saw the large elm tree in his courtyard,
which after long years had decayed and broken,
and pointed to it, saying:
"That tree lacks sentience,
yet still withers and rots.
Though humans may wish to nurture and preserve themselves,
how can they prevent their own decline?"
From Huán Tán's Xīn Lùn
Zhèng Zé was the governor of Wèi Commandery,
and the common people lacked timber,
so he assigned them to plant elms as hedges.
Records of Wèi
Emperor Huán of Wèi once suffered from poisoning,
and on the ground where he vomited,
an elm tree still grew.
Since there were no elm trees in the soil of Cānhé Slope,
people of the time found it extraordinary.
"Book of Wèi"
Emperor Tàizǔ Dàowǔ, personal name Guī,
was born on the seventh day of the seventh month north of Cānhé Pō.
The following year,
an elm tree grew in the depression where his placenta was buried,
which later developed into a forest.
The sovereign
Xíng Guǒ of Héjiān rebelled,
his followers exceeded one hundred thousand.
Previously,
people of Hénán often mocked those of Héběi for enjoying eating elm leaves,
thus the people of Qí nicknamed them
"the Elm-Licking Bandits"
They were suppressed by Yuán Tiānmù.
"Wei Biography Two" states: Licking,
pronounced as tà chuò.
Xú explained:
"It means like a dog taking food with its mouth.
In Hán's "Cáo Chéngyù Stele," it says licking followed Guānghuà.
The great river is north of the city gate of Jīnchéng.
It flows eastward,
and Liáng Quán flows into it,
which originates from the southern mountains of the county.
According to the elders: Liáng Huī,
courtesy name Shǐ'é,
was a descendant of Liáng Jì, the great general of the Hàn dynasty.
After Liáng Jì was executed,
he entered the Qiāng territory.
Later, his grandfather was supported by the Qiāng people,
becoming a chieftain and residing in this city.
The land was barren and the people were in turmoil,
so Liáng Huī planned to move to Táohǎn.
When he encamped at this mountain,
he was surrounded and pressured by a group of Qiāng people.
There was no water,
so Liáng Huī thrust the elm whip he held into the ground,
and prayed to the mountain with a black sheep.
A divine spring gushed forth,
and elm trees formed a forest.
《Water Classic》
Frequently seeing the strategies you proposed to benefit the people,
planting the elms of Jìnán,
and cultivating the lacquer trees of Hànzhōng.
Wèi Yú Qú's "Letter to Páng Huìgōng": peeling elm bark in the autumn frontier, digging up barbarian rats in the cold mountains.
Yǔ Xìn's "Thanks for the Gift of Vegetables":
Beans make one heavy,
elms make one sleepy,
which is known to both the foolish and the wise.
Jī Kāng's "Essay on Nourishing Life": Eating elm seeds makes one sleepy and unwilling to wake.
Jī Kāng's "Essay on Nourishing Life"
White Elm with Interlocking Branches: One hundred paces east of Zhèng County,
there is an old county town.
South of the county, in a village named Wǔbǎi,
stands a white elm tree with interlocking branches,
where different roots merge into a single trunk,
reaching a height of over forty-four zhang.
The local people honor it as a shrine.
"Jīngzhōu Tújì"
There is the Gūyú,
and the Lángyú.
The Lángyú has no pods,
and villagers use it for carts, making excellent hubs,
produced in Bóhǎi's Dōngguāng,
to supply the government.
"Guǎngzhì"
The willow is called the heavenly bramble,
and the wolfberry willow is also called the marsh willow.
Comprehensive Records
Yáng,
is the river willow.
Chēng,
is the tamarisk.
Liǔ,
is the small yáng.
"Shuōwén"
Zhǎnqín's home had a willow tree,
he personally practiced benevolent virtue,
thus he was called Liǔxià Huì,
also said to be the name of a town.
"Huáinán Zhù"
King Āi of Wèi appointed Tián Xū as his chancellor,
and Huìzǐ said to Xū:
"You must diligently serve those around you!
Now consider planting a poplar tree:
lay it sideways and it will grow,
break it and plant it again, and it will still grow.
However, if ten people plant poplars
while one person uproots them,
then no poplars will survive.
Although you have planted yourself firmly with the king,
if there are many who wish to remove you,
you will certainly be in danger.
From the "Annals of the Warring States Period"
During the reign of Emperor Zhāo,
a large willow tree in the Shànglín Imperial Park broke and fell to the ground,
but one morning it stood up again,
growing new branches and leaves.
Insects ate its leaves,
forming characters that read:
"Gōngsūn Bìngyǐ will ascend."
Mèng of Lǔ interpreted this as:
"Wood
symbolizes the common people,
indicating that someone from among them will receive the Mandate of Heaven."
After the deposition of the Prince of Chāngyì,
Emperor Xuān was enthroned instead,
whose original name was Bìngyǐ.
In the Hàn garden there is a willow,
shaped like a human,
called the human willow.
It sleeps and rises three times a day.
"Sānfǔ Gùshì" How can it compare to the Ox Star by the river,
that is heard only once every other year?
Unlike the willow within the palace,
which manages three sleeps all morning long.
Yùxīshēng "Jiāng Wényān Fù"
Zhāng Chǎng served as the Metropolitan Governor.
At that time, when court assemblies were dismissed,
he would pass by Zhāngtái Street on horseback,
where there were willow trees,
known in the Táng Dynasty as "Zhāngtái Willows."
From "Shì Shuō."
Sūn Jìng arrived in Luòyáng,
settled his mother in a small house near the Imperial Academy,
and then began his studies.
He wove willow slips to copy classics,
and when sleepy, he would hang his head from a roof beam.
"Biographies of Virtuous Men of Chǔ"
Jī Kāng was exceptionally skillful by nature,
and was capable of forging.
There was a willow tree at his home,
which was very lush,
so he channeled water to encircle it.
Every summer month,
he would stay beneath it to roam, play, and forge.
Lǚ Ān admired Jī Kāng's lofty character,
and each time he missed him,
he would order a carriage to travel a thousand miles to visit.
"Book of Jìn"
Wáng Gōng,
styled Xiàobó.
Someone admired his handsome appearance,
saying he was as fresh and elegant as a willow in the spring moon.
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World."
Gù Yuè and Jiǎnwén were the same age,
yet his hair turned white early.
Jiǎnwén said:
"Why has yours turned white first?
He replied:
"The nature of the willow,
is to wither at autumn's approach;
the substance of the pine and cypress,
becomes more luxuriant after frost.
In Shishuo, Gù Kǎizhī wrote of his father:
"You maintained integrity as the world declined.
When he visited the Prince,
the Prince's hair showed no gray strands,
while yours was already streaked with white.
Asked about your age,
he then said:
"Why has yours alone turned white early?
You replied:
"The nature of the pine and cypress,
remains luxuriant despite frost;
I, being of willow's substance,
wither first at autumn's approach.
Such is the difference in our endowed natures.
The Prince praised this for a long time.
Note
Huán Wēn set out north on an expedition from Jiānglíng,
passing through Jīnchéng,
where he saw the willows he had planted when he was young and served as the governor of Lángyá,
all of which had grown to ten arm-spans in girth.
He sighed with deep emotion, saying:
"If trees can grow like this,
how can humans bear the passage of time?"
He grasped the branches and twigs,
shedding tears with a sorrowful expression.
From "Liú Yìqìng's Records"
Táo Kǎn served as the Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
stationed in Wǔchāng.
He once directed the various camps to plant willow trees.
Commandant Xià Shī secretly uprooted the willow trees by the west gate of the commandery at night
and planted them as his own.
Later, when Táo Kǎn stopped his carriage at Xià Shī's gate,
he asked:
"These are the willow trees from the west gate of the commandery.
Why did you steal and plant them here?"
Xià Shī was terrified
and apologized for his offense.
People at the time feared Táo Kǎn.
"Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū"
Gù Kǎizhī was naively credulous of minor tricks.
Huán Xuán once gave him a willow leaf, deceiving him by saying:
"This is a cicada's hiding leaf;
use it to conceal yourself."
Xuán then urinated on him.
Kǎizhī believed he couldn't be seen,
and treasured it even more.
Popular tradition holds that Kǎizhī possessed three exceptional qualities,
this foolishness being one of them.
(From A New Account of the Tales of the World)
When Liáng's Zhāng Tiānxí succeeded to affairs,
willows transformed into pines,
and fire emerged from mud.
Wáng Jìngzé once went on a mission to Wei,
and planted willows at the northern lodge.
Later, when Vice Director Yú Chángyào returned from a northern mission, Jìngzé asked him:
"Those willows I planted in the past,
how big are they now?"
Chángyào replied:
"The northerners regard them as sweet pear trees."
From the Book of Southern Qi
Táo Qián's residence was bordered by five willow trees,
and he once authored "The Biography of Master Five Willows" himself.
"History of the Southern Dynasties"
When Liú Quān served as the Inspector of Yìzhōu,
he presented several Shu willow trees,
with branches extremely long,
appearing like silk threads.
At that time, the Fragrant Forest Garden of the old palace had just been completed,
and Emperor Wǔ planted them in front of the Tàichāng Línghé Hall.
He once admired them and sighed, saying:
"These willows are charming and delightful,
resembling Zhāng Xù."
At that time, they were so cherished and admired.
"Book of Qí, History of the Southern Dynasties"
Liú Huán and his two brothers shared a single thatched hut,
yet never ceased their studies.
They gathered disciples to teach,

Carpenter Shí went to Qí,
arriving at Qūyuán,
where he saw the Guardian Lì Tree.
It was so large it could shelter a herd of cattle;
measuring it, it was a hundred arm-spans around,
its height reached the mountain's summit, towering eighty feet before branching out,
and there were more than ten limbs that could be used to make boats.
Crowds gathered to see it as if at a market,
yet Carpenter Bó did not even glance at it,
and continued on without stopping.
His disciples, having gazed their fill at it,
ran to catch up with Carpenter Shí,
and said:
"Since we took up our axes to follow you, Master,
we have never seen timber as magnificent as this.
Why is it, sir, that you refused to look at it,
and walked on without stopping?
What is the reason?"
He replied:
"It is a useless tree.
If used to make a boat, it would sink;
if used for a coffin, it would quickly rot;
if made into utensils, they would soon break;
if used for doors, they would ooze sap;
if used as pillars, they would be infested with insects.
This is a tree of no worth.
Because it is of no use whatsoever,
it has been able to live to such an old age."
When Carpenter Shí returned home,
the Guardian Lì Tree appeared to him in a dream,
saying:
"Are you comparing me to those cultivated trees?
Had I been of any use,
could I have grown to be so large?"

"Inner Biography"
Confucius was seated in attendance with Duke Āi of Lǔ.
The duke presented him with peaches and millet.

The attendants on both sides covered their mouths and laughed.
Duke Āi said:
"The millet
is not for eating;
it is for cleansing the peach.
Zhòngní replied:
"Qiū knows this.
Now millet
is the foremost of the five grains,
and in sacrifices to ancestors it serves as the principal offering.
There are six categories of fruits,
and the peach is the lowest among them;
it cannot enter the temple in sacrifices to former kings.
Qiū has heard it said
that a noble person uses the inferior to cleanse the superior,
but has not heard of using the superior to cleanse the inferior.
Now to use the foremost of the five grains to cleanse the lowest of fruits
is to make the superior serve the inferior.
Qiū considers this contrary to righteousness,
and therefore dares not place it before the temple's principal offering.

The flat peach originates from Persia,

Lán Chāo replied:

From "Famous Sites of the Realm"
During the reign of Emperor Wǔzōng,

Yuáncháng received the order and left.

The envoy from Yuè, Zhū Fā, holding a plum blossom branch, presented it to the King of Liáng.
A minister of the King of Liáng, named
"Hánzǐ,"
turned to his attendants and said:
"How can there be such a thing as presenting a single plum blossom branch
to the ruler of a feudal state?
I ask to make you all ashamed of this.
He then went out and said to Zhū Fā:
"Our great king has commanded:
if a guest wears a cap, he will be received with courtesy;
if he does not wear a cap, he will not.
Zhū Fā replied:
"That land of Yuè is also a fief granted by the Son of Heaven.
It does not possess the provinces of Jì or Yǎn,
but lies on the remote shores of the sea,
dwelling as an outer barrier state.
Moreover, flood dragons compete with us for territory,
therefore we cut our hair and tattoo our bodies,
creating brilliant patterns,
to resemble the offspring of dragons,
in order to ward off water deities.
Now your great state commands that with a cap, one is received with courtesy,
without a cap, one is not.
Suppose an envoy from your great state
were to visit our humble city,
our humble ruler would also command, saying:
'The guest must cut his hair and tattoo his body,
only then may he be received.'
What would your great state think of that?
If you find it acceptable,
I am willing to borrow a cap to have an audience;
if you find it unacceptable,
I hope not to alter our state's customs.
When the King of Liáng heard this,
he threw on his robes and came out to receive Zhū Fā,

During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty,

One day,

he saw a beautiful woman among the pine forest,
wearing light makeup and plain clothes, coming out to greet him.
At that time, the lingering snow had not yet melted,
and the moonlight was faintly bright.
Shīxióng spoke with her,
only sensing an overwhelming fragrance,
and her speech was exceptionally clear and elegant.
Thus, he went with her to a tavern to drink together.
After a short while, a child in green clothing arrived,
laughing, singing, and dancing playfully.
Soon, they fell asleep drunk,
only feeling the chill of the wind for a long time.
By then, the eastern sky was already bright.
Rising to look around,
he found himself beneath a large plum tree,
with kingfishers chirping noisily above,
gazing at the setting moon and the slanting stars.
All he felt was deep melancholy.

he managed to preserve Héng.

to Fànzhōu in Lóngyáng, Wǔlíng to build a residence

one's family should be enfeoffed.'
I replied, '
Moreover, people should worry about lacking virtue and righteousness,
not about not being wealthy.
If one can remain humble despite nobility, that is true goodness.
What is the use of this?'
By the end of the Wú period, Héng's oranges matured yearly,

bearing a mandarin fruit as large as a chicken egg,
which ripened late,
and had tiny holes as fine as needles.
All the officials found it strange,
and just as they were about to present it,
they delayed for a long time before giving up.
When they cut it open,
they found a red-spotted snake inside,
over a foot long.
Later, Lǐ Chóngzhēn was killed by soldiers.

all wrapped in paper.
Later,
the local official disliked the paper as disrespectful,
replacing it with fine cloth.
Then he feared the tangerines might be damaged by the cloth,
and often felt anxious.
Suddenly, the imperial inspector Gān Zǐbù arrived.
The official thought he was investigating the cloth-wrapped tangerines matter,
and exclaimed in fear:
"Indeed, I'm being investigated."
When Zǐbù reached the post station,
the official explained that wrapping tangerines in cloth was meant as respect.
Zǐbù initially didn't understand,
only realizing after some time.
Those who heard couldn't help but laugh heartily.

During the Tiānbǎo era,
the Secretariat-Chancellery memorialized:
"We, your subjects, today while reporting matters received the virtuous words:
'I have heard that south of the river it becomes an orange,
north of the river it becomes a trifoliate orange,
this is because the terrestrial influences differ,
and the nature of things consequently changes.
I recently planted several sweet orange trees within the palace,
and since this autumn,
they have borne one hundred and fifty fruits,
which are no different from those presented from south of the river and the Shǔ region,
this can indeed be considered somewhat extraordinary.'"
The Old Táng History records the ministers congratulating the emperor,
saying:
"Where rain and dew spread evenly,
they blend with the celestial realm and are equally bestowed.
Plants and trees possess their nature,
relying on terrestrial influences to subtly communicate.
Thus, this precious fruit from beyond the river
becomes an excellent produce within the forbidden palace.
With green stems holding frost,
their fragrance flows through ornate halls;
golden skins gleaming in sunlight,
their colors beautify vermilion courtyards"
and so forth.
Thereupon, they were distributed to the great ministers,
and outside there was one double-joined fruit,
which the Emperor and the Consort held and admired together.
The Emperor said:
"This fruit seems to understand human intentions,
I and you are fundamentally of one body,
therefore it forms a double-joined fruit."
Then they sat close together and ate it.
Consequently, he ordered a painting made,

Within the husk lies over a liter of juice,
clear as water,
yet sweeter than honey.
Eating the husk alleviates hunger,
but drinking the juice increases thirst.
There are also two spots resembling eyes,
commonly called the "King of Yuè's head."
Records of Extraordinary Things: Long ago, the King of Linyì bore an old grudge against the King of Yuè,
and sent an assassin to behead him.
The head was hung on a tree,
and soon transformed into a coconut.
Enraged, the King of Linyì
ordered it hollowed out as a drinking vessel.
Southerners have imitated this practice ever since.
At the time of the assassination,
the King of Yuè was heavily intoxicated,
hence the liquid inside remains like wine.
Accounts of Southern Flora and Fauna
In the country of Hēlíng, it is customary to make wine from coconut palm flowers.
The tree produces flowers over three chǐ long,
with fruits as large as a human brain.
When cut open,
the sap is extracted to make wine.
It tastes sweet,
yet drinking it can also cause intoxication.
Book of Táng
The coconut has sap;
cut its flower and use a bamboo tube to collect its juice,
make wine and drink it,
which can also cause intoxication.
From "Jiāozhōu Jì"
In the desolate lands of the southeast, there exists a coconut tree,
standing twenty to thirty zhang tall,
or over ten zhang,
with a circumference of over one zhang,
or seven to eight chi.
Its branches rise tall and straight.
At two hundred years old, its leaves fall and flowers bloom,
the flowers shaped like sweet melons.
After another two hundred years, they fall entirely and calyxes form,
bearing fruit below,
which matures in three years.
After ripening,
it neither grows nor shrinks,
the fruit shaped like a winter melon,
resembling a wax gourd.
It is seven to eight cun long,
four to five cun in diameter,
with the calyx covering its top.
If this fruit is not harvested,
it remains unchanged for myriad generations;
if the fruit is picked while the calyx is left,
the calyx will bear fruit again as before.
The fruit is shaped like a sweet melon,
its pulp sweet and delicious as honey.
Eating it
moistens one's body,
but no more than three sheng should be consumed,
as it causes deep intoxication,
from which one awakens only after half a day.
The tree is tall,
making it unreachable by people.
Only beneath it grows the duōluó tree,
which people can climb to reach it,
also called "leafless,"
or "yǐjiāo."
Zhāng Màoxiān said:
"The jiāo stands straight and cannot be bent.
Later generations, not seeing its leaves,
call it leafless.
Another name is "qǐgǎo,"
and people who see it without leaves call it qǐgǎo.
Shényì Jīng
Yúfù County has many papaya trees,
with fruits as large as a wǔ (jar),
bearing white-yellow fruits,
very bitter yet fragrant.
This is what the Ěryǎ calls "mào."
Shuǐ Jīng
Qí Xiàozhāo launched a northern expedition against the Kùmòxī.
Upon reaching Tiānchí,
he used papaya ashes to poison the fish,
which all died and floated to the surface.
The Kùmòxī secretly remarked to one another:
"The pond harbors divine fish;
to harm them brings ill fortune.

fleeing northward.
The ruler of Qí dispatched troops in pursuit,
capturing seventy thousand cattle and sheep,

Empress Yáng craved sour flavors,

"Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng Huáng"
The stone bridge on Tiāntāi Mountain,
with its steep and perilous beams,

causing travelers' hearts to tremble with fear.
Among the crevices of the rocks grow quinces,

(From "Fāng Yǔ")
People in Xuānzhōu grow papayas,

Lotus,
also known as fúqú.
Its stem is called jiā,
its leaves are called xiá,
its rootstock is called mì,
its unopened flower is called hàndàn,
its fruit is called lián,
its root is called ǒu,
its seed is called dì,

Lǐ Xún said:
"Hánqú
is its general name,
with an alternative name fúróng.

people in the north simply call the root ǒu hé,
and also call the fruit lián hé;
people in Shǔ call the root ǒu jiā,
some use the mother plant to name the flower,
others use the root and seed to name the mother plant and leaves.
These are all cases of confused names,
customary transmission errors,
losing the correct form.
The "Ěryǎ" states: fúqú,
stem called hé.
Its unopened flower is called hàndàn,
and when opened, it is called fúqú.
Its fruit, the lián, has green skin with white seeds called dì,
inside the dì is a green part three fen long like a hook called yì,
as the saying goes, "bitter as yì."
The "Shī Yì Shū" says: its leaves are named hé.

"The Seven Stimuli":

During the time of Huángdì,

blue in color,

"Records of Omissions"
Queen Mother of the West and King Mù of Zhōu shared a jade tent.

The white lotus,

The Upper Yù River lies east of Mount Pángtáng,

what is called the "surging flow,"

Hán Tuìzhī's poem:

"Guān Lìng Nèi Zhuàn"
In the first year of Emperor Zhāo's Yuánshǐ era,

each stem bearing four leaves,

When the sun shone, the leaves lowered to shade the roots and stems,
resembling sunflowers guarding their base,
and they were named "Low-Light Lotuses."
Their seeds were like black pearls,
suitable for adorning pendants.
Even when the flowers and leaves withered,
their fragrant aroma permeated over ten li,

benefiting the skin and texture.
The palace ladies valued them highly,

they would always chew them when coming and going,

using them for amusement.
As described in the "Chǔ Cí,"
"plucking lotus leaves to make garments,"

"Records of Omissions" Emperor Zhāo visited the Willow Pond,
where there were lotus flowers,
pure white in color,
as large as dou measures,
with sweet, edible flowers and leaves,
their fragrance detectable within ten li,
and lotus seeds like pearls.
Seen in the imperial literature "Chūxué Jì."
The Mysterious Northern Ridge is one hundred and seventy thousand li from Kōngtóng,
where the sun and moon do not reach,
yet the land is self-illuminated.
There is a Purple River ten thousand li long,
with foaming waves a thousand zhang high,
in which grow cold-resistant lotuses

"Records of Penetrating the Hidden"
Emperor Líng planted lotuses in the canal of the Western Garden,

named Yèshū Lotus.

thus also called Wàngshū Lotus.
from "Shí Yí Jì"
Wáng Dūn was in Wǔchāng,

The Emperor
Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐ Mào, courtesy name Yúnchāng,
was a son of Emperor Wǔ.
At the age of seven,
his mother Ruǎn Shūyuán was critically ill,
so monks were invited to perform rituals.
Someone offered lotus flowers for Buddha worship.
The monks placed them in a bronze jar filled with water,
and the flowers grew even fresher.
Zǐ Mào wept and paid respects to Buddha,
vowing:
"If my aunt is blessed with recovery,
may these flowers remain fresh until the end of the fast."
After seven days,
when the fasting period concluded,
the flowers had become even brighter red.
Looking into the jar,
they noticed small roots had sprouted.
Ruǎn's illness soon recovered.
The world praised this as a testament to his filial piety.
From "Fǎyuàn" and Wú Jūn's "Zhai Chūnqiū"

North of Lìchéng's second lǐ lies Lotus Seed Lake,
encircling twenty lǐ in circumference.
The lake abounds with lotus flowers,
their red and green hues alternating brightly,
suddenly evoking the image of rinsed brocade.
Moreover, fishing boats are partially obscured and reflected,
with nets spread across the slopes.
From a distance,
they resemble spider webs floating on cups.
Wèi Yuánfān once held a feast by the lake,

it indeed succeeded.
At that time, Prince Qīnghé found it strange and remarkable,

The Duke said:

Qīnghé laughed and agreed,
but in truth, he did not comprehend.
After the gathering dispersed,
he spoke to Chief Clerk Fáng Shūdào,

"Regarding the matter of the lake's eyes,
I truly do not grasp it.
Shūdào replied:
"Lotus root can disperse blood,
and the lake's eyes refer to lotus seeds,

Qīnghé sighed and said:

One came out holding a plum blossom,

He replied:
"A plantain."
Another came out holding a pine or cypress,
and also answered "plantain."
After this repeated several times,
someone slapped his face,

"This is such-and-such flower,
this is such-and-such tree—
why do you call them all plantains?"
He responded:
"I only see things anxiously procured,
all ending up withered."

also softened somewhat.

Zhū Rúzǐ was

One day,
while washing vegetables by the stream,
he suddenly saw two small spotted dogs chasing each other on the bank.
Rúzǐ found this strange,
so he followed them into a clump of wolfberry bushes.
Returning, he told Xuánzhēn,
who was also amazed.
Thereupon, he went with Rúzǐ to wait and observe,
and again saw the two dogs playing and leaping about.
When they approached, the dogs went back under the wolfberry bushes.
Xuánzhēn and Rúzǐ searched and dug together,
and found two wolfberry plants,
their roots shaped like spotted dogs,
and hard as stone.
They washed them, took them back,
and boiled them to eat.
Shortly after,
Rúzǐ suddenly ascended flying to the peak ahead.
Xuánzhēn was astonished for a long time.
Rúzǐ bade farewell to Xuánzhēn,
and rose on a cloud and departed.
Nowadays, people commonly call that peak the Youth Peak.

Emperor Gāozōng said to Empress Wǔ Zétiān:

Scholar Xǔ Shènxuǎn was unrestrained and unconventional,

Shènxuǎn remarked:

Among flowers, few have six petals;

Their leaves were lush and drooping,

The flowers were brilliantly red with six petals,

When they bore fruit,

《Yěrén Xiánhuà》: In the eighth year of the Guǎngzhèng era, in the tenth month,

Nine li west of Guǎngzhōu City is Huātián.

The Nàsīmíng flower

Southerners, admiring their fragrance,

As Lù Jiǎ's "Records of the Southern Yue Journey" states: In the lands of Southern Yue,

thread the flower hearts with colorful silk

The Mòlì flower resembles the white rose,

This flower is extremely delicate and tiny,

Jīnyínhuā,

when the year will be evil,

Jílì Cǎo,

One application healed him completely,
and the entire region relied on this remedy.
From History of the Southern Dynasties
Liáng Jíshì Zhān dreamed of obtaining a pile of deer hides,
and upon counting them,
found there were eleven pieces.
When he awoke,
he joyfully said:
"Deer symbolize
official emolument.
Does this mean I shall hold eleven official posts?"
From the time he began his official career, it had already been long,
and when appointed as governor of Xīyáng and Wǔchāng commanderies,
he felt troubled about it,
and upon falling ill, refused treatment.
In the seventh year of the Pǔtōng era,
he died in his commandery.
From History of the Southern Dynasties
Huìjī's Kǒng Yòu possessed such profound virtue that it connected with the divine.
He lived in seclusion in the valleys of Sì Míng Mountain.
He had several hundred hu of coins,
which he regarded no differently than tiles or stones.
Woodcutters vied to take them,
but upon touching them, the coins instantly turned into gravel.
Once, a deer wounded by an arrow came to seek Yòu's help,
and Yòu nurtured and treated it.
Only after it recovered did the deer leave.
During the Tiānjiàn era,
there was a man named Shào Wénlì
whose family had for generations made their living by cooking and butchering.
Once, when he was about to kill a deer,
the deer knelt down and shed tears.
He considered this an ill omen.
The deer was pregnant with a fawn,
soon to give birth.
Yet it was taken to the kitchen and butchered,
and together they were cut open and slaughtered.
Because of this, he fell ill,
and deeply reproached himself with regret.
He then donated his residence to become a temple, which is the present Xiǎo Zhuāngyán Temple.
"Record of Temples in the Liáng Capital"
Zhēnshān is in Pílíng.
During the Liáng dynasty,
a villager named Hán Wénxiù saw a deer give birth to a girl on the ground,
so he took her in and raised her.
When she grew up,
she was different from ordinary girls,
so she became a female Daoist priest.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng built a separate Daoist temple for her,
naming her Lùniáng (Deer Maiden).
After her death, when she was placed in a coffin,
Emperor Wǔ offered sacrifices,
but only an extraordinary fragrance was smelled,
and no skeletal remains were seen.
It is said she achieved liberation from the corpse,
so the coffin was buried in Pílíng.
Hence, the burial site was named Zhēnshān.
From "Shù Yì Jì".
Jīnyáng Gate Poem:
"The long-lived deer gaunt, a bronze plaque hanging low."
Annotation: The Emperor once captured a white deer in the Fúróng Garden,
only the mountain hermit Wáng Hào recognized it,
saying:
"This is a deer from the Jìn Dynasty."
The Emperor found it extraordinary,
ordered his attendants to examine it thoroughly,
whereupon they found a bronze plaque among the snow-white hair at the base of its antlers,
inscribed with the words:
"White deer of the Yíchūn Garden."
The Emperor thus grew even fonder of it,
moved it to the northern mountains,
and named it Shānkè (Mountain Guest).
The "Xuānshì Zhì" attributes this poem to Zhāng Guǒ about Hàn Wǔdì's deer.
Emperor Xuánzōng of the Táng dynasty visited the hot springs,
where he witnessed a white deer ascending to heaven,
and subsequently changed the name of Huìchāng to Zhāoyìng County.
The "Huìchāng Jiěyí" states that Huìchāng
is the present-day Xīnfēng.
Táng Jīngshī Ānguó Sì Shí Yuánkāng, during the Zhēnguàn era, traveled to study in the capital city,
gaining a reputation for diligence and talent.
He initially dwelled in the mountains and wilderness,
where he encountered a deer
with antlers branching into eight tines,
its form exceptionally unique.
He soothed and tamed it until it submitted,
and thus he raised and cared for it.
Riding it to distant places,
it never showed signs of weariness.
He loaded the texts of the Three Treatises on its back,
and also tied small scrolls to its tail.
Dragging them into the upper capital,
he intended it as a playful jest.
People were all astonished and watched in amazement.
"Song Biographies of Eminent Monks"
Chǔ Wúliàng was mourning his mother's passing,
so he resigned from his official position,
and built a hut beside her tomb.
The pine and cypress trees he had planted there
were sometimes damaged by deer.
Wúliàng wept and said:
"The mountains have plenty of grass and plants,
how could you bear to damage the trees at my ancestor's grave?"
He then kept watch throughout the night.
Soon a herd of deer grew tame and restrained,
and no longer caused any harm.
Because of this, Wúliàng never ate venison for the rest of his life.
From the "Book of Táng"
In the first month of the eighth year of the Zhèngyuán era,
Hé Shìgàn, the Surveillance Commissioner of Èzhōu, presented a white deer.
The Emperor said:
"Upon my ascension to the throne,
auspicious signs are immediately presented.
Shìgàn has offered this white deer—
what would he think if I returned it to him?
He ought to feel ashamed and fearful, so I shall keep it."
Though distant and nearby regions continued presenting offerings,
he ultimately refused to view them,
and subsequently released the deer into the imperial park.
From "Táng Huì"
Lù Shào, the Director of the Bureau of Forestry's younger brother, was the County Lieutenant of Lǔshì County.
He often watched hunters hunt.
Suddenly, they encountered five or six deer.
Approaching the stream, they saw the deer were not frightened by people,
their spotted fur was like a painting.
Lù found it strange that the hunters did not shoot,
so he asked them.
The hunter replied:
"These are immortal deer.
Shooting them cannot harm them,
and it will bring misfortune.
Lù did not believe it,
and insisted.
The hunter, having no choice, shot one arrow,
and the deer ran away with the arrow.
Upon returning,
the shooter fell off a cliff and broke his left foot.
Under the hoof was a pierced ring. When Hú Xiàng was in Guózhōu,
a hunter killed a deer weighing one hundred eighty jin,
under whose hoof was a pierced bronze ring,
on which were seal script characters,
which even those knowledgeable in natural studies could not decipher.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
During the Bǎolì era of the Táng dynasty,
Zhū Kèróng, the military governor of Fànyáng, hunted and captured a deer.
Inside the deer's gallbladder, he found a pearl,
the size of a pellet,
black in color,
soft at first but later hardening,
shining like stone.
Kèróng considered it an auspicious sign for himself,
and someone asked Má Ānshí,
saying:
"What omen is this?
Ānshí replied:
"This matter has never occurred since ancient times,
allow me to reason by analogy.
The deer (lù)
represents official salary (lù).
The deer's death
means the salary is exhausted.
The pearl being soft initially then hardening
indicates the pearl is changing.
With salary exhausted and pearl transformed,
there must be changing events,
an omen of decline and fall.
From then on, Kèróng became careless in speech.
That same year in May,
his army rebelled,
and his entire family was killed.
"Collection of Auspicious Signs"
In the seventh year of the Kāibǎo era,
a deer in the imperial gardens of Jīnlíng suddenly began speaking like a human one morning.
When the herders scolded it,
the deer scolded them back,
saying:
"On this day next year,
you will all become ghosts.
With the gardens fallen into desolation,
how could you possibly confine me?"
The following year,
the Sòng army crossed the river,
the herders all died fighting the enemy,
and the gardens were abandoned.
"Records of Jīnlíng"
In Jiānglíng, Sōngzī, and Zhījiāng villages along the Pìn River, deer hunters
often use pelican leg bones as pipes,
with fat membranes from deer hearts as reeds,
to mimic deer calls when blown.
There are large and small types,
producing varied yōuyōu sounds.
Some imitate the call of a doe,
attracting all stags to gather,
lured by the female's voice,
enabling hunters to draw bows and shoot them.
Deer abound in the southern regions,
where a single male
mates with hundreds of females.
By spring, they grow thin and weak,
due to excessive mating.
Come summer,
they regain plumpness by feeding solely on calamus.
When their antlers are tender,
the velvet causes great pain,
and if encountered by hunters,
the deer dare not flee,
crouching motionless.
Hunters tie ropes to their antlers,
cutting them off to take.
First, they taste the blood,
then kill the deer.
How the deer suffer!
Like the golden monkeys, musk deer, and peacocks,
their usefulness brings them harm,
truly pitiable.
"Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Herd of hundreds of elks,
dig and eat grass roots,
the place becomes muddy,
called "mí jùn".
People follow these tracks,
plant rice without plowing,
yet harvest a hundredfold yield.
"Records of Broad Learning"
The deer is
an immortal beast,
often naturally joyful in nature,
following the clouds and springs.
Upon reaching sixty years,
it inevitably carries jade beneath its antlers.
The antlers have purple spotted patterns like dots,
and when moving, saliva may emerge from its mouth,
no longer able to run swiftly.
"Tiānxuán Catalog of Beasts"
Buddhist texts refer to deer as Yīní.
Shāngǔ's poem reads: "Shining on the beach, the crab scuttles;
burning the wilds, one obtains the deer."
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra states the eighth of the Tathāgata's thirty-two marks is called shuāng shuàn,
slender and curved like a Yan deer.
Wáng Yī states it is Mìlìjiāluó.
"Fānyì Míngyì"
Hú Jūshì once remarked that deer have a spirited and vigorous nature,
and they are adept at distinguishing wholesome plants,
consuming only nine types of vegetation,
refusing to taste any others.
These nine plants are: firstly, kudzu leaves and flowers,
deer medicine,
white mugwort,
water celery,
licorice,
uniform-headed mugwort,
mountain ear,
and she gan.
Their meat is used in offerings to deities
because of its pure and potent nature.
Those taking medicinal herbs should avoid eating deer meat,
as deer often graze on detoxifying plants.
"The Mountain Valley"
In Shǔjùn there is Yìmù Mountain,
on which there is a cave,
resembling the mouth of one yearning,
hence the name.
It stands seven hundred and twenty zhang high,
with cliffs sheer and steep,
and has a level ground over a hundred paces wide,
flat and squarely shaped.
Deer from various mountains
gather there once a day,
called the Deer Market.
"Illustrated Classic"
Yúnnán Commandery produces cháshǒu,
which is pronounced as Cài Mào,
and is the name of a two-headed deer.
This beast is a deer with two heads,
and the fetus from its womb,
often taken in the middle of the fourth month,
can be used to treat the venom of snakes and vipers.
Yǒngchāng also has them.
"Records of Diverse Matters": In Yúnnán Commandery, there is Xióngcāng Mountain,
on which dwells a divine deer,
with one body and two heads,
primarily feeding on poisonous plants,
and is named the poison-eating deer.
Wèi Hóng's "Records of the Southern Regions": West of Wǔlíng Commandery, there is a mountain,
where a beast like a deer resides,
with heads at both the front and the back,
often using one head to eat
and the other to move.
It is occasionally seen by people in the mountains.
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Records of Jīngzhōu":
Spear the iron-eating beast,
shoot the poison-devouring deer.
Deer come at night to rest,
forming a deer-antler encampment.
The larger ones stand with antlers facing outward in a circle,
while the smaller ones gather in the center,
encircled like a fortress.
Nowadays people imitate this by making wooden deer-antler barriers.
"Suǒ Suì Lù": Jiāng Tóngzǔ passed through Tuōdǐ Village Station in Jīngshān, Yǐngzhōu.
The station attendant said deer were forming an encampment ahead,
so he went out to observe them.
They covered several miles in view,
countless large deer,
forming concentric circles,
with antlers facing outward.
There were several dozen layers with two fawns
playing and jumping in the dusty central area.
Nearby farmland
was completely trampled,
leaving the crops entirely destroyed.
Hunters gathered around the periphery,
saying one couldn't approach,
as those who came close would be gored and often killed.
The next morning they began to leave,
with hunters carrying bows, arrows, spears following them,
waiting until the larger ones moved farther ahead
before daring to hunt the young and weak,
each returning with some game.
"Yí Jiān Zhī Bǐng"
The Zìtǒng states: Cū,
means alert and defensive,
for deer by nature eat back-to-back,
guarding against harm from humans or beasts.
Lì means traveling in company,
for it is the nature of deer to travel together when urgently seeking food.
The ritual of presenting betrothal gifts includes paired hides,
which are precisely deer hides.
*Shuōwén Jiězì*
In Shèng County, Shàn Mountain,
also known as Lùtāi Mountain,
once a hunter named Chén Huìdù shot a deer on this mountain.
The deer was pregnant and wounded,
and after giving birth,
it licked its fawn dry before the mother died.
Chén Huìdù then renounced the world and became a monk in a temple.
Later, grass grew where the deer died,
named lùtāi grass.
"Zhèjiāng Chronicles"
In the Records of Kuàijī, the Lánshì Mountain in Shàngyú,
where Gé Xuán lived in seclusion,
had a hidden armrest that transformed into a deer.
When the deer cried,
it meant the county magistrate had committed a crime.
From the "Records of Unique Phenomena"
Zhāngyè's southern mountains,
also called Tiānshān,
also called Xuěshān.
Produce red deer,
with short legs and bodies as large as oxen,
weighing a thousand jīn in meat.
"Universal Geography"
Táo Yǐnjū states: In ancient times, deer that resembled horses were said to be worth
a hundred gold pieces.
Now in the Jīng-Chǔ region,
there are deer that closely resemble horses,
especially when they shed their antlers,
making them indistinguishable from a distance.
Locals call them "horse-deer,"
which shows that when Zhào Gāo called a deer a horse,
he was merely categorizing by resemblance.
From "Ěryǎ Yì"
The deer resembles a horse yet is swifter than a horse,
the jackal resembles a dog yet is stronger than a dog.
A state may possess a horse worth a thousand gold coins but not a deer worth a thousand gold coins,
a household may possess a dog worth a thousand gold coins but not a jackal worth a thousand gold coins,
for dogs and horses are useful while jackals and deer are useless.
From "Liúzǐ"
In the summer of the eleventh year of the Yingli era under Emperor Mùzōng of the Liáo dynasty,
he shot a salt-licking deer at Jade Mountain.
"Record of Imperial Excursions" He had a fondness for salt,
sprinkling wine on the ground
to lure deer and shoot them.
"Glossary of National Language" The character 䑛 is interpreted as "lick".
The Mingyuan states: The large deer is called a zhǔ,
and herds of deer follow it,
all watching where the zhǔ goes,
taking the direction its tail turns as their guide,
hence debaters wave it.
Its tail repels dust,
and when placed among madder-dyed silks,
it can prevent the colors from fading over the years.
Using it to brush felt,
it keeps the felt moth-free.
The Enping County Register says: The water buffalo is called huí,
the yellow cattle are called mò,
the zhǔ is called huāng,
and the deer is called zhuó.
The roe deer has no soul,
the white gazelle is easily frightened.
"Daoist Texts"
Mí róng tonifies yang,
lù róng tonifies yin.
"Suǒsuì Lù"
The musk deer is not among the celestial animals,
and belongs to no trigram in the Eight Trigrams.
Therefore, Taoists permit it to be made into dried meat.
"Mr. Táo's Writings"
Among the beasts of the mountains and marshes,
none is more cunning than the elk.
The elk knows that the hunters set nets in front and drive it toward them,
so it deliberately turns and runs back,
dashing against people repeatedly.
The hunters, aware of its trick,
pretend to raise the net and advance toward it,
thus capturing the elk.
"Chǔ Cè"
On the coastal islets of Hǎilíng,
reeds stretch endlessly,
where herds of elk swiftly gallop.
When people attempt to capture them,
not even fawns can be caught,
for they often travel in pairs, carrying their young on their backs.
"Records of Tàizhōu"
The musk deer of the northwest
devour snakes and eat cypress,
thus forming their fragrance.
In the southeastern mountains and streams, there are pines but no cypress,
so the musk deer do not develop fragrance.
From Zhào Pìgōng's "Miscellaneous Discourses"
In the Shāngrǔ Mountains, there are many musk deer,
who treasure their musk glands above all else.
Whenever they are pursued by people,
and the situation becomes critical,
they throw themselves off high cliffs,
using their claws to tear out the musk,
then die where they fall,
still curling their four legs,
to protect their musk glands.
Lǐ Shāngyǐn wrote in his poem:
"The musk deer leaps from the cliff, abandoning its scent."
Yáng (sheep),
signifies auspiciousness,
its form resembles the head, horns, feet, and tail.
Confucius said: The characters for ox and sheep,
are formed based on their shapes.
Among the six domestic animals,
the sheep primarily provides food.
A large sheep is considered beautiful,
hence the character includes "dà" (large).
Léi,
means emaciated,
a sheep being thin is seen as a sickness.
Gāo,
refers to a lamb.
Miē,
is the sound of a sheep bleating.
Shān,
describes the smell of sheep.
"Shuōwén" states: Dá,
is a small lamb.
Xué Zǒng replied to Wéi Zhāo saying: A newborn lamb is called gāo,
an immature sheep is called zhù,
a grown one is called yáng,
these are different names for various stages of growth.
"Shī Shēngmín Shū" notes: A large sheep is called qián, measuring six chǐ.
"Shīzǐ" mentions: A small lamb is called zāng.
"Jíyùn"
In all sacrifices to the ancestral temples, the sheep
is called soft fur.
"Qūlǐ"
The sheep is also known as the bearded registrar.
According to the "Gǔjīn Zhù", a sheep without horns is called gǔ.
The sheep is also called the bearded gentleman,
and also known as the blue bird.
The jiāo sheep resembles a sheep but has no horns,
and eating it is poisonous.
All offerings to ministers use a lamb.
The lamb has horns but does not use them,
like those who are fond of benevolence.
When held, it does not cry out,
when killed, it does not curse,
resembling those who die for righteousness.
The lamb kneels when suckling from its mother,
resembling those who know ritual.
The word for sheep (yáng) is similar to auspiciousness (xiáng),
thus it is used as an offering.
"Chūnqiū Fánlù" Qiáo Zhōu's "Fǎ Xùn" says: The sheep has the ritual of kneeling to nurse,
the chicken has the awareness of timely crowing,
the wild goose has the etiquette of orderly formation,
and humans take these as models.
Zhèng's "Hūnlǐ Yèwén" eulogy says: They gather without forming factions,
kneeling to nurse shows respect,
ritual deems them fit for offerings,
appropriate for auspicious affairs.
There was a person with a yellow head and large belly,
who emerged to govern in harmony with heaven,
ruling for three hundred and four years.
The "Chūnqiū Mìng Lì Xù" records the divine sequence as follows:
"The August Spirit emerged from Huái,
driving six flying sheep,
governing for three hundred years.
Five generations lasted fifteen hundred years.
During the reign of King Chéng of Zhōu,
the Eastern Yí presented a six-horned sheep.
In the first year of King Lì of Zhōu,
foreign states offered a three-horned sheep.
"Shù Yì Jì"
Quǎn Xū paid homage to the Son of Heaven by the Léishǒu River,
and presented four teams of fine horses.
The Son of Heaven ordered Kǒng Yá to receive them,
saying:
"In the Léi River waters,
there are black oxen with white horns,
and black sheep with white blood?"
The Biography of King Mù of Zhōu
The state of Qí attacked the state of Lǔ,
so Lǔ sent Liǔxià Huì to Qí.
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Is your lord of Lǔ afraid?"
Liǔxià Huì replied:
"When Qí and Lǔ were first enfeoffed,
they went out together through the southern gate of Zhōu,
cut open a sheep and made a covenant, saying: 'From now on, for our descendants,
whoever dares to attack the other,
may their punishment be like this disemboweled sheep.
Therefore, my lord is certainly not afraid because of the disemboweled sheep.
Upon hearing this, the Marquis of Qí withdrew his troops three hundred lǐ.
From "Shuō Yuàn"
Once there was a sheep thief,
who gave a sheep's head to Jìn Shūxiàng.
Shūxiàng's mother buried it without eating it.
Three years later,
the sheep theft incident came to light,
and authorities pursued the Shūxiàng household.
Upon inspection, the sheep's flesh and bones had completely decomposed,
with only the tongue remaining.
The people of the state found this extraordinary,
and thus adopted "Yángshé" (Sheep's Tongue) as their surname.
Duke Dìng of Lǔ met the Jìn army at Wǎ.
Fàn Xiànzǐ held a lamb,
while Zhōngháng Wénzǐ and Zhào Jiǎnzǐ both held geese.
From then on, Lǔ began to esteem the lamb.
Previously, Lǔ had used the same ceremonial gifts,
and only then did they realize the prestige of holding a lamb.
During the reign of the Marquis of Lǔ,
he wished to appoint Confucius as Minister of Education,
and planned to summon the Three Huán to discuss it.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng said:
"The people of Zhōu had a fondness for fine furs and delicacies,
wishing to make a robe worth a thousand gold pieces,
yet sought the fox's counsel for its skin;
desiring to prepare the delicacies of a shàoláo sacrifice,
yet consulted the sheep about its meat.
Before the words were finished,
the foxes fled one after another beneath the heavy hills,
and the sheep called to each other hiding deep within the forest.
Thus the plans of the Zhōu people came to nothing.
Now you wish to make Confucius Minister of Education,
and summon the Three Huán to discuss it—
is this not also seeking the fox's counsel for furs,
and consulting the sheep about its meat!"
From "Fúzǐ"
Jì Bǎizi dug a well and obtained something like an earthen vessel,
inside which there was a sheep.
He sent someone to ask Zhòngní (Confucius),
saying:
"I dug a well and got a sheep,
why is that?"
He replied:
"From what I have heard,
it is not a sheep.
The monster of wood and stone
is Kuí,
called 'Wǎngliǎng';
the monster of water
is the dragon,
called 'Wǎngxiàng';
the monster of earth
is 'Fényáng'
《Family Sayings》 Duke Āi of Lǔ sent someone to dig a well,
for three months they didn't get spring water,
but obtained a live sheep.
The duke had a shaman dance to make it ascend to heaven,
but the sheep couldn't ascend.
Confucius saw it and said:
"The essence of water becomes jade,
the essence of earth becomes sheep,
this sheep's liver is earth."
The duke had the sheep killed,
and upon examining the liver, it was indeed earth.
《Han Shi Wai Zhuan》 Someone asked Zhòngní:
"I dug a well and got a dog,
why is that?"
Zhòngní said:
"From what I have heard, it is a sheep."
《Sōu Shén Jì》
Jìn Wénzhòng grew vegetables,
Zēngzǐ raised sheep,
not because they were inherently foolish and incapable of handling affairs,
but because they managed grand matters and were unaccustomed to trivial tasks.
Liúzǐ's "Guān Liàng Piān" states that they cut up sheepskins and used them with soil for planting.
Note
Qí Zhuāng Gōng's minister Wáng Guóbēi,
who had been litigating with Zhōnglǐ Xí for three years without a verdict,
fearing the guilty might escape,
had the two men share one sheep,
and swear an oath at the altar of Qí.
The two men followed each other,
sprinkling the altar with the sheep's blood,
and when Wáng Guóbēi's oath was fully read,
before Zhōnglǐ Xí's oath was half finished,
the sacrificial sheep rose and butted Zhōnglǐ Xí.
The people of Qí considered it divine.
"Mòzǐ"
Tú Yáng Yuè,
a man of Chǔ,
lived in obscurity working in a butcher's shop.
When King Zhāo lost his state,
Yuè went to follow the king.
After the king regained his state,
he wanted to reward Yuè,
but Yuè said:
"When Your Majesty lost the state,
I lost my butchering job;
now that Your Majesty has regained the state,
I have also returned to butchering.
My position and income have already been restored,
what need is there for further reward?"
The king sent Minister Sīmǎ Zǐqí to offer him a high official position with three jade tokens,
but Yuè said:
"I only wish to return to my butcher's shop for good."
Thus he did not accept the offer.
From "Biographies of Noble Scholars"
Wèi Wénhóu saw that Sòng Língzǐ had declined three official appointments.
Wénhóu asked:
"Why are you so poor?"
Sòng Língzǐ replied:
"Your Majesty, consider the wealthy man from Chǔ
who herded ninety-nine sheep but desired a hundred.
Once, while visiting an old friend in the town,
he encountered a poor neighbor
who owned a single sheep.
The wealthy man bowed and said:
'I have ninety-nine sheep,
and now with your one,
it would complete my hundred,
making my flock complete.'
The neighbor gave it to him.
From this we can see that
the wealthy are not truly wealthy,
nor are the poor truly poor.
From "Fúzǐ"
Zāng and Gǔ, two men together herding sheep,
both lost their sheep.
Asked what Zāng had been doing,
he was holding a bamboo slip reading a book.
Asked what Gǔ had been doing,
he was playing at dice for amusement.
The two men's activities were different,
but their losing the sheep was the same.
Zhuāngzǐ
Yáng Zhū visited King Huì of Liáng,
and said that governing the world was as easy as turning something in the palm.
The king said:
"You, sir, have one wife and one concubine,
yet cannot manage a garden of three acres,
and yet you speak of governing the world—
how is that?"
Yáng Zhū replied:
"Have you seen a shepherd?
A hundred sheep form a flock,
and a child of five feet tall can carry a whip and follow them,
making them go east or west as he wishes.
But if Yáo were to lead one sheep,
and Shùn were to follow with a whip,
they would not be able to make it move forward.
From the "Lièzǐ"
Zhāng Yí said to the King of Chǔ:
"Those who form alliances,
are no different from driving a flock of sheep to feed a live tiger.
It is clear that the tiger and the sheep cannot contend.
Now Your Majesty does not side with the tiger but with the sheep,

saying:

stretching out its left leg,
bending its right foot.

when it saw people observing fasting, it would also observe fasting.
If food was offered at improper times,
it would not eat,
only wanting to drink pure water.
By the following day,
in the morning,
when the fast was broken and congee was given,
it would then begin to eat.

left his room again.
After Lǐ saw the dog depart,
he arranged pillows with towels and combs,

and covered them with a quilt,
making it appear as if someone was sleeping.
Then Lǐ hid elsewhere to observe.
After a short while,
the dog entered his room,
thinking Lǐ was already asleep,
it jumped onto the bed
and bit at the throat area.
After biting,
realizing its mistake,
the dog got down from the bed,
leapt about furiously, howled and barked, then died.

In the Northern Dog Country,

covered in long hair without clothing,
they fight fierce beasts with their bare hands,
and their speech resembles the howling of dogs.
Their wives are all human,
capable of speaking Chinese,
giving birth to sons as dogs
and daughters as humans,
who intermarry among themselves,
dwelling in caves and eating raw food,
while the wives and daughters consume human flesh.
It is said that once a person from China reached their country,
and his wife took pity on him,
enabling him to escape back,
giving him over ten chopsticks,
instructing him to leave one chopstick every ten or so li,

Wú Yòu,
courtesy name Jìyīng.
At age twenty, he lost his father,

Sūn Qī
was a native of Jìyīn.
In his youth, he was a Confucian scholar,
but his family was poor.
He served his mother with utmost filial piety,
herding pigs in the great marshes
to provide for her.
Those who came from afar to study under him
would all carry their classics along the field ridges to follow him,
and the village was transformed by his benevolence and humility.
When the Yellow Turban rebels arose,
they passed through his village paths
and agreed among themselves not to violate Master Sūn's home.
He was recommended for the "Fāngzhèng" erudite selection,
and officials were sent with sheep and wine to invite Qī,
but he drove his pigs into the grass
and paid them no heed.
Minister over the Masses Huáng Wǎn specially summoned him,
yet he did not take up the post,
and eventually passed away at home.
"The Biography of Hermit Huángfǔ"

A few days later,

Huī, in turn, generously thanked him.

"Records of the Strange"
Lǐ Fén played the qin on Sìmíng Mountain.
On a moonlit night,
a woman arrived,
exceedingly beautiful,
except he noticed her mouth appeared wrapped in high black silk.
She stayed overnight,
and they were immensely joyful.
Fén secretly took one of the woman's green felt shoes,
and she wept, begging for its return, but he refused.
By dawn,
he saw fresh blood covering the ground,
and upon examining the shoe,
it turned out to be a pig's hoof shell.
Fén was terrified,
and following the blood, he reached the Zhang family's pigsty in front of the mountain,
where he saw a sow,
with one shell missing from its hind foot.
The pig glared at Fén, roaring and snarling,
as if filled with anger.
Fén reported the incident to Old Man Zhāng, who immediately killed it, and Fén then abandoned the mountain monastery to wander elsewhere.
From "In Search of the Supernatural" (similar to the story of Yǐn Zòng in "Records of the Mysterious and Strange").
The deposed emperor was insane and devoid of virtue,
imprisoning his uncles in the palace halls.

he was placed in a bamboo cage and weighed,
and mockingly called the "King of Pigs."

mixing in various scraps of food,
stirring them together into a mash.
A pit was dug in the ground,
filled with mud and water,
and Emperor Míng was stripped naked and forced into the pit.
The mixed trough food was placed in front of him,
and he was ordered to eat directly from the trough with his mouth,
all for the amusement and laughter of others.
At that time, the court official Liú Méng's concubine was in her final month of pregnancy,
so she was brought into the inner palace,
in the hope that she would bear a son,
whom they intended to establish as the crown prince.
Once, Emperor Míng offended the deposed emperor's decree,

saying:
"Today, we slaughter the pig."
Xiùrén laughingly said to the emperor:
"The pig should not die today."
The emperor asked why,
and Xiùrén replied:
"Wait until the crown prince is born,

The emperor's anger then subsided,
and he said:

Guō Yuánzhèn, during the Kāiyuán era, failed the imperial examination,
and was traveling from Jìn to Fén by night,

with towering gates and halls,
where candles burned in the main hall, yet it was silent and devoid of people.
Suddenly, he heard a woman weeping,
and Guō asked:
"Are you human?
Or a ghost?"
She replied:
"In my village, there is a General Wū,
who can bring fortune or disaster upon people.
Each year, the villagers select a beautiful maiden to marry him.
My father, coveting the villagers' gold,
secretly offered me for the selection,
and left me drunk in this room.
The general is due to arrive at the second watch."
Guō, greatly angered, said:
"If I cannot save you by force,

Not long after,
carriages and horses crowded the area,
and a clerk in purple entered,

"The Prime Minister is here."
Soon, the general entered,

saying:
"I hear there is a joyous ceremony tonight,

The general, pleased, invited him to sit.
Guō drew his dagger,
chopped off the general's wrist,

At dawn,

Guō explained everything to them,

The monk Biàncōng traveled to Wǔtái Mountain,
and was about to return to the capital.
An old monk entrusted him with a letter,
on which was written
"Seek Bóhè in the northern part of the Eastern Capital and deliver this."
The monk secretly opened the seal,
looked at it,
and it said
"Once you have delivered all sentient beings,
come back early.
If you insist on staying longer,
I fear you will surely create karma."
He resealed it.

named Bóhè,

who had also transformed and departed.

In the past, there was a man named Si Yuan,
who was hunting with fire in the wilderness.
A deer fled eastward,
and Si Yuan chased it with shouts.
A crowd from the west was pursuing a pig;
hearing Si Yuan's shouts,
they all raised their voices in response.
Si Yuan, hearing the multitude of voices,
