(Qiān Zǎi)
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Bì Háng, the Vice Censor-in-Chief, served as the Prefect of Wèi Prefecture.
He was captured by Ān Lùshān's rebels,
and soon planned to return to allegiance,
but though compliant, he had not yet acted.
After several days,
he suddenly saw little people in the courtyard,
five or six inches tall,
hundreds of them,
playing as if nothing was wrong.
His family members struck and killed them.
The next day,
all the little people were dressed in white mourning clothes,
and weeping,
they carried the dead in funeral carriages with burial implements,
exactly like the arrangements for a scholar's funeral.
They then built a tomb in the courtyard,
and after the burial,
they entered a hole in the southern wall.
Greatly astonished by this,
Bì Háng excavated the tomb,
and found a dead rat.
He then poured boiling water into the hole,
and after some time, dug it out,
finding hundreds of dead rats.
More than ten days later,
Bì Háng failed in his plan,
and his entire family was killed.
"Guǎng Yì Jì"
Lǐ Zhīwēi was strolling beneath Wénchéng Palace at night,
the crescent moon faintly bright,
when he saw several dozen little people,
each only a few inches tall,
gathered under an ancient locust tree.
One wearing purple robes
was attended by ten others.
The rest were slightly taller,
and one announced to the elder:
"I shall be a Secretary of the Western Pavilion.
Another said:
"I shall be a Recorder before the Hall.
Another said:
"I shall be a Clerk of the Literary Bureau.
Another said:
"I shall be an Assistant Scribe of the Southern Palace.
Another said:
"I shall be a Commandant of the Imperial Way.
Another said:
"I shall be a Registrar of the City Administration.
Another said:
"I shall be an Envoy of Roaming Fields.
Another said:
"I shall be a Halberdier of the Eastern Wall.
After speaking, they led each other into a burrow and departed.
The next day,
he dug to investigate
and discovered they were rats.
Records of Hédōng
During the Bǎoyìng era,
there was a family named Lǐ who had lived in Luòyáng for three generations without keeping a cat.
Suddenly one day,
the Lǐ family gathered many relatives and friends,
feasting together in their private hall.
After they had taken their seats,
hundreds of mice appeared outside the door,
all standing on their hind legs like humans,
clapping with their front paws,
as if overjoyed.
The servants were astonished,
and reported this to the Lǐ family.
The Lǐ family and their guests then evacuated the hall,
and watched from a distance.
Once everyone had left,
the hall suddenly collapsed,
and no one in the family was injured.
Alas, mice are humble creatures indeed,
yet they can recognize kindness and know how to repay it—
how much more should humans?
"Records from the Xuānshì"
Lù Jìngchún was appointed as the magistrate of Suì'ān.
Previously, many magistrates had died,
and Jìngchún wanted to decline the post,
but his wife said:
"If you do not die,
and the prison is kept intact,
isn't it that life and death are fated?
He followed her advice.
Upon assuming office,
an owl hooted at his screen,
dozens of mice ran in front of him,
his attendants tried to drive them away,
but they clung to the staffs and screamed.
Jìngchún was not afraid,
and after a long time, he was promoted to the position of wèi magistrate.
"New Book of Tang"
Wáng Xiàojié served as the commander of the Clear Border Circuit.
Initially,
when advancing the army to Píngzhōu,
white rats entered the camp during the day and crouched down.
Everyone said:
"Rats are spirits,
symbols of the northern tribes.
Their white color signifies submission,
an omen of heaven's destruction of them."
But when the battle came,
it was Xiàojié who was defeated.
The emperor
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty, Táng Jìn was about to attend court
when suddenly a rat appeared from his front satchel,
over a foot long,
and leaped out.
He was greatly frightened
and said to his son:
"Despite my lack of talent,
I wrongly hold the position of high minister;
I am noble without virtue.
I have long feared unexpected calamity,
and now such an ominous sign appears.
Is this not a harbinger of impending disaster?
A few days later,
he was indeed found guilty
and demoted to Prefect of Jìnyún.
(Xuānshì Zhì)
Xǔchāng Xī Shàngshū Shìměi,
during the late Yuánhé era served as the surveillance commissioner of Èzhōu.
One day,
after rising early to attend to official duties,
having already fastened his belt,
while holding his boot with his left hand before slipping his foot in,
suddenly a large rat crossed the courtyard facing north,
standing with clasped paws and dancing.
The minister grew furious,
shouting at it in alarm,
yet it showed no sign of fear.
He threw his boot to strike it,
whereupon the rat fled,
and a venomous snake fell out from inside the boot.
Had it not been for the rat's strange behavior,
this would have caused the disaster of a swollen finger or festering foot.
From "Quē Shǐ".
Jìnshì Lǐ Zhāogǔ,
after ten attempts at the imperial examinations had not yet passed,
at the time the year's successful candidates had already been determined by the examiner,
and there was no opportunity for recommendation or influence.
The examiner was fully asleep,
when suddenly he glimpsed a scroll of examination papers in front of his pillow,
looking at where it was titled,
it was indeed Zhāogǔ's paper.
He ordered it moved to the shelf,
and went back to sleep.
Secretly observing,
there was a large rat,
that took his paper,
holding the scroll rod in its mouth,
returned it before the pillow,
repeating this several times.
Zhāogǔ passed the examinations the following spring,
the examiner asked about the reason,
it turned out his family for three generations had not kept cats,
all said it was the rat's repayment.
"Records of Hearing Marvels" "Yùquánzǐ"
At the end of Emperor Xīzōng's reign,
a beggar from Guǎnglíng named Dù Kějūn,
once visited a wine shop owned by someone surnamed Lè west of the city during heavy snowfall,
seeking a drink.
He saw the manager exchanging clothes for wine with a white man,
but the storage was careless,
and mice gnawed the clothes.
Dù immediately had a clean room prepared,
and said:
"I recall a talisman from years past,
capable of repelling mice.
I shall try writing it;
if it proves effective,
this room may forever be free of mice.
The scholar obtained the talisman and burned it,
whereupon the mice vanished.
"Guìyuàn Cóngtán"
During the Tiānfù era,
a great famine struck the Longyou region.
That autumn,
the crops appeared very abundant,
but just before harvesting,
more than half of them turned out to have no ears.
Someone went to the field edges,
dug into rat burrows to search,
and obtained a great amount.
Thereupon, every household excavated the burrows,
some harvesting five to seven hú.
It was traditionally called "plundering the rats' granaries."
The starving people all went out to seek food,
and many were saved and kept alive.
Dòu Pán had long failed the imperial examinations,
but in his later years he married the daughter of Yǔwén Yì,
and subsequently passed the exams.
At that time, Dù Shàng's residence caught fire,
which was said to have been caused by a mouse's tail catching fire.
Wéi Shuō therefore remarked
to Pán:
"When a fish is about to transform into a dragon,
thunder burns its tail.
It seems recently mice also have their tails burned,
at which Pán felt greatly ashamed.
From "Suǒ Yán"
The Director of the Bureau of Forestry, Zhōu Rényuàn, was overseeing the Ever-Bountiful Granary.
A visitor requested an audience,
identifying himself as Chǔ Chāng, a Presented Scholar from Jiāngzhōu.
When he was received,
he appeared like a ten-year-old child.
He presented a letter as a gift,
saying:
"Dim light in a dark room,
a dried-up drop from a cold spring.
Zhuāng Zhōu's valley is already empty,
where has Kǒng's chariot gone?"
Yuàn asked:
"The chariot of Kǒng Xù—
what is the story behind that?"
The person replied:
"Yáng Sān,
Yáng Sān,
you are the grandson of Yáng Mài,
the son of Yáng Zhōng.
The matter of Kǒng Xù—
why must you ask?"
Yuàn became angry,
and wanted to strike him.
The person suddenly collapsed to the ground,
revealing only his turban and headcloth.
Yuàn immediately chased him,
and he transformed into a large rat,
running beneath the granary.
Chén Tài was a poor man who loved to give alms.
One night, he saw a white mouse,
snow-white in color,
climbing along his tree,
sometimes up and sometimes down,
for a long time,
waving it away but it would not leave.
Chén told his wife and children,
saying:
"It is said that where there is a white mouse,
there is hidden treasure."
So they dug there,
and indeed obtained fifty ingots of white silver.
《Bǎoguāng Lù》: A white mouse with fur as bright as snow,
red ears and feet,
and crimson eye sockets—
this is the essence of gold and jade.
Watch for where it emerges,
dig there,
and you shall obtain gold and jade.
It is said that when a mouse reaches five hundred years, it turns white;
if its ears and feet are not red,
then it is an ordinary mouse.
《Lù Yì Jì》
In the Southern Hàn, Liú Bīn,
originally named Hóngdù,
was the son of Yǎn.
When Yǎn fell ill,
lying in his bedchamber,
he summoned the Right Deputy Minister Wáng Fān to speak with him, calling
Hóngdù by his childhood name,
and said:
"Though Shòu and Juàn are older,
neither is fit to handle my affairs.
Only Hóngcháng resembles me,
and I wish to establish him.
Yet, alas, my descendants are unworthy;
in later generations, they will be like rats entering an ox horn,
and the situation is bound to gradually decline.
With this, he shed tears and sobbed.
From the "History of the Five Dynasties."
The mouse's gallbladder is in its head,
it can be obtained by taking it alive.
"Miscellany"
Fén shǔ,
a rodent that travels underground,
transformed from bǎiláo birds,
also called fén shǔ.
"Zì Lín"
Humans eat arsenopyrite and die,
while silkworms eat it and do not hunger.
Fish eat croton seeds and die,
while mice eat them and grow fat.
"Huáinán Shuō Lín"
On the night of Jiǎzǐ,
rats hide;
on the night of Gēngshēn,
bats hide.
From "Suǒsuì Lù"
The sage took bees as his model to establish the relationship between ruler and subject,
took spiders as his model to establish nets and traps,
took the bowing mouse as his model to create rites,
and took warring ants as his model to set up military.
Wénzǐ states: The bowing mouse,
shaped like an ordinary mouse,
moves through the fields,
and upon seeing people, it stands up with its front paws clasped together.
When people approach intending to catch it,
it immediately leaps away.
Such mice are found in Qínchuān.
Lù Yì Jì records: The Xiàng Shǔ has a dignified posture,
yet humans may lack propriety.
Lù Jī states: In Hédōng there is a large rat
that can stand like a human,
crossing its front paws above its head while dancing,
and is skilled at vocalizing.
Hán Tuìzhī's quatrain from "South of the City" says:
"The polite rat stands bowing.
Sūn Yì states: Xiàng is a place name,
according to geographical records, Xiàng Prefecture
borders Hédōng,
thus it is known that Xiàng Prefecture has this kind of rat,
and the poet likely drew an analogy from it.
If, like the Máo school, we interpret xiàng as "to look at,"
then observing that creatures have dignified postures
and fur,
all could be used to illustrate propriety,
so why specifically choose the rat?
The red flying squirrel,
mostly found in Jiāozhǐ,
and Guǎng, Guǎn, and Lóng prefectures.
Its back and belly have thick fur,
soft and dense,
only the wing membranes are light black,
often perching in pairs among red banana flowers.
If hunters capture one,
the other will not leave.
Women in the southern regions all buy and wear them,
believing they bring charm and delight.
"Lǐngbiǎo Lùyì"
The mole-rat has a head and tail like a mouse,
is bluish-black in color,
has short legs,
a hundred-toed form,
and can weigh over a thousand pounds when fully grown.
It appears within the boundaries of Línglíng Commandery,
but its origin is unknown.
When the people suffer disasters or commit evil deeds,
the mole-rat enters their fields,
shakes off its fur, which all turns into small mice,
and devours their seedlings before leaving.
If someone catches a mole-rat,
treats its skin,
and eats it as a belt,
it is quite effective in curing hangovers,
because its three hairs emerge from a single pore,
which differs from ordinary skin,
and people often treasure it.
"Record of Extraordinary Things"
People in Lǐngnán eat rats,
calling them house deer.
"Juànyóu Lù"
The Liǎo people of Língnán enjoy making honey-squeaks,
which are fetal mice whose eyes have not yet opened,
still red and wriggling all over.
They are fed with honey,
nailed to the banquet table,
where they crawl about squeaking.
Using chopsticks to pick them up,
biting into them produces squeaking sounds,
hence the name "honey-squeaks."
From "Qiān Zǎi": The Nóng people of Guǎngnán Prefecture have no delicacies in their diet.
They once pickled shrews,
and caught flying insects to eat.
From "Yúnnán Zhì"
The bamboo rat,
as large as a small dog,
feeds on bamboo roots.
It is found in Fēngxī County.
According to the "Jiāozhōu Records," the bamboo rat
is a rodent that eats bamboo,
living deep in mountain valleys and bamboo forests of uninhabited areas,
consuming nothing but bamboo,
and is as large as a wildcat.
Its meat is plump and crisp,
highly valued by mountain dwellers.
In the Western Regions there is a Kingdom of Rats,
where rats as large as dogs,
wear golden hoop collars,
medium-sized ones are like rabbits,
small ones resemble ordinary rats,
all with white heads.
When merchants pass through this kingdom,
if they do not first perform sacrificial rites,
the rats will gnaw at their clothing.
If they obtain sand and recite incantations,
they will remain unharmed.
Shì Dào'ān once witnessed this personally in the Western Regions.
A common saying states:
"When a rat obtains the essence from a dead person's eyes, it becomes king."
From Yì Yuàn and Records of the Various Countries in the Western Regions.
According to an old theory, the king of rats transforms one drop of its urine essence into a rat.
Another theory states that the rat mother has a head and feet resembling those of a rat,
a bluish tail,
a sharp mouth,
and is as large as a water buffalo.
It has a natural fear of dogs,
and one drop of its urine can form a rat.
When rat disasters occur,
they often originate from the rat mother.
Wherever the rat mother goes,
it can generate tens of thousands of rats,
and its meat is extremely delicious.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The Great Qín Kingdom produces mice that ward off poison.
In the sixteenth year of the Wǔdé era, the state of Jìbīn presented a rùtè rat,
which had a large beak and a red tail,
and was capable of eating snakes.
If someone was bitten by a snake,
the rat would immediately emit a foul odor and urinate on the wound,
and the sore would then heal.
"Old Book of Táng"
Shì Shànwúwèi,
arrived in the country of Wuchang,
where there was a white mouse
that tamely circled around and daily offered golden coins.
from the "Song Dynasty Biographies of Eminent Monks"
The Khitan nation produces a large rat,
called pílí,
which resembles a large rat but has short legs,
and is extremely fat.
Their country considers it a rare delicacy,
digging it out from burrows,
to supply the sovereign's meals.
From the dukes and ministers downward,
none are permitted to taste it.
They often feed it with goat's milk.
Recently, a northern envoy once brought some to the capital,
cooked and presented to the emperor.
Our dynasty's envoys to their country,
also all get to eat it,
as it is extremely treasured.
"Mianshui Yantan" Diāo Yuē, as envoy to Khitan,
playfully wrote a poem saying:
"Hosting the banquet, Yilibi,
guarding the quarters, Hebazhi.
Farewell gifts of three bolts of silk,
secretly bestowed ten pílí.
Pílí,
resembles a rat but larger,
lives in burrows,
eats fruits and grains,
tastes like suckling pig but crisp.
The Khitan regard it as a precious dish.
"Xu Huixi" Shaped like a large rat,
extremely plump,
very afraid of sunlight,
if struck by a ray of light,
it dies immediately.
"Lu's Old Anecdotes" There is the Bilinbang,
with a morsel of its meat,
placed in the cauldron of food,
it instantly tenderizes,
hence it is cherished.
Fúxiū "Record of Mission to Liao" "Liao History Glossary" explains: Yilibi means assistant administrator.
Quoting Diāo Yuē's poem saying.
The Book of Master Shī states: The squirrel among the pines and cypresses,
knows not of the beautiful firs in the hall-like mountains.
Shuōwén explains that mountains resembling halls are called "mì."
In Xuāndà there is produced a yellow rat,
which the natives prize.
Those who catch them
always keep several pine-tailed rats,
called night monkeys.
These can smell out the yellow rat's burrow,
and know whether it is there or not.
If it is, they go in, bite its nose, and come out.
Yēlǜ Déguāng took off his white sable,
and gave it to Jìn Gāozǔ to wear.
The History of the Five Dynasties records: North-west of Qìdān as far as Yūjuélǜ,
there are many black, white, and yellow sables and squirrel pelts,
which are sufficient for all the northern kingdoms.
According to the Account of the Captured Territories.
The *Shuōwén* states: Mǎ (horse),
signifies fury,
and martial prowess.
A horse at one year is called zhù,
at two years, jū,
at three years, táo,
at eight years, bā.
One measuring six chǐ is called jiāo,
seven chǐ, lái,
eight chǐ, lóng.
Ào,
is a steed,
which died on a rénshēn day,
and is considered taboo when riding a horse.
Yīn combines with eight,
eight combines with Yáng nine,
eight nines are seventy-two,
two represents earth,
earth governs the moon,
the moon's essence becomes the horse.
The moon's number is twelve,
thus horses are born in twelve months.
Humans ride horses to govern the world,
kings drive horses,
therefore the character for horse incorporates the character for king.
《Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yōu》 The earth's essence becomes the horse,
born in twelve months,
responding to Yīn and recording Yáng,
to combine achievements.
Thus humans drive horses,
bearing heavy loads to reach distant places,
to benefit the world.
The moon moves swiftly,
therefore horses are good at running.
《Chūnqiū Shuōtící》 Nourished by the bright moon and thus born,
originating from the River Chamber and receiving endowment.
Zhāng Shìjiǎn's "Dance Horse Rhyme-prose"
The Book of Hàn states: The four stars in Hànzhōng are called Tiānsì,
with one adjacent star named Wángliáng,
Wángliáng whipping his horse, chariots and cavalry fill the wilds.
Yuánmìngbāo says: The four stars in Hànzhōng are called cavalry,
also known as Tiānsì.
The Chūnqiū Héchéng Tú states: Wángliáng governs the heavenly horses.
The Huainanzi states: When the Yellow Emperor governed the world, the azure dragon came to draw his chariot,
and the Feihuáng served in the stables.
It also says: When the world follows the Way, the Feihuáng serves in the stables.
The Ruìyìng Tú says: Chénghuáng,
when the ruler's chariots and robes
are in proper measure, it arrives.
The Fúruì Tú says: Ténghuáng is
a divine horse.
Its color is yellow,
and it appears when the ruler's virtue governs the four directions.
Also named Jíguāng,
this horse never dies.
Also called Chénghuáng,
or Feihuáng,
sometimes written as Jíhuáng,
or called Cuìhuáng.
Also named Zǐhuáng,
its appearance resembles a fox's back,
with two horns on it.
It comes from the land of the Báimín,
and riding it grants a lifespan of three thousand years.
The Yellow Emperor rode it across the realm.
The Běijīng states: In the land of the Quǎnróng, there is a patterned horse,
with a pure white body and mane,
eyes like gold,
named Jíliàng (also written as Jíliáng).
Riding it grants a lifespan of a thousand years.
The Zhōushū says: The patterned horse of the Quǎnróng,
with a red mane and white body,
eyes like gold,
is named the steed Jíhuáng.
It was presented during King Chéng's reign.
Guō Pú stated: Jíliáng, Jíhuáng, Jīsī, and Chénghuáng
are all the same creature.
The "Shang Shu Zhong Hou" states: Emperor Yáo built an altar by the River Luo,
and in the second month on a Xīn day, the ceremonies were fully prepared.
When it reached the time of Rì Jì,
glorious light emerged from the river,
and a dragon-horse, holding a shell in its mouth,
changed to a green color,
approached the altar,
and spat out the shell diagram.
Sòng Jūn said: Jì
means side.
Zhèng Xuán said: It has red patterns on a green ground,
meaning red patterns on a green background.
The "Ruì Yìng Tú" says: The dragon-horse
is a benevolent horse,
the essence of the river water.
It stands eight feet five inches tall,
with long shanks,
a body covered in scales and armor,
wings on its frame,
hanging hair on its sides,
its cry is not mournful,
and it treads water without sinking.
It appears when there is an enlightened king.
Fēitù is
the name of a divine horse,
capable of traveling thirty thousand lǐ in a day.
When Yǔ controlled the floods,
he toiled diligently for years,
saving the people from calamity.
Heaven responded to his virtue and sent it.
Sūn's "Illustrations of Auspicious Signs"
The Biography of Zōu Yáng states: Sū Qín served as prime minister of Yān,
and someone slandered him to the King of Yān.
The King of Yān gripped his sword in anger,
then fed him with juétí horses.
Lǐ Sī's letter says: Fine steed juétí horses
are not kept in the outer stables.
Mèng Kāng states: Juétí
are fine horses
that can outrun their mothers seven days after birth.
The Book of Zhōu states: Due north offered juétí as tribute.
The Guǎngyǎ states: Horses
are a category.
Sūn's Illustrations of Auspicious Signs states: Juétí
are beasts of the earth deity,
capable of speech on their own.
When the ruler is benevolent and filial towards the people,
they appear.
Yǔ came because of his merit in controlling the floods.
In the wilderness of Jiǔdài, where the horses greatly rejoice,
Xiàhòu Qǐ danced the Jiǔdài here,
with horses riding two dragons.
《Classic of Mountains and Seas》: Xiàhòu, with two dragons, drove atop the Xuāntái.
Preface by Wáng Yuáncháng
The Annals of Lü Buwei states: Yī Yǐn advised Tāng, saying:
"The Son of Heaven cannot obtain the ultimate flavors,
therefore he needs the pair of Qīnglóng,
and the steed Yífēng."
Gāo Yòu's commentary says: These are all names of horses,
swift as if racing with the wind.
Yán Shǐgǔ says: When horses run swiftly,
they often outpace the wind,
thus leaving the wind behind.
The Writings of Shīzǐ states: When people speak of ruling the world,
they mention Qílín and Qīnglóng horses,
yet Yáo used plain carriages and unadorned horses.
King Zhòu of Shāng imprisoned Earl Xī of Zhōu in Yǒulǐ,
so Jiǎng Zǐyá and Sǎn Yíshēng used a thousand yì of gold
to seek rare treasures from across the land,
in order to absolve their lord's offense.
Thus they obtained the patterned horse of the Dàchéng clan,
with its dappled body and crimson mane,
eyes like yellow gold,
and a neck like a pheasant's tail.
It was named the Jīsī Steed,
and was presented to King Zhòu of Shāng.
From "Jiǎng Zǐyá's Six Secret Teachings"
The "Diagram of Auspicious Responses" states: The Yaoniǎo is
a divine horse,
similar to the Feitu,
signifying that an enlightened ruler possesses virtue.
The "Xiàhóu Geographical Records" say: On Wēng Zhōu stands the city of King Xú Yǎn.
Legend holds that in the past, when King Mù of Zhōu was touring his domains,
the feudal lords collectively honored King Yǎn.
Upon hearing this, King Mù
ordered Zàofǔ to drive the Yaoniǎo horse,
which traveled a thousand lǐ in a day,
and returned personally to campaign against him.
Yìng Shào said: In ancient times, there was a superb horse
named Yaoniǎo,
with a red beak and black body,
capable of covering fifteen thousand lǐ in a single day.
The Son of Heaven commanded a chariot drawn by eight steeds,
with Huáliú on the right and Lǜ'ěr on the left,
Chìjì as the right outer horse and Báiyì as the left.
The Son of Heaven presided over the chariot,
with Zàofǔ as the charioteer,
the secondary chariot's team,
had Qúhuáng on the right and Yúlún on the left;
Dàolí as the right outer horse and Shānzǐ as the left.
Bó Yāo presided over the chariot,
with Cān Bó as the charioteer,
and Bēn Róng as the right guard.
Traveling east to Huángzé,
he had the court musicians perform.
The ballad went: In the ponds of Huáng,
the horses kick up sand,
the sovereign's majestic demeanor;
in the marshes of Huáng,
the horses kick up jade,
the sovereign's longevity and prosperity.
"Records of Emperor Mu" Upon ascending the throne for thirty-two years,
Emperor Mu toured the world.
Driving a chariot of gold and jade,
riding the winds alongside the mists,
he rose from the mountains of the morning sun,
from dawn to dusk without end,
to the edges of the universe.
He drove eight dragon-like steeds:
the first named Juédì,
whose feet never touched the ground;
the second named Fānyǔ,
outpacing flying birds;
the third named Bēnxiāo,
traveling ten thousand miles by night;
the fourth named Chāoyǐng,
chasing the sun as it moved;
the fifth named Yúhuī,
with fur radiantly gleaming;
the sixth named Qǐguāng,
casting ten shadows from one form;
the seventh named Téngwù,
galloping upon the clouds;

My sons

they can be told how to recognize good horses,

named Jiǔfāng Gāo,
whose skill with horses is no less than mine.
I request that you grant him an audience."
Duke Mù met with him,
and sent him to find a horse.
After three months he returned,
and reported:
"I have found one,
at Shāqiū."
Duke Mù asked:
"What kind of horse is it?"
He replied:
"A yellow mare."
They sent someone to fetch it,
but it turned out to be a black stallion.
Duke Mù was displeased,
and summoning Bólè, said to him:
"A failure!
The man you sent to find a horse
cannot even distinguish the color or gender correctly,
so how could he possibly know anything about horses?"
Bólè sighed deeply and said:
"Has it really come to this?
This is precisely why he surpasses me
a thousand or ten thousand times over.
What Gāo observes
is the innate nature;
he grasps the essence and forgets the coarse details,
concentrates on the inner qualities and ignores the external appearance,
sees what he needs to see,
and does not see what he doesn't need to see,
looks at what should be looked at and overlooks what should not.
In Gāo's judgment of horses,
there is something more valuable than the horse itself."
When the horse arrived,
it indeed proved to be a horse of exceptional quality under heaven.

Zàofù served as the charioteer for the King of Qí,

and when the training was completed,
he tested the chariot in the garden,
where the thirsty horses saw the pond,
abandoned the chariot and ran to the pool,
causing the chariot to fail.
Another account says that Wángzǐ Yúqī was the charioteer,
not using reins or whips but indulging the horses' desires,
monopolizing the benefits of fodder and water.
Yet when the horses passed by the garden pond, the chariot failed,
not because the benefits of fodder and water were insufficient,
but because their attention was divided by the pond.
Wáng Zǐ Yúqī served as charioteer for Zhào Jiǎnzhǔ,
vying to cover a thousand lǐ on the imperial road.
At the start of the journey,
he hid in a ditch,
and Wáng Zǐ Yúqī aligned the reins and whip to urge the horses forward.
Suddenly a boar charged out from the ditch,
frightening the horses and causing the chariot to overturn.
Another account says Zào Fǔ drove a team of four horses,
galloping and maneuvering freely as he pleased with the horses.
To have free control over the horses,
one must master the reins and whip.
However, when the horses were startled by the emerging boar,
even Zào Fǔ could not restrain them,
not because the reins and whip lacked strict control,
but because his authority was compromised by the boar's sudden appearance.
The governance of a sage ruler,
is akin to Zàofǔ's handling of the reins.
He aligns them at the bits and bridles,
and moderates their pace with the harmony of his lips;
he sets the proper measure in his heart,
and controls the rhythm within his grasp.
Internally, he attains it in his mind,
and externally, he aligns with the horses' will.
Thus, advancing and retreating follow the line,
and turning in curves matches the compass;
taking the path to reach afar,
his energy and strength remain abundant.
Truly, he has mastered the art.
Therefore, power and authority
are the ruler's chariot;
the great ministers
are the ruler's team of horses.
If the body is separated from the chariot's stability,
and the hands lose the hearts of the horses,
yet one can avoid peril,
such a thing has never existed in past or present.
Hence, if the horses are not well-tuned,
even Wáng Liáng cannot take the right path;
if ruler and ministers are not in harmony,
even Táng Yáo and Yú Shùn cannot achieve good governance.

Duke Dìng of Lǔ asked Yán Huí, saying:
"Have you, sir, also heard of Dōngyě Bì's skill in charioteering?"
He replied:
"Skilled he certainly is,
nevertheless,
his horses will surely bolt."
The duke's countenance showed displeasure,
and he said to his attendants:
"Can a gentleman indeed slander others?"
Three days later,
the groom came to report,
saying:
"Dōngyě Bì's horses have bolted, with the two outer ones breaking free,
while the two inner ones dragged the carriage back into the stable."
Hearing this,
the duke hastened to summon Yán Huí.
When Huí arrived,
the duke said:
"How did you know this would happen?"
He replied:
"I knew it from principles of governance.
In ancient times, Emperor Shùn was skilled in employing the people,
while Zàofǔ was skilled in employing horses.
Shùn never exhausted the people's strength,
and Zàofǔ never exhausted his horses' strength.
Therefore, Shùn had no rebellious people,
and Zàofǔ had no runaway horses.
Now, in Dōngyě Bì's charioteering,
when he mounts the chariot and takes the reins,
the bits and harness are properly adjusted;
in walking, trotting, and galloping,
all proper techniques are fully applied;
when traversing dangers and going long distances,
the horses' strength is completely spent,
yet he still incessantly demands more from them.
It was by this that I knew."
The duke said:
"Excellent!
It is truly as you have said.
Might you elaborate further?"
Yán Huí said:
"I have heard that birds, when desperate, will peck;
beasts, when desperate, will snatch;
people, when desperate, will deceive;
and horses, when desperate, will bolt.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been one who exhausted those below him yet could avoid peril."
The duke was pleased,
and subsequently reported this to Confucius.
Confucius replied:
"That which makes him Yán Huí
consists precisely of such insights."

but now old and worn out, no longer of use,

Tiánzǐfāng said:
"To covet its strength in youth,
yet abandon its body in old age—
this is something a benevolent person would not do.
He then used a bundle of silk to ransom it.
When Bàwǔ heard of this,
he knew where to place his allegiance.
《Huáinánrén Jiě Hánwàizhuàn》
Tiānxià mǎ Xú Wúguī yīn Nǚ Shāng jiàn Wèi Wǔhóu,
yuē:
"Wú xiàng mǎ: zhí zhě zhòng shéng,
qū zhě zhòng gōu,
fāng zhě zhòng jǔ,
yuán zhě zhòng guī.
Shì guó mǎ yě,
ér wèi ruò tiānxià mǎ yě.
Tiānxià mǎ yǒu chéng cái,
ruò xù ruò shī,
ruò sàng qí yī,
ruò shì zhě,
chāo yì jué chén,
bù zhī qí suǒ.
Wǔhóu dà yuè ér xiào.
"Zhuāngzǐ"
Rú Ěr persuaded Wèi Sìjūn,
who was pleased yet sighed deeply.
His attendants asked:
"Why do you not appoint him as chancellor?
The lord replied:
"A horse that resembles a deer
may be priced at a thousand gold pieces.
Yet there are horses worth a hundred gold,
but no deer worth even one gold piece -
because horses serve human purposes,
while deer do not serve humans.
Now Rú Ěr is chancellor material for a kingdom of ten thousand chariots,
and has ambitions toward greater states.
His heart is not in Wèi.
Though eloquent and wise,
he would not serve me,
which is why I do not appoint him chancellor.
Hánzǐ
Sū Dài wished to see the King of Qí,
and said to Chúnyú Kūn:
"A man had a fine horse,
which he wished to sell.
He saw Bó Lè and said: 'For three mornings I have stood in the market,
but no one has spoken to me.
I wish you would walk around and look at it,
then leave and glance back at it.
I would then offer you the earnings of one morning.'
Bó Lè did as he said,
and in one morning the horse's price increased tenfold.
Now I wish to present my fine horse to the king,
but have no one to introduce me.
Would you be willing to act as my Bó Lè?
I would offer you a pair of white jade discs,
and ten yì of gold,
as fodder for the horse."
Chúnyú Kūn spoke to the king and had him received.
Note: 'Fodder for the horse' is used to avoid direct mention of the bribe.
From the "Chūnqiū Hòuyǔ".
In ancient times, those skilled in judging horses: Hánfēng Shì assessed the mouth and teeth,
Má Zhāo assessed the cheeks,
Zǐnǚ Lì assessed the eyes,
Wèi Jì assessed the mane,
Xǔ Bǐ assessed the rump,
Tóufá Hè assessed the chest and flanks,
Guǎn Qīng assessed the lips and muzzle,
Chén Bēi assessed the thighs and legs,
Qín Yá assessed the front parts,
Zàn Jūn assessed the hind parts.
All these ten individuals,
were master craftsmen of the world.
Their methods of judging horses,
did not rely on observing just one characteristic of the horse,
yet they could discern the height of its bone joints,
the smoothness or roughness of its hooves,
the firmness or brittleness of its physique,
and the length of its endurance.
This is not only true for judging horses.
Indeed, humans also have their characteristics.
"Lǚ Guān Biǎo"
Near the frontier lived a man
who was skilled in managing horses,
but his horse ran away for no reason into the land of the Hú.
Everyone consoled him,
but his father said:
"How do we know this won't turn out to be a blessing?"
After several months,
his horse returned with a fine steed of the Hú,
and everyone congratulated him,
but his father said:
"How do we know this won't turn into a misfortune?"
With a wealthy household and excellent horses,
his son loved riding,
but fell and broke his thigh.
Everyone consoled him,
but his father said:
"How do we know this won't become a blessing?"
After a year,
the Hú people invaded the frontier in great numbers,
and all able-bodied men took up their bows to fight.
Of those living near the frontier,
nine out of ten perished.
Only because of his lameness
did the father and son preserve each other.
The "Yōu Tōng Fù" says: The old man of the north understood the interdependence of fortune and misfortune.
From "Huái Rén Jiàn"
Emperor Wǔ issued an edict stating:
"Some horses may kick and gallop yet cover a thousand miles;
some scholars bear the burden of public criticism,
yet achieve merit and fame.
As for unruly horses
and unrestrained scholars,
it all depends on how they are managed."
The Book of Hàn
The General of Agile Cavalry challenged the various scholars,
and Dōngfāng Shuò responded:
"Gānjiàng and Mòyé,
the sharpest swords under heaven,
can cut through swans and wild geese in water,
and sever horses and oxen on land.
But when used for mending,
they are not as good as an awl worth one coin;
Qíjì and Lù'ěr,
the finest horses under heaven,
when employed to catch mice in a deep palace,
are truly not as good as a lame cat.
"Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò"
In the garden of Empress Wèi, there were ten funeral carriage horses from the burial procession,
kept well-fed and cared for by subordinate attendants,
yet they were unfit for riding,
and the horses died only at sixty years of age.
From "Huán Tán's New Treatise": Hán Zǐzhì once fed fifty-year-old horses with rehmannia and licorice,
and they bore three foals again,
dying only at one hundred and thirty years of age.
From "Bàopǔzǐ": Zhāng Nèzhī, the governor of Dé Prefecture, had a white horse,
its color like white silk.
His father, Zhāng Xióng, served as governor of several prefectures,
and often rode it.
After Xióng passed away,
his son Jìngzhī, as Director of the Bureau of Evaluations,
was reassigned as governor of Shòu Prefecture,
and also rode this horse.
After Jìngzhī passed away,
his younger brother Nè, from the position of Supervising Secretary,
was reassigned as governor of Dé Prefecture,
then entered court as Chancellor of the National University,
later served as governor of Cháng Prefecture,
and the horse remains to this day,
estimated to be over eighty years old,
extremely plump and robust,
with no signs of lameness in its legs.
From "Records of Court and Commoners"
Guǎnghàn's Yáng Wēngwěi could understand the language of birds and beasts.
While riding a lame horse in the wilderness,
there was a person grazing horses in the fields,
several miles away,
their calls could be heard by each other.
Wēngwěi said to his driver:
"That horse grazing there is blind in one eye.
His driver said:
"How do you know?
He replied:
"It scolded this horse in our carriage saying: 'Lame horse.
The lame horse also scolded it back: 'Blind horse.
The driver didn't believe him,
and sent someone to check,
and indeed the horse was blind in one eye.
《Lùn Héng》 Lǐ Nán was riding a red horse on the road,
when he met someone riding a white horse,
the white horse neighed first,
and then Nán's red horse neighed in response.
Nán said to his attendant:
"That horse said: 'You will soon meet a yellow horse,
blind in the left eye,
that is my son,
please tell him to hurry,
so we can travel together.
The attendant didn't believe him,
but after traveling two miles,
they indeed encountered a yellow horse blind in the left eye.
Nán's horse neighed first,
and the blind horse responded.
When they asked its owner,
it indeed turned out to be the offspring of that white horse.
《Bào Pǔ Zǐ》
Emperor Shìzǔ gathered his generals,
inquiring about the spoils seized from the defeated rebels.
Only Lǐ Zhōng alone had taken nothing.
Emperor Shìzǔ said:
"I wish to specially reward Zhōng—
would you all not resent this?"
He then bestowed upon him his own great black horse, embroidered quilts, and clothing.
"Basic Biography"
Mǎ Yuán attacked Jiaozhǐ,
and said to his officials:
"My younger cousin Shǎoyóu
often lamented my great ambitions,
saying: 'A gentleman lives but one lifetime,
he should only seek adequate clothing and food,
ride in a simple carriage,
drive a slow horse,
serve as a local official,
guard the ancestral graves,
be called a good man by his village,
this is enough.
To seek more surplus
only brings hardship upon oneself.
Records of the Eastern Han
For traversing the heavens, nothing compares to the dragon,
for traversing the earth, nothing compares to the horse.
The horse is
the foundation of military arms and armor,
a great asset to the state.
In times of peace, it serves to distinguish the order of nobility and commonality,
in times of change, it aids in overcoming difficulties from near and far.
Quoting from the "Memorial on the Bronze Horse Model"
Yú Zhī,
was appointed by the provincial government as an assistant in Nányáng.
The Grand Administrator Zhāng Zhōng was connected by marriage to the royal family,
and his crimes were severe.
Zhī handled the case according to the law.
The Inspector feared Zhōng's influence,
summoned Zhī,
to which Zhī responded:
"My years are advancing and my aspirations are spent;
like an old horse worth eight hundred coins,
life and death hold the same value.
I only wish to achieve something in this enlightened era."
Thereupon, he cast aside his official seal and left.
From "Chronicles of the Elderly of Chángshā."
Sūn Jiān campaigned against the Yellow Turbans,
pressed his advantage and advanced deep,
but met with defeat at Xīhuá,
was wounded and fell from his horse,
lying in the grass.
His troops were scattered,
and none knew Sūn Jiān's whereabouts.
The dappled horse Sūn Jiān had ridden
galloped back to camp,
pawing the ground and neighing loudly.
The officers and soldiers followed the horse into the grass,
and thus found Sūn Jiān, supporting him back to camp.
From the "Wú Shū".
An old steed in the stable may stay,
But its aim is to gallop a thousand li away.
A noble-hearted man though advanced in years,
Never abandons his proud aspirations.
Cáo Cāo, "Yuèfǔ" Dù Zhì's "Poem to Mǔqiū Jiǎn" says: A fine steed untested,
Lingers idly by the trough and stable.
A warrior's ambition unfulfilled,
Faces hardship and much bitterness.
"Wénzhāng Xùlù"
Sūn Quán attacked Héféi and was defeated.
He reached the bridge on horseback,
but the southern section of the bridge had been dismantled for over ten feet,
with no planks remaining.
Gǔ Jílì was behind his horse
and instructed Sūn Quán to hold the saddle and loosen the reins,
while he whipped the horse from behind
to boost its momentum,
enabling it to leap across the gap.
From "Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn"
Zhū Jiànpíng was skilled at judging horses.
When Emperor Wén was about to depart,
he had a horse brought in from outside.
Jiànpíng encountered it on the road
and said:
"This horse's features indicate
it will die today."
As the emperor prepared to mount it,
the horse disliked the scent of his perfume
and startled, biting the emperor's knee.
The emperor angrily had it killed.
(Records of Wèi)
Huán Fàn went out to join Cáo Shuǎng.
Xuānwáng said to Jiǎng Jì:
"The wise advisor has gone.
Jì said:
"Fàn is indeed wise.
But a jade horse yearns for stable beans,
Shuǎng will certainly not be able to use him.
From Gān Bǎo's Records of Jìn
In Zhōnglú County, within the western mountains, there is a path.
During the Han Dynasty, several hundred horses once emerged from it,
and it is now called the Horse Cave.
People would rest their horses here overnight,
hence it was named the Riding Pavilion.
The horses were all small in shape,
resembling those of Bādiān.
During the Three Kingdoms period,
when Lù Xùn attacked Xiāngyáng,
dozens of horses again emerged from this cave.
Xùn transported them back to Jiànyè.
When an envoy from Shǔ arrived,
a soldier from one of the five military families in Zhēnchí,
recognized the color of one of the horses,
saying it was the one his deceased father had ridden.
Facing it, he shed tears.
Thus, the underground passage was named the White Horse Pit.
"Records of Xiāngyáng": Thirty li north of Yílíng County, there is a stone cave,
named Horse Passage.
A white horse often emerged from the cave to graze,
and when people chased it back into the cave,
it would travel underground and emerge in Hànzhōng.
When people in Hànzhōng lost horses,
they would also often appear from this cave,
spanning a distance of several thousand li.
"Water Classic, Chapter 24"
Zhāng Zhèn, styled Wángzǐ, could mold horses from clay,
which could travel a thousand li in a day.
From Gé Hóng's "Biographies of the Divine Immortals"
Wáng Jì was skilled at understanding horses' temperaments.
He once rode a horse
that wore a coin-patterned mudguard.
When they came to a body of water ahead,
the horse refused to cross all day.
Wáng Jì said:
"This must be because it treasures the mudguard.
He had someone remove it,
and the horse crossed directly.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Wǔzǐ had a passion for horses,
and was also quite discerning about them.
Hence Dù Yù remarked that Wáng Wǔzǐ had an obsession with horses,
while Hé Chángyú had an obsession with money.
Emperor Wǔ asked Dù Yù:
"What obsession do you have?"
He replied:
"Your subject has an obsession with the Zuǒ Zhuàn."
"Yǔ Lín"
Wáng Zhàn, courtesy name Chǔchōng,
resided by a grave mound.
His elder brother's son Jì came to visit him.
Jì had a fondness for horses,
and the horse he rode was swift and spirited,
which he cherished greatly.
Zhàn remarked:
"This is a fine young horse,
but its strength is insufficient to endure hardship.
Recently, I saw the Inspector's horse,
which should surpass this one,
only it hasn't been properly cared for."
Jì acquired the Inspector's horse,
fed it grain for over ten days,
and tested it with Zhàn.
Zhàn had never ridden a horse before,
yet he suddenly galloped off,
his movements no different from Jì's,
and the horses were evenly matched.
Zhàn said:
"Now we're just riding on the main road,
how can we distinguish which horse is superior?
We must go to the ant mound!"
So they rode around the ant mound,
and the horse indeed stumbled and fell.
From Dèng Càn's "Records of the Jìn Dynasty"
Wáng Wǔzǐ was reprimanded and moved his residence to the foot of Běimáng.
At that time, there were many people and land was expensive.
Jì enjoyed horse archery,
so he bought land to build a racecourse.
He arranged coins in a circle around the entire racecourse.
People at the time called it the "Golden Moat."
In the Shìshuō, it is referred to as a moat,
but another version says racecourse.
Wáng Róng was outstandingly talented,
yet he did not adhere to formal etiquette or appearance,
and he enjoyed riding a white horse from Bā.
Although he held the position of one of the Three Excellencies,
he would casually travel privately,
inspecting his fields and gardens,
without a single attendant,
tucking his own handkerchief into his waistband.
"Discourses on the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove"
Chén Ān served as an attendant for Héjiān King Sīmǎ Yǒng,
being exceptionally strong and robust.
He often rode a horse,
which was extremely swift and fast.
Later, the horse died,
and two red snakes emerged from its nostrils.
"Records of Spectral Spirits"
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Jìn,
someone presented a horse,
dreaming that the River God requested it.
When it turned out the emperor had the same dream,
he cast the horse into the river to offer it to the god.
Initially, Grand Tutor Chǔ Bào also favored this horse,
but the emperor said it had already been given to the River God.
After Chǔ Bào's death,
soldiers claimed to see him riding this horse.
"Records of the Strange"
Zhī Dàolín often kept several horses.
Someone remarked:
"It is unbecoming for a monk to keep horses."
Zhī replied:
"I value their divine vigor."
《Shishuo》 Zhī Dào'ān was located on the southern peak,
anciently known as Zhīxíng Mountain.
Now there is White Horse Gully,
where Zhī watered his horses.
Beside the hermitage on a rock,
there are four horse hoof prints,
said to be the hoofprints of Dàolín's flying steed.
《Wújùn Zhì》
During Fú Jiān's reign,
Dà Yuān presented heavenly horses and thousand-mile colts,
all of which sweated blood,
had crimson manes,
phoenix chests of five colors,
and bodies of qilins.
He ordered his ministers to compose poems halting the horses and sent them back,
demonstrating his lack of desire.
"Jīn Zǎi Jì"
Fú Jiān was attacked by Mùróng Chōng,
and Fú Jiān galloped on a piebald horse,
but fell into a ravine.
The pursuing troops were nearly upon him,
and he had no way to escape.
The horse then hesitated by the edge of the ravine,
lowering its bridle toward Fú Jiān,
but Fú Jiān could not reach it.
The horse knelt down to offer it again.
Fú Jiān grasped it,
managed to climb ashore,
and fled to Lújiāng.
From "Yì Yuàn"
In the fourth year of Taishang,
Wang Pú of Yǎnzhōu led two thousand followers to surrender,
presenting a beautiful woman,
one horse,
and a goat whose beard trailed nine inches from the ground.
He was appointed Commandant of Chángshuǐ
and Duke of Lǐnqiū.
Cuī Hóng's "Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms"
The white horse ridden by Hóu Jǐng,
whenever about to win a battle,
would prance and neigh,
its spirit proud and graceful;
but when facing defeat,
it would lower its head and refuse to advance.
At the battle of Shítóu,
its morale was dejected,
lying down and unwilling to move.
Hóu Jǐng had his attendants bow and plead with it,
or even whip it,
yet it ultimately refused to go forward.
History of the Southern Dynasties
Quán Huì served as the Erudite of the National University.
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
while returning home from his office,
his horse suddenly collapsed on the road without reason,
and he consequently lost the ability to speak,
dying abruptly.
Huì had always feared horses throughout his life,
yet as his rank and reputation rose,
he had no choice but to ride them,
and indeed met his end because of this.
Wáng Shìchōng's nephew, the false Prince of Dài Wáng Wǎn,
was on a mission to Dòu Jiàndé's army,
riding the dappled horse once mounted by Suí Yángdì,
his armor exceedingly splendid,
stood out before the troops,
to boast before the masses.
Tàizōng said:
"What he rides,
is truly a fine horse.
Yùchí Jìngdé requested to go and seize it,
then with Gāo Zèngshēng and Liáng Jiànfāng, three swift steeds,
charged straight into the enemy army,
captured Wǎn,
and led his horse back.
"Old Book of Táng"
Yǐn the child prodigy often told how Bólè had his son hold the Classic of Horse Physiognomy,
using illustrations to seek a horse,
but for a whole year, he found none that resembled the descriptions.
Returning home, he reported this to his father,
who then ordered him to search again.
Going out, he saw a large toad,
and said to his father:
"I've found a horse,
roughly matching the description,
but not entirely complete.
Bólè asked:
"How so?
He replied:
"This horse has a bulging forehead and sunken eyes,
a contracted spine,
only its hooves aren't like piled-up wine vessels.
Bólè said:
"This horse is good at leaping and tossing,
but it's unfit for riding.
His son laughed and stopped.
(Records of Affairs from the Court and the Country)
During the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
a palace report stated:
"In the performance of dancing horses,
their graceful movements followed the rhythm perfectly.
When the drinking music played,
they would hold cups in their mouths,
lying down and then rising again.
The Tibetans were greatly astonished.
From "Jǐnglóng Wénguǎn Jì" Emperor Xuánzōng once ordered four hundred horses to be trained for dancing,
divided into left and right groups,
named as someone's favorite,
someone's darling.
At that time, fine horses were also presented as tribute from beyond the frontier,
and the emperor had them trained,
each mastering the art to perfection.
He then commanded them to be adorned with embroidered trappings,
decorated with golden bells,
ornamented on their manes,
and interspersed with pearls and jades.
The music for them was called "The Pouring Cup Music."
When the melody was played,
they would raise their heads and wag their tails,
moving back and forth in time with the beat.
Moreover, on a three-tiered wooden platform,
the horses would mount it,
spinning as if flying.
Sometimes, strong men were ordered to lift a couch,
and the horses would dance upon it.
Dozens of musicians stood to the left, right, front, and back,
all dressed in light yellow robes,
with patterned jade belts,
selected specifically for their youth and handsome appearance.
Every Qiānqiū Festival,
they were often commanded to perform below the Qínzhèng Tower.
Later, after the emperor fled to Shǔ,
the dancing horses were scattered among the people.
Ān Lùshān once witnessed their dance
and grew fond of them.
From then on, he took several dozen and kept them in Fànyáng.
Afterward,
they came into the possession of Tián Chéngsì,
who was unaware of their nature.
Mixing them with warhorses,
he placed them in the outer stables.
One day,
during a grand military feast,
as music played,
the horses began to dance uncontrollably.
The stable hands thought they were bewitched,
and struck them with brooms.
The horses, believing their dance was out of rhythm,
adjusted their movements with rising and falling cadence,
still retaining their former demeanor.
The stable officials found it extremely strange
and reported it to Chéngsì.
He ordered them to be whipped severely.
The more orderly the horses danced, the harsher the whipping became,
until they eventually died under the lash.
Some people at the time knew they were dancing horses,
but fearing Tián's tyranny,
they never dared to speak up.
From "Mínghuáng Zálù"
Prince Níng was just gathering guests for porridge,
when a horse broker named Qū Shénnú
came to present two horses.
Prince Níng immediately examined and tested them in the central hall,
and the seated guests found them indistinguishable.
Prince Níng turned to Shénnú and said:
"What are their prices?
The broker first pointed and said:
"This one is a thousand strings of coins.
Then he pointed and said:
"This one is five hundred strings.
Prince Níng was pleased,
and paid as quoted.
The guests couldn't fathom the disparity in price.
He then had the horses saddled and raced,
back and forth several times,
and smiling said to the seated guests:
"Can you tell which is superior?
They all said:
"We cannot.
Prince Níng then looked at the thousand-string horse,
saying:
"This horse, whether slow or fast over a hundred rounds,
raises not a speck of dust beneath its hooves.
Then he looked at the five-hundred-string horse,
saying:
"This horse, after just ten passes back and forth,
already stirs up dust under its feet.
Thus their prices are ranked accordingly.
The seated guests were then convinced.
"Records of Marvels"
The young gallants of Cháng'ān,
every springtime,
would form groups and alliances,
each procuring a short horse,
adorned with embroidered saddles,
golden bridles side by side,
coming and going beneath the flowering trees,
with servants following carrying wine vessels,
and whenever they encountered a beautiful garden, they would halt their horses to drink.
"Tiānbǎo Reminiscences"
Liǔ Zōngyuán's "Ode to the Dragon-Horse Painting" states: During Emperor Míng's reign,
an extraordinary horse was obtained from the river in Língchāng Commandery,
its appearance featured dragon scales,
a serpent's tail,
curly hair,
round eyes,
and a fleshy mane.
It resided in the imperial stables for twenty years.
When calamity struck,
the emperor fled westward,
and the horse reached west of Xiányáng,
entered the Wèi River,
transformed into a dragon,
swam away,
and its final whereabouts remained unknown.
Ān Lùshān was obese,
and every time he traveled by post to court,
he had to change horses midway,
which was called the "Minister's Horse-Changing Platform."
Otherwise,
the horse would collapse,
so the horse had to be capable of carrying five shi while galloping to bear the load.
*New Book of Tang*
Táng Lángzhōng Zhāng Yuānyī, considering Táng Bōrě short and squat,
deemed himself a depressed and stunted Shǔ horse.
"Records of Court and Country"
Liú Cóngjiàn governed Luzhou in Dàmǎ,
presenting a nine-foot horse,
but Emperor Wǔzōng did not accept it.
The Book of Táng states: Xiájiásī, the ancient Jiānkūn nation,
raised exceptionally robust horses,
selecting the best fighters as lead horses.
The Huíhé Chronicles record: In the Western Regions, there were horses
over ten feet tall,
under whose bellies people could walk
unhindered back and forth.
The Guīxīn Miscellany notes:
In his previous life, Liú Sānfù, who was known to Lǐ Déyù for his literary talent,
could recall events from three lifetimes.
He said he had once been a horse,
and the horse would often neigh in pain when thirsty for water at the post station,
with its hooves causing heart-wrenching pain.
Later, when Sānfù rode a horse,
he would always loosen the reins on rough terrain,
and remove any stones in the path.
His household did not install door thresholds,
fearing they might injure the horse's hooves.
"Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Lù Yán moved from Chéngdū to Zhǔgōng,
the horse he was riding suddenly spoke in human language,
saying:
"Reed catkins bloom,
after these flowers blossom, Lù will have no home.
Not long after, he met with disaster.
In Hédōng, Péi Guāngyuǎn served as the magistrate of Wèinán in Huázhōu.
He was exceptionally greedy and cruel by nature,
and particularly fond of playing polo.
Even during the sweltering heat of midsummer,
he never took a break.
He kept a white horse,
handsome and strong, capable of galloping,
but it ultimately succumbed to exhaustion in the scorching summer heat and died on the open field.
He also plotted to kill the village head Wáng Biǎo,
and seized his son.
In the year Dàshùn Xīnhài,
Péi fell ill for over a month.
At times, it seemed as if he was being tormented by spirits,
and he would speak alone, saying:
"Wáng Biǎo has come."
After a short while, he would say:
"The white horse has come."
He then impersonated both Wáng Biǎo and the horse, reproaching himself in their voices.

staking ten million coins against it."

Note:
Shí Chòng's ox was inferior in appearance and strength to Wáng Kǎi's ox,
yet when Wáng Kǎi went on an outing,
he set out very late to race into Luò City.
Chóng's ox, dozens of paces behind,
swift as a flying bird,
left Kǎi's ox unable to catch up despite running at full speed.
So Kǎi secretly bribed Chóng's driver,
asking:
"How is the ox made to run so fast?"
The driver said:
"The ox is not slow by nature,
but it's because the driver fails to control it properly.
In urgent moments, if you let it pull with a tilted shaft,

Kǎi followed this advice,
and thus won the race.
Shí Chòng later found out,
and killed the informant.

Yuán Hǔ rashly replied:

Duke Huán, stern and with a changed countenance,
looked around at those seated and said:

He had a large ox weighing a thousand jīn,
consuming ten times more fodder and beans than an ordinary ox,
yet when bearing heavy loads for long distances,
it could not even match a weak cow.
When Cáo Cāo entered Jīngzhōu,
he had it cooked to feast his soldiers.

How does this compare to Yuán?"
All those seated were both startled
and lost color.

He begged to appoint Huán Chōng as governor of Jiānglíng.

Mount Mín has many kuí niú.
The "Classic of Mountains and Seas" notes: In today's Shǔ mountains,

Local people shot it with crossbows and obtained thirty-eight dàn of meat,
which is what the "Ěryǎ" calls wéi.
In the region of Líntáo,
there was a mountain dweller named Zhòng Xiǎoxiǎo,
known among the people as Zhòng Yěniú.
He made his living by gathering and hunting.
West of Líntáo,
reaching the areas of Diéyán and Pānmín,
there were several tracts of fertile farmland
that, since the time of Ān Lùshān,
had fallen into desolate wilderness.
In these areas, bamboo cattle, also called wild cattle, were abundant.
Their color was jet black,
and their size could rival six or seven camels,
with meat weighing up to ten million jin.
Their horns
could be lifted by two strong men.
Wherever they drank and grazed,
trees and dense bamboo
were trampled into dust.
Hunters would first set dogs to chase them,
waiting for them to flee in panic,
then poison their arrows
and seize the opportunity to shoot.
Once hit by an arrow,
they would track the trail
and follow slowly.
Where the arrow poison took effect, the cattle would die,
collapsing like mountains,
piling up meat like mounds.
A single ox could yield several thousand jin of meat,
which was exceptionally delicious when fresh,
with fibers like red silk threads.
During the Qiánníng era,

At the end of the valley,
they reached a southern cliff.
As the dogs pressed urgently,
the cattle crowded and pushed against each other.
The one at the front
lost its footing and fell off the cliff.
Those following behind,
unaware their companions had fallen,
continued one after another in succession,
until thirty-six heads
all perished at the base of the cliff,
piling meat beyond measure.
The people of Qín, Chéng, and Jiē prefectures
could not carry it all even with shoulder poles.

mistaking them for ghosts riding dragons.
Hence it was named Chénglóngzhōu (Riding Dragon Isle).
from "Records of the Known World"
An envoy in charge of camels was sitting at night when
he heard voices outside the door saying:
"Tomorrow, the gentleman will be sent on a ten-thousand-mile mission,
but he will avoid this hardship.
What shall I do then?
A reply came:
"Censor, please comfort yourself,
you will surely be exempted eventually.
The envoy secretly peered out
and saw that they were two camels in the courtyard.
The next morning,
an imperial decree ordered one camel to carry military uniforms to Shǔ,
and it subsequently died in Shǔ.
"Qīngmíng Tóuxiá Lù"
The great Yuèzhī country of the Western Regions produces single-humped camels.
Note: They have one hump on their back,
the term "hump" referring to its elevated shape resembling a mound of earth.
Nowadays, it is commonly called the "humped cattle."
The Book of Hàn records that the single-humped camels of Tǔfān can travel a thousand lǐ in a day.
From Dūnhuáng, crossing the Western Flowing Sands leads to foreign lands.
The Flowing Sands stretch over a thousand miles,
with no water in between,
though hidden water sources exist at times,
unknown to people.
All travel by camel,
which know the water veins;
when they reach such a spot, they halt and refuse to move,
stamping their feet on the ground.
People dig at the stamped spot,
and water is always found.
From "Bówùzhì"
Shànshàn,
was the ancient kingdom of Lóulán.
To its northwest lie several hundred li of shifting sands,
where hot winds blow in summer,
posing a hazard to travelers.
When the wind is about to arrive,
only old camels know it,
immediately braying and standing abruptly,
burying their mouths and noses in the sand.
People often take this as a sign,
and likewise cover their noses and mouths with felt,
as the wind speeds swiftly by,
passing completely in a moment.
If one does not do this,
it will certainly lead to peril and death.
"Accounts of Foreign Lands from the Later Zhōu Dynasty"
In Yútián there are small deer,
with slender and long horns,
which mate with camels to produce offspring,
called wind-footed camels.
They can travel seven hundred lǐ in a day,
swift as the wind.
"Records of Harmonious Observations" Persia produces famous horses and large camels,
and there are often camels that can travel seven hundred lǐ in a day.
Wealthy families may own several thousand of them.
"History of the Northern Dynasties"
The Huáguó
is a branch of the Chēshī people.
They have two-humped camels,
and wild donkeys with horns.
From the *Nán Shǐ*
The smoke from camel dung,
rose straight up like a wolf's signal smoke.
When the camel's hump droops, its teeth are old;
when young and healthy, the hump stands straight.
From "Suǒsuì Lù"
The "Yì Xùn" says: The sound of an ox is "moo,"
the sound of a camel is "tuó."
In the country of Jūyí in the Western Regions,
there is a stone camel on the mountain.
Water flows from beneath its belly;
if one catches it with a golden vessel or hands,
it immediately passes through.
However, if it is contained in a gourd,
one can then drink it,
causing the body to become fragrant and pure, enabling one to ascend and become an immortal.
The country is mysterious,
and encounters are rare.
"Yì Yuàn"
The donkey, also known as Hànlí,
its offspring is called Lí.
From Hé Chéngtiān's "Compiled Texts"
The Xiongnu's extraordinary livestock,
are donkeys and mules.
"Records of the Grand Historian"
Emperor Líng drove four white donkeys in the Western Garden of the palace,
personally holding the reins,
galloping and circling about,
considering it great amusement.
Thereupon, the high officials and noble relatives imitated one another,
even riding in curtained carriages,
using them as mounted attendants,
mutually encroaching and seizing,
until their price equaled that of horses.
Now, the donkey,
is a beast of burden for heavy loads and long distances,
ascending and descending mountain valleys,
used only by rustic folk.
How could there be emperors or gentlemen harnessing them?
This dull-witted creature,
now esteemed,
seems to indicate Heaven's will that the state will fall into great disorder,
with the wise and foolish inverted.
All those in power
are like donkeys.
"Later Records of the Five Elements" states: Hàn Emperor Líng raised several hundred donkeys,
often riding them himself,
galloping throughout the capital.
Sometimes he drove four donkeys into the market.
"Jīn Lóu Zǐ"
Jì Zǐxùn drove a donkey cart,
and went with his disciples to visit Xǔ.
On the way, they passed by Xíngyáng,
and stopped at a host's house.
Suddenly, the donkey he was driving stiffened and died,
with maggots flowing out.
The host hurriedly informed him,
and Zǐxùn said:
"Is that so?
He calmly sat still,
finished his meal,
then slowly went out,
tapped it with his staff,
and the donkey immediately sprang up,
walking as before.
They then continued on their journey.
Those who followed to watch
often numbered in the thousands.
From the Book of the Later Han.
Zhūgě Kè's father, Zhūgě Jǐn,
had a long face resembling a donkey.
Sūn Quán held a grand assembly of his ministers,
and had someone lead a donkey in.
A long tag was attached to its face,
which read:
"Zhūgě Zǐyú."
Kè knelt and requested a brush,
adding two characters beneath it,
so it read:
"'s donkey."
The entire assembly laughed heartily,
and so the donkey was given to Kè.
From "Records of Wú."
Wáng Jì passed away.
When he was about to be buried,
all the distinguished individuals had gathered.
Sūn Chǔ, who deeply admired Jì, arrived later,
wept bitterly for him,
and none of the guests could hold back their tears.
After weeping,
he turned to the funeral bed and said:
"You always enjoyed my donkey bray,
so I shall perform it for you."
His imitation was lifelike in both form and sound,
causing all the guests to laugh,
but Chǔ looked at them and said:
"Are all of you not dead yet,
yet you let Wáng Jì die?"
From the "Jìn Shū"
The head should resemble a pig. At the end of Emperor Wǔ's reign, he once saw a donkey.
Xiè Dàzhuàn asked His Majesty:
"From a distance, what does its form
seem to resemble?"
Emperor Xiào Wǔ covered his mouth and laughed,
and replied:
"The head should resemble a pig."
"Shì Shuō"
Wáng Dǎo said to Zhūgě Huī:
"People say 'Wáng-Gě',
not 'Gě-Wáng'."
Huī replied:
"People say 'donkey-horse',
not 'horse-donkey',
but does that mean donkeys are superior to horses?"
Book of Jìn
Shì Dào'ān, whose virtue was revered throughout the land, once rode a red donkey,
traveling between Jīngzhōu and Xiāngzhōu,
seen morning and evening.
Now atop the Hédōng Temple stands a Donkey Terrace,
while south of Xiàn Mountain lies Zhōnglǘ Village.
The Historical Records claim these accounts may be fictitious,
