Emperor Hòufèi raised thousands of donkeys in the Yàolíng Hall.
"Book of Sòng"
The Prince of Dōng Hǎi was mediocre and inferior,
the Former Deposed Emperor called him the Donkey Prince.
"Biography of Liú Xiù Rén" Wèi Yuán Tǎn was arrogant, wolf-like, fierce, and crude,
Prince Ān Fēng Yán Míng often sternly reprimanded him,
saying:
"In the past, the Sòng Dynasty had the Prince of Dōng Hǎi, Yī,
whose will and nature were mediocre and inferior,
and people called him the Donkey Prince.
I have closely observed your actions,
and I fear you too cannot avoid the title of donkey.
Those who heard it at the time called him the Donkey Prince.
"History of the Northern Dynasties"
Wáng Huàn was first appointed as the Minister of Works.
Liú Xiáng and Huàn's son, Róng, were traveling together in a carriage,
when they reached the central hall,
they saw a passerby driving a donkey.
Xiáng remarked:
"Donkey,
you'd better do your best,
for with your talent,
you could have already become a minister.
(From the Book of Southern Qí)
Gōngsūn Guǐ,
styled Yuánqìng,
served as the garrison commander of Hǔláo.
When Emperor Tàiwǔ was about to launch a northern campaign,
he requisitioned civilian donkeys to transport grain,
and assigned Guǐ to oversee the allocation in Yōngzhōu.
Guǐ ordered each donkey owner to contribute an additional bolt of silk,
before accepting their service.
The common people remarked:
"Whether the donkey is strong or weak,
it carries silk to prove its worth."
The public ridiculed him for this,
and he was recalled to the capital as a result.
Book of the Later Wei
After Chén Hòuzhǔ entered Suí,
Emperor Wéndì asked the supervisor:
"What does Shūbǎo enjoy?"
The reply was:
"He enjoys donkey meat."
Asked how much he drank,
the answer was:
"He and his younger brothers drink one dàn daily."
Emperor Wéndì was greatly astonished.
From History of the Southern Dynasties
Sū Shìcháng had an ugly appearance,
but was quite knowledgeable,
possessed a humorous nature,
and his speech was mixed with witty remarks.
During the Dàyè era of the Suí dynasty,
he served as the Commissioner of Waterways.
Emperor Yáng once said to him:
"Why does your face resemble that of a donkey driver?
Shìcháng bowed twice,
shouted,
placed his hands on the ground,
wrinkled his neck and distorted his face,
imitating the appearance of a donkey driver.
The ministers covered their mouths and laughed,
Emperor Yáng was greatly pleased,
and bestowed upon him one hundred bolts of silk.
From the Old Book of Táng.
When Empress Wǔ first proclaimed the Zhōu dynasty,
she feared the people's hearts were unsettled,
so she ordered individuals to recommend themselves for official posts.
Beyond the regular officials, many supernumerary positions were created, such as Lǐxíng, Shíyí, Bǔquē, and Censorial Officials.
This reached the point where
there was a saying,
"Enough to fill carts and be measured by the bushel."
Once, a clerk from the Censorate was about to enter his office
when he encountered several Lǐxíng Censors standing together inside the gate.
The clerk did not dismount from his donkey
but charged right through their midst.
The Censors were furious
and prepared to cane him.
The clerk said:
"Today's offense truly
lies with this donkey.
I beg you to reprimand it first,
and then I will accept my punishment."
The Censors agreed
and said to him:
"Your skills are evident,
but your wits are exceedingly dull.
What kind of donkey beast
dares to proceed among the Censors?"
Thereupon, they felt ashamed and stopped.
From "Records of Our Dynasty."
Táng Yáng Jiǒng often called court officials "unicorn props."
Someone asked him about it,
and he said:
"Those who pretend to display unicorns nowadays
must meticulously adorn its form,
drape it over a donkey,
making it appear as a marvelous creature.
But once the hide is removed,
it's still just a donkey.
Those without virtue yet clad in crimson and purple robes—
how are they any different from this?
From "Qiān Zǎi"
Wáng Jíshàn later became the Right Minister,
but implemented no significant policies.
He only prohibited clerks from bringing donkeys into the hall,
spending all day chasing them out,
earning the nickname "Donkey-Chasing Minister."
The Emperor
Guō Yīngyì,
was the son of Zhīyùn.
While governing Jiànnán,
he was quite unrestrained and dissolute,
taking women
and making them ride donkeys to play polo,
using jeweled inlays for the donkey saddles,
and spending enormous sums on rewards,
all for his amusement.
"Book of Táng"
During the late Xiàntōng era,
the authorities, considering the extravagant attire of examination candidates,
submitted a petition to prohibit them from riding horses.
At that time, there were no fewer than a thousand candidates in the examination grounds,
all riding long-eared donkeys.
Someone mocked them, saying:
"This year, by imperial decree, all ride donkeys;
short reins and long cruppers fill the nine thoroughfares.
The lean young men can still manage,
but among them, Zhèng Chāngtú is utterly distressed."
Zhèng Guāngyè
had a large and tall physique,
hence the remark.
From "Records of the Selected"
Táng Xiàhóu Jí studied chanting poetry,
traveled to Xīchuān,
and relied on a meritorious official to serve as an aide in his staff.
At that time, people called him Xiàhóu Lǘzi,
meaning he was vulgar.
"Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn was garrisoning Tàiyuán,
while Zhōu Tàizǔ served as the Hàn guard,
he had the young Emperor Yǐn oversee the seals and tallies,
and they often jested familiarly with each other.
Later, when they campaigned against Yèchéng together,
they attended day and night side by side.
One day, the young emperor said to Tàizǔ:
"Last night I dreamed you were a donkey,
carrying me up to heaven.
After I dismounted from you,
you suddenly turned into a dragon,
leaving me behind as you went south.
What omen is this?"
He replied:
"Your Highness means: 'The donkey,
with its humble form,
knows not to be toyed with in vain.'"
They clapped their hands and ended the conversation.
From the "Cèfǔ"
Lù Zhěn states that during the Tiānshèng era,
the Attendant-in-Chief Féng Zhěng passed away.
The following year,
a household near the Xīqìng Courtyard in the southern part of the capital gave birth to a donkey,
with white hair on its belly forming
the characters "Féng Zhěng"
in two words.
The Féng family ransomed it with gold,
secretly raising it indoors.
People from all directions knew about it.
"Bó Zhái Biān"
In Lǐngnán there was a post station,
named Cuìlán,
where many travelers would stable their horses in the main hall.
The station official tried to stop them but they would not listen,
so he wrote on the wall:
"Dogs and horses are not beasts for the hall,
Do not say the postal station is just a place you pass through.
Generally, humans and beasts must be distinguished;
If you won't heed the oriole's song, what can be done?"
The phrase "heed the oriole's song"
refers to an ancient story about a donkey
that ate peonies.
A poetic description says: Spreading its iron-hard double hooves,
it startled butterflies from their dreams;
Raising its boat-like pair of ears,
it would not heed the oriole's song.
The station official's words came from this.
"Mòkè Huīxī"
The reason for calling a donkey "wèi"
Now that donkeys are produced in Wèi territory,
does the meaning lie therein?
One theory suggests that because it has a saddle and a trough,
akin to the various guards having stomach and departments,
it is thus designated as "wèi."
《Zīxiá Jí》 Alternatively, it is said that because Jìn's Wèi Jiè enjoyed riding them,
they were named after him.
《Ěryǎ Yì》
Yì yǐ yà yà,
is the braying of a donkey,
usually occurring at noon and the beginning of the fifth watch.
There was a donkey immortal,
enjoying five hundred coins,
carrying loads without ceasing,
passing through without a fixed master,
traveling the great post roads under heaven.
"Fúzǐ"
In the country of Wūcháng, on Mount Tètán,
there is a temple in the mountains,
with a great many monks.
Every day, donkeys transport food,
with no one controlling or driving them.
They come of their own accord,
leave the food, and return,
but no one knows where they go.
From "Records of the Western Regions"
Sòng Yuán Shū's Collection of Humorous Writings: The Inscription on the Bestowal of Nine Honors to the Lord of Lúshān states.
At the beginning of the Kāichéng era,
a commoner in the East Market lost his father,
and rode a donkey to the market to buy funeral items.
After traveling about a hundred paces,
the donkey suddenly said:
"My surname is Bái, given name Yuántōng,
I have repaid my debt to your family enough,
do not ride me again.
The bran seller in the South Market owes me five thousand four hundred coins,
and I owe your family the same amount in cash,
so you may sell me now.
The man was astonished,
immediately led it away,
and quickly found a dealer to sell it.
The donkey was quite sturdy,
but the offered price was only five thousand coins.
He went to the bran shop,
where they paid exactly five thousand four hundred coins,
so he sold it there.
Two days later, the donkey died.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The Jìn monk Lǎng resided on Jīnyú Mountain.
After his death,
the donkey he used to ride went missing on the mountain.
There were people who saw it at the time,
and it had turned into a golden donkey.
Woodcutters would often hear its braying.
The locals said that whenever the golden donkey brayed once,
the world would be at peace.
End
The steed hangs its ears low, alas!
On the slope it stumbles and slows;
A lame donkey pulls the carriage, alas!
Its uselessness daily grows.
From "The Songs of Chǔ"
A mule is
the offspring of a male donkey and a female horse.
A hinny is
the offspring of a male horse and a female donkey.
According to Shuōwén,
when a donkey is the female
and a horse is the male,
they produce a mule.
When a horse is the female
and a donkey is the male,
they produce a hinny.
In Gǔjīn Zhù,
a hybrid is the offspring of a male donkey and a female cow.
Yùpiān records that in a county in Shǔ,
horses and cows mate and produce offspring,
always with the cow as the female and the horse as the male,
which is why mules are now produced in Chuān and Guǎng.
Those born in Guǎng
have light hooves;
those produced in Shǔ
have heavy hooves,
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ had two white mules,
which he cherished deeply.
Yángchéng Xūqú resided
in the palace at Guǎngmén.
One night, he knocked at the gate and requested an audience,
saying:
"Your servant Xū is ill,
and the physician instructed that obtaining the liver of a white mule
would cure the disease,
but without it, I shall die."
The gatekeeper entered to report this,
while Dǒng Ānyú attended by the ruler's side,
and angrily said:
"Ah!
It is Xūqú.
He seeks to deceive our lord—
I request that he be punished immediately."
Jiǎnzǐ replied:
"To kill a human to save an animal—
is that not inhumane?
To kill an animal to save a human—
is that not humane?"
Thereupon, he summoned the cook,
slaughtered a white mule to obtain its liver,
and gave it to Yángchéng Xūqú.
Not long after,
the army of Zhào mobilized to attack the Dí.
From the left of Guǎngmén, seven hundred men,
and from the right, seven hundred men,
all scaled the walls first and captured armored heads.
How can a ruler not cherish his people?
Lǚlǎn
In the fourth year of the Yuánfēng era,
the state of Xiūmí presented a dappled mule,
ten feet tall,
with reddish and patterned fur,
all resembling mountain colors,
swirling to form images of the sun and moon.
It was often fed with fodder in vessels made of gold and jade,
and kept in the imperial stable.
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"Among the lower ranks of the six domestic animals,
there is no need for deep affection.
In the past, Xiàhóu indulged in wild beasts,
and lost his state because of it.
Moreover, the Róng and Dí tribes present their vulgar beasts,
wasting wealth and damaging virtue,
which is not the way to set an example for the world.
King Chǔ Zhuāng loved horses,
and Shū'áo knew it was a failure in governance.
I hope Your Majesty will reflect on material things,
and preserve the critical affairs of the state.
The mule,
a vulgar beast,
should be placed in a burden-bearing role;
if not used, it should be abandoned in the wild.
The emperor then released it.
Later, a rustic saw a red snake descending from the sky to the ground,
with clouds and mist swirling around the earth.
As the clouds slowly dispersed,
it transformed into a red dragon,
and he rode it into the clouds.
Someone came to report this,
and the emperor said:
"That jester made me lose a dragon.
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"What is so hard to find about a dragon?
I fear that Your Majesty's expenditure on gold and jade will ultimately turn into donkeys and mules.
The emperor accepted his words but deeply resented him.
"Records of the Obscure"
The King of Qiūcí, Jiàng Bīn, paid homage to the Han court,
admiring the clothing and institutions of the Han,
and upon returning to his kingdom, built palaces following Han customs.
Foreigners from the Western Regions remarked:
"Neither donkey,
nor horse.
As for the King of Qiūcí,
he is what we call a mule.
Records of the Han Dynasty. Gāo Chāng's nature was difficult to subdue,
so a song was composed:
"Neither donkey,
nor horse.
Meaning Gāo Chāng resembled a mule.
The Emperor
General White Mule Emperor Míng Huáng was about to ascend Mount Tài to perform the fēngshàn ceremony.
Yìzhōu presented a white mule,
pure, bright, plump, and sleek,
extraordinary and majestic.
The emperor then personally rode it.
It was gentle, accustomed, comfortable, and convenient,
unaware of the toil of ascending and descending.
After the ceremony was completed,
he rode it back down.
Just as they reached the foot of the mountain,
the emperor had not rested for long
when the officials reported that the white mule had died without any illness.
The emperor sighed in amazement for a long time,
bestowing upon it the posthumous title
"General White Mule,"
and ordered the officials to prepare a coffin and build a stone tomb.
The tomb is located several miles north of the fēngshàn altar,
and it remains there to this day.
From "Records of Messages from the Kaiyuan and Tianbao Eras"
Wú Shǎochéng occupied Càizhōu.
Since the region had few horses,
he extensively raised mules instead,
training them for warfare while riding them,
calling them the "Mule Army."
They were especially renowned for their bravery and fierceness,
and their armor and weapons were all painted with thunder god and star patterns,
intended as talismans against evil.
According to the Old Book of Tang, when Wú Yuánjì rebelled,
one of his generals, named Dǒng Zhòngzhì,
guarded Huíqū.
His troops rode mules into battle,
and were called the "Mule Brigade."
They were the most formidable and fierce,
so government troops were always on high alert against them.
End.
Jìnshì Lǐ Zhān throughout his life widely sought unique flavors.
He would tie a mule in the courtyard,
surround it with fire,
and when the mule grew thirsty and drank,
he would cleanse its intestines with limewater,
then take wine mixed with various pungent flavors,
and make it drink again.
Before the mule had died, pressured by the fire,
its outer flesh was already cooked.
This method was passed down by Di Shènsī the junior remonstrance official,
but not long after, both died.
From "Yùquánzǐ"
In the first year of the Jìngkāng era,
the Jīn people attacked Xùnzhōu.
Emperor Huīzōng left Tōngjīn Gate in plain clothes,
boarding a small boat that was approaching Yōngqiū,
but the vessel ran aground and could not proceed.
At night, he went up the embankment,
riding a dappled mule
named Bógēqīng,
and fled toward Suīyáng.
"Huīchén Lù"
Qián Áng governed the commandery with a notable reputation,
and was praised for his ability and talent during the Chóngníng and Dàguàn eras.
He once commanded Qínzhōu as a military commissioner,
at a time when Tóng Guàn had just begun to enjoy imperial favor,
and was handling border affairs in Xīhé.
Relying on his favor, Tóng Guàn was arrogant and haughty,
and everyone vied to flatter him without respite,
yet only Qián Áng never showed him special respect.
Qián Áng was short in stature but vigorous and capable,
remaining energetic and sharp even in old age.
One day,
when he went to Tiānníng Temple for a Buddhist ceremony,
he waited for Tóng Guàn to arrive,
but it was a long time before he came.
Qián Áng said:
"Your Excellency, why have you come so late?"
Tóng Guàn replied:
"It so happened that the mule I rode,
being small and difficult to mount,
insisted on bucking and jumping.
Just as I was about to settle in the saddle,
it suddenly circled around the courtyard for a very long time,
which is why I was delayed."
Qián Áng asked:
"Your Excellency's mule,
is it male
or female?"
Tóng Guàn said:
"It is male."
Qián Áng remarked:
"If that's the case and it's so unruly,
why not have it castrated?"
Although Tóng Guàn felt shamed and angry at the moment,
he could not retaliate.
Later on,
when Tóng Guàn rose to great power,
he ultimately caused Qián Áng to be demoted and reprimanded.
A horse's strength is in its front shoulders,
a donkey's strength is in its thighs,
and a mule's strength is in its loins.
Riders adjust their pace according to these strengths.
The mule's hip has a clavicle,
which prevents it from reproducing.
Its larger bone,
resembles a mortar with a small opening.
The smaller bone resembles a pestle,
with a large head.
The small opening cannot accommodate the large head,
so it cannot come out.
This is why mules do not multiply.
"Ěryǎ Yì"
Of the three hundred sixty scaled creatures,
the dragon is their chief.
The "Elder Dai's Book of Rites" states: The dragon,
chief of the scaled creatures,
can be obscure or luminous,
can be small or large,
can be short or long.
At the spring equinox it ascends to heaven,
at the autumn equinox it enters the abyss.
The "Shuōwén" says:
The jiāolóng,
is a divine creature among water-dwelling beings.
When it rides upon water, its divinity is established;
when deprived of water, its power is lost.
Hence it is said: "When the jiāolóng obtains water, its divinity can be established."
From "Guanzi: Circumstances and Conditions"
The dragon, adorned with five colors, roams freely;
thus, when it wishes to be small, it transforms like a silkworm or caterpillar,
when it wishes to be large, it extends to the ends of the world,
when it wishes to ascend, it soars above the clouds,
when it wishes to descend, it enters the deep springs.
It changes without fixed days,
rises and falls without set times,
this is called divine.
"Guǎnzǐ: Shuǐ Dì"
Those with scales are called jiāolóng,
those with wings are called yìnglóng,
those with horns are called qiúlóng,
those without horns are called chīlóng.
According to the "Guǎngyǎ," a dragon that has not yet ascended to heaven is called a pánlóng.
The "Fāngyán" states that heaven has nine dragons,
and the yìnglóng has wings.
From "Xiàng Dài."

In the past, there was an old woman of the Wēn family,

She often lived by the stream,
catching fish to support her daily needs.
Suddenly, by the waterside, she encountered an egg,

After about ten days,

When it grew to about five feet,
it could already enter the water to catch fish,
yielding over ten fish a day.
As it grew to about two feet more,
the number of fish it caught gradually increased.
It often swam in the waves,
circling and lingering by the old woman's side.
Later, when the old woman was preparing fish,
she accidentally cut off its tail,
and it hesitantly left,
returning only after several years.
The old woman saw its radiant, gleaming colors

"Dragon child,

"This is a dragon child,

Today, when people make boats with a dragon's stub tail,
it originates from this.

forming this pool.
From "Shānchuān Jìyì" (Records of Extraordinary Mountains and Rivers).
Táo Kǎn often caught fish,
and once obtained a weaving shuttle,
which he hung on the wall.
After a short while,
during a thunderstorm,
the shuttle transformed into a red dragon,
leaping up from the house and flying away.
"Yì Yuàn"
Lǚ Guāng attacked Qiūcí,
stationing his army south of the city.
At night outside the camp, there was a black object,
as large as a broken dike,
swaying with a head and horns,
its gaze like lightning.
By dawn, clouds and mist surrounded it,
and it was no longer seen.
In the morning, looking at the spot,
it stretched five li from north to south,
and over thirty paces from east to west,
where the traces of scales and armor were imprinted on the ground,
clearly still visible.
Lǚ Guāng laughed and said:
"It is a black dragon."
Soon, clouds gathered from the northwest,
and a heavy rain erased its traces.
Dù Jìn said to Lǚ Guāng:
"The dragon,
a divine beast,
is an omen of a ruler's auspicious encounter.
The Yìjīng says: 'Seeing a dragon in the fields
means virtue spreads widely.'
This truly shows that you, General, embody spiritual harmony,
and your virtue aligns with both hidden and visible realms.
I urge you, General, to strive and achieve great fortune."
Lǚ Guāng's face showed delight.
From the Jìn Zǎijì.
In the fifth year of the Lóngjiǎo Yǒngmíng era,
a dragon horn was presented,
measuring nine chi and three cun in length,
red in color with patterns.
"History of the Southern Dynasties"
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's Empress Xī was extremely jealous.
Upon her death,
she transformed into a dragon,
entering the rear palace,
and communicated with the emperor through dreams.
Sometimes she appeared in a radiant form,
and when the emperor was about to fall ill,
the dragon would stir the water, causing it to surge and leap,
so a hall was built over the open well,
with piles of clothing,
and a silver pulley and golden vase were always placed there,
filled with a hundred flavors for sacrifices to her.
"History of the Southern Dynasties": Empress Xī was of a jealous nature.
When Emperor Wǔ first ascended the throne,
before she could be formally installed,
in a fit of anger,
she suddenly threw herself into the well in the palace courtyard.
The attendants rushed to the well to save her,
but the empress had already transformed into a venomous dragon,
with flames and smoke soaring to the sky,
and no one dared approach.
The emperor lamented for a long time,
then posthumously honored her as the Dragon Heavenly King,
and erected a shrine by the well.
"Records of the Two Capitals"
Wèi Cuī Tǐng, styled Shuānggēn,
served as the governor of Guāngzhōu.
Several miles northwest of the old city of Yè in the province lay Fǔ Mountain,
with towering peaks and ridges,
facing the vast sea to the north
and overlooking Dài Mountain to the south.
Tǐng intended to construct
a temple on its summit. The elders remarked:
"On this ridge,
torrential rains are frequent during autumn and summer.
Legend has it this is a dragon's path,
fearing this temple may not stand long."
Tǐng replied:
"How distant are humans and dragons?
Dragons appear and vanish swiftly—
could they be confined to a single path?"
Thus, he proceeded with the construction.
Over the following years,
there were indeed no unusual storms or rains.
After Tǐng was replaced,
the temple was destroyed by wind and rain,
and could no longer be rebuilt.
The people believed it was influenced by his virtuous governance.
From "The History of the Northern Dynasties"
In the third year of the Tiāntǒng era of Qí,
the Vice Director of the Mobile Department Lú Qián stationed troops in Wǎn.
At that time, dragons roared within the city,
which Lú Qián considered an ill omen.
He relocated the army outside,
and thus it was named Lóngmíng Chéng (Dragon Roar City).
"Records of the Universe"
In the second year of Emperor Liáng Yuándì's Chéngshèng era,
a dragon soared from the moat of Jiānglíng City,
radiant with five colors,
leaping majestically into the clouds.
Six or seven small dragons followed it in flight,
while schools of fish leaped up,
falling to their deaths on the land paths.
The place where the dragon had resided formed a cavern,
as large as several hundred hú containers.
From the "History of the Southern Dynasties".
In the third month of the second year of the Chéngshèng era,
two dragons emerged from the river west of the city,
soaring and leaping into the sky.
Their five colors were distinct,
reflecting distantly upon the river water.
All the common people looked up and watched them,
while some elders gathered and mourned,
secretly saying to one another:
"The earth dragon has departed;
will our state perish?"
From "The Biography of Wáng Sēngbiàn": The elders secretly wept together,
saying:
"In former years, dragons appeared at the Huái River in Jiànkāng,
and the world fell into great chaos.
Now they have appeared again;
disaster will be upon us any day now."
The emperor heard of this and was troubled by it.
Within a year, calamity befell him.
From "The Annals"
Lù Fǎhé refused to engage Rèn Yuē and proceeded to Ānnán,
entering Chìtíng Lake.
Lù Fǎhé rode in a light boat,
wearing no armor,
sailing down the river.
He approached within one lǐ of Rèn Yuē's army before turning back,
and said to his officers and soldiers:
"Their dragon lies asleep and motionless,
while the dragon of our army
is capable of leaping vigorously.
If we wait until tomorrow to attack them,
we should defeat the enemy without losing any of our own troops."
From "Records of the Three Kingdoms"
As the Sui army crossed the river,
Lǚ Sù of Jīngzhōu fled to defend after his defeat.
Biéshuài Liào Shìlóng of Yánzhōu,
commanding a large vessel, feigned surrender,
intending to burn the Sui fleet,
and then fight a decisive battle to the death.
At that moment, five yellow dragons and multicolored elephants,
each over ten zhàng long,
raised their heads in succession,
flowing eastward with the current,
as fierce winds and waves arose,
with clouds and mist darkening the sky,
striking terror into the Chén troops,
who unknowingly set themselves ablaze.
The Sui forces, aboard tall warships,
unleashed large crossbows against them.
The Chén army suffered a major defeat,
and the wind and waves immediately ceased.
Thus, Emperor Wén of Sui issued an edict,
to announce it at the suburban altar and ancestral temple.
from The Book of Chén
During the Zhēnguàn era,
Fénzhōu reported sightings of azure and white dragons.
The white dragon spewed an object into the air,
glowing like fire,
which sank two chǐ into the ground upon landing.
Excavation revealed it to be dark gold,
with a round and oblique shape,
over a chǐ in width,
and six to seven cùn in height.
From the Old Book of Táng.
Jìn Wú Cāngyīng donated his residence to establish a temple,
and personally traveled to Yángjùn to acquire scriptures and statues.
While crossing the great river,
the boat suddenly tilted dangerously.
Suddenly, a pair of bones appeared,
each measuring ten feet long,
floating and surging with the waves,
and swiftly entered the boat.
Immediately, the river calmed,
and upon reaching shore, he reported the matter to the authorities.
Officials examined the bones,
and they turned out to be dragon teeth.
From "Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks: Biography of Sēng Míng"
Dào Zhuó of the temple in Luò County, Yìzhōu, built a wooden pagoda,
which was protected by a dragon,
residing in a well at the southwest corner,
where signs would occasionally appear.
Beside it were three ponds,
inhabited by three dragons.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
the three dragons fought fiercely,
with thunderclaps striking,
water and fire flying alternately,
and after a long time, it calmed down,
the pagoda remaining as before.
People all picked up dragon hairs,
about three chǐ long,
yellowish-red and lovely.
"Fǎyuàn": During the Zhōu dynasty,
a monk named Cè at Língguǒ Temple in Tóngzhōu,
following Yá's nirvana,
held an alms-giving in the market,
and just before the meal,
suddenly saw black clouds coming from the east,
obscuring the sun and casting shade,
then it rained dragons,
their hairs distinctly five-colored,
the longest being five,
the shortest still five cùn.
"Shàng Sēng Yá Xià"
Seafarers say that dragons always lay two eggs,
one of which is the jídiào.
They often emerge from the water at Lùtái,
or are left as drippings by the water's edge.
When encountering drifting wood, they adhere to branches,
resembling the shape of cattail hammers,
their color slightly bluish-yellow,
or similar to gray,
and are called zǐshāohuā.
They enhance male vitality,
and can be used in medicine.
"Běi Mèng"
In Yīnpíng County there is dragon blood,
and the mountain is also called Lóngxiàng Cliff,
with sheer cliffs and towering crags
over ten thousand zhàng high.
There are four stone dragons
within the stone cliff.
In the past, a group of dragons fought together;
four dragons became exhausted and wounded,
vomited blood and died,
then transformed into stone.
Their blood turned into black jade,
suitable for making utensils,
but it cannot withstand wind and sunlight.
"Yuánhé Annals"
During the Later Jìn Dynasty, in Zhènzhōu bordering on Xíngtái,
a dragon was once killed in a fight.
A local magnate named Cáo Kuān,
witnessed it,
took its pair of horns,
and in front of the horns there was an object,
blue in color,
with a pattern resembling tangled brocade,
which no one could identify.
Cáo Kuān was killed by bandits a year later,
and the military governor of Zhènzhōu was also executed.
From "Běi Mèng"
During the Kāiyuán era,
Qí Huàn, considering Xúchéng's terrain perilous and urgent,
petitioned to excavate the Hé River.
Cuī Yánhuī, the Deputy Magistrate of Zhēnyuán County, dug several thousand paces
and discovered a dragon hall.
At the start of the excavation,
they thought it was an ancient tomb,
but its appearance was as if newly built, clean and pure.
Looking around the northern wall,
they found a five-colored dormant dragon below,
over ten feet long,
with five or six carp beside its head,
two spirit turtles,
and fur nine inches long.
(Guǎng Yì Jì)
In the country of Jùmíng, a merchant was herding eight cows to graze in the marsh.
At that time, a Liccha caught a dragon,
intending to eat it.
The merchant exchanged his eight cows for it,
released it into another pond.
Suddenly, the dragon spoke in human language,
inviting him into its palace,
where there was a dragon maiden.
She gave him eight gold ingots,
saying:
"This is dragon gold,
cut it and it regrows,
sufficient for your parents and relatives,
lifelong use without exhaustion.
From the "Fǎyuàn"
In the eighteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
thunder struck in Wènshuǐ County,
and a stone fell from the clouds,
as large as a mortar pestle,
with a high ridge and a flat belly.
County Magistrate Zhāng Xiàojìng reported this to the emperor.
At that time, an elder monk from the Magadha Bodhi Temple in the Western Regions arrived in the Western Capital,
renowned for his extensive knowledge.
By imperial decree, he was consulted,
and he explained that it was a dragon's food, fallen due to a struggle between two dragons.
Thus, it had fallen.
The emperor
The wife of Liú Jìng, the magistrate of Shǔ County, fell ill.
Míng Chóngyǎn, the Grand Master for Proper Consultation, diagnosed her,
saying:
"You must obtain a live dragon's liver;
eating it will surely cure her."
Liú Jìng believed it impossible,
but Míng Chóngyǎn then wrote a talisman, rode the wind, and released it to the heavens.
In a moment,
a dragon descended,
entered the water in a jar,
and had its liver excised.
After eating it, she recovered.
From "Qiān Zǎi." During the Spring and Autumn period,
Marquis Zhōu, governing Huá, had been ill for a long time.
He told the physician:
"Only by obtaining a dragon's liver for treatment can I recover;
without this, it cannot be cured."
Marquis Zhōu inquired of his attendants,
who scolded him, saying:
"A dragon coils in the moat of the city;
each year during droughts, prayers to it are answered.
Slaughter it and take its liver—
it can be done."
The Marquis ordered it to be taken.
That day,
frightening thunder and fierce winds arose,
and the transformed dragon went away from the south,
crashing through a breach in the city wall.
To this day, whenever the breach is repaired,
it breaks again as before.
From "Tú Jīng."
Zhāng Lùsī
was a native of Yǐngshàng.
He passed the imperial examination in the classical canon during the early Suí dynasty,
and during the Jǐnglóng era,
he served as the magistrate of Xuānchéng.
His wife, Shí shì, was from Guānzhōu,
and they had nine sons.
After leaving his post in Xuānchéng and returning home,
he often fished in the shade of the Jiāo shì platform.
One day,
he noticed that at his fishing spot, there were palaces and towers,
so he entered and lived there.
From then on,
he would go out at night and return at dawn,
and upon returning, his body was always cold and wet.
His wife, alarmed, asked him about it,
and he replied:
"I am a dragon.
Liǎo rén Zhèng Yǎngyuǎn,
is also a dragon.
He rides a white ox and occupies my pond,
calling it the Zhèng Gōng Pond.
I have fought him many times but have not yet won.
Tomorrow, when I go to battle,
you can have our nine sons assist me.
The one wearing crimson silk
is me;
the one wearing blue silk
is Zhèng."
The next day,
the nine sons shot arrows at the one in blue silk,
hitting him, and he left in anger.
Zhāng Lùsī pursued him,
and wherever they passed, valleys were formed,
reaching all the way to the Huái River.
The one in blue silk plunged into the western mountains of Héféi and died,
becoming Lóngrǒng Mountain.
The nine sons all transformed into dragons.
Zhāng Lùsī's elder brother served as the commissioner of cavalry and infantry,
and his descendants scattered and settled in Yǐngshān,
where their tombs remain to this day.
From Zhào Gēng's "Stele of Lord Lóng."
During the Kāiyuán era,
Master Yè Tiānshī was expounding scriptures in Fènghuà County of Míngzhōu,
when suddenly an old man appeared claiming to be the guardian dragon of the treasure vault,
who had guarded it for a thousand years,
just managing to avoid the punishment of fiery sands.
Now a foreign monk was chanting spells over the water,
attempting to seize the treasure that governs heaven and subdues the seas.
Master Tiānshī saved him with a talisman,
calming the waves and stilling the winds.
The old man wept in gratitude.
The immortal master commanded a clear spring to be brought forth,
which then formed a stone channel,
that never dried up even in winter.
To this day it is called Master Tiānshī's Channel.
"Records of the Mysterious and Strange" "Collected Biographies of Immortals"
Northwest of Beiting in Shazhou there was a Black River,
where a giant dragon caused calamity,
and the people suffered greatly from it.
All officials assigned to this land
would first prepare sacrificial animals and wine to offer by the riverbank,
and only then dare to administer governance.
During the Kaiyuan era,
Zhāng Sōng from Nányáng served as Protector-General,
and he immediately ordered a sacrifice to be made,
while secretly commanding his attendants to prepare bows and arrows and wait by his side.
Soon a giant dragon, a hundred feet long,
leapt out from the waves,
lowered its head onto the mat,
and stretched out its tongue, which was several feet long,
intending to eat.
Before it could,
it was killed by arrows.
At that moment,
its right side quickly collapsed onto the ground,
with a sound like a mountain crumbling.
After the dragon died,
onlookers gathered as if at a market.
Zhāng Sōng ordered its belly cut open and prepared a memorial to present to the emperor.
The emperor admired his decisiveness and courage,
and issued an edict to place its tongue in a box and bestow it upon Zhāng Sōng,
furthermore issuing a commendatory decree to reward him,
thus granting him the honorary name "Zhāng of the Dragon's Tongue."
(From "Accounts from the Xuan Shi")
Grand Marshal Fáng Guǎn once pursued his studies in a valley of the Zhōngnán Mountains.
Suddenly, he heard a sound resembling the resonance of striking bronze,
which he had never heard before.
He inquired of the elderly,
who said it was the chant of a dragon,
and that rain would soon arrive.
Guǎn looked up at the sky,
where clouds slowly billowed and spread,
and indeed, a sudden downpour began.
From then on,
he heard it again, and the omen proved accurate without fail.
Later, he struck a red gold alms bowl to mimic the dragon's chant.
From "Collection of Supernatural Tales"
During the Tiānbǎo era,
the young dragon of Xīngqìng Pond once ventured out into the palace's southern moat,
its sinuous and wondrous form
seen by all.
When the imperial carriage journeyed westward,
the dragon rode the clouds and rain one night,
departing from the pond toward the southwest.
Upon reaching the Jiālíng River,
as the emperor was about to board a boat,
a dragon flanked the vessel, advancing alongside it.
The emperor shed tears,
turning to his attendants to say:
"This is the dragon from my pond."
He ordered wine to be poured as a libation,
whereupon the dragon shook its scales and departed.
From "Old Accounts of the Liǔ Family"
Táng Yángchéng was appointed as the governor of Dàozhōu.
Upon reaching Xiāngyáng,
five elderly men came to greet him,
claiming to be from Chōnglíng.
Yángchéng gave them silk fabric,
and inquired about their residence.
They replied:
"Five miles northwest of the city.
When he arrived, he searched for them,
but found only the Five Dragon Well,
with the silk fabric still there.
Consequently, he erected a temple for them,
which occurred in the nineteenth year of the Zhēnyuán era.
From "Yàn Shū's Classified Essentials"
In Mount Máo's dragon pool,
the dragons resemble lizards,
yet radiate five colors naturally.
In the past, Yán Fèng during the Zhēnguàn era was ordered to fetch a dragon offspring for observation,
and the emperor composed a song for its return.
Taoist followers vied in marveling at its divinity.
Lǐ Déyù, fearing it would delude the world,
once captured and dried it into jerky.
The dragon ultimately proved incapable of divinity.
From "Casual Talks under the Military Tent"
When Niú Sēngrú governed Xiāngzhōu,
there was a prolonged drought,
and prayers brought no response.
A recluse who claimed to be a dragon keeper
was asked by the lord to bring rain.
The recluse said:
"There are no dragons in the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
only a black dragon in a certain deep pool.
If forced to drive it out,
I fear it may cause disaster,
and be hard to control."
The lord insisted on his request,
and indeed heavy rain fell,
causing the Hàn River to flood,
drowning ten thousand households.
The recluse, fearing punishment, secretly fled.
"Yùquánzǐ"
The monk Sēngqié was resting at leisure when
he saw a deity announce to him:
"Heaven is excessively scorching,
the people's crops are dying.
Why are you hiding your lazy dragon?"
He replied:
"What can be done about it?"
The deity said:
"Tonight,
just put your little finger outside the window crack,
what could happen to a person?"
Sēngqié followed this instruction.
That night, thunder struck unusually fiercely,
at dawn he examined his finger,
and found a faint red vein-like mark on it.
From "Biographies of Eminent Monists" (The incident of Xuānlǜshī of Nánshān riding a dragon into his middle finger joint is similar.
At the end of the Xiántōng era,
Kǒng Wēi, the prefect of Shū Prefecture, presented a dragon skeleton.
A memorial was submitted recording the event,
stating: Hú Jǔ, a commoner from Shànzhèng Village in Tóngchéng County of the prefecture, witnessed a blue dragon fighting to death in his courtyard.
It was the fourth month,
with silkworm trays still in the yard.
Suddenly, storm clouds arose violently,
and the sound of clashing was heard in the clouds.
Blood fell like heavy rain, sprinkling on the silkworm trays.
The blood did not stain the trays
but gradually gathered and coagulated,
so that it could be picked up and held in the palm.
In a moment,
it caused a chilling pain that penetrated to the bone.
Initially,
the dragon dragged its tail along the ground,
coiled around a slop bucket,
then soared into the clouds.
When the rain came,
it was entirely slop.
After the dragon died,
it was dissected,
revealing a large sore in its throat.
The dragon measured over ten feet in total length,
with its body and tail being equal in length.
The base of the tail was flat and thin,
its scales and mane were like those of a fish,
but it had whiskers two zhang long.
Its feet were covered by a red membrane,
and its pair of horns were each two zhang long.
Its belly showed signs of self-conflict or misalignment.
At the time, the Grand Cloud Granary Commissioner was dispatched to supervise and transport it to the prefecture.
Because the flesh was too heavy to move whole,
it was cut into several tens of segments
and carted to the authorities.
"Supplemental Records of the Táng Era"
South of Hǎizhōu there was a canal,
which connected to Huáichǔ upstream,
serving as a route for both official and private water transport.
During the Bǎoyìng era of the Táng dynasty,
the dam broke and the water dried up,
halting the passage of fishermen and merchants.
The prefecture appointed Lǐ Zhīyuǎn, magistrate of Dōnghǎi, to oversee the repair work.
Each time the dam was nearly completed, it would collapse again,
and this happened repeatedly.
The expenses incurred were considerable,
causing Zhīyuǎn great concern.
Someone suggested that when Emperor Wǔ of Liáng built the Fúshān Dam,
it frequently suffered breaches and damage,
so they filled the base with tens of thousands of catties of iron,
and only then was the dam completed.
Upon hearing this,
Zhīyuǎn followed the advice and plugged the gaps with iron.
Initially,
when the dam was about to fail,
a rumbling like thunder was often heard from below,
but after this, the sound shifted several miles upstream.
This is because metal and iron have a pungent quality,
and pungency can harm the eyes.
The flood dragons, protecting their eyes,
avoided it and moved away,
thus allowing the dam to be completed.
During the Dàlì era,
Chéng Hào, a vice director of the Ministry of Justice, had a home in Xiàngzhōu,
with a small pond in front of the residence.
Someone forging a sword
quenched it in the pond,
causing all the snakes and fish to die.
At Yǎn's family home, there were several dozen fish in the well.
Due to an urgent matter,
a family member threw a medicine pestle into the well.
After two nights,
all the fish floated to the surface,
revealing that fish also fear iron.
From "Féngshì Jiànwén"
South of the great river,
among the reeds and rushes,
sleeping dragons were often burned.
At the end of the Later Liáng dynasty,
a commoner named Xiàng Shì from Chénzhōu accidentally burned a dragon.
From all sides came wind and thunder,
yet heavy rain could not extinguish the flames.
Soon it was reduced to ashes,
but its horns remained unconsumed,
gleaming white like jade.
Xiàng Shì treasured them and kept them hidden.
Gāo Yù, a military commander in Húnán, offered a high price and forcibly took them.
At that time, a mystic said:
"Commander Gāo is inviting disaster!
Why use an ominous object to hasten it?"
Soon after, he was executed.
(From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán")
During the reign of Zhuāngzōng,
a monk from Wǔtái Mountain named Chéng Huì called himself the Dragon-Subduing Master.
The emperor held him in high esteem,
often kneeling to show respect,
while princes and consorts all bowed to him,
yet Chéng Huì remained seated arrogantly to receive their homage.
Earlier,
when he visited the emperor from Táishān,
Wáng Róng of Zhènzhōu did not show him courtesy.
Chéng Huì grew furious,
saying:
"I command five hundred venomous dragons;
if I order one to lift a stone slab,
will the province not become a marsh?"
A year later,
the Hū River flooded massively,
destroying Zhènzhōu's outer walls.
Those who heard his words
increasingly regarded him as divine.
Hence, the emperor revered him even more devoutly.
The History of the Later Hàn records: Zhènzhōu suffered a great flood,
which ruined its southern city.
Chéng Huì remarked:
"They lacked faith,
so I sent a small dragon to warn them."
He claimed this was due to his ability to command venomous dragons.
At the beginning of the Tóngguāng era, when he arrived at the court,
powerful nobles all bowed to him,
but Guō Chóngtāo, knowing his true nature,
refused to bow throughout.
When the capital faced a drought,
he was invited to Luòyáng to pray for rain,
yet for dozens of days, there was no sign of response.
Upon hearing threats of being burned,
he fled in fear,
returning to his temple where he died of shame and anger.
A stupa was erected for him,
titled "Master Fǎyǔ"
—how absurd!
The Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán notes: Below the North Peak of Wǔtái Mountain lies the Green Dragon Pool,
covering about two acres,
said in Buddhist scriptures to be where five hundred venomous dragons are confined.
At high noon each day,
when the dense fog briefly clears,
only bhikkhus and pious laymen may glimpse it.
If bhikkhunīs or women approach,
thunder, lightning, wind, and rain
immediately erupt violently;
should anyone get close to the pool,
they are inevitably drawn in by the toxic miasma,
and swiftly vanish.
According to traditional accounts.
During the Tóngguāng era,
a commoner's son from Cāngzhōu encountered a white snake on the road,
bound it with a rope,
and swung it until its head fell off.
Shortly after,
a thunderbolt lifted this youth into the air,
where he was burned to death by lightning fire.
When he fell to the ground, vermilion writing was found on his back, stating:
"This person killed Ān Tiānlóng,
and has now been executed by celestial mandate.
From "Běi Mèng"
When Qián Liú of Wúyuè was young in the army, he never slept.
In his later years,
when slightly tired,
he would carve a wooden pillow
to alert himself,
or order his grandsons to recite poetry until dawn.
During the Tiānfú era of the Jìn dynasty,
when the Khitan envoys arrived at the court,
Lǐ Yǒng, a close attendant, was appointed as the supervising escort.
A Khitan deputy envoy,
from Yōujì,
said to Yǒng:
"Has Wúyuè ever not slept?
Yǒng asked the reason,
to which he replied:
"I once heard Prince Master of Wǔtái Shān speak of the sleepless dragon in Zhèzhōng,
who has now returned.
Upon inquiring further,
it was after the Rénchén year of Chángxīng.
From "Jiǔguó Zhì"
Liú Dòngwēi excelled at painting dragons.
One day,
a couple came to his door to view his paintings,
and remarked:
"Dragons have male and female,
their appearances differ.
The male,
has horns with rugged ridges and steep hollows,
deep-set eyes and flaring nostrils,
pointed manes and dense scales,
broad above and tapered below,
with blazing crimson flames;
the female,
has smooth horns and gentle ridges,
wide eyes and straight noses,
rounded manes and thin scales,
with tails stouter than their abdomens.
Liú felt unsettled by this,
and questioned them,
to which the person replied:
"We ourselves are dragons,
please observe us.
Thereupon they transformed into a pair of dragons and departed.
"Records of Extraordinary Events" Liáng Shí Fǎcōng accompanied Prince Jìn'ān to White Horse Spring,
where a white turtle came to Cōng's hand to take food,
and he told the Prince:
"This is a male dragon.
Later at Lingquan Spring,
a multicolored crucian carp also came to his hand to eat,
Cōng said:
"This is a female dragon.
The Prince and his ministers bestowed rich rewards before returning.
"Dharma Garden"
Héjīn is also known as Lóngmén,
where the traces of the giant spirit remain, with water cascading down.
Note: There is a mountain beside it,
blocking both land and water routes,
so creatures like turtles and fish
cannot ascend.
Large fish from rivers and seas
gather below the gate,
thousands unable to climb.
Those that ascend become dragons,
while those that fail remain fish.
Hence the saying, "Exposing gills at Lóngmén,
hanging ears under the cart shaft."
From the "Records of the Three Qín": Below Lóngmén,
each year in late spring,
two yellow carp,
from the sea and various rivers, compete to come here.
In one year, those that scale Lóngmén
number no more than seventy-two.
Upon first ascending Lóngmén,
wind and rain arise,
followed by celestial fire burning their tails,
and they transform into dragons.
From Lín Dēng's "Records of Broad Knowledge": Sturgeon emerge from the Gǒng Cave in March,
then ascend to cross Lóngmén,
succeeding in becoming dragons.
Otherwise, they return with scarred foreheads.
If not for the cycle of coming and going,
how could such a name exist?
From the "Commentary on the Waterways Classic": In Fēngxī County of Jiāozhǐ, there is a dike guarding Lóngmén,
where the water is a hundred fathoms deep.
Large fish that climb this gate
transform into dragons;
those that fail to pass
expose their gills and scar their foreheads,
bleeding.
This water often appears crimson.
The pool has Tàiqián River emerging with foam,
the mountain divides into ninety-nine streams,
converging into one mouth over three hundred lǐ.
From the "Records of Jiāozhōu": Observing Lóngmén,
one fish, flapping scales and bristling fins, ascends Lóngmén to become a dragon.
Yet another mystic,
treading waves without sinking,
shakes a bell, sings, and drifts upon Lóngmén's currents,
lingering all day without transforming.
They share the same endeavor but achieve different outcomes,
their paths alike yet principles distinct.
Why is this? Is it not because the fish responds with sincerity,
while the human seeks with falseness?
From "Fúzǐ".
According to old accounts, during the spring flood season,
when fish leap at the Dragon Gate,
some transform into dragons.
To this day, in the mountain caves of Fénjìn,
dragon molted bones and horns are abundant,
collected for medicinal use,
some being of five colors.
"Supplement to the National History": The land of Wǔchéng County in Shǔ corresponds to the Heavenly Gate.
The Heavenly Gate
is where dragons fail to ascend to heaven,
fall dead to this place,
hence dragon bones are excavated,
unceasingly in winter and summer.
"Records of Huáyáng": "Records of Omissions" states: East of Fāngzhàng Mountain lies a dragon ground,
covering a thousand li in area,
where dragon skins and bones pile up like hills,
scattered over more than a hundred qǐng.
"Records of the Strange": Pǔníng County has a Dragon Burial Isle,
where elders say dragons molt their bones in the waters north of the isle.
Dragon bones remain plentiful there today.
Note that mountains, hills, and ridges capable of producing clouds and rain
all contain dragon bones,
some deep, some shallow,
mostly within the soil.
Teeth, horns, spines, and feet
are all distinctly present.
Large ones measure tens of zhàng,
or fill ten zhàng;
small ones are merely one or two chǐ,
or three to four cùn,
with complete bodies.
They have been seen during collection.
Recently, a household in Púzhōu dismantling a thatched roof
found dragon bones on the ridgepole,
about one chǐ long,
fully formed.
"Classic of Resonance"
Zhāng Zé,
residing in the eastern part of Yùnzhōu,
found a dragon's slough among tree branches,
only as large as a newly emerged cicada's shell,
complete with head, claws, horns, and tail,
hollow inside yet firm.
When tapped,
it produced a sound like jade,
not only lustrous and covered with eyes,
but also glowing brightly in the room when it encountered darkness,
so he secretly kept it at home,
and it became a celebrated curiosity.
Another person, Shěn Me,
served as an assistant official in Qīngzhōu during the Shàojīn period,
and found a dragon's slough on a grape trellis in his courtyard,
fully intact but without any glow.
"Chūnzhǔ Jìwén"
The nature of the dragon is crude and fierce,
yet it fears beeswax,
loves jade and azurite, and is fond of roasted swallow meat.
Therefore, people who have eaten swallow meat
must not cross the sea.
"Southern New Book"
Ānqīshēng often rode a dragon to pay homage at the Jade Capital,
hence he was called the Jade Capital Child.
"Records of Marvels"
In ancient times, there were the Dragon Tamer Clan,
and in Cháng'ān, there were households that raised dragons.
By observing the water, they could discern the presence or absence of dragons' colors and eyes,
knowing it all completely.
During the reign of Emperor Yì,
the Dragon Tamer Clan reported that two dragons had escaped from the dragon pond.
They searched for several tens of days toward Guāndōng,
and spotted them in the Wèiwáng Pond of the Eastern Capital,
capturing and returning them to the capital.
While passing through Huàzhōu,
Lǐ Nè was the prefect of Huàzhōu.
Nè's father was named Lǐ Jiànbiāo,
who was a close friend of Bái Jūyì.
Nè was an upright and honest man,
and upon hearing that dragons had been obtained,
he considered it utterly absurd,
ordering them to be brought to the government office for inspection.
There, they were poured from a small bottle into a basin,
revealing two fine loach fish.
Nè glared angrily,
saying:
"What proof is there?"
The person replied:
"Proof is not difficult;
please dig a hole about a foot deep,
and pour water into it."
They collected the loaches and tossed them into the water.
The fish fell into the water,
chasing each other in circles,
their tails touching the four corners of the hole,
and with each touch, the hole sank deeper,
while the water also surged violently.
In a short while, the hole had widened to several feet.
The person consulted Nè, saying:
"I fear if the hole expands further,
it will be hard to control."
So, they grasped and put them back into the bottle.
Only then did Nè find it marvelous,
generously gifting them money and silk,
and they carried them back to the capital.
"Tales from the Central Court"
Western sorcerers who could perform divine incantations
would pace like Yǔ at the water's edge and blow breath,
whereupon dragons would emerge afloat.
When first emerging, they measured over ten zhàng in length.
Thereupon the sorcerer would blow again;
with each blow the dragon would shrink accordingly,
until only a few cùn long,
the sorcerer would pick it up and place it in a pot.
Sometimes there were four or five dragons,
kept alive with a little water,
the mouth of the pot sealed.
When these sorcerers heard of places suffering drought,
they would take the dragons there to sell them,
one dragon being worth dozens of jīn of gold.
The entire region would pool resources to pay the price in full.
Then the sorcerer would open the pot and release a dragon,
placing it into a deep pool.
Again pacing like Yǔ and blowing upon it,
each blow caused it to emerge and grow,
reaching several tens of zhàng in length,
and in moments clouds and rain gathered all around.
"Bàopǔzǐ"
At the Mǐcāng Píhēluó Temple, there was a divine dragon
residing in the rice granary.
When servants came to take rice,
the dragon would retreat backward.
If the servants took too much rice,
the dragon would not give it.
When the rice in the granary was about to run out,
the servants would bow to the dragon,
and the granary would immediately overflow.
"Accounts of Foreign Lands"
Dragon fire blazes upon encountering water,
while human fire is extinguished by it.
From the Buddhist Canon
In the country of Bōzhī there are three pools.
Tradition says the largest pool has a dragon king,
the next one a dragon wife,
and the smallest one a dragon child.
Travelers must make offerings before they can pass,
otherwise they often encounter wind and snow.
Book of Later Wèi
In Buyeo County, Cháoxiǎn, at the foot of Fúsū Mountain, there was a strange rock,
spanning across the river islet,
on which were marks of a dragon's claws.
Legend has it that during the Táng Gāozōng era,
Sū Dìngfāng set out to conquer Bǎijì,
and as he approached the river intending to cross,
suddenly a great storm arose.
Using a white horse as bait,
he hooked a dragon.
Soon, the river calmed and became passable,
allowing his army to cross and conquer it.
Hence, the river was named White Horse Rock,
and the place was called Dragon Fishing Terrace.
From "Cháoxiǎn Zhì".
In the west of the Western Wūchǎng Kingdom, there is a pond
where the Dragon King resides.
Beside the pond stands a temple
with over fifty monks.
Whenever the Dragon King performed divine transformations,
the king of the country would pray and request,
casting gold, jade, and treasures into the pond.
Later, they would surge forth,
allowing the monks to retrieve them for the temple's clothing and food,
relying on the dragon to aid the world,
and people named it the Dragon King Temple.
"Records of Monasteries"
The eyes of the Lílóng can see tiny objects from a hundred miles away.
The dragon can transform water,
humans can transform fire;
the dragon cannot see stone,
humans cannot see wind.
Fish cannot see water,
ghosts cannot see the earth,
sheep cannot see rain,
dogs cannot see snow.
"On the Natural Changes of Yīn and Yáng"
The hidden spirits await auspicious clouds to soar aloft,
The roosting birds rely on fierce winds to ascend the void.
The "Rectifying Errors" chapter states: The roosting birds of the Mystic Garden,
The hidden spirits of the Nine Abysses.
The "Master Who Embraces Simplicity"
Nàqié,
Qín yún lóng.
Nàqié cháng zài dìng,
wú yǒu bù dìng shí.
《Fānyì》
In Chéngdū's Zhuólóng Pond,
Suí Shǔ King Xiù excavated earth to build the Guangzi City,
thus forming the pond.
A foreign monk saw it
and said:
"Mahā Kumbhīra."
For the foreign monk called "mahā" great palace,
"kumbhīra" dragon,
meaning this pond was vast and had a dragon.
The "County Records" translated it as
"Palace Kumbhīra Dragon"
On the mountain of Wǔhuāshù Lóngchí,
the four sides are high,
and in the center there is a pool,
seven hundred li square,
where groups of dragons dwell.
There are many five-flower trees,
which the groups of dragons eat.
It is forty-five thousand li from Kuàijī.
"Kuàdìtú"
During the Qiánfú era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a monk who devoted himself daily to chanting scriptures.
While traveling down the gorge,
he moored his boat at Báidì City.
Late at night during his chanting,
he suddenly detected a foul, fishy odor,
and saw a figure on the water surface
gradually approaching the boat.
The monk asked who it was,
and the figure replied:
"I am not human;
my surname is Xǔ, given name Dàokūn.
In the early Táng dynasty, I served as governor of Kuízhōu,
but due to greed, cruelty, and tyranny, I died
and received karmic retribution as the Yànyù Duī Dragon King for three thousand years.
It has now been two thousand and forty years.
Just now I heard your reverend chanting,
so I came to express my gratitude."
The monk said:
"The gorge route is perilous,
with frequent capsizings and drownings.
Could you command the dragons to restrain themselves?"
The figure answered:
"These creatures are truly numerous,
all acting through karmic retribution—
it cannot be restrained by ordinary power."
As the monk prepared to ask further,
the figure suddenly vanished.
From "Records of Karmic Retribution"
Jiāo,
belongs to the dragon category.
Those without horns are called jiāo,
when the pond fish reach three thousand six hundred,
the jiāo comes to lead them.
It can lead the fish in flight,
but placing a fish trap in the water makes the jiāo leave.
"Shuōwén"
The jiāo resembles a snake,
with four legs and a slender neck,
its neck has a white bulge, the larger ones,
measuring several arm spans around,
are oviparous,
their eggs like one or two hú jars,
able to swallow people.
—Guō Pú
A huǐ transforms into a jiāo after five hundred years,
a jiāo transforms into a lóng after a thousand years,
a lóng becomes a horned lóng after five hundred years,
and after another five hundred years, it becomes a yìnglóng.
Pythons have round eyes,
while jiāo have connected eyebrows.
"Shù Yì Jì"
At the end of Jié of Xià's reign,
a woman in the palace transformed into a dragon,
which could not be approached.
Shortly after,
she turned back into a woman,
extremely beautiful but cannibalistic.
Jié appointed her as his concubine Jiāo,
who informed Jié of auspicious and ominous matters.
"Shù Yì Jì"
When Dàntái Zǐyū was crossing the river carrying a jade worth a thousand gold pieces,
the River God desired it,
so the waves of Yánghóu rose up,
and two flood dragons flanked the boat.
Zǐyū held the jade in his left hand,
and with his right hand wielded his sword to strike the flood dragons,
killing them both.
After crossing the river,
he threw the jade into the river three times,
but the River God made it leap back to him three times.
So Zǐyū destroyed the jade and left.
"Records of Diverse Matters"
There was a man named Cì Fēi from the state of Jīng,
who obtained a precious sword at Gānsuì.
On his return, while crossing the river,
he reached the middle of the stream,
where the waves of the river god Yáng Hóu
caused two flood dragons to encircle his boat.
Cì Fēi declared with indignation:
"These are but rotten flesh and decaying bones in the river.
If I must abandon the sword,
why should I cherish it?"
He drew his sword and plunged into the river to stab the dragons,
killing them.
The king of Jīng heard of this
and appointed him to the office of Zhí Guī.
From "The Annals of Lǚ."
In the Eastern Sea there was a warrior named Zīqiū Xīn,
renowned throughout the world for his valor.
He came upon a divine abyss and said:
"Water the horse.
His servant said:
"If you water the horse here,
the horse will surely die.
He said:
"Water it with Xīn's command.
His horse indeed sank.
Zīqiū Xīn removed his court robes,
drew his sword and entered,
for three days and three nights,
killing three jiao and one dragon before emerging.
The thunder god pursued and struck him for ten days and ten nights,
blinding his left eye.
"Han's Outer Traditions"
In the fifth year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Hàn Wǔdì,
he personally shot a flood dragon in the river while sailing from Xúnyáng,
and captured it.
When the Hùzǐ River breached its banks,
a dragon accompanied by nine offspring
emerged from the breach and swam upstream into the Yellow River.
Its churning wake created surging waves
that extended for dozens of miles.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Emperor Zhāo of Hàn often roamed the Wèi River,
having his ministers fish for amusement.
At that time, there was a senior official named Rén Xù
who caught a white flood dragon,
three zhǎng in length,
resembling a large snake,
without scales or armor,
with a single horn on its head,
two chǐ long,
and fangs protruding beyond its lips.
The Emperor said:
"This is akin to a loach fish,
not a rare auspicious sign.
He then ordered the imperial chef to prepare it as zhǎ (fermented fish),
its bones were blue and flesh purple,
with a very delicious taste.
Later, the Emperor longed for it again,
sending netters to search once more,
but they never found it.
"Shí Yí"
Cáo Gōng was intelligent and brave from a young age.
At the age of ten,
he often bathed in the Qiáo River.
Once a flood dragon approached menacingly,
he fought back vigorously from the water,
causing the dragon to submerge and retreat.
Thereupon he finished bathing and returned,
but never spoke of it.
Later, when someone was seen fleeing from a large snake,
Cáo Cāo laughed at him,
saying:
"I was attacked by a flood dragon and felt no fear,
so why should one be afraid of a mere snake?"
Only then did the crowd learn of his earlier encounter,
and all were astonished.
《New Sayings》
In the seventh month of the third year of the Chìwū era of Emperor Wú Dàdì,
a man named Wáng Shù
was gathering herbs on Tiāntāi Mountain.
As it was hot at the time,
he rested beneath a bridge,
when suddenly he saw a small green-clad youth in the stream,
just over a foot tall,
holding a green cattail and riding a red carp,
heading straight into the clouds,
gradually disappearing from sight.
After a long while, Shù climbed a steep cliff,
gazing in all directions,
and saw a cold wind rising over the sea,
followed instantly by thunder and lightning roaring together,
quickly approaching.
Shù grew frightened,
and hid inside a hollow tree.
When the sky cleared, he again saw the youth who had ridden the red carp,
returning into the stream,
only to reveal it was a black flood dragon.
"Zhāng Sān's Wú Records"
At the east gate of Xúnyáng City, where the main bridge stood, there was often a flood dragon,
which brought harm to the common people.
Dǒng Fèng wrote a talisman and sank it into the water,
and shortly after, a dead flood dragon was seen floating to the surface.
From "Records of Xúnyáng."
Under the long bridge at the stream islet of Yìxīng Commandery, there was a dark-scaled flood dragon
that devoured people.
Zhōu Chǔ, grasping his sword,
waited by the side of the bridge.
After a long time,
he encountered it emerging,
whereupon he leaped from the bridge,
landed on the flood dragon's back, and stabbed it multiple times.
Blood flowed into Jīng Stream,
and it died only when it reached from the commandery islet to Lake Tài.
"Records of the Strange"
Dèng Xiá of Jìn,
courtesy name Yìngyuǎn,
possessed extraordinary courage and strength,
his valor overshadowed his contemporaries,
who compared him to
Fán Kuài in governing the commandery.
Renowned as a celebrated general,
he served as the Grand Administrator of Xiāngyáng.
In the foul waters north of the city dwelled a flood dragon,
which often harmed people.
Xiá then drew his sword and entered the water,
where the dragon coiled around his legs.
Wielding his sword, Xiá severed the dragon,
causing it to bleed profusely,
turning the river water crimson throughout.
Hence, the place was named Zhǎnjiāo Zhǔ,
also called Zhǎnjiāo Jīn.
"Xiāngyáng Records of the Elderly"
Perfected Lord Xǔ,
named Xùn,
styled Jìngzhī,
was originally from Rǔnán.
Later in Yùzhāng, he encountered a youth,
whose appearance was refined and neat,
who called himself Shènláng.
Lord Xǔ spoke with him
and knew he was not human.
In the blink of an eye,
the youth...
The Perfected Lord said to his disciples:
"The youth who just came
is actually the essence of a flood dragon and clam-monster.
I recall that Jiāngxī has repeatedly suffered from floods,
if we do not eliminate him,
I fear he will escape."
The clam-monster essence knew the Perfected Lord had recognized him,
so he hid in Lóngshā Isle,
transforming into a yellow ox.
The Perfected Lord observed from afar,
and said to his disciple Shī Dàyù:
"That essence has transformed into a yellow ox,
I will now transform my body into a black ox,
and tie a handkerchief on my neck,
to use as identification.
When you see the oxen charging and fighting,
you must intercept him with your sword."
The Perfected Lord then transformed and left.
Shortly after,
they saw a black ox chasing a yellow ox,
Dàyù swung his sword at the ox,
hitting its left thigh,
whereupon it threw itself into the well west of the city,
following this well directly back to Tánzhōu,
where it transformed back into human form.
Previously, the clam-monster essence had transformed into a handsome youth,
using treasures and wealth worth tens of thousands,
managed to marry the daughter of Tánzhōu Governor Jiǎ Yù.
At this point,
the Perfected Lord sought an audience with Governor Jiǎ,
saying to him:
"I heard you have an esteemed son-in-law,
may I briefly meet him?"
Lord Jiǎ then ordered Shènláng to come out,
but Shènláng was terrified,
feigning illness to hide.
The Perfected Lord declared sternly:
"This is a creature that harms rivers and lakes,
an old monster flood dragon and clam,
how dare you hide your form?"
Thereupon the clam-monster essence resumed its original form,
writhing in the hall,
and was soon killed by officers and soldiers.
The Perfected Lord also made its two sons come out and sprayed water on them,
whereupon they immediately turned into small clam-monsters.
The Perfected Lord said to Jiǎ Yù:
"Your family members were nearly turned into fish and turtles.
Now you must move quickly,
without delay."
Jiǎ Yù hastily relocated.
In a short while,
the official residence collapsed and submerged,
white waves surging upward.
Even now,
the old traces remain clearly visible.
"Biographies of the Twelve Perfected Lords"
At Huīshè Huángdūn Lake,
also known as Jiāo Lake,
there lived a giant clam in the lake,
which often fought with the giant clam of Lǚ Lake.
Chéng Língxiǎn, who was brave and skilled in archery,
dreamed that the clam transformed into a human and told him:
"I am plagued by the giant clam of Lǚ Lake,
if you assist me,
I will surely repay you generously.
The one bound with silk and white silk,
is me.
The next day,
Língxiǎn drew his bow and shot,
hitting the clam behind.
Later, a Daoist
taught Língxiǎn to seek a favorable burial site.
Língxiǎn followed Emperor Wǔ of Chén and achieved merit,
becoming a founding minister.
Zhào Yù once lived in seclusion on Qīngchéng Mountain.
Emperor Yáng of Sui appointed him as the governor of Jiā County.
At that time, an old flood dragon was causing harm in the Qiánwéi Pond.
Yù led a thousand armored soldiers,
lining the riverbanks and raising a clamor.
Yù took his sword and entered the water.
After a while,
the river water turned completely red.
Yù held the flood dragon's head in his left hand,
his sword in his right hand,
and surged through the waves to emerge.
When the Sui Dynasty fell into great chaos,
he withdrew into seclusion,
and no one knew how or when he died.
Later, when the Jiālíng River flooded,
the people of Shǔ saw Yù riding a white horse in a blue mist,
followed by several hunters,
passing over the waves.
Emperor Tàizōng of the Song Dynasty conferred upon him the title of Divine and Valiant Great General,
and a temple was established in his honor at Guànjiāngkǒu.
"Fángyú Shènglǎn"
Sū Tǐng of the Táng dynasty first served as the wèichéng of Wūchéng.
On a day off,
he once went boating along the creek with his colleagues,
reciting poems while intoxicated,
and thus arrived at Dàojī Temple.
In front of the temple was the deepest part of the Zhà Creek,
where local legend held that the water was unfathomable,
and inhabited by flood dragons,
which had plagued people for generations.
Sū Tǐng, still drunk, walked back,
returning from Luòtuó Bridge,
but fell into the water while crossing the bridge,
sinking straight to the bottom of the pool.
Someone in the water ordered him to support the minister out,
so he gradually rose to the surface,
and Sū Tǐng was thus saved.
"Guǎng Yì Jì"
Táng Lù Yīn's "Continuation of the Water Classic" states: When a snake and pheasant leave eggs on the ground,
after a thousand years they become flood dragons.
It happened that Emperor Wǔ of Hàn personally shot a flood dragon in the Xúnyáng River,
which was the day the snake emerged from its shell,
bringing harm to the region,
with floods raging and sweeping through,
the people of Wú called it "fāhóng" (flood outbreak).
I, while at Yīshān in Xīnchéng County of Hángzhōu,
suddenly saw a pair of pheasants in the lush grass,
flying up over ten feet high,
their wings and feathers in disarray,
then descending back into the grass,
repeating this several times without ceasing.
After a long time without emerging,
I cleared the grass to look closely,
and found a giant snake and a female pheasant coiled and entangled together,
with saliva and foam scattered messily.
In a moment,
the pheasant startled and flew away,
and the snake also slipped into the grass.
Only then did I verify Yīn's account.
"Yù Shì Qīng Huà"
During the reign of the Former Shu's founding emperor,
while repairing the plank roads in Fèngzhōu, the garrison commander Bái Mǒu
was overseeing the project.
When they reached Wǔxiū Pond,
he saw a woman floating toward them on the water.
Thinking she was drowning,
he ordered laborers to pull her ashore with hooks.
Suddenly she transformed into a giant snake
and vanished into the pond.
Bái considered this ominous
and consequently fell ill.
I recited for him Cén Shēn's rhapsody:
"East of Qútáng,
there dwells an ancient flood dragon of a thousand years,
which transforms into a woman
adorned in colorful garments and exquisite makeup,
floating by the water's edge."
Upon hearing this,
Lord Bái realized it was a flood dragon,
and his illness soon healed.
Additionally, the palace official Sòng Yùzhāo himself recounted being beckoned by two or three women
on the Liǔzhōu riverbank, when local villagers shouted to stop him—
they were also flood dragons.
From "Beimeng Suoyan": Héjiān Hūchí
often had flood dragons entering the river.
They would frequently appear violently in May,
then transform into humans,
walking alongside people on the bank
until reaching a steep cliff,
where they would push them off together.
From "Yudi Zhi"
Wúhú has Xiāojī.
Xiāo,
is a hairy dragon.
Xiāo resembles a snake,
has four legs,
and can harm people.
As Jiǎ Shēng said,
"secluded with xiāo and otters in hiding"
《Fāng》
If a dragon has no horns and is yellow in the north,
it is called a tŭlóu.
"Shuōwén"
The Jìsūn clan seized the ducal house's power.
When Confucius wished to discuss statecraft, he was treated as an outsider,
so he accepted support and thus became persuasive,
yet the state of Lǔ criticized Confucius.
Confucius said:
"The dragon feeds in clear waters and swims in clear waters,
the hornless dragon feeds in clear waters but swims in turbid waters,
the fish feeds in turbid waters and swims in turbid waters.
Now I, Qiū, am not as exalted as the dragon above,
nor as lowly as the fish below—
am I then the hornless dragon?
Those who wish to achieve merit,
how can they always follow the straight line?
One who rescues a drowning person gets wet,
one who pursues a fugitive must run."
From "The Annals of Lü Buwei"
Now when the red hornless dragon and the blue horned dragon roam Jìzhōu,
the sky is clear and the earth is still,
they sip sweet flavors and taste sweetness,
taking steps not beyond the area of a small field,
so snakes and eels belittle them,
thinking they cannot compete with them in the rivers and seas.
But when it comes to the pure morning of dark clouds,
where yīn and yáng struggle with each other,
they descend with the supporting wind,
mingled with freezing rain,
and soar upward on whirlwinds,
their majesty shakes heaven and earth,
their roar resonates throughout the land,
while snakes and eels lie buried in the mud a hundred fathoms deep.
From "Huáinánzi: Surveying Obscurities"
Yáng Xióng's "Response to a Guest's Objection" states: When the emerald dragon and crimson serpent are about to ascend to heaven,
they must first raise their bodies from the depths of Cāngwú.
Without stepping on floating clouds,
or relying on swift winds,
to rise emptily upward,
they cannot pierce the vast firmament and soar through the nine gates.
"Hànshū"
On the third level of Kūnlún Mountain, there is a hundred-li-wide pool of chī dragons,
populated by many dragons and chī,
all of them white in color,
which shed their internal organs once every thousand years.
To the left of this pool, there are five-colored stones,
said to be the petrified intestines of the white chī.
"Records of Omissions"
Driving azure dragons, with white serpents as outriders,
I journey with Chónghuá to the garden of jade.
"Crossing the River" from The Songs of Chǔ
I ride a jade chariot drawn by four azure dragons.
"The Rhapsody on Gaotang"
Zhāng Huàn's memorial states: The snake can bend and stretch,
matching the dragon's soaring and hibernation.
《Hòu Hàn》
Mǎng,
the king snake.
Note: The largest of snakes,
hence called the king snake.
Guǒ Zàn said: The sovereign among snakes,
this is called the giant mǎng.
Small ones measure several xún,
large ones may reach a hundred zhàng.
The "Ěryǎ"
Téng,
the téng snake is a type of dragon,
capable of summoning clouds and mist to move within them.
The "Ěryǎ" states: the téng snake moves by swimming through the mist,
while the yìng dragon rises by riding the clouds.
The "Huáinánzǐ·Zhǔshù" notes: the téng snake swims through the mist to strike the centipede.
The "Shuōlín" says: if a rabbit does not mate,
or a téng snake does not copulate,
they cannot be considered chaste.
From the "Bàopǔzǐ".
Yì slew the Ba Snake at Dòngtíng,
its bones formed a mound,
hence it was called Bālíng.
The "Records of Xún River" states: He beheaded the long serpent at Dòngtíng.
The "Huáinánzi" says: The Ba Snake swallowed an elephant and regurgitated its bones after three years.
If a nobleman consumes it,
he will suffer no ailments of the heart or abdomen.
The "Classic of Mountains" records: Slaying the Ba Snake,
revealed the elephant's skeleton.
From the "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú."
One who excels at employing troops is like the Shuàirán.
The Shuàirán
is a snake from Chángshān.
Strike its head and the tail will respond;
strike its tail and the head will respond;
strike its midsection and both head and tail will respond.
From "Sūnzǐ's Art of War". In the western mountains, there is a snake
with a disproportionately large head and tail,
adorned with five colors.
When a person or creature touches it,
hitting the head brings the tail to strike,
hitting the tail brings the head to strike,
hitting the waist brings both head and tail to strike simultaneously.
It is named Shuàirán.
This snake is most abundant in Chángshān of Kuàijī,
hence "Sūnzǐ's Art of War" states: A general commanding three armies
should position them like the Shuàirán.
From "Shényì Jīng".
In ancient times, the round hill had many large snakes,
and also grew fine medicinal herbs.
When the Yellow Emperor was about to ascend it,
Guǎngchéngzǐ taught him to carry realgar, and all the snakes departed.
Nowadays, carrying five taels of Wǔdū realgar, which is as red as a rooster's comb,
when entering the mountains and forests, one need not fear snakes.
If a snake bites a person,
applying a small amount of realgar powder to the wound
will cure it immediately.
From Bàopǔzǐ
Crown Prince Shēnshēng of Jìn Xiàngōng arrived at the Spirit Tower,
where a snake coiled around the left wheel of his chariot.
The charioteer said:
"Your Highness, dismount and pay homage.
I have heard that when a snake coils around the left wheel of a ruler's son,
he will swiftly obtain the state.
The crown prince then did not proceed,
but returned to his residence.
The charioteer went to see the crown prince,
who said:
"If I now obtain the state,
this means our ruler will lose his peace;
to see the benefit for the state but forget the ruler's peace,
is not the way of a son;
to hear of gaining the state and pay homage for such an omen,
is not the ruler's desire.
He drew his sword intending to die,
but the charioteer stopped him,
saying:
"Portents and anomalies,
are the way of Heaven;
reverently receiving the mandate,
is human conduct;
paying homage to auspicious signs and guarding against calamities,
is ritual propriety;
reverently receiving the mandate,
not causing the ruler grief through one's own person,
is filial piety.
Now Your Highness sees good fortune but does not pay homage,
losing ritual propriety,
and seeks death to grieve the ruler,
losing filial piety.
The crown prince did not proceed,
but fell upon his sword and died.
From "Xīn Xù"
Duke Wén of Jìn went out hunting,
when his vanguard returned to report:
"There is a large serpent ahead,
as tall as a dike,
lying across the road."
Duke Wén said:
"Turn the chariots around and return."
His charioteer said:
"I have heard that when encountering auspicious signs one should welcome them,
but when seeing ominous creatures one should confront them.
Now there is an omen ahead,
I request to attack it with our followers."
The Duke said:
"That will not do.
I have heard that when the Son of Heaven has bad dreams, he cultivates the Way;
when feudal lords have bad dreams, they improve their governance;
when high officials have bad dreams, they repair their residences;
when common people have bad dreams, they cultivate their virtue.
If this is done,
then calamity will not come.
Now I have committed faults,
and Heaven has sent this omen to warn me.
If I attack it,
this would be defying Heaven's mandate."
So he returned to fast and pray at the ancestral temple,
saying:
"I, the unworthy ruler, have committed errors,
Heaven's punishment should fall upon my person.
I dare not fail to reform,
and reverently prepare sacrificial animals to announce this."
Then he withdrew and improved his governance.
After three days, he dreamed that Heaven executed the great serpent,
