saying:
"How dare you block the path of an enlightened ruler?"
Duke Wén awoke,
sent someone to check,
and the serpent had already putrefied.
Duke Wén was greatly pleased.
From "Jiǎzǐ"
When Sūn Shū'áo was an infant,
he once returned from an outing,
worried and refusing to eat.
His mother asked him the reason,
and he replied tearfully:
"Today I saw a two-headed snake,
and I fear my death is imminent.
"Where is the snake now?
He said:
"I've heard that whoever sees a two-headed snake will die,
but I feared others might see it too,
so I killed it and buried it.
His mother said:
"Do not worry,
you will not die.
I have heard that those who perform hidden acts of virtue
are rewarded with blessings by heaven.
When people heard of this,
they all understood his capacity for benevolence.
When he later became prime minister,
even before governing, the people already trusted him.
Yán Yuān and Zǐ Lù sat together at the gate of their master's residence.
A ghostly apparition sought an audience with Confucius,
its eyes were like the sun,
and its form was immense.
Zǐ Lù lost his spirit,
his mouth was sealed and he could not speak.
Yán Yuān then wielded his sword and advanced, striking its waist,
whereupon its form transformed into a snake,
and he immediately beheaded it.
Confucius came out to observe,
and sighed, saying:
"The brave do not fear,
the wise are not confused,
the benevolent possess courage,
but the brave do not necessarily possess benevolence.
"Yǐn Yún Xiǎoshuō"
In the first year of Duke Dìng of Lǔ,
nine snakes coiled around a pillar,
which was interpreted as an omen that the temple of the ninth generation would not be sacrificed to,
so the Yáng Palace was established.
From "Sōu Shén Jì".
King Huì of Qín intended to attack Shǔ.
The King of Shǔ was fond of women,
so (Qín) presented five beautiful women.
The King of Shǔ dispatched the Five Dīng to welcome the women,
and upon returning to Zǐtóng,
they saw a large snake entering a mountain cave.
One man pulled its tail but could not extract it,
so the Five Dīng pulled the snake together,
causing the mountain to collapse,
crushing the Five Dīng,
who stamped on the snake and cried out loudly.
"Annals of the Kings of Shǔ": In Miánzhú County, there is a Jade Consort Stream.
Initially,
the Jade Maiden and the Five Dīng strongmen were born together.
Their mother first gave birth to a lump,
which the father considered strange,
so he abandoned it in the stream.
Later, he heard crying sounds,
went to look,
and found one girl and five boys,
so he took them back to raise.
When they grew up,
the girl became the consort of the Marquis of Shǔ,
and the boys became the Five Dīng,
who opened the road
for the golden ox to enter.
Chīyí Zǐpí served Tián Chéngzǐ.
When Chéngzǐ left Qí,
he fled to Yān.
Chīyí Zǐpí carried the travel pass and followed him.
When they reached Wàngyì,
he said:
"Have you not heard of the marsh-drying snakes?
When the marsh dried up, the snakes were about to migrate.
A small snake said to a large snake: 'If the large snake travels and the small snake follows it,
people will think we are just ordinary traveling snakes,
and someone will surely kill you.
You would do better to carry me in your mouth as we travel.
Then people will surely regard me as a divine lord.'
So they carried each other and crossed the public road.
Everyone avoided them.
Now you are handsome while I am ugly.
If you serve as my superior guest,
you appear as a lord of a thousand chariots.
If you serve as my envoy,
you appear as a minister of a ten-thousand-chariot state.
You would do better to be my retainer."
Tián Chéngzǐ then carried the travel pass and followed him.
When they reached an inn,
the innkeeper treated them with great respect,
and offered them wine and meat.
From "Hánzǐ"
Zhāo Yáng led the Chǔ army to attack Wèi,
destroying their forces and killing their general,
then shifting his troops to attack Qí.
Chén Zhěn, as an envoy of the King of Qí,
went to see Zhāo Yáng and said:
"In Chǔ, there was a man hosting a sacrifice,
who gave a goblet of wine to his retainers.
The retainers discussed among themselves: 'If several people drink it, there won't be enough;
if one person drinks it, there will be some left over.
Let us each draw a snake on the ground,
and whoever finishes the snake first will drink the wine.'
One man finished first,
took the wine and was about to drink it,
but then, holding the goblet in his left hand,
he used his right hand to draw on the snake,
saying: 'I can add legs to it.'
Before he finished adding the legs,
another man completed his snake later,
snatched the goblet from him, and said: 'A snake originally has no legs;
how can you add legs to it?'
So he drank the wine.
The one who added legs to the snake
ultimately lost his wine.
Now you, sir, attacked Wèi,
shattered their army and killed their general,
and are about to shift your troops to attack Qí.
Qí fears you greatly,
but if you do not know when to stop after winning a battle,
it is just like adding legs to a snake.
Zhāo Yáng then disbanded his army and returned.
《Strategies of the Warring States》
In Dōngyuè's Mǐnzhōng region, Shàowǔ County had Yōng Ridge,
also known as Black-Headed Ridge.
In the northern marshlands dwelled a giant serpent,
measuring seventy to eighty zhǎng in length,
over ten arm-spans in girth,
which plagued the land.
Commandants and senior officials
often fell victim to it.
Through dreams, shamans and wizards revealed
its desire to devour young maidens.
The commandant and magistrate thus purchased servant girls from indebted families to raise them,
sacrificing them to the serpent in the eighth month,
delivering them to its lair,
where the serpent would swallow them,
having already consumed nine maidens.
At that time, Lǐ Dàn of Jiānglè County had six daughters,
but no sons.
His youngest daughter, named Qí,
volunteered to go,
requesting the purchase of a fine sword and a serpent-biting hound,
along with several hú of rice cakes,
which she coated with honey.
Arriving at the cave entrance,
as the serpent emerged its head,
large as a granary door,
like a two-chǐ mirror,
it first devoured the honeyed cakes.
Lǐ Qí then set the hound upon the serpent,
while striking from behind with her sword,
causing the serpent to leap out,
dying upon reaching the courtyard,
where nine maidens' skulls were recovered.
The King of Yuè marveled at her,
taking her as his queen.
"Sōu Shén Jì" "Kūnyuán Lù"
Beside the Zhuóshuǐ River in Suí County, there is a place called Broken Snake Mound.
Long ago, the Marquis of Suí went out and saw a large snake cut in half.
Suspecting it was divine,
he had someone apply medicine to seal its wound,
and the snake was then able to leave.
Hence, the place was named Broken Snake Mound.
Over a year later,
the snake returned with a pearl in its mouth to repay the kindness.
The pearl was an inch in diameter,
pure white,
and emitted light at night,
shining like the moon.
It was called the Marquis of Suí's Pearl,
also known as the Divine Snake Pearl.
South of the mound lies the pond of Jìliáng, a senior official of Suí.
From "Shuō Yuàn," "Sōu Shén Jì," and "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù."
Minister Jìn Shàng of Chǔ, having slandered and caused Qū Yuán's death,
was punished by Heaven,
transformed into a great python,
which dwelled in a cave behind the mountain.
People erected a temple for it.
"Records of Shè [□]"
Xiǎohuáng County was
the region of Huángxiāng in the state of Sòng.
When Duke Pei raised an army for open-field battles,
he lost his deceased mother in Huángxiāng.
After the empire was pacified,
he dispatched envoys with a catalpa-wood coffin to summon her spirit from the desolate wilderness.
Thereupon, a crimson snake washed itself in the water
and entered the catalpa coffin.
At the bathing site, strands of her hair remained,
hence she was posthumously honored as Lady Zhāolíng.
(From "Chénliú Customs and Traditions")
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Zhāng Kuān served as the Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Previously, there were two old men disputing over mountain land,
and various prefectures contested the boundaries,
remaining unresolved for years.
When Kuān arrived,
they came again.
Kuān observed that the two old men’s appearances were not human,
so he ordered soldiers to hold halberds and escort them in,
asking:
"What kind of spirits are you?"
The old men tried to flee,
but Kuān shouted and blocked them,
whereupon they transformed into two snakes and slithered away.
"In Search of the Supernatural"
In Qióngdū County, there lived an old woman,
who was poor and alone.
Every time she ate,
a small snake,
with horns on its head,
would appear by her bed.
The woman took pity on it and fed it.
Later, it gradually grew larger,
eventually reaching over ten feet in length.
The magistrate had a fine horse,
which the snake then sucked to death.
The magistrate, greatly enraged,
demanded that the woman produce the snake.
She said it was under the bed,
so the magistrate ordered the ground dug up,
but the deeper they dug, the larger the hole became,
with no sign of the snake.
The magistrate, redirecting his anger, killed the woman.
The snake then manifested its spirit through a person,
saying:
"Angry magistrate,
why did you kill my mother?
I will avenge my mother."
After this, every night,
sounds like thunder or wind were heard,
for about forty days.
When people met each other,
they were all startled and said:
"Why is there a fish on your head?"
That night,
an area of forty square li,
along with the city, suddenly sank into a lake.
The locals call it
"the sunken lake."
Only the old woman's house remained,
unharmed and still standing to this day.
Fishermen gathering catches
would always stay there overnight.
Whenever there were wind and waves,
they would stay by the house,
where it was calm and safe.
When the wind was still and the water clear,
the city walls and watchtowers could still be seen distinctly.
Now, when the water is shallow,
the locals dive down
and retrieve old wood,
which is hard, genuine, glossy, and black as lacquer.
Nowadays, enthusiasts give it as gifts to use as pillows.
Lǐ Yīng's "Records of Yìzhōu": In the old seat of Wǔqiáng County, there is the Wǔqiáng Abyss.
The elders say that a villager traveling on the road
saw a small snake,
suspected it had spiritual power,
took it and raised it,
naming it Dànshēng.
When it grew up, it devoured people,
causing distress in the village.
They captured it and imprisoned it,
but Dànshēng carried the prison and fled,
and the town sank into a lake.
The county magistrate and his officials all turned into fish.
Now, about half a li northeast of the county seat is submerged,
the abyss water flows southeast,
collecting to form a lake,
also called the Lángjūn Abyss.
The elders of the town also say that on the day the county sank,
the magistrate's son fled east,
and it also sank here,
hence the abyss got the name Lángjūn.
Lì Dàoyuán's "Commentary on the Water Classic"
Mǎ Yuán campaigned against the Wūxī Mán,
advancing to encamp at Hútóu.
He fell ill from heatstroke,
so he carved a chamber into the cliffside,
to escape the scorching heat.
A saying in Wǔlíng goes: By Hútóu Mountain there is a stone cave,
which is the chamber Mǎ Yuán carved.
Inside the chamber was a snake,
as large as a hundred-hú boat.
It is said this was the lingering spirit of Yuán.
From "Records of Wǔlíng"
General of Chariots and Cavalry Féng Gǔn of Bā Commandery, styled Hóngqīng,
while serving as a court gentleman, opened his seal-ribbon case.
There were two red snakes,
about two feet long,
that crawled away to the north and south respectively,
causing him great worry and fear.
Diviner Xǔ Shì interpreted this and said:
"This is an auspicious sign.
In three years, you will become a frontier general,
with 'east' in your title.
After five years, you will become a general-in-chief,
and be appointed as the governor of Liáodōng."
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* records: when an outer snake fought with an inner snake,
during Emperor Wén's reign, a similar event occurred.
Historical records document these occurrences,
yet only Hóngqīng's case ended auspiciously.
Could this be what is called 'some obtain divine favor and prosper'?
*Fēngsú Tōng*
Dòu Wǔ's mother gave birth to Wǔ,
and also gave birth to a snake,
which was sent into the forest.
Later, when his mother passed away,
and before her burial was completed,
a large snake emerged from the thickets and grass,
went straight to the funeral site,
struck the coffin with its head,
shedding tears and blood,
bending and twisting its body,
as if displaying a mournful weeping expression,
and after a while, it left.
People at the time understood it as an auspicious sign for the Dòu family.
"Book of the Later Han"
Lǐ Yīng's "Records of Yìzhōu" states: At Míng Hè Mountain in Jìnyuán,
it was the place where Zhāng Líng ascended to immortality.
Legend says qílín and white cranes often roamed and soared above it,
with an inscription recording that Zhāng Líng was sucked in by a venomous snake,
and his disciples believed he had achieved immortality.
"Universal Geography"
When Emperor Huán ascended the throne,
a great snake appeared in the Yángdé Hall.
Chúnyú Yì, the market official of Luòyáng, said:
"The snake has scales and armor,
which is a symbol of weaponry.
Its appearance in the palace precincts
indicates that influential ministers from the imperial consorts' families will face execution by arms.
He then abandoned his official post and fled.
By the second year of the Yánxī era,
Grand General Liáng Jì was executed,
his family members were arrested and punished,
and troops were deployed in the capital.
From Gàn Bǎo's "Sōushénjì"
Tiānmén Mountain,
is rugged and beautiful,
with winding rocky valleys,
and a great cliff rising straight up for thousands of ren,
where trees and grasses intertwine,
and clouds and mist shroud it.
Below, there is a narrow path,
and when travelers pass,
they suddenly fly up and emerge above the forest,
as if ascending to immortality,
thus leaving the mortal world.
Such occurrences gradually became too numerous to record,
and people traveling north and south
called it the Valley of Immortals.
At that time, those devoted to the Dao
came from thousands of li away,
bathed by the cliffs,
seeking to ascend to immortality.
Beneath this forest,
none failed to fly away.
One evening,
a wise man said to others:
"This must be the work of a monster,
not the path to immortality."
So he tied himself with a stone,
and dragged a zhang into the valley,
but again he flew away,
realizing it was an evil aura sucking him in.
He then sent word to nearby villages,
recruiting hundreds of young men,
armed with weapons,
and carrying large clubs.
First, they set fire to the grass,
and cut down the bamboo and trees,
then went to the mountainside to observe,
and saw from afar a creature,
tens of zhang long,
looming high and low,
with its head hanging down, looking below.
As they drew closer,
they saw it was a giant python.
So they ordered the young men to beat drums, leap, shoot arrows,
and then hack and stab.
Its mouth gaped over a chi wide,
still trying to harm people,
but its strength was no match for the crowd,
and after a long time, it finally died.
The bones it had swallowed and the remains of other animals
lay piled up like hills on either side.
"Bówùzhì"
Along the roadside in Jìnxìng Commandery, five or six lǐ away, there was a creature,
with a girth of a hundred arm-spans,
and a length of several dozen zhàng.
Travelers passing by to look at it
would go and never return,
and this had been the case for many years,
with a great many people lost.
Dǒng Fèng was coming out from Jiāozhōu,
passing through this ridge,
and upon seeing it, was greatly startled,
saying:
"This is a snake.
While on his journey,
he cast a talisman and issued a command,
and after staying overnight, went to look:
the snake was already dead.
Those around him said:
"The white bones have piled up into a mountain.
Guǎngzhōu Jì
Emperor Zhào Wǎng Lún usurped the throne.
In the palace hall, there were large and small pythons,
with flesh hanging between their ears,
resembling heavy mourning headbands,
and the small pythons were the same.
"Jìn Shū"
Yán Hán's sister-in-law fell ill,
requiring the gallbladder of the bearded snake,
but it could not be obtained.
Yán Hán worried and sighed for many days.
A young boy came holding a blue pouch and gave it to Yán Hán.
Yán Hán looked inside,
and it was indeed a snake gallbladder.
The boy transformed into a blue bird and flew away.
From the "Zhōngxīng Shū": In Jiāozhǐ, the mountains have many large snakes,
named bearded snakes,
ten zhàng in length,
seven to eight chǐ in girth,
often waiting in trees for deer and other animals.
When a deer or animal passes by,
they lower their heads and coil around them.
After a while,
the deer dies,
first moistening it with saliva until wet,
then swallowing it whole.
The antlers and bones pierce through the skin as they emerge.
When the mountain tribes see the snake motionless,
they pierce the snake from head to tail with large bamboo spikes,
kill and eat it,
considering it a rare delicacy.
Thus, Yáng's "Nányì Yìwù Zhì" says: The bearded snake is huge,
both massive and long.
Its colors are mottled and striking,
its patterns like brocade.
It eats ashes and swallows deer,
its fat nourishes wounds.
It is truly a feast for banquets,
served in vessels and cups.
It is said that when it is nursing its wounds,
its fat is very plump.
If you strike it,
and throw women's clothing at it,
it will coil up and not flee,
making it easy to capture.
From the "Shuǐ Jīng": Quánjiàn Province presented rán snake gallbladders.
They are collected on the fifth day of the fifth month.
The two lobes of the gallbladder are five to six chǐ apart.
Strike the snake's head and tail,
and use a stick under its belly,
tapping back and forth,
the gallbladder will gather.
Cut it out with a knife for medicine,
seal the wound and release it,
and it will not die.
It can be collected again later.
If you see a scar under its ribs, release it.
From the "Qiān Zǎi": The rán snake's gallbladder is near the head in the first ten days of the month,
near the heart in the middle ten days,
and near the tail in the last ten days.
From the "Yǒuyáng": The gallbladder is about the size of a duck egg.
Cut it out,
then place it back into the liver and abdomen,
sewing the wound with thread,
and the snake will revive.
Carry it back and release it into rivers and marshes.
The gallbladder is dried quickly,
to be used as local tribute.
Some say that after a snake has its gallbladder taken,
if it sees the captor another day,
it will turn sideways from afar to show the abdominal wound,
proving it has no gallbladder to escape further harm.
From the "Lǐngbiǎo Lù Yì": The rán snake's fangs are six to seven cùn long,
highly valued by the locals,
said to ward off misfortune,
and beneficial for long journeys.
Selling one can fetch several oxen.
From the "Kuòdì Zhì": Eating snake meat wards off gǔ poison.
From the "Zhèngsú Yīn": Its fat is traditionally said to be harmful to people.
Its skin can be used to make drums,
now made in Cháozhōu with scales intact,
producing a very loud sound,
similar to elephant skin drums.
From the "Běihù Lù": Its fat, if it touches human bones,
makes them soft,
and can also cause impotence,
lasting a lifetime.
From the "Píyǎ": Yú Yuàn served as the governor of Jìn'ān.
The commandery historically produced bearded snakes,
whose gallbladders could be used for medicine.
Someone offered one to Yú Yuàn,
but he could not bear to kill it,
so he released it thirty lǐ away.
Overnight, it returned to the original spot.
Yú Yuàn had it sent elsewhere,
but it came back again.
People believed this was due to his benevolent heart.
From the "Qí Shū": Lú Yuánqīn of Quánzhōu suffered from leprosy,
with only his nose not yet collapsed.
On the fifth day of the fifth month, he obtained a rán snake gallbladder intended as tribute,
but someone said the meat could cure the disease.
So he cut a piece of snake meat and ate it.
After three to five days,
he felt his condition gradually improving,
and in a hundred days, he recovered fully.
From the "Qiān Zǎi":
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
there was a giant serpent over ten zhǎng long.
It blocked the road,
and whenever passersby approached,
it would suck them in with its breath and seize them,
having already devoured hundreds of people.
Travelers avoided the road entirely.
The Daoist priest Wú Měng went with several disciples intending to kill the serpent.
The serpent hid in a deep burrow and refused to emerge.
Měng summoned the local deity of Nánchāng with a talisman,
whereupon the serpent emerged from its burrow.
Its head rose several zhǎng high.
Měng climbed along its back from the tail and pressed its head to the ground with his foot,
while his disciples struck it dead with an axe from behind.
Měng said:
"This serpent is the essence of Shǔ.
With the serpent dead,
the rebels in Shǔ shall be pacified."
Soon after,
Dù Tāo was indeed vanquished.
From "Records of Yùzhāng"
The Shu ruler Lǐ Shì's palace attendant Zhāng shì had a bewitching appearance,
and Shì favored her.
One day,
she transformed into a large patterned snake,
over ten feet long,
and was sent to the imperial garden,
but at night she returned to sleep under the bed.
Shì became frightened,
so he killed her.
There was also a beauty named Zhèng,
whom Shì also cherished and loved,
who transformed into a tigress,
and one night ate Shì's favored concubine.
Not long after,
Shì was overthrown by Huán Wēn.
"Records of Unique Strange Events"
During the Eastern Jìn Dynasty,
Venerable Bátuóluó was translating scriptures by the Green Lotus Pond at Tiānníng Temple in Guǎnglíng.
Suddenly, two green snakes emerged from a well,
transforming into two young boys.
From dawn, they swept, cleaned, and burned incense for the Venerable,
until dusk when they waited for him to put away the sutras before leaving,
and so it went day after day.
Once the translation of the scriptures was completed,
the green-clad youths were nowhere to be found.
From "Bǎoyòu Guǎnglíng Zhì".
Empress Xì Shì
was the wife of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
Several months after her passing,
the emperor was in his resting hall
when he heard rustling sounds outside.
Looking,
he saw a python coiling and crawling up the hall,
its eyes gleaming and mouth gaping toward the emperor.
Startled and terrified, the emperor jumped up
and said:
"The palace is strictly guarded;
it is no place for your kind.
Is this a demon seeking to harm me?"
The snake spoke in human language:
"This python
was once Xì Shì.
In life, I was consumed by jealousy,
harming others and destroying things;
for this crime after death,
I was condemned to become a python.
A python,
unlike ordinary snakes,
can also transform itself.
Neither the imperial palace nor the weighty affairs of Liáng could hinder me.
Moved by Your Majesty's past kindness,
I have revealed this ugly form to you,
begging for any meritorious deeds to save and deliver me."
The emperor was deeply moved and sorrowful.
Then he searched for the python,
but it was nowhere to be seen.
The next day, he told this to Master Zhì,
who replied:
"Only through Buddhist rites, repentance, and sincere devotion can this be resolved."
The emperor then composed ten volumes of penitential texts
to perform repentance rituals for her.
Another day,
a wondrous fragrance filled the palace,
growing more exquisite over time,
with no known source.
The emperor looked up
and saw a celestial being,
dignified and beautiful in appearance,
who said to him:
"This is the python's later incarnation.
Thanks to Your Majesty's meritorious deeds,
I have been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Now I manifest my true form as clear proof."
She expressed heartfelt gratitude,
and after speaking, departed.
"Preface to Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's Repentance"
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, along with palace attendants, visited Xuánzhōu Garden,
where they saw a large serpent coiled on the path,
surrounded by numerous small serpents,
all of black color.
A palace attendant remarked:
"I fear this may be the Coin Dragon.
The emperor then had one hundred thousand strings of coins buried at the serpent's location,
to suppress it.
(From *History of the Southern Dynasties*)
In Wǔdāng County of Nányáng, there was a cypress tree,
forty arm-spans in girth.
When Xiāo Xīn of the Liáng dynasty served as the commandery governor,
he had it cut down.
It is said that a huge snake fell from the hollow of the tree,
several arm-spans thick,
and thirty feet long,
followed by dozens of other snakes that entered the southern mountains,
with a sound like wind and rain.
Before the tree was felled,
it had appeared in Xiāo Xīn's dream,
but he paid no attention to it.
After the tree was cut down,
Xiāo Xīn indeed died at his official post.
The "Tújīng" states: The official died shortly after.
The "Shuǐjīng" records:
In the first year of Emperor Xiàojìng of the Eastern Wèi,
a large snake was seen on the city of Wǔláo,
Gāo Zhòngmì rebelled at Wǔláo.
Later, when Sīmǎ Xiāonán took office,
the snake appeared at Wǔláo again,
and Xiāonán also rebelled.
People referred to it as a female dragon.
"Wèi Shū"
In the final years of Hòuzhǔ's reign,
Fù Zǎi, the Imperial Librarian, submitted a memorial to remonstrate with the emperor,
and Hòuzhǔ had him bestowed death in prison.
After his death, a vicious snake with a coiled tail
came up onto the funeral bed,
positioning itself to receive the sacrificial offerings.
It would leave only to return again,
and this continued for over a hundred days,
with snapping sounds heard from time to time,
before Chén soon perished.
From *History of the Southern Dynasties*
Xuē Jùn in his childhood was playing with children from his clan by the stream bank,
when he saw a yellow snake with horns and feet.
He called the other children to look at it,
but none of them could see anything.
Jùn considered this an ill omen,
and returned home feeling worried and dejected.
His mother pressed him until he told her,
and Jùn answered truthfully.
It happened that a foreign monk came to their house begging for food,
and Jùn's mother, frightened, told him about it.
The monk said:
"This is actually an auspicious sign for the child.
He will achieve fame and position early, but his lifespan will not exceed six or seven."
Having said this, he went out,
and suddenly disappeared.
Everyone at the time found this strange.
Later, Jùn died at forty-two,
thus verifying the prediction about six or seven.
"Book of Sui"
At the end of Emperor Yáng's Dàyè era,
Zhái Ràng first met Lǐ Mì,
whose clothes were hanging on a rack,
when Mì's belt transformed into a red snake.
Ràng found this extraordinary,
yet he ultimately ended up being killed by Mì.
Above
In Search of the Supernatural: A snake that has lived for a thousand years will sever itself,
and then reconnect.
Huáinánzǐ states: The divine snake severs its own body,
and rejoins itself.
Emperor Yáng dispatched people to the remote mountains along the coast of Lǐngnán to seek this snake,
and after several attempts, it arrived in Luòxià.
The one obtained
was about three chǐ long with a yellow-black color,
its head had brocade-like patterns,
completely resembling the color of gold,
unable to poison people,
and it understood how to eat meat.
If one wished to make it sever its own body,
one would first provoke it with wine to anger it,
causing it to be unable to bear its furious poison,
then it would sever itself into three or four pieces.
The places where it severed
were as if cut by a knife,
revealing the patterns of its skin and bones,
and there was also blood.
However, after the prolonged anger subsided,
the three or four severed pieces gradually came together and reconnected,
the body restored as before,
also as if it had never been severed.
Suí Dynasty Editorial Director Dèng Lóng said this type of spiritual snake severs itself,
and it does not necessarily have to be a thousand years old.
"Qióngshén Mìyuàn"
Tài Zōng was stationed at Bǎi Bì,
and often wished to spy on the enemy.
He secretly dispatched troops to raid from afar,
causing the cavalry to scatter in all directions.
Tài Zōng and one armored soldier ascended a hillock and fell asleep,
when suddenly enemy troops converged from all sides like gathering clouds,
yet they remained unaware of it.
It happened that a snake was chasing a rat,
and the rat bumped into the armored soldier,
startling him awake.
He immediately reported to Tài Zōng.
They both mounted their horses and galloped over a hundred paces,
but were overtaken by the enemy.
Tài Zōng shot a large-feathered arrow at them,
killing their valiant general,
whereupon the enemy cavalry retreated.
At the time, this was regarded as a miraculous event.
"Old Book of Táng"
Yú Shìnán was enfeoffed as a County Duke in the eighth year of the Zhēnguàn era.
At that time, large snakes were frequently sighted,
which troubled the Emperor.
He consulted Shìnán about it,
who replied:
"During the reign of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
a green snake appeared on the imperial throne;
in the time of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
a great snake three hundred paces long
was seen in Qí,
passing through the market and entering the temple.
Snakes ought to dwell in the wilderness yet entered the market—
that is why it was considered ominous.
Now the snakes appear in the mountains and marshes,
exactly where they belong.
I fear there may be unjust imprisonments or wrongful detentions,
so it would be appropriate to review the cases of prisoners."
At Zhìxiàng Temple in Cháng'ān, there was a virtuous man
who had been practicing Daoism at the Western Chán Monastery since his teens.
Under the seat in the monastery's Buddha hall, there was always a snake.
When the virtuous man first began his practice,
the snake was as thick as one encircling arm,
but after more than forty years,
it had grown as large as a hall pillar.
Though they saw each other, they never bore ill will.
During the Kāiyuán era,
the virtuous man went to the Buddha hall at night to pay respects.
The hall had no lamp, yet it was filled with brilliant light,
which he found very strange.
He then searched where the snake emerged
and found something like a pearl an inch in diameter.
He took it to the market and set a high price,
hoping to find someone who recognized it.
After a few days, a foreign trader came to trade,
fixing the price at a million coins.
The virtuous man said:
"This is a luminous pearl,
which should be priceless.
Why is the offer so low?"
The foreigner replied:
"Clam pearls are precious,
but this is a snake pearl,
worth at most a thousand strings of coins."
The virtuous man sighed in admiration
and sold it.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
During the Tiānbǎo era,
in Luòyáng there was a giant snake,
over ten feet tall,
a hundred feet long,
that emerged from beneath Máng Mountain.
The foreign monk Wúwèi,
upon seeing it, said:
"This creature intends to breach the waters and flood Luò City.
He then used Indian methods to chant spells over it,
and after several days the snake burst open.
In the summer of the second year of the Jiànzhōng era,
north of the Shā River in Níngjìn County, Zhàozhōu, there was a very lush pear tree,
which the people worshipped as a deity.
Hundreds and thousands of snakes came from the east and west, heading toward the northern bank,
gathering under the pear tree into two piles;
those remaining on the southern bank
formed one pile.
Suddenly, three tortoises, each about an inch in diameter,
circled around the piles,
and after all the snakes had died, each climbed onto its respective pile.
A villager reported this,
noting that the snakes' bellies all had wounds,
as if struck by arrows.
The prefect Kāng Rìzhī,
recorded the event in a drawing,
and presented the three tortoises as an offering.
Lǐ Zhōu's younger brother suffered from rheumatism.
Someone suggested snake wine could cure it,
so he sought a black snake,
placed it alive into a covered jar,
and added yeast.
After several days,
the snake's hissing never ceased,
and when fully fermented,
the aroma became intensely potent.
Filling a cup to the brim and drinking it,
in a moment,
his body entirely turned into liquid,
leaving only his hair behind.
"Supplement to the National History" Medical Officer Lù Shào mentioned recording a case where someone brewed snake wine,
having killed dozens of snakes previously.
One day,
while personally approaching the jar,
he peered inside and noticed something in the wine,
which leaped out and bit his nose.
As it was about to fall off,
upon inspection,
it turned out to be a snake's skull.
Consequently, the wound destroyed his nose,
as if sliced off.
"Yǒuyáng Miscellany"
Wéi Gāo governed Western Shǔ.
At that time, a yellow mandarin tree was just ripening,
when suddenly over several nights all the fruits fell,
except for one stem remaining at the treetop,
as large as a bowl,
with lush branches and leaves,
different from ordinary ones.
The garden official reported this to Governor Wéi,
who personally went to inspect it,
and said:
"This is a remarkable fruit,
unsuitable for a subject to eat."
He proposed to present it to the emperor,
ordering it to be broken off about a foot from the stem,
whereupon the fruit fell off by itself from the stem.
A skilled physician named Zǎn Yīn was standing by in attendance,
and said:
"When any fruit falls before its time,
and the stem detaches on its own,
it indicates an ailment in the fruit.
Allow me to test it with a needle."
After repeated requests, Governor Wéi finally consented.
Zǎn Yīn took a needle,
approached the stem and pricked it,
whereupon the fruit immediately rotated at the touch,
and Zǎn Yīn swiftly made another puncture,
causing blood to spatter and soak his sleeve.
Governor Wéi was greatly astonished,
and thus ordered it to be cut open,
revealing it to be a two-headed snake.
From "Records of the Northern Households."
At the beginning of the Kāichéng era,
a yellow snake appeared in the palace,
emerging at night from the treasure vault,
roaming between the steps and courtyard,
its radiance shining brilliantly,
making it impossible to capture.
A palace attendant threw a coral jue at it,
whereupon it vanished along with the jue.
The vault keeper reported the incident in detail,
and the emperor ordered a thorough search of the vault,
where a golden snake was found,
with the coral jue piercing its head.
The emperor examined it closely
and said:
"Long ago, when Suí Yángdì was the Prince of Jìn,
he presented a golden snake to Lady Chén.
I wonder where this snake came from."
His attendants then noticed beneath its chin
the characters
"Ā Mǐn"
inscribed.
The emperor started and exclaimed:
"Indeed, it confirms my suspicions!"
"Ā Mǐn"
was
Suí Yángdì's childhood name.
The emperor's vast learning and keen perception
were often demonstrated in such matters.
He then ordered a glass chain
to be attached to the front leg of a jade pig,
after which the snake was never seen again,
as pigs are known to devour snakes.
From "Dū Yáng Biān"
Jiǎ Gōnglù arrived at Léizhōu,
moored his boat by the opposite shore,
awaiting favorable winds.
He saw a group of children crowding around two giant snakes,
each over ten feet long.
One had the iridescent colors of a peacock,
its gold and emerald hues dazzling to the eye;
the other was vermilion red,
as vivid as fresh blood.
There were also over ten white snakes,
following one after another,
as if forming an escort procession,
all entering a hollow in a banyan vine,
and never emerging again.
Thus it is known that snakes have four types—wood, herb, water, and earth—
their varieties are inexhaustible.
"Records of the Northern Households"
During the Guānghuà era,
Yáng Shǒuliàng guarded Bāo.
One day, a snake,
lay across the road of Xiégǔ Ridge,
standing seven to eight feet tall,
with no one knowing its head or tail,
surrounded by countless small snakes
flanking it like wings.
Each time it dragged its body,
the trees and woods would break and collapse.
It took nearly half a month to pass completely,
blocking travelers.
They gathered grass and burned it at the roadside,
fearing any lingering venom,
before proceeding.
The following year,
Yáng was executed.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Liáng Niú Cúnjié governed Yùnzhōu,
and built a grand mansion at the southwest corner of the inner city.
During the rammed earth construction,
they unearthed a snake den,
with countless snakes large and small.
Cúnjié ordered them killed,
and transported to the wilderness—
it took over ten cartloads to remove them all.
Someone remarked at the time:
"These snakes
are a gathering of spirits."
That same year,
Cúnjié died from a carbuncle on his back.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Initially, a yellow snake appeared in the stele tower,
which Wáng Chùzhí regarded as a hidden dragon and worshipped it;
then hundreds of wild magpies nested in the wheat fields,
and Chùzhí considered this the result of his own virtue, thus feeling assured.
Everyone knew these were ominous signs,
saying:
"Snakes dwell in mountains and marshes but now occupy human dwellings,
magnies nest in trees but now settle in fields.
When petty men usurp positions and rise above,
it is a sign that they will lose their proper place."
Soon after,
Chùzhí was indeed deposed and died.
History of the Five Dynasties
Jǐng Huàn served as the magistrate of Báishí in Bìzhōu.
While traveling, he crossed the Bā Ridge,
reaching the Jade Maiden Temple,
where a giant serpent lay coiled across his path,
its body measuring over seven feet in diameter,
with scales larger than door panels,
a massive head,
and a tail extending down the mountain,
accompanied only by the sound of crashing trees echoing through the valley.
His attendants were terrified,
unable to proceed,
so they temporarily took shelter in a mountain cave,
and from a high vantage point observed it,
only seeing its tail by the end of the day,
thus realizing that fish large enough to swallow boats and birds vast enough to obscure the sky truly exist.
From "Casual Tales of Idle Men"
During the Xuānhé era,
a scholar's household in Càizhōu had a small snake suddenly appear in their study.
Its patterns were brilliantly colored,
winding between desks and shelves.
It showed no fear upon seeing people,
nor did anyone dare harm it.
It would only appear daily during the sì hour (9-11 AM),
and by noon it would vanish,
repeating this pattern every day.
The scholar found this strange,
so he waited for its appearance and captured it,
placing it in a wire basket.
When he checked at noon,
it had turned hard and cold, transformed into stone.
Its substance was exquisitely formed by nature,
surpassing even ghostly craftsmanship.
The next day at the sì hour,
it would wriggle again,
then once more become stone,
with its coiling and stretching postures
changing daily.
The scholar treasured it,
brought it to the capital,
and showed it to the court eunuch Liáng Shīchéng.
Liáng exclaimed in admiration:
"This is where the divine work of creation resides!
In the palace, there are jade rats and jade rabbits
that appear at their designated hours—
this is one such object."
The scholar then presented it as a gift.
(From Yǔ Jiǎn)
Initially,
Wú Lín served as the Grand Military Commissioner in Shǔ,
and because the Shā Jīn Píng area was densely overgrown,
he feared that bandits might hide within it,
intending to burn it but had not yet made it public.
Suddenly, an old woman with a child came straight to the camp gate,
saying:
"I've heard the Commissioner plans to burn the mountain;
this is a military order I dare not obstruct,
but my mother and child have long lived here,
and we cannot leave immediately.
I beg for a brief delay of one day,
to allow us to move away,
so that my child and I may preserve our lives."
Wú scolded her:
"What kind of demon are you?"
The woman replied:
"If you must kill me,
I can destroy your entire clan."
Enraged, Wú ordered his guards to seize her,
but she suddenly vanished,
so he set fire to the mountain from all sides.
The next day,
a large snake was found burned to death under the cliff,
tens of zhang in length;
and a smaller snake,
over one zhang long.
When the fire was set,
a burst of black smoke rose in the flames,
heading southeast.
At that time, the Commissioner's son Tǐng's wife was pregnant,
and she gave birth to Xī,
precisely when the mountain was burning.
Xī later became the Military Commissioner of Sìchuān,
betrayed the court,
accepted a noble title from the Jīn,
and was enfeoffed as the King of Shǔ.
In Xīngzhōu, two suns were seen rubbing against each other,
the night sky turned red as blood,
and the light illuminated the ground like daytime.
"Records from the Rivers and Lakes" Ān Bǐng Zǐwén, along with Yáng Jùyuán and Lǐ Hǎoyì, conspired to forge an edict and execute him.
The edict stated:
"With arms, I reflect on my own person,
I have been blind to the sages' warnings;
though even dogs and horses know their master,
you willingly became a subject of barbarian slaves!
The state has constant punishments,
your crime is beyond pardon."
These words were from Hǎoyì's brother-in-law Yáng Jūnyù.
"Jade Dew from Crane Forest"
The two-headed snake,
these are common beyond the mountains.
Sometimes there are ones as thick as a small finger,
over a foot long,
with red scales on the belly,
and brocade patterns on the back,
one head having a mouth and eyes,
the other resembling a head but lacking a mouth and eyes.
It is said that both heads can move forward and backward,
but this is also incorrect.
In the past, Sūnshū Áo considered seeing it unlucky,
so he killed and buried it,
fearing others might see it and suffer its misfortune.
Southerners see it as ordinary,
so where does the misfortune lie?
"Lǐngbiǎo Lù Yì": The two-headed snake is also named Yuèwáng's tied hair,
and folklore considers seeing it inauspicious.
"Jiān Míng Yuàn": The two-headed snake is non-venomous,
and indigenous people use it as bait.
"Nányuè Zhì": Jì Sēngzhēn encountered his mother's funeral,
and upon opening the tomb, found a five-colored two-headed snake.
"Nán Shǐ"
The Hàn River again flows east and converges with Luò Valley,
where the valley has two sources that join,
together pouring into one ravine west of Shénshé Shù.
On its left and right, the mountain streams abound with multicolored snakes,
which are tame and gentle by nature,
and do not harm other creatures.
The "Water Classic"
In Diānchí and Huángjīn River there is a giant serpent,
named Qīngcōng,
which enjoys devouring humans.
There is also a large serpent concealed in trees,
waiting for deer to pass by,
coiling around them,
and swallowing them only after the deer dies.
After swallowing,
the serpent also coils around the tree,
causing the antlers and bones to pierce through its skin,
nearly killing the serpent.
Once the wound heals, it resumes killing and swallowing deer.
"Records of the Universe"
In the Jiǔzhēn region's Long River, there is a hook snake,
which eats humans.
If one kills this snake,
it will cause death;
if not,
it will pursue and take revenge on the person,
never ceasing.
Even among a crowd of people,
it will go to harm the killer,
with almost no chance of failure.
It is also said that the hook snake is several zhang long,
with a hook at the end of its tail,
which it uses to catch people and livestock on the shore to eat them.
In the Shànghuìchuān Xìnggǔ Commandery, there is a large snake,
several zhang long,
with a forked tail like a hook,
which uses its tail to hook people and horses on the shore from the water to eat them.
"Records of the Commanderies and States"
Féiyí On Mount Tàihuà there is a snake called Féiyí,
with six legs and four wings.
When it appears, there is a great drought under heaven.
From the "Classic of Mountains"
Mount Lín has many Míngshé,
their form like snakes,
with four wings and a sound like chime stones,
when they appear, there is great drought.
Above
I, the solitary one, on the day of Sì, in the mountains, am called the solitary one;
I am the snake in the shrine.
The Bàopǔzǐ states that on the day of Sì, it is not appropriate to kill snakes.
The Yǒuyáng
If a snake refuses to come out when dragged backward,
prick its tail with a needle and it will emerge immediately.
From "Suǒsuì Lù"
To distinguish a snake's gender,
use a soft, fine object to place on the snake.
If it becomes agitated and restless,
it should be known as male;
if it remains still and unmoving,
it should be known as female.
As stated in the Zá Bǎozàng Jīnglǜ:
"Testing a snake with white cotton
reveals differences in its movement or stillness."
Nèidiǎn
Planting millet attracts snakes,
burning goat horns and hair
will make snakes dare not come.
"Qiǎn Zǎi"
In autumn, the venom of vipers is at its peak,
and if they have nothing to bite, they release their venom onto plants and trees.
The plants and trees immediately wither and die.
If woodcutters gather these plants and trees
and happen to be injured or pricked by them, it can also be fatal.
"Records of Diverse Matters" Liu Yao led his troops into Féngyì.
Emperor Mǐn sought reinforcements from Prince Bǎo of Nányáng,
but Bǎo's advisors debated, saying:
"If a viper bites your hand,
a brave man cuts off his wrist.
Let us cut off the Lǒng road
and observe how the situation develops."
Attendant Gentleman Péi Shēn said:
"If the snake has already bitten your head,
can you cut off your head?"
"Biography of Lǐ Jìng of Jin" The King of Qí said:
"If venom stings your hand, cut off the hand;
if it stings your foot, cut off the foot.
Why? Because they endanger the body."
"Former Biography of Tián Dān"
The Fish Star governs yin and yang and knows the timing of clouds and rain.
Thus it is praised saying:
"The Fish Star in Hànzhōng is like clouds and rain.
The divination states: When the Fish Star is bright and large,
rivers and seas all overflow.
It is also said: When the Fish Star is bright and large, then yin and yang are harmonious;

"Duàn Chéngshì's Poem"
Zhān Hé used a single cocoon filament as his fishing line,
a fine needle as his hook,
a slender mulberry branch as his rod,
and split grains as bait,
to land a cart-filling fish from the hundred-fathom deep abyss.
In the rushing currents,
his line did not break,
his hook did not straighten,
his rod did not bend.
When King Chǔ heard of this, he found it remarkable,
summoned Zhān Hé to inquire about the reason.
Zhān Hé said:
"I heard from my late father's words
about Pú Qiězǐ's archery:
with a weak bow and fine silk cord,
riding the wind he released it,
piercing two cranes amid the blue clouds.
His mind was focused,
his hand movements even.
I followed this principle,
emulated it and learned fishing for five years,
before fully mastering the way.
When I stand by the river holding my rod,
my mind has no distracting thoughts,
only the thought of fish.
I cast the line and sink the hook,
my hand neither light nor heavy,
nothing can disturb it.
When fish see my hook and bait,
they appear like sinking dust and gathering foam,
swallowing them without suspicion.
This is how one can use weakness to overcome strength,
use lightness to bring forth heaviness.

In Kūnmíng Pond there is a numinous marsh,

The pond connects to White Deer Plain,
where a man was fishing,
and his line broke as he left.
He appeared in Emperor Wǔ's dream,
asking to remove the hook.
Three days later,
while amusing himself by the pond,
the Emperor saw a large fish holding the line in its mouth,
and said:
"Is this not the fish from my dream yesterday?
So he took the hook and released it.
After two days,
the Emperor again visited the pond,
and by the bank obtained a pair of bright pearls,
upon which he said:
"Could this be the fish's repayment?

Gěng Huìchāng during the Five Phoenixes era again proposed tripling the sea tax,
and the emperor approved his plan.
Xiāo Wàngzhī memorialized:
"The former censor's subordinate Xú Gōng, whose home was in Dōnglái,
said that when the sea tax was increased in previous years,
fish stopped appearing.
The elders all said that during Emperor Wǔ's time when the government once engaged in fishing itself,
sea fish disappeared;
later when fishing was returned to the people,
fish then reappeared.
The interaction of yīn and yáng,
the mutual response among creatures,
applies to all matters.

Yáng Xù was fond of eating raw fish,
while serving as the Assistant to the Grand Administrator of Nányáng.
Fàn Zuò Jiāo Jiǎn presented him with a carp,

When Jiǎn offered another one,
Yáng Xù then showed him the dried fish he had hung up,
to deter his intention.
"Xiè Chéng's Records" Wáng Shěnzhī gave fish to his assistant Huáng Tāo,
and Xú Yǎn drafted a thank-you note on his behalf,

placed on the carved plate,

Zuǒ Cī,
courtesy name Yuánfàng,
was once in Cáo
Cāo's presence when Cáo said:

Thereupon, Zuǒ Cī requested a bronze basin filled with water,
and using a bamboo rod with bait, fished in the basin.
In a short while,
he pulled out a perch.
Cáo Cāo said:
"One fish is not enough for all present at the banquet;
can you get more?"
So he baited the hook again and cast it into the water,

he pulled out more fish,

From the "Book of the Later Hàn."
Gě Xuán saw a man selling a large fish,
and Xuán said to him:
"May I trouble this fish to go to the River Earl's place for a moment?
The fish owner said:
"The fish is already dead.
Xuán said:
"No problem.
He wrote with cinnabar on paper and placed it in the fish's mouth,
then threw it into the water.
After a short while,
the fish leaped back onto the shore,
spitting out ink writing,
blue-black in color,
that flew away like tree leaves.
Another time, Xuán was sitting in a tower with the King of Wú,

Xuán said:
"Rain is easy to get.
He immediately wrote a talisman and placed it in the water,

heavy rain came pouring down.
The Emperor said:

Xuán wrote another talisman and threw it into the water,
and in a moment,
hundreds of large fish appeared.
He had people prepare them.
"Records of Former Worthies of Rǔnán"
Jiè Xiàng was discussing with the King of Wú,
when grey mullet was mentioned as the finest delicacy.
So he dug a pit in the palace courtyard,
filled it with drawn water,
and asked for a fishing rod.
After Jiè Xiàng baited the hook,
he caught a grey mullet in no time.
The astonished and delighted emperor
then ordered the cook to slice it.
Jiè Xiàng also went to Shǔ to buy ginger,
and returned after a short while.
From "Biographies of the Divine Immortals."
Gān Shǐ said,
take a pair of carp,
make one of them hold medicine in its mouth,
and throw both into boiling oil.
The one with the medicine thrashed its tail and flapped its fins,
swimming and diving,
as if in a deep pool,
while the other was already cooked and ready to eat.
I then asked:

"This medicine comes from over ten thousand miles away,

Cáo Zhí's "Discourse on Discerning the Way"
Hǎo Lóng served as General Huán's Southern Barbarian Adjutant.
On the third day of the third month during a gathering,
they composed poems,
and those unable to do so were penalized with three shēng of wine.
Hǎo Lóng initially accepted the penalty for being unable,
but after drinking,
he grabbed a brush and immediately wrote one line,
saying
"The jūyú leaps in the clear pond."
General Huán asked:
"What is a jūyú?"
He replied:
"Barbarians call fish jūyú."
General Huán said:
"Why use barbarian language when composing poetry?"
Hǎo Lóng said:
"I traveled a thousand lǐ to serve you,
only to become a barbarian office adjutant—"
"how could I avoid using barbarian language?"
From A New Account of the Tales of the World.
Yú Xiàofù served as Shìzhōng,
and was favored by Xiàowǔ.
Once, while attending a banquet,
the emperor casually asked,
"You are in the household,
have you never offered any suggestions or critiques?"
Xiàofù's home was near the sea,
and suspecting the emperor had some request,
he replied,
"The weather is still warm,
and the zé fish and shrimp sauce cannot yet be procured,
soon there will be something to present."
The emperor laughed heartily,
then drank until he was quite drunk,
going out to bow but unable to rise,
so the emperor said,
"Assist Shìzhōng Yú."
Xiàofù said,
"I am not yet in a position to assist,
nor am I too drunk to cause disorder,
such a gift beyond my station,
I dare not accept."
The emperor was very pleased.
"The Book of Jìn" states that the jì fish is found in Dōnglái.

"Zé"
is also written as
"jì"
character,
pronounced 'jì,' also pronounced 'zhì.'

roasted it's sweet and delicious.

than to give up the zé fish forehead."
"Records of Strange Things from Línhǎi"
During the Lóng'ān era,
a commoner named Chén Xìng from Dāntú built a fish weir by the river.
When the tide receded,
he found a woman in the weir,
six chǐ tall,
with a beautiful appearance,
no clothes,
motionless as the water withdrew,
lying on the sand,
and unresponsive when spoken to.
One of the men proceeded to rape her.
Chén Xìng dreamed at night:
"I am Jiāng Huáng,
yesterday I lost my way,
and fell into your weir,
the water people insulted me,
now I shall kill him."
Chén Xìng dared not return,
waited for the tide to come,
and followed the water away.
The rapist soon fell ill and died.
From "Records of Heard Knowledge": Mermaids,
the larger ones from the Eastern Sea,
are five to six chǐ long,
shaped like humans,
with eyebrows, eyes, mouth, nose, hands, and head all like a beautiful woman,
nothing lacking.
Their skin and flesh are white as jade,
scales with fine hair,
multicolored,
light and soft,
one to two cùn long.
Hair like a horse's tail,
five to six chǐ long.
Their private parts are no different from those of men and women.
Widowers and widows along the coast often capture them,
raising them in ponds,
during intercourse,
no different from humans,
and they do not harm people.
When the court official Chá Dào was sent as an envoy to Gāolì,
he anchored at a mountain one evening,
and saw a woman in the sand,
in red garments, bare-shouldered,
her hair disheveled,
with slight red scales on her elbows.
Chá ordered the boatman to push her into the water with a pole,
taking care not to injure her.
The woman, upon reaching the water,
turned over on her back,
looked at Chá, bowed with hands clasped, danced with emotion, and disappeared.
The boatman said:
"I have been at sea,
but never understood what this thing is."
Chá said:
"This is a mermaid,
capable of intercourse with humans.
In water,
they resemble human nature."
From "Records of the Unusual."
Lú Xún, in the fifth year of the Yìxī era, sailed down from Guǎngzhōu,
anchoring his ships west of the river,
where many of his troops died of plague.
After the matter was settled,
people who went to Càizhōu
found all the hair of the dead,
transformed into sheatfish.
Also, Sīmǎ Zhāng Shìzhān, gazing at the lake's edge,
saw a coffin,
on the head of which was a sheatfish.
The crowd tried to have it removed for a look,
and it turned out to be hair,
with some not yet fully transformed.
One account says that during life, washing the hair with glutinous rice water,
after death, the hair turns into shàn.
Also, in the past, there was a person who could not eat without shàn,
and after death, when the coffin was opened, it was full of shàn.
Shàn,
is the same as sheatfish.
"Yì Yuàn"
Xiè Língyùn was governing Yǒngjiā when,
he visited the Stone Gate Cave,
and by the side of Mùhè Creek,
he saw two women washing yarn.
Their faces were delicate and beautiful,
unlike ordinary mortal appearances.
He teased them with a poem,
saying:
"I am Xiè Kānglè,
with one arrow I shoot two cranes;
may I ask you yarn-washing maidens,
where did the arrow land?"
The two women paid him no attention, aloof and indifferent.
He teased them again, saying:
"Whose daughters are you, washing yarn?
Your fragrant sweat dampens the new rain,
silent and wordless before others,
what matter makes you endure such hardship?"
Then the two women softly chanted:
"We are the crucian carps in the deep pool,
temporarily out by the stream to feed.
After feeding, we return to the pool ourselves;
how could one find our cloud-like traces?"
After chanting, they vanished.
Kānglè then turned back.
"The Qīngtián Records"
In the Bright Moon Gorge, there are two streams,
flowing east and west.
In the second year of the Shēngpíng era of Emperor Shùn of the Sòng dynasty,
a man named Wēishēng Liàng from the streams caught a white fish,
three chǐ long,
and placed it in his boat,
covering it with grass.
When he returned to cook it,
he saw a beautiful woman beneath the grass,
pure, fair, and graceful,
around sixteen or seventeen years old.
She claimed to be the daughter of Gāotáng,
who had temporarily transformed into a fish to swim
and was caught by him.
Liàng asked:
"Since you are human,
can you become my wife?"
The woman replied:
"Our hidden bond has made it so,
why would it be impossible?"
For the next three years, she was Liàng's wife,
then suddenly said:
"My allotted time is complete,
I must return to Gāotáng."
Liàng asked:
"When will you come back?"
She answered:
"When feelings cannot be forgotten,
I will return with longing."
After that, she came and went three or four times a year,
and her eventual fate is unknown.
From "Records of the Three Gorges"
Chǔ Yànhuí was appointed Supervisor of the Secretariat and Palace Attendant during the Yuánhuī era.
At that time, Huáiběi was under Wèi control,
and jiāngnán had no abalone.
Occasionally some would be arduously obtained and brought there,
with one piece worth several thousand coins.
Someone presented thirty pieces of abalone to Yànhuí.
Though Yànhuí held high rank then, he was extremely impoverished,
and a disciple suggested selling them,
saying:
"We could get ten million coins.
Yànhuí's countenance changed,
and he said:
"I consider this to be food,
not wealth or goods.
Moreover, I didn't know it could be sold for money,
and simply accepted it.
Though I am indeed poor and lacking,
how could I sell provisions to obtain money?
He shared them all with relatives and friends to eat,
and they were finished within a few days.

In the ninth year of the Yǒngmíng era,
at Shípǔ in Yánguān County, a sea fish came riding the tide,
and when the water receded, it could not leave.
It was over thirty zhǎng in length,
black and scaleless,
and while still alive, it made a sound like an ox.
The locals called it a "hǎi yàn,"
and they took its meat to eat.
"Wǔxíng Zhì of the Southern Qí"
When Wáng Sù first arrived in the country,
he did not eat mutton or dairy products such as yogurt,
often having crucian carp soup for meals instead.
After several years had passed,
Sù attended a palace banquet with Emperor Gāozǔ,
where he consumed a large amount of mutton and yogurt porridge.
Emperor Gāozǔ found this strange
and said to Sù:
"You are accustomed to the flavors of the Central Plains;
how does mutton compare to fish soup?"
Sù replied:
"Mutton
is the finest of land products;
fish
is the best among aquatic creatures.
Preferences differ,
yet both are considered delicacies.
In terms of taste,
they are indeed superior or inferior:
mutton is like the great states of Qí and Lǔ,
while fish resembles the small states of Zhū and Jǔ."
Prince Péngchéng said to Sù:
"Why do you favor the small states?"
He replied:
"What is cherished in one's hometown,
one cannot but favor."
Records of the Buddhist Monasteries of Luoyang
In the third year of Tàihé era,
Empress Dowager Wénmíng, Madame Féng, visited the hot springs at Mólín Palace in Jīnhé Prefecture,
where she caught a pair of carp,
each three chǐ long.
She pierced their gills with golden locks
and released them into the pond.
Later, they grew to five chǐ long,
submerging and surfacing together.
On the fifth day of the fifth month in the first year of Zhèngguāng era,
the sky was clear and the air crisp.
A clanging sound was heard from the pond,
the water churned violently,
and in moments, thunder and lightning struck.
One carp soared into the sky, transforming into a five-colored rainbow and departing,
vanishing only after a long while.
The other remained in the pond.
By the sixth month of the first year of Xiàochāng era,
Yuán Yuān, the regional inspector on a northern campaign, stopped here
and drained the pond to catch the fish.
Its scales were extraordinary,
so Yuān ordered it killed,
yielding two jīn and eight liǎng of gold.
The following year, Yuān was killed by Gé Róng.
From "Jìzhōu Tújīng" and "Jùnguó Zhì".
According to Xíng Zǐlì's Geographical Records: At the beginning of the Yánxīng era of the Northern Wei Dynasty,
a man named Sūn Yuàn from Wén'ān was fishing in the Wǔqú River.
A school of fish came from the west in the water,
and together they blocked it with firewood.
Suddenly, someone said to Yuàn:
"In a moment,
you will catch a big fish.
If you desire more gains,
you should not kill it.
Yuàn offered to share a meal with him,
but only noticed that his breath was slightly fishy and his clothes were stained with grease.
When he was about to leave,
Yuàn offered him fish as a gift,
but he firmly declined.
After he left,
Yuàn cast his net and indeed caught a big fish,
which resembled a carp but was larger.
Yuàn considered it a valuable catch,
so he killed and ate it.
Suddenly,
wind and rain darkened the day,
and the sound of flying birds was heard.
When the wind subsided,
and the rain cleared,
someone arrived by boat,
and ahead, countless fish were seen
flying into the sea.
Yuàn then gave up fishing altogether.
Thus, the place where they entered the sea was called "Flying Fish Mouth."
From "Xuānshì Zhì".
At the foot of Xiàn Mountain, in the Hàn River, emerges the bream fish,
plump and delicious.

using wooden stakes to block the river, hence called "stake-headed bream."
During the Song dynasty, Zhāng Jìng'ér served as governor,

Jìng'ér built six large ships,
loaded them with fish and presented them,
saying:
"I offer one thousand six hundred stake-headed, short-necked bream."

someone presented him with two live carp.

"This is what I sensed in my dream.

saying:
"We will ensure your longevity.

From "Liáng Shū" quoting "Yù Lǎn"

the common people were terrified,

In the fourth year,
in Liángjùn there was Qīnglíng Water,
its surface spanning about two lǐ,
which was the place where Wèi Píng obtained the great turtle.
South of Qīnglíng Water there was a transverse canal,
running southeast to Yáshān County,
and entering the Tōngjì Canal to the west.
At that time, there was much rain,
and the ditches and canals were all full.
Suddenly, a large fish resembling a carp,
but with a single horn on its head,
over a chǐ in length,
and scales of bright red,
emerged from Qīnglíng Water,
with a head about three chǐ long.
It entered the transverse canal and swam northwest against the current for over ten lǐ,

At that time, several hundred people followed along the banks to watch,
all saying:
"A red dragon with large scales,
emerging from the depths,

During the reign of Emperor Suí Yángdì,
Cháng Jùn was sent as an envoy to the Chìtǔ Kingdom.
Upon returning and entering the sea,
he saw green fish flying in groups above the water,
floating on the sea for over ten days.
Reaching east of Línyì,
they sailed along the mountains,
the seawater appearing yellow in color,
with a foul, fishy smell.
After sailing for a day without it ceasing,
it was said to be the excrement of a giant fish.
"History of the Northern Dynasties" In the past, someone traveled the Eastern Sea,
then encountered fierce winds,
and the ship, being patched up, could not be controlled,
drifting with the wind and waves,
not knowing where they were headed.
After a day and a night,
they found a solitary islet,
and the companions rejoiced,
dropping stones and mooring the cable,
they went ashore to cook food,
but before the food was cooked, the islet sank.
Those on the ship cut the cable,
and the ship drifted again.
The former solitary islet
was actually a giant fish,
which, enraged,
raised its tail and fins,
sucking in and spitting waves,
moving swiftly as the wind,
and those on the islet
suffered over ten deaths.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital" Lǐ Chóngjǔ saw a giant fish on a sand island in the sea,
cut open its belly,
and found a small boat inside,
along with three dead people,
their clothes still intact.
"Casual Talks from the Secret Pavilion" The sea whale,
is the largest creature in the sea,
even the smaller ones are over a thousand feet long.
The saying that it can swallow a boat
is certainly not false.
Every year, Guǎngzhōu often dispatches ships,
to trade past Nán'ān.
A person from Běihǎi happened to join this voyage,
and within a year, his hair turned speckled with white,
saying they passed through the deep and wide area of Tiáolí,
and saw over ten mountains,
some emerging, some submerging,
at first greatly surprised by it.
The boatman said:
"Those are not mountain islands,
but the backs of whales.
Indeed, they saw eyes flashing,
fins like winnowing baskets.
In a moment of peril,
at noon, a sudden drizzle fell,
the sailor said:
"This is the whale spraying water,
dispersing into the air,
blown by the wind,
resembling rain.
As they approached,
the fish drummed against the ship and made noise,
then suddenly submerged and left.
"Strange Records from Lǐngnán" Wáng Shīzhōng was the prefect of Dēngzhōu.
One day,
an unusually strong wind arose,
he called and asked the elders,
who said:
"A sea whale is about to pass here,
it always brings strong winds first.
The next day,
Shīzhōng climbed Pénglái Pavilion to wait for it.
After a short while,
the fish arrived,
its head unseen,
but its back like a mountain,
emerged from the water,
vaguely moving from north to south,
taking two days to finally see its tail.
"Supplementary Records of Collected Tales" Shěn Zuòzhé once welcomed relatives by the sea,
reaching Pǔtuó Mountain,
he saw flags and banners miles away in the sea,
like an army of tens of thousands of cavalry,
churning and surging eastward.
He asked the locals,
who said:
"That is a giant fish.
What looks like flags and banners,
are actually its scales and fins.
After a short while,
it came closer,
and the mountain rocks shook from it.
"Simple Notes from Lodgings" In the south, it was once clear,
and two mountains in the sea appeared like dark eyebrows,
seafarers said they were six hundred lǐ from shore on each side,
when suddenly a storm with thunder and rain occurred,
the fog and dew all turned foul,
mixed with mud and slime,
lasting for seven days before stopping.
It happened that someone came from the mountain,
saying a giant fish roared and blew foam,
one of its gills caught on the mountain peak for seven days,
causing the mountain to break,
and it couldn't leave,
its cries became thunder,
its breath became wind,
its foam became fog.
"Records of Strange Things from Lǐngnán" In Zhēnlà Kingdom, there is a fish called jiàntóng,
with four legs and no scales,
a nose like an elephant,
sucking water and spraying it up,
reaching fifty or sixty feet high.
There is also the fúhú fish,
shaped like a loach,
with a beak like a parrot,
and eight feet,
often half of a giant fish emerges,
looking like a mountain from a distance.
"History of the Northern Dynasties, Chapter 83" The largest in the Eastern Sea,
is the fish of the Eastern Sea.
Travelers at sea meet its head on the first day,
and its tail on the seventh day.
When the fish gives birth for three days,
the blue sea turns red because of it.
"Records of the Mysterious Middle" A seafarer and a mountain dweller debated their local products.
The seafarer said:
"Across the sea, there is a fish,
with a forehead like the peak of Huàshān,
sucking in waves covering ten thousand qǐng.
The mountain dweller said:
"In the Dèng Forest, there is a tree,
with a circumference of thirty thousand xún,
reaching straight up for a thousand lǐ,
shading several countries beside it.
Someone said:
"At the eastern extreme, there is a giant,
who cuts trees for a whip,
but they are too short to support;
fishes for food,
but it's not enough to satisfy hunger.
"Master Sūn Zǐ" Mountain dwellers do not believe in fish as large as trees,
large as wood,
and seafarers do not believe in trees as large as fish.
"Family Instructions of the Yán Clan" The Black River,
is the North Pole,
its water thick and stagnant,
with dense clouds emerging above.
There is a black kūn a thousand feet long, like a whale,
often flying and swimming in the Southern Sea.
"Records of Omissions Collected" Yíngzhōu, also called Soul Island,
or Huán Island.
Beside the island is a deep abyss,
a thousand lǐ wide,
where a fish resides.
It is a thousand zhàng long,
with brilliantly colored scales,
a horn on its nose,
often dancing and playing in groups.
Some who watch from afar
see five colors in the water,
and clouds descending upon it,
which are actually this fish spraying water to form clouds.
Once, five hundred merchants went to sea to seek treasures,
encountered the Makara fish king opening its mouth,
the ship sped away quickly,
the shipmaster asked those on the deck:
"What do you see?
They replied:
"We see three suns,
and a great white mountain.
The water flows rushing,
as if into a large pit.
The shipmaster said:
"The three suns:
one is the real sun,
two are the fish's eyes.
The white mountain is the fish's teeth.
The rushing water is entering the fish's mouth.
We are doomed.
At that time, there was an upāsaka on the ship,
who told everyone to chant "Namo Buddha" together,
and the fish closed its mouth,
saving everyone's lives.
"The Great Treatise" There are three salty flavors in the sea:
one is from the giant fish in the sea,

"Sūtra of the Storehouse" The Buddha said the wish-fulfilling pearl

The fish's body is two hundred eighty thousand lǐ long,

The Tang Code stipulated: If one catches a carp, it should be released immediately;

Tàizōng observed fish at the Western Palace,

Zhōu Lìzhēn,

The provincial governor dined on vegetables with Lìzhēn,

Lìzhēn said:

In the twenty-first year of the Kāiyuán era,
a fish with an inscription was caught in Qúzhōu
and presented as tribute.
Attendant-in-Chief Péi Guāngtíng and others submitted a memorial of congratulations,
stating:
"Fish and dragons form auspicious diagrams,
emanating from the Hé and Luò rivers.
Compared to this glorious brilliance,
how could others be worthy of mention?
The court received Zhāng Jiǔlíng's "Congratulatory Ode on the Auspicious Fish Inscription," which said:
"The fish serves as an emblem of the dragon,
already revealing the origin of the Mandate of Heaven;
the inscription forms enduring script,
further signifying the eternal bestowal of years.
When Hán Yù first arrived in Cháozhōu,
he inquired about the people's hardships,
and they all said:
"The Èxī has crocodiles,
which have nearly devoured all the livestock,
leaving the people impoverished.
A few days later,
Hán Yù personally went to inspect it,
ordering his subordinate Qín Jì to throw a sheep and a pig into the river and offer prayers.
On the evening of the prayer,
a violent storm with thunder and lightning arose from the river,
and after a few days, the water completely dried up,
shifting sixty li westward.
From then on, Cháozhōu was free from the crocodile menace.
"The Book of Táng" records: Wáng Qízhí, while governing Cháozhōu,
caught a crocodile,
as large as a boat,
and had it painted as a picture.
Its shape resembled a tuó (Chinese alligator),
with a beak half the length of its body,
teeth like a saw's teeth,
and a tail with three hooks,
extremely sharp.
When encountering deer or pigs, it would use its tail to spear them for food.
It laid many eggs,
some of which became fish or tuó,
but only one or two developed into crocodiles.
"Lǐngbiǎo Zhì" states: The crocodile's body is earth-yellow,
with four legs,
a long tail,
and a shape like a tuó,
but it moves swiftly.
Its mouth is full of sharp teeth,
often harming people.
Deer in the south are most afraid of this creature.
When deer run along the cliffs,
and a group of crocodiles roar below,
the deer become terrified and fall off the cliffs,
often caught by the crocodiles—
an example of one creature subduing another.
Thus, when Grand Marshal Lǐ Déyù was demoted to Cháozhōu,
passing by Crocodile Beach,
his boat was damaged,
and his lifelong treasures, ancient books, and paintings were lost in the water.
He then summoned a Kunlun slave from the ship to retrieve them,
but they saw many crocodiles
and dared not approach,
realizing it was a crocodile den.
"Lǐngbiǎo Lù Yì" notes: In the South Sea, there are crocodiles resembling tuó.
If their heads are cut off and dried,
their beaks lose teeth but regenerate,
repeating this three times before stopping.
"Bówù Zhì" says: Crocodiles like to lay eggs on sand,
as large as goose eggs,
which are edible.
"Jiāozhōu Jì" records: People in Guǎngzhōu say crocodiles can chase cattle and horses on land,
capsize boats in water,
and kill people, but when encountering nets,
they dare not touch them,
showing such caution.
"Gǎnyìng Jīng" mentions: Crocodiles are also called Hūléi,
and bears can subdue them,
gripping their snouts to the shore,
tearing and eating them.
Another name is Gǔléi,
which transforms into a tiger in autumn,
emerging with three claws.
They are abundant in Yīngpān Village near the sea in Sīléi and other prefectures of the South Sea.
"Héwén Jì" describes: In the south, there are crocodiles
with beaks eight feet long,
most active in autumn.
If people are by boats,
the fish may emerge to eat them,
so people carry spears by the boat's side for defense.
"Yú Xǐ Zhìlín" states: Large crocodiles are two to three zhàng long,
with four legs,
resembling a gecko,
and often swallow people.
King Fàn Xún of Fúnán ordered them captured,
placed in moats,
and those he was angry with
were bound and fed to the crocodiles.
If the person deserved death,
the crocodile would not eat them,
and they were released,
considered innocent.
"Wú Shí Wàiguó Zhuàn" notes: In Línyì Kingdom, crocodiles were kept in city moats,
with tigers enclosed outside the gates.
Those guilty were fed to the fierce beasts.
If the crocodiles did not eat them,
they were deemed innocent,
and released after three days.
"Nánshǐ" records: In Zhànchéng Kingdom, there was a crocodile pond.
For disputes the officials could not resolve,
they had the two parties ride water buffaloes across the pond.
The guilty one would be emerged and eaten by the crocodile,
while the innocent could pass multiple times,
and the crocodile would emerge but not eat them.
"Yíngyá Shènglǎn"
White birds fly by Xīsài Mountain's side,
Peach blossoms fall on streams where mandarin fish grow fat.
"Yī Pǐn Jí" records: Mandarin fish have large mouths and fine scales,
with rounded fins and spines,
yellow bodies marked with black patterns,
thick skin and firm flesh,
distinctly different from ordinary fish.
In summer's intense heat,
they prefer hiding in rock crevices,
where people approach to catch them.
Those with particularly bright markings
are males;
those slightly duller
are females.
Fishermen thread a rope through a male's gill and place it by the stream,
where groups of females come to bite it,
clinging stubbornly when pulled,
allowing them to be captured,
often yielding over ten fish.
While most fish lack stomachs and cannot chew,
mandarin fish possess stomachs capable of chewing.
"Ěr Yǎ Yì" notes:
Lǐ Déyù had a giant fish rib bone,
two zhang and five chi long,

it was delivered from Hǎizhōu.
"Jù Tán Lù"
Fēng Yǎn, while a guest in Hǎizhōu, saw someone holding a bundle of black objects,
shaped like bamboo slivers.
He asked the person,
and it turned out to be hair from the gills of a sea creature,
intended to be used as decorative inlays for a screen.
When asked how it was obtained,
the person said that decades ago, a large fish in the Eastern Sea
died on the shore of a mountain,
and this was collected from it,
only suitable for use as screen inlays.
Countless pieces had been used before and after,
and now, for official screen-making,
this unique pattern and unusual color were sought out.
Its texture resembled water buffalo horn,
the small end was like bristles,
the large end was square,
four to five inches long,
and about an inch wide—
truly extraordinary.
Nowadays, the fan-like hairs in the gills of large fish among people are less than an inch long,
but this object was four to five inches long,
indicating the fish was enormous.

The state of Cáo was located north of the Cōnglǐng Mountains,
which was the state of Jìbīn during the Hàn Dynasty.
On the Cōnglǐng Mountains stood a temple dedicated to Shùntiān,
in front of which lay a fish spine bone
with a hollow passage through it,
allowing horses and riders to pass through.
From the "History of the Northern Dynasties"

Rebellious-scale fish,

"Records of Anecdotes"
During the reign of the Qián family's state,
they levied a tax on the fish of West Lake.
Fishermen were required to submit several catties daily,
which was called
"the official household fish."
Those who could not meet the quota by the end of the day
had to buy fish to fulfill it,
causing much grievance and lament among the people.
One day,
when Wǔsù was hosting a grand banquet,
a painting depicting Jiāng Zǐyá fishing with a straight hook at Pánxī was presented.
Wǔsù pointed to it and ordered Luó Yǐn to compose a poem.
Luó Yǐn immediately responded:
"In those days, Lǚ Wàng displayed his grand strategies,
Who could match his skill in fishing for a state?
But had he been born by West Lake's shore,
He too would have had to offer the official household fish."
Wǔsù burst into laughter,
and from then on, the tax was entirely abolished.
From "Casual Conversation Records"
The Gēng family dug a pond and constructed a bamboo railing,
and when stepped on, it made a *cè cè* sound.
The Xīn family dug a pond and constructed a wooden railing,
and when stepped on, it made a *táng táng* sound.
Both families raised fish in their ponds,
and whenever they leaned on the railings to cast feed,
the fish would leap out eagerly.
Over time, merely hearing the *cè cè* and *táng táng* sounds,
even without casting feed, the fish would still leap out eagerly.
Thus, the Gēng family's fish could be named *Cè Cè*;
the Xīn family's fish could be named *Táng Táng*,
a transformation through feeding.

someone brought a giant fish into the capital,

was caught in a fisherman's net,

The Dragon King sends word, missing you here a thousand times over;
the crab is most anxious,

It then leaped into a pond,
and could not be caught again.
That year,
the Yellow River burst its banks massively,
flooding the capital city,

The sturgeon emerges from the rivers and seas,
and in mid-March it ascends from the river.
Its body resembles a dragon,
with a sharp head,
a mouth located beneath the jaw,
and armor covering both its back and belly.
It measures about four to five feet in length and width,
and nowadays it is caught by fishing on the rocky shoals east of Méngjīn.
The larger ones weigh over a thousand pounds,
and can be steamed into a thick soup,
or made into fermented fish,
while their roe can be used to make sauce.
The "Shī Yì Shū" states: Its long nose and soft bones
are edible,
commonly referred to as jade slabs.

The "Pí Yǎ" notes: Nowadays, in Jiāngdōng, sturgeon is called huángyú (yellow fish),

"Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital": The royal sturgeon dwells in caves.
Mountains have caves called xiù,
and this cave is located at Xiǎopíng Mountain south of the Yellow River.
Elders say the royal sturgeon fish
comes from the south,
emerges from this cave,
enters the river water,

floats on the water surface,

Fishermen see it,
catch it to present as tribute,

The larger ones are called royal sturgeon,
the smaller ones are called wèi-wěi,

The flesh is white in color,
but the flavor is not as good as the huso sturgeon.

Zhòngmíng

In Jiāngdōng, the bream fish is called biān,
also known as pī.
