broad and thin yet plump,
calm with little strength,
with fine scales,
it is among the most delicious fish.
The bream from the Liáng River in Liáodōng is especially plump and thick,
even more exquisite than those in the Central Plains.
Hence, the local saying goes:
"For provisions, settle in Jiùliáng,
for bream, the Liáng River's is the one.
The "Explanation of the Book of Songs" notes that a separate market was established south of the Lè River,
named the Four Directions Market,
commonly known as the Yǒngqiáo Market among the people.
Fish from the Yī and Luò rivers
are mostly sold here.
When scholars and commoners need sliced raw fish,
they all go there to obtain it,
as the fish is exceptionally delicious.
A saying in the capital goes:
"Luò carp and Yī bream,
are more prized than cattle and sheep.
From "The Record of the Buddhist Temples in Luòyáng."
The Xù resembles the Fáng but has a large head,
and is an unappetizing fish.
Hence the local saying goes: When buying fish, if you get a Xù,

In Xúzhōu, it is called Lián or sometimes Yōng.
The "Shī Yì Shū" states: With a thick line and heavy bait,
fine fish will take it;
with a fine line and fragrant bait,
common fish will take it.

The jiāyú emerges from the Bǐng Cave.
"Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ" states: To the southeast, one reaches the mouth of the Bǐng River,
which originates from the Bǐng Cave above,
from where the jiāyú emerges.
It typically comes out in the third month
and returns to the cave in the tenth month.
The cave entrance is five to six feet wide,
and seven to eight feet above the ground.
A spring cascades down,
and the fish pass through from below the cave.
The cave entrance faces the bǐng direction (south-southeast),
hence it is called the Bǐng Cave, which flows down into the Bāo River.
"Water Classic" notes: The fish of Bǐng Cave feed on milky water,
and consuming them brings warmth.
"Yǒuyáng" records: The Bǐng Cave is located in Jǐngxiá of Míngtōng County, Bā Commandery,
with a total of ten caves,
among which produce jiāyú.
Their emergence is limited to the Lóngjǐ Shoal of Bāqú,
with black spots on their heads,
said to form from reflecting and interacting with celestial constellations.
They have long bodies and fine scales,
flesh as white as jade,
naturally salty in taste,
likely from consuming salt-like substances.
"Survey of Scenic Spots" describes: Jiāyú have fine scales,
resembling trout.
In Shǔ mountains, they are called zhuōyú.
Rèn Yù's "Records of Yìzhōu" states: Many waters in Yǎzhōu have jiāyú,
some say the flavorful fish in the Yellow River are of this kind.
"Records of Yúnnán" notes: In Lǐ Shàn's annotation on "Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ," it is said: The fish emerge from the cave on bǐng days,
but this is not the case now.
Bǐng refers to
a south-facing cave,
where such fish often thrive;
how could the fish choose bǐng days?
"Běncǎo" by Chén Cángqì states: Current editions do not include this phrase about bǐng days.
Among all fish, only the black snakehead has a gallbladder that is sweet and edible.
It has a tongue,
its scales are fine and patterned,
also named the patterned fish,
it shares energy with snakes,
its head bears stars,
and at night it faces north.
Nowadays, Taoists avoid it,
because its head supports the Dipper.
It is also designated as a taboo creature,
hence there is the saying: the sky taboos the wild goose,
the earth taboos the dog,
and the water taboos the black snakehead.
All are forbidden to be eaten.

The cuttlefish was traditionally called Hé Bó's minor official,
and whenever it encountered large fish, it would release ink,
covering an area of several feet,
to conceal itself.
Some people from Jiāngdōng would use its ink to write contracts to swindle others of their property,

Fishermen say that in the past, when the Qín emperor traveled east,

The Yǒuyáng records that whenever this fish encounters fishing boats,

all with long tails and four legs,
red bellies,

In Nányáng, the Dān River produces dān fish.
Ten days before the Summer Solstice,
keep watch at night.

there was an old woman from Xiāng who often used red seal script charms to cure people's illnesses.
One day,
she told the villagers:
"I must go to Dòngtíng Lake to save hundreds of lives.
A local named Zhāng Gǒng prepared a boat to escort her.
One day before reaching Dòngtíng Lake,
a great storm had tossed a large vessel,
stranding it on Jūnshān Island where it shattered,
carrying nearly a hundred people,
who scattered to dwell across the island.
Suddenly, a white sturgeon,
over ten feet long,
swam along the river.
Dozens of people intercepted it,
beat it to death, and divided its meat to eat.
The next day,
a city wall white as snow
encircled the island,
gradually narrowing and tightening,
trapping the people clustered within,
reducing the space to less than thirty feet.
People from Yuèyáng also glimpsed the snowy wall from afar,
but none could comprehend it.
The old woman then landed on the island and flew her sword to strike it,
the white wall let out a thunderous roar,
and then collapsed,
revealing a giant white sturgeon,
over a thousand feet long,
writhing as it died.
The old woman was none other than Fán Fūrén, wife of Liú Gāng.

crouching under the bed.
They were greatly alarmed,

After slaughtering a soft-shelled turtle,

"Records of Diverse Matters"
The yuán looks like a soft-shelled turtle,
those with red undersides are yuán,
while white ones are soft-shelled turtles.
It is commonly said that the yuán's body has twelve zodiac-associated meats,
and when fishermen catch them,
even if dismembered and cut into pieces,
regardless of size,
those not yet thrown into the boiling pot
can still jump and flee.
Though both soft-shelled turtles and yuán can grow very large,
if bitten by mosquitoes or gnats,
they may die within a day.

A man from Chǔ presented a giant soft-shelled turtle to Duke Líng of Zhèng.
Gōngzǐ Sòng and Zǐjiā were about to have an audience
when Gōngzǐ Sòng's index finger moved involuntarily. He showed it to Zǐjiā, saying:
"Whenever this happens to me,
I am sure to taste some rare delicacy."
When the cook was about to butcher the turtle,
they looked at each other and smiled.
The Duke asked the reason,
and Zǐjiā told him.
When it was time to eat,
the Duke summoned the ministers to share the turtle,
but deliberately excluded Gōngzǐ Sòng.
Furious, Gōngzǐ Sòng dipped his finger into the cauldron,
tasted the soup, and stormed out.
The Duke was enraged
and wanted to kill Gōngzǐ Sòng.
Gōngzǐ Sòng then conspired with Zǐjiā and assassinated Duke Líng in summer.

Duke Jǐng of Qí was crossing the Jiāng and Yuán rivers,
when a giant turtle seized the left outside horse of his team and submerged with it.
Everyone was terrified,
whereupon Gǔ Yězǐ drew his sword and pursued it,
moving diagonally for five lǐ,
then upstream for three lǐ,
until reaching beneath Dǐzhù Rock,
where the turtle was.
He grasped the turtle's head with his left hand,
and held the left outside horse with his right hand,
leaping like a swallow and soaring like a swan, he emerged,
shouting loudly up to the heavens,
causing the water to reverse its flow for three hundred paces,
onlookers all mistook him for the River Earl.

In the Later Hàn Dynasty, the Xī barbarian Tián Qiáng sent his son Lǔ to occupy the Upper City,

and his youngest son Cāng to occupy the Lower City,

From "Yǒuyáng"

"Běi Hù Lù Zhù"
Once there was a man and his servant who both suffered from a heart and abdominal illness,
and treatment could not cure them.
The servant died,
so they cut open his abdomen to examine it,
finding a white turtle inside,
with red eyes,
very vivid.
They tried putting various medicines into the turtle's mouth,
but it still would not die.
Later, someone riding a white horse passed by,
and the horse's urine splashed onto the turtle,
causing it to retract its head and hide in the blood.
They then tried using the urine to pour over it,
and it suddenly dissolved into water.
The patient immediately drank a liter of it,
and was cured.
"Records of the Strange" states: Fāng Gé said that when eating turtle, one must not eat amaranth.
Because he consumed both together,
he began to suffer from severe abdominal pain.
At the time, he almost didn't know the cause,
and people suspected it was due to the turtle and amaranth.
So they had a young servant eat both items,
and the servant then fell ill,
with symptoms similar to Gé's and becoming weak and exhausted,
even more severe,
and soon died abruptly.
They carried the body and placed it in the horse stable,
before it was encoffined,
suddenly countless small turtles surged out from the nine orifices,
scattering and running under the stable,
but whenever they encountered horse urine,
they immediately turned into water.
Gé heard of this,
went to see for himself,
gathered the many turtles,
and poured horse urine over them,
all of which turned into water.
Thereupon, Gé drank horse urine,
and was then cured.
Some say that white horse urine is especially effective.

Zhāng Zé served as an assistant to Fáng Zhīwēn,
and had always been fond of eating turtle.
Suddenly he died a sudden death,
but revived after one night,
saying that he had been summoned by the Lord of Mount Tài to be held accountable for his excessive consumption of turtle.
He was sent by a group of ghosts to be thrown into a boiling cauldron,
where his limbs were dismembered and cooked,
just as one would prepare a turtle.
Once cooked,
he was divided and eaten by the ghosts.
The cruelty, poison, and suffering
were beyond description.
He endured this nearly several dozen times,
before the Lord finally forgave him,

"Having suffered all these torments,
do you dare to offend again?"
He replied:
"I dare not."
Only then was he ordered to be sent back.

Huáng Déguī's family was cooking a turtle,

The family pitied it,

Quēzǐ said:
"The people of Yìqú
cook turtles and terrapins until they are underdone,
so that they are foul and stinking;
the people of the Central States,
even if they have starved for three days without opening their mouths to eat,
would rather die than consume them.
Wú Zhāng and Zhuāng Jí accepted them and blended them,
and when sick people ate them,
their bodies became light;
when the sovereign of ten thousand chariots ate them,
his anger was dispelled.
Thus, turtles and terrapins are extremely foul and stinking,
and cannot be improved.
Yet sick people, by eating them, have their bodies lightened,
and the sovereign of ten thousand chariots, by eating them, has his anger dispelled;
why is this?
It is because the blending of Wú Zhāng and Zhuāng Jí remains.

which were harvested from the Héjiān region.
Every year they were presented as tribute,
breaking ice and using fire for illumination,
hanging aged dog meat
so that when the crabs detected the dog meat they would surface and could be captured.
Each one was worth a hundred coins,
wrapped in felt and honey and sent by courier stations,
galloping on horseback to the capital.
From "Yǒuyáng"
In recent times, a Persian sailed by ship across the sea toward India,
drifted into the vast ocean,
and reached an island,
where he obtained many treasures.
They set sail and traveled with the wind,
when from afar they saw a red object on a peak resembling the shape of a snake.
After a while, it gradually grew larger.
The Persian said:
"The mountain spirit treasures its valuables,
and has come to pursue us.
What can we do about it?"
Everyone on the boat trembled with fear.
Suddenly, they saw two mountains emerge from the sea,
hundreds of zhang high.
The Persian said joyfully:
"These two mountains
are the claws of a giant crab.
This crab often enjoys fighting with the mountain spirit,
and the spirit rarely wins,
fearing it greatly.
Now that its claws have emerged,
we have nothing to worry about."
Soon the great snake arrived,
and the crab engaged in a coiled battle with it for a long time.
The crab clamped the snake's head,
and it died on the water,
looking like a continuous mountain range.
Thus, the people on the boat were saved.
(Guǎng Yì Jì)
Once a man sailing the sea reached an isle,
where the woods were exceedingly lush.
So he moored his boat and went ashore,
and cooked by the water's edge.
Halfway through cooking, the woods submerged underwater,
so he hastily cut the cable and managed to depart.
Upon closer inspection,
it was a giant crab.
"Records of Extraordinary Things"
The Minister Yán Xù held a high position but was unlearned,
and was despised by his contemporaries.
Jiāng Wénwèi composed "The Crab Rhapsody" to satirize him,
saying,
"Outwardly it has many legs, yet inside not an inch of gut.
Its mouth utters irresponsible words,
often losing its way yet puffing warm breath on others.
Within its breast, armor and weapons,
it often gathers its kind to run amok.
Yán Xù was deeply ashamed of this.
"The Wild Record of Xiāngshān"
Táo Gǔ was sent as an envoy to Wúyuè,
where King Zhōngyì hosted a banquet for him.
While eating the mud crab,
he inquired about its varieties,
and Zhōngyì ordered over ten types to be presented, from the mud crab down to the smallest crab.
Gǔ remarked:
"This is truly what is called each generation is worse than the preceding one."
From "Shèng Sòng Shí Yí": Ài Zǐ, why is each crab inferior to the last?
Yúháng wèi Fàn Dá yè mèng jiǎzhòu ér bài yú tíng běi qī rén,
yún:
"Mǒu děng jiē Qián shì shí guīshùn rén,
jīn hǎi xíng shī dào,
sǐ zài jūn shǒu,
xìng jiàn dài yě.
Jì jué,
rén yǒu yǐ yóumóu qī méi wèi xiàn,
yīn qiǎn zòng zhī yú jiāng.
"Chūn Zhǔ Jì Wén"
Zōu Hào was resented by Cài Jīng,
and was exiled to live in Zhāozhōu.
He had a laborer dredge the Gǎnyìng Spring by one or two feet,
and beneath the chaotic rocks, they found a single crab,
which he released into the river himself,
saying:
"Since arriving at the Five Ridges,
I haven't seen this creature for several years.
Beneath the chaotic rocks,
is not a suitable place for it to dwell either,
so how did it emerge from there?
Does not the Yìjīng say,
things cannot remain in difficulty forever,
thus it is followed by the hexagram 'Jiě' (Release).
The crab (xiè),
symbolizes release (jiě),
Heaven has truly revealed this to me.
I shall receive grace and return,
and standing in attendance is something to be anticipated.
Thus, I record this.
From the "Dàoxiāng Collection"
According to ancient lore, in the valley of Nánxīng Shànglǐ in Jiànyáng County, the water was extremely clear and cold,
and it once produced white crabs
with the peculiarity of moving straight forward.
In years of drought,
the villagers would enter the valley,
catch them in basins and carry them back,
and rain would immediately follow.
From "Jiànníng Zhì"
Lǚ Kàng, the prefect of Táizhōu,
commissioned artisans to create a crab chart,
which included twelve species in total: first, the swim crab;
second, the rowing crab;
third, the sword-holding crab;
fourth, the peng crab;
fifth, the jiepu crab;
sixth, the sand dog crab;
seventh, the tide-watching crab;
eighth, the leaning-gaze crab;
ninth, the stone crab;
tenth, the bee river crab;
eleventh, the reed tiger crab;
twelfth, the fiddler crab.
Additionally, maritime merchants reported that east of Chánbì Island in the sea lies another island abundant with crabs,
of remarkably diverse species,
including some with tiger-like heads,
some with wings capable of flight,
some that can catch fish,
and some with shells spanning over a foot in size.
From Fù Jiāyòu's "Treatise on the Twelve Species."
Hóngxiè ké,
yānhóng sè,
jù zhě kěyǐ zhuāng wèi jiǔbēi yě.
Hǔxiè ké,
shàng yǒu hǔ bān,
kě zhuāng wèi jiǔqì,
yǔ hóngxiè jiē chǎn Qióng Yá hǎibiān,
suī fēi zhēnqí,
yì bù yì cǎi dé yě.
"Lǐngbiǎo Lù Yì"
The mantis shrimp,
the larger ones are over a foot long,
with two extremely strong claws.
In August, they can fight tigers,
and the tigers are no match for them.
They molt with the ebb tide,
shedding once to grow once.
"Yǒuyáng"
In August, crabs have awns inside their bellies.
These awns,
which are genuine rice awns,
are about an inch long,
and are offered to the sea god facing east.
If the awns have not been offered,
the crabs should not be eaten.
Upon opening them, seawater is still found inside the belly.
From the "Běncǎo".
Crabs with hair on their underside
can kill people.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The lodestone attracts iron,
and the crab spoils lacquer.
Even if one knows the reason clearly,
they do not know why it is so.
Huainanzi: Like the crab transforming lacquer,
or hemp ruining wine,
these cannot be explained by reason.
Baopuzi: Crab and lacquer combine to form liquid.
Records of Diverse Matters: The nature of the crab spoils lacquer,
and burning it attracts rats.
Materia Medica: If a crab is thrown into lacquer,
it turns into liquid,
and consuming it grants longevity.
If a black dog's blood is poured over it for three days,
then burned,
all rats will gather.
Immortal's Prescription:
To abandon the great Way and rely on petty techniques
is no different from employing a crab to catch rats
or a toad to catch fleas.
This is insufficient to prohibit wickedness and block
evils, and thus disorder grows even more rampant.
Note: By burning mugwort on the crab's shell
and placing it in a burrow,
it will then run frantically through the burrow
and manage to catch just one rat.
《Huái—》
The "Guǎngzhì" states: Pú,
a small crab,
is as large as a coin.
Also, the crab barnacle is like an elm seed,
located in its abdomen,
inseparable in life and death.
"Běihù Lù"
The sea mirror,
called by the people of Guǎng as the glossy leaf plate,
is formed by two shells joined together,
its round shell is very smooth and translucent inside,
when sunlight shines on it, it glows like mica,
inside there is a little flesh like a mussel embryo,
in its abdomen there is a small red crab,
as small as a yellow bean.
The crab has fully developed pincers on the sea mirror,
when hungry, the crab comes out to gather food,
when the crab is full and returns to the abdomen,
the sea mirror is also full.
If pressured by fire,
the small crab will come out,
once it leaves the intestines and abdomen, it immediately dies.
If dissected alive,
the small crab is still alive in the abdomen,
but after a short while, it also dies.
From "Lingbiǎo Lù Yì"
In the South Sea, there is a water creature,
named Kuǎi,
which belongs to the clam category.
Inside it resides a small crab,
as large as an elm seed.
When Kuǎi opens its shell to feed, the crab also emerges to eat;
when Kuǎi closes its shell, the crab returns inside.
It is captured along with Kuǎi and brought back,
remaining inseparable until death.
"Records of Diverse Matters"
The hermit crab has a crab in its belly,
the jellyfish has shrimp for eyes.
From "Rhapsody on the River": The hermit crab,
is over an inch long,
with larger ones being two to three inches long.
Inside its belly, there is a small crab,
resembling an elm seed,
living together in symbiosis,
both helping the hermit crab obtain food.
From "Records of the Southern Yue": When a tree is cut down, its parasitic plants wither;
when grass is weeded, the onion threads wilt;
if the river crab does not return, the hermit crab perishes;
if the mulberry tree is severed, the borers are destroyed.
From "Baopuzi."
The crab's carapace, large and small, is mostly adorned with twelve deep rouge-colored spots,
just as the carp has thirty scales.
Its shell resembles that of the tiger crab or the horseshoe crab,
suitable for making stacked boxes,
while parrot-shaped wine vessels and spiral cups
cannot be mentioned in the same breath.
From the "Records of the Northern Households."
Hào,
a large shrimp,
two or three zhàng in length,
with whiskers several chǐ long,
now in Qīngzhōu called
"xiā yú"
as
"hào"
From the "Ěryǎ"
Shùn acted as the Son of Heaven and had drooping ears,
the people of Guànxiōng came to present pearl shrimp.
From "Jīn Lóu Zǐ"
There is a Dānxiā,
ten zhang long,
with whiskers eight chi long,
having two wings,
its nose like a saw,
it dwells in the purple cassia forests,
using its whiskers to wrap itself in swift currents,
taking this as a resting place.
Mǎ Dān once broke off a Dānxiā whisker to use as a staff,
later discarded the staff and flew away,
the whisker transformed into a cinnabar stone,
by the seaside.
from "Records of the Obscure"
Wú Nányáng Téng Xiū was the governor of Guǎngzhōu.
Someone told Xiū that shrimp whiskers could be as long as one zhàng,
but Xiū did not believe it.
Later, the person intentionally went to the Eastern Sea to obtain shrimp whiskers,
which measured four zhàng and four chǐ in length,
and sealed them to show Xiū.
Only then did Xiū accept it as true.
From "Jiāo Guǎng Jì"
In the South Sea, shrimp heads are made into cups,
with tentacles several feet long,
decorated with gold carvings.
The Governor of Kāngzhōu during the Jìn dynasty often presented one as a tribute,
which Emperor Jiǎnwén used to hold wine.
Before he could drink from it,
the cup leaped outside.
At that time, Qū Ānlián, the Governor of Lújiāng, was quite skilled in divination,
so he was ordered to perform a divination,
and he said:
"Within thirty days,
there will be a report of an anomaly from the rear court."
Indeed, a child was born,
with a human face and the body of a dog.
From "Records of Nányuè."
In the early Dàzú era,
a scholar accompanied an envoy from Silla.
A wind blew them to the Land of Long Beards,
a place called Fúsāng Continent.
Its official ranks included titles like Master Artisan, Wave Suppressor, Servant Official, and Island Patrol,
and the scholar was appointed as Director of Winds,
concurrently holding the position of Royal Son-in-Law.
Seeing that all the consorts and concubines had beards,
he composed a poem:
"Flowers without pistils lack beauty,
women without beards are likewise plain.
If my lord were to send all beardless ones away,
they might not compare to those fully adorned."
The king laughed heartily
and said:
"Could it be that our son-in-law remains captivated by the sight beneath our daughter's chin?"
Later, when visiting the Dragon King of the Sea,
he saw cauldrons filled with shrimp,
among which five or six,
red-colored and as large as arms,
leapt at the sight of guests as if pleading for rescue.
The guide explained:
"These are the shrimp kings."
The Dragon King ordered their release.
From "Yǒuyáng Zálǔ".
Liú Huǐ,
boarding a sea vessel,
suddenly saw two giant lobster shells hanging on the window panel,
complete with heads, tails, pincers, and legs,
each measuring seven to eight feet long,
with the head occupying one portion of it;
their beaks were sharp as blades,
and on the tips of their beaks were feelers,
like red chopsticks,
each two to three feet long,
their paired legs had pincers,
as thick as a person's thumb,
over two feet long,
covered with sharp spines,
like rose branches,
red, sharp, and hard,
untouchable by hand;
their brain shells, baked through, curved over a foot long,
far exceeding the size of cups or bowls.
"Lingbiǎo Lù Yì"
On Guǎngzhōng's Yōngróng Road, snails and clams often arrive with the rain,
called "sky shrimp" and "sky clams."
People gather and salt them,
but if left uncollected, they dissolve away,
likely carried there by sea winds.
From the "Pānyú Jì"
Red prawns come from Cháozhōu, Fānzhōu, and Nánbā County,
with the largest being two feet long.
The locals often carve them into cups,
sometimes inlaying them with white gold,
and exchange them as gifts.
"Records of the Northern Households"
Jellyfish, jellyfish,
in Guǎngzhōu they are called shuǐmǔ,
in Mǐn they are called tuó.
From the Lǐngbiǎo Lùyì: In the Eastern Sea there is a creature,
shaped like coagulated blood,
measuring several zhàng in length and breadth,
square and round,
named zhǎyú,
with no head or eyes,
no abdomen or internal organs,
and many shrimp attach to it,
following it east, west, south, and north.
The Yuè people boil and eat it.
From the Bówùzhì: Zhà is also called chūpúyú,
living in the Eastern Sea,
like a blood clot.
Large ones are like a bed,
small ones like a dǒu,
with no abdomen, stomach, eyes, or vision,
using shrimp as eyes.
When the shrimp move, the zhà sinks,
hence it is called shuǐmǔ (water mother).
The shrimp serving as eyes is like the relationship between jùxū and qúyù,
mutually dependent.
From the Běncǎo: In the southern regions, people enjoy eating it,
saying it has a warm nature,
and it treats illnesses caused by river fish.
From the Lǐngbiǎo Lùyì: The sea mirror crab serves as its abdomen,
the jellyfish shrimp serve as its eyes.
From the Yuèjuéshū.
In Mǐnzhōng there are five-colored shrimp,
over a foot long,
displaying five colors.
Plum shrimp appear during the rainy season.
Reed shrimp are green in color,
traditionally said to transform from reeds.
White shrimp and green shrimp are named after their respective colors.
Mud shrimp are said to transform from rice blossoms,
mostly found in field mud,
also called seedling shrimp.
Moreover, in the sea there are mantis shrimp,
shaped like centipedes,
known as tube shrimp.
"Yǎ Yì"
The Biē Rén official in charge of sacrifices,
supplies clams, snails, and ant eggs,
to be given to the Hǎi Rén official.
Zhèng Sīngōng states: Pí,
means clam.
Dù Zǐchūn states: Pí,
means mussel.
The Rites of Zhōu
When Gōngshū Bán saw a snail peeking out,
he stealthily traced it with his foot,
and the snail withdrew and closed its door,
never to open again.
Thus, he imitated it,
installing it on doors,
intending for closures to be as secure and tight as this.
From "Fēngsú Tōng": Even today, doors still use snails as knockers,
a tradition passed down from ancient times.
From "Yǎ Yì"
The Record of Zhennü Gorge in Guìyáng states: During the Qín dynasty, several women were gathering snails here,
when they encountered a storm,
and one woman suddenly turned into a stone figure.
Its present form stands seven feet tall,
resembling a woman.
From the Shǐxīng Jì
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn visited the Hùzǐ River,
where he heard the sound of string music and singing from beneath the water.
An old man emerged and presented the emperor with a purple conch,
inside which was a substance
resembling ox fat.
The emperor asked Dōngfāng Shuò,
"What is inside the purple conch shell?
Shuò replied,
"It is the marrow of a flood dragon.
When applied to the face,
it improves one's complexion.
Moreover, if a pregnant woman uses it,
she will give birth with ease.
The emperor ordered women in the rear palace experiencing difficult labor to try it,
and it proved remarkably effective.
When the emperor applied the fat to people's faces,
their skin became fair and lustrous.
From "Yōu Míng Lù".
During the Tàikāng and Yǒngxī eras of Wèi Guàn,
his family's cooked food fell to the ground,
and all transformed into snails,
which extended their feet and crawled away.
Guàn ultimately met execution.
"Shì Shuō": During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
when Péi Kǎi's family cooked millet in a steamer,
some of it transformed into snails,
and that same year, Kǎi passed away.
Shí Chóng's family rice transformed into snails,
and Chóng was also executed.
"Guǎng Wǔxíng Jì"
During the Guāngqǐ era of the Táng dynasty,
a severe famine struck Rùnzhōu.
A certain household had stored a large quantity of grain,
selling it at five hundred wén per dǒu,
with prices fixed in advance.
When people crowded around waiting for the granary to open,
they discovered all the grain inside had transformed into small snails.
Everyone was astonished,
though some gathered and took portions away.
To this day, there are still those who possess these snails.
(From "Records of Transmissions")
A monk from Lóngtán Temple under the patronage of the Prince of Guǎnglíng dreamed of hundreds of people begging for aid.
The next morning, he saw people carrying snails and clams to the market.
Suddenly recalling his dream,
he redeemed and released them into the pond.
A few days later,
he unexpectedly found a small basin by the pond.
It was neither bronze nor tin,
neither pottery nor stone.
He took it back to use as a washbasin.
One morning, when he went to fetch it for washing,
he suddenly saw it filled with grains of limonite.
Upon asking his disciples,
they said someone had placed only a few grains there the previous day.
The monk did not believe them.
He tried storing beans, wheat, and silver in it,
and by the next day, it was all fully replenished.
The monk then treasured it.
With the accumulated wealth, he extensively renovated the temple.
When the monk grew old and ill,
his disciples argued over the vessel.
The monk said:
"This is a divine object from the water palace;
it must not be wasted on trivial matters."
He then took it and threw it into the pond,
where it transformed into a golden wild goose and flew away.
People named the place
"Jīnyàn" (Golden Wild Goose)
From "Geographical Records"
In Nánkāng there was a woman
who made her living gathering snails.
One night while staying at a pavilion,
she heard the sound of wind and rain,
and saw numerous snails opening their mouths and approaching,
chaotically devouring her flesh.
By the next day,
only her bones remained there.
Therefore, the pavilion was named
"Snail Pavilion"
Records of the Strange states: The Nánkāng records are somewhat similar.
Jìn'ān scholar Xiè Duān obtained a large conch on the seashore,
as big as a stone-measure dou,
cut it open,
and found a beautiful woman inside who said:
"I am the White-robed Plain Maiden from the Heavenly River,
The Heavenly Emperor takes pity on your pure integrity,
and ordered me to become your wife."
Xiè Duān thought she was a demon,
and rebuked her.
The maiden sighed,
rose on a cloud and departed.
The above account is slightly similar to that in In Search of the Supernatural,
see also
"Heavenly River section"
Yìxīng's Wú Kān served as a county clerk,
and his home bordered the Jīngxī stream.
One day, he unexpectedly obtained a large spiral shell,
which soon transformed into a woman,
known as the Snail Woman.
The county magistrate heard of this and demanded her,
but Wú Kān refused.
The magistrate then tormented Wú Kān with a task,
saying:
"Now I demand the hair of a toad and the arm of a ghost—two items.
If you fail to procure them, you will be punished."
Wú Kān told the Snail Woman,
and she immediately produced them.
The magistrate then deceitfully said:
"I further require a Huòdǒu."
Wú Kān again told the Snail Woman,
and she replied:
"This is a beast."
In a moment, she led it in;
it resembled a dog but consumed fire,
and its excrement became fire.
The magistrate tested it with fire,
when suddenly it discharged excrement that burned down the county offices,
and the magistrate along with his entire household perished in the flames.
"Records of Original Transformations"
The nautilus,
has a spiral tip that curves and is red like a parrot's beak,
hence it is named after this.
Its shell is predominantly bluish-green with patterns,
and the largest ones can hold up to two liters of meat.
The interior is glossy and translucent like mica,
and it is fashioned into wine cups,
making it unique and delightful to admire.
"Lingbiǎo Lù Yì" When the mollusk leaves its shell to feed,
it returns to the shell once full.
If it is eaten by a fish,
the shell floats to the surface,
and is then obtained by people.
Its substance is white with purple patterns,
resembling the shape of a bird,
and it is no different from a wine vessel.
Thus, because it resembles a bird,
two eyes and two wings are crafted on it.
"Yìwù Zhì" The mollusk often sheds its shell to roam.
In the morning when it leaves,
there are insects similar to spiders
that enter its shell.
When the mollusk returns in the evening,
these insects then exit.
As Yǔ Chǎn said, the nautilus roams within,
residing temporarily and carrying its shell.
"Yì Yuàn"
The size of the hóngluó is similar to that of the yīngwǔluó,
its shell is thin and red,
and it can also be used as a wine vessel.
Carving small shells into feet,
and attaching them with glue and lacquer,
makes it even more exquisite and admirable.
"Lǐngbiǎo Lù Yì"
There are several kinds of Hǎiwén lí,
the larger ones can hold one dǒu,
southerners use them as wine cups.
"Guǎngzhì"
Southerners call the patterned conch
the cloud conch,
using it to serve wine.
From "Annotation of Lù's Poetry"
The green hawk conch,
is used by people in Jiāngdōng as bowls.
"Records of Extraordinary Things"
When conches sound,
it foretells strong winds.
When snails emit light,
it foretells overcast rain.
When clams close tightly,
it foretells rebel armies rising in chaos.
"Mystic Pearl"
There are three kinds of clams,
all born in the sea.
Gé lì clams,
are transformed from thousand-year-old birds;
hǎi gé clams,
are transformed from hundred-year-old swallows;
kuí gé clams,
also called fù lěi,
are transformed from old bats.
"Shuō Wén"
In the Huái River,
the yellow sparrow transforms into a clam by autumn;
by spring it becomes a yellow sparrow again.
After five hundred years, it transforms into a mirage clam.
From "Shù Yì Jì".
Dōngyuè hǎi gé.
《Zhōu Shū Wáng Huì》
The Queen Mother of the West said:
"Among the elixirs of immortality is the White Water Spirit Clam.
Han Wu Nei Zhuan
Zhēnlà Kingdom presented a Ten-Thousand-Year Clam and a Never-Night Pearl,
whose radiance was like moonlight shining,
making everyone appear beautiful regardless of their actual looks.
The emperor bestowed the clam upon Fēiyàn,
and the pearl upon Jiéyú,
saying:
"When I gaze upon the empress by day, she is not as beautiful as when I see her by night,
and it makes me feel dazed as if lost."
Jéyú then presented the Never-Night Pearl to the empress as a birthday gift,
but never revealed the emperor's words.
《The Unofficial Biography of Empress Zhào》
The Treatise on Empresses and Consorts in the Book of Jin states: Emperor Hui's discernment was dim,
as frogs croaked to signal the dusk,
and the patterned clam submerged its light.
It mentions the patterned clam,
which is the very patterned clam consumed by the people of Wu.
In the summer of the first year of the Zhōu Tiānhé era,
a person from Qí Jìzhōu obtained a pair of jade rings from a clam.
"Records of the Three Kingdoms"
During the Linde era of the Tang Dynasty,
bright water was used for the Feng and Shan sacrifices.
Lǐ Jìngzhēn once obtained clams measuring one chi and three cun in the eighth or ninth month,
and experimented with them according to the prescribed method.
By midnight,
he had obtained four or five sheng of water.
"Tang New Tales"
In the sixth year of the Kāibǎo era,
the Hànyáng army presented a clam,
on which a dragon was faintly visible in relief,
about five cùn long,
with golden scales and armor gleaming brightly.
Lǐ Bù Shìláng Lǐ Cháng said that Junior Supervisor Sūn Shēnlǎo's estate was situated by the Gāoyóu Lake.
One evening when it was overcast and dark,
the estate's servant reported that a pearl had appeared in the lake.
He went with several companions to the water's edge,
where they saw a faint glow,
which soon became as bright as the moon.
In the gloomy mist,
they could see each other's faces.
Suddenly, they spotted a clam as large as a reed mat,
with one shell floating on the water
and the other shell spread like a sail.
It moved as swiftly as the wind.
Boatmen raced after it in small boats,
but ultimately could not catch up.
Once it was far away, it sank beneath the surface.
From "Wénchāng Miscellaneous Records."
The Xīn'ān barbarian women hang golden rings on their ears,
stringing together qín and sè ornaments attached beside their coiled buns,
and also wind their waists with threaded conches and clams,
calling them kē pèi.
"Yúnnán Jì"
There is a clam in the East Sea,
often eaten by birds.
When its flesh is completely consumed,
the shell floats up and emerges,
becoming thinner on the sandy shore.
Tides wash over it repeatedly,
polishing it white as snow.
It is most refined for medicinal use,
superior to those collected from dead clams.
"Records of Diverse Matters"
Ducks and geese often feed on the sand by the riverbank,
where the sand and stones all dissolve and decay.
Only the clams they consume remain undigested,
passing out with their droppings.
When used as medicine,
they are far more effective than ordinary ones.
"Notes on Past and Present"
All creatures of the clam family,
when opening their shells hear the thunder's roar,
will never close them again.
From the Records of Nányuè.
In October, pheasants enter the Huái River and become shèn.
Shèn refers to
the bulrush reed.
From the "Dàdài Lǐ"
Shēntú Dí said to the Duke of Zhōu:
"How can the lowly be despised?
The divine frog of Zhōu emerged from earth and stone,
The bright moon of Chǔ came from clams and oysters,
Minor families and great nobles arose from muddy marshes,
Yet all the feudal lords under heaven consider them treasures.
I, Dí, now ask to withdraw.
Mòzǐ
The *Shuōwén* states: Jié,
is a clam.
The *Hàn Lǜ* records: Kuàijī presented two shēng of jié paste.
An annotation in the *Hànshū* states: Yín has a Jiéqí Pavilion.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Jié, pronounced as "jié," is a clam,
one cùn long,
two fēn wide,
with a small crab inside its abdomen.
Qí refers to a curved bank,
where many jié clams are found,
hence the pavilion was named after it.
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ ordered the subordinate prefectures to provide clam sauce,
for offering in the ancestral temple.
Fearing that the flavor might become bland and thin,
his subordinates were apprehensive and dared not rest.
"Guǎngchuān Shū Bá"
During the Daguan era,
Shào Zōngyì of Wúxīng was preparing to eat a mussel he had cut open,
when inside appeared a pearl bearing the image of an arhat,
with the right shoulder uncovered,
head tilted and gazing leftward,
the lines of the robes fully detailed.
Monks and laypeople, witnessing this marvel for the first time,
then reverently presented it to the Cígǎn Temple.
The temple overlooked a stream.
During the Jiànyán era,
while Surveillance Commissioner Yáng Yìngchéng and guests were passing it around for admiration,
it unexpectedly leaped over the railing into the water.
They urgently prayed to the Buddha for its recovery,
amid the vast, misty waves.
With one attempt, they retrieved it.
Yè Shǎoyùn and Zēng Gōnggǔn both wrote poems praising it.
"The Yellow and the Female of the Literary Garden"
The retired scholar Lǐ Pú resided in Shòuchūn.
One day,
he ascended his tower and saw a dragon soaring from the Huái River shallows amid thunder and rain.
After the rain cleared, he walked along the shallows
and found a clam,
quite large,
and happened to pick it up to examine it.
Inside, the coiled trace of a dragon was vivid,
with scales, mane, claws, and horns all complete.
"Old Study Hut Notes"
There was once a giant clam in Lake Dòngtíng,
as large as a sail.
Late at night, it would stand sideways on one shell,
riding the wind through the misty waves,
spitting out a huge pearl from within,
which shone in reflection with the moonlight.
Fishermen tried to capture it for a whole day,
but could not get close,
and it eventually disappeared from sight.
"Yuèyáng Local Records"
In the southern region of Línyì, there are giant clams large enough to fill a cart;
pearls reaching an inch in length are not considered valuable,
and the people of the country do not gather them.
From "Shíyílù"
A clam contains a paste.
A clam,
is the same as a giant clam.
The "Erya"
The small clam is called yáo,
also known as jade yáo,
which can be used to adorn sword scabbards.
The commentary on the Book of Songs states:
"The Son of Heaven has a jade béng and a yáo bì"
refers to this.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas records: On Zégāo Mountain,
the Gāo River originates there,
flowing east into the Jīrǔ River,
where many clams and yáo are found.
The Erya and Strange Names of Marine Creatures note: The river's bèizhù, whose shell is as beautiful as jade,
has ten meaty columns and outer skin,
called jiāngyáozhù.
Guō Jìngchún's "Rhapsody on the River" writes: Jade yáo and hǎiyuè,
tǔròu and shíhuá.
Hán Tuìzhī referred to mǎzhùjiǎ as this.
People do not use this
"yáo"
character,
which shows their lack of knowledge.
The Record of the Houqing Feast
People in the southeast eat aquatic products,
while those in the northwest eat the products of six domestic animals.
Those who eat aquatic products
consider turtles, clams, snails, and mussels as delicacies
and do not notice their fishy smell;
those who eat the products of six domestic animals
consider badgers, onions, rabbits, rats, and sparrows as delicacies,
and do not notice their gamy, burnt taste.
"Bówù Zhì"
Birds lack stomachs and lungs,
clams and oysters lack internal organs.
Leeches live by being hollow inside,
silkworms grow without stomachs.
From Péi Wěi's "Treatise on Honoring Being"
Hānkuí,
the "Lù Běncǎo" states: The kuí's form resembles a sea clam,
round and thick on the outside,
with patterns running both vertically and horizontally,
which is the present-day hān.
The "Zìshū" states: Hān,
is a clam,
originating from Kuàijī,
edible.
"Ěryǎ"
Wǎ wūzi,
refers to creatures like clams.
In the south, they were formerly called hānzi for a while,
but when Minister Lú Jūn took office as governor,
they were renamed wǎ wūzi,
because their shells have ridges resembling roof tiles,
hence the name.
Inside the shell, there is purple flesh that fills the belly broadly,
and people particularly value it.
They are often roasted to accompany wine,
commonly known as "heavenly sliced roast."
Eating too much can cause qi stagnation,
with back and shoulder aches and discomfort,
though its inherent nature is not fully understood.
From "Lingbiǎo Lù Yì"
Regarding the Sea Clams During the Yuánhé Era,
the military governor of Lǐngnán, Cuī Yǒng, died.
The ministers' proposed candidates were all unacceptable,
so the emperor said to Péi Dù:
"There was once someone who remonstrated against presenting sea clams and mussels,
whose words were very upright and just.
You should find this person and appoint him."
Péi Dù went out to inquire among people,
and someone mentioned that it was Kǒng Kuí who had remonstrated.
Péi Dù reported this the same day,
and the emperor then appointed him.
"History of the Táng Dynasty"
Yuán Zhēn served as the Surveillance Commissioner of Zhedong in Mingzhou,
where the annual tribute of clams required
a labor force of ten thousand couriers,
who could not endure the exhaustion.
Zhēn memorialized to abolish it.
Purple clams are as large as ditches,
and giant clams can fill a cart.
"Rhapsody on the River" states: Clams measure four chi in diameter,
with shells resembling roof tiles,
bearing patterns.
"Records of Products from Linhai's Land and Waters" notes: The "Jade Compendium" mistakenly classifies them
"under mussels,"
which is an error.
Using its shell as wings, the clam anticipates wind and rain,
and can fly using its shell as wings.
From "Yǒuyáng"
Emperor Wénzōng was fond of eating clams.
One day,
his attendants presented them on a square tray,
among which one unopened clam did not crack.
The emperor, suspecting it was unusual,
then burned incense and prayed to it.
Shortly after,
it opened by itself,
revealing two figures inside,
with elegant eyebrows and refined features,
their bodies fully formed,
adorned with spiral topknots and jeweled necklaces,
their feet treading on lotus blossoms,
whom they called bodhisattvas.
The emperor then placed them in a golden sandalwood box,
covered it with jade-threaded silk,
bestowed it upon the Xìngshàn Temple,
and ordered it to be venerated.
By the Huìchāng era,
when Buddhist temples were destroyed,
its whereabouts became unknown.
From "Dū Yáng Biān." The account of Suí Emperor Yáng's fondness for clams is somewhat similar.
From "Yǒu Yáng."
Northerners enjoy frying food with sesame oil.
During the Qinglì era,
a group of scholars gathered in the Yùtáng,
and had someone procure a basket of fresh clams,
ordering the cook to prepare them.
After a long wait with no arrival,
they sent someone to check,
only to be told they were burnt,
yet still not fully cooked,
causing all the seated guests to burst into laughter.
From "Bǐtán"
The oyster, also known as lì gé,
is called mǔ gé.
Táo Yǐnjū stated that it is transformed from a hundred-year-old diāo.
It attaches to rocks to grow,
with lumpy shells connected like rooms,
hence the name lì fáng,
pronounced like Ēpáng's fáng.
It is also called háo shān.
People from Jìn'ān call it háo pú.
Initially growing by the sea,
it is as small as a fist-sized stone,
gradually expanding on all sides,
some reaching one to two zhàng in size,
standing rugged like mountains, with each cluster forming a "room."
Inside, there is a piece of oyster meat,
the size of the meat
depends on the room it grows in.
Large rooms are like horse hooves,
while small ones are like a person's fingertip.
Every time the tide comes, all the rooms open;
if small insects enter, they close,
using them to fill their stomachs.
Sea gatherers harvest them,
prying open the rooms with intense heat,
and scooping out the meat.
Shells that curve to the left are male,
while those curving to the right are female oysters.
The "Běncǎo" mentions female oysters as mǔ,
not meaning male.
Among shelled creatures, only oysters are formed by saltwater.
"Yǒuyáng"
Nánshān calls oysters "háojiǎ,"
which are oysters.
Héjiànzhōu's round oysters,
are highly valued by the locals,
as the saying goes:
"Obtaining a single oyster from Héjiàn,
though not enough to make one wealthy,
can still elevate one's status.
"Nányuè Zhì"
Hé Yìn was extravagant in his tastes,
and his meals would always cover a square zhang.
Later, he gradually wished to eliminate the more extreme items,
but still ate whitefish, minced eel, and candied crab,
believing these were not living creatures he had seen.
He hesitated about eating clams and oysters,
so he had his disciples discuss it.
His student Zhōng Wán said:
"The eel being minced
suffers greatly in its bending and stretching;
the crab about to be candied
is even more violently disturbed.
A benevolent person's consideration
should deeply harbor compassion and grief.
As for clams and oysters,
they lack eyes and eyebrows internally,
shaming the marvel of primordial chaos;
coarse shells seal them externally,
unlike the caution of the golden man.
They neither wither nor flourish,
truly inferior even to plants and trees;
they have no fragrance or odor,
how do they differ from tiles and gravel?
Therefore, they should always fill the kitchen,
and perpetually serve as food."
Jìnglíng Prince Zǐliáng saw Wán's argument,
and was greatly angered.
Rǔnán's Zhōu Yǒng wrote "A Letter to Yìn" urging him to eat vegetables.
Yìn in his later years finally abstained from meat.
From History of the Southern Dynasties
In Yuèchéng County, at Xīnxīkǒu, there is an Oyster Islet,
covering several dozen acres, surrounded by oysters on all sides,
their flavor is particularly excellent.

Ancient shell lime,
Oyster shell.
"Records of Rare Things"
The chariot clam is a large clam,
also called shèn,
capable of spitting vapor,
forming towers and pavilions in the sea.
During spring and summer, along the shores of islands,
this vapor is often seen.
Běncǎo (Materia Medica)
Lúlíng Wáng Sòng Yìzhēn was appointed as the Governor of Nán Yùzhōu,
with Liú Zhàn serving as his Chief Clerk.
When Yìzhēn departed,
he resided in Gāozǔ's mourning quarters,
and ordered his attendants to prepare a meal,
but Zhàn forbade it.
Yìzhēn then set up a separate kitchen tent within his study,
and as Zhàn entered,
he was warming wine and roasting clams.
Zhàn sternly said:
"You should not have such arrangements at present."
Yìzhēn replied:
"The morning is very cold—
what harm is there in a cup of wine?"
When the wine was served,
Zhàn stood up and said:
"You neither abide by propriety yourself,
nor extend it to others."

On the twelfth of last month I arrived at Yǒngjiā Commandery,

Above,

"Línhǎi Shuǐtǔ Wùzhì"
The toad,
also known as the toad,
also called chú,
also named qùfǔ,
also known as kǔlóng.
Its fat, when applied to jade, carves it like wax,
hence it is said to be able to join jade and stone.
However, the fat is hard to obtain in large quantities,
so take a plump one, chop it, boil it into an ointment, and apply it to jade;
it also becomes soft and smooth,
making it easy to cut ancient jade artifacts.
Some unique pieces that are not the result of human carving
are mostly engraved with the Kūnwú knife and toad fat.

calling it chánsū.

Toads have no intestines,
they belong to the dragon and snake category.

the moon's essence, the toad,
